### Series Title Page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all extant monuments of Catholic tradition through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and most diligently corrected; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the most extensive editions produced in the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following the individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters duly set within the text itself, and likewise with headings distinguishing the upper margin of the individual pages and indicating the subject treated; enlarged with works both doubtful and apocryphal, yet possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one, namely, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father wrote upon any topic may be seen at a glance; the other, of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers, and in which places in their works, commented upon the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture. A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others, if the following be weighed: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of the reprinted works, the most convenient format of the volumes, constantly uniform throughout the whole course of the work, the modest price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time brought together in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, form, and kind.**

# [The Complete Works of Peter Lombard]

## Prolegomena

[Col. 0009]

## Historical Notice

(*Ancient Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 68, under the bishops of Paris.)

[Col. 0009A] When Theobald died, Philip, son of Louis the Fat and brother of Louis VII, was appointed to his place by the unanimous votes of the canons. He had first taken a wife; but after the marriage had later been dissolved, and after he had undertaken the profession of sacred knighthood, he succeeded his brother Henry—who had entered the Cistercian order—in holy orders. At the time of his election as bishop, he held the office of archdeacon, not dean, as Robert of Mont has it, in the Church of Paris.

But such were Philip’s virtue and modesty that he willingly relinquished the dignity in favor of Peter, formerly his teacher. He died as archdeacon in 1161, is commemorated in the Necrology on the day before the Nones of September, and was buried behind the high altar beneath the shrine of St Marcellus, with this epitaph:

> Here lies Philip, son of Louis [Col. 0009B] the Fat, king of the Franks, archdeacon of the Church of Paris, who died in the year 1161.

Peter, therefore, was called Lombard because he was born at Novara among the Insubrians, a province later inhabited by the Lombards. He first devoted himself to studies at Bologna; then, inflamed by a love of learning, he came to France, commended to St Bernard by letters from the bishop of Lucca, so that Bernard might provide him with what was necessary in France. After spending some time at Rheims, he conceived the desire to go to Paris. Bernard therefore wrote Letter 410 to Gilduin, abbot of Saint-Victor, asking him to provide Peter with sustenance until the Nativity of the Blessed Mary.

Peter made such progress at Paris that he not only remained there, but also undertook the office of teacher. In this [Col. 0009C] occupation he spent much time and gained great renown for learning. Therefore Philip, having been elected by the clergy of Paris, gladly yielded his position and dignity to his former teacher, now a canon of Chartres. Peter held it from 1159 to 1160, as is clear from the chronicle of Nicholas Trivet [Note: [Col. 0009D] *Spicilegium*, vol. VIII, p. 445.]; from a charter in the Victorine annals, in which Peter grants the canons of that house a tithe at Rezias in 1159, the first year of his episcopate; and from an instrument by which he invested the nuns of Edera with a third part of the tithe at Athias, issued at Saint-Victor in 1159, the first year of his episcopate. This is also confirmed by the years of Maurice, who began his episcopate in 1160. John of Paris records the death of this same [Col. 0009D] Peter.

Few memorials of his episcopate survive, since its duration was short; but this one, and a magnificent one, will suffice in place of many. It is taken from the *Chronicle* of Ricobaldo of Ferrara, in Claude Etiennot, vol. VII of *Historical Fragments*, p. 186:

> At this time Peter Lombard, from the territory of Novara, was distinguished by his talent. He composed the book of *Sentences* and was a learned and humble man. While he was bishop of Paris, certain leading men of the district in which he had been born set out for Paris to greet him, taking his mother with them. Because his mother was poor, they dressed her, as they thought fitting, in fine clothing. But she said to them: “I know my son; he will not be pleased by this attire.”
>
> Having come to the bishop, they presented his mother to Peter. Looking at her, he said: “This is not my mother, for I was the son of a poor woman,” and turned his eyes away from her.
>
> At last the mother said to her companions: “Alas! I told [Col. 0010B] you that I knew my son and his ways. Let me put on my customary clothes; then he will recognize me.” Once she had resumed her usual dress, she was brought back to her son. When Peter saw her thus, he said: “This is my mother; this is the poor mother who bore me, nursed me, cherished me, and raised me.” Rising, he received her into his embrace and had her sit beside him.

He also expounded the Epistles of the Apostle Paul profitably. After his death Peter was buried in the collegiate church of the suburb of Saint-Marcel. The following inscription is still read upon his tomb:

> Here lies Master Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, who composed the book of *Sentences*, glosses on the Psalms and the Epistles, and whose day of death is the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August.

[Note: [Col. 0010D] Sauval, vol. I, p. 432.]

To this inscription the year 1164 was wrongly added in later centuries.

[Col. 0010C] No one even slightly versed in theology has failed to hear of Lombard. Matthew Paris, Trithemius, St Antoninus, Sixtus of Siena, the continuators of Affligem and Anchin, Henry of Ghent, Opmeer, Cardinals Baronius and Bellarmine, Genebrard, Possevino, Masson in his *French Annals*, and six hundred others have praised him in the highest terms. Alberic, in his *Chronicle*, enumerates the excellent labors of so great a man: the book of *Sentences*, the *Gloss* on the Epistles of Blessed Paul, and a fairly large work on the Psalter—this is what is called in the schools the *Major Gloss*.

Aubertus Miraeus adds, on the authority of the *Belgian Chronicle*, that Lombard compiled from the sayings of the holy Fathers—namely Ambrose, [Col. 0010D] Hilary, Augustine, and Cassiodorus—the commendable work of the *Sentences*; that he was exceedingly diligent and notably learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect, [Col. 0011A] and transmitted his name to posterity with such glory that the schools of theologians, everywhere exercised upon his little works, call him “the Master” with singular veneration.

His books of *Sentences* were elucidated by commentaries from the most learned scholastics: William of Auxerre, Albert the Great, St Thomas, St Bonaventure, William Durand, Giles of Rome, Gabriel the Greater, Scotus, Ockham, and William Estius. Eisingrenius asserts that Lombard wrote several sermons. His books of *Sentences*, partly corrupted and altered through scribal fault and partly afflicted, through Lombard’s own good faith but insufficient caution, by many false citations and other errors—since he borrowed much from Hugh of Saint-Victor and the Ordinary Gloss—were restored to the standards of truth both by John Aleaume and by the scholars of Louvain. Richard of Le Mans, moreover, annotated and published the commentaries on the Psalms, called the *Hymns*, and the *Soliloquies*.

Since he was the first to undertake the whole vast sea of theology, it is not surprising if a man otherwise most learned occasionally struck upon some reefs of error. See the passages indicated by Sixtus of Siena in Books V and VI of the *Sacred Library*, notes 62 and 71.

When he was accused before Alexander III of heresy for teaching that Christ as man was not “something,” the supreme pontiff directed William, archbishop of Sens, to strive in an assembly of bishops at Paris to abolish utterly this doctrine of Peter, formerly bishop of Paris, and to order theologians to teach [Col. 0011C] that Christ, as perfect God, is likewise perfect man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh.

Joachim, abbot of the monastery of Flora, also wrote a little book against Lombard; but at the general Roman council in 1215 Joachim himself, the accuser, was condemned. The same teaching of Peter Lombard was vigorously attacked by Walter, the sixth prior of Saint-Victor at Paris, in four books not yet published, preserved in the Victorine library. In them he ranks Lombard with Peter Abelard, Peter of Poitiers, and Gilbert of Poitiers, calling them “the four Labyrinths of France,” and vehemently attacks them because they measure the highest mysteries of faith by Aristotelian dialectic.

Others accuse Peter Lombard of plagiarism, saying that he profited considerably from Peter Abelard’s books of *Sentences*, [Col. 0012B] and that a certain Bandinus, an obscure theologian, copied him almost entire in the four books of *Sentences* published at Vienna in 1519. See Jacob Thomasius, *On Literary Plagiarism*, sections 493–502.

In chapter *Fraternitatem*, in the *Extra* on donations, a former manuscript codex of Saint-Germain-des-Prés contains Alexander III writing to the bishop of Paris that P. (Peter Lombard), his predecessor, had made burdensome grants to his canons, without consulting them, to the detriment of the church.

As for those who wish Peter Comestor and Gratian to have been Lombard’s brothers, born of adultery, St Antoninus rejects this as a fable: Lombard was a native of Novara; Gratian, compiler of the *Decree*, was Etruscan; and Peter Comestor was from Troyes.

[Col. 0011]

## Historical-Literary Notice

(*Literary History of France*, by Benedictine religious, vol. XII, p. 585.)

### § I. — History of the Life of Peter Lombard

[Col. 0011C] Peter Lombard took his surname from Lombardy, where he was born, in the territory of the city of Novara.

[Note: [Col. 0011D] Paul Jovius (*History*, Book III) says that Peter Lombard was born in a village commonly called *Lumen omnium* (“Light of all”), and that for this reason, he adds, Peter gave himself the title *Lumen omnium*. We think that the village in question is Lumello in the Milanese territory, which geographers identify with the ancient town of Laumellum. This village lies on the river Grogna, between Valence and Vigevano.]

His family was poor and obscure.

[Note: [Col. 0011D] We shall not pause here to refute the fable which [Col. 0012D] makes Peter Lombard, Gratian, and Peter the Eater three uterine brothers, born of an adulterous woman. The distance between their birthplaces is enough to destroy this fiction. Peter Lombard was from Novara, Gratian was Tuscan, and Peter the Eater was from Troyes in Champagne.]

Yet he had the good fortune to find a protector who enabled him to undertake his first studies at Bologna. From there [Note: [Col. 0012D] Dubois, *Ecclesiastical History of Paris*, vol. II, p. 121.] he went [Col. 0011D] to France to perfect them, taking with him letters of recommendation from the Bishop of Lucca to St Bernard. Bernard sent him to the school of Rheims, where Lotulf was probably teaching at the time; being himself from Novara, Lotulf must have taken particular care of his fellow countryman.

The renown of the teachers at Paris subsequently drew him to that city. His purpose was not to reside there [Col. 0012C] for long. St Bernard so informed Gilduin, abbot of Saint-Victor, in a letter (Ep. 410), asking him to provide for Peter’s maintenance for several months. But the attractions of a residence already so convenient and advantageous for men of letters soon held him there and no longer allowed him to leave. Ardent in work, his progress, matching his efforts, earned him a chair of theology, which he filled for several years with the greatest reputation.

It is claimed that, during the course of his lectures, he was given a canonry in the Church of Chartres. But this favor, as Du Cange proves [Note: [Col. 0012D] *Latin Glossary*, under *Archiater*.], fell to another person of the same name, who served as physician to King Louis the Younger.

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Baronius likewise erred in confusing him with Peter Lombard, friend of St Thomas of [Col. 0013D] Canterbury and John of Salisbury, who wrote him a letter in 1167, the thirty-second in the second book of the holy prelate’s letters. This Peter Lombard was subdeacon of the Roman Church and became cardinal and bishop of Benevento. (Pagi, under the year 1167, no. 22.)]

A far greater [Col. 0013A] reward awaited him, notwithstanding the obstacle apparently posed by his obscure birth combined with his status as a foreigner. This was the bishopric of Paris, which became vacant in 1159 through the death of Theobald and was first offered to Philip, brother of King Louis the Younger.

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Robert of Mont, under the year 1159.]

But this prince, who had not considered beneath him the post of archdeacon of Paris, which he then held, judged the office of chief pastor of this church beyond his strength and declined it. On his advice and at his request, Peter Lombard was substituted for him, since Philip regarded Peter’s virtue, talents, and services as better suited to that dignity. Thus a contemporary author recounts the latter’s election.

Walter, prior of Saint-Victor in the same century, on the contrary accuses him of having attained the bishopric through simoniacal means.

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Egas. Bul., vol. II, p. 858.]

But this writer, as will be seen below, displays so much animosity against the memory of this prelate that he deserves no credit without supporting evidence in such a matter. Peter did not enjoy the episcopate for long, and in the following year, 1160, he was replaced by Maurice de Sully.

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Dubois, *Ecclesiastical History of Paris*, vol. II, p. 122.]

Almost nothing is known of his administration, owing to its brevity. But the incident reported by the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* shows that the wisdom which had placed him upon his episcopal seat did not abandon him there.

[Note: [Col. 0013D] See above the notice extracted from *Gallia [Col. 0014D] Christiana*. Editor.]

We are not unaware that the same incident is attributed to other prelates; but there is no objection to its having been repeated, and in any case we give it as we found it.

The body of our prelate was buried in the choir of the church of Saint-Marcel near Paris, where the following epitaph may still be seen on his tomb:

[Note: [Col. 0014D] Corrozet, *Antiquities of Paris*, ch. 744.]

> Here lies Master Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, who composed the book of *Sentences*, the Glosses on the Psalms and the Epistles, and whose day of death is the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August.

[Col. 0013C] The theological school of Paris has never ceased to honor the memory of this great man. From time immemorial it has required its bachelors seeking the license to attend the service which it has celebrated for him every year on 29 July.

[Note: [Col. 0014D] “In the choir of the collegiate church of Saint-Marcel at Paris is a representation of the tomb of the celebrated Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris. This figure and inscription, although ancient, are not from the time of his death, but more than a hundred years later, as may be judged from the height of his mitre.” Le Beuf, *History of Paris*, vol. I, p. 196.]

### § II. — His Printed Writings

1. Two methods prevailed in the schools of theology when Peter Lombard entered the field as a teacher. The first, that of antiquity, consisted in explaining in order the doctrine contained in Scripture, from Scripture itself and tradition. This was a simple, sure, peaceful, and illuminating method, which maintained in purity the deposit of revelation, edified while instructing, and fixed for the human mind the limit at which it should stop in its search for the truths of salvation.

The second method, which our author had almost seen arise, was to treat religious subjects as philosophical subjects, controversially [Col. 0013D] and through reasoning. Cumbrous and quibbling, better fitted to satisfy curiosity than to nourish piety, it broke down the barriers separating reason from faith, opened the door to endless questions, and, being less concerned with the principal matter than with accessories, cast shadows over the former through the efforts of its adherents to shed light on the latter.

[Col. 0014A] Everything was made a matter of dispute in this new theology, later called Scholastic because everything in it was treated contradictorily, from the existence of God to the loftiest of our mysteries. The field thus widened opened a vast space in which every school advanced its own particular opinions—often absurd, sometimes dangerous, and almost always useless—occupied itself in supporting them with specious sophisms, and at the same time labored to destroy, by similar means, the opinions opposed to them.

Peter Lombard, a witness to this license, had the good sense to perceive its disadvantages and the zeal to work toward remedying them. To carry out this design, he gathered from the Fathers and ancient doctors the most precise passages concerning the questions then debated in the schools, and arranged them by subjects. In this way he sought to form a body of clear, authoritative, authentic decisions, capable, in a word, of removing all doubts and restoring every mind to uniformity of doctrine.

The work produced by this labor is entitled the *Sentences*, a title which, as has been seen above, was not new. It is divided into four books, each comprising a large number of distinctions. The author’s procedure is first to establish, for each subject, the state of the question; then to set out the opinions on both sides with the authorities supporting them; and finally to deliver the judgment that seems to him most consonant with the spirit of antiquity.

“All learning,” he says in his Preface, “has things or signs as its object. Things are divided into those which are to be enjoyed and those which are only to be used”—that is, God and creatures. Signs are likewise of two kinds: some terminate in signifying without conferring what they signify, as do the sacraments of the old law; others confer it, namely the sacraments of the [Col. 0014C] new law. These are the four matters included in the author’s design.

The first book, comprising forty-eight distinctions, concerns the attributes of the Divinity. But before entering upon this subject, Peter raises the question whether it is lawful to enjoy virtue for its own sake. He decides negatively, on the principles of St Augustine whom he cites, and proves that virtue must be referred to God as its final end.

From there he proceeds to the mystery of the Trinity, which is the subject of the second distinction. Having established it by the authority of the Old and New Testaments, he investigates in the third distinction what images of the Trinity may be found in creatures. The generation of the Word occupies the next six distinctions. Among the questions raised there, the most subtle, in our judgment, is this (Distinction 7): Did the Father have the power and will to beget his Son? If the answer is affirmative, it follows that the Father has a power and a will which the Son does not possess.

This difficulty is resolved by saying that, although the Father begot voluntarily, the generation is not an effect of will but of nature. For he is Father in the same manner in which he is God (Distinction 6). Now his divinity does not proceed from his will. The same must therefore be said of his fatherhood (Distinction 7).

The procession and mission of the Holy Spirit furnish [Col. 0015A] the subject of ten distinctions, from the tenth through the nineteenth inclusive. Thereafter the absolute and relative properties of the three divine persons are treated, ending with the thirty-fourth distinction. In the following distinction, and until the end of the book, the discussion concerns certain attributes of the Divinity requiring special consideration: namely, God’s knowledge, providence, predestination, and omnipotence.

Because all things are present to God’s knowledge, the question is raised (Distinction 36) whether they should be admitted to be in the divine essence. The answer is negative: although God’s knowledge is his essence, everything in that knowledge does not belong to God’s essence; otherwise all things would be coessential and of the same nature with him, which is absurd.

This divine essence is present in every place and enclosed in none. It is neither local nor circumscribable. It is otherwise with spirits. Although they are not susceptible of dimension (Distinction 37), they are nevertheless bounded and circumscribed in a place; but in such a way that, if several spirits—even all spirits—were assembled in the same place, they would not press upon one another or prevent as much matter from existing there as could exist if the place were entirely empty.

God’s foreknowledge may be understood in two ways (Distinction 38): either as simple knowledge of future things or as the determination of those things. In the first sense it is not the cause of future events, although it embraces all of them, good and evil. In the second sense it extends only to those of the former class, and knows them by determining them.

The difference between predestination and reprobation (Distinction 40) consists in this: by the former God foresees what he is to do in the elect; by the latter he knows the evils which the reprobate will do, and of which he is not the author. Predestination then had opponents who claimed that it imposed necessity on human beings. They reasoned thus: what is impossible now has been impossible from eternity. But it is now impossible for one predestined not to be saved; therefore it has never been possible for that person not to be saved; therefore it is absolutely necessary that the person be predestined.

“For resolving this difficulty,” our author says modestly, “I would rather hear others than speak myself.” Then, after showing that the same objection can be raised concerning foreknowledge, he answers directly by making a distinction. “One who is predestined,” he says, “cannot at the same time be non-predestined”; that is, predestination and reprobation can never fall upon the same subject—this is granted. But it is denied that God could not, at every time, have refrained from predestining the one whom he has actually predestined; and since power is always the same, it is still true now that he could have refrained from forming this predestination. Here appears the distinction between the composite and the divided sense, expressed by the author with the terms *conjunctim* (“conjointly”) and *divisim* (“separately”).

Omnipotence (Distinction 43) gives rise to several questions, of which the following are the most notable. Some modern theologians, of whom Abelard was the leader, maintained that God can do only what he does. Besides reasons already seen above, they supported themselves by certain passages from St Augustine:

[Note: [Col. 0015] *Enchiridion*, ch. 96; *Confessions*, Book VII, ch. 4.]

Augustine says there that God is called almighty only because he can do all that he wills, and that his will is no greater than his power. Our author replies (Distinction 44) [Col. 0016A] that these propositions mean only that everything God wills lies within his power; they do not mean conversely that he wills or actually does everything which he has the power to do.

Can God make things better than they are? This follows from the preceding question. Peter declares for the affirmative, and argues thus against those who hold the negative: Why do you say that an individual creature, or even the totality of creatures, cannot be better than it is? Is it because it is so supremely good that no perfection is lacking to it? But then you make the creature equal to the Creator. Is it because it cannot receive the greater good which it lacks? In that case this is a defect in it, not a perfection; and it could certainly be better if it were made capable of a greater good. Therefore God can make a thing better than it is. He can also make it in another and better manner—provided, of course, that this manner is referred to the thing itself; for if it is referred to the wisdom of the maker, one must admit that there is no other or better manner than that which he employs.

The last four distinctions concern God’s will. The author recognizes only two kinds: the will of good pleasure, which is will properly so called, and the will of sign, which is merely metaphorical. The former, which must be regarded as the universal cause of all things, is one (Distinction 45) and admits neither multiplicity nor mutability, because it can never fail to be fulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 0115] “It is one, and admits neither multiplicity nor mutability, because it cannot be unfulfilled.”]

The will of sign is fivefold: command, prohibition, counsel, operation, and permission. This is why Scripture sometimes names the wills of the Lord in the plural.

The author then raises several [Col. 0016C] difficulties concerning the supreme efficacy of the will of good pleasure (Distinction 46). First, Christ says to Jerusalem that he often wished to gather its children as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, but Jerusalem did not will it. Second, the Apostle declares that God wills the salvation of all human beings, yet not all are saved. Peter answers by using the explanations St Augustine gives to these two passages in his *Handbook on Faith* (chs. 67, 98, 109).

But does God also will that evil should happen? After reporting different opinions on this question, the author concludes:

> “Let us therefore say that God does not will that evil be done, without adding, however, that he wills evil not to happen. For whatever he wills to be done is actually done; and whatever he does not will to be done is not done.”

A human being sometimes wills by a good will something other than what God wills, and sometimes wills by an evil will what God wills by a good will (Distinction 48). For example, a dutiful son wishes his father to live, while God often does not will it. An unnatural son, conversely, desires his father’s death, and God also wills it. There is therefore a great difference between what it is fitting for a human being to will and what it is fitting for God to will; and the end to which a human being refers the will must be the rule by which that will is approved or condemned.

Sometimes God’s good will is fulfilled through the evil will of human beings, as in the crucifixion of his Son. But, it is said (ibid.), if God willed the passion of his Son, then he either did or did not will that he should suffer it at the hands of the Jews. In the first case, did he therefore will that the Jews put him to death?

Peter first replies simply by granting that God willed Christ to suffer and die, because his passion was good for us and the source of our salvation. But when it is added that God therefore willed him to be put to death by the Jews, he distinguishes: God willed that his Son should suffer the passion and crucifixion inflicted upon him by the Jews—this he grants. God willed the Jews to put his Son to death—this he denies. For, he says, God did not will the act of those Jews, which was evil; but he willed the passion of Jesus Christ, which was good, and this will was fulfilled through the evil will of the Jews.

Thus ends the first book.

The second book, divided into forty-four distinctions, concerns creatures. The first treats of the end for which man and angel were created. The following ten concern the angels. At the twelfth distinction it begins the Work of the Six Days, which it follows through the sixteenth. Man occupies [Col. 0017B] the rest of the book. To be brief, we shall pause only at this latter subject. After setting out the prerogatives of innocent man, it asks (dist. 24) what grace was necessary for him to persevere in that state. The answer is that man, like the angel, received at his creation a grace by which he could preserve himself—that is, not fall away from what he had received—but could not, without a new grace, merit eternal salvation. “The grace of his creation,” says the author, “gave him the power to resist evil; but it did not give him the power to accomplish good. Yet by means of this assistance he could in a certain way live well, because he could live without sin. But without the help of another grace, he could not live spiritually in such a way as to merit eternal blessedness.”

Free choice is defined (ibid. and dist. 25, at the beginning) as a faculty of reason and will by which, with the help of grace, one chooses [Col. 0017C] good, and without this grace inclines toward evil. But this definition, the author adds, fits neither God nor the glorified saints, who, precisely because they are incapable of sinning, possess free choice all the more perfectly. “Therefore [Note: [Col. 0017D] *Unde, si diligenter inspiciatur, liberum videtur dici arbitrium, quia sine coactione et necessitate valet appetere vel eligere quod ex ratione decreverit.* ‘Hence, if the matter is examined carefully, choice appears to be called free because, without compulsion or necessity, it is able to seek or choose what it has determined by reason.’] if one examines the matter more closely, free choice appears to be called such only because it can, without compulsion or necessity, seek or choose what reason has directed.”

Grace is divided into operative and cooperative grace (dist. 26). The former precedes the good will, for by it the human will is freed and prepared to be good and to will the good effectively. The latter follows the will once made good and helps it to act. But how does grace precede the will? [Note: [Col. 0017D] *Si diligenter attendas, nihilominus tibi monstratur quae sit ipsa gratia voluntatem praeveniens [Col. 0018D] et praeparans, scilicet fides cum dilectione.* “If you attend carefully, you are nevertheless shown what that grace is which precedes and prepares the will: namely, faith together with love.”] By inspiring in it a faith accompanied by love. It is disputed whether operative grace and cooperative grace are two really distinct graces. The author inclines toward [Col. 0017D] those who think that they are one and the same grace, and that the entire distinction lies only in their effects. Grace, he says, is called operative insofar as it frees the will and disposes it to will the good; and cooperative insofar as it helps it not to will in vain—that is, to accomplish the good work.

The question of original sin is one of those which the author treats most fully and carefully (dists. 30–33). In the four distinctions devoted to this doctrinal point, after proving the [Col. 0018A] transmission of original sin, he investigates its nature and shows from Saint Augustine that it is concupiscence itself, which the Apostle calls the law of sin. The question is asked: what is this concupiscence in children? It is not an act, he says, but a vice which makes the child disposed to desire, and which causes the adult actually to desire. But, it is objected (dist. 32, at the beginning), baptism wipes out original sin, and yet concupiscence remains after that sacrament. The author replies that although baptism does not destroy concupiscence, it nevertheless diminishes it and prevents it from ruling and reigning. Thus, what remains of it is no longer imputed as sin, but is merely the punishment of sin, whereas formerly it was both punishment and sin. Does concupiscence have God as its author? Yes, he says (ibid.), as punishment; but as sin, it is the work of the devil.

The examination of original sin is followed by that of [Col. 0018B] actual sin. The author (dist. 41, at the beginning), discussing whether all actions performed without faith are evil, says that the affirmative view [Note: [Col. 0018D] *Quod a quibusdam non irrationabiliter adstruitur, qui dicunt omnes actiones et voluntates hominis sine fide malas esse, quae fide habita bonae existunt.* “This is maintained not unreasonably by some, who say that all human actions and volitions are evil without faith, though they are good when faith is possessed.”] is plausibly upheld by some; he adduces their reasons, drawn from Saint Augustine; then reports the opinion of those who held the negative and decides nothing.

The Incarnation, the three theological virtues, the four cardinal virtues, the Ten Commandments of the Law, and the difference between the two Covenants are the subjects filling the third book, composed of forty distinctions.

One of the questions greatly agitating the schools in Peter Lombard’s time was whether the divine nature, or only the person of the Son, had become incarnate. Reasons drawn from the Fathers were alleged on both sides. Having weighed them, the author concludes that one must say that the person of the Son assumed human nature, and that in the Son the divine nature [Col. 0018C] was united to that human nature; and for this reason, he adds, one truly says that the divine nature assumed flesh. As for the statement, he continues, that the Son alone assumed the form of a servant, this does not mean to exclude the divine nature, but only the persons of the Father and the Holy Spirit. Finally, in response to the objection that what is proper to the Son, and not what is common to the Godhead, clothed itself with humanity, he replies that the divine nature was united to human nature in the proper hypostasis of the Son, and not in those of the three persons collectively.

There was also vigorous dispute concerning the adoration of Christ’s humanity (dist. 9). Some maintained that it was owed not the worship of *latria*, but only the worship of *dulia*, of which they distinguished two kinds: one that may be rendered to every holy creature, and another fitting only to the creature par excellence, namely the body and soul of Jesus Christ. This was the opinion of Gilbert of Poitiers. Others held that one and the same adoration should be rendered to both natures; this is the opinion adopted by our author (dist. 10), after supporting it with very precise passages from antiquity.

Another question making a great noise in the schools was this: is Jesus Christ, insofar as he is man, a person or a thing? The arguments for and against balance each other, says our author. For it is proved that he is a person by the following reasons: if insofar as man he is something, he is either a person or a rational substance; but if [Col. 0019A] he is a rational substance, he is at the same time a person. For the definition of person is nothing other than a rational substance of an individual nature. Therefore, once it is granted that he is something insofar as man, one is compelled to concede that he is a person. But this concession leads to a difficulty. For if, insofar as man, he is a person, then he is a fourth person of the Trinity; therefore he is God through his humanity. In order to avoid this difficulty and others, he adds, some maintain that Jesus Christ, insofar as man, is neither a person nor something. Peter then shows the falsity of the reasoning which concludes from the fact that the man in Jesus Christ is a rational substance that he is therefore a person in that respect. For, he says, Christ’s soul is a rational substance. Yet it is not an isolated thing, unjoined to another. Moreover, [Col. 0019B] he adds, this description of person does not fit the three persons of the Trinity. He reinforces this response with an argument drawn from the fact that Christ was predestined to be the Son of God, from which it follows that he is something insofar as man. But he immediately contests this proof, saying that he is not the Son of God by reason of his humanity: *Non enim quo homo est, eo filius Dei*—“For he is not Son of God in respect of that by which he is man.” This is where he ends the question, suggesting that he inclined toward the opinion of the Nihilists—that is, those who claimed that Jesus Christ was not something according to his humanity (dist. 14).

Hugh of Saint-Victor had endeavoured to prove that divine knowledge and human knowledge are equal in Jesus Christ. Peter Lombard takes a middle position between this opinion and that of theologians who maintained that Christ’s soul is ignorant of something. He grants that, through the wisdom it has [Col. 0019C] received by virtue of its union with the Word, it knows all that God knows, but does not comprehend it as perfectly as God does. From this he infers that the wisdom of this soul is not equal to the wisdom of the Word, because, he says, the latter is far more excellent and comprehends all things in a far more perfect manner. It was objected that if Christ’s humanity knows all things, it follows that it can also do all things. Peter denies the consequence, because omnipotence is an incommunicable attribute of the divinity, whereas apprehensive knowledge of all things can be granted to a creature and has in fact been granted to Christ’s soul, according to the testimony of Scripture.

In treating of Christ’s death, Peter raises the question whether, in that state, the divinity was or was not separated from the humanity. Several theologians maintained the affirmative. He reports their arguments (dist. 21), refutes them, and proves by explicit authorities that the soul and flesh of the Saviour, [Col. 0019D] though divided by death, were neither of them separated from the Word.

Jesus Christ, being endowed with the fullness of virtues and graces, did he have faith, hope, and charity? It is on the occasion of this question, and before answering it, that the author discusses the theological virtues (dist. 23), at considerable length. “Faith,” he says, “properly has as its object things which are not seen.” He distinguishes two kinds of faith: one unformed and common to evil Christians and demons, namely faith devoid of charity; the other particular to the good and characterizing them, namely faith formed by charity. The first, in his view, is not a virtue, though it is nevertheless a gift of God. Hope concerns invisible and eternal goods. It cannot exist without love. Jesus Christ possessed neither of these virtues (dist. 26), because he had clear and distinct knowledge of [Col. 0020A] their objects, which they see only as in a mirror and in an enigma. But he had charity, and in the highest degree. Can this virtue, which consists in loving God for his own sake and one’s neighbour for God’s sake or in God, be lost once received? Peter affirms that it can (dist. 32), and proves this against certain doctors who denied it. Yet he admits that perfect charity is not lost, or is lost only rarely.

The fourth book, comprising fifty distinctions, embraces the sacraments of the old and new law, the Last Judgment, the resurrection of the dead, the blessedness of the saints in heaven, and the punishments of the damned in hell.

The author maintains (dist. 1) that circumcision had the same efficacy as baptism for the remission of sins, but not for conferring grace. Baptism administered in the name of Jesus Christ alone is valid, in his view (dist. 2). In his time it was still administered [Col. 0020B] only by immersion, and the usage of the Gallican Church was to repeat this immersion three times in honour of the Trinity. Nevertheless, he considers it permissible to use only one immersion, provided that the custom of the Church in which one finds oneself does not oppose it.

Regarding confirmation (dist. 7), he considers holy chrism essential to this sacrament, for which he recognizes no minister other than the bishop.

He makes the form of the Eucharist consist (dist. 8) in these words: “This is my body; this is my blood.” “For when they are uttered,” he says, “the bread and wine are changed into the body and blood of Jesus Christ; the rest serves only to honour God.” He vigorously attacks the heresy of Berengar (dist. 10); but he wrongly maintains (dist. 13) that the power to consecrate resides only in Catholic priests, and that no real change of the bread and wine occurs in the sacrifice offered [Col. 0020C] by heretical or excommunicated priests.

In penance he distinguishes three acts (dist. 17): contrition, confession, and satisfaction. But are they equally essential to this sacrament? Opinions already varied on this subject. Peter declares for the opinion maintaining that contrition alone, without oral confession, wipes out sins. “For as soon as a truly contrite penitent,” he says (dist. 18), “resolves to confess, God forgives his sins, because at that point there is confession of the heart, though not of the mouth, by which the soul is purified from its faults and the debt of eternal death is remitted to it . . . . The penitent must therefore confess, if he has the opportunity; but before he makes confession aloud, if he has the desire in his heart, he has already received remission of sins.” But further down it is asked: if sin has been remitted by contrition as soon as the penitent has resolved to confess, what can the priest [Col. 0020D] remit to him (in the tribunal of penance)? “Some,” he answers, “think that the sinner is bound by a double bond, namely by the stain of the soul and by the debt of eternal punishment: God himself releases him from the first bond, and the priest from the second. Others say that God alone remits the eternal debt, just as he alone inwardly gives life to the soul through himself.” Having cited several authorities in support of this latter view, the author concludes as follows: “It is plainly evident from this that God himself absolves the penitent from the debt of punishment; he absolves him, I say, when he inwardly enlightens him by inspiring true contrition of heart. Reason supports this view. For no one is truly contrite . . . . unless he has charity. Now one who has charity merits eternal life; and no one is at once worthy of life and of death . . . . It does not follow from this that we deny to priests the power to remit and retain sins, [Col. 0021A] that is, to declare sinners bound or loosed . . . . For they bind when they impose penitential satisfaction on those who confess, and they loose when they relax some part of it or admit penitents, once purified, to participation in the sacraments.” This passage shows two things: first, that Peter Lombard admitted only one kind of contrition in penance, namely perfect contrition, to which he attributed the power to wipe away sins along with the desire for the sacrament. This was Hugh of Saint-Victor’s opinion, and it was that of several great theologians down to the Council of Trent, and even of some since then. Second, he regarded sacramental absolution only as a juridical act by which the priest declares that sins are forgiven. Both opinions, despite the names and number of their defenders, are universally rejected today, and rightly so, as opposed to [Col. 0021B] the spirit of the Council of Trent and the decisions of several Fathers of the Church.

Peter says nothing about Extreme Unction except what is admitted by all theologians.

Concerning Orders, he discusses only one controversy (dist. 25): that concerning ordinations performed by heretics. He admits that this question is extremely difficult and that there are very strong reasons both for and against the validity of such ordinations. He is content to report them without deciding anything.

Peter uses sixteen distinctions to explain the sacrament of marriage. Its institution, essence, benefits, diriment impediments, duties, and indissolubility are the chief matters included in this treatise. Examining the question of the marriage of unbelievers (dist. 29, toward the end), he asks whether it may be dissolved by the conversion of one party to the Christian religion. Having set out the arguments for the affirmative, he [Col. 0021C] says “that it is indeed permissible for the husband who has become a believer to send away his unbelieving wife, even though she consents to live with him; but while she lives he cannot marry another. As for one,” he adds, “who withdraws voluntarily, he is not bound to follow her; and while she lives he may contract a new marriage. But this,” he continues, “must be understood only of those who married in unbelief. If, however, both subsequently convert to the faith, or if they contracted their marriage while already believers and afterwards one of the two, apostatizing, leaves the other out of hatred for that same faith, then the one abandoned must not follow the one departing; but so long as the latter lives, the abandoned party may not remarry, because there is between them a ratified marriage, *ratum*, which cannot be dissolved.” This is approximately the same doctrine as that of Hugh of Saint-Victor on the dissolubility of marriages of unbelievers. It is found [Col. 0021D] in all the scholastics who have followed down to the present day.

Among the decisions our author gives concerning the state of human beings after this life, the following seemed to us most noteworthy (dist. 43). All human beings will rise in the state of the perfect man, to the measure of the full age of Jesus Christ—that is, at about thirty years of age. But they will not all be of the same height, and the taller will not be shortened to bring them to Christ’s stature; for he himself says that they will not lose a hair from their heads. They will rise without any bodily defect, and God will do, as Saint Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0021D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 89.], by gathering together all the parts of their bodies scattered [Col. 0022A] throughout the universe, what a sculptor does when he wishes to recast a misshapen statue. After breaking it up, he throws all its pieces into a more regular mould, where they are arranged differently from the first time and take on a new form. It is the same statue in substance; it differs only in form.

The saints in heaven hear the prayers offered to them on earth (dist. 46); and this is by no means impossible to believe, because in the light of the Word that enlightens them they know those things below which can delight them or in which they can help us. They intercede for us in two ways: through their merits, which add value to our prayers; and through their affection, by desiring and asking for the fulfillment of our wishes—though they do so only in subordination to the divine will. Peter Lombard thinks (dist. 47) that the damned do not suffer all the punishments they strictly deserve, and that [Col. 0022B] God lets them experience certain effects of his mercy.

Such are the matters that struck us most in the four books which we have just surveyed: a work that earned its author the title Master of the Sentences, served as the text for theology professors’ lectures for several centuries, and whose renown the enlightenment of recent times has not eclipsed. The number of commentaries made upon these books would be almost infinite to enumerate. Pitseus counts as many as one hundred and sixty composed by Englishmen alone [Note: [Col. 0021D] *Script. Angl.*, p. 947.]. But who could enumerate those produced by theologians of other nations?

Not content with adorning the *Summa of the Sentences* with commentaries, people even sought to lend it the graces of versification. The libraries of Caius-Gonville and of Saint Peter’s, Cambridge, each preserve a manuscript titled [Col. 0022C] *Quatuor libri Sententiarum versificati*—“The Four Books of the Sentences Versified” [Note: [Col. 0021D] *Cat. mss. Angl.*, part III, nos. 1143 and 1774.].

Before passing to our author’s other works, we must not conceal the doubt raised by Doctor Echius, Chelidonius, and Thomasius concerning the true author of the work just described [Note: [Col. 0022D] Pez, *Anecdota*, vol. I, introductory dissertation, pp. XLV, XLVII, no. 67.]. Having found at Melk Abbey a manuscript entitled *The Summa of Master Bandini*, the first read it attentively, he says, and noticed with surprise that, except in style, it differed almost in nothing from Peter Lombard’s *Sentences*. “I compared it at once with a printed copy,” he adds, “and it appeared to me that one of the two writers must be considered a plagiarist; yet I cast no suspicion upon either one. For Peter Lombard has for so many centuries passed so universally as the author of this *Summa* that it cannot be taken from him without the clearest and strongest reasons. Yet Bandini’s manuscript is ancient and is found [Col. 0022D] among the manuscripts of a very ancient monastery. Moreover, the work is composed in such a manner that it seems easier to have added to it than to have subtracted from it: *Tali formula concinnatus, ut quis facilius addiderit quam detraxerit*—‘Composed in such a form that one could more easily add than take away.’” Chelidonius, abbot of the Scottish Benedictines at Vienna, having obtained access to this manuscript, had it printed in that city by Johann Singrenius in 1519, in a folio volume with a dedication addressed to Emperor Maximilian. This editor does not at all doubt that Bandini’s *Summa* is the original of the books of the *Sentences*, and Thomasius, as stated above, seems to support this opinion. But a thirteenth-century manuscript discovered by Dom Bernard Pez [Note: [Col. 0022D] Ibid.] in the library of Oberaltaich Abbey entirely disperses [Col. 0023A] the cloud. It bears the title: *Abreviatio magistri Bandini de libro Sacramentorum Magistri Petri Parisiensis episcopi fideliter acta*—“A faithfully made abridgment by Master Bandini of the Book of Sacraments of Master Peter, Bishop of Paris.” Thus neither Peter Lombard nor Bandini is guilty of plagiarism; rather, the latter made, quite permissibly, an abridgment of the former’s work.

2. Peter Lombard is the author of a Commentary on the Psalms and Canticles, in which he uses and expands Anselm of Laon’s Interlinear Gloss. This Commentary, says Alberic of Trois-Fontaines [Note: [Col. 0023D] Under the year 1156, p. 328.], is what the schools today call the Great Gloss: *haec est in scholis quae dicitur Magna Glossatura*—“this is what in the schools is called the Great Gloss.” Gerhoh, provost of the Regular Canons of Reichersberg in Bavaria, in his letter to Pope Alexander III concerning the errors current in his own time [Note: [Col. 0023D] Pez, *Anecdota*, vol. V, p. 535.], criticizes a proposition in this work in which the author seems to advance that Christ’s humanity is owed only the simple worship of *dulia*, rather than worship of adoration. [Col. 0023B] But the orthodox way in which Peter Lombard explains himself on this subject in his *Summa of the Sentences* (book III, dist. 10) requires that this proposition be interpreted favourably. Or else it must be said that, since the Gloss on the Psalter was written before the *Summa*, he retracted in the latter what he had rashly ventured in the former on this point.

3. He wrote a Commentary on Gospel Harmony, concerning which we can say nothing, because we have not seen it and no bibliographer has described it.

4. We have another Commentary by him on Saint Paul’s Epistles, drawn largely from the Fathers, especially Saint Ambrose, Saint Jerome, and Saint Augustine. This work is clear and methodical and contains, besides the thoughts of the Fathers, very good insights proper to its author.

§ III.—His manuscript or lost works.

[Col. 0023C] The works of Peter Lombard that have not yet been published are:

1. Glosses on Job, of which a copy is preserved among the manuscripts of Savigny Abbey in the diocese of Avranches [Note: [Col. 0023D] Le Long, *Biblia Sacra*, vol. II.].

2. Sermons for the Sundays and feasts of the year, found in the library of Erfurt Cathedral [Note: [Col. 0023D] *Cat. mss. Angl.*, part IV, p. 1645.] and in that of Alne, or Aune, Abbey in the diocese of Liège [Note: [Col. 0023D] Sand., *mss. Belg.*, part II, p. 244.]. They are also found in the Royal Library, in one and the same volume, while the Sermon on the Eucharist is separately in another (no. 3588).

3. Two letters to Philip [Note: [Col. 0023D] There was no Archbishop of Reims named Philip in the twelfth century. This is [Col. 0024D] apparently Philip, archdeacon of Paris.], Archbishop of Reims, and one to Arnoul, provost of the Church of Metz [Note: [Col. 0024D] Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae latinitatis*, vol. V, p. 782.]. The latter is a response to the letter Arnoul had written to our author. According to Fabricius, these three pieces exist in a single manuscript in the Pauline Library at Leipzig.

4. Among the manuscripts of Afflighem Abbey [Col. 0023D] [Note: [Col. 0024D] Sand., ibid., part II, p. 147.] is found *Petri Lombardi methodus practicae theologiae*—“Peter Lombard’s Method of Practical Theology.” This title probably indicates a work different from the *Sentences*.

5. Leland [Note: [Col. 0024D] *Script. Britan.*, p. 227.] testifies that he had in his hands Peter Lombard’s apology, composed by Lombard himself against the charges of error levelled at him by John of Cornwall, who had been his disciple. In this work, says Leland, Peter Lombard answers his opponent’s objections exactly, forcefully, and subtly, and treats him with the superiority [Col. 0024A] of an old soldier over a champion just entering the arena. We do not know what became of this work. But it is certain, as will be seen, that John of Cornwall did not consider himself defeated and did not lay down his arms.

§ IV.—His doctrine, learning, genius, and manner of writing.

It is principally from the *Summa of the Sentences* that Peter Lombard’s literary merit must be assessed. An account has been given above of the course of this work and of the principal points of doctrine it contains. Its constant renown in the schools has also been discussed. It is now appropriate to recall the objections it encountered and to indicate in detail what occasioned them. Under the pretext of the Nihilism implied in it, John of Cornwall, mentioned above, undertook during the author’s lifetime and after his death to have him condemned. To this end he addressed to Pope Alexander III a writing full of gall and violence, and for about twelve years made various efforts to attain this goal. At last, in 1170, he obtained from the pontiff a rescript forbidding all professors to teach that Jesus Christ, insofar as man, is not something. Such was this disciple’s gratitude toward his master, and such was the outcome of his efforts. Soon after, Walter, prior of Saint-Victor, renewed the same attacks with equally little restraint in his treatise against the Four Labyrinths of Theology. A third opponent of our author arose from Italy at about the same time [Note: [Col. 0024D] d’Argentré, *Collectio judiciorum novorum*, vol. I, pp. 219–220.]. This was the famous Joachim, abbot of Flora in Calabria. He accused the Master of the Sentences of admitting a quaternity among the divine persons, because he had said (*Sentences*, book I, dist. 8) that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are a certain supreme thing, *quaedam summa res*, which neither begets, [Col. 0024C] is begotten, nor proceeds. Absurd as the accusation was, he undertook to prove it in a book that he presented to the Lateran Council held in 1179. Occupied with other matters, the assembly did not think fit to rule on this point; but that which met in the same place in 1215 openly defended the denounced proposition and branded the accuser’s pamphlet with an ignominious censure [Note: [Col. 0024D] Matthew Paris, under the year 1179.].

More moderate and equitable than these three rivals of Peter Lombard, the Parisian masters of theology drew up, around the year 1300, a list of articles in the work of the *Sentences* which they did not approve, and agreed not to teach them. But, according to M. d’Argentré, it should be noted that this list was not drawn up in an assembly of the University; that the articles it contains ceased to be taught only by a private arrangement; and that no decree is known, [Col. 0024D] either of that school or of any other, which proscribed them. They number sixteen, of which the most noteworthy are:

1. The charity by which we love God and neighbour is not something created, but the Holy Spirit himself. (Saint Thomas nevertheless gives this proposition a favourable interpretation, saying [II–II, q. 23, a. 2] that “the Master’s intention is not that the movement by which we love God should be the Holy Spirit himself, but that it comes immediately from the Holy Spirit and not through the mediation of any habit, [Col. 0025A] as do the acts of the other virtues, such as faith and hope.”)

2. Angels increase in merit with respect to their essential reward until the Last Judgment.

3. Before sin, man enjoyed the intuitive vision of God.

4. Those baptized with John’s baptism, without placing their hope in it, were not obliged to receive that of Jesus Christ.

5. Schismatics, heretics, excommunicated persons, and those who have been deposed do not consecrate Christ’s body.

6. Bishops in the same situation lack the power to confer orders.

To these sixteen articles modern writers have added ten others, the same ones that we noted in the analysis of the *Sentences*. Such are the author’s positive errors.

Besides this, he is reproached [Note: [Col. 0025D] Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, no. 34.] with important omissions—for example, on Holy Scripture, the Church, papal primacy, and councils: matters [Col. 0025B] which he does not address at all; with forced allegories which he sometimes offers as proof of his assertions; and finally with a lack of critical discernment, which led him to accept spurious documents such as the False Decretals.

Despite these blemishes, Peter Lombard, as has been said, has always been regarded, and will never cease to be regarded, as the leader and model of the School. He indeed deserves this double title: by the excellence of his method—the best, not to say the only one, to which one can adhere; by the soundness and acuteness of his mind, evident in almost all his decisions; by the extent and select quality of his learning, striking examples of which appear in the prodigious number of passages from Scripture and the Fathers that he ordinarily employs in his books with taste and discernment; and finally by the clarity of his style, which, with a few exceptions, is the best suited to the kind [Col. 0025C] of subjects he treats. Why, then, has this guide, so venerable and so respected, always been so little followed? Why has this Master par excellence made almost no disciples? A surprising thing! The School, wholly occupied with turning over, explaining, commenting upon, and analyzing the *Summa of the Sentences*, generally abandoned its method and plan. This work, made to banish from theology all useless and often dangerous questions, to mark the boundaries within which the human mind ought to confine itself in studying this divine science, and to make known the essential sources from which it must be drawn—this work, I say, so well conceived in the judgment of its interpreters, nevertheless had consequences wholly contrary to its purpose. Never, indeed, was freedom of opinion greater than after it had appeared. Never did the scholastics study pagan philosophy more ardently, or make greater [Col. 0025D] use of it in matters of religion, than after Peter Lombard had shown them its danger. Never was the study of the Fathers more neglected than after he had demonstrated its necessity by his principles and made its usefulness felt by his example. Shall we dare say it? It was the degree of perfection to which our author seemed to have carried his work that caused the path he had traced to be abandoned. In those times, devoid of criticism, people imagined that he had exhausted in his books the whole doctrine of antiquity, and therefore believed themselves excused from resorting to the original sources. Indolence maintained this prejudice; the rage for disputation strengthened it. For what was one to do in a populous school, how was one to exercise oneself and distinguish oneself there, without the aid of disputation?

It was at the same time and from the same causes that the study of canon law was seen to degenerate. [Col. 0026A] Gratian, a contemporary of our author, made, under the title of the *Decree*, a compilation of ecclesiastical laws which had the same success and produced the same effects as the *Summa of the Sentences*. From then on, people ceased to read the councils and the ancient Decretals. This new *Decree* took the place of a universal code and became the text of an infinite number of voluminous commentaries, in which men occupied themselves only in imagining new cases, obscuring those that antiquity had decided, and making a science peaceful by its institution into an inexhaustible source of litigation. Thus two works intended to restore sound learning became the occasion and the epoch of its decline.

## § V.—Editions of His Works

Since one of our obligations is to make known the editions of our authors’ works, we confess that it is impossible for us to satisfy it [Col. 0026B] fully with respect to Peter Lombard’s *Sentences*. Since, as has been said, for several centuries and almost down to recent times they were the sole text on which theological lectures turned, they had to be reproduced in every country a number of times that is not easy to imagine. We therefore ask our readers to be content with the editions or reprints that have come to our knowledge after careful research. We shall arrange them under the names of the places where they were made, taking care to name the authorities for those we have not seen ourselves.

At Venice, three folio editions: namely, in 1477 by Vandelin of Speyer; in 1480, with the exposition of Nicholas of Orbellis and the conclusions of Henry of Gorichem; and in 1514 by Gregory de Gregoriis. One quarto edition of 1507; two octavo editions, the first of 1563 by François Laurent, [Col. 0026C] the second of 1584 by Marc-Antoine Zalterio.

At Basel, eight folio editions. The first six, issued from the presses of Nicolas Kesler, are dated 1486, 1487, 1492, 1498, 1502, and 1510. The seventh, of 1513, is accompanied by the Commentaries of Giles of Rome and the additions of Henry of Vrimaria. The eighth was issued in 1516 by Peter of Lagendorff, through the care of Daniel Agricola, a Franciscan.

At Geneva, the first book of the *Sentences* was published in 1580 by Eustache Vignon, in octavo, with Lambert Danaeus’s Commentary and Prolegomena, which attempt to show the origin and progress of scholastic theology. This edition was placed, as it deserved, on the Index.

At Louvain, a fine folio edition, corrected by Jean Aleaume, issued by Bartholomew Gravius in 1546. In the same place and by the same printer [Col. 0026D] appeared seven quarto editions: in 1546, 1552, 1556, 1557, 1567, 1568, and 1574.

At Mainz, Herman Maresius printed the *Sentences* for Herman Masius, in octavo, in 1632.

At Cologne, four octavo editions: the first in 1509; the second in 1566, by the widow of Jean Birkman, corrected by Antoine Democharès; the third by the same widow in 1576; the fourth in 1604.

At Paris, three folio editions: the first, of 1535, by the heirs of Josse Bade Ascensius; the second, of 1546, by Jérôme and the widow Denyse de Marnef; the third, of 1564, by Sébastien Nivelle. Seven quarto editions: in 1516 by Louis Tilletan for Jean de Roigny; in 1537 by the same; in 1538 by Nicolas Buffet for Jean Petit and Jean Macé; in 1539 by Chevallon; [Col. 0027A] in 1542 by Nicolas de Guingant, corrected by Dr. Jean Aleaume; in the same year by Jean Foucher; and in 1550 by the widow of Maurice de la Porte. Twenty-one octavo editions issued in 1514 by François Regnault and Geofroi de Marnef; in 1517 by Jean Petit and François Regnault; in 1528 by [lacuna]; in 1536 by Jean Petit, corrected by Democharès; in 1541 by Poncet le Preux; in 1542 by the widow of François Regnault; in 1543 by Oudin Petit; in 1548 by the widow Charlotte Guillard, and in the same year by Mathurin Dupuys; in 1550 by Jean Macé, and in the same year by Jean de Roigny; in 1553 by Mathurin Dupuys; in 1557 by Gilles Corbin, and in the same year by Oudin Petit; in 1558 by Jérôme de Marnef; in 1560 by Gabriel Buon and Maurice Meunier; in 1563 by the widow of Maurice de la Porte; in 1564 by Maurice Meunier for Jean Macé; in 1565, corrected by Jean Bauge, by [lacuna]; and in 1573, 1574, and 1575 by [Col. 0027B] Jean-Jacques Dupuys. Besides this, Claude de Lépine, a Dominican, issued an abridgment of the *Sentences* in 1551, in octavo, by Jean Foucher. Another abridgment of the same work appeared in 1554, in sixteens; two duodecimo editions, each in two volumes, also appeared: one by Jean Petit, without date, the other by Denys Rou in 1508.

At Lyons, David la Mouche, for Vincent Portonaire, printed the *Sentences* twice in quarto, namely in 1525 and 1528. Four octavo editions or reprints appeared in the same city: the first in 1581 by Antoine [Col. 0028A] Tardif; the second in 1593 by Pierre Landry, through the care of Pierre Wiart; the third by the same in 1594; the fourth in 1618 by Jean Royaux for Claude Landry.

At Rouen, Antoine Ferrand and Jean Behours reproduced in 1651, in one quarto volume, the edition of the *Sentences* issued by Dr. Jean Aleaume.

To these editions must be added one without place or printer, made in 1499 through the care of Jean Pyvard.

The other writings of our author have by no means caused the press to groan as often.

Only three editions of his Commentary on the Psalms are counted, all three issued at Paris in folio: the first in 1533 with Haimon’s Commentary; the second in 1537 by Chevallon, under the direction of Richard of Le Mans, a Franciscan; the third in 1541 by Louis Tilletan for Poncet le Preux.

[Col. 0028B] Lipenius announces two editions of the Commentary on the Harmony: one from 1483, the other from 1561.

We know of eight Paris editions of the Commentary on Saint Paul: the first, a folio of 1535, by the heirs of Josse Bade Ascensius; the second, of 1537, in the same format, by Claude Chevallon; the third, of the same year, in octavo like those following, by Jean Petit; the fourth, of 1538, by the same; the fifth, of 1541, by [lacuna]; the sixth, of 1543, by Poncet le Preux; the seventh, of the same year, by Jean Foucher; the eighth, of 1555, by [lacuna].

## NOTICE FROM FABRICIUS

(*Bibliotheca mediae et infimae latinitatis*, vol. V, p. 262.)

[Col. 0027C] Peter Lombard [Note: At the same time there was a certain Lombard, a familiar of St. Thomas and a deacon of the Roman Church, whose letter to Alexander III is extant. See Pagius under the year 1167, no. 22.], from a town near Novara, which Jovius and others testify was called “the Light of All”; head of the theological school, or Scholasticus, at Paris; and thence, from being a canon of Chartres, bishop of Paris from 1159; he died 20 July 1164. On him see Vincent of Beauvais, *Mirror of History*, XXIX.1; Antoninus of Florence, *Sum of Histories*, title 18, chapters 6 and 7; and, besides Labbe, Cave, and others, Hottinger, *Ecclesiastical History*, part III, p. 72 ff.; the Sammarthani, vol. I, p. 435; Lazarus Augustinus Cotta, *Museum of Novara*, etc.

Nothing of Lombard’s is more celebrated than the four books of the *Sentences*; hence among the scholastic doctors he is especially well known by the surname “Master of the Sentences.” These books contain a sum of theology selected from the writings of the Fathers and arranged according to scholastic method: thus, in Book I, through forty-eight distinctions, the doctrine of God, one and triune, is expounded; in Book II, the topics [Col. 0027D] of creation, angels, and fallen man, through forty-four distinctions; in Book III, the incarnation of the Word and the love of God and neighbor, through forty distinctions; [Col. 0028C] in Book IV, the Sacraments [Note: This is the great volume on the sacraments, concerning which see the appendix to Henry of Ghent, chapter 11.] and the four last things, through fifty distinctions. It is not unbelievable that Lombard profited, as from other sources, so also from John Damascene’s [Note: Adam Tribechovius, *On Scholastic Doctors*, p. 285.] books *On the Orthodox Faith*, then recently translated from Greek; and likewise from the books of his teacher Peter Abelard [Note: Jacob Thomasius, *On Scholastic Doctors*, §9], or, if one prefers, even from the theological *Sum*, or the four books of *Theological Sentences*, of Master Bandinus [Note: The same, *On Literary Plagiarism*, §493 ff.], later printed at Vienna in 1519. Yet he seems to me by no means to be chargeable with plagiarism on that account, especially since it is not sufficiently established whether Bandinus wrote before Lombard; rather, Bandinus’s work may appear to be a kind of epitome of Lombard’s *Sentences*. We should not, however, suppose him identical with the younger Bandinus, on whom see above, vol. I, p. 169, and the bolder conjecture of Oudin, vol. II, p. 1222.

It is impossible either to count the editions or to give a distinct account of the commentaries on this work, which are innumerable. For since for several centuries it held sway in the schools [Note: Erasmus, on Matthew 1:19: “Peter Lombard, the rhapsodist of that work called the *Sentences*, is a theologian not to be despised. I judge that he was both an upright man and, as that age allowed, learned. And would that his labor had succeeded as happily for the Christian world as it was undertaken by him in pious zeal! For it is evident that he intended, by collecting once for all the matters relevant to the subject, to exclude every question. But the result turned out otherwise. For we see from that work not mere swarms, but seas, of interminable questions burst forth.”], approved by Scotists no less than Thomists, [Col. 0029A] it is not surprising that it had so many editors and interpreters. This *Bibliotheca* alone supplies hundreds of them, to be noted in the index, so that even a diligent man might readily grow weary in listing them. I find the older editions mentioned at Nuremberg, 1474, 1478, 1499, folio.

Venice, 1477 and 1480, folio; and 1507, quarto, with the interpretation of Nicholas of Orbellis, the conclusions of Henry Gorichem, and Thomas’s problems. Basel, 1486, 1492, 1498, 1502, 1513, folio, with certain errors condemned at Paris in 1277, and the Articles [Note: Jean Launoy, *On the Varied Fortune of Aristotle*, p. 71: “As regards Peter Lombard, his opinions were debated at the Roman council held by Alexander III in 1179; and he also wrote to William, archbishop and legate of Sens, concerning certain propositions of Lombard (this is available in the volumes of councils under the year 1170). This controversy lasted for several years. Then Joachim, abbot of the monastery of Floris, attacked Lombard and his *Sentences* rather fiercely, but Innocent III finally restrained the attack at the Lateran Council over which he presided in 1215. However that may be, Prior Walter and Abbot Joachim—or at any rate others—finally achieved this result: that from Lombard’s *Sentences* there was afterward made a list of certain propositions that were by no means to be taught. At the end of the *Sentences* these are designated thus: ‘Articles in which the Master of the Sentences is not commonly upheld.’ There are twenty-six of them, whereas in Antoninus of Florence’s *Theological Sum*, part IV, title 11, chapter 8, only fourteen are rejected. Compare what Edmund Martène says on the Council of Tours of 1163 and that of Paris of 1178, *Anecdota*, vol. V, pp. 1655, 1657, and *New Collection*, vol. II, p. 844; vol. I of the *Anecdota*, p. 517; on John of Cornwall, vol. IV, p. 67 ff.; on Joachim, p. 41; on Walter, prior of St Victor at Paris, vol. III, p. 118; Oudin, vol. II, p. 1223 ff., etc.] in which the Master is not commonly upheld in the *Sentences*. These are twenty-six, whereas in Antoninus of Florence’s *Theological Sum*, part IV, title 11, chapter 8, only fourteen are rejected.

Paris, 1528, octavo; 1536, octavo.

Corrected by Jean Aleaume: Louvain, 1546, folio; Paris, 1550, quarto; 1564, octavo. Louvain, 1546 and 1568, quarto.

Venice, 1570, octavo, revised by Bartholomew Gravius and other learned [Col. 0029B] men.

Cologne, 1566 and 1576, octavo, revised by Antoine of Monchy, Democharès, Ressonnaeus, doctor of the Sorbonne; Lyons, 1594, octavo; 1618, octavo.

With a brief exposition of the letter and questions that may be raised concerning it, by Juan Martínez de Ripalda, S.J.; Lyons, 1636, octavo.

The first book with Lambert Danaeus’s threefold commentary. Geneva, 1580, octavo, etc.

Commentaries on the Psalter, or the Masterly Gloss (*Major Glossatura*), from selected and orthodox authors. Nuremberg, 1478, folio; Basel, 1486; and revised by Fr. Richard of Le Mans, Franciscan. Paris, 1541, folio. François Pithou, *Pithoeana*, [Col. 0030A] p. 20: “Please buy for me Peter Lombard on the Psalms; it is a very good book. Everything Lombard did is excellent. He was a very worthy man,” etc.

James Le Long, p. 901 of the *Exegetical Biblical Library*, mentions unpublished Glosses on Job from the Savignian Library.

*Collections on All the Epistles of Paul*, from the holy Fathers—Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and others; Paris, 1535, folio, and 1537, folio; 1541, 1543, 1555, octavo. See Richard Simon’s *Critical History of the New Testament*, III.33.

Henry of Ghent, chapter 31, mentions sermons written by him on various feasts, not yet, I believe, published.

In the Pauline Library at Leipzig are manuscripts, according to Feller, p. 182: a letter of Arnold, provost of the Church of Metz, to Peter Lombard, and two letters of Lombard to Philip, archbishop of Rheims. [Col. 0030B] [For a long time suspicion has arisen against this writer that he plundered the work of Master Bandinus entitled *Theological Sum*, in which the sacraments are discussed in the same manner and in the same order as in Lombard’s fourth book. Thus there was just and proper reason for doubt as to which had borrowed from the other, until Fr. Pez finally decided the case against Bandinus in the introductory dissertation to the first volume of the *Anecdota*, p. XLV. For he says that in a monastery formerly in Bavaria he found a manuscript written in the thirteenth century bearing this title of Bandinus’s work: “Abridgment by Master Bandinus of the Book on the Sacraments of Master Peter of Paris.” —Mansi.]

# COMMENTARIES ON THE ENTIRE PSALTER OF PETER LOMBARD, FORMER BISHOP OF PARIS, MASTER OF THE SENTENCES

Compiled in his customary manner from selected and orthodox authors, and woven into this felicitous rhapsody with just and new diligence; carefully revised in no ordinary fashion by Brother RICHARD OF LE MANS, doctor of theology of the Franciscan order, with the names of the authors indicated in their proper places; now published for the first time. Interwoven by the same editor is a defense of the ecclesiastical edition, without prejudice to Hebraism, and a comparison of different translations in the manner of an apology, wherever the Vulgate reading seemed to differ from the Hebrew truth or otherwise vary.

(From the Paris edition of 1541, published by Poncet le Preux, “under the Wolf,” printed by Jean-Louis Tilletan, in small folio, with the privilege of the King and Senate.)

## Dedicatory Letter of Brother Richard of Le Mans, Doctor of Theology and Least of the Friars Minor, to the Most Reverend Father Vincent Lunel, General Minister of the Entire Order of Friars Minor, a Man of Manifold Learning

Divine praise, most observant Father, ought by every vote to hold first place (*ta prōteia*, “the first honors”); upon it depends the one hinge of Christian religion. No labor can be beneficial—indeed, it is known to be especially harmful—unless through it, according to our weakness, we learn ever more fully to praise God, the Best and Greatest. This is, in truth, the angels’ *ambrosia*; the perfected happiness of the saints: “Blessed,” he says, “are those who dwell in your house; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Psalm 83). Meanwhile, in this vale of tears, in this most wretched exile, what can more nearly transform us, poor little human beings otherwise fastened to the earth that flows away beneath us, into that heavenly disposition, than to celebrate, proclaim, and exalt our Creator and Redeemer with spiritual songs and joyful hymns—whereby human beings become gods and all sons of the Most High? And, as Basil says, “God, raising our thoughts to what is on high, has not left them cast down upon the ground and worthy to be trampled, in order that, ever tending upward, we may set ourselves on an equal level with the summits of the highest things.”

Yet it is not from my own rashness that I would attempt to attain, even in the least degree, with human words—and indeed with these trifling words of ours—a matter incomprehensible in itself, if anything in divine praises can be called small. Rather, the subject of the task undertaken, so often imposed on me by your obedience, rightly compelled my stammering speech to this purpose. For God’s goodness is so great that he deigns to hear what our infancy labors to utter concerning his majesty in uncouth and soiled speech, though not with a soiled mind. It was fitting, certainly, that one who by God’s gift toils over the Davidic psalms, which embrace the entire force of Scripture through the most delightful theme of praise, should begin by taking, however he could, his subject matter from them. For, according to Basil, “the book of Psalms has gathered up what is useful from all things and is a common treasury of good teachings, discovering for each person what suits his attention.”

Moreover, while three years ago we were frequently turning over, with eager hand, the treasure of the Library of St Victor, there came to hand the Psalter of our lyrical David, illuminated by the noble equipment of commentaries of that excellent man, the Master of the Sentences: his own and not his own—his own, because of a most apt, concise, and singular collection of sayings (*gnomologia*) from Catholic doctors; not his own, because by laborious craftsmanship he had industriously excerpted them from the writings of others.
