When the brethren of that monastery, being most devout and greatly disposed [Col. 0033] to spread learning, willingly shared these with me, we began to taste the very abundant fruits of those commentaries. Before us also, several grave men, who had discovered like copies in certain public libraries, had found this work—constructed from a harmonious accumulation of diverse flowers—to be very celebrated. Accordingly, there was an urgent and ardent desire that it be committed to the press and published for the no small benefit of all, especially since nothing occurs more frequently on believers’ lips, nor can anything be found more suited to advancing the worship of God and expressing his ineffable glory in sung hymns, than the ineffable jubilation of the psalms. For the whole earth is invited to this by the divine Psalmist: “Let all the earth adore you and sing psalms to you” (Psalm 65). When, according to the Apostle, this is sung with the spirit, it is also sung with the mind (1 Corinthians 14). Who could express in words how great is the joy by which the inward person is refreshed—so great that no one knows it except the one who receives it? The account written concerning King Saul (1 Samuel 16) is ready to hand: tormented by an evil spirit, he suffered more lightly when David struck the harp with his hand, and the evil demon (*kakodaimōn*) withdrew from its harsher assault. Every tongue and every intellect is surpassed by the power of the Psalms, “for here is perfect theology.” Yet it is far better to experience this with the fear of God than merely to sound it forth in speech.

But, to return to the point from which we digressed, we were finally persuaded that this very rich work should be printed, with the doctors whom it had drawn together into a kind of miscellany identified according to such vigilance as we could provide. Thus it came about that what others had commented on separately in the Psalms, he embraced collectively in a certain brevity. This is the value of such commentaries. Since, however, it was not sufficiently clear which passages corresponded to their authors and how fully, because they were sometimes marked in a haphazard fashion, it was necessary to go through one by one the authors whom he cited, as if syllable by syllable, as our longer preface will show, although the proofs needed for exactness (*tekmēria pros to akribes*) were not observed as I would have wished.

Furthermore, we saw that the ecclesiastical edition called the Vulgate might almost fall into contempt; indeed, we found that this had nearly happened. Through the introduction of so many new translations, it was as though David were alien to us and to the songs hitherto celebrated among Christians, so that someone might now think the genuine reading of the Psalms to have been adulterated in the common psalmody of churches and monasteries, which is most powerfully offered to God the Lord by day and night. I am not unaware, however, how much light the comparison of different translations brings. Saint Augustine testifies to this in Book II, chapter 14, of *On Christian Doctrine*: “The great number of translators, when manuscripts are compared, examined, and discussed, is very helpful; far from falsehood!” Nevertheless, it did not seem unfitting to defend the most sacred practice of the Church, so far as our slender ability allowed, if these men had burdened their pages with novelties in such a spirit that the Vulgate translation—the one used by the entire order of the Church—might be overthrown. Just as it would not show a candid heart to publish their own work with that purpose, so we did not wish to pronounce anything unfavorable about them, although it is clear that some of them do not enjoy a wholly good reputation.

Therefore, for each verse we appended a comparison wherever anything happened to vary. By God’s grace, we endeavor thereby to reconcile our reading with the Hebrew truth, as interpreters of old did—a point readily accepted by those whose judgment is less corrupted and who favor the ecclesiastical rite with Christian affection. But where the difference between our reading and the others was very slight, it had to be passed over. We nonetheless hesitated for a long time, and not without reason, over undertaking so difficult a work, weighing the smallness of our own ability and considering that it would be most difficult even for those highly practiced in such matters; nor do I claim such skill in languages that I can pass even the slightest judgment on the others. Yet because the aim on which we fixed our whole gaze is unshakable—namely, the most firm strength of ecclesiastical custom, by which even the Apostle was not afraid on occasion to confirm his sayings: “We have no such custom, nor has the Church of God” (1 Corinthians 11)—we were given courage, not too rashly, to launch our little vessel upon the sea without contention, trusting him who says: “These signs shall follow those who believe in me: they shall speak with new tongues; they shall take up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it shall not harm them” (Mark 16).

I do not doubt that those who devote entire days to Hebrew studies could have advanced this task with less effort and greater praise. Far be it from any one of them to have hastily condemned an edition devoutly impressed upon and received by Latin ears through so many centuries. Nor would I have any calumniator snatch from my words the claim that the Church, otherwise secure in itself, needs me as her defender. But let him remember that those were also received who offered even goats’ hair for making the tabernacle of the Lord. In truth, however, I had not yet firmly resolved in mind to undertake this office until your most reverend fatherhood added the yoke and merit of obedience, which I was certainly not free to refuse. But if any rash audacity lies concealed in human self-love (*philautia*), the tenor and command of obedience will at once excuse it.

It will excuse it in such a way, however, that I do not wish stubbornly to defend my errors or cover them with any coloring. Rather, I wish frankly to confess the fault of my ignorance wherever it is discovered, ready to retract anything discordant that I may have written through lack of skill or thoughtlessness. For what is written that ought not to be left, in all submission and modesty, to the judgment of the Church and the examination of learned men? Therefore I owe this first offspring, however produced through my own exertions from the labors of others, to your most devout fatherhood, since without your command—and that command so often repeated—it would have been too frightening for me to come forward in public. And whatever it is, your obedience has brought it about; and it is most fitting to dedicate all our works to it.

A most apt congruity was also present: the studies on praise should be consecrated to him whose general office depends upon the single state of divine praise and piety. For what do you now traverse almost the whole Christian world in apostolic course, with unexhausted labors? What do you seek with such painstaking effort, except that God, the Best and Greatest, may be praised—not only among the Franciscan brothers, whose whole ministry you diligently exercise, but also among every class of human beings; and that you may advance God’s honor with manifold increase through the ever-present grace of the Holy Spirit? This grace has made the supreme pontiff and the greatest princes of the Christian faith, insofar as they are inclined to orthodox religion, favorable to you. You enjoy so good a reputation among them as I would wish this little monument of our modest talent, whatever it may be, always to find in a fair reader. Let it therefore go forth safe under your auspices—something which it will be as easy for you to defend against the leonine and calumnious teeth as your abundance of learning is rich and varied.

Paris, in the year of Christian salvation one thousand five hundred and forty.

# PROLOGUE TO THE MASTER, OR A COMPARISON OF THE DIFFERENT TRANSLATIONS OF THE PSALTER AND A DEFENSE OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL READING IN VERSES THOUGHT TO DIFFER FROM THE TRUTH OF THE HEBREW SOURCE

By Brother Richard of Le Mans, Doctor of Theology, of the Order of Friars Minor.

[Col. 0035]

[Col. 0035A] Although no understanding of things can be had without knowledge of words, indeed even of syllables, such treatment by itself would be somewhat barren. It therefore seemed fitting to insert our annotations into the commentaries of Peter Lombard, formerly bishop of Paris, rightly called the Master of the Sentences, now published for the first time. Accordingly, let the reader expect nothing in these scholia beyond what the title promises. Let him first nourish his mind with the learned expositions of the psalm; then, if he doubts the fidelity of the Vulgate edition or is pleased to compare the recently produced different translations, perhaps he will find what he seeks and will not regret the reading—provided only that he bring a fair and by no means contentious disposition.

Since at the threshold of his prologue the Master touches briefly on the number of books in the Psalms and their authors, it will not be unfitting to take up the subject and the dispute more deeply. At the same time, certain prefatory matters must be set forth, which are judged necessary for establishing the purpose of the undertaking [Col. 0035B], lest, as they say, we begin the course of our modest night-work with unwashed feet.

First, as to whether there are several books of Psalms, Saint Jerome seems variable and inconsistent with himself if one reads him inattentively. For what the Master cites in his prologue is found in Saint Jerome, volume III, in a certain letter to Marcella, whose words we append:

> “Amen”; in the Septuagint, *genoito*, that is, “let it be done.” Hence also at the end of the books—for the Psalter is divided among the Hebrews into five volumes—they translated “Let it be done, let it be done,” where the Hebrew reads “Amen, amen,” so that the things said above may thereby be confirmed as true.

So he writes.

The same opinion may be inferred from what he writes to Marcella in volume I concerning Leah’s death:

> “When, about the third hour of the present day, we had begun to read the seventy-second Psalm—that is, the beginning of the third book—and were compelled to explain that a part of its title belongs to the end of the second book and to the beginning of the third book,”

etc.

From these passages it is apparent that Saint Jerome held the Psalter to be divided into books. Yet he follows the contrary opinion when, writing to Sophronius in volume III, he says:

> “I know that some think the Psalter is divided into five books, so that wherever the Septuagint translators write *genoito, genoito*—that is, ‘Let it be done, let it be done’—there is the end of a book; whereas in Hebrew ‘Amen, amen’ is written. But we, following the authority of the Hebrews, and especially of the apostles, who always name the Book of Psalms in the New Testament, maintain that there is one volume of Psalms.”

And again, a little later:

> “For if ‘Amen,’ for which Aquila translated *pepisomenōs* (‘faithfully’ or ‘certainly’), were placed only at the end of books, and not sometimes at the beginning or end of a discourse or statement, the Savior would never say in the Gospel, ‘Amen, amen, I say to you’; nor would Paul’s Epistles contain it in their midst. Moses also, Jeremiah, and the others would in this manner have several books, since they frequently insert ‘amen’ in the middle of their volumes. Moreover, the number of the twenty-two Hebrew books and the mystery of that number would be altered. For the Hebrew title itself, *Sepher Tehillim*, which is translated ‘Book of Hymns’ and agrees with apostolic authority, shows not several books but one [Col. 0036B] volume.”

These are Jerome’s words. But do these statements seem to you to express a contradiction? For in the first passage he said: “The Psalter is divided among the Hebrews into five volumes,” and now he says: “Following the authority of the Hebrews, we maintain one volume of Psalms.”

But however Saint Jerome understands this and remains consistent with himself, you may consider it from his exposition of the eighty-ninth Psalm, addressed to Cyprian in volume III, where he argues as follows:

> “The Hebrews say that one volume of Psalms contains five books: from the first to the fortieth; from the forty-first to the seventy-first; from the seventy-second to the eighty-eighth; from the eighty-ninth—which is the beginning of the fourth book and which we are now discussing—to the one hundred and fifth. At the end of all these, a double ‘Amen’ is placed, which the Septuagint translated ‘Let it be done, let it be done’; and from the one hundred and sixth to the end, after the pattern of the Twelve Prophets, who, although they themselves issued separate books, are contained under the name of one volume.”

And further, in the preface to the Books of Kings:

> “The second [order begins] with David, whom they comprehend in five divisions and one volume of Psalms.”

You see, then, that just as the Twelve Prophets are joined in one volume, so the five divisions [Col. 0037A] of the Psalms are joined in one volume.

## Disputation Concerning the Authors of the Psalms
There is a great controversy among learned men concerning the authors of the Psalms. But for the sake of discussion I shall say two things, prejudging no one’s opinion. First, although St Jerome seems more inclined to the opinion which holds that the Psalms have several authors, yet at times he follows a different view. Second, if one looks more closely into the statements of Jerome and Augustine, one may perhaps find that they agree with one another in this controversy.

Accordingly, that Jerome seems to think that not all the Psalms are David’s is shown from volume III, in the letter to Cyprian: “We should also know that those err who suppose that all the Psalms are David’s, and not the works of those whose names they bear in their titles.” Again, in the same volume, to Sophronius: “We attest that all the Psalms belong to the authors named in their titles—namely David, Asaph, and Idithun, the sons of Korah, Heman the Ezrahite, Moses and Solomon, and the rest whom Ezra comprises in the first book.” Again, to Cyprian: “But whereas in most codices the ninety-eighth Psalm bears the title, ‘A Psalm of David,’ this is not found in the Hebrew; Scripture having the custom that all Psalms which lack a title stating whose they are are assigned to those whose names occur in the preceding Psalms.” Finally, in the prologue to Malachi: “We have said, concerning the Psalms which have no titles, that they should be believed to belong to those whose names are prefixed to the preceding Psalms.” Thus Jerome.

Nor is the evasion valid by which one might say that Jerome does not speak according to his own view, but according to the opinion of his Hebrew teacher Bar-Hanina, or of others. For, interpreting Matthew 13, “That what had been spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying, ‘I shall open my mouth in parables,’” etc., he says: “I have read in certain codices, ‘through Isaiah the prophet’; but because this is by no means found in Isaiah, I suppose it was removed by prudent men. Yet it seems to me that it was originally published thus: ‘through Asaph the prophet, saying’; for the seventy-seventh Psalm, from which the testimony was taken, is entitled, ‘Of Asaph the prophet.’” Thus Jerome. When he says, “It seems to me,” he sufficiently indicates his own opinion.

But let us prove that he sometimes speaks in accordance with another opinion. In volume III, to Fabiola, On the Forty-Two Stations, concerning Psalm 77—which, according to the Evangelist Matthew, we believe was spoken in the person of the Lord—the history of the ten plagues in Egypt and Israel’s departure into the wilderness is narrated. Then, after inserting a few words, he adds: “For the same prophet had said elsewhere: ‘I have dwelt with those who dwell in Kedar; my soul has long been a sojourner’ (Psalm 119). Unable to endure absence from the Holy Land, he groans mournfully and says: ‘I remembered these things, and poured out my soul within me, until I pass over into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even unto the house of God, amid the sound of exultation and confession, the noise of one feasting’ (Psalm 41). And in another Psalm: ‘Unveil my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law’ (Psalm 118).” Thus there.

From this it is evident that Jerome assigns the Psalms cited—namely the seventy-seventh, the one hundred and nineteenth, and the one hundred and eighteenth—to the same prophet; which cannot be so unless he means David. For, as has been seen, the seventy-seventh is Asaph’s; the forty-first belongs to the sons of Korah; and the one hundred and nineteenth and one hundred and eighteenth have no proper title. But if Jerome’s view, mentioned above, is true, they belong to the person to whom the preceding Psalms are ascribed. Now the first preceding Psalm which has a title is Psalm 109, which is plainly attributed to David.

Again Jerome, volume III, to Fabiola, On the Priestly Garment, says: “And therefore David prayed in the Psalm: [Col. 0038A] ‘Unveil my eyes,’” etc. And, in volume I, To Paulinus, On the Education of a Monk: “Everything that we read in the divine books indeed shines and gleams even in its outer covering, but it is sweeter in the marrow. He who wishes to eat the kernel must break the nut. ‘Unveil,’ says David, ‘my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law.’ If so great a prophet confesses the darkness of ignorance, in what night of ignorance do you suppose that we, little ones and almost infants, are surrounded?” Thus Jerome. Here you see that this Psalm is expressly assigned to David, though above he had said that the same prophet spoke in Psalm 77 and Psalm 41.

Moreover, Jerome cites Psalm 72, entitled “Of Asaph,” as spoken in David’s person in Ecclesiastes, chapter 4: “David in Psalm 72, and Jeremiah in his own book, investigate this passage more fully.” And in his Commentary on Ephesians, chapter 3: “David, expressing their words in his own person, says: ‘How good is God to Israel,’” etc. Likewise in Matthew: [Col. 0038B] “As it is written in David: ‘They passed into the disposition of the heart.’” But these words occur in Psalm 72. Further, in volume III, to Dardanus: “David sings in another Psalm: ‘Glorious things have been spoken,’” etc. Yet that Psalm, Psalm 87, is manifestly entitled “Of the sons of Korah.” In addition, Psalm 88 is entitled “Of Ethan the Ezrahite”; and yet Jerome, volume III, to Damasus, On the Two Sons, takes several verses from it as spoken to David: “According to that which I spoke to David: ‘If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, if they profane my statutes.’”

Someone might say: because David composed the greater part of the Psalms, the whole Psalter is therefore often called “David.” Thus St Jerome speaks in the prologue prefixed to the Books of Kings: “Among the Hagiographa, the first book is Job and the second David.” For sometimes he cites them otherwise than by David’s name, as in the second book Against the Pelagians: “Asaph says: ‘You fed us with the bread of tears,’” etc. This [Col. 0038C] is taken from Psalm 79, which is entitled to Asaph himself.

Yet even if you escaped in that way, you would not altogether satisfy all the points touched upon, since he said that the same prophet spoke in Psalm 77 and the others which I have adduced. And, that no occasion for evasion may be given, how will you resolve what St Jerome himself writes in volume III to Cyprian? There he would contradict the Apostle in Hebrews 4 unless you said that Jerome had changed his opinion, and that the passages mentioned above show this: taking David as a person, not in the Psalter.

But let us see how otherwise he would contradict the Apostle in his letter to Cyprian. He says thus concerning Moses: “From his mouth we have learned the creation of the world—that is, of those things only which are visible—the creation of man, and the truth of all earlier history. He left us not only five books, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, but also eleven Psalms, [Col. 0038D] from the eighty-ninth, whose opening is, ‘Lord, you have become a refuge to us,’ through the ninety-ninth, which is entitled, ‘A Psalm of Confession.’” Thus Jerome.

But the Apostle, in Hebrews 4, plainly attributes Psalm 94—which is shown to be among those eleven—to David: “For since,” he says, “it remains for some to enter into it, and those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief, he again appoints a certain day, ‘Today,’ saying in David after so long a time, as has been said above: ‘Today, if you hear his voice,’” etc. From this it is plain that the Apostle does not assign this Psalm to Moses, since in chapter 3, speaking of Moses, he says: “And Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony to the things that were to be spoken.” Then shortly afterward he adds: “Wherefore, as the Holy Spirit says: ‘Today, if you hear his voice,’” etc.

Discussing these words in chapter 4, the Apostle shows, by the ordered and fitting sequence of the context, that the Holy Spirit spoke through Moses concerning the creation of the world; and then, after so long a time, again in David: “Today, if you hear,” etc. Attend therefore to the order of the Apostle’s argument: “And the works having indeed been completed from the foundation of the world. For he said somewhere concerning the seventh day thus: ‘And God rested on the seventh day from all his works’; and again in this place: ‘They shall not enter into my rest.’ Since therefore it remains for some to enter,” etc. Here one must consider that the Holy Spirit said in David, after a long time had elapsed since he had spoken through Moses concerning the creation of the world. Therefore it follows that the Psalm was composed not by Moses but by David, whom the Apostle sufficiently identifies personally when he mentions the great interval of time between the two prophets.

You might nevertheless evade this by referring “he said” to Moses, not to the Holy Spirit, according to the literal sense: Moses said that God rested on the seventh day; [Col. 0039B] and after so long a time the same Moses appointed a certain day, “Today,” in David—that is, by the use of “today” in the Psalter which is called David’s, as was certainly current in the Apostle’s time. Yet this exposition would, in my judgment, be somewhat forced.

It remains to demonstrate the second principal point: namely, that perhaps St Jerome and St Augustine do not disagree with each other on this subject. From their words it is easy to see that the inscription of a title may signify either by whom a Psalm was composed or by whom it was recited. For St Augustine plainly adopts this view when he discusses at the beginning why the first Psalm has no title: “There is no doubt that there are one hundred and fifty Psalms; and the title-inscription shows both which number each Psalm is and by whom it was recited. For not all the Psalms were composed by David. David himself chose from the whole people four chief men cleansed by the Holy Spirit, whose names are Asaph, Heman, Ethan, and Idithun, so that whomever the divine Spirit entered might sing a hymn to God. David therefore alone sang nine Psalms with his own mouth; but the rest were spoken by those four chief men, according to the title-inscriptions.” Thus Augustine.

You see that he says not all Psalms were produced by David, especially with respect to their performance in song. Nor is St Jerome’s statement to Sophronius, already cited above but treated without distinction, far from this view. He says: “We attest that all the Psalms belong to the authors named in their titles—namely David, Asaph, Idithun, the sons of Korah, Heman the Ezrahite, Moses and Solomon, and the rest whom Ezra comprises in the first book.” In the final clause he finds that certain Psalms belong to persons whose names are unmentioned, and whom he says Ezra comprises in the first book. For Ezra says, in 1 Esdras 2: “The singers, the sons of Asaph, one hundred and twenty-eight.” It is clear that the Psalms [Col. 0039D] cannot belong to those whom Ezra comprises except as singers, when the Law and Psalms were restored. This is supported by what is written in Nehemiah 12: “In the days of David and Asaph, from the beginning, leaders of the singers were appointed, in the song of those praising and giving thanks to God.” And in 1 Chronicles 25: “Therefore David and the commanders of the army set apart for the ministry the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Idithun, who were to prophesy with lyres, harps, and cymbals, serving in their appointed office according to their number.” Then, after listing their sons who prophesied before the king, he adds: “All were under the hand of their father for singing in the temple of the Lord, distributed among cymbals, harps, and lyres, for the services of the house of the Lord, under the king, namely Asaph, Idithun, and Heman.””

Therefore, just as St Augustine must be explained in book XVII of *The City of God*, chapter 14, so that he may not contradict what he said in the prologue to Psalm 1, so St Jerome too, where he names many authors of Psalms, must be understood in a manner that agrees with this: [Col. 0040A] as we have mentioned before, a Psalm’s inscription denotes either its author or its singer. St Augustine says in the book cited above: “Those seem to me more credible who judge that all those one hundred and fifty Psalms should be assigned to David’s work, and that he prefixed some with the names of others representing something relevant to the matter.” Thus there. How these words ought to be reconciled with his other statements, seek if you can; we have opened a path already touched upon by some, although I have passed over in silence a great part of the authorities of both doctors.

Our view is further supported by the fact that the title of Psalm 38 reads: “For Idithun; a song of David”; and of Psalm 71: “For Idithun; of David himself.” Yet concerning Idithun, beyond the passages we have cited, 1 Chronicles 25 says: “Idithun, who prophesied with the lyre concerning those who gave thanks to and praised the Lord.” Nor does the title of Psalm 76, “For Idithun, a Psalm of Asaph,” stand in the way, as though Asaph were the principal author and Idithun the singer. For [Col. 0040B] Asaph could have begun the Psalm by singing and Idithun replied, just as it is said in 2 Maccabees 1: “Jonathan beginning and the others responding.” Similarly the title of Psalm 87 should be understood: “A song, a Psalm of the sons of Korah; an instruction of Heman the Ezrahite.” Hence in Hebrew it is said, “For answering: an instruction of Heman.”

But you will say: if we suppose David to be the author of all the Psalms as to their subject matter, a difficulty remains as to how the title of Psalm 71, namely “Of Solomon,” and of Psalm 89, “A prayer of Moses, the man of God,” should be understood, since these two cannot be fitted in as conveniently as the others who performed the office of singers and were contemporaries of David.

As to the first, the end of the Psalm declares its author: “The praises of David, son of Jesse, have ended.” Therefore the title “to Solomon” is understood as “for Solomon” or “concerning Solomon,” who was a figure of the true Solomon, the peaceable king, of whom the subject matter of the whole Psalm fittingly speaks. The Hebrew also indicates this: *LISLOMOII* [probably *li-Shelomoh*, “for/concerning Solomon”]. For *lamed*, according to Pagninus, book I of the *Hebrew Institutions*, sometimes denotes material cause, as in Exodus 4, *LENACHASCH*, “into a serpent”; and the Seventy Interpreters, in the superscription, said: “A Psalm concerning Solomon,” *εἰς Σολομῶν ψαλμός*. The title of Psalm 126 may be understood similarly: “A song of ascents, of Solomon.”

As to the second, concerning the title of Psalm 89, St Jerome, writing to Cyprian, reports the solution of those who suppose all the Psalms to be David’s, although Jerome himself perhaps thought otherwise, as we have indicated. “Therefore,” he says, “they wish this Psalm also, under Moses’ name, to have been composed by David: namely, because the lawgiver describes in sacred utterance the common misery of the human race and then the expectation of salvation.” Nor would the objection of the Lord Lyra refute this, namely that this same subject matter is also mentioned in many other Psalms, because that argument is not treated so briefly and continuously, nor in the manner of a prayer, elsewhere. Hence the Hebrew has *LEMOSCHEH*, “to Moses.” The titles of the other Psalms may be treated in their proper place.

## On St Jerome’s Commentaries on the Whole Psalter

Moreover, because the Master very frequently cites St Jerome in his exposition of the Psalms from commentaries which some rashly assign among pseudepigraphal works, it will not be out of place to show that these commentaries are not falsely inscribed with St Jerome’s name, as they dream and impudently assert—such as Erasmus and Bruno Amorbachius.

The former, reviewing the list of works of others, as he calls it, among writings ascribed to Jerome but mixed in, as he would have it, says: “The commentaries which we possess on the entire Psalter under the title of St Jerome openly show on their face that they are not the work of a single author. If anyone asks my judgment, I think that there is nothing there by St [Col. 0041A] Jerome. One part is indeed by some man, whoever he was, plainly learned and polished in expression, yet very far removed from St Jerome. For this writer has less brilliance and smoothness, more sinew; moreover, he is everywhere more copious and painstaking, and more given to displaying his resources. The other part is by some garrulous fellow—I might almost call him a pettifogger.” See what a great injury Erasmus dares to inflict upon these commentaries, besides what he adds at the end of that review.

The latter, in the letter prefixed to the Psalter addressed to the reader, says: “This eighth volume, excellent reader, contains commentaries on the Davidic Psalms. Although they are not devoid of learning, they have hitherto been falsely inscribed to St Jerome.” You have heard their judgment; let us see how blind they are.

Let the most holy Jerome himself speak and defend himself against such troublesome critics. For in book I of the *Apology against Rufinus*, he refutes their excessive boldness—answering Rufinus indeed, but plainly condemning such Aristarchuses: “He is also said to criticize this: that, in interpreting the second Psalm, instead of what we read in Latin, ‘Lay hold of discipline’ (Psalm 2), where the Hebrew text has *NASEQU BAR*, I stated in my little commentaries, ‘Worship the Son’; and again, when I translated the whole Psalter into Roman speech, as though forgetful of my earlier exposition, I wrote, ‘Worship purely’—which is plainly contradictory to itself, as everyone sees.” He then discusses at greater length and clears himself of this calumny, from the multiple interpretation of the venerable sense of the verse and the equivocation of the Hebrew idiom.

It is certain that the commentary on Psalm 2, on the verse “Lay hold of discipline,” reads thus: “In Hebrew one reads *NASEQU BAR*, which may be translated, ‘Worship the Son.’” Rufinus criticized this interpretation. Yet these gnawing critics say that in these commentaries—which St Jerome openly acknowledges as his own—there is nothing by Jerome. What shamelessness! [Col. 0041C]

Furthermore, St Augustine quotes St Jerome’s commentaries extensively on Psalm 93, in the same order, with the same wording, the same form of expression, and the same meaning, expressly naming St Jerome and his commentaries. For Augustine, in Letter 111—which in ancient codices is numbered 198—disputing against the Anthropomorphites, teaches that whenever Scripture mentions limbs of God, they are to be understood spiritually, as all those understand who resist the Anthropomorphites by spiritual interpretation. Then he adds the following word for word:

“From their writings, lest I cause too much delay by mentioning many things, I introduce this one passage of St Jerome, so that this brother may know that he ought no more to contend with me than with our predecessors in this matter, if something moves him to the contrary. Therefore, when that most learned man in the Scriptures was expounding the Psalm where it is said: ‘Understand therefore, you senseless among the people; and you fools, at last become wise. He who planted the ear, does he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, does he not see?’ (Psalm 93), among other things he said: ‘This passage is particularly effective against those who are Anthropomorphites, who say that God has the limbs which we too have. For example, they say that God has eyes: “The eyes of the Lord behold all things”; that the hand of God does all things; and that Adam heard the sound of the Lord’s feet walking in Paradise (Genesis 3). They hear these things simply and transfer human weaknesses to God’s majesty. But I say that God is wholly eye, wholly hand, wholly foot. He is wholly eye because he sees all things; wholly hand because he works all things; wholly foot because he is everywhere. Therefore see what he says: “He who planted the ear, does he not hear?” He did not say: “He who planted the ear—therefore does he himself not have an ear?” He did not say: “Therefore does he himself not have eyes?” But what did he say? “He who planted the ear, does he not hear? He who formed the eyes, does he not see?” He employed limbs; [Col. 0042A] he gave the powers.’”

Augustine has copied this extensively from St Jerome’s commentaries on the whole Psalter, in which the same view is also briefly touched upon at the verse of Psalm 65: “His eyes are upon the nations,” etc. Let rash critics now go and say that there is nothing of Jerome there. Let them deny Augustine; let them deny Jerome himself, who has given plain testimony on his own behalf against impostors mad with a desire to bite. What is more, scarcely is there a Psalm in whose interpretation Augustine does not insert several things taken word for word from those commentaries, though he expands them more broadly—as you will prove by reading both.

Indeed, Augustine repeatedly seems to have wished to point out those commentaries of Jerome when, on Psalm 50, at the verse “and strengthen me with a principal spirit,” he says: “Some therefore understand the Trinity to be referred to here: the Son in the upright spirit, the Holy Spirit in the holy spirit, and the Father in the principal spirit.” For Jerome himself appended to that passage an interpretation entirely corresponding to Augustine’s words: “But you,” says Jerome, “who read Holy Scripture, understand the Holy Trinity here: the principal spirit, the Father; the upright spirit, the Son; and the holy spirit, the Holy Spirit.” He further discusses the same interpretation in the chapter on Galatians 4. Cassiodorus, interpreting this passage, plainly confirms the same point; he flourished, unless I am mistaken, more than nine hundred and sixty years ago, and adduces Jerome to the same sense, so that you may clearly recognize how many centuries ago such commentaries had an undisputed author.

Add that Gregory, on the same Psalm, at the verse “a contrite heart,” names Jerome. Since Erasmus found a certain letter to Damasus, clearer than daylight in testifying concerning the commentaries on the Psalmist, he attacked it with so many insults and so much furious abuse that it is tiresome to repeat them. The letter appears in volume IV as follows:

“To the most blessed Pope DAMASUS, of the Apostolic See of the city of Rome: the humble HIERONYMUS. I have read the letters of your apostolic office, asking that I should hasten to interpret the Psalmist, singing according to the simplicity of the Seventy Interpreters, because of the fastidiousness of the Romans, so that where obscurity hinders, the sense may be rendered more openly and in Latin. Your client therefore prays that this voice of those who sing Psalms may be sung day and night in the Roman See, and that your apostolic authority command the following to be joined to the end of every Psalm, whether at morning or evening hours: ‘Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. As it was in the beginning, and now, and always, and unto ages of ages. Amen.’ Command this hymn to be joined to every Psalm, so that the faith of the three hundred and eighteen bishops of the Council of Nicaea may also be declared in fellowship with your voice.” Thus there.

This is also supported by what Sigebert relates in his *Chronicle*: that Pope Damasus established at Jerome’s request that “Glory be to the Father,” [Col. 0042D] etc., should be sung in the church at the end of Psalms. Strong confirmation of this is supplied by its observance among Latins throughout all lands.

Therefore, lest simple people be deceived by the utterly trifling lies of these critics, it is appropriate to overthrow their credibility by the clearest arguments, leaving no room for evasion, so that from one notable lie, so shamelessly fabricated, they may readily be held suspect in other matters. Let us digress a little so that we may return the sooner, and show that Erasmus often did not read the works which he presumed to kill by his criticisms; but, excessively credulous, he entrusted the matter to men of his own stamp, who, having read works asleep with excessive stupidity, reported sheer lies to their Erasmus, and thus everything was stamped with Erasmus’ name.

Lest I seem to invent this, hear the criticism of a certain Erasmian, prefixed in volume VII to Solomon’s Proverbs in Jerome: “It has not escaped me, candid reader, that the commentaries on the Proverbs of Solomon, to which we have given the first place in this volume, are not Jerome’s. For this may be detected even from the fact that the whole manner of expression differs in every way from Jerome’s diction; indeed, Gregory is cited once and again in this work. The most ancient parchment manuscripts attributed them to Bede.” Thus he.

Now let us hear Erasmus himself in volume I, when reviewing Jerome’s works, whether genuine or, as he wishes, spurious: “Three books on Solomon’s Proverbs, which are evidently not Jerome’s even from this fact, that Gregory is cited in them, although in every other respect they differ everywhere and completely from Jerome’s writings. The man who prepared the Venetian edition thinks it a weighty argument that certain passages are cited under Jerome’s name in the decretal letters. He suspects that the work was collected from various sources by Bede; and I do not greatly object to that conjecture.” Such are the judgments of learned men.

Let us grant them, then, that those books are Bede’s or anyone else’s; but far be it from us to grant them the sheer inventions which they fabricate with excessive brazenness. For I have anxiously read through the entire commentary once and again, and not even once—so may God love me—is Gregory cited. Augustine, however, is cited twice, namely in chapters 6 and 24. Indeed Jerome himself is cited in chapter 30. It is remarkable where their minds were wandering when this point, above all others, would have served their criticism. From this one may infer either that he did not read it, or, if he did read it, that his judgment was excessively hasty and blind—if one wishes to excuse his thoughtlessness in so serious a matter. If anyone thinks that here I am divining what he does in other matters without deeper consideration, then, if space permitted, it would be very easy to demonstrate how often he has erred as widely as heaven from earth, and has foully confused and disfigured pious authors with lying criticisms.

Now let us return to Jerome’s commentaries on the Psalter, and, so far as possible, remove the things that could incline anyone in the other direction, lest the authority which is frequently adduced in this book under Jerome’s name be despised. Someone might hesitate because Jerome explains certain Psalms differently in other treatises, and sometimes rejects an interpretation found in these commentaries. For instance, the words of Psalm 44, “My heart has uttered a good word,” he interprets as spoken in the person of the Father, who begot for himself the Word equal to himself; yet he rejects this interpretation in volume III, to Damasus, On the Two Sons. He says: “You understand with me, faithful reader, that, being filled with fatness, we burst forth into a belch of his praise, saying: ‘My heart has uttered a good word; I speak my works to the king’; although certain persons, more superstitiously than truly, not considering the context of the Psalm, think that this should be understood in the person of the Father.” Thus Jerome there.

He replied similarly to Rufinus, as mentioned above, when Rufinus accused him of having translated the Psalter into Latin in a manner contrary to what he had discussed in the commentaries. Add that, to the virgin Principia, he explains this verse in two ways, adducing the differing views of those who interpret it: “Some,” he says, [Col. 0043D] “wish it to be understood as spoken in the person of Christ, others in the person of the Father: that from the deepest vital parts and hidden recesses of the heart he brought forth his Word, which had always been within him, according to the prophecy of another Psalm: ‘From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you’ (Psalm 109); so that, just as ‘womb’ does not signify a womb—for God is not divided into members—but demonstrates the identical substance of Father and Son, so heart and word are brought forth from heart in order to show the Father and the Son,” etc. By rejecting neither interpretation, he sufficiently approves both. And Augustine certainly interprets it of the eternal generation of the Word of God.

But Erasmus repeatedly impresses upon us the difference of style. I answer that the commentaries contain much learning, as these censorious men do not deny; nor must a writer always preserve the same character of expression. Rather, according to the subject matter or the usefulness of reading, he often lowers his style. Lest you think this my invention, hear Jerome himself, with purified ears, writing to Paul of Concordia, On the Life of the Monk Paul: “Meanwhile we have sent you yourself—that is, the elder Paul to the older Paul—in which, for the sake of simpler people, we have labored much at lowering our style.” Thus he. Had he not written this, Erasmus would have said that the *Life of the Monk Paul* was not composed by St Jerome because of its divergence, as he is wont to say, in diction.

It was also fortunate that St Jerome added for us, near the end of his letter *On Avoiding Suspicious Cohabitation*: “Therefore I have briefly touched upon Scripture and have not woven my discourse, as I am accustomed in other books, with its flowers. The composition was extemporaneous, and flowed with such ease by the light of a little lamp that the hand of the secretaries outran my tongue.” If these words had not been added, Erasmus would not have permitted the letter to be assigned to St Jerome when he departed from his customary manner.

Moreover, Erasmus himself has miserably stabbed himself with his own sword in the judgment which he prefixed to Augustine’s work *On the Morals of the Church*, volume I: “He exposes the mysteries of the Manichaeans, and does so with a marvelous elegance of style—which I wish he had been permitted to employ in his other writings. In this work he has certainly shown that whatever offends learned men in his diction arose not from ignorance but from charity, by which he lowered his style to the understanding of the unlearned. For, that the usefulness of reading might be evident, he changed his style to suit the capacity of the common people in the later work; and he seems to have done this in very many of his works.” Thus Erasmus.

What St Jerome says in *On the Best Method of Translating* suits him most aptly. What are you doing, O pillar of letters and Aristarchus of our age, who pronounce judgment upon all writers? If then it is clear that St Augustine lowered his diction for greater benefit to readers, what prevents St Jerome from having sometimes done likewise, in addition to the points already mentioned? Especially since he writes to Pammachius in volume II: “Ecclesiastical interpretation, even if it possesses elegance of speech, ought to conceal and avoid it, so that it may speak not to idle schools of philosophers and a few disciples, but to the whole human race.” Again, against Pelagius, to Ctesiphon: “Hear ecclesiastical simplicity—or ignorance, as it seems to you.” And in book I against Jovinian: “In the simple words of the divine Scriptures, there is always a more restricted sense.” Very helpful is what he says in the prologue to book III on Galatians: “The harshness of Hebrew reading has sullied all elegance of speech and all the grace of Latin eloquence.” And what he afterwards adds to the same effect. Likewise at the end of the commentary on the prophet Haggai: “I beseech you, reader, to pardon one dictating in hurried language, and do not look for elegance of expression, which I have lost through long study of the Hebrew language.” Finally, to Marcella, On the Ephod: “We, as you know, held fast by Hebrew reading, have contracted rust in the Latin language.”

What wonder, then, if St Jerome is more polished in [Col. 0044D] some works than in others, so as to seem almost another person? But if you bring against us St Jerome in book II of the *Apology against Rufinus*, openly teaching that a certain letter had not come from his workshop but was fabricated under his name, and deriving the argument solely from the difference of style, this does no harm. For that letter assumed the person of St Jerome as repenting because, led by Hebrews, he had translated Hebrew books in which there was no truth. If this had been so, St Jerome would have betrayed himself wholly and plainly as the man he was held by all to be—namely, most eloquent—lest, in a letter in which he was singing a recantation, he should conceal himself, as it were, under a disguised form of speech, not daring plainly to confess his error, as though in a kind of darkness. The situation is otherwise when the matter itself, humility, or the benefit of reading required speaking in one fashion or another.

Erasmus would have acted more wisely had he maintained here the same opinion which he openly states in his annotations on the New Testament, namely on Acts 13 and Hebrews 2. There he frankly attributes all the commentaries to St Jerome and supports his own statements by them—unless one prefers to say that in the annotations he recanted what he had written against St Jerome. For St Jerome’s works are noted as having been printed in 1526, but the fourth revision of the annotations in 1527. We have wished to examine these matters at some length, lest anyone be offended while reading the explanations of the Master of the Sentences, who everywhere cites St Jerome from commentaries which recent critics have dared to disparage as spurious.

Nevertheless, I would not have you immediately infer from this that the books are invariably by the authors under whose names they are inscribed, as though there had nowhere been error and there were no spurious works; rather, my purpose was to prevent rash judgment.

[Col. 0045B] Moreover, a difficulty might be raised by what we shall often say: namely, in reconciling the ecclesiastical edition with the Hebrew truth, that the Hebrew codices we possess were corrupted after the Seventy Interpreters, or otherwise altered. This seems especially troublesome since St Jerome himself, in his translation according to the Hebrew standard, writing to Sophronius, generally follows the reading of the Hebrew codices of our own age. We shall meet this difficulty with two axioms. First: St Jerome had already begun, even in his own age, to regard the Hebrew codices as suspect in certain passages. Second: after St Jerome, Hebrew books abound in manifest errors and stand far removed from the original integrity of Scripture. These claims must be supported by proofs.

As to the first: St Jerome, expounding Micah chapter 5, “And thou, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah,” says: “We read, only according to the Seventy Interpreters, in Joshua—where the cities and towns of the tribe of Judah are described—among other things also this: ‘Theco and Ephrathah, this is Bethlehem,’ [Col. 0045C] etc.; which is found neither in the Hebrew nor in any other translator. And whether it was erased from the ancient books through the malice of the Jews, lest Christ should appear to have been born from the tribe of Judah, or added by the Seventy, we do not know anything certain with clear assurance.”

Again, discussing the Apostle’s words in Galatians 3, “Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree,” he asks why the Apostle omitted “by God,” which occurs in Deuteronomy chapter 21. He answers in two ways. First, thus: “It seems to me either that the old Hebrew books differed from what they now contain; or that the Apostle gave the sense, not the words; or—what is more likely—that after Christ’s Passion the name of God was inserted by someone both in Hebrew and in our codices, in order to fasten disgrace upon us, who believe in Christ as cursed by God.”

He then argues that nowhere in Scripture can anyone be shown explicitly to be cursed by God, with the divine name expressly added. To establish his opinion—that this was added by the faithless—he says: “Therefore I enter this contest with bold step: I appeal to the books that nowhere is it written, ‘cursed by God.’ And wherever a curse is set down, the name of God is never joined to it.” Afterwards he adduces many authorities. “Cursed art thou above all beasts” (Gen. 3) is said to the serpent; and to Adam, “Cursed is the earth in thy works,” etc. (ibid.).

Perhaps you will object more forcefully with what St Jerome says on Isaiah chapter 6: “And if anyone should say that the Hebrew books were afterwards falsified by the Jews, let him hear Origen, who answers this small question in the eighth book of his Explanations: that the Lord and the apostles, who rebuke the Scribes and Pharisees for their other crimes, would never have kept silent about this crime, which was the greatest. But if they say that the Hebrew books were falsified after the coming of the Lord and Saviour and the preaching of the apostles, I shall be unable to restrain my laughter: that the Saviour, apostles, and evangelists should have produced testimonies in such a way that the Jews would afterwards falsify them.” Thus St Jerome there [Col. 0046A].

But if you attend carefully, you will discover that this does not conflict with the aforementioned opinions of Jerome. It would indeed be absurd to say that the Jews falsified books in passages bearing witness to Christ or to Christ’s mysteries—passages that had not been in their codices before Christ and the apostles cited them, but which they had added on the basis of the apostolic preaching: “Out of Egypt I called my Son” (Matt. 2); “For he shall be called a Nazarene” (ibid.); “Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7); “They shall look on him whom they pierced” (John 19); and other similar texts. St Jerome had set these out before the question under discussion; the meaning of his words is readily gathered from their sequel.

The second axiom is proved. On Matthew 16, “Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?” Jerome says: “Observe that wherever ‘Son of Man’ is written in the Old Testament, ‘son of Adam’ stands in the Hebrew. Likewise, what we read in the Psalm: ‘Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?’ (Ps. 4), is said in Hebrew as ‘sons of Adam’; yet in the extant Hebrew codices one reads *bene ish*, that is, ‘sons of a man.’” [Col. 0046B]

I do not know, however, why it has happened that the same reading occurs in St Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew, if indeed that translation is genuine, although the difference has little bearing upon the sense. Bruno Amorbach, too, in the epistle prefixed to his threefold Psalter, quite plainly admits that Hebrew codices were altered. For he says: “What of the Hebrew truth, as they call it, which we have found somewhat altered—so we suspect—in favour of the Jews of our own time by someone learned in Hebrew? For it greatly favours their expositions. Indeed, the Venetian exemplar did not agree in many places with the most ancient codices of St Jerome.” So he says.

But let us proceed to show plainly that the Hebrew exemplars are corrupted. In Genesis chapter 8, according to the truth, we read that the raven was sent out by Noah and [Col. 0046C] did not return. Yet all the Hebrew codices now available give the contrary sense: namely, that it went out and returned, *vaiet ze iatzo vaschob*, that is, “which went out, going forth and returning.” But the Seventy Interpreters read it with the negation, *ouch hypestrepsen*, “it did not return.” St Jerome follows them in *Against the Luciferians*: “The raven is sent out from the ark and did not return; afterwards the dove announces peace on the earth.” Likewise, writing to Oceanus: “And immediately, when the foulest bird has been driven away, the dove of the Holy Spirit flies down to him.”

Josephus the Jew also supports this in book 1, chapter 5 of the *Antiquities*: “After a few days, as the water receded still further, he sent out a raven, wishing to learn whether any part of the earth had been left clear of water and whether it now seemed safe to go out. Finding everything still flooded, it did not return to Noah.” Thus Josephus.

Sanctes, therefore, should not in the epistle to Clement VII prefixed to his new publication have singled out this passage as though the ecclesiastical reading were falsified. I should rather say that the Hebrew texts are corrupt than repudiate an ancient reading, esteemed for so many centuries. Nor does Augustine of Eugubium accomplish anything by maintaining—although otherwise a defender of Jerome’s edition—that this passage was corrupted by copyists or through the long duration of time. He adds that utterly fabulous interpretations were brought in by commentators, namely that the raven was detained by feeding on a corpse. Yet St Augustine, the light of the Church, does not shrink from this interpretation, which Eugubinus calls a fable: “It is asked whether the raven died or might somehow have remained alive. For if there had been land where it could rest, the dove likewise would have found rest. Hence many infer that the raven might have settled upon a corpse, which the dove naturally avoids.” [Col. 0046D]

St Ambrose also alludes to this in book *On Noah and the Ark*, chapter 17, and makes clear [Col. 0047A] that he too read the passage with the negation. For, discussing why the raven was sent out and did not return, he says: “A higher meaning signifies that every righteous person, when he begins to cleanse himself, first casts away from himself what is dark, unclean, and rash. For every shamelessness and fault is dark, and feeds upon the dead like a raven; but virtue is near to the light, shining with purity and simplicity of mind. Therefore fault is, as it were, sent out and driven away, and separated from innocence, so that nothing dark may remain in the mind of the righteous man. Finally, once gone forth, the raven does not return to the righteous person, because every fault that flees all righteousness seems compatible neither with uprightness nor with justice.” Thus St Ambrose. These things certainly are not, and should not be called, fabulous.

But Eugubinus himself objects: “Then, if he denied that the raven returned, how does this cohere with what is immediately added: ‘Until the waters were dried up’? For what does it mean: ‘it went forth and did not return until the waters were dried up’? Did it perhaps [Col. 0047B] return after they were dried up? Even the dove did not do that.” St Ambrose answers this objection and removes the whole difficulty: “We must also consider,” he says, “why he said that the raven did not return until the water was dried from the earth, as though it afterwards returned. But this is a familiar idiom of divine Scripture. For in the Gospel you have it written of holy Mary that Joseph did not know her until she bore a son (Matt. 1), though certainly neither afterwards did he know her.” Thus far he.

Therefore the negation should not be erased from our codices, as Eugubinus wishes. He likewise maintains that St Jerome’s exemplars in the *Hebrew Questions* are corrupted where they contain the negation. For there the passage is read thus: “After forty days Noah opened the door of the ark which he had made, and sent out the raven; and it went out and did not return to him until the water was dried from the earth.” Thus spoke the Seventy; Jerome then adds his own account: “For ‘door,’ ‘window’ is written in Hebrew; and concerning the raven it is said otherwise: ‘He sent out the raven, and it went forth—going forth and not returning.’”

Eugubinus was moved to call even the codices handed down to us from Germany corrupt because Jerome wrote, “and concerning the raven it is said otherwise.” But it would be astonishing to condemn all exemplars, both ancient and recent. Therefore, unless I am mistaken, just as “window” and “door” are close in meaning, yet Jerome notes that *door* was used for *window*, so the Seventy said of the raven, “it went out and did not return,” whereas the Hebrew reads differently, “it went forth, going forth and not returning,” which Sanctes and Münster translate “going out and returning.” Jerome’s word *otherwise*, then, is used not so that you should understand a contrary sense, as Eugubinus supposed, but another reading. [Col. 0047C]

Thus St Augustine does not write fabulously when, on Psalm 102, he interprets the negation mystically: “Brothers, do not delay to turn to the Lord. There are those who prepare their conversion and defer it, and the raven’s cry comes to be theirs: ‘Tomorrow, tomorrow.’ The raven sent from the ark did not return. God does not seek delay in the raven’s cry, but confession in the dove’s groaning.” [Col. 0047D]

Further, in Job 13 we read: “Even if he should kill me, I shall hope in him.” The Hebrew has a desperate and wholly contrary sentence: namely, “I shall not hope.” Here an error is manifest, unless someone chooses to be foolish for no reason. The error entered because “in him,” or “upon him,” and the adverb of negation do not differ among the Hebrews in sound, but in writing: the former is written with *lamed* and *waw*, the latter with [materially uncertain OCR: Hebrew letters omitted]. Hence Sanctes translates: “Behold, he will kill me; I shall not hope.” Münster too, perceiving that the straightforward sense sounded blasphemous, was compelled to say either that one term had been put in place of the other or that it ought to be read interrogatively, so that the same sense might be restored. These men cry out at Genesis chapter 8 that the negation must be erased and that our edition is corrupt; but there they permit themselves whatever they wish when they find no answer.

Finally, other matters which are to be resolved through variation or equivocation will, God willing, be examined as far as possible in our scholia. For in discussing many things it must be carefully observed, as St Jerome states in book 1 of his *Apology against Rufinus*, how great a forest of ambiguous names and words exists among the Hebrews. This gave material for divergent interpretation, while each translator, amid uncertainties, rendered what appeared to him the more coherent sense. [Col. 0048A]

We must also answer the amazement that arises in some minds when, in the following pages, we frequently attempt to defend the ecclesiastical translation, and, when maintaining that it does not differ from the Hebrew truth, explain that the Seventy read otherwise. For St Jerome confidently testifies to Sophronius, and cites many witnesses of his work, that he altered nothing in meaning from the Hebrew truth. And wherever his edition differs from the older versions, he sends the reader to any Hebrew, so that the reader may plainly see that Jerome is attacked by his adversaries in vain. Yet St Jerome’s translation, corresponding directly to the Hebrew, very often differs widely from the customary reading. Therefore, it seems that we labour in vain to prepare such reconciliations.

The answer is at hand, if you understand that St Jerome did not present the edition he had elaborated from the Hebrew as one to be retained and embraced in common use. Rather, he supplied it especially to a private individual, so that he might answer Jews who maliciously alleged that Hebrew was read differently. Sophronius complained that at almost every point they mocked him; faith was consequently held in contempt. Yet, by following the Hebrew reading which they approve, testimony for Christ’s faith could immediately be drawn against them—testimony which they obstinately denied to Sophronius, who was unskilled in Hebrew letters.

I have thought it good to set down the words to Sophronius: “Since therefore you were now disputing with a Hebrew and had brought forward from the Psalms certain testimonies for the Lord and Saviour, and he, wishing to mock you at almost every phrase, asserted that the Hebrew did not contain what you alleged from the Seventy Interpreters, you earnestly requested that after Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion I should translate a new edition into Latin.” After a few intervening words he adds: “Nor do I say this in order to bite my predecessors or to think that anything should be taken away from those whose translation, most carefully corrected, I formerly gave to men of my own language. But it is one thing to read Psalms in the churches of those who believe in Christ; another to answer Jews who maliciously challenge every word.”

Further, in book 2 of his *Apology against Rufinus*: “Have I said anything against the Seventy Interpreters? Many years ago I gave them, most carefully corrected, to students of my language; daily I expound them in the assembly of the brethren; I sing their Psalms in continual meditation. Was I so foolish that, as an old man, I should wish to forget what I learned in childhood? All my treatises are woven from their testimonies.” Thus Jerome.

From this it is plain that the Church reads the Psalms according to the Seventy, apart from a few passages; nor did St Jerome wish otherwise, unlike those who wish from their Hebrew to impose a rule upon the Church. We know indeed that Aristeas, Josephus, and the whole school of the Jews attribute only the five books of Moses to the Seventy Interpreters—something Jerome reports on Ezekiel chapter 5 and Micah chapter 2. But it is clear that Jerome does not follow that opinion, not only from the authority just cited, but a thousand times over from his commentaries, his letter to Sunia and Fretela, and many other passages.

There is therefore no difficulty if, by way of disputation rather than as a settled conclusion, we attribute the divergence of the Septuagint edition from the Hebrew to a variation of reading which can be derived from similarity of letters, difference of strokes, clearer expression of the sense, multiplicity of equivocation, corruption of exemplars, or any other plausible conjecture. Yet we submit everything to better judgment.

[Col. 0049A] The chief divergence, however, seems to have arisen from the addition of vowel-points, which I am not yet persuaded existed in the time of St Jerome. For you will never find him naming *pathaḥ* or *qameṣ*, or vowel movements of that kind, which later Hebrews have handed down to us. Indeed, from his commentaries in several places it may plainly be inferred that he translated Bibles not at all marked off by points.

First, on Habakkuk chapter 3, “Before his face death shall go”: “For what we have translated ‘death,’” he says, “three letters are set down in Hebrew—*daleth*, *beth*, *resh*—without a vowel. If they are read *dabar*, they signify ‘word’; if *deber*, ‘pestilence.’” Here the printers have added points.

Again, on Isaiah chapter 9, “The Lord sent a word into Jacob”: among the Hebrews, *dabar*, written with three consonantal letters—*daleth*, *beth*, *resh*—according to the circumstances of the passages, if read *dabar*, signifies “word”; if *deber*, “death and pestilence.” Therefore many, troubled by the ambiguity of the expression, do not say that a word was sent, but death. [Col. 0049B]

And on Jeremiah chapter 9, “Speak: thus says the Lord, and human mortality shall fall”: the Hebrew word is written with three letters, *daleth*, *beth*, *resh*—“for it has no vowels in the middle”—and, according to the sequence of speech and the reader’s judgment, if read *dabar* signifies “word”; if *deber*, “death”; if *dabber*, “speak.”

From this it becomes plain that, if vowel-points—as they are now called—had existed, and if the printers had attached them to Jerome’s works, it would not lie within the reader’s discretion what should be read, contrary to the prescribed vocalic movements. This is made still clearer from the letter to Evagrius, in which Jerome discusses whether Salem ought to be called *Salem* or pronounced *Salim*, the city of Melchizedek, king of Salem. “It makes no difference,” he says, “whether it is called Salem or Salim, since the Hebrews very rarely use vowel letters in the middle; and the same words are pronounced with different sounds and accents according to the choice of readers and the diversity of regions.”

[Col. 0049C] Many examples of this kind occur in his *Explanations*. St Jerome calls “vowels” what Hebrew scholars now call gutturals, as is clear from the prologue to the prophet Amos, where he says that this Amos is not the one whom we read as Isaiah’s father. “For the latter is written with the first and final letters of his name, *aleph* and *tsade*; the former with *ayin* and *samekh*.” He then adds: “We do not have so great a difference of vowel letters, and especially of the letter which among the Hebrews is threefold.”

Sebastian Münster, in the preface to his newly issued edition, though he contends with all his powers that vowel-points were not recently introduced, reports that some consider them to be inventions of those dwelling at Tiberias, who were always more cultivated and polished in the sacred language. At last he acknowledges that St Jerome lacked a codex marked by points, and that formerly almost all exemplars lacked points. [Col. 0049D] He goes so far as candidly to assert that there was a cabbalistic tradition which priests were obliged to know and explain to ordinary people. But when, with the passage of time and because of their sins, many tribulations befell them, they were scattered throughout the world, and learned men diminished; they were compelled to commit to writing many things which had previously been known by tradition alone. Thus he.

Then there is a great controversy among the rabbis concerning the uninjured and genuine integrity of the reading. Consequently, those who prescribe laws to our edition out of what I may call the superstition of their points accomplish nothing. Rabbi David Kimhi, of no ordinary authority among Jews and Hebrew scholars, says in the preface which he placed before the Prophets, and on 3 Kings 18—as Münster translates him—that in the first captivity the exemplars were corrupted: they drew one reading from one exemplar and another from another; and where they could not obtain a clear sense, they wrote one word in the text and another in the margin. The exemplars perished and were scattered; and when the wise men who held the sense of Scripture died, those of the Great Synagogue attempted to restore the Law to its ancient state. Finding disagreements among the exemplars, they trusted the reading supported by the greater number. But wherever they could not obtain clear knowledge, they wrote one word without points, or wrote it in the margin rather than in the text. [Col. 0050A]

Rabbi Jacob, son of Hayyim, rejects this opinion of Kimhi and the other rabbis as follows: “Their opinion is far from me. For I cannot be induced to believe and confess with my lips that Ezra the scribe found the book of the divine Law and the books of the prophets doubtful, corrupted, and confused. Rather, it is my opinion that Ezra and his colleagues found the sacred Bibles whole and unharmed, and that Ezra by his own judgment recognized which books had been written through that excellent wisdom.”

See: Hebrew scholars do not agree concerning the fidelity of their own codices. [Col. 0050B] I would not doubt, however, that they were sound in the age of the apostles; but concerning the marks of the points, as we said above, this has not yet been demonstrated. While we were writing these things, the long-desired little book of Elijah the Jew, published on accents and translated by Münster, came into our hands. In it he confirms our view concerning the question of the points in every way, so copiously and lucidly that no scruple can remain.

At last, after much discussion, he persuades us that vowel-points were invented and added to the Bibles by the masters of the Masorah, Tiberian men from Mysia in Asia Minor, as we touched on above, highly practiced in sacred Scripture. This took place after the four hundred and thirty-sixth year from the destruction of the Second Temple, and therefore after the four hundred and sixty-eighth year from the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. Among other arguments, he says that a large part of the names of the points are Syriac and Babylonian. This Elijah is still alive, second to none in grammatical learning, as all candidly proclaim. [Col. 0050C]

Perhaps you will object: in Matthew chapter 5 it is written, “Amen I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, one iota or one apex shall not pass from the Law until all things are fulfilled.” But the Hebrews call vowel-points “apices”; therefore, if points existed in Christ’s time, they could not have been invented by later Jews. Yet the Gospel does not use *apices* for their points, but for the smallest part of a letter. This is evident from St Jerome himself on the same passage: “The form of the letter shows that even those things thought least in the Law are full of spiritual mysteries.”

Again, on the sole chapter of Obadiah: “What is written in Isaiah, ‘The burden of Dumah,’ may be read, with a small stroke changed, as *Roma* instead of *Duma*: *resh* in place of *daleth*. For the letter *waw* is used in their language both for *v* and for *o*.”

And on Zephaniah chapter 3, “I will restore to the peoples a chosen lip”: “The Seventy read *bedorah*, *resh* instead of the letter *daleth*, judging, because of the great similarity of the letters, which are distinguished by a small stroke.”

Likewise, on Isaiah chapter 27, “Whom shall he teach knowledge?” The Hebrew word *de‘ah*, which all translated “knowledge,” the Seventy alone interpreted as *kaka*, that is, “evils.” The error is plain. For the first letter, *daleth* or *resh*, is distinguished by a small stroke. Thus, if *de‘ah* is read, it means “knowledge”; if *ra‘ah*, “wickedness.” Hence the Ordinary Gloss: “An apex is the uppermost small part of a letter; it signifies the least commandment, or the least part of a commandment.”

Indeed, St Jerome in *Against Helvidius* seems to take *apices* for the letters themselves: “Will not the letters themselves speak to me and refute me for folly—that he is called firstborn who opened the womb, not one who has brothers?” [Col. 0050D]

You will again raise an objection from St Jerome on Ephesians chapter 3, “that the Gentiles are fellow-heirs, fellow-members of the body, and fellow-partakers”: “I know,” he says, “that the addition of the conjunction by which one says ‘fellow-heirs, fellow-members, and fellow-partakers’ makes the sentence inelegant in Latin; but because it occurs in Greek, and in the divine Scriptures individual words, syllables, apices, and points are full of meanings.” [Col. 0051A] Here St Jerome appears to distinguish *apices* from *points*; but no points other than those called vowel-points among Hebrew scholars are found. Therefore, they were not of recent origin. Nor is it enough to say that St Jerome speaks of points—that is, Greek accents—because he is interpreting the Epistle to the Ephesians, which was written in Greek. For he adds “in the divine Scriptures,” showing that he is speaking generally.

But these considerations do not compel that conclusion. For perhaps from the beginning the Hebrews, like the Greeks, possessed certain marks of accents, which may be understood as points. Thus St Jerome, on Ezekiel chapter 27, writes: “Hebrew names are frequently interpreted in different ways because of differences of accents and especially because of changes in vowel letters, which among them have their own particular properties.”

Or he may have used *points* in the sense in which, writing to Evagrius concerning various opinions about Melchizedek, he says: “I have read these things in Greek volumes, and have wished to set forth, as it were, the broadest regions of the earth upon a little tablet—not extending the spaces of meanings and treatises, but signifying infinite matters through certain points and summaries, so that in a small letter you might learn at once the opinions of many.” [Col. 0051B]

In a similar sense one must take the same author’s words on Malachi chapter 3: “From this it is clear that the apostles, evangelists, and the Lord and Saviour himself did not follow the authority of the Seventy Interpreters, which those possessing knowledge of the Hebrew language do not need; rather, they translated from the Hebrew what they had read, not concerning themselves with the syllables and points of words, provided that the truth of the meanings was translated.” And even more clearly, in the prologue to the prophet Malachi: “I do not know that I have read other commentaries on this prophet, except a short booklet of Apollinaris, which ought to be called not so much an interpretation as the points of an interpretation.”

## On the Commentaries: Whether They Are the Master’s

[Col. 0051C] Finally, that we may at last cease prefacing and come nearer to the matter: let us discuss the grounds on which we have concluded that these various extracts, assembled with great care into one body, are by Peter Lombard. A reasonable doubt might arise because the four exemplars which we were permitted to inspect lack the author’s name.

But Abbot Trithemius in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* will satisfy you: “Peter Lombard,” he says, “wrote, with discerning study, from the sayings of the holy Fathers, the commendable work of the *Sentences*, four books; one book upon the entire Psalter, whose opening is: ‘Since all the prophets,’ etc.”

No less trustworthy evidence is supplied by the very carefully compiled catalogue of the library of the most devout monastery of the Fathers of Saint Victor, from which we received a codex through spontaneous and kindly familiarity. It expressly attributes these commentaries to Peter Lombard by name.

Add also that, in one exemplar [Col. 0051D] communicated to us, an ancient hand had begun to mark the letter **M** in the margin wherever it saw various interpretations by different doctors stitched together, as though indicating the Master’s painstaking diligence. Perhaps overcome by the weariness of a rather long labour, it finally ceased to proceed; yet sometimes, as though roused again, it repeatedly made the same mark. Add that a certain codex had at its end, although in a different hand: “Psalter from Lombard’s glosses.”

The reader should further be warned that, in different exemplars, the names of the authors cited in the *Explanations* were marked in various ways at the heads of pages. In some, Haymo is indicated; in others, nowhere. In these, Gregory, Remigius, and Isidore appear; in those, not at all. And however authors were cited, the order was disorderly and unsettled, leaving the reader uncertain where they spoke when he came to the context of the commentaries, how much of a given opinion and how far it should be assigned to its author. [Col. 0052A]

Although, in our exemplar, certain marks of points were written here and there above the sequence of lines, by which one might distinguish whose words were written below, we could have distinguished from the points the extent of the marked author’s exposition if we had found everywhere that nothing had been omitted and how far the interpretation extended. The points showed me who had begun to speak, but not how far. For among the successive little marks there are very often intermingled many matters that required marks of their own. Moreover, we discovered that such signs frequently went astray and were omitted in many places. From this one may suspect either that such marking points were not originally supplied, or that they were copied corruptly.

The same must be said concerning the title and number of the cited authors. Even if in certain exemplars authors are noted in regular order in the margin and in the passages beneath, the difficulty already mentioned remains. Therefore persistent labour was necessary, so that we might draw [Col. 0052B] from the original sources what ought to be affixed in the proper places. Thus, for example, when you see Augustine, Jerome, and others simply cited in an open codex, understand that they are cited from their writings on those Psalms. But if passages had to be sought from their other volumes, they are marked in the margin, as far as possible. A few things that might delay the reader, create obscurity, require a brief explanation, or raise a difficulty are briefly clarified.

Further, because the doctors are not always quoted word for word, but their thought is gathered and constructed—now from the beginning, now from the end, then again from the beginning and middle of their works—we preferred to note in the margin, point by point, “from such-and-such an author,” rather than cite them in the direct grammatical form. And where Cassiodorus and later writers agree with Augustine, it was necessary only to identify Augustine, since, drawing from him, they should be considered as one.

Although Jerome is older than Augustine, where they agree we indicate Augustine rather than Jerome, because [Col. 0052C] where Jerome discusses something briefly, Augustine, in his manner, expands upon it at length. Augustine is also continuous throughout this work beyond the others, who are cited intermittently and in separated passages, except that Cassiodorus occurs very frequently. Where individual authors say something distinctive, they are indicated separately. If an opinion is drawn jointly from two, they are linked by one conjunction. Finally, when we have not found an author cited, we attribute it to the Master, indicated by the letter **M**. This is very rarely done, and was omitted by the printer through a certain inadvertence.
