Moreover, we very frequently cite Alcuin and the interlinear gloss; by this understand that by “Alcuin” we mean the ordinary gloss, following the statements of the historians Antoninus of Florence and Robert Gaguin. The latter, speaking of Charlemagne, says: “He cultivated his mind in the liberal disciplines, first under Peter of Pisa, then under Alcuin the Englishman, a man exceedingly learned in divine and human matters. Antoninus of Florence reports that he was the author of the glosses on the Bible [Col. 0052D] (which they call the ordinary gloss), namely in Part Two, Title 14, Chapter 5. This is supported by what Sigebert writes in his *Chronicle*.”

Alcuin, otherwise called Albinus, a native of Britain and the cherished master of King Charles, excelled in literary learning in Gaul. Under his instruction in particular the king himself learned all the liberal arts. He wrote many things, among which especially notable are the books on the Holy Trinity written for the king himself; likewise, at the king’s command, he corrected the sacred history. Yet Abbot Trithemius raises a difficulty by affirming that Strabo was the compiler of such a work. “This Strabo,” he says, “is recorded as having been the first to assemble, from the sayings of the holy Fathers, the gloss now called ordinary, upon the whole Bible.” The statements called the *Chronicle of Chronicles* agree sufficiently with this. Strabo, a most diligent commentator and pupil of Rabanus, commented very beautifully upon the books of the Bible.

Whatever the case may be, it is most certain that such compilations were enlarged and expanded by later hands beyond both Alcuin and Strabo [Col. 0053A]. For Rabanus, who was Alcuin’s pupil, is often indicated; so is Strabo; and Alcuin himself is called Rabanus’s scribe—persons whom it is more probable were added by later writers than by themselves. Add that Isidore, who preceded them all, is cited very often. Haymo, Bede, and Remigius are occasionally alleged: the latter is later; the former are sufficiently close to the men already named. Trithemius agrees with us on this point, saying that others later enlarged this gloss by adding sayings of the Fathers.

Moreover, in copies printed from type we have far more than in older handwritten books. Nevertheless, we preferred to adopt “Alcuin” rather than “the ordinary gloss,” or any other name, because in some copies of this collection of maxims Alcuin was sometimes marked. Besides, the Master, in Book II of the *Sentences*, Distinction 12, expressly cites Alcuin on Genesis; and this is read in the ordinary gloss. Again, in Book III, Distinction [Col. 0053B] 18, Ambrose is cited; the Master appears to have taken Ambrose’s view from the ordinary gloss on Chapter 9 of the Epistle to the Hebrews, since Ambrose’s commentary on that epistle is lacking. [Note: [Col. 0053C] It is now said to have been printed.]

Furthermore, in Book IV, Distinction 4, the Master appears to call the ordinary gloss “authority”; for, introducing Hebrews chapter 6, he says: “Hence authority says that the Apostle used the plural, ‘foundations of baptisms,’ because there is baptism in water, in blood, and in repentance,” etc. You will find all these things in the ordinary gloss on that chapter.

Nor should you wonder that, in this miscellany of the Master, almost everything found in the ordinary and interlinear glosses is read nearly word for word. Since in both cases the same material was taken up, it could not happen otherwise than that a patchwork gathered from similar joinings should advance at equal pace toward the same aim. But the materials that lay in the ordinary and interlinear glosses like sand without lime, he here reduced beneath the text into order by applying a subtle binding mixture.

[Col. 0053C] Add that whoever finally prefixed the name-headings by which cited authors could be recognized [Col. 0054A] in the confused heap of the ordinary gloss, very often listed them most confusedly and incorrectly. For where Augustine ought to be noted, he assigns Cassiodorus, and conversely. Where the beginning or end of a statement belongs only to one interpreter or another, he so marks the name as though the entire statement belonged to the person indicated. Indeed, where one author interprets a matter in one way and another in the opposite way, he sometimes attributes their writings in reversed order, so that each has the opinion opposed to his own. In addition, he leaves places anonymous very frequently, as though their author were uncertain, although they claim a proper author for themselves, like other passages, and perhaps sometimes more certainly than those he labels. You will readily verify all this by reading. These things are so evident that it would be superfluous to dwell upon them longer.

In handwritten books, however, the authors’ names were very rarely appended. It was therefore no idle task, but an exceedingly laborious one, to restore citations to those cited, lest something like a confused chaos arise. Finally, to conclude: [Col. 0054B] as regards the interlinear gloss, we are sufficiently persuaded that it is older than this kind of compilation, lest anyone suspect that what the Master comments upon was transferred into glosses of this kind rather than the reverse. For this gloss is inserted in ancient books and libraries, especially because those ancient authors, owing to scarcity of writing materials and the narrowness of writing space, delighted in brevity.

John Trithemius also supports us in many respects. Among ecclesiastical writers he lists Anselm of Laon, a man keen in intellect, scholastic in speech, distinguished no less by life than by learning, who by a new manner of exposition explained the Scriptures of both Testaments with interlinear and marginal glosses drawn from the writings of the Fathers. From the same author we gather that he flourished about thirty years before the Master of the *Sentences*. Finally, you will learn from these commentaries matters so excellent, which are not found in other bundles of glosses, that you will not regret frequent reading. Enjoy them, therefore, and fare well in the crucified Jesus, friendly reader.

## TO THE READER

[Col. 0053]

How much fruit and advancement in learning this Peter Lombard of ours will bring you, friendly reader, can be sufficiently taught even by the forest of worthy authors whom you see cited. Further, you will find here not merely the thought of one doctor, as commonly happens elsewhere, but a certain oracle—as I might call it—of the holy men: an exposition settled and sanctioned among those saintly and ancient doctors, approved by him to whom the name “Master” is rightly given, like a judgment delivered by the chief senator after the votes of those sitting with him.

Whatever you may draw from this work, do not suppose it sought from stagnant pools, from muddy streams, or from the Egyptian and bitter rivers of heretics. Everything is full of that ancient and primal teaching by which the Church flourished when it shone with the old doctors like jewels and pearls. If Lombard had written only his own opinion, his learning and judgment would surely not have been so inferior that his studies could not have been counted among the monuments of the doctors. But when by his own judgment he has approved as sacrosanct the interpretations of other—and not ordinary—authors, what worthy of a good and modest man, what ancient and received doctrine, will you not be able here either to hear or read?

Indeed, in place of so many commentaries on the Psalter, this one alone may suffice you; thus you may dispense with the others, since in this work you possess together all those whom the most learned judge selected. Add that the Psalm titles have been collected so fully, learnedly, and usefully that you will find nowhere else such a storehouse of riches; and afterward you will acknowledge that nothing more readily prepares, in brief compass, a path to the true understanding of the Psalms. So much for the commentaries.

But with regard to the apology of that excellent and most learned doctor Richard of Le Mans, I would address a few words to two classes of persons: first, those who have until now been content with our Vulgate edition; second, students of the Hebrew language. Let the former not despair as soon as they see a few Hebrew or Greek words, as though they could derive no benefit from them because they have made no progress in those languages. Let them read carefully the apology, which he calls a “comparison,” compare it with the verse under discussion, and read the commentary on that place. They will then see how ridiculous it is, on slight grounds and deliberately, to disparage as foolish and unworthy of being held in Christians’ hands the ecclesiastical edition which all the ancients have highly praised, which Jerome, Lyra, and several other men skilled in Hebrew have received, approved, and illuminated with commentaries.

They will also find here a most ready objection against certain shallow pedants of this age. Having scarcely learned the first elements of the sacred language, they babble against the Latin edition whenever word does not answer word, or when phrases—of which the Hebrews abound in astonishing number—are not sufficiently unfolded among us. Such people, forsooth, cultivate modesty: they arrogate to themselves what even those most expert in that language and possessed of the keenest judgment do only with restraint.

Finally, I ask candidates for Hebrew learning to pardon the author of this apology if he rebukes certain persons more sharply than they would wish. A candid man, impatient of headlong novelty, perhaps feared that Christianity would be endangered by this path. Consider what the unlearned multitude may think when overwhelmed by so many translations differing not only from the Vulgate but also from one another by the widest interval. I would certainly venture to declare that good men do not act modestly when they so easily and freely depart from the common edition, or force upon the public their own version as perfect and as the only one.

It is one thing to point out a Hebraism and separately explain that the same passage can be translated in different ways; it is another, through private desire and with the slightest judgment in a most weighty matter, to publish one’s own fancy and vomit it before the public like undigested food. Would that those in Paris who are most accomplished in this language, but most modest, might sometime deliver their judgment—keen as it is—on such matters. Then it would be possible to observe that many petty scholars of this age have rushed into producing various editions more for novelty and display of intellect, not to mention profit, than in order that we might possess pure and complete Scripture. For one who wishes to be useful and is not mad manages the matter so that, precisely when undertaking it, he causes no trouble and does not produce a great disadvantage from promised benefit.

Use these commentaries, then, friendly reader, and embrace the apology, if you value the authority of the Church and do not wish the commentaries of the ancient doctors on the Psalter to be ruined. Yet if printers sometimes deserve indulgence because they cannot print everything so correctly, John Louis Tiletanus, even if he does not request it—confident in his diligence—justly deserves pardon. The labor expended on the old handwritten copy could not easily be expressed. Besides swarming with innumerable errors, both in spelling and in the establishment of divisions, it was so difficult to read that a good many words had to be guessed rather than read.

In the Hebrew words, however, we noted no errors, although a mistake occurred on a few pages because it was not possible to be present promptly with the printer when he began printing the first sheets. But this happened rarely and only in a very few pages first given to the press. Farewell.

# PETER LOMBARD’S COMMENTARY ON THE PSALMS OF DAVID

## PREFACE

[Col. 0055]

[Col. 0055A] Although all the prophets are known to have spoken by revelation of the Holy Spirit, David, the outstanding prophet, prophesied in a certain more worthy and excellent manner than the others, like a trumpet of the Holy Spirit [Cassiodorus]. For the other prophets prophesied deeds and sayings through certain images of things and coverings of words—that is, through dreams and visions. David, however, set forth his prophecy by the impulse of the Holy Spirit alone, without any outward aid.

Accordingly, this book is appropriately called the *Book of Soliloquies*. [Jerome and Remigius.] It is also called the *Psalter*, a name taken from a musical instrument called in Hebrew *nablum*, in Greek *psaltērion* (ψαλτήριον), from the Greek ψάλλειν (*psallein*), “to touch”; in Latin it is called *organum* (“instrument”). It has ten strings and gives forth sound from above through the touch of the hands. The book is literally named from that instrument because David sang psalms to the sound of it before the ark in the tabernacle of the Lord. And just as each melody of that instrument was called a psalm, so each section or clause of this book is called one.

In spiritual understanding too it fittingly takes its name from that instrument: as the instrument has ten strings, so this book teaches observance of the Ten Commandments. And as that instrument gives forth sound from above through the touch of hands, so this book teaches right action, not for earthly things but for the heavenly things which are above.

[Col. 0055C] This book consists of one hundred and fifty psalms, not without a reason of deeper significance. [Col. 0056A] For this number is marked by very notable mysteries. It consists of eighty and seventy; and eighty signifies the same as eight, while seventy signifies the same as seven. Eight signifies the eighth age, that of resurrection: since there are six ages of those living and seven of those dying, the eighth age will be that of those rising again. This began when souls began to rest at Christ’s Passion. Seven signifies the time of this life, which is lived through the recurrence of seven days. The book is therefore rightly composed of this number of psalms, whose parts signify the aforesaid mysteries, because it teaches us so to work and live in the sevenfold course of this life that in the eighth age of resurrection we may not [Col. 0056B] be clothed in the double garment of confusion, but in the robe of double glorification.

Or it was composed in this number of psalms because, as we have said, this number consists of eighty and seventy, which signify the same as eight and seven. [Augustine.] Eight signifies the New Testament. For the fathers of the New Testament serve the *ogdoad*, that is, the number eight: they observe the eighth day of Christ’s resurrection, namely Sunday, and the octaves of saints, while awaiting the eighth resurrection. Seven, however, signifies the Old Testament, because the fathers of the Old Testament served the *hebdomad*, that is, the number seven. They observed the seventh day, the seventh week, the seventh month, [Col. 0056C] the seventh year, and the seventh year of the seventh decade, which is also called the Jubilee. Thus Solomon says: “Give portions to seven, and also to eight” (Eccles. 11); and Micah: “We shall raise up over them seven shepherds and eight princes” (Mic. 5). This book, then, was rightly issued in this number of psalms, whose parts signify the teaching of both Testaments, so that it may be shown that the commandments of both Testaments are contained in this book.

This book is also divided into three fifties, signifying the three states of the Christian religion: the first in repentance, the second in righteousness, and the third in the praise of eternal life. Therefore the first fifty ends with repentance, namely, “Have mercy upon me, O God, according to …” (Ps. 50); the second with righteousness: “I will sing of mercy and judgment unto thee, O Lord” (Ps. 100); the third with the praise of eternal life: “Let every spirit praise the Lord” [Col. 0057B] (Ps. 150). Because David teaches these things in this book, this threefold division of the psalms is made.

[Remigius.] It should also be noted that this Scripture is used more than the others in ecclesiastical offices. This is because in this book lies the completion of the whole theological page: here are described the rewards of the good, the punishments of the wicked, the rudiments of beginners, the progress of those advancing, the perfection of those arriving, the life of the active, and the contemplation of the contemplative. Here too is taught what sin takes away, what repentance restores, what a penitent conscious of sin should say—namely, “O Lord, rebuke me not in thy wrath,” etc. (Ps. 6), and elsewhere, “Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great …” (Ps. 50)—and what the penitent obtains through repentance. It continues: “I will teach the wicked thy ways, [Col. 0057C] and the ungodly shall be converted unto thee” (ibid.).

This shows that no one, however greatly he has sinned, should despair of pardon and God’s mercy if he takes up the humility of repentance. For when we see David, a murderer and adulterer, made through repentance a teacher and prophet, no place for distrust is left to anyone concerning the performance of repentance. So too Saul’s conversion and his elevation to apostleship fully assure us of God’s mercy. Therefore the Church uses his Epistles more than those of others in its offices, just as it uses David’s prophecy.

This prophecy is also in more frequent use because it excels the others in clarity of expression. What the other prophets said obscurely and as if through riddles [Col. 0057D] about Christ’s Passion and resurrection, eternal begetting, and the other mysteries, David—the most excellent of the prophets—opened so manifestly that he seems rather to proclaim the Gospel than to prophesy. Having considered these matters, it remains to see what its title is, what its subject matter is, what its intention is, and what its mode of treatment is. Its title is as follows:

> The Book of Hymns, or Soliloquies, of the Prophet concerning Christ begins.

It says “book,” not “books,” against those who maintained that there are several books because of the five divisions of psalms marked by “Let it be, let it be.” Jerome too agrees with them, but their reason is not valid. Though there are five divisions, there are not therefore to be called five books, just as there are several divisions of Paul’s Epistles and yet one book. This is also clear from David’s own words, when speaking in the person of Christ he says: “In the beginning of the book it is written of me.” [Cassiodorus.] He says “of the book,” not “of the books,” indicating that there would be one book, not several. Hence it is also said in the Acts of the Apostles: “As it is written in the book of Psalms” (Acts 1); it does not say “books.” Thus it is one book, although Jerome says there are five because of the five divisions.

“Hymns, or Soliloquies.” [Augustine.] A hymn is praise of God with song. A song is an exultation of the mind concerning eternal things, breaking forth into voice. This book is therefore aptly called a book of hymns, because it teaches us to praise God with exultation concerning eternal things, [Col. 0058B] not only in heart but also in voice, so that whoever hears may say, “Come” (Rev. 22), curtain may draw curtain, and our fountains may flow abroad. These hymns are written metrically among the Hebrews, though this could not be preserved in translation.

Or, “Soliloquies.” [Cassiodorus.] Here one must see what prophecy is, in what ways it occurs, and according to what times. Prophecy, then, is divine inspiration or revelation announcing events with unchangeable truth. Thus prophecy is called vision, and a prophet is called one who sees. It occurs in four ways: through deeds or sayings, through things seen to be said or done—that is, through dreams and visions.

Through deeds: as through Noah’s ark, which signified the Church; and through the iron griddle placed between the prophet Ezekiel and the city. Through sayings: as through what the angels said to Abraham and other faithful persons, for example, “In thy seed shall all nations be blessed” (Gen. 22), and such things. Through visions: as happened to Jeremiah, who saw a pot kindled from the face of the north; and to Moses, who saw the burning bush that was not consumed; and Ezekiel saw a wheel within a wheel. [Col. 0058C] Through dreams: as through Nebuchadnezzar’s dream, in which he saw a stone cut from a mountain without hands. What was a dream to the king was prophecy to Daniel. Likewise Pharaoh’s dream, in which he saw seven cattle and seven ears of grain, was prophecy to Joseph, who understood spiritually.

Besides these, there is another mode of prophecy, more worthy than the rest: when one prophesies by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit alone, with every external aid of deed, saying, vision, or dream removed. David prophesied in this way, namely by the impulse of the Holy Spirit alone. Hence in what follows: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me” (Ps. 84). For this reason it is called a soliloquy, as though the utterance of the Holy Spirit alone. Although in titles and in certain psalms he alludes to various histories, nevertheless he learned nothing from them; rather, in them he understood as figured what he had previously known through the Holy Spirit.

Or they are called soliloquies as though utterances concerning Christ alone. For the others prophesied about Christ obscurely and as if through riddles, but David discussed most manifestly his incarnation, Passion, eternal begetting, and resurrection; thus it is called the Book [Col. 0059A] of Soliloquies. Just as prophecy occurred in different modes, so it also occurred according to different times. One prophecy concerns the present, another the past, another the future. Of the present: Elizabeth’s words, “Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1). Of the past: Moses’s words, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). Of the future: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” etc. (Isa. 7).

Prophecy may be through good persons, such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, and others; and through evil persons, such as Balaam, Caiaphas, and others. Again, one prophecy is according to the foreknowledge of God and must be fulfilled in every way, even according to the tenor of the words, as: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive” (ibid.). Another is according to threat, as: “Forty days remain, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah [Col. 0059B] 3); this is fulfilled not according to the surface of the words, but according to the import of an unspoken meaning.

When “the Prophet” is said by excellence, with no proper name added, David is understood; just as when “the Apostle” is said, Paul is understood, and when “the City” is said, Rome. This is said against certain persons who maintained that there were several writers or authors of the Psalms because names such as Asaph, Heman, Ethan, and Jeduthun occur in their titles. We shall show in the book that this was done for the signification of mysteries perceived from the interpretation of the names. Those persons, therefore, were not authors of the psalms; the placement of their names serves the rationale of the mysteries.

“Concerning Christ.” Behold whom the Soliloquies concern: the whole Christ, that is, head and body.

[Col. 0059C] The subject matter of this book, then, is the whole Christ, namely bridegroom and bride. Its intention is to conform human beings, deformed in Adam, to Christ the new man. Its mode of treatment is as follows. At times it treats Christ according to the head, at times according to the body, and at times according to both. It treats Christ according to the head in three ways: at times according to divinity, as, “With thee is the beginning” (Ps. 109); at times according to humanity, as, “I lay down and began to sleep” (Ps. 3); and at times by transference, when he uses the voice of the members, as in, “Far from my salvation,” etc. (Ps. 21), and “O God, thou knowest my foolishness,” etc. (Ps. 68). Likewise, it treats the Church in three ways: [Col. 0059D] at times according to the perfect, at times according to the imperfect, and sometimes according to the wicked who are in the Church in body, not in mind; in name, not in divine reality.

It is also customary to ask concerning the order of the psalms, which differs from the sequence of history, why they are not arranged in the order in which they were composed. Clearly they are not: for the history treated in “Have mercy upon me, O God” (Ps. 50) preceded that treated in “O Lord, how are they multiplied?” (Ps. 3); and “Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands,” etc. (Ps. 17), was composed before both the aforesaid psalms. The reply is that, though a reason for the order can be given in some cases, it cannot be given in all. Yet they are not arranged so without reason.

For Ezra the prophet, who restored by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit the Psalter and the whole library burned by the Babylonians, arranged the psalms in this manner by revelation of the same Spirit, and added the titles to them. These are, as it were, keys to the psalms: just as one enters a house through a key, so the understanding of the psalms set beneath becomes clear through fitting expositions of their titles. These matters are to be observed concerning the entire book.

In addition, certain particular matters must be considered in individual psalms.

[Jerome, Commentary.] Therefore, concerning the first psalm, let us see why no title is prefixed to it as to the others; what its subject matter is; what its intention is; and what its mode of treatment is. [Cassiodorus.] A title is not appended to the first psalm because this psalm is the beginning, preface, and head of the book, as is said in the following passage: “In the beginning of the book it is written of me.” It treats of him who is the beginning of all things, namely Christ, who has no beginning. [Jerome, Commentary.] Thus it lacks a title lest the title written before it should seem to be the book’s head and beginning; or also because this psalm is, as it were, the title and prologue of the work that follows. For it contains the summary and subject matter of the entire book.

The subject matter of this psalm is the same as that of the whole book: the complete Christ. Its intention is likewise the same. Its mode of treatment is as follows. The psalm has two parts. First, it treats of the blessed man, alluring us by blessedness. Second, it treats of the punishments of the wicked, frightening us by adversities, at the words: “Not so are the wicked, not so.” It treats of the blessed man in this manner: in the first verse it shows him free from every evil; in the second, full of every good in himself and thereafter useful to others, up to the division.

To show him free from every evil, it uses a comparison with the old man, Adam, showing that he was full of every evil. For nothing better demonstrates the excellence of anything than when the baseness, oppression, or lowliness of its contrary is not left unmentioned. It shows, then, that the old Adam sinned in a threefold manner: namely in thought, will, and act; in the teaching or habitual practice of speech. Again, “thought,” taken broadly, embraces three things: the first movement of the soul, which is venial fault; pleasure; and consent, which are mortal sins. Thus whoever sins by consent sins also in thought; but whoever does not sin even in thought does not sin by consent or pleasure.

It marks these three kinds of sin by three words: “went,” “stood,” and “sat.” By “went,” sin of the will; by “stood,” sin of deed; by “sat,” sin of speech or habitual practice. Adam therefore went away from God—not in place, [Cassiodorus] but in unlikeness—when, assenting to the persuasion of the devil and Eve, he departed from God. [Alcuin.] He stood when, eating the forbidden fruit, he took pleasure in sin. He sat when, excusing himself and referring blame to the Creator, he was confirmed in pride (Gen. 3), saying, “The woman whom thou gavest me deceived me.” [Augustine.] He could not return except by being set free through him who had none of these things.

[Col. 0061A] This is said by comparison with exiles: while they are still on the road they are more easily recalled; once they stand still, with greater difficulty; finally, with greatest difficulty when they have already become teachers and masters there. Likewise, one who sins by will alone returns more easily; one who sins by deed, with greater difficulty; but one who sins by habitual practice or by the teaching of speech is recalled with the greatest difficulty. [Augustine, Book I, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, and Sermon 90, *On Time*.] These are the three dead persons whom the Lord raised: in the house, at the gate, and in the tomb. This is the three-day period in which Moses wished to lead God’s people out of Egypt.

Again note: “of sinners, of the ungodly, of pestilence.” For the ungodly person sins against God; the sinner against himself; the pestilential person against his neighbor. Adam sinned against God, against himself, and against his neighbor.

[Col. 0062A] [Remigius.] As though he said: The first human being was miserable and unhappy, who went in the counsel of the ungodly. [Interlinear Gloss.] That is, of the serpent and Eve: that is, he sinned by consent of will; he stood in the way of sinners, that is, he sinned by deed. [Alcuin.] And he sat in the chair of pestilence, giving others an example of sinning—that is, sinning by teaching or habitual practice. For a chair properly belongs to teachers, as a throne to kings and a tribunal to judges. [Remigius.] Behold, he has shown that the first human being sinned in three ways. Sin is committed in thought, deed, and words, by teaching. Now the things which increased in their order in the first human being must be removed in the second. As though he said: The first human being was unhappy—he went, stood, and sat—but the second is blessed.

# PETER LOMBARD’S COMMENTARY ON THE PSALMS OF DAVID

[Col. 0061]

## PSALM ONE

[Col. 0061B]

**VERSE 1.**—“Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, and has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the chair of pestilence.”

[Cassiodorus.] Blessed is said of one to whom everything desired comes successfully: namely, a man firm against prosperity and adversity, who has not gone [Interlinear Gloss] away from God into the region of unlikeness—that is, who did not sin in thought—although he was placed in the counsel of the ungodly, that is, although the ungodly plotted this. This is more praiseworthy. [Augustine and Jerome.] This man did not go away as Adam did, who consented to his wife, deceived by the devil. The ungodly who plotted this are demons, scribes, and Pharisees.

“And has not stood in the way of sinners.” [Augustine.] The way of sinners is the world, in which indeed he was born and lived among sinners; yet the allurements of the age did not hold him. [Interlinear Gloss.] Or, the way of sinners is perverse action which leads to death. Thus, “he has not stood in the way of sinners” means: neither in the world nor in perverse action did he stand.

“And has not sat in the chair of pestilence.” [Augustine.] That is, he did not desire an earthly kingdom. Pestilence is a disease widely spreading and involving all or nearly all; it is said to derive from *pastus* (“feeding”), as though *pastulentia*. This is the love of ruling, which scarcely anyone lacks. Or, more fittingly, the chair of pestilence is perverse and destructive teaching, which creeps like a cancer. Thus, “he has not sat in the chair of pestilence” means that he taught not destructive teaching but saving teaching. Behold, in this first verse he is shown free from every evil by the removal of the things which were in the first human being.

[Col. 0061D]

**VERSE 2.**—“But his will is in the law of the Lord; and in his law he shall meditate day and night.”

“But in the law of the Lord.” [Remigius.] Here Christ is shown [Col. 0062B] to be full of every good in himself, because it is not perfect praise to flee blameworthy things unless praiseworthy things follow. Therefore, after showing his freedom from evil, he adds, “But in the law,” as though saying: He did not go, stand, or sit, but his will was in the law of the Lord. [Augustine.] It is one thing to be in the law and another to be under the law. One who is in the law acts according to the law, voluntarily obeying it; one who is under the law acts according to it under compulsion from fear. The former is free; the latter a slave.

Again, one thing is the law of the letter, written for a slave; another is the law of holiness, perceived in the mind by a child, who has no need of letters. “Law is not laid down for the righteous,” as the Apostle says (1 Tim. 1). Thus he says “in the law of the Lord” because his will—that is, Christ’s will—served voluntarily, not under the law as though serving from sorrow and fear. [Cassiodorus.] He says “will” to show that labor was no weariness to him. This will is neither idle nor momentary. [Augustine.]

“But he shall meditate day and night”: that is, continually, in prosperity and adversity. Day signifies joy; night, adversity. [Cassiodorus.] “In his law”: certainly not in the letter of the law, but in holiness of purpose. This meditation on the law is continual observance of holiness. See how these answer the preceding statements. There it says, “he did not go”; here, “his will is in the law.” There, “he did not stand in the way of sinners” and “did not sit in the chair of pestilence”; here, “he shall meditate continually in the law of the Lord.”

**VERSE 3.**—“And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of waters, which shall give its fruit [Col. 0062D] in its season.”

And he shall be like a tree that is planted. [Alcuin.] Above he showed Christ exempt from every evil and [Col. 0063A] filled in himself with every good; here he is shown as useful to us, and in three ways: namely, by giving the fruit of life, leaves, and shade. Note that all these things do not belong to every blessed man, but to Christ alone. This is a full definition of the blessed man, as though he said: “He shall meditate day and night, and he shall be like a tree.” He speaks of Christ by comparison with the tree of life which stood in the midst of Paradise; if obedient man ate from it, he would live for ever. So whoever spiritually receives Christ shall never see death [Gloss, in loc.]. And as that tree was greener than the others, so Christ was greener than all other saints, to whom the Spirit was not given by measure [Jerome]. Therefore he was like a tree—that is, truly the tree of life—as Wisdom says: “It is a tree of life to all who embrace it” [Col. 0063B] [Gloss, in loc.].

“Like” sometimes indicates mere resemblance; sometimes it expresses reality; and sometimes both, as here. For it indicates resemblance in such a way as not to exclude the expression of reality [Augustine]. “Which is planted,” that is, made man or incarnate, whereby we may approach him. And this is “beside streams of waters” [Alcuin and Augustine]. The waters signify the Holy Spirit, according to the saying: “He who believes in me, from his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7). They are set against the heat of vices, as water is against the heat of thirst. Thus, “it is planted beside streams of waters,” that is, he will become man through the operation of the Holy Spirit, who descended upon him most fully. Therefore it adds “streams of waters,” in order to indicate fullness [Alcuin].

Or, by water is understood the wisdom of God, [Col. 0063C] because the inward man is refreshed, just as thirst is refreshed by water. Thus, “planted beside streams of waters” means: according to Wisdom, which assumed humanity; that is, he will become man united to the wisdom of God. And it rightly says “beside the water,” because God was not made man by the mutability of one nature into another, but by the union of person [Augustine].

Likewise, the waters are the mortal human race. Hence John in the Apocalypse says: “Many waters, many peoples” (Rev. 17), because they flow down into death as water flows into the sea. Thus, “planted beside streams of waters” means: amid the flowing multitude of peoples, because he appeared “in the likeness of sinful flesh” [Gloss, interlinear].

“That tree shall give its fruit,” that is, eternal life, “in its season,” that is, in the time of fullness, when the entrance to Paradise was opened, [Col. 0063D] concerning which [Augustine] says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6).

Or thus: “He shall give his fruit,” that is, establish churches, “in its season,” that is, after the resurrection and ascension, when the Spirit had been sent. Or thus: “He shall give his fruit,” that is, he will send the Holy Spirit, “in its season,” that is, after his glorification. Hence in the Gospel: “The Holy Spirit had not yet been given, because Christ had not yet been glorified” (John 7).

Note that this tree is rational, from the fact that it says “shall give” [Cassiodorus]. For giving belongs to rational awareness and to the will of the one who offers.

VERSE 4.—“And his leaf shall not fall, and whatsoever he does shall prosper.”

[Augustine.] “And his leaf shall not fall,” that is, [Col. 0064A] his word shall not be ineffectual, but shall lead to life. Hence: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24). [Cassiodorus.] Words are aptly called leaves, because just as leaves cover their fruits, so the Lord’s words preserve his promises [Alcuin].

And what does each expression mean? [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Gloss, interlinear.] “And whatsoever he does shall prosper,” that is, fruits and leaves—deeds and words—shall prosper for him, in contrast to Adam’s fall, and for his members. And it rightly says “whatsoever,” because even though he should die, all that he does shall nevertheless prosper, since his death is the salvation of the world.

PART II, VERSE 5.—“Not so the ungodly, not so; but they are like dust which the wind casts away from the face of the earth.”

“Not so the ungodly.” Here is the second part, in which he treats [Col. 0064B] of the punishments of the wicked and terrifies them with adversities. Fear of these makes the promises more welcome, as though he said: “All things belonging to him shall prosper. But the ungodly are not so, because they shall be able to attain nothing.” Note that by this repetition unshakable firmness is shown.

“Not so”; rather, they are like dust, because they yield to evil suggestions and do not possess the moisture of God’s grace. “The wind casts it away,” that is, pride, which is compared to wind because it seeks lofty things and puffs up; “from the face of the earth,” that is, from the presence of eternal stability [Augustine], which is called earth by comparison, because just as this earth nourishes and sustains the outward man, so that one nourishes and sustains the inward man.

VERSE 6.—“Therefore the ungodly shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.”

“Therefore the ungodly shall not rise.” Since the wind casts them away, [Col. 0064C] that is, because they were given over to a reprobate mind, therefore the ungodly do not rise in the first resurrection, which is by faith—namely, from sins. And this is “in judgment,” that is, so that they may judge and accuse themselves.

For there are two resurrections. One is of the soul, in the present, by which a person rises from sins. Hence the Apostle says: “Awake, you who sleep, and Christ shall enlighten you” (Eph. 5). The other is of the body, in the future, by which it shall become impassible and immortal. Here he treats of that of the soul.

“Nor shall sinners themselves likewise rise in the counsel of the righteous,” so as to prefer God’s will to their own wills; this is the counsel of the righteous. Or, “in the assembly,” another reading, “of the righteous,” that is, in the concordant multitude of the righteous; and the meaning is the same as the preceding one [Col. 0064D], taking “sinners” and “ungodly” as the same persons.

Or thus: he says that what the proud desire is taken away from them—namely, the power to judge. He speaks of the resurrection of the body and the future judgment, as though he said: Since the wind casts them away, therefore the ungodly shall not rise “in judgment,” that is, in order to judge. This he repeats more plainly [Augustine]: “nor shall sinners themselves rise in the assembly of the righteous,” that is, in the judgment, in order that they may judge together with them. He calls judgment a “counsel” by comparison, because God’s judgment will be as it were a council, in which different sins will be punished by different penalties.

Or thus, let us understand “ungodly” as one group and “sinners” as another. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The ungodly are unbelievers, idolaters, and apostates; when they rise, they shall not be judged, because they have already been judged. Sinners are false Christians. Thus: because the wind casts them away, therefore the ungodly—that is, those wholly without faith—[Col. 0065A] shall not rise in judgment in order to be judged, because they have already been judged; nor shall sinners—that is, false believers—rise in the counsel of the righteous in order to judge, but shall only be judged.

[Jerome and Augustine.] Note that there will be four orders at the judgment. Some will judge and will not be judged, such as the apostles and others most perfect. Others will neither judge nor be judged, because they have already been judged. For the sentence of their condemnation is known to the whole Church, as in the case of unbelievers. Others will be judged and saved, as those moderately good; others will be judged and condemned, as those moderately evil. Therefore Job says: “He does not save the ungodly, and grants judgment to the poor” (Job 36). For those who are wickedly oppressed will then come as judges [Col. 0065B] over their oppressors.

[Gregory and Jerome.] There are indeed two divisions: the elect and the reprobate; but two orders are contained in each division. Some are judged and perish; others are not judged and perish; others are judged and reign; others are not judged and reign.

Those are judged and perish to whom, by the Lord’s denunciation, it is said: “I was thirsty, and you gave me no drink. Depart, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). But others are not judged and perish at the last judgment, concerning whom the prophet says: “The ungodly shall not rise in judgment,” and the Lord says: “He who does not believe has already been judged” (John 3). And Paul says: “Those who sinned without the law shall perish without the law” (Rom. 2). Yet all rise, even unbelievers, but for torment, [Col. 0065C] not for judgment.

2 For their case is not then examined when they come before the sight of the strict Judge already bearing the condemnation of their unbelief. Those, however, who retain the profession of faith but do not have works corresponding to that profession are rebuked so that they may perish, as moderately evil persons. But those who did not even hold to the sacraments of faith will not hear the Judge’s rebuke in the final examination, because they have already been condemned in the darkness of their unbelief; they do not deserve to be rebuked by the denunciation of him whom they despised. At least those hear the Judge’s words who have held his faith at least in word. These do not receive even the words of the eternal Judge in their condemnation, because they refused to preserve reverence for him even verbally.

The former perish under the law, because they sinned while placed under the law. To the latter nothing is said concerning the law in their destruction, because they made no attempt to possess any law. For a ruler governing an earthly commonwealth punishes differently a citizen who offends within it and an enemy rebelling outside it. In the former case he consults his laws and condemns him under the words of a fitting denunciation. Against the enemy, however, he wages war, employs instruments of destruction, and repays torments deserved by that enemy’s wickedness. The law does not inquire what charge it has against his evil.

Thus, at the final judgment, the legal denunciation strikes the one who departed in action from what he held by profession; while the other is destroyed without a judicial denunciation, because he is not bound by the law of faith. But among the elect, some are judged and reign: those who wipe away the stains of life with tears. [Col. 0066A] Redeeming their earlier evils by later deeds, they cover before the Judge’s eyes whatever unlawful thing they once did by the added covering of alms. To these, standing at the right hand when the Judge comes, he says: “I was hungry and you gave me food,” and so forth (Matt. 25).

Others, however, are not judged and reign. By the power of perfection they transcend even the commandments of the law, because they are not content merely to fulfil what the divine law commands all persons to fulfil, but in a more excellent desire seek to offer more than they could hear in the general commandments. To these the Lord says: “You who have left all things and followed me, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, shall yourselves sit upon thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19). And concerning them [Col. 0066B] the prophet says: “The Lord will enter into judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. 3). And of them Solomon, speaking of the bridegroom of holy Church, adds: “Her husband is noble in the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. 31).

These, therefore, are not judged and reign in the last judgment, because with their Author they come also as judges. For in leaving all things, they have performed by their own devotion more than they heard commanded generally. The special command given to a few more perfect persons, and not to everyone generally, is what the rich young man heard: “Go and sell all things,” and so forth (Matt. 19). For if the general command bound everyone under this precept—that is, this counsel—it would certainly be a sin for us to possess anything in this world. [Col. 0066C] But one thing is said through Holy Scripture to all, and another is commanded specially to the more perfect.

These, therefore, are rightly not held under the general judgment, because by their way of life they have surpassed even the general commandments. For just as those who, persuaded by unbelief, disdain to keep the law are not judged and perish, so those who, persuaded even by piety, fulfil more than the general commandments of the divine law are not judged and reign. Hence Paul too, transcending special commandments, performed more labor than he received from the ordinance of law and permission. [Augustine.] For though he had received the right that, while preaching the Gospel, he should live by the Gospel, and had given the Gospel to its hearers, he nevertheless refused to be supported at the Gospel’s expense.

Why then should this man be judged in order to reign, who received less that he was obliged to observe, but found a greater rule by which to live? Judgment is rightly granted to the poor, because the more they were despised in this world with great humility, the more, when they receive seats, they rise then to a higher summit of power. Hence it is elsewhere said: “Until righteousness is turned into judgment” (Ps. 93). Righteousness is thus turned into judgment, because those who now live justly and blamelessly then receive the power of judging.

Hence the Church of Laodicea is told: “To him who conquers I will grant to sit with me upon my throne, as I also conquered and sat with my Father upon his throne” (Rev. 3). The conquering Lord declares that he sat on the throne with his Father, because after the struggles of his passion, after the palm of his resurrection, he judged it fitting to make clear to all [Col. 0067A] that he was equal to the Father’s power; and, having trampled down the sting of death, he made known that he was not unequal to him. Hence he says to Mary, who did not yet believe him to be equal to the Father: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20).

For us to sit upon the Son’s throne is to judge by the authority of the same Son. Because we receive the primacy of judgment through his power, we sit as it were upon his throne. Nor is it inconsistent with truth that elsewhere he testifies that the disciples will come upon twelve thrones, while here he declares that they will sit upon his throne. By the twelve thrones, universal judgment is shown; by the Son’s throne, the particular height of judicial authority is indicated.

Or thus, taking the same ungodly and sinners: because the wind casts them away, “the ungodly shall not rise in judgment,” that is, to judge in the future. [Col. 0067B] This agrees with the second interpretation, but what follows differs: “And therefore sinners themselves shall not rise in the counsel of the righteous,” that is, to rest, once judged, in the fellowship of the saints. Or, “in the counsel of the righteous” has the same meaning: in the eternal good, which it is the counsel of the saints to pursue.

VERSE 7.—“For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the path of the ungodly shall perish.”

“For he knows,” as though he said: The ungodly do not rise with the saints in judgment, because God loves the works of the righteous but not those of the ungodly. This is the meaning of “for he knows,” and so forth.

Or, connect it with the first preceding interpretation: They do not rise here in the soul because God does not approve their works; for he approves those of the righteous alone. This is the meaning of: “For the Lord knows the way [Col. 0067C] of the righteous,” as his own, and approves it; “but the path,” that is, the work, “of the ungodly shall perish.” He says “shall perish” in place of “the Lord does not know,” but this is stated more plainly, because what perishes is that which is not known by the Lord, while to be known by the Lord is to remain and to exist.

COLLATION ON PSALM I: “BLESSED IS THE MAN.”

VERSE 1.—“He has not sat in the seat of pestilence.” Our translator seems to have expressed the Hebrew and Greek term more significantly, marking the utterly corrupt destruction of heretical perversity, than if he had said “of mockers,” Hebrew LETZIM, or translated “of pestilences,” Greek λοιμῶν. For in simply reading “of mockers,” or in reading the plural “of pestilences,” perhaps one does not receive such force of emphasis as the Prophet intends and as Saint Jerome explains on Isaiah 66: “I will choose their mockers, or their mockeries, [Col. 0067D] and bring upon them the things they feared.”

“He gives the reasons,” Jerome says, “why they were delivered over to their mockers, the Scribes and Pharisees, concerning whom the first psalm, according to the Hebrews, sings: ‘He has not sat in the seat of mockers’; the Seventy call them pestilent, such as were the sons of Eli, sons of pestilence. Likewise, on Isaiah 3, ‘And effeminate men shall rule over them,’ he says that in Hebrew TAALULIM is written, which the Seventy and Theodotion translated ‘mockers.’ He then adds: We may call mockers also the teachers of the people of Israel, who devour God’s people as bread for food, perversely interpret the Holy Scriptures, and mock the foolishness of their disciples. Again, on the same prophet’s words, ‘My people, those who call you blessed,’ and so forth (Isa. 3), he had called the Scribes and Pharisees exactors, not teachers, and above, mockers.” So he says.

These remarks clearly suggest that our edition, besides other things, prophetically censures the pestilent leaven of the Pharisees, of which the Savior says in Matthew 16: [Col. 0068A] “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Luke 12). Moreover, Jerome himself, commenting on this passage of the psalm, says:

“For ‘pestilent,’ the Hebrew has ‘mockers,’ because a perverse teacher mocks all disciples. The Hebrew root from which the word is derived also signifies to interpret wordily: Job 16, ‘My verbose friends,’ MELITZAIREHAI. For what are heretics but hunters after words, according to Proverbs 19: ‘He who pursues only words shall have nothing; but he who possesses understanding loves his own soul’? Do you not now plainly see heretics, with bombastic and foot-and-a-half-long words and distorted interpretations, scorning all the ceremonies of the Church as though in unrestrained laughter and with wrinkled, sneering noses? By these they infect wretched souls with an incurable corruption, to the common destruction of all, if it were possible. Therefore, to gather together what has been scattered: the heretical, superstitious, and windy doctrine which David wished to be absent from the blessed man at the beginning is most fittingly designated by the single name ‘pestilence.’ For from any one of those things, unless care is taken, a most pestilent corruption spreads widely. Therefore perverse teachers, having fallen into such madness of wickedness, are to be rejected with such detestation that they are called not evil men but wickedness itself; not pestilent men, not mockers, but, singularly and in the highest degree, pestilence. Learn, then, to venerate our translation, which in so small a word comprehends so great a matter, the deeply hidden meaning with which the Hebrew word LOTZ was pregnant.”

VERSE 5.—“Not so the ungodly, not so.” The Hebrew reads it only once: “not so,” *lo chen*. The Seventy or other Greek versions indicated by repetition the weight of the statement, as in Psalm 21: “My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” where the Hebrew does not have “look upon me.” For the weight of the matter is more deeply felt by that vocal addition, owing to the immeasurable sorrow of Jesus Christ suffering grievously on the cross, of whose wondrous endurance that entire psalm speaks.

Saint Jerome adduces a similar instance in *On the Best Method of Translating*, addressed to Pammachius, from Mark 5: TALITHA QUMI, which is translated: “Little girl, I say to you, arise.” “Let Jerome be accused,” he says, “of falsehood because he added ‘I say to you,’ when the Hebrew has only ‘Little girl, arise.’ But in order to make it more emphatic, ἐμφατικώτερον, and to express the sense of the speaker and translator, he added ‘I say to you.’” So he says.

Nevertheless, as regards the present passage, Jerome asserts that he found “not so” only once in Origen’s Hexapla. “Which the wind casts away from the face of the earth.” In Hebrew one finds only: “which the wind casts, or will cast, away”—*ASCHER TID PENNU RUACH*. The Seventy, in agreement with our edition, add ἀπὸ προσώπου τῆς γῆς, “from the face of the earth,” in order to express the latent meaning contained in the Hebrew words. [Col. 0068D]

But the rendering “chaff” by Sanctes, followed by the interpreter for Cajetan; “straw” by Münster; and “stalk” by the paraphrase of Campensis, does not fit the Prophet’s meaning as well as “dust,” which our version has, as do Jerome according to the Hebrews, Conrad, and Pratensis. For although MOTH may mean indiscriminately chaff, fine straw, dust, or refuse, the wind does not ordinarily cast common chaff away from the face of the earth; rather, a winnowing fan or threshing instrument casts it away from the face of the threshing floor. But the wind everywhere, as is evident, continually stirs up dust. By this the inconstancy of the ungodly and their perpetual separation from the stability of eternal life are most significantly denoted, according to Lamentations 1: “Jerusalem has sinned grievously; therefore she has become unstable.”

Nor do I see why these men rejected the edition which they call the Vulgate. Certainly, the more common it is, the more acceptable it is. New things require much longer proof than old things, [Col. 0069A] which have been tested through so many years. And those new things would have no authority, or at least less authority, unless they became old.

VERSE 6.—“Nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.” The Master interprets *concilium* as both that which belongs to the will and that which belongs to an assembly, in the double sense in which the Seventy understood it. For it is known that βουλή means both. Nor is the Hebrew ADATH, that is, “assembly,” harmed by this, since the Lord’s counsel is the congregation of the righteous, who do not depart from his will by so much as a fingernail’s breadth. Hence Psalm 88, “God who is glorified in the council of the saints,” may be read in two ways, either with *s* or with *c*, even from the Hebrew BESOD, so that you understand “the congregation of the saints,” whose saving counsel is to glory in the Lord once they have acknowledged their own frailty.

SECOND PSALM.

[Col. 0069]

3 TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0069A]

“Why have the nations raged?” [Cassiodorus.] This psalm is second in order and first in title. Hence it is also called the first in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 4). The prophet Ezra appended titles to the psalms; they are like keys and doorways of the psalms. For through their understanding the meaning of the psalms set beneath them becomes clear. Although history is frequently touched upon in the titles, or certain names are placed there concerning which the psalms do not speak literally, nevertheless history mystically understood and names suitably interpreted disclose the content of the psalms.

Thus here David is named. His name is interpreted “strong in hand, desirable in appearance,” and he signifies Christ, who is truly strong in hand in defeating the powers of the air, and desirable in appearance—that is, one into whom the holy angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1). A psalm denotes good action. Literally, a psalm was a melody produced by touching ten [Col. 0069C] strings; so too good action is performed through observance of the Ten Commandments.

The meaning of the title is: this psalm—that is, this treatise—is called a psalm because it exhorts to good works; it is attributed to David, that is, to Christ, who here speaks of himself as king. In its intention it exhorts us to submit to him. Its structure is as follows: the psalm has three parts. First, it rebukes and threatens the persecutors, and Christ or the Prophet speaks. Second, it introduces Christ’s words concerning his almighty kingdom and his unfailing generation, where we learn much concerning his divinity and humanity: “But I have been appointed,” and so forth. Third, after these mysteries have been disclosed, it admonishes all to obey him humbly, persuading them by what is useful—namely, lest they perish—and by what is honorable, because “Blessed are all who trust in him”: “And now, O kings.” Therefore, rebuking the persecutors, the Prophet, or Christ, says:

VERSE 1.—“Why have the nations raged, and the peoples devised vain things?”

[Remigius.] “The nations,” that is, the Roman soldiers, the crucifiers, [Cassiodorus,] “raged” [Remigius] like irrational beasts; for raging is the action of beasts. [Cassiodorus.] “And the peoples,” namely, the Jews, [Gloss, interlinear,] “devised vain things” [Alcuin], that is, false things from the Scriptures, concerning the Messiah yet to come, whom they await. For they are Abraham’s children, waiting with the she-ass.

[Remigius.] Or, “devised vain things,” that is, to hold Christ in death. Or, “they devised vain things,” namely, that the world should not go after him. [Augustine.] And why? That is, with what advantage to themselves? As though he said: In vain, because they did not achieve their purpose that Christ should be extinguished.

[Col. 0070A] VERSE 2.—“The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ.”

[Remigius.] “The kings stood,” as though he said: Not only the peoples and nations—that is, the lesser persons—[Col. 0070B] rose against Christ, but also the greater, because “the kings of the earth stood,” as if with delay; for delay is indicated in this phrase. [Gloss, interlinear.] “The kings of the earth,” namely Herod, and “the rulers,” namely Pilate. [Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, book 3, chapter 16.] The plural is used for the singular by synecdoche.

Or, “the kings of the earth” means the earlier Herod, who killed the infants, and the later Herod, his son, who concurred with Pilate in Christ’s death. [Cassiodorus, Remigius.] “They stood,” and “the rulers”—namely, the priests, Annas and Caiaphas—“assembled together,” that is, in one evil will.

[Cassiodorus.] A foolish presumption: the kings of the earth assembled against the King of heaven. This he explains by saying, “against the Lord,” that is, against the Father. For whoever contradicts the Son also contradicts the Father. Therefore, “against the Lord,” that is, because “against his Christ,” that is, against me, insofar as Christ speaks.

VERSE 3.—“Let us break their bonds asunder, and cast their yoke from us.”

VERSE 4.—“He who dwells in the heavens shall laugh at them, and the Lord shall mock them.”

“Let us break their bonds,” as though he said: They say this. [Gloss, interlinear.] But, O my own people, says Christ, do not consent to my death; and this is: “Let us break their bonds,” that is, their flatteries and threats, “and let us cast their yoke from us,” [Remigius, Gloss, interlinear,] lest they rule over us.

“He who dwells in the heavens.” The connection according to this interpretation is: Christ says, “Let us break them,” because he who dwells in the heavens. [Augustine, Remigius, Cassiodorus.] Otherwise, from the words “Let us break their bonds”: although this may be said in Christ’s person, as we read it, these words fit better those who do not wish to submit to Christ’s yoke—that is, Christ’s persecutors. Christ or the Prophet says, as though they had assembled together, kings and rulers, saying: “Let us break their bonds,” [Alcuin] that is, their arguments—those of God and Christ, or Christ and his disciples—by which they wish to bind us to themselves; “and let us cast their yoke from us,” [Remigius] that is, the law.

They say these things; but surely he who dwells [Augustine, Alcuin]—that is, the Lord—“in the heavens,” namely the spiritual heavens, that is, holy souls and angels, shall laugh at them as it were with his cheeks. This occurred when, guards having been set, he rose again. And the Lord shall mock them as it were with his nose; this occurred [Col. 0071A] when they were scattered throughout the world.

[Jerome.] For laughter is made with the cheek, but mockery is expressed with a wrinkled and contracted nose. These things, however, must in no way be understood carnally of God; they are anthropopathic, ανθρωποπαθῶς, that is, expressions of human feeling attributed to God.

Otherwise [Augustine], God’s laughter is the power of foreknowledge which he gives to the saints, so that, seeing Christ’s name destined to be among all nations and his dominion to spread among future generations, they may understand that those men devised vain things. “He who dwells in the heavens” remains unchanged. “He shall laugh at them,” that is, he shall give his saints understanding that they are to be laughed at and have devised vain things. “And the Lord shall mock them” is a repetition.

VERSE 5.—“Then he shall speak to them in his wrath, and in his fury he shall trouble them.”

“Then,” that is, moreover; and then, namely when he shall laugh, “he shall speak to them in his wrath.” This is anthropopathy, ανθρωποπάθος, that is, a human emotion, when what belongs to the creature is attributed to the Creator. [Augustine.] For God’s wrath is a movement arising in a holy soul which knows God’s law when it sees that law transgressed by an evil person. By this movement many acts of vengeance are performed, as Moses did when he descended from the mountain and saw the people playing before the calf: girded with a sword, he went from gate to gate. So too Phinehas, when he pierced the Jew and the Midianite woman engaging in shameful intercourse.

Thus, “he shall speak to them in his wrath,” that is, he shall rebuke and punish them through saints who will be moved by their sins. He explains this more plainly afterwards, saying: [Col. 0071C] “And in his fury he shall trouble them.” [Augustine.] Both the wrath and fury of God are the darkening of the minds of those who transgress the law. Thus, “then he shall speak to them,” that is, he shall blind them.

Or, this verse is read partly of the present and partly of the future, thus: [Gloss, interlinear.] “Then,” that is, when he shall laugh, “he shall speak to them” through prophets and through Holy Scripture, and this “in his wrath,” that is, in the threatening of punishment; and in the future “he shall trouble them” in body and soul, “in his fury,” that is, in eternal punishment.

Or, the whole passage from “He who dwells” is read of the future in this way: [Remigius.] “He who dwells in the heavens” remains unchanged. “He shall laugh at them,” that is, he shall make them worthy of laughter in the future. He then repeats the same thing: “And the Lord shall mock them.” Then, namely in the future, “he shall speak to them,” who now seems silent while he endures them, “in his wrath, and in his fury he shall trouble them.” [Augustine.] God’s wrath and fury are not a disturbance, which is wholly absent from him, but his power—that is, his might—by which he justly punishes. Thus, by his power he shall punish them.

VERSE 6.—“But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his commandment.”

“But I.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] Here is the second division, where he introduces Christ’s words concerning his almighty kingdom and ineffable generation, in which we learn much concerning Christ’s divinity and humanity. As though he said: They shall indeed be troubled; but “I,” says Christ. [Augustine, Gloss, interlinear.] “I” is said with emphasis, as though he said: I whose yoke and bonds they wished to cast off, “have been appointed [Col. 0072A] king by him,” the Father, “over Zion, his holy mountain”—that is, over the Church from the Jews, which is called the holy mountain because it first receives the rays of faith, as mountains first receive the rays of the sun. This accords with: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15).

[Jerome, Cassiodorus, Remigius.] “Proclaiming his commandment,” that is, the Gospel, or that spiritual commandment concerning which he says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13). [Gloss, interlinear.] He is not king over the Jews only, but also over the nations. The author proves this by the Father’s authority, since it was doubtful; and this is the meaning: I am truly king even over the nations, because:

VERSE 7.—“The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you.”

[Col. 0072B] VERSE 8.—“Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession.”

The Lord—the Father—said to me [Alcuin], that is, promised me. Note that the person reigning speaks here, that is, Christ as reigning; or the person of the ruler, that is, the Father, promised what I have said. That is: the Father promised me, “Behold, I will give you the nations,” [Gloss, interlinear,] that is, the nations of the world, “for your inheritance,” which you may cultivate. “Your inheritance,” as though he said: an inheritance which is yours insofar as you are God. [Cassiodorus.] An inheritance is so called from *herus*, “master,” because the master rules over it in free power.

“And I will give you the ends of the earth.” [Augustine.] Here he puts “ends of the earth” for what he had above called “nations,” but more clearly, so that you may understand all nations—not a part of the earth, but the whole possession—which you may possess for their advantage and salvation, and that they may bear good fruit for you. I call it “your possession,” as though he said: I shall give you the nations, which nevertheless you possess together with me as God.

[Gloss, interlinear.] “And in order that I may give to you, ask of me,” that is, obey by suffering and dying, that you may thus be able to ask. [Augustine.] For the words “ask of me” belong to the assumption of humanity—that is, to human nature—which took place for the salvation of humankind; according to that nature he intercedes for us, and this is what it means to ask.

The reason why I will give you the nations as an inheritance rather than to some other obedient person [Alcuin] is that you are my Son, consubstantial by nature, by an ineffable generation; and truly so, because I, coeternal with you, have “begotten you today,” [Col. 0072D] that is, eternally. [Gloss, interlinear.] This generation is not new, but was accomplished from eternity. [Augustine.] Although “today I have begotten you” could literally be understood of the day on which Christ was born according to his humanity, nevertheless, since “today” signifies presence and whatever is eternal always is, it is rightly understood divinely of the eternal generation of the wisdom of God.

Note that in some of the foregoing things Christ agrees with others. [Alcuin.] For he was appointed king by God, as the kings of the earth too were appointed by him; and he preached over Zion, [Cassiodorus] as the prophets preached. He is the Son, as Israel also is called a son. Hence the Lord says to Pharaoh through Moses: “Let my firstborn, Israel, go.” But “Today I have begotten you” belongs to Christ alone. [Remigius.]

[Col. 0073A] Otherwise, by Zion, which is interpreted “watchtower” or “contemplation,” is understood the universal Church, which contemplates God’s glory and is a mountain by the eminence and firmness of its virtues. Thus: “But I have been appointed king by him”—this remains unchanged—“over Zion, his holy mountain,” [Augustine] that is, over the holy universal Church, which contemplates God and is firm and lofty in virtues. “Proclaiming his commandment” also remains unchanged. I rightly say that I have been appointed king by him because the Lord said to me: “I will give you the nations for your inheritance,” and so forth. These and what follow remain unchanged.

Note, however, that the Father’s “saying” is understood in several ways: as disposing, making, begetting, and promising. Here it may be understood as disposing or promising.

[Col. 0073B] VERSE 9.—“You shall rule them with a rod of iron, and you shall break them like a potter’s vessel.”

Rule them with an iron rod. [Cassiodorus.] As if he said: “I will give you the nations, and deservedly so, because you will rule them.” [Cassiodorus.] That is, you will not be a tyrant with an iron rod, [Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, with inflexible justice or royal power; and you will break them unto life like a potter’s vessel, [Augustine] that is, insofar as they are a potter’s vessel—that is, clay—you will crush in them whatever they have contracted from the sinful mire. [Alcuin.] Or thus, so that it is understood partly in a good and partly in an evil sense, according to Simeon’s saying: “Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many” (Luke 2); so that “he who is righteous may still be justified, and he who is filthy may still become filthy” [Col. 0073C] (Rev. 22). [Cassiodorus.] Thus: “You will rule them,” that is, the good, “with an iron rod”: this is Christ’s royal power. “And you will break them,” namely sinners, by permitting them to become still more filthy; they are like a potter’s vessel, being both earthen and easily broken.

**VERSE 10.** “And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth.”

And now, O kings. [Cassiodorus.] Here is the third division, in which, after these matters have been disclosed, he admonishes all humbly to obey him. He persuades from what is useful—namely, lest they perish—and from what is honorable: because “Blessed are all who trust in him.” Note that in the first part the Prophet speaks in a certain manner of expression; in the second, Christ alone; here, in the third, the Prophet again speaks after Christ in a certain manner of expression. [Cassiodorus.] [Col. 0073D] In the first part, therefore, he comes forward as a Prophet, that is, he speaks before Christ, as the prophets prophesied before Christ. In this part he speaks after Christ as an apostle, that is, bearing the figure of the apostles who preached after Christ.

As if he said: “The clay has been crushed. And now, since the clay in you has been crushed, and you have been renewed and made kings,” [Augustine] that is, now able to rule yourselves—you “who judge,” that is, condemn, “the earth,” [Remigius] that is, earthly things within yourselves—“understand what has been said.” And if you are not sufficient by yourselves, be instructed by others. He calls the saints “kings”; and Christ or the Prophet speaks. [Gloss, interlinear.] Alternatively, Christ speaks: “Thus the Father promised me; but you who have been made kings, namely you who judge the earth”—these things are unchanged from the first explanation—“now,” [Col. 0074A] that is, through what has been said, understand how great are the things the Son accomplishes; [Augustine] and, if you are not sufficient by yourselves, be instructed by others. Lest they should grow proud on that account, he adds:

**VERSE 11.** “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling.”

[Augustine.] Serve the Lord, who does not permit one to sin, in fear, so that “he who stands may take heed lest he fall.” [Cassiodorus.] But lest this appear a wretched servitude, he adds, “and rejoice in him,” [Augustine] because the fear of the Lord is not misery but joy. Yet lest one again fall into recklessness, he adds, “with trembling,” lest the rejoicing be negligent.

[Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Alternatively, the whole passage is Christ speaking to the kings of the earth, as if to say: “I have been appointed king; and now that I have been appointed king, you kings who judge the earth [Col. 0074B] literally should not be distressed, but understand and be instructed. For it is advantageous to you to be subject to him from whom come understanding and instruction; and it is advantageous not to rule rashly, but to serve the Lord of all and rejoice in blessedness.” This is what follows: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling.” And—

**VERSE 12.** “Lay hold of discipline, lest at any time the Lord become angry, and you perish from the righteous way.”

Lay hold of discipline, even if God’s discipline—namely adversities—flees from you. [Gloss, interlinear; Augustine.] “Lay hold,” I say, as upon a defense and safeguard. “Lest at any time the Lord become angry”: he says “lest at any time” doubtfully. [Augustine.] [Col. 0074C] Yet this doubt is not in the Prophet, but in those who think of God’s anger with uncertainty. [Cassiodorus.] Or he says “lest at any time” because of God’s patience, since in this age he endures for a long time. “Lest you perish from the righteous way,” that is, being removed from Christ, or from good action. [Augustine.] To fall away from this is a great punishment for those who have tasted the sweetness of righteousness.

**VERSE 13.** “When his wrath shall blaze forth swiftly, blessed are all who trust in him.”

“When it shall blaze forth”: as if he said, “Lay hold, lest you perish—and so that you may be blessed, which is more.” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] For when it blazes forth, it does not burn now, when he chastises as a father; but it will burn in the future, when there will be no patience. “Swiftly,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] because he will examine not each of these things separately, but all together at once. Or, “swiftly,” although they think his wrath—that is, the punishment of the wicked—to be far off: all who trust in him will be blessed. The sense is: [Augustine] when it shall blaze forth, that is, when the punishment of the wicked comes, it will not merely fail to touch those who trust in God; they will also be blessed, because they will attain the kingdom.

## Comparison on Psalm II, “Why Have the Nations Raged,” etc.

**VERSE 6.** “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain.” The Hebrew: *NASACTI MALCHI AL TSION HAR QODSHI*: “I have appointed my king over Zion, my holy mountain,” or “the mountain of my holiness.” But the Septuagint, and consequently our translation, rendered the sense in the passive, with the third-person pronoun referring to the Father, because of the immediately preceding verse: “Then he will speak to them,” [Col. 0075A] so that the statements might cohere more suitably. For David had named God in the preceding lines in the third person; therefore, after threatening evils with punishment, he aptly added: “I have been appointed king by him,” in the person of the Son, notwithstanding the counsel of the wicked.

The verse which immediately follows is likewise connected in that arrangement: “The Lord said to me”; for, if one anxiously follows the Hebrew reading, the speech passes from the third person of the verb into the first, and immediately from the first into the third, as the impulse of the Spirit suggested, who “breathes where he wills” (John 3) and touches the prophet’s mind. Good interpreters, however, though touched by the same Spirit, adapt themselves more closely to ordinary human usage—something which the Spirit himself commonly does, though at times also exceeding human understanding.

Here Faber prefers the reading which he found in a copy belonging to the Celestines of Paris: namely, “But I have anointed my king,” above all the other readings. [Col. 0075B] For Jerome, according to the Hebrew, translates: “But I have appointed my king.” Pellicanus, Sanctes of Prato, and Münster, being especially devoted to Hebraism, follow him: “I have appointed my king.” Campensis and the interpreters for Cajetan have: “I have set my king over”; nevertheless, Campensis has “I shall anoint” in his version.

But Faber meanwhile followed—as he loudly proclaims—the authority of the prince of the apostles, who in Acts, chapter 4, openly cites this psalm: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers assembled together against his Christ.” Then, as though alluding to Faber’s interpretation, he adds: “For truly Herod and Pontius Pilate assembled in this city against your holy child Jesus, whom you anointed,” etc. Yet, although nothing is truer than that the Father anointed his Son Jesus with the Holy Spirit, it was necessary to observe that the prince of the apostles has in view the name *Christ*, which he had just mentioned; [Col. 0075C] nor was he compelled to be understood as referring to a verse later in the psalm, which Peter himself did not cite.

Moreover, the Hebrew word *NASAC*, according to Münster’s scholia, means “to pour out as a libation” and “to pour.” Since kings were anointed with oil when they were set over a kingdom, the Prophet here uses the word *NASAC*.
