This shows that it makes little difference to the meaning whether one reads “I have anointed” or “I have appointed”; nevertheless, one ought not to be wise in one’s own eyes.

In the same verse: “Declaring his decree.” Hence in Hebrew the verse begins in the first person: *ASAPPERAH EL-HOQ ADONAI*: “I will declare the decree of the Lord.” Each construction accords with its own person, notwithstanding the unaltered sense, as was stated above. There is nothing surprising in the different division, since this commonly occurs; we shall shortly give the reason. Since, however, a most weighty and more than difficult subject was being begun—namely, the eternal generation of the Son—the Septuagint certainly could appropriately begin the verse from that point, so that the opening of the discourse might correspond to the opening of the thought.

[Col. 0075D] Since the name of God was used only once, the Septuagint added “his” to clarify the sense. Jerome and Pellicanus have “the decree of God”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “the decree: Messiah, Lord,” etc. Sanctes simply has, “I will declare the statute,” making a pause, then: “The Lord said,” etc. Pratensis similarly; but Münster ventures more boldly: “I will declare as a statute what the Lord said.” And Campensis: “I will instruct him in the law of the Lord. Thus also I think: You are my Son,” etc.

Behold, you see at last to what madness we shall come unless we direct ourselves toward the one aim of the Church’s rite: everything will certainly be confused and uncertain. But since, as one proceeds, one division after another of the verses often appears in the Latin and Hebrew editions, it is worthwhile both to untie this knot and, once this has been said here, to repeat it elsewhere where the matter demands it.

For the Hebrew Psalter consists of lyric verse; therefore its metrical feet could not correspond equally in Latin or Greek. If you do not believe me, let Jerome speak in his letter to Paulinus, volume III: “David, our Simonides, Pindar and Alcaeus, as also Flaccus, Catullus, and Serenus, sings Christ upon the lyre.” The same author, in the prologue to the Book of Job: “If anyone finds it incredible that there are metres among the Hebrews, and that, in the manner of our Flaccus and the Greek Pindar, Alcaeus, and Sappho, either the Psalter or the Lamentations of Jeremiah, or nearly all the songs of Scripture, are composed in metre, let him read Philo, Josephus, Origen, Eusebius of Caesarea; by their testimony he will prove that I speak the truth.”

Again, on Jeremiah 10: “And David sings in lyric verse: ‘The steps of a man are directed by the Lord,’ etc.” (Psalm 36). Likewise, on Jeremiah 25: “Thus in the Psalter they wrongly seek the historical order of the psalms, since this is not observed in lyric song.” Again, on Ezekiel 30: “To omit other matters contained in the order of the psalms, the question is asked how the third psalm is placed before [Col. 0076B] those psalms in which David changes his appearance before Abimelech; and concerning Doeg the Idumean; and when he was found in the cave; and the fiftieth psalm of repentance, whose title indicates that he went in to Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah—when these psalms precede the third, in which he is said to flee from the face of his son Absalom. But in the psalms the answer is easy: it is lyric poetry, and in such a work the order of history is not sought, but songs of individual deeds.”

**VERSE 9.** “You will rule them with an iron rod.” Why do Münster translate “you will break,” Sanctes “you will crush,” Pratensis and the interpreters for Cajetan “you will break,” and Campensis “you will rule” and “you will break,” when it is too well known to need saying by me that *TERO‘EM* among the Hebrews means “you will rule them,” or, as Jerome translates, “you will feed them”? For “to feed” and the Greek *poimainein* mean to govern with authority. Hence the Lord said to Peter, John 21: “Feed my sheep.”

To the point: Pellicanus, in this place, has “You will rule them,” with us, even as Münster and Pratensis plainly translate Psalm 22: “The Lord is my shepherd,” and Sanctes, “The Lord feeds,” where there occurs the same root of the word as here, *ADONAI RO‘I*. We do not deny, however, that it sometimes means “to crush”; but here they ought not to have shown a spirit of contradiction, if indeed they did. Add that St. John, in Revelation 19, seems to cite this verse according to our reading.

**VERSE 12.** “Lay hold of discipline.” Hebrew: *NASEQU BAR*, which Sanctes, Münster, Pratensis, and the interpreter for Cajetan render “Worship the Son”; Jerome in his Commentaries: “Worship the Son,” as we mentioned above in our prologue. In his version according to the Hebrew: “Worship purely.” Pellicanus: “Kiss purely.” All these meanings may be drawn from the Hebrew words. *NASCAQ* sometimes means [Col. 0076D] “to be armed”: 1 Chronicles 12, *NOSQEI QESHETH*, “armed with the bow,” or “drawing the bow.” But *BAR*, with no Hebrew authority dissenting, denotes now “son,” now “purity,” now “food,” now “chosen.”

Thus, according to the sense “to be armed” in *NASCAQ*, the Septuagint correctly rendered the meaning: “Lay hold of discipline,” as though: arm yourselves with the Son; take delight and be strengthened in Christ’s discipline by chosen purity, as by food. For Jerome writes to Sunnias and Fretela: “This too is the rule of a good translator: that he should express the idiom of one language by the proper character of his own language. We prove that Cicero did this in Plato’s *Protagoras*, Xenophon’s *Oeconomicus*, and Demosthenes’ speech against Aeschines; and Plautus, Terence, and Caecilius, most learned men, did likewise in translating comedies. Nor should anyone think the Latin language extremely narrow because it cannot translate word for word, since even the Greeks render many of our expressions by circumlocutions and endeavor to express Hebrew words, not by fidelity to a literal translation, but by the properties of their own language.”

Therefore, we ought with all sinews and strength—which arms aptly imply—to cling tenaciously to Christian discipline. Its sum lies in confessing and worshipping Christ’s name, in kissing his holiness—“of whose [Col. 0078A] fullness we have all received” (John 1)—and in wholly embracing it with the affection of love, according to the saying in Song of Songs 1: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Thus the Septuagint fittingly, in a phrase worthy of kissing, said: *draxasthe paideias*, “Lay hold of discipline.” We pass briefly over the quibbles of the clever. The Chaldee paraphrase plainly supports us: “Receive instruction.”

## PSALM III

[Col. 0077]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF DAVID, WHEN HE FLED FROM THE FACE OF ABSALOM HIS SON.”

[Col. 0077A]

“O Lord, how they are multiplied!” Title: “A Psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom his son.” Ezra took from the history a covering for mysteries. For [Col. 0077B] we read in the Book of Kings that Absalom, David’s son, pursued his father and sought to kill him. David yielded to him with his followers, leaving the city of Jerusalem barefoot, understanding that this had happened to him because of the adultery committed with Bathsheba and the murder perpetrated upon Uriah, as the prophet Nathan had foretold, saying: “The sword shall not depart from your house, and the Lord shall raise up your seed against you” (2 Kings 12).

While Absalom pursued David with an army turned against him, Absalom turned his back in flight and, carried by the impetus of a mule, was caught in a spreading oak. Its branches encircled his neck, and, his head having been caught there, he hung there and was killed by Joab, commander of David’s army. [Col. 0077C] When Absalom was dead, David was restored to the kingdom and reigned in peace.

The title alludes to this history, though the psalm does not treat of it, but of what the history signifies: namely, Christ’s passion and resurrection. [Augustine.] For David is Christ, and Absalom his son is Judas. Christ calls Judas a son with the other apostles in the Gospel, saying: “Can the sons of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (Luke 5). Christ fled from Judas when Judas departed to the scribes and Pharisees and he withdrew with the remaining apostles to the mountain; or rather, he fled from him when the wisdom of God abandoned Judas’s mind, so that he might be wholly and completely the devil’s. This abandonment is called a flight because of its swiftness. Hence the Lord said to him: “What you are doing,” that is, what you intend to do, “do quickly,” [Col. 0077D] that is, you will do it (John 13).

And as David showed peace to his wicked son Absalom, commanding the people going to battle to preserve the young man Absalom, and, when Absalom had been killed, saying, “Who will grant me that I may die for you, my son Absalom?” (2 Kings 18), so Christ showed peace to Judas the traitor at the supper, in the kiss, and in other ways. Therefore Absalom is fittingly called such: it is interpreted “peace of the father”; for *aba* means “father,” and *salem* means “peace,” whence Absalom is said as though *Absalem*. And as Absalom did, so Judas also perished by hanging. When he was dead, Christ reigned in peace, because he rose in glory.

Therefore Ezra, understanding that the event signified the mystery of Christ’s passion and resurrection, which the psalm treats, set the words of the title from the history. [Remigius.] It is as if David himself, understanding this only through the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0078A] alluded in the sequence of the psalm’s words to the history. The meaning of the title is: this psalm is attributed to David, that is, to Christ, who speaks here—a psalm treating what was prefigured when he fled from the face of Absalom his son, [Augustine] that is, of Christ’s passion and resurrection, signified in that history.

[Col. 0078B] This psalm is the first among those which treat briefly of Christ’s passion and resurrection. [Cassiodorus.] The Prophet’s intention is to refute, especially, the pagans who do not think that the glory of majesty can descend to lowliness—that God can become man, suffer, and die. Its method is as follows. The psalm has two parts: first, it sets forth two opposing sides, like combatants: on one side, the multitude of persecutors; on the other, Christ armed with prayer and secure in God as his protector. Second, the outcome is shown, namely the resurrection, which is the completion of the passion. Thus he proposes that there is no need for fear, at the words, “I slept.” Therefore Christ, speaking to the Father and wondering, as it were, why he has so many persecutors when he has come to save, says:

**VERSE 1.** “O Lord, how they are multiplied who afflict me! Many rise up against me.”

“O Lord, they are multiplied who afflict me,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Remigius] so that the number of persecutors might increase from the number of disciples. And why? Surely because I have deserved no evil from them. “They are multiplied,” I say, [Gloss, interlinear] because, behold, many rise up, seeking to cast me down, that is, that they may cast me down, against me—and truly so.

**VERSE 2.** “Many say to my soul: There is no salvation for him in his God.”

For many who lie in wait for my soul say this in the evident reality of the matter—that is, showing it by word and deed. [Cassiodorus, Gloss, interlinear.] Note that “many” is repeated to indicate the great number of persecutors. What do they say? “There is no salvation for him in his God,” that is, in him whom he makes his God. The persecutors say this. Unless they had despaired that he would rise again, Judas would not have betrayed him, nor would they have killed him. [Augustine.] The sense is: God will not save him, nor is he the Son of God.

**VERSE 3.** “But you, O Lord, are my protector, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head.”

“But you, O Lord.” He has set the multitude of enemies against himself; here he shows the other side, namely his own against them. As if he said: They are so; [Cassiodorus] but you, Lord, eternal Word, Son of God, says Christ the man, are my protector, [Augustine] that is, protector of my humanity—not indeed of a person, but of human nature. [Gloss, interlinear; Remigius.] The taking up of man—that is, of human nature—is “the Word became flesh,” that is, the incarnation of the Word.

Notice that he speaks of God by comparison with an advocate, a judge, and a physician. [Cassiodorus.] An advocate takes up an accused person in order to defend him; a judge, in order to spare him; a physician takes up a sick person in order to heal him. “My glory”: [Augustine] behold, he proceeds by increase: you are my glory, because that man is one God with him who takes him up, that is, with the Word which assumed the humanity of that man. “And you lift up my head,” that is, my mind, which is not cast down by so great a passion. This is deservedly mine, because:

**VERSE 4.** “With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain.”

“With my voice,” [Gloss, interlinear] the voice of the heart, which sounds to God: with this voice Moses, though silent with his mouth, cried to the Lord when it was said to him, “Why do you cry to me from the earth?” [Augustine, Gloss, interlinear.] Susanna also, crying with this voice, was heard. With this voice, I say, I cried to the Lord. Prayer is called a cry because of the force of its intentness.

“And he heard me from your holy mountain,” that is, from me, who was the holy mountain in which he dwelt; of whom Isaiah says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be on the summit of the mountains, and all nations shall flow to it,” etc. (Isa. 2). This is the small stone cut from a mountain without hands, which grew into a great mountain and occupied the whole face of the earth, as Daniel says (Dan. 2). [Augustine.] Or, “from his holy mountain,” that is, from his righteousness. For it was just that he should raise the innocent one, who chose to die for others, not for himself.

### PART II

**VERSE 5.** “I slept and was lulled to sleep; and I rose again, because the Lord took me up.”

“I slept.” [Alcuin.] Here is the second part of this psalm, in which the outcome of the matter, namely of the passion, is shown. [Gloss, interlinear; Alcuin.] Thus he proposes that there is no need for fear. As if he said: “He heard me.” In what? In this: that I rose from death, and that the Lord took me up into his kingdom, whence, after sending the Spirit, he confirms the preachers. And deservedly, because I willingly accepted death. This is what he says: “For I slept,” that is, I willingly allowed myself to undergo the passion, “and was lulled to sleep.”

Another reading: [Augustine, Gloss, interlinear] “And I took sleep,” that is, death followed, just as one passes from drowsiness to sleep. Alternatively, according to the sequence of the letter: as if he said, “They rage against me; but I would not sleep unless I willed it.” And “I” should be pronounced with emphasis, as though he said, “I, who am so great.” “I slept,” that is, I was subjected to injuries; “and was lulled to sleep,” buried in the heart of the earth; and afterward I rose again, because the Lord took me up.

**VERSE 6.** “I shall not fear thousands of people surrounding me; arise, O Lord, save me, my God.”

“I shall not fear.” As if he said: And therefore, because I have now been delivered, I shall no longer fear the thousands of people surrounding me as I hang upon the cross—how great a multitude stood around the crucified one! After the resurrection they could do him no harm. [Augustine.] And so that I may not fear, “Arise, O Lord.” He does not say “Arise” to a sleeping God; but it is the custom of sacred Scripture to attribute to God what he himself does in us. [Col. 0080A] Thus: “Arise, O Lord,” that is, cause me to rise from death. He makes this clear by adding, “Save me, my God.”

**VERSE 7.** “For you have struck all who oppose me without cause; you have broken the teeth of sinners.”

“For you have struck”: this does not refer back, that is, it is not connected with the preceding words, nor is the reason for the preceding clause given here. For he does not save because he struck; rather, the teeth have been broken—that is, the slanderous words rendered ineffective—because he struck. Thus: “Save me, my God; and when I have been saved, you have broken the teeth of sinners,” that is, rendered ineffective the slanderous words by which the wicked tear Christ and Christians apart. [Gloss, interlinear.] [Col. 0080B] Or, the teeth are the leaders of sinners, who cut some people away from the number of the saints and incorporate them into the wicked.

And this follows from the fact that “you have struck all who oppose me without cause; you have broken the teeth of sinners,” [Augustine] that is, all heretics who are within the Church with us in body, though not in mind.

**VERSE 8.** “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people.”

“Salvation belongs to the Lord.” [Gloss, interlinear.] He turns his words to human beings, as if to say: Since this is so, as I have said, O people, you must believe this: salvation belongs to the Lord. [Augustine.] Then prayer is made for them to the Lord, to whom Christ speaks thus: “And, O Lord, let your blessing be upon your people,” that is, upon those who hope [Col. 0080C] for salvation from you, not from another.

This psalm may also be read in another way, so that the whole of it is Christ speaking here, that is, the Church and her Head placed amid storms of persecutions. Accordingly, David in the title means the Church with her Head; Absalom means the persecutors of the Church. The title means: this psalm is attributed to David, that is, the Church, and treats of what happened when David fled from the face of Absalom his son, that is, from the presence of persecutors.

Therefore the Church, in fear, says: “O Lord, how they are multiplied who afflict me!” And why? Truly because many rise against me, desiring to extinguish the Christian name. “Many say to my soul: There is no salvation for him in his God.” Otherwise, [Col. 0080D] the persecutors would not hope to destroy the Church, flourishing abroad so widely. They say: “But you, O Lord, are my protector,” because the Church has been assumed in Christ the man and exalted with him. Hence it follows: “And you are my glory, and lift up in heaven my head,” that is, Christ, who first ascended into heaven.

And deservedly, because “with my voice I cried to the Lord”: this is unchanged. “And he heard me from his holy mountain,” that is, from Christ or from his righteousness. What did he do for you? [Jerome, Augustine, Alcuin.] Behold: “I slept,” formerly in the torpor of vices, “and was lulled to sleep; and afterward I rose again,” according to the saying: “Awake, you who sleep, from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.” And this was not because of me, but because the Lord took me up.

Therefore, “I shall not fear thousands of people surrounding me,” [Col. 0081A] that is, nations which endeavor to extinguish the Christian name. And that this may happen: “Arise, O Lord,” namely Christ, my Head, in whose resurrection is salvation. Hence: “Save me, my God.” And the Church says, while I reign: “You have struck with confusion all who oppose me without cause.” And because you have struck all who oppose me without cause, you have therefore broken the teeth of sinners—that is, slanderous words or their leaders. And because the Lord has done this, therefore believe, O people, that salvation belongs to the Lord; and, O Lord, your blessing is upon your people.

This psalm may also be read morally, in the person of every believer attacked by vices and desires. Accordingly David means any believer, and Absalom means carnal vices and desires. Therefore the faithful person, feeling the battle of vices, says: “O Lord, how they are multiplied who afflict me! Many rise against me. Many say to my soul: There is no salvation for him in his God.” For from the heaping-up of vices despair of healing steals in, as though the vices were taunting the soul—or indeed as though the devil and his angels did so by their suggestions.

“But you, O Lord, are my protector, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head,” that is, Christ in heaven, or my mind which serves the law of God. And deservedly, because “With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain”: this is unchanged. “I slept and rose again; the Lord is my protector”: this is unchanged. Therefore I shall not fear thousands of people surrounding me. Here the people consist of vices and demons. “Arise, O Lord; save me, my God”: this is unchanged.

“For you have struck all who oppose me without cause.” This is rightly said of the devil and his angels in predestination, that is, according to what God has predestined and what will happen to them. “The teeth of sinners,” that is, the authors of vices, who attempt to cut him away from Christ’s body—namely, those who slander him. “Salvation belongs to the Lord.” Pride must be avoided, and everything given to God. “And your blessing is upon your people,” that is, upon each one of us.

## Comparison on Psalm III, “O Lord, How They Are Multiplied”

**VERSE 3.** “But you, O Lord, are my protector.” Hebrew: *MAGEN BA‘ADI*. Jerome, according to the Hebrew: “a shield around me”; Pellicanus, Sanctes, and the interpreters for Cajetan: “a shield for me”; Pratensis and Campensis: “a buckler for me.” These come to the same meaning as our reading. Certainly, the root from which that noun is derived means “he protected.” *MIGGEN*, and hence *MAGEN*, “protector” or “defender,” most aptly corresponds to that to which shield or buckler alludes, as Münster translates: “You are protection around me.” Nevertheless, the Septuagint and Latin edition correspond much more closely to the mystery of the Incarnation, as is clearly seen in the explanation of the text.

**VERSE 6.** “I shall not fear thousands of people,” etc. Hebrew: *LO IRA MERIBABOTH*. Sanctes and Münster: “I shall not fear ten thousands,” with whom the Septuagint agrees: *apo myriádōn*, “from ten thousands.” It is customary for “thousands” to be used indefinitely. Hence Jerome, according to the Hebrew, and Pellicanus simply translated “thousands.” Campensis has “a hundred thousand,” and Pratensis “battles,” using paraphrase; but the sense is not altered.

**VERSE 7.** “You have struck all who oppose me without cause.” Hebrew: *HIKKÎTA ETH KOL OYEVAI LEHI*. Pratensis, Sanctes, Münster, Pellicanus, the interpreters for Cajetan, and Campensis translate “on the cheek” or “upon the cheek.” The Hebrew *LEHI* denotes a contemptuous blow, which also refers to blasphemies, according to Job 16: “Those reproaching me struck my cheek.” Sanctes does not deny this in his *Thesaurus*, nor Münster in his *Scholia*. Who does not see how aptly this applies to Christ the Lord? Though entirely innocent, he was struck with slaps and blows by the impious Jews, loaded with blasphemies, and spat upon in the face as upon the vilest little man, though no deceit was found in his mouth (1 Peter 2).

Hence he answered that utterly wicked servant who struck his cheek: “Why do you strike me?” (John 18). For what sin had he committed that he should be struck without cause? It strongly supports this that which is written in Luke 6 and Matthew 5: “If anyone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also.” Augustine, in Book II of *On the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount*, teaches learnedly that this is not to be understood literally. For when the Apostle says in 2 Corinthians 11, “You endure it if anyone strikes you in the face,” Augustine says that this signifies being scorned and despised; otherwise the Lord would not have fulfilled what he commanded, since he did not offer his other cheek to the servant of the priest, but instead reproved him.

But if you translate as the Hebraists wish, “You have struck all my enemies on the cheek,” then the contradictions and insults are not referred to Christ suffering but to the destruction of Christ’s Jewish enemies, as Münster likewise interprets in his scholium: “You laid low my adversaries with a disgraceful blow.” According to the sense of Catholic psalmody, many suitable things are then connected concerning the Jews and heretics, as though a punishment of retaliation corresponded to the insulting blows inflicted on Christ. For Wisdom 11 says: “By the things through which one sins, by these also one is tormented.” They struck Christ’s cheek, contradicting him without cause; therefore, by just judgment, the teeth of sinners ought to be broken, so that they may pay the penalty due to their fault in the proper order, according to Psalm 57: “He will break their teeth in their own mouth.”

Jerome said: “You have struck the cheek of all my enemies.” This may mean: you took notice of that blow by which malicious men, without any cause, struck me, though innocent, with contempt.

## PSALM IV

[Col. 0081]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “FOR THE END: A PSALM, A SONG OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0081D]

When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me. Title: “For the end: a psalm of David’s song.” [Aug. Hier. Alc.] “End” is understood in two ways: as cessation and as completion—that is, when something fails, or when it is perfected. It means cessation when one says, “The candle is finished,” or “The expense is ended.” It means completion when one says, “The house is finished,” “The book is finished,” that is, completed. [Col. 0082D] [Aug.] In the titles of the psalms, however, it is taken in the sense of completion, and signifies Christ, who is the completion of the faithful: in the present, unto righteousness; in the future, unto the crown. [Gl. int.] Or it signifies the fullness of time. Hence the Apostle: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, [Col. 0083A] made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. IV).

[Cassiod.] The phrase here, “a psalm of a song,” must be carefully noted. For in the titles of psalms sometimes only “psalm” is placed, sometimes only “song,” and at times both, though in different order. Ezra sometimes set down “a song of a psalm,” sometimes “a psalm of a song.” To make the reason for this difference clear according to the literal sense, it should be known that sometimes the psalm before the ark in the tabernacle of the Lord was sung to the sound of the instrument alone, called the psaltery, without the choir’s voice; sometimes by the human voice without an instrument; sometimes by instrument and choir’s voice together. When both were used, sometimes the sound of the instrument led and the choir’s voice answered; at other times the choir’s [Col. 0083B] voice led and the instrument followed. When it was sung by the instrument alone, it was called simply a “psalm,” because *psalmus*, literally, is the sound and modulation of an instrument. [Aug., Cassiod.] When it was sung by voice alone without an instrument, it was called simply a “song,” for a song is the sound of the human voice. When the instrument led and the voice followed, it was called “a song of a psalm,” or “a psalm’s song.” But when the choir’s voice led and the instrument followed, it was called “a psalm of a song,” or “a song’s psalm.”

Although this seems to have occurred according to the literal rationale just described, Ezra nevertheless employed this variation in the titles chiefly for its mystical signification, just as David employed the aforementioned instrument in [Col. 0083C] a great mystery. [Aug. on Ps. LXXVII; Cassiod.] For, as we said above, a psalm denotes good action, while a song indicates the gladness of mind possessed through eternal things. Thus “psalm” is used where good action alone is treated; “song,” where the exultation of the mind alone is discussed. “A song of a psalm,” or “a psalm’s song,” occurs where good action is first discussed and then the mind’s joy; “a psalm of a song,” or “a song’s psalm,” where the mind’s joy is treated first and then good action—as here. For he first says that he was heard and enlarged in tribulation; afterwards he treats of repentance and the sacrifice of righteousness.

This is a psalm concerning morals, because it instructs us in good conduct. The meaning of the title is therefore this: this psalm is called a “psalm” because it exhorts us to act well; I say, a psalm “of a song,” because it treats of the gladness of the mind, making mention of eternal joy. I say, a psalm directing us unto the end, that is, unto Christ, who is the completing end: in the present unto righteousness, in the future unto the crown. Or, “unto the end,” that is, unto the fullness of time, because it concerns things accomplished in the time of fullness. It belongs to the prophet David, who speaks here in his own person, or in that of some perfect man. [Alcuin.] Its intention is to urge the abandonment of false gods and the vanities of the age, that is, temporal things.

The arrangement is as follows. The psalm is in three parts. [Cassiod.] First, by his own example he rebukes unbelievers concerning false gods and false goods. Second, setting forth the new man, he commands them to put off the old man, at “And know ye that …” [Col. 0084A] Third, having put off the old man, we are commanded to offer ourselves to God in sacrifice, because we are certain concerning the goods, at “Sacrifice …” Therefore the prophet, rebuking idolaters and recalling them from the superstition of idolatry, says:

**VERSE 1.**—“When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me; in tribulation thou hast enlarged me.”

“When I called, he heard me.” As though he said: Your gods, O idolaters, when they are invoked, cannot hear, because they do not truly live. But God—the giver of my righteousness, that is, he who justifies me, from whom my righteousness comes—heard me when I called upon him. [Aug.] That is, having grace inwardly in my mind, I called for a greater grace to be bestowed. Or, according to another text, it is read in the second person, “thou hast heard [Col. 0084B] me”: thus, O God of my righteousness, thou hast heard me when I called upon thee; and the meaning is the same as in the former reading.

“In tribulation thou hast enlarged me”: that is, thou hast brought me from the narrowness of sorrow into the breadth of joy. This joy arises from a pure conscience and from hope of eternal life. Hence the Apostle: “We glory in tribulations also, knowing that tribulation worketh patience; and patience, trial; and trial, hope; and hope confoundeth not, because the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts” (Rom. V). This produces enlargement of heart and drives away straits. By this holy men are inwardly refreshed even if outwardly afflicted; those who lack it are constricted in their inmost parts. These are the priests’ walks in Ezekiel’s temple (Ezek. XLII). Hence elsewhere: “I walked in the innocence of my heart.” [Col. 0084C]

Observe the change of person. From the third person, where he says, “He heard,” he passes to the second, where he says, “Thou hast enlarged me.” He first announced to men that he had been heard; then, as though he already had in his heart the Lord of whom he had previously spoken, he addresses him familiarly in love. In this the enlargement of the heart is shown.

**VERSE 2.**—“Have mercy on me, and hear my prayer.”

“Have mercy.” [Alcuin.] As though he said: Thou hast shown mercy through righteousness and enlargement. [Aug.] Again, still have mercy on me against the miseries of this life, so that what has been begun in me may be completed. Hear my prayer, which concerns the goods to be sought, says the righteous man. And since this is so concerning me, O—

**VERSE 3.**—“Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?”

“Sons of men.” [Gl. int.] As though he said: You who ought to employ reason. Or, sons of men—namely, of Adam and Eve, not of God. For Adam was a man, not a son of man; his sons are those who bear his image. You, I say, are heavy of heart: that is, your heart is weighed down by the burden of sins and the weight of iniquity, by which it is sunk into the depths. For in the prophet Zechariah, iniquity is read to sit upon a talent of lead (Zech. V). Therefore Pharaoh and the Egyptians are said to have been submerged like lead in very violent water (Exod. XV), [Col. 0085A] because the heart of Pharaoh and the Egyptians was made heavy.

Peter also, as though having something of lead, was afraid while walking on the water; yet, since he was not weighed down by its weight, he was not submerged by the waters, but was drawn out when the Lord stretched his hand toward him (Matt. XIV). But the Lord Christ, free from every contagion of sin, walked fearlessly upon the waters, as having nothing of leaden heaviness. Hence Isaiah says: “The Lord ascendeth upon a light cloud” (Isa. XIX), because he assumed flesh which provides us refreshment against the incitements of vices, free from every harmful burden.

You, I say, sons of men, are heavy of heart; and how long will this be? [Aug.] That is, at least at the advent of the Son of God, with truth present, let your error cease. “Why do you love?” As though he said: Truly [Col. 0085B] you are heavy of heart, because you love—that is, embrace by desire—and laboriously seek vanity and falsehood. [Cass.] That is, idols, which are vain, namely alien from true being, and falsehoods because they are not God as they are said to be.

And why do you do this—why do you love or seek vanity and falsehood? [Aug.] That is, earthly things, which are vain because they pass away like a shadow. For all things under the sun are vanity and falsehoods, [Rem., Aug.] because they do not make people what they promise, namely happy. And why do you do this? Why do you wish to be happy through earthly things, which are vain and passing? Truth alone makes happy, and from it all things are true. Why then are you held by love of temporal things? Why do you follow last things as though they were first?

[Col. 0085C] **PART II. Diapsalma.**

**VERSE 4.**—“And know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful; the Lord will hear me when I cry to him.”

“And know.” [Hier., Aug.] The second part, in which, having set forth the new man, he commands the old man to be put off. It should be known that where we have *diapsalma*, the Hebrews have *SELAH*, which is translated “always.” It confirms and commends what precedes or follows. [Hier.] In places of this kind, while the psalms were sung before the ark of the Lord, a silence was inserted into the singing, and there was a certain interruption of the words, as though the following words were understood to contain something different from the preceding ones, marked by a special praise.

[Aug.] Therefore the Septuagint translators, attending more to the meaning and sequence of the matter than to the Hebrew word’s strict propriety, did not translate *SELAH*, but put *diapsalma* in its place. By this word is signified a division of voices in singing: *psalma* is what is sung, while *diapsalma* is the silence inserted in singing. Thus *sympsalma* [σύμψαλμα] means the joining of voices in song. It is certain that wherever a *diapsalma* is placed, a change of subject and person occurs. Thus, after rebuking unbelievers, he proposes Christ, through whom God hears, saying: “Know.”

Note also that a conjunction is customarily placed at the beginnings of prophetic Scriptures, so that it may join what is said to the vision that is in the heart. For one often finds beginnings such as, “And the Lord said to him,” or, “And the word of the Lord came to him.” So here. [Col. 0086A] Or it may be joined thus with what precedes: as though he said, “Do not love vanity. And know why: because the Lord has made his holy one wonderful; the Lord will hear me,” and so forth. But the intervening *diapsalma* forbids this joining. For the nature of a *diapsalma* requires not the connection of lower and upper words, but their separation, though this is observed almost nowhere. Indeed, although a *diapsalma* intervenes, what follows is nevertheless joined in wording with what precedes.

Hence the text may also be continued here differently. [Cassiod.] As though he said: Know that these things are vain, and know also what you ought to follow. For the Lord the Father made his holy one wonderful, namely Christ, who is the Holy of holies. [Aug.] That is, he showed him wonderful by raising him and placing him at his right hand; you ought to turn to him from love of the world. Of him it is said: “When the Holy of holies shall come, your anointing shall cease” (Dan. IX). Therefore, just as he is called Lord of lords and God of gods, so he is Holy of holies: holy in himself and sanctifying others. [Gl. int.] And through him the Lord will hear me concerning eternal rest when I cry—or, “when I shall cry”—to him. So he will also hear you if you cry. Therefore cry, and thus you will be worthy of hearing: namely, if you cry and do what follows.

**VERSE 5.**—“Be angry and do not sin; what you say in your hearts, be pierced with compunction for in your beds.”

“Be angry.” As though he said: But in order that you too may deserve [Col. 0086C] to be heard, be angry and do not sin. [Aug.] That is, if a movement of the mind arises which is not within our power, let reason not consent to it. [Cassiod., Alcuin.] Anger is venial when it is not brought into effect. It should be known that the first movement of the mind is not in our power, but by God’s grace we can moderate it. [Cassiod.] Therefore he permits what belongs to habit—that is, he does not forbid it—but forbids what belongs to fault, namely mortal sin. As though he said: Be angry indeed in the first movement, which is unconquerable; [Aug.; Hier., *Against the Pelagians*, II] and if you are angry, do not sin by consenting and bringing it into effect.

The Apostle teaches the same when he says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. IV). By these words he implies [Col. 0086D] that it is altogether sin—even a light sin—to be angry, while righteousness consists in assuaging anger by swift repentance. [Aug.] Or: “Be angry” with yourselves concerning past sins, and do not sin further. [Gl. int.] Or: Be angry at the first movements, resisting them, and do not sin—that is, do not bring them into effect.

After anger he also removes hypocrisy, saying, “What you say.” [Aug.] Say with your lips also what you say in your hearts, lest you be among those of whom it is said: “This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. XV). “And in your beds be pierced with compunction”: that is, in your hearts be pierced by the sorrow of repentance, so that the soul, punishing itself, may be pierced, lest it be condemned and tormented in God’s judgment.

Or, “be pierced with compunction in your beds”: that is, stir yourselves as though by certain [Col. 0087A] goads applied—not for sorrow over sins, but for seeing the light of Christ; namely, not for the lower watering, but for the upper watering, so that you may burn with love for invisible things. Or thus: I say, do not sin; and if you have sinned, be pierced by repentance for those things which you say in your hearts. [Cassiod., Rem.] That is, for the things you deliberate in your heart, which God also knows: that is, for consent and for the things you have willed.

“In your beds,” that is, concerning the pleasure of the flesh, in which reason is held captive like a wild beast in its lair. Or beds are the thoughts of fierce persons, such as thoughts of murders, robberies, and the like. Thus: be pierced with compunction for what you say in your beds—that is, be pierced with compunction for your most atrocious thoughts.

[Col. 0087B] **PART III. Diaphalma.**

**VERSE 6.**—“Sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord; many say, ‘Who will show us good things?’”

“Sacrifice,” the third part. [Cassiod., Alcuin.] Having put off the old man in the preceding part, here we are commanded to offer ourselves in sacrifice, because we are certain concerning the good things. As though he said: Be pierced with compunction, be angry, and sacrifice—that is, offer—not animals, in which God does not delight. Hence through Isaiah: “My soul hateth your sacrifices” (Isa. I). Rather, sacrifice sacrifices of righteousness, which is a contrite spirit, so that a person punishing himself through repentance may immolate himself to God. Hence elsewhere: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. L). [Aug.] This is rightly called a sacrifice of righteousness. For what is more just [Col. 0087C] than that each person should be angry with his own sins rather than another’s, and should offer himself to God by punishing himself through repentance and satisfaction?

Or thus: Be pierced with compunction and sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness—that is, after repentance and lamentation perform just works. Perhaps the inserted *diapsalma* denotes this: that one should pass from the old life to the new; namely, that when the old man has been extinguished through repentance, the sacrifice of righteousness according to the regeneration of the new man should be offered to God. For thus the soul itself, now washed, offers itself upon the altar of faith, kindled by the divine fire, that is, by the Holy Spirit. Thus after Passover, when they roasted ears of grain by fire and rubbed them in their hands, Pentecost follows, when they offered new loaves from new harvests. These signified works of righteousness.

I say, sacrifice, [Col. 0087D] [Aug., Cassiod.] and thus hope in the Lord for eternal gifts. For you will not receive them here. But because scarcely anyone loves inward goods, which alone ought to be loved, while other things are to be used for necessity, not enjoyed as a source of delight, he adds: “Many say.” As though he said: I say, “Hope,” but many say, “Who will show us good things?” [Aug.] Namely, future goods, concerning which they doubt and despair. Therefore they say: “Who knows whether they are true?” or “Who has come back from the lower world to report these things?” To them the prophet answers the question being asked—“Who will show us good things?”—briefly showing what goods ought to be sought, by adding:

**VERSE 7.**—“The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us; thou hast given joy in my heart.”

“It is marked.” As though he said: They say this, but now, O Lord, the light of thy countenance—that is, the light of thy grace, by which thy image is re-formed in us and by which we are like thee—has been marked upon us. That is, it has been impressed upon reason, the higher power of the soul by which we are like God, just as a seal is impressed on wax. [Col. 0088A] Therefore our reason is understood as God’s countenance, because just as someone is recognized by his face, so God is recognized through the mirror of reason; and just as one face is made like another by conformity, so by reason we are like God, according to the saying: “God made man in his image and likeness” (Gen. I).

This reason was deformed through human sin, by which man became unlike God; but through Christ’s grace it was re-formed or recovered. Hence the Apostle: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind,” etc. (Eph. IV). Thus the grace by which the created image is renewed is here called light. For there is a threefold image: the image of creation, the image of re-creation, and the image of likeness. The image of creation is that in which man was created, namely reason. The image of re-creation is that through which the created image is re-formed, namely God’s grace infused for the restoration of the mind. The image of likeness is that to which man was made; for he was made in the image and likeness not of the Father only, or of the Son only, but of the whole Trinity. [Aug.] By memory he is like the Father; by understanding, the Son; by love, the Holy Spirit. Hence: “May I remember thee, understand thee, [Col. 0088C] and love thee.”

The light of the countenance, then, is justifying grace, by which the created image is stamped. This light is the whole and true good of man, by which he is stamped like a coin with the king’s image. For man was made in God’s image, which he corrupted by sinning but is stamped anew by being born again. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII). [Alcuin.] As if he said: Just as one renders to Caesar his own image, so render the soul to God, enlightened and stamped with the light of his countenance.

Or thus, taking the phrase intransitively: “the light of thy countenance,” that is, thy countenance is luminous and enlightens us; namely, the image by which you shall know, now in a riddle, and in the future as thou art. “It is marked upon us”: that is, it has been impressed upon [Col. 0088D] our soul. [Hier., Cassiod.] He calls reason “the light of the countenance,” because it is luminous and enlightens man; and “God’s countenance,” because, as said above, God is seen through it.

Or the light of the countenance is called the cross of Christ, impressed upon us inwardly and outwardly—namely, on the brow of the mind and the brow of the body—as the sign of our king. [Aug.] For as an imperial coin bears the emperor’s image, so the marks of the heavenly ruler are impressed upon the faithful. This cross is the true light, because God shines upon such persons through it. And by this light thou hast given spiritual joy—not outwardly and in vain things, but inwardly in my heart, where God dwells. Joy must be sought there, for inwardly are true and certain goods, which the wicked do not see as they pursue temporal things, concerning whom he rightly adds:

[Col. 0089A] **VERSE 8.**—“They have been multiplied by the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil.”

“By fruit,” or “by the time of grain.” [Alcuin.] As though he said: Thou hast given me joy within, but those who say, “Who will show us good things?” are many because of grain, wine, and oil—that is, temporal grain, wine, and oil. Or: “By the fruit of grain, wine, and oil,” because they suppose that in these is fruit, that is, the complete good. He adds “their,” not without reason; it must be referred to all three, so that one says “their grain, their wine, their oil,” to mark a difference. [Aug.] For there is another grain that is not theirs, namely the bread of God that came down from heaven. There is also another wine that gladdens the heart of man. And there is God’s oil, concerning which it is said: “Thou hast made my head fat with oil” (Ps. XXII).

Observe that he sets down these three, as the more necessary for human use, in place of all the greater riches by which those many people who do not seek the true good have been multiplied. For those who do not see that the kingdom of heaven is within them are multiplied in these things—not indeed in truth, but multiplied in distraction and misery. Multiplication does not always signify abundance; rather, it often signifies dispersal among many things, when the soul given over to temporal matters is always inflamed by desire and cannot be at leisure, but is distracted by manifold and miserable thought. It is not permitted to see the simple good. Therefore, distracted by innumerable phantasms, such people do not seek the simple good in simplicity of heart, acting contrary to the command: “Serve the Lord in goodness, [Col. 0089C] and seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. I). This multiplicity is strongly opposed to that simplicity by which the simple and true good is sought, concerning which the good man exults, saying:

**VERSE 9.**—“In peace, in the selfsame, I shall sleep and rest.”

“In peace, in the selfsame.” [Cassiod.] As though he said: Thou hast given me joy, certainly joy in this: that I may sleep in peace which is also “in the selfsame,” that is, unchangeable, withdrawn from every tumult of the world. This will be when this mortal shall put on immortality; and I shall rest, that is, enjoy the blessed life. [Alcuin.] And this is true, because hope which does not confound already exists. This is what he says:

[Col. 0089D] **VERSE 10.**—“For thou, O Lord, hast established me singularly in hope.”

“For thou, O Lord,” etc. [Rem., Cassiod.] Or thus: “In peace.” As though he said: They labor to be multiplied in these temporal things, but I shall sleep in peace of mind, here forgetting the world and tending toward “the selfsame,” that is, toward that good which is “the selfsame”: that which is altered by no change, but remaining itself abides in immutable eternity. And I shall rest in the future. This will truly be so, because thou, O Lord, hast already established me. Or: thou hast caused me to dwell singularly in hope—that is, in the one hope by which the one and true good is uniquely hoped for, not in the multiplicity of the world. And what is hoped for will assuredly be. He appropriately says “singularly,” in contrast to the statement that [Col. 0090A] they “have been multiplied by the time of grain, wine, and oil.” For this multiplicity perishes, while singularity is maintained in the saints, of whom it is said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul in God” (Acts IV). For, set apart from all things born and dying, lovers of eternity and unity ought to cling to the one God.

## Comparison on Psalm IV: “When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me”

**VERSE.**—“When I called, he heard me.” Hebrew: *AVENI*. Münster, Sanctes, and Campensis: “Hear me.” Jerome, according to the Hebrew, seems to have read *AVITANI*; and Pellican, by a double *qamets*, *AVANI*. This proves that the manuscripts varied, since they translated, “Thou hast heard me” and “He heard me.” But Pratensis and the interpreters for Cajetan gratuitously translate [Col. 0090B] “Answer me,” since for God to answer us is to hear prayers. Whichever you read—“he heard,” “hear,” “thou hast heard,” “answer”—the sense is not impaired. Faber nevertheless preferred that churches should sing “Thou hast heard me,” in the second person. But why? “From the Greek,” he says, “and the Roman translation.”

Had he compared manuscripts, some having *εἰσήκουσέν μου* (“he heard me”), others *εἰσήκουσάς μου* (“thou hast heard me”), he would not have preferred another translation to our Vulgate. The blind Burgos man suffers from the same blindness in a certain apology, whose title is: “Apology of Peter de Ponte, the Blind Man of Burgos, against those who perversely and stubbornly cling to their obstinate errors concerning many terms and meanings of the divine sacrifice.” He wished, with Faber, for “Thou hast heard me” to be read in the second person. How blind he is in this matter we have demonstrated. Yet everything which this man criticizes in them he has gleaned from Faber with scarcely a letter changed.

**VERSE 3.**—“Sons of men.” In Hebrew, [Col. 0090C] *BENE ISCH*, that is, “sons of a man.” Jerome likewise translates it in this manner according to the Hebrew. Yet in his commentary on Matthew XVI: “Whom do men say that the Son of man is?” “Observe,” he says, “that wherever ‘sons of men’ is written in the Old Testament, ‘sons of Adam’ is also written in Hebrew,” expressly mentioning this passage. Therefore we have concluded more clearly than daylight that manuscripts varied even in Jerome’s age, and the Septuagint translated *υἱοὶ ἀνθρώπων*, “sons of men.”

“How long [will you be] heavy of heart?” Hebrew: *AD MEH QUEBODI LICHIMMAH*. Jerome, in the version which we often cite as addressed to Sophronius, renders it thus: “How long, my illustrious ones, do you love disgrace?” etc. Pratensis: “How long [shall] my glory [be] a reproach?” Sanctes uses a paraphrase: “How long will you turn my glory into disgrace?” Münster: “How long will my glory be in disgrace?” The interpreter for Cajetan: “It shall be for disgrace.” Campensis’s paraphrase: “You will seek to inflict insult.” Pellican agrees: “How long [shall] my glory [be] unto disgrace?” The translator following Campensis: “How long [will you despise] my greatness?” This great variety and divergence from the Vulgate reading arises from the equivocation of the Hebrew word *CABAD*, which sometimes means “was heavy,” at other times “to be honourable.” Hence *CABOD*, “glory,” and *CEBODI*, “my glory.”

But we rightly ask: whence do we derive “heavy,” or “heavy of heart,” *βαρυκάρδιοι*? It is clearer than daylight that the Septuagint read *AD MEH CABOD LEB LAMMAH*, that is, “How long [will you be] heavy of heart?”, placing a division. Then they followed with “Why,” etc., so that what is now read as one word they distinctly read as two, *LEB LAMMAH*, especially since *beth* and *caph* have no small resemblance and it is easy for one to slip in place of the other. But the Septuagint join *LAMMAH*, which is part of the word, with what follows, “Why?”, whereas others read it differently, joined as *LICLIMAH*, [Col. 0091A] after first making a division at *IN LEB*, that is, “in heart,” where others read *LIC*, the beginning of the word in the reading they transmit to us. Jerome, satisfying the Jews for Sophronius, as we explained in the preface, joined *LICLIMAH* to the verb “you love,” and took *QUEBODI* adjectivally when he translated “my illustrious ones,” where others say “my glory.”

**VERSE 4.**—“Has made wonderful.” I cannot sufficiently wonder why Sanctes, Münster, Pratensis, and the interpreters for Cajetan wished to translate “has set apart” or “has separated,” when they themselves attest that the word here used, *HIPHLA*, means beyond controversy both “to make wonderful” and “to set apart.” Jerome too said, “He made wonderful,” although it matters little for the sense, since we make wonderful things superior to others and separate them by exalting them. Yet they show that they voluntarily depart from the common and correct reading. There are also many matters of this sort, too trivial to be noted.

**VERSE 5.**—“Be angry and do not sin.” In Hebrew, as to the first word, *RIGZU*: Pratensis, Münster, and the interpreter for Cajetan render “tremble” or “be afraid”; Sanctes, “be fearful,” so that people ought to fear under the name of sin; and Campensis expresses this in his paraphrase: “Take diligent care not to sin.” Although this is very true, it does not suit the apostolic interpretation in Ephesians IV, where he understands this verse as concerning the restraint of anger. For after setting down *ὀργίζεσθε καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε* (“Be angry and do not sin”), he immediately explains what he means: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger.” Jerome plainly gives this understanding in Book II against the Pelagians; hear his words without reluctance:

> “God’s anger is just, but a man’s anger proceeds from a disturbed mind. Hence it is also said in the psalm: ‘Be angry,’ etc. The Apostle teaches the sense of this verse: ‘Let not the sun go down upon your anger’; so that it is altogether sin even to be angry slightly, while righteousness is to temper it by swift repentance.”

He gives the same opinion in his Commentary on Ephesians:

> “No one doubts that this is taken from the fourth psalm; and it seems contrary to what is said elsewhere: ‘But now put away also all anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and foul speech from your mouth’ (Col. III). Taken simply, it is harmful, since the reins of anger are thought to have been loosened. But the term ‘anger’ is understood in two ways, not only among us but also among the philosophers: either when, provoked by injury, we are stirred by natural impulses; or when the onset has subsided and rage has been extinguished, the mind can retain judgment and yet desire vengeance upon one thought to have injured it. I therefore think that the former anger is meant here, and that we, as human beings, are permitted to be moved at the sight of something unworthy, and for the tranquility of mind to be disturbed as by a light breeze; yet we must by no means be lifted up by the swelling whirlpools of fury.”

These are the words of holy Jerome. They do not correspond at all, or only slightly, to those persons’ translation, which disagrees with the Apostle’s sense and thus perhaps either corrupts or obscures the psalmist’s genuine meaning. Hence Jerome too, in the version according to the Hebrew, wrote “Be angry,” and not, like these others, “Be fearful” or “Tremble.” Pellican likewise has “Be angry.” Although fear can be reconciled with anger so as to yield a worthy interpretation, it is not the same affection of the mind.

“What you say in your hearts, and in your beds be pierced with compunction.” Hebrew: *IMRU BILBABCHEM AL MISSCABCHEM VEDOMMU*, that is, “Speak in your heart upon your bed, and be silent,” as the candidates for Hebraism contend. Four things in our edition and the Septuagint produce the difference: namely, the relative “what,” not present in Hebrew; secondly, the indicative form, “you say”; thirdly, the transposed copulative conjunction “and”; [Col. 0092A] lastly, the verb “be pierced with compunction.”

That this number varies here or there does not alter the sense, since in sacred writings one is very often used for the other. As to the first point, a relative pronoun—of whatever case, gender, or number—is commonly understood among Hebrews, as is clear, for example, in Psalm VII: “In the command which thou hast commanded,” and “he fell into the pit which he made”: in Hebrew the relative is not present. As to the second, the four letters *aleph, mem, resh, waw*, without distinction of points, may be understood as *amru*, in the indicative mood—that is, “you have said” or “you say,” with the past used for the present. Münster likewise understood the beginning of Psalm II this way, translating “Why do the nations gather for tumult?” where it is certain that the Hebrew reads the past *RAGESCHU*.

There need be no great contention regarding the transposed conjunction, since, according to the good judgment of the interpreter, it may refer either to what precedes or to what follows. Finally, the verb *DAMAM*, “he was silent,” whence *DOMMU*, is referred to the compunction of the heart, which occurs in secret and is known to God alone. For the silence of the heart is secretly to go and turn to God in one’s inmost depths, according to Psalm XXXVII: “Lord, before thee is my desire, and my groaning is not hidden from thee.” Seek further material in the commentary.

**VERSE 7.** “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us.” They read in Hebrew *NESAH*, which, with great agreement, they translate “lift up” or “raise over us,” from the stem *NASAH*, with *sin* and *aleph*, that is, “I raised.” It appears that the Septuagint read this word nominally for “sign,” though, weighing the sense, they translated “it is marked.” For beyond dispute the Hebrews affirm that *NES*, from the root *NASAS*, means “a standard,” which is undoubtedly raised up. From this noun the Septuagint not inappropriately derived *NESAH*, “a sign,” and translated *ἐσημειώθη*, “it has been marked.” In Isaiah XLIX we read *ARIM NISI*, that is, “I shall raise my standard.” [Col. 0092C]

What then prevents the Septuagint from using it in this way, especially since that light of which the Psalmist sings, descending from the Father of lights, pertains to the knowledge and contemplation of God—a knowledge which exalts a person in a manner known to no one except the one who receives it? Add that the root from which the word proceeds, as Sanctes proves by authorities cited in his *Thesaurus*, properly signifies, among many other things, “to receive” and “to give”; and this very well suits the image which we naturally bear and by which we partake of God.

### Verse 8

“From the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil they have been multiplied.” The Hebrews read: *MEETH DEGANAN VETIROSCHAN RABBU*, which may be translated, “From the time when their grain and their new wine were multiplied,” or, as in Jerome’s version, “In time their grain and their new wine were multiplied.” Pagninus has “when”; Sanctes and Münster, “when their grain and wine were multiplied.” The interpreter for Cajetan does not add “when,” since it is not present in the Hebrew either. Pellican: “more than when their grain and new wine are multiplied.”

Those translators who said “from the fruit,” etc., expressed the force of the sentence more closely. For what does it mean to be multiplied “from the time of their grain,” except by the produce gathered in its proper season? Campensis fittingly shows this *paraphrastically*: that grain and wine came forth for them abundantly, as they had desired, and that they became rich.

Faber wishes the word “oil” to be struck out gratuitously, as superfluous. “Nor,” he says, “did sacred Jerome find that word when he had revised the ancient Psalter of Origen’s Hexapla, which had been corrected by Jerome’s own hand; nor is it found in the Hebrew, nor in the other editions, nor among the Septuagint. Therefore the churches need not fear immediately to amend that passage and uproot the word ‘oil,’ and henceforth sing: ‘From the fruit of their grain and wine they have been multiplied.’”

So Faber. O good man, why does so soft a word as “oil” burden your throat? Surely in the Old Testament the Lord commonly indicates an overflowing abundance of goods by these three together—grain, wine, and oil—as in Joel 2: “Behold, I will send you grain, wine, and oil, and you shall be filled with them.” Allow, therefore, the ecclesiastical chant to be anointed with the oil of gladness, since without oil there is no melody in the Church.

Nor should Jerome’s statement trouble us. Although he does not wish that word to be struck out or uprooted, as Faber exaggerates, if it is sung in the Church—even if it is not included—it ought to be understood as signifying the abundance of every kind of wealth, as Pellican seems to suggest in his *Scholia*. We rejoice far more in your spiritual consolation than those worldly persons rejoice in a most abundant harvest and vintage. It is clear, moreover, that “vintage” may be extended to other things.

Jerome, in Question 10 to Hedibia, further declares that nothing pleases him except what is ecclesiastical and what he does not fear to say publicly in the Church. Nevertheless, the manuscripts evidently differed, since we now read ἐλαίου, “of oil,” in the Greek. If it is absent from certain others, that does not matter where the sense is sound and comes to the same thing.

Indeed, if what we cited in the prologue from Rabbi David Kimhi is true—that there were disagreements among the copies and that certain words had been written in the margin—it is not altogether improbable that in some manuscripts merely one letter, namely *nun*, was added at the end of that word, so that, instead of *tirossam*, “their wine,” one reads *tirossamen*, a compound expression meaning “their wine and oil.” It is easy either to add or remove one letter.

Nor does it object that, on following that reading, neither the second conjunction nor the suffix, or pronoun, would be present; for translators supply this, especially since the Psalter is a lyric poem, as we proved in the preface. In this verse Münster and Sanctes added “when”; thus in the first Psalm Münster said: “The wicked are not so, but are driven toward evil, like chaff.” Yet “but are driven toward evil” is not in the Hebrew; nevertheless, he shows that it must be understood.

### Verse 9

“In peace, in the selfsame [reality], I shall sleep and rest.”

A twofold division may be made: first, “in peace, in the selfsame [reality]”; then, “I shall sleep and rest.” Or thus: “In peace, in the selfsame [reality], I shall sleep; and I shall rest.” The blind Burgensian attacks the former division in his *Apology* and mocks the ecclesiastical chant at Compline and other prayers, in which they suspend the voice at “in peace, in the selfsame,” as though they ought to sing “in peace, in the selfsame I shall sleep,” after making a pause.

But neither division should be rejected. For if you consider what *in idipsum*, “into the selfsame,” means, perhaps you will approve the first division more than the second. Augustine, indeed, interpreting that verse of Psalm 121, “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in the selfsame,” teaches that “the selfsame” is that which cannot change, and signifies the very name of God, who is: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3). All other created things can be in one way or another; but he who created them cannot be in one way or another, because it is said of them: “You shall change them, and they shall be changed; but you are the same” (Ps. 101).

Therefore, since Christ is our peace, “who made both one” (Eph. 2), and that peace is eternal, surpassing every understanding (Phil. 4), and immutable, in which we are all one: does it not seem most fitting to you that “the selfsame” belongs to this peace, and that we rejoice “in peace, in the selfsame”—in the peace which alone is undisturbed and immortal?

If you inspect more closely the word used in Hebrew, you will see that it is not simply *IAHAD*, “together,” but with the pronominal *waw*, signifying “with,” namely *IAHADAN*; this the Septuagint translators rendered ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό, “unto the same [thing],” to indicate the highest unity. These matters might have been passed over in silence, had others remained silent. Yet I do not forbid correction wherever there is an evident error in pauses or elsewhere, provided it is done neither ignorantly nor thoughtlessly.

## Psalm V

[Col. 0093]

### Title of the Psalm: “For the End, for Her Who Obtains the Inheritance”

[Col. 0093C]

“My words.” Title: “For the end, for her who obtains the inheritance.”

[Remigius.] The title of this Psalm alludes to the history in Genesis, where we read that Abraham had two sons: one by the slave-woman Hagar, namely Ishmael; the other by the free woman Sarah, namely Isaac. Ishmael, who was older, persecuted Isaac while playing with him. Sarah, therefore, understanding Ishmael’s play with Isaac to be persecution, said to her husband: “Cast the slave-woman and her son out of the house” (Gen. 21). Thus the slave-woman was cast out of the house with her son, and the free woman with her son obtained the inheritance.

The title seems to look back to this history, to which certain words of the Psalm also allude. Yet this Psalm concerns not the history, but rather what it signifies. The free woman Sarah, who bore not according to nature but through God’s grace, signifies the Church, which begets spiritual children for God, not by the power of the flesh but by God’s grace. The slave-woman signifies the Synagogue, which serves for temporal things, and the whole body of the wicked, who, though fruitful and abounding in earthly goods, persecute the Church and her children with torments and mockery. Yet the Church obtains the eternal inheritance, while they are excluded.

The meaning of the title is therefore this: this Psalm directs us toward the end, that is, toward the eternal inheritance, which is consummation. It is for that free woman—that is, for Sarah, who is to be honored; that is, it concerns the Church to be honored, signified by the free Sarah.

[Remigius, Alcuin.] Here the Church is honored, since she is affirmed to possess the inheritance, from which her rival is excluded. Hence follows why she obtains the inheritance—not so the Synagogue, which is cast out of the house.

[Augustine.] The Church is the one that receives the inheritance, that is, eternal life, that is, God himself, who is called our inheritance because he nourishes and sustains us. We too are called God’s inheritance, because he manages and governs us.

[Cassiodorus.] The Prophet’s purpose is to assure the faithful concerning the inheritance they are to receive. The method: the Psalm has three parts. First, he speaks of the inheritance which he seeks for himself and declares that it is given to him, saying that the rival is excluded. Second, he asks for help against the things which the rival brings forward: “Lord, lead me.” Third, he displays the rewards of the good, so that, as punishment frightens, rewards may attract: “And let them rejoice.” In this way Cassiodorus divides the Psalm.

Augustine, however, makes five divisions: first, the Church prays that she may be heard; second, that she may understand what hinders her from seeing God, or that she may recognize that she has been heard: “For to you I shall pray”; third, she promises that she will become God’s house: “But I”; fourth, she prays for inward aid: “Lead me”; fifth, she prophesies what punishment awaits the wicked and what reward the just: “Judge them.”

[Cassiodorus.] Therefore, the Church, called by God, offers here a threefold prayer: she asks to be separated from the wickedness of the world and to come to God, saying:

### Verse 1

“My words receive with your ears, O Lord; understand my cry.”

Lord, receive the words of my mouth—

[Cassiodorus.] —that is, my psalmody—and understand my cry, that is, the affection of my heart by which I cry to you.

[Augustine.] Moses cried thus in silence, as did Susanna when she was accused by the elders. Understand, I say, and receive with your ears—that is, by the presence of your majesty. By saying “understand,” he rightly shows that this is a spiritual, not a vocal, cry, one that is understood. Thus God’s ear is understood not as a bodily instrument but as the presence of divine majesty. A bodily voice is heard by a bodily ear; a spiritual voice is understood. Note, therefore, the fitting distinction of the words: “Receive the words; understand the cry.” And because I cry with mouth and heart:

### Verse 2

“Attend to the voice of my prayer, my King and my God.”

“Attend to the voice of my prayer,” or, according to another reading, “Hear my prayer.”

[Cassiodorus.] Behold, he prayed three times concerning the same matter, directing his prayer to the Holy Trinity, saying: You, I say, who are my King, namely Christ; and you who are my God, namely the Father.

[Augustine.] The Son is properly called King according to the customary language of Scripture, perhaps because, according to his humanity, he was anointed with spiritual oil. The King is rightly named first, because through him we go to the Father. Hence follows, “and my God.” Yet he does not say, “Attend,” in the plural, but “Attend,” in the singular. For the Catholic faith proclaims not two or three gods, but the Trinity itself as one God; not in the sense that the same Trinity can at one time be called Father, at another Son, and at another Holy Spirit, as Sabellius believed; but so that the Father is none but Father, the Son none but Son, and the Holy Spirit none but Holy Spirit. Yet this Trinity is one God, because he truly is one God.

[Augustine, Tractate 36 on John.] Therefore Christ the Lord says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). Hear both words and observe both, “one” and “are,” and you will be delivered from Charybdis and Scylla. For “one” delivers you from Arius; “are” delivers you from Sabellius. If “one,” then not different; if “are,” then both Father and Son. He would not say “we are” determinately of one person, nor “one” of what is different.

Let the Sabellians therefore be ashamed, who say that he who is Father is himself the Son, confusing the persons; they are called Patripassians because they say that the Father suffered. The Arians, however, say that the Father is one thing and the Son another: not one substance, but two; the Father greater, the Son lesser. Do not say this, Catholic Christian; for the substance of Father and Son is one, their divinity one, their coeternity one, their equality perfect, and there is no dissimilarity.

If, therefore, you believe Christ to be other than the Father, yet in some respect distant from him in nature, you have escaped Sabellius’s Charybdis but have been shipwrecked upon Arius’s Scyllaean rocks. Sail in the middle, then; avoid both dangerous sides, and say: “The Father is Father; the Son is Son; the Father is one person, the Son another, but not another thing—indeed, the very same [in substance]—because [they are] one God.”

### Verse 3

“For to you I shall pray, O Lord; in the morning you will hear my voice.”

“For to you.” This is the second part according to Augustine. Thus far is the Church’s prayer that she may be heard; here is her understanding of the things that hinder her from seeing the Lord—or, that she may know herself to have been heard.

The Church, previously desiring as though in the present to be heard, said, “Hear my prayer,” in which she displayed her own calling. But, dimmed amid the storms of this age, she feels that she does not see what she desires, though she still hopes. She knows why she does not see: because the night of sins still remains for her. She therefore says: “For to you”—as though she said, “I prayed and was not heard; yet I shall not cease. Rather, I shall pray to you, O Lord. Not in the night of sins, but in the morning you will hear my voice.” Not in the night, because sins have brought it about; but when they have ended, you will be seen.

[Alcuin.] Morning is the end of darkness and the beginning of light, which continually increases, so that even beginners are not excluded: as the habit and love of sin depart like darkness, they begin to see the Lord and gradually make progress in him.

[Augustine.] Since she has not yet been heard but says she will be heard, why did she first say, “Hear,” and not, “You will hear”? Perhaps because she cried above, desiring to be heard in the present; therefore she said, “Hear.” But because she cried in the night, she was not heard. And because she was not heard, she perceives what she must pass through in order to be heard. Hence she says, “You will hear.”

Or she has been heard above but does not understand that she has been heard, because she does not yet see the one who hears unless she cleaves to him. The sense is: “I prayed and do not feel that I have been heard; yet still, O Lord, I shall pray to you.”

[Alcuin.] And because I shall pray to you, “in the morning”—this does not change—“you will hear my voice,” that is, I shall understand that I have been heard. And in this:

### Verse 4

“In the morning I shall stand before you, and I shall see that you are not a God who wills iniquity.”

“In the morning.”

[Augustine.] I shall not be a person of the hour, but shall stand before you perseveringly; and through purity of life I shall not lie in earthly things, seeking blessedness in them. By saying “I shall stand,” he denotes two things: the directing of the mind toward eternal things and perseverance. “And I shall see,” that is, I shall know, that you are properly he who, remaining stable, causes all things to move. You are God. Therefore you do not will iniquity.

[Alcuin.] To be God and to take pleasure in iniquity can never agree.

[Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] Note each word. He says “you are,” which properly belongs to God. Likewise, “I shall stand before you.” A person who is pure stands before God as present.

[Jerome and Augustine.] And this is “morning,” namely, as soon as he abandons the darkness of vices. Or thus: “In the morning I shall stand before you”—this does not change—and then I shall see you. For he who clings to earthly things does not see God, but the person who stands before God in the morning of virtues does. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,” etc. (Matt. 5). Therefore: “In the morning I shall stand, that I may see you, because you are God who does not will iniquity.”

Iniquity—lying, murder, deceit, and the like—is the night. When it passes, morning comes, so that God may be seen. Here he gives the reason why he will stand in the morning and see: because God does not will iniquity. For if God willed it, he could be seen by the wicked without morning. You truly do not will iniquity, because:

### Verse 5

“Neither shall the malicious dwell beside you, nor shall the unjust remain before your eyes.”

“The malicious”—

[Gloss, interlinear.] —the person who wills evil to his neighbor, even if he cannot accomplish it—“shall not dwell beside you,” that is, he shall not see you in such a way as to cleave to you. Hence follows: “Nor shall the unjust remain.” An unjust person is one who does not do what he ought. “Before your eyes,” that is, before your light; because the eyes of their minds, through the darkness of sins, cannot endure the light of right understanding. Even if they sometimes see the true light, they do not remain, because they love things that turn them away from the truth. But if this night passes, morning comes for them, so that they may see and cleave to the truth.

Or thus: he says “morning” when eternity begins. The meaning is: “I shall pray to you, O Lord; and because I shall pray to you”—this does not change—“in the morning,” that is, at the beginning of eternity, “you will hear my voice.”

[Remigius.] And in that morning I shall stand before you as present. Then I shall fully see that you are God who does not will iniquity—that is, I shall understand that the wicked do not please you. And truly so, because then the malicious person shall not dwell beside you; rather, “let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the grace of God.” Then the unjust shall not remain before your eyes, even if here they received his mercy, he “who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil.”

[Alcuin.] The unjust are those who do evil. Truly they shall not remain, for:

### Verse 6

“You have hated all who work iniquity; you will destroy all who speak lies.”

“You have hated all”—

[Remigius, Augustine.] —that is, you appear to hate them when you separate them from yourself. Hatred does not occur in God, if he is said to hate the wicked, because he does not allow them to remain in himself. “All,” I say, “who work iniquity.”

[Jerome.] He does not say “those who have worked,” lest he exclude repentance, through which sinners are justified; but “those who work iniquity.” He takes iniquity generally as whatever is foreign to the divine commandments, and it is worked by the person to whom it is pleasing.

[Gloss, interlinear.] But if it displeases him, even though he falls, the weakness of nature causes it; he himself does not do it. Hence the Apostle: “Now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me” (Rom. 7).

It follows: “And you will destroy all”—not only those who work iniquity, but also those “who speak lies.”

[Augustine.] For this is contrary to truth. Truth concerns what is; falsehood is not a substance or a nature—that is, it does not concern what naturally is, but what is not. And rightly is that person destroyed who turns aside from what is to what is not.

It must be known that lying and speaking a lie are not altogether the same thing.

[Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 18; *On Lying*, chapter 12.] To lie is to speak contrary to what one thinks in one’s mind. Indeed, someone sometimes lies while saying what is true, because he speaks contrary to his conscience; and someone is sometimes truthful while saying what is false, because he does not speak contrary to his conscience. A lie, however, is a false signification by speech, with the intention of deceiving. Therefore, for there to be a lie, falsehood must be present and it must be spoken contrary to conscience.

What is said here should not be understood generally of every lie, just as neither should that saying: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1). For there are three kinds of lies.
