Some are told for another’s safety or advantage—not out of malice but kindness—such as the midwives are recorded to have done in Exodus, when they told Pharaoh a falsehood in order to save the children of the Hebrews (Exod. 1). Such lies are praised not in their actuality, but in the cunning or disposition involved. In those who lie in this manner, not the falsehood but the cunning—that is, prudence or disposition—is praised, because those who lie only in this way will someday deserve to be freed from every lie.

There is also another kind of lie, made in jest, which does not deceive. For the person to whom it is said knows that it is said in jest. These two kinds of lies are not without fault, but not serious fault. Yet the perfect ought not to lie, even in order to preserve someone’s temporal life, for by that person’s death his soul is not killed—whether it is the soul of a righteous person who remains silent or of another person who is killed.

They may, however, if they do not tell a falsehood, keep the truth silent. Thus, if someone does not wish to deliver a person over to death, let him conceal the truth but not tell a falsehood, lest he kill his own soul for another’s body. For there is no fault in sometimes concealing the truth, as the Lord also showed his disciples in the Gospel, saying: “I have many things to say to you which you cannot bear now” (John 16).

That case in which there is no double heart ought not to be called a lie. For example, if someone entrusts me with a sword and I promise to return it when he asks for it: if he asks for it while mad, I ought not return it, lest he kill himself or another. There is no double heart here, because, when I promised to return it, I did not think that he might demand it while mad.

If, therefore, someone cannot avoid all lies, let him at least have only lies of this necessity, so that, once freed from even these if they alone remain, he may deserve to receive the strength of the Holy Spirit, by which he may despise whatever must be endured for truth. But the third kind of lie proceeds from malice and duplicity, and must be avoided by all, especially and entirely.

### Verse 7

“The Lord abhors the man of blood and deceit.”

### Verse 8

“But I, in the multitude of your mercy, shall enter into your house; I shall worship toward your holy temple in your fear.”

“The man of blood”—

[Cassiodorus, Augustine.] —that is, the murderer—repeats what was said above, “those who work iniquity”; and “deceitful,” namely one who deceives his neighbor, is what was said above: “those who speak lies.” These, I say, the Lord abhors—that is, he disinherits them. Those who are disinherited are customarily called abhorred.

But the Church, which obtains the inheritance, rejoices in hope, saying: “But I.”

[Augustine, at the conclusion of this Psalm.] This is the third part according to Augustine, where the Church promises that she will become God’s house and will approach him in fear before the future consummation that casts fear out.

As though she said: “The malicious and unjust shall not remain before your eyes; but I, in the multitude of your mercy”—that is, not by my merits but by your abundant mercy—“shall enter into your house.”

[Remigius.] That is, into the heavenly house. Or the multitude of God’s mercy is the many perfect saints whom the Church now bears. With them the Church says: “I shall enter in the multitude of your mercy,” that is, with the multitude of perfected and blessed people, who are such through your mercy.

[Gloss, interlinear.] “I shall enter into your heavenly house,” as a stone into a building. Here is marked the reception of the free Sarah—that is, of the Church—as above was the exclusion of the slave-woman: “The malicious shall not dwell beside you,” etc.

In this entrance is perfection, as is shown by “I shall enter,” because “I shall worship toward your holy temple,” the heavenly one.

[Augustine.] That is, properly, toward the temple, not in the temple: I approach it by good works and prayers, praying that I may be in its building. This is said of progress, which comes before consummation is given. “I shall worship,” I say, “in your fear,” which is a great safeguard for those advancing toward salvation, but is cast out for those who arrive. For those who are already friends do not fear, to whom it has been said: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15), when, that is, they have been brought to what was promised.

### Verse 9

“Lord, lead me in your righteousness; because of my enemies, make my way straight in your sight.”

“Lord, lead me.” This is the fourth part according to Augustine, where the Church, advancing amid obstacles, prays to be helped inwardly, lest she be turned aside by deceitful tongues. According to Cassiodorus and Alcuin, this is the second part, where the Church asks for help against the assaults brought by her rival, through which that rival will perish.

As though she said: “I shall enter; in the future I shall worship. But now, amid adversities, O Lord, lead me,” that is, make me advance.

[Alcuin and Gloss, interlinear.] Being led is fitting for one making progress. By this she declares herself to be on a journey—that is, advancing toward perfection, not yet in perfection itself.

[Cassiodorus, Augustine.] “Lead,” I say, “in your righteousness,” by which you receive penitents and suppliants; not in human righteousness—that is, that which appears righteousness to a human being, where evil is repaid with evil. This appears just to people, but God does not act so. Even when he punishes, he does not inflict his own evil but leaves people to their own evils, casting them out into what they have chosen. A human being, however, when punishing, acts from an evil will; therefore, he himself is already evil, since he desires to punish evil.

Then he gives the reason why he ought to be led: “Because of my enemies,” to confound or convert them; “and make straight my way,” by which one goes to you, “in your sight”—that is, in the conscience, where no human being sees, but you alone do. A person who praises or blames is not to be trusted, because he does not see into the conscience, in which the way toward God is made straight. Hence follows:

### Verse 10

“For there is no truth in their mouth; their heart is vain.”

“For there is no truth in their mouth; their heart is vain.”

[Jerome.] Or thus, according to another reading, in which the text is also divided as follows: “Because of my enemies, who lie in wait for me, make straight”—that is, show—

[Remigius.] —“my way,” that is, your commandments, “in your sight,” so that I may have these commandments before my eyes. Govern me through them, so that I may not turn aside into heresy, either to the right hand of prosperity or to the left hand of adversity, but may walk the royal way, which is Christ, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14).

“For there is no truth in their mouth”—

[Augustine.] —namely, in the mouth of my enemies, whose judgment is not to be trusted. Therefore one must flee to the conscience, where God sees. Nor is it surprising that truth is absent from their mouth, because “their heart is vain.” “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Luke 8).

Their heart is vain because it deceives itself about sin, thinking certain sins not to be sins, and something to be sin which is not sin; and because it deceives itself concerning the punishment of sin, promising itself impunity. And not only is truth absent from their mouth, but also:

### Verse 11

“Their throat is an open sepulchre; with their tongues they dealt deceitfully. Judge them, O God.”

[Jerome, Remigius, and Alcuin.] Their throat is an open sepulchre—that is, comparable to an open sepulchre—because they bring forth foul things in order to corrupt others. When they do not succeed by their tongues—that is, by evil tongues—they act deceitfully. For if they cannot deceive suitably, they act with deceit, clothing false things under the appearance of truth.

Note that he says “they dealt,” because they not only devise deceits but accomplish what they intend when they seduce others.

Or thus: “Their throat is a sepulchre,” because of their greed, for which they lie by flattery. He adds “open” because their greed is always gaping, just as an open sepulchre is ready to receive corpses.

Or thus: “Their throat is an open sepulchre.”

[Augustine.] Because liars draw people to themselves by pleasant flattery and devour them by making them like themselves; when those people are dead, the liars are their sepulchres. It follows: “With their tongues they dealt deceitfully”—this does not change.

“Judge.” This is the fifth part according to Augustine. It is a prophecy, predicting the punishment of the wicked and the reward of the just. This is not a wish; rather, according to God’s righteousness, he sees what will happen. As though he said: “And because they are such, O God, judge them.” He does not wish it; he predicts what will be.

“Judge,” I say, in this way:

### Verse 12

“Let them fall from their thoughts; according to the multitude of their impieties cast them out, because they have provoked you, O Lord.”

“Let them fall from their thoughts,” that is, let them be frustrated in their opinions.

[Cassiodorus, Augustine.] One falls when one is frustrated in one’s hope. Or thus: “Let them fall,” that is, let them be condemned; and this “from their thoughts,” their conscience bearing witness against and accusing them. Let them so fall.

“Cast them out,” though they imagine themselves admitted, “according to the multitude of their impieties”—that is, far away, as their many impieties deserve. Drive them from the eternal inheritance, possessed by seeing God. For they will be cast out more or less according to the quantity and quality of their sins.

Therefore cast them out because, O Lord, “they have provoked you,” or “made you bitter”: by sinning, they have made you, the sweet food of truth, bitter to themselves. For the bread which came down from heaven, though sweet in itself and life to the sick, is made so bitter by sins that they cannot endure it.

### Verse 13

“And let all who hope in you rejoice; forever they shall exult, and you shall dwell in them.”

“And let them rejoice.” Here is the third part according to Cassiodorus, where, after the recompense of the wicked, he adds the rewards of the good, so that, as punishment frightens, rewards may attract.

[Jerome, Augustine.] As though he said: “Let those persons fall, but, on the contrary, let the good rejoice in the future because they have obtained the inheritance—all who now hope in you.” To those who taste you, you are sweet. Hence: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33).

“I say, let them rejoice,” and I say it without doubt—

[Cassiodorus.] —because “they shall exult forever,” not merely temporarily. Why shall they exult? Behold: “and,” that is, because “you shall dwell in them.”

[Augustine.] This is their eternal exultation: when the just become God’s temple and their joy is his dwelling in them.

### Verse 14

“And all who love your name shall glory in you, because you will bless the righteous.”

And then all who love your name shall glory in you, as possessing for enjoyment what they love. This is the eternal inheritance of which the Psalm is entitled. Therefore they shall glory, because “you will bless the righteous”—that is, you will give the righteous eternal blessing.

[Augustine.] Blessing is to glory in God and to dwell from him [perhaps “in him”; Latin: *habitare ab eo*]. But because calling, which belongs to grace, comes before this, he adds:

### Verse 15

“O Lord, you have crowned us as with the shield of your good will.”

“O Lord, you have crowned us as with the shield of your good will”: that is, your good will, by which you called us, is for us like a shield against the enemy, by which we are protected; and it is like victorious weapons by which the enemy is conquered.

[Augustine, Cassiodorus.] For God’s good will precedes our good will, so that he may call us to repentance; these are the weapons by which the enemy is overcome.

[Augustine.] This is the shield against the one who, in tribulations and temptations, suggests despair.

The meaning is: your good will, by which you call us, protects us and makes us conquer; and the whole is understood of the present.

[Cassiodorus.] Or thus: in one expression he indicates the benefits of God in both present and future time when he says, “You have crowned us as with the shield of your good will,” etc. It is understood partly of the present and partly of the future. A shield, named from its roundness and round in David’s homeland, does two things: it protects the body and crowns the head. Thus God’s gratuitous will, by which he calls us, is here a defense against all things and in the future a crown: like a shield fitted to the head, it is a crown; to the heart, a defense. “And, O Lord, you have crowned us as with the shield of your good will”: that is, your good will is for us in the present like a shield, and in the future like a crown.

## Comparison on the Psalm: “My Words,” etc.

[Col. 0102B]

### Verse 9

“Make my way straight in your sight.” In Hebrew the expression is inverted: *HANESCHAR LEPHANAI DARCHECA*, “Make my way straight in your sight.” Jerome, in his letters to Simia and Fretella and in Book III *Against the Pelagians*, attests that the manuscripts varied and that the sense comes to the same thing. For he says:

“Solomon says: ‘Be confident in the Lord with all your heart. But do not exalt yourself in your own wisdom. In all your ways know him, that he may make your paths straight.’ Understand what he says: we must not trust either in our own wisdom or in any virtues, but in the Lord alone, from whom a person’s steps are directed. Finally, we are commanded to show forth our ways and make them our own, though they are made right not by our own labor but by his help and mercy. Hence it is written: ‘Make your way straight in my sight,’ or, as other copies have it, ‘Make my way straight in your sight,’ so that what is right to you may also seem right to me.” Thus Jerome.

Indeed, God’s way is our way. It is God’s way which he commands and shows; it is our way by which we tend toward him. Hence in Psalm 118: “I have kept your commandments and your testimonies, because all my ways are in your sight.”

In this Psalm and all the rest, recent translators use words other than those of the Vulgate. But since the sense is not harmed, I do not wish the reader to be troubled by these trifles, although, in my judgment, they ought to have deferred to the common edition—provided, however, that they omit its wording with no purpose of condemning it, which we do not readily believe of them all.

Yet verse 10 warns us, where we have “their heart is vain,” while the Hebrew is *QUIRBAM HAVOTH*, “their inward part is perversities.” Though the sense does not differ, Jerome asserts that *QUIRBAM* is better in Hebrew. Jerome does not say that “inward part” is translated better than “heart,” but that it sounds better in Hebrew. For he immediately adds in his little commentary on this passage: “For the heart of heretics truly lies in wait for all whom it deceives.”

The reason has already been given above why the same divisions and parts of verses do not always occur. Therefore it is the mark of an idle person to contend too anxiously over matters of this kind.

### Verse 12

“They have provoked you, O Lord.” You need not wonder that “O Lord” is not in the Hebrew but is in the Septuagint and in our text, so as to give greater force in declaring the arrogant rebellion by which evil servants provoke so good a Lord.

For those translators freely allow themselves similar and dissimilar additions; for example, in Job 15, where our reading has: “He runs against him with neck outstretched,” etc., Sanctes translates: “God will run against him to strike him on the neck.” Münster: “Therefore the hand of God hastened against him, to seize him by the neck.” You see that the sense has been altered because they added “God” or “the hand of God,” which was not read in that place. The reader ought to remember this, lest we be compelled to sing the same song too often whenever opportunities for such remarks arise.

### Verse 13

“As with the shield of your good will.” Pagninus: “as with a shield, with love”; Jerome: “with the shield of graciousness.” The Hebrew word *ZATZON* is a devout disposition of mind or, as Pellican says, benevolence. One translated it in the genitive, another in the ablative. Since the Hebrews do not have such varieties of cases, they nevertheless have the construct state; hence it appears that the former expression was read: *CATZNATH*, “you have crowned us.”

*TAATRENNU*, that is, “you will crown him,” was undoubtedly read by the translators without the point in the belly of the letter *nun*, the point which the Hebrews call *dagesh*. If that point is inserted in the middle of the letter, it signifies “him”; without it, it signifies “us.” Faber’s statement that “us” is found in certain Hebrew manuscripts helps the sense very little: “you have crowned the righteous man” or “you have crowned us,” unless it is referred to Christ as crowned.

One should not dispute about the difference of tense. For the Hebrews very commonly use one tense for another, especially in the prophets.

## Psalm VI

[Col. 0103]

### Psalm VI. Title: “For the End, a Psalm of David, for the Octave.”

[Col.

0103B]

“Lord, not in fury.” Title: “For the end: a psalm of David, for the octave.” [Aug.] Some call the coming of the Lord for judgment the octave, because, they say, the Lord will come to judge the living and the dead after seven thousand years. But this time is known to no one, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows—not even an angel, nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Matt. 24). And the Apostle says: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thess. 5). The Son is said not to know, not because he himself does not know it within himself, but because he makes those know it not for whom it is not expedient to know. Hence the presumption of certain persons seems excessively rash, who, having calculated the years, confidently expect the day of the Lord to come after seven thousand years.

Rather, the eighth day [Col. 0103C] is called the day of judgment, because all times revolve in the recurrence of seven days, after which there will be that day which has no variation. Or the day of judgment is called the eighth because it will follow two lives, namely the carnal and the spiritual. For there are two lives lived in the present. One consists in the delight of the flesh and belongs to the body, which is the outer and old man; to this man, living according to the body, the Old Testament was given, and in this life death reigned. The other life belongs to the mind, which is the new man, regenerated through Christ. Now the number four belongs to the body, because it consists of four elements, is affected by four qualities—dry, moist, hot, and cold—and is governed by the four [Col. 0103D] seasons of the year: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. But the number three belongs to the soul because of its threefold power: rational, irascible, and concupiscible. Therefore, when both lives have been completed, as though the number seven had passed, the eighth day of judgment will come, when each will be repaid according to his merits.

Therefore the Church, fearing and repenting, prays here. The meaning is this: this psalm, which is called a psalm because it urges right conduct, directs us to the end, that is, to Christ, who is the completion of believers: in the present, toward righteousness; in the future, toward the crown. It is attributed to David, that is, to the penitent man who speaks here, repenting and fearing on account of his sins. [Cassiod., Alcuin.] I say, it is a psalm composed for the octave, that is, for fear of judgment. The octave is the coming of the Lord, in [Col. 0104A] which the sinner fears being reproved and therefore repents. And this [Col. 0104B] is the first of all the penitential psalms, of which there are seven. This is so as to show that, through the sevenfold Spirit, whatever is committed during the sevenfold course of this life may be blotted out; and because there are especially seven modes of remission through which sins are erased: baptism, almsgiving, martyrdom, the conversion of an erring brother, forgiving one who sins against oneself, weeping and satisfaction for sins, and communion in the body and blood of the Lord.

The form of these penitential psalms is such that they begin with tears and the bitterness of repentance and end in the certainty of pardon, as is clear here. There is also here a supplicatory confession, in which sin is acknowledged and pardon requested. Though such a plea has no place before secular judges, it nevertheless has great force before God, to whom the confession and condemnation of sin are pleasing.

[Col. 0104C] Intention: He urges repentance. Method: There are four divisions. First is the opening, in which he seeks favor from the person of the Judge through His power, and from his own person through his weakness; likewise from the Judge’s habitual mercy, since He does not wish to be entreated by the dead but by the living. Second, he sets forth the miseries of the penitent, at “I have labored.” Third, he shows himself corrected, so that he may be separated from the wicked, at “Depart from me,” and so forth. Fourth, he prays for the conversion of his enemies, at “Let them be ashamed,” and so forth. Thus, in the person of the penitent, who fears punishment in judgment, he prays, saying, O—

### Verse 1

> “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger.”

O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury. [Aug.] *Fury* is the same thing as *anger* in Greek; hence the terms are variously used here. For in some manuscripts *fury* is found first, then *anger*; in others the reverse, *anger* first and then *fury*. In others, *indignation* or *bile* is given instead of *fury*—a different reading.

But anger and fury are movements of the mind prompting the infliction of punishment; yet such a movement does not apply to God. Of Him it is written: “But you, Lord of powers, judge with tranquillity” (Wisdom 12). What is tranquil is not disturbed. Therefore disturbance does not apply to God as Judge; but His fury is understood as His anger, namely, the judgment in which He will appear as though angry and enraged toward the wicked.

To be rebuked and to be corrected are different. To be rebuked is more severe than to be accused; consequently condemnation is feared. To be corrected is milder, that is, to be amended or instructed. Those who have no foundation of faith will therefore be rebuked in judgment, that is, condemned. But those who have built wood, hay, and stubble upon that foundation will be corrected, that is, purified.

Therefore, unwilling to be among those who are rebuked or corrected, and knowing that “it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God,” this man prays, [Alcuin, Gl. int.] saying: O Lord, who are mighty, cut me here, burn me here; but do not rebuke me in your fury or indignation—that is, in the future judgment, where you will condemn the wicked as though I were to be condemned—nor even correct me, which is less severe, as though I were to be chastised, in your anger, that is, in judgment. It is as though he said: Heal me here, lest there be need there. [Aug.] For where health is, neither death nor the hand of a physician who burns or cuts is to be feared. Hence he adds:

[Col. 0105B]

### Verse 2

> “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak; heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled.”

### Verse 3

> “And my soul is exceedingly troubled; but you, O Lord—how long?”

[Rom., Hier.] “Have mercy”: as though he said, Do not rebuke me, but rather, O Lord, have mercy on me, wretched as I am, in this life. And this is necessary, [Cassiod.] because I am weak by nature and by vice, so weak that I cannot endure righteousness. Nor am I weak merely a little: weakness has reached even to my bones, that is, to the strength of my soul, and this exceedingly. [Aug.] This is what he says: Truly I am weak, “for my bones are troubled,” that is, the strength of my soul.

Then follows an explanation of “bones,” when he says [Col. 0105C]:

“And my soul”—behold the bones—“is troubled,” and this exceedingly. And because I thus disclose my sickness to you, heal me, O Lord. [Hier.] It is as though he said: Cure me as a wise physician, for I am sick and you are the physician; I possess weakness, you possess health; I am weak because of sin, you heal through mercy. I pray that you may heal me, and you, O Lord, delay—but how long?

[Aug.] He suggests that he has long struggled with vices. Yet God’s delay is not cruelty; rather, He delays in order to make the soul realize into what evils it has hurled itself. He delays also because this man does not yet pray so perfectly that it may be said to him: “While you are still speaking, I shall say: Behold, I am here.” He delays also so that, through the difficulty of healing, the person may henceforth guard himself more carefully. What is easily healed is not much guarded against. But from the difficulty of healing there comes more diligent protection of health once restored. And this is so that the punishment awaiting those who do not turn may be shown, if those who do turn are healed with such difficulty. Hence elsewhere: “If the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and sinner appear?” (1 Pet. 4).

Or it may be read thus: “Have mercy on me, O Lord.” This does not change. And it is necessary, because I am weak. [Alcuin.] The soul is weakened by guilt. From that guilt, heal me, O Lord. [Rem.] And you ought to do so, because my bones are troubled—that is, my mind is troubled unto repentance. And my soul, that is, even my sensuous nature, is exceedingly troubled unto repentance. [Alcuin.] Therefore, how long, O Lord, do you delay? It is as though he said: What remains to prevent your healing me? Nothing. Therefore, since you are merciful, do not delay; but rather, O—

[Col. 0106A]

### Verse 4

> “Turn, O Lord, and deliver my soul; save me for the sake of your mercy.”

[Aug.] Turn, O Lord, toward me, from whom you had turned away, so that I may turn to you, according to that saying: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you, says the Lord” (Zech. 1). Yet God is always ready for our perfect conversion, as the prophet says: “We shall find him prepared like the dawn” (Hos. 6). What prevented us from receiving Him was not His absence—He who is everywhere—but our own turning away.

It seems better, however, to say: “Turn, O Lord,” that is, make me turn perfectly. Here he recognizes the labor involved. For it is hard and laborious to be turned back from the darkness of earthly desires to the serenity and tranquillity of the divine light. [Col. 0106B] Therefore, after saying “Turn,” he adds: “and deliver my soul,” bound by sins, as though, in turning, hindered and oppressed by many enemies, like one entangled in the perplexities of this age and suffering, in the very act of conversion, thorns of tearing desires. “And save me,” that is, make me advance unharmed in goodness by giving me virtues. And do this for the sake of your mercy, not for my merits, because just condemnation is due to one who sins and transgresses a commandment that has been given.

[Cassiod.] Or thus: Turn, O Lord, from vengeance; deliver my soul from impending death; save me for the sake of your mercy. This does not change. It follows:

### Verse 5

> “For in death there is no one who remembers you; but in hell who will confess you?”

[Cassiod.] “For there is no one”: as though he said, Therefore I hasten to be forgiven here, because after death, or in hell, confession is not accepted. This is the meaning: “for in death there is no one who remembers you” for pardon, namely, in death—that is, after he has died. [Aug.] For he understands that this is now the time of conversion, because once this life has passed, nothing remains except recompense. “There is no one who remembers you in death; but in hell who will confess you?”

[Cassiod.] No one will confess you for pardon, namely, after judgment. This does not conflict with the rich man in the Gospel, who confessed in hell when he saw Lazarus at rest, though from the deep; compelled by comparison with Lazarus, he confessed his [Col. 0106D] evils, so much so that he even asked that his brothers be forewarned of them. But after judgment the ungodly will be in deeper darkness, where they will see no light of God to whom they might make any confession.

Or he calls sin “death,” sin committed in contempt of the divine law, just as we call the sting of death “death,” because it produces death. For “the sting of death is sin”; in sin, the person who despises God’s commands is forgetful of God. He calls “hell” the blindness of mind which one incurs when one despairs. For the blindness of despair receives and envelops the sinner—that is, the dying person—so that he is given over to a reprobate mind.

The wording is connected thus: Therefore I groan and grieve so over sin, because in hell—that is, in sin, by which the divine law is despised—there is no one who remembers you. But in hell—that is, in the blindness [Col. 0107A] of despair which envelops the dead person—who will confess you? No one.

## Part II

### Verse 6

> “I have labored in my groaning; every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall drench my couch.”

“I have labored.” [Cassiod., Alcuin.] This is the second part, in which he relates the miseries by which the penitent is worn down. It is as though he said: No one remembers you in death or in hell; [Aug., Gl. int., Cassiod., Alcuin.] but, that I may be delivered from it, I have labored in making satisfaction, “in my groaning,” that is, the groaning of my heart. He groans when he sees what he has done and what punishment is to come. And, as though this had profited too little, he adds:

[Aug., Hier., Cassiod.] “And afterward, every night I shall wash my bed”: literally, I shall weep in bed through the nights because of my sins. He repeats the same thing in other words: [Col. 0107B] “With my tears I shall drench my couch.” Here *couch* is understood as the same thing as the preceding *bed*: it is as though he said, I shall soak with my tears the covering laid upon my bed; that is, I shall shed many tears.

[Rem., Alcuin.] Or he calls the conscience the bed: for some it is rest, and for others torment. The pure in heart rest there; the ill-disposed are tortured there. He calls sensuous nature the couch. The meaning is: “I shall wash my bed,” that is, cleanse my conscience. [Rem.] “Every night,” that is, in respect of every sin. 13 [Rem., Alcuin.] “And with my tears,” that is, with the bitterness of repentance, “I shall drench my couch,” that is, my sensuous nature; I shall make it fruitful, though it was formerly dry of good works.

[Aug., Cassiod.] Or the bed is bodily pleasure and worldly delight, in which the sick soul rests and the human being is relaxed. The couch is the accumulation of sins, like a heap of garments; when this heap is loosened by the rain of tears, a new harvest of virtues springs up. The meaning is: “I shall wash,” that is, erase with tears of repentance, [Aug., again,] “my bed,” that is, bodily pleasure and worldly delight, which the person washes who strives to withdraw himself from it. And I shall do this “every night,” that is, for each sin arising from it.

He says “every night” in order to convey that he suffers, as it were alternately, days and nights. For one who is willing in spirit perceives some light of truth, yet sometimes rests in the delight of this world because of the weakness of the flesh, and is compelled to suffer days and nights by alternating inclination. He suffers nights when he serves the law of sin with the flesh, and perceives days when he serves the law of God with the mind. [Cassiod.] “With my tears I shall drench my couch,” that is, with the shower of tears I shall dissolve the accumulation of sins, so that afterward a harvest of virtues may germinate.

Notice that he says, “I shall drench,” though he said above, “I shall wash.” For drenching is more than washing: something can be washed on the surface, but drenching reaches inward parts. By this he signifies that weeping remains even in the depths of the heart.

### Verse 7

> “My eye has been troubled by fury; I have grown old among all my enemies.”

[Aug.] “My eye has been troubled by fury,” or by anger. Fury or anger here is understood either as God’s or as the person’s own. Again, God’s anger is twofold: that which will be at the judgment, and that which is present here, in the blindness of mind, when sinners are given over to a reprobate mind. There will be outer darkness then, because sinners will then be wholly outside God—that is, outside the light—because they will be in utter blindness. For what is it to be wholly outside God but to be in utter blindness? God indeed dwells in inaccessible light. But these darknesses begin already here in the sinner, when he is shut out from God’s inward light; yet not wholly, while he remains in this life.

Therefore he says that the eye is troubled, not extinguished. It is as though he said: Therefore I wash, because my eye, that is, my reason, has been troubled by God’s fury—both the future fury which I fear and the present fury which I feel. His eye has also been troubled by his own anger, which, by disturbing the inward sun—that is, the wisdom of God—prevents it from seeing; and the mind, which is not permitted to see it because of its own disturbance, imagines that it undergoes a sunset within itself. Hence the Apostle says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger.”

The meaning is: Therefore I groan thus, because my eye, namely reason, has been troubled by fury, or by my own anger. It has been troubled, and deservedly, because “I have grown old among all my enemies,” namely, vices or wicked persons, who are truly enemies of those turning to God. Every good person is separated from them, not in place but in mind. And he adds “all,” as though he said: I have grown old even among all of them; I was exempt from none, but consented to all.

Or it may be read thus: Therefore I labor in this way because I have grown old, having become a member of the old man. He says this by comparison with an old garment, which is fit neither for adornment nor for use, among all my visible and invisible enemies, to whom I consented. By this he shows himself subject to every vice. He says this lest anyone despair because of the gravity of sins.

But why did this happen? Because my eye, that of reason, was troubled by the fury inflicted upon the first parent, [Alcuin.] that is, by the punishment laid upon the first man and transmitted through him to all his posterity. For he is the root, and we are the branch of punishment. [Aug., Alcuin.] Yet because the labor of repentance is not fruitless after labor, groaning, and the most frequent showers of tears, he indicates that he has been heard, adding:

### Verse 8

> “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.”

“Depart from me.” [Cassiod.] This is the third part, in which the correction of the man who prays is shown, so that he may be separated from those evils now in mind and in the future also in place—their company having been that in which he sinned—and may hold fast to God’s commands. Or this is not a wish but a prophecy, because this will happen at the judgment, when the ungodly will be separated from the righteous. Or it is happening even now on the threshing floor, where the grains are already bare and separated in mind from the chaff, though they may be hidden among it and contained in the same gatherings.

Thus this penitent says, signifying that after such great difficulties he has been heard: “Depart from me, now in mind and in the future also in place, all you who work iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.”

### Verse 9

> “The Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has received my prayer.”

The Lord has heard, by forgiving, [Col. 0109A] my supplication, which is for putting away sins. [Rem., Aug.] The frequent repetition here of the same thought comes from excessive feeling, because for one who rejoices it is not enough to say only once what gives joy. Hence he adds: The Lord has received, [Cassiod., Rem.] as an offering, my prayer, [Gl. int., Alcuin.] which is for obtaining virtues. For supplication is for the removal of evils; prayer, for the bestowal of goods. [Cassiod.] By these words he gives an example that those who pray faithfully are heard. Notice that “Lord” is used three times here, showing that the holy Trinity was present to the prayers. He begins with tears and, being heard, rejoices, as also happens in the other penitential psalms.

### Verse 10

> “Let all my enemies be ashamed and exceedingly troubled; let them turn back and be very quickly ashamed.”

“Let them be ashamed.” This is the fourth part, in which, now free from sins and rejoicing in the conclusion, he prays for his enemies to be converted, so that, like himself, they may have pardon. It is as though he said: Since the Lord heard me when I repented, then let all my enemies, by my example, turn back and be ashamed—that is, of their deeds, because they are evil—and be troubled by fear of judgment unto repentance. And let this be done vehemently, that is, with vehement groaning.

[Aug.] The perfect man prays here that the wicked may be ashamed of their sins, repent, and turn back, [Cassiod.] lest they go where they were heading; and that this not be delayed, but that they be very quickly ashamed. [Aug.] This may refer to the effect desired, or to Christ’s power, who in so swift a time quickly turned the nations to faith. Or thus: let them turn quickly from evils. And after conversion, let them be greatly ashamed in the recollection of their sins, which is the safeguard of virtues.

Or this is prophecy, not a wish: he foretells what will happen to the enemies who here refuse to repent of their sins. It is as though he said: The Lord heard me, but all my enemies, and so forth—that is, they will be greatly ashamed and troubled in the future. This certainly does not happen here, where the wicked instead mock those who abandon everything and, by their mockery, cause the weak to be ashamed of Christ’s name. But [Col. 0110A] it will occur at the judgment, when, ashamed, they will say of the good, as it is written:

> “These are they whom we once held in derision and made a proverb of reproach. We fools considered their life madness and their end without honor. Behold, how they have been numbered among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints! What did pride profit us, or what did the boasting of riches bring us? All those things have passed away like a shadow” (Wisdom 5).

“And let them turn back and be ashamed”: it is as though he said, Let their turning be unto confusion, since they refused to have unto salvation that which is most just. And let all these things happen very quickly, because when they begin to despair of judgment and say, “Peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them (1 Thess. 5). When it comes, it will be perceived that an entire life has not been long; for just as its coming seems slow to those who desire it, so it will seem swift to those in despair.

This psalm is sung at funeral rites, because through groaning of this kind and penitential lamentation the faithful obtain after this life what they long desired long and earnestly in this life; while the wicked experience what they did not fear here but despised.

## Comparison on Psalm VI: “Lord,” etc.

### Verse 3

In this psalm the more recent translators use different words, though the meaning remains untouched; nor is it our purpose to hunt down every syllable. It will suffice to examine those renderings which differ more widely and substantially, occasionally noting lighter matters as we move on to others. Sanctes added of his own: “you will crush”; Münster: “you will afflict.” But: “How long, O Lord, will you crush me?” Cajetan’s translator has, “Will you be angry?” although the explanation of Jerome and Augustine tends toward the implied meaning: “you do not deliver,” “you do not correct.” If the Latin translator had added this, I do not know whether they would have loudly protested that it was not in the Hebrew and therefore had to be slain, torn out, or pierced through.

### Verse 5

“In hell who,” etc. What came into the minds of Sanctes and Münster, that they should translate *pit* and *grave* in place of *hell*, when they themselves teach that *Sheol* signifies pit, grave, and hell, confirm this from passages of Scripture, and Jerome, Pratensis, Pellicanus, Campensis, and Nebiensis have used *hell*?

# Psalm VII

[Col. 0109]

## Title of the Psalm

> “For the end: a psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord concerning the words of Cush, son of Gemini.”

[Col. 0109D]

“Lord my God.” The title: “For the end: a psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord concerning the words of Cush, son of Gemini.” [Note: [Col. 0109] From Augustine; but Jerome disapproves this explanation of the title.]

The history from which the prophet took the occasion may easily be learned in the Second Book of Kings. There it is read that David, fleeing from his son Absalom, left the city barefoot. At David’s counsel, his friend Cush went over to Absalom’s side in order to spy out the plans and report what Absalom was plotting against his father, under the instigation of Ahithophel, who had abandoned David’s friendship and was instructing the son, by every counsel he could, against his father. Among all else, Ahithophel gave him this counsel: that Absalom should permit an attack [Col. 0110D] to be made on his father and have him killed. This was changed by Cush’s prudence: he advised David and secretly instructed him to flee from the plains into the wilderness. Moved by grief, Ahithophel then hanged himself with a noose.

The title alludes to this history, though the psalm does not treat of it. Rather, the prophet took from the history a veil for mysteries, which are explained according to the interpretations of the names. For *Chusi* means “silence”; *Gemini*, “right hand”; and *Achitophel*, “the ruin of a brother.” By this is signified the crime of Judas—that is, the criminal Judas who betrayed the Lord to the Jews and thus became the ruin of his brother, namely Christ. Christ’s disciples are called not only sons but also brothers, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Go and tell my brothers” [Col. 0111A] (Matt. 28). And the Apostle says: “[that he might be] the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. 8).

And as David fought against Ahithophel and Absalom through Cush’s counsel, so the Lord fought against all the deceits of Judas—that is, of Judas and the Jews—through Cush, that is, through silence: the profound secret by which blindness came upon Israel, “so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter in, and thus all Israel might be saved” (Rom. 11). Marveling at this silence rather than explaining it, the Apostle cries out: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God,” and so forth (ibid.).

By this silence the Lord, concealing from Judas and the Jews the sacrament of the Passion, turned the “ruin of a brother,” that is, Judas’s crime, into mercy; and what Judas did for the destruction of one man, the Lord bent toward the salvation of all. Therefore the faithful person to whom the words of Cush have been made—that is, to whom the manifestation of this silence, this secret, wrought by God’s favorable right hand, has been given—sings this psalm to the Lord. For it was not to be concealed from those for whom it was accomplished.

Therefore the mystery of the incarnation and Passion was silence to the Jews, but revelation to the faithful, to whom Christ made known all that he had heard from the Father (John 15). And just as Judas is signified by Ahithophel, so the Jews are signified by Absalom. For as David suffers from his wicked son, so Christ endured suffering from the people he had nurtured, as he says through Isaiah: “I have nourished and raised up children, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1).

[Rem.] The meaning of the title is thus: This psalm, which directs us to the end, that is, to Christ, is attributed to David, that is, to the faithful person to whom the revelation of the mystery was made; that faithful person sang the psalm to the Lord, that is, in honor of the Lord, “concerning the words of Cush,” that is, concerning the manifestation of the profound silence by which Christ [Col. 0111C] fought against the Jews while concealing the mystery of the Passion. Cush is called “son of Gemini,” that is, of the right hand, because God’s right hand—that is, God, favorable and merciful—opened that silence to this faithful person.

[Aug., Cassiod.] Literally, Cush is said to be the son of Jemini, that is, of the right hand, because he advised what was necessary for David’s salvation by a necessary act of betrayal. This psalm is the first of those in which future mysteries of the Lord are signified broadly and openly through David’s actions. In the third psalm, likewise, Christ’s mysteries are signified through David’s actions, but briefly and obscurely.

Intention: He urges thanksgiving for the manifestation of the silence. Method: There are five divisions. First, he asks to be delivered from all persecutors or persecutions. Second, he asks that the glory of Christ’s resurrection may come to his aid, at “Arise, O Lord.” Third, he treats of the judgment of one who has returned, at “The Lord judges the peoples.” Fourth, he frightens by fear of the future judgment while promising hope to those who return, at “The Lord is judge.” Fifth, a joyful conclusion concerning the granting of praise is set forth, at “I will confess.” Thus this faithful man, not presuming upon himself, prays to be delivered by the Lord, putting forward his merit in this manner: O—

### Verse 1

> “O Lord my God, in you I have hoped; save me from all who persecute me, and deliver me.”

[Gl. int.] Lord of all by power, to whom *dulia* is due; God of all by re-creation, to whom *latria* is due. And you are my Lord and God by my will. I have hoped in you, not in myself. [Hier., Cassiod., Remig., Gl. int.] Behold, he puts forward his merit; then he asks to be delivered from vices and the devil, saying: “Save me from all who persecute me,” that is, from all spiritual wickednesses, namely vices and sins. “And deliver me.”

### Verse 2

> “Lest at any time he seize my soul like a lion, while there is none to redeem or save.”

[Hier., Aug.] “Lest at any time”: that is, lest at some time he—the devil, who “goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5), and who fights in them—seize me like a lion. For he uses vices and sins as weapons to attack the faithful. [Gl. int.] Let him seize, I say, my soul. This man does not care if his body is afflicted.

[Cassiod., Alcuin.] Notice that he uses distinctive words when he says “deliver” and “seize.” It is the Lord’s work to deliver; the lion’s, to seize. Observe also the fitting sequence: first he names the persecutors, then the lion. [Aug., Alcuin.] For one cleansed of all spiritual wickednesses, that is, the filth of transgressions, is delivered from the devil.

[Gl. int.] Or otherwise, so that “persecutors” and “lion” are understood as the same thing: the envious one, namely the devil. For the perfect man speaks here; having already conquered vices, he has no battle but against the devil, saying: “Save me from all who persecute me,” and so forth—that is, from the devil and his angels. [Aug.] As though every warfare of vices had been overcome, nothing now remains for the perfected man except the envious devil.

Then what he had said in the plural he adds in the singular: “Deliver me, lest at any time,” that is, at some time, “the lion,” that is, the devil, “seize my soul.” Let him seize it, I say, while there is none to redeem except Christ. It is as though he said: If you do not redeem, he seizes; nor is there anyone who can save—that is, by giving eternal life—except the one who redeems, namely Christ. For unless Christ redeems and saves, the devil seizes.

And so that it may be evident that this is said by the perfect man, against whom only the most deceitful snares of the devil must be guarded, he adds:

### Verse 3

> “O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands.”

“O Lord my God,” and so forth. [Gl. int.] Here again he puts forward merit, namely that he is innocent and patient. [Col. 0112D] It is as though he said: Deliver and save me, because, O Lord my God, and so forth. [Aug., Alcuin.] “I have not done this,” namely that universal sin which he stated without naming: pride, the root of all evils, the first vice of those who depart and the last of those who return. “And there is no iniquity in my hands,” that is, in my works.

Or thus: “I have not done this.” [Alcuin.] He then explains what he said, “I have not done this”: namely, what follows, “there is no iniquity in my hands,” which is said and understood of every sin. Then repeat according to the sequence of each individual phrase: O Lord my God, “if I have done this.” [Aug.] Or: the universal sin, because he stated it without naming it. Or: what follows, namely, “if there is iniquity in my hands,” and so forth.

[Col. 0113A]

### Verse 4

> “If I have repaid evil to those repaying me [with] evil, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies.”

“If I have repaid evil,” namely, to those who repaid me evil for good. [Aug.] It is greater patience not to repay those who repay evil for good than to endure those to whom one has done no good. This is to say: If I have not imitated in patience what you worked for me in that silence, so as to endure most patiently the deceits of your betrayer, may I deservedly fall.

He does not invoke this upon himself by an oath, but says what happens to those who avenge themselves. Thus he prophesies; he does not swear by imprecation, as he seems to do. Such swearing is the gravest kind of oath, when a person says: If I did that, may I suffer this. I say, may I fall, conquered by my enemies and made empty. For whoever secretly avenges himself is conquered by the devil, made empty through vain and proud joy because he was unable to be conquered. But whoever does not repay evil conquers anger. And he who conquers anger is better than one who takes a city, as Solomon says (Prov. 16).

It is clear here that the perfect man speaks. For no one but the perfect man can say: “If I have repaid evil to those who repaid me evil,” knowing that Christ did this. [Cassiod., Alcuin.] Or it may literally be understood of David, who committed nothing against Absalom for which Absalom ought to inflict evil upon him, when he said: “O Lord my God, if I have done,” and so forth—that is, if this evil which I suffer happens to me because of a past fault which I committed against Absalom. Or if now there is iniquity in my hands, and so forth—that is, in my works—for which this happens to me. Or, “if I have repaid evil to those who repaid me evil”: which is called justice among human beings, may I deservedly fall, even if it does not appear so to people. I say, may I fall, conquered by my enemies, namely Absalom and his accomplices, and made empty of the fruit of meekness, which abounded in David.

Then, in the person both of David himself and of the perfect man, he adds:

[The source proceeds directly to verse 6.]

### Verse 6

> “Let the enemy pursue my soul and seize it, and trample my life to the earth, and bring my glory down into the dust.”

[Aug.] “Let him pursue”: it is as though he said, I said, “May I fall empty,” and, what is more serious, may the enemy pursue me—namely the devil, who is uniquely the enemy and was above called the lion. [Gl. int.] Let him pursue my soul, against which human beings have no power. They can indeed rage against the flesh, but cannot have the soul in their power.

The devil pursues the soul by attacking it, namely by suggestion, and seizes it when he deceives it. Hence he adds: “and seize it,” that is, deceive it through consent; “and trample my life to the earth,” that is, by trampling it, make my life earth, namely food for himself. For he is not only the lion, as was said above, but is also called the serpent. To him it was said in the curse: “You shall eat earth” (Gen. 3). And to the sinner it was said: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (ibid.).

[Alcuin.] Therefore the life of the sinner is food for the serpent, that is, the devil, because it is earth, that is, earthly. [Cassiod., Aug.] Therefore he says here: “Let him trample my life to the earth,” that is, incorporate my soul, reduced to earth, into himself, and let it be contemptible there. Hence he adds: “and bring my glory,” that is, me, a human being made in God’s image, “down into the dust,” as though he said, reduce me to nothing.

Or thus: “my glory,” which ought to be in the conscience, where God sees, and firm in the Lord, so that “he who glories may glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10), “bring down into the dust,” that is, into pride and boasting, so that I may wish to glory before human beings. For dust, which the wind casts about, is the boasting of the proud. He therefore wishes his glory to be firm within, where God sees. It is dust if he glories before human beings. Behold how greatly pride must be guarded against.

### Verse 7

> “Arise, O Lord, in your anger; and be exalted at the boundaries of my enemies.”

[ Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] “Lord, arise.” This is the second part [Col. 0114B], in which he asks that the glory of Christ’s resurrection may come to his aid. [Glossa interlinearis.] As though he said: “If I have done this, let this happen to me.” [Augustine.] But because I have not deserved it, O Lord, arise—that is, appear in the flesh. For he sleeps while, hidden in his secret counsels, he remains unknown. [Cassiodorus.] Appear, I say, in your wrath—that is, in vengeance against the devil. For this perfect man does not here pray against human beings, but against the devil, that he may lose his possession—that is, sinners and ungodly persons, who are his possession. [Augustine.] For when an ungodly person is justified, he passes from the devil’s possession into the temple of God. And because the removal of a human being is punishment for the devil, God’s wrath against him is therefore spoken of. Hence he adds: “And be exalted in the borders,” [Glossa interlinearis, Augustine.] in the possession of my enemies—that is, of the devil and his angels—so that there you may be honored by converts [Col. 0114C], who were formerly the devil’s possession. And because the proud devil is overcome through humility, showing in what manner he wishes Christ to appear, he adds:

VERSE 8.—“And arise, O Lord my God, in the command which thou hast commanded; and the synagogue of the peoples shall surround thee.”

“And for its sake return on high; the Lord judges the peoples.”

“And arise”—that is, appear—“O Lord my God, in the command of humility which thou hast commanded.” [Augustine.] That is: because you command humility, fulfill it first yourself; appear humble, so that others may learn from you to overcome pride, lest they be possessed by the proud one. I say, appear humble, [Alcuin, Glossa interlinearis, Augustine.] and thus the synagogue—that is, the assembly [Col. 0114D]—of the peoples shall surround you, some in love, some in persecution. For the peoples surrounded Christ: either despising him as humble, in persecuting him; or loving him, in believing.

And, O Lord, return—by rising again and ascending—on high, that is, into heaven, for its sake: that is, for the sake of the synagogue that will believe, so that from on high you may send the Spirit by whom the assembly comes into being. Or, for its sake—namely, for the persecuting synagogue—return on high by withdrawing yourself from it. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] As though he said: since you have no place among the wicked, withdraw yourself from them.

Or thus from the words, “Arise in the command”: here he prays for Christ’s resurrection, as in the preceding verse for his incarnation. As though he said: “Appear in the flesh.” And, O Lord my God, arise [Col. 0115A]—[Remigius, Alcuin.] that is, by rising make yourself known throughout the whole world. And do this by fulfilling the command which you gave: that is, cause human beings to fulfill the command of humility which you commanded. Thus the following clause proceeds: because the synagogue of the peoples—that is, from diverse peoples, or specifically from the Jews—shall surround you, loving or persecuting you, as was said above. And for its sake, namely for the loving synagogue, return on high: that is, make those who love you know your omnipotence—you who descended in order that they might see you. Or, for its sake—that is, for the persecuting synagogue, in which you find no place—return on high: that is, withdraw yourself from those who persecute you. This interpretation partly agrees with the preceding one.

Or thus from the words, “Arise, O Lord, in thy wrath”: the Church says, “Exercise [Col. 0115B] your wrath against my enemies, namely the Jews.” [Augustine.] Then, as if explaining, she adds: “And for this reason be exalted in the borders of my enemies, O Christ”—that is, become high and unknown to my enemies, who are your enemies, so that they do not understand you. This is the “silence” from which the psalm takes its title, so that they may thus crucify you. “And arise, O Lord my God, in the command which thou hast commanded”: that is, when you appear humble—you who command humility—be high. For he was exalted by humility, that is, not understood. And because the Jews who crucify you do not understand you, the Gentiles will believe in you. Thus the synagogue of the peoples—that is, the fullness of the Gentiles—shall surround you in faith. And for its sake—that is, for the synagogue of the Gentiles [Col. 0115C]—return on high: that is, again cease to be understood, because it too will offend against you at the end and will depart from the faith. Hence he says in the Gospel: “Do you think that, when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18). For the charity of many will grow cold, and iniquity will abound (Matthew 24). And the Lord will return on high, so that sincere faith, cleansed from the stain of every perverse opinion, may be held by a few.

However this passage is interpreted, what follows is fitting:

“The Lord judges the peoples.” [Cassiodorus.] This is the third part, treating of the judgment of him who has returned—that is, of Christ—whose return has been explained above in several ways. [Augustine.] After this he fittingly adds concerning judgment. For after the ascension into heaven, understood as a return, he plainly adds concerning judgment, because from there he will come to judge [Col. 0115D] the living and the dead. Or, when he abandons sinful Christians to their lack of understanding of the truth—which too is called a return, according to another interpretation—he will come to judge. As though he said: “I said, ‘Return’; and after the return the Lord judges, or will judge, the peoples.” The perfect man, unafraid of this judgment, dares to pray:

VERSE 9.—“Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness and according to my innocence over me.”

“Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness,” [Remigius.] which consists in doing good things; “and according to my innocence,” etc., because I am free from evils, because I have not repaid evil to those repaying me with evil. [Augustine.] Note that above, in the penitential psalm, the penitent said: “Save me for thy mercy’s sake” [Col. 0116A] (Psalm 6), in which he calls sinners to repentance and makes no mention of any merit of his own. But now, already called, because he has kept the commandments, he asks to be judged according to righteousness—“over me.” As though he said: “My righteousness and my innocence are over me,” since even that righteousness and innocence are from God, not from me.

VERSE 10.—“The wickedness of sinners shall be brought to an end, and thou shalt direct the righteous man, O God who searchest hearts and reins.”

“The wickedness shall be brought to an end.” [Augustine.] As though he said: “The Lord will judge; and meanwhile the wickedness of sinners shall be completed,” that he who is filthy may become filthier still (Revelation 22), so that at last just judgment may come. He predicts this; he does not desire it. [Remigius.] And because, as the envy of the wicked increases, the merits of the righteous increase, [Col. 0116B] it is added: “And thou shalt direct.” As though he said: “The wickedness of the wicked will be completed; and from this you shall direct the righteous man, so that the righteous may be justified still more.” And because, owing to dissimulation, a human being cannot know where true righteousness lies, he adds what belongs to God alone. You, I say, O God, search hearts and reins: that is, thoughts and delights, which he searches in secret, where none sees save him who beholds hearts—that is, God. For he alone searches hearts, namely what each person thinks, and reins, namely what delights each person; for the end of care and thought is delight, which each strives by care and thought [Col. 0116C] to attain. Delight is understood through the reins because the pleasure of generation is in the reins, through which human nature is transmitted by succession of offspring into a life of misery and deceptive joy. Human beings can see our works, consisting in words and deeds; but God alone sees with what disposition they are done and what end they seek, he who, when he sees that the heart is in heaven and delights not in the flesh but in the Lord—[Augustine.] that is, when thoughts and their ends are good—directs the righteous man. Nor does he only direct him, but also helps him; hence follows:

VERSE 11.—“My help is righteous from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart.”

“My help from the Lord is righteous.” [Augustine.] It is righteous because it is now given to the righteous person. It is like medicine: one kind preserves health; another produces it. For medicine has two functions: to cure illness [Col. 0116D] and to preserve health. According to the first function he said in another psalm: “I am weak; heal me,” etc. (Psalm 6). According to the other, the perfect man says here: “My help is righteous,” etc. Both kinds of medicine save; but one transfers from sickness to health, while the other preserves a person in health itself. The former provides a remedy for escaping illness; the latter, a remedy lest one return or relapse into illness. By the former we, being sick, are healed; by the latter, being healthy, we are preserved. And observe that he says “upright in heart,” and does not add “and in reins,” because where the heart is, there also is delight, when eternal things are contemplated; and because delight in the good pertains not to the reins but to the heart.

PART IV. VERSE 12.—“God is a righteous judge, strong and patient; does he become angry every day?”

[Col. 0117A] “God is judge.” [Cassiodorus, Glossa interlinearis.] This is the fourth part, in which he terrifies by fear of future judgment and promises hope to those who return. As though he said: “My help is from him. But, O wicked persons, whose wickedness is here being brought to completion, God has brandished the sword”—namely, at the judgment. And truly, because he himself is judge; he himself is righteous, rendering to each according to merits. [Augustine.] He himself is strong, one whom none can resist; and although he is now patient, enduring in much patience vessels of wrath. And truly he is patient: for does he become angry every day? No; rather, he awaits repentance. Hence he punishes them more severely afterward if they do not turn. [Augustine.] And according to another text: “Does he bring wrath every day?” Thus it is found in Greek: μὴ ὀργὴν ἐπάγων, “not bringing wrath”; and this is said more significantly than “does he become angry,” because the wrath by which he punishes is not in God himself [Col. 0117B] but in the angels of wrath through whom he punishes. They delight in human punishment, not because of the justice in which they take no delight, but because of malice. Therefore God does not bring wrath every day—that is, he does not daily gather his ministers for vengeance—but by patience invites people to repentance.

VERSE 13.—“Unless you are converted, he has brandished his sword; he has bent his bow and made it ready.”

[Remigius.] “Unless you are converted”: as though he said, “He is now patient; but unless you wicked persons are converted, he has brandished his sword,” or, “has made his blade glitter.” Another reading: the sword of God is Christ, [Augustine.] who in his first advent was hidden as in a sheath of humility; but in the second he will flash forth light to his own and terror to the ungodly. [Col. 0117C] Or: “He has brandished his sword”—[Remigius.] that is, he will execute manifest vengeance. Nor has this been left unannounced, for “he has bent his bow and made it ready.” He calls Sacred Scripture the bow, in which the hardness of the Old Testament is bent and tamed by the string of the New Testament. Therefore he has bent the bow by tempering the Old Testament through the New. He has prepared the bow by an explanatory exposition, through which he made it intelligible. He says this by comparison. [Alcuin.] For as one who bends a bow threatens, so God threatens the wicked through Sacred Scripture, lest God’s patience be thought lax.

VERSE 14.—“And in it he has prepared instruments of death; he has made his arrows for those who burn.”

[Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] “And in it he has prepared”: so that he may be thought about to send [Col. 0117D] an arrow immediately, just as one prepares a bow in order to shoot an arrow. And “in it,” the bow—[Augustine, Alcuin.] that is, in Sacred Scripture—“he has prepared instruments of death,” namely heretics, who poison souls out of the Scriptures and are therefore called instruments of death. He prepares them in Scripture, not by making them, but by permitting them to err. And from that same bow he shoots his arrows, namely the apostles, of whom it is elsewhere said: “Sharp arrows of the mighty one” (Psalm 119). He made these arrows—that is, he brought them about—for those burning with love of God. Wounded by these arrows, they burn with such love for the kingdom of heaven that they despise everything opposing or recalling them from their purpose, saying: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” (Romans 8).

Or, he takes “instruments of death” and “arrows” for the same thing—[Col. 0118A] namely, certain obscure passages of Sacred Scripture. [Alcuin.] From these comes death to heretics who understand them perversely; but to those burning with zeal, the same passages are arrows, because they are exercised by the very difficulty of understanding them, so that they may comprehend soundly and explain them to others. [Augustine.] Or, he calls “instruments of death” and “arrows” the heretics, who leap from the same bow of Sacred Scripture into souls, not to inflame them with charity but to destroy them with poisons. This does not occur except according to human deserts. For God prepares and ordains that certain people, reading with an evil intention, should through their sins understand wrongly what is in the Scriptures; this is a punishment for their sin. And they, like thorns and arrows, rouse the good children of the Catholic Church from sleep, so that they may keep watch in understanding the Scriptures, so that those approved may be made manifest as silver. But this [Col. 0118B] is attributed to divine ordering, not because God himself makes people sinners, but because, when they have sinned, he orders something out of their evils. Or both terms may be understood of the good. For the same persons are instruments of death to some and arrows to others, according to the Apostle’s saying: “To some we are an odor of death unto death; to others, an odor of life unto life” (2 Corinthians 2). The sense is: in that bow, that is, in Sacred Scripture, he has prepared instruments of death, namely apostles who are to some an odor of death; and he has made the same persons his arrows, namely an odor of life unto life, for those burning with love of the Word. But after this ordering, just judgment will come for the sins of the wicked. Of it it is said that it is not the peace of God and ineffable light that brings forth from itself the means by which the wicked are punished; rather, sins themselves are turned into punishment for a person, so that [Col. 0118C] what were delights to the person committing them become instruments for God as punisher.

VERSE 15.—“Behold, he labors to bring forth injustice; he has conceived pain and has borne iniquity.”

[Alcuin.] “Behold,” he says, “he labors to bring forth injustice.” As though he said: “God has prepared this in the Scriptures, from which he seems to be the cause of the condemnation of wicked people. But behold, it is manifest that the cause of condemnation comes not from God but from the human being, because the wicked person is like one opening and digging a pit and falling into the hole he has made.” [Glossa interlinearis, Augustine.] And truly, because he has conceived from the devil—namely, through suggestion—pain, that is, desire for temporal things. It is called pain because wicked persons feel pain at the loss of earthly things, for the sake of which they devise evils. These are [Col. 0118D] the seed from which iniquity—that is, injustice—is born. Hence he adds: “And he labors to bring forth,” that is, he strives to accomplish injustice, namely to deceive his neighbor. And a person of this kind at last “has borne,” that is, has made and brought forth, iniquity. Iniquity is the same as injustice. Therefore he has borne what he labors to bring forth; this denotes the sin of an accomplished deed. For he has brought forth iniquity when he has carried it into action. And in the iniquity brought forth there is a pit—that is, a precipice—for others. Hence follows:

VERSE 16.—“He opened a pit and dug it, and fell into the hole which he made.”

“He opened a pit.” As though he said: “He conceived, labored to bring forth, and bore; and so now he opened a pit.” [Alcuin.] That is, he is comparable to one opening a pit by conceiving—that is to say [Col. 0119A], he began deceit. [Augustine.] This is by consenting to the suggestion of earthly desires. “And he dug it”: [Alcuin.] that is, he is like one digging by laboring to bring forth, namely by persisting in the work of deceit. “And he fell into the hole which he made”: that is, he is like one falling into the pit by bearing, namely by perpetrating deceit. [Augustine.] For the deceiver is first harmed by the loss of innocence before another is harmed by loss of money.

VERSE 17.—“His pain shall return upon his own head, and his iniquity shall descend upon his own crown.”

His pain, which he conceived, shall return upon his head—that is, upon his mind; and his iniquity, which he bore, shall descend upon his crown—that is, upon his reason, which [Col. 0119B] he had called his head. [Augustine, Glossa interlinearis.] This is because he did not wish to escape sin but to be sin’s slave, lust ruling over reason. Therefore he who is lower is weighed down by iniquity, which sits upon the talent of lead in the prophet Zechariah, and it shall descend upon him and burden him, so that he may not fly back to the rest of the saints.

Or distinguish “head” from “crown,” and “shall return” from “shall descend.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] The head is the soul; the crown is reason. Sins rule over and prevail over each, and afterward shall come down upon them when they thrust them into punishments. The sense is: his pain which he conceived, and the iniquity which he bore, shall return upon his head—that is, upon his soul—and upon his crown—that is, upon his reason, over which they rule here. [Cassiodorus, Glossa interlinearis.] And afterward pain and iniquity shall descend with [Col. 0119C] violence upon head and crown, when eternal punishments subject him.

VERSE 18.—“I will confess to the Lord according to his righteousness, and I will sing praise to the name of the Lord Most High.”

“I will confess to the Lord.” [Cassiodorus.] This is the fifth part, the conclusion of the psalm. Gathering everything into a summary, he says that he will readily confess. As though he said: “Because my help is from the Lord, therefore I will confess to the Lord,” that is, praise the Lord. [Augustine.] And this “according to,” that is, because of his righteousness. For this confession is not a confession of sins but of the righteousness of God, who inwardly protects the righteous and punishes the wicked according to their wickedness. Against this praise, the blasphemies of the ungodly avail nothing. Unwilling to attribute their sin to their own fault, they excuse their evils by fortune, fate, the devil—whom one can resist—or by some other nature not from God. Such persons wander [Col. 0119D] in fluctuation rather than confessing to God so that he may forgive them. But one who sees the merits of souls so ordered by God that, while what is due is allotted to each, the beauty of the universe is violated in no respect, praises God in all things. He distinguishes between God’s making and ordering one thing—namely, the whole good universe—and not making, but ordering, another thing—namely evil. “And I will sing praise by my works to the name of the Lord Most High.” [Cassiodorus.] Singing praise belongs to joy, as penitence for sins belongs to sorrow. This psalm may also be understood in the person of Christ, if what is said humbly is referred to our weakness, which Christ himself bore [Col. 0120A].

## COLLATION ON PSALM VII: “O LORD MY GOD, IN THEE HAVE I HOPED”

VERSE 2.—“While there is none to redeem or save.” Hebrew: **POREQ VEEN MATZIL**, that is, “tearing,” or “may tear,” and there be none to deliver, as the Hebraists wish. Yet this is not necessary, since **PARAQ** means “he delivered” or “redeemed,” in Psalm 135: “And redeemed us from our enemies,” where the same word is read as here. But the Septuagint understood the negation as applying to both the preceding and following terms.

VERSE 4.—“If I have repaid evil to those repaying me.” Pagninus: “If I have repaid evil to one at peace with me”; Sanctes: “If I have repaid evil to one living peaceably with me”; [Col. 0120B] Münster: “But I repaid evil to my peaceful one”; the translator for Cajetan: “If I repaid evil to my peaceful one.” Campensis arrives at the same sense only in his paraphrase, which differs greatly from the Latin. But the Hebrew word is ambiguous: **SCHOLMI**, “my peaceful one,” or “one repaying me,” from the root **SCHALAM**, “he was peaceful” or “he restored.” Jerome according to the Hebrew, and the Septuagint, adopted the latter meaning; I care very little about the variation.

The translator following Campensis is almost with us: “If I have repaid those bringing me harm, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies.” Hebrew: **VAAHALTZAH TZORERI REQUAM**. Jerome: “I dismissed my enemies empty”; Pagninus: “I oppressed those opposing me without cause”; Münster: “I even delivered from affliction one opposing me without cause”; Sanctes: “I delivered my enemy gratuitously”; the translator for Cajetan: “And I delivered my oppressor in vain”; [Col. 0120C] Pellicanus: “And if I did not deliver my enemies without cause”; the translator following Campensis: “If I rashly despoiled my enemy.” How do these agree? This discord both of words and sense has arisen from the equivocation of two small words. The verb **BALATZ** is polysemous: sometimes it means “he turned aside,” as in Hosea 5, “They shall go to seek the Lord and shall not find him; he has withdrawn from them.” In Hebrew this particle is used, yet it bears the same sense: “He has withdrawn from them,” and “he has turned aside from them.” Likewise, to turn aside empty from enemies means nothing other than to be overcome by them, as the Septuagint understood it. At other times the word means “he delivered,” “he stripped,” or “he armed.” The second term, **REQUAM**, sometimes denotes “in vain,” “gratuitously,” or “without cause,” and sometimes “empty,” as in Deuteronomy 15: “You shall not allow him to depart empty”; the same particle occurs in Hebrew. “Empty” and “vain” are the same.

VERSE 6.—“Be exalted in the borders of my enemies.” [Col. 0120D] The Septuagint has—unless the manuscripts deceive—τῶν ἐχθρῶν σου, “of your enemies,” as is also read in the Roman psalmody; and the copies evidently vary. For in verse 9 of this psalm, “Judge me according to my righteousness,” Simia and Fretella put a question to Jerome himself: why in Greek did it read κατὰ τὴν δικαιοσύνην σου, that is, “according to your righteousness,” although we read “my righteousness”? But if in the preceding verse they had had a similar variation, they might perhaps have raised a similar question about the same pronoun. Add that in our manuscripts the verse about which Simia and Fretella inquired has μου, “my,” not σου, “your,” a very clear argument for variation. But whether you read “my enemies” or “your enemies,” the sense is not changed. For the enemies of the righteous are also the enemies of God, according to Acts 9: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” This is because of the unity of body and head.

The Hebrews seem to have something quite different because of the particle **BEABROTH**. Jerome according to the Hebrew has “rise up in indignation”; [Col. 0121A] Pagninus, “rise up among the wraths of those afflicting me”; Campensis’s paraphrase, “May the furies of my enemies move you”; Münster, “Rise up because of the indignations of my enemies”; Sanctes, “Raise yourself up because of the indignations of my enemies”; Pellicanus, “Rise up in the transgressions or wraths of those afflicting me”; the translators for Cajetan, “In the indignations of my oppressors”; Nebiensis, “Rise up in wrath against those troubling me”; the Chaldean, “Rush upon the oppressors in fury.” The equivocation of the word **ABAR** produced the variation. For since it sometimes denotes passing beyond—whence, according to some, the Hebrews are called “those from beyond the river”—and boundaries are points to which we always pass, the Septuagint learnedly translated according to the sense, “in the borders.” Augustine interprets these as God’s possession, which through conversion has passed from the devil’s dominion into the temple of God. This is a blessed passage, beyond which no other need be sought. The same word also means “to be angry,” [Col. 0121B] whose sense others followed. Thus what I cited in the prologue from Jerome Against Rufinus, book I, is entirely true: what a forest of ambiguous Hebrew nouns and verbs there is, furnishing matter for divergent interpretation while each translator, among uncertainties, renders what seems to him more fitting.
