VERSE 10.—“The wickedness of sinners shall be brought to an end.” Nebiensis: “May it be completed, I pray.” Chaldean: “Let wickedness now be destroyed,” **IIGMOR NA**. Pagninus, Sanctes, the translator for Cajetan, and Campensis take it actively: “Evil shall consume the ungodly.” Jerome according to the Hebrew, Pellicanus, and Münster translate it passively: “May the evil of the ungodly, I pray, be consumed.” According to Münster, the Greek has the passive συντελεσθήτω, “let it be completed,” with a double *m*, according to Augustine’s exposition: “He who is filthy, let him become filthier still” (Revelation 22). Yet this is not required by the Hebrew **GAMAR**, whence **IIGMOR** is here spoken in the future tense.

[Col. 0121C] “God searching hearts and reins.” The Hebrews connect the first word of the following verse in the Latin version with the end of the preceding verse, thus: “The righteous God who searches hearts and reins”; then, “My help,” etc. In Greek some copies have at the end of the verse ὁ Θεὸς δικαίως, “God justly,” adverbially; others δίκαιος, “righteous”; others, namely the Aldine edition, have at the beginning of the following little verse δικαία ἡ βοήθεια, “the help is righteous,” as we read. Take either: God is righteous—indeed, righteousness itself—and his help is righteous.

VERSE 12.—“God, a righteous judge, strong and long-suffering.” “Long-suffering” is not in the Hebrew; the Septuagint added μακρόθυμος. Yet they did not do so superfluously, because God’s righteousness is never separated from his mercy. [Col. 0122A] Ambrose, *Hexameron*, book III, says: “We find that many things have not idly been added and joined by the Seventy men to the Hebrew reading.” Jerome has “strong”; the others repeat “God,” but the Hebrew word **EL** says either. Münster: “God is a righteous judge.” So Pagninus and Pellicanus. But Sanctes, Campensis, the translators for Cajetan, and Nebiensis have: “God judges the righteous,” in an ambiguous sense. Let them see how correctly they have translated. For it can be taken in either sense: that God judges a righteous human being, or a righteous matter.

“Does he become angry every day?” The Hebrews read it without a question. Jerome according to the Hebrew: “Threatening all day”; Münster: “He is moved every day”; Sanctes adds from his own: “He is angry with the wicked every day”; the rest are to the same sense. The Septuagint evidently read twice, without points, **ALEPH** and **LAMED**, so that the first is **EL**, “God” or “strong”; the second [Col. 0122B] **AL**, not taken interrogatively, as Münster wished the phrase in Job 13 to be understood: “Though he kill me, shall I not hope?” There our edition lacks the negation, and the same sense returns if it is read interrogatively with the negation. However it may be, the meaning does not vary: God threatens every day, and yet does not become angry by immediately punishing sinners.

VERSE 13.—“Unless you are converted.” Hebrew: **IM DO JASCUB**, that is, “unless he shall have turned,” in the singular number. But translated in that manner, the sentence is ambiguous: namely, whether it should refer to God, the sinner, or the sword. In the plural, however, the meaning is given much more clearly, where the singular number would understand “the ungodly person”: if he does not repent, God will execute his vengeance upon him. Therefore the Septuagint, in the manner of a good translator, removed the ambiguity by rendering it in the second person plural. Hence Jerome renders by a participle: [Col. 0122C] “For one not turning, he shall sharpen his sword,” although it is manifest that the Hebrew is in the future of the fourth verbal order. The Chaldean agrees with our edition: “If he does not return to his honor.” Nebiensis differently: “Certainly he will not return.”

VERSE 13.—“He made his arrows for those who burn.” Why should Sanctes, Münster, Pagninus, and the translators for Cajetan have rendered “persecutors” or “those persecuting” instead of “those who burn,” when **DALAQ**, with no one disputing it, also means “he burned”? Jerome translated “for burning”; Pellicanus, “burning persons”; Campensis embraces both: “Those who pursue someone most ardently.” How “he made arrows for those who burn” should be understood—whether *ardentibus* is ablative (“by/with burning persons”) or dative (“for burning persons”)—you have above in the exposition of the Commentary.

# PSALM VIII

[Col. 0121]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID, FOR THE WINEPRESSES”

[Col. 0121D]

“Lord, our Lord.” The title: “Unto the end, a psalm of David, for the winepresses.” [Augustine, Alcuin.] Nothing is said in the text of this psalm about visible winepresses, but about spiritual ones, signified by visible winepresses—that is, the churches. For it treats here of the Church’s establishment and of the cause of that establishment, namely Christ’s ascension and the sending of the Holy Spirit. When the Lord ascended after the resurrection, he sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles and other believers; filled by him, they gathered churches through preaching. [Augustine.] The Church is called a winepress [Col. 0122D] for the same reason that it is called a threshing floor. For the same reality is often conveyed in Scripture through many and diverse comparisons. It is compared to a threshing floor or a winepress because, as grain is separated from chaff on the threshing floor, and wine from grape-skins in winepresses, so in the Church the good are separated from the evil by the work of their ministries—not in place but in disposition—and are cleansed, as it were, from coverings: as grain is cleared from chaff on the threshing floor and wine is stripped from grape-skins in winepresses. Yet these were necessary, so that they might be born and grow together and reach maturity. So in the Church the mixture of the evil is necessary for the good: they begin, grow, and come to completion together, but the good in good and the evil in evil. In the future, however, [Col. 0123A] they will also be separated in place: the grain will be stored in barns, but the chaff burned in unquenchable fire.

Or the Church is called a winepress because in it the understanding of God’s word, while it is conveyed through the sound of the voice, is as though wine contained in grape-skins; it is thus carried to the ears, as to a winepress, where it is distinguished. For sound has force upon the ears, but understanding is received by the hearers’ memory as in a certain vat. From there it passes into the habit of the mind and the discipline of conduct, as from the vat into cellars, where, if negligence does not make it sour, it is strengthened by age.

Or winepresses are also martyrdoms, where the bodies of those who are trodden under the afflictions of persecution for Christ’s name remain upon the earth like grapes, while their souls flow forth to the rest of the heavenly dwelling. And because these things occur in the churches, the churches themselves are called winepresses. [Col. 0123B] The sense of the title is: this psalm of the prophet David, tending unto the end—that is, unto Christ—[Cassiodorus, Glossa interlinearis.] because it treats of Christ’s exaltation according to his two natures, and concerning the winepresses—that is, the churches—of whose establishment and cause of establishment it treats. The Prophet’s intention here is to refute the error of the Jews, who say that God is known only in Judaea, and of the Donatists, who say that he is known only in Africa, and of their like. [Cassiodorus.] Method: the psalm has two parts. First, Christ’s praises are described, namely his majesty and sublime operation; second, it says that human nature, once fallen, has been exalted above all things in Christ, at the words, “What is man?” Therefore, beginning with praise, the prophet says: O—

[Col. 0123C] VERSE 1.—“O Lord, our Lord, how admirable is thy name in all the earth!”

[Remigius, Glossa interlinearis.] Lord of all according to power, who are especially our Lord according to reception and worship: your name—that is, your glory and renown—is admirable because of the creatures you have made and govern. And “how admirable”: as though he said, infinitely so. For no one is sufficient to know all creatures, in which we marvel at you. I say, it is admirable in all the earth, not only in Judaea, as the Jews say, nor only in Africa, as the Donatists say. Therefore, lest Jews or anyone else claim for themselves as peculiar what belongs commonly to all, which is the intention of the psalm, the discourse is directed to God the Trinity; then he sets forth in part that through which it is admirable, speaking to God the Father.

VERSE 2.—“For thy magnificence is exalted above the heavens.”

“For thy magnificence is exalted.” As though he said: “It is admirable for this reason, because your magnificence”—[Remigius, Cassiodorus.] that is, your Son, God and man—“has been exalted from earthly humility above the heavens,” literally: the God-man sitting at the right hand of God the Father. Or, “thy magnificence is exalted above the heavens,” [Augustine.] that is, above the Scriptures, because it surpasses all the utterances of the Scriptures. Or, “is exalted” means in incomprehensibility; “above the heavens,” [Remigius.] means above all rational creatures. Or “thy magnificence,” that is, your renown and glory—what he had earlier called your name—“is exalted above the heavens,” that is, above the Scriptures, by which it is not fully expounded. The Scriptures are called heavens because they conceal divine mysteries. And, O Lord, thou:

VERSE 3.—“Out of the mouth of infants and nursing children thou hast perfected praise because of thine enemies, that thou mayest destroy the enemy and the avenger.”

[Cassiodorus.] “You have perfected praise from the mouths of infants.” He calls them infants and sucklings not by age, but by simplicity, as Peter says in the Catholic Epistle: “As newborn babes,” etc. (1 Pet. 2)—that is, those who are not yet able to take solid food, but milk. [Augustine.] Such were those to whom the Apostle gave milk, saying: “As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3). They were prefigured by those who praised the Lord as He came to His Passion, and the Lord employs this testimony concerning them when, in answer to the Jews who told Him to rebuke them, He said: “Have you never read: From the mouths of infants,” etc. (Matt. 21).

Appropriately, however, He did not say, “You made,” but “You have perfected.” For God perfected praise from these, because, if only the perfect were in the churches, they would not provide for humankind as they do now, when even those not yet capable of knowledge of spiritual and eternal realities are nourished on faith in temporal history and praise God. The sense is: “You have perfected praise from the mouths of infants and sucklings.” [Cassiodorus.] That is, You are preached not only by the perfect but also by the unlearned; and You have done this because of Your enemies, in order to destroy the enemy and avenger—or defender, according to another reading. [Augustine.] Enemies in general are all who speak against the dispensation accomplished through the Crucified One. Heretics seem to be defenders of faith, and philosophers defenders of wisdom, although the former attack true faith and the latter true wisdom.

Or He calls the Apostles infants and sucklings, because “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1). [Remigius.] Hence the praise is more perfect, because one comes to it not by human wisdom but by divine grace. Thus: “From the mouths of infants and sucklings,” that is, of the Apostles, “You have perfected praise.”

[Cassiodorus, Remigius.] Or this may be understood of the Hebrew children, because from the words of those children praise was perfected. What seemed to be done childishly was done through the prompting of the Holy Spirit. The sense is: “From the mouths of infants and sucklings You have perfected praise,” that is, from the words of Hebrew children You have perfected praise. And all this was done to confound Your enemies—perhaps the pagans. [Cassiodorus.] For this reason He wished to be praised by such persons, lest this wisdom should appear human rather than divinely bestowed. And You did this in order to destroy the enemy, that is, the Jew, and the avenger or defender. For the Jew is God’s enemy while he defends the Father alone, since “he who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father” (John 5). Or he is an enemy by his intention, and an avenger, namely, a defender of his own sect.

### VERSE 4.—“For I shall behold Your heavens, the works of Your fingers, the moon and the stars which You have founded.”

“For I shall behold,” as though he said: Truly You have perfected praise and will destroy the enemy, because I shall behold Your heavens. [Remigius, Alcuin.] That is, through the Holy Spirit I already foresee the Apostles, and I shall also behold them bodily in their successors. This is particularly fitting language for the earliest believers. I call them heavens, for they are the works of Your fingers. [Cassiodorus.] They are instructed through the cooperation of the Trinity, which is here signified by three fingers, as in: “Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers?” (Isa. 40).

[Jerome, Augustine, Alcuin.] And through those heavens I shall see the moon built up—that is, the universal Church—and the stars, that is, individual churches in various places, or other teachers. Yet You, not they, founded the moon and stars. For the Apostles are ministers of the building, whereas You are its author or founder.

Or, from the words “From the mouths,” the discussion returns to that sense in which he called the Scriptures “heavens.” [Augustine.] Since he had said that Christ surpasses the utterances of all Scripture, someone might perhaps suppose that little ones could not arrive at, or ascend to, knowledge of Him through the Scriptures. Removing this doubt, he says that Christ also lowered the Scriptures to infants, so that they too might grasp God’s magnificence and enemies might be destroyed.

This is the meaning: the Son was exalted above the Scriptures; yet through those Scriptures You have perfected praise from the mouths of infants and sucklings—that is, You inclined those Scriptures down to infants and sucklings so that they might ascend. Thus praise might be perfected through the Scriptures which He bent down to infants. Hence elsewhere: “He bowed the heaven and came down” (Ps. 17). And You did this because of Your enemies, namely, in order to destroy the enemies of Christ’s cross.

As though explaining this, he adds: “in order that You may destroy the enemy and defender.” By “enemy and defender” he means the same persons whom he called all enemies, namely, those who oppose Christ’s cross. They are destroyed when the Scriptures are seen—that is, understood—having been brought down to the capacity of infants; and through them such persons are nourished unto strength and raised to the loftiness of understanding. Of these he adds: “For I shall behold Your heavens.” And truly You will destroy them, says the Prophet in the person of the Church, because “I shall behold Your heavens.” [Remigius.] That is, I shall understand the sacred Scriptures, which are the works of Your fingers—that is, made by the Spirit of God, whose gifts are seven, though He is one Spirit, just as there are many fingers on one hand. [Augustine.] “And I shall behold the moon,” that is, the universal Church; “and the stars,” that is, individual churches or teachers, which—or which stars—You have founded in the heavens, or established in those same Scriptures, which we believe to be denoted by the name “heavens.”

### VERSE 5.—“What is man, that You are mindful of him? Or the son of man, that You visit him?”

“What is man?” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] This is the second part, in which he says that human nature, once corrupted, is in Christ exalted above all things. He had first displayed the omnipotence of the Godhead; accordingly, in this part he treats of the exaltation of humanity. But beforehand he speaks of the humiliation of all human nature, showing that there is absolutely no merit in man worthy of God’s favour. [Interlinear Gloss.] As though he said: Since all these things are through the Son, therefore, “What is man?” etc.

Or the connection is this: “Your magnificence has been exalted; and what is man, that You are mindful of him? Or the son of man?” [Augustine.] By “man” sinners are understood; by “son of man,” spiritual persons. For the disjunction indicates a difference between man and son of man. Every son of man is a man, but not conversely—for example Adam, who was a man but not a son of man.

Thus “man” here means everyone bearing the image of the earthly man, that is, every carnal sinner; “son of man” means everyone bearing the image of the heavenly man, that is, Christ. And rightly the new man is called son of man, because the new is made from the old by a certain transformation. For spiritual regeneration, through which one is renewed by the transition from secular life to eternal life, is begun by God. God’s mercy looks upon both; but the former as one far removed from God, and the latter—the son of man—as one present before Him.

[Cassiodorus.] Therefore, uttering the words with contempt, he says: “What is sinful, earthly man, that You are mindful of him,” as of one far off? God is mindful of him [Augustine] by giving temporal salvation, namely, the blessing of the left hand. Hence elsewhere: “The Lord will save men and beasts” (Ps. 35). Or: “What is the son of man,” that is, the spiritual person who bears the image of the heavenly man, “that You visit him?” [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss.] He is visited as one present, since he is near God through purity of life. He is therefore visited as present—that is, enlightened by the light of God’s countenance. Hence elsewhere: “The light of Your countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us” (Ps. 4); whereas salvation is far from sinners.

Or by “man” he means any human being generally, and by “son of man” Christ as man. The sense is: “What is man”—[Cassiodorus] any lowly and miserable human being—“that You are mindful of him?” God is mindful of him through mercy. “Or the son of man”—here the voice should rise—namely Christ the man: what is He, that through Him You visit man? This occurred when “the Word was made flesh” (John 1). [Augustine.] In this incarnation the heavenly physician came to the sick; the Son of God became the son of man. Concerning Him, because of the weakness of His flesh, he adds:

### VERSE 6.—“You have made him a little lower than the angels; You have crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of Your hands.”

[Augustine, Cassiodorus.] “You have made Him lower,” as though he said: Human nature is humbled not only in others, but also in Christ Himself, because You made lower Him who is the head of all believers. “Lower than the angels,” [Interlinear Gloss] because He was capable of suffering and mortal; yet only a little lower, because in other respects He surpasses the angels over whom He commands. I say, You made Him lower; but afterward You “crowned Him with glory,” namely, the incorruptible brightness of His body, “and honour,” so that He may be venerable to all.

[Cassiodorus.] He fittingly says, “You crowned,” because the circuit of the world, which is in a manner like a crown, came to His faith. “And You set Him,” that is, established Him, “over the works of Your hands.” [Augustine.] Since the angels too are works of God’s hands, the only-begotten Son of God has been set above them.

### VERSE 7.—“You have subjected all things beneath His feet: all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field.”

“All things,” etc. [Interlinear Gloss.] I say that You set Him over all works, because You subjected them beneath His feet—that is, beneath His dominion and power—and he enumerates what they are: sheep, etc. [Augustine.] Why, omitting higher beings, namely the hosts of angels and human beings themselves, does he name these lowly creatures? It must be understood mystically.

By sheep he means the innocent. By oxen he means those who labour and cause earthly things to bear fruit. This is said concerning angels and human beings, to show through all things that they are subject to Christ. Thus: You subjected to Him sheep, that is, innocent persons, both human and angelic; and oxen, namely those ploughing and threshing, who in the Lord’s vineyard tear up the shrubs of sin with the spiritual ploughshare.

[Augustine, Alcuin, Remigius.] “All” oxen: he uses the feminine gender in order to denote fruitfulness, those who make human hearts fruitful with the seed of God’s word; and these are human beings and angels. “Moreover,” etc.—as though he said: You subjected not only oxen to Him, but also the beasts of the field. [Augustine.] By saying “moreover,” he distinguishes these from the saints mentioned before. For these are dregs, just as those former are wine. Thus he indicates that even the evil are subject to Christ, a point which might seem less apparent. He signifies this by “beasts of the field,” that is, carnal persons amid the expanse of pleasures, as though in the breadth of fields, not dwelling on the mountains of virtues.

Therefore the beasts of the field are people who live in the flesh, where they undertake nothing arduous and ascend nothing laborious; rather, the broad way to which they cling leads to death. Thus Abel too was slain by his brother in the field. And You have subjected to Him:

### VERSE 8.—“The birds of heaven and the fish of the sea, which pass through the paths of the sea.”

“The birds of heaven,” that is, the proud. [Augustine, Alcuin.] The proud are aptly signified by the birds of heaven, concerning whom it is said: “They have set their mouth in heaven” (Ps. 72). Their head says: “I will ascend into heaven and exalt my throne,” etc. (Isa. 14). “And the fish of the sea,” that is, the curious, “which pass through the paths of the sea”—those who, in the deep of this age, seek with obstinate zeal temporal things, which, like paths upon the sea, quickly vanish.

For this reason he rightly says not merely “they walk,” but “they pass through”: by this he shows the most stubborn eagerness of those who seek vain and transient things. These three kinds of vice—pleasure of the flesh, pride, and curiosity—contain all vices. As John says, they are “the lust of the flesh, the ambition of the world,” that is, pride, “and the lust of the eyes” (1 John 2). For curiosity is especially powerful through the eyes. In these three respects the Lord and Saviour was tempted and overcame; by these the first man was conquered and fell.

### VERSE 9.—“O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is Your name in all the earth!”

“O Lord, our Lord, how…” [Interlinear Gloss.] Behold the conclusion of the psalm; behold the goal toward which all tends. As though he said: Since You have done all these things, therefore, O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is Your name in all the earth! [Augustine.] He appropriately repeats the beginning, showing that both the beginning and the end of good must be referred to God.

## COLLATION ON PSALM VIII: “O LORD, OUR LORD”

### VERSE 3.—“From the mouths of infants and sucklings You have perfected praise.”

Would that the modernizers who Hebraize had translated without presumption, “You have perfected strength” or “might,” instead of “You have perfected praise.” Let them therefore rebuke the Evangelist in Matthew 21—indeed Christ Himself—who turned this passage against the Jews who were finding fault: “Have you never read,” He says, “From the mouths of infants and sucklings You have perfected praise?” Behold, Christ says “praise,” while you, wiser than Christ or than the interpreter John the Evangelist—who, according to Theophylact’s report, rendered Matthew into Greek, according to some, though it is more probable that Matthew wrote in Hebrew—wish to translate “strength” or “might” better!

What wonder, then, if you do not fear to undermine other passages, when you do not even spare the Evangelists? What will men of war not dare next? Does one not read in Matthew 21, in Greek, κατηρτίσω αἶνον [“you have perfected praise”]? What, then, came into Münster’s mind when he translated “strength,” both in the Psalmist and in Matthew? We indeed know that the interpretation is worthy: Christ’s strength is established to such a degree that it is invincible and is confirmed by the testimony of children. See, however, whether Jerome translated anything other than “praise” according to the Hebrew. Nebiensis agrees with us.

### VERSE 6.—“You have made Him a little lower than the angels.”

Many, such as Faber and the Blind Burgundian, insist that it should firmly be read “than God,” because the Hebrew has *Elohim*. They have rushed into such madness that they have said and written that the passage of the blessed Paul, Hebrews 2, must be recalled to the anvil—that is, revised—criticising its translator, whom some allege to have been Luke, because it is wrongly read “than the angels.” Henceforth, they say, it should be sung in the churches: “You have made Him a little lower than God.”

To examine the present passage, first, there should be no dispute about the word, which no one doubts signifies God, as well as judges, princes, and men distinguished by awe and strength—and indeed angels themselves. In Exodus 21, “His master shall bring him before the gods”; and in Exodus 22, “You shall not speak evil of the gods”: *elohim* is used.

The main issue concerns the meaning of the Prophet and the Apostle, which, I think, Faber has by no means attained. Indeed, his interpretation conflicts in many respects with the prophetic and apostolic meaning, if the preceding and following passages are examined more carefully. For David began by greatly wondering at and admiring that union of human nature with the Word: “What is man”—human nature so frail, so despised—“that You are mindful of him,” through abundant mercy, so as to assume it into the dignity of hypostatic union?

Then, so that opposites may illuminate one another by their proximity, he shows Christ’s mortality, abasement, and capacity for suffering, so that he may immediately join the glorious exaltation, in accordance with Philippians 2: “He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming obedient unto death.” Then follows: “Therefore God also exalted Him,” etc. The Prophet therefore says: “You made Him a little lower than the angels,” because of mortality and passibility, to which angels are not subject. Although He was mortal and thereby lower than angels, nevertheless, after an inexpressible triumph, He sits above angelic nature at the right hand of the Father.

Accordingly he immediately adds: “You crowned Him with glory and honour, and set Him over the works of Your hands.” Nor does it prevent Christ, in another respect, from being superior to angels, by the grace of headship and the fullness of His influence, even insofar as He is man, according to Ephesians 1: “To restore all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth, in Him”; and Colossians 1: “And through Him to reconcile all things unto Himself, making peace through the blood of His cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven.”

But perhaps some contentious person will say: How can He be said to have been made only a little lower than angels, when Psalm 21 says: “A worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people”? This statement seems to mean that He was lowered far more than a little beneath angels. This argument certainly refutes the opinion that He is said to have been made lower than God, which cannot be understood according to the divine nature. Therefore it must refer to the human nature, which bears no proportion to the divine—nor even after it has assumed the robe of immortality’s glory.

Against the other interpretation, however, nothing objects if you consider the Prophet’s sense more carefully. For we acknowledge that Christ was regarded as lower than the most abject people according to the estimation of wicked Jews and unbelievers, while in reality He was holiness and goodness itself. Therefore the Prophet says most fittingly, “a little lower,” because although the Lord freely subjected Himself to mortality and was thereby beneath angels, nevertheless, if you fix the eyes of your mind upon that most blessed union, that abasement will seem to have been only slight.

Nor is it discordant that Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret it in terms of duration. Christ indeed put on our mortality, but, in view of the glorification that followed, He was worn down by our miseries for a short time. Yet Faber rejects this interpretation in vain, saying that Hebrew *meʿat* does not refer to a measure of time but of quantity. For in Psalm 36, “Yet a little while, and the sinner shall not be,” the Hebrew reads *meʿat*. And in Psalm 2, “When His anger is kindled in a short time,” these words plainly concern duration. The Greek agrees: Βραχύτι, “for a short time.”

But you will protest and cry out that Jerome translated, “a little lower than God,” according to the Hebrew. This objection was answered in the prologue: Jerome provided that translation for Sophronius while he was disputing with a Jew who, wishing to mock Sophronius in almost every phrase, asserted that the Hebrew did not read as Sophronius alleged. “It is one thing,” Jerome says, “to read the Psalms in churches of believers in Christ, and another to answer Jews who cavil at every individual word.” You see, then, that Jerome translated thus because of cavillers.

Accordingly, in his Commentary on this passage he says: “In the Hebrew, where it reads ‘than angels,’ who are called *malachim*, it has God, that is, *elohim*.”

[Note: [Col. 0129.] Observe here that Erasmus, on Hebrews 2, believed Jerome’s commentaries to be genuine and approved them, although he subsequently attacks them, as is explained in the prologue.]

“This passage the Apostle interprets in the Epistle to the Hebrews concerning Christ.” Here you see Jerome’s view: the Apostle interprets Hebrew *elohim* as “angels.” For Jerome was not ignorant of the Greek reading of the Epistle to the Hebrews. In it the Apostle says: “But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour.”

It is helpful that Pellicanus, Sanctes, and Münster translate “than angels.” Here, in the scholia, he teaches that *malachim* is to be understood in place of *Elohim*; and the Hebrew interpretation and the Chaldee paraphrase plainly have “than angels.”

# PSALM IX

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END, FOR THE HIDDEN THINGS OF THE SON: A PSALM OF DAVID.”

“*I will confess to You.*” The title is: “Unto the end, for the hidden things of the Son: a psalm of David.” When “Son” is said without adding whose son, as here, Christ is understood by excellence, He who is the only-begotten Son of God; just as He Himself says of Himself without further qualification: “If the Son shall make you free, you shall be truly free.” [Augustine.] Or He is also David’s son, because He was born from David. By saying “for the hidden things,” and naming the hidden things of the Son, he indicates that some of His things are manifest.

It should therefore be known that there are two comings of Christ. The first is in humility, which was hidden from the Jews and, when the Jews were blinded, benefited the Gentiles. Hence: “Blindness has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter in” (Rom. 11). The second is in majesty, which will be manifest to all.

There are also two judgments of God: the hidden judgment now taking place, which begins with the house of God. That is, God’s hidden judgment is the punishment by which every person is now either exercised for purification or admonished toward conversion. Or, if he despises the discipline of God who calls him, he is blinded unto condemnation. The manifest judgment will be at the end, when God will repay each person according to his merits.

Thus he treats here of hidden things: the humble coming, which benefited the Gentiles when the Jews were blinded; and the punishment by which God judges in purifying, converting, and blinding. The title means: This psalm of the prophet David, who here speaks in the person of the Church, directing us unto the end, that is, toward Christ, concerns the hidden things [Interlinear Gloss] of the Son, namely of God—or of David himself, from whom Christ was born according to the flesh.

The intention is to admonish us not to believe that the world is governed by chance or fate, but by God’s just judgment. The method has five divisions. [Cassiodorus.] First, the Prophet joyfully sings because the worship of the devil is destroyed by Christ’s coming, and Christ reigns, judges, and helps. Second, he calls the faithful to praise: “Sing to the Lord.” Third, he predicts the end of evils for sinners together with Antichrist: “Let sinners be turned back.” Fourth, he considers the evils of Antichrist’s time: “Why, O Lord?” Fifth, he prays that judgment may be hastened so that the evils of the saints may end: “Arise, O Lord.” [Augustine.] Thus the Prophet speaks here against those who complain about the flourishing of the wicked and the suffering of the good, supposing that this happens not through divine ordering but by chance.

### VERSE 1.—“I will confess to You, O Lord, with my whole heart; I will recount all Your wonders.”

“I will confess to You,” as though he said: Some complain and speak evil, but I will confess to You, O Lord—that is, I will praise You, whoever may speak evil. [Interlinear Gloss.] And I shall do so “with my whole heart,” not merely in part, as do those who approve some works of the Lord and blaspheme others. Rather, I will confess with my whole heart. [Augustine.] For in no respect do I doubt God’s providence; I perceive that all things are done rightly which fools rashly suppose to happen by chance.

And I shall also recount to others Your wonders, not ours, and all of them—visible and invisible. For the person who passes from visible things to invisible recounts all things: for example, one who says that He raised Lazarus in body and raised Paul in mind, which is greater and more excellent. Or: “I will recount all Your wonders,” that is, whatever I say about Your works is wonderful.

### VERSE 2.—“I will be glad and rejoice in You; I will sing to Your name, O Most High.”

“I will be glad.” [Interlinear Gloss.] I shall not only recount Your wonders to others, but shall also be glad and rejoice, which is more than being glad. [Cassiodorus.] Rejoicing is the most intense gladness. I shall be glad and rejoice in You, [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss] not in worldly things or in the pleasure of perishable things, but in the hidden things of the Son; elsewhere there is no true gladness. And I shall sing through my deeds to Your name, rejoicing, O Most High, so that by this example others too may sing. Then he gives the cause of his praise:

### VERSE 3.—“When my enemy is turned backward, they shall be weakened and perish before Your face.”

“When…” etc. [Interlinear Gloss.] Here is why he does the things just mentioned. As though he said: Therefore I shall be glad and sing, because, when You turned my enemy backward—[Jerome, Remigius, Interlinear Gloss] namely the devil, who before Christ’s coming went before as guide upon the road of death, but lost his claim when You turned him back—the wicked shall be weakened. [Augustine.] That is, they are weakened so that they can neither do nor will anything against the pious. And they shall perish, because they shall no longer be wicked, according to: “Turn the wicked man, and he shall not be” (Prov. 12:7). And this is “before Your face,” namely before the knowledge of God, because He will not remember their iniquities. Thus that person perished who said: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2).

Or it may be understood in an evil sense: because You turned the devil to flight, and therefore his members shall be weakened in evil [Jerome, Remigius, Alcuin], so that they can do no harm to the good; and they shall perish on the day of judgment “before Your face,” that is, through Your assault, when You say: “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25). Then, showing how the devil was turned backward, he adds:

### VERSE 4.—“For You have accomplished my judgment and my cause; You have sat upon the throne, judging righteousness.”

“For You have accomplished,” as though he said: The enemy has been turned backward and the wicked have perished. [Interlinear Gloss.] But how and by what means? Here it is: “You have accomplished my judgment”—namely when Christ was judged and sentence given against Him—“and my cause,” which Christ conducted against the wicked while accused. I call them my judgment and my cause, because they served me and benefited me. [Augustine.] Sailors similarly call a wind “their wind” when they use it to sail well.

“You have sat,” or “You sit,” as though he said: You accomplished my cause because You, God the Father, sat—or sit—upon the throne, [Remigius] that is, upon Christ’s soul, because God, namely the Father, “was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself” (2 Cor. 5). You, I say, sat, O Father, who judge righteousness—namely, that Christ should die for the human race. And thereby:

### VERSE 5.—“You have rebuked the nations and the wicked has perished; You have blotted out their name for ever and unto ages of ages.”

“You have rebuked,” that is, frightened the nations concerning their sins. Or the address is directed to Christ: “You have sat,” as though he said: You have accomplished judgment; [Augustine] and You, O Christ, after the resurrection, have sat—or sit—upon the throne, that is, at the Father’s right hand. You sit, I say, who judge—that is, who will judge—righteousness at the end, because Christ will judge justly at the end, He to whom the Father has given all judgment (John 5).

I say that You sit at the Father’s right hand, and therefore, sending the Holy Spirit into the Apostles and through the Apostles, You rebuked the nations for their sins. Thus the wicked person perished, having become pious. Or the wicked one, that is, the devil, perished when his power was taken away by God. The wicked one perished because You blotted out their name, the name of the wicked. For those who believe God are not called wicked.

And this is “for ever,” or “unto the age,” namely this present age, “and unto ages of ages,” namely eternity. An age is this present age, which revolves through the succession of changing times; the age of ages is eternity, which abides in unchangeable eternity, of which this age is an image and shadow. Or “unto ages of ages” defines and explains the preceding “for ever,” lest, when saying “for ever,” you should understand the present age. Therefore You have blotted out the name of the wicked for ever and unto ages of ages, [Interlinear Gloss] because henceforth they shall be able to do nothing among God’s peaceful people. And truly, because:

### VERSE 6.—“The enemy’s swords have failed utterly, and You have destroyed their cities.”

“The enemy’s swords” is in the genitive case. [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss.] That is, the devil’s rebellions and the various errors by which he kills souls have failed “unto the end”: through Christ, partly at His first coming and completely at His second. [Augustine.] This end is that sword which God has openly brandished when You judge. Thus above, in another psalm, he said: “He has brandished His sword,” He who now judges secretly. Until He judges openly in the future, the enemy’s swords retain some power; but then they will fail completely, when it is brandished openly.

And while He now judges secretly, “You have destroyed their cities,” that is, their strongholds—[Jerome, Augustine] namely those persons in whom the devil reigns, where deceitful and fraudulent counsels occupy the place of a court. The functions of the individual members attend this rulership like attendants and ministers: the eyes for curiosity, ears for lust, hands for robbery; and in this manner the remaining members serve tyrannical rule, that is, perverse counsels.

The populace, as it were, of this city consists of all luxurious affections and turbulent motions of the mind, stirring up daily seditions within a person. You have destroyed these cities, therefore, where king, court, minister, and populace are found, so that, with the devil expelled, they may serve righteousness. And therefore:

### VERSE 7.—“Their memory has perished with a noise; but the Lord remains for ever.”

“Their memory has perished.” [Interlinear Gloss.] Before God, so that He may not punish them. Or “their memory,” that is, the memory of the wicked, has perished: their rites will be cut off. It has perished, I say, “with a noise” or tumult—that is, both the noise and the tumult of impiety have perished. [Augustine.] Or he says “with a noise” because when impiety is overthrown there is a tumult: no one comes to perfect peace except by struggling against vices amid great turmoil.

Or everything from that point may be understood of the future. [Cassiodorus.] “The enemy,” that is, the devil; “his swords,” that is, the devil’s power, “shall fail unto the end,” that is, they shall be destroyed at the end of the age; “and You have destroyed their cities,” that is, his peoples, meaning You will destroy them. Note that he says “their” in the plural, although above he said “enemy” in the singular; for, although demons are many, they are alike in wickedness and are as one.

It follows: “Their memory has perished,” that is, will perish in the future, “with a noise,” that is, with a great cry, as happens when prosperous affairs are brought to a grievous end. [Augustine.] But, by contrast, “the Lord remains for ever”; therefore the wicked oppose Him in vain.

### VERSE 8.—“He has prepared His throne for judgment, and He Himself will judge the world in equity; He will judge peoples in righteousness.”

“He has prepared His throne.” [Augustine.] I say that He remains for ever and will judge, because He has prepared His throne, that is, judicial power, in judgment—that is, when He was judged. [Cassiodorus.] For through patience He acquired heaven and the authority of judgment: because He was judged in humility, He will judge in majesty. [Augustine.]

Thus he adds that He Himself will at last openly judge the world—that is, the world itself, so that it may possess incorruptible qualities and be purified. [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine.] Or, concerning the whole world: He will judge all nations, rendering to their merits what is due in equity. He repeats the same in other words: “He will judge peoples” means what he said, “the world”; “in righteousness” means what he said, “in equity.”

### VERSE 9.—“And the Lord has become a refuge for the poor, a helper in due times, in tribulation.”

“And He has become…” [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss.] As though he said: He will judge in the future; and meanwhile, lest the enemy who has been turned backward should harm them, the Lord has become a refuge in avoiding evils. But this is only for the poor, that is, for the one who loves nothing among transient things. How fitting for Him who is Judge also to be a refuge for the poor, who desires nothing of the world! He is likewise a helper in doing good.

He is helper and refuge “in due times,” that is, in circumstances where help is needed. He then explains these due times: for one placed in tribulation, He is helper and refuge. Sweet is the help and refuge given in necessity. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] He fittingly calls tribulations “due times,” because no more fitting means tears a person away from the world than that toil and pain should be mingled with these trivial and harmful pleasures.

### VERSE 10.—“And let those who know Your name hope in You, because You have not forsaken those who seek You, O Lord.”

“And let them hope.” [Interlinear Gloss.] As though he said: Since You are refuge and helper, therefore, O Lord, let those who know Your name hope in You, not in the world. [Augustine.] They do so when they cease to hope in worldly things; for then, when they have turned from the world and seek somewhere to fix their hope, knowledge of God’s name receives them.

A name is known when the one whose name it is is known. God’s name is “Lord.” Hence: “He who ascends above the setting: Lord is His name” (Ps. 67). He rightly knows that name who gladly serves Him as Lord. Or God’s name is “He Who Is.” Thus the Lord says to Moses: “I am who I am”; and “Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you” (Exod. 3).

The person rightly understands this name who does not place hope in things which pass away in the changing course of time, possessing almost nothing except “will be” and “has been.” For what is future in them, when it comes, immediately becomes past; it is awaited with desire, lost with sorrow, and not possessed with certainty. Therefore let no one hope in transient things, but in Him whose essence knows neither past nor future. For “You have not forsaken,” [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss] as though he said: Truly You are helper and refuge, because You have not forsaken—although for a time it may seem so—those who seek You, O Lord. With Him no one can seek transient things, for “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6).

## PART II. VERSE 2.—“Sing to the Lord who dwells in Sion; proclaim among the nations His works of zeal.”

“Sing to the Lord.” [Augustine.] This is the second part, in which the Prophet calls the faithful to praise, looking to the benefits of the present age and of the age to come. As though he said: Since the Lord has not forsaken those who seek Him, therefore, O you whom He has not forsaken while seeking Him, sing to the Lord. [Jerome.] That is, praise the Lord by preaching Him and by fulfilling in deed what you preach.

I say, sing to the Lord “who dwells in Sion,” that is, in the Church of the present time, [Augustine] which now beholds God through a mirror. For just as Jerusalem, which is interpreted “vision of peace,” signifies the Church above in heaven, so Sion bears the image of the Church which now exists. For Sion is interpreted “contemplation,” which is practised now so that we may arrive at the vision of peace—that is, from Sion to Jerusalem.

Every diligent contemplation, however, falls into error unless the Lord dwells in it. “Proclaim among the nations His works of zeal,” the works of zeal which He has toward His own. What are they? Namely these:

### VERSE 12.—“For He who requires their blood has remembered them; He has not forgotten the cry of the poor.”

For he himself, seeking the vengeance which he inflicts upon the slayers, has remembered their blood, that is, the blood of those slain—comforting and glorifying them. [Col. 0134D] Or thus: “Proclaim among the nations his ordinances,” [Jerome, Augustine], that is, his commandments, in which one must diligently apply oneself. But, as though those sent to preach the Gospel should say, “No one believes us, and we are killed,” he replies: Those sent by Christ are not killed without the fruit of eternity. For the Lord, seeking vengeance—that is, their blood at the future judgment, where punishment will belong to the killer and glory to the slain—has remembered his own, glorifying and comforting them, and terrifying their persecutors by punishment. He says “has remembered,” not because forgetfulness can befall God and he becomes mindful after forgetting, but because the judgment will come after a long time. This is said according to the feeling of the weak, who think him forgetful because it does not happen as quickly as they wish. To this he adds: “And he has not forgotten the cry of the poor,” as though to say: [Col. 0135A] I said, “He has remembered,” which seems to imply that he had forgotten; yet he has not forgotten the cry of the poor, as you suppose. And if I said “has remembered,” this was directed against those who, because of the delay, think that God has forgotten. He shows what that cry of the poor is:

**VERSE 13.**—“Have mercy on me, O Lord; behold my humiliation from my enemies.”

“Have mercy on me,” etc. [Interlinear Gloss.] Behold, that is the cry. One speaks on behalf of all, etc.; in his own person he says what each person asks, namely: Have mercy on me, O Lord; behold with a merciful gaze my humiliation. God’s regard is help: being light, he drives away darkness by making the mind serene. The sense is: Behold my humiliation, that is, help my humiliation; and how great it is is measured by my enemies. [Col. 0135B] For the humility of the sufferer is measured by the pride of the enemy, since these are humbled as much as those are exalted. You, I say, behold it.

**VERSE 14.**—“Who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may declare all thy praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion.”

[Augustine, Cassiodorus.] “Who lift me up,” that is, who remove me far from the gates of death, namely, from all depraved desires through which one goes to death. Death itself is the delight already possessed in this life through enjoyment of things desired. Hence the Apostle: “The widow who lives in pleasures is dead” [1 Tim. 5]. One comes to such pleasures through desires, as through gates of death. You therefore remove me from them, so that I may declare all thy praises. [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine.] For whatever I say is praise of God. I declare, I say, being and speaking among those who are, in the gates of the daughter of Zion. The gates of the daughter of Zion are the excellent pursuits through which, in the holy Church, one comes to the vision of peace, where nothing is as though it were not yet, nor has been as though it were no longer; but there is only that which is, and this itself is eternity. Therefore all God’s praises are fittingly declared in these gates, so that what is holy may be given to those who ask, and not to dogs (Matt. 7), who prefer stubborn barking to earnest seeking. These gates are opposed to the gates mentioned above. Those are gates of death; these, gates of life. The daughter of Zion is the Church; for Zion bore all the churches of the world, because Christ was born there and faith began there.

Or, the gates of death are the bodily senses, [Col. 0135D] from which those are lifted up who seek not the things seen but the things unseen. The gates of the daughter of Zion are the sacraments and the beginnings of faith, which are opened to those who knock, so that they may reach hidden things which eye has not seen nor ear heard (1 Cor. 2). The sense is: You lift me up from the gates of death, that is, from desire for temporal things subject to the five senses. For what purpose? That I may declare all thy praises to those who are in the gates of the daughter of Zion, that is, in the sacraments and beginnings of faith.

Otherwise. [Jerome, Interlinear Gloss.] The gates of death are heretics, or their doctrines. The gates of life are the prophets, apostles, and their teaching, who lead to life through sound doctrine, just as heretics draw men to destruction through evil teaching. Thus: You lift me up from the gates of death, that is, from the teaching of heretics; [Col. 0136A] and place me in the gates of the daughter of Zion, that is, among the prophets and apostles—that is, in the teaching of the prophets and apostles—so that there I may declare all thy praises.

**VERSE 15.**—“I will rejoice in thy salvation; the nations have been fastened in the destruction which they made.”

“I will rejoice.” [Augustine, Alcuin.] Up to this point has been the cry of the poor, which God does not forget. Thereupon the afflicted Church says that she rejoices and asserts that she is saved: “I will rejoice.” As though to say: Because you lift me up from the gates of death, therefore I will rejoice in thy salvation, that is, in Jesus Christ. For by hope the Church is already saved. I will rejoice; but the nations, wishing to kill the bodies of the saints, have been fastened in the destruction of their souls, nailed, as it were, by certain nails of sins; [Col. 0136B] that is, they die in soul. In the destruction, I say, which they made. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] For each person’s iniquity is his own punishment. Then he shows how each is bound by his own sins, saying:

**VERSE 16.**—“In this snare which they hid, their foot has been caught.”

[Augustine.] In this snare also which they hid—that is, in the fraud they conceal—their foot has been caught, that is, their affection. A hidden snare is deceitful thought; the foot of the soul is love. If this is crooked, it is called cupidity or lust; if straight, charity. For by love the soul is moved, as if toward the place to which it tends—that is, toward good or evil delight—and it rejoices through love that it has arrived there. Therefore in this snare [Col. 0136C] which they hid, that is, in their fraudulent plan, their foot—that is, the love which through fraud comes to empty delight—has been caught, because that delight binds them so that they do not dare break away their love from it and turn it toward what is beneficial. For if they try, it pains them to abandon the things that delight them, and that pain does not allow them to depart. These things occur by God’s hidden judgment, by which he judges now. Therefore he adds:

**VERSE 17.**—“The Lord shall be known, making judgments; in the works of his hands the sinner has been caught.”

“The Lord shall be known.” [Interlinear Gloss.] Here, by his own, making true judgments, separating—namely, here, by merit rather than place—the evil from the good. Then, to show how the wicked are tortured here [Col. 0136D] and what judgments he makes, he adds: “In the works of his hands.” As though to say: These are the judgments he makes: the sinner has been caught in his works, etc. This does not proceed from God, as that by which he tortures them, but from themselves, because their very sins are their torments and punishments. Then, not as a wish but as a prediction, there follows:

**PART III. VERSE 18.**—“Let sinners be turned into hell, all the nations that forget God.”

“Let them be turned.” This is the third part according to Augustine, and here is the song of the *diapsalma*; that is, in this third part there is a *diapsalma*, where there is also a song, namely a kind of hidden joy in the separation which is made here between good and evil, not [Col. 0137A] by place but by disposition. Therefore, predicting their separation, the Prophet says: Let sinners be turned into hell, that is, let them be ensnared by deadly delight. And he explains whom he calls sinners: namely, all nations that forget God. As though to say: “Just as they did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge, so let God give them over to a reprobate mind.”

Or the whole may be understood of the future judgment from the words “The Lord shall be known.” [Cassiodorus.] As though to say: Here their foot has been caught in the snare, but in the future they will be condemned. For in the future judgment the Lord, making true judgments, will be known by all, when he will separate the evil from the good also by place. The Lord will then be known to make true judgments because the sinner has been caught in the works of his hands; that is, the sinner will be bound by his own works. [Col. 0137B] He will not be punished merely by the remembrance of them, as some falsely suppose, but, according to the nature of his works, being condemned to outward punishments.

“Let them be turned.” This is the third part according to Cassiodorus, in which he predicts the end of evils for sinners together with Antichrist. As though to say: Meanwhile, the nations are fastened in destruction and their foot is caught in the snare; but at last let sinners be turned—that is, sinners will be turned—so that they may not rejoice in their pleasures. They will be turned, I say, into hell, lest they suppose that they are to be sent elsewhere: namely, all the nations that forget God.

**VERSE 19.**—“For the poor man shall not be forgotten for ever; the patience of the poor shall not perish for ever.” [Col. 0137C]

“For not unto the end.” As though to say: God has not forgotten the cry of the poor, and truly so, [Augustine,] because the poor man’s forgetfulness is not with God unto the end, or at the end; that is, the poor man will not at the end be in oblivion, even if he seems so here, while the wicked flourish in worldly prosperity and the righteous suffer. At the end of the world the poor will not be despised; and this is because of patience. Hence he adds: “And the patience of the poor shall not perish for ever.” For this reason especially God will remember the poor, namely, because of patience, which is now needed to endure the wicked, already separated in their wills, until they are finally separated locally at the last judgment. [Col. 0137D] Of that judgment he speaks next.

**VERSE 20.**—“Arise, O Lord; let not man prevail; let the nations be judged in thy sight.”

“Arise, O Lord.” [Cassiodorus.] Here the Prophet prays for the future judgment. Speaking of the end of the age, he foresaw by illumination of heart the coming of Antichrist. [Interlinear Gloss.] Therefore, as though terrified, he cries out: “Arise, O Lord.” As though to say: I say that the patience of the poor will not perish. But that it may not perish, arise, O Lord, to judge; and let not man prevail, [Cassiodorus] that is, let mere man—not God, as he will pretend—fail to prevail over them. But first, let the nations be judged, that is, let them through him be plunged into sin. And what is said of Antichrist is [Col. 0138A] “in thy sight,” [Augustine] that is, in what is hidden, which few holy and righteous persons see and understand. And, O—

**VERSE 21.**—“Set, O Lord, a lawgiver over them, that the nations may know that they are men.”

[Interlinear Gloss, Jerome, Augustine.] O Lord, because they refused you and your law, set Antichrist, a wicked lawgiver, over them—that is, for their ruin—and so let the nations, that is, those living as Gentiles, know, that is, learn by suffering, that they are men, namely, that they have been foolish. As though to say: Because they will not be sons of man—that is, new men—let them be old men, serving the old man, that is, sin.

**PART IV. VERSE 22.**—“Why, O Lord, hast thou withdrawn far off? Dost thou despise in due times, in tribulation?” [Col. 0138B]

“Why, O Lord?” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] The fourth part, in which he discusses the evils of that time; moved by their excessiveness, he says to God: “Why, O Lord,” etc. [Augustine.] Because he will be allowed to do such great things that he will be thought God, he introduces, as it were, the voice of those groaning and complaining over the delay of judgment: “Why,” etc. As though to say: Let the nations indeed be judged; but why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far from your own? [Cassiodorus.] This appears to be so when he delays in bringing help. The Prophet asks this to instruct simple saints; and immediately, as though he had suddenly understood—or as one who knows, in order to teach what he knows—he resolves the question by adding, “Thou dost despise,” etc. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As though to say: Behold why you have withdrawn [Col. 0138C] far off: because you despise at the fitting times, that is, you fittingly disregard and permit tribulation. He says “despise” according to what appears to those who groan while help is delayed, or delayed even for a short time; but he does it fittingly, namely, so that:

**VERSE 23.**—“While the wicked is proud, the poor is inflamed; they are caught in the counsels which they devise.”

“While the wicked is proud, the poor is inflamed.” [Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] As though to say: For this purpose you disregard and allow tribulation: that the poor may be inflamed with desire for your coming, because while the wicked is proud, the poor in spirit is inflamed with love of God. Or, “is inflamed” means “is purified”; for the furnace of tribulation turns the wood of vices to ashes and purifies the gold of virtues; or it corrupts the wicked and purifies the good. [Augustine.] From this it is clear that God’s providence works wonderfully through evils. In comparison with sinners, the good are kindled by great zeal of good hope to live rightly, just as knowledge of truth grows through heresies and becomes more welcome. The wicked themselves are caught in the counsels—that is, the thoughts—in which they intend to catch the saints. For evil thoughts are their bonds. And as though someone asked why these things happen to the wicked, he replies:

**VERSE 24.**—“For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the unjust man is blessed.”

“For he is praised,” etc. As though to say: Therefore the wicked is proud, or is caught, because the sinner [Col. 0139A] who sins in himself is praised by his own people and is not corrected, in the desires of his soul—that is, in the fulfilment of the desires of his sensuality. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] This is a great wrath of God: correction is absent and flattery present. [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Alcuin.] The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins. [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss.] A person delights in doing what he does when he not only fears no reprover but also hears a praiser. Therefore he adds: “And the unjust man,” that is, one unjust by harming others, “is blessed,” as though he were God. And by this means the sinner, namely Antichrist—

**VERSE 25.**—“The sinner has provoked the Lord; according to the multitude of his wrath he will not seek.”

“He has provoked the Lord,” [Jerome] that is, he has provoked the true God to anger so that he may be punished by him. Or: I said that the sinner is praised in his desires, and this he certainly deserved because the sinner, namely Antichrist, has provoked or angered the Lord, so that he suffers these things—[Col. 0139B] that is, that the scourges of correction are withheld from him. He has provoked him so greatly that Antichrist will not seek God according to the multitude of Antichrist’s wrath, [Cassiodorus] who will do everything turbulently and cruelly. Or it is God, who is accustomed to seek out others and call them back from evil: he will not seek him, [Augustine] that is, he will not heed his sins in order to avenge them here, since he will punish him more grievously in the future. And this is according to the multitude of his wrath, that is, God’s wrath. This is because God is exceedingly angry with him when he allows him to reach riches and honours through frauds and crimes. For it is a great wrath of God when he does not correct a sinner but permits him a wandering licence to rush into sin. Hence he says to the sinful synagogue: “My jealousy has departed from thee. I will not punish your daughters and your wives when they have committed fornication” (Hos. 4). And God’s wrath—or Antichrist’s own wickedness—is so great that:

**VERSE 26.**—“God is not in his sight; his ways are defiled at all times.”

“God is not in his sight.” [Augustine.] It is a great evil to be forsaken by the light of truth, although people think the blindness of bodily eyes, by which the visible light is withdrawn, a great evil. [Augustine, Alcuin.] The cause of his wickedness is that he does not have God before his eyes. Therefore his ways—that is, his thoughts, counsels, and deeds—are defiled, [Col. 0139D] that is, foul, throughout all his time, that is, throughout the whole time of his life. Or “at all times” means in comparison with all who have existed at any time. This results because, O God:

**VERSE 27.**—“Thy judgments are removed from before his face; he shall rule over all his enemies.”

“Thy judgments are removed from before his face,” that is, he thinks that God does not judge; because judgment is delayed, he does not think that he will be punished. And therefore his ways are defiled also because he will rule over all his enemies. For he is said to overcome all kings, so that he alone may reign and sit in the temple of God, exalting himself above everything that is worshipped and called God (2 Thess. 2). And because he will attain that empty height and dominion through impious and evil arts, he adds:

[Col. 0140A] **VERSE 28.**—“For he has said in his heart: I shall not be moved from generation to generation without evil.”

“For he has said in his heart,” [Interlinear Gloss] as though to say: Truly he will rule, because of evil arts. For he has said in his heart, that is, within himself; outwardly he says other things in order to seem good. What has he said? “I shall not be moved from generation to generation without evil,” [Augustine] that is, my fame will not pass from this present generation to posterity unless by evil arts I obtain such a summit and such exalted rule that posterity cannot be silent about it. For a ruined mind, devoid of good arts and alienated from the light of justice, contrives through evil arts a way for itself to fame so enduring that it may even be celebrated among posterity. And those who cannot become known honourably desire people at least to speak ill of them, provided their name travels far and wide.

Or thus: He said, “I shall be moved from the mortal generation into the immortal generation, but not without evil,” that is, not without evil arts. For Antichrist will think that by evil arts, and in no other way, he will come bodily from the mortal generation into eternity, from earth to heaven. Simon Magus likewise thought that through criminal arts he would attain heaven and, by magical arts, pass from the human generation into the divine.

Or thus: “He shall be moved from generation to generation,” that is, I shall occupy all nations, but not without evil, that is, without sin, which is proper to him. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] Or thus: “I shall not be moved”—here make a pause—that is, I shall not be disturbed; rather, advancing from the present generation [Col. 0140C] into the generation to come, I shall always be without evil, [Remigius and Alcuin] that is, without disturbance. He then sets out his wickedness, saying:

**VERSE 29.**—“Whose mouth is full of cursing, bitterness, and deceit; beneath his tongue are toil and pain.”

“Whose mouth is full of cursing,” etc. [Interlinear Gloss.] As though to say: This man permits himself such things, whose mouth is full of cursing, that is, blasphemies and insults. [Augustine.] Cursing is rightly said to be within his mouth, not outside it, because it lacks effect. It will have power only to destroy him and will not harm the elect. [Col. 0140D] His mouth is full of bitterness, that is, bitter words and threats, and of deceit, [Augustine and Cassiodorus] that is, flatteries; for by bitterness and deceit, that is, by anger and snares, he will turn others. And toil—that is, iniquity—and pain—that is, the destruction which will follow from it—are beneath his tongue, not upon it, because he will think these things silently within himself. He will speak otherwise outwardly to people so that he may seem just. [Cassiodorus.] Or “toil and pain are beneath his tongue,” that is, his thoughts concern the toil of the saints and bodily suffering, because he will devise how to afflict and kill the saints, as is evident in the martyrs killed by him and his followers. Or the toil of the saints and the pain which is outward in bodily punishments are beneath his tongue; that is, his tongue is that of worldly people, which inwardly harms the soul through those outward things, [Alcuin] because [Col. 0141A] his words, by which the soul will be cast down, will be more feared and more harmful than blows. [Cassiodorus.] Then, comparing him with a robber who lies in wait on hidden roads to kill the innocent, he says:

**VERSE 30.**—“He sits in ambush with the rich in secret places, that he may kill the innocent.”

“He sits.” [Remigius, Augustine.] As though to say: He remains in ambush with the rich of this world, whom he will enrich and heap with gifts, displaying their false prosperity in order to deceive others. The ambushes, I say, are laid in hidden places—that is, in ambiguities, where it is not easy to discern what should or should not be desired. Why does he sit there? That he may kill the innocent by making the innocent guilty. Then he explains his ambushes, saying:

[Col. 0141B] **VERSE 31.**—“His eyes look upon the poor; he lies in wait in secret, like a lion in his den.”

“His eyes look.” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] As though to say: They look upon the poor with mercy and affection. Or he deceives others in this way because his eyes look cruelly upon the poor in spirit. [Augustine.] For he will especially persecute the just and poor in spirit, whose is the kingdom of heaven. And he lies in wait in secret because the person deceived does not know it. He himself is like a lion because of force, in his den because of deceit. [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine.] He is rightly compared to a lion in a den, because force and deceit will operate in him: force in his dominion, deceit in his miracles. This is the third persecution, compounded of force and fraud. There are two before the persecution of Antichrist. The first was violent, when martyrs were driven by proscriptions, tortures, and slaughter to sacrifice to idols. The other is deceitful, occurring now through heretics and false brethren; but that one will be both violent and deceitful. Force is signified by the lion, deceit by the den. Both will be in Antichrist. Then, setting out his intention in both deceit and force, he repeats:

**VERSE 32.**—“He lies in wait to seize the poor: to seize the poor, while he draws him.”

“He lies in wait.” As though to say: For what purpose does he lie in wait? [Augustine.] Behold, he lies in wait to seize the poor by deceit. Behold the deceit. [Interlinear Gloss.] Likewise, he lies in wait to seize the poor by violence, [Col. 0141D] while he draws him to himself by tortures. Or, conversely, it may be said that he first speaks of force and then of deceit, thus: He lies in wait to seize the poor by force. Likewise, he lies in wait to seize the poor by deceit, while he draws him to himself through flatteries; yet this is no less a seizure. He then adds more plainly concerning those two things, first concerning deceit:

**VERSE 33.**—“In his snare he will humble him; he will bow down and fall when he has ruled over the poor.”

“In his snare.” [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss.] Behold the deceit: his own, namely, one belonging to himself; or in his trap. He will not indeed ensnare him so that he falls in soul, but he will humble the poor man. [Augustine.] For the more wonderful the signs he performs, the more the saints opposed to him will be despised [Col. 0142A] and counted as nothing; but he will bow down and fall when he has inflicted punishments on the saints. Hence he adds: “And he will bow down and fall.” [Cassiodorus.] For when excessive prosperity has relaxed his mind into ease, he will fall by sudden destruction. He will fall, I say, when he has ruled over the poor. Behold the force. [Augustine.] For just as the trap aptly signifies ambushes, so dominion most clearly implies terror. And rightly he will fall.

**VERSE 34.**—“For he has said in his heart: God has forgotten; he has turned away his face, lest he see unto the end.”

“For he has said,” etc. Or the connection may be thus: Truly he will bow down and fall. [Interlinear Gloss.] For in this way he has said in his heart: God has forgotten the poor, so as to save them. Or: God has forgotten me, so as to punish me. [Augustine.] To think oneself unpunished is bowing down and falling. Again he says: God has turned away his face, lest he see me or them, unto the end, that is, until the day of judgment. [Interlinear Gloss.] Or: “He has turned away his face, lest he see unto the end,” that is, lest he see what is done on earth and in the world. [Augustine.] Those deny that God sees unto the end who say that he does not care for human affairs, because earth is the end of things and the final element, in which nothing happens without order; but people do not see him, since this belongs to the hidden things of the Son. Therefore, while the Church labours in that time, like a ship amid great waves and storms, it rouses the Lord as though sleeping, that he may command the winds and calm may come, saying:

**PART V. VERSE 35.**—“Arise, O Lord God, and let thy hand be exalted; do not forget the poor.”

[Col. 0142C] “Arise, O Lord.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] The fifth part, in which he prays for judgment, so that these exceedingly great evils may soon end—so great that no one would wish the time in which they occur to be prolonged. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though to say: Antichrist will say and do such things; but, O Lord God, now arise—that is, come swiftly—and make your power manifest. Now vengeance against Antichrist is at issue. “And let thy hand be exalted,” that is, thy power and judgment. [Jerome.] “And do not forget the poor,” as Antichrist and his accomplices think, saying, “He has turned away his face,” etc. [Augustine.] Therefore, the Church, understanding and rejoicing in that judgment, now says:

**VERSE 36.**—“Why has the wicked provoked God? For he has said in his heart: He will not seek.”

[Col. 0142D] Why has the wicked man, Antichrist, provoked God—that is, what did it profit him to commit such great evils? I say that he provoked him, and indeed he said in his heart: “There is no God,” [Remigius, Cassiodorus] not believing in God as punisher. “God will not seek out what I do.” Thus Antichrist says; but, O God:

**VERSE 37.**—“Thou seest, because thou considerest toil and pain, that thou mayest deliver them into thy hands.”

“You see,” that is, you know how you may deliver them—namely, Antichrist and his accomplices—into thy hands, that is, into thy acts of vengeance. [Jerome.] Why? Because you consider the toil and pain which he inflicts on the saints. Above it was said of this: “Beneath his tongue are toil and pain,” which they think [Col. 0143A] God does not know; but truly he does know.

Or thus: He said in his heart, “He will not seek.” Yet you see that you consider toil and pain, or anger, so that you may deliver them into thy hands. [Augustine.] For people sometimes do not take vengeance for all injuries done them because they fear toil or anger; and so this wicked man thinks that God cannot punish so many evils without toil and anger. This sense requires a particular punctuation; if it is mistaken, the sense is obscured. For the wicked man said thus: “God will not seek,” as though God considered toil and anger in order to deliver them into his hands—that is, as though he feared to toil and be angry. He will therefore spare them, lest he tire himself by punishing them and be disturbed by anger, as people sometimes do when they suppress vengeance so as not to labour or be angry. The sense is: Antichrist said, “God will not seek out the evils that I do.” And he said that you, O God, see—that is, endure—evils and leave them unpunished, because you consider toil and pain, or anger, in delivering them into thy hands; that is, because you fear to toil and grow angry if you punish them. But do you fear this? Far be it!

**VERSE 38.**—“The poor man has been left to thee; thou wilt be a helper to the orphan.”

“The poor man has been left to thee.” As though to say: Do not forget the poor, nor ought you to do so, because the poor man has been left to thee. [Augustine.] He is poor precisely because he has left all the temporal things of this world, so that you alone may be his hope. And you, no other, will be helper to the orphan, whose father—the world, by which he was carnally begotten—dies, so that he may say: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6). [Alcuin.] Note that he terrifies by punishments and soothes by benefits. [Col. 0143C] And because the poor man has been left to thee, therefore:

**VERSE 39.**—“Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked man; his sin shall be sought, and shall not be found.”

“Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked man,” [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss] that is, the power of that worst man, who is a sinner in himself and wicked toward others; or a sinner in force and wicked in fraud. Then he affirms what he prayed: “His sin shall be sought,” that is, he shall be judged concerning his sin, “and shall not be found,” [Remigius, Alcuin] that is, he himself shall perish because of his sin. Or, [Augustine] his sin shall be sought—whether it is still needed, as before, for purifying the good. Hence above: “While the wicked is proud, the poor is inflamed.” And it will not then be found [Col. 0143D] necessary, because there will no longer be anyone in whom there is a place for his sin, all the just then having been purified, just as a file is not needed for smooth iron.

**VERSE 40.**—“The Lord shall reign for ever and ever; you nations shall perish from his land.”

**VERSE 41.**—“The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; thine ear has heard the preparation of their heart.”

But the Lord shall reign for ever and ever. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] This kingdom will be more welcome because of the evils that precede it; it will come when Antichrist has been destroyed. But you nations—that is, all sinners who are without God’s law—shall perish from his land, namely from the land of the living; that is, you shall perish from this kingdom. [Col. 0144A] But the poor will possess it, because the Lord has heard the desire of the poor, with which they burned amid the evils of this age, longing for the day of the Lord.

Then, turning his address to God, he says: “And thine ear,” that is, thy power by which thou hearest, or thy mercy. [Augustine.] For it is not permissible to understand a bodily member in the Godhead; rather, when the members visible and bodily in us are named, the powers of operations must be understood. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] Thy ear, I say, “has heard the preparation of their heart,” that is, the heart prepared to serve, waiting through patience. Or, according to another reading, thy ear has heard the preparation, or desire, of their heart—that is, the ardour of their desire: this occurs when something is sought more fervently with all the powers of the soul. Or, it has heard the preparation of their heart, that is, that which God himself prepared in their hearts. Or, “Thine ear has heard the preparation of their heart,” that is, God hears as soon as they wish to ask.

**VERSE 42.**—“To judge for the orphan and the humble, that man may no longer add to magnify himself upon earth.”

“To judge for the orphan.” [Augustine.] Behold the desire of the poor. For their desire is that you judge, that is, that you may judge for the orphan, who is not conformed to the age, and the humble, who is not proud. For it is one thing to judge the orphan, another to judge for the orphan. Even one who condemns judges the orphan; but one judges for the orphan who pronounces sentence on his behalf. It should be noted that here the second coming for judgment is mentioned, which will be manifest, [Col. 0144C] although this psalm concerns “the hidden things of the Son,” as the title indicates.
