Yet that coming too is rightly now placed among the hidden things of the Son, because no one knows of it—not the angels, nor the powers, nor the Son of Man—not indeed in respect of knowing, but in respect of disclosing it to us—so that he may no longer add. [Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus.] As though to say: Therefore they desire you to judge, so that man, namely that proud Antichrist—who is mere man, not God—may no longer add, as he did on earth, to magnify himself upon the earth. For then all evils will end, when man, the author of evils, is condemned with his people.

## COLLATION ON PSALM IX, “I WILL GIVE THANKS”

As regards the title, which the Septuagint rendered “for the hidden things of the Son,” the rabbis and the newer versions have produced monstrous and confused interpretations. One says that it concerns the death of a certain enemy of David called Laben; he maintains a metathesis, *Laben* for *Nabal*. Another writes that it is the name of a singer. Pagninus renders it “for the death of the fool”; Pellican, “for the victory of youth, for the son.” The interpreters for Cajetan render it “concerning death, for the son”; Jerome, however, “concerning the death of the son.” Sanctes and Münster leave the Hebrew *ALMUTH, Labben*. If *almuth* is read as one word, it can mean “hidden,” as the Septuagint understood it from the root *ALAM*, “he hid”; if it is divided into two parts, it means “concerning death,” as Jerome translated it.

**VERSE 4.**—“For thou hast made my judgment and my cause.” I do not know on what impulse Pagninus translated “my strictness” for “my cause,” when all the Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins whom I have been able to consult render [Col. 0145A] “my cause.” In Hebrew it is *DINI*. In Greek: *tēn dikēn mou* (τὴν δίκην μού), “my cause” or “my judgment.”

**VERSE 6.**—“The enemies have failed; their swords unto the end.” Pagninus, Münster, Nebiensis, Sanctes, and Campensis rendered “O enemy,” in the vocative. Yet Jerome and Pellican, with the Septuagint, give the genitive. Then, for “swords,” Jerome says “desolations,” while nearly all the others say “devastations” or “destructions,” in the same sense. The Hebrew word *HORABOTH* is ambiguous between “swords” and “desolations.” Hence Pellican and Pagninus translated “swords.”

**VERSE 7.**—“Their memory has perished with a sound.” Hebrew: “with them.” Whence, then, did the Septuagint derive “with a sound”? Observe, however, that the Septuagint took *HEMAII* not as it is a pronoun, but as a noun derived from the root *HAMAH*, meaning “to sound,” “to roar,” “to make a tumult.” This is evident from Psalm 45: “Their waters sounded and were troubled.” The Hebrew has that word for “sounded.” Campensis’s paraphrase appears [Col. 0145B] to allude to this when it says, “with the astonishment of those passing by.”

**VERSE 17.**—“The sinner has been caught in the works of his hands.” The Hebrews add *HIGAION*, which means “with meditation.” But the Septuagint omitted it, as also the word *SELAH*, which is not part of the textual sequence of the psalm. Rather, as Jerome writes to Marcella, it is a *diapsalma*, by which we observe that what precedes and what follows are connected together, or at least are taught to be eternal.

**VERSE 21.**—“Set, O Lord, a lawgiver over them.” Jerome, Sanctes, Münster, and Campensis have “terror”; Pagninus, “yoke”; the interpreters for Cajetan, “dominion.” This results because the word *MORAH* may be derived from the root *IARE* with *aleph* at the end, and will then mean “terror”; or from the root *IARAH* with *heth* at the end, meaning “he taught,” so that *morah* or *moreh* means “teacher” or “lawgiver.” *Aleph* and *heth*, [Col. 0145C] among the Hebrews, are letters commonly interchangeable.

VERS. 24.—For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man blesses. Then there follows, in our text and in the LXX, the beginning of another verse: “the sinner has provoked the Lord.” The Hebrew codices, with a different division, bring back the two words of the following verse—namely, “has provoked the Lord”—to the preceding verse, and translate them variously: Jerome, “the covetous man, applauding himself, has blasphemed the Lord”; Pagninus, “the wicked man blesses one who blasphemes the Lord”; Münster, “and he blessed the covetous man whom God curses”; Sanctes, “and he blessed the covetous man; he made the Lord angry”; the interpreter for Cajetan, “the covetous man has blessed; he has despised the Lord”; Pellican, “the covetous man blesses; he blasphemes the Lord”; the paraphrase of Campensis, “nor are there lacking those who flatter, in hope of plunder, that impious man who so openly blasphemes the Lord”; Nebiensis, “blessing the robber, he has blasphemed the Lord”; the Chaldee, “he who blesses a robber rejects God.” But where, finally, are we to turn? [Col. 0145D] The Septuagint read BARUCH, that is, “is blessed” or “blessed,” not BERECH, “he blessed,” with a different division, as occurs because of the metrical character of the poem by which the Psalter is numbered, as we have taught above.

VERS. 26.—His ways are defiled at all times. From the ambiguity of the Hebrew word HOL, or HALAL, arises great diversity among translators. Since those roots signify to defile, to suffer, to bring forth, and to prosper, Jerome and Nebiensis translate, “his ways bring forth”; Pagninus and Sanctes, “shall prosper,” following the Chaldee interpreter. Münster: “his ways are troublesome,” to which Campensis alludes. The edition, however, still has, in our manner, “his ways are profane”; Pellican: “his ways shall suffer,” JAHILU DERACAU.

VERS. 30.—He sits in ambush with the rich. Pagninus: [Col. 0146A] “in the ambushes of villages”; Sanctes and the interpreter for Cajetan, “of country houses”; Münster, “of hamlets”; Pellican, “of courts”; Jerome, “of vestibules.” The LXX read HATZERIM with aleph, HATZERIM, from the root ATZAR, “he stored up.” The word is the same apart from aspiration. And indeed, mutual interchange among the gutturals, as they are called, is easy. But concerning the discrepancy among manuscripts, enough has already often been emphasized, not without purpose; and this will be made clearer still below.

VERS. 31.—His eyes look upon the poor. Jerome alone, so far as could be seen, translating according to the Hebrews, rendered LEHELECACH, “upon thy strong ones.” Hence it is clearer than light that Jerome read two words, or one word compounded from two, and derived the first from HAIIL, that is, “strength,” while taking the other with a prefixed, non-essential servile CAPH. He does the same in verse 38, “the poor man is left to thee,” where he translated, “thy strong ones are left to thee.” In our Hebrew Bibles we have HELECA.

[Col. 0146B] VERS. 33.—When he shall have gained dominion over the poor. Hebrew: BAATZUMAU HELCAIM. Jerome: “powerfully in his strength.” Pagninus: “the army of the crushed shall fall in his strength”; Sanctes: “the assembly of the poor shall fall with his mighty ones”; Münster: “that the assembly of the poor may fall into the hand of his mighty ones”; Pellican: “he shall cast down the impoverished by his strength.” Campensis likewise alludes to this. These versions refer “shall fall” to the assembly of the poor. The Septuagint refer it to the person of Antichrist, because they interpreted the servile letter beth as “when,” as the Hebrews not infrequently take it in verse 23, and supplied the substantive verb: namely, “while there is an army of the poor or innocent in the strongholds of Antichrist.” But because this would have been somewhat obscure, they expressed it by a verb and participle: “when he shall have gained dominion over the poor.” A faithful interpreter ought not render word for word. Jerome attended to the word [Col. 0146C] as though it were compounded from HAIIL, as he was troubled by it in the immediately preceding verse, and CAAH, that is, “he suffered” or “was oppressed,” since he translated “powerfully.”

In the same verse Faber says that in this clause, “He shall bow himself down,” the words “he shall bow himself down” ought to be deleted on the authority of the Greek and Hebrew. How false this is is shown by the root SCHOAH, that is, “he bowed himself down”; nor do teachers of Hebrew disagree. And the Greek κύπτω means “to bend oneself down.”

VERS. 36.—In his heart he will not seek. The Hebrews now read, “thou wilt not seek,” in the second person, LO TIDROS; yet Jerome, according to the Hebrew, translates it with the LXX in the third person. And although the sense comes to the same thing, this is, among other arguments, evidence that the Hebrew reading corresponding to Jerome’s version is not altogether genuine, even if it is German.

VERS. 39.—Break the arm of the sinner and the malignant man; his sin shall be sought and shall not be found. Jerome: “Break the arm of the ungodly and malignant man; thou shalt seek [Col. 0146D] his ungodliness and shalt not find it.” The same sense is followed by Münster, Nebiensis, and the Chaldee interpreter. Pagninus, Pellican, and the interpreter for Cajetan make a different division and interpretation. The first: “Break the arm of the ungodly, and thou shalt seek evil; thou shalt not find his ungodliness.” The second: “Break the arm of the ungodly, and pursue the malignant man.” The third: “Break the arm of the ungodly, and thou shalt seek evil.” Sanctes added something of his own: “Thou shalt seek his ungodliness, which he said thou shalt not find.” Consider what and how much the modern teachers allow themselves: whatever they dream.

VERS. 42.—That man may no longer presume to magnify himself upon the earth. Nebiensis comes fairly close: “that man of the earth may no longer presume to be proud.” Pagninus: “that he may not continue further to crush man out of the earth.” Sanctes approaches this: “that the wicked man may not add further, so as to crush man out of the earth”; or, as the interpreter for Cajetan has it, “he shall no longer add to breaking man from the earth.” These make a different [Col. 0147A] sense from ours, though they tend toward the same end. But the Hebrews do not have inflections of cases in the Latin manner; therefore “man” may be taken either in the nominative or accusative case. Hence Jerome translated, “that man of the earth may by no means further be proud,” which does not differ from the meaning of our edition, as the paraphrase of Campensis also indicates: “that the wretched little man born of the earth may no longer attempt to trust in his own strength.” Münster differs: “and that man of the earth may no longer add to raging against them.” Pellican: “that man of the earth may no longer be added to be dismayed in spirit.” Münster refers “man” to Antichrist or a tyrant; Pellican, to the poor man. And the word [lacuna] ARATZ is ambiguous.

## PSALM X

[Col. 0147]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0147A]

I trust in the Lord. The title: “Unto the end, a psalm of David.” Here the Prophet speaks of heretics, who, as rotten members within the Church, falsely claim to possess Christ and endeavor to turn and tear others away from the breasts of the one true mother, the Church, drawing them to themselves [Col. 0147B] and asserting that Christ is with them. They admonish us, as though with piety and zeal, that by crossing over to them we should pass over into Christ. To these the Prophet replies here, in the person of one of the faithful, rebuking them and teaching that they must be resisted. The meaning of the title is: This psalm, directing us unto the end, that is, unto Christ, is of David the prophet. [Cassiodorus.] Its purpose is to teach resistance to heretics. The psalm has a twofold arrangement. First, it treats of heretics who seek to convert Catholics to their perversity; second, it says what God will give to each group, namely the good and the evil. There: “But the righteous…” Therefore, replying to heretics with rebuke, he says:

VERS. 1.—“In the Lord I trust: how do you say to my soul, ‘Pass over to the mountain like a sparrow’?”

[Col. 0147C] I trust in the Lord. [Augustine.] As though he said: There is one mountain, namely Christ, in whom I trust and whom I hold; he is the mountain at the summit of the mountains. How, then, do you say? Behold the rebuke: to my soul, what do you say? “Pass over to the mountain,” that is, to the Christ who is among us. In other words, how do you advise me to cross over to you, as though there were many Christs? As though he said: It is astonishing. You give this advice; but if I did these things, I would be like a sparrow—that is, a bird, unstable and flighty—if I crossed over. [Cassiodorus, Remigius.] For the species is put for the genus.

Or thus: “You say to my soul, ‘Pass over to the mountains,’” another reading, [Augustine,] that is, to us who are mountains. Mountains indeed we are, through pride, not through humility as the righteous are. And you ought to cross over to us because you are like a sparrow, that is, winged with virtues and commandments. But the things you put forward to make me cross over to you do not permit me to cross, because, if I am a sparrow, I have a house where I may rest, according to the words: “For even the sparrow has found herself a house” (Ps. LXXXIII). But what house? The Lord, who is a refuge for the poor. How, then, do you say that I should cross over to you?

Or thus: “You say to my soul, ‘Pass over from your low place to the mountain,’” that is, to the eminence of understanding which we possess. And so you will be like the sparrow which nests on high. And how do you say this? As though he said: This is astonishing. Then the faithful person, in whose person the Prophet speaks, turns to others and says:

VERS. 2.—“For behold, sinners have bent [Col. 0148A] the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, that they may shoot the upright in heart in the dark.”

For behold. As though he said: Someone might ask, “To whom are you saying this, and why?” He answers: [Gloss, interlinear.] “Behold, I say this to sinners, because behold, sinners have bent the bow,” etc. Or the connection is thus: Therefore [Col. 0148B] I trust in the Lord. For behold—as though he said—it is plain that sinners, [Jerome, Remigius,] that is, heretics, have bent the bow, that is, they have distorted Sacred Scripture toward themselves, according to their own will, so as to wound the souls of the simple. [Cassiodorus, Gloss, interlinear.] Or, “they have bent the bow,” that is, in the holy Scriptures they have acquired an understanding subtle in their own estimation, while they judge others to have a dull one; “and they have prepared their arrows in the quiver,” [Augustine,] that is, they have poisonous words ready in their heart. For what purpose? “That they may shoot the upright in heart in the dark,” [Jerome,] that is, those dwelling in a simple understanding. Or: “that they may shoot the upright in heart in the dark,” that is, amid their ambiguous and obscure opinions. They do this by means of the bow, not because Scripture serves this purpose—that is, not through a defect in [Col. 0148C] Scripture—but:

VERS. 3.—“For they have destroyed what thou hast perfected; but what has the righteous man done?”

For they have destroyed. [Cassiodorus, Remigius.] By expounding badly, that is, they have perverted the things which thou hast perfected, namely the Scriptures which thou hast perfectly set forth. Or, “thou hast perfected” by fulfilling in thyself the things foretold in the Scriptures.

Or according to another reading: “That they may shoot the upright in heart in the darkened moon.” The moon fittingly signifies the Church. There are two opinions about the moon, and which of them is true cannot altogether, or can only with difficulty, be known. Some say that it has its own light, but that one half of its globe shines and the other is dark. When it gradually turns the shining part toward the earth so that it may be seen, it appears horned; thus it increases until that whole part is seen. And when it turns again, the dark part begins to appear, until it is wholly withdrawn from us again. This is the Church: on the spiritual side it shines, and on the carnal side it is dark. The spiritual part sometimes appears to people through good works, and sometimes is hidden in a conscience known to God alone, though it is seen only in the body. This occurs when we pray in our heart and seem almost to do nothing, though we direct our hearts not toward earth but upward to the Lord.

Others say that the moon has no light except from the sun; but when it is with the sun, it has toward us the part which is not seen by the sun and therefore does not shine upon us. But when it withdraws from the sun, it is illuminated on the side it has [Col. 0149A] toward us, until, at the sun’s setting, it rises full from the east. When from the other side it begins to approach the sun, its upper part is illuminated and its lower part darkened. This likewise accords well with the Church, which has no light except from the sun of righteousness, that is, Christ, who is allegorically called the sun in many places of Scripture. Therefore, whichever of these two opinions be true, the moon is suitably understood allegorically as the Church. But if anyone does not wish, or lacks leisure, or lacks the mental capacity, to exercise his mind in these obscurities, which are more laborious than fruitful, it is enough, omitting obscure explanations, to observe with ordinary eyes the waxing and waning of the moon. If it declines in order to be renewed, it signifies the Church in which the resurrection of the dead is believed to be yet to come. Behold how the moon signifies the Church.

Now we must see how the darkness of the moon signifies the darkness of the Church. The moon is dark, or becomes dark, in three ways: either it comes to an end in its monthly courses; or its brightness is interrupted by cloud; or it is in eclipse, when it appears blood-red. [Augustine.] Likewise the Church was dark when, in the beginning of the faith, it was still new and had not yet shone widely over the earth; or when, covered by the clouds of blasphemers, it is reviled; or when it is bloodied by the slaughter of martyrs. Amid these terrors and darknesses of the Church, the wicked cast their deceitful words like arrows in order to pervert the upright, because they know these times are suited to deceiving the weak. Therefore he says: “That they may shoot the upright in heart in the darkened moon,” that is, in [Col. 0149C] the darkness of the Church, which is darkened in the three ways mentioned above.

Or the Church is called dark when her children sin and many ignorant and carnal persons abound in her. Then, taking occasion from the darkened moon, wicked heretics hurl reproaches at Catholics because they live with such persons and receive sacraments from them. But one who trusts in the Lord need fear nothing. Let him fear who trusts in man, who then says that sacraments are holy when they are given by holy persons. The meaning is: “That they may shoot the upright in heart in the darkened moon,” that is, when, owing to the many carnal and ignorant persons, they perceive that they cannot be refuted because the light of the Church has been obscured. “For they have destroyed what thou hast perfected”: this does not change.

Or thus, from the words “For behold”: these are the terrors and threats of heretics concerning sinners, unless we pass over to them as though they were righteous. For they say: You ought to come over to us, “for behold, sinners have bent the bow,” that is, they interpret the Scriptures carnally. “And they have prepared their arrows in the quiver,” that is, poisonous words in their hearts. For what purpose? “That they may shoot the upright in heart in the dark”: this does not differ in meaning from the first reading. “What thou hast perfected”: the faithful man turns his speech away from those heretics, to whom he had formerly been speaking, toward God. As though someone should say: Why do they tell you, “Pass over”? Why do they frighten you with sinners, since they aim to shoot the upright? He answers: Because the things which thou hast perfected—that is, the praise which God has perfected out of the mouth of infants—they have destroyed, so far as in them lies, in their assemblies. There they shoot at or harass with empty and scrupulous questions little ones [Col. 0150A] who ought to be nourished with the milk of faith; and they kill them with the poisons of perverse doctrines, thereby striving, as it were, to prevent you from giving praise.

[Cassiodorus.] “But the righteous man…” This is the second part, where he says what God gives to each group—the good and the evil—and threatens judgment, so that at least through fear they may abandon falsehoods. As though he said: Thus heretics offend and trouble us. But what has the righteous man, that is, Christ, done? In respect of both groups, namely good and evil, [Augustine,] as though he said: If heretics offend you, does not Christ give you peace? He says: “My peace I give to you; my peace I leave to you” (John XIV). He indeed gives peace, which heretics violate by their abominable dissension. Christ displayed such great peace that he endured even Judas, his betrayer, with wonderful patience; he sent him with the other apostles to preach the kingdom of heaven; and he gave him the Eucharist, as he did to the rest, though he had earlier named him betrayer [Col. 0150B] and devil. He granted him these things in order to show that God’s gifts reach those who receive faith, even if the person through whom they receive it is like Judas. [Alcuin.] Note that by this question he invites both parties to the answer that follows.

VERS. 4.—“The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord, his throne is in heaven.”

The Lord is in his holy temple: here he shows what he does for the good. And at the words “he shall rain upon sinners,” he says what he does to the evil. First, then, answering the preceding question, he shows what he does for the good: [Col. 0150C] “The Lord is in his holy temple.” [Alcuin, Augustine.] That is, he is in his own people, so that he makes them his temple. This temple is also heaven, as he adds. The Lord does this also—as though he said—“his throne is in heaven”; that is, those whom he makes a temple he also makes heaven, that is, hidden mysteries. [Augustine, Gloss, interlinear.]

Or it may be divided thus: The Lord is Lord of all generally by power; but specially he is “in his holy temple,” that is, in the faithful. Hence it is said, “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (I Cor. III); nowhere else is God so present as he is in his temple. Then he repeats: “In heaven,” that is, his throne is among the saints.

VERS. 5.—“His eyes look upon the poor; his eyelids examine the sons of men.”

[Col. 0150D] His eyes. [Remigius, Gloss, interlinear.] As though he said: Thus he acts toward the greater persons, namely by making them a temple and heaven; but toward the poor man, that is, the lesser persons: [Jerome, Augustine,] “his eyes,” that is, his mercy, look upon him, and this is light to that poor man. For God’s regard is both help and light to his own. Therefore the tumults of tribulations arising in the nets need not be feared before the shore of eternity is reached.

Or by “the poor man” he signifies the same people whom he signified by “heaven” and “temple.” As though he said: Some are temple and heaven. And this too, no less than the other things, is from the Lord, because his eyes, that is, his mercy, look upon the poor man, through which he becomes heaven. And “his eyelids,” that is, the frequent opening of Scripture in some passages and its opening through other passages—Scriptures which are, as it were, the eyes of God—[Col. 0151A] examine, that is, test, the sons of men, namely those renewed from their old state through faith. In other words, they test the good, because the good are not wearied by obscurities but exercised by them; they are not puffed up by knowledge but strengthened. And likewise:

VERS. 6.—“The Lord examines the righteous and the wicked; but he who loves iniquity hates his own soul.”

The Lord examines, [Jerome, Gloss, interlinear,] that is, through tribulations and heresies he tests the righteous and the wicked. [Augustine.] Why then do you, righteous man, fear that the wicked man who does not sincerely share in the sacraments will harm you, when the Lord examines both you and him? [Cassiodorus.] Or, “the Lord examines the righteous and the wicked,” because the Lord alone judges the consciences of both. The Lord examines each; and by examining he finds this: that he who loves iniquity hates his own soul. [Augustine, Alcuin.] That is, the lover of iniquity harms his own soul, not the righteous man who believes God. Why, then, do you fear if an unjust man is bodily present with you?

Notice that he says, “he who loves iniquity,” not “he who commits it.” [Gloss, interlinear.] Iniquity is the same as sin; hence John: “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity” (John VIII). But no one lives without sin. He, however, loves iniquity who sins from desire and affection; even if he lived forever, he would wish to sin forever.

VERS. 7.—“He shall rain upon sinners snares, fire and sulphur; and a spirit of storms is the portion of their cup.”

[Col. 0151C] He shall rain upon sinners. Up to this point he has said what the righteous man does for the good. [Alcuin.] Here he says what he will render to the evil. As though he said: The Lord is in the temple and in heaven. The Lord will also rain snares upon sinners. Or join it thus: I say that he who loves iniquity hates his own soul, and the result demonstrates this, because the Lord will rain snares, that is, ensnaring doctrine, upon sinners. [Augustine, Gloss, interlinear.] The Lord rains these snares from clouds, namely pseudo-prophets who mingle falsehoods with truths; or also from good prophets, from whom snares flow when their teachings are wrongly understood. But the Lord rains these snares only upon those who are sinners. Hence, “to some we are an odor of life unto life; to others, an odor of death unto death” (II Cor. II). Therefore all who water souls by the word of God, whether good or evil, may be called clouds. From them the Lord rains upon sinners so that they may thereby be without excuse. This rain is a snare to them because they either do not understand soundly or do not fulfill it in deed.

Then the punishment of blasphemers is described when he adds, “fire,” [Augustine, Jerome,] namely of covetousness; “and sulphur,” that is, the stench of evil works; and “a spirit of storms,” which shall be in the future, that is, that final separation from the righteous. These are the portion of their cup, that is, their punishment. [Augustine.] He calls their punishments a cup because their punishments too are according to the manner and measure of their merits. Here is marked the order of the punishments suffered by the wicked. First they are ravaged by the fire of covetousness; then, by the stench of evil works, they are cast away from the saints; then they are plunged into eternal punishments. [Cassiodorus.] Or, with the rest unchanged, [Col. 0152A] “a spirit of storms” may be understood of the present: a tumultuous mind.

VERS. 8.—“For the Lord is righteous and loves righteous acts; his countenance has seen equity.”

For the Lord is righteous. [Augustine.] As though he said: The Lord will render these things aforesaid to good and evil. And why will he do this? Because the Lord is righteous and loves “righteous acts,” that is, righteous persons. He said “righteous acts” in the plural, so that you may understand righteous persons, in whom there are many acts of righteousness, though there is one righteousness of God in which all participate. “And his countenance has seen equity.” Or: his face, that is, equity, has been seen in his face, that is, in his knowledge. For his face is his knowledge, that is, his power by which he makes himself known to the worthy. Or “his countenance has seen equity” in relation to both groups, namely good and [Col. 0152B] evil, because he does not give himself to be known by the evil but by the good; and this is equity.

This psalm may also be read otherwise, as referring to Christ’s passion. Christ speaks according to his human nature, as is customary, against the errors of the Jews: “I trust in the Lord: how then do you say to my soul, ‘Pass over to the mountain like a sparrow’?” That is, agree with us in legal observances and the rest. Therefore I trust in the Lord, because behold, sinners—the scribes and Pharisees—have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver in order to shoot the upright in heart in the dark, that is, they wish to shoot the faithful in the darkened moon, that is, the synagogue filled with sinners. [Jerome, Augustine.] Another reading: “For they have destroyed what thou hast perfected,” that is, me, whom thou hast made perfect. The Jews destroyed me insofar as they thought me a destroyer [Col. 0152C] of the Law. But what did the righteous man, whom they despised as a destroyer of the Law, do? Behold, the Lord is in his holy temple, that is, the Word of the Father is in man; or the Son of Man is in heaven at the Father’s right hand. And he repeats: “His throne is in heaven.” And his eyes look upon the poor man, whom he took upon himself according to his divine nature; or for whose sake he suffered according to his human nature. And his eyelids examine the sons of men. Christ’s eyelids are the opening and closing of his eyes, that is, his death and resurrection, by which he tested the sons of men, namely his disciples. And the Lord, now ruling the Church from heaven, examines the righteous and the wicked; and by examining, he finds this, that he who loves iniquity hates his own [Col. 0152D] soul. And he teaches why this is so. For he shall rain upon sinners. This and the remaining material to the end do not differ from the preceding exposition.

## COMPARISON ON PSALM X: “IN THE LORD I TRUST”

VERS. I.—How do you say to my soul: “Pass over to the mountain like a sparrow”? Pagninus: “Pass over from your mountain like a sparrow.” Sanctes agrees; and Münster is not far from them: “Fly away from your mountain like a sparrow.” The interpreter for Cajetan: “Wander about your mountain, bird.” He immediately reports the Hebrew wording or reading, which does not expressly contain either a preposition or a mark of comparison. Pellican translates, “a sparrow to their mountain,” although the Hebrew now reads HARCHEM, “your mountain.” But Jerome according to the Hebrew, without the pronoun: “Fly across to the mountain like a bird.” Here you see that the Rabbis and their followers wish the preposition “from” or “away from” to be understood. The Septuagint, Jerome, [Col. 0153A] and Pellican read the preposition “in” or “to”; nor does Jerome read “your,” any more than the LXX do. The translator for Campensis: “Go hence at once to your mountains, more swiftly than a bird.” And the paraphrase: “Flee from mountain to mountain, as you are accustomed to do with your companions, and hide yourself somewhere in a cave, as a sparrow is wont to do.” But if each person continues to produce the notions of his own brain, whole cartloads of diversities will be piled upon Holy Scripture, so that readers will finally carry away nothing but confusion and the instability of a bird flying hither and thither.

VERS. 2.—They prepared their arrows in the quiver. Here one might overlook the fact that sworn Hebraists put “sinew” or “string” in place of “quiver,” were it not that an arrow fitted upon the string seems a more immediate danger than one stored in the quiver, though the point of the sense is the same. Yet, since Augustine interprets this of the snares of heretics, so that the quiver may be understood as their heart, in which they devise perverse thoughts against the simple, by which afterward they may mortally [Col. 0153B] wound the unwary, the quiver is more suitable to this meaning than an arrow already placed on the string. Moreover, the Hebrew particle IETER may readily be applied to the violence of the wicked and their hidden deceits. Jerome certainly translated this particle in Job XXX as “quiver”: “He opened his quiver.”

VERS. 3.—For they have destroyed what thou hast perfected. Jerome: “The laws have been scattered.” The meaning does not vary, because the laws of God are the things which he perfects and which perfect us. The translations of Pagninus, Augustine, Nebiensis, Münster, and the interpreter for Cajetan amount to the same thing—namely, “foundations”; or, as Pellican wishes, “those things which have been set.” Sanctes alone translates “nets,” following certain Rabbis. I do not know how the translator for Campensis and the paraphrase tear apart and fragment the sense. The former translates, “that they may utterly destroy”; the latter, “in the very attempt, their counsels were rendered vain.”

VERS. 5.—His eyes look upon the poor. [Col. 0153C] The Septuagint added τὸν πένητα, “the poor man,” by way of clarification, as later translators very frequently do.

VERS. 6.—But he who loves iniquity hates his own soul. Because the Hebrews lack variation of cases, the converse sense may be rendered in this way: “His soul hates the one who loves iniquity.” The change of case makes our version refer to the sinner, who by sinning hates his own salvation; the other version, which Jerome and the rest give, refers to God, who pursues sinners with hatred. Each has the dignity of its own interpretation. Only this stands in the way: SANEAH, “he hated,” is feminine in gender, so that it can refer only to “soul,” which is said to be God’s. Yet this could easily happen, where points are not written, if the letter he belonged to the next word NAPHSSO, by reading HANAPHSSO, while the preceding word remained to be read SANA.

It is astonishing how tragically Faber and the Blind Burgensis attack the Latin reading, as though it contradicted the Gospel diametrically when it admonishes that whoever hates his soul shall keep it unto eternal life (John XII), as if “soul” must always be understood as bodily life. What then is that saying in Proverbs XXIX: “He who shares with a thief hates his own soul”? And: “My soul thirsted for thee, O God” (Ps. LXII). Since “soul” is so often used in Scripture in a good sense, they ought to have noticed that the Gospel explains itself when it adds: “He who hates his soul in this world.” Then these warlike men strive to excuse the Septuagint, who recoiled from attributing a soul to God, only immediately to overthrow that excuse by admitting that the prophets did not fear to attribute a soul to God, when Isaiah said: “My soul hated your solemnities”—as though the LXX had not written, “My soul hates your feasts,” τὰς ἕορτὰς ὑμῶν μισεῖ ἡ ψυχή μου, in Isaiah chapter one. [Col. 0154B]

Because of this lack of distinction between cases, it has come about that in the following verse, “He shall rain upon sinners snares, fire, sulphur; a spirit of storms, the portion of their cup,” some have translated “fire and sulphur” in the accusative and then “a spirit of storms” in the nominative; others have translated everything in the accusative. Whom, finally, shall we follow? So that we may not waver, we have the usage of the Churches, which wavers in no respect.

VERS. 8.—His countenance has seen equity. Jerome according to the Hebrews, and Pellican, translate “their faces” or “their countenances.” The Hebrews read PANEMO. But the Hebrews are accustomed at times, according to the logic of government, to take it so that it means “them” or “their”; thus the sense would refer to the righteous, whose faces have seen what is right. Yet the LXX took PANEMO in place of PANAU, that is, “his countenance.” That this may not seem my invention, Münster does not deny it in his scholia. Sanctes, Pagninus, and the interpreters for Cajetan translate similarly. Nevertheless, either sense is fitting.

## PSALM XI

[Col. 0153]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID, FOR THE OCTAVE.”

[Col. 0153C]

[Col. 0153D] Save me, O God. The title: “Unto the end, a psalm of David for the octave.” [Augustine.] As was said concerning the sixth psalm, the octave is understood as the day of judgment, because after this time, which passes in seven days, the Lord will come for judgment. Above, the sinner conscious of guilt feared the octave, lest he be punished there. Here the Prophet, in the person of a perfect man, prays for it to come. [Cassiodorus.] For here the Prophet asks that the iniquity of the world may be destroyed, so that he may attain the truth of the promise to come. The meaning is: This psalm, directing us unto the end, is of David the prophet, who here speaks in the person of a certain righteous man, in character (habitus). It is for the octave, that is, for the day of judgment, which he desires, so that the iniquity of the age may be destroyed and the promised truth may come. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] Its purpose is to call people back from the falsehoods of the age to the utterances of God, in which salvation is found. [Cassiodorus.] Its arrangement is twofold. First, he asks to be saved from the perversity [Col. 0154D] of the age; second, Christ, sent by the Father against the evils of the age, is shown forth, whose utterances are true. There: “Because of the misery,” etc. Therefore, seeing the vanity of the age multiplied, the holy man, as though afraid, suddenly cries out because of the magnitude of the danger, saying:

VERS. 1.—“Save me, O Lord, for the holy man has failed; for truths have been diminished from among the sons of men.”

Save me, O Lord. [Cassiodorus.] Then he explains what he feared, gathering many things into one so that the danger may appear greater, saying: “For the holy man has failed.” As though he said: Therefore I cry, because the holy man has failed, that is, no holy man is found in this world where there are so many evils. This was also Elijah’s opinion when he said: “Lord, I alone am left” (III Kings XIX). Or, “the holy one,” that is, God, who is present everywhere, [Alcuin,] has failed in relation to human beings because he is scarcely acknowledged by man. Therefore he has failed in relation to those who do not believe in him. [Augustine.] And truly the holy one has failed because truth has failed. This is what is meant by: “For truths have been diminished from among the sons of men.” He says “truths” in the plural because he is dealing with human truths. God’s truth is one, and holy souls are illuminated by it; but there are many truths in human beings, just as many images appear in mirrors from one face. [Cassiodorus.] Note that he does not say “in the sons,” but “from the sons of men,” because God’s gifts are corrupted and diminished by their fault. It follows:

[Col. 0155B] VERS. 2.—“Each one has spoken vain things to his neighbor; with deceitful lips, with heart and heart, they have spoken.”

They have spoken vain things, etc. [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: Truly truth has been diminished, because falsehood has increased. Or connect it thus: Truths have been diminished; and, moreover, each one has spoken vain things in order to deceive his neighbor, that is, any human being. [Augustine.] For every human being is a neighbor by the condition of first birth. Therefore one must act wrongly toward no one. Or he understands “neighbor” as someone joined to us by some opportunity, whom they also use for deception; and that is worse. [Alcuin.] It should be known that “neighbor” is said in three ways: by the condition of first birth, in which sense every human being may be called a neighbor; by kinship of flesh, according to the saying, “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy” (Luke X); and by the rendering of a benefit and compassionate mercy. Thus the Gospel says, in the parable of the wounded man: “Who seems to you to have been a neighbor to him?” “He who showed mercy to him” (ibid.). I say, they have spoken vain things, being themselves deceitful lips, [Gloss, interlinear,] that is, talkative for reviling, and deceitful for deceiving. [Augustine.] And they are truly deceitful because “with heart and heart they have spoken,” that is, with a double or manifold heart. For the repetition signifies a double heart. It follows:

VERS. 3.—“May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips, and the tongue that speaks great things.”

“May [the Lord] destroy.” As though he said: They are talkative and deceitful; but may the Lord destroy deceitful lips—not the persons themselves, but their deceits and garrulousness. [Cassiodorus.] And he adds, all, lest any deceitful person exempt himself—that is, suppose himself excepted—as though those who agree in one perversity should perish everywhere. And may he destroy the boastful tongue, that is, the proud tongue. [Remigius.] These are hypocrites, having an appearance in speech in order to deceive people, yet not subject to God. Or philosophers are signified by the boastful tongue, on account of their eloquence. He then states how hypocrites or philosophers possess a boastful tongue:

**VERSE 4.**—“Who have said: ‘We shall magnify our tongue; [Col. 0156A] our lips are from ourselves. Who is our lord?’”

Who have said this, namely: “We shall magnify our tongue.” [Cassiodorus, Remigius.] And they do so, because they exalt themselves by their loquacity and place in their own power what they do not think they have received from God. For they have said this and another thing: “Our lips are from ourselves,” that is, our eloquence is from ourselves, not from God. [Cassiodorus.] For they boast of the power of their lips, as though it were not from God. [Interlinear Gloss.] Hence they say, “Who is our lord?”—that is, whose rule are we subject to? As though to say: No one.

## PART II. VERSE 5.—“Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I shall arise, says the Lord.”

[Col. 0156B] “Because of the misery.” The second part, in which, against the evils of the age, Christ is said to be sent by the Father; his utterances are true, just as those of the ungodly are false. As though he said: [Jerome, Cassiodorus.] The wicked say and do these things already mentioned, but against them the Lord the Father says this: “I shall arise,” that is, I shall appear in the Son—now, in this time of grace, which he did not do among the earlier people. And this is in order to remove the misery and groaning of the needy—that is, of the Gentiles—and of the poor—that is, of the Jews. [Remigius.] The Gentiles are rightly called needy, since they had neither Law nor prophets; the Jews, poor, since they did not understand the Law spiritually. The sense is: [Augustine.] Because of the lack and poverty of spiritual goods suffered by Jews and Gentiles, I shall send the Son. Or by “the needy and poor” [Col. 0156C] he signifies the same persons. The sense is: I shall send the Son to remove the misery of the needy, [Interlinear Gloss.] that is, mortality and susceptibility to suffering. And I shall do this because of the groaning of the poor, who groan over evils and are contrite for sins; otherwise they would not be worthy of help. What he will do when he arises he adds, saying:

**VERSE 6.**—“I shall set [him] in salvation; I shall act confidently in him.”

“I shall set [him] in salvation,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] that is, in Jesus, not in servants. He does not say what he will set there, but it should be understood as belonging to the consolation of the poor. As though he said: I shall place in Jesus the consolation of the poor. [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss.] “And I shall act confidently,” that is, powerfully, [Col. 0156D] in him, because nothing will resist him. Indeed, he will teach, not as the scribes and Pharisees, but as one having authority (Matt. 7), adding to the Law and changing certain things by his own will, as the author of the Law. Therefore he says, “I shall act confidently in him,” which I do not do in servants.

**VERSE 7.**—“The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings: silver tested by fire, proved from the earth, purified sevenfold.”

“The sayings of the Lord.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Up to this point these were the Father’s words concerning the Son. But the Prophet now speaks in his own person, commending the words of Christ’s preaching and showing their sincerity and usefulness. As though he said: The Father will send the Son. [Augustine.] And the sayings of the Lord, namely of the Son, are pure sayings, [Col. 0157A] that is, free from the corruption of pretense. For many preach truth, but not purely, because they sell it for the price of the desires of this age. [Cassiodorus.] He says this in opposition to what was said above of the wicked: “They spoke vanity.” The silver of the Lord’s utterance is tested by fire, [Cassiodorus.] because the Lord’s sayings are proved through the fire of tribulations, contrary to what was said above: “Deceitful lips spoke in heart and heart.”

Divine speech is compared to silver because, just as among all metals nothing rings more sweetly than silver, so among all utterances the divine word sounds most sweetly in the mind. [Interlinear Gloss.] And that silver is “proved from the earth,” that is, having nothing earthly from the earth; the genitive is here used for the ablative, in the Greek manner. And it is purified [Col. 0157B] sevenfold, that is, perfectly. [Alcuin.] For the number seven signifies perfection and universality. [Augustine.] Or it is purified sevenfold: the Word shines and gleams through the sevenfold Spirit—namely through the fear of God, piety, and the other gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are seven. Through them the divine utterance shines, while the preachers of God’s Word are radiant with these charisms. [Augustine.] Thus it is shown that what they preach is holy.

Or it may be understood specially of the Lord’s discourse delivered on the mountain to the disciples. As though he said: That silver of the divine utterance is sevenfold, because there are seven degrees of blessedness, concerning which the whole Sermon on the Mount was set forth—namely poverty of spirit, meekness, mercy, and so forth. And that silver is purified [Col. 0157C] sevenfold, that is, in a sevenfold manner: each of the seven is purified through the fire of persecution, which is treated in the eighth beatitude, when it is said: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5), etc. The eighth beatitude, then, is endurance of persecution, by which the silver is as though purified by fire sevenfold—that is, according to those seven things which precede in the discourse. For by this fire the poor, the meek, the merciful, and the others are purified. Therefore the seven virtues, also called beatitudes, which perfect and make blessed, are first set forth in the discourse. But the eighth, which returns to the beginning, tests, clarifies, and reveals whatever is perfect.

[Col. 0157D] **VERSE 8.**—“You, O Lord, will preserve us, and guard us from this generation forever.”

“You, O Lord.” [Cassiodorus.] Here he shows the usefulness of the divine sayings, turning to the Lord. As though he said: Such are the Lord’s sayings. And, O Lord, whose sayings are pure, you—not we ourselves—will preserve us through those sayings here and in the future. Above he said of the wicked, “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips”; here, speaking of the good, he says that he may preserve them. It follows: “And you will guard us.” [Augustine.] Here as needy and poor; in the future as wealthy and rich. You will guard us, I say, leading us away from this generation, namely that of this age, forever—that is, to eternal blessedness. [Cassiodorus, Remigius.]

**VERSE 9.**—“The ungodly walk in a circle; according to [Col. 0158A] your height you have multiplied the children of men.”

“In a circle.” As though he said: You will preserve us; but the ungodly walk in a circle, [Augustine.] that is, in the desire for temporal things, which revolve in the recurrence of seven days. Therefore they do not attain the eighth—that is, eternity, which will be given in the eighth; hence this psalm is so entitled. Solomon speaks of this circle in Proverbs: “A wise king is a winnowing fan for the ungodly, and brings upon them the wheel of evils” (Prov. 20), [Augustine.] that is, the circuit of changeable things which turn like a wheel.

It follows: “According to your height.” The ungodly are in a circle, but you have multiplied the children of men, not indeed in temporal things, but according to your height—that is, in virtues, through which you make them ascend to contemplate [Col. 0158B] you on high. He adds this because there is also a multiplication in temporal things which turns people away from the unity of God. But the righteous are multiplied according to God’s height when they go from strength to strength. Or thus: [Cassiodorus.] You have multiplied the children of men like the stars of heaven, according to the promise made to Abraham; and this, not according to their merits, but according to your height—that is, as befits you on high.

## COLLATION ON PSALM XI: “SAVE ME.”

**VERSE 6.**—“I shall act confidently in him.” The Hebrew has *IAPHIAII LO*. Pratensis: “He will speak for him.” Münster added something of his own, or wished it to be understood, and rendered: “from him who blows upon him,” or “who sets a snare for him.” The Interpreter for Cajetan translates more simply: “he will blow upon him.” Sanctes ventures further: “from him who [Col. 0158C] mockingly blows upon him.” Pellicanus otherwise: “there will be blasts.”

What are we to do here amid so many uncertain windings of roads? Let us hold fast what is certain and leave what is uncertain. It is certainly the case that *POHACH* means “to blow” or “to speak”; but the Septuagint, by a not unsuitable metaphor, took “to blow” or “to breathe upon someone or something” to mean to put into him—that is, to suggest and say, as it were, into his ear what ought to be done. Jerome’s version sufficiently indicates this, namely “their help,” as though he had read in the Hebrew *MO* in place of [uncertain reading]. And the Septuagint has *APHIACH LO*, that is, “I shall breathe upon him,” if one renders word for word. We have argued, on grounds not frivolous, that such things occur not infrequently—if only they find a fair-minded reader.

**VERSE 7.**—“Silver tested by fire, proved from the earth.” The translator follows a Greek manner of expression, now received in many instances into ecclesiastical usage, such as: “In turning back the Lord the captivity [Col. 0158D] of Zion” (Ps. 125); “In turning back my enemy” (Ps. 9); “I go fishing” (John 21); and many expressions of that kind. Yet Faber and his blind follower despise this reading excessively. Latin idiom more readily accepts Jerome’s rendering: “separated from the earth.”

It is astonishing how the modern Hebraists differ among themselves. Münster says, “in a carefully selected place of earth”; Sanctes, “from the Lord of the earth.” Likewise Pratensis and the interpreters for Cajetan: “from the roof of the earth”; Pellicanus: “by an earthly alchemical process”; the Campensian Paraphrase: “by art and instruments suited to the purpose, whatever impurity of earth it contained has been removed.” Others say: “in the goldsmith’s little furnace formed of select earth”; the Chaldean and Nebiensis: “silver purified again in a melting-pot from earth.” In Hebrew there are only two words, *BAELIL LAARETZ*, which will produce as many dreams as people please, if we fall asleep with respect to the ecclesiastical reading.

[Col. 0159A] **VERSE 9.**—“According to your height you have multiplied the children of men.” Hebrew: *CERUM ZULLOTH LIBNE ADAM*. Jerome, according to the Hebrew, rendered it thus: “when the vilest of the children of men have been exalted”; Pratensis: “when reproaches are exalted for the children of Adam”; Münster: “when they are exalted in disgrace, they are children of men”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “as though raising up vilenesses for the children of Adam”; Sanctes: “when they have been exalted, vileness belongs to the children of men”; Pellicanus: “when they have been exalted, revelries belong to the children of men”; the Campensian paraphrase: “when those who are most depraved among men have gained supremacy”; the edition corresponding to it: “when vanity is exalted among the children of men”; Nebiensis: “when they have been exalted, the children of men will be despised”; the Chaldean paraphrast: “like a leech that sucks the blood of the children of men.”

But let us weigh the ecclesiastical reading. First, insofar as it concerns exaltation: whether you render it by a verb, a participle, or a noun, you still retain the same sense. [Col. 0160A] But a difficulty remains about the following word, *ZULLOTH*. If you derive it from the root *ZALAL*, it means revelries or vilenesses; and the point called *dagesh* in the middle of the letter *lamed* indicates, in its customary manner, that another *lamed* is missing. But if you derive *ZULLOTH* from the root *NAZAL*, that is, “it flowed down,” then *zuloth* means streams or outflowings. Thus “the streams of the children of men” are aptly understood as generations of men, multiplied like the stars of heaven and flowing like waters, according to Ecclesiastes 1: “A generation passes away, and a generation comes”; and 2 Kings 14: “We all die and flow away like water upon the earth which does not return.” Moreover, if you translated word for word, you could render it: “according to your height, the streams of the children of men.” And the Septuagint, that the sense might be clearer, expressed it more plainly by a verb: “You have multiplied the children of men.” Nor is this unsuitable.

# PSALM XII

[Col. 0159]

## PSALM XII. TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0159B]

“How long, O Lord?” The title: “Unto the end, a psalm of David.” This title is clear. [Cassiodorus.] This psalm concerns the love of Christ, in which is the perfection of the whole Law; whoever possesses it does not love the world. [Alcuin.] For here the Prophet, full of love and eagerly awaiting Christ’s Incarnation, through which he understands the future redemption, speaks in the person of the ancient Fathers as though complaining of delay. In this is also shown love of neighbor, for whose salvation this is desired: that, superstition having been cast away, the worship of the one God may be received.

Or he speaks in the person of modern saints, desiring Christ’s second coming, when they are certain of salvation. For as intensely as the ancients desired the first advent, so intensely do the moderns [Col. 0159C] desire the second, according to the words: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1).

**Intention.** He invites to the same desire.

**Method.** The psalm has two parts. The first is a complaint concerning the delay of the first coming, according to the ancients, and of the second, according to the moderns. [Cassiodorus.] Secondly, he prays to be enlightened, lest he yield to the enemy’s deceits: “Look upon [me],” etc. Therefore the Prophet first says, in the person of the ancients complaining of the delay of the Incarnation:

**VERSE 1.**—“How long, O Lord, will you forget me unto the end? How long will you turn your face away from me?”

**VERSE 2.**—“How long shall I lay up counsels in my soul, sorrow in my heart day by day?”

“O Lord, will you forget me,” that is, will you withhold from me the presence of the Incarnation [Col. 0159D] unto the end, [Cassiodorus.] that is, unto the time of fullness? Hence the Apostle: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son,” etc. (Gal. 4). How long will this be awaited? Then he repeats it in other words: “How long will you turn your face away from me?” [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss.] namely, the presence of your Son, who is your face, to be seen by human beings. And how long will this be?

“And how long shall I lay up counsels,” [Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus.] namely, varied counsels, as one anxious in my soul? [Col. 0160B] Here is shown the great ardor of one enduring delay, who says that counsel is lacking to him whereby—that is, how—he may lessen his longing to see [him]. When anxiety is great, to desire a good thing and endure it for a longer time makes desire grow into sorrow, because hope is deferred. Hence he adds: “And how long shall I lay up sorrow in my heart?” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] And this “day by day” absolutely, that is, each day. And:

**VERSE 3.**—“How long shall my enemy be exalted over me? Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God.”

“How long shall my enemy be exalted over me?” [Cassiodorus.] That is, the devil over me. He says this because before Christ’s coming the devil held human beings captive. Or, “over me,” that is, over my faith: [Col. 0160C] he is worshiped throughout the world, while my faith is found among few. And because the world thus perishes, this saint weeps. “Look upon [me] and hear [me].” The second part. After his complaint, he prays that he may be enlightened, lest he who trusts in mercy yield to the enemy’s deceits. As though he said: Now there is sorrow, since your face is turned away and the enemy was exalted; but, O Lord, whose servant I am, who are my God, whose creature I am, look upon me—that is, send him whom you are going to send—and hear me. This man speaks for all those for whom he petitions generally.

**VERSE 4.**—“Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death; lest at any time my enemy say: ‘I have prevailed against him.’”

“Enlighten my eyes.” [Jerome, Augustine.] The inner eyes, [Col. 0160D] so that, if we do not see with the body, we may at least see with the mind.

Otherwise, the whole passage is read in the person of modern saints desiring Christ’s second coming, that they may live blessedly with him, and complaining of the delay. Thus: “O Lord, how long will you forget me unto the end?” should be understood as: How long do you defer my understanding Christ spiritually, who is the Father’s wisdom and the true end of every intention? [Augustine.] He repeats: “How long will you turn your face away from me?” That is, how long will you not grant my soul knowledge [Col. 0161A] of you? Scripture speaks in our customary manner when it says that God forgets or turns away his face. This is said not according to the proper nature of things, but by likeness to creatures: for forgetfulness does not occur in God, nor does any change.

“And how long shall I lay up counsels in my soul?” Counsel is needed only amid adversities. The sense is: How long shall I lay up counsels, etc.—that is, how long shall I be amid adversities? This he explains by adding: “How long shall I lay up sorrow in my heart day by day?” He uses “day” for this present time, from which he desires to be released in sorrow and prayer, longing for eternal things. Or “day by day” means continually.

Or the phrase “How long shall I lay up [counsels]” is not said as a question, but is an answer to the preceding question. As though he said: You will forget and turn your face away for as long as I shall lay up counsels—that is, for as long as it will be [Col. 0161B] necessary for me to take counsel in my soul. For unless each person takes such counsel in his soul, namely to practice mercy, God will not direct him unto the end, nor give him full knowledge of himself, so that he may see him face to face. Then follows, “How long shall I lay up sorrow in my heart,” etc.; this does not change.

It follows: “And how long shall my enemy be exalted over me?” namely, the devil, or carnal habit. But that this may be removed: “Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God,” etc. He says “Look upon me” in opposition to what was said above, “You turn your face away from me”; and “hear me” in opposition to “You forget me.” Enlighten the eyes of my heart, lest I ever sleep through the desire arising from myself, in death—that is, lest those very eyes be closed by the pleasure of sin. [Cassiodorus.] For the eyes [Col. 0161C] sleep in death when the light of faith is buried and they are closed by carnal pleasure. Or, “lest I ever sleep in death,” that is, lest I be enveloped in any mortal sin. [Remigius, Interlinear Gloss.] Or, “in death,” that is, in sin against the Holy Spirit, of which John says: “There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John 5). I say: lest I sleep, not through myself, nor even through another. And this is: “lest at any time my enemy say,” [Cassiodorus.] namely, the devil, who triumphs when he captures. What will he say? “I have prevailed against him.” [Augustine.] Behold the devil’s taunt, which is greatly to be feared. Therefore I say, lest the enemy say this, because:

**VERSE 5.**—“Those who trouble me will exult if I am [Col. 0162A] moved; but I have hoped in your mercy.”

“Those who trouble me,” [Augustine.] namely, the devil and his angels, will exult if I am moved from the stability of faith. As though he said: [Alcuin.] You ought to enlighten me not only for my sake, but also lest the enemy rejoice. It follows: “But I”—as though he said: They trouble me, but I have hoped in your mercy, [Augustine.] not presumed upon myself; for even that very fact, that one is not moved, he attributes not to himself but to God. Or, “in your mercy,” namely in the coming of the Son. For although this holy man hastens, he is nevertheless patient: [Cassiodorus.] even if what he desires is delayed, he remains firm in hope; and, inwardly already seeing him whom he desires to see in the flesh, he rejoices. Hence he adds:

[Col. 0162B] 27 **VERSE 6.**—“My heart will exult in your salvation; I shall sing to the Lord, who has granted me good things, and I shall make melody to the name of the Most High Lord.”

“My heart will exult,” or “has exulted.” [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss.] As though he said: I have hoped in mercy; therefore my heart will exult in your salvation, that is, in Jesus, whom I behold in my mind as one who is to come. [Alcuin.] Therefore this man, who earlier complained, says that good things have been given to him, adding: The Lord has granted me spiritual good things, not belonging to a human day. And to the Lord who has granted me good things I shall sing with my heart, [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] namely with the heart’s joy, which belongs to the contemplative life. Note that he says “has granted,” not “will grant”; this indicates the great power of faith. He already possesses [Col. 0162C] what is future.

It follows: “And I shall make melody in deed,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] which belongs to the active life. I shall make melody, I say, to the name of the Most High Lord. The sense is: I shall sing and make melody to the name of the Most High Lord—that is, I shall give thanks joyfully in heart and deed. If, then, this faithful man so greatly desires and so serves Christ who is still to come, what must be done now that he has been received? [Cassiodorus.] Certainly, he must be served in every way.

## COLLATION ON PSALM XII: “HOW LONG?”

“I shall make melody to the name of the Most High Lord.” We do not read this in Hebrew. If it has been added in Greek from the combination of certain other psalms, it causes no inconvenience.

# PSALM XIII

[Col. 0161]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0161D]

“The fool has said.” The title: “Unto the end, a psalm of David.” [Cassiodorus.] The face whose coming the Prophet desired in the preceding psalm is here shown to have come, and to be destined for contempt by the Jews. Therefore the Prophet, speaking in his own person or Christ’s, rebukes here the folly and hardness of the Jews, who do not believe in Christ present, whom they had desired. This is the first psalm concerning the rebuke and conversion of the Jews. And the sense of the title is: This psalm, directing us to the end, is of David—that is, of Christ or of the Prophet. [Col. 0162D]

**Intention.** The Prophet’s intention is to refute the Jews, despisers of Christ.

**Method.** The psalm has three parts. The first is a rebuke of the Jews, describing their wickedness. Secondly, he threatens judgment: “Will not all those who work iniquity know?” Thirdly, their conversion is foretold: “Who will give salvation out of Zion?” Therefore, imprecating against the hardness of the Jews, he says:

**VERSE 1.**—“The fool has said in his heart: ‘There is no God.’”

“The fool has said.” [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: The earlier Fathers awaited Christ who was to come; but when he [Col. 0163A] appeared, the fool—that is, the Jew—said in his heart, not merely with his mouth: This man is not God. They said this because:

**VERSE 2.**—“They have become corrupt and abominable in their pursuits; there is none who does good, not even one.”

“They have become corrupt.” [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss.] Deprived of every power of reason, they have become abominable—that is, reprobate. [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss.] And this is “in their pursuits,” that is, because they love the world rather than God, and withdraw from Christ: among them there is none who does good.

Or this may be understood of Gentiles, who think there is no God. [Augustine.] The fool—that is, the Gentile—has said, “There is no God.” And he has said this in his heart, not with his mouth, because no one dares to say—though he may think—“There is no God.” They say this because [Col. 0163B] they have become corrupt—that is, blind—so as to say, “There is no God”; and they have become abominable—that is, reprobate. For just as they judged it unworthy to have God in their knowledge, so God gave them over to a reprobate mind. And this is in their pursuits or affections, because they love the world and not God. Thus there is none, whether among Jews or Gentiles who do not believe, who does good. “Not even one,” I say—that is, not even a single one. Or, “not even one” means “except one,” namely Christ, without whom no one does good, because no one can do good unless he himself has shown it.

**VERSE 3.**—“The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God.”

[Col. 0163C] “The Lord from heaven.” [Augustine, Alcuin.] From this place he speaks particularly of the Jews. As though he said: None of them does good; but this is why they are without excuse: the Lord, namely Christ, looked down from heaven, [Remigius, Alcuin.] that is, from the human nature which he assumed, excelling through the power of divinity and acting divinely. He looked, I say, upon the children of men. [Augustine, Alcuin.] Or “from heaven” means through holy souls he looked down; for nothing is hidden from him in himself. Heaven is called God’s seat, and the soul of the righteous is God’s seat. Therefore by “heaven” he here signifies holy souls through whom he looked upon the children of men. He does not say “upon men,” but “upon the children of men,” [Augustine.] that is, the Jews, whom he names more honorably because of their worship of one God.

[Cassiodorus.] Or, the Lord—the Father—looked down from heaven by sending the Son upon the children of men, that is, he had mercy on the Jews, to whom he sent the Son bodily. [Remigius, Cassiodorus.] He looked down for this purpose: “to see,” that is, to make it evident whether anyone understands in his heart that God is in man, or seeks God [Col. 0163D] by following his commandments. [Jerome.] But he found this:

**VERSE 4.**—“All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one.”

**VERSE 5.**—“Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully; the poison of asps is under their lips.”

“All have turned aside.” Or join it thus: He saw whether anyone [Col. 0164A] understands or seeks; [Augustine.] and this indicates that a person does not understand because he does not seek but turns aside. And truly so: all have turned aside. [Interlinear Gloss, Jerome.] The Jews have become such as the Gentiles, of whom he said above: “The fool has said, ‘There is no God,’” etc. [Jerome, Augustine.] And together with that turning aside they have become unjust—that is, harmful to themselves and others; they have turned away from God. Hence there is none who does good, not even one, [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] that is, except the one, because none does good without the one, namely Christ.

“An open tomb,” etc. These three verses, extending to the second division, are said not to be from the Hebrew; nevertheless, the Apostle adduces them in the Epistle to the Romans [Col. 0164B] against the Jews. They are said to have been put together from many psalms and added even by the seventy translators. Hence this psalm, when repeated later, does not contain them. They show how those who have turned aside are useless to others and themselves, and first how they are useless to others. [Cassiodorus, Remigius.] As though he said: They have become useless to others because their throat is an open tomb—that is, they are like an open tomb. [Augustine.] These words signify either the greed of a gaping appetite, or that they kill others with the foul things they utter and, as it were, devour those to whom they commend the perversity of their character. [Cassiodorus.] For just as an open tomb exhales foul odors, so does their throat exhale pestilential words. [Col. 0164C] “With their tongues they acted deceitfully,” flattering others. [Augustine.] For flattery accompanies the greedy and all evildoers. [Interlinear Gloss.] Or, they acted deceitfully, commending evils under the appearance of good. “And the poison of asps,” that is, the deceit of asps, is beneath their lips—that is, in their heart—which is worse than being in the mouth. [Remigius.] The asp stops its ears so as not to hear the enchanter’s voice. [Augustine, Jerome, Interlinear Gloss.] They are therefore rightly compared to an asp, because they refuse to hear the commandment of the Law, but return evils to those who preach it. Hence follows:

**VERSE 6.**—“Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood.”

“Their mouth is full of cursing,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] that is, reproaches and blasphemies; this is the poison [Col. 0164D] of asps. And it is full of bitterness, that is, threats. Their feet—that is, their will and affections—are swift because they do everything rashly; [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss.] or “swift,” that is, ready through the habit of doing evil, to shed the blood of Christ and his people.

**VERSE 7.**—“Destruction and unhappiness are in their ways; and they have not known the way of peace; there is no fear of God before their eyes.”

“Destruction,” etc. [Jerome.] Here he shows how they were useless to themselves. As though he said: Because they are such, therefore destruction and unhappiness are in their ways—that is, in their works. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] For all the ways of the wicked are full of pains and misery. The way of the ungodly is rightly [Col. 0165A] called destruction, and unhappy destruction, because it both crushes and is crushed, while it harms others and itself. Or because punishment exists here and will be inflicted in the future. There is unhappiness because it leads to hell, and the wicked do not return from these ways. Therefore: “They have not known the way of peace,” [Augustine.] that is, Christ; or the way of peace, namely the Gospel, of which the Lord said: “My yoke is easy,” etc. (Matt. 11).

Or it may be said specially of the Jews. As though he said: They were useless to themselves because destruction and unhappiness are in their ways: [Alcuin.] they were destroyed for their deeds through Titus and Vespasian, and are unhappy because they are scattered everywhere. Or destruction is now in their ways, and unhappiness in the future. [Remigius.] For now the cornerstone, namely Christ, falling upon [Col. 0165B] them, will crush them by blindness; but unhappiness will be in hell, when they are condemned in soul and body. And all this is because they have not known the way of peace; this remains unchanged. And all these things are because they do not fear God. This is: “There is no fear of God before their eyes.” [Augustine.] These do not say, like the Gentiles above, “There is no God”; yet they do not fear him.

## PART II. VERSE 8.—“Will not all who work iniquity know, those who devour my people as bread for food?”

“Will they not know,” etc. [Augustine.] The second part. He threatens judgment upon the ungodly. As though he said: They commit the evils foretold and do not fear that they will be punished for them in the future. [Cassiodorus.] [Col. 0165C] But will not those who work iniquity know that the Lord is in the righteous generation? As though he said: They will then know what they now refuse to know, namely that the Lord is in the righteous generation, not in the generation that loves the world and killed me, Christ says. He inserts what iniquity they commit: [Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus.] “Those who devour my people,” by deceiving or killing them, “as bread for food”—that is, so that the deception of Christians may be a satisfaction to them. [Augustine.] Or, they devour the people as those do who use their ministry to obtain advantages from people, rather than for the salvation of people or the glory of God. They do this “as bread for food”: just as bread is daily food, so by daily plunder they swallow up simple Christians. [Col. 0165D] Why do they do this?

**VERSE 9.**—“They have not called upon the Lord; there they trembled with fear where there was no fear.”

“They have not called upon the Lord.” [Augustine.] For those who love things displeasing to God do not truly call upon God. Therefore their destruction is increased, [Cassiodorus.] because they do not call on the Lord; for it is necessary that the proud should do evil when they refuse to call upon God. And because they did not call upon God, “there they trembled with fear where there was no fear,” [Augustine.] that is, they trembled at the loss of temporal things. The Jews feared to lose their earthly kingdom, where there was no need for fear; and they did not fear to lose heaven, where they ought to have feared. [Cassiodorus.] Note that, just as it is prudence to fear at the right time, so it is cowardice to tremble inappropriately, as the Jews did for [Col. 0166A] nation and place after casting away the fear of God. For they said: “If we leave him thus, all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11). It follows:

**VERSE 10.**—“For the Lord is in the righteous generation; you have confounded the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his hope.”

“The counsel of the poor.” [Cassiodorus.] Having set out the sentence of common condemnation against the Jews, he now attacks them particularly, saying: “You have confounded the counsel of the poor.” As though he said: The Lord is in the righteous generation; but you miserable Jews have confounded the counsel of the poor, [Augustine.] that is, you despised Christ’s humble coming, undertaken so that those whom he called might place their hope in God alone and not in the passing world. [Col. 0166B] Therefore the coming itself is called “counsel.” [Cassiodorus.] Behold the charge against the Jews, to whom it is obscurely said: “You have confounded the counsel of the poor,” that is, of Christ; you refused to receive him, although he came to deliver you. It is to be read as an exclamation.

Or it means the counsel of any poor person who is a member of Christ. You did this because the Lord is his hope. [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss.] That for which he ought especially to have been revered is the very reason he is more despised.

## PART III. VERSE 11.—“Who will give salvation to Israel out of Zion? When the Lord has turned away the captivity of his people, Jacob will exult and Israel will rejoice.”

“Who will give?” [Cassiodorus.] The third part. Finally, the conversion of the Jews is foretold, which will occur when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in. [Remigius, Augustine.] As though he said: [Col. 0166C] You have confounded Christ’s counsel; but who else, coming forth from Zion—that is, from the Jews—will give salvation to Israel, that is, save believers, unless, understand, he whom you despised in humility? For he himself will come in glory for judgment. As though he said: No other will save; but he will save in the future, because when the Lord Christ has turned away the captivity of his people, [Cassiodorus.] that is, when he has condemned the devil who held God’s people captive, Jacob will exult and Israel will rejoice. [Augustine.] This is a repetition, as frequently occurs: “Jacob will exult” is, I think, the same as “Israel will rejoice.” Note that the Apostle also adduces this testimony from Isaiah concerning the Jews: “There will come out of Zion one who will turn away captivity,” or “ungodliness,” [Col. 0166D] from Jacob (Rom. 11), just as it is here set forth concerning the Jews.

## COLLATION ON PSALM XIII: “THE FOOL HAS SAID IN HIS HEART.”

Verses 5, 6, 7, whose openings are “Their throat is,” etc.; “Destruction,” etc.; “Their mouth,” etc., are not found in the Hebrew or in the Greek at this point, but have been taken from other places in Scripture. Jerome plainly indicates this in the preface to his commentary on Isaiah the prophet, chapter 16, replying to the virgin Eustochium, who had objected to him the Apostle’s passage in Romans 3, where he expressly cites these verses. It will not be burdensome to hear Jerome’s words.

“Surveying the whole of Scripture in my mind, I observed that, just as almost the entire Epistle to the Romans is constructed from the Old Testament, so this testimony too is woven together from the Psalms and Isaiah. For the first two verses—‘Their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they dealt deceitfully’—are from the fifth psalm [Col. 0167A]. What follows—‘The venom of asps is beneath their lips’—is from the one hundred and thirty-ninth psalm. Again, the words ‘Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness’ are taken from the ninth psalm. But the three following verses—‘Their feet are swift to shed blood; destruction and misery are in their ways; and they have not known the way of peace’—are found in the prophet Isaiah. The final verse—‘There is no fear of God before their eyes’—is at the beginning of the thirty-fifth psalm. I think your question has been resolved, and that our rule concerning the translation of the Old Testament has been shaken rather than moved; and that the Apostle did not so much take from Psalm 13 what is not found in the Hebrew as those who did not know the Apostle’s art of weaving Scriptures together sought an appropriate place in which to put the testimony he had employed, since they did not think it had been placed in Scripture without authority. Finally, all the commentators who have left us learned commentaries on the Psalms note these verses and pass over them, openly confessing [Col. 0168A] that they are not found in the Hebrew, nor among the Seventy Translators, but in the Vulgate edition, which in Greek is called the *koinē* [common edition], and is different throughout the whole world.”

These are Jerome’s words, and he holds the same opinion in Isaiah, chapter 59. Yet there is no danger if we chant these verses here, although they are not from this passage; Jerome himself did not reluctantly expound them in his commentary on this psalm, indicating that they were taken from other places.
