VERSE 9.—“There they trembled with fear where there was no fear.” In the Hebrew one reads only, “There they trembled with fear,” and the latter part appears to be taken from Psalm 52. What if the Hebrew has to be understood as containing what the translators expressed? For the Chaldee has, “whom it was not fitting to fear.” As for the different punctuation, this has already been noted once and again. Even if it sometimes produces a different sense, it is helpful so long as the sense remains sound; but let it never be employed for the sake of faults. For the Spirit of wisdom is manifold, unique, holy, subtle, and mobile (Wisdom 7).

## PSALM XIV

[Col. 0167]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0167B]

“Lord, who shall dwell?” Title: “A Psalm of David.” “Father” is the title. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] This psalm is properly a moral instruction and a restraint upon presumption, treating of the unity of the present Church and of the peace to come. For in the present Church, because the bodily coexistence of evil persons with good does not permit us to know who truly belongs to the unity of the Church, certain people, though unworthy, boast that they belong to the Church when in truth they do not. Therefore the Prophet, crushing their presumption, asks, like a priest standing before the propitiatory, who are worthy to serve God in the present Church and to rest in future blessedness.

God gives him a fully definitive answer [Col. 0167C], clearly showing who truly belong to the present Church and are to be made blessed in the future. The Prophet’s intention is to restrain those who boast that they belong to the Church when they do not. The arrangement is in two parts. First, the Prophet asks—[Cassiodorus] as though a priest standing before the face of the Lord and seeking an answer, wishing to know whom God judges worthy of his Church. Second, the Lord’s answer is added: “He who walks without blemish.” Thus the Prophet, like a priest seeking an answer, says:

### VERSE 1.—“Lord, who shall dwell in thy tabernacle? Or who shall rest upon thy holy mountain?”

[Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Lord, who shall dwell worthily, namely [Col. 0167D] in thy tabernacle—that is, in the present Church, where we fight against the devil? For although “tabernacle” is sometimes used for the everlasting dwelling-place, it is properly associated with warfare and soldiers. Hence soldiers sharing quarters are called *contubernales*, as though having tents together. This interpretation is supported by what another translation contains: “Who shall sojourn in thy tabernacle? Or who shall rest upon thy holy mountain?” [Augustine, Cassiodorus] That is, in eternal blessedness, where there is the vision of peace and the surpassing height [Col. 0168B] of charity; where no one struggles in combat, but rests in everlasting peace.

### PART II. VERSE 2.—“He who walks without blemish and works righteousness.”

“He who walks.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] The second part, in which the Lord’s answer is given. He says, following the pattern of the Decalogue, that one reaches his courts by ten virtues. Note that he here calls “ten virtues” ten effects of virtues, all of which are referred to the four principal virtues: justice, temperance, prudence, and fortitude. Some of these ten are specially referred to one of these four virtues; others belong commonly to several. Likewise, some are appropriate only to the perfect, while others suit the imperfect, as will be shown in the exposition [Col. 0168C] of the psalm. Therefore the Lord, answering from the sanctuary of his court, says: “He who walks without blemish”—as though to say: He shall dwell and rest who enters the tabernacle without blemish, that is, innocently. [Remigius, Gloss, interlinear.] Behold the first virtue, that is, the first effect of virtue, in which temperance is indicated. [Jerome, Remigius.] The second virtue follows: “and works righteousness,” because it is not enough to abstain from evil; and this is referred to justice. He then explains these more fully—that is, these two virtues—adding their other effects.

### VERSE 3.—“He who speaks truth in his heart; who has not practised deceit with his tongue.”

“He who speaks truth.” [Interlinear Gloss.] Behold the third effect of virtue: truth conceived in his heart [Col. 0168D]. [Augustine.] That is, one who knows and speaks the truth; prudence, and also justice, are indicated in this. He fittingly adds “in his heart,” since someone may at times think that he is deceiving, yet speak the truth. Such a person has truth on his lips but not in his heart. [Interlinear Gloss.] For example, someone may deceitfully point out a road to another, supposing that robbers are on it, and say: “If you take this road, you will be safe from robbers”; and it may happen that there really are no robbers there. He has spoken truth, but not in his heart. The fourth virtue follows: “who has not practised deceit with his tongue.” [Augustine.] This is a part of innocence [Col. 0169A], that is, of temperance. Deceit is on the tongue when one thing is said and another is in the breast. The fifth virtue follows.

### VERSE 4.—“Nor has done evil to his neighbour, and has not received reproach against his neighbours.”

“Nor has done evil to his neighbour.” [Interlinear Gloss.] This too is a part of innocence. [Augustine.] “Neighbour” is understood of every human being. The sixth follows: “and has not received reproach against his neighbours,” that is, he does not rashly or willingly believe an accuser. The seventh follows.

### VERSE 5.—“The wicked man is brought to nothing in his sight; but he glorifies those who fear the Lord.”

[Col. 0169B] “The wicked man is brought to nothing.” [Interlinear Gloss.] Behold fortitude. As though to say: He has not accepted reproach; rather, the wicked man—that is, the devil, or a person making evil suggestions—is brought to nothing, that is, he cannot be compelled to harm anyone. And this is “in his sight,” namely, that he knows why the wicked man is wicked. [Augustine.] This is great perfection: that the wicked man has no power in a person, and that this is in his sight—that is, that he knows with certainty that no one is wicked [Interlinear Gloss] unless he turns from the Creator to the creature. “But he glorifies those who fear the Lord.” [Augustine.] He set forth above seven virtues belonging to the perfect; now he presents three others suitable to beginners. As though to say: God will glorify not only the perfect, who possess the foregoing things, but also glorifies those who fear the Lord [Col. 0169C], that is, beginners, since fear is the beginning of wisdom (Ecclus. 1). Thus, as the preceding matters belong to the perfect, so those which he is about to mention belong to beginners. The eighth follows.

### VERSE 6.—“He who swears to his neighbour and does not deceive; who has not given his money at interest, nor accepted gifts against the innocent.”

“He who swears to his neighbour and does not deceive.” [Interlinear Gloss.] He who swears does not harm his neighbour but assists him. He swears firmly to his neighbour—that is, he promises—and does not deceive, because he fulfils what he promised. The ninth follows: “who has not given his money at interest” [Remigius, Interlinear Gloss], that is, does not seek temporal profit. The tenth follows: “nor accepted gifts against the innocent.” [Augustine.] That is, he does not oppress the cause of an innocent person for the sake [Col. 0169D] of someone’s gift. These three are not great things; but one who cannot do even these is much less able to speak truth in his heart, not practise deceit with his tongue, and not do evil to his neighbour. Yet he concludes these lesser matters as follows:

### VERSE 7.—“He who does these things shall not be moved for ever.”

“He who does these things shall not be moved for ever.” [Augustine.] That is, he will attain those greater things in which there is unshaken stability. Hence he speaks in the future tense, “shall not be moved,” whereas in the earlier conclusion he used the past tense, when he said, “The wicked man is brought to nothing in his sight.”

Alternatively: “He who walks,” etc., is read particularly of Christ, who observed all these things most fully. [Col. 0170A] As though you ask: Who shall dwell? Who shall rest? Certainly he who walks without blemish—that is, Christ, [Cassiodorus] who, properly speaking, entered the temple according to the Law as a lamb without broken limbs, not to be expiated, as the rest were, but without blemish, that is, free from sins; and who works righteousness, as when he drove sellers and buyers from the temple (Matt. 21); who speaks truth. Truth exists when a thing is as it is said to be. Christ did this in the strict sense. It adds, “in his heart,” because Christ sometimes kept silent before unworthy persons deceitfully seeking an answer. “And has not practised deceit with his tongue,” because he made known to his disciples, without any addition or withholding, everything he heard from the Father that was to be made known to them (John 15). “Nor has done evil to his neighbour,” that is, to the Jews, his neighbours according to the flesh [Col. 0170B]: he did them no evil, but prayed for them. “And has not received”—that is, did not regard as acceptable—“reproach against his neighbours.” This is clear from the fact that he did not tear Judas apart with biting rebuke. And: “The wicked man is brought to nothing in his sight” (Ps. 72), that is, the devil is despised by him, as when he said, “Get behind me, Satan” (Matt. 4). Conversely, Christ glorifies those who fear the Lord.

“He who swears to his neighbour and does not deceive.” Christ swore when he promised the apostles with most certain truth: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15). It follows: “Who has not given his money at earthly interest.” For money is twofold: either earthly, which is absolutely forbidden to be lent at interest, since the Lord entrusted it to Judas to distribute to the poor [Col. 0170C], not for interest, but for the instruction of people; or spiritual, which is commanded to be given at interest, that is, the preaching of God’s word, which yields the gain of souls’ salvation. “And has not accepted gifts against the innocent.” Christ did indeed accept gifts, such as those from the Magi and the daily devout offerings of believers in the Church, but not against the innocent; indeed, he gave his life for them.

It follows: “He who does these things.” Behold the complete answer to the questioner. This is the conclusion of the psalm. As though to say: As I have said concerning Christ, likewise whoever does these things for his neighbour shall not be moved for ever—that is, shall not be separated from God himself, but shall rest upon the mountain of eternal blessedness. Note that it says, “does these things,” in order to invite us to action, and not merely to the singing [Col. 0170D] of these words.

## COMPARISON ON PSALM XIV: “LORD, WHO SHALL DWELL?”

VERSE 5.—“The wicked man is brought to nothing in his sight.” [Jerome:] “The ungodly man is despised in his eyes.” Sanctes: “He who despises himself in his own eyes casts himself away.” Pratensis: “The abominable man is disregarded in his eyes.” Münster: “He who is despised and contemned in his own eyes.” So too nearly all the others in the same manner, except that some distinguish at the point, “in his sight” or “in his eyes,” whether “his” or “their own.” Others join the phrase “wicked” or “ungodly,” “abominable” or “contemned,” together, so that Münster, in order to remove ambiguity, wished to add a coordinating conjunction to indicate the distinction; yet this is not found in the Hebrew, nor is the relative pronoun “who,” except insofar as it may be understood from what precedes. Its addition disturbs [Col. 0171A] the order of the sense.

As for the first term, which they render “to be despised” or “disregarded,” while we say “is brought to nothing,” this arose from the equivocal nature of the Hebrew word *NIBZEH*. If it derives from the root *BAZAH*, it means “disregarded” or “despised.” But if from the stem *BAZAZ*, it is correctly rendered “is brought to nothing,” whose root signifies “to lay waste” and “to plunder,” even though it could not be a participle in such a form, for one would have to say *NABAZ*. Or it may be derived from the former root, as though one said: “The wicked man is of no account in his sight.”

VERSE 6.—“He who swears to his neighbour and does not deceive.” Hebrew: *NISEBA LEHARA VELO IAMIR*. Jerome: “He who swears in order to afflict, and will not change.” Münster: “He swears to inflict evil and does not change.” Pratensis: “He swore to afflict and will not change.” Sanctes: [Col. 0172A] “He who swore to afflict himself and did not change.” Nebiensis: “He swears in order to afflict himself and does not vary.” The translator for Cajetan: “He swore to do evil to himself.” He treats the final expression as a little gloss.

The ambiguous reading produces the variation: namely, *HARA*, or, with transposed letter, *RAAH*, or, if you prefer, *REEH*; it may also be read thus for “neighbour” or “companion,” *LEHAREA*. The second reading, however, plainly represents “neighbour,” as the Seventy understood it, and Pellican and the Campensian paraphrase agree with them. For the latter explains it thus: “He has firmly resolved to persevere in a friendship once entered into with someone, and will not change his purpose.” The alternative, “He who swears to his neighbour and will not change,” likewise conveys the same understanding as “does not deceive.” For one who violates an oath changes; and for that reason deceives the person to whom he swore. Hence the Chaldee translator says: “and shall not swear falsely.”

## PSALM XV

[Col. 0171]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “THE INSCRIPTION OF A TITLE, FOR DAVID HIMSELF.”

[Col. 0171B]

“Preserve me, O Lord.” [Title: “the inscription of a title, for David himself.”] This title is taken from the Gospel, not from the Old Testament. [Jerome, Cassiodorus.] For in the Gospel we read that, when the Lord had been crucified, Pilate placed above him this title: “JESUS OF NAZARETH, KING OF THE JEWS.” When many of the Jews wanted to remove it, saying: “Do not write, ‘Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews,’ but, ‘He said, I am King of the Jews,’” Pilate replied: “What I have written, I have written.”

[Cassiodorus.] There, though Pilate did not know it, God signified that Christ’s kingdom was not weakened but confirmed by the humility of the Passion. This psalm concerns that kingdom, whose confirmation was marked by the unaltered title. Therefore Ezra prefixed this psalm with the inscription of that title [Col. 0171C], which he foresaw by the Holy Spirit would come to pass, [Alcuin] showing that Christ’s kingdom, signified by that inscription, is discussed here.

The sense is: “The inscription of a title”—that is, the victory and kingdom marked by the title’s inscription—is attributed or belongs to David. [Cassiodorus.] Not to that actual son of Jesse, but to David himself in the true sense—that is, Christ, who speaks here according to his humanity. [Augustine.] The royal title stood out concerning him in his Passion, written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, in order to show that he is king of all who are truly Jews—that is, confessors. [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss.] Just as at Rome an inscription was written on a triumphal arch to display the triumphs of kings, so a title was inscribed for Christ as the sign of his victory. [Col. 0171D] [Jerome.] There are three kinds of titles that are written: one over the tombs of the dead; another on the thresholds of cities or houses; a third for a king’s victory. Here, then, he speaks of the title of our King.

[Cassiodorus.] This psalm is the second among those which briefly concern Christ’s Passion and Resurrection. Its purpose is to urge all people not to oppose Christ’s kingdom or title. Its arrangement is in two parts: first, Christ, showing the true nature of his humanity, asks to be preserved amid dangers, declaring that all he endured was brought to the glory of his inheritance. Second, he gives thanks to the Father for the understanding granted to him and for his Passion and Resurrection, beginning with “I will bless the Lord” [Col. 0172B], etc. Therefore Christ, praying to the Father according to his humanity, says: “O—”

### VERSE 1.—“Preserve me, O Lord, for I have hoped in thee. I said to the Lord: Thou art my God, for thou hast no need of my goods.”

[Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss.] Lord Father, preserve me amid dangers; and thou shouldst do so, because I have hoped in thee, not in myself. Behold the merit by which he ought to be preserved. I say that I have hoped, and rightly, because thou art my God, [Cassiodorus] that is, the God of my humanity; and I said this to thee, Lord, not with my lips, but with the affection of my heart. Or thus: “I have hoped in thee, and I said to thee, Lord, ‘Thou art my God,’” [Augustine] insofar as I am human; and thou art truly God, because thou hast no need of my goods—that is, thou dost not await being made blessed by my good things.

[Cassiodorus.] But if God has no need of Christ’s good things, and yet has everything from him, human arrogance and the heresy of the Pelagians are overthrown; for they think that some good can be accomplished by their own powers, whereas even Christ, in respect of his humanity, has no good from himself. It follows:

### VERSE 2.—“For the saints who are in his land, he has made all my desires wonderful in them.”

“For the saints who are.” Christ has explained how he prayed; now he begins to relate what good things the Lord has done for him. As though to say: I have said these things to the Lord, but God has made all my desires wonderful [Alcuin]—these are my good things. Christ calls his desires all his wishes: the wish to die and to rise again. [Cassiodorus.] These are wonderful because, through obedience to them, earthly people become heavenly, and children of the devil become children of God. These desires, I say, he made wonderful in the saints who are in his land—that is, in the land which is blessed, not in the land of curse; not those boasting in the compass of this world, but those who are in his land [Col. 0172D], [Augustine] that is, those who have fixed their hope in the land of the living, which is an anchor for them amid the waves of this world.

He made all my desires wonderful: that is, the wish to die and to rise again. [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine.] These desires are planted and fulfilled in them—that is, in their progress, in which both beginners and the perfect have perceived what his humility, by which he died, and his power, by which he rose again, have profited them. Or: “He made all my desires wonderful in them,” that is, among those who saw and understood these things. It follows:

### VERSE 3.—“Their infirmities were multiplied; afterwards they hastened.”

“Their infirmities were multiplied.” As though to say: He made my desires wonderful in the saints, whose carnal weakness had previously been multiplied through the severity of the Law, in order that they might desire the grace of the New Testament. And this is the meaning: He made them wonderful in the saints; but first their infirmities were multiplied [Augustine], because when the Law was given their weakness increased—not indeed for destruction, but so that they might hasten to the physician. Hence it adds: “Afterwards they hastened,” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] running to the physician.

Or he speaks of outward affliction, by which they were often chastised in order that they might be healed. The sense is: Their outward infirmities [Col. 0173B] were multiplied through salutary affliction, under God’s providence. [Remigius.] And, having been chastised, they afterwards hastened—but not in their former manner—because:

### VERSE 4.—“I will not gather their assemblies from blood offerings, nor will I remember their names with my lips.”

[Interlinear Gloss.] “I will not gather their assemblies,” established by blood offerings; that is, their assemblies shall not be carnal, nor shall I be propitiated by the blood of animals. “I will gather them”: as though to say, I shall not deal with them according to the legal rite. “Nor will I remember their names,” but through spiritual transformation they shall forget what they were; for they will no longer be called sinners, enemies, or human beings, but will be called righteous, brothers, and children of God.

Or: “I will not remember their names” as formerly in the Old Testament [Col. 0173C], [Alcuin] when he gave particular designations either to a people, as: “Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel”; or to an individual, as to Moses; or to a tribe, as: “Speak to the house of Judah, to the house of Benjamin.” But now there is no respect of persons: in every nation, the one who fears the Lord is acceptable to him.

“I will not remember their names with my lips,” my own lips, by which I shall say in the future to the wicked: “Depart, ye cursed, into everlasting fire” (Matt. 25)—which I shall not say to them. Or, “with my lips,” that is, through the apostles, through whom God speaks. [Cassiodorus.] Or he calls the two Testaments “lips,” which speak with one voice and through which his desires are revealed. [Cassiodorus.] But neither the apostles nor the Testaments threaten judgment to such persons. [Col. 0173D] It follows:

### VERSE 5.—“The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup; thou art he who wilt restore my inheritance to me.”

“The Lord is the portion.” As though to say: I will not remember their names, but instead they shall have with me an inheritance: God himself. [Augustine.] The phrase is read intransitively: “The Lord Father is the portion of my inheritance,” that is, he is the hereditary portion of me and mine. [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine.] Let others choose for themselves other things to enjoy; but God is the portion of me and of the saints. “And the Lord is the portion of my cup,” that is, he is my cup. [Augustine.] Let others therefore drink poisons and deadly pleasures; but I and mine shall drink God.

Then, turning his speech to God, he says: “Thou art”—as though to say [Col. 0174A]—thou, O Lord, art the inheritance, and thou art also its restorer. This is the meaning: Thou, O Father, art he who wilt restore to me my inheritance—that is, knowledge of my inheritance, namely of my glory. Thou wilt not restore to me in myself anything that I have lost, for I have lost nothing; but thou wilt restore to mine, among whom I am and with whom I am one, the knowledge of my glory, which they lost through sin. This glory was with thee before the world was made (John 17). Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Glorify, Father, thy Son with the glory which he had with thee before the world was made.”

[Jerome.] Or by “inheritance” he means the light of glory—that is, the glory of immortality—which we lost in Adam, which was restored to Christ in his Resurrection, and will be restored to us in ours. Hence he says elsewhere: “And my flesh flourished anew” (Ps. 27). It follows:

### VERSE 6.—“The measuring-lines fell to me in splendid places; indeed, my inheritance is splendid to me.”

“The measuring-lines.” [Augustine.] As though you say: Thou wilt restore an inheritance which is splendid. For the measuring-lines, that is, the boundaries of my possession, have fallen to me by lot into thy splendor, just as God is the possession of the priests and Levites. I rightly said “in splendid places,” for indeed my inheritance is splendid to me—not, certainly, to everyone, but to those who see, in whom I am. And therefore I say, “to me”:

### VERSE 7.—“I will bless the Lord who has given me understanding; moreover, even unto night my reins have reproved me.”

[Col. 0174C] “I will bless the Lord.” [Augustine.] As though to say: It is splendid to those who see; but I will bless the Lord who has given me understanding, by which this inheritance can be seen and possessed. Hence: “And this is eternal life, that they may know thee,” etc. (John 17). “Moreover, even unto—”: as though to say, he gave me understanding; but moreover—that is, beyond understanding—and even unto night, that is, unto death, my reins reproved, instructed, or corrected me. [Augustine, Alcuin.] That is, even unto death my lower part, namely the assumption of flesh, instructed me, so that I might experience the darkness of mortality; this darkness that understanding does not have, because through it he could neither be disturbed nor fail.

Or thus, from the words “The Lord is the portion,” he understands by the inheritance the converted nations—that is, all the faithful, who are Christ’s inheritance. [Alcuin.] As though he said: I will not gather those who shed blood, but those who choose God as their portion. And this is the meaning: The Lord is the portion—that is, the share and reward—of my inheritance [Cassiodorus], that is, of the saints, who are my inheritance. And he is the portion of my cup, that is, the reward of my Passion; for inheritance pertains to the nations and the cup to the Passion, and the cup, when drunk, gives resurrection.

And thou, O Lord Father, art he who wilt restore the inheritance to me, Christ; or my inheritance—that is, the human race, which thou gavest me as inheritance and kingdom, that I might cultivate it and reign in it, though it had perished through the devil’s work. [Jerome.] But let no one consider himself an inheritance unless he is splendid, because “the measuring-lines fell to me in splendid places,” that is, in the saints. [Col. 0175A] [Cassiodorus.] He says “measuring-lines” because the saints become Christ’s inheritance, as though by lot; this signifies divine election, by which they passed into Christ’s portion, just as the lot fell upon Matthias, who had been chosen from eternity. [Jerome.] Each receives according to his measure, that is, according as God’s grace measures out to each.

It follows: “Indeed”—as though to say: I rightly said, “in splendid places,” [Remigius] for indeed my inheritance is splendid to me. Although some regard the saints in the world as abject, yet to me they are splendid. “I will bless the Lord.” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] The second part, in which Christ gives thanks to the Father for understanding and for the Passion, in which he conquered through the Father’s favour, and for the Resurrection and confession. These are the means by which the inheritance is restored, so that he may be King of the Jews, as the title says. As though to say [Col. 0175B]: My inheritance has been restored to me. But I will bless the Lord who gave me understanding, [Cassiodorus] by which Christ saw all things true and holy.

Moreover, I shall bless him because my reins—that is, the Jews who are from Judah, from whom I am, and from whom I came according to the flesh, namely my kindred—reproached me with injuries and through temptations and sufferings. This is “even unto night,” that is, even unto death. But in these things always:

### VERSE 8.—“I kept the Lord always before my sight, because he is at my right hand, that I may not be moved.”

“I kept the Lord, who always is, before my sight,” [Augustine] that is, even when I came into things that pass away, I did not remove my gaze from him who always is; I kept watch in order that, when temporal things were accomplished, I might return to him. Observe that he says: “I kept the Lord always before my sight.” [Cassiodorus.] Draw from this an example for avoiding sins. For one who always beholds God with the mind’s gaze is not defiled by sins. I attend to God because he is at my right hand, that I may not be moved [Augustine, Cassiodorus], that is, he favours me so that I may remain stable in him, and therefore no adversity prevails against me. And because he is at my right hand:

### VERSE 9.—“Therefore my heart rejoiced and my tongue exulted; moreover, my flesh also shall rest in hope.”

“Therefore my heart rejoiced and my tongue exulted,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, there is exultation also in thoughts [Col. 0175D] and words. This is complete joy, received both in a cheerful heart and expressed in lively speech. Moreover, my flesh shall not fail in destruction but shall rest [Augustine], that is, shall sleep in hope of the Resurrection. [Cassiodorus.] Observe that here, speaking of joy and rest, he says “moreover,” just as above, speaking of sufferings, he said: “Moreover, even unto night my reins reproved me,” so that heavenly joys of humanity may correspond to the measure of its troubles. It follows:

### VERSE 10.—“For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, nor wilt thou give thy Holy One to see corruption.”

“For thou wilt not leave.” [Augustine.] As though to say: In what hope shall it rest? In this: that neither the soul shall be given up to possession in hell [Col. 0176A], nor wilt thou permit the holy body, through which others also are to be sanctified, to decay. This is the meaning: Thou hast not left, according to the common condition of others, my soul—which I possess as a true human being—in hell; [Cassiodorus] nor wilt thou give thy Holy One, namely my body sanctified by thee, to see corruption, that is, putrefaction. Elsewhere he says that he suffers corruption, that is, wounding: “What profit is there in my blood, when I go down into corruption?” (Ps. 29). I say, “Thou wilt not give”; indeed:

### VERSE 11.—“Thou hast made known to me the ways of life; thou wilt fill me with joy in the presence of thy countenance, delights at thy right hand unto the end.”

[Augustine.] Thou hast made them known through me, to me—that is, to mine, in whom I too am. I say “to me thou hast made known,” and I say that thou hast made known the ways of life, that is, the ways of humility, by which human beings may return to life, from which they fell through pride. And thou wilt fill me—that is, mine in the future—with joy in the presence of thy countenance, so that, when they see thee face to face, they may desire nothing further. Because I am in them, I say: thou wilt fill me. Meanwhile they have delights [Interlinear Gloss] on the journey of this life. [Augustine.] And this is at thy right hand, that is, in thy favour and graciousness. These delights lead them unto the end, that is, unto the consummation of eternal blessedness. The sense is: [Cassiodorus.] In thy favour, on the journey of this life, they have delight that leads them to the end: the glory of beholding thy countenance.

Or Christ speaks of himself: “Thou wilt fill me with joy in the presence of thy countenance; delights shall be for me at thy right hand”—that is, joy and delight shall be for me in thy session, withdrawn from human sight [Col. 0176C]. And this shall be unto the end, that is, perfectly and eternally.

## COMPARISON ON PSALM XV: “PRESERVE ME, O LORD.”

According to Jerome, the title is that of David, humble and simple; he reads two words, or one word compounded from two: namely, *MACAC* and *TAM*. The former means “he humbled,” the latter “simple and pure,” yielding *MICHTAM*. Others, however, took it as a simple though derived word, and translated “insignia” or “ornamented with finest gold.” Hence the Seventy said *stēlographia*, that is, “an inscription of a title”; the Chaldee, “an upright engraving,” is not far from them.

VERSE 1.—“I said to the Lord: Thou art my God.” Thus Jerome. But Pratensis, Sanctes, Pellican, Münster, the translators for Cajetan, and Campensis translate it in the second person: “Thou hast said,” referring this to the soul as though addressing itself; the Chaldee translator likewise has: “Thou hast spoken, O my soul.” In Hebrew a very small point changes person and gender: those who give the first person read *AMARTI*; by adding one point and removing *yod*, it becomes second-person feminine, since Hebrew verbs, like nouns, have gender. Yet the sense wholly agrees.

“Thou hast no need of my goods.” Jerome: “There is no good for me without thee.” Therefore Faber and the blind Burgensian criticise the Seventy, as though they had altered the Prophet’s meaning. But it is rather they who are ignorant of Hebrew learning and were able to say this with rash boldness. The Hebrew has *TOBATI BAL ALECA*, which, if rendered word for word, means “my good,” or “my goodness, is not upon thee.” This expression certainly contains either interpretation and causes no difficulty. Hence Münster translates: “My good adds nothing to thee”; [Col. 0177A] Pratensis: “My goodness contributes nothing to thee.” Pellican and Campensis mean the same. Sanctes, with Jerome, follows the other sense: “My good is not except from thee.”

VERSE 2.—“He has made all my desires wonderful.” The Seventy took *HEEDIR* as a verb in what they call the *Hiphil*. Others take it as the noun *ADDIRE*, that is, “magnificent,” “admirable,” “mighty,” etc. Or, more probably, the Seventy connected that noun with “desires,” as though: “my admirable desires are in them.” They expressed this idiom by a verb without changing the sense. The others, however, refer *ADDIRE* back to what precedes, so that one may say: “All my desire is in the magnificent saints.”

VERSE 3.—“They were multiplied into their infirmities.” Jerome and the translators for Cajetan: “their idols.” The others translate “anxieties,” “pains,” or “troubles,” because *ATZAB* means “he afflicted” or “he carved.” Hence *ATZABAH* means “affliction” or “idol,” because an idol brings great affliction upon those who worship it, as Münster maintains in his lexicon. Therefore Jerome says in his commentary on this passage that the Seventy translated “idols” as “infirmities.” [Col. 0177B] The Chaldee too translates “idols.”

“Afterwards they hastened.” Jerome: “following behind.” To follow behind is to return quickly, as he himself indicates in his commentaries: “The Gentiles,” he says, “leaving idols, returned to me most swiftly.” This does not disagree with “Afterwards they hastened.” Münster and Sanctes, adding words of their own, turned the sense elsewhere: the former, “May their pains be multiplied, who have bestowed [their devotion] upon another god”; the latter, “The anxieties of those who hasten after a foreign god shall be multiplied.” Pratensis comes close: “They hastened after another”; and Nebiensis: “They make haste after a stranger.” Pellican and the translators for Cajetan agree with us: “Afterwards they hastened,” namely, to the worship of the one God. [Col. 0178A] The Hebrew has *IIRBBU ATZEBOTAM AHER MAHARU*. The Chaldee translator: “Afterwards they hasten to sacrifice sacrifices.”

VERSE 4.—“I will not gather their assemblies from blood.” Heb. *BAL ASSIC NISSCEHEM*. And they translate: “I will not pour out their libations”; or, as Nebiensis prefers, “I will not mix their mixtures with blood,” so as to signify that henceforth carnal observances will not be acceptable to God. But since the ecclesiastical reading agrees to the same effect, [31] there is no need for anxious investigation, although a reconciliation could also be made in the literal sense by examining the roots *NASAC*, which denotes “to pour out a libation” and “to mix,” and *SACAC*, which can mean “he gathered together.” However that may be, the sense remains unharmed:

VERSE 9.—“My tongue rejoiced.” Hebrew: *QUEBODI*, that is, “my glory.” But since the word *QUIBBED* means “he glorified,” and we glorify someone with the tongue, the interpreters preferred to translate it [Col. 0178B] by “tongue”; this accords most fittingly with the sense of the preceding and following words. For they first set down the joy of the heart: “Therefore my heart rejoiced.” And since the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart, it is most suitably added: “My tongue rejoiced,” in accordance with Psalm LXII: “As with marrow and fatness let my soul be filled, and with lips of exultation my mouth shall praise thee.” Then follows at last: “And my flesh shall rest in hope,” that they might complete the praise in heart, tongue, and every work. Moreover, if the interpreters had read *LESCHONI* (“my tongue”) in place of *QUEBODI* (“my glory”), ought they to be called to account? In any case, the sense points to nothing else.

## PSALM XVI

[Col. 0177]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PRAYER OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0177C]

“Hear, O Lord.” Title: “A Prayer of David.” [Cassiodorus.] This psalm is the first of those entitled by the name of prayer; four others follow which are appropriately prefaced by “prayer,” because, although prayer is inserted among the others, in these it is almost continuous. [Jerome.] But in this psalm Christ prays according to his humanity, joining to himself the voice of his body, which is the Church. This psalm makes us attend to the true nature of Christ’s humanity: in the same voice he here prays with his members, not for his own benefit but for our need. [Alcuin.] For Christ’s prayer is instruction for the faithful. Thus, by weeping for Lazarus, he taught us to possess love for our neighbour; and by fleeing his persecutors, he removed from us the rashness of exposing ourselves imprudently to danger. [Col. 0177D] So he prayed, in order to set before us a pattern of prayer. [Augustine.] And this is the sense of the title: the prayer of this psalm belongs to David—that is, to the person of the Lord with the Church joined to him, which is his body. [Cassiodorus.] Intention: it exhorts to prayer. Method: the psalm has three parts. First, he asks that recompense be made to him according to justice. Second, he asks to be delivered from the plots of the Jews, at “I have cried.” Third, he prays that recompense be made to himself and to his adversaries, at “Arise, O Lord.” Christ, therefore, praying to the Father according to his humanity, with the voice of his body joined to him, says: O

VERSE 1.—“Hear, O Lord, my righteousness; attend to my supplication.”

“O Lord, hear my righteousness.” [Cassiodorus; Gloss, interlinear.] For righteousness has a voice before God which pierces heaven. And, in place of “righteousness,” attend to my supplication, which concerns the avoidance of evils. And do not merely attend, but:

VERSE 2.—“Receive with thine ears my prayer, not from deceitful lips.”

“Receive with thine ears,” [Cassiodorus.] as though he said: Not cursorily, so that my prayer, which concerns his good things and their bestowal upon him, may quickly pass away. [Interlinear Gloss.] I call it a prayer uttered “not from deceitful lips,” like the prayer of those who unjustly condemn me and mine. [Cassiodorus; Remigius.] Or like the prayer of those who say, “Lord, Lord,” and do not do the will of the Father (Matt. VII). It follows:

VERSE 3.—“Let my judgment come forth from thy countenance; [Col. 0178D] let thine eyes behold equity.”

“From thy countenance.” [Interlinear Gloss.] Behold what he asks in his prayer. As though he said: Hear my prayer, in which I ask this: Let my judgment—the judgment by which I was judged by Pilate and the Jews—come forth, O Lord; [Remigius.] that is, let it appear to have proceeded “from thy countenance,” that is, from thy sight, by which thou seest all things and needest no one else’s testimony. [Cassiodorus; Remigius.] That is, according to what thou knowest in me, who have no sin, let it appear to have proceeded, not from their disposition—that is, according to the purpose and will of the Jews. This was plainly accomplished in the resurrection, when, contrary to their expectation, he rose from the dead. And let thine eyes, O Lord, behold equity, so that thou mayest give remedy to me and punishment to the Jews, as they have deserved. [Interlinear Gloss; Alcuin.]

[Col. 0179A] Or thus: “My judgment,” Christ the man says, “by which I discern all things, let it come forth from thy countenance,” that is, from the illumination of thy knowledge, so that I may judge the truth. “And my eyes”—another reading, [Augustine; Interlinear Gloss]—namely, the eyes of the heart, “have seen equity.” [Augustine.]

Or, while retaining the same sense, divide the text thus: “Receive my prayer”—make a pause here. Then follows: “Not from deceitful lips; let my judgment come forth from thy countenance,” namely, in judging I shall utter from my lips nothing other than what I understand from thee. “Let my eyes behold equity”: this is unchanged.

VERSE 4.—“Thou hast proved my heart, and visited it by night; thou hast tested me by fire, and iniquity has not been found in me.”

“Thou hast proved”—therefore do what I ask, because thou hast proved [Col. 0179B] my heart and visited it by night. [Augustine.] That is, my very heart was tested by the visitation of tribulation; this tribulation is called not only night but also fire: night, because it disturbs; fire, because it burns. Hence he adds: “Thou hast tested me with the fire of tribulation.” [Cassiodorus.] He says this by comparison with a furnace which purifies metal. “And there has not been found in me”—as though he said: Thou hast tested me by tribulation, but in it I was found righteous. And that is because no iniquity was found in me for the burning to consume. I am so righteous and free from iniquity that:

VERSE 5.—“That my mouth may not speak the works of men; because of the words of thy lips I have kept hard ways.”

“And that my mouth may not speak the works of men,” [Augustine.] that is, that nothing may proceed from my mouth except what belongs [Col. 0179C] to thy glory and praise, and not to the works of men, which they do apart from thy will—that is, I have spoken nothing but good.

Elsewhere, however, it is written: “From the mouth of the Most High” (Lam. III)—that is, from the humanity of the Son of God—“neither good nor evil shall proceed.” When he stood before Herod, namely when he was questioned by him with many questions and words, he answered nothing (Luke XXIII), but was silent as a sheep before its shearer (Isa. LIII). Or “from the mouth of the Most High,” that is, of Christ ascending into heaven, neither good nor evil shall proceed, because at his ascension he is not recorded to have spoken anything, though he had said much before. Or “from the mouth of the Most High,” that is, of Christ who will judge in majesty, neither good nor evil shall proceed in judgment—that is, good and evil shall proceed. For two negations complete the sense of one affirmation. [Col. 0179D] He will say good things to the good: “Come, ye blessed” (Matt. XXV); and evil things to the evil: “Go, ye cursed” (ibid.). Or “from the mouth of the Most High,” that is, of God the Father, neither good nor evil shall proceed in judgment, because the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John V).

“Because of the words”—as though he said, [Interlinear Gloss]: And although I am thus innocent, Christ says, nevertheless I have kept. Or connect it thus: “Let not my mouth speak the works of men, but rather I have carefully kept hard,” or laborious, ways, [Augustine.] namely the ways of mortality and passion. Or, according to another reading, [Remigius.] “I have kept the ways of the robber,” that is, I undeservedly endured what a robber deserved to endure; and this was not for my own fault but because the words [Col. 0180A] of thy lips were to be fulfilled. [Augustine; Remigius.] That is, in order that the words of thy peace, signified by the lips and promised in his words, might be fulfilled; this promise is called “words of peace.” Or: “because of the words of thy lips to be fulfilled,” that is, of the prophets. It follows:

VERSE 6.—“Perfect my steps in thy paths, that my footprints may not be moved.”

“Perfect,” or, “for the perfecting of my steps,” etc.—as though he said: I kept hard ways, indeed for the perfecting of my steps in thy paths. [Augustine.] That is, that the love of my Church might be perfected, by which one comes to thy rest through narrow ways, that is, through stricter precepts. For by this I taught that the Church cannot come to thee except by the narrow way; and “that my footprints may not be moved,” that is, the marks of [Col. 0180B] my journey, impressed by the sacraments and apostolic Scriptures, so that those who wish to follow me may look upon and observe them.

Or: I therefore kept hard ways, and my steps were perfected, that now “my footprints may not be moved,” that is, that I may remain steadfast in eternity after I have completed the hard ways and perfected my steps.

Otherwise, from the words “that my mouth may not speak,” as though he said: [Cassiodorus.] No iniquity has been found in me, as thou knowest, even if I am silent. And this is what he says: Thou knowest what I say, so that—that is, although—“my mouth may not speak,” that is, even if I am silent. And this is what he says: Thou knowest me to be pure. The text is divided there: “my mouth.” Then follows “works,” etc., as though he said: And although I am so pure, nevertheless, because of the words of thy lips, this is unchanged: I have kept [Col. 0180C] hard ways, namely “the works of men,” that is, what men’s works deserve: namely passion and death, and the remaining sufferings and miseries.

[Jerome.] Or he calls the virtues “hard ways,” because they are difficult to men, not to Christ. And this is the sense: I have kept the ways of virtues, hard to men—namely, “the works of men,” that is, those which men ought to imitate; for to them the way of vices is easy and that of virtues difficult.

Or thus: I say, “iniquity has not been found in me,” [Alcuin.] yet I say this “that my mouth may not speak,” that I may not say this boastfully, which is “the works,” that is, the work of man—namely, to speak boastfully.

Or thus: [Remigius.] I am so righteous that my mouth may not speak anything improper—that is, that I may not sin with my tongue, which is “the works,” that is, the work of man—namely, to sin with the tongue. What follows is not changed in sense from the first exposition down to “perfect”: as though he said, And because I kept hard ways, therefore perfect my steps. [Cassiodorus.] That is, bring my human actions to completion, even to the end, namely to passion and death; for before that there is only a beginning. I say, perfect them in thy paths, that is, in thy stricter precepts. Perfect them for this purpose: that my footprints may not be moved, that is, that those who wish to imitate me may not be moved away from thee. [Remigius; Interlinear Gloss.] Or by “footprints” he means the good works he performed and the teaching he handed down. And this is the sense: Therefore perfect them, that my footprints, in which the pattern of righteousness is impressed, may not be moved away from the good who wish to imitate me.

## PART II. VERSE 7.—“I have cried, because thou hast heard me, O God; incline thine ear unto me, and hear my words.”

“I have cried,” etc. [Cassiodorus.] This is the second part, in which Christ asks that his purity may be delivered from the plots of the Jews. As though he said: I have kept hard ways and perfected my steps. I too, says the whole Christ, have cried—that is, I have directed prayers to thee with free and earnest intention—therefore because thou hast heard me, O God, that is, because I most certainly know that I shall be heard. [Cassiodorus.] Only a righteous person can say this, one who prays confidently because he knows that he is heard; who, reversing the order of the words, can say: [Augustine.] “Because thou hast heard me, I have cried.” Otherwise it would seem more appropriate to say, “Because I have cried, thou hast heard me.”

Or thus: “I have cried”—this is unchanged. Therefore, indeed, because, in order that I might be able to do this, O God, [Col. 0181B] thou didst hear me when formerly I prayed more weakly. [Augustine.] Christ says this properly in his members. And because I have cried, therefore incline thine ear—that is, [Interlinear Gloss] the ear of thy clemency and mercy—to me, [Cassiodorus.] namely to me who am humble; and hear my words: let thy hearing not abandon me in my humility. What words? These:

VERSE 8.—“Make wonderful thy mercies, thou who savest those who hope in thee.”

“Make wonderful thy mercies.” [Augustine.] Wonderful things are new things. These are the things which Christ performed in the flesh, to the amazement of the Jews. And this is the sense: Make thy mercies wonderful—that is, do new things at which even the wicked may marvel, lest mercies become cheap and be loved less. Thou, I say, who savest those who hope in thee.

VERSE 9.—“From those who resist thy right hand keep [Col. 0181C] me as the pupil of the eye.”

[32] “From those who resist thy right hand,” [Augustine.] that is, from those who resist thy right hand, namely the favour by which thou favourest me. [Cassiodorus.] Or, “thy right hand,” that is, me, thy Son. And keep me as the pupil of the eye—that is, preserve me according to my humanity. [Augustine.] For the pupil is extremely small, and yet through it the ray of light is directed, by which light and darkness are distinguished. So through Christ’s humanity his deity distinguishes between good and evil human beings, because it numbers among the lot of the good those who have faith in his humanity, but the others among the fellowship of the evil. [Cassiodorus.] He asks that it be preserved in this manner:

VERSE 10.—“Protect [Col. 0181D] me under the shadow of thy wings, from the face of the ungodly who have afflicted me.”

[Augustine.] Protect me as a hen protects her chicks under the shadow of thy wings; [Cassiodorus.] that is, within the defense of thy love and mercy. For mercy and love are the Father’s wings, by which he protects us. Protect me, I say, from the face—that is, from the assault—of the ungodly, namely demons and Jews, who afflicted me, thus:

VERSE 11.—“My enemies surrounded my soul; they enclosed their fat; their mouth spoke pride.”

“My enemies,” [Cassiodorus.] namely the Jews, surrounded my soul with their schemes—that is, my life—wishing to take it away; and “they enclosed their fat.” [Augustine.] That is, they were covered with their rich joy after their desire had been satisfied by wickedness. For once Christ was seized, they displayed outwardly the joy conceived within in fullness.

[Alcuin; Cassiodorus.] Or, by comparison with animals which are puffed up with fat and become wanton, he says: “They enclosed their fat,” that is, they retained pride; they were not lean—that is, humble—but swollen with pride. Or: “They enclosed their fat,” that is, they retained a fat and carnal understanding. Or: “They enclosed their fat”: satiated with crimes, they lost true understanding. [Cassiodorus; Augustine.] Hence it remained for them to speak pride. And therefore “their mouth spoke pride,” saying: “Hail, King of the Jews” (Matt. XXVII), and the like. [Cassiodorus.] He says “mouth,” not “heart,” because the wicked often condemn in their hearts what they defend with their mouths. It follows: And

[Col. 0182B] VERSE 12.—“Casting me out, they have now surrounded me; they fixed their eyes to bow down to the earth.”

“Casting me out,” [Augustine; Interlinear Gloss] outside the city, as though the place might be defiled by me. The wicked tenants, because they had first killed the servants sent into the vineyard (Matt. XXI), now surrounded me, the Son and heir (ibid.), upon the cross—not in service but in fury, assembling as though for a spectacle. And they did this because they fixed the eyes of their heart upon the earth, namely lest they lose place and nation. For they said: “If we let him thus alone, the whole world goes after him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John XI).

Or: “They fixed their eyes to bow down to the earth,” [Augustine.] that is, they bent the intention of their heart toward earthly things, thinking that he who was being killed suffered evil, while they who killed him suffered none. And as though someone should ask: Whence came this opportunity to them? He answers:

VERSE 13.—“They received me as a lion ready for prey, and as a lion’s whelp dwelling in hiding places.”

“They received me,” [Alcuin.] that is, they eagerly received me from God, whose purpose was that he should die; [Remigius; Cassiodorus.] or from Judas the betrayer, or from Pilate the judge. Who were they? The rulers, who were like a lion—that is, the devil—ready for prey, who goes about seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. V). [Cassiodorus.] That is, they were to be compared to the devil as a lion, at whose instigation they acted. And [Col. 0182D] not only the rulers, [Augustine.] but also the people, who were like a lion’s whelp—that is, a son of the devil, to whom it was said, “You are of your father the devil” (John VIII)—dwelling in hiding places, that is, persisting and plotting in ambushes. [Cassiodorus.] For it is the custom of evil persons to conceal their designs, that they may secretly bring them to completion. [Augustine.] Therefore they devised snares by which they might entrap and destroy the righteous one.

## PART III. VERSE 14.—“Arise, O Lord; go before him and overthrow him; deliver my soul from the ungodly man, thy sword from the enemies of thy hand.”

“Arise, O Lord.” [Cassiodorus.] This is the third part, containing a prayer concerning recompense for himself and his adversaries. As though he said: [Augustine.] They act thus, but thou, O Lord, who seemest to sleep and not to care for the iniquities of men, [Col. 0183A] arise in vengeance against the Jews, and go before him—the people—or them, namely the Jews. He speaks by comparison with a runner. [Alcuin.] For the people runs to crucify; God the Father runs to avenge; but God goes before them by blinding them. For no one sins first against another before sinning against himself—that is, every person by sinning harms himself before another. And “go before him” means, [Augustine.] let the punishment of blinding go before their deed, and thus overthrow them.

Or: “Overthrow him,” by comparison with a wrestler; that is, make them ineffective and cast them down, so that they may lose the place and nation for retaining which they killed Christ. Hence he adds:

VERSE 15.—“O Lord, divide them from the few of the earth in their life; their belly is filled from thy hidden things.”

[Col. 0183B] “O Lord, from the few of the earth”—but he inserts concerning himself, “deliver my soul,” as though he said: [Augustine.] Overthrow them, but deliver my soul from enemies, from the devil, by raising me from the death inflicted by the ungodly. Then he explains what he had said: “Deliver thy sword from the enemies of thy hand.” My soul is thy sword, which thy hand—that is, thy eternal power—assumed, in order by it to overcome the kingdoms of iniquity and to divide the righteous from the ungodly here in affection and hereafter also in place. Therefore deliver this soul of mine, thy sword, from the enemies of thy hand—that is, of thy power—that is, from my enemies, I who am thy hand.

“O Lord, from the few”: after praying for his own concerns, he adds concerning the recompense of his adversaries and develops what he had said, “Overthrow”; as though [Col. 0183C] he said: Overthrow them in this way: O Lord, thou wilt destroy them from the earth, or “divide them in their life,” another reading. As though he said: O Lord, thou wilt destroy them from the earth which they inhabit and scatter them throughout the whole world in this life, which they alone regard as theirs who despair of eternal life. Nor will this visible punishment alone be theirs: “their belly is filled from thy hidden things,” that is, their memory is full of sins which, like darkness, are hidden from the light of thy truth, so that they forget God.

VERSE 16.—“They are filled with children, and have left their remnants to their little ones.”

[Augustine.] “They are filled with children,” that is, with evil works. For we understand children as works: as good works are good children, so evil works are evil children. [Jerome.] Or: “they are filled with swine’s food,” [Col. 0183D] that is, with uncleanness, trampling underfoot the pearls of God’s words.

Otherwise, from “O Lord, from the few,” and our reading is read: O Lord, divide them—that is, the Jews—from the few, that is, from the elect, according to the manners by which they are defiled. [Alcuin.] Or, from the few faithful persons who, on the angel’s warning, when the destruction of the Jews was imminent, withdrew into the kingdom of Agrippa, where they remained safe. [Note: [Col. 0183] From Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, III, chap. 5; and Peter Comestor, from *History of the Acts of the Apostles*, chap. 69.] I mean the Jews, removed from the land for which they killed me. Divide them, I say, throughout the world, and do this in their present life. What, then, will be theirs after this life? Complete misery.

“From thy hidden things,” as though he said: This comes deservedly upon them, because “from thy hidden things”—that is, from uncleannesses [Col. 0184A] which indeed God does not know, that is, which he forbids—“their belly is filled,” that is, their carnality has been satiated. [Cassiodorus; Alcuin.] Or it may be understood in a good sense: “from thy hidden things,” that is, from the precepts of the Law and Christ’s miracles. [Cassiodorus.] “Their belly,” that is, their carnal understanding, is filled with these good things; yet though they have been fed by them, they “are filled with swine’s food,” that is, uncleanness, and “have left their remnants,” namely the remnants of sins, to their little ones, [Augustine; Jerome.] that is, to their descendants, crying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” [Alcuin.] Or: “They are filled with children,” that is, for the work of children. It is a comparison from something which is not the case: for children are filled by no feast. And they are so filled that they “have left their remnants,” [Col. 0184B] namely the remnants of their curse, to their little ones, that is, to their descendants.

[Remigius.] Or: “They are filled from hidden things,” that is, from sins; and this “with children,” that is, for the benefit of children, who are the remnant to be saved, of whom Isaiah said: “The remnant of Israel shall be saved” (Isa. X). Hence he adds here: “And they have left their remnants to their little ones,” that is, to their descendants, from whom that remnant will come. It follows:

VERSE 17.—“But I shall appear in righteousness before thy countenance; I shall be satisfied when thy glory appears.”

“But I,” as though he said: [Augustine.] This will happen to them; but I, who did not appear to them because with a filthy and darkened heart they do not see the light of truth and wisdom, shall appear in thy righteousness—that is, according to thy righteousness—before thy countenance, or in [Col. 0184C] thy sight. And although they are filled with uncleanness, so that they did not know me, I shall be satisfied with purity—that is, in those who understand me, namely the saints—when, or while, thy eternal glory shall appear or be manifested to the saints in judgment.

## COMPARISON ON PSALM XVI: “HEAR, O LORD, MY RIGHTEOUSNESS; ATTEND.”

VERSE 3.—“Thine eyes have seen equities.” The Roman Psalter has “my eyes”; but Jerome corrects it in his letter to Sunnias and Fretela.

VERSE 4.—Verses 4 and 5, because they may be divided in different ways, repeatedly yield a different sense. First, thus: “Thou hast tested me by fire, and thou wilt not find; I have thought,” or, as Jerome prefers, “thoughts shall not pass through my mouth,” or “not pass through my mouth,” ending the fourth verse here. Then, as the [Col. 0184D] fifth verse begins: “in the works of men.” In accordance with the Hebrew, our interpreters too made the division: “Thou hast tested me by fire, and thou wilt not find iniquity.” Or, which comes to the same thing: “Iniquity has not been found in me,” because *ZAMAM*, though it denotes “he thought,” does not always do so absolutely, but rather “he devised wickedness or crime.” Then let the beginning of the fifth verse be: “That the works of men may not pass through my mouth.” Thus “to pass through” is suitably understood as “to be entertained in the mouth”: therefore, “Let not my mouth speak the works of men.” This interpretation and the former one do not differ from the Spirit of truth, who is manifold and one (Wis. VII).

VERSE 5.—“I have kept hard ways.” Jerome: “the ways of the robber,” or, as others prefer, “the ways of the destroyer.” But *PARITZ* or *PERETZ*, from the same word *PARATZ*, sometimes means a broken and shattered path, which is usually hard. Nebiensis translates [Col. 0185A] “ruined ways.” Besides, the ways of the robber are laborious, as is explained in the interpretation concerning Christ, who suffered ignominiously as though he were chief of robbers.

VERSE 11.—“They enclosed their fat.” Faber and Caecus argue that the churches ought to chant, “They enclosed with their fat,” using the ablative, so that “my soul” is understood as the accusative object. This is what they want according to their own fancy; but it can be understood that they enclosed their body with fat, as Sanctes translates, from whom Munster does not differ in translating passively: “They are enclosed with their fat.” Campensis tends in the same direction in his paraphrase: “They are well fed and obese.” This is what it is to enclose one’s fat. Pratensis indeed translates, “They enclosed with their fat,” but so that the verb passes to the following expression, namely “their mouth,” contrary, however, to the sense of the Hebrew pause—though the Chaldean distinguishes it in this manner: “Their fat covers their mouth.”

VERSE 12.—“Casting me out, they have now surrounded me.” If we read *ASSURENI* with *yod* at the end, [Col. 0185B] meaning “steps against me,” as the Septuagint read it, and as Jerome more plainly translated: “casting me out,” or “walking against me.” Nebiensis likewise. [33] Other Hebraists read *NU* at the end with *waw*, so that it means “our steps.” Similarly, in the following word one must distinguish *SEBABUNI*, as the Septuagint, Jerome, Nebiensis, Sanctes, and Pellicanus read it, or *SEBABUNU*, as Munster, Campensis, and the interpreters for Cajetan read it. You see how easily manuscripts vary.

VERSE 13.—“They received me as a lion ready for prey.” Hebrew: *DIMIONO*, that is, “his likeness is like that of a lion,” etc. The interpreters read it with a final *yod*, not a *waw*, as often happens among the Hebrews. And because it would have been somewhat obscure to say, “my likeness” or “the likeness of me, like a lion ready for prey,” they made the meaning clear: “They received me as a lion.” It is as if you were to say: This image of a lion ready for prey is applied to me, while my enemies raged against me after the manner of a raging lion.

[Col. 0185C] VERSE 14.—“Deliver my soul from the ungodly man, thy sword from the enemies of thy hand.” The difficulty in this verse, and properly in the one following, lies in the different division and rendering of the words. For those following the Hebrew text make the end of the verse at “thy sword.” Jerome translates thus: “Deliver my soul from the ungodly man, who is thy sword,” which the versions of others imitate. The Septuagint understood “thy sword” as an accusative, referring it to “soul,” as Augustine explains. For this reason they divided the sequence of verses differently, as they also do not infrequently for the reasons stated above.

In the same verse, whose beginning according to the Hebrew is the end of verse 14 according to the Latin texts: “from the enemies [Col. 0186A] of thy hand.” Jerome: “from the men of thy hand,” as Nebiensis also has it. Or, as others render it: “from men who are thy hand,” or “thy scourge, deliver [me],” as Sanctes translates. But since the Hebrew word *MATHIM*, according to Rabbi David, denotes men devoted to the desires of this age, they will certainly be enemies of the Lord’s hand, which especially bestows spiritual gifts upon its friends. Hence Pellicanus explains: “from those,” he says, “upon whom thou takest vengeance.”

VERSE 15.—“O Lord, divide them from the few of the earth in their life.” Sanctes: “from men of the world, whose portion is in life”; Pratensis: “from men of time, whose portion is in life”; the interpreter for Cajetan: “from men of the world, whose portion is in lives”; Pellicanus: “from men of scant subsistence, their portion in lives”; Munster: “from men, I say, and from the wicked age, whose portion is in life”; Nebiensis: “from men of the age, whose portion is in their life.” Far otherwise Jerome: “who have died in the deep, whose portion is in life.” Let us weigh each expression separately in the reading we have. “From [Col. 0186B] the few”: in Hebrew the same word is repeated which the Septuagint translated as “enemies” in the preceding verse, as has been explained. But since it also signifies men of scant subsistence, as Pellicanus translated it, our reading does not violate Hebrew truth.

Then the following expression, namely “of the earth,” *HELED*, in Hebrew indicates the duration of the life of this age. Therefore there is no discrepancy if the sense is reconciled. Munster, moreover, in his earlier lexicon writes that it means “the depth of the world,” in the sense adopted by Jerome, who, as is clear, also read *METHIM* with long *e*, which they now call *tsere*, and which means “the dead,” as Jerome translated it. The others read it with short *a*, called *hateph pathah*. Finally, “divide them in their life”; the Hebraists have, “whose portion is in life.” But this also departs in no way from the Hebrew source. For *HALAQ* means “he divided,” and *HELEQ*, “a portion.” Hence *HELQUAM* may be “their portion,” or *HOL QUAM*, “divide them.”

[Col. 0186C] VERSE 17.—“I shall be satisfied when thy glory appears.” Jerome: “when I awake, with thy likeness.” Or, as others have it: “when I awake to thy likeness” or “image.” The sense is altogether the same. For the glory which almighty God promised you is that one should be transformed into the image of his Son, according to Romans VIII: “Whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.” And again, 1 John III: “When he appears, we shall be like him.” I know, however, that some interpret “thy image” as “the soul.” But we are not bound to this. Moreover, the fact that the Septuagint spoke in the third person and others in the first arises from the Hebrew infinitive form, which can be adapted to any person: *BEHAQUITZ*.

## PSALM XVII

[Col. 0185]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END, FOR DAVID THE SERVANT OF THE LORD, WHO SPOKE TO THE LORD THE WORDS OF THIS SONG, IN THE DAY WHEN HE DELIVERED HIM FROM THE HAND OF HIS ENEMIES AND FROM THE HAND OF SAUL; AND HE SAID:”

[Col. 0185D]

“I will love thee, O Lord, my strength.” Title: “[Unto the end, for David the servant of the Lord, who spoke to the Lord the words of this song, in the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of his enemies and from the hand of Saul; and he said.]” We read in the Book of Kings that Saul, a wicked king, persecuted David, who was gentle and meek. When Saul had died, David was delivered and reigned in peace. [Jerome and Remigius.] David seems to have sung this psalm to the Lord for that deliverance. But because the title has “[unto the end and of a song],” we are led away from the historical account. [Interlinear Gloss; Cassiodorus; Alcuin.] For the end is Christ, [Col. 0186D] while song is exultation concerning eternal things. It is therefore better understood of the whole Christ, namely head and members, whom the Lord wholly delivered on the day of Christ’s resurrection from the hand of enemies—that is, Jews and demons—and “from the hand of Saul,” that is, death. [Jerome; Alcuin.] For Saul signifies death. [Augustine.] Saul, indeed, is interpreted “petition,” because the people extorted this king from God; he was not chosen to remain, [Alcuin.] but permitted to reign for a time, as is said in Job: “God makes the hypocrite reign because of the perversity of the people” (Job XXIV). But God chose David to remain, and from him Christ was born, king forever. Yet David did not possess the kingdom until he had been delivered [Col. 0187A] from his persecutors. As David first endured Saul before he reigned in peace, [Alcuin.] so Christ first endured death before he reigned in repose; and so too did his body, which is the Church. And Saul, David’s persecutor, is fittingly called death, because death alone persecutes us. For unless we were mortal, the enemy could do nothing to us. And just as God did not choose that king, so God did not make death (Wis. I); rather, the ungodly summoned it by hands and words.

[Jerome; Augustine; Remigius; Cassiodorus.] And this is the sense of the title: the words of this song, which is called a song because it treats of the joy of Christ’s resurrection and the establishment of the Church. [Jerome.] This is stated lest it be understood of David’s history. I say, of a song tending unto the end, that is, unto Christ, and belonging to David, that is, to Christ according to the head and [Col. 0187B] according to his body, the Church. I say, David, servant of the Lord God the Father, of whom Isaiah says: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. IX). These words the whole Christ spoke to the Lord, [Interlinear Gloss; Augustine.] that is, in honour of the Lord. For Christ and the Church—that is, the whole Christ—say this. I say, of a song uttered in the day, that is, on account of the day of Christ’s resurrection, on which day the Lord Father delivered him, that is, Christ according to head and body, from the hand of his enemies, that is, from the power of the Jews according to the head, and from the power of demons according to head and members. [Augustine and Cassiodorus.] For on the day of resurrection Christ was delivered from the devil and his members were released; and from the hand of Saul, that is, from the power of death, he delivered Christ in actuality [Col. 0187C] and his members in hope, and will at last deliver them in actuality. [Remigius.] It is fitting that he first says “from enemies,” and afterward “from death,” because death, the last enemy, shall be destroyed. And for this spiritual deliverance the whole Christ, giving thanks to God, said: “I will love thee, O Lord.” Intention: [Cassiodorus.] it exhorts to thanksgivings for spiritual deliverance.

Method: There are four divisions. First, the Prophet gives thanks for deliverance, gathering together the sum of God’s benefits. Second, he deals with the calamities of the human race before Christ’s coming and with how the Lord showed mercy there, at “They surrounded me.” Third, Christ speaks of his own strength and power, at “God who girded me.” Fourth, the joyful Church praises God’s gifts, at [Col. 0187D] “The Lord lives.” Therefore the whole Christ, giving thanks for spiritual deliverance, says: O

VERSE 1.—“I will love thee, O Lord, my strength: the Lord is my firm support, my refuge, and my deliverer.”

“O Lord, I will love thee,” [Remigius.] which alone remains after deliverance from all things. He adds the reason: because thou art my power or strength, [Augustine.] by which I am strong over my enemies. “The Lord is my firm support”; or, “O Lord,” another reading—as though he said: And, O Lord, thou art my firm support, that is, thou hast made me firm. And this is because thou art my refuge, because I fled to thee; and I fled, and—that is, because thou art my deliverer from enemies, because thou hast delivered me. Then, changing person, he says: And

[Col. 0188A] VERSE 2.—“My God, my helper; and I will hope in him.”

“My God,” [Jerome; Cassiodorus.] that is, my Creator, “is my helper.” As though he said: He who creates me helps me; and with him helping, I shall hope in him, as though he said in the second person: [Augustine.] Thou who createst art my helper, who first freely bestowed upon me the help of calling, that thereby I might be able to hope in thee. And thou art:

VERSE 3.—“My protector, the horn of my salvation, and my upholder.”

“My protector against snares,” [Cassiodorus; Augustine.] because I did not presume upon myself, raising against thee, as it were, a horn of pride; rather, I found thee to be the height of salvation. Hence he adds: And thou art the horn—that is, the firm height—[Col. 0188B] of my salvation for scattering enemies; and that I might find this, thou art my upholder, [Cassiodorus; Augustine; Interlinear Gloss] that is, thou hast received me through grace. And therefore:

VERS. 4. — “Praising, I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies.”

“Praising”: [Augustine, Gloss interlinearis] seeking not my own glory but that of the Lord, I will call upon the Lord for perseverance; and thus I shall be saved from my enemies—that is, the error of ungodliness will not harm me. [Augustine]

Or the whole passage may be read in the person of David himself. He says: “I shall love you, O Lord, who are my strength,” or “my might,” that is, the source from which I am strong. Then, changing person, he speaks of him to men, saying: “The Lord is a firm support,” by which he stood firm in battle. [Col. 0188C] “And my refuge,” [Cassiodorus] because, when counsel was needed, he fled to him and found it; “and my deliverer,” as a powerful person might free one captured by enemies; “and my God, and my helper, and I shall hope in him, and my protector” against snares, “and the horn of my salvation” for scattering enemies, “and my upholder,” as a physician supports a sick man. [Remigius, Cassiodorus] “Praising”: after all these benefits, he does not boastfully exalt himself, but ascribes all things to God, saying: “Praising, I will call upon the Lord.” And therefore I shall be saved from my enemies. For whoever acts otherwise, left to himself, perishes, even if he seemed to have conquered. It follows:

PART II. VERS. 5. — “The pains of death surrounded me, and torrents of iniquity troubled me.”

[Col. 0188D] “They surrounded me.” [Cassiodorus] This is the second part, in which the Prophet, speaking in the person of the righteous who lived before Christ’s coming, treats of the calamities of the human race, of how God had mercy through the mystery of the Incarnation, and of how in baptism he gathered Christians from the whole world. [Alcuin] Observe the rule of the unity of head and body, that is, of Christ and the Church. For head and body are as though one person, and therefore the head speaks with its members in one voice, although the things said refer to different persons. Some things belong to the head alone; some to the members alone; some to head and members alike. Likewise, among things belonging to the members, some concern those of the past, some the present, some the future; some the perfect, and some the imperfect. [Col. 0189A] Yet amid such diversity there is one voice, and as though one person seems to speak, so that, just as two are one flesh—namely bridegroom and bride—so they may also be one voice. For see here: though he begins to speak in the person of the ancients and afterwards deals with the mystery of the Incarnation, he carries the narrative so far that he uses the words of the present Church, gathered from the whole world in baptism, at: “He sent from on high,” etc. [Cassiodorus] Thus the continuous literal sense proceeds. He had said, “I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies.” Now, as if someone should ask, “It is remarkable that you say this. What has happened to you?” He answers: Behold what: “The pains of death surrounded me”—not pains arising from worldly matters, but of death, that is, of the devil, through whom death came. That is, the devil, as the Apostle says, before Christ’s advent reigned almost everywhere and in all persons [Col. 0189B] (Rom. V); among them the righteous were few, and they were troubled by swiftly rushing iniquities. Hence he adds: “And torrents of iniquity troubled me,” that is, iniquities abundant and rapid as torrents troubled me.

VERS. 6. — “The pains of hell surrounded me; the snares of death came before me.”

“The pains of hell”: [Cassiodorus] that is, the Gentiles, destined to be tormented in hell with deserved pain, surrounded me. And besides this, “the snares of death came before me,” that is, original sin, whence death bound me before I could sin by my own power. But:

VERS. 7. — “In my tribulation I called upon the Lord, and I cried to my God.”

[Col. 0189C] “In this great tribulation of mine,” that is, in this great necessity, where one seeks with all one’s strength, “I called upon the Lord,” [Cassiodorus] which is the sole remedy amid evils. I say, the Lord—not indeed one alien to me, but “my God.” And this is what he adds: “And I cried to my Lord,” which is more than calling upon him.

VERS. 8. — “And from his holy temple he heard my voice; and my cry entered before him into his ears.”

And God himself “heard my voice from his holy temple,” [Cassiodorus] that is, from heaven, or from Christ’s body to come, in whose Incarnation they obtained the effect of being heard. “And my cry,” that is, [Col. 0189D] the cause of my righteousness, which rightly enters to God because it pleads for the ruin of the world—this cry is “before him,” [Augustine] that is, I possess it inwardly in my conscience, not before men—and it entered, by the likeness of a faithful messenger, into the ears of his power and mercy. It follows:

VERS. 9. — “The earth was shaken and trembled; the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken, because he was angry with them.”

“The earth was shaken.” [Cassiodorus] Having recounted the sorrow which God’s people endured before Christ’s advent, he comes to the secrets of the Incarnation, which are properly indicated when he says, “He bent down the heavens”; but he first sets forth the things that occurred at the time of the Incarnation, saying: “The earth was shaken.” Behold how he heard the preceding sorrow: [Col. 0190A] namely, through the Incarnation, which he describes by the things then accomplished. “The earth was shaken,” as if to say: he heard in this manner, because at the time of the Incarnation the earth—that is, sinners—was inwardly moved to repentance. [Augustine, Cassiodorus] And afterwards it trembled outwardly because of sins. [Cassiodorus] For sinners must necessarily tremble at the presence of the Judge. “And the foundations of the mountains,” [Augustine] that is, the hopes of the proud in this world, “were troubled.” The foundations of mountains are the presumptions of the proud, and such things upon which they relied. But these were troubled and shaken, so that worldly hope should no longer have a firm support in human hearts. [Cassiodorus] For the hope of the world, which God hates, departed. And why was this? “Because he was angry with them,” that is, because God’s wrath became known to them. And thus:

[Col. 0190B] VERS. 10. — “Smoke went up in his anger, and fire blazed out from his face; coals were kindled by him.”

“Smoke went up,” [Augustine] that is, the tearful supplication of penitents, “in his anger”—namely, in the punishment of the judgment foreseen, that is, when they learned what God threatens. And afterwards, “fire blazed out from his face,” that is, burning charity blazed forth after repentance from knowledge of him. Thus “coals were kindled”: that is, those who had already been dead, extinguished from God’s fire and from the light of righteousness, and had remained cold and dark, were kindled anew, illuminated, and revived. [Cassiodorus] And this was “by him,” that is, by the Lord’s coming. But did he come? Certainly he came, because:
