VERS. 11. — “He bent down the heavens and came down; and [Col. 0190C] darkness was beneath his feet.”

“He bent down the heavens,” or “heaven”: [Cassiodorus] that is, the Word of God humbled himself in order to take flesh; and “he came down,” that is, he came to us clothed in flesh.

Or thus: “The coals were kindled,” [Jerome] that is, those formerly extinguished were kindled by him with the fire of charity. But how were all these things done? Behold, God the Father “bent down the heavens,” [Gloss interlinearis] that is, humbled heavenly things by sending the Son, of whom he adds, “and he came down to us.” He then humbled heavenly things because he subjected angels to human nature. And “darkness,” [Cassiodorus] that is, the devil who darkens minds, “is beneath his feet,” because he is trampled under the Lord’s power.

VERS. 12. — “And he ascended above the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds.”

[Cassiodorus] He who descended also ascended above the heavens when, before the apostles’ eyes, he ascended; and “above the cherubim,” which is interpreted “fullness of knowledge,” means that he surpasses every mode of knowledge. [Augustine, Cassiodorus] For who can attain this mystery: that mortal and passible flesh has been so exalted? “And he flew”: his fame flew. “He flew,” repeated again and again; for the word signifies the very great speed with which his fame ran throughout the whole world. Hence he adds, “upon the wings,” that is, the swiftness, “of the winds.” For his fame outstrips winds, than which nothing is swifter; thus, immediately after he was born, he was announced to the Magi by a star.

VERS. 13. — “And he made darkness his hiding place; his tent was round about him: dark water in the clouds of the air.”

“And darkness,” that is, the mystery of the Incarnation, which is deep and obscure to us, “he made his hiding place,” [Col. 0191A] [Cassiodorus] that is, the secret place of his majesty, which was covered by the cloud of flesh. He will reveal this when we see him face to face. “His tent,” that is, the Church which serves in his army, “is round about him,” that is, close to him. And therefore, although it does not yet see by sight, nevertheless it does so by faith.

Or thus, from “They surrounded me,” the passage may be read in the person of Christ, without change of voice. Recounting his Passion, he says: “The pains of death surrounded me,” [Augustine] that is, pains of the flesh, which are most grievous. “And torrents of iniquity,” that is, the wicked crowds of the Jews, stirred up for a time but soon to cease, like rain-fed streams, [Col. 0191B] “troubled me,” that is, they acted so as to trouble me. “And the pains of hell surrounded me,” that is, among those surrounding me in order to destroy me were pains of envy, which work death and lead to hell. “And the snares of death,” namely the Jews, who through a show of righteousness recommend evil, whence death comes, “came before me,” so that they wished to harm me first—a thing which will afterwards be repaid to them.

Or thus: “The pains of death surrounded me, and the pains of hell surrounded me,” that is, the Jews grieving over me—which is for them a cause of inward death and of hell—surrounded me.

Or thus: “The pains of death surrounded me,” that is, the pains of the dying, namely those which dying persons are accustomed to suffer. And these pains which surrounded me are “fixed,” another reading, [Alcuin] that is, on account of my lower part, namely the weakness of my humanity. “And torrents of iniquity,” [Gloss interlinearis] that is, the passing assaults of the wicked, troubled me, according to: “Jesus began to be afraid and distressed” (Mark XIV). And all these things occurred because “the snares of death came before me,” that is, because mortality and passibility had taken hold of me beforehand. But “in my tribulation I called upon the Lord”: this does not change. “And I cried to my Lord”: this also does not change. “And the Lord heard my voice from his holy temple,” [Augustine] that is, from my heart, in which he dwells; and “my cry,” which is “before him,” that is, which I have inwardly in my conscience and not before men, “entered into his ears.” [Col. 0191D] This does not change, except that here the cry is for resurrection. It entered, I say, whence I was glorified.

Or thus: “The earth was shaken and trembled.” For when Christ had been glorified, sinners were shaken and trembled toward repentance; “and the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken, because God was angry with them.” This does not change. And “smoke went up in his anger,” and “coals were kindled by him”: understand this as before. “He bent down the heavens,” or “heaven,” shows how God’s wrath became known to them and how the aforesaid things were done: for “he bent down heaven and came down,” that is, he humbled the righteous man, so that he himself might descend to human weakness by teaching simple things. “And darkness is beneath [Col. 0192A] his feet,” that is, the ungodly who savor earthly things, blinded by the darkness of their own wickedness, did not know him. For the earth is the footstool of his feet, because earthly people are not raised to contemplate him. “And he ascended above the cherubim,” that is, he was exalted above the fullness of knowledge, which is charity, so that no one might reach God except through charity. “And he flew,” because he shows himself incomprehensible to his lovers, lest they seek to comprehend him by bodily images. He flew, I say, “upon the wings of the winds,” because his incomprehensibility surpasses the powers of souls, which, as though by wings, raise themselves from earthly fears into the breezes of freedom.

“And he made darkness his hiding place,” that is, hidden hope in the heart of believers, where he remains concealed without abandoning them. “And he made darkness his hiding place,” that is, the obscurity of the sacraments in which he is hidden. For divinity lay hidden in flesh; forgiveness of sins in baptism; Christ on the altar under the sacrament of bread. Or, “he made darkness his hiding place,” that is, he lies hidden amid these darknesses of mortal life, where we walk by faith and not by sight; where we hope for what we do not see and wait for it in patience. And although he is hidden, nonetheless [Col. 0192B] “his tent is round about him,” that is, converts among whom he dwells and serves in this present time surround him as their center, because he favors all equally. Yet even through the Scriptures they do not now see him by sight, because “dark water,” that is, obscure teaching, is “in the clouds of the air,” that is, in the prophets and in all preachers who, raised above earthly things, rain the word of God upon those below. It is obscure, I say:

VERS. 14. — “Before the brightness in his presence, clouds passed over: hail and coals of fire.”

“Before the brightness which will be in his presence,” [Augustine] that is, in comparison with the brightness which will be in his manifestation. For now we see through a mirror, but then face to face (I Cor. XIII). [Augustine] Therefore, lest anyone think himself to be in the future light merely because he rightly understands the Scriptures, it follows: “clouds passed over.” As if to say: dark water is in the clouds; these clouds, that is, preachers of the divine word, passed over [Col. 0192C] to the Gentiles and are no longer only in Judaea.

[Jerome] Otherwise, from “He bent down the heavens”: that is, he humbled preachers from the contemplative life to the service of the active life, so that Rachel might yield her husband to Leah. And through their teaching he himself descended into the understanding of certain simple persons unable to grasp greater things. Hence it says, “he descended”; or, “he bent down the heavens,” [Alcuin] that is, he humbled preachers to bear troubles. “And he descended,” suffering himself in them, with whom he is one. Hence he is said to suffer in them, as he himself says: “Behold, I am coming to Rome to be crucified again.” [Note: [Col. 0191D] From the history of the Passion of the Apostle Peter.] It follows: “And his darkness,” that is, those in darkness who even persecute, “is beneath his feet,” [Alcuin] that is, under his power. Or “darkness,” that is, those who believe simply, are beneath his feet, that is, subject to him. It follows:

[Col. 0193A] “And he ascended,” [Jerome] as it were in certain persons through the heavens, that is, through preachers; namely, he descended in the weak. But there are others in whom he ascends through those same persons. This is: “And he ascended above the cherubim,” [Alcuin] that is, he makes certain persons full of knowledge, in whom he is preeminent; yet even they do not wholly comprehend him, because “he flew upon the wings of the winds,” [Augustine] that is, he surpasses the swiftness of their understanding. “And he made darkness his hiding place,” [Alcuin] that is, he secretly employs those in darkness, as he himself says through the prophet: “Assyria is the rod of my anger; but he himself did not know” (Isa. X). For through the Assyrian—that is, through Sennacherib or Nebuchadnezzar—God afflicted the Jews who sinned against him, and many others; nor did the Assyrian understand why this was done, or by whose power. But [Col. 0193B] “his tent” [35] “is round about him,” [Alcuin] that is, his soldiers know what is being done through the wicked.

It follows: “Dark water in the clouds of the ether.” Another reading, according to what is found in the Hebrew: “Before the brightness in his presence, clouds.” Here make the division. As if to say: through the heavens, that is, the teachers of the New Testament, he descends into the knowledge of the lesser; but he ascends into the knowledge of the greater. But through the clouds of the ether, that is, through the prophets—in which clouds there is dark water, [Cassiodorus] that is, obscure teaching—he does not ascend and descend in the same way, because, covered by the shadow of figures, they did not irradiate others with the light of doctrine. But clouds which are not of the ether, that is, the apostles, are “before the brightness”—one expression—that is, exceedingly bright. “In his presence,” that is, [Col. 0193C] contemplating him more closely. And these clouds passed over, because the preachers passed from Judaea to the Gentiles. Here the reading is brought together into one.

And from those who passed over came forth “hail and coals of fire,” [Augustine] that is, rebukes which, like hail, strike hard hearts. But if the fire of charity melts their hardness, it becomes water that satisfies in a gentle mind. And they are coals because hearts kindled by that fire revive.

VERS. 15. — “And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice: hail and coals of fire.”

“And he thundered”: as if to say, the clouds passed over, and through those who passed over the Lord, who is “from heaven,” [Gloss interlinearis] that is, exalted, thundered with threats concerning eternal punishments. And the Most High—this is what he had called “from heaven”—gave [Col. 0193D] his sweet voice, which concerns eternal rewards.

Or thus: “The Lord thundered from heaven,” [Augustine, Gloss interlinearis] that is, the Lord sounded from the heart of the righteous when he speaks great mysteries; this is the confidence of the Gospel. Through this, both the preachers themselves preach more confidently and the hearers believe the preachers more trustingly. “And the Most High gave his voice,” [Augustine] so that we might hear heavenly things in the depth of the world.

Or literally, the Lord thundered from heaven, [Cassiodorus] as when thunder was heard, as is read in the Gospel, God the Father saying: “I have glorified him, and I shall glorify him again” (John XII). “And the Most High gave his voice” when he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III). From this came “hail and coals of fire,” as explained above. It follows:

[Col. 0194A] VERS. 16. — “And he sent his arrows and scattered them; he multiplied lightnings and troubled them.”

“And he sent.” As if to say: the Lord thundered and the Lord sent. [Alcuin] As if to say, they do not pass over at random, but are sent; for the apostles’ passage to the Gentiles did not always appear certain or reasonable. Therefore he says: “And he sent his arrows,” [Augustine] that is, evangelists flying straight with the wings of virtues; “and he scattered,” or dispersed, those to whom he sent them, so that to some they might be an odor of life unto life, to others an odor of death unto death (II Cor. II). “He also multiplied lightnings,” that is, miracles which render people astonished. Hence he adds: “and troubled them.”

VERS. 17. — “And the fountains of waters appeared, [Col. 0194B] and the foundations of the world were revealed.”

“And the fountains of waters appeared,” [Cassiodorus] that is, the truth of preachers, who are compared to waters because they water others with doctrine. [Augustine] Or, “fountains of waters appeared,” fountains springing up unto eternal life, which were made in the preachers; “and the foundations of the world were revealed,” [Augustine, Gloss interlinearis] that is, the prophets were revealed—that is, those who had formerly not been understood—upon whom the believing world is built, namely the Church, called “the world” because it is gathered from the whole world. And he fittingly says “revealed”: [Cassiodorus] for at Christ’s coming it became clear what the divine utterance had concealed. Thus, on the day of the Passion, those sacraments are uncovered in the Church which, during the preceding forty-day period, had been covered.

[Col. 0194C] VERS. 18. — “At your rebuke, O Lord, at the breathing forth of the spirit of your anger.”

“At your rebuke.” [Alcuin] Here there is a turning toward God himself, to whom he speaks as though in thanksgiving. As if to say: all these things were done, O Lord, by your rebuke, [Augustine] that is, by you crying out: “The kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. IV); and by the breathing forth of the spirit of your anger, that is, by you saying: “Unless you repent, you shall die by death” (Luke XIII). [Cassiodorus] He understands Christ’s rebuke and breathing forth as preaching, because by preaching he rebuked sinners and inspired them to fear the wrath to come. It follows:

VERS. 19. — “He sent from on high and took me; and he drew me out of many waters.”

[Col. 0194D] “He sent from on high.” [Cassiodorus] Up to this point he has dealt with the Lord’s coming. From here he treats of Christian times, in the person of the present Church, without changing voice. As if to say: all this was done because God the Father sent Christ “from on high,” that is, from heaven; and he took me, the Church his bride, and drew me out of many waters, that is, from the waters of baptism. [Augustine]

Or, “he took me,” the glorious Church, first by calling her from the Gentiles into his inheritance. Hence he adds: “and he drew me out of many waters,” that is, from a multitude of peoples. [Alcuin]

Or thus: he sent the Holy Spirit, who is a gift, from on high, that is, from above, because he is equal to the Father and the Son. For the Holy Spirit is one God with the Father and the Son, and a gift because he can be given, and is given when he begins to be present in someone according to [Col. 0195A] the charisms of grace. Although these are bestowed alike by the Father and the Son, they are nevertheless frequently called gifts of the Holy Spirit because they are granted to us from love; and the Holy Spirit is the love of each, namely of the Father toward the Son and of the Son toward the Father, and the bond joining both. It follows: “And he took me,” as if a fugitive; and “he drew me up” to the height of virtue and good work. And this “from many waters”: this does not change.

VERS. 20. — “He delivered me from my very strong enemies, and from those who hate me, because they were strengthened against me.”

“He delivered me from my very strong enemies,” that is, from riches, which harm above all enemies; and from those who hate wickedness, [Alcuin] that is, from external enemies—human beings and demons—which was necessary, because formerly “they were strengthened against me,” [Augustine] so long as I was under them and did not know God. He speaks of himself according to his state before conversion. In what respect were they strengthened? Behold:

VERS. 21. — “They came before me in the day of my affliction, and the Lord became my protector.”

“They came before me,” that is, they prevailed over me, “in the day of my affliction,” [Gloss interlinearis] in the time of my carnality.

Or, by “enemies” and “those who hate,” he means persecutors; and the Church speaks of herself according to her state after conversion, saying: [Augustine] “He delivered me from my enemies,” who envied me when I now desired him; “very strong,” because they temporarily prevailed in afflicting and perverting this temporal life of mine; “and from [Col. 0195C] those who hate me,” because I desire him. I say that he delivered me through the fact that “they were strengthened against me.” For he delivered me all the more through their being strengthened. [Cassiodorus] For when the Church is afflicted, it grows more. “And they came before me,” [Gloss interlinearis] that is, they harmed me first, by comparison with runners; and this was not in a time of joy but “in the day of my affliction,” that is, during the time of flesh in which, [Augustine] namely, I bear a mortal and laborious body. “And the Lord became my protector” against miseries and pleasures. It follows:

VERS. 22. — “And he brought me out into a broad place; he saved me, because he willed me.”

“And he brought me out.” As if to say: when I suffered the narrownesses of the flesh, God brought me out into spiritual breadth against [Col. 0195D] the straits of the flesh, to enlarge me in merit and number. [Cassiodorus] For through evils God enlarges charity; indeed, through the cruelty of the wicked the Church increases in merit. And “he saved me,” which occurred [Cassiodorus] when I came to faith. For as unbelief is the death of the soul, so faith is its life. Hence: “My righteous one lives by faith” (Heb. X). And he did all this because “he willed me” before I willed him—that is, he chose me freely.

VERS. 23. — “And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the purity of my hands he will repay me.”

“And he will repay.” [Gloss interlinearis] As if to say: he gave all these things freely, namely faith and charity. But afterwards he will repay me here in the present life according to my righteousness, [Col. 0196A] [Augustine] that is, according to the righteousness of good will—he who mercifully gave me to will what is good—and he will repay me here according to the purity of my hands, [Cassiodorus] that is, of my deeds—he who gave me to act, by bringing me out into breadth. That is, he repays me according to the righteousness of good will and according to works which follow God’s first benefits, namely faith and charity, which God grants freely, without preceding merit. [Alcuin] Then, for these—namely faith and charity—and for the works arising from them, he repays spiritual goods as though for merits. Here in the present life, namely perseverance and other things. Hence he adds:

VERS. 24. — “For I have kept the ways of the Lord, and have not acted wickedly in departing from my God.”

[Col. 0196B] “For I have kept.” [Augustine] As if to say: he will repay this because I have kept the ways of the Lord, so that long-suffering in perseverance may attain breadth of works; and I have not acted wickedly by departing from my God.

Or thus: “The Lord will repay me according to my righteousness and according to the purity of my hands,” [Alcuin] that is, he will repay me according as I am righteous and pure, that is, innocent. I am righteous because I have kept the ways of the Lord. I am pure because I have not acted wickedly by departing from my God. And both these things are so because I considered God’s judgments, both present and future; I saw that they were just, found them just, and did not reject them—that is, they pleased me—and thus I kept them. This is what he says:

VERS. 25. — “For all his judgments are before me, and I have not cast away his ordinances from me.”

[Col. 0196C] “For all his judgments are before me,” [Augustine] that is, I always attend to and consider with persevering contemplation the rewards of the righteous, the punishments of the ungodly, the chastisements of those needing correction, and the trials of those being proved. “And his ordinances,” [Cassiodorus] that is, those judgments found to be just, “I have not cast away from me,” as does one who fails under their burden and returns to his vomit; or one who, overcome by the weakness of the flesh, abandons what he had begun. It follows:

VERS. 26. — “And I shall be spotless with him, and I shall keep myself from my iniquity.”

“And I shall be.” [Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinearis] As if to say: I lived thus formerly; and as I began, so afterwards I shall be “with him,” that is, adhering to him, spotless. [Alcuin] Not that I shall be wholly [Col. 0196D] without stain, [Cassiodorus] but because I shall keep myself from my iniquity, lest I fall again through mortal sin, which is the death of the blessed person. It follows:

VERS. 27. — “And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the purity of my hands before his eyes.”

“And he will repay me.” [Cassiodorus] Above he said that he would be repaid in the present life for faith, charity, and works; here he speaks of the future, and adds that he will be repaid for the same things, where a reward will also be rendered for the long-suffering of perseverance, which, as said above, is rendered in the present life for faith and works. This is: “And the Lord will repay me,” in the future, “according to my righteousness and according to the purity of my hands.” [Augustine] Therefore, not only on account of the breadth of faith which works through love (Gal. V), but also [Col. 0197A] on account of long-suffering, he will repay me, who am “before his eyes.” [Cassiodorus] This can be said only by the righteous: as they continually behold the Lord, so may the Lord continually look upon them.

Or he defines what God will repay him: namely that which is “before his eyes,” [Augustine] not what people see, but what God alone sees; for the things seen by people are temporal, whereas the unseen are eternal (II Cor. XIV). To this pertains the height of hope.

VERS. 28. — “With the holy you will be holy, and with the [36] innocent man you will be innocent.”

“With the holy, holy.” [Alcuin] He had said that he would be repaid according to his righteousness. Now, so that grace may be seen together with free choice, he shows how righteousness is possessed; and there is a turning toward the Lord, as though in thanksgiving. As if to say: although I said, “He will repay me according to my righteousness,” nevertheless, O Lord, you will be holy with the holy—that is, you help the holy person in holiness—[Jerome] because you are holy by nature and sanctify others by grace; and “with the innocent man you will be innocent,” that is, you help the innocent person in innocence, because you are innocent.

VERS. 29. — “And with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will be perverted.”

“And with the chosen you will be chosen,” [Augustine] that is, you are chosen by the one whom you choose; “and with the perverse you will be perverted,” [Alcuin] that is, you pervert the perverse person, that is, you allow him to be perverted. Note that according to two judgments—the hidden one, namely [Col. 0197C] which is now taking place, and the manifest one which will occur in the future—God repays good and evil persons in two ways. Here he repays so that the righteous may become more righteous, and the one who is filthy may become filthier still (Rev. XXII). Thus he says here: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will be perverted.” In the future, he will repay the good with reward and the wicked with punishment. Thus there he says:

VERS. 30. — “For you will save the humble people, and you will humble the eyes of the proud.”

“For you [will save] the humble people.” [Cassiodorus] As if to say: here you will act thus toward good and evil persons; and this is because in the future you will save the humble people and humble the eyes of the proud, [Augustine] who, ignorant of God’s righteousness, wish to establish their own (Rom. X), [Col. 0197D] [Cassiodorus] however high they may be.

Or thus, “with the holy,” and he speaks to men. As if to say: just as I shall be spotless with him, so you, whoever you are, will be holy with the holy one, namely Christ, who is the Holy of holies—that is, through his gift you will be holy; and with the innocent man, namely Christ, you will be innocent; and with the chosen one, namely Christ, you will be chosen; and with the perverse one, the devil, you will be perverted, that is, you will be perverse. This is an argument from association, because character is formed by association: “He who touches pitch is defiled by it” (Ecclus. XIII). And all this is so because you, O Lord, will save the humble people.

Or thus: “With the holy you will be holy.” As if to say: it is hidden that you will repay the saints in the future. [Augustine] There is also a hidden depth in which it is understood that “with the holy you will be holy,” namely sanctifying him, because you are understood; holy with the holy because you sanctify; and in which it is understood that “with the innocent man you will be innocent,” because you harm no one, but each person is bound with the cords of his own sins; and “with the chosen you will be chosen,” that is, you are chosen by the one whom you choose; and “with the perverse you will be perverted,” that is, you appear perverse to the perverse, because the wicked say: “The way of the Lord is not right” (Ezek. XVIII). [Col. 0198A] And this is because you will save the humble people. [Augustine] To them it appears perverse that you save those confessing sins and humble the eyes of the proud. This does not change.

VERS. 31. — “For you enlighten my lamp, O Lord my God; enlighten my darkness.”

“For you enlighten.” [Alcuin] What he had stated above concerning certain members who are chosen and sanctified, here he prays concerning others; [Cassiodorus] and thus the Church proceeds. For above it affirmed that he sanctifies saints; here it prays that he may enlighten others who are darkness, speaking to the Father thus: O Lord, Father, who are my God, you enlighten my lamp, that is, the apostles and the other earliest preachers. [Cassiodorus] For preachers were lamps, in whom was light, that is, knowledge of truth, through which they enlightened others, just as a lamp contains light in an earthen vessel. Hence the Apostle says: “Having this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Cor. IV). Since you enlighten my lamp, that is, the preachers, [Alcuin] through them enlighten my darkness, [Col. 0198C] that is, those who are still in darkness. I call them “my darkness” because, although they are in darkness, they are nevertheless mine by predestination.

Or thus, so that no distinction is made between “lamp” and “darkness”: [Augustine] the same persons are signified by each expression, though under different aspects. For we are called a lamp because we do not possess light from ourselves, just as a lamp does not shine of itself; but we are called darkness because we are dark through our vices. Thus: “For you enlighten my lamp, O Lord,” that is, because our light is not from ourselves but from you; “you who are my God, enlighten my darkness,” that is, enlighten us who are darkness through our sins.

VERS. 32. — “For in you I shall be delivered from temptation, [Col. 0198D] and in my God I shall pass beyond the wall.”

“For in you.” [Augustine, Gloss interlinearis] As if to say: I ask you, and with good reason, because in you, that is, through you, I shall be delivered from the devil’s temptation. [Cassiodorus] Then, changing person in joy, he says: “And in my God,” not in myself, “I shall pass beyond the wall,” [Augustine] which sins have built between human beings and heaven. Note that he does not say, “I shall destroy it,” but “I shall pass beyond it.” [Cassiodorus] For a human being cannot utterly destroy it; but with God’s help he passes beyond the wall, that is, the obstacle of sins.

VERS. 33. — “My God: his way is unstained; the words of the Lord have been tested by fire; he is the protector of all who hope in him.”

God, as though he said: “Truly, O God, I shall be delivered in you, because you, my God, will deliver me from the contentions of the people.” [Col. 0199A] [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] Thus far the grammatical construction extends: he inserts the rest in commendation of him, changing person and speaking of him to others thus: “My God will deliver me.” And his way is undefiled, that is, he proceeds only by a pure way, [Augustine] because he does not come to human beings unless they cleanse the way of faith by which he may come, since his way is undefiled. Hence: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Isa. 40). And elsewhere the prophet cries: “Choose out the stones from the streets” (Isa. 62). From this comes the custom that, on the principal feasts, man-made churches are cleaned and adorned so that the high priest may enter with a procession. Thus you too should adorn the bridal chamber of your mind, so that the eternal priest, with the fullness of graces, may enter into you and gradually make you advance from strength to strength. [Col. 0199B] It follows: “and the words of the Lord are tested by fire,” [Augustine] that is, they are proved by the fire of tribulation. And “the Lord is the protector of all who hope in him,” that is, tribulation will not consume those who hope not in themselves but in him. And rightly he deals first with faith and afterwards with hope, because hope follows faith. [Cassiodorus.] He adds, “of all”: for no one is excluded except one who refuses to hope.

Or thus: “My God.” As though he said: “In my God I shall pass over.” For my God has this, that his way is undefiled—[Alcuin] namely, that he himself is the undefiled way by which one goes to heaven. [Jerome.] Or he has this, that his way by which he came into the world is undefiled, namely, the holy and immaculate Virgin Mary; and according to this interpretation the grammatical construction does not look back to what precedes. It follows: “And the words of the Lord,” [Col. 0199C] that is, of Christ, “are tested by fire,” that is, by the Holy Spirit. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] That is, whatever he said was examined by the Holy Spirit—that is, useful and honourable—just as a wise person judges beforehand within himself whatever he is about to say.

**VERSE 34.**—“For who is God except the Lord? Or who is God except our God?”

“For who,” as though he said: “My God”—and rightly so. “For what other God is there except the Lord,” that is, except him who is Lord over worldly things? Or “who is God except our God?” [Cassiodorus.] That is, he who was born in Judaea? The gods of the Gentiles are not gods. He says this against pagans, who invent many gods for themselves.

Or thus, since the connection is not changed: as though he said, [Col. 0199D] [Augustine] “I say, God, because who else is God except our Lord, whom we serve by obligation? Or who is God on account of our God, whom, after good service, we sons possess as a separate inheritance?”

## PART II. VERSE 35.—“God, who girded me with strength and made my way spotless.”

“God who girded me.” [Alcuin.] The third part. He still commends him, beyond the general matters, by particular ones. For he had said that he is protector and helper; now he teaches specifically how and in what respects he is helper and protector. [Jerome.] As though he said: “I rightly called him my God.” For God is he who girded me, that is, armed me beforehand. Or, “girded,” by comparison with a runner, lest the flowing folds of desire impede the steps, that is, [Col. 0200A] good works. [Augustine.] He girded me, I say, with strength, so that I may be strong; and here the Church speaks. It follows: “and made my way spotless,” namely the charity by which I may ascend to him. For just as faith, by which he came to me, is spotless, so too is the charity by which I go to him. It follows: he is

**VERSE 36.**—“Who made my feet like those of harts, and sets me upon high places.”

“Who made my feet,” [Augustine] that is, my love, by which I go to him, “like those of harts,” that is, for passing beyond the thorny and shadowy entanglements of the age. And he is the one who sets me upon high places, that is, fixes the intention of my heart in heaven. And he is

**VERSE 37.**—“Who teaches my hands for battle, [Col. 0200B] and made my arms like a bronze bow.”

[Augustine.] “Who teaches my hands for battle” against vices and demons; that is, he teaches us to work so as to overcome enemies who strive to block the way to heaven. Then, changing person, he adds: “and you made my arms like a bronze bow,” that is, you gave me an unfailing resolve for good works and conduct.

**VERSE 38.**—“And you gave me the protection of your salvation, and your right hand upheld me.”

“And you gave me the protection of your salvation,” [Augustine] that is, you protected me unto salvation, because the things mentioned above are insufficient unless God’s protection is present; “and your right hand,” that is, the favour of your grace, upheld me.

**VERSE 39.**—“And your discipline corrected me unto the end, and that same discipline will teach me.”

[Col. 0200C] “And your discipline,” [Alcuin] as though he said, “you will protect me,” certainly not so that I suffer nothing—yet suffering is for progress. And “and,” that is, “because,” “your discipline corrected,” or directed, or raised me up, “unto the end”: that is, your correction does not allow me to stray, [Augustine] so that whatever I do I refer to that end in which one cleaves to you. “And that same discipline will teach me” to persist in better things; [Gloss, Augustine] that is, the same discipline will teach me to reach the place toward which it directed me, nor do bodily hardships hinder me. For:

**VERSE 40.**—“You enlarged my steps beneath me, and my footprints have not been weakened.”

“You enlarged my steps beneath me,” [Augustine] that is, you made charity broad, working cheerfully even through those things which are beneath me, namely mortal [Col. 0200D] things and members. “And my footprints have not been weakened by the evils of the world,” that is, my paths, or the marks which I left for imitators. [Alcuin.] From these words it is evident that tribulation is correction, instruction, enlargement, and strengthening. “They have not been weakened,” I say, but:

**VERSE 41.**—“I shall pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I shall not turn back until they fail.”

“I shall pursue my enemies,” [Augustine] that is, my carnal affections, “and overtake them,” so that they may be consumed and not overtake me. “And I shall not turn back from this intention until they fail” in rebellion—those which now make resistance.

[Col. 0201A]

**VERSE 42.**—“I shall break them, and they shall not be able to stand; they shall fall beneath my feet.”

“I shall break them, and they shall not be able to stand,” that is, they shall not endure against me; “they shall fall beneath my feet,” that is, I shall prefer to them the loves by which one goes into eternity. And all this comes from him because:

**VERSE 43.**—“And you girded me with strength for battle; you tripped up beneath me those rising against me.”

“You girded me with strength for battle,” [Augustine] that is, you bound up the flowing desires of the flesh with strength, lest I be hindered in battle. “You tripped up beneath me those rising against me.” These words suit Christ the Head, in whose person the whole may also be understood from the place, “God who girded me with strength.”

[Col. 0201B]

## PART II

[Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which Christ speaks of his strength and power, saying: God the Father is he “who girded me with strength.” By this he indicates dignity and might, fitting for one who will judge the world by his own power; “and made,” that is, established, “my way spotless,” that is, without sin; “who made my feet like those of harts.” For as a hart leaps over thorns and rough places, so Christ avoided the thorns and pits of sins. “And he sets me upon high places.” As though he said: as the hart seeks the heights, so Christ ascended above all creatures. And he is the one “who teaches,” making me wary of threatening snares, “my hands,” that is, works or wills, “for battle against the devil”; “and made my arms like a bronze bow,” that is, [Col. 0201C] you gave me unremitting strength. [Alcuin.] And this is a likeness of something which does not exist.

[Cassiodorus.] Or Christ’s arms are the prophets and apostles through whom he works. They are a bronze bow because, in preaching, they do not grow soft but continually, with strength, shoot forth words of salvation. “And you gave me the protection of your salvation,” that is, the glory of the resurrection; “and your right hand,” namely your divine power, “upheld me,” that is, placed me, a man, on high. “And your discipline corrected,” or directed, “me unto the end,” and so forth—this as regards the effect, because the result of correction and instruction was found in Christ, who nevertheless was neither corrected from evil nor taught what he did not know. “You enlarged my steps beneath me,” that is, you made known throughout the world even the works of my lower nature, [Col. 0201D] namely, humanity; “and my footprints have not been weakened,” that is, the signs which he left for imitators. And because you thus established me in strength, “I shall pursue my enemies,” [Jerome, Alcuin] that is, the Jews, reproving them and wearying them with diverse afflictions, “and overtake them,” that is, encompass them with true arguments. “And I shall not turn back from this work until they fail” in rebellion. “I shall break them,” [Cassiodorus] that is, afflict them with various miseries; “and they shall not be able to stand” against me, “and they shall fall beneath my feet,” that is, I shall subject them to myself. And this is because “you girded me with strength for battle,” against demons and Jews. “And you tripped up those rising against me, so that they might be beneath me,” [Augustine] that is, you caused my pursuers to be deceived, so that those who wished to prevail over me might be subject to me.

[Col. 0202A]

**VERSE 44.**—“And you gave my enemies their back to me, and you destroyed those who hated me.”

“And you gave my enemies their back to me,” that is, you caused them to follow me; and “those who hated me,” [Augustine, Gloss] that is, those persisting in hatred, you destroyed throughout the whole world. There, that is, in that dispersion:

**VERSE 45.**—“They cried out, and there was none to save them; to the Lord, and he did not hear them.”

[Augustine.] They cried out to other gods, and there was none to save them. For another could not do so: who could save those whom you did not save? Afterwards they cried to the Lord, and he did not hear them, that is, he did not judge them worthy to be heard. As though he said: another cannot save; you are unwilling to save, because they do not withdraw from their wickedness.

[Col. 0202B]

**VERSE 46.**—“And I shall grind them as dust before the face of the wind; I shall wipe them away as the mud of the streets.”

“And I shall grind them.” [Gloss, Alcuin.] As though he said: “You destroyed them, and beyond their dispersion I shall grind them as dust before the face of the wind,” that is, I shall take away their virtues, so that they may yield to every wind of doctrine and suggestion. And so it came to pass, [Augustine] because they are dry, without the rain of God’s mercy, so that, lifted up and puffed up by pride, they may be swept away from firm hope, as from the solidity of earth. Behold the same action of Father and Son. [Alcuin.] For above he had said to the Father, “you destroyed”; here he says, “I shall grind.” “And I shall wipe them away as the mud of the streets,” [Augustine] that is, I shall wipe them away as luxuriant and slippery persons walking through broad ways which lead to death.

[Col. 0202C]

**VERSE 47.**—“You will deliver me from the contentions of the people; you will establish me as head of the nations.”

“You will deliver me.” [Alcuin.] Here again the passage is understood in the person of Christ the Head. As though he said, concerning them: [Augustine] “but you will deliver me from the contentions of the people,” the Jews, who said: “If we let him go on thus, the whole world will follow him” (John 11); “and you will establish me as head of the nations,” that is, so that I may be head of the nations. And truly, because:

**VERSE 48.**—“A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me.”

[Augustine.] “The people of the nations whom I did not know,” that is, whom I did not visit in bodily presence, nor in the Law and the Prophets, “served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me.” [Col. 0202D] [Jerome, Augustine.] They did not see with their eyes, but obeyed through preachers. [Alcuin.] Note that this sequence contains the exaltation of the nations and the humiliation of the Jews, concerning whom he adds:

**VERSE 49.**—“Foreign sons lied to me; foreign sons grew old, and they limped from their paths.”

“Foreign sons.” As though he said: “The people of the nations obeyed, [Alcuin] but the sons”—that is, the Jews, whom I nourished and exalted—“having become foreign, lied to me,” that is, concerning my honour. Hence elsewhere: “Through the greatness of your power, your enemies will lie to you” (Ps. 65). Or thus: they are to be called not my sons [Augustine] but foreign sons, that is, the Jews, to whom it is said: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8). “They lied to me.” Of them Isaiah says: [Col. 0203A] “Woe to the sinful nation, to a people full of sins, to foreign sons!” (Isa. 1). [Jerome.] For previously the Jews were called sons because of the prerogative of their father, as he says through Moses to Pharaoh: “Dismiss Israel, my firstborn” (Exod. 4). But through sin they became foreign. And he repeats it in reproach: “foreign sons grew old,” [Augustine] that is, they remained in the old man, though I came to renew them; “and they limped.” As though he said: weak in one foot, because while holding the Old Testament and rejecting the New, they became lame, possessing one foot and lacking the other. And even in that which they possess they are lame, because “they limped even from their paths,” that is, even in the old Law they are lame, following their own traditions rather than God’s.

**VERSE 50.**—“The Lord lives, and blessed be my God, [Col. 0203B] and let the God of my salvation be exalted.”

“The Lord lives.” [Cassiodorus.] The fourth part, in which the exulting Church praises in summary God’s gifts. As though he said: because God does the things mentioned above, it is evident that the Lord lives, because he gives life to all things; and my God is blessed, because he blesses all things. Therefore “let the God of my salvation be exalted,” that is, let him be believed in throughout the whole world.

Or thus: “The Lord lives,” because by firm faith he is seen by me as present in my heart. “And let my God be blessed,” that is, praised. “And let the God of my salvation be exalted,” [Augustine] that is, let him give me salvation in the height, not in the depth—that is, heavenly and not temporal salvation. For I shall not think of the God of my salvation in an earthly way, nor of salvation itself as earthly; rather, I shall hope in him on high. Then, turning his speech toward God, he says:

[Col. 0203C]

**VERSE 51.**—“God, who gives me avengings and subjects peoples beneath me, my deliverer from my wrathful enemies.”

“God who gives,” as though he said: “I exhort you to bless God, and with good reason, because you, God, are he who gives”—the Church says—“avengings to me,” [Augustine] by subjecting peoples to me. Hence, as though explaining, he adds: “and you subject peoples beneath me.” [Cassiodorus.] It is a pious vengeance when a rebel is made subject. You, I say, are “my deliverer from my enemies,” not enemies of just any sort, but wrathful ones. It is greater glory to be delivered from evils that burn fiercely.

**VERSE 52.**—“And you will exalt me above those rising against me; you will deliver me from the unjust man.”

“And you will exalt me above those rising against me.” [Cassiodorus.] [Col. 0203D] For the more fiercely one rises in anger, the more greatly is the one exalted who endured it. “And from the unjust man,” [Remigius] that is, from any schismatic, “you will deliver me.”

**VERSE 53.**—“Therefore I shall confess you among the nations, O Lord, and sing a psalm to your name.”

“Therefore,” [Remigius] that is, because of the things said above, “I shall confess to you among the nations, O Lord,” both praises and sins; “and I shall sing a psalm to your name,” [Augustine] that is, you will become more widely known through my good works.

**VERSE 54.**—“Magnifying the salvations of his king and showing mercy to his anointed, David, and to his seed for ever.”

“Magnifying salvations.” The grammatical construction refers back to the preceding words: “let the God of my salvation be exalted.” I mean God, “magnifying,” that is, who magnifies “the salvations of his king,” [Col. 0204A] Christ—that is, makes wonderful the salvations which his Son gives to believers. And I mean God “showing,” that is, who shows mercy “to his anointed David,” that is, to the deliverer himself, mighty of hand, who conquered this world; “and to his seed,” that is, those whom he begot as believers in the Gospel. And this is “for ever,” that is, without end.

[Jerome.] Or it may be understood from the point where Christ the Head speaks to the Father: “O God the Father, you are he who gives me avengings upon the Jews and subjects peoples,” that is, nations, “beneath me. You,” I say, are “my deliverer from my wrathful enemies,” [Augustine] the Jews, who during the Passion cried: “Crucify, crucify” (John 19). “And you will exalt me above those rising against me,” while I suffer, by raising me or causing me to ascend; “and you will deliver [Col. 0204B] me from the unjust man,” that is, from their unjust kingdom. “Therefore I shall confess you among the nations, O Lord,” that is, the nations through me will confess you; “and I shall sing a psalm to your name,” that is, you will become more widely known through my good works. “Magnifying”—after inserting the Head’s words, the Church returns to what it had begun: as though it said, “Let God be exalted”—I mean God, “magnifying the salvations of his king and showing mercy to his anointed David and to his seed for ever.” These words are unchanged.

## Comparison on Psalm XVII: “I Will Love You”

**VERSE 4.**—“I shall invoke the Lord, praising.” Jerome, Sanctes, Münster, the interpreter for Cajetan, and Campensis say: “I shall invoke the Lord as praised,” or “worthy of praise”; yet the text in Campensis has, “when I sing with praises, the Lord”; Pratensis: “I shall invoke [him] as praised,” and so forth. The Septuagint and Pellican have “praising.” In Hebrew the letters are entirely identical whether the sense is “praising” [Col. 0204C] or “praised.” The vowel points make the distinction: it may be read *MEHULLAL*, that is, “praised,” or *MEHALLEL*, that is, “praising.” Since the Hebrews lack case-declension, some translated, “praised, I shall invoke,” which is less suitable; others, “I shall invoke [him] as praised.” Owing also to a different pronunciation of the points, it could be rendered “praising,” as we read it. The Chaldee too interprets: “While praising, I shall pray before God.”

**VERSE 9.**—“He was angry with them.” Faber judges that the pronoun “with them” is superfluous. Hebrew reads *HARAH LO*, which, rendered word for word, means “he was angry with him,” so that it refers to the earth mentioned a little earlier; Nebiensis and the Chaldee interpreter understand it in this way. Yet it seems to be opposed by the fact that “earth” is feminine in Hebrew, although Sanctes, Pratensis, and Münster take it to mean that God himself was angry. Jerome, however, in the Hebrew version [Col. 0204D] has with us, “he was angry with them,” if indeed our manuscripts are accurate. From this you may know that he read *LAMO*, that is, “with them.” I wished to pass over this very small point, since it disturbs nothing in the sense, had I not found persons wishing to pierce it with a spit.

**VERSE 15.**—“The Most High gave his voice: hail and coals of fire.” Here Faber and Caecus criticize this as an unsuitable construction, since according to Latin usage it should properly be said, “he gave his voice, hail and coals of fire,” with an apposition in the accusative case. As though one could not understand the verb “they descended,” as Münster indicates and Pratensis and Sanctes understand. And although Jerome translates with the accusative, he did not reject the other version entirely. This is clear from his treatise to Sunnia and Fretela, where he answers why the Greeks do not have this verse, “hail and coals of fire,” in the second Psalm, after two verses have intervened. “But it must be known,” he says, “that it was added under an asterisk in the Septuagint translation from the Hebrew and from Theodotion’s edition.” [Col. 0205A]

**VERSE 32.**—“For in you I shall be delivered from temptation.” Jerome, following the Hebrews, has “in you I shall run girded,” and Pellican follows him. Others translate, “I shall break a troop,” or “an army,” or “a wedge of soldiers.” The Septuagint made explicit the sense of that metaphor. But since *GADAD* signifies “he girded himself for battle,” Jerome took the participle not as a noun—as when it is read [reading uncertain in the source]—that is, “a girding for battle,” which very fittingly corresponds to temptation, which tests a human being and summons him to battle. For Job 7 says: “Human life upon earth is warfare.” Therefore Faber had no reason to criticize this edition in this place, he who wishes that it refer solely to Christ, who ascends unencumbered to God the Father. Rather, he should have noticed the unity of body and head, because of which Scripture regularly passes back and forth from one to the other. [Col. 0205B] Augustine teaches this practice more frequently, and here too interprets the passage concerning the members.

**VERSE 37.**—“You made my arms like a bronze bow.” Jerome, in the Hebrew version, does not disagree. The others convey the meaning by translating: “a bronze bow was broken by my arms.” They take the word set down in Hebrew, *NIHATAH*, as inflected from the root *HATATH*. The Septuagint interpreters, with Jerome, derived it from the stem *NAHAH*, that is, “he led,” so that the letter *nun* is radical and it is read *NAHITA*, meaning “you led,” or, as Pellican translates, “you stretched my arms like a bronze bow.” The Chaldee says: “Strengthen my arm like a steel bow.”

**VERSE 39.**—“And your discipline corrected me unto the end.” This is not found in Hebrew manuscripts. But Faber’s addition that it is not found in Greek either is false, since we read, *καὶ ἥ παιδεία σου ἀνώρτωσε με εἰς τέλος*: “and your discipline raised me up unto the end.” Perhaps Faber used another manuscript. Moreover, it appears that the Septuagint wished to explain what immediately follows: “your discipline itself will teach me.” Or, as those more closely following the letter translate: “will multiply me.” How the Church increased through persecutions by tyrants, attacks by heretics, and temptations from the wicked is shown by the advancement of the saints from the beginning of the world, who, instructed by the Lord’s discipline, were multiplied like the stars of heaven. Nor is this hindered by the fact that Jerome, following the Hebrew with the others, has “your gentleness [Col. 0206A] will multiply me,” because the Hebrew word *INACH*, or *ANACH*, sometimes means “he afflicted”; from it is derived the particle used here, *ANAVAH*. Thus it does not prevent it from likewise signifying the affliction by which we are otherwise tested by God together with gentleness. For “whom he loves he rebukes, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12).

**VERSE 49.**—“They limped from their paths.” Jerome gives almost the same rendering for the first word, namely “they shall be contracted.” Pellican agrees wholly with us in both respects. The others say “they shall fear” or “be terrified”; Nebiensis, “they shall be girded”; the Chaldee paraphrast, “they shall depart from their palaces.” Yet they do not deny, especially Münster, that the Hebrew word *HARAG* may be understood by metathesis in place of *HAGAR*, which means “to limp” or “to be contracted,” as the same witness states in his lexicon. Afterwards, the phrase that follows, “from their paths,” they translate “from enclosures,” “inner chambers,” “prisons,” or “hiding places”; Jerome, “in their straits.” But since this passage, according to Augustine and Jerome, refers to the Jews abandoning the spiritual meaning and wholly clinging to the letter of the Law and to carnal observances, interpreters preferred “paths” to “prisons” and “enclosures,” which are the literal sense. Thus the faithless Jews may be understood as contracted in one foot, failing to attain the true spirit of Scripture, [Col. 0206B] so that they now walk only upon the slippery surface of the letter, which kills (2 Cor. 3). Jerome almost indicated this when he said, “in their straits.” For what is narrower than to bind the understanding of Scripture so tightly in the chains of that deadly letter?

**VERSE 51.**—“My deliverer from my wrathful enemies.” The final term, “wrathful,” was added by the Septuagint, as Jerome testifies in his work to Sunnia and Fretela: *ὁ ῥυστής μου ἐξ ἐχθρῶν μου δυνάτων*, “my deliverer from my powerful enemies.” Our manuscripts have *ὀργιλῶν* in place of *δυνάτων*, that is, “wrathful.” And Jerome, following this, shows that some copies read “nations” instead of “enemies”; this is still found in the Roman psalmody.

**VERSE 54.**—“Magnifying the salvations of his king.” Faber’s codex was defective: in Jerome it read “to one magnifying,” and in what follows, “showing mercy,” and so forth, it read “from one showing,” whereas corrected books have the nominative case in both places. Others likewise translate in the same construction, because of the Nebiensis and Chaldee editions. The sense is not changed.

# PSALM XVIII

[Col. 0205]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID”

[Col. 0205C]

“The heavens declare.” Title: “Unto the end, a psalm of David.” [Cassiodorus.] This psalm concerns Christ’s first coming, through which the tyrant devil falls and humankind is released [Col. 0205D] from sin and death. By “the end” is understood Christ, or the time of fullness. Of this it is said: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6). [Alcuin.] And this is the meaning of the title: this psalm is attributed to David as looking toward the end, that is, toward Christ, who is the end of every consummation, or toward the time of fullness. For this Prophet looks toward the end, that is, toward Christ, or toward the last times, in which the events treated here took place.

Purpose: he urges us, abandoning the oldness, to approach the new person, or the new Law.

Method: the psalm has three parts. First, the Prophet, speaking of Christ’s incarnation, commends the preaching of the new Law. [Cassiodorus.] Second, he praises the commandments of both the New and Old Testaments, at “The law of the Lord.” Third, he asks to be cleansed of vices, that he may be worthy to recount such great mysteries, at “Who can understand sins?” Therefore, commending the preaching of the new Law, he shows in the first part who preach, what they preach, and to whom they preach with discernment; and how wonderfully and widely they preach, saying:

[Col. 0206D]

**VERSE 1.**—“The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the works of his hands.”

“The heavens declare,” [Augustine] that is, the apostles, in whom God dwells as though in heavens, “declare the glory of God,” that is, they expound Christ’s glory, in which he is equal to the Father, and that he is God and freely forgives sins. Or, “the glory of God,” that is, the glory by which the Son himself glorified the Father upon earth. “And the firmament,” that is, those same apostles, strengthened by the Holy Spirit and made heaven—who formerly through fear were also earth—“announces the works of his hands.” [Gloss.] That is, the works of the Lord’s mighty deeds which he performed according to his humanity: namely, his birth, Passion, death, and such things. [Alcuin, Augustine.] Thus they are first [Col. 0207A] called “heavens,” that is, lofty, because they announce lofty things. In the latter expression they are “the firmament,” that is, strengthened, because it was necessary for them to suffer for him. For they did not suffer because they preached the Word in the beginning with the Father, but because they announced that the same Son of God had become man, suffered, and died. Hence the Apostle: “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel” (1 Cor. 5). And elsewhere: “We preach Jesus Christ crucified: to the Jews indeed a stumbling-block, but to the nations foolishness” (1 Cor. 1). Behold who and what they preach.

Or literally, “the heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the works of his hands,” [Augustine] because the heavens sent forth a new star announcing the rising of the highest King, which led the Magi to the manger.

**VERSE 2.**—“Day pours forth the word to day, and night shows knowledge to night.”

“Day to day.” [Col. 0207B] [Alcuin, Augustine.] Behold how discriminately they preach. They do not say everything to everyone. Rather, “day,” that is, the bright to the bright—namely, holy persons to holy persons—“pours forth,” as though bringing forth from fullness, “the word,” that is, God’s wisdom, begotten of the Father. As though he said: the spiritual person brings forth to spiritual persons the fullness of wisdom, which is the Word in the beginning with God the Father. “And night,” namely the mortality of flesh—that is, the same persons condescending to the mortality and weakness of flesh and becoming as it were night, that is, as it were carnal—shows to “night,” [Remigius, Augustine] that is, to dark and carnal persons, as though far away, not the Word of the Father but knowledge concerning human things, that is, Christ’s humanity. Or “shows [Col. 0207C] knowledge,” that is, by instilling faith in his humanity, it announces the future knowledge—namely, that through these lesser things one will come to greater things. [Remigius.] The Apostle teaches that he had this discernment in preaching when he says: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified; but we speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2). And elsewhere: “Whether we are carried away, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Cor. 5). They are carried away when in mind they ascend as far as the Word of the Father, whom God spoke once; they are sober when they accommodate themselves to little ones. Hence the Lord says: “Who do you think is the faithful and prudent servant, whom …” and so forth (Matt. 14). [Augustine.] For few are faithful, and fewer still are prudent in administering God’s word. [Col. 0207D] Rare indeed is the teacher who does not mix some adulterating opinion with divine utterances; rarer still is one who judges what is suitable for each individual. Such people, therefore, are not stewards but prodigal destroyers: they irreverently reveal things that should be concealed to those for whom they are not fitting, and recklessly flood without measure those who seek things that require diligent pursuit; they intoxicate with wine those who ought to be nourished with milk, caring more to display their ingenuity than to benefit their neighbours.

> **Note:** [Col. 0207D] From Gregory, *Morals*, book 20, on Job 29: “And my speech distilled upon them.” Likewise, *Morals*, book 39, chapter 6.

Therefore in the tabernacle of the Lord, upon the table, there were bowls, cups, and goblets with which libations were offered. In bowls is signified harsh and biting preaching in threats; in cups, abundant preaching; in [Col. 0208A] goblets, the least and slenderest preaching. For in the teaching of sacred discourse there must be offered not only great and hidden things which intoxicate, but also small and slender things which, as if by a taste, provide knowledge. The wise must be instructed differently from the foolish, the old differently from the young, the celibate differently from the married. And thus, “day pours forth the word to day,” and so forth.

Or, literally, “day pours forth,” and so forth. [Alcuin.] For this teaching is continued through days and nights down to posterity. And it is so wondrous that they spoke in all languages. This is what he adds:

**VERSE 3.**—“There are no languages or speeches in which their voices are not heard.”

“There are no languages.” [Alcuin.] As though he said: They declare, and do so so wonderfully that there are no “languages,” [Col. 0208B] that is, tongues, “in which,” that is, through which, and no “speeches,” [Gloss] that is, modes of speaking—namely the low, middle, and high styles—“in which their voices,” the voices of those heavens, are not heard. [Augustine.] That is, there are no tongues or modes of speech through which the voices of the apostles have not been heard. For the Holy Spirit caused the first teachers to speak in all languages, since he was going to gather all nations into one.

> **Note:** [Col. 0208D] From Augustine, *Tractate 32 on John* and below in this Psalm, verse 10.

And just as one person then spoke in all languages, so now one person too—namely the whole Christ, Head and body—speaks in all languages, because the one holy Church consists of persons from every nation. [Cassiodorus.] Or “languages” are understood as public persuasions addressed to a crowd; “speeches,” as ordinary narratives offered daily and to each individual.

[Col. 0208C]

**VERSE 4.**—“Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

“Into all the earth.” [Alcuin.] Here he shows how widely they preached. As though he said: They preached so wonderfully, and also so widely, that “their sound,” that is, the fame of the apostles, [Gloss] went out “into all the earth,” that is, into every part of the earth’s circuit, even if not their bodily presence; and “their words,” the very things they said, went forth “to the ends of the world,” that is, even into the earth’s remotest corners.

**VERSE 5.**—“In the sun he set his tabernacle; and he himself as a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber.”

[Col. 0208D]

“In the sun he set.” [Cassiodorus.] What the Prophet praises others for doing, he himself does: he preaches the Incarnation. And as though someone asked the Prophet how these things came about, he answers, “in the sun.” [Gloss.] Or these may be the words of the apostles themselves, by which what they preach is disclosed. As though they said: “Their words went out to the ends of the earth,” speaking thus: [Augustine] the Lord, intending to wage war against the kingdoms of temporal errors, set his tabernacle—that is, as it were, a military dwelling—namely the dispensation of his incarnation, in which he came to overthrow the world’s errors. [Alcuin.] “In the sun”: the sun does three things—it shines, burns, and creates the succession of seasons. He therefore set his tabernacle in the sun, [Augustine] [Col. 0209A] in time, because he assumed flesh subject to temporal changes. Or “in the sun,” that is, openly, [39] namely in the public view of the world. Hence he says: “A lamp does not come to be placed under a bushel, but upon a lampstand.” Or “in the sun,” [Alcuin] that is, in labour, because he freely endured the heat of labours. And he set “his tabernacle,” [Augustine] that is, the Church, “in the sun,” that is, openly, not secretly so as to remain hidden, according to the saying: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5). [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] “And he himself as a bridegroom,” because, so often promised by the prophets, he came forth “from his chamber,” that is, from the virginal womb, where God was joined to human nature as a bridegroom to a bride. [Cassiodorus.] Here is a great and fitting likeness of the sacrament, that is, of sign and thing signified. [Augustine.] For he was born of a Virgin in order to signify that he would join the Church to himself as a virgin. Behold Christ’s mercy was humble, but his majesty mighty. Therefore he adds:

**VERSE 6.**—“He rejoiced as a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the summit of heaven.”

[Col. 0209B]

“He rejoiced,” and so forth. [Gloss.] As though he said: He came forth from the chamber; and in coming forth “he rejoiced,” because he did not unwillingly undertake labour, “to run a course,” not to dwell upon it, because he did not remain upon the world’s way. [Augustine.] He rejoiced, I say, “as a giant,” that is, as the mightiest one, surpassing all human beings in incomparable power. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] He is fittingly compared to a giant because, untroubled and irrevocable, he surpasses human nature by his power. [Col. 0209C] “From the summit of heaven”—as though he said: What course did he run? [Augustine.] Behold, he who eternally came forth from the Father came into the world, becoming man; and again, leaving the world, ascended to the Father. And this is what he says: “from the summit of heaven,” that is, from the Father—namely, from equality with the Father—is his going forth, not temporal but eternal, by which he was born of the Father; he, understand, in time became man.

**VERSE 7.**—“And his meeting is unto its summit, and none is hidden from his heat.”

And his return, as a man made, is unto his highest point, the Father; that is, he as man comes, in the fullness of divinity, unto equality with the Father. “Return,” therefore, belongs to Christ according to his humanity, when, ascending to the Father’s throne, he comes to it. But he ascended according to his humanity. By saying “unto his highest point,” he indicates that, insofar as he is God, he is equal to the Father. What the Prophet says here, Christ says of himself in the Gospel: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John XIII). And there is no one who can hide himself, after the incarnation of the Word, from his heat. For the Word, made flesh and assuming our mortality, allowed no mortal to excuse himself by the shadow of death—that is, by sins—because he penetrated even that shadow, and the heat of the Word dissolved it: that is, the love or grace of Christ, when “a light arose for those sitting in the region of the shadow of death” (Luke I). Or the heat is the Holy Spirit, whom, after his ascension, Christ sent to the apostles on his return to heaven; no one is hidden from him, because, as God, he knows all hearts and is able to convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment (John XVI). In these words the Trinity, unity, and both natures of Christ are shown. Where he says “from the highest heaven,” the Father is understood; where he says “his going forth,” the eternal generation of the Son is understood; when he says “his return,” the same Son according to his humanity is understood; when he says “unto his highest point,” that same one is understood as equal to the Father insofar as he is God; when he says “from his heat,” the Holy Spirit is understood. By saying “his,” he indicates the unity of the Trinity.

## Part II. Verse 8

> “The law of the Lord is spotless, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, granting wisdom to little ones.”

[Col. 0210B] “The law of the Lord is spotless.” [Alcuin.] The second part, in which the precepts of the New and Old Testaments are praised. As though he said: No one can hide himself from the heat, that is, from the Holy Spirit. [Augustine.] This Spirit is the law of the Lord, and testimony, and righteousnesses, and commandments, and fear, and judgment. These are said to be the Spirit because he performs the things which each of them commends; and first, the law. As though he said: The bridegroom came forth from the bridal chamber and gave gifts through the Holy Spirit to his bride. What gifts? The law and five others. And the law of the Lord, given through Moses, is spotless, or irreproachable—that is, altogether true—and converts souls, correcting them by its strictness and sending them to Christ’s grace. The testimony of the Lord is faithful and grants wisdom concerning divine things to the little ones, not to the proud. For all the testimonies he gave to Israel are full of truth, and he gave wisdom to the humble, not to the proud. [Glossa interlinearis.] The testimony of the Lord is therefore called faithful because what it promises to all who observe it shall be fulfilled. And:

## Verse 9

> “The righteousnesses of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts; the commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes.”

The righteousnesses of the Lord are right; that is, both the law which makes righteous and whatever it commands are just. The righteousnesses, I say, gladden hearts with hope of reward. “The commandment of the Lord”: up to this point he has commended the Old Testament; from here he commends the New.

Or otherwise, from the words “the law of the Lord”: as though he said: I say that Christ’s heat penetrated the shadow of death, and truly did so, because Christ himself is the law—not human law, but the Lord’s law—who came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matt. V); spotless, because he “did no sin” (1 Pet. II), and makes others spotless, which the earlier law did not do. He, I say, converts souls by freedom to imitate himself, not by oppressing them with the yoke of servitude. [Augustine.] Note that he says “souls,” that is, wills, not merely hands; for the old law chiefly restrained the hand, not the mind. He himself is the faithful testimony of the Lord, because “no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. X). He, I say, grants wisdom concerning divine things to little ones, because the things hidden from the wise have through him been revealed to little ones—that is, to the humble, not the proud. And the righteousnesses of the Lord—all are in him—are right, because he did not teach what he did not do, so that those who imitate him might rejoice in heart in the things which they do freely and with charity, not slavishly and in fear. The righteousnesses, I say, gladden hearts with hope of eternal reward, not terrifying them with fear of punishment as the old law did. And the commandment of the Lord—that is, Christ—is bright, that is, without the veil of carnal observances; a commandment, I say, enlightening the eyes, that is, the sight of the inward person, rather than dulling it, as Moses did, upon whose face the children of Israel could not gaze, and therefore he placed a veil over his face (2 Cor. III).

## Verse 10

> “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever; the judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves.”

The fear of the Lord is holy: namely, loving freely, fearing not punishment but separation; that is, serving not from fear of punishment but from fear of losing the highest good. This is chaste and filial fear. [Note: Col. 0211. Book III of the *Sentences*, partly from Augustine and partly from Cassiodorus on Psalm CXXVII.] For there are four fears besides natural fear: worldly fear, by which we fear losing worldly goods; servile fear, by which fear of punishment restrains us from evil deeds; initial fear, in which one serves partly from fear of punishment and partly from love of righteousness; and filial or chaste fear, by which we fear offending the bridegroom and being separated from him. It is this fear that is treated here. For the penal fear connected with earthly things, for love of which the soul commits adultery, is not holy; but chaste fear is holy, by which the more the Church loves, the more diligently she guards against offending the bridegroom. Thus this fear is not cast out by perfect charity (1 John IV), but endures. Perfect charity casts out initial fear, which is present in charity but not in perfect charity; even imperfect charity removes servile and worldly fear. [Cassiodorus.] The fear of the world, therefore, is not holy, because it is not beneficial but changes with temporal things—that is, it makes people change according to things temporarily possessed or lost. But the fear of the Lord is without all disturbance, because it is love mingled with awe: if it fears the Judge, it knows him to be merciful. Therefore fear endures for ever and ever because its fruit endures eternally. Or fear itself endures in some use without end, or until the end.

And the judgments of the Lord—that is, of the Father, who judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son—are true in Christ, because, whether he threatens or promises, he deceives no one; and they are justified in themselves. Or, another reading has “in the same thing,” that is, unchangeably, because no one takes away the rewards or punishments which he gives. [Jerome, Remigius.] Or they are justified in themselves because they require no authority besides that of the Lord himself in order to be firm.

## Verse 11

> “More desirable than gold and much precious stone; and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.”

“More desirable.” He still commends God’s judgments. As though he said: Because God’s judgments are such, therefore they are much more desirable than gold and precious stone; or, than gold and a very precious stone. Whichever way the wording is arranged, the meaning is this: They are more desirable than gold and much precious stone—that is, than all the splendors of this age, for which the judgments of the Lord are sometimes not desired but feared, despised, or disbelieved. These splendors are signified by the two things, gold and stone. The sense is: The judgments of the Lord are more desirable than everything sought for wealth, signified by gold; power, signified by precious stone; or pleasure, signified by honey and honeycomb. Hence he adds that they are sweeter than honey and honeycomb: that is, than every sweetness of temporal pleasure.

[Cassiodorus.] He prefers the judgments to honey according to the New Testament, in which, like strained honey, God’s judgments are manifest without figures. He prefers them to the honeycomb according to the Old Testament—that is, according to what is contained in the Old Testament—where they are enclosed, as it were, in the cells of figures. Yet the comparison with honey and honeycomb is made because the judgments, open in the New Testament and covered in the Old, taste sweeter to the palate of faith than honey or honeycomb to the throat of the flesh.

[Augustine.] Or thus: by gold and stone, and honey and honeycomb, the saints are understood. The judgments are more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and honeycomb; that is, if anyone is gold, stone, honey, or honeycomb, he desires God’s judgments more than himself, setting God’s will before his own; and they are sweeter to him than he is to himself. Gold and precious stone are that stone which is not to be consumed by fire, but is to be received pure into God’s treasury. God’s food, moreover, is the one who is honey: that is, one already freed from the bonds of this age, awaiting the day when he comes to God’s banquet. The one who is honeycomb is he who is still enfolded by this life, as honey in wax: not hardened fast to this life, nor wholly free from carnality, and needing the pressure—not of a crushing but of an expressing hand of God—so that he may be directed from temporal life to eternal life.

## Verse 12

> “For your servant keeps them; in keeping them there is great reward.”

“For.” Truly they are sweet, because your servant not only says so but also keeps them in deed: sweet now and wholesome afterward. Thus he proves them sweet not by speaking but by keeping them. He keeps them, I say, and the reward is great—so great that its measure cannot be stated. [Cassiodorus.] It is “in keeping them,” that is, in the very act of keeping them, not merely in something external. [Augustine, *Glossa interlinearis.*] While they are kept in this life, one rejoices in them; they please through themselves. Therefore he does not say “for keeping them,” but “in keeping them.” [Remigius.] For not only will reward be rendered for them in the future, but here too the keeping of my commandments is great joy. For to serve God is to reign.

## Part III. Verse 13

> “Who understands transgressions? Cleanse me from my hidden faults; and spare your servant from alien sins.”

“Transgressions.” [Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which the Prophet asks to be cleansed from vices so that he may be a Psalmist worthy to relate these mysteries. [Augustine.] As though he said: Truth is sweet to a mind that sees; judgments are sweet. But what sweetness will there be for one who does not see? None. Why does he not see? Because of transgressions. Nor is this surprising. For who understands transgressions—that is, all of them? As though he said: No one understands them all. Some are known, and therefore no one understands all transgressions. For just as darkness enfolds the eyes, so transgressions do not permit the mind to see either the light or itself. Therefore he prays concerning transgressions, adding: “From hidden faults”—as though he said—“that I may understand and praise you, O Lord, cleanse me from hidden faults, and spare me from alien sins.”

[Cassiodorus.] He includes all sins under two categories: hidden and alien. Hidden sins are original sins and those which arise by a secret will, hidden from many before the deed is done; if they are perhaps recognized, as Solomon says, “do not follow those desires” (Ecclus. XVIII, 1). Yet we must observe that there are many sins of which we are wholly ignorant and whose sources and stealthy incursions we cannot recognize. Alien sins are those committed at the urging of evil persons or of the devil.

[Augustine.] Praying concerning both, therefore, he says: “Cleanse me from hidden faults,” that is, from desires hidden within me—my own, namely, which arise from me. For my own things defile me. Cleanse me from my own faults so that I may not be deceived by alien sins, since one who is cleansed from his own sins is not captured by alien ones. Hence he suitably adds: “And from alien sins”—that is, sins that come from elsewhere—“spare me.” Alien sins afflict me. Therefore, spare me, your servant: not one proudly belonging to myself and desiring to be under my own power. From those hidden sins, cleanse me by removing evil thought from my heart.
