From these alien sins, spare me by repelling the tempter, because I am now your servant, not free as my own master. If they do not rule me, then I am clean. Hence he adds:

## Verse 14

> “If they do not rule over me, then I shall be spotless; and I shall be cleansed from the greatest transgression.”

“If they do not.” [*Glossa interlinearis.*] As though he said: “Spare me from alien sins,” not by removing them altogether, which is impossible, but by preventing them from ruling; for if those alien sins do not rule over me, then I shall be spotless from deadly sin. [Augustine.] Or thus: Cleanse me from hidden faults; spare me from alien sins, namely so that they do not rule over me. For if my own sins do not rule over me—another reading has “hidden sins,” namely, and alien sins—then I shall be spotless from deadly stain. For there is no more certain source of sin than the hidden sin by which the devil fell, and the alien sin by which humanity was deceived and, by consenting, made it its own. “And I shall be cleansed”: as though he said, if my own sins do not rule over me, I shall be cleansed from the greatest transgression, namely the sin of pride, which is the last sin for those returning to God and the first for those departing from him. This truly is the greatest sin. For there is no greater sin than apostasy from God, which was the beginning of pride in angel and human being. Pride is the beginning and cause of every sin; one who lacks it is truly spotless.

## Verse 15

> “And the words of my mouth shall be pleasing, and the meditation of my heart always before your sight.”

“And they shall be”: as though he said, “I shall be spotless and cleansed, and then the words of my mouth shall be such as to please in your sight, not in the sight of human beings.” But if I am not cleansed from pride, my words will please in the sight of people, not of God. If I am cleansed, however, not only my words but also the meditation of my heart will be such—not so as to please people, since pride will no longer exist—but always before your sight, for you see within and inspect the conscience. “Before your sight,” I say, O:

## Verse 16

> “Lord, my helper and my redeemer.”

Lord, who are my helper in doing good—my helper, that is, of me as I strive toward you—and this because you are my redeemer from evils, so that I might strive toward you. Therefore let everyone beware lest, by attributing to himself his conversion to you or his attainment of you, he be rejected as proud.

## Comparison on Psalm XVIII: “The heavens declare the glory”

### Verse 3

> “There are no speeches nor words whose voices are not heard.”

This verse has been fiercely attacked by Faber and his Caecus. “It is,” they say, “an absurd statement with no sense at all; nor should we hesitate or fear to correct this error in our books, so that henceforth the divine psalmody may be sung correctly and intelligibly to the honor of him who inspires it.” Fine words indeed, illustrious gentlemen: please prescribe for us a rule of speaking. One of them says that it ought to read “by whom,” or more suitably “from whom their voices are not heard,” because Jerome, according to the Hebrews, rendered it thus: “by whom their voice is not heard”; and because the Greek reads, “whose voices are not heard” (*hōn ouchi akouontai hai phōnai autōn*).

Do you, good Faber, wish *aph’ hōn* (“from whom”) to be understood, to satisfy your taste? Then Augustine is absurd. Then, in your judgment, so great a doctor speaks correctly on no occasion; let us hear the absurdities which you allege are his, in his exposition of this place: “Whose, if not of the heavens which declare the glory of God? ‘There are no speeches nor words whose voices are not heard.’ Read the Acts of the Apostles: when the Holy Spirit came upon them, they were all filled with him and spoke in the languages of all nations, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance. Behold, there are no speeches nor words whose voices are not heard. Yet they did not sound forth only in the place where they were filled.” These are the words of holy Augustine, the great luminary of the Church.

What more need be said? In Hebrew no relative pronoun is explicitly supplied, so much so that some simply translated, “their voice is not heard”; others, “that their voice may not be heard”: *beli nishma qolam*. Yet the Hebrews commonly leave implicit the relative pronoun “who,” “which,” or “that,” as the logic of the sense requires. For this reason either “whose” or “by whom” may be understood, so that the genitive or ablative refers to the speeches of all nations, through whom the apostles’ voice was heard throughout the earth. In the Master’s explanation, the genitive is used in place of the ablative, in Greek fashion: *hōn*, “whose,” that is, “through whom,” as Augustine interprets it.

### Verse 4

> “Their sound went forth into all the earth.”

Munster: “their direction”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “their line”; Sanctes: “their measuring line”; Pagninus: “their course”; Pellican: “their rule.” Hebrew: *qawwam*. These men ought not to have censured the Apostle in Romans X: “For how shall they believe,” he says, “unless they are sent? And indeed, their sound went forth into all the earth” (*phthongos autōn*). Certainly, with their newly born translations they diminish the apostolic preaching, which immediately sounded throughout the whole world with a kind of thunderclap. This too was signified on the holy day of Pentecost, by that sound which most clearly testified to the coming of the Holy Spirit (Acts II). See whether Jerome translated otherwise—he rendered “sound,” or, according to the Hebrew.

You make it impossible for anyone to trust you in translating the Hebrew, since you preferred to depart from the Apostle rather than from your rabbis, who, lacking the rule of faith, interpret it as the rule or line of the spheres stretched out over the letter. This is to Judaize. Campensis spoke more truly: “their doctrine traversed the whole earth”; another: “their speech.” Here Eugubinus rightly observed that it is not inappropriate to suppose that the Seventy, adding one small letter, namely *lamed*, read *qawwah qolam* in place of *qawwam*. Or, if you add a stroke at the top of the *vav*, you will have *qolam*.

### Verse 5

> “In the sun he placed his tent.”

Hebrew: *la-shemesh sam ohel bahem*. The first particle can equally be taken in the dative or ablative, and the last either reflexively or simply relatively. Hence it may be translated thus: “He placed a tent for the sun among them,” or “In the sun he placed his tent”; translators vary accordingly. The former rendering, however, is more difficult to understand, even if it is sound, and tends toward the idea that Christ, that sun, dwells in the apostles. Our reading, however, is clear from Augustine’s meaning, as you have it in the exposition.

Moreover Augustine of Eugubio is less pleased with Augustine, while holy Aurelius Augustine pleases us. For he scorns our reading as poorly attached, because it does not correspond with what precedes: “For who,” he says, “is he who placed a tent in the sun, when until then he had mentioned no one except the heavens?” He wonders what thing it can be that places a tent in the sun. But was it not said a little earlier: “Day pours forth speech to day”? And that Word placed his tent in the sun, as holy Augustine argues at greatest length and with the greatest wisdom.

### Verse 11

> “More than gold and much precious stone.”

In the second phrase some translate “pure gold,” namely *obrizon*. The Hebrew *paz* is ambiguous between refined gold and precious stone. Hence in our manuscript Jerome, according to the Hebrew, has “precious stone”; in Faber’s copy, *obrizon*. Yet the meaning is entirely the same.

### Verse 12

> “For your servant keeps them.”

Jerome: “will teach them”; Pagninus: “was cautious in them”; Pellican: “will be cautious in them”; Munster: “is warned by them”; Sanctes: “is enlightened in them”; the interpreter for Cajetan: “is stirred up by them”; Campensis: “is instructed by them.” The Hebrew reads *nizhar bahem*. The root means “to observe” or “to teach.” Hence in Ezekiel XXXIII, where we read, “and he did not take warning,” the Hebrew has the same expression as in the present passage. This merely shows that the interpreters and Jerome translate actively, while others translate passively according to the Hebrew conjugation called *niphal*. It appears that the interpreters and Jerome read *yizzāhēr* in the future, which among the Hebrews is not often used for the present; although the sense is the same: “he has been kept in them,” or “he has taken heed in them,” and “he has kept them.”

### Verse 13

> “From alien sins, spare your servant.”

Jerome: “from the proud.” The Hebraists agree. Or it is clear from this place that the interpreters read *zārîm*, with the letter *resh*, rather than *zēdîm*, with *daleth*. Such interchange is easy because of the very close resemblance of the two small letters, which are distinguished by a slight stroke, as even beginners in the alphabet know. If you read with *resh*, it plainly means “aliens”; with *daleth*, “the proud” or “insolences.” So far as the sense is concerned, however, there is no discrepancy, since by “aliens” proud demons are understood, from whom we pray that we may be spared, because God’s power repels them from us. Thus, “From alien sins spare your servant” means, with the other translators, “restrain or hold back your servant”; or, with Jerome, “deliver your servant.”

# Psalm XIX

[Col. 0215]

## Title of the Psalm

> “Unto the end, a psalm of David.”

[Col. 0215C]

“May he hear you.” The title, “Unto the end, a psalm of David,” is clear. Here the Prophet treats of Christ as a priest about to sacrifice and a king about to fight. In the form of a wish, he sings of things that were to happen to Christ in the time of his affliction, which lasted until the Passion, and in the time of joy, which followed the Resurrection. His purpose is to urge the faithful to the same desire. The psalm has two parts. First, he states the things which he wishes to happen to Christ in the time of tribulation. Second, he desires and affirms what will happen in the time of glory, at “May he grant you.” [Jerome.] Therefore, desiring that Christ’s voice as priest may be heard, he says: O Christ:

## Verse 1

> “May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you.”

[Augustine.] May the Lord, the Father, hear you in the day of tribulation, when you said: “Father, glorify your Son” (John XVII). May he hear you, I say, and thus may the name of the God whom you serve protect you—the God, I say, of Jacob, that is, of the younger people. Therefore may he protect you, because the people born later belongs to you, the people for whom you fight. This is the Christian people. And:

## Verse 2

> “May he send you help from the sanctuary, and defend you from Zion.”

May he send you help from the sanctuary; that is, may he help you by making for you a sanctified body—the body, that is, the Church—and may he defend you from Zion. Zion is interpreted “watchtower” or “contemplation.” As though he said: From Zion, therefore, God protects Christ when he makes secure, by lofty contemplation, the Church which is his body. And:

## Verse 3

> “May he remember all your sacrifice; and may your holocaust be made fat.”

May the Lord remember all your sacrifice; that is, may he make us remember all the injuries and insults which you endured for us. And may your holocaust be made fat: that is, may it become pleasing to God; that is, may he turn the cross upon which you were wholly offered into the joy of the resurrection.

Otherwise, the whole passage “May he hear you” can also apply to the Church. [Cassiodorus.] For out of exceeding charity the Prophet desires the Church to receive prosperously the things which he saw were to come through Christ, saying: O Church, may the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation, in which we pray to God with greater longing. Thus may the name of the God of Jacob protect you; thus may he do for you what he did for Jacob, so that, as he gave Jacob the grace of blessing and set him before the Jews, just as he set him before his elder brother Esau, rejecting Esau and choosing Jacob (Gen. XXVII), so, having rejected the Jews, he chose the Church of the Gentiles, according to the saying: “The last shall be first and the first last” (Matt. XX). And, O Church, may the Father send you help from the Holy One—that is, from the Son whom he sent—and defend you from Zion: that is, may he send you from contemplation and make you secure. May he remember all your sacrifice, in order to reward you. The Prophet foresaw by the Holy Spirit the sacrifice which the Church offers—not the sacrifice of animals, but of Christ’s body and blood. And may your holocaust, in which one’s intention is wholly inflamed with love for God, be made fat: that is, pleasing to God.

## Part II. *Diapsalma*. Verse 4

> “May he grant you according to your heart, and confirm all your counsel.”

“May he grant you.” [Alcuin.] The second part, in which he desires and affirms the things he wishes to happen to Christ in the time of glory. As though he said: May he hear you and grant you according to your heart—that is, according to your intention, you who knew the worth of the Passion—not according to the heart of those who desired to destroy you. May he confirm your counsel—that is, fulfill it—because Christ does all things by lofty counsel. He adds “all”: not only the counsel by which you laid down your life for the life of many, so that the grain of wheat, having died, might rise more abundantly; but also that by which blindness happened in part to Israel, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter and thus all Israel might be saved (Rom. II).

## Verse 5

> “We shall rejoice in your salvation, and in the name of our God we shall be magnified.”

“We shall rejoice.” [Augustine.] As though he said: This is why I pray these things, O Christ: because we shall rejoice in your salvation—that is, in the fact that death will not harm you, by which you make it unable to harm us—and we shall be magnified in the name of our God, namely Christ, being called Christians from his name. Or, “in the name of our God we shall be magnified”: that is, confession of your name will not destroy but magnify us. In saying “we shall rejoice” and “we shall be magnified,” the Prophet shows that he is one member of the Church so long before Christ.

## Verse 6

> “May the Lord fulfill all your petitions; now I know that the Lord has saved his anointed.”

“May he fulfill.” As though he said: Why enumerate them individually? May the Lord fulfill all your petitions—not only those which you made on earth, but also those which you make in heaven, interceding for us. Nor do I doubt this, because already now I know, having been shown it so long beforehand by prophecy, that the Lord has saved—that is, will save—his anointed: that is, the Lord the Father will raise Christ. And:

## Verse 7

> “He will hear him from his holy heaven; in powers is the salvation of his right hand.”

“He will hear him from his holy heaven.” [Augustine.] Not only from earth, where he asks to be glorified, but also in heaven, where he intercedes for us at the Father’s right hand, sending from there the Holy Spirit upon believers. “In powers”: as though he said, he will indeed hear him in this, that in our powers is the salvation of his right hand; that is, our powers are the salvation of his favor, for we are made powerful by the help of his grace, since even in tribulation he gives us help, so that when we are weak, then we may be powerful. For the salvation of man, which belongs to the left hand, is vain. Pride arises from it when sinners exalt themselves because they are safe for a time. Of them he adds:

## Verse 8

> “These are in chariots, and these in horses; but we shall invoke the name of the Lord our God.”

“These are in chariots.” [Cassiodorus.] Or thus: Because he had said that Christ asks and is heard, thereby showing him to be true man, he adds “in powers,” in order to show him also to be almighty God. As though he said: He will ask and be heard as true man; nevertheless, he himself is almighty God, because salvation belongs to his right hand—that is, salvation is in the right hand of his divinity: he has in his deity what he asks from the flesh. This salvation is not temporal or subject to any evil, but consists in powers: that is, he makes his own people powerful in eternity.

[Alcuin.] The salvations of the left hand are temporal things, in which those who are not his will be powerful. This is what follows: “These are in chariots.” As though he said: The salvation of his right hand is in powers, but those who are not his are in chariots—that is, they are borne along by the shifting succession of temporal goods—and rejoice in worldly power; and “these are in horses,” that is, they rejoice in proud honors. He touches on the two kinds of triumph among the ancients, one greater and one lesser. [Cassiodorus.] The greater triumph, called the laureate triumph, was performed in a chariot; the lesser, called an ovation, was performed on horseback. [Alcuin.] By these things the Prophet despises those who presume upon earthly rank. “But we”: as though he said, they exult in such things, but we shall invoke the name of the Lord our God, fixing our hope upon eternal things and seeking not our own glory but God’s.

## Verse 9

> “They are bound and have fallen; but we have risen and have been raised upright.”

“They are bound.” [Cassiodorus.] Here he shows how vain human salvation is. As though he said: They are in chariots and horses; therefore they are bound by earthly desires, namely by covetousness for temporal things, unwilling to spare the Lord lest they lose their place and nation (John XI). Rushing against the stone of stumbling and rock of offense (1 Pet. II), they fell from heavenly hope into the death of blindness, though they appear to stand upright; for blindness has happened in part to them, as they are ignorant of God’s righteousness and desire to establish their own (Rom. X). But we—as though he said, the Jews, bound, have fallen, but we, the people of the Gentiles, raised from stones into children of Abraham, have risen from vices and death. [Cassiodorus.] And this is not by our own strength: justified by faith, we have been raised upright to things above.

## Verse 10

> “Lord, save the king; and hear us in the day when we call upon you.”

“Lord.” This is the conclusion of the psalm. And because it will be so—that is, because when the King is saved, we shall be saved—therefore, O Lord, save the King, Christ, so that he who by suffering gave us an example of battle may, as priest raised from death and established in heaven, offer our sacrifices also. And since he now offers for us, hear us, as through him our advocate, on the day when we call upon you: that is, on the day when we truly believe that he has risen, for this is truly to call upon you.

## Comparison on Psalm XIX: “May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation”

### Verse 3

> “May your holocaust be made fat.”

I greatly wonder why Munster, Sanctes, Nebiensis, Pagninus, and the interpreters for Cajetan wished to translate “may he reduce your holocaust to ashes,” even though *dassen* in Hebrew, with no one dissenting, means both “to grow fat” and “to reduce to ashes,” even in the conjugation called *piel*. The Seventy, Jerome, the Chaldee translator, Pellican, and Campensis understood it in the former sense. If the interpreters had given “may he reduce it to ashes,” I fear they would indeed have translated “may it be made fat,” lest I say that they despise the ecclesiastical reading.

### Verse 5

> “In the name of our God we shall be magnified.”

Jerome: “we shall lead choruses.” Others translate: “we shall raise a banner,” or “we shall triumph.” *Dāgal* in Hebrew means “to raise a banner.” It is agreed, moreover, that the interpreters understood it as though the letters had been transposed into *gādal*, “he was magnified”; in the future, *nigdol*, “we shall be magnified.” Yet “to raise a banner” and “to be magnified,” or “to triumph” and “to lead choruses,” are not far apart.

### Verse 8

> “But we shall invoke the name of the Lord our God.”

Hebrew *nazkîr* literally means “we shall remember” or “we shall cause to remember.” But the interpreters have conveyed the sense. For how shall we remember God’s name unless by invoking it in tribulations? Hence Nebiensis translates: “we shall place [it]”; the uncertain printed form is *Thiera*.

### Verse 10

> “Lord, save the king.”

In Hebrew the division of the clause is placed after the verb *hôshî‘āh*, “save,” so that thereafter “king” is arranged in the nominative case. The Seventy differ. But one must not immediately infer from Hebrew that, if a clause-mark is placed after a verb, the sentence must likewise be interrupted at that point. For in Psalm XXI, “My heart has become like melting wax,” the major clause division is placed in Hebrew thus: *kaddōnag names*; yet the reading should not pause at “wax,” but be read continuously, if we agree with Jerome’s rendering, “like melted wax.” Therefore in the present passage either reading may have its own sense and justification.

But Faber and Caecus suppose that our reading is virtually blasphemous, because it seems to imply that the Prophet prays for Christ: “Lord, Father, save the king,” that is, Christ. O delightful men! Why do you not look at the beginning of the psalm itself: “May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation; may he protect you,” etc.? Therefore here the Prophet prays to God the Father for Christ. Do you not know that expressions of this kind are often said by congratulatory acclamation, or are prophetically put in place of the future, as in: “Judas, what you are doing, do quickly”? There are hundreds of such cases.

In what follows—“and hear us in the day,” etc.—Jerome reads, “you will hear us”; the others, “may he hear us.” The variation may lie in the initial letter of the word: if one writes *ta‘anēnû*, as Jerome read it, it means “you will hear us”; or *ya‘anēnû*, as the others understood it; or *wa‘anēnû*, with *vav* for *yod*, as often occurs, meaning “hear us,” as the Seventy read it. Nebiensis translates “answer us”; the Chaldee translator, “receive our prayer.” In meaning, however, this makes no difference.

# Psalm XX

[Col. 0219]

## Title of the Psalm

> “Unto the end, a psalm of David.”

[Col. 0219C]

“Lord, in your strength.” Title. “To the end, a psalm of David,” is clear. [Cassiodorus.] This is the third psalm among those treating of the two natures in Christ; two on this subject have preceded it, namely the second and the eighth, and several others on the same matter still follow. In all of them the one person of Christ is shown, subsisting in two natures, [Note: [Col. 0219] The Nestorians divided the person; the Eutychians confused the natures.] against heretics who either divide the person or confuse the natures in an impious conjunction. Here the Prophet describes Christ as the heavenly King, true God and true man, so that the world may believe him upon hearing whom the Jew despised upon seeing. Intention: He admonishes us to believe that Christ is God and man. Method: The psalm has three parts. First, it sets forth the sum: in brief, [Col. 0219D] the merit and the reward. Second, it describes Christ’s powers and glory, at “For thou hast gone before him.” Third, it treats of the punishments of his enemies, at “Let thy hand be found.” What he prayed concerning Christ in the preceding psalm, he here proclaims, beginning thus:

VERSE 1.—“O Lord, the king shall rejoice in thy strength; and in thy salvation he shall exult exceedingly.”

[Col. 0220C] O Lord, that is, Father: the king, namely Christ as man, shall rejoice in thy strength, [Augustine.] namely, that of the Word—that is, in the fact that the Word was made flesh. This is rightly called thy strength, because he is co-omnipotent with thee. [Cassiodorus.] Behold the merit: Christ as man did not presume upon himself, but attributed everything to the Word. [Alcuin.] Hence he received this reward, that through him all things were saved. Therefore he adds: “and in thy salvation,” [Augustine.] that is, in this, that he shall give life to all things through him, “he shall exult exceedingly,” [Cassiodorus.] because the matter is great. And this is so because:

VERSE 2.—“Thou hast given him his heart’s desire; and hast not defrauded him of the wish of his lips.”

Thou hast given him his heart’s desire, [Jerome, Augustine.] namely, to eat the Passover with his disciples, which he desired, [Col. 0220D] and, when he wished to lay down his life and take it up again and redeem the world. “And hast not defrauded him of the wish of his lips,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] that is, of his words—that is, of the words he uttered. For whatever he said was done. For he said: “My peace I leave with you” (John 14), and it was done. His word was also fulfilled in casting out demons and healing the sick, and his preaching too was received.

[Col. 0221A] PART II. Διάψαλμα [Diapsalma]. VERSE 3.—“For thou hast gone before him with blessings of sweetness; thou hast set upon his head a crown of precious stone.”

“For thou hast gone before him.” [Cassiodorus.] The second part, in which his powers and glory are described. As though he said: Whence has this come to him? “For thou hast gone before him with blessings of sweetness.” [Remigius.] By blessings he means immunity from sin, with which Christ was endowed even in his conception, so that sin might not later harm him. [Gloss, interlinear.] It is called a blessing “of sweetness,” because all was by grace. Therefore, while others are preceded by Adam’s bitterness, thou alone hast gone before him with blessings of sweetness—that is, immunity from sin, which is from grace; [Augustine.] and, because he was preceded by immunity from sin, the gall of our sin did not harm him. “And thou hast set upon his head a crown of precious stone,” [Col. 0221B] [Gloss, interlinear.] that is, making him king, after the likeness of a conqueror. Or: “Thou hast set upon his head a crown of precious stone,” that is, at the beginning of his preaching precious stones surrounded him—[Augustine.] namely, the apostles, from whom the preaching was to take its beginning. [Note: [Col. 0221] From Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chapter 2.] These are the twelve precious stones in the breastplate of judgment, engraved with the names of the twelve sons of Israel, which the high priest, when entering the tabernacle, wore upon his breast; because the teacher of the Church ought to examine both the life and doctrine of the saints who have gone before, diligently investigate those who especially flourished in works of virtue and shone in the teaching of truth, gather all these things in the secret place of his breast, and bring them forth in the performance of his work. [Cassiodorus.] [Col. 0221C] He calls it a crown because the circle of apostles surrounded Christ as he taught, like a crown.

Or thus: “Thou hast gone before him with blessings of sweetness,” [Alcuin.] that is, thou didst first and more fully confer upon him the gifts of grace, in whom all are made alive; to whom the Spirit was not given by measure, and from whose fullness we have all received (John 1). Hence: “Therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows” (Psalm 44). For in him the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily, so that he might himself be the firstborn among many brethren (Colossians 1–2), that is, having the Spirit above the rest, and rising before the rest as impassible and immortal. [Alcuin.] Those whom, after their experience of death, thou didst fit to him as a crown to its head. Hence he adds: “Thou hast set upon his head a crown [Col. 0221D] of precious stone,” [Cassiodorus.] because the whole circle of the world—that is, the universal Church—surrounds him in faith, as a crown surrounds the head. It follows:

VERSE 4.—“He asked life of thee, and thou gavest it him: length of days for ever and ever.”

He asked life—that is, resurrection—of thee, saying: “Father, glorify thy Son” (John 17). And thou gavest it him. He asked it for his Church, and thou gavest it length of days for ever and ever: that is, the long times of this age, which the Church possesses; and afterward eternity. And further:

VERSE 5.—“Great is his glory in thy salvation; glory and great beauty shalt thou lay upon him.”

Great is his glory, that is, thou shalt give him the name which is above every name (Philippians 2). And this is “in thy salvation,” [Col. 0222A] [Gloss, interlinear; Augustine.] that is, in the fact that thou hast raised him, because although he possessed the name of God before, it became known in the resurrection. A thing is said to come about when it becomes known. Thus he himself, now risen, says: “All power is given unto me in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 28). And thou shalt yet lay upon him [Augustine.] that is, add to him, glory and great beauty, when thou shalt place him in heaven at thy right hand. And truly it shall be so.

VERSE 6.—“For thou shalt give him blessings for ever and ever; thou shalt make him glad with joy with thy countenance.”

“For thou shalt give him blessings for ever and ever,” [Augustine.] that is, he himself shall be in blessing without end; and this will be that blessing, because thou shalt make him glad, according to the manhood which thou hast raised up to thee, so that he may be in joy with thy countenance—that is, with thy presence.

[Gloss, interlinear.] Or thus from the words “Great is his glory”: the glory of Christ as man is “in thy salvation,” that is, in the Word of the Father. [Cassiodorus; Gloss, interlinear.] What glory comes from this? Behold: thou shalt lay upon him glory from judgment, because in his divinity he shall judge, and great beauty in the majesty which will then appear. Note that here Christ is said to be about to judge in divinity, while elsewhere he is said to judge in humanity; both are true. He shall judge in humanity because the form of a servant will appear to all at the judgment; but in divinity because from it he possesses the power of judging. Or “glory and great beauty,” [Alcuin.] means glorious and beautiful persons, such as Peter, by whose shadow the sick were healed (Acts 5). “Thou shalt lay [Col. 0222C] upon him,” beyond whom there is no other foundation, as the Apostle says: “A foundation is laid which no one can change, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 3). Therefore, “upon him.”

“For thou shalt give him blessings for ever and ever,” namely, so that through him all nations may be blessed, as God promised Abraham: “In thy seed shall all nations be blessed” (Genesis 22). “And thou shalt make him glad with joy with thy countenance,” [Alcuin.] that is, because his own people will rejoice in thy presence, when thou shalt be all in all (1 Corinthians 15). It follows:

VERSE 7.—“For the king trusteth in the Lord; and in the mercy of the Most High he shall not be moved.”

“For the king.” [Gloss, interlinear.] He gives the reason for all that precedes. As though he said: Rightly have I done these things, because the king—[Augustine.] namely, Christ as man—does not exalt himself but, being humble in heart, trusts in the Lord; and in the mercy of the Most High he shall not be moved, that is, nothing shall disturb his humility and obedience even unto death. Or divide it thus: “And in the mercy of the Most High he shall not be moved.” The sense is the same.

PART III. VERSE 8.—“Let thy hand be found by all thine enemies; let thy right hand find all that hate thee.”

“Let thy hand be found.” [Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which the Prophet treats of the punishments of Christ’s enemies, as above he treated of his praises; and he speaks to Christ. As though he said: And because thou art such, O Christ the King, let thy hand—[Augustine.] that is, thy power—be found, when thou shalt come to judgment, by all thine enemies, who did not recognize it in thy humility; and let thy right hand, that is, the splendor by which thou reignest at the Father’s right hand, find for punishment on the day of judgment all who hate thee, because they themselves do not now find it.

Or he speaks to the Father, and the passage is understood partly of the present in a good sense, partly of the future in an evil sense; and by hand and right hand he means the Son. [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: Such is the King, O [Col. 0223B] Father: let thy hand, that is thy Son, be found through faith by all thine enemies, so that they may believe. And if thy right hand—that is, the Son himself—is not found by anyone, it shall find, [Jerome.] on the day of judgment, all who hate thee, for punishment. And this will happen, because:

VERSE 9.—“Thou shalt make them as a fiery furnace in the time of thy countenance; the Lord in his wrath shall trouble them, and fire shall devour them.”

“Thou shalt make them as a fiery furnace,” [Augustine.] burning inwardly in the consciousness of their own impiety. And this shall be “in the time of thy countenance,” that is, at the time of thy manifestation. Then, changing person, he shows that they will also be tormented outwardly, adding: “The Lord,” etc. As though he said: The fire of conscience will torment them inwardly; and further, “the Lord, in his wrath,” [Cassiodorus.] that is, at the future judgment, [Col. 0223C] when he will seem to be angry with the wicked, “shall trouble them,” when he says: “Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire” (Matthew 25); and immediately the fire of hell shall devour them, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. [Augustine.] The order of condemnation is shown: after the accusation of conscience, having been troubled, they will be consumed by God’s vengeance in eternal fire. Hence the prophet Zephaniah says: “There shall be a cry from the first gate, and a howling from the second” (Zephaniah 1). As though he said: [Note: [Col. 0223D] From Jerome’s Commentary on Zephaniah.] There are two gates, sight and hearing. Therefore from the first gate, which is sight, there shall be a cry when the ungodly see all their evils, their own consciences accusing them. Hence: behold the person, and all his works before him. But from the second gate, that is, from hearing, there shall be howling—that is, vehement pain—when at last [Col. 0223D] they hear this sentence of condemnation, namely: “Depart, ye cursed,” etc. And:

VERSE 10.—“Their fruit shalt thou destroy from the earth; and their seed from among the children of men.”

“Their fruit, because it is of the earth,” [Augustine.] that is, earthly, “thou shalt destroy from the land of the living.” [Alcuin.] That is, they shall have no fruit of blessedness in the land of the living, because they loved earthly things. “And their seed,” that is, their works or those whom they have led astray, “thou shalt destroy from among the children of men,” [Augustine.] that is, thou shalt not reckon them among the heirs of the kingdom. This punishment, however, shall befall them because:

VERSE 11.—“For they have turned evils upon thee; they have devised counsels which they could not establish.”

[Col. 0224A] [Augustine.] “For they have turned upon thee” the evils which they thought would threaten them from the Romans if thou shouldst reign—that is, they directed them against thee to be killed. [Gloss, interlinear.] Or: they turned upon thee the evils which were in themselves—that is, they laid them upon thee, saying: “Thou hast a devil” (John 7), and such things. “And they have devised counsels,” namely these: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people” (John 12), and that the world should not go after him. [Augustine.] Yet all these things perished. Hence he adds: “which they could not establish” according to their own will, not knowing what they were saying. Yet some spoke truth, though they did not understand it.

VERSE 12.—“For thou shalt make them a back; in thy remnants thou shalt prepare their face.”

“For thou shalt make them a back.” [Alcuin.] Having spoken of their future punishment, he now speaks of the present cause of that punishment. As though he said: Therefore these things shall happen to them in the future, because in the present thou shalt make them a back—[Augustine.] that is, thou shalt order them among those blinded persons from whom, having set them aside and despised them, thou shalt turn away. And “in thy remnants,” that is, among those whom thou leavest and rejectest—in the desires for an earthly kingdom, which thou dost not love—thou shalt prepare for thy passion “their face,” that is, their shamelessness, while, through desire to retain their kingdom, they killed Christ. He patiently endured this for our salvation, as had been ordained.

Or thus. [Alcuin.] As though he said: Because the Jews do these things, thou shalt make them a back—that is, thou shalt drive them away from thee—“in thy remnants.” And because thou shalt make them a back—that is, because these will be driven away from thee—“in thy remnants,” that is, among those from the nations whom thou dost leave for thyself to be received, [Col. 0224C] thou shalt prepare “their face,” that is, the knowledge of thee. I call it their face, that is, the face which ought to have been theirs, because to them were entrusted the oracles of the Law and the Prophets (Romans 3), and Christ came to them.

Or, the Jews are the back, because they contemplate earthly rather than heavenly things. And this shall happen to them in the future because thou shalt make them a back—that is, thou shalt allow them to be bent down toward the earthly things which are behind; and their face, [Cassiodorus.] that is, their evil intention, thou shalt prepare in thy remnants—that is, thou dost prepare it for thy passion, so that, when they supposed that they were killing thee, the salvation of the world might come about. Christ therefore prepared their intention by ordaining good from it.

VERSE 13.—“Be thou exalted, O Lord, in thy strength; we will sing and chant thy powers.”

“Be thou exalted”: the conclusion of the psalm. As though he said: They thus devised their plans; but thou, O Lord, whom they did not recognize as humble, be thou exalted—that is, rise in glory [Augustine.]—and this in the strength of thy humility, which they considered weakness. And we will sing and chant thy powers: that is, we will celebrate with heart and deed and make known thy wonders.

COLLATION ON PSALM 20: “O LORD, THE KING SHALL REJOICE IN THY STRENGTH.”

VERSE 2.—“And hast not defrauded him of the wish of his lips.” Jerome translates in the same manner. Others, however, render it: “Thou hast not withheld or denied the testing of his lips.” The Hebrew word placed here is found nowhere else in Scripture. For this reason it would have been better for these Hebraizers to follow the Septuagint and Jerome in the meaning of that word rather than the Jews, even though they agree with them: “the wish of the lips,” and their free utterance. And indeed it is not unsuitable that the Septuagint and Jerome read *ARESSUTH* for *ARESSETH*, with an added initial aleph; for *RESSUTH* among the Hebrews means free capacity, which wonderfully accords with Christ’s preaching, which was completely free, without any respect of persons.

VERSE 12.—“For thou shalt make them a back.” Münster, Nebiensis, Pratensis, and Campensis: “thou shalt put them aside”; Jerome, Sanctes, Pellicanus, and the interpreters for Cajetan: “shoulder” or “back.” Since therefore the Hebrew *SCHECHEM* has both meanings, why do they contend without reason against [Col. 0226A] the Vulgate edition? Certainly, if the interpreters had rendered it “thou shalt put them aside,” perhaps the ancient translators might have been expected to render, “thou shalt make them a back.” So great is the desire to contradict. Yet I prefer to persuade myself that they did this not out of eagerness to condemn, but for the elegance of variety.

“In thy remnants thou shalt prepare their face.” Jerome, Nebiensis, Sanctes, and the interpreters for Cajetan put “cords” in place of “remnants.” Münster, Pratensis, Pellicanus, and the paraphrase of Campensis understand it as the string of a bow or crossbow. But the Hebrew word *IETHER* chiefly has three meanings: at times “remainder” or “remnants,” as the Septuagint understood it; at times “cord,” as Jerome understands it; thirdly “string,” as those who translate it so intend. And this threefold meaning can readily be adapted, according to the exposition of blessed Augustine, to indicate the destruction of the obstinate Jews.

PSALM XXI.

[Col. 0225]

TITLE OF THE PSALM: “TO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID, FOR THE MORNING ASSUMPTION OR RECEIVING, OR FOR THE MORNING HIND.”

[Col. 0225B]

“My God, my God, look upon me.” Title. “To the end, a psalm of David, for the morning assumption or receiving, or for the morning hind.” [Cassiodorus.] This psalm is the first of those which principally and extensively treat of Christ’s passion. [Alcuin.] Although this psalm would suffice as testimony to the Lord’s passion, lest anyone have any excuse or any uncertainty, four others openly written on the same subject follow: the thirty-fourth, fifty-fourth, sixty-eighth, and one hundred eighth. Their common character is this: they begin from groaning and activity and end in the salvation of humankind, [Col. 0225C] lest the faithful, hearing of the Passion, despair, but rather believe that true salvation arises from it.

Yet in the title there is no mention of the Passion, but of the resurrection, when it says “for the morning assumption or receiving.” [Cassiodorus.] But by that which follows, namely assumption, that which precedes is indicated, namely the Passion. Thus, when someone is said to have been manumitted, he is understood to have been a slave; likewise, when Christ is said to have risen, he is understood to have died. [Augustine.] The morning assumption or receiving means Christ’s resurrection, which occurred in the morning, while it was still dark, when human nature was assumed into glory. [Alcuin.] It is so called by likeness to the sun, which is gradually taken up as it rises [Col. 0225D] until it shines everywhere. So Christ ascended from Passion to resurrection, thence into heaven at the right hand of the Father. Hence, after sending the Holy Spirit upon the apostles, he illuminated the world with the rays of faith.

And because the principal subject here is the Passion, in which Christ prayed for resurrection, it rightly says not “of the assumption” but “for the assumption.” And this is the sense of the title: This psalm, tending to the end—that is, to Christ—whose Passion it treats, is David’s, that is, Christ’s, who here speaks in his own person or under the person of the old man, [Augustine.] that is, the Church, which is old in guilt and punishment. For our oldness consists in two things, [Col. 0226B] namely punishment and guilt. Christ consumed both these things in us through his single oldness; hence he lay in the tomb for one day and two nights, signifying that by his own single oldness he would consume our twofold oldness. For as the Apostle says: “Our old man is crucified with him” (Romans 6). Hence the prophet Hosea: “I will be thy death, O death” (Hosea 13): I mean the Christ who prays for the morning assumption—that is, who treats of the Passion, in which he prays for the resurrection accomplished in the morning.

[Cassiodorus.] Thus Christ’s assumption is prayed for here—that is, his resurrection—for which the Passion is first set forth, so expressly expounded that it seems an evangelical history rather than prophecy. And rightly is it narrated so carefully, because the Passion itself is the salvation of the world. Others have “for the morning hind,” which is the same thing by another likeness. [Alcuin.] For the hind is Christ’s human nature, which leapt over the mud and thorns—that is, sins—and was taken up, as it were, on high in the morning of resurrection glory. In its intention, it admonishes us to suffer with Christ, that we may reign with him. [Cassiodorus.] Method: The psalm has three parts. First, lament over abandonment is set forth, together with prayer, as in all psalms concerning the Passion. Second, the Passion is described, and resurrection is prayed for, at “They surrounded,” etc. Third, the fruit and power of the Passion are shown, at “I will declare,” etc. [Augustine.] Christ, therefore, under the person of the old man exposed to punishment and guilt, cries out:

VERSE 1.—“My God, my God, look upon me: why hast thou forsaken me? Far from my salvation are the words [Col. 0226D] of my transgressions.”

[Alcuin.] “My God, my God.” He repeats “God” from feeling. Or: “God,” of all through the power of creation, who art properly “my God” through worship, “look upon me.” This is not in the Hebrew, but was added by the Septuagint interpreters, following the sense rather than the words. Look upon me, I say; and this is necessary because “thou hast forsaken me,” that is, thou hast exposed me to punishment and guilt. And why is this? According to the Hebrew, connect the wording thus: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”

[Augustine.] It is wonderful how Christ says, “Thou hast forsaken me,” when God was with him. For God had not forsaken him, since the Word of God was God; but he says this for us, who are one in him as members and are his body. For Christ’s body is the Church, for which he speaks here and for which the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us (John 1): “Far.” Here is the solution. As though he said: Behold why: namely because thou art far from my salvation, the salvation of me as the old man, because salvation is far from sinners (Psalm 118). And these words—namely, “thou hast forsaken me,” “far,” and “why”—are not words of righteousness but “of my transgressions,” that is, they show that I am not righteous but a sinner.

Or, with one punctuation: “The words of my transgressions are far from my salvation,” that is, Christ says in the person of the old man: my words, which are foolish and transgressions, are the reason why thou art so far from my salvation.

VERSE 2.—“My God, I shall cry by day, and thou wilt not hear; and by night, and it is not unto foolishness for me.”

“My God.” [Augustine.] Again, Christ says this in the person of the old man. As though he said: They are so far from salvation that I shall cry to thee, O thou who art my God, by day—that is, in prosperity, that it may not depart—and by night—that is, in tribulation, that it may depart; and thou wilt not hear me crying in this way, because I cry with words of transgression. How can he say this who “did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2)? But he says it of us, his body—of me, of you, of that person—for he bore the person of his body, that is, the Church. So too elsewhere, when he said, “Let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26), he spoke for us, unless perhaps one thinks that he feared to die—that is, that he said it through fear of his own death.

[Augustine.] But God did not truly fear to suffer, since he would rise on the third day, while Paul burned with desire to depart and be with Christ. A soldier cannot be stronger than his commander; it is enough for the servant to be like his lord. Therefore the soldier who is to be crowned rejoices to die, while the lord who is to crown him fears death? Rather, representing our weakness, he said this for his weak members who fear death: it was their voice. So here too it is the voice of the members, not of the head: “I shall cry by day and night, and thou wilt not hear.” For many cry in tribulation and are not heard.

But it should be carefully observed that Augustine here [Note: [Col. 0227] Augustine on Psalm 93, on the verse “How long shall righteousness,” etc.] [Col. 0227D] seems to say that Christ did not have true sorrow or fear, whereas he himself elsewhere says that Christ assumed true sorrow or fear just as he assumed true flesh; and the Gospel too says: “Jesus began to be afraid and to be distressed” (Matthew 26). Therefore let the reader distinguish how both statements are made, and understand that both are true. For he truly did not fear death—that is, through necessity of condition he was not subject to that defect, because he was without fault and sin—and yet he assumed real fear and sorrow in himself, just as real flesh, but solely by the will of compassion, not by necessity of condition.

Therefore, possessing true fear of death, he said, “Let this cup pass [Col. 0228A] from me” (ibid.), but especially for his weak members. So here too, in the person of his members, he says that he will not be heard. But this is for salvation, not for foolishness. Hence he adds: “and it is not unto foolishness.” As though he said: I cried in prosperity and adversity, and was not heard; but neither of these is unto foolishness for me, but unto wisdom—namely, that I may know what ought to be cried for and how: [Augustine.] namely, not with words of transgression and out of desire for temporal life, but with words of conversion to thee for eternal life. By this, therefore, I understand that God does not hear according to one’s wish but according to salvation, just as a physician does not act according to the sick person’s wish but according to health.

VERSE 3.—“But thou dwellest in the holy place, the praise of Israel.”

[Col. 0228B] “But thou.” As though he said: I shall cry to thee day and night, and am not heard. [Augustine.] But thine own understand why this happens: because thou dwellest in the holy—that is, in those sanctified by thee. Therefore thou dost not hear words of transgression, but those crying with words of eternal life; namely, those whom thou makest understand that, for salvation, thou sometimes dost not hear saints, as Paul (2 Corinthians 12), and that, for condemnation, thou sometimes dost hear the wicked, as thou didst with the demons, permitting them to enter the swine (Matthew 8), or to tempt Job (Job 1). Thou, I say, who art “the praise of Israel,” that is, of the one who sees thee, not of the one who wished to hide himself from thy sight.

VERSE 4.—“Our fathers trusted in thee; they trusted, and thou didst deliver them.”

[Col. 0228C] “Our fathers trusted in thee.” [Gloss, interlinear.] Christ still speaks in the person of the old man. As though he said: Thou didst not hear me, but thou didst hear and deliver the fathers who went before. Why, then, dost thou not hear me, or us? As though he said: It is wonderful. And this is what he says: “Our fathers trusted in thee,” [Augustine.] the ancient ones, namely the righteous, trusted. As though he said: Deliverance comes from hope. And thou didst deliver them: the people of Israel from Egypt (Exodus 14), the three youths from the furnace (Daniel 3), Daniel from the lions’ den (Daniel 6), Susanna from a false accusation (Daniel 13), and such persons.

[Augustine.] Why then dost thou not likewise deliver us? Let all who come to Christ know that this happens because the Christian is tested in tribulation, if he does not forsake his God. For a furnace turns straw into ashes but removes dross from gold; thus those in whom God dwells become better in tribulation, tested as gold. He who made us knows, therefore, what he is doing; the good builder who builds the house also knows how to restore us. And if anything falls, he knows how to repair it. It follows:

VERSE 5.—“They cried unto thee, and were saved; they trusted in thee, and were not confounded.”

“They also cried unto thee,” [Augustine.] certainly not with words of transgression, from which salvation is far, “and were saved” immediately—I do not mean only in the future. And he repeats: “They trusted in thee.” [Cassiodorus.] Observe that there is great beauty in the expression when he repeats “they trusted”; and [Col. 0229A] “were not confounded” concerning their reward, [Augustine.] because their hope was not in themselves but in thee.

VERSE 6.—“But I am a worm and not a man; the reproach of men and the outcast of the people.”

“But I.” [Augustine.] Up to this point Christ has spoken in the person of the old man. Here Christ now speaks properly in his own person. As though he said: Thou didst deliver the fathers but not the Church, which is wonderful. And not only is this wonderful, but also what thou hast done to me: for thou hast made me, who am greater than all, more despised than others. He marks his excellence when he says: “But I am a worm and not a man”; his abasement when he says: “the reproach of men.” And this is the meaning: “But I am a worm,” because I was born of the Virgin without male seed, that I might be above men in honor. [Col. 0229B] Hence he adds: “and not a man” only, because I am also God. Therefore, after saying “worm,” he adds “and not a man,” so as to mark the distinction: for Adam too was a human worm, since he was not from the seed of a man, and a mere man; but Christ is “a worm and not a man,” because “the Word was in the beginning with God.”

[Cassiodorus.] Or, “not a man” means not a sinner. And though I am such and so great, I, who am greater than all, while I was in this dignity, became “the reproach of men” amid spittings and blows, and “the outcast of the people,” when they chose Barabbas in preference to him. [Cassiodorus, Gloss, interlinear; Augustine.] Behold how great are Christ’s sufferings while the fathers were delivered. He therefore speaks of his own abasement so that, even in this way, human pride may imitate God made humble.

Or all the foregoing may be understood in the person of Christ, who, expressing the true nature of humanity, says: “My God, my God.” These are the words that he cried while hanging on the cross: “Eli, Eli, why hast thou forsaken me?” This is what he said there: *lamma sabacthani* [“why hast thou forsaken me?”] (Matthew 27). When he said these things on the cross, he indicated that this psalm was written of himself: “Far from my salvation.” As though he said: Behold why: because the words—that is, the petition—of “my transgressions,” [Cassiodorus, Gloss, interlinear; Alcuin.] that is, the transgressions of my members, demanding my death, without which there is no salvation, are far from my bodily salvation. That is, they are the reason why I suffer, because in this manner—that is, by the Passion—the transgressions of my people are to be removed. Note that he calls our transgressions his own: he made them his, not to possess them, [Col. 0229D] [Augustine.] but to destroy them, that he might make his righteousness ours.

[Cassiodorus.] They are so far that I shall cry to thee. As though he said: Thou art my God; I shall cry “by day,” because there were no darknesses in him, and “by night,” that is, in tribulation, in which those who cry are accustomed to be heard. Yet thou wilt not hear me so as to prevent my being crucified. For Christ was not heard unto bodily salvation. Carefully note that he says here that Christ was not heard, agreeing with what Christ himself says in the Gospel: “Let this cup pass from me, if it be possible; nevertheless, not my will but thine be done” (Matthew 26). From these words it seems that Christ asked and willed what he did not obtain.

But statements in another psalm seem contrary: “Thou hast given him his heart’s desire; and hast not defrauded him of the wish of his lips” (Psalm 20). And elsewhere: “May the Lord fulfill all thy petitions” (Psalm 19). We must know, therefore, that in accordance with the two natures there were different wills in Christ. For he willed one thing by the will of divinity, with which the rational affection agreed in all respects; another by the affection of sense. By the will of divinity and reason he willed to die for humankind’s salvation; by the affection of sense he did not will it. Yet both were good, but the one was better: namely, that he should die. Therefore he brought that one into effect.

Nevertheless, it must not be said that in Christ the spirit lusted against the flesh, or the flesh against the spirit, or against God, because it was God’s will that according to the flesh he should will and ask this, so that the truth of humanity in him might be expressed. [Col. 0230B] Attending to this, therefore, we say that Christ, according to the affection of the flesh, willed and asked something which he did not obtain, because neither did he will to obtain it according to the will of divinity and reason. Why then did he ask it? So that he might give you a model of crying to God in tribulation and of subjecting your will to the divine will. For whatever he willed according to divinity and reason was done.

Therefore, because here according to the affection of sense he cried for temporal safety, which he did not obtain, he rightly says: “I shall cry and thou wilt not hear”; and this “will not be unto foolishness for me.” [Cassiodorus; Augustine.] Rather, it will be so that humankind may be wisely liberated by my blood. For no mode of our liberation was more fitting: that the human being who fell through pride should rise through humility.

[Col. 0230C] “But thou.” As though he said: I say, “Thou wilt not hear”; but although thou dost not hear, nevertheless thou dwellest in me, the Holy One, because “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5). Thou, I say, art “the praise of Israel,” [Cassiodorus; Alcuin.] that is, thou who praisest the one seeing thee. “Our fathers trusted in thee.” As though he said: I say that thou dwellest in me, the Holy One, and so it is wonderful: for thou didst deliver the ancient fathers but not me. But I am a worm and a reproach. [Gloss, interlinear; Cassiodorus.] And this is what he says: “Our fathers trusted in thee,” Christ says—those who were less than I, who were my fathers according to the flesh—trusted, and thou didst deliver them. This does not change. “They also cried unto thee and were saved; they trusted in thee and were not confounded”: understand these as before.

“But I am,” etc. As though he said: Thou didst deliver them, but “I am a worm and not a man,” [Cassiodorus.] that is, so contemptibly trampled as though I were a worm and not a man. Or, “I am a worm,” [Augustine; Cassiodorus.] because I am mortal, born from flesh without intercourse and concupiscence, like a worm from the earth; humble, lowly, and creeping silently. Yet I am not merely a man, because I am also God. And I am “the reproach of men,” etc.

VERSE 7.—“All that saw me mocked me; they spoke with their lips and shook their heads.”

[Cassiodorus; Augustine.] All the wicked, namely, seeing me such as this, mocked me; and they spoke with their lips, not only in their heart, saying: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matthew 27). [Cassiodorus.] [Col. 0231A] And they shook their heads, mocking or as though threatening, not exercising judgment, and said ironically:

VERSE 8.—“He trusted in the Lord; let him deliver him; let him save him, because he wills him.”

[Gloss, interlinear.] “He trusted in the Lord,” as he says; “let him deliver him from our hands.” Or, if he does not deliver him, let him save him—that is, raise him—“because he wills him,” as he says. [Cassiodorus.] This is the irony of the Jews. Behold, it is as though historical narration, not prophecy, so that there may be no excuse and no uncertainty.

VERSE 9.—“For thou art he who drew me out of the womb, my hope from my mother’s breasts; upon thee was I cast from the womb.”

For you are: here he shows the cause of the reproaches. [Aug.] As though he said: This is why they say these things: because [Col. 0231B] you are he who drew me from the womb—that is, because I became man by your working. For they would not say such things to the Word who is in the beginning with God (John 1). For that Word, through whom all things were made (ibid.), was not drawn from the womb, except because the Word was made flesh (ibid.). And you are my hope, or, my God—another reading—and this from my mother’s breasts; that is, according to the humanity by which he sucked his mother’s breasts. From the breasts, therefore, you are my hope and my God, who before the ages are my Father according to divinity. And I was cast, or hurled, upon you from the womb, so that you alone might be my hope, since I am now man, now weak, and you are my God.

VERS. 10.—“From my mother’s womb you [Col. 0231C] are my God; do not depart from me.”

From my mother’s womb, etc.—that is, according to what I have from my mother, not according to what I have from you. [Aug.] For from you you are my Father, but from my mother you are my God, that is, Creator, insofar as I am man; but insofar as I am God, I am begotten from you. And therefore, do not depart from me.

Or thus, and the order of the wording is changed as follows: [Cassiod.] They do these things to me; but you, do not depart from me, because you have already begun to be with me. And this is what he says: “For you are he who drew me from my mother’s womb,” not a man, because by your power—not by a man’s act—I was born while the womb remained closed. He says this lest the Virgin’s childbirth be doubted. For all was done by God’s power. And you are my hope [Col. 0231D] from my mother’s womb. True humanity in Christ, and great perfection, are here indicated; for from the breast he did what scarcely anyone already mature can do, etc.: “I was cast upon you from the womb,” not into the sin of man; for others are cast into Adam’s sin, by which they are held guilty. But I was cast upon you, that I might hope in you alone; and you are not only my hope from the breasts, but also: “You are my God from my mother’s womb.” As though he said: Neither was the conception accomplished without God, nor was I conceived in sin as a man; but I was conceived and born of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Angel says to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1).

Or thus: “For you are,” and it is read allegorically, where the Synagogue is understood by “mother.” As though he said: This is why they [Col. 0232A] do these things to me: because you are he who drew me from the womb. [Aug.] Not only from that virginal womb, which is the law of birth for all, but also from the darkness of the Synagogue, by which whoever trusts in the legal observances of Sabbath, circumcision, and the rest is covered over and has not yet been born into the light of Christ. And you are my hope, or my God, from my mother’s breasts—not from the time I began to be nursed at the Virgin’s breasts, for you were so even before that—but from the breasts of the Synagogue, from which, as from the womb, you drew me, as I said above, lest I should suck a carnal habit. And I was cast upon you from the womb of the Synagogue, whose womb—that is, the Scribes and Pharisees—did not bear me, but hurled me away. Nor did its womb cause me, like an infant, to forget you; rather, you are—that is, [Col. 0232B] you were—my God from my mother’s womb, the Synagogue. Therefore, do not depart from me. He ends the complaint in prayer and adds the reason.

VERS. 11.—“For tribulation is near, and there is none to help.”

“For tribulation is near,” [Aug.] in my body; or, “is near” in time, because it is imminent. And again, for this reason: because there is no other to help, if you do not help.

PART II. VERS. 12.—“Many calves have surrounded me; fat bulls have besieged me.”

They have surrounded me. [Cassiod.] The second part, in which Christ’s Passion is described; prayer brings it to an end. To convict the Jews, it reports future events as though past. As though he said: Tribulation is near. For [Col. 0232C] many calves surrounded me, in their counsels or with swords and clubs—[Aug., Cassiod.] that is, the multitude of a luxuriant people, who were without God’s yoke. And fat bulls—that is, proud rulers, more fierce because of their fatness—besieged me, by comparison, as though I were a fortress, lest I escape.

VERS. 13.—“They opened their mouth against me, like a lion tearing and roaring.”

[Cassiod., Aug.] They opened their mouth against me, like wild beasts wishing to devour me; their mouth, namely, opened not by God’s wisdom but by their own wicked thought. I mean, they who were like a lion tearing at the arrest, and roaring when they said, “Crucify, crucify” (John 19). For it was like a lion’s [Col. 0232D] tearing when I was seized, and roaring when they cried, “Crucify, crucify.” Compare the words and assign each to its proper counterpart. [Cassiod.] “Like a lion tearing”: they surrounded me; “like one roaring”: they opened their mouth. It follows:

VERS. 14.—“I have been poured out like water, and all my bones have been scattered.”

“Like.” As though he said: They besieged and surrounded me, and even killed me—and so contemptibly that I was poured out like water; that is, I was killed by them as contemptibly as water is poured out. [Gl. int.] Not without reason does he use the pouring out of water in comparison with his death. [Aug.] For when water is poured out, it does three things: it washes, waters, and makes the feet slip. So, when Christ was poured out, the filth of vices was washed away, minds were watered with virtues so as to germinate, and the persecutors also fell, because for the sin of Christ’s killing they are punished inwardly and outwardly, as are the Jews. And from fear of the Passion all my bones were scattered, [Aug., Hier.] that is, my disciples were scattered, who were to be the supports of my body, that is, of the Church, because, leaving him, they fled. Hence elsewhere: “You have removed friend far from me” (Ps. 87). And therefore the disciples fled, because:

VERS. 15.—“My heart became like melting wax in the midst of my belly.”

My heart became like melting wax in the midst of my belly; that is, my teaching, by which I had confirmed them, when the Passion came upon it as though fire, vanished and failed among the weak, [Alcuin.] who are signified by the belly. [Col. 0233B] And also for this reason, because:

VERS. 16.—“My strength dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue clung to my jaws; and you led me down into the dust of death.”

My strength, formerly proved by miracles, dried up—[Alcuin.] that is, became despised—like a potsherd, which is something most worthless. My strength dried up also—that is, because—my tongue clung to my jaws; that is, I did not answer them a word. Hence: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he was silent” (Isa. 53). And it dried up also because, according to the Jews’ opinion, you led me down into the dust of death, [Hier.] namely, into which the dead are reduced. And all this proceeded from that.

[Col. 0233C] VERS. 17.—“For many dogs have surrounded me; the counsel of the wicked has besieged me.”

“For many dogs have surrounded me.” Or thus from the passage, “I have been poured out like water”—another reading. A great mystery is here indicated when he says, “Like water,” namely, the washing away of sins. [Cassiod.] And this occurred because the apostles were scattered through the world to preach; they are understood by the bones, and they too are said to be poured out like water that washes and waters. As though he said: They surrounded me and even killed me; and when I suffered, all my bones—that is, my steadfast apostles—were scattered, [Aug.] that is, sent everywhere by the Lord to preach, when he said to them: “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves” (Matt. 10). And those bones were poured out like [Col. 0233D] water, [Cassiod.] because the apostles washed away the filth of vices and watered minds, as water washes and waters. And through them my heart became like, etc.—that is, it brought forth the secret meaning of Scripture; [Hier., Aug., Cassiod.] for Scripture, that is, the wisdom and will of Christ, which had been enclosed in the Scriptures, was melted like wax when the Lord was crucified, so that all the weak might understand. Hence he adds: “In the midst of my belly.” The belly, being the soft part of the body, signifies the weak in the Church, to whom Christ’s wisdom and will were likewise revealed. Or, “in the midst of my belly,” that is, in the memory of the Church. [Aug.] For as the belly receives food, so memory holds knowledge of things. And fittingly he compares the mysteries of the Law to wax, which gives light when dissolved by heat; [Cassiod.] [Col. 0234A] so, when the fire of Christ’s Passion was applied, the mysteries of the Scriptures were laid open, that they might shine upon all in the Church. And for this reason the veil of the Temple was torn from top to bottom (Matt. 27); and through the same Passion, “my strength dried up like a potsherd,” [Hier., Cassiod.] that is, my name, which before the Passion was despised, is afterward honored more firmly. And therefore he does not say “like hay,” but “like a potsherd,” because, as a potsherd becomes firmer in the fire, so Christ’s strength was, as it were, hardened and made solid by the fire of the Passion. And my tongue—that is, my preachers—clung to my jaws, that is, they attended to my words in order to receive wisdom from my inward parts. Or, “my tongue clung to my jaws,” that is, the apostles through whom I was to speak kept my commandments within themselves. [Col. 0234B] And through them you led me down into the dust of death, [Aug.] that is, into the ungodly, whom the wind drives from the face of the earth and who are destined for death; [Gl. int.] that is, into the knowledge of those who were the dust of death. I was led by the preaching of the apostles, because they surrounded me. As though he said: I was poured out, and this because many dogs surrounded me—[Aug., Cassiod.] namely, Jews barking and biting not for truth but from custom, as dogs follow custom. And the counsel—or “assembly,” another reading—of the wicked, that is, Jews devising evil, [Cassiod.] so as to seize and kill me by deceit, besieged me in the Passion, in which the spiritual city Jerusalem is besieged. [Gl. int.] Or, “the assembly of the wicked,” that is, of the Gentiles, besieged me. Or:

VERS. 18.—“They pierced my hands and my feet; they numbered all my bones.”

“They pierced my hands.” [Aug.] Behold the Gospel narrative. For these things are read to have happened in the Gospel: Gentile soldiers pierced my hands and feet with nails. [Gl. int.] Note that he does not say “they transfixed” or “they wounded,” but “they dug,” [Cassiod.] because, as dug earth produces fruit, so Christ when wounded gave the fruit of life. And “they numbered,” that is, they made all my bones countable. [Aug.] The punishment of the cross is properly described here; nor could the stretching of the body upon the wood be described better than by saying, “They numbered all my bones.” [Cassiod.] [Col. 0234D] Although these words may rightly be understood literally, the digging of his hands nevertheless suggests that they did not believe his works; and the digging of his feet, that they tore the apostles to pieces. Likewise, “they numbered my bones,” that is, the apostles: seeking to prevent them from growing to a greater number, they tried to extinguish them, so that they might be few and unchanging. And they did not only do the things foretold; but also:

VERS. 19.—“But they considered and gazed upon me; they divided my garments among themselves, and upon my clothing they cast lots.”

They, the Jews, [Aug.] unchanged from their wickedness, considered what was happening and did not understand; and they gazed upon me—they saw only as far as the flesh with the eyes of the body, not as far as the Word with the eyes [Col. 0235A] of the heart. Or, “they considered and gazed upon me,” that is, with diligence and pleasure they looked upon me suffering such things, though eyes ordinarily turn away from a cruel sight. [Cassiod.] See how obstinate the Jews were: nothing happened by chance, nor were their hearts softened by so many miracles. “And they divided my garments among themselves,” literally into four parts, as John the Evangelist says (John 19); “and upon my clothing they cast lots.” This was the seamless tunic, woven from above throughout. [Cassiod.] These things may also be understood mystically. By Christ’s garments are understood the Scriptures or the Church’s sacraments; by the seamless tunic, upon which the lot was cast, charity or the Church’s unity is understood; by those who divided the garments are understood corrupters [Col. 0235B] of the Scriptures. Therefore, as those men actually divided the garments, so those who do not aim at unity have divided my garments—the spiritual sacraments and holy Scriptures—by corrupting them. For his sacraments and Scriptures could be divided through heresies; but not the tunic from above, that is, woven so completely throughout. [Aug.] This is the charity or unity of the Catholic Church, which no one can divide. For ecclesiastical charity is not torn apart, but comes to certain persons by lot and God’s gift. Whoever has it is secure, and no one moves him from the Catholic Church; and if he begins to possess it outside, he is admitted, as an olive branch carried by a dove was brought to the ark (Gen. 8).

[Col. 0235C] VERS. 20.—“But you, O Lord, do not remove your help far from me; look to my defense.”

But you. After the narrative he prays. As though he said: Though they act thus, you, O Lord, do not delay your help from me until the common resurrection of all; [Aug.] rather, raise me immediately. And so it happened, because after three days he rose; and look to my defense, lest they harm me in any way.

VERS. 21.—“Deliver my soul, O God, from the sword; and my only one from the hand of the dog.”

Deliver—As though he said: Do not delay, but deliver, O God, my soul from the sword; [Aug.] that is, from death. For *framea* is a sword, by which he intended death to be understood. Or, from the sword, that is, from the tongue of dissension. [Col. 0235D] And deliver my only one, that is, the Church, from the hand of the dog, that is, from the power of Jews barking like dogs and without discernment. As though he said: Deliver head and body. For by “soul” and “only one” the head and body are understood; and, since it is one, it rejects divisions. [Hier.] Therefore he fittingly prays for both together. Or, the only one is Christ’s soul, which alone is free from sin.

VERS. 22.—“Save me from the mouth of the lion, and my humility from the horns of unicorns.”

Save me from the mouth of the lion, [Aug.] that is, the devil, who goes about like a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5). Or, from the mouth of the lion, that is, from secular rule; [Col. 0236A] and from the horns—that is, the heights or pride—of unicorns, that is, the Jews, save my humility. [Note: [Col. 0235D] From Pliny, book VIII, chapter 21.] The unicorn is a most proud animal, said to die of indignation if it is held against its will, and it has one horn. [Alcuin, Hier.] By it are signified the Jews, who are rightly called unicorns, as though seeking only earthly things, or boasting uniquely of God’s worship, or being uniquely proud, having killed the Son after the servants as well. [Aug.] Unicorns are also all proud persons who set themselves up singularly and do not tolerate companions. Thus, “from the horns of unicorns” means from the heights of the Jews, or of any proud persons who exalt themselves singularly and do not tolerate companions.

[Col. 0236B] PART III. VERS. 23.—“I will declare your name to my brethren; in the midst of the Church I will praise you.”

I will declare your name. [Aug.] The third part, in which the fruit of the Passion is shown. Up to this point he has said what he suffered and what he prayed. See now why he suffered; for unless he willed it, he would not suffer. [Cassiod.] See the fruit of the Passion, lest the hearts of believers be disturbed by hearing of the Passion. As though someone asked: With what fruit do you suffer these things? Answer: [Aug.] These fruits: namely, “I will declare your name to my brethren,” that is, to my apostles, who love one another as they are loved by me. And through them I will praise you, O Father, not in one part only, but in the midst of the Church for which I suffered. But what is that Church? Wherever God is feared and praised, there is the Church. The seed of Jacob, the seed of Israel, is the Church. Hence he adds: [Col. 0236C] And you:

VERS. 24.—“You who fear the Lord, praise him; glorify him, all the seed of Jacob.”

You who fear the Lord, praise him, not yourselves. [Aug.] He calls those who fear God to praise. [Cassiod.] For human fear produces not praise but blame. And you who are the seed of Jacob, to whom the greater shall serve, all of you—that is, from every nation; that is, you who are the people of the faithful gathered from every nation, to whom the greater Jewish people serves—glorify him. Those whom he previously called the seed of Jacob he makes clear by adding:

VERS. 25.—“Let all the seed of Israel fear him, because he has not spurned nor despised the supplication [Col. 0236D] of the poor.”

Let all the seed of Israel fear him, [Aug.] that is, all born unto new life [Cassiod.] and restored to the vision of God; for the stranger does not know how to fear. [Gl. int.] Then he adds the reason why they ought to glorify him: namely, because, although he was exalted, he did not spurn or despise [Aug.] the humble supplication of the poor—not of one who cries the word of the beloved from a vain life, but of the poor person or poor persons, that is, the supplication of anyone who does not presume upon himself and is not puffed up by worldly display.

VERS. 26.—“Nor has he turned his face from me; and when I cried to him, he heard me.”

[Col. 0237A] Nor has he turned his face from me, [Aug.] as from that former one, who said above: “I shall cry, and you will not hear.” And when I cried to him, he heard me. For what purpose is he heard? Because:

VERS. 27.—“With you is my praise in the great Church; I will pay my vows in the sight of those who fear him.”

[Aug.] With you is my praise, O Lord, because I do not seek my praise, because you are my praise. You dwell in me as holy, and now hear me, holy, praying. He places praises with God who teaches that no confidence should be placed in man. Or join it thus: I say, “he heard me,” and therefore “with you is my praise,” that is, I will praise you. And this in the great Church, that is, throughout the whole world, not merely in Africa, as the Donatists say. How will the [Col. 0237B] praise be? See: “I will pay my vows,” that is, the sacrifice of my body and blood, which Christ offered to God, [Aug., Gl. int.] and which the faithful know, in the sight of those who fear him, so that they may understand both that it is the true body and that through it they are saved. And these are the sacrifices of my body and blood.

VERS. 28.—“The poor shall eat and be satisfied; and those who seek him shall praise the Lord; their hearts shall live for ever and ever.”

The poor shall eat, [Aug.] that is, those who despise the world and are humble, and shall be satisfied. Those who imitate the rich are not satisfied, because they do not hunger for the Lord’s supper and Passion. But those who imitate him in suffering are satisfied and praise him with overflowing speech.
