For such poor persons neither desire the abundance of this world nor fear want; [Col. 0237C] concerning them he adds: “and those who seek him shall praise the Lord.” [Aug.] The poor praise God; the rich praise themselves. For this reason they are poor: because they praise God in order to seek him, and he is the wealth of the poor. The rich seek to fill a chest with earthly riches; the poor seek to fill the heart with God. [Gl. int., Aug.] Therefore, even if their bodies die, their hearts shall live; in this the others, outside, are rich. Therefore he says “hearts,” because that food is food for the heart. “They shall live,” I say, “for ever and ever.” The rich live in this age, but afterward die without end. By contrast, the poor shall live eternally.

VERS. 29.—“All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord.”

[Col. 0237D] They shall remember. [Gl. int.] Here the Church speaks, as though saying: Who are the poor, and how will they praise? It answers: The poor are all the ends of the earth and all the families of the nations. And they will praise in this way, because they shall remember, etc. Or join the wording thus. Above Christ said that he would declare God’s name to his brethren, that is, the apostles, and through them praise God in the midst of the Church; here he adds that through these same men many will be converted. [Aug.] And this is “through them I will praise you,” and afterward through these praisers, all the ends of the earth—that is, the Church from the whole world—shall remember God, because God had slipped from their minds, and shall turn to the Lord.

[Col. 0238A] VERS. 30.—“And all the families of the nations shall worship before him.”

And all the families of the nations, [Gl. int.] that is, some from every family and from every end of the earth, shall worship before him, [Aug.] that is, in their consciences, where true worshipers worship the Father, not before men. [Gl. int., Cassiod.] Or, they shall worship before him, because they behold him as Lord. Or, they shall worship before him, that is, they shall worship in the understanding of faith, through which they behold God; for the sight of God is only by faith.

VERS. 31.—“For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he will rule over the nations.”

“For the Lord’s.” [Aug.] As though he said: And he ought to be worshiped. [Col. 0238B] For the kingdom belongs to the Lord, not to proud men. [Gl. int.] Formerly the Jews renounced the kingdom for him, saying: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). [Aug.] But Christ alone is our king, as the title on his cross indicates; we are marked with his name and image, as a coin is marked with the king’s name and title. Therefore heretics who possess Christ’s baptism, if they come to the Church’s unity, are not altered by us; rather, we recognize in them the titles of our king. Of him he adds: “and he will rule over the nations,” not only over the Jews.

VERS. 32.—“All the fat ones of the earth have eaten and worshiped; before him all who go down into the earth shall fall.”

They have eaten. [Cassiod.] Here he shows that the sacrament [Col. 0238C] of the body is shared even by the wicked, but does not benefit them as it does the good. As though he said: Not only will the poor eat, but all the fat ones of the earth—that is, the rich of the earth—have eaten Christ’s body of humility; [Aug.] yet they have not, like the poor, been satisfied unto imitation, but have merely worshiped. [Note: [Col. 0237] Augustine, Psalm 48, at the verse “Together, rich and poor”; and cited in *De consecratione*, distinction 2, canon “Non prohibeat.”] And this is what he adds: “and worshiped.” They worship God only outwardly, but do not show brotherly humanity. From this it is evident that good and evil alike share in the sacrament of life. Hence Augustine says elsewhere: “Let not the steward forbid him to eat, but let him warn the exacter to fear; yet if anyone manifestly persists in a grievous sin, he must be prohibited.” But one whose sin is hidden is to be admonished before him. As though he said: The wicked eat with the good. But all who go down into the earth—that is, who love earthly things—will fall because they receive unworthily. [Aug.] Before him, that is, before God, because God alone sees how those fall who, abandoning heavenly things, choose to be made happy on earth. [Cassiod.] The Church receives both, namely the worthy and the unworthy; but he sees and distinguishes who receive unto life and who unto death.

VERS. 33.—“And my soul shall live for him, and my seed shall serve him.”

And my soul—[Aug.] as though he said: The fat ones fall, [Col. 0239A] but my soul, which in contempt of the world seems to men to die, shall live not for itself but for him—that is, it has life not from itself but from God; nor does it attribute life to itself, but to him. And my seed, that is, my works, or those believing through me, shall serve him, that is, shall praise God. [Gl. int.] He says this lest anyone doubt the Church’s continuance. It shall serve, I say, because:

VERS. 34.—“A generation to come shall be declared to the Lord; and the heavens shall declare his righteousness to a people that shall be born, whom the Lord has made.”

It shall be declared, [Gl. int.] that is, by proclamation a coming generation shall be converted to the Lord, that is, to the Lord’s honor: the generation of the New Testament, which will be regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit. [Cassiod.] Or thus: My soul shall live to God and serve him, and thus shall come to the Lord. And a generation to come shall be declared to the Lord by angels (John 3), to him, because angels offer the prayers of men to God, not for instruction but in ministry (Tobit 12). And the heavens, [Hier., Cassiod.] that is, the Evangelists, shall declare his righteousness, that is, the Son of God, or his commandments. They shall declare, I say, to a people. Who is that people? [Aug.] The people who shall be born to the Lord by faith. How shall it be born? Behold, the people whom the Lord has made, [Cassiod.] that is, whom the Lord made a second time, namely by regeneration; for he who first made us that we might exist, made us a second time that we might be righteous. Note that the psalms concerning the Passion, as we have said, end in the great hope of Christians, so that it may be known that salvation comes from the Passion.

## COLLATION ON PSALM XXI: “MY GOD, MY GOD, LOOK UPON ME.”

[Col. 0239C]

In the title, the Septuagint has: “For the aid of the morning.” Jerome: “For the morning stag,” or, as others say, “for the hind,” or “concerning the hind of dawn.” Münster says in a scholium that the Hebrew word is uncertain among the Hebrews as to its meaning; but it sometimes denotes strength or a circumstance in which, without difficulty, that strength of Christ in the morning resurrection may be understood, by which he was received into immortality, as Augustine interprets it. The rest may be found in the exposition, lest we repeat what has already been done.

VERS. 1.—“My God, my God, look upon me.” The final part is not found in the Hebrew, and therefore seems especially to be removed, since Jerome writes in chapter 21 of Matthew: “And what is read in the middle of the verse, ‘look upon me,’ is superfluous.” The same Jerome replies in the tract *On the Best Method of Translating*: “Let my detractors ask and understand that in the Scriptures one must consider not words but meanings. The beginning of the twenty-first Psalm according to the Hebrew is exactly what the Lord spoke on the cross: ‘Eli, Eli,’ etc., ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’ Let them explain why the Seventy Translators inserted ‘look upon me.’ For thus they translated: ‘My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?’ They will surely answer that no harm is done to the meaning if two words are added. Let them hear from me also that the state of the churches is not endangered if, through speed of dictation, I have omitted some words. It would take too long now to set forth how much the Seventy added of their own, how much they omitted, and what in the Church’s copies is marked by obeli and asterisks.” Thus he.

“Words of my sins.” Jerome according to the Hebrew, and all the others whom we frequently cite, have: “words of my roaring,” or “of my lamentation.” Saint Jerome, in commenting on this place, approves and interprets both [Col. 0240A] translations: “Aquila,” he says, “has interpreted this passage thus: ‘Far from my salvation are the words of my roaring’; Symmachus: ‘the words of my groanings’; the fifth and sixth editions: ‘the words of my cry.’ And according to the other interpreters the sense is: My groans and efforts, by which I sought to save the people of Israel, have become far from my salvation, which I desired to bestow upon the people, because they themselves were unwilling to receive healing. But according to the Seventy Interpreters, the sense is this: When I pray for salvation and complain that I have been forsaken, I do not speak in my own person, but in that of the people, whose sins I myself took upon my body. Hence I say: Far from my salvation are the words that I utter. For I, being God, seek salvation for myself not so much as for the people who need salvation.”

VERS. 2.—“I will cry by day and you will not hear; and by night, and not unto foolishness to me.” Good heavens! How fiercely Caecus Burgensis (“the Blind Man of Burgos”), following Faber, fumes here, claiming that the Latin reading is incongruous and absurd because the expression *clamabo per diem et nocte* (“I shall cry through the day and at night”) is solecistic. It ought, he says, to be *per diem et nocte*, or *die et nocte*. Why then did Jerome and Augustine, educated among rhetoricians and grammarians, not perceive such absurdity? Certainly, if it had been said continuously, “by day and by night,” he would have had greater occasion for barking; but where two clauses intervene, the preposition *in* could be understood, so that it means “in the night,” especially since the coordinating conjunction is repeated—not only in the Latin edition but in Greek and Hebrew. Indeed, there is no need for the preposition *in* to be understood: “I will cry by day, and you will not hear; and I will cry by night,” etc.

What follows in the same verse makes this clearer: “and not unto foolishness to me.” Jerome and the Hebrews have *VELO DUMIAH LI*, that is, “nor is there silence for me.” Jerome, in his commentary on the present [Col. 0240C] passage, shows that the Septuagint expressed the sense: “Hanging in the day,” he says, “he is not heard by the Father; at night he rises victorious from the dead.” Otherwise: “He who is not heard in joy is heard in tears.” Hence he says, “not unto foolishness to me,” that is, I did not cry in vain. And Aquila translated from Hebrew, saying: “And by night you will not be silent,” that is, you will hear me, answer me, do what I prayed. Here you see that the phrase “by night” may refer to what follows, so that there is no silence for Christ in the night of tribulation, in which he was heard because of his reverence. For God is said to be silent when he does not hear; and we cry “unto foolishness” when we pray in vain and God is silent to us.

VERS. 18.—“They pierced my hands and my feet.” Even from this passage it is most clearly evident that the Jews corrupted the Hebrew manuscripts, which the present verse openly convicted: they could not show where David had had his hands and feet fixed; yet from this prophecy we could cast before them the most dreadful crime which David had foretold so many ages earlier was to be committed by the ungodly. Their mouth was stopped, unless they avoided the Scripture. It is probable that the manuscript Jerome used was genuine, since he prepared his translation according to the Hebrew at the request of Sophronius, who was in daily conflict with the Jews; whenever he brought forward anything from the Psalter concerning Christ the Lord, the faithless would object that it was not found in the Hebrew as he cited it. Therefore they tried to evade Sophronius in every discussion, for which [Col. 0240D] reason Jerome states that he prepared that edition and changed nothing from the Hebrew, lest Sophronius thereafter be deceived by the Jews’ falsehoods. Hence we argue that the passage had not yet been corrupted, since we know that he translated it according to our reading; otherwise he would have supplied them with greater occasion for calumny.

For this reason Münster, in his scholia, warns that one must have recourse to ancient manuscripts. I have not thought it burdensome to attach his words, because they serve the aim of our undertaking, in which we often maintain that manuscripts have varied or been corrupted through malice, negligence, or in some other way. But let us hear Münster himself: “The Hebrews here commonly read, ‘like a lion, my hands and my feet’—supply, ‘they watched,’ lest I should defend myself with my hands or flee with my feet. But the ancient translators read *CARU*, ‘they pierced,’ for *CAARI*. And indeed in this place the most ancient Hebrew manuscripts ought to be consulted in order to investigate the truth of this matter. I have here nothing but Nizabon’s mockery, who heaps insults on us on account of the foolish translation of this passage, as though the ancients had deliberately made *CARU* here from [Col. 0241A] nothing.” Thus he.

But the edition seen beside Campensis’s Paraphrase also plainly Judaizes: “He breaks,” it says, “my hands and feet like a lion.” Nebiensis holds the manuscripts to be corrupt, but the construction to be defective, so that “they pierced” must nevertheless be supplied, and the sense is: “The ungodly, like a lion, pierced, mangled, and fastened my hands.” Likewise, what follows in the same verse: “they numbered all my bones.” The Hebrews read in the singular, “I will number all,” etc.; yet the sense agrees. And, as Jerome teaches in *On the Best Method of Translating*, variety of expression agrees in unity of spirit.

VERS. 22.—“And my humility from the horns of unicorns.” Hebrew: *ANITATI*, if taken verbally, means “you have heard me,” or “you have answered me,” as the newer translators rendered it. Jerome, however, said “hear me,” so that he seems to have read *ANENI*. Yet nothing prevents its being taken nominally, as Pellicanus did in translating “my humility,” from the root *ANAH*, which sometimes denotes “he afflicted” or “he humbled.”

VERS. 28.—“Their hearts shall live.” Here manuscripts vary. Jerome according to the Hebrew, in Faber’s copy, has “their heart.” Likewise the interpreters cited by Cajetan and Nebiensis. [Col. 0242A] But the Hebrews read *LEBABCHEM*, “your heart.” If, however, you say *LEBABHEM*, it is “their heart.” But because the sense is sound, this could be passed over, as must often be done with trifles that would burden more than benefit; though certain matters must sometimes be touched on lightly, on account of those who are excessively fastidious.

VERS. 33.—“And my soul shall live for him.” The Hebrew appears diametrically opposed: *NAPHSSO LO HIIAH*, “his soul shall not live,” or “his soul shall not be made alive,” taking the past for the future. But where pronunciation is the same and writing similar, error in such matters is easy. For in Hebrew “for him” and “not” are pronounced differently and nearly written alike: the negation has an *aleph*, thus *lo*, while the dative pronoun has a *waw*, thus *lo*, as the Septuagint read. Again, *waw* and *yod* are interchangeable and neighboring letters in Hebrew; therefore there is no need to dispute why the Septuagint said “my soul,” while others say “his soul,” *NAPHSSO* or *NAPHSSI*. Pellicanus explains both readings, with respect to affirmation or negation: “his soul shall not live,” that is, it has no strength from itself and will not be preserved because of its own abasement; or, “it shall live for him,” through him, for him. Campensis explains the negative reading otherwise: because he did not disdain to spend his own life for them.

VERS. 33. — “A generation yet to come shall be proclaimed to the Lord.” The Hebrews make a different division and say: “It shall be proclaimed,” or “it shall be reckoned, into the generation.” Then begins the opening of another verse: “They shall come and proclaim,” etc. But the Septuagint, dividing it differently, understood the relative pronoun “which,” as commonly happens in Hebrew: “The generation which shall come,” that is, the generation to come. Nor is it an objection that *generation* is singular while *IABOU*, “they shall come,” is plural; for where there is a collective noun, it is sometimes joined with a plural. As in: “Sing joyfully to God, all the earth” (Ps. LXV).

## PSALM XXII

[Col. 0241]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0241C]

“The Lord governs me.” Title: A Psalm of David. [Alcuin.] Under the figure of the Jewish people returning from the Babylonian captivity under Zerubbabel and Jesus the high priest, the prophet here foretells the return of the faithful people from the Babylon of this age, through Christ, to the house of God. For this psalm treats of Christ’s mercy, by which this return is effected, enumerating ten graces through which, as by stages, a person returns to the Lord. Its sense is: This psalm is attributed to David, that is, to the Church, in whose person the Prophet speaks here. Its purpose is to exhort all to hope in God’s mercy. Its method: there are ten divisions, as also ten graces. [Aug.] The first grace is the place of pasture, that is, the divine word, which fattens those who meditate upon it; [Col. 0241D] we shall deal with the others in their places. And because spiritual return is effected through Christ the high priest, [Aug.] the Church therefore speaks of Christ himself thus, saying:

VERSE 1. — “The Lord governs me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture there he has placed me.”

The Lord, [Aug., Cassiod.], that is, Christ, governs or feeds me; that is, Christ is my shepherd, in whom I am safe and also fully supplied. Hence it adds: “and I shall lack nothing” in the future. [Cassiod.] It says this because it believes that spiritual substance [Col. 0242C] will be conferred upon it by God. Christ, I say, has already led me into a place of pasture, that is, into understanding of the divine word, instructing those who are beginning in the faith—or, those beginning to believe. [Aug., Alcuin, Gl. int.] In this place of pasture I am certain of fullness; and there, that is, in that same place, he has placed me to be nourished—not I myself. For the divine word does two things: it instructs beginners, as he indicated by saying, “he will lead me into a place of pasture”; and it more fully strengthens and nourishes those already faithful in the faith, as he indicates when he says, “there he has placed me.”

### PART II. VERSE 2. — “He has led me beside the water of refreshment; he has converted my soul.”

“Beside the water.” [Cassiod., Gl. int.] The second part, in which the second grace is indicated: namely, the water of refreshment. It is as though he said: He instructed me in the faith. [Cassiod., Col. 0242D Aug.] And afterward he led me, gradually, as children are led, beside the water of refreshment, that is, of baptism, by which those who had lost their wholeness and strength are restored. And the soul, sterile through the dryness of sins, is made fruitful.

### PART III. — “And my soul.” The third part, in which the third grace is indicated: after baptism the contracted soul becomes without wrinkle; that is, from sinful it becomes righteous, through growth in virtue and good works. [Cassiod.] It is as though he said: He led me in baptism. And afterward “he converted my soul,” so that afterward it might be holy and righteous. Behold, we have shown the first grace to be understanding of the divine word; [Col. 0243A] the second, regeneration by baptism; the third, sanctification after baptism. [Alcuin.] Yet to some the order of these graces appears reversed: for the third seems first, and the first third. For a person first turns to God, then is regenerated, and afterward is nourished by understanding of the divine word. According to this reading, it is as though he said: He led me to a place of pasture; [Gl. int.] and previously he led me beside the water of refreshment. The sense of the words is not changed; but first he converted my soul, turned away in Adam, as a shepherd turns a sheep.

### PART IV. VERSE 3. — “He led me along the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.”

“He led me.” [Cassiod.] The fourth part, in which the fourth grace is indicated: namely, that he led him upon the precepts of charity, [Col. 0243B] that he might be rooted and perfected in charity. It is as though he said: He led me, he converted me, and then he led me along the paths of his righteousness; that is, he made me persevere in the precepts of charity. Or: “He led me along the paths of his righteousness,” that is, he brought me to such knowledge that, like a master, I teach his precepts. [Aug.] Or by “paths of righteousness” he means the stricter commandments and more perfect counsels, along which few righteous people walk as on narrow paths, since paths are narrower than roads. Yet he says that he has kept these things by God’s grace. Hence he adds: “for his name’s sake”; as though he said: He led me, and this for his name’s sake, not because of my merit. [Gl. int.] Even if merit seems to appear here, it should not be regarded as appearing in the others, but grace alone.

[Col. 0243C]

### PART V. VERSE 4. — “For even if I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, because you are with me.”

“For even if.” [Cassiod.] The fifth part, in which the fifth grace is indicated: that in the shadow of death one does not fear evils, that is, the perverse persuasions of heretics and schismatics. It is as though he said: He truly led me; for, that is, because even if I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death—that is, if I live among those ignorant of God. Or, “in the midst of the shadow of death,” [Aug.] that is, in the midst of this life, which is the shadow of death, because it is dark with the gloom of sins and leads to death. Or, “in the midst of the shadow of death,” [Cassiod.] among heretics and schismatics, who are the shadow of death because they bear the figure [Col. 0243D] of destruction, that is, the image of the devil. If, I say, I walk among these things, I shall fear no hidden or manifest evils, [Aug.] because you are with me in my heart through faith, so that after the shadow of death I may be with you through sight.

### PART VI. VERSE 5. — “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me.”

“Your rod.” [Cassiod., Aug.] The sixth part, in which the sixth grace is indicated: correction, called rod and staff. By “rod” he means mild discipline, such as is suited to sheep. By “staff” is meant strong discipline, administered to more grown children. It is as though he said: I shall fear no evils; and truly, for your rod and your staff—that is, discipline, which is a rod for sheep, that is, for the simple and weak, and your staff for more mature [Col. 0244A] children, who grow from an animal to a spiritual life—have not afflicted me, but rather have comforted me by instructing me, because in them I understand that you remember me. [Cassiod.] Or, the rod is severe strictness, of threat and punishment, which breaks vices to pieces. [Jerome.] The staff is governance, that is, gentle correction joined with the sweetness of persuasion, which supports—that is, keeps—the faithful in goodness.

### PART VII. VERSE 6. — “You have prepared a table before me against those who trouble me.”

“You have prepared.” The seventh part, in which the seventh grace is indicated: [Cassiod.] the Lord’s table, that is, blessed banquet, fullness of faith, heavenly food, of which the Apostle says: “Whoever eats the Lord’s flesh unworthily eats and drinks death for himself” (I Cor. XI). It is as though he said: By what means [Col. 0244B] have they comforted me? Because you have prepared for me a table, namely, communion in Christ’s body. [Alcuin.] And this “before me,” not before the ungodly, because I understand that I ought to imitate the footsteps of Christ’s passion. Thus it is said in Proverbs: “You have sat at the table of a rich man,” that is, of Christ; “consider what is set before you, and know that you too ought to prepare similar things,” that is, to suffer as he did (Prov. XXIII, according to the Septuagint). Therefore the prophet says elsewhere: “What shall I repay to the Lord? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the Lord’s name” (Ps. CXV). And this table is “against those who trouble me,” [Aug.] because it harms the ungodly when they receive it unworthily: they eat and drink judgment upon themselves, since even good things unworthily received harm the wicked.

We read of three tables. The first was in the Law, the second in the Gospel, the third in heaven. [Col. 0244C] Of the first Moses says in Exodus, where one reads of a table placed in the tabernacle near the entrance; upon it were twelve loaves of presentation made from fine flour, and on each a golden dish with a handful of incense (Exod. XXIV). Of the second the Apostle says: “You cannot partake of the table of Christ and of the table of demons” (I Cor. X). Of the third the Lord says: “That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke XXII). The first table showed refreshment but did not provide it; the second satisfies, the third glorifies. The first was in the letter, the second in the Spirit, the third in direct sight. The first taught, the second helps, the third brings to completion.

Or, he takes “table” here to mean the stronger doctrine upon which not little children but more mature persons feed. [Col. 0244D] It is as though he said: By what means have they comforted me? [Aug.] Because after the rod, by which, still little and animal-like, I was fed as though upon the pasture of milk, you prepared before me a table, that is, stronger food, so that I might no longer be fed with milk as a little child, but as one more mature might approach the Father’s table. And by this I have been strengthened against those who trouble me.

### PARTS VIII–IX. VERSE 7. — “You have anointed my head with oil; and my cup, making me drunk—how excellent it is!”

“You have anointed.” [Cassiod.] The eighth part, in which the eighth grace is indicated: the anointing of the head, namely Christ, which was not dried up by any barrenness of sins and from whose anointing the other members rejoice. [Alcuin.] For the ointment descends from the head into Aaron’s beard [Col. 0245A] and to the hem of his garment (Ps. CXXXII). The sense is: “You have anointed my head with oil,” that is, you have filled Christ with spiritual grace, from whose fullness we have received (John I). Or, by “head” the righteous man means his mind. Thus: “You have anointed my head with oil,” [Aug.] that is, you have gladdened my mind with spiritual joy. “And my cup.” [Cassiod.] The ninth part, in which the ninth grace is indicated: the cup of blessing, that is, Christ’s blood, which so intoxicates as to make sober. Thus: “Your cup,” or “my cup”—yours because you give it, mine because I receive it—“making me drunk,” [Aug.] that is, giving forgetfulness of empty delights, “how excellent it is!” [Cassiod.] For it gives the brightness of eternal life.

Note that he sets the cup, that is, Christ’s blood, by itself, as though it were a grace distinct from the table, that is, from the flesh; although flesh cannot exist or be received without blood, nor blood without flesh, and there are not two sacraments there but one. [Alcuin.] Yet because flesh is not blood, nor blood flesh; because bread is changed into flesh and wine into blood, and not conversely; and because each is received under distinct species, he distinguishes table and cup here as different graces.

### PART X. VERSE 8. — “And your mercy shall follow me all the days of my life.”

“And your mercy.” [Cassiod.] The tenth part, in which the tenth grace is indicated: mercy following for preservation, which goes before in order to confer grace. [Note: [Col. 0245D] Cassiodorus, in the Collect for the Sixteenth Sunday after Pentecost.] Hence: “May your mercy, O Lord, go before us and follow us”: go before by inspiring; follow [Col. 0246A] by helping. It is as though he said: You have done all these things for me, and after all these things your mercy shall follow me all the days of my life—not of yours, [Cassiod.] that is, so long as one lives in this mortal life. [Aug.] May it not merely follow me in order to preserve the preceding gifts, but also:

VERSE 9. — “And that I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days.”

[Aug.] “And that I may dwell,” in the future, “in the house of the Lord,” not made by hands. And there, “for length of days,” that is, eternally. [Alcuin.] Or this verse may be connected differently with what precedes. For this verse may be joined to all the foregoing. It is as though he said: You placed me, led me, guided me, and so forth, in order that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days [Col. 0246B] of my life, for length of days.

This psalm is sung at the funerals of the faithful departed, because through the graces enumerated here, as by certain stages, one ascends to eternal life, which is then desired and prayed for the faithful.

### COMPARISON ON PSALM XXII: “THE LORD GOVERNS ME, AND NOTHING”

VERSE 22. — “My cup, making me drunk—how excellent it is!” The Hebrews end the verse at “making me drunk,” and then begin the following verse: “Yet goodness,” etc. But the Septuagint joined the Hebrew *AK TOB* (“surely goodness”) to the same verse, especially since the particle *TOB* means “good,” “beautiful,” and “well-known,” and since the Psalter is known to proceed in lyric verse, as was shown above once and again. It conveys “goodness,” however, when it has what they call *vau sured*, according to Rabbi David in the Book of Roots: *TUB*.

## PSALM XXIII

[Col. 0245]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF DAVID ON THE FIRST DAY OF THE SABBATH.”

[Col. 0245C]

“The earth belongs to the Lord.” Title: A Psalm of David, on the first day of the Sabbath. “The first day of the Sabbath” is called the first day after the Sabbath. [Note: [Col. 0246D] From Jerome, Question 4 to Hedibia.] For because of the Sabbath’s dignity, the Hebrews call all the other days by the name of the Sabbath, saying the first of the Sabbath, the second of the Sabbath, and so forth, just as the Gentiles called days by the names of planets, saying the day of the Moon, the day of Mars, the day of Mercury, and so on. Christians, however, call the days *feriae*, because on all days we ought to abstain from servile work, that is, from sin.

[Cassiod.] On the first day of the Sabbath the world was created, light was separated from darkness, and things confused and formless received their forms. On that same day Christ, having put off the darkness of mortality, was glorified; and humanity, the gloom of sins having been driven away, was restored through Christ’s resurrection. [Aug.] This psalm treats of that glorification of Christ and restoration of humanity. The meaning of the title is: This psalm belongs to David, who speaks here in his own person or in that of the Church. This psalm, I say, concerns the Lord’s glorification and humanity’s restoration, accomplished on the first day of the Sabbath, [Cassiod.] which is called the Lord’s Day, [Col. 0246C] the same day that was first in the primal creation of things. [Alcuin.] Its purpose is to exhort us to welcome Christ the conqueror in triumph. [Cassiod.] Its method is as follows: the psalm is in three parts. First, it says that the whole world belongs to God, so that just as no one is outside his dominion, so no one may be estranged from faith in him. Second, it determines with what virtues those in the Church are endowed, at “Who shall ascend?” Third, it calls the superstitious away from perversity, that with hearts opened wide they may receive Christ, at “Lift up the gates.” Therefore the Prophet, after the manner of a herald who proclaims after the triumph that the whole earth belongs to the victor, contemplating the glory of Christ’s resurrection, says:

VERSE 1. — “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness; the inhabited world, and all who dwell in it.”

“The Lord’s,” that is, Christ’s—he is Lord of lords—[Col. 0246D] “is the earth,” [Cassiod.] that is, the fruitful Church. This is the good earth upon which the Gospel seed fell and brought forth fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold; “and its fullness,” that is, all with which the Church is filled, namely all the saints and the charisms of graces. And this earth, that is, the Church, is not small, but comes from the whole world and from all [Col. 0247A] who are in it. Hence he adds: “and it itself is the inhabited world, and in it are all who dwell therein.” [Aug.] For when the glorified Lord is proclaimed to the faith of all nations, then the whole world becomes his Church; that is, in the whole world and from the whole world his Church is made. And rightly is the Church the Lord’s.

VERSE 2. — “For he founded it upon the seas and prepared it upon the rivers.”

“He founded it,” [Aug.] that is, he most firmly established it upon the seas, that is, above all the waves of this age, so that it may overcome them and they may not harm it; and “he prepared it upon the rivers,” [Jerome] that is, the Church, upon the rivers—that is, upon those greedy for this age. [Aug.] For as rivers flow into the sea, so greedy people slip down into the world; and the Church overcomes even these, having, through God’s grace, conquered worldly desires and been prepared in charity to receive mortality. [Col. 0247B]

### PART II. VERSE 3. — “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? Or who shall stand in his holy place?”

“Who shall ascend?” [Cassiod.] The second part, in which he determines with what virtues those in the Church are endowed. It is as though he said: The inhabited world, that is, the Church from the whole world, belongs to the Lord; yet no one is there except the innocent. He says this interrogatively to make his hearers attentive: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” etc.

Or the preceding words may be understood literally. “The earth is the Lord’s,” which he created, “and its fullness,” that is, everything with which he adorned it. [Jerome.] Nor merely part of the earth, but “the inhabited world,” that is, the whole world, “and all [Col. 0247C] who dwell in it,” that is, all its inhabitants, belong to the Lord. And rightly so, because “he founded it upon the seas and prepared it upon the rivers,” etc. [Alcuin.] That is, he established it so that it might not be overwhelmed by the sea or rivers.

“Who shall ascend the mountain?” It is as though he said: [Jerome.] The world and all its inhabitants belong to the Lord, [Cassiod.] but no one is upon the mountain of his righteousness except the innocent. He employs a question for this purpose, saying, “Who shall ascend?” [Jerome.] It is as though he said: Great effort is needed. “Who” here is used to indicate rarity, not impossibility: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” [Aug.] that is, the lofty righteousness of the Lord. Or “who shall stand,” after ascending, “in his holy place,” prepared above the seas and rivers? [Aug.] That is, who shall remain where he ascended? [Jerome.] It is as though he said: Few ascend, and fewer remain. For many ascend [Col. 0247D] who do not persevere. Then he answers the foregoing question, saying:

VERSE 4. — “The innocent in hands and clean of heart, who has not received his soul in vain, nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbor.”

“The innocent in hands,” etc. [Alcuin.] He says that the one who will ascend and remain is certainly innocent toward his neighbor [Jerome] in three ways: by hand, that is, in deed; by heart, as indicated by “innocent in hands and clean of heart”; and innocent in words, as he says there, “nor sworn deceitfully,” etc. And he is innocent toward himself as well. [Alcuin.] This is what he says in “who has not received,” etc. It is as though he said: The question is who shall ascend and stand? Certainly the one who is innocent in hands, [Aug.] that is, pure in works, since works are understood by hands; who is clean in heart, that is, pure in thoughts; and who has not received his soul in vain, that is, who has not assigned his soul to things transient and perishing, but, knowing it to be immortal, has desired eternal things. Therefore he has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbor. For just as eternal things are simple and do not deceive, so he has conducted himself toward his neighbor. [Alcuin.] He promises nothing by which to deceive him. Lest he make matters worse, he permits simple oaths and forbids deceitful ones. Note that he does not say simply, “he has not sworn,” but “he has not sworn deceitfully.” This shows that he permits simple oaths and forbids deceitful ones. [Cassiod.] A person swears deceitfully who will act otherwise than he promises, since perjury is wickedly to deceive one who trusts. [Jerome.] The one who does not swear deceitfully proclaims what he thinks and fulfills it in deed.

Or here he takes “soul” to mean one’s sensual faculty. Thus: he who has not received his own sensual soul—that is, sensuality, the lower power of the soul—as acceptable, in vain, [Gl. int.] that is, in sin; [Jerome] who has not stained it after baptism with any filth of sins. “Nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbor”: this is unchanged.

VERSE 5. — “He shall receive blessing from the Lord and mercy from God his Savior.”

“He shall receive.” It is as though he said: Everyone ought to be innocent both toward himself and toward his neighbor, and from this come these rewards for him; because this man, such as ascends the mountain of the Lord, [Cassiod.] that is, to the height of righteousness and faith, has this indeed from the Lord. This is what he says: “He has received blessing from the Lord,” [Gl. int.] that is, by receiving the Lord’s blessing he will ascend and stand in God’s lofty righteousness.

Or thus: it is as though he said: The person who has the foregoing qualities shall ascend. But he does not have them from himself, but from God, because “he shall receive blessing,” that is, the aforesaid goods, from the Lord. [Cassiod.] This blessing is given through mercy, not through merits, because God first forgives sins through mercy. This is what he says: “And he shall receive mercy,” that is, remission of sins, by mercy shown by God his Savior, that is, by Christ. And lest you think that the foregoing things are to be received by Christ alone, because:

VERSE 6. — “This is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob.”

[Col. 0248D] “This generation,” that is, such is the generation of all together who seek him, or God. It is as though he said: Although I said in the singular, “he shall ascend,” “the innocent shall receive,” yet such people are not few but are a generation, [Cassiod.] that is, a multitude reborn in baptism, and they seek only God. Therefore he says, “of those who seek him.”

Or the connection is this: Truly the blessing shall be through mercy. For thus [Aug.]—that is, by mercy—those who seek him are born in baptism. This is the meaning: “This is the generation of those who seek him,” not indeed for worldly favor or earthly riches, but who seek God—so that they seek the face of God, [Remigius] that is, his presence and knowledge—the God, I say, of Jacob. [Cassiod.] That is, who seek God as Jacob sought him. [Col. 0249A] This is done by those who wish to be set above others in greater fervor, so that he may grant them primacy as he did Jacob, whom he set before Esau and whose birthright he inherited. [Aug.] Thus God gives primacy, taken away from the Jews—that is, Christ—to the Christian people born later. Hence Isaiah says: “I shall take away from Jerusalem head and tail” (Isa. IX).

### PART III, *DIAPSALMA* (“interlude”). VERSE 6. — “Lift up your gates, O princes; and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter.”

“Lift up.” [Cassiod.] The third part: having set forth the Christian religion, he calls the superstitious away from perversity, that they may admit Christ with hearts opened. It is as though he said: Since no one ascends or stands except the innocent and pure, therefore, O princes of the world and superstitious persons, [Col. 0249B] such as the leaders of hypocrisy, lift up—or take away—that is, remove from your souls your gates, [Cassiod.] that is, gates of death, which were set by the prince, the devil, and through which he enters hearts. Those gates are vices and sins, by which room is made for the devil in human hearts. And in opposition to those gates of death, “be lifted up,” that is, be exalted in human hearts, O everlasting gates—namely, every grace given when Christ came, who, full of the Spirit of grace, watered others with grace in order to drive spiritual wickedness from the hearts of his own. “Be lifted up,” I say, and so the King of glory shall enter hearts: [Aug.] that is, Christ, in whom we glory without pride, who came girded with humility, like a strong athlete, to conquer the pride of the devil.

VERSE 7. — “Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.”

“Who is this?” [Cassiod.] The Prophet asks here not because of his own ignorance, but to convict the pride and unbelief of the Jews. [Alcuin.] And so as to commend Christ more fully and invite others to love him, he says: “Who is this King of glory?” [Cassiod.] Who is to enter hearts? He answers, describing him by his powers, as by his proper name: [Cassiod.] He is absolutely the Lord of all, strong in deeds, even though you seized him with swords; and mighty, even though you handed him over to Pilate. He is the Lord mighty in battle, where he fought against the devil and against the Jews. Therefore, Jews, do not suppose that you overcame him in battle, even if you seem for a time to have prevailed against him. [Col. 0249D]

VERSE 8. — “Lift up your gates, O princes; and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter.”

“Lift up,” or “take away,” your gates, O princes; and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and he shall enter, etc. This is repetition. [Cassiod.] For he repeats what was said in order to determine more fully who the King of glory is—not item by item as before, saying “mighty,” “strong,” and so forth, but, as previously, first putting forward the Prophet’s question:

VERSE 9. — “Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts—he is the King of glory.”

[Col. 0250A] “Who is this King of glory?” [Cassiod.] He answers briefly and completely: the Lord of the heavenly hosts, that is, of angels; or of virtues, [Alcuin.] that is, of graces, because he gives every gift to all; or the Lord of hosts, [Jerome] that is, of earthly rulers—he is the King of glory. Where we have “of hosts,” the Hebrew has *sabaoth*, interpreted “of armies,” “of forces,” or “of hosts.”

Otherwise: “Lift up,” or “take away,” etc. By “princes” he means demons, who wish to rule human beings. He says, therefore: O princes of darkness, who seek primacy over human beings, take away the gates, O princes—that is, remove the entrances of desire and fear which you have established in human souls in order to enter through them and deceive people; let them not impede the Lord who comes. [Aug.] For people fear what should not be feared [Col. 0250B] and desire what should not be desired. And you, everlasting gates—that is, the approaches to eternal life, namely renunciation of the world and conversion to God—be lifted up, [Gl. int.] that is, exalted in human hearts. Thus the King of glory shall enter: [Aug.] that is, Christ, in whom we glory without pride. He has overcome the gates of death and opened for himself the heavenly doors, fulfilling what he said: “Rejoice, because I have conquered the world” (John XVI).

“Who is this?” [Aug.] Mortal nature trembles in amazement when it hears that the King of glory is to enter and asks, “Who is this King of glory?” The Prophet answers: He is strong and mighty, whom you thought weak and oppressed. He is the Lord mighty in battle, where he fought against death; and, when the scar has been drawn together [Col. 0250C] and hardened, you shall find yourself restored when immortality is given back. For when the weakness of humanity, which was owed to the earth, was dissolved in the place where battle was waged with death, the Lord’s glorification was made firm.

“Lift up,” or “take away.” Above he spoke against demons; from here the way goes to heaven—that is, he addresses the heavenly angels, who used to be worshiped by humans. And the Prophet again cries out: You also, heavenly princes, take away your gates which you have in the minds of people who worship the host of heaven. Before Christ’s coming, good angels allowed themselves to be worshiped with the worship called *dulia*, not *latria* (Gen. XVIII; Joshua V), so that reverence might be shown by people to them rather than to evil angels. [Note: [Col. 0249D] From Gregory, Homily 8 on the Gospels.] But after the incarnation, in humility [Col. 0250D] and submission, which they owe to their Lord, they forbid people to worship them, that people may understand that human nature in Christ has been exalted above every creature. Hence in Revelation the angel said to John: “Do not worship me, for I am your fellow servant and of your brothers” (Apoc. XXI).

“And be lifted up, O everlasting gates,” that is, the gates of eternal righteousness, charity, and chastity, through which the soul may love the one true God and not commit fornication beneath the many who are called gods. Thus the King of glory shall enter the mind, that he may intercede at the right hand of the Father (Heb. VII), that is, that he may be believed to intercede for us. “Who is this King of glory?” [Aug.] Even the prince of this air, who formerly held primacy in humanity, marvels and asks: “Who [Col. 0251A] is this King of glory?” The Prophet answers: The Lord of hosts, namely heavenly or earthly ones—he is the King of glory. Even with his body glorified above you, he goes on; he who was tempted stretches beyond all angels, he who was tempted by the transgressing angel. Therefore let no evil prince set himself in the way or bar his path to us, so that, as God, he may dwell in us and be worshiped.

Or otherwise, “Lift up,” or “take away.” David the prophet speaks these words, assuming the person of the angels who preceded Christ as he descended to hell or ascended into heaven. Therefore the angels going before Christ to hell say to the powers of Tartarus: [Jerome.] O princes of hell, take away your gates, that is, remove your power by which until now you held all people in hell. And those same angels going before Christ in his ascension say: And you everlasting gates, which until now were closed—namely, the entrances of heaven and the entry of paradise—be lifted up, that is, be opened, and the King of glory, that is, Christ, shall enter heaven. He is the high priest who, under the old Law, entered once a year with blood into the holy of holies (Heb. IX).

The demons marvel and ask: “Who is this King of glory?” [Jerome.] It is as though they said: We have our king, namely the devil. Who is this King of glory? The angels preceding Christ to hell answer: He is the Lord strong and mighty, who conquered death and the devil; the Lord mighty in battle against the devil, your prince, because he bound the strong man and now [Col. 0251C] comes to overthrow his house and plunder his vessels—that is, to break the bars of hell and lead captivity captive.

[Jerome.] “Lift up your gates.” The ministering powers preceding Christ in his ascension call out to the other heavenly powers that they may open the way to the Lord who comes and meet him: O princes of heaven, lift up your gates, that is, unbar the heavenly entrances for the coming Lord. And you everlasting gates, be lifted up, that is, let the approaches to heaven and the eternal entrance stand open. Let the ethereal doors be opened and the gates of the everlasting dwelling places. And the King of glory shall enter heaven to intercede for us at the Father’s right hand [Aug., Jerome]. The angelic powers themselves, astounded at the new mystery of one clothed in flesh, ask in amazement: “Who is this [Col. 0252A] King of glory?” Others answer them: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory.”

Or otherwise, by “princes” he here means the saints, of whom it is said elsewhere: “And now, O kings, understand” (Ps. II); and Peter says: “You are an elect race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (I Pet. II). [Gl. int.] It is as though he said: Since no one ascends except one who is innocent and clean, therefore, O princes—that is, faithful people, who are an elect race and royal priesthood—lift up your gates, that is, enlarge the good works through which God enters. “And be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter.” These and what follows are not changed from the first exposition as far as “Lift up,” where the preceding words are repeated, through to the end.

### COMPARISON ON PSALM XXIII: “THE EARTH IS THE LORD’S”

[Col. 0252B]

VERSE 4. “Who has not received his soul in vain.” Some translate “my soul,” others “his soul,” others “his own soul,” as do the Septuagint and Jerome. The diversity arose from the Hebrew particle written with final *vau* but pointed with *hireq*: namely, *NAPHSCO* or *NAPHSCI*.

VERSE 5. “And mercy from God his Savior.” Jerome, from the Hebrew, has “righteousness,” as also the more recent translators render it. But *TZEDAQAH* is sometimes understood as almsgiving, which is a work of mercy. Add that the crown of righteousness which the Lord will render to those who love his appearing (II Tim. IV), and which corresponds to our good works, has more of divine generosity and grace than of debt, according to Titus III: “Not from works of righteousness which we did, but according to his [Col. 0252C] mercy he saved us.” This righteousness is also faith, God’s gift, through which we are mercifully made righteous, because, in Hebrews II, without faith it is impossible to please God.

VERSE 6. “Lift up your gates, O princes.” Jerome and the others translated: “Lift up your heads, O gates.” This happened because of the polysemy of the Hebrew word *ROSH*, which no Hebrew denies often signifies “a prince.” But the variation of case endings among Latins and Greeks is not the same among Hebrews. Therefore, according to the sequence of the discourse, now one case is rendered, now another; and this or that reading does not prejudice the sense, whether you take “gates” for the dominion of earthly desire or for any sins which impede the entrance to the kingdom of heaven.

## PSALM XXIV

[Col. 0251]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0251D]

“To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.” Title: Unto the end, a Psalm of David. This psalm is the consolation of the faithful against the adversities of the world. [Alcuin.] Behold, this is the prayer of the Church, grievously afflicted in this world, as though the prayer of a people grievously situated in Babylon. For here the Church speaks as one grievously scourged in penitence, who is set before others lest they murmur amid adversities; having experienced in herself God’s mercy and justice, she encourages by mercy and terrifies by justice. [Cassiod.] This is the first psalm arranged according to the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, though not by all of them. [Col. 0252D] For some are written through all the letters, while some are not. Those written through all signify those who, perfected in every virtue, sing God’s praises. Those not written through all signify less perfect praisers.

The meaning of the title is: This psalm directs us unto the end, that is, to Christ; it is attributed to David, [Gl. int.] that is, to the Church, which speaks here in the person of a penitent corrected by scourges. Its purpose is to exhort us not to murmur amid adversities, but to look to God. The psalm has three parts. First, because it is raised up to the Lord, it asks to be taught God’s ways. Second, it prays for the forgiveness of sins, both former sins [Col. 0253A] and those committed daily, at “Remember,” etc.

Third, he treats of eternal things, showing how they are obtained, at the words, “Who is the man?” Therefore, so that the Church may safely ask for what follows, she first states her desire and the love she has for God, speaking thus to him: O

VERSE 1.—“To thee, O Lord, have I lifted up my soul: my God, in thee I trust; I shall not be put to shame.”

[Jerome.] O Lord, I have lifted it from the earth by spiritual desire, after the likeness of a grain which, having sprung up in the earth, rises on high. But if it lies low, it is trampled underfoot and rots. What have I lifted? My soul, [Augustine.] which, trampled down by carnal desires, was pressed to the earth. To whom have I lifted it? [Cassiodorus, Ordinary Gloss.] To thee, that I may embrace and contemplate thee [Col. 0253B]. [Alcuin.] He easily despises earthly things who raises himself to behold divine things; and, O my God, [Augustine.] having experienced my own weakness amid evils, I now trust in thee, not in myself—I who formerly, trusting in myself, wished to be like God. Hence, brought by my pride to this weakness of the flesh, I was ashamed. Now, therefore, I trust in thee alone. And therefore I shall not be put to shame through a sin proceeding from myself, so as to lose that in which I trust—which would happen if I lost it. For hope does not put to shame. Nor shall I lose it through a sin arising from the suggestion of enemies. This is what he says:

VERSE 2.—“Neither let my enemies mock me; for all who wait for thee shall not be confounded.”

[Col. 0253C] Neither let my enemies mock me, [Ordinary Gloss.] that is, let them not prevail against me. This prayer has the force of an assertion, as though he said: My enemies of every kind shall not prevail against me—[Augustine.] namely, visible and invisible enemies, and especially those who, plotting and insinuating by serpent-like, hidden suggestions, cast me down into these evils. [Alcuin.] And I am certain of that for which I ask, because he deceives no one who patiently waits for him. [Ordinary Gloss.] This is what he says: for all who wait for thee—that is, who patiently bear the burden of the day and the heat (Matt. 20), namely, present tribulation, until thou comest—shall not be confounded, whether by themselves or by enemies; that is, by sin coming from themselves or from enemies.

[Col. 0253D] VERSE 3.—“Let all who act wickedly in vain be confounded.”

Let them be confounded. [Ordinary Gloss.] As though he said: Those who wait for thee shall not be confounded; but let those be confounded—here, healthfully, on account of their sins; or, if they refuse here, at last in eternal punishment. He adds who they are and why: [Augustine.] namely, all the wicked, or those doing wicked things, because they act unjustly in order to acquire things that pass away. Their actions are wicked because they act in vain—that is, they labour over vain things—because all things alien from God are empty and fruitless.

VERSE 4.—“Show me thy ways, O Lord, and teach me thy paths.”

Thy ways—as though he said: I shall not be put to shame. And lest this happen, O Lord, show me thy ways, that is, the lighter precepts [Col. 0254A]. [Ordinary Gloss.] As though he said: those which lie before the sight, just as something placed before the eyes is ordinarily indicated by the hand. [Cassiodorus.] Ways, then, are instructions concerning the order of life fitting for everyone, even the simple. Paths are those things which are hidden and narrow, such as the mystical understanding of the Law, known to few. Hence he adds: and teach me thy paths—that is, the narrow understandings of the Law, hidden and known to few—as though he said: those things which are concealed; and, O Lord,

VERSE 5.—“Direct me in thy truth, and teach me; for thou art God my Saviour, and for thee have I waited all day.”

[Augustine.] Direct me, fleeing errors, in thy truth, that I may live rightly and piously, as thy truth requires; and teach me truth itself, that I may understand what I believe. [Col. 0254B] Therefore, I say, teach me, because of myself I have known nothing but falsehood. Distinguish: he asks two things, to be directed and to be taught. [Cassiodorus.] “Direct” belongs to a good life; “teach” to true knowledge; in these lies perfection. It follows: “For thou art”—as though he said: Therefore do what I ask, because thou art God my Saviour, not I myself; [Augustine.] because I was driven from thee out of paradise into a far country, and I cannot return by myself unless thou meetest me as I wander. Likewise, for this reason too: because I have waited for thee all day—that is, throughout the whole course of worldly time—my return awaits thy mercy. Here he sets out two commendable things in saying, “Thou art my Saviour” and “I have waited for thee.” [Cassiodorus.] For there are two things that make people good: believing that God is our Saviour, and patiently awaiting his recompense.

[Col. 0254C] VERSE 6.—“Remember thy compassions, O Lord, and thy mercies, which are from of old.”

Remember. [Alcuin.] The second part, in which he prays concerning former sins and those committed daily, appealing to the mercy shown of old, and because he fears the true Judge. As though he said: Thou oughtest to direct and teach, because thou art God and because I have waited for thee; [Alcuin.] and if this is insufficient, O Lord, remember—though men suppose thee forgetful because thou delayest—thy compassions, [Cassiodorus.] that is, works of mercy, and thy mercies, naturally inherent in thee. For compassion properly consists in the bestowal of good things; mercy is naturally in God and is God himself. These mercies and compassions are from the age, from the beginning of the age. [Augustine.] For thou hast never been without mercy, nor has thy compassion failed sinful humanity: thou didst subject even sinful humanity, not indeed to vanity, but in hope. [Alcuin.] Therefore, let not that which was begun at the beginning of the age fail in my case.

VERSE 7.—“Remember not the offences of my youth and my ignorances.”

Offences. As though he said: Remember mercy, and through thy mercy do not remember—that is, do not preserve for everlasting vengeance—[Augustine.] the offences by which I abandoned the way of righteousness, of my youth; [Cassiodorus.] that is, of my self-confident and rash boldness; [Augustine.] nor my ignorances. Or, “my ignorances” means sins which I committed unknowingly, or which I committed before [Col. 0255A] I believed. [Cassiodorus.] Offences occur when the way of righteousness is knowingly abandoned. “Youth” here is not age, but the boldness of rashness, which exists when the disposition of the mind exceeds modesty. By “ignorances” he means sins done unknowingly; for we do things we do not know to be evil, even after baptism and faith. Or he calls “ignorances” sins committed before faith. [Jerome.] Or, by “the offences of youth” he means sins which he committed, as it were, in adolescence, namely before he left the house of his wicked father, that is, the devil, of whom it is said: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8). “The offences of ignorance” means those found in little children, who are held even by original sin. Thus: “The offences of my youth,” [Cassiodorus.] that is, those which I did while still young in [Col. 0255B] the house of my former master, namely the devil; and “the offences of my ignorance,” that is, original sin in little children—do not remember these, that is, do not reserve them for eternal punishment.

VERSE 8.—“According to thy mercy remember me, for thy goodness’ sake, O Lord.”

According to thy mercy—as though he said: I say, do not remember; rather, remember me, [Ordinary Gloss.] that is, mercifully see how frail my nature is. [Augustine.] Thou whose work it is to show mercy and to forgive sins, remember me—not according to the wrath I deserve, [Alcuin.] but according to thy mercy, by which thou didst deign to seek me, as befits thee. As though he said: As great as thy mercy is, so abundantly have mercy on me. [Ordinary Gloss.] And, O Lord, remember [Col. 0255C] me not because of my merit, [Alcuin.] but because of thy goodness naturally inherent in thee, by which thou didst make all things from nothing. Distinguish between mercy and goodness. [Cassiodorus.] Mercy is properly exercised toward the wretched; goodness toward anyone whatsoever. God does good both when implored by the wretched and when moved by goodness. For none is good of himself except God alone (Luke 18).

VERSE 9.—“The Lord is sweet and upright; therefore he will give the law to those who sin in the way.”

Sweet and upright. [Ordinary Gloss.] Here the discourse turns toward people, to whom this faithful person speaks, showing with what confidence he asks so insistently. As though he said: I ask with this confidence because the Lord is sweet, [Col. 0255D] [Augustine.] since he forgives all former sins to sinners and ungodly persons: here is grace without merits. And he is upright, [Alcuin.] because after the mercy of calling and forgiveness, he will require deserving merits at the final judgment. He says this lest God’s gentleness make us secure and idle. [Augustine.] And therefore, namely because he has first granted mercy, in order to bring them into the way, he will give the law to sinners: [Jerome.] that is, correction, or charity, by which people are joined and reconciled to God; [Alcuin.] yet only if they are in the way, that is, in faith. Or: he will give the law in order to set them in the way, that is, in God’s commandments. Or, he will give it in the way of this life, in which right living is both possible and necessary. And the Lord

VERSE 10.—“Will direct the meek in judgment; he will teach the gentle his ways.”

[Col. 0256A] He will direct the meek in judgment, [Augustine.] those who do not resist him at the future judgment; that is, he will not disturb in judgment those who follow his will and do not resist him. And here he will teach the gentle his ways: not those who wish to run ahead, as though they could govern themselves better, but those who do not lift up their neck or kick back when a light yoke and a light burden are placed upon them.

VERSE 11.—“All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, to those who seek his covenant and his testimonies.”

All: [Augustine.] as though he said: What ways will he teach them? Mercy, by which he is gracious, and truth, by which he is incorruptible. And all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] which, though they are infinite, are nevertheless contained in these two: the one he displays by forgiving sins, the other by judging merits. Mercy forgives sins; truth judges merits. Therefore all the ways of the Lord are the two comings of the Son of God: one of mercy, the other of judgment; that is, in these two comings he plainly displays mercy and truth to us. In the first, mercy; in the second, truth. Yet these two are together in every work of the Lord, even though they are not plainly evident to us. He holds his ways who, having experienced mercy, lays aside pride, seeing that he was freed by none of his own merits, and thereafter fears the severity of the Judge. It follows: “To those who seek,” etc. As though he said: I say that all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth; and although this does not seem so to others, it is evident to those who seek his covenant, [Jerome.] that is, his passion and death, through which we were redeemed and promised life was restored to us. Those who seek his covenant, [Augustine.] that is, who attend to what he testified in the prophets and evangelists, understand Christ as merciful in his first coming and as Judge in his second. The gentle seek his covenant, namely his death, when by his blood he redeemed us into new life; and they seek his testimonies in the prophets and evangelists, where he promises life to those believing in his death, but threatens eternal death to unbelievers.

Or thus, from the words “sweet,” etc., the whole passage may be read of the present time: As though he said: I ask with this confidence because the Lord is sweet and upright. [Cassiodorus.] Sweet, because he gives pleasant things; upright, because he corrects. And therefore, because he is sweet and upright, not from cruelty but from kindness, he will give the law of correction or charity to sinners—provided, however, that they are in the faithful way, [Alcuin.] or in order that they may be in the way of God’s commandments. Or, he will give it in the way of this life, in which one must live rightly. He will give the law, I say, [Cassiodorus.] and in the present judgment, in which he judges while punishing and correcting. He will direct the meek toward better things, [Alcuin.] that is, if those who are corrected are meek: tamed from being wild, so that they patiently endure the lash of their correcting Father and the cautery of the physician who burns to heal. And if they are gentle—that is, mild in disposition, as though naturally possessing this—[Col. 0257A] he will teach them his ways, that is, his commandments, through neglect of which the chastisements came. “All”—as though he said, he will teach his ways, that is, his commandments. But all the ways of the Lord, that is, all his commandments, are mercy and truth, that is, full of mercy and truth; this is certainly evident to those who seek his new covenant, [Cassiodorus.] aptly called a covenant, because in it there is a clear and certain promise of inheritance, which is also confirmed by the death of the testator; and his testimonies, namely the testimonies of the Old Testament, in which the prophets were witnesses of the promises.

VERSE 12.—“For thy name’s sake, O Lord, thou wilt be gracious to my sin; for it is great.”

For thy name’s sake, O Lord, [Ordinary Gloss.] that is, because thou art sweet and upright, thou wilt do as I have prayed: thou wilt forgive the sins that I accuse. [Augustine.] And this is it: O Lord, thou wilt be gracious, when the sacrifice of a contrite spirit is offered to thee, [Alcuin.] to my sin. Thou wilt do this for thy name’s sake, for thy glory, so that thou mayest be praised by humankind. The reason is referred to the Lord. And this is because I do not neglect or minimize my sin; rather, I think that it is great.

Or thus: [Cassiodorus.] Because thou art sweet, O Lord, for thy name’s sake—[Augustine.] which is Jesus, namely “Saviour,” that is, in order to fulfil the reality denoted by thy name—thou wilt be gracious, through the sacrifice of a contrite spirit, to my sin, committed not only before faith but also after faith. And this is necessary, [Augustine, Alcuin.] because it is great, that is, because that sin is grave: for even on the way of faith, offence is not absent. Therefore unless it is removed by thee, it will not be blotted out: thou forgivest not only sins committed before faith, but also that which is great, [Cassiodorus.] namely what is committed daily. Therefore, for thy name’s sake, spare me. He says this because he does not dare ask that he be spared on his own account, since his sin increases daily. In this the Cathari are refuted. [Note: [Col. 0257D] From Isidore, *Etymologies*, VII.24, question 3, chapter “Quidam.”] For there was a sect of heretics who most arrogantly called themselves by this name, as though on account of purity. They deny forgiveness of sins to sinners, do not admit second marriages, and proclaim themselves purer than others. Hence they called themselves *Cathari*, as though “the pure”; but if they wished to know their own name, they ought rather to call themselves worldly than pure.

[Col. 0257D] PART II, VERSE 13.—“Who is the man who fears the Lord? He will appoint for him a law in the way which he has chosen.”

Who is the man? [Alcuin.] The third part, in which he treats of eternal things, showing how they are obtained, labouring and praying that he himself and all Israel may be delivered from these evils. He begins with fear, which is the beginning of wisdom. As though he said: The Lord will give the law; and since this is so, do you wish to know to whom he will give it? [Cassiodorus, Ordinary Gloss.] And, as though someone had answered, “I do,” he adds: Who is the man—that is, the rational person who fears the Lord, not being self-secure? [Augustine.] Fear is that by which one begins to approach wisdom. Therefore he sets it forth. And as though someone said, “Why do you ask this?” he answers: Here is why: because the Lord will appoint for him, [Col. 0258A] namely for the person who fears him, a law—that is, correction, so that he may no longer sin with impunity. Or, “law” means the fulfilment of the law, which is charity, for the person [Ordinary Gloss.] set in the way of faith which he has chosen: that is, which he freely embraced, or chose as safe after learning through chastisements that one must not depart from it. Then he adds concerning the reward, saying:

VERSE 14.—“His soul shall abide in good things, and his seed shall inherit the earth.”

[Cassiodorus.] His soul, after the dissolution of the body, shall abide in good things. For although immediately after the body it does not possess perfect blessedness, nevertheless it shall abide in good things, having the single robe until the time of the resurrection, when the body will be glorified. [Jerome, Alcuin.] Hence he adds: and at last [Col. 0258B] his seed, his good work from which fruit is gathered, shall inherit the earth; [Augustine.] that is, it shall possess the solid inheritance of the restored body, when, on account of the merit of the good work done here, it receives the second robe of the glorified body. Meanwhile:

VERSE 15.—“The Lord is the support of those who fear him, and his covenant is made manifest to them.”

The Lord, [Cassiodorus.] not a changeable human being, is the support of those who fear him. [Augustine.] Fear seems to belong to the weak. Yet the Lord is the support of those who fear him, [Cassiodorus.] because fear of God gives firmness, whereas human fear produces distrust. And the Lord causes his covenant to be made manifest to them, [Augustine.] that is, causes to be made manifest to them what he himself testified: [Col. 0258C] namely, that the nations and the ends of the earth are Christ’s inheritance. Or thus: the soul of the person who fears God does not now return to Egypt, to the flesh-pots, to delight in the darkness of sins, but shall abide in good things, [Alcuin.] that is, it shall remain among the commandments as among delights. Or now it shall abide, in hope if not in reality, in future good things. “And his seed shall inherit,” etc. [Jerome.] That is, through the merit of his good work—that is, by doing good, whereby he merits life—he cultivates the earth. [Alcuin.] Another reading: “Eve,” that is, the flesh, by mortifying its vices and lusts. And besides these things, the Lord is a support to those who fear him. [Cassiodorus.] Man indeed is changeable, but God strengthens the person who fears him, lest he yield to evils. The sense is the same as above. And his covenant is this, that it may be made manifest to them; [Alcuin.] that is, he will manifest himself to them, as he promised when he said: “If anyone keeps my words, I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14). Therefore, whatever others may do,

VERSE 16.—“My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he himself will pluck my feet out of the snare.”

My eyes, [Jerome, Ordinary Gloss.] namely the eyes of the heart, of which Solomon says: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head” (Eccles. 2), that is, in his heart—indeed, all my gazes are always toward the Lord. [Cassiodorus.] For I do not look upon the ground, nor attend before me to my feet, as some do lest they fall into snares or pits. Rather, looking upward to the Lord, I do not fear [Col. 0259A] earthly dangers, because he whom I behold will pluck my feet, that is, my affections, from the snare of vices. Or, “he will pluck my feet from the snare,” [Ordinary Gloss.] that is, from passion and death, which holds people bound. It is said by comparison, as though one held by death were chained by the foot.

VERSE 17.—“Look upon me and have mercy on me, for I am solitary and poor.”

Look upon me. [Ordinary Gloss.] As though he said: And because my eyes are toward thee, therefore look upon me, etc. Or connect it thus: My eyes are toward the Lord—the eyes, I say, of one who says: [Cassiodorus.] “Look upon me,” looking upon thee, “and have mercy on me, because I am wretched”; and there is room for mercy because I am solitary, [Ordinary Gloss.] that is, not divided among many things, but remaining in unity. [Augustine.] For no schisms or heresies hold the Church; and I am poor in the things of the world. [Col. 0259B] Therefore he calls himself solitary and poor, in order to win God’s mercy. [Cassiodorus.] For an only child is loved more, and a poor person is more pitied. There is also another reason, namely:

VERSE 18.—“The tribulations of my heart have been multiplied; deliver me from my necessities.”

The tribulations of my heart have been multiplied: [Ordinary Gloss, Augustine.] that is, the calamities of the world are so many that their anguish reaches even to the heart, while iniquity abounds and the charity of many grows cold. [Alcuin.] And, O Lord, deliver me from my necessities, that is, from adversities, which are necessary for all who wish to live piously in Christ. [Augustine.] He therefore fittingly calls them necessities, [Col. 0259C] because it is necessary for him to endure them to the end in order to be saved. And:

VERSE 19.—“See my humiliation and my labour, and forgive all my offences.”

See, [Ordinary Gloss.] that is, regard favourably, my humility, because boasting in righteousness does not tear me away from unity; and my labour, [Augustine.] by which I endure the undisciplined people mingled with me. Appeased by these sacrifices, forgive all my offences: not only those which I committed before faith, [Augustine.] but also those which I commit after faith through weakness or the darkness of this life. Then he prays for his enemies, saying: And also:

VERSE 20.—“Look upon my enemies, for [Col. 0259D] they are multiplied, and they hate me with unjust hatred.”

Look upon them, [Cassiodorus.] that is, convert, my enemies. Or, because we do not know what we ought to pray for, the sense may be this: Look upon my iniquity, [Ordinary Gloss.] that is, deal with them as thou knowest how, since they are multiplied. [Augustine.] Not only are there unbelievers outside, but false brothers are also not lacking within the Church. [Cassiodorus.] And the destruction of so many people cannot be without grief. Therefore he prays for those of whom he adds: [Augustine.] they hate me with unjust hatred, though I love them. But from them:

VERSE 21.—“Guard my soul and deliver me; I shall not be put to shame, because I have hoped in thee.”

[Ordinary Gloss, Cassiodorus.] Guard my soul by preserving it in the good things I have possessed, so that I may not turn aside [Col. 0260A] to imitate them; [Augustine.] and deliver me from the perplexity in which they are mingled with me. Deliver me, I say, and cause me not to be put to shame if perhaps they rise against me. And thou shouldst do this because I have hoped in thee, not in myself. Or thus: “I shall not be put to shame,” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] as though he said: I say, “Deliver me,” and if not for another reason—or that is, at least for this reason—so that I may not be put to shame because I have hoped in thee; that is, lest my hope in thee result in shame for me. Therefore deliver me, because:

VERSE 22.—“The innocent and upright have cleaved to me, because I have waited for thee.”

[Alcuin.] The innocent and upright have cleaved to me through good works amid tribulations; that is, they are not merely mingled with me in bodily presence, but also in agreement of heart. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The wicked indeed are tolerated, [Col. 0260B] but they have not cleaved to me in mind; the upright in heart have cleaved to me. [Augustine.] And this is because I did not fail in goodness by following them, but because I waited for thee, awaiting the winnowing of thy final harvest, that is, judgment. And thou, O

VERSE 23.—“Deliver Israel, O God, from all his tribulations.”

O God, deliver Israel: that is, those who are Israel, [Augustine.] the people whom thou hast prepared for thy vision. Deliver them, I say, from all their tribulations, whether outward or inward.

## Comparison on Psalm XXIV: “To thee, O Lord, have I lifted up”

VERSE 2.—“Neither let my enemies mock me.” The Hebrews have [Col. 0260C] *al yaʿaltsu oyebai li*, “let not my enemies rejoice over me,” that is, at my expense. It is evident that the evil spirit cannot truly rejoice within himself, since his perpetual damnation is an abyss of unspeakable sorrow; but his joy is spoken of according to its effect, when he deceives us while we are unwary. Thus, for him to rejoice over us is to mock us, and his mockery is deceitful deception, as the Septuagint declared, without departing from the Hebrew truth.

VERSE 6.—“And thy mercies, which are from of old.” In Greek, ὅτι, that is, “because they are from of old.” In Hebrew likewise, that is, “because.” Augustine too reads it in the same way in his exposition of this psalm. Therefore it seems that scribes have mistakenly written *quae* (“which”) for *quia* (“because”), although the sense suffers no harm whatever. Hence the translator for Campensis rendered it thus: “Be mindful of thy mercy and goodness, which thou hast exercised from eternity”; and the Paraphrase: “Call to mind, O Lord, thy clemency and kindness [Col. 0260D], which in former ages thou hast so generously exercised toward thine own.”

VERSE 7.—“Remember not the offences of my youth and my ignorances.” In the use of the word “ignorances,” there seems to be a conflict with the meaning of the Hebrew word *pessaʿ*, which is derived from the root *pashaʿ*. It means to sin and rebel out of deliberate malice; and everyone recognizes that this is opposed to ignorance. Yet there is a kind of ignorance which theologians call affected ignorance, according to Psalm 35: “He would not understand, that he might act well.” This is the most dangerous kind. Nevertheless Jerome, writing to Cyprian, interprets it as ordinary ignorance, saying: “Remember not the offences of my youth and my ignorances,” etc. And again: “Who understands offences? Cleanse me, O Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare me from those of others,” etc. For faults are alien to us which we commit sometimes deliberately, sometimes through ignorance and error. Yet even where there is no will in the crime, error remains blameworthy.

[Col. 0261A] 52 VERSE 14.—“The Lord is the support of those who fear him.” Jerome and the other Hebraists read, “the secret of God,” etc.: *sod Adonai*. Although there is some slight difference in the words, they agree in meaning. For *sod* is secret counsel; if you give it to the weak, you make them stable and strengthen them.
