Add that *yasad* among the Hebrews unquestionably means “to found.” And because, says Münster, counsel is no less necessary in every work than a foundation in a building, it also means “to take counsel.” What, then, prevents *sod* from denoting a foundation or support, when the word from which it may be derived means “he strengthens”? We pass over certain minor points, though we are aware of them.

## Psalm XXV

[Col. 0261]

### Title of the Psalm: “A Psalm of David”

[Col. 0261A]

“Judge me, O Lord.” Title: “A Psalm of David.” [Augustine.] David here does not mean Christ, the mediator between God and humankind, but the perfect man, [Ordinary Gloss.] who asks to be separated from the wicked in place in the future, from whom in the present he is separated by merit. The sense is: This psalm is attributed [Col. 0261B] to David, [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] that is, to the perfect man who speaks here. Its purpose is this: the psalm warns us to avoid the company of the wicked and to join ourselves to the righteous, because character is formed by association. Its arrangement: the psalm has two parts. [Cassiodorus.] First, the righteous man says that he has no share here with the wicked and asks to be separated from them in the future. Second, he asks not to be mingled with the wicked at judgment, beginning at “O Lord, I have loved.” Note the difference between the first and second parts. In the first he says little about judgment and much about his innocence; in the second, he treats of both, touching on them almost equally. In the first he speaks first of judgment and afterward of his innocence; in the second, conversely. [Augustine.] Therefore, seeing that good people are now with evil people, grain with chaff, so that little or no grain appears—as Elijah thought himself left alone (3 Kings 19)—this holy man prays to be locally separated in the future, saying:

VERSE 1.—“Judge me, O Lord, for I have entered in my innocence; and trusting in the Lord, I shall not be weakened.”

O Lord, judge me, [Augustine.] that is, distinguish me in place from the wicked, who are now together with us in the Church, lest we go together into eternal fire. In saying “judge,” [Cassiodorus.] the righteous man does not presume; rather, he has certainty in God’s mercy, as he shows where he says, “trusting in the Lord.” He then sets out his merit: “For I,” etc. [Augustine.] As though he said: I say, “Judge me.” Why? Because, after the mercy which thou hast first granted me, I possess the merit of my innocence, whose way I have kept. This is what “I have walked” means: I have entered the way of moral conduct. [Ordinary Gloss.] Or, my innocence among sinners [Alcuin.] is not the innocence of angels. But what sort of innocence is human innocence? [Ordinary Gloss.] To say this is not self-exaltation, but the confession of one who is not ungrateful. [Augustine.] Though I am innocent and righteous, I shall not hope in myself but in God. “And trusting in the Lord, I shall not be weakened,” that is, I shall not stagger among [Col. 0262A] sinners. [Augustine, Ordinary Gloss.] Otherwise, unless he trusted in the Lord, he would stagger among the wicked; though they fall, he stands, because he trusts not in them but in the Lord. Or, another reading: “I shall not be moved,” locally, among sinners. [Augustine.] Rather, I shall remain among them in body but not in mind, something which certain people refuse to do so that they may appear good. Those who, though supposedly good, refuse to be among the wicked are schismatics; they are worse than the wicked and, like chaff, are swept away by the wind of pride even before the winnowing itself.

VERSE 2.—“Prove me, O Lord, and try me; burn my reins and my heart.”

Prove me—as though he said: I said that I am innocent and righteous; but because no one understands his own offences, lest anything of my hidden faults lie concealed from me, prove me, O Lord, and try me—that is, prove me by temptations. [Augustine.] That is, judge me as proved, not for thyself, since thou knowest all things, but for me and for people, lest any fault remain. [Cassiodorus.] He says “try” because, unless we were tried, we would be negligent. [Alcuin.] Note that God tries, man tries, and the devil tries, but God, man, and devil do so differently. God tries in order to instruct; man tries in order to learn what he does not know; the devil tries in order to seduce. [Cassiodorus.] God’s trial is therefore a proving, as when God tried Abraham. [Alcuin.] Observe that here the perfect man prays for tribulations, lest anyone murmur at them. Hence he adds: “Burn,” namely with the fire of tribulation, [Col. 0262C] my reins and my heart. [Augustine.] Apply the healing purgatory of tribulation to my pleasures, so that no evil thing may delight me, and to my thoughts, so that I may think no evil. For he used “heart” for thoughts and “reins” for pleasures.

VERSE 3.—“For thy mercy is before my eyes, and I have been pleasing in thy truth.”

[Col. 0262D] “For thy mercy”—as though he said: Therefore I say, “Burn,” because thy mercy is before my eyes. [Augustine.] That is, I attend not to my merits but to thy mercy, which made me such a person, lest I be consumed by that fire. Or thus: “Prove me, O Lord, and try me” [Note: [Col. 0261D] From Gregory, *Morals*, book II, chapter 11.], that is, first examine my strength, and then permit me to be tried only as I am able to endure. And “burn my reins,” that is, my pleasures, with the fire of thy word, of which the Lord said: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12). [Augustine.] With this fire he burns pleasures: the good ones by enkindling them, the evil by consuming them. And burn my heart, that is, my thoughts: enlightening the good and consuming the evil. Burn them with the warmth of the Holy Spirit, from whom no one can hide. [Col. 0263A] “For thy mercy”—as though he said: I ask that thou not permit me to be tried beyond my strength; and thou certainly wilt do this, because thy mercy is before my eyes, that is, I behold thy mercy with my whole heart, which does not permit one to be tried beyond one’s strength. Or connect it thus: as though he said: Therefore I say, “Burn,” because that burning itself is thy mercy before my eyes; that is, it appears to me as mercy rather than harshness, because in it he recognizes God as merciful to himself. [Augustine, Ordinary Gloss.] And I have been pleasing to myself within, where thou seest; I do not fear if I displease where people see. I have been pleasing, I say, in thy truth, that is, thy good things delight and please me. He speaks by a comparison. For he is inwardly pleasing to himself as though someone saw a tomb in a mirror. Observe that he did not say *placui* (“I pleased”) but *complacui* (“I was well pleased”). For the person to whom his own falsehood is displeasing and God’s truth pleasing, is pleasing to himself with that truth and in it.

VERSE 4.—“I have not sat with the council of vanity, and I shall not enter in with those who practise iniquity.”

“I have not sat.” [Alcuin.] As though he said: I have been well pleased in truth, and this is indeed so, because I have not sat and have hated—which is to avoid evils—and I shall wash my hands—which is to do what is right. This is: I have not sat with the council of vanity; [Augustine.] that is, I have not set my heart upon it or consented, even if I entered bodily. To sit is to consent with those who sit there. If you are physically present and do not do this, you have not sat there. If you do it while absent, you have sat there in heart, though not in body. Therefore he says: “I have not sat with the counsel or assembly of vanity”; that is, I have not set my heart upon those who devise ways to become happy [Col. 0263C] through transient things, which is the cause of all wicked people—that is, all wickedness. As though he said: I have avoided the deliberation of the wicked and have not even begun their deeds. Hence he adds: “And I shall not enter in with those who practise iniquity,” [Cassiodorus.] that is, I do not share the consciousness of their work; that is, I shall not even begin to commit iniquity with them, although I am among them. And because it is not enough to have avoided them, he adds:

VERSE 5.—“I have hated the assembly of evildoers, and I shall not sit with the ungodly.”

I have hated the assembly. As though he said: I have not only avoided the counsel of vanity, but I have also hated the very assembly of evildoers, [Augustine.] that is, the gathering of the wicked which is formed so that people may arrive at a counsel of vanity. Although they are of us in body, they are not of us in mind; they are of us in number, not in merit; in name, not in divine reality. [Col. 0263D] And I shall not sit with the ungodly, that is, I shall not take pleasure in them. [Cassiodorus.] Distinguish between the vain, evildoers, and ungodly. The vain labour over perishable and transient things. The ungodly are heretics who corrupt the sacred Scriptures. The former seek superfluous things, the latter poisonous things, so that they wound hearts as if with different weapons of error. [Alcuin.] Evildoers are those who do evil to their neighbours.

VERSE 6.—“I shall wash my hands among the innocent, and I shall compass thine altar, O Lord.”

I shall wash. Having shown how he avoids evils, he adds how he does what is right. As though he said: I shall not consent to the ungodly; rather, I shall wash my hands, [Jerome.] that is, by repenting and confessing I shall make my works clean. [Augustine.] I say this while associating with the innocent [Col. 0264A] always in mind and often in body. And, O Lord, I shall compass thine altar—that is, my mind or faith, [Alcuin.] where vows are offered to God. [Jerome.] For there is no place of true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church, that is, outside the faith of the Catholic Church. I shall compass it, [Alcuin.] that is, adorn it with virtues. [Jerome.] Therefore I shall associate with the innocent.

VERSE 7.—“That I may hear the voice of praise, and declare all thy wondrous works.”

[Aug.] So that I may hear from them the voice of praise—that is, learn with what voice you are to be praised, namely, how I should praise you and not myself; so that I may not presume upon myself because of the good itself, but upon you who gave it. [Rem.] Therefore, the person who understands how God is to be praised is the one who attributes his good to God [Alcuin.], not to himself. Or: “that I may hear [Col. 0264B] the voice of praise,” that is, the voice of the Holy Spirit, who teaches me to praise you; [Aug.] and, when I have learned, “that I may recount,” that is, explain to others, all your wonders, not my own.

Or thus: by the altar let the heavenly Jerusalem be understood. No one embraces that altar except one who washes his hands among the innocent. For many unworthy persons touch this visible altar, and for a time God endures injury being done to his sacraments; but will the heavenly Jerusalem be so? No. For just as you are now received together with the wicked within these walls of the Church, so you will not be received with the wicked into the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, into Abraham’s bosom. Therefore this man says: “I shall wash my hands,” that is, my works; when these have been washed, “I shall encompass your altar, O Lord,” that is, I shall embrace with my desire and hope—and in the future also in actuality—[Hier., Cassiod.] your sublime things, [Col. 0264C] namely the heavenly altar, into which Christ our priest entered for us. “I shall encompass,” I say, “that I may hear the voice of your praise,” which is sung by the angels, [Alcuin.] namely, “Holy, holy, holy,” etc. Or: “that I may hear the voice of your praise,” that is, the voice by which you will say in the future: “Come, blessed of my Father,” etc. (Matt. XV). And here I shall recount all your wonders. These points do not change.

## PART II. VERSE 8.—“O Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house, and the place where your glory dwells.”

“O Lord, I have loved.” [Cassiod., Alcuin.] The second part, in which he asks that he may not be mingled with the wicked in judgment, because he agrees not with them but with God’s house. As though he said: I shall wash my hands and encompass the altar; and I shall do this because [Col. 0264D] I have loved, O Lord, the beauty of your house—[Hier.] that is, I have loved to make myself a beautiful house for you—and the place where your glory dwells, [Alcuin.] that is, the place in which you dwell gloriously, so that I may receive something of the glory and essence of the Godhead.

Or thus: the Church is God’s house; the saints are the beauty of this house, and they themselves are the place where your glory dwells. [Aug.] Thus: “I have loved the beauty of your house,” which is found in the saints; even though the Church still has evil persons, that is, I have loved the good who are in the Church, whose life and teaching make the Church herself beautiful. “And the place where [your glory] dwells”: the beauty of the house is the place where glory dwells—that is, the saints, who are the beauty of the Church and are the place where glory dwells, because they seek not their own glory but God’s glory. This is the meaning: “And I have loved the place where your glory dwells,” that is, [Col. 0265A] those in whom, by dwelling, you are glorified, so that glory may be given not to themselves but to you. Therefore he does not simply say “the place where [you] dwell,” but adds, “of your glory,” namely, where your glory dwells.

Or thus: “I have loved the beauty of your house,” [Cassiod.] that is, the good deeds by which your house is adorned, according to the saying: “So let your works shine before men, that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V). “And the place where your glory dwells,” that is, the secret place of the heart, where the seat of devout thoughts is. And because I have thus disposed myself, grant me these things:

### VERSE 9.—“Do not destroy my soul with the wicked, O God, nor my life with men of blood.”

[Aug., Cassiod.] “Do not destroy,” in the future, O God, [Col. 0265B] my soul, which has loved the beauty of your house, together with the wicked who hate you—those with whom I do not share fellowship of mind here, even if I do in body. Therefore, although you now permit good and evil persons to be together, do not destroy them together in the future.

> [Note: [Col. 0265D] From Augustine, in the preface to the second exposition of the same psalm.]

On the threshing floor, grains cannot be distinguished from chaff at a distance; so too there is an opinion, arising from the abundance of many people’s wickedness, that there is no good person at all. This opinion was present even in Elijah when he said, “Lord, I alone am left” (III Kings XIX). Yet in the future the mixture of the wicked will not harm the good, because God does not err in judgment, but will repay each according to merits.

“And [do not destroy] my life with men of blood,” [Cassiod.] namely, those who live carnally and hate their neighbor. Thus the wicked and the men of blood are those who act against the two commandments of love, and so, as far as lies in them, dishonor and defile God’s gift. [Aug.] For God’s house is adorned by the two commandments of love, namely love of God and of neighbor.

### VERSE 10.—“In whose hands are iniquities; their right hand is full of gifts.”

“In whose.” He shows who the wicked and men of blood are: those in whose hands are iniquities, [Aug.] that is, whose deeds are wicked; and “their right hand is full of gifts,” that is, whatever good they do, they do for gifts—money, human praise, fear of offending a rich person, or unjust pity. For someone, lest he be reproached for what he has done against a poor person, suppresses justice and pronounces judgment against truth, sparing the poor in a bad cause. Or thus: he is as though he received a gift from [Col. 0265D] the poor person, because he is not accused of acting against the poor. But blessed is the person who shakes his hands free from every gift. For gifts blind the eyes and bend the force of authority [Col. 0266A] (Deut. XVI). Hence the Lord says through Isaiah: “Woe to you who justify the ungodly for gifts” (Isa. XXXIII).

Or: their “right hand,” that is, their reason, “is full of gifts,” that is, it has been rewarded with present goods. As though he said: what was given them for obtaining eternal salvation, they turn toward receiving the gifts of this age, considering godliness a means of gain (I Tim. VI).

### VERSE 11.—“But I have walked in my innocence; redeem me, and have mercy upon me.”

“But I,” [Cassiod.] as though he said: They have been enriched by gifts. But I, by contrast, “have walked in my innocence,” that is, I have been enriched with the riches of innocence and spiritual treasures. Therefore he says, “Redeem me.” This man sees the price of Christ’s blood, by which the world is redeemed. [Col. 0266B] Therefore he says: “Redeem me,” [Aug.] that is, may the price of so great a blood avail for my reward or for the completion of my deliverance; “and have mercy upon me,” that is, may your mercy not abandon me amid the perils of this life, but accompany me in all things—which you ought to do. “For,” that is, because.

### VERSE 12.—“For my foot has stood upright; in the churches I shall bless you, O Lord.”

“My foot,” [Aug., Alcuin.] though shaken on every side by scandals, “has stood upright,” that is, my love and affection, which is apt easily to slip, has not departed from your righteousness. [Cassiod., Alcuin.] Rather, it has stood unmoved against every scandal, stretching forward and persevering in uprightness. In this he shows that he loves God. [Aug.] Then he adds concerning love of neighbor: “in the churches.” [Col. 0266C] [Cassiod.] As though he said: Therefore redeem me also, because, if you redeem me, O Lord, I shall bless you, not myself. He says “in the churches” in the plural because there are many throughout the world. [Aug.] As though he said: I join love of neighbor to love of you, because I shall not conceal from those whom you have called your blessing, so that through me you may be blessed by those who are formed by example and teaching to bless. For to bless the Lord in the churches is to live in such a way that God is blessed through each person’s conduct. Whoever blesses the Lord with an unmade tongue does not bless truly.

## COLLATION ON PSALM XXV: “JUDGE ME, O LORD.”

### VERSE 3.—“I have been well-pleasing in your truth.”

Hebrew: *HITHALLACHTHI*, that is, “I have walked.” The interpreters have learnedly explained the metaphor. For what could sound more fitting than that to walk with [Col. 0266D] God means to please him through diligent conduct? Thus Genesis V: “Enoch walked with God.”

# PSALM XXVI

[Col. 0265]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “FOR THE END; A PSALM OF DAVID, BEFORE HE WAS ANOINTED.”

[Col. 0265D]

“The Lord is my illumination.” Title: “For the end; a psalm of David, before he was anointed.” [Hier.] This title is taken from the history in the Book of Kings, where David is said to have been anointed three times. First, at Bethlehem by Samuel, in the house of his father Jesse—not indeed as king, but as a sign of the future kingdom (I Kings XVI). From that day the Spirit of the Lord was directed upon him. Second, he was anointed king at Hebron after Saul’s death, and [Col. 0267A] reigned over the tribe of Judah (II Kings II). But after Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, who reigned over the other tribes, had been slain, David was anointed there a third time, to reign over all Israel (II Kings V). Going up to Jerusalem, he reigned in peace. Yet the last two anointings are reckoned as one. [Alcuin.] After his first anointing David had enemies; after the second he reigned in peace. The title alludes to this history.

But since all these things happened to them figuratively (I Cor. X), it must be known that formerly two persons were anointed: [Aug.] king and priest, in whom the one Christ, king and priest, was signified. He is king because he rules and leads us; priest because he intercedes for us and offered sacrifice to God—not another sacrifice, but himself. We, however, are Christ’s body, and in him we are Christ, because we are all anointed from the fullness of his anointing, from which he is called Christ. For Christ is named from chrism. Therefore, in receiving Christ, may we all both be Christ’s people in him and be Christ, because in a certain sense the whole Christ is head and body.

And as David was first anointed as a sign, then twice as king, while those two anointings are reckoned as one, so we too are first anointed here as a sign of the future kingdom, when we receive the grace of the Holy Spirit in baptism and the other sacraments (Rom. VI); but secondly we shall be anointed as kings in the future, when we receive the freedom of the glory of the children of God and the redemption of our body. As David had enemies after his first anointing and reigned in peace after the second, [Alcuin.] so, after sacramental anointing, we labor under enemies [Col. 0267C] and groan while awaiting the adoption as children (Rom. VIII); after the second, we shall rest. And as David was twice anointed king, so the anointing of our glorification, by which we shall be anointed as kings, is a twofold robe: that of soul and body. But these two are reckoned as though one.

[Aug.] Therefore, for us the anointing is now in the sacrament, by which what we shall be is prefigured. Hence it is said, “before he was anointed.” The meaning of the title is this: [Gl. int.] this psalm, directing us to the end of future consummation, is attributed to David, that is, to every faithful person. It is a psalm, I say, dealing with the state “before he was anointed” a second time—that is, with the state before complete anointing, while he had enemies. [Aug.] Thus, in the sacrament—that is, in sacramental anointing—this faithful person speaks here while groaning and laboring, that he may rejoice in actuality; he declares that he desires something ineffable, showing for what he endures everything.

Purpose: it warns that no one should grow sluggish after the first anointing, but should diligently prepare for the second. Structure: the psalm has two parts. [Alcuin.] First it treats of the first anointing, by which the second is assured. [Cassiod.] Secondly, it tells what labor and groaning there are before the second, so that it may be attained, beginning at “Hear, O Lord.” [Aug.] Therefore the faithful person, anointed with the first anointing, speaks as a novice of Christ:

### VERSE 1.—“The Lord is my illumination and my salvation: whom shall I fear?”

[Col. 0268A] [Gl. int.] The Lord dwelling in me is my illumination; [Aug.] or my light, against the darkness of my ignorance. [Hier.] I am not light to myself, but he is the one who enlightens every person coming into this world (John I). He is also my salvation against weakness, [Aug.] so that I may now be able to resist sin. [Gl. int.] It is as though he said: The Lord has given both knowledge of himself and salvation; whom then shall I fear? No one, because no one can prevail against him. And:

### VERSE 2.—“The Lord is the protector of my life: from whom shall I tremble?”

The Lord is the protector of my life, [Alcuin.] that is, he gives me the life of virtues [Aug.] and protects it by repelling every assault and ambush. [Cassiod.] Without his protection all his gifts are lost. Therefore it is not enough for him to give unless he also protects. Hence he does not say “giver,” but “protector of my life.” Or, because the Lord protects me, from what person—or from what thing—shall I tremble? That is, whom or what shall I fear? [Aug.] As though he said: neither anyone nor anything. For I belong to the almighty One, more powerful than all, who enlightens, saves, and protects. Therefore I fear no one except him, walking steadfastly in the light of grace.

Or these two verses may be understood of the future. In the first verse he indicates the sabbath-rest of the soul; in the second, the sabbath-rest of the body. As a figure of this, as was said above, David’s final two anointings preceded.

> [Note: [Col. 0267] From Bede, on Exodus XVI. That there was a board divided through the middle is found in Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book III, chapter 7.]

The same thing was signified in the tabernacle of the Lord by the one-cubit board divided through the middle and placed at the corners of the western side; it received the two walls of the tabernacle on either side and joined them to the western front. This signified that believers from each people hope to have a twofold glorification after the setting of the body; therefore they persevere steadfastly in good until the end.

This is the meaning: “The Lord will be my illumination,” or my light, after this life, and my salvation according to the soul, which he will glorify and illuminate so that it sees God face to face. Whom then shall I fear? As though he said: no one. For who is there for the soul to fear when God dwells in it? Then he adds concerning the sabbath-rest of the body: “And the Lord is the protector of my life,” [Aug.] that is, he will protect me with the life of immortality. “From whom then shall I tremble?” Whom could the flesh fear when it has put on incorruption? [Col. 0268D] No one.

### VERSE 3.—“While evildoers draw near against me, to eat my flesh.”

“While they draw near.” Here he shows why he does not fear. According to the first interpretation, this text is connected with what precedes as though he said: I shall fear neither anyone nor anything, because those who persecute me—namely, my evildoers and enemies—fall, and take away only my flesh; when they are ended, I shall be spirit, that is, spiritual. This is what he says: “While they draw near,” etc.

According to the other, future interpretation, connect it thus: The Lord will protect me in the future; [Aug.] and truly, because he already does this: evildoers fall. This is what he says: [Col. 0269A] “While they draw near,” etc. The order of the words is as follows: the evildoers—by their intention, though not in effect—have been weakened and fallen; and this happens “while they draw near.” [Gl. int.] He fittingly says this because he already feels them in himself. They “draw near,” I say, “against me,” [Aug.] namely, in order to set themselves above me in insult; God turns this to good, so that by their reviling tooth they consume, not me as they wish, but my carnal desires. Thus he adds: “to eat my flesh.” Here *ut* (“to”) is effective or consequential, not purposive: they do not draw near with this aim, but by God’s counsel it is brought about through them that they injure not the soul but eat the flesh, that is, destroy carnal desires.

### VERSE 4.—“My enemies who trouble me, they themselves have been weakened and have fallen.”

“Who trouble me.” [Gl. int.] As though he said: Not only those who seem friends and desire to deceive by flatteries fall, but also my manifest enemies, who openly trouble me out of hatred: they themselves have been weakened and have fallen, [Aug.] in what they wickedly defended, so that they may now believe better things. [Hier., Alcuin.] For when Christ takes flesh, enemies were made wavering concerning what they had formerly defended; afterward they fell, that is, they submitted their necks to faith. This is understood in a good sense.

Or it may be understood in an evil sense: “they themselves have been weakened,” that is, gradually debilitated, “and have fallen,” [Alcuin.] that is, they have come to the ruin of the soul.

Or let the same people be understood by “evildoers” and “enemies,” thus: the evildoers, namely my enemies who trouble [Col. 0269C] me, etc. This does not change, with the intention—that is, the purpose and desire—of eating my flesh, [Cassiod.] that is, of taking delight in my bodily death. Here the cruelty of enemies is indicated: they tear flesh because they cannot injure souls. Therefore they are not to be feared, according to the saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. X). [Hier.] What evil, then, do they do us? Can they take away hope? Can they take away what the Almighty gives? [Aug.] If a gift can be taken away, its giver is overcome. But just as the giver cannot be overcome, so what he gives cannot be taken away. Therefore let us fear no one except the Lord. Whatever another may rage, whatever another may proudly do against us, let us not fear. And while the wicked draw near, they themselves have been weakened and have fallen. Therefore, having received such great confidence:

### VERSE 5.—“If camps should stand against me, my heart shall not fear.”

[Col. 0269D] “If camps should henceforth stand against me,” [Aug., Cassiod., Gl. int.] that is, a conspiracy of opponents, hostile machinations, “my heart”—[Aug.] that is, reason restored—“shall not fear” so as to desert to them. And likewise:

### VERSE 6.—“If battle should rise against me, in this I shall hope.”

“If battle,” [Aug., Cassiod.] that is, worldly persecution, namely the conflict of persecutors, “should rise”—[Gl. int.] suddenly, or grow immeasurably—against me, [Cassiod.] I, for whom God is protector, shall hope in the Lord in this battle; [Alcuin.] that is, [Col. 0270A] I shall have in the Lord hope of victory and hope of eternal reward. And this is fitting, because:

### VERSE 7.—“One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.”

“One thing I have asked,” etc. [Aug.] Or: “in this,” that is, in this one petition which I consider, “I shall hope,” that is, I shall fix my hope. For “I have asked one thing.” Although he should have said in the neuter, *unum petii* (“I asked one thing”), he said *unam petii*, using a feminine adjective substantively according to popular speech, in which we customarily say *duas* (“two,” feminine), not *duo* (“two,” neuter), and *unam* (“one,” feminine), not *unum* (“one,” neuter).

[Hier.] In this manner, he says: “one [thing],” namely a thing—that is, God himself—I have asked of the Lord. [Cassiod.] The wicked seek many things; I, however, one. “And this I shall seek,” in order that I may dwell all the days of my life in the house of the Lord, [Aug.] namely, in the present Church: that is, so long as I live, no adversity may exclude me from the unity of the faithful, who throughout the world maintain the unity and truth of the Lord’s faith; rather, may I always remain in it. And:

### VERSE 8.—“That I may see the will of the Lord, and visit his temple.”

[Cassiod.] “That I may see the will of the Lord,” which is seen by one who understands the commandments. The meaning is: that I may understand his commandments spiritually, and with the mind, though not with bodily eyes, visit his temple—[Alcuin.] that is, the body of Christ, which is the temple of divinity. Or, “visit his temple,” [Hier.] that is, make myself his temple; for he rests only upon the humble and quiet person (Isa. LXVI). This I can do, because “he hid me in his tabernacle,” etc.

Or thus: “I have asked one thing,” as though he said: I have asked one petition from the Lord, and I shall seek it all the days of my life. He explains what that petition is: [Aug.] “that I may dwell in the house of the Lord not made by hands,” namely, in the heavenly Jerusalem, where there is nothing evil. I desire to be there so that I may see there the will of the Lord as it is. [Alcuin.] For the Lord’s will is fulfilled more fully in a human being there than here. Hence it is said: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth” (Matt. VI): that is, as it is done among the angels and saints who are now with you, so may it be done also in other human beings, so that in nothing [Col. 0270D] they may disagree from your will, as they now do.

“And visit,” that is, behold with desire and frequency, “his temple,” that is, the heavenly Jerusalem, namely the assembly of the heavenly court; or Christ’s human nature, in which divinity dwells as in a temple. I seek this with this confidence because “he hid me,” etc.

Or thus: “I have asked one thing.” Here “one thing” and “house” are understood as the same, namely the heavenly Jerusalem. Thus he says: “I have asked one thing of the Lord, and this I shall seek.” [Aug.] This one thing is the eternal house in which one remains forever; [Alcuin.] there are eternal days there, of which it is said, “And your years shall not fail.” Hence he adds: “that I may dwell in the house of the Lord not made by hands, all the days of my life,” that is, eternally. Why there? “That I may contemplate the delight of the Lord.” [Aug.] Another reading: that is, to this end [Col. 0271A] that the desirable hope may at last appear to me, which I shall see face to face; this is the true good. “And that I may be protected by his holy temple,” that is, that I may be clothed with immortality, having become his temple.

Another reading has: “And may his temple protect,” or “his temple will protect.” This does not alter the preceding sense, but confirms it thus: therefore I desire always to dwell in the house, that I may contemplate the delight of the Lord—that is, enjoy contemplation of that supreme, unchangeable, eternal Good, from whom all good things come—and more securely enjoy these delights. And so that no affliction may come upon me and no suggestion turn me aside, he himself, his temple, will protect me. Therefore I desire not only to contemplate him, but also that he, his temple, may protect me by granting impassibility. One of these belongs to the glorification of the mind, the other to the brightness of the body. There is perfection of joy; here, incorruptibility of health. These two we also distinguished in the first verses of the psalm. Therefore he grants me these things unto the end.

### VERSE 9.—“For he hid me in his tabernacle in the day of evils; he protected me in the secret place of his tabernacle.”

“For he hid [me].” [Aug.] Therefore I do not rashly ask for the one thing, even though I am a sinner. He hid me, I say, in his tabernacle, that is, in the dispensation of the incarnate Word. [Cassiod.] There he hid me so that I might not be seen by the enemies seeking me, just as, figuratively, David hid himself in hiding places when fleeing Saul so that he might not be seen (I Kings [Col. 0271C] XXIV). [Aug., Hier.] The tabernacle of divinity is Christ’s flesh, in which he defeated the powers of the air and in which, through faith and hope, he concealed me so that the evils of this age might not harm me. Hence the Apostle says: “Now your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III). [Aug.] For through faith and hope in hidden things we are already with Christ in God’s sight.

“He hid [me],” I say, “in the day of evil persons,” that is, in the present day, in which the evil flourish. Or: “in the day of evils,” [Gl. int.] that is, in the time of temptations to which my mortal life is subject; [Aug.] these are the days of my life. [Gl. int.] “And he protected me,” lest I be harmed, “in the secret place of his tabernacle,” [Cassiod.] that is, in the secret place of divinity, where the mind of the just person always is. And:

### VERSE 10.—“He exalted me upon a rock; and now he has exalted my head above my enemies.”

“He exalted me upon a rock.” [Aug.] He speaks from the analogy of commanders providing higher positions for their soldiers: so also the Lord exalted me upon a rock, that is, in the strength of virtues. Or he exalted me in Christ through the advancement by which I progress from virtue to virtue, and made me, as it were, beyond ordinary human beings. And now, the prophet says, looking toward his own time—that is, before the time of the Incarnation—he has exalted my head, [Cassiod.] that is, my mind, above my enemies, that is, above vicious desires.

Or “now,” namely while it is the day of evils. Therefore it is all the more remarkable: “he exalted my head above my enemies,” that is, he so illumined my mind that I foresee the future condemnation of the wicked. Then he adds his joy at these benefits, by which [Col. 0272A] he is also certain—that is, through this joy he shows himself certain of the second anointing, as through what was said before. For he would not rejoice unless he were certain. He adds, speaking of true joy:

### VERSE 11.—“I went around and sacrificed in his tabernacle a sacrifice of shouting; I shall sing and make psalmody to the Lord.”

“I went around.” As though he said: The Lord did the things aforesaid for me, and after all these things I “went around,” that is, I examined all his benefits by bringing them to mind; and, not ungrateful, I sacrificed in his tabernacle—[Aug.] that is, in the Church spread throughout the whole world—a sacrifice of shouting or jubilation, that is, of ineffable praise, so that when speech fails, jubilation alone remains. Thereafter I shall sing to the Lord, namely with the fruitfulness of contemplation, and “make psalmody,” that is, [Col. 0272B] make my work manifest. [Aug., Cassiod.] The sense is: I shall rejoice in the Lord in heart, and by deeds and words I shall proclaim God’s glory—and by actions.

Another interpretation from “He protected me in the secret place of his tabernacle.” [Aug.] He says “in the secret place,” as though he said: It has many parts, namely outer parts and the inner sanctuary; and this is indeed so. For we are like the outer parts, since we are children through adoption. Christ himself, the priest, is the hidden tabernacle in which our life is hidden. Thus the body and head too—that is, the whole Church—is one tabernacle, whose inner sanctuary is Christ, whom he immediately calls the rock when he says: “Upon a rock.” The sense is: “He protected me in the secret place of his tabernacle,” that is, in Christ; [Col. 0272C] “upon a rock,” that is, in the same Christ, “he exalted me”; and “now,” [Gl. int.] that is, in the present before I come to the house, “he has exalted my head,” that is, Christ, above my enemies. For although I still suffer, Christ is above, and he is the pledge of our exaltation.

Or: “He protected me in the secret place of his tabernacle,” that is, in the heart that believes unto righteousness. And so that what I believed might become publicly known unto salvation, he “exalted me upon a rock,” that is, in his firmness he made my confession prominent. “And now,” in this life, where the body is dead because of sin, “he has exalted my head,” that is, my mind, above my enemies, that is, vices; because my mind serves God’s law and is not captive under the law of sin.

And I, not ungrateful, seeking, as it were, matter for praising God, “went around,” that is, I surveyed in mind [Col. 0272D] all created things. All things say: “God made me.” All things delight me, in which the craftsman is commended; from every side all things resound with their Creator. The very forms of creatures are like certain voices praising their Creator. In these things so great a praise of God is found that it cannot be expressed in words. Hence he adds: “And I sacrificed in his tabernacle,” that is, in the Catholic Church, a sacrifice of jubilation, that is, ineffable praise. For jubilation is joy or praise that cannot be explained in words. What follows does not change.

Or: “I went around,” that is, I considered the faith of the world in which the head is exalted above my enemies; this is the honor of the Church, exalted in him. And in that very tabernacle of his—that is, in the Church spread throughout the world—I sacrificed a sacrifice of shouting or [Col. 0273A] jubilation, that is, I praised the Lord ineffably.

Or: “I went around,” that is, I considered the believing world—the same sense as the preceding, but what follows changes. [Aug.] For by “his tabernacle” Christ’s Incarnation and Passion are understood, in which he conquered the devil. This is the meaning: “in his tabernacle,” that is, in my own, because the Lord was humbled for us; while I attend to that, “I sacrificed a sacrifice of shouting,” that is, rejoicing, I praised him; for he delights in such a sacrifice.

Or: “I went around,” he says this by comparison with a good soldier, who carefully guards the camp and ensures that there is no entrance for an enemy. Thus this man says: “I went around,” as though he said: Because he has given himself to me as leader, I give myself to him as soldier, that I may fight for him against enemies, cautiously guarding the walls of my mind. “And in his tabernacle,” that is, in the Church, “I sacrificed,” [Col. 0273B] etc. The rest does not change.

Or: “I went around,” that is, I searched my mind, so that I might fulfill all its desires. The rest does not change.

Or: “I went around.” [Hier.] That is, I looked about at the examples of preceding saints, by which I might shape my life. There I found ineffable praise. Hence he adds: “And I sacrificed in his tabernacle,” etc. The rest does not change.

## PART II. VERSE 12.—“Hear, O Lord, my voice with which I have cried to you; have mercy upon me and hear me.”

“Hear.” [Cassiod., Alcuin.] The second part shows what labor, groaning, and prayer exist before the second anointing, in order that it may be attained; and by the spirit of prophecy he promises this anointing to himself at “I believe [that I shall] see.” [Aug.] As though he said: In the future I shall have the one thing, when I contemplate God’s love and am protected in incorruption; but before one rejoices in that one thing, there is the groaning of the miserable and the prayer of the needy. Therefore, among the others, groaning and praying, I cry: O Lord, hear me.

[Alcuin.] Or the text is connected throughout with all that precedes: assuredly I have asked for one thing, and I shall still ask. [Aug., Gl. int.] And you, O Lord, hear my inner voice, with which I cried to you in intense longing for that one thing; and have mercy upon me, so that your mercy may accompany my merit, by which I may be in that one thing; and hear me. [Cassiod.] He presses his prayers concerning that one thing when he says, “Hear; have mercy upon me,” because the more he has received, the more ardently he desires; for desire has neither end nor satiety.

### VERSE 13.—“My heart said to you: my face has sought you; your face, O Lord, I shall seek.”

[Col. 0273D] “To you [my heart] said.” [Cassiod., Alcuin.] As though he said: Therefore hear me, because my heart has spoken to you—that is, the heart’s desire which speaks to God. Or reason, taught by you, converses with you concerning that one thing and meditates on nothing but what you teach. [Aug.] Or: I desire, and did not display myself to people, but in the heart, where you alone hear, I said—what? This: “My face has sought you,” not something outside you; that is, my presence has sought yours. [Alcuin.] Or, my beauty, by which I am notable, has sought yours, which is the one thing spoken of above, “that I may contemplate the delight of the Lord.” “Your face,” [Aug., Cassiod.] as though he said: I have sought it; and, O Lord, I shall seek your face, that is, I shall persist steadfastly [Col. 0274A] in this seeking. But that I may find what I seek, you, O Lord:

### VERSE 14.—“Do not turn your face away from me; do not turn aside in anger from your servant.”

Do not turn your face from me in the future, because it is not in my power to obtain what I ask; and do not turn aside in anger from your servant in the future, [Aug.] lest, in seeking you, I fall into evil. For you are the one thing that I ask; I desire to possess nothing else and fear to lose nothing but the one thing. This holy man has fixed his desire and petition intensely upon this one thing; he asks for nothing else: one thing suffices him. Another asks God for these temporal goods and rejoices in what is given; this man seeks only the one thing. Another who possesses such goods fears God’s anger lest he take them away; this man thinks there is no anger except if God turns his face away from him. Even if God should punish something in him, he could say nothing more divine.

Or this may be understood of the present: “Do not turn aside,” as though he said: I pray that you will not turn your face away in the future; therefore meanwhile, do not turn aside in anger from your servant. He did not simply say, “Do not turn aside,” but added, “in anger.” For from some he turns aside in anger, from others not in anger. He turns aside not in anger when he turns his face away from sins in order to blot them out, not from the sinner in order to destroy him; he turns aside in anger when he does not pardon the sinner. [Alcuin.] Or he turns aside not in anger when he permits someone to fall, so that the person may rise more cautious and stronger. Accordingly, explain it thus: Do not turn aside from me, your servant—that is, do not allow me to fall—in anger, so as to punish me eternally, but so that our weakness may become more cautious. Do not turn aside, I say, but:

### VERSE 15.—“Be my helper; do not forsake me, nor despise me, O God my savior.”

[Col. 0274C] “Be my helper,” [Aug.] because, although I am free and set upon the way, I am not sufficient for myself. When shall I find you unless you help me? Without you I shall fail. Therefore I pray also for this: [Gl. int.] that on this way you may not forsake me. [Aug.] As though he said: Do not interrupt what you have begun. You have already set me on the way, but I shall wander if you leave me. You have given me free will, but without you my effort is nothing. “Nor despise me,” that is, do not scorn that I, a mortal, dare seek you, the eternal one, because you are the God who created me and my Savior, who heals the wound of sin. As though he said: You created and recreated me in vain if you despise mortals. You ought not do so, because it is not my own fault but inherited fault by which I fell into this mortality. This is what he says:

### VERSE 16.—“For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up.”

[Col. 0274D] “For my father,” [Alcuin.] namely Adam, “and my mother,” namely Eve, “have forsaken me,” that is, by sinning they exposed me to this misery; but the Lord, having taken flesh, took me up into immortality.

[Hier.] This may literally apply to David, who, being the youngest of his brothers and despised by his parents, was chosen by the Lord through Samuel (I Kings XVI). Mystically it may also be understood thus: the evil father was the kingdom of the world, or the devil; the mother was the city of the world, namely Babylon—that is, the society of the wicked. As though he said: Therefore do not despise me, because my father, namely the kingdom of the world or the devil, and my mother, namely the city of the world from which I was born, forsook me when I sought you and despised them, since they could not give what I seek. But the Lord took me up, for he can give me what I seek, and even now gives what is necessary.

See the great humility by which this man made himself little before God: he made God his father and mother. He is father because he created, calls, commands, and governs; he is mother because he cherishes, nourishes, suckles, and sustains. Therefore he says: “The Lord took me up,” namely to govern and nourish me, as father and mother.

### VERSE 17.—“Set a law before me, O Lord, in your way; and direct me in the straight path because of my enemies.”

Legem. [Aug.] As though he were saying: “Since I am tending toward you, therefore, O Lord, set a law before me as I tend toward you and am already set upon the way”; that is, grant correction which will not allow me to stray. Therefore, set a law, lest your discipline abandon me when I stray. The one assumed [i.e. Christ] may say this: “Set [a law] before me,” I say, “as I am placed in your way,” that is, in Christ, in whom there is law together with mercy, who is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14). He is Wisdom, of whom it is written: “She carries law and mercy upon her tongue” (Prov. 31, according to the LXX). For if you stumble in the law, he who shed his blood for you forgives you when you confess to him. [Col. 0275C] Then he adds concerning mercy, saying, “and further direct me in the straight path,” that is, in the uprightness required amid afflictions; for it is not enough to begin, since enemies do not cease until one arrives. Hence he adds, “because of my enemies,” who never cease to lay snares.

Note that he says two things: namely, “set a law,” and “direct.” The former belongs to precept, because correction is contained in precept; the latter belongs to mercy, through which one is directed toward what is better. And:

### VERSE 18.—“Do not deliver me over to the souls of those who afflict me; for unjust witnesses have risen up against me, and iniquity has lied to itself.”

“Do not deliver me over to the souls of those who afflict [me],” [Aug.] that is, do not allow them to be satisfied by my evils, so that I consent to them, even if you give my flesh into their hands. Hence it is said in Job: “The earth has been given into the hand of the wicked” (Job 9), that is, the flesh has been delivered into the hand of the sinner. Deliver, then, if it please you, my flesh into the hands of those who afflict me; but do not deliver my soul to their souls. Let flesh devour flesh, earth earth; let that soul be kept unharmed for you.

And as though someone asked, “Why do you say this?” he answers: “Behold why: because unjust witnesses have risen against me,” that is, men saying false things about me to myself, in order to unsettle and draw me back from you, as though I sought glory from men. But I would thus be delivered to their souls if I were false with them and sought human glory; “and iniquity lied to itself,” not to me—that is, it delighted in its own lie. Yet it did not move me; hence my reward in heaven is greater. Or, “iniquity lied to itself,” [Hier.] that is, to its own harm. [Col. 0276A] For every sin returns upon its own author.

[Cassiod.] This can also be said historically in the person of David, thus: “Do not deliver me to the souls of those who afflict me,” namely Saul and his helper. “For unjust witnesses have risen against me,” such as Doeg the Edomite and the other accusers of David (1 Kings 21). “And iniquity lied to itself,” as when they said that the priest Abimelech had given David counsel against Saul and had consulted the Lord for him (ibid.). It lied, I say, to itself—that is, to its own harm—because they were false.

### VERSE 19.—“I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

“I believe that I shall see.” [Aug.] Here he returns to that one thing for which he longs, as though saying: “So many dangers, so many labors [Col. 0276B] assail me on every side; and amid these dangers and hardships, under God’s guidance, I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord,” who himself first suffered these evils and afterward was glorified, according to the saying: “He shall drink from the torrent in the way,” etc. (Ps. 109).

[Alcuin.] And I, after the tongues of those who bite and slander, believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord, which are true and eternal. [Aug.] They recommend blessedness in this land, which is the land of the dying; but those good things for which I wait are in the land of the living, where there is no place for falsehood.

### VERSE 20.—“Wait for the Lord; act manfully. Let your heart be strengthened, and endure the Lord.”

“Wait for the Lord,” [Alcuin.] as though he were saying: “Since I am certain of that one thing, so you, whoever have been anointed, [Col. 0276C] wait for the Lord.” [Aug.] Wait confidently for him who does not deceive: the omnipotent one has promised, the reliable one has promised, the truthful one has promised—he who cannot lie.

Or connect the text thus, as though he were saying: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord.” But even if this is slow in coming to one who loves, wait for the Lord, [Aug., Cassiod.] who does not deceive; and, in order that you may attain it, do not act slackly, but act manfully or courageously—that is, endure the burning of outward things manfully, and the burning of the heart bravely. Hence he adds: “and let your heart be strengthened,” [Gl. int.] namely, lest you grow weary; and, even if evils occur, endure the Lord perseveringly—not for three days, but unto the end.

[Cassiod.] Distinguish between “wait for the Lord” and “endure the Lord.” “Wait for the Lord,” that is, for what you believe and hope concerning the Lord; “endure the Lord,” that is, what you suffer for the Lord and from [Col. 0276D] the Lord. He also takes “endure the Lord” and “wait for the Lord” in the same sense, so that it is a repetition for emphasis: as though saying, “Act manfully and be strengthened, and thus endure the Lord.”

[Aug.] Do not think that what you have not yet received has been denied: if it is delayed, it is not taken away. Therefore do not fail through despair, because it has been said, “Endure the Lord.” For by enduring you will possess him whom you endure. Expect something else; desire something else, if you find something better, greater, or sweeter. But because the Lord alone is good and sweet to all (Ps. 144), endure and desire him, lest you be among those to whom it is said: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Ecclus. 2).

## COLLATION ON PSALM 26: “THE LORD IS MY LIGHT”

[Col. 0277A]

### VERSE 8.—“That I may see the will of the Lord.”

It appears that through a scribal error *voluntatem* (“will”) was written for *voluptatem* (“delight”), especially since the particles are very similar. This is strongly supported by the Greek reading τερπνότητα, that is, “delight,” according to the unanimous agreement of all authorities; and this is fully confirmed by Augustine’s reading and interpretation: “that I may contemplate the delight of the Lord.” Jerome, according to the Hebrew, translates “beauty” or “pleasantness.”

Nevertheless, since the Hebrew root NAAM means “was beautiful” and “pleased,” both may rightly be said: “that I may see the will and the delight.” For Jerome’s commentary on this passage also interprets it as “that I may see love,” in accordance with what is written in 1 John 3: “We shall see him as he is.” Unless one says that Jerome likewise has a scribal error, *dilectionem* (“love”) for *delectationem* (“delight”). Finally, it makes no difference to the sense.

[Col. 0277B]

### VERSE 11.—“I went around and sacrificed.”

The beginning of this verse, in the Hebrew and in the translations, looks back to the end of the preceding sentence: “Now he has raised my head above my enemies who are around me.” It is probable, however, that the translators read SABBOTI, that is, “I went around,” where others read SEBIROTAI, that is, “my circuits” or “those around me,” and supplied the preposition “in”: “in my circuits,” literally.

### VERSE 13.—“My heart said to you, it sought,” etc.

Jerome, according to the Hebrew, reads: “my face sought,” without the pronoun “you.” Although he does not reject the other reading, in his letter to Sunia and Fretela he [Col. 0278A] prefers this one. Yet one thing is certain: Jerome used a manuscript different from the Hebrew ones now extant, because they have BAQQUESSU, that is, “seek.” Thus the modern translators render: “Seek my face.” If Jerome’s manuscript had BIQQUESCH, then it is “it sought,” as the LXX read, adding “you”—ἐξεζητήσεως (“you may seek out,” reading uncertain)—for the sake of intelligibility.

So also in Psalm 18: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults.” The pronoun “my” is not in the Hebrew, though it is plainly to be understood; Münster indicates this in his version. In Greek manuscripts we find added, κύριον ζητήσω, that is, “I shall seek the Lord.” Augustine, however, with the Roman psalmody, reads: “I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I shall seek.” Certainly the variety of expressions agrees in unity of spirit.

### 56. VERSE 8.—“Iniquity lied to itself.”

In the Hebrew, in place of the pronoun “itself,” there stands a particle belonging to the following verse, namely LULE, that is, [Col. 0278B] “unless.” Because the sense was obscure, Münster added from his own words: “I should have failed,” he says, “if I had not believed that I would see the good things of the Lord.” Jerome does not appear to have read this little word; for after ending the preceding usage with “in open falsehood,” he immediately continues: “But I believe,” etc.

The LXX, however, may reasonably have read simply LO, that is, “to itself,” or LO LO twice for greater emphasis, rather than LULE, as the manuscripts now have. Above we have also shown from Münster that with aleph [it is] sometimes written for LO without aleph.

# PSALM 27

[Col. 0277]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM FOR THIS DAVID”

[Col. 0277C]

“To you, O Lord, I shall cry.” Title: “A Psalm for this David.” [Alcuin.] By David is sometimes understood the head, that is, Christ; sometimes the body, that is, the Church; and sometimes both together, that is, the whole Christ. [Cassiod.] But where “himself” or “to himself” is added in the title, Christ is understood, as here.

And the sense is: This psalm is attributed to this David, that is, to Christ, who speaks in this psalm. This psalm is the third among those that deal briefly with Christ’s Passion and Resurrection. [Alcuin.] Here Christ is set forth as not trusting in himself, though so worthy, but asking everything from God; this is a useful example for the righteous.

**Intention.** [Cassiod.] He warns those who wish to reign with Christ to endure adversities.

[Col. 0277D] **Method.** It is divided into two parts. First, the prayer offered in the time of the Passion is set forth. Second, having been heard concerning his resurrection, he gives thanks, at “Blessed,” etc.

[Alcuin.] Christ, certainly insofar as he is man, setting himself forth as an example to the righteous, humbly says to the Father: “O—”

### VERSE 1.—“To you, O Lord, I shall cry: my God, do not be silent toward me; lest at any time you be silent toward me, and I become like those who go down into the pit.”

“Lord my God,” [Gl. int.] I, a man, shall cry—or have cried—to you. [Aug.] And you, O God, “do not be silent toward me,” that is, do not separate the unity of your Word from that which I am as man; “lest at any time you be silent toward me.”

[Alcuin.] This is not in the Hebrew, but was added by the LXX; Jerome marked it, with an obelus prefixed, as though it should be struck out. It is strange that he should say it is not found in the Hebrew and was struck out by Jerome, since it is read there and Jerome translates it [Col. 0278C] according to the Hebrew. Yet it is true that the Roman Psalter does not read it. The Hebrew has it thus; and therefore you should continue as though it had not been inserted: “and I shall become like”—as though saying, “I say, do not be silent.”

[Jerome.] And this is because, if you are silent, “I shall become like those who go down into the pit.” [Aug.] That is, [I shall become like those who descend] into the misery of this life. For because the Word is always united to me, I am not such a man as other men, who are born into the profound misery of the world, where, as though you were silent, your Word is not recognized.

[Alcuin.] Or both expressions may fittingly be read: “do not be silent” and “lest at any time you be silent,” which the LXX did not add without reason. For they understood Christ in that one prayer, “Do not be silent,” to ask two things: namely, that in his Passion the Father would glorify him by protecting him, [Col. 0278D] and that in the Resurrection he would glorify him by raising him from death. They therefore distinguished these two things by different words.

[Gl. int.] In the first, indeed, he asks to be glorified in the Resurrection; in the second, in the Passion. Thus: “Do not be silent toward me” in the Resurrection, but answer me by granting [my request], that is, by raising me. And not only this, but “lest at any time,” that is, not even for an hour, “be silent toward me”; but also here, [Jerome] that is, in the Passion, glorify me by protecting me, and afterward in the Resurrection, for which he had prayed above.

Then he gives the reason, as though saying: “Therefore do not be silent, because if you are silent, I shall become like those who go down into the pit,” that is, into hell, that is, like those held in hell.

### VERSE 2.—“Hear, O Lord, the voice of my prayer, while I pray to you, while I lift up my hands toward your holy temple.”

[Col. 0279A] “Hear.” [Cassiod.] As though he were saying: “Do not be silent, but hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication.” This is so “while,” that is, because I pray to you. [Aug.] Christ did this before his betrayal for those who would believe. [Jerome.] And also “while,” that is, because I lift up my hands, literally, upon the cross. And this is not for my own guilt, but in order to establish your holy temple, [Gl. int.] that is, in order that I may establish the Church for you. As though saying: “I do this for the salvation of those who become your temple.”

Or, “I lift up my hands,” that is, I do not lower my works, “toward your holy temple”; this meaning does not change. [Cassiod.] Or, literally, “I lift up my hands toward your holy temple,” which is in Jerusalem. He says this according to the custom of the Jews, who were commanded, wherever they might be, to pray toward that direction [Col. 0279B] in which they knew Jerusalem to be; Jesus too did this in fulfilling the law. Or, in prayer I lift up my hands toward the temple, that is, toward heaven, which is the custom of the faithful, because we hope for help from there.

### VERSE 3.—“Do not deliver me up together with sinners, and do not destroy me together with those who work iniquity.”

“Do not [deliver me up] together [with them].” As though he were saying: “I say, hear me, lest you deliver me to death together with sinners,” [Gl. int.] that is, with the intention with which they are delivered. As though saying: “Even if you deliver me to death, do not do it with the purpose for which they do, because they are sinners and you are truth. And do not destroy me by condemning me as guilty with those who work iniquity,” that is, as they intend, because they themselves work iniquity—that is, my death—and because they speak [Col. 0279C] peace deceitfully. Hence he adds:

### VERSE 4.—“Who speak peace with their neighbor, but evils are in their hearts.”

[Aug.] “Who speak peace,” saying: “We know that you have come from God, teacher” (John 3). They speak, I say, “with their neighbor,” that is, with me, who am near to them by the flesh and also by the mercy I have bestowed; for I did not pass by on seeing the man wounded by robbers, as did the priest and Levite, but, as a true neighbor, I drew near in order to show him mercy. “But evils”—as though saying, they speak good things and peace with their lips; but evils, that is, hatred, are in their hearts. And therefore:

### VERSE 5.—“Give them according to their works, [Col. 0279D] and according to the wickedness of their contrivances.”

“Give them according to their works,” [Cassiod., Alcuin.] that is, according to what they intended, not according to what resulted from it. This is a prediction, not a wish. [Aug., Rem.] Or he desires that God’s justice be observed in this, because this too is just; as though saying: “O Lord, I agree with your justice, which pleases me, even though I do not delight in their punishment.” “And give them according to the wickedness of their contrivances.”

[Gl. int.] For they did evil and devised evil, saying that I was a deceiver and not God (Matt. 23). [Aug.] Another text has: “according to the malignity of their dispositions,” because those who desire evil cannot discover good. The sense does not differ from [Col. 0280A] the former reading. And he repeats this in order to mark the stubbornness of their malice, saying:

### VERSE 6.—“Render to them according to the works of their hands; repay them their recompense.”

“Repay them according to the works of their hands.” [Aug.] Even if what they did benefits others unto salvation, nevertheless render to them according to the works of your hands—that is, according to the intention of their own deeds. He says “works of hands” because they were zealous in these matters: they seized [him], crucified [him] with their tongues, if not with their hands, by instigation if not by actual deed—things which are among their worst works. He says this lest they excuse themselves on account of others.

[Cassiod.] He adds further concerning their punishment, saying: “Repay them their recompense.” [Aug.] Because they return evil to me for good. Repay them this: just as they returned deceit to me for truth, so may their deceit deceive them. And that this happened to them is manifest.

### VERSE 7.—“Because they have not understood the works of the Lord, and in the works of his hands you will destroy them, and you will not build them up.”

“Because they have not understood the works of the Lord.” Or: “in the work of the Lord,” namely, the Word’s having become man. [Aug.] This is indeed their very recompense: that they did not recognize as God the one whom they tested with malicious intent, nor the purpose for which the Father sent him incarnate. Nor did they understand [Col. 0280C] “the works of his hands,” the visible works; that is, they were not moved even by the visible works set before their eyes, through which they might have been led to invisible things, but did not understand.

And therefore, “you will destroy them,” or “destroy them,” so that they may harm neither me nor, beforehand, my Church; “and you will not build them up” afterward, as you used formerly after captivities, but from this captivity they will not be brought back.

[Alcuin.] Or thus: “because” gives the reason why they ought to be repaid, as though saying: “And he will repay them deservedly, because, even if the works which they committed were lacking, this alone would suffice for their condemnation: that they did not understand, through the law and prophets by which they were rebuked, the works of the Lord,” that is, the invisible things which God works through me. “And [they did not understand] the works of his hands,” [Cassiod.] that is, not even the visible things which God works through me. Therefore, “you will destroy them, and you will not build them up”: that is, you will not destroy them so as [Col. 0280D] to build them up into something better, as you destroyed Paul and many others to make them better, according to Jeremiah: “I have sent you to uproot and pull down, to destroy and demolish, to build and to plant” (Jer. 1).

[Gl. int.] Or, “destroy them, and you will not build them up,” that is, blind them—not for a time, but unto the end.

## PART II.—VERSE 8.—“Blessed be the Lord, because he has heard the voice of my supplication.”

“Blessed.” [Cassiod.] The second part, in which Christ, heard concerning his resurrection, gives thanks and adds concerning the salvation of believers. As though saying: “I do not pray in distrust, because the Lord has heard the voice of my supplication; therefore let him himself be blessed.” He has heard [me], I say, in such a way that:

[Col. 0281A]

### VERSE 9.—“The Lord is my helper and my protector; in him my heart hoped, and I was helped.”

“The Lord is my helper,” [Aug.] that is, the helper of me suffering so greatly, “and my protector,” that is, the protector of me rising into immortality; “and in him my heart hoped, and I was helped.”

### VERSE 10.—“And my flesh has blossomed anew, and of my own will I shall confess to him.”

“And has blossomed anew.” As though saying: “I was helped, and in such a way that my flesh blossomed anew,” through freedom from sin—[Gl. int.] flesh which withered in Adam through sin. The flower, therefore, which it lost in the first man, it recovered in me, who was conceived without defect and sin and born of the Holy Spirit.

Or, “my flesh blossomed anew,” [Col. 0281B] that is, it flowered again in the Resurrection, namely when it rose; [Cassiod.] it had previously flourished in freedom from sin at the conception. Therefore, once the fear of death had been consumed, “I shall confess to him,” and this “of my own will.” [Aug.] That is, my own people, in whom I am, will confess to him; and this not from the compulsion of fear, as under the law, but with free will under the law.

### VERSE 11.—“The Lord is the strength of his people, and he is the protector of the salvations of his Christ.”

“The Lord is strength.” Here he adds concerning the salvation of believers. As though saying: “And deservedly they will confess,” [Cassiod.] because the Lord—the same one who is my helper and protector—[Alcuin.] is strength in battle against the devil for his people, [Aug.] namely, those who trust in him. Therefore let not the people think themselves strong, so as to presume to establish their own righteousness, but let them submit themselves to the righteousness of God.

And he is “the protector of the salvations of his Christ,” [Gl. int.] that is, he protects in this struggle those whom Christ has chosen for salvation, lest they be harmed by the devil. Or this may be understood of the future: [Aug.] as though saying, “In battle he is the strength of his own; and after the battle he will protect with immortality the salvations of his Christ,” that is, those made safe through his Christ. This I, already raised and with my flesh already blossoming anew, intercede and pray for, thus: “O—”

### VERSE 12.—“Save your people, O Lord, and bless your inheritance; rule them, and lift [Col. 0281D] them up forever.”

[Gl. int.] “O Lord Father, save from the evils of this age your people,” [Gl. int.] who are also mine, because all that is mine is yours; “and bless your inheritance,” [Aug.] that is, increase your inheritance in virtues and in number. [Gl. int., Aug.] It is also mine, because you said: “I will give you the nations,” etc. (Ps. 2).

Behold how great is the hope of believers when he who suffered prays for them, being their judge and advocate. “Rule them” in this temporal life, [Alcuin.] lest they turn aside to evil; “and lift them up,” [Aug.] from earthly things unto eternity, that is, to desire eternal things. Or, lift them up in understanding, namely of the Scriptures, and in good work. And this “forever,” that is, throughout this whole age, unto the end. Or, “lift them up forever”: [Col. 0282A] [Cassiod.] take them hence unto eternity, that is, into eternal life.

## COLLATION ON PSALM 27: “TO YOU, O LORD, I SHALL CRY”

### VERSE 1.—“Lest at any time you be silent toward me, and I shall become like,” etc.

Here Faber and the Blind Man of Burgos attack the Greek and Latin edition, as though it produced a sense contrary to the Prophet’s meaning. In their view, he fears that he will be made like the dead and the despairing if God does not answer—that is, hear—his prayer; and our reading seems to affirm what must be avoided.

Yet Augustine, Pellicanus, and Pratensis follow it. Thus Faber and the Blind One hold, for the safety both of grammar and meaning, that it should be read: “lest at any time you be silent toward me, and I may become like those who go down into the pit”; lest, if “and I shall become like” is said, an assertion be understood contrary to the truth.

Had they seen Jerome’s explanation of this passage, they would not have condemned the Greek construction, [Col. 0282B] καὶ ὁμοιωθήσομαι, “and I shall become like.” Indeed it corresponds word for word to the Hebrew VENIMSSALTI, “and I shall become like.” Jerome accordingly understands it thus: “Lest at any time you be silent toward me”—that is, if you are silent, I shall be like those who perish. This explanation becomes clearer than light, and is explained more fully above in the exposition.

### VERSE 3.—“Do not destroy me together with those who work iniquity.”

The final phrase, “do not destroy me,” is not in the Hebrew, but was understood from the preceding clause, “do not deliver me up together with sinners.” “We find many things not idly added by the Seventy to the Hebrew reading,” says Ambrose, *Hexameron*, book 3. For example, in Psalm 20, “they devised plans which they could not [carry out],” the LXX also added, quite suitably, the word “to establish,” which was not in the Hebrew; Münster did the same.

Perhaps the preceding words in the same verse, “do not deliver me up together [with them],” were written by a scribal error in the LXX for “do not draw me away together [with them].” For the Greeks read μὴ συνελκύσῃς με, “do not draw me along,” and the Hebrews [Col. 0282C] AL TISMECHENI; Münster says, “do not draw me.” Jerome, however, and Pratensis have “do not deliver me,” unless you suspect the same error. In any case, the sense is the same.

### VERSE 7.—“You will destroy them, and you will not build them up.”

The Hebrew manuscripts have the third person: “he will destroy them, and he will not build [them] up.” Yet Jerome and the LXX read the second person. For if you say IEHERSEM, it means “he will destroy them”; but TEHERSEM means “you will destroy them.” There was no need to mention this unless because some are accustomed to cry out, “It is not thus in the Hebrew.”

### VERSE 10.—“And my flesh has blossomed anew.”

The Hebrews say, “my heart exulted” or “rejoiced”: IAALOZ LIBBI. Yet ALAZ not unfittingly signifies “to blossom,” especially since this concerns Christ’s Resurrection unto immortality. For in Psalm 95, “the fields shall rejoice”; in Hebrew, IAALOZ SADAI. And what does the joy [Col. 0282D] of the field mean except the springing forth and verdure of herbs and flowers?

The LXX, in order to indicate the emphasis and weight of joy, put the effect—namely, the exaltation of the flesh before the heart’s gladness—when, in Christ, the majesty of divinity in the Resurrection overflows abundantly into the body. For a joyful mind makes one’s age flourish, Proverbs 18; especially since it had just preceded: “in him my heart hoped, and I was helped.”

The LXX, believed to have been inspired by the Holy Spirit, most fittingly added concerning the resurrection of the flesh, “and my flesh blossomed anew”; and immediately afterward there follows again concerning the heart’s joy: “and of my own will,” without “with my song,” as the Hebrews wish, “I shall confess to him,” so that the glory of the body, as though placed in the middle, may be surrounded by the triumph of incorruption. For they were not ignorant of what was said in Psalm 15: “My flesh shall rest in hope.”

### VERSE 11.—“The Lord is the strength of his people.”

The Hebrews now read OZ LAMO, that is, “strength to them” or “their strength.” Hence it is evident that the LXX read AMMO for LAMO, that is, “his people.” Jerome read OZ LI, because he translated “my strength.” Sanctus reads OZ LO, because he translated “his strength.” Hence I am readily led to think that the LXX likewise had another word quite close to the term [Col. 0283A] discussed a little before, where they read “flesh.” This could be indicated, if necessary, under the meaning “garment”: LEBUSSI, “my garment,” by which the flesh is signified (Phil. 2). For although AMO and LAMO may here correspond in sound, there is nevertheless a greater difference in writing; yet you see one plainly put in place of the other, so that the constant argument which we often make is undoubtedly established: manuscripts were formerly different.

# PSALM 28

[Col. 0283]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF DAVID AT THE COMPLETION OF THE TABERNACLE”

[Col. 0283A]

“Bring to the Lord.” Title: “A Psalm of David at the completion of the tabernacle.” In the Book of Kings it is read that, in the time of Eli the priest, the sons of Israel fought [Col. 0283B] against the Philistines and were defeated by them (1 Kings 4). Eli’s two sons also, namely Hophni and Phinehas, fell in battle; the ark of the Lord was captured by the Philistines and carried to Ashdod. The Philistines placed it beside the idol Dagon.

But on the next day they found Dagon prostrate before the ark, and raised it up. Likewise on the following day they found it prostrate and raised it again. On the third day they found it once more prostrate before the ark, with its head and the palms of its hands cut off. [Note: [Col. 0283] According to the LXX interpreters, at Dagon’s second raising.]

The ark remained in the regions of the Philistines for seven months, and they were struck with a severe plague. For mice swarmed out of the earth and devastated them, gnawing away their protruding buttocks. [Col. 0283C] Struck and compelled by this plague, they finally returned the ark to Gibeah; and, to heal the plague brought by their sin, they sent with the ark, according to the number of provinces, five female donkeys and as many golden mice.

When David was prosperously reigning, after the death of Saul and his son Ishbosheth, he took the ark from Gibeah and brought it to Jerusalem. When it had been brought back, he made a tabernacle for it and offered burnt offerings. [Jerome.] Literally, this seems here to exhort others to bring sacrifices; but the subject is rather the signifying tabernacle, that is, the Church.

[Jerome, Alcuin.] For just as the ark was brought back from the Philistines and David spread a tabernacle for it, so Christ brought the Church back from the devil’s dominion and bestowed upon it gifts of grace. The Prophet here speaks of its perfection: namely, that Christ fills it with the seven gifts [Col. 0283D] of the Holy Spirit, confirms it in them, thus advances it, and afterward rewards it.

The sense of the title is: This psalm belongs to David the prophet, who speaks here, composed “at the completion of the tabernacle,” [Aug.] that is, treating of the perfection of the Church in this age, in which warfare against the devil is conducted within it. Therefore it is called a tabernacle, [Cassiod.] just as in its future state it is called a house, because there it will rest.

**Intention.** [Alcuin, Cassiod.] He exhorts the faithful to offer themselves to such a perfecter.

**Method.** The psalm is in three parts. First, he exhorts the faithful to offer sacrifices. Second, he treats of the establishment of the Church, enumerating the seven gifts of the Holy [Col. 0284A] Spirit, at “The voice of the Lord is over the waters.” Third, he says what happens to the Church once established, at “The Lord [sits] upon the flood.”

Therefore, as the Prophet exhorts the faithful to bring spiritual sacrifices to God, he says: [Gl. int.] “O sons of God, not [sons] of wrath or perdition.”

[Col. 0284B]

### VERSE 1.—“Bring to the Lord, O sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams.”

[Jerome, Aug.] “Bring to the Lord” yourselves, in faith and good works. In this sequence he shows to whom, who, what, how, where, and why they ought to offer. To whom? To the Lord. Who? Sons of God. What? Sons of rams. How? “Bring to the Lord glory and honor.” Where? “In his holy court.” Why? “The voice of the Lord.”

Having said who should offer and to whom, he adds what they should offer: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams,” [Aug., Gl. int.] that is, yourselves, uncorrupted by errors, whom the apostles—leaders and guardians of the flocks—begot through the Gospel. They guard the flock with anxious diligence because assaults by heretics are not lacking.

Therefore he says, “Bring,” namely yourselves, “to the Lord, [Col. 0284C] sons of rams,” [Cassiod., Alcuin.] that is, as sons of the apostles, whom you ought to imitate.
