They are called rams because, with the two horns—that is, the authorities of both Testaments—they prevailed against heretics, and with a hard brow demolished superstitions and idols.

[Alcuin.] Hence the pontifical mitre has two horns, because every scribe taught in the kingdom of heaven brings forth from the treasure of his heart things new and old (Matt. 13). And the seventh stopping-place of the children of Israel coming from Egypt was Elim, where there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees (Exod. 15), which both by its name and by the nature of the place signifies the apostolic order. For Elim is interpreted “rams.”

These are the apostles, leaders of the faithful flocks. The twelve springs are the twelve apostles first chosen by the Lord, from whom flows living water springing up into eternal life (John 4). The seventy palm trees are the other seventy-two disciples designated in Luke’s Gospel and sent to preach, who announced to the whole world the palm of Christ’s victory. It should be known that “the Lord” here means the whole Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

### VERSE 2.—“Bring to the Lord glory and honor; bring to the Lord glory to his name. Worship the Lord in his holy court.”

“Bring to the Lord,” [Aug.] namely to the Trinity, “glory and [Col. 0285A] honor,” so that through our good works God may be glorified and honored. He repeats: “Bring to the Lord glory,” in such a way that you also bring it to his name, namely, that through you God may be gloriously made known throughout the world. [Jerome.] For nothing accrues to God from us, but [glory accrues] with respect to others who profit thereby.

He says that we should bring glory to the Lord and to his name. Or in this sequence “the Lord” may be understood as Christ. For although the essence of the three persons is undivided, [Cassiod.] different passages of Scripture are applied to different persons. Thus here we understand the Lord as Christ, who strengthens the Church with virtues. To this Lord, therefore—that is, to Christ—bring yourselves, O sons of God; bring yourselves to this Lord, sons of rams. The meaning of the words is unchanged.

[Gl. int.] Then he adds how they ought to bring [this offering]: “Bring to the Lord,” to Christ, “glory,” by preaching that he is equal to the Father; “and honor,” because he is the one who has dominion over all things. “Bring to the Lord,” to Christ, “glory,” in such a way that it is brought also to his name, that God may be gloriously made known throughout the world.

[Aug.] Then he shows where they ought to bring it, saying: “Worship the Lord in his holy court,” or “in his holy hall,” [Aug., Gl. int.] that is, in the enlarged and sanctified heart, because all holiness comes from charity.

## PART II. VERSE 3.—“The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the God of majesty has thundered: the Lord is over many waters.”

“The voice of the Lord.” [Cassiod.] The second part, where he treats of the establishment of the Church, in which he enumerates with great proclamation the seven virtues of the Holy [Col. 0285C] Spirit. He begins from the lowest, namely the spirit of fear, and ascends to the highest, namely the spirit of wisdom.

[Gregory.] Isaiah, however, enumerating the same gifts in reverse order, descends from the highest to the lowest, saying: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.” Isaiah enumerates them in descending order because he treats of Christ’s Incarnation, in which he emptied himself by taking—or assuming—the form of a servant. But here the Psalmist ascends from the lowest to the highest because he treats of the Church’s establishment, which begins from fear, the beginning of wisdom, and gradually rises to greater things.

He shows here why an offering should be made to the Lord, as though saying: [Col. 0285D] “Therefore bring [offerings], because the voice of the Lord,” [Aug., Gl. int.] that is, of Christ, “has come upon the waters,” that is, upon the Jews, who were in the flux of the age; and “upon the waters of the sea,” [Aug.] that is, upon the peoples of the Gentiles.

He shows how that voice came when he says: “The Lord, the God of majesty, has thundered,” that is, Christ, who is the King of glory, preached repentance terrifyingly from the cloud of the flesh and inwardly terrified human minds. [Alcuin.] That is to say, Christ’s preaching gave the spirit of fear to Jews and Gentiles; nor did Christ cease thundering until he gave strength, that is, piety. This is what follows.

### VERSE 4.—“The voice of the Lord is in strength; the voice of the Lord is in magnificence.”

“The voice of the Lord,” [Alcuin.] that is, Christ’s preaching, [Col. 0286A] “came in strength”: it gave piety, which, when compared with fear—that is, in relation to fear—is called strength. For piety is worship toward God, which they render after they begin to fear offending God.

God also adds magnificence, that is, knowledge, the third grace, which makes men magnificent, so that one engaged in the worship of God may know how to conduct oneself in the present life. This is what follows: “The voice of the Lord has come in magnificence,” that is, Christ’s preaching gave the spirit of knowledge, by which we know how to live rightly amid this crooked and perverse generation (Phil. 2).

This also:

### VERSE 5.—“The voice of the Lord breaks the cedars; and the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon.”

The voice of the Lord is that which breaks the cedars. [Augustine, Alcuin.] That is, the Lord will break through repentance and humility the cedars—that is, the lofty among the Gentiles—and the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon—that is, the lofty among the Jews—at the time of the final ingathering, when the remnant will be saved (Rom. II), so breaking and humbling them that they will not shrink from suffering whatever adversities may come. That is to say: he will give the Spirit of fortitude to Gentiles and Jews, so that they may be strong in those things which they recognize by the Spirit of knowledge. [Cassiodorus.] The cedar aptly signifies pride, because it is a very tall tree, especially in Lebanon, where the cedars are taller. Unless cut down, this tree remains useless; abiding in its root, it bears no useful fruit. So pride, which brought sin upon us, while it remains rooted, bears useless fruits; when it is cut down, the fruits of grace grow up.

[Col. 0286C] VERS. 6.—“And he shall crush them like a calf of Lebanon; and the Beloved like the son of unicorns.”

Once pride has been cut down and broken in them, he shall crush—that is, humble—them like a calf. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] On Lebanon, a mountain fit for pasture, calves were raised for sacrifice, because that mountain is rich in grasses, watered by springs, and planted with trees. Those humbled from pride are compared to this: like a calf, they are prepared to die for Christ. Therefore he shall crush them like a calf of Lebanon—that is, he shall humble them so completely that, if need be, they may be sacrificed for Christ.

And because he had said, “he shall crush” and “he shall break,” without saying who would do so, he now specifies it: and the Beloved [Col. 0286D] shall do this—that is, Christ will crush pride. Of him the Father says: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. III). He is like the son of unicorns—that is, according to the flesh, the son of the Jews, who take pride in one Law and are therefore called unicorns.

Or thus: “and the Beloved.” That is, they shall be broken and crushed; and what wonder if they are crushed? It is no wonder. For the Beloved himself—that is, Christ—shall be crushed, that is, humbled even unto death. And this is so as the son of unicorns: that is, insofar as he is the son of the Jews, insofar as he is man. For, being God, he could not otherwise seem capable of being crushed. He next speaks of the Spirit of counsel, saying:

VERS. 7.—“The voice of the Lord cutting off the flame [Col. 0287A] of fire; the voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness, and the Lord shall move the wilderness of Kadesh.”

The voice of the Lord cuts off the flame of fire. [Alcuin.] Fire is the tinder of sin; the flame which issues from it is consent to the act and habitual practice. Yet the Lord does not extinguish this flame; rather, he interrupts and cuts it off, by giving the Spirit of counsel, lest it reach consent, action, or habit. This befits the strong, lest, if they are idle, flame burst forth from the fire.

He next speaks of the Spirit of understanding: “the voice of the Lord shakes the wilderness”—that is, moves the Gentiles to faith. [Augustine.] He calls the Gentiles a wilderness because they had been without Law, without God, and without prophets. “And the Lord shall move the wilderness of Kadesh”—that is, the Jews. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] [Col. 0287B] Kadesh, literally, is the place where water was given from the rock; this happens there even now in the literal sense, and spiritually happens today in the Church when hard hearts also are converted to faith and pour forth living waters. Kadesh means “holy of the Law.” Thus the wilderness of Kadesh means that the Jews are deserted by the holiness of the Law: they do not possess the holy thing of the Law, that is, the spiritual understanding of the Law.

But the Lord moves and shakes both them and the Gentiles, as a farmer shakes barren ground so that it may bear fruit. That is, he gives understanding, so that they may grasp the Scriptures also according to anagogy; and this takes place in a mind well settled by counsel. Through this understanding of Scripture he advances them as far as the Spirit of wisdom and makes them stags, who climb the mountain of wisdom, which concerns the divine essence. This is what follows:

[Col. 0287C] VERS. 8.—“The voice of the Lord preparing stags, and he shall reveal the thickets; and in his temple all shall speak glory.”

The voice of the Lord—that is, the preaching of Christ—prepares stags. [Jerome; Alcuin, Jerome, Augustine.] That is, it grants the Spirit of wisdom to certain persons who overcome and repel the poisonous tongues of heretics. [Cassiodorus.] They are therefore compared to stags. [Alcuin, Augustine.] And he grants this not only to the Gentiles, but will also reveal to the Jews at the end the things concerning divinity which are thickly veiled. He will open for them the obscurities of the books and the shady coverings of the mysteries, where they may feed freely.

[Alcuin.] Observe that, beginning with fear, he rises as far as wisdom. For with all these stages of gifts is joined chaste fear, [Col. 0287D] which is not cast out even by perfect charity.

This sequence may also be read without the indicated distinction of the seven gifts, as follows. “The voice of the Lord”—that is, Christ’s preaching—is upon the waters, that is, upon peoples. [Augustine.] For here no distinction is made between Jews and Gentiles. He then says how it came about: “the God of majesty”—that is, Christ—“thundered,” that is, from the cloud of flesh he preached repentance in a terrifying manner. And by this means the Lord—that is, Christ—dwells over many waters, that is, many peoples. For after Christ sent forth his voice to the peoples and terrified them, he converted them to himself and dwells in them through faith, hope, and charity; and he received them through waters, and through many waters.

And the voice of the Lord—that is, [Col. 0288A] of Christ now dwelling in them—is “in power,” making them powerful. And the voice of the Lord is “in magnificence,” of miracles or works, that is, performing in them miracles or works. And the voice of the Lord breaks the cedars: Christ’s preaching, through contrition of heart, humbles the proud. And the Lord will break, through repentance, the cedars of Lebanon—that is, those exalted by the brilliance of earthly nobility. [Alcuin.] Lebanon means “whitening,” signifying worldly splendor; those who shine with it and are exalted will be confounded and broken by the lowly things of the world which he chose (II Cor. I).

[Augustine.] Once their pride and loftiness are removed, he shall crush those cedars—that is, those exalted by worldly riches—like calves: he will cast them down and humble them to imitate his own humility, he who, like a calf, [Col. 0288B] was led to the victim of the cross by the nobles of the world, signified by Lebanon. Hence the Prophet: “The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers,” etc. (Ps. II). And it is no wonder if they are crushed: for he himself, the Beloved—that is, Christ, the Father’s only Son—crushed himself, that is, emptied himself of his nobility, and became man, like the son of unicorns: that is, like the son of Jews ignorant of God’s righteousness and proudly boasting of their supposedly singular righteousness.

And the voice of the Lord cuts off the flame of fire: that is, it passes, without any injury to itself, through the most vehement burning rage of its persecutors. Or it divides their furious wrath, so that some are converted and others are not. Thus it cuts off their tumult, drawing some to its charity while leaving others in their malice. The voice of the Lord [Col. 0288C] shakes the wilderness—that is, moves to faith the Gentiles, who were without God, Law, and prophets. And then the Lord shall move the wilderness of Kadesh: that is, he will make the holy content of his Scriptures celebrated, which was abandoned by Jews who did not understand it; that is, he will make the words of the Law intelligible.

The voice of the Lord prepares stags: that is, it perfects those who overcome and repel poisonous tongues. And he will reveal to them the thickets—that is, the obscurities of books and the shady coverings of mysteries—where they may feed freely. [Alcuin.] “And in his temple”: up to this point he has shown how Christ perfects the Church by the seven gifts; here he says what occurs in it. He calls it the temple which, in the title, was called the tabernacle. As though he said: Thus Christ has perfected the Church, [Col. 0288D] and all who are in his temple, thus perfected, shall speak glory. Or, according to another reading, “every one shall speak glory.” [Augustine, Alcuin.] For each person praises the Lord for his own gift. Whoever, therefore, does not speak glory is not truly in the temple; therefore, give glory.

PARS III. VERS. 9.—“The Lord causes the flood to be inhabited; and the Lord shall sit as king for ever.”

“The Lord, the flood.” [Alcuin.] The third part, in which he says what becomes of the Church once established. As though he said: Therefore give glory, because the Lord causes this temple—that is, the saints established in the Church like Noah’s ark—to inhabit the flood of this world. [Augustine, Jerome, Alcuin.] That is, he will cause them to dwell unharmed among those who flow about and submerge others, just as he preserved Noah’s ark amid the waves and inundations of water.

[Remigius.] Or, the Lord causes the flood—that is, those wicked persons who were submerging others in sin—to inhabit this temple, namely the Church, because he converts even such persons to the unity of the holy Church. Or, according to another reading, “the Lord inhabits the flood.” [Cassiodorus.] That is, he inhabits the waters of baptism, which cleanse the world’s crimes, just as the world was cleansed through the Flood.

“And he shall sit.” He has shown how Christ perfects the Church; here, how he advances it. As though he said: And then, in that temple, the Lord shall sit as king for ever, [Augustine, Alcuin.] that is, reigning in them eternally—being powerful and governing them—until eternity comes. And he will truly rule, because:

VERS. 10.—“The Lord will give strength to his people;  
the Lord will bless his people in peace.”

The Lord will give strength to his people. [Augustine.] They are contending against [Col. 0289B] the storms and whirlwinds of this world, for there is no peace in this age. He then adds concerning recompense: and at last the Lord will bless his people in eternal peace, giving them peace in himself. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John XIV).

## COMPARISON ON PSALM XXVIII: “BRING TO THE LORD, O SONS OF GOD.”

VERS. 1.—“Bring to the Lord, O sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams.” Some render only the latter part: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams”; such are Jerome and Sanctes. Others render only the former part: “Bring to the Lord, O sons of gods,” that is, as they maintain, of nobles, princes, or strong men. In Hebrew it is **BENE ELIM**. *Elim* signifies [Col. 0289C] God, angels, princes, rams, strong men. Our translators embraced both senses in a double clause and rendered both.

VERS. 2.—“In his holy court.” Hebrew: [.....] **BEHADRATH**. If *he*, that is, *h*, is a radical aspiration, the interpretation is “in beauty” or “in magnificence,” as Jerome and the modern translators have it. But if it is servile, to use their terminology, and is declined from the stem [.....], it will mean “dwelling,” and consequently “court,” as the translators understood it. Yet there is no need to labor excessively over such matters, since God’s court is his own magnificent glory. In verse 4 of the same psalm the translators have rendered the same word.

VERS. 6.—“And he shall crush them,” or “her,” “like a calf [of] Lebanon.” Because the Hebrews lack distinct case endings, Jerome translates in the nominative case, and Sanctes [renders] “a calf,” so that it may refer to Christ, who was a calf in the humility of his Passion, in order to crush our pride. Other Hebraists translate it in the fourth case [the accusative], according to our usage, but place the division after the word “calf,” or refer “Lebanon” to what follows, as Jerome also does. They differ, however, because he uses the nominative where the others, apart from Sanctes, use the accusative. Thus the diversity may be uncertain both in case and in the division of pauses.

Hence Campensis’s Paraphrase: “and he shall cause Lebanon to leap like a calf.” But where we say “and he shall crush them,” the modern translators render “he shall cause [them] to leap.” Yet because Jerome translated according to the Hebrews, “he shall scatter them,” Nebiensis agrees; I do not think they always attained the full meaning of the words. The translator following Campensis said: “he shall trample Lebanon like a bull.” Finally, nothing prevents the meanings from converging. For the voice of the Lord—that is, Christ’s preaching—crushes the Gentiles when it [Col. 0290A] softens their hearts and, through inward sorrow, induces them to sacrifice themselves to him. This spiritual sacrifice is signified by the calf. And how could a heart thus cleansed fail to be exalted in its God, and fail to glory in being crucified with Christ, in the mortification of the flesh and the Passion of the true Calf?

On the same passage: “And the Beloved like the son of unicorns.” Hebrew: **VESSIRION IZEMO BEN REMIM**, that is: “And Sirion, like *filius* (‘a son’) or *filium* (‘a son,’ in the case required by the construction), of unicorns or of a rhinoceros.” For either can be derived from the Hebrew. And Jerome sometimes translates it in one way, sometimes in the other. **SIRION** or **SARJON**, when it is a proper name, means a mountain called Hermon. It can, however, be derived from the verb **SCHOR**, which means “to sing,” “to contemplate,” “to offer a gift”—all of which befit the Beloved, who is to be proclaimed and honored with gifts. The Septuagint seems to have had this in view.

VERS. 7.—“The voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness.” [Col. 0290B] Some translate, “causing the wilderness to bring forth”; and Sanctes added on his own initiative, “causing the wild beasts of the wilderness to bring forth.” Others [translate], “the wilderness trembles,” which is the same as our reading. The difference arises from the many meanings of the Hebrew particle **HOL**, which can signify “to make tremble,” “to conceive,” “to bring forth,” and many other things. The interpretation, however, can readily be harmonized.

VERS. 8.—“The voice of the Lord preparing stags.” Jerome: “the voice of the Lord acting as midwife for does”; or, as others wish, “causing does to bring forth,” or “causing stags to tremble.” It has already been said that the word **HOLEL**, used here, is highly equivocal: one takes one sense, another another. Faber and Caecus insist, not without irritation, that “does,” rather than “stags,” ought to be read, because stags do not give birth. To this we say that it is true if the translation must be “he shall cause [them] to give birth.” But if we translate “to prepare,” there is no objection to rendering “stags,” since **AIAL** is common to both, even though, perhaps, **AIALIM** would have to be said for “stags” in the masculine.

The voice of the Lord prepares stags when it makes people, through their merits, loving and eager, like stags renowned in song for their swiftness.

VERS. 9.—“The Lord causes the flood to be inhabited.” This passage refutes the slander by which some caviller might perhaps accuse us: we often rightly complain of a word’s ambiguity, and for that reason defend the Latin reading and try to show that our translators followed another meaning, even if Jerome translates otherwise in order to satisfy Sophronius against the Jews, with whom he frequently disputed. For Saint Jerome, replying to Sunnia and Fretela, who asked about this verse, writes as follows:

> “The Lord causes the flood to be inhabited, in place of which you say that you have read, *κύριος τὸν κατακλυσμὸν κατοικεῖ*, that is, ‘the Lord inhabits the flood.’ The former concerns the grace of believers; the latter, the dwelling-place of him in whom they believe. But because the verb *IASSAB* is ambiguous and can have either meaning—for sitting and dwelling are both expressed by it—and because in the same psalm the grace of baptism is spoken of—‘the voice of the Lord upon many waters,’ and ‘the voice of the Lord preparing stags; and he shall reveal the thickets; and in his temple every one shall speak glory’—we wish these things to be understood of those who glorify the Lord, and we have translated: ‘The Lord causes the flood to be inhabited.’”

Thus Saint Jerome. Yet without inconsistency, according to the Hebrews he translates, “the Lord inhabits the flood”; and the Hebraizing moderns, “he sits,” or “sat,” over the flood. This deceived Faber, who says: “It seems more correct from the Hebrew to say ‘he inhabits’ rather than ‘he causes [it] to be inhabited,’ since he himself deigns personally to inhabit minds purified and sanctified by the washing of waters.”

# PSALM XXIX

[Col. 0291]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF A SONG AT THE DEDICATION OF THE HOUSE OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0291A]

“I will exalt you.” Title: “A psalm of a song at the dedication of the house of David.” We do not read that David made or dedicated any house to the Lord. It must therefore be understood of the spiritual house. [Alcuin.] For the whole Christ—that is, Bridegroom and Bride—is the one house of God: in Christ the Head the fullness of divine grace dwelt, and from his fullness we all received (John I). This house has been built and dedicated in respect both of the Head and of the members. In respect of Christ, it was built at his conception; [Cassiodorus.] it was dedicated at his resurrection, when, rising from the dead, he was confirmed by the grace of immortality.

But in respect of the Church, it is built daily while it labors in this life. [Jerome.] It will be dedicated in the future, when the saints, rising from the dead, stand in great steadfastness, shining like the sun. [Alcuin.] This house is also called a tabernacle, as in the title of the preceding psalm. It is called a tabernacle according to its present state, when warfare is carried on within it; for a tabernacle properly belongs to war. It is called a house according to its future state, when rest will be enjoyed in it, as is said in this psalm’s title.

For above he treats of the completion of the tabernacle in time of war; here, however, is a psalm of song, [Augustine.] that is, of joy experienced at the dedication of the house of David—that is, for the dedication of the house of Christ. This dedication has now taken place in the Head; [Col. 0291C] it will take place hereafter in the members. Hence there is joy because the house is dedicated—that is, confirmed. With a renewed body, not only Christ’s but that of the whole Church, it will abide in eternal peace.

Or the whole Christ speaks in this psalm, [Alcuin.] because some words of this psalm apply to the Head, others to the body, and others to both. It is a brief psalm concerning Christ’s Passion and resurrection, so that the Passion may not terrify those whom the hope of resurrection makes glad.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] From Cassiodorus, at the conclusion of the psalm.] Purpose: through the hope of the dedication already accomplished in Christ, he exhorts the faithful to praise. Method: the psalm has three parts. First, Christ treats of his own dedication, commanding the saints, who hope for the same, to offer praise. Second, he says how he deserved that dedication, at “But I.” Third, how he received it, at “The Lord heard.” Therefore Christ, inasmuch as he is man, giving thanks to God for his dedication, says:

VERS. 1.—“I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have taken me up, and have not made my enemies glad over me.”

O Lord, I will exalt you, [Augustine.] that is, I will praise your exaltedness, because in the resurrection you took me up, dedicating me by the glory of impassibility. This is said in the person of the foundation—that is, Christ the Head—which has already been dedicated. Afterwards, that is, [Col. 0292A] in the future, it will be said in the person of the whole house, when it has been dedicated in the general resurrection.

Again, in the person of the Head he adds, “you have not delighted,” or “made glad, my enemies over me.” Another reading: “You did not permit my enemies—namely, the Jews and demons—to delight or rejoice over me.”

VERS. 2.—“O Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me.”

“O Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me.” [Augustine.] These do not seem to be Christ’s words—namely, “you did not make glad,” and “I cried.” One seems false, the other impossible. It appears false that his enemies were not made glad over him, when the Gospel records that he was scourged, struck, and crucified. Likewise, it seems contrary—indeed impossible—that Christ should cry out and pray, since he is almighty God, who fulfills the prayers of the faithful and through whom all natural things were made.

But it must be known that Christ is neither God only nor man only, as various heretics have taught. Rather, he is true God and true man. Yet he is not two Christs, but one Christ, who is weak not insofar as he is God, but because he is man. By this also he prays for us and is mediator between God—the Trinity, that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and sinful human beings, having affinity with both. In that he is weak, he is near to us; in that he is not iniquitous, he joins us to God. Yet even as man he presides [Col. 0292C] over us as the Head, in whom all the senses are found for the other members.

Therefore it is neither unfitting nor impossible that he should pray according to the humanity he assumed, since he is the one to whom prayer is made according to his divinity. And his enemies did indeed rejoice over him on the cross; likewise they rejoice over his people in their sufferings, but not at the dedication, whether over him or his people. Therefore what he says is true: “you have not delighted,” or “made glad, my enemies over me”—that is, you did not permit them to rejoice over me at the dedication, although they did so before.

He then states the taking-up, saying: “O Lord my God, I cried to you” in the Passion, “and you healed me” in the resurrection; for I now bear no diseased body but a glorious and immortal one. And:

[Col. 0292D] VERS. 3.—“O Lord, you brought my soul up from hell; you saved me from those going down into the pit.”

“O Lord, you brought my soul up from hell.” This requires no exposition. [Augustine, Jerome.] For it is plain that Christ’s soul was brought by God out of hell together with the souls of the saints. “And you saved me from those going down into the pit,” [Augustine.] that is, from those persecutors who descend into the depth of the world. For the pit is the depth of the world: namely, the abundance of luxury [Col. 0293A] and wickedness. Those who immerse themselves in sensual pleasures and earthly desires descend into the pit. Such people persecuted Christ, but he was saved from them in the resurrection, so as no longer to be with them.

Or: “You saved me from those going down into the pit,” that is, from the condition of profound blindness, because he is free from sin and from corruptible flesh, since he is impassible. Or: “Save me from those going down into the pit,” [Jerome.] that is, from the pit of hell, where the souls of sinners are, lest I, like them, fall headlong into death.

VERS. 4.—“Sing psalms to the Lord, you his saints; and confess to the remembrance of his holiness.”

“Sing psalms.” [Augustine.] After the song comes the psalm. Here it is the voice of the Church or of the prophet, observing in the members what has already come before in the Head, and therefore exulting and exhorting others to exult. As though he said: Because our Head rose again, you other members should hope for this also; what you see accomplished in the Head, hope for yourselves, who believed it in the Head, because the same thing has been promised to us. Having, therefore, these promises, sing psalms to the Lord by your deeds, O you his saints.

[Interlinear Gloss, Jerome.] Or the whole may be said in the person of the Church speaking to Christ thus: “I will exalt you, O Lord,” that is, I will gloriously praise your exaltedness, because you have taken me up in dedication: that is, you will receive me in reality in the future, and have already received me in hope. “And you have not delighted,” or “made glad, my enemies over me,” [Augustine.] that is, then you will not make glad over me those who throughout the world have tried to crush me through various persecutions. For then enemies will not rejoice over us as they do now.

He then explains this taking-up: [Interlinear Gloss.] “O Lord, my God, I cried to you” here, “and you healed me” already in hope, and in the future you will heal me in reality. And, O Lord, you brought my soul up from hell, [Jerome.] because he both brought out the souls of the righteous who were held there and, freeing others from sins, prevented them from being sent there. Hence he adds: “And you saved me from those going down into the pit of hell.” Therefore sing psalms to the Lord, [Jerome.] by doing good, you his saints, and confess to the remembrance of his holiness: [Augustine.] that is, praise him because he remembered to sanctify you—that is, because throughout all this time, which seemed excessively long to our longing, he did not forget the holiness by which he sanctified you. You had forgotten him, but he did not forget you.

Or: “Confess to the remembrance of his holiness,” [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss.] that is, praise him because, in his goodness and holiness, he remembered us. Therefore sing psalms and confess:

VERS. 5.—“For anger is in his indignation, and life in his will.”

“For anger,” [Augustine.] that is, the punishment by which he avenged in you original sin, which you discharged by death, “was in his indignation”—that is, in his despised threat, when he said to the first parents: “On the day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. II). [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss.] But they touched and died, and were expelled from Paradise. Thus his rejection of humankind was because of sin, yet there is hope: “and”—that is, because—“life is in his will.” [Augustine.] Eternal life he gave, not through our powers or merits, but because he willed it; you could not return to it of yourselves, [Col. 0294A] but he restored you and saved us freely, for we were not worthy. What is a sinner worthy of but punishment? Yet he justified the ungodly through faith and gave them life.

VERS. 6.—“Weeping shall linger at evening; and joy at morning.”

“At evening,” etc. [Augustine.] To the two statements just given he adds two others in this way: because anger is in his indignation, therefore weeping shall linger at evening; and because life is in his will, therefore there shall be joy at morning. Follow the order of the text and the exposition of its words thus: anger proceeded from his indignation, and that anger is not brief but long. For weeping—that is, every kind of human misery, both of guilt and punishment—beginning at Adam’s evening, both temporal and inward, shall linger until morning.

Evening is when the sun declines to setting. At that time Adam sinned, and the light of that sun—that is, Christ, who is the Sun of righteousness—and the light of hearts set from him, while the sun of time was then declining to its setting. Hence in Genesis: “When the Lord walked in Paradise in the breeze after midday, Adam was afraid and hid himself” (Gen. III). Already that sinner covered himself among the trees of Paradise; he did not wish to see the face of God, in whose presence he had been accustomed to rejoice. The Sun of righteousness had set for him; he did not rejoice in God’s presence. From that point this whole mortal life began: day turned into night, joy into weeping.

Therefore weep, O human race, because you are born from Adam. For we all were made from Adam, as were all who have begotten children and all who will beget them, since they themselves were created from him. Evening, then, began after midday, when the light of wisdom departed from sinful man and he was condemned to death. From then weeping has endured and will endure as long as the people of God await, amid labors and temptations, the day of the Lord—that is, morning.

This, then, is the weeping: the whole misery of humankind, beginning at Adam’s evening, when he sinned and inward light departed from him. It shall linger, [Interlinear Gloss.] that is, remain long and among many people: long, because complete restoration did not immediately follow the Lord’s being handed over; and among many, because all of us are born from him in sin [Col. 0294D] and punishment. It shall linger, I say, until morning, [Augustine.] that is, until the day of the Lord, when our resurrection will take place—a resurrection prefigured in Christ’s morning resurrection. Then, namely at morning, we shall have everlasting joy, because then the Lord will wipe every tear from the eyes of the saints (Rev. XXI).

Otherwise, according to the moral sense. [Augustine.] Morning, or dawn, means the arising of faith and charity: namely, when the light of grace rises for the believer, which sets for the sinner. By this light we rise again in soul, according to the saying: “Rise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” (Eph. V). To signify this resurrection, the Lord rose in the morning, promising us the same through his resurrection, which is the efficient [Col. 0295A] cause of the present resurrection of the soul and of the future resurrection of the body.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] From Gregory, *Dialogues*, book I, chapter 9.] For Christ, whose action is our instruction, did not without a reason of celebrated mystery choose to be buried at this evening when Adam sinned, and to rise in the morning—on the morning of the third day. [Augustine.] He was buried in the evening to show that he died not for his own fault but for us, who were buried in the evening in Paradise—that is, through Adam’s committed sin. In Paradise we were buried at evening in guilt and punishment. He rose in the morning so that we may rise in the morning, when the light of grace rises in a person’s mind.

He rose on the morning of the third day; likewise, we rise on the third day, that is, in the time of grace, which follows the time before the Law and the time under the Law. What your Head showed in himself during those three days, then, will be shown in you during the three ages of the world. For if you consider the world, the first day is before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace. Thus the weeping which began at evening shall linger. This does not change until morning—that is, until the light of faith rises through Christ’s morning resurrection—and then there shall be joy.

Or: “Weeping shall linger at evening,” [Jerome, Cassiodorus.] because, when the Lord had suffered and been buried, the apostles and women remained in weeping and mourning; “and there was joy at morning,” because, coming to the tomb in the morning, they received the glory of the resurrection. And it was said to the women: “Go, tell my brethren to go into Galilee; there they shall see me” (Matt. XXVIII). In the evening they wept for him dead; in the morning they exulted at the resurrection.

[Col. 0295C] PART II. VERS. 7.—“But I said in my abundance: I shall never be moved.”

“But I.” [Alcuin, Interlinear Gloss.] The second part, in which Christ says how he acted and merited dedication before it. As though he said: From Adam’s evil motion came weeping; but I, in my abundance, [Cassiodorus.] that is, in confidence in the divinity whose fullness dwells in me, [Interlinear Gloss.] said this: “I shall never be moved from God,” as Adam was moved. And just as I said, you,

VERS. 8.—“O Lord, in your will you have given strength to my beauty.”

O Lord, [Interlinear Gloss.] you did this because you gave me beauty, namely because I was free from sin. And you gave strength to that beauty, namely because it also worked miracles. [Cassiodorus.] I did not have this from human nature, but “in your will,” that is, from your will, from you; which is proved by this:

VERS. 9.—“You turned your face away from me, and I became troubled.”

You turned your face away from me, exposing me to the Passion, and I became troubled: that is, when you oppose me, the weakness of my flesh is troubled. Hence Jesus began to be afraid and distressed (Mark XIV). From where, then, does man presume, when he hears Christ say such things concerning himself?

VERS. 10.—“To you, O Lord, I shall cry, and to my God I shall make supplication.”

“To you, O Lord.” [Interlinear Gloss.] As though he said: You turned your face away [Col. 0296A] in the Passion, and then I said: “I cried to you, O Lord,” concerning the glory of immortality to be bestowed; “and I shall make supplication to my Lord,” concerning mortality to be removed, saying:

VERS. 11.—“What profit is there in my blood, while I descend into corruption?”

“What profit,” etc. These may also be understood in the person of the members: “But I.” The reason why weeping lingers is shown. [Augustine.] As though he said: There is weeping at evening, but it is because of my fault; for I, that people who spoke from the beginning while existing in Adam, said in my abundance—that is, while I had abundance in Paradise and suffered no want—this: “I shall never be moved” from this good in which I had sufficiency, because I enjoyed God. I said this to you while believing the devil, who said: “You shall not die by death, but you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III).

But because God was about to take from the proud what he had given to the humble, it follows: “O Lord, in your will.” As though he said: In Paradise I had abundance, but this abundance, O Lord, was from you, not from me; for in your will you gave strength to my beauty. That is, I was not good and strong from myself, but from you. To show this, you turned your face away from me—that is, you sent me out of Paradise—and I became troubled. But now, placed here, I shall cry. This is: “To you, O Lord, I shall cry.” In Paradise you did not cry but praised; you did not groan but enjoyed. But once set outside, groan and cry, because tribulation is near to one who serves a proud person. [Col. 0296C] For God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (Jas. IV).

Then, in the person of the Lord—that is, of our very foundation—“What profit is there in [my] blood,” etc. [Augustine.] Alternatively, from the words “You turned [your face away],” as though: You gave me beauty and strength. I learned this from the fact that you at some time turned your face away from me—that is, the light of your knowledge—from me, sinful man. Hence human disturbance arose, as he says: “and I became troubled,” when the light of your knowledge departed from me.

Recalling this time of my disturbance and misery, and being situated in it, I hear the voice of my Head, who is to die for me and says in the Passion: “To you, O Lord, I cried,” concerning glory; “and to my God I shall make supplication,” concerning immortality, saying: “What profit will there be in my blood,” [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss.] that is, in the shedding of my blood, which was shed without fault of mine, while I descend, as though through certain stages of evils, into corruption? As though he said: none. For if I do not rise immediately and my body becomes corrupt, I shall proclaim no one, gain no one, and so confession will perish. This is what he says:

VERS. 12.—“Will dust confess to you, or will it declare your truth?”

Will the dust—[Augustine], that is, the multitude of the ungodly whom I shall justify by my resurrection—confess to you either praises or sins, or proclaim your truth for the salvation of others? [Col. 0297A] [Alcuin.] As though he said: By these words he does not indicate a necessity that would prevent the Father from allowing him to descend into corruption. Or thus: as though he said, Truly there will be no profit if the body decays, because, if I remain dust, will anyone confess to you or proclaim your truth? As though he said: There will be no confession or proclamation to you. [Augustine.] And it should be known that confession is twofold: either of sin or of praise. Let us therefore never be without it. When we fare badly amid tribulations, let us confess our sins; when we fare well, in the exultation of joy let us confess praise.

PART III. VERSE 13.—“The Lord heard, and had mercy on me; the Lord became my helper.”

[Col. 0297B] The Lord heard. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] The third part, in which he says how he received dedication. As though he said: I prayed, and the Lord heard me praying and had mercy on me, so that the Lord became my helper. [Augustine.] For he did not allow his Holy One to see corruption (Ps. XV), but dedicated me with the glory of immortality. Then, speaking to the Father himself, he says:

VERSE 14.—“You turned my mourning into joy for me; you tore open my sackcloth and girded me with gladness.”

You turned. [Jerome.] As though he said: You became my helper in this way: namely, because you turned my mourning, in which I said, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” [Col. 0297C] (Matt. XXVI), into the joy of resurrection. [Gloss, interlinear.] Or: “You turned my mourning into joy,” that is, you caused the Apostles, who grieved for me, to rejoice. This was because “you tore open my sackcloth,” etc. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] Sackcloth is a rough garment used for labour or in a time of sorrow, as by the Ninevites, who, clothed in sackcloth, performed repentance. This is the human flesh which Christ assumed; it was torn by dying, and grain came forth—that is, the gift of the glorious resurrection. Or the Godhead appeared; hence he adds, “and you girded me with gladness.” Or sackcloth is the penalty of sin. For sackcloth is made from goats and kids; [Augustine] and goats and kids signify sinners, because they were offered under the Law for sins. Sackcloth, therefore, is the mortality [Col. 0297D] which Christ drew or received from sinners. For he assumed sackcloth, but not the merit of sackcloth—that is, sin, which is the cause of death. In this sackcloth of mortality, divinity lay hidden like grain. Hence elsewhere: “While they troubled me, I clothed myself in haircloth” (Ps. XXXIV), that is, in the sackcloth of mortality, so that what was within might not be seen.

This sackcloth, [Augustine, Alcuin] that is, this mortality, was torn in the resurrection—that is, destroyed. Once it was torn, divinity was brought forth, 61 that is, manifested, though it had previously been hidden: just as an intact sack conceals what is within, while a torn one reveals it. This is the meaning of “you tore open my sackcloth”: you destroyed the mortality of flesh in the resurrection. “And you girded me with gladness,” [Augustine] that is, with the glory of immortality.

[Col. 0298A] VERSE 15.—“That my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced with compunction; O Lord my God, I shall confess to you for ever.”

That this very glory of mine may sing to you, [Augustine] that is, may be the reason why you are praised by me and by my people. And truly you have girded me with gladness, because I shall no longer be pierced with compunction—that is, I shall die no more, since Christ suffered once and dies no more. And now, finally: “O Lord my God, I shall confess to you for ever,” that is, I shall praise you.

Or these may be the words of the Church, beginning from “You turned.” The voice does not change because of the unity of head and body. As though she said: My foundation has been dedicated, that is, Christ has been established in the glory of immortality; I, the Church, have attained him as firstborn from the dead—now in hope and hereafter in reality—[Col. 0298B] in the dedication of your house which went beforehand in my head. I say, “You turned my mourning,” which is for sins, “into joy for me,” which is from absolution, because you “tore open my sackcloth,” that is, the veil of sins and the sorrow of mortality; and “girded me with gladness,” that is, you clothed me with the first robe, with immortal gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and humility may no longer mourn. And this is because I shall no longer be pierced with compunction, either by consciousness of sin, fear of death, or fear of judgment. And, O Lord my God, I shall confess to you for ever. This is my glory: to confess to you for ever that nothing comes to me from myself, but all things from you, who are God, all in all.

## COLlation ON PSALM XXIX: “I WILL EXALT YOU, O LORD, BECAUSE …”

[Col. 0298C]

VERSE 5.—“For anger is in his indignation.” Hebrew: *KI REGA BEAPPO*, “for a moment is his anger.” Jerome: “his anger is for a moment,” or “his anger is momentary.” The translators, by metathesis, took *GEAR*, that is, “anger, rebuke,” in place of [uncertain reading], which Münster specifically indicates may sometimes occur in this root in his lexicon.

VERSE 8.—“You gave strength to my beauty.” Jerome and the Hebrew: “strength” or “might to my mountain.” Here it is clear that the translators read *HADRI* instead of *HARRI*, *daleth* for *resh*, letters which are closely alike or differ only minimally.

VERSE 13.—“The Lord heard, and had mercy on me.” Hebrew: “Hear, O Lord, and have mercy on me.” The sense is complete in either case. Yet it is not difficult to read [Col. 0298D] *SCHAMA*, “he heard,” for *SCHEMA*, “hear”; especially where vowel points are not attached, the reading is wholly indifferent. Likewise, *HANNANI* for *HONNENI*: “he had mercy,” for “have mercy.” One ought to close one’s eyes to such things, unless I observed that some persons are inflamed with a perverse zeal for the letter.

VERSE 15.—“That my glory may sing to you, and I may not be pierced with compunction.” Hebrew: *LO IIDDOM*, that is, “may it not be silent,” or “it shall not be silent.” The same reading occurred in Psalm IV. But the silence of the heart is secret compunction, which God alone hears in secret; whereas in glory every lament and the gnawing remembrance of sin cease. The Septuagint evidently read, in the first person, *LO EDDOM*, or simply as a participle. Finally, if one divides it, “let glory not be pierced with compunction,” it differs in no respect from saying that a person already resting in that blessed state is beyond every risk of compunction. I add that Sanctes, in his *Thesaurus*, [Col. 0299A] teaches that “glory” in Hebrew is sometimes taken for “soul,” and further, more plainly, that it is sometimes used for the whole person. Therefore, “that my glory may sing to you” means “that I may sing and praise you”; and then “and I may not be pierced with compunction” readily follows.

## PSALM XXX

[Col. 0299]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “FOR THE END: A PSALM OF DAVID, FOR ECSTASY.”

[Col. 0299A]

“In you, O Lord, I have hoped.” Title: “For the end: a Psalm of David for ecstasy.” *Ecstasy*—Greek ἔκστασις—is called in Latin *excessus*, “a departure beyond oneself.” [Augustine.] It is an experience of the mind, occurring in two ways: either through fear of earthly things, or when the mind is caught up to heavenly things and, forgetting lower things, abandons the care that it bestows on ordinary business. In this psalm, however, ecstasy is chiefly understood as fear arising from the persecution of God’s people [Col. 0299B] among all nations, and from the disturbance caused by the failure of faith throughout the world. [Alcuin.] Here the humiliation of Christ and of the holy martyrs is described; hence exaltation follows.

[Note: [Col. 0299D] From Cassiodorus at the conclusion of the psalm.] This psalm expresses human weakness and God’s benefits, so that, seeing himself, a person may not be proud, and, seeing God’s mercy, may not be afraid. The sense of the title is: this psalm, directing us to the end—[Augustine] that is, to Christ—is David speaking here in the person either of Christ himself, or of David, or of the Church. It is entitled “for ecstasy,” that is, dealing with the departure beyond oneself that occurs when the mind fears earthly things.

Its intention is to warn that no one should presume upon himself, but upon God’s mercy. Its structure is threefold. [Cassiodorus.] Against fear, hope is first set forth, and prayer with confidence of deliverance and joy. Second, it enumerates how many and how great are the things that trouble; against these there is prayer, at “Have mercy on me.” Third, it states what God’s goods are, set against evils, at “How great.” [Augustine.] It should be known that certain words of this psalm suit the Head, certain words the members, and certain words the Prophet. First the Redeemer speaks; then the redeemed, giving thanks for their deliverance, at “You redeemed.” Then these same persons speak at length about their disturbance: “Have mercy on me,” and so forth. The Prophet’s voice is inserted on account of “the end” and “for the end,” at “How great” and at “Love the Lord.” Yet amid so great a variety the voice does not change: head and members use the same voice, saying “I,” “me,” and “to myself,” because of the exceedingly great unity of head and body—that is, Christ and the Church, [Col. 0299D] bridegroom and bride—which charity brings about.

For just as the tongue takes up the voice of all the members, saying, “You tread on me for the foot,” rather than “You tread on the foot,” and “You wound me for the hand,” rather than “You wound my hand,” so Christ fittingly uses the words of his members, not separating himself from our words. [Augustine.] For he who deigned to become man for us and to put on the form of a servant does not disdain to transform us into himself. He does this in several ways: when he does or says something for the instruction of his members, as when he fasted, prayed, and was tempted (Matt. IV); when he speaks in the person of the members, or about the members in his own person, as when he said, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” [Col. 0300A] (Acts IX); or when he shows something to be in himself which he does not have by the nature of his own condition, but has mercifully assumed from the corruption of our weakness—as when he says that he is sorrowful or afraid, and the like. Therefore, since he has thus transformed us into himself, he does not disdain to speak in our words, so that we too may speak in his.

This is a divine exchange, these are divine transactions, enacted in this world by the heavenly merchant. For [Col. 0300B] the heavenly merchant came to receive insults and give honours; to drink in pain and give salvation; to undergo death and grant life. He dies, then, from what is ours—that is, from our flesh, which he possessed. He was afraid not in himself but in us. For what you fear is yours; what you hope is God’s gift. You fear, that you may know yourself; you hope, that you may glorify the divine mercy that consoles you in fear.

Thus Christ speaks here in the prophet and in the members. Even if some statements in this psalm seem incapable of fitting the Head, Christ nevertheless speaks, because Christ exists in his members. Bridegroom and bride—that is, Christ and the Church—are, as it were, one person. Hence Isaiah, commending this unity, says: “As a bridegroom he bound a mitre upon me, and as a bride he adorned me with ornaments” [Col. 0300C] (Isa. LXI). He calls himself bridegroom and himself bride because of the most excellent unity of head and body. The Lord himself also observed this unity when he spoke through Adam concerning marriage: “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II). Explaining this, the Apostle says that it is a great mystery in Christ and in the Church (Eph. V). Therefore, because bridegroom and bride are two in one flesh, these two rightly speak with one voice. [Jerome.] Therefore he begins in the person of the Head, speaking thus to the Father:

VERSE 1.—“In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be confounded; deliver me in your righteousness.”

In you, Lord Father, I have hoped according to my humanity; [Col. 0300D] let me never be confounded, [Augustine] that is, may I never be confounded while, as a man like other men, I am insulted. [Cassiodorus.] “In your righteousness deliver me”: raise me from death.

VERSE 2.—“Incline your ear to me; hasten to rescue me.”

“Incline your ear to me,” [Augustine] that is, draw near to me who am lowly; “and hasten” in doing, [Alcuin] that is, in those things which must be done—in releasing souls from hell and such matters. “That you may rescue me”: by raising me from death on the third day. Do not delay until the general resurrection, or until the end of the world, to separate me from sinners; and that this may be so:

[Col. 0301A] VERSE 3.—“Be to me a protecting God and a house of refuge, that you may save me.”

“Be to me a protecting God,” [Alcuin] that is, be to me, O God, as great a protector as it befits God to be; “and a house of refuge, that you may save me.” [Augustine.] That is, be to me as a house to which I flee and in which I am saved. Therefore I seek you, and no other.

VERSE 4.—“For you are my strength and my refuge; and for your name’s sake you will lead me and nourish me.”

[Gloss, interlinear.] “For you are my strength” to endure sinners or persecutors; [Augustine] “and you are my refuge.” [Cassiodorus.] This is for leaving them at the end of evils, namely the end that comes through death. “And for your name’s sake,” [Augustine] that is, so that through me you may become known [Col. 0301B] to all nations, “you will lead me,” or “you will be my guide”—another reading—that is, I shall follow your will in all things; “and you will nourish me,” that is, by gradually gathering saints to me, you will complete my body. [Gloss, interlinear.] And you will also rescue me from sufferings, as he says:

VERSE 5.—“You will bring me out of the snare which they hid for me, because you are my protector.”

“You will bring me out of the snare which they hid for me,” [Cassiodorus] that is, you will raise me from death to things above, so that the counsels of the Jews may be in vain. You will bring me out, I say, because you are my protector, against whom no adversity can prevail. Hence, as he cries out in the Passion:

VERSE 6.—“Into your hands I commend my spirit; you have redeemed me, O Lord God of truth.”

“Into your hands I commend my spirit,” [Augustine] [Col. 0301C] that is, I commend it to your power, soon to receive it back. Note that he speaks here who uttered the same words in the Passion. For by the words Christ spoke on the cross he indicates that he was speaking in this psalm. Then the faithful people, redeemed by Christ’s Passion and joyful at the resurrection of the Head, gives thanks, saying: “You have redeemed me, O Lord God of truth,” who do not deceive in your promise, because you do what you promise.

The foregoing may also be understood in the person of that same people—that is, the Church—which, trembling in ecstasy, nevertheless begins with hope, saying: O Lord, I have hoped in you, not in myself. For this fear is not without hope. If there is disturbance, divine consolation is not absent. And therefore, “I shall not be confounded for ever.” For I dread that confusion [Col. 0301D] which is eternal. There is, however, a certain temporal confusion, lasting only for a time, which is beneficial: namely, the disturbance of mind that looks upon its sins, shudders at their sight, blushes from horror, and corrects itself through blushing. This person wishes to be confounded with such confusion, but not eternally; from that eternal confusion he prays to be delivered, adding: “In your righteousness deliver me,” 62 that is, in that righteousness which you give me, deliver me, [Gloss, interlinear] because you find in me no righteousness but a proud and false one. Hence it is said: “Ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they are not subject to God’s righteousness” (Rom. X).

[Augustine.] If, therefore, you consider my righteousness, you condemn me. A human righteousness is that by which one thinks oneself justified by one’s own powers, not seeking to be saved freely. Who is saved freely? The one in whom the Saviour finds not something to crown but something to condemn. He finds no merits deserving good, but merits deserving punishment. If he acted with strict justice, the sinner would be condemned. And if he acted thus, whom would he deliver? No one. For he finds all sinners, coming into the world himself alone without sin. Therefore the grace of God through Jesus Christ delivers. Why grace? Because it is given freely. Why is it freely given? Because your merits did not precede it, but God’s benefits came first. Therefore he says, “In your righteousness deliver me,” that is, let this be why he delivers me: because he justifies me, making the ungodly godly, the unrighteous righteous, and the blind seeing.

“Incline your ear to me,” that is, your mercy. God did this when he sent his Son. For what mercy is greater than to give his only Son for us? Here is prayer; as at the beginning of the psalm, hope has been set before it: “Hasten to rescue me,” that is, from evils. He says “hasten” to indicate that what ends does not last long, and that what seems slow and long to you is brief in God’s sight. Still praying, he says: “Be to me a protecting God,” that is, protect me as befits you, my God, and “be to me a house of refuge,” because I flee to you when I am in danger. There are others who flee from you, though they cannot hide from you; wherever they turn, they find God angry. Hence elsewhere: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?” (Ps. CXXXVIII). Nothing remains, therefore, except to flee to you, not from you, before whose eyes all things are naked.

Observe the order of the prayer. [Alcuin.] How does it ascend? He said: give righteousness, rescue from sins, protect. Here he says: “Be a house [Col. 0302C] of refuge.” [Cassiodorus.] The house of refuge is the Church, in which people are saved as they were saved in Noah’s ark. And the meaning is: “Be to me a house of refuge,” that is, be a refuge to me in the house of the Church, so that you may save me. Therefore I seek you and no other, because you, and no other, are my strength and my refuge.

“And for your name’s sake,” [Augustine] not for my merit, not because I am worthy, but that you may be glorified, “you will lead me,” or “you will be my guide,” lest I wander from you; “and you will nourish me,” that I may become strong enough to receive the food with which you feed angels. For he who promised us heavenly food nourished us here with milk and employed a mother’s mercy. A mother nursing a little child passes food, which the infant is not fit to chew, through her flesh and pours milk into the child, who thereby receives the very same thing that he would receive at table. So the Lord, clothed in flesh, came to make his wisdom—the food of angels—into milk for us. [Alcuin.] Thus, as little children, we may be nourished on the great food of angels transformed into milk, until at last, grown strong, we are refreshed by that same food.

Observe that here he affirms the deliverance about which he also says, “You will bring me out of the snare.” [Augustine.] He calls the snares and temptation of the devil a “snare,” for the devil tempts through two gates: desire and fear. Through the gate of desire he first tempted Christ in three ways: gluttony, avarice, and vainglory. When he found that gate shut, he afterwards tempted the same Christ through fear of the Passion. Thus he tempts all saints through these same gates. Therefore let the whole body of Christ say: “You will bring me out of the snare which they hid for me,” or “the trap which they concealed for me,” that is, from the snares which the devil and his own secretly lay for me. You will bring me out because you are my protector. And this is truly so because you, O Lord God of truth, have redeemed me, as Christ cries, “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII). Then the same people speaks.

VERSE 7.—“You have hated those who observe vanities in vain.”

“You have hated,” etc. As though he said: You redeemed me, [Augustine] but indeed you hate those who observe vanities—that is, the false happiness of the world—which is observed not merely vainly but superfluously, [Augustine, Gloss, interlinear] when a person acts wickedly even for the sake of life by pursuing vanity, and nevertheless loses that very life.

VERSE 8.—“But I have hoped in the Lord; I shall exult and rejoice in your mercy.”

“But I,” who do not observe vain things, “have hoped in the Lord.” [Augustine.] If you hope in money, honour, some exalted human authority, or some powerful person, you observe vanity. For in all these things, when you hope, either you expire and leave them here, or, while you live, they all perish and you fail in your hope. Hence Isaiah: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass withered and its flower fell, but the word of the Lord remains for ever” (Isa. XL). Therefore he says, “I have hoped in the Lord,” who is not [Col. 0303C] vanity but truth and life. And therefore, “I shall exult and rejoice in your mercy,” [Augustine, Gloss, interlinear] which does not deceive, not in my own righteousness. [Cassiodorus.] Distinguish between “I shall exult” and “I shall rejoice”: to exult is to rejoice with great alacrity of mind; to rejoice is to be glad with a measured affection of mind. [Alcuin.] Observe that here he treats of the joy he has because he hopes in the Lord, who hates vain persons.

VERSE 9.—“For you have looked upon my humility; you have saved my soul from necessities.”

“For you have looked upon.” [Gloss, interlinear.] He explains mercy. As though he said: Your mercy is apparent in this: that you have looked upon my humiliation, by which you subjected me to vanity in hope. Humility is understood [Alcuin] both as weakness and as the virtue of humility itself. [Col. 0303D] “And you have saved”: as though he said, because humility pleases you, therefore you have saved my soul from necessities. [Gloss, interlinear.] The necessities are innumerable: not to know another’s heart; to suspect evil of a faithful friend or good of an unfaithful one; not to know what you will be tomorrow; to be unwilling to die yet nevertheless to die; to follow old habits. Hence the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII). [Alcuin.] Whoever is thus humble is saved in part in the present and fully in the future. Or: you have saved me from those descending into the pit of legal fear, so that, having overcome necessities, I may serve freely in charity.

VERSE 10.—“And you have not shut me up in the hands of the enemy; you have set my feet in a spacious place.”

“And you have not shut me up,” [Augustine] so that I could not breathe freely, “in the hands of the enemy,” that is, in the devil’s power: he ensnares through desire of life and terrifies through death. Those who live well and die well are delivered from his hands; but those who live badly are shut up here, in order that they may be condemned with him at the end. “And you have set my feet in a spacious place,” that is, you have led my charity from the narrowness of fear into freedom; and this occurred in Christ’s resurrection, which is promised likewise to me. For you have now made righteousness easy for me, though once it was difficult. The path is indeed narrow to one who labours; but the very same path which is narrow becomes broad to one who loves.

Or this may be said in the person of Christ: “But I have hoped in the Lord; I shall exult and rejoice in your mercy, because you have looked upon my humility.” These statements are plainly about Christ, who further says: “You have saved me from those descending [Col. 0304B] into the pit”—[Cassiodorus] that is, from sins, from which a human being cannot free himself—“and you have not shut me up in the hands of the enemy,” [Gloss, interlinear] that is, in the devil’s power, who has nothing in me. “And you have set my feet,” that is, my affections, “in a spacious place,” [Cassiodorus] that is, in the country of virtues, in charity, which is a spacious place and the region of the blessed: a place free from the devil’s power. But because flesh is weak and evils press hard, he adds in the person of the members:

PART II. VERSE 11.—“Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am troubled; my eye, my soul, and my belly are disturbed in anger.”

“Have mercy on me.” [Alcuin.] The second part, in which fear is now recounted—that is, how many and how great evils trouble; against these there is also prayer. As though he said: “You have set my feet in a spacious place,” [Augustine, Gloss, interlinear] but, on the contrary, evil people strike fear into me. Therefore I pray: “Have mercy on me, O Lord”; and it is necessary, “for I am troubled.” I do not say that I am dying, [Augustine] but that I am troubled: for I no longer fear death, but torments and the excesses of evils.

It seems remarkable that he says here, “I am troubled,” when shortly before he rejoiced at being delivered from the enemy’s hand, by a gift of God the Giver infused into him, and said, “You have set my feet in a spacious place.” But we must understand that, in one case, he spoke in reference to certain members of the same body, which is the Church, and here in reference to other such members. To some there is a spacious place through joy at deliverance; [Col. 0304D] to others, tribulation and narrowness. According to the latter he says: “For I am troubled by God, so that my eye”—that is, reason—“is disturbed in anger,” [Cassiodorus] that is, because of the anger and fury of persecutors. For in the anger of persecutors my eye, that is, my reason, is troubled; likewise my soul, [Alcuin] that is, sensibility; and my belly, that is, my flesh.

Or by “eye” and “soul” spiritual teachers are indicated: others see through their teaching and live by their example. By “belly” the weak are understood. “My eye is disturbed in anger,” that is, those through whom others see; “and my soul,” that is, those by whose example others live; “and my belly,” that is, the weak. He includes them all, so that God may be sought from every rank. Hence come disturbance and fear.

[Col. 0305A] VERSE 12.—“For my life has failed in pain, and my years in groanings.”

“For my temporal life has failed in the pain of torments,” [Gloss, interlinear] that is, through long and grievous sufferings the present life has been brought to death; “and my years,” [Cassiodorus] that is, the long life lasting amid punishments, “are in groanings”; they are not removed by death.

VERSE 13.—“My strength has been weakened in poverty, and my bones have been disturbed.”

“My strength has been weakened,” or “my vigour has been weakened”—another reading—“in poverty” or “want”—another reading. [Augustine.] For I lack bodily health, yet torments are not spared; I lack dissolution, yet death is spared. In this my strength, that is, my confidence, has been weakened; “and my bones have been disturbed,” that is, my firmness has been disturbed.

Or he speaks of God’s anger, [Cassiodorus] who in anger exposes the saints at times to great tribulations. As though he said: I am so troubled that my eye—[Jerome] that is, the understanding by which I contemplated you, O God—is disturbed in your anger; likewise my soul and my belly. [Augustine.] For in anger you disturbed the eye which I had fixed upon you. “And my soul,” that is, sensibility; “and my belly,” [Alcuin] that is, memory, by which I held what you endured for me and what you promised me. [Cassiodorus.] For the understanding is disturbed and the mind confused when dangers are feared to which God exposes the saints. The belly is disturbed, that is, memory, which receives knowledge of things as a belly receives food. This memory, [Col. 0305C] holding God’s promises stored within it, is disturbed by imminent dangers. Hence come disturbance and fear.

“For my life,” [Augustine] that is, confession of faith and of your name, O God, “has failed in the pain of torments”; “and my years,” [Cassiodorus] that is, the periods I spend here for a longer time, “are in groanings,” not in clear voices. And my strength—the strength of the mind—has been weakened so that I am even weary of living; [Alcuin] and this is “in poverty” or “want,” that is, in lack of fullness, [Cassiodorus] because human frailty has no good in itself. “And my bones have been disturbed,” that is, bodily strength has been disturbed. This shows that no human presumption can exist either in soul or body.

Or this holy man here speaks of his own anger. For one kind of anger is just and another unjust: one arises from vice, the other from zeal. Just anger is that [Augustine] by which one is angry at one’s own sins and those of others, seeing people confess God with their mouths yet deny him by their conduct; renounce the world in words but not in deeds; seeing brothers plotting against brothers, giving a kiss yet not keeping faith. Such people this man begot, existing like grain among chaff and like a lily among thorns; he grieves for them and is angry out of charity. Hence elsewhere: “Zeal for your house consumed me, and the reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me” (Ps. LXVIII). Solomon says: “Open correction is better than hidden love” (Prov. XXIII), because the fitting anger and harsh rebuke of a holy man are better than the gentle assent of a flatterer who conceals truth. Hence: “Let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” [Col. 0306A] (Ps. CXL). And elsewhere: “Better are the wounds of one who loves than the deceitful kisses of one who hates” (Prov. XXIII). And elsewhere: “Honey drips from the lips of a harlot. But in the lips of the saints there is death, or a sword, by which they strike sinners as though angry.” This anger is good.

But unjust anger is that which passes into hatred. Hence the Apostle: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. IV). [Augustine.] The sun goes down upon that anger which harbours hatred of one’s brother; this extinguishes the eye. [Alcuin.] Anger arising from vice blinds the eye of the mind. Anger arising from zeal causes disturbance, because even this, by shaking the mind, disperses contemplation, which exists only in a quiet mind; yet shortly thereafter it contributes more greatly to seeing God, like eye-salve applied to the eyes: it first disturbs the sight [Col. 0306B] but afterward makes it clearer.

This man speaks of this anger when he says: “My inner eye is disturbed in anger,” that is, because of my anger; “and my soul,” that is, sensibility; “and my belly,” that is, all my inward parts. [Augustine.] For he is angry at the sins of the chaff, yet he does not hate them, for then the eye would be extinguished. “Belly” is used for the inner parts, which are disturbed when the ungodly cannot even be rebuked; he does not cry out to them plainly, but groans within, saying: “For my life has failed.” As though he said: Thus my eye has been disturbed because my life has failed in sorrow. The life of the perfect is the progress of others. Hence the Apostle: “Now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord” (1 Thess. III). And again: “I desire to depart and be with Christ; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. [Col. 0306C] III). When someone sees that people do not progress through his ministry, labours, and preaching, he grieves and says, “My life has failed in sorrow,” seeing no progress in those to whom he preaches; “and my years,” that is, the times I spend here, are “in groanings,” not in clear voices, because the iniquity of many abounds. “And my strength has been weakened in poverty” or want, because the charity of many grows cold; “and my bones have been disturbed,” that is, even the strong are troubled on account of sinners.

VERSE 14.—“I have become a reproach above all my enemies, very much so to my neighbours, and a fear to those who know me.”

“Above all.” Again this is the voice of the Church, [Augustine] [Col. 0306D] that is, of the faithful people, which says: “I have become a reproach above my enemies,” that is, above all the wicked who are tortured for their crimes up to confession. I surpass their reproach, since my confession is followed not by death but by torture. He specifies to whom he has become a reproach, saying, “to my neighbours,” that is, to those already near to my faith; “and a fear to those who know me,” that is, I have struck fear into those acquainted with me by the example of dreadful tribulation.

Or thus: “I have become very much a reproach,” and this because of those enemies who are “above all my enemies,” that is, worse than all my other enemies. The pagans and Jews are enemies, but false Christians are worse than all. For bad Christians live more wickedly than pagans and Jews. The prophet Ezekiel compares them with branches [Col. 0307A] (Ezek. XV). These branches excel wild trees on the vine because they bear fruit; once cut off, fire alone awaits them, since the craftsman can make nothing from them. Christ is the vine, who says: “I am the true vine, and you are the branches” (John XV). The faithful who remain in this vine bear the fruit of salvation; but those cut off are fit for the burning of eternal fire, whereas something may yet be done with pagans and Jews. For when what is knotty, crooked, and bark-covered in them has been hewn and smoothed, they may be put to use in the spiritual building, as forest timber is suitable for the construction of buildings.

Bad Christians are exceedingly bad figs; just as the truly good are exceedingly good figs. Of these Jeremiah writes: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” He says: “I see baskets of figs: very good figs, and very bad figs” [Col. 0307B] (Jer. XXIV). Peter says of the bad: “The latter things have become worse for them than the former. For it would have been better for them not to know the way of righteousness than, having known it, to turn back” (2 Pet. II). [Augustine.] They are like a dog returning to its vomit, and like a washed sow in a wallowing of mud.

Then he adds to whom he has become a reproach: “to my neighbours.” That is, I have become a reproach to those already wishing to believe, who are deterred by the evil life of false Christians weighing down the ship, that is, the Church. This is Peter’s ship, which was weighed down by the multitude of fish so that it was nearly sunk. These are the many evil people in the Church; because of them, even those who know are afraid lest everyone be like them, and almost all good people fall under evil suspicion. For people say: “What sort of a man was he? How did he fall? How was he found in that shameful act, that crime, that evil deed? Do you think they are not all like that? Surely they are.” Therefore he adds: “And I became a fear to those who know me.” He calls the same people “those who know me” whom he had called “neighbours.”

VERSE 15.—“Those who saw me outside fled from me; I was given over to forgetfulness as one dead from the heart.”

“Those who saw me,” [Augustine] that is, those who did not understand my invisible hope, “fled from me outside,” that is, they fled to outward and visible things, away from hope in invisible things; they declined from the Catholic faith into heresies and schisms. This is especially to be mourned and grieved over: even those who knew what the Church is [Col. 0307D] fled outside by making schisms and heresies. “And I was given over to forgetfulness,” or “I was forgotten,” like one dead from the heart—that is, I passed so completely into their oblivion, and they forgot me so completely, as though I had died from their heart.

VERSE 16.—“I became like a lost vessel, because I heard the reproach of many who dwell round about.”

“**I became like a lost vessel**,” [Aug., Gl. int.], that is, I seemed to myself to have perished: though living for the Lord’s uses, I was producing no gain, or was not retaining those whom I had won. I say this because I heard—and kept silent concerning—the reproach of many who dwell round about. [Aug.] For many reproach me, following the circuit [Col. 0308A] of temporal things and unwilling to return with me to the fatherland. For, on account of evil Christians, all good Christians are reproached by those who go round about and never enter into truth. Many speak evil of bad Christians, and those slanders reach all Christians. For one who slanders or reproves, as it were, does not separate or distinguish the good from the bad, or the bad from the good. He does not say, “See what evil men do,” but, “See what Christians do.” Yet it is those who go round about and do not enter who say these things. Why do they go round about and not enter? Because they love the wheel of time; they do not enter into truth because, given over to temporal things, they do not love eternity, being constrained like a wheel. Of them it is said elsewhere: “Set their princes like a wheel” (Ps. 82). And elsewhere: “The ungodly walk round about” [Col. 0308B] (Ps. 11): such men, by reproaching us faithful people, wish to drive us from truth and from the Church. Hence he adds:

### Verse 17.—“While they were gathering together against me, they took counsel to seize my soul.”

In that [Aug.] reproach, while they gathered against me, [Cassiod.] and this all together—not a few—it is the more grievous because it is undertaken by the counsel of many. While they gathered together, I say, they took counsel to take away my life: [Aug.] that is, to make my soul consent to them.
