Lest death should set my soul free, they devised a plan by which they would not allow it to die. But what did I do in opposition? What counsel did I find? Behold:

### Verse 18.—“But I hoped in thee, O Lord; I said, Thou art my God; my lots are in thy hands.”

But I hoped in thee. [Aug.] As though he said to them [Col. 0308C]: “But amid these reproaches, amid these scandals, amid these dissensions, knowing that the power of such persons is nothing, [Cassiod., Aug.] I hoped in thee, O Lord, not in man.” Nothing is more healthful, nothing safer, than to hope in the Lord, since everyone who puts his hope in man is cursed. [Hier.] For if you attend to a human being and wish to make your hope depend upon him, you still wish to be nourished on milk, and you will become a *mammotreptus*—as children are called who suck for a long time—which is unfitting. Therefore become fit for the table, where you may be fed with stronger food. Perhaps for this reason God allowed you to encounter an evil man whom you thought good: so that you might find bitterness in the breast, as it were, of a mother, be repelled by that offense, and [Col. 0308D] be invited to stronger food—that is, to God. Nurses do this to children long dependent on the breast: they put something bitter upon their nipples, so that the offended little ones recoil from the breast and come to the table. Say therefore, like one somewhat more grown: “But I hoped in thee, O Lord.” In this no one is deceived; in inviting others to trust, we are often deceived.

And I said to the Lord: “Thou—not any man—art my God,” because thou art unchangeable. Or rather, thou neither advance nor fail: thou dost not advance, because thou art perfect; thou dost not fail, because thou art eternal. Or, “Thou art my God,” that is, my Savior; and wilt thou not save me, thou who now dost correct me? As though he said: “Thou surely wilt.” And “my lots are in thy hands,” not in the hands of men: that is, the cause and order of election, hidden from men, are in thy power and knowledge. [Col. 0309A] For I do not see why thou hast chosen me from among the ungodly. “And these are my lots,” as though he said: although with thee there is a just and hidden order of election, I, to whom this is hidden, came by lot to the seamless garment of the Lord—that is, to the unity of the Church—namely, by the grace of election.

Literally, a lot is not something evil, but a thing which, amid human uncertainty, indicates the divine will. For the apostles also cast lots when Judas, having betrayed the Lord, perished; and it then began to be asked who should be ordained in his place. Two were chosen by human judgment, but one of those two was chosen by divine judgment. God was consulted concerning which of the two he himself wished, and the lot fell upon Matthias. Therefore, as I think, “lot” here means the grace of God, which without merits chooses whom it wills. [Col. 0309B] This is what is meant by “my lots are in thy hands”: that is, my gratuitous election, because my election comes through God’s will and hidden justice.

Or, according to another reading, “in thy hands,” that is, in thy power, [Cassiod.] are the times of life, because we live or die whenever thou wilt. And therefore:

### Verse 19.—“Deliver me from the hand of my enemies, and from those who persecute me.”

Deliver me from the hands of my enemies, [Aug.] that is, from the devil and his ministers, who begrudge us the kingdom of heaven, from which they were cast out, and who persecute us. Hence he adds: “and from those who persecute me.” Above all, those Christians who refuse to live rightly persecute the Church. Through them the Church incurs reproach, and from them it endures enmities, [Col. 0309C] when they are rebuked and are not permitted to live wickedly. Among such persons this mourner says:

### Verse 20.—“Make thy face shine upon thy servant; save me in thy mercy, O Lord: let me not be confounded, for I have called upon thee.”

Make thy face shine upon thy servant, [Aug.] that is, make known to men, who think that I am neglected, that thy face is directed upon me and that I serve thee. For now there is confusion, since evil persons are mingled with good; as though he said: “Let it appear what belongs to thee, though now there is confusion.” Hence he says in another psalm: “Distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. 42).

Yet, lest he seem to justify himself, he adds: “And save me, O Lord,” not in my righteousness, not [Col. 0309D] in my merits, but in thy mercy. Not because I am worthy, but because thou art merciful: do not hear me according to judicial severity, [Aug.] but according to thy most merciful goodness. “And let me not be confounded,” that is, let me not blush before evil men who insult me, because—that is, because—I have called upon thee, not upon another.

Or, this is the reason why I shall not be confounded; as though he said: “For this reason I shall not be confounded, because I have called upon thee”—properly called upon thee, unlike the wicked. For you call upon the Lord when you call God into yourself, when you invite him into the house of your heart. But that house must first be cleansed of every defilement and deceit; otherwise you do not truly call upon him. If you call upon God in order that he may give you profit, you call upon profit, not upon God. Therefore call upon God freely, O covetous one, so that God himself may fill you. Do you not wish him to come to you without [Col. 0310A] gold and silver? What, then, of the things God does for you can suffice one for whom God himself does not suffice? Rightly, therefore, he here asks: “Let me not be confounded, for I have called upon thee.” Call upon God, then, if you wish not to be confounded.

### Verse 21.—“Let the ungodly be ashamed and be brought down to hell; let deceitful lips become dumb.”

Let them be ashamed, [Cassiod.] as though he said: “I pray that I may not be confounded; rather, let the ungodly who call upon stones be ashamed and be brought down to hell,” that is, be joined to the shades of hell. Such was the confusion this man feared. [Aug.] And let deceitful lips, which here are talkative because they do not fear judgment, become dumb in their punishments, so that they may instead say: “We fools accounted their life madness,” etc. (Wis. 5). The lips, I say, are:

### Verse 22.—“Those which speak iniquity against the righteous [Col. 0310B] in pride and misuse.”

Those which speak against the righteous one, [Gl. int.] that is, against Christ, or also against his own people. [Cassiod.] Observe how fittingly he opposes iniquity to the righteous. They speak, I say, “in pride,” because the creature exalts itself against the Creator; and “in misuse,” [Alcuin.] that is, with a perverse use of God’s benefits. For, contrary to the proper use by which men are ordinarily grateful for benefits, they acted when they crucified him who came for their sake.

Or, according to another reading, they “speak iniquity in pride and contempt,” [Aug., Gl. int.] that is, being proud and despising Christ as though he were a mere man who had been crucified, while they themselves flourish in the world. Against them the Prophet cried out, saying: “How great,” etc.

[Cassiod.] These matters may also be understood in the person of Christ, from the words, “Above all my enemies.” Christ says, insofar as he is man: “I became a reproach above all my enemies,” that is, in the sight of all my enemies; and I became also an extreme reproach to my neighbors, and a terror to those who knew me. The division is made at the word “reproach.” Or thus: “I became a reproach above all my enemies,” that is, I was held in greater reproach than those who deserved it—as when the Jews chose Barabbas and rejected Christ. Then he adds to whom he became a reproach: “to my neighbors exceedingly,” that is, to my relatives or to those who were now to believe; and “a terror to those who knew me,” that is, to those familiar with me. And “those who saw me outside,” that is, those who thought me a mere man, as I appeared outwardly, [Col. 0310D] fled from me, like the apostles, who, when they saw Christ seized in his Passion, left him and fled.

[Cassiod., Alcuin.] “And I was given over to oblivion,” or “I fell away,” as one dead from their heart: that is, I fell from their mind as a dead man, whose memory is buried with his body and whose restoration is despaired of. “And I became like a lost vessel,” [Cassiod.] because Jesus, being dead, was thought fit to be cast away. And this was because I heard and kept silent concerning the reproach of many who dwell in the circuit of error: those, namely, who understand the Law carnally and not spiritually, or who do not attain any point of truth in me. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2). [Aug.] Or “in the circuit” means in the desire for temporal things.

And in that [Col. 0311A] reproach, while they gathered together—that is, all of them—they took counsel against me to take away my life: [Cassiod.] that is, to make my soul consent to them. But I, knowing that such persons have no power, hoped in thee, O Lord. And I said: “Thou art my God; my lots,” or the times of life, “are in thy hands.” This does not change. “Deliver me,” as though he said: “I have hoped in thee; therefore deliver me from the hand of my enemies and from those who persecute me”—namely, from the hand of the Jews and demons. And “make thy face shine upon thy servant,” that is, make manifest thy favor toward me, so that, as they despair concerning one who dies, so they may have confidence concerning one who rises again. Hence he adds: “And save me in thy mercy, O Lord,” by raising me; “and let me not be confounded, because I have called upon thee.” This does not change.

But let the wicked Jews and other unbelievers be ashamed and be brought down into hell [Aug.] after this life; and meanwhile here, let deceitful lips which devise falsehoods concerning me be made dumb—when, namely, thy mysteries are made manifest: those of the Passion, Resurrection, and redemption of humankind. The lips, I say, which speak iniquity against the righteous one—namely, against me—and this in pride and contempt, as explained above. Seeing and admiring these things, therefore, the Prophet exclaims:

## Part III. Verse 23.—“How great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord, which thou hast hidden for those who fear thee.”

How great. [Alcuin.] The third part, in which he states what God’s good things are, set against the evils mentioned above, which alleviate those evils. As though he said: “They speak against the righteous and are proud. But, O Lord, how great is the multitude of thy sweetness!” [Cassiod.] That is, how abundant in many ways is thy sweetness, by which thou correctest, sparest, and promisest; [Aug.] by which thou greatly lovest even those whom thou correctest. Yet the ungodly man does not perceive it, having lost the palate of his heart through the fever of iniquity. But lest they should become carelessly secure, thou hast hidden from them the sweetness of thy love, though it is useful for them to fear thee. This is what follows: the sweetness, namely, which thou hast hidden. [Cassiod.] That is, thou hast concealed it so that it may be desired more; but in the future it will be revealed. Thou hast hidden it, I say, “for those who fear thee,” that is, for thine own, to the end that they may fear thee. Or, thou hast hidden it for those who fear thee: thou hast reserved it for them and not denied it them, [Aug.] so that they alone may attain and possess it, and it may not be shared with the ungodly. This sweetness thou hast:

### Verse 24.—“Perfected for those who hope in thee, in the sight of the children of men.”

Perfected, [Hier.] that is, thou wilt perfect it, withholding it not from those who not only fear thee but also hope in thee—namely, those who wait to the end. They hope, I say, “in the sight of the children of men,” [Aug.] that is, they hope in such a way that they are not ashamed of their hope and faith, but confess before men. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever has confessed me before men, I too will confess before my Father” (Matt. 10).

Or thus: thou hast perfected this sweetness for those who hope, and this is indeed “in the sight of the children of men,” that is, it is not hidden from those who live not according to Adam but according to the Son of Man, although many doubt it.

### Verse 25.—“Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy face, from the disturbance of men.”

Thou shalt hide them, as though he said: “Their sweetness is thus perfect because thou shalt hide them, lest they be seen by the ungodly, in the secret of thy face,” [Gl. int., Cassiod.] that is, of thy knowledge: namely, so that they may see thee face to face, though now thou art hidden. Thou shalt hide them, I say, “from the disturbance of men,” that is, while evil men are disturbed when condemned. [Aug., Cassiod.] Or, “from the disturbance of men,” so that they themselves may now suffer no human disturbance. This may also be understood of the present time: for even now, though afflicted and harassed by the reproaches of men, by entering in mind to the countenance of God they are not [Col. 0312B] disturbed.

“Thou shalt protect them”: since he had promised the preceding things for the future, lest the future promise itself should cause disturbance, he now speaks of the present.

### Verse 26.—“Thou shalt protect them in thy tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues.”

Thou shalt protect them, [Aug.] as though he said: “In the future thou shalt hide them; and here meanwhile, while they are pilgrims and cursed tongues make a din, denying future things, thou shalt protect them so that they are not harmed, in thy tabernacle”—namely, in the tabernacle of faith in those things which the Lord did and endured for us; that is, in the Catholic Church, which is the tabernacle of faith. A tabernacle is the dwelling of soldiers engaged on campaign; a house is the dwelling of those at rest. Therefore let the pilgrim fight on campaign, protected in the tabernacle, [Col. 0312C] so that he may rest gloriously in the house of heaven not made with hands.

But from whom wilt thou protect them? Behold: “from the contradiction of tongues,” namely, from all schisms and heresies. For diverse heresies and schisms resound, contradicting true Christian doctrine. Therefore run to the tabernacle of God; hold fast the Catholic Church; do not depart from the rule of truth.

[Cassiod., Alcuin.] “Blessed”: he has concluded the fullness of the benefit in praise, comparing it with his own weakness. The Prophet, or the faithful people, speaks as though saying: “What more shall I say? Nothing remains except to praise God.” And:

### Verse 27.—“Blessed be the Lord, for he hath made his mercy wonderful to me in a fortified city.”

[Col. 0312D] Blessed be the Lord, that is, praised, [Aug.] because after the correction of persecutions he made his mercy wonderful to me, that is, made his mercy marvelous to all—not only in Jerusalem, but “in a fortified city,” or in “the city round about,” according to another reading; that is, throughout the whole world. For, after the Holy Spirit was sent, he filled the whole world, which is called “the city round about” because it surrounded Judaea, where the people of God were. As though he said: “In the midst of the nations, there God’s praises were uttered, sacrifices were offered, prophecy did not cease; but now among all the surrounding nations is the people of God, upon whom mercy has been poured out—mercy first poured out upon that Jerusalem.”

As though he said: “The ointment of Christ was contained in a vessel; [Col. 0313A] but now, as from a broken vessel, the ointment has been diffused throughout the world.” Hence in the Song of Songs: “Thy name is ointment poured forth” (Song 1), because the apostles, anointed with the Holy Spirit, proclaimed the great works of God everywhere; and, driven from Jerusalem like timbers burning with divine fire, they set the entire forest of the world ablaze with the fervor of the Spirit and filled it with the light of truth. Again, the same world is rightly called a fortified city because it was armed against God with carnal wisdom and philosophical tradition.

[Cassiod.] Or God the Father made his mercy wonderful—that is, the incarnation of the Word—in the city round about, that is, in Jerusalem, [Aug.] which lies amid the nations, as a temple of faith. From there truth flowed out to the surrounding nations, because there Christ taught, suffered, rose again, and completed the other mysteries. The faithful people who spoke before now speaks here, comparing God’s benefit with its own weakness, as though saying: “The Lord made his mercy wonderful.”

### Verse 28.—“But I said in the excess of my mind: I am cast away from before the face of thine eyes.”

But I. The faithful people, speaking above, says: “I said in the excess,” or ecstasy, “of my mind,” and in my terror, when the nations raged terribly against me. This terror is called “excess,” [Alcuin.] because in fearing it departs from reason: “I am cast away,” according to punishment and according to guilt, “from before the face of thine eyes.” [Aug.] “For if thou wert looking upon me, thou wouldst not permit me to suffer these things; if I were before thy face, [Col. 0313C] I would not fear so greatly.” But it is said in another psalm: “When I said, My foot has been moved, thy mercy, O Lord, helped me” (Ps. 93). Hence he adds here also:

### Verse 29.—“Therefore thou hast heard the voice of my prayer, while I cried unto thee.”

Therefore thou hast heard, etc., as though he said: “Because I confessed my fall, because I was not proud but accused my own heart, because, wavering in tribulation, I cried to thee, [Gl. int.] therefore thou didst not cast me away in fear and faint-heartedness, but didst hear the voice of my prayer,” [Aug.] setting a limit to the correction and showing that I belong to thee. And thou didst this without delay, “while I cried,” that is, while I directed myself intensely toward thee. For crying to God is not done by the voice but by the heart: [Col. 0313D] many who were silent with their lips cried out, while many who made a noise with their mouths, their hearts turned away, were able to obtain nothing. Cry out, therefore, within, where God hears.

See this whole matter in Peter, in whom a figure of our fear appeared beforehand. Seeing the Lord walking upon the waters, he thought him a phantom; but the Lord said to him: “It is I; do not fear.” Peter trusted and said: “Lord, if it is thou, command me to come to thee upon the waters” (Matt. 14), as though saying: “By this I shall prove that thou art he: if by thy word I can do what thou canst do.” And he said, “Come”; and by the word of him commanding, power was given to him obeying. Peter descended and began, fearless as one hoping in him. But seeing a strong wind coming, he was afraid; and when he began to sink, he cried out, saying: [Col. 0314A] “I perish.” This is what this man says: “I said in the excess of my mind, I am cast away from before the face of thine eyes.” This is also what is said in another psalm: “I said, My foot has been moved” (Ps. 93). But Jesus, stretching out his hand to Peter, raised him. This is what follows here: “Therefore thou hast heard the voice of my prayer.” It is the same thing as is said in the other psalm: “Thy mercy helped me” (Ps. 93).

Or, “the excess of mind” here means that which occurs when the mind is caught up to heavenly things. Hence he recognizes the misery of this pilgrimage. For, his mind having been caught up above, he saw the height of God, [Hier., Alcuin.] from which he perceived that, while in this life, he is cast very far away from contemplation of God’s light. And because he humbly laments this and prays that the good lost in the first parent may be restored to him, he is therefore heard by God. Hence he adds: “Therefore thou hast heard the voice of my prayer, while I cried unto [Col. 0314B] thee.”

[Aug.] Here is the hortatory conclusion. For the Prophet now exhorts again, as though speaking on account of the things stated above:

### Verse 30.—“Love the Lord, all ye his saints, for the Lord will require truth; and will repay abundantly those who act proudly.”

Love the Lord. [Aug.] Or here the faithful people speaks, which, having experienced the things stated above, now exhorts you, as though saying: “I was afflicted, I cried, I feared, yet I was not confounded.” [Cassiod.] So you too will be heard if you love God. Therefore love the Lord, the author of so great a benefit, [Aug.] all you his saints, whose task it is to love God, who do not love the world [Col. 0314C] nor the things that are in the world (1 John 2). [Alcuin.] For a friend of this world is made an enemy of God. [Aug.] Learn, therefore, not to love the world, so that you may learn to love God. Turn away, that you may be converted; pour out, that you may be filled.

Therefore love him, because the Lord will require truth. [Gl. int.] Truth is that the creature should serve the Creator. The Lord will require this in the future, even from the saints, when the righteous man shall scarcely be saved. [Aug.] And if the righteous is scarcely saved, where shall the ungodly and sinner appear? (1 Pet. 4). Then he will repay abundantly those who act proudly: [Cassiod.] he will rage against those who despise him by doing what is contrary to God’s commands. [Aug.] That is, he will give recompense to those who act in abundant pride, who do not turn even when convicted, because [Col. 0314D] they are exceedingly proud.

[Cassiod.] Moreover, all act in abundant pride who do not promptly repent of any mortal sin. For pride is put for every vice, because it is the root of all vices. Even in the present, the Lord sometimes repays some persons in order to humble the proud. [Aug.] This is done because, if he did it to no one, divine providence would not seem vigilant; if he did it to everyone, divine patience would not be preserved. Therefore, that he may appear patient and just, he repays some here, but not all.

### Verse 31.—“Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all ye who hope in the Lord.”

Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, etc. [Gl. int.] As though he said: “He will repay in the future. Therefore meanwhile [Col. 0315A] [Cassiod.] act manfully, lest love be idle.” [Aug.] Rather, let them work good unceasingly, so that, doing good without failing, they may in due time reap without failing. [Cassiod.] And if grievous things occur, of the kind I spoke of above, let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord. This verse expresses the virtue and intention of the entire psalm: that the frailty of the flesh may not fear the many evils of this age.

## Comparison on Psalm 30: “In thee, O Lord, have I hoped; let me never be confounded.”

### Verse 4.—“Thou shalt lead me and nourish me.”

Jerome and Campensis have the same. But Sanctes, Pratensis, Münster, and the interpreters for Cajetan render it “thou shalt lead and guide me.” Yet, since Jerome translated a similar expression in Psalm 21, “He led me out upon the waters of refreshment,” as “he nourished me,” this more fittingly corresponds [Col. 0315B] to the grace of Christ, which nourishes us so that we may be strong, as he commented on this passage. It would have been better not to alter the Septuagint version, even if the sense can be reconciled.

Pellican reads the Hebrew word found here with a strong aspiration rather than with *he*, that is, with a light aspiration, because he translated: “Thou shalt possess me as an inheritance”: **TENACHALENI** for **TENAHALENI**. And this seems to come closer to the notion of nourishment or leading.

### Verse 6.—“Into thy hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit.”

The Hebrew has **APHQUID**, and the Septuagint, **παραθήσομαι**, “I shall commend,” in the future tense. It appears that Christ the Lord, while hanging on the cross, changed the tense. Although Greek manuscripts in Luke 23 have the future tense, I would judge them corrupt, because the ancients cite the Evangelist in the present tense. Jerome, *Against the Pelagians*, book 3, and in his commentary on this passage; Augustine, *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, chapters 9 and 10, and in his exposition of the psalm; Ambrose, on the indicated passage of Luke; and again Theophylact on the same passage—unless the manuscript deceives—support this.

The Apostle did something similar in Ephesians 4: looking back to the fulfillment of the event, he changed what the psalm had said, “He received gifts among men,” and put **ἔδωκε δόματα**, “he gave gifts.” Yet the Campensis translation has the present tense. Nor is it unusual in Hebrew for the future to serve in place of the present. Hence Münster translates, “I commend my spirit.”

### Verse 15.—“Those who saw me fled outside from me.”

Faber and Caecus wish the Latin reading to be corrected so that the particle *foras* (“outside”) is not joined to *fugerunt* (“they fled”), but to *videbant* (“they saw”), producing the more Latin expression *foris videbant* (“they saw outside”), because Jerome said, “They saw me in the streets.” Yet Jerome in his commentaries, and Augustine, refer it to the verb “they fled,” as is clear from their interpretation. Campensis likewise says: “They fled outside, leaving me alone.” Nor does the fact that a note of division is placed with the word **BAHUTZ** stand in the way, because, according to Campensis’s testimony, it has no separating force in the Psalter.

### Verse 16.—“I heard the reproach of many who dwell round about.”

Sanctes, Pratensis, Münster, and the interpreters for Cajetan render: “the reproach or infamy of many; terror, or terror all around,” putting “terror” in place of “those who dwell.” Jerome, according to the Hebrew, renders it: “a gathering round about”; Pellican: “which goes about in a circuit.” The Hebrew term **MAGOR** [Col. 0316A] sometimes signifies a dwelling and sometimes terror, from the root **GOR**, “he dwelt” or “he feared.” Therefore innovators wrongly and gratuitously depart from the Latin edition, if they do so out of contempt.

### Verse 18.—“My lots are in thy hands.”

The Hebrew **ITTOTAI** means “my times.” The sense comes to the same thing: for our lot, that is, our election, is in the hidden power of God; while time, by its own nature, indicates what God disposes or ordains. Hence the Campensis translation: “My acts are in thy hand.”

### Verse 21.—“Let the ungodly be ashamed, and be brought down to hell.”

The Hebrew **IIDEMU LISSEOL** means: “Let them be silent in the pit,” that is, in hell. Sanctes, however, translates: “Let them be cut off in hell.” As regards the matter itself, the difference is very slight. Even if **DOM** perhaps does not mean “he brought down,” yet to be silent unto hell is to have no ground of defense against the sinner’s being sent and brought down to hell. Thus that silence is a just condemnation, to which you have nothing to reply, [Col. 0316B] according to Matthew 22: “But he was speechless.” The Campensis translator has: “Let them be put to sleep in the pit”; and Münster: “Let them be restrained.”

“Those which speak iniquity against the righteous.” The Hebrew **ATHAQ** sometimes signifies something weighty and hard, and sometimes something old; therefore Jerome’s version according to one manuscript has “old things,” and according to another “hard things.” Pratensis, Sanctes, Münster, and the interpreters for Cajetan follow the latter sense. Pellican says “ancient.” How antiquity and weight may properly be said of sin, however, Scripture shows everywhere; and what should be understood by them, the Septuagint has aptly made plain in its translation.

### Verse 25.—“From the disturbance of men”: **MERUCESC IS**.

Jerome: “from the hardness of man”; Sanctes, Pratensis, and the interpreters for Cajetan agree. Pellican: “from the exaltations or prides of man”—that is, of men, says Sanctes in his *Thesaurus*, where he also reports the rabbis’ interpretation. Rabbi Solomon: “from the associations or societies of the ungodly.” The Targum: “from the armies of the mighty.” Rabbi Himmaniel: “from the hardnesses and strengths of man.” Münster, closer to the Septuagint: “from the provocations of anyone.” But this “disturbance of men” includes all these meanings.

### Verse 28.—“I said in the excess of my mind.”

Jerome: “in my stupefaction.” Several translate: “in my precipitancy,” or “while I was hastening.” Pellican gives both, precipitancy and terror. On this we say nothing other than what Jerome replies to Sunia and Fretella:

> “But I said in the excess of my mind, for which in Latin manuscripts was read, ‘in my terror.’ And we translated according to the Greek, **ἐν τῇ ἐκστάσει μου**, that is, ‘in the excess of my mind.’ For Latin speech cannot otherwise express **ἔκστασις** than as ‘an excess of mind.’ But I knew that I had read otherwise in Hebrew: ‘in my stupefaction and amazement.’”

So he says. But the Campensis translation has “in my despair”; Campensis himself, “in extreme anxiety.”

### Verse 30.—“For the Lord will require truth.”

The Hebrew **EMUNIM NOTZER** means “he preserves the faithful,” or “he preserves truths.” But in what way does the Lord preserve truths except by strictly examining a truthful life at the last judgment? Hence he preserves truths because he continually requires how they are kept, leaving nothing unexamined—not even the smallest thought. If that thought contains anything wrong, it will be weighed exactly, by the rule of truth, before the Judge from whom nothing can be hidden.

# Psalm 31

[Col. 0315]

## Title of the Psalm: “A Psalm of Understanding of David.”

[Col. 0315D]

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven.” The title: “A Psalm of Understanding of David.” [Aug.] This psalm treats of the grace [Col. 0316D] and mercy of God by which we are Christians. Hence the Apostle, in the Epistle to the Romans, draws from this psalm an argument for grace against those who boast of works [Col. 0317A] of the Law and parade their merits, saying that blessedness belongs to the man to whom God reckons righteousness, as the Prophet says: “Blessed are those,” etc. (Rom. 3).

[Alcuin.] This psalm especially treats against the vices of persons who either do not know their sins, or, when they know them, defend them and boast of their merits. [Aug.] On the contrary, it teaches us to acknowledge ourselves sinners, accuse our sins, and attribute good things to the grace of God. [Note: [Col. 0317D] From Cassiodorus on verse 3 of this psalm.] Therefore this psalm is set against human vices, lest anyone suppose that what he keeps hidden in his conscience is hidden from God.

The meaning of the title is: [Gl. int.] “This is David’s understanding,” that is, the understanding of the penitent, in whose person David speaks here; [Cassiod.] that is, here you are taught what you ought to understand if you are truly penitent, or wish to repent. [Aug.] First, understand that you are a sinner; then, if you begin to do good, do not attribute it to your own powers, justifying yourself by word, but to the grace of God, so that there may be no deceit in your heart. This is the second of the penitential psalms and differs from the first. For in the first, the penitent weeps through fear of judgment; in this one, grievously afflicted, he is compelled to confess the sins that he had kept silent.

**Intention.** He exhorts to repentance.

[Cassiod., Alcuin.] **Method.** There are four parts. First, he says that the beginning of good is through God’s forgiveness; that he himself, following the human vice just mentioned, had been miserable, but by God’s mercy had been converted to true understanding; and that, having experienced a fall, he more fittingly calls back others who have been deceived, and strengthens those who stand firm. Second, [Col. 0317C] he treats of confession, whence forgiveness comes, at “I have made known my transgression.” [Cassiod.] Third, he commends repentance, at “For this shall everyone pray.” Fourth, a joyful ending is given, where God is said to give understanding, at “I will give thee understanding.”

The Prophet, therefore, commending grace, shows that the beginning of good is through God’s forgiveness, saying:

### Verse 1.—“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered.”

Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven. [Aug.] He does not say, “those in whom he found no sin,” for he finds sin in all; rather, “those whose sins are forgiven.” You have done nothing good, and forgiveness of sins is given you. From your guilt vengeance was owed you; from his grace he gives pardon. For condemnation is owed for your evil works, just as the kingdom of heaven is owed for good works. If, therefore, what is owed you is rendered, you must be punished. God does not render to you the punishment owed, but gives both forgiveness and unowed grace. Let no one, therefore, boast of his works before faith; let no one be lazy in good works after receiving faith. For God grants forgiveness to the ungodly and justifies them by faith. Thus the justification of faith begins through forgiveness.

[Alcuin.] By “iniquities” he means the tinder of sin, namely concupiscence, which before baptism is not only punishment but also guilt—not actual guilt, certainly, but original guilt; after baptism, however, it is punishment and not guilt. [Note: [Col. 0317D] From Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, chapter 25.] For in baptism original sin is destroyed—not so that it does not exist, but so that it is no longer sin. Therefore he fittingly says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven,” that is, mitigated through grace, so that they do not reign in the mortal body (Rom. 6). The reason for this is that sins are covered in baptism. Hence he adds: “and whose sins”—namely original sins, and any actual sins—“have been covered.” [Aug.] That is, covered over and abolished. For if God has covered sins, he has not wished to take notice of them. If he has not wished to take notice, he has not wished to punish them; he has not wished to acknowledge them, but to forgive them. Therefore he does not say that sins are covered as though they remain and live there, but that they are so destroyed that God does not see them—that is, does not punish them eternally. For God’s seeing sins means punishing them. Hence elsewhere: “Turn thy face away from my sins” (Ps. 50). This is said by analogy. [Gl. int.] For sins are covered in baptism as the Egyptians pursuing Israel were covered in the Red Sea (Exod. 14).

Nor is it enough that sins be covered in baptism, unless thereafter one guards against that which God imputes—that is, mortal sin. Hence he adds:

### Verse 2.—“Blessed is the man to whom the Lord hath not imputed sin, and in whose spirit there is no deceit.”

Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin: he who guards himself against mortal sin, which is imputed for eternal punishment. [Cassiodorus] Or, even if, after iniquities have been forgiven and sins covered, some lighter sin remains—as in Job and Nathanael, whom the Lord praises—the Lord has not imputed sin to them. [Note: [Col. 0318D] From Jerome on Hosea, ch. VIII.] Or he calls “iniquities” the sins committed before faith or baptism [Col. 0318C], and “sins” those committed after faith or baptism. Thus: “Blessed are they whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered,” that is, those to whom God forgives sins committed before faith. For those in whom he covers sins after faith are not blessed through themselves, lest those sins be revealed at judgment. Thus no sin will be imputed to them for punishment. [Alcuin] Hence he adds: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin.” For to some who possess grave sins God imputes them; to others, by mercy, he does not impute them, even if they have some sins—namely, those who do not proclaim themselves righteous while they are evil, but, acknowledging themselves, make satisfaction. Hence he says, “and in whose spirit there is no guile.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus] Here he shows to whom God does not impute sin: namely, to the one in whom there is no guile. For, being a sinner, he accuses himself; in his heart he holds what he confesses with his mouth [Col. 0318D]. Guile consists in a sinner proclaiming himself righteous. But one who accuses himself is free from guile. Such was Nathanael, of whom the Lord said: “Behold, a true Israelite, in whom there is no guile” (John 1); and that humble publican who said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18).

VERSE 3.—“Because I kept silence, my bones grew old, while I cried out all day long.”

Because I kept silence. [Jerome] As though he said: “I now make confession in this way; but formerly, because I kept silence, my bones grew old.” Or connect it thus: This is the blessed man in whose spirit there is no guile, [Augustine] because I, formerly not confessing to God, fell [Col. 0319A] into sin. This is what he means when he says, “Because I kept silence”: I kept silent concerning what ought not to have been concealed, namely confession of sin. “My bones grew old,” that is, my inward strength failed. Had he acted otherwise, vigorous strength in the Lord would have been renewed. For if I had cried out my sins, I would have been found weak in myself, but made strong in the Lord. Instead, perversely, he kept silent about sins and cried out about merits. Hence he adds: “While I cried out all day long.”

I said what ought not to be said about my own righteousness; therefore there is no contradiction in his saying, “I kept silence while I cried out.” He kept silent about some things and did not keep silent about others; he kept silent about what would have profited him, and did not keep silent about what would have caused his failure; he kept silent concerning confession and cried out presumptuously concerning merits. He showed sound limbs to the physician and concealed the wounded ones. Therefore he was not healed or restored to health, but [Col. 0319B] “grew old,” that is, remained in oldness, because in confessing he did not love newness. Whoever does not wish to confess sins labors in vain to defend them; while he boasts of merits, his strength fails more and more. For he aggravates guilt while defending it; he repels grace while boasting of merits.

Therefore, even if a person is conscious of no sin, he should nevertheless not proclaim himself righteous: “Who can understand transgressions?” (Ps. 18); or, “Who boasts that he has a pure heart?” (Prov. 20). Whoever says that he has no sin is a liar (1 John 1). Hence the Apostle says: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4). And Solomon: “There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness” (Ecclus. 7)—that is, one who presumes upon his righteousness, like the Pharisee who said, “I am not like other men,” [Col. 0319C] etc. (Luke 18). Or thus: “I kept silence” verbally concerning sin, while “I cried out all day” in my inward feeling that I was a sinner, because the punishment of sin or inward blindness showed me to be a sinner.

VERSE 4.—“For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; I was turned in my misery, while the thorn is driven in.”

For day and night. As though he said: “Keeping silent about sins and boasting of merits, I grew old; but, O Lord, because your hand was heavy upon me, to humble me in my pride”—[Augustine] because your vengeance touched me—and this “day and night,” that is, continually, “I was turned in my misery,” that is, I recognized that I was miserable, “while the thorn is broken,” or “driven in,” that is, while conscience was pierced. Then I felt pain and [Col. 0319D] discovered my weakness.

[Cassiodorus] Or: I recognized that I was miserable “while the thorn is broken.” [Note: [Col. 0319] In the Roman Psalter one reads “is broken.”] This thorn is that which raises up the whole body, namely pride; when broken, it does not cast a person down into destruction, but raises him to salvation. Or read the text thus: “I cried out and kept silence,” which I ought not to have done, “and therefore your hand was heavy upon me day and night.” The sense of these words does not change: as though he said, “You struck me continually, and not without cause, because I was turned in my misery,” [Augustine] that is, I became miserable. And it truly is my misery and wretchedness “while,” that is, because, “the thorn,” namely sin, “is driven in,” that is, carried as far as consent, [Col. 0320A] habit, and act.

[Alcuin] Of these thorns it was said to the first man when he sinned: “Your land shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3). And elsewhere: “Thorns and thistles grow in the hands of a drunkard” (Prov. 16). Or the thorn means reason: it is “broken,” that is, broken and bent down toward earthly things, though it ought to be raised upward, just as the spine of the back holds a human being upright.

PART II. Diapsalma.

VERSE 5.—“I made my transgression known to you, and I did not conceal my injustice.”

“My transgression,” etc. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] The second part, in which confession of sin is commended, from which comes pardon. Thus above he said that growing old resulted from concealment. [Note: [Col. 0319] From Gregory’s exposition of the seven penitential psalms, and from Cassiodorus.] As though he said: “I was turned in [Col. 0320B] misery; my conscience was pierced; and thus, by confessing, I myself made known to you my transgression”—namely, what I committed by acting, that is, by keeping silence about sins—“and I did not conceal my injustice,” namely, what I did when I ought not to have done it, that is, when I cried out about merits. [Augustine, Gloss] That is, I did not cover it, but uncovered it, so that you might cover it; I revealed it, that you might conceal it. For when a human being uncovers, God covers; when a human being covers, God lays bare; if a human being acknowledges, God forgives.

VERSE 6.—“I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the impiety of my sin.”

“I said: I will confess.” [Gloss] As though he said: “I made it known, and truly so. For first I said”—[Alcuin] that is, I resolved [Col. 0320C] within myself—this, namely: “I will confess,” or declare, “my injustice to the Lord,” acting against myself concerning my injustice. [Gloss] That is, acting contrary to my former conduct. Formerly I had kept silence; now I will declare it.

Or thus: “I will confess my injustice to the Lord,” [Augustine] declaring it to be against myself, that is, attributing it to myself and not to God or to nature; for that too is to attribute it to God. Thus now I will confess against myself, [Gloss] whereas previously I acted against God. [Augustine] For many confess their iniquity, but against God. When they are found in sins, they say: “I did not do this,” or “This is not sin, but God willed it.” Others say: “Fate did this to me; the stars did this to me.” And thus, circuitously, they wish to arrive at accusing God, rather than take the direct way to appease God. [Col. 0320D] For he himself made and ordered the stars. Thus through them they seek to show that God caused them to sin.

Let them instead say: “Lord, have mercy upon me and heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40). Let the sick person cry thus to the physician and say: “God created me with free choice; therefore, if I have sinned, I sinned—not fate, not fortune; nor did the devil compel me. Rather, I consented to the one persuading me.”

“And you forgave.” [Gloss] As though he said: “Thus I spoke, and thus I resolved; and you even forgave the impiety of my sin”—namely, my resolve to conceal my fault and my wicked boasting of merits. The great mercy of God is here displayed, [Cassiodorus] [Col. 0321A] in that he forgave sin at the promise alone. For a vow is reckoned as an act. [Augustine] Great, then, is his saying: “I said: I will confess,” or, in another reading, “I will declare.” He has not yet declared it; he promises that he will declare it. Yet God already forgives, because this very saying, “I will declare” or “I will confess,” is in some way a declaration—not with the mouth, but with the heart. The voice has not yet reached the mouth so that a human being may hear the confession, but God hears it.

PART III. Diapsalma.

VERSE 7.—“For this shall every holy person pray to you at a fitting time.”

“For this shall [one] pray.” [Cassiodorus] The third part, in which, commending its fullness, he says that it is common to all the saints, though various sects reject it. Against them he has recourse to God. [Alcuin] As though he said: “You forgave [Col. 0321B] the impiety of my sin.” [Augustine] And for this forgiveness, once granted, every holy person shall pray to you. For by this one is holy, and on this account prayer is made: because you have forgiven. Otherwise no one would be holy or worship you, because all are sinners and lack the glory of God. And when shall he pray? “At a fitting time.”

The fitting time is the time of grace, newly manifested to you, when Christ’s grace was revealed (Rom. 3). Of this the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time came, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. 4). From what did he redeem them? From the devil, from destruction, from sins, from the burden of the law which oppressed them and proved them guilty. It did not help the thorn of sin: it showed it, but did not [Col. 0321C] consume it. [Alcuin] Thus it almost compelled them to cry out for grace and for the physician; but grace heals.

VERSE 8.—“Yet in the flood of many waters they shall not draw near to him.”

“Yet.” [Alcuin] As though he said: “Though a saint prays, though it is a fitting time,” [Augustine] yet those who are “in the flood of many waters,” that is, flowing away in carnal desires—or who are in the flood of many waters, [Alcuin] that is, in the errors of different sects and the multiplicity of vain doctrines, such as philosophers who assign salvation to free choice, Jews who assign it to carnal observances, [Augustine] and others who impute sins to fate, fortune, or similar things—[Col. 0321D] though the one teaching of God concerns humility of heart and confession of sin: all these, I say, “shall not draw near to him,” that is, to God. For he here changes person, as he often does, as in: “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people” (Ps. 3).

Those who are in the flood of diverse teachings do not draw near to God: such as those who say, “Fate made me sin,” or “Fortune, which governs all things,” or “the race of darkness, which rebels against God.” These waters are diverse and bitter. But that is the true and sweet water which flows from the innermost fountain of pure truth: the water of confession of sins and humility of heart, the saving life of a person who casts himself down, presumes nothing from himself, and attributes nothing to his own power and pride. This water flows from [Col. 0322A] him who, though exalted, became humble for our sake—that is, from Christ. Or, “they shall not draw near to him,” that is, to the saint, by imitation. But this is within the flood which resounds on every side.

VERSE 9.—“You are my refuge from the tribulation that surrounded me; my exultation: deliver me from those surrounding me.”

“You are my refuge,” etc. [Gregory] For I, being in this flood, walking in this world, do not listen to such people, but flee to you. [Jerome] Or thus: For this, namely, that impiety may be removed, every holy person shall pray to you, because no one is without sin. He shall pray, I say, “at a fitting time,” in this life, where it is permitted. “Yet”—as though he said—“I say that the saint prays,” whereby he is shown to have sins; but nonetheless, in the flood of many waters, that is, when punishments and distresses overflow at judgment, [Col. 0322B] those very punishments shall not draw near to the saint, just as the waters did not draw near to Noah in the flood (Gen. 7).

“You are”—as though he said—the saint will pray thus: “O Lord, you are my refuge, not my own strength, nor another god; but you alone are my refuge.” [Augustine] You are my refuge from the tribulation of this world, or from sins, which surrounded me; and you are my exultation. For I rejoice in hope of the future good which you promise and in your sparing mercy. Therefore, O Lord, deliver me from those who surround me, because although I rejoice in hope, I still remain amid evils.

PART IV. Diapsalma.

VERSE 10.—“I will give you understanding and instruct you in this way in which you shall walk; I will fix [Col. 0322C] my eyes upon you.”

“I will give you understanding,” etc. [Alcuin] The fourth part, in which a joyful end is shown. It is said that God gives understanding. Hence this person exhorts others to the same thing, as though he said: “You, deliver me, who promised me this: ‘I will give you understanding.’” [Cassiodorus] Or Christ replies to the penitent who had asked to be delivered, and the Lord answers him: “I will give you understanding,” [Augustine] namely, so that you may know yourself and understand that all things are from grace, and rejoice in hope. This explains why it is called a psalm of understanding, as the title shows: here understanding is said to be given to the penitent, [Alcuin] lest the suppliant be thought neglected, God himself bearing witness; “and I will instruct you, lest you stray,” as though unarmed against the sword.

[Augustine, Cassiodorus] [Col. 0322D] “And this in the way,” namely, God’s way, “in which you shall walk,” not in error; “I will fix my eyes upon you,” lest anyone harm you—that is, I shall not afterward withdraw my eyes from you, [Augustine] because you always lift your eyes to me, [Cassiodorus] now justified. See how great is the glory of the penitent.

VERSE 11.—“Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding.”

“Do not become,” etc. [Augustine] Having received understanding, this penitent turns to the proud who defend their sins and shows us what understanding is. [Alcuin] As though he said: “The Lord did this for me; therefore, O you whom I invite, do not become like a horse.” He does not say “like an ox,” which is humble, but “like a horse,” which walks with uplifted neck: by it the proud are signified. By the mule are signified [Col. 0323A] the foolish and slothful. Thus: “Do not become like horse and mule,” that is, proud and foolish, because such people have no understanding.

[Jerome] Or by horse and mule two peoples are understood. By the horse is meant the untamed Gentile; by the mule, the Jew slow to believe. Thus: “Do not become like horse and mule,” that is, do not become like the Gentiles or like the Jews, who have no understanding. What, then, do such people suffer? Behold: “With bit,” etc.

Or thus: “Do not become like a horse.” A horse indiscriminately accepts a rider; a mule accepts any burdens. [Cassiodorus] Thus neither has understanding: the former concerning riders, the latter concerning burdens. Therefore he forbids people to be ridden by the devil and loaded with vices, lest otherwise the horse be restrained with a bridle and the mule with a bit. Thus: “Do not become like horse and mule,” that is, do not receive the devil as rider or take on the burden of vices, because such people have no understanding, like horse and mule. Hence he adds, “which have no understanding.” [Augustine] “If he has refused to yield, O God, do for them what you did for me,” says the penitent, namely:

VERSE 12.—“With bit and bridle restrain their jaws, those who do not draw near to you.”

“With bit and bridle,” that is, with greater and lesser tribulation, restrain—or break—[Alcuin] or “you will break,” that is, draw back and confine—their jaws, that is, their boasting about their own powers and merits. [Augustine] For if you do not have Christ as rider, the mouth with which you boast of merits and keep silent about sins will be broken. Therefore, if you do not wish your mouth to be broken, do not be like horse and [Col. 0323C] mule, but like the ox that knew its owner (Isa. 1).

Or: “With bit and bridle [restrain] their jaws,” with which they chew. “Break [them],” [Cassiodorus] that is, give them food more sparingly, so that, compelled at least by necessity, they may return, like animals which endure bridles and whips until they hold to the path. “Their jaws,” I say, [belong to] those who will not draw near to you by humbling themselves. For there are some who, though they sin through weakness of the flesh, nevertheless do not withdraw from devout prayers.

These may also be Christ’s words: “Do not,” etc. He above answered the penitent, saying, “I will give understanding,” etc.; and he speaks this to others, urging them toward the same end, saying, “Do not,” etc. Afterwards he turns his words to the Father when he says, “Restrain,” etc. The sense of the words is unchanged.

[Col. 0323D] VERSE 13.—“Many are the scourges of the sinner, but mercy shall surround one who hopes in the Lord.”

Even with the bridle, the sinner has many scourges. [Augustine, Alcuin] Behold: after the bridle, scourges are added to tame him, lest he be among those unpunished people to whom freedom is now given to wander along their own path. Thus he above said that he himself had been tamed, when he said, “Your hand was heavy,” etc. [Augustine, Jerome] It is therefore no wonder if scourges follow once the bridle has been applied. For this man desired to be an untamed animal: he wished to govern himself not by God’s will but by his own impulse, and to rush unbridled into lust. Therefore he is tamed by bridle and scourge—and may he be thoroughly tamed! For one must take care lest, by resisting too much, he deserve to be left untamed and go onto the wandering [Col. 0324A] road leading to death.

Or this can be understood of the future: “Here you will restrain them, and in the future [there will be] many scourges for the sinner.” [Jerome and Alcuin] Or it can be understood both of the present and the future: “Do not become like horse and mule, because many are the scourges of the sinner,” here and in the future; but mercy shall surround on every side the one hoping in the Lord, [Gloss] who gives all things freely, [Cassiodorus] so that no place may remain for the enemy; [Augustine] this mercy consists in consolations. The Law is in scourges; the Gospel is in consolation. And because mercy surrounds, therefore you who were formerly ungodly and proud [should rejoice].

VERSE 14.—“Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous; and glory, all you upright in heart.”

“Rejoice in the Lord,” [Gloss] you who formerly rejoiced in yourselves, [Col. 0324B] “and exult in the Lord,” because you are now righteous—not through your merits, but through grace—you who formerly were sinners. Distinguish: to rejoice is to delight in a quiet sweetness; to exult is to rejoice with the ardent excitement of a stirred-up spirit. “And glory” because you are subject to him; do this even amid tribulations, [Augustine] all of you who are upright in heart, that is, not resisting God.

Those are crooked in heart who say either that God does not exist, or that he is not just, or that he does not govern these things, when they see the wicked prosper and the good suffer. Those are upright in heart who direct their heart according to God’s will, preferring it to their own, as Christ also taught when he said, “Not as I will, but,” etc. (Matt. 26), transforming his own people in himself; as also there: “Saul, Saul, why do you [Col. 0324C] persecute me?” (Acts 9).

## Comparison on Psalm XXXI: “Blessed Are They Whose”

VERSE 2.—“And in whose spirit there is no guile.” The Latin edition, even though it generally follows the Greek copies we possess, does not do so consistently. For here we read, **οὐδέ ἐστιν ἐν τῷ στόματι αὐτοῦ δόλος**, that is, “and in his mouth there is no guile.” Jerome, in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela, indicated that this belonged to Symmachus alone. Otherwise the Septuagint translators, Theodotion, the fifth and sixth editions, Aquila, and the Hebrew text itself have “in his spirit.” There are also several other places in the Greek which differ from the Latin.

VERSE 4.—“I was turned in my misery.” All the more recent translators here abandon the Vulgate reading, together with Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew, because they translate “my sap,” “moisture,” or “freshness,” rather than “my misery” or “wretchedness.” The matter becomes very clear: Jerome and the Septuagint understood *lamed*, the letter called servile, whereas others [Col. 0324D] take it as radical in *lessaddi*, because *lasad* means “moisture.” But if you derive it from the root *shadad*, “he devastated,” it signifies “misery,” and *lamed* will be the sign of the ablative or accusative: “in my misery” or “toward my misery.”

That Jerome understood it thus is clear not only from his translation from the Hebrew, but also from his discussion addressed to Sunnia and Fretela, whose words I append:

> “You suggest that in the Greek ‘my’ is absent from ‘I was turned in my misery’: **ἐστράφην εἰς ταλαιπωρίαν, ἐν τῷ ἐμπαγῆναί μοι ἄκανθαν**, that is, ‘I was turned in misery, while a thorn is driven into me’; this has been added from the Hebrew and from Theodotion’s translation. And in Hebrew one reads *LESSADDI*.”

Here you see Jerome asserting that in the Hebrew “my” is added to “misery,” on account of the *yod* at the end of that word. But had he taken the *lamed* as radical, he would neither have translated it thus nor indicated that the suffixed pronoun was added to that meaning.

[Col. 0325A] “While the thorn is driven in.” Jerome translated, “when it was inflamed”; others, “into the droughts of summer.” The diversity arose because it can be translated literally as “in the swords of the thorn,” which the Septuagint rendered not inappropriately, “while the thorn is driven in.” For *harbon* or *hereb* means “drought” or “sword,” and *qayits* or *qots* may ambiguously mean “summer” or “thorn.” The Septuagint followed the latter sense.

VERSE 7.—“You are my refuge from the tribulation that surrounded me.” For “surrounded,” they translate “you will guard”: *TITZRENI*, from the root *NATZAR*, means “you will guard me.” Yet with different pointing, from the root *TZOR*, it may meanwhile mean “you will surround me,” or, in the feminine, “she will surround me,” *TETZURENI*. Enough and more has been said in the preface concerning the rationale of the points and their invention. The translator attached to Campensis agrees with us. For he translates: “You are my refuge from the tribulation that had surrounded me.”

“My exultation, deliver me from those surrounding me.” Jerome has: “My praise, saving [me], you will surround me.” Others translate: “You will surround me with songs or cries of one delivered, or of deliverance.” These versions aim at the same sense. Jerome, however, and the interpreters working for Cajetan read *RONI*, since they say “my exultation” or “my praise,” where the others [Col. 0326A] read *RONE*. Further, *PALLET* means “deliver,” “of delivering,” or “of deliverance.” But Jerome appears to have understood *POLET*, that is, “saving,” even if modern translators wish it to be neuter; rather, one should say *MEPHALLET*.

VERSE 10.—“I will fix my eyes upon you.” Jerome: “I will think of you with my eye.” The rest: “I will refuse” or “I will take counsel for you with my eye.” These are closely related, and with the same interpretation refer to God’s guardianship and providence toward the converted sinner, lest he thereafter fall back; this is God’s most steadfast counsel. The translation attached to Campensis has: “I will fasten my eyes upon you.”

VERSE 14.—“Glory, all you upright in heart.” It is quite intolerable that Sanctes and the interpreters for Cajetan should have translated, “praise all the upright,” using the accusative, when no reason whatsoever, not even the least, compelled them to do this. Therefore Jerome added *eum*, “praise him, all you upright in heart,” as though warning that no one should refer this praise to the upright, but to God, who makes them upright. Yet I suspect that the accusative in the text of Sanctes is due to scribal error, since in his *Thesaurus* he translates with the nominative. The Cajetan translation also can easily be restored to the sense of the Latin reading when it says, “cause all the upright of heart to praise.”

# PSALM XXXII

[Col. 0325]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0325B]

[Cassiodorus] “Exult, you righteous, in the Lord.” Title: “Unto the end, a psalm of David.” The title is clear. In this psalm, however, the Prophet commends God’s mercy and power and recounts his works, treating of the works of creation and re-creation, so that his power by which he creates may be feared, and his mercy by which he re-creates may be loved.

Intention: he invites people to praise, showing who ought to praise, whom they ought to praise, how, and why. Method: the psalm has three parts. First, he urges the righteous or upright to praise. Second, he calls blessed the one who attains the worship of God, at “Blessed is the nation.” Third, he adds what he thinks concerning the matters already mentioned, at “Our soul.” Therefore, showing who ought to praise, the Prophet urges the righteous to praise, saying:

VERSE 1.—“Exult, you righteous, in the Lord; praise befits the upright.”

You righteous, exult even in adversities—not in yourselves, [Augustine] nor in the world which perishes, as the unrighteous do, whose exultation ends with the world—but [Col. 0325D] in the Lord, in whom nothing displeases them. He to whom God is pleasing is pleasing to God; and, since God remains, the exultation of the righteous will remain. Since we cannot exult in him except by praising, he says, “Praise befits the upright.”

The one who praises is upright, that is, subject to God; otherwise he is distorted and crooked. The crooked person praises God when things go well for him and blasphemes when things go badly; but the upright person praises always, that is, in prosperity and adversity, as Job did. Therefore those are upright who direct their heart according to God’s will, which is the rule, and prefer the will of the better to their own will: that is, the will of almighty God to the will of a weak person, the will of God to the will of man. For as far as God is from man, so far is God’s will from human will.

Hence Christ, taking human nature and setting before us the rule, both teaching and enabling us to live, showed us a certain private human will, in which he represented both his own and ours. He is our head, and we belong to him as members. He said: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26). This was human will, desiring something proper to itself and, as it were, private. But because he wills that man be upright and directed to him who is always upright, he adds: “Not what I will, but what you will, Father” (ibid.). It is as though he said to man: “See yourself in me. You may will something proper to yourself, although God wills something else; this is granted to human weakness, namely, to will something proper to oneself. But immediately consider what is above you—namely God: consider him above you and yourself below; him the Creator and yourself the creature; him the Lord and yourself the servant; him almighty and yourself weak. Then you will submit your will to his will and be upright.”

[Cassiodorus] Therefore he says, “Praise befits the upright,” not merely “praise,” but “praise together,” on account of the unity of the Church.

[Col. 0326D] VERSE 2.—“Give thanks to the Lord with the harp; sing psalms to him upon the ten-stringed psaltery.”

“Give thanks.” He has said who ought to praise and whom they ought to praise; here he says how they should praise. Thus the Lord is to be praised: “Give thanks to the Lord with the harp.” The harp sounds from below and belongs to the earth. [Augustine] Thus we ought to praise: that is, through earthly prosperity and adversity, which come to us from him. Thus: “Give thanks to the Lord with the harp,” that is, praise the Lord whether prosperity abounds or adversities arise; “and sing psalms to him,” or “to that one,” “upon the ten-stringed psaltery.”

The psaltery gives forth sound from above and has ten strings. It signifies heavenly doctrine, which is from above and calls you to heaven, briefly set forth in the Ten Commandments. Thus: “Sing psalms to him on the ten-stringed [Col. 0327A] psaltery,” that is, praise him while attending to the higher things he has given you, namely heavenly doctrine.

Or the harp signifies the flesh, which is the lower nature of man. [Jerome] The psaltery signifies charity, contained in the two commandments of love of God and neighbor. To these belong the Ten Commandments of the Law: three on the first tablet concerning God, seven on the second concerning one’s neighbor. Thus: “Give thanks to the Lord with the harp,” [Augustine] that is, offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, mortifying the flesh with its vices and desires. “And sing psalms to him upon the ten-stringed psaltery,” that is, let your members serve charity, in which the three and seven commandments are fulfilled, upon which the whole Law and the Prophets depend.

[Alcuin] And because it is insufficient unless your righteousness abounds beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees, he adds:

VERSE 3.—“Sing to him a new song; sing well to him with joyful acclamation.”

“Sing to him,” [Augustine] not only with the tongue but with your life, “a new song”: namely, the song of grace, the song of faith and charity; [Cassiodorus] the song of the Incarnation, at which the world rejoices and of which the angels too sang. This is the new song brought by the new man. For there is a new king and a new law: “Behold, all things have become new” (Rev. 21).

[Jerome, Augustine] None sing this song except new people, renewed by grace, who belong to the New Testament. Therefore sing to him a new song, put off oldness [Col. 0327C] and put on newness; for the New Testament belongs only to the new. [Cassiodorus] And sing to him well, not badly, through good works. If you ask how to sing well, behold: “Sing to him with joyful acclamation,” or jubilation, that is, with unspeakable joy or exultation, so that what is understood and rejoiced in cannot be expressed in words. [Augustine] This befits the ineffable one whom you cannot speak of, yet must not keep silent about. Nothing therefore remains but that you should jubilate: that is, rejoice in heart even if not in words, and let the boundless breadth of joys have no limits of syllables.

VERSE 4.—“For the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works are in faithfulness.”

“For the word is upright.” [Alcuin] Here he states why God is to be praised. Above he set out the manner of praise; now he gives the reason why God should be praised. As though he said: “Therefore you ought to praise, because the word of the Lord is upright,” [Augustine] that is, his promise is true in all things and deceives no one. Hence God is called faithful (1 Cor. 10; John 2), though a faithful human being is called so in another sense. God is faithful in giving to man what he promised; man is faithful in believing God who promises. By virtue of his promise, God is our debtor, not by virtue of anything committed to him; for we have entrusted nothing to him by which we may hold him as debtor, since from him we have all the things in which we rejoice. Therefore let us hold fast to the most faithful debtor, because we hold fast to the most faithful promiser. “And all his works are in faith,” that is, faithful; he promises nothing that he does not fulfill, because:

[Col. 0328A] VERSE 5.—“He loves mercy and judgment; the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.”

“He loves mercy,” [Augustine] which consists in promising, “and judgment,” which consists in fulfilling. Or by “word” is understood the law of God, namely the law of the Gospel. [Gloss] As though he said: “Therefore praise, because the word of the Lord is upright,” [Augustine] that is, God’s law is upright; or, the Lord’s speech is upright, namely, for making you upright, which you cannot accomplish by yourselves. Thus it is upright in itself and upright in its effect. “And all his works are in faith,” [Cassiodorus] because he works for salvation only in the faithful. Hence in the Gospel: “Your faith has saved you” (Luke 7).

Or thus: “The word of the Lord is upright”—this does not change—“and all his works,” supply, “are upright.” Here distinguish. [Alcuin] That is, whatever works he commands are upright in themselves, as is evident from the words “in faith.” Or all the works that he loves and eternally rewards proceed from faith; and because this faith is from God, all good works are from God. He says this lest anyone suppose that he has arrived at faith by the merits of works, when all the works that God loves—that is, rewards—are in faith.

Therefore praise him, who not only does the things just mentioned, but also loves mercy—for he frequently acts mercifully. [Augustine, Alcuin] That is, out of love for us he grants mercy now on the way, calling and justifying. And he loves judgment, which will occur in the future, when he exacts what he has bestowed beforehand, because there too he will repay good and evil people according to their merits, exacting with interest the talents entrusted to us [Col. 0328C] (Matt. 25).

See that the Lord loves mercy and judgment; you too must observe both, because both concern you. Otherwise the Lord would not rebuke the Pharisees by saying: “You omit the weightier matters of the law, namely mercy and judgment” (Matt. 23). Take care, therefore, lest, having lost judgment, you show mercy to a poor person in an evil cause. For your God says to you: “You shall not show partiality to the poor in judgment” (Exod. 23), so that you may not encourage his evil cause and cover his iniquity. If you spare his purse, you strike his heart, because he remains unjust and therefore becomes worse, seeing that justice seems to favor him.

“The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.” As though he said: “He truly loves mercy, because the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord”: everywhere sins are forgiven to human beings; everywhere the Gospel is preached. Therefore he says, “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.” He says “earth,” not “heaven,” because heaven does not need mercy, where there is no misery. Human misery abounds on earth, and the Lord’s mercy superabounds. The earth is full of human misery and the Lord’s mercy, not heaven, which does not need mercy, though it needs the Lord’s governance. For all things need the Lord, both miserable and blessed things: without him the miserable are not raised up, and the blessed are not governed. Thus heaven also needs the Lord. For it did not give itself its own stability, but:

VERSE 6.—“By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power.”

The heavens were established [Augustine] not by themselves but by the word [Col. 0329A] of the Lord, that is, by the Son of the Father. And by the spirit of his mouth—that is, by the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Son, who is the Father’s mouth—all their power was made firm, and all of it, not merely part; for they possessed nothing of themselves, as though God had to supply something lacking. Note that the work of the Word, that is, the Son, and of the Holy Spirit is one and the same. For “all their power” and “they were established” are the same thing. Therefore the Son and the Holy Spirit accomplish this. But is it without the Father? Certainly not: the Father works through the Word and through the Holy Spirit. This Trinity, therefore, is one God.

VERSE 7.—“Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin; placing the depths in treasuries.”

“Gathering.” He still continues concerning natural works which pertain to power, [Jerome] saying: He himself gathers the waters of the sea as in a wineskin; literally, he confines the sea with shores. And he places the depths in his treasuries, according to that saying: “He brings forth the winds from his treasuries” (Ps. 134). Therefore:

VERSE 8.—“Let all the earth fear the Lord; let all the inhabitants of the world be moved by him.”

Let all the earth fear the Lord, [Aug.] that is, let the sinner cease from sinning; and if not through love, at least through fear. Or, in a mystical sense, earth, heavens, and so forth may be understood. [Hier., Aug.] As though he said: He truly loves mercy, because the earth—that is, the Church throughout all lands—is full of the Lord’s mercy; [Aug.] for everywhere the Gospel is preached in the Churches, forgiveness of sins is granted, and salvation is proclaimed everywhere. But how is this so? Because the heavens—that is, the apostles, who [Col. 0329C] shower us with teachings so that the Church’s crop may spring up throughout the whole world—were established by the Word of the Lord, that is, by the Father’s wisdom: they were fully instructed by bodily companionship with Him who is the Father’s Word, who taught them by inward inspiration and outward preaching. And afterward their strength, which they possessed, was strengthened by the spirit of His mouth, that is, by the Spirit of the Son, from whom it had been given; and not a part, but all of it: both their teaching and their miracles were given and confirmed by the Holy Spirit. They were so thoroughly confirmed by Him that they went confidently among wolves and, though living among them, endured.

From whom did they receive so great a power, if not from Him who sent them? “Behold,” He says, “I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves” (Matt. 10). Observe whom He sends, and where He sends them. He certainly sends sheep, and sends them into the midst of wolves. If one wolf were sent into the midst of innumerable sheep, which of them could resist him? What would he not throw into confusion? He would devour them all—unless perhaps he were quickly satisfied. But Christ sent weak persons among the savage, who seized them, handed them over to authorities, and inflicted afflictions upon them. Yet by a power not their own, but that of the Spirit speaking in them, they did not fail: the sheep conquered the wolves, and filled with sheep a world full of wolves. At that time the sea of persecutors raged with enormous waves; the earth thirsted for the heaven of God. But now, through the sufferings of those who broke through the battle-line, Christ’s name has been glorified and raised above the heads of the swelling billows. Hence the salt water of the sea that remains in Christians no longer dares to rage openly; [Col. 0330A] rather, a hidden murmur roars within them, and the enclosed brine growls beneath mortal skin.

Therefore he adds, “Gathering,” etc., as though he said: The apostles’ strength was established by God’s Spirit; and once it was established, the Lord also became one “gathering the waters,” etc. For if bitterness is afterward covered by skin, a deadly plague covers bitter thought. For now the wicked, fearing for their own skin, keep within the evils which they dare not emit; concerning them the Lord utters: “May He who knows the secrets of all hearts correct you.” Hence he adds: “placing the abysses,” that is, the very wicked, “in His treasuries,” because for a time He grants them power to do and say things by which the good are instructed. And because there is still water in the bottle, although enclosed, therefore let all the earth fear the Lord: let there be no carefree and sluggish [Col. 0330B] joy; and if it rejoices in the mercy with which the earth is full, let it fear lest its joy be proud. This is so because the water is in the bottle, and the abysses are in treasuries.

Or thus: “gathering,” as though he said: He established the heavens—that is, the apostles—and through the heavens so established He gathers the waters of the sea as in a bottle: [Cassiod., Alcuin.] that is, He gathers and makes firm the fluctuating peoples in the unity of faith, hope, and charity—that is, in the Church, in which the flesh is dead. He also places the abysses—that is, those deep in the darkness of vices—in treasuries: [Alcuin.] that is, He places them among those who are a treasure, through whom He enriches others with wisdom. Such was Paul, who from an abyss became a treasure: from a persecutor, an apostle; from crystal, a morsel (bucella). Therefore, “Let all the earth fear the Lord,” etc.: that is, the Church made from the sea, that is, from the fluctuating people.

Or, “in His treasuries” means in the treasuries of His wisdom and knowledge—[Cassiod.] that is, in His Scriptures, containing His wisdom—“You place abysses,” that is, profound heights, so that whoever examines the Scriptures with zeal for piety may prove them. [Hier., Alcuin.] Or thus: “gathering,” as though he said: The heavens—that is, the apostles—were established by God’s Word; and He is not merely powerful over those whom He loves and establishes, but also gathers the waters of the sea as in a bottle. That is, He holds the open persecutors of the Church as in a bottle, since they do nothing except what they are permitted; and He places them in His treasuries, in order to bestow gifts upon His soldiers from them, while allowing them to scourge the sons whom He receives. Therefore let all the earth fear not them but the Lord.

[Col. 0330D] This interpretation differs from the second, because there the waters of the sea signify evil Christians and heretics, whereas here they signify open persecutors, such as Jews and Gentiles. Or thus: He is “gathering the waters of the sea as in a bottle,” that is, gathering the peoples of the world in the confession of sin put to death, lest they flow away freely. And He places the abysses in treasuries, because He keeps His hidden things for them as riches—things which eye has not seen nor ear heard (1 Cor. 2). Therefore let all the earth fear the Lord, and nothing else; that is, every human being.

I say, let it fear—indeed, let it be moved, as if by the hand of God’s mercy. [Alcuin.] This is said by comparison with a sleeping person who is shaken in order to awaken: so God’s grace moves people so that they may keep watch, mingling love with fear. As though he said: [Gl. int.] Certainly all who inhabit the world, namely [Col. 0331A] the universal Church—that is, all who stand in the perfection of the other faithful—must be moved. I say, moved not by another, but by Him alone. [Cassiod.] He says this because something may also be moved by the devil; but what is moved by God is moved beneficially, and what is moved by the devil is moved uselessly. [Aug.] Therefore let them be moved by Him, not by human terrors or by any creature—lion, serpent, devil, and the like. If such things rage, fear God, not them, because all things are under Him. And what is there to fear from all these things? Nothing.

### Verse 9

> “For He spoke, and they were made; He commanded, and they were created.”

“For He spoke and they were made.” [Aug.] As though he said: Therefore they can do nothing except what He permits.
