You may have the desire to harm through yourself; but unless He gives you the power to harm, you do not have it, because “there is no power except from God” (Rom. 13); but wicked desire, which is not from God, does exist. Yet it does no harm if He from whom all power comes does not permit it. Therefore God, standing as man before a man, said: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19). For a human being does not have such power unless he receives it from above. Nor could even the devil take away one little sheep from the holy man Job unless he first said: “Stretch out Your hand” (Job 1), that is, give permission. Therefore Job himself, instructed by this, did not say, “The Lord gave and the devil took away,” but, “The Lord gave, and the Lord took away” (ibid.).

Therefore let all be moved by Him. By Him, because no other made the things [Col. 0331C] they fear, but He alone created them. “For He spoke,” [Gl. int.] that is, willed, “and they were made,” that is, formed from unformed matter; “He commanded,” [Alcuin.] that is, commanded by His Word, “and they were created,” unformed from nothing. These words indicate the creation and formation of things. Or they indicate creation and formation together, and re-creation. First, creation and formation when He says, “He spoke and they were made,” that is, created and formed. Then re-creation when He says, “He commanded,” namely, the law [Cassiod.] through the prophets; “and they were created,” that is, believers were created through it in good works.

### Verse 10

> “The Lord frustrates the counsels of the nations; moreover, He rejects the thoughts of peoples, and [Col. 0331D] rejects the counsels of rulers.”

“The Lord frustrates.” [Cassiod., Alcuin.] As though he said: He not only permits the wicked, when He wills, to do harm; He also makes the wicked cease from doing harm when He wills. This is what He says: “The Lord frustrates” the counsels made against Himself and His own, so that they have no effect. The counsels, I say, “of the nations”: [Aug.] that is, of the Jews, who seek not His kingdom but their own. And He not only frustrates them, but also rejects “the thoughts of peoples,” that is, of the Jews, who think of earthly matters. For although the Jews devised many schemes to remove the Christian name from the earth, the Church nevertheless grew.

Or distinguish nations from peoples, so that by “nations” you understand the Gentile people and by “peoples” the Jewish people. Thus: He “frustrates the counsels of the nations,” that is, of the Gentile people, [Cassiod.] when He destroyed idolatry. “Moreover, He rejects the thoughts of peoples,” [Aug.] that is, of the Jews: although their will was fulfilled in killing Christ, it was rejected in His resurrection. And He rejects also “the counsels of rulers,” that is, the tyrants of this age, or the demons who seek to rule such peoples.

### Verse 11

> “But the counsel of the Lord remains forever; the thoughts of His heart from generation to generation.”

“But the counsel of the Lord.” [Aug.] As though he said: He rejects their counsels; but the Lord’s counsel, by which He makes no one blessed unless that person is subject to Him, remains forever, [Cassiod.] because it is dissolved by no passage of time. And “the thoughts of His heart,” [Aug.] that is, the thoughts [Col. 0332B] of His wisdom, are from generation to generation: that is, they are not changeable but eternal.

Or, “the counsel of the Lord remains forever”: [Cassiod.] the mystery of the Incarnation, in which He takes thought for humankind, remains forever and avails for our attaining eternal salvation. And “the thoughts of His heart are from generation to generation,” [Aug.] that is, His predestination is immutable, and all things are laid up in it; they remain exactly as they were foreseen.

### Verse 12

> “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord; the people whom He chose for His inheritance.”

“Blessed is the nation.” [Cassiod.] This is the second part, in which he calls blessed the person who attains God’s worship. This happens in Christian times, in which the nations have been converted. These are the righteous and upright, whom praise befits. [Col. 0332C] As though he said: “The counsel of the Lord remains forever”; this is God’s counsel: that “Blessed is the nation,” etc., that is, only the one who obeys Him is made blessed.

Or continue thus: because the Lord’s counsel is forever, therefore this nation alone among all nations is blessed, whose God is its Lord: [Aug.] that is, which chose no lord for itself except its own God, from whom it lives and whom it worships. Thus God is its possession and inheritance; nor was it chosen from itself, but by God, so that it might itself be God’s inheritance, and thereby blessed. Hence follows: “Blessed is the people whom the Lord chose for His inheritance,” which He cultivates, so that by possessing it He may not allow it to remain uncultivated and wretched.

Behold, the needy person possesses God, and is likewise possessed by Him. Thus God is both possessor and possession: possession, because we live from Him as from our bread; possessor, because He cultivates us as His land and uproots what is crooked. In both respects it is not God but the human being who profits. Blessed is the nation because God is its possession; blessed is the people because God is its possessor. For no human being is blessed except through that which is better than himself, by which the human being himself may become better. If, therefore, you wish to become better than you are, seek what is better than you; from it you will become better than yourself, and blessed.

But do not seek that thing outside yourself, because what you seek is within yourself, if you desire to be blessed. Do not seek it in your body; seek in your very soul what is better. For all blessedness is in your soul, because the soul is naturally capable of blessedness, able to enjoy it; and through the illumination of grace it understands what true [Col. 0333A] blessedness is and merits it. Through that illumination the body subject to it also merits incorruption, so that the restoration of the lower—the body—may take place through the better, the soul. For the body becomes better and glorious through the soul, which is better than the body; and a human being is never made blessed through what is lower than himself or herself. Therefore this does not occur through anything earthly, nor even through an equal, such as the angels, with whom human nature will be made equal when it has been rendered incorruptible, but through that which is better than the soul, which is above it.

This is God, who made him, and He Himself is blessedness. You will see Him; you will possess Him. Raise yourself, then, to Him, whom you will have whenever you will it, because the restorer of your soul comes to you—the One who was formerly its maker. The soul is not made better through the body; rather, through the righteous soul the body will become immortal. But the soul is righteous from God, whose image is in it, by which it is like the angels. Therefore God is the human being’s highest good.

### Verse 13

> “From heaven the Lord looked down; He saw all the children of men.”

[Aug.] “From heaven” shows how God chose a people for His inheritance: namely, from heaven—that is, from Christ as man—the Lord looked down at the coming of the Son, [Cassiod.] and mercifully saw, not sins, from which He turns away His face, [Aug.] but all the children of men: that is, all who wish to be reborn into new life and belong to the Son of Man. And:

### Verse 14

> “From His prepared dwelling-place He looked upon all who inhabit the earth.”

[Col. 0333C] “From His prepared dwelling-place.” [Aug.] That is, from the dwelling-place of assumed human nature, which God prepared for Himself; [Alcuin.] for it came to be only through the Father’s preparation. Or, “prepared” means [Cassiod.] foreseen for the salvation of the world. God “looked,” [Aug.] that is, mercifully saw, “upon all,” so as to preside over and govern those who inhabit the earth, that is, throughout all lands. Or, He looked upon “those who inhabit the earth,” that is, those who cultivate the flesh. And this is true because He is:

### Verse 15

> “He who formed their hearts one by one; He who understands all their works.”

“He who formed,” [Aug.] that is, fashioned by the hand of grace, “their hearts one by one,” giving to each individual particular gifts, because He bestows proper gifts upon each individual heart. [Col. 0333D] [Gl. int.] Yet through this the unity of the body—that is, the Church—comes about. And He is the one “who understands all their works,” that is, knows how each person uses those gifts.

Or, by “heaven” and “dwelling-place” holy angels may be understood. Thus: “From heaven,” [Aug., Alcuin.] that is, from the righteous soul and angelic mind, the Lord looked mercifully; and “He saw all the children of men.” This does not change. “From His prepared dwelling-place”: God’s dwelling-place is the angels and all whom He sends to preach, especially the apostles, prepared by the teaching and grace of the Holy Spirit for the calling of others, through which He had mercy upon all. This is the meaning: “From His prepared dwelling-place,” from the angels and all whom He sends, “He looked upon all who inhabit the earth,” that is, He had mercy upon all who cultivate the earth of the flesh, [Col. 0334A] whom through them He called to life. Nor did He merely call them through these messengers: He Himself “formed one by one,” that is, their individual hearts; [Cassiod.] that is, He inspired every good will in them. And He Himself “understands,” [Aug.] that is, more secretly and inwardly sees all their works and the end for which they are done; for with Him their works are acts of understanding, that is, He knows the intentions of those works as He knows the works themselves.

Or, literally, “He formed their hearts”: [Hier.] that is, He created souls, “one by one,” that is, each separately from nothing, not from Adam, as some say, imagining that soul comes from soul. And He “understands all His works,” that is, He knows all souls together and their actions.

### Verse 16

> “A king is not saved by great power, nor shall a giant be saved by the abundance of his strength.”

“He is not saved.” [Alcuin.] Having said that spiritual things come from God, he now adds that bodily things too come from God: namely, bodily safety and the other things contained in these three categories—power, bodily strength, and riches. He indicates these three by the three words he introduces: king, giant, horse. As though he said: God gives not only spiritual things but also outward safety. For no one has it except from Him. Thus one powerful as a king is not saved with bodily safety through great power, that is, through his own power; a giant—that is, some proud person exalting himself against God, strong in bodily powers as a giant—shall not be saved by the abundance of his own strength. Nor will a rich person be saved [Col. 0334C] by his riches, which are signified by the horse. Hence follows:

### Verse 17

> “The horse is deceptive for safety; and in the abundance of its strength it shall not be saved.”

“The horse is deceptive.” [Aug.] A horse is an animal in whose speed and strength one puts confidence; figuratively, it denotes every worldly eminence by which one is made proud. But the higher you raise yourself in it, the more grievously you fall. [Cassiod.] Human prosperity is therefore appropriately called a horse: it carries people, and while it hastens too greatly, it falls like a horse and loses its rider.

Read the text and supply “but” from the lower [reading; perhaps “higher”]: as though he said: Safety lies not merely in power or bodily strength; the horse too is deceptive for safety—that is, the proud power of worldly prosperity deceives and lies to a human being concerning outward safety. For its rider is not saved “in the abundance of its strength”; [Hier.] that is, the rider of it is not saved through it. The horse is the human body, which, however beautiful and well-formed it may be, is nevertheless deceptive [Col. 0334D] for spiritual or bodily salvation.

Or thus: “He is not saved” concerns spiritual things here. For just as above he said how the righteous are made by God through grace, so here he says that, after being made, they are aided by the same One beyond what they have become, and preserved in the good. As though he said: The righteous are made, but even once made, they are not saved by their own strength, because “a king is not saved,” etc.

Or continue thus: since good will and every good thing come from God, [Aug.] therefore whoever is a king—that is, whoever rules his own flesh by mortifying its vices and desires—is not saved through his own great strength, if he presumes on his own power and ascribes it to himself rather than God, because he will not gain a reward from his own strength. And the giant—that is, whoever fights against the devil or against his own desire—shall not be saved through the abundance of his own strength, if he attributes it to his own courage and not to God.

“Deceptive,” as though he said: he will not be saved by his own strength; rather, if he mounts a horse—that is, the proud opinion that he is saved by his own strength—he is deceived. For the horse, that is, proud opinion, is deceptive for salvation. Whoever thinks that he is saved through himself or through a human being is deceived, because he will not be saved, even if he possesses strength not merely in part but “in abundance,” so as to ascribe it to himself. From where, then, are we saved?

### Verse 18

> “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear Him, and upon those who hope in His mercy.”

“Behold, the eyes of the Lord.” Or join it thus: No one is saved by his own strength; [Cassiod.] but behold whence salvation comes: the eyes of the Lord—that is, God’s love, namely, the regard of divinity which protects—are upon those who fear Him, not upon those who presume on themselves, and upon those who hope not in their own powers or merits, but in His mercy. Observe that fear of God and hope are always joined. The Lord’s eyes are upon those who fear and hope in order that:

### Verse 19

> “He may deliver their souls from death and feed them in famine.”

He may finally deliver their souls from death, giving them eternal life, and meanwhile here feed them with His Word and eternal truth, [Col. 0335C] since they are in hunger for righteousness: that is, they hunger and thirst for righteousness. [Cassiod.] These are the two desires of the faithful, indicated here: that in the judgment they may be delivered from eternal death, and that here they may be nourished with spiritual things, where there is need of good things.

Or the whole passage may be taken as referring to the present: that He may deliver their souls from death here, not their bodies, and feed them in famine. These points do not change.

## Part II. Verse 20

> “Our soul waits for the Lord, for He is our helper and protector.”

“Our soul.” [Alcuin.] This is the third part, where he shows what he thinks of the matters already stated. It is, as it were, a conclusion of what precedes. [Aug.] As though he said: He now feeds us in hunger, but in order that our soul may afterward be perfectly satisfied with incorruptible foods, it waits for the Lord. [Col. 0335D] Or continue thus: “that He may deliver from death”: expecting this, our soul waits for the Lord. Or thus I say, He delivers the soul; for this reason our soul meanwhile waits for the Lord—that is, is patient. And it can wait because He is our helper while we strive toward God, and our protector while we resist the enemy.

### Verse 21

> “For in Him our heart shall rejoice, and in His holy name we have hoped.”

“For in Him,” etc. [Gl. int.] As though he said: Therefore we must wait, because our heart shall then rejoice fully in Him, [Aug.] not in ourselves, where there is want; and now we have hoped that we shall come to God in the future, not through our own merits but in His holy name—that is, [Col. 0336A] because, while we were absent through faith, He sent us His name, that is, His Son. Then he adds a prayer:

### Verse 22

> “Let Your mercy be upon us, O Lord, according as we have hoped in You.”

“Let Your mercy be.” As though he said: As we have hoped, let Your mercy, O Lord, be upon us: that is, through Your mercy let this be fulfilled in us, namely that in the future we may rejoice in You. By what merit? Behold, “according as we have hoped in You”; for hope does not disappoint.

Or thus: [Cassiod.] “for in Him”: because he had said that we wait, lest anyone murmur at patience, he adds the gift, namely that the heart rejoices here in the Lord. As though he said: Therefore we must wait, because, while we wait, our heart shall rejoice in Him, [Aug.] not in ourselves, where there is great want without Him. And “we have hoped in His holy name,” [Cassiod.] namely, in the name of Christ, whose coming the Prophet joyfully awaited in patience.

By “we have hoped,” he indicates the continual time of hope in which the ancient righteous desired Christ’s coming until He came, because it is not permitted to cease from hope until its fulfillment. It follows: “Let [Your mercy] be,” as though he said: As we have hoped, so let Your mercy, O Lord, be upon us. The Prophet desires the incarnation of Christ to be fulfilled, so that he may be made perfect. By what merit? “According as”: let it be so, and let it occur for this reason, because we have hoped not in another but in You. He says this in order that every superstition and perversity may be excluded.

## Comparison on Psalm 32: “Rejoice, O righteous.”

[Col. 0336C] **Verse 7.** “Gathering the waters of the sea as in a bottle.” Those who read **NED** render it “as a heap” or “mass.” But those who read **NOD** translate it as “a bottle,” as Jerome and the Seventy do; Nebiensis agrees. The difference is of little importance for the sense, just as in verse 9 the Hebrews say, “He commanded and it stood,” where we say, “He commanded and they were created”; for the meaning agrees, though the manner of expression differs. This indicates that nothing can subsist apart from God’s power: for as soon as God withdraws His hand, all things would immediately be reduced to nothing.

**Verse 15.** “He who formed their hearts one by one.” Hebraists render **JAHAD** as “together” or “simultaneously,” whereas we say “one by one.” But because the Hebrew particle is ambiguous, signifying singularity as well as equality—or, if one may speak so, simultaneity—the Seventy interpreters more suitably translated it “one by one” or “individually,” lest they seem to lend support to two errors. The first, later attributed to Origen and the Priscillianists, asserts that souls existed [Col. 0336D] before being infused into bodies. The second, which Augustine writes in chapter 86 of *On Heresies* was originated by Tertullian, maintains: “The error was that the child’s soul is generated from the father’s soul, just as body from body.” But when you hear the Seventy say that He “formed their hearts one by one” or “individually,” they leave no support from this passage for such madness. Nebiensis agrees with us.

**Verse 17.** “In the abundance of its strength it shall not be saved.” The Hebrews have the active form, “it shall not save.” Munster adds “anyone” on his own authority. Faber mocks our reading as though it meant that the horse, incapable of blessedness, was not saved—a statement, he says, unworthy of a prophet, since no philosopher, however dull, ever failed to know that. Therefore, to avoid this difficulty, he urges that henceforth we should sing, “In the abundance of its strength it shall not save.” The blind Burgensis has kneaded the same dough. O charming intellect! Do you not understand that, according to Augustine’s interpretation, the horse is taken metaphorically [Col. 0337A] for every worldly eminence and proud dignity? Certainly the higher it is, the more dangerous it is. As for the Hebrew grammatical point, the letters are altogether the same [Col. 0338A] in the active and passive senses. You may read **JEMALLET** or **JEMULLAT**, the former actively and the latter passively.

# Psalm 33

[Col. 0337]

## Title of the Psalm

> “A Psalm of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, and he dismissed him, and departed.”

[Col. 0337A]

“I will bless the Lord.” The title: “A Psalm of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, and he dismissed him, and departed.” [Aug.] This title makes us attentive and asks for those who knock. It is drawn from the history in the book of Kings, where it is written that, while David was fleeing Saul his persecutor, [Col. 0337B] he went to Achish, king of Gath—that is, king of a certain people neighboring the kingdom of the Jews—and hid there to escape Saul his persecutor.

It was reported to the king that he had with him the man who had received great glory among the Jewish people. And they said to him: “This is David, for whom the Israelite women made a chorus, saying: ‘Saul struck down a thousand, and David ten thousand’” (1 Sam. 21). On hearing this, David perceived the king’s envy and feared him. Since Saul had begun to envy him because of this glory, David had every reason to fear that the king to whom he had fled might also wish to destroy one whom he could have as a nearby enemy if he kept him safe. [Hier.] Saul had also sent messengers to him, that Achish might hand David over to them [Col. 0337C] to bring to Saul, who wished to kill him. But through God’s providential mercy, which showed him a way of escape, he escaped by feigning madness.

[Aug.] For he changed his countenance before Achish: he acted wildly and drummed at the city gates; he was also carried in his own hands, fell down at the doorway of the gate, and saliva ran down over his beard. When King Achish saw him, he said to his servants: “Why have you brought me this madman? Is he about to enter my house?” And so he dismissed him, casting him out; David departed thence unharmed (1 Sam. 21).

The title appears to refer to this history, nor is there disagreement, except that the one here called Abimelech was properly named Achish, as the history relates. [Col. 0337D] [Alcuin.] But Ezra changed the name for the sake of the sacrament, and we should not suppose that history alone is being narrated. For “all these things happened to them in figure” (1 Cor. 10). [Aug.] We should therefore know that David signifies Christ, and the change of countenance signifies the transformation of the old sacrifice into the new. [Alcuin.] The old sacrifice is called the “countenance” because, in a sign, it indicated God’s will.

Abimelech means “the kingdom of my father” (Luke 1), and signifies the Jews, who were the kingdom of their father, namely David, who was Christ’s father according to the flesh, according to the saying: “God will give Him the throne of David His father.” [Aug.] The Church is a kingdom, not of David its father, but of God the Father. Achish means “How is it?” and thereby are signified those slow disciples to whom, when the Lord said, “Unless you eat [Col. 0338A] My flesh and drink My blood, you have no life in you” (John 6), it seemed that He would give His flesh to be eaten bit by bit. They said: “How can this man give us His flesh to eat? This saying is hard” (ibid.).

In this change of countenance Christ was also ‘affected’ (affectabat)—that is, full of compassionate feeling, because He had compassion on us even to death; and He drummed, because He was stretched out upon the cross like a skin upon wood. And this was at the city gates—that is, at hearts closed to God—in order to open them by the cross. He was carried in His own hands, which cannot be understood literally; but He was carried in His hands when, at the Supper, He offered His body and blood to the apostles, thereby commending humility to humankind. The saliva ran upon His beard: that is, the childish and weak words of the speaker, “This is My body” (Matt. 26), concealed His power, which is understood by the beard. By all these things He fell down at the doorway of the gate: that is, He humbled Himself to the beginning of our faith. For the doorway of the gate is the beginning of faith, where the Church begins and proceeds to sight.

The meaning of the title is this: [Gl. int.] This psalm [Col. 0338C] is attributed to David, that is, to Christ, because the Christian also speaks in Him. For the words of this psalm suit both the members and the head. I say, it is a psalm concerning what He did when He changed His countenance: [Aug.] that is, transformed the old sacrifice into the new. He showed this transformation at the Supper, when, by giving His body and blood to the disciples at the Supper, He commended humility.

I say, He changed it before Abimelech, that is, before the Jews; and David dismissed Abimelech—that is, Christ dismissed the Jews—and went to the Gentiles. Likewise He changed it before Achish, that is, before the ignorant disciples. And Achish, or Abimelech, dismissed David; and he departed—that is, those ignorant disciples dismissed Christ on account of the changed sacrifice [Col. 0338D] and went backward. Or Christ departed from their hearts. Literally, the meaning concerning David is clear: he changed his countenance before Abimelech; Abimelech dismissed him; and David departed unharmed.

This is the second of the psalms written through the imperfect alphabet. **Intention.** [Cassiod.] He urges the mind, not the foot, to approach the new sacrifice. **Method.** [Cassiod.] There are four divisions. First, the Prophet gives a summary preface of praise, urging the meek to do the same. Second, he exhorts the faithful to communion in the new sacrifice, at “Come near.” Third, he instructs beginners from what they must refrain, at “Come, children.” Fourth, he deals with the recompenses of the good and evil, at “The eyes of the Lord.” Thus, beginning from praise, Christ speaks—and the Christian in Him.

[Col. 0339A]

### Verse 1

> “I will bless the Lord at every time; His praise shall always be in my mouth.”

“I will bless,” [Hier.] that is, praise, “the Lord” [Aug.] in heart, mouth, and deed; and not only in prosperity [Gl. int.] but “at every time,” in prosperity and adversity. This did not occur in the time of the former countenance, that is, of the old sacrifice, when carnal persons served for carnal things.

Observe that the Church sings this verse at Sext, the hour when Christ suffered and was lifted up upon the cross. The sun burns hot, because Christ’s passion, proceeding from the fervor of charity, is for us a cause and material of praising the Lord with most ardent love. [Cassiod.] “His praise shall be in my mouth,” in order that I may instruct others. [Aug.] And this “always,” because all that He thinks or says [Col. 0339B] is without fault; and therefore God’s praise is always in Him. But because this is impossible except for one who is humble and commends humility, he adds:

### Verse 2

> “My soul shall be praised in the Lord; let the meek hear and rejoice.”

“My soul shall be praised,” [Cassiod.] not here in myself or in outward things, [Aug.] but in the Lord. For its praise is the proclamation of its Lord, as a good servant glories in the good reputation of his master. [Gl. int.] Whoever does not wish to be praised in the Lord is not meek but proud.

Or it may be understood of the future, as though he said: “I will bless”; therefore, in the future, “my soul shall be praised in the Lord.” Let the meek hear this—not the learned, not those who fast, because they are proud; [Col. 0339C] [Aug.] but the meek, who possess moderation in all things and are gentle in spirit. For one who is not meek becomes angry. [Gl. int.] Let them hear, I say, and not be saddened by this change, but rejoice, because the matter is pleasing to the soul. [Cassiod.] And because spiritual grace does not wish to accomplish alone what benefits many, He calls others, saying: And, O meek ones:

### Verse 3

> “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt His name together.”

“Magnify the Lord.” [Aug.] He says this from the fervor of charity. “Magnify,” I say, “with me”; for He is not a limited thing, but suffices for all. “Let us all exalt His name together,” that is, into one, so that one may be made from all. [Cassiod.] In order to draw all whom he invited, he recounts the good things that came to him from this, adding:

### Verse 4

> “I sought the Lord, and He heard me; and from all my tribulations He delivered me.”

[Aug.] “I sought” inwardly with a clean conscience, not gold or anything else, but the Lord Himself; “and He heard me.” From this it is clear that one who is not heard did not seek Him Himself. “And from all my tribulations”: he says this because, after a pure heart and a clean conscience, tribulations remain. But this holy person says, “from all He delivered me”: that is, He will deliver me in the future, when this mortal nature has put on immortality. [Cassiod.] “From all” is said universally because the deliverances cannot be stated particularly, that is, one by one: how many things he has obtained, or from how many things he has obtained deliverance, he who sought nothing other than God.

## Part II. Verse 5

> “Come near to Him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be put to shame.”

Draw near. [Cassiodorus.] In the second part, after the praises already set forth, he now individually urges the saints concerning the new countenance; [Alcuin] he exhorts them to communion in the true sacrifice. [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: I say, “Magnify,” and if this seems at first unpleasant, draw nearer to him. He exhorts others by saying what he himself has experienced. [Augustine.] Or connect it thus: I say, “Magnify”; and in what order? [Alcuin.] Behold: draw near to him, [Augustine] by cleaving to him in faith and running with the two feet of double love; and, receiving him, be enlightened, lest you become blind like the Jews, who were darkened concerning the Crucified One [Col. 0340B]: we, by eating and drinking the Crucified One, are enlightened. And after the light, your faces, [Cassiodorus] that is, your minds, shall not be put to shame at the future judgment; nor shall they be disappointed in their expectation, for those who are deceived blush, but you shall obtain what you seek. Or even here in the present, your minds shall not be put to shame amid adversities. [Augustine.] For whatever happens here to the righteous person, he is not ashamed: even if among men he is judged inferior to his enemy, he is nevertheless always superior before God. But the proud person is ashamed in adversity, because he has not drawn near to the Lord. [Gloss, interlinear.] Or, if you draw near in faith, your minds shall not be put to shame, like those who, when they heard that Christ would give his flesh to be eaten, said, “This saying is hard” (John 6), and went back in confusion.

[Col. 0340C] VERSE 6.—“This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him; and saved him out of all his tribulations.”

This poor man, [Jerome] as though he said: Truly those who draw near shall not be put to shame, because this poor man—that is, the spiritually poor man, namely I, David, or Christ, or the Church—cried, and the Lord heard him. [Augustine.] Here he shows how you are heard: namely, if you are poor in spirit; the rich person is not heard. But this is the manner of being heard: if someone is spiritually poor. [Cassiodorus.] Hence he draws near to God and is enlightened; nor does he blush, because when he cries out, he is delivered from all the straits of this age, while he now passes over to God; and he saved him out of all his tribulations [Col. 0340D], as he passes over to himself at death. But how is this? Behold:

VERSE 7.—“The angel of the Lord shall encamp round about those who fear him, and shall deliver them.”

The angel of the Lord shall encamp. Or continue it thus. [Alcuin.] I say, “Draw near”; and just as this poor man cried and was heard, in the same way the angel of the Lord, [Augustine] that is, Christ, who is the Angel of Great Counsel; or some angel from heaven, who is the rampart of the Church; [Jerome] or a man who is a minister of God’s will, shall encamp. [Cassiodorus.] That is, he shall make an encampment purely around those who fear him, in order to fortify them here; and in the future he shall deliver them. [Alcuin.] Other interpreters agreeing with this sense have translated: “The angel of the Lord encamps in a circle around those who fear him.” [Augustine.] But some corrupt manuscripts [Col. 0341A] have: “The Lord sends an angel,” etc.

VERSE 8.—“Taste, and see that the Lord is sweet; blessed is the man who hopes in him.”

Taste. [Augustine.] Here he plainly treats of the sacrament which was carried in the hands. [Gloss, interlinear.] As though he said: Do not merely draw near in order to believe, but taste the flesh and blood of Christ, and thus see—[Cassiodorus] that is, understand—that God is sweet; [Alcuin] that is, a sweet food, which is life to the one receiving it, banishing every affliction in the future. [Cassiodorus.] For God is life and truth. [Augustine.] And because God is life, the flesh which he united to himself is life-giving. But if you do not yet understand these things, Achish—that is, ignorance—reigns in you, and David—that is, Christ, the truth—has departed from you. Blessed, [Col. 0341B] etc.: as though he said, I say, “Taste,” and hope in that which you taste, because blessed shall be the man who hopes in that which he tastes: through this hope, that is, eternal life, in the future. Or thus: “Blessed”—as though he said, the Lord is sweet, and hope in him, because even now blessed is the man who hopes in him; miserable is the one who hopes in himself or in other people. [Gloss, interlinear.] But one who hopes in him is already blessed, because in hope he already possesses him who is every good. And because he wishes all to be watchful, he adds: “And, O you,”

VERSE 9.—“Fear the Lord, all his saints, because there is no want to those who fear him.”

[Gloss, interlinear.] All his saints, fear the Lord, [Cassiodorus] so that one who stands may see that he does not fall. [Jerome.] And he adds “all,” so that no one, however well deserving, may cease from this [Col. 0341C] or presume upon security. Therefore fear the Lord, because those who fear him have no lack of temporal things. Others are in want of something, but his saints are not, to whom he himself says: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added unto you” (Matt. 6). [Augustine.] Did the Lord feed the person who despised him and abandon the one who feared him? Therefore do not abandon God, lest you suffer hunger. For many abandon God lest they become poor. [Alcuin.] But he promises not superfluities, but necessities, because those who fear God lack nothing; but:

VERSE 10.—“The rich have lacked and hungered; but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing.”

The rich of this age, [Gloss, interlinear] that is, the proud, have lacked and [Col. 0341D] hungered, because they even lack temporal bread and sometimes suffer want. Or rather, this must be understood of spiritual goods. [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: Therefore fear him, because those who fear him have no lack of spiritual and true good; but the rich of this age—that is, the proud—have lacked inward goods. For you must not think this is said of earthly things, which are of no value, but of spiritual things. [Augustine.] Look, indeed, at many wicked rich men dying amid their riches, who did not become poor while they lived; but they are borne through great abundance of wealth to the very end of life, breathe out their last on ivory beds with their household flowing about them, have a magnificent funeral procession celebrated, and after a splendid funeral are carried to the tomb by their own people. Therefore do not let Scripture deceive you here: understand spiritually [Col. 0342A] what it says, “The rich have lacked.” [Cassiodorus.] For they do not possess faith, which is the substance of things hoped for (Heb. 11). And “they have hungered,” [Alcuin] because they are not filled with the Lord’s body. For what do they possess who do not possess God? Or, “the rich have lacked,” that is, in the future they shall be deprived of the highest good, namely God, though they hunger—that is, desire it. [Gloss, interlinear.] Hence it adds, “and yet they have hungered,” that is, they have desired by the endowment of nature. “But those who seek.” [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: The rich have lacked; but those who seek—that is, seek the Lord wholly earnestly, and nothing else—shall lack no good thing; that is, without diminution they shall possess the good which is every good, because in God are all good things, since he is the author of all and complete sufficiency.

[Col. 0342B] PART III, *diapsalma*, VERSE 11.—“Come, children, hear me: I will teach you the fear of the Lord.”

Come. [Cassiodorus.] The third part. Having discussed above the sacraments of the Church, he now admonishes those as though they were outside—that is, beginners receiving the first rudiments of faith—what they should abstain from. As though he said: I say, “Fear”; but that you may know how to fear, O children, that is, learners—for it is the prophetic custom to call disciples children—come. [Jerome.] Hear me in faith, that is, learn from me; and lest the name of fear be dreaded, he adds, I will teach you, children, [Cassiodorus, Gloss, interlinear] whom I would not teach unless it were something useful, namely the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom. [Jerome, Gloss, interlinear.] As though he said: Learn fear, and you ought to do so, because in it is life; as he says thus:

[Col. 0342C] VERSE 12.—“What man is he that desires life, and loves to see good days?”

Who is the man who desires eternal life, and who loves to see good days, which are never found in this age? [Augustine.] All confess that they wish this: they desire a good thing, but do not seek it in its own country. It is as if you sought some righteous man, but not in the land where he lived, and you were told: “You seek a good and great man, but do not seek him here, where you will not find him.” Thus we too should seek life, but not here. And as though someone said, “Why do you seek this?” he answers:

VERSE 13.—“Keep your tongue from evil, and let not your lips speak deceit.”

[Col. 0342D] Keep your tongue, showing how they ought to fear. [Alcuin.] As though he said: Whoever you are who desire eternal life, fear in this way: namely, keep your tongue, concerning which Solomon says in Proverbs, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. 18), from every evil. [Jerome.] Lest you speak evil openly, keep your lips from speaking deceit—that is, from speaking good things deceitfully. [Gloss, interlinear.] Note that he says first, “Restrain the tongue,” and then, “the lips,” [Cassiodorus] because when we intend to speak, we move the tongue first, and afterward the lips follow the tongue’s movement.

VERSE 14.—“Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace, and pursue it.”

Turn away from evil and do good, [Augustine] that is, harm no one by deed. And because this is not enough, he adds, “and do good.” It is too little not to strip a clothed person; clothe the naked person. If you have not stripped him, you have turned away from evil; but you do not do good unless you clothe the naked and receive the stranger into your house. [Cassiodorus.] Therefore there are two good acts: turn away from evil and do good. The former avoids guilt; the latter earns the palm.

And note that there is one manner of turning away from evil by which punishment alone is avoided, and another by which life too is acquired. For if someone, with no occasion provoking him to evil, turns away from an evil deed, he certainly avoids the punishment that he would have incurred had he committed it. But if, provoked or harmed by an invisible or visible enemy, he does not repay evil, or does not consent to evil, he has turned away from evil and earned the palm. Or thus: Turn away from evil, [Jerome] that is, destroy vices within yourself; and [Col. 0343B] do good, that is, build virtues; and thus seek peace, [Cassiodorus] that is, desire that your spirit may have peace with the flesh. He says “seek” because here the righteous person never has complete peace with his body, but is always at war with vices. Therefore he commands that peace always be sought here, even though it cannot be fully possessed here. Hence he adds: “And pursue it” as it flees—that is, persevere in seeking it. Otherwise it will not be attained in the future. Or, “Seek peace,” [Augustine] that is, God himself, who is our peace. And because you will not have it here, pursue it into heaven, where it has gone before.

PART IV. VERSE 15.—“The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are unto their prayers.”

The eyes of the Lord. [Cassiodorus.] The fourth part, where he treats of the tribulations of good and evil persons, lest the righteous person grow weak in any uncertainty amid dangers. As though he said: I say, “Turn away from evil; seek peace”; and lest you lose confidence because of your weakness, the eyes of the Lord, [Augustine] that is, the gaze of God’s mercy, are upon the righteous. Even though, like a physician, he cuts and burns, and thus seems not to hear, he does this in order to heal and bring forth unto eternity; and his ears are unto their prayers, so that he grants what they ask, [Gloss, interlinear] namely grace for grace. And note that he does not say “to their prayers,” but “in their prayers,” [Cassiodorus] indicating the swiftness of his hearing, since the hearer dwells within the prayers themselves. [Augustine.] But perhaps the wicked person says: “I safely do evil, because the Lord’s eyes are not upon me; God attends to the righteous, but he does not see me.” Therefore he adds:

[Col. 0343D] VERSE 16.—“But the countenance of the Lord is upon those who do evil, to destroy their remembrance from the earth.”

But the countenance. [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: God regards the righteous; but neither should the wicked suppose that he is unknown, because the countenance of the Lord—that is, God’s knowledge—is upon those who do evil. Yet he does not look on them mercifully, namely in order to hear them, but knows them in order to punish them. Hence he adds: “To destroy their remembrance from the land of the living,” [Alcuin] namely that no mention—that is, no intercession—may be made for them among the good. God’s justice so greatly pleases the good. Hence Abraham says to the rich man in the Gospel: “A great chasm has been fixed between us and you” (Luke 16), so that the good cannot cross to them with any fellow-feeling because of the disgrace of the sins which they have committed. [Col. 0344A] And truly the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, because:

VERSE 17.—“The righteous cried, and the Lord heard them, and delivered them out of all their tribulations.”

The righteous of old, [Gloss, interlinear] such as Abraham and the rest, cried to the Lord for their deliverance; and the Lord—that is, Christ—heard them in his resurrection, and delivered them out of all their tribulations when he led captivity captive (Eph. 4). Or he delivered them bodily: [Augustine] thus the flame could not harm the three children in the furnace, and in their praises the fires grew cold; so he delivered others also.

VERSE 18.—“The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit.”

The Lord is near. [Alcuin.] As though he said: As the Lord heard the righteous in the Old Testament, so also in the New Testament the Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart—not to all troubled in body, but to those troubled in heart, namely those who wear down the hardness of their heart—and he will save those humble in spirit, not merely humble in words; which is necessary, because:

VERSE 19.—“Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and out of all these the Lord will deliver them.”

Many are the tribulations. Or this may be understood of modern righteous persons, and of the spiritual deliverance by which they have been delivered, [Cassiodorus] not so that they did not feel tribulations, but so that, by bearing them bravely, they did not succumb. And this is what it means: “The righteous cried, and the Lord heard them.” [Col. 0344C] [Augustine, Alcuin.] He heard them in such a way that he delivered them, not bodily, but by giving them patience. And this is what follows: “And out of all their tribulations he delivered them,” at least spiritually. And truly he delivered them, for he is inclined to do this. And this is what he says: “The Lord is near”; or it is an allusion to what he had said, “The righteous cried,” as though he said: They cried, and the Lord is near to those troubled in heart. [Augustine.] The Lord indeed is high, but he draws near to the humble person and not to one who exalts himself. Hence he adds: “And he will save the humble in spirit”; this does not change. “Many are the tribulations”: as though he said, he will save the humble, certainly not so that they suffer nothing, because the tribulations of the righteous [Cassiodorus] are many: from the devil, from envious people, [Col. 0344D] and from themselves. Therefore whoever does not suffer is not righteous, because the tribulations of the righteous are many. [Augustine.] By contrast, those of the wicked are fewer; and out of all these the Lord will deliver them in the future. The Lord is a mighty deliverer; meanwhile:

VERSE 20.—“The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them shall be broken.”

The Lord guards all their bones, that is, the supports of faith—namely patience and the other virtues—and not one of them shall be broken. [Augustine.] That is, not even patience shall perish. This was signified in the paschal lamb, concerning which Exodus says: “You shall not break a bone of it” (Exod. 12). This was fulfilled in our Lord Jesus Christ, whose legs were not broken on the cross, and is fulfilled in his saints, whose patience [Col. 0345A] is exercised amid tribulations but not overcome.

VERSE 21.—“The death of sinners is most grievous; and those who hate the righteous shall offend.”

The death of sinners: as though he said, the Lord guards the righteous and will deliver them; [Augustine] but the death of sinners is not merely evil but most grievous, because it carries them off to hell. Even if it ends amid riches, perfumes, and the lamentations of people, it is nevertheless most grievous because it is in sins and draws them to the underworld. And he says this in contrast to what he had said of the good: “He will deliver them.” And because all are sinners, he specifies whose sinners’ death is most grievous, saying: “and those who hate,” etc. And as though someone said, “Whose sinners’ death is most grievous?” the answer is: Not everyone’s, [Col. 0345B] because all are sinners, but that of those who hate the righteous one, that is, Christ, who justifies; whoever is not reconciled through him perishes. For they shall offend—that is, abandon the Lord—by hating the good. This is contrary to what he had said above of the good, namely, “The Lord guards all their bones.”

VERSE 22.—“The Lord will redeem the souls of his servants; and none of those who hope in him shall offend.”

The Lord will redeem. [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: The death of sinners is most grievous, but the Lord will redeem, at the price of death, the souls not of freedmen—that is, of those who from being servants of God have made themselves free—but of his servants who obey him; and all who hope in him, though they are not without sin, nevertheless shall not offend, [Col. 0345C] [Remigius] that is, shall not sin unto death. For this is the measure of human righteousness: however much mortal life progresses, since it cannot be without sin, it does not offend in this—that is, it guards against this mortal sin—while, that is, because it hopes in him in whom there is remission of sins.

## COLLATION ON PSALM XXXIII: “I WILL BLESS THE LORD”

In the title: “Your countenance.” Jerome: “his mouth”; Sanctes: “his word”; Münster: “his utterance”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “his meaning”; Pagninus: “his taste.” Münster indicates, following the opinion of some, that it signifies vision or counsel. Pellicanus also teaches that it can be understood as “rite and custom.” Finally, what is to be understood, and how, you have clearly in 1 Samuel 21, lest you be tossed about amid so great a variety.

“Draw near to him and be enlightened.” Jerome: “Look to him and stream together”; Pagninus: “They looked to him and ran”; Münster, Sanctes, and the interpreters for Cajetan: “They looked to him and were enlightened.” First, Jerome and the Septuagint translated in the imperative, second person, whereas the other modern translators use the indicative, third person. This arose from the likeness of the persons in the two moods, especially if the vowel-points are not supplied. For *habbîṭû* means “look”; and because this looking is an approach to God through conversion, grace, faith, and contemplation, they fittingly said, “Draw near.” But if you read *hibbîṭû*, it means “they looked.” Moreover, the particle *naharû*, from the root *’ôr*, as R. Kimhi maintains, Münster reporting it in his scholia, means “they were enlightened,” with *he* standing for *aleph*. But if it is from the stem *nahar*, it signifies “run” or “stream together,” as Jerome and Pagninus translate. Pellicanus suggests both senses. Nebiensis and the Chaldean interpreter agree with us: “Look to him, and be enlightened.”

VERSE 10.—“The rich have lacked and hungered.” Hebrew: *kephîrîm*, that is, “lion-cubs” or “lions”; the meaning of the name suits no one better than the rich of this age, who are high-minded and, like lions, ravenously and violently tear away the goods of the poor. [Col. 0346C] For this reason they have not unreasonably changed “lions” into “rich.” Hence the translator according to Campensis renders: “The violent shall lack and hunger.” And the song of the Virgin Mother of God alludes to this: “He has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty” (Luke 1).

## PSALM XXXIV

[Col. 0345]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF”

[Col. 0345C]

Judge, O Lord. Title: “Unto the end, a psalm of David himself.” [Augustine.] By David, whose name is interpreted “strong of hand” or “desirable in appearance,” Christ is understood: in conquering the devil, he is strong of hand; in promising eternal life, he is desirable to behold. [Col. 0345D] For what hand is stronger than that which overthrew the enemy, not armed, but pierced with nails upon the wood? What is more desirable than he, upon whom angels desire to look, and whom martyrs, though not seeing him, wished to die in order that they might deserve to attain the sight of him? He therefore is truly desirable, since he promises life; and this is the subject treated in this psalm. For here Christ calls upon God against the persecutors of head and body, and through tribulations promises life to all. Its sense is: This psalm, directing us unto the end, is ascribed to David himself, that is, Christ, who speaks here now in his own person, now in that of his body. [Cassiodorus.] This is the second of those psalms which deal extensively with Christ’s Passion.

Purpose: it admonishes us to bear adversities. Method: the psalm has three parts. [Col. 0346C] First, it begins with prayer, praying for both parties: for himself and for his adversaries, with a recounting of their guilt. Second, having set forth hope of good and joy, it narrates how maliciously they behaved toward Christ, at “But my soul.” Third, it treats of the fruit of the Passion, promising the confession of the whole Church, at [Col. 0346D] “I will confess thee.” Therefore, beginning with prayer in the person of himself and his members, he says: “O”

VERSE 1.—“Judge, O Lord, those who harm me; fight against those who fight against me.”

O Lord, judge—[Cassiodorus] condemn—those who harm me in intention; and fight, [Augustine] that is, conquer, those who fight against me in deed. Behold, God fights for us. “If God is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. 8).

VERSE 2.—“Take hold of arms and shield, and rise up to help me.”

Take hold. [Gloss, interlinear.] This is first read in the person of the members. As though he said: I say, “Fight”; but how will you do this? Take up arms and shield for me. It is a great spectacle to see God armed on your behalf. [Augustine.] He who has arms and a shield strikes enemies with arms [Col. 0347A] and protects us with the shield. But what is God’s shield, and what are his arms? The shield is the protection of God’s good will, by which he defends us. Hence elsewhere: “You have crowned us as with the shield of your good will” (Ps. 5). We are God’s arms, because as we are armed by him, so he arms himself with us, by whom he strikes enemies. Thus, “Take up arms and shield” means, [Cassiodorus] help and fortify us by your good will so that we may both strike enemies and be protected from their darts. Or he calls the soul of the righteous person, or of Christ, God’s arms, [Alcuin] by which he defeated enemies; it does nothing unless God fights by means of it. Therefore he says, “Take hold of arms and shield,” that is, so rule and defend Christ’s soul that through it you may subdue adversaries and protect us. “And rise up to help me.” [Augustine.] God is said to sleep when we sleep, and to rise when we watch and are awakened. Hence elsewhere: “Rise up, why do you sleep, O Lord?” (Ps. 43). Thus the Gospel says that Jesus slept in the boat, and then the boat was tossed by waves (Matt. 8): if he were awake, it would not be tossed. The boat is your heart; sometimes therefore God sleeps in the boat, that is, faith in your heart grows lukewarm, and then the boat is tossed. Observe the shipwreck and awaken the sleeping Christ—that is, faith; if it keeps watch, tranquility will come. For all temptations will depart, or at least have no power, when Christ—that is, your faith—keeps watch in your heart. Say therefore: “Rise up,” that is, make yourself known, appear, make yourself felt in helping me, and against the others:

VERSE 3.—“Draw out the sword, and shut in against [Col. 0347C] those who persecute me; say to my soul: I am your salvation.”

Draw out the sword, [Jerome] that is, multiply vengeance; and against those who persecute me—that is, visible and invisible enemies—shut in, that is, bring matters to a conclusion, lest they range about harming you. [Augustine.] Or the sword is the same as the arms, namely the soul of the righteous person. This sword is drawn out when, through righteous persons abounding, good life shines forth. Thus the enemy is shut in, having nothing evil to say about us. And because invisible enemies suggest to my soul, “There is no salvation for him in his God,” you, against them, say to my soul in the reality itself, so that I may hear in you—what?—“I am your salvation,” in both ways: namely, in the present and the future, in temporal and eternal things, so that apart from you I may seek no one. Or Christ says this in his own person: “Take up arms,” as though, “Judge my enemies.” [Alcuin.] But do for me what I ask: namely, take up arms—that is, cause me to have arms, namely teaching and miracles—and the shield, that is, constancy; and rise up to help me, that is, cause me to use what I have received, namely the arms and shield. And draw out the sword, and shut in against those who persecute me: that is, make me, who am now obscure, manifest—so evidently that you confine and convict my enemies, leaving them nothing to bark against; and say to my soul so that all may know: “I am your salvation.”

VERSE 4.—“Let those who seek my soul be confounded and put to shame.”

Let them be confounded and put to shame. Here he foretells the evils of enemies. [Augustine.] It is prophecy, not a wish. As though he said: Save my soul, so that those who seek to destroy it may be confounded. And this is what follows: let those seeking to destroy my soul be confounded and put to shame—that is, let them fear punishments—and not seek to imitate it. And:

VERSE 5.—“Let them be turned backward and confounded, who devise evils against me.”

[Jerome.] Let them be turned away from God, so that they are backward; and let those who devise evils against me be confounded with death-bringing confusion. Or rather this is said of those to be converted, for whom he prays. [Augustine.] As though he said: Save my soul; and let them be confounded, even healthfully unto repentance, and put to shame—that is, fear punishments—who seek my soul. And let them be turned backward, that is, let them follow and not go before; let them not give counsel, [Col. 0348B] but receive it. For Peter, in going before, was Satan; in following, he was a disciple. And let those who devise evils against me be healthfully confounded, that is, now following, they shall deliberate good things; but those stubborn in wickedness:

VERSE 6.—“Let them become as dust before the wind, and the angel of the Lord afflicting them.”

Let them become, etc. [Augustine.] This is prophecy by which he foretells evils for the wicked, not a wish that he desires them to happen thus. Or the prophet, in the Spirit of God, says these things in the manner in which God does them—that is, permits them to happen by a certain judgment, just, holy, and serene—not in disturbed anger or with a mind bent on exercising enmity, but in the justice of punishing vices. The prophet wishes this justice to be preserved in him who rejoices with it, not delighting [Col. 0348C] in the evil of a creature. Nevertheless, it is prophecy even so. He therefore says: [Augustine, Gloss, interlinear.] Let them become like dust before the face of the wind—that is, temptation—so that they easily yield to temptation, or even the slightest suggestion, as if they did not wait. “The face of the wind” means the presence of a more grievous temptation, but they go before it through a lesser one; and let the angel of the Lord, namely an evil angel, afflict them along with that very suggestion. And if at any time they resist by reason:

VERSE 7.—“Let their way be darkness and slipperiness, and the angel of the Lord pursuing them.”

Let their way—that is, their reason—be darkness and slipperiness, that is, obscure and slippery, that is, unstable. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Or “darkness” means ignorance, [Col. 0348D] and “slipperiness” lust; let their way be such that in these vices they descend as into an abyss of death. This is a dreadful way: who would not dread slipperiness and darkness? Who would not beware of setting foot there? These are two great evils and punishments of human beings. And let the angel of the Lord pursue them, not allowing them to stand until light shines before their feet. He says this by comparison with someone who is easily thrown down in darkness and slipperiness because he cannot see where to move his foot. Or perhaps he does this so that he may wait until it grows light. [Gloss, interlinear.] But the angel of the Lord does not permit these persons to stand until the light of grace rises upon them, but casts them headlong into various evils.

VERSE 8.—“For without cause they hid for me the destruction of their snare; in vain they reproached my soul.”

[Col. 0349A] For without cause. Here he recounts the guilt of enemies. And as though someone asked, “On what ground are such great evils theirs?” he answers: Hear on what ground. [Augustine.] For without cause, because I did them no harm, the Jews hid—as they supposed, though I knew their hearts—for me, Christ, the destruction wrought by their snare, [Gloss, interlinear] that is, the counsels and plots by which they would kill me. Yet their snare became destruction for them, not for me. For it shall be the destruction not of the one dying, [Cassiodorus] but of the one sinning. [Augustine.] Hence another edition has: “They hid for me the trap of their corruption, and reproached,” that is, accused, “my soul”; and this “in vain,” that is, uselessly, saying false things and proving nothing. And therefore:

VERSE 9.—“Let the snare which he does not know come upon him, [Col. 0349B] and let the trap which he hid catch him; and let him fall into the snare itself.”

Let the snare which he does not know come upon him. [Augustine.] Let their own snare hold them. Behold a fitting recompense. For nothing is more just than that what they hid should happen to them. For they are deceived by that by which they wished to deceive; they are harmed by that by which they wished to harm. Hence he adds: “And let the trap which he hid catch him,” so that they may be bound by the cords of their own sins, which they produced while secretly devising how to seize and terrify Christ; and let him fall into the snare—not another one, but the very snare which they spread for me. It is as if someone prepared a cup of poison for another and, forgetting, drank it himself. Thus it happened to the Jews who prepared a snare for Christ himself: they fell into it. For no one is evil without first harming himself. Think of malice as of fire. If you want to burn something, that which you bring near the fire burns first; unless it burns, it does not burn another thing. For example, when you put a torch to fire, it burns first so that it can burn something else. Thus malice proceeds from you, and before it devastates the one toward whom it extends its branch, it harms you; it does not harm where it has its root. Indeed, I say that it can happen that your malice does not harm another; but it cannot happen that it does not harm you. Or according to another reading, “Let him fall into the snare, into it,” neutrally understood: [Jerome, Gloss, interlinear] that is, by the very fact that they prepare a snare for me, let them fall inwardly. Or it can be understood of the outward punishment by which the Jews were punished [Col. 0349D] for the sin of Christ’s death, thus: Let the snare of captivity, which he does not know, come upon him; and let the trap which he hid for me catch him—that is, let him similarly be captured unexpectedly by Titus and Vespasian, as they captured me; and let him fall into the snare of death itself, namely that which they prepared for me. Let them be killed in the same manner as they kill me. And so it happened: some were captured and some killed. Or “snare” and “capture” may be understood in a good sense. [Cassiodorus, Gloss, interlinear.] He says this while desiring that good might come to them from Christ’s death. As though he said: They prepared death for me, and from it let that snare which he does not know come—that is, let the snare of truth, which the sinner does not know, bind them, so that, attached to the devil by its bond, they may become attached to God; and let the trap which he hid, [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] that is, the hidden trap, Christ’s death, [Col. 0350A] catch him, so that he is not abandoned to his own crimes. And let him fall into the good snare, by which they may be restrained from evils. And this in it—that is, from that very death.

PART II. VERSE 10.—“But my soul shall rejoice in the Lord, and shall delight in his salvation.”

My soul, etc. [Alcuin.] The second part, where, having set forth hope of good and joy, he recounts how maliciously they act toward the gracious one. Here Christ speaks first. As though he said: These foretold things shall happen to them; but my soul shall rejoice—as one that hears, “I am your salvation”—shall rejoice, I say, in the Lord, seeking no external riches, not seeking to overflow with pleasures [Col. 0350B] and earthly goods, but setting before itself him alone, than whom nothing is sweeter. He who made all things does not fail. Therefore seek him, and in him you shall have all things; and it shall delight. As though he said: But my soul shall rejoice in the Lord. Whence follows that it shall also delight in its salvation, [Gloss, interlinear] that is, in its salvation, which was accomplished for it in the resurrection. By which resurrection:

VERSE 11.—“All my bones shall say: O Lord, who is like thee?”

All my bones, [Jerome] that is, my disciples, have been strengthened and shall say, giving thanks: “O Lord,” etc. And those who are my bones—that is, the steadfast—shall say this. Though flesh yields, the bones, [Augustine] that is, the righteous, nevertheless praise in words. Flesh, [Alcuin] that is, the carnal and weak, has no words of praise and confession, because the weak are entirely silent before you; but the strong praise and fear you as great. Or it may be spoken in the person of the Church: [Augustine.] “But my soul shall rejoice in the Lord” remains unchanged; “and shall delight in his salvation,” etc., that is, in Christ, of whom it is elsewhere said: “My eyes have seen thy salvation” (Luke 2). And “all my bones shall say,” that is, all the strength of my mind shall say, [Augustine] because no one else can say what follows: “O Lord, who is like thee,” or “like unto thee”? No one. For nothing among gods or creatures is like him, [Augustine] because he alone rescued humankind from the mighty hand. Hence follows: Thou art:

[Col. 0350D] VERSE 12.—“Rescuing the needy from the hand of those stronger than he; the poor and indigent from those who despoil him.”

Rescuing, through the Word’s incarnation in deed, [Cassiodorus] that is, humankind, from the hand of those stronger than he: the devil, who held humanity. But Christ, strong of hand, bound the devil, [Augustine] who was stronger than man; he himself conquered the needy and poor man from those who despoiled him, that is, from the devil and his members. “Needy,” “indigent,” and “poor” signify the same thing, [Cassiodorus] namely humankind, which is as though one needy, indigent, and poor person: needy because mortal; indigent because in the sweat of its face it seeks bread (Gen. 2); poor because, cast down from pure wisdom, it possesses a thin and shadowy reason.

[Col. 0351A] VERSE 13.—“Unjust witnesses rising up questioned me concerning things which I did not know.”

### Psalm 34 (Vulgate): “Judge, O Lord, Those Who Wrong Me”

**VERSE 13.**—“Unjust witnesses rose up; they questioned me about things that I did not know.”

“Unjust witnesses rose up.” [Cassiodorus.] Having described the calamities of man, lest Christ himself seem exempt from them, he sets forth his own Passion. It is as though he said: Not only have others suffered calamities, but I also; for unjust witnesses rose up—suddenly, as it were, and without restraint. They were unjust because they bore witness against what was right. They questioned me, not convicting me, concerning things which I did not know in practice: namely, sins which Christ did not know how to commit. Thus one commonly says of someone, “He does not know how to do good,” because he does not do good. [Augustine.] So Christ, who knows the iniquities which he judges, is said not to know sin—not because he does not see or judge it, but because he does not commit it. For it is foreign to his action and to his conscience.

[Col. 0351B] Therefore he says, “I did not know,” in the way that an art is said not to know a fault which, nevertheless, through that art is recognized and avoided. Thus he says: “They questioned me about things that I did not know”—that is, they questioned me concerning iniquities, intending to prevail against me, but they could not, [Gloss, interlinear] because I am the Art itself, in which every learner learns only to do good. And when I had come to save them and had healed their sick, for these good deeds

**VERSE 14.**—“They repaid me evil for good, barrenness to my soul.”

“They repaid me evil for good,” namely, barrenness to my soul. When I had brought fruitfulness, [Augustine] they repaid barrenness. I brought life; they repaid death. I brought honors; they brought insults. I brought medicine; they brought wounds.

The Lord cursed this barrenness in the fig tree, where, when he sought, he did not find: it had leaves but no fruit (Mark 11). That is, there were words in the Synagogue but no deeds. Observe, indeed, abundance in words and barrenness in deeds. For the Apostle says: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal?” and so forth (Romans 2).

**VERSE 15.**—“But I, when they troubled me, clothed myself in sackcloth.”

“But I.” As though he said: They acted thus; but I, when they troubled me, [Augustine] and raged against me, clothed myself in sackcloth—that is, in my divinity I lay concealed beneath mortal flesh. I did not exercise my power, and therefore I was unknown to them. For the flesh of Christ is called sackcloth because of its likeness to sinful flesh. Sackcloth [Col. 0351D] is made from goats’ hair, and goats were offered for sins under the old Law. And likewise:

**VERSE 16.**—“I humbled my soul in fasting, and my prayer shall return into my bosom.”

“I humbled,” that is, afflicted, “my soul in fasting.” [Augustine.] What sort of fasting was Christ’s: bodily or spiritual? Christ did indeed wish to eat, when he sought fruit on a tree; he also wished to drink, when he said to the Samaritan woman, “Give me to drink” (John 4). But this passage concerns neither that thirst nor that fast, but another fast signified in him by these things.

For Christ hungered and thirsted for our salvation and our good. He fasted, therefore, because he found no good works among the Jews: the apostles had fled from him and hidden themselves in the crowd; [Col. 0352A] Peter, who had promised to persevere even unto death, had already denied him three times. He scarcely found one thief, whom he tasted upon the cross. Therefore the holy Church observes the strictest fast on the day of the Passion, in remembrance of this event.

“And my prayer”—as though he said: I humbled myself by fasting, and also prayed—“shall return into my bosom,” or, “into my bosom.” [Augustine.] Christ says this as man, insofar as he prays: he prayed to no one other than him who was personally united to him. But the prayer returns into the bosom, that is, to the Word in whom the Father was. For the bosom is the secret place in which we are commanded to pray, where Susanna prayed (Daniel 13). The secret place of Christ is his divinity, to which his humanity prays.

[Augustine.] Christ, insofar as he is the Word, does not pray, [Col. 0352B] but hears prayer. Nor does he seek help for himself, but with the Father helps all. Thus, “My prayer shall return into my bosom” means that in himself the man intercedes with the divinity.

Or: “My prayer shall return into my bosom”; or, “my word,” [Gloss, interlinear] that is, it will benefit only those who are predestined, who will be household members and sound in the bosom of holy Church. They had gone out from it and become leprous, like Moses’ hand: when it appeared outside his bosom it was leprous, but in the bosom it was made sound (Exodus 4).

**VERSE 17.**—“As for a neighbor, and as for our brother, so I was pleasing; as one mourning and sorrowful, so I was humbled.”

“As for a neighbor,” etc. [Cassiodorus.] One case is used for another: the accusative for the ablative. The sense is: Even though the Jews troubled me, I nevertheless so found pleasure [Col. 0352C] in them as in a neighbor and as in our brother—that is, as concerning a neighbor and concerning our brother. I so found pleasure in them—that is, I rejoiced in their kinship—although they persecuted me. [Gloss, interlinear.] Behold grace in return for hatred; a benefit in return for injury.

Or, I pleased my Father by possessing them—supply, “thus”—as a neighbor and as our brother. Yet, although I did all these things, [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] they were unwilling to turn. And because they would not turn, I was thus humbled—that is, I grieved as a father mourning a son, sorrowful at a son’s death. Other interpreters say: “As a mourning mother, I bent over them.”

Or this may be said in the person of the members: “And my prayer”—as though he said: Christ speaks in the person of his members, “I humbled my soul,” and also prayed for the Jews, “and my prayer shall return into my bosom.” [Jerome.] Although it did not benefit them, I was nevertheless not deprived of my reward, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Into whatever house you enter, say: Peace to this house. And if those in it do not receive it, your peace shall return, or be brought back, into your bosom and to you” (Matthew 10). That is, [Cassiodorus] if it does not benefit them, it will benefit you. So his prayer, which he prayed in his members, not accepted by the Jews, returned to him as to a neighbor.

Again, here he speaks in his members, among whom some are very near to God, never having been stained by a grievous blot; others are far away through sin. For the former there is joy; for the latter mourning and sorrow. He first deals with those who are near, using one case for another. This is the meaning: “I was so pleasing,” to God, “as for a neighbor and as for our brother,” that is, as for a neighbor and brother. This may fittingly be said by one approaching God, rejoicing, and pleasing God, as to a brother and neighbor—one who is approached not by places but by actions.

[Augustine.] For we do not approach or withdraw from God, who is everywhere and contained in no place, by moving through places. Rather, to approach him is to become like him; to be far from him is to become unlike him. Thus, when you see two things closely alike, you say, “This is near to that”; and when they are unlike, even if held in the same place and in one hand, you say, “This kind or thing is far from that.” And as one who is like him rejoices, so one who is unlike him groans. Therefore he adds: “As one mourning and sorrowful,” etc. This applies to one who is not far away, so that he may thus draw near.

**VERSE 18.**—“And they rejoiced against me and assembled; scourges were gathered against me, and I did not know.”

“And against me.” [Cassiodorus.] Here Christ speaks, setting forth how impiously the Jews acted against him. It is as though he said: I grieved over their destruction, but they rejoiced against me. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] That is, they are glad, while I am sad; for while I grieve piously, the Jews rejoice impiously. “And they assembled” in a council, “and scourges were gathered against me,” [Gloss, interlinear] that is, they prepared torments. “And I did not know,” according to their opinion.

Or another reading has, “they did not know”: [Cassiodorus] namely, whom they were acting against, why they acted, or that these things would return upon them.

[Col. 0353C]

**VERSE 19.**—“They were scattered and were not pierced with compunction; they tested me, mocked me with mockery, and gnashed their teeth over me.”

“They were scattered,” [Cassiodorus] that is, dissolved or stupefied at the miracles seen during the Passion; nevertheless, through the hardness of their hearts, they were not pierced by penitence. Or, “they were scattered,” [Alcuin] that is, dispersed by the Romans throughout the whole world. Yet they were not pierced with compunction—that is, they did not repent. Or, they were scattered, that is, divided: for some said, “He is good,” while others said, “No, but he deceives the crowds” (John 7). “And they were not pierced with compunction; and they tested me,” saying, “Tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 27); “and they mocked me,” [Augustine] saying, “He saved others; himself he cannot save” (ibid.).

“They mocked me,” I say, “with mockery.” This form of speech, namely repetition, is used when a thing seems to have been done abundantly, as in: “In blessing I will bless you,” and “Rejoicing, I shall rejoice.” “And they gnashed their teeth over me,” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] as savage beasts do in their cruelty: when reason fails, they gnash their teeth and, remaining silent, show what they desire. [Augustine.] These things reported here as done to Christ on the cross are done everywhere to his body. This prayer ends by adding:

**VERSE 20.**—“Lord, when will you look? Restore my soul from their malice, my only one from the lions.”

“Lord,” etc. As though he said: The wicked do these things to me, says Christ; but, O Lord, when will you look, [Col. 0354A] so as to raise me again? [Cassiodorus.] That is, do not delay long, but restore my soul to my body on the third day. I mean the soul delivered from their malice; and from the lions—that is, from raging powers—deliver my only one, namely the Church, or my flesh, which was without sin.

Or he speaks in our person, for whom it seems long: “Lord, when will you look?” [Augustine.] That is, when shall we see vengeance upon those who insult us? When will the judge, overcome by the widow’s persistence, hear her? Our Judge delays our salvation not from weariness but from love; not through inability, but with reason: so that we may desire it more eagerly and the full number of us may be completed unto the end. Yet out of longing we say: “Lord, when will you look? Restore my soul,” etc.—that is, the Church.

[Col. 0354B]

### Part III

**VERSE 21.**—“I will confess you in the great assembly; in a weighty people I will praise you.”

“I will confess.” Third part. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] He now treats of the fruit of the Passion and promises the confession of the whole Church. From there he prays, with recollection of his fault, for the confusion of his persecutors and the exultation of believers. It is as though he said: [Gloss, interlinear] I say, “Restore,” and if you do this, I will confess you in the Church—this is the only one. He adds “great,” because it consists of all nations; and “in a weighty people,” namely one not carried away by the wind of temptation, I will praise you in the whole multitude.

[Augustine.] There is confession both among grain and chaff, but praise belongs to the weighty, to the grain, not to the chaff. Chaff flies away; wheat remains, because it is weighty. This is a good weightiness, far removed from that of which it is said elsewhere: “How long will you be heavy of heart?” (Psalm 4). This weightiness strengthens; the other weighs down and plunges into the depth—namely, the depth of the world—where they are not sunk like lead in mighty waters. And that I may confess him:

**VERSE 22.**—“Let not those who oppose me unjustly exult over me, those who hate me without cause and wink with their eyes.”

“Let not those who oppose me unjustly exult over me.” [Augustine.] For they insult me because of my chaff, and they also hate me, [Gloss, interlinear] which not all opponents do; and they hate me without cause, because I did them no harm. Christ here repeats matters from his Passion, [Jerome] so as to add their punishment. I say they oppose and hate me, and yet they wink with their eyes, [Augustine] like hypocrites and pretenders, declaring by their faces what they do not possess in their hearts. [Cassiodorus.] Or, they wink with their eyes when they mutually prompt one another by silent signals to deceive and test me. And indeed they wink at me as hypocrites.

**VERSE 23.**—“For indeed they spoke peaceably to me; and, speaking in the wrath of the earth, they devised deceits.”
