“For indeed they spoke peaceably to me,” saying: “We know that you are truthful, Master, and teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?” (Matthew 22). [Augustine.] These are the ones who winked, who spoke such things; and while speaking in that manner, [Cassiodorus] that is, while speaking peacefully, they devised deceits. And this “in wrath,” that is, destructively. For one devises a deception who does not wish to kill; this was the wrath [Col. 0355A] “of the earth,” [Gloss, interlinear] that is, for the sake of the earth, namely lest they lose their place and nation.

**VERSE 24.**—“And they opened their mouth wide against me; they said: ‘Good! good! Our eyes have seen.’”

Those who had previously winked and devised deceits afterward openly opened their mouths wide [75] against me, loudly and openly calling for death: “Crucify him, crucify him” (Luke 23). In death itself they said: “Good! good! It is well for us; our eyes have seen in you what we wished, what we desired.”

Or they said mockingly, “Good! good!” [Augustine.] It is a voice of derision and insult: “Now our eyes have seen your deeds and wonders. This is the Christ; and if he is Christ, the King of Israel, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matthew 27).

**VERSE 25.**—“You have seen, O Lord; do not be silent. O Lord, do not depart from me.”

“You have seen.” As though he said: They acted thus; [Gloss, interlinear] but you, O Lord, have seen my obedience and their iniquity. [Cassiodorus.] This is said when we wish to call something to mind. As if he said: You have seen how cruel they are and how patient I am. Therefore do not be silent, [Augustine] that is, do not delay in giving sentence; [Jerome] but judge. O Lord, do not depart from me in the Passion, but, O

**VERSE 26.**—“Rise up and attend to my judgment, my God and my Lord, to my cause.”

“Lord,” [Cassiodorus, Gloss, interlinear] you who seem to lie down, rise up [Col. 0355C] in order to repay both me and my adversaries; and attend to my judgment—whether read *judicium meum* or *judicio meo*. [Alcuin.] Give me the name that is above every name; since I have been attentive, attend deservedly to my cause—the cause, [Augustine] namely, of my Passion and death, in that I suffer and die for the redemption of the human race. You, I say, attend, who are my God and my Lord.

Or he speaks in the person of his members: “Lord, do not depart from me until judgment comes, as you promised me: ‘Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age’” (Matthew 28). But rise up, O Lord, to help and reward me. “And attend to my judgment,” in that I have been afflicted and tormented by labors and pains. But because many wicked persons also suffer these things, he adds, “Attend to my cause,” for which I suffer. For the punishment is similar for criminals and good persons, but not the cause; therefore it is not punishment but cause that makes a martyr. Therefore:

**VERSE 27.**—“Judge me according to your righteousness, O Lord my God; and let them not exult over me.”

“O Lord, judge me,” [Gloss, interlinear; Augustine] whom they judge unjustly, not according to punishment but according to your righteousness, which you have given me; or mine, which is in me. This is my cause. [Augustine.] Judge, I say, O Lord—you who are my God—and judge me according to this, namely, that you are my God. [Gloss, interlinear.] I say: judge me according to your righteousness, [Col. 0356A] and according to that same righteousness judge those who persecute me. “And let them not exult over me,” [Cassiodorus] that is, let them rather mourn than rejoice at having accomplished their evils.

**VERSE 28.**—“Let them not say in their hearts, ‘Good! good for our soul’; nor let them say, ‘We shall devour him.’”

“Let them not say in their hearts,” [Gloss, interlinear] even if they say with their mouth: “‘Good! good!’ for our soul,” [Augustine] that is, “It is well for us, because we have done what we wished.” The meaning is: Show them that they have accomplished nothing, so that they may not rejoice or say, “We shall devour him,” [Gloss, interlinear] so that he might not rise again, but rather:

**VERSE 29.**—“Let all those who rejoice at my evils be ashamed and fear together.”

[Col. 0356B] “Let them be ashamed” at the glorification of my resurrection, and “fear,” that is, let all who rejoice at my evils fear punishments together, [Jerome] not only those who commit those evils.

Or he says this concerning, or in, his members: “Let them not say”; and he speaks of the persecutors of the Church, such as Jews and Gentiles. As though he said: Let them not rejoice; and in order that this may be so, let them not say, “We shall devour him,” or “We shall swallow him.” [Augustine.] Those incorporated into evils devour the righteous. For just as those whom Peter kills or eats are restored to life, so those who are transformed into the body of the wicked are swallowed up.

“Let them be ashamed.” As though he said: Let them not say this; rather, let them be ashamed of their sins, so that we may swallow them, as Israel swallowed the crushed calf which Aaron had molten in the fire. Moses, descending from the mountain, cast it into the fire, destroyed its form, then crushed it, cast it into water, and gave it to the people to drink (Exodus 32). This signifies the body of the ungodly.

> **[Note: Col. 0355D. From Isidore, on Exodus 32.]**  
> The holy preachers destroy the image of its malice with heavenly fire and, once cleansed through the water of baptism, bring it into the fellowship of the Church.

That this may happen, he prays here, saying: “Let them be ashamed.” [Cassiodorus.] He who is ashamed of his deeds condemns them by his own judgment; but because someone may be ashamed without having reverence, he adds, “and fear together,” to indicate conversion, since reverence is fear of the Lord joined with love. He then identifies those whom he wishes to be ashamed: “those who rejoice at my evils.” Next he states more plainly what he had said:

[Col. 0356D]

**VERSE 30.**—“Let those who speak evil against me be clothed in shame and reverence.”

“Let them be fully clothed in shame,” or disgrace, [Cassiodorus] as in sackcloth of repentance and the garment of mourning, and in reverence. Shame counters the boldness they displayed in raging; reverence counters the shamelessness of falsehood. They ought to possess these, so that they may cure those faults by them.

Or it may be taken in an evil sense: “Let them be clothed.” As though he said: Let them be ashamed here unto salvation, and let them fear. But if they are unwilling, [Jerome] let them at last be clothed in the evil shame of hell, and in fear—those, namely, who speak evil, or great things, that is, proud things, against me.

[Col. 0357A]

**VERSE 31.**—“Let those who desire my righteousness exult and rejoice, and say: ‘May the Lord, who desires the peace of his servant, always be magnified.’”

“Let them exult.” [Cassiodorus.] He ends, as do other psalms concerning the Passion, in the great hope of believers. As though he said: Let those people be ashamed and confounded; but let those rejoice and exult who seek not to establish their own righteousness, [Gloss, interlinear] but to imitate my righteousness; and who by it desire the peace of his servant, [Jerome] that is, of Christ—[Gloss, interlinear] that is, my peace, which I came to bring to earth, toward God and neighbor.

And rejoicing, let them say: “May the Lord always be magnified,” that is, may he thus be magnified until the end of the age, just as he is already magnified in the conversion of some. There is a great difference [Col. 0357B] between these rejoicing persons and those mentioned before. The latter curse: “Good! good! for their own soul”; [Cassiodorus] their joy swiftly passes away. But the former do not say this for their own soul; rather, they turn their prayers toward God and place their joy in his praises, not in themselves—and that joy is everlasting.

**VERSE 32.**—“And my tongue shall meditate on your righteousness, your praise all the day.”

“And my tongue.” As though he said: I will confess; I will praise; and my tongue shall meditate upon your righteousness. Meditation belongs to the heart, not the tongue; but Christ’s voice is so consonant with his heart that what belongs to the heart is given to the mouth, when he says, “My tongue shall meditate on your righteousness.” His tongue meditated upon God’s righteousness [Cassiodorus] when he preached the New Testament to the peoples. “And your praise all the day,” [Augustine] because in all his words and deeds he praised God. For one praises all day who does everything well. One does not cease praising who does not cease acting well; one does not cease acting well who does not cease being righteous. Therefore do every good thing, and you have praised the Lord all day.

Or, [Jerome] “tongue” means the inward tongue, namely the tongue of the mind rather than the body. “My,” that is, of my faithful people, Christ says, “shall meditate on your righteousness.” Thus elsewhere: “Your law is my meditation.” [Alcuin.] Or the preachers are understood as Christ’s tongue, through whom he teaches others. As though he said: Let what I have said happen, and my tongue—that is, my preachers—shall diligently proclaim you righteous, since you fulfilled your promises; and they shall proclaim universally [Col. 0357D] all the things in which you are to be praised.

### Comparison on Psalm 34: “Judge, O Lord, Those Who Wrong Me”

**VERSE 3.**—“Bring forth the spear.” Almost all except Jerome translate it “the spear.” The sense does not differ, for a *framea* is a spear. They might therefore have followed the Fathers. The Campensis translation has “draw the blade,” and the Nebiensis, “take up arms.”

**VERSE 8.**—“They reproached my soul.” Jerome, with others, has “they dug for my soul.” But *HAPHAR* is ambiguous, as is clear also from verse 5 of the same psalm, even if it is neuter there. Yet the meaning here is not foreign, nor is there any difficulty if the Septuagint understood *HAPHERU* actively.

**VERSE 12.**—“Delivering the needy from the hand of those stronger than him.” Faber and Caecus contend, for the convenience of Latin expression, that one should read *fortiorum eorum*, “those stronger than them.” But we have already observed that ecclesiastical usage has admitted, in some places, the Greek form; as in 1 Corinthians 13: “Charity is greater of these” (*major horum est caritas*) rather than “greater than these,” if one wishes to speak more purely to Latin ears—unless one takes the comparative in place of the superlative, which is sometimes customary among Latin writers. Such matters ought to have been ignored, had the detractors not treated them as though they were some great offence. Finally, Saint Augustine states, on Psalm 82, verse 4, that an interpreter sometimes translates a Greek expression which is unusual in Latin.

**VERSE 15.**—“But I, when they troubled me.” The Hebraizing moderns have: “When they were sick,” or “when they themselves were sick.” The Hebrew word *BAHALOTHAM* may be understood, because of the final *mem* and the infinitive form, either in a neuter or in a passive sense. Jerome supports this in the Hebrew version, [Col. 0358B] where he rendered it in this manner: “when I was deformed by them,” and thus, “when they troubled me,” although the other interpretation has the opposite meaning.

**VERSE 14.**—“As for a neighbor, as for our brother, so I was pleasing.” Jerome: “As toward a friend, as toward my brother, so I walked.” Sanctes: “As for a friend, as for my brother, I walked.” Pratensis and the interpreters for Cajetan: “As, or like, a companion; like my brother, I walked.” Pellicanus: “As a friend, as a brother, I displayed myself upright in my conduct.” Münster: “Just as if any one of them had been my friend and my brother, so I walked.”

In Hebrew there are only four words: *BEREA KEAH LI HITHHALACHTI*. The first means “friend”; the second, “brother”; the third is a first-person pronoun, which may refer to either the preceding or following word; the last means “to walk.” The Septuagint interpreters rightly understood this figuratively as “to be pleasing.” For one is said to walk in the way of God’s commandments when those commandments greatly please him; Scripture frequently uses this trope. The only difficulty is the apparently improper expression, “I pleased my brother.” Yet Augustine perceived no difficulty in his exposition, where he repeatedly uses that reading. For he seems to supply an infinitive in this way: “I was pleasing,” that is, “I rejoiced to be near God,” that is, to draw near.

From his interpretation, as you have it in the Exposition, it plainly follows that the criticism of Faber and Caecus is demolished. They reject “our brother” and adopt “my brother,” because, they say, we share no kinship with the Father, whom Christ addresses here. Yet “our brother,” not “my brother,” expresses the fellowship of human nature by which he is joined to us. This entire argument collapses if one reconsiders Augustine’s explanation, apart from the fact that the preposition *ad*, “toward,” is understood.

[Col. 0358D]

“As one mourning and sorrowful.” In Hebrew they put “mother” for “sorrowful”: *EM*, that is, “mother.” Since Hebrew lacks variation of cases, Jerome, the interpreters for Cajetan, Pellicanus, and Nebiensis translate it in the nominative: “as a mourning mother,” understanding “her son.” Conversely, Sanctes, Pratensis, and Campensis refer the mourning to the son, with an accusative: “as one mourning his mother,” namely, a son. The Chaldee Paraphrast has: “as one mourning and sorrowful over his mother.” Therefore Münster translated: “according to a mother’s mourning,” so that it could be understood either way.

The interpreters read *IM* for *EM*, since there is absolutely no distinction between the letters, and either may be read without pointing. And they said “and sorrowful,” not taking care to translate more literally, “I was humbled with sorrow.” Sanctes renders “sorrowful” as “clothed in black”; the interpreter for Cajetan, “dark”; Pratensis, “very black.” The interpreters followed the metaphor, since blackness is a symbol of sorrow. [Col. 0359A] Thus Jerome said “sad,” and Münster, “mournful.”

**VERSE 18.**—“And they rejoiced against me.” Jerome: “in my weakness,” or “in my adverse health”; according to Münster, Sanctes, and Pellicanus: “at my limping”; Pratensis: “when I had been crushed.” The Hebrew *TZELA* sometimes denotes a side or rib, as in Genesis 2 concerning Adam’s rib; at other times, a fracture, blow, or limp. Thus “against my side” does not conflict with “against me,” nor are the other versions far removed.

**VERSE 15.**—“Scourges were gathered against me.” What Jerome and the interpreters for Cajetan render “those striking for scourges” is not far from the sense which the translation of Sanctes reverses: “Those struck assembled against me.” Pratensis and Pellicanus have “the lame”; Münster, “the cast down”; the Chaldee, “the impious.” *NECHIM* is derived from the root *NACHA*, “he struck,” “he weakened.” Therefore the interpreters correctly expressed the sense.

**VERSE 16.**—“They were scattered and were not pierced with compunction.” Jerome: “tearing apart, and not being silent.” The interpreters for Cajetan come quite close: “They tore apart and did not keep silence.” So too Pellicanus and Münster: “They stretched wide their mouth and did not keep silence.” Sanctes agrees: “They laughed loudly and did not keep silence.” Pratensis has: “They opened.” The Hebrew *QUARA* means “he tore,” “he broke,” “he opened.” Metaphorically, according to Sanctes citing Rabbi David, it means “he laughed loudly,” as though in wordiness he tore flesh apart.

The Septuagint understood it according to its proper meaning and in the neuter. They customarily translate the second clause metaphorically, as do others: *LO DAMU*, “they did not keep silence.” For Jews, worn down by many distresses, do not cease blaspheming and are not pierced with compunction by any scourges. Silence of the heart, however, is compunction.

“They tested me, mocked me with mockery.” [Col. 0359C] Jerome: “in the pretence of feigned words”; Pellicanus: “with pretenders of mocking feasting”; Pratensis: “with pretenders of food-related mockeries”; Sanctes: “with impious mockers who indulge their belly”; Münster: “with flatterers they were talkative mockers”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “with blandishments, the mockery of empty chatter.” The Hebrew has *BEANPHE LAAGE MAOG*. The first word means to pretend and assume roles, which fits especially the Scribes, Pharisees, and Herodians testing Christ the Lord in Matthew 22 in order to catch him in speech: “Master, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth, and you care for no one, for you do not regard the person of men,” and so forth.

The Septuagint interpreters appear to have read *BEAHANPHI*, that is, “with my pretenders” or “hypocrites.” Yet they expressed it more clearly in the words, “They tested me.” The other two words beyond all dispute mean mockery, although the last also denotes certain other things. Therefore these innovators had no reason to undermine the Latin reading—if indeed they had translated differently with that intention—in the present verse: “They were scattered and were not pierced with compunction.”

It is astonishing that Faber and Caecus babble against the Septuagint—who nevertheless, as Jerome attests in his preface to the books of Chronicles, were filled with the Holy Spirit—accusing them of great rashness, because they rather boldly overturned the meaning of the Holy Spirit and supplied their own. “For how,” they ask, “if they were scattered, is it immediately added, ‘They were not pierced with compunction; they tested me, mocked me with mockery, and gnashed their teeth over me’? For the preceding and following matters conflict.” This reasoning is feeble, since in the words [Col. 0360A] of the prophets it is customary for the past tense to be used in place of the future, as in what follows, given as the cause of vengeance: “They tested me,” etc. The Master’s exposition shows their arguments to be worthless; so does Jerome: “They were scattered,” he says, “from the bond of charity.”

**VERSE 17.**—“Lord, when will you look?” This is the prayer of an afflicted person awaiting the time when he desires to be more quickly delivered. The Hebrew has *CAMMAH*, meaning “how much?” or “how long?” or “when will you look?” Thus it may refer to the magnitude of the mockeries and persecutions which the afflicted man asks either to end or at least to be diminished. Both interpretations aptly apply to Christ as man, detesting the blasphemies of the Jews, grieving over their destruction, and nevertheless seeking just vengeance. Since the Hebrew word is ambiguous, Faber ought not to have railed against our edition.

**VERSE 20.**—“For indeed they spoke peaceably to me.” The Hebrew has a negation, which produces the opposite meaning, namely, “they will not speak peace”; Jerome rendered this according to the Hebrew. But I do not doubt that the Septuagint read *LI* instead of *LO*: the former means “to me.” Thus in Job 13 the Hebrew reads the negation, “I shall not hope,” while we read, “I shall hope in him,” or “I shall hope in it.” But Faber and Caecus object: How can they speak peace and then immediately add, “They opened their mouth wide against me and said, ‘Vah, vah, our eyes have seen’”? These are words of hatred, not peace. The commentary fully resolves this question. [lacuna] “Speaking in the wrath of the earth.” Jerome and Nebiensis: “in plunder.” Others translate: “against the meek or humble of the earth,” and so forth. The polysemy of the word *REGA* produces the variation.

**VERSE 24.**—“Our eyes have seen.” I do not know what moved the interpreters for Cajetan to translate, “They saw our eyes,” using the accusative. Not only did they do this, [Col. 0360C] but Cajetan himself followed it in his Exposition. All the others, however, translate it in the nominative, in accordance with the interpretation given in the commentary.

**VERSE 24.**—“Judge me according to your righteousness.” Here Faber is utterly wrong. He says that the Hebrew reads not “your” but “my.” Yet the Hebrew reads *CETZIDQUECA*, “according to your righteousness,” and Jerome translates it thus. Faber was misled by a corrupt manuscript.

**VERSE 25.**—We read “Good! good!” twice, just as in verse 24 Faber’s manuscript has it repeated in Jerome’s translation; our manuscript has it only once, as we now read it in Hebrew. The Septuagint could quite suitably repeat it for emphasis. Faber and Caecus argue that it ought to be “Vah, vah!” because, in the Gospel context, *euge* is an exclamation of rejoicing whereas *vah* is one of insult. But they did not understand that the Hebrew particle *AH* has two senses. If an aspirate *he*, *i*, or *h* is prefixed, so that it is lightly aspirated as *HEAH*, it is usually understood as “Good!”—as we read in the Hebrew here.

**VERSE 31.**—“May the Lord always be magnified, those who desire the peace of his servant.” The Hebrew has, “who desires the peace of his servant,” singular, so that it refers to the Father, whose good pleasure it was to save his Christ. We have frequently noted that the resemblance of the words causes the number to appear now one way and now the other. For the forms differ only by a final *yod*. The former may be plural; the latter is singular. The latter is pointed *HEHAPHETZ*; the former, *HAHAPHETZE*.

## Psalm 35

[Col. 0361]

### Title of the Psalm: “Unto the End, for the Servant of the Lord, a Psalm of David”

[Col. 0361A]

“The unjust man said.” Title: “Unto the end, for the servant of the Lord, a psalm of David.” [Alcuin.] This psalm concerns the error of certain people who say that all evils arise from the defect of nature and our creation, while good things arise from free choice. Here the Prophet refutes this, saying that all evils are from ourselves, whereas good things are from God through grace. Thus in the title the faithful person who speaks in this psalm is rightly called “servant of the Lord,” because he attributes good things to God and evils to himself.

This psalm tending unto the end is attributed to David—that is, to a certain faithful person, who speaks in this psalm as a servant of the Lord, namely as one who rightly understands concerning God that good things are to be attributed to God and evils to himself.

[Cassiodorus.] Or David here signifies Christ, who is called the servant of the Lord, that is, obedient to the Father unto the end. The words of this psalm also suit him. This psalm tends unto the end; it is attributed to David, that is, to Christ, the servant of the Lord, obedient unto the end to God the Father.

**Purpose.** It urges us to attribute evils to ourselves and good things to God.

**Method.** The psalm has two parts. [Alcuin.] First, it asserts that evils arise from man. Secondly, it says that good things come from God through mercy, at: “Lord, in heaven,” etc.

[Cassiodorus.] It should be noted that there are two kinds of sinners. Some, through the weakness of the flesh, cannot follow the commands of the Law. Hence it is said in the Book of Wisdom: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind that thinks many things” (Wisdom 9). Others are blasphemers, namely those who sin willingly and freely, as though to say: God does not care about these things. It is concerning such persons that the psalm speaks.

**VERSE 1.**—“The unjust man said, in order that he might sin, within himself: there is no fear of God before his eyes.”

“**The unjust man has said, etc.**” [Aug.] Here is a description of the wicked man. As though he said: The unjust man, that is, the class of unjust persons, “has said,” that is, has resolved, “within himself,” namely privately and not in public; that is, he has set it before himself where no human being sees. What? “That he may transgress,” that is, sin freely. I say, “within himself,” where, even if God sees, he does not care, because “there is no fear of the Lord before his eyes.” Men fear to profess wickedness publicly; they do not fear God, as though to say: God will not investigate or care.

Or connect it thus: “The unjust man has said,” etc., “that he may transgress.” Whence does this come to him? Because “there is no fear of the Lord before his eyes.”

**VERSE 2.**—“Because he has acted deceitfully in His sight, that his iniquity may be found unto hatred.”

“Because, in His sight,” [Aug.] namely that of God, whose fear is not before his eyes, “he has acted deceitfully,” that is, he has acted deceitfully in his heart. For he is not ignorant—indeed, he knows—that God is there, that is, that God sees in the heart; yet he wills evil. In this he acts deceitfully: that he might find his iniquity and hate it.

Another reading: he acted deceitfully in this respect, that, seeking his iniquity with deceit, [Col. 0362A] he did not wish truly to find and hate it. For many inquire into their own iniquities, but deceitfully, not wishing truly to find and hate them. When they recognize them, they do not abandon them but defend them. But if they sought sincerely, they would find and hate them. Thus they are truly concealed from them; yet they act against themselves unwillingly, unwilling to understand truly, although they inquire and cannot excuse themselves on the ground of ignorance.

Otherwise, from the words “because he has acted deceitfully,” etc., as though he said: [Cassiod.] There is no fear, because he has acted deceitfully in God’s sight; that is, he did not wish to devote himself to God’s law, “that his iniquity might be found unto hatred,” that is, that through that law he might discover and hate his own iniquity—as though he could be excused through ignorance.

Otherwise, the whole passage: as though he said: The wicked claim that they sin either by fate, by the stars’ configuration, or by the necessity of providence; [Col. 0362B] [Alcuin.] but rather he “has said,” that is, resolved, “within himself,” that is, from his own will. Nothing compelled him “to transgress,” that is, to fall away from that for which he was created. By this he is unjust, and thus it is clear that there is no fear of God, in actual practice, before his eyes—that is, before him. This fear hangs over all, because all profess to fear God, but do not show it in their conduct.

“There is no fear of God before his eyes, because he has acted deceitfully,” that is, he obeys the flesh rather than God, although reason suggests something different—that which is in God’s sight; that is, what God sees, even if no one else does. Or, “in his sight,” namely in that of the unjust man: that is, what the unjust man himself sees, he knows from God, so that his iniquity may be found by that same person “unto hatred”; that is, so that he may recognize that his iniquity ought to be hated by God and by all [Col. 0362C] good persons—yet he has not hated it.

**VERSE 3.**—“The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit; he would not understand, that he might do good.”

“The words of his mouth.” [Alcuin.] Here he shows wickedness in its parts: namely, in words, thoughts, and evil deeds. Thus, “the words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit,” that is, iniquitous and deceitful, or openly evil. Or, if apparently good words are uttered deceitfully, his thought also, though it could be good and concerned with good things, is concerned with wicked things.

Thus: “he would not understand.” I do not deny that he could understand; but I say that he was unwilling. What was he unwilling to understand? “That he might do good.” I do not say that he was unwilling to understand what he could not understand, but what he could understand. Thus he acts more ruinously against himself, since he is unwilling to understand what he is able to understand.

[Aug.] There are indeed certain things which men cannot understand even if they wish to, such as “In [Col. 0362D] the beginning was the Word” (John 1). But although he could not understand “In the beginning was the Word,” he could nevertheless understand so as to act rightly; yet he was unwilling, and therefore has no excuse. [Cassiod.] Pardon is sometimes granted for lack of understanding, but punishment is always due to an evil will. “He would not understand,” but rather:

**VERSE 4.**—“He devised iniquity upon his bed; he stood in every way that was not good; but he did not hate malice.”

“He devised iniquity upon his bed,” [Aug.] that is, in his heart, in which he takes pleasure, in which, if it were clean, [Col. 0363A] he would rest. There the Lord commands prayer, with the door of the mind shut against importunate thoughts (Matt. 6), so that we may ask nothing external of God. For if we seek such things, the door of the heart stands open; a crowd of evil thoughts sees it and enters. Hence Solomon: “Dying flies destroy the sweetness of the ointment” (Eccles. 10:1), that is, importunate thoughts succeeding one another drive out the sweetness of pure prayer.

The Lord removed this crowd when He raised the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter in the house (Matt. 9 [printed: XIX]). Moses likewise, when about to receive the law and speak with the Lord, left the crowds at the lower part of the mountain and ascended to its summit (Exod. 19). Ish-bosheth also, Saul’s son, was slain by enemies because the maidservant who kept the door did not guard it well (2 Kings [Samuel] 4).

[Aug.] Thus “upon his bed” here is what was said above, “within himself,” that is, in the heart, where those of clean heart rest as it were in a bed. Therefore, if there is tumult outside—or at least—let there be rest in the bed. This will exist if there is there a good wife, namely God’s wisdom and a pure conscience. But if there is an evil wife there, there is no rest even there, and consequently nowhere.

There are three things which do not allow a person to rest in his house: smoke, dripping water, and an evil wife. Smoke is sins born of desire, which darken the mind; dripping water is sins flowing in from elsewhere; an evil wife is the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God, or an evil conscience, which resists reason. If anyone is troubled, therefore, by his own vices or those of others, let him flee to his bed; there, if he receives a good wife, he will rest, but if [Col. 0363C] an evil one, he will be troubled still more.

“He stood.” As though he said: His words and thoughts are evil, and his deeds also are evil. Thus, “he stood,” that is, with zeal and persistence, perseveringly, “in every way that was not good”; [Aug.] that is, he was inclined to perform wicked acts. “But he did not hate malice”; rather, he loved it. Behold the height of evil. For one who cannot wholly be without malice ought at least to hate it—the very malice which God hates—so that in his mind he may serve the law of God. This man did not do so: he found and knew evil to be evil, and yet did not hate it.

## Part II. Verse 5

**VERSE 5.**—“O Lord, Thy mercy is in heaven, and Thy truth even unto the clouds.”

“O Lord, Thy mercy is in heaven.” [Alcuin.] This is the second part, in which he says that good things come from God through mercy. [Col. 0363D] As though he said: Evils come from man, but good things come from God’s mercy. Thus: O Lord, “in heaven,” that is, among those who are heaven, who know hidden things, is Thy mercy; and that those same persons are clouds comes from Thee. Thus: “Thy truth reaches even unto the clouds.” [Aug.] The clouds are teachers.

**VERSE 6.**—“Thy righteousness is as the mountains of God; Thy judgments are a great deep.”

“Thy righteousness is as the mountains of God,” that is, Thy righteous ones, who are the spiritual mountains of God, are compared to actual mountains, [Aug.] because they are illuminated before others by the light of the true sun. [Jerome, Alcuin.] And as Thou hast chosen these who are mountains and clouds, so Thou rejectest others; and thus Thy judgments—namely, that Thou hast mercy on these and blindest those—are “a great deep,” that is, wholly [Col. 0364A] unsearchable to anyone. And although Thou raisest these and rejectest others, Thou nevertheless preservest both. Thus:

**VERSE 7.**—“Men and beasts Thou wilt save, O Lord, according as Thou hast multiplied Thy mercy, O God.”

“Men and beasts,” that is, the elect and the reprobate, “Thou wilt save, O Lord”; [Alcuin.] the latter only bodily, namely the reprobate, but the former also spiritually, namely the elect. In this great mercy appears. Hence he says in wonder, “according as,” etc.

Otherwise, connect the text thus: [Cassiod.] There, “men”: Thy judgments are incomprehensible because Thou wilt save, O Lord, “men,” [Jerome] that is, rational beings, “and beasts,” that is, irrational beings. The sense is unchanged: “Thou wilt save according as Thou hast multiplied Thy mercy, O God.”

According to this reading, proceed to the following verse as though he said: Thou wilt save men and beasts; but beyond beasts, that is, beyond the temporal salvation granted to beasts—that is, to the reprobate—are “the sons of men,” etc.

Otherwise, the whole passage from “O Lord, Thy mercy is in heaven”: [Aug.] As though he said: Evils are from man, but both spiritual and temporal good things are from God. He teaches first concerning spiritual goods, then concerning temporal goods. Thus: Evils are from man; but, O Lord, Thy mercy, namely that which Thou givest to the saints, is “in heaven,” that is, heavenly, not earthly, like the temporal mercy common to good and evil alike.

But how could a human being recognize heavenly mercy unless God announced it to him? He announces it by sending truth even unto the clouds. Thus: [Col. 0364C] “Thy truth has come even unto the clouds,” that is, to preachers, through whom God thunders threats, flashes miracles, and rains teaching. They are therefore rightly called clouds. Hence: “Who are these that fly as clouds, and as doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60). And elsewhere: “I will command My clouds that they rain no rain upon it” (Isa. 5).

The sense is: Thy truth has come even to the clouds; that is, Thou bestowest Thy truth on the clouds, and through the clouds on all others, so that by it they may understand Thy heavenly mercy. These same clouds are “Thy righteousness,” that is, they are filled by Thy righteousness. They are mountains of God, not mountains of the world. The mountains of the world are Arius, Maximianus, Donatus, Sabellius, and other heretics; anyone steering a ship among them would suffer shipwreck.

Teachers too are rightly called mountains: first the sun of righteousness, that is, Christ, clothes them with the light of wisdom; then that light descends from them—or, rather, not from them but from the lowest valleys, that is, into the hearts of inferior persons. I say “from them,” yet not “from them,” for they are ministers of teaching, not its authors. Being enlightened by righteousness, they become mountains; and through Thy judgments others become a deep, that is, profound in sins. This deep is great because such persons are many, while the mountains are few.

“Men.” Above he showed that spiritual goods are from God; here he says that temporal goods are from the same source. As though he said: Not only spiritual goods, but temporal ones also, are from God, because “men and beasts,” that is, fleshly persons who love such things along with beasts, “Thou wilt save, O Lord,” just as beasts, only temporally. [Col. 0365A] As though he said: He who made both preserves both temporally. For temporal goods, which He gives them in common, are also from God. He calls only fleshly persons “men”; “beasts” he takes literally: “Thou wilt save according as Thou hast multiplied Thy mercy, O God.”

**VERSE 8.**—“But the sons of men shall hope in the shelter of Thy wings.”

“But the sons of men.” [Aug.] As though he said: Thou wilt save men, namely fleshly persons, only bodily, along with beasts; but “the sons of men,” that is, the good, shall hope. Those who are according to Adam, that is, who bear the image of the old man, are called simply men; here those who are according to Christ, that is, who bear Christ’s image, are called sons of men. Yet “sons of men” also means human beings generally.

“In the shelter of Thy wings,” [Aug.] he says this from the likeness of a bird; and he says “wings.” [Jerome:] the Old and New Testaments. Thus, “in the shelter of Thy wings,” [Gloss] that is, in the protection of the Old and New Testament, they shall hope for future goods. While those who are according to Adam rejoice in present things, those who are according to Christ hope for the mercy that is in heaven, announced through the clouds.

**VERSE 9.**—“They shall be inebriated from the abundance of Thy house, and Thou shalt give them drink from the torrent of Thy delight.”

“They shall be inebriated.” [Aug.] He speaks by a comparison, because the reality cannot be expressed; through this likeness he indicates that, being filled with grace, they lose their mind’s fleshly affection, so that they no longer recognize carnally their own fathers, [Col. 0365C] sons, or friends. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who does not hate father and mother, or brothers or sisters, for My sake, is not worthy of Me” (Matt. 10).

This inebriation is “from the abundance of Thy house,” namely of the present Church. “And Thou shalt give them drink from the torrent of Thy delight,” [Cassiod.] that is, from the Holy Spirit. [Aug.] As though he said: There will be an outpouring of grace and mercy to make them drunk. [Alcuin.] Or “the torrent of delight” means God’s will in a human being, breaking through every obstacle. Thus: “from the torrent of Thy delight,” etc., that is, Thy will, like a torrent within a human being, will break every obstacle.

Or the torrent of Thy delight is called Christ’s wisdom because it is sudden and swift. [Cassiod.] Thus: “from the torrent of Thy delight,” that is, from Thy wisdom, Thou shalt give them drink.

Or this may be understood of the future: “They shall be inebriated from the abundance of Thy house,” [Col. 0365D] [Aug.] of the future Jerusalem. [Alcuin.] Then they shall be drunk in reality, that is, filled, whereas now they hope. And “from the torrent of Thy delight,” that is, of Thy pleasure—which is called a torrent not because blessedness will pass away, but because it is abundant—Thou shalt give them drink; and Thou wilt be able to do so.

**VERSE 10.**—“For with Thee is the fountain of life, and in Thy light we shall see light.”

“For with Thee,” [Aug.] O Christ, “is the fountain of life,” that is, the source of every good; and “in Thy light,” O Christ, “we shall see light,” because through His preaching we now see the light of the Father and the Holy Spirit. Therefore, “extend Thy mercy,” so that our way through this age may be safer.

Or thus, so that the speech from the words “for with Thee” is addressed to the Father: as though he said, Thou shalt give them drink—and truly, because with Thee, O Father, is the fountain of life, that is, [Col. 0366A] Christ, who is also the light. Hence follows: “and in Thy light,” that is, through Christ, [Jerome] who is light from light, “we shall see light,” [Aug.] namely the Father, in the future. Note that He who is the fountain is also the light: a fountain because He satisfies; light because He illumines. Meanwhile, however:

**VERSE 11.**—“Extend Thy mercy to those who know Thee, and Thy righteousness to those who are upright of heart.”

“Extend Thy mercy to those who know Thee,” namely to those who believe rightly [Aug., Gloss]: that good things are from Thee and evils from themselves. And extend “Thy righteousness,” namely uprightness of life, to those “who are upright of heart,” who direct themselves to God’s will [Cassiod.] and do not bend it toward themselves, so that in all things, [Aug.] namely both prosperity and adversity, they may praise God.

**VERSE 12.**—“Let not the foot of pride come to me, and let not the hand of the sinner move me.”

“Let not [the foot of pride] come.” [Aug.] As though he said: I hope, I am made drunk; and therefore let not “the foot of pride” come to me. [Cassiod.] That is, let not proud desire come, the foot by which one goes away from God—that is, withdraws from Him. [Aug.] This is what he says in another psalm: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults” (Ps. 18 [19]). “And let not the hand,” that is, the impulse, “of the sinner,” that is, of the devil, move me. This is what he says elsewhere: “And spare Thy servant from strangers” (ibid.).

Thus God does for us what this man asks. [Gloss.] For God removes also the evils which arise from ourselves or from the devil. Note the proper order: first he says, “Let not pride come”; then, “Let not the hand of the sinner move me,” because if you are proud, [Col. 0366C] the operation of one who gives evil counsel quickly moves you. Otherwise, no. Therefore I fear that the foot of pride may not come to me, because:

**VERSE 13.**—“There the workers of iniquity have fallen; they have been cast out, and shall not be able to stand.”

“There they have fallen,” [Aug.] that is, in the foot of pride. [Gloss.] As though he said: From on high those who still work iniquity fell—[Aug.] namely the devil and the first man. [Gloss.] They were cast out of paradise, first the devil and afterward man; nor could they stand by their own strength.

Or this may be understood of philosophers: [Aug.] Therefore let not the foot come, because “there,” that is, through the foot of pride, they have fallen, because “when they knew God, they glorified Him not as God” (Rom. 1). They are those “who work iniquity,” according to the words: “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts,” etc. (ibid.). “They have been cast out and could not stand”; [Col. 0366D] this remains unchanged.

## 78. Comparison on Psalm 35: “The Unjust Man Has Said”

**VERSE 2.**—“Because he has acted deceitfully in His sight, that his iniquity may be found unto hatred.” The Hebrew infinitive, used in place of the Latin gerund and corresponding to the words “that it may be found,” permits **LIMTZO** (“to find”) to be rendered either actively or passively: “for finding,” that is, as Jerome translates it, “that He might find iniquity,” namely God, “in order to hate it.” Pratensis also translates actively. Sanctes likewise used the active and added words of his own, changing the sense thus: “that he may find his own iniquity, so that he may hold good in hatred.” For because of the reflexive pronoun, the meaning necessarily had to be referred to the wickedness of the sinner who flatters himself concerning sin.

Among the Hebrews, however, affixes or pronouns of this sort can, as the matter requires, establish either a reflexive or a simple reference; the same is true among the Greeks. Therefore [Col. 0367A] Augustine reads: “that he might find his own iniquity and hate it,” in accordance with the exposition given in the gloss. For the Greek reads: **τοῦ εὑρεῖν τὴν ἀνομίαν αὐτοῦ καὶ μισῆσαι**—“to find his iniquity and to hate [it].”

Münster does not differ from the Septuagint: “Until,” he says, “his iniquity is found worthy of hatred.” Pellicanus and the Campensian paraphrase agree.

# Psalm 36

[Col. 0367]

## Title of the Psalm: “A Psalm of David”

[Col. 0367A]

“Do not emulate.” The title is “A Psalm of David.” [Alcuin.] This psalm is the third among those written according to an incomplete alphabet, and it is wholly concerned with the correction of morals. For this psalm is like Christ’s garment and a drink for His body: a garment which covers His whole body with precepts, protects it against adversities, and cherishes it as in the fold of counsel.

[Aug.] [Col. 0367B] It is a drink for the weak, who murmur at the prosperity of the wicked and the toil of the good, as if all things occurred by chance. The psalm remedies their error like a health-giving antidote, teaching that all things, even these lower things, are governed by divine providence and do not happen by chance.

**Purpose.** [Alcuin.] It urges us, having despised the world, to cling to God.

**Structure.** The psalm has three parts. [Cassiod.] First, the Church, in whose person the Prophet speaks, urges that no one imitate evildoers, but that whatever good is hoped for be sought from the Lord, who gives things profitable and eternal. Second, it says that the wicked are tormented by envy toward the good, at the words “The sinner shall watch.” Third, it treats of how the righteous are never abandoned here, mingling the rewards of the good with the punishments of the wicked, with interspersed exhortations, at the words “I have been young,” etc.

Therefore, as the Church discourages the imitation of evildoers, she says:

**VERSE 1.**—“Do not emulate evildoers, nor be jealous of those who do iniquity.”

“Do not,” [Gloss] O weak person, who are accustomed to do this, “emulate,” [Jerome] that is, be indignant at, “evildoers,” [Gloss] that is, at the sight of evildoers because they flourish. “Nor be jealous,” [Jerome] that is, do not love or imitate, “those who do iniquity,” [Gloss] because they oppress the good. Why?

**VERSE 2.**—“For like grass they shall quickly wither, and like the green herbs they shall soon fall.”

“For like grass,” [Aug., Gloss] which flourishes today and is cast into the oven tomorrow, the wicked “shall quickly [Col. 0367D] wither,” that is, the wicked shall quickly fall; “and like the green herbs,” or plants of the meadow.

Another reading: [Aug.] “worthless” plants, which have no deep root. Therefore they are green in winter and dry up in summer. Grass and green herbs are taken in the same sense, and the wicked are rightly compared to them: they flourish in winter, but dry up in summer. Now, therefore, is winter; summer is the day of judgment, when the wicked, no longer green, shall fall and wither, because they have no deep root through charity.

By contrast, the tree of deep root through charity is now dry, because “what we shall be has not yet appeared”; then it will be glorious, because then the dignity of flowers will clothe us round about and the abundance of fruit will enrich us. Even if this seems long to one who endures it, it is swift to God. Therefore join yourself to God, and it will be swift for you.

That day is unknown, because it shall come like a thief, [Col. 0368A] according to the words: “Of that day no one knows, neither the Son, nor the angel, nor man” (Matt. 24). But how is the Son said not to know, when He knows all that the Father knows? Just as a day is called cheerful because it makes people cheerful, and cold is called sluggish because it makes people sluggish, so the Son is said to know or not know for us, to whom He was sent as teacher, making us know or not know. Thus He knows it for Himself, but not for us.

[Cassiod.] Otherwise, by grass are understood nobles, who easily prosper in temporal matters. By herbs, not garden herbs but wild plants—namely the most worthless plants which spring up of themselves in fields—are understood persons of middling rank. Yet both those, that is, nobles, shall quickly wither, and these, that is, persons of middling rank, shall fall. Why? Because those who are like grass, that is, nobles, shall quickly wither, and those who are like green herbs, that is, persons of middling rank, shall fall. They are so; but you:

**VERSE 3.**—“Hope in the Lord and do goodness; dwell in the land, and thou shalt be fed by its riches.”

“Hope in the Lord”; they hope in vain things. [Aug.] For hope is the entry-point of faith and the beginning of salvation. [Cassiod.] Through hope one enters into seeing that which is believed. At the beginning of faith we are taught to hope in God; and “do goodness,” [Col. 0368C] because faith without works is dead. [Aug.] They, by contrast, do evil. “And dwell in the land,” lest you do good outside the Church; [Aug., Cassiod., Jerome] “and thou shalt be fed,” even unto fullness and sweetness, “by its riches”—the riches of that land being God Himself, or the Holy Scriptures.

**VERSE 4.**—“Delight in the Lord, and He will give thee the requests of thy heart.”

“Delight in the Lord.” [Aug.] Behold the riches of the land: delight in the Lord, so that His delight or remembrance may be sweet to you. [Cassiod.] Love Him whom you fear, having cast aside the pleasure of the world, and He “will give thee the requests of thy heart,” that is, of your reason, not of the flesh. And in order that He may give:

**VERSE 5.**—“Reveal thy way to the Lord, and hope in Him; and He Himself shall act.”

“Reveal thy way to the Lord,” [Aug.] that is, tell Him what you suffer in the flesh, namely the corruption of the flesh, and that you wish to be delivered from it. “And hope in Him,” and He who is able shall act; that is, God’s grace shall deliver you from this body of death.

Or thus, from “Hope in the Lord”: hope for eternal things, which are in the Lord. And in order that you may hope, “do goodness,” that is, good deeds. In order that you may do these, cultivate the land. Another reading: “Eve,” [Alcuin] namely the body, lest it bring forth thorns and thistles. Thus thou shalt be fed by its riches, that is, by its virtues. Therefore delight not in yourself but in the Lord—that is, be delighted in Him. If this is so, He will give thee the requests of thy heart, namely the eternal things which reason seeks.

These foregoing things I say to the righteous; but if you are a sinner, “reveal thy way to the Lord,” that is, confess your sins. And then likewise “hope in Him,” that is, for the good things that are in the Lord; and “He Himself shall act,” that is, shall give. What?

**VERSE 6.**—“And He shall bring forth thy righteousness as light, and thy judgment as the noonday: be subject to the Lord, and pray to Him.”

“And He shall bring forth from the darkness of this age thy righteousness,” [Cassiod.] that is, faith, which is here as though under a bushel, “as light,” [Aug.] that is, into the light of judgment, where all things will be manifest. For now righteousness, that is, the faith by which you act justly, is hidden, because you do not yet see what you believe; and so is “thy judgment,” by which you judge and choose to follow what you do not see, and which is now mocked by the wicked. He shall bring it forth “as the noonday,” not merely as light [Col. 0369B] but as bright light.

Meanwhile you ought to do this: “be subject to the Lord,” that is, obey His commands, “and pray to Him” until He gives what He has promised. [Cassiod.] Behold a good rule: that we do good and pray continually.

**VERSE 7.**—“Do not emulate him who prospers in his way, the man who does injustices.”

“Do not.” [Gloss.] Here he explains whence indignation is usually born. Do not emulate him who prospers in his way, [Aug.] and not in God’s way, in which you are. This man prospers on the road, but at his arrival—that is, when he reaches the end—he will be unhappy; with you, the righteous person, it is the reverse. Therefore do not emulate him who prospers, namely “the man who does injustices.” But you:

**VERSE 8.**—“Cease from anger and forsake wrath; do not emulate so as to act wickedly.”

“Cease from anger,” [Aug.] lest your eye be disturbed by anger. Look upon truth, that is, Christ, who suffered much and never prospered, yet was not angry. Therefore do not be angry at the flourishing of the wicked, because to be angry and indignant at this is to murmur against God and nearly to blaspheme. “And forsake wrath.” [Cassiod.] Note the distinction between anger and wrath: anger is sudden; wrath lasts longer. Yet both must be forsaken, since through both one sins.

[Aug.] This is said to one who is still weak and swollen with the question why goods are not given to him which even the wicked possess. “And do not emulate so as to act wickedly,” that is, so as voluntarily to become wicked by imitating the one who, through malicious action, flourishes for a time.

Or thus, from “Do not emulate”: as though he said, pray to Him, and do not emulate him who prospers in his way; that is, let not the prosperity of the wicked move you from perseverance, nor be disturbed by the man doing injustices—that is, if they do unjust things to the righteous. Even if they do something to you, “cease from anger,” that is, do not be angry. Even if they do great things, “forsake wrath,” that is, do not become furious; above all, do not emulate so as to act wickedly, that is, so as to become malicious in the same manner.

**VERSE 9.**—“For those who act wickedly shall be cut off; but those who wait for the Lord shall inherit the land.”

“For those who act wickedly,” [Gloss] that is, who are evil, even if they flourish now, “shall be cut off” in the future, that is, condemned outside the boundaries of the land of the living. [Col. 0370A] But those “who wait,” [Cassiod., Gloss] namely who bear adversities and despise present things, for the sake of the Lord, who does not deceive and can do all things, “shall inherit the land” of the living. But how long must this be endured? [Aug.] What seems long to the weak will soon come. Thus:

**VERSE 10.**—“Yet a little while, and the sinner shall not be; and thou shalt seek his place and shalt not find it.”

“And yet.” As though he said: You have already endured, and there still remains “a little while,” that is, a short time. [Gloss.] Therefore do not grow weary. “And the sinner shall not be,” for whom you grieve; that is, the dominion of the sinner shall not be, who now lives for the godly person, that is, for the godly person’s benefit, whom he purifies for a short while. The “little while” extends to the end of each person’s life, when the saints are set free.

[Aug.] After this brief life, however, you will not yet be where the saints will be, to whom it shall be said: “Come, ye blessed of My Father” (Matt. 25); that is, you will not have the double garment which the saints shall have in the resurrection. But you may be in that rest in which the proud and barren rich man saw Lazarus, ulcerated and poor (Luke 16), and in that rest safely await the day of judgment, when, having received your body again, you shall be made equal to angels.

But how was Lazarus in rest when the sacrifice had not yet been offered? [Alcuin.] Entirely in hope; partially in reality, because he felt neither material fire nor the gnawing worm of conscience. “And thou shalt seek.” As though he said: Thus the sinner shall not be, because “thou shalt seek his place and shalt not find it”; that is, if you sought it, you would not find it. [Aug.] For then he shall not have the use which he now has, when God uses him to test the righteous; for God makes a scourge out of evil persons, by which He chastises His children.

**VERSE 11.**—“But the meek shall inherit the land, and shall delight in the abundance of peace.”

“But the meek,” [Cassiod.] not merely any persons who endure, but those who endure patiently, “shall inherit the land” of the living. And what shall they have there? [Aug.] “They shall delight in the abundance of peace.” The wicked delight in external things; for you, O righteous person, all things are peace.

## 79. Part II. Verse 12

**VERSE 12.**—“The sinner shall watch the righteous man, and shall gnash his teeth at him.”

“The sinner shall watch the righteous man.” [Cassiod.] This is the second part. Having said that the good ought not to emulate the wicked, he now adds that the wicked are tortured by envy toward the good because they are unlike them. Therefore it is shameful to emulate them—that is, the wicked. As though he said: Then they will have peace, but now there is war, because the sinner shall watch the righteous person, as though by hidden snares, in order to entice him. He watches him because, when he sees the righteous person, he believes himself accused by him. But if he cannot entice him, “he shall gnash his teeth at him,” like a raging beast. [Aug.] As though he said: Whom he cannot overthrow, he attempts to kill.

**VERSE 13.**—“But the Lord shall mock him, because He foresees that his day shall come.”

“But the Lord shall mock him,” [Gloss] that is, He sees him as ridiculous and causes His own people to see him thus. Therefore, as God does, so we also, seeing that the wicked will perish, should mock them. [Cassiod.] This is also a great consolation in present circumstances. He shall mock him because He foresees, [Aug.] what the sinner himself does not see, that his day will come. See this also with God: the day on which recompense shall be rendered to him.

For vengeance is always taken upon the ungodly, either here or in the future. If he converts himself, vengeance is taken upon him here, as upon Paul, who, cast down by the divine voice, came to his senses. If he does not convert himself, vengeance shall be taken upon him in the future. [Alcuin.] If neither favors nor threats prevail, punishment attacks. Hence follows:

**VERSE 14.**—“Sinners have drawn the sword; they have bent their bow.”

“Sinners have also drawn the sword.” [Aug.] Behold open assault. [Alcuin.] But if they accomplish nothing even thus, they lie in wait with deceits, when by speaking well they intend evil. Thus: “they have bent their bow,” [Aug.] that is, their deceits. Behold hidden assault, which occurs through ambushes. Afterwards he assigns each item to its corresponding purpose. As though he said: They have bent their bow:

**VERSE 15.**—“That they may deceive the poor and needy; that they may slaughter the upright in heart.”

“That they may deceive the poor,” [Gloss] who is not sufficient for himself, “and needy,” who has no hope from another. “They have drawn the sword that they may slaughter the upright in heart,” [Cassiod.] namely the martyrs. But:

**VERSE 16.**—“Let their sword enter into their own hearts, and let their bow be broken.”

“Let their sword enter into their own hearts,” from which it came. [Cassiod., Gloss.] As though he said: By killing in the body, he had killed himself in mind. This does not harm the saints; rather, their deceit becomes futile, as is said in what follows. “Let their sword enter into their own hearts,” [Col. 0371C] and so it comes to pass. [Aug.] For outwardly they harm you, O righteous person; inwardly they harm themselves. Thus they are mad, as though someone were to thrust a sword through his own body in order to cut another person’s cloak. “And let their bow be broken,” that is, let their ambushes be frustrated, so that they do not harm the righteous man, who, even if plundered, says:

**VERSE 17.**—“A little is better for the righteous than the great riches of sinners.”

“A little is better for the righteous,” etc. Or connect the text thus: Though the impious man acts thus toward the righteous, [Gloss] nevertheless the little which the righteous person possesses “is better than the great riches of sinners,” because, even if things now go well for the wicked, they will not always go so. [Alcuin.] Note that a little earlier he dealt with the malice of sinners and the endurance of the good; here, with the wealth of the former and the poverty of the latter. Truly it is better:

**VERSE 18.**—“For the arms of sinners shall be broken, but the Lord strengthens the righteous.”

“For the arms,” that is, the power, “of sinners shall be broken”; [Aug.] “but the Lord strengthens the righteous” in adversities through hope, through examples, and especially through the example of His own cross. For the cross has ended in punishment but remains in glory: it has passed from places of execution to the foreheads of emperors. He who has given such honor to His own sufferings—what will He do for His faithful people?

**VERSE 19.**—“The Lord knows the days of the undefiled, and their inheritance shall be for ever.”

“The Lord knows.” [Aug.] As though he said: How does He strengthen them? Because the Lord knows—what man cannot know—the days of the undefiled, and although they appear miserable to the ignorant, God knows what will serve their good. Or “knows,” [Jerome] that is, approves, “the Lord [knows] the days of the undefiled,” that is, the life of the undefiled; and “their inheritance,” [Gloss] which shall be given in return for their undefiled days, “shall be for ever.”

**VERSE 20.**—“They shall not be confounded in an evil time, and in days of famine they shall be satisfied, because sinners shall perish.”

“They shall not be confounded.” [Aug.] The person is confounded who hopes in man, whether in himself or in another. Hence: “Cursed is the man who makes flesh his arm” (Jer. 17). In an evil time, that is, in present tribulation, in which they rather glory; and in days of famine, which are now, when there is no full refreshment and there is much misery, they “shall be satisfied” [Col. 0372B] in hope—and truly so, because only sinners shall perish, those who, when external things are removed, possess nothing within: they are troubled outwardly and inwardly alike. For:

**VERSE 21.**—“But the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they have been honored and exalted, failing away, shall fail like smoke.”

The enemies of the Lord indeed, [Jerome, Interlinear Gloss] that is, in truth, as soon as they have been honoured with honours and power, and exalted in glory, fail inwardly and utterly fail in every virtue, just as smoke fails. [Augustine] The more widely smoke spreads, the more it vanishes; so too do the wicked. For the higher the rank, the more grievous the fall. Or thus from that place: “They shall not be confounded in the evil time” (Ps. XXIV). And it is read partly [Col. 0372C] of the present and partly of the future, thus: “They shall not be confounded in the evil time” (ibid.), that is, at the future judgment. [Cassiodorus] “And in the days of famine,” that is, in this life, which is a day of famine, when the good hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt. V), “they shall be satisfied”: through the Scriptures and examples, and through the Lord’s promises. To these two things he afterwards opposes two others, dealing with the wicked: [Cassiodorus] namely, “sinners shall perish,” in contrast to what he had said, “they shall not be confounded”; and “the enemies indeed,” in contrast to what he had said, “they shall be satisfied.” Thus the good shall not be confounded in the future, because sinners alone shall perish at the judgment; the good shall be satisfied here, but the enemies of the Lord, as soon as—that is, immediately after—they have been honoured and exalted, shall fail; that is, as soon as they ascend on high, so soon do they fall from truth. And the word *ut* (“as”) is not in the text, as [Note: [Col. 0371] the Greek nevertheless suggests it, as though it belonged to the text: ἅμα τὸ δοξασθῆναι αὐτοὺς, “at the very time when they are glorified.”]. [Col. 0372D] I say that they fail, so that not even sound judgment remains. And this is “like smoke,” because the more they are raised, the more swiftly they fall, like smoke. [Jerome] Or thus: let the first verse be read wholly of the future, and the second of the present: “They shall not be confounded in the evil time,” that is, at the judgment; and “in the days of famine,” namely, when the wicked shall hunger in the future, “they shall be satisfied.” For then sinners shall perish; and not only then, but even meanwhile, “the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they have been honoured,” etc. This is unchanged. Therefore these things happen to the wicked, because:

**VERSE 22.**—“The sinner shall borrow and shall not repay; but the righteous shows mercy and gives.”

“The sinner shall borrow and shall not repay.” [Augustine] Here he receives [Col. 0373A] body, mind, and other things from God, and gives no thanks. Or, “the sinner shall borrow,” [Cassiodorus] that is, he hears the word of God and does not repay—that is, does not render in works what he received by hearing. As though he said: he brings back no profit. [Augustine] “But the righteous shows mercy and gives” from those things which he receives from God. [Cassiodorus] Note that mercy toward those who lack comes first, and then he gives. Mercy therefore precedes in inward disposition, and generosity follows in outward action. Thus he first said “shows mercy,” and afterwards “gives.” [Augustine] There is always something for him to give, at least prayer. Therefore he shows mercy and gives, because he knows that those who bless the Lord shall inherit the earth, while those who curse shall utterly perish. And this is:

**VERSE 23.**—“For those who bless him shall inherit [Col. 0373B] the earth, but those who curse him shall utterly perish.”

“For those who bless him,” [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss] namely, giving thanks in all things and following his commands, “shall inherit the land of the living”; but those who curse him by their shameful life—of whom it is said, “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles through you” (Rom. II)—shall utterly perish. Even when they become persons who bless, they perish in evil, according to the saying, “Turn the wicked man, and he shall not be” [cf. Ps. XXXVI]. Therefore one must bless, because:

**VERSE 24.**—“With the Lord the steps of a man shall be directed, and he shall will his way.”

“The steps of a man,” [Cassiodorus] which were crooked of themselves, because human beings are born in sins, “shall be directed,” or “shall be directed with the Lord,” [Interlinear Gloss] that is, by the Lord. [Col. 0373C] This is said by comparison with a king or a commonwealth arranging affairs. [Jerome] By “steps” he means works and their effects; and through this a man shall will God’s way, even if it is hard. [Augustine] The way of earth is not hard, but it is full of robbers; the way of the Lord, however, is safe, though hard. Or, “his way,” [Alcuin] that is, the man’s way, God shall will. On this way of God:

**VERSE 25.**—“When he falls, he shall not be dashed down, because the Lord supports his hand.”

“When he falls,” [Cassiodorus] that is, when he suffers adversity in the body, he shall not be dashed down in mind. [Jerome] Or, if he falls by committing a venial sin, he is not broken by crimes, because the Lord supports—[Interlinear Gloss] he says this by comparison—“his hand,” that is, his help.

**PART III. VERSE 26.**—“I was young, and indeed I have grown old; and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed [Col. 0373D] begging bread.”

“I was young,” etc. The third part. [Cassiodorus] Here he treats of the righteous person as never forsaken, mingling the rewards of the good and the punishments of the wicked with intervening exhortations. As though he said: He supports his hand; for “I was young, and indeed I have grown old.” [Alcuin] The Church here speaks as one person: she was a child in Abel; in the prophets and patriarchs, young; in the time of the martyrs, as though old; and in a fruitful old age, at the end of the world, she will be as though in decrepit age. The prophet does not distinguish these four ages here, setting forth only two, youth and old age; and he uses youth for childhood. [Augustine, Cassiodorus] For the Church, as one person, was young in the earliest times, when she received the beginnings of the natural law in Adam; now, at the end of the age, she has grown old [Col. 0374A] in fruitful old age, when, spread abroad among all nations, she received Christ at a venerable age. And in these ages “I have not seen the righteous forsaken by God, nor his seed.” [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss] That is, his works or imitators, “begging spiritual bread”; [Augustine] that is, lacking the bread of the Word, because the Word of God is always with him. Truly he does not lack it, because:

**VERSE 27.**—“All day long he shows mercy and lends, and his seed shall be in blessing.”

“All day long.” Or join the text thus: Because he does not lack, therefore “all day long he shows mercy” in the disposition of mercy, and afterwards lends earthly things so that he may receive eternal things. [Augustine] Or, he shows mercy by admonishing and lends by teaching. [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss] This may be said either of actual almsgiving, which begins with mercy and then [Col. 0374B] opens the hand; [Cassiodorus] or of spiritual things. “And his seed,” which he sows in order to reap, [Augustine] that is, good works or imitators, “shall be in blessing,” [Interlinear Gloss] that is, in increase; [Augustine] because “he shall come with rejoicing, carrying his sheaves” (Ps. CXXV). And therefore, whoever you are:

**VERSE 28.**—“Turn away from evil and do good, and dwell for ever and ever.”

“Turn away from evil and do good,” [Augustine] that is, harm no one, but do good. He first says, “turn away from evil,” and afterwards, “do good,” because a wicked person cannot immediately desire good things. [Cassiodorus] For no one becomes beautiful all at once. Do not suppose that you have lost anything; rather, through this you shall live. And this is “dwell in the land of the living,” [Augustine] “for ever [Col. 0374C] and ever.” [Interlinear Gloss] Behold the reward: “Turn away from evil and do good.”

**VERSE 29.**—“For the Lord loves judgment; and he will not forsake his saints; they shall be preserved for ever.”

“For the Lord loves judgment,” [Augustine] by which he permits the saints to be afflicted; for even if he allows the saints to suffer, he judges justly nonetheless. [Cassiodorus] And because the Lord loves judgment, you too should love it, so that you may rejoice in your good things. “And he will not forsake his saints”; [Interlinear Gloss] even if he permits them to be afflicted, he nevertheless does not abandon them. Or, “the Lord loves judgment,” [Cassiodorus] that is, discerning persons who distinguish good from evil. “And he will not forsake his saints,” because they shall be preserved for ever, even if they die here. [Col. 0374D] In contrast:

**VERSE 30.**—“The unjust shall be punished, and the seed of the ungodly shall perish.”

“The unjust shall be punished” for their wicked deeds. “And the seed of the ungodly,” [Interlinear Gloss] that is, their works, “shall perish,” that is, they shall bear no fruit, because they shall be without the fruit of blessedness. Or, “the seed of the ungodly shall perish,” [Augustine] that is, their imitators shall perish with them, just as conversely the seed of the righteous shall be in blessing.

**VERSE 31.**—“But the righteous shall inherit the earth, and shall dwell upon it for ever and ever.”

[Augustine] “But the righteous shall inherit the land of the living,” which is eternal. Hence it follows: “and shall dwell upon it for ever and ever.” Rightly do these things belong to the righteous, because:

[Col. 0375A] **VERSE 32.**—“The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment.”

The mouth of the righteous person’s heart shall meditate wisdom, [Interlinear Gloss] which concerns God himself and eternal things; and his tongue shall speak judgment for the instruction of others, that is, what God commands one to hold fast and to flee. [Augustine] But lest you suppose that these are among those of whom it is said, “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. XV):

**VERSE 33.**—“The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps shall not be tripped up.”

“The law of his God,” [Interlinear Gloss] that is, God’s commandments, is in his heart. As though he said: the heart accords with the tongue. And what profit does this bring him? “His steps shall not be tripped up.” [Cassiodorus] To trip up is to set a pit of ambush before one’s feet. And the meaning is: [Augustine] the word in the heart [Col. 0375B] delivers one from the snares of sins. Nevertheless, his steps shall not be tripped up.

**VERSE 34.**—“The sinner watches the righteous, and seeks to put him to death.”

“The sinner watches the righteous,” [Augustine] that is, lies in wait for him, because the righteous is burdensome for him to behold: “his life is unlike that of others.” And therefore he seeks to put him to death.

**VERSE 35.**—“But the Lord will not forsake him in his hands, nor condemn him when he is judged.”

“But the Lord will not forsake him in his hands,” [Augustine] that is, in his power, as regards the soul, so that the righteous should consent to him. For as Job says: “The earth [Col. 0375C] has been given into the hand of the wicked” (Job IX), that is, the flesh, upon which he can rage; but God brings forth the soul unconquered, lest it yield to them. Nor will the Lord condemn the righteous, [Interlinear Gloss] even if he is condemned here by a human being, when the righteous is judged in the future, that is, when judgment concerning him takes place before Christ’s tribunal. That judgment shall be for that righteous person, that is, for his benefit. Behold the consolation of the righteous. Or thus: the Lord will not condemn him, that is, he will not permit the righteous to be condemned when he is judged by the wicked; that judgment shall be for that wicked person, [Alcuin] that is, for his harm. [Augustine] And because the Lord so acts toward the righteous, therefore now:

**VERSE 36.**—“Wait for the Lord, and keep his way; and he will exalt you, that you may inherit the earth; when sinners perish, you shall see it.”

[Col. 0375D] “Wait for the Lord”; and even if you suffer long in waiting, keep his way, that is, his commandments. And what then is in it for me? He “will exalt you” by merits, [Cassiodorus] because no one can possess the heavenly homeland unless exalted. Hence he adds, “that you may inherit”—as though he said: he will so exalt you that you may inherit, that is, securely possess, the land of the living. [Interlinear Gloss] Even if you do not now know what he promises, you shall later learn it by experience. Hence he adds: “when sinners perish, you shall see” in reality what you now believe concerning the rewards of the good and punishments of the wicked. He notes the joys of the good in two ways: first, because they shall then feel how great their delights are; then because they shall see the punishments of the ungodly. [Cassiodorus] Blessedness is therefore more pleasing to those delivered from such evil. Or, you shall see here in the present with the eye of faith. [Augustine] Whoever lacks that eye delights [Col. 0376A] in the prosperity of the ungodly. Will they perish? Certainly, because:

**VERSE 37.**—“I saw the ungodly exceedingly exalted, and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon.”

“I saw the ungodly.” [Cassiodorus] This is said against the notion that God is not displeased with one who enjoys prosperity here: he was “exceedingly,” that is, beyond measure, exalted in honours, and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon. He speaks by comparison. [Interlinear Gloss] Lebanon is a mountain on which there are tall cedars, which are cast down by the wind. Its name is interpreted “whiteness,” by which the brightness of this world is signified. And he is raised above the cedars of Lebanon, that is, in the brightness of this world, which is swiftly cast down.

**VERSE 38.**—“And I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found.”

[Col. 0376B] “And I passed by to his last things.” [Augustine] He passes by who attends not to the present but to the last things. Hence elsewhere: “This is a labour before me, until I enter into the sanctuary of God,” etc. (Ps. LXXII). “And behold, he was not” powerful, because his place was not found. Hence follows: “And I sought him,” whether the ungodly person lives there with the godly, that is, for the godly person’s benefit. “And his place was not found,” namely, a place of ruling. Or thus, from the passage “I saw the ungodly”: he was exalted above the humble and raised up above—according to another reading—the cedars of Lebanon, [Cassiodorus] that is, above the lofty, so that he might be loftier than the lofty. “And I passed by” the world, tending toward God in a better manner of life, becoming a true Hebrew. This is a good passing-over: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. LXXVI). Hence: “Let us pass over [Col. 0376C] to Bethlehem and see this thing which has come to pass” (Luke II). And in passing by I saw this: “Behold, he was not.” As though he said: I saw that he could do nothing, since all the things in which a human being glories are nothing. “And I sought him,” that is, I recalled him to mind, because then the good grieve more over the wicked, that they are separated from them, when they are changed for the better. “And his place was not found.” [Cassiodorus] The place of the wicked is the world, which too shall be dissolved.

The whole passage may nevertheless be understood of the devil, whose opportunity for harming has been taken away when he was bound—already in part, and wholly in the future. Hence Jeremiah cries: “The partridge gathered what she did not lay; she made riches not with judgment; in the middle of his days they shall leave him, and at his latter end he shall be found a fool” (Jer. XVII). And Joel: “I shall drive away from you him who is from the north” [Col. 0376D] (Joel II). This is: “I saw the ungodly,” that is, the devil, exalted above others, especially before Christ’s advent—before the Law and under the Law—when he drew people after himself as though a flock. But at the third time, namely of grace, and on the third day, namely Christ’s resurrection, the proud one was humbled and turned back, as a stronger man plundered his goods (Luke XI). Hence in the Rogation processions the dragon, on the first two days, precedes the cross with its tail full; on the third it follows, with that tail emptied. “And raised above the cedars of Lebanon,” that is, above the lofty. What follows is unchanged from the first reading.

**VERSE 39.**—“Keep innocence, and behold equity, for there are remnants for the peaceable man.”

[Col. 0377A] “Keep.” [Interlinear Gloss] As though he said: Since such things happen to the ungodly, be unlike them. And this is: “keep,” [Augustine] lest he wrest from you innocence—not earthly innocence. Then keep it, [Interlinear Gloss] and, even if you are burdened, understand that this is just. And this is: “behold equity.” [Cassiodorus] Or otherwise, according to another reading: “keep truth”—this is another reading—so that you may not be concerned with worldly things. And “behold uprightness,” another reading, so that God may not be considered unjust [Augustine] when he favours the ungodly and afflicts the righteous. As though he said: [Interlinear Gloss] whatever God wills, will it yourself, for otherwise you are crooked. Or, “keep innocence” with regard to God, and “behold equity” with regard to your neighbour. [Augustine] And lest you suppose that a human being is finished, attend to the last things, and you shall see that “there are remnants for the peaceable [Col. 0377B] man”: after this life good remains for him; he has not utterly perished but lives. [Augustine] The remnants are the good things left after this life to the good, that is, eternal things, or a good memory after death. [Cassiodorus] These, however, belong to the peaceable person. The peaceable person is one who preserves and makes peace among those at discord. [Cassiodorus] Note to whom this virtue belongs: he is placed in the rank of the blessed. Hence: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. V). But conversely:

**VERSE 40.**—“But the unjust shall utterly perish together; the remnants of the ungodly shall perish.”
