“But the unjust shall utterly perish together,” [Augustine] or “into the same thing,” according to another reading, that is, for ever. Or, they shall all perish together, into one; and “the remnants of the ungodly,” that is, their earthly things, [Col. 0377C] “shall perish.” Or distinguish it thus: [Alcuin] “The unjust shall utterly perish, and together with them the remnants of the ungodly,” namely earthly things, “shall perish.”

**VERSE 41.**—“But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord, and he is their protector in the time of tribulation.”

“But the salvation.” [Interlinear Gloss] As though he said: All these things belong to the righteous, yet the whole is from the Lord. And he gathers it up briefly. And this is salvation: the command, “Keep innocence, behold equity,” [Cassiodorus] is possible only through God, whose salvation of the righteous is from the Lord, [Interlinear Gloss] not from another source; and he is their protector if anyone attacks them in the time of tribulation.

**VERSE 42.**—“And the Lord shall help them and deliver them; he shall rescue them from sinners, and save them, because they hoped in him.”

[Col. 0377D] “The Lord shall help them,” [Interlinear Gloss] that is, shall work together with them; and “the Lord shall deliver them” from the labour of the vineyard in the future. Or this may be understood of the present: “the Lord shall deliver them,” that is, make them free and secure, as though there were no adversary; and “he shall rescue them,” [Cassiodorus] lest their faith be perverted by sinners. As though he said: he preserves them unharmed from the hostility of the world; and he shall save them in the future, not because they have not sinned, but because they hoped in him.

## Comparison on Psalm XXXVI: “Do Not Be Envious”

**VERSE 1.**—“Do not be envious of evildoers.” Sanctes and the interpreters for Cajetan rendered this “do not mingle yourself with them,” without reason, because the root *TAHAR* is ambiguous. Jerome and Praetensis say, “do not contend,” which accords with the meaning of our edition: namely, that no one should be disturbed, provoked, angered, [Col. 0378A] or contend because the way of the ungodly prospers. Jerome, in his Commentaries, embraced both meanings of the Hebrew word. “Envy,” he says, “has many interpretations, which ought to be understood or explained in their proper place. For here it says: Do not be a participant with evildoers, neither unto zeal nor unto envy, because zeal is wrath, according to that which the Lord said through the prophet: ‘In evil indignation I have been jealous for Zion’” (Zech. VIII). Thus he. It may also be understood to mean that no one should become like evildoers, a point touched upon by the Chaldee Paraphrast and Nebiensis.

**VERSE 3.**—“You shall be fed on his riches.” Some translate, “feed on faith,” or “on truth,” as Jerome does; some, “feed faith” or “truth,” as Praetensis and Sanctes do. But because in Hebrew the pronoun “yourself” is understood, as in “feed yourself on truth,” it was rightly said, “to feed” or “you shall be fed on faith or truth.” Yet since the particle *EMUNAH*, which they translate [Col. 0378B] “truth,” derives from the root *AMAN*, which sometimes means “to nourish,” as is proved from Lamentations IV, the Septuagint not inappropriately said “riches,” by which a human being is nourished; and the Apostle likewise calls the faith by which the righteous lives “the riches of the world,” in Romans II: “If their offence is the riches of the world, and their diminishment the riches of the Gentiles, how much more their fullness?” In every respect Nebiensis agrees in his annotations. “The Hebrew word,” he says, “means faith as much as riches. From this it is understood that, in this world, the riches of God are faith. For the one who lacks faith is most poor and miserable.” Stapulensis and Caecus call the translator to account, saying that according to the rules of Latin speech he ought to have said *pasce* (“feed”), in the imperative, since “dwell in the land” came before and the conjunction should have like moods. We reply, however, that the translator often speaks in the Greek manner, which has been received in no small degree into the Church’s usage, as, “I go fishing” (John XXI). Nevertheless, the rule of Roman usage requires [Col. 0378C] that we say “for fishing” or “to fish”; but the Greeks have this form: κατασκήνου τὴν γῆν καὶ ποιμανθήσῃ, “Dwell in the land, and you shall be fed.” Nor do I see that it is unfamiliar to Latin ears for the conjunction *and* to require corresponding moods when it signifies the consequence of a thing, as here: “Hope in God, and do goodness, and dwell in the land.” And certainly it follows from these things that “you shall be fed on his riches.”

**VERSE 5.**—“Be subject to the Lord, and pray to him.” Hebrew: *DOM LAIDONAI VEHITHHOLEL LO*, that is, “Be silent before the Lord, and wait for him.” Yet the sense comes to the same thing. For what is that silence understood here, except perfect obedience toward God without any murmuring or complaint? As for the translators’ rendering, “pray to him,” it is clear that they read *he*, the soft aspiration, in place of *chet*, the strong aspiration: *HITHHOLEL*, “praise,” though it also has another [Col. 0378D] meaning. These aspirates are not immediately distinguishable.

**VERSE 15.**—“That they may slaughter those upright in heart.” Hebrew: *IISSRE DAREC*, that is, “the righteous in way,” which the translators understood spiritually, as they ought, in place of “heart.” For the way is the spiritual disposition of the heart. Hence “foot” is customarily used in Scripture for the inward disposition, as in John XIII: “He who has bathed needs only to wash his feet” (John XIII). And Münster did not translate altogether badly when he rendered it, “those of upright conduct.” Hence Jerome, to Sunia and Fretela: “While we pursue the *kakozēlia* [affected imitation] of translation, we lose every grace of translation.”

**VERSE 17.**—“A little is better for the righteous than the many riches of sinners.” Münster, Praetensis, Pellicanus, and the translators for Cajetan refer the final term, “many,” to sinners rather than riches, in this manner: “than the riches of great or many ungodly persons.” This ought not to have been done. For Jerome [Col. 0379A] translates differently according to the Hebrew: “Than the many riches of sinners,” he says. The Chaldee and Nebiensis agree with him, and Sanctes and the Campensian Paraphrase do not differ from them. Perhaps one may tolerate departure from the Vulgate edition when the Hebrew reading seems far removed; but where it is ambiguous or close, it cannot please an impartial judge.

**VERSE 21.**—“But the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they have been honoured and exalted, shall fail; like smoke they shall fail.” Jerome: “The enemies of the Lord, glorying like unicorns, shall be consumed; like smoke they shall be consumed.” Münster: “The enemies of the Lord shall be consumed like the choicest part of lambs; they shall perish with smoke.” Sanctes: “The enemies of the Lord shall be like precious lambs; they have failed,” etc. Praetensis: “They have failed like the fat of lambs.” And the other Hebraizing interpreters likewise. Such translations differ from our edition in two words, namely “honoured” and [Col. 0379B] “exalted,” for which two other words answer in Hebrew: *KIQUAR* and *CARIM*. The first, if rendered strictly word for word, means “according to price” or “glory.” Therefore the interpreters most rightly translated “when they had been honoured”; and Jerome rendered “glorying,” to avoid the *kakozēlia* of translation.

The second word, *CARIM*, may be compounded from *RAM*, “high,” or from *REM*, “unicorn.” Jerome undoubtedly understood it in the latter sense, and it fully accords with the meaning of the Latin edition. For the monoceros, or unicorn, is an untameable animal; and the enemies of the Lord imagine themselves invincible in human glory and pride. As for the others’ rendering “like the fat of lambs” or “the precious thing of lambs,” this resulted because they took the letter [uncertain OCR: the letter itself is omitted] as essential and not auxiliary—a distinction recognized by students of Hebrew. For *CARIM*, taking the first letter as belonging to the essence of the word and not as forming a compound, means “lambs”; and *ICQUAR*, as stated above, means “price.” Their sense is: just as the fat of lambs placed upon the altar is immediately burned, so the enemies of the Lord shall fail with smoke.

**VERSE 23.**—“For those who bless him shall inherit the earth, but those who curse him shall perish.” Jerome and others read it passively: “Those who are blessed by him shall inherit the earth, and those who are cursed shall perish.” Campensis, however, reads it actively; Nebiensis likewise translates it in both active and passive senses. There is absolutely no difference in the letters. Added points make the distinction, about which there is fuller discussion in the prologue; indeed, even now the Jews do not read the Bible in their synagogues with the markings of the points. It may be read [Col. 0380A] *MEBORACAU* or *MEBARACAU*. Yet this matters very little for the understanding, since those who bless the Lord are in turn blessed by him, and those blessed by the Lord in turn bless him.

**VERSE 25.**—“When he falls, he shall not be dashed down, because the Lord supports his hand.” Because Hebrews properly lack the reflexive pronoun, namely “his own,” they use the pronoun without distinction according to the sense and sequence of the discourse. Therefore it may be translated “he puts his own hand beneath,” namely God’s; or “he sustains his hand,” namely that of the righteous man, lest he slip. Yet the sense agrees entirely.

**VERSE 37.**—“I saw the ungodly exceedingly exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon.” Jerome: “like a flourishing native.” Others: “like a laurel” or “a leafy tree.” *EZRAII* is ambiguous. It means “native,” as in Exodus XII, according to Jerome. But, as Münster says in his scholium, Hebrews take it for a tree [Col. 0380B] always green and sappy, such as the laurel, box-tree, cedar, and the like. Metaphorically, according to Rabbi David, it signifies a man who flourishes and is conspicuous to all by his nobility and lineage. Jerome calls him a “native,” that is, a citizen, who is called a green tree. For just as a green tree is conspicuous on account of its beauty and verdure, so a citizen is known to all—who he is and of what family. You see that the diversity of expressions agrees in unity of spirit.

**VERSE 38.**—“I passed by, and behold, he was not.” Jerome, Praetensis, Pellicanus, Campensis, and Nebiensis read with the Septuagint in the first person; Münster, Sanctes, and the translators for Cajetan read “he passed by,” in the third. The meaning certainly comes to the same thing. We wished to pass it over, but it is appropriate to give frequent warning about the diversity of manuscripts or readings, lest we seem to be guessing. And certainly immediately afterwards the first person is unquestionably added: “I sought,” etc.

**VERSE 39.**—“For there are remnants for the peaceable man.” [Col. 0380C] Hebrew: *AHARITH LEISCH SCHALOM*. The first word means “last” or “final”; the second means “man,” understood as “anyone,” and functions as a dative marker; the third means “peace.” Jerome therefore translates, “At the end, peace for the man.” Sanctes, alluding to what is rendered to a person at the last, says, “Because peace is each person’s reward.” Münster: “Whatever final thing is given, for such a man it is peace.” Praetensis, somewhat less aptly: “The final thing for the man of peace.” They aim at the same meaning as the Septuagint, which calls that final thing awaiting a person “remnants,” because after death nothing remains to the righteous person except innocence, simplicity, and peace of conscience. Hence the Chaldee: “The end of a man is peace.”

## Psalm XXXVII

[Col. 0379]

**TITLE OF THE PSALM:** “A PSALM OF DAVID, FOR THE REMEMBRANCE OF THE SABBATH.”

[Col. 0379D]

“Lord, do not in wrath.” The title. “A Psalm of David for remembrance.” [Cassiodorus] This psalm is third in the order of the penitential psalms. It teaches that we should always keep in memory the sin which we are wholly unable to escape—not in order to commit it, but so that we may at least restrain ourselves from its frequency. This means that this psalm belongs to David, that is, to the penitent, and is made “for remembrance,” that is, teaching us to remember sin in order that we may beware of it. Or, “for remembrance of the Sabbath.” [Augustine] The Sabbath is the rest of eternity, which he desires to possess and fears to lose. Thus this penitent man, placed amid evils, fearing worse things yet mourning, remembers the eternal Sabbath; conscious of sin, he fears to be deprived of it [Col. 0380D] and, grievously afflicted, desires to enjoy it. [Cassiodorus] For here the psalmist introduces the penitent as tormented in many ways, so that he seems to set before novices, as an example, Job himself, who conquered the incitements of the flesh and enormous sufferings, that they may gladly embrace torments less than their deserts—that is, less than they themselves have deserved—through which they are delivered from eternal punishment.

And this is the meaning: this psalm belongs to David, that is, the penitent, and is made “for remembrance of the Sabbath,” that is, it concerns remembrance of the Sabbath which the penitent desires. **Purpose:** it exhorts to penitence. **Method:** it has four divisions. First, he seeks mercy through punishments stated in summary. Second, a narrative is set forth in which miseries are enumerated, at “My scars have become putrid and corrupt.” Third, because amid so many [Col. 0381A] evils he hoped in the Lord, he declares that he will be heard, with mention of amendment, at “For in thee, O Lord, I have hoped.” Fourth, an exultant conclusion concerning salvation is given, so that hope may be certain for those who imitate him. Thus it is in all the penitential psalms: at “Forsake me not, O Lord my God,” etc. Beginning therefore with prayer and tears, he says:

**VERSE 1.**—“O Lord, do not rebuke me in thy fury, nor correct me in thy wrath.”

“O Lord, not in thy fury,” [Augustine] or “in thy indignation,” according to another reading, “rebuke me”; that is, do not let me be among those to whom at the judgment you shall say: “I was hungry, and you gave me not to eat. Depart, ye cursed, into everlasting fire” (Matt. XXV). “Nor correct me in thy wrath,” or “amend me,” according to another reading; that is, do not let me be among those [Col. 0381B] who, corrected through fire, shall be saved. Instead, correct me here, because the fire is then more grievous. Here wrath and fury are understood as the same thing, namely, the day of judgment, when God will seem angry to the wicked. Or thus: [Cassiodorus] He asks that an angry Judge may not inflict torments for destruction, but a merciful one for correction. The meaning is: O Lord, do not rebuke me in thy fury nor correct me in thy wrath; [Jerome] rebuke me in such a way that the punishment may be merciful and corrective, not wrathful and vindictive.

**VERSE 2.**—“For thy arrows are fixed in me, and thou hast made firm thy hand upon me.”

“For thy arrows,” etc. [Augustine] Here the penitent enumerates the evils that he suffers, so that, because they are many, they may be enough—that is, sufficient for God—and he may not suffer worse things. As though he said: Do not rebuke me in fury, because what I suffer can suffice thee. And this is: “For thy arrows are fixed in me.” The arrows are God’s punishments, namely pains of mind and body. For just as arrows are drawn and fixed, so punishments were made intense in Adam by the threat with which God threatened Adam, saying: “In whatsoever day thou shalt eat, thou shalt die the death” (Gen. II). And because he ate, they were fixed in us also through punishment and guilt. He was the origin of this misery; we are his offspring. They are fixed, and not for an hour; rather, thou hast made them firm for a long time, namely, that they should endure to the end of the age and in many parts, namely, in flesh and soul, and in those same parts in many ways, as will be shown [Col. 0381D] in what follows. [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss] “Thou hast made firm,” I say, “thy hand upon me,” that is, thy punishment. Here he seeks mercy from the Judge’s power. Thou hast made it firm to such an extent that:

**VERSE 3.**—“There is no health in my flesh because of thy wrath; there is no peace in my bones because of my sins.”

“There is no health in my flesh.” [Augustine] For he bears a mortal body subject to so many miseries that even when it is called sound, it is not truly sound, since it can readily be harmed. Hence he says here: “There is no health in my flesh because of thy wrath”; [Cassiodorus] that is, because of the force of punishment exercised in Adam. Here he seeks mercy from his own weakness, a punishment which is not unjust, [Augustine] because it is for sins. And this is: “There is no peace [Col. 0382A] in my bones.” He takes bones for flesh and explains what he had said, saying it otherwise: “because of my sins.” As though he said: my sins are the cause of this thing.

**VERSE 4.**—“For my iniquities have passed over my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me.”

“For my iniquities.” He repeats what he had said, explaining it more clearly: “My iniquities have passed over,” or “lifted up, my head.” This is what he had earlier said: “because of my sins.” Therefore, “like a heavy burden,” or “a heavy load,” “they have weighed upon me.” This is what he had earlier said: “There is no peace in my bones.” The meaning is: “For my iniquities have passed over my head, like a heavy burden,” etc. [Col. 0382B] [Augustine] That is, because iniquity raised the proud person’s head against God, God weighed him down with the mass of punishments, as with a load, and pressed him down so that he could no longer rise. Note also that he fittingly says that iniquities have weighed upon him, because iniquities, which are light and pleasant while they are being committed, are burdened with afflictions—that is, they become burdensome and heavy.

[Interlinear Gloss] Or thus from “There is no peace,” where he shows the soul’s affliction after displaying the flesh’s weakness. The meaning is: “There is no health in my flesh; and also there is no peace in my bones,” that is, not even in reason is there peace, because the flesh attacks it. And this is “because of my sins,” that is, because of the urgency of my thoughts and suggestions. There is no peace because sin reigns in the mortal body (Rom. VI). And this is what he says: “For my iniquities have passed over [Col. 0382C] my head,” that is, my reason. The rest is unchanged.

[Cassiodorus] Otherwise, the whole passage from “For thy arrows”: he calls the arrows words of God, which pierce human hearts and inflict the wound of love, not of envy. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded by love.” These words, fixed in the penitent person’s heart, cause him to remember the eternal Sabbath. As though he said: Do not rebuke me, because “thy arrows are fixed in me,” that is, thy words are fixed in my heart and make me remember the Sabbath. And because he does not yet possess what he loves, he groans. Hence follows: “Thou hast made firm thy hand upon me,” namely thy punishment, because I do not possess what I love. Thus “there is no health in my flesh,” that is, I know that there is no salvation of the flesh in comparison with the future. There is no health, and this is “because of thy future wrath,” [Col. 0382D] [Cassiodorus] that is, because I have foreseen the face of wrath. That is: because thou threatenest, lest I see wrath. This man is so terrified by fear of future wrath that there is no health in his flesh, after the manner of a modest servant who is afflicted by future lashes. “And there is no peace in my bones”: as though he said, grievous pain reaches even to the inward parts. And this is “because of my sins,” because a saint is afflicted by sins more than by bodily punishments, thinking that he deserves more grievous things. “For my iniquities,” etc. As though he said: I have not suffered unjustly, but I impute everything to my sins, whereby he more effectively seeks mercy. And this is: “For my iniquities have passed over,” etc. These things are unchanged.

**PART II. VERSE 5.**—“My scars have become putrid and corrupt because of my foolishness.”

[Col. 0383A] “They have putrefied,” etc. [Cassiodorus.] The second part, where there is narration, in which miseries are enumerated. As though he were saying: “My iniquities have gone over my head, because my scars”—[Glossa interlinearis], that is, the wounds of sins—“which had been healed through baptism, have putrefied,” when one now consents again to sin, “and have become corrupt,” when it is brought into action. [Note: [Col. 0383D] From Gregory, in the exposition of the seven psalms.] And all this is “because of my folly,” that is, through my own stupidity, because I have not employed the powers received in baptism. This I ascribe to myself, not to God. And this is the same as what he said above, “because of my sins.” [Glossa interlinearis.] Alternatively, “my scars,” or “my bruises”—another reading—[Cassiodorus], that is, “my sins,” “have putrefied,” [Augustine] in others through example. And “they have putrefied” is another reading. It is evident to me myself that this man is not sound, because he has scars [Col. 0383B] which have putrefied for others and stink to him, so that, turning away from them, we may breathe in the fragrance of the eternal Sabbath and, running with the bride after the fragrance of the ointments, may groan. “Because of my folly” remains unchanged.

VERSE 6.—“I have been made miserable and bent down utterly; all day long I went about sorrowing.”

“I have been made miserable.” [Alcuin.] He said how his iniquities had gone over him; here he says how they weighed him down. As though he were saying: Because they have putrefied, therefore “I have been made miserable,” [Augustine] that is, I have been afflicted with miseries, “and I have been bent down” from pride; for everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled (Luke 18). This man has been bent by God so that he cannot raise himself, like the bent woman whom the Lord found [Col. 0383C] bent for eighteen years and raised up. Or, “I have been bent down,” [Augustine] that is, devoted to earthly things. Hence also “I have been made miserable,” that is, sad.

“I have been made miserable,” and this “unto the end,” that is, unto death; “and all day,” that is, throughout my whole life, namely continually “I went about sorrowing,” because I remembered the Sabbath of which I was deprived; yet I went about, or walked, [Cassiodorus] along the way of this life without despair. “I have been sorrowful,” therefore,

VERSE 7.—“For my loins have been filled with delusions, and there is no health in my flesh.”

“For my loins have been filled.” [Augustine.] Or, “my soul has been filled with delusions, and there is no health in my flesh.” Thus there is nowhere in the whole human being from which full joy may come, until the soul is stripped of delusions and the body clothed with health. The delusions of the soul [Col. 0383D] are countless; they sometimes scarcely permit one to pray. Images of bodies present themselves, and you pass from one to another; forgetfulness comes, and you remember this in place of that, and so forth. These will be driven away when we see the truth as it is. Hence the Apostle: “Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7.) “The grace of God.”

Or thus: [Jerome, Glossa interlinearis] by “loins” let us understand carnality, that is, sensuality, which is harassed by the devil and the body is afflicted. As though he were saying: I sin not only through my own weakness, but also through the devil—[Cassiodorus], that is, through the devil—who afflicts the body and harasses the soul with various imaginations. And this is what “my loins,” or “my soul,” that is, “my carnality,” [Col. 0384A] “have been filled with delusions,” namely diabolical ones, means. And meanwhile through this, “there is no health in my flesh,” which the devil afflicts, just as above, through the arrows, there was no health in it.

VERSE 8.—“I have been afflicted and exceedingly humbled; I roared from the groaning of my heart.”

“I have been afflicted.” [Cassiodorus.] To the two things set forth he supplies two corresponding explanations: “there is no health in my flesh,” because I have been afflicted in body; “my soul is filled with delusions,” and that is because “I have been humbled” in mind, so that nothing in me may be free from punishment—“exceedingly,” because calamity is on every side.

Or thus: [Glossa interlinearis.] I have been sorrowful and afflicted through repentance, and “I have been exceedingly humbled” by the humility of repentance; “I roared from the groaning of my heart.” [Alcuin.] Groaning is usually made in the heart, roaring in the voice. But this man roars [Col. 0384B] from groaning, not in his voice. And “I roared” means, [Glossa interlinearis] I sought refreshment for the soul with great longing. [Cassiodorus.] This is by comparison with a lion and other beasts, to which he compares himself in order that the groaning may be shown stronger. And that roaring came from groaning. Behold, the strength of patience is shown: he breaks forth into groaning, not into words.

And the sense is: [Augustine.] I desired and sought the Sabbath, and because I did not obtain it, I groaned. And that groaning was “of my heart,” [Jerome] that is, of reason. For there is a groaning of the flesh and a groaning of the mind. Every groaning that arises from outward things is of the flesh; but that which is for the Sabbath, which the flesh does not attain, is of the heart.

VERSE 9.—“Lord, all my desire is before thee, and my groaning is not hidden from thee.”

“Lord, before thee.” As though he were saying: “I roared from the groaning of my heart,” [Augustine] a groaning which man does not know. But, O Lord, before thee, who seest the heart, is all my desire. If desire is before God, then so also is the groaning that accompanies it. Desire indeed is prayer; and one who does not cease to love never ceases to pray. For charity is love.

Or thus: [Glossa interlinearis.] “All my desire, O Lord, is before thee,” that is, I desire nothing except to be before thee. And “all my desire is before thee,” [Cassiodorus] that is, it is of such a kind as deserves to be before thee, because I groan for sins. Therefore “my groaning is not hidden from thee,” [Augustine, Alcuin] and not from men, but is heard, because [Col. 0384D] it is devoutly directed toward the liberation of the soul, not toward earthly things but toward heavenly things. God does not heed other groanings.

VERSE 10.—“My heart is troubled; my strength has forsaken me; and the light of my eyes, even that is not with me.”

“My heart.” Here he explains the pains of the soul. “My heart is troubled within me.” [Cassiodorus.] As though he were saying: Hence come pain and groaning, because my heart is troubled within me. [Augustine.] Fear and anxiety are inflicted from every side. And this is because “my strength has forsaken me,” the strength which I had before sin. Had that strength remained, nothing would terrify me. Why did this strength also leave? [Augustine.] Because “even the light of my eyes is not with me,” [Col. 0385A] that is, the light which is God is not with me, ever since Adam fled into the shadow, fearing the face of God. No one sees this light in the present by direct sight; for although they are now Christians, they do not yet see it, nor will they see it in the future.

Or thus: [Cassiodorus.] “My heart is troubled within me,” that is, my mind has succumbed to passions, because my strength—that is, the strength of patience—has forsaken me; and “the light of my eyes is not with me,” that is, untroubled reason, which he does not retain amid such immense troubles.

VERSE 11.—“My friends and my neighbours drew near against me and stood.”

“My friends.” [Augustine.] Thus far he has confessed what he suffers inwardly from himself; now he tells what he suffers outwardly, from those among whom he lives. Hence elsewhere it is said: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare thy servant from strangers” (Ps. 18 [19]). And therefore, speaking in the person of the Head, he expounds Christ’s passion, not separating his own voice from the Head. For just as the Head calls our sins his own, so we should call the sufferings set forth here his own, because the voice of the whole is one. These things also suit every person living among others.

He therefore says in the person of the Head: “My friends,” false friends, “and my neighbours,” namely his kinsmen, the Jews, “drew near against me,” crucifying him, and with counsels and deceits [Gregory] “stood” perseveringly.

VERSE 12.—“And those who were near me stood afar off; and those who sought my life used violence.”

“And those who were near me,” [Augustine] namely the apostles, [Col. 0385C] “stood afar off,” fearing death; and “those who sought my life” to take it away, not to imitate it, “used violence,” that is, crucified me.

VERSE 13.—“And those who sought evils for me spoke vanities and devised deceits all day long.”

“And those who sought evils for me,” [Augustine] because they found no crimes, “spoke vanities,” that is, fabricated falsehoods; and they “devised deceits,” that is, frauds, all day long. How many false testimonies did they utter before the cross, and after the resurrection through the bribed guards? Of these Isaiah says: “I will appoint wicked men for his burial” (Isa. 53). For, corrupted by money, they sowed a lie, saying: “While we slept [Col. 0385D] his disciples came and took him away” (Matt. 28).

VERSE 14.—“But I, like a deaf man, did not hear; and like a dumb man not opening his mouth.”

“But I, like a deaf man, did not hear,” [Augustine] that is, I did not answer, as though I did not hear; “and like a dumb man not opening his mouth.” And not only did I not hear, but also—

VERSE 15.—“I became like a man who does not hear and who has no rebukes in his mouth.”

“And I became like a man who does not hear,” [Augustine] that is, I became as though I could not hear, “and having no rebukes in his mouth.” Thus he was silent against them, [Col. 0386A] as though he had nothing with which to accuse them—though he had done so before. But that had to be fulfilled: “Like a sheep before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53).

“For in thee, Lord, I have hoped.” As though he were saying: Therefore I was silent in the Passion, because “in thee, Lord, I have hoped; thou wilt hear me, O Lord my God.” If one’s conscience is good, there is nothing to fear and nothing about which to hesitate.

“Because I said.” Again here the Head speaks concerning weak feet, that is, the members, just as previously he spoke concerning himself; for although he is in heaven, he does not abandon those whom he has on earth. As though he were saying: Therefore thou wilt hear, because I said: “Let not my enemies ever rejoice over me,” that is, over my members, so as to prevail against them; for this is what they strive for. And because, while my feet—that is, my weak members—are moved, at times into some sin, [Col. 0386B] my enemies “have spoken great things over me,” that is, the most wicked tongues of enemies rise up, when pity would rather have been fitting.

[Cassiodorus.] Alternatively, from the passage “My friends”: the grievously afflicted penitent says these things, so that Job himself seems to utter these words: “My friends and my neighbours.” Humanity rejoices in these two consolations, but these people become an accumulation of sufferings. Hence it follows: “They drew near and stood against me,” reproaching me; thus the stroke came upon me and I failed. “And those who were near me stood afar off,” including even my wife. Hence he himself says: “My wife abhorred my breath” (Job 19). “And those who sought my life used violence,” that is, the devil with his servants, who, the more they strive after the death of the soul, the more they see someone standing firm.

[Col. 0386C] “And those who sought evils for me,” such as his wife and friends, “spoke vanities,” because, counselling for the body, they suggest things opposed to the soul—namely, that he should speak against God. “They devised deceits all day long.” “But I, like a deaf man” to the counsel of those urging iniquity, “did not hear. And I became like a dumb man not opening his mouth.” He calls him dumb and says “not opening his mouth,” because even if a dumb person does not speak plainly, he at least murmurs in stammering. This penitent likewise said nothing harsh, nothing against God.

Notice that against wicked thoughts this man is silent, whereas above against bodily pains he roared. “And I became like a man who does not hear,” thereby being a man [Alcuin], that is, rational. As though he were saying: I was made like one who pretends [Col. 0386D] not to hear insults, wherein he is a man, that is, rational, lest by this he fall into something worse; “and not having rebukes in his mouth”: I was silent as though there were nothing I could justly answer. Behold the great strength of hearing harmful things and not replying in return.

PART III. VERSE 16.—“For in thee, Lord, I have hoped; thou wilt hear, O my God.”

“For in thee, Lord, I have hoped.” [Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which he affirms that he will be heard, with remembrance of amendment, because amid so many evils he hoped in the Lord. As though he were saying: They do these things to me, but I have hoped. It is a saving remedy amid evils to hope and not fail—in thee, Lord, who changest sad things into joyful ones. Repeat: And because “in thee, Lord, I have hoped,” “thou wilt hear me, O Lord my God.” Therefore thou wilt hear—

[Col. 0387A] VERSE 17.—“Because I said: Let not my enemies ever rejoice over me; and while my feet are moved, they have spoken great things over me.”

“Because I said: Let not my enemies ever rejoice.” [Augustine.] Amid evils the saint especially guards against the enemy’s exulting over his fall. I said this, and yet perhaps it happens for correction. And this is what is meant by “while my feet are moved,” that is, my actions. [Cassiodorus.] And while this happens, “they have spoken great things over me”: if they are ever moved through human weakness, the ungodly mock, whereas the godly grieve. Therefore thou wilt also hear.

VERSE 18.—“For I am ready for scourges, and my sorrow is always before me.”

“For I am ready,” [Augustine] knowing that I have sinned, [Col. 0387B] “for scourges.” As though he were saying: I was born for this, to bear scourges. For God scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. 12). Therefore let not my enemies exult; “and my sorrow is always before me.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] He grieves because he has sinned; the ungodly person defends himself, while the righteous person is angry against himself.

VERSE 19.—“For I shall declare my iniquity, and I shall be concerned for my sin.”

“For my iniquity.” [Augustine.] As though he were saying: What causes the sorrow? Not the scourge, which is medicine, but the wound of sin; for unless he grieved, he would not accuse himself thus. And this is what “I shall declare my iniquity” means: I shall confess it. And because confession is not enough, he adds, “I shall be concerned,” that is, I shall be anxious [Col. 0387C] and diligently act for the healing of my sin. There are two modes of perfect repentance: confession and amendment, which is effected by tears, almsgiving, and such things as are indicated here.

VERSE 20.—“But my enemies live and are strengthened against me, and those who hate me unjustly are multiplied.”

“But my enemies,” [Cassiodorus] sent by thy permission to test me, “live,” [Augustine] that is, enjoy the world, because they fare well in the age in which I labour and roar; and they “are strengthened” in lies. Or, “have grown strong,” another reading; “they are against me,” [Glossa interlinearis] in persecution—which is more grievous. This contributes to obtaining aid. And they are not few, but “those who hate me unjustly are multiplied,” that is, become more numerous each day—which is most grievous—[Col. 0387D] [Augustine] repaying evils for good. Hence follows:

PART IV. VERSE 21.—“Those who repay evils for goods slandered me, because I followed goodness.”

“Those also who repay evils for goods slandered me.” Why? [Augustine.] “Because I followed goodness.” This is why he said, “evils for goods.”

[Col. 0388A] PART IV. VERSE 22.—“Do not forsake me, O Lord my God; do not depart from me.”

“Do not forsake me.” [Cassiodorus.] The fourth part, where there is a rejoicing conclusion, so that there may be sure hope for those who imitate him. As though he were saying: The evils just mentioned are brought upon me, [Gregory] but because these evils are unbearable to a human being, “do not forsake me.” Or the text may be joined thus: [Cassiodorus.] Here the penitent, freed from past sins and joyfully confessing with thanksgiving that God is the author of his salvation, cries out that he may no longer be abandoned, saying: “Do not forsake me, O Lord my God,” [Gregory] because an offence after pardon is grievous. And if thou forsakest me for an hour, do not depart utterly from me; but rather—

[Col. 0388B] VERSE 25.—“Attend to my help, O Lord, God of my salvation.”

“Attend to my help,” [Cassiodorus] while I fight against the enemy, “O Lord, God of my salvation,” giver of eternal salvation.

[Augustine.] Alternatively, “Do not forsake me” may be understood as words of Christ. For we say these things in him who intercedes for us, that is, in the person of Christ saying: “Do not forsake me, O Lord my God.” But since he says here, “Do not forsake me, do not depart from me,” how then did he cry above: “Why hast thou forsaken me?” (John 19). What is said here seems contrary to that cry, but it is not. There the voice is that of the old man, crucified with him; that is, there he spoke in the person of the Church, which is old in guilt and punishment, whose oldness was consumed on Christ’s cross. Here [Col. 0388C] he speaks in his own proper person: “Attend to my help, O Lord, God of my salvation,” [Cassiodorus] because he saved both my soul and freed body and soul from sufferings.

COLLATION ON PSALM 37: “O LORD, NOT IN THY WRATH.”

VERSE 7.—“My loins have been filled with delusions.” Münster translates “thighs” for “loins.” Pagninus, Sanctes, and Campensis in his paraphrase translate “the flanks or entrails.” I do not know by what ingenuity. For although the Hebrew word *KESALAI* also signifies that, it at the same time denotes “loins,” as Jerome, Pellicanus, the interpreters for Cajetan, the Chaldee paraphrase, and Nebiensis translate it. But for “delusions,” Jerome gives “disgrace”; Pellicanus, “baseness”; others, “burning” or “combustion.” It is easy to adapt these to the exposition of the context. The Chaldee also agrees with us.

VERSE 11.—“My friends and my neighbours drew near against me.” Hebrew: “my beloved ones and my friends stood against my leprosy,” or “opposite my wound.” *Negaʿ* is a noun signifying a scabby wound, and *nigʿî*, “my wound,” as the Hebrews have understood it. But *nāgaʿ* as a verb signifies “to draw near” and “to strike,” and *nāʾû*, “they drew near,” results from reading *waw* in place of *yod* and disregarding the vowel points. How easy this is among the Hebrews is well known.

PSALM 38.

[Col. 0387]

TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END: A CANTICLE OF DAVID FOR JEDUTHUN.”

[Col. 0387D]

“I said.” The title: “Unto the end: a canticle of David for Jeduthun.” [Col. 0388D] It is read in Chronicles that, when the ark of the Lord had been brought back from the Philistines, David appointed before it four thousand singers and an equal number of gatekeepers. Over these he set the sons of Korah; over the singers he placed two hundred and eighty-eight men, among whom were Asaph, Heman, Ethan, and Jeduthun. Ezra frequently placed their names in the titles, both for the honour of the mystery and because of the meanings of the names, by which the sense of the psalms set beneath them is opened—as the meaning of this psalm is opened.

By this name Jeduthun, which is interpreted “leaping over those,” that is, those remaining in the world and clinging to earthly things, is meant the one who leaps over them, concerning whom this psalm speaks. For this psalm teaches the mind to leap from love of the world to God’s law, and thence to eternity. And because this is pleasant to the mind, though burdensome to the flesh, “canticle” is fittingly added in the title. The sense is: This canticle is called a canticle because it mentions [Col. 0389B] eternal blessedness, for the sake of which it is pleasant for the mind to leap over, though it be burdensome to the flesh. It directs us “unto the end,” that is, unto consummation; it is of David the prophet. And it is “for Jeduthun,” [Glossa interlinearis] that is, concerning one who leaps over.

Purpose. [Cassiodorus.] This psalm warns us to preserve restraint of the tongue among blasphemers and wicked persons, and to restrain contests and quarrels. Such silence is greatly useful.

Arrangement. The psalm has three parts. First, it treats of restraint of the tongue among blasphemers and revilers, and thus desires to know the end, where these evils are absent. Second, it says how all are subject to vanity and contingency; therefore it adds that it awaits the Lord and asks to be delivered, at “Nevertheless, in an image.” Third, amid all the evils of the world it asks that God be present and sins forgiven, so that it may depart with a favourable [Col. 0389C] end, at “Hear my prayer.”

[Augustine.] This leaper-over, renouncing earthly attractions, always incurs the envy and slander of the wicked through his good reputation. Therefore he resolves to be silent among evil people, lest he say anything wrongly, beginning thus:

VERSE 1.—“I said: I will keep my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue.”

“I said,” [Cassiodorus] that is, I deliberated in my heart, where wise people deliberate before they speak. He first deliberates because what he begins is difficult. Explaining what it is, he adds: “I will keep.” He says this [Augustine] because perhaps he had already fallen in speech: “my ways,” that is, my actions and words. I say, “my ways,” now good ones, [Cassiodorus.] [Jerome.] Therefore I shall keep them [Col. 0389D] “that I may not sin with my tongue” through foolish or idle speech—which is difficult. [Augustine.] For the tongue is not in a moist place without reason: it slips easily. Therefore perfect is the person who does not sin with the tongue (James 3). “My tongue,” [Glossa interlinearis] that is, under my control.

VERSE 2.—“I set a guard upon my mouth when the sinner stood against me.”

“I set a guard upon my mouth.” [Augustine.] As though he were saying: After I passed beyond earthly delights, and by good words incur envy and slander from them, understanding before God suffices me, lest by speaking I give an opening to slanderers. In this there is often disturbance, so that things are said which ought not to be said; against this the better remedy is silence. Therefore he says here: “I set a guard upon my mouth.” As though he were saying: I said, “I will keep,” and I set a guard upon my mouth lest unsuitable words [Col. 0390A] should go forth.

“I set a guard,” not because of diligent people ready to hear, but “when [the sinner] stood,” namely with persistence. As though he were saying: I did this when it was most necessary. The sinner, namely one who does not perceive the things of God’s Spirit and slanders: to persons of this kind—proud, slanderous, quarrelsome—nothing ought to be said. Thus the Lamb, namely Christ, was silent without a voice before his shearer; he also withheld things to be said later from his disciples, though they were ready to hear much. I say, “stood against me,” seeking an occasion for slander; the sinner is deceived by the silence of the one who has leapt over, being unable to catch him in words. Hence follows:

VERSE 3.—“I was dumb and humbled, and I kept silence from good things; and my sorrow was renewed.”

“I was dumb.” [Jerome.] As though he were saying: I set a guard [Col. 0390B] to such an extent that “I was dumb,” that is, wholly silent, “and I was humbled.” This is said so that you may understand the silence to be pure, not deceitful. Or, “I was humbled,” [Jerome] that is, I endured reproaches from them; [Cassiodorus] “and I kept silence from announcing good things.” Or, “from good people,” because one should not give what is holy to swine nor cast pearls before dogs (Matt. 7). He was silent, therefore, from good things, lest he teach one who despises them and seeks a cause for contention.

[Augustine.] Thus “my sorrow,” which he suffered in speaking and from which he rested in silence, “was renewed.” His sorrow arises because he withholds from fellow servants the food of the word. Therefore—

VERSE 4.—“My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation fire shall blaze.”

“My heart grew hot within me,” [Cassiodorus] that is, it grew warm in every part with the fire of God, that is, love of heavenly things. [Col. 0390C] And this “within me,” [Alcuin] that is, in reason, so that he might think upon heavenly things. Notice that he thought inwardly before he went outward in speech.

Or “my heart grew hot within me,” [Cassiodorus] that is, through the inward grace of the Holy Spirit; “and in my meditation,” that is, in my deliberation. He says this lest the burning intensity of his love should seem mad: “fire shall blaze,” namely the fire of love.

VERSE 5.—“I spoke with my tongue: Make known to me, O Lord, my end.”

“I spoke.” [Cassiodorus.] He said that he thought inwardly. [Alcuin.] Here he says that he spoke outwardly. As though he were saying: After I considered within myself, I also spoke “with my tongue,” that is, with the tongue of those who leap over. [Augustine.] He did not speak in order to instruct a hearer, [Cassiodorus] but to God who hears him. From him I hear inwardly that I was unwillingly silent among the wicked, but I spoke to the Lord, driven by the heat of charity. What did I say? Namely: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end,” [Augustine] that is, Christ, who is our end: consummation unto righteousness in the present and unto a crown in the future.

VERSE 6.—“And what is the number of my days, that I may know what is lacking to me?”

“Also make known to me what is the number of my days.” [Augustine.] He wished to know this not from desire for this life, [Cassiodorus] but from longing for Christ, that it might appear whether he could see Christ’s coming, which the ancient Fathers longed greatly to see. Hence: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see,” etc. (Luke 10). Hence the aged Simeon cried out, “Shall I see?” etc. (Luke 2). Hence also, before the Lord’s Nativity, those antiphons are sung in the person of the ancient Fathers, [Cassiodorus] namely, “O Adonai,” “O Wisdom,” and so forth.

[Augustine, Alcuin.] Therefore I wish to know the number, that I may know what is lacking to me for life before Christ’s coming. Before him much is lacking for life, because before him are Adam’s old days, which lead to death, and not the new generation which leads to life. Hence follows:

VERSE 7.—“Behold, thou hast made my days measurable, and my substance is as nothing before thee.”

“Behold.” [Glossa interlinearis.] As though he were saying: Is anything lacking? Certainly, because behold, thou hast made my days—or, according to another reading, my old days—[Cassiodorus] short and empty; the text then reads “my feet,” an apparently corrupt reading. And my substance, condemned when Adam sinned, “is as nothing” of itself, because it passes quickly, and while it exists, it is nothing. [Cassiodorus.] Good actions indeed are something, because they confer life. It is nothing, I say, and this “before thee,” who truly seest; [Cassiodorus] as though he were saying: Even if the acts of one who leaps over are something, his substance is nevertheless nothing before God.

VERSE 8.—“Nevertheless, every living human being is altogether vanity.”

“Nevertheless.” [Cassiodorus.] This man, seeing Christ’s coming, which he had asked to see, yet not possessing the eternal good, returns to the weakness he has amid virtues, saying: Great are the things we have said and believe; nevertheless that eternal reality is not yet here. Rather, all things are vanity because of their changeableness. And [Col. 0391C] because they are mutable and passing, behold, this man who desires eternal things reproaches the human life to which he is subject. He says this lest anyone suppose saints to be free from temptations.

[Glossa interlinearis.] To this vanity belongs man, not God, not every spirit, [Jerome] that is, both the good and the bad. If one is evil, he is vain in worldly matters; but if he is good, this life is vain to him who wishes to be with Christ. I mean a human being living in this world.

Alternatively, from the passage “I was dumb,” or “I became deaf.” This one who leaps over says that he kept silence from good things while fearing that he might speak evil. “I kept silence,” [Augustine] that is, I kept silent even about good things to the converted, while I feared that I might speak evil. And because I do not distribute to the poor the talent entrusted to me, [Col. 0391D] the rich Lord does not entrust it to me. And this is “I became deaf,” another reading: I began no longer to hear from God. For he has been placed between the rich God and the poor human being. The leaper-over runs between God and man, that he may receive from God and distribute to man his master’s money. But while he fears being lavish and wasteful, he becomes a miserly steward by not distributing to others (Matt. 25). Therefore it is withdrawn from him by the Lord. He confesses that he suffered this, teaching us to beware lest we imitate it.

[Augustine.] But if this slothful servant is condemned because he does not distribute, what will that person suffer who wastes through luxury? Thus “I was humbled” by God; I did not humble myself. And so “my sorrow was renewed”: he grieves that he kept silent about what ought to have been said. Because he saw evils, he kept silent even about good things and toward good persons; hence, because he was silent, “zeal for thy house consumed me” [Col. 0392A] (Ps. 60 [69]), that is, love for the neighbours to whom he was silent distresses him.

Hence follows: “My heart grew hot within me.” His heart began to be restless, seeing dangers on both sides. “And in my meditation fire shall blaze,” that is, agitation, while I see dangers in both alternatives—speaking and being silent—amid turbulent and slanderous people and those ready to hear. In this heat I “spoke with my tongue,” that is, I sought a better place, where I would not suffer these things: namely, the end, that is, eternal life. And this is: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end.” [Glossa interlinearis.] As though he were saying: Although I have passed over many things, there still remains an end where there are no scandals.

“And the number”: behold, as though the end were known, he desires more and passes over everything; for he desires to know more perfectly concerning the end. And this is: “Make known to me the number [Col. 0392B] of my days.” [Augustine.] This is the number without number, which is truly a number of days and does not pass away. But the number of the present days is not truly a number for one who leaps over; it only appears to be so to one who clings.

“That I may know what,” that is, how much, “is lacking to me here in the present.” A person who knows these things is more humble. “Behold, measurable”: as though he were saying, with the end known, he considers these temporal things which he leaves behind and compares them with one another. Someone might say: Why did you say that those days are, as though these temporal days were not? What do you think of these passing days? [Glossa interlinearis.] “Behold, thou hast made my days measurable,” though thou hadst given them immeasurable duration if man had remained steadfast. Or, “my old days,” another reading: [Augustine.] Thou hast made my days measurable because bodies are corrupted by sin and punishment.

“And my substance [Col. 0392C] is as nothing before thee,” that is, whoever has seen that this substance is nothing sees before thee, sees where thy eyes are, not where human eyes are; that is, he agrees with thy vision. [Alcuin.] Or, “my substance is as nothing before thee,” that is, in comparison with that substance which shall hereafter be before thee.

[Augustine.] “Nevertheless”: as though he were saying, although I have passed over so many things, although I long for eternal things, nevertheless, while I live here, where there are so many scandals and temptation, “every living human being is altogether vanity,” both the one who leaps over and the one who clings; that is, they still belong to total vanity, because all things under the sun are vanity. Everything visible is under the sun; invisible things, however, are not under the sun—that is, faith, hope, and charity. Here Jeduthun has a place beyond the sun, whose citizenship is in heaven (Phil. 3).

[Col. 0392D] Or thus: although days are measurable and substance is nothing, nevertheless “every living human being is altogether vanity”; that is, there is total vanity in the rational creature, which according to different persons seeks total vanity. This man groans over this, just as he burns with the love of things above.

Or thus: although substance is nothing, nevertheless every person living [Glossa interlinearis] as though pleasantly in the world which he serves is “altogether vanity”: he is vanity itself, not merely vain. This is said for emphasis.

PART II. *Diapsalma* (Interlude). VERSE 9.—“Nevertheless, man passes through in an image; but he is also troubled in vain.”

“Nevertheless.” [Cassiodorus.] Here is the second part, in which he says how all are subject to vanity and contingency. Therefore [Col. 0393A] he sets himself in contrast as one who awaits the Lord and asks to be delivered. As though he were saying: Although man applies himself so eagerly to vanity, nevertheless “man passes through,” [Alcuin] that is, passes quickly, “in an image,” that is, comparably to the image in a mirror, which quickly disappears. Hence Job: “Man comes forth like a flower and is crushed, and flees,” etc. (Job 13).

Or thus: Though he applies himself to vanity, nevertheless man passes through. This remains unchanged. I mean, he is placed in God’s image, that is, in reason; and it is therefore astonishing that this does not draw him away from vanity. Yet “he is troubled in vain”: [Cassiodorus] he is led away from purity of mind into worldly pursuits, because with labour and misery he desires earthly things. And this is “in vain,” that is, uselessly, because all things pass away.

Alternatively, according to another reading: “Although man walks in an image, nevertheless he is vainly troubled.” And the sense is: Man is vanity, [Augustine] yet he walks in God’s image. Although man walks in the image, namely of God, that is, in reason, which is beyond the sun and is truth because it desires invisible and true goods, nevertheless he is vainly troubled, that is, with vain desires, [Cassiodorus] namely concerning food, clothing, and such things.

VERSE 10.—“He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he shall gather it.”

“He stores up treasure.” [Augustine.] As though he were saying: Hence comes vain disturbance, because he stores up treasure. [Cassiodorus.] Behold, among the remaining vices the prophet chose avarice to show what he intends. For it is the root of all evils. “And he does not know for whom he shall gather it.” [Augustine.] For he does not know whether a son who himself passes away will possess it.

VERSE 11.—“And now what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? And my substance is with thee.”

“And now what is [my expectation]?” [Augustine.] Having seen this vanity, from which he has leapt over, and looking toward the truth to which he stretches, he says, as though placed between the two: And now, after passing over so many things, what is my expectation, that is, my end—concerning which he said above, “Make known to me, O Lord, my end”? He says “expectation,” [Cassiodorus] because no one here is perfect. Is it not the Lord, who is above all? That is, Christ. As though he were saying: My expectation is the expectation of Christ’s first or second coming. It is called expectation because it comes with delay, and [Col. 0393D] because meanwhile one endures many things.

“And my substance”—as though he were saying: Truly, O Lord, thou art my expectation, because my substance is considered as being with thee, [Alcuin] that is, according to what it will be in the future, when it also will be impassible and immortal.

Or thus: “My substance is with thee,” that is, David says that he foresees his substance as being with thee through the union of person.

Or he calls “substance” not that actual substance contracted from Adam, but the possession of a good conscience. And this is “my substance”: not that old substance of Adam, but the possession of a pure conscience, by which the inner person is sustained and nourished. It is with thee, not in our temporal age; [Augustine] but before God, to whom it is pleasing.

Or thus: “My substance is with thee,” that is, as it tends toward thee, it already begins in some measure to exist. But [Col. 0394A] because no one is without sin, however far he has leapt over, I ask:

VERSE 12.—“Deliver me from all my iniquities; thou hast made me a reproach to the fool.”

“Deliver me from all my iniquities.” [Augustine.] Or join it thus: I await thee; therefore deliver me from all my iniquities, because they are many, even in the righteous person. “From all,” I say: not only from those which I have passed over, lest I roll back into them, but entirely from all. To think in this manner does not hinder perfection but produces it. For imperfect is the person who has not yet received what he desires; yet he is perfect because he knows that very thing which is lacking to him.

“Thou hast made me a reproach to the fool.” As though he were saying: And because I act thus, I am a reproach, etc. Or join it thus: Therefore thou oughtest to deliver me, because thou hast made me a reproach to the fool, [Col. 0394B] [Cassiodorus] that is, to the foolish person. The fool who remains in vanity mocks those whom he knows to possess good morals: against him.

### Verse 13.—“I became mute and did not open my mouth, because you did it; remove your blows from me.”

“I became mute.” [Alcuin.] Being made an object of reproach, I kept silent; I did not contend angrily against them, and I did not open my mouth—that is, I did not murmur against God. And this came from you, “because you did it”: you made me such, giving me patience; and because I am such, remove your blows from me. [Interlinear Gloss.] Or connect it thus: deliver me from the iniquity of sin and also remove your blows—that is, suffering and death. You can do this, because you made them. [Cassiodorus.] And this is what follows: “your,” that is, made by you. It is necessary [Col. 0394C] that you remove them, because I have failed. And this is:

### Verse 14.—“By the strength of your hand I have failed under rebukes; because of iniquity you corrected man.”

For by the strength of your hand—that is, by your mighty power—I have failed under this rebuke by which you rebuked the human race. Yet this is deserved by us, because it is on account of our iniquity. I say “under rebukes,” which nevertheless aim at correction, because through them you corrected man. Otherwise iniquity would remain uncured. [Cassiodorus.]

Another interpretation begins at “I became mute”; and another reading is found there, namely, “I became deaf.” [Jerome.] As though he said: “You gave me as a reproach to the fool; at his insults I became deaf and did not open my mouth”—that is, [Interlinear Gloss; Col. 0394D] I did not even attempt to speak, because I would speak in vain, since they are incorrigible—and “which you made.” “Remove your blows from me,” [Augustine] that is, your scourges: because you made me, do not destroy me. Strike only so that I may make progress, not fail; prune only so that I may grow, not be crushed. As though he said: He who created should re-create.

“By the strength”—as though, “remove the blows.” I mean blows grievously inflicted. “By the strength of your hand,” [Cassiodorus] “I have failed under reproofs,” another reading; [Augustine] that is, when you rebuke me, I fail. But your rebuking is instruction because of iniquity. Hence follows: “Because of iniquity.” As though he said: Because I have failed, you rebuke me; but I have not failed and become weak without cause—rather, it is because of iniquity. And in this you instructed man. Another reading: “you did not condemn.” [Col. 0395A] Thus your rebuke is both punishment and grace. Hence elsewhere: “you who fashion pain in the commandment” (Psalm 93 [94]); that is, you shape my pain, which you have inflicted. For one pain is unformed and another formed. Unformed pain does not correct a person; formed pain imparts the form of instruction. Such pain is a commandment—that is, it has the force and image of a commandment, because it teaches one to depart from evils.

### Verse 15.—“And you caused his soul to waste away like a spider; nevertheless every man is vainly troubled.”

“And you caused [it] to waste away”: he shows the manner of instruction. [Alcuin.] As though he said: You corrected man so greatly because you caused his soul to waste away, that is, to be dried up from the moisture of virtues and knowledge of God, “like a spider,” [Col. 0395B] which weaves an empty web. So too this person labours vainly in gathering temporal things. Or, like a spider, because, just as the spider dies from the expenditure of its entrails, from which it weaves its web, [Cassiodorus] so man dies while drawing iniquity out from himself.

Or it may be understood positively. For the spider has a slender body; it stands not on the ground but aloft, and by the expenditure of its entrails it weaves webs. So the soul of a converted and afflicted person leaves earthly things, standing aloft in heavenly conduct, and performs subtle works, wasting away—that is, humbled—through fear of God. [Augustine.] Or man is compared to a spider because, just as the spider is something frail and weak, so the human soul is instructed through weakness and humility, lest one presume upon oneself, having displeased through strength and pride. And this is the meaning: thus you instructed him, because [Col. 0395C] you caused his soul to waste away like a spider; that is, you caused the soul to waste away, to become weak, having cast off pride through humility, like a spider, than which nothing is more frail, and which collapses when lightly touched by a finger. This weakness is good, just as proud strength, which existed before, was a vice.

“Nevertheless every man is vainly troubled.” [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: Although man is corrected, although rebuked, although made to waste away, nevertheless every man living amid uncertainty is vainly troubled—that is, through human weakness he is disturbed by vain things. [Cassiodorus.] No one is exempted from this vanity except one who contemplates God with a pure mind.

### Part III. Diapsalma. Verse 16.—“Hear my prayer, O Lord, and my supplication; [Col. 0395D] give ear to my tears.”

“Hear.” And here is a *diapsalma*. [Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which, amid so many evils of the age, he asks God to be present to him and his sins to be forgiven, so that he may come forth with a prosperous end, since all things are vanity. [Augustine.] Placed among these things, therefore, and passing beyond them, already acting in hope regarding higher things, he says, “Hear.”

Or the connection is this. [Alcuin.] These things are vain; but because I neither seek them nor grieve for them, hear me, O Lord. The more things this man vows, the more he supplicates. “My prayer”: prayer is when we disclose our vows to God; “and my supplication.” [Cassiodorus.] Supplication is frequent entreaty from the depths of the heart. But lest you think that he prays only in words, he adds also “my tears,” which are powerful in prayers to move mercy. And this is what follows: [Col. 0396A] “give ear to my tears.” [Augustine.] For although he has passed beyond so many things, he nevertheless has reason to weep: what he desires is absent; scandals increase; iniquity abounds; charity grows cold (Matthew 24).

### Verse 17.—“Do not be silent; for I am a stranger with you and a sojourner, like all my fathers.”

“Do not be silent.” [Augustine.] As though he said: I pray, I entreat, O Lord, do not be silent—that is, make me hear you. [Cassiodorus.] For God speaks secretly in the heart of the faithful: “I am your salvation” (Luke 2); this is the voice he desires. Or, “Do not be silent,” that is, say to me: “Your sins are forgiven you”; or, “Do not be silent in the future,” that is, say to me: “Come, blessed ones,” and so forth (Matthew 25).

“Do not be silent, for I am already with you in hope,” [Augustine] but I am still [Col. 0396B] a stranger or resident alien—that is, one who has no settled abode here, because I am to pass hence to eternal things, where I shall not be a resident alien. And I am a pilgrim—understand, with you—because some are pilgrims with the devil, that is, the wicked; but others are with God, with whom they are in hope, not in possession. For as long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord (2 Corinthians 5), like all my fathers, who departed to life. It is therefore established that the same is true of me. [Cassiodorus.]

Or thus: “Do not be silent, for I am a stranger with you,” that is, I do not remain in the devil’s city, but have been received into yours; I have been transferred from Babylon to Jerusalem; I forsake my kingdom for yours. “And a pilgrim,” not choosing an abode here for myself, because my homeland is there, not here. “Like all my fathers”: he says this lest anyone think himself exempt from this condition.

[Col. 0396C]

### Verse 18.—“Forgive me, that I may be refreshed before I depart, and shall be no more.”

“Forgive me.” [Cassiodorus.] Here he asks that he may be forgiven, in order to come assuredly to judgment. [Augustine.] As though he said: Since I am about to depart, this remains to be asked: forgive me, and so forth. Or connect it thus: Because I am with you, therefore forgive me, who am burned by cares, that I may be refreshed through mercy; for he has the heat of vices. Hence he says: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive,” and so forth (Matthew 6). “That I may be refreshed,” I say, before I depart from this life, [Augustine] lest I depart with sins. I say, forgive; otherwise—that is, if you do not forgive me so that I may be refreshed—I shall depart from this life and shall no longer be in the true being which is with God.

## Comparison on Psalm 38: “I Said: I Will Keep Guard”

[Col. 0396D]

### Verse 3.—“I became mute and was humbled.”

For the second clause the Hebrew reads *dumiyyāh*, and they translate it “silence,” so that the sense is, “I became mute in silence.” But because the root *dāmah* or *dīmach*, among other meanings, signifies “he oppressed,” the Septuagint did not unreasonably render “I was humbled” for “I became mute through humiliation.”

### Verse 7.—“In my meditation fire shall blaze.”

Here Faber philosophizes that the Hebrew more aptly expresses intensity as “in my meditation I was kindled with fire.” Yet according to the very letter, so to speak, the Hebrew now reads *baʾagigi tivʿar ʾesh*: “in my meditation fire shall blaze.” Nor does it matter that Jerome, disregarding the affected literalism of translation, rendered it in the manner Faber read it. Yet Jerome did not know that he would have such a prophet, unless Jerome read [Col. 0397A] *ʾevʿar* in the first person, a thing which we frequently find to have been done.

### Verse 6.—“That I may know what I lack.”

Jerome fully agrees. Others translate, “how brief a time I am.” Clearly *ḥādal* means “he ceased,” while *ḥeled* means duration, through transposition of the letters *lamed* and *daleth*. Therefore, had not the Septuagint said, *ti hysterō egō*—“what do I lack?”—one might suspect a scribal error: *desit*, “he lacks,” from *deesse*, in place of *desiit*, “he ceased,” from *desinere*. But that our days quickly come to an end and that we run swiftly through them agree well enough. The Chaldean and Nebiensian versions say, “that I may know when I shall fail.”

### Verse 11.—“You made me a reproach to the fool.”

The Hebrews, it appears, read the opposite sense: “Do not make me a reproach to the fool,” *ʾal teşîmēnî*. There seems to be opposition in the sound of the words; but when you consider the desire of the sinner turned to God, imploring with all his affection to be delivered from all iniquities because of which he felt himself handed over to the reproach of the foolish evil spirit, you will find that he confesses that before repentance, while pricked by the sting of conscience, he had been given to the fool—with God permitting it—so that, having recognized the enemy’s tyranny, he might come to his senses and thereafter pray to God that, by returning to his vomit, he might not again be handed over to the fool’s reproach and to diabolical delusions. Thus, in summary, the sense is: “Deliver me from all my iniquities”; and above all he entreats God for this very thing, because on account of my sins you justly gave me as a reproach to the fool. But, good God, if henceforth you preserve me from sin, I may safely say: “Do not make me a reproach to the fool.”

But if I seem to you to wrench an opposing Scripture, I shall offer a similar instance from Jerome’s little work *On the Best Method of Translating*, and from his Commentary on Isaiah, chapter 8. In the former, wishing by many arguments to demonstrate the duty of a good translator, so as most clearly to teach that a true translator ought not to serve the slumbering letter or be tortured by the stale affected literalism of words, he adduces among other things the testimony of the Septuagint on Isaiah 8, which seems diametrically opposed to the Hebrew truth, as also to the Apostle Paul and Peter:

> “For the Apostle Paul, in Romans 9, taking his example from Isaiah, says: ‘Behold, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence.’ He differs from the Old Translation and yet agrees with the Hebrew truth. For in the Septuagint the sense is opposite: ‘You shall not encounter [him] as a stone of stumbling, nor as a rock of ruin’; while the Apostle Peter likewise, agreeing with the Hebrew and with Paul, writes: ‘But for unbelievers, a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence’ (1 Peter 2). From all these passages it is evident that the apostles and evangelists, in interpreting the old Scriptures, sought the sense and not the words; nor did they greatly concern themselves with order and phrasing, provided the meaning was clear.”

These are Jerome’s words. Here you see that the Septuagint has a negation and the Hebrew truth an affirmation, [Col. 0397D] which are contradictory. Yet what he did not reconcile here, he brought into harmony in his commentary on Isaiah 8. For he says:

> “Therefore they are commanded to hear the Lord and to fear him alone. For if they trust in him, they will have him for sanctification and will not strike against him as against a stone of stumbling or a rock of ruin. From this place the Apostle also takes testimony that Christ became a scandal to the Jews but foolishness to the Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1). And again: Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain to the law of righteousness. Why? Because not from faith but, as it were, from works of the law, they stumbled at the stone of stumbling, as it is written: ‘Behold, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence; everyone who believes in him shall not be confounded’ (Romans 9). See, these two statements conflict: ‘He shall be to you a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence’; and, ‘You shall not encounter [him] as a stone of stumbling, nor as a rock of ruin.’ But when it is understood, ‘if you trust in him, you shall not encounter [him] as a stone of stumbling,’ all things agree.”

Thus it applies to our point: if the Lord delivers me from my iniquities, there is no reason why I should be handed over to the reproach of the fool. But if I embrace sins, it follows that I shall be handed over [Col. 0398B] to the reproach of the fool.

Finally, since the negation and the name of God differ in nothing when written without vowels, could not the Septuagint have read *El*, “God,” rather than *ʾal*, “not,” so that the sense would be: “God, you gave me as a reproach to the fool,” although “God” is not expressed?

### Verse 16.—“You caused his soul to waste away like a spider.”

Jerome and nearly all the others render “moth” instead of “spider,” a sense not inappropriate, although the little word *ʿāsh* also means spider or spider’s web, as Pellicanus translates it, and as the Chaldean version has it. But why is it that where we have “his soul,” others say “his desired thing,” “his desirable things,” or “his precious thing”? Münster added something of his own: “his desirable strength.” Certainly, if we weigh the dignity of the soul and the value that we ought to place upon it, there is no need to hunt after letters and syllables while retaining the meaning. The Chaldean Paraphrast and Nebiensis speak differently: [Col. 0398C] the former says “his flesh,” the latter “he whose body is broken.” But let us follow the Septuagint, if we cherish unity.

“Every man is vainly troubled.” Neither in Greek nor in Hebrew is “troubled” read. Jerome reports to Sunia and Fretella that it was added in the edition which he calls the *koinē*—the common edition—to the Septuagint, under the obelus. Yet do not immediately conclude that it ought to be erased; we should remember what he says in the same treatise: “And I ask you to avoid such trifles and superfluous disputes where there is no alteration of meaning.”

### Verse 18.—“Forgive me, that I may be refreshed.”

Jerome: “Spare me, that I may smile.” Others: “Turn away from me,” or “cease,” or “turn aside,” “and I shall be strengthened.” Regarding the first, the agreement between “forgive,” “spare,” and terms of that kind is clear. Regarding the second, smiling and being strengthened are not far from refreshment; Münster says the same in other words: “Cease from me, that I may recover my strength.” And if the Hebrew word *bālag* means “to strengthen,” “to smile,” or “to refresh,” according to the vocabulary of the Complutensian Academy, [Col. 0398D] surely a person is made firm and strengthened as one who, his sin remitted, rejoices in the oil of heavenly grace and the refreshment of divine mercy.

## Psalm 39

[Col. 0397]

### Title of the Psalm: “For the End: A Psalm of David”

[Col. 0397D]

“I waited expectantly for the Lord.” Title: “For the end: a Psalm of David.” “The end” in psalm titles is understood in different ways. Sometimes it signifies Christ; sometimes the fullness of time; sometimes the New Testament; sometimes Christ’s passion or resurrection. Here it is understood as the New Testament, which brings to completion that into which the Old [Col. 0398D] Testament is shown to have been transformed. The Church waited a long time for it, desiring Christ and, with him, the New Testament. In that expectation she endured much from the devil, secretly and openly; nor, even after Christ’s coming and the reception of the new law, was she altogether free from them, entirely escaping neither the devil’s open nor hidden snares.

[Augustine.] For the devil is a lion and a dragon: a lion when he rages openly, as he did in the time of the martyrs, when patience is required; a dragon when he secretly lays snares, stirring up scandals and temptations, as he does now, when vigilance is required. He is more to be feared when he deceives as a dragon than when he rages as a lion. There he compels; here he teaches people to deny Christ. Yet amid these things she did not cease to wait, until she received both.

The meaning of the title is therefore: this psalm directs us toward the end, [Interlinear Gloss] that is, toward the New Testament which brings to completion, because it treats of the transformation of the Old Testament into the New. It is attributed to David—that is, to Christ, who saves. This the law does not do, nor the gods of the Gentiles. [Interlinear Gloss.] He speaks in this psalm from the members—that is, in the person of his members.

Purpose. [Jerome.] It exhorts people, abandoning the ceremonies of the law and the superstition of idolatry, [Col. 0399B] to approach the New Testament.

Method. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] The psalm has two parts. First, it introduces the Church as having waited for God, received him, and received from him the New Testament, which many will also follow. Hence it strikes at every superstition and invites people to God’s wonders. [Cassiodorus.] Second, it explains the wonders: the incarnation, the righteousness of preaching, the deliverance of human beings from iniquities, the confusion of enemies, and the joy of those who hope—beginning at “I proclaimed.” Since it was difficult to recall the Jews from their customary ceremonies and the Gentiles from idolatry to the New Testament, the author therefore employs the authority of the ancient Fathers, saying:

### Verse 1.—“I waited expectantly for the Lord, and he inclined toward me.”

“I waited expectantly.” [Cassiodorus.] By this repetition more is understood than if it were said simply. One waits even when one is ungrateful; but one who “waits expectantly” waits meekly and with desire. Thus, “I waited expectantly,” [Jerome] means: I waited meekly and continually with desire in Abraham and the other patriarchs, and in the promise of the prophets. [Alcuin.] Behold, authority from the ancients. For what did I await? Not the law, through which iniquity or transgression abounds; not a human being, [Augustine] who can deceive and be deceived and who is needy with me; not anything else; but the Lord, who can save.

And what did he do? “He inclined”; he did not turn away, but inclined toward me—that is, toward my benefit, namely, so as to help me. He does not say “he inclined me,” as he also inclines the wicked, but not for the wicked’s benefit. Thus, the Lord was attentive and kindly disposed toward them. He then adds how he inclined, namely, by hearing them and bringing them out. This is:

### Verse 2.—“And he heard my prayers, and brought me out of a pit of misery and from the mud of dregs.”

“And he heard.” [Jerome.] He who concealed himself from the prophets heard my prayers; they do not cease waiting for him.
