And what did he do? “He brought me out of a pit of misery,” [Augustine] that is, out of the depth of carnal desires; “from the mud of dregs,” or slime, that is, from evil works, which defile and hold fast the feet of the affections and are base like dregs in comparison with wine. Or the pit is the darkness of iniquities—that is, unbelief and ignorance; the mud is carnal desire. Thus, “he brought me [Col. 0400A] out of a pit of misery and from the mud of dregs,” that is, from the depth of iniquity and carnal desires. [Interlinear Gloss.] Or by the pit of misery and the mud of dregs, hell is understood; he brought out the captive righteous whom it held there. Thus, “he brought me out of the pit of misery,” and so forth—that is, out of hell.

### Verse 3.—“And he set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps.”

“And he set [them],” [Augustine] so that I may now walk by making progress, “upon a rock,” that is, Christ, “my feet,” [Jerome] that is, my senses, which were previously with the devil. [Cassiodorus.] Note that God gives beneficial things in two ways. First he brings one out of the misery of the world, which is the pit and mud of dregs. Then he sets one upon the rock when we walk in Christ’s commandments. Sins, like the mud of a pit, stink and engulf; the rock stands opposed to that mud. [Jerome.] The Gentiles who worship idols, or all who love earthly things, are in the pit and mud of sins. “And he directed,” so that I should not look back, “my steps,” that is, those of my works. For Lot’s wife looked back and was turned into a pillar of salt; and no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.

### Verse 4.—“And he put into my mouth a new song, a hymn to our God.”

“And he put”: as though he said, he set and directed, and so put in the preaching of the New Testament, namely, “a new song,” that is, joy in the new grace, not the old song from the Mosaic law. For people of the Old Testament sang the old song: “eye for [Col. 0400C] eye, tooth for tooth, life for life” (Deuteronomy 11); moreover, they descended to hell, the gate of the kingdom being closed to them, with the cherub barring the entrance to paradise, in whose hand was the flaming sword (Genesis 3).

[Augustine.] But people of the new law sing the new song which the new man brought. For there is a new king, a new law; behold, all things have become new (Revelation 21). [Jerome.] Therefore the new people sing new things concerning the Lord’s incarnation, resurrection, ascension, and such matters. Hence, especially on these solemnities, the ministers of the Church, clothed in white or silken vestments, sing and read, so that no one may presume to sing the new song unless renewed.

“I mean a song, namely a hymn, a song pleasing to God.” [Jerome.] As though he said: It is not a shameful song or one for the theatre; it belongs to the New Testament. It pleases, I say, our God, not foreign gods, [Cassiodorus] but God who is ours through worship, not another’s.

### Verse 5.—“Many shall see and fear, and shall hope in the Lord.”

“They shall see.” [Augustine.] As though he said: many later peoples shall see what was said concerning those earlier ones—that is, they shall see that the Christ foretold has come, [Jerome] whom the earlier ones awaited. [Cassiodorus.] Or many shall see the wonders performed at the time of the incarnation. Or thus: many followers shall see, [Augustine] that is, imitate the preceding people of patriarchs and prophets; they shall fear to follow evil ways, recognizing themselves as sinners; [Jerome] and, having become Christians, they shall hope for the forgiveness [Col. 0401A] of sins in the Lord, not in those who went before, [Augustine] namely, the patriarchs and prophets, because God alone forgives sins.

### Verse 6.—“Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not looked to vanities and lying follies.”

“Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord.” He calls the name “Saviour.” The meaning is: blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord—that is, who does not hope from him for temporal things, but for what his name signifies, [Augustine] namely salvation; that is, who hopes for God himself, not something else from him. And “his” is superfluous; for in Hebrew genitives are often doubled in this manner.

[Alcuin.] Or thus, so that “his” is not superfluous: “Blessed is the man whose name is the Lord.” [Augustine.] Make the division here: that is, he in whom is the praise of God, so that he believes salvation comes from God alone, from whom also comes his hope—that is, from whom comes to him hope of life. “And he has not looked to vanities,” whither—that is, toward which vanities—many go. [Jerome.] Earthly things are vain. “And [Col. 0401B] lying follies”: [Cassiodorus] follies are angers and quarrels; or lying follies are idols, which deceive away from truth. Thus folly is false, [Augustine] because it is not what it is thought to be; salvation is true. Or follies are found in the deceitful spectacles of actors and theatres, and in 87 other pleasures. [Augustine.] He used the plural so that it may be understood of everything pertaining to pleasure. Thus, “he has not looked to lying follies,” which are found in the pleasures of this world. [Augustine.] But one who does not look to these has something to marvel at and behold, because:

### Verse 7.—“You, O Lord my God, have done many wonders; and none is like you in your thoughts.”

[Augustine.] “For you have done many,” and so forth. Or connect it thus. [Cassiodorus.] These are false things, but your works are wonders, namely heaven and earth. Here he overthrows superstitions. [Augustine.] Thus: “You, O Lord God, have done many wonders,” both bodily and spiritual. Bodily wonders include heaven, earth, and Peter walking on the waters (Matthew 14), which was a sign of this spiritual wonder: that you make us walk with dry feet in this world—that is, amid the waves of the world. Therefore you do something greater than an actor: he learned to walk upon a rope; you make a person [Col. 0401D] walk above the sea. You did these things “in your thoughts,” [Interlinear Gloss] that is, not through another’s counsel, but by your own wisdom. Hence, “Who has been his counsellor?” And none is like you: among all those things, no authors of arts are comparable to you.

### Part II. Verse 8.—“I proclaimed and spoke; they have been multiplied beyond number.”

“I proclaimed.” The second part. [Alcuin.] Here are the wonders: the incarnation, the righteousness of preaching, deliverance of people from iniquities, the confusion of enemies, and the joy of those who hope. Note that in the first part the untrained and unformed were prepared so that they might gladly receive Christ’s words. [Augustine.] Christ speaks the matters contained in the second part partly in the head—that is, in his own person—and partly in the members. As though he said: You have done many wonderful things, [Col. 0402A] and I, Christ, have proclaimed these wonders, and so forth.

Or connect it thus: What are those wonders? Behold the wonders of God. “I proclaimed” first through the prophets, and afterward “I spoke” [Cassiodorus] myself; and the wicked have multiplied beyond the number of those to be saved. [Augustine.] Jerusalem—that is, the predestined—has a fixed number; but beyond this number chaff is mixed in, [Interlinear Gloss] that is, the wicked. For many are called, but few chosen (Matthew 19). Or, “they have been multiplied beyond number,” [Cassiodorus] that is, beyond what anyone can count. Or: I spoke in such a manner, and while I was speaking, they were multiplied beyond number—that is, more believed than formerly.

### Verse 9.—“You did not desire sacrifice and offering, but you perfected ears for me.”

“Sacrifice.” As though he said: What need was there for speaking, when legal observances sufficed? Because you no longer desired sacrifice, which was made from animals, or offering, which was made from other things such as fine flour, incense, and oil, after the reality had been presented. [Augustine.] Once the reality came, God no longer desired those legal observances, which were like words making promises. He is a promiser only until he gives; when he has given, he changes his word: he no longer says, “I shall give,” but “I have given.” Therefore, when he himself came, he no longer desired what was his figure.

Hence at the Nativity of the Lord the Mass of promise is sung, namely, “A light shall shine”; and afterward it is not repeated, whereas the Mass of the fulfilment of the promise, namely, “A child is born,” and so forth, is repeated later. See the change of words: there is a promise of the future; here, thanksgiving for one already born. Hence also the prophecy is sung before the Epistle on that same day, just as a base is set beneath a column in the tabernacle of the Lord.

But if someone says that those legal observances still endure among the Jews because they practise circumcision and certain similar things, it is not true. For they have been removed for the most part. They have neither king nor priest nor anointing nor ephod nor teraphim. [Augustine.] Some things nevertheless remain which they observe, lest they remain wholly without a sign. For as God placed a sign upon Cain so that no one should kill him—for he was a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth, trembling in his head—so the Jew remains with the sign of circumcision and similar things and has not yet been killed, retaining his sign. But Cain was cursed from the ground which received the blood of his brother, which he shed. Hence the Lord said: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground” (Genesis 4). That is, the Jew is cursed by the Church, which received the blood of Christ shed by the Jew; and from this ground that blood cries to God while it is daily offered to God in the Church for the expiation of humankind. But the Jew who shed it is deaf and does not hear spiritually. These are God’s wonders and thoughts, to which none is comparable.

“But you perfected ears,” or “a body.” As though he said: You did not desire those things, but you perfected a body for me, [Alcuin] that is, you gave me a perfect body, namely, without sin. For this reason you did not desire those things. Or, “you perfected ears,” that is, you made me perfectly understand what you willed. Or, according to another reading, “but you prepared a body for me.” [Col. 0403A] Thus the Apostle states it in the Epistle to the Hebrews: you gave me a body fit to be offered.

### Verse 10.—“You did not require holocaust and sin-offering; then I said: Behold, I come.”

“Holocaust.” [Augustine.] Here he explains the preceding verse and says “holocaust,” which earlier was “sacrifice,” and “for sin,” which above was “offering”; accordingly “for sin” is one expression. Properly, however, a holocaust is called that which was entirely burned; for *holos* is Greek for “whole,” and *cauma* means “burning”; hence *holocaust*, “wholly burned,” for sin—as with the *apopompaean* goat, that is, the scapegoat, which was sent into the wilderness with the sins of the people.

Or “for sin” may be two words. Thus: “holocaust and also for sin,” that is, what was offered for sin and was greater and more worthy under the law, as with the red heifer (Numbers 10), [Col. 0403B] you did not require. “Then I said”—as though, because you did not desire these things and prepared a body, then I said, “Behold, I come immediately,” [Cassiodorus] because it is time for the promised things to come, since the things that promised them are removed. [Augustine.] Therefore, when sacrifices cease, it is evident that Christ has come. “I come,” because:

### Verse 11.—“At the head of the book it is written concerning me: I desired to do your will, my God, and your law is in the midst of my heart.”

“I desired to do your will,” [Augustine] because thus it is written concerning me at the head of this book of Psalms; or thus, it is written concerning me—that is, predetermined—“at the head of the book,” [Alcuin] that is, with God the Father, who is my head, says Christ, I who am the book of humankind, in whom each person ought to read; that is, I am the pattern of righteousness for humankind. What is written? [Interlinear Gloss.] “That I may do your will,” wholly obedient, offering myself. And, O my God, I desired this. [Augustine.] This is what is said in the first Psalm: “in the law of the Lord,” to do his will; “and I desired your law in the midst of my heart,” [Interlinear Gloss] that is, in the fullness of my heart. [Augustine.] Hence in the same Psalm he says: “And in his law he shall meditate day and night.”

### Verse 12.—“I proclaimed your righteousness in the great assembly; behold, I will not restrain my lips; Lord, you have known.”

“I proclaimed.” Christ says these things in the members, [Augustine] that is, in the person of the members. As though he said: formerly I spoke through myself; afterward, also in the members, I proclaimed to others that righteousness is yours, [Interlinear Gloss] that is, righteousness comes from you. I did this in the great assembly, [Augustine] namely, that which is throughout the whole world, not small as it formerly was. And if anything rises up against me, fear does not prevent speech. This is: “Behold, I will not restrain my lips” from speaking, as though I did not have it only in my heart and keep silent from fear. He says this against worldly fear: “Lord.” As though he said: I shall also do this without pretence, because, Lord, you have known my heart. As though he said: lips sound to people, but you, Lord, know my heart. He says this lest the proclamation be only in the lips, since one believes in the heart unto righteousness, while confession is made with the mouth unto salvation. [Alcuin.] He says this against hypocrisy. Or thus: “I will not restrain [my lips], and, O Lord, you have known”—that is, you are witness that fear does not prevent speech. Or: “I will not restrain [them],” and this is through you, because you, Lord, have known—that is, you predestined it would be so; and I am not slow in this, because:

### Verse 13.—“I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation.”

“I have not hidden in my heart,” [Cassiodorus] when I could benefit others, “your righteousness”—or my own, [Augustine] that is, I confessed faith without concealing it through fear, as though it were enough to retain it in the heart. [Interlinear Gloss.] This is said against the slothfulness of the flesh: I did not hide it, but declared “your truth,” [Alcuin] that is, the fulfilment of promises, “and your salvation,” that is, your saving work. Or “your truth and your salvation,” [Augustine] that is, Christ, I declared—[Interlinear Gloss] that is, I preached—nor did I desist because of the counsel of many. This is:

### Verse 14.—“I have not hidden your mercy and your truth from the great council.”

“I have not hidden your mercy,” [Augustine] by which he forgives sins, “and your truth,” by which he renders rewards, from the great council—that is, because of the many who conspire.

### Verse 15.—“But you, O Lord, do not remove your compassions far from me; your mercy and your truth have always sustained me.”

“But you, O Lord, because I have not concealed your mercy and truth, do not make your compassions distant from me, lest they be without effect in me; [Interlinear Gloss; Col. 0404C] that is, do not remove your mercies from your wounded members—because your mercy and truth,” [Augustine] namely from the first righteous person onward, “have sustained me.” Therefore let what you have begun not be vain.

[Remigius.] Distinguish what he says, “mercy and truth have sustained [me].” [Augustine.] Mercy sustained me, because I would not dare to turn to you unless I were secure of forgiveness—as though he said: You are good, and I love you. Truth sustained me, because I would not persevere unless secure of the reward—as though he said: You are just, and I fear you. The meaning is: your mercy and truth—that is, love and fear—lead me to you. As though he said: these always sustain me, and I always look to them. And this is necessary:

### Verse 16.—“For evils without number have surrounded me; my iniquities have overtaken me, and I was unable to see.”

For evils have surrounded me. [Cassiodorus.] That is, sins beyond number among men, because there are sins committed by ourselves and by others. [Augustine.] What, then, if mercy should cease? [Interlinear Gloss.] Or, evils have surrounded me, that is, punishments. And my iniquities have seized me in the very act itself; [Augustine] oppressed by them, the eye cannot see, though with a purified heart a person will see God. Hence follows: “And I could not do,” understand, “so that I might see.” As though he said: They have seized me so completely that not even by exertion could I see you; for:

VERSE 17.—“They have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head, and my heart has forsaken me.”

[Col. 0405A] My iniquities have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head. [Alcuin.] That is, so as to exceed those who are the hairs of the head, [Augustine] namely, the faithful who are rooted in Christ and adorn him by living well. Or, literally, this is said by comparison: “They have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head,” that is, beyond counting. Take care, therefore, if you have avoided grave sins such as adultery and murder, lest you be overwhelmed by a sand-heap of lesser sins: they seem small indeed, but they are many. [Cassiodorus.] Appropriately, moreover, hairs are mentioned in comparison with offences. For this is why priests in the Old Testament were shaved: that they might appear thereby to have put away the vices of the flesh. And my heart—that is, my reason—has forsaken me, because it does not seek what would profit it. Or, “my heart has forsaken me,” [Augustine] that is, the heart does not know itself, as when Peter [Col. 0405B] said: “I will not deny you” (Matt. XXV). Note that he says, “has forsaken.” This blindness was not natural in man; [Interlinear Gloss] rather, through sin we were made blind by the first parent, who transmitted to us both punishment and guilt. Therefore:

VERSE 18.—“May it please you, O Lord, to rescue me; O Lord, look upon me to help me.”

O Lord, may it please you, [Cassiodorus] that is, may it jointly please the Trinity—you, the one God. For by saying “you,” in the singular, he indicates unity of essence; by saying “may it please,” he indicates the Trinity of persons. May it please you, I say, to rescue me from evils. [Augustine.] Note that he says “may it please,” not doubting God’s power if his will be present. As though he said: If you will, you can. O Lord, 88 look upon me to help me in cooperation for good, [Cassiodorus] as though he said: Look upon those who repent in their sorrow. God’s regard is our help.

VERSE 19.—“Let those who seek my life in order to take it away be confounded and ashamed together.”

Let them be confounded. [Cassiodorus.] Here Christ speaks, as though he said: Look upon me; but, on the other hand, let them be confounded by the wondrous working of miracles, and let them together be ashamed at the glory of the resurrection. [Augustine.] And so it happened: they rejoiced when he laid down his life, but were confounded when he received it again—those who seek my life, not in order to enjoy it, but to take it away by killing me.

VERSE 20.—“Let those who wish me evil be turned backward and ashamed.”

[Col. 0405D] Let them also be turned backward, [Augustine] that is, let those who were proudly perishing follow humbly. Christ says this of the members in a good sense. And let them be ashamed—not only those who say or do evil, but those who wish me evil; that is, who, even when they bless, nevertheless wish evil.

VERSE 21.—“Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ bear their shame without delay.”

Let them bear, as an immense burden, their shame without delay, [Cassiodorus] lest their evil become more burdensome through longer delay—those who flatteringly say to me, “Well done, well done,” that is, those who applaud me as though with a good intention. [Augustine.] Note two kinds of enemies, against whom one must especially beware: the one who says good things with evil intent—hence above he said, “who wish me evil”—and the one who says evil things [Col. 0406A] by deceptive praise—hence here he says, “who say to me, ‘Well done, well done.’” Each is evil and must be avoided.

VERSES 22, 23.—“Let all who seek you exult and rejoice in you, and let those who love your salvation always say: ‘Let the Lord be magnified.’”

Let them exult. [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: Let those be confounded; conversely, let all who seek you, founded upon you, exult and rejoice in you—[Augustine] that is, glorifying not me but you in me—and let them say: “Let the Lord be magnified,” [Interlinear Gloss] namely, in his members, though he cannot become greater in himself. [Cassiodorus.] This is their exultation. For this confession has made Christians rejoice eternally. “Let the Lord be magnified,” [Augustine] I say, always: because, if a person is a sinner, it calls him to repentance; if righteous, to a crown. [Cassiodorus.] And lest just anyone say this, [Col. 0406B] he adds: “those who love your salvation,” that is, me.

VERSE 24.—“But I am needy and poor; the Lord is mindful of me.”

But I. [Cassiodorus.] Christ says this of himself in the form of a servant, lest anyone arrogate to himself the glory of the aforesaid rejoicing. Let them speak thus; but I, to whom they said, “Well done, well done,” say this of myself: namely, that I am needy insofar as I am human. The needy person asks from another, and the poor person is not sufficient for himself; but the Lord is mindful of me, that is, he cares for me.

Or thus: [Augustine.] That it may be understood of the members, as though he said: Let them always say this concerning you: “Let the Lord be magnified,” etc. But let them say this concerning themselves: “But I am needy and poor,” that is, there is nothing in me to be praised; from myself I am destitute and poor, like the tax collector who [Col. 0406C] did not dare raise his eyes to heaven, with whom I say: “Be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII). I am not rich, because I am not proud like the Pharisee who said: “I am not like the rest of men,” etc. (ibid.); but the Lord is mindful of me.

VERSE 25.—“You are my helper and my protector; my God, do not delay.”

My helper. [Augustine.] Here the whole body of Christ prays: one needy person with Christ, and one poor person. As though he said: I am poor; and, O Lord, you are my helper and protector. [Interlinear Gloss.] As though he said: This is certain. But this which follows I ask: “My God, do not delay,” [Augustine] that is, do not let us remain long in evils, but bring them swiftly to an end—especially in the time of Antichrist, when tribulation will be so great that, if possible, even the elect will be shaken (Matt. XXIV). Hence: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved,” and then “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing” (ibid.). Or this may be understood of the present thus: “My God, do not delay in helping us now,” because even now there is woe to those who are pregnant—that is, those who conceive desires for others’ possessions—and to those who bark, that is, who now nourish what they have sought.

## Comparison on Psalm XXXIX: “I waited expectantly for the Lord.”

VERSE 6.—“Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord.” Hebrew: “Blessed is the man who has made the Lord his hope.” The difference in meaning is very slight; nevertheless, it is known that the Septuagint read *shem*, “name,” where others read *sam*, “has made.”

[Col. 0407A] VERSE 7.—“You have done many wonderful things, O Lord my God, and in your thoughts; none is like you.” Jerome: “and your thoughts for us, I find no order before you”; Pellicanus: “and your thoughts toward us, no one reaches to you”; Pratensis: “and your thoughts toward us, there is no comparison with you”; Nebiensis: “there is no proportion to you”; Sanctes: “and your thoughts for us cannot be set in order before you”; Münster: “as also your thoughts which are toward us, and there is no one who,” supply “the wonderful things,” “sets them in order before you”; the translators for Cajetan, adhering more than is fitting, according to their custom, to captive letters: “You have done many things, you, O Lord my God—your separate things—and your thoughts to us, without reckoning them to you.”

The Hebrew is more exact. For that reason a paraphrase may range around this or that sense; it is enough for us, however, to defend our own. For Campensis says: “The thoughts by which you diligently care for us are so many and so wonderful that no human being can understand how much he owes you for them.” But the Chaldee is briefer and different: “It is not possible,” it says, “to set your praise in order.” First, *umachshebotheca*, which may be translated “and your thoughts,” or “your thoughts,” or “by your thoughts,” according to the differing construction. Then *elenu*, that is, “toward us,” “concerning us,” or “for us,” as the context requires. Likewise *en arok*, that is, “without comparison,” as though one said: “Your thoughts, if compared with us or with ours, have no equality or proportion.” This sense is plainly conveyed by our reading: “In your thoughts there is none like you.” Hence the translator after Campensis: “Your counsels among us lack an equal.”

VERSE 8.—“I have proclaimed and spoken; they have multiplied beyond number.” Jerome: “If I should wish to recount and number them, they are more than can be recounted.” Others tend to the same sense. The Hebrew reads: *agidah va’adaberah atzmu missaper*. This is also, word for word: “I shall recount and speak; they have multiplied,” or “they have been multiplied” (either may be said indiscriminately), “beyond number,” or “from being numbered,” so that our edition refers the multiplication to human beings. Other versions refer it to God’s wonderful works. Faber and Caecus approve the latter view, but only insofar as they condemn the Latin edition as incongruous and as a corrupted understanding. The exposition plainly refutes the rash trifles of such critics. Jerome on the same verse, followed also by Augustine: “They have multiplied beyond number—the Jews in their wickedness.” Or, “beyond number,” that is, sinners are beyond number, and they are outside the number because they are not worthy to be counted among the righteous. According to this interpretation, “they have multiplied” does not refer to the wonders in the preceding verse, but to what immediately precedes: “I have proclaimed,” etc. [Col. 0408A] Jerome states this plainly in the same place: “Hence the Lord himself began thus to his Father, saying: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near’” (Matt. III). Afterwards he shows that, nevertheless, many remained unbelieving beyond number. I know, however, that the other interpretation has the worth of its own meaning. Both, therefore, are sound. The differing division of verses has been discussed here and elsewhere once and again, with reasons given.

“But you have fashioned ears for me.” The Septuagint translates *sōma*, that is, “body,” and the Apostle cites it thus in Hebrews X. The meaning is the same. For through perfect obedience, which is most fittingly understood by “ears,” Christ had a mortal body, so that you may understand the whole by the part, and by that part which bears the weight of the matter. The Hebrews also say *oznaim karitha li*: “You have dug out,” or “prepared, ears for me.”

VERSE 11.—“In the head of the book it is written of me.” Hebrew: *bimgillath sepher*, that is, “in the scroll of the book.” The former word properly signifies a rolled-up sheet. Hence the Septuagint translated “in the head,” as though: from the first leaf, as soon as you begin to unroll the book, you will find written concerning me. This becomes still clearer from the explanations of Jerome and Augustine, from whom you may learn it. Nevertheless, if it were necessary, we could show from Hebrew that that particle may not inappropriately be understood also as “head,” because the meaning of “head” and “scroll” is derived from nearly the same root, namely *galal*, “he rolled, turned, folded.” For it signifies the skull and the shell of the head, and is sometimes used for the whole head because of its spherical shape.

VERSE 18.—“Look upon me to help me.” Jerome and others translate “hasten.” For the Hebrew says *tuschab*; yet Jerome himself approves the Septuagint’s “look upon,” replying to Sunia and Fretella, who had read *speuson*, “hasten,” in the Greek. But, he answered, the Septuagint reads *proschye*, that is, “give heed.” Hence [Col. 0408C] the discerning reader may see that, even if the older readings agree more closely with the Hebrew truth than with the Septuagint, it does not immediately follow that they should be erased—especially where the sense suffers no harm.

VERSE 21.—“Let them bear their shame without delay.” Recent Hebraists render “reward” instead of “without delay,” giving: “Let them be desolated because of the reward of shame or confusion.” Yet they do this gratuitously, because *eqeb* is ambiguous, meaning “heel,” “end,” and “reward.” Thus “upon the heel,” or “upon the end,” is rightly understood as “swiftly” or “without delay,” as the Septuagint understood it. Jerome’s rendering alludes to this: “Let them perish after their shame.” Hence the translators for Cajetan translated: “They are forsaken upon the heel of their shame.” Finally, however one reads it, the sense appears to look to the same point.

# Psalm XL

[Col. 0407]

## Title of the Psalm: “Unto the end, a psalm of David” (or, as Jerome translates: “Unto the end, an understanding for the sons of Korah”).

[Col. 0407D]

“Blessed is he who understands.” Title: “Unto the end, a psalm of David,” or, as Jerome translates, “Unto the end, an understanding for the sons of Korah.” This little clause, “or, as Jerome translates,” etc., is an addition. For we have seen another handwritten manuscript in which it is absent; moreover, Jerome himself gives no such title either in volume VIII or in his translation according to the Hebrew. Nor likewise does the Septuagint; but this title occurs in Haymo. Thus perhaps someone wrote “Jerome” in place of “Haymo.”

The same error occurs in the Ordinary Gloss. Korah, as is read in Numbers XVI, stirred up rebellion against Moses and Aaron along with Dathan and Abiram. Therefore Dathan and Abiram, with their entire household, were swallowed alive by the earth. But Korah and the 250 men with him who had taken censers to burn incense before the Lord were killed by divine fire, because they had appropriated to themselves the office of Aaron and his sons (Num. XXVI). Yet certain sons of Korah did not imitate their father’s wickedness. Therefore they were later taken by David into the service of the house of the Lord, and were blessed by the Lord with eternal joy. For this reason they are often mentioned in psalm titles, but especially because of the interpretation of their name, [Col. 0409A] 89 from which, as here, the spiritual understanding of the psalm is derived. [Jerome.] For Korah is interpreted “Calvary,” the place of the Lord’s Passion. Therefore Christ’s Passion is understood through “Calvary.” This is read in volume IV, in a certain exposition of Psalm XLI which is not attributed to Jerome; Saint Augustine says the same in the title of the following psalm, and Jerome has it below, on Psalm LXXXIV.

The sons of Calvary, therefore, are the sons of the Passion, the sons of the cross, who glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ with the Apostle saying: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI). To such persons is assigned the understanding of this psalm: those who believe that Christ, although poor and dead, is nevertheless true God. This is the meaning: the understanding of this psalm, tending unto the end—that is, unto Christ—is assigned to the sons of Korah, that is, the sons of the cross.

Purpose: it exhorts that, although Christ is poor and suffered, he should nevertheless be believed to be God. [Cassiodorus.] Method: the psalm has three parts. First, the prophet celebrates with divine praise the one who understands the needy and poor person. Second, Christ speaks of his Passion, which belonged to his condition as needy, at the words: “My enemies,” etc. Third, he speaks of the resurrection, which is the glory of the needy one, to confirm the hope of the faithful, at the words: “But you, O Lord.” Note that in this psalm the voice is that of the whole Christ, that is, head and body, as though of one person. Some words of this psalm suit the head, some the members, and some the prophet. [Jerome.] First the prophet speaks for himself in his own person. Afterwards he introduces Christ speaking [Col. 0409C] both in the members and in himself: in the members, at “I said”; in himself, at “My enemies,” etc. Therefore the prophet says:

VERSE 1.—“Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor; on an evil day the Lord will deliver him.”

Blessed is he who understands. [Augustine.] As though he said: He who worships one who is poor and dead is mocked; but blessed in eternal things is he who understands Christ, even though he sees him needy and poor—[Jerome] because he is also God, who so believes him to be human as also to understand him to be the same God. This may also be understood of Christ’s members. [Augustine.] Attention must indeed be given to the needy, so that something may be given to them; and this too belongs to him. This is the sense: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and [Col. 0409D] poor.” Note that he does not say “who gives,” but “who understands,” so that even those who do not ask may be given to. [Cassiodorus.] For one who gives to a petitioner does well indeed; but one who perceives the silent person is undoubtedly blessed. Hence blessed is he who anticipates the voice of one about to ask. He explains here the blessing: “On an evil day,” that is, the day of judgment, “the Lord will deliver him.”

VERSE 2.—“May the Lord preserve him, enliven him, make him blessed upon the earth, and not give him over to the will of his enemies.”

May the Lord preserve him and enliven him. [Augustine.] Here the prophet rightly wishes for the one who understands the needy and poor person what is a sure promise. [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: In the future he will deliver him; meanwhile, [Col. 0410A] may the Lord preserve him amid the evils of the world, [Jerome] lest he fall away from this understanding; and, while remaining in it, enliven him. Hence follows, “enliven him,” [Augustine] in the future life, or here through justification. And lest they think that benefits are given to them only in the future and that they are neglected here, he adds: “and make him blessed upon the earth,” that is, in this life. He fittingly promises goods both in the present and in the future, [Interlinear Gloss] because godliness has promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come. “And do not give him over to the soul,” that is, the will, of his enemies—even if [you give him] into their hands—[Augustine] namely, the devil and his servants.

VERSE 3.—“May the Lord bring him help upon his bed of pain; you have turned all his bed in his weakness.”

May the Lord bring help. [Cassiodorus.] Do not suppose that the blessed person has rest here: he prays that his pains may be relieved, lest human weakness be overcome by hardships. As though he said: Do not give him over, but rather let the Lord bring him help upon his bed of pain. As though he said: These temporal goods are a bed of rest, but God makes them full of pains, lest hope be placed in them. Therefore he says here, “upon his bed of pain.” [Augustine.] Why then, when God brings help, do they suffer so much? Turning his speech to God, he explains the design of his healing, saying: “You have turned all his bed.” As though he said: I rightly called it a bed of pain: you have turned all his bed—of man, that is, worldly prosperity—into his weakness, that is, you have providently changed it into his distresses. A bed is some earthly thing which an infirm person, even a good one, chooses for himself [Col. 0410C] in order to rest: a wife, children, and other lawful things, when he cannot continuously endure the labour of a mind stretched toward God. But God, wishing us to have no love except for eternal life, mixes bitterness with these pleasures and turns them into our weakness, lest we love as the home of eternal dwelling the inn where, on the road by which we are pilgrims from the Lord, the Samaritan commanded care to be given to the wounded man who fell among robbers (Luke X). [Cassiodorus.] Troubled by these things, the man asks for mercy, because, knowing that he had sinned, he feared that he might justly be handed over to them. Hence he adds:

VERSE 4.—“I said: O Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.”

I said. As though he said: You have turned it, but knowing that I had sinned, I said: “O Lord, have mercy on me.” [Augustine.] [Col. 0410D] Christ the head says this in the members: Have mercy in this way—heal my soul through scourges—because I by no means excuse sin, but accuse it, saying: “Because I have sinned against you.” I do not blame fortune; I do not say: “Fate does this to me”; I do not say: “Venus made me an adulterer, Mars a robber, and Saturn a miser.” Note that this verse is sung at Terce, because the soul is healed from sin through faith and the working of the Trinity. [Cassiodorus.] But lest God’s servants, afflicted by these things, appear therefore to have been deserted by God—when the Lord himself endured such things—he says: “My enemies said.” And Christ says this of himself.

Or otherwise, from the words, “May the Lord bring him help.” [Augustine.] The bed of pain is said to be the flesh in which sin is found, and upon which the godly person groans like a paralytic in bed, while the ungodly rejoices. The sense is: Do not give him over, but rather, upon his bed of pain, that is, upon the weakness of the flesh which weighs down the soul, [Jerome] may the Lord bring him help, so that, like a healed paralytic, he may carry the bed by commanding the flesh rather than serving it. But whence the pain? Because “all his bed.” [Alcuin.] By “all his bed” he means vegetative and sensual nature, which in Paradise was subject to reason and was a bed of joy and rest; but because of sin God changed it to the contrary, so that it now fights against reason and inflicts pains. This is the meaning: “You have turned all his bed,” that is, you have allowed sensuality to resist reason. And this occurred in his weakness—that is, in man’s, [Alcuin] when Adam was made weak by transgression. [Augustine.] But when a person knows that he suffers this because of sins, let him turn and say: “I said: O Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.”

## Part II. Verse 5.—“My enemies spoke evil things against me: When will he die and his name perish?”

My enemies. [Cassiodorus.] The second part, in which God himself speaks of his Passion, which belonged to his state as needy. As though he said: Blessed is he who understands the needy and poor one. But when my enemies saw the people following Jesus, they spoke evil—[Augustine] that is, false—things against me, namely: “When will he die?” They said this because he was troublesome to them and grievous to behold (Wisdom II). They also feared that they themselves would lose their place and nation. “And his name will perish,” so that he may have no renown. Note that they say, “He will die, and his name will perish,” because, seeing him die, they thought the people would know that they had falsely hoped in him; thus they curse him. These words are said particularly of Christ, but may also be said of the members. For persecution occurs today in order that Christ’s name may be extinguished; yet through his death and that of his own, the Church has grown all the more. Hence: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John XII). And elsewhere: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. CXLVIII).

VERSE 6.—“And if he came in to see, he spoke vain things; his heart gathered iniquity to itself.”

And if he came in. [Alcuin.] As though he said: Not only open enemies, but even those who pretended to be friends spoke evil things. [Augustine.] This is the meaning: “And if someone, such as Judas, came in,” and this was “in order to see,” that is, to spy; so the Apostle also says of false brothers secretly introduced: “They came in secretly to spy out our freedom” (Gal. II). He “spoke vain things,” that is, pretended things; and “his heart gathered iniquity,” [Interlinear Gloss] preparing a slander which it ought to have laid aside there. And this “to itself,” [Augustine] that is, its own evil, because it harms itself, not me. And because he entered in order to see:

VERSE 7.—“He went out abroad, and spoke the same thing.”

[Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss.] He went out from the bosom of truth, or from the friendship which he pretended, abroad—that is, to those opposed to Christ—or so as to become an open enemy. [Cassiodorus.] [Col. 0412A] Behold, his entrance is evil and his assault is evil. “And he spoke the same thing,” [Interlinear Gloss] namely, vanity—that is, false and vain things.

VERSE 8.—“All my enemies whispered against me; against me they devised evils for me.”

Against me. [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: Not merely those who came in, but all my enemies—although few are usually the perpetrators of crimes—whispered against me, murmuring to one another’s ears. For those who share in crime do not dare reveal their designs. [Augustine.] Or distinguish the wording thus: “He went out abroad and spoke.” Make a division here, and the sense does not change: “The same thing”—in one plan—“all my enemies whispered against me, and against me they devised evils for me.” [Interlinear Gloss.] If one could find more evil than another, the evils, I say, were intended for me, [Augustine] though they would rather finally be evils for themselves.

VERSE 9.—“They established an unrighteous word against me: shall not one who sleeps add that he may rise again?”

“They established an unrighteous word against me,” [Cassiodorus] namely: “It is expedient that one man die for the people” (John XI), etc.; “If you let this man go, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John XIX). These are the wicked tenants who, after killing the servants, resolve to kill the householder’s son, saying: “Let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance” (Matt. XXI). They say so, [Augustine] but shall not he who has power to lay down his life also have power to take it up again? (John X). This is the meaning: Shall not one who sleeps—not dead by necessity or unwillingly, as you suppose, but voluntarily asleep and soon to awaken—add that he may rise again? Note that he says “sleeps,” because just as from the side of sleeping Adam, who was a figure of him to come, a rib was taken, from which Eve was formed, so Christ slept the sleep of death, so that from the side of the sleeper—from which flowed blood and water, the sacraments of our redemption—his bride, the Church, might be formed.

VERSE 10.—“For even the man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, magnified treachery against me.”

For even. [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: And whence came that sleeping? From the betrayer. “For even the man”—or connect it thus: [Col. 0412D] “They established an unrighteous word against me,” because even the man “who dips his hand with me in the dish” (Matt. XXVI), [Alcuin] through whom they were given that opportunity of crucifying me. This is the meaning: “For even the man of my peace,” namely Judas. [Augustine.] Behold the prophecy of the kiss with which he betrayed him. “In whom I trusted,” as it seemed; or, “I trusted,” according to what I deserved. [Cassiodorus.] Or, “in whom I trusted,” in the members, [Interlinear Gloss] because other brothers hoped something in him, since he appeared to be like the rest. [Augustine.] Thus Christ says that he hungers in the poor; and “who ate my bread” (John XIII). Behold the prophecy of the morsel by which the Lord identified him. [Cassiodorus.] Or, “he ate my bread,” that is, along with the others he received my teaching, and “magnified,” that is, made great, treachery against me. [Col. 0413A] [Augustine.] Or, according to the letter, “he raised his heel against me,” that is, lifted his foot to trample me.

## Part III. Verse 11.—“But you, O Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up, and I shall repay them.”

But you, O Lord, have mercy on me. [Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which he speaks of the resurrection, which is the glory of the needy one, to confirm the faithful in hope. As though he said: They act thus; but you, O Lord, have mercy on me, [Augustine] who am needy and poor. Note that Christ asks as man for what he accomplishes as God. Have mercy, and in this, raise me up; and I shall repay them in the present, that they may be scattered, and in the future, that they may be condemned. For their scattering throughout the world is for warning, not yet for condemnation; and this you will truly do.

[Col. 0413B] VERSE 12.—“By this I have known that you have willed me, because my enemy will not rejoice over me.”

By this I have known that you have willed me. [Interlinear Gloss.] That is, I have known that I have always pleased you, because my enemy will not rejoice over me; [Augustine] that is, because you will raise me up, and thus they will not rejoice. They rejoiced at the death, but were ashamed at the resurrection. Or thus: “By this I have known that my enemy will not rejoice over me,” [Cassiodorus] that is, because you have raised me up. “I have known that you have willed me,” that is, you love me. For the Father’s love appears in his raising him up.

VERSE 13.—“But you have received me because of my innocence, and established me before you forever.”

But me. [Alcuin.] Here he affirms what he prayed for: “But you have received me because of my innocence,” [Augustine] that is, because I am without sin, in the resurrection. [Jerome.] “And you have established me” in the glory of impassibility. [Cassiodorus.] Hence it is said: “Death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI). You established me also by giving the name which is above every name (Phil. II). “You established me,” I say, “before you forever.” [Augustine.] Before human beings and for a time, you first made me weak.

VERSE 14.—“Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from age to age: So be it, so be it.”

Blessed be the Lord. [Cassiodorus.] This is a laudatory conclusion after the Passion and resurrection have been expounded. As though he said: You received and established me; therefore praise belongs to you. [Interlinear Gloss.] This is the meaning: Blessed be the Lord, to whom *dulia* (service) is due [Note: [Col. 0413] Here *dulia* is understood as noted on Psalm VIII.]; God, to whom *latria* (worship) is due. God, I say, of Israel—that is, of those who see him. These are not the Jews, [Col. 0414A] but we, who are the younger son—that is, the younger people, younger not in faith but in time—to whom the elder serves, namely the Jewish people, elder in time. [Augustine.] For the Jews are our book-carriers, who carry the codices for us; but we are Israel. Otherwise the pagans would have thought that what is said about Christ and the Church was invented, but they are overcome by the testimony of their enemies. “Blessed,” I say, “from age to age,” [Cassiodorus] that is, from the time when all things began to be ordered until the age to come, where all things are already eternal. “So be it, so be it.” This repetition shows that all ought to do this. [Jerome.] For “So be it, so be it,” the Hebrew has *amen, amen*, which Aquila translated “truly,” that is, “faithfully.” Here Jerome says that the first book of the Psalter ends.

## Comparison on Psalm XL: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor.”

[Col. 0414B]

VERSE 1.—“Concerning the needy and poor.” In Hebrew only “concerning the poor” occurs. But the Septuagint could add “needy,” just as Münster could add: “Blessed is he who looks out for one oppressed by infirmity,” to express the force of the word *dal*.

VERSE 7.—“He went out abroad and spoke the same thing.” The Hebraists refer the final phrase to the following verse: “the same thing,” that is, “together they whispered against me.” Faber adopts this view, virtually ridiculing the other punctuation: “For what sense,” he says, “would there be in: ‘He went out abroad and spoke together’?” If Stapulensis had observed the Scriptural manner of speaking, which comprehends many under one person, he would not have attacked the Latin reading in such a hostile spirit. Hence the text of St Augustine and the Roman psalmody use the plural, though they follow the Hebrew reading. In Hebrew, however, “to enter,” “to go out,” and “to speak” are read in the singular. They are understood of Christ’s enemies, but singularly and especially of Judas the traitor. Therefore Münster, in the preceding verse, translates “and if he came in to see” as: “and if one of them comes, in order to see.” How Judas plotted the betrayal within himself, so that it is true that he “spoke the same thing,” the Gospel plainly testifies: “When the devil had put it into Judas’s heart,” etc. (John XIII). Moreover, we have repeatedly observed that divisions of verses and also pauses often vary; this is also clear from the preceding verse. For some connect “heart” with what precedes, while others with what follows: “And if he came in to see, he spoke vain things; his heart.” Or thus: “His heart will gather iniquity to itself.” The Master follows the second reading.

VERSE 9.—“Shall not one who sleeps add that he may rise again?” The Septuagint, by means of a question, heightens the force of the matter, whereas the Hebrews, reading with a simple statement, seem almost cold: “He who slept shall not add that he may rise again”—as though these were the words of the Jews denying Christ’s resurrection. The first interpretation reproaches their unbelief.

# Psalm XLI

[Col. 0413]

## Title of the Psalm: “Unto the end, an understanding,” or “by understanding, for the sons of Korah.”

[Col. 0413D]

As a stag longs for streams of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.

**Title of the Psalm:** “For the end; an understanding, or with understanding, for the sons of Korah.”

Korah, as we said above, is interpreted “baldness” [Note: Jerome, on Psalm 33, Col. 0413D]; this was the place of the Lord’s Passion, which occurred at Calvary [Col. 0414D]. The sons of Korah, therefore, are sons of the bald one—that is, of Christ, prefigured in bald Elisha. When Elisha was going up from Jericho to Bethel, forty-two boys came out from Bethel, mocking Elisha and saying, “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead!” [Col. 0415A] Then Elisha commanded two bears to come out of the wood, and the boys were killed by them (4 Kings 2). Thus too, when Christ went up to Bethel [Note: Augustine, on Psalm 44, Col. 0415D]—that is, when, having assumed flesh, he came to the Synagogue, formerly the house of God, which is what Bethel means—he was mocked by little ones shouting, “Away! Away! Crucify him!” (John 19): that is, by Jews shouting in childish folly. They are devoured by two bears [Note: Jerome, as above, Col. 0415D]: namely, by the devil and his angels, or by Titus and Vespasian, whom God sent for the destruction of the Jews in the forty-second year after Christ’s resurrection, just as those forty-two boys were devoured by two beasts.

[Augustine.] The sons of Korah, then, are those who have received Christ’s trophy—that is, the sign of the cross—upon the brow of heart and body. This psalm is assigned to them [Col. 0415B]. The sense of the title is: the understanding of this psalm, directing us to the end—that is, to Christ—belongs to the sons of Korah, that is, of the cross which was on Calvary. Or, according to the other reading, “which is with understanding,” with “psalm” understood: thus this psalm, directing us to the end, belongs to the sons of Korah, that is, of Christ, “with understanding,” so that they may understand spiritually.

For this psalm suits every Christian who is inflamed with the fire of divine charity, and this is the first psalm here concerning that subject—that is, the charity of God [Note: Cassiodorus, Psalm 84; this appears more fitting where he writes “for the sons of Korah,” Psalm 133, a Song of Ascents, Cols. 0415D, 0416D]. Two others follow, namely Psalms 83 and 133. [Jerome.] This psalm is directed against worldly sorrows, lest they draw us away from God. It contains the voice of a believer longing for God, who has lived amid vices [Col. 0415C] and tends toward the font of baptism [Note: Cassiodorus, at the conclusion of the psalm, Col. 0416D]; or of one who, having exhausted his vices, rises to the contemplation of God. He sets forth his desire by the carefully chosen example of the hind, and the mockery of the wicked confronts him. But lest worldly sorrow should draw his mind into despair or weariness, he later consoles his soul.

**Purpose.** He warns that worldly sorrows should not draw anyone away from holy longing.

[Cassiodorus.] **Division.** The psalm has two parts. First, all this believer’s desire is said to be directed toward God. Second, it treats of disturbances, against which reason strengthens the sensuous soul through hope in God: “Why are you sad?” and so forth. Accordingly, showing his desire, he says:

### Verse 1

> “As the stag longs [Col. 0415D] for streams of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.”

**As the stag longs.** [Augustine, Alcuin, Jerome, Gloss interlinear.] This voice suits catechumens, and also all believers still journeying as pilgrims. “As the hind longs”: behold the carefully selected comparison of the stag. For although by many other characteristics the stag is compared to the believer, it is because of this quality, as the more outstanding and expressive, that it is brought forward here.

When a stag is weighed down with age, with its hair and antlers grown out, it drags out a serpent. Having dragged it out, it burns from the venom through its nostrils, and therefore longs most ardently for a spring from which to drink. Once it has drunk, it sheds its antlers and hair. This fittingly applies both to the believer and to the catechumen, and to the perfect person, though in differing ways.

The likeness is applied to the catechumen in this way: just as the stag, burning after it has dragged out the serpent, seeks a spring to extinguish its heat, so the catechumen, recognizing that he burns from the venom of vices contracted from the earth, seeks and desires the font of baptism. There he lays aside the hairs of vice and the antlers of pride, and thus grows young again, having become a new human being.

[Jerome, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear, Augustine.] It applies to the perfect person in this way: as the stag drags out the serpent and kills it once drawn out, and, once it is killed, seeks a spring in order to drink, so the believer, having consumed the vices and sins within himself, longs for the spring of contemplation [Col. 0416B], where he may be refreshed.

Yet both the perfect person and the catechumen tend toward the same fountain—Christ, who is the fountain of living waters. Thus: as the stag, after drawing out the serpent, longs to come to streams of water so that it may grow young again, so my soul longs for you, O God, says the catechumen. Or, so that it applies to the perfect person: as the stag, after killing the serpent, longs to come to streams of water, so, with vices consumed, my soul longs with a more ardent longing than before to come to you, O God.

Note that, because this concerns catechumens seeking the font of baptism, this psalm is sung on the Saturday of Easter and Pentecost, when the sacrament of baptism is celebrated. But because it also concerns perfected persons longing to see God [Col. 0416C], it is sung at funeral services. What they had previously desired, they then possess.

### Verse 2

> “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?”

**It thirsted.** [Augustine, Jerome, Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine, Jerome, Augustine.] Here he defines his desire, since the hind might desire the spring either in order to drink or to wash. He shows that it desires the spring chiefly for drinking. As if he said: My soul longs for you. It has thirsted, indeed—and long ago, not merely for the first time—for God, the fountain, or the strong one: that is, for Christ, who is the fountain of flowing waters [Col. 0416D], from whom all good things flow; the living one, not the dead idols of the nations.

And for what has it thirsted? To come and appear. This is what is meant by, “When shall I come?” As if he said: “I desire to depart” (Philippians 1), because I thirst while on pilgrimage, I thirst while running; I shall be satisfied when I arrive. But when shall I come? He says this because what is soon to God is slow to human longing. “And appear,” because then we too shall appear, who now lie hidden before God’s face, because then we shall see him as he is (John 3). Such a stag, while it runs, suffers those who mock it.

### Verse 3

> “My tears were my bread [Col. 0417A] by day and by night, while it is said to me daily, ‘Where is your God?’”

**My tears were my bread.** [Gloss interlinear, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As if he said: In the future I shall appear; but on the way, my tears were my bread by day—that is, amid prosperity, which this person despises—and by night, that is, amid adversity. These tears were not bitterness or destruction to me, but bread—that is, refreshment—because the Christian is instructed by afflictions.

The cause of these tears is the continual taunting of the wicked. Hence it follows: “while it is said.” As if he said: This is why I have tears: because it is said to me every day, while they point out their god with a finger, “Where is your God?”

### Verse 4

> “I remembered these things and poured out my soul within me, because I shall pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God.”

**I remembered these things, or meditated upon them.** [Augustine.] As if he said: They ask, “Where is your God?” And while they ask these things, I too have meditated through all visible things upon this: “Where is my God?” I examined the visible things of the world through the windows of my senses, in order that through them I might know the invisible Creator. Nor did I seek God only through those visible things, but also through my own soul, so that through these—that is, through outward things and my soul—I might find the invisible things of God.

This is what is meant by, “I poured out my soul”: that is, in order to attain and understand God, I expanded my soul. For, having left behind those outward instruments subject to bodily senses [Col. 0417C], my mind returned to itself and began to contemplate itself: that it might see itself within itself, know itself in itself, and understand whether its God is anything of such a kind. Behold the “understanding” of the title.

But since it found God neither in outward things nor in the soul, because the unchangeable God transcends these changeable things, it adds: “above myself.” As if he said: I expanded my soul so as to understand above itself. For if the soul remained in itself without transcending itself, it would not see God, who is beyond it. But why did it do this? Because in this manner I shall pass—or enter—into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God.

God’s tabernacle on earth is the faithful, in whom this person now admires many things: namely, that sin does not reign in the body, but rather the weapons of righteousness; that the soul obeys God, endures hardships, tends upward, and the like [Col. 0417D]. He passes beyond these things also, reaches in mind to the heavenly house of God, and marvels. This is what is meant by: “Therefore I poured out my soul, because in this manner I shall pass”—or enter—by examination and contemplation.

[Cassiodorus, Augustine.] “Into the place of the wonderful tabernacle”: that is, into the present Church, which is a kind of image and appearance of the Jerusalem to come. When it is seen, that other Jerusalem is desired more greatly, and there is greater groaning in this one. Therefore he says, “I shall enter into the place of the tabernacle,” because anyone seeking God outside the place of this tabernacle goes astray. I say that he reaches in mind as far as the house of God, not being ensnared by worldly desires. How do you reach the secret place of God’s house?

### Verse 5

> “With the voice of exultation and confession: the sound of one feasting.” [Col. 0418A]

**With the voice of exultation.** [Augustine, Jerome, Augustine, Alcuin.] Something of the eternal feast sounds forth—a melody sweet and tuneful to his heart—by which he is drawn and delighted, like the hind toward streams of water. And there is the sound of confession—that is, of eternal praise, sung to God by angels—which brings him wondrous sweetness. This is said by comparison with those celebrating feasts, whose custom was to arrange musical performances before their houses. I say, “with the voice of exultation and confession”: that is, the sound of one feasting, namely of those sounding forth and feasting, rejoicing in eternal refreshment. Or, “which confession is the sound of one feasting”; but the sense does not change.

[Jerome, Alcuin.] Otherwise, from the words “I remembered these things.” As if he said: They reproach me in this way; and remembering these reproaches, I poured out my soul—that is, I rejoiced with joy, and my soul melted. And this took place within me: it does not leap about outwardly, but, pierced with compunction, returns into itself. For one kind of compunction belongs to joy, another to sorrow.

Why was I rejoicing thus? Because I shall pass to the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God: that is, because I consider that, although I do not now see God visibly, nevertheless through the Church, in which the saints are wonderful, I shall reach the heavenly Jerusalem. I say that I am in the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting: that is, seized by the sweetness of angelic praise, which is received in the mind.

## Part II — Verse 6

> “Why are you sad, [Col. 0418C] O my soul? And why do you trouble me?”

**Why are you sad?** [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin, Gloss interlinear.] This is the second part, in which he treats of disturbances, against which reason strengthens the sensuous soul by hope in God. As if he said: I have passed from here as far as God’s house; but because the world clamors and the flesh weighs down the soul, comparing these sad things with those joyful ones, he says: “Why are you sad?” As if he said: Since I have passed as far as that house, O my soul, when you behold joyful things and do not doubt concerning God, who is present, why are you sad? And why do you trouble me? As if he said: If you seek a reason, there is nothing in the world for which you ought to do this.

### Verse 7

> “Hope in God, for I shall yet confess to him: the salvation of my countenance, and my God.”

**Hope in God.** [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As if he said: Lest the soul say, “I trouble you because I am not there, where I was carried in passing; and here I am burdened,” he says instead: Hope meanwhile in God. Behold the saving remedy: hope. For I shall yet confess to him—not fully now, but in the future—in reality. For I am not yet saved in every respect; but I shall confess in hope. What shall I confess? That he himself is the salvation, and so forth.

Or thus: Hope, and you can hope, because I shall yet confess to him in the present—that is, I shall repent of sins, so that I may not stand against you. To him, I say, I shall confess, who is salvation, from whom—and not from myself—I have salvation. I call him “the salvation of my countenance,” because of our form which he assumed [Col. 0419A]; and he is also my God, that is, my Creator.

### Verse 8

> “My soul has been troubled within myself; therefore I shall remember you from the land of Jordan and Hermonim, from the little mountain.”

**Within myself.** [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] This person, converted toward God, says that disturbances arise from himself, but their end comes from God. Therefore his hope is in God. This is what is meant by: “My soul has been troubled within myself,” or “by myself.” As if he said: My soul is sad, but my soul has been troubled within me, or by me. The soul that is refreshed by God is troubled in relation to me. I have no firmness or hope in myself; therefore I shall never presume upon myself, but shall hope in God.

See how he who above corrected his soul, returning to the condition of a human being, here says that the soul is troubled by himself. Unless the vices of the flesh were present, it would remain tranquil. See of what diversity the human being consists. “Therefore,” as if he said, because my soul is troubled in relation to me; “therefore”—that is, because of the soul’s disturbances—I shall remember you: I hasten to you, who exclude all evils. Here is the remedy by which tribulations are escaped.

But whence—that is, on account of what—will he remember God? He adds, “from the land of Jordan.” In Jordan, whose name means “descent,” the Lord consecrated baptism. In it the humbled are washed and become fruitful earth, yielding thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold fruit. Descend, then, in order that you may be raised. Thus: “I shall remember you from the land of Jordan,” that is, from baptism, where there is forgiveness of sins: because in baptism you forgave my sins, humbled me, and made me fruitful earth [Col. 0419C]. One who remembers these things is not troubled by evils.

“And I shall remember you from the land of Hermonim, from the little mountain.” Hermon is a small mountain near the Jordan, and its name means “anathema” or “curse.” Therefore anathematize yourself by displeasing yourself, so that you may please God; anathematize the devil also, by renouncing him. The meaning is: “I shall remember you from Hermonim, from the little mountain,” because you caused me to displease myself, to renounce the devil, and to be lofty in virtues yet humble; for remembrance of God is not among the proud, but among the humble. Note the fitting connection of the words: “Jordan and Hermonim, from the little mountain” [Col. 0419D]. No one runs to forgiveness, as to Jordan, unless he is displeased with himself and confesses himself a sinner; this is signified by Hermonim. And no one confesses himself a sinner unless he humbles himself; this is signified by “little.”

### Verse 9

> “Deep calls to deep, in the voice of your cataracts.”

**Deep.** [Jerome, Alcuin.] As if he said: It is fitting that I remember you; for “deep calls to deep”: that is, the Gospel and the Law agree in this, and this calling is made “in the voice of your cataracts,” that is, through the teaching of the prophets and apostles, from whom God’s streams flow. Hence they are called cataracts. Literally, cataracts are the outlets of rivers from which water flows. And therefore I shall remember you, because:

### Verse 10

> “All your heights and your waves have passed over me.” [Col. 0420A]

**All your heights and your waves which were over me.** [Alcuin.] That is, the greater and lesser punishment which overwhelmed me have so passed over me—that is, they will pass over me. He uses the past for the future with prophetic certainty. Therefore I shall also remember you, because:

### Verse 11

> “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night his song.”

**By day,** [Alcuin, Augustine, Jerome] that is, amid prosperity, the Lord commanded his mercy: God commanded the bearing of evils, which is mercy, by which he chastises every son whom he receives. And by night—that is, amid adversity—he commanded his song: that is, he commanded us to rejoice in Christ himself. Hence the Apostle says, “Rejoicing in tribulations” [Col. 0420B]; and because of all these things I pray amid adversities (Romans 12). This is what is meant by “with me is prayer.”

Or thus, from the words “deep calls to deep.” This person, remembering God and marveling how all things invite to God—even human beings, one another—says to God: As if I ought to remember you, because “deep calls to deep”: that is, one human being calls another to God when he preaches something of the truth. Such a person is called “deep,” because neither the heart of the caller nor that of the called can be known: for “the heart of man is deep and unsearchable” (Jeremiah 17). Hence, “Man shall approach the deep heart” (Psalm 63), and elsewhere, “He is a human being: and who shall know him?” One person calls another. And this occurs not in his own voice, but in that of your cataracts: that is, in the voice of the Holy Spirit divinely infused into him, from whom flow waters springing up to eternal life (John 4) [Col. 0420C].

Or “deep” means the two judgments of God, namely the first and second, by which this person is frightened. Hence elsewhere: “I feared because of your judgments” (Psalm 120). As if he said: My soul was troubled and I was humbled, because the deep—that is, the judgment which God inflicted upon sinful humanity, from which labor and death come to us here—calls to the deep: that is, it points to the other judgment by which the wicked will be condemned. For if God punished humanity so severely, what will he do in the future to those who do not repent? This is what the speaker feared when he said, “My soul is troubled within me.” Thus he is humble, because he fears the judgments.

These two judgments trouble him, and this occurs “in the voice of your cataracts”: that is, through the teaching of your preachers, who announce these things to people [Col. 0420D]. This is clear from the fact that “all your heights”—or, according to another reading, “all your overhangings”—that is, the future evils which you threaten; “and your waves,” namely, the pains which I feel, have already in reality passed over me: that is, they now oppress me. One of these comes to me from the first judgment, the other from the future judgment. But the more frequent evils are, the sweeter mercy will be. For “by day”—that is, in prosperity—“the Lord commanded his mercy”: that is, he teaches his mercy, namely that mercy which delivers from tribulation.

For the law of the Lord, who promises the mercy of deliverance, is learned in a quiet time; but he does not reveal that mercy—that is, its fruit—except in the night of adversity. Thus he says here: “By night,” that is, amid adversities, “he revealed,” according to another reading [Col. 0421A]: that is, in adversities its fruit is revealed. Then he comes to help, and God proves true what he commanded by day. Hence, “The mercy of God is beautiful in the time of tribulation, like a rain-cloud in a time of drought.”

Therefore, like the ant, we ought amid prosperity to learn and collect what may sustain us in adversity. The ant gathers during summer what will benefit it in winter; so you too, amid prosperity, learn mercy. This—namely God’s mercy—ends disturbances.

### Verse 12

> “With me is prayer to the God of my life; I shall say to God: You are my protector.”

**With me.** [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As if he said: Though evils are everywhere, what then do you do in this pilgrimage? I tell you: prayer is mine amid these disturbances [Col. 0421B]. This prayer is “with me”: that is, I have within myself what I may offer. I do not bring God incense and spices from afar, nor a calf or ram from the flock. Within myself is that by which I may please God; I do not seek it outside myself.

This prayer is offered to the God of my life, that is, to him who gives life. But prayer without almsgiving and fasting is empty. For the justice of a person in this life consists in fasting, almsgiving, and prayer, which flies to God with those two others. I shall say to my God: “You are my protector,” because through baptism you received me, to place me in your homeland.

### Verse 13

> “Why have you forgotten me? And why do I go grieving, while the enemy afflicts me?”

**Why have you forgotten me?** [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Because he delays what he has promised. This is the burden: he seems to have forgotten. The meaning is: “Why have you forgotten me? Why do you now permit me to be vexed by these miseries?” This person saw what sweetness the homeland possesses and dreaded the perils of the world. “And why do I go grieving?”—according to the perception of the flesh, which dreads these hardships. I go to you grieving because the enemy, namely the devil, afflicts me through temptation and tribulation [Col. 0421C]. As if he said: I go grieving while, because iniquity abounds, the charity of many grows cold (Matthew 24).

### Verse 14

> “While my bones are being broken, those who trouble me—my enemies—reproached me.”

**While they are being broken.** [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As if he said: The enemy so afflicts me because my bones are being broken: even the strong members of the Church yield to scandals. For the bones are, as it were, broken when the strength of patience is afflicted and grows lukewarm; and the wicked mock this [Col. 0421D]. Moreover, those who trouble me, my enemies, reproached me. They reproached me in this manner:

### Verse 15

> “While they say to me every day: ‘Where is your God?’”

**While they say to me every day.** [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin.] This is said especially to believers amid the Church’s temptations. What do they say? “Where is your God?” This is that reproach: “Where is your God?”—as if either he does not exist, or does not care for you; and if he cares, let him deliver you, if he can. Thus they speak. Yet nevertheless:

### Verse 16

> “Why are you sad, O my soul? And why do you trouble me?”

**Why are you sad, O my soul?** [Augustine.] Or the connection may be given thus: They say these things to me, and since because of them my soul is troubled within me, what should I counsel it except what I said above: “Why are you sad, O my soul, and why do you trouble me?” This is a repeated encouragement against frequent tribulations. But lest you say, “I am troubled because I suffer evils here,” rather:

### Verse 17

> “Hope in God, for I shall yet confess to him: the salvation of my countenance, and my God.”

**Hope in God, for I shall yet confess to him** [Gloss interlinear, Augustine], in the future or now. What shall I confess? That he himself is “the salvation of my countenance and my God.” Here he states the confession itself and repeats the confirmation of hope.

## Comparison on Psalm 41: “As the stag longs”

### Verse 1 — “As the stag longs,” etc.

Jerome translates: “As a plot prepared for irrigations of water” [Col. 0422B]. The other translators agree with our edition, although they differ slightly in wording. Thus, since *AIAL* can ambiguously mean either “stag” or “hind,” and “plain,” though some posit a difference in the vowel points—which, as was demonstrated in the Prologue, St Jerome did not read—he followed the other meaning and read *AIIL*. Likewise, where we read *TAAROG*, “it will cry out like a hind,” which we translate “it pants” or “it longs,” so that without objection the future may stand for the present, Jerome took it for *ARUGAH*, meaning a line or bed of plantings, to which St Jerome alluded. For a thirsty and dry bed of plants aptly corresponds to the soul supremely longing for God.

### Verse 2 — “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain.”

It may appear to be a scribal fault that “fountain” was written for “strong one,” as Lyra thinks, because of the resemblance of the words, especially since in Hebrew *LELOHIM LEEL* is read twice continuously [Col. 0422C], signifying “for God, for the strong one”; this is also how St Jerome translates it, and the Greek has ἰσχυρόν, “strong one.”

Certainly, as St Jerome writes to Sunnia and Fretela, if anything has been altered through a copyist’s error, we ought not defend it by foolish contention. Yet, upon considering the matter more deeply, it has seemed to me unnecessary to say that a changed word is a lapse caused by neighboring syllables. Rather, the Latin reading originally had “God” only once: “My soul thirsted for the living God,” as may still be seen in the Roman psalmody and in Augustine’s text. Later, from the coherence of wording and sense, it is not improbable that Latin writers added “fountain,” without thinking of “strong one,” as though they had substituted one for the other, but rather to make a connection with the preceding verse.

For more than six hundred years ago, Haymo read and explained “fountain”: “My soul thirsted to possess God—God, I say, the fountain, because he is the source of every good.” Likewise St Augustine, in Book I of the *Soliloquies*, or whoever else is its author, chapter 35, after citing the verse, immediately cries: “O fountain of life, vein of living waters, when shall I come to the waters of your sweetness?” Furthermore, whoever finally published the exposition on this psalm in volume IV of the works of St Jerome, after explaining that three fountains are appropriate—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—immediately, when turning to the second verse, interprets “the living fountain” as baptism itself [Col. 0422D].

From these facts it abundantly appears that this reading was accepted through long usage, and its own authority should be granted to it, especially because of its euphony. For in some cases we know that similar changes were made by Latin writers themselves for the sake of harmonious sound, and yet are not rejected.

Indeed, Sunnia and Fretela had asked Jerome why in Psalm 39 the Latins said, “And your law in the midst of my heart,” whereas in Greek they had found: *Καὶ τὸν νόμον σου ἐν μέσῳ τῆς κοιλίας μου*, “And your law in the midst of my belly,” which corresponds to what is written in Hebrew, *BETHOC MEAI*. But among the Latins, because of euphony, it was translated “in the heart”; yet we must not remove what is true. These are his words; and καρδίας (“of the heart”) and κοιλίας (“of the belly”) are quite close. Moreover, St Augustine, discussing the reasoning behind the title of Psalm 51, in which *Achimelech* occurs for *Abimelech*, says that Jerome held that this error, which had crept in through the resemblance of the Hebrew letters *kaph* and *beth*, should not be changed, maintaining that there is a mystery in it.

But if anyone is not satisfied and insists that the Church ought absolutely to sing, “to God, the strong and living one,” let him at least satisfy Augustine in what he especially wished to be corrected, in Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 13. But what does he say?

> “Even that phrase which we can no longer remove from the mouths of the singing people, ‘Upon him shall my sanctification flower,’ certainly takes nothing from the sense.
