Yet a more learned hearer would prefer it to be corrected, so that not *floriet* but *florebit* should be said; and nothing prevents correction except the custom of singers. Such matters, therefore, may easily be disregarded by anyone unwilling to avoid them, since they detract nothing from sound understanding.”

These are St Augustine’s words [Col. 0423B]. Likewise Jerome himself, in the letter said to be addressed to a certain rustic, cites it according to the Vulgate reading, both in the earlier and the later Froben edition, the latter praised as most painstakingly produced; and again in the editions most recently printed at Paris.

Finally, if the Greek witnesses we possess did not object, one might easily conjecture that *EL* was read for *ED*, which our translator renders “fountain” in Genesis 2. This conjecture would be strengthened by the fact that if the top point of the letter *lamed* is cut off, the letter *daleth* remains—a thing we see done in printed books. See the example before your eyes: remove the topmost tip, and the letter *daleth* remains. But let each person enjoy his own judgment.

### Verse 4 — “I shall pass into the place of the tabernacle.”

Pratensis, Sanctes, Münster, and the translators for Cajetan [Col. 0423C] render, instead of “into the place of the tabernacle,” “in the number” or “into the number.” Jerome and Pellican agree with us. The latter translates “covering,” the former “shelter.” For *SAC* is indifferent in meaning between “shelter” and “number,” whence the Chaldee has “in shelters.”

But what follows immediately presses the matter more strongly: “wonderful, even to the house of God,” instead of “of the wonderful one.” Jerome said, “I shall be silent.” Here *EDDADEM* seems to have been derived from *DOM*, “he was silent,” with the *daleth* doubled [Col. 0424A]. The other translators seem to have done something similar, except that they read *resh*, that is *r*, in place of *daleth*, because of the likeness of the letters. Since *RAM* means “lofty,” and hence “wonderful,” the reading would be *ERAREM*.

The other Hebraists translate “I shall walk,” or something similar, and derive it from the root *NADAD*, with the *pe* lacking, as they speak, according to the indication of that conjugation; then they join the final *mem*, that is *m*, to it as an added, non-essential letter, as they call it. The Chaldee paraphrast comes quite close to the sense of our reading: “walking alone in the camps of the righteous.”

### Verse 5 — “With the voice of exultation and confession: the sound of one feasting.”

Jerome: “of a multitude celebrating a feast”; Pratensis: “a great throng of people dancing.” You may reconcile these in this way: *HAMON HOGEG*. The former word sometimes means “sound,” sometimes “multitude”; and the verb *HAGAG* properly means to celebrate feasts with banquets and rejoicing.

But the Latin reading appears faulty, in which “sound” seems to be read corruptly as a nominative in place of “of sound” or “of a sound” in the genitive. This is clear from the Greek ἤχου and from Augustine’s text, as well as from Jerome’s translation, which has *multitudinis*, “of a multitude,” as a genitive [Col. 0424B]. Yet this is not necessary from the Hebrew, since it may be nominative, genitive, or accusative as the construction requires. For Sanctes translates: “and confession, a dancing multitude”; the translators for Cajetan likewise; Münster: “in the voice of exultation and confession, leading, I say, a hastening crowd.”

### Verse 7 — “The salvation of my countenance.”

The Hebrew reads *PANAU*, “his countenance.” The translators read *PANAI*, as in the final two verses of this psalm and of the following psalm, which are entirely alike. What follows—“and my God”—according to the Latin reading belongs to the end of this verse; according to the Hebrew reading, it belongs to the beginning of the following verse. The reason for the difference has been discussed several times.

### Verse 10 — “All your heights and your waves.”

For the first word Jerome gives “whirlpools”; and Nebiensis likewise, together with the Chaldee. Sanctes and Pagninus agree with them, rendering “floods” or “waves.” The others translate “breakings” or “mockings.” Augustine has “suspensions,” which he interprets as God’s threats. The Hebrew word *MISSBAR* is ambiguous [Col. 0424C]. Because of this ambiguity, it is not difficult to reconcile the translations.

## Psalm 42

**Title of the Psalm:** “For the end: a psalm of David.”

**Judge me. Title: “For the end: a psalm of David.”** [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] By David is understood here the Church, which is Christ’s body. It groans here among the tares—that is, among the wicked—with whom it shares many things: birth, death [Col. 0423D], prosperity and adversity, peace, war, health, and plague. Yet it does not share with them the same ground of merits. Therefore it asks to be separated from them in the future.

This psalm tends toward the end; it is David’s—that is, it belongs to Christ’s body, which speaks here. This psalm is directed against worldly pressures, lest they too draw us away from God.

**Purpose.** He warns that we should not fail under pressures.

**Division.** The psalm has two parts. First, he complains of association with the wicked and prays to be separated. Second, he treats of final joy—that is, the joy which shall be at the end—for which he offers praise amid tribulation: “And I shall enter.” Seeing, therefore, the good now joined with the evil, desiring to be separated from them bodily, now in spirit and in the future also in place, he cries:

### Verse 1

> “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation; rescue me from the unjust and deceitful person.” [Col. 0424C]

**O God, judge me,** separating me from the wicked in the future. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Seeing mercy, this person does not fear judgment. Therefore he says, “Judge me.” As if he said: I do not fear judgment because I know your mercy; I do not dread the avenger because I acknowledge the forgiver. I might fear if you dealt strictly with me. But, “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord” (Psalm 142); I need your mercy. For if you exercise judgment or justice without mercy, where shall I go? “If you observe iniquities, who shall endure it?” (Psalm 129).

Therefore we must hope in your mercy and persevere in humble confession; thus the fear of judgment is removed or mitigated, so that hope of glory almost overcomes fear. Yet every human being dreads judgment. What will the reed of the desert do when the cedar of paradise is shaken?

And distinguish here and now, if not my place [Col. 0425A], at least my cause—that is, my merits, which are the cause of life—from the unholy nation, with which I have equal weakness but unlike conscience and desire: namely, from the unjust and deceitful person. This is the unholy nation. The unjust person openly does evil; the deceitful person secretly. Rescue me in this present life, lest I be corrupted by them.

Or the whole may be understood of the future, thus: “Judge me, O God.” In saying this, he does not ask that his sins be examined—which is dangerous, since the stars are not clean in God’s sight and he finds perversity in the angels (Job 24)—but asks to be separated from the wicked in the cause of his recompense, so that, with the goats placed at the left, he may be at the right with the elect. Hence he adds, “And distinguish my cause from the unholy nation,” explaining it thus: “Rescue me in judgment from the deceitful and unjust person.” The unholy nation consists of the unjust and deceitful persons, from whom he is separated in judgment.

### Verse 2

> “For you are, O God, my strength: why have you cast me off? And why do I go grieving, while the enemy afflicts me?”

For you are. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though he said: Deliver me, because you, O God, are my strength; I do not claim for myself the strength needed amid these scandals. Why then have you rejected me, as it appears? Since he longs for it, he thinks himself rejected because he does not immediately receive what he desires. And why do I go sorrowful? He is sorrowful because, even if he is not overcome, [Col. 0425C] he is at least endangered—that is, he suffers dangers. This man seeks the cause of his sorrow, which is sin, just as righteousness is the cause of joy. Hence Isaiah says: “I made every breath; because of sin I made him sorrowful for a little while” (Isa. 57). Thus God punishes for sin; therefore he goes sorrowful while the enemy—that is, the one who afflicts me here in the present with temptations, which he will not do there, in the future—afflicts me. This is said so that “enemy” may be excluded.

VERSE 3.—“Send forth your light and your truth; they themselves have led me and brought me unto your holy mountain and into your tabernacles.”

Send forth, for judgment. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] He prays for this because, when Christ comes for judgment, every sorrow will be taken away from the saints: your light and your truth, that is, Christ. For Christ is the light of the world and the truth of the Father. Coming in his first advent, he now distinguishes the case of merits; and in the second he will deliver from the wicked and deceitful man, because he will send separating angels, who will separate wheat from chaff and tares, so that they may gather out of his kingdom all scandals (Matt. 13). Send forth: and so it shall be, because we already possess a certain pledge, since they themselves—that is, the light and truth—have already led me away from sins and brought me to your holy mountain, that is, to the present Church, which is likewise your tabernacle. Hence it follows: and into your tabernacles, which belong to those who are pilgrims and soldiers; for as long as we are in the body, we are pilgrims away from the Lord, fighting against the devil (2 Cor. 5).

[Col. 0426A] PART II. VERSE 4.—“And I shall enter unto the altar of God, unto God who makes my youth glad.”

And I shall enter. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] The second part, in which he treats of final joy. For its sake he praises God in tribulation, whereas above he was sorrowful. Thus he strengthens himself. As though he said: You have led me into your tabernacles, where, being placed, we hope that I shall also enter from his holy mountain—that is, from the holy Church—unto the altar of God, namely that invisible altar of the heavenly Jerusalem, to which no unrighteous person approaches. But whoever approaches it is taken up as a whole burnt-offering, wholly kindled by divine fire; unto this altar I shall enter, just as the high priest alone entered into the Holy of Holies.

[Alcuin, Augustine.] Note that the priest, ascending to celebrate Mass at the altar, says, “I shall enter,” etc. [Col. 0426B] For through desire and love of the higher, invisible altar, he ought modestly to approach this visible altar, intending to seek eternal, not perishable, things, so that in humility he may follow Christ’s exaltation. What that altar is, he explains when he says: unto God, namely him who makes my youth glad—that is, my newness—who previously made old age sorrowful. And therefore:

VERSE 5.—“I will confess to you upon the harp, O God, my God: why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you trouble me?”

I will confess to you upon the harp. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The harp sounds from below, just as the psaltery sounds from above. Therefore, one who performs God’s commandments and does not suffer confesses upon the psaltery. But one who both performs them and suffers—which belongs to the lower nature—confesses upon the harp. The meaning is: I will confess to you upon the harp, O God, my God; that is, I will give you thanks in tribulation. Hence above he said: “I go sorrowful.” See how he, formerly sorrowful because of the evils of the world, makes joy for himself through good understanding. But why sorrowful, etc.? Or connect it thus: Because I shall confess, therefore why is my soul sorrowful? He says this because he wishes to raise it toward better things; or perhaps he fears because he cannot avoid all sins. For it is difficult to find a life wholly purified when the judge is one who knows how to judge with exactness and purity. Even if a life has now become commendable among human beings, so that they have nothing left to criticize, God nevertheless justly finds in a human being something to criticize—something perhaps not even seen by the person who is to be judged. Fearing these things, the soul [Col. 0426D] is troubled. Hence he adds: And why do you trouble me? He frequently and vehemently urges that the sorrow of this world be avoided, because it extinguishes patience, charity, and hope, and rather throws the whole life into confusion.

VERSE 6.—“Hope in God, because I shall yet confess to him: the salvation of my countenance, and my God.”

Hope in God, not in yourself. [Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Augustine.] For what are you in yourself? What are you from yourself? Let him be health within you who accepted wounds for your sake. And you can hope, because I shall yet confess to him. What will you confess to him? This: You are the salvation of my countenance, because you will heal me; and my God, because you created me. As one sick I speak to you; I acknowledge the physician and the disease; I do not boast of being [Col. 0427A] well. Hence elsewhere: “I said: Lord, have mercy upon me; heal my soul,” etc. (Ps. 40).

This utterance, brothers, is safe; but be watchful in good works. Touch the psaltery by obeying, and touch the harp by enduring sufferings; break your bread for the hungry. And Isaiah says: do not suppose that fasting without almsgiving and prayer is sufficient (Isa. 58). Fasting disciplines you, but it does not refresh another. Your hardships will be fruitful if you grant spaciousness to another. Therefore give to others what you have denied yourself. For how many poor people can the meal omitted today feed! Fast in such a way, then, that, while another eats, you may rejoice that you yourself have eaten: for God loves a cheerful giver (1 Cor. 9). If you give bread sorrowfully, you have lost both the bread and the merit. Therefore act wholeheartedly; persevere in prayers. How swiftly the prayers of those who do good works are received! And this is human righteousness in this life: fasting, almsgiving, and prayer. Do you wish your prayer to fly to God? Make for it two wings—fasting and almsgiving—by which it may fly to God. May the light and truth of God find us such that they find us secure when he comes to deliver us from death—he who has already come to undergo death for us.

COLLATION ON PSALM 42: “JUDGE ME, O GOD.”

VERSE 4.—Who makes my youth glad. The Hebrews have *gīlî*, that is, “my exultation.” But a person’s exultation is youth itself, which by its own nature is inclined toward things that bring joys. And because the translators wished to suggest newness, they did so more suitably by means of “youth.”

## PSALM 43

[Col. 0427]

TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END: A PSALM FOR THE SONS OF KORAH, FOR UNDERSTANDING.”

[Col. 0427B]

God, we have heard with our ears. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] “Unto the end: a psalm for the sons of Korah, for understanding.” It should be known that in the Old Testament God bestowed temporal goods abundantly upon many, as upon the immature and those to be attracted to service; and he permitted a few to be afflicted. But in the New Testament the Church grants worldly prosperity to few believers, and withdraws it from many, permitting them to be afflicted, chastening them as sons, so that they may be sons of Korah—that is, of suffering—and may learn that other goods are to be sought, goods not shared with the wicked: spiritual and eternal goods, which are prefigured by the temporal goods given to an immature people. Therefore the title appropriately includes [Col. 0427C] “for understanding.”

The meaning of the title is: This psalm, directing us unto the end, namely Christ, is sung or assigned to the sons of Korah, that is, of suffering—namely, the holy martyrs, whose voice is here—for understanding: that they may understand why God seems to abandon martyrs, by withdrawing temporal things and allowing them to be afflicted, when he helped the ancient Fathers with a mighty hand and bestowed temporal things upon them. God does this because he does not listen to temporal things, so that eternal things may be desired from him and temporal things not loved. Understanding this, they should not seek to have it done to themselves as it was done to the immature. To those God granted prosperity so that they might believe; upon these he brings adversities so that they may seek the future. But they should know that their spiritual things are prefigured through the temporal things of the former.

This psalm is thus a consolation for the weak. [Col. 0427D] Intention: it urges contempt for earthly things and desire for heavenly things. Method: the psalm is in three parts. First, it distinguishes God’s benefits, showing what has been given in the world to beginners and what will be given in heaven to the perfect. Second, it recounts the evils which the good endure here, at “But now.” Third, it prays for help: that Christ may aid those afflicted here at the time of resurrection, at “Arise, why.” The Prophet, therefore, speaking in the person of the martyrs, recalls the past—so that the abandonment of present saints may seem all the more astonishing—saying:

VERSE 1.—“O God, we have heard with our ears; our fathers have declared unto us.”

God. [Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear.] He says “God” first, as a person accustomed to do when joyful or gravely afflicted. “We have heard with our ears,” that is, we have understood by the discernment of reason, while the fathers taught us. He says “we have heard” so that the matter may receive greater credence and not be thought uncertain. From whom did you hear it? From fathers—not young men—so that they may appear trustworthy: our fathers, who would tell their own people only what was certain, declared to us, that is, related to us, what?

VERSE 2.—“The work which you wrought in their days, and in the days of old.”

[Col. 0428C] The work which you wrought. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Although God always works, he is said to work when he displays some sign of newness. Therefore he says here, “the work which you wrought,” such as the leading forth from Egypt and the bringing into the land of promise, “in their days,” namely in days of old. You wrought this work, namely:

VERSE 3.—“Your hand destroyed the nations, and you planted them; you afflicted peoples and cast them out.”

Your hand—or the work—which you wrought in their days. This is not altered. [Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] And also that which you wrought in ancient days, such as the creation of heaven and earth—all of which are fulfilled spiritually in us. Your hand: he sets forth the work which God performed in the days of the fathers. Your hand—that is, your power—destroyed by death [Col. 0428D] and in other ways the nations of the land of promise, namely the Amorites, Hivites, Hittites, and others; and you planted them, namely the fathers. Nor did you easily afflict the peoples who were there, who otherwise would not have believed, because they were strong; and you expelled them from the land of promise. You did these things.

VERSE 4.—“For they did not possess the land by their own sword, nor did their own arm save them.”

[Col. 0429A] For they themselves did not possess the land by their own sword. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] He says this because perhaps they might have been considered strong. And their arm—that is, their strength—did not save them. As though he said: They neither possessed the land through themselves nor were saved through themselves.

VERSE 5.—“But your right hand, and your arm, and the illumination of your countenance, because you were well pleased with them.”

But your right hand, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] that is, your power, saved them; and your arm, that is, the Son; and the illumination of your countenance, that is, the favor of your presence. For God was present to them through such signs so that he might be understood to be present, since he does not show us his presence except through the effect of miracle. For we cannot see his presence face to [Col. 0429B] face. And this was not by their merit, but because you were pleased with them; in other words, you acted thus with them so as to please others through them, so that whoever observed them might say: “God is with them.”

Or according to another reading: “It pleased you in them,” that is, it pleased you to do these things for them alone. Otherwise, from the words “But your right hand”: your right hand means the good success which you gave them; your arm, the strength you gave them; and the illumination of your countenance, the wise counsel given to them by you. These saved them—all of which you did because you were pleased with them, that is, through your good will.

VERSE 6.—“You yourself are my king and my God, who command salvations for Jacob.”

You yourself, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine,] who did these things for them, [Col. 0429C] are my king, who are accustomed to rule me, and my God, who are accustomed to aid me. He says “God” so that you may not doubt concerning God the Christ—that is, that Christ of whom he speaks is God. Note that the same God is ours and theirs. The times have changed, but the author does not change. You, I say, who command—through another, not by yourself—bodily salvations for Jacob, that is, for those ancient people. For you appeared to them through a subjected creature, not through yourself, that is, through your essence; this is reserved for the righteous in the resurrection.

VERSE 7.—“In you we shall winnow our enemies with the horn; and in your name we shall despise those who rise up against us.”

In you, our enemies, [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Augustine, Cassiodorus, [Col. 0429D] Gloss interlinear.] As though he said: What you did for them then temporally, you will do for us spiritually at the judgment; therefore, afflicted as they are, they console themselves and take courage again. This is the meaning of “In you, our enemies”: As you helped them, so also help us. In you we shall winnow our enemies as chaff is separated from grain, with the horn, that is, with strength. And in your name—that is, because we are called as belonging to your kingdom—we shall in the future despise evil spirits who now rise up in us, because they will not be able to harm us. I bless in you.

VERSE 8.—“For I shall not hope in my bow, nor shall my sword save me.”

For I shall not, etc. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Or you will rightly do these things for us. For I shall not hope in my bow, just as the fathers did not hope in theirs, and my sword shall not save me. [Col. 0430A] The bow, of less force in war, signifies lesser human strength; the sword, believed to have greater force in war, signifies greater human strength. But he hopes in neither.

VERSE 9.—“For you have saved us from those who afflict us, and have put to shame those who hate us.”

You have saved us, [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] that is, you will save us: he uses the past for the future. It is so certain as though it had already happened, just as what has been cannot not have been. You will save us from those who afflict us—that is, from unclean spirits that afflict us here—and you have put to shame those who hate us, that is, you will put them to shame when they are condemned. And then:

VERSE 10.—“In God we shall be praised all the day, and in your name we shall confess for ever.”

[Col. 0430B] In God we shall be praised. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin.] These persons do not arrogate to themselves glory from the future things which he combines. Note also that past tenses are to be understood as futures. We shall be praised, I say, all the day—that is, in an eternity not interrupted by nights, but wholly day. And we shall confess—that is, praise you, which is their glory—for ever, that is, without end; hence: “They shall praise you for ever and ever” (Ps. 8). And this is in your name, which is Jesus, namely Savior, because you have delivered me from all things.

Or, from “For you have saved us,” it may be read in the present. As though he said: My sword will not save me, but you will, because in this age you have saved us from those who afflict us, lest they draw us after themselves; and you have put to shame those who hate us, that is, you have caused those who hate us to be ashamed. And therefore [Col. 0430C] then we shall be praised in God all the day, and in your name we shall confess for ever. These things are unchanged.

PART II. VERSE 11.—“But now you have rejected and put us to shame; and, O God, you will not go forth with our armies.”

But now. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The second part, in which he recounts the evils that the good endure here, though they have not forgotten God. As though he said: These things will truly be future, and the others were heard from the fathers; but now, namely in the middle time between their past and our future, you have rejected us. They say these things because the promise is deferred, while here the wicked are held in contempt; and you have put us to shame, not in conscience but before human beings. [Col. 0430D] Notice that he magnifies his evils here, in order to win the judge’s favor.

God did this in order to teach them to despise these things and seek eternal things. This is the understanding in the title, to which the sons of Korah are directed. He also did it so that it might appear whether God is worshipped freely—he from whom man has freely been saved. God is not to be worshipped for earthly things. And because he will give things like these eternally, but not earthly things. Yet if you think carnally about eternal things, perhaps you will say: “I worship him because he will give me an estate.” You still bear a temporally corrupt mind. For you do not worship with chaste love; in the future age you do not wish to receive a reward which you must leave behind here. You wish to exchange carnal pleasure, not to cut it off. Therefore do not hope that God will give such things as he commands you here to despise. These were the hopes of the Jews, [Col. 0431A] who expect such present things to be restored to them multiplied in the future, such as a golden Jerusalem and the like. But one who worships God in this way is not praiseworthy, just as fasting is not praised in the person who reserves his stomach for a luxurious supper. Such fasting is not fasting of continence but of luxury. Therefore God must be worshipped freely, not for anything else obtained from him. And you will not go forth, O God, openly. I say, you will no longer go forth, as you formerly did for the Jews, with our armies—that is, in our hosts. And by this we are weak against enemies.

VERSE 12.—“You have turned us back behind our enemies; and those who hate us plundered for themselves.”

You have turned us back. [Augustine, Gloss interlinear.] He explains how they were put to shame [Col. 0431B] and rejected. You have turned us back behind our enemies, because there they are victors and we defeated; and he says this concerning those who fall away from the faith. Hence follows: Those who hate us plundered for themselves, that is, they drew us into their own camp of wickedness.

VERSE 13.—“You have given us as sheep for food, and have scattered us among the nations.”

You have given us. [Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] He says this because all things happen by God’s power, that is, by the power God gives: as sheep for food, not for offspring—that is, sheep meant for food, not for the offspring of spiritual works. He laments those who suffered in such a way that they were turned into the body of the nations, as if consumed by them; and you have scattered us among the nations.

Or, from “You have turned us back,” he speaks of those who remain steadfast, yet sometimes yield by flight to the fury [Col. 0431C] of persecutors. And this is the meaning: You have turned us back behind our enemies. To turn back is to flee an enemy, according to: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 10). And those who hate us plundered for themselves. This happens to fugitives: they fall as prey because they cannot resist their enemies. You have given us, who remain steadfast in the faith, as sheep for food. Here different martyrs are indicated, that is, different kinds of martyrdom: some became food for beasts; others were handed over to the nations into slavery. Hence he says, “as sheep for food,” where the slaughter of some is indicated. And you scattered us among the nations. Here persecution is indicated.

VERSE 14.—“You sold your people without price, and there was no multitude in their exchanges.”

[Col. 0431D] You sold your people, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] that is, the martyrs, when they are handed over to foreigners, and this without price. For we see whom you gave, but not whom you received, because no one is acquired; this happens for testing or correction. Hence follows: And there was no multitude in their exchanges, because either no one is acquired in exchange for them, or, if anyone is, they are nevertheless few.

Or according to another reading: [Note: [Col. 0431] Augustine took ἀλάλαγμα from ἀλαλάζω, “I rejoice,” not from ἀλάττω, “I change.”] “And there was no multitude in their rejoicings,” because during persecution they did not assemble to rejoice to God, as happens in peace.

[Col. 0432A] VERSE 15.—“You have made us a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those around us.”

You have made us, [Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus.] as though he said: Besides harsh things, we suffer shameful things also, because you have made us, as though fixed in this condition, a reproach to our neighbors, who are soon to be converted. Affliction inflicted by neighbors is grievous, because that which is inflicted by those standing around is not said only in passing. And you have made us mockery, which is made by wrinkling the nose, or contempt. Another reading has: “and derision,” which is made with the mouth. Derision is the voice of confused joy, declaring insult by unrestrained mirth. Contempt is degrading vileness before those who are around us and never with us.

[Col. 0432B] VERSE 16.—“You have made us a byword among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples.”

You have made us a byword among the nations, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine,] so that they take from us a formula of cursing against others, saying: “May you perish as Lawrence did,” and the like. Or: you have made us a likeness of Christ among the nations. They were made a likeness of Christ among the nations when they inflicted on them punishments comparable to his. And you made us among the peoples a shaking of the head—that is, an occasion for their insulting us—as they insulted Christ in his passion, shaking their heads.

VERSE 17.—“All the day my shame is before me, and confusion of face has covered me.”

All the day my shame is against me, or [Col. 0432C] before me. [Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus.] A grievous shame is shown, one that remains all day. It was against the saints, or before the saints—that is, before the eyes of the saints—when they saw those whom they knew to be wicked insulting them. Or he says it is against himself, that is, against his being good, because he had done nothing for which he ought to be ashamed. Describing the shame, he adds: And confusion of my face has covered me. He says that his countenance is covered by a kind of mantle of confusion, when the face burns red with a bloody cloud. But in saying “has covered me,” rather than “my face,” he indicates horror not only of the countenance but of the whole body. And this confusion proceeds:

VERSE 18.—“From the voice of one reproaching and reviling, from the face of the enemy and persecutor.”

[Col. 0432D] From the voice of one reproaching, [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] that is, insulting, and reviling, that is, bringing an accusation. To reproach is to curse to one’s face; to revile is to speak ill of one absent and bite deceitfully. He then adds who the reproacher and reviler is: from the face, that is, from the pressing presence, of the enemy who hates, and of the persecutor in action. And:

VERSE 19.—“All these things came upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, nor have we acted wickedly in your covenant.”

All these things, [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Gloss interlinear.] as though he said: They came upon us not separately but together [Col. 0433A], because they were not in us through fault. They came, I say, like a wild beast or a torrent; yet we have not forgotten you, because we understand that you are to be worshipped freely for your own sake. See how great is the constancy of the martyrs. And we have not acted wickedly. As though he said: How then are we not bound? Because we have not acted wickedly in your covenant, that is, in the law whose commandments we keep. Or “in your covenant” means in the pact which we made with you in baptism.

VERSE 20.—“And our heart has not turned back; and you have turned our paths aside from your way.”

And our heart, [Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine,] that is, our reason, has not departed so as to turn backward—namely, by despairing of God’s goodness. Even if it sometimes descends from contemplation of truth, it does not [Col. 0433B] nevertheless turn back. Therefore he did not merely say, “has not departed,” but added, “back.” And while we walk thus in the narrow way, you have turned aside—that is, removed—our paths from your way. For our paths lay in the prosperities and pleasures of the world. But you removed them from your way and showed your narrow way, which leads to life. Therefore you have turned aside:

VERSE 21.—“Because you have humbled us in a place of affliction, and the shadow of death has covered us.”

Because you have humbled us in a place of affliction, [Gloss interlinear, Jerome, Alcuin, Gloss interlinear, Augustine,] that is, in the world, whence contrition and repentance arise. But you will exalt us in the place of strength, namely in the future.

Or thus: “And you have turned our paths aside from your way,” that is, you have caused our works to depend upon your law; the rest is unchanged. Or thus it may be read: “And you have not turned aside”—that is, you have not permitted our paths, namely our works, to turn aside and stray from your way, that is, from the law. Therefore you have not turned them aside, because you have humbled us in a place of affliction; this is unchanged. And the shadow of death has covered us, that is, human beings dying through ignorance of the truth and drawing others into the darkness of their death. Or this mortality is the shadow of death. True death, however, is condemnation with the devil.

VERSE 22.—“If we have forgotten the name of our God, and if we have stretched out our hands to a strange god.”

If we have forgotten. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear.] Here is the understanding [Col. 0433D] of the sons of Korah: amid all these evils they do not forget God, knowing that God will search out these things. As though he said: We have not forgotten you, because if we have forgotten, etc. Or connect it thus: We have not forgotten; but if we have forgotten the name of God, and if we have stretched out our hands—literally. The description is of one praying, who by outstretched hands forms the cross which he has received upon his forehead. Or hands signify works. The meaning is: If we have stretched out our hands to a strange god, that is, if with our works we have devoted ourselves to an idol.

VERSE 23.—“Will not God search out these things? For he himself knows the secrets of the heart.”

Will not God search out these things? [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Namely, he will make them manifest. As though he said: It is serious before God to sin in his religion; the force of the emphatic utterance shows this. Truly he will search out and disclose these things, because he knows even hidden matters: for he himself knows the secrets of the heart. [Col. 0434A] Religion is practised more by this heart than by bodily devotion. Note that he says “knows.” God is said to know what he causes you to know. Hence he said to Abraham: “Now I have known that you fear the Lord” (Gen. 22), that is, I have caused you and others to know it. Thus God knows how he searches out; that is, he is said to know in the same manner as to search out—not merely for himself, but also for you, when he causes you to discover yourself and to give thanks to him who made you discover yourself, as happened in Peter, who tested what he was capable of. And:

VERSE 24.—“For for your sake we are put to death [Col. 0434B] all the day; we are accounted as sheep for slaughter.”

For your sake. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] As though he said: What are those hidden things? Behold: because we are put to death all the day by prolonged sufferings. And this is for your sake, not for our crimes, but so that your faith may increase among the nations; and the fact that we are put to death for you belongs among those hidden things. For people see that we die, but no one except God sees the reason. We are accounted as sheep for slaughter, that is, we are killed without any resistance.

Or read this verse thus. “For your sake”: hitherto they have said that they have not forgotten; here they ask that they may persevere in what they have said, that we have not forgotten. And that we may persevere: “Arise,” and you ought to do so. “For your sake we are put to death [Col. 0434C] all the day; we are accounted as sheep for slaughter.” The meaning of these words is unchanged.

PART III. VERSE 25.—“Arise: why do you sleep, O Lord? Arise, and do not reject us unto the end.”

Arise. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which he prays for help: that Christ may aid those afflicted here at the time of resurrection. As though he said: We suffer such great things; but, lest we fail, arise—that is, strengthen those who stand. I say, arise, because you sleep, O Lord—that is, you seem to be neglectful. This appears to be so when what is awaited is deferred. And why? Although we do not know this, you know why. For it is either because of fault or for benefit. [Col. 0434D] If because of fault, would that it were absent! But if for benefit, would that it were present! Arise by restoring those who fail, and do not reject us unto the end. And if you reject us here, do not do so unto the end.

VERSE 26.—“Why do you turn away your face? Do you forget our poverty and our tribulation?”

Why? [Alcuin, Gloss interlinear.] He gives two further answers to the two matters stated before. As though he said: You reject some because you turn away your face, that is, withdraw your knowledge from them. You sleep with respect to some who groan over evils because you forget our poverty—that is, you do not give the spirit of strength, without which we are poor—and our tribulation, because you do not relieve it. And why is this? As though he said: We do not know, but let us inquire, because you act only justly and mercifully. Note that [Col. 0435A] to say this is not a complaint but the devout supplication of a pure heart.

VERSE 27.—“For our soul is humbled in the dust; our belly is glued to the earth.”

For. [Alcuin.] You turn away your face because, with your knowledge withdrawn, our soul is humbled in the dust—that is, in thoughts of worldly things, which are comparable to dust. And our belly—that is, sensuality—is glued to the earth, that is, clings to earthly things. And since this is so necessary—that is, since we so need help:

VERSE 28.—“Arise, O Lord, help us; and redeem us for your name’s sake.”

Arise, [Alcuin, Jerome,] that is, make us rise from earthly to heavenly things; and help us when raised; and redeem us—that is, liberate us when helped, so that we may be without fear. And do all this for your name’s sake, that is, freely, not because of our merit.

[Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Or, from “For our soul is humbled”: the holy martyrs, whose voice is here, prayed above; and although he delays to hear them, after that delay they nevertheless do not despair, but continue in prayer. Sprinkling ashes upon themselves, they torment their souls with remembrance of sins, according to the custom of penitents. For ashes and sackcloth are the weapons of penitents. Hence during Lent ashes are sprinkled upon penitents’ heads, on account of humility and remembrance of their fragile [Col. 0435C] condition. This is the meaning: You ought not to forget, because our soul is humbled in the dust—that is, with ashes sprinkled upon us, we are pricked to repentance. And our belly is glued to the earth, that is, the belly has adhered to the earth, as happens to persons prostrated, who stretch themselves out in the complete casting-down of the body. By saying this he displays the utmost humility. One who presses knees to the ground has some further way to humble himself; but one so humbled that even his belly clings to the earth has no further degree of humility possible. He therefore expresses excessive humiliation, so that, because he has reached the utmost point, God’s mercy may now be present.

Or thus: do not forget us because our soul is humbled in the dust—that is, for those who are dust. As though we pray not only for ourselves but also for those [Col. 0435D] who readily yield to unlawful habits and cling to earthly things. And our belly is glued to the earth, that is, carnal persons have adhered to earthly things; and we humble ourselves and pray for them. Arise, O Lord, help us: here “arise” is used without the word “sleep”; it pertains to Christ’s resurrection, in which lies the hope of all the faithful, in which human captivity is destroyed, and through which we too are helped and set free. As though he said: Since we are thus humbled, arise from death, O Lord Christ, and thereby help us and redeem us from captivity. And do this for your name’s sake.

[Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Otherwise, the whole passage from “Arise, why”: the holy martyrs pray that Christ may arise through faith among the nations, because they know that Christ does not sleep and has risen for them. Yet they pray that he may arise through faith, not for themselves but for the nations which think him dead. For if those nations too believed that he had risen, they would not persecute believers in him; rather, they themselves would believe. As though he said: We are put to death all the day, and, that these things may end, arise through faith among the nations, because you, O Lord, sleep not for us but for the nations which do not believe. And why? He repeats “arise” out of earnest feeling. And do not reject us unto the end. For if Christ arises among the nations, persecution ceases. Why indeed do you turn away your face? As though he said: You are not absent as you seem to be while you delay to help. And why do you forget, as though you had forgotten our poverty, which you are accustomed to relieve, and our tribulation, of which you are always the merciful observer? Therefore do not forget us, because our soul is humbled [Col. 0436B] so that we may invoke you for help, in the dust—that is, amid the hands of dust; for dust persecutes us, that is, the wicked, of whom it is said: “Not so the wicked, not so; but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1). And our belly is glued to the earth: here he laments those who are belly, that is, carnal, and have adhered—that is, consented—to wicked persons. But, that these things may end, arise through faith among the nations; when they cease from persecution, even those who had adhered to the earth are delivered, repent, and are restored to Christ’s body. Hence it follows: and thus help us and redeem us from the hand of the nations, for your name’s sake, not for our merit.

COLLATION ON PSALM 43: “O GOD, WE HAVE HEARD WITH OUR EARS.”

[Col. 0436C] **VERSE 10.**—“In God we shall be praised.” Jerome: “In God we shall rejoice.” In Hebrew the verb is in the past tense, *HILLALNU*, that is, “we have praised.” Sanctes and Münster take it in the present sense, that is, “we glory.” But since it is more correctly understood of future glory, according to Augustine, the Septuagint translators and Jerome rendered it by the future; they, however, used the passive form *HULLALNU*, in which there is absolutely no distinction apart from the addition of vowel-points. Yet, since praising God pertains more to that glory than being praised, “we shall be praised” might seem to be a copyist’s error for “we shall praise,” unless the preceding phrase, “in God,” opposed this; otherwise one would have to say “God” if it had been translated “we shall praise.” Moreover, the Greek has the future passive, *epainethēsometha* [“we shall be praised”]; and everything said to be done in God is referred to God. For all our praise proceeds from him who will say to the saints those sweetest words, surpassing every praise: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” [Col. 0436D] (Matt. 25). Add that to say “to be praised in God” and “to glory in God” is no different, or they aim altogether at the same thing.

**VERSE 20.**—“And our heart did not turn back, and you turned aside 96 our paths from your way.” In the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin edition alike, the negation which preceded is understood in the second clause, “and you turned aside,” so that Scapulensis and Caecus accomplish nothing by supposing that the negation is expressed twice in Hebrew. This is false; rather, it must be repeated. Therefore it is not surprising if they cry out that we read a sense opposite to the Hebrew, although blessed Augustine interprets it affirmatively; yet he took “paths” in a bad sense, whereas, when taken with the negation, they ought to be understood in a good sense, so that the interpretation may agree with it.

**VERSE 21.**—“You humbled us in the place of affliction.” Hebrew: *TANNIM*, “of dragons”; the Septuagint aptly explained the figurative expression.

## PSALM XLIV

[Col. 0437]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “FOR THE END, FOR THOSE WHO SHALL BE CHANGED; FOR THE SONS OF KORAH, FOR UNDERSTANDING; A SONG FOR THE BELOVED.”

[Col. 0437A]

“My heart has poured forth a good word.” Title: “For the end, for those who shall be changed; for the sons of Korah, for understanding; a song for the beloved.” [Aug., Cassiod., Gl. int., Aug.] This concerns the holy marriage of bridegroom and bride—that is, of Christ and the Church; namely, of king and people, Savior and those to be saved. Thus this song is also called an *epithalamium*, that is, a praise of the bridal chamber, because the praise of bridegroom and bride is sung here. For at weddings certain songs are customarily sung in honor of the bridegroom and bride; these are called *epithalamia*, that is, praises of the bridal chamber. The Prophet sings similar things at this marriage. For at this marriage the prophets, apostles, [Col. 0437B] and all the saints cry aloud with holy exultation, with timbrels, harps, and other instruments; hence the hearer is nourished.

The grace of God made the union of this marriage in the Virgin’s bridal chamber, when the Word became flesh and human nature was united to the divine; and bridegroom and bride were joined, now by charity and afterward also by immortality. The sense of the title is: Understand that this psalm, directed toward the end—that is, toward consummation—was written for the sons of Korah, that is, of Christ, for the understanding of so great a mystery, of so great a beauty: namely, the union of Christ and the Church. And it is a song [Note: [Col. 0437D] Jerome, to the virgin Principia.], because here is exultation concerning eternal things. [Aug., Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod.] I say, a psalm composed for those who shall be changed from the old person into the new, and for Christ the Beloved, of whom the Father says: “This is my beloved Son” [Col. 0437C] (Matt. 3). For it describes him through whom they shall be changed. The praise of bridegroom and bride is sung here.

Or thus, without supplying “psalm”: “A song,” this one tending “for the end,” that is, toward Christ; or composed for the consummation of eternal blessedness, “for those who shall be changed,” that is, for those to be changed, and “for the beloved,” that is, for the one who changes them—namely, bridegroom and bride—is written “for the sons of Korah, for understanding,” that they may understand and venerate so great a mystery. Its purpose is to exhort to the praise of bridegroom and bride.

Method. The psalm has three parts. First, the Prophet, filled with heavenly banquets, promises that he will pour forth the praises of God. Second, he begins the praise of the bridegroom, praising him in four ways: from beauty, power, judgment, and [Col. 0437D] adornment, at “Beautiful.” Third, the bride’s praise is sung more humbly, likewise in four ways: from beauty, glory, companions, and offspring, at “Hear, daughter.” Therefore the Prophet, desiring, as it were, to be admitted to this marriage, says that he wishes to sing to the bridegroom, so that the way may be opened to him:

### VERSE 1.—“My heart has poured forth a good word; I speak my works to the king.”

“My heart,” [Cass.] that is, my mind, full within, has poured forth [Note: [Col. 0437D] Jerome, to Principia.], as from fullness, “a good word,” that is, a hymn to God. Just as one who blasphemes pours forth an evil [Col. 0438A] word, [Aug., Hier., Cassiod.] so the Prophet pours forth abundant praise of God from within and wished to sing that hymn to the king. Hence it follows: “I speak,” that is, I eagerly desire to speak my works to the king, that is, to his praise, because I have them from him. By “works” he means this psalm. For he eagerly wished to speak to the king that work which he had conceived in his mind. But lest you think he speaks anything from himself, he compares himself to the pen of a scribe, for he is guided by the Holy Spirit. This is:

### VERSE 2.—“My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe.”

“My tongue is the pen of a scribe,” that is, of the Holy Spirit, “writing swiftly.” [Hier., Cassiod., Aug.] For “he spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 32). Or he says “writing swiftly” in order to mark the power of prophecy, [Col. 0438B] which does not, under human strain, deliberate over what it discloses to others from the secret place of the Divinity. Or he compares it to a pen in order that through this one may understand that he wrote what he says. Thus: “My tongue is the pen of a scribe” [Note: [Col. 0438D] Jerome in the Commentary], because what I say and write is of one writing swiftly, because the things I write will come quickly.

## PART II. VERSE 3.—“You are beautiful in form above the children of men; grace has been poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever.”

“Beautiful.” [Cassiod., Hier., Aug., Alcuin.] The second part begins here, where he begins the praise of the bridegroom which he promised, first praising him from beauty. Thus, as though admitted to the bridegroom, he sings in praise of him: “You are beautiful in form,” because you are free from sin beyond the children of men. Certainly he is human; yet, though he himself is human, [Col. 0438C] he is not like just any human being. Therefore, to commend him by comparison with his own race, he does not say here “above the angels,” whom he also surpasses; but “above the children of men,” against those who, thinking him a mere human being, say in Isaiah the prophet: “We saw him as having neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53). Since beauty without wisdom and eloquence is insufficient, he adds: “Grace has been poured upon your lips,” because “the law indeed was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1); and this grace remits sins. He says “upon your lips,” because while he spoke, the world received the grace of reconciliation.

“Therefore”: all that has been said from the beginning of the psalm to this point is read in the person of the Prophet, as are the following words. Augustine, however, and Jerome [Note: [Col. 0438D] Jerome, vol. III, to Damasus, *On the Two Sons*.] say that some think [Col. 0438D] the Father is speaking these things, though more superstitiously than truly, since they do not consider the whole text, in which there are certain things unsuitable to the Father. They suppose these words should be understood in the person of the Father thus: The Father commends Christ according to both natures, and first according to the divine nature, saying: “My heart has poured forth a good word,” as though to say: I did not beget from an outward union, but from my heart, just as a person produces his plan from the heart: before the thing to be done exists, it exists as a plan. Now the Father’s plan is the Son, whom the Father begot from himself before all created things. [Alcuin., Cassiod.]

The sense is: “My heart has poured forth a good word,” that is, from my fullness and secret essence I begot the Word, that is, the Son. He is called the Word because through him the Father is known; and the Word is called good because the Son of God, in his own nature, is alone good together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Hence, “No one is good but God alone” (Mark 10). This Word is also good because through him all good things were made. It follows: “I speak,” that is, I bring forth the Word. Here he says the same as before, but adds: “My works to the king,” where he says that all God’s works are in the Word himself. Hence elsewhere: “What was made,” namely in time, “was life in him” (John 1), [Col. 0439B] so that nothing exists in the work which was not first in the plan. The sense is: “I speak my works to the king,” that is, I eternally beget the Word, with whom and in whom I order all things before they exist in actuality. Of this Word it is elsewhere said: “God spoke once,” etc. (Ps. 61).

Likewise he calls the Word his tongue, saying “My tongue,” as though to say: Not only do I order all things with him, but I also speak through him. Thus, he is my tongue; he is also the pen of my scribe. This is a fitting comparison. For as neither scribe acts without a pen nor pen without a scribe, so Father and Son work together. Note that he compares the Word not with a sound that passes away but with writing that remains, to show that the Son is coeternal with the Father. The scribe is “writing swiftly,” because the Father ordered not one thing after another but all things at once [Col. 0439C] in the one eternal Word.

“Beautiful”: above, the Father commended the Son according to his divine nature; here, according to his human nature. As though to say: The Son was begotten as God from my essence, and he himself, as human, is “beautiful in form above the children of men, and grace has been poured upon your lips.” These words do not change. “Therefore God has blessed you”: the former words were spoken by the Prophet in the person of God the Father, these in his own person; for it seems more fitting to take this from the person of the Prophet than from that of the Father, and sudden changes of persons are found altogether unexpectedly in the holy books of Scripture. Therefore the Prophet says in his own person: “Therefore,” that is, because of the grace through which the kingdom of heaven is given, whereas formerly earth was given, God has blessed you as human [Col. 0439D] forever, by giving you a kingdom whose end will not be.

### VERSE 4.—“Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one.”

“Gird yourself.” [Hier., Aug., Hier., Cassiod.] Here he praises him for power. As though to say: And you, being such, gird yourself, like one about to fight. For we gird ourselves for fighting, bind ourselves about for service, and tuck up our garments for travel. Gird yourself with your sword, by which he himself divides even son from father and daughter-in-law from mother-in-law (Luke 12), that is, with the Word of God, by which he struck down enemies, as Samson overcame enemies with the jawbone of an ass. Of this sword the Lord says in the Gospel: “I came not to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10). “Upon your thigh,” [Col. 0440A] that is, upon your flesh. For the thigh is the seedbed of human propagation, and therefore flesh is fittingly understood by it. He adds “O most mighty one,” so that you may hold him in reverence even according to the flesh, which is understood by the thigh. I say, “O most mighty one”:

### VERSE 5.—“In your splendor and your beauty, aim prosperously, proceed, and reign.”

“In your splendor and your beauty.” [Cassiod., Hier., Aug., Cassiod.] Distinguish here: namely, according to humanity and divinity. “Splendor” refers to humanity, in which he appeared to the world; “beauty” to divinity, by which all things are beautiful. “Aim,” that is, look compassionately upon perishing humanity.

Or thus: “splendor” and “beauty” are taken for the same thing, namely, the justice of God. As though to say: Gird yourself, and having girded yourself, aim, that is, look mercifully upon humanity. Do this “in your splendor and beauty,” that is, from your justice, by which you are splendid and beautiful. “Prosperously,” that is, liberating human beings, “proceed” [Col. 0440B] from the Virgin’s womb, like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber. Or, “prosperously proceed,” namely from those conquered to others yet to be conquered; “and reign,” that is, show your power in the faith of human beings—you who have always reigned in yourself. I say, proceed and reign; and this:

### VERSE 6.—“Because of truth and meekness and justice; and your right hand shall lead you wonderfully.”

“Because of truth,” [Hier., Aug., Cassiod., Alcuin., Aug.] that is, because through you and yours you teach truth, which destroys our falsehood; and because of meekness, because you are meek in bearing with the wicked, as when he prayed for enemies and said to the adulterous woman, “Neither do I condemn you” (John 8), and likewise to his own people. And because of justice, because he displayed the justice of life. All this is so because your right hand, that is, the power of the Word, shall lead you without stumbling through the course of your whole life, or from people to people, wonderfully: because all will marvel, or because it will work miracles.

Another interpretation, beginning at “Prosperously proceed and reign”: “Proceed and reign prosperously,” that is, proceed so prosperously that you reign by faith among the nations, which has now happened. And this is for the fulfillment of the truth of promises; the promises have now been fulfilled. And for the fulfillment of meekness in you and yours; and this has happened, because the martyrs suffered, through which the kingdom grew, just as he himself first suffered. [Col. 0440D] And for the fulfillment of justice; and this shall be, because he will come to judge according to each person’s works. And you are able to do this because your right hand shall lead you wonderfully. This sense does not change. And:

### VERSE 7.—“Your arrows are sharp; peoples shall fall beneath you, into the hearts of the king’s enemies.”

“Your arrows are sharp,” [Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] that is, your words, which pierce human hearts and swiftly reach wherever he wills, and are directed far off. Note that above a sword was set forth, which strikes near at hand; here an arrow, which strikes from afar. Thus Christ’s incomprehensible power is shown. And peoples wounded by these arrows shall fall beneath you, in heart, or into [Col. 0441A] hearts. Where they raised themselves against Christ, there they fall before him. I mean the hearts of the king’s enemies—that is, your enemies, you who are the great king—so that enemies may become friends, as Saul, formerly raised up against Christ, was struck in his heart by an arrow sent from heaven and fell in humility, saying: “Lord, what do you command me to do?” (Acts 9).

Or thus: the peoples of the king’s enemies—that is, many of your enemies—shall fall beneath you, that is, submit themselves to you. And this “in heart,” that is, by reason or will. This is what the title said: “for those who shall be changed, and for the sons of Korah.”

### VERSE 8.—“Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom.”

“Your throne.” [Aug., Cassiod.] Here he commends Christ from judgment, for a throne belongs to judgment. As though to say: God has blessed you forever, because your throne—that is, the throne of your kingdom, your judicial and royal authority—O God, endures for ever and ever; for whatever he has established is not changed. This befits you, because the rod—that is, the scepter and government—of your kingdom is a rod of uprightness, which sets straight those who are crooked. This is the rule of divine equity, truly straight and never bent. It governs the righteous and strikes the wicked. Therefore let no one flatter himself excessively concerning Christ’s mercy, because for him it is a rod of uprightness: if it governs some, it crushes others; it governs spiritual persons and crushes carnal ones. Love the merciful one in such a way that you wish him to be true. It truly is a rod of uprightness, because:

[Col. 0441C] ### VERSE 9.—“You have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.”

“You have loved justice.” [Aug., Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod., Alcuin.] For you are not only righteous in yourself, but you love justice in others; and you hate not human beings but iniquity. Otherwise justice is not loved perfectly unless iniquity is hated. Therefore, if a person hates iniquity in himself, he acts with God. God hates iniquity; you too should hate it, so that you both hate one thing. For you will be God’s friend if your own iniquity displeases you in yourself while his creature pleases you.

“Therefore,” namely in order that you might love justice and hate iniquity, he anointed you. Or continue it thus: “Therefore,” namely because you loved justice and hated iniquity, these rewards were given to you [Col. 0441D]: God, that is, your God, the Father, anointed you, O God the Son, according to your humanity—that is, he made you king, giving you the name which is above every name (Phil. 2). [Aug., Cassiod., Hier.] Note that he says, “God anointed you,” although divinity had no need to be anointed; but he says this because that human being is God—anointed insofar as he is human, anointer insofar as he is God. “God” is used twice, for Father and Son; and in Greek one is plainly vocative and the other nominative.

This anointed one is the stone—that is, the one signified by the stone—which Jacob anointed when he set it up as a pillar and poured oil on it (Gen. 28). By calling him anointed, he signifies that he is both king and priest, in whose figure kings and priests were anointed in the Old Testament [Col. 0442A] (1 Sam. 16; Exod. 29). I say, he anointed you with spiritual oil: oil of gladness because of purity of conscience and fullness of grace. And this was “above your companions,” that is, the apostles and other saints, to whom the anointing of grace would flow from him. For the Spirit was not given to him by measure (John 3); in him dwells bodily the fullness of divinity (Col. 2); and “from his fullness we have all received” (John 1).

### VERSE 10.—“Myrrh and stacte and cassia from your garments, from ivory houses, from which the daughters of kings delighted you in your honor.”

“Myrrh and stacte.” [Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod., Aug., Alcuin., Cassiod., Hier., Gl. int.] Here the Prophet praises the bridegroom from his bride and adornment, first from his adornment. As though to say: You possess not only the things just mentioned, but myrrh, stacte, and cassia shall breathe forth from your garments. The good fragrances of virtues are signified by these spices. Hence the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2). These fragrances are appropriately used for bridal joy, as is customary at weddings.

Stacte is also called ammoniacum; cassia is also called fistula. By them are signified the diverse fragrances of virtues. Myrrh, a bitter spice which drives away worms, is the bitterness of the flesh, which expels the worms of evil desires and a bad conscience and preserves from the decay of vices. Stacte dispels every swelling and tumor: that is humility, which heals hardness of heart. Cassia grows in watery [Col. 0442C] places, grows to an immense size, and gives off fragrance: this is faith, which grows through baptism. Christ’s garment, from which these flow, is the Church, which Christ washed with blood from stain and stretched out on the cross from the wrinkle of duplicity. The sense is: myrrh, namely mortification of the flesh; stacte, namely humility; and cassia, namely faith, shall breathe forth to others by good example “from your garments,” that is, from your saints, from your Church.

“From houses.” [Rem., Cassiod., Hier., Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] He calls the same persons houses whom he previously called garments: namely, the saints, who are called garments for one reason and houses for another; these houses are ivory. They are called Christ’s garments because they adorn him by life and teaching; houses because Christ dwells in them; ivory because they are chaste, just as the elephant is said by some to be a chaste animal. For ivory is cold by nature; hence chastity is signified by ivory. And as ivory, previously dark, becomes bright through files, saws, or carving tools, so the saints, polished by the perfecting and wearing away of diverse sufferings, become bright through a variety of virtues. This is the meaning: I say that these things shall breathe forth from your garments, namely from ivory houses—that is, from the hearts of the saints in whom God dwells—ivory because of chastity or the beauty of virtues.

Another interpretation begins at “myrrh and stacte.” “Garment” is understood as Christ’s body, by which his divinity is concealed. From it comes myrrh, because he died for all human beings; stacte flowed, because by his preaching he softened hardness of heart; cassia came forth, that is, redemption through the water of baptism. This is the meaning: myrrh, stacte, and cassia [Col. 0443A] shall breathe forth from your garments, that is, from Christ’s body, by which divinity is concealed as by a garment. And these things do not come from Christ’s body alone, but also “from ivory houses,” that is, from the saints. Here the meaning does not change.

Enticed by these fragrances, the daughters of earthly kings follow Christ, disregarding the honor of their fathers. This is the meaning: these spices breathe forth from your garments, and “from which”—that is, from the spices of virtues—the daughters of earthly kings delighted in you, that is, held you delightful. And this is “in your honor,” namely because they did not care for the honor of their fathers, but for that of Christ. He calls the apostles kings, because they rule both themselves and others by virtues; their daughters are all who are begotten through them in faith, whom they begot in Christ’s honor and not their own. For Christians are called from Christ, not Petrines from Peter [Col. 0443B] or Paulines from Paul.

This is drawn from the old law. For it is written in the Law: “If a brother dies without offspring, his brother or another nearer relative shall take his wife, in order to raise up offspring, not for himself but for his brother; and the child born shall bear the name of the deceased” (Deut. 25). This spiritually applies to Christ, who is the first brother and firstborn among many brothers (Rom. 8), who says through the Prophet: “I shall declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. 21); and in the Gospel: “Go and tell my brothers” (Matt. 28). He died without offspring, because while hanging on the cross he scarcely gained one thief alone. Hence he says: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. 140). [Col. 0443C] Elsewhere: “All day I stretched out my hands to an unbelieving people” (Rom. 10).

But offspring is raised up for him by a brother who takes his wife—that is, by the apostles, who undertake to govern Christ’s bride, the Church. They are not bridegrooms but friends of the bridegroom, for “he who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3). Through their preaching, a multitude of nations entered to Christ. And the child bears the name of the deceased: that is, those converted to faith bear the name of Christ crucified, from whom they are called Christians. This is the meaning: “from which,” namely the spices, “the daughters of kings,” namely of the apostles, delighted in you. I say daughters “in your honor”: you are the first brother, from whom they have their name and whose glory they seek.

### VERSE 11.—“The queen stood at your right hand, [Col. 0443D] in a gilded garment, surrounded with variety.”

“She stood.” [Cassiod., Aug., Gl. int., Aug., Cassiod.] Here he commends the bridegroom from his bride. As though to say: You are such, and such is the bride who stood—not bent down in fear, but raised up in hope—the queen, who rules under the king, namely the bride, the Church, “at your right hand,” that is, in hope of eternal things. But she who is at the left, where the goats shall be, is not a queen but a handmaid who shall be cast out of the house with her son (Gen. 21), when it shall be said: “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25). But to the queen it shall be said: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess,” etc. (ibid.).

I say, she stood “in a gilded garment,” that is, in the teaching of wisdom, “surrounded with variety,” that is, diversified by all languages. Yet the garment of Catholic teaching is one, because it is without a seam. [Col. 0444A] Hence the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles in fiery tongues divided among them (Acts 2).

Or thus, garments signify works, and it is called gilded, not golden. Charity is understood in gold. What is golden consists wholly of gold; what is gilded has gold and something else. Thus: The queen stood in the garment of good works, gilded, not golden, lest charity alone be present, but the other things which charity adorns also be present. I say, she is surrounded with variety of merits. Although there is unity in charity, the queen is nevertheless adorned with gold, that is, the teaching of the apostles; scarlet, that is, the confession of martyrs; gems, that is, the purity of virgins; and purple, that is, the lament of penitents. Hence in the Old Testament the curtains of the tabernacle were woven from four precious colors: twisted fine linen, twice-dyed scarlet, hyacinth, and purple [Col. 0444B] (Exod. 26).

## PART III. VERSE 12.—“Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, forget your people and your father’s house.”

“Hear, daughter, and see.” [Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod.] The third part begins here, where the bride’s praise is sung, but more humbly—that is, less excellently—than the bridegroom’s praise above. He praises her in four ways: from beauty, glory, young women, and offspring. The Prophet addresses the queen as one of the Fathers—that is, of the apostles, whom he previously called Fathers. As though to say: The queen stood at your right hand. And, O queen, my daughter—that is, begotten by my preaching—hear inwardly and see God himself. As though to say: The Jews saw and killed; you, hear the Gospel and by believing you shall see God: here through an image, hereafter face to face.

Or, hear the prophecies which foretold Christ’s Incarnation, see that they have been fulfilled, and incline your ear, that you may hear humbly. For it is little to hear unless one hears humbly. Forget your people, namely the people of Babylon, from which the Church came; that is, forget the rites of the Law or of idolatry by which you serve the king of Babylon. And forget the house—that is, the manner of life and fellowship—of your father the devil: that is, Babylon, which is opposed to Jerusalem. This is the preceding exposition, and thus faith is beautiful.

### VERSE 13.—“And the king shall desire your beauty, [Col. 0444D] because he is the Lord your God, and they shall worship him.”

“And the king shall desire the beauty which he himself made in you.” [Aug., Cassiod., Hier., Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] Here he praises her from beauty. I say, the king shall desire it—which is a great thing—because he, not the former father, namely the devil, is not merely any king but your Lord God, not only your bridegroom; and all the peoples of whom you are made shall worship him, namely your king.

### VERSE 14.—“And the daughters of Tyre with gifts; all the rich of the people shall entreat your face.”

“And also the daughters of Tyre,” [Aug., Hier., Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] that is, of the nations: the whole is understood from a part. For by Tyre, neighboring Judea, he denotes the nations that will believe in Christ. Hence the Canaanite woman who came out from those borders (Matt. 15) is a figure of the Church. These daughters of Tyre, that is, the nations, shall come to that king of yours “with gifts,” namely to offer themselves or to give alms, by which they may obtain the kingdom of heaven. Therefore he says “with gifts,” because he wishes us to lay up treasure in heaven by giving temporal goods. The daughters of Tyre are all the rich of the people, the noble, wise, and such persons.

Or according to the interpretation of the name: Tyre means “distress.” Thus, “the daughters of Tyre,” that is, of the distress of sins—the nations who are in the distress of sins—shall come with gifts, namely all the rich of the people. This does not change the preceding sense. And these, worshipping with gifts, [Col. 0445B] shall entreat your face, O queen: that is, conformity with you, lest they act as outsiders, but in the bride’s presence—that is, within the unity of the Church. For the face of the Church benefits those who give alms, lest they do so outside the Church’s nest, so that the glory may be God’s and not their own.

### VERSE 15.—“All the glory of the king’s daughter is within; in golden fringes, clothed about with varieties.”

“All glory.” [Cassiod., Aug., Hier., Aug., Cassiod., Gl. int., Hier.] Here is the bride’s praise from glory, as the bridegroom’s above was from power. As though to say: I said that the king shall desire your beauty; this beauty is only inward, because all her glory, that is, the king’s daughter’s, is within or inwardly—that is, in your conscience. Therefore let your almsgiving be in secret, where God sees and loves the inward beauty which he sees. Or “inwardly” means not in outward circumcision, as under the old Law, but in spiritual things.

I say, the queen exists “in golden fringes,” that is, in the teaching of wisdom; she is “clothed about with varieties,” that is, of diverse languages. Diversity of languages is an adornment of teaching, but it does no good unless glory is within. Or fringes, which are the end of a garment, signify the end of the world or of a human life. He calls them golden, not gilded as above, but golden, because at the end is all perfection, where full charity is found. Thus, the queen’s glory is within, and this glory is “in golden fringes,” that is, at the end of the age or of each person, when charity shall be perfected; she is [Col. 0445D] clothed about with varieties of virtues or nations.

### VERSE 16.—“Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be brought to you.”

“They shall be brought.” [Cassiod., Aug., Alcuin., Cassiod.] Here he praises the bride from her companions, as above he praised the bridegroom from judgment. As though to say: The queen, having forgotten her father’s house, came to the king. After her, the first and universal mother of the faithful, virgins—that is, chaste minds—shall be brought by God’s grace. For they do not possess this from themselves. These virgins are the queen’s companions, that is, not strangers to her but belonging to her. Turning his words to the king, he says: “And these shall be brought to you, O king!” Note the difference of words: “they shall be brought,” as coming by suitable preaching; “they shall be carried,” as converted through unsuitable [Col. 0446A] preaching.

Or, by “virgins” let the strong be understood, and by “companions” the weak. Thus: After her, the queen, virgins shall be brought to the king, as strong and courageous people; and her companions, namely widows and chaste women of the second rank, and other weak persons, as though wearied by weakness, shall be carried to you. Note that first the Church’s unity is stated when he says “her”; afterward the enumeration of its parts is distinct when he says “virgins” and “companions.” He adds:

### VERSE 17.—“They shall be brought in gladness and exultation; they shall be led into the king’s temple.”

“They shall be brought,” [Cassiod., Aug.] even by the ministries of angels, in gladness and exultation, because that frail sex overcame the grave sufferings of the body. Thus they shall be led as living stones into the king’s temple, not merely into his presence but into the king’s inner sanctuary, that is, the future Jerusalem. Or, “into the king’s temple,” that is, into the present Church. It is not enough that they are virgins unless they are brought into this temple, for there are heretical virgins outside this temple, whose bond is charity.

### VERSE 18.—“In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth.”

“In place of your fathers.” [Cassiod., Hier., Aug.] Here he says how greatly the bride has advanced in increase and praises her from her offspring. As though to say: They shall be brought; for in place of your fathers, namely the ancient fathers, worshippers of idols, sons have been born to you—that is, apostles, princes of preaching. Or, after the prophets came the apostles, and after the apostles, in place of the apostles, bishops and others whom the Church has begotten and appointed in office. Hence it follows: “You shall appoint them princes over all the earth”—not in one place only in the Church.

### VERSE 19.—“They shall remember your name in every generation and generation.”

“They shall remember your name, O Lord.” [Hier., Cassiod.] Or, another reading has “I shall remember,” according to which the Christian people speaks thus: You shall appoint them princes, and through their preaching I shall remember your name, O Lord—that is, the Christian people which perseveres through every succession in their preaching. Or, those princes themselves shall remember your name, O Lord, in every generation and generation.

[Col. 0446D] ### VERSE 20.—“Therefore peoples shall confess you for ever, and unto age upon age.”

“Therefore.” [Hier., Aug., Alcuin.] Because you shall appoint them princes, peoples shall in one confession confess to you their sins or praises.
