This confession avails for unity and is therefore pleasing to God. And this is “for ever” in the present age, “unto age upon age,” that is, in the future, where praise is eternal.

It should be noted that this psalm is sung at the Nativity of the Lord because it treats of the praise of bridegroom and bride and of the marriage of Christ and the Church, whose betrothal took place in the Incarnation of the Word. It is also sung on the feast of the Blessed Virgin because what is said here of the Church in general may be referred particularly to Mary. It is also sung for virgins, because it says, “Virgins shall be brought to the king”; and for apostles, because it says, “Sons have been born to you.”

## COLLATION ON PSALM XLIV: “MY HEART HAS POURED FORTH,” ETC.

The title in the Septuagint: “For those who shall be changed,” *hyper tōn alloiōthēsomenōn* [“for those who shall be altered/changed”]. Hebrew: *AL SCHOSCHANIM*, “upon lilies,” or “for lilies”; by which virgins are fittingly understood—especially Christ the bridegroom and the Church the bride. Through virginity, human beings become equal to angels. Thus they shall be changed when this mortal thing has put on immortality. “In heaven they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 22). Hence St. Jerome testifies that he wished to expound this psalm for the virgin Principia because he found in its title “lilies and flowers,” which pertain to the immortal beauty of virginity.

**VERSE 4.**—In verses 4, 5, and 6, Hebraists divide the text differently [Col. 0447B]. For that reason the sense is confused by being turned back and forth, and here he sets one construction beside another according as it pleases him more. Let us follow our Fathers.

### Verse 5

Where we read, “direct,” the Hebrews again repeat it. And in thy beauty, *vahadareka*. The translators read the final *kaph* as essential, not merely auxiliary, in the verb which they call *Hiphil*, from the root *darach*, that is, “he proceeded” or “went.” Hence *hidrîk*: “he directed,” “he aimed”; in the imperative, *hadrek*: “direct.” This seems to be how the translators understood it. Then follows, “proceed prosperously.” This meaning is conveyed by a single particle. Immediately after comes *rekab*, that is, “ride.” Understanding its emphasis, the Septuagint aptly said, “reign,” or “triumph.”

### Verse 7

“Thy arrows are sharp; peoples shall fall beneath thee, into the hearts of the king’s enemies.” What have Faber and Caecus not advanced here? For they maintain that the ablative *corde*, “in the heart,” ought to be read; that it should refer to the word “sharp,” rather than to the verb “shall fall”; and that the intervening phrase should be treated parenthetically, thus: “Thy sharp arrows—the peoples shall fall beneath thee—in the heart of the king’s enemies.” We have no need of such philosophy. What Augustine understood is stated clearly in the Gloss.

Therefore Sanctes, in order to show that it refers to the verb “shall fall,” repeated that verb, although it occurs only once in Hebrew: “Thy arrows are sharp; peoples shall fall beneath thee; they shall fall into the heart of the king’s enemies.” Munster translates, “they shall be fixed fast”; the Chaldee, “they shall pass through into the hearts of those who hate the king.” Nor does it matter that the expression is singular in Hebrew and Greek. In Greek it is *en kardia*, “in the heart”; in Hebrew, *beleb*, which may indifferently mean either “in the heart” or “into the heart.”

“For, as Jerome says to Principia, ‘The Hebrew translation differs in words, not in meaning. He immediately adds this verse, in which some formerly read: “Most mighty one, thy arrows are sharp; most mighty peoples shall fall beneath thee, [the] king’s enemies.” In the Hebrew there is no “most mighty one.” The rest is similar.’” Thus he.

### Verse 9

“Therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee.” Augustine must have used Greek manuscripts different from those we have seen. For he took the first name, “God,” in the vocative from the Greek, with a correct interpretation; Jerome too has this altogether in his letter to the virgin Principia. But he took the second “God” as nominative. “Yet,” says Augustine, “in Latin the same case of the noun appears to be repeated. In Greek, however, the distinction is entirely clear.”

Nevertheless, our manuscripts read *ho Theos, ho Theos sou*, “God, thy God,” so that St. Jerome, writing to Principia, wonders why Aquila rendered “thy throne, O God” in the preceding verse as *Thee*, but in the following verse repeated *Theos*, “God”—although now in our copies the latter form appears in both verses. From this a clear argument is drawn that manuscripts have varied.

Nor should it pass unnoticed that Jerome says he could have used *thee*, “O God,” for the sake of the meaning—[Col. 0448A] a form which Latin usage does not admit—lest anyone should suppose, perversely, that God is twice called the Father of the beloved and most loving king.

### Verse 11

“The queen stood at thy right hand, in a garment embroidered with gold, surrounded by variety.” The Hebrew lacks the two words at the end of the verse. Yet the Greeks and Latins now read them, because of the forcefulness of the sense and the more explicit meaning of the terms. For the first signifies a mass of gold, indeed a distinguished one, *kethem*. The second is jewelled gold, or, as Jerome wishes, a diadem. All these sufficiently indicate variegated beauty.

Jerome records and interprets both readings in his letter to the virgin Principia: “The queen stood at thy right hand in a garment embroidered with gold. And what follows, ‘surrounded by variety,’ no translator rendered except the Vulgate edition. In Hebrew: ‘The consort stood at thy right hand in a golden diadem.’ Where we translate ‘consort,’ the Hebrews read *shegal*, for which Aquila has *synkoitēn*, that is, ‘bedfellow’ or ‘concubine’; Symmachus and the Fifth Edition, *pallakēn*, that is, ‘mistress’ or ‘concubine.’ The Septuagint, Theodotion, and the Sixth Edition translate ‘queen.’

“Then, where I put ‘in a golden diadem,’ Symmachus translated ‘in first gold.’ Aquila, the Fifth, and the Sixth Edition: ‘in dye,’ or ‘in Ophir gold,’ such as belongs to daughters of kings and is prepared for the embraces of a bridegroom. By drops of myrrh, cassia, and ivory houses they delight him whose throne is for ever and ever.

“But the Catholic Church, now founded with firm root upon Christ the rock, one perfect and near dove, stands at the right hand and has nothing sinister in herself. She stands in golden garments, passing from the words of Scripture to their meaning, and full of every virtue. Or, as we translated it, ‘in a golden diadem.’ For she is queen, reigning with the king; and by her daughters we may understand both the souls of believers generally and, specifically, the choirs of virgins. Ophir is a kind of gold, named either from a region of India or from its colour. Among the Hebrews there are also seven names for gold. We understand both wife and concubine from the Song of Solomon: she cannot sleep without her bridegroom or husband.” Thus Jerome.

### Verse 13

“And they shall worship him.” The Hebrews read, “Worship him,” because they read *vehishta‘ani* with a final *yod*; the Septuagint without a *yod*, but with doubled *waw*.

### Verse 14

“The daughters of Tyre with gifts.” Jerome, according to the Hebrews, has “daughter of the mighty one.” Thus he appears to hold, in his letter to the virgin Principia, that there is an error in the Latin or Greek language due to the ambiguity of the word—provided that he calls the equivocation an “error.” For when we read and chant this passage, he also interprets and discusses it mystically and beautifully. It was not burdensome to copy down his words:

“‘The daughters of Tyre with gifts,’ etc. The Hebrew word which we read in Ezekiel according to the Septuagint can be translated ‘Tyre,’ ‘tribulation,’ ‘most mighty’ or ‘most mighty woman,’ and ‘flint,’ that is, a very hard stone. Hence an error has arisen in the present passage. Aquila, the Septuagint, Theodotion, and the Fifth Edition translated ‘Tyre.’ The Sixth retained the Hebrew word *tzor*; Symmachus, *kratiston*, that is, ‘most mighty.’

“We referred the same word to God, so that she to whom He had above said, ‘Hear, O daughter, and see,’ may be called daughter of the Most Mighty One; or, certainly, may herself be most mighty because she has imitated her mighty Father. The rich of the people shall entreat her countenance with various gifts: rich in every good work and in knowledge; or those considered rich in this age, wise men of this world and persons educated in the disciplines of philosophers.

“Or, better, those who had previously been rich, possessing the oracles of God, the covenants, and the prophets—that is, people from Israel. For just as before the Saviour’s coming those who were from Tyre, that is, from the Gentile people, and wished to become proselytes, entreated the rich people of Israel and through them were admitted into the Temple, so after the Lord’s coming, whoever of Israel may wish to believe—once rich through intimacy with and protection by God—will come [Col. 0449A] to the daughter of Tyre. Offering varied gifts of virtues and confession in Christ, they will entreat her, that they may find among the Gentiles the salvation they lost in Judaea.” Thus he.

But the Latin edition, which reads the plural “daughters of Tyre,” refers to the end of the preceding verse—namely, “they shall worship him”—according to both Jerome’s and Augustine’s explanation in their Commentaries. Had Stapulensis and Caecus wished this, they would not have so sharply attacked the Vulgate reading as disturbed and confused—indeed, as absurd. For who would speak thus: “The daughters of Tyre with gifts shall entreat thy face,” rather than, as Latin usage requires, “your face”?

But they are mistaken in arranging the order. Nor is it an objection that Hebrew and Greek say “daughter of Tyre” in the singular, as though vocative, since the Church is mentioned, which is one and many according to different considerations; and the varied relation in the coordination of words produces a multiplicity of interpretations. Yet nowhere is the interpretation unworthy.

### Verse 15

“All the glory of the king’s daughter is hers.” The pronoun *eius* (“his” or “her”) was added from Roman psalmody or from other editions, which must have been numerous. This may perhaps have happened because, if it is read with the point called *mappiq* in the letter *he*, that is, with the aspiration placed at the end of the word *kebudach*, it means “his/her glory.” But if points were not written, as is more probable, it could more easily have been translated with *eius* (“his/her”).

### Verse 19

“They shall remember thy name, O Lord.” Thus we read in the Roman edition. For the Hebrews too have—as Jerome testifies in his letter to Principia—*azkirah*, that is, “I shall remember.” Yet because it is the future of the verb called *Hiphil*, it could not inappropriately be translated, “I shall cause to remember.” How fitting this is for the apostles, to whom the Spirit of Christ Jesus suggested all things whatsoever they had said, no one fails to see. Thus they remembered His name, God inspiring them and refreshing and strengthening the remembrance of what had gone before.

## Psalm XLV

[Col. 0449]

### Title: “Unto the end. A Psalm of David, for the hidden things.”

[Col. 0449B]

“God is our refuge.” [Jerome, Alcuin, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Title: “Unto the end. A Psalm of David, for the hidden things.” This psalm deals with the hidden mysteries of the divine dispensation: that God became man; that salvation was promised to both peoples; that blindness happened in part to Israel so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter; that the apostles passed over to the Gentiles; and that there was extraordinary peace on earth at the time of the Lord’s birth. Hence Isaiah: “They shall beat their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into sickles” (Isa. II).

Its sense is: This psalm, tending toward the end—that is, Christ—is David’s, that is, of some faithful person from Judaea, so that the testimony may be more certain. I say, a psalm composed “for the hidden things,” that is, dealing with the manifestation of hidden things.

Or according to another translation, which reads: “At the end, a psalm, for the sons of Core, for the hidden things.” The sons of Core are the sons of the cross, who speak of the hidden things, that is, of Christ’s coming and the other matters predicted. Thus this psalm, tending toward the end, is attributed to the sons of Core, who speak here. I say, a psalm composed for the hidden things.

Its intention is to exhort to faith. Its method: the psalm has three parts. First, it shows that all hope must be placed in the Lord’s coming and in the apostles’ passage to the Gentiles. Second, it says that the Church is founded upon Christ, to whom nations and kingdoms are subjected: “The river’s stream.” Third, it recounts the great works done at the time of the Incarnation: “Come and see.”

Therefore the prophet, at Christ’s coming, seeing many tribulations rise up, first sets consolation before them; speaking in the person of the sons of Core, or of some faithful person from Judaea, he says:

### Verse 1

> “God is our refuge and strength, a helper in the tribulations which have found us exceedingly.”

“God is our refuge.” [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] As though he said: Other gods are not a refuge, but our God—that is, the God common to us through His assumption of flesh—is a refuge while He delivers from danger, and strength. He adds this because there is a refuge where one fears more; if anyone should sometimes flee to such refuges, he becomes weaker. But here he is strengthened. Therefore one must flee to Thee, because Thou art a helper in tribulations, since Thou helpest us overcome them.

And Thou art not only a helper in overcoming other trials, but also in those which are “exceeding,” that is, in the conscience; for the things within us weigh too heavily upon us. For there is no greater tribulation here than the conscience of sins. But our God helps even there, because He forgives sins.

These tribulations found us, not we them: that we might repent through ourselves, where nevertheless He too must be entreated; but the tribulations themselves found us when others urged us to repent. Therefore sometimes a person finds the tribulation of sins, when without another’s admonition he considers his errors and so repents, saying: “I found tribulation and sorrow” (Ps. XIV). Sometimes tribulation finds a person, when he repents through another’s persuasion, recognizing sin. In both cases God must be entreated.

Or thus: “tribulations” may mean punishments; and the words are read consecutively: “He is a helper in tribulations; these tribulations have found us.” For we were fleeing from them. Or, “they have found us,” because through Adam we were exposed to them. They found us exceedingly, because here we perish beneath the weight of punishments. All the more powerful is He who delivers.

### Verse 2

> “Therefore we shall not fear when the earth is troubled and mountains are moved into the heart of the sea.”

“Therefore.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Because such is our security, we who agree with the mountains—that is, the apostles—shall not fear. Let their opponents fear when, at the novelty of the miracle in Christ’s coming, the earth is troubled: that is, Judaea, as dry land, without idolatry, surrounded by the bitterness of the Gentiles as land by the sea, and the mountains—that is, the apostles—are moved, according to: “Because you have rejected the word of God, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII).

“Into the heart of the sea,” that is, into the faith of the Gentiles, because the Gentiles believe them. Or the sea is this world; the heart of the sea is the fierceness of the Gentiles. [Col. 0451A] For they passed over to fierce and barbarous Gentiles, in which transfer:

### Verse 3

> “Their waters made a sound and were troubled; the mountains were troubled in its strength.”

“The waters made a sound,” opposing them, “and were troubled”—their waters, or “its” waters, according to another reading, that is, the waters of the sea. [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss, Alcuin, Interlinear Gloss.] “The mountains too were troubled,” that is, the powers of the world, “in its strength,” that is, in the strength of God, who is refuge and strength.

Or from the words “they made a sound,” as though the mountains were moved: in that transfer the mountains themselves, the apostles, made a sound by preaching, and “their waters were troubled.” The reference is made according to the sense, not the grammatical wording: that is, the waters of the sea, namely the peoples of the Gentiles, or their teachings, which were made foolish when the Saviour’s teaching flashed forth. Hence: “Their judges were swallowed up, joined to the rock” (Ps. CXL). This is Moses’ rod, which swallowed the rods of Pharaoh’s magicians. For God made foolish the wisdom of this world. “Where is the wise man? Where the scribe? Where the inquirer of this age?” (I Cor. I). Hence the prophet Obadiah: “I shall destroy the wisdom of the wise and reject the prudence of the prudent” (Obad. VIII).

“The mountains were troubled”: that is, externally the apostles were troubled, “in its strength,” that is, under the overwhelming persecution of the sea.

## Part II. *Diapsalma.*

### Verse 4

> “The river’s stream makes glad the city of God; the Most High has sanctified His tabernacle.”

“The river’s stream.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The second part, in which he says that the Church is founded in Christ, and the nations and kingdoms are subjected to it. As though he said: The sea rages thus, but amid these waves and sounds those who have fled to that refuge do not fear, because the river’s stream—that is, the overflowing of the Holy Spirit—makes glad the city of God, namely the Church. And the Most High has sanctified His tabernacle, that is, the Church or the body which He assumed from the Virgin. And:

### Verse 5

> “God is in her midst; she shall not be moved. God shall help her at morning dawn.”

God remains in the midst of that city, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] because He provides equally for all and does not accept persons. Just as what is in the middle has equal distances to every boundary, so God is said to be in the midst because He provides equally for all. Therefore that city shall not be moved; hence, “the gates of hell shall not prevail against her” (Matt. XVI).

God shall help her in the labour of the world “at morning,” that is, at the very beginning of a good work; and this “at dawn,” that is, through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, who is light like the day. Or another reading: “God shall help her with His countenance,” that is, through the presence of the Incarnation. Or “with His countenance,” that is, by showing His help—when by helping He makes Himself known. And thus:

### Verse 6

> “The nations were troubled and kingdoms were bowed down; He gave forth His voice, and the earth was moved.”

“The nations were troubled” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus] beneficially. The kingdoms too were bowed down, so that they might worship and not stand erect in pride. For “He gave”; he does not say “He uttered,” but “He gave,” as though His voice were a great gift: that is, preaching, when He thundered from the clouds, that is, the preachers, who are called clouds and mountains—mountains because of their height and steadfastness, clouds because of rain and fruitfulness. Hence the earth was moved: that is, the earthly person trembles in fear of the Judge. Who gave His voice?

### Verse 7

> “The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our defender.”

“The Lord of heavenly hosts,” [Jerome, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus] “who is with us” through assumption of flesh—as if adding the proper name, Emmanuel. For Emmanuel means “God with us.” In these words he briefly defines what Christ is when he says, “Lord of hosts, with us.” As though he said: He who formerly sent angels has now Himself come. He is with us, and by this He is our defender.

Therefore let no weakness terrify us; ours are none but the sons of the cross. He, I say, is the God of Jacob, that is, of those signified by Jacob. As though he said: He who will give us things as great as those He gave Jacob is not God of Jacob alone.

## Part III. *Diapsalma.*

### Verse 8

> “Come and see the works of the Lord, the wonders He has set upon the earth, removing wars unto the end of the earth.”

“Come and see.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin, Jerome, Augustine, Jerome, Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which he recounts the great works done at the time of the Incarnation. As though he said: What did the defender do? Great works. “Come” by faith and “see,” that is, understand the works of the Lord.

Or the connection is thus: because He is with us and is our defender, therefore come by faith. As though he said: Now secure, I invite you. “And see,” that is, understand the works which the Lord performed at the time of the Incarnation, such as the extraordinary peace, and the like, which He set over the whole earth. These works were wonders because they foreshadowed something. What? Namely, that He Himself is removing spiritual wars—that is, wars of evil will—unto the end of the earth.

This has already happened in some who do not resist God, because through Christ’s coming the idolatry and superstition of the whole world have perished. This was signified by the actual peace which existed throughout the world at the time of the Lord’s birth. Hence the angels then first sang the song of peace: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will” (Luke I). For He was born who is peace, who makes both one (Eph. II), who said: “My peace I give to you; my peace I leave to you” (John IV). He truly removes wars, because:

### Verse 9

> “He shall break the bow and shatter weapons; and He shall burn shields with fire.”

“The bow,” [Augustine] that is, snares, He shall break; “weapons,” that is, open attack, He shall shatter; and “shields,” that is, the protection of vain presumption. Hence Job says: “He ran against God with the thick neck of his shield” (Job XV). He shall burn them with the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that we may be armed with the evangelical weapons described by the Apostle.

### Verse 10

> “Be still, and see that I am God; I shall be exalted among the nations, and I shall be exalted in the earth.”

[Col. 0453A] “Be still and see.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Jerome, Remigius, Augustine.] As though he said: He gave His voice. What voice? “Be still” from the devil’s weapons, namely from vices and contentious tumults, so that you may attend to your weakness. For you are weak through yourself: that is, you must become weak so that you may be strong through God.

Or from the words “Come”: there is the Lord’s voice, and it deals literally with the things done at Christ’s coming. As though he said: He gave His voice. And that voice is: “Come and see the works of the Lord.” The sense of these words is unchanged. “Which He set upon the earth”: as signs for summoning a straying people to the way of truth; these were wonders, as it were *prodigia*, indications of a future newness, such as the Virgin’s childbirth, the star, the extraordinary peace, and the rest.

“Removing”: behold the works and wonders, namely that He Himself is removing wars literally unto the end of the earth, because at that time the world was at peace because of His presence; for He “shall break the bow and shatter weapons and burn shields with fire.” All these things occurred literally at Christ’s coming, according to: “They shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles” (Isa. II).

Therefore, if weapons have been burned, be still, O people, from wars, having nothing with which to fight. And see, that is, understand that I am God—not he who deceived you, nor you yourselves, but I who made and renew you. Therefore do not exalt yourselves on account of your works, because I shall be exalted among the nations when they are converted to faith; and after the fullness of the nations has entered (Rom. XI), I shall be exalted in the earth, that is, in Judaea. The nations are the sea because of idolatry. Therefore one may say:

[Col. 0453C]

### Verse 11

> “The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our defender.”

The Lord of hosts is with us, and the God of Jacob is our defender: namely, He who makes the Christian people, signified through Jacob although later in time, victorious.

## Comparison on Psalm XLV: “God Is Our Refuge,” etc.

The title is translated by the Septuagint, Pellicanus, and Praetensis as “for the hidden things.” Jerome and the translator for Cajetan rendered it “for maidens” and “for young women.” Munster and Sanctes retained the Hebrew word *alamoth*, as though it were a musical instrument. The Hebrew is ambiguous: *alam* means “he hid,” and *almuth*, “youth,” although the pointing marks vary when they are written. St. Jerome alludes to the second meaning. Yet the sense comes to the same thing: for the psalm treats of the beginning of the Church being born, as it were of her youth, strengthened by the hidden and inward growth of the Holy Spirit.

### Verse 1

“God, our refuge.” Faber affirms that from the Hebrew it ought to be said, “God, our refuge,” because Jerome says, “God, our hope.” In Hebrew is *lanu*, that is, “to us” or “for us,” which may refer either to God or to hope, a difference of little consequence to the sense.

“In tribulations which have found us exceedingly.” *Nimitsa* may be a future tense, as Sanctes understood it, translating, “we shall find,” namely strong help in God, so that the verb does not refer to tribulations. Or it may be what they call *Niphal*, and then it means “is found,” so that it may be referred to God or to tribulations by supplying a relative pronoun, as Hebrews commonly do. As if you said: “In tribulations, in which help is found in great measure.” But so that the sense might be clearer, the Septuagint said, “which found us exceedingly,” or “in which we were found exceedingly,” using the singular in place of the plural—which is not unusual.

Or the Hebrew *me’od*, which signifies intensity, may take the place of a noun, so that you understand: “in tribulations in which intensity is found,” that is, “which press us severely.” Thus, whether you translate that God is our help and is very timely in tribulations, as many render it, or that He is a helper in tribulations which grievously afflict us, both understandings are worthy and sound.

### Verse 4

“The Most High sanctified His tabernacle.” The translators, as appears, read *qiddesh*, verbally, that is, “he sanctified,” and *mishkano*, that is, “his tabernacle.” For the Hebrew is now read as *qedosh mishkene ‘elyon*, that is, “the holy tabernacle of the Most High.” The sense is: “The river’s stream,” or divisions, or rivulets, “make glad the holy”—supply “place,” according to Munster—“of the tabernacles [Col. 0454C] of the Most High.”

### Verse 8

“Which He set as wonders upon the earth.” Jerome: “desolations,” or, as others wish, “wastelands in the earth.” The Hebrew word is ambiguous, from the root *shamem*, “he was desolate,” or *shamam*, “he was amazed.” Yet those wonders are the desolations of the earth, that is, of earthly affections, which Christ trampled underfoot at His coming, casting out the prince of this world.

### Verse 9

“He shall burn shields with fire.” The Hebrew *agaloth* is translated “wagons.” But since *agal* means “round,” and they maintain that the word used here denotes wagons because of their roundness, why may not the Septuagint, on the same reasoning, translate “shields,” which are likewise made round? Especially since, under either rendering, military equipment is indicated, whether by wagons or shields.

## Psalm XLVI

[Col. 0453]

### Title: “Unto the end. A Psalm of David, for the sons of Core.”

[Col. 0453D]

“All nations.” [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss, Jerome, Cassiodorus, Jerome.] Title: “Unto the end. A Psalm of David, for the sons of Core.” The nations whom in the preceding psalm he called to faith, now converted, he invites in this psalm to praise. Or these are the sons of Core, that is, the sons of suffering.

Its sense is: This psalm belongs to the prophet David, who here speaks in the voice of the apostles. It was composed for the sons of Core—that is, for directing the converted nations—unto the end, that is, to Christ’s praise.

Its intention is to exhort to praise. Its method: the psalm has two parts. First, he invites to God’s praise the nations to whom grace has passed. Second, God’s ascension and kingdom are described; hence he urgently exhorts them to sing: “God has ascended with jubilation.” Therefore, in the voice of the apostles exhorting the nations to praise, he says:

### Verse 1

> “All nations, clap your hands; rejoice unto God with a voice of exultation.”

“All nations.” [Augustine.] As though he said: Even if the boys—that is, the Jews—mock and say, “Go up, baldhead” (IV Kings II), you—all nations to whom grace has passed, not Jews alone—clap your hands, that is, rejoice in good works; rejoice unto God with a voice of exultation. As though he said: Let hand and tongue agree: let the one act, the other confess. Hence in Leviticus the head of the turtledove is commanded to be twisted toward the armpits (Lev. V). Our edition has “toward the little wings.”

### Verse 2

> “For the Lord is most high, terrible, a great king over all the earth.”

“For.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] These are the reasons for rejoicing and clapping: because the Lord whom the boys mocked is most high, that is, powerful to do what He wills, and terrible in ascending to heaven, though He previously appeared contemptible. Or He is terrible because He will judge in power, and a great king because He governs His own, over all the earth, not merely over the Jews. This was shown by the title set above the cross, inscribed in three languages.

### Verse 3

> “He has subjected peoples to us, and nations beneath our feet.”

“He has subjected peoples to us.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Remigius.] He speaks in the person of the Church. As though he said: Therefore clap your hands also because He has subjected peoples to us, that is, to the universal Church. For all the faithful may say this in common, since all outsiders belong to them in a certain sense. For how many non-Christians now run to the Church, asking the Church’s help! They wish to receive temporal assistance, even though they do not yet wish to reign with us eternally. “And nations beneath our feet.” For the Church has been so exalted that it has all who do not yet believe beneath its feet, because they seek the Church’s help and serve it temporally.

Or he speaks in the person of the apostles: “He subjected to us, apostles from Judaea, the peoples of the Gentiles.” For, suffering from their own people, they are honoured by the Gentiles. “And nations beneath our feet,” that is, beneath our preaching. Understand preachers by “feet,” to whom the peoples are subjected.

Or again, in the person of the same apostles: God subjected peoples, that is, the Jews, to Himself, to be joined with us; and nations, that is, believing Gentiles, beneath our feet, that is, beneath our preaching, which they obey. And:

### Verse 4

> “He chose for us His inheritance, the beauty of Jacob whom He loved.”

“He chose,” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine] not by our merit but by His grace, says the Church, namely to give us—and though He came to the Jews—His inheritance, that is, eternal life: which inheritance is the beauty, that is, the splendour, of Jacob, that is, of the later people. Or, “whom Jacob loved.” The heavenly inheritance is the beauty of the Christian people, in which it will be beautiful, shining like the sun, though it is now despised.

Or in the person of the apostles: He chose to give us His inheritance of many peoples, that we might cultivate it, striking their hearts with the sword of preaching and destroying wickedness. This is the beauty of Jacob, that is, those like Jacob or signified by Jacob: namely, those who give earthly things for heavenly things, as Jacob did when he gave a dish of lentils for Esau’s birthright (Gen. XXVII). This came by grace, because He loved him, Esau having been rejected (Mal. I). Hence there follows here, “whom He loved.”

## Part II. *Diapsalma.*

### Verse 5

> “God has ascended with jubilation, and the Lord with the voice of a trumpet.”

“God has ascended.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The second part, in which the ascension and kingdom of God are described; hence he urgently exhorts them to sing. As though he said: He subjected them to us, and He was able to do so because God—that is, Christ—ascended in jubilation, because the joy of the astonished apostles could not be expressed. For jubilation is ineffable joy, which can neither be kept silent nor expressed. The Church represents it on the chief solemnities by forming varied melodies around the same sound, as is sung at the Lord’s Nativity: “Like a bridegroom,” as though, sensing joy concerning himself, he could not express the gladness due to His merits.

So Jeremiah says: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God! I am a child; I do not know how to speak” (Jer. I). And Moses, after he began to speak with the Lord, says that he had become slower and more impeded in speech (Exod. IV), though he had been instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. For when anyone approaches the understanding and speaking of the Word which was in the beginning (John I) with the Father, the mind fails and the voice falls silent.

“And the Lord with the voice of a trumpet.” For there was heard the trumpet’s voice: that is, the clear voice of angels crying, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand here looking into heaven?” etc. (Acts I). This happened so that the world might believe more firmly, confirmed by such heralds, namely apostles and angels. Therefore:

### Verse 6

> “Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises.”

“Sing praises to our God,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, praise Him through works. Those outside mocked Him as a man, but He is also God. Sing praises continually to our King, that is, Christ; sing praises. It is most salutary that this is now repeated so often. Therefore sing praises.

### Verse 7

> “For God is King of all the earth; sing praises wisely.”

“For.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] He is God, who creates, and King, governing what He has created. He is now King of all the earth, because He is acknowledged by all the earth. He is not king merely of a portion of the earth, as Jupiter of Crete or Mars of Thrace. I say, sing praises wisely. Here he teaches how one ought to sing praises: wisely. Formerly they sang without understanding while worshipping stones. No one acts wisely in what he does not understand. And you ought to sing praises because:

### Verse 8

> “God shall reign over the nations; God sits upon His holy throne.”

“God shall reign,” or “has reigned,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Jerome] as though he said: Those who despise Him when humble should at least submit to His power. He shall reign over all nations, though formerly over the one people of the Jews. Now this prophecy has been fulfilled: God sits upon His holy throne, that is, in heaven, reigning at the Father’s right hand for ever.

Or the holy throne consists of thrones, virtues, and saints. Thus He is upon His holy throne, that is, over the angels and righteous souls. How shall He reign? Because even:

### Verse 9

> “The princes of the peoples have gathered [Col. 0457A] with the God of Abraham, because the mighty gods of the earth have been greatly exalted.”

“The princes of all peoples,” [Augustine, Jerome, Alcuin] not of one particular people only—that is, the firstfruits of every nation—“have gathered,” that is, have assembled in faith with the God of Abraham, that is, in Christ, who is the God of Abraham and who has children from stones (Matt. III). As though he said: With the Jews expelled, the Gentiles coming from east and west succeed to the sons of Abraham, possessing the promise (Matt. VIII).

Hence follows, “because the gods”: as though he said, they gathered for this reason: because “the mighty gods of the earth,” that is, Jews, who presume upon themselves as earth, “have been greatly exalted,” that is, have become exceedingly proud. As though he said: The branches were broken, so that the humble wild olive might be grafted in (Rom. XI).

Or thus: they gathered because “the gods of the earth,” that is, the strong apostles, whom neither death nor life shall separate from Christ’s love (Rom. VIII), have been greatly exalted through doctrine and miracles.

## Comparison on Psalm XLVI: “All Nations,” etc.

### Verse 4

“He chose for us His inheritance.” *Nahalathenu*, that is, “our inheritance,” according to the Hebrew as we see it. Or *nahalathennu*, with the little point *dagesh*, that is, “His inheritance,” or “His own,” according to the Septuagint. Nor does the difference equally affect the sense. For the inheritance is God’s effectively and causally, and it is ours by gift also.

### Verse 9

“The princes of the peoples have gathered with the God of Abraham.” Jerome and most others: “The princes of the peoples have gathered”—supply, “so that they may be”—“the people of the God of Abraham.” Or, as Munster wishes, “they are joined to the people of the God of Abraham.”

Here it is plainly seen that the Septuagint read the preposition “with” in place of “people,” because in Hebrew two little letters, namely *ayin* and *mem*, without added pointing marks may, at the reader’s discretion, form either the preposition “with” or the noun “people.” Thus, if you read *im*, “with,” as the Septuagint rendered *IM*; if you read *am*, “people,” as the others understand *AM*.

For the mighty gods of the earth have been greatly exalted. Jerome: “For the gods, the shields of the earth, have been greatly exalted.” Sanctes: “For the shields of the earth belong to God; He has been greatly exalted.” Pellican: “The protectors of the earth belong to God; He has been greatly exalted.” Münster, in order to make clearer the sense he conceived, added words of his own thus: “because it belongs to God, as with a shield, to protect the earth—He who is greatly exalted.” But if you render the Hebrew word for word, you may say: “because the gods, the shields of the earth, have been greatly exalted”; and because this was somewhat obscure, the Septuagint rightly made the sense clearer: “For the mighty gods of the earth have been greatly exalted.” Nebiensis comes fairly close: “The gods, the shields of the earth, have been greatly exalted.” The Greek manuscripts, however, read: τοῦ Θεοῦ οἱ κραταιοί, that is, “the mighty ones of God”—in the author's gloss, “mighty gods.”

## PSALM XLVII

[Col. 0457]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM, OR A PRAISE OF A SONG, OF THE SONS OF—OR FOR THE SONS OF—KORAH, ON THE SECOND DAY OF THE SABBATH.”

[Col. 0457C]

**Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise.** [Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] The title: “A psalm, or a praise of a song, of the sons of—or for the sons of—Korah, on the second day of the Sabbath.” As we read in Genesis, on the first day God made light and separated it from darkness, when things confused and without form were receiving their forms (Gen. VII); so, on the Lord’s Day—which was the first day in the first creation of things—He raised Christ from the dead and separated the light of immortality from the darkness of mortality.

On the second day of the Sabbath, that is, on the second day, God made the firmament. Thus, after Christ’s resurrection, He made the Church—the body for its head—which was established after Christ’s resurrection upon the firm rock, from which it cannot be moved. Hence the Apostle says, “which is the pillar [Col. 0457D] and foundation of the truth” (1 Tim. III); and of this Church the song is sung for the sons of Korah.

The meaning of the title is: This psalm, or praise of a song, belongs to the sons of Korah, or is sung for the sons of Korah. I call it a psalm set on the second day of the Sabbath, when the firmament—that is, heaven—was made; that is, it treats of the Church, which was confirmed after Christ’s resurrection, and which it calls a city. It commends this city and the Lord of the city.

It commends the city in five ways: from the dignity of its Founder, its location, its extent, the king’s kindness, and its everlasting stability. Its purpose is to urge all people to magnify it. Its method: the psalm has two parts. First, it treats of the city’s foundation, describing it commendatorily. Second, it gives thanks for Christ’s coming and urges that the ranks [Col. 0458B] of the Church be apportioned, by which the Savior may [Col. 0458C] be recognized: “We have received, O God.” Therefore the Prophet, first commending the city from the dignity of its Founder, says:

### VERSE 1.—“Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, in the city of our God, on His holy mountain.”

Great is the Lord, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin,] who was formerly humble: He is great because He made all things mightily. And He is worthy of praise because He made them exceedingly—without limit or end—beautifully and wonderfully. Where is He worthy of praise? In the city of our God, not in Babylon, which is the city of the wicked. For God is blasphemed among the wicked.

This city is situated on His holy mountain. This city cannot be hidden (Matt. V); it is renowned among all. This is that mountain which, as Daniel says, was a small stone cut from a mountain without hands, which afterwards grew [Col. 0458D] into a great mountain and filled the whole earth (Dan. II): that is, Christ, born from the Jewish people without male seed, upon whom the Church is founded. But lest you suppose that this city exists only in one place, he adds:

### VERSE 2.—“It is founded in the joy of the whole earth: Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great King.”

“It is founded in joy.” [Jerome, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As if to say: This city is founded in the joy of the whole earth. For she who formerly, subjected to curses, grieved under the reproach of barrenness, now rejoices everywhere in fruitful offspring. Here she is commended for her extent.

Or according to another reading: “Founded in the joy of the whole earth.” [Col. 0459A] As if to say: The Lord is great—the Lord, I say, who is founded in the joy of the whole earth. Another translation agrees with this sense, for others render it: “Extending the joys of the whole earth.” He is Christ, who spreads joys throughout the whole Church.

“Mount Zion,” etc. He shows in parts what he had said: by Mount Zion he signifies the Jews; by “the sides of the north,” the nations that cling to the devil, who is signified by the cold and harsh north wind. For he himself says: “I shall ascend into heaven, and I shall set my throne toward the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). Hence in the Song of Songs: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind” (Song IV). Hence Jeremiah: “From the north every evil shall be opened over the face of the earth” (Jer. I).

[Jerome, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As if to say: Truly the whole earth [Col. 0459B] is founded, because Mount Zion—that is, the Jews—and the sides of the north—that is, the nations—are included. For all who cling to someone are called that person’s “sides.” Thus we are accustomed to say: “He is a good man, but he has corrupt associates,” namely, those wicked people who are joined to him. Thus the nations were the devil’s sides. These, I say, are the city of the great King, that is, of God. Other kings are not great.

The meaning is: The two walls came together in the cornerstone, who made both one (Eph. III), so that there might be one fold and one shepherd (John X). And:

### VERSE 3.—“God shall be known in her houses, when He receives her.”

God shall also be known in the houses of this city. [Interlinear Gloss, Jerome, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss.] He says “houses” in the plural because there are now several houses in this city. There are many orders of churches, yet one Church. I say He shall be known, but this is through the grace of Him who receives her. That is, when He receives her as a physician receives one to be healed.

Or it may be read of the future, according to another reading: “God shall be known in the future in her ranks,” that is, according to degrees of merits, because He shall give each person a distinct knowledge of Himself. “When He receives her” into eternal blessedness. Here she is commended for the king’s kindness.

### VERSE 4.—“For behold, the kings of the earth have assembled; they have come together as one.”

“For behold, the kings.” [Augustine.] These are the sides of the north. As if to say: Truly the sides of the north are the city [Col. 0459D] of God, for behold, the kings of the earth have assembled with the other faithful in the unity of faith. They have come together upon the cornerstone, and this “as one,” that is, into unity of faith and conduct. In this unity there is no place for heretics, divided into factions by corrupt doctrine, who say, “Behold, here is Christ; behold, there” (Matt. XXIV). And so:

### VERSE 5.—“They, seeing thus, were amazed; they were troubled, they were moved, trembling seized them.”

They became people who see, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine,] and thus—that is, seeing—they were amazed at Christ’s glory and miracles. After admiring Christ’s glory and miracles, they were troubled because of their sins, and they were moved, that is, changed toward good things; trembling seized [Col. 0460A] them because of the consciousness of their offences. Their fear was so great that they even trembled bodily.

### VERSE 6.—“There were pains there as of a woman in labour; with a vehement spirit You shall shatter the ships of Tarshish.”

“There,” [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Cassiodorus,] that is, in that disturbance, were the pains of repentance. Pains, I say, like those of a woman in labour: grievous, but useful, because from them fruit proceeds. Hence Isaiah: “From fear of You, O Lord, we conceived and gave birth to the spirit of salvation” (Isa. XXVII).

How shall the whole be accomplished? Because “with a vehement spirit,” that is, through the Holy Spirit, or in the mighty fear of You who shall judge, You shall shatter the ships of Tarshish—that is, You shall overthrow the pride of the nations. Cilicia is called Tarshish from Tarsus, its chief city; and by this the nations are understood: the whole from a part.

[Col. 0460B] Or Tarshish is Carthage, which long flourished through trading ships. By those ships is signified the pride of the nations, which trusts in the uncertain riches of this world as though in gusts of wind. But now there is a firm seat in Zion, not upon the sea. We must be established there, not blown about by every wind of doctrine (Eph. IV). Note that He says “You shall shatter”: He speaks by comparison with those shipwrecked.

Or according to the interpretation of the name: Tarshish means “the exploration of joy.” Therefore the ships of Tarshish are those who wander about, seeking out joys in various parts of the world. The Lord will shatter them, so that they may cease from such pursuits.

Alternatively, from the words “when He receives her”: as if to say, God shall be known in the houses, and this when He receives the city for protection. And why is there need for Him to protect it? There is great need: for behold, the kings of the earth, [Col. 0460C] that is, of the nations, have literally assembled and come together as one against this city, to remove it. But afterwards they themselves, seeing by faith that this city is so worthy, were amazed; and after their amazement they were troubled. This and the rest which follows do not differ from the previous interpretation.

Alternatively, this is treated literally of Herod, and the history of the Lord’s Nativity is expounded. As if to say: Truly He will receive her, because through the Incarnation—which shall truly take place—behold, the kings, that is, the Jewish rulers, gathered when Herod stirred them up to identify the place of the Lord’s birth. And they came together as one, agreeing that it was in Bethlehem of Judah (Matt. II), according to the Scriptures. They themselves, seeing the event take place as they had read in prophecy [Col. 0460D] (Mic. V), were amazed at so great a glory—not lightly or idly, but troubled for their sins and moved to faith. Their terror was so great that their bodies trembled; whence follows: “Trembling seized them; there were pains as of a woman in labour,” that is, repentance, because seeing these things, they were so troubled unto repentance. But “with a vehement spirit”—Herod’s—“You shall shatter the ships of Tarshish”: the ships at Tarsus in Cilicia, by which the Magi returning by another way were believed to have crossed over to their own country, were broken up by Herod.

### VERSE 7.—“As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God: God has founded her for ever.”

“As we have heard.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine.] [Col. 0461A] Having run through all that was done at the time of the Incarnation, he concludes. As if to say: Since it is so, therefore, as we heard in prophetic promises—such as “All nations shall worship Him, and all kings shall serve Him” (Ps. XCVII), and “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXIII)—so we have seen in fulfilment. For all kings and all nations worship Christ; Christ reigns at the right hand of the Father in the city, in the Church, of the Lord of hosts, because there He appoints angels as guardians.

He repeats this, saying, “in the city,” that is, in the catholic Church of our God—he says “our God” lest an assembly of heretics claim this name for itself. Whoever is in this city hears and sees; whoever is outside is blind. Lest this city be thought temporal, he adds: God Himself founded [Col. 0461B] that city firmly. Therefore do not fear that the firmament may ever fall. He founded her, I say, for ever, not for an hour, like Moses’ former tabernacle (Exod. XXVI).

### PART II. VERSE 8.—“We have received, O God, Your mercy in the midst of Your temple.”

“We have received.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] The second part, in which, giving thanks for Christ’s coming, he urges that the ranks of the Church be apportioned, through which the Savior may be known. The connection is: In what order was this city founded? Behold, “we have received,” etc. Or: What have we heard and seen? Behold, “we have received,” etc. Or: He founded her—and truly, because we who are good, O God, grains among chaff, a lily among thorns, a beloved among daughters (Song II), have received. What have we received? Your mercy, [Col. 0461C] not only the sacraments but also the reality of the sacraments. For grains and chaff share in the sacraments, but only the good receive the reality of the sacraments.

Where have we received it? In the midst of Your temple—that is, in the midst of the people who do not receive mercy, the chaff. Through the sacraments in which they share, they are God’s people and temple. Of them the Apostle says: “Having an appearance of godliness, but denying its power” (2 Tim. III). This people of chaff is so numerous that no grains appear to be present; yet some grains are there, because:

### VERSE 9.—“According to Your name, O God, so also is Your praise unto the ends of the earth; Your right hand is full of righteousness.”

[Col. 0461D] According as Your name, O God, is, so also is Your praise unto the ends of the earth. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss.] By this it is shown that the city is not founded in a narrow place.

Or thus, it treats of Christ’s actual reception, when He was received by Simeon and others, when He was presented in the temple (Luke II). The meaning is: “We have received, O God, Your mercy,” that is, Your Son, in the midst of Your temple, which was in Jerusalem. By this, those who despise Him are more gravely accused, since He was seen in their midst; and Christ’s Incarnation is indicated, since, as man, He was presented in the temple.

Or it treats of receiving Christ through faith, by which He is received by all believers. “We have received by faith, O God, Your mercy,” that is, Your Son, in the midst [Col. 0462A] of Your temple, that is, in the common body of Your people. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] And this is according to Your name, O God, which is spread everywhere, because no one fails to submit himself to this name, even if he does not know its worship. Therefore, according to Your name—that is, as reverence for Your name is enlarged—so Your praise, which is truly found only among the saints, has been enlarged unto the ends of the earth: that is, praise is given to You in the Church spread throughout the whole world. For there are not lacking those who praise You in every land, because Your right hand—that is, Your propitiation—is full of righteousness: it has justified many, all of whom praise You.

Or Your right hand—that is, eternal blessedness, in which the righteous are placed—is full of righteousness, that is, full of righteous persons, because many righteous shall stand at the right hand. Hence:

[Col. 0462B]

### VERSE 10.—“Let Mount Zion rejoice, and let the daughters of Judah exult, because of Your judgments, O Lord.”

Let Mount Zion rejoice, [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Jerome,] that is, Judaea, which received the first rays of faith; and let the daughters of Judah—that is, of confession—exult: the nations begotten through confession from Judah, that is, from the apostles. And this is because of Your judgments, O Lord, by which blindness happened to Israel, so that the fullness of the nations might enter in (Rom. XI). And you, O nations:

### VERSE 11.—“Surround Zion and embrace her; proclaim in her towers.”

Surround Zion, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Jerome, Cassiodorus,] the elect from among the Jews. Surround her, I say, not with scandals, but embrace her in the arms of charity.

Or, from “let Mount rejoice,” Mount Zion is understood as the universal [Col. 0462C] Church. For Zion means “watching-place.” Thus: Let Mount Zion rejoice, namely, she who is in the people’s watchfulness. And let the daughters of Judah—that is, of Christ—exult, namely, holy women. By Judah their descent is indicated, because Christ was from Judah; and these women exult, so that the Church may exist in both sexes.

The cause of joy is God’s judgments; hence follows, “Because of Your judgments, O Lord.” As if to say: Let Mount Zion rejoice and exult because of Your future judgments, O Lord, in which they know that they are destined for future blessedness. As if to say: Even if the righteous now labour among thorns, nevertheless let them exult because God does not err in judging, but will separate all grains from the chaff. Therefore, though born mixed together, let them live distinctly; let them not judge rashly now. It belongs to them now to gather; but it belongs to God to give hope, now in merit and in the future in reward.

Let those within rejoice and exult; but you reprobate persons, in whose midst mercy is received, who are outside because you do not possess the reality of the sacraments, surround Zion—not with scandals, but by showing honour—and embrace Zion, that is, the good, with charity. And you preachers, proclaim, that is, preach her praises to others. Do this in her towers: that is, in the height of her fortifications, in the concord of the apostles, who are the towers of this city. For just as, in an earthly city, towers serve for defence, for observing hostile attacks, and for speaking to outsiders, so in this city apostolic towers fittingly serve as [Col. 0463A] defences against heretics and as elevated places from which outsiders may be addressed, so that outsiders may hear.

But lest, through joy, they grow lax and indolent, he urges them to set their hearts upon the Church’s strength. Hence he adds:

### VERSE 12.—“Set your hearts upon her strength, and distribute her houses, that you may recount it to another generation.”

Set your hearts. [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As if to say: Proclaim, not so that you may have an appearance of godliness while denying its power; but set your hearts, not merely your mouths, upon her strength, that is, upon charity (2 Tim. III). For charity is the city’s strength, which nothing conquers. Hence Solomon says: “Love is strong as death” (Song VIII).

And, having charity, distribute—that is, distinguish—her houses: distinguish the house [Col. 0463B] from the house which has merely an appearance, and the house which, together with the appearance, possesses godliness. Do not confuse them as though they were one. As if to say: If you possess charity, you will not judge rashly, and you will see that the wicked do not harm the good.

Or thus: “Distribute her houses,” namely, the houses of circumcision and uncircumcision (Gal. II), so that Paul may go to the nations and others to the circumcision. They divided the administration, but united charity. This fits better; that is, this interpretation agrees more closely with the wording. Hence follows: so that in this way you, O preachers, may recount it to another generation, that is, down to posterity.

Or according to another reading: “Distribute her ranks,” that is, arrange the distinct offices in ordered fashion—presbyters, deacons, and the like—so that through them [Col. 0463C] you may recount the mighty works of God to another generation, namely, the Christian people, which is second after the Hebrew people whom God first chose.

### VERSE 13.—“For this is God, our God, for ever and ever; He Himself shall rule us for ages.”

“For this is.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Here he shows what must be proclaimed. The statement is brief, but encompasses everything. As if to say: Proclaim this: that this Christ, present, seen on earth and conversant with human beings (Baruch III), is God—our God—even though He is hidden in a human being; and this is for ever, not temporarily like false gods. He says this against those who made mortal human beings gods.

And “for ever and ever”: He Himself will rule us lest we fall, because Christ is King. He is God and our King: because He is God, He protects us lest we die; because He is King, He rules us lest we fall. And this is for ages, that is, without end.

## COLLATION ON PSALM XLVII: “GREAT IS THE LORD,” ETC.

In the title the Septuagint mystically added “on the second day of the Sabbath.” For the firmament was made on the second day, and by it is understood the Church, of which the psalm treats most nobly.

### VERSE 2.—“It is founded in the joy of the whole earth.”

Here the translators differ remarkably. Jerome: “with a beautiful shoot, [Col. 0464A] the joy of the whole earth”; Sanctes: “beautiful in situation, the joy of the whole earth”; Pratensis: “a beautiful nymph, the joy of the whole earth”; Münster: “a beautiful place, and the joy of the whole earth”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “a beautiful bride gladdening the earth”; the Campensian Paraphrase: “an elegant region, in the joy of the whole earth”; the translator of the same: “she is a beautiful nymph and the glory of the whole earth”; the Chaldee: “beautiful as a bridegroom, the joy of all inhabitants of the earth”; Nebiensis: “with a most beautiful shrub, gladdening all the earth.”

Where shall we turn amid such diversity? Let them contend as much as they please. It is known that this variety arose from the Hebrew particle *NOPH*, which has many meanings: to lift up, a shoot, a bride, a region, a honeycomb. The Septuagint adopted the first meaning: “it is lifted up in the joy of the whole earth,” which cannot be soundly accomplished without a foundation. Yet all these versions can be brought into one. For the holy Church, established upon the firm rock, puts forth [Col. 0464B] leafy, flourishing branches; blooms with fragrant roses; is a spiritual region; and finally is Christ’s most beautiful bride.

### VERSE 4.—“For behold, the kings of the earth have assembled.”

“The earth” is read neither in the Septuagint nor in the Hebrew. Jerome writes to Sunia and Fretela that he removed it from the old Latin manuscripts. Sunia and Fretela read “of her earth” in place of “of the earth.” The Roman Psalter and Augustine’s text have “of the earth.” Since it has been received into the Church’s use, it should not be cut out; indeed, Jerome himself interprets it in his commentaries as “the kings of the earth,” that is, “the rulers of the age.” And in the Greek manuscripts which I was able to examine, we read: οἱ βασιλεῖς τῆς γῆς, “the kings of the earth.”

### VERSE 6.—“With a vehement spirit.”

Jerome: “with a scorching wind”; others: “with an east wind”; the Chaldee and Pratensis: “with the south wind”; and the translator of Campensis: “with a south windstorm.” But the east wind, called *Eurus* or *Vulturnus*, is hot and dry and is therefore scorching and vehement.

### VERSE 11.—“Proclaim in her towers.”

Since *SAPHAR* is indifferent between “to recount” and “to count,” the Septuagint, taking the former meaning, understood the preposition “in.” Other translators render: “Count her lands.” In either case the interpretation is worthy.

### VERSE 13.—“Distribute her houses.”

*PASEGU*, that is, “strengthen” or “exalt,” as the recent Hebraizing translators render it. Jerome and the Septuagint seem to have read *PALEGU*, since the Septuagint renders, “distribute,” “those things separated.” There is little difference in sense, just as where we say “houses,” they put “palaces,” *ARMENOTHEHA*. Finally, it is not improbable that the first word means “to distribute,” as the lexicon of the Complutensian Academy reports. Nebiensis accordingly translates, “separate.”

### VERSE 13.—“He Himself shall rule us for ages.”

*ALMUTH*, that is, “until death,” “over death,” or “in death,” as Jerome, Münster, Sanctes, and the Campensian Paraphrase render it. But Pellican and the interpreters for Cajetan render “eternally”; the translation of Campensis, “for ever.” Moreover, “until death,” this kind of expression, sufficiently indicates God’s eternal providence toward His saints. The Praetorian translator renders “through youth”; the Chaldee and Nebiensis likewise, taking *almuth* as one word. For thus it means “youth,” by which Rabbi Solomon, according to Lyra, metaphorically understands sweetness: understand that God leads us gently, as a child of good disposition is sweetly and humanely treated by a wise father.

## PSALM XLVIII

[Col. 0465]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END, FOR THE SONS OF KORAH, A PSALM OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0465A]

**Hear these things, all nations.** [Alcuin, Augustine, Jerome, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Title: “Unto the end, for the sons of Korah, a psalm of David.” Here the Prophet treats of those who love this world, showing that they will perish together with their glory; and of Christ the Redeemer—not of them, but of those who despise the world. He reproves those who worship God so that things may go well for them here: those who murmur against or blaspheme God because the wicked flourish while they themselves are oppressed, as if God were ignorant of these things or did not care for them, lest He trouble Himself with seeing or correcting them. Against these persons the Prophet speaks here to the sons of Korah.

The meaning is: This psalm of David, directed to the end—that is, to Christ—is sung for the sons of Korah. Its purpose is to admonish the person cast down in the world not to value highly those who are exalted in it. Its method has four divisions. First, he makes his hearers attentive to the new and great things he is to say. Second, he begins to pursue them, saying that Christ will not redeem the ungodly: “Why shall I fear?” Third, he treats of what shall be rendered to the ungodly and the righteous: “Like sheep.” Fourth, he warns that the powerful should not be feared, since they leave everything behind with the light: “Do not fear.” Therefore, first making them attentive, he says:

### VERSE 1.—“Hear these things, all nations; give ear, all you who inhabit the world.”

Hear these things which I am about to say. [Augustine.] Here he makes attentive all nations, that is, all the wicked. Even today, what is said here is heard through readers. For we see that this psalm, which formerly was not recited [Col. 0465C] except among the one Jewish nation, is now recited throughout the whole world, namely, in all churches. Receive it with ears made for hearing.

As if to say: Do not listen in passing, all you who inhabit the world; that is, all the righteous, who are masters rather than slaves of things. For those inhabit the world who are not held by the world or entangled in its errors. He then explains what he said:

### VERSE 2.—“Both earthborn men and sons of men; rich and poor alike together.”

“Both earthborn men.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] He understands by “earthborn men” the wicked, and by “sons of men” the righteous. Or thus: by “nations” and “those who inhabit” he understands all human beings generally: “Hear these things, all nations”—I exclude no one, because God does not accept persons; He is available to all, and the Incarnation is a universal benefit. And to make clearer what he said, he adds: “Receive with ears for hearing, all you who inhabit the world.”

“Both,” etc. Here he explains in parts those whom he had previously called earthborn men, that is, the wicked. Earthborn men are those who follow earthly vices, as though born from the earth. They belong to Adam’s portion, for Adam was a man, not the Son of Man. “And sons of men, hear,” that is, the righteous, who belong to Christ’s lot, for He was the Son of Man and bore the image of man (2 Cor. XV). He then adds: “Both earthborn men and sons of men”—for this refers to both. As if to say: I withhold my discourse from no one. Let the heir of earth listen on account of judgment—that is, that he may know by what he shall be judged and thus fear; and the righteous for the sake of the kingdom—that is, that he may know by what he shall reign and thus love.

Then follows a brief exposition concerning the righteous, when he adds “rich and poor.” The rich person refers to the earthborn, the poor to the sons of men, etc. “Rich,” that is, earthborn, and “poor,” that is, the Son of Man: hear, you who are “alike together,” that is, not separated until the harvest. For then you will not be together, when the tares are separated from the wheat (Matt. XIII), and the sheep from the goats (Matt. XXV). Therefore let them now hear, “alike together,” that is, not separately; and let lambs and goats feed together until He comes who will separate some to the left and others to the right (ibid.).

[Col. 0466B]

### VERSE 3.—“My mouth shall speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart understanding.”

“My mouth.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] He commends what he is to say. As if to say: Therefore listen, because my mouth shall speak wisdom, that is, Christ. Wisdom pertains to divine matters. And lest you suppose that he speaks only with his mouth and not from his heart, he adds: “and the meditation of my heart shall speak understanding,” namely, concerning morals, which consists in providing for the future. For understanding pertains to the instruction of morals. In these two is indicated the whole divine discourse; and this is not from me, but:

### VERSE 4.—“I shall incline my ear to a parable; I shall open my proposition upon the psaltery.”

“I shall incline my ear to a parable,” [Jerome, Alcuin, Jerome, Augustine, Jerome, Augustine,] that is, I shall humble [Col. 0466C] myself before the truth speaking within, which teaches me to speak in parables so that it may not lie open to all. Or: “I shall incline my ear to a parable,” that is, I shall humble myself before the truth which teaches me through parables and riddles. For now we see through a mirror in a riddle (1 Cor. XIII). Whatever we now see is through a riddle.

“And I shall open upon the psaltery,” that is, I shall show by deeds my proposition: what I set before myself above all things, namely, eternal blessedness. The meaning is: By deeds I shall show what I say.

### PART II. VERSE 5.—“Why shall I fear in the evil day? The iniquity of my heel shall surround me.”

“Why shall I fear?” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] The second part, in which he begins to state what he promised above, saying [Col. 0466D] that Christ will not redeem the ungodly. Here the Prophet, treating the general cause in his own person, asks the cause of the condemnation and fear of the wicked, which is iniquity. Thus: Why should I fear on the evil day, that is, on the day of judgment? It is called a “day” because all things shall then be open, and “evil” with respect to the unrighteous, who shall then be condemned. Behold why I shall fear: because of iniquity, etc.; that is, I shall fear because of an iniquity which I can avoid.

The death which people fear is the separation of soul from flesh. But the true death which they do not fear is the separation of soul from God. Both, however, were offered to humanity through the devil’s persuasion.

[Col. 0467A] As if to say: There is no reason for me to fear—that is, no reason why I need fear—if I wish, since it lies within my power to avoid iniquity, the cause of fear. Only for this shall people fear on the last day, which will be evil for the condemned, not for the righteous. Therefore whoever does not avoid it when able shall justly be punished. And this is why I shall fear: because the iniquity of my heel shall surround me.

He alludes to the words which the Lord said to the serpent in Genesis: “I shall put enmities between you and the woman; she shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. III). In each of us are this woman and her husband. Eve is our flesh, which seduces the husband, that is, reason. Through the flesh, man falls; and that fall is here signified by the heel, which the devil watches in order to cast him down. Or, by the heel is understood the end of life, at which the devil especially lies in wait; and by the serpent’s head, the beginning of the devil’s suggestion. Hence it is said: “She shall watch your head, O serpent,” [Note: [Col. 0467D] Augustine, on verse 14 of this Psalm.] [Augustine,] that is, the beginning of the suggestion, lest delight arise; “and you shall watch her heel,” that is, the fall of the flesh, or [104] the end of life, in order to lie in wait.

And this is “the iniquity of my heel”: that which comes to me from the fall of the flesh, which the devil watches. For the devil watches when you slip, in order to throw you down; you should watch his head, that is, the beginning of his suggestion. Or: “The iniquity of my heel,” which shall be mine at the end, shall surround—that is, oppress—me and make me afraid.

### VERSE 6.—“Those who trust in their own strength and glory in the multitude of their riches.”

“Those who trust.” [Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] These are those whom the iniquity of the heel shall surround: namely, those who trust in bodily or mental strength, in riches or friends, in which the sum of all earthly goods is contained. As if to say: Fear comes from iniquity, and iniquity from earthly things, in which people are so foolish because there are some who trust in their own strength—that is, presume upon their bodily strength or intelligence—and others because they glory in the multitude of their riches, that is, glory in abundant riches, from which they become proud. For from what is a person more puffed up than from riches?

Note that after internal things, signified by the term “strength,” he sets external things, understood by “riches.” And there are others who trust in friends; this must be understood, but in vain, because:

### VERSE 7.—“A brother does not redeem; shall a man redeem? And he shall not give to God his propitiation.”

“A brother,” [Augustine, Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine,] literally, does not redeem him. And truly he does not: for shall a mere man redeem him? As if to say: No, because no brother or other human being shall give God his propitiation, that is, that by which God is appeased.

Or thus, from “those who trust”: As if to say: One surrounded by iniquity has reason to fear; and he explains the parts of this iniquity, saying whom iniquity surrounds: those who trust and glory, etc. For those [Col. 0468A] who trust in their own strength and glory in the multitude of their riches—this is unchanged.

“A brother,” that is, Christ—this should be pronounced with admiration—who is the firstborn among many brothers (Rom. VI), and who after the resurrection said, “Go and tell My brothers” (John XXI): that great Brother does not redeem. And if that Brother, Christ, does not redeem, shall the man who wounded him redeem? As if to say: no human being will redeem him. Therefore whoever trusts in this Brother will not fear on the evil day, unlike the others. A man does not redeem because a human being will not give God his propitiation, that by which He is appeased.

### VERSE 8.—“And the price of the redemption of his soul; and he has laboured for ever, and shall yet live unto the end.”

[Col. 0468B] And he shall not give the price of the redemption of his soul, [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Jerome, Alcuin,] that is, that by which a human soul may be redeemed, because no offering can equal the price of Christ.

Or, therefore the brother—that is, Christ—does not redeem such a person, because such a one, who trusts in strength, riches, or friends, will not give God his propitiation, that by which he may bend God concerning his sins; nor will he give God the price of his soul’s redemption, that is, alms by which he may redeem his soul. Therefore such a person shall labour for ever. His labour shall not end; his life shall end. Yet he shall still live unto the end, that is, after the end of his bodily life. He shall live in soul, because the soul does not perish with the body, but is reserved for suffering until, when it receives the body, both may be tormented. Therefore he shall labour, because:

[Col. 0468C]

### VERSE 9.—“He shall not see destruction when he sees the wise dying; the foolish and the senseless shall perish together.”

He will not see destruction, [Aug., Alcuin.], that is, he will not understand what true destruction is. And this is because he sees the wise dying: that is, because he sees good and evil people die alike. For he says: “If the wise man who worshipped God devoutly has died and cannot escape, why should I follow him? I will make things pleasant for myself while I live.” Thus he does not know what true destruction is—the eternal destruction that awaits him. Yet the wise person passes into life; but the foolish person, that is, one who does not provide for himself with regard to the future, and the stupid person, namely one who does not know in what evil he now stands—or, the foolish person who does not attend to present or future evils, and the stupid person who, even if he does attend to them, does not guard against them—shall perish together.

VERS. 10.—“And they shall leave their riches to strangers; and their tombs shall be their houses for ever.”

And they shall leave behind the riches [Alcuin, Aug., Gl. interlin., Aug.] for which they committed evils. I say, their own riches—that is, riches not according to God’s will—to strangers. Even if they leave them to their children, they nevertheless leave them to strangers, since such heirs are strangers who provide them no help. And their tombs are their houses: they who built palaces to endure throughout this age remain in tombs, not in the palaces they constructed. Or thus: their tombs, in their own opinion, are their houses for ever [Col. 0469A]; that is, they think that the tombs which they build, as though eternal houses for their memorial, will always be houses for them, although they dwell rather in hell.

VERS. 11.—“Their dwelling-places endure from generation to generation; they have called their names upon their lands.”

Their dwelling-places also [Aug., Gl. interlin., Aug.], in which they are only temporary residents—that is, the houses which they leave to heretics—they think will endure through the generation of their sons and the generation of their grandsons. Further, they have called their names upon their lands: that is, they seek to have their names invoked from their houses. Yet this is no great thing, because this invocation was only within their own lands, that is, in their own provinces; their fame did not reach foreigners [Col. 0469B].

Or, according to another reading: “They invoked their names in their lands.” This is what heirs do: at the tombs of the dead they intoxicate themselves in remembrance of them. Yet not even a drop reaches the tongue of the one burning in hell. Thus they serve their own bellies, not the spirits of the dead; for nothing reaches the spirits of the dead except what those persons did while alive. And both in this and in other matters:

VERS. 12.—“Man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them.”

Man did not understand [Aug., Alcuin, Aug., Alcuin, Gl. interlin.], that is, he did not act intelligently when he builds tombs as if eternal and causes his name to be invoked [Col. 0469C], whereas he ought rather to seek eternal things, though he was in honour—that is, made in God’s image, not indeed in strength but in rational understanding.

Or thus: as though he said, “Man devotes himself so earnestly to vain things; and God is not to be blamed for this, but man, because, though man was in honour, that is, made in God’s image, he did not understand his dignity: namely, that by understanding man is superior to beasts, not by strength.” As though he said: “He did not act intelligently, but, having lost reason, he was compared to senseless beasts”—that is, not in some other respect, but in senselessness. And deservedly: “and,” that is, because through his own fault, not by nature, he became like them—namely, the beasts.

VERS. 13.—“This way of theirs is a stumbling-block to them; [Col. 0469D] and afterward they shall take pleasure in their own mouth.”

This way. [Cassiod., Aug.] Here he gathers together into one all that has been said. “This way”: as though he said, “Thus do those people act.” And this way—that is, this life—is called a way because it leads to death. This way, I say, is theirs, not God’s; it is a stumbling-block, that is, a goad and pain, not security, because they are tormented by their own deeds, that is, by evils. Let it not be so with you, that you should think such people happy. The life of the wicked is a stumbling-block.
