Hence Habakkuk: “Because of iniquity I saw the tents of Ethiopia; the skins of the land of Midian shall be troubled” (Hab. III). [Note: [Col. 0469D] Jerome, in his Commentary on Habakkuk III, book II.] The Ethiopians are black demons, darkening the minds of seducers with the blackness of sins and the gloom of vices. Hence: “You gave him as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians” (Ps. LXXIII). Their tents and tabernacles are wicked people who labour for wealth or honours, just as the good, who seek eternal things, are the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. III). They are likewise “the skins of the earth,” because they love earth rather than heaven; they do not give earthly things for eternal ones, as Job says: “Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his soul” (Job II). “Skin for skin”: all that a man possesses—namely, the ugly skin of earthliness and mortality—for the glorious skin. Therefore I saw that the tents of Ethiopia, namely the skins of the earth, would be troubled, and this because of their iniquity.

By what shall they be troubled? [Jerome, Alcuin, Aug.] By Midian, that is, by judgment, through fear of which they shall be tormented both now and in the future. “And afterward they shall please others,” that is [Col. 0470B], they bring others to ruin with themselves. Or: they shall take pleasure in their own mouth, where pretence resides, because they cover over their evils. Thus they please themselves, not in heart but in mouth.

Or, according to another reading, “they shall bless.” As though he said: since they are such that they seek only temporal goods, they also become hypocrites and bless God with their lips, not with their heart. For when they hear of eternal life and contempt for the world, they pay no heed; but lest they be ashamed or reproved, they bless God with their mouths. They are worse than openly wicked people, and the latter state becomes worse than the former. Or, they bless God when their desires are fulfilled. This is the custom of sinners: when their wishes are fulfilled, they give thanks to God, but they do this “in their own mouth,” according to the saying: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. XV).

[Col. 0470C] PART III. *Diapsalma.* VERS. 14.—“Like sheep they are set in hell; death shall feed upon them.”

Like sheep. [Cassiod., Aug., Gl. interlin., Aug., Alcuin, Cassiod., Alcuin.] The third part, in which he says what shall be rendered to the righteous and the ungodly. As though he said: “They boast thus, but those who attend only to present things are already set in hell in their minds, just as the righteous in their minds dwell in heaven.” I say, they exist like sheep, that is, sluggish sheep; and death, that is, the devil, is their shepherd. According to another reading, as Christ is life, so the devil is death; he is their shepherd, as of sheep whom he leads to the pastures of death.

Or thus: they boast in this manner, but it is already clear to me that they are set—that is, that after this life they shall be placed—in hell like sheep. For sheep, once their wool has been removed, remain; so in these people punishment finds, without the consumption of their substance, what it may torment [Col. 0470D]. “And death shall feed upon them.” This is said by comparison with cattle, which do not pluck herbs up by the roots but crop their tops, so that the herbs grow again for food. Thus those fed upon by death live again, because they do not fail. Or, “it shall feed upon them,” that is, it shall lead them from pasture to pasture, from punishment to punishment.

VERS. 15.—“And the righteous shall rule over them in the morning; and their help shall grow old in hell, away from their glory.”

And the righteous shall rule over them. [Cassiod., Jerome, Aug., Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod.] That is, they shall be above them [Col. 0471A] and judge them in the morning, that is, at the resurrection, when all things shall be made manifest. For now it is night, while the merits of the righteous do not appear and the apparent prosperity of the wicked is called happiness. And their help, which they possessed here in the glory of this age, which came from their glory—that is, from their strength, money, and friends—shall grow old in hell, like a garment.

Or: “their help shall grow old in hell”; and this “from their glory,” that is, in proportion to their glory. For insofar as any wicked person was seen to have glory among people, so much corruption shall he suffer in hell. Or distinguish it thus according to another reading: “Their help shall grow old in hell”; then separately, “they have been driven out from their glory,” or “from their own glory”—this is another reading. Those people are so, but I am not. And this is:

VERS. 16.—“But God shall redeem my soul from the hand of hell, when he shall receive me.”

But God shall redeem my soul. [Cassiod.] As the terror of the things foretold crushes the wicked, so the hope of redemption lifts up the good. He shall redeem it, I say, from the hand of hell, that is, from the power of the devil, who before Christ’s coming held souls, when he shall receive me—that is, flesh from me.

PART IV. *Diapsalma.* VERS. 17.—“Do not fear when a man has become rich; 105 and when the glory of his house has been multiplied.”

Do not fear. [Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod.] The fourth part, containing the warning not to fear the powerful in this world, who leave all things behind with the light. For why such things are permitted to sinners is a common complaint. As though he said: “Because the wicked perish thus, and God redeems his own, do not fear to be good when a man becomes rich, although you, being righteous and yet poor, may seem to have laboured in vain.” It is no great thing that he is rich; even the base possess this. He then adds what is greater: “when glory,” namely glory consisting in worldly honours, “has been multiplied.” I say, not only his glory, but that of his house as well; for not he alone, but also all belonging to him, are honoured. He says that this too is to be counted as nothing. Therefore do not fear:

VERS. 18.—“For when he shall perish, he shall take none of all things with him; neither shall his glory descend with him.”

[Col. 0471D] For when he shall perish, he shall take none of the things possessed here with him [Aug., Cassiod.]; nor shall his glory descend with him to the lower world, because he shall fall into the abyss. Therefore it says, “shall descend.” And therefore he shall descend:

VERS. 19.—“Because his soul shall be blessed during his lifetime; he shall praise you when you have done well to him.”

Because his soul [Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod., Aug.]—his sensual soul, not his reason—shall be blessed, that is, exalted, during his lifetime, because while he lived he benefited himself; in death his soul shall be tormented. Or, it shall be blessed not on account of a good act, certainly, but on account of pleasures. For it is blessed by the favour of the luxurious, who, amid feasts, wish their hosts well. Therefore he shall also descend, because he shall praise you—that is, praise you, O God—when you have done well to him, that is, only in prosperity; in adversity he blasphemes [Col. 0472A]. But the praise brought about by prosperity is contemptible; that praise is of great merit which the force of suffering does not remove.

Nor is his own wickedness enough for him; indeed, he also:

VERS. 20.—“He shall enter even to the generations of his fathers; for ever he shall not see light.”

He shall enter even to the generations of his fathers [Aug., Jerome], that is, he shall imitate his ancient wicked fathers, and therefore he shall not see light. For those who imitate the worst fathers are to be condemned in their company. I say that he shall not see light for ever, because even here he is in inward darkness, and afterward he shall suffer outer darkness (Matt. XXII). But why is this so? Because:

VERS. 21.—“Man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts [Col. 0472B] and became like them.”

Man, though he was in honour, did not understand. [Aug., Cassiod.] As though he said: “God is not to be blamed for it, but man.” And therefore he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them. Here he repeats human deformity, so that the wicked man may cease from wickedness.

## Comparison on Psalm XLVIII: “Hear,” etc.

VERS. 1.—“All you who inhabit the world.” Jerome has “inhabitants of the west”; Pratensis and Pellicanus render “time” and “age” instead of “world”; Sanctes and the others have “world,” with the Seventy. Yet since we are temporal and mortal, and since the word *heled* signifies the time in this age in which we perish, the sense is not injured. Rabbi Emmanuel says that it means the world as capable of generation and corruption, and Jerome aptly suggests this by “the west.”

[Col. 0472C] VERS. 7 and 8.—“A brother does not redeem; shall a man redeem? He shall not give God his propitiation and the price of the redemption of his soul.” In order that the immediately preceding negation may be repeated, the second clause, “shall a man redeem?” should be read exclamatorily or interrogatively, according to Augustine. Our edition corresponds almost word for word to the Hebrew, *ACH LO PHADOH IIPHDOH ISCH*. Jerome translates otherwise: “Redeeming a brother, a man shall not redeem, nor shall he give God propitiation for him, and the price of the redemption of their soul”; here he reverses the order by transferring the earlier negation, which in Hebrew is drawn back to the first particle.

Similarly Münster, though with a different translation: “But a brother, by redeeming, cannot redeem anyone, nor can he give God his redemption; for the redemption of their soul is precious.” Pratensis: “A brother not redeeming, shall a man redeem; and he shall not give God his redemption, and the redemption of their soul shall be precious.” Pellicanus: “A brother by not redeeming shall redeem a man,” etc. Nebiensis: “By no redemption shall a man redeem a brother.” He also reports the opinion of certain Hebrews who think that *AH*, “brother,” is used for *EHAD*, “one,” so that the sense is: “One does not redeem; let each person redeem,” or “let individuals redeem.” Sanctes: “A brother not redeeming, shall someone redeem,” etc. The interpreters for Cajetan: “A brother not redeeming, shall a man redeem,” etc. The translation according to Campensis: “No one can by any means redeem his brother, nor give an account to God on his behalf.” Amid the perplexities of so many versions, no one need investigate further, since the ecclesiastical reading is sufficiently clear and corresponds most closely to the Hebrew truth.

VERS. 8.—“And he shall labour for ever.” Jerome and those adhering to Hebrew idiom seem to give the opposite sense: “but he shall rest,” or “shall cease for ever,” although labour and rest are opposed. Faber and Caecus attacked this passage fiercely. According to Augustine, it is understood of one who, while living, trusted in his strength and gloried in the abundance of his riches [Col. 0473A]. But when, after life has ended, he must render account before the tribunal of the Judge, he finds nothing by which to redeem his soul; and therefore he shall labour for ever. His pleasure-loving life, which he led amid delights, comes to an end; now condemned for damnation, he shall cease from those joys in which he was intoxicated, and shall thereafter be unable to avoid misery or find a place for repentance.

He sets forth the notable example of the feasting rich man and the ulcer-covered Lazarus, whose conditions were reversed in death. The latter had laboured until the end and shall live for ever; the former had lived until the end and shall labour for ever. From these things you see how “labour” and “cease for ever” are to be understood.

VERS. 10.—“Their tombs are their houses for ever.” Jerome: “their inward parts, their houses in the age,” so that these words are referred to the preceding verb, “they shall leave.” Pellicanus, Pratensis, Sanctes, and the interpreters for Cajetan: “their inward part, their houses for the age.” Münster: “and yet their thought is that their houses remain for ever.” The Hebrew particle *QUEREB*, since it signifies the middle and everything innermost, can readily be applied to a tomb, a thought, or anything else that suits the argument. The Chaldean and Nebiensis agree with us. How the sense should be understood is given in the exposition of the verse.

VERS. 12.—“Man, though he was in honour, did not understand.” At the end of the psalm the same verse is repeated, where they read *LO IABIN*, “he shall not understand,” or “he did not understand,” so that the future stands in place of the past or the present, according to Münster’s translation. In the present place, *LO IALIN* is read, “he shall not remain” or “he shall not lodge overnight.” *Iabin* and *ialin* are not far apart; thus it is highly probable that the interpreters read *iabin* in both places. Yet the meaning can be reconciled in this way: “Man was created in honour, endowed with reason; but alas, he did not remain in that honour, because he quickly transgressed, entrusting and yielding his will to the counsel of a woman rather than of reason.”

[Col. 0473C] “He became like them.” Pratensis and Münster translate: “like those,” namely the beasts, “which were destroyed” or “perished.” Jerome agrees with us: “and he was made equal.” Sanctes and others: “they are alike,” or “the beasts were made equal to men”; the sense is the same. Nebiensis: “he was made like dumb beasts.” *NIDMU* derives from the root *DAMAH*, which is ambiguous between “to destroy” and “to make like”; hence the variation arose.

VERS. 13.—*VEAHAREHEM BEPHIHEM IIRTZU*, that is, “afterward,” or “their descendants,” “in their mouth,” or “in their mouths,” or “according to them,” “shall be pleased” or “shall run.” Because of the multiplicity of meanings of the particles and their usages, one translates this way, another differently, another differently again. Nowhere does the meaning depart from sound understanding, provided that the reading received in the Church’s use is not condemned; it should deservedly be preferred to others, lest we drift through precipices. It is clear that *IIRTZU* is the future of the verb *RATZAH*, “he willed” or “he was pleased.” For if it were from the stem [uncertain: the source omits the term], “he ran,” it would be read *IARUTZU*, even if the earlier word is sometimes taken to mean “to walk.”

VERS. 14.—“And the righteous shall rule over them.” Jerome, in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela, teaches here, as in many other places, that the translator’s task is to express not word for word but sense for sense. Thus he writes: “You say that for ‘righteous,’ *οἱ εὐθεῖς*, that is, ‘the upright,’ is read in Greek; but this was rendered into Latin so for euphony’s sake. Otherwise, even in the place where we read, ‘Behold, it is written in the book of *εὐθέων*,’ we understand ‘the book of the righteous’; and we should not express word for word in such a way that, while following syllables, we lose the sense.” Thus he.

[Col. 0474A] VERS. 15.—“And their help shall grow old in hell.” Jerome: “and their form shall be worn away in hell.” Pratensis: “and the pit shall consume their strength.” Pellicanus: “and their strength unto destruction.” He then refers “hell” to what follows. Sanctes: “their form, to grow old, shall go forth to the pit.” Münster: “their form shall be for failure in the grave, into which every one goes,” etc. The interpreters for Cajetan: “their form, for the pit to consume.” The translator according to Campensis: “the treasure of these persons shall grow old.” In Hebrew it stands thus: *VETZURAM LEBALLOTH SCHEOL* [Col. 0474B]. The first particle is highly ambiguous: it may mean help, strength, form, and many other things. The second is an infinitive form, which ought to be explained by a gerundive. The third means pit, grave, hell. Since Hebrew lacks declensional variation, one interpreter refers it to what precedes, another to what follows; and lest the sentence be incomplete, each supplies what seems more suitable to him, taking the verb passively or actively, while another devises something else. Our reading and Jerome’s version come nearer to Hebrew truth, according to the varying significance of the first word. The others confuse the reader, though perhaps they aim at the same end.

“From their glory.” The Greek adds *ἐξώθησαν*, “they were driven out,” and this is read in the Roman Psalter. It is not found, however, in Hebrew or in the Vulgate edition. The Hebrew is *MIZZEBUL LO*: rendered word for word, “from a dwelling for him.” Jerome: “after his dwelling”; Pratensis: “for his dwelling”; Sanctes: “from the dwelling that was for him”; Münster: “from his dwelling”; Pellicanus: “hell is their dwelling-place.” The Latin Psalter corresponds sufficiently to the Hebrew, except that it puts “glory” in place of “dwelling-place.” But if “dwelling-place” is understood as the body, for the care of which alone worldly people tarry and glory, then they rightly said “glory” instead of “dwelling-place”: it shall grow old in hell, so that shame and contempt will be greater in proportion as their worldly glory was greater.

VERS. 19.—“He shall praise you when you have done well to him.” Jerome from the Hebrew: “They will praise you when you have done well to himself.” The others are similar, so that the sense is that the ungodly praise those who, following their example, benefit their own souls—that is, devote themselves to the pleasures of life. Yet the final letter *kaph* differs little from *vav*, and thus manuscripts may have varied between *LAC* and *LO*, that is, “to you” or “to him.” As for certain expressions in Hebrew put in the plural where we render them in the singular, this is of little consequence, since the meaning is certain.

106 VERS. 21.—“He became like them.” This has been discussed above at verse 12. But note that there Jerome translated “he was made equal”; here, “he shall be silent.” Therefore here he derives *NIDMU* from the root *DOM*, “to be silent.” Yet grammatically it would have to be expressed differently, unless one says that *DAMAH* also signifies “to be silent,” as Sanctes attests in his *Thesaurus*.

## Psalm XLIX

[Col. 0473]

### Title of the Psalm: “A Psalm of Asaph”

[Col. 0473D]

God of gods. [Cassiod.] Title: “A Psalm of Asaph.” As we said above, Asaph, together with many others, was set over the singers in the tabernacle of the Lord, and he is frequently mentioned in the psalm titles, both for the reverence due to his office and for the interpretation of his name. Asaph, in Hebrew, means in Latin “assembly,” in Greek *synagōgē* (“synagogue” or “gathering”) [Col. 0475A]. Here the Synagogue speaks according to its faithful part, the part that awaited Christ. By its voice the unbelieving Jews are more effectively refuted; and because its testimony is more certain, the Prophet uses it here while treating of the change of legal sacrifices into the sacrifice of praise, just as above he treated of the change of those same sacrifices into the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood. He also treats of both comings of Christ: by the first he gently invites, by the second he terrifies.

The sense of the title is: this psalm is attributed to Asaph, that is, to the faithful Synagogue, in whose person the Prophet here speaks. His intention is to warn that no one should return to sacrifices now brought to an end. Method: the psalm has three parts. Asaph, about to introduce God’s voice in the second part concerning the change of sacrifices, first—that is, in the first part—treats of both his comings, inviting by the first and frightening by the second. Second, the voice of Christ is introduced, warning that, when sacrifices of cattle have been abandoned, a sacrifice of praise should be made: “Hear, my people.” Third, he says from whom he desires sacrifice, when wickedness is imputed to the sinner: “But to the sinner,” etc. But lest anyone think too meanly of the Incarnation, the power of the incarnate One is proclaimed, so that all unbelief may be removed, when he says:

VERS. 1.—“The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and called the earth.”

God, [Aug.] namely the Word made flesh, who is the maker of gods—that is, who deifies human beings; for he gave power to those who believe in his name to become children of God (John I). He is also Lord of lords, and has spoken through himself and through heralds; formerly he spoke in many ways through the prophets. Note that “God” is said in three ways: substantially or naturally, as God—the Trinity, namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; by adoption, as saints are called gods through the grace of adoption; and by mere designation, as idols and demons. “And he called”: before saying what he spoke, he says what he did by speaking. As though he said: “I say, ‘He spoke’; and in speaking he did this: he called the earth,” not one land only, but all that is:

VERS. 2.—“From the rising of the sun to its setting; from Zion is the beauty of his splendour.”

[Col. 0475D] From the rising of the sun to its setting [Gl. interlin., Aug.], having sent witnesses to the ends of the earth. Therefore he did not call Africa alone, as Donatus says; he did not separate it, because he left no region that he did not call by his call. He called as much as he created.

And from where did he begin? From Zion, that is, from Jerusalem, because from there began to be proclaimed the beauty of his splendour—that is, his splendid beauty—for he was beautiful beyond the sons of men. As though he said: “He who called all nations began from Jerusalem, because the apostles, going out from there, proclaimed Christ’s beautiful form throughout the world.” Hence Isaiah: “The law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II). For the glory of the Gospel began from Zion. From there he who was beautiful in form beyond the sons of men began to be proclaimed, because there the Holy Spirit was given to the apostles so that they might be witnesses in Jerusalem and throughout the earth [Col. 0476A]. I say that God spoke and called; and though at that time he was hidden through the likeness of sinful flesh, and still sits at the Father’s right hand, nevertheless:

VERS. 3.—“God shall come manifestly; our God, and he shall not keep silence.”

He shall come manifestly for judgment [Aug.], because he is God. He is God—not just any one, but our God, who is the true God. And at the judgment he will not keep silence, as he does now, when even punishments are admonitions; for now he waits for repentance.

VERS. 4.—“A fire shall blaze before him, and a mighty tempest round about him.”

A fire before him. [Cassiod., Aug., Alcuin, Aug., Cassiod.] Here he shows how he shall come to judgment: a material fire, or the fire of an evil conscience, shall blaze. Therefore let the chaff fear that it will be burned—that is, it will torment the wicked. It shall blaze before him, that is, when they behold the Judge. Or, according to another reading, “Fire shall go before him.” This fire will be material; by it the face of this world will be burned, and the wicked will be burned, while the good will be purified. Therefore let punishment frighten those whom rewards do not invite.

And a mighty tempest shall be round about him. This tempest is God’s judgment; it will not be produced by winds but by God’s power, through which it will happen that his threshing floor is winnowed and the grains separated from the chaff. It is called a tempest because it will come unexpectedly and swiftly seize those whom the fire will burn [Col. 0476C]. [Aug., Cassiod., Aug., Gl. interlin.] And it shall be round about him—that is, among the saints and angels, who are called his surrounding company, because the righteous sitting with him shall judge and the angels, the reapers, shall separate good from evil (Matt. XIII). The tempest, that is, the judgment and sentence of equity, is called a tempest by analogy, because it shall come unexpectedly and suddenly seize; it is mighty because it shall separate the good, and it shall be from the wicked; it is round about him, that is, in the saints and angels. For the separating angels and the saints are around him. But when he comes for judgment:

VERS. 5.—“He called heaven from above, and the earth, to distinguish his people.”

He called, [Jerome, Aug., Jerome, Gl. interlin., Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod.] that is, he shall call heaven: all the perfect who shall sit above with him in judgment, namely upon twelve seats, to judge the twelve tribes of Israel. And he shall call earth, that is, all those to be judged. For what purpose? To distinguish his people, so that heaven with him may distinguish his people [the following words are corrupt or uncertain in the source]. For heaven distinguishes earth with him.

At the judgment, some shall only judge; these he here calls heaven. Others shall be judged; these he here calls earth. Yet among these latter some shall be saved; these he calls his people. Of those to be condemned he says nothing. Or, let heaven mean all righteous persons who are to be saved, and earth all sinners who are to be condemned. Then “from above” is read thus: the Lord, coming from above, that is, from the Father, called—that is, shall call—heaven, that is [Col. 0477A], all the righteous, and earth, that is, sinners. For what purpose? To distinguish his people, that is, to divide evil people from good.

Notice that he first called all the mixed multitude together, “from the rising of the sun to its setting.” But then he will call in order to distinguish. For tares grow together with wheat, and the master of the house does not allow them to be uprooted (Matt. XIII). Peter likewise enclosed large and small fish in nets cast into the sea and dragged them to shore while the net was almost breaking (Luke V). And in the Gospel, the master of the house sent servants to the crossroads to summon to the wedding whomever they found (Matt. XXII).

VERS. 6.—“Gather to him his saints, who establish his covenant upon sacrifices.”

Gather. [Aug., Jerome, Aug., Alcuin, Cassiod.] Seeing future things as present, the Prophet exhorts the gathering angels and applauds. As though he said: “And because it shall be so, therefore, O angels who reap, gather to him his saints, who establish his covenant”—that is, the New Covenant—“upon sacrifices,” that is, above the Old Testament.

Or, “who establish his covenant,” that is, who think upon his promises, “upon sacrifices,” that is, upon the works which they perform, which are sacrifices to God. As though he said: those who say, “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come” (Rom. VIII). Or: those who establish his covenant upon sacrifices are those who say that after labour follows the denarius. Or: they are those who esteem works of charity more highly than sacrifices of cattle.

[Col. 0477C] VERS. 7.—“And the heavens shall declare his righteousness, for God is judge.”

And they shall declare. [Gl. interlin., Aug.] As though he said: “He shall come manifestly and judge; and the heavens”—that is, the apostles—“shall declare this righteousness of his to the whole world.” We see this already fulfilled. For the heavens have already declared to us this righteousness of God: some shall be at the right hand and some at the left. Then no grain shall be with chaff, although they are now mixed, because God, who is not deceived, is judge—that is, one who distinguishes.

PART II. VERS. 8.—“Hear, my people, and I will speak; Israel, and I will testify to you: I am God, your God.”

[Col. 0477D] Hear, my people. [Cassiod., Jerome, Aug., Jerome, Gl. interlin.] The second part, containing Christ’s voice warning that sacrifices of cattle should be left behind and a sacrifice of praise made. Here he says what the God of gods has spoken. As though he said: “God has spoken. What has he spoken? These words: Hear with the ear of the heart, you who are my people.” In the same expression he shows both who ought to hear and why. As though he said: “If you are my people, hear. And if you hear, I shall speak to you.” Otherwise, if you do not hear, even if I speak, I do not speak to you.

He repeats this under another term: “Hear, Israel,” that is, “as Israel,” namely a man seeing God. As though he said: “If you are Israel—that is, if you see me—you do not neglect to hear me.” “And I will testify to you,” that is, through the Scriptures and miracles I will show you [Cassiod., Jerome, Aug., Gl. interlin., Aug.] that I am that universal God, who is God of all through power, and your God properly and more intimately because I have you as a servant, and because I was promised to you in the prophets. Therefore he says “I am,” because being belongs properly to deity. Hence: “I am who I am,” and “He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. III).

Notice that he first says simply, “I am God,” and afterwards says, “I am your God.” As though he said: “Even if I am not your God, I am nevertheless God: I am God to my own benefit; to your harm I am not your God.” And I myself:

VERS. 9.—“I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices; but your burnt offerings are always before me.”

For your sacrifices [Aug., Aug., Alcuin, Aug.] not offered, I will not rebuke you, because I do not seek animals for sacrifice. I do not want these; rather, I desire your burnt offerings, that is, those that are always within your control, not merely temporary, and which are before me, that is, pleasing to me. By burnt offerings he means the soul entirely enflamed with the fire of charity. Hence elsewhere: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. L). In that psalm he says that he does not desire animals as sacrifice or burnt offering. If the soul is enflamed, it draws the bodily members into its own service, so that they may not serve desire. Thus Leviticus commands the offering of fat with the kidneys (Lev. III), by which inward charity is signified. But lest you suppose these burnt offerings to be animal offerings, he adds:

VERS. 10.—“I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks.”

I will not take calves from your house. As though he said [Col. 0478C]: “I will not rebuke you if you do not offer them; and if you do offer them, I will not accept calves in sacrifice.” I mean calves from your house. I would accept calves signified spiritually, not those from your house. Hence the prophet: “We shall render to God the calves of our lips” (Hosea IV). In saying this he foretells the New Testament, in which all figurative sacrifices cease; nor shall I take goats from your flocks. Therefore I will not receive from you:

VERS. 11.—“For all the wild beasts of the forests are mine, the cattle on the mountains, and the oxen.”

For they are mine. [Aug.] As though he said: “Because they are not yours but mine, why should I seek from you what is mine, I who created it?” And this is: all the wild beasts of the forests are mine [Col. 0478D], that is, those which you do not possess, namely the untamed ones, are mine. And also the cattle 107 which you feed upon the mountains, and the oxen. As though he said: “The tame animals which you nourish and possess are also mine.” Or, according to another reading: “Wild horses and oxen, and even the birds, are mine,” because:

VERS. 12.—“I have known all the birds of heaven, and the beauty of the field is with me.”

I have known [Aug., Gl. interlin.] from eternity that no human being made all the birds of heaven, what they are and how many. As though he said: “The birds too are mine.” And the beauty of the field, that is, the abundance of all things growing on earth, is with me, that is, it serves me. Or, it is with me because I am everywhere. Hence in the prophet: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII). Or, it is with me because nothing escapes my notice: no future thing is future to him, and things now past are not removed from him; with him are all things future in the ineffable knowledge of God’s wisdom. And therefore:

VERS. 13.—“If I should hunger, I would not tell you; for the world is mine, and its fullness.”

If I should hunger [Aug., Jerome]—which never happens—this is said to convict one small in understanding. I would not tell you to feed me. As though he said: “If you give these things, perhaps you think I am hungry; that is madness. For the world is mine; therefore do not seek something to give me, since without labour I have what I wish, and its fullness,” that is, all creatures. But:

VERS. 14.—“Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?”

[Col. 0479B] “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though he said: I desire these things not in sacrifices, but in the poor. Mystically, by these likenesses he signifies the Church. The wild beasts are the Gentiles; the beasts of burden upon the mountains are the simple who stand upon the height of faith; the oxen are the apostles and prophets; the birds are the heavenly powers of angels; beauty is the converted Gentiles, who are the adornment of the earth—that is, the Church. The Lord hungers for the salvation of all human beings and is satisfied by all. But he does not desire the flesh of bulls in sacrifices, but in the poor.

VERSE 15.—“Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and render your vows to the Most High.”

Offer to God. [Cassiodorus.] Having rejected the old rite, speaking of himself as though of another, he indicates what we should do for him. [Col. 0479C] As though he said: I do not want these things, but offer to God—he does not say “to me,” but speaks of himself—as another, as afterwards when he says: “But God said to the sinner”; he does not say, “I said”—a sacrifice of praise, which is within you yourself, namely, that you give thanks in all things. Behold what he requires; and likewise, again and again, render to the Most High your vows, which are within you, not outside you.

VERSE 16.—“And call upon me in the day of tribulation; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me.”

And then call upon me. [Augustine, Gloss interlinear.] For you ought not to presume upon your own strength in the day of tribulation—that is, adversity—which is given for this purpose, that a person may call upon God. Or, our tribulation properly concerns fear for salvation, not carnal matters; and I will deliver you, lest you fail. Behold the reward of the offering. And thus you shall glorify me, so that you no longer depart [Col. 0479D] from me. Or, “you shall glorify me” means: among others you shall be a cause of honour to me.

PART III. VERSE 17.—“But God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my just acts, and take my covenant upon your mouth?”

To the sinner. [Cassiodorus.] Here begins the third part, in which he says from whom he wishes sacrifice, where the sinner’s wickedness is charged against him, because God seeks praise, lest a foul person think this is commanded to him. He forbids the tongue to presume to give praise when a corrupt conscience contradicts it. Yet praise is not forbidden to those converted to repentance, but to those who forget God, as he says below. As though he said: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise”; but see that you do not sing well and live badly, because God said to the sinner: “Why do you recount my just acts?” Therefore let him not be secure, as though [Col. 0480A] he were saved by this alone, that he has taught well.

Or the sequence may be taken thus: He said these things to his people, but not to his own—that is, God said to the sinner. This is said against the preacher; nevertheless, let the hearer be secure, whoever it may be from whom he hears good things, according to that saying: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23). This, I say, he said: “Why do you recount my just acts,” when you do not fulfil them in deed? That is, why do you bring forth in public discourse—namely, to the people—something concerning my majesty? “And take,” that is, irreverently presume to preach my holy covenant with your polluted mouth to others? [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] As though he said: Nor should a polluted mouth presume to teach holy words. Or this means the mouth of a heretic; for reading is not forbidden to those who are to be corrected. Hence the Apostle says: “I chastise my body [Col. 0480B] and bring it into bondage, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9). Therefore let wicked persons not mingle themselves with divine discourses. For this reason, in the Old Testament there was a bronze basin at the entrance of the tabernacle, where the priests washed their hands when about to enter the tabernacle and when departing. Hence: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52).

VERSE 18.—“But you have hated discipline, and cast my words behind you.”

But you. As though he said: You speak rightly with your mouth, but deny it by your deeds. And this is what is meant: You have hated discipline, because when I correct you, you murmur; you praise me when I spare you; you murmur when I chastise you. You have cast my words behind you, [Augustine] that is, you put behind yourself the things you speak. You do not see them; and do not say that you have not done this, because:

[Col. 0480C] VERSE 19.—“If you saw a thief, you ran with him; and you placed your portion with adulterers.”

If you saw a thief. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] Literally, you ran with him by consenting and praising; and you placed your portion with adulterers by some form of agreement. For in these two crimes he denotes all offences, taking the whole from a part.

Or thus: If you saw a thief of the sound understanding of Scripture, you ran with him by consenting; and with adulterers—that is, those who impose a false interpretation upon the Scriptures—you placed your portion by some assent: that is, you were an accomplice in the deed. And:

VERSE 20.—“Your mouth abounded in malice, and your tongue fashioned deceits.”

Your mouth abounded in malice, [Augustine, Cassiodorus] because [Col. 0480D] it not only does not rebuke, or keeps silence, but even praises; and it does so even when it knows the thing is evil, so that it is deceit. Hence follows: “And your tongue fashioned deceits.” He accuses both conscience and tongue. He says “fashioned,” because it is the habit of a deceiver so to arrange falsehoods that they flatter by the charm of their words. And this person does this even against his brother. Hence follows:

VERSE 21.—“Sitting, you spoke against your brother; and against the son of your mother you laid a stumbling-block. You did these things, and I kept silence.”

Sitting. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though he said: You take pleasure in doing this at leisure. For he does not disparage another by accident, but deliberately. What someone does while passing or standing, he does not do deliberately. But you, sitting, spoke against your brother—that is, every human being, [Col. 0481A] because every human being is a brother by the condition of first birth; and against the son of your mother—that is, of holy Church, to whom we are joined by charity—you treacherously laid a stumbling-block, that is, heresies and other things by which an innocent person may be ensnared.

Or thus: “Sitting, you slandered your brother.” Another reading: “Brother” here is understood as someone who walks rightly and teaches rightly; when a learned person slanders him, he lays a stumbling-block before the weak person, who is here called the son of the mother. And “sitting” means, as though he said: Deliberately you slandered your brother who teaches and walks rightly. And while doing this, you laid a stumbling-block against the son of your mother—that is, some weak person who still needs milk, that is, lesser teaching. For when one who appears learned slanders a brother perhaps teaching rightly or walking rightly, he lays [Col. 0481B] a stumbling-block before the weak person, who does not know how to judge. Therefore he is called the son of the mother, needing, that is, the milk of the Church, not yet coming to the Father’s table to be fed with his bread—that is, with the food of stronger teaching. Therefore he is unable to judge.

You did these aforesaid things, O wicked person, and I kept silence; that is, I delayed punishment, awaiting repentance, but you turn this into impunity.

VERSE 22.—“You wickedly supposed that I would be like you. I will reprove you and set you before your face.”

You supposed. [Augustine.] As though he said: I kept silence, from which you, O wicked person, supposed that I would be like you, consenting to evils, because you think evil things please me, since you do not believe me an avenger. But I will reprove you, and by reproving I will set you before your face: that is, I will show you to [Col. 0481C] yourself, and you will displease yourself—which you would do now if you saw yourself. But you would please me if you saw yourself. As though he said: What you placed behind your back I shall place before your face, so that you may know that you have acted wickedly and may see your foulness, in order that you may blush. And since the Lord has said this, therefore you:

VERSE 23.—“Understand these things, you who forget God, lest at any time he snatch you away and there be none to deliver.”

You who forget God, [Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Alcuin, Cassiodorus] whom no one can resist—that is, you who do not believe that I am God—understand what I have said, namely, that I desire praise, but not from a sinner. Let no one say that he was not forewarned. Therefore understand, lest at any time God—that is, I—snatch you away for punishment, and there be none to deliver. [Col. 0481D] When the devil snatches someone away, God delivers; when God snatches someone away, no one has power to free him. Understand this, namely, that:

VERSE 24.—“A sacrifice of praise shall glorify me; and there is the way by which I shall show him the salvation of God.”

A sacrifice. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine, Alcuin.] Not what wicked people sing, but a sacrifice of praise—not of animals—shall glorify me. No one offers this sacrifice and is wicked, because no one praises unless he is good; for if he praises, he also lives well. For no one praises if he speaks well yet lives badly; nor does one who lives well if he attributes what he has to himself, or exalts himself above another, to whom he ought rather to ascribe what he possesses.

Therefore let him cease from evils and offer a sacrifice of praise; and there—that is, in the sacrifice of praise—is the way, because this sacrifice is the path to God. This is Jacob’s ladder, by which the angels descend and [Col. 0482A] ascend: that is, the faithful ascend to praise of Christ’s divinity and descend to praise of his humanity. By this path I shall show him—that is, the one who praises—the salvation of God, that is, myself. Christ is the salvation of God, who comes with grace; one does not know him who attributes anything to another than grace.

## Comparison on Psalm XLIX: “God of Gods”

VERSE 6.—“Gather his saints to him.” Hebrew: “Gather to me.” But an easy error occurs between *li* and *lo*, that is, “to me” or “to him,” while the sense remains sound in either case. Likewise in *hasidai* and [unprinted Hebrew], that is, “my saints” or “his saints.”

VERSE 9.—“I will not reprove you for your sacrifices; but your burnt offerings are always before me.” Sanctes, Münster, and the interpreters for Cajetan translated it thus, so that the preceding negation is repeated in the second clause: as though the burnt offerings of the old rite were not before God, because they no longer please him. The sense is pious; nevertheless, others do not understand it thus. How it should be understood affirmatively, seek from the foregoing gloss. Or: those burnt offerings are before me because I have no need of them. The translator for Campensis read it interrogatively: “Shall I reprove you on account of sacrifices, or on account of a continual burnt offering being offered before me?” The Chaldean Paraphrast gives a very different sense: “I do not rebuke you because of your sacrifices, which you did not sacrifice to me in captivity, but because of the burnt offerings which your fathers continually sacrificed before me.”

VERSE 11.—“Beasts upon the mountains, and oxen.” Jerome and others, except Pellican, say “a thousand” instead of “oxen.” For if you say *aleph*, it means “a thousand”; if *alluph*, “an ox,” as the Septuagint appears to have understood it. And where there are no vowel-point marks, according to the reader’s choice and the suitability of the sense, [Col. 0482C] either meaning is understood.

VERSE 12.—“I know all the birds of heaven.” Hebrew: *harim*, that is, “of mountains,” through which the aerial heaven may be understood, unless perhaps the Septuagint took the prefixed, as they say, servile letter *he*, and then *rim* from the root *ram*, that is, “high, exalted.” It would then be as if one said, “birds of the height,” which means heaven. Hence the Chaldean: “those which fly in the air of the heavens.”

“The beauty of the field is with me.” Jerome: “the totality of the field.” Pagninus, Sanctes, Münster, and Campensis: “the wild beast,” or “wild beasts, of the field.” Pellican: “the pleasantness of the field,” with the Septuagint. The interpreters for Cajetan: “the moving thing of the fields.” *Ziz* has two meanings. The first is the same as “splendour” or “appearance,” and thus they aptly translated it “beauty.” The second is a general name for wild animals; therefore Jerome translated it “the totality of the field,” as if embracing both meanings. Others followed the other sense. The translator for Campensis has: “The little birds of the field are not hidden from me.”

[Col. 0482D] VERSE 21.—“Sitting, you spoke against your brother.” We have often pointed out from Jerome that a good translator ought not make himself a captive by serving the letter more than is fitting. Jerome himself taught this also in the present place to Sunia and Fretela, saying:

“You say that you have read *kateláleis* (κατελάλεις) in Greek, and you think it has not been correctly translated because we said, ‘You spoke against your brother,’ whereas we ought to have said, ‘You slandered your brother.’ That this is faulty and cannot stand in our language is evident even to fools. Nor are we ignorant that *katalalia* (καταλαλία) is called ‘slander’; but if we should wish to use it, we cannot say, ‘You slandered against your brother,’ but ‘You spoke ill of your brother.’ Yet if we did this, again a contentious critic would ask why we did not say *kata tou adelphou sou* (κατὰ τοῦ ἀδέλφου σου), that is, ‘against your brother.’ These things are superfluous, and we ought not torment ourselves with a putrid word-for-word interpretation when there is no loss in the meaning, because every language, [Col. 0483A] as we have said before, speaks according to its own idioms.”

VERSE 24.—“There is the way by which I shall show him the salvation of God.” Jerome: “To him who orders his way, I shall show the salvation of God.” Sanctes: “To one placing God’s way before himself, I shall show God’s salvation.” So too the others understand it in the same sense, except Pellican, who with us has, “There is the way.” The difference arose from a double reading of a single word having only two letters [the Hebrew characters are not printed]. For if [Col. 0484A] you place upon the first—namely, [unprinted Hebrew character]—the point called *smol*, that is, “left,” making *sam*, it signifies “to place” or “to set.” But if by *yamin*, that is, a point on the right-hand side, it is *sham*, it signifies “there,” as the Septuagint and Pellican understood it. The translation for Campensis agrees: “By this way I shall show him the salvation of God.”

## Psalm L

[Col. 0483]

### Title of the Psalm: “A Psalm of David, When Nathan the Prophet Came to Him, When He Entered in to Bathsheba”

[Col. 0483A]

“Have mercy upon me, O God.” Title: “A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, when—or because—he entered in to Bathsheba.”

We read in the Book of Kings (2 Kings [Col. 0483B] 11, etc.) that David, prosperously reigning and sitting in his palace, saw Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, washing herself; he desired her and, having summoned her to him, knew her. When he learned that she had become pregnant by him, he recalled Uriah from the campaign, in the hope that he might go in to his wife and that she might be thought pregnant through intercourse with him. But Uriah refused while the people of the Lord were suffering in the camp. Therefore the king wrote to Joab, commander of his army, that Uriah should be placed in that part of the battle where he would be killed. Uriah received this letter concerning his own death and delivered it to Joab, who did as David commanded; and Uriah fell.

Thus, after David had concealed the guilt of adultery, Nathan the prophet, sent by God, came to him and sought his judgment concerning a rich man who, though he had a hundred sheep, took from a poor neighbour the one little ewe that he possessed. When David judged this man worthy of death, Nathan answered: “You too have done this: though you had many wives and concubines, you took the one whom Uriah possessed.” At the prophet’s rebuke David repented, and, confessing his sin before all, cast himself down as guilty. This is what the title says: This psalm is attributed to David the prophet. I say, a psalm dealing with the repentance and humility which David displayed when Nathan the prophet came to him, sent by God to reprove him, who set forth the parable of the poor man’s sheep. He came, I say, to rebuke him for the sin he committed when he entered in to Bathsheba; or, to reprove him for this, because he entered in to Bathsheba.

[Augustine, [Col. 0483D] Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The peace of prosperity conquered him whom wars had not conquered. David, however, is set forth here as an example—not of falling nor of seeking the ease of prosperity, but of rising again if you have fallen. Nor should you despair because of the enormity of sin when you see that David, after the guilt of murder and adultery, pleased God through the humility of repentance. For when Nathan the prophet rebuked him, the king was not ashamed to confess his sin publicly. He did not excuse himself, as people usually do, but exacted from himself penalties which scarcely anyone would endure under compulsion. Before all he cast himself down as guilty, though all feared his judgment.

Hence the humility that is so powerful for penitents is specially shown here. Therefore this penitential psalm is used in the Church more frequently than the others [Note: [Col. 0483D] Cassiodorus, at the conclusion of this psalm], because humility is more fully displayed here; and because this is a moderate form of supplication, which even the weak can fulfil, [Col. 0484B] since nothing difficult is said here, as in others:

“Every night I shall wash my bed” (Ps. 6);
“Your hand has been made heavy upon me” (Ps. 31);
“My wounds have become putrid and corrupt” (Ps. 37);
“I ate ashes as bread” (Ps. 101);
“Out of the depths I cried” (Ps. 129);
“The enemy has persecuted my soul” (Ps. 142).

But here he asks mercy from the merciful one. Elsewhere, therefore, stricter demands are provided for the stronger; here, moderate ones for the weak. Perhaps this is why he will say, “I shall teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly shall be converted to you”: because he foresaw that many would seek pardon through this psalm.

This psalm is fourth in the order of the penitential psalms, and fiftieth in the order of the psalms, according to the manner of jubilee, because this is a psalm of remission. For the jubilee year in the Law was the fiftieth year, [Col. 0484C] in which all debts were remitted and alienated possessions restored (Lev. 25). [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] Hence jubilee was called “beginning” or “remitting.” So through penitential humility, of which this psalm treats, full remission of sins is granted to such persons.

Purpose: It exhorts to repentance. Method: There are five divisions. The first part is a plea, in which he seeks favour from the character of the Judge, through the mercy and justice by which he ought to punish, unless this person makes satisfaction; this is to seek favour from his own character. Secondly, confidence of cleansing is shown from the authority of God who reveals, at “the uncertain things,” etc. Thirdly, secure in confidence, he asks for love for all sinners and complete restoration, at “Turn away your face.” Fourthly, he says what he will repay when restored, at “I shall teach.” Fifthly, he prophesies concerning the building of Jerusalem, at “Deal graciously, O Lord.”

David, therefore, not excusing his sin but confessing it publicly, says:

VERSE 1.—“Have mercy upon me, O God, according to your great mercy.”

Have mercy upon me, O God. [Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] In saying this, he removes any place for judgment—that is, for examination—because the deed is admitted. “According to your great natural mercy,” whose mercy is the divine nature. As though he said: I flee to your mercy, that you may pour the healing draught of remission upon my grave wounds. [Col. 0485A] I call it great mercy because my misery is great and therefore requires great medicine. For one would have to despair of grave sin unless there were great mercy, whose greatness cannot be defined. He fittingly says “great”: the mercy which brought God down from heaven and clothed him in flesh in order to suffer and die. Through it David believed that he could readily be absolved; through it he knew that the human race would be freed. What then could God not give when he is asked to forgive according to his own nature?

VERSE 2.—“And according to the multitude of your compassions, blot out my iniquity.”

And have mercy upon me according to the multitude of your compassions [Note: [Col. 0485D] E. Gregory, *On the Penitential Psalms*], shown from the beginning of the age; that is, according to the multitude of your deeds, [Col. 0485B] which surpasses every magnitude of sins. [Cassiodorus, Gregory, Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear.] Behold, by mercy and compassion he asks. Mercy is in the nature; compassion is in its effect. He shows how he wishes God to have mercy: “Blot out,” so that no trace of sin may remain, “my iniquity,” committed against my neighbour. He will show below what manner of blotting out he desires:

VERSE 3.—“Wash me yet more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin.”

Wash me from the iniquity [Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear, Augustine, Alcuin, Jerome, Cassiodorus] by which I sinned against Uriah. He says “wash,” because he saw by the Spirit the washing of baptism, in which there is full cleansing and remission, and he asks to be washed in this manner. “And wash me from my sins,” namely, that which was in me through pleasure of the flesh. I say, “wash me more” than from the act of sin, because I sinned more than merely in the act: I knowingly and willingly committed both offences. Therefore wash me more, so that you may wipe away not only the guilt of the deed but also the liability of my will.

Or: “Wash me more” than I can understand how to ask. Wash me, I say, and cleanse me—that is, wash me in such a way as to make me clean. For some things are washed which nevertheless are not clean.

VERSE 4.—“For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me.”

For my iniquity, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] for which he asks mercy that God may forgive it—because he knows God to be just, so as to punish sins—he adds: “For my iniquity.” For one might say to him: You ask for sin to be blotted out through mercy; what then will become of justice? Will justice perish through mercy, so that this offence goes unpunished? No, because I punish it. And this is what is meant: Therefore do not punish, because I know my iniquity. [Col. 0485D] As though he said: Forgive, because I acknowledge it and do not conceal it; and my sin is always before me. He has done to himself what God will do at the judgment. Hence above: “I will reprove you and set you before your face” (Ps. 49).

Or, according to another reading, “my sin is always before me”: he does not have sin behind his back, as he had formerly when he neglected it. For he had sin behind his back when, as king, he passed sentence upon the rich man who took the poor man’s sheep, forgetting himself.

[Col. 0486A] VERSE 5.—“Against you alone have I sinned, and done evil before you; that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.”

Against you alone. [Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus.] I say, “Cleanse me”; and rightly I ask you to cleanse me, because I sinned in myself through pleasure of the flesh, but against you alone, because the king is superior to all and therefore ought to be punished only by God, who is greater than he. If one of the people goes astray, he sins both against God and against the king. But the king has no human being to judge his deeds. Therefore he says: “Against you alone have I sinned,” and “the evil”—committed against my neighbour—“I have done before you.” He says this because he knows that God is everywhere. Hence he accuses himself because he was not ashamed to act in God’s presence.

“Against you alone have I sinned,” because God is righteous, “that you may be justified,” that is, found righteous and true, “in your words,” that is, in the sayings which you have spoken; your words do not pass away but are fulfilled. Hence: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Luke 21). And you are so righteous that you prevail—that is, surpass others in righteousness—“when you are judged,” that is, when you are compared with me and others in judgment. For God is of such justice that he is willing to be judged with a human being. Hence in Isaiah: “Judge between me and my vineyard” (Isa. VI); and afterwards, as if setting forth his case before a judge, he says: “My people, [Col. 0486B] what have I done to you, or in what have I troubled you? Answer me” (ibid.). Therefore, against him whom he made king from being a shepherd, God has such justice that he prevails if judgment is held between himself and David.

[Augustine, Jerome, Augustine.] Or thus, from “against you alone”: David says this prophetically—that is, in the spirit of prophecy—to Christ, who has no sin. “Against you alone,” as though he said: Therefore I say to you, “Cleanse me,” because I sinned in myself, and against you alone, because you alone are without sin, and therefore a righteous punisher. For he punishes justly who has nothing in himself that deserves punishment; he is a just reprover who has nothing in himself deserving reproof. Among human beings Christ alone is this one, of whom Isaiah says: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. 53). “And I have done evil against my neighbour before you,” that is, in your presence.

“Against you alone have I sinned,” you who are so righteous that you may be justified—that is, found alone to be true—in your words, because you alone, in all things, could say “one” as God and man; therefore “God is true, but every human being a liar” [Col. 0486D] (Rom. 3). Or: You are so righteous that you prevail over all injustices; for you surpass all human beings and all judges, and one who thinks himself righteous is unrighteous before you. Before whose sight the stars are not clean (Job 25), who find wickedness in your angels (Job 4). Therefore you alone judge justly when—that is, although—you are judged unjustly: that is, when you have been judged unjustly by Pilate and the Jews.

[Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Gregory.] Or thus: You are so righteous that you prevail over the devil, death, and the Jews when you are judged in the judgment in which you were judged. For he sees the future righteous Judge to be judged by sinners, and victorious in that judgment—he who “ascended above the setting.” For by dying he became victorious. Hence: “O death, I will be your death” (Hos. 13).

Or thus, from “that you may be justified in your words,” etc.: He shows the Father to be true in the promise by which he had promised that Christ would be born from David’s stock. Some said that because of David’s sins God would not fulfil this promise; against them David says, speaking to God the Father: Therefore cleanse me, so that when I have been cleansed you may be justified—that is, found true—in your words, which concern the promise of Christ that you made to me; and may prevail—that is, show them to be liars—when you are judged by them for not doing what you promised.

Or thus: He argues against those who said that God would not pardon David because he had offended God so grievously. David therefore prays that God may spare him, and thus fulfil what he promised concerning pardon for one who groans in repentance, saying: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, I will remember none of his iniquities” [Col. 0487B] (Ezek. 18). As though he said: Therefore cleanse me, so that you may be justified in your words concerning the promise of pardon for the penitent groaner, and may prevail—that is, convict them—when you are judged by them for not sparing me.

VERSE 6.—“For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me.”

For behold. [Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] He said that Christ is righteous and prevails over others in righteousness. But lest it be thought that he prevails only over those who committed great offences, and not over those who, from their birth, committed nothing of the kind, he adds, presenting in himself the person of the whole human race: “For behold.” As though he said: Truly you prevail. “For behold.”

Or the connection may be taken thus: I have sinned, and it is no wonder, because behold, I was conceived in original and actual iniquities: that is, I was so conceived that I am both held by the stain of original sin and disposed toward actual sins. He says that he was conceived in iniquities not because union between spouses is a sin, since it is for the sake of offspring; but because what takes place—that is, what is conceived—takes place from flesh subject to punishment. And what is sown from a body dead through sin is born with the bond of original sin, and of temporal and eternal death. Therefore he does not say he was conceived in iniquities because he was born of adultery—indeed, he was born of holy Jesse and his wife—but because in all persons iniquity and the bond of death are drawn from Adam. [Col. 0487D] For no one is born without carrying both punishment and the merit of punishment, except you, who were conceived of the Holy Spirit. Therefore you impute sins even to those who have committed no actual sin. For in all are the bonds of sin, the propagation of death; you, O God, prevail, because you were conceived of the Holy Spirit.

The humility of the penitent must be noticed: he confesses that all things have been transmitted from his parents, whereby the odium of sin is diminished. For if he is a sinner from the root—that is, because he confesses himself a sinner from the root—such a humble confession of so many sins moves the mercy of the merciful Judge. He is accused of one offence and confesses all.

“And in sins of lust my mother conceived me,” or nourished me in her womb: that is, the concupiscence of lust, which is sin unless excused by the goods of marriage. [Col. 0488A] For this act, chaste in a spouse, has no fault; but the origin of sin in offspring carries with it the punishment due. Therefore I confess that I have sinned in this way, because:

VERSE 7.—“For behold, you have loved truth; you have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.”

Behold, you have loved truth in what is manifest. [Gloss interlinear, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] As though he said: I do not cast blame upon you, but confess the truth which you love. Here the penitent, because in confessing he has spoken the truth which God seeks above sacrifices, asks that God come to his aid.

Or thus: Therefore I punish my sin in this manner because, behold, you have loved truth in what is manifest—the truth by which you punish sin, although you are a merciful pardoner. For God grants mercy in such a way that he preserves truth, so that the sins of the person whom he forgives are not unpunished. For he forgives one who punishes himself. Mercy, therefore, is that a human being is delivered; truth is that sin is punished.

“The uncertain things”: according to some, this is the second part, in which confidence of cleansing is shown from the authority of God who reveals hidden things. As though he said: I pray that you spare me because you have already made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom—namely, the coming of your Son, which was uncertain to some and hidden from others—through the spirit of prophecy. [Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine.] For by this he indicates prophecy, through which it was revealed to David that God had a Son and that he would be born from David’s seed; thus he had greater need to beware of sin.

Or thus: “The uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom,” that is, of your knowledge—that is, things concerning your knowledge which are hidden from others—you have made known to me. Or, “the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom,” that is, the remission of sins revealed to me through wisdom, you have made known to me [Col. 0488C] through Nathan the prophet, who said to me when I repented: “The Lord has taken away your sin” (2 Kings 12). It is uncertain and hidden that God forgives such persons. Under this uncertainty the Ninevites repented, saying: “Who knows whether God may turn and forgive?” (Jonah 3). But David knew this, because Nathan the prophet said to him as he confessed: “Your sin is forgiven you” (2 Kings 12). Therefore he says confidently:

VERSE 8.—“You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.”

You shall sprinkle me. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Jerome, Cassiodorus, [Col. 0488D] Augustine, Augustine.] Here, according to some authors, the second division of this psalm is said to begin: confidence in God’s mercy, which is highly useful lest despair enter in, a sin graver than all others. As though he said: You have made known the uncertain and hidden things to me; and therefore I am certain that you, Lord, will sprinkle me with hyssop—that is, with Christ’s blood and the humility of charity—so that I may be fixed in Christ by the root of charity.

For hyssop is a lowly but medicinal herb, whose root is said to cling to a rock. Thus a person sprinkled with it in mystery becomes humble, fixed by the root of charity in humble Christ, and is thereby cleansed. This herb is also said to cleanse the lungs, in which swelling resides; so humility drives away pride. Thus I shall be cleansed; and he adds how: You shall wash me with the water [Col. 0489A] of baptism—that is, as in the time of grace you wash the faithful in baptism. Or: You shall cleanse me. Another reading: “And I shall be made whiter than snow,” that is, incomparably so.

Or he says “beyond snow” in order to indicate that he is to be the Lord’s garment, and therefore without spot and wrinkle; for Christ’s garments at the Lord’s Transfiguration became white as snow, by which the saints are signified. Hence: “As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. V). “Though their sins be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow” (Isa. 1). And this is what is meant: “I shall be made whiter than snow,” so that I may be the Lord’s garment without spot and wrinkle. Hence Christ’s garment shone like snow on the mountain. And thus I shall hear, and:

VERSE 9.—“You shall give joy and gladness to my hearing, [Col. 0489B] and the humbled bones shall rejoice.”

You shall give joy to my hearing. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine.] Notice that this person is humble. As though he said: I shall hear you humbly; I shall not speak against you proudly by defending my fault. And to this hearing of mine you shall give joy concerning the absolution of sin, by saying: “Your sin is forgiven you” (2 Kings 12); and gladness concerning the eternal things which you promise me. For one who humbly hears and learns rejoices inwardly in the truth. Hence the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears: he stands and does not fall by speaking, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice. And because I am now humble, the bones—that is, my inward parts—shall rejoice, having been humbled because they are without arrogance and have no swelling; for swelling repels what is poured in.

[Col. 0489C] PART III. VERSE 10.—“Turn away your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities.”

Turn away. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Jerome, Augustine.] The third part, in which, confident and secure, he asks for the blotting out of all sins and complete restoration. As though he said: The bones have been humbled, and therefore turn your face away from my sins, not from me, because I have them before my own face. For if a human being turns toward his sin, God turns away his face so as not to punish. Therefore turn toward your sin, so that God may turn away; lest, by turning toward it, he himself take notice of it—he who is the wakeful rod. Hence Jeremiah is told: “What do you see, Jeremiah? I see a wakeful rod” (Jer. 1). God is the wakeful rod, who watches over his people to punish them if they sleep in confessing; but he sleeps if they are watchful.

I say, turn away, and by turning away blot out all my iniquities from your knowledge. This man presumes more than [Col. 0489D] concerning that great sin of murder and adultery, and this through God’s great mercy. Charged with two offences, he wisely prays for all. I say, blot them out; and once evils are blotted out:

VERSE 11.—“Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inward parts.”

Create in me, O God, a clean heart, as though it were something new. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] But because even before sin he had been innocent, he adds: “Renew my spirit, making it right,” because the uprightness of my spirit had become crooked [Col. 0490A] toward earthly things. The spirit is right when God is good to it in every respect, as David was afterwards, even amid adversities. And do not renew me only in spirit, but also within my inward parts, whence adultery proceeded. [Note: [Col. 0489D] Gregory, Homily 13 on the Gospels.] For the loins are the seat of pleasure. Hence the devil is said to be one “whose strength is in his loins and in the navel of his belly” (Job 40). Therefore he asks for the remedy of healing in both parts, namely soul and flesh, because he sinned in them. He so desires to be cleansed that he appears to wish to commit nothing of this kind ever again.

VERSE 12.—“Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.”

“Do not cast me away.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As if he said: “Turn your face away from my sins, but do not cast me away from your face, from which light and healing come.” Fearing to lose that face [Col. 0490B], he calls upon that face, and says: “Do not take your Holy Spirit,” that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, “away from me.” He says “take away,” because he already possesses the Spirit’s gift: one who confesses and repents cannot do so by himself. For whenever a person is angry with himself and displeased with himself, this is not possible without the gift of the Holy Spirit. Or: “Do not take from me the spirit of prophecy,” which he asks above all else not to be taken away, while saying nothing about other things; “do not take away the Spirit,” and, through him,

**VERSE 13.**—“Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a ruling spirit.”

“Restore to me,” [Augustine, Jerome,] because by sinning I lost the joy of your salvation, that is, of Christ. By faith in his future coming those before us were saved, just as we are saved through faith in the event now accomplished [Col. 0490C]. The times have changed, not the faith. And “with a ruling spirit,” that is, with the Holy Spirit—by the grace of the Holy Spirit through which you forgave me—strengthen me. Not only do not take it away, but also strengthen me.

Or thus: because he says “spirit” three times, some find the Trinity here in God, who is spirit, not body. They call the “right spirit” the Son; they understand the Holy Spirit under his own name; and by the “ruling spirit” they understand the Father.

## PART IV. VERSE 14.—“I shall teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly shall turn to you.”

“I shall teach.” [Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Gloss, Cassiodorus.] The fourth part, in which he says what he will render in return when restored: having first wept, he now becomes a teacher. I say, “Strengthen me” [Col. 0490D] in the grace by which you forgave me; and, strengthened, I shall not be ungrateful, but shall teach either by example—for when pardon is granted to him, hope is given to others—or by word, since afterward he proclaimed the mighty works of God. I shall teach the wicked who remain in the faith yet sin, your ways, that is, mercy and truth. Those whom he had called wicked, he afterward calls the same persons ungodly, adding: “and the ungodly,” such as I am. Or, the ungodly are those wholly without God, that is, unbelievers; and these ungodly persons, I say, shall turn to you. Behold the profitable fruit of preaching: namely, that the ungodly turn to you. To say this is not self-exaltation but foresight, because through these words many who prayed have been released. “I shall teach,” which, in order that I may be able to do,

**VERSE 15.**—“Deliver me from blood-guiltiness, O God, God [Col. 0491A] of my salvation; and my tongue shall exult in your righteousness.”

“Deliver me from blood-guiltiness, O God, God.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] We all know that in Latin one does not ordinarily say *sanguines* (“bloods”), but *sanguinem* (“blood”); yet although the plural is less Latin than the singular, he spoke more properly in the plural, indicating that many sins are drawn from the origin of fleshly sin—that is, from flesh corrupted through original sin. Hence: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15), that is, the sins which arise from the corruption of flesh and blood. And this is the meaning: “Deliver me from bloods,” O God, that is, from fleshly sins, which are many, so that I may now cease from them.

Or thus: “Deliver me from bloods,” that is, from every corruption of punishment and guilt, and give me incorruption [Col. 0491B], which will be fulfilled in the future. Hence what follows: “O God, God, giver of my salvation”—that salvation will consist in incorruption, when this mortal thing puts on immortality; at present it already exists in hope. And thus my tongue shall exult, that is, with exultation it shall proclaim your righteousness. Otherwise, unless I have first been cleansed, I fear what was said above: “Why do you recount my justices?” Note that he praises righteousness when he ought rather to give thanks for kindness or mercy; yet it was an act of righteousness to receive one who confesses. And these two things are always joined in the Lord’s judgment; nor do I doubt of you, because, O

**VERSE 16.**—“Lord, you shall open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.”

“Lord, you shall open my lips,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus,] [Col. 0491C] closed because of sins; “and my mouth,” including the hidden recess of the heart, “shall proclaim your praise”: namely, that you created me, that you did not abandon me while sinning, that you prompted me to confess, and that you commanded it. I offer this as my plea because you do not desire animal sacrifices.

**VERSE 17.**—“For if you had desired sacrifice, I would surely have given it; you will not delight in burnt offerings.”

“For if you had desired sacrifice,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Jerome,] such as at that time was paid for expiation, “I would surely have given it.” The prophet saw the time of grace, when these figurative observances would cease. “If you had desired it, I would have given it”; but you will not delight in sacrifices, not even in burnt offerings, which are more worthy, and which are rejected by Christ’s coming [Col. 0491D]. What then must be offered? Not cattle, not a goat, but

**VERSE 18.**—“A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.”

The sacrifice of sinners [Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus] which pleases God is a troubled spirit, in which hope of pardon is given to those turning back, if they are willing to repent. A joyful, wanton spirit binds a person to sin; but a crushed spirit is the sacrifice by which sins are loosed. The promise concerning this sacrifice follows: “O God, you will not despise a heart contrite through repentance.” God despises a bull and a goat, and so forth—things which had their time while they promised something future—but does not despise a heart humbled by confessing to God, not exalted by excusing sin [Col. 0492A]. He says first “contrite” and afterward “humbled,” because it cannot be humbled unless it has first been broken.

## PART V. VERSE 19.—“Deal graciously, Lord, in your good will with Zion, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built.”

“Deal graciously.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine, Gloss, Augustine, Gregory.] The fifth part, now rejoicing over the building of Jerusalem, that is, of the Church, in which the sacrifice of righteousness is offered. As if he said: “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to you; and, that this sacrifice may be offered to you, O Lord, deal graciously with Zion,” that is, with the Church. Above, one person—the prophecy—was praying for himself. But now there is here a type and image of the Church, figured by Zion, for which the Prophet prays [Col. 0492B] in his own person or in that of the Church, saying to this Zion, that is, to the spiritual Zion, namely the Church, which contemplates something that it hopes for: “Deal graciously,” that is, send the Son and forgive sins. And do this “in your good will,” so that she may not attribute any merits to herself; “that the walls of Jerusalem may be built”—that is, that the defenses of our immortality, destroyed through the first human being and to be given in the future, may be established in faith, hope, and charity. These are the good merits by which immortality will be safeguarded for us in the future. He prays that this may be brought to completion, and

**VERSE 20.**—“Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and burnt offerings; then they will lay calves upon your altar.”

“Then,” [Augustine, Gloss, Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Jerome, Cassiodorus,] [Col. 0492C] namely, when many have been built up—that is, in the future—“you will accept,” that is, the sacrifice of righteousness, of praise, will be acceptable to you. Now a sacrifice is offered to you for iniquity: a contrite heart. But then there will be sacrifice of praise alone, which is the sacrifice of righteousness.
