“And then you will accept offerings and burnt offerings,” that is, the saints, who will be burnt offerings, so that the divine fire—the fervor of charity—will consume them wholly; and thus the burnt offering will be raised up, so that they become spiritual and death is swallowed up in victory. Then the harvesting angels will lay calves, that is, new peoples in innocence, namely of the new age, their necks free from the yoke of Law and sin, upon your altar, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem.

Or thus, and this is read of the present: I say, “Let Jerusalem be built”; and when you have built the Church [Col. 0492D], then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, that is, righteousness will be a sacrifice to you. And then you will accept offerings and burnt offerings, that is, lesser saints, understood by “offerings,” and the perfect, offered to you as “burnt offerings.” Then priests will lay calves, that is, the innocent and mature, free from the yoke of sin, upon your altar, that is, upon faith.

Or, the calves are preachers who fill the world with the lowing of preaching, and who are laid upon the altar of the Church by their elders, as by the apostles. The meaning is: then the greater prelates will lay calves, that is, preachers, upon your altar, that is, the Church.

Or, calves are those who offer themselves to God in sacrifice, that is, martyrs. The meaning is: they will lay themselves, calves, upon your altar—that is, they will offer themselves to you.

Or [Col. 0493A] thus, so that “the sacrifice of righteousness” is understood as the Passion of the Son, that is, of Christ, while “offerings and burnt offerings” pertain to believers. The meaning is: then the Passion of Christ will be acceptable to you as the sacrifice of righteousness; and you will accept offerings and burnt offerings, that is, believers suffering for your name will be pleasing to you. The remainder is unchanged.

## COMPARISON ON PSALM 50: “HAVE MERCY,” ETC.

**VERSE 1.**—“Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.” The Septuagint added “great,” to indicate the weightiness of the matter. Indeed, in some manuscripts it is read in the plural: “according to your mercies.” The plural has emphasis: *QHEHASDECA* [“according to your mercies”]. Hence Jerome, in Book II Against Jovinianus:

> “David is afterward tempted by the devil, and after his sin speaks in repentance: ‘Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.’ A great sin desires to be blotted out by great mercy.” [Col. 0493B]

**VERSE 5.**—“And prevail when you are judged.” In Hebrew, Greek, and Latin it is uncertain whether the verb *you are judged* is to be understood actively or passively, because in Greek and Hebrew the infinitive is used. If you translate word for word: “in judging,” or “when you judge,” *ἐν τῷ κρίνεσθαί σε*, *BESSOPHTECA*. Jerome, “according to the Hebrews,” rendered it unambiguously in the passive: “when you are judged.” His explanation on this verse also makes this clear. Moreover, in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 23, he cites it thus: “And prevail when you have been judged.”

Yet Jerome himself, in Book II Against Jovinianus, interprets it with an active meaning:

> “I suspect,” he says, “that you have sometimes lied as a human being; for every human being is a liar, so that God alone may be true and may be justified in his words and prevail when he judges.”

So too the modern translators take it actively, apart from Pellicanus. Campensis’s paraphrase likewise seems to take it passively [Col. 0493C]; he says, “you will be judged most justly.” But either sense is fitting: either that God may appear righteous when faithless heretics judge him for not forgiving repentant sinners, or—as Ambrose interprets it in his commentary on Luke, chapter 9—that when we sin, this must be attributed wholly to us, while all things that are just in themselves belong to God. For he says:

> “Therefore the Lord has mercy, lest anyone fail on the way. If anyone therefore fails, he fails not through the Lord Jesus but through himself; nor have you anything to ascribe to the Lord, who prevails when he is judged. For what can you say to him who has bestowed on you every foundation of the virtues? Did he not beget you? Did he not feed you? His food is virtue; his food is strength. But if through your negligence you lost the virtue which you had received, it was not the supports of heavenly nourishment but those of your own mind that failed you.”

So he says. Now it is evident that judging properly belongs to the Most Just One, in whom sin can have no place—that is, openly punishing sins and sinners. But where we have “and you prevail,” Hebraists, apart from Jerome, render it “you are pure” or “you appear clean,” *TIZKEH*. Jerome says with us, “you prevail.” And certainly *ZICAH*, if we trust the vocabulary of the Spanish edition, sometimes means “to conquer.” Münster too attests this on the authority of Aruc, that is, the Chaldaic dictionary. However this may be, the sense does not differ greatly. For the victory of a judge over the guilty person consists in his being free of the crime which he must punish. No one doubts how closely this agrees with God, who is justice itself [Col. 0493D–0494A].

**VERSE 6.**—“For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me.” It is quite unconvincing when Faber and Caecus contend that “iniquity” and “sin” should better be read in the singular because of original guilt. For they ought to have observed that David assumes the person of the human race and of the root of all sinners. Further, their argument from Hebrew—that “my mother bore me” should be read instead, so that David may express his humiliation more clearly by showing that he was not sanctified in the womb like Jeremiah and John the Baptist—achieves nothing, because the Hebrew word *IAHAM* properly means “to grow warm” and “to conceive.”

[Col. 0494B] **VERSE 7.**—“For behold, you have loved truth; you have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.” Modern translators, punctuating differently, also translate differently: “For behold, you have loved truth in the inward parts,” or “in the kidneys,” or “in the inner being; and in secret you will make wisdom known to me.” Jerome, according to the Hebrews, agrees with us: “For behold, you love truth; you have made manifest to me what is hidden and secret.” The Hebrew particle *TUHOTH* means “kidneys, inward parts”; and, according to Münster, it is taken for pure thoughts and affections. These are uncertain and hidden to us, as the translators rendered according to the sense rather than the words. Hence Jerome, writing to Sunia and Fretella:

> “We were unwilling to alter what had been read by the ancients; and the sense was the same, although in this place he says it differently.”

**VERSE 15.**—“And strengthen me with a ruling spirit.” Jerome: “Strengthen me with a powerful spirit”; Pellicanus: “You will sustain me with a spirit of freedom” [Col. 0494C]; Pratensis: “with a generous spirit”; so also Münster, and others. Sanctes: “May a willing spirit strengthen me.” The translators for Cajetan: “with a spontaneous spirit,” and so forth. But *NADIB* means a princely, generous, liberal person, so that the interpretations return to the same sense. Hence Campensis’s paraphrase: “Fortify me with that princely spirit”; Nebiensis: “with a noble spirit”; and so forth. The Chaldean reads: “A prophetic spirit will strengthen me.”

**VERSE 17.**—“For if you had desired sacrifice, I would have given it.” Hebrew reads: *KI LO TACHPOTZ ZEBAH VELTENACH*. If you render it anxiously, “You do not desire, or will not give, sacrifice, and I shall give,” the meaning is obscure unless it is read as a question, as Sanctes does: “And shall I give?” Hence, so that the sense might be clearer, the translators rendered it aptly. Thus Jerome: “For you do not desire that I should offer a victim.” So also Nebiensis. Münster, expressing this, translated: “For you do not desire sacrifice; otherwise [Col. 0494D] I would give it.” The translation according to Campensis agrees with ours: “For if you loved a victim, I would offer it.”

# PSALM 51

[Col. 0493]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “FOR THE END, A DAVIDIC INSTRUCTION, WHEN DOEG THE EDOMITE CAME AND REPORTED TO SAUL AND SAID: DAVID HAS COME TO THE HOUSE OF ABIMELECH.”

[Col. 0493D]

“Why do you glory in malice?” The title: “For the end, a Davidic instruction, when Doeg the Edomite came and reported to Saul and said: David has come to the house of Abimelech.” We read in the Book of Kings that David, fleeing from Saul, came to Nob, a city, to the priest Abimelech [Col. 0494D], from whom he sought bread and a sword. He gave him the loaves of offering and Goliath’s sword, and sent David to Achish king of Gath. Now when Abimelech gave David the sword and the bread, Doeg the Edomite, Saul’s chief shepherd, was present. When Saul one day complained that no one had informed him about David, Doeg said: “I saw the son of Jesse in Nob with Abimelech, who consulted the Lord for him [Col. 0495A], gave him provisions, and gave him Goliath’s sword” (1 Kings 22). Therefore Saul commanded his agents to kill Abimelech and all the priests who were in Nob. But since they refused to stretch out their hands against the priests of the Lord, Saul said to Doeg: “Fall upon the priests”; and Doeg fell upon them and slaughtered eighty-five men wearing the ephod (*Ephoth*) (ibid.). He also killed the men who were in Nob, the women and children, and the animals. Abiathar alone, the son of Ahimelech, escaped and fled to David.

[Augustine, Jerome, Augustine, Jerome, Augustine.] This title touches upon that history and does not differ from the truth of the history, except that the Book of Kings reads Ahimelech, whereas the title of this Psalm has Abimelech. Jerome likewise says that the Hebrew has Ahimelech. That indeed was the priest’s name; but because of the similarity of the letters *beth* and *caph*, which differ by a small stroke, Abimelech is substituted. Or perhaps, as above the title of the preceding Psalm has “before Abimelech” rather than “before Achish” (Ps. 33), with the name changed in order that you may not follow the historical event but the mystery, so here as well.

Therefore, pursuing the mystery, let us first consider the interpretations of the names and then their mystical meanings. Abimelech is interpreted “the kingdom of my father,” and signifies the Jews. The house of Abimelech is the kingdom of the Jews, which the Father established. Doeg means “movement”; Edomite means “earthly,” from Edom, the name given to Esau. Saul means “request,” and signifies death, which sinful humanity sought by word and deed, just as the people extorted Saul as king from the Lord [Col. 0495B] (1 Kings 18). David means “strong of hand,” or “desirable in appearance” (Gen. 22).

[Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] Doeg betrayed David and killed the priests, not David. Just as a ram was sacrificed for Isaac, not Isaac: in both acts, that is, in both instances of shed blood, the resurrection and life of Christ were signified. It was signified that Christ, although according to his humanity he would shed blood and suffer—as the ram’s sacrifice and the killing of the priests signify—nevertheless according to his divinity lived impassible and unharmed, as David’s escape signifies.

Doeg the Edomite—that is, “movement” and “earthly”—is the race of evil human beings: earthly, shifting, and not enduring forever. David the king ate the loaves of offering [Col. 0495D], which no one but priests may eat (Lev. 24), and thus prefigured not only the person of a king but also that of a priest. David, then, is Christ and his body. Here are mingled the earthly kingdom and the heavenly: that is, the good, who are God’s kingdom, and the evil, who are the devil’s kingdom. This Psalm deals with these two kinds of people; it is not a prayer for the wicked but a prophecy declaring what will happen to them.

The sense of the title is this: the instruction of David the prophet, directing us toward the end. Here is shown what he understood concerning what happened when Doeg—that is, “movement”—the Edomite—that is, “earthly,” that is, the race of the evil—came and reported it to Saul, because he betrayed Christ to death. What did he report? “David,” that is, Christ, “has come to the house of Abimelech,” that is, to the Jews [Col. 0496A], because Christ was then betrayed to death when he came to the kingdom of the Father, that is, the kingdom of the Jews, which the Father established. And this was prefigured in that history.

Alternatively, Doeg the Edomite, David’s adversary, whose name means “movement” and “earthly,” signifies Antichrist, who will move the whole world and who will come with signs and miracles before the coming of judgment. Seeking aid from Saul, that is, from the devil, he will announce that David has come to the house of Abimelech: that is, that Christ has come to the Church, which is the kingdom of God the Father. The sense is: the instruction of David the prophet, directed to the end. Here is disclosed the meaning of what occurred when Doeg the Edomite, that is Antichrist, came and reported it to Saul, that is the devil: “David,” that is Christ, “has come to the house of Abimelech” [Col. 0496B], that is, to the Church. The past tense is used for the future.

The purpose is to strengthen believers against Antichrist and his accomplices. The method: there are four divisions. First is an invective against Doeg, to strengthen believers. Second, it treats of the swift end of the wicked: “Therefore God will destroy you utterly.” Third, mockery is set forth because of his overthrow: “They shall see.” Fourth, it says how the good person conducts himself against him: “But I.” The Prophet therefore, making an invective against Doeg, says: O Doeg,

**VERSE 1.**—“Why do you glory in malice, you who are mighty in iniquity?”

“You who are mighty in iniquity,” [Augustine,] which is a very small thing: “Why do you glory in malice?” As if he said: One ought to glory in goodness, which is great. He explains what this iniquity is by adding:

**VERSE 2.**—“All day your tongue devised injustice; like a sharp razor you have wrought deceit.”

“All day,” [Augustine, Jerome, Augustine, Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin,] that is, without interruption. Behold the iniquity: “Your tongue devised injustice,” that is, its speech displays meditation upon evil. This shows a frivolous mind and rash utterance, because it does not think before it speaks. Hence Solomon says: “The heart of fools is in their mouth” (Ecclus. 2). Such a person, if he cannot do evil, speaks evil; but if he cannot even do that, he at least thinks it, so that when some evil is absent from his hands, it may not be absent from his heart.

He adds what this accomplishes: “You have wrought deceit [Col. 0496D] like a sharp razor,” that is, as promptly as a sharp razor, which shaves quickly and easily. Or, as a razor shaves off superfluous and useless hairs, so evil people shave the saints’ hairs, that is, they take away useless and superfluous things: evil desires and present goods, which the saints despise, along with life itself, so that they may be sons of Korah, to whom it is said: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10). The meaning is: “You have wrought deceit like a sharp razor,” because it takes away useless things and purifies the mind.

Or: “You have wrought deceit like a sharp razor,” which, while promising renewal, cuts; so also that deceitful one, namely Antichrist, promises his followers blessedness and kills them.

**VERSE 3.**—“You have loved malice more than goodness, [Col. 0497A] iniquity rather than speaking equity.”

“You have loved.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As if he said: You have not merely done evil but have also loved malice. One who loves it more than goodness does not abandon evil, because even if goodness sometimes touches his mind, he recoils from it. Note that he says: “You have loved malice more than goodness.” As if he said: You have both before you, but perversely choose this—malice. Thus you act as if you preferred water to oil and earth to heaven; but with these, that is, after their likeness, you fall lower, because just as they are borne downward by their own weight, so you, preferring malice to goodness, rush into the deep, since you embrace the talent of lead upon which iniquity sits, as the prophet Zechariah says [Col. 0497B] (Zech. 5).

“You have also loved to speak iniquity more than equity,” as though you do not even conceal evils under fair words, but

**VERSE 4.**—“You have loved all the words of your ruin, deceitful tongue.”

“You have loved all the words of ruin,” [Jerome, Gloss, Augustine,] your own and others’. I say, you have loved them, you who are a deceitful tongue, that is, talkative and deceitful. Or thus: “You have loved all the words of ruin.” These are words of ruin: “a deceitful tongue,” that is, deceitful words, instruments of fraud, spoken by those who harbor one thing in their heart and utter another with their mouth.

## PART II. VERSE 5.—“Therefore God will destroy you utterly; he will pluck you out and remove you from your tent, [Col. 0497C] and your root from the land of the living.”

“Therefore.” [Cassiodorus, Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The second part, where he treats of the swift end of the wicked. As if he said: You have loved these things; therefore God will destroy you utterly, even if not immediately, because first he will pluck you out, that is, take away your rank, and afterward remove you, that is, cause you to be transferred from your tent, that is, from this vain glory in which you remain for a time.

Or, “from his tent.” Another reading also takes the tent as the present Church, where Doeg the Edomite is now with David, whom he plots against: that is, chaff with grain, servants with sons, who will not remain in the house forever (John 8). This is the meaning: “He will remove you,” that is, cause you to depart from his tent, that is [Col. 0497D], from the present Church, where chaff is among the grain. As if he said: Now you are in the tent, but a servant does not remain in the house forever. If a servant now does any good deeds, he receives his reward; and he will pluck up your root from the land of the living, that is, from the blessedness of the saints.

Our root is charity, by which we are rooted in the land of the living. The root of this man—that is, his will—is uprooted from it, because it is not fixed more deeply through charity, but is in dry and barren rock, upon which scattered seeds withered because they had no moisture (Luke 8). Behold Doeg, that is, “movement,” of whom the title speaks. For he is the dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth. Or, the root of evil is greed, which does not bear fruit in the land of the living. Or the passage speaks especially of Antichrist [Col. 0498A], whose root is his ministers, who will have nothing with him among the saints.

## PART III. VERSE 6.—“The righteous shall see and fear, and shall laugh over him and say: Behold the man who did not make God his helper.”

“They shall see.” [Cassiodorus, Gloss, Augustine, Gloss, Augustine, Gloss.] The third part, where the mockery made by the saints over his overthrow is shown. As if he said: The evil will suffer these things, but not without benefit to the godly; for the righteous shall see now, that is, they now see what will happen to the wicked in the end, and shall fear, that is, they fear lest they too fall. In the future they shall laugh over him, that is, shall pronounce him worthy of mockery.

But here they weep, for now they walk, as Peter says, “attending to the prophetic word as to a lamp in the night, until day dawns and the morning star arises in our hearts” [Col. 0498B] (2 Pet. 1), that is, until Christ appears, who is our light. Therefore one must fear now, because events occur in the night. But then it will be day, and therefore they will then laugh over him, because there will then be no place for correction. And they will say: “Behold the man,” not God, “who did not make God his helper,” but made himself a god. As if he said: He did not hope in God but in riches. Hence follows:

**VERSE 7.**—“But he hoped in the abundance of his riches, and prevailed in his vanity.”

“But he hoped in the abundance of his riches.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] It does not say, “he possessed riches,” because one person may possess them without loving them, while another burns with avarice even without possessing them. “And he prevailed in his vanity,” because nothing is more vain than one who thinks a trifle of greater worth than God. Or this concerns Antichrist especially: “He prevailed in his vanity,” because more than all evil persons he will deceive the faithful.

## PART IV. VERSE 8.—“But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in the mercy of God for ever and ever.”

“But I.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The fourth part, where he says how a good person stands against him. Note that up to this point there has been condemnation of that party; here is praise of the opposing party. Behold a complete contrast. The evil hope in riches, but I—says the faithful people—who am in the house of God, that is, in the Church, am like an olive tree [Col. 0498D], green in winter and summer, fruitful, from whose shoot Christ comes. The people of God are this olive tree, from which the proud branches—that is, the Jews—were broken off, and the humble wild olive of the Gentiles was grafted in (Rom. 11).

I, then, who am the olive tree, have hoped in God’s mercy; that man, namely Doeg, in riches. I mean mercy enduring forever. What he said, “forever,” he repeats: “and unto age of age,” that is, forever and ever, so that by repetition he may confirm how firmly founded he is in love of the heavenly kingdom. Or thus: “I have hoped in the mercy of God,” not in order to gain earthly things, but for those things which are eternal, “forever and unto age of age,” that is, eternal things. And

**VERSE 9.**—“I shall confess to you for ever, because you have done it; and I shall await your name, because it is good [Col. 0499A] in the sight of your saints.”

“I shall confess to you for ever,” [Augustine, Gloss, Cassiodorus, Augustine,] that is, I shall praise you forever, because you have done the things foretold: namely, that I am an olive tree and that I have hoped in God’s mercy forever. “And I shall await”—I shall not be hasty—“your name,” that is, the reality denoted by your name, namely Jesus: that is, that I shall then be saved. Therefore I shall await your name, because it is good. The name is delightful, but only to one who tastes it; the world, however, is bitter. I say it is good, but only in the sight of your saints, not in the sight of the ungodly, who do not taste it through love.

## COMPARISON ON PSALM 51: “WHY DO YOU GLORY,” ETC.

**VERSE 1.**—“Why do you glory in malice, you who are mighty in iniquity?” Jerome and the Hebrew render the second clause in an almost opposite sense, as follows: Jerome, “mighty in the mercy of God all day,” so that the beginning of the following verse may refer to the end of the preceding one. Modern Hebraists place a pause at “mighty”: “Why do you glory in malice, O mighty man? The mercy or kindness of God is with me”—supply, “throughout the whole day.” But are not kindness and iniquity utterly opposed?

One should know, however, that in Hebrew the same word, *HESED*, denotes both kindness and vice. Then, where they now read *EL*, “God,” before the words “all day,” referring it to the preceding “kindness,” the Septuagint read *EL*, “to,” as though saying “unto the whole day,” otherwise “all day.” There is no difference at all in the letters; a dot and a third *yod* make the difference [Col. 0499B–0500A]. Because of the variant reading, it was necessary to follow one or the other division in relation to what precedes and follows, and to render the ambiguous word in one meaning or the other. The translator following Campensis took *el* not as “God” but as “giant”: “O criminal giant,” he says.

**VERSE 4.**—“You have loved all the words of ruin.” Jerome: “for devouring.” Or, as the translators for Cajetan render it, “words of swallowing”; Pratensis, “of oppression”; Sanctes, “all scattered words.” *BALA*, according to Hebrew, means “he devoured, swallowed”; and one who speaks rashly, as it were, swallows words. In the second conjugation it also means “he rebuked, destroyed, ruined.” Hence *BELA*, “corruption, ruin.” The meaning ultimately comes back to the same thing. For Matthew 12 says: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” And when someone, burning with a perverse heart to injure a neighbor, brings forth with wicked mouth as rashly as possible what he harbors in his malicious heart in order to overthrow him, it is fitting that the words immediately added are [Col. 0500B]: “a deceitful tongue,” *LESCHON MIRMAH*. From Hebrew this can be rendered in the instrumental or vocative case, though the Septuagint reads *γλῶσσαν δολίαν*, “a deceitful tongue,” either governed by the preceding “you have loved,” or with the preposition understood, *κατὰ*, “through a deceitful tongue,” as in the Roman translation, “in a deceitful tongue.” And certainly the interpretation corresponding to the Chaldean entirely agrees with our reading.

**VERSE 7.**—“He prevailed in his vanity.” Jerome: “in his plots.” Nebiensis similarly: “Others say, in his perversity.” The word *HAUATH*, according to Hebrew tradition, means corruption and perversity, and the malice of heart and deed. As to the sense, it matters little. But the Chaldean says, “in his money”; the Gospel teaches how vain it is to hope in that.

# PSALM 52

[Col. 0499]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “FOR THE END, A DAVIDIC INSTRUCTION, FOR AMALECH, OR FOR MAELETH.”

[Col. 0499C]

“The fool has said.” Title: “For the end, a Davidic instruction, for Amalech.” In the Book of Kings we read that David, fleeing from Saul, went with six hundred men to Achish king of Gath. He gave him the city of Ziklag, which the Amalekites invaded and burned while David was absent; they also carried away captive his wives and those of the others, together with sons and daughters. When David learned of this upon returning from King Achish’s army, he pursued and struck them, and recovered everything they had taken (1 Kings 27–30).

[Remigius, Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] This title refers to that history. The Amalekites, whose name means “a people licking the earth,” signify Antichrist and his followers, lovers of earthly things, who will as far as they are able ravage the Church at the end of the world. But David—that is, Christ, truly strong of hand—will free her after striking the Amalekites, that is, Antichrist and his followers. The meaning is this: this is the instruction of David the prophet, directing us toward the end, that is, toward Christ, which he had concerning Amalek, that is, concerning the Amalekites who ravaged Ziklag; through them he understood the members of Antichrist who would ravage the Church, and who are refuted here.

Or according to another reading cited by Augustine: “for Maeleth.” Maeleth means “sorrowing” or “in labor,” and signifies the Church, which grieves because the charity of many grows cold and labors until Christ is formed in them (Gal. 4). For her, namely for the Church in labor [Col. 0500C], the Prophet treats here of evil people, threatening and rebuking them, among whom she groans in travail. The sense is: this is the instruction of David the prophet, directed toward the end, composed for Maeleth—that is, for the woman in labor or in sorrow, who is the Church—for whose sake people among whom she groans are rebuked here.

It should be noted that the same Psalm occurred above as regards the surface wording. But it differs from this one in title and subject: there it concerns the incarnation of the Lord; here it concerns the coming of judgment. The Prophet’s intention is to strengthen and console the Church against the wicked; this consolation is shown at the end of the Psalm. The Psalm has a threefold structure. The first part is a rebuke of the wicked. The second is a threat concerning the end, at “Do they not know?” The third declares that salvation belongs to the woman in labor, at “Who will give?” Therefore, first rebuking and reproaching the wicked, he says:

**VERSE 1.**—“The fool has said in his heart: There is no God.”

**“The fool has said.”** [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine] Among these fools there is cause for grief; for, although the term is spoken in the singular, many are understood. *The fool*, therefore—that is, everyone who lives wickedly—has spoken, since God hears even though a human being does not; thus what is said is heard “in his heart,” though he does not dare utter it aloud. What has he said? “There is no God.” For one who thinks that evils please God does not think Him to be God. So also one who says that He spares everyone. For God’s being God is identical with His being just, since justice in God is God. Therefore, one who denies that He is just denies that He is God. Now he denies Him to be just who thinks that evils please Him, or that He does not punish them. This is the person to whom it was said above: “You thought that I should be like you” (Ps. 49 [50]). He says, “There is no God.”

Or, *the fool*, that is, the Jew, said in his heart—that is, with the deliberate purpose of malice—“This man is not God.” The wicked say the same today. Why so? Because:

**VERSE 2.—“They have become corrupt and abominable in their iniquities; there is none that does good, no, not even one.”**

**They have become corrupt.** [Interlinear Gloss, Jerome] Or the connection may be made thus: they say these things, and therefore they have been corrupted from every power of reason; and, what is worse, all who say, “There is no God,” have become abominable [Col. 0501B]. And this is so in their iniquities, to such an extent that among them there is none who does good. But:

**VERSE 3.—“God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God.”**

**God from heaven**, [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Interlinear Gloss, Alcuin] by sending His Son, looked down upon the children of men—that is, He had mercy on those who ought to be children of men, bearing the image of the new man (1 Cor. 15). Or, *from heaven*, that is, through holy souls, He looked down upon the children of men, that is, He admonished them, “to see,” that is, to make it be seen, whether there is someone understanding through knowledge, or seeking God through action. Or thus: whether there is one who understands, or, if he does not understand, whether at least he is seeking to understand God. I say that He looked down; but:

**113 VERSE 4.—“All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none that does good, no, not even one.”**

**All have turned aside.** [Augustine, Jerome, Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus] As though to say: In looking down, I found this: and together with their turning aside, they became useless to themselves and to others. Hence there is none who does good of himself—that is, led by reason. And, as if from grief, He repeats: “No, not even one,” that is, not one. For if He were excepting even one, He would say, “except one.” A fitting order is noted here: first they turn aside; then they become useless; thence follows [Col. 0501D] that there is none who does good.

**PART II. VERSE 5.—“Will not all those who work iniquity know, who devour my people as the food of bread?”**

**Will they not know?** [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin] The second part, in which the wicked are threatened with the end. For He who speaks on behalf of the travailing woman threatens them. As though He said: They say, “There is no God.” But will not all those who now refuse to know come to know in the future—those who work iniquity and devour My people, who travail and grieve, wishing to consume them? I say that they devour them as the food of bread, that is, continually. Will not all these, I say, know that God truly exists? As though He said: They will certainly know by the experience of punishments. And this is deservedly so, because they:

[Col. 0502A] **VERSE 6.—“Did not call upon God; there they trembled with fear, where there was no fear.”**

**They did not call upon God.** [Augustine] Each person calls upon that which he wishes to possess. By saying this, He consoles those who groan, lest they imitate those who prosper; for such persons did not call upon God, and therefore will soon perish. Hence follows: “And therefore they trembled with fear where there was no fear,” that is, they fear earthly things which ought not to be feared, but not those things where fear was appropriate, namely eternal things. So too the Jews killed God lest they lose their place and nation (John 11). Why is this so?

**VERSE 7.—“For God has scattered the bones of those who please men; they have been put to shame, because God has despised them.”**

[Col. 0502B] **For God has scattered their bones**, [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin] that is, their inward goods—those of persons who please men, that is, seek to please them. But no one broke His bone, that is, Christ’s, who was unwilling to please men, while the bones of the two crucified with Him were broken (John 19). Good people displease themselves when they discipline the flesh; wicked people please themselves. “They have been put to shame, because God has despised them.” This refers particularly and literally to the Jews, because they lost the place for whose sake they killed Christ. Or it refers generally to all the wicked. He uses the past for the future: “They have been put to shame,” that is, they shall be put to shame because they will be separated from the kingdom of God. “Because He has despised them,” that is, He will despise them. But Israel will be saved. Hence follows:

[Col. 0502C] **PART III. VERSE 8.—“Who will give salvation to Israel out of Zion? When the Lord has turned back the captivity of His people, Jacob shall rejoice and Israel shall be glad.”**

**Who will give from Zion?** [Cassiodorus, Augustine] The third part, in which he says that salvation will come to the travailing Church. As though he said: You have said, “There is no God”; but, O fools, who, proceeding from Zion—that is, from among the Jews—will give salvation to Israel? Is it not this one alone, to whom you said, “He is not God”? Certainly He alone will give it, when the Lord—who is now held captive in your hands—has turned away the captivity of His people. Then the true Jacob, that is, the Christian people, whom the elder shall serve (Gen. 25), shall rejoice here because it understands these things; and, having itself become Israel, it shall be glad in the future, because it shall know [Col. 0502D] perfectly.

## COLLATION ON PSALM 52: “THE FOOL HAS SAID,” etc.

Jerome interprets the title **AL MAHALATH** as “choir”; others, as “inheritance.” Some take it as a musical instrument. Münster says that it is uncertain what the Hebrew signifies. In Greek it is read: **ὑπὲρ Μαελέθ**, “for Maeleth.” Hence in Latin manuscripts it appears to have been read incorrectly as *Amaleth* instead of *Maeleth*, and this may have deceived some persons. Augustine’s own interpretation, therefore—*Maeleth*, that is, “a woman in labour”—from the Hebrew root **HALAL**, shows that the printed exemplars are corrupt, since in the title they have *amaleth*, whereas the interpretation appended protests in favour of “the travailing woman.”

**VERSE 4.—“Together they have become useless.”** **NEELAHU**, that is, “they have become putrid,” “they have become corrupt”; Jerome: “they have adhered.” For the root **ALAH**, by metathesis—that is, transposition of letters—is said, according to Rabbi David Kimhi in the *Book of Roots* [Col. 0503A], in place of **HALA**, which means “he oppressed” or “he was weakened.” Hence **HELEATHAH**, that is, “rust,” according to Jerome; and rust adheres to metal so as to corrupt and consume it. Thus the ungodly, through mutual participation in malice, ruin and corrupt one another, so that they stink before God.

**VERSE 7.—“For God has scattered the bones of those who please men.”** Jerome translates: “the bones of those surrounding [Col. 0504A] you”; Pratensis, Sanctes, Münster, and the interpreters following Cajetan, to the same effect. The Hebrew reads **HONAC**, from the root **HANAH**, “he besieged,” “he encamped.” Therefore it appears that the Septuagint read **HONEN**, that is, “those who curry favour,” and used a periphrasis in order to make the sense clearer, saying: “those who please men.” Pellicanus reads it as though the final letter *caph* were radical rather than incidental, because he translates “the bones of dedication,” from the stem [uncertain Hebrew term], “he dedicated.”

# PSALM 53

[Col. 0503]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END, IN SONGS OR HYMNS, AN UNDERSTANDING OF DAVID, WHEN THE ZIPHITES CAME TO SAUL AND ANNOUNCED TO SAUL: ‘IS NOT DAVID HIDDEN AMONG US?’”

[Col. 0503A]

[Col. 0503B] **“O God, save me by thy name.”** Title: “Unto the end, in songs or hymns, an understanding of David, when the Ziphites came to Saul and announced to Saul: ‘Is not David hidden among us?’” In the Book of Kings it is read that David, fleeing from Saul, came into the wilderness of Ziph and hid there. Then the Ziphites came to Saul and said: “Behold, David is hiding among us; come down, that we may deliver him into your hands.” And Saul came down. When this was reported to David, he withdrew from there and fled to the very secure places of Engedi, where, hidden in a cave, he escaped. Thus their betrayal did not benefit the Ziphites, nor did it harm David. For Saul was given into David’s hand in the cave; when Saul had gone aside there to relieve himself, David cut off the edge of his cloak, showing that he did not wish to kill him when he was able [Col. 0503C] (1 Sam. 23–24).

The title is taken from this history, though the psalm does not treat that history itself, but rather its meaning. For *Ziphites* means “flourishing ones,” and signifies those who flourish here in the present life and seem green with an abundance of temporal goods, whose glory is like the flower of grass (Isa. 41 [an apparent citation error in the source]): it flowers today and tomorrow is cast into the furnace. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] David is hidden among them, that is, the saints who are dead to the world and whose life is hidden with Christ in God (Col. 3). The Ziphites betray these to Saul when they endeavour to draw them into the kingdom of death. Their flower and peace are not to be loved, because they pass away like hay. David understood this in that event.

And this is the meaning: here is set forth the understanding of David the prophet, or of any spiritual person, who understands that the flower of the wicked [Col. 0503D] will pass away; for the foolish man does not know how the flower of the world perishes. I say, an understanding which he had concerning what occurred when the Ziphites came to Saul. Literally, the Ziphites came to Saul; their betrayal did not benefit them, and it did not harm David. For there, as we have already said, Saul was given into David’s hand in the cave. These are those through whom are signified the persons flourishing in the world, of whom this psalm speaks. And they announced to Saul: “Is not David hidden among us?” Now David is hidden, that is, those whose life is hidden with Christ, among the flourishing persons of this age. Among them they are despised and rejected, and these people betray them to Saul while striving to draw them into the kingdom of death.

And this understanding is “in songs or hymns,” that is, in praises, because one who understands this also knows [Col. 0504A] that God must be praised amid adversities. He knows this who directs the gaze of the mind toward the end, that is, toward final things, not present ones.

**Purpose.** He also exhorts us to praise God amid adversities.

**Method.** The psalm has two parts. [Col. 0504B] First are the words of the Church praying and hidden among the Ziphites, whose good is inward and whose reward concealed. Second, it tells what God does for it and for the Ziphites; therefore it offers praises, at the words, “For behold.” Thus the Church, praying while hidden among the Ziphites, says:

**VERSE 1.—“O God, save me by thy name, and judge me in thy strength.”**

**O God, save me**, [Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine] in the world. And do this “by Thy name,” which has been preached to the world. As though she said: Others ask to be delivered by one thing or another; I ask by Thy name, namely that name of humility which is salvation. Save me here, that is, fulfil in me the reality of Thy name; and afterward I shall not fear to be judged in strength. Hence follows: “And in Thy strength,” that is, in the future judgment, where Thy strength will appear, “judge me,” that is, separate [Col. 0504C] me from the Ziphites, so that, when their grass withers and their flower falls, my flower, which is in the courts of the house of the Lord, may remain for ever.

**VERSE 2.—“O God, hear my prayer; give ear to the words of my mouth.”**

**O God, hear.** [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] Again, He repeats “God,” the name of power, lest aid be delayed. And, O God, hear my prayer, because I do not ask Thee for the flower of the Ziphites; and give ear—that is, lay up in Thy mind—the words of my mouth, because the heart is also shown through words. Therefore receive them Thou; even though the Ziphites hear them, they do not understand them, since they have known nothing but temporal things.

**VERSE 3.—“For strangers have risen up against me, and the mighty have sought my soul; and they have not set God before their sight.”**

**For strangers.** [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus] This is the cause of the prayer, and the Church speaks. As though she said: Therefore I pray, because strangers, that is, wicked persons, have risen against me; and the mighty, that is, persecutors, have sought my soul; and they have not set God before their sight, because they think that God does not know what they do—people who behold nothing but the world: how coin may be added to coin, how flocks and wealth may be increased. Or David speaks in his own person. As though he said: Therefore I pray, because strangers, that is, the Ziphites, rose up against me. But it does not seem that the Ziphites were strangers to David, since they were of the same tribe (Josh. 15). For Ziph was a village belonging [Col. 0505A] to the tribe of Judah, the tribe from which David came. Yet they were strangers through the flourishing of their malice, for they betrayed him—not strangers by tribe or place. “And the mighty,” that is, Saul and his servants, “have sought my soul, and have not set God before their sight.” This remains unchanged.

**PART II. Διάψαλμα (Diapsalma). VERSE 4.—“For behold, God helps me, and the Lord is the protector of my soul.”**

**For behold, God.** [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] The second part, in which he says what God does for him and for the Ziphites. Therefore he gives praise. **114** As though he said: They have not set God before their eyes, as is evident from this: “For behold, God helps me” inwardly, where no one sees, where our glory does not lie in outward bloom. Those among whom I lie hidden do not know this; yet they would see that He helps me [Col. 0505B] if they set God before their eyes. Therefore He helps me, as I labour to bear what they inflict. May He help me in this way; and this is because “the Lord is the protector of my soul,” even if He abandons the body.

Or thus: He turns evils upon my enemies and will destroy in His truth those who flourish in the happiness of the world. And he says this while speaking to God.

**VERSE 5.—“Turn evils upon my enemies, and in thy truth destroy them.”**

**Turn.** [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus] He predicts, he does not wish for it. This is the meaning: O God, “turn,” that is, Thou wilt turn, evils upon my enemies—that is, Thou wilt turn them away from me and upon them—and in Thy truth destroy them. As though he said: They flourish for a time; let them perish eternally. That is, they flourish in false goods but perish in true punishments. It is prophecy, not a wish. [Col. 0505C]

Or according to another reading: “And in Thy strength destroy them,” those whom Thou hast tolerated in Thy weakness. Or he prays for their conversion, and this is the sacrifice which he offers to God for his deliverance, saying: O Lord, turn evils upon my enemies, and destroy them with respect to their former disposition; “in Thy truth,” that is, so that they may come to Thy truth. And then:

**VERSE 6.—“I will freely sacrifice to thee; I will confess thy name, O Lord, because it is good.”**

[Col. 0506A] **I will sacrifice to Thee**, [Augustine] a sacrifice of praise, not cattle, and freely, because I love gratuitously that which I praise: I praise it for its own sake, not for something else which I may wish to receive from it. One who praises for another reason praises from necessity; if he possessed that other thing, he would not praise. But to me, even the things He has given are pleasing because of the Giver. And I will confess Thy name, O Lord, that is, I will praise it, because it is good: I find nothing better than that name. This is to confess freely: namely, to confess because it is good, not because it gives temporal things. Therefore I shall confess Thy good name.

**VERSE 7.—“For thou hast delivered me from every tribulation, and my eye has looked down upon my enemies.”**

**For Thou hast delivered me from every tribulation.** [Augustine] [Col. 0506B] In this he has proved the name good; if he had known otherwise, tribulation would not have been necessary to him. And my eye, lifted upward over my flourishing enemies, has looked down: caught up in mind to God, it sees that every flower is like grass.

## COLLATION ON PSALM 53: “O GOD,” etc.

**VERSE 5.—“Turn evils upon my enemies.”** Faber and Caecus think this passage corrupt, indeed even at variance with the true sense, which is immediately displayed when the words “destroy them” are added. For this reason, as they wish, one ought to say: “Turn *toward* my enemies evils,” especially since Jerome says from the Hebrew: “Render evil to those who lie in wait for me.” **IASSIB**, according to Sanctes in his *Thesaurus*. After Kimhi it is written with *vav* and read with *yod*, because it may be in the verb-form called **qal**, or in **hiphil**, meaning “he turned” or “he turned away.” [Col. 0506C] He turns evils upon my enemies and turns away from me the evils which He brings upon my enemies. This sense expresses God’s mercy and justice more fully: mercy toward David, who is delivered; justice against the Ziphites, who had deceitfully wished to destroy him. That we express this in the second person and imperative does no harm to the meaning.

**VERSE 7.—“My eye has looked down upon my enemies.”** The Hebrew simply says: “My eye has seen my enemies.” But the interpreters rightly said that this seeing means looking down upon them. Hence Sanctes used a periphrasis: “And my eye has seen in my enemies what I wished.” Münster is similar, and the translation according to Campensis has: “May my eye look down upon my enemies.”

# PSALM 54

[Col. 0505]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END, IN SONGS OR HYMNS, AN UNDERSTANDING OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0505D]

**“Hearken, O God, to my prayer.”** Title: “Unto the end, in songs or hymns, an understanding of David.” [Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus] By David here is understood the Church, which must earnestly consider the evil in which it now is, and from which it desires to be delivered, mourning among the evils of the world; for in the present sojourn there is no place for joy, but for sorrow. And this is the meaning: here is shown the understanding of David, that is, of the Church—what it ought to understand. For the Church must carefully understand the evil in which it now is, and from which it desires to be delivered. For one who understands mourns amid the evils of the world, because this country is not one of joy but of sorrow [Col. 0506D]; another does not understand.

And this understanding is “in songs or hymns,” that is, in praises, so that one who understands here always praises God, whether He instructs us in adversities or comforts us in joys. This happens if the gaze of the mind is directed to the end, that is, to Christ, or to the future consummation. Throughout this psalm the Church speaks, either in its own person or in that of Christ. When it speaks in its own person, it speaks as a man faint-hearted amid a storm, who, while tossed and submerged in the waves of the world, like Peter on the sea (Matt. 14), cries to Jesus and determines in his weakness to separate himself from so many scandals, lest he neither profit them nor harm himself—like David, who fled into solitude because of the annoyance of his fellow citizens. But when it speaks in Christ’s person, the complete character of the servant’s form in Christ is described, so that an example of humility may be given us, since Christ, though so exalted, humbled Himself so greatly. Accordingly, this psalm is the third among those which treat more fully of Christ’s passion and resurrection.

[Augustine, Cassiodorus] **Purpose.** It exhorts the Church to attend to its evils and to mourn amid them.

**Method.** The psalm has three parts. The first is a preceding prayer against the evils or waves of the world. The second concerns this faint-hearted man, now safe in solitude, who hopes for God’s help and utters imprecations in return, at the words, “I awaited.” The third declares, proceeding alternately, what happens to himself and to them, at the words, “But I.” Therefore the Church, labouring among the waves of the world, prays, saying:

[Col. 0507B] **VERSE 1.—“Hearken, O God, to my prayer; and do not despise my supplication. Attend to me, and hear me.”**

**Hearken, O God, to my prayer.** [Augustine, Cassiodorus] These are the words of one afflicted and desiring deliverance. And then: “Do not despise my supplication,” as happens to those whose prayer, once fulfilled, is afterward despised because it was not for eternal things. For even if God gives temporal things to someone who asks, nevertheless that person’s prayer is not acceptable to Him, because it lacks its proper end. “Attend to me and hear me.” For what is happening to You? Behold:

**VERSE 2.—“I have been made sorrowful in my exercise, and I have been troubled by the voice of the enemy and by the tribulation of the sinner.”**

**I have been made sorrowful in my exercise**, [Augustine] that is, in the things which the wicked inflict, as he will say openly afterward. By these wicked persons every good person is exercised: the wicked person lives either that he may be corrected, or that through him the good person may be exercised. “And I have been troubled in the sea of the world by the strong wind of tribulations.” Just as Peter, seeing a violent wind arise, was afraid (Matt. 14), so this man was troubled in the struggle itself by which he is exercised among the wicked. While he wishes to love his enemies, whose correction he loves, the abundance of their malice begins to make him hate them. Thus he begins to sink in the waves. Hence: “I have been troubled by the voice of the enemy and by the tribulation of the sinner.” This is the exercise in which he was grieved: it troubles the eye of the mind by anger as a speck of straw does, yet does not extinguish it by hatred as a beam would. Afterwards he assigns each point to its corresponding phrase, showing how he has been troubled by the voice of the enemy and by the tribulation of the sinner. As though he said: I have been troubled by the enemy’s voice.

[Col. 0507D] **VERSE 3.—“For iniquities have turned against me, and in anger they were troublesome to me.”**

**For they have turned against me their iniquities**, [Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus] which were their own. Therefore He says, “They have turned,” because the onset of their malice is like the course of a stream. And this is “by the tribulation of the sinner”; and, that is, because in their anger—that is, in their fury, not because I deserved it—they were troublesome to me, but destructive to themselves. And through this:

**VERSE 4.—“My heart has been troubled within me, and the fear of death has fallen upon me.”**

**My heart has been troubled within me.** [Augustine] This is what is said elsewhere: “My eye has been troubled because of anger” (Ps. 6). Hence follows the fear of death. The death of the soul is hatred, just as life is love. Hence he adds: “And the fear of death has fallen upon me,” because:

[Col. 0508A] **VERSE 5.—“Fear and trembling have come upon me, and darkness has covered me.”**

[Jerome, Augustine] Fear of the mind and trembling of the body came upon me, and darkness covered me. Darkness means wicked people, who persecute the Church and cover it with hatred, because “he who hates his brother is in darkness” (1 John 2). But in this weakness what does he say?

**VERSE 6.—“And I said: Who will give me wings like a dove’s, that I may fly away and be at rest?”**

[Col. 0508B] **And I said: Who will give?** [Augustine] Seeing evils everywhere, and seeing that he makes no progress with the wicked while the wicked harm him, this man considers what he should do. He wishes for a time to separate himself from these scandals, lest by remaining among them he increase the sins of the weak. Hence he asks for the wings of virtues, by which he may fly away to solitude and ascend to the height of contemplation.

God gives these wings of virtues to one who does not possess them. But to one who has them, a prelate of the Church sometimes gives them when he releases wings that have been bound. For some possess these wings but have them bound by pastoral care and office; they cannot use them to fly away into solitude unless they are first released. Thus one who releases bound wings gives wings which, though present, were not available for use and did not belong to the person possessing them in this respect.

Adorned with these wings, Isaac went out into the field to meditate (Gen. 24); and Mary sat at the Lord’s feet, attending to what He said, while her sister was distracted by many concerns (Luke 10). Desiring these wings, then, he says: “And I said: Who will give me the wings of virtues? And having them, I shall fly away into solitude, and there I shall rest in contemplation.” This man desires solitude. “Give me,” I say, wings like a dove’s, not like a raven’s. For the raven, sent forth from the ark, did not return afterward; but the dove, sent forth carrying an olive branch, returned (Gen. 8). The dove seeks to fly away from troubles, but does not lose love and always mourns. So too a good person wishes to separate bodily from those whom he cannot benefit, yet not in love: he loves their correction and grieves at the ruin of their transgression. For he lives devoutly in Christ.

To this inward disposition belongs what the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Or who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (1 Cor. 11 [an apparent citation error in the source]). Thus others’ evils are to him like a persecution, as Lot was tormented in Sodom by the evil life of the Sodomites (Gen. 19). Therefore he desires to flee and remain in the wilderness because of the multitude of tribulations and scandals. Yet at times he is bound, not by the birdlime of covetousness, but by pastoral care and office, so that he cannot leave unless he is released. If he is not released, then let him say: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1); “but it is necessary to remain for your sake.” Thus there is merit for him in his desire.

Alternatively, this man desires death, through which he may be separated from the wicked, and says by comparison: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, that I may fly away and rest?” **115** That is, who will give me wings so that I may be dissolved [Col. 0509A] and thus fly away from them and rest with Christ?

**VERSE 7.—“Behold, I have gone far away in flight, and I have remained in solitude.”**

**Behold, I have gone far away in flight.** This man asked for wings and received them, but not in the manner in which he had asked—namely, that he might bodily fly away from them. God did something better for him than he asked. [Augustine] By grace God so strengthened him that, while bodily among the wicked, he himself might advance, even if they did not; and that the charity of the good might not be broken. This is the meaning: I said, “Who will give me wings?” and I received them, because, behold, fleeing, I have gone far away from the wicked—not by place, lest the charity of the good be broken, and lest the exercise provided by the wicked be lost, whom God mingles with others as He did Judas with the apostles. [Note: [Col. 0509D] Gregory, *Morals*, book IV, chapter 35.]

The person who flees and goes far away is one who lifts himself from the multitude of earthly desires into the lofty contemplation of God. It follows: “And I remained in solitude,” [Augustine] the solitude of the mind, where no one is with him except God, where there is rest. [Note: [Col. 0510D] Gregory, as cited above.] For he remains in solitude who perseveres in the mind’s withdrawn attention.

Alternatively, the whole psalm is read from its beginning in Christ’s person, in whom the servant’s form is described. Therefore Christ says, according to His humanity: “Hearken, O God, to my prayer, and do not despise my supplication; attend to me,” [Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus, Jerome] because I am one to whom Thou shouldst attend; “and hear me,” who am worthy. For what is happening to Thee? “I have been made sorrowful,” through human weakness, “in my exercise.” Under this one term Christ’s whole life is set forth: He never relaxed from what He had undertaken through any idleness. In what was He sorrowful? Because the faithless did not bear fruit. “And I have been troubled by the voice of the enemy,” who called Me a Samaritan and one having a demon (John 8). “And by the tribulation of the sinner.” [Interlinear Gloss, Jerome, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Jerome, Cassiodorus] This was not through My deserving but through their wickedness. “For iniquities have turned against me,” because they imputed their evils to Me; “and in their anger they were troublesome to Me,” but destructive to themselves.

And through this “my heart has been troubled”: by the law of the flesh the mind is troubled. And this occurred “within me”; it did not proceed from Me—that is, I was troubled not through necessity or My own deserving, but by My free will. “And the fear of death fell,” as a weight, “upon Me.” Or, “it fell upon Me” because there death perishes over which it has no right. Hence: “O death, I will be thy death” (Hos. 13) [Col. 0509D]. “And fear” of the mind “and trembling” of the body came upon Me. It is a property of death that we first fear it and then tremble at it. “And darkness covered Me,” according to another reading; that is, death followed.

And while placed in this turmoil I said: “Who will give Me, unless Thou, Lord Father, wings like a dove’s, that I may fly away and rest?” That is, that I may fly away from the unbelieving Jews and rest among the believing Gentiles. [Alcuin, Jerome, Cassiodorus] For as the dove sent forth, finding muddy places, returned to the ark, so Christ, finding the hearts of the Jews muddy, flew away to the Gentiles. Hence follows: “Behold, I have gone far away in flight,” from the Jews, “and remained in the solitude,” of the Gentiles. Hence Isaiah says: “Let the wilderness rejoice and blossom like the lily” (Isa. 35) [Col. 0510A]. And elsewhere: “Rejoice, thou barren woman that dost not bear,” etc. (Isa. 54).

This also touches literally upon the fact that He avoided His persecutors in order to remove an occasion for anger, and remained in deserted places praying. In this He taught us to rest in the secrecy of conscience when we are pressed by the wicked.

**PART II. Διάψαλμα (Diapsalma). VERSE 8.—“I awaited him who saved me from faintness of spirit and from the storm.”**

**I awaited Him.** [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss] The second part, in which, now safe in solitude, he hopes for God’s assistance and utters imprecations against his fellow citizens. The treatment proceeds first according to the first reading, which is in the Church’s person, in this way: as though she said, “I remained in the solitude [Col. 0510B] of the mind, where there is rest. But because tribulation is outward, I awaited Him who saved me.” Christ saves us when He is awakened in us, that is, when faith in Him burns brightly in us, and when we see what He endured for us—as Peter too was delivered when he awakened Him who slept, saying: “Lord, we are perishing” (Matt. 8). Therefore, if the little boat of your heart is troubled by waves, awaken Christ—that is, awaken the faith of Christ in yourself—and you will be saved.

From what did He save me? “From faintness of spirit,” by which above he said that he was troubled, “and from the storm,” that is, seditions. This is the storm in which Peter cried out: “Thou hast saved me.” But against those who exalted themselves, he says:

**VERSE 9.—“Cast them down, O Lord; divide their tongues, for I have seen iniquity and contradiction in the city.”**

**O Lord, cast them down**, [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin] lest they fortify their plans by devising schemes, as though by some contrivance; and divide the tongues of those who wickedly conspired to build the tower of pride, lest there be a proud unity and their malice attain its effect. Their figure was those who moved their feet from the East and came into the land of Shinar to build a tower against the Lord reaching to heaven, so that their name might thereby be celebrated. But there their language was confounded, lest they accomplish what they wished (Gen. 10–11). Thus he asks that this be done to the wicked.

Therefore divide them, because “I have seen iniquity,” that is, the faithlessness of those who do not believe, “and contradiction,” [Col. 0510D] because they act against Christ’s mysteries, “in the city,” Babylon, which builds the tower of pride. Because I have seen these things, I fled into solitude. This is the city of which the Lord says through the prophet: “I am God and not man, and I will not enter the city” (Hos. 11). There is another city, which God inhabits, of which it is said: “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5). And this city:

**VERSE 10.—“Day and night iniquity shall surround her upon her walls; and labour and injustice are in her midst.”**

**Iniquity**, [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Interlinear Gloss] not merely for an hour but day and night, that is, continually, shall surround her, namely Babylon. These things commonly trouble the righteous person, so that he wishes to fly away. I say, iniquity existing “upon her walls,” that is, upon the princes of that city, who are its fortifications. They will fall like the walls of Jericho when the ark goes around them on the seventh day (Josh. 6), that is, at the judgment, when, after this life which is conducted through seven days, Christ will examine each person’s merits. “And labour is in her midst,” that is, among the common populace. Labour is in the middle, and, that is, because injustice—that is, iniquity—is there. But rest is in humility. Behold, iniquity is among both great and small.

Or, labour consists in oppressing others, and injustice in conducting judgments. This is what “in her midst” means, by comparison: as though throughout the entire city.

**VERSE 11.—“And usury and deceit have not failed from her streets.”**

**And they have not failed**, [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Jerome, Cassiodorus] because usury always continues: it exacts more, whether through injury or in any matter whatever, than it has received; it does not forgive in order that it may be forgiven. And deceit remains, because they deceive others. These things are not hidden from her streets, even though they are evil, but are done publicly. As though he said: They made gain openly and deceived openly—both of which the law forbids.

**VERSE 12.—“For if my enemy had reviled me, I would surely have borne it.”**

**For if my enemy.** [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus] Up to this point the Church has spoken of open enemies; now it speaks of hidden enemies. As though she said: Do thus in the city—namely, cast them down and divide their tongues—because in it there are not merely open enemies but hidden ones as well, who harm more greatly. For if my enemy, someone manifest, had reviled me with taunts, I would surely have endured it, because the evil would not have been unexpected.

[Col. 0511C] **VERSE 13.—“And if he who hated me had spoken great things against me, perhaps I would have hidden myself from him.”**

**And if he who hated me** had openly spoken great things against me, [Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, proudly insulted me, magnified himself over me, and threatened me with all he could do, perhaps I would have hidden myself from him among those who are inwardly with me, namely in the Church, away from one who is outside. I say, “perhaps.” Or, according to another reading which others give, “certainly.” Here the great patience of this person is noted: he would so make way for words as to hide himself, lest he see that adversary endure them.

**VERSE 14.—“But thou, a man of one mind, my guide and my familiar.”**

**But thou, a man of one mind**, [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss] formerly one who at some time gave good counsel; “my guide,” who at some time gave good advice; and “my familiar,” who was in the same Church with me. You, I say, being such a one, are not to be endured. Since there are wicked persons within, what remains except solitude? For no pestilence is more effective in causing harm than a familiar enemy. Hence: “A man’s enemies shall be those of his own household” (Matt. 10). And elsewhere: “From her who sleeps in your bosom, guard the doors of your mouth” (Mic. 7) [Col. 0512A].

**VERSE 15.—“Who together with me didst take sweet food; we walked in the house of God with one accord.”**

**Who together**, [Augustine] dwelling with me in the Church along with others, didst take sweet spiritual food. Hence: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33 [34]). “And we walked with one accord in the house of God,” that is, in the Church. But because you are now outside, not in body but in mind, therefore there is disagreement between us.

[Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Jerome, Cassiodorus, Jerome, Gloss, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] Alternatively, the whole passage from “I awaited him” is read in the person of Christ. As though he said: [Col. 0512B] “I remained in solitude.” And there likewise, “I awaited him,” namely God the Father. As though he said: In solitude, not secure in myself, I awaited the Father’s protection; he saved me from faintheartedness of spirit, lest I yield to evils in the Passion and storm, lest I become angry. It follows: “Cast them down, O Lord; divide their tongues,” that is, let them be scattered through divided tongues.

Or Christ speaks specifically of the Jews, who are entangled in many seditions and schisms, ever since they said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). He adds why these things occur: “For I have seen iniquity and contradiction”—this does not change—“in the city,” Jerusalem; and not merely for an hour: indeed, “day and night iniquity shall surround it,” Jerusalem. The iniquity, I say, existing upon its walls, and toil and injustice in its midst. These do not [Col. 0512C] change. “And usury and deceit have not departed from its streets,” Jerusalem. Nor does this change.

“For if an enemy”—here Christ speaks particularly against Judas, and this is a reproach directed at Judas, or against any Jewish man who acts as a familiar enemy toward him—As though he said: Do this in the city of Jerusalem, because there I have familiar enemies, who are intolerable. This is the meaning: “For if my enemy,” an open enemy, “had done evil to me, I would surely have endured it. And if one who hated me,” that is, one who had no knowledge of me, “had spoken great things against me, I might perhaps have hidden myself from him,” that is, I would not have taken vengeance.

“But you, O Jewish man, were of one mind,” you to whom the oracles of God were entrusted (Rom. 3); “my guide,” because I made you a guide [Col. 0512D] over my people; “and my acquaintance,” because you are of the same nation as I. Why, then, do you seek to kill me? “You who together with me received sweet foods,” that is, the ordinances of the Law, which I expounded to you; “and in the house of God,” that is, in the Temple at Jerusalem, “we walked in concord.”

Or he speaks particularly against Judas, saying: “But you, O man,” namely Judas, “of one mind,” because he was among the apostles; “my guide,” because he was sent ahead to towns and villages; “and my acquaintance,” because he foreknew him as his betrayer. Why, namely, do you betray me, “you who together with me received sweet foods”? Bodily foods, namely the morsel: foods which alone could be sweet to the wicked. Yet the force of wickedness is usually softened by shared meals. Therefore his guilt is the graver. “And in the house of God,” that is, in the Temple at Jerusalem, [Col. 0513A] “we walked in the concord of bodily association,” because Judas was in his company.

### Verse 16. “Let death come upon them; and let them go down alive into hell.”

“Let death come.” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine, Alcuin.] As above he imprecates against open enemies, so here against hidden ones; and, lest it be thought that he was speaking of one person only, he makes the Jews share the punishment—that is, he pronounces the curse generally upon Jews together with others.

He touches upon the beginning of schism, when Dathan and Abiram raised sedition against Moses and Aaron, as is related in Numbers: the earth swallowed them alive, together with their tents and all their possessions. Korah also, and two hundred and fifty men with him, following their wickedness, took censers [Col. 0513B] to burn incense before the Lord. They were consumed by divine fire; and this also destroyed fourteen thousand seven hundred of the people (Num. 16). Thus a new death came upon them.

So he calls down punishment upon the wicked; and Christ and the Church speak with one voice. As though he said: Because they are such, therefore let a new death come upon 116 them, as a new death came upon Dathan and Abiram, who began the schism and proudly separated themselves. For the earth opened itself and swallowed them alive. Hence, by way of exposition, he adds: “And let them go down into hell,” that is, into the abyss of earthly desire. Let them go down, I say, “alive,” that is, sinning knowingly, knowing that they are perishing. Yet, while perishing, let them be swallowed by the gaping mouth of earthly desire. [Col. 0513C] This is the new death; and he speaks generally of leaders and followers.

Or distinguish between leaders and followers, as there was such a distinction in that schism. The leaders were swallowed by the earth, while the following people were destroyed by fire. So here he calls down a divided punishment upon the authors of evil and their supporters, saying: “Let death come upon them,” that is, upon the lesser persons who consent to their superiors: let the fire of destruction come upon them, just as fire came from heaven upon the people. “And let them go down,” namely the leaders who author evil, “alive into hell,” the hell of earthly desire—that is, sinning knowingly—as the earth swallowed their leaders.

For they, that is, the lesser persons, consented and followed; and, inflamed by eagerness to agree, they would not withdraw from their leaders. Therefore [Col. 0513D] the burning of destruction came upon the burning of dissension; but the leaders were swallowed by the earth. Thus these knowingly sinning persons go down. And rightly so, because of this:

### Verse 17. “For wickedness is in their dwellings, in their midst.”

“For wickedness is in their dwellings,” or “lodgings,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin], that is, in this life, where they are strangers and passing through. For they will not remain here forever; why, then, do they press on so? And this wickedness is “in their midst,” that is, in their heart.

He says that wickedness is in their lodgings because it is foreign to them, not natural, but received into a lodging, as something adventitious. Or: first wickedness is “in their dwellings,” that is, in secret; and afterwards “in their midst,” that is, publicly and openly.

[Col. 0514A]

## Part III. Verse 18. “But I cried to the Lord, and the Lord saved me.”

“But I.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which, proceeding by alternation, he declares what will happen to himself and to them. Here the body of Christ, that is, the Church, speaks. They will perish in this way; “but I cried to the Lord” amid the disturbance of my trial, “and the Lord saved,” or “will save,” me—which necessarily follows. And I, lest I should be ungrateful:

### Verse 19. “At evening and morning and noon I shall recount and proclaim; and he will hear my voice.”

“At evening,” [Augustine, Jerome, Augustine], that is, concerning past things, “I shall recount”; “and in the morning,” that is, concerning future things, “I shall proclaim to him”; “at noon,” which does not turn the sun toward setting, that is, in [Col. 0514B] eternal things, which ever endure: “you will hear my voice.” In this interpretation, the several terms correspond to the several terms, and the three times are distinguished.

Or it may be interpreted so that the respective terms correspond without a distinction of times: for the Lord was at evening on the cross; in the morning, in the resurrection; at noon, in the ascension. He says therefore: “At evening I shall recount”: I recount the patience of one dying at evening. “And in the morning I shall proclaim,” that is, I proclaim the life of the resurrection accomplished in the morning. “And he will hear my voice” at noon, that is, when seated at the right hand of the Father, where he intercedes for us, and to which he ascended at noon.

See what great consolation this affords him amid the storm, against the wicked who are outside and inside—that is, openly and secretly. Thus let us too, amid the wicked, pray and lament with him, and confidently say:

[Col. 0514C]

### Verse 20. “He will redeem my soul in peace from those who draw near to me, because they were among many with me.”

“He will redeem in peace.” [Gloss, Augustine, Jerome, Alcuin, Augustine.] As though he said: He will thus hear me, because he will redeem my soul, to be placed in eternal peace. This is against those who do not love peace; therefore my soul is in peace, because I loved peace.

He will redeem it, I say, “from those who draw near to me,” that is, from false Christians, who deceive more than open idolaters. They draw near, therefore, in name, not in divine reality; in body, not in mind; in number, not in merit. And they truly draw near, “because they were among many with me.” Or, they were with me in many sacraments—namely baptism, the reading of the Gospel, feast days, [Col. 0514D] and such things—but they were not with me in the few things: in all the sacraments with me, but not in faith, hope, and charity, without which all those things are nothing.

Or “they were among many with me,” that is, among the chaff, which is plentiful. They were with me, not among the grains, which are few; that is, they were not with me among the few elect. For they belonged to the multitude of those called, not to the small number of the elect (Matt. 22). And fittingly he says, “with me”; for chaff is also near wheat. For they arise from one seed, take root in one field, are nourished by one rain, are gathered beneath the same reaper, undergo the same threshing, and await the same winnowing; yet they do not enter one barn. So also these are with me in many sacraments, or among the chaff.

[Col. 0515A]

### Verse 21. “God will hear and humble them—he who is before the ages.”

“He will hear.” [Gloss, Augustine.] I say that he will hear me; and he will not merely hear me praying for my exaltation, but God will also hear me praying for the humbling of enemies, and—that is, because—he will humble by affliction those who trust in a leader who began only yesterday. He will humble them, I say, he “who is before the ages,” because “in the beginning was the Word” (John 1). This is not apparent to them, because Christ was born in time from the Virgin. And he will rightly humble them.

### Verse 22. “For there is no change in them, and they did not fear God; he stretched out his hand in repaying.”

“For there is no change in their perverse understanding,” [Col. 0515B] [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Gloss]; rather, they remain in perversity. They die in schism because they do not change for the better, but for the worse: neither while they are here nor in the resurrection, because the understanding of the faithless is unchangeable.

“And they did not fear God.” A human being is converted by this remedy, namely by fearing God; and punishment follows for these things, though it is not something different. Hence follows: “He stretched out his hands,” after the likeness of one wishing to strike, who raises his hands in order to strike more heavily; and this “in repaying,” that is, in order to repay them.

### Verse 23. “They defiled his covenant; they were divided by the wrath of his countenance; his heart drew near.”

“They defiled,” [Augustine, Jerome, Gloss, Augustine, [Col. 0515C] Alcuin, Augustine], and it was not enough for them not to fear or to change. They even defiled the covenant of his promise, which the Lord himself spoke to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22); whoever contradicts it pollutes it.

Or, “they defiled his covenant,” that is, they perverted the Scriptures. Or, as far as lay in them, they defiled the Scriptures by acting contrary to them. Therefore they were divided through heresies “by the wrath of his countenance,” or on account of wrath: that is, by him being angry, who gave them over to the desires of their heart (Rom. 1).

“And they drew near.” As though he said: Because they defiled, and because they are armed and divided, the righteous are armed still more, and the weak are delivered, who place their care in God. This is the meaning: they defiled; and through this, “his heart,” that is, the secret will of God contained in the Scriptures, [Col. 0515D] drew near to his faithful ones, so that we may understand his will: by cutting them off from the Catholic faith, he pierces the good to the heart, and the good who have been proved are stirred up still more. And the will of God that lay hidden becomes understood in the Scriptures.
