Hence elsewhere: “The assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples, that those who have been tested by the silver of the divine utterance may be excluded”—that is, may stand out and appear (Ps. 67).

### Verse 24. “His words were softened above oil, and they are darts.”

“Softened.” [Augustine.] Truly it will draw near, because his words—God’s words—were softened above oil. For hard and obscure things in the Scriptures are softened when expounded, and penetrate even to the bones. Hence it follows: [Col. 0516A] “And those same words are darts,” because, though softened, they do not lose their power. Rather, the evangelists are armed by them; they strike human hearts toward the love of peace and free the weak from the tangled questions of heretics.

I say that the words are softened; but if they are still hard for you, a child nourished on the milk of lesser teaching, do not be angry with the breasts of the Church, but:

### Verse 25. “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will nourish you; and he will not give the righteous person wavering for ever.”

“Cast your care upon the Lord,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin], or upon God, not upon another who is a rock to a ship, not a harbor to one tossed about in the world. And he will nourish you with the milk of simple understanding, until you advance to the bread of a more mature understanding.

[Col. 0516B] It is wholesome counsel to cast one’s care upon the Lord, who nourishes. Worldly care, like our worm, consumes us. But if care is cast upon the Lord, he nourishes. Hence Solomon: “As a worm harms wood and a moth a garment, so a man’s sadness harms his heart” (Prov. 25). Cast care upon the Lord as into a harbor, because “he will not give the righteous person wavering for ever.”

Thus the preceding words were words of wavering: “I was grieved in my agitation and troubled.” Alternatively, the whole passage from “But I cried to God” is in the person of Christ. Christ said: “But I cried to God, and the Lord—the Father—saved,” that is, will save, “me.” And because he will save me, therefore: “At evening,” when I shall be seized; “and morning,” when I shall be judged; “and noon,” when I shall be crucified, [Col. 0516C] “I shall recount” past works, “and I shall proclaim” the powers and works that he will perform; and therefore “he will hear my voice.”

[Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine, Gloss, Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] Or thus, so that the verbs correspond to the nouns: recounting belongs to evening, when he said everything that Judas was plotting. Proclaiming belongs to morning, when he said to Pilate: “For this I was born, that I should bear witness to the truth,” etc. (John 18). “He will hear” belongs to noon, when he gave up the Spirit. See how great mysteries are briefly stated.

Or thus, divide the text: “The Lord will save me at evening and morning.” Divide the text here. Therefore I, not ungrateful, “shall recount and proclaim,” and he “will hear my voice.” “He will redeem my soul in peace.” He will redeem it, I say, “from those who draw near to me,” that is, those who falsely [Col. 0516D] praise me, saying: “We know that you are truthful,” etc. (Mark 12). “Because they were among many with me,” that is, not with the few elect. And he will hear not only for my sake but for theirs also. “God who is before the ages will hear me.” He will humble them from pride so that they may believe. Or, he will humble them “so that they may take away both place and nation” (John 11); and rightly so.

[Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] “For there is no change in them, and they did not fear God; he stretched out his hand in repaying.” These things do not change. And because such persons are divided “by the wrath of his countenance,” that is, he himself, being angry, will divide them from the grains in the future. For wrath is the avenging judgment by which the good are divided from the wicked, as grain from chaff. Then “his heart will draw near,” that is, the will of God, announced through prophets and apostles, will be known to all.

Or the heart of God is the righteous, who know the secrets of their God. They will draw near to God when those others are divided. Therefore these things happen to them, because “his words were softened above oil,” or, according to another reading, “they softened,” by flattery; and yet those same words are darts when they say: “He is guilty of death” (Matt. 26). Since they are such, therefore cast your care not upon them but upon the Lord, and he will nourish you. And he will not give the righteous person wavering for ever. These things do not change.

### Verse 26. “But you, O God, will bring them down into the pit of destruction.”

“But you.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Gloss, Augustine.] These, then, will not waver; but what will happen to the wicked who defiled the covenant? The wicked will be led down into the pit of Gehenna. This is the meaning: “But you, O God, will bring them down.” [Col. 0517B] This is the end of defilement: “into the pit of destruction,” that is, into the darkness of submersion. Nor will it be delayed, because:

### Verse 27. “Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days; but I, O Lord, shall hope in you.”

“Men of blood,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine], who sometimes kill souls and bodies, “and deceitful men” in their seduction, “shall not halve their days,” that is, the days they choose for themselves, not those appointed by God. Nor will they complete what they suppose they will, [p. 117] but will perish before the time, because they hope.

Or thus: he will bring them down into the pit because “they shall not halve their days” [Note: [Col. 0517D] Gregory, *Moralia*, book V, chapter 28]—that is, they will not spend the remaining days, after those passed in evil, in good, “redeeming the time” (Eph. 5), but continue altogether in evil.

[Alcuin, Augustine.] Some do not begin good days, but persist continuously in evils; others halve their days; others complete good days. For some die in Egypt, others in the wilderness, and others in the Holy Land. Those die in Egypt who continue in the darkness of vices to the end of life. Those die in the wilderness who, having departed from the confusion of sin, amend their errors through repentance. Those complete their days who persevere without crime in works of righteousness to the end of life.

These three kinds of persons were symbolized by what was shown written in the scroll of Ezekiel, where these three things were written: “a song, a lamentation, and woe.” The prophet was told to devour the scroll, that is, to bring the mysteries of these three things into the understanding of his mind (Ezek. 2). They sing a song who have not experienced the fall into sins. There is lamentation [Col. 0517D] because they rise again from sins through the lament of repentance. Woe to those who sin and do not repent: they shall not halve their days. “But I, O Lord, shall hope in you”—which they do not do; and therefore they do not reach the eternal day.

## Collation on Psalm LIV: “Hear,” etc.

### Verse 5. “And darkness enfolded me.”

Jerome: “gloom.” Others translate *pallatzuth* as “horror” or “trembling.” But since earlier there had already occurred, “Fear and trembling came upon me,” the Septuagint and Jerome rightly understood the following expression as “darkness,” since in death, spiritual as well as bodily, light fails—though death is terrible even in name alone.

### Verse 8. “I awaited him who saved me.”

Hebrew: *AHISSAH MIPHLAT LI*. If rendered word for word: “I shall cause salvation to hasten for myself”; and this is accomplished through firm hope in him. The sense “I awaited,” etc., has therefore not been rendered inappropriately.

“From faintheartedness of spirit and storm.” The edition of Praetensis: “from a violent spirit and storm”; Sanctes: “from a wind raised by a whirlwind”; Pellicanus and the interpreters for Cajetan: similarly. Münster: “because of the wind of whirlwind and storm.” In meaning there is no difference. Yet I wished to recount their renderings, because no conjunction is supplied in the Hebrew: some of them wished one to be understood, others did not.

The translator for Campensis follows himself: “to escape more quickly from the rapid wind and storm.” What Jerome understood may be found in his letter to Sunnias and Fretela: “You say that in the Greek you have found ἀπὸ ὀλιγοψυχίας, which is properly called ‘faintheartedness.’ But it should be known that, in place of ὀλιγοψυχία, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Fifth Edition rendered ἀπὸ πνεύματος, that is, ‘from spirit.’ And in Hebrew *MERUAH* is written. Accordingly, their entire sense reads thus: [Col. 0518B] ‘I shall hasten that I may be saved from the spirit of storm and whirlwind.’”

### Verse 14. “But you, O man of one mind.”

Jerome likewise: “according to my equality”; Sanctes: “according to my equality”; Pellicanus and Praetensis: “according to my rank.” There is discrepancy in the words, but the sense agrees. Hence the interpreters for Cajetan say, “as my estimation”; Münster: “but you, man, were according to the estimation of my heart”; Nebiensis: “a man of my worth”; the Chaldee: “like me”; the translator for Campensis: “but you, O companion-in-arms, my colleague.”

Three or four interpreters have comprised these meanings in one word. I do not see by what spirit these men are moved if they do this from contempt for the ecclesiastical reading—a conclusion I do not wish to persuade myself of in every case.

### Verse 15. “You who together with me received sweet foods.”

Jerome: “we who together had sweet secret counsel.” So likewise all the other Hebraizing interpreters. The Septuagint seems to have read *soc* for [uncertain reading]; the former means “counsel, secret,” the latter “anointing,” which is understood as refreshment and food. So in 4 Kings 4: “Unless there is a little oil with which I may anoint myself,” that is, “be somewhat refreshed.” [Col. 0518C] Although the Hebrew has only “a vessel of oil,” the Septuagint nevertheless has ὃ ἀλείψομαι ἔλαιον, “oil with which I may anoint myself.” Nor is “sweet secret counsel” far removed from familiar table fellowship, so that the meaning comes to the same thing.

“We walked in concord.” Jerome: “in terror”; the others: “in a crowd,” “together,” or something similar. The particle *REGESCH* is ambiguous between “noise” and “gathering,” whence the divergence. The Chaldee has “with haste.”

### Verse 19. “I shall recount and proclaim.”

Pellicanus: “and, troubled, I pray”; Münster: “and, urgently, I pray”; Praetensis: “I shall make a noise”; Sanctes: “I shall make tumult.” Jerome, however, the interpreters for Cajetan, and Nebiensis have “and I shall resound,” which is certainly to proclaim. This also concerns the future, according to the exposition; *HAMAH* has various meanings. The Chaldee says: “I shall cry out.”

### Verse 20. “He will redeem my soul in peace from those who draw near to me.”

Praetensis, Sanctes, Münster, and Campensis, instead of the second clause, translate: “from the battle that is against me,” or something similar. The Hebrew word *QUAROB* or *QUERAB* is ambiguous between “battle” and “near.” Hence Jerome, the interpreters for Cajetan, Pellicanus, and Nebiensis have: “they were with us.” The understanding, however, tends to the same result.

“Because they were among many with me.” Lefèvre and Caecus judge this verse, read in this manner, to be contrary to the truth of the Hebrew. Why? Because Jerome translated from the Hebrew: “For many were against me.” Certainly they ought not to be angry with our reading. *IMMADI* can be understood either way. Hence Pellicanus, Münster, Sanctes, and the interpreters for Cajetan translate “with me.”

### Verse 22. “He stretched out his hand in repaying.”

Jerome: “against his peaceful ones”; the remaining Hebraizing interpreters tend in the same direction. The interpreters had regard to the root *SCHILLEM*, that is, “he repaid.” Others, however, to the root *SCHLAM*, that is, “he was peaceful.”

### Verse 23. “They were divided by the wrath of his countenance.”

*HALCU MAHAMAOTH PIU.* Jerome: “his mouth [was] smoother than butter”; Nitidius: “his mouth [was] butter”; Pellicanus: “they were softer than butter in his mouth”; Praetensis: “it was softer than butter in his mouth.” The others similarly. The ambiguities of Hebrew words produced this variation. For *HALAQ* sometimes means “was divided,” as the interpreters understood it; at other times, “to flatter,” “to soothe,” or “to soften,” as others understand it. Moreover, *HALAQ*, with the same letters distinguished by a single point, sometimes denotes “smooth.”

Then *HEM’AH* means “butter.” But *HEMĀH*, and in construction *HAMATH*, means “wrath”; in the plural, *HEMOTH*. The Septuagint appears to have read the latter, while the others read the former.

“His heart drew near.” Praetensis: “the inmost part of his [Col. 0519B] heart”; Sanctes and the modern translators: “his heart makes war,” or “his heart fights.” *QUARAB* means “drew near”; [Col. 0520A] *QUERAB*, “battle”; *QUEREB*, “the inmost part.” One follows one meaning, another another. Hence in some copies of Jerome one reads, “his heart fights”; in others, “his heart draws near.”

### Verse 25. “Cast your care upon the Lord.”

*IEHABCA*, that is, “what he has given you.” Hence Jerome translates “your charity,” which we ought especially to care for. Romans 3: “The fulfillment of the Law is love.” Others translate “your burden” or “your weight,” namely, so that God may bear you. This sense is not remote from ours. The translator for Campensis has: “Entrust to him care for yourself.”

Sanctes, in his *Thesaurus*, reports that Rabbi David explains it thus: “Cast upon the Lord what he has given you up to this day. Cast upon him what you need, and he will sustain you, as he has done until now.” This is his explanation. And he adds: “Our masters,” he says, “did not know what *IEHABECHA* was. They heard an Arab woman saying to her husband, *SCHAQUOL IEHABIC*”—“Release your burden.” Certainly I marvel that a little woman should know it and the rabbis not.

## Psalm LV

[Col. 0519]

### Title of the Psalm: “For the end; for the people who have been made far from the holy ones; upon the inscription of the title; to David himself; when the Philistines held him in Gath.”

[Col. 0519B]

“Have mercy on me, O God.” Title: “For the end; for the people who have been made far from the holy ones; upon the inscription of the title; to David himself; when the Philistines held him in Gath.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.]

This title is taken partly from the Gospel and partly from the Old Testament. For in the Gospel we read that, when the Lord was crucified, Pilate placed above him a title in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. Certain Jews wished to erase it, saying: “Do not write, ‘Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews,’ but that he said, ‘I am King of the Jews.’” Pilate answered: “What I have written, I have written” (John 19). For it had been prophesied by the Holy Spirit in the titles of other psalms: “Do not corrupt the inscription of the title,” by which Christ was shown to be king. This is from the Gospel.

But in the book of Kings it is read that David, fleeing Saul, came to Achish king of Gath, a city of the Philistines, where he is said to have been a sojourner but not held captive (1 Sam. 21). Therefore David here signifies Christ, born from his seed, whom the Philistines—that is, foreigners, namely persecutors of the Christian name—held of old in himself and now in [Col. 0519D] his members, “in Gath,” that is, in the winepress, namely in the pressures of tribulations. These are called a winepress because they are useful: through them the merits of the saints are increased and the wine of righteousness flows out.

The Philistines and the people who have been made far from the holy ones are the same. The sense of the title is: This psalm, tending toward the end—that is, toward Jesus himself—is for the salvation of the people. Or “for the people” means “against the people,” namely the people who have been made far from the holy ones. Those who receive Christ in the inscription of the title draw near to the holy ones. The people made far from the holy ones in the inscription of the title is every Jew, and everyone else, who rejects Christ as king; and these are the same persons who trouble the Church, that is, [Col. 0520B] the Philistines.

I say, “the inscription of the title made to David himself,” that is, to Christ: not altered in accordance with the reality of the thing, though this was the Jews’ wish. “To David himself,” that is, to Christ: for they wished to change it, but it was not changed. [Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] For the inscription of the title was not erased even though the people pressed for this, because in another psalm it was prophesied: “Do not corrupt the inscription of the title.”

The people made far from the holy ones are persecutors who tread the Church like grapes, so that the wine of righteousness may come forth. Note that up to this point the title is from the Gospel; what follows—namely, “when they held,” etc.—is from the Old Testament. As though he said: The people was made far from the holy ones when, that is, because, the Philistines, meaning foreigners—that is, persecutors—held him, namely Christ in the head and in the members, in Gath, that is, in the winepress.

Literally, David is read to have sojourned in that city but not to have been held; but Christ, born from his seed, is held not only formerly in himself but still now in his body, amid pressures that are useful. Before the winepress the grape is intact, yet nothing flows from it; when pressed it is not barren, because wine comes forth.

The Prophet’s intention is to strengthen the Church against persecutors. Method: the psalm has three parts. First, the Church prays, like a grape pressed by the Philistines, briefly touching upon the tribulations in which it is; through hope in God she concludes that she does not fear, that is, at the end of the first part she says that she does not fear. Second, she enumerates the evils which she suffers and the conversion of enemies, at “All day.” Third, now freed from the evils of the world, she promises to sing praise in future blessedness, or even here, at “In me.” Therefore the Church, like a grape pressed in the winepress, cries out:

### Verse 1. “Have mercy on me, O God, for man has trampled me down; all day long, attacking me, he has afflicted me.”

“O God, have mercy on me,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus], lest I fail under trampling. Why do you cry out? “For man,” namely the one who has been made far from the holy ones—and not man only, [Col. 0521A] but also the devil, of whom the Gospel says: “An enemy, a man, did this” (Matt. 13)—“has trampled me down,” like a grape in the winepress, so that wine may flow forth.

He repeats the same thing more explicitly: a man attacks visibly, or the devil invisibly, and is therefore more dangerous. “All day long he has afflicted me,” that is, throughout all time. For no one lives in Christ without tribulation.

### Verse 2. “My enemies have trampled me down all day long, because many make war against me.”

“They have trampled me down.” [Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin, Gloss.] They do this deservedly not because of anything in me, but because they are my enemies, namely those far from the holy ones. They are members of the devil. And these have trampled me down as grapes beneath their feet.

“All day,” I say: have mercy. And you must have mercy, “because many who wage war have stood against me,” and these same persons are lofty. Yet they are not lofty for long, but only for a day.

### Verse 3. “Because of the height of the day I shall fear; but I shall hope in you.”

“Because of the height,” [Alcuin, Gloss, Cassiodorus, Augustine]: but I shall fear because of the height of the day, that is, because of the height of those who trample me down. They are lofty, but not for long: only for a day. I shall fear their power, granted for an hour, as though the height of the day were the world—that is, worldly height, where there is fear of pride.

In order to show the tribulation to be more severe, he says that he is trampled by proud persons. “I shall not fear”; rather, “I shall hope in you,” in whom no one who hopes has anything to fear.

Or the text may be read and divided differently, while retaining the same sense. As though he said: “The enemies who trampled me down are many. But shall I fear because many wage war against me? No; rather I shall hope in you.”

Or thus, according to another reading: “My enemies trampled me down all day because of the height of the day.” Divide here: “because many who make war against me shall fear; but I shall hope in you.” This text is explained thus: “My enemies trampled me down all day.” And this was “because of the height of the day,” because they did not recognize the day—that is, Christ—shining loftily. For Christ is the day. The twelve apostles are the hours of this day. Hence the Lord himself says: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” (John 11). The enemies could not attain the height of this day. Hence during Christ’s Passion darkness came to pass (Matt. 27).

Or, “they trampled me down because of the height of the day,” that is, because those who trample are lofty, though only for an hour—that is, only for a day, not for long. Yet they need not be feared, because the many who make war against me will fear when their day has passed, namely when the time of their height has ended.

But I do not say, “I shall not fear,” lest I seem to presume upon myself with foolish arrogance; rather, “I shall hope in you,” which is the cause of not fearing. One who does not fear because of hardness of heart or pride is like a senseless person. Insensibility is not feeling; it is not health.

Note that there are three states of the body: health, insensibility, and immortality. In insensibility the body does not suffer pain; neither does it in immortality. But in insensibility it does not suffer pain because it does not feel; in immortality, because it has been made wholly firm. Health, if it is afflicted, has pain. Yet the insensible person should not think himself nearer immortality than the healthy person.

So too there are three dispositions of the soul: prudent caution, foolish arrogance, and secure glory. Foolish arrogance resembles insensibility, when someone, presuming upon himself, neither fears nor takes care. Therefore, lest he should seem through foolish arrogance to resemble an insensible person, he did not say, “I shall not fear,” but “I shall hope in you.”

### Verse 4. “In God I shall praise my words; in God I have hoped; I shall not fear what flesh may do to me.”

“I shall praise my words in God,” [Augustine], attributing to him the fact that I speak well, because I have it from him. I call them my words because I received them. As though he said: They are God’s because he gives them, and mine because I receive them.

I said, “I shall hope”; but even before—that is, long ago—I have hoped in God. Therefore, through hope of what is to come, “I shall not fear.” This person does not fear, though above, seeing the future evils of the world, he was afraid and prayed. “I shall not fear,” I say, “what flesh may do to me,” because, if it tramples, wine comes forth from the trampling.

## Part II. Verse 5. “All day long they cursed my words; all their thoughts are against me for evil.”

“All day.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The second part, in which she enumerates evils, by suffering which the conversion of enemies comes about. Therefore she concludes, as before, through hope in God that she will not fear. I say: “I shall not fear what flesh may do to me.” For what does flesh do? “All day long they cursed my words,” even if they come from God. And all their thoughts, being directed to evil because they devise nothing good, are against me. For when words are rejected, the person speaking is not free from insult. If they abhor the bread itself, how can they spare the vessel in which it is served?

### Verse 6. “They will dwell and hide themselves; they themselves will watch my heel.”

They shall dwell, [Augustine, Cassiodorus] or “they dwell.” Another reading. As though he said: Their thoughts are bent upon evil, and these are hidden. This is what “they shall dwell and hide” means: because they are strangers in this world, where there is nothing but pilgrimage and sojourning, where no one sees another’s heart, whatever evil they devise is concealed. Or thus—and he speaks of false brethren, who secretly enter in order to harm. As though he said: Some attack openly, but some among them are far [Col. 0522D] from the saints—namely, the counterfeit ones—who shall dwell, or “sojourn,” that is, shall enter deceptively, and shall conceal their deceits because they do not dare to oppose openly. Such people do greater harm than manifestly wicked persons, as did Judas, who was a devil (John 6). He was chosen with the other eleven and sojourned for a time. He chose one whom he knew, not for the work of testing, as the others, but for the work of temptation, so that he might give you, who do not know whom to choose, consolation: that you might “cultivate” (*coleres*) as he did [object unstated]. For if they say false things about you, they do not take heaven away from you, nor do such men harm you. And such persons themselves shall watch my heel, that is, my foot so as to cause it to stumble, that they may bring accusations. For they hunt for every word, seeking snares somewhere and trying to make tangled accusations; yet they themselves are caught first, so as to perish, before they catch others so as to destroy them. Or, “they shall watch [Col. 0523A] my heel,” that is, the end of my life, since we are judged according to our end. Therefore the devil lies in wait for the heel.

VERSE 7.—“As they have borne down my soul, for nothing thou shalt save them; in wrath thou shalt break the peoples.”

“As they have borne down.” [Remigius, Augustine] As though he said: They act thus, as those who have borne down my soul as though it were a heavy burden—that is, as those to whom I am burdensome to behold. Hence in the Book of Wisdom: “Let us oppress the righteous man; for he is grievous to us even to behold” (Wisdom 2). Such are they; yet thou, O Lord, shalt save them. And this “for nothing.” Or thus, according to another reading: “As they have borne down my soul, for nothing thou shalt save.” [Col. 0523B] Here the Church speaks to Christ, saying: My soul has endured robbers openly and those who hide within; and, as I have endured, so thou, O Christ, shalt save them—that is, do thou endure and pray for them, and they shall be saved. Thou shalt save them, I say, and this for nothing, because it entails no labor for thee, as though it were nothing to thee; for, if they are desperate cases, thou healest them by a word. Or, “for nothing thou shalt save them,” as though for none of their merits, but freely, through mercy. Or, thou shalt save by this very means, because thou shalt break them. Or, thou shalt lead the peoples in wrath—namely, when through God’s scourges they come to their senses; for thou terrifiest them by tribulations, and thus leadest them to thyself. For there is a wrath of consummation, by which children are scourged for correction; and a wrath of destruction, by which evil men are punished unto their undoing. [Col. 0523C] Or, “thou shalt break the peoples in wrath,” that is, while they foresee the coming wrath of God.

VERSE 8.—“O God, I have declared my life to thee; thou hast set my tears in thy sight.”

“O God, my life.” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus] Note that human life is threefold: the life of nature, by which we live and breathe; the life of grace, by which we live in Christ; and the life of sin, which is lived in vices. Two are from God and are good: the life of nature and that of grace. The third is from man and is evil. We ought to declare all these to God, beginning with the life of sin. See how it is to be declared to God. As though he said: Thou shalt break the peoples, and I, for their instruction, have declared to thee my life, which has always been evil. He declares his life to God who confesses his sins [Col. 0523D] to God—not teaching God, but condemning himself, so that he may thus be released. Or it is understood of the life of nature and grace, thus: As though he said: Thou shalt break them; but I, lest I be ungrateful, have declared to thee, O God—that is, have ascribed to thee—my life, both natural and gracious, because thou hast made me live. Therefore I declare my life to thee, not to myself, so that others may follow this example. For it profits God’s gains that you invite others to receive the life which you have received, so that one who lives may no longer live for himself, but for him who died for all (2 Corinthians 5); and so do I. And thou hast set my tears in thy sight, that is, as they were in thy promise: thou hast heard me entreating thee, as thou hadst promised to hear one who weeps. I found thee merciful in promising, faithful in fulfilling. Observe how devout are tears which pray for [Col. 0524A] enemies. Therefore they are acceptable to God, as he himself promised. Or divide the wording thus: “Thou hast set my tears in thy sight”; divide here, while the meaning remains the same.

VERSE 9.—“As also in thy promise; then my enemies shall turn back.”

“As also in thy promise,” etc. [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine] As though he said: Thou shalt save and break them, as is also in thy promise, because thou didst promise Abraham: “In thy seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 22). And then, namely when thou breakest them, my enemies shall turn from their error, so that they are “backward,” that is, they follow whom they wished to go before. And

VERSE 10.—“On whatever day I call upon thee, behold, I have known that thou art my God.”

[Col. 0524B] “On whatever day,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] namely, whether in childhood, in middle age, or at the end of life, I call upon thee, seeking nothing other than thee, behold, I have known that thou art my God. Behold great riches. However avaricious you may be, God suffices for you; for avarice sought to possess the whole earth. Add heaven as well. Add what is greater: him who made heaven and earth. And the sense is as though he said: Whenever I call upon thee, thou wilt hear me. In this the wondrous clemency of God is perceived: he awaits whatever time of our conversion, and whenever he is entreated, he grants pardon. Note too that he says, “Thou art my God.” As though he said: Although the God of all, thou art properly mine, since thou helpest me, I worship thee, and I love thee; the others are strangers. And therefore

VERSE 11.—“In God I will praise the word; in the Lord [Col. 0524C] I will praise the speech; in God I have hoped; I shall not fear what man may do to me.”

“I will praise the word,” [Augustine, Jerome, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Cassiodorus] that is, doctrine, in God, by ascribing it to him. He says the same as he said above. And “the speech,” that is, whatever I may say above, I shall praise in the Lord—that is, I shall ascribe it [to him]; and if anything presses upon me, I have hoped in the Lord. Therefore I shall not fear, etc. Or thus: in God the Father I shall praise the Word, that is, the Son; because whatever is said of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit according to substance is said of the power of the Word, by which he is coeternal and consubstantial with the Father. Afterwards he adds concerning his humanity: “in the Lord,” that is, in Christ, who is the Word made flesh, I shall praise “the speech,” that is, the preaching by which he gave the world a rule of life and salvation. This man preaches these two things: the power of the Word and Christ’s humanity. Or thus, so that the Trinity of persons may be denoted by the three expressions he uses: “In God the Father I shall praise the Word,” 119 that is, the Son; “in the Lord, and the Holy Spirit, I shall praise the speech,” that is, the Son, because whatever I say according to substance concerning one person I say also concerning the others. And if anything presses upon me, I have hoped in God; I despise worldly things. Therefore I shall not fear what man may do to me, because, although he takes away outward things, he does not take away inward things: he takes away nothing except worldly things. The end of this part is the same as that of the first.

PART III. VERSE 12.—“Thy vows are upon me, O God: I will render praises to thee.”

[Col. 0525A] “They are upon me,” etc. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin] The third part, in which the Church, now freed from the evil ages, says that in future blessedness—or even here—it will sing God’s praise. As though he said: I shall not fear, because thy vows, O God, are in me. They are within, things which never depart from us. I do not seek outside myself what I may offer, because from the altar of the heart, from the storehouse of conscience, comes everything that must be kindled with charity. These vows are praises. Or another reading has, “vows of praise to thee.” Which vows shall I render to thee, in eternity or even here. Therefore I shall praise here,

VERSE 13.—“Because thou hast delivered my soul from death, and my feet from slipping, that I may please God in the light of the living.”

“Because thou hast delivered my soul from death,” [Augustine, [Col. 0525B] Jerome, Cassiodorus] because through myself I was dead. Through thee is the life which I declare to thee; and [thou hast delivered] my feet from slipping. Another translation has: “My eyes from tears, my feet from slipping.” Here, in hope, thou hast delivered [me] for this purpose: that I may please God, not strangers—namely, the Allophyles, who are far from the saints and have no light by which to see. I say this as one existing in the light of the living. He is in the light who loves God freely; this no one knows—not even the devil—but God alone. Or it may be understood of the future, thus: Therefore I shall praise in the future, because thou hast delivered—that is, thou shalt deliver—my soul from eternal death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from slipping, so that I may please God in the light of the living. This will be in the future, where neither does the soul die by sinning, [Col. 0525C] nor do eyes weep evils, nor do feet stumble. That is not so here, where one nevertheless pleases God perfectly. Hence he adds: “That I may please God in the light of the living eternally.”

COLLATION ON PSALM 55: “HAVE MERCY,” etc.

The title is given thus in the Septuagint: “Unto the end, for the people,” etc., as you have it in the Master. In Hebrew: “For the victor, concerning the silent dove,” or “for the silent dove among those afar off,” or “of distant ones” or “of removals”; or, according to Jerome: “because he had gone far away,” David’s inscription, *Michtam*. Jerome renders it “simple and humble,” concerning which something was said above on Psalm 15. As regards the Hebrew phrase “for the silent dove of removals,” it could also be rendered “for removals,” or “for those who are removed from the silent dove.” The former version will be taken in a good sense, namely of Christ or the Christian people, who inwardly preserve innocence and place their trust in distant things, that is, in heaven. [Col. 0525D] The latter will be understood in an evil sense, against the Jews who removed themselves from the silent dove—that is, from the simplicity which is in Christ Jesus—while attempting to destroy David’s inscription, that is, the writing of the title. For they said: “Do not write, ‘The King of the Jews’” (John 19). And this seems to be how the Septuagint understood it. The remaining matters are explained in the gloss.

VERSE 3.—“From the height of the day I shall fear; but I will hope in thee.” The beginning of the third verse in our text is, in Hebrew, the end of the second verse, according to the division of the copies which we use. But *marom*, understood as a particle in a different manner, caused the Septuagint to take it as though the letter *mem* were the preposition “from,” which is very familiar in Hebrew. Pellican did the same when he rendered it “from on high.” The others take the letter *mem* to be, as they call it, a hêemantic sign, that is, the mark of a derived noun; therefore they translate: “O Most High,” “O exalted one,” or “in the height.” Sanctes gives the last, in a sense contrary to the others’ version: “Many fighting [Col. 0526A] for me, in the height.” For this is set against: “Many fighting against me, O Most High.” Nebiensis translates: “against me, exalted one.” Nor should the variation in the division into verses disturb us, for it frequently leaves a sentence dependent on what follows, especially in poetry. Moreover, if “day” belongs to the continuation of the third verse, it requires the genitive case according to the Septuagint. But if it pertains to the beginning of the verse, since it has neither preposition nor inflectional ending, they translate: “I shall fear the day,” or “by day,” “in the day,” or “on whatever day I shall fear.” Münster, “although I should fear by day,” added the latter phrase of his own accord. Jerome, in his letter to Sunia and Fretela, gives the sense of our reading more plainly, teaching that a negation has been added in Greek: “I shall not fear,” οὐ φοβηθήσομαι. And the order is: “Because many fight against me, yet I shall fear thy exalted light.”

VERSE 4.—“In God I will praise my words.” In Hebrew, “his word.” But *yod* is commonly found in place of *waw*, and conversely, because of the likeness of the letters: *debaro*, “his word”; *debari*, “my word”; *debarai*, “my words.” [Col. 0526B]

VERSE 5.—“All day long they cursed my words.” Here Faber is wholly mistaken, daring to assert that *mea*, “my,” is superfluous in place of *nomen*, although *debarai* is most plainly read in this Hebrew verse. Stapulensis was wrong because he did not find it in the text of Jerome’s translation. Yet it is certain that Jerome employed a primitive pronoun in place of a possessive one, because he rendered: “They afflicted me with words.” Other Hebraists follow the Septuagint. The translation according to Campensis nevertheless says: “At all times they afflict my affairs.”

VERSE 7.—“As they have borne down my soul, for nothing thou shalt save them.” Pratensis: “When they have awaited my soul, deliverance for them because of iniquity.” The interpreters for Cajetan: “As they have awaited my soul, escape is theirs because of iniquity.” Pellican similarly. Sanctes, Münster, and Campensis read the second part interrogatively or admiringly: “When they await my soul, shall there be escape for them because of iniquity?” Yet the first particle of the whole verse, *caasser*, may mean “as” or “when.” Accordingly, if interpreted in the former manner, the sense of the Latin reading will be: “As they have borne down”—or, as others have it, “awaited”—my soul, namely by persecuting it, so thou shalt save them for nothing. That is, as Jerome renders it: “because none among them is safe.” But where we say “for nothing,” and Jerome “none,” others have “because of iniquity”; hence they were obliged to understand it as a question. The variation occurred because *auen* means both “vanity” and “iniquity.” The Septuagint, as also Jerome, had regard to the former sense. As though one said: “Over or for vanity, their Savior,” that is, their salvation is vain and nonexistent. Augustine, however, expounded it in a good sense: “for vanity” or “for nothing,” that is, freely.

“In wrath thou shalt break the peoples.” Jerome seems to criticize [Col. 0526D] this passage in his letter to Sunia and Fretela, as though the Latin reading were corrupt—indeed, the Greek as well. For he says: “In wrath thou shalt break the peoples.” For this, Greek reads ἐν ὀργῇ λαοὺς καταξεῖς, that is, “thou shalt break.” And among the Latins, in place of “thou shalt cast down,” that is, καταβαλεῖς, error has wrongly prevailed with κατάξεις, that is, “thou shalt break.” For in Hebrew there is *IHORED*, which we may render “cast down.” Symmachus also translated κατασεῖσαι, “to shake down.” But it should be known that Jerome sometimes calls there to be an error in the words, not in the sense; when that is so, he did not wish to change the translators’ established usage, as he said a little earlier: “Therefore we did not wish to alter what had been read from the ancients, since the meaning was the same.” And he repeatedly stresses the same point, as elsewhere to Sunia and Fretela: “Wherever the meaning is the same, we did not wish to alter the usage of the ancient translators, lest by excessive novelty we frighten the reader’s interest.”

VERSE 8.—“O God, I have declared my life to thee.” [Col. 0527A] Jerome: “Thou hast numbered my more secret things”; Pratensis: “Thou hast numbered my wanderings”; Sanctes: “migrations”; Pellican: “Thou hast numbered my distress”; others: “my roaming” or “my pilgrimage,” etc. The Hebrew word *nod* means migration, movement, and roaming. All these suit our mortal and perilous life so aptly that the Septuagint, following their own line of reasoning, understood “life” not wrongly at all, and were by no means enslaved to the stinking letter; for as pilgrims and strangers we have no abiding city in this age, but seek the one to come (Hebrews 13). Job also [says] in chapter 13: “Man never remains in the same condition.” Jerome’s use of “secret” for “life” or “wandering” resulted from his reading *sodi* rather than *nodi*, that is, “my secret.” Sanctes indicated this in his *Thesaurus*. “I have declared to thee,” where we read it, and “thou hast numbered,” where others have it, are reconciled without any difficulty, since *saphar* signifies both; and if the points are not written, the first and second persons differ only slightly, generally not in the word *sapharta* or *sapharti*; and in the first person the very small letter *yod* is added, where now there is a paragogic *he*. In either case the reading will finally have its own meaning. [Col. 0527B]

“Thou hast set my tears in thy sight.” Recent translators have, in place of “in thy sight,” “in thy bottle.” It is not implausibly shown that the Septuagint read *negdeca* rather than *nodeca*. The former means “thy sight,” the latter “thy bottle.” Jerome’s Hebrew version, which agrees with the Septuagint, confirms the argument—unless one wishes to say that they rendered an explained metaphor, which was conveyed by a bottle in which something is kept for preservation. God keeps our tears so that, for the groans which we send forth in expiation of sins, he may give recompense. For this reason they are said to be in his sight, because they please him from the heart. [Col. 0528A]

VERSE 9.—“As also in thy promise.” The Hebrew is read interrogatively: “Are they not in thy numbering,” or “thy account,” or “thy book?”—supply: “these things are recorded,” as Münster wishes. There is no loss in meaning if you simply read in the Septuagint’s manner. God’s book is his promise, which is also set forth in the Scriptures. Nebiensis translates: “indeed, in thy book”; and the Chaldean [translation]: “indeed, in thy accounts.” Jerome stated it absolutely, but not “in thy account,” which is more obscure. For what does “Thou hast numbered my tear, but not in thy account” mean, unless perhaps it alludes to the Apostle’s words in Romans 8: “The Spirit intercedes for us with unutterable groanings”?

[Col. 0528B] VERSE 12.—“Upon me, O God, are thy vows, which I will render to thee as praises.” In Greek, and in the Roman psalmody, it reads αἰνέσεως, “of praise.” In Hebrew, however, *todoth* occurs in the plural: “praises” or “thanksgivings.” Yet I do not see why the relative *quae*, “which,” in our reading ought to be marked with an obelus, as Faber and Caecus decide. For it is not contrary to Latin usage for vows to be called praises or thanksgivings by apposition. Not to mention that, in translating foreign languages, some departure from the idiom of Latin must be allowed—especially in sacred texts, in which, according to Jerome, every single word, when of the finest kind, contains individual mysteries.

PSALM 56.

[Col. 0527]

TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END: DO NOT DESTROY or CORRUPT DAVID IN THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE, WHEN DAVID FLED FROM THE FACE OF SAUL INTO THE CAVE.”

[Col. 0527C]

“Have mercy on me, O God.” Title. “Unto the end: Do not destroy or corrupt David in the inscription of the title, when David fled from the face of Saul into the cave.” We read in the Book of Kings that David, fleeing from Saul, came to the very secure places of En-gedi, where he lay hidden in a cave (1 Kings 24). The title touches upon this history, but the words concerning the inscription of the title draw us away from the history. [Augustine, Cassiodorus] For we read of no title inscribed upon David which Saul wished to corrupt; but a title was inscribed upon Christ, who was born of David, which the Jewish people wished to corrupt. Yet because, through the Holy [Col. 0527D] Spirit, “Do not corrupt” had been written, Pilate said, “What I have written, I have written” (John 19). The cave is understood as his flesh or his tomb, in which Christ lay hidden, concealed from or unknown to the Jews. Therefore the Prophet, foreseeing this future event through the Holy Spirit, says: “Do not corrupt.” And the sense is: This psalm directs us unto the end, that is, unto Christ. It says this: “Do not, Pilate—or whoever you are—destroy or corrupt David,” that is, Christ, “in the inscription of the title,” that is, by denying that Christ is king. The inscription of the title confirmed this, the inscription having been changed according to the Jews’ wish, when he fled—that is, because he fled from the face of Saul, that is, from the Jews’ recognition, into the cave of flesh, namely when, veiled in flesh, he was not known. For “had they known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2). Or, they wished to alter it when he fled, that is, because he fled from Saul’s face, that is, from the Jews’ recognition, into the cave, that is, into the tomb. Veiled, because, when he is not delivered from the cross or tomb, he is not thought to be the Son of God. This psalm briefly treats Christ’s passion and resurrection, in which Christ, insofar as he is human, prays concerning the passion so humbly that he seems like one of the faithful crying out. Intention: it warns that no one should oppose the title of the cross, but should believe Christ to be king. Method: the psalm has three parts. First, the Prophet, speaking in the person of the Lord—because the Lord speaks in him—cries out amid evils, as it were, and foretells deliverance. Secondly, he says by what means he is delivered and from whom, at “He sent, O Lord.” Thirdly, after the resurrection he proclaims praises, at “My heart is ready.” Therefore Christ, insofar as he is human, praying to the Father, says:

VERSE 1.—“Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me, because my soul trusts in thee.”

“Have mercy on me, O God.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] Christ says this to the Father on our behalf, teaching us to pray, he who has mercy on us together with the Father. And he repeats, “Have mercy on me.” The doubled repetition shows the greatness of the danger. Therefore have mercy, because my soul trusts in thee. This is the reason why he ought to obtain [mercy]. Here the voice of the body is now joined to the head; and, speaking in the person both of the members and of himself, he says how he may be delivered.

VERSE 2.—“And in the shadow of thy wings I will hope, until iniquity pass away.”

[Col. 0529A] “And in the shadow of thy wings,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Interlinear Gloss] that is, in the protection of thy maternal tenderness, I will hope. He does this continually also in his members. I will hope, I say, until iniquity pass away; this will be wholly accomplished in the members at the end. For until the end of the age, neither will iniquity, which oppresses, be lacking, nor righteousness, which suffers. I say, I will hope, and I shall not be idle; indeed,

VERSE 3.—“I will cry to God Most High, to God who has done me good.”

“I will cry to God Most High,” [Augustine] that is, to God who is most high. But if he is most high, how will he hear you crying? Experience gives confidence. I mean God, who has done me good; as though he said: I have learned by experience, because he has done good to me, that he will also hear me when I cry. For if he sought out the ungodly who did not seek him, and [Col. 0529B] willed to die for the ungodly, how will he fail to hear those who cry to him?

VERSE 4.—“He sent from heaven and delivered me; he gave those who trample me to reproach.”

“He sent.” [Jerome, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus] First, in the person of the Church, he has done me good thus: so well that the Father sent the Word from heaven, that is, from his hidden essence and from the secret knowledge of the angels. And thereby he delivered—that is, he will deliver—me. As though he said: Because he has already sent the Word, it is already certain, as though it had already happened, that he “delivered,” that is, will deliver, and “gave,” that is, will give to reproach those who trample me. Or thus, in the person of the Head: he has done me good in this way, because he sent me help from heaven, and through this heavenly help he delivered me, raising and [Col. 0529C] exalting me. And those who trampled upon me, namely those who mocked him when dead, he gave over to reproach, dispersing them everywhere—especially when they see the resurrection of him whom they thought they had destroyed being worshipped.

PART II. *Diapsalma.* VERSE 5.—“God sent his mercy and his truth, and delivered my soul from the midst of lion cubs; I slept, troubled.”

“He sent from heaven.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine, Jerome, Augustine, Alcuin] The second part, in which he now declares what he sent and from whom he delivered [me]. He speaks in the person of the members. As though he said: He sent from heaven. But what did he send? God the Father sent, I say, his mercy, that is, Christ, the Father’s Word, in whom God dealt mercifully [Col. 0529D] with us; for Christ has compassion upon us and, out of mercy, died for us. Therefore he is called his mercy and his truth, that is, Christ, who repays according to merits and rose in truth in order to justify us, as he had foretold. In him too the promises are fulfilled. Therefore he is called truth: both are contained in him, and neither exists without the other. For if there were mercy alone, we would have license to sin; but if truth alone, humankind could not endure. “And delivered”: this is said of the Head, because he sent the Word for precisely this purpose. And, that is, because he delivered my soul—behold, he raised himself. For Christ speaks, and speaks of the one sent; therefore he speaks of himself. From what did he deliver [it]? From the midst of lion [Col. 0530A] cubs, that is, from the people led astray by their rulers. What then did he suffer? Behold, I slept in deep rest, easily to be awakened, like one asleep. David, literally, did not sleep in the cave, but Christ slept in death. Hence it is plain that this must be understood of Christ. I slept, I say, and was troubled—not indeed troubled in my reason, but while they disturbed [me] by their own opinion. Or, “I was troubled,” according to the flesh, through the fear and anguish of the passion. Hence: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26); and elsewhere: “Jesus began to be afraid and distressed” (Mark 14). Who troubled [him]?

VERSE 6.—“The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.”

“The sons of men,” [Interlinear Gloss, Alcuin, Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus, [Col. 0530B] Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, the Jews, who ought to be sons of men. The straightforward order of the words is: The sons of men prepared a snare; but he inserts how they troubled [him], saying that their teeth—that is, their mockeries—were weapons in respect to their designs, and arrows in respect to their words. Therefore let not the Jews excuse themselves: though their hands were unarmed, their mouth was armed. Hence he adds: “And their tongue [was] a sharp sword,” when they cried, “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 23). For those cries, namely “Crucify” and the like, made death swift, like a sharp sword.

VERSE 7.—“Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let thy glory be over all the earth.”

“Be exalted,” [Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus] words of Christ to the Father. As though he said: They act thus; but, O God the Father, [Col. 0530C] be exalted above the heavens—that is, make it appear in me that thou art high above the angels; make me rest, rise, and ascend. And through this thy glory shall spread over all the earth. “Thy glory,” that is, all the inhabitants of the earth shall glorify thee. Or these words are understood as spoken by the Prophet to Christ. The preceding words were spoken by the Lord—by the Prophet, indeed, but in the Lord’s person. And rightly, because the Lord speaks in the Prophet; even when the Prophet speaks in his own person, the Lord speaks through him, since he dictates to him. Therefore the Prophet, through the Holy Spirit, seeing Christ’s injuries and seeing that by the resurrection the Jews were proved vain, joyfully cries out: O Christ, who seemest merely human, hanging on the cross, be exalted so that thou mayest appear to be God; be exalted so that thou, hanging [Col. 0530D] on the cross, mayest be known to reign in majesty with the Father. For he is exalted not with respect to himself but with respect to humankind. Be exalted, I say, above the heavens—literally, because he sits at the Father’s right hand, to judge the Jews on earth; and above the heavens, that is, even above spiritual beings, because he has angels subject to him. Thus thy glory may also be spread through all the earth, that is, extended everywhere—which is now fulfilled, because the whole world is subject to him.

VERSE 8.—“They prepared a snare for my feet, and bowed down my soul.”

“They prepared a snare,” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Interlinear Gloss] after interposing something concerning his exaltation, he continues the narrative begun. The sons of men [Col. 0531A] prepared a snare, secretly as it were, for my feet. The Lord’s feet are his rebukes of the wicked and his promises to the faithful. With these “feet,” as it were, he walked when he rebuked the wicked and promised rewards to the good. The Jews prepared deceits against them in the case of the adulterous woman whom they brought before him, seeking to entrap him in an inescapable dilemma: either that he would act contrary to the Law if he said she should be dismissed, though the Law commanded her stoning; or that they might mock him as a liar if he condemned her to death, he who preached gentleness (John 8). And they bowed down my soul, when, in compassion for them, [his soul] was made barren by them. Or, “they bent down my soul,” that is, they wished, as it were, to press me down from heaven to lower things. They prepared a snare, but not without my knowledge.

[Col. 0531B] VERSE 9.—“They dug a pit before my face, and fell into it.”

“They dug a pit,” [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss, Augustine] that is, by shouting the sentence of death; “before my face,” because he knew everything they were plotting. This happened when they said of him: “He is guilty of death” (Matthew 26). In doing this, they harmed not me but themselves. Hence follows: “And they fell into it,” into the pit they had dug—that is, blinded in a cauterized and darkened conscience.

PART III. *Diapsalma.* VERSE 10.—“My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody.”

“My heart is ready.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Interlinear [Col. 0531C] Gloss] The third part, in which, after the resurrection, he promises praises. [As though he said: That man prepares a pit, but my heart, O God, is ready for endurance; therefore he falls in, while I shall sing. And he repeats it for confirmation: “My heart is ready,” as though so very ready. Or, “My heart is ready” to give thanks. And because thanks are given in word and deed, he repeats, “My heart is ready,” so that one occurrence may be referred to deed and the other to word. And how? “I will sing and make melody,” that is, I shall give thanks by words and works. He thereby returns the two terms to the preceding doubling, because he is ready for both. Then, rejoicing, he addresses the flesh, saying: O

VERSE 11.—“Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp; I will arise at dawn.”

“My glory,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, O my flesh, [Col. 0531D] which art the cause of my glory, arise—mightily, as if to perform a miracle. This is an expression of rejoicing, because he is certain; hence, affirming by repetition and adding something else, he continues: “Arise, psaltery and harp.” The psaltery gives sound from above, the harp from below. By the psaltery and harp, the one flesh of Christ and two kinds of deeds are understood. Therefore Christ’s one flesh arose; with it two instruments arose. For in Christ’s flesh are two kinds of acts: miracles, signified by the psaltery, and sufferings, signified by the harp. And these arose because both are preached among the nations. Therefore the psaltery and harp arose, and shall confess the Lord. This is the meaning: “Arise, psaltery,” that is, flesh performing divine acts; and “arise, harp,” that is, flesh [Col. 0532A] suffering humanly. Arise, I say, because I am even certain of the hour: for I shall arise at dawn; this is the hour of Christ’s resurrection. Or another reading has, “Arise at dawn.” And so [the sense is as stated].

VERSE 12.—“I will give thanks to thee among the peoples, O Lord; I will make melody to thee among the nations.”

“I will give thanks to thee.” [Cassiodorus] Christ says this in his members, that is, I shall praise thee among the peoples, O Lord, 121 and make melody to thee—that is, I shall render to thee a heavenly act—among the nations, that is, in the midst of the nations. Here the reason for confession and psalmody is shown. As though he said: Therefore I shall give thanks and make melody.

VERSE 13.—“For thy mercy has been magnified even unto the heavens, and thy truth unto the clouds.”

[Col. 0532B] “For thy mercy has been magnified unto the heavens,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, because the humanity of the Son has literally been brought up even to the heavens; and thy truth has come even to the clouds, that is, to the preachers. The clouds are prophets and other teachers, who, filled with the rain of the Holy Spirit, rain teachings upon others. Hence: “Who are these that fly like clouds?” (Isaiah 60); and elsewhere: “I will command my clouds that they rain no rain upon them” (Isaiah 5). Or thus, so that angels are understood by “heavens” and preachers by “clouds,” because the heavens are above the clouds, and in those heavens is the dwelling of the angels. Therefore angels are fittingly understood by “heavens.” The clouds are lower than the heavens, that is, human preachers, lower than angels, still in fleshly obscurity. [Col. 0532C] They possess within themselves the light of knowledge, but concealed; through them the Lord flashes in miracles, thunders in threats, and rains in doctrines. Therefore truth pertains more to the heavens, that is, the angels, and mercy to the clouds, than mercy to the angels and truth to the clouds, that is, to preachers. For the angels see the form of truth without obscurity; and mercy is not needed where there is no misery. Yet it is fittingly said here that truth refers to the clouds and mercy to the angels, because truth—that is, knowledge of truth, which excels in angels—also descends to human beings; nor has God deprived us of it, to whom Truth itself, born of the Father, came veiled in flesh. Again, angels seem not to need mercy; but although angels do not need mercy, nevertheless, when [Col. 0532D] miserable human beings through mercy become equal to angels in the resurrection, God’s mercy ascends even to the heavens, that is, to the angels. Therefore, giving thanks, let us say with the Prophet, who said the same thing above:

VERSE 14.—“Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let thy glory be over all the earth.”

“Be exalted above the heavens, O God.” He repeats what was said before, confirming our faith: “and thy glory over all the earth.”

COLLATION ON PSALM 56: “HAVE MERCY ON ME, O GOD,” etc.

The discussion of the title was given above, and in connection with Psalm 15.

VERSE 2.—“Until iniquity pass away.” Hebrew *hauoth*; Jerome and Nebiensis: “until snares pass away”; Pratensis: “perversity”; Münster: “tyranny”; [Col. 0533A] Pellican: “the immensity of perversities”; Campensis: “a flood of crimes”; the translator following him: “Until malice pass away”; Sanctes: “Crushings”; the Chaldean: “tumults.” All these are in the nominative case. Only the interpreters for Cajetan translated in the accusative: “Until my soul shall pass beyond”—supply, “the crushings.” Finally, these are reconciled without very great difficulty.

### Verse 3

**“To God, who has done good to me.”** Jerome: “my avenger”; Pellican: “God bringing completion upon me”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “God fulfilling [his purpose] upon me”; Pagninus: “repaying upon me”; Sanctes: “repaying me”; Münster: “who pierces through the cause impending over me”; the Campensian Paraphrase: “who will accomplish what he has begun in me.” In the Hebrew there are only two words, *GOMER ALAI*. The first signifies to complete and accomplish, to render and repay. Hence Rabbi David, as Sanctes himself testifies, explains it as “rendering mercy”; and this doubtless occurs when He executes vengeance upon the evil demons and the enemies of our souls, which is to do us good and to plead our cause. Certainly our reading does not depart at all from the Hebrew truth. For this reason we wish to review the various renderings, lest anyone who encounters any one of them suppose that the Hebrew contains something other than what we read quite simply. For some permit themselves a long circumlocution in translating, and scarcely allow even a small addition for the sake of clearer sense in the Vulgate edition.

### Verse 4

**“He sent from heaven and delivered me; he gave those who trampled upon me over to reproach.”** The second clause, namely, “he gave those who trampled upon me over to reproach,” has in Hebrew only two words: *HEREPH SOAPH*. The first means “he put to shame”; the second, “one trampling upon me” or “devouring me.” Therefore both could be joined to the preceding statement and referred to the verb “delivered,” immediately before it; or they could be distinguished separately. [Col. 0534A] For this reason some necessarily either supplied something in sense or simply left the reader in suspense. Thus Pagninus: “he will save me from the reproach of one swallowing me up”; Sanctes: “from the reproach of one wishing to gulp me down”; Münster: “from the reproach of one devouring me.” Yet the Hebrew phrase did not compel this. For Jerome rendered it thus: “He will reproach those trampling upon me”; Nebiensis: “He will reproach one swallowing me up”; Pellican: “putting my trampler to shame”; the Campensian Paraphrase: “He will make infamous the one who tries to trample me.” But what else does the Vulgate edition give? “He gave those who trampled upon me over to reproach.” And the Chaldee: “He confounded those trampling upon me.” Our reading was therefore sufficient and ought not be despised if someone chooses to disturb it.

### Verse 5

**“He rescued my soul from the midst of lion cubs; I slept troubled.”** Jerome: “my soul slept in the midst of raging lions”; Pagninus: “in the midst of those who burn”; Pellican: “in the midst of those who burn the children of men,” [Col. 0534B] so that “they burn” looks back to the opening of the following verse, as Münster also wishes: “I lie among the children of men set ablaze by flame”; Sanctes: “I lie among the burning.” The Septuagint wished to explain the figurative expression “lying among raging lions,” as Jerome translates it, or “among burning ones,” according to the others. How fitting this is to Christ according to the dispensation of his humanity, no one fails to know who understands John 12: “Now my soul is troubled,” etc. And how in the tomb he was troubled among the guards, you may find in Augustine. Then, in what follows, “the children of men,” etc., properly has its place, rather than being gratuitously drawn back to the preceding words. Yet there the Septuagint indicated that the verb “he rescued” is to be understood, as Hebraizing translators frequently do whenever it seems convenient to them. A reader of our comparisons will encounter this everywhere.

## Psalm LVII

[Col. 0533]

### Title of the Psalm

**“Unto the end: Do not corrupt, or destroy, David, in the inscription of the title.”**

[Col. 0533C]

### “If indeed you speak righteousness”

Title: “Unto the end: Do not corrupt, or destroy, David, in the inscription of the title.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Here the Prophet commends righteousness to humankind, admonishing them to speak righteousness truly; and he reproves those—especially the Jews—who do not speak righteousness truly. For the Jews who had earlier said, “Master, we know that you are truthful and have come from God” (Matt. 22), cried out for his death and renounced his kingdom, saying, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). These are reproved here.

The sense of the title is: This psalm directs us to the end. It declares: Do not, Pilate or Jew, destroy or corrupt David in the inscription of the title, [Col. 0533D] that is, do not deny Christ the King whom the title declares him to be. The intention is to warn that no one should oppose Christ’s kingdom. The psalm has three parts. The first is a rebuke of the Jews, that we may not do similar things. The second declares what their recompense will be: “God shall break their teeth.” The third shows the correction of the righteous through the punishment of the wicked: “The righteous shall rejoice.”

Christ, therefore, speaking against the Jews, says:

### Verse 1

**“If indeed you speak righteousness, judge rightly, O sons of men.”**

**Sons of men.** [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine.] That is, sons of the prophets: you indeed speak righteousness with your lips—as though it were enough merely to speak it. For all can easily speak righteousness, since Truth has written in every heart: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another.” And he repeated this upon tablets, because they did not read it in their hearts, so that, when the voice was applied from without, transgressors might return to the heart and find within what they read without.

I say, you speak righteousness; but speak righteousness truly, so that it may be righteousness not of the lips but of deeds—that is, so that what is in the heart may be in the mouth. Therefore judge uprightly, or rightly. Let the lips be known by deeds. For if you act otherwise than you speak, you speak good things but judge evil things. For you act as you judge.

When asked which is better, gold or fidelity, you set fidelity before gold. A friend comes and entrusts gold to you with no witness; he departs and dies. He leaves an heir, a son, who does not know what his father entrusted to you. Consider that you likewise had entrusted something to another, told no one, and left a son: what would you wish your friend to provide for him? Answer. What does your thought answer you? Judge that in the case of your friend’s son. You previously said that fidelity was better; but avarice, by which you consider denying the gold to your friend’s heir, commands something else. You previously said within yourself that fidelity is better, and in your judgment you said—or considered—gold better. You have not judged as you spoke. You spoke truly; you judged falsely.

Truth sees all speaking righteousness lest they be called unrighteous, and cries to all: “If you truly speak righteousness—if not falsely, if one thing is not on your lips and another in your heart—judge uprightly, or rightly, [Col. 0535A] O sons of men.” Set fidelity before gold and all other temporal things, and likewise in other such matters. Otherwise you are hypocrites. If you say, “Master, you are truthful,” do not judge me worthy of death, because I am your King, as the title says.

But the Jews judged Christ in such a way that they are proved to have spoken falsely concerning him and are accused by their own words. Therefore I admonish you thus, namely that you may judge rightly, because iniquity is in your heart, your mouth, and your hand. And this is:

### Verse 2

**“For in your heart you work iniquities upon the earth; your hands devise injustices.”**

**For you work iniquities in your heart.** [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Those in whose heart and hand is iniquity cannot judge rightly. I say that you work upon the earth, that is, because you see me as earth, namely as a human being. Or because you love earth, that is, earthly things; and your hands devise injustices, as though assembling them from many parts. As if he said: Your deeds agree with your wicked thought, because the hand follows the heart. Yet if the hand is lacking, you are not therefore without guilt, because God reckons as done whatever you will but cannot do.

Now devising is perversity assembled from many parts. Or, according to another reading: “Your hands bind injustice together,” namely, they join one sin to another. Hence Isaiah: “Woe to those who draw sins as with a long rope” (Isa. 5). And sins are aptly compared with a rope. For each person is bound fast by sins, which bind a human being as chains do. Hence it is said at the end: “Bind his hands and feet,” etc. (Matt. 22). Because of sins committed in thought and deed, the sinner will be condemned; yet meanwhile he is also struck by those same sins. Hence the Lord, with a scourge made of cords or little ropes, struck those buying and selling in the temple. Behold, they are wicked both in heart and in hand. Whence comes this to them? Because:

### Verse 3

**“Sinners have been estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehood.”**

**Sinners have been estranged from truth.** [Augustine.] And I say, sinners from their mother’s womb—that is, from their very origin—not because they sinned from that time, but because God foreknew from the womb that they would be sinners. Thus he said to Rebecca while she was still pregnant: “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25). What follows explains this: “They have gone astray from the womb,” that is, they were foreknown from the womb as those who would go astray; and what was foreseen occurred, because they spoke falsehood. Behold iniquity in the mouth; and not only do they fail to do good, but they will not even hear it, because:

### Verse 4

**“Their fury is according to the likeness of a serpent, like that of a deaf asp which stops its ears.”**

**Their fury, etc.** [Augustine.] Or thus from the words “they have been estranged.” The womb, or belly, is understood as the love of the Church, in which converts are conceived and born, as they receive the rudiments of faith and are gradually nourished until, with truth formed in them, they are brought forth into the light.

Note that, just as a bodily mother observes five stages and seasons in the development of a bodily child, so in spiritual rearing [Col. 0536A] the holy Church observes the same. First, a child is conceived—that is, it is born in the womb; second, it is nourished in the womb; third, it is brought out into the light; fourth, it is carried in its mother’s hands so that it may grow; fifth, it is weaned, so that it may come to its father’s table and thus be nourished with stronger food.

Thus those whom holy Church rears first are, as it were, born in the womb—that is, conceived—when they receive the rudiments of the Christian faith in catechesis and exorcism. They are first, as it were, fed in the womb when they are more fully instructed in these rudiments. Third, through baptism and the reception and understanding of the other sacraments, they are, as it were, brought forth into the light, now that truth has been formed in them. Fourth, they are, as it were, carried in the Church’s hands and fed or nourished with milk, while they are instructed in the simpler teaching of the Church, until from the milk of simple understanding they come to the Father’s table to eat strong food, namely the bread of angels: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1).

These things are still observed today in the celebration of the sacraments. For when, on the Wednesday of the fourth week, Christ’s champions are called to the warfare of Christianity, they are, as it were, born in the womb. From then until the Saturday of Easter, they are, as it were, nourished in the womb. On Saturday they are, as it were, born into the light through baptism. Thereafter they are, as it were, carried in the hands and nourished with milk, until on Pentecost they are clothed from on high with the power of the Paraclete; and, having been granted various tongues, they speak the mighty works of God (Acts 2). Hence Abraham made a great feast when Isaac was weaned (Gen. 21), which he had not done at the circumcision or other occasions, because Isaac was then a little child.

Therefore, between Easter and Pentecost no difficult observances are imposed, namely fasting and vigils in the untimely night, because “our sister is little and has no breasts” (Song 8), and Christ rose at dawn. But these persons either are not conceived in the womb or are not born from the womb. And this is: “Sinners have been estranged from the womb” of the Church, which conceives those who are converted and nourishes those already born in it—and even those not yet born from it—until truth is formed in them and then gives them birth in perfection.

But these, though conceived, because through impatience they shake their mother’s womb before they are formed, contradicting the teaching of truth, are expelled as miscarried offspring. Therefore let your mother bring you to birth, lest she cast you off. And be patient until the teaching of truth is made sure in you. But if, in impatience, you shake your mother’s sides, she casts you out; yet this harms you more than her.

It follows: [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] “They have gone astray from the womb,” because they followed things contrary to their mother. And because they go astray from the belly in which truth is, they spoke falsehood. They are inexcusable in this, because they refuse to believe truth. And this is: “Their fury is according to the likeness of a serpent,” because the anger of the obstinate is irrevocable. Of what serpent? “Like that of a deaf asp.” Why deaf? Behold, it stops its ears with earth and its tail. For it is said to press one ear to the ground and stop the other with its tail so that it may not hear the voice of the charmer. Thus these persons, lest they hear truth, stop the ears by which they hear with earth and tail—that is, with present and past sins. [Col. 0537A] Earth means present things in which a person delights; the tail means past sins. It should be noted that Scripture does not praise everything from which it draws a comparison, as in the case of the unjust judge who heard the widow who petitioned him, though the Lord does not commend him (Luke 18). So also here.

### Verse 5

**“Which will not hear the voice of charmers, nor of the enchanter who charms skillfully.”**

Because the asp stops its ears, it will not hear the voice of charmers so as to be brought back to the light, nor the voice of an enchanter who charms skillfully, insofar as concerns his art. [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine, Alcuin.] So too these people do not hear the voice of Christ and the apostles, who are charmers wise in the ears, that they may come out into the light.

Or, according to another reading: “of the medicated remedy prepared by the wise one.” [Col. 0537B] The words show what sort of voice the charmers have. For it is a prepared remedy. The prepared remedy is all the commandments of the Law and the Prophets. All commandments were a remedy before Christ’s coming, but not a medicated one, because no one was healed by it. But by Christ’s coming it was medicated, for he fulfilled the Law and the Prophets.

For when wood was put into Marah, the water was sweetened so that the children of Israel could drink it, whereas before they could not taste it because of its excessive bitterness (Exod. 15). This is the bitterness of the Law, sweetened by the grace of the Gospel. And what had lain hidden in the legal sacraments has been brought into the light. The city set upon a mountain, which cannot be hidden, has been shown to us (Matt. 5): that is, the Church; and the lamp placed upon the lampstand, [Col. 0537C] that is, the teaching of truth, is manifest.

For where was the Church of Christ hidden, and where Christ’s truth? Is he not himself the mountain which grew from a little stone and filled the face of the earth? Is he not the serpent raised upon the wood, by looking upon whom those bitten by serpents are healed? He therefore is the wise one by whom the remedy is medicated.

## Part II. Verse 6

**“God shall break their teeth in their own mouth; the Lord shall shatter the jaws of lions.”**

**God shall break [them].** [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] This is the second part, in which it is said what their recompense will be. As if he said: They despise in this way, but God will break their teeth—that is, their deceitful words—whose fury is like that of an asp. And this will be in their own mouth, because he will catch them in their own words. For in their own speech they speak against themselves.

Those who were compared to asps are now also compared to lions, as he adds: “The Lord shall shatter the jaws of lions,” that is, the cries for death made by the Jews, so that they may not take effect. Note that the Jews were asps when they tempted him deceitfully; they were lions when they cried out for his death. Their jaws were broken when he rose again. He explains this more openly as he continues: those who are such are, although torrents now, nevertheless:

### Verse 7

**“They shall come to nothing like water that runs away; he has bent his bow until they are weakened.”**

**They shall come to nothing like water that runs away.** [Cassiodorus.] Behold, here they are also compared to torrents, because they are noisy, unlooked-for, headlong against the rocks of pride. But they swiftly pass away: they are compared to so many evils. [Col. 0538A] They thus run down; but on the contrary God, in mercy and for their salvation, bends his bow—that is, the threats by which he terrifies—until they are weakened, that is, until they are converted, as Saul was weakened when he heard: “Why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9). He who cried this from heaven was bending the bow. Many, therefore, have been weakened, terrified by his bending of the bow. But what will those who are not weakened suffer? Behold:

### Verse 8

**“Like wax which melts, they shall be taken away; fire has fallen upon them, and they have not seen the sun.”**
