**Like wax which melts, they shall be taken away,** [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine] that is, they shall perish through the fire of desires; for as fire consumes a garment, so lust consumes the soul. Or thus: God bends his bow, that is, vengeance, until they are weakened inwardly and outwardly; and this is understood in an evil sense, and that they may be taken away from God’s sight, sent into Gehenna. Or, “they shall be taken away” here in the present life from their land, like melting wax: “fire has fallen upon them,” etc.

It should be known that between the first sin, which is pride, and the last punishment, which is eternal fire, there are certain intermediate things which are both sins and punishments. Of these he says: “Fire has fallen upon them,” namely the fire of pride, desire, and anger. Therefore they have not seen the sun, namely of righteousness, concerning which the wicked say in the Book of Wisdom: “We have strayed from the way of truth, and the sun of righteousness has not shone upon us” (Wis. 5).

Here is read first, according to another text, which is:

### Verse 9

**“Before your thorns understood the buckthorn, while still living, so in wrath he swallows them up.”**

**Before the buckthorn produces your thorns, while still living he swallows them up in wrath.** [Augustine, Alcuin.] There sins are understood by the buckthorn, and the piercing of eternal condemnation by thorns. For the buckthorn is a plant initially soft but later turning into thorns; likewise, sins delight now but pierce later. This is what he says: “Fire”—of vices—“has fallen upon them.” And that fire swallows them up, that is, devours them “while still living,” that is, while they still live. Nor does he merely say “living,” but adds “while still,” because the life of the ungodly is not true but false. They seem to live and do not live.

He adds, “in wrath.” He does not say simply, “in wrath,” for God judges tranquilly. Or because the present is not wrath by comparison with the life to come. I say he swallows them up “before the buckthorn produces your thorns,” turning his speech toward them—that is, before the torments of pleasures arise. For while they still live, the fire of vices which has fallen upon them in God’s wrath devours them and conceals the buckthorn, that is, the thorn of the buckthorn, namely the final piercing of sin, so that it is not now seen.

Or, according to our text, sins are also understood by the thorn, and final condemnation by the buckthorn. And the meaning is: “Before your thorns,” that is, your sins, “understand the buckthorn,” that is, sharp condemnation, even at the end the fire of vices swallows them up—that is, devours them—while still living. Thus in wrath he swallows them up. This is unchanged.

## Part III. Verse 10

**“The righteous shall rejoice when he sees vengeance; he shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner.”**

[Col. 0539A] **The righteous shall rejoice.** [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] This is the third part, showing the correction of the righteous through the punishment of the wicked. As if he said: Fire swallows up the wicked. Yet this is not without fruit for the good. As if he said: The righteous person who has faith, even if something in him needs washing, shall rejoice. Even if pressed by troubles, when he sees this present vengeance he nevertheless does not rejoice at their punishment, but because he is not in it. Rather, he shall wash his hands—that is, his works—in the blood of the sinner, that is, in the punishment and death of the sinner which he sees. Hence Solomon: “When the fool perishes, the wise man will be wiser” (Prov. 19).

### Verse 11

**“And man shall say: If indeed there is fruit for the righteous, indeed there is a God judging them upon the earth.”**

**And he shall say,** [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss, Alcuin, Augustine] that is, a human being—that is, a rational being—will reflect within himself that this did not happen to them by chance but as punishment for sin. For he will say: “Indeed, there is a God judging them,” that is, the wicked, “upon the earth,” even this earth, where they seem to flourish. He proves this from the opposite: “if,” that is, because “indeed there is fruit even here for the righteous,” although he is oppressed here. As if he said: Just as by God’s just judgment the righteous person becomes still more righteous, so by the same justice it is permitted that the filthy become still more filthy (Rev. 22).

Or thus, according to another reading cited by Augustine: “And man shall say: Therefore there is fruit for the righteous; therefore there is a God judging them upon the earth.” He draws the inference from the two preceding statements. For he said that the wicked are swallowed up here and that the righteous wash themselves. And this is: the rational human being will say, because the righteous wash their hands, therefore there is fruit for the righteous here. And because fire swallows up the wicked, therefore there is a God judging them upon the earth, even this earth where they appear to flourish.

## Comparison on Psalm LVII: “If indeed you speak righteousness,” etc.

### Verse 1

**“If indeed you speak righteousness.”** There is one Hebrew particle here, namely *ELEM*, which sometimes means “assembly,” sometimes “indeed,” and at other times “mute.” Thus Pagninus translates: “Do you indeed speak mute righteousness?” Sanctes and Münster put instead of “indeed”: “O assembly, O council.” Jerome, Nebiensis, Pellican, and the interpreters for Cajetan say: “truly indeed.” The Chaldee agrees. Although the interpretation of the others has merit, if we choose to confuse everything in this way, there will never be an end.

### Verse 2

**“Their fury is according to the likeness of a serpent.”** Sanctes, Münster, the Chaldee, the interpreters for Cajetan, and the Campensian version give “venom” instead of “fury.” [Col. 0539D] Jerome, Nebiensis, Pagninus, Pellican, and the translator for Campensis give “fury” itself, like the Septuagint, because the Hebrew word *HAMATH* is ambiguous.

### Verse 5

**“Which will not hear the voice of charmers, nor of the enchanter who charms skillfully.”** The versions agree sufficiently. Pagninus: “so that it does not hear the voice of charmers, the charms of a learned enchanter”; Münster: “which refuses to hear the voice of charmers, and of the magician who is learned in magical arts.” The rest similarly. Jerome: “so that it does not hear the voice of whisperers, nor the skillful charms of an enchanter.”

Augustine used another edition, because his text and interpretation have together: “and of the medicated remedy prepared by the wise one.” For the Greek reads differently, *φαρμακοῦτε φαρμακευομένη παρὰ σοφοῦ*, that is, “charmed by a wise sorcerer,” and “of the enchanter, which is charmed by the wise one.”

### Verse 7

**“They shall come to nothing like water that runs away.”** Thus Jerome and Nebiensis: “Let them dissolve like waters which flow away.” [Col. 0540A] In Hebrew, instead of “running away,” there are two particles, *IITHHALCU LAMO*, literally, “they shall go for themselves.” Certainly the Septuagint and Jerome interpreted rightly. Others wish otherwise. Münster: “and let them pass away in themselves”; Pagninus: “let them go away for themselves like water”; Sanctes: “they shall walk for themselves”; Pellican: “let them go away for themselves.” The Campensian Paraphrase agrees better with the Septuagint and Jerome: “let them flow away like water, naturally unstable.” The other translations seem to suggest, I know not what, a different sense—perhaps attending to the Hithpael, which according to Elijah sometimes signifies a kind of pretense or opinion, that is, one who seems to himself to walk rightly.

**“He has bent his bow until they are weakened.”** Jerome agrees: “He bends his bow until they are crushed,” so that the verb “bends” refers to God. Pagninus, Sanctes, Münster, and Campensis translate it in the plural and refer it to the arrows: “Let them aim their arrows; let them be as though cut off,” or “as though shattered.” Münster: “While they aim their arrows, let them be destroyed.” By this device they alter the sense. I cannot sufficiently wonder at this, since it is manifest that in the Hebrew scrolls the single word *IIDOC*, “he bends,” is read. If it is permissible to play with the Scriptures in this manner, there will finally be as many senses as there are heads. I would not have this said to anyone’s injury.

### Verse 8

**“Like wax which melts, they shall be taken away.”** Jerome: “Let them pass away like a worm melted away”; Sanctes: “like a snail which dissolves, let it go on”; Pagninus: “like a snail which dissolves, let it go on”; Münster: “let each of them depart like a flowing snail.” And the others likewise. Hebrew: *SCABELUL TEMES*. Leaving the verbal shell, the Septuagint carefully attended to what this comparison suggested, namely the destruction of the ungodly, aptly signified by melting; and whether it be of a worm, wax, or something of that sort makes no difference to the sense. [Col. 0540C]

Jerome has already repeatedly stressed this point, or something like it: while we follow the *κακοζήλια*—the slavish imitation—of translation, we lose all the elegance of translation. The duty of a good translator is to express the idiom of another language in the proper character of his own language. You have an example in 1 Samuel 24: the Hebrews say “to cover his feet,” while we translate “to relieve the bowels”: *LAHASEC RAGLAU*, “to cover his feet.” And in Judges 3, *MESIC RAGLAU*, “covering his feet.” Our edition has “relieving his bowels.” Therefore, when the sense suffers no loss, Hebrew figures should be explained, even though one must depart from the sound of the words.

**“Fire has fallen upon them, and they have not seen the sun.”** Jerome: “like the miscarriage of a woman.” Likewise the others: “a miscarriage,” or “a mole,” which do not see the sun. Although the sense tends to the same point, namely that whenever the fire of divine vengeance or of desire falls, the ungodly person is reduced to nothing, there may nevertheless be a variant reading in Hebrew. For the Hebrew word without vowel points can be read *NEPHEL*, that is, “miscarriage,” or *NAPHAL*, that is, “he fell”; and *ESCH*, simply, “fire”; or *ESCHETII*, that is, “woman” or “mole.”

### Verse 9

**“Before your thorns understood the buckthorn.”** All agree except Sanctes and Münster, who translate thus: “Before your kettles,” or “your pots,” “feel the fire of buckthorn.” Hebrew *SIROTECHEM* is ambiguous.

**“While still living, so in wrath he swallows them up.”** It seems quite intolerable that Sanctes and Münster translated here as follows: the former, “like raw flesh, so wrath like a whirlwind will destroy them”; the latter, “like something raw, so fury agitates him.” I suppose they understood *BASAR*. For *BASAR HAI* is fresh raw flesh. Why they did this is not clear. I believe that if they had found anything similar in the Septuagint, [Col. 0541A] they would accuse it, as it were, of sacrilege. For Hebrew, however plain, did not compel them to do this at all. Hence Jerome translates: “like living beings, like a tempest in wrath it will snatch them away.” And the others likewise, with words slightly altered but the meaning unchanged. It is certain that Sanctes and Münster borrowed this from Rabbi David.

### Verse 10

**“He shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner.”** [Col. 0542A] Hebrew *PEAMAU* means “his feet” or “his steps,” but *PAAM* is very polyvalent. At times it signifies “to strengthen,” as in Judges 13, where we have “the Spirit of the Lord was with him”; the Hebrews say, *LEPHAAMO*, “to strengthen him.” Moreover, strength and works are frequently understood in Scripture through hands.

## Psalm LVIII

[Col. 0541]

### Title of the Psalm

**“Unto the end: Do not corrupt, or destroy, David, in the inscription of the title, when Saul sent and guarded his house in order to kill him.”**

[Col. 0541A]

### “Deliver me from my enemies, O my God”

Title: [Col. 0541B] “Unto the end: Do not corrupt, or destroy, David, in the inscription of the title, when Saul sent and guarded his house in order to kill him.” We read in the Book of Kings that Saul, seeking to kill David, sent his attendants to guard David’s house so that they might kill him when he went out in the morning. When his wife Michal, Saul’s daughter, learned this beforehand, she lowered him through a window by night, and thus he escaped (1 Sam. 19).

[Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The title alludes to this history, though the psalm does not treat the history itself but its meaning. David signifies Christ; his house, Christ’s tomb; Saul, the king of the Jews; and the kingdom of the Jews, those who sent men to guard the tomb. But it does not seem fitting that it is said “so that Saul might kill him.” Christ had already been killed when they sent them. Yet they sought to kill him, not bodily but spiritually: that is, to extinguish his name and reputation among the nations so that they might not believe in him. They were nevertheless unable to accomplish this. For the King lives over Jews and Gentiles. Here the Holy Spirit also foretells this through the Prophet.

The sense is: This psalm tends toward the end, that is, Christ. It declares: Do not, Pilate or Jew, corrupt or destroy David in the inscription of the title. This same thing had been stated above in other titles. In vain, therefore, does anyone attempt to destroy what divine authority so often forbids. But when Pilate said, “What I have written, I have written” (John 19), what is said here was fulfilled: namely, “Do not corrupt or destroy David in the inscription of the title.”

Do not corrupt him because Saul—that is, the Jewish kingdom—sent men and guarded his house—that is, Christ’s tomb—in order to kill him, that is, to take away his name and reputation so that he might not be believed in. Having been delivered from those whose attempt was frustrated, he is here shown to possess renown among all nations. Here Christ speaks whole, namely Head and body. The intention is to warn that no one should oppose Christ. The psalm has three parts. First, he prays to be delivered, ascending from the low places to the heights. He also prays for the salvation of the Gentiles. Second, he confirms the salvation of the Gentiles and prays for the salvation of the Jews: “They shall return.” Third, the salvation of the Jews is affirmed, and with both walls gathered together, thanks are given: “They shall return.” Thus the whole Christ, as though besieged by enemies, cries out, saying:

[Col. 0542A]

### Verse 1

**“Deliver me from my enemies, O my God; and free me from those who rise up against me.”**

**Deliver me from my enemies, O my God.** [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Jerome, Cassiodorus.] This happened in Christ’s flesh and will happen in his members, while he who is without stain asks this. It shows what we necessarily await. For our enemies—the devil and his angels—do not cease daily to rise against us, to mock the weakness and frailty of our nature, and to ensnare us by deceits, suggestions, temptations, and every kind of snare, while we still live upon earth.

Note that four kinds of adversaries are distinguished here: enemies, who have the wish to harm but do not pursue it ardently; those who rise up, who are already stirred and prepared in mind; workers, who with hardened mind now carry their wickedness into action; and men of blood, who not only heap insults upon others but shed blood. The Jews did this: first they killed Christ, and afterwards the apostles. Of these, then, he says: “Deliver me from my enemies,” who hate me, “O my God; and free me from those who rise up against me,” who harm by words.

### Verse 2

**“Deliver me from those who work iniquity, and save me from men of blood.”**

**Deliver me from those who work iniquity,** [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine] namely those who strike with their fists, etc., and perform such acts; “and save me from men of blood,” namely those who killed the righteous one, that is, Christ, and afterwards his own people.

### Verse 3

**“For behold, they have seized my soul; the mighty have rushed upon me.”**

**For behold, they have seized [my soul].** [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Here Christ speaks in his own person. As though he said: Deliver and save me. For what do they do to you? Surely evil, because “behold, they have seized my soul,” namely my bodily life, since the mighty have rushed violently upon me in humility—the mighty in temporal things, namely those who abound, who do not set God as their helper but, hoping in riches, have prevailed in their vanity.

Or they are also mighty because they are proud and presume upon their own righteousness. They deride Christ as he dines with sinners, who have no need of a physician; yet they killed him as a criminal in the guise of righteous men. But there is no iniquity in him. And this is: “The mighty have rushed upon me,” that is, those proud of their righteousness, as though upon a criminal; but they found no sin in me. Hence he adds:

### Verse 4

**“Neither my iniquity nor my sin, O Lord; without iniquity I ran and directed [my course].”**

[Col. 0543A] **Neither my iniquity,** [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine, Alcuin] which I committed against them, was the cause why they rushed upon me; nor my sin, which might in any way be in me. Or: neither my iniquity—that is, malice—was the cause, nor my sin in deed. O Lord, but without iniquity I ran the course of this world. Hence elsewhere: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18). And I set the crooked straight, as far as lay in me.

Or, according to another text: “And I was directed toward you.” And therefore:

### Verse 5

**“Rise up to meet me, and see; you, O Lord God of hosts, God of Israel.”**
Rise up, [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine]—you who seem to be asleep—that is, help me. Rise up, I say, to meet me: as though I run toward you in sorrow, do you run to meet me [Col. 0543B] and render according to desert. And see—that is, make it seen—how I run to you and direct others, lest they think crooked what is straight and follow it. Or thus: rise up to meet me and see—that is, make yourself known, and make it apparent that you rise up to meet me, that is, that I am equal to you. For “to meet” is said only of equals. Christ did not cease to be equal to the Father, although for our sake he became weak, emptying himself by taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2).

Thus in the Gospel he compares himself to a hen, saying: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wished to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matt. 23). No bird appears so weakened on account of its young as a hen: its voice grows hoarse, its whole body becomes rough, its wings droop, and its feathers hang loose. Such maternal affection, or charity, is found in weakness. So too Christ was weakened for our sake in order to take away our weakness; yet in that weakness he comes as equal to the Father. For he assumed what he was not without losing what he was. Thus he emptied himself in such a way that he did not display to us the dignity which he possessed with the Father.

Therefore, in that very weakness he must be recognized as equal to the Father—not by bodily sight, but by faith—so that what we have not yet been able to see, we may at least believe. And while we believe this within ourselves, he ascends to the Father. Hence he said to Mary Magdalene, to whom he first appeared after the resurrection: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father” [Col. 0543D] (John 20). What does “Do not touch me” mean? Did not the women later return from the tomb, worship him, and hold his feet? (Matt. 28). But here he speaks of the mind’s touch, not that of the body: that is, do not believe merely what you see, lest your gaze—like your touch—cling too closely to my humanity. I say this because I have not yet ascended to my Father, certainly in your heart: because, after seeing me die, you do not yet believe that I am equal to the Father.

Observe by what steps he ascends. He began from weakness, and gradually ascended to the glory of the resurrection and arrived at equality with the Father. Then follows prayer for the conversion of the nations: “And you, Lord God of the heavenly hosts, God of Israel”—that is, you who seem to be the God of one nation, which worships you—

[Col. 0544A]

**VERSE 6.**—“Attend to visiting all the nations; have no mercy on all who work iniquity.”

“Attend to visiting all the nations,” [Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus] because all are weak, so that all may be gathered to the wedding feast (Matt. 22). I say, attend; and yet “have no mercy on all who work iniquity,” in such a way as to leave their sins unpunished; rather, pursue, punish, convert. And so he does: he leaves no sins unpunished, because either the human being repenting, or God the judge, punishes them.

Or thus: there is a certain iniquity, and God does not have mercy unto salvation on one who commits it. This is the defense of sins, when a person defends what God hates. Hence: “There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John 5). And the sense is: “Have no mercy on all who work iniquity,” namely, that sin which is unto death and for which prayer is not to be made. Or: visit all the nations; yet do not have mercy on all Jews, though on some of them you do.

## PART II. Διάψαλμα (*Diapsalma*).

**VERSE 7.**—“They shall return at evening, and suffer hunger like dogs; and they shall go around the city.”

“They shall return.” [Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus] The second part, in which the salvation of the nations, prayed for, is affirmed, and the salvation of the Jews is prayed for. I said, “Attend,” and truly you will attend, because the nations “shall return” from idols “at evening,” that is, in the last age of the world. And, seeking to convert others, they “shall suffer hunger,” grieving if they cannot convert them, “like dogs,” namely by barking against enemies; and [Col. 0544C] “they shall go around the city,” that is, they shall fortify the Church against heretical attacks. And:

**VERSE 8.**—“Behold, they shall speak with their mouth, and a sword is upon their lips; for who has heard?”

“Behold,” [Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear, Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Augustine] that is, openly, “they shall speak with their mouth,” for the instruction of believers and the refutation of heretics; and the sword of the Holy Spirit, which is the word of God—or, according to another reading, “death,” which is the same thing—will be upon their lips. With that sword they kill the wicked so that they may live; the good strike in order to heal. And truly, “for who has heard such things?”—according to another reading—such things, that is, as they will preach? No one. Thus all will marvel. Or, according to our text: therefore frequent preaching is on their lips, because “who has heard them?” That is, few will hear them.

[Col. 0544D]

**VERSE 9.**—“But you, Lord, will laugh at them, and reduce all the nations to nothing.”

And [Cassiodorus, Augustine] those who will not hear, you, Lord, will laugh at in the future. And all the nations which do not worship you, you will then reduce to nothing.

Or, from the words “They shall return,” he here speaks of the Jews. Thus: I said, “Have no mercy”—on all Jews; yet you will have mercy on some of them, because they “shall return at evening,” that is, rather late, after the ascension and the sending of the Spirit—something which they ought to have done before they crucified him. And, seeking to convert others, they “shall suffer hunger like dogs.” Previously the nations were called dogs because of their uncleanness; but the Jews too recognize themselves as dogs, that is, sinners, like the Canaanite woman, who humbly acknowledged herself and said: “Even the little dogs eat from the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table” [Col. 0545A] (Matt. 15). She hungered for the heavenly bread. Thus these also, because they acknowledge themselves to be dogs, hunger and act well. But those act badly who, filled with their imagined righteousness, say with the Pharisee: “I fast twice in the Sabbath” (Luke 18).

“They shall go around,” by evangelizing, “the city,” that is, the surrounding region—the world which surrounds on every side—Judaea, where these things were said. “Behold, they shall speak with their mouth,” that is, they will be indignant and angry against those slow to believe, saying: It is no wonder that we are indignant and angry, “for who among the Jews has heard us?” That is, who among the Jews has believed our report? As though he said: Few Jews believe. Yet, although the Jews do not believe, the nations are proclaimed to through believing Jews. Hence he says: “And a sword,” or “death,” is upon their lips. This is the two-edged sword, cutting with either Testament, by which Peter slays the creeping things shown to him on the sheet, when he was told: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” [Col. 0545B] (Acts 10).

“And you, Lord”—as though they themselves speak against the sluggish—“will laugh at them,” that is, you will regard them as nothing. They say, “Who has heard?” Why will you laugh? Because “you will reduce all the nations to nothing”: you will regard them as nothing in order to convert them; that is, you will easily convert all nations, because it will be easy for you to make all nations believe in you. As though he said: All nations will become Christian. And you say, “Who has heard?” This was said earlier in the person of the Church: thus they are strong, presuming upon themselves. “But I”—

**VERSE 10.**—“I shall keep my strength for you, because God is my defender; my God, [Col. 0545C] his mercy will go before me.”

“I shall keep my strength for you,” [Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Augustine] that is, I shall not depart from you by presuming upon myself. For they fell, though strong, because they did not keep their strength for you. And I shall rightly keep it for you, because “you, God, are my defender,” because he has taken me up from my lowliness to his height—“my God.”

Then, changing person, he adds: “My God,” spiritually speaking, because “his mercy will go before me.” I brought nothing on account of which he should have mercy; for no one merits God’s gifts. And that it is mercy which goes before me is shown in this:

**VERSE 11.**—“God will show me concerning my enemies: do not kill them, lest at any time they forget my people.”

“God will show me concerning my enemies,” or, according to another reading, “to my enemies,” [Augustine, Alcuin, Gloss interlinear] that is, through my enemies: he has shown me how great was the mercy he had toward me, in those toward whom he did not have it, because from the same mass he made one vessel for honor, another for dishonor. Hence the Apostle: “He endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order to make known his riches upon vessels of mercy” (Rom. 9).

The Church immediately prays for those enemies, saying: O God, do not kill them—even their sins—namely, lest they forget your law. Another reading gives this: their forgetting the law of the Lord would be their being killed; that is true death, in the abyss of the wrath of sin.

Or, from “my strength,” it is spoken in the person of Christ and concerns the Jews. As though he said: The strong rushed upon me, namely the Jews; although I could destroy them, nevertheless [Col. 0546A] I shall keep my strength for you, that is, according to your ordering. Though I could scatter the Jews, I nevertheless permit them to live, keeping my strength for you—that is, for your ordering. I ought to do this because God has shown me, as I consider my enemies, what must be done concerning them; to whose counsel I must submit, because he is God, my defender and my God, and his mercy will go before me, because he went before Christ beyond his companions (Ps. 44), to whom he gave the Spirit without measure (John 3).

And this God—repeat—has shown me concerning my enemies, that is, the Jews, what is to be done about them. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin] What he showed you was what was to be done about them when I prayed for them, that they should not be killed; and he showed this not by word but by deed. [Col. 0546B] He prays for them to the Father: O God the Father, do not kill them. This may be understood especially of the Jews. This is what the Father showed him: “Do not kill them.” He asks that the Jews not utterly perish. They have indeed been scattered, so that they may be summoned to conversion; or so that the Church may have from its enemies the testimony of the Old Law.

Therefore he prays for them, saying: “Do not kill them who killed me, but let the Jewish people remain, bearing the sign of circumcision, Sabbath, and Passover, just as Cain bore a sign so that no one should kill him” (Gen. 4). Thus that people, possessing its sign, has not been killed, because it is necessary for believers; and in those branches cut off is shown what mercy belongs also to those grafted in. Therefore, do not kill them, lest at some time “my people,” even if not now, forget me—if they are not witnesses of the Law and of Christ’s death. Do not kill them, [Col. 0546C] but:

**VERSE 12.**—“Scatter them in your power, and cast them down, O Lord, my protector.”

“Scatter them among all nations,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine] namely the Jews, who carry the books for us. And do this “in your power,” because you are strong, not they; and “cast them down,” or, according to another reading, “lead them down”: that is, do not abandon them, but lead them onward by preserving them. In this you are “my protector, O Lord,” that is, you protect me so that I may have testimony from them.

Or according to our text: “Cast them down,” so that they may be a reproach to all. Or: cast them down in what is evil in them, so that they may rise good; as happened in Paul, for Paul would not have risen unless Saul had first fallen [Col. 0546D] (Acts 9). You, I say, cast them down—you who are my protector, O Lord. The text is obscure. For the things said here are obscure, and I fear they may not be adequately set forth. As though he said: Do not kill them, but:

**VERSE 13.**—“The sin of their mouth, the word of their lips; and let them be caught in their pride.”

“Kill the sin of their mouth,” [Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Augustine] that is, pardon it; and kill the very word of their lips, that is, render it unfulfilled, so that they may fear the one whom they wished to destroy when raised again, and may marvel that the one whom they despised on earth is adored in heaven by all nations.

Or thus: cast them down, and also cast down the sin of their mouth, namely the sin of thought, and the word of their lips, that is, the sin [Col. 0547A] of speech; and thus, converted, let them be caught in their pride. Someone is caught in his pride when, observing the enormity of his sin, he sees that he acted proudly. For some converted Jews learned that this was so: namely, that their deed came to nothing and sin remained upon them. Thus they were caught in their pride. And this is the sense of “let them be caught in their pride,” in which they seemed to prevail: let them know that they acted proudly and vainly, because the strong rushed upon him in vain. They killed not life but death. For death was extinguished in the one dying, and life rose again in the one rising on the third day.

Thus they found that they had condemned nothing and done nothing; and they were more humbled by the greatness of their sin, and by that humility more fully brought to completion—that is, perfected. Nothing impedes perfection so much as pride. Envy is pride’s companion; nor can it happen that a proud person does not envy. Thus the devil, who fell through pride, envied humankind. The crime, that is, reflection upon the greatness of the crime, brought about pride, just as an angel of Satan did for Paul (2 Cor. 12). But forgiveness effaced the crime.

**VERSE 14.**—“And because of cursing and lying they shall be proclaimed in the consummation; in the wrath of consummation, and they shall be no more.”

“And because of cursing.” [Gloss interlinear, Jerome, Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear, Augustine] As though he said: They have been caught in pride, and thus, because of the curse in which the Jews are among the nations—or because he cursed Christ—and because of the lie by which they perverted the Scriptures, they shall [Col. 0547C] be proclaimed by the apostles and others as an example. “In the consummation”; or, according to another reading, “consummations shall be proclaimed”: that is, the apostles will preach that where the offense of cursing and lying abounded, the grace of perfection superabounded (Rom. 5), and that this pertained to the healing of the humility and weakness of humankind.

Or according to the other reading: “because of the curse,” namely that by which you think one hanging upon a tree accursed (Deut. 21); “and because of the lie,” namely that you gave money to the guards that they might lie (Matt. 28), they “shall be proclaimed in the consummation”—that is, they are all the more perfected because they have been caught in these things. All this happened “in the wrath of consummation,” that is, in God’s vengeance by which he brings to completion. [Col. 0547D] For there is a wrath, that is, a vengeance of God’s bringing-to-completion, by which God sometimes avenges in order to perfect; and there is a wrath of destruction, as when he says: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25). I say that they are caught in their pride, and thus they will no longer be people in the pride in which they were caught.

**VERSE 15.**—“And they shall know that God shall rule Jacob and the ends of the earth.”

“And then they shall know that God shall rule Jacob,” [Augustine] that is, the Jews, “and the ends of the earth,” that is, the nations whom they despised as dogs. For previously the Jews seemed righteous to themselves; but it is shown to them that they are not so apart from Christ, who rules Jacob. Having laid aside pride, they know themselves equal to the nations, because all have sinned.

## PART III. Διαψαλμα (*Diapsalma*).

**VERSE 16.**—“They shall return [Col. 0548A] at evening and suffer hunger like dogs; and they shall go around the city.”

“They shall return.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] The third part, in which the salvation of the Jews is affirmed and, with both walls gathered together, thanks are given. As though he said: Let them be caught in their pride. And thus they shall fully return at evening, that is, at the end of the world. Or: they shall return, even though at evening—that is, after Christ’s killing, though they ought to have done so earlier—and they shall suffer hunger “like dogs,” that is, as sinners rather than sheep, recognizing themselves as weak so that they may become healthy. For no one is more incurable than one who thinks himself healthy; but those who recognize themselves as weak are healed. Hence: “Their weaknesses were multiplied; afterward they hastened” (Ps. 15). “And they shall go around the city,” as above. And:

**VERSE 17.**—“They themselves shall be scattered for eating; but if they are not satisfied, they shall murmur.”

“They themselves,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Alcuin, Augustine] now made worthy, will certainly be scattered in order to eat, so that they may gain others. But if they are not satisfied with the faith of the peoples, they will then murmur, just as they formerly murmured in the wilderness. Or, “they shall murmur,” that is, grieve, and not merely be scattered. Or, “they shall murmur” against the sluggish, that is, rebuke others unwilling to believe. He says “they shall murmur” because above he also mentioned their murmuring as they said: “For who has heard?”

**VERSE 18.**—“But I shall sing your strength, and in the morning I shall exalt your mercy.”

[Col. 0548C] “But I.” [Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus, Jerome] Here this psalm concludes, where, with both walls joined in the cornerstone, the whole Church now rejoices. As though he said: Both walls were previously far apart, but I, now the whole Church, shall sing your strength, by which you raise up the nations and humble the Jews. And “in the morning,” namely when trials have passed, when the night of this age has gone by, when we shall no longer fear the ambushes of robbers—that is, of the devil and his angels—when we shall behold the very Word of God as the sun: in that morning, I say, I shall exalt your mercy, just as Christ rose in the morning. Hence: “Weeping will remain at evening, but joy at morning” (Ps. 29). The apostles wept at evening for him dead; in the morning [Col. 0548D] they rejoiced in him risen. And I shall rejoice, I say, receiving your mercy, which will be given in recompense. Or: I shall rejoice on the morning of the Lord’s Day, receiving your mercy, that is, Christ’s resurrection. I shall rejoice.

**VERSE 19.**—“Because you have become my defender and my refuge in the day of my tribulation.”

“Because you have become my defender,” [Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus] as the Church is raised from lowliness to height; “and my refuge in the day of my tribulation,” when that is welcome. And, O God, who are:

**VERSE 20.**—“My helper, I shall sing psalms to you, because God is my defender; my God, my mercy.”

“My helper,” [Gloss interlinear, Augustine] that is, my fellow-worker, “I shall sing psalms to you,” that is, I shall act, not merely sing, [Col. 0549A] because you, God, are my defender. It is a great thing that you are God and defender; and you, the same God, are “my mercy” in every respect, because you give all things freely. Although he has said much, he has not said everything; but in this one thing he comprehends everything, because all is from God’s gift. Therefore, filled with his good things, he finds no name for him except “his mercy.”

## Comparison on Psalm LVIII: “Deliver me from my enemies,” etc.

**VERSE 4.**—“Without iniquity I ran and set straight.” Hebrew: **BELI AVON IERUTZUN VIICONANU**, that is, “without iniquity they ran,” or “they will run, and they will set straight,” or “be made ready.” If you refer this to David or Christ, “my works” must be understood: “my works ran without iniquity.” Therefore the Seventy, so that the sense might be clearer, rendered it in the singular, in the first person [Col. 0549B]. For it would be difficult to refer it to the guards who surrounded David, or to the treacherous Jews raging against Christ. For how could it be “without iniquity”? For this reason Jerome marked a division here: “I have not acted unjustly,” by one word; then he added, “and they run and prepare themselves.” This is supported by Nebiensis. But Münster, because of the absurdity of the sense, was compelled to add the pronoun *my*, or to understand: “without my iniquity, they run together and arrange themselves.” The Chaldee did the same, so that the absence of iniquity might refer to David or the righteous person, whose innocence, though perfect, did nothing to prevent the wicked from persecuting him hostilely, with no regard for justice.

**VERSE 7.**—“They shall suffer hunger like dogs.” Hebrew: **ICHEMU CACALEB**, “they will make an uproar,” or “cry out,” or “bark,” according to Jerome. But the translators of the Seventy conveyed the very force of the expression in fitting words: what hungry dog does not run about when it barks? This is made clearer [Col. 0549C] by verse 17 of this psalm. For after the similar verse it is said below: “If they are not satisfied, they shall murmur.”

**VERSE 10.**—“My strength, for keeping.” Thus Jerome. They now read in Hebrew **UZO**, that is, “his strength,” which is more difficult, instead of **UZI**, that is, “my strength.” We have pointed out several times how easily *vav* changes into *yod*, and conversely; yet that “my strength” fits more suitably than “his strength,” I think is clear. Hence the translator following Campensis: “My strength, I bring it acceptably to you”; and the Chaldee paraphrast: “My strength, I will watch for you.” Nebiensis translates: “Their strength, I will watch for you,” and explains the phrase as defective and exclamatory. As though he said: “Because of their immense strength, I will watch for you.”

“My God, his mercy will go before me.” From this passage, among countless others, it is inferred that even the Hebrew manuscripts varied. For Sunia and Fretela had first read [Col. 0549D]: “My God, his will shall go before me.” Jerome, replying to them, says: “Where the Greek has written ἔλεος αὐτοῦ προφθάσει με, that is, ‘his mercy shall go before me,’ which is also truer, the Hebrew reads: ‘The mercy of my God shall go before me.’” Yet we now see otherwise in Hebrew copies. Some have **ELOHE HASDI**, others **ELOHE HASDO**. Accordingly Münster and Sanctes said, “God of my mercy,” or “of my loving-kindness.” The Chaldee: “God, my goodness”; Nebiensis: “God, my mercy”; the others: “God, his mercy shall go before me”; and the interpreters for Cajetan, departing from customary expression: “God of his grace shall go before me”; the translator following Campensis: “God, your goodness converts me.” Yet this is the verse mocked by Faber and Caecus. As to the sense, finally, it makes little difference.

[Col. 0550A]

**VERSE 11.**—“Lest at any time my people forget.” Concerning this verse, let us state what Jerome writes to Sunia and Fretela: “‘Lest at any time they forget your people.’ For this the Greek has written μή ποτε ἐπιλάθωνται τοῦ νόμου σου, that is, ‘lest they forget your law.’ But neither the Seventy nor the Hebrew has ‘your people,’ but ‘my people’; and we have translated it so.” Thus he. Here he seems to take *my people* in the genitive case, though others take it in the nominative. Hence, to remove ambiguity, they translated: “Lest my people forget at any time.” In Hebrew, however, the verb “to forget” is put in the plural, **IISCHKEHU**; in the master’s exposition *my* is, as it were, joined to the construction, so that it is a primitive pronoun and refers to God. It should further be known that Greek manuscripts, Augustine, and the Roman Psalter read “your law.” Hence this is evidence that the genuine reading of the Seventy is not consistently preserved here.

**VERSE 13.**—“The sin of their mouth, the word of [Col. 0550B] their lips.” So that the sentence may not remain unfinished, something must be supplied to suit the reader’s understanding. Sanctes and Münster supply a preposition: “Because of the sin of their mouth,” etc.; but Jerome supplies the preposition *in*: “In the sin of their mouth.” Our translators refer these cases back to the preceding verb, namely, “cast down,” etc. In Greek, however, they are read in the nominative case. All these interpretations agree without great difficulty.

**VERSE 14.**—This verse admits a different division in our edition from that in the Hebrew. For the Hebrews end the verse at the word “they shall be proclaimed.” And if they read “they shall proclaim” or “they shall recount,” actively, **IESAPERU**, the Seventy apparently read it passively, **IESUPERU**. Such a change is easy, especially where vowel points are not written. Then they used **CALLEH**, “consummation,” as an infinitive in place of a noun, which is not unusual among the Hebrews; others take it verbally as an imperative: “Consume.” This resulted in the Seventy joining to the verb “they shall be proclaimed” the phrase “in consummation.”

**VERSE 15.**—“And they shall know that God shall rule Jacob, and the ends of the earth.” Jerome, writing to Sunia and Fretela, says that he is held in amazement by the arrangement of this verse, for which he says: “In Greek it is written, καὶ γνώσονται ὅτι ὁ θεὸς δεσπόσει τοῦ Ἰακὼβ, καὶ τῶν περάτων τῆς γῆς, that is, ‘and they shall know that God will rule Jacob and the ends of the earth.’ But the conjunction *and* has been added, and the order is: ‘They shall know that the God of Jacob will rule the ends of the earth.’”

But in Hebrew it is read thus: **VEIJEDEU KI ELOHIN MOSCHEL BIIAACOB LEAPHSE HAARETZ**. There the Hebrew participle *ruling* is placed between the name of God and Jacob. Moreover, with the word *Jacob* a prepositional sign is added—not to mention that, if Jacob were a genitive in the construct state, one would not say *elohim* but *elohe*. Jerome himself, [Col. 0550D] in his translation from the Hebrew, rendered it: “And they shall know that God shall rule Jacob and the ends of the earth.” Likewise all the others: “even to the ends of the earth.” Therefore I suspect that Jerome approved one reading without disapproving the other, especially in Greek.

**VERSE 18.**—“They shall murmur.” Pratensis and Nebiensis: “They shall sleep”; Münster and the interpreters for Cajetan: “They shall spend the night.” **LON** or **LAN** is ambiguous. Therefore Jerome, Sanctes, and Pellicanus follow the Seventy. Nor is the sense that, if they are not satisfied, they ought to sleep equally fitting; indeed the opposite would suit better, even if they could devise their interpretation.

# PSALM LIX

[Col. 0551]

## Title of the Psalm

“Unto the end, for those who shall be changed, in the inscription of the title, to David himself, for instruction; when he set Mesopotamia of Syria—or Syrian Sobal—on fire, and when Joab turned back and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt Pits, twelve thousand.”

[Col. 0551A]

“God, you have cast us off.” The title: “Unto the end, for those who shall be changed, in the inscription of the title, to David himself, for instruction; when he set Mesopotamia of Syria—or Syrian Sobal—on fire, and when Joab turned back and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt Pits, twelve thousand.”

In the Books of Days—that is, Chronicles—and in the Book of Kings, we read that, after Nahash king of the Ammonites died, David sent messengers to comfort his son Ammon. His princes, or Ammon’s, suggested to him that [Col. 0551B] David had sent them in order to spy. Therefore Ammon shaved David’s servants, cut off the hair of their heads, cut their garments from the buttocks down to the feet, and sent them away thus. Then, seeing that he and his people had wronged David, Ammon hired an army from every quarter, with chariots and horsemen from Mesopotamia, Syria, and other places. When David heard this, he sent Joab, the commander of the army, against them in battle and put them to flight by the edge of the sword (1 Chron. 19; 2 Sam. 10).

We read in the Book of Kings that, when David reigned prosperously after Saul’s death, he defeated Hadadezer, king of Sobal, which is a part of Syria, and Syria became tributary to David. After Syria had been captured, he struck down twelve thousand from Edom. On returning, he placed garrisons in Idumaea, and Idumaea became subject to him and paid tribute (2 Sam. 8). [Augustine] This title touches upon those histories; but because the history does not relate that David turned Joab back, or that he set anything on fire in the aforesaid devastations, leaving the surface of the history—as often happens elsewhere—we are directed to a spiritual understanding, drawn from the interpretations of names.

Mesopotamia is interpreted “an exalted calling”; Syria, “sublime”; Sobal, “vain antiquity”; Joab, “enemy”; Edom, “earthly.” By all these are signified those puffed up by the greatness of earthly vanity. Christ sets them all alight with the fire of love, which he deigned to send upon earth; he turns Joab—the enemy, either the devil—to flight, or a human being to faith; and he strikes Edom [Col. 0551D], that is, earthly people, so that they may live as heavenly ones.

The sense is this: this psalm, directing us to the end—that is, Christ—concerns those who shall be changed from an old life to a new one, “in the inscription of the title” received through faith; that is, those who shall be changed into Christ’s kingdom. The inscription, I say, is made “to David himself,” that is, Christ. Or thus: those who shall be changed into the kingdom, from an old life into a new one, “in the inscription of the title,” through faith—that is, those changed into Christ’s kingdom. The inscription, I say, is made to David himself, that is, Christ. Or thus: “those who shall be changed in the inscription of the title”—here make the division—that is, they shall be changed into Christ’s kingdom. I say, not for themselves but for David himself, that is, Christ: so that they may live for him, they shall be changed by entering into his instruction. For anyone who wishes to bear his title must pass into his instruction.

But how would he change them unless he sent fire upon the earth? (Luke 12). In no way. Therefore it adds: “When he set Mesopotamia on fire,” and when David, literally, defeated all these. But the statement that he set these provinces on fire cannot be understood historically; it is made for its signification, for which he is accustomed to depart from history. As though he said: They shall be changed. For this reason—that is, because he set Mesopotamia of Syria, or Syria, on fire with God’s fire.

In Mesopotamia is the exalted calling: namely, the whole world, raised by the holy calling of the apostles, which Christ set on fire with the fire of love. Syria is interpreted “sublime”; but what was previously sublime with vain height is, when set alight, humbled so that it may be exalted more truly. “And Syrian Sobal”: Sobal means vain antiquity, which is stretched out so that it may be moved. The sense is: he set on fire those first sublime, that they might be humbled; and those vain and old, that they might become new. And he turned Joab, that is, the enemy, who is the devil or a human being: if the devil, into flight; if a human being, he is converted to faith. And with the sword of the Spirit and the word of God he struck Edom, that is, earthly life. For the earthly person is struck, killed so that he may live as heavenly.

And when he struck Edom, he struck twelve thousand in the Valley of Salt Pits. [Note: [Col. 0551] In 2 Sam. 8, eighteen thousand are given. So also in 1 Chron. 18. We must therefore recur to the mystical sense, as Augustine does.] Twelve thousand is a perfect number, to which the number of the apostles is assigned: they call believers from the four regions of the world to the Trinity. Therefore twelve thousand is the whole world struck down. A valley is humility. Salt pits signify the savor of wisdom. These two are rightly joined, because many are humbled vainly and in an old manner, suffering for earthly things. Heretics too have suffered; but it is good to be humiliated wisely, that is, for the Lord. The sense is: he struck twelve thousand, that is, all from the four regions of the world, called by apostolic teaching to faith in the holy Trinity. And this was in the Valley of Salt Pits, that is, in humility that is wise and discerning.

[Col. 0552D]

**Purpose:** He teaches that the breaking of the world is blessed, and through it demonstrates that people are to be changed for eternal things.

**Method:** [Cassiodorus, Augustine] The psalm has three parts. First, persecutions are recounted, endured in order to avoid eternal punishments. Second, it treats of deliverance, which it asks for and affirms, at “That your beloved may be delivered.” Therefore the prophet, in the voice of those struck and changed for the better, says:

[Col. 0553A]

**VERSE 1.**—“O God, you have cast us off and destroyed us; you were angry and had mercy on us.”

“O God,” [Note: [Col. 0553D] From Jerome, in the *Epitaph of Paula* and elsewhere.] “you have cast us off” from evils, us who were evil; and “you have destroyed us,” badly built as we were, so that you might raise us into a good building. This is the city with three names, which was first called Jerus, then Salem, and then Jerusalem. *Jerus* means “trampled down”; *Salem*, “peace”; Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace.” [Note: [Col. 0554D] From Jerome, *On Hebrew Names*.] First the vices in us are trampled down; then, in the peace of righteousness, the structure of good works is built; finally we shall be caught up to the vision of ineffable peace.

[Alcuin, Augustine, Alcuin] These three are marked here by the words “you have destroyed us” and “you have had mercy on us.” Hence the Lord says: “Behold, today and tomorrow I cast out demons and accomplish healings, and on the third day I am consummated” (Luke 13). These are Passover, Pentecost, [Col. 0553B] and the Feast of Tabernacles. They are also the three days of the Lord’s passion: repentance, righteousness, glory. “You were angry and had mercy on us.” For you do not have mercy unless you are angry. Anger is the old state, so that it may perish; mercy renews the inner person, although the outer person is wasting away (1 Cor. 4).

Or thus: “O God, you cast us off,” in Adam, away from yourself; and “you destroyed us” from immortality, because you were angry with us for our sins; yet you had mercy on us through the Son. Thus:

**VERSE 2.**—“You have shaken the earth and troubled it; heal its fractures, because it has been shaken.”

“You have shaken the earth,” [Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Augustine] from error toward repentance, brandishing the sword of the Spirit, when you said: “Repent, and believe the Gospel; for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Mark 1). And you troubled it toward repentance, while conscience accused it of sins. Therefore, as you began, so bring it to completion: namely, “heal its fractures,” that is, its suffering and death, because it has been shaken. Otherwise it is not worthy to be healed unless it has been shaken. Heal it; and this is necessary, because:

**VERSE 3.**—“You have shown your people hard things; you have given us wine of compunction to drink.”

“You have shown hard things,” [Alcuin, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine] that is, the miseries of this time, which through love are delightful to us, though through the weakness of the flesh they are burdensome, to your people now, after they have conquered. For if a person is not changed, he is not at once made eternal. Once a person has been changed for the better, there follows what is said in the book of Jesus son of Sirach: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Sir. 2). The first labor is to conquer sins, so that you may be changed; the second is, because you have been changed, to endure adversities to the end.

“And you have given us wine to drink”—not that wine in which is debauchery, but wine “of compunction,” that is, tribulation, by which the sufferer is cleansed, just as a wound is cleansed with wine. You have given us spiritual wine to drink, from which not vices but compunction arises. For it is not a destroying death, but a burning medicine. And why do you do this? Because through this:

[Col. 0554A]

**VERSE 4.**—“You have given those who fear you a signification, that they may flee from the face of the bow.”

You gave those who fear you a sign. [Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] By the present tribulation you have given a sign to those who fear you, so that they may flee from the face of the bow—that is, from the assault of future vengeance, namely the future judgment. This bow, as though already drawn, now threatens but does not yet strike: judgment terrifies us but does not condemn us. Its signification is given to us through present events; for if God punishes us so severely here, what will he do at the future judgment? Judgment is aptly called a bow, because the farther a bow is drawn back, the more forcefully its arrow is driven forward; so too, the longer judgment is delayed, the more grievous will be its coming. Or the “sign” is understood as the banner of the cross, given to us as a sign [127], so that we may follow Christ’s sufferings; by it we shall escape the face of the bow, because if we are companions in sufferings, we shall also be companions in the resurrection (II Cor. I). Thus: You gave those who fear you a sign—that is, the banner of the cross to imitate—so that through it they may flee from the face of the bow, that is, judgment. Or: You gave those who fear you a sign, that is, the Scriptures, so that through them they may flee from the face of the bow.

## PART II. Diapsalma. VERSE 5.—“That your beloved may be delivered, save your people, and hear me.”

That they may be delivered. [Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear, Augustine.] The second part, in which he treats of the deliverance that he prays for and affirms, for the sake of which the blows are welcome. You gave those who fear you a sign, that they might flee—and that in the future they may be delivered from the miseries of this world. “Save me,” says the righteous person in general, by placing me at your right hand, where true salvation is. As though he said: Make us stand at your right hand; concerning temporal safety, let your will be done. He has the taste of the Valley of Salt who seeks eternal things. The righteous person is always heard concerning such things, but concerning earthly matters only insofar as these are beneficial. “And hear me,” because I now ask for what you wish to give. And this is necessary, because:

## VERSE 6.—“God has spoken in his holy one: I shall rejoice and divide Shechem; and I shall measure out the valley of the tabernacles.”

God has spoken in his holy one, [Augustine] that is, he has promised salvation in Christ. He spoke to the Holy One, from whom salvation comes. From whom, namely? Because God has spoken, this will happen: I shall rejoice. He does not state God’s words, but what follows from God’s words. This is the voice of the Church: “I shall rejoice.” Or thus: I pray in this confidence, because God has spoken in his holy one, that is, he has promised in Christ. What? That I shall rejoice—that I shall do what will result in joy for me—thus: because I shall apportion, or divide, Shechem.

Shechem is the place where Jacob, returning from Laban, made shelters for his sheep and cattle, and called it Succoth, that is, “Tabernacles.” There also he hid the idols which he had brought from Syria, where he had long lived as a sojourner, burying them beneath a terebinth tree (Gen. XXXIII). According to the historical sense, therefore, by Shechem he signifies the nations, which are divided, because faith is not possessed by all: some believe, others do not. But according to its interpretation, Shechem means “shoulders,” which are divided—that is, burdens are apportioned in such a way that sins weigh some down, while others bear Christ’s light yoke (Matt. XI). Accordingly, by Shechem are understood in general all Christ’s burdens, good and bad—that is, those of Christ and of the devil. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Augustine.] Or by Shechem only the good shoulders are understood: Christ’s burden, which the Church distributes to each according to their strength.

“And I shall measure out the valley of the tabernacles.” The valley of the tabernacles, because of Jacob’s sheep, signifies the Jews, who too are divided, because some believe and others do not. Thus: “I shall measure out the valley of the tabernacles,” that is, I shall have not a few from among the Jews. Or, because tabernacles belong to those serving as soldiers, by the valley of the tabernacles are understood all who serve God. Thus: “I shall measure out the valley,” that is, I shall measure out those who humbly serve God, according to the measure of the predestined.

Gilead is the mountain where Laban overtook the fleeing Jacob, together with all that Jacob had acquired in Mesopotamia. There, after quarrels and disputes, they were reconciled and entered into a covenant of friendship. Having gathered stones, they made a mound and ate upon it. Laban called it “The Mound of Witness,” and Jacob “The Heap of Testimony.” And Laban said to Jacob: “This mound shall be a witness between me and you; but if I cross it in going against you, or if you pass beyond it with evil intent toward me …” (Gen. XXXI). Therefore it was called Gilead, that is, “Mound of Witness” or “Heap of Testimony.” By it are understood the martyrs, in whom there is a heap of testimony, while amid every reproach directed against the Christian name they steadfastly confessed Christ.

## VERSE 7.—“Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; and Ephraim is the strength of my head.”

Gilead is mine, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine] that is, the heap of testimony is mine: the true martyrs are mine. And Manasseh is mine. Manasseh was Joseph’s firstborn, whom he called by this name, saying: “God has made me forget my labors and my father’s house” (Gen. XLI). Therefore his name is interpreted “forgetful.” By him are signified the faithful, who have forgotten their former disgrace, because the Christian name is now an honor. Hence the Apostle: “For we are not ashamed of the Gospel” (Rom. I). Or, Manasseh is every person who, forgetting his former life, stretches forward with the Apostle toward what lies ahead (Phil. III). Or by Manasseh is understood the Church of the nations, which was formerly barren and subject to curse and reproach, but now, because she bears children, has forgotten her reproaches and shame. Hence Isaiah: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear, because the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. XXXIV). “You shall forget the shame of your youth, and you shall not remember the reproach of your widowhood.”

“And Ephraim is mine.” Ephraim was Joseph’s other son, whom he named thus, saying: “God has made me fruitful in the land of my poverty” (Gen. XLI). Therefore his name is interpreted “fruitfulness,” which the fruitful grain produces. Hence it follows: “Ephraim is mine,” that is, fruitfulness. And this fruitfulness is “the strength of my head,” that is, of Christ, says the Church. For the grain that dies had power within itself to bear fruit (John XII).

## VERSE 8.—“Judah is my king; Moab, the pot of my hope.”

Judah, [Jerome, Augustine, Alcuin] that is, Christ, is my king. For Christ was born from Judah; therefore he is aptly signified here by him. Hence Jacob, blessing him in the figure of Christ, said: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you,” etc. (Gen. XLIX).

“Moab, the pot of my hope.” Moab is a people descended from Moab, whom Lot’s elder daughter conceived by abusing her drunken father. By him is understood everyone who misuses the Law. For just as the daughters, misusing their father, bore the Moabites, so one who misuses the Law produces evil works, just as one who uses it rightly produces good works. From those who misuse the Law arises the pot, that is, the tribulation of the Church. This is the boiling pot from the north, that is, from the devil. Hence Jeremiah: “I see a kindled pot, and its face is from the face of the north” (Jer. I). And elsewhere the same Jeremiah says: “From the north every evil shall be opened” (ibid.), that is, from the devil, who said: “I shall set my throne in the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). From him, therefore, the pot causes tribulation to boil up in the Church; but under Christ’s leadership the burning pot of iniquity has become a pot of hope, not of destruction, because “tribulation produces patience; patience, tested character; and tested character, hope” (Rom. V), when the flame of charity, poured out in hearts, burns against the pot of iniquity.

The meaning is: Judah, that is, Christ, is my king. Under his rule Moab—that is, one who misuses the Law—is a pot because he brings tribulation. And this tribulation belongs to my hope, because it makes me hope more fully, rather than fail. Or Moab is put for the nations; that is, the nations are understood through Moab. By the pot is understood refreshment. Of the nations, some have been converted, and these are burned by tribulation; others have not been converted, and they burn others by tribulation. Yet both—the burners and the burned—are a pot, that is, refreshment, for Christ and the Church, because she receives consolation from the burned and benefit from the burners. The meaning is: Moab, that is, the nations—whether burning others by tribulation or burned themselves—is the pot, that is, the refreshment, of my hope, from which I have hope of life. The Church speaks:

## VERSE 9.—“Over Idumea I shall stretch out my sandal; foreigners are subject to me.”

Over Idumea. [Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear, Augustine, Jerome.] As though she said: I said, “I shall rejoice, I shall divide,” because I shall stretch out my sandal—that is, the Gospel, by which the life of those walking in the world is fortified. Or, “sandal” means Christ’s humanity, in which his divinity lay hidden. Or by the sandal, which is made from a dead animal, is understood Christ’s Passion, which I shall spread by preaching even into Idumea. Idumea means “earthly,” that is, even to earthly persons. As though she said: Even if the world boils with scandals, nevertheless I shall stretch out my sandal even to people living an earthly life. And thus foreigners, or the Allophyli, who belong to my race, are subject to me. For many worship Christ who will not reign with him—that is, hypocritical Christians. Or by foreigners he understands the nations, who were formerly strangers but are now subject. Thus: foreigners—that is, Gentiles formerly alien—are now subject to me. Hence: “I shall call not-my-people my people,” etc. (Hos. II). I say, “I shall stretch out,” but:

## VERSE 10.—“Who will lead me into the fortified city? Who will lead me even into Idumea?”

“Who will lead me into the fortified city,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus] or “the surrounding regions,” according to another reading, except God? That is, into the nations surrounding central Judea. This city, “the surrounding regions,” is the whole world, which elsewhere is called the wheel. Hence: “The sound of your thunder was in the wheel” (Ps. LXXVI), that is, among the Gentiles. “Who will lead me into Idumea,” so that I may reign, namely among earthly people, who are not of me and do not wish to profit from me?

Or thus: “Who will lead me into the fortified city?” That is, into the future Jerusalem, except you, God. “And who will lead me even into Idumea?” That is, even to earthly people, to whom he desires to be brought, so that when the full number of the predestined has been completed from among them, he may come with them together to blessedness. I say, “Who will lead me?”

## VERSE 11.—“Is it not you, God, who cast us off? And you, God, will not go forth with our armies.”

Is it not you, God, who will lead us—you who cast us off, [Augustine] because you allow us to be afflicted? This is what he said at the beginning of the psalm. And you, O God, will not go forth with our armies: you will not visibly appear against those who say, “Where is the God of gods?” as you once did for the fathers, not displaying your power such as you displayed in David, Moses, and Joshua son of Nun, before whom the nations gave way and, after great slaughter, they gained possession of the promised land. But you will work within us and thus lead us better, because in this way they appear to fight not for temporal life but for the life to come. And because you will lead us, therefore:

## VERSE 12.—“Give us help from tribulation, for human salvation is vain.”

Give us help. [Gloss interlinear, Augustine.] Or the connection is thus: You will not go forth, but there is no need for concern, because in this way God’s help is greater—namely, when he helps inwardly. Therefore, O God, give us help from tribulation: help us from the very source from which you are thought to abandon us. This I seek, not temporal safety; that is, because human temporal salvation is vain. This is vain antiquity, namely Zobal.

## VERSE 13.—“In God we shall do valiantly; and he himself will bring to nothing those who afflict us.”

We shall do valiantly, [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear] conquering the devil in God—not by the sword, not externally, but inwardly—because God will be both our army and our victory. Hence he adds: “And he himself will bring to nothing those who afflict us,” even though we may be of no account, by blotting them out, namely from the book of life, where they appear to themselves to be written. Or, “he will bring [them] to nothing” in our estimation, so that we may regard them as nothing.

## 128. COMPARISON ON PSALM LIX: “O GOD, YOU HAVE CAST US OFF,” ETC.

### VERSE 1.—“You have had mercy on us.”

Pratensis and Pellicanus have rendered the opposite sense. The former translates here, “you have surrounded us,” as though God had been unwilling to dwell in our midst; the latter, more plainly, “you will fail us.” The translator for Campensis has “you turn away.” But all the others agree with us: “you will return to us,” or “you have turned us.” This conveys mercy and corresponds to the Hebrew: “you have turned.” Let us continue to follow our own brains; we shall give sleep without understanding.

### VERSE 3.—“You made us drink the wine of compunction.”

This is understood in a good sense. But those who translate “of poison,” or “deadly wine,” employ it in an evil sense. Jerome does not depart from our meaning when he says “sleep-inducing wine”; Sanctes follows him. Pratensis: “wine producing anxiety.” Münster, in his Scholia, and Sanctes, in his Thesaurus, teach that *TARELAH* is variously explained by authorities.

### VERSE 4.—“That they may flee from the face of the bow.”

Pratensis, Nebiensis, Sanctes, and Pellicanus: “that they may be lifted up or exalted”; Münster: “that they may triumph”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “that they may be marked out.” In Hebrew it is *LEHITHNOSES*. But *NASAS* also means “to flee,” as Münster too testifies; and Jerome translates it thus, although “to be raised up” may also be accommodated to a swift flight. Furthermore, it might trouble one more that where we say “from the face of the bow,” the Hebrews have *MIPENE QUOSCHET*, that is, “from the face of truth”—which means “because of truth,” as they now translate it. It is now clearer than daylight that the Septuagint, whom Jerome follows word for word, understood the Hebrew letter *ṭeth* in place of the letter *taw*, which are sometimes interchangeable. For it is plain that *QESHETH* means “bow” among the Hebrews. Indeed Münster, in his Lexicon, does not deny that the former form, *quoschet*, is more customary among Chaldeans than among Hebrews.

### VERSE 8.—“Moab, the pot of my hope.”

Jerome: “of my washing”; and the rest in the same way: *RAHATZI*, “of my washing.” But it should be noted that this word means “confidence” in Chaldee, as Münster indicates on Daniel III. I think no one is unaware that the Chaldean language is in large part related to Hebrew. And just as *BAR*, which the Hebrews used for “son,” though it is more customary among Chaldeans than Hebrews, came into use, so the same might have happened with this word in this sense.

### VERSE 8.—“Foreigners are subject to me.”

Here the Hebrew has a certain word indifferent between “to join oneself,” or “to make a covenant,” and “to cry aloud in joy”: *HITHROAI*. Hence Jerome translates: “Philistia is allied with me.” Nebiensis and Pellicanus add: “make a covenant”; Campensis: “seek my friendship.” How these correspond to subjection, I think is clear. Others, according to another sense, translated: “cry aloud” or “sound the trumpet.”

# PSALM LX

[Col. 0557]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “FOR THE END, IN HYMNS: A PSALM OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0557D]

Hear me, O God. Title: “For the end, in hymns: a psalm of David.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] In this psalm the voice is that of the Church laboring upon earth. It is as though the voice of one person, yet it is not one person, because it cries from the ends of the earth. Although it labors amid the hindrances of this world, it nevertheless never ceases to praise God. This psalm, directing us to the end—that is, to Christ—is therefore “in hymns,” that is, in praises offered to David, that is, Christ.

Purpose: it urges praise. Method: the psalm has two parts. First, the Church, pressed on every side, prays and indicates that she will persevere, and by what means. Second, now heard concerning the inheritance she is to receive, she declares that she will offer praises; this begins at “For you, O God.” Therefore the Church, from the whole world as though one person, cries:

## VERSE 1.—“Hear, O God, my supplication; attend to my prayer.”

Hear, O God, my supplication. [Gloss interlinear.] A supplication is persistent and may also be offered to human beings, though not to God alone. A prayer is that which is offered purely to God. Therefore “attend,” because:

## VERSE 2.—“From the ends of the earth I cried to you, while my heart was distressed; you exalted me upon the rock.”

I cried to you from the ends of the earth, [Augustine] that is, from every quarter of the whole earth, because the Church is spread to earth’s furthest bounds. Why do you cry? Behold, I cried while my heart was distressed—that is, I cried in distress. For one cries when distressed, namely amid temptations, which certainly promote growth. No one knows himself unless he is tempted; no one can be crowned unless he conquers; no one can conquer unless he fights; and no one can fight unless he has enemies and temptations.

Then follows the hearing of the cry: “upon the rock,” etc. As though he said: The heart is distressed, but I am not therefore overcome, because you exalted me from the depths of vices upon the rock, that is, Christ, of whom he himself says: “Upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. XVI). By this person’s example great hope of being heard is afforded to others. You exalted me, and one thus exalted says:

## VERSE 3.—“You led me, because you became my hope; a tower of strength against the face of the enemy.”

You led me, through yourself the way, to yourself the truth and the life. How do you lead? Because you became my hope, you who exalt those who hope. Otherwise you would not be our guide unless you had become our hope. We hope that you will not destroy those for whom you delivered up your own Son. And you are a tower of strength, because you defend your own against every scandal, while a person reflects that Christ himself suffered first, and for what end he suffered. You are a tower, I say: the defense of your own against the face of the enemy, that is, the devil, who prowls about seeking someone to devour (I Pet. V). You are the tower, and I, fortified by this tower:

## VERSE 4.—“I shall dwell in your tabernacle for ages; I shall be sheltered under the covering of your wings.”

I shall dwell, [Augustine, Cassiodorus] or, according to another reading, “I shall be a sojourner,” that is, a temporary resident, in your tabernacle. Whatever the enemy may do, this person trusts in God’s benefits, so that amid the world’s perils he may remain safe in God’s tabernacle. And this is “for ages,” namely until the ages have run their course, so that the Church may continually gather her children who are born. Observe that it is not one person who remains through the ages, but one Church, which dwells on earth until the end of the world and is never uprooted by adversities; she cries from the ends of the earth, and to her it is said: “What hope do you have amid so many evils?” Certainly a sure hope: because, even though many are against me, I shall be sheltered against the heat of this world under the covering of your wings—that is, in the protection of your mercy and power, which are compared to wings because they do not burden and avert every injury.

Or connect the text thus, assigning each phrase to its corresponding phrase while retaining the same meaning: because you exalted me upon the rock and led me, therefore I shall dwell, or be a sojourner, in your tabernacle for the age. And because you are a tower of strength, therefore I shall be sheltered under the covering of your wings.

## PART II. Diapsalma. VERSE 5.—“For you, my God, have heard my prayer; you have given an inheritance to those who fear your name.”

“For you are God,” etc. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Gloss interlinear.] The second part, in which the Church, now heard concerning the inheritance possessed or to be possessed, states the basis on which she promises praises. As though she said: “From the ends of the earth I cried to you.” And you, O God, heard my prayer, with which she began at the start of the psalm. And truly, because you have given an inheritance to those who fear you—that is, the future kingdom. Therefore he says “you have given,” in the past tense, because it has already begun in some. Or he uses the past for the future because of the fullest certainty. Thus: You have given—not, I say, “you will give,” for I am so certain as if it had already happened—an inheritance to whoever fears your name. For there is no distinction, because “in every nation whoever fears God is acceptable to him” (Acts X).

## VERSE 6.—“You will add days upon days to the king; his years unto the day of generation and generation.”

Days upon days. [Gloss interlinear, Alcuin, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine.] Here he shows what the inheritance is in Christ the King, because it is the same in the soldier. We shall indeed be heirs of God and co-heirs of Christ. Thus, when he says what the king’s inheritance is, he also indicates what the soldier’s is. As though he said: You gave an inheritance—but what inheritance? That which the king himself possesses. And what does he possess? Behold, you will add eternal days to the king above the king’s temporal days. By this he signifies Christ’s eternity, he who is our King. For the Father gave Christ the King days without end beyond these days in which the Church reigns in the present, so that he may reign not only in these days in the Church, but the saints may also reign with him forever.

Then he repeats the same thing in other words: “And you will add his years upon years,” beyond those years in which he is with us in the present. Observe that the Lord’s eternity is called by many names. For whatever one says concerning eternity—years, days, one day—what one says is less than it; yet something must be said, to provide material for thought concerning what cannot be expressed.

Or thus: he calls the days of the king, that is, Christ, the days of the good people who lived here by imitating him; and he calls the same days “years,” because here some lived longer than others. Thus: He will give this inheritance because, beyond the days of the king, that is, Christ, which they lived here in goodness, you will add to them his days, in which he lives to God. And because some lived here longer, he adds “his years.” As though he said: You will add to them his years, in which he himself lives to God, beyond years, that is, beyond the longer life of some persons. And these days and years extend to the day of this present generation and of the future generation—that is, they are one day, a single day containing and surpassing the ages of the present and future generation. This day is eternity. I say that you will add the king’s years and days—which is a great thing—because that king:

## VERSE 7.—“He remains forever in the sight of God; who shall seek out his mercy and truth?”
