He remains forever. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Augustine, Alcuin, Jerome.] So they too shall remain. Here he shows what that eternity is when he says, “he remains forever.” This is the other generation, namely the eternal one. I say, he remains in the sight of God, where he is ready to show mercy to all. For what reason does he remain there? For the mercy to be shown to us here and for the truth to be fulfilled in the future. But “who shall seek out his mercy and truth for him,” according to another reading—that is, in order to imitate him in these things? As though he said: Few. He therefore added “for him,” lest anyone suppose that he should learn these things from books and then live for himself, not for him. His mercy is that he forgives sins and promises life not by merits but by goodness. His truth is that he does not deceive but gives what he promised. We ought to follow mercy toward the weak and even toward enemies; we ought to keep truth by not sinning, so that a person may thereby be righteous.

Or thus—and here is the conclusion of the psalm—because the soldier will possess the king’s inheritance, who will seek out his mercy and truth in eternal life? As though he said: no one. For eternal blessedness will be so sufficient that no one will seek mercy there, where no one will be miserable; no one will seek truth there, where all will see God. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “On that day you will ask me nothing” (John XVI). And because that will then be so, whatever others may do, I:

## VERSE 8.—“Thus I shall sing a psalm to your name for age upon age, that I may fulfill my vows from day to day.”

Thus I shall sing a psalm to your name, [Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine] that is, I shall work for your honor in such a way that whoever seeks may do likewise by my example. And this “for age upon age,” that is, as long as this age endures, because this must not be done merely for a time. Thus, I say, I shall sing psalms, so that I may fulfill my vows from day to day—that is, so that I may continually render what I vow.

Or thus, so that it is understood partly of the future and partly of the present: “Thus I shall sing a psalm to your name for age upon age,” that is, I shall thus sing praises to you in eternity, so that here in the present I may render to you the vows of my good works, until I come from the present day to the future day. Therefore, if you wish to sing eternally, fulfill your vows in this day until you reach that day. Here, then, I shall render vows; there, joyful praises. Hence, after everything in the Church’s offices, it is said: “Let us bless the Lord,” because for every good thing that we do in the present, we shall praise God perpetually in the future. Children say this because then we shall be companions in angelic purity. For no one shall enter the kingdom of heaven unless he is a little child (Mark X).

## COMPARISON ON PSALM LX: “HEAR ME, O GOD,” ETC.

### VERSE 2.—“You exalted me upon the rock.”

In Hebrew the meaning may be ambiguous: *BETZUR IARUM MIMENNI TANEHENI*. For the first word, *tzur*, means both “rock” and “strong one”; therefore it can in different ways be understood either favorably or unfavorably: by “rock,” Christ or his help; by “strong one,” the devil or an adversary, or some serious affliction. Jerome therefore takes it in the second sense: “When the strong one rises against me, you will be my guide,” drawing the beginning of the following verse back to the end of the preceding verse, where we read, “you led me.” Others take the first sense and supply a relative pronoun: “Lead me to the rock which is higher than I.” The Septuagint joined the two words together without a supplied relative. However one expresses it, God’s power and present help are steadfastly celebrated.

### VERSE 6.—“Who shall seek out his mercy and truth?”

*HESED VEEMETH MAN IINTZERUHU*: “Prepare mercy and truth,” supplying “which,” as they maintain, “will preserve him.” Jerome, however, plainly says, omitting the word *MAN*, while others translate, “Prepare [them]: mercy and truth will preserve him.” The translator for Campensis: “goodness and faithfulness will guard him.” But it is conjectured that the Septuagint read *MAM* for *MI*, that is, “who?” or, in Chaldee, *MAN*, “who?” Those who translated “prepare” departed from the root *MINNAH*, “he prepared.” The attached pronoun found in the verb “they will preserve” was placed by the Septuagint so as to be joined to *EMETH*, “truth,” yielding: “Who will preserve his truth?” and consequently, “Who will seek it out?” Or the possessive pronoun “his” is understood in the middle. For Augustine’s text reads: “Who shall seek out his mercy and truth for him?” And the final phrase was omitted by the Septuagint. The Roman Psalter reads: “Who shall seek out theirs?”

# PSALM LXI

[Col. 0561]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “FOR THE END, FOR IDITHUN: A PSALM OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0561D]

“Shall not my soul be subject to God?” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Title: “For the end, for Idithun: a psalm of David.” As we said above, Idithun was director, with certain other singers, in the tabernacle of the Lord (I Chron. XVI). Mention of them is frequently made in the titles of the psalms (Ps. XXXVIII), both because of the dignity of their office and because of the interpretations of their names, through which the meanings of the psalms placed under them are explained. Thus Idithun is set here; his name means “leaping over those,” namely those remaining in the world and clinging to earthly things. This psalm concerns that one who leaps over: the Prophet who in mind has leapt from earthly to heavenly things, exhorting the sluggish to follow him there and praising the Lord’s place to which he arrived by leaping over. For this leaper is above something in such a way as to be beneath something else. The sense is: This psalm is of David the prophet, who here speaks in the person of one who leaps over. I say that the psalm is assigned to Idithun, that is, that it treats of the one who leaps over.

[Col. 0562D] He leaps over, I say, unto the end, that is, unto Christ. Purpose: he urges us, after despising these transient things, to hope for eternal things.

Method: the psalm has three parts. First, the one who leaps over answers envious persons who wish to deceive him. Second, he exhorts himself to be subject and urges the rest to the same, at “Yet my soul is subject to God.” Third, he reproves those who go astray and warns them to trust in God, not in transient things; this is the purpose of the psalm, at “Yet they are vain.” This leaper, seeing so many obstacles meet him, subjects himself to God, who is above him, and, as though from on high, replies to those beneath him by rebuking them.

## VERSE 1.—“Shall not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation.”

[Col. 0563B] Shall not my soul be subject to God? [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As though he said: Although you act so that I may be moved, and although I leap over many things, nevertheless my soul will always be subject to God, desiring nothing apart from him. He says this lest, in leaping over, he become exalted; for whoever exalts himself will be humbled (Luke XVIII). And, “Shall it not be subject?” It certainly shall, because from him, namely God the Father, is my salvation—that is, the Son, who is the author of my salvation. Truly he is the author.

## VERSE 2.—“For he himself is my God and my savior; my protector: I shall no longer be moved.”

For he himself is my God. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Jerome, Cassiodorus.] He says this lest he be thought inferior to the Father. Or it may be taken so that no distinction of persons is made. Truly it will be subject, because from him, God, is my salvation—that is, my deliverance. As though he said: I know who is above me. And truly so. For he himself, who is God of all by power, is mine by a certain special possession, namely by grace; he is my savior, that is, my redeemer through the Incarnation; and my protector unto glory. Or, according to another reading, “my helper,” namely in the labors of this world; and therefore I shall not be moved. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though he said: You act so that I may be moved; but fortified under the covering of his wings, I shall no longer be moved away from him, whereas in Adam I was indeed moved. Or: I shall no longer be moved as I was formerly moved through the infirmity of the flesh. Here he says the same as in another psalm. For what he says here, “Shall not my soul be subject to God?” is what is said elsewhere: “Let not the foot of pride come against me” (Ps. XXXV). And what is said here, “I shall no longer be moved,” is what is said there: “And let not the hand of the sinner move me.”

## VERSE 3.—“How long do you rush upon a man? You all kill, as against a leaning wall and a thrust-down fence?”

[Col. 0563D] How long? [Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Augustine.] As though from a tower—that is, from the citadel of contemplation—he speaks to those below, namely to those clinging to earth. As though he said: And because I shall not be moved, how long do you rush upon a man, as a river or a wild beast? Certainly not upon the soul, but upon the flesh, because power has been given to you over the body, not over the soul. Hence Job: “The earth is given into the hand of the wicked” (Job IX). Observe that he says “How long,” etc. For they began this from the blood of Abel (Matt. XXIII). But did those persons belong to the man who speaks here? Certainly they belonged to this universal man, that is, to the Church, which says here what it says elsewhere: “Sinners built upon my back; they prolonged their iniquity” (Ps. CXXVIII). This Church is one with her head, Christ, who is the head of all the faithful. Thus he says: How long do you rush upon the man, as though from the blood of Abel, because the members that came forth before the head belong to the head? But did any come forth before the head? Certainly, because the head says in another psalm, “My mother is Zion” (Ps. LXXXVI). Why would he call Zion his mother unless some had preceded, from whom he might be born? He says “mother,” but this is said by the man born in her—that is, it is said by the head insofar as he is a man born in her, not insofar as he is the Most High who founded her.

[Col. 0564B] You rush upon him, [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine] and not lightly, but you kill the innocent one—namely, according to another reading, you rush upon him as though you were going to cast him down. I mean you who press upon him as upon a leaning wall and a fence, because you suppose that he has no defender and that he readily falls like a leaning wall, which would fall even if it were not struck; and like a fence, which is a construction of stones without a binding of cement, such as is around gardens and vineyards. And lest you think it firm because of its very newness, he adds, “thrust down,” or “struck,” or, according to others, “while the others remain.” Thus our text reads literally: “You all kill.” [Jerome, Augustine.] As though he said: You rush upon the man; but you ought not rush upon him, because in rushing upon the man you kill yourselves, all of you, even those who consent.

Or thus, according to another reading: “How long do you heap things upon a man?” The meaning is the same as in the preceding reading. For they heap evils upon the man, that is, upon the Church—the burdens of sufferings—so that each faithful person may fulfill in his body to the end what is lacking of Christ’s sufferings (Col. I). Then, as though in derision, he adds, according to another reading: “You all kill the man.” As though he said: All of you kill that man, insofar as he is man; but not all one man, rather all the Church. But because God is my protector, I shall not be moved, as was said above, as against a leaning wall and a thrust-down fence. This does not change. Persecutors can do nothing against me.

## VERSE 4.—“Yet they devised to drive away my price; I ran in thirst; with their mouth they blessed, and in their heart they cursed.”

Nevertheless, the pretended and hidden ones devised to cast away my price, because the poison lies concealed in their heart, even if they do not dare to utter it: to cast away my price, that is, Christ, so that men might not worship him. Or, they devised to take from me eternal blessedness. Or, according to another reading: “They devised to cast away honour,” that is, Christ. For since they cannot extinguish Christ’s name, they dishonour the exalted true Joseph. Note the different kinds of enemies. Violent persecutors rush upon him; heretics and hypocrites devise to cast away the price. Such are they. Yet I thirsted for their salvation. And this is: “I ran in thirst,” because, although he continually drinks them in, he continually thirsts for more. But they blessed with their mouth [Col. 0565A]. Since they cannot do so through open evils, they try to seduce him by blandishments; and in their heart, where they devised to cast away the price, they cursed. This man thirsted for them.

It should be understood that two spiritual cities are signified here: one of the evil, called Babylon, which begins with Cain; the other of the good, called Jerusalem, which begins with Abel. The king of the former is the devil; the king of the latter is Christ. The citizens of Babylon are those who rush upon others and devise to cast away the price; the citizens of Jerusalem are those who thirst and drink them in unto the end. These two cities are intermingled in body but divided in mind.

The city of the evil is signified by that city which Cain first built, where previously there had been no city, and which he called Enoch, that is, “dedication,” because evil people dedicate themselves to temporal things, while in this present life—which comes first—they plant the root of their heart, because “that which is animal comes first.” But the city of the good is signified by Jerusalem, which was built later, not where there had previously been no city, but where there was Jebus, whence the Jebusite. For it had three names: namely Jebus, Salem, and Jerusalem. Jebus is interpreted “trampled down”; and appropriately Salem, or Jerusalem, is built there when that city has been overthrown [Col. 0565B], because from the old man, overthrown and trampled down, the new man is made.

The bodily intermingling of the two cities results in those who belong to Jerusalem—that is, the good—sometimes administering the affairs of Babylon, and those who belong to Babylon—that is, the evil—administering the affairs of Jerusalem: for example, the three youths in Babylon, and evil men reigning in Jerusalem. Of the former God says: “I am God and not man, and I do not enter into the city” (Hos. 11). Of the latter the Prophet says: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 86).

## PART II. Διάψαλμα [Diapsalma].

### VERSE 5.—“Nevertheless, be subject to God, my soul, because my patience is from him.”

Nevertheless. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The second part, in which he again urges himself—that is, his soul—to be subject to God. As though he said: Such are they. Nevertheless, whatever they do, be subject to God, my soul. This repetition instils strength into our mind. And you ought to be subject, because my patience, which I possess amid such great scandals, is from him. For a human being could not endure these things by himself. From whom is it? Behold: from God. And truly,

### VERSE 6.—“For he is my God and my saviour; my helper: I shall not depart.”

For he is my God [Col. 0565D]. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Therefore he calls me. And he is my saviour; therefore he justifies me. He is my helper; therefore he glorifies me. And I shall not depart. From the place where I am glorified I shall depart from sojourning; I shall not depart from the heavenly dwelling. Or, according to another reading: “I shall not be a deserter.” Thus: because you are my helper, I shall not desert this firmness of faith, because

### VERSE 7.—“In God are my salvation and my glory; the God of my help, and my hope is in God.”

My salvation is in God [Col. 0566A], that is, my deliverance—not death, as in the gods of the Gentiles. And not only shall I be saved in God, that is, made righteous from being ungodly; but my glory too shall be in God, here and in the future—that is, I shall be glorious in him. And truly, because he is the God of my help.

Or thus, so that the whole is understood of the future: My salvation is in God in the future, so that I shall not merely be saved, but my glory also shall be in the future: then I shall be saved and glorious in him. And what of the present? God himself is my helper in the contest. He says this lest a human being attribute anything to himself. And my hope is in God until perfection is reached, namely that glorification in which the righteous “shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13).

### VERSE 8.—“Hope in him, every assembly of the people; pour out your hearts before him: God is our helper for ever.”

Hope [Col. 0566B]. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Interlinear Gloss.] Having made his own faith public, he admonishes all who labour under superstitions: hope in the Lord. As though he said: My hope is in God; following that example, hope in him. As though he said: Imitate me, Jeduthun, every assembly of the people. As though he said: Be one, and thus you will be able to hope.

How ought one to hope? “Pour out your hearts before him” [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine], that is, pour out your perverse thoughts by confessing sins, hoping for good things, asking forgiveness, and weeping over ruin. For by tears the heart is poured out. Therefore pour it out; do not retain the poison of sin within. This pouring out is signified by striking the breast. For when penitents outwardly strike their breasts, they show how greatly the consciousness of sin wounds the soul. Hence: “Prick the eye, and it produces a tear; prick the heart, and it produces knowledge” (Ecclus. 22).

Likewise, in this striking of breasts there is a sound, by which are signified the sound and cry of the confession of sins. I say, pour out your hearts; and what you pour out does not perish, because God is a helper for ever. What, then, should you fear among the wicked?

## PART III. Διάψαλμα [Diapsalma].

### VERSE 9.—“Nevertheless, the sons of men are vain in the balances, that they may deceive; they themselves, from vanity, into one and the same thing.”

Nevertheless. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Interlinear Gloss, Jerome, Alcuin.] The third part, in which he reproves the erring and warns them to trust in God, not in perishable things—the point intended by the psalm. As though he said: They rush upon others and kill; nevertheless, you good people, as though set on high, pity those whom you formerly feared, and say from charity: “The sons of men are vain.”

Or the connection is this: I have thus admonished you, namely, “Hope; pour out your hearts.” Nevertheless, they are vain, etc. Or join it thus: “God is our helper.” And although God so works for us, nevertheless the sons of men, namely the children of Eve and Adam, are vain, seeking earthly things in themselves; and the sons of men are liars in the balances—that is, in the rectitude of the Scriptures—because they pervert the Scriptures by which they may prove falsehoods.

Or, “they are liars in the balances” [Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine, Cassiodorus], that is, in unjust weights by which they deceive buyers. Hence Solomon says: “Weight and weight, measure and measure—the smaller, namely that with which you sell, and the larger, that with which you buy—both are abominable before God” (Prov. 20); and likewise: “A deceitful balance is abominable to God, but a just weight is his will” (Prov. 20).

Both interpretations proceed together in this way: Why do they do this? “That they may deceive others,” I say, “they themselves being from vanity into one and the same thing,” namely one thing. For though they differ in their perverse pursuits, they are nevertheless one in vanity. Hence the foxes which Samson tied together in order to burn the crops of the Philistines met together at their hind parts, while their faces were different (Judg. 15). For heretics resemble foxes: they agree in the perversity of error; but, teaching contrary things and fighting against one another, they bring about the victory of the Church.

Or thus, and it concerns hypocrites, who are one thing and wish to appear another. This is what is meant by “the sons of men are liars”: they deceive those who look upon them by a false weighing, because they wish to appear righteous [Col. 0567B] when they are liars. And this is what follows: I say that they are liars in the balances, that is, in the scale of justice, by which they more easily deceive, so that, themselves deceived by vanity, they may deceive others “into one and the same thing,” that is, by the very fact that they are believed to be just.

### VERSE 10.—“Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire robberies; if riches abound, do not set your heart upon them.”

Do not. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] Here the thirsty man turns to them, as though he said: My hope is in God; but you, O sons of men, do not hope in iniquity. Rather, as my hope is in God, so let yours be. And you who do not possess, as though from necessity you were about to plunder, do not desire robberies—where rather the devil plunders you.

O ruinous gains! You find money; you lose righteousness. For the prey you wish to seize is in a trap: you hold what belongs to another, and you are held by the devil. The sense is: neither hope for nor desire things which are gathered by robbing others.

Lest he seem to say this only to the poor, he adds: And you who possess, if riches abound—that is, overflow, as though flowing from a full fountain—do not set your heart upon them [Col. 0567C], that is, do not hope in the uncertainty of riches (1 Tim. 6). This is addressed to the rich. Therefore, let the one who does not possess not covet; let the one who possesses not be proud. Note that he does not say, “Do not have,” but “Do not set your heart upon them.” For he does not condemn riches, by which we may merit heaven, but the heart set upon them, which does not spend but stores up.

### VERSE 11.—“God has spoken once; these two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and mercy to you, O Lord, because you will render to each according to his works.”

“God has spoken once,” etc. He said two things, namely, “Do not set your heart upon riches,” and “Hope”; to these he supplies two corresponding points, giving the reason for the preceding statements. As though he said [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine]: Do not set your heart upon riches—why? Because the power of vengeance belongs to God, namely to the Son. He said, “Hope.” Why should one hope? Because mercy for rewarding belongs to you, O Lord; in this, power and mercy are made manifest. Behold, because you will render to each according to his works [Col. 0568A].

This shows that these things are said of Christ, because “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). How do you know this? Because God “spoke once,” that is, eternally: he disposed all things, among which I heard these two things, namely that power, etc.

Or thus, according to the sequence of the text: Hope in God, because God spoke once, where I heard these two things. It appears contrary that God should speak once and two things be heard. What also is meant by what is read in the Apostle: “God, who in many portions and in many ways spoke in former times” (Heb. 1)? Among human beings God speaks in many ways, but with himself once, because he begot the one Word, through whom all things were made and in whom all things were disposed together. Among all these things, he heard these two things which need to be stated here, though he heard many other things which need not be mentioned here.

Those two things are power and mercy. All the Scriptures concern these two; for these two the Law and Prophets exist; for these two Christ himself and the apostles were sent. Therefore let power be feared and mercy loved; let power not be despised because of mercy, nor mercy despaired of because of power. This is what is meant by: Hope in God, because God spoke once—that is, he eternally begot the Word, in whom he made and disposed all things.

This is that Word concerning whom the shepherds said: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this Word which has been made” (Luke 2). This Word is not merely ineffable; even his name, written on the golden plate of the high priest (Exod. 28), was the tetragrammaton—that is [Note: [Col. 0567D] From Bede on Exodus 28, unless the ordinary gloss is mistaken.] four letters: *iod, he, vau, heth*, that is, “the beginning of the passion of this life.” The name composed from these letters, as some report, is *ia ia*, or *ie ie*. It is called ineffable because, whereas the other names of the Lord signify an ineffable reality, this name signifies a more ineffable reality, according to the interpretations of the letters.

As though he said: The one whose name this is, is the beginning of the life lost through Adam, and this is through the humility of his passion. What, indeed, is more wonderful than that by suffering and dying he freed us from death? Ineffable, therefore, is the generation of the Word, whose name too is ineffable. Yet this man, grasping something of it, says: “God spoke once” [Col. 0568C], that is, he eternally begot the Word in whom he disposed all things.

[Note: [Col. 0567D] See Jerome, Letter to Marcella, *On the Ten Names of God*, and Letter to Damasus, beginning “And it came to pass…”; likewise Jerome on Ezekiel 16, at the words “And a crown of beauty upon your head.”]

He saw this when raised above all things, even transcending the angels and arriving at that clarity where the One begot the One. “Among all things I heard these two things,” in that height to which I leapt; as though saying, “I do not say this from myself, but heard it, caught up to the only-begotten Word.” What things? “That power belongs to God,” that is, to the Son, who not only has power in himself but also grants it to others, because no one has any power except from the just God, even if his justice is hidden from you. “And mercy belongs to you, O Lord, because you will render to each according to his works.”

These things do not change [Col. 0569A]. [Augustine.] With him is power; with him is mercy. It belongs to his power to condemn the wicked. Therefore tremble at his power. The devil, then, is a certain power, yet he often wishes to harm and cannot, because this power is under another power. He presses only so much upon the leaning wall as he receives power to do. For he who gives the tempter power himself provides mercy for the tempted. “There is no power except from God.” Do not say: Why does he give such great power to the devil, without giving power in return? He who gives power possesses justice. Therefore do not fear the enemy. He does only as much as he has received power to do.

## COLLATIO ON PSALM 61: “SHALL NOT MY SOUL BE SUBJECT TO GOD,” ETC.

[Col. 0569]

### VERSE 1.—“Shall not my soul be subject to God?”

Some translate, “my soul is silent”; others, “my soul looks toward”; some, “my soul waits.” All these aptly indicate peace of conscience and the soul’s perfect obedience toward God. This translator, following Campensis, has: “My soul will observe God alone.”

### VERSE 3.—“You kill, all of you.”

The Septuagint and Jerome read the verb actively. For Sanctes, in his *Thesaurus*, reports that some read *THERATZEHU* in the *piel* form, that is, “you will kill”; others in *paul*, that is, “you will perish,” passively. The modern translators indeed follow this latter reading—lest for the moment I call them perverters. Campensis, however, and the Paraphrase and translation of 131 have the active form. Similarly, the Chaldee has: “You will commit murders.”

### “Like a leaning wall and a thrust-down fence.”

If you read in the nominative, “like a leaning wall and a thrust-down fence,” you may supply the substantive verb, “you shall be” or “you may be.” In our reading, the understood verb is “lean upon” or something similar, as is gathered from Augustine’s interpretation, lest Faber and Caecus, after their fashion, destroy the ecclesiastical psalmody.

### VERSE 4.—“They devised to cast away my price.”

Jerome: “his portion,” if one reads *MASEATI*, that is, “my gift” or “my portion”; but if *MASEATO*, it means “his gift” or “his portion,” according to Jerome. But where one reads *MISEETO*, it means “from exaltation,” as the modern Hebraizing interpreters employ it and variously render it, tossing the meaning now here, now there.

Pratensis: “On account of his exaltation they formed a plan to cast him out.” Sanctes: “From the greatness of God himself they devised to drive one another out, lest they should thrust away the God whom they exalt and against whom they plot and scheme.” Pellicanus: “From elevation they formed a plan to cast out.” The interpreters for Cajetan: “From his height”—supply, “the man’s”—“they devised to thrust him away.” Campensis’s Paraphrase: “Because they saw him increasing through God’s help, we foolish men, having formed a plan, were trying to overthrow him in order to prevent this.” The Translator: “They formed a plan merely to cast him down from his standing.” Nebiensis: “For his exaltation, that they might cast him away.” The Chaldee Paraphrast: “On the day of good action they take counsel to strike.”

### “I ran in thirst,” *IIRTZU CAZAB*.

That is, “they were pleased in falsehood,” or “they wished for falsehood.” *RATZAH* is used both for “to take pleasure” and “to run.” The Septuagint attended to the second sense, though not wholly word for word. Then *CAZAB* indeed denotes falsehood; but sometimes it means a spring which fails to provide water, especially with *aleph* prefixed, as in Jeremiah 15, where we read: “You have become to me as the falsehood of waters.” The interpreters plainly had this sense in view.

### VERSE 7.—“The God of my help, and my hope is in God.”

Here one is ashamed to report Caecus’s mockery, following Faber, against the translators: that the sense “The God of help is in God” does not fit very well—though the sequence of that little verse seems to lead to it. But from the Hebrew one must say: “the strength,” or “rock, of my strength; and my hope is in God.” Hebrew *TZUR* means a strong rock, and it is God; he is called “the God of help,” that is, God the helper. So what absurdity is there in “God is my helper, and my hope is in God”? Where is the awkwardness of expression which offends you?

### VERSE 8.—“Hope in him, every assembly of the people.”

The Hebrew is: “Hope in him at every time, peoples.” In Hebrew the particle “peoples” is so placed that it is uncertain whether it belongs to what precedes or what follows. According to the demands of construction and the suitability of the meaning, it may be translated either in the singular or plural, and in either case. I do not know whether the translators read *ADATH*, “assembly,” in place of *ETH*, “time.” For they differ by a single letter, although “a people of every age or time” is not far from “every assembly.”

### VERSE 9.—“The sons of men are liars in the balances, that they may deceive; they themselves, from vanity, into one and the same thing.”

Hebrew: *CAZAB BENE ISCH BEMOZNAIM LAALOTZ HEMAH MEHEBEL IAHAD*: “The sons of a man are liars in balances for ascending.” Jerome translates this “in deceitful balances,” since fraud is usually practised when the balance rises. *MEHEBEL IAHAD* means “from vanity together,” or “into one and the same thing.” Jerome explains it thus: “fraudulently together”; Pratensis: “they themselves are rather vanity together”; Sanctes: “if they rise in the balances, they are lighter than vanity together.” Likewise do the rest of the newly born Hebraizers.

The result is that the letter *mem* is now the preposition “from,” “away from,” or “of,” and now the mark of comparison, which the Hebrews lack. It is enough that our edition does not disagree with Hebrew truth.

### VERSE 10.—“Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire robberies.”

The Hebrews join *BEGAZEL*, that is, “in robbery,” with the immediately preceding words: “Do not hope in iniquity without fraud and robbery.” The Septuagint joins it to what follows and seems to have read *heth* for *he*, that is, a strong aspiration in place of a weak one, since *TECHEBALU* differs only slightly from *TEHEBALU*. The former sometimes means “to strive,” “to travail,” and hence “to desire,” especially in the conjugation they call *piel*; the latter, “to vanish,” so that the sense is, “Do not become vain.” Jerome translates this: “Do not be frustrated.” The Chaldee agrees with us regarding the meaning of the word, unless the translation misleads.

### VERSE 11.—“God has spoken once; these two things I have heard.”

Jerome, Pellicanus, and the interpreters for Cajetan render it in the same way. Nebiensis comes close enough. But Pratensis and Sanctes have: “I heard these things twice”; Münster: “He spoke once and a second time, which I also heard”; Campensis: “God spoke one thing, but I heard it very often”; the Translator: “God spoke once, which I heard again and again.” Because of men’s cleverness, everything is confused when Hebraism does not compel it.

The Chaldee Paraphrase translates thus: “God spoke one Law, and we heard it twice from the mouth of Moses.”

# PSALM 62

[Col. 0569]

## A PSALM OF DAVID WHEN HE WAS IN THE DESERT OF IDUMAEA.

[Col. 0569D]

“God, my God.” Title: “A Psalm of David when he was in the desert of Idumaea.” As is read in the book of Kings, David, fleeing from Saul’s presence, hid himself in the desert of the Idumaeans [Col. 0571A]. The psalm does not deal with that event, but with what it signifies.

[Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] By David the Church is understood, which, like one in a desert, thirsts amid the dryness of the age and asks mercy from God with devout prayers, until it receives eternal things, teaching us by its example to conduct ourselves rightly amid this crooked and perverse generation. The sense is: This psalm is attributed to David, that is, to the Church, which speaks here. I say, a psalm composed concerning what it endured while in the desert of Idumaea—that is, in the desert of this age, where they are.

This psalm is understood as spoken in the person of the head and the members. For his voice is ours, and ours is his. Its intention is to admonish us to live rightly amid a perverse generation. Its structure is twofold. First, the Church says how it is situated in the desert of this age: namely, the bride desires to see God, whom she praises, and desires to do so more fully. Second, it sets forth the good and evil of the two parties, at “If I have been mindful.” Therefore the Church, burning amid the necessities of this life, says:

### VERSE 1.—“O God, my God, at dawn I keep watch for you.”

God [Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine], common to all by your power, you are my God in a somehow more special sense, namely by worship and holy desire. Observe the affection of devout entreaty in this repetition: “I keep watch for you from the light,” or, according to another reading, “at dawn”—literally, in the morning hour, when Christ rose, so that the Church may then praise him, when he stirred it to rise by the example of his resurrection. Hence this psalm is sung in morning praises.

Or, morally, “light” means the light of grace, which makes us keep watch for God. One person keeps watch for God, namely one who truly remembers God; another sleeps with respect to God, namely one who forgets God. One sleeps to the world, or with respect to the world, while forgetting the world; another keeps watch for the world while loving it. Therefore this man says, “I keep watch for you,” while I sleep to the world, not loving the things of the world but desiring you alone. Conversely, one sleeps to God who, devoted to earthly things, forgets God.

“I keep watch,” I say, and this “from the light,” because the light of grace rises for me. For you would not keep watch unless the light rose which awakened you. I say that I keep watch for you, and that my soul and body thirst. This is what follows:

### VERSE 2.—“My soul has thirsted for you; in how many ways my flesh has thirsted for you.”

My soul has thirsted [Augustine] for you for many reasons, because what is in you is one and blessed. Others desire other things, but my soul desires none but you. The soul thirsted for many reasons, but the flesh thirsted because of more things. This is “in how many ways”: for its manifold deficiency, my flesh, which has greater need, thirsted for you and not for another thing. For it suffers many deficiencies and changes its stages of life; it also thirsts for resurrection, because resurrection is promised to it and it desires it, just as blessedness is promised to our soul.

Or thus of the present: In how many ways my flesh thirsted for you in relation to present things [Col. 0572A]. For even here the Lord’s flesh thirsts while it seeks from him necessities here; then he adds where it thirsts.

### VERSE 3.—“In a deserted, pathless, and waterless land, thus I appeared to you in the sanctuary, that I might see your power and your glory.”

In a deserted land. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Here one must thirst. This age is a desert; this is Idumaea. The title speaks of it, which is rightly called a deserted land, where no saint dwells. He adds “pathless,” because there is no way out of it; and “waterless,” because while you remain there, there is no water.

This desert is evil, dreadful, and fearful; yet God has made a way for you here, namely Christ, who is the way, truth, and life (John 14); and he has sent the water of his word, filling preachers with the Holy Spirit, so that there might be in them “a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4).

“Thus I appeared to you in the sanctuary.” As though he said: My soul and flesh thirsted, and thus, then, I appeared to you: in holy desire, that is, through holy desire. Unless someone first fails in evil, he never reaches the good, which is God. “And I appeared to you,” not, I say, that you might see me, for you see all things, but “that I might see your power and your glory,” that is, Christ. As though he said: You saw me so that I might see you. For no one sees God unless God first appears to him—that is, unless he is seen by God. The sun makes us see by its light; so also does God. Therefore let us appear to God in holy desire, so that he may appear to us.

Let the one to whom God does not appear be in holy desire, and Christ’s majesty and equality with the Father will appear to that person, though he was human. Therefore I do all these things:

### VERSE 4.—“For your mercy is better than lives; my lips shall praise you.”

For your mercy [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine], that is, the life of grace which is given through mercy, not through merits, is better than human lives, even though long and prosperous. These are many: the life of a soldier, a farmer, and others. What you give to those corrected is better than what the perverse choose. “My lips”: after God’s benefits, he promises praise. As though he said: Because your mercy is above lives, therefore my lips shall praise you to my neighbour, for whom I am also concerned. Unless your mercy had preceded me, I could not praise you. Thus I praise with my lips.

### VERSE 5.—“Thus I will bless you in my life, and in your name I will lift up my hands.”

Thus I too will bless you already in my life [Col. 0572D] [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin], namely the life which you gave me, not the life I chose for myself. Or thus: Because your mercy is above lives, thus—that is, therefore—I shall bless you in my life, that is, by living well. Or thus: Through your mercy I shall praise you; and, as you gave me through mercy to praise you, so I shall bless you in my life, that is, I shall attribute to your mercy my life in which I shall praise you.

And in your name, that is, for your honour, I shall lift up my hands in prayer, literally. I shall also lift them up in good works, as Christ lifted up his hands upon the cross for us, so that our hands—those of the body and those of good action—may be stretched out to God. He lifts up his hands in God’s name who, persevering in good works, prays to God with outstretched hands in the form of a cross. Hence the Apostle says: “Lifting up pure hands in prayer, without anger and disputation” (1 Tim. 2).

As a figure of this, Moses is recorded in Exodus as having done this [Col. 0573A]: while in prayer he lifted his hands to the Lord, God’s people conquered Amalek; but when he lowered his hands, Israel was overcome (Exod. 13). For while someone performs good works for heavenly things, he conquers Amalek—that is, the crowd of demons that licks the blood of our destruction; but when he lowers his hands, that is, works for earthly things, he is conquered by Amalek.

### VERSE 6.—“May my soul be filled as with fat and richness, and my mouth shall praise you with lips of exultation.”

“As with fat,” etc. [Augustine, Jerome, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] This is what is sought with hands lifted in prayer. As though he said: I shall lift my hands, and ask this: Would that my soul were filled as with fat and richness. Literally, these formerly pleased God in sacrifices. Fat is in the entrails; richness is in the flesh. Beneath their covering he desires certain spiritual things.

By fat is understood wisdom, which is hidden and is the richness of the soul; without it the soul grows thin, or is so frail that it quickly fails in good works. By richness is understood strength of spirit or devout cheerfulness. Therefore he added “as,” and did not say simply “with fat and richness” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Jerome, Interlinear Gloss, Augustine].

The sense is: May my soul be filled as with fat and richness, namely with knowledge and devout cheerfulness, or strength of spirit, here where thirst and prayer with lifted hands exist. When thirst and prayer have passed, praise will follow. Hence he adds, “and with lips.” As though he said: I say that the soul should be filled, and then my mouth shall praise you with lips of exultation, because of a pure conscience, whose companion is exultation. Or, according to another reading: “With lips of exultation I shall praise your name.” The meaning is the same. For dry lips cannot praise.

Or thus, so that the whole is understood of the future, and “fat” and “richness” are taken as the same thing, namely eternal joy. The sense is: May my soul be filled as with fat and richness, that is, with the blessed joy which shall be in eternal satiety; and then, with lips of exultation, it shall praise your name [Col. 0573D].

## PART II.

### VERSE 7.—“If I have been mindful of you upon my bed, in the mornings I shall meditate upon you, because you have been my helper.”

If I have been mindful. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The second part sets forth the good and evil of the two parties, namely in opposition to the difficulties of the age that it suffers here. He says that his security is from God, in which he remembers him, remembers that enemies will perish, and rejoices that the king will rejoice with the saints.

As though he said: My mouth shall praise you, because on my bed and in the morning I have been mindful of you. “Upon my bed” means in the repose of prosperity, lest prosperity itself dissolve me and make me forget God. And if I have remembered you in repose, then in the mornings too—that is, in good actions—I shall meditate upon you; for actions are understood by “morning,” because each person begins to work well in the morning. He rightly says, “on my bed and in the morning.” For if you are not mindful in repose, neither are you mindful in action; but if in leisure, then also in activity.

Lest he fail in action, he adds, showing why he does not fail and remains mindful: “because you have been my helper” [Col. 0574A]. Unless God helps us here, we cannot fulfil good things.

Or thus according to the moral meaning, and it agrees partly with the preceding interpretation. As though he said: I shall praise you if—that is, because—I have been mindful of you upon my bed. Understand the bed on which we rest to mean prosperity, in which this man remembers God, something a human being scarcely does. “And in the mornings I shall meditate upon you,” that is, as the light of grace shines upon me. Evil things are done in the night; but with Christ showing the way, as in light, we ought to do good things. No one acts in the morning unless he acts in Christ. Therefore “in the mornings,” that is, in the light of Christ, I shall meditate upon you, as he said above: “From the light I keep watch for you,” so that the son of light, namely of Christ, may keep watch for the author of light, namely God. Therefore I meditate upon you, because you have been my helper amid the dangers of Idumaea.

### VERSE 8.—“And in the covering of your wings I shall exult; my soul has clung after you; your right hand has received me.”

And if anything arises, I shall exult in good works, in the covering of your wings, that is, in your protection, because I am a chick. If you do not protect me, the kite carries me off. Therefore I shall exult, because my soul has clung in charity after you [Col. 0574C], that is, has so clung to you in charity as to love you above itself. [Alcuin.] Or, “after you,” namely so as to follow you, not wishing to go before you, as Peter wished to do (Matt. 16). Therefore I shall exult, and therefore my soul has clung to you, because your right hand—that is, your propitiation—has received me under its wings to cover me from dangers.

### VERSE 9.—“But they themselves sought my soul in vain; they shall enter into the lower parts of the earth; they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes.”

But they themselves [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine], as especially notable persons, sought my soul in vain, because I escaped. Or this is said in the person of the whole Christ, that is, head and body. As though he said: Therefore I shall exult, because your right hand—that is, your wisdom, your Word—has received me, the whole Christ. For in Christ the man is the wisdom of God, and we are in him and are assumed with him, though in a different way: he through the union of person; we through adoption.

Thus they sought my soul in vain, that is, in vanity—the soul in which all live. This is Christ’s soul, because they accomplished nothing against the soul united to God, though seeking to destroy it. They, namely any persecutors, and especially the Jews, notable for wickedness, sought our soul in the head and in the apostles. Therefore they shall enter, in mind and desire, into the lower parts of the earth [Col. 0574D], that is, into earthliness. For they feared losing the land and therefore killed Jesus; and they went under the earth, by which the thing proposed to them ruled them. Rather than being carried to heaven, they are swallowed up by earth. Their evil thoughts, because born from the earth, tend down into the depths of the earth, as into mud.

Yet what they feared happened to them, because afterwards they lost even their land. Hence follows: “They shall be delivered,” etc., because they were conquered by enemies. Or, “they shall enter into the lower parts of the earth,” that is, into hell, and therefore here “they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword,” that is, into the power of Titus and Vespasian; and “they shall be portions for foxes,” that is, for worldly rulers, who are compared to foxes, as the Lord says of Herod: “Tell that fox,” etc. (Luke 13).

The Jews, I say, shall be the portions of these rulers because they did not wish Christ as king, saying: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss.] They rejected the lamb and held the fox. Or, foxes signify the deceitful. Therefore they are portions for foxes while they join themselves to deceitful men by a perverse will. Or, they shall be portions for foxes—that is, demons [Col. 0575B].

### VERSE 10.—“But the king shall rejoice in God; all who swear by him shall be praised, because the mouth of those who speak iniquities is stopped.”

The King indeed—that is, Christ, who truly is the King rejected by the Jews—will rejoice, though they seemed to have prevailed, in God the Father. Hence: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14). And all who swear in him—that is, who make promises to him and vow a good life—will be praised, that is, will be praiseworthy: those who chose Christ, not the fox. Note that he says, “swear in him,” not “swear through him,” lest the oath seem to be commanded through him; rather, he says, “those who swear in him,” by promising him obedience. He then gives the cause of the joy: “because the mouth of those who speak wicked things has been stopped,” or “blocked up”—that is, it will be stopped at the judgment, where all iniquity, overcome, will fall silent: the mouth of Jews and pagans speaking wicked things. For then they, not the Christians, will be destroyed. Note that in these two verses he contrasts the good and evil of the different parties.

## Comparison on Psalm 62: “O God, my God,” etc.

[Col. 0576A]

**Verse 1.—“At daybreak I keep watch for you.”** Why have Nebiensis, Pratensis, Sanctes, and the interpreters for Cajetan simply and plainly said, “I shall seek you,” when *schachar* means “to seek early in the morning,” and Jerome rendered it, “I shall rise at daybreak to you”? Münster: “I shall seek you in the morning.” Campensis and Pellicanus likewise. The Chaldee: “I shall come before you in the morning.” The translator for Campensis said, “I shall come to you early.” If they did this out of dislike for the Latin reading—which we do not believe—it would appear to have the semblance of a contradiction.

**Verse 2.—“How manifoldly my flesh longs for you.”** It is evident that the interpreters took *camah* as a compound expression, meaning “how often,” or “how manifoldly.” For if it were the verb *camach*, meaning “has desired,” how could the others have translated, “my flesh desires”?

**Verse 3.—“Thus have I appeared to you in the sanctuary.”** Hebrew: *hazîtîkha*, that is, “I saw you,” or “I contemplated you.” But the sense is easily reconciled. The translator for Campensis has, “In like manner I appear before you,” namely in the sacred sanctuary.

**Verse 7.—“Thus I remembered you,” etc.** Perhaps *sic* may seem an error for *si*, “if,” because Greek reads εἰ, “if.” Sanctes, Nebiensis, Pellicanus, and the interpreters for Cajetan translate, “If mindful,” or “if remembering.” Yet the Hebrew particle often means “truly” and “certainly”; therefore it may also mean “thus.” Hence Pratensis wrote, “certainly mindful”; and Münster, “Have I not remembered you?” by an interrogative which requires an affirmative answer. Jerome renders neither “if” nor “thus,” but simply, “remembering you.” The Master, with Augustine, reads “if,” yet explains it as “because,” not conditionally. Budé also teaches in his *Commentaries on the Greek Language* that εἰ is sometimes taken in the sense of ὅὴ [probably ὅτι, “because”].

**Verse 9.—“In vain they sought my soul.”** [Col. 0576C] *Leshoah*, that is, “unto desolation”; Jerome rendered it by the paraphrase, “they sought to kill my soul.” Our edition does not deny that the faithless sought to destroy his soul, but it also explains that their efforts were frustrated. Nor is that futility inappropriately denoted by the Hebrew word. For what greater devastation and desolation is there than what is vain, or vanity?

# Psalm 63

[Col. 0575]

## Title of the Psalm: “Unto the end, a Psalm of David.”

“Hear, O God.” Title: “Unto the end, a Psalm of David.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] This psalm briefly treats of Christ’s passion and resurrection, in which the whole Christ speaks, namely head and body. For as our head does, so we too pray in tribulation. This psalm directs us unto the end, that is, unto Christ; it is attributed to David, that is, Christ, who here speaks with the voice of his body joined to himself. Its purpose is to urge us to hope in the Lord amid sufferings. Its arrangement is twofold. First, it recounts what he endured and how he bore it, so that we may hope in the Lord amid sufferings. Second, it mocks the perversity of the Jews, at “The arrows.” Therefore the whole Christ prays in his passion, saying:

**Verse 1.—“Hear, O God, my prayer when I make supplication; deliver my soul from fear of the enemy.”**

“Hear, O God, my prayer when I am troubled,” another reading. [Col. 0576C] [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Gloss.] In the words, “Hear; deliver my soul,” he does not ask to be delivered so that he may not die, but from fear of the enemy: that he may not fear those who can kill only the body, but may fear you, who can kill and destroy both body and soul. Thus he is delivered even when killed. For he neither fears man nor yields to him.

Or, according to our text, the wording may be divided differently: “Hear, O God, my prayer, that you may exalt me; and deliver my soul from fear of the enemy”—even if not from fear of death, since every human being dreads death—“when,” that is, because, “I make supplication,” that is, pray with all my strength. I say, “Deliver”: this shall be because—

**Verse 2.—“You have protected me from the assembly of the wicked, from the multitude of those who work iniquity.”**

“You have protected me from the assembly,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, from the counsel of the wicked, as from the councils of the Jews, and from the multitude of those actively working iniquity, namely in order [Col. 0577A] to kill him who had done them so many good things. What is said here—“You have protected”—was accomplished in the Head, no less than it is experienced by the members. By this example the rest are strengthened.

**Verse 3.—“For they sharpened their tongues like a sword; they bent their bow, a bitter thing, so that they might shoot the blameless one in secret.”**

“For,” or, “those who sharpened.” [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine.] As though he said: What indeed did they do to you? Certainly evil: for they sharpened their tongues like a sword. By openly shouting for his death, they killed him with their tongues if not with their hands. Christ speaks here. “And they bent their bow,” that is, their deceits. For the bow strikes secretly and the sword openly: a bitter thing, though [Col. 0577B] the words are sweet; for they carry honey in the mouth and a sting on the back. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though he said: They prepared hidden snares, namely that he should be betrayed through a disciple—a bitter thing, that a table-companion should be a traitor. For what purpose did they bend it? “That they might shoot the blameless one in secret,” according to their own judgment: through a disciple and such means, doing everything so that they might appear to have done nothing. Whom did they seek to shoot? The blameless one. For this reason they ought to have feared. The great iniquity of the Jews is here displayed, and therefore they are inexcusable: they bent the bow, and will thus carry it out, because—

**Verse 4.—“Suddenly they will shoot him, and they will not fear; they have strengthened for themselves an evil word.”**

“Suddenly.” [Augustine.] Or “all at once”: that is, deceitfully, as though [Col. 0577C] unexpected and not foreseen, they will shoot him as one ignorant of it—as seems to them, who believe that they can deceive God. As though he said: They will carry out their crime and will not fear because of it. O hard heart: to wish to kill a man who raised the dead, and not to fear for it! They do not fear because they have strengthened themselves by obstinacy, not by truth. In no way were they willing to desist, not even through the judge, who did much to restrain them; nor were they moved by miracles, from their evil, or wicked, word: “He is guilty of death” (Matt. 26); or, “It is expedient that one man should die for the people” (John 11). And this was for themselves—that is, to their own harm—not for the Lord, whom they did not injure but themselves, when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27). He then explains how they bent the bow.

[Col. 0577D]

**Verse 5.—“They discussed how to hide snares; they said, ‘Who will see them?’”**

“They discussed,” [Gloss, Cassiodorus, Gloss, Augustine] or “arranged”: first among themselves, afterwards with the disciple, how they might hide snares, saying: “If the disciple betrays him, if the Romans crucify him, what is that to us?” This is the custom of evil persons. Whoever devises deceit thinks he is escaping notice. Hence follows: “They said, ‘Who will see them?’”—namely, the snares—that is, “Who will be able to avoid them?” They thought that the one whom they killed was hidden from them. Therefore they thought that he did not see, because—

**Verse 6.—“They searched out iniquities; those searching searchings failed.”**

“They searched out iniquities,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] namely how they might accuse the righteous man through false witnesses, or [Col. 0578A] how they might destroy him and prevent the world from going after him. For they said: “Let him be betrayed through a disciple; let him be killed by a judge.” Or thus: “It is nothing to us”; they searched, but those who searched failed in their searching, that is, in their perverse counsel. Or thus: They searched out iniquities—I mean, searching out searchings, that is, bitter and hidden counsels—but the more keenly they think, the more they fail from truth and equity. They are plunged into darkness because they do not see God, and therefore think that they are not seen by God.

**Verse 7.—“Man shall approach the deep heart; and God shall be exalted.”**

“Man shall approach the deep heart,” or “and the deep heart.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though he said: He who searches out evil fails; but, conversely, the person searching for good will approach [Col. 0578B] the deep heart—that is, the profound understanding of the heart—as one who investigates divine things, which is to go to the deep heart. There he does not fail, but grows. And he comes so far as to believe that God is supreme and almighty. Hence follows: “And God shall be exalted,” namely in that person’s heart. For God becomes great not in himself, but in the human heart.

Or thus: They searched, but in vain, because the man, Christ—who could not suffer unless he were man—will willingly approach his passion. “And the heart was deep for him,” that is, it was a secret heart, because he did this according to a profound counsel: exposing to them the man, that is, human form, on which they might rage, while preserving within God, that is, the form of God, by whose power he would rise again. And God will be exalted in the resurrection. As though he said: He is killed as man in the passion, and that same one [Col. 0578C] is exalted as God in the resurrection.

Or thus, with the sense unchanged: Since Christ knew their snares, why then did they prevail? Because he willed it. And this is what is meant by “Man, Christ, shall approach,” etc.

## Part II

**Verse 8.—“The arrows of little children became their wounds, and their tongues were weakened against them.”**

“The arrows of little children.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The second part, in which he mocks the enumerated perversity of the Jews, who were more disturbed when the resurrection was announced; while the righteous rejoiced. As though he said: They searched, but their wounds became like the arrows of little children—that is, they did no harm, like children’s reeds—and likewise their tongues. To the guards they said: “Say, ‘While we were [Col. 0578D] asleep, his disciples came and stole him’” (Matt. 28). Their tongues were weakened against them, that is, to their shame. For if they were asleep, how could they have seen? But if they saw nothing, how were they witnesses? Therefore, by lying, they spoke against themselves. Or, their tongues were weakened against them by the power of my resurrection in all that they said against me. Here it is clear that they “strengthened for themselves an evil word.” I say that God shall be exalted; and, God having been exalted and the miracles seen—

**Verse 9.—“All who saw them were troubled, and every man feared.”**

“All who saw them troubled,” [Augustine] that is, who understood that they had failed: others are troubled on their account, though they themselves do not repent. Those were troubled [Col. 0579A] who, seeking counsel for their salvation, said: “What shall we do, brothers?” (Acts 2). And every man—that is, every person using reason—feared God. Therefore whoever did not fear was not a man, that is, did not use reason. But if a person fears God, he should not allow man to frighten him away from proclaiming, like the apostles, whom the chief priests threatened, ordering them not to preach in the name of Jesus; yet they did not cease preaching for that reason (Acts 5).

**Verse 10.—“And they proclaimed the works of God, and understood his deeds.”**

“And they proclaimed.” [Augustine.] The preachers, delivered from fear of the enemy but fearing God, proclaimed the works of God—that is, the resurrection and ascension, and so forth—and understood his deeds to be divine, not human. [Col. 0579B] Why did he suffer? Why did he not come down from the cross? Because he had to die and rise again. This was not then understood.

**Verse 11.—“The righteous shall rejoice in the Lord and hope in him; and all the upright in heart shall be praised.”**

“The righteous shall rejoice.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Here the promise to the righteous is shown, and this is the conclusion from what has preceded. As though he said: Christ rose again, and therefore the righteous shall rejoice in the Lord. The righteous person is no longer sorrowful as when the Lord was crucified, but rejoices and hopes, because all things are manifest. “And he shall hope in him”; and in the future, when the perverse are condemned, all upright in heart—those to whom God is pleasing in all things—shall be praised, or exalted. He adds “all,” lest anyone suppose that this is said only of the apostles.

## Comparison on Psalm 63: “Hear, O God, my prayer,” etc.

[Col. 0579C]

**Verse 2.—“From the assembly of the wicked.”** Hebrew: *missôd*, that is, “from secrecy,” “from counsel.” The sense aims at nothing else, since the wicked Jews repeatedly gathered their synagogue to deliberate about the Lord’s death, as is more than sufficiently evident from the Gospels.

“From the multitude of those who work iniquity.” *Merigshath*, which they translate “from the tumult” or “uproar.” Certainly the tumult of those working iniquity is nowhere made more gravely than in a popular disturbance. Indeed, the word literally means “multitude”; for *ragash* sometimes means “he gathered.” The interpreters for Cajetan rendered it “from the assembly.”

**Verse 6.—“Those searching searchings failed.”** The modern translators give the opposite sense: namely, “They accomplished by searching what had been devised,” *tamnu chephes mechuppas*. But [Col. 0579D] Jerome entirely agrees with us in this respect, because *tamam* signifies both “to complete” and “to fail” or “be consumed.”

**Verse 7.—“Man shall approach the deep heart.”** Jerome: “to the thoughts of individuals and the deep heart”; Sanctes and Münster: “the inmost part of each person and the deep heart”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “the midst of a man and the deep heart,” “in the belly of a man and the sharp heart.” All these [Col. 0580A] are far from the Vulgate reading.

Now *veqarab* may be read without distinction of vowel-points, and it means “and he shall approach.” Or it may be read *veqereb*, and will mean “the inmost part,” “an inward thought.” Again, *ish*, properly “man,” is nevertheless commonly understood of each individual. “To the deep heart” appears to be a scribal error for “and the deep heart.” For the Hebrew is *veleb ‘amoq*, and the Greek καὶ καρδία, “and heart.” For this reason the Master records both readings.

Nevertheless, Augustine makes it clear that the reading is “to the deep heart.” For he says: “The man approached those very counsels; he approached all those sufferings. The man approached the deep heart, the secret heart: exposing the man to human eyes, while preserving God within”; and he pursues the rest in the same way. Saint Hilary agrees. Having interpreted this psalm, when he came to this passage, besides the fact that his text more than once reads, “Man shall approach the deep heart,” he explains it thus: “Through the man instructed in God’s teaching, and lifting the humility of his heart on high, these proclamations of the divine operation will be brought forth.” [Col. 0580B]

It is not improbable that the difference arose because *kardia* in Greek may be nominative or dative in the same sound, differing by the iota subscript: καρδία or καρδίᾳ. Finally, neither reading changes the sense: “man and deep heart,” that is, a man of deep heart. This also seems to have been Hilary’s view in the passage cited, as though rejecting neither reading but approving both pronunciations: “For when the failure of those who search has been recognized, and when the man of deep heart approaches, the magnificence of divine goodness is acknowledged.” Thus Hilary.

“And God shall be exalted.” Jerome, with the other Hebraizing translators: “God will shoot them.” The Septuagint took a future form from the root meaning “he was exalted,” so that it is *vaiarom*. Others, however, took the final *mem* as auxiliary and incidental, from the stem *yarah*, “he shot.”

[Col. 0580C]

**Verse 8.—“The arrows of little children are their wounds.”** The Hebrew connects the words above in a very different sense, and says: “With a sudden dart he will shoot them,” or, as Nebiensis has it, “Their blows will be a sudden dart.” Jerome rendered it similarly. But there are two very closely related words, *pith’om* and *petha’im*. They differ almost only in their vowel-points, and *yod* and *waw* commonly interchange. Again, the *aleph* absent from the second term—as is customary among Hebrews—is enclosed in the great vowel called *qamets*. Now *pith’om* means “suddenly,” while *petha’im* means “little children.”

**Verse 9.—“All who saw them were troubled.”** Some say, “All will flee” or “draw away”; others, “They will be moved,” which is “they will be troubled,” or, in the past tense, “They were troubled.” Such tenses commonly perform the reciprocal function of one another. But *yithnodedu* also bears [Col. 0580D] either meaning, or at least a related one.

“And every man feared.” Or, in the plural, “All men feared,” as Jerome, Sanctes, the Chaldee, Nebiensis, and the interpreters for Cajetan render it. Münster, Pellicanus, and Campensis, however, give “they will see.” *Va-yir’u*, if derived from the stem *ra’ah*, means “they will see”; if from the root *yare’*, it means “they feared,” unless someone wishes superstitiously to bind himself to observance of the vowel-points.

# Psalm 64

[Col. 0579]

## Title of the Psalm

[Note: [Col. 0579] This title was added by the Greeks under the teaching of the Holy Spirit, as it is right to believe.]

“Unto the end, a Psalm of David. A song of Jeremiah and Haggai, or Ezekiel, concerning the word of pilgrimage, or concerning the people of the migration when they began to depart.”

[Col. 0579D]

“It is fitting that a hymn be sung to you.” Title: “Unto the end, a Psalm of David. A song of Jeremiah and Haggai, or Ezekiel, concerning the word of pilgrimage, or concerning the people of the migration when they began to depart.”

As is read in the histories of the Old Testament, Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians, took the children of Israel captive and, after Jerusalem had been overthrown, carried them away to Babylon; in that captivity they were held for seventy years (2 Kings 25). The literal cause of that captivity was a statement made in Nebuchadnezzar’s court. When it was said that all nations ought to be subject to him, it was stated that the Jews were rebellious; therefore he captured them. Hence the title says, “concerning the word of pilgrimage.” [Augustine.]

Jeremiah foretold that this captivity would come, saw it when present (Jer. 25 and 29), and lamented it when past in the fourfold alphabet of Lamentations. Jeremiah also prophesied that after seventy years the people would return to Jerusalem. Among the captives, moreover, were certain prophets, namely Haggai, Ezekiel, and others, who understood and foretold the return from Babylon to Jerusalem. When the seventy years of captivity had been completed, some of them returned to Jerusalem with the permission of Cyrus, king of the Persians; and, at Haggai’s and other prophets’ exhortation, the temple was restored. [Col. 0581A] The title alludes to this history.

But since all these things happened to them as a figure of us (1 Cor. 10), they should rather be referred spiritually to us. It must therefore be known that at present there are two spiritual cities: one of the evil, which began with Cain and is called Babylon; the other of the good, which began with Abel and is called Jerusalem. Desire makes citizens of the former; love makes citizens of Jerusalem. Although they are mingled bodily, they are separated in mind: one of them journeys in the other and is held captive there. For as long as we are in this body, we are away from the Lord (2 Cor. 5), we who sigh from Babylon toward Jerusalem—[Gloss] [Col. 0581C] that is, from the world and the body of sin toward heaven.

The cause of this pilgrimage and sighing was the word which the devil spoke to our first parents: “You shall be as gods” (Gen. 3). [Augustine.] Yet one begins to return from this captivity when one begins to love. For love sets the foot in motion toward return. And just as the children of Israel returned after seventy years had been completed, under Jesus the high priest, so we begin to return under Christ our leader, who, according to Luke, was born in the seventy-seventh generation (Luke 3), until in the future, when this life’s period of seven has been completed and the goats have been placed on the left, we are placed at God’s right hand.

The prophets just named understood that this spiritual return was prefigured in that historical return, and especially rejoiced over it. Hence “song” is placed in the title. Its meaning is: This psalm, which directs us unto the end, that is, unto consummation, belongs to David and is a song, that is, rejoicing—the voice of a people returning. This song concerns the people of migration, that is, those who migrated from heaven to earth, from perfection to misery or confusion; or it concerns the word of pilgrimage, that is, the people journeying by reason of that word, “You shall be as gods.” [Gloss, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus.]

I say that the song was uttered when they began to depart in mind from the Babylon of this world. As though he said: The song does not arise because they journeyed away, but because they begin to return. One begins to go out when one begins to love. Love makes a citizen of Jerusalem; desire, a citizen of Babylon. Therefore, although they are bodily intermingled, they are separated in desire. [Col. 0582A]

This is the song of Jeremiah and Haggai, or, literally, of Ezekiel. Jeremiah means “exalted,” and signifies those who say, “Our citizenship is in heaven.” Haggai means “feast of God,” and signifies those who rejoice in hope, who keep a feast-day for the Lord amid the remnant of their thoughts. Ezekiel means “God has strengthened me,” and signifies those strengthened in the Lord. This song belongs to such persons. Or, literally, it is the song of those prophets who prophesied the return to Jerusalem, in which they understood the spiritual deliverance over which they especially rejoiced.

The prophet’s purpose is to comfort us in this exile, lest anyone despair, because he assures us of the return, of the one through whom it occurs, and of the riches possessed by those who return. The psalm is in two parts. First, he affirms the return and prays; second, he describes God’s praises and powers, at “The hope of all.” Therefore, in the voice of those returning, the joyful prophet sings:

**Verse 1.—“A hymn is fitting for you, O God, in Zion; and a vow shall be paid to you in Jerusalem.”**

“A hymn is fitting for you.” [Alcuin.] Since we have mentioned the seventieth, it should be known that three seventieth periods are commemorated in the holy Church: one signified, and two signifying. One of the latter preceded as a figure, namely the seventy of the Jewish captivity; the other is observed by the Church in representation, beginning at “They surrounded me” and ending on Saturday in White, which the Church observes as a representation of our spiritual captivity. We are captive while in the body and absent from the Lord; this same captivity was figured by the seventy of the Jews. [Col. 0582C]

Just as the Jews, before the completion of seventy years, had permission and opportunity to return through Cyrus’s permission, and returned fully when the same seventy years were complete, under Jesus as leader, so, before the completion of this sevenfold period of our pilgrimage, freedom to return has been granted to us through Christ, by whose death we have been redeemed—already freed in soul and hope. But when this life’s period of seven is complete, we shall be wholly free, both persons made glorious.

Therefore the Church, beginning at “They surrounded me” and continuing until the Paschal Sabbath, sets forth the miseries and labours of our sojourn, while falling silent concerning the song of joy, namely Alleluia, “Glory to God in the highest,” and the like. But on the Paschal Sabbath, having obtained through Christ’s passion the power to return, and thus rejoicing in hope, she sings Alleluia. Yet because she is still weighed down by the burden of corrupt flesh and suffers the snares of robbers, after Alleluia there remains the tract, “Praise,” because we must still be drawn through long labours; and in the following week we sing the gradual with Alleluia, journeying on the laborious way. Therefore we grieve in reality but rejoice in hope.

But on Saturday in White, as though the seventy of this captivity had ended, we sing two Alleluias, wholly joyful for the twofold robe of our glorification, by which we shall be glorified in the future. Now, however, as partly freed and joyful in hope, like persons returning from Babylon, we sing: “O God, a hymn is fitting for you”—a hymn sung by the one who truly loves God. Where? In Zion, that is, in the heavenly homeland, where we are now in hope. [Augustine.] Therefore we do not sing in Babylon, where we hung up our instruments. [Col. 0583A]

The meaning is: Those who are in Zion either in mind or in reality ought to praise you. “Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15). “And a vow,” that is, the mortal soul and body, “shall be paid to you in Jerusalem,” that is, in the heavenly homeland. Here, in the present, we vow by doing and thinking well; there we shall pay our vows by praising God for both. Note that the heavenly homeland is Zion, and the same is Jerusalem. It shall indeed be paid, because—

**Verse 2.—“Hear my prayer; all flesh shall come to you.”**

“All flesh,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, human beings of every kind—poor, rich, men, women, learned, unlearned, children, old persons—shall come to you, who took the firstfruits of our flesh, that is, assumed flesh free from sin. This also is the tithe of the tithe which, under the old law, the lesser priests gave to the high priest (Num. 18). This also is the light cloud upon which the Lord ascended in order to enter Egypt (Isa. 19). Therefore the rest shall gather to you as eagles to the body (Matt. 24), so that the whole burnt offering may be completed.

And because you bring others back, bring me back with them. That is: Hear my prayer, so that you may bring me back with the others. Or thus: Zion is understood as the present Church, Jerusalem as the heavenly one. Hence Isaiah: “The Lord lives, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31). Here the love of God is like fire; in the future it is like a furnace. And this is the meaning: O God, a hymn is fitting for you, not for the gods of the Gentiles, and only in Zion—which means “watching,” that is, only in contemplation, that is, in faith. And from good works [Col. 0583C] a vow, that is, praise, shall be paid to you in the heavenly Jerusalem—such praise as they used to offer, after battles, to Mars and the other gods.

And now hear my prayer here, that you may spare me there, where I know that all shall come, so that each may receive the things proper to the body (2 Cor. 5). Behold, this man first does what he says the rest must do: namely, he invokes and praises God. “All shall come to you.” As though he said: With what hope do you pray this? Because all flesh shall come to you—not the soul only, but every evil person as well. And you must hear, because—

**Verse 3.—“The words of the wicked have prevailed over us; and you will be propitious to our impieties.”**

“The words of the wicked,” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine] that is, of the devil and the first parents, Adam and Eve, prevailed over us like a sea overwhelming us: they cast us into this exile. Or thus: I say, “Hear,” although we are unworthy. The words indeed of wicked persons—that is, the evil rites and customs of our parents—prevailed over us, because we, born on earth, followed the customs of our Gentile parents, who surpass children in authority as in age. The pagans commended their rites to their children. But in contrast, you, O Son, Word of God, will be propitious, in the sacrifice of Christ the man, to our impieties; you are propitious when you forgive and grant pardon. Therefore the words of the wicked do not crush us. This propitiation occurs through the sacrifice which Christ the priest offered. Thus he is both priest and victim. I say, “You will be propitious,” and—

[Col. 0584A]

**Verse 4.—“Blessed is he whom you have chosen and taken up; he shall dwell in your courts.”**

Blessed is every person whom you have chosen by grace from the mass of the lost. Hence: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15). And you have taken him up into your own inheritance, that is, into eternal rest. For Christ adopts as a son every person whom he receives into blessedness. Why is he blessed? Because he shall dwell, never to be moved, in your courts, namely of Jerusalem, to which those sing who begin to leave Babylon. And we, having returned—

**Verse 5.—“We shall be filled with the good things of your house; your temple is holy, wonderful in righteousness.”**

“We shall be filled,” etc. [Augustine, Alcuin, Jerome, Cassiodorus.] Or thus, beginning with “Blessed”: As though he said: You will be propitious, [Col. 0584B] and this through the blessed man.
