For blessed is the man whom you have chosen—that is, the one with whom you clothed yourself in time, though in the beginning you were the Word—and whom you took up into the unity of person, joining the nature of that man to yourself, not a person. For he assumed human nature, and is therefore said to have assumed a human being, not a human person. Such a one shall dwell in your courts, that is, in your assembly.

And through him one shall be filled with the good things of graces, which are the good things of your house—that is, of the present Church, which abounds in the different good things of spiritual gifts. What are these good things? They are holiness in itself and equity toward one’s neighbour. And this is your temple, namely the temple of the righteous person—that is, the Church. For she herself is the house; the temple of God is holy in itself and wonderful in equity [Col. 0584C] toward one’s neighbour.

Or, concerning the future: “We shall be filled” in the good things of your house, that is, of the future Jerusalem, which cannot be spoken. How great are those good things? Behold, your heavenly temple is holy and wonderful, [Augustine, Jerome, Cassiodorus] not in outward things, like earthly buildings resplendent with columns and marble, but in equity, or, according to another reading, “justice,” which is more beautiful and admirable to the inward eye. We ought now to hunger for it, so that we may be satisfied by it.

Or the house and temple are understood as Christ’s flesh, with whose good things we are filled, because “of his fullness we have all received” (John 1). This temple is holy. Hence: “The holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Lord’s” (Luke 1). And it is wonderful in righteousness when it gives each person what is due. To him also he says:

## Part II

**Verse 6.—“Hear us, O God our Saviour, the hope of all the ends of the earth, and of those far away upon the sea.”**

“Hear us,” etc. [Gloss, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though he said: That we may be filled with such good things, hear us. So long before the Incarnation he asks to be heard: O God, who are our Saviour, namely Jesus. Behold the one of whom he said above, “All flesh shall come to you.” “The hope of all.” The second part, in which God’s praises and powers are described. As though he said: Hear us—you who are the hope not merely of Judaea or Africa, but of all the ends of the earth. Behold why he said above, “All flesh shall come to you,” etc.; and you are also the hope of those who are far away on the sea, that is, literally, on islands.

Or thus, the sea may be understood as the world. The sense is: You are the hope of all those far from their homeland. They are far away because they are on the sea, that is, in the world. For the sea figuratively signifies this world, bitter through falsehood and stormy through the waves of temptations, where fish devour one another. He then adds how he is the hope of all. As though it were through this that you are the hope of all: because you are—

**Verse 7.—“Preparing mountains in your strength, girded with power; you who trouble the depth of the sea, the sound of its waves.”**

“Preparing,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] namely to act against the candidates for baptism, mountains—that is, preachers, whom he sent to preach—and this in your strength, not theirs, because through them he worked miracles. How did you prepare them? You prepared them by being girded with power, that is, with divinity, because the humanity of the Word was encompassed by majesty, so that divinity might give what the man did not possess of himself.

“You who trouble”: behold what God did through those prepared mountains. You trouble to repentance the depth of the sea—not its surface, as it were, but hearts sunk more deeply in sins—and you trouble to repentance the sound of its waves, that is, those resounding in contradiction and surging in persecution. He then repeats the same thing more openly.

**Verse 8.—“The nations shall be troubled, and those who dwell at the ends shall fear because of your signs; you shall delight the goings forth of morning and evening.”**
“The nations shall be troubled,” etc. [Aug.] Or, from that passage [Col. 0585C], “Girded.” Another reading, cited by Augustine, is: “girded round with thy power.” Thus thou preparest the mountains, thou who art girded round—that is, surrounded on every side, after the manner of the mighty—by thy power, that is, by all believers. For Christ is in the midst of the Church, surrounded on every side, because all of us who believe in him hold him in common. But because faith is not from ourselves but from him, he is said to be girded by his own power.

[Note: [Col. 0585D] From Bede or Alcuin, on Exodus 25.] This is the lampstand in the tabernacle of the Lord, having three branches on one side and three on the other, and in each, at three places, cups, spheres, and lilies; because all the saints, whoever they were before Christ’s coming or after it, belonged to three orders of the faithful—namely, married persons, continent persons, and rulers—and are rooted in Christ. Hence: “Those who went before [Col. 0585D] and those who followed cried out, saying: Hosanna in the highest” (Matt. 21).

I say, “preparing mountains.” And from this the sea of the world was stirred, and began to trouble and persecute the saints. This is what is meant by “who troublest,” for the persecution of the saints, “the depth of the sea,” that is, the hearts of rulers and likewise of all the ungodly, from whom every disturbance arises. [Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] These were troubled when they saw their gods and their hopes brought to nothing. And who can endure “the sound of its waves”? Another reading. No one can do so of himself, but only by God, who prepares the mountains in his strength. Therefore they will be troubled all the more when they see that these men are more powerful than their own gods. Hence follows: “And the nations shall be troubled.” First—not [Col. 0586A] the mountains being troubled. For the mountains remained unshaken; but the nations will be troubled first, and even “those who dwell at the ends of the earth” will fear. For Christians are now feared everywhere. Why will they fear? “At thy signs,” that is, the miracles performed through the apostles, not through preaching alone.

First they will be troubled, and afterward “thou wilt delight the goings forth of morning and evening,” that is, thou wilt make them steadfast in prosperity and adversity. Morning is prosperity, because morning is glad after the sadness of night; evening is adversity. In these two a human being is tested; but an exit is granted, so that he may not be captured by gains—he whose riches are God—and so that he may not be terrified even by adversities, since God suffered for him. The sense is: “the goings forth of morning and evening,” that is, of prosperity and adversity, “thou wilt delight,” that is, thou wilt make them delightful already in this life. [Col. 0586B] For unless the very escape delights a person, he does not labor to escape from it, but is captured by gain. He to whom Christ’s promise is not pleasing, and whom adversities terrify, is not delighted by him who was willing to suffer for him in order to provide him an escape. How this has been done he adds, as though saying: How wilt thou do this? Because:

### Verse 9.—“Thou hast visited the earth and made it drunk; thou hast multiplied to enrich it.”

“Thou hast visited the earth,” [Aug., Alcuin., Cassiod.] that is, thou hast sent clouds which rained upon the earth, and through their preaching and teaching thou hast made the earth drunk. Or thus: Thou wilt do this through preachers. For inwardly thou teachest those to whom they preach; and this is: “Thou hast visited the earth,” that is, human beings by thy coming; and thou hast made them drunk inwardly [Col. 0586C] with the Holy Spirit, and “thou hast multiplied to enrich it,” or, “to make it wealthy,” that is, thou hast honored it with many kinds of gifts. Whence dost thou enrich it with waters? This is what follows:

### Verse 10.—The river of God is full of waters; “thou hast prepared their food, for such is its preparation.”

“The river of God,” [Aug.] that is, the former people of God—the faithful, namely, who were in the primitive Church, deep in their capacity to receive—“is full of waters,” that is, of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, from which others drink and are watered, according to the saying: “He who believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7). For thou hast prepared their food, that is, the bread of life and understanding of the Scriptures. I rightly say, “thou hast prepared,” because such is the preparation of that river: that thou givest through mercy, not because [Col. 0586D] they deserved it. Thou hast prepared; and, O Lord, thou hast made drunk with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, namely, the chief ones.

### Verse 11.—“Make its streams drunk; multiply its offspring; in its little drops the thing that sprouts shall rejoice.”

“Its streams,” of the river, [Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod.] that is, the teachers. As though he said: Let the first believers be made drunk. Or, according to another reading, “making its furrows drunk”; the sense is the same. “And multiply its offspring,” that is, grant mature imitators, begotten from the streams, so that, as it were, from believers others may believe. And “the thing that sprouts,” namely the beginner who is still unformed, “shall rejoice in its little drops,” that is, in the drops of its teaching, because by them he progresses. For certain things, though smaller, are distilled to little ones [Col. 0587A] one by one. “Thou wilt bless the crown.”

Or, from the passage, “The river of God”: by the river is meant God’s mercy. Whence, “thou hast multiplied to enrich”? Behold: “The river of God,” that is, the mercy of God, compared to a river in full flood, “is full of waters,” that is, is filled with refreshment for each individual. For it is sufficient for all and cannot be exhausted. After drink, he adds concerning spiritual food, namely Christ’s body, saying: “Thou hast also prepared their food,” namely the food of salvation. Or this whole passage may be understood of Holy Communion, when we are fed by his body and given his blood to drink. Thus: “The river of God is full of waters,” and the mercy of God fully ministers to us the drink of blood. “Thou hast also prepared their food,” that is, thou hast prepared for them the food of the Lord’s flesh. And lest anything be thought to happen by chance [Col. 0587B], he adds: truly thou hast prepared it, “for such is the preparation” of that food, as God ordains it; without him nothing takes place there.

And, O Lord, “making its streams drunk,” that is, the apostles and others who have drunk from the river of God’s mercy, so that they may suffice for themselves and others, “multiply its offspring,” so that preaching may not fail through successive generations. The sense is the same as before. “In its little drops the thing that sprouts shall rejoice.” Nor is this altered. And truly thou wilt do this because:

### Verse 12.—“Thou wilt bless the crown of thy goodness-year, and thy fields shall be filled with abundance.”

“Thou wilt bless the crown of thy goodness-year,” [Alcuin., Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] that is, the multitude of the faithful acquired in the year of thy goodness, that is, in the cycle from Christ’s coming until the end of the world, namely [Col. 0587C] the time of grace, in which thou hast sown the seed of the word and what is sown grows. Therefore the crown of the year of goodness is the whole world, in which the Church exists, and the circuit from Christ’s coming to the end of the world. It is called a crown because it is the victor’s glory for conquering the devil. And this crown is called the goodness of God, lest anyone boast of his own merits. “And thy fields,” that is, people full of fairness of heart and equality of justice, namely the righteous, “shall be filled with abundance” of good things, or of imitators.

### Verse 13.—“The beautiful places of the wilderness shall grow fat, and the hills shall be girded with exultation.”

“The beautiful places of the wilderness,” [Aug., Cassiod., Aug., Cas.] that is, of the Gentile world, shall also grow fat. For all nations are a wilderness, to whom no prophet was sent. These [Col. 0587D] received fatness when the apostles came to them, through whom they were made beautiful. Thus, where the prophets had not resounded, the Lord of the prophets was received. “And the hills,” that is, those whom God raises through humility—for God raises the humble—“shall be girded,” that is, strengthened to preach to others. And this “with exultation,” because they come to the kingdom; and:

### Verse 14.—“The rams of the sheep have been clothed, and the valleys shall abound with grain; they shall cry out; indeed, they shall sing a hymn.”

“The rams of the sheep,” [Aug., Cassiod., Aug., Alcuin.] that is, the apostles, leaders of the flock, “have been clothed with exultation,” because they rejoice in their fruits. Or, they “have been clothed with the wedding garment,” that is, charity. “And the valleys,” that is, humble peoples, “shall abound with grain,” that is, with the harvest of good [Col. 0588A] works, because they bear much fruit; and they shall cry out, not in blasphemy against God but in a hymn: “indeed, they shall sing a hymn.” And because of this they shall abound with grain.

This psalm is sung at the funerals of the faithful departed, because it treats of the return from the Babylon of this world to the heavenly homeland, to which the saints, drawn forth from the flesh at death, happily pass, immediately receiving the single robe, until at the resurrection they are glorified with the robe of twofold blessedness.

## Comparison on Psalm 64: “Thee becometh,” etc.

### Verse 1.—“Thee becometh a hymn, O God, in Zion.”

Jerome: “Praise is silence for thee,” etc. Nebiensis, Pellicanus, and Sanctes follow him: “Praise is silent for thee,” etc. [Col. 0588B] Münster, translating for Cajetan, has: “Praise awaits me, O God”; the Translator: “Praise is attributed to thee”; Pagninus agrees with our reading: “Praise becometh thee.” *Dumiyah* is a homonym meaning silence, expectation, and fitness. The words differ, but the meaning is the same. By this we recognize that all praise belongs to God’s magnificence, before which every tongue is silent. Ecclesiasticus 43: “Exalt him as much as you can; he is greater than all praise.” But “in Jerusalem” was added by the Septuagint for the sake of clearer understanding, and not inappropriately.

### Verse 5.—“Thy temple is holy, wonderful in righteousness.”

Jerome translates: “in the sanctification of thy temple”; Sanctes: “of thy holy temple”; Pratensis: “with the holy [one] of thy temple” [136]; Pellican: “in the sanctuary of thy temple”; the translators for Cajetan: “in the holiness of thy temple.” The Chaldean translator does likewise. Münster: “in the holy place of thy temple.” *Qedosh*, “holiness,” or *qadosh hekaleka*, “thy temple is holy.” The Septuagint followed the second pronunciation [Col. 0588C] and therefore joined it to the following clause in the same verse. But by following the other pronunciation there is a pause and the verse ends with “in the holiness of thy temple.” Then begins the opening of another verse: “terrible,” Jerome; “terribly,” Pagninus; “in terrible things,” Sanctes himself; “terrible things,” according to certain others. Each translates what seems to him more suitable.

### Verse 6.—“And in the distant sea.”

Faber and Caecus attack the translator, who ought, they say, to have written with Jerome, “and of the far-off sea.” Otherwise the awkwardness of the expression and the improper joining of the construction are not avoided. In Hebrew, in what we might call a slavish imitation of the letter—*kakozēlian* (κακοζήλιαν)—it reads: “and of those far away in the sea,” *ve-yam reḥoqim*, that is, of those who dwell remotely in the sea, as the gloss also explains: those who are far away on islands. Where, then, is the absurdity of the expression?

### Verse 7.—“Who troublest the depth of the sea.”

Jerome and others have: “restraining the sound of the seas,” [Col. 0588D] so that the sense seems opposite, although both troubling and restraining the sea’s storm are God’s work when he wills it. Yet it appears that the Septuagint read *tsade* in place of *shin*, letters not so very different in pronunciation; and *he* in place of *ḥet*, where the writing is close enough that perhaps *matzbeh*, “making to swell,” stood for *mashbia*. Among the Hebrews it is a rule that letters produced by the same outlet or organ are interchanged. Moreover, it is not uncommon in Hebrew for the same word to signify opposites, as *berekh*, “he blessed” and “he cursed,” and *qiddesh*, “he sanctified” and “he profaned.” And Sanctes cites the Septuagint in relation to the root of which we are speaking.

### Verse 9.—“The nations shall be troubled.”

Hebrew: *ve-hamon le’ummim*. Jerome, Pagninus, and Sanctes render “the multitude of nations and peoples,” to correspond to the preceding verb, “he restrains.” But [Col. 0589A] *hamon* also means a roar or tumult, as Münster, Pellican, Nebiensis, the translators for Cajetan, and Campensis likewise render it; therefore it could be translated by matching word with word: “and the roar of nations.” What the Septuagint rendered, “the nations shall be troubled,” is not unsuitable.

“Thou wilt delight the goings forth of morning and evening.” Through his excessively compressed version, Sanctes has left no room for the wider sense which the Hebrew allows. For instead of “the goings forth of morning and evening,” which are expressly found in Hebrew, he translated “morning and evening stars”; and the reader is compelled to understand it narrowly. Yet the phrase is not enclosed within such confines. For where then would Augustine’s interpretation stand, of the morning going forth as prosperity and the evening one as adversity, when the Hebrew nevertheless says *motsa’e*, that is, “goings forth”?

### Verse 10.—“Thou hast prepared their food.”

The Hebrew says “their grain,” *deganam*. This might have been passed over, since the full sense of each remains intact; [Col. 0589B] nevertheless it should be lightly touched upon, so that we may always remember what has often been repeated: that a skilled translator should chiefly express meaning by meaning, as learned persons also unanimously maintain.

### Verse 11.—“Multiply its offspring.”

Jerome: “multiply its fruits”; Pagninus: “level its heaps”; Sanctes: “make it descend into its furrows”; Münster: “thou sendest rain down into its little valleys”; Pellican: “press down its clods”; the translators for Cajetan: “depress its heaps”; Campensis’s paraphrase: “harrow its clods.” To the same effect are the Chaldean translator, “thou shalt restrain its birds,” and Nebiensis, “lay down its plots.” *Naḥeth gedudeha* (“lower its ridges”). Turn it and turn it again as much as you wish: in the end you will reach no other conclusion than the one to which the translators led you—namely, that from the abundance of divine grace the gain of souls may increase more and more through successive generations.

[Col. 0589C] ### Verses 11 and 12.—“In its little drops it shall rejoice.”

Jerome and Nebiensis: “water it with rains”; Pagninus: “make it slippery with showers”; others: “melt it” or “make it soft with showers or stars.” The sense is not changed. For fertile earth is metaphorically said to rejoice, as in:

> What makes the crops glad, etc.  
> (Vergil, *Georgics*, book 1, verse 1.)

But what immediately follows, “sprouting,” the Hebrews join by the introductory particle to the beginning of the next verse, which they divide differently. Thus they say: “And bless its sprouting,” where we join “sprouting” to [Col. 0590A] “shall rejoice,” ending the verse there, and then begin: “Thou wilt bless the crown.” Now if we read *tzimeḥah*, that is, “its sprout”; but if we say *tzomeaḥ*, that is, “sprouting,” then “thou wilt bless the crown.” The Hebrews begin the verse, “Thou hast crowned,” leaving “thou wilt bless,” as stated, at the end of the preceding verse. Further, without vowel points, it may be pronounced *‘atereth*, “crown,” or *‘ittarta*, “thou hast crowned.” Therefore the division of the verses ought to have been adapted to the differing reading. Yet the sense is nowhere harmed: only the words differ or are differently arranged. Hence Jerome expressed the Prophet’s thought thus: “The year shall roll on in thy goodness.”

### Verse 12.—“Thy fields shall be filled with abundance.”

Jerome: “Thy tracks shall drip with fatness.” Or, as Pagninus, Pellican, and the translators for Cajetan prefer: “thy tracks,” or “thy paths.” The Chaldean: “the treading of thy journey shall drip with fatness.” The translator following Campensis: “the tracks of thy chariot drip with fatness.” For “tracks” or “fields,” Sanctes renders “heavens”; Nebiensis and Münster, “clouds.” But *ma‘gal* properly means a path or track. Thus the metaphorical expression is explained: the abundance will be so great that thy steps will sooner wear down the overflowing plenty of crops than thy heels will wear the earth. Sanctes understood “heavens” from roundness, because the root from which that noun is derived, namely *‘agol*, means “round.” And what do those who translate “they drip” or “they distill fatness” mean except abundance of produce?

### Verse 13.—“The beautiful places of the wilderness shall grow fat.”

Pagninus, Münster, the translators for Cajetan, and Campensis’s paraphrase translate “the dwellings of the wilderness.” If *ne’oth* is written with *aleph* in place of *waw*, thus *neuoth*, as some maintain, Münster testifies in his lexicon that it means “dwellings.” But if it is derived from the stem *na’uch*, “he was beautiful,” then it means pleasant places and pasturelands, or places where livestock graze. Accordingly Jerome rendered it [Col. 0590C] thus: “the pastures of the wilderness shall grow fat.” Nebiensis agrees. Pellican: “the beautiful places of the wilderness shall be watered.” Sanctes: “they have distilled in the plains of the wilderness.” The translator following Campensis: “beautiful pastures.” Everywhere the interpretation is worthy.

### Verse 14.—“The rams of the sheep have been clothed.”

Jerome translates: “The flocks shall be clothed with lambs.” It is well known that Hebrew lacks inflection for cases, which often produces a differing syntactic relation; and more recent students of Hebraism translate “the plains shall clothe the livestock,” or “the fields shall be clothed with flocks.” But *karim* is ambiguous, meaning both “rams” and “fields.” The Chaldean paraphrast gives another meaning, as he often does elsewhere: “The rams shall ascend over the livestock.”

## Psalm 65

[Col. 0589]

### Title of the Psalm: “Unto the end: a song of a psalm of resurrection.”

[Col. 0589D]

“Make a joyful noise unto God, all the earth.” Title: “Unto the end: a song of a psalm of resurrection.” [Aug., Cassiod.] The Jews, by the righteousness of the Law, hoped for temporal goods for themselves and for the resurrection to a blessed life, although in that resurrection they did not understand that there were goods other than those found here. Hence they could not answer the Sadducees’ question about the woman with seven husbands, who asked whose wife she would be of the seven in the resurrection (Matt. 22). Later, resurrection also began to be promised to the Gentiles who believed in Christ, who rose again. Thus this psalm opposes the pride and presumption of the Jews and supports the faith of the Gentiles called to the same hope of resurrection: that the humility of the flock may follow where the exalted Head has gone before. [Col. 0590D] Thus it is fitting that a song is added in the title.

The sense is: This song, directing us unto the end—that is, Christ, or the consummation of future blessedness—is a song of resurrection, because here is exultation concerning the resurrection of the Head which has preceded us and of the body which is to come. It is a song of a psalm because, on account of the resurrection, it urges us to work well. Intention: it urges joyful praise and psalmody because of the hope of resurrection. Method: there are four divisions.

First, it urges all to rejoice in Christ’s resurrection, which gives life to all. Second, it invites beginners to consider God’s works, that one faith may unite those whom one reward awaits, at “Come and see.” Third, it urges the nations to bless God, who, although he tests them by tribulations, nevertheless leads them to the kingdom, [Col. 0591A] at “Bless, O nations.” Fourth, it again urges those who are no longer untrained but devout, by the example of their own deliverance, to trust more fully in the Lord, at “Come and hear.” Therefore the Church, rejoicing in the hope of resurrection and inviting all to song and psalmody, says:

### Verse 1.—“Make a joyful noise unto God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise.”

“All the earth,” [Aug.] not Judaea alone, “make a joyful noise unto God” with ineffable affection because of the joy of the resurrection. For jubilation is ineffable joy, which can neither be kept silent nor expressed. This is done for God, who perceives it. “And sing a psalm” by the work itself, in such a way that people may hear, that is, perceive. And do this with expressible affection. For psalmody is done by works, and it is done for people who recognize it. Do it “to his name,” not to your own, so as to seek your own [Col. 0591B] glory. “And give glory to his praise,” not to your own skill, because God chose the weak and the things which are not, lest anyone glory in himself but in the Lord (1 Cor. 1). Therefore do not act like the Jews, who attribute righteousness to their own merits and begrudge grace to the Gentiles. I say, rejoice and give glory. And:

### Verse 2.—“Say unto God: How terrible are thy works, O Lord; through the multitude of thy power thine enemies shall lie unto thee.”

“Say unto God: O Lord, how terrible are thy works!” [Cassiod., Aug., Hier., Aug.] Briefly he speaks of the mysteries of the Incarnation. [Col. 0591C] For these are the terrible works: that God became man, that he suffered, that he died, and such things. They might be called lovable, but he calls them terrible so that you may fear. For if you rejoice because of the things already mentioned, fear lest what was given to the humble be taken from the proud, as happened to the Jews. Therefore do not boast over the broken branches, but fear lest perhaps he spare not you either (Rom. 11). Thy works are terrible, and these works are “in the multitude of thy power,” that is, they are many and great according to thy power. Yet, although the works are many, “thine enemies shall lie unto thee.”

Or thus, and he speaks of works and miracles done among the Egyptians and the children of Israel: O Lord, how terrible, that is, fearsome, are thy works concerning the children of Israel and the Egyptians, which were done “in the multitude of thy power,” which then appeared! And yet thine enemies lied to thee, despite seeing thy power, when they saw the mighty acts in Egypt and the signs [Col. 0591D] at the Red Sea. They lied when they said: “All that God has commanded us we will do and hear” (Exod. 24).

Or thus, and the text is divided differently: “How terrible are thy works, O Lord.” Here the text is divided. The sense of these words is not changed. “Through the multitude of thy power thine enemies lie unto thee.” As though he said: The works are terrible. What works? “Thine enemies lie unto thee,” and this is “through the multitude of thy power,” that is, thine enemies will lie to thee in order that the power of thy strength may appear—a power which appeared most especially in the resurrection, which he here intimates, when the Gentiles are admitted after the lying Jews have been excluded.

Therefore, from the lie of the Jews, who said, “While we slept, his disciples stole him away” (Matt. 28)—and who had earlier [Col. 0592A] lied in many matters, saying, “By Beelzebub [137] he casts out demons” (Luke 11)—thy power is greatly displayed. The enemies of anyone commonly lie in order to diminish his power; but the opposite happens in thy case, because thy power would appear less if thine enemies had not lied to thee. Christ’s greatest power according to his humanity appeared in the resurrection, whence the psalm receives its title. Therefore the Lord commends this resurrection, the special sign of his power, by the likeness of Jonah, saying: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale,” etc. (Matt. 12). Likewise: “Destroy this temple,” etc. (John 2). No sign is more powerful than this. For the saints—or rather, God in them—performed many miracles: they raised people and the dead rose, yet only to die again; but no one rose into eternal life.

[Col. 0592B] Therefore the lie of the Jews, by which they brought him to the cross so that he might thus rise, served to commend this power. The lie of the false witnesses about destroying the temple also served, for they were believed and Christ was condemned (Matt. 26). But he rose, and they were false. The guards of the tomb also joined in the lie and were proved false. The number of lies was increased so that the reward of believers might be increased. They lied, and Christ appeared against the liars to those who were truthful. Therefore, leaving them in their lie:

### Verse 3.—“Let all the earth adore thee and sing to thee; let it sing a psalm to thy name.”

“Thee,” [Hier., Cassiod., Aug.] [Col. 0592C] whose power they lied against, let all the earth adore in faith, having been substituted in their place; and let it sing to thee by works, and sing a psalm to others, that is, for the instruction of others. And let it do this “to thy name,” O Most High, who a little before wast most lowly among liars.

### Part II, Verse 4.—“Come and see the works of God: terrible in his counsels over the children of men.”

“Come and see.” [Cassiod., Aug.] The second part, in which he invites beginners to consider God’s works, so that one faith may unite those whom one reward awaits. Explaining those works, he openly says that the resurrection belongs to the Gentiles, while the Jews are rebuked. As though he said: The enemies have lied. And, O Gentiles, leave the lying Jews. “Come,” confessing your sins, “and see,” that is, know, the works of God, in which he is [Col. 0592D] terrible, because he is terrible in the counsels held over the children of men, that is, over the Jews. The children of men had counsels to destroy him; he had a counsel to blind the proud, that they might afterward be humbled, and to save the humble. And what did he do? Behold, by his counsel he did this: he is:

### Verse 5.—“Who turned the sea into dry land; they shall pass through the river on foot; there shall we rejoice in him.”

“Who turned the sea,” [Aug., Alcuin., Aug.] that is, the bitter world, “into dry land,” namely, that it may thirst for sweet water; and those who have been turned into dry land shall pass through the river on foot. The river is the mortality of the world, where some come and others succeed them. Everyone born from earth must give place to one who is born, and [Col. 0593A] this whole course of passing things is like a certain river. But whoever believes in Christ passes through on foot, that is, the humble person passes easily and more safely; he does not seek to cross on the horse of pride. Thus: those turned into dry land shall pass “on foot,” that is, easily, “through the river,” that is, through the passing world. For although their sins have been forgiven, they are still in the course of mortality; they do not become immortal at once. And there, namely, when we have crossed the river and are no longer mortal, we shall rejoice in God himself, not in ourselves, when he himself shall be all in all (1 Cor. 15). In whom shall we rejoice? In him:

### Verse 6.—“Who ruleth by his power for ever; his eyes look upon the nations; let not those who provoke him be exalted in themselves.”

[Col. 0593B] “Who ruleth,” etc. [Cassiod., Hier., Cassiod., Aug.] Or thus without a break, join the words: “There shall we rejoice in him who ruleth by his power.” The sense is the same.

Otherwise, the entire passage from “Come”: As though he said: The works are terrible; that you may know what they are, come, you who are far off, and see, that is, recognize, the works of God in which he is terrible, because he is terrible in counsels held over the children of men. And he speaks of actual deeds formerly done among the people of Israel. He then states what those works are: he is the one who literally turned the Red Sea into dry land; and at the river Jordan the children of Israel passed over on dry foot. There, in those works, we shall rejoice, “in the same thing,” according to another reading—that is, in what they signify. For we rejoice in those works not for their own sake but because of their sacraments, [Col. 0593C] that is, their meanings. Therefore when he says “in the same thing,” he now shows the sacraments of those works, that is, their meanings, in which Christians rejoice. For the crossing of the sea signifies baptism, by which the river of this world can be crossed without danger. Christians rejoice in these things.

And he is the one “who ruleth by his power for ever,” which no human being does. For what power do we have? Is it eternal? If our power were eternal, we would not have slipped or fallen into sin. But we shall be strong in him if we share in him. Nor does he grant this to Jews alone, because “his eyes look upon the nations,” that is, he enlightens the Gentiles, lest you suppose the promises already stated to be empty. [Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod.] [Col. 0593D] Therefore let the Jews, who provoke God—or, according to another reading, “stir him to anger”—“not be exalted in themselves,” that is, in their descent and fleshly observances; let them not be exalted because of the Law, as though more were owed to them. For all have sinned; but let those humble in themselves be exalted in Christ. Note that one who provokes God is accustomed to exalt himself by wishing to defend his sins; this is what is prohibited here.

### Part III. Diapsalma (musical interlude). Verse 7.—“Bless our God, O nations, and make the voice of his praise heard.”

“Bless, O nations.” [Cassiod., Aug., Alcuin., Cassiod., Aug.] The third part, in which he urges the nations to bless God, who, though he tests them by persecutions, nevertheless leads them through temptations to the kingdom. For these things seem [Col. 0594A] to conflict with the promised resurrection. As though he said: “His eyes look upon the nations.” And because he has enlightened us, O nations, bless our God, in whom you are blessed. Hence: “In thy seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22). And openly make others hear “the voice of his praise,” so that one who loves God may love his neighbor also, by declaring to him whatever is useful: namely, the voice which the Father speaks concerning the Son, “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3). It is as though he said: Praise not yourselves, but him by whose grace we are what we are. I mean, the voice of that praise:

### Verse 8.—“Who hath set my soul unto life, and hath not suffered my feet to be moved.”

“Who hath set my soul unto life,” [Aug.] which was dead in itself but lives in him. [Col. 0594B] Here he enumerates the reasons why he ought to be proclaimed. He has set my soul unto life; and afterward it is necessary that it persevere unto the end. He has granted this and “has not suffered my feet to be moved.” What then is the cause of your being moved? Behold:

### Verse 9.—“For thou, O God, hast proved us; thou hast tried us by fire, as silver is tried.”

“For thou, O God, hast proved us,” [Alcuin., Cassiod., Aug.] or thus continuously: Thou hast not allowed us to be moved because thou hast proved us, O God; thou hast not cast us headlong, but hast tested us by adversities. And thou hast tested us with the fire of charity, which does not allow us to feel torments. Or thou hast tested us with the fire of tribulation: thou hast not turned us to ashes, but removed our impurities by applying fire to us. I say, thou hast tested us “as [Col. 0594C] silver is tried,” not as hay, which is wholly burned.

### Verse 10.—“Thou hast brought us into a snare; thou hast laid tribulations upon our back; thou hast set men over our heads.”

“Thou hast brought us into a snare,” [Aug., Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] that is, into chains, not so that, captured, we might die, but so that, delivered from them, we might be proved. This snare does not deceive but tests. And thou hast laid “tribulations,” that is, scourges, “upon our back,” so that we, badly raised up through pride, may be bent down into humility. And thou hast set—because by thy will it is permitted to happen—men, namely murderers, over our heads: for we endure as superiors those whom we know to be worse. [Col. 0594D] Thou hast done all these things, and we:

### Verse 11.—“We have passed through fire and water, and thou hast brought us out into refreshment.”

“We have passed through fire and water,” [Gl. int., Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] that is, through adversity and pleasant things. By the analogy of one who does not leave the road because of either heat or rain, so neither are we delayed by prosperity or adversity, signified by fire and water. For fire burns—that is, adversity; water corrupts—that is, prosperity. Observe the fitting order: first he places fire and afterward water. A vessel hardened by fire does not fear water; but if it has not been hardened by fire, water dissolves it like clay. So also, if you are baked in the fire of adversity, you will not be dissolved by the water of prosperity.

Hence, in the Church’s sacraments, [Col. 0595A] namely catechizing and exorcism, fire is first applied, so that the unclean spirit cries, “I am burning”; afterward one comes to the water of baptism, and from water to refreshment. What happens in the sacraments happens to us in temptations. For if, having been baked by the fire of adversity, you do not crack, neither will you be dissolved by the water of prosperity, and you pass into refreshment.

Or literally: by these elements the deaths of martyrs have often been accomplished. “And thou hast brought us out,” in hope, after the heat of tribulations, “into refreshment,” that is, eternal rest, where there is a desirable fire that consumes everything fragile in us, so that nothing of our own remains, but death is swallowed up in victory. Hence follows:

### Verse 12.—“I will go into thy house with burnt offerings; I will pay thee my vows, which my lips have distinguished.”

[Col. 0595B] “I will go in,” [Cassiod., Alcuin., Aug., Alcuin.] at last in reality, into thy future house. Behold the refreshment. Here he says what God’s goods are, set against the preceding evils. “I will go in with burnt offerings,” that is, so as to offer myself before thy presence. Or, with burnt offerings of good works first performed in the present; and then, namely when I enter, I will pay thee, together with the angels, my vows—that is, vows of praise—which I vow here, that is, promise here, “which my lips have distinguished.” He does not pay who does not distinguish; he distinguishes who says that he is nothing, that God is all, and that he needs God, not God him.

Or thus: I shall enter into thy future house; and meanwhile here I shall pay thee my vows, namely myself. “Which my lips have distinguished,” that is, which my reason has preferred [Col. 0595C] above all things. Cain rightly offered, but did not rightly divide (Gen. 4), because he offered a creature to the Creator but withheld himself, which was dearer. I say: I will pay my vows, “which my lips have distinguished.”

### Verse 13.—“And my mouth hath spoken in my tribulation.”

“And which my mouth hath spoken,” [Gl. int., Alcuin.] that is, my heart has spoken, that is, promised, “in my tribulation,” because tribulation is sweet in hope. Or: “which my mouth hath spoken,” that is, which I openly declared to people to prevail over all other vows, “in my tribulation,” not conquered by tribulation. And what has it spoken? Behold:

### Verse 14.—“I will offer unto thee fat burnt offerings with the incense of rams; I will offer unto thee bullocks [Col. 0595D] with goats.”

“Burnt offerings.” [Aug., Hier., Cassiod., Aug., Alcuin.] Or thus continuously: I will enter with burnt offerings because, while I live, I will offer thee my burnt offerings, that is, myself with the marrow of inward love. For charity is within me, not on the surface, as it is in those who please people. And I will offer these to thee “with the incense of rams,” that is, with the prayer of the apostles, who are leaders of the flock, because what is done according to their tradition pleases God.

Or according to another reading: “With incense and rams.” The sense is: I will offer thee a burnt offering with incense, which is prayer—as though he said, with prayer. And I will do this with rams, that is, with the apostles, because, as leaders of the flock, they especially pray [138] [Col. 0596A] for the flock. “And I will offer thee bullocks,” namely teachers who labor in the Lord’s vineyard, “with goats,” that is, with sinners who redeem sins by almsgiving. For if those who thresh are offered, they do not nevertheless remain sinners; rather, healed by repentance, they too are offered—not by themselves, but joined rather with the bullocks, because they have made friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity.

Or thus: according to another reading, “I will offer thee bullocks with the incense of rams,” that is, with the burning and destruction of brutishness and resistance. Or: I will offer thee bullocks, that is, stiffness of neck, with goats, that is, wantonness, by slaughtering these vices within myself.

## PART IV. Interlude (*Diapsalma*). Verse 15.—“Come, hear, and I will recount, all you who fear God, what great things he has done for my soul.”

[Col. 0596B] Come. [Cassiodorus, Gloss, interlinear, Augustine.] The fourth part: having now set everything forth, he again exhorts not the untrained, but the devout, that by the example of his own deliverance they may trust the more in the Lord, blessing him for having heard him. As though he said: Thus do I; and you, all nations, come in faith and hear with the mind, and I will recount. I mean you who fear God. For if you do not fear God, I shall not recount, nor will you hear; for the fear of God opens the ears. I will recount what great things he has done for my soul. If you wish, he will do the same for your souls. Then, explaining what great things he has done for his soul, he adds:

### Verse 16.—“To him I cried with my mouth, and I exalted him beneath my tongue.”

To him I cried with my mouth. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As though he said: He did this for my soul, that I should cry to him, [Col. 0596C] whereas the nations cry to dumb idols. And he did this, that I exalted him beneath my tongue—that is, what I possess inwardly, I speak outwardly. The sense is: I cried and exalted him; that is, I preached him publicly, and in secret confessed that what is in my mouth is also in my heart. Hence the burnt offerings are “fat” or “marrowy”: by these two things the Christian is made perfect. And he did this, that:

### Verse 17.—“If I had regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not hear.”

I did not regard iniquity in my heart. [Augustine, Alcuin.] For when he says, “If I had regarded iniquity in my heart,” he does not mean that it was not suggested to him, but that it was not loved—that is, that I did not love iniquity in my heart. For many love within themselves what they condemn in others, [Col. 0596D] perhaps being ashamed before men. If, I say, I had regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not hear me; for the purity of prayer is heard in this way—that is, by not regarding iniquity—and in no other way. Note that he says, “in my heart.” For the heart is one’s own when it is not perverse. Behold, this man sets forth his merit, that others may learn first to labour before seeking a reward. Hence he adds concerning the reward:

### Verse 18.—“Therefore God heard; and he attended to the voice of my supplication.”

He heard. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though he said: Because I did not regard iniquity, therefore God heard me and attended to the voice of my supplication. Behold the reciprocity: God attends to one who attends to him. These good things God did for my soul. Hence:

[Col. 0597A] ### Verse 19.—“Blessed be God, who has not removed my prayer and his mercy from me.”

Blessed be God, [Augustine, Cassiodorus,] because by hope I have thus arrived at the resurrection: he has not removed my prayer and his mercy from me, but continually causes me to pray, so that I may not grow lukewarm in prayer, and continually shows mercy. If prayer has not been removed, be assured that neither has mercy, which, if it delays what is to be given, does not take it away. For these two are joined together: if prayer is not suspended, mercy is not prolonged.

## Comparison on Psalm LXV: “Make a joyful noise unto God,” etc.

### Verse 4.—“Terrible in counsels toward the children of men.”

Sanctes reads “a terrible work”; the Praetensis, Münster, and the interpreters for Cajetan, “terrible in work.” *Nora alilah.* The first element may refer either to God or to the work, so that the construction varies while the meaning remains. Further, *alilah* does not simply mean “work,” but a deliberate contrivance; hence it has aptly been rendered “counsel.” The Chaldee has “author of contrivances.” Hence Jerome: “terrible counsels,” followed by Pellicanus and Campensis.

### Verse 6.—“Who rules in his power for ever.”

Faber and Caecus maintain that this does not concern God’s eternal power but a temporal rule, forming their judgment from Jerome’s version, “who rules in his strength for an age.” As though it said: He who governs this world by his command. Yet the Hebrew word *OLAM*, found here, quite properly signifies perpetuity, especially when written with the letter *waw*. That they oppose Jerome diametrically is clearly demonstrated by Jerome himself, so to speak. In interpreting Galatians 1, “that he might deliver us from this present evil age,” he discusses it thus:

> One must also inquire what the difference is between “age” and “age of age,” or “ages of ages”; and where it is used of a short period of time and where of eternity. For in Hebrew “age,” that is, *OLAM*, where it has the letter *waw*, signifies eternity. But where it is written without *waw*, it means the fiftieth year, which they call the Jubilee. For this reason, the Hebrew servant who, because of his wife and children, loves his master and is bound to service with his ear pierced, is commanded to serve “for an age,” that is, until the fiftieth year.

Thus far Jerome.

### Verse 10.—“You brought us into a snare.”

Jerome and [Col. 0598A] Nebiensis translate “siege.” The other translators agree with us, but Jerome understood *METZUDAH*, from the root *MATZAD*, “he besieged.” Otherwise, from the stem *TZOD*, it properly means “a snare.”

“You laid afflictions upon our back.” Jerome, alluding to scourges, reads “you laid a creaking sound”; Nebiensis likewise. Others have “a chain”; some, “distress upon our loins.” The matter itself does not depart from this sense.

“You set men over our heads.” *HIRCABTA*, that is, “you caused [them] to ride,” as Sanctes, Nebiensis, and the interpreters for Cajetan render it. Jerome and the other modern translators, recognizing the figurative expression, agree with us. Hence the translator for Campensis: “you lay [them] on us as upon a beast of burden,” etc.

### Verse 11.—“You brought us out into refreshment.”

So Jerome, Pellicanus, and Campensis; Sanctes and the theologians of Cajetan: “into a watered land”; [Col. 0598B] Praetensis: “abundance”; Münster: “into a fruitful place”; Nebiensis: “satiation”; the Chaldee: “breadth.” But what do these express except the rich repose suggested by the image of refreshment? The translator for Campensis says “refreshment.”

### Verse 14.—“I will offer you fat burnt offerings with incense of rams.”

Jerome, in his letter to Sunia and Fretella, teaches that the Greek reading “with incense and rams,” *μετὰ θυμιάματος καὶ κριῶν*, is erroneous, because the Hebrew is *IM QUETORETH ELIM*.

### Verse 16.—“I rejoiced beneath my tongue.”

The Hebrew has *VEROMAM*, that is, according to Jerome, “I exalted.” Or, as others wish, “he was exalted,” namely by me, and therefore, “I exalted.” The Greek reads *ὕψωσα*, “I exalted.” Thus I do not wish, through foolish contention, to defend the corruption of the printers. And it appears that ancient copies had “I exalted,” since the marginal gloss writes, [Col. 0598C] “elsewhere, I exalted.”

Yet I know this one thing: as regards the sense of the matter, “to rejoice” is sometimes used for “to exalt” or “to praise.” Lest you doubt it, the Chaldee translates, “his praise is beneath my tongue.” Again, Psalm 58, verse 19: “But I will sing of your strength, and in the morning I will rejoice in your mercy.” The Greek has *ἀγαλλιάσομαι*, “I shall rejoice,” and not *ὑψώσω*, “I shall exalt,” so that no one may suppose that “I shall rejoice” was written in error for “I shall exalt,” although the sense tends in that direction; for the Hebrews there say, “I shall praise,” *ARANNEM*.

Therefore, if “to rejoice” is also used for “to praise,” as in Psalm 50, “My tongue shall rejoice in your righteousness,” *ἀγαλλιάσεται ἡ γλῶσσά μου τὴν δικαιοσύνην σου*, I see no danger in reading, “I rejoiced beneath my tongue,” although word for word “I exalted” would be more correct. Yet I would not serve contentious disputes.

## Psalm LXVI

[Col. 0597]

### Title of the Psalm: “Unto the end, in hymns: a psalm of David’s song.”

[Col. 0597D]

### “God have mercy on us.”

Title: “Unto the end, in hymns: a psalm of David’s song.” [Cassiodorus, interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus.] After the song of the resurrection, the Prophet adds his own supplication, praying that those who have been blessed may be led to the knowledge of God, and prophesying the blessing of all nations through Christ’s coming; hence he exhorts them to praise him.

The sense of the title is: This psalm, which exhorts to good works, is “of a song,” because here there is rejoicing over blessing; and it sends us to the end—that is, to Christ. It is “in hymns,” that is, in praises to be offered to David—that is, Christ.”

Intention: he exhorts to praise. Method: the psalm has three parts. First, he prays that we may be blessed, so that knowledge of the Saviour may be possessed. Second, he exhorts us to confess, for the sake of guidance and judgment, at “Let the peoples confess.” Third, the same exhortation is given, but tending to another point, at “Let the peoples confess.”

Since in the preceding psalm he had exhorted us to bless God—which we cannot do unless he first blesses us—he therefore here prays to be blessed, saying:

### Verse 1.—“God have mercy on us and bless us; may he cause his face to shine upon us, and have mercy on us.”

God have mercy on us and bless us. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] For God’s blessing is first in us, like rain watering the soil of [Col. 0599A] our mind. Then we bless him, which is like fruit; and in both cases we grow, not he. Therefore let one desiring the rain of the Lord’s blessing say: May God first have mercy on us, and afterward bless us.

For God first has mercy on the erring person by bringing him back to the way. Afterwards he blesses him by increasing his good things. The Creator blesses the creature by increasing it in number and merit. The creature blesses the Creator by praising him in heart, voice, and deed, and by ascribing to him every good thing it possesses.

But because many wish to be blessed with an abundance of temporal goods—children and other such things—which indeed all come from God but are common to good and evil alike, he adds what belongs properly to the righteous: “May he cause his face to shine,” etc. This is the blessing of the right hand, which belongs only to the good. The blessing of the left hand is common to good and evil.

For if God gave worldly goods only to the good, the wicked person would suppose that God ought to be worshipped for their sake. But if he gave them only to the wicked, the weak person would fear to turn to God lest these things fail him. Therefore the husbandman first nourishes him by not taking these things away. He gives them to the good, that they may be consoled as they enter; he gives them also to the evil, that the good may learn to seek other things not shared with the evil. He removes them from the good, that they may prove themselves strong, like Job; he removes them from the wicked, so that the weak person may not fear to lose what he sees the wicked lose, while the wicked person has nothing left within. But this person, if he perseveres, has something within with which to console himself. Otherwise he will be empty in both respects. Behold why these things are given [Col. 0599B] or, commonly, taken away from good and evil alike. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.]

Therefore, desiring the blessing of the right hand, he says: “May he cause [his face] to shine.” As though he said: May he so bless us that he causes his face to shine upon us; that is, may God the Father show us his face, namely the brightness of his Son, who is the Father’s face. May he enlighten us, that we may receive light from him; for no one can see him unless flooded with his brightness or charity.

It is not said, “May he cause his face to shine,” because his face, which is light from light, lacks light, but in order that what it is may be revealed over us. Therefore he does not simply say, “May he cause his face to shine,” but adds, “upon us.”

Or thus: by “face” may be understood the image of God which he impressed upon us, that is, reason. The sense is: May wisdom enlighten his face impressed upon us—that is, his image—lest it remain in darkness, so that we may know that we were made in God’s image and, if it has been disfigured by us, may be re-formed by him. [Col. 0599C] “And have mercy on us”: behold whence he began. For mercy begins, and mercy preserves us. May he enlighten us for this purpose:

### Verse 2.—“That we may know your way upon earth, your salvation among all nations.”

That we may know, [Augustine,] O God, your way—that is, the way leading to you, whither and by what way we are to go, which cannot be done in darkness—namely Christ, on earth, that is, in this life, as he is known in heaven. In what earth? Namely, among all nations. What way? Your salvation—that is, Christ.

## PART II. Verse 3.—“Let the peoples confess to you, O God; let all the peoples confess to you.”

[Col. 0600A] Let them confess. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The second part, in which, after knowledge, he exhorts the peoples to confess to God for guidance and judgment. As though he said: And because Christ is known among the nations, which have found the way, let them confess to you, etc.

Or the sequence may be taken thus: I say, “that we may know”; and when they have known, O God, let the peoples confess to you—that is, accuse themselves and praise you. And not only the peoples of one land, but let all peoples confess to you, lest it be said that the Church is not spread everywhere. And if they confess:

### Verse 4.—“Let the nations be glad and rejoice, because you judge the peoples with equity and guide the nations upon earth.”

Let them be glad, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine,] because this confession does not lead to punishment. For those who have already confessed do not fear future judgments as persons to be condemned there, since Christ is their advocate and pardoner, not an avenger or punisher. And let the nations rejoice, because he to whom confession is made is good. For he frees those who confess and condemns the proud.

Hence he immediately adds, turning his address to God: “Because you judge”—that is, you will judge in the future judgment—the peoples with equity. And that equity is not to be feared by the good, because he now guides them. Hence he adds: “And you guide the nations upon earth” toward good things.

## PART III. Verse 5.—“Let the peoples confess to you, O God; let all the peoples confess to you: the earth has yielded her fruit.”

Let them confess. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Jerome.] The third part, in which the same exhortation is given, but [Col. 0600C] tending to another point—namely, that the earth has yielded its fruit—so that, although the beginning is the same, the meaning tends in different directions.

Rejoicing, therefore, he says: Let the peoples confess to you, O God; let all peoples confess to you. He repeats in exhortation what he had said above, adding another matter, namely the earth’s fruit; and by the repeated word he asks that we may be blessed. Hence follows, “The earth has yielded.”

As though he said: Therefore let them confess, because the earth has yielded her fruit; that is, Mary has borne Christ. This earth, from our clay, from our mud, from Adam, brought forth the first flower, who says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2). This flower therefore became fruit, that we might eat it, that we might eat his flesh.

This fruit, then, is virgin from Virgin, Lord from handmaid, God from man, son from mother, fruit from the earth. And in this fruit and in this seed:

### Verse 6.—“May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us; and may all the ends of the earth fear him.”

May God bless us. [Jerome, Augustine, interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Jerome, Augustine, Cassiodorus.]

Or thus: the earth—that is, the human being, Christ—has yielded his fruit, namely restoration and blessing. Hence: “May God bless us.”

Or “earth” may be understood as the Church, which was once full of thorns; but the call of the divine majesty came, and thus it bore good fruit—thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold. And this is the earth that first brought forth thorns—that is, the Church—which [Col. 0601A] in confessing gave its fruit, namely good works: in Jerusalem it first gave fruit, because there it was first watered by the gift of the Spirit; there miracles were performed; they spoke in the languages of all; those converted distributed all their possessions to the poor.

But not only that Church which is in Jerusalem ought to do this; rather, may God bless us also, etc.

Or the sequence may be taken thus: The earth yielded fruit, but only through God’s blessing; therefore, that we may yield fruit, may God the Father also bless us; God the Son, who is ours, not the Gentiles’; and may God the Holy Spirit bless us again and again and multiply us.

For by the threefold use of “God” the Trinity of persons is indicated; by saying “him” and not “them,” the unity is indicated. Hence follows: “And may they fear him.” As though he said: What is the value of blessing? It leads to fear. Therefore let all the ends of the earth fear him, because the Judge will come—he who first came humble. Let us recognize him humble, lest we dread him exalted.

Behold, the fear of God is sought among other benefits, so that what has been entrusted may be carefully kept. The fear of God begins and completes; whoever knows how to fear does not cease to love.

This psalm is joined at Morning Lauds to the psalm sung in the third place, because in this psalm the blessing of the Trinity is invoked, whose essence is one and the same, without diversity. In that psalm—namely, “O God, my God, to you I keep watch from the dawn”—[Col. 0602A] thirst and dryness are explained. But in this one the rain of the Lord’s blessing is sought to refresh thirst; therefore it is sung in conjunction with it.

## Comparison on Psalm LXVI: “God have mercy on us,” etc.

### Verse 1.

The closing clause repeated at the end, “And have mercy on us,” is an addition intended to arouse a more fervent affection. This was not unusual for the Septuagint translators to do for a definite purpose, though one unknown to us. For I see that certain others more often append additions which either produce a different meaning or at least divert to another meaning.

For example, in Psalm 35 we read: “Let not the foot of pride come against me.” Münster says: “Let not the proud foot of enemies come against me.” And in another preceding psalm: “They repaid barrenness to my soul.” Münster: “They tried to deprive me of my soul.” Again, Psalm 45: “Be still and see.” The same translator: “Abandon [Col. 0602B] your undertaking, and know,” etc.

### Verse 6.

The Hebrews divide the final verse into two little verses, as regards the division of the writing; but as regards the sense, it must be one verse. Otherwise the mystery of the Trinity together with the unity of essence would be suggested separately, which is neither so pleasing nor fitting; yet Jerome refers us to this passage: “See the mystery of the Trinity comprehended in one little verse.”

Let this be noted, lest anyone suppose that a division of meanings must always be made according to the division of verses. We have partly given the reason for this above.

## Psalm LXVII

[Col. 0601]

### Title of the Psalm: “Unto the end, a psalm of David’s song.”

[Col. 0601C]

### “Let God arise,” etc.

Title: “Unto the end, a psalm of David’s song.” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] Here the prophet treats of the exaltation of Christ and the Church, in this world and in the world to come, and of the overthrow and ruin of enemies, in order to terrify the wicked and gladden the good. Hence, both in the title and in the psalm, he exhorts them to sing to God and rejoice.

The meaning is: This psalm of song, directing us to the end—that is, to Christ—is by the prophet David, who here treats of the exaltation of Christ and his people and of the ruin of their adversaries, shaping his manner of speech from what once happened to Moses and the children of Israel when they fought against their enemies.

For when the ark of the Lord was raised, they overcame their enemies; and Moses is said to have used words like these when the ark was raised: “Let God arise,” etc. (Joshua 6). The ark signifies Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God (Colossians 2). The Prophet here prays for his resurrection, through which enemies are scattered.

Intention: he exhorts all to sing to God. Method: there are six divisions. First, with Christ rising again as though the ark were raised, he says what will happen to the good and evil, both here and in the future, to terrify the latter and gladden the former. Second, he treats of the word of the Gospel, at “O God, when you went forth.” Third, he treats of Christ’s gifts when he ascends, at “While he divides.” Fourth, he explains God’s works, at “Our God.” Fifth, he prays and affirms that the Church may be enlarged and strengthened, at “In [Col. 0602C] the churches.” Sixth, he says that Christ, who ascended, will come for judgment, at “Sing praises.”

Therefore the Prophet, praying that Christ may be exalted through the resurrection, says:

### Verse 1.—“Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered; and let those who hate him flee from before his face.”

Let God arise, [Cassiodorus, interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus,] that is, let Christ rise from death. The Prophet confidently desires what he knows will happen. “And let his enemies be scattered,” here in Christ’s resurrection and afterward at the future judgment. This has already happened, because Christ rose and the Jews were scattered among all nations.

“And let those who hate him,” namely those obstinate in evil, “flee from before his face,” not in place, for he is present everywhere, but in fear of mind: that is, by fearing, not by hiding. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The sense is: Let them withdraw in mind, through fear and will, from the presence of him—namely, God—who is present everywhere. It is a grave curse and a dreadful rebuke for them to will and attempt what cannot possibly occur.

Or thus: it treats of the presence of God by which he comes in the saints. Hence: “From now on you shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven” (Matthew 26). The sense is: “Let them flee from before his face,” that is, from his presence—not from that presence which they do not see, by which he is everywhere, but from his presence by which he comes in the clouds (Revelation 1), that is, in his preachers. In other words, let them fear before the presence of the saints.

### Verse 2.—“As smoke vanishes, let them vanish; as wax melts before the face of fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God.”

Let them vanish as smoke vanishes. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Jerome.] Smoke proceeding from flame vanishes as it rises; thus, issuing from the flame of wickedness, they produce smoke and fail away through that very self-exaltation. For they lifted themselves up with the fires of hatred and insulted the Crucified One; and thus they soon vanished, and will vanish in the future.

Thus let sinners perish before the face of God as wax melts, that is, is annihilated before the face of fire. For at the judgment the wicked will be taken away from the face of God, who will be fire for the punishment of the impious and light for the righteous.

Or it may be said beneficially of penitents. As though he said: Let those who hate flee and be scattered; but let others vanish as smoke vanishes, not so as to be reduced to nothing, but so that they may cease from their sins. And thus let sinners perish in that in which they are evil, before the face of God—that is, before the presence of his grace—as wax melts before fire, so that their hardness may be dissolved through tears of repentance, when the fire of the Holy Spirit is applied.

### Verse 3.—“And let the righteous feast and rejoice in the sight of God; and let them delight in gladness.”

And, on the contrary, let the righteous feast, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus,] that is, be gladdened by the contemplation of God here and in the future; namely, let those who laboured in the vineyard be refreshed in the delights that are in the sight of God.

And let them rejoice now or then, not as though before men through empty boasting, but in the sight of God, who beholds without error. And in the future let them delight in gladness: let them no longer rejoice with trembling. Their being glad may then delight them, because their gladness, unlike that of the world, will not end.

### Verse 4.—“Sing to God; sing a psalm to his name; make a way for him who ascends above the west; the Lord is his name.”

Sing to God. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] He turns to those to whom he has given such great hope, or exhorts them. As though he said: The Lord has risen; therefore sing to God by living in the spirit, and sing a psalm to his name—that is, perform righteous works for his glory.

Thus make a way for him into the hearts of believers. Or prepare your hearts that he may enter, because his way is undefiled. Therefore make a way for him “who ascends above the west.” For the setting of the death—that is, of vices and sins—gives place to him above whom the sun of righteousness rises, because new life does not receive a person unless the old has died.

Or, “he ascends above the west,” [Isidore,] because in rising again he conquered the fall of the body. For by his death he consumed our death; hence Moses’ serpent swallowed the serpents of Pharaoh’s magicians (Exodus 7). [Cassiodorus, Augustine.]

And lest you doubt who this is, “the Lord” is his essential name: the one whom the Jews killed as an ordinary man is Lord essentially. Had they known this, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2).

Hence the Lord said to the two disciples whom he sent into the village: “If anyone says anything to you, say that the Lord has need of them” (Matthew 21). And even while making the way, troubles arise:

[Col. 0604A] ### Verse 5.—“Rejoice in his sight; they shall be troubled before the face of him who is the father of orphans and judge of widows.”

Rejoice, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine,] and do not grow faint, in his sight, not in men’s sight—that is, in consideration of the future reward, which lightens hardships. Therefore rejoice, because those who trouble you in men’s sight shall be troubled before his face.

Whose face? The face of the Father of orphans. As though he said: You are not abandoned as people suppose. Those are orphans whose father—namely, the world and the devil—has died, and whose mother is desire; and he is judge of widows, namely, of those deprived of hope in this world, for whom error also dies as a husband.

In such people God dwells; he gathers and draws them, because from widows and orphans he makes a temple for himself. In this temple there is the subject of what follows:

### Verse 6.—“God is in his holy place: God, who makes those of one manner dwell in a house.”

God is in his holy place. [Augustine.] In what place? Not outside us, but within us. For God is the one who makes men of one manner dwell in a house—that is, united in mind, thinking one thing (Philippians 2), gathering them into one.

This is God’s holy place: not all who are in the house, in which there are also vessels for dishonour (Romans 9). Therefore he builds for himself a place in which to dwell, for he rests only upon the humble and quiet person (Isaiah 66). Grace builds this place, not merits. Hence follows:

### Verse 7.—“Who brings out those bound in strength, likewise those who provoke him, who dwell in tombs.”

Who brings out those bound, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine,] because he looses the bonds of sins. Hence elsewhere: “You have broken my bonds” (Psalm 115), in his strength, by which those who formerly were not strong become strong.

Or he brings out from hell to heaven those held bound there, in his strength, by which he bound the strong one, that is, the devil. Likewise he brings out those who provoke him, namely blasphemers against God; or those who provoke him by persecuting the good and resisting righteousness, although they are altogether dead in dead works.

Hence follows: “Who dwell in tombs,” that is, who are buried in carnal, foul, and dead works, so that they neither will nor can walk. Those who are bound, however, will but cannot; yet these are loosed by grace, while the others are raised.

## PART II. Interlude (*Diapsalma*). Verse 8.—“O God, when you went forth before your people; when you passed through the wilderness.”

God. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The second part, in which he treats of the word of the Gospel presented to humankind by Christ’s going forth—that is, by Christ’s incarnation.

As though he said: Truly you bring out, because, O God, when you went forth—or “shall go forth,” according to another reading—before your people, that is, when you appeared to people through your works. For God goes forth when he appears in works, but only to those who know how to contemplate his works; these are his people: namely, that he looses the bound and raises the dead.

And when you passed through—or “shall pass through”—in the wilderness, or “the wilderness,” that is, to the nations: that is, when you preached to the nations.

### Verse 9.—“The earth was moved; for the heavens distilled before the face of the God of Sinai, before the face of the God of Israel.”

The earth was moved, [Augustine,] that is, earthly people were stirred to faith. But whence came this? “For,” that is, because the heavens, namely the apostles, distilled rain, namely grace. And this was from the face of God: not from themselves, but from God, who is in them.

“Mount Sinai,” before the face of the God of Israel—understand, “distilled.” As though he said: And more than the others, Mount Sinai, according to another reading, distilled before the face of the God of Israel; that is, Paul, the apostle of the nations, who distilled drops of teaching more than them all (1 Corinthians 15). He is suitably signified by Mount Sinai because he was formerly doubled, or begotten into bondage, from the law which was given on Mount Sinai (Galatians 4).

Or thus, according to the same reading—“Mount Sinai distilled before the face of the God of Israel”—the heavens and mountains are the same: that is, the apostles themselves are signified by heavens and mountains. Yet it does not say “mountains,” but “mount,” expressing in the singular number what it means in the plural, as elsewhere when it says: “The heavens declare, and the firmament announces” (Psalm 18): it signifies the same thing by “heavens” and “firmament.” Thus “Mount Sinai,” that is, the apostles, distilled before the face of the God of Israel.

Some Greek and Latin books, however, do not have this reading, namely, “Mount Sinai before the face of the God of Israel,” but have “before the face of the God of Sinai,” or “Sinai before the face of the God of Israel.” The sense is: The heavens, namely the apostles, distilled before the face of God. Whose God? The God of Sinai—or Sinai—before the face of the God of Israel: that is, the one who gave the law to the people of Israel, because he who gave through Moses the law by which he might terrify also gives through the apostles the blessing by which he might free.

The Roman Psalter reads “Mount Sinai” with Augustine and Cassiodorus. The Septuagint, which we follow, does not have “mount”; the variation seems to have arisen from the Hebrew word *ZEII*, a demonstrative pronoun. It could therefore be understood either as “this mount” or as “this is in Sinai,” as Jerome translates it; in the second position he repeats “God” only once, although the Hebrew now says twice, “God, God of Israel.” What did they distil?

### Verse 10.—“You will set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance; and it was weakened, but you made it perfect.”

Rain, that is, doctrine: the willing grace of the Holy Spirit, which is given without merits by God’s will alone. For he willingly begot us by the word of truth (James 1). You will set apart—or “have set apart”—this rain, O God, for your inheritance, [Augustine,] namely the faithful, upon whom the rain descends in abundant watering; and that inheritance was weakened, that is, it acknowledged itself to be nothing of itself. But you made it perfect, because strength is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12). And:

### Verse 11.—“Your living creatures will dwell in it; in your sweetness, O God, you have prepared for the poor.”

Your living creatures, that is, the gentle nations, will dwell in that inheritance: that is, they will be that inheritance.

[Augustine.] All these things are read mystically, as we have said; but some interpret them figuratively—that is, historically—in this way: “O God, when you went forth before your people, and when you passed through the wilderness,” before Israel in the pillar of fire and cloud (Exodus 13), “the earth was moved,” that is, people were moved when they saw the miracles.

“For the heavens distilled manna,” namely before the face of the God of Sinai, before the face of the God of Israel, because manna was given from heaven; this he subsequently calls rain, saying: “You will set apart a voluntary rain,” namely that which satisfied the desire of the Jews. “For your inheritance,” O God, because this rain was given to Israel alone.

But Israel was weakened by disgust with that food, desiring the flesh of Egypt. Hence follows: “It was weakened; but you made it perfect.” This cannot stand literally, because that people was struck by [Col. 0606B] God, not made perfect. For a great plague followed those murmurings and expressions of disgust. All fell in the wilderness and did not enter the land of promise, except two. Thus this directs us to the mystery which we first expounded.

Or perhaps it may also be understood historically in this way: that Mount Sinai signifies the law which brings forth into bondage (Galatians 4). The sense is: O God, when you went forth before your people, in a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night, and when you passed through the wilderness, literally, Mount Sinai—that is, the law of Moses, given on Mount Sinai—distilled before the face of the God of Israel.

“For,” that is, because the heavens distilled that very law while the Lord spoke to Moses. Hence the earth was moved, because people are troubled, being unable to fulfil the law. This law is the rain that he gave only to Israel.

Hence follows: “You will set apart a voluntary rain,” that is, the law which the people desired, saying: “All that the Lord has said to us we will do and hear” (Exodus 24). And elsewhere: “There is no lack of one to fulfil it, but there is a lack of one to command it” (Romans 5).

You will set it apart, O God, for your inheritance, because it was given to Israel alone; and it was weakened, whether the law or the inheritance. The law, because it threatens and does not help, and thus makes people weak. The inheritance, that is, the people, was weakened because transgression abounded when the law was given.

But you, O God, made it perfect: either the law, through the Holy Spirit given, by whom the mysteries of the law were opened; or the inheritance, that is, the people, in whom after transgression grace abounded still more. Hence elsewhere: “From cursing and falsehood they will be announced at the consummation” (Psalm 58).

And your living creatures, subject to you and not free for themselves—that is, the converted nations—will dwell in it, the inheritance or the law.

[Cassiodorus.] Another interpretation of the whole passage: it is read continuously, both according to the history and according to the allegory, in the Father. As though he said: Truly, O God, you lead forth, because this was prefigured. O God, when you went forth before your people, and when you passed through the wilderness—literally, God went before Israel when he appeared in the pillar of cloud and fire, and in the wilderness satisfied them with manna. Allegorically, he went forth when he appeared to human beings through his humanity; or when he leads out those in bonds and raises those who were buried. He passed through the wilderness when he came to the nations; and then the earth was shaken [Col. 0607A], because, upon seeing such great wonders, the people of the earth were moved. For the heavens distilled manna, because manna descended from heaven like dripping rain. And this came from the presence of God, whose presence was known by the pillar. And Mount Sinai smoked before the God of Israel—another reading—namely when Moses received the Law there.

“You will set apart a voluntary rain,” that is, what the heavens distilled, namely manna, a rain freely given, which satisfied that people’s desire to eat greedily; “for your inheritance,” O God, because he gave to no other nations what he then gave to the Jews. And the inheritance was weakened for a time, while it did not believe in Christ. But you, O God, perfected it—the inheritance—when you admitted the nations to make up its fullness.
