Then he adds: whence you perfected it. “Your living creatures,” that is, the nations that are yours [Col. 0607B] when they believe, “will dwell in it,” in the inheritance, that is, in the Church. He explains what those creatures are and how they dwell there. As though he said: How will this happen? [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Behold, O God, you have prepared this for the poor person, who is weak in himself; that is, you predestined the poor person for this, that he might belong to your inheritance. By this he indicates the predestined, who were prepared from the origin of the world. And this is not in that person’s own capacity, but in your sweetness—not the sweetness of the world, which is bitter, but that, namely, which you give. God’s sweetness is that by which good is done, not from fear of punishment, but from love and affection for righteousness. By whom will this be done? By the evangelists, to whom—

### VERSE 12.—“The Lord will give the word to those who proclaim the gospel [Col. 0607C] with great power.”

“The Lord will give the word.” [Augustine.] And this is the meaning: the Lord—the Father, or Christ—will give the word, namely provisions by which his living creatures may be fed, to those proclaiming the gospel. See what the living creatures do: they proclaim the gospel, and this “with great power,” namely with great steadfastness of faith; or, “with great power,” namely that of miracles. [Note: [Col. 0607D] Cassiodorus and the Roman Psalter.] Alternatively, according to another reading: “The Lord will give many powers for proclaiming the word.” Who is this Lord?

### VERSE 13.—“The king of powers of the beloved, of the beloved; and to divide the spoils for the beauty of the house.”

“The king of the powers of the beloved,” [Augustine, Jerome, Augustine] namely of the only Son: that is, the Father, who is king of the Son’s powers, because power is governed by him and serves him; from him it is given, [Col. 0607D] and receives powers—miracles and powers of mind. Or the king of powers and the beloved may be one and the same, namely Christ. The sense is: Who is the Lord? The king of the powers of your beloved, that is, Christ, king of your powers, that is, of his apostles. This is said in the manner of ancient Scripture, as is read in the Old Testament: “Moses did as the Lord commanded Moses.” Or thus: the king of the powers of the beloved, who is the Father of the angelic powers, which also belong to the beloved himself, because he commands them, and he too is the beloved.

Then he repeats “of the beloved” [Note: [Col. 0608D] The repetition of *dilecti* is not in the Greek.], which is done for emphasis. Yet this repetition is not in all books; but whether it is present or absent, the sense is this: “of the beloved,” not only for other purposes but also—that is, even—for [Col. 0608A] dividing, that is, for dividing the spoils, namely those snatched from the devil. He divided them, making some apostles and others prophets. I mean spoils “for the beauty of the house,” that is, those by dividing whom he made the Church beautiful. Or thus: the Lord will give the word to the evangelists, and he will also give them power to divide the spoils for the beauty of the house. Or the preceding reading is divided thus: “The king of the powers of the beloved, of the beloved.” Pause here: “And to divide the spoils for the beauty of the house.”

### VERSE 14.—“If you sleep between the midst of the lots, the wings of the silvered dove; and the rear parts of her back in the brightness of gold.”

“If you sleep between the midst of the lots.” [Augustine.] First the meaning of each word must be noted, and then the construction of the words. The dove is [Col. 0608B] the Church, of which it is said in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one” (Song II). It is silvered, that is, instructed by divine utterances. For divine utterance is signified by silver. Hence elsewhere: “The utterances of the Lord are silver,” etc. (Ps. II). The dove’s wings are the teachers of the Church, through whom the Church is raised aloft and ever flies to heavenly things; by their preaching, the Church’s glory is borne to heaven. Or the wings are the two commandments of love, on which all the Law and the Prophets hang (Matt. XXII).

“The rear parts of her back,” that is, the dove’s back, which is its hind part, are love. This is said by analogy. For the rear parts of the back are where the roots of the wings are fixed, or where a burden is carried; thus the Church’s wings—that is, the two precepts of love—are joined in love, and [Col. 0608C] love itself, fulfilled in these precepts, is that through which every burden of the commandments is light. For whatever is difficult in a commandment is light to one who loves. Hence: “My burden is light” (Matt. XI), namely through the Holy Spirit, from whom comes love. Gold signifies wisdom. Therefore there, that is, in the rear parts of the back, is the verdure of gold, that is, the vigor of wisdom. The vigor of wisdom, however, is love: thus love is appropriately understood through the rear parts of the back by analogy, not by a property of substance.

[Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Or, the rear parts of this dove are the final times of the Church, namely those which will be at the general resurrection or at each person’s end. These will shine with the appearance of gold, because after it departs from the world it shines above gold [Col. 0608D]—that is, incomparably—in love, which never fails (1 Cor. XIII). Here, therefore, it is compared to silver on account of eloquence; there, to gold on account of the fullness of love.

As for the phrase “between the midst of the lots,” it must be understood that Latin usage would say simply “between the lots”; but where Latin has “the Lord among us,” or “between me and you,” Greek has “between our midst,” or “between my midst and yours.” Here, therefore, it says “between the midst of the lots,” that is, between the midst of the lots—a manner of speaking used of things that are accustomed to have agreement with one another. Thus, when the Lord speaks to Abraham about the sign of circumcision, saying, “This shall be a covenant between me and you” (Gen. XVII), the Greek has [Col. 0609A] “between my midst and yours,” to express agreement.

By “lots” he here means the two Testaments, through which an inheritance is given, called in Greek *klēronomia*. But *klēros* in Greek is rendered in Latin not “testament,” but “lot” or “lots.” In the Old Testament, the portions of inheritance, namely the promised land, are so called, since they come from God’s promise as though by lot. He fittingly calls the two Testaments “lots,” therefore, because through them eternal inheritance is given. To sleep between the midst of the lots is to rest in the authority of the two Testaments and to acquiesce peacefully.

Or “lots” means the inheritances themselves: the Lord gives one earthly inheritance in the Old Testament and another, eternal inheritance in the New. He sleeps between them who no longer ardently seeks the earthly one and patiently awaits the heavenly. For whoever still longs after the earthly [Col. 0609B] never rests, but is tossed about by many desires. Or he sleeps between these inheritances who perseveres until the end of life in contempt for earthly things and hope for heavenly things.

The sense of the individual words has now been explained. But the construction, since it is manifold, either depends on what precedes and is contained beneath the first verse, or extends to the following verse. Which way of speaking is more fitting is uncertain; for either can soundly be said. Turning his words, then, toward those of whom the beauty of the house is made, he says: “The Lord will give the word to those proclaiming the gospel with great power.” He will surely give it if you, O wings of the silvered dove—that is, teachers of the Church instructed by divine utterances—sleep between the midst of the lots, that is, in the authority [Col. 0609C] of the two Testaments; or between the two inheritances, earthly and heavenly, not ardently desiring the former and patiently awaiting the latter. Or if you persevere until death in contempt for earthly things and desire for heavenly things.

Or the construction may extend to the next verse: the beloved divides the spoils for the beauty of the house. And, O you who are divided as spoils for the beauty of the house through diverse gifts, if you sleep between the midst of the lots, then the wings of the silvered dove will be made white in Selmon—that is, you yourselves, who are wings, will be made white. Or thus, so that the sentence begun here is ended in the following verse: If you, O wings of the silvered dove, sleep between the midst of the lots, then others, namely human beings who receive through grace the remission of sins, will be made white as snow in Selmon. Or thus: O you who are divided as spoils for the beauty of the house, if you sleep between the midst of the lots, you will be wings of the silvered dove—that is, you will be raised on high; or the wings of the silvered dove, namely the two commandments of love, will belong to you. In these ways the text is arranged. Which interpretation should be preferred is uncertain, but in each case the sense follows well.

“And the rear parts of her back shall be in the brightness,” or “verdure”—another reading—“of gold”: that is, love, which is the vigor of wisdom. The back belongs to the Church for the aforesaid analogical reason. Or “the rear parts of her back” are the final things of the Church, which will be at the general resurrection. [Cassiodorus.] Or they will be at the end of each individual. [Col. 0610A] “In the verdure,” or “brightness, of gold”: that is, they will shine in love above gold, incomparably.

## PART III. Interlude (Διάψαλμα).

### VERSE 15.—“While the heavenly one distinguishes kings over her, they shall be made white as snow in Selmon: the mountain of God, a rich mountain.”

“While he distinguishes.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which he treats of the gifts of Christ ascending, who alone can do this, and no other. As though he said: If you sleep, you will be wings; as though he said: this is possible only through the one who distinguishes, because while the heavenly one—that is, Christ, who ascended above all the heavens—distinguishes kings, distributing grace to each as he wills, over her, the dove or inheritance—that is, while rulers are distinguished over the Church by the grace of the Holy Spirit—those rulers or other persons will be made white [Col. 0610B] through the remission of sins, “as snow,” that is, incomparably, “in Selmon,” that is, in the shadow of grace which comes from Christ’s body.

For Selmon is interpreted “shadow”: that is, in the grace of the Holy Spirit, because they are distinguished not by their own merits but by the Spirit shading them from the heat of the flesh. The shadow of grace is a defense for us against the incitements of vices and fleshly desires. Of this the angel says to the virgin who was to give birth: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I), that is, will make a shadow for you. A shadow, moreover, comes from a body and light. The light is the Word; Christ’s flesh is the body. Light came to the body, that is, the Word to the flesh: “For the Word was made flesh” (John I). We who believe in him are protected by this shadow, which flows from Christ’s body, from whose fullness we have received.

[Col. 0610C] He then adds praise of the mountain, saying: This Selmon, that is, this one in whom is the fullness of grace and from whom a shadow is made for us, is the mountain of God set upon the summit of the mountains, to which all nations will flow (Isa. II), and a rich or fertile mountain, from which flowing, sweet waters issue. Thus:

### VERSE 16.—“A curdled mountain, a rich mountain. Why do you gaze suspiciously upon curdled mountains?”

“A curdled mountain,” [Augustine, Jerome] because it nourishes little children with the milk of gentler teaching; and “a rich mountain” in its fertility, because it feeds the mature with the bread of more solid teaching. This is the mountain which in Ezekiel wounds the prince of Tyre. “Why do you gaze suspiciously upon curdled mountains?” Or “cheesed mountains,” another reading.

### VERSE 17.—“The mountain in which it pleased God to dwell in it; indeed the Lord will dwell unto the end.”

“The mountain,” [Col. 0610D] or “in the mountain,” another reading, “in which it pleased God,” etc. As though he said: Since this mountain is such, why then do you suppose other curdled—or cheesed—mountains to be this mountain? He says this lest anyone dare compare him with the rest, because some said that he was John, others Elijah (Matt. XVI); he rebukes them here. Do not suppose it. For he alone is the one in whom it pleased God—that is, the Word—to dwell in him, in his own person; in others he dwells through him. For the Lord—that is, the Word—was pleased to dwell in him, namely the man Christ, unto the end, because he is personally united with him, in whom “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II). The Word was indeed in the flesh in such a way that the Word alone was said also to have become flesh: that is, the human being was joined into the one sole person of Christ.

Or thus: none is like him; for this mountain, namely the Lord Christ, dwells—or will dwell—in the other mountains, that they may be something, though without him they are nothing, until he leads them to the end, that is, to the contemplation of God in himself. Therefore, because he dwells in the other mountains, they become:

### VERSE 18.—“The chariot of God is manifold by tens of thousands, thousands of rejoicing ones; the Lord is in them, in Sinai, in holiness.”

“The chariot of God,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] because it carries God and, joined in unanimity by love, is guided by God for the service [Col. 0611B] of his will. By dwelling in them and governing them, he leads them to himself as their end, as a chariot to its appointed place. This chariot is manifold by tens of thousands—that is, from innumerable peoples, from a great multitude of saints—which are “thousands of rejoicing ones,” because they rejoice in hope until they are brought to the end. Why do they rejoice in the end? Because the Lord is already in them; and he will also be the end of their consummation in Sinai or Sina, “in holiness” or “holy,” that is, by fulfilling the commandment which is holy. For what profit is a commandment unless the Lord is there, who gives both willing and working? (Phil. II.) Otherwise the letter kills (2 Cor. III), but through the Holy Spirit the Lord gives the love by which it is fulfilled. Therefore the thousands rejoice.

[Col. 0611C] [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Jerome.] Or thus, beginning at that place: “Why do you gaze suspiciously upon curdled,” or cheesed, “mountains?” Understand: “to be like this mountain.” Do not suppose it, because this mountain alone is the one in whom it pleased God the Father to dwell, he who pleased the Father that the Father might dwell in him. Hence: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV). It pleased the Lord to dwell in him, Christ, unto the end—that is, unto the limit, namely unto equality with his majesty—which is an end without end and the fullness of all things.

But the other mountains are the chariot of God, through which God is conveyed throughout the whole world. This chariot is manifold by tens of thousands. This does not change: because the Lord is in them, and this is “in holy Sinai,” that is, in the holy commandment fulfilled. Sinai is the mountain [Col. 0611D] on which the Law was given and is interpreted “commandment”; when it is fulfilled, the Lord rests therein, since God’s presence is customarily beheld in holy commandments when they are fulfilled. Or thus: the Lord is in them, that is, in the saints; he who formerly gave the Law on Mount Sinai is the same one who is “in the holy one,” that is, in Christ, the Holy of holies.

### VERSE 19.—“You ascended on high; you took captivity captive; you received gifts in human beings.”

“You ascended.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] He turns his words toward the Lord himself. But how did this occur? Behold: You, O Christ, ascended on high in place and dignity. He who descended in order to instruct us ascended above all the heavens to the Father’s right hand. And before you ascended, you “took captivity captive,” that is, those who were held captive in the lower regions [Col. 0612A]. These are the spoils; the figure is that of a triumph. The Apostle interprets this of Christ (Eph. IV).

Or, “you took captivity captive” means: you took human beings who had been captives under the devil through sin, and happily made them captives. They are called captives because they were caught, namely in Peter’s nets. Hence Peter too was told: “From now on you will be catching people” (Luke V). They were put beneath a light yoke. Hence in this chariot there are thousands rejoicing, not weeping. [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine.] “And you received gifts from the Father in human beings to be received,” that is, by receiving human beings, you received human beings as gifts. Or, you received gifts from the Father in human beings, namely gifts to be given to the human beings received: that is, gifts which you would give to those whom you received. Or, according to another reading, “you gave,” as God, gifts to human beings—[Col. 0612B] which also happens in triumphs.

Although this reading is found in few manuscripts, Paul nevertheless says with apostolic authority: “He gave gifts to human beings,” insofar as the Son is God with God the Father. He gave them by sending the Holy Spirit, who is of the Father and the Son. But insofar as the same Son is in the Church, he received gifts in his members, while the members themselves receive them, with whom he is one, according to: “What you did to one of the least of these, you did to me” (Matt. XXIII). I say, “you took,” which was necessary.

### VERSE 20.—“Indeed, the unbelievers also, that the Lord God might dwell.”

“Indeed,” [Jerome, Augustine] that is, because there were unbelievers who did not believe that God, namely the Word, dwelt in the Lord Christ as man. Or the connection is: “You received gifts in human beings,” indeed, that is, because you received even unbelievers so that the Lord might dwell in them. These are those whom he happily captured and made into his chariot. Therefore the Prophet, full of joy, pours forth a hymn:

### VERSE 21.—“Blessed be the Lord day by day; God of our salvations will make our journey prosperous.”

“Blessed,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Jerome] as though he said: Christ ascended on high, and where he has gone before he will make us follow; therefore let the Lord be blessed. Here is praise for the triumph, “day by day,” or “from day to day”—another reading, of the same force—that is, continually, because every day he captures captives until the end. And because he leads that chariot to its end, he adds: he who has done such things will make prosperous for us the journey of going to himself; that is, he will make for us the course of life, which is truly prosperous when its guide is the Savior. Who will do this? “The God of our salvations,” that is, of our deliverances, because he frees us from many dangers and also calls unbelievers to faith.

## PART IV. Interlude (Διάψαλμα).

### VERSE 22.—“Our God is a God of saving; and to the Lord, the Lord, belong the issues of death.”

“Our God,” etc. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The fourth part, in which he explains God’s works that arise from the matters just mentioned: the crushing of enemies, the conversion of sinners, and martyrdoms among both sexes. As though he said: I call him “the God of salvations”: God, I say, who is ours, not just anyone’s God, will save. [Col. 0613A] Here he commends grace, because no one is saved except through him. He saves those who nevertheless should not be surprised to die, since the Lord—the Lord himself—had no exit from this life except through death, by which he frees us.

Yet he died willingly, so that humanity might not fear death. And though he is the author of salvation, still “to the Lord, the Lord,” etc.: the same sense. Or thus: God saves, and do not complain about death. Rather hope, because Christ came forth from it and enabled us to come forth from it. This is the meaning of “and to the Lord, the Lord, belongs the issue of death”: namely, the resurrection, by which he came forth from death. But lest you think the evils of the obstinate go unpunished, he adds:

### VERSE 23.—“Yet God will shatter the heads of his enemies, the hairy crown of those walking on in their offenses.”

“Yet.” [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though he said: Though he died, or though he is Savior, nevertheless God will shatter—or crush—either here, that they may be humbled, or in the future, that they may be cast into Tartarus, the heads, that is, the pride, of his enemies. Or he will shatter the authors of Jewish sedition, or the authors of heresies, namely heresiarchs. And he will shatter the crown of the head, that is, the proud exaltation of people who exalt themselves excessively, “walking on,” [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine] that is, persevering, or falling from vice into vice, in their offenses, in which they ought at least [Col. 0613C] to humble themselves, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII). Yet even there they are proud and plunge into many sins, according to: “Foolish thought, which led to faults.”

Or, he will shatter “the hairy crown,” that is, the subtleties of empty questions. There are those who seek such petty grounds for accusation that they seem even to examine hairs. I mean the crown of people walking on in their offenses. This remains unchanged. He will shatter their heads, because:

### VERSE 24.—“The Lord said: From Bashan I will turn back; I will turn back into the depth of the sea.”

“The Lord said.” [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine.] Or the connection is: The Lord will shatter the heads of the Jews and will also convert many from the nations, because the Lord said: “I will turn human beings back from Bashan,” that is, from the shame of sins, because one who prays for sins is ashamed of them. For Bashan is interpreted “confusion” or shame; or Bashan is interpreted “dryness.” And from dryness, that is, need, the Lord turns those who do not think themselves full of righteousness when they are empty. For “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. V). The dry soul says: “I stretched out my hands to you; my soul is to you as land without water” (Ps. CXLII). The full soul says: “I am not like other people” (Luke XVIII).

“And I will turn back those who lie in the depth,” or “deep,” or “depths of the sea,” that is, of the world. Or, according to another reading, “I will turn myself,” to those who are from Bashan, because God turns toward those who are ashamed of sin [Col. 0614A], or who, being dry, desire the rain of grace. Under this interpretation follows: “I will turn myself to the depth of the sea,” that is, to those who were most utterly desperate. Or: I will turn them back, or turn myself toward them.

The Roman Psalter reads “I will turn myself”; the variation seems to have arisen because the Hebrew *ASCIB* may be understood as belonging to the verb which they call *qal*, in which case it is “I will turn myself,” or to the conjugation which they call *hiphil*, in which case it will be “I will turn back,” although the former is generally found with *waw*.

### VERSE 25.—“That your foot may be dipped in blood; the tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him.”

“That your foot may be dipped.” [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine.] Yet it is not God but the Prophet who says this, turning toward him. As though he said: Thus you will turn them, O God—or turn toward them—so that your foot may be dipped in blood: that is, so that those who were formerly enemies may become your foot, preaching you even to blood, namely unto death. And the tongue of your dogs will become, or be, from enemies, because through conversion enemies will become dogs barking for the Lord against his foes. These are good dogs, who eat of the crumbs (Matt. XV): praiseworthy, not detestable dogs. Thus he did not merely say “dogs,” but “your dogs”; nor are their teeth praised, but their tongue—and surely not without reason or without a great mystery.

Gideon was commanded to take out only those who lapped the water of the river like dogs; and in such a great multitude no more than three hundred were found (Judg. VII). In that number is the sign of the cross, because the letter *tau* signifies three hundred in Greek numerical notation. Thus only those are to be admitted to the office of governing who preach to others what they receive and who carry out by the works of their hands what they teach by word of mouth. Hence in Leviticus: “The mouth of the turtledove is bent back toward the shoulders” (Lev. I). And as though someone should ask: How can it be so great a good that they should be his dogs when they were his enemies? He says: “from him,” that is, by his grace, not from themselves; or “from yourself,” another reading, that is, from your part, O God. The sense is the same.

### VERSE 26.—“They have seen your goings, O God: the goings of my God, my king, who is in the holy place.”

“They have seen,” etc. [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Interlinear Gloss.] As though he said: Your foot will be dipped, because they see that you have gone before, [Col. 0614D] O God. This is the meaning: “They have seen your goings,” or steps, O God. Or, according to another reading: “Your steps have been seen, O God,” by which you came into the world. This grace lay hidden in the Old Testament; now it is manifest, when the Son sent forth is proclaimed among the nations. They have seen the goings of that God—“my God” in creation, namely the Word; “my king” in governance—who is God in the holy temple, that is, in the saints. [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss, Alcuin.] Or, “in the holy one,” namely in the body, though the faithless do not see him according to the body in which he suffered. And in this, namely in suffering or believing:

### VERSE 27.—“The princes went before, joined with those who sing psalms; in the midst of young women beating tambourines.”

[Col. 0615A] “The princes,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, the apostles, went before them, namely other people. Or thus I say, “the goings of my God”: in order that those steps might be seen, the princes, that is, the apostles, went before you, O God, in praise, so that the peoples might follow. Nor did they come alone, but “joined with those who sing psalms,” that is, with those who sound forth God’s praises by doing good works for God’s glory.

The princes are also “in the midst of young women beating tambourines,” that is, they are ministers and overseers of new churches praising God, with the flesh subdued, the skin dried of the moisture of sin and stretched free from the wrinkle of duplicity. For a tambourine is made from dried and stretched skin. Or understand this literally of holy women, lest you exclude the female sex, who also receive from them—that is, from the apostles—the pattern for praise and suffering.

## PART V. Interlude (Διάψαλμα).

### VERSE 28.—“In the churches bless God the Lord, from the fountains of Israel.”

“In the churches.” [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss, Augustine.] The fifth part, in which he prays and affirms that this beginning of the Church may be extended and strengthened, and that heretics may consequently be destroyed. As though he said: Since the Lord converts in this way, therefore, O you converted from Bashan, bless God, to whom *latria*—worship—is owed, and the Lord, to whom *dulia*—service—is to be rendered; and do so not elsewhere nor in other conventicles, but in the churches. These are the young women beating tambourines, lest anyone imagine bodily dances of luxury. For churches are young women, namely adorned with new grace; they are also tambourine-beaters, with the flesh chastened and spiritually resonant.

[Alcuin, Remigius, Augustine.] [Col. 0615C] “Bless,” you who have drunk from the fountains of Israel, that is, from the apostles’ teaching, so that in imitation of them you may preach that Christ first chose from Israel in order to make them fountains of living water springing up into eternal life (John VII).

### VERSE 29.—“There is Benjamin, a young man, in an ecstasy of mind.”

“There,” [Cassiodorus] that is, among the fountains, or in the churches, or in the temple at Jerusalem, is Benjamin, namely the apostle Paul, the last of the apostles, “a young man,” that is, chosen last, who was of the tribe of Benjamin (Phil. III). Hence in Genesis: “Benjamin is a ravening wolf; in the morning he will eat the prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoils” (Gen. XLIX). [Note: [Col. 0615] From Augustine’s sermon on the conversion of Paul, and from Remigius.] This is Paul, who in the morning of his life persecuted the saints, but in the evening of his conversion to God divided the spoils snatched from the devil among diverse offices. He is “in an ecstasy of mind,” his mind withdrawn from the senses of the body, as when he was caught up to the third heaven. [Augustine.] Or, “in alarm of mind,” another reading, with all being terrified at so great a miracle in his calling. There also are:

### VERSE 30.—“The princes of Judah, their leaders; the princes of Zebulun, and the princes of Naphtali.”

“The princes of Judah, the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.” [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss.] By these tribal names he indicates Christ and the apostles; perhaps apostles were from these tribes. And these are leaders of those who bless the Lord in the churches. But the sense drawn from the interpretation of the names, which suits the Church, is more pleasing: Judah means confession; Zebulun, dwelling-place of strength; Naphtali, enlargement. These fit the Church’s rulers. For in martyrdoms confession comes first; for its sake, whatever happens must be endured courageously. When distresses have ended, enlargement follows in the reward. Thus: there are princes of Judah, that is, of confession; princes of Zebulun, that is, of strength; princes of Naphtali, that is, of enlargement.

Or the passage treats of the three virtues signified by these interpretations: confession is in faith, strength in hope, and breadth in love, because they love [Col. 0616B] God and neighbor. The meaning is: Bless God from the fountains of Israel, which is fitting because there are there princes of Judah, princes of Zebulun, and princes of Naphtali—that is, princes of faith, hope, and love. These are the leaders of those in the churches; and through this each of them is Benjamin, that is, son of the right hand, a young man, having put away the oldness of malice, “in an ecstasy of mind,” that is, with the mind borne upward. And through these, O—

### VERSE 31.—“Command, O God, your power; confirm, O God, what you have worked in us.”

“O God, command your power,” [Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin] that is, make known and commend to us Christ your Son. As though he said: Accomplish, O God, what I proclaim will happen; confirm among the nations what you have worked in us Jews, namely the faith which you have worked in us. And so he does: for God commends his love toward us, because while we were sinners Christ died for us (Rom. V). He prays this well and confidently. For if Christ died for us, how then did God not give us all things with him? (Rom. VIII.) In this way God commands, or commends, his Christ. Note the distinction of the words: “command,” by teaching through preachers; “confirm,” by helping through grace.

Or thus, according to another reading: O God, command your power, that is, enjoin your strong ones to proclaim you, and through them confirm, etc. Or: O God the Father, command your work to your power, that is, to the Son and Holy Spirit; and through the Son and Holy Spirit, O God, confirm what you have worked [Col. 0616D] in us. This remains unchanged. You will truly do this, because:

### VERSE 32.—“From your temple in Jerusalem kings will offer gifts to you.”

“Kings.” [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Alcuin, Remigius, Augustine.] Or the connection is: If you do this, earthly or spiritual kings will offer you gifts, namely sacrifices of praise; and this will be “from your temple,” from nowhere else, which is in the heavenly Jerusalem, “which is free and is our mother” (Gal. IV), and which is also the temple from which every good gift descends (Jas. I), and for which every good work is done. Or divide the sentence thus: “What you have worked in us,” beginning from your temple, which is in Jerusalem, that is, beginning from the Jews; this will come to pass because kings will offer gifts to you. But because heretics interrupt this praise, he adds:

### VERSE 33.—“Rebuke the beasts of the reed; the assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples, that they may exclude those tested by silver.”

“Rebuke the beasts of the reed,” [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine] that is, heretics, who are called beasts because they harm through lack of understanding. I mean beasts “of the reed,” or pen, because they pervert the Scriptures, which are written with a reed; or because they are light and unstable; or because they are among those moved by every wind of doctrine (Eph. IV). Rebuke them, therefore, because “the assembly of bulls,” that is, heretics proud and of untamed neck, is among “the cows of the peoples,” that is, among those who are easily deceived and light, like little women. Hence the Apostle: “Among them are those who enter houses and lead captive little women” (2 Tim. III). But they cannot deceive those who are stable and weighty; hence: “I will praise you among a weighty people” (Ps. XXXIV).

Yet this does not occur without benefit to the godly. For through this it comes about that “those tested by silver,” that is, in God’s utterances, are brought forth or stand out. This is what the Apostle says: “That those who are approved may become manifest” (2 Cor. V). In the silversmith’s craft, those are called *exclusores* who know how to bring forth the shape of a vessel from an undifferentiated mass. Or explain the heretics’ intention thus: they assemble in order to exclude from the cows those tested by silver, namely Catholic teachers. Rebuke the beasts; also scatter those who agree with them. This is:

### VERSE 34.—“Scatter the nations that desire wars; envoys will come from Egypt; Ethiopia will hasten her hands to God.”

“Scatter the nations,” etc. [Alcuin, Interlinear Gloss, Remigius, Augustine.] Or the connection is: They act thus; but lest your flock be scattered, scatter the nations, that is, heretics and others who agree with them. He calls them nations because of the kinds of their diverse sects; lest, where there is a succession of descent, error be confirmed. They “desire wars” because they devote themselves not to correction but to contention. This will happen because envoys, that is, heralds of reconciliation, will come to Christ bringing gifts from Egypt, that is, from the darkness of the nations. By the name Egypt or Ethiopia he signifies the faith of all nations through a part for the whole. Thus he prophesies not that heralds will come from Jews alone but from the nations: “Ethiopia,” that is, the Gentile world, “will hasten her hands to God,” that is, before his vengeance. Through confession it will hasten before it, lest, remaining in sins, it be punished.

### Verse 35

“Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord.”

Sing to God, kingdoms of the earth; and accordingly the words “to God” belong either at the beginning of the following verse or, more properly, at the end of the preceding verse. [Aug., Cassiod., Alcuin., Cassiod.] The faith by which a person is justified without preceding works, and which afterwards begins to work through love (Gal. 5), is commended. The meaning, then, is: Ethiopia—that is, the Gentile world—cleaving to God by faith, that is, believing God, shall forestall her hands, that is, her works [Col. 0618A] (which is unambiguous in Greek): by believing in God she shall anticipate her own works, believing first and acting afterwards.

Or Egypt may be understood as the Synagogue, which Ethiopia—that is, the remotest part of the Gentiles—outstrips by believing. Thus: “Envoys shall come from Egypt,” that is, from the Synagogue, which was in darkness; and Ethiopia, that is, the remotest part of the Gentiles, coming to God, shall forestall Egypt’s hands—that is, the legal works of the Synagogue—because she shall be justified through faith without works of the Law.

Or, according to another reading: “Ethiopia,” namely the Gentile world, black with sins, “shall hasten to give hands to God,” that is, to submit herself to God. The comparison is with the conquered, who, laying aside their arms, surrender their hands to the victors lest the kingdoms of the earth perish.

Having run through all the things which we now see fulfilled, he exhorts us to praise Christ and foretells His future coming. As though he said: Since matters are as we have said, therefore, kingdoms of the earth—that is, Egypt and Ethiopia, namely every race of humankind—sing to God with purity of mind; sing psalms to the Lord in deed.

### Part VI — Diapsalma

### Verse 36

“Sing psalms to God, who ascends above the heaven of heavens, toward the east.”

Sing psalms to God. [Cassiod., Alcuin., Aug., Alcuin., Hier.] This is the sixth part, in which he says that Christ, who ascended to the place where He will bring the saints to perfection, will come for judgment. As though he said: I say, sing psalms, I say, to God—that is, to Christ—who ascended insofar as He is man. For insofar as He is God, He is equal to the Father, above the heaven of heavens—that is, above all heavens—at the Father’s right hand, [Col. 0618C] above the highest creatures, so that He should have nothing above Him except Him who created Him.

Whence did He ascend? “Toward the east,” or “from the east.” Another reading specifies the place where He rose and from which He ascended, because Jerusalem, where He rose and ascended, lies in the east. Or He ascended toward the east of our illumination, that is, so that He might cause the light of grace to rise for us. Or “the East” is understood as the Word begotten of the Father, by whose power that man ascended. Thus, He ascended toward the East, that is, by the power of the Word; and because He will come from there to judge, he adds:

### Verse 37

“Behold, He will give to His voice a voice of power; give glory to God over Israel; His magnificence and His power are in the clouds.”

[Col. 0618D] Behold, at the judgment He will give to His voice—or, His own voice—a voice of power: the efficacy of raising all the dead. Formerly, like a lamb voiceless before its shearer, He kept silence; but then He will come with the sound of a trumpet. I say, sing psalms and give glory to God. I say that He will give a voice; and then His magnificence over the Israel of God will be manifest, since there will no longer be any mingling of the wicked with the good. His power will be in the clouds, because He will not come alone for judgment, but with the elders of the people, who are the clouds. Lest you understand these otherwise, he adds:

### Verse 38

“God is wonderful in His saints; the God of Israel Himself will give power and strength to His people. Blessed be God.”

God, the God of Israel, will be wonderful in His saints. [Col. 0619A] [Aug., Cassiod.] Then every good person will truly be Israel, because he will see God as He is. God Himself will give power and strength in the flesh, which even in the resurrection will be incapable of suffering. Hence the Apostle says: “Through the power of His resurrection”; and even to His people, now weak, He will give strength by which death, the last enemy, shall be destroyed (1 Cor. 15).

Or the phrase “He Himself will give” may be understood of the present. He has promised great things; and lest anyone despair, on account of human weakness, of attaining such rewards, he submits: He Himself will give power and strength here to His people. Therefore, blessed be God.

## Comparison on Psalm LXVII: “Let God arise and let them be scattered,” etc.

### Verse 4

“Make a way for Him who ascends above the west.” [Col. 0619B] Hebrew: *Sollu la-rocheb ba-araboth*.

For “make a way,” Sanctes, Münster, the interpreters for Cajetan, and the Campensian paraphrase render “exalt Him,” although the Hebrew word unquestionably signifies what we read. Jerome, Pratensis, and Pellican likewise say, “prepare the way”; and the translator at Campen has, “fortify a way for Him,” which conveys no different interpretation in the commentary.

Then Jerome renders the following words, “for Him ascending through deserts,” and Pellican, “in wildernesses.” Pratensis leaves the Hebrew word *araboth*. Sanctes translates, “who ascends above the heavens”; the interpreters for Cajetan and Nebiensis, “equity in the heavens.” Münster adds: “He rides upon the spheres of heaven as upon a horse.” The Campensian gives two alternatives: “who, like the sun, is brought to us at its setting,” and in the paraphrase, “who uses the clouds as His vehicle.”

The sole source of confusion is that *ereb*, plural *araboth*, is a Hebrew homonym and ambiguous. For at one time it signifies “evening,” as is plain from Genesis 1; at another it means “desert.” Hence the Hebrews sometimes take it to denote the outermost sphere surrounding the others, because it is a desert of stars. There is therefore no reason now to hesitate about the Vulgate edition.

“Lord is His name.” Jerome: “In the Lord is His name”; Pellican: “With the Lord is His name”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “In God, His name”; Sanctes, Pratensis, and Münster leave the Hebrew word *Jah*: “in Jah, His name.” The reader should remember that it has often been emphasized that Hebrew lacks variation of cases. But since *beth*, a letter denoting the preposition “in” or “with,” is used here, Jerome quite suitably translates, “In the Lord is His name.” We may otherwise say, “The Lord is His name,” or, as the interpreters have it, “His name is for Him.” Campensis agrees with us: “whose name is Lord,” or “whose proper name is Savior God.”

### Verse 5

“They shall be troubled before His face.”

The interpreters rendered at once the two meanings of the same word. For *lephanaw* can mean both “at His sight” and “at His anger.” Thus they translated: “Rejoice in His sight; and they shall be troubled before His face.” No other translators include the final clause, except Pellican, for some reason unknown to me; after writing “rejoice before Him,” he immediately adds, “and His enemies perish before Him.”

I do not know what edition Jerome follows in the commentaries when he translates, “the fathers of the fatherless and judges of widows shall be troubled.” For it is certain there were several editions: namely, Lucian’s, the Septuagint’s, Aquila’s, Symmachus’s, and Theodotion’s. There were also a fifth and a sixth.

### Verse 7

“Who brings out those in bonds with strength.”

Pratensis, Sanctes, Münster, and the Campensian paraphrase read, “in fetters.” Pellican, Nebiensis, and the interpreters for Cajetan: “in fitting circumstances.” The Campensian text alludes to this when it reads, “He brings out conveniently.” Yet Jerome himself agrees with us. Certainly these were fetters that could not be loosed without God’s most strong and most timely hand.

“Likewise, those who embitter, who dwell in tombs.” This first clause may be referred back to the preceding verb, “who brings out,” though in Hebrew it may also be expressed in the nominative case. [Col. 0620A] [144] Therefore others translate “unbelievers,” “rebels,” or “stubborn persons,” which does not differ from “those who embitter.”

But the phrase added, “in tombs,” they translate “in a dry place” or “in dry regions,” *tzehihah*. Yet this does not prejudice the rendering “tombs,” which are not absurdly represented by barren places dead through drought, since they are also full of the dry bones of the dead. And, if one must philosophize, earth occupies the highest degree of dryness.

### Verse 11

“Your animals shall dwell in it.”

*Haithca*, “your animals,” is the reading of our text and of Jerome, Nebiensis, and Pellican; or “your congregation,” according to Pratensis, Münster, Sanctes, and the interpreters for Cajetan. Campensis indicated both, because of the ambiguity of the particle.

### Verse 12

“The Lord will give the word to those who proclaim the good news with great power.” [Col. 0620B]

The various arrangement of clauses and cases, whose Hebrew endings are alike, caused translators to preserve one or another structure of the sentence. Jerome: “Lord, You will give a word to female heralds of very great strength.” Pellican: “The Lord will give the word of the Gospels of great power.” Pratensis: “The Lord will give the word of heralds of a great host.” Sanctes: “Of those who proclaim: the host is great.” Münster: “The host of heralds was great.” The interpreters for Cajetan: “The Lord will give the saying of the heralds of a great host.” The Campensian text, farther from the literal sense: “Lord, You entrust to those who announce a great army the command.” Its paraphrase differently: “The Lord will furnish an effective word to the female heralds of His might.” Nebiensis: “Lord, You will give a word to female heralds of a great host.” The Chaldee paraphrase: “God gave the words of the Law to His people through Moses and Aaron, who announced God’s word to the great host of Israel.”

You see, excellent reader, into what a forest translations wander when each person contributes his own invention according to mere choice. It remains only to explain why *hammebassroth*, “female proclaimers of good news,” stands in the Hebrew plural and feminine. Jerome fully explains this manner in the Commentaries: “In Hebrew it has, ‘those who are evangelized,’ that is, the women who proclaimed the good news to the apostles, where it says, ‘Go, tell my brothers,’ etc. (Matt. 28); or it signifies souls that believed in Christ. But according to the Septuagint interpreters it is said to the apostles, because the Lord gave them power to preach the Gospel.”

### Verse 13

“The king of powers of the beloved, beloved.”

Two Hebrew roots have poured out a confused mass, as it were a cloud, of interpretations. For the words here read as *Iiddodun iiddodun* are derived by the Septuagint and Jerome from the root *dod*, “beloved,” “allied,” common in the Song of Songs. Hence Jerome translated, “Kings shall make alliances, shall make alliances,” using a verb where the Septuagint uses a noun. Pratensis, Sanctes, and Campensis say, “They shall flee, they shall flee.” Münster: “Those fleeing escaped.” Pellican: “They shall be routed, they shall be routed.” All these derive it from the verb *nadad*. The interpreters for Cajetan: “They shall be moved, they shall be moved.” Nebiensis: “They shall turn back, they shall turn back.”

“And the beauty of the house, to divide spoils.” The commentary explains how the order of the sentence must be arranged for coherence. Others translate in the nominative case, because the word *nevath* is ambiguous. Jerome and Pellican, with the Septuagint, translate: “The beauty,” or “splendor, of the house, to divide spoils.” Others translate “the female inhabitant,” “the dwelling,” “the mistress,” or “the household of the house.”

### Verse 14

“If you sleep between the midst of the lots.”

In Hebrew, *scephataim*. Jerome, Nebiensis, Pellican, and the interpreters for Cajetan translate “boundaries” or “borders,” which do not differ from our sense: namely, that these are the two Testaments, or the Church militant and triumphant, as has been explained. But since this word sometimes also means “pots,” Sanctes, Münster, Pratensis, and the Campensian paraphrase translate “tripods” or “cooking-pots.” “If you lie among blackened tripods, you shall be like the wings of a dove, which is read as having silvery feathers.” They understand the substantive verb “you shall be,” for ease of interpretation, as if the meaning were: “Even if you have been tested by such affliction that you seem blackened as with soot, yet afterwards, by God’s kindness, you shall shine with a new splendor of joy and enjoy it.”

The Campensian edition indulges itself too much: “Then you will rest just as a river between its banks; between the wings of a dove, white above silver,” although the word itself sometimes signifies the banks of rivers.

“The hind parts of her back in the pallor of gold.” Since the Hebrew *ebroth* can be understood in two ways, as “back” or as “wings” and “feathers,” the interpreters, Jerome, and Pellican translated “hind parts” and “shoulders”; the rest translate “feathers” or “plumage.” The wings are, supply, “like tawny gold,” or “distinguished by the greenness” or “pallor of gold.” The edition appended to the Campensian paraphrase appears to include both senses when it says, “whose back surpasses the brightness of gold and which hangs in the air.”

### Verse 15

“While He distinguishes heavenly kings over her.”

Münster: “When the Almighty scattered kings on her account.” Similarly, the interpreters for Cajetan: “When the Almighty breaks kings in her.” Yet *paras* also means in Hebrew “he stretched out” or “he distributed.” Jerome and the other Hebraists therefore agree with the Septuagint, with a few words changed but the sense preserved.

“They shall be whitened with snow in Selmon.” Because Selmon here appears to be an appellative rather than the proper name of the mountain mentioned in Judges 9, some retained the word itself, while others translated “darkness.” Nebiensis: “shadow of death.” Yet the Prophet seems to have alluded to the mountain. The blind Burgensian wished “mountain” placed in the accusative, otherwise the absurdity of the expression, “in Selmon, a fat mountain,” could not be avoided. But no Greek, Hebrew, or Latin author translates thus, because it does not depend upon what precedes but looks to what follows—except that Augustine indicates that some manuscripts have “mountain” in the accusative and others “mountain” in the nominative, because Greek *oros* is neuter.

“Why do you suspect, you curdled mountains?” Faber and Caecus attack the translator because it ought to be pronounced “mountains” in the vocative, since Jerome translates “lofty mountains.” Augustine, however, both reads and explains “mountains” in the accusative. But what is better known than that the Hebrews decline their cases alike? It is permissible, according to the requirement of meaning and syntax, to express it in one case or another.

But Jerome has “you contend”; others, “you leap,” others, “you envy.” From this it is plainly clear that “mountains” cannot be understood with those verbs except in the vocative. *Teratzedun* is derived from the verb *ratzad*, which Hebrews explain in three ways: “to leap,” “to lie in wait,” and “to await,” especially according to a certain rabbi cited by Sanctes. Hence Pellican translated, “Why do you look enviously at mountains of elevations?” though he seems to interpret it from the vocative. Yet in saying “you look,” he does not differ from our reading, nor does the Chaldee, “you marvel.”

Moreover, some read “humped mountains,” “mountains of elevations,” or “lofty mountains,” while we read “curdled mountains,” that is, “cheese-like mountains.” This is not surprising, since *gabenunim* has both meanings in Hebrew; hence Nebiensis, “mountains of curds.” Since Jerome had once translated “you contend,” in order that the connection of the sentence might stand, he added the preposition “against,” making it: “You contend against the mountain,” etc. If you do not wish to supply the preposition, you may say with Münster, “This is the mountain,” etc., since Hebrew speech is often so compressed that, for completeness of sense, some fitting word must be supplied.

### Verse 18

“God’s chariot is manifold: ten thousand, thousands of those rejoicing.”

The translators render this variously, but agree in this: it is not a numerical count of God’s ministers. Therefore there was no need to burden the reader with a less necessary matter. Still, I shall cite Jerome: “The chariot of God is innumerable, thousands of the abundant.”

### Verse 19

“You received gifts among men.”

Jerome, explaining Ephesians 4, teaches why the Apostle, quoting this very passage, changed “You received” into “He gave,” although Hebrew reads *laquata* and Greek *elabes*:

> “He elegantly says here, ‘He gave gifts among men,’ whereas in the Psalter it is written, ‘He received gifts among men.’ There, because it had not yet happened but was promised as future, He is therefore said to have received. But here, when the Apostle writes, because He had already given and churches had been established throughout the whole world, He is said not to have received but to have given.”

Thus far Jerome. Pellican nevertheless translates, “You taught gifts in man,” alluding to *lequach*, “teaching.”

### Verse 21

“God of our salvations will make our way prosperous.”

Jerome: “He will carry us.” Pellican agrees: “He will support us.” If we are borne by Almighty God, what prosperity will not be granted to our way? Yet *amas* means both “to load” and “to bring,” and the word “salvation” can also be taken in different cases. Hence other translations arise from human preference: Pratensis, “God will burden us with our salvation”; Sanctes, “God will bring us our salvation”; Pellican, “God, our salvation”; the interpreters for Cajetan, “God will load our salvation”; Münster, “May He load us with His benefits, He who is the God of our salvation.” Campensis agrees. All such translations yield a worthy sense. But what need is there for such confusion, by which the Vulgate edition may perhaps become distasteful to some weak persons?

### Verse 24

“I will turn into the depths of the sea.”

Hebrew: *mimmezuloth*, that is, “from the depths of the sea.” “I will turn into the depths” and “I will restore from the depths” seem to conflict. Yet Jerome, in the Commentaries, takes it thus: “I will turn my people from Bashan; I will turn them into the depths of the sea,” that is, “I will turn my people from the profound vices and sins of this age, from agitation and waves.”

### Verse 25

“The tongue of your dogs from enemies, from him.”

Some refer “from him” to the blood spoken of earlier in the same verse—“that your foot may be dipped in blood.” Thus Münster renders: “The tongue of your dogs is red from enemies because of that blood.” Others give it to God, which Jerome seems to do when he says, “from Yourself,” if Augustine’s discussion pleases us; for Jerome himself, in the Commentaries, refers it to the blood. Sanctes changes it to the plural: “from the enemies themselves.”

### Verse 26

“They saw Your goings, O God.”

Jerome, writing to Sunia and Fretella, corrects the Greek manuscript in which stood *etheorethesan*, “they were seen,” as our copies now have it, in place of *etheoresan*, “they saw.” He confesses that he found the latter in the Septuagint and the Hexapla, although he does not deny that the usage had prevailed by which *etheorethesan* was retained.

### Verse 27

“The princes went before.”

Others read “singers.” For *scharim*, with the point on the right side, means “singers”; but *sarim*, marked with a point on the left side, means “princes,” which is how the Septuagint and the interpreters for Cajetan pronounced it.

### Verse 28

“From the fountains of Israel.”

Münster wished to add or insert his own invention, “from the origin of the heart of Israel,” although in Hebrew there is no mention of the heart and no other interpreter I have seen has introduced it.

### Verse 29

“In an excess of mind.”

If *rodem* is derived from the root *radah* and the letter *mem* is an affix, it means “ruling.” Therefore Pratensis, Sanctes, Münster, and the interpreters for Cajetan translate “ruling them” or “their ruler.” But if the same word is derived from the primitive verb *radam*, so that *mem* is radical, it means “to slumber.” Hence the Septuagint said, “in an excess of mind.” Pellican and the Campensian paraphrase support this. The former says, “he is seized by sleep”; the latter, “in ecstasy.” Jerome’s rendering, “containing them,” does not differ from this sense, namely the fountains [145] of Israel mentioned above, so that Paul the Apostle’s rapture may be indicated: in that ecstasy he abundantly drew streams of divine wisdom.

### Verse 30

“The princes of Judah, their leaders.”

Hebrew *rigmatham* or *regamah* is a homonym meaning “purple,” “destruction,” “company,” or “assembly.” Therefore different translators render it differently. Jerome: “The princes of Judah in their purple”; Sanctes agrees with us. Pratensis, Nebiensis, and Pellican: “their destruction” or “their stoning.” Campensis approaches Jerome: “their ornament.” Münster and the interpreters for Cajetan: “their counsel” or “their astonishment.”

### Verse 31

“Command, O God, Your strength.”

The Hebrews read in the past tense and third person: “Your God has commanded”; then follows *uzzecha*. [Col. 0623C] Since the case is not distinguished by its ending, some translate “strength”; Jerome, “from Your strength”; some others, “strength for You”; Campensis—being paraphrastic—“to add strength to You.”

When the verb is read as “he commanded,” in the third person, the strength of man is meant, which is given or established by God. But in the second person it refers to God’s strength, which Augustine says is Christ. Yet the Hebrews write the past tense and imperative with precisely the same letters. It may be pronounced *tzirah*, “he commanded,” or *tzauweh*, “command.” The imperative suits excellently, since the same mood immediately follows in the other clause: “Strengthen, O God,” or “confirm,” etc.

### Verse 32

“From Your temple, which is in Jerusalem.”

Münster, owing to an assumption which he inserted, forces and draws the reader to his own imagination. For he says: “May Your strength come forth from Your temple in Jerusalem.” But according to the mind of the other interpreters, once the added words which are not from the Prophet have been removed, the reader is free to extend the phrase to what follows: “Kings shall offer gifts to You.” Otherwise, under Münster’s forced version, it must necessarily cling to what precedes.

It should be observed that the supplemental letter *mem* may be taken as “in”; otherwise it marks the ablative. For most translate “in the temple,” though in Hebrew it is written with *mem*. Let us recall what was not idly noted at verse 24 of this psalm: where we read “into the depths of the sea,” Hebraists said “from the depths of the sea,” solely because the letter *mem* was prefixed.

### Verse 33

“Rebuke the beasts of the reed.”

Jerome, Nebiensis, Pellican, Pratensis, and the interpreters for Cajetan follow the Septuagint. Sanctes differently: “Rebuke or destroy the congregation of the reed,” *gear haiath*. Münster differs greatly: “Scatter the company of those who use spears.” Campensis agrees: “Lay waste the multitude armed with the spear.” The Campensian edition imagined a special sense for itself: “Drive the beasts with a reed,” as though it wished to suggest a shepherd of such power and gentleness that the animals obey his nod without kicking back. The sense is indeed pious, though I do not know whether it is in its proper place.

But to return to the point: it should never escape memory what Jerome writes against Rufinus in the first book. I have recalled above how great a forest of ambiguous nouns and verbs exists among the Hebrews, furnishing material for different interpretations while each person, amid uncertainty, translates what seems more fitting to him. Now the word *quaneh* is used by the Hebrews for “reed,” “congregation,” and “spear.”

“The congregation of bulls among the cows of the peoples,” with “is” understood. Others translate it in the accusative, to correspond to the preceding verb, “rebuke.” Since *abbirim* means strong bulls, they sometimes translate simply “bulls,” sometimes “strong ones.” Faber, in his usual manner, diminishes the authority of the Vulgate edition, which has “cows” for “calves.” He philosophizes that this is more fitting because calves are wantonly playful, whereas cows are not, but rather sluggish and idle. Would that he had seen Jerome’s comment on that place! Certainly he would not have attacked the interpreters.

Hear Jerome’s words: “He signifies the heretics themselves, because they cannot deceive anyone except the simpler and smaller persons—that is, the lesser cows. For they cannot deceive bulls, that is, the great.” Augustine also elegantly explains why cows are used. I indeed know that Hebrew reads *egle*, “calves.” Yet the weakness and frivolity of the peoples are thereby indicated; and that these are more plainly signified by the feminine need not detain us longer.

“That they may exclude those who are tested by silver.” Hebrew: *mithrapes*. The translators differ remarkably regarding the first word. Jerome, for “that they may exclude,” has “of kicking,” namely, of calves. Nebiensis agrees. The interpreters for Cajetan: “trampling,” namely the congregation. Pratensis and Pellican: “desiring” or “striving.” Münster: “he will humble himself,” to which Campensis alludes: “until, made suppliants, they pay tribute.” Sanctes: “boasting,” or “trampled with incisions.”

It is not my intention to pursue every translation. Our purpose is, as far as we can, to examine our edition. There is one interpretation answering to the Vulgate reading, provided Augustine is right in explaining that “to exclude” here means “to appear” or “to stand out.” Some indeed translate, “boasting in portions of silver.” But if “exclude” is taken in an unfavorable sense, the interpreters would have had to read final *mem* in place of *samekh*, letters which are very closely related. This is plausible, since that letter at the end of words means “them,” whereas it would not do so if read with *samekh*. This will also be true if *mithrapam* is derived from the root *raphah*, which sometimes means “he loosened” or “he weakened.” If heretics are understood to devise means of drawing even those more learned and foremost in God’s Church into their error, then it fits that those who had been stronger should be weakened.

As to the second clause, “those tested by silver,” Jerome translated “silver wheels.” Nebiensis, Pratensis, and Pellican follow him: “numberings of fragments of silver.” Sanctes: “with silver incisions.” The interpreters for Cajetan and Münster agree. The Campensian edition uses a paraphrase and understands nations devoted to wealth. Hebrew reads *beratze keseph*. Jerome derives *ratze* from the stem *rotz*, “to run,” whereas those who translate “fragments” derive it from *ratzath*, “he broke.” The sense is the same: the apostles, called wheels because of the swift course of Gospel preaching, were broken and tested like gold in a furnace; through them are likewise understood those who cling to apostolic teaching unto death.

### Verse 34

“Envoys shall come from Egypt.”

Pratensis, Nebiensis, Sanctes, Münster, and Campensis do not differ from us, taking *chashmannim* as “envoys,” “nobles,” or “princes.” But Pellican and the interpreters for Cajetan say “fat persons,” plainly having read *he* instead of *chet*, a soft aspiration instead of a hard one, from the stem *schamen*, “he became fat,” with *he* as a servile letter.

Jerome differs: instead of “envoys,” he reads “speedily.” I suspect he used one word compounded from two: *nosh*, “he hastened,” and *monim*, “which signifies portions of time.”

“Ethiopia shall forestall her hands to God.”

It is certain that “hands” here is plural in Hebrew, *iadau*, and accusative in Greek, *cheira*, or in other manuscripts *cheiras*. But it is uncertain what the Latin pronoun “her” refers to; the ambiguity is removed in Greek by the feminine *autēs*. In Hebrew, however, *waw* is instead a sign of masculine gender, although *Kush*, Ethiopia, does not resist the masculine.

Meanwhile, it is clear that Augustine, in the *Expositions*, explained “her hands” as God’s hands. If it read “her own hands,” as Augustine more strongly approves later, every difficulty would be removed. But the earlier interpretation would have no place in this passage. Jerome certainly simply wrote “hands,” without any pronoun. Likewise Origen, in Homily 1 on the Song of Songs, seems to refer the pronoun “her” to the Synagogue, confirming this by Scriptural authority. Jerome translates it there in the same way as we read and sing it here, and the Master indicates it in the following verse.

### Verses 35–36

“Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord; sing psalms to God,” etc.

The third clause, “sing psalms to God,” at the beginning of verse 36, is an addition from the old Psalter, according to Jerome writing to Sunia and Fretella:

> “You say that in this verse, ‘Sing psalms to the Lord’ is not written, because immediately after the diapsalma follows, ‘Sing psalms to God, who ascends above the heaven of heavens toward the east.’ Yet this verse should rather read according to the Hebrew truth: ‘Sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord.’ And the words which follow at the beginning of the other verse, ‘Sing psalms to God,’ are not in the authentic books, but marked with an obelus. Therefore you also should rather read what is true, lest, while accepting an addition, you omit what was written by the Prophet.”

Thus far he. From this it is understood that the manuscripts used by Sunia and Fretella did not have the second clause, “sing psalms to the Lord,” but that the verse ended with the statement, “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God”; then the diapsalma was inserted, so that the next verse began, “Sing psalms to God.” We now read the added words, without nevertheless overlooking the Hebrew truth.

“Who ascends above the heaven of heavens toward the east.” Jerome, with most others, translated “from the beginning.” Sanctes and Pellican adhere to the Septuagint. For *qedem* may mean either.

## Psalm LXVIII

[Col. 0625]

### Title of the Psalm

“To the end, for those who shall be changed: a psalm of David himself.”

[Col. 0625C]

“Save me, O God.”

Title: “To the end, for those who shall be changed: of David himself.” [Aug., Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod.] There are two changes. One is from good to evil, by which Adam was changed from God’s image into a worse state, and in him all die. The other is from evil to good, by which the faithful are changed from evil to good and from good to better through Christ’s grace, in whom all are made alive. The cause of this change is Christ’s Passion.

For through it Christ Himself passed from the world to the Father; and in Him He caused us also to pass from death to life, from earth to heaven. Hence He Himself descended to those who had fallen in order to raise them up. This passage—namely, the passage [Col. 0625D] itself—is called *Pascha* in Hebrew. Thus Exodus says: “For it is the Phase, that is, the passage of the Lord” (Exod. 12). Among the Greeks, however, *Pascha* signifies suffering.

The order of the title is this: this psalm, directing us to the end—that is, Christ—is attributed to David himself, that is, Christ, who speaks here according to Head and Body, acting for those—that is, concerning those; that is, concerning the cause of their change, namely the Passion of Christ—who shall be changed from evil to good, from fear to security, from the world to heaven.

This psalm is the fourth among those treating more extensively of Christ’s Passion and resurrection. Its intention is to urge praise for the change that has taken place. Its method comprises five divisions. First, He prays to be saved, because He suffers many things in His own regard without cause, yet pays what another stole. Second, He explains what He has paid, at “God, You know.” Third, He sets prayer against the evils mentioned, at “But I indeed.” Fourth, He prophesies against His adversaries, at “Let their table become.” Fifth, He expounds the dispensation of the Incarnation and the holiness of His purpose, at “I am poor.”

Therefore Christ [146], in His Passion, cries to the Father:

### Verse 1

“Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even unto my soul.”

“God, save me.” [Aug.] This is the voice of the despised mustard seed as it is buried in the garden, though it grows into a great plant. Indeed, the mustard seed is tiny, dark, and entirely contemptible; and it was said of Christ: “We saw Him, having neither beauty nor comeliness” (Isa. 53). Yet, having become a great mountain, He filled the face of the earth.

Why do You cry? “For the waters”—that is, the uprising and agitation of the people—“have entered even unto my soul,” to take it away; that is, the Jewish crowds prevailed not merely to seize and bind Christ, but even to kill Him. In saying and crying thus, Christ conforms His members to Himself: that is, He gives His members a pattern of crying, for whom the passage through death is bitter, though by it we cleave to Christ.

He has gall and vinegar, which were given to the Lord in His Passion. Therefore He cries so that His own may cry, lest they yield to iniquity from fear of death, beyond which the wicked have nothing they can do to them.

### Verse 2

“I am fastened in the mud of the deep, and there is no substance.”

“ I am stuck fast in the mire with my body.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though he said: “They held me fast in the mire of the deep,” that is, of Jewish iniquity. Man is mire, and is from the mire of earth; but not from the deep: that is, he was made from what is not corrupt, but by falling away from righteousness through original and actual sins, he became the mire of the deep—that is, of iniquity. Whoever does not yield to this mire when it persecutes him is changed from mire into gold.

“And there is no substance.” Wealth, by which a person is sustained, is called substance. Thus “there is no substance” means: I have come to poverty. Hence below: “I am poor and sorrowful.” Or, “there is no substance.” This is rather difficult to understand [Col. 0627B] and needs a little commendation and explanation. Substance is understood as that which I am from God. Natures themselves are called substances: man, beast, heaven, earth, and all such things are substances precisely insofar as they are. For things which are nothing are altogether nothing in substance. Substance, therefore, is something. God is a certain substance. Hence also, against the poisons of certain heretics, we are so instructed in the Catholic faith as to say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one substance. Whatever the Father is as God, that is the Son, that is the Holy Spirit. Yet when he is Father, he is not that which he is [i.e. not “Father” as an essential predicate]. For “Father” is said not with reference to himself but to the Son; whereas “God” is said with reference to himself. [Col. 0627C]

Therefore, in that by which, or in that which, he is God, he is substance; and because the Son is of the same substance, undoubtedly the Son also is God. But because “Father” is not the name of a substance, but is referred to the Son, we do not say that the Son is Father in the way that we say that the Son is God. You ask what the Father is: the answer is, God. You ask what the Son is: the answer is, God. You ask what the Father and Son are: the answer is, God. Asked about each separately, answer, God. Asked about both, answer, God—not gods.

It is not so among human beings. You ask what Abraham is: the answer is, a human being. You ask what his son Isaac is: the answer is, a human being. Abraham and Isaac are of the same substance. But if you ask what Abraham and Isaac are, the answer is not “a human being,” but “human beings.” [Col. 0627D] It is not so in divine things. For there is so great a communion of substance there that it admits equality but not plurality.

If, then, someone says to you, “When you say that the Son is what the Father is, surely the Son is the Father,” answer: I said that the Son is what the Father is according to substance, not according to that which is said in relation to another. For God is said with reference to himself; the Son is said in relation to the Father. Again, the Father is called God with reference to himself, and Father in relation to the Son. In that he is called Father in relation to the Son, the Father is not the Son; in that the Son is called Son in relation to the Father, he is not the Father. But in that the Father is said with reference to himself, and the Son with reference to himself, Father and Son are one and the same—that is, God.

What, then, does this mean? “I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no substance.” Substance means that which each thing is from God. God made man [Col. 0628A] a substance. Would that he had remained in what God made! For if man had remained in what God made, he would not have been stuck in the mire, he whom God brought forth. Substance means that which every thing is insofar as it was made by God. Thus the Gospel says: “All things were made through him” (John 1), that is, all natures, all substances which praise God—not because all things have awareness to praise him, but because things well conceived bring forth praise, and through contemplation of creation the heart is filled so as to pour forth a hymn to God. Creeping things also praise him—but not avarice, envy, and the like, which God did not make.

God therefore made man a substance, naturally good; but because he did not remain in that condition and instead fell into iniquity, which is not a substance but the perversity of man, “there is no [Col. 0628B] substance”—that is, there is not the condition in which he was made by God. In this perversity the Son of Man, the Son of God, was fixed, because he was fixed in their iniquity. “There is no substance in them” [Cassiodorus, Jerome, interlinear gloss], that is, I did not find in them what I made; for they were not made such by God, but something else accrued from elsewhere.

Or thus: “There is no substance for me,” that is, no bodily strength to escape the Passion. Or, “There is no substance for me,” that is, no stability of life, because:

### Verse 3.—“I came into the depth of the sea, and the storm overwhelmed me.”

“I came willingly into the depth of the sea,” [Augustine, Jerome, Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, into the place in which we were shipwrecked—the depth of the age and of the mad people. “And the storm,” that is, the uprising and passing violence, [Col. 0628C] namely, the voices crying for death, “overwhelmed me” in death. Behold Jonah swallowed by the whale, yet vomited forth on the third day. And though they acted thus, nevertheless I:

### Verse 4.—“I laboured crying out; my throat became hoarse; my eyes failed while I hoped in my God.”

“I laboured crying out,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] admonishing them; for he cried for a long time: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. 23); and: “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. 18). He laboured in this because he was not received. For one who cries out and is not heard labours; one whose request is fulfilled does not labour.

“And my throat became hoarse.” This is not read literally in the Gospel, but he became hoarse in relation to them, because he was not understood by them. “My eyes [Col. 0628D] failed while I hoped in my God.” Another reading: that is, the disciples despaired, just as the eyes of the two disciples were held back when, on the road, they did not recognize Christ; despairing, they said: “We had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel” (Luke 24). What was inwardly present was outwardly effected in them: the blindness of the heart appeared in their eyes. But he restored their hope when he offered them his scars to touch; having touched them, Thomas returned to hope, crying: “My Lord and my God” (John 20). Thus he touched the form of a servant and recognized the form of God.

Therefore the Law says: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Alcuin]: that is, you shall not introduce the Passion and death to the apostles while they are still tender and weak, because they would have been lost in such a state.

Or thus: “My eyes failed,” that is, [Col. 0629A] I died. Then it gives the reason: “while I hope in my God,” that is, because I await mercy and not power from him.

### Verse 5.—“Those who hate me without cause are multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.”

“Those beyond the hairs,” etc. [Alcuin, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine.] What he had previously said figuratively—the waters, the mire, the depth of the sea—he now says plainly in fact: “Those who hate me without cause,” that is, without reason, “are multiplied,” so that even a disciple was among them. “Beyond the hairs of my head” is said for an innumerable multitude.

He compares enemies with the hairs of the head because they were deservedly shorn away from Christ when Christ was crucified at Calvary. Hence Christ was stripped of his garments during the Passion, clothed in others, and afterward resumed [Col. 0629B] his own; likewise, the altars are uncovered during the time of the Passion and are covered again when the Resurrection approaches. For during the Passion the Jews withdrew from Christ, and so too did the apostles. When he rose, however, the apostles returned, but the other Jews did not. Therefore he was clothed with other garments, namely, the Gentiles. But at the end, through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, all Israel will be saved; then he will receive his own garments.

The transfer of the book signifies the same thing: it is first placed on the right side of the altar, then transferred to the left; near the end of Mass it is returned to the right.

Or, the hairs signify the good; and this is the meaning: “Those who hate me are multiplied beyond the hairs of my head,” [Cassiodorus] that is, they are more numerous than those who serve as an adornment, just as hair adorns the head. The enemies are numerous, and harmful as well. [Col. 0629C] Therefore he adds:

### Verse 6.—“My enemies who unjustly persecuted me were strengthened; then I paid what I had not seized.”

“My enemies, who also persecuted me unjustly, were strengthened.” [Augustine.] This is what he had said: “without cause.” The praise of Christ and of the martyrs lies in the goodness of their cause, not in the bitterness of their punishment. For the cause makes the martyr, not the punishment.

“Then I paid what I had not seized.” As though he said: I did not sin, yet I paid the penalty. For Adam and Eve, presuming as the devil did, seized at divinity. They wished to seize divinity and lost blessedness.

## Part II. Verse 7.—“O God, you know [Col. 0629D] my foolishness, and my offences are not hidden from you.”

“O God, you know.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The second part, in which he explains what he paid: namely, the foolishness and offences of his own people.
