And because he paid for others, he prays that the ancient ones who were waiting, and the others who seek—that is, those of the present time—may not be disappointed in him, since he bears such great things with such equanimity.

As though he said: “I did not seize,” because, O God, “you know my foolishness.” Christ says this from the standpoint of his members: “my” means “my people’s.” That is, you know that they are ignorant of God; and “my offences”—that is, those of my people, which I took upon myself to destroy, not which I committed (for he was a bearer of offences, not their perpetrator)—“are not hidden from you.” This is said concerning the foolishness and offences of his people. These are those who are changed into wise and righteous persons.

[Col. 0630A]

### Verse 8.—“Let not those who wait for you be put to shame in me, O Lord, Lord of hosts.”

“Let them not be put to shame.” [Cassiodorus.] Here he shows what he had above said about the members. As though he said: Since I paid for others, let not those who wait for you with longing, O Lord—that is, the prophets and ancient righteous persons, who wait for what they could not see with their eyes—be put to shame in me, in my death. Therefore, lest anything occur otherwise than the Holy Spirit foretold through them, O Lord, or God of the heavenly or earthly hosts, namely he to whom nothing is impossible.

Then he prays for those of the present time who seek him, saying:

### Verse 9.—“Let not those who seek you, O God of Israel, be confounded because of me.”

[Col. 0630B] “Let not those who seek you, O God of Israel”—that is, God of those who see God—“be confounded by insults because of me in my death.” [Interlinear gloss, Cassiodorus, Remigius, Augustine.] He says this so that those unable to behold his divinity may not be misled by the weakness of his flesh.

Or thus, beginning from “O God, you know”: As though he said: I made payment, and I did so because it is pleasing to you. Christ speaks of himself: “O God, you know,” that is, you approve my foolishness—that which appears foolish and absurd about me, namely, the mockery and death that I endure—according to: “What is foolishness in God is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1). Those who seemed wise to themselves mocked this in me, but you knew why it would happen. “And my offences,” that is, those of my people, “are not hidden from you.” This does not change. [Col. 0630C]

Since I paid for others, therefore let those who wait for you, O Lord of hosts, not be ashamed at my death; that is, let it not be said to them: “Where is your Christ? Where is he who said, ‘You believe in God; believe also in me’” (John 16)? He speaks of the righteous who lived after Christ’s coming, concerning whom he also adds: “Let not those who seek you, O God of Israel, be confounded by insults.” This does not change.

Or here he speaks in the person of the Church; and the Church prays that she may not be oppressed by the scandals of heretics, so that her children should be ashamed. Thus: “Let not those who wait for you be ashamed in me,” that is, in my humiliation, etc.; the rest does not change.

### Verse 10.—“For for your sake I endured reproach; shame covered my face.”

[Col. 0630D] 147. “For your sake.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, interlinear gloss, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] He gathers together the many things he suffered to arouse indignation against the Jews. As though he said: They are rightly not confounded because of me, for I endured reproach in insults, such as what they themselves say: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub” (Luke 10), “He is a glutton and a drunkard” (Matt. 2)—for your sake, not through any fault of mine or for another reason.

As though he said: It is no great thing that I endured, but that I endured it for your sake. “And shame covered my face,” spat upon. This often happens to the righteous when they are slandered: they commonly become more sorrowful for a time, the more they know that false evil is being fabricated about them.

Or, according to another reading, the whole Christ speaks: “Disrespect,” that is, the boldness which we must [Col. 0631A] have among those to whom Christ is displeasing, “covered, as it seemed, my face,” so that we may not be ashamed of him; and:

### Verse 11.—“I became a stranger to my brothers, and a foreigner to the sons of my mother.”

“I became a stranger to my brothers by kinship of the flesh,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus] like Joseph to his own, because they do not believe me; “and a foreigner to the sons of my mother,” that is, of the Synagogue—or, in another reading, a guest, namely one received into the house temporarily, not as a most beloved brother. As though he said: I was such to them; I became a foreigner to them when they said: “We do not know where this man is from” (John 9). But why?

### Verse 12.—“For zeal for your house consumed me, and the reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me.”

[Col. 0631B] “For zeal for your house,” [Alcuin, Augustine, interlinear gloss] that is, the indignation by which I was angry with them for your house. Or “zeal,” that is, love for your house, “consumed me,” because I pursued their iniquities among them, when, having made a whip from cords, I scourged those behaving wickedly in the temple, driving out buyers and sellers, and saying: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. 21).

Or distinguish it thus: This happened because I had zeal for your house. And that zeal “consumed me,” that is, became the cause of my death. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] He adds what follows from this zeal: “And the reproaches of those who reproached,” or reviled, “you long ago in the wilderness fell at last upon me,” because, reproved, they hurled insults at him like darts: “Is not this the son of Joseph?” (Luke 4).

Those “reproaching you” did so when they said: “Can he prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Ps. 77), and: “These are your gods, O Israel” (Exod. 32). And therefore he says that the same insults now fall upon himself which they formerly cast in reproach, so that you may see that they did this from an impious habit rather than for the first time.

Or thus: the reproaches of those now reproaching you in me fell upon me, because whoever reproaches Christ also reproaches the Father; they fell upon me because they found me. Evils fall upon us when we cannot avoid them. They fell upon Christ, therefore—that is, they took effect.

### Verse 13.—“And I covered my soul with fasting, and it became a reproach to me.”

“And I covered my soul with fasting,” [Cassiodorus, interlinear gloss, Alcuin, [Col. 0631D] Augustine] as with a cloak of sorrow—that is, my will. Or, “I covered my soul,” that is, I did not exercise my power in taking vengeance. And this was in fasting for their salvation: for just as Christ hungered and thirsted for their faith and salvation, so Christ’s fast was when those who had believed in him failed.

And just as, in the Passion, when gall and vinegar were offered to him as drink, he tasted but would not drink, so he chose rather to fast than to receive gall or vinegar—that is, the old and bitter people who do not enter his body. This is what it means that I fasted from them: I did not assent to them. It “became a reproach to me,” a matter of detraction and mockery. As though he said: They insult me because I lay exposed to spitting, blows, and the like. Why did it become a reproach?

[Col. 0632A]

### Verse 14.—“And I made sackcloth my garment, and I became a proverb to them.”

“And,” [Augustine, Jerome, Remigius, Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, because “I made sackcloth my garment”: I set before them my mortal flesh, upon which they might rage, and I concealed divinity under a sack. For sackcloth is mortal flesh, which Christ put on in order to condemn sin through sin. Sackcloth is sorrowful flesh, as shown by his weeping over Jerusalem and for Lazarus.

Or thus: they are such persons, and yet “I made sackcloth my garment,” that is, I wished them, harsh as they were, to be my garment; and “I became a proverb to them,” a derisive saying—that is, a likeness of a curse, so that when cursing anyone they might say: “May it happen to you as it happened to Christ crucified.”

Or, “I became a proverb to them” because I taught them by [Col. 0632B] parables. Hence: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables,” etc. (Luke 8). And then:

### Verse 15.—“Those who sat in the gate spoke against me, and those who drank wine sang about me.”

“Against me.” [Interlinear gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Remigius.] Or connect it thus: Who did this to you? Behold, “those who sat in the gate spoke against me,” that is, in public. Those sit in the gate who, through eager curiosity, mingle in human gatherings. He says, then, that his Passion was the talk of the Jews, so that no one was excepted who was not involved in this conversation. Thus Cleopas says: “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem and do not know the things that have happened there in these days?” [Col. 0632C] (Luke 24). As though he said: Since you are a stranger, perhaps you do not know; but others do.

As though he said: They discussed me in public assemblies and at banquets. Hence he adds: “And those who drank wine sang about me,” that is, my mockery was their psaltery—their song—when I was fasting; those who drank wine were those intoxicated with temporal pleasure. Behold, song is turned against him who forbids vain songs.

Or, those who drank the wine of error, impiety, and pride spoke against me while sitting in the gate of the city, [Jerome, Cassiodorus] where judges customarily sit to judge cases—that is, in public judgment—as did the scribes and Pharisees, who had the key of knowledge yet neither entered nor allowed others to enter (Luke 11). These spoke against me. And “those who drank spiritual wine sang about me” by doing good works. For they fittingly sing psalms to God through approved work who drink spiritual wine that gladdens the mind.

## Part III. Verse 16.—“But I direct my prayer to you, O Lord: O God, it is the time of favour.”

“But I.” [Cassiodorus, interlinear gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which prayer is set against the evils predicted above, for his own part—that is, Christ’s—so that we may learn to oppose prayers, not quarrels, to disputes. As though he said: They rage against me in this way; but I, while the ungodly thus insulted me, directed my prayer to you, O Lord. When the wicked are not corrected, nothing remains except to pray, even for them.

And because I pray to you, therefore hear me. Hear me because, O God, now is [Col. 0633A] “the time of favour,” that is, of grace and reconciliation, through the Incarnation, through the blood, through death; for when the grain dies, fruit arises (John 15). Hence the Apostle: “Behold, now is the acceptable time,” etc. (2 Cor. 6). He then explains how this time came about. This time comes:

### Verse 17.—“In the multitude of your mercy hear me, in the truth of your salvation.”

“In the multitude of your mercy,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, in your great mercy, which stands against the multitude of our iniquity. This is why it is called the time of favour. Therefore repeat: “Hear me in the truth of your salvation,” that is, in the perfect Resurrection, so that you may give salvation in the Resurrection, as you promised through the prophets.

Note that, having first mentioned mercy, [Col. 0633B] he adds truth, because all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth: mercy in forgiving sins, truth in fulfilling promises.

### Verse 18.—“Deliver me from the mire, that I may not be stuck fast; free me from those who hate me, and from the depths of the waters.”

“Deliver me.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Here Christ speaks from the weakness of his members. As though he said: Hear me in this: “Deliver me from the mire,” in which he had previously said that he was stuck fast bodily, not mentally, “that I may not be stuck fast”—or, in another reading, “cling”—in mind. As though he said: If the body is held, let not the soul be held. Above, speaking of himself, he said that he was stuck fast bodily in the mire of the deep; but he says this from the weakness of his members. Thus: “Deliver me from the mire [Col. 0633C] that I may not be stuck fast,” or “cling,” that is, from muddy desires, lest I consent in mind. “Free me from those who hate me, and from the depths of the waters,” so that I may not consent to evils.

### Verse 19.—“Let not the flood of waters overwhelm me; let not the deep swallow me up; nor let the pit close its mouth over me.”

“Let not [the flood] overwhelm me.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] According to the spirit he was above submerged; according to the flesh, let not the flood of water submerge it in the depth of mire in mind; “nor let the deep”—the depth of sins which swallows souls—“swallow me up.” Hence: “When the sinner comes into the depth of vices, he despises” (Prov. 18). These perils threaten his members, for whom he says these things.

“Let it not swallow me up,” just as “let the pit not close its mouth over me.” That is, let not the pit—the depth of human iniquity—close its mouth over me. Even if you have fallen, the pit does not close its mouth over you if you do not close your own mouth; rather, confess and say: “Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord” (Ps. 129), and thus you escape. It closes its mouth over one who despises while in the deep, from whom, once dead as though he were not, confession perishes. [Col. 0633D]

Or the whole may be understood in the person of the Head as follows: “Deliver me from the mire, that I may not be stuck fast.” [Augustine, interlinear gloss, Cassiodorus, Jerome, Remigius.] Then he explains what he said, adding: “Free me,” in the Resurrection, “from those who hate me”—these are the mire—“and from the depths of the waters,” that is, from the Jews. For the Jews are deep in the malignity of their counsel and turbulent in their seditions. [Col. 0634A] Hence he adds: “Let not the flood of waters overwhelm me” irretrievably, that is, the assault of the Jews; “nor let the deep,” that is, hell, “swallow me up; nor let the pit,” that is, hell, “close its mouth over me,” that is, let it not so swallow me that it shuts me in.

### Verse 20.—“Hear me, O Lord, for your mercy is kind; according to the multitude of your compassions look upon me.”

“Hear me.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Having set forth the perils of humankind, again in the voice of the members he prays, saying: “Hear me, O Lord.” This is the reason for hearing: “for your mercy is kind,” or sweet, not because I deserve it. Mercy is sweet to the afflicted as bread to the hungry. [Col. 0634B] The Lord commends this sweetness to us through affliction imposed and deliverance delayed. For tribulation comes, and God delays help, in order to stir longing. Thus help becomes sweet, for once it arrives there is no longer anything to delay.

“And look upon me,” not upon my sins, “according to the multitude,” not of my sins, but “of your compassions,” to which sins, though numberless, yield.

### Verse 21.—“And do not turn your face from your servant; for I am afflicted: hear me speedily.”

“And do not turn away.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The whole Christ speaks. “From your servant,” Christ, of whom the prophet says: “Behold my chosen servant, whom I have chosen” (Isa. 42). He is rightly called *puer*, “servant” or “child,” from purity, because of his freedom from sin. Or, “from your servant,” that is, from any holy person, [Col. 0634C] one who is lowly and not proud, from whom the discipline of tribulation removes pride. But “hear me speedily”: there is no reason to delay, for I am afflicted; my affliction has gone before, let your mercy follow. Then follows the voice of the Head:

### Verse 22.—“Attend to my soul and deliver it; rescue me because of my enemies.”

“Attend to my soul and deliver it because of my enemies,” [Augustine] that is, so that my enemies may be confounded by my deliverance, or converted. This is a remarkable petition and not one to be passed over hastily: he makes the cause of his rescue the confusion or conversion of his enemies, as though otherwise he would not be delivered. If neither occurs, then, will he not be delivered? He certainly will. [Col. 0634D] But he says this 148 in order to distinguish two deliverances, hidden and manifest.

There is a certain hidden deliverance in the soul, which occurs for the sake of the saints themselves. Thus the seven brothers, the Maccabees, were delivered when they were consumed by fire while their mother exhorted them to choose death for God’s laws rather than assent to people against those laws (2 Macc. 7). There is another, manifest deliverance, which occurs for the sake of enemies, whether to punish or to deliver them. Thus the three youths were delivered from the fiery furnace; as a result Nebuchadnezzar himself was converted and proclaimed their God, whom he had formerly despised (Dan. 3).

Distinguishing both deliverances here, therefore, he says: “Attend to my soul”: this pertains to the hidden deliverance of the soul. “And deliver it,” [Col. 0635A] that is, grant that deliverance which you alone know. Then he adds concerning the visible deliverance: “Rescue me,” visibly in the Resurrection, “because of my enemies.” This pertains to the manifest deliverance: namely, that the flesh may rise and, ascending, send the Spirit. Hence the enemies were converted, to whom it would be of no benefit if you delivered the soul alone. Therefore rescue me, because:

### Verse 23.—“You know my reproach and my shame and my humiliation.”

“You know my reproach,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] which occurs in words, as when they said: “He has blasphemed” (Matt. 26); “and my shame,” which came to me in the Passion from reproach; and “my humiliation,” or modest shame. Other interpreters call it “disgrace,” such as slaps, scourges, and his being handed over to Pilate as an accused person. [Col. 0635B] He endured all these things not for his own guilt but for us, in order to instruct us in enduring such things. Therefore, speaking to the Father, he says: “You know my reproach, my shame, and my humiliation,” because you know why these things are mine, whereas my enemies do not know. And also rescue me, because:

### Verse 24.—“All who afflict me are before your sight; reproach and misery awaited my heart.”

“All who afflict me,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] my enemies, “are before your sight,” though they do not know why I suffer these things. Therefore they cannot either be confounded or corrected unless you visibly rescue me. Thus he says, “because of my enemies.”

Or thus: [Col. 0635C] they inflict these things on me, and do so in your presence; this is what he means when he says, “All who afflict me are before your sight.” By saying this he arouses indignation against them because they commit so great a crime in God’s presence.

Or, the whole is in the person of the members: “O God, you know my reproach,” or, in another reading, “my disgrace.” Reproach is what an enemy casts in one’s teeth; shame is what bites the conscience; and modest shame is when even an honourable brow blushes over false accusations. All these things are in the body of Christ, not in Christ himself. For Christians are taunted with the name of the crucified Christ; but for the strong, it is Paul’s glory, who says: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6). [Col. 0635D] And elsewhere: “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel” (Rom. 1). Such persons could have reproach cast at them, but neither shame in a sound mind nor embarrassment in their countenance.

But when some are accused of having killed Christ, they are pierced by an evil conscience and are beneficially ashamed and converted, so that they can say: “You have known my shame.” Others believe but are ashamed to confess, human speech holding more power with them than the divine promise; such persons are commended to God, not that he may leave them in that condition, but that, helping them by his divine promise, he may enable them to advance.

“All who afflict me are before your sight.” The meaning of “reproach” does not change. As though he said: They heaped reproach upon me, yet not upon one ignorant or unwilling. Indeed, my heart awaited their reproach, which, though foreseeing it, I was unwilling to avoid, because it foresaw and foretold what was to come; and my heart came to this because it endured willingly, according to: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you” (Luke 22). [Col. 0636A] And it awaited “misery,” which nevertheless belonged more to those crucifying him than to himself, since in compassion he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23). And just as I awaited and foretold, so what follows was fulfilled:

### Verse 25.—“And I waited for one to grieve with me, and there was none; and for one to comfort me, and I found none.”

“And I waited, and there was none,” [Jerome, Cassiodorus, Augustine] from so great a multitude, from among all the persecutors, “to grieve with me”; rather, they joyfully carried out their crime. “And I found none to comfort me.” One who improves comforts the physician; instead, “they gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” This is the consummation of the Passion. For when he said, “I thirst,” they offered gall with vinegar (John 19), thereby revealing their own most bitter dispositions.

Or it may be understood of the disciples and women. Although they grieved, they did not grieve “with” him—that is, in the same way. This is the meaning: “There was none to grieve with me.” The disciples and the women who wept over him grieved, but not in the same way; for they grieved carnally over the mortal life that was to be transformed by death, whereas they ought to have grieved over the blind people who were killing the physician—something no one then did. “And I found none to comfort me” by making progress. And because I found none both grieving with me and comforting me, this was gall to me—that is, bitter—[Col. 0636C] because of their oldness. This is what follows:

### Verse 26.—“And they gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”

“And they gave me the gall of bitterness for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” Literally. [Augustine.] The Gospel says gall was offered him, but as a drink, not as food. Therefore this is said mystically. It aptly says not, “They gave gall as food,” because the Lord had already received food: he had eaten the Passover with his disciples, where he showed the sacrament of his body. This is sweet food, pleasant food, the food of Christ’s unity, which the Apostle commends when he says: “Because we who are many are one bread and one body” (1 Cor. 10).

Into this food—that is, upon the sweet food which is the food of Christ’s unity—they cast gall, that is, bitterness, by resisting truth and contradicting the Gospel. The despiser of him who sits in heaven still does this today, and sins more grievously than the one who crucified him while he walked on earth. Therefore, just as the Jews then gave him a bitter drink, so today those who by wicked living cause scandal in the Church, and bitter-making heretics, give him bitter drink. Yet the Lord tasted it, teaching us to taste—that is, to endure—such people; but he did not drink it, because such people cannot be received into the body. This therefore is mystically foretold, just as it was mystically performed in the Passion. “And in my thirst,” in which I desired their faith, “they gave me vinegar to drink,” that is, old sourness, because I found in them nothing but oldness.

[Col. 0637A]

## Part IV. Verse 27.—“Let their table become a snare before them, and a recompense, and a stumbling block.”

“Let their table become [a snare].” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The fourth part, containing prophecy against the adversaries. As though he said: They gave me vinegar to drink. Therefore let their table become a snare to them: the snare which they set for me by giving me such a drink, let such a snare be theirs—that is, let their malice become a snare of death to them. And let this be “before them,” because they see that it is evil and yet do it, going down alive into hell. Hence: “Let them go down alive into hell” (Num. 16). And likewise: “If the Lord had not been in us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (Ps. 135). That is, they know they ought not to assent to them and yet do assent. [Col. 0637B] “And for recompenses,” of afflictions, because they repaid me thus; “and for a stumbling block,” that is, an offence. They themselves are their own stumbling block.

[Cassiodorus.] Otherwise, the whole passage: the table is Holy Scripture, because just as various dishes are placed upon a table for the refreshment of the body, so in Holy Scripture various teachings are set forth for the nourishment of souls. Thus, in the tabernacle of the Lord, after the entrance there was a table with four feet, upon which were set twelve loaves of fine flour before God; upon each was a golden dish with a handful of incense (Exod. 25; Lev. 24). The twelve loaves are the twelve apostles and their successors, who ought to apply themselves diligently and watchfully to theological pages, so that they may be ready [Col. 0637C] to give an account of faith and hope (1 Pet. 3). Hence: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge,” etc. (Mal. 2).

The Jews had this table while they observed God’s commandments; but after they fasted from faith, this table was given before their eyes to the Gentiles, that they might grieve more severely. This is the meaning: let the table—that is, their Scripture, which was set before them and given to the Gentiles before their eyes—become a snare to them, that is, a rebuke, so that those who bound others by the letter of the Law might themselves be bound and fall by it. And let it become “a recompense,” because its being taken away from them and given to the Gentiles was a recompense of evils, since, unwilling to feast upon it through spiritual understanding, they were excluded from it; and “a stumbling block,” because by abandoning the author of peace, they stir up quarrels and perverse pursuits for themselves. And:

### Verse 28.—“Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bow down their back continually.”

“Let their eyes be darkened,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, their mind, because they did not wish to attend, “that they may not see,” that is, recognize the true sun. As though he said: Because they did not see without cause, let it befall them not to see. “And bow down their back,” that is, the minds of these same people, continually toward earthly things. This follows upon the darkening of their eyes: because they do not see heavenly things, they think of lower things.

Note that this is predicted concerning those who do not repent. Or, by “eyes” are understood the greater persons, namely teachers; by “back,” the lesser. Thus: let their eyes—the teachers who lead the way—be darkened so that they may not see, that is, lose the light of knowledge; and bow down their back—that is, the lesser persons—continually. [Col. 0638A] When those who lead lose the light of knowledge, their followers bend down to bear the burdens of sins and to desire earthly things; and further, they must be punished outwardly in this life and in the life to come. This is what follows:

### Verse 29.—“Pour out your wrath upon them, and let the fury of your wrath overtake them.”

Pour out your wrath, [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus,] so that, like a river, it may be abundant upon them, overwhelm them, and the fury of your wrath—that is, your vengeance—may overtake them as they flee. Here it pursues; there it overtakes, so that escape is impossible. Thus fury overtakes when that which is feared comes to pass.

VERSE 30.—“Let their dwelling-place become desolate, and let there be none to inhabit their tents.”

[Col. 0638B] Let their dwelling-place become desolate. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] This is now manifest. For just as above his deliverance was shown, not only hiddenly, when he says, “Attend to my soul,” but openly as well, when he said according to the body, “Deliver me because of my enemies,” so here he first foretells hidden calamities, which consist in the blindness of their mind, concerning which he previously said, “Let their eyes be darkened,” etc.; and afterwards open calamities, whence he now adds: “Let their dwelling-place,” namely their private houses, “become desolate,” as has now happened, when they lost the place in which they had been proud; and let none of their number inhabit their tents, that is, the Temple and royal palace. Observe that, concerning the Temple and palace, he uses “to inhabit,” which occurs through the affection of a devout mind; concerning houses, he uses “to dwell,” which occurs through bodily residence. Why is this done to them?

VERSE 31.—“For they persecuted him whom you struck, and they added to the pain of my wounds.”

For they persecuted him whom you, [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine,] not through his own fault, struck with suffering and mortality, which is the penalty of the human race, for the redemption and salvation of the nations. As though he said: What God did for good, they carry out for evil with cruel intent. And to the pain of my wounds—that is, the pain I endured because of their betrayal and sins—they added by bringing death upon me. Or: to the pain of my wounds, which they inflicted upon me with lance and nails, they added the guards at the tomb. Or: “to the pain,” that is, to the punishment for my wounds, that is, my sins—he says this on behalf of the members—they added persecution; that is, in addition to the punishment which is mine because of sins, they added persecutions. And therefore:

VERSE 32.—“Add iniquity to their iniquity, and let them not enter into your righteousness.”

Add iniquity. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Remigius, Gloss interlinear.] He foretells, as something just, that God permits vice to be added to vice, upon their iniquity. For their iniquity was that they killed a man. Upon this God added that they should kill his Son, so that, just as they had killed the servants sent beforehand, so also they killed the heir himself [Col. 0639A] (Matt. 21). Or he added wicked sons to wicked fathers, so that they may not enter into your righteousness, that is, into the straight way of life, having abandoned their own righteousness, which is from the law (Rom. 10). And:

VERSE 33.—“Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous.”

Let them be blotted out of the book of the living. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Jerome.] The book is God’s knowledge, by which he predestined for life those whom he foreknew would be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. 8). It must not therefore be understood as though God writes someone in this book and later blots him out; rather, it must be understood thus: let them be blotted out of the book of the living according to their own expectation, because they suppose themselves to be written there—that is, let it become evident even to them that they are not written there. Hence elsewhere: “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand” [Col. 0639B] (Ps. 90); that is, many will be scandalized from among those who hope that they will sit with you and stand at the right hand. This he subsequently explains when he says: “And let them not be written with the righteous,” according to your equity. He denies this only to those who are not changed, as the title says. Or distinguish thus, with the same meaning: let them be blotted out from the book of the living of old—that is, of Abraham, Isaac, and the others—and let them not be written with the righteous, namely the new apostles and other later saints.

PART V. VERSE 34.—“But I am poor and sorrowful; your salvation, O God, has upheld me.”

But I am poor. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] [Col. 0639C] The fifth part: here he expounds the dispensation of the incarnation and the holiness of its purpose, declaring what is the end of the Passion. As though he said: Such is their condition; but I—the whole Christ speaks—am poor, that is, humble, and sorrowful in the Passion, according to the Head. For he himself suffered pain for all. Hence: “He himself bore our pains” (Isa. 53). No other can therefore say this; “I,” by way of distinction, says the same thing of his body: “I am poor,” whence: “Blessed are the poor” (Matt. 5); and sorrowful, whence: “Blessed are those who mourn” (ibid.). In the voice of the Head: “Your salvation, O God, has upheld me,” so that I am no longer poor or sorrowful.

VERSE 35.—“I will praise the name of God with song, and will magnify him with praise.”

I will praise, [Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear,] in myself and in the members, [Col. 0639D] the name of God with song, that is, with delight, because even if everything else is lacking, God is nevertheless with me; and I will magnify him in praise before my neighbor.

VERSE 36.—“And it will please God more than a young calf bringing forth horns and hoofs.”

And [Augustine, Cassiodorus] this—that I shall praise him—will please God more than a young calf, which was offered under the law; that is, it will please him more than all legal offerings, because the sacrifice of praise will be more acceptable than the sacrifice of a calf. For praise from a pure heart will please more than the slaughter of cattle. I mean a calf bringing forth horns and hoofs. This is the literal sense.

[Col. 0640A] VERSE 37.—“Let the poor see and rejoice; seek God, and your soul shall live.”

Let the poor see, [Cassiodorus, Alcuin,] namely that the offering is now in the mind, where the poor person is equal to the rich, not in external possessions. Let them therefore rejoice; and, O poor, do this solely with a view to God. He says this as follows: “Seek God, and your soul shall live,” even if the body does not.

[Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Otherwise, and this is understood of the future: “I will praise the name of God with song, and magnify him with praise,” in the future. And that praise will please God more than a young calf offered for sins. Under the law a young calf was offered (Num. 19), signifying the new life of grace which was to follow. And just as a calf tosses its adversary with its horns and stirs the ground with its hoofs, so the new life possesses horns of defense, by which it may toss the heretic who contradicts it; and it has protections for the feet—that is, for the affections—like hoofs, by which it may tread upon the roughness of the age [Col. 0640B] and stir up the person who does not contradict, yet meanly savors earthly things. As though he said: It ought to stir him with its hoofs. And concerning this young calf—that is, concerning the new life which exists in the present—Christ says in the members: “My praise with the angels will please God,” where there will be neither an adversary to toss nor a sluggard to be stirred from the earth. Observe that he says “bringing forth,” because, while the faithful person daily increases by God’s power, he brings forth horns and hoofs. Let the poor see these things—that is, believe them—so that they may be filled and rejoice, that is, delight in hope. And so that you may see, O poor, seek God: hunger and thirst after the food [Col. 0640C] of the mind, because he is the living bread that came down from heaven (John 6). And thus your soul shall live, even if your body does not: seek him.

VERSE 38.—“For the Lord has heard the poor, and has not despised his bound ones.”

For the Lord has heard, [Gloss interlinear, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear,] the poor at all times. Otherwise he would not hear them. Thus he will hear you also, and has not despised his bound ones in mortality, by which, when the Lord was offended, he shackled his servants; rather, he hears them crying out from it. The person who seeks more than necessities makes these shackles burdensome; but let the evil of the day suffice for the day (Matt. 6). Or, “his bound ones” means those bound by sins, his own—that is, those to be freed by him. Or, “his bound ones” means those bound by his laws; he has not despised them.

[Col. 0640D] VERSE 39.—“Let the heavens and the earth praise him, the sea and all creeping things in them.”

Let the heavens praise him, [Alcuin, Remigius,] whom he previously exhorted together and now separately to praise, saying: Let the heavens praise him, that is, the apostles; and the earth, that is, the Jewish Church; and the sea, that is, the nations; and all creeping things, that is, all kinds of persons monstrous in sins, clinging to earthly things—which are in them, that is, in the earth and sea. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Jerome, Cassiodorus.] Or let this all be taken literally: let heaven, earth, and sea—that is, heavenly things, earthly things, and swimming creatures—praise him. These praise him when the Creator is praised from them. These are the true riches of the poor person: namely, to see created things and from them praise the Creator, etc. As if he said: to him let every [Col. 0641A] knee bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2); and, to include everything perfectly, he adds: “and all creeping things which are in them.” Thus every creature is invited to praise God.

VERSE 40.—“For God will save Zion, and the cities of Judah shall be built.”

For God. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As though he said: When these created things are considered, God is praised; but there is another reason why God should be praised: for God will save Zion, that is, the Church, and save her eternally. Although she is afflicted here, now throughout the world the cities of Judah—that is, the Churches of Christ, who is from Judah—will be built. They are built through the confession of humility, so that those who are ashamed to confess may remain outside them. Observe that the psalm ends in the hope [Col. 0641B] of the faithful people. Wonderful is the building of the Church; hence all creatures are exhorted to praise.

VERSE 41.—“And they shall dwell there, and acquire it as an inheritance.”

And [Cassiodorus] the poor, namely, shall dwell there with steadfast mind—that is, in that Zion—and shall acquire it as an inheritance, or acquire the inheritance, when they reach the heavenly Jerusalem. Who are they? Behold:

VERSE 42.—“And the seed of his servants shall possess it; and those who love his name shall dwell in it.”

And the seed of his servants, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine,] that is, imitators of their faith or good works, shall not merely acquire [Col. 0641C] it, but shall also possess it—that is, Jerusalem. Who does this apply to in detail? All who love his name shall dwell in it. These are the seed of his servants, not those who are sons according to the flesh, because the servants too loved his name. Therefore, whoever do not love his name should not call themselves the seed of his servants; and those who love his name should not deny that they are the seed of his servants. The final verse explains the preceding one, lest perhaps you should think this is said about the Jews.

COLLATION ON PSALM 68: “SAVE ME, O GOD,” etc.

The reason for the title, “For those who shall be changed,” although the Hebrews say, “for lilies,” was discussed in Psalm 44 [Col. 0641D].

VERSE 13.—“I covered my soul in fasting.” Jerome: “and I wept for my soul in fasting.” Sanctes and Münster add something of their own: “and I wept, and afflicted—or chastised—my soul by fasting.” Yet what does it mean that the soul is covered in fasting, except that, afflicted on every side, it hungers and thirsts for salvation? Nevertheless, the Septuagint may have derived EBKEH from the root BUC, meaning “to be perplexed and confounded, shut in by distresses,” which corresponds to a soul overwhelmed by sorrow, even if perhaps it should be pronounced ABUCAH.

VERSE 16.—“But I, my prayer is to you, O Lord.” Faber and Caecus accuse the translator because he rendered an accusative, which requires a verb borrowed from elsewhere in order for the sentence to stand complete; this would not have been necessary if he had translated in the nominative case, as Jerome does: “My prayer is to you, O Lord.” We say this: although that expression in the nominative case is more customary, yet, with the first-person pronoun, which is undoubtedly read in the Hebrew, the wording “But I, my prayer is to you, O Lord,” would have been more unnatural than the other: “But I direct my prayer to you, O Lord,” since the pronoun sufficiently suggests its own verb, especially in the Hebrew idiom. For this reason Münster rendered it: “But I pour out my prayer to you”; and Sanctes: “With my prayer I turned myself to you.” Hence Jerome himself omitted the pronoun because he had rendered the phrase in the nominative; for the Hebrews have thus: **VAANI TEPHILLATHI**. And Augustine, reading, “But I, my prayer is to you, O Lord,” was almost compelled to interpret it thus: “But I was toward you in prayer.”

VERSE 21.—“Reproach awaited my heart, and misery.” **HERPAH SCABERAH**: that is, “reproach crushed my heart,” or, to avoid ambiguity, “my heart was crushed by reproach.” It is most certain that the Septuagint took the Hebrew word so that its first letter is pronounced by the dot called *smol* on the left horn, because **SIBBER** means “he awaited,” even though it is not difficult to bring “he crushed” and “he awaited” into agreement. Nevertheless, our reading more significantly and suitably indicates the voluntary Passion of Christ the Lord, and a less compelled bearing of the cross than the other reading, since he foreknew everything. Further, where we read “misery,” Jerome has “I am in despair,” with which Pellican agrees. Others interpret **VAANUSCHAH** as “I languish.” But the verb has several meanings among the Hebrews. One thing alone could disturb someone: how can despair suit Christ? Certainly Christ was abandoned as hopeless by the apostles fleeing and by the Jews crucifying him as a mere man. Otherwise it may be a figurative expression of the same sort as the Lord Jesus’ words while hanging on the cross for the expiation of our sins: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” [Col. 0642C] (Matt. 27).

VERSE 23.—“For recompenses and for a stumbling-block.” Because of the homonymy of **LISCHLOMIM**, some translate “recompenses,” such as Jerome and Sanctes; some render it “peaceful things,” as Pratensis and Münster do, so that you may understand that things which ought to have served peace become an occasion of offense. The Chaldee translates “sacrifices.”

VERSE 27.—“They added to the pain of my wounds.” **VEEL MACHEOB HALALECA IESAPERU.** Jerome rendered it thus: “and, in order to afflict them, they told of your wounded ones”; Sanctes: “they will tell over the pain of your wounded ones.” Pratensis and the interpreters for Cajetan agree in the same sense. Pellican: “and they will speak abusively to your wounded ones in their pain.” Münster: “they speak of the pain of your wounded ones.” Now, because **HALABECA** can indifferently mean “the wounded” or “wounds,” the preceding statements have been framed so as to cohere with this or that rendering, according to whichever seemed more consequential and more closely connected. Hence the Campensian edition and the paraphrase, understanding “wounds,” render it in this way: “and they count the blows which you inflicted.” Or thus: “They recounted with pleasure the severity of the wounds by which you wounded me.” Moreover, what we read as “they added” corresponds to the meaning of the verb **SIPER**, that is, “he counted” and “he recounted.” But number increases through addition: one who counts adds. Therefore the Septuagint rightly says: “They added to the pain of my wounds.”

VERSE 33.—“Your soul shall live.” Hebrew: **LELABECHEM**, that is, “your heart.” Yet it is written in Proverbs: “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds.” Therefore “heart” is rightly taken for “soul,” as Jerome also did in his version according to the Hebrew. Campensis agrees.

PSALM 69.

[Col. 0643]

TITLE OF THE PSALM: “FOR THE END: A PSALM OF DAVID, FOR THE REMEMBRANCE THAT THE LORD SAVED HIM.”

[Col. 0643A]

“God, to my aid.” Title: “For the end: a psalm of David, for the remembrance that the Lord saved him.” [Cassiodorus.] Memory is understood in two ways: either when, remembering sins, we fear God’s judgment—of this he treated above in Psalm 37—or when we retain the promised good things in our hearts and are secure. It is understood here in the latter sense, as is shown by what follows in the title: “that the Lord saved him.” The sense of the title is: This psalm, directing us to the end, that is, to Christ, is attributed to David, that is, to Christ and to every righteous person who speaks here, being concerned with remembrance—not indeed of sins, but of this fact: that the Lord has saved him by hope and certainty. As though he said: Even if they have been changed, which was treated in the title of the preceding psalm, they should nevertheless glory not in themselves but in God who saves. Observe fittingly that, just as above Christ our Head spoke of his Passion and added the hope of resurrection, so likewise his members in this psalm declare both their sufferings and take up hope of resurrection. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] This, then, is the voice of those afflicted with Christ and of martyrs preaching amid sufferings; but together with them, trusting in Christ the Head, it is also the voice of every righteous person, for whom, owing to abounding charity, even the wrongdoing of Christians is a source of suffering. Thus Lot endured no bodily suffering or persecution from anyone, but suffered from their evil deeds; he was not even told where he should not dwell [Col. 0643C] (Gen. 19). The devil, who takes many forms, inflicts this persecution. For he is a lion when raging openly and a dragon when lying secretly in wait. Therefore the persecution of the righteous comes either from the lion, in assault, or from the dragon, in ambush. Hence all cry out with one voice: “God, to my aid,” etc.

Purpose: He exhorts us to glory in God, not in ourselves. Method: The psalm has two parts. First, in the person of all the righteous, he asks for help and for the wicked to be put to shame. Secondly, he exhorts the good, whom God helps and frees when needy, to rejoice: “Let them exult and rejoice.” Therefore, in the person of all the righteous, he says:

VERSE 1.—“God, attend to my aid; O Lord, hasten to help me.”

God, [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin,] who are accustomed to help, attend—that is, look—to my aid against dangers. We always need God’s help in this age, and especially in tribulation. Help, and quickly. This is what is meant by: “O Lord, hasten to help me.” Thus he asks as though, if mercy delayed, his torments would increase. Observe that every affirmation begins with this verse. Hence tribulations need not be feared. Observe also that this verse is said before all the Hours—that is, at their beginning—because when we ought to pray, then most of all the devil strives to tempt us, so that dead flies may spoil the sweetness of ointment (Eccl. 10). [Col. 0644A] Therefore, against his assaults, before all else we ask God for help. And, O Lord:

VERSE 2.—“Let those who seek my soul be confounded and afraid.”

Let those who seek my soul in order to crush it—namely, by killing—be confounded. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] To be confounded is to be disturbed by one’s perversity. Before their confusion, they defend their sins or deeds as though glorious; afterwards they are converted. Hence he adds: “and let them fear.” To fear is to fear that punishment will follow for injured righteousness.

VERSE 3.—“Let those who desire evil for me be turned backward and blush.”

Let them be turned backward, [Augustine,] not go before but follow; not live by their own counsel but by that of the saints. [Col. 0644B] And let those who desire or devise evil for me blush. Observe that there are different periods in the Church. At first there was the assault of persecutors; hence above he said, “who seek my soul.” Now the malevolence of thoughts remains; hence here he says, “who desire.”

VERSE 4.—“Let those who say to me, ‘Aha, aha,’ be turned back at once, blushing.”

Let those who say to me, “Aha, aha,” be turned back at once, blushing, [Cassiodorus, Augustine,] whether mockingly or flatteringly. For there are two kinds of persecutors: those who censure and those who flatter. For just as gold is tested by fire, so is a man by the tongue of flatterers (Prov. 27). The tongue of a flatterer harms more than the hand of a persecutor. Both censure and flattery are fire. He enters this fire who is tested by blame [Col. 0644C] or praise; he emerges unharmed who is caught by neither, like Paul, who rejected those saying, “I am of Paul” (1 Cor. 1).

PART II. VERSE 5.—“Let all who seek you exult and rejoice in you; and let those who love your salvation always say: ‘Let the Lord be magnified.’”

Let them exult. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The second part, in which he exhorts the good, whom God helps and frees when needy, to rejoice. When all these have been turned away and confounded, let all who seek—not human beings, but you, who first sought them—exult and rejoice in you, in whom there is light and not elsewhere; and let them say—for one who does not say this does not seek God—what? “Let the Lord always be magnified.” It is said in our manner of speaking, whereby someone grows through praises; God is not magnified, but we profit by praising. [Col. 0644D] Therefore he is magnified not in himself but in us. Let them therefore say, “Let the Lord always be magnified,” because he calls the sinner, grants pardon to one confessing, then makes that person live justly, and finally glorifies him. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Or distinguish it thus: “And let them always say”—what?—“Let the Lord be magnified.” Let those who love your salvation say this always, because they should never cease from his praise, since their salvation is from him, not from themselves.

VERSE 6.—“But I am needy and poor; O God, help me.”

But I. [Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] [Col. 0645A] As though he said: You exhort others to say, “Let the Lord be magnified”; what then do you yourself do? But I do what I exhort others to do. I say that I, even now righteous, am needy or a beggar—that is, one who asks—because the law in my members still resists the law of my mind (Rom. 7), and I hunger for righteousness (Matt. 5); while he is rich, lacking nothing, my light. Or continue thus: Let them say that of God, but let them think this of themselves, so that each may say: “I am needy,” etc. Or thus: This person takes upon himself the words of God, who in the preceding psalm said these same things concerning himself: “Those who seek my soul are rich, but I am needy,” that is, asking, “and poor,” that is, insufficient for myself, because he has neither worldly resources; and inwardly, where he is rich, he always seeks, desires, and receives. But, O God, help me in the world’s tribulation. Behold where he began. Or, according to another reading: “God helps [Col. 0645B] me.” And:

VERSE 7.—“You are my helper and my deliverer; O Lord, do not delay.”

Be my helper, [Gloss interlinear, Augustine,] so that I may conquer. Even the righteous must always say this. Or, according to another reading: Therefore help, because you are my helper and deliverer from so many bonds of cares. And lest I fall, you—not another—are my hope. Therefore, O Lord, do not delay. What is sought with great desire seems delayed; nevertheless, he does not wish God to come before the time he has appointed, but seeks patience. Thus, “O Lord, do not delay” means: do not let what you will come seem too late to me. This happens through patience; one who lacks it thinks it late and turns away from him, just as Lot’s wife looked back and became a pillar of salt (Gen. 19), so that she might season you. For she is an example to you: do not look back.

COLLATION ON PSALM 69, “GOD, ATTEND TO MY AID,” etc.

The title in Hebrew was simply set down as **LEHAZKIR**, “for remembrance.” Therefore the Septuagint did not idly explain this indefinite remembrance as “for the Lord to save me” (*eis to sōsai me kyrion*; εἰς τὸ σῶσαί με κύριον).

VERSE 4.—“Let them be turned back at once, blushing.” [Col. 0646B] This verse contains the word **EQUEB**, which is ambiguous between “footstep” and “reward” or “recompense.” Hence Jerome translates, “at the footstep of their confusion,” which means “at once,” namely, immediately upon the footstep, as is read word-for-word in Hebrew. It is a figure indicating something about to happen immediately. For what is it to tread upon another’s heel except to follow him closely? Others, retaining the other sense, translate with fitting meaning: “as the reward of their confusion,” or, “let them be ashamed as much as they deserve.”

PSALM 70.

[Col. 0645]

TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF DAVID, OF THE SONS OF JONADAB AND OF THE FIRST CAPTIVES.”

[Col. 0645B]

“In you, O Lord, I have hoped.” Title: “A psalm of David, of the sons of Jonadab and of the first captives.” [Augustine.] This psalm commends grace, which is commended here in almost every syllable. For whatever good we are, we are so by God’s mercy; whatever evil we are from ourselves, so that all our hope may be in God and not in our own strength. As to the mention of the sons of Jonadab in the title, one should know that Jonadab is commended by Jeremiah, because he commanded his sons not to drink wine and to live not in houses but in tents (Jer. 35); and they obeyed him as though God himself had commanded it. Although God did not command this, he did command that children obey their parents—which they ought to do unless their fathers command something contrary to God. Hence God blessed them for their obedience, [Col. 0645D] and did so through Jeremiah. He reproaches the children of Israel, who refuse to obey God their spiritual Father, whereas those men obeyed their carnal father. Jeremiah therefore urges the children of Israel to prepare for captivity and not resist God’s will. From this, then, the title of this psalm seems to have been taken.

When it had said, “of the sons of Jonadab,” it added, “and of those first led captive,” not because the sons of Jonadab were led captive, but because they are contrasted with the children of Israel, who were to be held captive for the sin of disobedience. For the children of Israel were carried captive first, second, and third; but the psalm does not speak of these. Rather, it speaks of us, who are held captive under the law of sin which is in the members (Rom. 7). Thus the grace of the Deliverer is more highly commended: we are sons of Jonadab, that is, of the willing one. For Jonadab means “the Lord’s willing one,” that is, one who serves voluntarily. The sons of Jonadab, therefore, are sons of obedience, namely those who serve from love; and they too are captives under the law [Col. 0646C] of the flesh. But why are we called the first captives? It is now clear: because through the disobedience of the first man, in whom all sinned, we are captives; and in comparison with the sons of Jonadab, all obedience has been found blameworthy. We are thus rightly called the first captives, because the first man was earthly, from the earth, and we are like him. The second man is heavenly, from heaven, and through him we are freed.

The sense of the title is: This psalm is of David the prophet, for the sons of Jonadab and the first captives—that is, the sons of the willing one, the sons of obedience. This psalm is sung also to those who were first led captive, namely those belonging to the first man; because of the first man they are the first captives, since what is animal comes first, and because of the second man they are redeemed second. It is sung to them so that those who are evil of themselves may learn to return through grace. [Cassiodorus.] Or thus: by the sons of Jonadab let us understand all obedient people, and by the first captives all disobedient people. For the title admonishes us to have the devotion of the sons of Jonadab, not the stubbornness of the Jews, who deserved to be captives because, although frequently admonished, they would not be corrected. The history is related thus in the books of Kings (2 Kings 17, 25).

Therefore, because they despised the Lord’s law, the Jews were handed over to the first, second, and third captivities. Yet, so that they might be corrected, before the first came it was foretold through the prophet; but they remained, in their habitual wickedness, obstinate. Thus the sons of Jonadab are set in place of all obedient people, and the first captives in place of all stubborn people. The sense is: [Gloss interlinear, Haymo, Alcuin.] This psalm of David is for the sons of Jonadab, that is, the obedient, to whom it is sung that they may persevere; and for the first captives, that is, the disobedient, to whom it is sung that they may desist. Or, the first captives are in this world, from which escape is possible; the second captives are in hell, from which escape is impossible. The sense is: This psalm of David is for the sons of Jonadab, that is, obedience, and for the first captives, that is, those held in the first captivity, which is in this world. Or, “the first captives” means those who were captured by vices before they became Christ’s children.

[Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Here the universal righteous person speaks, from the beginning of the world until its end, placing all hope in God and earnestly commending the grace of God, which is given freely, lest we presume falsely in ourselves. This is the purpose of the psalm. Method: the psalm has three parts. First, he asks to be delivered from all evils and filled with praise. Secondly, he treats of the grace to be given in the time of old age and senility: “Do not cast me off in the time of old age.” Thirdly, he states to what person grace belongs and what grace it is: “O God, who is like you?” Therefore the universal righteous person, from the captivity into which he was born from Adam, cries to God, saying:

VERSE 1.—“In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be confounded. In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me.”

O Lord, I have hoped in you, not in myself. [Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] For if I hope in myself or in worldly things, which are perishable, I am confounded. Therefore I shall not be confounded forever, even if here I am ashamed because of sin, having no fruit in those things of which I am ashamed. Yet I shall not be confounded forever—that is, in the future. Or thus: I was already confounded in Adam, but in Christ I shall not be confounded forever. We must therefore depart from Adam and draw near to Christ. Deliver me from dangers, and rescue me from the power of the devil, in righteousness not my own—if I establish it, I am not subject to God’s righteousness (Rom. 10)—but yours, that is, the righteousness I have from you. For I do not glory in myself, nor do I reject your grace. Or “in your righteousness” means according to what your righteousness requires. For your righteousness is that you spare the person who prays; and this is mercy as well. And, O Lord, although I am unworthy:

VERSE 2.—“Incline your ear to me, and save me.”

Incline toward me, [Cassiodorus, Augustine,] as I lie sick, your ear—that is, your mercy; for merit does not reach to him. This is a confession of humility. Whoever says this confesses that he lies like a sick person prostrate before a physician who stands; and save me from the inward sickness. Hence elsewhere: “Cleanse me from my hidden sins” (Ps. 18). And:

VERSE 3.—“Be to me a protecting God and a fortified place, that you may save me.”

Be to me a protecting God, [Augustine,] so that the enemy’s darts may not reach me. I say, protect me, because I cannot protect myself; and you who were terror to Adam as he fled, now be to me a fortified place [Col. 0648A] or refuge, to which whoever flees is safe, because he is so high that he fears nothing. Hence he adds: “that you may save me”; for in another place I cannot be safe.

VERSE 4.—“For you are my strength and my refuge.”

For you are my strength. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] He gives two corresponding grounds for the two previous requests. As though he said: Be to me a protecting God, and you will be, because you are my strength—that is, through you I am strong against every temptation. This refers to “protecting.” I say, be to me a place of refuge, and you will be; and that is, because you are my refuge, and no other. For whenever I have been weakened in myself, still held captive, I flee to you; for however strong I may be by grace, so long as life is conducted in the body of sin, one must always fear. [Col. 0648B] This refers to the fortified place.

VERSE 5.—“My God, rescue me from the hand of the sinner, and from the hand of one acting against the law and of the unjust.”

My God, rescue me. [Gloss interlinear, Augustine.] He repeats what he said above, specifying from whom he asks to be rescued. As though he said: Because I have hoped in you, therefore, my God, rescue me from the hand—that is, from the power—of the sinner in general, lest by force or guile he lead me into sin. Here the person who is now to be freed from captivity suffers; that is, free me from outward enemies. Hence elsewhere: “Spare your servant from strangers” (Ps. 18). Then he divides “sinner” into categories, saying: “and from the hand,” that is, from the power, “of one acting against the law,” that is, a transgressor, “and of the unjust,” that is, one who sins simply without the law. For there are two kinds of sinners: some have received the law, as Jews and Christians; others have not, as pagans. Therefore I say: rescue me.

VERSE 6.—“For you are my patience, O Lord; O Lord, my hope from my youth.”

For you are my patience, O Lord, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine,] because it is not in me to endure them, but from you. You are my patience because you are my hope, O Lord, from my youth. Or rather thus: You are my patience; and because you are patience, therefore you are my hope, O Lord, from my youth—that is, from my conversion. Or, because in youth a person is fit for battle, he says: “You are my hope from my youth,” that is, from the time I began to hope in you and fight against the devil. I did not yet hope, but you were my protector, who brought me safely to the time when I might learn to hope in you. Therefore you are my hope from youth, that is, from the time you armed me with faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues to fight against the devil. A young man fights, but falls unless God is his hope. And you have helped me not only from youth but also from infancy, because:

VERSE 7.—“In you I have been strengthened from the womb; from my mother’s belly you are my protector.”

In you I have been strengthened, [Cassiodorus,] not weakened, from the womb: namely, while in the womb of the Church we are conceived by the first elements of faith, and afterwards regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit. Hence he adds: when I was born, I came forth from my mother’s belly; you are my protector. Because of this:

VERSE 8.—“My song is always in you; I have become as a portent to many, and you are a strong helper.”

In you, [Gloss interlinear, Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus,] not in false gods, is my song—that is, my praise. And this is always so: both in the present, while I walk by faith, and in the future, when I shall see by sight; because not even then, when made equal to angels, shall I forget the grace that delivered me. Or thus: You are my protector, and my song is in you—that is, it delights me to be in you. And this is always so, as your benefits are unceasing. Hence: “I have become as a portent to many.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Or continue thus: I will praise both in the present and in the future; but here, in the time of hope and the time of groaning, I have become as a portent to many, who mock me because I believe what I do not see and reject their ways. [Col. 0649B] Yet I shall not fear, because you are a strong helper, that I may conquer—not merely a protector. Therefore their reproach, or assault, must be disregarded where God’s power gives support, against which nothing can stand.

VERSE 9.—“Let my mouth be filled with praise, that I may sing your glory, your greatness all the day.”

Let my mouth be filled with praise. [Cassiodorus; Gloss, interlinear; Cassiodorus.] He has spoken of God’s benefits; now he asks that he may be able to give thanks. For unless God fills the mouth, desire does not burn. As though he said: Because you are a helper, therefore let my mouth be filled with praise—that is, make me praise you unceasingly before my neighbour. Or the connection is this: “My song is in you.” Therefore, that I may be able to sing, let my mouth be filled with praise, that I may sing your glory. [Col. 0649C] Glory is praise celebrated by the mouths of many. And “all the day,” [Augustine; Cassiodorus] that is, without interruption: in prosperity, because you console; and in adversity, because you correct. May I sing your greatness, because before I existed you made me; when I existed, you gave me salvation; when I sinned, you forgave me; when converted, you gave me life; when persevering, you crowned me. Thus under the name of greatness he includes everything.

PART II. VERSE 10.—“Do not cast me away in the time of old age; when my strength fails, do not forsake me.”

Do not cast me away. [Cassiodorus; Remigius; Augustine.] The second part, in which he treats of the grace to be granted in old age and extreme old age. As though he said: You have been my hope from my youth. You also, [Col. 0649D] do not cast me away in the time of old age, when exhausted strength needs greater help. And what is old age? Behold: “when my strength fails,” that is, when patience under assault becomes weak, O God, do not forsake me, because then it has greater need of help. Or, “when my strength fails,” that is, the strength of my own self, so that I may not presume upon myself—O God, do not forsake me. Here God answers you: indeed, then my strength will be in you when yours has failed, so that you may say with the Apostle: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12). But why do I say this?

VERSE 11.—“For my enemies have spoken evil against me; and those who watched my soul took counsel together.”

“For my enemies have spoken evil against me,” [Gloss, interlinear; Cassiodorus] that is, they discouraged me; and those who watched [Col. 0650A] my soul with intent to deceive—that is, those who lay in wait for me—took counsel together. For a burden not divided is heavier; that is, they spoke with common counsel. I say, they themselves—

VERSE 12.—“Saying, God has forsaken him. Pursue and seize him, for there is none to deliver him.”

“Saying,” [Augustine; Cassiodorus] in their heart, among themselves: That God, namely the one whom he makes his God, has forsaken him. Seeing him worn down by calamities, they suppose that he has been abandoned by God. Therefore pursue him, as one slow to escape; and seize him, as one powerless, because there is none to rescue him once seized. Thus they say, but—

VERSE 13.—“O God, do not be far from me; my God, look to my help.”

[Col. 0650B] O God, do not be far from me, [Cassiodorus] so that I may be exposed to graver afflictions; rather, be near. He considers God far away while He delays. My God, look to my help, because I know that I am to be afflicted.

Or all this may be understood in the person of Christ, beginning at “Do not cast me away.” Hence Jerome expounds this entire psalm as concerning Christ. Thus he says in Christ’s person: “Do not cast me away in the time of old age.” [Augustine; Cassiodorus.] Old age was also in Christ, when he was made a portent, when he was weakened on the cross and mocked. This is called old age because he assumed it from our oldness. Hence the Apostle: “Our old man was crucified with him” (Rom. 6). “When my strength fails,” namely that of his humanity, O God, do not forsake me. I say this because “my enemies spoke evil against me, [Col. 0650C] and those who watched my soul took counsel together.” This is said concerning Christ, who became weak in his enemies’ hands and was seized as though he could do nothing; he had such things in our person. Hence it may also be understood of his members, as we said before: “They took counsel together, saying, God has forsaken him.” Thus elsewhere Christ says: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27)—that is, why do these people think that I have been forsaken? Certainly to their own harm. For “if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2). Therefore, “Pursue and seize him, because there is none to deliver him.” Thus one deliberates because one judges by outward appearance. They say so, but: “O God, do not be far from me, my God,” and so forth.

[Col. 0650D] VERSE 14.—“Let those who slander my soul be confounded and fail; let those who seek evils for me be covered with confusion and shame.”

Let them be confounded. [Gloss, interlinear; Cassiodorus.] First, this is said in Christ’s person as follows: “Look to my help”; on the contrary, let those who slander my soul be confounded, since you come to my aid. And so it happened, because God’s decrees do not change. And let those slandering my soul fail while I suffer—namely the Jews, who bark against the upright. And lest they recover their senses, let those who seek evils for me be covered with confusion and shame, because they have failed—namely the Jews.

VERSE 15.—“But I will always hope, and I will add to all your praise.”

“But I will always hope, and I will add to all [Col. 0651A] your past praise,” [Augustine; Jerome; Augustine] so that what your law commanded to be offered to you in visible sacrifices, I, with the redeemed people, will bring it to you in conduct. Or, “beyond all your praise,” that offered to you by others—that is, although God is praised in all other things, He was not yet praised for raising mortal flesh to eternal life. This praise was added to God through Christ’s resurrection. Therefore this addition of praise is praise for the Incarnation and Resurrection, after the creation and governance of all things, as what follows shows.

This whole passage can likewise be understood in the person of the Church. “Let them be confounded”: contrary to their presumption in their own justice and powers, so that they may recognize their sins. It is a prayer for evildoers: and let those who slander my soul fail in their perverse [Col. 0651B] powers; or, those who commit my soul—that is, provoke us to resist God. This is to wage war against God, as those do to whom God does not seem good amid their adversities, which is to consider Him unjust. [Cassiodorus; Augustine; Cassiodorus; Augustine.] The soul is also committed if it hates those from whom it suffers. And let those who seek evils for me be covered, as though by a veil of shame, with confusion arising from their evil conscience of sins; and with shame, or modest embarrassment, for the sake of restraint. Job’s own wife did this when she said: “Say something against God and die” (Job 2). And Tobit’s wife: “Where are your righteous deeds?” (Tob. 2). She said this in order that the God who had made him blind might displease him. Thus, those who seek evils for me—that is, those evil counsellors—commit the soul and seek evils. But I will always [Col. 0651C] hope, as they despair; and I will add to all your praise. That is, beyond perfect praise: for your praise would be complete, that is, perfect, and nothing would be lacking to it, if you condemned sinners, since that would be justice; but because you also deliver these, I will add to all your praise.

VERSE 16.—“My mouth shall proclaim your righteousness, your salvation all the day.”

“My mouth.” [Gloss, interlinear; Cassiodorus; Augustine.] Here the Church speaks. As though she said: This I shall do in myself, and I shall not praise only within myself, but also before my neighbour. And this is what is meant: my mouth shall proclaim to the Gentiles your righteousness—that is, Christ, through whom righteousness was fulfilled. But lest you understand otherwise, he adds, “your salvation,” and this “all the day,” that is, in prosperity and adversity, because neither prosperity nor adversity will draw me away from praise.

Or thus: “the whole day” is called the day together with its night, because night serves day, not day night. Our flesh is night, while righteousness is day. Therefore whatever is done in the flesh, as in the night, should serve righteousness, as the day; and whatever is done at God’s command should not be done for the flesh’s profit, lest day serve night, but for righteousness’ sake, so that night may serve day. Therefore it shall proclaim your salvation all the day—that is, so that whatever I perform in the flesh may serve righteousness. Or thus: the addition to praise lies in this, that “my mouth shall proclaim that righteousness is yours, not mine,” because your righteousness is in me, not my own; and that I proclaim salvation to be yours, not mine, because salvation belongs to the Lord, not to man. And this is unchanged all the day: I shall proclaim your salvation all the day.

[Col. 0652A] VERSE 17.—“For I have not known learning; I will enter into the powers of the Lord. O Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone.”

“For I have not known learning.” [Augustine.] Another reading: “I have neither done nor approved the things which greedy merchants do.” For one greedy of gain blasphemes because of loss, lies about the prices of goods, and swears falsely. Thus all the day God’s praise is not in his mouth. But these vices belong to the person, not to the craft, which can be pursued without them; just as wrongdoing occurs in every craft, not because of the crafts themselves but because of people. For a craft does not know vice. Therefore he speaks here of another kind of trading.

The Greek word for “trading” is derived from activity; the Latin from *negotium* (“business”). Traders, then, are active people—namely Jews and others who presume upon what they do and praise their own works. Therefore they do not attain [Col. 0652B] grace, which is commended here so that no one may glory in himself. But whoever glories like a trader is driven from the Lord’s temple, for He cast the sellers and buyers out of the temple (John 2). By contrast, rest is in God, who justifies. Such traders are restless rather than good workers. They are called *negotiatores* because they deny leisure, concerning which it is said: “Be still, and see that the Lord is gracious” (Ps. 45). Thus, “I have not known trading” means: I have not known those who presume upon their actions and seek righteousness from their own works.

Or thus, according to our text. Where some codices have “trading,” others have “learning,” a diversity of translators which perhaps indicates one meaning rather than introducing an error. Let us therefore inquire into the “learning” which this man, whose mouth always has praise, did not know. There is a certain learning of the Jews. For the Jews had received the Law, which the Gentiles had not; yet they gloried not in grace but in the letter, which convicts but does not help, reveals the disease but does not cure it, exposes the weak but does not heal them. This is the pool which, in five porticoes, held a multitude of sick and infirm persons awaiting the movement of the water; but the angel of the Lord descended into the pool, the water was stirred, and one person was healed (John 5). For the Mosaic Law, in the porticoes of its five books, possesses the sick and does not heal them. But when the Angel of Great Counsel (Isa. 9), that is, Christ, came, the water was disturbed—that is, the Jews crucified him—and the unity of Christ’s body was healed.

The Law is also Elisha’s staff, sent through the servant to raise the dead person, but the dead person did not rise by it. Therefore Elisha himself came; and, being alive and grown, Elisha contracted his greatness and fitted himself to the dead child, and the dead child rose (4 Kings 4). This is Christ, who through his servant Moses sent the staff, that is, the Law, to raise one dead in sin. But because the staff of the Law could not give life, Elisha himself—that is, Christ—came and contracted his greatness to the littleness of the dead, because “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2), and fitted himself to the dead because “he was found in appearance as a man” (ibid.); and thus the dead person rose. But when Elisha sent the staff to raise the son of the hostess, he did not know what he was doing—that is, what was signified by that action.

[Col. 0653A] The sense is: Why shall I proclaim your salvation? Because I have not known “learning”—that is, I have not approved that anyone is justified by works of the Law (Rom. 3), but I have rejected those who presume upon the letter of the Law, recoil from grace, and pursue the Law’s figures. These are the traders who exalt their own works. And through this I shall enter into power—that is, into the Christian strength which belongs to the Lord, not to me, unlike those who glory in themselves. And, O Lord, then I shall remember your righteousness alone, not the righteousness of worldly law, because of myself I am absolutely nothing. Therefore I shall remember it, because, O—

VERSE 18.—“O God, you have taught me from my youth; and until now I will proclaim your wonders.”

O God, you have taught me, [Cassiodorus; Augustine] through books or by inspiration, what I was and what your righteousness has given, so that [Col. 0653B] I might remember your righteousness alone. “From my youth,” that is, from the beginning of the faith by which you renewed me, though you had made me; “and until now,” that is, even after faith, because as you were necessary at the beginning of faith, so you are necessary afterward, since even now I can do nothing by myself. And I, lest I be ungrateful, will proclaim your wonders: namely, that you govern me, that you have set me in the way, that you make me live, whom you raised in soul. This is wonderful. For what is more wonderful than raising the dead in soul? One raised in body lives even in the bodily absence of the one who raised him, as Lazarus did while Christ was bodily absent (John 2), because the soul is the life of the body. But the soul of one raised does not live without God, who is its life. This, then, is the wonderful grace: that He raises the dead, and afterward remains with us lest we die. This is what “from my youth” means, and so forth. [Col. 0653C] And now, O Lord, as you have begun, so bring it to completion. And this is—

VERSE 19.—“And unto old age and grey hairs, O God, do not forsake me.”

“And unto old age and grey hairs,” [Augustine; Cassiodorus; Augustine; Cassiodorus; Augustine] that is, unto my last things, O God, do not forsake me, because unless grace remains with me until my very end, I shall be nothing.
