Or four periods of the Church are distinguished here, like four ages. The youth of the Church was in the time of the martyrs, when they were strong. As time advances there is the “now,” that is, the present time. For “now” signifies time advancing, the time which presently exists, while faith progresses through the churches. Then comes old age, namely gravity, when charity will begin to grow cold [Col. 0653D] as the ages of the world decline. Finally, at the end of the age, there will be extreme old age, that is, decrepitude, when, because iniquity abounds, the charity of many will grow cold (Matt. 24), when Antichrist comes and life is closed with its desired end. These things needed to be said in Scripture because of those who say that Christians will exist only for a short time. Against them the Lord says: “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

As though he said: I will remember your righteousness alone because you, O God, taught me, as we said above, “from my youth”—that is, from the time of the martyrs, when I began to fight—and “until now,” that is, until the advancing time which now exists. Through the stretches of time doctrine has increased, and I, being taught, will proclaim your wonders: namely, that from being wicked I have been made righteous, [Col. 0654A] which is the same as was said above. And because, taught from youth, I have proclaimed God’s righteousness, “unto old age,” when faith will begin to grow cold, “and unto grey hairs,” that is, unto the end of the age, O God, do not forsake me. That is, do not abandon me either in mature age or when I am already near my end, so that those who say, “Christians will exist for a time,” may not rejoice, and so that I may proclaim praises to the end. Hence he adds:

VERSE 20.—“Until I proclaim your arm to every generation that is to come.”

“Until I proclaim.” [Cassiodorus; Augustine.] Others note here only three periods or ages of the Church, signifying the same thing by “now” and “old age.” “Until I proclaim.” As though he said: Do not forsake me until I proclaim your arm—that is, Christ—to every generation, through succession, [Col. 0654B] which is to come until the end of the age.

VERSE 21.—“Your power and your righteousness, O God, unto the heights, you who have done great things.”

“Your power.” [Augustine; Cassiodorus; Gloss, interlinear; Cassiodorus.] Here he shows what the arm has accomplished. As though he said: Do not forsake me, O God, until I proclaim your power to deliver, by which through the Incarnation you free captives; and your righteousness to punish, by which you condemn sinful humanity in just judgment. I say that I carry my preaching “unto the heights,” above which is the Son of God—that is, even to the man exalted above the heights, because God-man sits at the Father’s right hand, reigning with Him. I say that I shall proclaim power and righteousness, you who have done these two great things. [Col. 0654C] For both are wonderful: that a human being condemned by righteousness is redeemed through grace. By righteousness He expelled Adam from Paradise; by grace He received the thief.

Or thus: Do not forsake me until I proclaim your power, by which a human being is enabled to be good—your power, not that of man, because man is nothing of himself—and your righteousness, by which a human being is righteous—your righteousness, not that of man, O God. And do not suppose that man alone needs grace: for your grace reaches “unto the heights, you who have done great things,” because God made great by grace, when they did not exist, those who are in the heights—that is, all the heavenly orders—and preserves them in what they are, living justly and blessedly.

PART III. VERSE 21.—“O God, who is like you?”

[Col. 0654D] “O God, who is like you?” [Cassiodorus; Alcuin; Augustine.] The third part, in which he says to what person grace belongs—namely, to captive humanity—and what grace it is: the twofold resurrection, of mind and body. Hence he promises thanks. As though he said: Your power is in the heights. And since this is so, O God, who is like you in nature or power? No one, because nothing is like you. Yet foolish man exalts himself and believes the devil when he suggests: “You shall be like gods” (Gen. 3); and thereby he is made captive. For every Adam, while perversely wishing to be like God, falls into captivity. Therefore let him cry to Him from whom he fell: “O God, who is like you?”

There is, however, another, good likeness: the righteous person who loves his enemies and does good to them is like God, in whose likeness and image he was made, who makes [Col. 0655A] his sun rise upon the good and evil and sends rain upon the just and unjust (Matt. 5). This is likeness through obedience, not pride; through imitation, not equality. Thus that person is rightly like God who believes God to be supreme and in need of nothing, while he himself exists not through himself but through God. But one who wishes to exist through himself as God does exists through no one; he perversely desires to be like God, as the devil did, who refused to be under Him, and as man did, who as a servant refused to be bound by the commandment, but wished to be like God, with no ruler over him. This is perverse likeness.

For God, who needed nothing, commanded him not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 2), to test how great was the good of obedience. Whatever the tree was, and whatever fruit it bore, it was called the tree of the knowledge of good or evil because the person who refused to distinguish good from evil through the commandment would distinguish them through experience of evil, so that, by touching what was forbidden, he might find punishment. The tree was good in its own nature, and its fruit was good. Thus the good of obedience could never have been more perfectly [perhaps “more clearly”] demonstrated than by forbidding what was good, so that the punishment might arise only from disobedience and not from an evil thing, and the reward from obedience. For if the thing forbidden were evil, it would seem to be avoided even without prohibition, and punishment would follow not from disobedience alone but from failure to avoid an evil thing. But now, since a good tree was forbidden, it is clear that obedience alone has found its reward and disobedience alone has incurred punishment. Therefore this captive cries: “O God, who is like you?” No one.

[Col. 0655C] VERSE 22.—“How many great and grievous tribulations you have shown me; and, having turned, you have given me life, and from the depths of the earth you have brought me back again.”

But to me, who wished perversely to imitate you, how many tribulations have you shown—[Augustine; Cassiodorus; Augustine] that is, justly inflicted—namely sufferings. And rightly so: one who departs from Him who is goodness and blessedness in Himself is miserable. He says “shown” because he knows that these things are beneficial: “many” in quantity and “grievous” in quality. Behold justice in sinners. But this discipline by which you scourged me was an admonition to conversion, not abandonment of a captive. Hence it follows: “And yet, having turned”—[Cassiodorus; Augustine; Cassiodorus; Augustine] that is, having converted me—“you have given me life.” Behold mercy in those converted.

[Col. 0655D] “And from the depths of the earth,” that is, from the overthrow of sin, “you have brought me back again” in hope. For when our nature, united to the Word of God, rose for our sake, we were brought back from the depths of the earth. Hence, when we believe in Him, we return in Him, and the first resurrection of the soul occurs, which has already risen with Him in hope. Thus the Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ,” etc. (Col. 3). Therefore he says here: “You have brought me back again.” Likewise, a second time we shall again be brought back when we rise in body. Hence he will say afterward—or “again” means often: you have brought me back, and thus in those already brought back in hope—

VERSE 23.—“You have multiplied your magnificence; and, having turned, you have comforted me.”

“You have multiplied,” [Cassiodorus; Augustine; Cassiodorus; Augustine] because God comes to aid in diverse ways, “your magnificence,” [Col. 0656A] or justice, namely scourges, because you do not spare even your children the scourge. “And, having turned, you have comforted me” through the Scriptures and rewards. He says “comforted” because, although He chastises strictly, He nevertheless does not permit them to remain sad. Hence the universal righteous person confesses that he sings the truth. “For I also”—or, according to some, the text is thus: “You have comforted me, and from the depths of the earth you have brought me back again.” This restoration will be in the future, I mean according to the body: “You have comforted me,” which I show from its effect.

VERSE 24.—“For I too will confess to you in the instruments of psalm your truth, O God; I will sing to you on the harp, O Holy One of Israel.”

“For I also.” [Cassiodorus; Gloss, interlinear; Augustine.] Or the connection is thus, according to another text: “You have brought me back, but I will confess to you in the instruments of psalm or of psalms.” [Col. 0656B] Psalms are aptly called vessels of truth, like spiritual casks preserving the Lord’s wine. Thus: I will confess to you, O God, your truth—that is, that you are truly God—in the instruments of psalm, that is, in the singing of psalms, which are vessels of truth.

Or, “in the instruments of psalm,” that is, in the enlivening of the spirit. For the instrument of psalm is the psaltery, namely, the instrument which sounds from above, by which the spirit is signified; it has already risen with Christ in hope. The harp sounds from below and signifies the body, which also will rise. Hence he adds: And I will sing to you in deed, O you who are the Holy One of Israel, on the harp—that is, in the mortification of the flesh. [Gloss, interlinear; Cassiodorus; Remigius; Gloss, interlinear.] Or: “I will confess to you in the instruments of psalm,” that is, in the contemplative life; “and I will sing to you on the harp,” that is, in the rendering of temporal service. And I will do this rejoicing. Hence he adds:

VERSE 25.—“My lips shall rejoice when I sing to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed.”

“My inner lips shall rejoice,” [Gloss, interlinear; Augustine] namely the lips of the soul, which has already been brought back the first time, when I sing to you—that is, when I praise you in preaching—and my soul, which you have redeemed, which rejoices with those inward lips by which it silently cries to the Lord. Nor will the redeemed soul alone rejoice in God.

VERSE 26.—“But my tongue also shall meditate all the day on your righteousness, when those who seek evils for me have been confounded and put to shame.”

“But my tongue also,” [Augustine; Cassiodorus] namely that of the body, which shall be brought back a second time—“again,” that is, whose [Col. 0656D] restoration is signified by “a second time”—shall meditate on your righteousness all the day, that is, without end, in eternity. When will this rejoicing be? “When those who seek evils for me have been confounded and ashamed,” or have blushed—that is, those who now insult me. This will be at the end, namely of the age, when they see with their eyes things which they never believed would happen. For then the saints have a place of secure rejoicing, when the wicked are not permitted to rule.

## Comparison on Psalm LXX: “In you, O Lord,” etc.

No title is prefixed in the Hebrew. But it should be believed that it was added by the Seventy. For, as Jerome writes in *On the Best Method of Translating*, it would be too long now to unfold how much the Seventy added of their own and how much they omitted, matters which in the Church’s copies are marked by obeli and asterisks. Yet antiquity gave them authority, as the same witness states in his comments on Ezekiel, chapter 5. Indeed, he also explains this title to Paulinus in *On the Training of a Monk*.

Moreover, what Augustine says in *City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 43, should not be passed over: “Whatever is in the Hebrew codices and is not in the Septuagint, the Spirit of God did not choose to say through these interpreters, but through those prophets. But whatever is in the Septuagint and not in the Hebrew codices, the same Spirit chose to say through these rather than through those, thereby showing that both were prophets. For in this way He said some things through Isaiah, some through Jeremiah, some through one prophet and another; or, differently, He said the same things through this one and that one, as He willed. But whatever is found in both, He willed to say through both, one and the same Spirit, yet so that those went before in prophesying and these followed by prophetically interpreting them.” Thus far St Augustine. I add that after the title the Greek appends: *anepígraphos par’ Hebraíois*, “without a title among the Hebrews.”

[Col. 0657B] VERSE 3.—“And into a fortified place.” The Hebrew is *LABO TAMID*, that is, “that I may enter continually,” or “to which I may always come.” But what does a fortified place mean except possessing a place into which, whenever necessary, you can safely withdraw? This was not badly explained by the Campensis edition: “You are for me a strong rock, into which I always flee.” It seems borrowed from the Chaldee: “Be,” it says, “for me a strong rock for continual refuge.” Then, where we read “that you may save me,” the Hebrews have a little more: “You have commanded,” or “appointed,” “that you should save me”—*TZIVITHA LEHOSSIENI*. The sense seems fuller, unless it should be said that the certain and unquestionable protection of a stronghold includes the same thing.

VERSE 17.—“For I have not known learning.” Jerome supports this. The others translate from the Hebrew: “I have not known numbers,” so much so that Münster, to make the sense he intended clearer, introduced from his own resources: “I do not know the number of God’s benefits.” But since *SEPHOROTH* signifies both writing or learning and reckonings, and consequently trading, which is conducted through profitable numbers and accounts, it provides material for differing interpretations. On this point Augustine says of this verse: “Where some codices have ‘trading,’ others have ‘learning’; how they agree is difficult [Col. 0658A] to discover. Yet the diversity of translators perhaps indicates a meaning and does not introduce an error.”

VERSE 20.—“Until I proclaim your arm to every generation that is to come.” But the Hebrew is such that you may place a slight pause at the word “generation” and read: “Until I proclaim your arm—to the present generation,” as Münster wishes. Then understand “to every one that is to come” as “to posterity.” Jerome also does not reject this reading: “Until I proclaim your arm to the generation, and your powers to all who are to come.” Yet it is certain that in the Hebrew, immediately after “generation,” follows the mark of the universal signification, *LEDOR LECAL*, even though a clause, as it is called, is supplied; this is something I find interpreters commonly observe less carefully.

VERSE 22.—“How many great and grievous tribulations you have shown me; and, having turned, you have given me life; and from the depths of the earth you have brought me back again.” [Col. 0658B] In three places the pronoun is placed in the first-person singular. In the first place Jerome reads, as we do, the first-person singular; in the other two he has the pronoun in the first-person plural. Pratensis, however, everywhere gives the first-person plural pronoun; Nebiensis likewise. The others, however, retain “me.” Hence one may infer that the copies vary, or that *yod* is used in place of *waw*, or conversely. And indeed I saw three differing codices. One consistently had *waw* with the vowel point *ḥireq*; another had *yod* once and *waw* twice; the third had *yod* everywhere: *HIREITANI* or *HEREITANU*, “you have shown us” or “me”; *TEHAIENI* or *TEHAIENU*, “you will give life to us” or “me”; *TAALENU* or *TAALENI*, “you will cause us” or “me” to ascend.

These matters might be idle, since they have no bearing on the meaning, unless I perceived that some persons are, if I may put it so, overly scrupulous in hunting for tiny details. But these remarks are made chiefly because of the following verse, where we read, “You have multiplied your magnificence,” while the Hebrew has “my magnificence,” or “my greatness”: *GEDULLATHI*. Even though the resemblance is not equally close here and there, it is nevertheless most certain that the glory of the Son is the glory of the Father, and conversely, according to John 17: “All mine are yours, and yours are mine.”

## PSALM LXXI

[Col. 0657]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “CONCERNING SOLOMON”

[Col. 0657C]

“O God, give your judgment.” Title: “Concerning Solomon.” [Augustine; Cassiodorus; Jerome.] Solomon means “peaceful,” a name which most truly and fittingly belongs to him through whom, as Mediator between God and human beings [Col. 0657D] (1 Tim. 2), we are reconciled to God from being enemies, having received remission of sins (Eph. 2). He himself is that peaceful one who made both one, breaking down the middle wall of partition, and reconciled both to God; upon the peace of reconciliation he will give the peace of immortality (ibid.). Hence: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave with you” (John 14).

This fourth psalm is directed to this Solomon—that is, to this true peace-maker—because here he is commended according to each nature. This is the fourth psalm concerning Christ’s two natures. Purpose: it exhorts us to believe that Christ the king is true God and true man. Method: it has seven divisions. First, it deals with the judgment, desiring that it be given to the Son. Second, it treats of the same judgment, affirming what it had desired, at “He will judge [Col. 0658C] the poor.” Third, it states who and what sort of king will come beforehand, who is to judge in the future, at “He shall descend like rain.” Fourth, it treats of his works, at “For he shall deliver.” Fifth, it treats of the king’s honour, at “And he shall live.” Sixth, it exhorts all to offer praise to him, at “May his name.” Seventh, it gives praise from its own side, at “Blessed be the Lord.”

The prophet, therefore, speaking to the Father concerning Christ, says: O—

VERSE 1.—“O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son.”

O God the Father, give your judgment to the king, that is, to Christ. [Gloss, interlinear; Augustine; Jerome; Augustine; Cassiodorus.] As though he said: Let what I foresee as future come to pass. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John 9), not because the whole Trinity judges together, but because the person of the Son alone, according to his humanity, will be seen by all in judgment. And to show the earnestness of his petition, he repeats the same thing in other words by the figure of *epimone*, saying: “And your righteousness,” that is, give just judgment to the king’s son—that is, [Col. 0659A] your Son, for you are king. Therefore he does not usurp the kingdom, because he is the king’s son, as we have said. This is *epimone*, that is, frequent repetition. Repetitions, whether made with the same or with different words, greatly commend the divine utterances; they occur especially in the Psalms and in that kind of discourse through which the soul’s affections are moved. I say, “give judgment”—for what purpose?

VERSE 2.—“To judge your people in righteousness, and your poor in judgment.”

“To judge,” [Augustine; Cassiodorus] that is, for judging your people in righteousness, who are also his own—namely, that he may separate them from those who are not his—and your poor in judgment. These are God’s people, namely the humble, not the proud. By saying “your people” and “your poor,” he shows that all things belonging to the Father also belong to the Son, and conversely.

[Col. 0659B] VERSE 3.—“May the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness.”

“May they receive.” [Gloss, interlinear; Augustine; Cassiodorus; Augustine.] As though he said: Grant these things, but first let the Judge be made known through messengers. And this is what is meant: may the mountains—that is, the greater ones, namely the prophets and apostles, who approach heaven in their height—receive peace, that is, Christ. I mean the peace to be proclaimed to the faithful people; and may the hills, namely the lesser ones, receive righteousness, that is, Christ.

Or thus, so that a distinction is made between peace and righteousness. May the mountains, namely the greater ones, receive the peace of humility for the people—that is, for the sake of the people—so that they may not exalt themselves because of their greater rank. For those eminent in the Church ought to provide for peace with vigilant attention, lest, acting proudly because of their honours, they make schisms by breaking the bond of unity. And may the hills, that is, the lesser ones, receive righteousness by imitation, so that they do not put servants before the Lord, but follow the greater ones by imitation and obedience in such a way as always to place Christ before them. Or, may the mountains—that is, the greater ones—receive peace, that is, the word of reconciliation, namely the word of the Gospel, in order to proclaim it to the people; and may the hills—that is, the lesser ones—receive righteousness, that is, obedience, so that they may obey the teaching of truth.

PART II. VERSE 4.—“He will judge the poor of the people, save the children of the poor, and humble the slanderer.”

Judges. [Cassiodorus, Haymo, Augustine.] The second [Col. 0659D] part, in which he again treats of the same judgment, affirming that it will take place. After the prayer, he states by prophetic power what is to be accomplished at the Lord’s coming. As though he said: “Give judgment,” and you will truly give it, because he will judge the poor of the people. Or, alternatively, let both kinds of preachers of evangelical peace be understood by “mountains and hills”—those preceding, such as the apostles, and those following, such as their successors. Thus the wording is distinguished: the mountains, that is, the earlier preachers, and the hills, that is, the later preachers, shall receive peace, that is, Christ, to be proclaimed to the people.

Then, according to another reading, follows: “The righteous shall judge the poor of the people.” But those manuscripts are more approved which [Col. 0660A] have what we explained above: “He will judge the poor of the people,” that is, those who are poor among the people, in whom good and evil are mingled. Thus he will judge; and—that is, because—he will save the children of the poor, separating them from the wicked. These are the same as the poor, just as Zion and the daughter of Zion are the same city.

Or distinguish between “the children of the poor” and “the poor.” By “the poor” he means the Fathers, namely the prophets and apostles; by “the children of the poor,” those who make progress under them. The Lord will judge all these in such a way as to save them. And in the present life he will humble the accuser, that is, the devil. For while a human being lives by God’s grace so as to worship God freely, the devil is humbled—the devil who says, “Does Job worship God for nothing?” (Job 1). Or the devil was humbled in Christ’s Passion, when he fell through the accusations of the Jews against Christ, in whom he possessed no right; and so he deservedly lost those in whom he is recognized as having some right. [Col. 0660B] [Cassiodorus.] He is rightly called an accuser because he strives to draw the innocent into guilt, which is what it means to accuse falsely. Christ humbled him in the Passion, yet he has not been wholly destroyed. Hence elsewhere: “You have humbled the proud one as one wounded” (Ps. 88 [89]). Hence Jeremiah: “The partridge cries out: she gathered what she did not bear; she made riches without judgment; in the midst of her days she shall leave them, and at her end she shall rise up foolish” (Jer. 17).

[Note: [Col. 0659D] From Augustine, *On Pastors*, book 12.]

Or, in the future judgment, he will humble the accuser, that is, the devil.

### Verse 5

> “And he shall endure with the sun, and before [Col. 0660C] the moon, from generation to generation.”

And he shall endure. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Here he shows him worthy to judge. As though he said: The king will judge, and he himself will endure with the sun, that is, as long as times revolve. Times are signified by the sun because they change and are distinguished according to the sun’s course. It is not, however, a great thing for him to endure with the sun, through whom all things were made; but this is a prophecy that the religion of the Christian name will always endure, against those who say that the Church will at some time fail.

Therefore he shall endure with the sun, that is, he shall endure in and with the Church, which is his body, for as long as times revolve. And before the moon: he could have said “with the sun and before the sun,” that is, with times and before times, before which he is eternal. [Col. 0660D] But by the moon, which waxes and wanes, he preferred to designate the increase and decline of mortals. The sense is: he shall endure before the moon, that is, by his immortality he precedes all mortal things.

He then explains what he called “the moon.” “The moon,” I mean, “of generation and generations,” according to another reading: that is, he endures before the generations of generations which pass away through the departure and succession of mortals.

Or thus: by the sun, God the Father is understood, with whom the Son endures, as the brightness and ray of the sun. The sense is: “He will humble”—and defeat—the devil in the Passion. And when the devil has been defeated, the brightness, that is, the Son, will endure with the sun, that is, with the Father, seated at the Father’s right hand [Col. 0661A] forever. And this is before the moon of generation and generations, because he is the firstborn from the dead, preceding the Church, which passes through the departure and succession of human beings.

Or “generation of generations” means the future generation in which we shall be begotten immortally. Thus: “the moon,” I mean, “of the generation of generations,” that is, which will be begotten immortally in the regeneration.

Or, according to another reading: “He shall endure from generation to generation”; or, “for ever and ever”; or, “unto generations of generations,” that is, without end. This explains the foregoing.

### Part III. Verse 6

> “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece, and like dripping showers falling upon the earth.”

He shall descend. [Cassiodorus, Gloss.] The third part. Behold [Col. 0661B] who and what kind of king this is who is to judge. As though he said: How will this kingdom begin? Behold, it will begin with the Jews and be completed among the nations. This is: “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece.”

It alludes to the action of Gideon, recorded in the Book of Judges. About to fight against the Midianites, he asked the Lord for this sign of victory: that a fleece of sheep placed upon the threshing floor should be drenched while the floor remained dry; and so it happened. Afterwards he asked that the floor be watered while the fleece was dry; and it was so (Judg. 6). This mystically signified that the Jewish people would first be irrigated by Christ’s grace while the threshing floor of the Gentiles remained dry; and afterwards that the Gentiles would be drenched while the fleece of the Jews was dry.

For by the fleece Judea is understood, which was to be stripped of the authority of teaching, like a sheep of its fleece. Or it is so called because it retained within itself the rain [Col. 0661C] of doctrine, which it did not wish to be preached to the Gentiles, just as fleece retains rain. Thus that king says: “He shall first descend upon the fleece like rain,” that is, Christ’s grace shall first descend upon the Jewish people. Hence he chose his mother and his apostles from among them, while the threshing floor of the whole world was dry, just as rain first descended upon Gideon’s fleece. And afterwards “he shall descend like dripping showers falling upon the earth,” that is, upon the Gentiles, while the fleece of the Jews was dry—just as afterwards Gideon’s floor was drenched while the fleece was dry. Behold where the kingdom will begin and where it will be completed; and that kingdom will be beneficial, because “righteousness shall arise,” and so forth.

[Gloss, Cassiodorus, Jerome.] Or thus: he treats of Christ’s birth after having spoken of the future judgment. As though he said: Christ will judge in the future, and first he will come in utmost humility and gentleness. This is: “He shall descend into the womb of the Virgin like rain upon the fleece.” For Christ, whom nothing could withstand if he wished to be known by manifest power, willed gently to descend into the Virgin’s womb without any disturbance, as rain descends upon fleece, [Col. 0661D] so as to display his power more fully by tempering it. The comparison is fitting. Wool, in receiving water, is not broken but remains whole; so too in the Virgin, her integrity remained whole before childbirth, in childbirth, and after childbirth.

He confirms the same point with another comparison, adding: “And he shall descend like dripping showers falling upon the earth,” which descend like dew with the greatest gentleness. Who, then, after such evident comparisons, could doubt the Virgin’s childbirth? He next sets forth [Col. 0662A] what he himself brought forth in rising, what shoots sprang up from the showers, saying:

### Verse 7

> “In his days righteousness shall arise, and an abundance of peace, until the moon is removed.”

“In his days righteousness and an abundance of peace shall arise, until the moon is removed, so that it is no more.” [Augustine.] That is, peace will remain until death has been destroyed and the mortality of the flesh, signified by the moon, no longer exists. The moon also signifies the Church. Another reading has “is exalted”: some translators rendered it “is removed,” while others rendered it “is exalted.” Thus: “until the moon is exalted,” that is, until the Church is raised through the glory of the resurrection.

### Verse 8

> “And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth.”

[Col. 0662B] And he shall rule. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Here he shows the extent of the kingdom. As though he said: The kingdom is so beneficial and so broad because he shall rule from sea—that is, from any boundary of the earth—to sea, that is, to every boundary of the earth: the Church will spread so widely. And he shall rule from the river Jordan, where the Father’s voice sounded over Christ: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3). His teaching began there; from there the authority of the Teacher is extended to the ends of the earth through the preaching of the Gospel of Christ’s kingdom. From there the rule of baptism flowed throughout the whole world. Therefore he shall rule to the ends of the earth on every side. This is what he previously said: “from sea [Col. 0662C] to sea.” Observe that in few words he teaches great mysteries.

### Verse 9

> “Before him the Ethiopians shall fall down, and his enemies shall lick the earth.”

Before him. [Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] What he had said universally, he shows in particular, saying: “Before him the Ethiopians shall fall down,” that is, the Ethiopians, who are at the ends of the earth and are very dark, shall worship him—that is, the Gentiles; the whole is named from a part. And his enemies, namely stubborn schismatics who envy Christ’s glory, shall lick the earth in the manner of the serpent, to whom it was said, “You shall eat earth” (Gen. 3). That is, they will love earthly things, which are their penal food. Or “they shall lick the earth” means that they will love schismatic people [Col. 0662D] and find them pleasing, though under their leadership they oppose the divine utterances.

### Verse 10

> “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring offerings.”

The kings of Tarshish. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin, Jerome, Gloss.] Tarshish is interpreted “contemplation”; the faithful fixed in contemplation offer gifts when they serve with devout minds. The sense is: The kings of Tarshish, that is, the faithful fixed in contemplation, are called kings because they rule their vices; and the islands, that is, those who exclude from themselves the surrounding vices of the world, shall offer gifts—that is, themselves—by serving devoutly. The kings of Arabia and Sheba: these lands delight the nostrils with various fragrances, and signify those who indulge themselves softly in earthly pleasure. But now they are kings of Arabia and Sheba because they subject these allurements to strict discipline. [Col. 0663A] And they shall bring offerings, that is, they shall bring others with them into the fellowship of the Church.

Or this can be understood of evil kings who persecute and kill martyrs. Thus: the kings of Arabia and Sheba, that is, ignorant persecutors, bring offerings because, in sacrificing martyrs, they brought them forth.

Or the whole may be understood from interpretations of the names. Tarshish means “the searching out of joy”; Arabia, “humble” or “of the plain”; Sheba, “burning” or “conversion.” Thus: The kings of Tarshish are those who search out true joy; the islands are those who exclude vices from themselves: they shall offer gifts, namely themselves and others. The kings of Arabia are the humble, or those full of justice and equity; and the kings of Sheba are those kindled by divine fire, or converted to God: they shall bring offerings, namely themselves and others.

Or it may be understood historically of the kings who came to worship Christ with gifts, who came from these provinces, and with whom came the islands, that is, even the remotest peoples. Hence this psalm is sung on the feast of the Epiphany. What do the individual details signify?

### Verse 11

> “And all kings shall worship him; all nations shall serve him.”

And all the kings of the earth, [Cassiodorus.] who seem worthy of worship, shall worship him. Here he shows what the king’s household is: and all nations, which have earthly lords, shall serve him, because there is no nation which does not, in some portion of its people, worship the Creator.

### Part IV. Verse 12

> “For he shall deliver the poor from the mighty, and the poor man who had no helper.”

For he shall deliver. [Cassiodorus.] The fourth part, in which he treats of his works. As though he said: Why so great an honor for him? Because he shall deliver—or has delivered—the poor, that is, the people of believers, among whom there are kings, from the mighty one, that is, the devil. Not his own strength, but human sins made him mighty. He then repeats himself in order to specify which poor person he delivers, saying: “and the poor man who had no helper,” because neither a righteous human being nor an angel nor the Law nor free choice could deliver him, but only the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Rev. 5). And although he delivers, sins, for which they were held, do not please him; but:

### Verse 13

> “He shall spare the poor and needy, and shall save the souls of the poor.”

[Col. 0663D] He shall spare. [Augustine.] By redeeming from usury—that is, he will forgive sins. Whom? The poor and needy: those who do not trust in themselves but in grace.

Or the sense continues thus: I say that he will deliver the poor; and if the delivered poor person sins, he will spare the poor and needy. This is necessary, since all sin and lack the glory of God (Rom. 3). And he will save the souls of the poor from iniquity, that is, by giving them grace to do righteousness and to avoid iniquity. For two forms of the help of grace are commended here: forgiveness of sins, when he says, “He shall spare the poor”; and participation in righteousness, when he adds, “He shall save the souls of the poor.” He next gives two equivalent expressions for these two, saying:

### Verse 14

> “From usuries and iniquity he shall redeem their souls; and their name shall be honorable before him.”

[Col. 0664A] From usuries, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] that is, from sins, he shall redeem their souls; and this is what he said above, “He shall spare the poor.” Sins are called “usuries” because more evil is found in their punishments than was committed in the sins themselves. For example, when a murderer destroys only a human body and does no harm to the soul, yet that person’s own soul and body shall be destroyed in Gehenna. Thus he shall redeem them from usuries by forgiving the sins that deserved greater punishments. And he shall redeem their souls from iniquity by the price of his blood, namely by helping them through grace to do righteousness.

The same things are thus repeated as were said above: by sparing, he redeems from usuries; by saving, he redeems from iniquity. Therefore what was above, “He shall spare the poor,” is here, “From usuries he shall redeem”; and what it says there, “He shall save the souls of the poor,” is here, “From iniquity he shall redeem.”

Or thus, so that “he shall save the souls of the poor” is understood of the future—namely, not merely that he now spares. Here follows: from usuries, that is, eternal punishments, and iniquity, that is, the very sin for which punishment was owed, he shall redeem their souls by the price of his blood. And their name, namely the Christian name, though contemptible to the wicked, shall nevertheless be honorable before him, because in his kingdom they will live before him.

Or, according to another reading: “their name shall be honorable before themselves,” because they will give thanks for benefits, giving [Col. 0664C] glory to his name.

### Part V. Verse 15

> “And he shall live, and there shall be given to him of the gold of Arabia; and they shall worship concerning him always; all day they shall bless him.”

And he shall live. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The fifth part, in which he treats of the king’s honor. As though he said: Although by his death he redeemed the poor, nevertheless he shall live without end, though he was despised in dying. And there shall be given to him of the gold of Arabia, that is, the wise people of the world shall believe in Christ. Arabia signifies the Gentiles; gold, which excels among metals, signifies wisdom, which excels among teachings.

“And they shall worship concerning him always,” by his being multiplied, that is, by the multiplication of his body; or by attaining him, that is, according to his instruction, because he himself taught us to pray thus: “May your kingdom come,” and so forth. [Col. 0664D] All day, that is, throughout all time, they shall bless him by a good life; and rightly, because:

### Verse 16

> “There shall be a firm foundation in the land upon the summits of the mountains; his fruit shall be exalted above Lebanon, and they shall flourish from the city like the grass of the earth.”

“There shall be a firm foundation upon the summits of the mountains.” [Augustine, Gloss, Augustine.] The summits of the mountains are the authors of Scripture, namely the prophets and apostles. He confirms them because everything foretold by them has been fulfilled in him. And this is “in the land,” because everything was written for those who are on earth. Hence he also came to earth to fulfill these things. Therefore he is the firm foundation of the prophets because he fulfilled what they foretold.

Or thus: he himself shall be [Col. 0665A] the firm foundation, that is, the bread of faith strengthening the heart, upon the summits of the mountains—that is, in the apostles and other saints. And this is on this earth, which is remarkable: namely, that he strengthens them so here.

It follows: “And his fruit,” namely the good, “shall be exalted above Lebanon.” That is, he will raise his own above the cedars of Lebanon, literally: if Lebanon produces tall cedars, Christ carries his own up to heaven. Or this may be understood from the interpretation of the name. Lebanon means “whitening” and signifies the splendor and dignity of this age. Therefore “his fruit,” that is, Christ’s lovers, “shall be exalted above Lebanon,” that is, above the brightness of the age, because all worldly things are despised.

Or “his fruit,” that is, charity, shall be exalted above Lebanon, that is, above all other gifts. Of this the Apostle says: “I show you a still more excellent way,” and so forth (1 Cor. 12). And those who are from the city, namely the city of God, that is, from the Church, shall flourish most delightfully in the future, as the grass of the earth grows green. [Col. 0665B] [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] For it is not the age of grass, but its greenness, that is compared to the saints. Leaving this city of the present Church, they shall flourish in that heavenly blessedness.

Or “grass” may mean fruitful grass, that is, grain, just as in Genesis grain too is understood by the word “grass,” when it says: “God commanded the earth to bring forth every tree and every grass” (Gen. 2), without adding, “and every grain,” including it under the name of grass. Thus they shall flourish as the grass of the earth, namely fruitful grass, such as the grass of grain.

Or, because “city” has been placed ambiguously—the text has not added either “his” or “God’s”—the city of Cain may be understood, just as above it was explained concerning the city of God, that is, the Church. For there are two cities in the present world: Christ’s city and the city of the world. God’s city is the Church, which began with Abel; the city of the world is Babylon, which began with Cain. It is compared with grass, according to: “All flesh is grass” (Isa. 40). For all the splendor of the city which Cain began to build is like the flower of grass, which flourishes today and tomorrow is cast into the furnace (Matt. 6). [Col. 0665C] The sense of this and the preceding passage is therefore this: “His fruit,” that is, what is promised to us eternally, shall be exalted above Lebanon, that is, shall be proclaimed and commended above all things of the age. And those things which are from the city—namely Cain’s city—shall flourish like the grass of the earth: whatever is held great in the world shall be compared to the grass of the earth.

### Part VI. Verse 17

> “May his name be blessed for ever; before the sun his name endures.”

May his name be blessed. [Cassiodorus, Remigius, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The sixth part, in which he urges all to speak praise to him, because all shall be blessed in him. As though he said: Because his fruit shall be exalted and the flower of the world shall fall, therefore may his name be blessed for ever. That is: because he gives eternal glory, may he be glorified eternally. And his name, that is, the king’s Son, endures before the sun, that is, before times and before every creature—that is, eternally. He says this so that you may not suppose the Son of God to be temporal.

### Verse 18

> “And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him; all nations shall magnify him.”

And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him, [Augustine.] as was promised to Abraham: “In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22). And lest you understand only the twelve tribes, he adds: all nations—namely, all who are blessed—shall magnify him, making him great.

### Part VII. Verse 19

> “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wonders.”

Blessed. [Augustine, Alcuin.] The seventh part, in which he praises from his own position. Having said all these things, he pours forth a hymn. As though he said: Because all shall be blessed in him, blessed be the Lord God of Israel. Observe that this is an exclamatory blessing, with exhortation and [Col. 0666B] prophecy: “who alone does wonders,” because whoever does them, he does them in that person.

### Verse 20

> “And blessed be the name of his majesty for ever; and the whole earth shall be filled with his majesty. Let it be, let it be.”

And blessed be the name, [Gloss, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] that is, the glory of his majesty, which is greater than all names; or, “the name of majesty,” namely the Christian name, which is derived from Christ himself. And this is forever, that is, as long as the age endures, and for ever and ever, as some translators add. And the whole earth, namely the saints, shall be filled with his majesty—or, according to another reading, his glory—that is, with his own glorification.

“Let it be, let it be.” [Gloss, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Behold, as it were, the ruler’s signature and the hearers’ assent. It is magnificent that he concludes thus: to say “let it be” once belongs to one who wishes; to repeat it belongs to one who desires exceedingly. As though he said: What you have commanded, Lord, so let it be, let it be, until what began from the river reaches the ends of the earth.

Jerome: “It should be known that Psalm 71 is the end of the second book, and therefore at its conclusion it has ‘Let it be, let it be,’ whereas in Hebrew it says ‘Amen, amen.’ This too must be observed more carefully: ‘The hymns of David, son of Jesse, have ended’ belongs to the end of Psalm 71. What follows—‘A psalm of Asaph’—is the beginning of the following psalm.”

## Comparison on Psalm 71: “O God, give your judgment to the king,” etc.

[Col. 0666D] **Verse 5. “And he shall endure with the sun.”** The Hebrew has: “They shall fear you with the sun.” That is, according to Jerome’s translation, “as long as the sun exists.” Since this fear ought to be understood as the religion of the Christian name, which is never to cease, it is fittingly signified by perpetual stability. But when *israuca* is read, I do not know whether the translators took *caph* as a servile prefix, and thus *sic* as essential, and [whether they relied] on the Chaldaic word *ierac*, which means “he prolonged.”

**“Before the moon.”** Faber argues that “beyond the moon” is said better and more divinely, so as to show that Christ’s kingdom will not cease when the world ceases, but will endure perpetually after the consummation of the age. Yet “before the moon” does not have quite the same force. Nevertheless, the Hebrew word in question properly means “before,” “in front of,” or “in the presence of”; with the broad agreement of the Hebrews it denotes *liphne yareah*. Jerome’s rendering, “beyond the moon,” looks to what immediately follows, namely “unto generation of generations,” so that, in explaining what the Prophet meant by “moon,” he might add “from generation to generation.”

[Col. 0667A] **Verse 6. “He shall descend as upon the fleece.”** So Jerome, Sanctes, and Nebiensis render it. But whereas holy and catholic teachers who treat this passage refer it by mystical allusion to the delightful history of Gideon—as do St Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose in the preface to book 1 of *On the Holy Spirit*, Chrysostom in a homily especially devoted to this subject, Arnobius, and most other learned and holy men—it seems unfair that certain modern Hebraizing scholars have so narrowed their translations that they leave no place for the mystery of the fleece, of which Judges 6 speaks. This is the more objectionable because, without any damage to the truth of the Hebrew, they could have translated either “fleece” or, more generally, “a shearing.” For *gez* properly means this, and no one disputes it.

But Pratensis renders it: “He shall descend like rain [Col. 0667B] upon cut grass”; Münster: “upon a mowing of grass”; the edition at Campen: “like rain upon a cut field”; the Campen paraphrase: “upon harvested grain.” Quite otherwise the Septuagint: “He shall come down like rain upon fleece” (*καταβήσεται ὡς ὑετὸς ἐπὶ πόκον*). If their authority is rejected in a matter that declares itself so plainly, what then will be done in obscure passages of Scripture, or passages needing investigation?

**Verse 7. “In his days righteousness shall arise.”** The Hebrews read *tzadiq*, “righteous [man].” It appears that the Septuagint read *tzedeq*, that is, “righteousness,” perhaps not without a more fitting correspondence. For since Christ himself, supremely righteous, had already arisen, what remained but that righteousness should spring up in us? If you read “righteous [man],” referring it as required to the faithful, nevertheless righteousness must precede, by which we are made righteous. And the immediately following clause, “an abundance of peace,” seems to indicate the same thing: first justifying grace, then peace itself, which is grace completing and perfecting us wholly.

[Col. 0667C] **“Until the moon is removed.”** In Hebrew it is plainly *ad beli yareah*, that is, “until there is no moon.” Why, however, some Latin manuscripts have “may it be taken up” or “may it be exalted,” and some “may it be removed,” Augustine explains in these words:

> “What has been rendered ‘may it be taken up,’ others translated ‘may it be removed,’ and others ‘may it be exalted,’ each translating as he thought fit the one Greek word placed there, *antanairesē* (*ἀνταναιρεθῇ*). But those who said ‘may it be taken up’ and those who said ‘may it be removed’ do not differ very greatly. For ‘taken up’ is more commonly said in the sense that something is removed and ceases to be, rather than in the sense that it is raised higher. ‘Removed,’ indeed, can be understood in no other way than as destroyed—that is, as ceasing to be; but ‘exalted’ means nothing other than raised higher.”

So far Augustine. Certainly Jerome in his commentaries explains it: “Let the Church be exalted.”

**Verse 9. “Before him the Ethiopians shall fall down.”** Pellicanus translates “solitaries”; Sanctes, “inhabitants [Col. 0667D] of the desert.” The translator for Cajetan agrees. Münster reconciles this in his scholium: they are taken as inhabitants of the wilderness, such as Ethiopians are. Nebiensis translates “peoples.” The Chaldee interprets it as “nobles.”

**Verse 12. “He shall deliver the poor from the mighty.”** Jerome and the translator for Cajetan support this. Modern translators render “the one crying out” or “the one calling” in place of “the mighty,” since *meshawea* and *shoa* can mean both “rich, wealthy, powerful” and “crying out.”

**Verse 14. “And their name shall be honorable before him.”** The Hebrews have: “Their blood is precious before his eyes,” *ve-yaqar damam be-‘enav*. It appears that the Septuagint read *shemam*, that is, “their name.” For they could not have been ignorant of what *damam* meant. Yet if the Hebrew *daleth* had a soft sound, it would sound almost like *ch*, inclining toward the pronunciation of *shim*.

**Verse 15. “And they shall worship concerning him always.”** Jerome likewise agrees, and “concerning him” refers to [Col. 0668A] Christ. Others render “for him,” as some did even in Augustine’s age. Augustine found that constricted, as though it meant, “They shall worship,” or—as the Hebrew has—“They shall pray for him,” namely Christ. He proceeds to dissolve this difficulty thus:

> “What the Greek has, *peri autou* (*περὶ αὐτοῦ*), some translated ‘concerning him,’ some ‘for her,’ or ‘for him.’ But what is ‘concerning him,’ unless perhaps what we pray when we say, ‘May your kingdom come’ (Matt. 6)? How ‘for him’ is to be understood is constricted, unless it is because, when prayer is made for the Church, prayer is made for him, because it is his body. For concerning Christ and the Church the great mystery was stated beforehand: ‘The two shall be one flesh’ (Gen. 2).”

These are Augustine’s words. Modern translators, moreover, render it in the singular: “He shall pray for him always,” so that we say that Christ the Lord always prays for that poor man. Yet because Jerome translates in the plural, and the Hebrew verb *yithpallel* has a passive sense, it seems more consistent that “for him” should refer to Christ the Lord. Hence Pellicanus rendered it thus: “Prayer shall always be made through him.” This corresponds to “they shall worship concerning him always.” The Campen paraphrase in turn agrees with the context: “May he be worshipped without end.”

[Col. 0668B] **Verse 16. “There shall be a firm foundation in the land upon the summits of the mountains.”** Hebrew: *pissat bar*. Jerome: “There shall be notable grain in the land upon the top of the mountains.” Paul of Burgos, a Jew converted to Christianity: “There shall be a small cake of wheat.” To commend the awesome sacrament of the most holy Eucharist, he also says that the Targum, that is, the Chaldee translation, says, in place of what we have “upon the summits of the mountains,” “upon the heads of the priests.” Pratensis: “There shall be an abundance of grain.” Sanctes, Münster, and almost all others say: “There shall be a handful of grain.”

Lyra says: “The common translation seems corrupted by the similarity of the words, having *firmamentum* [firm foundation] in place of *frumentum* [grain].” He says well, “seems,” in an outward sense, lest he assert it. For the Septuagint clearly has *stērigma* (*στήριγμα*), that is, “firm foundation.” Now *pissat* is polysemous among the Hebrews. Properly, however, it is explained as “the strength of refreshment.” For the Chaldee, *said lahama*, interprets it as “the firm foundation of refreshment,” or “substantial bread.” Hence Psalm 103: “Bread may strengthen the human heart.” How closely this corresponds to the whole sacrament of Christ’s body, the most solid foundation of Christian religion, cannot be adequately expressed in human words.

[Col. 0668C] **“His fruit shall be exalted above Lebanon,” etc.** Hebrew: *yiresh*. Modern translators render it “shall be shaken” or “shall be battered”; Nebiensis, “shall swell,” whereas Jerome, together with the Septuagint, explains it as “shall be raised.” But it is an allusion to the tall trees of Lebanon, which, because of the height of both mountain and trees, are shaken against one another by the force of the winds.

**Verse 17. “Before the sun his name endures.”** Hebrew: *yinon shemo*, which word for word might be rendered, “His name shall be sonned” [or “shall be propagated as a son”]. That is, according to Jerome’s translation, “his name shall endure”; or, as Münster says, “his name shall be propagated.” Nor is Sanctes’s rendering unattractive: “His name was begotten before the sun.” For this wonderfully commends that eternal and incomprehensible generation of the Son of God.

[Col. 0668D] **Verse 19. “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel.”** I do not know by what accident it happened that neither Greek nor Latin manuscripts have the name “God” repeated—“Blessed be the Lord God, God of Israel”—although this is plainly seen in Hebrew, so that the mystery of the Trinity may be judged to be expressed in full praise. St Jerome writes concerning this to Sunia and Fretela: “You say that ‘God’ is not found twice in Greek, whereas it is both in Hebrew and in the Septuagint; and the very manifest threefold naming of Lord, God, and God is the mystery of the Trinity.”

# Psalm 72

[Col. 0669A]

## Title of the Psalm

> “The praises, or hymns, of David son of Jesse have ended. A psalm of Asaph.”

[Col. 0669A]

“How good is God to Israel!” [Augustine.] The title: “The praises, or hymns, of David son of Jesse have ended. A psalm of Asaph.” [Augustine.] A hymn has three elements: praise, praise of God, and song. For unless it is sung joyfully, it is not a hymn. Nor does one sing joyfully who does not love. Thus, if there is praise but it is not of God, it is not a hymn; and if it is of God but not with song, it is not a hymn. Therefore, for it to be a hymn, it must have these three things: praise, God, and song. In the praise of one confessing is proclamation; in the song of one loving is loving affection.

Beyond the usual practice, it adds “son of Jesse.” The name David is often found in the titles, but “son of Jesse” is never added except here; this was not done without reason. David [Col. 0669B] was a certain man, son of Jesse (1 Sam. 16), who reigned in Israel in the time of the Old Testament. The New Testament was in that Old Testament, but hidden, just as Christ was in David and Abraham, but hidden: as fruit is in the root but does not appear. Yet a few prophets knew that both Christ and the New Testament were hidden there, and foretold that both would be revealed.

Therefore, at that time, when spiritual things lay hidden, the carnal people praised God for that kingdom in which the man son of Jesse reigned and for other such carnal things. But when that kingdom and the remaining temporal things failed, the praise failed—not the praise of David, Son of God, but of David, son of Jesse: that is, the praise of the carnal people. When these carnal things failed, which God removed so that those things hidden beneath them might be sought, Asaph speaks—that is, the Synagogue, but the faithful Synagogue. Even before, it worshipped God devoutly, although for earthly things; but it sought these from God, not from demons as the Gentiles did.

But when Asaph observed blasphemers abounding in the things for which it had formerly served, it began to waver, like certain persons from the same people, not knowing what lay hidden in these figures—as though there were no better gift which God could give. Yet prompted by the removal of these things to seek what it did not hold in common with the wicked, Asaph reproves itself for its error and says: “How good is God to Israel!”

The sense of the title is therefore this: here it is treated how the praises or hymns of David—not the Son of God but the son of Jesse, that is, the Jewish people signified by King David—have ended. Its praise ended because God no longer gives pleasant things as to children, to entice them to service. This psalm is attributed to Asaph, [Col. 0669D] that is, to the faithful Synagogue, which says this and now bears testimony against what it formerly did, so that it may be more credible.

[Intention: Augustine, Cassiodorus.] He exhorts us to praise God not for temporal things but for eternal things.

Method: There are four divisions. First, Asaph describes the wickedness of evil persons and says that he envied their prosperity, but was corrected from this and, having been corrected, corrects others. Second, explaining his own and others’ error, he says that he returned from it [Col. 0670A] to a better counsel, at “Therefore they shall be converted.” Third, he reveals what he learned in God’s sanctuary, at “Nevertheless.” Fourth, he compares the heavenly reward with his earthly desire and reproves himself, at “For what have I?” Thus Asaph, recalling his error, repenting of it, and reproving himself, says with astonishment:

### Verse 1

> “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart!”

“How good,” [Gloss, Augustine.] that is, how delightful God is to Israel. This was not always apparent to me. But to whom? To those who are upright in heart; he appears perverse to the perverse.

### Verse 2

> “But as for me, my feet were almost moved; my steps almost slipped.”

Me, however. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though he said: [Col. 0670B] Now I confess that God is good; but formerly, when my heart was not upright, my feet were almost moved—that is, toward error; my steps were almost poured out—that is, toward a fall. My feet were not wholly moved. Or, “my steps were poured out,” but “almost,” because I had begun to err but had not erred; I had begun to fall but had not yet fallen. Feet and steps are the same thing, namely the affections. Or “feet” denotes the judgment of the mind, which had departed from truth. “Steps” are evil actions, which were poured out, that is, rushed headlong. And he says “almost,” because he quickly returned. Why, then, were his feet moved?

VERS. 3.—“Because I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners.”

Because, fixing my attention on the wicked, I was jealous, [Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, I envied them and took it grievously. [Col. 0670C] What did I envy in them? Behold, I speak of the temporal peace of sinners—fleeting and perishable—which I used so earnestly to seek, and for which I even served God: seeing it, but not understanding. For this peace appears to be peace, but is not understood; it deceives the eyes, for it is fleeting and perishable.

VERS. 4.—“For there is no regard for their death; and there is firmness in their scourging.”

“For there is no regard.” [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine.] He briefly explains why this peace has been given to them: namely, because there is no turning aside from their death—another reading—that is, because a certain and eternal death awaits them, which does not turn away from them, nor they from it; and there is firmness in their scourging, that is, their lash is firm, not temporal but eternal. Therefore they are not now [Col. 0670D] afflicted.

VERS. 5.—“They are not in the labour of men, nor shall they be scourged with men.”

“In the labour of men,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin] that is, of the saints. For they are not now scourged together with the saints because eternal punishment is being prepared for them.

Or, according to our text: They possess this peace because God has no merciful regard for their death; that is, he does not free them from the death of sin. Nor is there firmness, that is, healing consolidation, in their scourging. By their death and scourging he means their sins, which God does not regard in order to heal them. [Col. 0671A] The meaning is: God does not show them mercy by making their wounds whole.

Or thus: “There is no regard for their death.” He says this by comparison with an incurable patient, from whom nothing is withheld. So too God, seeing them incurable, does not draw them back from evils, but gives them over to the desires of their heart (Romans 1); the other expressions do not change.

Or explain it thus: What peace the wicked have. [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: I saw this peace of sinners: namely, because there is no turning aside from their death—that is, they do not die soon, but live long. And there is no firmness, or scourging, in their wound, because even if at times a blow is inflicted upon them, it is not made firm so that the correcting lash may endure. Hence it follows: “They are not in the labour of men,” namely of the saints; they recover quickly from sickness and wounds, unlike [Col. 0671B] righteous persons, who are shaken by the lashes of tribulations. Hence he adds: “Nor shall they be scourged with men,” for correction; and because things thus go prosperously for them now:

VERS. 6.—“Therefore pride has held them fast; they are covered with their iniquity and impiety.”

Therefore pride has held them fast, [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus] as though with certain hands, so that they cannot escape. It is worse to be held fast by pride than to be proud in any manner; hence they themselves are wicked. This is the meaning of “they are covered”: I do not say merely clothed, as though they had a free head; rather, they are wholly covered, on every side, lest they come to their senses. Hence another reading has: “They are wrapped about,” with iniquity toward their neighbour and with their own impiety, because they blaspheme against God. Thus they neither see nor are their inward parts [Col. 0671C] seen. They are not seen because those thought happy are miserable within; they do not see because unrestrained security nourishes contempt. To heighten their guilt, he adds:

VERS. 7.—“Their iniquity came forth as though from fatness; they passed into the inclination of the heart.”

“Their iniquity came forth as though from fatness.” [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus.] As though he said: They are wicked, and their wickedness has come openly forth, as though from fatness—that is, from abundance, not from the leanness of necessity. Some are evil from leanness, that is, necessity; others from abundance. Thus a poor man steals from want, while a rich man steals from greed. Such persons have passed beyond the straight way and the measure of human beings, because they do not think themselves equal to other people, despising the poor, though life receives both alike naked and decay after death consumes both equally. I mean that they press onward into the inclination of their heart, doing what pleases them. Or, “they passed”—that is, they rushed from vices into vices, away from straight paths, in order to fulfil the inclination [Col. 0671D] of the heart. As though he said: They do this from desire, not necessity. To show that they sinned more grievously than if they had acted unawares, he adds:

VERS. 8.—“They thought and spoke wickedness; they spoke iniquity on high.”

“They thought and spoke wickedness.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] It was not enough for them to have it within unless they poured it out externally and taught others. They spoke iniquities not fearfully but “on high,” that is, openly—in public, aloft, clearly, for all to hear, and proudly. Or, they spoke “unto the height,” that is, against the Most High: they blasphemed against God. And:

VERS. 8.—“They set their mouth in heaven, and their tongue passed over the earth.”

“They set their mouth in heaven,” [Alcuin, Interlinear Gloss, Augustine, Jerome, Cassiodorus] that is, they speak of heaven and lofty matters as though they were gods. Thus they either threaten or arrange whatever they please as though their dignity were immortal. Or, they set their mouth in heaven, that is, they speak proudly against God, blaspheming him by saying either that God does not know their evils or that he does not punish them.

“And their tongue passed over the earth,” or “was upon the earth,” [Augustine, Jerome] that is, they speak beyond the measure [Col. 0672B] of human nature, as though they were immortal. For they pass beyond all earthly things, since they do not consider that, as human beings, they may soon die; their tongue passes beyond human frailty. Or thus: “Their tongue passed,” or, in another reading, “walked about,” exceeding the proper measure; though they are on earth—that is, though they themselves are on earth—yet they exceed the measure. Or thus: their tongue, being on earth—that is, their speech having become earthly—“passed,” that is, failed, because it is feeble outside the reason of truth. Another reading has “walked about”; this is from Jerome’s translation according to the Hebrew, *tihalac*, “it shall walk.”

PART II. VERS. 9.—“Therefore my people shall return here, and full days shall be found in them.”

“Therefore [my people] shall return.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] [Col. 0672C] The second part, in which Asaph, explaining his own error and that of others, arising from the prosperity of the ungodly, says that he turned from it to a better judgment, entering God’s sanctuary in order to investigate the truth of the matter. As though he said: Since these temporal goods belong to the wicked, from which the evils mentioned above arise, therefore, having considered that these evils arise from prosperity, my people, who had departed from truth, shall return to it, so as to be “here,” that is, in this judgment in which I now stand. Or, “shall return hither,” that is, shall return to God, to truth.

But when shall they return? Behold: when “full days shall be found in them,” that is, when the fullness of time comes, and so forth, when the Son was sent, who taught them to despise these things and seek eternal things. For the days are full in which Christ came. Hence the Apostle: “When therefore the fullness of time had come,” etc. (Galatians 4). These, then, are those among the Jews who knew Christ. Or, my people shall return to truth, and thus full, [Col. 0672D] that is, perfect and eternal, days shall be found in them in the future, even if they do not now appear.

VERS. 10.—“And they said: How does God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High?”

“And they said.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Here Asaph explains how his people began to err. As though he said: Whence shall the people return? Behold, because before their conversion they said in such a thought—from which they have now returned, choosing true things—whether, that is, if, there is knowledge in the Most High, that is, in God: does God know these things or not? They do not yet say with a hardened mind, “He does not know,” but they still hesitate and are near to health; and from so grave an illness salvation is nearer, just as patients close to recovery are more violently distressed.

If someone answers, “He knows,” they ask again: “And how does God know?” Does he know in such a way as to care for these things, or in such a way as not to care? If someone asks them why they hesitate about this, they answer: God seems to us not to know, or not to care, because the wicked are happy.

VERS. 11.—“Behold, these are sinners, and abounding in the age they obtained riches.”

For behold, these sinners obtained riches by violence in the world, [Remigius, Augustine] and not small riches but abundant ones. As though he said: I was not a sinner in order that I might have riches; but I see the opposite occurring.

VERS. 12.—“And I said: Therefore in vain I have justified my heart, and washed my hands among the innocent.”

“And I said.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The following words are still spoken in the person of the doubting people: Therefore, since they do not serve and yet possess wealth, “in vain I have justified my heart.” He says that he was deceived by foolish thoughts, so that, having rejected them, he may have cured us better. Of these he adds: “And in vain I washed my hands among the innocent,” that is, my works, not merely my thoughts.

VERS. 13.—“And I was scourged all day long, and my chastisement was in the mornings.”

“And in vain I was scourged all day long.” [Augustine, Jerome.] [Col. 0673C] As though he said: I serve well and am scourged; the wicked person does not serve and is honoured. And in vain was my chastisement for evils committed, “in the mornings,” that is, diligent and prompt. For mine is not delayed, whereas theirs is either late or nonexistent; or it is in the morning prayers.

VERS. 14.—“If I said, ‘I will tell it thus’: behold, I rejected the nation of your children.”

“If I said.” [Augustine.] Behold, this man now restrains himself by the authority of the saints; and, now near to truth, he reasons thus: “And I said: If I shall tell,” that is, maintain, “thus”—namely, that God does not care for these matters and that someone lives justly in vain—“behold, I have rejected,” that is, abandoned, “the nation of your children,” that is, of the holy patriarchs and prophets. For all of them—Abraham [Col. 0673D] and the rest—teach otherwise; I must yield to them. I am not wiser than them all.

[Cassiodorus.] Or according to another reading: Where we have, “and my chastisement was in the mornings,” another reading has, “and my judge was in the morning.” The meaning is as follows. Until this point Asaph had hesitated in the uncertain matter of his deliberation. He now says through whose teaching he knew the truth. As though he said: While hesitating, I said these things. And in this hesitation Christ, who rose in the morning, was my judge. Behold, the remedy now: Christ is judge, because he showed the way of truth and, rising in the morning, lifted our hope from the world to heaven.

“And I said: If I shall tell thus.” This does not change. “Behold, the nation of your children, for which I had made provision,” [Augustine] or “to which I sang in harmony,” another reading—understand: it meets and confronts [Col. 0674A] me. That is, the earlier preaching which I gave to the Israelites confronts me: that they should worship God, who created all things and renders to each according to his works. The teaching of the Fathers, with which I agreed and to which I was fitted, confronts me, lest I should reject the nation of the Fathers or contradict my earlier teaching.

158 VERS. 16.—“I thought to know this; it is labour before me.”

“I thought,” or “considered,” or “to know,” or “to understand,” this; or, in another reading, “I undertook to know this,” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus] that is, the truth of the matter. He had not previously done this when he said that God did not care for these things. Now this man is being recalled from his fall, since he does not presume to know in opposition to the saints. He has now [Col. 0674B] the first degree of knowledge. The first degree of knowledge is when one knows that one does not know what one previously seemed to know.

[Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] The whole may also be understood otherwise: namely, that this foolish people did not doubt, but disputed against God, as follows. Whence shall they turn from such a thought? “And,” that is, because before their conversion they said, “How does God know?” How can he be said to know what happens here, when he does not punish? As though he who does not care for human affairs knows nothing whatever. And indeed, [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] if there is knowledge in the Most High, there is failure here; then God is unjust—understand, he who permits the wicked. Therefore God seems to them not to know these things, because behold, sinners themselves, abounding in the world, have obtained riches. This does not change.

To refute this foolish people, however, Asaph replies. As though he said: They said these things; and, to refute them, I said this: Therefore, if what you say is so—that God is unjust and ignorant—the following absurdities result: “In vain I have justified my heart,” and “in vain I washed my hands among the innocent.” This does not change. And: “In vain I was scourged all day long”; this too does not change. And in vain was my chastisement in my hands.

“If I said”: Here he shows another absurdity and begins to resolve the question by the most approved authority of the saints, showing that matters are otherwise than they say. [Augustine, Alcuin.] “And I said” against them: If I shall “tell,” that is, maintain, thus: “Behold, I have rejected the nation of your children,” that is, the teaching of the prophets and patriarchs, who all taught that God is just and knows all things. I have judged it to be rejected, though it is not; and thus through these absurdities it is plain that God is neither unjust nor ignorant.

“I thought,” or “considered.” As though he said: By the aforesaid absurdities I wish to prove that God is not unjust; but I am now considering how this may be so. I do not yet fully resolve how he is just while giving evils to the good and good things to the wicked; it is not yet plainly clear to me. But “I thought,” or “considered,” “to know,” or “to understand,” this—that is, the truth of this matter; and to know it “is labour before me,” [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine] that is, a laborious question before my eyes. For it is as though a wall stands before my face: how God cares for these matters while the wicked fare well and the good fare ill. [Col. 0675A] Or, “it is labour before me,” that is, as regards things before me, namely present things; if I attend to them, I cannot free myself from the labour of this question. Or, “it is labour before me,” that is, greater than I, overcoming me; unless God opens it, it is labour before me, though not before God. If therefore I shall be before God, it will not be labour even to me. For, attending to him, I shall pass beyond the wall of this question—which he does by entering God’s presence. For he adds: “It is labour before me.”

VERS. 17.—“Until I enter into the sanctuary of God and understand concerning their last things.”

“Until I enter into the sanctuary of God.” [Alcuin, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The sanctuary of God is Christ, in whom are all counsels concerning the children of men; as God he recognizes the deserts of each. [Col. 0675B] The meaning is: until I direct my mind to Christ, who here had no prosperity, but now reigns eternally with the Father.

Or the sanctuary of God means the Holy of Holies, that is, the secret of the divine dispensation. Or the sanctuary of God is called the divine law: one who contemplates it sees that they are condemned in judgment. And as though someone asked, “What do you do in that sanctuary?” he adds, “and I shall understand”: with the eye of my mind I look from there toward the end, where all are judged according to their merits. This is the meaning: not of myself, but stationed in the sanctuary, I shall understand through present things their last things, where the flower of worldly things withers.

PART III. VERS. 18.—“Nevertheless, because of deceits you set them there; you cast them down while they were being raised.”

“Nevertheless.” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] The third part. [Col. 0675C] Behold what this man learned in the sanctuary: namely, that the wicked are now deceived by prosperity, but afterward, in the end, must abandon every good; from this evil he himself was freed, though he too sought earthly things, yet from God. For here he says that even in this world the wicked are not exempt and unpunished, because, even if happy, they bear guilt and incur frequent ruin.

[Alcuin, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine.] As though he said: It will not only go ill for them in the future; nevertheless, even here you have set before them this flower of temporal things because of deceits: that is, because they are deceitful and in it suffer deceit themselves. They are fraudulent, committing fraud against humankind in all their wickedness; and they themselves suffer fraud, choosing earthly things and abandoning eternal goods. For while they deceitfully take something from others, [Col. 0675D] they destroy their own soul.

Another reading has: “You set them near a slippery place.” Temporal things are slippery, and those who love are near them fall. The sense is: You made for them a position near a slippery place, that is, near temporal things. You made them, as it were, deceitful by giving under the appearance of good what is evil for them, just as a deceitful person, wishing to cast another down, places him near a slippery spot. Hence follows: “You cast them down from on high.” “While they were being raised,” that is, in the very fact of their being raised—not, I say, after they have been raised, because such exaltation is a fall. Thus it is with them in the present, and likewise in the future.

VERS. 19.—“How have they become desolation? Suddenly they failed; they perished because of their iniquity.”

“How have they become.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] [Col. 0676A] He marvels at them, seeing their last things: they have become desolation, because at death they are abandoned by all things; and death comes upon them suddenly. Hence he adds: “Suddenly they failed,” as smoke fails while it rises; and they do not die in common with the good, but “they perished” eternally because of their iniquity. Thus they failed.

VERS. 21.—“Like the dream of those who rise, Lord, in your city you shall reduce their image to nothing.”

“Like the dream of those who rise,” it fails.
