[Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin.] Or, another reading: “those rising from sleep” fail; or, “the dream of one rising” fails—the person who in sleep seems rich to himself. He dreams that he possesses treasures, honours, and the like, but waking has nothing. So these persons, when they awake from this life, in which the blind sleep, [Col. 0676B] will find nothing but misery. The comparison is fitting. For we see, as though our eyes were shut, goods which, when our eyes are opened, we immediately do not find. In this life, then, it is a dream; in death they are awake and know indeed.

But lest what belongs to them now seem great, he adds: O Lord, you shall reduce their image to nothing—another reading—that is, the forms of deformity which they fashion for themselves in the city of Cain. One becomes a lion through ferocity, another a bird through fickleness, another a boar through the filth of lust. And this happens “in your city,” that is, in the sight of your people.

[Jerome, Alcuin, Augustine, Alcuin.] Or, “in your city,” that is, when your city is established from among them. Or, “in your city,” that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem, when they knock at the heavenly palace, you will say: “Depart from me, because I do not know you” [Col. 0676C] (Matthew 7).

Or by “their image” he means temporal glory, which is not true glory but merely an appearance of glory. The sense is: “You shall reduce their image”—that is, the temporal glory which they seek—“to nothing in your city,” that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem; because when the reality of the heavenly city is lacking to them, the image too will perish. Those who possess nothing of eternal blessedness will retain not even its likeness. God does this to them with justice in his heavenly city because they, in their earthly city, reduced the image of God—that is, reason—to nothing. Hence all are compared with beasts.

Or this may be understood of heretics, whose diverse images, the rich man says, are the diverse heresies and persons of heresiarchs which they have put on in various doctrines. God shall reduce these images [Col. 0676D] to nothing in his city, namely in the present Church or in the Church above the heavens. Therefore you will destroy them.

VERS. 22.—“Because my heart was inflamed, and my reins were changed; and I was reduced to nothing and did not know it.”

“Because through them my heart was inflamed with the zeal of envy,” [Cassiodorus] that is, I envied the prosperous; “and my reins,” by which one stands firm, “were changed” or loosened—that is, the constancy of my mind was loosened so that I might love prosperity. It is a grave fault to give others an occasion of sinning. “And I was reduced to nothing,” clinging to vain things and becoming wrongful toward God; “and I did not know” that I was sinning. It is great and profound ignorance not to know that you sin.

VERS. 23.—“I became as a beast before you, and I was always with you.”

[Col. 0677A] “I became as a beast before you.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] In God’s sight, those who think against holy things are in the condition of beasts. Yet, though I erred in these things and did not know God’s judgments, “I was always with you” in some fashion, because I remained apart from idols and believed in you. And you:

VERS. 24.—“You held my right hand, and in your will you led me; and with glory you received me.”

“You held my right hand.” [Augustine, Remigius, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine.]

The whole can be understood differently from the words, “Because my heart was inflamed,” and so forth. As though he said: You will not reduce only them to nothing; I too, who now say such things about the rich, once desired such things. Therefore I was then [Col. 0677B] reduced to nothing, when my steps were almost poured out, as I said above. Thus one should not despair even of persons of this kind.

This occurred because my heart was inflamed, or, in another reading, delighted, by earthly things; and then my reins—that is, carnal pleasures—were changed for the worse. That is, when earthly things pleased me, my reins were changed. “And I did not know”: namely, I was dull-minded. What does he mean by “I did not know”? Behold, “I became as a beast before you,” another reading, since in loving earthly things I did not know eternal things. Yet I did not wholly depart from God, seeking these temporal things from God rather than demons. Hence he adds: “And I was always with you.” And because, although a beast, I did not depart from God, “you held [my] hand,” and so forth.

Or the whole can be understood thus: “Because my heart was inflamed.” Behold the conversion of this Asaph. Here is shown the result of the investigation above—“How does God know?” and so forth. As though he said: You will reduce them to nothing; but I shall always be with you. Why? Because my heart was inflamed, or delighted, by love of God; and when the heart is delighted in God, my reins—that is, carnal pleasures and lusts—were changed into spiritual things: I became wholly chaste. Why were they changed? Because I was previously reduced to nothing; that is, I had earlier descended to things which are nothing. [Col. 0677C] [Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] And this was because I did not know them to be nothing. And afterward: “I became as a beast before you,” that is, I became gentle, bearing burdens.

Or the connection is thus: “Because my heart was inflamed, therefore I became as a beast before you.” [Col. 0677D] The meaning is the same. “And I shall always be with you. And you held my right hand,” or, in another reading, “the hand of my right,” that is, you guided the power of the right hand—namely, that I am with you and am a son. This is my right hand. On the left is the beast which loves these temporal things. The hand, then, is power; the right hand is that I am a son and that I am with you. For “he gave power to become children of God to those who believe in his name” (John 1).

Or, taken intransitively: “You held my right hand,” not my left. God holds the right hand when he directs one toward good works and rescues one lest one be submerged, as he rescued Peter. “And in your will,” not by my merits, “you led me” to true understanding; “and with glory you received me,” that is, you united human nature to the Word. What greater glory is there for a human being than that humanity should be united to the Word of God [Col. 0678A] and placed at God’s right hand? Or, “in eternal glory you received me,” that is, you will receive me in the resurrection, the past tense being used for the future.

PART IV. VERS. 24.—“For what have I in heaven, and what did I desire from you upon earth?”

“For what?” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The fourth part. Having seen the evil of the ungodly and his own good, he reproves himself for his former conduct—namely, for seeking earthly things from God—and changes to the contrary, comparing his earthly desire with the heavenly reward. As though he said: I blessed God for receiving me in glory, because what have I in heaven? So great and such a thing is prepared in heaven that it cannot be spoken: namely, you yourself. And what did I desire from you upon earth? How worthless a thing I desired—something which even the wicked possess. I desired what was great; and because such a reward is [Col. 0678B] mine in heaven, therefore:

VERS. 25.—“My flesh and my heart have failed; God of my heart, and God is my portion for ever.”

“My flesh has failed,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, carnal delight in action, “and my heart,” that is, evil thought. But God is the restorer, in the full chastity of my heart; he has made my heart so chaste that I now love God freely. “And God is my portion”: it is so great a thing. Others choose other things, but I choose God; this is what he has in heaven. I say, God existing for ever, unlike other things. Or, “God is my portion for ever,” because I shall never again be separated from him, but shall always be with him. Therefore the Lord is my portion.

VERS. 26.—“For behold, those who remove themselves far from you shall perish; you have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you.”

[Col. 0678C] “For behold, those who remove themselves far from you shall perish.” [Augustine.] Far from God are those who seek these temporal things not from God but from demons. He withdrew from God when he became as a beast, but he was not far away, for he says, explaining: “I am with you.” You have destroyed all who commit fornication after strange gods. Such persons are far from you. Contrary to this fornication is chaste love, which loves God freely and possesses all things in him. They act thus; but what do you do?

VERS. 27.—“But for me it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God.”

“But for me it is good to cling to God.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] In the future, because nothing is better than seeing God face to face; and now, while I am a pilgrim and have no possession, it is good for me to place my hope in the Lord God. That hope is like an anchor [Col. 0678D] cast forward onto land.

Or it may be understood of the present: “But for me it is good to cling to God” through worship. For although he erred, he did not depart from worship. The other expressions do not change. For what is this good?

VERS. 28.—“That I may declare all your preachings in the gates of the daughter of Zion.”

“That I may declare all your preachings.” [Augustine.] This is this man’s occupation in the meantime: namely, to praise God and make fellow-lovers. Where? In the gates, or courts, of the daughter of Zion, [Cassiodorus] that is, in the public assembly of the Church, which is the daughter of Zion—that is, of contemplation. For Zion is interpreted “contemplation.” Or, “in the gates of the daughter of Zion,” that is, in the concord of the apostles, who are the gates of the Church, because preaching outside the unity [Col. 0679A] of the Church is vain. Or, “in the gates of the daughter of Zion,” that is, in the virtues.

## Comparison on Psalm LXXII, “How Good Is God to Israel,” etc.

VERS. 4.—“There is no regard for their death.” The Hebrew is *EN HARSZUBOTH LEMOTHAM*. All the more recent translators render it “the bonds of death,” or “in their death,” or something similar. Because this presents obscurity, Münster added of his own: “They have no bonds of anxieties in their death.” The Campensis text reads: “There are no burdens under which they collapse”; the Paraphrase: “Worn out by age, they are extinguished without prolonged suffering.”

If we understand someone to be drawn back and to cease from sin through repeatedly reflecting upon death—to which, by nature’s condition, he is necessarily bound and subject as though by certain chains—we might appropriately say that he has “the bonds of his death.” Or, if he is allowed to live for a long time, even to grey hair, and is not pressed toward death, he would be regarded as departing, as it were, unbound and enjoying life’s sweetness, since he is not overtaken by sudden or early death. In this way, therefore, the translations of these writers could be brought into agreement with the Vulgate edition.

To the point: the wicked do not strive to keep their last day in view, but add sins to sins as though they would never die. It also often happens that the godly are snatched away by a premature death, while the utterly depraved live out their days happily and, unshaken by any tribulations, reach decrepit old age by an unimpeded course. But because St Jerome translated otherwise than the moderns and accords with our edition, when he says that they have not reflected upon their death, I not unreasonably conjecture that the Septuagint and Jerome read the Hebrew word *HARZUBOTH* as composed of two words. For *HAZATZ* in Hebrew sometimes means to determine or decree a judgment, and *BATH* sometimes means the pupil of the eye. How this corresponds to the “regard” spoken of by the Septuagint and to Jerome’s “reflection” is plain even without my saying so. The Roman Psalter and Augustine have another reading, which is explained.

“There is no firmness in their scourging.” Pratensis, Sanctes, Münster, and the interpreters for Cajetan render the final term “their strength”: “their strength is sound,” or something similar. Jerome, Pellicanus, Campensis, and Nebiensis understand it as “their vestibules” or “their palaces.” For these derive it from the root *ILLEM*, “he gathers sheaves”; whereas the former derive it from the word *AJAL*, “strength,” as Sanctes previously indicated in his *Thesaurus*. Finally, the Septuagint took *aleph* in place of *he*: *HULAM*, “their scourging,” from the stem *HALAM*, “he struck.”

VERS. 6.—“They are covered with their iniquity [Col. 0679D] and impiety.” The Hebrew word *SCHITH* is very ambiguous and has supplied material for many interpretations. Jerome agrees with us: “They surrounded themselves with iniquity.” Nebiensis agrees with us word for word. Münster is nearly of this sense: “A garment of violence envelops them.” Nor is Sanctes far away when he says: “He shall cover himself in order to take prey for himself.” Campensis comes very close. Some render it “firmament”; Pellicanus: “They shall cover the firmament, iniquity to them”; others, “ornament”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “He shall clothe himself with an ornament of iniquity for himself.” Pratensis is far different: “Their iniquity shall envelop their offspring.” Felinus does not depart from this. The Hebrew reads: *IATOPH SCITH HAMAS LAMO*. We must hold firmly to what is certain and leave uncertain what is uncertain.

VERS. 7.—“Their iniquity came forth as though from fatness.” Jerome: “Their eyes proceeded from fatness.” Nor do the other Hebrew interpreters disagree. It is not improbable to me that the Septuagint read *AVONEMO*, [Col. 0680A] “their iniquities,” for *ENEMO*, since the letters are almost the same; and, as has been proved above, confusion through the mutual interchange of *yod* and *waw* is easy.

VERS. 8.—“They thought and spoke wickedness.” For the word “they thought,” the Hebrew has *IAMIQU*, and they do not fully know what it signifies. Jerome translated “they mocked”; Pratensis, “they will cause [others] to waste away”; Sanctes, “they dissolved,” which he otherwise sought to render clearer through a more explicit paraphrase; Münster, “they make others unrestrained”; and Campensis, “they are a terror to all whom they meet because of their power.” Yet in its margin the edition has another reading: namely, “all things are foul to them.” The interpreters for Cajetan translate actively, “they shall liquefy”; Pellicanus, Nebiensis, and Felinus, passively, “they shall melt” or “be dissolved.” It would be better to believe either the Septuagint or Jerome.

Yet not one of these agrees with them, even if the ungodly, in their thoughts, are as it were liquefied until they bring them into action [Col. 0680B] and fashion others like themselves. This was indicated as a punishment immediately at the end of the preceding verse: “they passed into the inclination of the heart.” They also mock those whom they see to be unlike their own conduct.

VERS. 10.—“Therefore my people shall return here.” For the word “here,” Pratensis and Pellicanus render “shaken”—namely, the people. The rest follow the Vulgate reading, because *HALOM* is a locative pronoun, while *HALAM* means “he was shaken.” I do not know what the Campensis edition and the Paraphrase intend. The former says: “Therefore the flock of those who follow them is present here”; the latter: “Because of such persons, the people of God shall fluctuate, turning now this thing, now that, in their minds.” Yet Münster too explains in his scholia what we say: “My people shall return hither,” that is, they devote themselves to the same pursuits as those among whom the ungodly live. Felinus follows the same view; let them see to it. One thing is certain: they differ far and widely from the explanation of the saints.

When they say “his people,” this is because of the fluid or mutual interchange of *yod* and *waw*: *AMMO*, or *AMMI*.

“Full days shall be found in them.” Jerome: “Who shall be found full in them?” Therefore it is absolutely certain that he read *MI*, “who,” where the manuscripts now have *ME*, “waters.” The Septuagint, however, had *IEME*, “days.” Since *me*, “waters,” in the plural and construct state did not fit well with the immediately following word, namely “full,” through a paternal error Sanctes and Münster supplied “of a cup,” producing “waters of a full cup.” Again, where we say “shall be found”—and Jerome agrees—they render “shall be pressed out.” For they derived *IMATZU* from the verb *MATZATZ*, whereas the Septuagint and Jerome derived it from *MATZATH*, “he found.”

VERS. 13.—“And I said: Therefore in vain.” These two words, “and I said,” were added by the Septuagint to express what was understood but suppressed. The Campensis edition similarly does this in the following manner: “Thus therefore I reasoned with myself.” This sort of procedure has been mentioned more than once.

“I washed my hands among the innocent.” Faber and Coecus struggle in vain to maintain that it is better and more fitting to say, “I washed my hands in innocence.” The Hebrew indeed has *NIQAION*, “innocence.” If we interpret this of Christ our Saviour, the head, it is admittedly more fitting to say that he washed his hands in innocence than among the innocent, since all have sinned. But since the psalm is most plainly also about the members whose feet were almost moved by the peace of the wicked, so that they appear to waver and to doubt God’s providence—though carnal wisdom is speaking—it is appropriately said: “I washed my hands among the innocent.”

### Verse 15

“Behold, I have rejected the generation of your children.” Jerome and the other interpreters, in place of Cajetan’s rendering, have “I have denied.” These do not conflict. Pagninus has “I have transgressed”; Felinus, “I shall have acted unjustly”; Münster, “I have deceived.” Nebiensis agrees. Sanctes made the sense conform to his own opinion: “Behold,” he says, “the generation of your children will say that I have transgressed,” although, beyond doubt, *bagadti* means “I have rejected” in Hebrew, even if it may denote other things as well. For Jerome explains that rendering, “I have transgressed against the generation of your children.”

### Verse 18

“Yet because of deceits you have set them.” The Hebrew has “in slippery places,” instead of “because of deceits”: *bahalaqoth*, as Jerome and the others render it. But *ḥalaq* denotes “to smooth,” “to flatter,” “to cajole”; hence the derivative noun may suitably mean “frauds.” Thus Nebiensis translates, “in flattery.” The Master, however, in his exposition brings it into agreement with the other wording.

The construction offended Faber and Coecus so greatly that they finally insist on erasing the preposition “because of,” so that it should read, “you have set deceits for them”; otherwise the sense would remain incomplete. Or else the word “evils” should be added, as is read in Greek, *kaka* (“evils”), [Col. 0681B] and in the Roman psalmody. Yet Augustine’s exposition indicates that *deceits* ought, for the coherence of the sense, to be supplied a second time: “Because of deceits you have set deceits for them.” For he says: “Because they practise fraud, they suffer fraud.”

160. “You cast them down while they were being lifted up.” Jerome has “into destruction.” Others translate “into desolations” or “ruins,” which is what we express by “while they were being lifted up.” The Hebrew is *lemasschuoth*. Certainly, however, it makes clear that the elevation was unto a more grievous fall. Therefore there is no difference of meaning. Even if that word derived from *nasa*, with the point called *smol*, it would undoubtedly signify “elevations.”

### Verse 19

“They perished because of their iniquity.” Modern translators say, “They were consumed by terrors.” What, after all, is so dreadful as sinning and falling into the hands of the living God? Although *ballahoth* may be derived from *balal*, that is, “he confused.” [Col. 0681C] Hence Bel is the name of an idol. And from the same root, if Münster is to be believed, the Hebrews derive *tablith*, that is, “confusion,” “crime.” Moreover, Rabbi David, as reported by Sanctes, maintains that *ballahoth* is formed by metathesis in place of *behaloth*, as though the transposition produced that meaning. Yet Jerome translates, “they were consumed as though they were not,” so that the word appears to incline toward *balah*, “he grew old, became worn out,” or toward *habal*, “he acted vainly.”

### Verse 20

“In your city.” Sanctes alone, so far as I have been able to see, says, “when he has sustained them.” Why he does so, let that man look to his own judgment; for the Hebrew itself, *ba‘ir*, means “in your city.” It is true, [Col. 0682A] however, that the Chaldean paraphrast comes somewhat near to this: “On the day of the great judgment,” he says, “he will cause them to rise from the house of the grave.”

“You will reduce their image to nothing.” Jerome has exactly the same. The others translate, “you will despise” or “you will neglect”; yet Münster in his scholium interprets *tzalmam tibzeh* as “you will reduce their image to nothing.”

### Verse 21

“My heart was inflamed.” Many translate, “my heart will wither.” The Hebrew word *ḥametz* is understood in two ways: both as “it fermented” and as “it acted violently.” Hence Jerome translates, “my heart was contracted.” Our interpreters expressed the metaphor. Augustine and the Roman psalmody have, “my heart was delighted,” apparently in a contrary sense. For Scripture uses leaven sometimes in a good and sometimes in an evil sense: Matthew 16, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees”; again, Matthew 13, “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven.”

[Col. 0682B] “My kidneys were changed.” Modern translators render: “My kidneys were pierced with stings,” or “I was sharpened in my kidneys.” Although reconciliation is easy, it is nevertheless likely that the Septuagint confused closely related roots, namely *shanan* and *shanah*: the former means in Hebrew “he sharpened”; the latter, “he was changed.” Jerome, however, translated, “my loins were like smoking fire,” which the Targum nearly also does, according to Sanctes: “my kidneys were like fire.” Jerome evidently read the two words as *ashchan*. For *esh*, with the *tsere* point, means “fire,” and *ashchan* means “smoke.”

“I was reduced to nothing.” The Hebrews have *ba‘ar*. Hebraists render it “foolish,” “without understanding.” But since its root, *bi‘er*, means “he consumed” and “he destroyed,” what prevents the interpreters from translating it as “reduction to nothing”?

### Verse 24

“What have I in heaven?” Münster added “apart from you.” If he does this for clearer meaning, let him allow the same principle to the authority of the ancient interpreters. Immediately afterward, “And apart from you what have I desired upon earth?” is read simply in Hebrew: “and with you I have desired nothing on earth,” where something must be supplied; or, as Münster has it, “I have desired no one on earth.” The interpreters repeatedly did such things as seemed fitting. As to our reading it interrogatively while others make the latter clause declarative, the meaning is not harmed.

### Verse 25

“God of my heart.” *Tzur lebabi*: “the strength” or “fortitude of my heart.” It is well known, moreover, that “the strong one” and “the rock” are used of God.

### Verse 29

“In the gates of the daughter of Zion.” These words are omitted in the Hebrew; perhaps they have been added from the psalm.

### Verse 9

In Greek it is written: *en tais pylai tē[s] thygatros Siōn*—“in the gates of the daughter of Zion.”

## Psalm LXXIII

[Col. 0681]

### Title of the Psalm: “The Understanding of Asaph”

[Col. 0681D]

“Why, O God, have you cast us off unto the end?” [Aug.] The title is “The Understanding of Asaph.” *Asaph* in Hebrew, and *Synagogue* in Greek, is called in Latin *congregatio*, “assembly.” Although an assembly may be a collection of anything whatsoever—animals, persons, stones, or the like—the Synagogue is properly called the assembly of the people, the children of Israel. Thus Asaph—that is, the Synagogue, a name properly applied only to the Jews—speaks here; but according to the grain, not according to the chaff.

The Law was given to the Synagogue, indeed by God through Moses; but grace and truth came through Christ (John 1). Grace, because what was then commanded is now fulfilled through charity. Truth, because what was promised is bestowed. In the Law and the Prophets there were three things: commandments, sacraments, and promises. The commandments were almost entirely the same as those of the Gospel: the moral commandments were the same; the ceremonial ones were not. The sacraments were not the same, because those only promised, whereas these give salvation. The promises were not the same, because there earthly things were first promised to fleshly persons; here eternal things are promised to spiritual persons. There likewise, under the figure of temporal things, spiritual things were promised to spiritual persons; hence those temporal things were, as it were, sacraments of spiritual realities hidden within them.

Those temporal things, therefore, were taken away when truth came. There is no anointing, priest, prophet, or temple: all have been laid waste—the things on account of which they killed Christ. This desolation [Col. 0683A] or destruction is lamented here by Asaph—not foolishly, but with understanding, discerning earthly things from heavenly, and the Old Testament from the New, so that you may know what you ought to choose from them. The meaning is: this is Asaph’s understanding—that is, this psalm discloses what faithful Asaph understands: [Cassiod.] namely, that truth has come and figures have been removed, and that eternal rather than temporal things must be sought.

This is the first psalm of lamentation for Jerusalem; two others on the same subject follow, namely the seventy-eighth and the one hundred thirty-sixth. [Note: [Col. 0683D] From Cassiodorus, on the Psalms.] This is a kind of discourse full of charity. For it teaches us to weep with those who weep; and David here weeps with greater compassion than Jeremiah. David weeps while Jerusalem is still prosperous, before the captivity has been seen, [Col. 0683B] just as Jeremiah afterward wept when the captivity had been accomplished. The overthrow of the city is so often set forth in lamentation in order that the hardness of the Jews might be frightened by calamities.

[Aug., Cassiod.] Intention: he urges us, leaving figures behind, to pass over to truth. Method: the psalm has three parts. First, describing Jerusalem’s irreparable overthrow, he asks its cause, as though wondering and lamenting; he prays for the rejected people and for vengeance upon the destroyers—a vengeance useful to them and already accomplished. Second, he shows that salvation was wrought everywhere at Christ’s coming, at the words, “But God is our king.” Third, he prays that what is done everywhere may also be done for the Jews, at the words, “Remember.” Therefore, wondering and lamenting, he says:

### Verse 1

> “Why, O God, have you cast us off unto the end? [Col. 0683C] Has your wrath been angered against the sheep of your pasture?”

God, [Cassiod.] you who are our Creator, have cast us off as strangers to your protection. And this “unto the end,” that is, utterly; for not even your temple is spared. By this he signifies the destruction and captivity brought about by Titus. [Aug.] Or: you have cast us off until the end of the age. Or: you have cast us off in order to send us to the End, that is, to Christ, who is the End; and your wrath, or mind, has been angered.

[Gl. int., Cassiod., Aug.] He does not simply say, “You are angry,” or “You rage,” but “wrath has been angered,” so that by this doubling its extreme severity may be shown, against the sheep. He calls them sheep in order to move the mercy of the compassionate shepherd; “of your pasture,” or “of your flock,” he says because we punish more moderately those whom we remember once to have been ours. And “why?” As though he said: Why is this so? Is it because we did not know the shepherd? He does not reproach, but asks why.

### Verse 2

> “Remember your congregation, which you possessed from the beginning.”

“Remember.” [Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod.] He recounts benefits already bestowed, so that the judge may be more inclined to his customary mercies, and may consider his own benefits in them rather than their errors. Praying for them, therefore, he says: “Remember your congregation, Lord, which you possessed from the beginning”—that is, that people beginning with the patriarchs, who were its beginning. This is the people Israel, which he possessed, [Col. 0684A] not the Gentiles. Or, according to another reading: “which you created from the beginning.” Though he creates and orders all, he did so especially for the Jews, to whom he gave the Law. Remember, and you ought to remember, because:

### Verse 3

> “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance, Mount Zion, in which you dwelt.”

You redeemed it from Egypt. [Haym., Aug.] Behold another benefit. “The rod” or “sceptre of your inheritance,” that is, the hereditary kingdom—the Jewish people, not the Gentiles. For the congregation itself is called the rod of inheritance. Since God wished to possess it, he turned Moses’ rod into a serpent; but when it was grasped by the tail, it returned to a rod.

For when Moses said to God, “What sign shall I give the children of Israel, that they may believe you sent me?” God said to him, “What do you hold [Col. 0684B] in your hand?” He answered, “A rod.” And God said to him, “Throw it upon the ground.” He threw the rod upon the ground, and it became a serpent; Moses was terrified and fled. The Lord said to him, “Take hold of its tail.” He took hold of it, and it returned to its former condition, becoming a rod, just as it had been before (Exod. 4). It is for this reason that the congregation itself is called a rod.

Mount Zion—that is, this rod, inheritance, or congregation—is Mount Zion, where were the people, the temple, sacrifices, and all things promising Christ. Therefore they should not then have been abandoned. [Note: [Col. 0684D] From Jerome, *On the Psalms according to the Hebrew*.] Jerome gives another reading: “Mount Zion,” or “of Mount Zion,” or “in it.” Thus: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance,” namely Mount Zion. Or: “the rod of your inheritance,” namely of Mount Zion. [Cassiod.] By Zion he signifies Jerusalem.

Up to this point he has spoken of the deeds of the Old Testament, which the promised truth follows. Hence he adds: “in which”—on Mount Zion—“you dwelt, O Christ,” because there the presence of Christ in his humanity dwelt. By this he entreats that it not be given over to devastation. “In it” is either not present in that reading or is superfluous; and I pray not only for my own people, but also for the Gentiles. Hence he adds: “Lift up your hands,” etc. [Aug.]

Or it may be understood mystically. By the rod Christ is understood; by the serpent, death, because death entered the world through the serpent’s persuasion (Gen. 3). Thus, the rod in the serpent is Christ in death. Hence also the bronze serpent was raised upon wood in the wilderness, where people were bitten by serpents; whoever looked upon it was healed from serpents. That is, whoever believes in Christ dead [Col. 0684D] is delivered from eternal death.

Moses was afraid and fled. So too the apostles, when Christ died. When the tail was grasped—that is, the latter things—the serpent became a rod, because he was first killed and afterward rose again; this is the serpent’s transformation into a rod. Moses held the tail without fear because, once the resurrection was known, the disciples believed firmly. [Alcuin, Jerome, Aug.] The sense is: “Remember your congregation,” and you will remember it, because “you redeemed, at the price of yourself, the rod of your inheritance”; that is, you redeemed your inheritance through yourself as the price, through yourself as the rod. Of this rod Jeremiah says: “I see a rod of watchfulness” (Jer. 1).

Or by Moses’ rod is signified the stability of the human race, which it possessed before sin. The rod, falling to earth, was changed into a serpent, which moves by the winding turns of its body; because through the fall of sin, humanity was changed from the stability of life into the course of this mortality. When the tail is grasped, the serpent becomes a rod. The tail is the end of the age, in which we return to the hand of God and become the established kingdom of God, we who through death flowed away as through a serpent. For then humanity, returning to God’s hand in the resurrection, will receive its former stability.

The sense is: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance,” that is, you restored the former stability in humanity, so that it might be your inheritance. But because this will also be true of believing Gentiles, who are far more numerous than the Jews, he makes explicit of whom he says this: 161. “Mount Zion,” [Gl. int., Aug., Cassiod.] as though he said, “That inheritance is Mount Zion,” [Col. 0685B] that is, I do not say this concerning the Gentiles. Or: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance,” namely this Mount Zion in which you dwelt, through legal institutions that promised Christ before Christ’s advent, or through bodily presence. And while existing upon that mountain:

### Verse 4

> “Lift up your hands against their pride unto the end: how greatly has the enemy acted wickedly in the sanctuary!”

“Lift up your hands,” [Aug., Cassiod., Cassiod., Alcuin.] that is, your power, against the pride of those by whom Jerusalem was overthrown—the kings of the Gentiles—so that you may turn their pride into humility, leading them unto the End, that is, Christ, just as you were casting us off unto the End. We now see this fulfilled, because the Christian religion flourished at Rome. It is well said, “lift up,” because Rome, once very superstitious, became most holy.

Or thus: “Mount Zion”—as though he said, “Which inheritance is a mountain because of the loftiness of its virtues, Zion because of contemplation; in which,” that is, in which matter, or because of which matter, “you dwelt in it”; or “in it” is superfluous. “In it, lift up your hands against their pride.” This is not altered. In “how greatly” he briefly recounts the history of the destruction.

[Aug., Cassiod., Alcuin., Cassiod.] As though he said: Therefore lift up your hands, because the idolatrous and Gentile enemy acted wickedly—that is, worked maliciously—in the holy things, namely in the temple, priesthood, and the other sacraments, which were holy things belonging to you. God permitted this because, now that the reality had come, they no longer prefigured anything. “How greatly he acted wickedly” is said with astonishment: certainly, greatly; for the priests and temple ministries became spoil, and the whole people were either slain or taken captive. The enemy did this, namely the Roman army. To designate it, he has by prolepsis—that is, anticipation—used “their.” He says that the enemy acted wickedly “in the sanctuary,” in order that contempt for the holy temple, in which the Godhead seems despised, may arouse indignation against the presumptuous.

### Verse 5

> “And those who hated you gloried in the midst of your solemn feast.”

And they gloried in their victory. [Alcuin, Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod.] Here is proof that they acted not from good zeal. They gloried, although punishment ordinarily [Col. 0686A] follows crime; these turn it into glory, these haters of you, servants of demons who are in no way to be tolerated. And this occurred in the midst of your solemnity. Jerusalem was overthrown when the Paschal solemnity was being observed, at which they crucified the Lord. Gathered together, they raged; gathered together, they perished. Or, not in some remote place, but in the midst of your court, according to another reading, they committed sacrileges. And:

### Verse 6

> “They set up their signs as signs; and they did not recognize them as one does at the entrance above.”

“They set up their signs,” or trophies, [Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] namely Roman standards—the dragons and eagles used in battle—or statues and every sort of memorial of victory. They first placed these in the temple, and they were accustomed also to place them over gates as signs [Col. 0686B] of triumph. “Signs,” that is, conspicuous signs: with grief he repeats “signs,” in order to hasten vengeance, provoke the judge, and show that they attributed the deed to their own powers. Hence he adds, “and they did not recognize,” namely that this came from God and was accomplished by God’s ordinance.

As though he said: They did not consider it. They first set up signs in the temple just as statues of rulers are customarily placed at the entrance—that is, at gates—or in roads and streets. “Above,” that is, upon elevated places, on a tower or some lofty position. Or, according to another reading, “they did not recognize in the going forth from above”: they did not recognize that this permission proceeded from God. The meaning is the same. And:

### Verse 7

> “As in a forest of trees, they cut down its doors together with axes; with axe and adze they cast it down.”

[Col. 0686C] “As in a forest of trees,” [Cassiod., Gl. int., Aug., Cassiod.] that is, without any regard or reverence, “they cut down”—that is, shattered—its temple doors with axes, though formerly care had been devoted to adorning them. They did this “together,” that is, being united and steadfastly conspiring as one. Note that before the temple was constructed, he prophesies its overthrow. “With axe and adze,” or “with a hatchet,” according to another reading, “and with the breaker they cast it down,” namely the city. The axe cuts beams; the adze works more finely. By this he says that both great and small things were destroyed, so that the city might be utterly ruined and laid waste. First they were cut down; afterward fire devoured all. Hence it follows:

### Verse 8

> “They burned your sanctuary with fire [Col. 0686D] upon the ground; they defiled the tabernacle of your name.”

“They burned with fire.” [Cassiod., Gl. int., Cassiod.] What could not be cut down was burned: your sanctuary—not merely private houses—and they defiled upon earth the tabernacle of your name, which Solomon built in the Lord’s name. For they could not defile that which is in heaven; therefore everyone ought the more to labor for that heavenly sanctuary. Or: “They defiled the tabernacle of your name,” that is, they cast down to the ground the pinnacles raised in praise of God. He magnifies their crime so that vengeance upon them may be more severe.

### Verse 9

> “Their whole race said in its heart: ‘Let us cause all God’s feast-days to cease from the earth.’”

The Romans said in their heart, their whole race together, [Col. 0687A] [Gl. int.] that is, all of them together, not merely a few. What did they say? This: “Let us cause all feast-days to cease from the earth,” so that there may be no glory of God’s name on earth. I say feast-days “of God”; the phrase “of God” is interposed by this Asaph himself. For those who served idols did not call God the one whose temple they were overthrowing.

### Verse 10

> “We have not seen our signs; there is now no prophet, and he will no longer know us.”

“Our signs.” [Aug., Gl. int., Alcuin.] Behold Asaph’s understanding. The foretold evils are a lesson to him. In them Asaph understands that all signs were overthrown because the reality had come. As though he said: Everything has been overthrown; and when all this has happened, moreover, “we have not seen our signs.” That is: with all these things overthrown, the signs cease, because there is now no prophet, as there was in former captivities, to foretell their deliverance; “and he will no longer know us,” that is, God will no longer bring us back from evils—or “yet,” according to another reading—until the Jew acknowledges him.

Or it may be read rebukingly, according to another text: “Have we not seen our signs?” As though he said: These evils rightly happen to us, because have we not seen our signs? That is: We saw them and did not understand. And indeed we saw them, because this is the sign: that there is no prophet, priest, or anointing. Hence: “When the Holy of Holies comes, your anointing shall cease” (Dan. 9). “And he will no longer know us”: some prophet, or God through a prophet, will no longer make known that Christ is to come, because he has already come.

### Verse 11

> “How long, O God, will the enemy reproach? Will the adversary provoke your name unto the end?”

“How long,” etc. [Aug., Cassiod., Gl. int., Alcuin., Aug.] Asaph cries out as an abandoned sick man who preferred to dismiss the physician rather than be healed. As though he said: These evils are upon us; but, O God, how long will the enemy—that is, the Gentile people—reproach? And, as though he said, “He will soon know,” he adds, “How long?” “The adversary provokes.” That is: The enemy will reproach as long as the adversary, namely the Jew, provokes your name. Thus, while they provoke you, you angrily chastise the Jews through the Gentiles, doing this so that in this way you may make them know you by leading them unto the End, that is, Christ.

Or: the adversary provokes unto the end of the age, that is, until, with the tail grasped (Exod. 4), there is a return to the kingdom, when the remnant is saved (Rom. 11). And, O Lord:

### Verse 12

> “Why do you turn away your hand and your right hand from the midst of your bosom unto the end?”

“Why do you turn away your hand and your right hand,” [Aug.] that is, the Jews, “from the midst of your bosom,” not bringing it unto the End, that is, Christ? The hand and right hand are the Jewish people. After the sign of the rod mentioned above, the sign of Moses’ hand is added here. For after the event concerning the rod, God gave Moses another sign, saying: “Put your hand into your bosom.” He put it in; then God said: “Bring [Col. 0688A] it out.” He brought it out, and it was found white, that is, unclean (Exod. 4). For whiteness on skin is leprosy, not brightness. Again he said: “Put it back into your bosom”; he put it back, and it returned to its own color.

This hand is the people of God, which, sent out from him, became unclean; but called back into the bosom, it returned to its own color. He says, therefore: “Why do you turn away your hand and your right hand from the midst of your bosom?” That is: How long, and why, do you estrange your people from yourself, so that it remains unclean outside? How long do you not call back the hand, unto the End—that is, so that it may know the Savior?

[Rem., Aug., Cassiod., Gl. int.] Or the whole passage may be read as spoken in the person of despairing Jews, beginning at “They said.” The evils already expounded could have moved the judge to mercy, had Jewish pride not been obstinate. Angrily and madly, upon seeing the overthrow, their whole race said in its heart: “Let us cause all God’s feast-days to cease from the earth.” That is, let us cast away God’s law, which did not deliver us, since we do not even see our signs—those formerly performed for our fathers. They speak foolishly, as though, after their guilt, what had been done for devout ancestors were owed to them.

The words are still those of despairing Jews: “There is now no prophet for us to consult,” as formerly happened in adversities. Since after Christ they no longer had prophets, they said they had been abandoned. Hence follows: “And he will no longer know us.” These things are said lest it appear to be God’s harshness that Asaph was not heard for them, since they deservedly endure such things because amid them they do not repent.

They said these things; but how long will the enemy, namely the Jew, reproach you, O God? How long will the adversary provoke your name? That is, how long do you permit the reproaches of the Jews? He does not say this because he wishes them to perish, but to be changed for the better. Then he shows how long by adding “unto the End,” that is, unto the evening of the world, when the Jews will be converted. Then he asks why God casts them off until then, adding: “Why do you turn away your hand and your right hand from the midst of your bosom,” or “court,” “unto the End?”

## Part II. Verse 13

> “But God is our king before the ages; he has wrought salvation in the midst of the earth.”

[Col. 0688D] “But God.” [Alcuin, Aug.] In the second part, once the signs have been destroyed, he shows the reality itself: namely, that at Christ’s advent salvation was wrought everywhere. Understanding Asaph says: We, as though abandoned by God and without understanding, cry, “There is now no prophet,” etc. But God, our king, who is before the ages, is not temporal, because “in the beginning was the Word” (John 1). He wrought this in the midst of the earth, that is, everywhere: namely salvation. And we Jews sleep.

Or let us at last return to understanding, so that we may learn the salvation God has wrought. He wrought it so that human beings might learn to seek eternal rather than temporal things. Behold, blindness happened in Israel, so that the fullness of grace might enter and thus all Israel might be saved (Rom. 11). If Israel did not go before, let it at least follow.

[Col. 0689A] Or “he wrought salvation,” that is, the incarnation, [Note: [Col. 0689D] Jerome here and in Ezekiel 5 and 38.] “in the midst of the earth,” that is, in Jerusalem, which is said to be in the middle of the earth. As though he said: the navel of the world, where God became man. Then he explains what salvation God wrought:

### Verse 14

> “You established the sea in your strength; you shattered the heads of dragons in the waters.”

“You established,” [Aug., Cassiod.] as though he said: Our temporal salvation was overthrown; but you established in your strength, that is, your power, the sea—that is, the Gentiles who surrounded Judaea in the middle. And you shattered the heads of dragons, that is, the pride of demons, in the waters of baptism.

Or literally: you established in your strength the passage through the Red Sea, so that there might be a dry way through its midst. He then adds the mystery signified by that figure: you shattered, that is, annihilated, the heads of dragons, that is, unclean spirits, in the waters of baptism.

### Verse 15

> “You broke the heads of the dragon; you gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia.”

“You also broke the heads,” [Jerome, Aug.] that is, the powers, of the dragon, the prince of demons, namely Leviathan. Or, according to another reading, “the head of the dragon,” that is, the beginning of sin, which is pride; woman—that is, the Church, or sensuality—is commanded to watch against it.

“And you gave him,” namely the devil, “as food to the peoples of Ethiopia,” that is, of all the nations, which had formerly been black with sins but afterward were made white by the brightness of virtues. To them the devil is food of consumption, while Christ is food of consummation: Christ is food by which we are perfected; the devil is food by which we are consumed.

This is the meaning of the molten calf’s head which the children of Israel made, as is read in Exodus. While Moses was with the Lord upon the mountain for forty days, receiving the Law, he came down from the mountain and heard the sound of Israelites playing before the calf. Girded with a sword and accompanied by the children of Levi, he went from gate to gate and struck many Jews. Then he threw the calf into the fire, so that its very form might first be destroyed. Next he crushed it bit by bit, so that it might gradually be consumed until it became dust. Finally, he put it in water and gave it to the people to drink (Exod. 32).

What is this except that idolaters are the devil’s body, just as Christians are Christ’s body? But the Israelites—that is, the apostles, who came from that people—consume the devil’s body and destroy its form by fire when, through the love of God, they teach people to refrain from evil appearance. Then they grind it little by little when they lead people gradually to renounce evils. Then they put it in water and give it to the people to drink, when through the rain of grace and the water of baptism they incorporate them into Catholic unity.

Hence Peter was told, after reptiles of every kind had been shown on a sheet: “Slay—by overthrowing evils—and eat—by building up in good things” (Acts 10). This is what it is to grind and to drink. Thus the devil, having lost his members, is consumed like food [Col. 0690A] by the peoples of Ethiopia, that is, by converted Gentiles. The same thing was also foreshadowed when Moses’ dragon swallowed the magicians’ dragons. So even now the Gentiles who believe devour the devil’s body.

Or thus: “You gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia,” because just as food is bitten by the eater, so believers bite the devil himself by reproving, accusing, and blaming him. [Cassiod., Alcuin.] Or the devil, while tempting, is food to the faithful because they advance through his temptation: purified by his assaults, they attain what they desire. Or: “You gave him as food,” in which they might delight, “to the peoples of Ethiopia” unwilling to be converted.

### Verse 16

> “You broke open fountains and torrents; you dried up the rivers of Ethan.”

[Col. 0690B] “You also broke open,” that is, opened, “fountains,” [Aug.] namely good preachers, so that they might pour forth the liquid of wisdom and the riches of faith; and “torrents,” namely those who preach for a time but desist in time of temptation. There is therefore a distinction between fountains and torrents. In the former, the word of life becomes a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. In the latter there is a torrent, which is flowing water but dries up in summer.

These are those who, having received the word of preaching, run eagerly but yield to temptations. They do not possess the word so as to live well, but so as not to be silent toward others. Yet through both kinds the earth is watered by God. Or “torrent” is here used improperly, namely for “river,” and denotes the abundance of preaching by which good teachers pour out faith and wisdom copiously to others.

Taking fountains and torrents as the same persons: “You dried up the rivers of Ethan,” which means “strong” and signifies those who presume upon themselves. That is, you dried up all teachings of Gentiles, wicked persons, and Jews who presume upon their own righteousness.

[Cassiod.] Or all may be understood of the wicked in this manner: You broke apart fountains, that is, those whose evils flowed continually, and torrents, that is, those who sin suddenly and swiftly; you separated them from their source, the devil. You also utterly dried up the rivers of Ethan—that is, “the strong one”—namely the floods and counsels of the devil, who presumed upon himself.

### Verse 17

> “Yours is the day, and yours is the night; you fashioned dawn and the sun.”

[Col. 0690D] “Yours also is the day,” [Aug.] that is, spiritual persons illuminated by the sun of unchangeable wisdom, which is spoken among the perfect (1 Cor. 2). Hence: “Day utters speech to day” (Ps. 18), the Word which was in the beginning with the Father (John 1). “And yours is the night”: fleshly persons, of whom the Apostle says, “I could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as fleshly” (1 Cor. 3). The moon comforts them as night, namely the manifestation of the flesh: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). Hence: “Night declares knowledge to night” (Ps. 18).

Truly they are yours, because you fashioned dawn—or the moon—that is, the fleshly person, who changes like the moon, but must not be abandoned; [Col. 0691A] and the sun, that is, wise persons, who remain, according to the saying: “The wise person remains like the sun, but the fool changes like the moon” (Sir. 27). Or: you made dawn and sun, the beginning and perfection of wisdom—that is, the unwise and the perfect.

### Verse 18

> “You made all the boundaries of the earth; summer and spring, you formed them.”

“You made.” [Aug., Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod.] For by your grace we were all saved, as the Apostle says: “Created in good works” (Eph. 2). Thus you made all the boundaries of the earth, because each believer has his own gift from you (1 Cor. 7). Or the boundaries are apostles and prophets, because just as boundaries distinguish limits, so they guard the laws of faith. You formed summer—that is, those fervent in spirit—and spring—that is, those newly established in faith and moderate in gentleness. Or all these things may be understood historically from “Yours is the day,” etc.

## Part III. Verse 19

> “Remember this: the enemy reproached the Lord, and a foolish people provoked your name.”

“Remember.” [Cassiod., Gl. int., Aug.] The third part. What is already done everywhere, he prays may be done for the Jews. By enumerating benefits he urges the merciful judge to pardon. As though he said: Since you have done the things already mentioned, remember this. He does not say “whose,” but it must be understood as “this work of yours.” Hence others translate, “this creature of yours.”

Which creature? Behold, the enemy, namely the Jew, reproached the Lord in words—that is, his own nation reproached Christ, saying: [Col. 0691C] “This man is a sinner. We do not know where he is from. We know Moses, to whom God spoke” (John 9). “This man is a Samaritan” (John 8). Yet the root of the nation remains (Rom. 11). Behold, Asaph in understanding grieves over its former blindness.

[Cassiod. and Aug.] Thus he prays for the Jews by confessing their errors; he prays for what will come to pass. For among the Jews there were vessels of mercy, and the foolish people was then Asaph without understanding. “It provoked” your name by deeds, that is, embittered it, when they struck Christ and offered him vinegar (Matt. 27). But I who understand pray:

### Verse 20

> “Do not hand over to the beasts the souls that confess to you; and do not forget unto the end the souls of your poor.”

[Col. 0691D] “Do not hand over to the beasts,” [Aug., Gl. int., Aug.] that is, to the devil and his angels, “the souls that confess to you,” souls which penitently confess their sins; and do not forget to lead “the souls of your poor” unto the End, that is, Christ. Rather, give Christ’s benefits to the poor. For they are now poor who were formerly rich, namely those who established their own righteousness but now do not dare lift their eyes to heaven. And, O Lord:

### Verse 21

> “Look upon your covenant, for those who are darkened have been filled with houses of iniquity upon the earth.”

Look upon the covenant—not the Old Covenant, which concerns earthly things, but upon thine own, [Aug., Cassiod.] namely the New, [Col. 0692A] by which thou hast promised the kingdom of heaven; that is, fulfil what thou hast promised, so that thou mayest establish the New Covenant, which concerns eternal things. He recalls the promise because his merits fail him. For the same reason God ought again to remember, because they are filled with iniquity—that is, with iniquities. Hence darkness follows. Therefore he adds, “who have been darkened,” because they lose the light of knowledge, dwelling in houses of earth—that is, in an earthly habitation; that is, they are blind and given over to earthly things in which they delight.

Or thus: Look upon the covenant, that the remnant may be saved (Rom. XI). [Aug.] For many who attend to the earth have been darkened, because the dust of iniquity has entered their eyes. Hence: “Let their eyes be darkened,” etc. (Ps. LXVIII). And they are filled with earth—that is, with the love of earthliness. And this is because they dwell in houses [Col. 0692B] of iniquity, that is, because they have wicked hearts. For hearts are houses in which they gladly dwell; of these it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V).

VERS. 22.—“Let not the humbled, having been put to shame, be turned away; the poor and needy shall praise thy name.”

Let not [him] be turned away. [Gl. int., Cassiod., Aug., Gl. int., Cassiod., Aug.] As though he said: Since thou hast promised, therefore let not one who is ashamed be turned away. Shame belongs not to the humble but to the proud, who attributes [what he has] not to God but to himself. Therefore, “ashamed,” that is, one whom pride brings to shame. For pride puts to shame those who love earthly things. Let him, having been made humble by the rooting out of pride, not be turned away from thee.

Note that, in the manner of orators, he substitutes one person for another: “welcome” is used for “unwelcome,” so that love for the devout yet obstinate person may temper hatred. And if the poor in spirit—that is, the humble—and the needy—that is, those not swollen with temporal goods or with their own righteousness—are not turned away, these, I say, and not others, shall praise thy name by confessing their sins and seeking eternal things.

Behold, Asaph, now understanding, casts off the earthly promises of the Old Testament; but because he has not yet received the heavenly things promised him in the New, and because he suffers the reproaches of evil people, he seems forsaken. Therefore he cries out:

VERS. 23.—“Arise, O God; judge thy cause; remember thy reproaches—those uttered by the foolish all day long.”

Arise. [Gl. int., Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] As though he said: “Let not the humble be turned away. O God, arise to strengthen me, for I seem forsaken because I have not yet received what thou hast promised—those invisible things which are accounted nothing—and judge thy cause.” After all else, this man makes his cause that of the Judge, to whom the nature of the business is disclosed when he says, “thy cause,” which I defend against those who murmur against it. For they say: “Where is thy God?” Christ, walking on earth, was despised by the Jews; and, seated in heaven, by false Christians.

He therefore says: Judge thy cause; that is, cause my hope not to be disappointed—I who believed what I did not see—and let them proclaim the manifest truth which they formerly foolishly denied. [Cassiod., Gl. int., Aug.] This is the meaning of “Judge thy cause,” namely, the cause which the good defend, [Col. 0693A] while Asaph is mocked with the words, “Where is thy God?” God himself is also reviled, and for this reason it is called his cause.

“Remember thy reproaches”: Christ is still mocked, nor will vessels of wrath be lacking until the end of the age, saying that vain things are preached to Christians. [Alcuin., Aug., Cassiod.] “The resurrection of the dead is empty.” Remember: grant a crown to thine own and punishment to enemies—namely, [remember] the reproaches uttered by the foolish all day long. For mockers will not be lacking until the end of the age. He says this so that the very continuance of the reproaches might stir the patience of the enduring Judge. He still prays against the enemies, saying:

VERS. 24.—“Forget not the voices of thine enemies; the pride of those who hate thee ascends continually.”

Forget not the voices of thine enemies, [Gl. int., Cassiod., Aug.] but suppress their blasphemies, because their pride—namely, that of the Romans, who hate thee—rises continually and moves him against his enemies. At the end he places the detestable evil, pride.

Or it may be understood favourably according to another reading. As though he said: Remember thy reproaches, and do not forget also the voices of those who beseech thee humbly and devoutly; and the pride even of those who hate thee rises continually to thee. As though he said: Do not forget the pride of those who hate thee, but let it continually ascend to thee—which indeed it does, because thou either correctest or punishest it. [Col. 0693C]

## 63. Comparison on Psalm LXXIII: “Why, O God, hast thou cast off,” etc.

VERS. 3.—“Thou hast redeemed the rod of thine inheritance.”

Münster wishes the genitive case of “inheritance” to be referred to the verb of the preceding verse, namely, “remember.” Thus he renders it: “Remember thy congregation, which thou hast possessed from the beginning; and, which thou hast redeemed.” Then, adding two little words of his own, he says: “Remember, I say, the tribe of thine inheritance”—certainly, that is, quite voluntarily.

Again, his rendering of “tribe” for “rod” is not outside the meaning: *scebet* signifies both; and in the manner of Scripture a rod is commonly used for a tribe and for dominion.

“Mount Sion wherein thou hast dwelt therein.” This verse suffers a double accusation from Faber and Caecus. The first is that we sing it in the nominative, “Mount Sion,” whereas the sequence of the discourse and grammatical rule [Col. 0693D] demand the accusative, “Mount Sion,” on account of the preceding word “thou hast redeemed.” I know indeed that the structure of the sentence is suited in this order, and was so observed by Jerome and Augustine; yet the other order of reading ought not to be rejected altogether, since in Hebrew there is a major pause at the phrase “thine inheritance,” *nahalateca*.

Moreover, it is peculiar to the Hebrews to include the substantive verb within pronouns. Here, however, we read *har Tzion zeh*, “this Mount Sion,” so that one may say very well, “This Mount Sion is.” The Greeks frequently recognize this expression in their articles. The Master mentions three readings in his Exposition.

Secondly, they quibble over this kind of expression, “wherein thou hast dwelt therein,” as foolish and unheard by Latin ears. But Saint Augustine refutes this class of men, more superstitious than devout, by the remarkable force of his learning, in Book XXII of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 13, in these most memorable words:

> “What, then, is correctness of speech except the preservation of Latin usage, established by the authority of ancient speakers? Yet people are offended by it all the more as they are weaker; and they are weaker as they desire to appear more learned—not through knowledge of things, by which we are built up, but of signs, by which it is by no means difficult to become puffed up. Even knowledge of things itself often raises the neck, unless it is restrained by the Lord’s yoke. For what harms the understanding reader if it is written thus: ‘What is the land upon which these men sit upon it, whether it be good or bad?’ Or: ‘What are the cities in which they dwell in them?’ I judge that manner of speech to belong more to a foreign language than to convey some deeper meaning.”

Thus far Saint Augustine. Here the holy doctor almost prophetically already dispelled future cavils against this passage and figure of speech.

VERS. 4.—“Lift up thy hands.”

For “thy hands,” the Hebrew has *peameca*. Jerome, Sanctes, Münster, and the interpreters for Cajetan render it “feet” or “steps”; [Col. 0694B] Pagninus, “blows”; Pellican, “palpitations.” This was noted on Psalm LVII, verse 10. Finally, Jerome understood the preceding word, *harimah*, nominally—the term which, with others, we render “lift up” or “exalt.” He himself rendered it: “the height of thy feet.”

“Against their prides.” Jerome merely has “it has been destroyed,” having prefaced “height”; Münster, “that thou mayest lay waste.” The others render “ruins” or “desolations.” The Hebrew has *lemasschuoth*: pronounced with the point called *smol* over the letter *shin*, it signifies elevations, and thus prides, as we read it. But if pronounced with the other point, called *jamin*, it represents devastations and ruins, as the others understood it. Yet the sense is not difficult to reconcile in either way.

“How greatly the enemy hath done evil in the sanctuary.” Sanctes, Münster, and Felinus render this verse so that its wording and sense depend upon what precedes, [Col. 0694C] as though one said: “Lift up thy hands against their prides and against every enemy who has done evil in the sanctuary. Lift up, I say, thy hands, and lay waste.” The interpreters for Cajetan agree. But Jerome, with the others, separates this clause by itself and says: “The enemy has done all things wickedly in the sanctuary.” This more closely corresponds to the Hebrew reading, *cal hera oyev baqqodesch*.

VERS. 5.—“And they gloried.”

Jerome: “they raged”; others: “they cried out,” “they roared.” *Shaagu* properly denotes the roar of a lion, a fitting type of proud boasting.

“In the midst of thy solemnity.” Jerome: “of thy covenant”; others: “of thy churches”; one, “of thy temple”; another, “of thy tabernacle”; another, “of thy synagogues.” *Moadeca* accommodates every version from the Hebrew.

VERS. 6.—“And they did not know.”

Our reading appears strikingly at variance with the Hebrew, especially because we have a negation which the Hebrews do not recognize here at all; nor is it sufficiently clear whence the Septuagint drew it. Yet there is one Hebrew word variously rendered by those who profess Hebrew learning: *iiuada*. First, Jerome has “manifest,” so that “signs” is understood from what precedes; Münster, “it was known”; Pagninus, the interpreters for Cajetan, and Pellican, “it shall be known.” Sanctes’ version almost reaches the sense of our edition, though in different words, when he renders, “it has been crushed.” For the root *iada* sometimes signifies to overthrow or crush; and something may be so broken to pieces that scarcely a trace of it can afterwards be recognized. This fits the utter devastation of the city of Jerusalem, of which the Lord foretold that not one stone would remain upon another (Luke XVIV [sic]), and of which the psalm speaks. Indeed, the Chaldee has: “He will strike with a hammer.”

Therefore, to set the sense plainly before us, the whole verse may be repeated: “They set up their signs as signs.” Then read as though in parenthesis: “and they did not know”—why? Because all things have been crushed. “They set up,” [Col. 0695A] I say, “signs, as at the exit above,” so that they might be signs of victory and of a city levelled to the ground. Yet I am not unaware that Augustine interprets “they did not know” otherwise; nevertheless, the parenthetical explanation seems fitting.

But because our undertaking is to compare translations, we do not disagree with him who, in Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 15, admonished us to do this, saying:

> “But, as I said above, comparison even of those interpreters who adhered more closely to the words is not useless for often explaining the meaning.”

And in chapter 12 of the same book:

> “This circumstance indeed aided understanding more than it impeded it, provided only that readers are not negligent. For the examination of several manuscripts has often made some more obscure meanings clear.”

So he says.

“As at the exit above.” Jerome: “at the entrance from above”; Pagninus and the interpreters for Cajetan: “as one bringing [something] above or upwards”; Münster explains its sense in a paraphrase: “as one bringing timbers to some elevated thing”; Pellican: “as one bringing a summary.” Others have their paraphrases. The Hebrew has *kemebi lemaalah*. Jerome read *beth* for *caph* in the first word; they differ only slightly. Again, he understood *mebi* with the Septuagint, so that the letter *mem* is not the sign of the participle but is, as it were, constitutive of a substantive—of the noun called denominative. Nor should it offend us that where we say “at the exit,” he says “at the entrance,” as though the two were opposed; for the same place is entrance and exit according to different points of view. Finally, the interpreters of the Septuagint rendered the last word almost literally, and thereby nothing is taken from the truth of the Hebrew.

VERS. 7.—“As in a forest of trees, with axes they cut down its doors.”

The Hebrews end the verse with the word signifying “axes,” so that it refers to the preceding verb “they set up”: according to Jerome, “they set axes in a forest of trees,” with “they set” understood. Others render it so that it depends upon the participle which they rendered “bringing.” The Septuagint, following another division, added the verb “they cut down” for the convenience of the sentence and sense. Nor are they of less authority than Münster, who does not make “axes” call for some preceding verb, but supplies another verb of his own from without. He says: “those who sent axes into tangled trees.”

In Hebrew it is *bisadoc etz quardumoth*, where it appears that the Septuagint uses *caph* in place of *beth*, cognate letters, as often happens.

“Its doors.” Others say, “its carvings,” without change of sense; although the Hebrew word can bear either meaning: *pituah*, from *patah*, “he opened,” “he carved.” Felinus also agrees. And immediately afterward, in the phrase, “with axe and adze they cast it down,” translators generally agree. For some render “hammer” instead of “adze,” because *kelaphah* is common to either implement.

VERS. 9.—“Their kindred together.”

Jerome, the Chaldee, Nebiensis, Pellican, and the interpreters for Cajetan agree in translating “their descendants” or “their children.” But Pagninus, Sanctes, Münster, Felinus, and Campensis preferred to follow certain rabbis who explain the word used here, *ninam*, as “let us lay waste,” or “let us rage against them.” Sanctes nevertheless noted that it may derive either from the root *nin*, “son,” understanding posterity by “son,” or from the root *janah*, “he laid waste”; and thus he redeemed our labour.

“Let us make all God’s feast-days cease from the earth.” Pagninus: “They burned all God’s temples in the earth.” Sanctes says “tabernacles” instead of “temples”; Münster, “synagogues”; the interpreters for Cajetan, “assemblies”; Campensis embraces both, temples and solemnities.

Jerome discussed this passage as copiously as learnedly in his letter to Sunia and Fretella that we may add nothing. He says:

> “‘Let us burn all God’s feast-days from the earth’: for this, the Greek reads, δεῦτε καὶ καταπαύσωμεν πάσας τὰς ἑορτὰς τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς—‘Come, and let us cause all the feasts of God to cease from the earth.’ And we translated: ‘Come, and let us cause all the feast-days of God to cease from the earth.’ I am astonished that some rash person thought that our marginal note, which we wrote for the reader’s instruction, ought to be inserted in the body [Col. 0696A] of the text. We wrote it thus: ‘The text does not have *katapausōmen*, as some suppose, but *katakausōmen*, that is, “let us burn.”’ Since the holy priest Firmus, who was the supervisor of this work, told me that many had debated this question, it seems necessary to discuss it more fully. In Hebrew it is written, *sarephu cal moade el baaretz*, which Aquila and Symmachus rendered ἐνέπρησαν πάσας τὰς ἑορτὰς Θεοῦ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, that is, ‘They burned all the solemnities of God upon the earth.’ The Fifth [version]: κατέκαυσαν, that is, ‘They burned.’ The Sixth: κατακαύσωμεν, that is, ‘Let us burn.’ It is evident that the Septuagint also, according to the truth of the Hexapla, translated this. Theodotion likewise rendered ἐνεπυρίσωμεν, that is, ‘Let us set fire to.’ From this it is clear that it must be sung as we translated it. Nevertheless, one must know what the Hebrew truth has. For what the Septuagint translators rendered should, because of its antiquity, be sung in the Church; while scholars should know the other reading for their knowledge of the Scriptures. Therefore, if anything has been added in the margin for study, it ought not yet to be put in the text, lest the earlier translation be disturbed at copyists’ will.”

Thus far we have faithfully reported Jerome’s words. O words worthy to be marked with a white stone; O words that will perish in no age! They alone would abundantly suffice to blunt the obstinate defiance of certain persons who, if perchance they think the Hebrew reads otherwise than is sung in the churches, rage, fume, and cry out to excess: “This must be erased, uprooted, slain. The Holy Spirit did not say this; let us sing with the Prophet in this or that way.”

What do you say? Jerome did not wish even what was true, and noted in the margin for the reader’s instruction, to be thrust into the body of the text; indeed, he judged the person who had done this rash. And even if it is now received that we sing differently from the way he may have translated or interpreted it, he wishes the name of antiquity to retain authority. He praises knowledge of the Scriptures; he does not wish ecclesiastical usage to be rashly violated. [Col. 0696C]

VERS. 10.—“And he shall no longer know us.”

Jerome: “There is no one among us who knows how long,” so that one understands that there is no prophet who knows the end of these evils and how long they will rage. Yet that sense may be fittingly elicited here from the Hebrew, *velo itanu iodea ad maii*, especially if *od* were read for *ad*, where the letters are the same, although *waw* is more commonly inserted in *od*.

VERS. 12.—“From the midst of thy bosom unto the end.”

Jerome: “from the midst,” or, as Faber’s codex had it, “in the midst of thy bosom, consuming.” Sanctes and Münster added certain words, as they thought necessary for completeness of sense. [Col. 0696D] I shall repeat the whole verse, so that their meaning may appear more clearly. He has it thus: “Why dost thou draw back thy hand and thy right hand from the midst of thy bosom? Wilt thou not draw it out to consume enemies?” The other is not far from this: “Why dost thou turn away thy hand and thy right hand? Bring it forth to consume the enemy.”

The variation depends on the final word, *caleh*, which means “to consume,” “to complete,” “to finish.” According to the rule of Hebrew grammar, it is an imperative or infinitive; therefore it is aptly rendered “by finishing” or “by consuming,” “finish,” or “consume.” Jerome, however, not adhering to the letter, said “consuming” with a participle—though it is not improbable that he read *coleh*, in the verb called *qal*.

VERS. 14.—“Thou hast strengthened the sea in thy power.”

Jerome, with the others: “Thou hast divided.” The Hebrew writes *poradta*, and it signifies to separate, distinguish, spread out, or scatter. If the meaning of the verse [Col. 0697A] is referred to the passage of the children of Israel through the midst of the Red Sea, “thou hast strengthened” and “thou hast divided the sea” tend to the same sense. If Augustine in some fashion refers it to the conversion of the nations, surely fullness and contrition of heart scatter an evil conscience and strengthen a good one.

VERS. 16.—“Thou hast dried up the rivers of Ethan.”

It does not seem to be the proper name of a desert. For Jerome, and most others, render: “mighty rivers.”

VERS. 18.—“Thou hast formed summer and spring.”

The Hebrew has winter, *horeph*, in place of spring; we believe that it not unfittingly also signifies spring. For in Job XXIX, where we read, “As I was in the days of my youth,” the Hebrew has *horphi*. But what does the youth of a season signify except, as it were, the youthfulness of spring? Yet whoever says “summer and spring, thy creatures” must necessarily understand winter also between them.

[Col. 0697B] VERS. 20.—“Do not deliver to beasts.”

*Lehaiath*, that is, “to a beast” or “to a congregation,” for the word is ambiguous. The Septuagint, Jerome, Nebiensis, Pagninus, Pellican, the interpreters for Cajetan, and the Campensis edition follow the former sense. Sanctes, Münster, and the Campensian paraphrase prefer the latter; but, since the sense seemed incomplete if one merely said, “Do not deliver the soul to the congregation,” they added “of enemies.”

“Souls confessing to thee.” The Septuagint, as Sanctes himself notes, read *daleth* for *resh*. These are, as has often been said, very similar letters. For the manuscripts now have *toreca*, that is, “thy turtledove,” according to Pagninus, Sanctes, Pellican, Münster, Campensis, Nebiensis, and Felinus. But *todeca* means “confessing to thee,” or “which shall confess to thee.” Jerome and the interpreters for Cajetan, however, translate “a soul instructed in thy law,” reading indeed with *resh* but deriving it from *torah*, “law”: *toreca*—although Sanctes maintains that in that sense it ought to be said *thoratheca*. The Chaldee nevertheless has: “the souls of those learning thy law.”

“And the souls of thy poor.” They again render *haiath* as “congregation.” [Col. 0698A] Jerome has “life,” which without doubt means “soul.”

VERS. 21.—“Those darkened have been filled, earth, with houses of iniquity.”

Because the verse has been translated according to Greek word order, it is somewhat more involved; but when arranged thus—“those who have been darkened are filled with houses of iniquity of the earth”—no difficulty remains. Augustine and the Roman edition have: “Those darkened are filled with earth of wicked houses,” so that, in Greek fashion, the genitive is used in place of the ablative. The Master, retaining our reading, supplies “dwelling.”

In Hebrew the difficulty is greater. Jerome has: “The lands are filled with darkness; the wicked habitations are overthrown.” Pagninus otherwise: “The darknesses of the earth are filled with habitations of iniquity.” Sanctes: “The dark places are filled, the dwellings of the wicked.” Münster: “All things are filled with dark prisons of the earth and violent dwellings.” The others almost agree in the same sense.

Let us examine each point separately. All agree on the first word. [Col. 0698B] In the second there is disagreement—namely, “they have been darkened.” For the Hebrew expresses it with the single word *mahassake*, because the Septuagint understood it as a participle, altering the vowel points as though it were written in the verb-form called *hiphil*. In the third, namely *eretz*, Jerome differs by employing it in the plural; accordingly, for the demands of construction, he had to supply the second word. In the fourth and fifth, namely *neoth hamas*, they agree sufficiently, except that Jerome seems to have added “overthrown.” But the word *hamas* is ambiguous, meaning both “to act wickedly” and “to be scattered”; hence it is likely that he wished to encompass both meanings.

In his commentaries, certainly, I do not at all know what edition he followed, because he reads “thickets” instead of “houses of iniquity” and interprets them as thorns, although the density in brambles is not far from the darknesses of the earth.

VERS. 24.—“The pride of those who hate thee ascends continually.”

For “pride,” the Hebrew has *scheon*. Jerome renders “sound,” and the others do not differ. The Septuagint explained what sound or noise ought to be understood by using the term “pride.” Hence the Campensis edition has “the arrogance of those rising against thee,” and the paraphrase, “their insulting outcry.” Felinus agrees.

# PSALM LXXIV

[Col. 0697]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “UNTO THE END: DO NOT DESTROY, OR CORRUPT; A PSALM OF A SONG OF ASAPH.”

[Col. 0697C]

“We will confess to thee, O God.” [Aug., Alcuin., Cassiod.] Title: “Unto the end: Do not destroy, or corrupt; a psalm of a song of Asaph.” This psalm brings the medicine of humility against the swelling of pride.
