In it Christ is shown to be true God and true man, Judge of the living and the dead, so that the Jews may believe and may not corrupt their faith and hope in Christ, but await God’s promise with certain faith. And this is said by Asaph, that is, the faithful Synagogue.

[Gl. int., Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod.] The meaning is: This psalm, which exhorts to good works, is a song because it treats of eternal recompense; it belongs to Asaph, that is, to the faithful Synagogue. It teaches this: that thou, O Jew—or whoever thou art—mayest not corrupt or destroy, that is, violate the hope held in God’s promise; but that his promise may be certain to thee. And, in order to do this, look unto the end: behold the end, where thou shalt be happy, while those who laugh here are miserable. Therefore despise whatever prosperity or adversity now meets thee here; rejoice in God’s promise alone.

Intention: This psalm warns that no proud person should presume upon himself, nor any humble person despair of God; even when the latter is afflicted, a sure promise consoles him. Method: The psalm has two parts. First, the humble person is set forth, and he invites others also. Secondly, the proud person is frightened by the judgment which cannot be escaped, at the words, “When I shall receive the time.” Therefore Asaph, certain of the promises, begins thus: O—

VERS. 1.—“We will confess to thee, O God, we will confess, and we will call upon thy name.”

O God, we will confess our sins, [Aug.] having now become humble: not to another god, but to thee—not to a cruel avenger, but to a merciful forgiver. This confession is an emptying of evils; for all things are washed away in confession. Then he repeats, “we will confess.” Repetition is confirmation, lest thou repent of having confessed. Hence, in the Gospel of John, the Lord doubles the word for stronger confirmation: “Amen, amen” (John I, and elsewhere). And in the Psalms, “Be it done, be it done,” is doubled (Ps. LXXI, LXXXVIII). Joseph said concerning Pharaoh’s dream—who saw seven full ears and as many barren ones, and seven fat cows and as many lean ones (Gen. XLI)—that repetition is confirmation.

We are taught from many places in Scripture that firmness of statement lies in repetition: one occurrence would suffice to signify truth, but a second is added to signify firmness. Confession of sins once made to an earthly judge brings death; but confession frequently made to God produces life. Invocation follows confession. Therefore he adds: “And we will call upon thy name.” After confession, God may be invoked in a person thus cleansed. And as confession empties one of evils, so invocation fills one with goods. Narrative follows afterward; therefore he adds:

VERS. 2.—“We will recount thy wondrous works.”

We will recount. [Aug., Gl. int., Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod.] This man has belched forth from abundance, so that others may come, so that he who hears may say, “Come” (Rev. XXII), so that curtain may draw curtain (Exod. XXXVI), and our fountains may be spread abroad (Prov. V).

“Thy wondrous works”: this is the rule of holy devotion here set forth. First one must confess sins, by which we are emptied of evils; then call upon God for help, by which we are filled with goods; and finally, belching forth from abundance, we can recount. For God is invoked by one cleansed, as by one who is his own. But if an undevout person calls upon him, he calls down judgment. If, however, one who has been cleansed calls upon him, then he may recount; otherwise it is said to him: “Why dost thou recount my righteousnesses?” (Ps. XLVIII).

Hence also the place of prayer is first cleansed of filth, then adorned with curtains, afterward decorated with coverings of varied colours (Exod. XXVI), so that we [Note: [Col. 0699D] From Gregory, Homily 19 on Ezekiel.] who are the holy temple of God may first be cleansed of evils through confession; then be adorned by curtains of virtues through invocation; and thereafter shine before men, unto the glory of God the Father, with the varied colours of good works. [Cassiod.] By means of this perfect religion, moreover, this man immediately deserves to be heard. For he says that Christ responds to his prayers; in the person of this Christ he adds:

## PART II. VERS. 2.—“When I shall receive the time, I will judge justices.”

“When I shall receive.” [Cassiod., Alcuin., Aug., Gl. int., Aug.] The second part, in which the proud person is frightened by the judgment that cannot be escaped, and the pillars are strengthened in order to recall him; God also humbles him, whereas he exalts the humble person.

Or according to another reading, “I will recount” is said in the singular, although he had previously said in the plural, “We will confess” and “we will call upon.” For all are now one Christ, from whom the invocation is received. Christ speaks in the person of Head and members. As though he said: “I, the whole Christ, will recount thy wondrous works. If anyone does not hear, I—Christ, who now am not seen—will judge justices.” Or: “I, Christ, namely the whole [Christ], will judge,” because the saints also will judge with him. Therefore let those about to be judged pray beforehand to be acquitted.

“I will judge, when I shall receive the time” of judging. For now is the time for teaching and mercy; afterward will be the time for judging. But did Christ receive a time? The Son of God did not receive a time; but the Son of Man received a time—yet he is the same Son of God through whom we were made, and Son of Man through whom we were restored. Therefore, as Son of Man, he received the time; as Son of God, he governs times. Thus Christ received, according to his humanity, what God himself gives—namely, authority to execute judgment. For as Son of God, he never lacked authority to judge, and therefore did not receive it; but as Son of Man he received it. Therefore the whole Christ will judge in the future. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “You also shall sit on twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX). So it shall be in the future; but what is true now?

VERS. 3.—“The earth and all who dwell therein have melted away; I have established its pillars.”

The earth, once firm, has now melted away, [Alcuin., Aug., Alcuin., Cassiod.] that is, from steadfastness in virtue and righteousness it has flowed apart into diverse desires. Then he explains which earth he meant: “and”—that is, “all who dwell therein.” For the earth itself flowed away in those dwelling upon it: such earth I found. But I, not an exactor of punishments but a forgiver of sins, established its pillars, which wavered during the Passion—that is, the apostles, who were strengthened in the Resurrection.

Or thus: the earth, formerly bound by vices, melted at the breathing of the Holy Spirit, so that it might bring forth shoots of virtues. And “all who dwell therein”—that is, “I established its pillars.” These things are not changed. And through the strengthened pillars:

VERS. 4.—“I said to the wicked: Do not act wickedly; and to the sinners: Do not raise up the horn.”

I said to the wicked, [Aug., Alcuin., Aug., Cassiod.] to all evil people generally: “Do not act wickedly.” They had already fallen, already failed, already become guilty, already flowed away; and yet he says, “Do not act wickedly”—that is, do not persist in evil, but flee to the physician. For it is evil to sin; worse to persist; and more destructive still, in defending oneself, to cast blame upon God. Hence he adds: “and to the sinners,” that is, to those defending their sins, he said: “Do not raise up the horn”—that is, do not be proud of it, raising horns among yourselves in excuse. As though he said: If you have already committed iniquity through desire, do not defend it through pride; if you are sound, you did not listen. Or: You who lie fallen, rise; do not excuse yourselves. Excusing oneself is a very great vice. For he raises, as it were, a horn who strives to excuse his sins through others: through the devil, through other persuaders, or through the necessity of the stars. It follows:

VERS. 5.—“Do not lift up your horn on high; do not speak iniquity against God.”

Do not lift up your horn on high, [Aug., Cassiod., Alcuin.] that is, against God, as does one who murmurs against God in blasphemous thought. Then he explains in fact what he had said: do not speak in your heart, even if you do not speak with your tongue, iniquity against God. As though [you said]: “God does not know these things,” or “He does not care,” like one who says he suffers unjustly because more wicked people prosper—which is to make God unjust.

Or: Do not speak iniquity against God, as do those [Col. 0701A] who say they sinned not by their own fault but through the necessity of the stars, so that it may be imputed to God rather than themselves; or those who know their sins yet promise themselves impunity. Why ought you not do these things? Because the Judge is such that he cannot be avoided, because he is everywhere: for he is God. This is the meaning: Therefore do not do this:

VERS. 6.—“For neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains, since God is judge.”

For the Judge does not judge from the east, [Aug.] as though you might flee thence to the west; nor does he judge from the west, as though you might flee thence to the east. As though he said: He does not judge from any divided place, because he is not spatially confined; for as God he is present everywhere. Nor does he judge from desert mountains, so that you may flee thence into the midst of peoples. Why not? Because God is Judge. If he were in some place, he would not be God.

Or: the Judge is not absent from east, west, or desert mountains—that is, from secret places. Why? Because God is Judge: nearly the same sense as the former interpretation.

Or according to the mystical sense: [Cassiod., Alcuin., Aug.] the east consists of good people, upon whom the sun of righteousness rises, namely people conspicuous through the brightness of God; the west, however, consists of those upon whom the sun of righteousness sets, that is, evil people. Desert mountains are false preachers, proud heretics, who arrogate to themselves the place of mountains; but they are deserted by God’s truth. God is present to them, but not as he is present to the good—not merely by knowledge, but by grace.

And this is why you should not do these things: because God is absent neither from the east, that is, from the good; nor from the west, that is, from the evil; nor from desert mountains, that is, from false preachers. God is present to, and knows, every kind of human being, because he is Judge even of the things that are in the heart. And he, being such, humbles the proud and exalts the humble.

VERS. 7.—“He humbles this one and exalts that one, because a cup of pure wine, full of mixture, is in the hand of the Lord.”

“He humbles this one,” [Aug.] that is, the proud Jew, such as the Pharisee swollen with the righteousness of the law; “and exalts that one,” that is, the humble Gentile, such as the tax collector saying, “God, be merciful to me,” etc. (Luke XVIII). By what means? [Col. 0701D] By the law which is in the hand of God the Mediator (Gal. III), called a cup because it gives the souls of believers drink. This is the meaning: “Because a cup is in the hand of the Lord.”

VERS. 8.—“And he hath inclined it from this to that; nevertheless its dregs have not been emptied out: all sinners of the earth shall drink from it.”

And He has tilted it from this into that. [Augustine.] Thus far extends the force of the proof; but let us see what meaning the individual words contain. The cup is the Law and the whole Scripture of the Old Testament, in which the New is hidden, as it were, in the dregs of bodily figures. It is called a cup because from it God makes the minds of believers drunk. Therefore the cup of pure wine, that is, of the sincere Law, [Col. 0702A] is so with respect to the just and good moral precepts: “You shall worship one God,” and so forth. Or it is called a cup of pure wine with respect to its spiritual meaning, full of mixture—that is, of the dregs of bodily sacraments—which remain and settle among the Jews; and from it all spiritual understanding has been poured out and strained into the humble Gentiles. But among the Jews the dregs of the figure remained, and the unbelieving Jews drank from them. And this is: He humbles the Jew and exalts the Gentile. And this is through the Law, because the cup—that is, the Law and the whole Old Testament—is in the hand of the Lord, that is, in the power of Christ the mediator. I say, a cup of pure wine because of the sincerity of its moral precepts and spiritual sense; and that cup is full of mixture, that is, of the dregs of bodily sacraments. And what follows? And the Lord [Col. 0702B] has tilted this cup, that is, the Law, from this—that is, from the Jew—to this, or into this, namely the Gentile, into whom spiritual understanding has been strained. And by this it is clear that He humbles the one and exalts the other. And although He tilts it, nevertheless its dregs have not been emptied among the Jews, because the carnal sacraments remained among the Jews; and all sinners of the earth, that is, all unbelieving Jews, shall drink from that mixture, that is, from the dregs of the figures. Or they shall drink from that cup: that is, generally all sinners of the earth shall drink—both proud sinners and humble sinners. The Jews are proud sinners, but the Gentiles humble sinners: some, namely the humble sinners, drink the wine of the cup; others, namely the proud sinners, drink the dregs. All shall drink, but separately.

[Col. 0702C] VERS. 9.—“But I will declare for ever; I will sing to the God of Jacob.”

I, [Augustine, Cassiodorus] Christ with my body, will declare for ever, that is, as long as the world shall exist. Or, according to another reading, “I will rejoice for ever,” over the future promise at the end of the age, of which the title says: “Do not destroy,” etc. Or thus—and it agrees in part with the former sense. The cup is the Law; the pure wine is the heavenly mystery, that is, the spiritual meaning [Note: [Col. 0701D] Gregory, Homily 6 on Ezekiel], full because, although it is always drunk, it is never exhausted; with mixture, that is, with both Testaments, because the Old and New are together. Hence Ezekiel: “I saw a wheel within a wheel” (Ezek. I). [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] The Jews do not drink the mixture, because they receive the Old without the New; [Col. 0702D] nor do the Manicheans, who receive the New without the Old. “From this into that,” because He took it from the Jews and tilted it toward the converted Gentiles. “Nevertheless its dregs”: dregs are not here taken for filth, but signify the lowest and final part of the wine, that is, the final and subtler matters of the Law, which cannot be reached here. The meaning is: although He tilts it, nevertheless its dregs, which He has tilted, have not been emptied, because those more secret things cannot be wholly understood [Note: [Col. 0701D] From Gregory, *Morals*, book XX, ch. 9]. Hence, “If anything remains over, you shall burn it with the fire of the Holy Spirit” (Exod. XII), because the fullness does not fail for all who drink. And all sinners of the earth shall drink from it, from the full cup [Note: [Col. 0702D] From Cassiodorus and Isidore on Genesis]: that is, the Jews converted at the end, along with the others, shall drink, observing both [Col. 0703A] Testaments, when Abraham, after sacrificing the ram, returns with his son to the servants waiting with the ass (Gen. XXII).

Or thus: He humbles this one and exalts that one, because He can do so, since the cup is the power and ordering of judgment. I say, a cup of pure wine, that is, of just judgment, is in the hand of the Lord, [Alcuin] that is, of Christ, full of mixture, that is, of mercy and judgment: for to some there is death through justice, to others life through mercy; and He tilts and offers this mixture to all. This is: “And He tilts it from this into that,” that is, to all generally. For all shall experience mercy and judgment. And although He tilts this cup, nevertheless its dregs have not been emptied: that is, the severe punishment for those who drink shall not end for the wicked. From that cup all sinners of the earth shall drink the dregs—not only the sinful Jews [Col. 0703B] shall drink. But I with mine, Christ says, will declare, or rejoice, for ever; I will sing to the God of Jacob.

VERS. 10.—“And I will break all the horns of sinners; and the horns of the righteous shall be exalted.”

And I will break, at the end, all the horns of sinners which are raised here, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, ordinary gloss] namely the dignities of the proud, which now refuse to be broken. This is what He said before: “He humbles this one.” And the horns of the righteous—which are not here but shall be there, that is, the gifts of Christ, which are the exalted state of the righteous—shall be exalted in the future, where the proud person shall be humbled and the humble person exalted. This is what He said before: “He exalts that one.”

## Comparison on Psalm LXXIV: “We Will Give Thanks,” etc.

[Col. 0703C]

VERS. 1, alternatively 2.—“We will invoke your name.” *QAROB SCEMECA*: “your name is near,” or, as Jerome translated it, “beside your name.” It comes to the same thing. For “the Lord is near to those who call upon him,” Psalm CXLIV, although they wish it understood thus: that we should always perceive God’s presence.

VERS. 2, alternatively 3.—“When I receive the time.” *MOED* is rendered “time” by Jerome, the Chaldean, Pellicanus, Sanctes, and Campensis. Münster, Felinus, and the interpreters for Cajetan render it “assembly” or “gathering”; [Col. 0704A] Pratensis, “solemnity.” That particle is common to all these meanings. One must beware lest too many claim wisdom for themselves.

VERS. 5, alternatively 6.—“Do not speak iniquity against God.” *BATZAUAR ATHAQ.* Jerome renders “against God iniquity” as “with an old neck.” Pellicanus and Nebiensis follow him. Pratensis: “with an exalted neck,” so that “exalted” is governed by the verb “to speak,” or by “speaking”; Sanctes: “with a fat neck”; Münster: “with a broken neck.” The first element is from *TZOR*, “strong,” which is also God Himself, as the Septuagint seems to have taken it, since the letter *beth* prefixed to words sometimes means “against.” Then the second element signifies both a hard, heavy thing and an ancient thing; all these suit obstinacy, represented by the neck and fat neck.

VERS. 6, alternatively 7.—“Nor from deserted mountains.” Jerome, Nebiensis, Pellicanus, and the translator for Campensis agree with us. The rest render “exaltation”; [Col. 0704B] Sanctes: “nor shall exaltation come from the wilderness,” where he supplies “shall come” from his own resources. *MIMMIBDAR HARIM*: if the last word has the substantive letter *he*, as the Septuagint and their followers understood it, it rightly means “mountains.” Others, however, have taken it as an additional form from the root [uncertain OCR], “he exalted” or “was exalted.”

VERS. 7, alternatively 8.—“A cup in the hand of the Lord, full of pure wine mixed.” Jerome has almost the same wording: “A cup is in the hand of the Lord, mixed with wine of the finest quality even to fullness”; Nebiensis likewise. Some others seem verbally to differ, yet do not vary in meaning if considered more closely. Pratensis: “A cup in the hand of the Lord has become red, full of mixture.” Pellicanus: “A cup is in the hand; the wine has bubbled up, it has filled the mixture.” Münster and Sanctes: “The wine grew red,” or “grows red,” “with full mixture” or “a mixture.” *HAMAR* does indeed mean “grew red,” as it is read here; but from it is derived *HEMER*, meaning good wine, unmixed wine. Felinus, however, prefers “turbid wine,” but the Chaldean translation has “pure wine.”

[Col. 0704C] 166 VERS. 8, 9.—“Its dregs have not been emptied.” The Septuagint drew out the sense from the sense, which is made clearer by what immediately follows: “all sinners of the earth shall drink.” If they drink continually, it follows that the dregs of the cup of divine wrath are never emptied. I say this because the Hebrew seems almost contrary, since it is written without a negative, *iimtzu*, that is, “they shall suck out,” “press out,” “drink up,” yet in such a way that there is never not something left to suck out. The Septuagint wonderfully observed the weight of the statement.

# PSALM LXXV

[Col. 0703]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “FOR THE END, AMONG HYMNS; A SONG AGAINST THE ASSYRIANS; A PSALM OF ASAPH.”

[Col. 0703D]

“Against the Assyrians” was added by the Greek translators by the counsel of the Holy Spirit, as has been demonstrated above in several similar cases.

“God is known in Judah,” etc. Title: “For the end, among hymns; a song against the Assyrians; a psalm of Asaph” [Note: [Col. 0703] From Cassiodorus in the preface and conclusion of the Psalm, and from Alcuin]. Assyrians means “directing,” and signifies the Jews, to whom this term applies by antiphrasis—that is, by the contrary—because they are not directing but wandering. Or they may be called “directing” in the sense of “raising themselves up,” because they raise themselves against Christ, in that they seek salvation through legal observances without Christ’s grace. They are fittingly called Assyrians because they persecute Christ’s Church, just as the Assyrians of old persecuted the Jews. Here Asaph—that is, [Col. 0704D] the faithful Synagogue—speaks against them, refuting them and saying that the names of glory have been taken from them and transferred to others: Judah, Israel, Salem, and Zion; and it is proved that no good is possible without Christ’s grace. The meaning is: [ordinary gloss, Alcuin, Cassiodorus] this Psalm is attributed to Asaph, that is, to the faithful Synagogue which here speaks, directing us to the end, that is, to Christ. It is “among hymns,” that is, among praises; and it is a song because it treats of Christ’s benefits—namely, that He is known, dwells, enlightens, and saves. It is “against the Assyrians,” that is, against the Jews, who do not direct themselves to God but wander; or who raise themselves against Christ, establishing their own righteousness. Its intention is to refute the Jews and exhort the devout to pay their vows. Its method is threefold. First, it breaks the glory of the Jews. Second, it says that Christ enlightens, saves, and judges, [Col. 0705A] at “Enlightening.” Third, it exhorts those now devout to pay their vows, at “For the thought.” Therefore faithful Asaph, refuting the Jews, says:

VERS. 1.—“God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel.”

God is known in Judah. [Augustine.] As if he said: The Jew boasts that God is known to the Jew, as the Prophet says here, and it is true; but to the Jew inwardly, who is a Jew in secret—not to the Jew in the flesh, who is a Jew openly in name alone. For God is known, as this Prophet says, in Judah—true Judah, namely, that which confesses sins; for Judah means “confession.” As if he said: By the authority of the Prophet, from which the Jews are accustomed to boast and insult the Gentiles, I refute them. For if you are true Jews, then God is known [Col. 0705B] among you, as the Prophet says; but if He is not, then you are not Jews. Yet God is not known among them, because they acknowledged the Gentile Caesar, saying, “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX), and denied Christ, born from the tribe of Judah. From that tribe kings formerly came, and from it they were called Jews. The Jewish people had twelve tribes according to the number of Jacob’s sons, apart from the tribe of Levi, which served in the tabernacle and had no allotment in the land of promise (Num. XVIII). In the division of the land of promise, Joseph’s two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, were received in order that they might have an allotment in the land of promise and might each form a tribe. Tribes are, as it were, distinct districts and assemblies of peoples. Therefore, when Joseph’s two sons were received along with the other [Col. 0705C] sons of Jacob (Gen. XLVIII)—for in place of Joseph’s one tribe two tribes of his sons were added—there were thirteen; but when the tribe of Levi, which was priestly and lived from tithes, was included, only twelve remained, among whom the land was divided. Among these tribes is Judah, from which kings came. Hence Jacob, blessing his sons, said: “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes to whom it was promised” (Gen. XLIX). And all are called Jews from this tribe, from which also our Lord Jesus Christ came. Therefore, having acknowledged Caesar and not Christ, who is from Judah, the Jews should no longer be called Jews. Thus the kingdom of the Jews has been overthrown because they refused to recognize the true King, namely Christ; they renounced this name when they said: “We have no king but Caesar.” If they have no king but Caesar, the ruler has now failed from Judah. Therefore He to whom the promise was made has come. Thus those who believe in Him are more truly Jews. The true Judah is Christ’s Church, believing in Him who came from the tribe of Judah, in which God is truly known. It follows: And in true Israel, namely those who see God, great is His name [ordinary gloss]; it is not blasphemed, as it is through the wicked.

VERS. 2.—“And his place was made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion.”

And His place, God’s place, was made in peace, [Cassiodorus, Jerome, ordinary gloss, Augustine] that is, He has a place in the humble and well-pacified person. Other translators say, “His place is in Salem,” [Col. 0706A] but it is the same, because an interpretation is given here. For Salem means “peace.” And His dwelling is in true Zion, that is, in the Church which now beholds through faith; or in Zion, that is, in future contemplation, when we shall see Him face to face (I Cor. XV). Observe the fitting order of the words. Judah, that is confession, is first; then follows Israel, that is, the person who sees God, because first one must confess sins, through which God is seen, and then there is a place with God in peace. When peace follows Israel, afterward there shall be His dwelling in Zion—that is, in contemplation, where He will be seen face to face.

VERS. 3.—“There he broke the powers, the bow, the shield, the sword, and war.”

[Col. 0706B] There He broke. [Augustine, Jerome, Remigius, ordinary gloss, Cassiodorus.] As if he said: They possess these things only from God, because there—that is, in Judah, Israel, Salem, Zion—He broke the powers; or there, that is, in that eternal peace, He broke the powers, namely the bow, that is, deceits; the shield, that is, everything by which they proudly protect themselves; the sword, that is, everything by which they fight against God; and war, that is, every kind of resistance which they make against God by defending sins. For where God, the author of peace, comes, all these things flee.

## PART II. Diapsalma. VERS. 4.—“You enlighten wondrously from the eternal mountains; all the foolish in heart have been troubled.”

Enlightening. [Alcuin, Augustine, ordinary gloss, Haymo.] The second part, in which it says that Christ enlightens, the Jew sleeps; and that Christ judges, the Jew perishes. As if he said: You have broken the powers, and You enlighten from the eternal mountains—that is, through the eternal mountains, namely the apostles; You, not the mountains themselves, enlighten wondrously, that is, by miracles. You shall be terrible when You come to judgment; but he inserts why You shall be terrible in the future, saying, “They have been troubled,” etc.; and this is a parenthesis. Or, according to another reading, “enlightening”: [Augustine, Jerome, Cassiodorus] as if he said: You have broken the powers. And You enlighten, not the mountains themselves. The word “You” is said magnificently and with force, lest anyone suppose that the mountains enlighten Him. You enlighten wondrously, that is, through miracles performed by the hands of the apostles; You enlighten from [Col. 0706D] the eternal mountains, that is, through the eternal mountains, namely the prophets and apostles, who first receive the light, through whom those sitting in darkness are enlightened, and whose blessedness shall not end. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Therefore they are called eternal; and through them You promised eternal life to believers. But at this enlightenment all foolish in heart—that is, those following worldly desires—have been troubled, because another life, not found here, was announced to them. He next sets forth why He shall be terrible in the future; therefore he adds: “They have been troubled.”

VERS. 5.—“They slept their sleep, and all men of riches found nothing in their hands.”

They slept, [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin] resting in these present things, which had become delightful to them—that is, cooling toward eternal goods and yielding to the flesh, without foreseeing what would profit them—their own sleep, which differs from the rest of the good because this sleep is deceptive. For in sleep they see themselves possessing treasures; but when they awaken, they find nothing. Hence he says: And all men of riches found nothing. Here is a definition of the avaricious, that is, those intent upon riches. He does not say, “those having riches.” Many have them who do not love them; but “men of riches” are those who place all their hope in the uncertainty of riches. They found nothing, I say, in their hands. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, ordinary gloss, Augustine.] He says this as though they were still searching in their hands when they discover that they have held nothing. Thus the dream of this present life makes them rich; awakening after this life reveals them poor. [Col. 0707B] These words allude to the actions of dreamers, who on waking seek in their hands what they seemed to hold while asleep and grieve that they have lost it, though they realize that they had never possessed it at all. Such are those who entered this life and, through temporal desires, as it were fell asleep. Here riches and fleeting vain pomp receive them, and all things pass away. Thus they found nothing in their hands because they placed nothing in Christ’s hands, who says: “I was hungry,” etc. (Matt. XXV). For He who is rich in heaven is hungry in the poor. Or “men of riches” means those who consider themselves rich in free choice and the Law; and they found nothing in their hands because after this life they have no good thing. But their having slept is from You, because:

VERS. 6.—“At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, those who mounted horses have slumbered.”

At Your rebuke, [ordinary gloss, Augustine, Jerome, Augustine] that is, from the wrath and blindness by which You blind them, O God of Jacob, that is, of the younger people, they have slept with blindness of heart, like Pharaoh and the Egyptians, and like those who wander through worldly matters. For Pharaoh despised the Lord’s rebukes with an obstinate mind; so these likewise neglect the Lord’s holy admonitions. But who have slept? Those who mounted the horses of pride, that is, those who refused to be humble, whose pride increased when Christ humbled Himself, while they were not humbled. Hence the sons of Israel were commanded in the Law not to multiply horses for themselves (Deut. XVII). Solomon too did not have horses from Judea, [Col. 0707D] but bought them from Egypt (III Kings X). Consider the fearful thing. A rebuke has a sound, and the sound of rebuke usually wakes people. But so great is the weight of the rebuking God that those rebuked fall asleep: that is, their hearts are hardened. Hardness of heart is sleep. But what those now asleep do not feel, they shall feel at the end, because:

VERS. 7.—“You are terrible, and who shall resist you? From that time is your wrath.”

You shall be terrible at the coming judgment; and [Cassiodorus, Augustine] although here they resist in some way, then who shall resist You? No one. But “from that time is Your wrath.” For now they say what they please and dispute against God. What then shall happen? Behold, then shall be Your wrath, when:

[Col. 0708A] VERS. 8.—“From heaven you caused judgment to be heard; the earth trembled and was still.”

Coming from heaven, You caused judgment to be heard, [Alcuin, Haymo, Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, You shall cause it to be heard. But He uses the past tense as if it had already happened: judgment made known to all. The Lord shall come from heaven to judgment. Hence the Apostle says: “At the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven, coming with angels” (II Thess. I). Or, according to another reading: “You hurled judgment from heaven,” for He shall descend as though a missile sent by a most powerful hand. Then the power of the judgment is explained when it adds: “The earth trembled.” As if he said: You shall execute judgment. Therefore the earth trembled and rested from its evils: that is, earthly people shall be terrified and, their power destroyed, shall cease. But it would be better for them to fear and cease now than then.

[Col. 0708B] VERS. 9.—“When God rose up in judgment, to save all the meek of the earth.”

When God, [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, ordinary gloss, Cassiodorus] that is, Jesus Christ, rose up in judgment—or judging judgment severely—He who here remained still and endured everything. Or connect it thus: I say, judgment shall be executed when God rises in judgment, that is, when He who appeared humble appears powerful. The meaning is the same. Or thus, from the words “from heaven”: as if he said: There shall be wrath. Nor has this been unannounced, because from heaven—that is, from me, Asaph—you caused judgment to be heard as something to come. Therefore the earth, that is, man, trembled and ceased from evil. When did You cause it to be heard? When God, that is Christ, rose here from death, and afterward was to come in judgment, that is, to judge all [Alcuin, [Col. 0708C] Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, ordinary gloss]. But lest you suppose that judgment is made only for the condemnation of the wicked, he adds, “to save all the meek of the earth,” namely those who do not mount the horses of pride, but have confessed their sins in humility, who possess peace of mind and do not reject God’s yoke. I say, meek of the earth—as if he said: I do not mean the angels, who are the meek of heaven, not of earth.

## PART III. Diapsalma. VERS. 10.—“For the thought of man shall confess to you, and the remnant of thought shall keep a festival for you.”

For the thought of man. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, ordinary gloss, Alcuin.] The third part, in which he exhorts those now devout to offer vows. As if he said: He rightly saves the meek, [Col. 0708D] because the thought of the meek person shall confess to You—that is, the meek shall praise You in thought and also in deed. Hence he adds: “And the remnant of thought.” That is, the performance of a good work shall keep a festival for You: the meek shall cease from the servile work of sin, not attending to the world but at rest and intent upon good works. For thought is the conception of a vow; the remnant is the payment of the vow—the act remaining after the thought. And because He shall save, therefore, O people:

VERS. 11.—“Make vows and pay them to the Lord your God, all you who bring gifts around him.”

Make vows in your mind of any good thing, and after the vow necessarily pay them in deed. [ordinary gloss, Augustine.] It should be noted that some vows are common, concerning those things without which there is no salvation: such as vowing faith in baptism, [Col. 0709A] renouncing the devil and his pomps, not killing, not being proud, and the like. Even if we do not promise these, we must fulfill them; and this command is given concerning them to all: “Make vows and pay them.” Other vows are individual, such as chastity, virginity, and the like. He therefore invites us to make these vows; He does not command that we vow, but that we pay our vows. Vowing is left to the will, but after the promise of a vow payment is necessarily required. Therefore He does not say simply, “Make vows,” and “Do not make vows,” but “Make vows and pay them”—that is, if you vow, pay. Otherwise they are bound by the vow itself and incur condemnation, because they have made void their first faith, as the Apostle says (I Tim. V).

Or “first thought” is that by which we begin good things: namely, to repent of sin and confess to God. This produces [Col. 0709B] the remaining thoughts which keep festival. First it is necessary to condemn and dislike what we were; afterward we must remember what we were and what we have received. These are the remnants of thought, lest the wound which we had and the gift of healing which the Savior bestowed should fall from memory. Keeping these in mind, let us give thanks to our Deliverer; this is to celebrate solemnities. The order of the text does not depend on what precedes, so that the distinctive character of the diapsalma may be preserved, but looks to what follows, thus: [Augustine, Cassiodorus] The thought of man—namely the first thought, by which he condemns evils and begins good things—shall confess to You; and the remnants of thought, that is, the thoughts remaining after the first, namely that a person should always remember past evils in order to mourn, [Col. 0709C] and bestowed goods in order to hope, shall keep a festival for You by giving thanks. For a person realizes that he is free from sins, just as, after cleansing, the Jews were commanded in the Law to offer God a festal gift. And because the Lord alone is owed a festival, therefore, O people, make vows and pay them—this does not change—to the Lord your God, not merely to man, because He is not merely man but also God. [ordinary gloss, Remigius, Cassiodorus.] Pay them, all you who are around Him through faith, bringing gifts—that is, yourselves as gifts offered upon altars. Such persons are exhorted to make vows, not heretics or pagans. Or according to another reading, which is, “All who are around Him bring,” or “shall bring,” [Alcuin, Augustine] as if he said: I exhort you for this reason, because all who are around [Col. 0709D] Him as servants shall offer or bring gifts of humility; that is, all the humble confess Him and worship Him. Those who are, as it were, around Him in the middle understand that truth is common to all and do not, through pride, make it their own; these offer gifts because they possess humility. But those who make their own what is common to all, as though trying to draw to one side something set in the middle, shall not offer gifts. He has now said to whom they ought to offer, namely the Lord, and who are around Him; then he adds why, saying:

VERS. 12.—“To the Terrible One, and to him who takes away the spirit of princes; terrible among the kings of the earth.”

To the Terrible One. [ordinary gloss, Alcuin, Augustine.] As if he said: Make vows to the terrible Lord—that is, because He is terrible. If not through love, act through fear, for the good truly fear Him, whereas the wicked do not. And because He is terrible, let no proud person presume to make common truth his own; rather, let him be humble, understanding what is common to all and possessing God’s Spirit, not the spirit of princes, that is, a proud spirit. Hence he adds: And to Him who takes away the spirit of princes, that is, the boldness of the proud—the spirit of pride or of fear—by giving His own Spirit. Thus He makes them kings of themselves, who govern their own bodies. Hence he adds: “Terrible among the kings of the earth,” [Jerome, Haymo, Augustine] who govern themselves while subject to God, of whom it is said: “The king’s heart is in the hand of the Lord” (Prov. XXI). Or literally, He takes away the spirit, that is, the life, of princes—earthly princes. As if he said: He is terrible not only to others but also to the kings of the earth. Hence he adds: “Terrible among the kings [Col. 0710B] of the earth,” who are terrible to others.

## Comparison on Psalm LXXV: “God Is Known in Judah,” etc.

VERS. 3.—“There he broke the powers, the bow, the shield,” etc. In Hebrew and Greek these two terms, “powers, bow,” are arranged so that they stand in a genitive relation. Jerome formerly translated, “the missiles of the bow,” which others render in the same sense as “the arrows” or “darts of the bow”: *RISCHPHE QUACHETH*. Here the first word would plainly be pronounced *RESCHAPHIM* were it not in the construct state, as the Greek clearly shows: *τὰ κράτη τῶν τόξων* (“the powers of the bows”). Therefore someone might say that the Latin copies contain a scribal error in reading “powers, bow,” as Jerome also has and explains in his *Commentaries*: “There,” he says, “He broke the strengths of bows, those burning arrows which the devil sent.” Augustine reads it so as well; likewise Cassiodorus, “the horns of bows”; and Arnobius also. Yet I find that Gregory himself read the terms separately, as is clear from his individual interpretation of each, *Morals*, book XXIII, chapter 29, in these words: “Again, in respect to human resistance, through that Prophet, the shield is set forth, as he says elsewhere: ‘There He broke horns, bow, shield, sword, and war.’ For in horns is denoted the pride of the proud; in the bow, the snares of those striking from afar; in the shield, the obstinate hardness of defenses; in the sword, the blow nearby; and in war, the very movement of the mind against the Lord.” And after a few intervening words: “Again, through the same Psalm it is said: ‘He shall break the bow, shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire.’ For the Lord breaks the bow when He destroys the hidden contrivances of plotters,” etc. Haymo, explaining this passage, tends toward the same reading and distinction: “There, that is, in Zion, that is, in those who behold Him, God broke—that is, destroyed—the powers of the devil, and enumerates them by parts: the bow, that is, hidden [Col. 0710D] attack; the shield, that is, the defense of wickedness; and the sword, that is, manifest attack. And to include everything, He says ‘war,’ that is, every attack.” Thus Haymo. He most plainly distinguishes “powers” and “bow.” Now, since there have been many editions, what if some had *τὸ τόξον* (“the bow”)? I leave that for the reader to weigh. It is clear, however, that the Chaldean distinguishes, with a conjunction inserted, “arrows and bows.” The translation of Felinus agrees.

VERS. 4.—“You enlighten wondrously from the eternal mountains.” Jerome: “from mountains of captivity”; Pratensis: “of prey”; Sanctes: “from rapacious ones”; and the others similarly. The Hebrew word *TEREPH* undoubtedly means “prey.” But it is plain that the Septuagint read *TEREM*, differing by only one little letter, that is, “before”; and, to make this clearer, they said “from eternal mountains” rather than “from mountains before.”

“They have been troubled.” Others translate, “they have been despoiled,” or [Col. 0711A] “they have been given over to plunder”: *ESCTOLALU*, where at the beginning *aleph* is placed in place of *he*, as Münster indicates. But people exposed to plundering are everywhere troubled. Hence Nebiensis has “they have been cast down.”

“Foolish in heart.” Others say “strong” or “robust in heart,” or “fierce.” Jerome, however, gives “proud in heart,” followed by Nebiensis: *ABIRE LEB*. From this we may infer that nothing is more foolish than a proud heart, according to the Apostle’s saying in Romans I: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools.”

VERS. 5.—“Men of riches found nothing in their hands.” At this place the diversity of translations depends on two points. One is the word *HAUL*, polysemous, meaning at times strength, army, riches, and certain other things. The other is (as has often been observed) the equivalence of case-forms in Hebrew declension. Therefore, that you may see how this is true, consider the various translations. Jerome says: “All men of an army did not find their hands”; [Col. 0711B] Pellicanus: “Vigorous men did not find their hands.” Nebiensis and the interpreters for Cajetan say almost the same; Pratensis agrees with Jerome. Sanctes: “Strong men did not find strength in their hands”; Felinus: “All men equipped with military prowess could accomplish nothing with their hands”; Münster: “All men whose hands were mighty did not find [them].” Campensis’s paraphrase comes quite close. Yet it should be known that Jerome, in his letter to Sunnias, prefers the reading “their hands,” without a preposition, because Greek has simply *ταῖς χερσὶν αὐτῶν* (“their hands”), especially since he was criticized as if he had inserted the preposition in his Greek version. Nevertheless, in the same work he advises avoiding disputes where the meaning is the same.

VERS. 6.—“Those who mounted horses have slumbered.” Jerome, as likewise all others who follow the Hebrew, has: “Chariot and horse have been put to sleep”: *NIRDAM VERECHB VASUS*. The metaphor expressed in different words is brought back to the same sense. For it is certain [Col. 0711C] that the Psalm speaks of the pride of earthly power, since, Augustine says, sitting on horses is not sinful, but raising the neck of power against God and imagining oneself to be in some position of honour is sinful. Whatever term in our reading corresponds to the different meaning of each Hebrew word does sufficiently convey the sense.

VERS. 8.—“From heaven you caused judgment to be heard.” Faber teaches that, more correctly according to the Hebrew, it should be said in the future: “From heaven you will cause judgment to be heard.” We know that the past tense is used in place of the future; nevertheless, word for word the Hebrew has the past tense, *HISGHMATA*.

VERS. 10.—“The thought of man shall confess to you.” *HAMAH* is rendered “wrath” or “rage,” where we say “thought.” Yet if we say that it can be derived from the root *IAHAM*, which sometimes means “to conceive,” we shall find “thought,” which Augustine interprets in this place as the first conception of inward repentance. Thus we too ought to be angry at our sins, recalling in the bitterness of our soul the deeds of our former life, so that from this we may worthily speak praise to God and confess to Him without pretense.

[Col. 0712B] “The remnant of thought shall keep a festival for you.” Jerome: “You shall gird yourself with the remnant of wrath”: *SCHERITH HEMOTH TACHOZ*. Others render: “You shall gird yourself with the remnant of fury.” I think the Septuagint read *HAGAG*, with double *gimel*, meaning “to celebrate a solemnity,” rather than *HAGAR*, with a single *gimel*, “to gird.”

VERS. 12.—“To the Terrible One, and to him who takes away the spirit of princes.” Jerome explains why he added the pronoun “to him,” which was not in the Greek, indeed not in the Hebrew either. Thus he writes to Sunnias and Fretella: “You say that ‘to him’ is not written in the Greek, *τῷ φοβερῷ ἀφαιρουμένῳ πνεύματα ἀρχόντων*, that is, ‘to the terrible one and to the one taking away the spirits of princes.’ It is true. But unless we add ‘to him,’ Latin speech does not sound right. For we cannot say, ‘to the terrible one, and who takes away the spirit of princes.’” Thus Jerome. Less important is the fact that the Hebrews connect the word “terrible” with the preceding verse, when the clauses are joined together.

# PSALM LXXVI

[Col. 0711]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “FOR THE END, FOR IDITHUN; A PSALM OF ASAPH.”

[Col. 0711C]

With my voice I cried to the Lord. Title: “Unto the end, for Idithun; a psalm of Asaph.” [Aug.] Idithun, as we have often said above, means “one leaping over them”; Asaph, “assembly.” It is the faithful assembly that speaks here: leaping over all visible things in order to attain the end, which is Christ, whom Moses desired to see when he said, “Lord, show me your face” (Exod. [Col. 0711D] XXXIII). To him the Lord said, “No human being shall see me and live” (ibid.). The sense of the title is: This psalm is ascribed to Asaph—that is, to the faithful assembly which here speaks and acts on behalf of Idithun, that is, concerning itself as leaping over into the end, namely into Christ, beyond whom there is nothing. Its purpose is to teach us to trample underfoot the desires and allurements of the world and to set before ourselves nothing but him from whom all things are, as he himself does.

Method: [Cassiod.] There are four divisions. First, he says how, transcending all things, he seeks and finds God. Second, he considers whether God will restore him, at “They anticipated.” Third, he says what he discovered by considering, at “And I said: Now.” Fourth, he explains what Christ accomplishes in the world, at “The waters saw you.” Therefore Asaph, leaping over all things and seeking God alone, says:

[Col. 0712C] VERSE 1.—“With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice to God, and he gave heed to me.”

“With my voice,” [Alcuin., Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] that is, with the intention of devotion, “I cried to the Lord,” asking nothing other than him; for from him he seeks himself, and passes beyond whatever is below him. He then repeats, “With my voice I cried to God,” showing why he cries: namely, because he is Lord, because he is God. Or thus: First he says to whom he cries, and not what he asks, saying, [Col. 0712D] “With my voice to the Lord.” He does not say what he asks, because there is no need to say it to one who knows what is expedient. Then he adds why he cried: “And my voice is to God,” another reading; the voice is directed to that for which it is uttered. He adds this lest he be thought to cry to God for something other than God himself, above whom there is nothing.

[Gl. int., Aug., Cassiod.] Or our text is read in the same sense: namely, “I cried with my voice, being directed to God”; and, to show that he did not cry in vain, he adds, “and he gave heed to me,” because he is always present to those who seek him—but not to those who seek something other than him. Hence: “They cried, and there was none to save them” (Ps. XVII). Likewise: “They cried to the Lord, and he did not hear them” (ibid.). God’s giving heed is his granting all that is requested, even more than is requested.

[Col. 0713A] VERSE 2.—“In the day of my tribulation I sought God with my hands in the night before him, and I was not deceived.”

“In the day of my tribulation.” [Gl. int., Cassiod., Aug.] As if he said: I sought God not only with my voice, but also with my hands, that is, with works; and not only at another time, but also “in the day of my tribulation,” when others seek to escape from tribulation—those who do not leap over it. Forgetful of necessities, this man seeks God alone.

Or the connection is thus: How do all these things occur—namely, the crying and the hearing? Behold: “In the day of my tribulation,” that is, when I suffer tribulation, or in this life, which is wholly tribulation to one who longs for heaven, “I sought God.” From tribulation this man seeks God, that in him he may find rest. He seeks nothing other than him.

Note that up to this point [Col. 0713B] he has said who cried, to whom, why, and under what necessity. He next adds how he sought, when, where, and with what result. As if he said: How do you seek? “With my hands,” that is, with good works, not with an empty desire. When? “In the night.” Here “night” means the same as the preceding “day of tribulation,” namely this life. This world is tribulation to one who longs for heaven. And it is night because in it the lamp of God’s word is needed. Hence Peter says: “We have the more certain prophetic word, to which you do well to give heed as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawn and the day-star arise in our hearts” (II Pet. I). The true day, therefore, will come after this night; compared with that day, this life is night. Yet it is day in comparison with the life of unbelievers. Hence the Apostle: “Let us walk becomingly as in the day” (Rom. XII). Thus it is day in comparison with unbelievers and night in comparison with angels; and although it is the same thing that is called day and night, it is called day above for one reason and night here for another. Day denotes necessity; night, the time of crying.

Behold, he has said under what necessity, how, and when he seeks; and where do you seek? “Before him,” or “against him.” He seeks God before God himself, who does not perform his righteousness before people in order to be seen by them. Hence: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matt. VI). And: “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet,” etc. (ibid.). And with what result? “I was not deceived,” unlike those who seek something else, because I found what I sought.

[Col. 0713D] VERSE 3.—“I refused to be consoled in my soul; I remembered God and was delighted, and I was exercised; and my spirit failed.”

“I refused,” or, “I denied consolation to my soul,” or “my soul refused to be consoled.” [Aug.] Here he explains the tribulation that pierces him and in a sense presses upon him the necessity of leaping over. As if he said: I spoke of “the day of tribulation.” That tribulation was so great that my soul refused consolation—or I refused to console my soul—because evils surrounded me on every side. Such weariness and sorrow for sinners took hold of me that the soul closes itself against every consolation. For if anyone appears righteous, he who alone is often a consolation is found otherwise: this man experienced it, struck by scandals. Therefore he now fears to rejoice or take consolation in anything, [Col. 0714A] because he finds scandal in everything. Or he is afraid because he is secure in nothing. What relief, then, is there?

Behold, “I remembered God,” in whom is sweetness. Let the hands of the seeker find him in sorrow as their consoler, “and I was delighted”; or, “and I chattered,” another reading, that is, I exulted in speaking about God like a chatterer who, through joy, neither wished nor could be silent. For those are properly called chatterers who are so called in common speech: when joy comes upon them, they neither can nor wish to be silent. And in chattering my spirit again failed, having previously wasted away through weariness of evils. Therefore my spirit again failed, because—

PART II. Diapsalma. VERSE 4.—“My eyes anticipated the watches; I was troubled, and I did not speak.”

“My enemies.” [Aug.] Another reading: “All my enemies anticipated my watches,” seeking grounds for accusation in my words; that is, all my enemies kept watch over me—more than I did. My spiritual enemies forestalled me by laying snares, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the spiritual forces of wickedness” (Eph. V). They watched more to deceive than I did to guard myself; everywhere they place scandals, everywhere they set traps. For weariness is in the heart; one must fear lest sorrow swallow up joy. Or lest, through chattering in joy, the spirit fail, and a person say something which the enemy may seize upon, that is, censure; on this account he is troubled and [Col. 0714C] does not speak. Hence it follows: “I was troubled,” because it is evil to be silent and evil to speak. Therefore he turns back, adding: “And I did not speak.” Yet he does not cease: he tries to find a remedy and wishes to transcend this also. Hence he adds:

VERSE 5.—“I considered the days of old, and kept eternal years in mind.”

“I considered the days.” [Aug.] This man now acts, as one beaten outside, in the secret place of his mind, where no one barks against him. God helps him there; remaining there, he reflects upon eternal things—which can be done there, not outside amid the noise. And this is: “I considered the days of old, and eternal years,” where these evils are not; “I kept them in mind,” that is, in memory. He takes “days” and “years” in the same sense. This reflection on eternal things requires a great silence from every tumult [Col. 0714D] of human affairs, so that he may act safely within. Hence he adds:

VERSE 6.—“And I meditated in the night with my heart; I was exercised, and I searched my spirit.”

“And I meditated in the night with my heart,” [Aug.] where there is no place for a slanderer; “and I chattered,” another reading, no longer outside as before; but “I searched,” another reading, “my spirit,” where, if I speak and chatter with it, I may be able to discover much. And what did you find? That God will not reject a human being for ever. He says this in the form of a question:

VERSE 7.—“Will God cast off for ever, or will he not add to be more favorable still?”

“Will God cast off for ever,” [Aug.] a human being? Far be it! Observe the leaps of the one who leaps over. Above he had found weariness in this life: nowhere faith, nowhere consolation. Whichever people he regarded, he found scandal in them; nowhere, therefore, was he secure. Thus he leapt over to God, that there he might rejoice; but, chattering outside about God, he was reproached by enemies. Hence he returned to his heart. Yet because it was evil for him to be silent, lest he be silent about good things, greatly distressed in this life he thought much about the other life, where there is no temptation; nor did he cease leaping over even his own spirit until he came to the end of which the title speaks, where he discovered that God will not cast off for ever. [Rem., Cassiod.]

Otherwise, from “My soul refused consolation.” As if he said: Rightly was I not deceived, because I sought God from God; for [Col. 0715B] my soul refused consolation in things other than God. Therefore I remembered God, in whom is sweetness, and was delighted in him; and I was exercised in investigating the greatness of his wisdom and power, and my spirit failed because the matter is incomprehensible.

“They anticipated.” Second part. [Cassiod., Alcuin., Cassiod.] Having found God, who alone is good, he considers whether he will restore him, according to Augustine’s preceding reading. This is not a division; rather, it states how he was exercised: namely, “my eyes anticipated the watches of others,” as a person does who rises before the proper time for work. Or, “my eyes,” that is, my affections, “anticipated the watches,” that is, the diligence of others. [Col. 0715C] Or by “watches” he signifies the night offices, as we customarily call them, which we hold in the praise of God. As if he said: Before others, at the night offices, I praised God; and while awake I was troubled because I could not attain what I seek.

[Alcuin., Gl. int., Haym., Cassiod.] One who sleeps amid worldly things dreams that he is blessed. “And I did not speak,” that is, I did not murmur against God. And therefore he was troubled because, while in the secret night he searches his own mind, he sees the human race falling into sins; and, having already leapt over vices, he is tormented by pious grief for others. But he is silent and does not speak, because in the night he does not have the consolation of human conversation, at which time he reflects more cautiously. Hence he adds: “I considered.” [Cassiod., Alcuin.] As if he said: Therefore I was troubled because “I considered [Col. 0715D] the days of old,” of Adam, in which humankind fell from its stability; that is, I considered what befell Adam through disobedience, and from this I recognized this deficiency of humankind. And I kept in mind, by contrast, the eternal years which, if man had persevered, he would have possessed—something foolish people do not do. As if he said: I saw the goods that I lost and the evils that I found. Therefore this man is troubled, because humanity desires the days of old and neglects eternal years.

“And I meditated in the night,” that is, in this state of deficiency, “with my heart,” that is, with reason, considering silently with reason whether in some way I could return to the eternal years; for one who speaks silently with reason is exercised peacefully in it. “And I searched my spirit,” that is, I purified my mind so that I might see. Other interpreters say, “I winnowed my spirit,” that is, the strength of my soul. [Hier.] Turning it [Col. 0716A] this way and that expresses the act of deliberation. Or, “I searched,” that is, I dug into my spirit, [Alcuin., Cassiod., Aug.] considering within myself: “Will God cast off the human race for ever? And will he not add,” that is, will he not himself add, “to be more favorable still?” As he who was already favorable by his grace in the Old Testament, will he not add something greater in the New through the coming of the Son? This is the thought of one discussing mercy. Or, “be more favorable still,” that is, may he who was angry in rejecting and inflicting evils become gentler in delivering and recalling. For what we suffer was wrath.

VERSE 8.—“Or will he cut off his mercy unto the end, from generation to generation?”

Or will he cut off from humankind the mercy [Col. 0716B] of the incarnation—[Gl. int., Cassiod.] namely, that he was born of a Virgin? I call it “his” mercy because he himself is merciful by nature. And will he do this “unto the end,” that is, wholly, from the good as from the evil? Or “unto the end,” that is, in the fullness of time: will he not grant even at that time the benefit of the incarnation, namely, from the generation of the wicked into the generation—or from the first generation of the Old Testament into the final generation, namely that of the New Testament? He repeats the same thing in other words, saying:

VERSE 9.—“Or will God forget to have mercy? Or will he restrain his mercies in his wrath?”

“Will God forget to have mercy?” [Aug., Haym., Gl. int., Aug.] In another there is no mercy unless God gives it, and will he himself be without it? Does the stream flow while the fountain has dried up? For he is the fountain of mercy, [Col. 0716C] who possesses it naturally, and from whom it flows into others like a little stream from a spring. When he says, “Will he forget to have mercy?” he indicates that God has begun and is accustomed to have mercy. He repeats the same thing differently: “Or will he restrain his mercies in his wrath?” That is, will wrath conquer mercy? Rather, mercy will conquer wrath. Hence through Isaiah: “I shall not be your avenger for ever” (Isa. XXXVII). “Nor shall I be angry with you for all time.” Therefore he says first, “Will he restrain his mercies?” because he has already begun to have mercy. And therefore one must not give up.

PART III. Diapsalma. VERSE 10.—“And I said: Now I have begun. This is the change of the right hand of the Most High.”

“And I said.” [Alcuin., Cassiod.] The third part, in which he says what he discovered by deliberating: namely, that Christ changes and redeems human beings. As if he said: I was considering these things [Col. 0716D] within myself, and afterward I said—that is, I answered this meditation of mine: Now for the first time I have begun to understand; that is, I understood what had been hidden from eternal ages, namely, that humanity would be restored to eternal years. And what I now understand is an argument for future consummation: namely, that I shall be perfected in the future. “And this is the change of the right hand of the Most High,” [Gl. int., Cassiod.] that is, of God’s favor and graciousness. As if he said: It is not a change from mercy to wrath but from wrath to mercy: namely, that we are changed from servants into sons, as I was.

VERSE 11.—“I remembered the works of the Lord, because I shall remember from the beginning your works.”

“I remembered the works of the Lord,” [Cassiod.] that is, this change accomplished in me; I remembered it, never giving it over to forgetfulness, so that I might deserve better things. But lest he seem to rejoice only in himself, he adds: And truly I remembered this change, because I shall also remember your wonders from the beginning—that is, those things which God bestowed upon humankind from the beginning: that he made Adam in his image; that he accepted Abel’s offering; likewise what he did for Noah, in whose ark he saved diverse animals as a mystery of the Church; what he did for Abraham, whose offering of his son signified Christ’s incarnation and passion; and finally, that God himself came. These are the things that delight a holy man. Hence above: “And I was delighted.” Then he repeats it more generally.

VERSE 12.—“And I shall meditate upon all your works, and I shall be exercised in your inventions.”

[Col. 0717B] “And I shall meditate upon all your works, and I shall be exercised in your inventions,” [Alcuin., Rem., Cassiod.] that is, in the commandments which you have devised, or by which you shall devise; for all wisdom and prudence are from you. Or, “in your observances,” another reading—that is, in commandments that must be observed—I shall be exercised, because it is not enough to read the Scriptures; one must display the fruit of works. Instructed in these matters, he breaks forth into praise, saying:

VERSE 13.—“O God, your way is in the holy one; what god is great like our God? You are the God who works wonders.”

“O God, your way,” that is, the way of returning to you, “is in the Holy One,” namely Christ. [Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] Otherwise, from “And I said”: this man who leaps over, finding rest nowhere, did not cease to leap over even himself until he came to God. Deceived and wearied in other things, he has now found where he may be secure. As if he said: Thus I leapt over myself all the way to the end. “And I said, Now,” that is, I understood for the first time: when I leapt over myself and came to God, I began something in which I might be secure, where my enemies do not anticipate me, where there is now no danger. And I also said: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High,” that is, now the most high God has begun to change me through the right hand, namely through Christ. [Hier.] For the Son is the Father’s right hand. Hence: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII). And I know that he can change me because he created all things, whose works I remember.

[Haym., Aug.] And this is: “I remembered the works of the Lord.” This man now ranges through God’s works and rejoices securely, whereas above he failed while chattering outside. Now forgetful even of himself, he delights in God alone. Hence he adds: “Because I shall remember.” As if he said: I remembered and shall remember, which he says in this way because “I shall remember your wonders”; and not only shall I remember, but also “I shall meditate upon all your works and chatter about your affections,” another reading. [Aug.] Behold, the third “chattering.” First he chattered to people outside and afterward failed in his spirit, yet made progress; now he chatters about God’s works when he has reached the place toward which he tended. “In your affections,” not in mine. For human affections differ from God’s. Human affections concern earthly things: the table, the theatre, hunting, fowling, and the like. And as human affection exists in these earthly things, [Col. 0718A] so there is a certain inward affection in God’s works and meditation: when his gift is contemplated, and in created things the Creator is sought and found, nowhere displeasing but pleasing through all things and above all things—God in the holy one.

He now begins to show God’s works of mercy toward us, about which he chatters and exults, showing through whom the return to eternal years is accomplished. As if he said: By the things mentioned I am certain that I shall come. And I shall come under this guide: O God, in the holy Christ is your way, that is, the way of worshipping you and coming to you. For he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). Let transgressors therefore return to their heart (Isa. XLVI), and search their heart while recalling eternal years; thus they shall find mercy. Hence, rejoicing, this man sets God’s power above the idols falsely worshipped.

[Cassiod., Aug.] As if he said: Since these things are so, what god among the gods of the nations, which people worship with affection, is great like our God? As if he said: none; for you alone—not another—are God properly so called, who alone work wonders both in soul and body. The deaf, blind, sick, dead, and paralytic were healed (Matt. IV, II). These things were done in bodies; in the soul, those lately drunk are sober, and those lately worshippers of idols are faithful. You work wonders, so that—

VERSE 14.—“You made known your power among the peoples; with your arm you redeemed your people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph.”

“Your power,” [Cassiod., Aug.] that is, Christ, you made known when you sent him into the world; and through this this man also becomes one who leaps over, which is one of the wonders. “Made known,” I say, among both faithful and unbelieving peoples; but to unbelievers you made him known only so that they know Christ in the flesh, while to believers you made him known also in his divinity. He then adds what he accomplished through this power, saying: “With your arm,” that is, in Christ, “you redeemed your people,” namely the sons of Jacob, that is, believing Jews, and Joseph himself, that is, the Gentile people. For Joseph came among the nations, and his name means “increase”; thus he fittingly signifies the Gentiles, from whom God’s people was enlarged. Or Joseph means Christ, because as Joseph, sold by his brothers, was first humbled (Gen. XXXVII) and afterward exalted when he ruled in Egypt [Col. 0718D] (Gen. XLII), so Christ, sold by the Jews, passed over to the Gentiles, among whom he ruled, where he had first been humbled in the persecutions of the martyrs. Therefore the sons are those whom he chose from the Gentiles. The meaning is: “And you redeemed the sons of Joseph,” that is, the sons of Christ chosen from the Gentiles. Here we repeat “sons,” which we did not supply the first time.

PART IV. Diapsalma. VERSE 15.—“The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you and feared, and the depths were troubled.”

“They saw.” [Cassiod., Alcuin., Haym., Aug.] The fourth part, where he explains what Christ accomplishes in the world. As if he said: How did he make known his power? Behold, “the waters saw you,” etc. Or the connection is thus: He made Christ known, and through him the waters—that is, the peoples—saw you by faith, O God [Col. 0719A] the Father. Or thus: Because he made known his power, therefore, O God, Christ, who are power and arm, the waters—that is, the peoples—saw you by faith. He repeats it so that each people may be understood: “The waters saw you and feared” because of their sins, and “the depths,” that is, the deep masses of waters, were troubled by the prick of conscience. And these are not few, but—

VERSE 16.—“The multitude of the sound of the waters; the clouds gave their voice.”

“There is a multitude of the sound of the waters,” [Cassiod., Aug.] that is, of peoples resounding in confession of sins, groaning over faults, praises of God, and thanksgivings. Like a stormy sea, the various vows in the Church of peoples resound. But whence come these sounds of waters and this troubling of the depths? [Col. 0719B] Because “the clouds,” that is, the preachers of God’s word, “gave their voice,” preaching Christ among all nations. Of them the Lord says through the prophet: “I will command my clouds that they rain no rain upon it” (Isa. V). And indeed they gave their voice.

VERSE 17.—“For your arrows pass through; the voice of your thunder is in the wheel.”

“For,” [Aug., Cassiod.] that is, because “your arrows,” O God—that is, the voices of the clouds—pass, or have passed, as far as the heart. They did not remain in the ears but pierced hearts through. Note that the word of preaching is called both rain and an arrow: rain because it waters; an arrow because it strikes. Or, “the arrows,” that is, the Evangelists, passed from nation to nation. “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel.” What is this? How shall we understand it? Literally, the voice of thunder rolls, so that a rolling, winding sound is perceived. Thunder has a certain crash like that of vehicles. But are we to return to such childish matters? Certainly not. It must rather be understood allegorically. As if he said: The clouds gave their voice, and this voice of the clouds was not made in secret but was your thunder—that is, it was open—and it was in the wheel of the whole world. For the wheel is the circle of the earth; hence a little wheel is called an *orbiculus*, “a small circle.” He explains this afterward when he says, “to the world,” namely, the world which the clouds traversed, thundering commandments and flashing miracles.

VERSE 18.—“Your lightnings shone upon the world; the earth was moved and trembled.”

[Col. 0719D] “They shone.” As if he said: The preachers passed through, and through them your lightnings shone upon the world, [Cassiod.] that is, divine commandments which by miracles drove away the world’s darkness. Hence “the earth,” that is, those who dwell on earth, was moved to conversion and trembled. He calls the same thing “sea” in what follows:

VERSE 19.—“Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters; and your footprints shall not be known.”

“Your way is in the sea.” [Aug., Cassiod., Hier.] The earth itself is called sea by comparison, because human life is bitter and subject to storms, where the larger fish devours the smaller. Thus your way is in the sea, that is, in the hearts of people, whom you have subjected to yourself. This sea was bitter and dead; but that fountain of life came in order to sweeten and heal it. [Col. 0720A] Therefore, according to Ezekiel: “A fountain of living water shall go out from the temple of the Lord and shall go to the Dead Sea, which had nothing living” (Ezek. XLVII). No little fish could exist in the Dead Sea; nothing lived in it. But from the temple of the Lord—that is, from the Father’s bosom—the Savior came forth and sweetened the Dead Sea.

Or literally: [Cassiod., Alcuin., Aug.] “Your way is in the sea,” when Christ walked upon the waters of the sea. Or the Jews are understood by “earth,” and the Gentiles by “sea.” The meaning is: “The earth was moved and trembled,” that is, the Jews; “your way is also in the sea of the Gentiles,” that is, your Son. Behold, now your way is in the sea of the Gentiles. Long ago it was “in the holy one,” as was said above: “Your way is in the holy one.” This fits well, because that Holy One is in the sea. [Col. 0720B] For he walks upon the waters of the Gentiles, subjecting them to himself through faith. [Haym., Cassiod., Haym., Aug., Cassiod.] As a figure of this he walked upon the waters.

“And your paths,” that is, your commandments, “are in many waters,” that is, among many peoples—not among few Gentiles; nevertheless “your footprints,” namely your bodily presence, teaching, and miracles, “shall not be known” by the Jews. For he touched some—that is, Jews—who say, “Christ has not yet come.” They say this because they do not see him walking upon the sea of the Gentiles. This is a tacit rebuke of the Jews. As if he said: Though he openly came and showed himself by miracles, nevertheless he was not known by unbelieving Jews, whom he himself led by the hand of Moses and Aaron. Hence he adds:

[Col. 0720C] VERSE 20.—“You led your people like sheep, by the hand of Moses and Aaron.”

“You led.” [Aug., Cassiod., Aug., Alcuin., Cassiod.] As if he said: By whom shall they not be known? By those whom you led. For you led your people, namely the Jewish people, out of Egypt “like sheep,” because they were not truly sheep but goats; and this “by the hand of Moses and Aaron,” that is, by the working of the miracles which they performed. As if he said: You did this for that people, and it did not know you? It is astonishing. Here is a rebuke and reproach of the Jews through the names of these two, Moses and Aaron. Their names also signify the deeds they performed and the mysteries spiritually accomplished in the Church.

Moses means “taken from the river,” Aaron “mountain of strength.” By these names are signified the powers they performed. For among other things Moses made a way in the sea for the Hebrews, signifying that the people of believers are delivered through baptism; Aaron, with eminent strength, resisted those who murmured, in which he bore the image of the Church, compared to a most steadfast mountain.

## Comparison on Psalm LXXVI: “With My Voice to the Lord,” etc.

VERSE 2.—“I sought God with my hands,” that is, “my hand”; or *JADAI*, that is, “my hands.” For the primary meaning of *JAD* is “hand.” It is subsequently transferred to many meanings; and therefore Pratensis, Nebiensis, Sanctes, Münster, and Campensis said, “my stroke” or “my wound,” because a blow [Col. 0721A] is made by the hand itself. Jerome, Pellican, and the interpreters before Cajetan, however, translate “my hand.” The edition appended to Campensis translates “my strength.” For they refer these words, in the nominative case, to what follows, as will immediately be shown.

“In the night before him.” Jerome: “In the night it is stretched out,” namely, the hand. Others: “My wound flowed,” or “was moved,” because they read *NIGERAH*, which can mean “to flow,” “to be extended,” or “to be drawn.” I think, however, that the Septuagint read *NEGDAH*, that is, “before,” or *NEGDO*, “before him.” For it is evident that *resh* and *daleth* closely resemble one another.

“And I was not deceived.” Jerome: “My hand does not rest,” as above. Pagninus and certain others: “My wound will not subside” or “will not cease,” according to their understanding of the already mentioned word *JAD*, together with *LO TAPHUG*. The Septuagint, drawing out the sense from the sense, clearly explained what it means for our hands to be extended to God and not relaxed.

For when almighty God commands that, when we are harassed by distresses, we implore his immediate help with devout and unceasing prayers, awaiting no other refuge, yet by divine counsel it very frequently happens that, though intent upon prayer, we are shaken on every side by waves of tribulations, from which we desired to be freed by continually calling upon God’s mercy. This happens so intensely that Psalm XLIII cries out: “Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord?” What then? Has God deceived us, he who so often urges us to rise to him amid afflictions? Far be it! Therefore let the hands never be relaxed. Let hope always be raised toward God—a hope that does not put to shame (Rom. V). And even if God does not hear according to the petitioner’s will, he nevertheless hears according to the sick person’s health and what is fitting. He has not deceived us but tests us; he does not kill but chastens us.

Hence St Augustine: “In this night let us seek God with our hands; let works not cease. Let us seek God; let desire not be empty.” Thus he. Therefore, if surrounded by tribulations, we began to lift our hands to God, and then, as suffering grew more savage, failed and wasted away, our own sloth would shamefully accuse God, as though he were false in his promises.

VERSE 3.—“I remembered God and was delighted.” Jerome, in place of the final phrase, has: “I shall be troubled”; Münster: “I shall be restless”; Sanctes: “I shall be in tumult.” So also nearly all the others: *VEEHAMAIAH*. The sense would seem opposed unless such disturbance were understood in a good sense.
