For a memory filled with God draws the outer person away from worldly desires—whence the preceding “night,” “my soul refused consolation,” etc.—and immediately follows: “I was exercised, and my spirit failed.” Hence Jerome in his Commentary: “In Hebrew it reads differently: ‘I remembered God and was troubled.’ I considered his gentleness; I considered his mercy; I considered his purity; and, seeing myself unclean, I was greatly troubled.” Thus he.

Add that [Col. 0721D] that Hebrew word also means “to resound,” which can readily be applied to joy. But for “I was exercised,” Jerome translates, “I spoke within myself,” *ASIHAH*, which others also render “I shall speak.” Münster expressed what kind of speech by paraphrase when he translated, “I shall make complaints.” Nothing is inconsistent with the Hebrew word *SOAH*.

VERSE 4.—“My eyes anticipated the watches.” Jerome: “I restrained the looking-up of my eyes.” The other Hebraizing translators render: “You have seized the guards,” or “the eyelids,” of my eyes: *AHAZTA SCHEMUROTH ENAI*. Therefore, just as “to hold the watches” or “guards” of the eyes can make a double sense—either that we can keep them not yet opened or fixed upward, or that we keep them opened, watchful, and raised from drowsiness—so also the eyes anticipate watches either when someone prevents his eyes from lifting their gaze, or when, through diligence and solicitude, he forestalls others in lifting his eyes to God [Col. 0722A] while the rest sleep.

Jerome touches on both points in his Commentaries:

> “In Hebrew it reads differently: ‘I restrained the looking-up of my eyes; I was astounded and did not speak.’ What it says is this: Considering my sins, I did not dare lift my eyes to heaven. For God says to the sinner: ‘Why do you recount my righteous judgments?’ (Ps. XLIX). Therefore I was astounded, afraid, and unable to speak. This is according to the Hebrews. ‘My eyes anticipated the watches’: before anyone kept watch, I kept watch. We read also in Daniel: ‘And behold,’ he says, ‘*IR*, that is, WATCHER’ (Dan. IV). ‘He who guards Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep’ (Ps. CXX). Therefore the monk who does not keep watch cannot say this verse.”

Thus far Jerome. Finally, it is not clear which edition Augustine followed. For he has: “All my enemies anticipated my watches,” unless *INNAH* in Hebrew means “to afflict.”

### Verse 5

“I kept eternal years in mind.” This final phrase, “I kept in mind,” begins the following verse [Col. 0722B] according to the Hebrews: *ezkerah*, “I shall remember.” Then, where we read “I meditated,” they translate “upon my psalms,” or “upon my song,” *neginathi*. The Septuagint, however, took it as though it were a word from the root *nagan*, “he played musical instruments,” which differs little from “to meditate,” so that the song is understood spiritually, as the teaching indicates.

Yet, to remove further uncertainty, it will not be useless to report what Jerome wrote on this verse to Sunia and Fretella:

> “And I meditated by night with my heart, and I exercised myself and searched my spirit.” In place of this, in the Hebrew we read: “I shall remember your psalms in the night with my heart. I spoke and searched my spirit.” For “exercise” the Septuagint translated *adoleschian* [ἀδολεσχίαν], that is, a certain recitation or meditation; and for what we said, “I searched,” they wrote *eskallon* [ἔσκαλλον], which Symmachus translated [Col. 0722C] *anereunōn* [ἀνερεύνων], that is, “I was investigating” or “seeking.” The Fifth Version likewise. In Greek it reads: *kai etē aiōnia emnēsthēn kai emelētēsa, nyktos meta tēs kardias mou ēdoleschon, kai eskalle to pneuma mou* [καὶ ἔτη αἰώνια ἐμνήσθην καὶ ἐμελέτησα, νυκτὸς μετὰ τῆς καρδίας μου ἠδολέσχον, καὶ ἔσκαλλε τὸ πνεῦμά μου]: “And I remembered eternal years and meditated; by night with my heart I discoursed, and my spirit searched.” Properly, however, *skalosmos* [σκαλισμὸς] is an agricultural term, used of weeding, that is, hoeing. And just as weeds to be cut are sought there with a hoe, so he metaphorically represented the reconsideration of his agitations by means of a hoe. And it must be known that *eskallon* signifies not once only, but frequently.

Thus far Jerome. In his Commentaries he also explains what it is “to search the spirit”:

> “I searched my spirit,” he says, “that is, I dug it as though it were a field, in order to sow there the seed of the Lord’s teachings.”

So he says. The Hebrew is *vauhapescī rūḥī*, “my spirit searched,” as modern interpreters render it. Yet Jerome said above that the Hebrew read, “I searched my spirit,” in the first person. Again, he gave “your psalms” [Col. 0722D] where others have “my song.” Although, in his translation for Sophronius, he renders both in the first person: both “my psalms” and “I searched.”

### Verse 8

“Or will he cut off his mercy for ever, from generation to generation?” Two words appear here to be omitted near the word “cut off”: *gamar omer*, that is, “the word,” or “utterance,” “is ended.” The Greek is likewise shown to have them: *synetelesē rhēma* [συνετέλεσε ῥῆμα], and Jerome translated them, as did the others.

Jerome satisfies this difficulty in his letter to Sunia and Fretella as follows: “The phrase ‘from generation to generation,’ which, following the Greek, you say you find as *synetelesē rhēma*, that is, ‘he completed the word,’ is rightly absent from the Latin, because it occurs in none of the translators.”

### Verse 10

“And I said: Now I have begun.” *Vaomar hallothi*. Jerome: “and he said, this is my weakness”; Münster, Pellican, and the interpreters for Cajetan likewise: “this is my infirmity,” or “my sickness”; Pratensis: “and I said, this is my expectation”; Sanctes: “and I thought of killing myself.” Campensis agrees with this: “Indeed I said, unto death: this remembrance torments me still.” It is remarkable how the rabbis dispute among themselves over this particle *hallothi*. For if one derives it from the root *halal*, it is extremely manifold in meaning. Some derive it from the verb *halah*, “to be sick.” Finally, the Septuagint took it from the root from which comes *heḥel*, “he began,” so that it means, “this is my beginning,” that is, “I have begun.”

“This is the change of the right hand of the Most High.” Jerome, the Chaldee, Nebiensis, Pratensis, and Pellican support this. The interpreters for Cajetan, Sanctes, and Münster translate “years” in place of “change” or “changes.” But lest the sentence be incomplete, they add something of their own. Sanctes says it thus: “I thought of killing myself because of the years [Col. 0723B] of the right hand of the Most High”; Münster: “but I shall remember the years of the right hand of the Most High.” Campensis’s paraphrase has the same sense: “the remembrance of former years.” Although the translator elsewhere differs, for he says: “The right hand of the Most High changes turns.”

The Hebrew has *shenoth*, from the singular *shanah*, which means both “he changed” and “year.” Because of this ambiguity, so many human editions are confused. Certainly, if everyone proceeds to translate according to his own judgment, everything will be uncertain or confused, unless there is some edition which the Church prefers to the rest; the others, however, may properly be read for learning’s sake.

### Verse 11

“I shall remember the works of the Lord.” Jerome: “the thoughts of the Lord,” *ma‘ălê Yāh*, that is, “the works” or “contrivances of the Lord”; just as shortly afterward Jerome himself translates a similar word. “Contrivances” are works established by divine counsel.

### Verse 15

“The waters saw you, O God, and were afraid.” Jerome says that *yaḥīlū*, “they were afraid,” means “they travailed”; Sanctes, “they suffered”; others, “they were afraid.” The particle commonly conveys these meanings, even if the sense is the same.

### Verse 16

“The multitude of the sound of waters.” [Col. 0724B] *Zormu mayim aboth.* Jerome and Nebiensis: “The clouds shook out waters.” Others: “the clouds poured out,” or “caused waters to overflow.” The Septuagint expressed the sense and force of the Hebrew expression. For the Hebrews call *zerem* “a sound,” “an abundance of waters,” “an onrush,” “rain,” or “a storm.”

## Psalm LXXVII

[Col. 0723]

### Title of the Psalm

“An understanding of Asaph.”

[Col. 0723B]

“Give heed, my people.” Title: “An understanding of Asaph.” [Augustine.] This psalm recounts what was divinely done to the people in the Old Testament: namely, what benefits God bestowed upon them and what punishments he inflicted on the ungrateful. [Note: [Col. 0723D] From Cassiodorus, at the conclusion of the psalm.] But while the history of the Old Testament is related in this psalm, the grace of the New Testament is made manifest. [Col. 0723C] For it says that the Jews were expelled for their sins, and declares that Christians were brought in, so as to make the purpose of both laws converge in an exhortation to humility.

And because all these things happened to them as figures of us, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 10), those things which are historically related about them must likewise be spiritually understood concerning us. Hence the psalm is entitled “understanding.” The meaning is: [Augustine, Cassiodorus] this is the understanding of Asaph, that is, of the faithful congregation, because what is narrated here must be understood inwardly, not merely as a figure. Thus the understanding of Asaph is what the faithful Synagogue understood, or what it ought to understand spiritually. For the things which then happened to them mystically, that is, figuratively, now happen to us in reality. And just as God was not well pleased with all of them, [Col. 0723D] so neither is he pleased with all these; and therefore they must be admonished.

Or the title may be read so that “understanding” is in the genitive case, as is clear in Greek, while “psalm” or “words” is understood: “This is a psalm,” or “words,” “of understanding,” that is, of the understanding granted to Asaph. Thus it is determined from the Greek.

The intention is this: by the events among the ancient people, he intends to warn the new people not to be ungrateful for God’s benefits and provoke his wrath against themselves. Method: there are nine divisions. First, he makes them attentive, because things which seem plain are parables and riddles. Second, he briefly states what God did for the Jews, although they were ungrateful to him: “How great things we have heard.” Third, he recounts what God did for them from the exodus out of Egypt onward, yet they did not come to their senses: “Before their fathers,” and so forth. We shall pursue the other divisions in their places.

The faithful Synagogue also speaks in this psalm, reproaching the wicked. But, that greater reverence and authority may be added to its words, it first introduces the Lord himself as speaking:

### Verse 1

“Give heed, my people, to my law; [Col. 0724C] incline your ear to the words of my mouth.”

“My people,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] namely, you who obey me. Or: “O you who are my people.” We, namely, are that people, who are also Christ’s congregation. Give heed in your heart to my law, that is, to the truth of the matter which is covered in figures. This is spoken by God, who gave the law. And then follows: “Incline,” through humility, “your ear,” the ear of the heart, and thus you will give heed well. [Note: [Col. 0724D] Bede, on Exodus, chapter 27.] For fear repels what is poured in. Hence in the old law the altar of the Lord was commanded to be made hollow and four-cornered, so that our mind, strengthened by the four virtues, might through humility be hollow for receiving the divine word.

“I say, incline to the words of my mouth,” that is, so as to understand the words of Asaph. [Cassiodorus.] For Asaph is [Col. 0724D] the mouth of God, who will speak below: “How great things,” and so forth. Therefore give heed, because:

### Verse 2

“I shall open my mouth in parables; I shall utter propositions from the beginning.”

“I shall open my mouth in parables,” [Gloss, Cassiodorus] which are manifest, because parables are comparisons of things: when, by a comparison drawn from things, what is said concerning them is understood concerning others. “And I shall utter,” through Asaph, “propositions,” [Augustine] that is, riddles, from the beginning of the Old Testament, from when they departed Egypt. Propositions are what in Greek are called *problēmata* [προβλήματα], questions requiring solution by discussion. Therefore careful attention must be given to them, [Col. 0725A] so that their fruit may be received through understanding; in Hebrew they are called riddles.

### Part II. Verse 3

“How great things we have heard and known; and our fathers have related them to us.”

“How great things we have heard.” [Jerome, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The second part, where he briefly tells what God did for the Jews, although they were ungrateful to him; and, if it did them no good, he tells it for the sake of the children, that they may not become like their fathers. It should be noted that God first spoke in the human being. For the words already given were God’s words; now the human being himself speaks. For these are human words: “How great things we have heard.”

God spoke the preceding words on his own authority, lest his speech, when spoken after him by a human being, should be despised. Therefore he says with admiration: “How great things,” because of their multitude, “we have heard”—foretold in the Old Testament—and “known,” fulfilled in [Col. 0725B] the New Testament. And from whom have we heard them? Behold: “our fathers have related them to us,” such as Moses and the prophets. This man also foresees that the fathers related them to their children. I say, “they related”:

### Verse 4

“They have not been hidden from their children in another generation.”

These things have not been hidden from their spiritual children, [Cassiodorus] which he later explains as “another generation,” and as the generation of the Gentiles, which is begotten from water and the Holy Spirit and in which regeneration was bestowed.

### Verse 5

“Relating the praises of the Lord and his powers, and his wonders which he has done.”

“Relating the praises of the Lord.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] This is the order of the words: the Lord is praised that he may be loved; and his virtues, or powers—that is, the deliverances [Col. 0725C] by which he often delivered the people—and his wonders, namely, that he fed the people in the wilderness and overcame their enemies: things which he did, not merely promised.

### Verse 6

“And he raised up a testimony in Jacob, and established a law in Israel.”

“And he raised up a testimony.” [Augustine.] This testimony is the beginning of which he said above: “I shall utter propositions from the beginning.” The beginning, therefore, is the Old Testament, because there is fear in it, and fear is the beginning of wisdom (Ecclus. 1). The end, however, is the New Testament, because Christ is here: he is the end of the law unto righteousness for everyone who believes (Rom. 10), and gives the Spirit through whom love is poured into our hearts (Rom. 5), which, when perfected, casts fear out (John 4).

The old law is called a testimony of this [Col. 0725D] New Testament because the New Testament has testimony from the law and the prophets. Hence the tabernacle of the Lord was called the tabernacle of testimony, because it prefigured so many mysteries (Exod. 26). Therefore the Old Testament is called testimony insofar as it proves, law insofar as it commands. The same thing is thus signified by “testimony” and “law,” but in different respects.

Likewise, Jacob and Israel mean the same thing: namely, the Jewish people. He says, therefore: “And he raised up in Jacob,” [Augustine] that is, in the Jewish people, “a testimony,” that is, the law. I say, “he raised it up,” because through that testimony sin, which had lain concealed, appeared and revived. Hence the Apostle says: “That sin might appear as sin, working death in me through that which is good” (Rom. 7). Then he repeats it: “And he established a law,” [Col. 0726A] that is, a testimony, “in Israel,” that is, in Jacob. He says, “established,” as though it were a yoke, lest they should wander according to a roaming will.

There is therefore a difference between “raised up” and “established.” “Raised up” denotes one thing, “established” another, as we have said. Thus the law is, for those who use it well, a testimony by which they flee sins; for those who use it badly, it is that by which they are convicted as sinners deserving punishment. So Christ is for believers the cornerstone, while for unbelievers he is a stone of stumbling (1 Pet. 2).

Or thus: “He raised up a testimony,” that is, the law, in Adam as though dead and asleep, in Jacob, [Alcuin, Cassiodorus] that is, in the Jewish people, restoring in writing what had become obsolete in their blinded minds. Or perhaps he calls “testimony” what happened to Jacob when, wrestling with an angel, he was made lame by a touch to his thigh (Gen. 32). This signifies the Jews: some stand firm in faith, while some depart from salvation. Thus what happened to Jacob was a testimony of this. Behold the parable.

This testimony is raised up when the law is written, because it had previously lain dormant through ignorance; but from then on both the sign itself remained in memory and the thing figured began from then on. And this is the meaning: “He raised up a testimony in Jacob,” that is, the event which happened to Jacob as a sign, previously dormant through ignorance. And when did he raise it up? “When he established a law in Israel,” in which law:

### Verse 7

“How great things he commanded our fathers to make known to their children, that another generation might know.”

“How great things he commanded our fathers.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] These are the ancient people, who received the command from [Col. 0726C] God but nevertheless neither knew nor did it. Why, then, did he command them? “To make them known to their children.” The children are the new people of the New Testament, who knew and did the commandments; this he adds by way of explanation. They received them in order that another generation, namely the one gathered from the Gentiles, might know spiritually what those fathers did not know. Thus “the children” and “another generation” are the same: the people of grace, those who know.

### Verse 8

“The children who shall be born and arise, and shall relate them to their children.”

“The children,” [Cassiodorus, Gloss] that is, Christians, who will afterward be born a second time from water and the Holy Spirit, “shall arise,” having their hearts set on things above. But those who have been born and not reborn have not arisen; that is, their heart [Col. 0726D] is not above but has been upon the earth. “And they shall relate them to their children,” that is, to those who come after. God’s commandments have been transmitted through generations, lest anyone think they were given to one person alone. For what purpose?

### Verse 9

“That they may place their hope in God, and may not forget the works of God, and may seek his commandments.”

“That they may place their hope in God.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] This is the benefit of paternal preaching: in God, not in the law which punishes, lest they establish their own righteousness; and “that they may not forget the works of God” by boasting of their own works, which are nothing unless from God, or by worshipping idols, as the Jews did when they worshipped idols.

Then, showing what true remembrance of God is, he adds: “And may seek his commandments,” [172] by doing them. Those said above to have known are now said to seek, in order that, hoping [Col. 0727A] in God, they may be helped by him to fulfil his commandments in deed. I say, “may seek”:

### Verse 10

“Lest they become like their fathers, a crooked and provoking generation.”

“Lest they become like their fathers,” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] namely, the Jews: “a crooked generation,” which did not receive the truth, “and provoking” God, so much so that they armed themselves against the Savior, which was the greatest of all bitter acts. Hence the Lord says through Ezekiel: “Go, and say to the provoking house,” and so forth (Ezek. 2, 12). And because it is crooked, it is:

### Verse 11

“A generation which did not direct its heart, and whose spirit was not faithful with God.”

“A generation which did not direct its heart,” [Gloss, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine] that is, a distorted generation. Or the connection may be made thus: it is a crooked generation because it is a generation which did not direct its heart and hand toward divine things, so as to correct itself. For one has a distorted heart who does not correct what he has wrongly understood and does not fulfil what nature teaches.

Why is that generation such? “And,” that is, because, “its spirit was not faithful with God”; that is, if reason at any time counseled well, it did not yield to it. Or thus: that generation is such because its spirit was not faithful with God, because they did not possess the faith which obtains what the law commands, but sought righteousness as though from works.

But when the human spirit cooperates with God’s working Spirit, then what God commands is done. And this happens only by believing in him who justifies the ungodly. The crooked and embittering generation did not possess this faith. Therefore it was said: “Its spirit was not faithful with God.” This is expressed much more strongly in order to signify the grace of God, which not only effects remission of sins but also causes the human spirit to cooperate with God in good works—as though it said: “Its spirit did not believe God.”

For to have one’s spirit faithful with God is not to believe that one’s spirit can perform righteousness, or any good thing, without God, but with God; and this is to believe in God, which is certainly more than believing God. For we also believe a human being, but not in a human being. To believe in God is, by believing, to cling to him in order to do good. Hence the Apostle says: “He who cleaves to God is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 6).

But that generation, [Col. 0727D] whose example must be avoided, even if it believed God, nevertheless did not believe in God, because it did not cling to God by faith so that, healed by him, it might cooperate with God working in it.

### Verse 12

“The children of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back in the day of battle.”

“The children of Ephraim.” [Haymo, Augustine.] As if he said: Truly crooked and distorted, because even the children of Ephraim, from whom less might have seemed likely, “bending and shooting the bow”—that is, promising to keep the commandments in the day of hearing, when God heard them crying out to him in some adversity, as though practising with weapons—“turned back in the day of battle,” that is, failed in the day of temptation.

For to bend the bow, shoot, and turn back in the day of battle is nothing other than to give heed and promise in the day of hearing, and to abandon in the day of temptation. It is like practising with weapons and, when the hour of conflict arrives, refusing to fight. As for the words “bending and shooting the bow,” whereas it seems he should rather have said “bending the bow and shooting arrows”—for a bow is not shot, but something is shot from a bow—we should understand it figuratively: “shooting the bow,” because they shoot something by means of the bow.

Or the word order is obscure; its order is: “bending the bow and shooting”—supply, “arrows.” Some Greek manuscripts, however, have “bending and shooting with bows,” so that we unquestionably supply “arrows.”

By “the children of Ephraim”—who was also called Ephraim—he intended the entire embittering nation to be understood, signifying the whole by a part. This is because something especially good was to be expected from them. For they were born from that son of Joseph upon whom Jacob, in blessing him, placed his right hand, though he stood to the left; and he set him before Manasseh, Joseph’s elder son, when he blessed them both with crossed hands, placing his right hand on Ephraim and his left on Manasseh, who was placed at the right (Gen. 48).

Since this tribe is blamed here and is not shown to have displayed what that blessing promised, it is evident that Jacob then prefigured that the last would be first and the first last (Matt. 20) through the coming of the Savior. Of him John says: “He who comes after me has been made before me” (John 1). Thus Abel was preferred to his elder brother (Gen. 4), Isaac to Ishmael (Gen. 21), Jacob to his twin Esau—though Esau was born first (Gen. [Col. 0728C] 27)—and Perez to Zerah, who first put out his hand (Gen. 38), and David to his elder brothers (1 Sam. 16). Thus the Christian people was preferred to the Jewish people.

Therefore, signifying the whole crooked nation by a part, he says: “Even the children of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow,” that is, shooting something with the bow; or, “bending the bow and shooting arrows,” that is, promising to keep the law, openly saying: “All that the Lord has spoken to us we will do and obey” (Exod. 24). “They turned back,” that is, failed, “in the day of battle,” namely, of temptation. Hence the prophet Hosea says: “Ephraim has become like a foolish dove” (Hos. 7), [Jerome, Augustine] because it is not hearing but temptation that tests a promise of obedience. They turned back because:

### Verse 13

“They did not keep the covenant of God, and were unwilling to walk in his law.”

“They did not keep the covenant of God,” [Augustine] not because they could not, but because they would not. Hence he adds: “And they were unwilling to walk in his law.” Even if they sometimes walk in it, nevertheless they are unwilling, because they do not act from the heart. They do what they would rather not have been commanded to do; but what is done from fear of punishment rather than love of righteousness is in no way done from the heart. Those who do not steal through fear of punishment and those who do not steal through love of righteousness are alike in hand, but not in heart.

### Verse 14

“And they forgot his benefactions, and his wonders which he showed them.”

### Part III. Verse 15

“Before their fathers [Col. 0729A] he performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the field of Tanis.”

“Before their fathers.” [Cassiodorus, Gloss, Augustine.] The third part, where he now begins to recount what God did for them from their departure from Egypt; nevertheless, they did not cease from murmuring and tempting. As if he said: “They forgot his wonders.” What wonders, and where were they done? They were done in the land of Egypt. What were they? That he divided the sea and led them forth, and so forth. This is the meaning: “Before their fathers he performed wonders in the land of Egypt.”

Who are the fathers of this crooked generation, from whom he above dissuaded the children, lest they should become like those fathers, namely, like the crooked generation? Hence above: “Lest they become like their fathers, a crooked and provoking generation.” These fathers are different from those fathers. But who are the fathers before whom these things were done? If you take Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as the fathers, he did not perform wonders in Egypt before them, since they had already died—unless perhaps you say that they were present in spirit, whom the Lord says in the Gospel are alive (Luke 20). Or, more suitably, they are Moses and Aaron and the other elders who received of Moses’ spirit (Num. 2). These are their fathers, before whom he acted.

And the meaning is: “Before fathers who were worthy of belief,” namely, before Moses and the others who understood, “he performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the field of Tanis.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] To remove every doubt, he names both the country, Egypt, and the location of the deeds, Tanis, a city of Egypt.

It should be noted that the good and evil things done there are mystically done in us also: [Col. 0729C] good things by God’s grace, evil things by judgment. For this reason he above warned us to attend to parables and propositions and to place our hope in God, lest we be like them. (Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.) Egypt, then, which means “darkness” or “tribulation,” is the world. Tanis means “a humble command.” The field of Tanis is the plain of the humble command.

As God then performed wonders before those fathers, so Christ, placed upon earth before the fathers of the New Testament, taught the humble command, saying: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11 [printed: II]). Therefore, in the world we receive the humble command from Christ, that we may be exalted in the future.

### Verse 16

“He divided the sea and led them through; [Col. 0729D] and he set the waters as though in a wineskin.”

“He divided the sea,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] as though it were not liquid, and led them through; and “he set the waters,” as though enclosed in a wineskin. Mystically, he who then made the waters stand still and brought them across restrains the fluid desires of concupiscence when the world is renounced, so that, with all sins blotted out, the faithful people may be brought through baptism to the land of promise.

### Verse 17

“And he led them in a cloud by day, and throughout the whole night in the brightness of fire.”

“And afterward he led them,” [Gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin] before placing them in their homeland, “in a cloud by day, and throughout the whole night in the brightness of fire.” So too, after baptism, he leads believers upon the spiritual journey before placing them in their homeland: in this age, [Col. 0730A] as though by day, through the cloud—that is, the flesh—his sacrament having been revealed. But at the judgment, as though by night, he leads them in the brightness of fire, because then great tribulation, like fire, will shine upon the righteous and burn the unrighteous.

Or, according to the allegorical sense: “And he led them,” and so forth. These things indicated what was to come. For the day is Christ, although he is hidden from the faithless by the cloud of flesh. And as the pillar of cloud was to them a shade against the heat of the sun, so through the Incarnation he gives us refreshment against the heat of vices. “And throughout the whole night,” that is, throughout the whole time of life, “in the brightness of fire,” that is, in the radiance of his light; and that brightness is the fire of the Holy Spirit.

### Verse 18

“He split the rock in the wilderness, and gave them drink as from the great deep.”

“He split the rock.” [Augustine, Gloss, Augustine.] Earlier the water of the sea stood like a rock; now a rock becomes a spring. And this happened in the wilderness, where the gift necessarily appears more welcome. “And he gave them drink,” like cattle rather than human beings, because they gave no thanks, “as from the great deep”: by this he indicates abundance.

Mystically, this also concerns the rock which is Christ, who says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7), whose side was pierced upon the cross. In the wilderness of this age God brings forth for thirsty faith streams of the Holy Spirit, the wood of the cross being applied with Moses’ rod, so that grace might flow out for believers.

### Verse 19

“And he brought water out of the rock, and led forth waters like rivers.”

“And he brought out of the rock,” [Cassiodorus, Haymo, Cassiodorus] which is wonderful, “water,” which followed them wherever they went; “and he led forth waters,” not scantily but “like rivers,” that is, abundantly. Mystically, likewise, the water proceeding from Christ does not fail through any diminution, so that it may be “a fountain of living water springing up into eternal life” (John 4).

### Verse 20

“And they continued to sin against him; they provoked the Most High to anger in the waterless place.”

“And they continued.” [Haymo, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As if he said: God did these things for them. Yet they, namely the crooked generation, “continued still to sin against him,” that is, not to believe; that is, amid so many benefits they added unbelief. And, that this might be understood as the greatest sin, when the Lord said in the Gospel, “The Spirit will convict the world concerning sin” (John 16), he immediately added by way of explanation: “Concerning sin, because they did not believe in me” (ibid.). Therefore, as there he calls unbelief “sin,” so here he calls unbelief “to sin.”

“They provoked the Most High to anger,” not believing that God could do difficult things for them, which is mystically most grievous before God. So we too, freed through baptism, sometimes provoke God to anger. And this was “in the waterless place,” or “in dryness,” according to another reading: literally, in a wilderness; or rather, in themselves, dry for lack of the moisture of grace. For although their bellies were full of water from the rock, their minds were dry. Thus this must be understood more of the dryness of heart than of body [173] or place. How did they provoke the Most High to anger? Behold:

### Verse 21

“And they tempted God in their hearts, that they might ask food for their souls.”

“And,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, because “they tempted God in their hearts, that they might ask food for their souls,” that is, carnal food for their lives, not spiritual food. The sense is: in unbelief they asked for food, and that is to tempt God. For to tempt is to ask deceitfully, so that simplicity is in one’s words while malice is in one’s heart. Mystically, so too many today seek wisdom from God in temptation.

### Verse 22

“And they spoke evil of God, and said: ‘Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?’”

“And then they spoke evil,” that is, falsehood, “of God. They said: ‘Can God prepare a table in [Col. 0731B] the wilderness?’” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] As if to say, “No.” This distrust is an injury to God. Mystically, the table signifies the refreshment of wisdom or the body of Christ. Hence many distrust.

### Verse 23

“Because he struck the rock, and waters flowed, and torrents overflowed.”

“Because he struck.” [Cassiodorus, Haymo.] As if to say: God can do that, because he could also do this other thing: “He struck the rock, and waters flowed, and torrents overflowed.” Behold, they furnish an example of God’s power and despair of a similar act. Hence from their own person it follows:

### Verse 24

“Can he also give bread, or prepare a table [Col. 0731C] for his people?”

“Can he likewise give bread, or prepare a table,” that is, abundant refreshment, “for his people,” namely, for so many people? As if to say, “No.”

### Part IV. Verse 25

“Therefore the Lord heard and delayed; and fire was kindled in Jacob, and wrath rose up against Israel.”

“Therefore the Lord heard.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The fourth part, where he says that, delaying vengeance, God first gave what they asked, lest he seem unable. As if he said: They asked this; and lest he seem unable, therefore the Lord heard, granting them what they requested. “And he delayed” punishment, first giving what they asked, although they asked in temptation, lest he seem unable. And after he gave it, “fire,” that is, God’s wrath, “was kindled in Jacob.” Then he explains, saying: “And God’s wrath rose up against Israel.” Why?

### Verse 26

“Because they did not believe in God, nor hope in his salvation.”

“Because they did not believe in God,” [Cassiodorus] or, “did not believe God,” and “did not hope in his salvation,” Christ, that he was able to give.

### Verse 27

“And he commanded the clouds above, and opened the doors of heaven.”

“And he commanded.” [Augustine.] Both matters briefly mentioned—namely, that he heard and that wrath rose—he now begins to relate clearly. First he explains how he heard; afterward, in the following part, how he took vengeance. As if he said: Thus he heard, because “he commanded the clouds above and opened the doors of heaven.”

### Verse 28

“And he rained manna upon them to eat, and gave them the bread of heaven.”

[Col. 0732A] “And he rained manna upon them to eat.” [Haymo, Gloss.] He sets forth above what he called manna: “and he gave them the bread of heaven,” that is, manna, that is, bread prepared not by human labor.

### Verse 29

“Man ate the bread of angels; he sent them provisions in abundance.”

“Man ate the bread of angels.” [Augustine, Haymo, Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] By the name of the thing signified, the signifying thing is understood: that is, manna, by which the bread of angels, namely Christ, is signified. “And he sent them provisions in abundance,” namely provisions which the greedy could not consume.

All these things are mystical, so that evangelical grace may be declared beneath the history of the Old Testament. “And he commanded the clouds above,” that is, the preachers; “and opened the doors of heaven.” The doors of heaven are the preachers, by whom one enters heaven, or the Holy Scriptures. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin.] He opened these doors because he gave his own the Spirit to understand their Scriptures (Luke 24).

“And he rained manna upon them to eat.” Manna means, “What is this?” (Exod. 16 [printed: XXVI]), and signifies the bread which came down from heaven, that is, Christ, or Christ’s body. He is truly the food of angels, by which incorruptible beings are incorruptibly fed. That man might eat him, the Word was made flesh; he is rained upon the whole world through the evangelical clouds and, their hearts being opened as though they were heavenly doors, is preached to the believing Church, not to the tempting Synagogue.

Manna is well called “What is this?” because this food is sought with wondering inquiry, although it is known to be Christ’s body. “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels.” The bread of heaven is none other than Christ, by whose contemplation the heavenly beings, that is, the angels, are refreshed. And this bread, that is, the Word, by which angels are fed with great food, man eats as milk because it was made flesh.

### Verse 30

“He moved the south wind from heaven, and by his power brought in the southwest wind.”

“He moved.” [Haymo, Alcuin.] As if he said: How did he send them? Behold: “He moved the south wind from heaven,” so that it might blow beneath; “and by his power brought in the southwest wind,” that other wind, because the quails are there (Num. 11 [printed: XXI]).

### Verse 31

“And he rained flesh upon them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea.”

[Col. 0732D] “And he rained flesh upon them,” [Haymo, Remigius] namely quails, “like dust,” that is, abundantly. He then specifies the flesh he gave: “and winged birds like the sand of the sea.” It was marvelous that, although they were winged birds, they caught them as they wished. But he adds why this was so:

### Verse 32

“And they fell in the midst of their camp, around their tents.”

And they fell in the midst of their camp. [Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] They flew two cubits above the ground, so that there would be no difficulty for them in catching them; around their tents, for a day’s journey in every direction, there were quails. All this is mystical: by the south wind and the southwest wind are understood preachers, whom God transfers from heaven to earth when, descending from higher matters, they disclose lesser matters to lesser persons. Thus, “He transferred the south wind,” that is, preachers from heaven to earth. Hence the Apostle: “I could not speak to you as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal persons” (1 Cor. 3). And “he brought in the southwest wind,” that is, fervent and radiant preachers, in his power—lest the southwest wind attribute to itself what it has from God. “And he rained flesh upon them.” Thus God also nourishes the small faith of those who do not tempt but believe, by signs uttered in bodily voices and passing through the air like birds. Yet they do not come from the north, where there are cold and darkness—that is, from worldly eloquence—but when the south wind is transferred to earth, so that the little ones, nourished by hearing earthly things, may be fitted to grasp heavenly things. Hence the Lord: “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” [Col. 0733B] (John 3.)

Or, by “flesh” is understood small faith. Thus: “He rained flesh upon them,” that is, upon the weak he rained small faith, uttered in bodily voices, “like dust.” Here dust signifies the subtlety of understanding which ascends to things above. Thus, “he rained these things like dust,” that is, by leading us from lesser things to great and higher things. “And he rained winged birds like the sand of the sea.” Sand signifies an innumerable abundance of wisdom seasoned with the savour of salt. Winged birds are heavenly desires, by which the nourished soul grows rich. God bestows these upon us; but we cannot receive them except within the enclosures of the Church—that is, except in conformity with the faithful. Hence it adds: “And they fell in the midst of their camp, around their tents.” [Col. 0733C]

[Augustine, Alcuin.] Or this signifies that the winds—that is, the preachers—come willingly to people and carry to them words sent by God, so that people may hear them in their homes and around their tents, because “their sound has gone forth into all the earth” (Ps. 18). This is according to the literal sense only.

VERSE 33.—“And they ate and were exceedingly filled; and he brought them their desire, and they were not deprived of their desire.”

“And they ate and were exceedingly filled”: in their bellies, not in their minds. [Cassiodorus.] Behold, those who thought this impossible for God were convicted. “And he brought them their desire,” although it did them no good. For things that are not beneficial are sometimes granted; “and they were not deprived of their desire,” because many partook of that flesh. [Col. 0733D] This was done for them so that weakness might not appear to be in God.

PART V, VI. VERSE 34.—“While their food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God rose against them.”

“While still.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The fifth part, in which he treats of their punishments and their feigned returns, made from fear of penalties; nevertheless, God’s judgment is moderated by mercy. It should be noted that above he explained how God heard them; here, however, he says how the wrath which he had delayed rose up, saying: “While their food,” or “the food”—namely manna and quails—“of them,” that is, of the wicked and unbelieving generation, “was,” or “were,” still in their mouths, “the wrath of God rose against them.” Behold what he had delayed above.

[Col. 0734A] VERSE 35.—“And he slew their fat ones, and bound the chosen men of Israel.”

“And he slew their fat ones,” [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine] that is, the proud, of whom it is said elsewhere: “Their iniquity has gone forth as though from fatness” (Ps. 72). “And he bound,” or “fettered,” “the chosen men of Israel,” that is, the good—but others’ murmuring bound them, as Moses, who, because of their murmurings, said in doubt: “Can we bring water for you out of the rock?” (Exod. 17). Or their murmuring hindered the chosen men from benefiting those for whom they desired to provide with fatherly affection. Or rather, he fettered them so that, together with those who suffered as an example of God’s justice, the chosen too might endure affliction as an example of their patience. Thus their common punishment served as an example, not only of [Col. 0734B] God’s justice but also of the patience of the good. This sense is clearer from the Greek, where one reads not “he hindered” but “he fettered.” Yet:

VERSE 36.—“In all these things they still sinned, and did not believe in his wonders.”

Though corrected by all these things, they still sinned, [Alcuin, Cassiodorus] that is, that wicked generation sinned. After all these things, their sins were more grievous and continually increased; “and they did not believe in his wonders,” God’s wonders.

VERSE 37.—“And their days failed in vanity, and their years in haste.”

And therefore “their days failed,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] as if weakened by wasting disease, though by believing in truth they could have had days [Col. 0734C] without failing. And this happened “in vanity,” that is, for vanity, on account of which they perished more quickly. “And their days failed,” being “in vanity,” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus] like one who dies at birth, born in vain. “And their years [failed] in haste,” that is, even a life which appears longer quickly passed away. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Wicked men shall not halve their days” (Ps. 54). But:

VERSE 38.—“When he slew them, they sought him; and they returned and came early to him.”

“When he slew them, they sought him.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] Those killed did not themselves seek him, but those who remained did. Yet he speaks thus because they are one people; he speaks as though of one body. They sought God not for eternal life, but because they feared [Col. 0734D] being slain after the example of those already slain. The good, however, seek even without necessity. Here he treats of the Jews’ feigned returns. Hence it follows: “And they returned to him and came early to him,” that is, diligently; or, according to another text, “before the light,” that is, remaining in night and not in light. Hence elsewhere: “It is vain for you to rise before the light” (Ps. 126): the devout person is in the light; the ungodly person prays before the light. They did all these things in order to gain temporal goods and avoid temporal evils. Thus it was not God but those things that they worshipped; for that is worshipped which is loved.

VERSE 39.—“And they remembered that God is their helper, and that God Most High is their redeemer.”

“And they remembered that God is their helper,” [Col. 0735A] [Gloss interlinear] in good things, “and that God Most High is their redeemer,” from evils.

VERSE 40.—“And they loved him with their mouth, and lied to him with their tongue.”

“And they loved him with their mouth,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus] not in their heart, although all secrets lay naked and open before him, and without any obstacle he saw what they loved more. “And with their tongue they lied to him.” Thus it happens to those who believe from fear alone, not from love.

VERSE 41.—“But their heart was not right with him, nor were they found faithful in his covenant.”

“But their heart,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Jerome, Augustine] as though God did not know human hearts, “was not right with him,” because they did not seek God for God’s sake; [Col. 0735B] “nor were they found faithful in his covenant,” because they neither kept the commandments, as they had promised, nor desired heavenly things rather than earthly ones—nor the inheritance of the New Testament. Faith in this testament was present in the elect even then, when it was veiled; but now, when it has been revealed, it is not found in many who are called. For “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20). [Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] These men were not faithful because they did not perform works; for whoever truly believes performs works. Hence *fides*, “faith,” is so called because what is spoken is done. Above he says: “Nor were they found faithful in his covenant,” that is, in his commandments. Such persons:

VERSE 42.—“But he is merciful, and will be gracious to their sins, and will not destroy them.”

[Col. 0735C] “But he,” God, “is merciful, and will be gracious to their sins.” [Augustine.] From these words evil people promise themselves impunity. But it must be understood that mercy is also shown to evil people before judgment, because he makes his sun rise upon good and evil alike.

[Note: Col. 0735D. From Augustine, *On Psalm 120*.] This is mercy of the left hand, not of the right: temporal, not spiritual; common to good and evil alike. Thus God spared that wicked people too, lest he utterly uproot it; but it remains in the succession of descendants, as Cain received a sign so that no one might kill him. Therefore, when he says, “He will be gracious to their sins,” he speaks not only of the fathers but considers the people’s succession. Hence follows: “And he will not destroy them” utterly.

[Col. 0735D] VERSE 43.—“And he abounded in turning away his wrath, and did not kindle all his wrath.”

“And he abounded”—the mercy of God—[Augustine] “in turning away his wrath,” that is, the punishment which he had begun, when God said to Moses, as Moses prayed to him: “Let me alone, that I may destroy them and make you increase into a great nation.” Moses replied: “Either forgive them this offence, or blot me out of the book of life” (Exod. 32). “And he did not kindle all his wrath,” so as utterly to destroy them; that is, he did not punish them as much as they deserved. Or this may be understood especially of the good, to whom the Lord became merciful when, in this age of grace, a remnant was saved. Thus: “But he is [Col. 0736A] merciful” to the good, yet in this manner: “and will be gracious to their sins,” that is, to the people, which remains the same in the succession of its children. So later he says that he brought them out of Egypt and led them into the mountain of sanctification, although he did not lead into the mountain of sanctification the very persons whom he brought out of Egypt, except in the succession of their children. Thus here, when it says “he will be gracious to their sins,” we understand this also to have been fulfilled in those of whom the Apostle says: “A remnant shall be saved” (Rom. 11), who will believe in Christ. He foresaw this here; hence it adds: “and he will not destroy them” with eternal death. “And he abounded,” in mercy, “to turn away his wrath,” because the remnant was saved; “and he did not kindle all his wrath,” because he even forgave that sin by which they killed his Son.

[Col. 0736B] VERSE 44.—“And he remembered that they are flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return.”

“And he remembered that they are flesh,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, fragile; the frailty of sinners moved the merciful Judge. “And [the] spirit” of a human being “goes” by itself into sin and “does not return” by itself from sin. Therefore God recalls human beings by grace, because by themselves they cannot return. Hence of the way of iniquity it is said in Proverbs: “All who walk in it shall not return” (Prov. 2; Luke 15)—that is, by themselves, though they are recalled by God’s grace. This is the wandering sheep which was carried back to the flock on the shoulders of the merciful shepherd.

Or thus: “And he remembered that the spirit” of a human being “goes” from this world and “does not return” to the body in this world. Here is a brief definition [Col. 0736C] of death.

VERSE 45.—“How often they provoked him in the wilderness; in the waterless place they stirred him to anger.”

“How often.” [Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear, Alcuin, Augustine.] The sixth part: intending to recount the plagues inflicted on Egypt for their sake, and to compare their evils with God’s benefits, he says that they forgot and tempted God. As though he said: He spared them, and although he spared them, how often they provoked him. Or the connection is this: Since man is flesh and a spirit that goes, how often, therefore—as though many times, not only in the ways already mentioned—“they provoked him in the wilderness,” that he might take away good things; “they stirred him to anger,” that he might inflict evils, “in the waterless place,” where they ought rather to have been afraid. He repeats their unbelief, which he had foretold, [Col. 0736D] in order to remind them what plagues God inflicted on the Egyptians for their sake, and consequently that they ought not to be ungrateful. He then explains how they provoked him.

VERSE 46.—“And they turned back and tempted God, and provoked the Holy One of Israel.”

“And they turned back,” [Gloss interlinear, Haimo] because they had covenanted: “Whatever God commands us, we shall do” (Exod. 24). “And they tempted God and provoked the Holy One of Israel,” that is, him who sanctifies Israel; and thus:

VERSE 47.—“They did not remember his hand, the day on which he redeemed them from the hand of the oppressor.”

“They did not remember his hand,” that is, the power [Col. 0737A] displayed on the day when he redeemed them from the hand of the oppressor, that is, Pharaoh. Affliction is usually remembered, but it was not so for them. [Cassiodorus, Haimo.] He aptly contrasts God’s hand with Pharaoh’s hand, saying “his hand” and “from the hand of the oppressor,” because their operations differ greatly. He then shows what they did not remember—namely, they did not remember:

VERSE 48.—“How he set his signs in Egypt, and his wonders in the field of Tanis.”

“How,” in what manner, “he set his signs in Egypt.” [Cassiodorus.] Signs are, as it were, imprinted traces of a character upon hard hearts. And how he set “his wonders in the field of Tanis”: wonders are things which signified something future. Tanis is a city, and its name means “lowly command”; this is necessary for us here, [Col. 0737B] so that we may be raised up in the future.

VERSE 49.—“And he turned their rivers into blood, and their waters, so that they could not drink.”

“And he turned.” [Augustine.] Here he begins to explain the plagues inflicted in Egypt for the Jews’ liberation. He gives here ten plagues, as ten are given in Exodus. Yet he adds some which are not contained in Exodus; these we can interpret only figuratively, that is, spiritually. There even the things which were done are called parables, as Scripture often does: in many places it does not follow the sequence of the narrative but adds some things and changes others for their significance. He omits three which are read in Exodus—namely gnats, sores, and darkness—and gives three others not read there—namely rust, frost, and fire. Thus all must be expounded by allegorical interpretation. Historically, however, only those things are to be understood which are read in Exodus (Exod. 7).

[Haimo, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As though he said: He set his signs in Egypt, and these wonders: namely, “he turned their rivers into blood,” literally, and “their waters,” that is, their cisterns, so that they could not drink. Where we have “waters,” others read more accurately “outflows of water,” called springs—that is, waters bubbling up from below—because the Egyptians dug and found blood instead of water. This too must be understood mystically. Water turned into blood signifies those who think carnally about the causes of things. For just as elsewhere water is changed into wine (John 2), signifying the change of the people for the better, [Col. 0737D] so here it is changed into blood, by which flesh is understood, signifying that they understand spiritual things carnally. The second plague follows (Exod. 8).

VERSE 50.—“And he sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them; and the frog, and it destroyed them.”

“He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them,” [Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Augustine, Cassiodorus] which is called the dog-fly. Mystically, the dog-fly is dog-like behaviour, because dogs are said not to see their parents when they are born. Therefore he sent among them dog-like behaviour, so that they would not honour parents or prelates; “and he sent the frog, and it destroyed them.” Mystically, the frog is talkative vanity and signifies the babbling of heretics, which dwells in muddy notions, just as the frog lives in mud.

[Col. 0738A] VERSE 51.—“And he gave their fruits to rust, and their labours to the locust.”

“And he gave their fruits to verdigris,” or “rust”; [Haimo, Augustine] by “fruits” he understands things which grow of themselves. This is not read in Exodus; therefore it is set forth here only in a mystical interpretation. Rust (*rubigo*), which others render *aerugo* (“verdigris”), harms secretly; it is compared to a vice difficult to discern, such as excessive self-confidence. For this harmful breath works secretly in fruits, just as hidden pride exists in character when one who is nothing thinks himself something. [Haimo, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear.] “And he gave their labours,” that is, crops produced by human labour, “to the locust.” Mystically, the locust is malice that wounds with its mouth, namely through false testimony. [Col. 0738B] Since locusts devour one another, they signify detractors, who gnaw at another’s fruits with envy.

VERSE 52.—“And he destroyed their vineyards with hail, and their mulberry trees with frost.”

“And he destroyed their vineyards with hail,” that is, their good things. [Augustine.] Mystically, hail is iniquity that takes away others’ property; from it arise thefts, robberies, and plunder. Yet the plunderer himself is devastated even more by his own vice. In Exodus hail is placed first and then the locust (Exod. 9–10). For what hail could not harm—that is, the tender things—Exodus later says was eaten by locusts. It follows: “And their mulberry trees with frost,” which is very different from hail, and this too is not read in Exodus. Therefore it is expounded mystically. Frost is the vice [Col. 0738C] by which love of neighbour freezes amid the darkness of folly, as if in the cold of night.

VERSE 53.—“And he delivered their cattle to hail, and their possessions to fire.”

“And he delivered their cattle to hail.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Mystically, by the death of cattle is signified the loss of chastity. For the desire by which offspring arises is common to us and cattle; the virtue of chastity is to have it tamed and ordered, but to let it loose to every impulse is the death of the soul. Therefore by the death of cattle is shown the downfall of fools, who, living beast-like, do not restrain unlawful impulses with the bridle of self-control. “And [he delivered] their possessions to fire.” Nor is this read in Exodus, and so we are compelled to understand it only mystically. Fire—not found in Exodus except together with hail, in [Col. 0738D] flashes of lightning, to damage the crops, and not said to have burned their possessions—signifies the savagery of anger, which may even become homicide. [Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear.] Or fire is greed, which devastates one’s possession—that is, the condition of the mind—and every good bestowed by nature.

VERSE 54.—“He sent upon them the wrath of his indignation, indignation and wrath and tribulation, assaults through evil angels.”

“He sent upon them.” [Cassiodorus.] He has enumerated nine plagues; before explaining the tenth, he says this to intensify that tenth plague, showing by what ministers it was inflicted. He interweaves both those figurative plagues and these present spiritual [Col. 0739A] plagues, showing the order of punishment when he adds: he sent upon them wrath—not, certainly, for correction, but “the wrath of his indignation.” He explains what he has said by ascending in order: namely, he sent indignation, then wrath, and then tribulation. Behold the order of punishment. For he is first angry at sins when we are not pierced with compunction. Then, in his indignation, wrath, and tribulation, he abandons human wickedness to itself, so that those who do not obey God may be afflicted by their own perversities, as is said there: “Therefore God gave them up to dishonourable passions” (Rom. 1). Human indignation belongs to swollen pride; wrath, to abominable audacity; tribulation, to confused despair. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] God sent these upon them not by imparting wickedness, but by withdrawing grace and permitting them to fall into them.

Hence it adds: “And he sent upon them an assault,” or “assaults,” “through evil angels.” Once corrupted by these vices already mentioned, stripped of God’s protection, they are then driven by devils into unlawful assaults. Or: he sent upon them indignation and wrath and tribulation—that is, an assault; and I mean indignation, wrath, and tribulation inflicted through evil angels. Accordingly, these things were done among them by God’s judgment through evil angels, and they occur among evil people in this evil age, as though in Egypt and in the field of Tanis, where we ought to be lowly until the age comes in which we shall be exalted.

What is said in this psalm concerning evil angels does not seem to be something to pass over casually. [Col. 0739C] It must therefore be known that God uses even evil angels well, fittingly, and justly. As to their substance, he himself created them good; but he did not create them evil—just as a human being also uses God’s good creatures badly. God uses evil angels not only to punish the evil, as in the case of King Ahab, whom a spirit of deceit led astray so that he would fall in battle (3 Kings 22), but also to test and make known the good, as he did Job (Job 1). For just as a good or bad human being uses the visible elemental matter—earth, water, air, and fire—according to his ability, not only for necessary things but also for superfluous, playful, and artistic works, so good and evil angels use those same elements according to the power possessed by each; their power is greater than that of human beings, and [Col. 0739D] greater in the good angels than in the evil, yet always according to God’s will, though in different ways.

Among evil people, the devil has power as over his own cattle, except where he is forbidden by a greater authority, namely God. But among the good he has no power unless he is permitted it for testing, not for destruction—just as someone who wishes to do what he will with another’s cattle awaits power granted by its owner. It should also be noted that God punishes the evil through good angels, as at Sodom. But it does not occur to me that the just are tested through them. Therefore the hardening in the Egyptians occurred through evil angels, to whom vices and evil habits are congenial, signified by their plagues; through these same angels those things were inflicted. For when God [Col. 0740A] gave them over to desire, those angels were ministers in the material of their own work. We may therefore without doubt attribute to evil angels the deaths of cattle, the deaths of the firstborn, and the hardening of the Egyptians. God is said to bring about this most unjust and malicious obstinacy not by inciting or inspiring it, but by abandoning them, so that those angels may work in the children of unbelief what God rightly and justly permits.

But we do not dare attribute to evil angels those things which were wondrously done with created things. For if they are attributed to demons because punishments were inflicted, it follows that we must also believe that Sodom was overthrown by evil angels, and that the same angels were received as guests by Abraham and Lot—which is far from the truth! Therefore through evil angels God punishes both good and evil human beings, but the good only with bodily punishments; the evil, however, with bodily and spiritual punishments. Through good angels, on the other hand, he punishes only evil human beings, and with bodily, not spiritual, punishments.

[Col. 0740B] VERSE 55.—“He made a way for the path of his wrath; he did not spare their souls from death, and shut up their cattle in death.”

“He made a way for the path.” He shows whence evil angels have this licence. [Augustine, Haimo, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Haimo.] As though he said: These assaults having been sent, he made a way—that is, breadth and manifestation—for the path of his wrath, that is, of his hidden equity by which God was angry with the Egyptians. Otherwise the devil would not have been allowed to inflict those things. It is called the path of wrath because a path is straight [Col. 0740C] and hidden. There was indeed a path of God’s wrath, which by hidden equity punished the Egyptians’ impiety. He made a way for that path, so that through evil angels he might bring them out, as it were, from hidden places into open crimes, and thus most manifestly punish persons who had become most openly ungodly. “And he did not spare their souls from death,” or “their souls,” “and shut up their cattle in death”—the cattle along with their owners. As though he said: He made them manifest, because they were like cattle; and he explains this better when he adds:

VERSE 56.—“And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the firstfruits of all their labour in the tents of Ham.”

“And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt,” [Gloss interlinear, Augustine] that is, the firstborn of all things: he struck the firstborn both of human beings and of cattle. This is the tenth plague, namely the death of the firstborn. Mystically, the death of the firstborn is the loss of justice itself, by which each person is united in fellowship with the human race.

But whether these figurative meanings are so understood, or otherwise: [Note: Col. 0739D. Also Augustine, Sermon 59 *On Time*, and here.] it must be known that the Egyptians were struck by ten plagues in opposition to the ten commandments written on the tablets, by which the people of God are watered. Since elsewhere we have explained those plagues and commandments by comparing them to one another through contraries, there is no need to burden this exposition of the psalm with them. We only observe that here also there are ten plagues, although not in the order in which they are set out in Exodus (Exod. [Col. 0741A] 8–10). In place of the three found in Exodus—namely gnats, sores, and darkness—which are not here, there are three others here which are not there: rust, frost, and fire. Such things are frequently varied to suit the appropriate interpretation.

[Cassiodorus.] Or the firstborn are the highest commandments, such as “You shall love God with your whole heart,” and similar things (Deut. 6); if these are not kept, we are deprived of the offspring of reason. “And he struck the firstfruits of all their labour,” that is, of grain and the like: all things serving for human food or comfort were devastated. And this was “in the tents of Ham,” where the Jews were not.

PART VII. VERSE 57.—“And he took away his people like sheep, and led them like a flock in the wilderness.”

[Col. 0741B] “And he took away.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Augustine.] The seventh part, in which he says that he led the Jews out of Egypt into the land of promise, and that they again offended. Thus: “And he took away his people from Egypt like sheep.” He did this in the tenth plague. Mystically, this also occurs inwardly in us: rescued in mind from the power of darkness, we are transferred into God’s kingdom, as sheep into spiritual pastures. “And he led them like a flock in the wilderness,” which lay between the sea and Egypt. Mystically, he likewise leads us, labouring in the wilderness of this age.

VERSE 58.—“And he led them in hope, and they did not fear; and the sea covered their enemies.”

“And he led them in hope, and they did not fear.” [Augustine.] Thus we too have been saved in hope and ought not to fear. [Col. 0741C] “And the sea covered their enemies.” Thus in baptism our sins are also blotted out.

VERSE 59.—“And he brought them into the mountain of his sanctification, the mountain which his right hand acquired.”

“And he brought them into the mountain of his sanctification.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Literally, into Mount Zion. Yet he did not personally bring into it the very persons whom he took from Egypt; rather, he signifies them by name and nation. Nevertheless, many were converted to the holy Church, which he prefers to understand. For it is the mountain which Christ acquired—namely, “into the mountain which his right hand acquired”—literally by driving out the nations; allegorically, Christ acquired the Church.

[Col. 0741D] VERSE 60.—“And he cast out the nations from before them, and divided the land among them by lot with a measuring line of distribution.”

“And he cast out from the land of promise the nations from before them,” [Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, from the presence of the Jews. Mystically, the nations are vices and errors, or evil spirits; Christ cast all these out from before the faithful. “And he divided the land among them by lot with a measuring line of distribution.” The historical meaning is clear. Mystically, this signifies that the one and same Spirit works all things in us, distributing to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12).

VERSE 61.—“And he caused the tribes of Israel to dwell in their tents.”

“And he caused the tribes [Col. 0742A] of Israel to dwell in their tents.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] Mystically, by Christ’s grace we, who are tribes of those seeing God, are raised into heavenly glory, from which the angels were cast out; or virtues reign where sins formerly reigned. He did these benefits for them, and yet the wicked generation, misusing the benefits, still tempted him. Thus:

VERSE 62.—“And they tempted and provoked God Most High, and did not keep his testimonies.”

“And they tempted and provoked God Most High” in the land of promise. “And they did not keep his testimonies.”

VERSE 63.—“And they turned away and did not keep the covenant; as their fathers turned into a crooked bow.”

“And they turned away from God and did not keep the covenant which they had made,” [Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus] saying: “All that the Lord has said, we shall do” (Exod. 24). “As their fathers turned into a crooked bow.” A crooked bow is easily slackened, and they readily turned back. It should be known that throughout the psalm he speaks as though of the same persons; yet he now speaks of those in the land of promise, whose fathers were those who provoked him in the wilderness. Or a crooked bow is one which does not shoot from afar but turns its arrows upon itself—that is, it signifies the malice of the deceitful. Therefore they “turned into a crooked,” or perverse, “bow,” that is, into a perverse intention of mind, so as to act against God by worshipping idols—although he had said: [Col. 0742C] “You shall have no other gods” (Exod. 20). He makes this clearer by saying:

VERSE 64.—“They stirred him to anger in their hills, and provoked him to jealousy by their graven images.”

“They stirred him to anger in their hills,” [Cassiodorus] that is, in their proud thoughts, when they presume to worship idols. Hence “they stirred him,” because “by their graven images they provoked him to jealousy,” that is, to indignation. Or according to another text: “By their graven images they were jealous of him,” when they give God’s honour to others.

PART VIII. VERSE 65.—“God heard and rejected them, and greatly reduced Israel to nothing.”

[Col. 0742D] “He heard.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] The eighth part, in which he treats of punishment inflicted in the land of promise, which was also turned against those through whom he punished. As though he said: God heard the things mentioned above—that is, he turned away and punished them—and rejected Israel. When he rejects them, they are nothing, though through him they had been everything. This is what follows: “And he greatly reduced Israel to nothing.”

VERSE 66.—“And he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, 176 his tabernacle, where he dwelt among human beings.”

“And he rejected,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus] because of their idolatry, “the tabernacle of Shiloh.” Shiloh is a city in which the ark was. This occurred in the time of Eli the priest, when they were defeated by the Philistines, the ark of the Lord was captured, and they themselves were devastated by great slaughter (1 Sam. 4). But why did he reject it? Behold: he rejected “his tabernacle [Col. 0743A] where he dwelt among human beings,” that is, among people. He aptly explains why he rejected the tabernacle when he says, “where he dwelt among human beings.” Since they were not worthy persons among whom he might dwell, he rightly rejected that which he had established not for its own sake but for theirs. Mystically, so too, because of sins, he leaves our bodies, for he does not dwell in a body subject to sins (Wis. 1); the Holy Spirit inhabits those bodies when they are rightly governed.

VERSE 67.—“And he delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hand of the enemy.”

“And he delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hand of the enemy.” [Augustine, Alcuin.] He calls the ark their strength and beauty: by it they seemed invincible and honourable in their own eyes among the nations. Mystically, so too in the evil he diminishes freedom of choice and takes away virtues. This does not occur in the good, even though they are sometimes bodily taken captive together with the evil. For if good people are delivered together with sinners, it is their body that is subjected to captivity; they are not captives in mind or delivered to the enemy, but are free and united to God.

VERSE 68.—“And he shut up his people to the sword, and rejected his inheritance.”

“And he shut up his people to the sword,” [Cassiodorus, Haimo, Cassiodorus] whom he had chosen among many nations. Once the ark was captured, it followed that the people fell. Thus he permits the evil among his people to be shut up in the slaughter of the soul. He repeats the same thing, saying: “And he rejected his inheritance.”

[Col. 0743C] VERSE 69.—“Fire consumed their young men, and their virgins were not lamented.”

“Fire also consumed their young men,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, the rage of those fighting. For it is read in the Book of Kings that at that time thirty thousand foot soldiers of the people fell (1 Sam. 4). “And their virgins were not lamented,” because amid fear of the enemy there was no opportunity for this.

VERSE 70.—“Their priests fell by the sword, and their widows were not mourned.”

“Their priests fell by the sword,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, Eli’s sons, namely Hophni and Phinehas. The wife of one of them, Phinehas—widowed and immediately afterwards dying in childbirth because of the same distress—could not be mourned with the rites of burial. For when she heard that Hophni and Phinehas had fallen in battle and [Col. 0743D] that Eli, their father, had fallen from his seat and died with his neck broken because of it, Phinehas’s wife, already near childbirth, bent herself in grief, gave birth, and so died. “And their widows were not mourned.” Mystically, they signify those who have renounced the world.

VERSE 71.—“And the Lord awoke as one asleep, like a mighty man intoxicated with wine.”

And he was aroused. [Haymo, Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss, Augustine.] Here he shows that vengeance was turned back upon the adversaries themselves, and he attributes human traits to the Lord for the sake of explaining the matters at hand—that is, so that he may explain more clearly what he is about to say. This is anthropopathy, that is, a human [Col. 0744A] preliminary passion, when what belongs to a creature is attributed to the Creator. He says therefore: And God, who earlier was as though sleeping and as though overcome with wine. This is said in the person of the deranged, who think thus whenever he does not help those in danger. For he seemed to sleep when he gave his people into the hands of those whom he hates, when they say to them: “Where is your God?” (Ps. 41). They also suppose him to be as though overcome with wine. Thus it seems to exulting wicked men that he sleeps as though drunk, because he does not come to help so quickly. [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus.] And indeed, to those who think so madly, he sleeps and is distant, and so he is to the negligent and unbelieving, who rouse him by no utterance of praise or deed. The Lord, I say, was aroused for vengeance. And as one mighty. God is aroused to vengeance [Col. 0744B] by evil deeds, just as here he is aroused by the sins of those who placed the ark among idols. He is said to be aroused just as someone is ordinarily awakened by the lament of his household: so the Lord was roused both by the sins of his enemies and by the lament of his own people. And this, as one mighty, because people are then quick to anger and strong in action when they rise from sleep after drunkenness. As though he said: He took magnificent vengeance upon them. Hence he adds:

**VERSE 72.**—“And he struck his enemies in their hind parts; he gave them everlasting reproach.”

And he struck his enemies in their hind parts, [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin, Haymo] that is, in the more private part of their buttocks, where mice boiling up from the ground gnawed their protruding outer parts; he gave them everlasting reproach, because no one else was so punished. For they were struck in their seats, which appears to be a sign of that punishment by which everyone who looks back will be tormented—those things which, as the Apostle says, he ought to regard as dung (Phil. 3). For whoever receives God’s covenant in such a way that he does not cast off old vanity resembles the enemies of his people, who set the ark of the Lord beside the idol Dagon. And just as Dagon fell against their will (1 Sam. 5), so those old things also fall against their will. For all flesh is grass, and the glory of man is as the flower of grass. The grass withers, the flower falls; but the ark stands forever. Its secret—that is, the ark’s—is the kingdom of heaven, where the eternal Word of God is. But those who love the things behind [Col. 0744D] will be tormented by them. For he gave them everlasting reproach. Mystically, so too Christ, drunk with the wine of his passion, was raised from death, as one mighty in the resurrection, and struck his enemies in their hind parts, that is, cast down into Gehenna, because he gave them everlasting reproach, that is, eternal punishment.

**PART IX. VERSE 73.**—“And he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph; and he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim.”

And he rejected. [Alcuin, Haymo, Augustine.] The ninth part. Here he deals with King David and the seat of the kingdom, as though saying: He struck his enemies in this way, but rebuilt his own people, which he shows there: “He chose the tribe of Judah.” And this is: “And he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph,” literally, so that the king should not come from it; “and he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim,” so that kings should arise from it.

**VERSE 74.**—“But he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion which he loved.”

But he chose the tribe of Judah, so that kings might arise from it. [Augustine.] These things and what follows can be understood literally; but these words more fittingly signify that the Jewish people was rejected by God and that the new people of Christians was chosen. Thus he aptly did not say, “He rejected Reuben,” who was the firstborn (Gen. 29), nor the others who were before Judah, who deservedly appear rejected, since Jacob detested their sins. Nor did he say, “He rejected Benjamin,” from whom Saul came, who had been rejected in recent times. Thus, because of the nearness in time—when that man was rejected and cast off and David chosen—this could suitably have been said; nevertheless, it was not said.
