Rather, he named those who seemed distinguished by more illustrious merits: Joseph, who, though wickedly sold, was exalted because of his righteousness and fed his father and brothers; and Ephraim, descended from him, who was preferred to his elder brother by the blessing of his grandfather Jacob. Through these names of conspicuous merit, therefore, we understand that the whole old people was rejected by God; and Scripture testifies that the tribe of Judah was chosen, not because of Judah’s merits—for Joseph was far better—but that, through the tribe of Judah, since Christ was born from it, the new people of Christ was preferred to the old people, the Lord opening his mouth in parables (Matt. 13). [Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] Hence we understand Mount Zion as the Church, which looks ahead to what is to come, not [Col. 0745C] to earthly things. Thus the passage proceeds from the beginning of the election of the Hebrew nation to Christ. Therefore he says next: “And he chose David.” The sense is: “And he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, and he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim,” that is, the Jews, who labor for an increase of earthly goods and put their confidence in the fruitfulness of this age. For Joseph is interpreted “increase,” Ephraim “fruitfulness.” “But he chose the tribe of Judah,” that is, the Christian people—namely, “Mount Zion which he loved,” that is, the Church.

**VERSE 75.**—“And he built his sanctuary like a unicorn, in the earth which he founded for ever.”

And he built his sanctuary like a unicorn, [Augustine] or like unicorns, or one-horned creatures. Unicorns are those whose firm hope is raised toward that one thing of which it is elsewhere said: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek” (Ps. 26). The sanctuary is the holy people, a royal priesthood, as Peter says (1 Pet. 2). [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Where did he build it? In the earth—that is, in the present or heavenly Church—which he founded for ever. For although the present Church passes away mortally, it is nevertheless founded eternally. Through whom did he do this? Behold:

**VERSE 76.**—“And he chose David his servant, and took him from the flocks of sheep; from following the ewes with young he received him.”

And he chose David, [Augustine] who was of Judah and here signifies Christ; he adds, “his servant.” He does not say “his Son,” because the form of a servant is derived from David, not [Col. 0746A] the coeternal substance of the only-begotten Son with the Father. “And he took him from the flocks of sheep.” Literally, David was transferred from the pastoral occupation of tending livestock to the kingdom of men; and he received him from the place where he was, following the ewes with young. Christ, however, was transferred from people to people, that is, from Jews to Gentiles—yet, according to the parable, from sheep to sheep. For the Jewish churches are no longer what they once all were: they bore twin offspring. Hence in the Song of Songs: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep” (Song 4), coming up from the washing, all of which bear twins, and none among them is barren. The teeth of the Church are those through whom she speaks, or through whom, as if by eating, she brings others into her body. They are called a flock of shorn sheep because they laid aside the burdens of the age as if they were fleeces, and placed at the apostles’ feet the proceeds from the sale of their possessions. Coming up from the washing, namely baptism, they produce twins: the works of twofold love. Hence none among them was barren. Christ was therefore transferred from these, but he feeds the flock among the Gentiles, who are Jacob and Israel. Hence it follows: and from the place where he was, following the ewes with young—that is, after the primitive Church, from those who came after the first believers—he received him. For what purpose?

**VERSE 77.**—“To feed Jacob his servant, and Israel his inheritance.”

To feed, with heavenly bread, Jacob his servant, [Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, the Christian people. For it is not the children of the flesh but the children of the promise who are reckoned as offspring (Rom. 9). [Alcuin.] Then he repeats: “And Israel his inheritance,” unless perhaps it is said that, in this present condition, he is Jacob the servant; but when he sees face to face, he is called Israel, the inheritance. Hence he also received the name. For Israel is so called from the contemplation of God. He transferred him for this purpose: that he might feed them. And so he did.

**VERSE 78.**—“And he fed them in the innocence of his heart; and in the understandings of his hands he guided them.”

And he fed them in the innocence of his heart, [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine] because he was without sin and taught them what he himself did; and in the understandings of his hands—that is, in works intelligently performed by him—he guided them to life. By these words his active holiness is signified. Or thus: perhaps it seems to someone that it would have been more fitting to say “innocence of hands and understanding of heart” than “innocence of heart and understandings of hands.” But he preferred to say it thus because there are some who do no evil out of fear: such people seem innocent in their hands, but not in their hearts. Therefore he said, “He fed them in the innocence of his heart,” namely, of human beings—that is, making them innocent even in the thoughts of their hearts. “And he guided them,” to life, “in the understandings of his hands,” namely Christ’s: that is, by the understanding which he himself works in believers, as though by hands—something that David, who is the figure of this one, could not do.

## 177. COLLATION ON PSALM 77: “GIVE EAR”

**VERSE 11.**—“His spirit was not faithful with God.” Here Faber and Caecus display their ignorance. [Col. 0747A] For they write that the Hebrew would more correctly say actively: “His spirit did not believe God.” This is an obvious falsehood. For anyone who knows even the Hebrew alphabet knows that it is read passively in Hebrew: *NEEMENAH AEL EL RUHO*. Moreover, Augustine teaches in his exposition that it is better said, “His spirit was not faithful with God,” than “His spirit believed God.” Yet Jerome translates it actively from the Hebrew. He translates it thus, while nevertheless understanding that, as the Hebrews say, this word in the conjugation called Niphal signifies to be firm, stable, abiding, faithful, strong, and persevering. Hence the sense is: His spirit did not remain; it did not cleave to God.

**VERSE 14.**—“And they forgot his benefactions.” Jerome: “his changes”; others: “his deeds.” *ALILOTHAU*. God, supremely good and great, is accustomed to exchange past afflictions for more abundant benefits, so that, from evils experienced, a certain light may increase in the mind as it recalls divine benefits.

[Col. 0747B] **VERSE 16.**—“And he set the waters as in a wineskin.” The Hebrews say that instead of “as in a wineskin” it is “as a heap” or “a wall.” It is certain that the Septuagint read *NOD*, “wineskin,” in place of *NED*, “heap.” Because of the kinship of the words, the interchange is easy, even though the sense is not disrupted. For almighty God held the waters as in a wineskin when he restrained them until the children of Israel crossed the Red Sea with dry feet, while the Egyptian pursued them. Finally, the Chaldee too agrees with us.

**VERSE 20.**—“In a waterless place.” Jerome: “in a trackless place”; others: “in solitude” or “in the desert.” *BATZIAH*, from which *TZAION*, “a dry place,” and therefore it signifies either meaning, although the desert too is not usually a source of water.

**VERSE 24.**—“Or prepare a table for his people.” The Hebrews say “flesh” instead of “table.” Yet the word used here, *SCHEER*, signifies every kind of food. [Col. 0747C] Thus Pellican translates it, following the Chaldee, as “nourishment,” which the translators have certainly fittingly represented by “table.”

**VERSE 25.**—“Therefore the Lord heard and delayed.” Jerome had the opposite in our copy, namely, “and did not delay,” whereas the Hebrew reads without a negation, *VAIITHABAR*, which Hebraists translate “and he was angry.” Faber wrote in the margin beside Jerome’s text, according to his copy, “he delayed,” namely his kindled anger. Some have “he did not delay”; then understand it of giving them what they desired, so that there is no contradiction among the translations. So far that discussion. But *ABAR* often means “to pass over.” Hence the verb they call Hithpael will properly mean “to act rightly,” “to pass over,” which is “to delay.”

**VERSE 29.**—“Bread of angels.” *ABIRIM* is translated “of the mighty.” Yet, as Münster testifies in a scholium, the Chaldee interpreter translates it as food that came down from the dwelling-place of angels.

**VERSE 30.**—“He transferred the south wind from heaven.” Jerome [Col. 0747D] has “the east wind” for “the south wind.” The others likewise have “the east wind,” or *QADIM*. According to Aristotle, *Meteorology*, book 2, chapter 6, in his treatment of winds, we should place the Vulturnus as blowing from the winter sunrise and as neighboring the south wind. But Pliny, *Natural History*, book 2, chapter 49, writes that the Vulturnus is called Eurus by the Greeks. Therefore, with regard to the narrative, there is little difference between the south wind and Eurus. Furthermore, where in the second part we say, “in his strength he brought in the Africus,” Sanctes and Pellican translate “south wind.” Jerome and the others support our reading. For Africus, as the philosopher testifies in the place cited above, blows from the winter sunset. The Hebrew is *TEMAN*. But Jerome also translates the earlier word *QADIM* as “south wind,” in Ezekiel chapter 27: “The south wind shattered you.”

**VERSE 37.**—“Their years with haste.” Jerome, Sanctes, and the edition according to Campensis support this: *BABEHALAH*. Others translate “with terror” [Col. 0748A] or “with disturbance.” In Hebrew it conveys both meanings; for *BIHEL*, the root, means “to hasten” and “to overwhelm rashly.”

**VERSE 46.**—“They provoked the Holy One of Israel.” *HITHUU*. Modern translators render it “they marked,” understanding that they set a limit to God, not believing in his infinite power. The translator according to Campensis considers “to mark” to mean “to hold in derision.” Jerome, however, agreeing with the Septuagint, translates “they provoked.” For the sign of justice is the punishment of evildoers. And the Chaldee has “they trampled underfoot.”

**VERSE 49.**—“And that they should not drink their rains.” Since rains are rare in Egypt, which is fertilized by the flooding of the Nile, as Pliny writes, *Natural History*, book 18, chapter 18, it would seem more correct to say “streams” or “flowing waters,” as the Hebrew has: *NOZLEHEM*. Augustine also touches on this while explaining the passage: “Or rather,” he says, “the outflowings of waters, as some understand better what is written in Greek, *τὰ ὀμβρήματα*, which in Latin we call springs, waters bubbling up from below. For the Egyptians dug, and found blood instead of water.” Thus Augustine. Now the Latin *imber* is the same word as the Greek *ὄμβρος* or *ὄμβρημα*. Therefore it should rightly be understood as Augustine explains it.

**VERSE 50.**—“He sent among them the dog-fly.” Jerome: “every kind of fly.” The Hebraists agree: *AROB*. Jerome says of this in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela: “The *coenomyia* is not, as Latin translators have rendered it, called the dog-fly through the Greek letter *y*; rather, in accordance with the Hebrew sense, it should be written with the diphthong *oe*, as *κοινομυῖα*, that is, every kind of fly. But Aquila translated *παμμυῖαν*, that is, every sort of fly.”

**VERSE 51.**—“And he gave [them] to mildew.” The Hebrew has “he gave [them] to the *bruchus*,” *LEHASIL*. But because the root from which it comes, namely *HASAL*, means “he destroyed” in Hebrew, the Septuagint not inappropriately translated it “mildew.” [Col. 0748C] Nicolaus Perottus, however, prefers “rust,” which is also called in Greek *ἐρυσίβη*; but *aerugo* and *rubigo* are confused with one another.

**VERSE 52.**—“Their mulberry trees.” Jerome and the others similarly have “their sycamore trees.” *SCHIQMOTAM*. But it should be known that the Egyptian mulberry is exactly the same as the sycamore. Hence it is called by that related name because it is peculiar to Egypt. Theophrastus teaches this, book 4, chapter 1: “That individual plants require their own soil and a climate suited to them is very clearly apparent from the fact that some places bear certain things, while others bear neither what grows naturally of itself nor what is planted; and even if they take root, they produce no fruit at all—as with the palm and Egyptian mulberry.” And in chapter 2: “For there are very many trees in Egypt such as the mulberry”; and a little later: “The mulberry is in some manner similar to our native mulberry, being close to it in leaf, size, and appearance.” So he says. Moreover, how great the damage inflicted by a plague that killed sycamores with cold may be inferred from their fertile nature. For, as John of Ruell writes in book 1 of *On the Nature of Plants from Approved Authors*: “Its fruitfulness is so remarkable that it produces fruit seven times in one year, and where you have first plucked it, another immediately springs forth.” Then, having set out the properties of the sycamore, he adds among its very few most useful qualities: “Theophrastus also calls this the Egyptian mulberry; Celsus, *morosicon*; Dioscorides, Galen, and those later than Theophrastus call it *sycomorus*, a name formed from fig and mulberry. Ulpian further relates that this tree is frequent on the embankments of the Nile, and that severe penalties are imposed upon those who cut down sycamores. Its power too is intermediate between the mulberry and the fig, from which it also acquired the name sycamore.”

For the first [occurrence of] *HANAMAL*, Jerome, Pellican, the translators for Cajetan, Campensis, and Pratensis render “hoarfrost,” “cold,” or “frost,” and thus agree [Col. 0749A] with the Septuagint. Münster translates “a stone of ice.” Yet in his lexicon he says it is bitter cold or ice, by which the shoots of trees are devastated. Sanctes gives “locust” and “bruchus.” In his *Thesaurus* he cites many rabbis who disagree among themselves.

**VERSE 53.**—“Their beasts of burden.” Jerome translates “their pastures,” *BEIRAM*; the others, “their beast of burden” or “their cattle.” I think Jerome takes the place for what is in the place, because he immediately adds in the same passage: “and their beasts of burden to birds,” where we read, “and their possessions to fire,” *UMIQNEHEM LARESCHAPHIM*. As to the first term, they agree that it is common to cattle, wealth, and any acquired possession. Of the second, they say it means a burning coal, a demon or consuming plague, a fire that prevailed, hail, scorching, fiery darts and arrows, or sparks of fire. How Jerome understands himself is explained in his commentary on Habakkuk chapter 3, on the verse: “Let the devil go forth [Col. 0749B] before his feet.” “Aquila,” he says, “translated ‘bird’ for ‘devil.’ Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Fifth Edition [translate] ‘flying creature,’ which in Hebrew is called *RESCHEPH*. The Hebrews relate that, just as Beelzebub is called the prince of demons in the Gospel (Luke 11), so Resheph is the name of a demon who holds primacy among the others; and because of his excessive swiftness and his roaming in different directions, he is called bird and flying creature. They also say that he is the very one who spoke to the woman in Paradise under the form of a serpent, and that from the curse by which he was condemned by God he received this name. For *resseph* is interpreted ‘crawling on the belly.’” Thus far Jerome.

**VERSE 55.**—“Their beasts of burden.” Münster, Nebiensis, and Sanctes freely translate *HAIATHAM* as “their life,” since the word can represent either meaning. Jerome and the others say “their living creatures” or “their beasts of burden.”

[Col. 0749C] **VERSE 63.**—“They did not keep the covenant.” Jerome, in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela, explains why he translated “covenant,” although it was not in the Hebrew, saying: “I know that ‘covenant’ is not found in the Hebrew; but because all translated with a similar word, *ἠσυνθέτησαν*, and among the Greeks a covenant is called *συνθήκη*, it is expressed by one phrase: ‘They did not keep the covenant,’ although the Septuagint has *ἠθέτησαν*. But in Hebrew it is said in one word, *IBGEDU*.”

**VERSE 68.**—“He rejected his inheritance.” *HITHABAR*. Jerome translates “he did not delay,” as also in verse 65, although the manuscripts vary. Others: “he was angry.” But it is clear that God’s rejection is a severe punishment, which is rightly called the wrath of God. As for Jerome’s “he did not delay,” if you understand “his wrath,” the sense does not differ. This was noted on verse 25.

**VERSE 69.**—“Their virgins were not lamented.” Thus Jerome: “No one mourned his virgins.” The edition according to Campensis, Pratensis, Sanctes, the translators for Cajetan, and the paraphrase of Campensis follow with “they did not marry,” if you render *HULLALU* word for word, that is, “they were praised,” as the Chaldee and Nebiensis have. Münster expressed this in a single added phrase: “they were not honored by marriage.” But had he added “they were not honored by burial,” he would have agreed with the ecclesiastical reading and Jerome. Nor are we compelled to understand marriages rather than any other thing suitable to the context.

**VERSE 70.**—“Their widows were not mourned.” Jerome too does not differ: “They were not,” he says, “wept for.” [Col. 0750A] Others, except the translator according to Campensis, print the active form: “They did not weep.” But the active and passive are the same apart from the vowel points, depending on whether one writes *TIBKENAH* or *TIBACHENAH*.

**VERSE 71.**—“As a mighty man overcome with wine.” Different translators render this metaphor variously, while preserving its meaning. Jerome and Nebiensis: “like a strong man after a wine-bout”; the Chaldee: “like a strong man made drunk with wine”; Pellican: “like a strong man from a wine-bout,” or “rejoicing from wine.” So too the translators for Cajetan; likewise Pratensis: “rejoicing because of wine”; Sanctes: “crying out because of wine”; Münster: “like a strong man who shouts after wine”; the edition according to Campensis: “as a soldier is gladdened by wine”; the paraphrase: “as one who, overwhelmed by wine, after a long sleep returns to himself and, gladdening himself with wine again, boldly undertakes dangers.” In Hebrew: *MITHRONEM MIIAIIN*.

**VERSE 72.**—“He struck his enemies in their hind parts.” [Col. 0750B] *AHOR*, which others translate “behind” or “backwards,” was rendered by Münster in such a way as completely to block an understanding of this passage from 1 Samuel chapter 5, where the Philistines are related to have been struck by God in the more private part of their buttocks because they irreverently held the ark of the Lord. For when Münster translates in this fashion, “He struck his enemies as they turned their backs,” he signifies only enemies put to flight. But by following the Vulgate reading, which is close to the Hebrew idiom, he leaves the reader free to understand either sense. Augustine follows the former interpretation, and the paraphrase of Campensis agrees with him: “He wounded the buttocks of his enemies,” following, I think, the Chaldee paraphrast: “He struck them in the hind parts with hemorrhoids.” “And he built his sanctuary like a unicorn.” Jerome likewise: “And he built his sanctuary in the likeness of a monoceros.” Others translate “high places”; Sanctes and Münster add “palaces.” Hence it is clearer than light that Jerome and the Septuagint read *REMIM*, while the others [read] *RAMIM*, which indeed differ by a single point. The Chaldee agrees with us.

“In the earth which he founded for ever.” In Hebrew: “like the earth which he founded for ever,” so that you understand not the earth absolutely as founded in itself, but that the stability of the earth is compared with the stability of the tabernacle that was built. Hebrew: *KEERETZ*. Hence Jerome: “He founded it like the earth for ever.” But if the second clause depends on what precedes, and on the mark of comparison set above, the same sense will result: “as in the earth which he founded for ever.” It is certain, however, that *beth* and *caph* are very similar. For if it were said *BERETZ*, it would mean “in the earth.” St. Jerome explained this difficulty at length to Sunnia and Fretela concerning “in the earth which he founded for ever”: “You say that you have found written in its place, *ἐν τῇ γῇ ἐθεμελίωσεν αὐτὴν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα*, that is, ‘he founded it in the earth for ever.’ In Hebrew it is written as Symmachus translated it: *εἰς τὴν γῆν ἣν ἐθεμελίωσεν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα*, that is, ‘and he built his sanctuary like that of a unicorn in the earth which he founded for ever.’ But if it is not said of the earth that it was founded, but of some other thing which appears to have been founded in the earth, let them prove from what precedes and follows what the sense is, so that I know not what thing said to be founded may appear to be in the earth. But if the sanctuary is thought to be founded in the earth, it should have been written: ‘He founded it in the earth for ever.’” Thus St. Jerome.

## PSALM 78

[Col. 0749]

**TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF ASAPH.”**

[Col. 0749D]

“O God, the nations have come.” Title: “A Psalm of Asaph.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] This psalm [Col. 0750D] is the second lamentation, in which Asaph, out of zeal for piety, prays that Christ may come to the aid of his people, who are to be grievously afflicted for their hardness. It concerns either the captivity wrought by the Babylonians (2 Kings 25), or rather the devastation wrought by Antiochus Epiphanes in the time of the Maccabees, when he placed idols in the temple, defiled the law of God, and ravaged the people (1 Macc. 1). But he did not overthrow the city or the temple. By these things is signified the persecution of the Church under the hands of the Gentiles: she suffers, yet does not fail, though in some who fall away she is defiled. The sense is: This psalm is assigned to Asaph, that is, to the faithful Synagogue, which speaks here. Its purpose is to exhort people to rejoice in their neighbors’ good fortunes and to grieve over their calamities. The psalm has three parts. The first is a complaint, in which are enumerated the things Jerusalem suffered in the time of Antiochus—when it was not destroyed—by which the persecution of the Church is signified. The second is a prayer [Col. 0751B] on behalf of its own party against its enemies, beginning, “How long, O Lord?” The third is the exultant conclusion of the lament, beginning, “But we.” Thus Asaph, grieving with his people, sets their evils before God, saying:

**VERSE 1.**—“O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem a keeper’s hut for fruit.”

“O God, the nations have come into your inheritance.” [Augustine.] He does not say this to God as though God were ignorant—since he himself knows from God whatever he knows—but speaks with him in an affection of piety, representing in himself all who would be present when these things happened. For he speaks in the person of those to whom they happened. This is a lament over the things God did in taking vengeance, and a prayer is joined to it, as though saying: “Would that he might now have mercy and spare them.” These words are therefore spoken by him who foretells why they are said as though by those to whom they happened; and the lament itself is prophecy. As to the phrase “into your inheritance,” it should be understood that, among the people of Israel, God’s inheritance consists of the elect, not the blinded. Therefore these words cannot be understood of the times after Christ’s ascension, when they were devastated by the Romans. For then that people which remained in Jerusalem was not God’s inheritance. [Note: [Col. 0751D] From Eusebius, book 3, chapter 5.] For all the reprobate had been blinded, and all the faithful, when the Romans approached, had withdrawn into Agrippa’s kingdom at an angel’s warning. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Rather, this must be understood of the time before Christ came. For at that time that people was God’s inheritance: there were prophets and saints among them when they were carried off to Babylon, or especially under Antiochus, under whom the Maccabees suffered dreadful things and were crowned most gloriously. He therefore speaks of the devastation wrought by Antiochus, saying: “O God, the nations have come into your inheritance,” that is, into Jerusalem, where some good people were; by saying “your,” he moves the judge whose possession is injured. “And they have defiled your holy temple” by the images they placed there, but they did not destroy it. First comes the outrage against the temple, in which lies an insult to God. Here he accuses them of sacrilege. Note that the temple did not yet exist when the Prophet said these things; he relates as past what he saw in the Spirit as future. But now they have plainly been fulfilled. It follows: [Col. 0752A] “They have made Jerusalem a keeper’s hut for fruit,” that is, a place of desolation, as such shelters are abandoned once the fruit has been gathered. Hence Isaiah: “The daughter of Zion shall be left like a shelter in a vineyard, and like a hut in a cucumber-field” (Isa. 1). Then, after sacrilege, he adds murders, saying:

**VERSE 2.**—“They have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth.”

“They have given the corpses,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, the bodies of your servants who refused to use unclean things, “as food to the birds of heaven.” As though he said: They rage not only against the living, but against the dead. To bury is an act of piety; to cast out is an act of cruelty. Thus these things are understood literally of the devastation under Antiochus. But if anyone understands them as occurring after Christ’s resurrection and ascension, they should be understood of what idolaters inflicted upon martyrs, when the Church suffered many things amid so great a multitude of martyrs. For although Asaph properly denotes the Jews, the Church too is called an assembly, and she is also the inheritance into which the nations came—not by believing, but by persecuting; that is, they invaded her with the will to destroy and utterly ruin her. She is also the temple of God, which is defiled in those who fall away, whom persecutors compelled, by terror or torture, to deny Christ and, by vehement pressure, to attach themselves to idols. Hence he says here: “They have defiled your holy temple.” Thus the Apostle says: [Col. 0752C] “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 2). The same Church is also Jerusalem, our free mother (Gal. 4), of whom Isaiah says: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail; for the children of the desolate are more numerous than of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54). Hence he says here: “They have made Jerusalem,” that is, the Church, “a keeper’s hut for fruit,” that is, a place of desolation. For when, as the nations persecuted, the spirits of the martyrs passed to the heavenly table like many sweet fruits from the Lord’s garden, the Church appeared deserted. “They have given the corpses of your servants,” that is, the resurrection of the holy martyrs, “as food to the birds of heaven,” as though any part of them could perish, when he to whom even our hairs are numbered restores all things whole from the hidden recesses of nature. He then explains what he had said: “the flesh of your saints.” These are “the corpses [given] to the beasts of the earth.”

**VERSE 3.**—“They poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.”

“They poured out their blood.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] He heightens the language in order to move the judge. “Like water,” that is, abundantly and vigorously, as though it were as lawful to shed blood as water, without guilt; and this not only within the walls but also around Jerusalem, when they found persons to kill outside it. The abundance of slaughter in the city and beyond it is noted, so that no one had leisure to bury them, since danger threatened everyone. Hence he adds: “And there was no one to bury them.” This can also be understood of the Church, which suffered throughout the whole world, whose circuit is the entire globe wherever persecution occurs.

**VERSE 5.**—“We have become a reproach to our neighbors, a derision and mockery to those around us.”

“We have become a reproach.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] For Jerusalem’s glory was once wonderful throughout the world. Hence Jeremiah: “This is the city that was called the crown of glory; she has been turned into a reproach to her neighbors” (Lam. 2). This is more grievous than if it came from distant people, because these are continually present. Or the martyrs say this: “We have become a reproach to our neighbors,” that is, to those near us in affection, who already wish to believe; “we have become derision and mockery to those around us.” This increases the offense: “those around us” are the Gentiles around Jerusalem. Or the martyrs say: “We have become derision and mockery to those around us,” that is, to the enemies of the Church throughout the world, because the death of his saints is precious not in their eyes but in the sight of the Lord (Ps. 115).

**PART II. VERSE 6.**—“How long, O Lord, will you be angry unto the end? Shall your zeal burn like fire?”

“How long, O Lord?” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin.] Here is the second part, a prayer on behalf of its own party against enemies and insulting neighbors. As though saying: They rage against us thus; but, O Lord, how long will you be angry with us unto the end? As though saying: Do not be angry unto the end. He asks that God not remain angry unto the end—that is, that the devastation may not continue, but that he may moderate correction. Thus he now prays, though above he lamented; and he prays concerning what is to come, while some good people were then among them. “And your zeal”—namely, how long—“shall burn like fire; shall it burn unto the end?” Do not be angry. God’s wrath and zeal are not disturbances in him who judges with tranquillity; rather, by the name of wrath is meant the vengeance taken on wickedness, when he punishes us for our offense. By the name of zeal is understood the demand for chastity, lest the soul despise the law of its God and perish by committing fornication against its God, as happened in Job. Note that these things occur to human beings because of sins, even to the righteous: as the Maccabees amid savage tortures, the three youths amid destructive flames, and the holy prophets in captivity testify. Hence he aptly says, “like fire.” For the zeal and wrath of God truly burn like fire. They burn until the gold—that is, the perfection of virtues—is purified and the wood is reduced to ashes.

**VERSE 7.**—“Pour out your wrath upon the nations that have not known you, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name.”

“Pour out.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As though saying: Do not be angry [with us], but rather “pour out,” that is, abundantly, your wrath. This is not spoken out of malice; rather, things foreseen are stated. For the form of a wish predicts the future. “Pour out,” I say, “upon the nations,” so that, as they oppress us, so they may be oppressed by your power—those who have not known you, nor wished to know or fear you. The guilt of the Jews is made lighter by comparison with theirs; “and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name”—but [have called upon] demons or any creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Note that by “nations” he understands subjects, and by “kingdoms” the kings themselves.

**VERSE 7.**—“For they have devoured Jacob, and laid waste his dwelling-place.”

Because they devoured Jacob. [Aug., Cassiod., Alcuin., Aug.] I say that they did not invoke [you], but moreover attacked [him], because they devoured Jacob, that is, the Jewish people. This is the inheritance previously said to have been handed over to the teeth of wild beasts. Behold, in the manner of orators, a man is put for mankind: that is, the beloved patriarch for the offending nation, so that remembrance of him may mitigate the people’s sins. And they laid waste his place, by the overthrow of the city, [Col. 0754B] which was stripped of its citizens; or because they killed those substituted in the place of the slain citizens. For the place is the city where the Temple stood, to which they assembled for the feasts. This is also rightly understood of the Church: for they devoured Jacob—that is, the Church, which is the younger [son], to whom the elder shall be subject—by incorporating others into themselves or by killing them. “And they laid waste his place” is a repetition.

**VERSE 8.**—“Do not remember our former iniquities; let your mercies swiftly come before us, for we have become exceedingly poor.”

Do not remember. [Gl. int., Aug., Cassiod.] As though he said: Do this to the nations that did not know you; but do not remember, etc. Or the connection is thus: They inflict these evils upon us; but because I know that you chastise us for our sins and through them, I pray: Do not remember our iniquities. [Col. 0754C] This confession of offences calls forth pardon. *Former*: he does not say this only of sins past, since even at that time certain Jews followed idols; but “former,” that is, sins like the ancient ones, by which they sinned for countless years in following idols. And let your mercies swiftly come before us, namely before the judgment which every human being fears; for unless pardon goes beforehand at judgment, the guilty person is not acquitted. Therefore I plead for mercies, because we have become exceedingly poor in merits. Let no one presume upon his own deeds. I say, do not remember our iniquities, but:

**VERSE 9.**—“Help us, O God of our salvation; and for the glory of your name, O Lord, deliver us, and be gracious to our sins for your [Col. 0754D] name’s sake.”

Help us, [Cassiod., Aug.] in the war undertaken to defend the laws against Antiochus, because they trust not in their own powers but in God’s might. Hence he adds: O God of our salvation, which is necessary because we are weak; and, O Lord, deliver us for the glory of your name—not for our merit, but so that, once delivered, we may render honor to your name. And be gracious to our sins for your name’s sake, not for our own sake: that is, let what cannot be obtained by our deeds be granted us through the mercy of your name. Or these words may be understood in the person of the martyrs. “Do not remember our former iniquities,” that is, those coming from ancient parents, whether by descent or imitation. “Let your mercies swiftly come before us,” lest we come to judgment to be condemned, because we have become exceedingly poor [Col. 0755A] in doing good. But help us, O God: as though he said, let our poverty, that is, our weakness, be helped by your mercy in doing good. As though he said: Let grace help free will. For when he says, “Help us,” he is neither ungrateful to grace nor does he abolish free will. For one who is helped also does something himself. Our Savior, necessary to our weakness; and for the glory of your name, so that whoever glories may glory in the Lord, not in himself (1 Cor. X). O Lord, deliver us. God delivers us—that is, rescues us from evils—both when he helps us to do righteousness and when he is gracious to sins, without which no one lives here. Hence he adds: “And be gracious to our sins for your name’s sake”: do these things for us.

[Col. 0755B] **VERSE 10.**—“Lest perhaps they say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’ And let it become known among the nations before our eyes.”

Lest perhaps they say among the nations. [Aug., Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod.] As though he said: I ask this especially for the nations, who perish by despairing of God. What might they say? That familiar utterance of the faithless: “Where is their God?” As though to say: Either he does not exist, or he cannot help his own. This is an intolerable taunt.

**VERSE 11.**—“The vengeance for the blood of your servants which has been shed; let the groaning of those in fetters enter into your sight.”

The vengeance for the blood of your servants which has been shed. Temporal vengeance, namely, so that they may escape eternal vengeance. Let it become known [Col. 0755C] among the nations before our eyes: that is, let it happen swiftly that we may see converted those who now persecute. This may be understood favorably, as referring to present vengeance; or it may be understood of eternal punishment thus: “Let the vengeance for the blood of your servants which has been shed enter [into your sight]. Let it become known among the nations before our eyes.” [Aug.] That is, take vengeance upon the wicked who shed the blood of your servants; and so it shall be at the end, because either in those converted here wickedness is slain—which he had previously desired—or at the end they perish. He says this not as wishing it, but as prophesying it; for the righteous person does not delight in an enemy’s punishment, because he does not hate him, but in divine justice, because he loves God. By contrast, the unrighteous person wishes, “May it be so to the wicked.” But: “Let the groaning of those in fetters enter into your sight”—or into yours—those fettered by the corruptibility [Col. 0755D] of the flesh, which weighs down the soul and through which the persecutor sometimes prevails. No one feels these fetters except those who groan under their burden. The Apostle desired to be released from them and to be with Christ (Phil. I). Or the fetters are God’s commandments, by which the saints are bound; when patiently endured, they are turned into ornaments. Hence it is said: “Put your foot into her fetters” (Ecclus. VI). Or literally, he calls those persons fettered [Cassiod.] whom the Gentiles bound. They pray with groaning that the Church may not fail in its brethren, even though punishment consumes them. He then shows what the groaning of those in fetters asks; for this was what their groaning sought.

**VERSE 12.**—“According to the greatness of your arm, take possession of the children of those put to death.”

[Col. 0756A] Preserve, [Cassiod., Aug.] lest they be stained by some error; or, according to another reading, receive into adoption the children—that is, the descendants—of those put to death. The holy martyrs always prayed that their blood might not be fruitless for their descendants, so that a harvest might grow from the place where it was thought to perish. This is a devout prayer: that God may not cast away the children of those punished for him, but multiply them. And do this according to the greatness of your arm, that is, of your power. For so great a thing followed among Christians as their enemies would never have believed.

**VERSE 13.**—“And repay our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom—their reproach, which they reproached you with, O Lord.”

And repay. [Aug., Alcuin., Aug.] Again, he does not wish this, [Col. 0756B] but truly prophesies, saying: Repay our neighbors—of whom he spoke above, among whom the Church remains until the future separation—sevenfold. By the number seven, that is, by sevenfold recompense, he signifies the completeness of punishment, since fullness is commonly signified by this number. So also in reference to the good it is said, “He shall receive a hundredfold in this age” (Mark X), where this is used for all things: as though he said, “Having nothing, yet possessing all things” (1 Cor. VI). And [repay this] into their bosom, that is, in their hidden inward parts now in this life, so that afterwards it may become known among the nations before our eyes. For when a person is given over to a reprobate mind, he receives in his inward sense the deserving of future punishments. Or “sevenfold” is put for the infinite: “their reproach [Col. 0756C] with which they reproached you, O Lord.” As though he said: Repay them this, sevenfold into their bosom—namely, the reproach with which they reproached you, O Lord—that is, for this reproach, give them over to a reprobate mind. For there they reproached your name in your servants, believing that they would blot out your name from the earth.

[Cassiod.] Or this may be understood favorably, and as a wish: Repay our neighbors. Although God repays bodily, nevertheless it is for the salvation of their souls. Hence he adds, “sevenfold,” by which he signifies the perfection of the heavenly gift when we are filled with the Holy Spirit. And [repay it] into their bosom, that is, into the secret place of their minds, where conversion may occur. “And repay them the reproach with which they reproached you, O Lord”: that is, cause them, in return for the injuries and reproaches which they inflicted upon you, [Col. 0756D] to render praises. This is a glorious vengeance, when God is praised from the mouths of his enemies.

**PART III. VERSE 14.**—“But we, your people and the sheep of your pasture, will confess you forever.”

But we, your people. [Cassiod., Haym., Cassiod., Aug.] The third part, containing an exultant conclusion—not the conclusion of parents who have conquered, but the pleasant conclusion of lamentation. As though he said: So let it be with them; but we, whom they thought to destroy, who are your people by faith and the sheep of your pasture, that is, fed by your teaching—these are the remnant of the Jews gathered by Mattathias (1 Macc. II). Or this is to be understood generally of every class of devout persons and true Christians, so that the Christian people too is included there. [Cassiod., Aug.] This is the flock for which he prayed that God might not remain angry [Col. 0757A] for long. We, I say, will confess you—that is, praise you in ourselves. And this forever, because until the end of the world the Church shall not be blotted out, as is supposed.

**VERSE 15.**—“From generation to generation we shall proclaim your praise.”

From generation to generation, [Aug., Cassiod.] that is, in every generation. It is the same as what he had said: “Forever we shall proclaim your praise to others,” a praise which they tried to silence by putting an end to us. Or this can be understood of the future: “from generation to generation,” that is, in the age to come, we shall proclaim your praise, not for the instruction of others but as honor duly owed.

## Comparison on Psalm LXXVIII: “O God, the nations have come,” etc.

[Col. 0757B]

**VERSE 1.**—“They made Jerusalem a watch-hut for fruit.” The Hebrews say, “into heaps,” namely heaps of stones or ruins. Jerome, writing to Sunia and Fretela, shows that the sense is the same—desolation—in these words: “*A watch-hut for fruit*, which in Greek is called ὀπωροφυλάκιον (*oporophylakion*), cannot be translated otherwise than as we have translated it. *Oporophylacion* means the lookout which guards of crops and fruit customarily have, so that of a most extensive city scarcely a small hut remains. This is according to the Greeks. But in the Hebrew, *LEIIM* is written, which Aquila translated λιθόριον (*lithorion*), that is, a heap and mound of stones by which vineyards and fields are customarily cleared.” So he says. Hence the Chaldee [paraphrase] said, “desolation.”

“They laid waste his place.” Jerome and Nebiensis translate “splendor” for “place,” although other Hebraists render it “dwelling-place,” agreeing here with the Septuagint. But *NAUEH* is ambiguous: *NAUEHU*, “his dwelling-place,” or “his splendor.”

“Preserve the children of those put to death.” Jerome and Sanctes: “Leave the children of destruction,” or “those subject to death.” Münster, Pellicanus, and Campensis express the same meaning differently: “Make the children survivors,” or “preserve alive those devoted to death.” Pratensis and the interpreter for Cajetan: “Release the children,” etc. Whichever way it is taken, the sense comes to the same result. And if any diversity seems present, Sanctes explains its source in his *Thesaurus* in these words: “Yet there are,” he says, “*ra. da.* [probably ‘Rabbis’], who derive *HOTHER* from *IETHER*, which means ‘rope, cord,’ and explain it as though it said: ‘Break or loosen the rope and binding of the children of death.’ For he had said beforehand, ‘Let the cry of the bound enter before you.’ Therefore he said that he would release them from their bonds.” [Col. 0758B] Thus far he. Therefore, that word, derived from *IATHAR*, literally means, in the conjugation called *hiphil*, “Cause the children of death to remain.” This unquestionably occurs when we are claimed as a particular possession of God, powerfully snatched by God’s strength from the danger of death. The mystical sense may be found in the explanation of the passage.

**VERSE 15.**—“From generation to generation.” Faber and Caecus object to this expression as insufficiently Latin; otherwise one ought to say *in generatione et generationem*, or *in generationem et generationem*, as the Greeks have. That is a minor matter. Yet Jerome, in his *Commentaries*, is not so offended as not obscurely to suspect that some mystery lies beneath it: “That is,” he says, “from the prophets as far as the Gospels.”

## PSALM LXXIX

[Col. 0757]

### Title of the Psalm: “Unto the end, for those who shall be changed; a psalm for the Assyrians; a testimony of Asaph.”

[Col. 0757C]

“You who shepherd Israel, give heed.” Title: “Unto the end, for those who shall be changed; a psalm for the Assyrians; a testimony of Asaph.” [Aug.] Asaph, “the enlightened,” here treats of Christ’s first coming and of his vine. This is a good testimony concerning the Head himself and his body: King and people, Shepherd and flock. For Asaph here speaks of Christ’s coming, who converts humanity and establishes the vine brought forth from Egypt. The title means: This psalm, directing us to the end—that is, to Christ—is the testimony of enlightened Asaph for those who shall be changed, and for the Assyrians; that is, for those who will be changed for the better, so that they may no longer be the generation [Col. 0757D] that did not direct its heart, but one directing itself toward Christ.

[Alcuin.] For “Assyrians” means “those directing,” and they are the same as those who shall be changed. Or distinguish between those to be changed and the Assyrians: understand the former as those to be converted, and the latter as the Jews. For this psalm deals both with those who are changed and with the Jews, who set themselves against Christ through free choice and carnal observances. Thus this psalm of Asaph—that is, of the Synagogue—tending toward the end, is a testimony for those who shall be changed and for the Assyrians, both those to be converted and the proud. To the former, that is, the converted, it is a testimony of right faith; to the latter, that is, the proud, of unbelief.

Purpose: [Col. 0758C] [Aug.] It exhorts us to be changed for the better and directed to Christ.

Method: [Cassiod.] The psalm has two parts. The first is a prayer for the first coming, through which the human race is restored. The second treats of the vine, saying how it was begun and brought to completion, at “You brought a vine out of Egypt.” Thus Asaph, who in the preceding psalms had anxiously prayed for the sins of the Synagogue, now has confidence concerning its conversion; and, those changed for the better, he gives testimony of Christ’s coming, for which he prays, saying: O God,

**VERSE 1.**—“You who shepherd Israel, give heed; you who lead Joseph like a sheep.”

You who shepherd Israel, [Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod.] give heed to those who see you—that is, send your Son. According to this, the address is directed to God the Father. Or rather, the address is directed to the Son, whom they desire, await, and invoke to come, and whom he defines by his acts, saying: O God, you who shepherd Israel—that is, the Jews spiritually seeing you—give heed, that is, pour upon us the light of mercy, so that we who are dark through ourselves may be bright through you. You who lead Joseph, namely the people signified by Joseph, the faithful people from the Gentiles. For Joseph means “increase”; and when the grain of wheat died (John XII), God’s people grew greatly. With the two walls joined in Christ, the cornerstone (Eph. II)—that is, Jews and Gentiles, Israel and Joseph—you lead them as [Col. 0759A] sheep into God’s folds and pastures. These are the sheep of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd” (John X). Note that he assigns proper words to each: Israel, as the elder, is shepherded; Joseph, that is, the devoted people, is led.

**VERSE 2.**—“You who sit upon the cherubim, manifest yourself before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh.”

You who sit. [Aug., Alcuin., Cassiod., Aug.] As though he said: Give heed thus, O you who sit upon the cherubim—that is, upon those lofty powers of heaven—manifest yourself before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh, that is, before the Jewish people among whom these tribes are found. As though he said: You who are known to angels, make yourself known to human beings. [Col. 0759B] Asaph prays that God’s Son, who was in the hiddenness of majesty, may appear through the Incarnation before the Jews, as had been promised, producing in them the powers signified by the names Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. Ephraim means “fruitfulness”; Benjamin, “son of the right hand”; Manasseh, “forgetfulness,” so that, forgetting the things behind, they may stretch forth to those before.

It may also be read according to the meanings of the names: You who sit upon the cherubim, that is, in the fullness of knowledge, which is charity—for *cherubim* means “fullness of knowledge”—manifest yourself before Ephraim, that is, before fruitfulness, and Benjamin, that is, the son of the right hand, so that we too may be fullness of knowledge. This can be through charity, which is God. Hence, God is charity: whoever knows it, what does he not know? For charity is the name both of God and of the gift. And before Manasseh, that is, before the forgetful one, so that you may now come to his mind, according to: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn” (Ps. XXI).

**VERSE 3.**—“Stir up your power, and come, that you may save us.”

Stir up your power and come. [Alcuin., Cassiod., Aug.] He repeats more plainly what he had prayed. The order is this: Come, you yourself, in the flesh; and stir up your power, that is, show your power in the resurrection, since you seemed weak in the Passion, when it was said: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matt. XXVII). You seemed to have no strength; the persecutor prevailed over you. This was prefigured when Jacob prevailed over the angel, [Col. 0759D] the angel himself willing it; yet the defeated angel blessed the victor. For the victorious man held the angel and said: “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Gen. XXXII). Thus the defeated one blessed the victor, but made that same victor lame. For he touched the sinew of his thigh, and it withered. This is a great sacrament. The Jewish people does indeed limp, but there too is the blessed race of the apostles. Therefore stir up your power, [Gl. int.] that is, though crucified through weakness, rise through power (2 Cor. XIII). I say, come: for what purpose? That you may save us. Thus we shall be saved, O

**VERSE 4.**—“O God, convert us; show your face, and we shall be saved.”

[Col. 0760A] O God, convert us, [Aug., Hier., Aug., Gl. int.] who are turned away from you; otherwise we are not converted unless you do it. Then, addressing the Father, he says: Show—or illuminate—your face, veiled by the cloud of flesh; that is, your Son, who is your image. That face was veiled to Asaph in the time of Christ’s weakness, and then Asaph was sick, unable to behold it veiled by the cloud of which it is said: “The Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt” (Isa. XIX). But God illuminated that face when Christ rose and ascended. And so we are saved. Hence he adds: “And we shall be saved.”

Yet even after Christ’s coming, anger remains for those converted to Christ—in the body, indeed, not in the mind—but this will have its end through Christ at his second coming. For he who in his first coming removed part of the punishment will at his second consume every punishment in the good. Therefore he says:

**VERSE 5.**—“O Lord God of hosts, how long will you be angry with the prayer of your servant?”

O Lord God of the heavenly hosts, [Haym., Gl. int., Aug.] whose companions we shall be, how long will you be angry with the prayer of your servant, now your servant? And if you were angry with the prayer of one who was your enemy, do not be angry with the prayer of one now your servant. God’s anger has certainly in part passed away from the servant—not so that he does not chastise as a father, but so that he does not condemn. For anger continues even toward the converted, but as correction. For he chastises every son whom he receives (Heb. XII).

**VERSE 6.**—“You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us tears to drink in measure.”

[Col. 0760C] You will feed us. [Cassiod., Alcuin., Gl. int.] Here he explains the sufferings which the saints will endure at the time of the coming. As though he said: Although I desire Christ’s coming, nevertheless we shall suffer many things in that time, because you, O God, will feed us with the bread of tears. He said the same thing by another comparison: “And you will give us tears to drink.” [Aug., Alcuin, Haym.] For those tears will serve correction and perfection, not destruction. These tears will be “in measure,” that is, according to your strength, so that you may be instructed, not overwhelmed. Hence the Apostle: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able” (1 Cor. X). Or “in measure” means according to the measure of sins. He then explains the tears, saying:

[Col. 0760D] **VERSE 7.**—“You have made us a contradiction to our neighbors, and our enemies have mocked us.”

You have made us a contradiction to our neighbors. [Aug.] This certainly happened. For from Asaph were chosen those who went to the nations and preached among the nations; they were contradicted by those saying, “Who is this herald of new demons?” Thus they were fed with tears. For they preached that one who had died had risen. It was a new thing; but miracles gave credibility to the incredible report. Therefore they were opposed, but the opponent was overcome, and from an opponent became a believer. [Note: [Col. 0759] From Isidore, *On Judges* XIV; and Augustine, Psalm LXXX, verse 7.] For Samson broke the lion’s jaws when it met him as he went to take a wife from among foreigners. And [Col. 0761A] our enemies not only contradicted us but also mocked us, [Aug., Gl. int.] as though we worshipped one dead. But although we are to suffer such great things, we desire him no less on that account; rather, we pray again.

**VERSE 8.**—“O God of hosts, convert us; show your face, and we shall be saved.”

O God of hosts, convert us, and show your face, [Cassiod.] that is, Christ’s presence, and we shall be saved. It is the custom of one who desires earnestly to repeat frequently what he asks with such great prayers.

[Hier., Haym., Cassiod.] Alternatively, from the words “Stir up,” he prays that the power of miracles which God exercised in the ancient people may be stirred up—a power stirred up when the reality which they prefigured was displayed, that is, when the truth came. Therefore, praying for Christ’s coming, he says: Come, you yourself, O God. And stir up your power, namely that of the miracles which you once performed, whose power lies dormant until their reality appears. I say, come, that you may save us. See how great a benefit of the Incarnation he knew. Therefore he prays so earnestly. What desires could suffice to ask for these things? “O Lord God of hosts”—another reading. He calls God of hosts the one whom Asaph knew would perform miracles both in himself and in other human beings; for he alone frees people from unbelief. You, O God, convert us, who are distorted; and, once converted, show us your face, because God is accustomed to look upon those converted.

He then asks why God delays the coming so long, reckoning this delay as God’s anger against himself, saying: “O Lord God of hosts, how long will you be angry with the prayer of your servant,” so as not yet to perform what you promised? Asaph said this in the time when he asked him to come, while the coming was still delayed by God’s counsel. He calls God angry because he delays. See the piety and great longing of the petitioner. Thus he cries because he knew the coming was delayed. “You will feed us”: he enumerates the evils they endured meanwhile before the coming. As though he said: So long, until you come, you will feed us with bread of tears. The bread of tears is a life full of sorrows. Yet this too is food, since we are not thereby extinguished but instructed. He adds that it is also drink, saying: “And you will give us tears to drink.” He sets down these two because these are the two things by which every human being lives, and thus he signifies the sufficient and complete [Col. 0761D] instruction of chastisements. For what time is free from tears? Yet what tears do you give? “In measure,” that is, in a distributed proportion. Hence: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted” (1 Cor. X), etc. He then explains the tears: “You have made us a contradiction to our neighbors, and our enemies have mocked us.” While our neighbors, who are from among us, are against us, our enemies mock us. That we may be saved from all of them: O God of hosts, convert us and show us your face, that is, Christ, and we shall be saved.

**PART II. VERSE 9.**—“You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out nations and planted it.”

The vine. [Cassiod., Aug., Alcuin.] The second part. Here he deals with the vine, showing how it was begun and perfected. By the vine he means the Church, which began from the Jews and is completed among the nations. Yet it is one and the same vine, though one people gives the beginning and another the completion. Speaking, therefore, of the beginning of this vine, he says: “A vine,” etc. As though he said: We shall be saved, but you will destroy the Jews, for whom you did so much—not for a trivial fault, but because, ungrateful for your benefits, they did not recognize even Christ’s coming, among the other benefits bestowed upon them. [Aug., Cassiod.] I rightly said, among many other benefits granted to them: for you brought a vine out of Egypt into the land of promise; you drove nations out of the land of promise, namely Amorites, Jebusites, and other peoples; and you planted that vine there as a cultivator.

**VERSE 10.**—“You were a guide on its journey before it; you planted its roots, and it filled the earth.”

Guide on its journey. [Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] I have said whence the vine was brought out and where it was planted. He next adds how it believed, how greatly it grew, and what it occupied: Afterwards, so that the vine might embrace the world, you were a guide on its journey before it, appearing visibly to it in assumed flesh. Hence: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). Or, according to another reading, the address is directed to God the Father: You made a way before it—that is, you sent it Christ made visible, who says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). And you planted its roots, that is, the prophets, apostles, and other teachers. And just as that vine now filled the whole earth, that filling continues to the end of the world, while some are converted daily. It should be noted that he dealt briefly with the beginning of the vine when he said, “You brought a vine out of Egypt.” But “it filled the earth” was said of the completion of the same vine. He then repeats more fully about the beginning of the same vine, saying:

**VERSE 11.**—“Its shadow covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God.”

It covered the mountains. [Aug.] Afterwards he repeats concerning the completion of the same vine at “And perfect it.” That completion occurred when the Jews were rejected and the nations received. Yet it is one vine. Recalling this vine in this psalm often causes confusion to those who are inattentive. Therefore let us pay attention, lest darkness envelop our eyes. As though he said: The vine now fills the earth, but formerly the shadow of this vine, which now fills the earth, covered the mountains. The mountains are the prophets, whom the shadow covered because they spoke in figures. Its shadow is circumcision, the Sabbath, and such things (Exod. XXIV), of which the prophets spoke: “Keep the Sabbath; circumcise the infant on the eighth day; offer the sacrifice of a ram, calf, and others; do not move” (Lev. VIII). Therefore its shadow covered the mountains, and after the shadow came the reality (Acts I).

Or thus: Its shadow, that is, care and concern for them, covered the mountains, that is, the greater persons; and its shrubs, that is, their offspring and increase, cover the cedars of God, that is, the teachers. [Aug., Haym., Aug.] For this vine, as it grew, covered all the saints—prophets and patriarchs—with care and concern. He said “cedars of God” because there are cedars to be overthrown, namely the proud, who are cedars of the world but not of God. It follows:

**VERSE 12.**—“It stretched out its branches as far as the sea, and its shoots as far as the river.”

It stretched out its branches from Jerusalem, [Cassiod., Aug.] that is, its children, by comparison, as far as the sea, which is near the Jews, and its shoots as far as the river Jordan. For some Jews—two tribes and a half—were beyond the Jordan, but the whole people was on this side of the Jordan (Num. XXXII). This, then, is the beginning of the vine being discussed here. Its completion, which he foretold above in “it filled the earth,” is through Christ the way. This is what is said elsewhere: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. LXXI). The Jewish nation did not accomplish this. Yet it is not another vine, but the same one. For from there comes Christ, salvation from the Jews (John IV), and from there the apostles and other righteous persons, even if some branches have been broken off (Rom. XI).

**VERSE 13.**—“Why have you destroyed its wall, so that all who pass along the way plunder it?”

Why have you destroyed [it]? [Gl. int., Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] As though he said: The vine was thus extended. What then happened to it? That people was overthrown. This is what “you destroyed its wall” means: its protection. A wall is made only of stones around vineyards. And all who pass along the way plunder—that is, strip and rob—it: namely, the nations who worship idols and pass by the way, that is, the Law or Christ. Or those passing along the way are all who exercise temporal dominion. Why did this happen to it? Because it was proud even against its planter; it killed the servants sent to it, and even the Son, the heir. Therefore its wall was destroyed; the nations found the Church destroyed and laid it waste. Asaph first laments this, but not without hope; for he now speaks of those who direct their heart. He then explains how they plundered it.

**VERSE 14.**—“The boar from the forest ravaged it, and the solitary wild beast fed upon it.”

The boar from the forest ravaged it, [Cassiod., Aug.] that is, drove it beyond the boundaries of its homeland. The boar is Vespasian, powerful and cruel toward, and opposed to, them—that is, the Jews—who, among other things, regard this animal as unclean; he came from the forest (Deut. XIV). For the nations were forests. That one people alone was the vine; but when the nations believed, this was fulfilled: “All the trees of the forest shall exult” (Ps. XCV). And elsewhere: “We found it in the fields of the forest” (Ps. CXXXI). “And the solitary wild beast fed upon it,” [Cassiod., Aug.] that is, Titus, who consumed the Jewish remnant with dreadful devastation. [Col. 0764A] He is called solitary, that is, proud. For every proud person says, “I am, I am, and there is no other.” Or “boar” and “wild beast” are understood as the same thing: the solitary wild beast is the boar that devastated it, namely the Roman army. But to what good effect have we suffered these things? That we may thus be healed and converted. He says this in prayer: O

**VERSE 15.**—“O God of hosts, turn back; look down from heaven and see, and visit this vine.”

O God of hosts, etc. [Alcuin., Cassiod., Gl. int., Haym.] Or the connection is thus: The vine has been so devastated; but so that the remnant may be saved, O God of hosts, turn back from anger at the end of the world. Look down with a merciful gaze from the heaven of heavens; see us who pray, while you are serene; behold us changed for the better. This is the remedy for which Asaph prays. And see by what sins humanity languishes and perishes. Or “see” means cause it to know you or its own sins; and visit this vine, that is, heal it in its weakness.

**VERSE 16.**—“And perfect that which your right hand planted, and upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself.”

And perfect it, [Aug.] do not establish another, but perfect this one. For in it is the very seed of Abraham, in whom all nations shall be blessed (Gen. XXII). There is the root that bears the wild olive (Rom. XI). Perfect it, I say, because blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the nations should enter; and thus all Israel shall be saved (ibid.). That which your right hand—that is, your propitiation—planted, that is, began.

[Alcuin, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus.] Alternatively, the whole may be expressed thus: first the foundation of the historical sense concerning the Jews is laid; then the structure of spiritual understanding concerning the Church is added. For through mystical comparisons he speaks of what occurred: that is, he thus speaks of the things literally done among the Jews under the likeness of a vine, branches, and the like, thereby also suggesting a mystery, that is, a mystical sense. For there are comparisons which are not mystical—as if he were saying: We shall be saved because you thus prefigured it long ago, when you transplanted a vine from Egypt. This is to be taken literally: “You drove out nations and planted it,” nor is this altered in the historical sense. Literally, the vine is the Jewish people, as a type of the Church, [Col. 0764D] which is mystically understood by the vine, because amid the shadowy crowds of sinners it is adorned with the fruit of the saints, as a vine is adorned with fruit amid leaves; and, dug around by tribulations and pruned by martyrdom, it grows more abundantly, like a vine; and, pressed out in the winepresses of worldly oppression, it is conveyed into the heavenly storehouse.

[Jerome, Haymo.] Therefore, just as you transplanted those Jews from Egypt, so also you transplanted the vine, that is, the Church, from Egypt—that is, from the darkness of ignorance and blindness—and drove out the nations, that is, vices; and planted it in virtues. You were the guide of its journey before it: literally, while they travelled in the pillar of cloud and fire, he went before them. And you planted its roots, that is, the rulers of the Jews, and it filled the land of promise. Thereafter the following matters are not altered in their historical sense. [Col. 0765A] Mystically, the whole is understood of the Church as follows.

[Cassiodorus, Haymo, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] He shows how it was spread throughout the world, saying: “You were the guide of its journey,” while he leads it on its spiritual journey through this wilderness of the world; “and you planted its roots,” that is, the roots of the Church—that is, prophets, apostles, martyrs, and other steadfast persons—from whom it stretches out branches and occupies the world. Hence follows: “And it filled the earth,” that is, the inhabited world. “And its shadow covered the mountains”: here the height and breadth of the vine are explained. For that vine is heavenly and from above; it even overshadows the mountains, that is, those more exalted in life and knowledge—its shadow of spiritual grace warms, nourishes, and causes them to grow more abundantly.

[Haymo, Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] For in the unity of the Church all receive grace, [Col. 0765B] by which they are refreshed from the incitements of vices. “And its shrubs covered the cedars of God.” Vines which climb trees are called shrubs; by them the lesser members of the Church are understood. The cedars of God are not the proud, but those who are lofty in the Church, such as God’s martyrs.

[Remigius, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Therefore its shrubs, that is, its lesser members, cover the cedars of God, that is, its greater members, because the Church too protects these, as though in her bosom; for by her authority they confirm what they say. Otherwise nothing is held to be Catholic unless it is confirmed by the testimony of the universal Church. “It stretched out its branches.” Having explained the vine’s height, he explains its breadth, saying: “It stretched out its branches,” that is, its children, to the sea of all nations; “and its shoots,” that is, its children of regeneration, to the river Jordan, [Col. 0765C] from which they flowed forth, for there the rule of baptism began (Matt. 3).

And because the vine is such, therefore: “Why have you broken down its wall?” He marvels why the Lord’s defence has been withdrawn from such a vine. But he says this of the Church, not on account of the good, for “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2), but on account of the unbelievers who are in it—in name, not in divine power; in number, not in merit. “And all who pass along the road pluck its grapes,” that is, demons. He explains how: “The boar laid it waste,” that is, the strong and savage devil; “from the forest,” because his thoughts are wild and pathless. “And the solitary wild beast,” the same as the boar—that is, the proud devil—has fed upon it. But: “You, O Lord God of hosts, turn back; look down from heaven, and see, and visit [Col. 0765D] this vine.” These words are not altered. “And perfect that which your right hand planted,” that is, your propitiation. But where will you perfect it? Perfect it as founded upon yourself, and upon the Son of Man. Here Christ is openly shown, who was born of the Virgin Mary (Matt. 1). For he himself is the foundation, which no one can alter, whom you confirmed for yourself when you said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). In him Christ was confirmed among men, he who alone is the foundation (1 Cor. 3). And so it shall be, because:

### Verse 17

> “Burned with fire and dug up, they shall perish at the rebuke of your countenance.”

“Burned with fire and dug up”: [Augustine] that is, sins shall perish at the rebuke of your countenance. He calls sins “burned” and “dug up.” But the sins which burning desire causes are burned; those which ill-grounded fear causes are dug up. [Col. 0766A] These are all grave sins, because all sins are committed either through desire or through fear when desire does not prevail: fear prevails. Search your consciences; question your hearts whether sins can exist except through either fearing or desiring. Thus, all sins in a human being arise from two things, namely desire and fear; conversely, love of God and fear of him lead to every good.

For you love in order that things may go well with you; you fear lest things go badly with you. Do this with regard to God, not the world. Both kinds of love burn, and both kinds of fear humble, but in different ways. Thus, concerning good fear, the cultivator interceding for the tree that bore no fruit, lest it be cut down, says: “I shall dig around it and put on manure” (Luke 13). The ditch signifies the pious humility of one who fears; the manure, the useful filth of one repenting. Concerning the fire of good love it is said: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12). Therefore he says, “burned with fire,” that is, sins arising from love that burns wrongly—for both forms of love burn; “and dug up,” that is, sins arising from fear that humbles wrongly—for both forms of fear humble. “They shall perish at the rebuke of your countenance,” that is, of your Son.

[Haymo.] This is the countenance that blots out sins. For what did Christ rebuke except sins? Or thus: evils which arise through the fire of desire are called burned, which agrees with the preceding interpretation. “Dug up” are hidden evils, when a pit is deceitfully prepared for another. [Col. 0766C] These, however, shall perish in the future, when the wicked are condemned for them, and it shall be said to them: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25). But so that all these things may now be fulfilled:

### Verse 18

> “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the Son of Man whom you have confirmed for yourself.”

“Let your hand be.” [Haymo, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Or continue thus, as though he said: How long shall we be evil? Until the Saviour comes. Therefore let your hand, O God, be upon the man of your right hand. Let your mercy show itself; act beneficently toward your vine by showing your countenance, that is, your Word. “Upon the man of your right hand,” that is, the Son of the Virgin. A great sacrament is signified here, and God’s great gift is displayed, because [Col. 0766D] Israel’s salvation could be doubted so long as Christ had not come. But then the promise was fulfilled, so that the Church, joined to her bridegroom, might no longer depart from him.

Therefore he says: “Let your hand be upon the Son of Man whom you have confirmed for yourself,” that is, may your operation bring the promised effect to completion; and he prays for the operation of the holy incarnation. As if he said: How long do you rebuke and accuse us? O God, let your mercy be upon the man of your right hand. As I have prayed, so do these things.

### Verse 19

> “And we shall not depart from you; you will give us life, and we shall call upon your name.”

“And we shall not depart from you any longer,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] when we have the Son; “and you will give us life,” so that we may love you rather than earthly things, in which we were formerly dead. This is the benefit flowing from the coming of the Son. “And we shall call upon your name,” [Col. 0767A] that is, we shall love you; you will be everything to us and our help. And that this may be so:

### Verse 20

> “O Lord God of hosts, turn us back; show your countenance, and we shall be saved.”

“O Lord God of hosts, turn us back.” [Haymo, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus.] I shall end with that with which I began. “And show your countenance, and we shall be saved.” Great is the sweetness of this little verse; in it he sets forth the rule of all religion. First God turns us; then he shows us his countenance, that is, looks upon us with the light of mercy; finally he saves us. Therefore the prophet repeats this, because through it anyone may briefly ask for what is needful.

## Comparison on Psalm 79: “Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel; you who lead Joseph like a sheep”

[Col. 0767B]

(The significance of the title and its addition have been discussed several times in connection with the Septuagint.)

### Verse 5

> “Over the prayer of your servant.”

The Hebrew has “your people,” as all render **AMMECA**. Certainly the servants of God are the people of God. Hence the Greeks have the plural, **τῶν δουλῶν σου**, “of your servants.” Yet I suspect that the Septuagint read *aleph* in place of *ayin*. For **UMMAH** in Hebrew means “people,” while **AMAH**, with the same letters, also signifies “servitude.”

### Verse 6

> “You will give us tears to drink by measure.”

For “by measure,” Jerome offers three renderings; Pellican likewise. Nevertheless, that number is understood as denoting abundance. Hence others say “in the greatest measure,” **SCHALISCH**; both tend toward this meaning. But the fact that the Hebrew has “them” or “to them,” while we say “us” or “to us,” does not affect the sense, even though Jerome translated [Col. 0767C] as did the Septuagint. Therefore it is not unlikely that the manuscripts varied.

### Verse 14

> “The solitary wild beast has fed upon it.”

Jerome: “All the beasts of the field have fed upon it.” Nearly the same is found in the Pratensis, Münster, Pellican, and Campensis. Yet among the Hebrews there is controversy over what **ZIZ** properly means, although the more common opinion is that it is a general name for wild beasts. Sanctes, indeed, translates: “A wild bird has fed upon it.” In his *Thesaurus* he reports the opinion of a certain [Col. 0768A] rabbi, who thought it a huge bird which, when it spreads its wings, darkens the sun. I consider this fabulous. However that may be, it is certain that the psalm signifies some exceptional desolation. Moreover, the interpreters for Cajetan, in place of “beast of the field,” say “the creeping thing of the Almighty,” so that it appears that they read **SCHADAI** with the point called *yamin* (“right”), whereas others read **SHADAI** with the *smol sadai* (“left-side”) point.

### Verse 16

> “Perfect it.”

Jerome, in place of the imperative, puts the noun “root,” so that it belongs to the preceding verb “visit”; Münster has “the site of the vineyard”; Sanctes and Nebiensis, “the dwelling-place”; Pratensis, “the little plant”; the interpreters for Cajetan likewise. The Septuagint understood the Hebrew word **CANNAH** as an imperative from the verb **CON**, or **CAN**, that is, “he established,” “he prepared”—though contrary to the rule, as often happens among the Hebrews. Pellican translates “prepare.” The paraphrase of Campensis is “restore it to its former dignity.”

### Verse 16

> “Burned with fire and dug up, they shall perish at the rebuke of your countenance.”

[Col. 0768B] Jerome translates with the accusative: “burned with fire and cut down,” so that you understand “the vine” or “the plant,” and take the phrase as dependent upon the preceding words. Others translate in the nominative, though in the singular, and supply the verb “is” or “lies.” Then the words following, “they shall perish” or “may they perish at the rebuke of your countenance,” they refer either to those who did this or to the cultivators of the vine, who would necessarily perish when it had been burned. In fact, in Hebrew these two forms are singular and feminine: **SERUPHAH**, **KESUAH**.
