Similarly in Greek: **ἐμπεπυρισμένη πυρὶ καὶ ἀνεσκαμμένη**, “burned with fire and dug up.” Jerome understands it thus too in his short commentary on this passage; after citing it, he immediately adds: “The synagogue, certainly, together with the unbelieving Jews.” But Saint Augustine, taking it in the plural and neuter gender, does not depart from the sense; the Chaldean also gives that sense: [Col. 0768C] “burned with fire and cut to pieces, may they perish at the rebuke of your countenance.”

### Verse 20

> “We shall call upon your name.”

Jerome alone translated passively: “We shall be called by your name.” For this reason it is very clear that here also he read the text without points; for, without the assignment of points, the active differs in no way from the passive. You may pronounce **NIQRA**, “we shall call upon,” or **NIQQARE**, “we shall be called.” This matter has been discussed in the preface.

# Psalm 80

[Col. 0767]

## Title of the Psalm

> “Unto the end, for the winepresses. A psalm for Asaph, on the fifth day of the Sabbath.”

[Col. 0767D] “Rejoice in God.” Title: “Unto the end, for the winepresses. A psalm for Asaph, on the fifth day of the Sabbath.” [Augustine, Haymo, Augustine, Alcuin.] In this psalm many mysteries are gathered together, yet the threshold of the psalm indicates its inner meaning through the winepresses and the fifth day of the Sabbath. For on the fifth day of the Sabbath, that is, the fifth day, God created from the waters living creatures—namely creatures that swim and creatures that fly (Gen. 1), that is, fish and birds. In this the sacrament of baptism is signified: among those reborn, some are like birds, namely those who, despising temporal things, rise toward heavenly things; others are like fish, who remain inquisitive amid the waves of this world. By the winepresses the Churches are understood.

For this psalm says nothing of literal winepresses. Therefore it is clear that the winepresses here mentioned are spiritual, namely Churches, [Col. 0768C] because, as in winepresses there are three things—pressure, and from it two products, oil and dregs, one of which is stored away while the other is cast out; likewise wine and pomace—so in the Church there is the pressure of tribulations, the burden of sufferings, through which good and evil are distinguished, though the same sacraments join them together. [Col. 0768D] For just as a cluster on the vine contains both wine and pomace, and an olive on the tree both oil and dregs, so ecclesiastical sacraments are shared by good and evil alike.

[Augustine.] But just as wine and oil, strained out by the pressure of the winepress, are stored away, while pomace and dregs are cast out as filth to be trampled underfoot, so when the pressure of temptations comes, the righteous become more righteous, and the filthy become filthier still (Rev. 22). Therefore, if the pressures which blasphemers complain abound in Christian times are present, do not be troubled: [Col. 0769A] be oil, not dregs that are cast out. For here what was hanging together on the tree is distinguished. Therefore, for the pressure of tribulations which distinguishes them, this psalm is sung to Asaph, that is, to the Lord’s congregation, to those reborn through the water of baptism. Of these, some are oil and wine, birds—that is, spiritual persons—while others are dregs, pomace, and fish.

[Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] And the meaning of the title is: This psalm, directing us toward the end, that is, toward Christ, is sung to Asaph because historically this Asaph speaks to the Jews, and spiritually to Christians. For Asaph speaks to himself. I say this psalm concerns the winepresses, that is, Churches, in which is the pressure of tribulations; it is set on the fifth day of the Sabbath, that is, it speaks of those baptized and to be baptized with the water of baptism, [Col. 0769B] as was prefigured by the work of the fifth day of the Sabbath.

Intention: [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] He warns that after baptism we should despise these things and ascend in mind to heavenly things. Method: It has two parts. First, he says what must be done by the elect, who are oil, wine, and birds. Second, he deals with the dregs by rebuking the reprobate, at “Hear, my people.” Thus Asaph, as though setting before himself the image of a certain festival, urges the elect to celebration, saying: O birds, wine, oil—that is, congregation of God, for which this psalm is made:

### Verse 1

> “Rejoice in God our helper; sing joyfully to the God of Jacob.”

“Rejoice in God our helper.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, [Col. 0769C] Augustine.] Others rejoice in their deceiver, the world; or in a fictitious god, who is a mocker and deceiver or deserter. But you, rejoice in God our helper; sing joyfully with a joy which you cannot express to the God of Jacob, because you truly are Jacob, namely the lesser people whom the greater shall serve. And:

### Verse 2

> “Take up a psalm, and bring the timbrel; the pleasant psaltery with the harp.”

“Take up a psalm,” [Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus, Alcuin] that is, receive spiritual things. By “psalm” is understood the heavenly gift bestowed by God through grace. “And bring the timbrel,” that is, bodily things. By the timbrel is understood what is bodily and comes from you—that is, what you have in your purses. As if he said: Let the words of God and human deeds come together in one fellowship. [Col. 0769D] This is the peace of Jerusalem (Ps. 121). This is the principle of giving and receiving (Phil. 4). Hence the Apostle: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your bodily things?” (1 Cor. 9).

[Augustine.] Therefore join the timbrel to the psalm, because the psaltery—here used for “psalm”—is pleasant with the harp, which is used for the timbrel. As if he said: Let one who awaits heavenly things not be sluggish in performing earthly works; let us answer the preaching of God’s word with bodily deeds. He then adds:

### Verse 3

> “Sound the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of your feast.”

“Sound the trumpet.” [Alcuin, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine.] These words, up to the division, may either be understood simply and literally of the Jews, or allegorically of Christians. [Col. 0770A] Literally they are understood thus: “Sound the trumpet at the new moon,” or at the beginning of the month of trumpets, which is the same thing. For *neomenia* is Greek; in Latin it means “new moon.” *Neos* (**νέος**) means “new”; *mēnē* (**μήνη**) means “moon,” which marks the beginning of the month. From the first day of the seventh month the Jews were commanded to sound the trumpet for seven days, that is, at the beginning of the new moon. This was called the feast of Trumpets, which they celebrated in memory of the event in which the Lord showed Abraham a ram caught by its horns among briars, which he sacrificed in place of Isaac. Then, as though explaining, he adds: “On the notable day of your feast.”

Asaph speaks these same words spiritually to Christians. As if he said: Take up and bring; and do not be afraid, but sound the trumpet at the new moon—that is, in your renewal—announce and [Col. 0770B] preach to others more clearly and boldly the new life which the new moon signified, on which the Jews sounded trumpets for seven days. This signified that the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, by which we are renewed, was to be preached by the trumpet—that is, openly, through manifest works or loud cries. Hence Isaiah: “Cry aloud; lift up your voice” (Isa. 58), namely, like a trumpet. I say “at the new moon,” namely “on the notable day of your feast,” that is, in newness of life, where there is knowledge of truth and rest from evils.

### Verse 4

> “For it is a commandment in Israel, and a judgment of the God of Jacob.”

“For it is a commandment.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] First, historically, it is thus: Therefore the trumpet must be sounded because the law was given to the Jews through Moses, in which this is commanded. And this is the meaning: This must be done because it is commanded by God in Israel, that is, among the Jews. But where there is commandment, there is judgment also, because “those who sinned under the law shall be judged by the law” (Rom. 2). Therefore do this also because judgment belongs to the God of Jacob—that is, because he who commands this is to be judge. And:

### Verse 5

> “He appointed it as a testimony in Joseph, when he went out from the land of Egypt; he heard a language he had not known.”

“A testimony of the future event.” [Cassiodorus, Haymo.] He appointed that commandment—or, without “that,”—in Joseph, that is, among the Jewish people. When? “When he went out from [Col. 0770D] the land of Egypt”; “he heard a language he had not known,” that is, he heard the law given through Moses. And then the Lord:

### Verse 6

> “He removed his back from burdens; his hands served in the basket.”

“He removed his back from burdens,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] by which Pharaoh oppressed them in mud and brickmaking. For his hands, that is, the hands of the Jewish people, served in the basket. A basket is a vessel by which he carried earth while making bricks for Pharaoh.

### Verse 7

> “In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you; I heard you in the hidden place of the storm; I tested you at the water of contradiction.”

“In tribulation.” If the prophet speaks here, it will be said thus: He turned aside, saying: “In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you, and heard you in the hidden place of the storm.” [Col. 0771A] [Haymo, Cassiodorus, Haymo.] Literally, when they did not dare openly even to groan for fear of the Egyptians, while they were oppressed with the work of mud and brick, God’s benefits were reckoned against them, so that their offence might be considered more grievous. “I tested you at the water of contradiction,” where, despairing of my goodness and power, you said: “Can he bring forth water from the rock, or prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Ps. 77).

[Cassiodorus.] Or this whole passage is understood spiritually of Christians in this way: Therefore preach in newness of life, because this is commanded in Israel—that is, among the Jews—both literally and spiritually, and judgment belongs to the God of Jacob. This is unchanged. And he commanded not only Jews but also Gentiles. This is the sense of “And he appointed it,” the commandment—or without “it,” the meaning is the same: [Col. 0771B] “He appointed a testimony,” that is, a command under solemn attestation, in Joseph, that is, among the Gentiles who have been increased. For Joseph means “increase.” Therefore the Gentiles are Joseph, because “the children of the desolate are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54).

When did he appoint it? “When he went out from the land of Egypt,” and so forth. Behold the fifth day of the Sabbath, mentioned in the title. [Augustine, Alcuin.] When the multiplied people went out from the land of Egypt—that is, from the darkness of ignorance through baptism—then they hear and perceive mysteries which they had not known, where the heart ought to cleave. This is the meaning: “When he went out through baptism from the land of Egypt,” that is, from the darkness of ignorance, “he heard a language he had not known,” that is, the commandments of the Gospel, which they had not known before. Or this signifies that the apostles spoke in various languages the mighty works of God.

What benefit came to them from this hearing? Behold: “He removed,” he himself, or the Lord, “from burdens,” and so forth. Or continue thus: Was it necessary to go out? Certainly it was, because God removed his back—that is, the mind—from burdens, that is, the load of sins, which are also indicated by the pursuing Egyptians. Hence the Lord says: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11). From what kind of people did he remove it? Behold: “His hands served in the basket,” [Col. 0771C] [Augustine] that is, in servile work amid the impurities of sins, in earthly and muddy works, signified by baskets, by which dung is cleared away and earth carried. For sins are servile works, according to: “Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8).

“In tribulation,” God here speaks to the sinner, saying: Previously you served in the basket. But you called upon me in tribulation, pressed by sins, and I delivered you; and I heard you in the hidden place of the storm—[Augustine, Haymo, Cassiodorus] figuratively, not in a storm at sea, but in the storm of the heart, where you undergo the warfare of suggestion. There I heard you, so that “with the heart you may believe unto righteousness” (Rom. 10); “I tested you at the water of contradiction,” that is, among a contradicting people, so that with the mouth confession may be made unto salvation (ibid.). For God tests us in the contradictions of heretics.

[Augustine.] And indeed, one heard in the storm of the heart must be tested at the water of contradiction. Once one has believed and been baptized, and has begun to walk in God’s way, one has many agitators, scoffers, slanderers, discouragers, who oppose in many ways. [Col. 0772A] This is the water of contradiction experienced by the ancients, though it is now almost dried up. For then the waters of the peoples were troubled and fiercely resisted. Thus, when Samson, the strong man, was going to take a wife from among foreigners, a lion came to meet him, which he killed. That is, when Christ was going to take a wife, the Church, from the Gentiles, a roaring lion—that is, the people of the Gentiles—came to meet him; but he tore it apart like a kid goat, because that people was nothing but a feeble sinner. Once that savagery had been slain, it no longer roars or runs to meet Christ. Indeed, we now find within it laws in favour of the Church, like a honeycomb in the lion’s mouth.

Why, then, should the water of contradiction now be feared, since it is now almost wholly dried up? For formerly the water of contradiction existed even for Christ himself, even in his own person, as was said of his birth: “He shall be for the fall and rising again of many, and for a sign that shall be contradicted” (Luke 2). Thus the Jews contradicted the title of his cross, wishing to alter it. Pilate answered them: “What I have written, I have written,” and so forth (John 19). Therefore he who tests us at the water of contradiction experienced that same water, in order to make us unafraid of it.

## Part II. Διάψαλμα — “Interlude”

### Verse 8

> “Hear, my people, and I will testify against you; Israel, if you will hear me, there shall be no new god in you, nor shall you worship a strange god.”

[Col. 0772C] “Hear, my people.” [Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Alcuin, Augustine.] The second part: hitherto he has dealt with the oil of the winepress, that is, the good; now he deals with the dregs, that is, the reprobate, who are reproved here, and this is said as a warning. As if he said: Since I have bestowed so many benefits, O dregs, pomace, fish, who are my people—and even here “his own” means what belongs to the winepress—hear.

[Cassiodorus, Haymo.] That is, understand; and “I will testify against you,” or, in another reading, “I will bear witness to you,” that is, I will prove to you by the testimonies of Scripture what I say. Or “I will testify against you” means: I shall be a witness to the truth. Behold, the Lord of judgment makes himself witness of the truth both here and in the future, so that no one may any longer doubt, since before earthly judges witnesses are usually produced to establish the truth.

[Cassiodorus, Augustine, Jerome, Augustine.] He then adds what he wishes him to understand: “Israel, if you will hear me.” By calling him Israel he signifies that he is familiar to him and invites him to his commands. “There shall be no new god in you”—in your heart, where truth, not falsehood, ought to be. I do not say “with you,” as though it were outside; but “in you,” that is, in your heart, where, if you do not think rightly, there is an image of your own fantasy. For whatever each person desires and reveres is that person’s god.

What shall not be in you? A new god. He says this lest the Word of the Father be regarded as existing in time. For a new god is one made in time. But our God is not new; he is from eternity to eternity. For Christ our God may perhaps be new as man, but he is everlasting as God. Therefore no new god shall be in you. If you hear me, some indeed make new gods for themselves, either idols or a Christ unequal to the Father, calling him the Son of God [Col. 0773A] while denying him to be the Son of God. For if he is the only Son, he is what the Father is from eternity. But they imagine a new god and invent other such things in their hearts; thus they themselves are temples of images, which, even if not placed in temples, they have nevertheless placed—what is worse—in their own hearts.

Therefore it is a great task to break these idols within and give place in the heart to the living God, not a new god. For all such people, though holding this or that view and making various gods for themselves, and though altering faith itself through falsehood, appear to agree among themselves. For in all is earthly thought, diverse opinion, one vanity. Hence elsewhere: “In their vanity together” (Ps. 61). Although they disagree through variety of opinions, nevertheless they are bound together by similar vanity. Therefore Samson tied together the tails of foxes and fastened fire there, in order to burn the crops of the foreigners, namely the Philistines (Judg. 15).

Samson means “their sun,” that is, Christ, who is the sun of those to whom he himself gives light; he is not the sun of all, concerning whom the wicked will say: “We have wandered from the way of truth, and the sun of righteousness has not shone upon us” (Wis. 5). Elsewhere: “The sun of righteousness shall arise, and healing is in his wings” (Mal. 4). The foxes are the chief heretics, especially deceitful, lying hidden in twisting and cavernous recesses, deceiving and foul-mouthed. Of them the bride says in the Song of Songs: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song 2), that is, convict the heretics. Though they appear to disagree among themselves, they nevertheless agree in evil—that is, in their rear parts [Col. 0773C]—are held by like vanity, and by the corrupting fire which they drag in their tails burn the crops: not ours, for “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2), but those of foreigners, who are vessels of dishonour.

Speaking, then, to this people, he says: “If you hear me, there shall be no new god in you,” because “I am who I am” (Exod. 3). He does not say “with you,” as though an image had been introduced from outside, but “in you,” that is, in your heart—the image of a new god which you carry with you and so remain old. “Nor shall you worship strange gods.” [Cassiodorus.] For if you do not think of a false god, neither will you worship one that has been made. He calls a god “strange” when he is a god in name, not in essence. It is almost an equal crime to think a god new and to serve idols. I say that you shall not worship, nor ought you to worship, because I am who I am.

### Verse 9

> “For I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt; open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.”

“For I,” [Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus, Augustine] am not strange, and even if I am man, I am the Lord your God, who bestowed these temporal benefits upon you—namely, brought you out of the land of Egypt. Historically, this shows that he is not new. Allegorically: I brought you out through baptism from the land of Egypt, that is, from the darkness of ignorance; God is identified by his deeds. Open wide your mouth through desire—that is, your heart, where you suffer constriction, where vain images are. But open your mouth wide by confessing and loving; break the idol of the heart that constricts you; remove the new god from your conscience. And I will fill [Col. 0774A] it with the bread of life and understanding, because with me is the fountain of life. Thus I have warned.

### Verse 10

> “But my people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not give heed to me.”

“But my people did not hear my voice,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] though I gave them the law and did great things, so that their guilt might grow. For although I filled the mouths of the prophets, they were not heard by the dregs. For who did not hear his voice? Behold: “Israel did not give heed to me.” Ungrateful for so many benefits, it was unwilling even to pay attention. Hence the fitting punishment follows.

### Verse 11

> “And I dismissed them according to the desires of their heart; and they shall go in their own devices.”

“And I dismissed them.” [Augustine, Haymo.] Behold, the dregs run out [Col. 0774B] through the opened openings of the winepress. “According to the desires of their heart,” that is, I gave them over to themselves. Hence the Apostle: “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts.” “And they shall go in their own devices,” or “affections,” in another reading—of whatever sort—because through their traditions they rendered God’s commandments void (Matt. 15). But:

### Verse 12

> “If my people had heard me, if Israel had walked in my ways.”

“If my people had heard me,” [Haymo, Augustine] by believing. Then, explaining, he adds: “If Israel”—this is the people—“had walked in my ways”: this is what it means to hear me.

### Verse 13

> “Perhaps I would have humbled their enemies to nothing, [Col. 0774C] and laid my hand upon those afflicting them.”

“Perhaps,” [Remigius, Augustine, Haymo, Cassiodorus] means “truly,” though he speaks ironically: I would have humbled their enemies—enemies of every kind, foes of every kind, through whom they complain that they sin—enemies, I say, to be accounted as nothing. Or “for nothing” means that I would have done this freely. Or according to another reading: I would have humbled their enemies by reducing them to nothing, and would have laid my hand, that is, my vengeance, upon those afflicting them, whom I would have crushed by my power. From their example it is clear that if we resist God, he does not oppose our enemies, nor lay the hand of our defence upon them.

### Verse 14

> “The enemies of the Lord lied to him, [Col. 0774D] and their time shall be for ever.”

“The enemies of the Lord.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Again the prophet speaks after the inserted words of the Lord. As if he said: They complain of enemies through whom they sin, but they themselves have become enemies of the Lord, because they lied to him. Repeating the point: in baptism they renounced the devil and his pomps—that is, devilish deeds condemned by God—but return to them again, and “the last state is worse than the first” (Luke 11 [printed “Luc II”]). Behold, the dog returned to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in mud (2 Pet. 2).

[Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine.] Or, literally, this concerns the Jews, who lied to the Lord by not carrying out what they had promised. This does not apply to the pagans, who promised nothing. What then comes to them? Even if they are tolerated here, they are not saved by sacraments alone. This is what is said: And therefore, because they are such, the time of their punishment shall be for ever—that is, eternally—even if they flourish here. Or “their time,” that is, their alteration through punishments: for they shall pass from snowy waters to excessive heat (Job 24); it shall be for ever, that is, eternally. And who are these? Behold:

### Verse 15

> “And he fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock.”

“And he fed them,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] or continue thus: They are such, and yet he fed them with the fat of wheat—literally, with manna. Hence they are ungrateful. Or allegorically, he fed them with Christ’s body. For he joined them to his sacraments and gave Judas too the morsel. Or: he fed them with the fat of wheat, that is, with spiritual understanding. “And he satisfied them with honey from the rock”: literally, [Col. 0775B] in the wilderness he brought water, not honey, from the rock (Num. 20). Therefore it must be understood only mystically. Honey, then, is wisdom, holding the first place in sweetness among the foods of the heart. The sense is: he fed them not only with the fat of wheat, but also with honey flowing from the rock, that is, with the wisdom of Christ. For “the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10). He satisfied them so that they might delight in God’s word, in knowledge of the sacraments, and in the solution of parables; and yet they lied to him.

## Comparison on Psalm 80: “Rejoice in God,” etc.

### Verse 2

> “The pleasant psaltery with the harp.”

The wording translated from the Hebrew differs very little: **KINNOR NAIM IM NA BEL**, which Jerome translated, “a harp, pleasing with a psaltery,” [Col. 0775C] although the first term signifies an instrument, and the final term is disputed.

### Verse 3

> “On the notable day of your solemnity.”

Jerome: “In the middle of the month, on the day,” etc. Pratensis: “in the solemnity, on the day,” etc. Sanctes and Munster: “at the appointed time, on the day, or indeed on the day of solemnity.” *CESEII* signifies the appointed time of a solemnity. But since in Numbers 29, in the middle of the seventh month—that is, on the fifteenth day—the notable feast of Tabernacles was held for eight days, Jerome’s translation alluded to that, as did Pellican’s likewise. For he says: “On the covering of the festal day.” Add that *CISSEH*, with the same Hebrew letters, also means “throne,” and thus can correspond to the Vulgate reading, “on the notable day,” since a throne is a symbol of a certain majesty. Moreover, what we read as “of your festival,” and the Hebrew as “of our festival,” comes to the same thing.

### Verse 6

> “His hands served in the basket.”

One might say that the Hebrew has the opposite sense, for the Vulgate reading denotes the forced labor of slavery. Jerome from the Hebrew, and the others likewise, by contrast indicate liberation from slavery in their renderings. Jerome does so in this way: “His hands withdrew from the basket.” Likewise Nebiensis. Sanctes: “His hands passed away from the bronze vessel”; Munster: “His hands passed away from making pots.” Here he added “making” on his own authority. But since *TAABORNAH*, that is, “they passed,” and *TAABODENAH*, are closely related because of *daleth* and *resh*, letters distinguished by a small stroke, and since the latter word means “they served,” it is likely that the Septuagint had it thus, reading it with *daleth*. Yet the sense is in no way impaired, since that clause seems explanatory of the immediately preceding statement: “His back turned aside from burdens.” If anyone goes further and seeks to know more particularly what burdens were lifted from the backs of the children of Israel, he will immediately perceive from the baskets that, under harsh servitude, they were compelled to carry stones, excavated earth, and things of that kind, as is plain from Exodus. Moreover, the fact that others render “basket” as “pot” or “cauldron” does not alter the meaning, although the Hebrew word *DUD* is common to both senses.

### Verse 11

> “According to the desires of their heart.”

Jerome, Nebiensis, Munster, and Campensis: “in the perversity of their heart”; Sanctes: “in strength”; Pellican: “in rash impulses”; the Paraphrase: “in a hardened mind.” Certainly *SCHERIRUTH* means hardness, obstinacy, perversity, rashness—affections of the heart, as no one doubts. Yet the learned followers of Cajetan come closer to the Septuagint, for they translate: “in the direction of their heart.” As though you said: Because they refused to be ruled and governed by God, they were left to themselves and to their own judgment. Perhaps they understood it as derived from the word *SARAR*, “to rule,” with the *smol* point, that is, the left-hand point. The Chaldee is not far from us: “I cast them out into the thoughts of their heart.”

### Verse 13

> “Perhaps I would have humbled their enemies for nothing.”

Faber finds fault with this passage because of the particle “perhaps,” which is a mark of uncertainty and cannot belong to God. Again, “for nothing,” that is, gratuitously or in vain, is far removed from God. Therefore, with Jerome, it should be said: “I would have humbled their enemies as though to nothing.” Some translate: “because in a short time [I would have humbled] their enemies,” etc., because the Hebrew has *KIMAT*. Now, as to the mark of uncertainty, “perhaps,” it is a peculiarity in divine mysteries, as in Ezekiel 2: “Thus says the Lord God: Perhaps they themselves will hear, and perhaps they will cease.” And in Luke 20: “Perhaps, when they see him, they will respect him.” God the Father speaks of the Son. Saint Jerome explains this manner of speaking in Matthew 21: “God is said to be uncertain in order that the free will of man may be preserved.”

As to the second phrase, “for nothing,” although we need not explain it as “gratuitously,” but as “unto nothing,” or, as the Paraphrase of Campensis has it, “with no difficulty I would have destroyed their enemies,” or, as another says, “I would reduce their enemies to a few,” nevertheless, if it is interpreted as “gratuitously,” the sense would not be that God does anything without cause, but that he frequently bestows many things from his abundant generosity without any preceding merit of ours. Saint Augustine interprets in this way the verse of Psalm 55: “For nothing you will save them”; that is, he says, “with no preceding merits of theirs.”

## Psalm 81

### Title of the Psalm

> “A Psalm of Asaph.”

**God stood in the synagogue.** Title: *A Psalm of Asaph.*  
[Note: From Cassiodorus on the title and in the exposition of the psalm.]

This psalm concerns the two natures in Christ. In it Christ, or the Prophet speaking, reproaches Asaph, that is, the Synagogue, which both saw the Lord bodily and yet did not acknowledge him. Hence he says here: “God stood in the synagogue.” Its sense is: Let this psalm belong to Asaph, that is, to the Synagogue, which is here rebuked, so that it may at least now understand what it did not understand before.

Its purpose is to urge belief that Christ is true God and true man. Its arrangement is in three parts. First, it announces that God stood there and reproves the opponents. Second, it urges them to understand that Christ is God, even if he is poor and needy: “Judge,” etc. Third, it says what was set before them, though they nevertheless perished: “I said.”

Thus, first announcing God, he says:

### Verse 1

> “God stood in the synagogue of gods; but in the midst he judges gods.”

**God stood.** [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] It does not belong to God to stand—he who fills heaven and earth, who is within all things without being enclosed, and outside all things without being excluded. Yet by this word he briefly indicates God made man. Therefore God, made man, stood in the synagogue of gods, that is, among the Jewish people, where the Son of God stood according to his humanity, he who was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. 15).

But the spiritual presence of the Godhead, which is everywhere, does not properly belong to the Synagogue, nor is it changed by time. He calls them “gods,” whom he later calls sons of the Most High: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.” Of them too the Lord says through Isaiah: “I have nourished and exalted sons, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1). Jews are often called sons, not only by the grace of the New Testament, but by that of the Old, namely, because he delivered them from Egypt and gave them the land of promise.

Therefore it was not the Father, nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son who stood bodily in the synagogue of the Jews. But why did he stand there? Behold: “He judges gods,” according to his Godhead. The man stands; God distinguishes—that is, not by merits but by grace he distinguishes vessels, some for honor and others for dishonor (2 Tim. 2; Rom. 9). He does this while standing in the midst. Hence in the Gospel of John: “One stands in your midst, whom you do not know” (John 1). And thus it is said here in what follows: “They have neither known nor understood.” But the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice (John 3).

### Verse 2

> “How long will you judge unjustly, and accept the persons of sinners?”

**How long will you judge?** [Augustine.] This is the voice of one who distinguishes. As though he said: I sent the Law and the Prophets, and you resisted or killed them; but how long will these things continue? Even until the coming of the Son? I indeed sent the Prophets, but you injured them, killed them, or consented to those doing so. Yet those who did these things are not even worthy to be spoken to; you are those who kept silent and wished to imitate them—that is, you who wished to imitate as innocent those who then kept silent.

“How long will you judge unjustly, and accept the persons of sinners?” Is the heir also to be killed, who came for you (Matt. 21), who for you chose to be without a father, as an orphan? (John 4.) Who for you hungered and thirsted, as one needy? (Matt. 4.) Who for you became poor, though he was rich? (2 Cor. 8.)

[Haymo, Gloss.] Or distinguish between those who judge and those who accept the persons of sinners. By the judges are meant the greater persons, who judge unjustly; those accepting persons—that is, adopting the likenesses of sinners—are the lesser persons, who consent.

## Part II. *Diapsalma*

### Verse 3

> “Judge for the needy and the orphan; vindicate the humble and the poor.”

**Judge.** [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The second part, in which he urges them to understand that Christ is God even if he is poor and needy; and he says that they did not do this. As though he said: Do not judge unjustly or consent to those judging, but rather, “judge”—this is said to the greater persons—“for the needy and the orphan,” that is, for the honor of him who chose to be without a father for you. And “vindicate,” that is, proclaim as just Christ, made humble and poor for you, rather than proclaiming just those who are proud for themselves, together with you who are lesser persons.

### Verse 4

> “Rescue the poor and needy; deliver him from the hand of the sinner.”

**Rescue the poor and needy; deliver him from the hand of the sinner.** [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] This is said to the lesser persons. By this he shows that those who allowed the rulers to act against Christ were not free from so great a crime: although the rulers were feared because of the multitude, the multitude could have restrained them from the deed and themselves from consent. For whoever ceases to oppose when able, consents; but:

### Verse 5

> “They have not known nor understood; they walk in darkness; all the foundations of the earth shall be shaken.”

**They have not known.** [Augustine, Haymo, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] This applies to all, both prelates and subjects. For if they had known, neither would the former have crucified the Lord, nor would the latter have chosen Barabbas (1 Cor. 2). “Nor understood,” that is, they did not even take care to know, because they walk in darkness. They were stirred up; but through this blindness of Israel, all the foundations of the earth will be moved to faith—that is, the fullness of the Gentiles will enter into faith.

Or thus: They did not know; nevertheless, in Christ’s Passion all the foundations of the earth will be shaken, because at the Lord’s death the earth was shaken and the rocks were split (Matt. 27). Here it is clear of whom he had spoken before: this sign occurred at Christ’s crucifixion. Or, “the foundations of the earth” means those who are earthly were spiritually moved, at that time, upon seeing so great a miracle—such as the centurion who said, “Truly this was the Son of God” (ibid.).

Or, the foundations of the earth are those happy in an abundance of earthly goods, upon whom earthly people build as good people build upon the apostles, who are called the foundations of heaven. They will be moved, either by marveling that a poor dead man is worshiped, or by following him after despising earthly things. He adds “all,” because there is no one who does not marvel or convert. But pride is the kingdom of earthly happiness. Against it came Christ in humility, rebuking those whom he wishes to make high through humility, in these words:

## Part III

### Verse 6

> “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.”

**I said.** [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Remigius.] The third part, in which he says what was set before them, though they perished. As though he said: “They have not known nor understood”; nevertheless, I said: You good people are gods by the adoption of grace, and sons of the Most High, that is, heirs of God—all, that is, of every condition.

[Haymo, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] For all who keep the commandments receive these promises: namely, that they may be sons of God. This is said of the righteous, who are predestined to life.

### Verse 7

> “But you shall die like men, and you shall fall like one of the princes.”

**But you wicked people shall die like men.** [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine.] That is, like sinners who have not been redeemed. For this is said to the unrighteous. And you shall fall, not be lifted up to heaven, like one of the princes—that is, through pride of mind you shall fall like the devil, and like the host of demons that fell. He is called “one,” because alike in pride.

Or thus: You wicked people shall die through the weakness of the flesh, like men, and you shall fall through pride, like one of the princes—that is, like the devil. As though he said: Though you are soon to die like men, you still do not amend; but, like the devil, who does not die in the flesh, you exalt yourselves in order to fall, because through diabolical pride they envied Christ’s glory, and the humility of the cross was contemptible to them.

Or he says generally to all: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High,” that is, he promised heavenly things to all. [Jerome, Haymo, Augustine.] Then he speaks to the wicked, distinguishing between greater and lesser persons. First he says to the lesser: “But you shall die like men”—the first human beings, namely Adam and Eve, who sinned through the devil’s persuasion. And you greater persons “shall fall, like one of the princes,” that is, like the devil, who sinned through pride. Therefore, that this vice might be healed, the following is added in the person of the Prophet:

### Verse 8

> “Arise, O God, judge the earth, because you shall inherit among all nations.”

**Arise.** [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine.] As though he said: You shall fall; but you, O God, arise from the dead, and judge—that is, condemn—the earth which swelled with pride in crucifying you; that is, condemn these people. For, when they have been rejected, you shall inherit among all nations—that is, all nations shall be your inheritance.

Or, “judge the earth,” that is, the world, which you can do because it is yours. And this is the meaning of “because you shall inherit among all nations.”

Or according to another reading: [Augustine.] “Because you shall destroy among all nations.” What will you destroy among the nations? The earth itself, that is, those who savor earthly things—either by crushing them utterly and excluding them from the inheritance, or by consuming in them the affection of earthly desire and pride. This is understood in a good sense, according to which meaning it is also said: “You shall inherit among all nations.”

## Collation on Psalm 81: “God Stood,” etc.

### Verse 1

**God stood in the synagogue of gods.** In this passage Faber dared to affirm that the Septuagint translators had corrupted the letter of the text; and, exaggerating the point, he treats them impiously, writing that they were deceived and fell foully. He is slightly moved to this opinion by the fact that *EL* is singular, where we read the plural “of gods,” while Jerome translates: “God stood in the assembly of God.”

Why then was not the beginning of the psalm likewise translated in the plural, “gods stood,” since the Hebrew has *ELOHIM*, a plural form? Therefore, whether you express “assembly of God” or “of gods” in the singular or plural, those gathered are saints belonging to God, or princes who possess authority from God. But here, since the collective noun “synagogue” was immediately placed before it, why are the Septuagint translators summoned to account for understanding a multitude in a singular form? Hence many who are thoroughly skilled in Hebrew do not hesitate to translate it with a plural number.

Thus Sanctes says: “in the congregation of judges,” which Munster renders “a magnificent congregation.” The edition connected with Campensis reads: “in the assembly of the mighty.” The Paraphrase agrees, in its own way. The Chaldee paraphrast says: “God placed his divinity in the congregation of the righteous, who are mighty in the Law.” Nor does it object that Jerome translated it in the singular. For he translated it so as to approve such a rendering in its proper place. In his commentaries, when he repeated the verse, he added this interpretation: “Because they were gods, God therefore stood among them.” And a little later: “See the dignity of man: God stood in the synagogue of gods. He grants us the name in order that he may grant us merit also.” There can be no doubt how broadly and learnedly Saint Augustine develops the matter by means of the plural number.

## Psalm 82

### Title of the Psalm

> “A Canticle of Asaph.”

**O God, who is like you?** Title: *A Canticle of Asaph.* [Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] This psalm concerns Christ’s second coming for judgment, when the good who suffer here will be crowned, while the wicked who persecute them will be tormented. By this it deters the wicked from persecuting God’s people, whom the wicked afflict in many ways at present, especially in the time of Antichrist.

[Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The sense of the title is this: This canticle is called a canticle because it exhorts to good actions. It fittingly joins both, because divine contemplation must be present in active affairs. It belongs to Asaph, that is, to the people of God, who speak here. And since Asaph properly refers to the Jews, the prophecy is understood to be directed especially against the Jews.

Its purpose is to dissuade the wicked from persecuting the good, and to urge the good to patience. The psalm is in two parts. First, setting forth the fear of the future Judge, it describes the malice of enemies or wicked persons. Second, it treats of the vengeance upon enemies or wicked persons: “Do to them as to Midian.”

Thus faithful Asaph, foreseeing Christ judging in majesty, who was judged in humility, says:

### Verse 1

> “O God, who shall be like you? Do not be silent, nor be restrained, O God.”

**O God, Christ,** [Augustine,] even though you are a man like others, even though, being judged, you were counted among wicked thieves: who shall be like you in the form of a servant? I do not speak of the form of God, when you will judge in glory. This is not referred to the divinity, to which no one thought a human being comparable. And so it would not be a great thing if it were referred to the divinity. Rather, it is said to him who, taking the form of a servant, was made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man. Therefore he does not say, “Who is like you?” which surely would be said if it referred to the divinity; but he says, “Who shall be like you?” referring this to the form of a servant, which then will be unlike other human beings when the Judge appears in glory.

[Alcuin.] Or this may be referred to the divinity, according to the words: “O God, who shall be like you in the power of your divinity?” For Christ, whom the wicked saw outwardly, this man sees inwardly: namely, as almighty. “Do not be silent.” [Augustine.] As though he said: Because you will be such in the future, therefore then do not be silent in punishing, O God, who first kept silent, when, like a lamb before its shearer, you were without voice and did not open your mouth (Isa. 53). “Nor be restrained,” O God—or softened—from what you have begun, you who first restrained your power so that you could be seized and put to death, though you had earlier shown it when those seeking to apprehend you fell backward at your word (John 18). For how could you have been seized and suffered unless you had restrained and checked yourself, and in some way made yourself gentle?

### Verse 2

> “For behold, your enemies have made a noise, and those who hate you have lifted up their head.”

**For behold.** [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin.] To the two things previously said he gives two corresponding reasons, treating of the persecution that will occur in the time of Antichrist. As though he said: Therefore, do not be silent, because behold, your enemies—that is, the members of Antichrist—have made a noise by contradicting you. He indicates the last times of Antichrist, when things now repressed by fear will burst forth into free speech. Since this voice will be irrational, it is called noise rather than speech.

“And those who hate you.” As though he said: Therefore do not restrain yourself; and that is because those who have long hated you, not newly, “have lifted up their head”—that is, they will then lift up their head, not heads. But it is that head which “is exalted above everything called or worshiped as God” (2 Thess. 2), namely Antichrist. Those who hate are many; but their head is one, namely Antichrist, raised so high that he is called God. They have lifted up their head, but they have not crushed your people. Therefore he adds:

### Verse 3

> “They have devised malicious counsel against your people, and have plotted against your saints.”

**They have maliciously devised against your people,** [Augustine, Cassiodorus,] or, as some manuscripts have it, “they have craftily devised counsel” in order to deceive against your people. He says this mockingly. For they cannot harm God’s people, for whom God is present. Hence the Apostle: “If God is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. 8). “And they have plotted against your saints”: not merely against mediocre persons, but even against heavenly men.

### Verse 4

> “They said: Come, let us destroy them from being a nation, and let the name of Israel be remembered no more.”

**They said.** [Cassiodorus, Gloss, Cassiodorus.] Behold the counsel by which they meditated vain things. This is that noise which is not speech but makes an empty clamor. They also said, “Come,” seeking associates for themselves in this; “and let us destroy them from being a nation.” He says “nation” in the singular because all Christians are one nation, having been born from the one fountain of baptism.

Or he says “from being a nation” in the singular, signifying by “nations” all good persons, whom Antichrist calls one nation because of their one will. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Or according to another reading: “Let us destroy them from among the nations,” namely, so that they may not be among the nations—that is, let us remove them from the world. Behold the persecution of Antichrist, which intends utterly to abolish the Christian name as though it were evil. “And let the name of true Israel be remembered no more,” that is, the name of those who ought truly to be Israel.

### Verse 5

> “For they have plotted with one accord; together they have made a covenant against you: the tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites.”

**For they have plotted.** [Gloss, Augustine, Alcuin.] He explains who the malicious plotters are, or with what intention they acted maliciously; first, with what intention, saying: “For they have plotted with one accord,” that is, diligently; “together,” that is, all of them; and, as though they could be stronger than you, “they have made against you a covenant,” so that you might move against them. That is, a pact, an agreement among themselves. For in Scripture a testament is not called only that which is valid only after the testator’s death; every agreement and compact valid among the living is also called a testament. Thus Laban and Jacob made a testament that was valid among the living. So the wicked made, as it were, a pact among themselves that they would unanimously persecute the good.

Behold, he has explained with what intention they acted maliciously. Then he shows who these malicious persons are, saying: “The tents of the Edomites.” [Augustine, Alcuin, Jerome.] Here he begins to recount Christ’s enemies under certain names of nations which suit them mystically. For by such names, according to their interpretations, the enemies of truth are most fittingly represented. By these names he indicates Christ’s enemies, who in the time of Antichrist will be like these peoples in so many evils; for as these fought against Israel, so those will then wage war against Christians.

And the sense is: Those who plotted and made a covenant are, behold, the tents—that is, the assemblies—of the Edomites. The Edomites were named from Edom (Gen. 25), who is also Esau and was called Seir (Josh. 24; Gen. 36). Edomites are interpreted “earthly” or “bloody,” because they love earthly things and thirst for blood; and the Ishmaelites, who are named from Ishmael, son of Abraham and Hagar (Gen. 16), and are interpreted “obedient to themselves”—that is, not to God—because they follow their own evil thoughts.

### Verse 6

> “Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek; the foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre.”

**Moab.** [Augustine, Jerome, Augustine, Gloss, Alcuin.] The Moabites are named from Moab, whom Lot, while drunk, begot by his elder daughter (Gen. 19). Moab is interpreted “from the father,” which is understood in a bad sense. The father indeed was good, but the daughter used him unlawfully; just as the Law is good if one uses it lawfully, not incestuously. By Moab, therefore, are signified lawless nations which, departing from God the Father, are from their father the devil (John 8).

“And the Hagarenes,” who are named from Hagar (Gen. 16), and are interpreted “proselytes,” that is, newcomers or strangers. By them are signified false brethren, who are in the Church only in name (Gal. 2): they are not citizens, but enter stealthily with an alien mind to spy out the Church’s liberty, and, when they find an opportunity to harm, reveal themselves.

**Gebal.** Gebal is interpreted “vain valley.” For *ge* [γη] means “valley,” and *bal*, “vain.” By it are signified deceptively humble persons, that is, hypocrites.

**And Ammon.** Ammon (Gen. 19), from whom the Ammonites are named, was begotten by Lot, while drunk, from his younger daughter. It is interpreted “a troubled people” or “a people of sorrow,” and by it are signified madmen.

**And Amalek** (Gen. 36). Amalek was the son of Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn, from whom the Amalekites are named. The children of Israel fought against them and overcame them when Moses raised his hands (Exod. 17). [Jerome, Augustine, Haymo, Augustine.] Amalek is interpreted “a people licking the earth,” by whom are signified the covetous and avaricious, lovers of earthly things.

**Foreigners.** This is a Latin name, for which the Hebrew has *Philisthiim*. Thus, although by their Latin name they designate themselves strangers, and thereby enemies, in Hebrew they are called *Philisthiim*, that is, “falling through drink.” By them are signified those drunk with worldly luxury.

And all these made a covenant with the inhabitants of Tyre, that is, with those possessing earthly things, around which they are distressed. For Tyre in Hebrew is called *sor*, and is interpreted “tribulation” or “distress.” This suits the enemies of God’s people, according to the Apostle’s words: “Tribulation and distress upon every soul of man that does evil” (Rom. 2). Then, as though indicating why they are enemies of God’s people, he adds:

### Verse 7

> “For Assur came with them; they became a help to the children of Lot.”

**For.** [Jerome, Alcuin, Augustine.] As though he said: Why are these enemies of God’s people? For—that is, because—Assur came with them. Assur, literally Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians, is interpreted “oppressing” or “exalted.” By him the devil is signified, who works in the wicked, of whom he is prince, and whom he presses down into the depth of sin.

[Augustine.] All these, through the working within them of the prince, the devil, became a help to the children of Lot—that is, they assist the invisible enemies who attack God’s people through these persons. For Lot is interpreted “turning aside.” [Jerome, Augustine.] Therefore the children of Lot are apostate angels, children of defection, because by turning away from truth they departed into the devil’s retinue. Hence it is said in the Apocalypse: “The dragon fell and drew with him a third part of the stars” (Rev. 12). Of them the Apostle says: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers” (Eph. 6).

## Part II

### Verse 8

> “Do to them as to Midian and Sisera, as to Jabin at the torrent of Kishon.”

**Do to them.** [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Haymo, Augustine.] The second part, in which he treats of the vengeance upon the wicked; and it is a prophecy. For he predicts evils to come upon them under the figure of certain names. As though he said: They act thus against your people. Or: You, Lord, do to them—he predicts, not curses—as you did to Midian and Sisera, and as to Jabin at the torrent of Kishon.

All these, literally, the people of God, namely Israel, defeated and conquered. Midian was the son of Abraham and Keturah (Gen. 25). From him came the Midianites, who afflicted the children of Israel many times, but whom they finally defeated when they cried to the Lord.

For in the book of Judges, chapters 4 and 6, it is read that when Jabin king of Canaan afflicted the children of Israel, they cried to the Lord. Then Deborah the prophetess, who judged Israel at that time, commanded Barak son of Abinoam to take with him ten thousand warriors and go against Sisera, commander of Jabin’s army. He said that he would go if she went with him. So she went with him. But the Lord threw into terror the army of Jabin, which Sisera had gathered at the torrent of Kishon; and Sisera fled to the tents of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite. For there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite.

When Sisera, concealed there, had fallen asleep, Jael took a tent peg and, striking it with a hammer, drove it through Sisera’s brain into the ground; and thus he died. And behold, Barak came pursuing Sisera; Jael went out to meet him and said: “Come, and I will show you the man you seek.” When he entered with her, he saw Sisera lying dead, with the peg driven into his temples.

Thus God humbled Jabin king of Canaan on that day before the children of Israel. They grew stronger daily and oppressed Jabin king of Canaan with a strong hand until they destroyed him. Gideon also defeated the Midianites by night with three hundred men. When they fled, the men of Ephraim met them and captured Oreb and Zeeb, princes of the Midianites, whom they killed; and they brought their heads to Gideon. Gideon himself later killed Zebah and Zalmunna, princes of Midian, when their army, after a long flight, rested in security. Therefore he says: “Do to them as to Midian and Sisera, and as to Jabin at the torrent of Kishon.”

### Verse 9

> “They perished at Endor; they became like dung upon the earth.”

**They perished, literally.** [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] All these perished at the torrent of Kishon and at the spring of Endor. Therefore, as all those were figuratively conquered by God’s people, so he prays that these be overcome in reality: “They became like dung upon the earth,” while their corpses decayed. Do this to all of them in common, but especially:

### Verse 10

> “Make their princes like Oreb and Zeeb, and Zebah and Zalmunna.”

**Make their princes.** [Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine, Haymo.] This he desires for the soldiers of Antichrist, who will not be converted. Or these things may be said according to the interpretations of the names. Midian means “turning aside judgment”; Sisera, “exclusion of joy”; Jabin, “wise.” Of him the Apostle says: “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe?” (1 Cor. 1.) Kishon, where they were defeated, means “hardness.”

The sense is: Do to them as to Midian and Sisera, etc.—namely, as to persons who turn aside judgment and do not think that they themselves will be judged; who exclude future joy; who are puffed up with the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God; and whom hardness of an obstinate mind draws into destruction.

**They perished at Endor.** [Augustine, Haymo.] Endor, where they perished, means “spring of generation,” but carnal generation is meant. Devoted to this, they perished unregenerate. “They became like dung upon the earth,” because nothing proceeds from them except earthly fertility.

“Make their princes like Oreb and Zeeb, and Zebah and Zalmunna.” Oreb means “dryness”; Zeeb, “wolf”; Zebah, “a sacrifice”—that is, a sacrifice to the wolf, not to God; Zalmunna, “shadow of disturbance.” All these things befall the wicked, whom God’s people conquered in a good cause. The sense is: Make their princes like Oreb, as persons dry of God’s grace; and Zeeb, that is, ravenous; and Zebah, as persons already a sacrifice of the wolf, that is, the devil; and Zalmunna, that is, unstable, yielding to every evil suggestion.

### Verse 11

> “All their princes who said: Let us possess God’s sanctuary as an inheritance.”

**All their princes,** [Cassiodorus, Augustine,] that is, the authors of their counsels, make them as I have said. “Who said.” Behold the empty noise with which your enemies made a noise. What did they say? “Let us possess God’s sanctuary.” Of this the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3). These are the saints: let them be an inheritance, so that they may become subject to us. They invade God’s inheritance to make it their own. They said this, but:

### Verse 12

> “My God, make them like a wheel, and like stubble before the face of the wind.”

**My God, make them like a wheel,** [Augustine, Gloss,] that is, let them not be stable in what they devise. Or as a wheel rises from what is behind and falls forward, so they too are lifted up from what is behind—that is, from earthly things in which they increase; this indeed is true. And in mind let them fall away from what lies before, that is, from eternal things. “And make them like stubble before the face of the wind,” that is, before the presence of temptation, so that they yield to every movement of evil suggestion.

[Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Wind is used for temptation, by which light and empty hearts are punished; and the lightness of sinners is fittingly compared to wind, which flits here and there. By these comparisons he predicts many calamities for them, and grievous torment for the fickleness of sinners. Hence he adds:

### Verse 13

> “As fire which burns the forest, and as a flame burning the mountains.”

### Verse 14

> “So shall you pursue them in your tempest, and in your wrath you shall trouble them.”

**As fire.** [Haymo, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As though he said: In the present they will feel these evils, but in the future you will thus pursue them in your tempest, that is, in a judgment which will be sudden and grievous; and in your wrath, that is, in the justice of final vengeance, you will trouble them, as fire that burns the forest.

[Augustine, Cassiodorus.] He calls the wicked a forest because they are barren of righteousness; and he calls these same persons mountains because they are full of pride, “as a flame burning the mountains.” God, who punishes, is a flaming fire. Fire and flame are fittingly said to be at the judgment, because then the dense forests of sins and the mountains of pride will be burned.

### Verse 15

> “Fill their faces with shame, and they shall seek your name, O Lord.”

**Fill their faces,** [Cassiodorus, Augustine,] with the foretold punishments of the stubborn. He prays for those who will believe, who do not have flatterers of their crimes but reprovers; shame often corrects such people. This good and desirable thing is foretold for them. Nor would it be foretold for them unless, in that society of the enemies of God’s people, there were also such persons to whom this would be granted before the final judgment. For even now the same body of enemies exists, according to the envy by which they begrudge God’s people; even now the same body makes a noise and raises its head, though partially and not universally as it will at the end. Yet some of them are converted, and for them he prays here.

He says “their” because they are still one body with the wicked. And this is the meaning: “Fill their faces with shame,” [Gloss, Alcuin,] that is, make them appear shameful to themselves and to others. “And thus they shall seek your name, O Lord.” Note that it is better to fall in order to repent than to be proud under the appearance of religion. Hence the prophet says: “And you, daughter of Zion, shall come as far as Babylon; there you shall be delivered” (Mic. 4).

### Verse 16

> “Let them blush and be troubled for ever and ever; let them be confounded and perish.”

Erubescant. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] Here he deals with the wicked who will not be converted. As though he said: I say, “Let them seek your name.” But if they do not do so, let them be ashamed in the future for the evils they have done, and let them be troubled by the punishments which they will suffer. And this “for ever and ever,” that is, eternally. But those who seek the Lord’s name, even if they are now ashamed and troubled because of their sins, will nevertheless not be confounded eternally. [Col. 0786C] Again he returns to those who are confounded in the present, lest they be confounded eternally. As though he said: Let those people be troubled eternally. But let those who seek the Lord’s name now be beneficially confounded because of their sins, and perish insofar as they are evil, so that they may become good.

VERSE 17.—“And let them know that your name is Lord; you alone are the Most High over all the earth.”

And thus let them know that the essential name “Lord” belongs to you; [Augustine, Alcuin] for whatever others are called lords are called so neither truly nor in their own right, since they exercise lordship as slaves; and, compared with the true Lord, they are not lords at all. And let them know that you alone are the Most High throughout all the earth, or above all the earth. Or this may be understood of the wicked: “and let them be confounded.” As though he said: Let the wicked be troubled eternally, and then let those wicked persons be confounded [Col. 0786D] in soul and body, and perish altogether beyond repair; and then let them know what they now refuse to know—namely, that the name “Lord” belongs to you and is unchangeable, and that you alone are the Most High throughout, or above, all the earth.

[Augustine, Cassiodorus.] He is indeed Most High also in heaven and above every heaven. But he chose this expression in order that human pride might be humbled. For the earth—that is, man, to whom it was said, “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. III)—ceases to be proud when he knows that God is high above all the earth; that is, when he knows that no one can prevail against those of whom it is said: “If God is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. VIII).

It should be noted that Asaph has been introduced in the preceding eleven psalms, so that the hardness of the Jews might be softened by the repeated voice of the Synagogue itself, or that they might believe in the very name to which they seemed devoted. In the psalms mentioned above he dealt with the Lord’s incarnation, the faith of the Gentiles, and judgment—matters in which the Jews’ manifold transgression is reproved. Thus it is fittingly said that there are eleven.

[Note: Col. 0787D. Augustine, Sermon 15, On the Words of the Lord.] For the number eleven is the number of transgression, because it exceeds ten yet does not reach twelve. Hence there were eleven goat-hair curtains in the tabernacle of the Lord; and the apostles numbered eleven after the most unhappy Judas had been rejected at the time of the Passion, when they fell away from faith. Hence: “You made darkness, and night came to be” (Ps. CIII).

## Comparison on Psalm LXXXII: “God, who is like you?” etc.

VERSE 1.—“Who is like you?”

Jerome: “Do not be silent within yourself,” and nearly all the others likewise. Münster rendered it, “Do not restrain yourself,” yet in his scholium writes that its proper sense is “Do not be silent within yourself.” Pellican differs somewhat: “My silence is not toward you,” which he explains as: “I do not conceal my anguish.” Hebrew: **AL DOMI**. But according to the word itself, they derive it from the verb **DAMAH**, “he was made like” or “he was silent”; then **AL**, “do not,” “nor,” or “not,” so that the sense is, “There is none like you.” The translators expressed this emphatically in interrogative form.

VERSE 3.—“Against your saints.”

Jerome: “Against your secret.” The others: “Against your hidden ones,” or “those who are privy to your secrets.” **TZEPHUNECA**. The Septuagint correctly expressed the sense, as may also be inferred from Münster’s scholium on this passage: “That is,” he says, “those who are protected by you in secret.” Campensis responds: “Those entrusted secretly to your protection are undoubtedly the saints, who alone strive to please God in secret.”

# PSALM LXXXIII

[Col. 0787]

## Title of the Psalm: “To the end; for the winepresses; for the sons of Korah; a psalm.”

[Col. 0787B]

“How beloved are your tabernacles.” Title: “To the end; for the winepresses; for the sons of Korah; a psalm.” [Augustine.] Nothing in this psalm is said about visible winepresses. It is therefore clear that the winepresses are something else—spiritual winepresses—which the Spirit of God intended us to understand here. Accordingly, let us recall what takes place in these winepresses, and see how this happens spiritually in the Church.

A grape hanging on the vine and an olive on the tree enjoy the open air; before the pressure of the winepress, the former is not wine and the latter is not oil. So those whom God foreknew before the ages to be made conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. VIII), before they enter the service of God, enjoy a pleasant freedom in the world. [Col. 0787C] But when they enter God’s service, it is said to them: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. II). Behold the winepress. For they are crushed by the pressure of sufferings; they are stripped of the coverings of carnal desires, as though into grape-skins; they put off the old man (Col. III), and thus flow into God’s storehouse.

Since these things occur in the churches, the churches of the present time are called winepresses. But who are in these winepresses? The sons of Korah—that is, the sons of the Bald One, namely Christ. For bald Elisha, mocked by children crying, “Go up, bald one; go up, bald one” (IV Kings II), was a figure of Christ, who was crucified at Calvary (John XIX). The Christian is pressed here in order that he may seek the rest which is not here, [Col. 0787D] and that God may be his refuge. For the person who leans upon earthly things, trusting in the uncertainty of riches (I Tim. VI), leans upon a reed-staff, which breaks easily and causes the one leaning upon it to fall. Therefore do not entrust yourself to it: it is fragile, it breaks, and it destroys you.

The sense of the title is this: this psalm, directing us to the end—that is, to Christ—is set before the sons of Korah, that is, the sons of Christ crucified on Calvary. I say, a psalm “for the winepresses,” that is, dealing with the churches, in which are the pressures of tribulations aptly called winepresses, because just as the fruit of the grape or olive flows out in the winepress, [Col. 0788B] so in the pressures endured by the churches the merits of the saints become manifest, though they had lain hidden in peace. Therefore, although the Church is afflicted, let the son of Korah not grow cold.

This is the second psalm concerning the love of God.

Purpose: It exhorts to the love of eternal things.

Method: It has three parts. First, it treats of the inestimable longing for the eternal home. Second, it states by what help one comes to God’s house: “Blessed is the man.” Third, it prays and humbles itself in order to obtain it: “O Lord, God of hosts.”

Therefore this man, sighing from the winepresses toward the eternal tabernacles, says with wonder:

VERSE 1.—“How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs for and fails away toward the courts of the Lord.”

“O Lord of hosts.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] This man senses God’s power, which will appear in wrath in the future. Therefore, when he says, “O Lord of hosts, how beloved are your tabernacles,” it is as though their loveliness cannot be expressed in words. He speaks of the eternal tabernacles, where there is no pressure.

And they are truly beloved, because my soul longs for and fails away from itself—that is, from its own condition—while tending toward the eternal courts of the Lord. The soul fails as it tends toward the courts of the Lord, like a pressed grape failing away into wine. Thus this man, stretching toward the rest of the heavenly storehouse, languishes with longing and love.

This seems to him great sadness when he says, “My soul longs for and fails,” because it does not possess what it desires. But is it without joy? By no means: there is also joy in hope, and therefore it endures the pressure of the winepress.

VERSE 2.—“My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.”

“My heart.” [Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine, Haymo, Augustine.] That is, my reason, and my subdued flesh, have rejoiced—even though they are burdened—in the living God, who gives life; that is, they have rejoiced from this present state toward that eternal one. Whence have they rejoiced? Behold:

[Col. 0789A] VERSE 3.—“For even the sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest in which to place her young.”

“For even.” [Augustine.] That is, because the sparrow—that is, reason—has found itself, while seeking, a house not made by hands. It now exercises its wings in the virtues of this time—faith, hope, and charity—so that the sparrow may fly into the house in which it will remain.

Note that to the two things mentioned above he gives two corresponding images. He had said that his heart and flesh rejoiced; to these he corresponds the sparrow and the turtledove. For the heart is like a sparrow, and the flesh like a turtledove, to which he also assigns young. With the heart we think upon God, as the sparrow flies toward the Lord; with the flesh we perform works. And the turtledove—that is, chaste flesh—finds itself a nest in which to place its young, that is, its works. What nest does it find?

[Col. 0789B] VERSE 4.—“Your altars, O Lord of hosts, my King and my God.”

“Your altars, O Lord of hosts,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Haymo] that is, the heavenly homeland, where souls feast at the heavenly banquet; there the soul rejoices as in a house, and the flesh places its works. “My King,” because you rule; “and my God,” because you created.

Or it may otherwise be read concerning the present Church. Thus the tabernacles are blessed, which properly belong to those engaged in warfare. The meaning is: “How beloved are your tabernacles!” He says this of the service of the present Church, which is a pilgrim upon earth. “O Lord of hosts,” meaning heavenly hosts, namely angels. He says this to indicate that here God sends angelic powers to help.

They are truly beloved, because my soul longs for and fails away from itself while tending toward the courts of the Lord—the courts of the present Church. Behold, in this verse he shows how great that service is, that is, how lovable and loving. It truly longs, [Col. 0789C] because my heart—namely, reason—and my subdued flesh have rejoiced in the living God, because he gives life; for this reason they rejoice.

“For even,” that is, because the sparrow has found itself a house in the heavenly Church. The comparison is fitting. Just as a sparrow leaves the woods and, having found a house, rejoices where it does not fear snares, so the soul rejoices when it knows that a dwelling has been prepared for it in heaven.

And the turtledove—that is, the flesh—finds itself a nest, which exists only for a time, whereas the house is eternal. By the nest he means faith and conformity to the Church’s sacraments, a nest which the turtledove seeks, “in which to place her young.” For it does not cast them out anywhere at random; rather, it performs good works in the nest of the Church, works through which it will be saved. In this it differs from others who perform works, but not in the nest of faith. For pagans too perform works, because they clothe the naked and do other such things. Heretics also do many things, but not in the nest of the Church—that is, not in faith and participation in the sacraments—and therefore they are trampled down; their works are not preserved for life.

This flesh is the woman by whom the sparrow—that is, the man—is seduced. Thus the Apostle says: “Adam was not deceived,” that is, not first; “but the woman was deceived” (I Tim. II). Adam afterward consents to the woman. So too now no evil persuasion can gain power over you unless first the desire of your flesh has been stirred; and afterward, if you consent in mind, the sparrow too has fallen. But if the desires of the flesh are overcome, the weapons of concupiscence are removed, [Col. 0790A] and the turtledove begins to have her young.

Hence the same Apostle adds: “But the woman shall be saved through childbearing” (ibid.), that is, the flesh through the production of good works—provided, however, that it performs them in the nest, that is, if it remains in the Catholic faith, in the fellowship of ecclesiastical unity. God supplies the means by which the nest may be made. For he clothed himself in the hay of flesh in order to come to you. Therefore place the young of your works in this faith.

[Haymo, Augustine, Haymo, Augustine.] In this verse he shows how secure that service is. Then, as though you had asked what nest it has found, he adds: “Your altars,” that is, the Church’s sacraments; “God of hosts”; “my King,” because you rule; “and my God,” because you created.

But this nest is in pilgrimage, under pressure, amid sighs. There, the man who has been placed in it already meditates upon future joys and sighs after the promises from above, saying:

[Col. 0790B] VERSE 5.—“Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ages of ages they shall praise you.”

“Blessed are those who dwell in your heavenly house, O Lord,” [Augustine] where there is no fear. The good already possess this: that they dwell in your house. “For ages of ages they shall praise you.” This is what they do for you; this is the entire occupation of the saints there. There is no necessity there, which is the mother of all human actions. What would they do there, where no one lacks anything? Thus they possess and do that by which they are blessed. Everyone who is blessed is called blessed either through possessing or through doing.

[Alcuin.] In this verse he shows to what blessedness this service leads.

[Col. 0790C] PART II. VERSE 6.—“Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, in the place which he has appointed.”

“Blessed is the man.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The second part, where he states by what help and with whose aid one comes to the house. As though he said: Blessed are those who dwell in your house; but how shall we come to the house, when the body weighs down one who would fly? By your help. And blessed is that man, and so forth.

Or the connection may be read thus: Those who dwell there will be blessed in the future. And blessed even now is the man whose help is from you against the labors of this age. What good does this do him? Much, because he has arranged ascents—that is, steps by which he may ascend—because he always makes progress, in his heart. Therefore, the more you love, the more you ascend.

Where has he arranged them? [Col. 0790D] “In the valley of tears,” or of weeping. The valley of tears is the humility of the penitent. Behold the winepress. He has said what he arranged, namely ascents; where, namely in the heart; and in what region, namely in the valley of weeping. So that he may ascend where? Behold: “to the place,” or “in the place,” which God has appointed or arranged. This is the place which cannot be expounded, which eye has not seen nor ear heard (I Cor. IX): the future kingdom, which God has arranged and ordained, so that one may reach it by steps.

Or the valley of tears is the lowliness of this world, where one must weep and not laugh. The sense is: Where did he arrange them? In the valley of tears, or weeping, [Jerome, Alcuin, Augustine] that is, in this lowliness of the world. For here there is weeping where there is sowing. He explains what he had said: “in the place which God has appointed” for human beings, that there they might weep for their sins. Man himself appointed that place for himself when he sinned.

Whence comes this weeping? Because God afflicted us by the law, through which we learned that sin resists the spirit; for when the commandment came, sin revived (Rom. VII). Therefore we groan, shut up under sin. How then shall we come to the place which he has appointed? By his aid. And will he help? Certainly.

[Col. 0791A] VERSE 7.—“For the lawgiver will give blessing; they shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion.”

“For.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] That is, because the giver of the old law—which held the multitude of sick persons in the five porticoes of the five books of Moses, [Col. 0791B] yet did not heal them—will give the blessing of evangelical grace (John V), because after the law of death grace that justifies will come. Behold, Christ is author of both Testaments.

And what does the blessing of grace grant? Behold: through it the faithful shall go from strength to strength, until the God of gods is seen in Zion. For through grace many powers are given; through all of these one comes to Christ, the power of God and wisdom of God (I Cor. I), so that, when those powers have ended in accordance with these acts, Christ may be seen in Zion—that is, in the fullness of contemplation—as God with God, the Word with the Father (John I), who is the God of gods, that is, of Christians.

But in thinking on these joys, he returns to sighing, seeing [Col. 0791C] where he still is. And he says:

PART III. VERSE 8.—“O Lord, God of hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob.”
