“O Lord, God of hosts.” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Gloss, Augustine.] The third part, where he prays and humbles himself in order to obtain the gift. As though he said: God will be seen in Zion, and in order that I may see him, O Lord God, giver of those powers by which one ascends to see you—or God of the heavenly hosts, namely the angels, with whom I desire to be joined—hear my prayer, that you may join me to them. Give ear to my prayer, O God of Jacob, that you may help me in the struggle, as you helped Jacob, whom you made Israel when you appeared to him, whence he was called Israel (Gen. XXXII). Do the same for me, and make me Israel. And, O—

[Col. 0791D] VERSE 9.—“Look upon us, O God our protector, and look upon the face of your Christ.”

God the Father, our protector, [Haymo, Jerome, Augustine] the shadow of your wings, look upon us—that is, protect the human race. Or this is said through Christ himself: “Look upon the face of your Christ.” As though he said: If not for our sake, at least because we are conformed to the image of your Son, look upon us. For he himself speaks in us. Hence the Apostle says: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (II Cor. XIII); and he is received in you, as he himself says: “He who receives you receives me” (Matt. X).

Or thus: by the face we become known to others. Therefore, “Look upon the face of your Christ,” that is, make Christ known to all, so that we may go from strength to strength. For the Father always looks upon Christ; that is not what is prayed for here. The sense is: cause Christ to be regarded by the Gentiles through the presence of the Incarnation. Therefore I pray:

[Col. 0792A] VERSE 10.—“For one day in your courts is better than thousands.”

“For one day,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] immutable, namely without rising or setting, not yielding to the third day and not pressed by tomorrow, which is in your courts—this is that for which he sighs—is better than thousands of days that people desire, that is, than infinite present days which have an end. Why?

VERSE 11.—“I have chosen to be cast down in the house of my God, rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.”

[Col. 0792B] “I have chosen,” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine] even if I could reign, to be low in human estimation in God’s house—that is, in the Church—not outside its threshold, but within it. See how sweet it is to be pressed in the bundle of the winepress.

Or: “I have chosen to be cast down,” that is, to be humble in the valley of tears. This man has found the humility by which he may ascend, “in the house of my God,” that is, in the lowest place, from which he may be summoned higher (Luke XIV), rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners—that is, rather than to be powerful among sinners, in the glory of the world.

Therefore I prefer to be in God’s house rather than elsewhere, because in it he gives the mercy by which he justifies, and afterward the truth of the promised reward. This is:

VERSE 12.—“For God loves mercy and truth; the Lord will give grace and glory.”

“For God loves mercy,” [Augustine] by which he first comes to help and forgives, and truth, by which he afterward crowns. He loves truth in order to give the believer what he promised. And he will give grace here. Hence the Apostle: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Cor. XV). And he will give glory there, that is, in the future. Hence the same Apostle: “There remains for me a crown of righteousness” (II Tim. IV).

But to whom will he give them? To those who walk in innocence. This is:

[Col. 0792C] VERSE 13.—“He will not deprive of good things those who walk in innocence; O Lord of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes in you.”

“He will not deprive.” [Augustine.] Or the connection is thus: Since he will give, therefore he will not deprive those who walk in innocence of spiritual goods. Why then is innocence abandoned for earthly goods? What does one gain? What does one lose? One has gained profit of gold; one has lost innocence. What then remains for us during the time of pressure, that we may arrive there? To hope in the Lord. This is what he says, turning to God: since he will not deprive them, therefore, O Lord of hosts, who do such great things as cannot be spoken, blessed is the man who hopes in you—[Cassiodorus] that is, who places his hope in eternal things, not in things that perish. In few words he concludes everything.

## Comparison on Psalm LXXXIII: “How beloved,” etc.

VERSE 3.—“The turtledove [has found] a nest.”

Scholars of Hebraisms translate **DEROR** as “swallow” instead of “turtledove.” Jerome, however, used the general term “bird,” though in his Commentaries he also interprets it as “turtledove.” The reason Faber thinks “swallow” more appropriate—[Col. 0793A] namely, because it commonly builds nests around temples, of which the psalm was speaking—is weak. For if “swallow” must be used on account of that appropriateness, whereas St Augustine found a deeper adaptation in the sparrow and turtledove, the turtledove should rather retain its place, unless something else prevents it. Accordingly, the Chaldee plainly has “turtledove”: **SCHAPHNINA**.

VERSE 6.—“He has arranged ascents in his heart.”

They interpret **MESILLOTH** as “paths.” “Ascents” and “paths” do indeed differ somewhat; but since the root from which that word derives, **SALAL**, means “to raise” and “to exalt,” why should translators not say “ascents”? Nor did the translators for Cajetan recoil from this, saying after Rabbi David, “elevations.” The translator in Campensis adopted the metaphor he preferred, giving “praises” instead of “paths,” for “to exalt” is also said of praising. Hence Nebiensis says “praisings.”

[No. 189.] “He has arranged [them] in the valley of tears.” The Hebrew here begins [Col. 0793B] another verse; and the translators say, “passing through the valley of weeping,” so that, if you wish, you may refer it to the paths from the preceding words, or understand it of people passing through the valley of weeping. The Septuagint understood it so that “passing through” pertains to the ascents. If it were to be rendered word for word, the relative pronoun “whose” would have to be understood, making the sense: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you, and whose ascents are in the heart, passing through,” etc. They expressed the same sense, however, by saying, “he arranged ascents.”

But Münster did what I criticized here, for he rendered: “And in whose hearts are paths, passing through,” etc., whereas the Hebrew reads: **MESILLOTH BILBABAM OBRE**, “paths in their heart, passing through.”

“In the place which he has appointed.” The Hebrew writers understand it differently, namely: “They make it a spring,” **MAAIAN IESCHITHUHU**. But since they attest that **MAAIAN** can sometimes mean “surface,” besides its principal meaning, which is “eye” or “sight,” I do not see why the Septuagint wrongly rendered it “place,” which for philosophers is unquestionably a surface. The fact that the tense of the verb differs from the number causes no difficulty, provided we preserve the sense. Good translators are not slaves to syllables.

[Col. 0793C] VERSE 7.—“For the lawgiver will give blessing.”

Because the word **ATAH**, according to Sanctes’ *Thesaurus*, may be both transitive and intransitive, Jerome and most others translate it passively: “The teacher shall be clothed with blessing,” or “with blessings.” But if you state it transitively, say “he will cover with blessing,” or “he will clothe with blessing,” with the persons who are to share the blessing understood. Thus “to give blessing” comes to the same thing.

Sanctes and Münster give a very different sense in this way: “The pools will be covered,” or “the rain will cover them.” The variation arises entirely from two homonymous words. The first is **BERACOTH**, which is ambiguous. For if you derive it from **BEREC**, “he blessed,” you rightly obtain “blessings”; otherwise it denotes pools [Col. 0794A] and wine-vats. The other word is **MOREH**, ambiguous between “lawgiver” and “rain.” Let them enjoy their Judaizing rabbis; meanwhile, we follow most closely the ecclesiastical reading.

“They shall go from strength to strength.” The word used here in Hebrew is polysemous: **HAIIL**. First, it means “strength,” as the Septuagint, Jerome, Nebiensis, Pagninus, Pellicanus, the translators for Cajetan, and Campensis’ paraphrase understand it. Second, it means “army”; accordingly Sanctes renders “from army to army,” and Münster “from company to company.” Third, it means “riches”; therefore the translator associated with Campensis rendered “from wealth to wealth.” Fourth, it means “wall.” We await someone who, after all these, will translate “from wall to wall.” Finally, according to some, it sometimes means “a city ditch.” Let a new Hebraist therefore arise and say, “from ditch to ditch.” Thus we shall gain nothing but confusion and contention. The Chaldee paraphrast has: “from the house of the sanctuary to [Col. 0794B] the house of study.”

VERSE 11.—“He chose to be cast down in the house of my God.”

Jerome, the Chaldee, Nebiensis, and Pellican agree. The others understand it differently: “I chose,” or “I preferred, to keep the threshold in the house of my God.” Let **HISTOPHEPH** mean “to remain at the threshold.” Certainly our translators explained the metaphor elegantly; for lowly persons are permitted to stand at either threshold, whereas only household members and persons of honor are admitted to inspect and inhabit the inner and more private parts of the house. The translator associated with Campensis expressed this trope differently: “I prefer,” he says, “to be a doorkeeper in the house of my God.”

VERSE 12.—“For God loves mercy and truth.”

The Hebrew has **KI SCHEMESES UMAGEN ADONAI ELOHIM**, that is, “The Lord God is sun and shield.” Even without my saying anything, this metaphorical expression speaks its mystery, which the Septuagint has reverently and learnedly disclosed: through the sun it suggests mercy to us, in accordance with Luke VI: “Be merciful, as your heavenly Father is merciful,” who makes his sun rise upon good and evil people. [Col. 0794C] And what speaks better through the shield than God’s invincible truth? “His truth,” it says, “shall surround you with a shield” (Ps. XC).

VERSE 13.—“In innocence.”

You might suspect that the translators did not render this quite appropriately because of Jerome’s words in his Commentary on this passage: “The Hebrew reads better, ‘in perfection.’ For innocence is not a perfect virtue, since a person who is innocent but lacks prudence does not possess perfected and consummate virtue. Therefore he says also in the Gospel: ‘Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves’ (Matt. X.16).” So he says. Yet this should certainly not move you, since Jerome himself translated the same or a similar expression from Hebrew as “innocence”: Job II, **MAHAZIQ BETUMMATHO**, “holding fast to his innocence.”

# PSALM LXXXIV

[Col. 0793]

## Title of the Psalm: “To the end; for the sons of Korah; a psalm.”

[Col. 0793D]

“You have blessed, O Lord.” Title: “To the end; for the sons of Korah; a psalm.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine, Alcuin.] This psalm is the third concerning the first advent, through which comes the blessing of all nations, which had been subject to the curse through Adam’s sin. Its meaning is: this psalm, directing us to the end—that is, to Christ, through whom blessing comes—is sung for the sons of Korah, that is, for us, and deals with the new blessing given through Christ.

Purpose: [Alcuin.] It exhorts us to come to Christ through faith, [Col. 0794D] so that blessing may be received.

Method: [Cassiodorus.] The psalm has three parts. First, it treats of the turning away of iniquity. Second, of the turning away of wrath: “You have softened.” Third, it states from whom and through whom this comes, and what it grants: “I will hear what the Lord speaks.”

[Haymo.] Setting Christ’s blessing against Adam’s curse, of which it was said, “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. III), he says, O—

VERSE 1.—“You have blessed your land, O Lord; you have turned away the captivity of Jacob.”

[Col. 0795A] “O Lord, you have blessed.” [Haymo, Augustine.] Formerly you had indeed cursed; but now you have blessed your land through Christ, through whom blessing comes. And through him you have turned away the captivity that was under the devil, because the law of the members held people captive. I mean the captivity of Jacob, that is, of the new people.

VERSE 2.—“You have forgiven the iniquity of your people; you have covered all their sins.”

“You have forgiven.” [Augustine, Gloss, Augustine.] Note that he speaks of future things as though they were past: thus you have turned it away because you have granted forgiveness. This is: you have forgiven the iniquity of your people—that iniquity which held humankind captive—so that sin may not reign in this mortal body (Rom. VI). You have covered all their sins through baptism, so that you might not see them, that is, punish them.

[Col. 0795B] PART II. **Diapsalma.** VERSE 3.—“You have softened all your wrath; you have turned away from the wrath of your indignation.”

“You have softened.” [Cassiodorus, Haymo, Augustine.] The second part, where he treats of the turning away of wrath, that is, punishment. As though he said: You have blessed; you have forgiven; and thus you have softened all your wrath which is here. You have turned us away—that is, you will turn us away wholly at the judgment—from the wrath of your indignation, that is, the wrath which comes from your indignation. These are spoken of the future, though the verbs are in the past tense.

VERSE 4.—“Turn us, O God our savior, and turn your wrath away from us.”

“Turn us away from vices, O God our savior.” [Augustine.] As though he said: What I said as though it were past, I pray may come to pass; [Col. 0795C] he asks for what he knew was still future. He therefore spoke prophetically as though these things were past, but here prays for them as truly future, saying: “Turn us, and turn away [your wrath].” As though he said: I spoke as though they had happened because I see with complete certainty that they will happen; and because they have not yet happened, I pray that they may. Turn us away from vices, O God our savior, and thus turn your wrath away from us.

VERSE 5.—“Will you be angry with us for ever, or extend your wrath from generation to generation?”

“For will you be angry with us for ever?” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] God’s wrath is every punishment that we suffer, as was said to Adam when he sinned: “Cursed is the earth in your work, and in labor and in the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. III). Because of wrath, therefore, we are mortal and subject to suffering, though renewed in Christ.

This man foresees that this punishment will pass away. “For as all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ” (I Cor. XV). Or will you extend your wrath from the generation that existed from Adam to Christ into the generation that exists under the grace of baptism in the time of the Son? For the entrance to the kingdom of heaven was not opened to that generation as it was closed to the old generation.

Or the first generation is the present one, carnally born from Adam, mortal because of wrath. For we have all drawn punishment and guilt from him. Therefore whatever happened to Adam followed us also, so that we should die; for we all were in him when [Col. 0796A] he sinned. For those sins of parents do not pertain to children which parents commit after their children have already been born. God’s wrath, then, is God’s vengeance, which the first generation experiences.

But because it was to come about that we should be regenerated, made new through faith, and that in the resurrection all mortality should be consumed and complete newness restored, there will in the future be another, immortal generation by God’s mercy. Into it wrath will not extend. Yet we would not deserve even this mercy by turning ourselves to God; for he himself turns us.

VERSE 6.—“O God, when you turn, you will give us life, and your people will rejoice in you.”

“O God, having turned,” or “turning us.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] As though he said: You will not extend your wrath; rather, O God, when you turn us—another reading—you will give us life. As though he said: Just as life comes from you, so too does conversion. For God first gives the desire to be converted, and afterward leads to life.

Or, according to our text: O God, having turned from your wrath at the advent of your Son, you will give us life in hope for so great a time before the reality is possessed; and then your people will rejoice in you, though previously they rejoiced wrongly in themselves. A person rejoices wrongly in something else; he rejoiced in himself to his own harm, but shall rejoice in you to his own good. In order that this may happen:

[Col. 0796B] VERSE 7.—“Show us your mercy, O Lord, and give us your salvation.”

“Show us your mercy, O Lord,” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] that is, your Christ, bodily and spiritually. By praying he foretold this before it happened, though now it has already happened in part. Yet there are many who do not wish to be healed, so that they may spiritually see mercy already shown. But how will the blind see it even when it is shown? They will, well enough, if they wish, because the very light shown to them is also salvation. Hence he adds: “And give us your salvation.”

[Note: Col. 0795D. From Augustine, in the Preface to the Psalms.] A human physician shows light to an eye clouded over; but light is one thing and the physician another. Christ is both the light, which shows mercy—that is, himself—and salvation, that is, the physician, because he heals the inward eyes so that the mercy shown, or light which is Christ, may be seen.

For he himself said: “He who loves me keeps my commandments, and I will love him and show myself to him” [Col. 0796C] (John XIV). But did not those to whom he was speaking see him? How then does he say, “I will show myself to him”? Flesh saw Christ’s flesh; the heart did not see his divinity. Yet flesh saw flesh so that through faith the heart might be cleansed, whence God may be seen. Thus it is said: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts XV); and: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V).

Christ is called mercy because he shows us mercy, teaching that whatever good a person possesses comes from God; thus a person does not become proud, and thus, enjoying God, rejoices in him.

Or otherwise, this man asks that Christ be shown to him only spiritually when he says: “Show us your mercy, O Lord.” He knew that Christ would come, but he asks that we may behold him with a pure heart, not with bodily eyes like unbelievers. For the Jews saw him and crucified him. And “give us your salvation” in the future—that is, Christ, to be embraced [Col. 0797A] and possessed, so that he may no longer be taken from us. This is read partly of the present and partly of the future.

PART III. VERSE 8.—“I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me, for he will speak peace to his people.”

“I will hear.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Gloss, interlinear Gloss.] The third part, where he says how he knows these things, through whom what he prays for comes about, and what he himself grants when he comes. As though he said: Why are you confident about what you pray for? Because, away from the noise of the world which disturbs outside, I will hear what the Lord God speaks [Col. 0797B] inwardly in me—[Augustine, Cassiodorus, interlinear Gloss] namely, the Holy Spirit—because he will speak eternal peace, against which nothing is adverse. Hence: “He has made your borders peace” (Ps. CXLVII).

[Augustine, Alcuin, Haymo.] There is no blemish in the moon there. Nor will Belial pass through there. This peace is not here. Or “he speaks peace,” that is, Christ: peace toward God and neighbor through Christ, to his Jewish people.

VERSE 9.—“And upon his saints, and upon those who turn to the heart.”

And over his saints. This is his people, and also over those—or over all those—who, from every nation, are converted to the heart, because they had departed from reason. Or, according to another reading [Col. 0797C], “who turn their heart” [Aug.] to him, not to another or to anything else.

VERSE 10.—“Yet his salvation is near to those who fear him, that glory may dwell in our land.”

Yet. [Gl. int., Aug.] As though he said: He will speak peace over all; yet from Zion comes the beauty of his comeliness. That is: the salvation of God himself, that is, Christ in bodily form, will be near those who fear him—that is, the Jews who feared him. For demons were worshipped and feared everywhere. But among the Jewish people God was feared and worshipped, even if for earthly things. He was near to them, not to the Gentiles, who sought such things from the devil. Therefore, although mercy is universal toward all, something spiritual and distinctive was accomplished among the Jewish people. Hence he adds: “that glory may dwell in our land,” in which, the Prophet says, “I was born.” For there the temple and God’s sacrifices first existed; there were the patriarchs; there Christ was born from them; there Christ appeared; there countless miracles are performed.

Or the connection may be thus: [Alcuin.] although he speaks peace over all, nevertheless his salvation—that is, the salvation which is through him—will be near those who fear him: that is, only to those who, while they stand, take care lest they fall. It is such salvation “that glory,” namely of immortality, “may dwell in our land,” that is, in our body, now mortal.

VERSE 10.—“Mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have kissed.”

Mercy and truth. [Cassiod., Aug., Alcuin.] After saying from what people Christ was to be born, he adds what he was to bestow. As though he said: Christ is near to those who fear him; and mercy, revealed in the New Testament among the Gentiles who were far off, and truth—that is, the fulfilment of the promises of the Old Testament, fulfilled among the Jews who were near—have met one another, that is, have come together in Christ. Hence the Apostle says: “For I say that Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision, in order to fulfil the promises of the Father; but that the Gentiles might glorify God for mercy” (Rom. XV). And elsewhere: “He preached peace to those who were far off, and peace to those who were near” (Eph. II). Righteousness and peace with God have kissed: [Aug., Alcuin.] that is, they agree in human beings. For these two love one another, so that one who does righteousness finds peace—and not otherwise. But how have these things occurred [Col. 0798B]? See how, and through what means.

VERSE 11.—“Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven.”

Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from the heaven of heavens [Aug.]; that is, Christ was born of a woman so that righteousness might look down from heaven—that is, so that human beings might be justified by God. For truth possesses that which it might offer for the justification of human beings.

Or, “truth has sprung up from the earth”: that is, confession has arisen from sinful humanity, so that a person may accuse himself, recognizing that he is ashes and earth, to whom it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III). Thus “righteousness has looked down from the heaven of heavens,” just as the confessing publican went home justified. Righteousness looks down from heaven, as though God said: “Let us spare this man, because he does not spare himself; let us forgive him, because he acknowledges [Col. 0798C] his sin.” Therefore righteousness has looked down from heaven—that is, justification has been given by the Lord God to the penitent; righteousness is from heaven.

VERSE 12.—“For the Lord will give kindness, and our land will yield its fruit.”

For the Lord will give kindness [Aug.], or sweetness—that is, a good disposition, so that right action may delight us; and we cannot otherwise possess this unless he gives it. Thus our land will yield its fruit, that is, good works. Truly he will give kindness, because—

VERSE 13.—“Righteousness will go before him, and will set his footsteps in the way.”

Righteousness will go before him [Alcuin, Aug., Hier.], that is, it will increase or go in advance before him, preparing the way for him [Col. 0798D]. The first righteousness of a human being is to punish his evil self and make himself good. This is God’s way, that he may come to that person. For whoever hates his sins already begins to be like God, who hates them. Therefore make yourself like God, and prepare a way for him by confession of sins. Hence John says: “Prepare the way of the Lord” (Matt. III), by confessing and repenting. Hence Isaiah says: “Cast out the stones from the streets” (Isa. LVII), that is, sins from your hearts. And the Lord himself, coming and visiting, will set his footsteps in the way thus prepared. For his way is undefiled; therefore, casting stones, thorns, and briars from our hearts, let us prepare the Lord’s way, laying our garments, with the apostles, upon the ass on which the Saviour sat; and with the crowd strewing the way with garments, branches of trees, and [Col. 0799A] flowers, let us cry with them: “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matt. XXI).

## Comparison on Psalm LXXXIV: “You Have Blessed,” etc.

VERSE 1.—“You have blessed, O Lord, your land.” Jerome: “You have been appeased, O Lord, toward your land”; the Pratensian: “You have loved, O Lord, your land”; Pellicanus: “Your land has pleased you, O Lord”; Sanctes: “You have been well pleased, O Lord, with your land”; Münster: “You have become gracious, O Lord, toward your land”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “You have willed, O Lord, your land”; the translator in Campensis: “May you be favourable, O Lord, to your land”; the Paraphrase: “You have been reconciled, O Lord, to your land”; the Chaldee and Nebiensis: “Your will, O God, is toward your land.”

How rightly the Septuagint rendered the word *ratzitha* is shown by Jerome in his letter to Sunia and Fretella. There he also acknowledges that he produced the Latin found in the Vulgate edition:

> “For ‘You have blessed, O Lord, your land,’ in place of which it is ‘you have blessed,’ you say that in Greek [Col. 0799B] εὐδόκησας (*eudokēsas*, ‘you were well pleased’) is written, and you ask how this word ought to be expressed in Latin. If we scrutinize words and syllables contentiously, we can say, ‘Your land has pleased you, O Lord’; and while following the words, we lose the order of the sense. Or indeed something must be added so that the order of the expression may be preserved, and we must say, ‘Your land has pleased you, O Lord.’ But if we do this, we shall again be asked why we added ‘you,’ when it is found neither in the Greek nor in the Hebrew. Therefore the same rule of translation is to be followed which we have often stated: wherever the sense suffers no loss, the euphony, propriety, and elegance of the language into which we translate should be preserved.”

This exposition of the holy man refutes the affected pedantry (*kakozēlia*) of many translations.

VERSE 6.—“O God, having turned.” The Master reports and explains a twofold reading: “turning” or “having turned.” Augustine reads it actively, as does the Roman Psalter; Jerome and Nebiensis, according to the Hebrews, have “returning.” Modern Hebraizing translators render it passively, “be converted toward us.” Certainly the Hebrews say that *taschub* is now transitive, now intransitive. In Greek ἐπιτρέψας (*epitrepsas*, “having turned”) occurs actively, although in Matthew XIII we find ἐπιτρέψωσι (*epitrepsōsi*), that is, “they may be converted,” from Isaiah chapter VI—unless you prefer to understand “themselves,” so that it means “they may turn themselves.” Yet one may do the same in the case of “turning.”

VERSE 9.—“And upon those who are converted to the heart.” Jerome and the others: “lest they return” or “be converted to folly.” Here it is plain that the Septuagint took *el* in place of *al*, words which, without vowel-point writing, do not differ at all. The former means “to,” the latter “lest” or “not.” Again, they divided *lecislah* into two words, namely *les*, with beth, meaning “heart,” and not with kaph. The interchange of these letters is readily made because of their close relationship. Likewise, *selah*, which is *diapsalma*, commonly remains untranslated in the Psalms, as we touched upon somewhat above. Therefore the translators rendered only [Col. 0800B] the earlier particles, leaving *selah*. And so that the reader may more clearly recognize each reading, we give both. We now have: *al jaschubu lecislah*. The Septuagint has: *el jaschubu leb selah*.

VERSE 11.—“Mercy and truth have met one another.” Jerome explained to Sunia and Fretella why the pronoun *sibi* (“one another”) was added in Latin:

> “You say that in Greek *sibi* is not found: ἔλεος καὶ ἀλήθεια συνήντησαν, that is, ‘mercy and truth have met’; nor is it found in Hebrew. And in the Septuagint it is marked with an obelus. When these signs, through the negligence of copyists, are omitted by many as though superfluous, great error arises in reading. But unless *sibi* is added—‘mercy and truth have met one another’—they will be thought to have met not one another but someone else; nor will righteousness and peace be thought to have given a kiss to one another, but to another.”

So far he. Certainly nearly all modern translators have added *sibi*, whereas Hebrew simply has *niphgāshū* (“they met”).

# PSALM LXXXV

[Col. 0799]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PRAYER OF DAVID”

[Col. 0799C]

“Bow down, O Lord.” Title: “A Prayer of David.” [Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod., Alcuin.] This psalm is the second among those entitled by the name of prayer. In this psalm Christ, the Son of God and of man, one God with the Father and one man with humankind, prays in the form of a servant—he who, in the form of God, is prayed to by us. For he prays for us, prays in us, and is prayed to by us: he prays for us as our priest; he prays in us as our head; he is prayed to by us as our God. Christ’s prayer is moreover instruction for the faithful, and every act of his is a lesson for the Christian. Our prayer, however, is a cleansing from sins.

Christ prayed as he bore the cross: namely, for our necessity, not his own [Col. 0799D]; just as he wept for Lazarus [Cassiod., Aug.] in order to teach us to possess love for our neighbour, and as he fled in order to restrain the boldness of foolish and ill-considered rashness. The meaning is: this prayer is assigned to David, that is, to the whole Christ. For Christ says this in us, and we say it in him, because this voice suits both head and body.

Purpose: he urges prayer. Method: the psalm has three parts. First, he prays in ascending; then he concludes that all nations will worship. Second, he prays for all who already worship, at “Lead me.” [Col. 0800C] Third, he prays for himself, mentioning the passion and resurrection, at “O God, the wicked.” Therefore Christ, humbly praying to the Father in the form of a servant, says: “O—

VERSE 1.—“Bow down your ear, O Lord, and hear me, for I am needy and poor.”

O Lord [Aug., Cassiod.], who are high, bow down your ear—that is, your mercy—to me, who am weak. God draws near to the humble, not to the proud. And hear me: fulfil my desires. Bow down, because I am needy, having no help from another, and poor in myself. God bows down to such a one; he does not bow down to the rich.

VERSE 2.—“Guard my soul, for I am holy; save your servant, my God, who hopes in you.”

Guard [Aug.]—as though in this sense: “Hear me,” says Christ [Col. 0800D], with the voice of the body joined to himself; “guard my soul from all stumbling-blocks against those who lie in wait, for I am holy.” This properly applies to Christ. For Christ is properly holy, namely, the sanctifier; his own are also holy, namely, sanctified in baptism, according to: “Be holy, for I also am holy” (Lev. XIX). Therefore the whole Christ is holy, and one holy one; but the head in one way, the members in another. Thus the whole Christ may fittingly say, “For I am holy.” Yet this is not the speech of pride exalted, but the confession of one who is not ungrateful.

“My God, save” [Cassiod., Gl. int., Aug.], because salvation is not from a human being, “your servant,” not your free servant, as Adam was, “who hopes in you.” A holy person is not proud.

VERSE 3.—“Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I have cried to you all day; make glad the soul of your servant, for to you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.”

Have mercy on me, O Lord, because I have cried to you [Aug., Hier., Aug., Alcuin.] not merely once but all day—that is, at every time. Make glad the soul of your servant, sorrowful in the passion, because I have lifted up that soul of mine, which good affection lifts. For affection is a step; your will is your path. You ascend by loving; you descend by neglecting. Though standing on earth, you are in heaven if you love God. The heart is not lifted as the body is lifted, by a change of place; rather, the heart is lifted by a change of will. To where have I lifted it? “[To you, O Lord],” where there is joy; on earth, bitterness.

Observe the ascent: the manner in which he ascends by prayer. First he is called poor; then holy; then hoping; afterward crying out; finally, lifted to God. The correspondence of the words is fitting: bow down to the poor; guard the holy; save the one who hopes; have mercy on the one crying out; make glad the one lifted up.

VERSE 4.—“For you, O Lord, are sweet and gentle, and abundant in mercy toward all who call upon you.”

For you, O Lord. [Aug.] As though he said: “I lifted up my soul because you, O Lord, are sweet to your own,” and so I was able to lift my soul. Because you are sweet, therefore make my affection joyful amid weariness from worldly bitterness; and you are gentle toward those whom you await, bearing the human being until you perfect him, because he would fly away from himself unless he were borne by the Lord. For many things occur in the human heart by which it is moved wrongly. Just as entreaties are hindered by vain thoughts, so that the heart scarcely stands before its God in order to speak to him in prayer. For when you pray, you speak to God; when you read, God speaks to you. But when the phantasms of evil thoughts steal in, the human heart in some manner flees from itself, and finds neither rails by which to enclose itself nor barriers by which to restrain its flights and wandering motions.

Against this David says: “I found my heart to pray to you” (IV Kings VII). God hears that alone [Col. 0801D]. He says that he found his heart, as though it were accustomed to flee from him [Alcuin, Aug.]; and he follows it as a fugitive. A person finds it when, after the dying flies have been cast out—which spoil the sweetness of ointment (Eccl. X)—the whole affection of the heart is gathered for praying to God. God bears the human being and waits while he wanders. You are abundant in mercy against our abounding iniquity, toward those who call upon you—not upon something other than you; toward all: none is excepted. Therefore—

VERSE 5.—“Receive my prayer with your ears, O Lord, and attend to the voice of my supplication.”

Receive my prayer with your ears. [Aug., Cassiod.] Here the great affection of one praying is shown: that is, let it not leave your ears; fix it there. Observe the order of prayer. First, the voice of supplication was to ascend, when he said, “Bow down your ear”; then he asked that he might be heard, when he said, “Hear me”; now he adds, saying, “Receive my prayer with your ears.” He does not ask that it be received in passing, but that it be stored, as it were, in God’s bosom, just as something is impressed upon the heart through the ears. Hence he adds: “And attend to the voice of my supplication,” so that your attentive mind may open your hearing to my supplication. Then the reason for hearing is given:

VERSE 6.—“On the day of my trouble I cried to you, because you heard me.”

I cried to you on the day of my trouble. [Aug., Cassiod., Alcuin.] This trouble always exists in pilgrimage, until God gives himself to be enjoyed. Or, “on the day of trouble” means when adversity threatens, when one will cry out more earnestly. Above he said: “I cried all [Col. 0802B] day”; here he intensifies it, because one cries more in trouble. Then he adds why he cried: “because you heard me.” He says that he cried because he was heard, though crying out ordinarily precedes being heard. This reversal is fitting in the saints, who are heard both before crying out and afterward.

VERSE 7.—“There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, and none according to your works.”

VERSE 8.—“All the nations whom you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and shall glorify your name.”

There is none like you. [Aug., Haym., Cassiod., Aug.] The order is: because you heard me, all nations whom you have made will come and worship before you, O Lord—that is, all will come from their own worship to your worship. If there is a nation which God did not make, that nation will not worship God. But there is none which he did not make, because he made Adam and Eve, the source of all nations. From them all nations were propagated. By these words he announces the Church spread everywhere, which is now fulfilled. Note also that, as Scripture says, the glory of a king lies in a populous nation, while the diminution of a people is the grief of a ruler. “And they shall glorify your name,” that is, they shall proclaim how worthy you are to be named.

Or according to another reading: “They shall be honoured by your name.” Therefore they will come and glorify you because there is none like you among the gods, O Lord, and none according to your works. Whatever “gods” may mean, there is none like you in essence or operation. Thus the nations will find among their gods none like you in essence or operation. Then he answers each point by its counterpart: “There is none like you,”

VERSE 9.—“For you are great and perform wonders; you alone are God.”

For you are great [Gl. int., Aug.], as none other is. “There is none according to your works,” because you perform wonders; therefore you alone are God, and no other. Or according to another reading: “You alone are God, great.” This is said against those who would call themselves great through themselves rather than through God. For what is called great in comparison with God? Nothing. But because there were to be persons who would call themselves great and make God small, it is said against them: “You alone are God, great.”

## PART II. VERSE 10.—“Lead me, O Lord, in [Col. 0803A] your way, and I shall walk in your truth; let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name.”

Lead me, O Lord. [Cassiod., Gl. int., Aug.] The second part, in which he prays for all who already worship. He speaks in the members. As though he said: “The nations will come; that they may be able to do so, O Lord, lead me. I do not say, ‘lead me to the way,’ because I am not outside the way; but, already placed in your way, lead me in it, lest I slip.” It is one thing to be led to the way, another to be led along the way: the latter is to be helped so as not to fall in it. Human beings are everywhere needy, whether they are in the way or outside it.

The way is Christ, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). Hence he adds: “And I shall enter,” or “walk”—that is, I shall advance further as you lead me in your truth; this is the way. And then, “Let my heart rejoice,” yet in such a manner that it fears your name. In worldly fear, the cause of danger or distress comes first; but in the fear of God, joy comes first. Both must be mingled, so that we may fear under hope and rejoice under fear. For fear is now present in joy; in the future there will be joy without fear, where there will be full security, which is not yet ours.

[Alcuin.] Joy now draws us; fear does not allow us to depart from the way. Both, therefore, must be retained. These are the two millstones between which the Christian is ground, so that he may become Christ’s bread: namely hope and fear. Hence it was said in Deuteronomy: “Do not take as a pledge the upper or the lower millstone” (Deut. XXIV). The upper millstone is hope; the lower millstone is fear. Therefore one must not take either without the other. Whoever hopes and does not fear is negligent; whoever fears and does not hope is dejected.

VERSE 11.—“I shall confess to you, O Lord my God, with my whole heart, and I shall glorify your name forever.”

I shall confess to you, O Lord my God. [Gl. int., Cassiod.] As though he said: “Lead me, and, once led, I shall confess to you with my whole heart.” The person who places all his hope in the Lord confesses with his whole heart. And with the saints I shall glorify your name forever, that is, in eternal blessedness.

VERSE 12.—“For your mercy is great toward me, and you have delivered my soul from the lowest hell.”

For your mercy is great [Gl. int., Aug.] [Col. 0803D], and this is toward me, according to: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James I). This mercy is great in this: you have delivered my soul from the lowest hell. From the phrase “lowest hell,” we understand that there are, as it were, two hells: a lower and an upper. For why is one called lower hell unless there is an upper hell? The heavenly dwelling-place of angels, therefore, is where the life of ineffable joys is; where there are the immortality and incorruption of things above. The earthly dwelling-place, however, is where there are flesh and blood, departure and succession, mutability and mortality. There is a hell below this earthly dwelling-place: that is, from this hell one goes to the lower hell, from which the Lord delivered souls by sending his Son. Indeed, on account of these two hells the Son of God was sent, delivering from every side: he was sent to this hell by being born, and to that one by dying.

Or perhaps within hell itself there is some lower region for the wicked. Thus the rich man who was tormented in hell lifted up his eyes to Abraham, who was with the other righteous, as it were at the edge and in the limbo of hell, where he was seen by the rich man who was in the lower part of hell (Luke XVI). Into that part descend those who have sinned most grievously; and one delivered from sins is delivered from it, because he is not sent there. These, however, are opinions, not assertions.

## PART III. VERSE 13.—“O God, the wicked have risen against me, and the assembly of the powerful have sought my soul, and have not set you before their eyes.”

O God, the wicked. [Cassiod., Alcuin, Aug.] The third part, in which he prays for himself, here mentioning his passion and glory. Hence those for whom he prayed receive abundant mercy and are delivered from hell. As though he said: “Your mercy is great; you have delivered from hell. Yet, O God, the wicked”—that is, those perverting your law, namely the Jews—“have risen against me,” so that they might call me guilty. Or “against me” means against the whole Christ. “And the assembly of the powerful,” that is, congregations of the proud, “have sought my soul” by deceitful counsels. [Cassiod., Aug.] Then he adds what always results from wicked dispositions: “And they have not set you before their eyes,” that is, they did not understand God, so as to spare the human being. Thus they acted.

VERSE 14.—“But you, O Lord God, are compassionate and merciful, patient, abundant in mercy, and true.”

But you, O Lord, are compassionate [Cassiod.] in action and merciful by nature; patient, awaiting the wicked; abundant in mercy toward those converted; and true in your promises. Or “true,” that is, responding according to merits.

VERSE 15.—“Look upon me and have mercy on me; give your authority to your servant, and save the son of your handmaid.”

Look upon me [Cassiod., Aug., Gl. int.] as a human being, and have mercy on me as mortal; and give your authority—that is, the power of judgment—to your servant, to me, Christ, innocent. As though he said: “Let the time of patience pass; let the time of judgment come.” And save—that is, raise from death—the son of your handmaid, that is, Mary, who said: “Behold the handmaid [Col. 0804D] of the Lord,” etc. (Luke I).

This may also be said of Christ’s members: “Give your authority to your servant,” [192] that is, to the saints; for not Christ alone, but also the saints, will sit as judges (Matt. I), and they are sons of the handmaid, that is, of the Church. “And save the son of your handmaid”: that is, may what you give to the saints endure.

VERSE 16.—“Perform with me a sign for good, that those who hate me may see and be ashamed, because you, O Lord, have helped me and comforted me.”

Perform the sign of resurrection [Aug., Alcuin, Cassiod.], namely the sign of Jonah the prophet, which has already been accomplished in the head (Matt. XII) and will also be accomplished in the members. That is, perform the remarkable resurrection of head and members. I say, perform it with me. As though he said: [Col. 0805A] “I, as God, act with you.” For Christ, insofar as he is God, raised himself insofar as he is human. Perform, then, a sign “for good,” or “now,” that is, for the benefit of others. For the resurrection is a sign for good, by which both the power of God is made known and the hope of believers confirmed.

[Aug., Cassiod.] Therefore make the Jews who hate me see this: that you, O Lord, have helped me in the contest, in the things I did, and comforted me in the sorrow that is here, in the things I suffered. Let them see this and be ruinously ashamed in judgment—those who now refuse to be beneficially ashamed.

## Comparison on Psalm LXXXV: “Bow Down, O Lord,” etc.

VERSE 10.—“Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name.” Jerome: “Make my heart one”; or, as others prefer, “unite my heart”—*iahed*. What is this union except that joy of charity by which we love God alone, and which, from the fullness of common love, makes all the faithful rejoicing in the Lord one heart and one soul?

VERSE 15.—“Give your authority to your servant.” In place of “give your authority,” Jerome has “your strength,” and others follow him: *uzeca*. Faber and Caecus contend remarkably that henceforth one should not sing “give your authority,” but “give strength,” as though we sang contrary to the Prophet’s meaning. They say that Christ is here introduced asking the Father for help, in view of the immeasurable evils that threatened; and that Christ prays in humility, to whom, on this reasoning, the supreme power of the kingdom would not be fitting.

Therefore Augustine was much more mistaken, who reads “power,” as does the Roman Psalter, and yet interprets it as authority. How can he say, “Give authority to your servant”? “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V). He, rising again and himself coming to earth to judge, will himself be seen as terrible, he who had been seen as contemptible; he will display power, he who displayed patience. Augustine pursues many other points in this sense.

# PSALM LXXXVI

[Col. 0805]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “FOR THE SONS OF KORAH. A PSALM OF A SONG”

[Col. 0805B]

“His foundations.” Title: “For the sons of Korah, a psalm of a song.” [Aug., Hier.] This psalm is brief in number of words but great in weight of meaning. It treats of the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, the Church, the spiritual city, one part of which serves in battle on earth and one part triumphs in heaven. This psalm commends it according to its present and future state. Therefore both are placed in the title: “Psalm” and “song.”

[Col. 0805C] The meaning is: this psalm is called a “psalm” because it treats of the Church in its present state, where it performs works; and it is called a “song” because it treats of the same Church in its future state, where it rejoices. [Cassiod., Gl. int., Aug.] This is added in order that you may be raised from the earthly—that is, militant—Jerusalem to an understanding of the heavenly one; that is, the movement is proposed from action to contemplation. “For the sons of Korah,” that they may dwell in Zion: here through faith, in the future by sight. One part of it triumphs in heaven; one part fights on earth.

Purpose: he urges love for the heavenly Jerusalem. Method: the psalm has three parts. [Cassiod.] First, the Prophet proclaims the heavenly Jerusalem to the sons of Korah, commending it by its foundations, gates, and fame, so that their affection for it may increase. Second, the Lord himself speaks of that Jerusalem, at “I will remember.” [Col. 0805D] Third, he touches upon future blessedness, at “Like those who rejoice.” [Aug.] Therefore the Prophet, filled with the Holy Spirit and pondering much within himself concerning this city, of which no psalm had yet said anything, bursts out with this:

VERSE 1.—“Her foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the tents of Jacob.”

Her foundations. [Aug.] “Her” refers not to anything previously mentioned, but to the Prophet’s inward meditation: he had never ceased to speak of her in his heart, even if not with his mouth. Her foundations are in the holy mountains: in the prophets and apostles, and in Christ Jesus himself, the chief cornerstone (Eph. II), who alone is the foundation which no one can alter (I Cor. III).

[Cassiod., Aug.] Behold the first praise, drawn from the foundations, so that the firmness of the whole city may be noted. And as though someone asked, “Whose foundations do you mean by ‘her’?” he says, “Zion’s.” And the Lord loves Zion’s gates. The gates and the foundations are the same persons. He loves them, I say, more than all the figurative tents of Jacob. As though he said: he loves the spiritual city more than those things by which it was prefigured. Then follows praise from its renown:

VERSE 2.—“Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God.”

[Col. 0806C] City of God, glorious things have been spoken of you [Aug., Alcuin.], unlike that figurative city which fell. These are the things which the Lord foretold of her through the prophets.

## PART II. VERSE 3.—“I will remember Rahab and Babylon, who know me.”

I will remember. [Cassiod., Aug.] The second part, in which the Lord himself speaks of this Jerusalem and shows what the glorious things are. These are those things: “In that city,” says the Prophet in God’s person, “I will remember Rahab and Babylon,” which do not belong to the Jewish people. Rahab was the prostitute in Jericho who received the spies sent by Joshua; when they were sought, she hid them and sent them out by another way. She was told to put out scarlet thread through the window when the city was taken (Josh. II), so that her house might be recognized by the victors through that sign and she might thus be saved. She did so, and both she and her household were saved.

By her is signified the Church of the Gentiles, which has scarlet in the window—that is, has the sign of Christ’s blood on its forehead. Hence the Lord says to the boastful Pharisees: “Tax collectors and prostitutes will precede you into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XXI). [Hier., Aug., Haym.] The interpretation of the name likewise signifies the same. For *Rahab* means “breadth” or “impetus.” These are the Gentiles who wander widely and violently through vices. Babylon, however, is the city according to the world, to which all wicked persons belong, just as all saints belong to Jerusalem. As though he said: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, holy city, where not the Jew alone but [Col. 0807A] all nations are found. For I will remember Rahab and Babylon,” that is, all nations. “I will remember,” I say, those who know me—that is, the apostles, to whom I shall command concerning the receiving of those peoples.

VERSE 4.—“Behold, foreign peoples, and Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians: these were there.”

Behold, foreign peoples, etc. [Aug., Hier., Aug.] See what he signified by Rahab and Babylon. As though he said: “I will remember—and behold foreign peoples,” that is, the nations; “and Tyre,” that is, those who are in the straits of vices or of repentance. For Tyre means “straitness”; “and the people of the Ethiopians,” that is, nations extending even to the ends of the earth, including black peoples. “And these were there,” that is, in Jerusalem.

VERSE 5.—“Will Zion say: ‘A man, and a man, was born in her; and the Most High himself founded her’?”

Will Zion, etc. [Haym., Gl. int., Hier., Haym.] Here the Prophet resumes his words. As though he said: Glorious things have been spoken of that city, and this miracle also occurred in it: namely, that a man was born in it, and the Most High himself founded it—that is, as God, not as man. But will a human being persuade Zion, that is, the Synagogue, of what I shall say, namely, that a man was born, etc.? As though he said: the unbelieving Synagogue does not accept this.

Or: “Will a human being speak to Zion,” that is, to the Church? As though he said: a human being does not speak from himself; rather, God in the human being proclaims this: that a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her.

Or according to another reading: “The man will call Zion mother.” [Aug., Cassiod.] As though he said: How do foreigners come to Jerusalem? Behold, there is a certain man, namely Christ the man, who will say: “Zion,” that is, the Synagogue, “is my mother according to the flesh”; and through him all these persons come. And who is that man? He is the man who was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her; and he, being such, will call that city mother.

Or thus, according to the same reading: after commending spiritual Zion, that is, the Church, he here rebukes carnal Zion, that is, the Synagogue. As though he said: Christ is the foundation of that city; but Zion—that is, the Synagogue, mother of the Church—will say that Christ is only a human being, not God. Yet Christ both was born in her as a human being and is himself the Most High—that is, the God who founded her. And lest this miracle appear unbelievable to anyone, he says:

VERSE 6.—“The Lord will recount in the writings of peoples and rulers, of those who were in her.”

The Lord will recount, or has recounted. Or the connection may be thus: [Haym., Aug., Hier., Gl. int.] “How do you know this? Behold, the Lord will recount it in the writings of peoples and rulers,” that is, in the writings directed to the faithful peoples and produced by rulers—namely Moses, the prophets, and the apostles. “Rulers,” I say, “of those who were in that city.”

Or according to another reading: [Aug.] “Of which rulers? Of those who were made rulers in her”—that is, of those who were made rulers in that city. Before they were in her [Col. 0808A], they were not rulers, but were the despised things of the world. For he chose the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong.

## PART III. Diapsalma. VERSE 7.—“The dwelling of us all is in you, as of those who rejoice.”

Like those who rejoice. [Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] The third part, having gathered together all the joys spoken of the city, concludes in few words by touching upon future blessedness. As though he said: Such is the city. And, O Zion, the dwelling of us all will be in you. What sort? Like that of those who rejoice. This joy is not ours in this pilgrimage. He says “like those who rejoice” because the joy will be such as we do not know here; and therefore, since it cannot be expressed, he said what he could.

## Comparison on Psalm LXXXVI: “Her Foundations,” etc.

[Col. 0808B]

### Verse 3 — “I will make mention of Rahab.”

So also the Pratensian version. Jerome interprets **RAHAB** as “pride,” as do the translators for Cajetan. But Sanctes and Münster understand it as meaning the Egyptians, so called because of their pride. Hence the Chaldean paraphrast: “I shall commemorate the praises of the Egyptians and Babylonians.” In the end, the sense comes back to the same thing.

Yet it may cause difficulty that Jerome in his Commentaries, and Augustine—and even before them Arnobius—interpret it of Rahab, the woman of Jericho; since this is written with *cheth*, a strong aspiration, whereas the other is written with *he*, a gentle aspiration. The Greeks here have **ῥααβ**, but, to represent the woman, they write with a rough breathing, as best they can, **ῥαχάβ**. But even if one does not wish one aspiration to be substituted for the other, the meanings of both agree. For **Rachab** means “breadth” or “expansion”; while **Rahab** means insolence and recklessness. And no one is unaware how eagerly the proud strive to enlarge themselves. Indeed, the mystery sung in Psalm 193, concerning the Church gathered from the Gentiles who had been puffed up by the swelling of pride, corresponds to the exposition of the saints.

### Verse 4 — “These were there.”

Hebrew: “This one was born there”: **ZEH JULLAD SCHAM**. The sense is the same: “This people was born in Jerusalem,” or “these peoples were there.” Yet Faber proclaims a more divine sense if it is said, “they were begotten there,” so that spiritual regeneration may be suggested. Certainly no lesser dignity is indicated—indeed, perhaps a greater one—in saying that the Gentiles already belonged, by God’s eternal election, to that city Jerusalem before they had done anything good or evil, than in expressing their birth, even a spiritual birth. For God calls things that are not as though they were.

### Verse 5 — “Will Zion say: ‘Man and man was born in her’?”

First the Hebrew must be set down, so that we may see what is disputed: **ULETZION IEAMEAMER ISCH VEISCH JULAD BAH**.

Three difficulties present themselves in this verse. The first concerns the interrogation, which does not appear in the Hebrew. Hence Jerome translates “and to Zion,” and Münster “of Zion.” Yet although the interrogation is not marked by any sign, it is not contrary to Hebrew usage. Paul, the Hebrew of Burgos, testifies that, if it is not read interrogatively, it should nevertheless be understood admiringly—which amounts to the same thing.

The second difficulty concerns the meaning of the verb, which in Hebrew is passive: “To Zion it shall be said,” or “Of Zion it shall be said: ‘Man and man was born in her.’” Or, as Münster wishes: “This one and that one was born in her.” On this reading, the punctuation should be made at “it shall be said”: namely, “To Zion,” or “Of Zion, it shall be said: ‘Man and man was born in her,’” understanding by this figure that many and various persons were born there.

But as regards the punctuation, the Hebrew construction does not compel this, except perhaps because the sense of the verb, which seems impersonal, would require it if read passively. Yet without the vowel-points, the active and passive verb do not differ, so that the reader was free to take it in either way, adopting whichever worthy interpretation seemed more coherent. For it may be pronounced **IEAMER**, “it shall be said,” or **IOMAR**, “he shall say,” as the interpreters probably rendered it. Thus, in this way, the division may suitably be made: “Will Zion say: ‘Man and man was born in her’?” according to the explanation.

The third difficulty concerns the Greek reading, followed and interpreted by Augustine and found in the Roman psalmody: “Mother Zion,” **μήτηρ Σιών**. On this and other points St Jerome gives satisfaction in his Commentaries:

> “The Seventy Interpreters translated thus: ‘Will Zion say: Man?’ Many therefore stumbled and did not understand what **μήτι Σιών** means. They added an *r*: **μήτηρ Σιὼν ἐρεῖ ἄνθρωπος**. And they say this because there follows, ‘and a man was born in her.’ They thought that it ought to be said, ‘Mother Zion shall say: Man,’ because one born is called a son. Therefore they err in the word ‘mother.’”

Thus Jerome there. Nevertheless, he does not disdain to expound that reading; afterward he returns to ours, as follows:

> “Let us also speak according to the Hebrew truth: ‘Will Zion say: Man, and man was born in her?’ What it says is this: Who will be able to report to Zion? Who will be able to announce to her concerning men that a man shall be born in her and shall save her? That is, no human being can announce to her that Zion is saved by the man who shall be born in her.”

So far Jerome. These things are such that Faber’s philosophy accomplishes nothing here.

### Verse 6 — “The Lord shall recount in the writings of the peoples.”

Jerome and Nebiensis: “The Lord has counted, writing the peoples.” Münster: “The Lord shall recount, when he has written the peoples.” Nearly all the others render it similarly. The Hebrew word here is the infinitive **BICHTHOB**, so that one may freely translate either “while he was writing the peoples” or “in the writing of the peoples.” Pellicanus also noted this.

Then the words “and of princes” must have been taken by the Septuagint from the beginning of the following verse in the Hebrew, and brought here: **VESSARIM**, which is ambiguous between “princes” and “singers,” as the latter Hebraists understand it, although the difference lies in the smallest vowel-point.

Further, where we say “who were in her,” the Hebrew has **ZEH JULLAD SAM**, that is, “this one was born there.” But it is customary for Hebrews to use the singular in place of the plural, especially where the sense required by the context demands it. And if you insist that this passage ought to be understood of Christ himself, nothing prevents a transition from head to members and conversely, on account of their unity. This is so frequent in the sacred writings that I do not know whether there is any mode of speech more common.

The Septuagint, as said above, joined the first part of the last verse, according to the Hebrew, to the penultimate verse. Then follows: “as of those rejoicing,” **KEHOLLIM**. Jerome translates, “as in choirs”; Pratensis, “as choristers”; Sanctes and Münster, “as flute-players”; the translators for Cajetan, “as women in labor”; Pellicanus, “as those dancing”; Nebiensis, “as those leading a dance”; the Chaldean, “and they shall utter song in choirs.” Although the word is ambiguous, almost every rendering conveys no slight joy.

But **CAL**, the particle of universality, according to them refers to what follows: **CAL MAAIANAI BAC**, “all my fountains are in you,” as Pellicanus, Sanctes, the translators for Cajetan, and Münster translate—“all my springs.” In three copies known to Jerome I found “all my strong ones.” The first was Faber’s, which he testifies he drew from the libraries of the Carthusians and Celestines; the second was the Froben edition; the third, that of Chevallon of Paris; a fourth, among the more recent editions, had “fountains.” Hence perhaps “strong ones” had slipped in for “fountains.”

Finally, Pratensis has: “all my contemplations.” Rabbi Jonah, as cited by Sanctes, has: “all my providences,” as it were “my lookings,” from a word meaning “eye.” Yet in truth we dwell in heaven through contemplation and heavenly desire, according to Philippians 3: “Our citizenship is in heaven.” Therefore the Septuagint rendered the more fitting sense; and in the one in whom God dwells through faith and charity there shall be “a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4). The translator for Campensis likewise has “a dwelling is in you,” with the Septuagint, although at the beginning he had said that his edition was based on the Hebrew truth.

## Psalm 87

[Col. 0809]

> “TITLE OF THE PSALM: A SONG OF A PSALM FOR THE SONS OF KORAH, TO THE END, FOR MAELETH [Note: This was discussed under the title of Psalm 52, Col. 0809D], TO ANSWER; AN UNDERSTANDING OF HEMAN THE ISRAELITE, OR EZRAHITE.”

[Col. 0809C]

“Heman the Ezrahite” is better, for the Hebrew reads thus; and certain Greek manuscripts had **Αἱθὰμ τῷ ὁρακλήτῃ**, “Aitham the inspired speaker.” Others had **Αἰμὰν τῷ Ἰσραηλίτῃ**, “Aiman the Israelite.” The former have been corrupted by a copyist in two respects, the latter in one only; and Augustine’s exposition sometimes follows the latter.

### “O Lord, God of my salvation.”

Title: “A song of a psalm for the sons of Korah, to the end, for Maeleth, to answer; an understanding of Heman the Israelite, or Ezrahite.”

[Augustine, Jerome, Augustine.] As we have often said, “song” denotes exultation of mind, while “psalm” denotes good action. Therefore psalms which have both these terms in their titles concern good action and the gladness of mind, as does this psalm. The sons of Korah, as we said above, are sons of the cross, sons of the Passion; this has been fully treated above. And the meaning of “to the end” has also been expounded above.

What follows, “for Maeleth, to answer,” is unusual in this title. **Maeleth** means “choir,” called “to answer,” because the choir answers the singer by singing in harmony. We should believe that not this psalm alone but other psalms also were sung in this manner. For in the singing of this psalm and others the choir answered the precentor, although they received different titles. I think this was done for variety, to relieve weariness. Titles vary in order to relieve weariness, or perhaps for another reason not sufficiently known.

I shall explain the mystery which seems to me to be indicated by “for Maeleth,” that is, “for the choir,” “to answer,” that is, that the choir should answer the singer. Here the Passion of Christ is prophesied, to which we must answer by imitation, as Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his steps” (1 Peter 2). This is to answer. Hence John also says: “As Christ laid down his life for us, so we too ought to lay down our lives for the brethren” (1 John 3). This is what is meant there by “to answer.” But this is of no benefit unless it is done in a choir, that is, in the harmony of charity. Hence the Apostle: “If I should deliver my body to be burned, but have not charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13).

**Heman** means “his brother.” Christ’s brethren here are those who glory in the cross, like the Apostle who says: “But far be it from me to glory, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6). These are true Israelites, that is, those who see God. Or Heman is called “the Ezrahite,” that is, “the stranger,” for he is said to have been an Easterner.

The sense of the title is: This song, called a “song” because the joyful end of the Passion is shown here, and a “psalm” because it deals with good action, is sung for the sons of Korah, that is, the sons of Christ, directing them toward the end of heavenly crowns. For what purpose is it sung to them? To answer Christ: that they may answer Christ, as it were the precentor, by imitation or thanksgiving, imitating the footsteps of his Passion. And let them do this “for Maeleth,” that is, in Maeleth—in the choir, that is, in the harmony of charity.

And this is the understanding of Heman the Israelite: namely, of those who are Christ’s brethren, glorying in his cross and seeing God. Or literally: this is the understanding of Heman, that is, of the man who understood this mystery in the choir responding to the singers—an Israelite or Ezrahite, that is, a stranger from the eastern regions.

Its intention is to exhort us to imitate Christ’s Passion. Its structure has four parts. First, Christ, in the form of a servant, prays for help, reporting that he has been despised by enemies. Second, he tells what his friends did in the Passion, at “You have removed far from me,” and so on. Third, he shows to whom his works are of no benefit, at “Will you work wonders for the dead?” Fourth, he says what he suffers in his members, at “But I cry to you.”

Therefore, praying to the Father in the form of a servant, he says:

### Verse 1 — “O Lord, God of my salvation, I have cried by day and by night before you.”

“O Lord God,” author of my salvation, because all comes from him, “I have cried before you.” He says this in the form of a servant, “by day and by night,” because Christ prayed both amid prosperous things and amid adversities. Therefore:

### Verse 2 — “Let my prayer enter into your sight; incline your ear to my petition.”

“Let my prayer enter into your sight.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The entering of prayer is its acceptance. He then repeats it, saying: “Incline your ear to my petition.” The inclination of God’s ear is his merciful hearing. Here is marked the great power of pure prayer, which, like a person, enters to God and performs the commission to which flesh cannot attain. He adds why he prays:

### Verse 3 — “For my soul is filled with evils, and my life has drawn near to hell.”

“For my soul is filled with evils”—not vices, but sorrows, by which the soul suffers with the flesh. Bodily pain cannot exist without the soul. Yet the soul may suffer pain even when the body does not suffer. Therefore Christ’s soul was filled not with sins but with human evils, that is, sorrows. This is what he himself says: “My soul is sorrowful” (Matthew 26).

Or: “My soul is filled,” namely with the evils of the perishing people, through compassion; “and my life has drawn near to hell,” while I am handed over to death. This is what he says in the Gospel: “unto death” (ibid.). What he says there, “My soul is sorrowful,” is said here: “My soul is filled with evils.” And what follows there, “unto death,” is said here: “And my life has drawn near to hell.”

He took these affections of human weakness, like the flesh itself and death, not from the necessity of his condition but by the will of compassion, so that he might transfigure in himself his body, which is the Church. Thus, if any of his own should happen to be sad or to suffer amid human temptations, that person should not think himself alien from God’s grace; and, so that he might know these things to be not sins but signs of human weakness, the body would learn from its own Head, like a choir harmonizing with the voice set before it.

### Verse 4 — “I am counted with those who go down into the pit; I am made like a man without help, free among the dead.”

“I am counted.” [Alcuin, Augustine.] As if he said: I have suffered not only grievous things but shameful ones as well, because I “am counted with those who go down into the pit” of misery or the depth of hell—by those, of course, who did not know what they were doing. They thought that he died by necessity, as other people die.

“I am made,” that is, I am judged by the same ignorant persons, “like a man,” simply, “without help”; although I was “free among the dead,” that is, alone without sin among sinners, and able to lay down my life and take it up again (John 10). Again: “I am counted.”

### Verse 5 — “Like the wounded sleeping in graves, whom you remember no more; and they have been cast away from your hand.”

“Like the wounded sleeping in graves,” [Augustine] because he too was wounded by the lance and shut in a sepulchre. Yet he differs in what follows: “whom you do not yet remember,” according to another reading—that is, whose time of resurrection has not yet come. In this Christ is distinguished from the other dead: wounded and dead, he was placed in the tomb, but on the third day he awoke.

But those who did not know what they were doing thought him like others killed by wounds and sleeping in graves, whom God does not yet remember. Note that Scripture customarily calls the dead “those who sleep” (1 Thessalonians 4; John 11), because it wishes them to be understood as those who will awaken, that is, rise again; they will awaken in the resurrection (Matthew 25).

“And they”—those among whom I was thus made—“have been cast away, O God, from your hand,” that is, deprived of your help, for they thought that I was without God’s help. This does not refer to those sleeping in graves whom God does not yet remember, among whom are righteous persons. Though he does not yet remember them so that they may rise, nevertheless it has been said of them: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God.”

Or: “I am counted as wounded persons sleeping,” [Jerome] that is, as wicked persons; “sleeping in graves,” that is, lulled asleep by fleshly pleasure, buried in debaucheries and obscenities, whom God does not awaken, whom God does not remember. “And they”—either those sleeping, or those among whom I was thus made—“have been cast away from your hand.”

### Verse 6 — “They have laid me in the lower pit: in dark places, and in the shadow of death.”

“They have laid me in the lower pit,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin] that is, in the deepest misery of the world, because he was taken away by a shameful death; “in dark places,” that is, in the darkness of oblivion, where no one would seek him; “and in the shadow of death.” The shadow of death is the place of evils where they are punished.

Or: they placed me, in their opinion, in the lower pit of vices, “in dark places and in the shadow of death,” that is, in the death of impiety. Or they truly placed me in the lower pit, that is, in the pit of hell, namely in dark places and in the shadow of death.

### Verse 7 — “Your wrath has been established upon me, and you have brought all your waves over me.”

“Your fury,” or “your wrath,” or “your indignation,” O God, “has been established upon me,” so that they were angry when they saw him die a shameful death. They thought that God’s wrath had destroyed him and that God had brought all indignations upon him when he allowed him to be crucified.

“And you have brought all your waves,” or “your liftings up,” that is, sufferings, over me. In another psalm he says: “They passed over me” (Psalm 41). But here he says: “You have brought them over me,” signifying that all that had been prophesied concerning his Passion came to pass.

### Part II. Verse 8 — “You have removed my acquaintances far from me; they have made me an abomination to themselves.”

“You have removed far from me.” The second part, in which he says what his friends did in the Passion. As if he said: You have brought these things over me, and then you have made far from me those to whom I was known. He does not say “the acquaintances whom he knew,” [Augustine] because all then knew him as God, but those to whom he was known. Or by “acquaintances” he means the good, whom he approves.

“You have removed” them far from me in place and mind; “and they have made me an abomination to themselves”—either the acquaintances themselves, because they recoiled from this kind of death, or rather the persecutors.

### Verse 9 — “I was delivered up and did not go forth; my eyes languished through poverty.”

“I was delivered up,” namely by the disciple, “and did not go forth,” that is, I did not reveal who I was; I lay hidden within myself, I was not manifested or made known. Hence “my eyes languished through poverty”: the apostles, seeing him not in power but as though defeated, were weakened because their food, that is, their light, had been withdrawn.

### Verse 10 — “I cried to you, O Lord; all day long I stretched out my hands to you.”

“I cried to you, O Lord.” [Augustine.] He plainly did this upon the cross. “All day long I stretched out my hands to you,” because he did all things according to the Father’s will. For by hands stretched out is understood the continuance of good works, from which he never ceased. The stretching out on the cross did not last one whole day; nor can “the whole” be taken for “a part,” since he adds “all.” But because these works did not benefit everyone, he adds:

### Part III. Verse 11 — “Will you work wonders for the dead? Or will physicians raise them up, and will they confess to you?”

“Will you?” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The third part, in which he shows to whom his works are of no benefit. As if he said: I stretched out my hands; but, O God, will you work wonders for the dead? By “dead” he means not bodily but in heart. Christ’s miracles are indeed performed before them, but they do not benefit them because the things seen do not move them to the life of faith.

Wonders were performed for those dead in body when some rose again, and when the Lord entered hell and ascended from it as victor over death: a great miracle was done for the dead. He therefore says: Will you work wonders for those dead in heart, not body? As if to say: No. He does not say that they are done for those whom they do not benefit even if they are done; therefore they are not done for them, because people will not be raised by physicians in order that they may confess to the Lord.

This is what follows: “Or will physicians,” or “giants,” “raise persons, and will those raised confess to you?” No. For confession perishes from a heart that is dead; unless it is raised, it cannot confess. But physicians, or giants, will not raise people so that they may confess to the Lord.

It should be noted that the Hebrew has not “physicians” but “giants.” Yet both sound almost the same in Hebrew. Therefore the Seventy Interpreters, whose authority is so great that, because of their remarkable concord, they are believed to have translated by the divine Spirit, rendered “physicians” rather than “giants,” not through error but through the opportunity presented by the similarity of the words in Hebrew, where physicians and giants sound alike and are distinguished by a slight difference. They wished to signify how the giants should be understood.

If, therefore, giants here are understood as the proud—that is, as the wise of the world—they are aptly called physicians, because by their arts they promise health to souls; against them it is said, “Salvation belongs to the Lord” (Psalm 3). But if giants are understood as the good—that is, the great and strong—they too are aptly called physicians, who can heal by their ministry while people are living, but cannot raise the dead. For they are restored to life in faith by God’s grace alone. Hence: “No one can come to me unless my Father draws him” (John 6).

### Verse 12 — “Will anyone in the grave declare your mercy, and your truth in destruction?”

“Will anyone placed in the grave?” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The body is the grave of the dead soul. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says to such persons: “You are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to men, but inwardly are full of dead men’s bones and every uncleanness; so you also outwardly appear righteous to men, but inwardly are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (Matthew 23).

Will anyone placed in a grave, that is, in the ruin of the soul, declare your mercy? And will anyone placed in destruction, that is, hardened, declare your truth? As if he said: These will not declare it, but the living and faithful will.

It should be noted that Scripture, especially the Psalms, loves to join mercy and truth.

### Verse 13 — “Will your wonders be known in darkness, and your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?”

“Will they be known in the darkness” [Augustine] of unbelievers, “your wonders, and your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness,” which says, “There is no God”? These are the darknesses. Hence the Apostle: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5). Therefore the dead, those placed in graves, darkness, and the land of forgetfulness are the same persons.
