### Part IV. Verse 14 — “But I have cried to you, O Lord, and in the morning my prayer shall come before you.”

“But I have cried to you.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The fourth part, in which Christ says what he suffers in his members. Behold the choir answering the precentor. As if he said: Christ’s works do not benefit these dead persons. What use, then, do the dead serve? What does he do with them for the benefit of his body, that is, the Church? Much: for in them is shown what grace is in the predestined.

Therefore Christ speaks in the voice of the Church: “But I.” As if he said: We too were once with them by nature children of wrath, with whom we were one. Therefore he does not simply say “I,” but “I too”: I also was by nature a child of wrath, as were the rest. But “I cried,” that I might be saved, “to you, O Lord,” not to another, because none of the physicians raises the dead.

But whoever cries and calls upon God believes; yet he would not believe unless God’s mercy had raised him. When mercy goes before him, it is already morning for him after the darkness of unbelief. But because future glorification remains, now “my prayer goes before.” This is the meaning: I cried, and thus morning of light or faith came to me. And in this morning, my prayer, preceded by mercy, “shall come before you,” that is, before the future judgment. In order that this prayer may burn more fervently, the good thing is delayed and evils are multiplied.

### Verse 15 — “Why, O Lord, do you reject my prayer and turn your face away from me?”

“Why, O Lord, do you reject?” [Gloss, Cassiodorus.] As if he said: I cry, I pray, but now why, O Lord, do you reject my prayer? See how greatly he desires: in these words he proposes that the reason why what he seeks is delayed should be sought. It lies in the postponement of the good and the multiplication of adversities, so that prayer, seemingly rejected, may be inflamed more ardently.

“Why do you turn your face away from me?” God is said to turn away his face by not giving what people want, but what is not advantageous.

### Verse 16 — “I am poor and in labors from my youth; but having been exalted, I was humbled and troubled.”

“I am poor.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] He briefly sets forth the tribulations of Christ’s body, saying: I am poor in worldly goods, and “I am in labors from my youth.” Hence elsewhere: “Often have they attacked me from my youth” (Psalm 128). “But having been exalted in the world, I was humbled.” [Cassiodorus.] Certain members of Christ are exalted in the world so that their humility may be greater. “And I was troubled” by adversities.

Or: “I was exalted,” formerly in a swollen heart; afterward “I was humbled,” namely through confession; “and I was troubled,” that is, ashamed of sins, condemning them.

### Verse 17 — “Your wrath passed over me, and your terrors troubled me.”

“Your wraths,” [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine] that is, afflictions, coming upon me—inflicted upon me—“passed over,” because God’s wrath does not remain upon the righteous but passes over. For it was said not of the faithful but of the unbelieving: “The wrath of God remains upon him.” He scourges the sons whom he receives (Hebrews 12), but for correction, not destruction. Hence: “Those whom I love I correct, rebuke, and chastise” (Revelation 3); and elsewhere: “I will strike, and I will heal; I will kill, and I will make alive” (Deuteronomy 32).

“And your terrors troubled me.” Everything that can happen, even if it does not happen, is prudently feared. They troubled me so severely because:

### Verse 18 — “They surrounded me like water; all day long they encompassed me together.”

“They surrounded me like water,” which submerges. [Haymo, Augustine.] Sometimes the terrors themselves so disturb the mind of one who reflects, while evils hang about him, that they seem to flow around and surround from every side at once. Hence friends and acquaintances abandon him in fear. Thus the Apostle says: “All deserted me” (2 Timothy 4).

And this happens “all day long,” because evils are never absent from the Church at any time until the age is ended. Therefore he adds: “They encompassed me together.” But all these things occur so that the prayer of the Church may come before God, until that salvation arrives in which no evil exists.

Or thus: “Your wraths passed over me,” that is, present punishments; “and your terrors troubled me,” [Cassiodorus] namely the terrors of the future judgment which all flesh fears. [Note: From Gregory, *Morals*, book 7, chapter 3; Col. 0815D.] Note that he says, “wraths passed over,” but “terrors troubled,” because one thing we already suffer concerning condemnation, and another we fear concerning eternal vengeance.

“Sins surrounded me all day long like water that submerges.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] For sins hem us in from every side with their abundant flood. He repeats: “They surrounded me together.”

Or this may be understood in the person of Christ, who says to the Father according to the form of a servant: “Your wraths,” that is, the afflictions which I suffer by your will, not by my merit, “passed over me,” that is, came upon me but were not to remain. “And your terrors,” namely those which I suffer because it pleased you, not because of my merit, “troubled me,” according to the weakness of the flesh. “My enemies surrounded me like water all day long; they surrounded me together.” Then follows speech in the person of Head and members together.

### Verse 19 — “You have removed friend and neighbor far from me, and my acquaintances because of misery.”

“You have removed far from me my friend,” [Cassiodorus] who is joined to us by devout and faithful affection, “and neighbor” by kinship. Human services are often withdrawn from the righteous through fear; and “my acquaintances,” who knew us merely by report or sight, you have removed because of my misery.

## Comparison on Psalm 87: “God of My Salvation,” etc.

### Verse 4 — “I am counted.”

All whom it was possible to consult translate passively with the Septuagint. Sanctes alone translated actively, “I counted myself,” contrary, however, to the rule of Hebrew. For the word is in the *Niphal*. For this reason the interpretation of the saints, who expound this verse of Christ the Lord, collapses: he was counted by unbelieving and impious Jews as one of the other dead who violently descend into the pit of hell. But the Lord, having power to lay down his life and take it up again, declares himself “free among the dead,” whom death could not bind in its chains. Therefore **NEHESCHABTI** means “I was reckoned,” or something similar, as in the Septuagint.

But if anyone relies on his own judgment, he introduces every confusion into the hidden senses. If the Septuagint had written, “I counted myself,” what would the foolish not have cried out? Sanctes himself, nevertheless, has “I was counted” in his *Thesaurus*.

### “In the shadow of death.”

Jerome rendered this “in the depths.” The others agree. The Hebrews now read **BIMZOLOTH**, but the Septuagint read **BETZALMAUETH**, with transposed letters: “in the shadow of death,” and so forth. If deep places are understood here, they imply the horror of death.

### Verse 8 — “They made me an abomination to themselves.”

The Hebrew has “you made,” referring it to God the Father. But the faithless made Christ an abomination, and the Father also “made” him so by that kind of expression found in Matthew: “I will strike the shepherd.” Similar expressions occur very frequently in Scripture.

### Verse 9 — “I was delivered up.”

Jerome with the others translates: “I was shut up,” **CALU**, from **CALA**, “he prohibited” or “he shut up.” But one who is delivered to deadly enemies is not far from chains and prison.

### Verse 10 — “Will physicians raise up?”

**REPHAIM** can signify three things: giants and strong men, as Jerome translates; physicians, as the Septuagint understands it—with Pellicanus agreeing; and the dead, as others have translated. Thus the ambiguity of the terms supplies material for differing interpretations, according as each interpreter sometimes permits. Yet we must constantly remember what Augustine writes here concerning the authority of the Seventy.

### Verse 15 — “Do you reject my prayer?”

The Hebrews have **NAPHSCHI**, that is, “my soul.” If you understand “the soul praying,” the sense comes back to the same thing. But **NEPHESCH** signifies not only “soul,” but also breath and exhalation, by which prayer is readily suggested.

### Verse 16 — “From my youth.”

Jerome, the Chaldean, Nebiensis, Sanctes, Münster, the translators for Cajetan, and the Campensian paraphrase agree in saying “from adolescence.” Pratensis, Pellicanus, and the edition for Campensis have “after shaking” or “affliction.” For **NOAR**, like many words, is ambiguous.

[Col. 0818B]

“Exalted.” The Septuagint pronounced **NISSETHI**, passively, where others read actively **NASATHI**, that is, “I bore.” Then **EMECA**, which literally means “your terrors.” The Seventy, expressing the sense, said: “I was humbled,” that is, “I was afflicted.” Finally: “and I was troubled.” In Hebrew: “I shall fear,” “I shall doubt”—**APHUNAH**, in the same sense.

### Verse 18 — “My acquaintances because of misery.”

Jerome translated: “You have taken away my acquaintances,” rendering “because of misery” by the verb “you have taken away.” Nebiensis agrees. With reference to the word **MAHASCHAC**, our Hebraists translate “in darkness,” “in obscurity”; Münster adds “you place,” or, as others wish, “they are darkness,” that is, they are unknown.

But if we understand Christ’s acquaintances as the disciples who turned their backs so that they might not be seized amid the same misery or Passion, we find that they were taken away from everyone’s sight and hidden. While they concealed themselves through fear of the Jews, they sought pleasant darknesses—that is, hiding places—lest they be sought for torture and death together with their best teacher, Christ. Thus misery, obscurity, and removal tend to the same meaning. Although perhaps Jerome understood **HASAC**, with the left-hand point, meaning “he refrained” and “he avoided.”

## Psalm 88

[Col. 0817]

> TITLE OF THE PSALM: “AN UNDERSTANDING OF ETHAN THE ISRAELITE.”  
> [Note: In the Hebrew, “the Ezrahite” occurs; Col. 0817D.]

[Col. 0817C]

### “The mercies of the Lord.”

Title: “An understanding of Ethan the Israelite.”

[Cassiodorus.] Ethan, as stated above, was appointed over the singers with several others in the tabernacle of the Lord. His name means “strong,” and no one is strong except in hope of God’s promise. That is the subject here. For this psalm says much about Christian hope and the magnificence of the Lord. No one who worthily petitions him is deceived by him; this the true Israelite understands. And this is its meaning: this is the understanding of Ethan, that is, of the strong Israelite—[Augustine] one who truly sees God.

Its intention is to exhort us to place our hope not in ourselves but in God. Its structure: [Cassiodorus] it has six parts. First, the Prophet promises that he will sing of God’s mercy and truth. Second, he describes God’s praises and power in various ways, at “The heavens shall confess.” Third, he sets forth the Father’s promises concerning Christ, at “Then you spoke.” Fourth, he contrasts adversities with those promises, at “But you have cast off,” and so forth. Fifth, he says in what manner the promises have been fulfilled, at “How long?” Sixth, he shows that the promises are also fulfilled spiritually in the members, not temporally, at “Where are your mercies?” and so forth.

[Augustine.] Therefore the Prophet, strong not in himself but in God’s mercy, says:

### Verse 1 — “I will sing for ever of the mercies of the Lord.”

I will sing, [Haymo, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Remigius], that is, joyfully proclaim, the mercies of the Lord. Hence a man is strong when he is weak in himself. I mean mercies that will endure for ever. God’s wrath is for a time; God’s mercy is for ever. Or: “For ever I will sing the mercies of the Lord.” How does he sing the mercies for ever and give thanks who remembers no misery? [Note: Col. 0818D. From Gregory, *Morals*, book IV, chapter 42.] But how is bliss complete if the memory of guilt touches the mind? We may answer that, while joyful, [Col. 0819A] we often remember sad things; and while healthy, we remember pains without pain. From this we are the more joyful and grateful. Thus, the recollection of misery takes nothing away from blessedness.

VERS. 2.—“From generation to generation I shall proclaim your truth with my mouth.”

In the generation of the Jews and in the generation of the Gentiles I shall proclaim your truth, [Cassiodorus, Augustine], that is, the truth which is yours, without which I am false. For whoever speaks from himself speaks falsehood; but whoever speaks truth speaks from God. Therefore, O God, I shall speak truth from you. And this, “with my mouth.” As though he said: I too shall speak. There are two things: one is yours, one is mine. Truth is yours; the mouth is mine, so that I may be a servant—that is, so that by it I may serve you. [Col. 0819B] For my members obey the Lord, or rather ought to obey him. Or: “I shall proclaim your truth,” that is, the truth of your promises, “with my mouth”; it does not merely slip from the mouth, but dwells there long, as something sweet.

VERS. 3.—“For you have said: Mercy shall be built up for ever in the heavens; your truth shall be established in them.”

“For you have said,” etc. [Alcuin, Augustine.] Here he says whence this comes, and what are God’s mercies through Christ. As though he said: I shall sing, and securely, because “you have said,” etc. Or the connection may be made thus: What mercies and what truth shall I sing? Behold: because you have said, that is, have made them known to me through the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0819C] As though he said: I, a man, confidently say what you, God, have said to me. What? That your mercy shall be built up for ever. The building up of mercy is not temporal, just as the ruin of iniquity is temporal. For in some persons temporal iniquity is destroyed, so that eternal mercy may be built up in those same persons. Hence the Lord says to Jeremiah: “Behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms, to root up and to destroy, to ruin and to scatter, to build and to plant” (Jer. 1).

Therefore, because of those who are destroyed and built up, lest they should suppose that the building up in which they are built was temporal, as the ruin in which they are destroyed was temporal, this man, whose mouth serves the truth of God, held to God’s very truth. “It shall be built up,” I say. And this is “in the heavens,” that is, through the heavens which declare the glory of God [Col. 0819D] (Ps. 18), through whom mercy is built up; and your truth itself shall be established “in them,” that is, through those heavens—or “without them,” as some books read. It should be noted that he repeated both things which he had stated before, namely mercy and truth, because all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. 24). For truth would not be displayed in the fulfilment of the promises unless mercy had first gone before in the forgiveness of sins. Indeed, truth pertains to the Jews, to whom the promises were made; mercy befits the Gentiles, from whom God did not shut off the fountain of his goodness. Hence the Apostle says: “For I say that Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision, for the fulfilment of God’s truth; but that the Gentiles should glorify God for mercy” (Rom. 15).

[Col. 0820A] 196 VERS. 4.—“I have made a covenant with my chosen ones; I have sworn to David my servant: I shall establish your seed for ever.”

“I have made.” [Augustine, Jerome, Augustine.] As though he said: You said that truth would be established; you also said this: “I have made a covenant,” namely the New Covenant, by which we are renewed unto a new inheritance—not, certainly, with all who are descended in the flesh from Abraham or David, but “with my chosen ones.” “I have sworn to David my servant,” literally, to that king. This man is secure because God said it, but more secure because he swore it. God’s oath is the confirmation of his promise. From both things a man becomes Ethan, that is, strong. What did I swear? That “I shall establish your seed for ever,” which is Abraham’s seed (Gal. 3), that is, Christ.

[Col. 0820B] VERS. 5.—“And I shall build up your throne from generation to generation.”

“And I shall build up from generation to generation,” [interlinear gloss, Jerome, Augustine], that is, for ever, “your throne,” that is, your royal power. Or: “I have sworn to David my servant,” that is, to Christ, everywhere obedient to me. Then he adds what he swore: “I shall establish your throne for ever,” that is, believers. For we who believe are Christ’s seed. Then what he called “seed” he calls “throne,” adding: “And I shall build up your seed,” that is, the faithful, in whom Christ rests and reigns. For unless we were governed by him, we should cast ourselves down by ourselves. And this is “from generation to generation,” that is, in every generation. For “generation” cannot be repeated as often as [Col. 0820C] it passes away. Therefore the repetition is put for every generation.

Or two generations should be understood: one carnal, the other future in the resurrection. In both Christ is preached; but here Christ is preached in order that he may be believed, there he will be preached in order that he may be seen. This is what he said above: “From generation to generation I shall proclaim your truth.” Thus Christ now sits in us whom he governs; then too he will sit in the saints, in whom he will reign. Or thus: Christ’s throne will be built up from generation to generation.

PART II. Διάψαλμα [interlude]. VERS. 6.—“The heavens shall confess your wonders, O Lord; indeed, your truth in the assembly of the saints.”

“The heavens shall confess.” [Cassiodorus.] The second part, in which [Col. 0820D] he describes in various ways the praises and power of God. [Alcuin, Augustine.] As though he said: You said that mercy would be built up; and as you said, so it shall be, because the heavens, made certain by your speaking and swearing, “shall confess,” that is, praise—not their own merits, but “your wonders, O Lord,” namely that you redeem and justify through mercy. For in every mercy shown to the lost, in the justification of the ungodly, what do we praise except God’s wonders? You praise because the dead rose; praise more because the lost were redeemed. You see a man yesterday a gulf of drunkenness, today an ornament of sobriety. You see a man yesterday the mire of lust, today the glory of self-restraint; yesterday a blasphemer of God, today a praiser of God. You see a man yesterday a servant of the creature, today a worshipper of the Creator. [Col. 0821A] These are the wonders which the heavens confess. Where shall they confess them? “In the Church”; indeed—or without “indeed”—they shall confess your truth, that is, the fulfilment of promises, “in the assembly of the saints.”

Or they shall confess the wonders, namely how God does and governs all things everywhere. [Cassiodorus.] “Indeed, your truth in the assembly of the saints.” Truth is proclaimed in the Church, where it is believed that the Word became flesh (John 1), and that the Trinity is one God.

VERS. 7.—“For who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Who shall be like God among the sons of God?”

“For who?” [Augustine.] As though he said: They preach confidently concerning you, because who among the clouds—that is, among preachers, even if they are mighty—shall be equal in power [Col. 0821B] to the Lord, namely Christ, even though he himself is man, who also came in the cloud of flesh? Hence Isaiah: “The Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and shall enter Egypt” (Isa. 19). It should be noted that heavens and clouds are the same thing, namely preachers: they are called heavens because of the brightness of truth; preachers are called clouds, which are misty, because of flesh and mortality, and because they pass by—where, that is, in whom, things are hidden which will later be made clear at the judgment.

And who, among the many sons of God—that is, among beings above or among men—will be like the Lord, namely Christ, in essence? He is the only Son of God. As though he said: No one. Therefore, let him not be thought merely a man. For he is Son by nature; we are adopted sons. He is begotten; we are created. He is begotten from eternity; we were made in time. He is one; we are many. [Col. 0821C] And truly none is like him, because he is

VERS. 8.—“God, who is glorified in the counsel of the saints, great and terrible above all who are around him.”

“God, who is glorified in the counsel of the saints,” [Augustine] because they cannot be made equal to him. Their counsel is to believe in him and glory in him. He is great and terrible in power above all who are around him. “Around him” is said not because his divinity, whose greatness has no end (Ps. 144), is enclosed by boundaries. For that which is everywhere and bounded nowhere has nothing around itself, except that through the flesh he was in one place; and that place has around it all the nations, among whom, after the apostles had been sent, he was made great and terrible through miracles. [Col. 0821D]

Or, “above all who are around him he is great,” [Cassiodorus], that is, above angels or men, who are his attendants, not his equals, and who draw near to him through his gift. And truly above all, because, O

VERS. 9.—“O Lord, God of hosts, who is like you? You are mighty, O Lord, and your truth is around you.”

“O Lord, God of the heavenly hosts,” [Haymo, Cassiodorus], that is, of angels; or of the powers with which those around you are enriched: who is like you? No one. For you, O Lord, are mighty from yourself; [Augustine] but they are mighty from you, because you made all things, namely heaven and earth and everything in them. Yet greater for us is your mercy, which has displayed truth not merely in [Col. 0822A] the place where you were born; your truth has also been spread abroad among all who are around you. When you came in the clouds of heaven, that truth began to be preached, and the sea of Gentiles around the dry land of the Jews began to roar, like the lion against Samson when he went to take a wife from foreigners (Judg. 14). But there is no cause for fear, because

VERS. 10.—“You rule over the power of the sea; you calm the movement of its waves.”

“You rule over the power of the sea,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine], that is, over worldly honour. For the sea rises by your permission, you who do not permit a man to be tempted beyond what he can bear (1 Cor. 10). And you not only rule over it, but “you calm the movement of its waves,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] though you do not remove it utterly, so that a person may deserve the crown. [Col. 0822B] But, in order that the sea’s rage may be weakened within the sea itself,

VERS. 11.—“You have humbled the proud one like a wounded man; with the arm of your strength you have scattered your enemies.”

“You have humbled the proud one,” [Augustine], that is, the dragon made in the sea to be played with (Ps. 103), who is humbled through humble Christ, in whom others are humble. For Christ humbled himself in order to humble the proud one. The proud one held proud people, “like a wounded man.” [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine.] The devil is wounded when Christ is wounded. He is not yet wholly dead; therefore he was humbled by losing those whom he held wounded—not because flesh, which he did not possess, was pierced, but because the heart was struck, where he was proud.

“With the arm of your strength,” [Jerome, Cassiodorus, Alcuin], that is, in your [Col. 0822C] strength. Or, in Christ you have scattered your enemies, that is, the powers of the air. Or, you have scattered your enemies, that is, the Jews, throughout the world. Or, “you have scattered your enemies,” that is, from among men you have taken up some who are the devil’s spoils; others you have left, whom you permitted to follow after him. [Cassiodorus.] You have triumphed over the devil in heaven because

VERS. 12.—“The heavens are yours and the earth is yours; you founded the world and its fullness; you created the north and the sea.”

“The heavens are yours.” [Cassiodorus.] You have also triumphed on earth over the Jew because—and that is because—the earth is yours literally, and because heaven and earth are his. Why, then, should they be proud in what belongs to another? You founded, that is, established, [Col. 0822D] the world and its fullness. Why, then, do they raise themselves against him whose is the circuit of the world and all the creatures in it? You created the north, that is, the devil, and the sea, that is, the world. Therefore they foolishly raise themselves against him by whom they were created.

Or it may be read mystically thus. [Augustine, interlinear gloss, Augustine.] As though he said: “The heavens shall confess your wonders, O Lord,” and deservedly, because the heavens are yours, that is, the apostles, who rain truth upon others; and the earth is yours, which receives truth around you. By this rain you founded the world, that is, the whole Church, and its fullness, that is, the things or persons by whom it is daily filled; the north, that is, the devil, who said: “I shall set my throne in the north and shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14); and the sea, [interlinear gloss, Augustine], that is, bitter persons [Col. 0823A] by whom the Church is cleansed, you created. Therefore what you have done in them contributes more to your dominion than their own will contributes to their malice.

VERS. 13.—“Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in your name; your arm is with power.”

“Tabor and Hermon.” [Augustine.] These are mountains of Syria. Tabor is interpreted “the light coming”; Hermon, “his anathema,” namely, of the supreme Light which enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1). The light of grace came; when it came, there came to be his anathema—that is, the devil’s, who held us in his error or in his sorrow. This means: It is given us by you to be enlightened, so that we may pronounce anathema upon the devil. As though he said: You have done all these things; and therefore Tabor, that is, those to whom light comes from you, the supreme Light, [Col. 0823B] and Hermon, that is, those who pronounce anathema upon the devil, shall rejoice in your name, not in their own merits.

[Alcuin.] Or, because Tabor and Hermon are mountains of Syria, the Gentiles are understood through them—the whole from a part, by synecdoche—and they shall rejoice when Christ comes. Or it is read allegorically thus: Tabor, that is, the Jews, to whom the light first came; and Hermon, that is, the Gentiles, who were formerly anathematized, shall rejoice in your name, the two walls being joined in the corner-stone (Eph. 2). “Your arm.” [Augustine, interlinear gloss.] As though he said: We were made by you and also defended by you, because your arm, by which you humbled the proud one, is always with power, and always,

VERS. 14.—“Let your hand be strengthened and [Col. 0823C] your right hand be exalted; righteousness and judgment are the preparation of your throne.”

“Your hand,” [Cassiodorus], that is, your operation, let it be strengthened against the proud, so that they may be humbled; and let “your right hand” be exalted, that is, let the number of those who are to be placed at the right hand be made glorious and increased. But at the end there shall be righteousness and judgment, that is, the manifestation of your righteousness and your judgment, when the sheep, now hidden, are separated from the goats (Matt. 25). Then shall be the preparation of your throne. Certainly this shall be on the day of judgment. God’s throne is eternal, but at the judgment it will appear prepared, when he himself is seen to judge justly. That is, your throne will appear at the judgment prepared to execute righteousness and judgment, [Augustine] that is, [Col. 0823D] to judge justly. What, then, happens in the meantime? Behold:

VERS. 15.—“Mercy and truth shall go before your face; blessed is the people that knows jubilation.”

“Mercy and truth shall go before your face,” [Augustine], that is, the face of you who will judge afterward. As though he said: Meanwhile mercy goes before, by which you blot out sins, and truth, by which you fulfil promises, so that the judgments to come need not be feared. Since these joys cannot be sufficiently expounded, he says: “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation,” that is, which knows that there is something in him to be rejoiced over [197] which it knows cannot be expressed. For jubilation is joy that could not be explained in words and yet cannot be wholly kept silent. From where does jubilation arise? From grace, entirely from [Col. 0824A] God, not from you, O man. This is what follows:

VERS. 16.—“O Lord, they shall walk in the light of your countenance; they shall rejoice in your name all the day, and be exalted in your righteousness.”

“O Lord, in the light of your countenance,” [Jerome, Haymo, Augustine, [Col. 0824D] Jerome], that is, in the illumination of the Holy Spirit or of the Son, men shall walk, namely Tabor and Hermon. In these words he commends the grace from which jubilation comes.

Or, from the words “righteousness,” the passage may be read in the present tense: “Righteousness and judgment are the preparation of your throne,” that is, now, by discerning persons and adhering to just things, people prepare themselves as a throne for the Lord. And mercy and truth in people shall go before your face, [Alcuin, Cassiodorus], after the likeness of a forerunner preparing lodging for the Lord, [Col. 0824B] and from this there is cause for jubilation. Blessed is that people who knows jubilation. He knows jubilation who places his joy not in his own power but in the Lord’s; or who understands in his heart what he sings with his mouth. Hence this reward follows: “O Lord, they shall walk in the light of your countenance,” that is, they shall persevere here and in the future in contemplation of the Trinity. “And in your name,” [Jerome, Augustine], which is blessed on earth—that is, in the Christian name, not in themselves—“they shall rejoice all the day.” Whoever rejoices in himself does not rejoice all day, because he falls. But those whom he illumines and justifies “shall be exalted in your righteousness,” not in their own righteousness, in which they would be cast down, here and in the future. I say, in your righteousness,

VERS. 17.—“For you are the glory of their strength, and in your good pleasure our horn shall be exalted.”

“For [Col. 0824C] you are the glory of their strength.” [Interlinear gloss.] I say that they are blessed in your righteousness, because you are the glory, that is, the exaltation, of their strength: of those whom you not only illuminate but also empower. “And in your good pleasure,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus], because it pleased you, not because we are worthy. Or, “in your good pleasure,” that is, in Christ, “our horn,” that is, our power, shall be exalted. It is in him because he assumed our flesh, in whom all hope rests. He says this thus:

VERS. 18.—“For our assumption belongs to the Lord, and to the Holy One of Israel, our king.”

“For our assumption belongs to the Lord,” [Jerome, Augustine, Jerome], that is, the assumption of our flesh. Otherwise, when assailed, we should fall, because we should be weak. “And to the Holy One of Israel, our king,” that is, to him who sanctifies and rules Israel.

PART III. Διάψαλμα [interlude]. VERS. 19.—“Then you spoke in vision to your saints, and said: I have placed help in one who is mighty, and have exalted one chosen from my people.”

“Then you spoke.” [Augustine, interlinear gloss, Alcuin.] The third part, in which he sets forth the Father’s promises concerning Christ, thereby showing that the foregoing praise is not doubtful, since paternal authority confirms it. As though he said: O God, how do you know these things that were foretold? Behold the reason: because then, namely when you made the covenant—or then, namely when you spoke these things to me—you spoke to your saints, [Augustine, Alcuin], namely the other prophets. And this “in vision,” that is, secretly, in the revelation which you made to them; hence they are called prophets, that is, seers. [Col. 0825A] For they did not speak unknowingly, as Montanus and certain heretics maintained.

And you said, [Haymo, Augustine], openly through them: “I have placed the help of men in one who is mighty,” namely Christ. Who is that mighty one? The chosen one. Hence he adds: “And I have exalted the chosen one above every name” (Phil. 2), namely one free from sin, born from my Jewish people. Who is the chosen one? David, that is, Christ, because he is of David’s seed. And this is:

VERS. 20.—“I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him.”

“I have found David,” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine], that is, Christ. For David is interpreted “strong of hand”; [Col. 0825B] “my servant,” that is, obedient to me. Therefore I have placed help in him, and “with my holy oil I have anointed him,” according to his humanity. Hence elsewhere: “God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44). Therefore he is mighty, because

VERS. 21.—“For my hand shall help him, and my arm shall strengthen him.”

“My hand shall help him,” [Haymo, Cassiodorus], that is, the Word shall cooperate with him, according to his humanity, in works and sufferings. “And my arm,” [Cassiodorus, interlinear gloss], that is, the Word, which is my strength, shall strengthen him against adversities, so that he may carry out what he has begun; it shall strengthen him so far that

VERS. 22.—“The enemy shall gain nothing against him, and the son of iniquity shall not add to afflict him.”

[Col. 0825C] “The enemy,” [Jerome, Cassiodorus], that is, the devil, “shall gain nothing against him.” Hence he himself says: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14). “And the son of iniquity,” [interlinear gloss, Augustine], that is, Judas, “shall not add to afflict him,” that is, he shall not add effect to his wicked will. Or, after Christ’s resurrection, he shall not add to afflict him, as he delivered him up to suffering while he was still corruptible.

Or this may be said of Christ according to his members: “The enemy,” that is, the devil or persecutor, “shall gain nothing against him.” He indeed rages, exercises, and benefits, but does not harm. And “the son of iniquity,” that is, the enemy, “shall not add to afflict him”: he shall indeed do what belongs to him, but shall not harm him.

VERS. 23.—“And I shall cut down his enemies [Col. 0825D] before his face, and put to flight those who hate him.”

“And I shall cut down his enemies from their conspiracy.” [Augustine.] For they shall gradually believe, as though the head of the calf had been ground to powder, and shall come into the drink of God’s people, just as Moses ground the head of the calf and scattered it in the water and gave it to the children of Israel to drink (Exod. 32). [Cassiodorus.] And this is “before his face.” When his face looks upon sinners, they are separated from their crimes, for which there is no place in his presence. “And I shall put to flight those who hate him,” [Cassiodorus] so that they flee from him when angry to him when appeased.

VERS. 24.—“And my truth and my mercy shall be with him, and in my name his horn shall be exalted.”

“And my truth and my mercy shall be with him.” [Col. 0826A] [Augustine, interlinear gloss.] Nothing is divided between Father and Son: the powers which the Father has, the Son also has. It should be noted that mercy and truth are frequently commended to us, so that we may render them to God. For as he gave mercy to us by blotting out sins, and truth by fulfilling promises, so let us render mercy to God by having mercy on the miserable, and truth by not judging unjustly; and let neither impede the other, so that we may not be excessively lax in mercy or excessively rigid in truth. Otherwise we are not on God’s way, where mercy and truth met each other. “And in my name,” which is God, “his horn,” [Cassiodorus], that is, his power, shall be exalted.

VERS. 25.—“And I shall place his hand in the sea, and his right hand in the rivers.”

[Col. 0826B] “And I shall place his hand in the sea,” [Augustine, Jerome, Augustine, Cassiodorus], that is, he shall rule over the Gentiles, who are signified by the sea. Or, I shall show his works in the world. “And I shall place his right hand in the rivers,” that is, I shall subject even the covetous to him. For rivers run into the sea; so the covetous run into the bitterness of the world, and yet they are subject to Christ. Or, “in the rivers,” that is, in the waters of baptism, “I shall place his right hand,” that is, his operation. And this is because

VERS. 26.—“He himself called upon me: You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation.”

“He himself shall call upon me,” or “has called upon me,” saying: “You are my Father,” [Remigius, interlinear gloss], insofar as I am God; “and my God,” insofar as I am man; “and the protector of my salvation,” that is, the protector of me, weak as I am, unto salvation.

VERS. 27.—“And I shall make him the firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth.”

“And I shall make,” that is, appoint, him “the firstborn,” [Remigius, Augustine, Jerome], that is, honour him above others, by comparison with the honour customarily given to firstborn sons; and I shall make him exalted above the kings of the earth—or, in another reading, among the kings of the earth—which has already been fulfilled. And because this power is not temporal, he adds:

VERS. 28.—“For ever I shall preserve my mercy for him, and my covenant shall be faithful to him.”

“I shall preserve my mercy for him for ever,” [Col. 0826D] [Cassiodorus], to whom everlasting power has been given in heaven and on earth (Matt. 28). “And my covenant shall be faithful to him,” because everything foretold about him has been fulfilled wholly in him. Or, the covenant, that is, the promise of eternal inheritance, is faithful to him who is mediator of the same covenant, [Augustine] that is, its signatory, surety, and witness; and he himself is the inheritance.

VERS. 29.—“And I shall establish his seed for ever and ever, and his throne as the days of heaven.”

“And I shall establish his Christian seed for ever and ever,” [Augustine], that is, eternally, “and his throne as the days of heaven.” The thrones of earthly kings endure like the days of earth, which pass away; but the days of heaven are always present, where his throne shall be for ever.

[Col. 0827A] VERS. 30.—“But if his children forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments.”

“But if.” [Alcuin.] As though he said: I promise this not only concerning those who persevere, but also concerning those who fall. And this is: “But if his children,” Christ’s children, “forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments.”

VERS. 31.—“If they profane my statutes and do not keep my commandments.”

“If they profane my statutes,” [Haymo, Augustine], that is, offend against them by acting badly, “and do not keep my commandments,” I shall not therefore destroy them, but:

VERS. 32.—“I shall visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with stripes.”

[Col. 0827B] “I shall visit,” [Haymo, Augustine], as a physician, “their iniquities with a rod,” that is, with a light correction; and in the rod there is mercy: it strikes indeed, but restores the inheritance. For what son is there to whom his father does not give discipline? A father gives discipline so that he may not withdraw mercy; he strikes the stubborn so that he may return to the inheritance. “For whom the Lord loves he corrects, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12). Therefore mercy belongs not only to the one who calls, but also to the one who scourges and strikes. Hence it follows: “And with stripes,” [Haymo], that is, in more grievous tribulation, I shall visit their sins.

VERS. 33.—“But I shall not scatter my mercy away from him, nor shall I harm in my truth.”

[Col. 0827C] “But I shall not scatter my mercy away from him,” namely David, [Augustine], that is, Christ, from whose body—which is one with its head—he does not withdraw mercy. For he does not take mercy away from one who is indeed a Christian. But if a man is so wicked that he flees when the father approaches, he himself alienates himself from the inheritance; the father does not cast him off. “Nor shall I harm him in my truth.” For mercy that delivers is not withdrawn in order that truth that punishes may not harm.

VERS. 34.—“Nor shall I profane my covenant, nor make void the things that proceed from my lips.”

“Nor shall I profane,” [Haymo, Cassiodorus, Augustine], that is, violate, “my covenant,” that is, my agreement. A promise would be profane [Col. 0827D] if it remained unfulfilled; for I shall not be found false because his children sin. For I have promised [198] and I act. Even if the chaff departs, he is not thereby without an inheritance. Because of evil fish, shall nothing from that net be put into vessels? Surely the good fish will be put in, that is, those whom he predestined. [Cassiodorus.] For God’s covenant remains unchangeable. Then, for confirmation, he repeats what he said: “The things that proceed from my lips,” that is, from the prophets, “I shall not make void.” This repetition is confirmation.

VERS. 35.—“Once I have sworn by my holiness: If I lie to David, his seed shall remain for ever.”

“Once,” [interlinear gloss, Haymo, Cassiodorus, Augustine], as though he said: [Col. 0828A] Truly I shall not make them void, because I have sworn to David, the man, son of Jesse, once—that is, eternally or unchangeably. A human being swears frequently, but God only once, for he does not change. And this is “by my holiness,” that is, in my secret, from which the prophets drank. Or, “by my holiness,” that is, in the man Christ, in whom what I swore was to be fulfilled. What did I swear? [Cassiodorus, interlinear gloss.] That his seed, Christ, shall remain for ever in God’s kingdom. “If I lie to David”—an *aposiopēsis* [deliberate breaking-off], as though: I would be true to no one.

Or: I swore once, [interlinear gloss, Alcuin, Augustine, interlinear gloss], that is, unchangeably and eternally, to David, that is, Christ, by my holiness. What? That “his seed,” that is, Christians, shall remain for ever in God’s kingdom. “And if I lie to David,” that is, to Christ, I shall be true to no one; and this is an *aposiopēsis*. [Col. 0828B]

VERS. 36.—“And his throne shall be as the sun before me, and as the perfect moon for ever, and as a faithful witness in heaven.”

“And his throne shall be as the sun before me,” [Augustine], though this is not before human eyes: that is, those in whom he sits and rules—the members who bear the head—“shall shine as the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13). “And as the perfect moon for ever,” namely one that will not again wane. Therefore the saints in the future kingdom shall shine like the sun according to the soul, which shall then be glorified by God’s glorification or contemplation; and they shall shine like the moon according to the body, which is now changeable like the moon, [Col. 0828C] but shall then be unchangeable and perfect.

[Alcuin.] Then the saints shall be perfect in both respects, clothed and glorified with the twofold robe. This was signified in the Old Testament by the board one cubit wide, divided in the middle, placed at the corners of the western wall and holding the two walls of the tabernacle together (Exod. 26), because the faithful of both the New and Old Testaments shall, after the setting of death, be glorified with a twofold blessedness. And hence “the faithful witness is in heaven,” that is, Christ. [Augustine.] Since in nothing is the Christian faith so contradicted as in the resurrection of bodies, Christ himself raised his own flesh, in order to confront every opponent; and though he could have healed his members so that it would not appear that they had been wounded, he nevertheless kept the scars in his body in order to heal the wound of doubt [Col. 0828D] in the heart.

PART IV. Διάψαλμα [interlude]. VERS. 37.—“But you have rejected and despised; you have deferred your Christ.”

“But you.” [Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] The fourth part, in which he sets forth things that appear contrary to the promises previously mentioned, lest those promises be thought fulfilled in someone other than Christ who was then to come. As though he said: These foretold goods belong to Christians, but not to Jews, who deprived themselves of the promise. And this is: “But you have rejected your Christ,” that is, you rejected the anointed David from the kingdom because of the sin he committed against Uriah through Bathsheba (2 Sam. 11). “And you have despised,” or “spurned,” him, because he suffered many indignities; and you have deferred him from the kingdom, by permitting him to remain long in tribulation.

[Col. 0829A] VERS. 38.—“You have turned away the covenant of your servant; you have profaned his sanctuary upon the earth.”

“You have turned away the covenant of your servant,” [Cassiodorus], that is, the covenant made with your servant, because the promises brought to the Jews have passed to the Gentiles.

[Augustine.] Or thus, and it is read simply and literally concerning David and his kingdom. As though he said: You promised all those things, but did these contrary things, because you rejected and despised David and his kingdom, which you brought to nothing; and this is astonishing. For you who promised, who confirmed, who even swore because of human doubt, both promised those things and did these things. Where, then, shall I hold fast your oath? Where shall I find your promise? Why did God promise those things and do these things? He did these things in order to establish the promises. [Col. 0829B]

For David was the one to whom all things were promised, but they were to be fulfilled not in David himself but in his seed, which is Christ (Gal. 3). Therefore, lest, because they were said to him, they should seem to have been fulfilled in him, God destroyed them in David, so that those things which had necessarily to come about because God had sworn might be sought in another. Thus Solomon too, David’s son, who became so great in wisdom and prudence that God’s promise concerning David’s seed was thought to have been fulfilled in him, fell (3 Kings 2), lest he be thought to be David’s seed in whom the promise was fulfilled. Likewise, when it was said to Rebecca, “The greater shall serve the lesser” (Gen. 25), Jacob bowed to the greater Esau (Gen. 33), so that this promise might be awaited in others.

Thus you rejected and despised this David, in whom the ignorant hoped that God’s promises would be fulfilled, [Col. 0829C] [Cassiodorus, Augustine]; yet you did not take away but deferred your Christ, your Son, so that the promises might be awaited more firmly in another rather than in that David. Hence he adds: “You have turned away the covenant of your servant,” which had been made with your servant—namely, the Old Covenant of the Jews. Their kingdom no longer exists; neither their sacrifice nor priesthood nor altar exists. You have profaned “upon the earth,” that is, throughout the earth, his sanctuary, or the holy things which they had. God showed them that these things were earthly.

VERS. 39.—“You have destroyed all his hedges; you have made his stronghold a terror.”

“You have destroyed all his hedges,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus], that is, the fortifications by which you had protected them, so that they might be plundered by enemies once they had lost God’s protection. [Col. 0829D] “You have made his stronghold a terror,” so that it may be said to sinners: “If God did not spare the natural branches, which seemed a stronghold, neither will he spare you” (Rom. 2). Or: “You have made his stronghold a terror,” [Cassiodorus], that is, what had been their support became fear to them on account of guilt—namely God. And:

VERS. 40.—“All who pass by the way have plundered him; he has become a reproach to his neighbours.”

“They have plundered him,” [Augustine, interlinear gloss], namely David—that is, Israel scattered everywhere—“all who pass by the way,” that is, the Gentiles who pass through this life, providing nothing for the future. “He has become a reproach to his neighbours,” [Col. 0830A] that is, the Jews have been regarded as a reproach by the Gentiles.

VERS. 41.—“You have exalted the right hand of those who oppress him; you have made all his enemies glad.”

“You have exalted the right hand of those who oppress him; you have made all his enemies glad.” [Augustine.] We see all these things fulfilled in the Jews.

VERS. 42.—“You have turned away the help of his sword, and have not aided him in battle.”

The support of his sword you have turned away, [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] For formerly a few used to conquer many; now they are conquered and taken captive. For a people armed without God is unarmed. And you have not helped him in battle.

VERSE 43.—“You have destroyed him from cleansing; and you have dashed his throne to the ground.”

[Col. 0830B] You have destroyed him from cleansing. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] This is graver than all the rest: that is, the scourges do not cleanse them, because the Jew lacks the faith by which hearts are cleansed. And you have dashed his throne to the ground: that is, their kingdom has everywhere been destroyed, because there is now no ruler from among them.

VERSE 44.—“You have shortened the days of his time; you have covered him with confusion.”

You have shortened the days of his time, [Alcuin, Augustine, Alcuin,] because their kingdom would have stood for a long time if it had been under God. They also thought that they would reign forever; but you have shortened the days of their kingdom, so that it did not stand, according to their expectation. Nor did it stand as long as it would have stood had it been under God. You have covered him with confusion, [Cassiodorus, Augustine,] because they bear the reproach of unbelief. [Col. 0830C] All these things came upon the Jews—not, however, with Christ and the eternal kingdom taken away from them, but deferred. Therefore he says to God:

PART V. Interlude. VERSE 45.—“How long, O Lord, do you turn away unto the end? Shall your wrath burn like fire?”

How long? [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] The fifth part. Behold, here he says in whom the promises have been fulfilled: namely, in the substance of David, which lives and delivers the soul—that is, in Christ. As if he said: You have inflicted these harsh things upon the Jews; but how long, O Lord, do you turn Israel away from faith and salvation—unto the end, that is, forever? No, Lord: rather, let Israel be saved. For blindness has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter in, and thus all [Col. 0830D] Israel should be saved (Rom. II [11]). Meanwhile, however, your wrath shall burn like fire; [Gloss, interlinear] or, likewise as a question, it may be said: Shall your wrath burn, that is, consume, like fire? As if he said: No, Lord, but rather:

VERSE 46.—“Remember what my substance is; for have you established all the children of men in vain?”

Remember. [Augustine.] David says this, being in the flesh situated among the Jews, but in hope situated in Christ. What is my substance in Christ? Even if the Jews fail, my substance does not fail. The root from which Mary will come does not wholly perish; and from her will come the seed to whom the promise was made. For the Virgin Mary was from that people; from the Virgin Mary came Christ’s flesh. And that flesh is not sinful, [Col. 0831A] but the cleanser of sins. For have you established all the children of men in vain? All the children of men go in vanity; yet you did not establish them in vain. How, then, do you cleanse them from vanity? Have you kept nothing for yourself through which you may cleanse them? You cleanse them through the seed in which my substance is; concerning which he adds:

VERSE 47.—“Who is the man that shall live and not see death? Shall he deliver his soul from the hand of hell?”

Who is he? [Augustine.] That is, how great is the man who shall live, rising from the dead, and shall not see death, because he shall no longer die? Yet he was in death, but he shall deliver—or has delivered—his soul from the hand of hell. Behold, Christ is truly signified here as the one wholly and uniquely singular person. [Col. 0831B] For this suits no one but Christ. For although those who rise again shall live and shall no longer see death, they themselves will not deliver their souls from the hand of hell; rather, he who is able to lay down his soul and take it up again (John X [10]), from whom no one takes it away, delivers his own soul.

[Alcuin.] Or all these things may be understood of Christ and the Church. As if he said: You promised all those things, but you yourself have done these contrary things—which nevertheless are for salvation. And this is the meaning: Yet you have cast back your Christ to the cross, and have despised him—that is, have given him over to contempt—and have taken him away, or deferred him, from glory for a time. Or he says these things of Christ according to his members: You have overthrown the covenant of your servant—that is, the promise [Col. 0831C] which you had made to him seems overthrown. “I shall profane his sanctuary upon earth”: that is, his saints are regarded as profane. You have destroyed all his hedges, that is, the prelates, while they are slain; you have made his stronghold a terror: that is, those who strengthened others by teaching are now a terror to them while they are afflicted. And all who pass along the way have plundered him, that is, Christ, because some of them have now been plundered by those who pass along the way, which is Christ. He has become a reproach to his neighbors. You have exalted the right hand of those who oppress him; you have made all his enemies glad. These things are plain. You have turned away the help of his sword, that is, preaching, so that by it he might not prevail against his enemies. And you have not helped him in battle, but have given him over to sufferings. You have destroyed him from cleansing, and dashed his throne to the ground: that is, certain envious persons have failed and have been brought down to earth. [Col. 0831D] You have shortened the days of his time, as is supposed, while they are swiftly removed from life. And you have covered him with confusion. Behold, thus you have cast back your Christ and the Church. But how long, O Lord, do you turn away—that is, how long do you not raise Christ again? Is it unto the end? Far be it! How long shall your wrath burn like fire? It is a repetition. Remember what my substance is—that is, how frail it is, 199 how it is nothing unless it be redeemed through him; remember. For have you established all the children of men in vain? Therefore raise Christ again. For who among you is the man who lives and does not see death, and who shall deliver his soul from the hand of hell? No one. In these words he now asks help for man—that is, for the human race—or particularly for the Jews.

[Col. 0832A] PART VI. Interlude. VERSE 48.—“Where are your former mercies, O Lord, which you swore to David in your truth?”

Where are your mercies? [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] The sixth part, in which he says that the promises are fulfilled also in the members—not temporally, but spiritually. And he speaks in the person of the Church. The wording is connected thus according to the first reading: Behold, we now have that in which the promises are fulfilled; but we who believe still labor. Therefore on behalf of these he says, Where are your former mercies, O Lord? As if he said: You deliver, and yet for your sake we are put to death. Where, then, are your former mercies, O Lord—that is, those once made to the fathers? Why do you not do as you swore to David in your truth? Or it may be connected thus, according to [Col. 0832B] the second reading: [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] As if he said: No one shall live or deliver his soul. And since this is so, where are your former mercies, O Lord? Why do you not do as you swore to David in your truth? He now asks that the promises made to David be fulfilled.

VERSE 49.—“Remember, O Lord, the reproach of your servants, which I have borne in my bosom from many nations.”

Remember, O Lord, so as to reward. [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] For God seems to have forgotten while he delays: remember the reproach of your servants and of many nations—that is, remember the reproach inflicted upon your servants by many nations. For Christ now sits in heaven, and a charge is brought against Christians concerning Christ: that reproach I, the Church, have contained—or borne, or cherished—in my bosom, [Col. 0832C] that is, in the secret place of the mind, because she did not dare speak openly. For a long time Christians contained reproaches in their hearts and did not dare resist. But now the name of Christ is wonderful among the kings of the earth.

VERSE 50.—“Which your enemies, O Lord, have reproached; which they have reproached—the change of your Christ.”

That reproach your enemies, O Lord, [Augustine]—that is, Jews and pagans—have uttered, saying that Christ had perished. He repeats, “which they have reproached,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine,] magnifying their wickedness. What have they reproached? Behold: the change of your Christ. For they cast this against him: that Christ died, that he was crucified, [Col. 0832D] which is to be changed from temporal life to eternal life, from earth to heaven, from Jews to Gentiles. What, then, do the madmen allege? Is that which they allege a reproach? Would that they too might be changed in this way.

VERSE 51.—“Blessed be the Lord forever. Amen, amen.”

Blessed be the Lord. [Alcuin, Augustine.] This is an exclamation at the sight of Christ’s brightness. As if he said: Their reproach and curse are temporal; but the Lord is blessed forever, [Cassiodorus, Augustine,] against the curses of the nations. Amen, amen. Behold, it is like the prince’s subscription after his commands, which all make. And it is a confirmation.

## Comparison on Psalm LXXXVIII: “The Mercies of the Lord,” etc.

[Col. 0833A]

VERSE 3.—“For you have said.” The Hebrew now has, “this is what I said.” The sense is indeed not harmed. But if you attach fewer marks of punctuation, you remain free to pronounce either the second or the first person. Hence Jerome, in the Hebrew text in Froben’s edition, has *you have said*; others, *I said*.

“Mercy shall be built.” Here it is doubtful where the medial point of division should be placed: whether thus, “Mercy shall be built forever,” then, after a pause, “Your truth shall be established in the heavens”; or as we set it out in the earlier writing. Those who omit the final phrase, “in them,” certainly follow the second division; Augustine and Cassiodorus do this. For “your truth shall be established in the heavens in them” is an unusual expression, even though that phrase is accepted in many places. But in the Greek, “in them” is not read; the Hebrew, however, [Col. 0833B] has “in them.” The Chaldee and Nebiensis: “The world shall be built by mercy; in the heavens you shall establish, or fashion, your truth in them.” Arnobius, a very ancient author, divided it as we wrote at the beginning, because he included the clause “in them.” Hence Jerome, according to the Hebrew, to bind together the joints of the sentence, added the conjunction thus: “Everlasting mercy shall be built; you shall found the heavens, and your truth shall be in them.” Sanctes omitted “in them,” thus: “In the heavens you shall form your truth.” Munster, lest that phrase be omitted, said: “In the heavens themselves you shall form your truth.”

Augustine discusses at length the rationale of divisions in Scripture, in book III of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapters 2 and 3. It was fitting to transcribe his words here, because among Hebraists one will often encounter divisions of verses and sentences different from those found in the Vulgate reading. He says: “But where it can be explained neither by the rule of faith nor by the context of the discourse, it does no harm to punctuate according to whichever of the possible meanings is indicated. Such is that passage to the Corinthians: ‘Therefore, having these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of the Lord. Receive us: we have wronged no one.’ For it is doubtful whether ‘let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit’ means that cleansing is from defilement in both body and spirit; or whether ‘let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh’ is to be taken separately, with another sense following: ‘and, being spiritual, perfecting holiness in the fear of the Lord, receive us.’ Such ambiguities of division, therefore, lie within the reader’s power.” Thus the holy Augustine.

But in Hebrew a division is indicated, namely by the small circular mark attached to the letter *he* in *HABBANEH*, “shall be built.” This nevertheless would present no obstacle if we believe Campensis near the end of his grammar, where he says that this mark does not have a separating force in the Psalter, Proverbs, and the Book of Job. Furthermore, in what we render “forever,” Jerome, Sanctes, Munster, Campensis, the Chaldee, Nebiensis, Pratensis, Pellicanus, and the interpreters for Cajetan agree: “the world shall be built.” *OLAM* is undoubtedly ambiguous, but we ought not depart from the common reading. On this, see above.

VERSE 6.—“For indeed [you have said] your truth.” Faber boldly proclaims that the particle *etenim* (“for indeed”) should be struck through with an obelus on the authority of the Hebrew, although *aph* is read, that is, “also,” “indeed”; the Septuagint has *καὶ γάρ*, “for indeed.” What will rashness and the desire to criticize not dare? “Yet also” is milder. But Pellicanus too translates *etenim*, with the Septuagint.

[Col. 0834A] VERSE 12.—“The north and the sea.” Jerome and others have “the right [hand],” by which they understand the southern region, which is the right side of the world, just as the northern is the left. The Septuagint read it with *mem* at the end, that is, “sea” or “seas.” The Hebrew now has it with *nun*. The kinship of the words furnished occasion for the ambiguity.

VERSE 33.—“Nor will I harm,” etc. “[I] will not lie,” where we say, “I will not harm.” If anyone did not stand by his promises, he would greatly harm those who depend upon hope in the promises. And this would be to lie in his truth, that is, in his oath or promise. Again, if truth, which is God’s justice, were to exercise ultimate vengeance, would it rightly be said to harm? For this reason our reading, which breathes both meanings, is worthy and consonant with the Hebrew.

VERSE 37.—“You have deferred your Christ.” Jerome: “You have been angry against your Christ.” Others follow him. [Col. 0834B] This is from the point touched on above: since the root can mean “you have caused [him] to pass over,” which is the same as “you have deferred,” and likewise denotes being angry.

VERSE 38.—“You have turned away the covenant of your servant.” Jerome: “you have weakened”; Pratensis and Pellicanus: “you have laid waste”; Sanctes: “you have removed afar”; Munster: “you have dissolved”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “you have caused [it] to be called”; the edition according to Campensis: “you cut off”; the Paraphrase: “you seem to have violated.” *NEARTAH.* I do not see these as tending in divergent directions. For the Chaldee translation also has, “You have turned away his sanctuary.” Others have “his diadem” or “his crown,” from a root meaning “he consecrated”; either meaning is not unsuitable, nor is the sense different.

VERSE 39.—“You have made his stronghold a terror.” Pratensis, Sanctes, Munster, the teachers of Cajetan, instead of “terror,” give “breaking” or “ruin.” Jerome, Nebiensis, and Pellicanus, with the Septuagint, have “terror” or “fear”; it is ambiguous, although fear is instilled through the breaking down of fortifications and walls.

[Col. 0834C] VERSE 46.—“Remember what,” etc.; that is, “remember how long I am,” as they wish, “how short my life is.” Sanctes: “Remember what I am, what time [I am].” He understands a transposition of the words, as though the reading were otherwise arranged. Jerome translates: “Remember me from the deep.” But the Hebrew term is “time” and “the duration of this age.” Munster had also said in his earlier lexicon that it signifies “the depth of the world,” and this suits Jerome’s version. Finally, the Targum reconciles all [the readings], saying: “Remember that I am your creature from the dust.”

VERSE 49.—“Which I have borne,” etc. Jerome: “I have borne in my bosom all the iniquities of the peoples.” In Hebrew there is the universal particle *CAL* [*kol*, “all”], which permits the supplying of whatever is more suitable. Hence Munster, after the Chaldee: “I have placed all the reproaches of many peoples.” Jerome supplied “iniquities.” The Septuagint joined the universal sign to the following words, although word for word it should have rendered, “of all the many nations.”

[Col. 0834D] VERSE 50.—“They have reproached,” etc. Others, instead of “change,” from the Hebrew term, give “footsteps.” The Septuagint explains the phrase. For “footsteps” suggest a certain passage of Christ through crucifixion and death, which unbelievers reproach believers with as though it were disgraceful.

## Psalm LXXXIX

[Col. 0833]

### Title of the Psalm: “A Prayer of Moses, the Man of God”

[Col. 0833D]

Lord, a refuge. Title: “A prayer of Moses, the man of God.” [Gloss, interlinear; Augustine, Jerome, Augustine.] This psalm is the third of those prefaced with the title “prayer.” It is called the prayer of Moses, who was minister of the Old [Col. 0834D] Testament and prophet of the New. According to this dispensation the psalm must be considered—not because Moses composed it, but because this psalm treats of the things contained in what was given through Moses in the Old Testament. Therefore it is called a prayer of Moses. [Col. 0835A] For since the old and new life, mortal life and life-giving life, years reckoned as nothing, days in which we shall be filled with mercy and joy, the punishment of the first man, and the kingdom of the world are here openly distinguished, the psalm is fittingly entitled with Moses’ name, in order that those who rightly search the Scriptures may be told that the law given through Moses, in which earthly rewards seem to be promised, has beneath its veil something such as this psalm reveals. But when anyone turns to Christ, the veil is removed and his eyes are unveiled so that he may consider the wonders of God’s law. And the meaning of the title is: This psalm is a prayer—a prayer, I say, of Moses, that is, one displaying and treating those things which the law given through Moses contained beneath a veil. Or it is Moses’ prayer: that is, David prays in this psalm [Col. 0835B] what Moses also prayed earlier. Moses, I say, the man of God. He was indeed a man subject to suffering, yet one to be delivered by God’s grace. This psalm deals with the failing of the human race, which will be removed through Christ.

Purpose. [Alcuin, Haymo.] It exhorts to contempt for the old life and love for the new.

Method. [Remigius, Cassiodorus.] The psalm has three parts. First, it sets before temporal man an eternal refuge. Second, it expounds human weakness, asking that aid be given to it, at the words, “Turn not away.” Third, it prays for and affirms deliverance, at the words, “Your right hand.” Therefore, speaking in the person of the Church and beginning from hope, he says:

VERSE 1.—“Lord, you have become a refuge to us from generation to generation.”

[Col. 0835C] Lord, by becoming man, you have become a refuge to us in this rock of the age. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] He fittingly says “have become a refuge,” because by becoming man he began to be for us, in a fuller manner than before, what he was not—namely, a refuge. Yet, while a refuge, you are subject to no accident. “From generation to generation,” that is, in every generation; or in two generations, namely the old, of which Moses was minister, and the new, of which that same Moses was prophet. But lest he should seem not to have existed before he became our refuge, he adds:

VERSE 2.—“Before the mountains were made, or the earth and the world were formed, from age unto age you are God.”

Before, etc. [Augustine.] As if he said: You have become a refuge, [Col. 0835D] yet you yourself are before the mountains were made—that is, the angels. For what great thing would it be to speak of visible mountains, which are part of the earth? God is prior to earth and heaven and all bodily things, and before the earth was formed—that is, before human beings. Behold, every rational creature is distinguished by this difference: by the name “mountains” the loftiness of angels is signified, and by the name “earth” the lowliness of human beings. Therefore he fittingly distinguished the words so as to say that mountains—that is, angels—are “made,” and earth—that is, human beings—is “formed.” For “to be formed” or “fashioned” is commonly said in relation to bodies. Hence: “God formed,” or “fashioned, man from the clay of the earth” (Gen. II [2]); “to be made” is from nothing. And, to state the whole universe of things briefly, he adds, “before the world was made,” because “from age unto age you are God” would more aptly be said, “from eternity unto eternity.” [Col. 0836A] For God is not from an age, since he is before the ages; nor is he only unto an age, since he is without end. But because of the ambiguity of the Greek word *αἰών* (*aiōn*, “age” or “eternity”), Scripture frequently uses it so that the Latin translator renders either “age” for “eternity” or “eternity” for “age.” Here, therefore, “unto an age” is used for eternity. Most aptly he says, “You are,” namely, unchangeable; he does not say “you will be” or “you were,” since the unchangeable essence of God knows neither past nor future. Hence it was said: “I am who I am,” and “He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. III [3]); and: “You shall change them, and they shall be changed; but you are the same, and your years,” etc. (Ps. CI [102]). And truly you are, because you are God. Behold what eternity has become a refuge for us, so that we may remain in it. Let us flee from this mutability of time to it; but because we are here amid temptations, lest we be turned away from that eternity, the man of God prays, saying:

PART II. VERSE 3.—“Turn not man away into lowliness; and you have said: Return, children of men.”

Turn not away, [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin.] The second part, in which he expounds human weakness, for which he asks aid. As if he said: Since you are a refuge, do not turn man away from your eternal things into the lowliness of temporal things—that is, into earthly desire and contempt—so that he may desire temporal things and savor earthly things. Or, do not turn away man who is placed in lowliness, that is, in dejection: namely, man cast down, or now placed in good lowliness, that is, now humble, though formerly proud. [Col. 0836C] [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Therefore I pray, “turn not away”; and this is because you have said: “Return to me from love of the world, children of men.” As if he said: I ask from you what you commanded and what you are able to do. For he who taught us to seek heavenly things is himself able to free us from the world.

VERSE 4.—“For a thousand years before your eyes are as yesterday, which has passed away.”

For a thousand years. [Augustine, Gloss, interlinear; Jerome, Augustine.] As if he said: Therefore do not turn away, because, etc. Or connect it thus: Therefore from these transitory things there is need to turn to you. For a thousand years—that is, however long the present life may be—before your eyes, that is, in your eternal and wise consideration, are, in comparison with your eternity, [Col. 0836D] as yesterday, which has passed away. He does not even say, “like tomorrow, which is to come,” but “like yesterday, which has passed away”: that is, it is like yesterday in respect of its having passed away. For all things which are bounded by an end must be regarded as having passed. [Gloss, interlinear; Augustine.] As if he said: Man is nothing unless you grant him another life; yet a thousand years are not comparable even to the length of one day, but rather are:

VERSE 5.—“And a watch in the night; their years shall be regarded as nothing.”

And a watch in the night, [Augustine, Cassiodorus,] that is, like a night-watch, which has only three hours. And the present life is rightly compared to a watch in the night because of its anxiety, and because it is spent in the night of this age. [Col. 0837A] [Augustine, Gloss, interlinear; Haymo.] Afterwards he also adds concerning the misery of mortal life, saying, “which are regarded as nothing,” etc. As if he said: And, to say less, if you turn man away from your eternal things, their years shall be—that is, shall be reckoned among—those things which are regarded as nothing, [Augustine, Alcuin,] like dreams. And they rightly shall be reckoned among them, because before these years come, they are not yet; but when they have come, they will no longer be. As if he said: The present life is spent in darkness, anxiety, and trembling; and it is as though nothing.

VERSE 6.—“In the morning let him pass away like grass; in the morning let him flourish and pass away; in the evening let him fall, grow hard, and wither.”

In the morning let him pass away like grass. [Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] As if he said: I have said that years are regarded as nothing; but I have not said this in accusation of you as maker of mutable things—rather, assenting to divine justice. I say first: Let man pass away in the morning, that is, let man pass away while he lives. For morning is the time of life. Let him pass away, I say, like grass. A fitting comparison. [Alcuin, Remigius, Alcuin, Augustine, Alcuin.] As if he said: As grass is changed from the condition it has in the night to a worse one when the sun rises in the morning, so man is changed for the worse. As if he said: Let man pay what he has deserved. In the morning let him flourish and pass away into another condition; and afterwards in the evening, that is, at the end. For “evening” signifies the last things, namely the time when man dies. Let him fall into death, grow hard in the corpse, and wither into dust—just as grass at the end, when cut or broken. [Col. 0837C] [Jerome, Alcuin.] Or because he says “morning” twice, he indicates two ages: the first morning is childhood, which swiftly passes; the second morning is youth, which flourishes and passes. Evening signifies old age, when human vigor cools. And the first morning of man, that is, childhood, passes away like grass—that is, swiftly. For “all flesh is grass, and the glory of man is like the flower of grass; the grass has withered, the flower has fallen” (Isa. XL [40]). [Augustine.] The second morning, that is, youth, flourishes and passes away—that is, swiftly completes its flowering; and in the evening of cold old age it falls, grows hard, and withers. These things do not change. But this punishment comes from sin.

VERSE 7.—“For we have failed in your anger, and in your fury we have been troubled.”

For we have failed. [Augustine, Haymo, Augustine.] As if he said: I say, “let him pass away,” and he passes away, because we have failed—having been made mortal and passible through weakness—in your anger, that is, in the vengeance inflicted upon us. Yet we fear to bring that misery to an end through death. And in your fury we have been troubled. We have been troubled by fear of death: being weak, we tremble to bring weakness to an end. Hence the Lord says to Peter, “He shall lead you where you do not wish” (John XXI [21]); and the Lord, transfiguring us in himself, says of himself: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. XXVI [26]). Then he adds that this punishment is ours because of sin.

VERSE 8.—“You have placed our iniquities before you, our age in the light of your countenance.”

You have placed [them]. [Gloss, interlinear; Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] As if he said: We have indeed failed justly, because we sinned; and you have placed our iniquities before you: you have not overlooked them. He explains what he had said: You have placed our age—that is, our iniquities, our perverse life—in the light of your countenance, that is, before you. This is the same as what he said above, “before you.” Or “our age” means our descendants: you have placed in the light of your countenance—that is, before you—the sins of our descendants. Those things are covered which receive pardon, and those things are brought to light which are punished. This is proved from what follows.

VERSE 9.—“For all our days have failed, and in your anger we have failed.”

For all our days have failed, [Alcuin, Augustine, Cassiodorus,] that is, our knowledge has failed, reason being darkened through sin; and in your anger we ourselves have failed by loving things that pass away. Or: All our days have failed—that is, the time of our life has been shortened and has almost failed, because the days of our life have been reduced to few. Human life was shortened because of God’s anger, since men sinned through presumption of a longer life. And we ourselves have failed in your anger, that is, our very being has failed through miseries.

VERSE 10.—“Our years shall meditate like a spider; the days of our years are seventy years in them.”

Our years. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The misery and brevity of this life are expressed here through the likeness of a spider, which weaves empty webs in order to catch flies by deceit. [Col. 0838C] And the meaning is: Our years shall meditate—or did meditate—like a spider; that is, in our years we applied ourselves to deceitful and empty occupations, labored in corruptible things, and wove vanities. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] Hence he rightly says, “the years meditated,” or “shall meditate,” not “worked,” because they pass without usefulness and without the fruit of good work, as though under empty meditation. Or it may be taken passively: Our years shall be considered, or reckoned, like a spider—that is, as empty and useless—and the days of our years are completed in seventy years. Or: The days of our years are so brief that they are seventy years in length—another reading—this being the span in which men are said to be long-lived. As if he said: Even to eighty years they seem to retain some strength.

VERSE 11.—“But if they are eighty years in their powers, and beyond that, their labor and pain.”

But if people reach eighty years of life, [Gloss, interlinear; Augustine,] though this is unusually long, they may be in their powers—that is, they may retain some strength and capacities up to eighty.
