And if they live longer, theirs is labor and pain: that is, if life extends beyond seventy, labor and pain are multiplied. [Jerome, Augustine.] For old age itself is a disease. Thus these words may be understood literally. But because some are weak and old before seventy years, while some beyond eighty remain vigorous in strength, they are better understood mystically. Thus seventy and eighty make one hundred and fifty; in one hundred and fifty the same meaning is present as in fifteen, which number consists of seven and eight. Seven signifies the Old Testament because of the Sabbath which it commanded to be observed. [Alcuin, Augustine.] The fathers of the Old Testament observed the seventh day, the seventh week, the seventh month, the seventh year, and the seventh year of the seventh decade, called the jubilee. Eight, however, signifies the New Testament because of the Lord’s resurrection on the eighth day, which is observed in the New Testament, where the future resurrection on the eighth age is also awaited. Hence there are fifteen steps in Solomon’s temple; hence also fifteen Songs of Ascents in the Psalms; and hence the water of the Flood rose fifteen cubits above the highest mountains.

[Col. 0839B] Therefore by seventy and eighty the Old and New Testaments are signified. Note carefully also that he distinctly says, “in them” and “in their powers.” And the meaning is this: Our years shall meditate like a spider; and thus the days of our years—that is, our life—are in those seventy years, or, “in them,” which are seventy years: that is, in temporal things which were promised in the Old Testament, signified by seventy. Therefore he said seventy, because temporal things were promised in the Old Testament, and in them is our life, belonging to the Old Testament. But if our life is not in those years but in powers—that is, if it is not in temporal things, but in eternal and spiritual things—[Col. 0839C] then the days of our years shall be eighty years: that is, our life shall belong to the New Testament, signified by eighty or eight, because the New Testament is in hope of the resurrection in the future eighth age. “And beyond that, their labor and pain”: that is, whoever goes beyond this faith and seeks something further finds labors and pains.

Or it may be understood thus. As if he said: The life which is in powers belongs to the New Testament. And although people are in the New Testament, nevertheless beyond this theirs is labor and pain: that is, although we are in the New Testament, our life still has labor and pain while we groan within ourselves, awaiting the redemption of our body (Rom. VIII [8]). [Augustine, Alcuin.] Or by seventy years may be understood the desire for earthly things, which are done in seven days; by eighty, eternity is signified. And the meaning is: The days of our years—that is, our life—shall be in those seventy years, that is, in the longing and desire for temporal things. But if our life is in powers—that is, in virtues—then there are eighty years, that is, eternity is sought; and “beyond that, their labor and pain”: these words do not change.

VERSE 12.—“For gentleness has come upon us, and we shall be corrected.”

For [gentleness] has come upon us. [Augustine, Alcuin.] As if he said: Labor and pain still remain. But this belongs to God’s mercy, who scourges his children. For the gentleness of God has come upon us. [Col. 0840A] Gentleness, if it is God’s, is called clemency; if it is ours, it is called mastery. For he, gentle through clemency, has made us gentle by taming us. [Augustine.] And thus we shall be corrected. For whom God loves, he corrects and chastens (Heb. XII [12]). And since this is so:

VERSE 13.—“Who knows the power of your anger, and can number your anger according to your fear?”

Who knows the power of your anger? [Gloss, interlinear; Augustine.] As if he said: Blessed is the one who knows; for this belongs to few, namely, to know the power of your anger, because when you spare most people, you are more angry. When you punish certain others, it is gentleness. Hence: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” (Hab. III [3]). [Col. 0840B] [Gloss, interlinear; Augustine.] But you are more angry with those whom you spare, so that the sinner may prosper in his way and receive greater things at the end—that is, eternal punishment, which is the power of your anger. How difficult, then, it is to find! Who knows the power of your anger? That is, who knows your anger and the power of that anger—the force and greatness which you exercise against those whom you spare here? For the power of human anger is to kill the body and afterwards do nothing (Matt. X [10]). But God both punishes here and afterwards casts into Gehenna, and only a few instructed persons understand his greater anger. And who knows how to number—[Gloss, interlinear; Haymo] that is, distinguish—your anger: because you spare these for punishment and punish those for salvation, according to your fear, that is, so that they may fear you? As if he said: Few [do so].

PART III. VERSE 14.—“Make your right hand known, O Lord, in this way; and make those instructed in heart [known] in wisdom.”

Your right hand, O Lord. [Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which he prays for and affirms deliverance. As if he said: Since you correct gently, therefore, O Lord, make your right hand—that is, Christ—known in such a way that your people may learn through him rather to seek the unseen things belonging to the New Testament than present things belonging to the Old Testament. We see this prayer of the man of God fulfilled. For God made Christ known in such a way that, in his sufferings, he showed that eternal things, not present things according to the Old Testament, are to be sought.

Or the right hand of God is eternal blessedness, by which he will separate sheep from goats (Matt. XXV [25]). God fittingly makes himself known in this manner to one who is to sit there when he scourges the one whom he receives (Heb. XII [12]), does not permit him to prosper in evils, but corrects him so as to place him at the right hand. And the meaning is: Make your right hand—that is, eternal blessedness—known in such a way that people may number your anger according to fear; and make known those who are instructed, or fettered, in heart in wisdom. For the Greek word [Note: [Col. 0839] *πεπαιδευνους*, “instructed”; *πεπηδεμὲνους*, “fettered”] signifies both, namely “instructed” or “fettered.” Yet the two are the same, because those instructed in wisdom put the foot of the mind into the fetters of God’s commandments, lest they stray from his way. God made such persons known in the New Testament, so that for his faith they might despise all things held great in the Old Testament and seek eternal goods through death. Observing this, the man of God prays for those who suffer much from the world for eternal things, saying: And O…

### Verse 15

> “Turn, O Lord—how long? And be entreated on behalf of your servants.”

“Turn,” that is, temper your justice. Thus he speaks to God as though His face had turned away from those in tribulation. I say, “Turn”; and how long will you remain turned away? This is the voice and prayer of the righteous person, not the indignation of one who is impatient. Or, according to another reading: “Turn, O Lord, a little,” not wholly; for it is more profitable if some tribulation continually stirs us. “And be entreated concerning [Col. 0841B] your servants.” As though he said: Show yourself such that you may be entreated by sinners. But this man of God, already anticipating future goods in hope, speaks as though of things accomplished:

### Verse 16

> “We have been filled in the morning with your mercy; we have exulted and delighted in all our days.”

“We have been filled in the morning with your mercy,” that is, in eternity. Now it is night, in which we hunger and thirst. But then they shall be satisfied with the countenance of God. Hence: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16 [Vulgate]). And elsewhere: “In the morning I shall stand before you and see” (Ps. 5), that is, I shall be satisfied. There we exulted in your praise and delighted in a joyful reality, throughout all [Col. 0841C] our days. There all days exist together. They do not succeed one another, because they are one day—that is, eternity. But now, instead of this:

### Verse 17

> “We rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us, for the years in which we saw evils.”

“We rejoiced even for the days,” that is, in evil days, in which you humbled us—namely, the years in which we saw evils, that is, bodily distresses. In those days we say:

### Verse 18

> “Look upon your servants and upon your works, and direct their children.”

“Look upon your servants,” etc. As though he said: You have humbled us; but look upon your servants, and “upon,” that is, into, your works, because these servants themselves [Col. 0841D] are your works; and direct their children, that is, their imitators, so that they may be upright in heart, to whom God is good. Or, “their children,” that is, their works.

Or the Prophet here prays especially for the sinning Jews, saying: “Look upon your servants.” What God does in himself, the Prophet prays may be done for his people. He prays, namely, that God may spare the sinning Jews, if not for their merits, at least because of the works which He has performed in them. Hence he adds: “And look upon your works,” which you made in them, “and direct their children.” As though he said: If they themselves have been scattered because of their iniquities, at least may their children at the end be corrected in faith—those who in themselves are perverse and incapable of conversion.

### Verse 19

> “And may the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us; and direct upon us the works of our hands; yes, direct the work of our hands.”

“May the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us,” that is, may the light of your countenance—namely, the image of God renewing us, the grace of the Holy Spirit reforming us—be impressed upon our mind. For there is a threefold image: the image of creation, the image of re-creation, and the image of likeness. The image of creation is that in which we were created, namely reason. The image of re-creation is grace, through which the created image, namely reason, is reformed. The image of likeness is that for which we were made, namely the triune God, in whose likeness man was made: not in the likeness of the Father alone, or of the Son, or of the Holy Spirit, but of the Trinity—through memory like the Father, through understanding like the Son, and through love [Col. 0842B] like the Holy Spirit. Through this trinity, the created image is like the uncreated Trinity. Hence: may I remember you, understand you, and love you.

Or the brightness of God is upon us when we are adorned by the imprint of the cross and bear on our forehead the standard of triumph. “Direct the works of our hands,” so that we may do them not for earthly rewards but for eternal ones. Then, because all good works are directed to one end, he adds in the singular: “Direct the work of our hands,” that is, all good things are the one work of charity, that is, they are directed to one end.

## Comparison on Psalm 89: “Lord, you have been our refuge,” etc.

[Col. 0842C]

### Verse 3

> “Do not turn man back into lowliness.”

In the Hebrew there is nowhere a negation; rather it is read affirmatively: “You turn man back into lowliness,” or “into crushing.” But I shall explain how this reading arose. For the name *God* and the negation *no* differ only in pronunciation and in the marking of points: for example, *EL* means “God,” while *AL* means “do not” or “not.” Moreover, where the preceding verse ended—“from age unto age you are God”—some Greek copies did not have “God,” just as the copies current among us also do not have it. Then the particle without pointing could be read *AL*. Therefore, those who handed down this edition from the Hebrew joined it to the following verse.

What Jerome thinks of this, however, you will see in his letter to Sunia and Fretela. “You say,” he writes, “that in the Greek there is no ‘God’: ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος καὶ ἕως τοῦ αἰῶνος σὺ εἶ, ‘from age and unto age you are,’ which is plainly lacking among them [Col. 0842D]. For the Hebrew truth has it, as do all the other translators; and the Seventy likewise translated: ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος καὶ ἕως τοῦ αἰῶνος σὺ εἶ ὁ θεός, ‘from age and unto age you are God,’ which in Hebrew is *MEOLAM VEAD OLAM ATAH EL*.” Thus far St. Jerome.

Furthermore, in either case the sense is sound. According to the Vulgate reading, “lowliness” is interpreted as earthly desire. According to the other reading, it is understood as the dissolution of the body into dust, according to the condition of nature. It is therefore right for us to pray to God that He not turn us away from eternal things because of the former lowliness. The latter we must necessarily acknowledge.

But let us hear Jerome writing more expressly and clearly to Cyprian, and expounding the whole psalm. There he approves and interprets both readings; he also maintains that our reading is that of the Seventy, though he seemed to think otherwise in his letter to Sunia and Fretela:

> “You turn man back to crushing; and you say: ‘Return, children of Adam.’ The Seventy: ‘Do not turn man back [Col. 0843A] into lowliness; and you said: “Turn back, children of men.”’ According to the Hebrew, what is said means this: O God, who created man, and from the beginning are his refuge and dwelling, you turn him back unto crushing: you made and formed him so that he might return to death and your vessel be broken at the final time of its life. Since this condition hangs over him—that what is born may perish, and, though he live a long time, nevertheless at the final end be dissolved—you speak daily to him through the prophets: ‘Return, children of Adam,’ you who by your own fault have offended God and from immortal have become mortal. For you refused to hear the command of the One who commanded: ‘From every tree in paradise you shall eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat. For on whatever day you taste of it, you shall die by death’ [Gen. 2].

> “But what the Seventy translated, ‘Do not turn man back into lowliness; and you said: “Turn back, children of men,”’ has this sense: I beseech you, do not humble perpetually in sin the man whom you created in your image [Col. 0843B] and likeness, and whom you deigned so greatly to honor that from a servant you named him a son. May the ancient sentence not prevail over him: ‘You are earth, and into earth you shall go.’ For you promised repentance, saying: ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he turn back and live’ [Ezek. 32]. You have spoken through the utterance of all your saints: ‘Turn back,’ or ‘return,’ children of men, to the most merciful Father, who runs to meet those who come, offers the ring which they lost through their fault, and freely bestows the ancient robe of incorruption. For a thousand years in your sight, like yesterday which has passed, have passed away, like a watch of the night, or in the night. You summon us through the prophets to repentance, saying: ‘Return, children of men.’ We ask, as I have already said, that you not cause man to be held in perpetual lowliness. Nor do we think long the period in which you promise that salvation will be granted us after many times; compared with eternity, the length of all times is brief.”

Thus divine Jerome.

[Col. 0843C]

### Verse 5

> “Those which are accounted as nothing,” etc.

Here the force of the thought, not the sequence of the words, is preserved. Jerome has: “when you strike them, they shall be like a dream.” Yet he did not render it word for word. For *ZARAM* means “to flow with force”: *ZERAMTAM SCHENAH IIHEIU*. Münster: “you cause a violent rush to come upon them, and they shall be like a dream”; Sanctes: “you have flooded them; they are a dream”; the others likewise. But without vowel-points it may be pronounced *SCHANAH*, “year,” or *SCHENAH*, “dream.” Jerome nevertheless explains his version to Cyprian.

### Verse 6

> “In the morning let it flourish and pass away.”

Münster and Campensis put “grow” in place of “pass away.” Jerome has “depart,” and the others similarly, or something akin to it. *HALAPH*, the future form of this verb, Münster had shortly before rendered “be changed,” and now “grow.”

### Verse 7

> “We have been troubled.”

So Jerome also, and likewise [Col. 0843D] all the other recent translators. Yet Jerome prefers the translation of Symmachus and Aquila to his own. “Instead of what we rendered, ‘we have been delivered,’” he says, “Symmachus and Aquila translated, ‘we have hastened.’ It signifies the brevity of human life.” And shortly afterward: “It is well said that the Seventy do not have ‘we have been troubled,’ but, according to the Hebrew, ‘we have hastened’; so that, however long the age of human beings may seem, it is nevertheless brief in comparison with eternity. The distinguished poet also attests this when he says: ‘But meanwhile time flees, irretrievable time flees.’”

### Verse 8

> “Our age”: *ALUMENU*.

Jerome translated: “our negligences.” Sanctes: “our errors.” The rest: “our hidden things.” The Seventy looked to *OLAM*, “age.” Jerome and the others looked to the root *ALAM*, “he erred negligently,” and sometimes “he hid.” Jerome discusses this with Cyprian:

> “Where we, according to the Hebrew and Symmachus, set [Col. 0844A] ‘our negligences [p. 202],’ for which the Seventy translated ‘age,’ the Hebrew has *ALUMENU*, which the Fifth Edition interprets ‘youth,’ and Aquila παροράσεις, ‘oversights.’ We may translate it into our language as ‘errors’ or ‘ignorances.’ Yet I wonder why the Seventy wished to call *ALUMENU*, that is, ‘youth,’ which means negligences, errors, or ignorances, ‘age,’ unless perhaps because vices are committed in the age and time of this life.”

### Verse 10

> “Our years shall meditate like a spider.”

Jerome and the more recent translators mark the division otherwise. For they take actively the verb of the preceding verse, where we said “we have failed,” and join it to the following words in this way: “We have consumed our years like speech.” Jerome nevertheless adds “speaking,” for greater clarity of sense; the others do not add it. In Hebrew, *HEGEH* is derived from the root *HAGAH*, which sometimes means “to meditate.”

Jerome explains to Cyprian why the Seventy introduced the word “spider”:

> “For ‘speech of one speaking,’ the Seventy translated ‘meditation of a spider.’ For just as the speech of one speaking flies past, so too the spider’s work is woven in vain. Of it it is written concerning the person of heretics in Isaiah: ‘They weave a spider’s web’ [Isa. 59]. It can catch small and light creatures, such as flies, gnats, and the like; but it is broken by stronger ones. It resembles the weak and simple persons in the Church who are deceived by their errors, whereas they cannot win over men strong in the truth of faith.”

Thus he.

### Verse 11

> “In strengths”: *BIGBUROTH*.

Jerome translates “greatly,” adverbially. The others agree with the Seventy, and he himself explains his version to Cyprian:

> “Whatever life we live, and whatever is pleasant in the life of mortals, is contained within the span of seventy years. But if it be much—and, as Symmachus translated, beyond expectation—it is eighty years; whatever is beyond this is spent in sickness and weakness, the companion of old age.”

> “Moreover, their labor and pain.”

Jerome similarly. Pellican is not far off, having “more abundantly,” where we and Jerome have “moreover.” Others translate “pride,” “strength,” or “excellence” for “moreover.” From this it is clear that the Seventy, by metathesis, took *HORBAM* in place of *ROHEBAM*. The former means “their muchness” or “their abundance”; then follows “labor and pain.” Pratensis and Pellican: “labor and iniquity”; Sanctes: “perversity and iniquity”; the others are nearly with us: *AMAL VAAUEN*. Finally, there is no trouble or affliction more grievous than iniquity, which may therefore be called by that name here.

### Verse 12

> “For gentleness shall come upon us, and we shall be corrected.”

In the Hebrew scarcely anything appears akin to this sentence, if we consider the words outwardly: *KIGAZ HISCH VAANUPHAH*, which [Col. 0844D] Jerome renders: “For we have passed away and flown off.” The rest agree. First we must say what Jerome treats concerning this; then we shall offer what may be said toward reconciliation, without prejudice to those who judge better.

Jerome to Cyprian:

> “When we have passed quickly and flown away. The Seventy: ‘For gentleness shall come upon us, and we shall be corrected.’ In Greek παιδευθησόμεθα is written, a word which is ambiguous and signifies both correction and instruction or teaching. For ‘whom the Lord loves he corrects,’ or teaches, ‘and he scourges every son whom he receives’ [Heb. 12]. Symmachus translated the passage thus: ‘For we are cut down suddenly and fly away.’ The Fifth Edition: ‘For we have passed swiftly and are dissolved.’ The meaning is this: after seventy years, or at most eighty, in which human life is spent, when the soul has been separated from the body, we fly away like the wind; or because above he compares man to green grass, to the beauty of flowers, and to evening dryness, he now puts the cutting down of flowers in place of the evening’s dryness. And when everything that we live through has passed, he says, we are dissolved by sudden death.

> “But what the Seventy said, ‘For gentleness comes upon us and we shall be corrected,’ has this meaning: after seventy and eighty years, when gentleness comes and the day of death presses upon us, we shall be judged not according to merit but according to mercy. And what is thought to be correction is instruction and teaching. We are quite astonished why the Seventy, Theodotion, and the Sixth Edition wished to translate the Hebrew expression *GAZ HISCH* as ‘gentleness,’ when Aquila, Symmachus, and the Fifth Edition translated ‘haste,’ ‘suddenly,’ and ‘quickly.’”

Thus far Jerome. But if we read *GAZ*, or *GEZ*, from the root *GAZAZ*, “he sheared,” it means in Hebrew “fleece,” which is certainly a symbol of sweetness and softness, perhaps the allusion intended by the Seventy. Further, *HISCH* may mean “he hastened” or “quickly,” so that it reads, “the fleece hastened.” Thus “gentleness” is indicated on this account as coming upon us. *OPH*, however, properly means “to fly away,” then “to shine” or “give light.” Finally, the Seventy seem to have had the latter in view in translating, because instruction or affliction gives understanding, although “flying away” can also be fitted without difficulty to correction and instruction.

### Verse 13

> “To number your wrath.”

The final particle in Hebrew belongs to the following verse, and the Seventy made another division: *LIMNOTH*. St. Jerome also notes this to Cyprian, whose exposition is as follows:

> “Who knows the strength of your wrath, and, according to your fear, your indignation? The Seventy: ‘Who knows the power of your wrath, and before your fear, to number your wrath?’ The Hebrew and the Seventy divide the words differently. For the Seventy join the numbering with the fear and wrath of the Lord. But the Hebrew attaches it to the following verse, so that it continues: ‘Thus make known that our days may be numbered, and we shall come with a wise heart.’ What, briefly, seems to us to be said is this: Who can know how long your wrath, from which fear arises for the human race, will endure, unless you, who are God, teach us? Therefore I beseech you to show us the time of our life, so that with a wise heart we may prepare ourselves for your judgment. And in saying, ‘Who knows the strength or power of your wrath, and according to your fear your indignation,’ he shows that it is difficult to know the mystery and rationale of God’s wrath, fear, and indignation.”

Thus he.

### Verse 14

> “Your right hand.”

Hebrew: “our days.” Jerome clearly explains the origin of the variation in the same place:

> “Make known to us our days so that they may be numbered, and we shall come with a wise heart. The error is obvious: why the Seventy said ‘right hand’ instead of ‘days.’ *IAMENU* is a compound word meaning ‘our days’; but if it is written in the singular number, its final letter, called *nun*, denotes ‘right hand,’ as in the name Benjamin, interpreted ‘son of the right hand.’ But if it has [Col. 0845D] the other form, it means ‘day’ or ‘days.’ The sense is: show us the number of our years and days, during which you have decreed that we should live in this world, so that we may prepare ourselves for your coming, and, despising the error of mortals, hasten to go to you and desire your presence, that we may hasten to you with a wise heart.

> “Nothing deceives humankind so much as their ignorance of the span of their lives: they promise themselves a longer possession of this age. Hence the excellent saying that no one is so old, nor of such decrepit age, that he does not suppose that he will live yet another year or more. The saying belongs to this sense: ‘Remember your death, and you shall not sin.’ For one who remembers that he is to die daily despises present things and hastens toward things to come. This is what David prays in another place: ‘Do not take me away in the middle of my days, before [Col. 0846A] I go and am no more’ [Ps. 38]. It is expounded thus: Do not make me die at the time when I still thought I would live, so that I might correct my sins by repentance. For if you do this, I shall cease to be found in my sins—not that he denies the hope of resurrection, but that he denies that he can stand before Him in whose sight all who persist in vices are accounted as nothing.”

Thus he.

> “Those instructed in heart by wisdom.”

Jerome: “we shall come with a wise heart”; Pratensis: “we shall bring a heart of wisdom”; Sanctes: “we shall bring wisdom into the heart”; and likewise the others. Here you see that where we say “instructed,” they say “we shall bring,” “we shall come,” or “we shall offer.” Moreover, in *NABI*, if the first letter belongs to the root, it means “prophet,” as the Seventy understood it; for no one is more instructed in heart than the Prophet himself. Therefore Jerome in his Commentaries interprets it as “those instructed in heart.” The Chaldee paraphrast agrees, saying: “The prophet alone, whose heart abounds in wisdom.” But if it is a servile prefix, it means “we shall bring,” according to the others.

Augustine touches upon and reconciles the reading “fettered” for “instructed” found in some manuscripts:

> “For,” he says, “the Greek word sounds alike in both senses, differing slightly by one syllable.”

Jerome, however, attributes it to error:

> “Where we translated, ‘those instructed in heart by wisdom,’ others translated, ‘those fettered,’ deceived by the ambiguity of the word.”

For πεπεδημένους means “fettered,” whereas πεπαιδευμένους means “instructed.”

### Verses 16 and 17

> “We have been filled in the morning with your mercy; we exulted and delighted; we rejoiced for the days,” etc.

Faber and Caecus, in their usual way, accuse the translators, who, they say, ought to have rendered this in the optative: “Fill us,” “make us glad,” and the following clauses in the future: “we shall exult” and “we shall delight.” For how could those who in verse seven complained that they had failed because of wrath and were disturbed by its fury now assert that they had rejoiced and exulted? Especially since Jerome translated from Hebrew: “Fill us,” and so forth.

But let them hear Jerome himself reply on our behalf against their barking, in the same place:

> “Fill us in the morning with mercy, and we shall praise and rejoice in all our days. The Seventy: ‘We have been filled in the morning with your mercy, and we exulted and delighted in all our days.’ In almost all places the Seventy have this practice: what is put in the future among the Hebrews, they relate as though already done and past. Thus here they do not, as those men maintain, say that they have been filled with God’s morning mercy and have rejoiced. Otherwise, if this had occurred, how afterward do they entreat and say: ‘Look upon your servants and upon your works’? Rather, they pray for everything that they ask, in order that they may deserve morning mercy; and when they have obtained it, they may praise and rejoice throughout all the days of their life.”

Thus far Jerome. Nor does his saying, “as those men maintain,” stand in the way; it must be understood according to the sound of the words. For Jerome himself teaches that, owing to the usage of Scripture, the Seventy rightly render the past in place of the future, even where the future tense is literally read in Hebrew. To prevent doubt, hear what he says in Book II of his Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter 2:

> “The question is therefore asked how God, who saved us and raised us up, also made us sit together with Christ. One who is inclined to a simpler answer maintains that according to God’s foreknowledge He has spoken of what is future as though it had already happened. And because this is a custom of Scripture, that future things are sometimes expressed in the past tense—for example, concerning the Lord’s cross: ‘They pierced my hands and my feet’; elsewhere concerning his passion: ‘Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter’; and again concerning the injuries of the scourges: ‘By his bruise we have been healed’; and elsewhere: ‘He was led to death because of the iniquities of my people’—this is done so that, because future things are uncertain to human beings, hope may not waver and fluctuate. Things which God has known as future, and to whom nothing is uncertain, are recalled as though already done. Thus, because past things, according to the philosophers, cannot be made not to have happened, those who hear may hold as already accomplished what is future.”

So there. Yet what the Seventy expressed in the past—“like a sheep he was led to slaughter,” ὡς πρόβατον ἐπὶ σφαγὴν ἤχθη—the Hebrews have *KASSEH LATTEBAH JUBAL*: “like livestock he shall be led to slaughter.” Nevertheless Jerome adduces the Seventy to support the scriptural rule that, by use of the past, it sets before the eyes as certain an event still to come [p. 203].

### Verse 18

> “Look upon your servants and upon your works.”

In Hebrew: “Let your work appear to your servants.” The sense comes to the same thing. For the Lord looks upon His servants and works [Col. 0848A] when He causes them to appear and be looked upon, as in Genesis 22: “Now I know that you fear the Lord”—that is, “I have made it known.”

> “Direct their children.”

Jerome and the others have: “May your glory be upon their children.” The word placed here among the Hebrews, if we pronounce it without the marks above the letters, can be read in either way: either the final *caph* belongs to the root and the aspirate *he* is the sign of the conjugation called *hiphil*, so that one reads *VEHADREC* and rightly says, “direct”; or the *caph* is a grammatical suffix and the *he* is radical, and one reads *VADARCA*, which must be rendered “your glory.” We think that the Seventy adopted the former reading.

## Psalm 90

[Col. 0847]

### Title of the Psalm: “A praise of David’s song.”

[Col. 0847B]

“He who dwells.” Title: “A praise of David’s song.” Concerning this psalm the devil dared to tempt Christ; but Christ’s temptation is our instruction. For just as He, when first tempted, overcame the devil’s temptations by humility, so He taught and enabled us to conquer that same enemy—whom we can conquer if we are willing to imitate Christ, not in divinity, power, or miracles, as the first man wished to do, but in that in which He was made for us, namely humility. To this He calls us, saying: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11).

Whoever thus imitates Christ enters through the door. Christ is the door, who says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall enter and go out, and find pasture” (John 10). Therefore, to enter [Col. 0847C] through the door is to enter through Christ; and to enter through Him is to imitate Him, not in magnificence and miracles, but, as we have said, in humility and patience. Following Him in these, through Him and in Him we conquer the devil. This psalm concerns that victory of Christ and His own against the devil. Hence its title contains “praise.” Its sense is: this psalm is the praise of David, that is, of Christ.

There is indeed also human praise; but this praise is that of a song, because it is divine alone. For this psalm is a hymn—that is, praise of Christ against demons—because it displays the temptations of the devil as conquered by Christ and by His people who remain in the help of God. With this purpose it admonishes us also to learn, from Christ’s example, to overcome temptations.

Method: [Col. 0847D] the psalm is in three parts. First, the Prophet describes one who trusts in God alone, wholly enclosed by the protection of God. Second, he says that Christ, raised into heaven, cannot be touched by anyone; He also protects feet upon earth, but the presumptuous fall away from Him: “They shall fall at your side.” Third, he introduces the words of God consoling the Church: “Because you will hope in me.” The Prophet therefore says of any holy person:

### Verse 1

> “He who dwells in the help of the Most High shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven.”

“He who dwells in the help,” not his own but that of the Most High—that is, whoever always places all his hope not in himself but in God, whose hope is not in a human being but in God—shall abide in the protection of God; that is, he shall be protected by God in every way, [Col. 0848B] so that he is neither caught by the enticement of wrongly flattering pleasure nor broken by fear of adversity. Thus he does not turn aside to the right or the left, as the children of Israel were commanded in the Old Testament to walk on the royal road, turning neither right nor left (Num. 20; Deut. 5).

The royal road is the way of Christ our King, who ran the path of the world so that He was neither enticed by prosperity nor broken by adversity. We too must imitate Him. By “God of heaven” is meant He whose seat is heaven, that is, the soul of the righteous person. Notice how the words “dwells” and “shall abide” correspond to one another: if he always dwells, so he shall always abide. He then confirms that he dwells when he says:

### Verse 2

> “He shall say to the Lord: You are my protector [Col. 0848C] and my refuge; my God, I shall hope in him.”

“You are my protector,” etc. He promises that he will be protected when he says: “He will overshadow you with his shoulders and surround you with a shield.” First, therefore, he shows how he dwells in the help of the Most High—namely, by saying to the Lord this: He dwells because he is not proud in himself, like the first man, but in the help of the Most High. What shall he say to the Lord? This: Lord, you are the protector of me, who am weak and need healing; and you are my refuge, my God, from the storm of the world.

Whoever says this has cast himself wholly upon Him. Whoever says, “My God is my refuge,” seeks no other help against the storms of the world. And lest you think that nothing is to be sought after receiving protection and refuge, he adds: “I shall hope in him.” As though he said: Because He is protector and refuge, therefore I shall hope in Him. Thus this person will hope in God, lest he ever presume upon himself. Had Adam done this, he would have stood securely. Therefore, “I shall hope.”

### Verse 3

> “For he has delivered me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word.”

“For he has [Col. 0848D] delivered me from the snare” into which proud Adam fell. The snare is that of hunters, that is, demons, who stretch snares not upon the way, which is Christ, but beside the way: on the right, through prosperity that wrongly exalts; or on the left, through adversity that depresses. Therefore, if you wish to walk securely, do not turn aside to the right or left. Rather, let Him be your way—He who became the way for you, so that through Himself He may lead you to Himself.

And so you will not fear [Col. 0849A] the snares of hunters. Notice that in Holy Scripture hunters are scarcely found in a good sense; fishermen, on the contrary, rarely in a bad one. “And from the harsh word”: through a harsh word the devil has sent many into snares. Some fall through a harsh word—for example, those who refuse to be Christ’s because people insult the Christian name, and those who so fear people’s slanders that they abandon the way of God. The insults and slanders of unbelievers are therefore a harsh word.

Or, by the snare and the harsh word he signifies two modes of temptation. Temptation occurs either through deeds, here called a snare, or through words, here called “from the harsh word.” Though it may seem slight, temptation by a word is nevertheless serious. The snare, then, is the crafty action of spiritual or carnal enemies [Col. 0849B] in deeds. The harsh word is every saying which moves a person away from divine rules, whether abusive or flattering. Thus: “He delivered me from the snare of hunters,” that is, temptation occurring through deeds; “and from the harsh word,” that is, temptation occurring through words.

### Verse 4

> “He will overshadow you with his shoulders, and under his wings you shall hope.”

“With his shoulders.” Here He promises one who hopes that he shall abide. As though he said: I say, “He delivered”; and, in order to deliver, He “will overshadow you with his shoulders”—you who dwell in the help of the Most High—or “between his shoulders.” This is said lest you think that you can protect yourself. Literally, when He says, “He will overshadow you between [Col. 0849C] his shoulders,” it may be understood from behind and from the breast. The shoulders are indeed around the head; but because He adds, “Under his wings or feathers you shall hope,” it is clear that the protection is from the breast, as though you were placed amid wings spread out on either side.

The comparison is with a hen protecting her chicks beneath her wings against the kite. The sense is: He will overshadow you—that is, provide the shade of protection—between his shoulders, like a hen; that is, He will place you before His breast so as to protect you with wings, so that, set as it were in the middle, with wings or feathers spread and extended on either side, and with the enemy not daring to approach, you may fear nothing unless you go out from there.

It should be noted that no bird is so weakened with its chicks as the hen, which is entirely changed by affection for them; we observe this [Col. 0849D] in the loosening of its feathers and the weakness of its voice. So the Wisdom of God, because we were weak, was made weak for our sake (Matt. 25 [citation as printed]), because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1), so that we might hope beneath His wings: “under his feathers,” or wings, you shall hope in His mercy.

### Verse 5

> “His truth will surround you with a shield; you shall not fear the terror of the night.”

“With a shield.” Wings are also a shield. Both are spoken of God figuratively, since neither wings nor a shield properly exist in God—just as He is called stone and lion, lamb and calf, though He is none of these. For if He were truly a stone, He would not be a lion; if a lion, He would not be a lamb. Therefore He is called both lion [Col. 0850A] and lamb, and the like, because He is neither lion nor lamb nor anything of that sort. These are likenesses, not literal properties.

Thus His truth will surround you, that is, protect you, as with a shield of mercy. The truth of God does not regard persons, nor mingle those who hope in themselves with those who hope in God; rather, it distinguishes humble people from proud, the repentant from those who defend themselves.

Or thus: by “shoulders” he promises divine benefits to the faithful person who hopes. The shoulders are the workings of miracles, in which the power of God is displayed as upon shoulders. The feathers are the admonitions of the prophets, which bear people to heaven. Thus, “He will overshadow you,” so that neither the sun of Christ’s divinity nor the moon of His humanity may burn you, “with his shoulders,” that is, with miraculous workings. “And under his feathers,” that is, [Col. 0850B] in the prophetic admonitions in which there is protection, “you shall hope.” His truth, fulfilling promises—that is, Christ’s incarnation, as in “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. 84)—will surround you as with a shield. He has called the shield the same thing that he called feathers. For Christ’s incarnation both overshadows with shoulders and defends with a shield.

“You shall not fear the terror of the night.” Just as he has noted the kinds of protection, so he notes the kinds of danger, that deliverance may be more welcome. He distinguishes four kinds of temptation: light and hidden, signified by “the terror of the night”; light and manifest, signified by “the arrow flying by day”; grave and hidden, signified by “the business walking in darkness”; and grave and open, understood by “the noonday demon.” Thus, “He will overshadow you [Col. 0850C] and surround you.” And so you shall not fear “the terror of the night,” that is, a light temptation which befalls the ignorant. It is called the terror of the night by comparison with a danger from which fear alone arises. And:

### Verse 6

> “The arrow flying by day; the business passing through darkness; the assault and the noonday demon.”

From the arrow that flies by day—[Augustine] that is, from a light temptation that comes upon those who know. For one who sins in ignorance sins, as it were, at night, and is tempted by nocturnal fear. But one who sins knowingly sins by day, and is tempted by the arrow in daylight. By those two expressions, namely “fear” and “arrow,” he has indicated the two lighter kinds of temptation: the hidden and the manifest. [Col. 0850D] To these two light kinds he adds two more serious ones, saying, “from the business that walks in darkness,” that is, from a more serious and hidden temptation; and “from assault and demon,” that is, he will not fear the attacking noonday demon, that is, grave and open temptation—such as when the heat of persecution burns so fiercely that many yield. Light temptations do not press so hard as to compel, but may quickly pass away when avoided. Serious temptations, however, do: as when a persecutor fiercely presses those not yet firm in faith, who do not know, as Christians, how to despise present things and seek those to come. Such persons are tempted “by the business walking in darkness”; or when the persecutor presses these things so forcefully upon those who know them, that temptation is “the noonday demon.” It catches both kinds, the knowing and the ignorant. [Col. 0851A] Yet it does not catch those who dwell in the help of the Most High, but those who presume upon themselves, of whom he says:

## PART II. VERSE 7.—“A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand; but it shall not come near you.”

“A thousand shall fall at your side.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] The second part, in which he says that the head of the person trusting in God—that is, Christ, raised up into heaven—cannot be touched by anyone, and that he also protects his feet 204 upon earth; but the presumptuous fall away from him. Behold, certainty of protection is given through Christ to the one trusting in God. [Cassiodorus] As though he said: He who dwells in the help of the Most High will not fear the noonday demon; but, O Christ, a thousand shall fall at your side. The side of God is the company of the righteous, who will judge with him. Hence it is said in customary speech: [Col. 0851B] “Send men from your side,” that is, from those who deliberate with you. [Augustine] Therefore Christ’s side consists of those to whom Christ promised that they would judge with him: namely, the apostles and their imitators, to whom he promised, “You shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX). For we must not suppose that Christ promised this only to the twelve. Where indeed will Paul sit, who labored more than all, if only twelve are to sit there? The twelve thrones, therefore, are the perfection of the tribunal; upon them will sit a thousand—that is, all who have left everything and followed Christ, trusting in him and not in themselves, who have driven the root of charity deep and will not wither beneath the sun of tribulation.

By God’s “right hands,” however, eternal blessedness is understood. Now there are many [Col. 0851C] who suppose that they will judge with the Lord, and far more who suppose that they will be placed at his right hand and then saved. But because they presume upon themselves and do not have the root of charity fixed deep within them, they fall away from their own thoughts. And because fewer suppose that they will judge, while more suppose that they will be saved—although they will not be—he therefore puts a thousand in the former case and ten thousand in the latter. The meaning is: O Christ, a thousand shall fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand; that is, fewer who presume that they will judge with you, and more who presume that they will be at your right hand, will fall through the noonday demon, that is, through the grievous heat of tribulation. But it shall not come near you, O Christ, in your true members, with whom you are one—for you are in [Col. 0851D] your true members. Even if it injures the body and afflicts the flesh, it nevertheless has not injured faith.

## VERSE 8.—“Yet with your eyes you shall consider, and you shall see the recompense of sinners.”

“Yet.” [Cassiodorus] As though he said: Although you permit the ungodly to persecute your own, and although those who fall may, by your permission, try you with harsh things, still not without punishment: because with your eyes—that clear sight by which you judge human merits—you will consider the evil they intended, and see the recompense of sinners. Not the good that is done through those who do not know will be repaid to them, but the evil they intended. Thus also the saint who has the eyes of faith sees them now exalted and thundering, but at the end struck by lightning. He said this lest the weak be shaken.

Or the connection may be made thus, with the same sense remaining: [Augustine, Alcuin] As though he said: Even if [Col. 0852A] the demon does not come near you in your members—which is through the wicked, that is, what the wicked intend—yet you will consider not what they do, but what they intend. This is what he says: “Yet with your eyes you shall consider, and you shall see the recompense of sinners.” [Augustine] It should be observed that Christ is, as it were, one person—head and body. Scripture speaks of him sometimes as head and sometimes as body, without a change of person, because the two are one flesh (Matt. XIX). Rightly, therefore, there is also one voice. Accordingly, attend carefully to where it speaks of Christ according to the head and where according to the members.

## VERSE 9.—“For you are, O Lord, my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge.”

“For you are.” [Augustine, Gloss interlinear] Here he speaks of [Col. 0852B] Christ according to the head. As though he said: Therefore the righteous person does not fall through the noonday demon, because you, Lord Christ, according to the head, are my hope. You are hope in this respect: you have established for me inwardly your most high refuge; that is, you have shown me that, for the highest and hidden things—whether to avoid them or attain them—I must flee to you, namely, in order to escape eternal punishments. For God’s refuge is on high and exceedingly hidden, so that one may flee to him from wrath to come. Many, indeed, make God their refuge merely in order to flee temporal evils.

[Augustine] Therefore you have made the refuge most high: that is, by rising and ascending, you have made it high, or rather shown it to be a refuge, so that your people may now hope to follow where you went before. Therefore:

## VERSE 10.—“Evil shall not come near you, and [Col. 0852C] no scourge shall come near your tabernacle.”

“Evil shall not come near you,” [Remigius, Augustine, Alcuin] O Lord Christ, or your people; “and no scourge shall come near your tabernacle.” God’s tabernacle is the flesh in which he fought for us. Once that flesh had been raised above the heavens, scourges no longer approached it as they had formerly done on earth; and thus our hope is directed there. But the head is in heaven and has feet on earth, on whose behalf he says: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” There is distinction by location, but union by affection. Yet neither does a scourge come near these feet so as to shake their faith; therefore this is rightly understood of the whole Christ. Therefore it shall not come near:

## VERSE 11.—“For he has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may keep you in all your ways.”

[Col. 0852D] For God commanded his angels concerning you, that they might keep you in all your ways. [Cassiodorus, Augustine] Hence in the Gospel: “An angel stood by him, strengthening him” (Luke XXII); and this is an indication of human weakness. The tempter said this to the Lord when he tempted him, proposing it because he doubted his divinity. But we believe him to be both God and man. Christ was tempted for our sake, that in him we might learn to conquer the tempter; just as he also wished to be baptized by a servant, not from his own need but for humanity’s benefit, so that we might not disdain to be baptized by fellow servants.

The Lord came to the baptism administered by a servant, fulfilling humility in order to crush the pride of those to come, lest someone, superior to certain Christians in life and knowledge, should say: “What need have I [Col. 0853A] of the baptism which this man has, when I am already better than he?” But let him consider that he does not surpass that man by as much as the Lord surpasses him. Therefore let him seek the Lord’s baptism, because the Lord sought a servant’s baptism.

## VERSE 12.—“They shall bear you in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone.”

“In their hands.” [Haimo, Augustine] As though he said: He commanded the angels concerning you, that they might keep you; and they themselves shall bear you in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone. Christ was borne into heaven by angels’ hands, not because he would have fallen without them, but because they rendered service to their king; and one who is carried is greater than a beast of burden.

When Christ had been glorified, he sent the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost (Acts II), just as on the fiftieth day after the Passover lamb (Exod. XII)—that is, after the lamb’s sacrifice—the Mosaic law was given, written on tablets of stone by the finger of God, that is, by the Spirit of God (Exod. XXXIX). But the law was given in the punishment of fear. The Spirit, however, came in the fullness of love, so that the feet of the head seated in heaven—that is, the evangelists traversing the world—might not strike against the stone, that is, against the law written on stone, and might not be held guilty under it without grace; but might be freed from fear, fulfilling the law through the love of the Spirit.

Therefore you were borne into heaven by angels, lest perhaps your foot strike against a stone: so that, having sent the Spirit, you might free believers from the guilt of the law, lest your feet which are on earth be guilty under the law. And he did this, because by driving out fear he filled them with love, which cannot be overcome.

## VERSE 13.—“You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk; you shall trample down the lion and the dragon.”

“Upon the asp.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus] After Christ’s human weakness has been shown, his divine power is now displayed—power which commands such beings and acts in Christ according to his members. All these names apply to the devil. He is an asp when he strikes secretly; a basilisk when he poisons openly. For the basilisk is king of serpents and harms by its breath. He is a lion when he persecutes violently, for the lion, king of animals, harms by strength. He is a dragon when he devours the negligent. But at the Lord’s coming all these injuries have been thrown down beneath his feet—that is, by the saints. This is what he says: “You shall walk upon the asp.”

[Augustine, Gloss interlinear] The asp harms by venom and signifies the devil, the serpent who seduced Eve, whom the Church tramples underfoot because she guards against his craftiness; and you shall walk upon the basilisk, that is, the king of demons, who, like a basilisk, harms by his breath. “And you shall trample down the lion and the dragon,” that is, the devil, who is a lion when he rages openly against the martyrs and a dragon when he secretly lays snares through heretics to corrupt Christ’s virgin. Hence the Apostle: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear lest, as the serpent seduced Eve by his craftiness, so your minds may be corrupted” (II Cor. II).

## PART III. VERSE 14.—“Because he has hoped in me, I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he has known my name.”

[Col. 0854A] “Because he has hoped in me.” [Augustine, Alcuin] The third part. Here are now God’s words to the Church, whom he consoles, promising her protection here and rewards in the future. [Haimo, Gloss interlinear, Alcuin, Cassiodorus] As though he said: He commanded the angels, saying: “Because he has hoped in me,” in his members, “I will deliver him from the evils of the world; I will protect him.” Behold certainty of protection through God’s promise. I will protect him because he has truly known my name. And because:

## VERSE 15.—“He has cried to me, and I will hear him; I am with him in tribulation, I will rescue him and glorify him.”

“He has cried to me, and I will hear him.” [Gloss interlinear, Augustine] And even if I do not yet hear him, I am already with him in tribulation. Therefore you need not fear in tribulation. [Col. 0854B] For faith in you is God in you. If faith sleeps in you—that is, grows lukewarm—awaken it, just as Christ, sleeping in the boat, was awakened by the disciples, and they were saved (Matt. VIII). So too, if you awaken faith, you will be saved and not abandoned. And if he does not rescue you when you wish, do not therefore suppose yourself abandoned.

He delivered the three youths from the fire; but did he who delivered them abandon the martyrs? Far from it. He delivered both them and these; but he delivered the three youths bodily, that unbelievers might be confounded, whereas he delivers the martyrs spiritually, that believers may imitate them. “I will rescue him.” As though he said: I am with him in tribulation, and afterwards I will rescue him from the world and glorify him in heaven; and then:

## VERSE 16.—“I will fill him with length of days, and show him my salvation.”

[Col. 0854C] “With length of days,” [Augustine] that is, with eternal life, I will fill him, because what he will possess is sufficient; “and I will show him,” by sight and not by faith, “my salvation,” that is, Christ in majesty. This vision is the whole reward.

[Alcuin] It should be noted that the Church uses this psalm throughout the year, and especially in Lent. For then it is sung in the versicles, in the tract, and in many forms. This is because, when Christ was fasting, the devil tempted him from this psalm; and, his temptations overcome by Christ, the defeated devil departed. Therefore we use this psalm daily at Compline, and especially on fasting days, so that at the time when the devil strives more earnestly to deceive, we may not labor more earnestly [Col. 0854D] to resist.

## COLLATION ON PSALM XC: “HE WHO DWELLS IN THE HELP OF THE MOST HIGH,” etc.

### VERSE 2.—“He shall say to the Lord: You are my protector.”

Jerome, in his letter to Sunia and Fretella, explains why the Latin here adds *es* (“are”) and *tu* (“you”), which occurred neither in certain Greek copies nor in the Hebrew, although *es* is written in the Greek copies we have seen. His own words deserve hearing:

> “You say that *es* is absent in the Greek. I will tell you something further: among the Hebrews neither *es* nor *tu* occurs; but among the Septuagint and the Latins it has been placed for euphony (*εὐφωνία*) and for the sequence of the words.”

Moreover, Caecus Burgensis wrongly cries out that a pause should be marked at “my refuge,” followed immediately by “my God, I shall hope in him”; rather, he says, it should read: “my refuge, my God; then, I shall hope in him.” The contrary, however, is found in the context both of the Hebrew and of the Greek.

### VERSE 3.—“And from the harsh word.”

Jerome: “from the death 205 of snares”; Pagninus of Prato: “from the pestilence of evils”; Sanctes: “from the death of destructions”; Münster: “from harmful pestilence”; and the others similarly. It is certain that, if read *DABAR*, it represents “word,” but *DEBER* means “death” or “pestilence.” Therefore the Septuagint expressed the former. Next, *HAVOTH*, according to Kimhi, signifies malice of heart and deed. But if the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart (Matt. XII), no word is harsher than one that is deceitful and perverse.

### VERSE 5.—“He shall surround you with a shield,” etc.

The Septuagint rendered the sense, though not the words: *TZINNAH VESOHERAH AMITO*, “his truth is shield and buckler,” which Jerome rendered, “his truth is shield and protection.”

### VERSE 6.—“From the business.”

Jerome: “from pestilence”; the others likewise, “from pestilence” or “from death.” It has already been said [Col. 0855B] that the letters daleth, beth, resh admit an ambiguous reading: *MIDABAR*, “from business,” or *MIDEBER*, “from death.”

“From assault and the noonday demon.” *MIQQETEB IASCHUD TZAHORAIIM.* Different translators express the same meaning in different words; nevertheless, the entire basis of the variation depends chiefly on the first expression, *QUETEB*, which has several meanings and is variously expounded by rabbis in various [Col. 0856A] places. Jerome translates it thus: “from the bite of one raging,” or, as other manuscripts have it, “of one lying in wait at noon”; Pagninus of Prato: “from sudden sickness laying waste at noon”; Sanctes: “from the bite that devastates at noon”; Münster: “from destruction ravaging at noon”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “from cutting destruction at noon”; the translator for Campensis: “from harm that lays waste at noon”; Campensis’s paraphrase: “nor fear if anyone should attack you with a dart even in the middle of the day”; Pellicanus: “from the noonday devastating demon”; Nebiensis: “from the destroyer who destroys at noon”; the Chaldean: “from a band of demons who harm at noon.”

### VERSE 10.—“And scourge.”

Jerome: *NEGA*, “leprosy,” is a blow or plague, especially a scabby eruption.

### VERSE 13.—“The asp and basilisk.”

Pagninus of Prato: “upon the lion and asp”; Sanctes: “upon the lion and basilisk.” Thus the more recent translators agree in the first clause, rendering *SCHAL VAPHETEN*, “lion and asp.” [Col. 0856B] Nevertheless, we trust Jerome and the Septuagint, who consistently translate “upon the asp and basilisk,” especially since the second clause says, “you shall trample down the lion.” Nebiensis also supports us. Pliny, Book VIII, chapters 21 and 23, tells remarkable things of the asp and basilisk, entirely appropriate in every respect to the ancient serpent.

# PSALM XCI

[Col. 0855]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF SONG FOR THE SABBATH DAY.”

[Col. 0855B]

“It is good to confess to the Lord.” Title: “A psalm of song for the Sabbath day.” [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine] To remove weariness from people’s minds, the same matters are treated in diverse and varied ways. For no song other than that found in the other psalms is treated in this psalm; it is the same song, though [Col. 0855C] in a different manner—namely, the song of faith, hope, and charity.

When it says “for the Sabbath day,” it should be known that there is a threefold Sabbath: the Sabbath of time, the Sabbath of the heart, and the Sabbath of eternity. The Sabbath of time is the seventh day, on which God rested after the works of the six days, teaching his people to labor in the present so that they may rest in the future. This Sabbath was observed in the old law. But the Sabbath of the mind is the tranquility of a good conscience, in hope of the future, so that it is not disturbed by worldly affairs. This is the Sabbath discussed here. The first principle of this Sabbath of the heart is that you should attribute your good things to God and your evil things to yourself.

[Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus] The Sabbath of eternity is eternal rest, for which we ought in the present to do good works, observing the Sabbath of the mind. This Prophet also deals with that Sabbath of eternity. Therefore he treats here of a twofold Sabbath: that of the mind and that of eternity. Hence “a psalm of song” is fittingly placed in the title. Its sense is this: [Cassiodorus, Augustine] This psalm, by which spiritual activity is indicated, is “of song,” by which the exultation of the mind is indicated, because in it we ought always to sing to God and give thanks with exultation. And this is on the Sabbath day, [Alcuin] that is, concerning eternal rest, with tranquility of mind. The Prophet speaks here of that rest, showing that the righteous labor for six days—that is, through six ages—and rest in the seventh; while the wicked, contrariwise, rest here and labor there. His purpose is that we may gladly labor here for eternal things, keeping the Sabbath of the mind.

Method. [Cassiodorus] The psalm is divided into three parts. [Col. 0856B] First, it says how a good person, undisturbed, keeps the Sabbath of the mind, perceiving that God does all things well—something the fool does not know. Second, it declares that the wicked will perish, so that this may be a warning to the rest, at “When sinners shall spring up.” Third, it says that the righteous flourish in virtues, so that the devout may rejoice in this promise, at “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree.” [Col. 0856C]

[Augustine] Since we are Christians for the sake of the age to come, whatever the state of present things may be, let us be thankful: either for God’s consolation through pleasant things or for his justice through harsh things. Present goods granted to us by God are consolation, though justice comes from above. For God both consoles and corrects us. In both let us be grateful to him, saying:

## VERSE 1.—“It is good to confess to the Lord, and to sing to your name, O Most High.”

“It is good to confess,” [Gregory] with the voice, to the Lord, so that we attribute evils to ourselves and good things to God. The perverse and troubled, who are without the Sabbath of the mind, attribute good things to themselves; but evils either to Satan, as though he had compelled them, or to the fate of the stars—which is to accuse [Col. 0856D] the Creator—or openly to God, as if to say: “He himself willed this.” But this psalm teaches the contrary: namely, that one should confess to the Lord in both cases—in sin, because you yourself did it; in good, because he himself did it. And thus you sing to the Lord’s name, seeking God’s glory rather than your own. Hence he adds: “And it is good to sing by works to your name, O Most High.”

He then gives two further purposes for the two things previously stated. As though he said: I say that it is good to confess—for what purpose?

## VERSE 2.—“To proclaim your mercy in the morning, and your truth in the night.”

“To proclaim your mercy in the morning,” [Augustine] that is, when things go well, which is mercy. When things go well with you, proclaim—that is, praise—God’s mercy; “and to proclaim your truth,” [Col. 0857A] not cruelty, “in the night,” that is, in adversity. As though he said: When things go badly for you, praise the truth by which he justly chastises. The meaning is: In prosperity, signified by morning, and in adversity, signified by night, you ought to give praise.

## VERSE 3.—“Upon the ten-stringed psaltery, with a song upon the lyre.”

“Upon the ten-stringed.” [Gloss interlinear, Augustine] As though he said: It is also good to sing upon the psaltery, that is, in a quickened spirit. For the psaltery gives forth sound from above, and consequently the quickening of the spirit is fittingly understood by it. I mean a ten-stringed psaltery, that is, of the ten commandments, through obedience to which the human spirit—that is, reason—is quickened. One sings upon this psaltery when, with a quickened spirit and by keeping the Decalogue, [Col. 0857B] one acts well with cheerfulness. For cheerfulness belongs to singing. Therefore whatever you do with cheerfulness, you do well. But one who does good with sadness is acted through rather than acting himself; he carries the psaltery but does not sing upon it.

It is good to sing with song, that is, with speech, and upon the lyre, that is, with deed. If you speak well only, there is song without a lyre; if you act but do not speak, there is a lyre without song. Therefore both speak well and do good, that there may be a lyre with song. [Haimo, Cassiodorus] Or: it is good to sing with song upon the lyre, that is, with joy in mortifying the flesh and in outward actions. For the lyre gives forth sound from below. Therefore it is good to sing and confess, because you have done these things in me. This is:

## VERSE 4.—“For you have delighted me, O Lord, in your work; and in the works of your hands [Col. 0857C] I shall exult.”

“For you have delighted me, O Lord, in your work,” [Augustine] that is, in what you do in me. For you have acted, if I act well. Hence the Apostle: “We are his workmanship, created in good works” (Eph. II). Unless God reformed you for good works, you would know nothing but sin. Hence in the Gospel: “He who speaks falsehood speaks from his own” (John VIII). In the Gospel the Lord says this: Every sin is falsehood, because it is contrary to law and truth. Therefore the person who speaks falsehood speaks from his own—that is, whoever sins sins from his own resources; but whoever speaks truth speaks from God, because God alone is true and every human being false (Rom. III). This is good confession.

“And in the works [Col. 0857D] of your hands.” [Augustine] As though he said: And then I shall exult, not in my own prosperity, but in the works of your hands—that is, if I do any good, I rejoice because of you. But what of those who live wickedly and flourish? The mind is disturbed by this and loses its Sabbaths, because it sees itself bound to the ten strings—that is, the works of the law—and yet suffering evils; while it sees another without these flourishing. Hence he says:

## VERSE 5.—“How great are your works, O Lord! Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep.”

“How great are your works, O Lord! Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep.” [Augustine] By these thoughts you cause the good to labor and the wicked to flourish, because the latter are strangers and the former children. But:

[Col. 0858A]

## VERSE 6.—“The senseless man shall not know, nor shall the fool understand these things.”

“The senseless man,” or “the imprudent man,” [Remigius, Augustine, Cassiodorus] who does not provide for himself for the future, shall not know; and the fool, who does not know that he is being struck so that he may become an heir, while the disinherited person is spared the scourge, shall not understand these things that follow or those which have been said. Note: the senseless man is one empty of heavenly wisdom but full of human cunning, who does not know the works of God because he thinks all things happen by chance; the fool is brutish, one who does not even understand worldly matters.

[Jerome, Alcuin] It may be read otherwise from the passage, “For you have delighted me,” and thus concerns the works of creation, in which the Creator is to be praised. As though he said: Therefore I shall confess and sing, because you have delighted me in your work—that is, both in the beauty of the worldly fabric itself, and in its obedience, ordering, causes, and effects. And I shall exult in the works of your hands, which I use or admire. And I shall rightly exult because, O Lord, how great are your works—in substance, form, life, and all else. Your thoughts, by which you made and govern such things, have become exceedingly deep. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] Observe that the highest kind of knowledge is to know that God accomplishes such great things as human understanding cannot attain. You have delighted me in your works; but the senseless man shall not know, and the fool, who even if he knows does not guard himself, shall not understand these things—those said above or those said afterward.

[Col. 0858C]

## PART II. VERSE 7.—“When sinners shall spring up like grass, and all who work iniquity shall appear.”

“When they shall spring up.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] The second part, in which he asserts that the wicked will perish, so that it may be a warning to the rest. The order of the words is as follows: As though he said: The fool shall not understand these things—namely, how sinners perish for ever and ever, that is, without end—when sinners themselves have sprung up, [Augustine] that is, after they have grown in temporal prosperity, like grass: for they are green in the winter of this world and will wither in the summer of the future judgment.

“And when they have looked forth,” according to another reading, namely at those who spring up and flourish for a time, all who work iniquity—that is, all who do not think rightly about God in their hearts and imitate their flourishing. Thus [Col. 0858D] they perish with them eternally. Hence it is repeated:

## VERSE 8.—“That they may perish for ever and ever; but you, O Lord Most High, are for ever.”

“That they may perish with them for ever and ever.” [Augustine] But you—as though he said: Sinners now flourish and prosper, but you, O Lord, are Most High for ever. From your eternity you wait above until the time of the ungodly passes and the time of the righteous comes, because God is eternal. God patiently endures evils and sees what he reserves for them. Do you too, human being, wish to be long-suffering and patient? Join yourself to the Eternal. For while a human being swiftly passes like grass, the word of God remains for ever. If a human being is temporal and not long-suffering in himself, through God’s word he is eternal. [Col. 0859A] Therefore join yourself to the eternal Word, and you will patiently endure evils, seeing all the wicked beneath you, and you will say:

## VERSE 9.—“For behold, your enemies, O Lord; for behold, your enemies shall perish, and all who work iniquity shall be scattered.”

“For behold, your enemies, O Lord.” [Haimo, Cassiodorus] Or it may be read thus: As though he said: The fool shall not understand these things, namely, that sinners spring up here like grass. For here they flourish for a short time like grass. And when sinners have sprung up here like grass, afterwards all who work iniquity—that is, sinners—shall appear, that is, will be openly visible and conspicuous to all. This will not appear here, certainly not to their glory, [Col. 0859B] but in order that they may perish for ever and ever—that is, always. But you, Lord Christ, shall remain Most High for ever; it shall not be as the Jews supposed, namely, that you would die by the common lot.

[Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus] “For behold, your enemies”—shall sinners perish? Certainly: “for behold, your enemies,” and he repeats, “for behold, your enemies.” As though he said: I now see that your enemies, namely blasphemers—and “the friend of this world is God’s enemy,” as James says (Jas. IV)—shall perish: all who commit adultery with love of the world, who now flourish; and, separated from the Lord’s flock, all who work iniquity shall be scattered. These are the enemies.

## VERSE 10.—“And my horn shall be exalted like that of a unicorn, and my old age in abundant mercy.”

“And it shall be exalted.” [Alcuin, Gloss interlinear] As though he said: And if they shall perish, what hope is there for you who suffer? Behold, my horn also shall be exalted like that of a unicorn—that is, the strength of unity, which will then be exalted, which is like my horn, that is, like my monarch, my prince, who will be exalted when heresies have been destroyed. [Augustine, Cassiodorus] For sometimes the unicorn signifies pride, as in: “And from the horns of unicorns, my humility” (Ps. XXI); sometimes the exaltation of unity, as here, because unity shall be exalted like one monarch-prince. [Augustine] All heresies indeed shall perish. And when will this be? When my old age is in abundant mercy, that is, at the end. [Col. 0859D] All that the Church suffers is her youth; her final stage, however, is always her old age, which shall be in joy.

## VERSE 11.—“And my eye has looked down upon my enemies; and my ear shall hear those rising against me in malice.”

“And therefore,” [Augustine] already now my eye has looked down upon, or “looked upon,” my enemies—that is, all who work evil—whom it observes or despises while testing someone and finding enemies who had seemed friends. And against malicious persons rising against me, my ear [Gloss interlinear, Alcuin]—foreknowing and forewarned by the truth within—shall hear. What shall it hear? That which follows:

## PART III. VERSE 12.—“The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree; he shall increase like a cedar of Lebanon.”

[Col. 0860A] “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] The third part, in which he says that the righteous flourish, so that the devout may rejoice in this promise. Or it may be read thus, with “of” understood: As though he said: And concerning malicious persons who now rise against me, my ear shall hear in the future—[Augustine] that is, the ear of the one standing at the right hand. What shall it hear? “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). The righteous person will not fear this evil report.

[Cassiodorus, Augustine] Or, according to another reading: “My ear shall hear the malicious persons rising against me,” at the end, when they will rebuke themselves, saying, as Solomon says: “What has pride profited us, and the boasting of riches?” (Wis. V). Behold what shall befall them in the future. And what shall become of the righteous? “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree”; they, like grass. The righteous person is called a palm tree because of its height, because its root is rough, because it has a beautiful crown at the summit, and because it bears fruit late. Thus labor makes the righteous person rough here; above, the beauty of immortality will crown him; and, as though late, after long labors, he will receive the reward of his works.

Then another comparison follows: “And he shall increase like a cedar of Lebanon.” [Alcuin, Jerome, Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear] The cedar is evergreen and taller than other trees, especially in Lebanon, whose name means “whiteness”; thus the righteous person will be incorruptible, white in the garment of immortality. The righteous, therefore, are compared to these trees, because these trees do not wither with age as grass does, to which the ungodly person is compared because it quickly withers. [Augustine, Cassiodorus] But the righteous person is compared to the palm and to the cedar; and the cedar is much taller than the palm, especially [Col. 0860C] in Lebanon. And because not one but many will flourish, he adds the plural, explaining the preceding comparison. Now:

## VERSE 13.—“Planted in the house of the Lord, they shall flourish in the courts of the house of our God.”

“Planted in the house of the Lord,” [Augustine, Haimo] that is, in the Church, where the root is rough, the palm trees shall flourish; “in the courts of the house of our God,” that is, in the courts of heaven. A court is the entrance to a dwelling; the house is the inner place. [Cassiodorus, Gloss interlinear] Therefore they shall flourish in the courts, that is, at the very beginning of the resurrection, when they hear: “Come, blessed of my Father,” etc. (Matt. XXV). And as though someone asked, “Do they not already flourish?” he adds:

## VERSE 14.—“They shall still increase in abundant old age; they shall be patiently enduring, in order to proclaim.”

[Col. 0860D] “They shall still increase here,” [Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus] as though they possess something here, but more there. They shall increase, I say, in abundant old age: for the Church begins to be most fruitful when it has reached the end of the age. For then the number of the blessed will swiftly be completed through the sufferings of the elect. At the summit, the palm shall flourish, which conceived at the root; and meanwhile they shall be patiently enduring, or tranquil. [Augustine] Behold the Sabbath mentioned in the title: grass does not disturb them. For cedar and palm do not bend even in storms, but remain tranquil. For what purpose? That they may proclaim here—what?

## VERSE 15.—“For the Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity in him.”

“For the Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity [Col. 0861A] in him.” [Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus, Augustine] Whoever says that all things are not well ordered is grass. But whoever is in the Sabbath proclaims the contrary. Or it may be understood thus: Therefore they are tranquil now, so that in the future, when they receive rewards, they may proclaim this in perpetual praise. For then they will proclaim: “For the Lord our God is upright,” that is, he is just, fulfilling what he has promised to his own; “and there is no iniquity in him,” so that he should permit those who suffer for him here to go without adornment there. [Alcuin] Therefore he will be proclaimed upright because he rewards; and not unjust, as though he should defraud them of their reward, but generous, so as to heap it up.

## COLLATION ON PSALM XCI: “IT IS GOOD TO CONFESS TO THE LORD,” etc.

### VERSE 7.—“And they shall appear.”

The Septuagint has *καὶ διέκυψαν*, that is, “they looked forth,” as Augustine’s context and his interpretation have it. But the Hebrew is *VAIATZITZU*, which is in the Hiphil verb-form, as it is called. It may be explained as “to look forth,” as in Song II, *METZITZ*, that is, “looking forth”; or as “to show oneself,” or “to appear,” after the manner of flowers which come forth and show themselves.

### VERSE 10.—“My old age.”

Jerome, Nebiensis, Pellicanus, and likewise the edition for Campensis: “my old age”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “my mixture”; Pagninus of Prato, Sanctes, and Münster: “I am sprinkled” or “anointed.” [Col. 0862A] Those who say “my old age” derive *BALLOTHI* from the verb *BALAH*, which means “has grown old.” Others derive it from the root *BALAL*, that is, “he poured over” or “he sprinkled.”
