“In abundant mercy.” Jerome: “in abundant oil.” Pellicanus and Nebiensis agree; Pagninus of Prato and Sanctes have “green oil”; Münster, “ointment of green olive”; the interpreters for Cajetan, “fresh oil”; the translator for Campensis, “my sap shall grow green”; and his paraphrase, “with most fragrant oil”—*BESCHEMEN RAANAN*. But no one doubts that oil signifies mercy in Scripture; moreover, *RAANAN* means “leafy” and “green,” which aptly indicate abundance. Hence the Chaldean: “with fresh oil of a leafy olive.”

**VERSE 14.**—“In abundant old age.” The Hebrews divide these two words, so that the first belongs to what precedes and the second to what follows. Thus Jerome renders: “They will still bear fruit in old age; they shall be plump and flourishing.” [Col. 0862B] The Septuagint joined together *BESEBAH DESCHENIM*. Jerome indicates something similar in the preceding psalm, as was noted. Then, where we say, “they shall be long-suffering,” others put “green” or “flourishing.” But because patience has a perfect work (James 1), it makes the soul flourish spiritually and grow most joyfully green. Again, “that they may proclaim,” in the Hebrew, is arranged with the following verse; we conclude the earlier verse at this point. Many instances of this kind occur in the Psalms. We have given the reasons above once and again.

## PSALM XCII

[Col. 0861]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PRAISE-SONG OF DAVID, ON THE DAY BEFORE THE SABBATH, WHEN THE EARTH WAS FOUNDED.”

[Col. 0861B]

“The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with splendour,” etc. Title: “A praise-song of David, on the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was founded.” [Aug.] It is not difficult to recognize this title from the book of Genesis. For the day before the Sabbath is the sixth day, on which man was made in the image and likeness of God, after all the works that were very good had first been made; and afterward God rested on the Sabbath, ceasing from new works, foreshadowing that we shall rest in God if we do good works, which are performed with labor—a labor in which man would fail unless the hope of rest sustained him. And because these works have an end, the sixth day on which they are performed has an evening. But the Sabbath has no evening, since Scripture is silent about it in order to signify that the rest granted after the labor of works will have no end.

This is also why, on the day observed for the dead, [Col. 0861D] after the feast of All Saints, the Church does not perform the office for the dead in the evening: because the rest wished for them on that day has no evening. But on the sixth day, literally speaking, the earth is not said to have been founded; the statement is mystical. For just as God made man on the sixth day, so in the sixth age of the world—that is, the sixth era of the age, which the sixth day signifies—he came to remake man. The earth, therefore, is founded when man is established immovably in faith; and then man is made in the image and likeness of God, which had been disfigured in man through sin. This is what the sixth day signifies.

[Cassiod., Aug.] And this is the sense of the title: this praise-song—that is, divine praise—is offered to David himself, that is, to Christ, whose praise is here sung in the demonstrative mode, concerning what he did when the earth was founded on the day before [Col. 0862B] the Sabbath, that is, the seventh day—concerning what he did in the sixth age of the world, signified by the sixth day. For then Christ, the foundation, came and established man in faith. This is the subject of the Psalm. Its intention [Col. 0862C] is to treat and exhort toward praise.

Method: [Cassiod.] There are seven divisions, as also seven grounds of praise. The first ground of praise is beauty; the second, strength, at “clothed”; the third, works, at “for”; the fourth, power, at “established”; the fifth, the praises of the whole creation, at “the rivers lifted up”; the sixth, the truth of his words, at “your testimonies”; the seventh, praise of the house, at “your house.” The prophet, therefore, exhorting us to praise the Lord, employs the demonstrative mode, saying:

**VERSE 1.**—“The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with splendour. The Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself.”

The Lord Christ has reigned, [Cassiod., Aug.] that is, he has made known that he is king. Then, explaining the first ground of praise, [Col. 0862D] he adds: “He has clothed himself with splendour.” Or, “he clothed himself,” in another reading, in relation to those to whom he was pleasing and who praised him. For Christ is beautiful to those to whom good things are pleasing. Therefore he put on splendour, [Cassiod.] that is, he displayed the beauty of his majesty to those whom it pleased—as when on Mount Tabor he shone before three disciples (Matt. 17).

[Aug., Cassiod.] The second ground of praise from strength follows: “The Lord has clothed himself,” or, “he clothed himself with strength,” in relation to those to whom he was displeasing, who disparaged him. For he is strong against detractors. He therefore put on strength, as when those who came to seize him went backward, 207 or fell down. Thus he showed splendour to friends, strength to enemies. And with these two he girded himself, [Alcuin.] so as to be, as it were, ready and unencumbered [Col. 0863A] in subduing the world to himself.

Or thus: “He girded himself.” Observe that he does not say “he girded,” or “he tucked up,” or “he armed himself,” but “he girded himself beforehand.” We gird ourselves to work; we arm ourselves to fight; we tuck up our garments to travel; we gird ourselves beforehand to serve. [Aug.] Girding therefore signifies works, because someone girds himself when about to work. You arm yourself when you attach something to yourself. Hence: “Gird your sword upon your thigh” (Ps. 44), that is, let the sword by which the world is subdued now be powerful in the flesh, while hidden wickedness is slain—that is, let the Spirit of God be powerful in the truth of speech.

But you gird yourself beforehand when you place something before yourself, as the Lord also girded himself beforehand when he washed the disciples’ feet (John 13), displaying complete humility, in which all strength consists. Pride, however, is frail, and all strength [Col. 0863B] comes from humility. Speaking therefore of strength, he said, “he girded himself beforehand,” namely with the humility which he possessed and showed to others, setting it, as it were, before himself. Hence he girded himself with a towel and washed the disciples’ feet, because he was then humble, giving an example of humility, as he himself taught: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11).

Or something else may be understood in this expression: namely patience, which is understood through strength, and which is especially necessary among detractors who disparage persons present. For someone disparages you when you are absent; because you do not feel it, strength is not necessary for you. But someone also disparages you when you are present; then it is necessary for you to gird yourself beforehand with strength, lest you become angry, because one who conquers anger is better than one who takes a city. Therefore he girded himself beforehand with the strength of patience, [Col. 0863C] which he held before himself.

[Jerome, Alcuin, Aug.] Or, “he girded himself beforehand” with the company of angels when ascending to the Father; or, “he girded himself beforehand” with zeal in working. And as Christ was clothed and girded with strength, so let man be immovable through strength; and this is the world which shall not be moved. Of this he adds:

**VERSE 2.**—“For he established the world, which shall not be moved.”

“For he established the world.” [Cassiod., Aug.] Here is the third ground, from works. As though he said: He put on splendour and strength precisely in order to found the earth. Hence he adds: “for he established in faith the world which shall not be moved,” [Cassiod., Aug.] that is, throughout the whole world he prepared those who shall not be shaken by any disturbance. For throughout the world there are stable persons, and also movable chaff. Therefore the world which shall not be moved is the person believing in Christ, prepared neither to become weak through the tongues of those who praise nor to be broken through the tongues of those who blame. The fourth ground, from power, follows.

**VERSE 3.**—“Your throne is established from then; you are from everlasting.”

“Your throne is established,” [Cassiod., Aug.] on which you sit at the right hand of the Father; or, namely, in believers. For a tranquil and humble soul is God’s throne. Hence: “My Spirit rested upon the humble and quiet person” (Isa. 66). Therefore be humble and quiet, that God may dwell in you. It is established, I say, “from then,” or “from that time,” in another reading; by this he indicates the time of grace. Perhaps he understands this from the day before the Sabbath, that is, the sixth [Col. 0864A] era of this world, when the Lord came: that is, it was established from the Incarnation, when, having come, he taught men. But lest you suppose that he began when he came by being born: “you are from everlasting,” that is, from eternity.

Or the connection is thus: [Gl. int.] Although I said that your throne was established from then, nevertheless you are properly “from everlasting,” that is, from eternity.

**VERSE 4.**—“The rivers have lifted up, O Lord; the rivers have lifted up their voice.”

**VERSE 5.**—“The rivers have lifted up their waves because of the voices of many waters.”

“They have lifted up.” [Cassiod., Alcuin, Aug.] This is the fifth ground, from the praise of the whole creation; and the reading is: “The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, their voice because of the voices of many waters.” The intervening words [Col. 0864B] are not in the edition of the Septuagint translators which Augustine expounds. As though he said: The Lord came on the sixth day; and in coming he chose his disciples, whom he filled with the Holy Spirit. Hence they are called rivers, concerning which it is elsewhere said: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 86). These rivers, therefore—that is, the apostles, filled when the Spirit was sent—lifted up their voice, that is, spoke strongly and loudly, though at first they had been afraid.

But when they were filled with the Holy Spirit, the Jews summoned them and ordered them not at all to speak or teach in the name of Jesus. Peter and John said to them: “We cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Acts 4). Thus the rivers lifted up their voice because, released from the Jewish council, the disciples heard this and all together raised their voice to the Lord. But as the apostles lifted up their voice, many believed; and, filled with the Holy Spirit, they too cried out. Hence it follows: “And there was a cry because of the voices of many waters,” when all together, like many waters, lifted up their voice, and many rivers began to cry out from a few. But while they cried out:

**VERSE 6.**—“The swellings of the sea became wonderful; wonderful is the Lord on high.”

“The swellings,” [Aug.] or the upheavals, “of the sea became wonderful”—that is, of the age, which began to rage and persecute believers. But the Lord is wonderful on high; for he walks upon the waters of the sea, that is, upon the heads of earthly powers and kings, whom he subdues and presses down, [Col. 0864D] so that there may be peace for the Church. This was once signified when he walked upon the waters.

[Cassiod., Alcuin.] Or, according to the same reading, without changing the beginning, it may be read under another punctuation: “The rivers have lifted up their voice, O Lord.” This remains unchanged. But what follows—“the rivers have lifted up their waves”—is absent from other editions, as we have said: “Because of the voices of many waters, the wonderful swellings of the sea have come about.” The waters are the nations which praise God. Hence the sea, that is, the age, rises greatly when it is established in God’s commandments. But so that all these things may be referred to God, who makes all things good, he adds: “Wonderful is the Lord on high.”

[Rem.] Or according to our text, the whole may be read thus: The Lord established the world; and while he established it, “the rivers have lifted up, [Col. 0865A] O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voice,” that is, the philosophers lifted up against God a voice of contradiction. And “the rivers have lifted up their waves,” that is, these same persons raised the agitated waves of their persecution “because of the voices of many waters,” that is, of many peoples. And “the swellings of the sea,” that is, of the age, “became wonderful.” This does not differ from the first reading. The same is true of what follows: “Wonderful is the Lord on high.”

**VERSE 7.**—“Your testimonies have become exceedingly credible; holiness becomes your house, O Lord, unto length of days.”

“Your testimonies.” [Cassiod., Alcuin, Aug.] This is the sixth ground, from the truth of his sayings. As though he said: Because the swelling of the sea is wonderful, and because the Lord is wonderful on high, “your testimonies, O Lord, have become exceedingly credible.” For he had previously said all this: “In me you will have peace; in the world you will have tribulation.” Therefore, when they saw tribulations, they hoped also for crowns on the basis of the prediction; and thus your testimonies became exceedingly credible, through reason, authority, and miracles.

[Gl. int., Alcuin, Cassiod.] Or thus: The age has been established in God’s commandments and the nations give praise. Since these things are so, [Col. 0866A] your testimonies—that is, the testimonies of the prophets—have become exceedingly credible, that is, have become true, that is, fulfilled in Christ.

“Your house.” [Cassiod., Aug.] This is the seventh ground, from praise of the house. As though he said: What has come about through all these things? Your house—your house, O Lord, throughout the whole world which shall not be moved—is fittingly adorned by holiness, that is, by the blessing of your coming, which is the eternal glory of the Church. And this is “unto length of days,” because, although many fall, the house nevertheless stands for a long time.

[Aug., Alcuin.] Observe that this Psalm is sung before the others in the morning praises, because it contains, most fully though in brief words, Christ’s praise and the grounds of praise.

## COMPARISON ON PSALM XCII: “THE LORD HAS REIGNED; HE HAS CLOTHED HIMSELF WITH SPLENDOUR,” ETC.

[Col. 0866B]

**VERSE 5.**—“Their waves.” Jerome, the Nebiensian, Pratensis, and Pellicanus: “their whirlpools,” which is the same thing. Sanctes, Münster, and the translators for Cajetan: “their breaking” or “their dashing,” yet also “of waves,” so that the sense is altogether the same: *DOCIAM* [probably a Hebrew transliteration; “their crashings,” OCR uncertain]. Moreover, the clause “the rivers have lifted up their waves,” which the Master says is not found in the Septuagint, we now read: “ἀροῦσιν οἱ ποταμοὶ ἐπιτρίψεις αὐτῶν”—“the rivers shall lift up their crashings/dashings.” It is absent, however, from the Roman edition.

## PSALM XCIII

[Col. 0865]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF DAVID, THE FOURTH DAY OF THE SABBATH.”

[Col. 0865B]

[Col. 0865C] In many Psalms titles were added by the Septuagint, either for the sake of elegance or by the authority of the Holy Spirit, in accordance with what Jerome says in the second prologue to the books of Chronicles.

“God of vengeances, the Lord.” Title: “A Psalm of David, the fourth day of the Sabbath.” [Aug.] To weak persons, who murmur against God in heart or speech, God seems to neglect present affairs, where good and evil are indiscriminately given to the good and the evil—and where, still more, greater goods are given to the evil and greater evils to the good. Or he seems to treat the wicked and the good alike, or even to favor the wicked more. Because of this weak people murmur against God and, impatient as though they were good in vain, either openly commit evil deeds, like a lion; or, if fear of men prevents them from daring, they nevertheless harbor such evil inwardly, like a wolf, and when an opportunity for harm has been found, they do not become evil but reveal what they were already.

For wolf and lion do not harm in the same way, but they desire in the same way; their will is equal, though their power differs. The one fears a dog; the other does not. This whole Psalm therefore heals those who murmur in heart or burst forth in words or acts, teaching patience. Hence it is suitably entitled “The Fourth Day of the Sabbath,” on which God made the lights—the sun to rule the day, and the moon and stars to rule the night (Ps. 135). These are the saints, who shine in the midst of this crooked and perverse generation, without murmuring, fixed in heaven. To them the Apostle says: “Do all things without murmuring, placed in the midst of a crooked generation, where you shine as lights in the world” (Phil. 2). For their citizenship is in heaven (Phil. 3), [Col. 0866B] and thus they look down upon what is done on earth. As though he said: Let them not concern themselves with what they see done here, just as the heavenly lights calmly complete their courses whatever happens on earth. And this is the sense of the title: This Psalm belongs to David the prophet and is observed on the fourth day of the Sabbath, [Aug.] that is, it concerns the patience of the saints, who are signified by the lights made on the fourth day of the Sabbath.

Its intention is to exhort to patience. Its method: The Psalm has three parts. [Cassiod.] First, the Prophet takes up the complaint of weak persons—why sinners glory—and sets forth beforehand the means of their healing: namely, that the Lord will take vengeance upon them. Second, he attacks blasphemers, showing that God knows and cares for these things, at “Understand.” Third, he says that the evils of the age are inflicted upon the righteous through the wicked so that, pierced by them, they may cry to God, at “Who will arise?” Therefore, against blasphemers who think God does not exact vengeance, he begins:

[Col. 0866D] **VERSE 1.**—“The Lord is a God of vengeances; the God of vengeances has acted freely.”

“The Lord,” [Aug., Gl. int.] whom some suppose will not take vengeance, is “the God of vengeances”; and, to confirm it more fully, he repeats, “the God of vengeances.” [Alcuin, Aug.] As though he said: He was not thought to take vengeance even on the wicked, but he truly does take vengeance. Therefore do not hasten to punish another if he has injured you, just as you would not wish to be punished at another’s request when you have injured someone. Do not overthrow the bridge of mercy across which you have passed; and if he sins against you, do not sin more grievously by blaspheming God. Weigh in the balance of justice that thief and yourself, the blasphemer. For he thinks that you are asleep; but you think that God is asleep. He watches for a man’s sleep in order to steal something; and you say that God sleeps and does not see man.

Nor should you desire vengeance, [Col. 0867A] which, if it comes, may perhaps find you first. How do you know when he will take vengeance? For, speaking in the flesh, he acted freely—or “confidently,” in another reading—because he spared no one, cutting away the vices of men as a physician. He therefore acted freely in the time of weakness, as when he taught in the Temple as one having authority (Matt. 7), because neither his truth nor his power could be resisted. What, 208 then, will he do at the judgment? Certainly he who, while to be judged, did not spare in word, will not spare in deed when judging. Hence, turning to the Lord, he says:

**VERSE 2.**—“Be exalted, you who judge the earth; render recompense to the proud.”

“Be exalted.” [Alcuin, Gl. int., Aug.] As though he said: Although they thus killed you because you acted confidently, now be exalted, so that they may no longer be able to do anything against you. [Gl. int., Cassiod., Aug.] Or the connection is thus: And because you acted then, now be exalted—by rising and ascending—so that they may no longer be able to do anything against you, you who judge the earth, that is, earthly persons. And “render recompense to the proud,” not to those who repent. I say “render,” because:

**VERSE 3.**—“How long shall sinners, O Lord, how long shall sinners glory?”

“How long,” etc. [Aug.] Or the connection is thus: I say “render,” but when will this be? He asks on your behalf, that in him you may find what you do not know, though he does not fail to know. He asks, therefore, when it shall happen, saying: “How long shall sinners, O Lord, how long shall sinners—?” This repetition signifies the pain of waiting, [Cassiod., Gl. int.] because the boasting of the wicked is burdensome to the good. How long, [Col. 0867C] I say, “shall they glory,” rather than merely sin?

**VERSE 4.**—“They shall pour forth and speak iniquity; all who work injustice shall speak.”

“They shall pour forth and speak.” [Alcuin, Aug., Cassiod.] He explains their sins. As though he said: They truly are sinners, because they shall pour forth, that is, utter all perverse thoughts, and shall speak iniquity against God, saying, “God does not care about these things,” or “the things we do please him.” Or they shall pour forth public persuasions and speak iniquity, that is, private persuasions, so that no time may be free from guilt.

[Aug.] Or according to another reading, which is, “They answer and speak.” As though he said: They sin and glory. [Col. 0867D] And this is because they answer, that is, they have something to answer one who justly rebukes them, saying: “Why should I not do what I please? I am happy; your righteous person is miserable.” They devise arguments of this kind for their answer. And while answering thus, they speak iniquity, saying that God does not care for these matters.

[Cassiod., Gl. int.] Then he proceeds by intensifying the charge: “All who work injustice shall speak”—they do not merely speak injustice. Then he explains what injustice they commit, namely this:

**VERSE 5.**—“They have humbled your people, O Lord, and afflicted your inheritance.”

“O Lord, they have humbled your people,” [Aug., Cassiod.] that is, the righteous, over whom they wish to lord it proudly. Then he specifies the people, saying: “They have afflicted your inheritance”—this is the people—but have not destroyed it.

**VERSE 6.**—“They have slain the widow and the stranger, and killed peoples.”

“The widow and the stranger,” [Cassiod., Alcuin.] that is, the alien, “they have slain; and they have killed the fatherless” (Deut. 10), literally. God protects these persons and commands that they be helped; therefore the crime is greater. Or typologically, by “widow” are signified those for whom error, their husband, has died; by “strangers,” those who do not seek here a continuing city (Heb. 13); and by “fatherless,” those who are without the devil as father and without concupiscence as mother.

**VERSE 7.**—“And they said: The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.”

[Col. 0868B] “And they said”—behold the blasphemy—“The Lord will not see.” [Cassiod., Aug.] The wicked person says this because God is presently silent, not taking vengeance, and he supposes that the matter pleases him. “Nor will [he] understand.” As though he said: Even if he sees, he will not take it to heart; that is, he does not care. As though he said: He pays no attention to these matters, neglects them, does not attend so as to see; God does not care what I do, but attends to other things—“the God of Jacob,” [Cassiod., Gl. int.] that is, of Christians, of whom they ought not to say this.

**PART II. VERSE 8.**—“Understand, you senseless among the people; and you foolish, become wise at last.”

“Understand, you senseless.” [Alcuin.] The second part, in which he attacks blasphemers, showing that God knows these matters and cares for them, wisely and justly ordering the affairs both of the wicked, for whom a pit is dug, and of the good, who are afflicted patiently. His purpose is unknown to the wicked; he reveals it to his friends. As though he said: You wicked persons say this, but, O sinners, understand, you who are senseless, whose feet, namely, totter while envying those who prosper in evil. [Aug., Cassiod.] And this is “among the people,” because they teach doubly what they have learned wrongly. And you, foolish persons—the foolish are those who openly blaspheme, saying that God does not see—“become wise at last.”

[Aug., Gl. int.] Or thus: You senseless persons, that is, those who do not know, understand—you who, now living well, are among the people, that is, in the number of the good—and you foolish, that is, imprudent persons: even if you know, become wise at last. What is it that you should know? What follows:

**VERSE 9.**—“Will he who planted the ear not hear? Or will he who formed the eye not see?”

[Col. 0868D] “Will he who planted the ear,” so that you might hear, “not hear?” [Jerome, Aug., Cassiod.] I do not say that he does not have an ear, because God has these powers, but not bodily members. As though he said: Does he who made in you that by which you hear not possess that by which he hears? “Or will he who formed the eye not see?” Certainly he sees. For he gave no one as much as he has in himself. And will he not rebuke at the judgment?

**VERSE 10.**—“Will he who corrects the nations not rebuke? Or he who teaches man knowledge?”

“He who now corrects the nations.” [Alcuin.] As though he said: Will he who daily corrects the nations for original sin not rebuke them for sins added besides? Or according to another reading, “he who instructs the nations,” for whose instruction God sent his Son, and before him [Col. 0869A] and after him sent his servants, that is, prophets and apostles. Will he not therefore rebuke, that is, judge, those to whom he first sent the word of teaching?

A teacher instructing in school entrusts you with something to be rendered back. Certainly, when you receive from the teacher, you are instructed; the teacher entrusts to you what he gives, and will he not demand that you return it? And when you begin to return it, will you be free from fear of blows? Thus God will require what he has sown. For we who receive now shall afterward stand before the Teacher in order to render an account of all things. Hence the Apostle says: “We shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, that each may receive,” etc. And is he who teaches man knowledge himself without it? Is the one who makes you know himself ignorant? Far be it!

**VERSE 11.**—“The Lord knows the thoughts of men, [Col. 0869B] that they are vain.”

“The Lord knows.” [Gl. int., Aug., Cassiod.] As though he said: He truly knows, because the Lord even knows the thoughts of men. And he knows this: that they are vain. But you do not know the thoughts of God, that they are just. Yet he knows that the thoughts of men are vain; and indeed the thoughts of such people are vain—something they themselves cannot know of themselves, but the Lord knows them to be vain.

[Aug.] Therefore abandon these thoughts, that you may grasp the thoughts of God, which are wise. The person who is in the firmament of heaven grasps them, no other does; but when people have become his friends, God discloses to them his counsel, namely why he spares the wicked. Hence he adds:

**VERSE 12.**—“Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach from your law.”

[Col. 0869C] “Blessed is the man,” etc. [Alcuin, Gl. int.] As though he said: They are vain, but blessed is the man whom you, O Lord, instruct as a child through tribulations, and whom you teach from your law, not from vanity, as an adult—namely, one whom you establish by heavenly teaching. Observe that instruction takes place in two ways: by the discipline of tribulations, hence he adds, “whom you instruct”; and by teaching of the law, hence he says, “and teach him from your law.” [Note: [Col. 0869D] From Augustine, in the preface to the Psalm.]

Those who are instructed in this way are like lights in heaven. For God’s law is the heaven in which the lights—that is, the saints—are fixed by meditating on the law, lest they be moved. Hence we mentioned in the title this heaven, concerning which it is elsewhere said: “He stretched out the heaven like a skin” (Ps. 103). For here the book of God is stretched out like a skin, so that in it may be read what must now be learned by people who are to be taught. But when all shall know God in the future, heaven shall be folded up like a book. Therefore learn patience from God’s law, so that you may endure patiently until a pit is dug for the sinner. It is not yours to know how or why it is dug for him.

**VERSE 13.**—“That you may calm him from evil days, until a pit is dug for the sinner.”

“That you may calm him.” [Aug.] As though he said: You teach him for this purpose, certainly: that from evil days, in which the wicked flourish and the good suffer, you may calm him, so that he may patiently endure whatever happens here, just as the lights calmly [Col. 0870A] complete their courses, whatever occurs below or whatever men say against them. “Calm him until a pit is dug for the sinner.” The prosperity of the wicked is a pit; the suffering of the good is the Father’s scourge.

Prosperity is a pit because, when God spares a man, he becomes exalted through impunity; and when he thinks himself high, he falls. Hence elsewhere: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Ps. 72). Behold now God’s counsel, by which he spares the wicked. The wicked are spared so that a pit may be dug for them. The pit is still being dug for the sinner, and do you already wish to bury him? You are in too much haste. Wait until the pit is dug for the sinner—not indeed for every sinner, but for the proud person. Hence above he said: “Render recompense to the proud,” not to the tax collector who confesses, but to the Pharisee who boasts (Luke 18).

The proud person is one [Col. 0870B] who is not humbled to repentance; then one who attributes to himself whatever good things he possesses. Even if he attributes them to God, he insults those who do not possess them and lifts himself above them. Therefore first humble yourself in repentance; afterward, if you live rightly, give thanks to him from whom you have what you possess, and do not despise another. But if a pit is dug for him, what of me who labor? Behold a great thing:

**VERSE 14.**—“For the Lord will not cast off his people, nor forsake his inheritance.”

“For the Lord will not cast off.” [Aug., Gl. int.] Or the connection is thus: I rightly said, “that you may calm him,” because the Lord will not cast off his people as rejected, even though he disciplines them, so that he may give them an eternal inheritance. And he will not forsake his inheritance as unaided. He will not forsake it, [Col. 0870C] I say:

**VERSE 15.**—“Until righteousness is turned into judgment; and who are beside it? All who are upright in heart.”

“Until righteousness,” [Cassiod., Gl. int.] that is, those who are now righteous and therefore judged, “is turned into judgment,” so that they may judge, because then they shall be judges of those persons. Hence: “You also shall sit upon twelve thrones,” etc. (Matt. 19).

[Aug.] But lest you doubt who these are, he asks and answers, saying: “And who are beside it?” He answers: “All who are upright in heart,” that is, those who are without error. Or according to another reading: “And all who have it,” that is, righteousness, “are upright in heart,” that is, they will what God wills—namely, to wait for the wicked and things of that sort. For those who subject their crooked will to the divine will and direct it according to the rule of the divine will are upright in heart.

Christ taught us this in his Passion, expressing in himself two wills according to his two natures, and subjecting the human will to the divine will. In his body, that is, in the Church, he foreshadowed certain persons who would wish to do their own will but would afterward follow God’s will. For the Lord, foreshadowing weak persons in himself—that is, bearing the person of the weak and sympathizing with them—said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26). Here you have the human will, which he immediately [Col. 0871A] directed to the divine by saying: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (ibid.). Thus he signified human weakness.

For the Lord did not truly—that is, of necessity—fear suffering when he was to rise on the third day, whereas Paul ardently desired to depart and be with Christ (Phil. 1). Paul rejoices at being crowned, and the Lord is sad when he is about to crown others. Yet he assumed sadness just as he assumed flesh, namely by will, not by necessity. For he was sad, as the Gospel says. For if he was not sad when the Gospel says, “My soul is sad unto death,” then neither did Jesus sleep when it says, “Jesus slept,” nor did he eat when it says that he ate. Thus nothing sound will remain, so that it may even be said that his body was not real. Therefore whatever is written concerning him is true. It happened, then: he was sad, and he voluntarily received real sadness just as he voluntarily received real flesh.

**PART III. VERSE 16.**—“Who will rise up for me against evildoers? Or who will stand with me against workers of iniquity?”

“Who will rise up for me?” [Cassiod., Alcuin, Aug.] The third part, in which he says that instability and the waves of the age—that is, evils through the wicked—come upon the righteous so that, pierced by them, they may cry to God and nothing else may please them; then deliverance is more welcome. As though he said: Many everywhere advise evil, not knowing how God justly governs these worldly affairs; but who will rise up? As though he said: I am tossed about; I am almost conquered. Wherever I look, evils meet me. But by what means shall I conquer? How then shall [Col. 0871C] I be upright, when so many things oppose me? And this is: “Who will rise up for me,” [Cassiod.] that is, on my behalf, “against evildoers,” that is, demons? Or who will “stand,” that is, persevere with me in the battle, patiently? For he conquers who endures; he loses who strikes. He will stand, I say, “against workers of iniquity.” As though he said: No one except the Lord. For man cannot, but the Lord can, as he shows by the result.

**VERSE 17.**—“Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell.”

For unless this were so, that the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt, [Aug., Cassiod.] or “had dwelt,” in hell—that is, in the pit prepared for the sinner; that is, it had nearly consented, or did consent, to the ungodly. For it was already wavering, already almost consenting to evil. It might have been deceived by vain persuasions unless the Lord had delivered it. But:

**VERSE 18.**—“If I said, ‘My foot has been moved,’ your mercy, O Lord, helped me.”

“If I said, ‘My foot has been moved,’ your mercy, O Lord, helped me against my movement.” [Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] Behold how God loves confession: confess that you have been moved, and you escape. As soon as fault is not denied to the Judge, he delivers. Thus he delivered Peter, walking on the water, lest he sink. Peter said to the Lord: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.” The Lord said to him: “Come” (Matt. 14).

For just as Christ walks upon the sea by his own power, that is, treads upon the heads of the proud and the waves of the age, [Col. 0872A] so at his command Peter—that is, the Church—yet through weakness, staggers and cries: “Lord, I perish” (ibid.). And mercy stretches out its hand, just as the Lord stretched out his hand to Peter, saying: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (ibid.). Therefore what is said here, “My foot has been moved,” is there, “I perish”; and what is said here, “Your mercy, O Lord, helped me,” is there, “Jesus stretched out his hand.”

[Gl. int., Cassiod.] Dangers make the deliverer sweeter. Hence consolation against the evils of the age is added, and it is then more joyful. Therefore he says:

**VERSE 19.**—“According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul.”

“And your consolations have gladdened my soul,” [Aug., Cassiod.] even though the body is burned; they are according to [Col. 0872B] the multitude of my sorrows. The sorrows are many and bitter, but the consolations are many and sweet; they do not fail the person who labors, and these consolations are in my heart. By this he signifies that the thoughts are healthful: when he considered eternal rewards, he despised temporal evils. Your mercy helps me, but:

**VERSE 20.**—“Does the throne of iniquity cling to you, you who fashion trouble by commandment?”

Will the throne of iniquity cling to you? [Aug.] No wicked person sits with you, for there is no fellowship of light with darkness (2 Cor. 6). [Cassiod., Aug.] Or, the throne of iniquity is possession of the world with attachment to it; it does not adhere to God, who commands his own to flee these things. You who fashion. As though he said: From this I understand that no wicked person adheres to you [Col. 0872C], because you did not spare even us from the scourge. And this is: you are he who fashions—that is, makes and forms—labour, or pain, according to another reading, even for your children. For as Peter says: “Judgment now begins with the house of God” (1 Pet. 4), that is, with the faithful; and if the children are scourged, what ought utterly wicked servants to expect? And again: “If it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel?” (ibid.). And again: “If the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?” (ibid.). How, then, can the wicked be with you, when you spare not even your faithful from the scourge?

In a commandment. [Aug., Alcuin.] As though he said: You cause pain, and that pain or labour is in a commandment, that is, it performs the function of a commandment. For just as a commandment corrects, so the pain of the scourge reforms children. Hence he fittingly used “you fashion,” that is, “you make and form” [Col. 0872D]. For one pain is formed, another unformed. Formed pain is that which instructs and reforms, and that pain is a commandment; the other is unformed. [Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] Or thus: “You fashion labour,” or “pain, in a commandment,” that is, from labour or pain you make a commandment for us, so that the labour or pain itself may be a commandment. For his commandment contains the commandment: “Blessed are those who mourn, and those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5). He commands this deservedly, because labour is the price of the kingdom of God, by which it is bought as something for sale. Therefore God commands labour and pain, so that a human being may not be without fear, nor love anything else through forgetfulness of the true good. For in calm waters God—Christ—sleeps, and then a wave rises, in which he is awakened. Thus in some persons faith in Christ grows lukewarm in the calm of ease, and the wave of temptation rises [Col. 0873A]. Let them therefore awaken faith, and so they are delivered.

**VERSE 21.**—“They will take captive the soul of the righteous, and condemn innocent blood.”

They will take captive. [Alcuin.] As though he said: And since there is nothing in common between you and evil people, what purpose then do they serve? That through them you may prick the good, so that, being pricked, the good may cry out to you; and in the end these men may perish. These three things are shown in these three verses. [Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] As though he said: Thus you fashion labour and pain, because through evil people you exercise and instruct the good. “They will lie in wait against the life of the righteous.” Since they cannot bring true charges, they bring false accusations. And when they cannot injure the soul, they will condemn innocent blood—which would suit their crimes. [Col. 0873B] And why does God permit this?

**VERSE 22.**—“And the Lord became a refuge for me, and my God the helper of my hope.”

And, [Gloss interlinear; Aug.] that is, because: thus the Lord became a refuge for me, so that I am secure. For if you were not in danger, you would not seek a refuge; you are pierced by pain in order that you may seek a remedy; hope in the world recedes, and hope in God comes. And my God became the helper of my hope. For it is not yet the thing itself, but hope, in which he helps us, lest we fail in hope but attain what is hoped for.

**VERSE 23.**—“And he will repay them their own iniquity, and in their malice he will destroy them; the Lord our God will destroy them.”

[Col. 0873C] “And he will repay them their own iniquity.” [Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod., Gloss interlinear.] By this end every doubt is cured. For it is plainly shown that God does not now neglect matters, but repays at the fitting time. “And in their malice,” that is, not according to what he accomplishes for us through them, but according to what they intended, “he will destroy them,” that is, he will separate them from his kingdom; there—that is, in that separation—their misery will be incomprehensible. He can truly do this, because he who will destroy them is the Lord our God.

## Comparison on Psalm 93: “The God of Vengeances, the Lord,” etc.

**VERSE 1.**—He acted freely. *Hophia*, that is, “appear splendidly.” Or, as St Jerome has it, “show yourself.” [Col. 0873D] The rest are to be understood similarly. You will reconcile our reading without departing from the sense if you understand that the power of almighty God is openly displayed and set before the eyes, more conspicuously than light itself, when he freely inflicts vengeance according to his will and choice, with no fear and no one hindering him: openly to all, in the open, manifestly.

**VERSE 4.**—“They utter.” Jerome and some others: “they flow”; Sanctes, Münster, and the translator for Campensis agree with our reading. *Iabiu* is ambiguous, although “they flow” suits a perverse and slippery tongue especially well. Hence the Campensian paraphrase: “The wicked mind will burst forth into words.”

[Col. 0874A] “They speak iniquity.” Jerome translates *athap* as “ancient,” which Pellicanus follows; Pagninus, “lofty”; Sanctes, “hard”; Münster, “harsh to hear”; the interpretation for Cajetan, “perhaps.” All these correspond most aptly to iniquity—indeed, nothing more so. Hence Nebiensis translates it “inveterate malice.”

“All who work injustice will speak.” They understand the word “will speak,” corresponding word for word to *iithammeru*, as meaning “with boasting.” Thus Jerome said “they will chatter”; Münster, “they boast”; Pagninus, “they will magnify themselves”; and others give somewhat similar renderings. The Master’s exposition is fitting.

In this verse St Jerome teaches that sometimes certain words must be added in Latin which are not in the Hebrew or Greek, for the elegance of the expression. For he says to Sunia and Fretella: “‘Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord’: you say that the ‘you’ is not in the Greek, *makarios anthrōpos hon an paideusēs, Kyrie*, that is, ‘Blessed is the man whom indeed you instruct, O Lord.’ And this is true. But in Latin it has been placed for *euphōnia*, that is, harmony of sound. For if we say, ‘Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord,’ the composition will lack elegance. But when ‘O Lord’ is said, and an apostrophe is made to the Lord, the sense suffers no harm if ‘you’ is also inserted.” [Col. 0874B]

**VERSE 15.**—“Who [will follow] after it? All who are upright in heart.” Since “righteousness” and “judgment” had been set before in the preceding clause, it was open to say in the following one, “according to that righteousness,” or “according to that judgment.” Yet Faber attacks our reading as though it were absurd. Jerome, according to the Hebrew, said “that,” not “that one” [feminine]. Whether “that one” is feminine or neuter, it is acceptable. Hence Münster translates: “After that one all will walk.” And Augustine explained it more clearly than light as concerning righteousness: “Those,” he says, “who now possess righteousness do not yet judge. For first there is possessing righteousness, and afterward judging.” Arnobius likewise has this. But Faber objects that the Greek *autēs* is feminine, so that it refers to *krisin*, “judgment,” of feminine gender. *Idem* [“the same”] is sometimes used thus. [Col. 0874C] But why does he shut his eyes and refuse to see the other word for righteousness, *dikaiosynē*?

**VERSE 17.**—“My soul would almost have dwelt in hell.” All agree sufficiently, because *dumah* signifies “grave,” “silence,” “cut off,” “deserted,” all of which refer to hell; although, with the Septuagint, some translate “in hell,” others “in silence,” and some “my soul [would have been] cut down” or “deserted,” where we say, “my soul [would have dwelt] in hell.”

**VERSE 19.**—“According to the multitude of my sorrows.” Jerome and most others put “thoughts” in place of “sorrows,” *sareappai*; but thoughts of sorrow are meant, as is clear from the continuation of the sentence: “Your consolations have made my soul glad.” Hence the Campensian translation: “In the multitude of my inward torments.”

**VERSE 20.**—“You who fashion labour in a commandment.” Almost everyone translates *amal* as “labour” or “affliction.” [Col. 0874D] Sanctes translated “iniquity,” I suppose because it surpasses every affliction; and it should be pronounced interrogatively: “forming iniquity in a commandment.” Others understand it simply, though not all in the same sense. There are those who refer it to the throne of iniquity, which is accustomed to fashion labour in a commandment by imposing burdens, as the modern writers wish. The ancients—Jerome, Augustine, Arnobius, Gregory, *Morals*, book 18, chapter 12, and Cassiodorus—are more pleasing. They explain it of God, who fashions labour 210 in a commandment, through which he corrects the ungodly and rewards those corrected; so that you may say simply and plainly, “You who fashion labour in a commandment,” setting aside the interrogation which the former writers pursue.

# Psalm 94

[Col. 0875]

## Title of the Psalm: “[Note: [Col. 0875D] *Anepigraphos par’ Hebraiois*—Untitled among the Hebrews.] A Psalm of Praise, a Song, for David Himself.”

[Col. 0875A]

“Come, let us exult in the Lord.” Title: “A Psalm of Praise, a Song, for David himself.” [Alcuin, Aug.] This concerns the time of grace, in which through Christ one enters into rest. Therefore both title and psalm exhort us to praise God joyfully and devoutly. For praise signifies devotion, song joyfulness, so that we may praise with gladness. Praise of what? The psalm indicates: namely, of God. And the sense is: [Cassiod.] This praise of song—that is, of devotion and joyfulness—is made to David himself, that is, to Christ.

Purpose: An exhortation to exultation and praise.

Method: The psalm has two parts. First, the prophet, describing Christ’s praises, invites the Jews, whom he foresaw might resist Christ. Secondly, Christ himself warns the same people not to harden themselves, at “Do not.” [Aug.] Thus, as though inviting them to a great feast, he says: O you who are far off through unlikeness,

**VERSE 1.**—“Come, let us exult in the Lord; let us make joyful noise to God our Saviour.”

Come, [Haymo, Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] by faith, and let us exult in mind in the Lord, not in the world; let us make joyful noise in voice to God, our saving Jesus. As though he said: Let joy be so great that it cannot be expressed in words, yet let the voice outwardly bear witness to what is conceived within. And

**VERSE 2.**—“Let us anticipate his face with confession; and in psalms let us make joyful noise to him.”

His face, [Aug., Gloss interlinear, Cassiod.] that is, the presence of the coming Judge, let us anticipate, because he will come; lest the enemy forestall us by accusation, and lest there then be anything in us to be examined. [Aug.] And let us do this in confession, praising him and accusing ourselves: these are distinct vows. Of these it is said elsewhere: “I will pay you my vows, which my lips have uttered distinctly” (Ps. 65). He therefore distinguishes who praises God and accuses himself. For confession is twofold: of praise and of sin. Confession of sin belongs to the praise of the one who forgives, and it is this praise with which the psalm is concerned. “And in psalms let us make joyful noise to him,” that is, let us feel in jubilation what we say or do in psalms.

**VERSE 3.**—“For the Lord is a great God, and a great King over all gods.”

“For God.” [Aug.] These are those words which [Col. 0875D] belong to the praise of this song. As though he said: Therefore let us make joyful noise and exult, because God is a great Lord in supreme power, and a great King over all the gods of the nations. Or, more properly, by “gods” he means human beings over whom he is king, not demons.

**VERSE 4.**—“For in his hand are all the ends of the earth; and the heights of the mountains are his.”

“For in his hand are.” [Cassiod., Aug.] After his greatness, he turns to mercy. As though he said: Therefore rejoice, because in his hand are all the ends of the earth, that is, the nations. Or according to another reading, which adds: “For the Lord will not reject his people, because in his hand,” etc. As though he said: Therefore let us make joyful noise, because the Lord will not reject his people, that is, the Jews, who are properly his people. Though some branches of them were broken off, yet the olive itself remains, from which came the apostles and many others, and Christ himself. From this very place the Apostle took testimony in the Epistle to the Romans (Rom. 10). Again, because in his hand are all the ends of the earth, that is, the nations. For he is the cornerstone and joins others in himself, that is, the nations. And “the heights of the mountains,” that is, earthly powers formerly hostile, [Gloss interlinear] or the powers of heaven, that is, angels, are his. Again, therefore, let us make joyful noise.

**VERSE 5.**—“For the sea is his, and he made it; and his hands formed the dry land.”

[Col. 0876B] “For the sea is his,” [Aug.] that is, the world, “and he made it,” whose waves God restrains within a boundary, not allowing us to be tempted above what we are able to bear (1 Cor. 10); and, by God’s action, those waves even bring us profit. Therefore he brings it about that scandals do not harm you, since they receive their measure from God, because the sea is his by dominion. “And he made it”: [Cassiod., Aug.] this is added so that you may know it is subject to him. “And his hands formed the dry land,” that is, the dry ground of the human mind, which has received rain and bears fruit, and which he does not allow the waves of temptations to cover.

**VERSE 6.**—“Come, let us worship and fall down, and weep before the Lord who made us, for he is the Lord our God.”

[Col. 0876C] Come. [Cassiod., Aug., Gloss interlinear, Cassiod., Aug.] First he called the untaught to exultation. Now, after displaying God’s grace, he calls them to repentance, which is harder. As though he said: Because he does such great things, therefore come. He repeats the foregoing exhortation. As though he said: In view of the praises I have recalled, do not remain far away in life and conduct, but come nearer; and let us worship, which is greater, and fall down humbly before God. And if perhaps you are troubled concerning the sins that have made you far off, weep: let us do what follows, “And let us weep before God.” For a tear extinguishes the flame of sin that burns in the conscience. “Who made us.” As though he said: He does not despise his own work. Behold great confidence. For you can fail of yourself, but you cannot restore yourself. He who made you restores you. Therefore let us worship, because he is the Lord our God, who is to be worshipped.

**VERSE 7.**—“And we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand.”

But what are we, that we may safely weep and fall down? [Aug.] Behold: we too are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand. See how elegantly the order of words is altered. He did not say “the sheep of his pasture and the people of his hand,” which would seem more fitting, because pasture belongs to sheep. He did this so that you might understand that those who are the people of God are sheep. [Col. 0877A] He also called them “the sheep of [his] hand,” whom he made, because he made us to be sheep. He says this in distinction from sheep which we buy: they are not called sheep of our hands, because they are sheep bought by us; we did not make them. But he, by his grace, made us sheep.

**VERSE 8.**—“Today, if you hear his voice.”

Today, if [you hear] his voice. [Cassiod., Haymo, Aug.] As though he said: We are people and sheep, but a condition is set before all this. As though he said: I say this on the condition that, if today—that is, in the time of grace—you hear his voice, who now speaks in person, whereas formerly he spoke through a servant and sent heralds before himself, he himself deigned to come. Therefore, do not be hard as you then were. Then he adds what voice they ought to hear, namely this:

[Col. 0877B]

## Part II—“Do not harden your hearts.”

Do not harden [your hearts]. [Cassiod.] The second part. Christ himself now warns them not to be hardened, lest what befell their fathers happen to them: do not harden your hearts. Whoever does not believe is stony.

**VERSE 9.**—“As in the provocation, according to the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me; they tested me and saw my works.”

“As in the provocation,” etc. [Cassiod., Alcuin.] The very majesty of Christ speaking terrifies the obstinate through comparison with their fathers, so that at least in this way they might soften. Or it may be read in the person of the Prophet, with another division, thus: As though he said: Because we are God’s people and sheep, therefore today—that is, always—if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts [Col. 0877C], as your fathers did in the provocation. Here the Prophet speaks in the person of Christ. “Provocation,” I say, which occurred according to the day—that is, on the day—of temptation in the wilderness: then, if you are hard, you will be like them. [Gloss interlinear, Aug., Cassiod.] Behold, the fault of the ancestors is repeated so that their punishment may be feared: “where your fathers tempted me,” to see whether I was able. Be no longer children of such men—that is, imitators. They tested me to see what I could do, and saw with their eyes the works of my great power, but did not believe with their minds.

**VERSE 10.**—“For forty years I was offended with that generation; and I said: They always err in heart.”

For forty years I was close to that generation, [Aug.] in signs and miracles. Or, according to another reading, “I was offended,” [Col. 0877D] that is, I was implacably angry with that generation. [Aug., Alcuin.] This number is mystical. For by forty years all ages are signified. It consists of ten, which is the first limit of numbers and thus signifies fullness, and of four, which refers to the four seasons. Hence the Lord, in the sacrament of this number, fasted forty days when he was tempted (Matt. 4), and was with his disciples forty days after the resurrection (Acts 1), [Aug.] signifying that he is present with us as comforter and helper during this time of pilgrimage and temptation. As he himself says: “I am with you until the end of the age” (Matt. 28). [Cassiod.] Notice also that Christ, fasting forty days and conversing with the apostles forty days after the resurrection, caused the whole world to believe. [Col. 0878A] But the Jews did not yield even to the benefits of forty years. “And I said,” [Haymo, Gloss interlinear] rebuking through ministers: “They always err in heart,” that is, seriously; or, “with a heart given to them,” as though [it were the faculty] through which they should not err.

**VERSE 11.**—“And these have not known my ways, as I swore in my wrath: If they shall enter into my rest.”

“And these have not known my ways.” [Aug., Haymo, Cassiod.] And therefore, “if those hard people shall enter”: they will not enter into my eternal rest—*aposiōpēsis*, a rhetorical silence or omission. As though he said: They will not enter, just as—that is, as—I swore, that is, as I immovably determined. God swears not by another but by himself; for by himself he confirms threats as well as promises. I swore, I say, in my wrath. This is added because he sometimes swears while graciously disposed, as in: “The Lord swore truth to David” (Ps. 131). [Col. 0878B]

## Comparison on Psalm 94: “Come, Let Us Worship,” etc.

**VERSE 1.**—“Let us make joyful noise to God.” *Letzur*, that is, “to the rock” or “to strength,” by which Christ, true God and true man, is rightly understood: “And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

**VERSE 4.**—“The ends of the earth.” Jerome and the Campensian paraphrase: “the foundations of the earth”; Pagninus: “explorations”; Sanctes: “investigations”; Münster, Nebiensis, and Pellicanus: “the inner recesses of the earth.” *Meheqre aretz*, “investigations,” is conveniently explained by “ends,” which are known in themselves to God alone, according to every dimension. Hence Münster in his scholium: nothing in nature is so hidden or so evident that it is not in God’s hand. Moreover, this clause, “for the Lord will not reject his people,” occurs in the Roman psalmody, which the Church uses daily at the beginning of the morning office. Yet it is neither in the Hebrew nor in the Septuagint. Certainly it is significant that the Apostle, according to Augustine’s testimony, took the proof-text of this psalm from this place in Romans 11. Yet I found in a certain Greek copy: *hoti ou mē apōsetai Kyrios ton laon autou*—“for the Lord will certainly not reject his people.” [Col. 0878C]

**VERSE 6.**—“Let us weep before the Lord.” Jerome and others: “let us kneel.” *Nibrechah*. It appears that the Septuagint read *nibcheh*, without the *resh*, and this means “let us weep,” although reverence and fear of the divine majesty are expressed in either reading.

**VERSE 11.**—“For forty years.” In Hebrews 3 the Greek codices perhaps incorrectly connect this with what precedes, making it: “They saw my works for forty years.” For what follows protests against this: “But with whom was he offended for forty years?” Although perhaps 211 both may be referred to it: namely, that they saw God’s works for forty years while always ungrateful, for which reason God was also angry with them for forty years. [Col. 0878D]

“Was offended.” Jerome: “that generation displeased me”; Pagninus: “I was afflicted with vexation.” Nearly all others say much the same. Sanctes, however, says “I contended,” as do the interpreters for Cajetan and the Campensian paraphrase. But the sense tends toward the implication that such contention made God angry. Nor does our reading disagree. It only observes that the Roman edition, used by the Church at the beginning of the morning Hours, has “I was near,” which Augustine follows in interpreting of the signs and miracles that displayed God’s presence to that people. The Hebrew word *aqut*, however, signifies nothing of this sort, unless you understand that God was all the more hostile to that people because for forty years he did not cease to present himself in wonderful signs and inexhaustible benefits; and such a reading states the cause of wrath and provocation, whereas ours states the effect.

[Col. 0879A]

**VERSE 12.**—“If they shall enter into my rest.” Jerome indeed supplies the negation, “that they should not enter into my rest,” but so as to explain the force of “if they shall enter into my rest.” For although in Hebrew *im*, “if,” and in Greek *ei* are used, they are not marks of a condition but of one swearing and expressing abhorrence. [Col. 0880A] The Apostle clearly develops this in Hebrews 3 and 4, where he uses both “if” and “not.” For after first setting out “if they shall enter into my rest,” he infers: “But to whom did he swear that they should not enter into his rest?” And in what follows he repeats it by means of “if.”

# Psalm 95

[Col. 0879]

## Title of the Psalm: [Note: [Col. 0879D] *Anepigraphos par’ Hebraiois*—Untitled among the Hebrews.] “A Psalm for David Himself, When the House Was Being Built after the Captivity.”

[Col. 0879A]

“Sing to the Lord.” Title: “A Psalm of David, when the house was being built after the captivity.” [Cassiod., Alcuin.] We read in the Old Testament that the house of God, that is, the Temple destroyed by the Babylonians, was rebuilt after seventy years of captivity, when the children of Israel, with King Cyrus’s permission, returned to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest. [Col. 0879B] By this rebuilding is understood the rebuilding of the spiritual temple, of which the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3). This temple was overthrown by the devil through sin, and man was taken captive under the law of sin and death; but through Christ this temple is rebuilt throughout the whole world, and man is freed from captivity lest he perish. This psalm concerns this rebuilding, not that material one. And the sense of the title is: This psalm belongs to the prophet David, who here speaks concerning what occurred when the house of God was built after the captivity [Col. 0879C] which was under the devil through sin, just as Solomon’s Temple was literally rebuilt under Zerubbabel after the Babylonian captivity. This is the second psalm concerning both comings [of Christ].

Purpose: [Cassiod.] It exhorts to praise for the rebuilding.

Method: The psalm has two parts. First, it addresses prelates, that they may sing and proclaim to all. Secondly, it addresses subjects, at “Bring to the Lord.” In the preceding psalm it warned the Jews to lay aside hardness and believe in Christ; but since that hardness was to endure, it now exhorts all nations, saying universally to all:

**VERSE 1.**—“Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth.”

Sing with tongue and life to the Lord the Father a new song, [Cassiod., Remigius, Gloss interlinear] namely, putting off the old man with his deeds and putting on the new; the one who loves sings it. [Aug.] Desire sings the old song, but charity the new, which itself is the new song. To sing, moreover, is to build. Therefore whatever you sing from desire, you sing as old; whatever from charity, you sound forth as new. It is better to be new and silent than old and singing, because if you are new and silent to human ears, you sound in God’s ears. Hypocrisy too sings the old song [Note: [Col. 0880D] Augustine on the following verse.]. For hypocrisy is a whitewashed wall (Acts 23), bright outside but mud within. Of this wall it is said: if you make a door in a wall not joined to others but raised up separately [Col. 0880A], whoever enters it remains outside. This is the hypocrite who wishes to build a whitewashed wall, not one made solid. Therefore whoever imitates him, as though making a door in that wall, is found outside; for he himself does not enter through the door, and his door admits no one. Then he repeats: Sing to the Lord the Son. Then he shows whom he has instructed to sing, saying, “all the earth,” [Remigius, Cassiod.] that is, all human beings, from whom God’s house is rebuilt. Again he repeats it.

**VERSE 2.**—“Sing to the Lord, and bless his name; proclaim his salvation from day to day.”

Sing to the Lord, the Holy Spirit. [Remigius, Cassiod.] He says “Lord” in order to distinguish the persons of the Trinity, because praise of Christ is honour to the whole Trinity. This is the figure *epimonē*, that is, a frequent repetition of an expression, which intensifies praise or blame. “And bless his name,” which is Jesus, [Haymo, Alcuin, Cassiod.] that is, Saviour, by declaring him to be salvation. Then he addresses prelates, saying: Proclaim, O prelates; thus the building of God’s house grows. What are they to proclaim? His salvation. And this “from day to day,” that is, continually, [Jerome, Remigius, Cassiod.] or from the Son to the Father, or from the Old Testament to the New. The Old and New Testaments are days made bright by the eternal sun. The former foretells; the latter proclaims the event accomplished. [Jerome, Alcuin.] He therefore proclaims from day to day who employs the authority of both Testaments in proclaiming the Saviour. Those two Testaments, indeed, like two days, make one light; one does not shine without the other. Therefore in Leviticus every animal that divides the hoof and chews the cud is clean: that is, it has two hoofs, because the person who observes the two Testaments is clean; by them the feet of my affections are protected from the thorns of vices. The Jew has only one hoof and therefore is unclean. [Aug.] He then explains where it is to be proclaimed, as though someone asked: Where do you wish it proclaimed?

**VERSE 3.**—“Proclaim his glory among the nations; his wonders among all peoples.”

Proclaim his glory, [Aug., Gloss interlinear] not your own, among the nations, passing over the Jews because of their obstinacy. And lest you think that some are excluded, he adds, “among all peoples,” not merely among certain nations: [proclaim] my wonders. This is why:

**VERSE 4.**—“For the Lord is great and exceedingly praiseworthy; he is to be feared above all gods.”

[Col. 0881A] “For the Lord.” [Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] Christ is great in power, even though he became man, whereby he appeared small. He indeed became small for our sake: because you are small, understand the great one, and you will be great in him. And he is praiseworthy in goodness. [Cassiod., Aug., Gloss interlinear.] And this “exceedingly” cannot be said to the full extent. He is fearful to those opposed to him and to his own, he who was frightened among human beings. [Aug.] And he is above all the gods worshipped by the nations while they were in captivity. And he is truly above the gods of the nations:

**VERSE 5.**—“For all the gods of the nations are demons; but the Lord made the heavens.”

“For all the gods of the nations are demons.” [Gloss interlinear, Aug.] This is praise by comparison; and since it was too little merely to be above demons, he adds: “But the Lord made the heavens,” where demons cannot dwell; and he takes “the heavens” literally. Or he understands “heavens” as the apostles and angels. Thus: the Lord made the heavens; he does not merely sit in them. If he made the heavens, then he also made angels and apostles, who command demons.

**VERSE 6.**—“Confession and beauty are before him; holiness and magnificence are in his sanctuary.”

Confession. [Cassiod., Aug.] Having urged them to sing and proclaim, he adds what benefit follows from this. This, namely, is the benefit which comes to all who sing: confession and beauty result from it. [Aug.] By confessing, a person becomes beautiful from ugly. If therefore you love beauty, confess, and so become beautiful—that is, righteous. He therefore said confession first, and beauty afterward. [Note: [Col. 0881D] From Gregory, *Morals*, book 1, chapter 14.] Hence Rebecca leapt down from the camel when she saw Isaac, in order to be joined to him, because the Church descends through confession from the crooked humpedness of vices as she comes to Christ. It follows: and this confession and beauty are before him. [Alcuin, Gloss interlinear, Aug.] For such people behold him and are beheld by him. And holiness, or “sanctity,” according to another reading, and magnificence come from this, namely, from singing. This holiness is in his sanctification: that is, whoever wishes to be magnificent and powerful, as the angels are, must first be holy. This comes from his sanctifying; for you cannot be holy by yourself. Therefore, when he sanctifies, one becomes holy [Col. 0881D], and thus magnificent.

## Part II. VERSE 7.—“Bring to the Lord, kindreds of the nations; bring to the Lord glory and honour; bring to the Lord glory for his name.”

Bring. [Alcuin, Remigius, Cassiod., Aug.] The second part, where he addresses subjects. As though he said: And because the Lord is such, therefore, O kindreds of the nations—so that neither native nor foreigner may be excluded—bring [offerings]; this is what the nations to whom proclamation has been made ought to do. To the Lord, [Alcuin, Aug.] let your hope not be in a human being, nor in the Baptist. For “cursed is the man who makes flesh his arm” (Jer. 17). Then he repeats, “bring to the Lord,” not to yourselves, so that those who proclaimed [Col. 0882A] proclaimed not themselves but the Lord. What ought you to bring? Glory and honour. [Cassiod.] Glory is brought when a person lives well, through whom God is glorified; honour is brought when thanks are returned for the goods of grace. “Was no one found who gave glory to God except this foreigner?” (Luke 17). Again he repeats, “Bring glory to the Lord,” [Aug.] so that it may be for his name also, not the name of human beings.

**VERSE 8.**—“Take sacrifices, and enter into his courts; worship the Lord in his holy court.”

Take sacrifices. [Aug., Jerome.] As though he said: Do not enter empty-handed, but with sacrifices. A contrite spirit is sacrifice to God (Ps. 50); confession is a sacrifice to God. Therefore, if you enter with a humble heart, you enter with a sacrifice; but the proud person enters empty-handed. And enter—one enters who is being built—into his prophetic courts, and worship the Lord in his evangelical holy court. [Haymo, Gloss interlinear.] By “courts” prophecy is understood; by “court,” the Gospel. The courts also signify the present Church, the court the heavenly Church. Thus: I shall enter into his courts, which are on earth; [Cassiod.] be conformed to his people. Worship the Lord in his holy court, which is in heaven. Or the courts are the prophets and apostles, through whom one goes to God. From these courts—that is, from the prophets and apostles—one comes into the court of the Catholic Church, where majesty is worshipped. Thus: enter into his courts, that is, into the teaching of the prophets and apostles. Worship the Lord in his holy court, that is, in the Catholic Church.

[Col. 0882C]

**VERSE 9.**—“Let all the earth be moved at his presence; say among the nations that the Lord has reigned.”

Let [all the earth] be moved. [Alcuin, Jerome, Gloss interlinear.] Having admonished all, he makes a vow and expresses a wish. As though he said: I say, enter and worship, you good people. But let the earth—that is, lovers of the world—be moved, so that they may be converted to repentance, at his presence, [Aug.] that is, the presence of his grace; and not merely a part, but all the earth, so that no one may say, “Behold, Christ is here,” or, “Behold, he is there” (Matt. 24). [Cassiod., Alcuin.] Or it may be understood adversely: let all the earth, that is, lovers of the world, be removed at the presence of God. But that this may occur, O good people, say among the nations [Gloss interlinear, Cassiod.] that the Lord has reigned [Col. 0882D], corrected, and judged. And this is what follows: because the Lord—that is, Christ—having conquered the devil, has reigned; that is, he has become known to the world as king, though he always reigned with the Father. [Aug.] Or, according to another reading, “the Lord has reigned from the wood,” namely, the cross, by which a person crosses the sea and the world becomes immovable.

**VERSE 10.**—“For he has made firm the world, which shall not be moved; he shall judge peoples in equity.”

212 “For he has made firm,” after the resurrection, “the world,” [Gloss interlinear, Aug.] that is, the Church throughout the world, where the building takes place, which shall not be moved. Why then does the heretic say it has not only been moved but even diminished? [Col. 0883A] “And he shall judge peoples in equity.” Then those who did not wish to choose equity will grieve. Others add: “and the nations in his wrath.” [Cassiod.] Therefore he will judge peoples, that is, the good, in equity; nations, that is, the evil, in wrath. Hence:

**VERSE 11.**—“Let the heavens rejoice, and the earth exult; let the sea and its fullness be moved; the fields and all that is in them will rejoice.”

Let the heavens rejoice, [Aug., Gloss interlinear] which declare God’s glory, and let the earth rejoice, which the heavens water; and then let the sea—that is, the world—and its fullness, from greatest to least, be moved. For the whole world was stirred up against the Church when it spread throughout the world; he foretells this, he does not wish it. Yet though the sea is moved, the fields will rejoice. Or [Col. 0883B] the sea is moved in a good sense, [Cassiod., Aug., Haymo] that is, the world changes for the better, along with its fullness, namely the nations. And then the fields rejoice, that is, all who are gentle, meek, and equitable; and all that is in them, that is, every power, sense, and reason. And

**VERSE 12.**—“Then all the trees of the forest will exult before the Lord’s presence, because he has come, because he has come to judge the earth.”

Then, [Alcuin, Augustine] when he corrects them, all the trees of the forests—that is, the pagans, who were once trees of the forests but now are timbers of God’s house, cut down for the building of the Church—will exult, because they have been cut off from the wild olive and grafted into the good olive tree (Rom. 11). They will exult, I say, before, or in the presence of, the Lord. I rightly say, before the Lord, because he has come. [Col. 0883C] First he came in the Church, in the clouds—that is, in the apostles and the other saints—and filled the whole world. Hence in the Gospel: “From now on you see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven” (Matt. 24). Whoever believes in this coming will exult at the last coming, concerning which he adds: Therefore they too will exult, because he comes, [Cassiodorus, Haymo, Alcuin] that is, he will afterwards come to judge the earth, that is, the living and the dead.

Or all these things may be said of the second coming: Let the sea—that is, the world—and its fullness be moved to joy at the second coming. This will be so because the fields—that is, all the gentle and meek—and all that is in them, namely every faculty and reason, will rejoice. Then, that is, at the second coming, all the trees [Col. 0883D] of the forests—that is, the converted nations, which were found in the forest’s fields—will exult before the Lord, because he comes, that is, will come; and indeed because he comes, that is, will come, to judge the earth.

**VERSE 13.**—“He will judge the world in equity, and the peoples in his truth.”

He will judge the world, [interlinear gloss] for he comes to judge; and he will truly judge. For he will judge the whole world, [Augustine] not a part: he did not purchase a part; because he paid the price for the whole, he must judge the whole. By “world,” therefore, he means all the children of Adam—that is, all people who were in him as one man. He was then in one place, but now is scattered throughout the whole world, which Adam signifies in Greek. For Adam, in the Greek language, signifies the world [Col. 0884A] of lands. This name has four letters: alpha, delta, alpha, mu; and the four regions of the world have these letters at their beginnings: they call the east ἀνατολή (*anatolē*), the west δυσμή (*dysmē*), the north ἀρκτός (*arktós*), and the south μεσημβρία (*mesēmbría*). The name Adam is composed from the four letters with which these names begin.

[Cassiodorus] Therefore, when he says, “He will judge the world in equity,” he includes every human being universally, to be judged according to God’s equity. But he explains more plainly how he will judge, adding: “and the peoples in his truth.” [Augustine] For in that judgment there will be truth and equity. What could be more equitable and true than to gather the elect with himself for judgment and to separate the rest—those who performed mercy to the right hand, and those who did not perform it to the left? [Col. 0884B] (Matt. 25.) Therefore there will be truth and equity there, [Cassiodorus] because in that separation there will be two peoples, to whom he will give the sentence of truth, so that some go into life and others into punishments.

## Comparison on Psalm XCV: “Sing to the Lord a new song,” etc.

**VERSE 5.**—“All the gods of the nations are demons.” Münster, instead of “demons,” said “they are vain”; and the translators for Cajetan, “vanities.” Although they have not translated badly, I do not know whether they have not improperly altered the Vulgate reading. For *elilim* means idols, demons, and nothingness. Hence Jerome and the Nebiensian translate “carved images”; the Chaldee and Sanctes, “idols.”

**VERSE 6.**—“Confession.” Jerome and Sanctes: “glory”; Münster: “splendour”; the translators for Cajetan: “beauty.” The word is ambiguous. Pagninus gave “confession”; [Col. 0884C] the Chaldee, Nebiensian, and Pellican, “praise”; others, “thanksgiving,” *hod*. But all these follow one another in meaning.

“Holiness and magnificence.” Others: “strength without power,” and “glory” or “exultation,” *oz ve-tiphereth*. The reconciliation offers itself spontaneously. For “the strength of the simple is the way of the Lord” (Prov. 10). Moreover, the way of the Lord produces holiness; while glory and exultation belong together.

**VERSE 9.**—“Say among the nations: The Lord has reigned.” The Roman Psalter has the additional words, “from the wood.” I suspect that they were erased by unbelievers from both the Greek and the Hebrew. For it is the practice of the faithless—as Jerome indicates in the preface to his epistle to Titus—to erase whatever they see contrary to their doctrine. Let the reader patiently hear what has led me to this conjecture. Cassiodorus, an author not to be despised, commenting on this place writes: “Other translators indeed do not have ‘from the wood,’ but for us it is enough that it has been established by the authority of the Seventy interpreters.” Thus he speaks.

Now it is evident that Augustine too read and interpreted “from the wood.” Arnobius, likewise a most ancient interpreter, continues in his *Exposition* as follows: “And nation should say to nation that the one Lord reigns from the wood of the cross, because through the wood of desire the kingdom of God had departed from human beings; now through the wood of the cross the kingdom of God has returned.” Thus far he.

Indeed, Tertullian, earlier than all these, has strengthened this suspicion even more in Book III *Against Marcion*. There, discussing the power of the cross from many Scriptural passages which would seem ridiculous if understood according to the outer bark of the letter, he finally comes to this passage and, with a certain sharpness of expression, strikes the unbelieving ear: “Come now, if you have read in David, ‘The Lord reigned from the wood,’ I await what you understand—unless perhaps some timber-working king of the Jews is meant, and not Christ, who from that point, after suffering on the wood and overcoming [Col. 0885A] death, reigned.
