For death reigned from Adam until Christ: why should Christ not be said to have reigned from the wood, from the time when, dying on the wood of the cross, he excluded the reign of death?” Behold Tertullian.

Finally, the Church adopted this reading in the devout hymn on the Passion of the Lord composed by Theodulf, bishop of Orléans:

> Fulfilled are the things which faithful  
> David sang in song,  
> Saying among the nations:  
> God has reigned from the wood,

[Col. 0886A] and which she frequently sings after Easter in commemoration of the cross.

**VERSE 10.**—“He set right the world.” Jerome: “He suspended the immovable world.” The others approach this, transmitting something similar, such as “it will be made firm,” or “he will make firm,” or “he prepares.” *Ticon*, from the root *con*, means “to make firm, direct, prepare, set right.” All these things are indeed accomplished by correction in the Church of God, signified by the world in its fourfold extent.

# PSALM XCVI

[Col. 0885]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM

“[Note: [Col. 0885D] Ἀνεπίγραφος παρ’ Ἑβραίοις, ‘Untitled among the Hebrews.’] A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF, WHEN HIS LAND WAS RESTORED TO HIM.”

[Col. 0885A]

[Col. 0885B] “The Lord has reigned; let the earth exult.” Title: “A psalm of David himself, when his land was restored to him.” [Alcuin] In the literal sense, this touches upon the fact that after the death of Absalom, David’s wicked son, who while living persecuted his father, David’s land was restored to him and he reigned in peace. This is not treated here, however, but rather what it signifies (2 Kings 18).

[Augustine] For David signifies Christ, whom wicked sons—that is, the Jews—crucified and renounced as king. Yet the land was restored to him when Judaea, which had crucified him, believed; when the apostles, who had wavered, were strengthened; and when the other sheep from among the nations were brought in. Or the land was restored to him when his flesh rose again, after whose resurrection the things sung here took place.

And the sense is: This psalm is composed for David himself—that is, [Col. 0885C] Christ—and contains his praise and victory, treating of what happened when his land was restored to him: that is, when Judaea believed, or when his flesh rose again. Foreseeing these things in the Spirit, the prophets rejoiced; and, if it could have been, they wished to see them fulfilled. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many kings and prophets wished to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke 10). Therefore the saints now present are filled with great joy in this psalm, which bears the title concerning the promises of the restoration of the land. For to the palate of faith the honey of the divine promise tastes sweet.

This is the fourth psalm concerning the first coming, by which the world was delivered. [Cassiodorus] Intention: he urges exultation. Method: the psalm has two parts. First, describing the powers of the Lord, he shows that all things have been restored to him and [Col. 0885D] rebukes idolaters. Second, he displays the complete exultation which not even persecution may interrupt, at the words, “Sion heard and was glad.” Therefore, seeing the superstitions of the world abounding before Christ’s resurrection, the Prophet counters them, saying:

**VERSE 1.**—“The Lord has reigned; let the earth exult; let many islands rejoice.”

The Lord, [Augustine, Cassiodorus] he who was despised and slain, has reigned—that is, has become known as king. Who else, then, ought to be worshipped? As if he said: no one. I say, he has reigned: therefore let the earth exult. What then remains for idols? Nothing. “Let many islands rejoice,” [Augustine] that is, those who dwell on islands, because there are Christians even on islands.

Or “islands” means the Churches throughout the whole world that are amid temptations. They are called islands because they are surrounded by the roaring waves of temptations. [Col. 0886A] [Col. 0886B] Just as an island is beaten by the waves raging around it but is not broken, so the Church, extended throughout the whole world, suffers the persecutions of unbelievers but is not overcome; rather, like an island, it breaks the waves that come against it. He adds, “many.” [Cassiodorus] He does not say “all,” because of the assemblies of heretics. Then he says what the Lord is like in his first coming:

**VERSE 2.**—“Cloud and darkness are round about him; righteousness and judgment are the setting right of his throne.”

Cloud and darkness are round about him, [Augustine] that is, to the impious who are blind and do not understand him, he is cloud and darkness. [Cassiodorus, Augustine] That is, he is cloudy and dark to them, shining with no brightness. But righteousness and judgment are the setting right [Col. 0886C] of his throne: that is, to the good he is righteousness and judgment; they, having been set right, are his throne. They have righteousness because they have been justified from themselves, and judgment because through them he judges. And:

**VERSE 3.**—“A fire shall go before him, and shall set his enemies round about on fire.”

Before him, [Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, before his coming, fire will go, because the impious, inflamed with anger at the preaching of the prophets, planned their death. And that fire will inflame his enemies: that is, the impious were inflamed with indignation because of the prophets’ preaching. They are “round about” because the preachers were few and they were many.

[Col. 0886D] [Augustine] Or by fire charity is understood, concerning which the Lord says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I wish except that it should burn?” (Luke 12.) As if he said: Those who have been set right are God’s throne; but before God sits in them, the fire, the Spirit, goes before. This is what he says: the fire of charity shall go before him. This is a good fire, just as that sword is good of which the Lord says: “I came not to send peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10). This is the sword of God’s word, which separates those joined by carnal affection so that they may live spiritually. But the fire of charity burns, and this fire will inflame his enemies round about. [Augustine, Alcuin] Throughout the whole world, that which is against God burns. Once it is consumed, his lightnings appeared.

[Col. 0887A] **VERSE 4.**—“His lightnings shone upon the world; the earth saw and was moved.”

“His lightnings shone.” [Augustine] Or in this way he also speaks of a double fire which will be before Christ’s second coming: namely, the fire of charity, which will burn in the good, and the fire of anger and envy, which will consume the evil. But the final fire into which the evil are to be cast will be after him, not before him. This fire goes before: it is the punishment of the evil and the salvation of the good. For when Christ is preached, the perverse person is angry and the just person suffers. Anger, like fire, consumes the adversary, who is consumed like a torch; but green wood remains—that is, the just person who burns in charity. And this is the meaning: the fire of charity and anger will go before him in the second coming. And that fire will inflame his enemies round about.

[Col. 0887B] For enemies who worshipped idols are burned—if evil, for destruction; if good, for restoration. Moreover, his lightnings—that is, miracles—shone upon the world, that is, the whole world. The clouds, that is, the preachers, were despised because of their human appearance, but a marvellous brightness appeared in their words and deeds. And the earth was moved. It saw these miracles with the heart, and the earth was moved, [Cassiodorus] that is, terrified—the earth that worshipped idols. Hence:

**VERSE 5.**—“The mountains melted like wax before the Lord, before the Lord of all the earth.”

The mountains, [Augustine] that is, the proud—namely every height raised against God—melted like wax. Even if the pagan does not believe, yet he is overcome. And this came from the Lord’s presence: [Col. 0887C] God was fire to the hard-hearted. Before the Lord all the earth melted, even that of the nations. Why was this so? Because:

**VERSE 6.**—“The heavens proclaimed his righteousness, and all peoples saw his glory.”

The heavens, [Augustine] that is, all preachers, whose heart is above, proclaimed his righteousness. [Cassiodorus, Augustine] For which believer is silent about Christ? And all saw his glory with the heart. And because all peoples saw Christ’s glory:

**VERSE 7.**—“Let all who worship carved images be put to shame, and those who glory in their idols.”

“Let all who worship carved images be put to shame.” [Augustine] This has now happened. For idolatry now ceases, and those who worshipped stones blush, because those stones were dead; but we worship the living stone. [Col. 0887D] And let those who glory in their images, which lack spirit, be ashamed. But what sort of God is ours? He is the one whom even angels worship.

**VERSE 8.**—“Worship him, all his angels.”

“Worship him, all his angels.” [Augustine] Worship belongs to the one God, not even to angels, much less to idols or demons. Therefore the worship of angels ceases—but they worship. Evil angels indeed wish to be worshipped; good angels worship and do not allow themselves to be worshipped. Let idolaters at least cease by this example.

## PART II—“Sion heard and was glad.”

“Sion heard,” etc. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine] This is the second part, in which, after the restoration of the land, complete exultation is displayed, which not even persecution interrupts. As if he said: The heavens will proclaim; the angels will worship. [Col. 0888A] And Sion, that is, the Church of Judaea, heard these things foretold: namely, that the angels worship him, that the heavens proclaimed his righteousness, that all peoples saw his glory, and that worshippers of idols would be put to shame; and therefore she was glad. For Judaea formerly believed that she alone would come to Christ, but now rejoices in companions from the nations, as the brethren rejoiced over Cornelius, whom Peter baptized.

**VERSE 9.**—“And the daughters of Judah exulted because of your judgments, O Lord.”

And the daughters of Judah, [Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, those of Christ who exulted from Judah. For the apostles and the brethren who were in Judaea heard that the nations had received God’s word; and therefore they rejoiced and magnified God (Acts 8). And this was because of your judgments, O Lord, [Col. 0888B] namely, because God is no respecter of persons, but receives all who come to him. [Haymo, interlinear gloss] Or he calls it a judgment that blindness happened to Israel so that the fullness of the nations might enter in (Rom. 11). And as though someone asked, “What are those judgments?” he adds:

**VERSE 10.**—“For you, O Lord, are most high over all the earth; you are exceedingly exalted above all gods.”

For you, O Lord, are most high in power. [Augustine, interlinear gloss, Alcuin, Cassiodorus] And this is over all the earth, because you are not God of the Jews only, but also of the nations. And, O Christ, you are exceedingly exalted because you are equal to the Father, or by reason of your works. And this is above all gods. [Col. 0888C] As if he said: Not merely above all evil gods, but even above the good—that is, human beings and angels. Or understand sinners and just persons by “earth” and “gods.” Or by “earth” and “gods” he signifies that Christ rules things earthly and heavenly. And since he is such:

**VERSE 11.**—“You who love the Lord, hate evil; the Lord guards the souls of his saints. He will deliver them from the hand of the sinner.”

You who love the Lord, hate evil, [Cassiodorus] that is, the devil, with whom God is not loved. For no one can serve two masters (Matt. 6). [Augustine, Alcuin] But if, when you have begun to hate the evil one, persecutions follow, do not fear, because the Lord guards the souls of his saints. To take these souls away is the final kind of persecution. [Augustine] For more grievous is the persecution in which people attempt to take souls away; but the Lord guards them. Though bodies die, they cannot kill souls (Matt. 10). “From the hand of the sinner,” [Haymo, Augustine] that is, from the devil’s power, he will deliver them. And if perhaps you complain that you are losing this light, do not care, because the true light is yours.

**VERSE 12.**—“Light has risen for the just, and gladness for the upright in heart.”

For the light of faith has risen for the just; and for the upright in heart gladness has risen, [Augustine, interlinear gloss, Augustine] namely for those to whom God is pleasing in all things, through hope. For the afflictions of the saints are not truly misery: they are already saved in hope. Therefore:

**VERSE 13.**—“Rejoice, you just, in the Lord, and give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness.”

[Col. 0889A] Rejoice, you just, in the Lord, [Jerome, Augustine] not in the world, in which there are afflictions. And give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness: that is, praise him because he remembered to sanctify us; for unless he had willed it, you would not rejoice in him.

## Comparison on Psalm XCVI: “The Lord has reigned,” etc.

**VERSE 2.**—“The establishment of his throne.” Jerome, instead of “establishment,” gave “foundation,” and some others “dwelling-place” or “preparation.” But *mecon* properly corresponds to “direction,” which is correction, and cannot be weakened or shaken.

**VERSE 5.**—“Before the Lord, all the earth.” Here perhaps the scribe nodded, placing a nominative in place of a genitive: “before the Lord, all the earth,” instead of “before the Lord of all the earth.” For in Hebrew *Adon* is in the construct state, that is, “of the Lord.” And this is clearer in Greek: ἀπὸ προσώπου Κυρίου πάσης τῆς γῆς, “before the Lord of all the earth.” Indeed Augustine too interprets it as though he had read the genitive, although the nominative occurs in the text. [Col. 0889B]

[Col. 0890A] Nevertheless, I judge this reading to have been drawn from the old translation followed by Arnobius and Cassiodorus. They express it in the nominative, as is plainly established by the fact that they add one verb, so that it reads, “the earth trembles” or “the earth trembled,” where the fault cannot be that of the scribe, such as someone might allege in the other wording. Each reading has its own sense and appropriateness.

**VERSE 8.**—“Worship him, all his angels.” In Hebrew, *Elohim* stands in place of “angels.” Jerome translates it “gods”; and the other Hebraists do the same, except Sanctes, who follows the Septuagint. Jerome’s “gods” is unsurprising: it accommodated Sophronius, enabling him to answer Jewish slanderers. But we, who speak to and with Christians, ought to say “angels,” unless we wish to depart from the Apostle in Hebrews 1, who cited this passage concerning Christ in this way: καὶ προσκυνησάτωσαν αὐτῷ πάντες ἄγγελοι Θεοῦ, “and let all God’s angels worship him.” This too has been discussed elsewhere, on Psalm VIII. [Col. 0890B]

# PSALM XCVII

[Col. 0889]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM

“A PSALM OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0889B]

“Sing to the Lord.” Title: “A Psalm of David.” The title is clear. [Cassiodorus] This psalm is the third of those treating of both comings, in all of which there is cause for fear and hope: hope through the mercy of the first coming, fear through the judgment of the second. Though these things are often repeated, they are always new through their varied presentation. Intention: he urges praise and exultation. Method: the psalm has two parts. [Col. 0889C] First, it treats of the manifestation of the saving right hand. Second, it declares that he must be praised and proclaimed in every manner, at the words, “Make a joyful sound to God.”

[Augustine] Therefore, inviting to praise, he says: O you who are new in Christ, once old in Adam:

**VERSE 1.**—“Sing to the Lord a new song, because he has done marvellous things.”

Sing to the Lord, [interlinear gloss, Cassiodorus] in life and speech, a song concerning Christ’s incarnation and the redemption of humanity, new because the world has heard nothing like it. Why? Namely, because he has done marvellous things. What marvellous things? Not merely those which are common, but also this singular thing:

**VERSE 2.**—“His right hand and his holy arm have saved for him.”

[Col. 0889D] His right hand, [Cassiodorus] that is, Christ, who is called the Father’s right hand because of his marvellous operation; and his holy arm—the same Christ, who is called the arm because of his strength—has saved. He does not say what he has saved, but we understand it to be the world, which was a great miracle. For it is greater to raise the whole world from eternal death than to raise the dead. He has saved, I say, for God himself. He adds this because many are healed bodily, but for themselves rather than for him: for, having received bodily health, they become wanton. Those who were chaste while ill become adulterers when healed; and those who, while ill, harmed no one, having recovered their strength oppress the innocent. Such persons, therefore, have been healed, but not for him. But those healed inwardly through faith are thus healed for him.

[Interlinear gloss] Or, according to another reading: “His right hand will save him.” And as though someone asked where that right hand is, he adds:

**VERSE 3.**—“The Lord has made known his salvation; in the sight of the nations you have revealed his righteousness.”

The Lord has made known his salvation, [Augustine] that is, Christ. For that is the right hand or arm, and also the salvation, namely Christ. To whom did he make it known? Not here or there, but in the sight of the nations he revealed [Col. 0890C]—not under a veil—his righteousness, that is, his salvation. Christ is called salvation because he saves, righteousness because he justifies.

**VERSE 4.**—“He has remembered his mercy and his truth for the house of Israel.”

He has remembered his mercy, [Cassiodorus, Augustine] namely, so as to deliver humanity by becoming human; and his truth, which he will show in the future, when they see him face to face. But for whom has he remembered them? For the house of Israel, that is, for one who sees God. Or thus: “He has remembered his mercy.” Mercy is what he promised. Truth follows it, because he has fulfilled it. Hence he adds, “and his truth.” Mercy promised the promise; the promise yields truth. But to whom? To the house of Israel, which now sees truth through faith and afterwards [Col. 0890D] will see through sight. And lest you suppose Israel to be one nation in the literal sense, he adds:

**VERSE 5.**—“All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.”

All the ends of the earth have seen with the mind, [Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, from one end to the other. What? The salvation of our God, that is, Jesus. Thus he says “all,” [page 214] because Christ was not given to some only.

**VERSE 6.**—“Make a joyful sound to the Lord, all the earth; sing, exult, and make melody.”

“Make a joyful sound.” [Cassiodorus, Haymo] This is the second part, in which he says that praise and proclamation must be made in every manner because the judge comes. As if he said: Because he has done these things, therefore make a joyful sound to God with a wordless voice. For jubilation is joy which can neither remain silent nor be expressed adequately [Col. 0891A] when speech fails. He adds, “all the earth,” [Cassiodorus, interlinear gloss] because all have seen. Sing to God with words, where speech is adequate; exult with the heart; and make melody by works. In what ways?

**VERSE 7.**—“Make melody to the Lord with the harp and the voice of a psalm, with hammered trumpets and the sound of a horn trumpet.”

Make melody to the Lord with the harp. [Cassiodorus, Jerome] That is, by bodily action, namely the mortification of the flesh; and do divine works by feeding the poor, which are signified by the psalm. Then he adds the same things in reverse order: sing with the harp and the voice of a psalm. He reverses the order so that whichever comes first, all may belong to God. And with hammered trumpets, namely silver or bronze trumpets formed by hammering, and with the sound of a horn trumpet.

[Jerome, Cassiodorus] He refers to the Jewish custom: [Col. 0891B] for as is read in the book of Numbers, they had two kinds of trumpets: some produced from silver or hammered bronze, others of horn (Num. 10). [Augustine] By hammered trumpets are signified those who, afflicted beneath the hammer of the whole earth—that is, the devil—advance and sound God’s praises. Affliction is therefore hammering; advancement is shaping out. Job was such a trumpet: suddenly struck by such losses and by the bereavement of his children, he sounded like a hammered trumpet under the hammering of that great tribulation: “The Lord gave; the Lord has taken away. As it pleased God, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1). See what a sweet sound that trumpet gave.

But the horn rises above flesh: thus it is firm and capable of sound. It is the person who overcomes fleshly affections and desires, who does not savour earthly things but those [Col. 0891C] above; who walks in the flesh but does not wage war according to the flesh (Col. 3; 2 Cor. 10), just as a horn clings to flesh and rises above it. The sense is: Sing with trumpets, [Augustine, interlinear gloss] so that there may be preachers—hammered, that is, shaped and advancing under the devil’s hammer; and sing with the sound of a horn trumpet, that is, let them sound to others in such a way that they chastise in themselves the vices of the flesh.

**VERSE 8.**—“Make a joyful sound before the King, the Lord; let the sea and its fullness be moved, the world and those who dwell in it.”

“Make a joyful sound.” [Augustine] As if he said: What will happen when you act in this way? Behold, when the trumpets sound, God’s ears are delighted, and the waves of the sea—that is, of the world—are stirred. [Col. 0891D] And this is what he says: “Make a joyful sound before the King, the Lord,” whose ears are delighted. “Let the sea and its fullness be moved”: he predicts, not wishes. [Interlinear gloss, Augustine] For when the apostles preached as though they were trumpets, the sea of the world was moved and the waves of persecutions increased. He explains what he had called “the sea and its fullness”: [Haymo] “the world and those who dwell in it.” While they persecute:

**VERSE 9.**—“The rivers shall clap their hands together; the mountains have exulted before the Lord, because he comes to judge the earth.”

The rivers will clap with hands, or with hand: that is, saints full of God’s Spirit will rejoice in good works. [Augustine] And this will be “together,” or “unto one.” Or it may be read in a good sense: “Let the sea be moved,” as though trumpets were sounding: [Col. 0892A] let the sea of the Law, the legal bitterness, be sweetened by the wood of the cross placed in it, just as by Moses’ wood at Marah. For when the children of Israel came to Marah, where the waters were bitter, they could not drink because of their excessive bitterness; therefore the Lord showed Moses a piece of wood, and when it was put into Marah the water was sweetened (Exod. 15). This is the wood of the cross, which mitigated the legal bitterness that no one could bear, so that the sacraments of the Law may be opened to believers.

Then he adds, “and its fullness,” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus] namely all the sacraments of the Law; “let the world”—that is, the Gentiles—be moved toward conversion, “and those who dwell in it.” He adds this so that you understand as applying to human beings what he had said figuratively. Or thus: let the sea, that is, the world, be moved by fear of the coming [Col. 0892B] judgment, at which the impious are afraid; and its fullness, that is, the multitude of people full of sins, because there will be many sins there. And the world will be moved literally, because the world itself will then be changed into a new form, when there will be a new heaven and a new earth; and let those who dwell in it be moved with fear. But the rivers, that is, the good, will then clap their hands together, that is, rejoice in good works; for the mountains will exult before the Lord. [Augustine] For the good will rejoice at the judge’s coming, but the evil will tremble. Why will they exult? Because he comes to judge the earth, that is, every sinner. The mountains rejoice because he will not judge unjustly.

**VERSE 10.**—“For he will judge the world in righteousness, [Col. 0892C] and the peoples in equity.”

For he will judge the world, [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] that is, all earthly persons, in righteousness, because they did not deserve mercy. For judgment without mercy will be given to the person who did not perform mercy. Under an ignorant or unjust judge, [Augustine] even a good person would be afraid; now it is necessary that only the evil person be afraid. And he will judge the peoples, [Cassiodorus] that is, believers from Jews and nations, in equity, because they will receive things proportionate to their merits.

## Comparison on Psalm XCVII: “Sing to the Lord a new song, because,” etc.

**VERSE 2.**—“His right hand has saved for him.” Jerome likewise renders it this way. Faber argues that “his right hand has saved him,” with the Roman edition, is clearer, especially since Greek reads ἔσωσεν αὐτὸν ἡ [Col. 0892D] δεξιὰ αὐτοῦ, “his right hand saved him.” Yet two of our different manuscripts have αὐτῷ, the dative; a third had the accusative, and then the blind follower of Faber in this matter complains that “has saved for him” is less grammatical speech. But blessed Augustine copiously explains that God saves for himself when the health conferred returns to its author through thanksgiving. For some are healed who are not healed for God, but for their own pleasures and evil deeds; nor is this kind of expression unfamiliar.

**VERSE 7.**—“With hammered trumpets and the sound of a horn trumpet.” Although “hammered” and “of horn” are not stated in Hebrew, nevertheless, according to Paul of Burgos, a Hebrew, wherever *hatzotzeroth* occurs, silver or hammered trumpets are understood. Again, where Hebrew has *schophar*, a horn trumpet is understood.

# PSALM XCVIII

[Col. 0893]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM

“A PSALM OF DAVID.”

[Col. 0893A]

“The Lord has reigned.” Title: “A Psalm of David.” The title is clear. [Alcuin] Here the Prophet treats of Christ’s power and kingdom, so that he may be worshipped even in his humanity; and he says three things about him. For the Prophet describes Christ as king and giver of good things, whom the ancient fathers also served; and to these three points he adds three exhortations, as is clear from the sequence of the psalm.

[Augustine] The prophets foretold these future things concerning Christ under a veil, so that they covered their meanings with certain figurative matters; but the veil was removed when truth sprang up from the earth, so that righteousness might look down from heaven. Intention: he urges us to worship Christ as God and exalt him as king. Method: [Alcuin, Cassiodorus] the psalm has two parts. First, it shows Christ reigning [Col. 0893B] and exalted above all, whatever may oppose him; therefore it urges submission to him. Second, it urges his worship because the ancient fathers were his—that is, served him—at the words, “Exalt the Lord.” Therefore, showing Christ to be king, he says:

**VERSE 1.**—“The Lord has reigned; let the peoples be angry; he who sits upon the cherubim—let the earth be moved.”

The Lord, [Augustine] that is, Christ, though formerly humble, has reigned—that is, has become known as king after his resurrection and ascension. Therefore let the peoples be angry, however much they wish. This is mockery. As if he said: They may safely be allowed to be angry, since they can no longer harm him. Yet he says this by permitting, not commanding: he who sits upon the cherubim.

[Augustine, Alcuin] The one who reigns is he who sits upon the cherubim, literally upon the angelic powers; and earth can do nothing against him, even though he himself was on earth, where he suffered the people’s anger. “Let the earth be moved” means the same as what he said above: “let the peoples be angry.” He expresses who this Lord is, saying:

**VERSE 2.**—“The Lord is great in Sion, and exalted above all peoples.”

This Lord is he who is in Sion, [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] that is, who was literally born among the Jews. He is great and exalted above all peoples. He says this lest Christ be thought lowly because of his passion. Or thus: although the peoples are angry, the Lord is great in Sion, that is, in the Church of the Jews, and exalted above all the peoples of the nations.

[Col. 0893D] [Augustine] Or take the whole passage from “Let the peoples be angry” in this way. As if he said: After the resurrection, Christ became known as king, and for that reason the peoples are angry—that is, will be angry. The Prophet foretold this as future, but it has now occurred. For when Christ began to be preached after the resurrection, the peoples who worshipped idols became angry. Note that he does not say, “They will be angry,” but, “Let them be angry,” using this form of speech because he saw the good that would result. For through their anger God accomplished many good things: while they are angry, God’s servants are purified.

He who reigns is the one who sits upon the cherubim, that is, who rests and reigns in one who has charity. [Col. 0894A] For *cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge,” which is charity. Therefore the fullness of the Law’s knowledge, which is God’s throne, will be in you if you have charity, against which those who are angry can do nothing. What can earth do against heaven? Ask your heart, then, whether it has charity. If charity is there, the fullness of the Law is there (Rom. 13). Thus you have become God’s throne, as it is written: “The soul of the righteous is the throne of wisdom” (Isa. 75). And elsewhere the Lord says: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66).

“Let the earth be moved.” This does not change. “The Lord is great in Sion.” [Augustine] As if he said: I say that he sits upon the cherubim. But if you do not understand what “he sits upon the cherubim” means, consider this: the Lord is great in Sion—that is, in the soul which contemplates God, or in the Church. For Sion is interpreted “contemplation.” If therefore you belong to the Church, and he is great and exalted in you, then he is in you above all peoples who are angry or were angry. And because he is exalted above all peoples, [Cassiodorus] those peoples who were formerly blasphemous now:

**VERSE 3.**—“Let them give thanks to your great name, because it is fearful and holy; and the honour of the king loves judgment.”

Let them confess to your name, [Augustine] that is, to your renown and glory. I say, your name, now great; it was small when they were angry—that is, when it was maligned by few. But now it has spread through the whole earth, and you ought to confess it, because that name itself is terrible in the power by which it punishes, and holy in the goodness by which it spares; and the king’s honor. [Cassiodorus] Here he explains how they ought to confess—namely, discerningly, not merely honorifically. And this is the meaning: because the king’s honor, that is, glorious proclamation, loves judgment—that is, demands discernment—because what comes from him is not to be worshipped by a light impulse, but by settled deliberation. Hence he adds:

VERSE 4.—“You have prepared directions for the crooked; you have executed judgment and justice in Jacob.”

You have prepared righteous directions, etc. [Cassiodorus, Augustine] Or distinguish it thus: The Name is terrible, and the king’s honor is judgment—that is, the condemnation of the wicked; and he himself loves this judgment. Or thus: “and honor.” As if he said: His name is terrible, because, though he was crucified, he is preached as the Judge who is to come, and he will not err in judgment. And that is because the king’s honor loves judgment, not [Col. 0894D] mercy alone, by which he spares, but also the judgment by which he will repay each person according to merits. Therefore let no one foolishly presume upon mercy, because he will repay each according to merits. For judgment is not just unless each person receives his due according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil. Therefore, if you seek to be righteous, he is the one who accomplishes this, because he directs. Hence he adds: You have prepared directions for the crooked; [Augustine, Gloss, interlinear, Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, you have made these—judgment, so that we may discern between good and evil, and justice. Justice is when we do good and avoid evil. Where? In Jacob: not only in that patriarch, [Col. 0895A] but also in the people whom he signified. And you have done these things, which no other could do.

PART II. VERSE 5.—“Exalt the Lord our God, and worship his footstool, because it is holy.”

Exalt the Lord. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine] The second part, in which he exhorts us to worship him because the fathers were his. As if he said: Since he does these things in us, therefore exalt, according as he is God, the Lord our God—namely Christ, who works judgment and justice in us—and exalt him so far as to worship. And this is what he says: worship his footstool, or the support beneath his feet.

We must consider what he commands us to worship when he says, “Worship his footstool.” Elsewhere Scripture says that the earth is his footstool [Col. 0895B] in these words: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66). Therefore he commands us to worship the earth because it is his footstool. But Scripture elsewhere says: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone” (Deut. 6). Yet it must be understood that in Christ there is earth—that is, flesh—which is worshipped without impiety. For he took earth from earth, because flesh is from earth, and from Mary’s flesh he took flesh. This flesh, assumed by the Word of God, is worshipped by us without impiety, because no one spiritually eats his flesh unless he first worships it.

[Note: [Col. 0895D] This is explained better and more fully in Master, Distinction 9 of the Third Book of the Sentences.]

I do not mean that worship which is latria, due to the Creator alone, but that which is the more worthy form of dulia. For dulia is worship also rendered to a creature, [Col. 0895C] and it has two kinds: one rendered indiscriminately to all creatures; the other rendered to Christ’s humanity alone. Thus, “Worship his footstool” means the body of Christ, which is the footstool of the Divinity. [Cassiodorus, Augustine] For by “feet” the unfailing stability of the Godhead is understood; but the worshipper does not look upon the earth, but rather upon him whose footstool it is, and for whose sake he worships. Hence he adds: “Because he is holy,” in whose honor he worships the footstool. [Cassiodorus] As if he said: He worships not for its own sake, but for the sake of him whose footstool it is. He says “holy,” masculine, rather than “holy,” neuter, so that you may distinguish the body from the Godhead, even though there is one person in both. [Augustine] Or, according to our text, “because it is holy”: worship the footstool itself, that is, the body, because it is holy.

[Col. 0895D] VERSE 6.—“Moses and Aaron were among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name.”

Moses the lawgiver and Aaron the high priest were among the priests of Christ. [Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus, Augustine] Imitate them, as though these were great men who preached him. [Cassiodorus] Note that Moses is called a priest: although he did not offer sacrifices, he nonetheless offered vows to God and prayed for the people. And Samuel was among those who call upon his name.

[Note: [Col. 0896D] From Augustine, who nevertheless discusses this fully in Question 46 of the Old Testament.]

Note that Samuel is not numbered among the priests, because he was an Ephraimite; according to the law, a priest is not made from that tribe but from Levi. [Col. 0896A] Therefore he is placed among those who call upon God’s name. Nevertheless, he was a priest, as is read elsewhere; and these men already then

VERSE 7.—“Called upon the Lord, and he heard them; in a pillar of cloud he spoke to them.”

They called upon the Lord Christ, [Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus] and he who now speaks in a human being heard them—such is the power of sincere prayer—and he spoke to them in a pillar of cloud, [Augustine] that is, through figures in a dark cloud. But those utterances foreshadowed someone manifest—namely Christ. Therefore he spoke to them in the cloud, whereas he now speaks openly to us in the footstool, that is, in assumed flesh. Note that he did not say “in a cloud,” but “in a pillar of cloud.” [Cassiodorus] For a pillar signifies strength and the ornament of a house. In this form he spoke [Col. 0896B] to them, which announced the Church or Christ’s flesh; but he who then spoke in a cloud now speaks openly through the Son. And these men, great as they were,

VERSE 8.—“Kept his testimonies and the commandment which he gave them.”

They kept his testimony and the commandment which he gave them. [Cassiodorus] Distinguish testimonies from commandments. A testimony is a signification, set forth through certain signs, of an event that has gone before. Thus it is often said in the Law: “This shall be to us for a testimony,” as Jacob and Laban set up a heap of stones as a testimony (Gen. 31). [Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss] Commandments, however, are such as the commandments of the Law given through Moses: “You shall not kill,” etc. (Exod. 20). And because they kept them, [Col. 0896C] therefore, O

VERSE 9.—“O Lord our God, you heard them; O God, you were gracious to them, yet avenging all their devices.”

O Lord our God, you heard them, [Cassiodorus] in their righteous petitions. And, O God, you were gracious to them, forgiving their sins so that they might not harm them in the future. For God is not called gracious except in relation to sins: when he grants pardon, then he is called gracious. He was gracious in forgiving; he was also gracious in avenging. Hence he adds, “yet avenging,” [Augustine] that is, vindicating—which is also a form of propitiation. He also takes vengeance by chastening, lest people always delight in sinning and lest human pride creep in. Hence the Apostle: “There was given to me [Col. 0896D] a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me,” etc. (2 Cor. 12). Truly, then, God is gracious not only in forgiving sins but also in punishing and chastening them.

[Augustine] Behold: even if these men were so great, they nevertheless had some sin in all their devices, or affections, and he was avenging. By “affections” he means those dispositions which God alone knew to exist in their hearts, and for which their punishment was to endure those among whom they lived. For daily they endured peoples who resisted and lived wickedly, among whom they were compelled to live. Through charity they grieved over those persons’ sins as if they were their own. Behold how he took vengeance [Col. 0897A] upon all their affections. For, as many suppose, Moses’ punishment was not merely that he did not enter the promised land, into which even wretched persons entered. It was also a figure of the reality: namely, that those who were under the Law—because the Law was given through him—and who would not be under grace, would not enter eternal rest. And because he is gracious, therefore:

VERSE 10.—“Exalt the Lord our God; worship at his holy mountain, because the Lord our God is holy.”

Exalt the Lord, [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss] who caresses and yields as a father; he adds, “our God.” As if he said: Exalt him according as he is God, and worship the Lord—not apart from his mountain, but on his holy mountain, that is, in the body. [Augustine] This is that small stone [Col. 0897B] which, as Daniel says, grew into a great mountain and filled the whole face of the earth (Dan. 2). It was cut out—that is, born—from a mountain, that is, from the Jewish people, who worshipped one God. It is therefore said to be cut out without hands—that is, without human agency—because it was conceived of a Virgin without male seed. Therefore worship, because the Lord our God, who is on the mountain, is holy.

COLLATION ON PSALM 98: “THE LORD REIGNS; LET THE PEOPLES BE ANGRY,” etc.

VERSE 1.—“Let the peoples be angry.” Jerome has “let them be moved”; others, “let them tremble.” Both are true and convey the force of the Hebrew word *yirgezu*: “they roared,” “were terrified,” “were angry.” Faber achieves nothing [Col. 0898A] in trying to persuade us that we should read only “let the peoples be moved,” namely toward joy, and that “let them be angry” is unsuitable; nor does he thereby evade Augustine’s exposition showing that this is not commanded but predicted.

“You who sit upon the cherubim.” Many manuscripts have the third person, “who sits,” and it corresponds more fittingly to the connection, since “The Lord reigns” preceded. But “you who sit” is not to be rejected, for Cassiodorus reads and explains it thus: “Nor is it unusual among the prophets that they pass, as though abruptly, from one person to another; and, just as in the former reading—namely, ‘who sits’—St. Augustine repeated the word ‘reigns,’ so that the sense is, ‘he who sits upon the cherubim reigns.’” Likewise, if one reads “you who sit,” nothing prevents one from supplying “you reign.” In Hebrew and Greek there is a participle: *yosheb*, καθημένος, “sitting.” Therefore: “he who sits” or “you who sit.” The former, however, accords better with grammatical rules. The latter is not alien to prophetic [Col. 0898B] forms of expression.

VERSE 6.—“Worship his footstool, because he is holy / because it is holy.” It is not clear from the Hebrew whether it should be read in the masculine or neuter gender: “because he is holy” or “because it is holy.” For whether you pronounce it in one way or the other, Hebrew idiom is not harmed: *hadom hu*. Hence St. Jerome and most others translate it in the masculine, while some in the neuter. But from the Greek it seems that the masculine should be read, since ἅγιος (“holy”) and ὑποπόδιον (“footstool”) differ in gender. Finally, Christ is holy, and his holy flesh—which is called his footstool—is nonetheless to be worshipped, as Jerome teaches in his Commentary.

“Avenging all their devices.” Almost all agree, though they translate “works,” with the same sense: *alilotham*. Jerome seems to say something different in accordance with the sound of the word: “upon their changes,” he says. Yet transgressions which change a person are rightly understood.

PSALM 99.

[Col. 0897]

TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM FOR CONFESSION.”

[Col. 0897C]

“Make a joyful noise to the Lord, all the earth.” Title: A Psalm for confession. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] Confession is twofold: one is confession of praise; the other, confession of sins.

Confession of praise belongs to the perfect; confession of sins, to beginners. Both are treated here. For this psalm teaches us both to praise God gladly and to bewail our sins humbly, because in evils one must not despair, nor should the mind be lifted up in good things. The sense is: This psalm is “for confession,” that is, it treats of confession—namely, of praise, or of both kinds. Intention: it exhorts to confession. Method: The psalm has two parts. First, it prescribes for the perfect the chief kind of confession, namely praise. Second, it introduces the second kind of confession, namely that of sins, for those about to enter—that is, for beginners—at the words, “Enter into his presence” [Augustine]. Therefore, exhorting to praise, he does not urge one corner of the earth alone, but, just as he knows that blessing has been sown everywhere, so he demands rejoicing from every side, saying:

VERSE 1.—“Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth; serve the Lord with gladness.”

All the earth. [Augustine] Not a part, because blessing has been sown everywhere: make a joyful noise to the Lord, not to another. True jubilation, however, is made with voice and heart. As if he said: If the voice jubilates outwardly, let the heart understand inwardly. The sound [Col. 0898C] of the heart is understanding. Jubilation is a wordless sound of joy, because the joy of the mind cannot be expressed in words: when a person rejoicing in things that cannot be articulated in words bursts forth into some sound of exultation without words, so that it appears that he is rejoicing in the sound itself, but as though filled with excessive joy and unable to explain in words what he rejoices in.

This jubilation is made by the good in confession, but by the wicked in confusion, when they rejoice so greatly in earthly things—for example, when reapers or vintagers delight in an abundance of fruit and, rejoicing in the fertility of the earth, sing; and amid their songs insert certain wordless cries in the exaltation of an exulting spirit. Such jubilation is to be condemned. But the righteous rejoice as they behold with a pure heart who God is, how great he is, and [Col. 0898D] in what order and how wonderfully he has made all things. Therefore they sing exultantly, and this jubilation is to be crowned. “Serve the Lord,” [Cassiodorus] not from necessity but from charity, because you have been freed through Christ. Therefore serve with gladness, not murmuring, as the Jews murmured in the wilderness (Num. 14). [Augustine] This service is not one of bitterness or indignation, but of happiness and freedom. For it is pleasing to the redeemed to be servants. Let charity make you a servant, because truth makes you free. Hence the Lord says: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples, and you will know [Col. 0899A] the truth, and the truth will make you free” (John 8).

VERSE 2.—“Enter into his presence with exultation.”

Enter. [Alcuin, Cassiodorus] He said, “Serve the Lord,” and therefore adds the reward, saying: “Enter into his presence with exultation.” It is a great reward to rejoice in the presence of so great a Judge, and this is understood of the future. Or it may be understood of the present thus: “Enter into his presence with exultation,” [Augustine] that is, rejoice in conscience, where God sees; outwardly, it is easy for the tongue to rejoice.

VERSE 3.—“Know that the Lord himself is God; he made us, and not we ourselves.”

And know that the Lord himself is God. [Augustine] Who does not know that the Lord is God? But this is said concerning the crucified one, against the Jews. As if he said: Let not him whom you crucified and scourged seem contemptible to you, because he himself is God. And know this: “He made us, and not we ourselves,” that is, all our good comes from him, not from us: from him comes that for which we are crowned; from ourselves, that for which we are condemned. [Jerome] He speaks either of the good works of grace or of works of creation. “He made us, and not we ourselves,” that is, he created us, according to that saying: “All things were made through him” (John 1). [Cassiodorus] He says this lest anyone suppose that our creation should be credited to the fathers, who are servants, whereas God is the author.

VERSE 4.—“His people and the sheep of his pasture; enter his gates with confession, his courts; confess to him in hymns.”

[Col. 0899C] His people. [Interlinear Gloss] As if he said: He made us, who are his people. Or according to another reading: “But we are his people,” and he is king, and we are sheep while he is shepherd. “Of his pasture,” that is, of the Scriptures, in which he fattens the minds of the faithful. Enter. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] The second part, in which he introduces the second kind of confession for those who are entering. As if he said: I have exhorted you to enter into his presence, and let there be no doubt, because he has mercy. Therefore enter confidently; do not remain outside, where the enemies are, for outside the wolf finds you. Enter, I say, the gates of his mercy with confession. [Augustine] At the gates is the beginning, and the confession of sins, of which there is discussion here, is that by which we begin to enter the mercy of God. The meaning is: enter the gates of his mercy [Col. 0899D] with confession—that is, begin through confession to enter into God’s mercy. Since you were not made by yourselves, praise him by whom you were made, accusing yourselves, because our accusation also [Col. 0900A] pertains to the praise of him who forgives. Elsewhere it is said of this: “Begin to the Lord in confession” (Ps. 146). And when you have entered his courts—that is, the breadth of heavenly blessedness, after receiving the fullness of grace—confess to him in hymns, that is, in praises. As if he said: When you are entering, reproach yourselves; when you have entered, praise him, etc.

VERSE 5.—“Praise his name, because the Lord is sweet; his mercy is forever, and his truth unto generation and generation.”

Praise his name. [Interlinear Gloss, Augustine] Now and in the future, because while he is praised he becomes sweet. Hence he adds: “Because the Lord is sweet; his mercy is forever,” because both here he delivers and in the future crowns; and “unto generation and generation”—that is, into every generation, or into the earthly and heavenly generation, one which bears mortals and the other which bears eternal beings—his truth remains, fulfilling promises.

COLLATION ON PSALM 99: “MAKE A JOYFUL NOISE TO GOD, ALL THE EARTH,” etc.

VERSE 2.—“With exultation.” Or “with praise,” as Jerome and certain others have; or “with song,” as Münster and Pellican have. Most have “with exultation,” with the Septuagint, *birnanah*. It conveys all these senses, which agree with one another; for true praise of God is not without exultation.

VERSE 3.—“And not we ourselves.” Here Faber, taught by a certain Hebrew, as he says, asserts that no negative particle is found in the Hebrew. We examined seven different manuscripts, all of which consistently have [Col. 0900C] *velo anagnu*. He then adds that “we” ought to be in the nominative case, since no one is so dull as to suppose that he created himself, and because Jerome wishes us to sing, with the negation deleted, “and we are his.” As regards St. Jerome, I think that he read *lo* without aleph—that is, “himself” or “his”—as do the recent interpreters following Cajetan, for they translate, “we are his.” Moreover, we have repeatedly observed that the pronoun and the negation differ not at all in sound. In writing, it is *lo* with aleph, that is, “not.” As for the grammatical case, it is ambiguous. Yet the sense is not changed. For “we are not our own [makers]” and “we did not make ourselves” mean the same thing. It is certain that Augustine explains it as an accusative governed by the verb “to make.” Nor did he take it as though anyone could doubt that he was not made by himself, but so that we may not be proud and may rather acknowledge that whatever we have comes from our Maker. Furthermore, in Greek it is plainly nominative: καὶ οὐχ ἡμεῖς, “and not we,” yet in such a way that ἡμᾶς, “us,” which had just occurred, seems to be mentally repeated. Finally, on consulting the Spanish edition I found written *velo*, just as we said Jerome had read it.

PSALM 100.

[Col. 0899]

TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF.”

[Col. 0899D]

“Mercy and judgment.” Title: A Psalm of David himself. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] This psalm is the hundredth, and just as the number one hundred is perfect, so this psalm contains and teaches the pattern of perfect holiness. For here we are taught to seek good and reject evil, which is the perfect conduct of life. And because all our good must be attributed to Christ, the title therefore reads: “Of David himself.” The sense is: This psalm is attributed to David himself, that is, to Christ, so that all which we are taught here may be applied to Christ’s virtues, and nothing to that earthly king. Christ sings this, and we sing in him; for this voice befits head and body. It treats of mercy and judgment. [Col. 0901A] Intention: it exhorts us to seek good and reject evil. Method: [Cassiodorus] The psalm has three parts. First, it sets forth mercy and judgment. Second, it explains what the blameless way is, at “I walked.” Third, it says what the end of the wicked is, at “In the morning.” Therefore, setting forth mercy and judgment, he says:

VERSE 1.—“I will sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment.”

O Lord, I will sing, [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss] that is, I will joyfully proclaim mercy, which is now, and judgment, which will be in the future. And this is to you, that is, to your honor, since you use both praiseworthily. [Augustine] Therefore let no one despair of God’s mercy or presume upon impunity, because he has judgment; and let no one changed for the better fear judgment, because mercy will come first. These are always together in him. For God neither loses the severity of judgment in the goodness of mercy, nor, in judging with severity, loses the goodness of mercy.

Yet these two are distinguished in time according to their effects. For mercy is now offered to all and shown in many ways, whereas judgment is in the future. This is the time of mercy, when God’s patience leads sinners to repentance and grants temporal goods to good and wicked alike. But in the future will be the time of judgment, when he will repay each according to merits. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] These two are joined together in mutual fellowship. In them he briefly includes all God’s works. This is the cause set forth beforehand for why he behaves thus, as he later adds when he says:

VERSE 2.—“I will sing psalms and understand in the blameless way: when will you come to me?”

I will sing psalms and understand in the way. [Haymo, Jerome, Alcuin] As if he said: I will sing of mercy and judgment. And because of these two I will sing psalms—that is, I will perform good works gladly—and I will understand when you come to me in the second coming, or at the death of each person; I, I say, who am set in the blameless way. [Augustine, Interlinear Gloss] For to sing psalms is to work gladly, and one cannot understand except in the blameless way; but in that way it is understood when God comes to us.

Or thus: I will sing psalms and understand, being in the blameless way. The sense is unchanged: “I will sing psalms and understand” through this “when,” that is, because you will come to me; by your aid I will sing psalms and understand. [Cassiodorus] Or thus: I will sing psalms—that is, work gladly—and by this I shall understand; for singing psalms gives this, that I may understand in my mind what is not apparent to the eyes, that is, believe that he will come whom this man so greatly desires. This is the sense: I will understand, I say, when you come to me in the flesh at the first coming. You will come, I say, in the blameless way, because you passed through the world without sin.

PART II. VERSE 3.—“I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house.”

I walked. [Alcuin, Interlinear Gloss] The second part, in which he explains what the blameless way is. As if he said: I will sing psalms and understand in the blameless way; even before I understood, I walked, etc. Or the connection may be made thus: What is the blameless way? It is innocence. Hence he adds: “I walked in innocence.” [Augustine] As if he said: This blameless way begins and is perfected in innocence. There is no need for many words: be innocent, and you have fulfilled justice. But a person harms in two ways: if he makes someone wretched, or if he abandons someone wretched. Innocent, however, is the person who harms neither himself nor others. Hence he says: “I walked,” or “I paced about.” As if he said: The way is broad in the innocence of my heart; for all wickedness suffers narrowness, while innocence alone is broad, a place in which one may walk about as at leisure. These are the walks of the priests in Ezekiel.

He then explains what he had said, namely “I walked,” “in the midst of my house,” that is, my heart, in which one of good conscience dwells peacefully. Others, however, are driven outside [Col. 0902B] as by smoke, dripping water, or a bad wife; they rest outside among trifles. Those who are outside take delight in matters concerning the body, because they are not well within themselves, where they might rejoice in their own conscience. [Cassiodorus, Augustine] Or this may be read in the person of Christ: What is the blameless way? Innocence. And I walked in the innocence of my heart, as if to say: I did not seek transient things, but ran the course of the world while existing in the midst of your house—another reading—that is, the Church, in whose midst I stand as the example of all. Innocence can do this: it can make one dwell in the midst of God’s house, as one honored and an example to others.

VERSE 4.—“I did not set an unjust thing before my eyes; I hated those who commit transgressions.”

I did not set [before my eyes]. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] He explains innocence in parts. First he says that he has nothing to do with the wicked: “I did not set an unjust thing before my eyes,” etc., until “my eyes,” where he says that he has a share with the righteous. Then he says that he drives the devil’s wiles from his heart, at “In the morning,” etc. As if he said: “I walked in innocence.” This all Christ says: “I did not set an unjust thing before my eyes,” [Augustine] that is, I did not love an unjust thing, nor was another’s injustice pleasing to me. “Those who commit transgression”: he explains “an unjust thing.” As if he said: I did not love an unjust thing, but rather hated those who commit transgression, [Augustine] that is, those who do not keep God’s law, even if they are in the Church [Col. 0902D]; I rejected transgressors—not human beings, that is, not insofar as they are human, but because they are transgressors.

VERSE 5.—“A perverse heart did not cling to me; I did not acknowledge the wicked one who turns away from me.”

It did not cling. [Alcuin, Augustine] He then explains whom he called transgressors, adding: “A perverse heart did not cling to me,” that is, one who transgresses in heart; as if to say, I did not consent to what is not right. “The wicked one who turns away from me,” [Cassiodorus] that is, the heretical person who differs from Catholics and departs from straight paths, “I did not acknowledge,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, I did not approve him; he did not please me, because although they may be marked with the sacraments along with us, they are not thereby of us.

[Augustine] Or: “A perverse heart did not cling to me,” that is, a crooked [Col. 0903A] heart, such as belongs to one who does not will everything that God wills. Yet even if he is weak and afraid—as Jesus foreshadowed this in his fear—let him submit himself to God, saying with Christ: “Let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, let your will be done” (Matt. 26). Let him avoid evils as far as he can; if he cannot, let him endure them. “And I did not acknowledge the wicked one turning away”: everyone turns away who is unlike me, whom I previously set before them for imitation.

VERSE 6.—“The one who secretly slanders his neighbor: him I pursued.”

The one who secretly slanders his neighbor. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss] One who maintains falsehood does not dare to slander openly. “Him I pursued,” lest he do this.

VERSE 7.—“With a proud eye and an insatiable heart, I did not eat with him.”

[Col. 0903B] “With a proud eye,” [Cassiodorus, Haymo] that is, with an arrogant heart, “and an insatiable heart,” that is, with an avaricious person: I did not eat bodily or spiritual things, literally, with such a notable person. He avoided the company of such people. [Augustine] Or rather, this should be understood spiritually. For Jesus too is recorded as dining with the proud, as with the Pharisee (Luke 9), when the sinful woman Mary came to him (Luke 7). We also refrain from eating at the table of noteworthy brethren so that they may be corrected. We often do this for medicinal reasons; yet we eat with many outsiders, such as pagans and other impious and proud persons. What then does he mean when he says, “I did not eat with a proud eye and an insatiable heart”? The proud and insatiable heart has its own banquet [Col. 0903C] on which it feeds but is not refreshed. For the banquet of the proud heart, which is insatiable, is envy. Pride is the mother of envy, which feeds and delights itself upon others’ evils, yet is not satisfied. Therefore the righteous person is not fed upon this food of pride and envious wickedness, but upon the food of justice. Hence: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice,” etc. (Matt. 5). This is the meaning of “with a proud eye and an insatiable heart, I did not eat with him”: I was not fed on, nor did I delight in, the banquet of pride and envy.

VERSE 8.—“My eyes were upon the faithful of the earth, that they might sit with me; he who walks in the blameless way ministered to me.”

My eyes. [Cassiodorus] Here he carries out the other part of innocence, namely that he has a share [Col. 0903D] with the righteous. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Interlinear Gloss] As if he said: Since you did not eat with such people, on what then were you fed? Behold, the eyes of my heart were upon the faithful: that is, the faithful pleased me, says the righteous person generally. “The faithful of the earth,” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] that is, those dwelling on earth where there are so many enticements; therefore their crown is greater. Or, “upon the faithful of the earth,” that is, those throughout the whole world, “that they might sit with me,” namely, that they might remain with me in unity of faith. Or “sit with me,” that is, share with me in the eternal kingdom, in the person of this same righteous one. “He who walks in the blameless way”—he, and no other, ministered to me, literally. [Cassiodorus] This is especially fitting for priests, that they should not live with the perverse, but:

VERSE 9.—“He who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house; he who speaks unjust things did not stand upright before my eyes.”

“He who acts proudly,” [Cassiodorus] that is, any proud person, “shall not dwell in the midst of my house,” literally. He says this lest he seem to approve those whom he has as intimates, if they are wicked. [Augustine] Or it may be said in Christ’s person: “My eyes were upon the faithful of the earth.” This does not change. “That they may sit with me,” upon the twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. 19)—that is, that they may judge with me. “He who walks in the blameless way ministered to me”: he ministered the Gospel to me, not to himself, not seeking his own interests but those of Christ.

But “he who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house,” that is, in my heart, where the meek and quiet one dwells, pleasing me; but the proud person [Col. 0904B] rebounds from it. Or, “shall not dwell in the midst of my house,” that is, the Church. [Alcuin] Although such a person may be tolerated for a time for the sake of correction, he can in no way take precedence by merits. He is not grain in my people, but chaff. [Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus] It follows in the person of the whole Christ: “He who speaks unjust things”—any slanderer—“did not stand upright before my eyes,” because even if he is glorious in his own eyes and among fools, he is not glorious before me.

VERSE 10.—“In the morning I slew all sinners of the earth, that I might destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity.”

In the morning. [Augustine] The third part, in which he shows what the end of those evils will be; Christ speaks here. [Col. 0904C] Note that he has already said above that only the good cling to him. And as though someone said: Since only the good cling to you, why then have you tolerated the wicked in your city for so long? The answer is that it is the time of mercy: now it is night, and not all things are yet manifest. In this night temptations abound, in which the beasts of the forest and the lion cubs—that is, devils—pass by, seeking food for themselves from God, namely permission to tempt the faithful. Hence the Lord says to the disciples: “Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat” (Luke 22). Wheat is not eaten by a human being until it is first crushed, so that it may become bread. Likewise, the devil devours no one unless he has first crushed him through tribulation.

Therefore in this night I spare, tolerate, and correct; but in the morning, [Augustine] that is, when [Col. 0904D] the day of judgment arrives and all things now hidden are laid bare—while it is not known what one now good or wicked person will later become—“I slew all sinners of the earth,” that is, the wicked will be sent into eternal fire. For this reason the wicked are now tolerated by the long-suffering one: that they may be corrected. If they do not do so in the present time of mercy, they will afterward be slain. This is what he says: “In the mornings I slew all sinners of the earth,” that is, at judgment I shall send the wicked into eternal fire. Why? “That all who work iniquity might be destroyed from the city of the Lord,” that is, from the fellowship of the Church. For they are now in it, but they are spared because it is the time of mercy; at the time of judgment they will be separated. Behold, the psalm ends where it began: “I will sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment.” [Col. 0905A] [Alcuin, Haymo] This also applies to the righteous person, who foresees that this will happen. Therefore he behaves as he said above. The meaning is: “In the mornings I slew all sinners of the earth,” that is, I foresaw that all the wicked would be slain, so that I might destroy—that is, see destroyed—all who work iniquity.

[Cassiodorus] Or it may otherwise be said in the person of the righteous. Here the third part of innocence is shown: after avoiding wicked people, the righteous person, returning to himself, adds that he has expelled from his heart the suggestions of demons. As if he said: I have avoided not only wicked people but also vices, because “in the morning”—that is, at the beginning of a suggestion, when the first twilight of temptations begins to appear—“I slew,” by prayer, which is how they must be cast out lest they grow, all sinners of the earth, that is, [Col. 0905B] demons, who make all flesh sin. I slew them so as to destroy all workers of iniquity—that is, every assault, or instigation, of the devil—from the city of the Lord. The city of God is the soul of the righteous person, from which the devil is subjected and removed.

COLLATION ON PSALM 100: “MERCY AND JUDGMENT,” ETC.

### Verse 4.—“A perverse heart did not cleave to me.”

The Hebrews divide this clause into two parts, so that the first—namely, “did not cleave to me”—belongs to the end of this verse; then “a perverse heart” is joined to what follows. [Col. 0906A] But because “did not cleave to me” seemed to produce an incomplete sense, Münster added something of this kind, especially since he had immediately translated the preceding words thus: “I hated transgressions,” so that the verb “will cleave” would have nothing to which it could refer. Jerome, however, and those who translate similarly, were not compelled to do this. “I hated,” he says, “one doing, or doing, transgressions.” And what follows, “nor shall it cleave,” corresponds suitably. Moreover, this question has been discussed more fully above.

### Verse 6.—“With an insatiable heart.”

Jerome has “high in heart.” The others have “vast” or “broad in heart,” *rehab lebab*. Yet whether you understand this as “avaricious” or as one who is not sated by another’s evils, the Septuagint translates it well; and immediately afterwards: “with this I did not eat.” Jerome: “with this I shall not be able [to endure].” The others echo this, saying, “I shall not tolerate this,” or “I shall not be able to bear him.” We think that the Septuagint read *lo ’okal*, from the stem *’akal*, “he ate.” We now read *lo ’ukal* [Col. 0906B], from the root *yakal*, “he was able,” although the sense agrees in either case.

### Verse 9.—“He did not direct [himself] before my eyes.”

For the expression “he directed,” the Hebrews have a passive verb which, if you remove the vowel points, you may read indifferently either actively or passively: “he directed” or “he will direct,” “he will be directed,” “he will be established,” “he will be prepared.” Jerome, attending to the sense rather than the words, translated, “he will not please.” Thus, *lo yakun*, “he did not direct,” taking the future in place of the past. That is, in Cassiodorus’s interpretation, “he did not advance.” But *lo yikkon*, that is, “he will not be established,” preserves the sense.

## Psalm CI

[Col. 0905]

### Title of the Psalm: “A prayer of the poor man when he was distressed, and poured out his supplication before the Lord.”

[Col. 0905C]

“O Lord, hear my prayer.” The title: “A prayer of the poor man when he was distressed, and poured out his supplication before the Lord.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] This is the fifth penitential psalm, and the fourth called a prayer. The poor man of whom the title speaks is Christ, who, though he was rich—God with God, through whom all things were made (John 1)—became poor according to the form of a servant (2 Cor. 8). Yet he is poorer in his members, in whose need he concealed his own poverty, so as to communicate his riches to them. For where he prepared himself, he enriched his members; among them also are penitents whom he transformed into himself—that is, in whose [Col. 0905D] person he speaks, saying, “I ate ashes as though bread.” For he was not in such need that he could say these things in his own person, but he says them in his members.

See how the lowest is harmonized with the highest: that is, by unity of voice the members are joined to the head. For as the two are one flesh, so they are also one voice. Likewise, through the prophet Isaiah he is called both bridegroom and bride in these words: “As a bridegroom he bound me with a mitre, and as a bride he clothed me with adornment” (Isa. 61). He is called bridegroom with respect to the head, and bride with respect to the body. Yet the voice or person is not changed. Therefore Christ is poor in us, with us, and for us.

[Note: [Col. 0905D] From Gregory, on the seventh penitential psalm.] Here he prays in the person of the penitent who recognizes his own lowliness [Col. 0906C] and the cause of that lowliness, and asks to be delivered from sins and restored to his former state. The sense is: This psalm is the prayer of the poor man—[Alcuin] that is, Christ—who is poor both in himself and in the members, 218 in whose person he speaks. It is a prayer uttered when he was distressed: amid the miseries into which he was cast through the sin of the first man. And, in order to escape them, he poured out his supplication before the Lord, through whom alone he can be delivered.

**Purpose.** [Cassiodorus] He warns all to consider their own misery and to seek God’s mercy.

**Method.** There are four divisions. The first part is an entreating appeal. The second is a sorrowful narrative, at the words, “For my days have failed.” The third is assurance of obtaining pardon, at “But thou.” In the fourth he says that he passes from his own brevity [Col. 0906D] to eternity, at “He answered him.” And because he mentioned three things in the title—prayer, poverty, and distress—intending to pursue each in its proper place, he begins with prayer, saying:

### Verse 1.—“O Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come unto thee.”

“O Lord, hear my prayer.” [Cassiodorus] Here is the prayer; then he repeats, “And my cry.” See how the prayer has grown into a cry: “let it come unto thee.” Let not the cloud of sins hinder me, the cloud that obstructs the wicked. Hence Jeremiah says: “Thou hast set a cloud before thee, that prayer may not pass through” (Lam. 3). [Augustine] The prayer is doubled because this repetition displays the penitent’s feeling. And here, through three verses, there is the figure *epimone*, that is, frequent repetition of the same thought.

### Verse 2.—“Turn not away thy face from me: in whatever day I am troubled, incline thine ear unto me.”

“Turn not away,” etc. Because I pray and cry, give ear; above all, show your face, because I am troubled and call upon you. This is what follows: Turn not away from me, a penitent, thy face—but turn it away from my sins. [Cassiodorus] You do indeed reject the offering of the wicked, but not the repentance of the devout. “Incline unto me,” [Augustine] that is, unto me in my humility, “thine ear, in whatever day I am troubled.” He says this because, in his members, he is troubled not merely at one time but at every time, etc.

### Verse 3.—“In whatever day I shall call upon thee, [Col. 0907B] hear me speedily.”

“Hear me speedily,” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] because I, now redeemed, seek not earth as one earthly, but heaven. To this desire you say, “While you are still speaking, I shall say: Behold, I am here.” I say, hear me “in whatever day I shall call upon thee.” He says this because he calls upon God in all the faithful and at every time.

### Part II. Verse 4.—“For my days have failed like smoke, and my bones have dried up like firewood.”

“For they have failed.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] The second part contains the sorrowful narrative, in which he explains what poverty and what distress he suffers, and thus reveals why he cries. As though he said: Therefore I cry, because “my days have failed,” [Col. 0907C] [Augustine, Jerome, Cassiodorus] that is, not this visible light—the illumination of the air by the sun—but the times of my life. They have failed, I say, “like smoke,” that is, because of the exaltation of pride. For when Adam was lifted up, his days fail. “And my bones have dried up like firewood,” that is, the strength and firmness of the soul have contracted.

Misery can move a merciful judge; here poverty is indicated. Or thus: “And my bones,” [Augustine] that is, the strong who bear the flesh—that is, the weak—“have been crushed as in a frying-pan,” according to another reading. For all who are scandalized are their frying-pan; for the righteous and good man is fried in proportion as he loves. Hence the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11).

Or thus: [Cassiodorus] “And my bones have been crushed as in a frying-pan,” that is, the strength of the mind is, as though fried, contracted by the remembrance of sins or by fear of judgment. “My bones have been crushed.” For a person is already being fried when he fears that he will be burned.

### Verse 5.—“I have been struck down like grass, and my heart has withered, because I forgot to eat my bread.”

“I have been struck down,” [Augustine] that is, I became mortal in Adam, from whom misery has been propagated, “like grass.” This is well said, because “all flesh is grass” (Isa. 40). Grass indeed grows green, but, when struck, readily feels the injury; so human flesh, flourishing under the law of God, when cut down by that very law, withers. “And my heart withered” through the barrenness [Col. 0908A] of sin. [Augustine] But how did this happen? “Because I forgot to eat my bread,” that is, to keep the word of God; for he neglected the command which God had given and drank the serpent’s poison by consenting to its evil persuasion. But now that the Lord has been crucified, remembrance returns, and he eats the bread which came down from heaven (John 6).

Note that he says, “I forgot.” For the nature of sinners is shown: [Cassiodorus, interlinear gloss, Augustine] while sin is desired, contemplation of God is not retained. Why then? Because I forgot, I now groan—not for earthly things, but for eternal things, and for others who groan over earthly things.

### Verse 6.—“At the sound of my groaning, my bone cleaved to my flesh.”

[Col. 0908B] “At the sound of my groaning.” [Augustine] Not the groaning of those who mourn over earthly, not spiritual, things—those for whom this one groans. For they groan, and he groans; but they do so in one way, he in another. “At the sound,” I say, “of my groaning, my bone cleaved,” or “my bones cleaved,” “to my flesh”: that is, by such groaning it is made clear that the bones cleave to the flesh, the strong to the weak, by bearing their weakness. Hence the Apostle says: “We who are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak” (Rom. 15).

Or it may be read otherwise: [Note: [Col. 0907D] From Gregory, on the seventh penitential psalm.] “I forgot to eat my bread,” that is, to keep God’s command. And this happened “at the sound of my groaning,” that is, at the voice of the devil, from whom come my groaning and misery. Hence: “My bone cleaved to my flesh,” that is, reason consented to sensuality.

### Verse 7.—“I have become like a pelican of the wilderness; [Col. 0908C] I have become as a night-raven in its dwelling.”

### Verse 8.—“I watched, and became as a solitary sparrow upon the roof.”

“I watched and became as a solitary sparrow,” [Augustine] or singular, or alone, “upon the roof,” or “in its dwelling.” Three birds and three places are distinguished here. The birds are the pelican, the night-raven, and the sparrow; the places are wilderness, ruins, and roof. The pelican is said to be in the wilderness, the night-raven among ruins, and the sparrow on the roof.

The pelican is a bird dwelling in the wilderness. The night-raven, a watchful and ugly raven of the night, dwells among ruins, commonly called collapsed buildings, where walls stand without a roof; there lives the night-raven, the bird which loves the night. The sparrow loves roofs.

One person [Col. 0908D] or many may bear the character of the three birds; but the three places are three kinds of people. There is a wilderness where Christians are not and never have been; ruins where they once were but have fallen; and a roof where they have been and have not fallen, remaining in the house.

Therefore, if a true preacher comes among those where Christians are not, he is like the pelican of the wilderness. If, however, he comes to those who once were Christian and fell, he is like a night-raven in its dwelling, or among ruins, because he does not abandon even their darkness, but seeks to win them. But if he comes to those who believed and did not fall, remaining in the house of the Church, yet acting lukewarmly, he is a sparrow upon the roof and cries to those beneath the roof—that is, to those who grow dull under [Col. 0909A] the flesh—while he himself is above the flesh. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who is on the roof, let him not go down to take anything” (Matt. 24). And elsewhere: “What you hear in the ear, preach upon the roofs” (Matt. 10).

Or Christ is understood through these birds. He is called a pelican, although it is not certain whether it kills its young with its beak, mourns for three days, and then pours its own blood over them with its beak, whence they return to life. So Christ kills—as he did Paul the persecutor—and makes alive by his blood, according to the saying: “I will kill, and I will make alive; I will strike, and I will heal” (Deut. 32).
