He is said to dwell in the wilderness, which properly suits Christ because he alone was born of a Virgin. After his birth, however, he came to his passion, where he was slain by ruins—that is, by the Jews who had fallen through blindness. Yet the Lord also loves them, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 24). Thus he was then like a night-raven among ruins; but he who slept in the passion watched in the resurrection, and, flying into heaven, became like a singular sparrow on the roof—[Cassiodorus] that is, in heaven—where he intercedes for us.

Or by these birds he marks different kinds of penitents. Hermits are compared to the pelican, a bird of extreme leanness and solitary wandering. The person who has withdrawn from public life is likened to the night-raven: while others sleep in the night of this world, he watches [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] and seeks food for his mind. Though he is not among people, he is nevertheless outside and aloft, saying to them: “Those who sleep, sleep in the night.” Truly a sparrow is one who wisely flees to the heights of the virtues, where he is safe from snares; [Col. 0909C] he is called solitary, or singular, because charity makes one out of many. And he is said to be on a roof, or a building, because of the height of faith, so that he may not descend to take anything from the house (Matt. 24).

### Verse 9.—“All day long my enemies reproached me; and those who praised me swore against me.”

“All day long,” etc. [Interlinear gloss] Christ speaks here. As though he said: Because I kill and make alive, therefore my enemies reproached me all day long, [Augustine] because I make sinners my members, as when they said: “Why does your master eat with publicans and sinners?” (Matt. 19). And those who would praise me openly with their mouth, but falsely, “swore against me,” that is, conspired against me. Why?

[Col. 0909D]

### Verse 10.—“Because I ate ashes as bread, and mingled my drink with weeping.”

“Because I ate ashes as bread, and mingled my drink with weeping,” [Augustine, Alcuin] that is, because I chose to have these classes of people as my members: namely, penitents, signified by ashes and weeping. Ashes and sackcloth are indeed the weapons of penitents.

[Alcuin, Cassiodorus] Or the whole may be understood in the person of a righteous man, as though he said: Thus I am chilled for others and groan. And, to add to my evil, my enemies reproached me all day long. Since the devil cannot otherwise destroy them, he seeks to ensnare them by a certain art: he causes penitents to be mocked, as though mockers, who had praised them while they were [Col. 0910A] worldly people together, were swearing in detestation of them. Hence he adds: “And those who praised me,” while I enjoyed worldly life with them, “swore against me,” that is, conspired against me. Why? Because I “ate ashes,” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] that is, I consumed by repentance the remnants of sins as though bread; for even slight sins—that is, light ones—must be consumed through repentance. “And I mingled my drink with weeping.” Although this may be understood literally, it should rather be understood of the Lord’s cup, which tears make sweeter.

Or thus: “Because I ate ashes”—as though he said: My enemies reproached me, but I did not care, because I ate ashes as bread; that is, I found nourishment in that very lowliness. So pleasing was it to me. “And I mingled my drink,” that is, temporal delight, “with weeping.” Or “drink” means the desire for the heavenly homeland, which I mingled with weeping because of its delay—that is, I mingled it with tears. Or “drink” means the draught [Col. 0910B] of the sacred Scriptures, which recall ancient things; I mingled it with weeping when I considered the good things I had lost and the evils I had found. But whence comes this weeping to me?

### Verse 11.—“From before thy wrath and indignation, because, having lifted me up, thou hast cast me down.”

“From before thy wrath and indignation.” [Cassiodorus] Wrath is vengeance; indignation in us is a movement of the mind, since we are indignant even with our children. Wrath, however, is an impulse in punishing, which does not apply to God, but is an anthropopathism. The meaning is: “From before thy wrath,” [Augustine] that is, from the imminence of vengeance which was in Adam and with which we were born. [Col. 0910C] This wrath comes from the propagation of iniquity, from the mass of sin. Hence the Apostle says: “We too were by nature children of wrath” (Eph. 2). And the Lord says: “The wrath of God remains upon those who do not believe” (John 3). He does not say, “will come,” but “remains,” because the wrath into which a person was born is not removed.

“And [from before] thy indignation,” which I earned by actual sinning. [Interlinear gloss, Augustine] And here the Church speaks. I rightly say, “from before thy wrath,” because, after lifting me up by making me in honor according to thy image, by which we surpass all animals, thou hast cast me down more grievously. For no creature shares this misery of sin and Gehenna except man. What beast laments over sin? What bird fears the Gehenna of eternal fire? For no such creature has any share in the blessed life. Therefore they have no stings of misery. And thou hast truly cast me down, because:

### Verse 12.—“My days declined like a shadow, [Col. 0910D] and I withered like grass.”

“My days,” which are “like a shadow,” that is, dark and vain, [interlinear gloss, Augustine, Cassiodorus] “declined.” “Like a shadow,” that is, they pass away as though useless. As though he said: Because I declined from the true one, my declining days became like me, and I withered like grass, without the dew of grace.

### Part III. Verse 13.—“But thou, O Lord, remainest for ever, and thy memorial unto generation and generation.”

“But thou, O Lord.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] This is the third part, in which assurance of obtaining pardon is shown. The fallen one now rises to prophesy; the penitent now raises his head. As though he said: [Augustine] I suffer these things by thy just judgment, but thou art strong in order to deliver me, thou who wast strong in order to humble me. This is the meaning: “But thou, O Lord, remainest for ever.” Therefore let the eternal one preserve the temporal. For though I have fallen, thou hast not grown old. Thou art strong to deliver me because thou wast strong to humble me.

“And thy memorial,” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine] that is, the memorable promise concerning thee—namely, restoration—by which thou rememberest us, or we remember thee. Or, “thy memorial” means the remembrance by which thou art mindful of us, because thou dost not forget us. It is “unto the present generation and the future generation,” because “we have the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4). I rightly say “thy memorial,” for:

### Verse 14.—“Thou, rising up, wilt have mercy on Zion; [Col. 0911B] for it is time to have mercy on her, for the time has come.”

“Thou, rising up to reign,” [Augustine] who, as though sleeping, had delayed, “wilt first have mercy on Zion,” that is, Judea. From there came the apostles and the other brethren, whose heart and soul were one in God (Acts 4). “Thou wilt have mercy,” I say, “because the time to have mercy on her has come,” of which the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4). And he repeats: “Because the acceptable time has come.” Hence: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6).

Note that he says, “The time has come.” [Cassiodorus] He says this because God willed all things to be done in order and appointed a time for this, in which the fitting opportunity was properly ordered. And thou wilt indeed have mercy on Zion.

### Verse 15.—“For her stones pleased thy servants, and they shall have compassion on her earth.”

“For her stones pleased thy servants,” that is, the apostles: the stones of Zion, [Augustine] that is, the steadfast prophets, are pleasing. For in Zion there are stones, and there are also non-stones—namely, dust, earth. Hence he adds: “And they shall have compassion on her earth,” or, “her dust.” The stones please the servants, and the servants themselves have compassion on the earth. The stones are the prophets; there preaching was first set forth, and from there the evangelical office was taken. Therefore the servants—that is, the apostles—recognize in the stones, that is, in the prophets, the sayings of God; and from the earth they form God’s image, when earthly people are cleansed, and they have compassion on them. As [Col. 0911D] man was formed from the dust of the earth, so God’s image is refashioned from the dust of fallen ruins (Acts 2). Thus, when the Holy Spirit was sent, many of those who had crucified the Lord believed; for from that dust came many thousands of believers, laying the prices of their possessions at the apostles’ feet (Acts 4).

But this did not happen only in Zion; indeed, another wall came from the Gentiles. Hence he adds:

### Verse 16.—“And the nations shall fear thy name, O Lord, and all the kings of the earth thy glory.”

“And the nations,” [interlinear gloss] who now do not know how to fear, shall fear thy name; and all the kings of the earth shall fear thy glory, greater than their own. This is why:

[Col. 0912A]

### Verse 17.—“For the Lord has built Zion, and he shall be seen in his glory.”

“For the Lord has built,” or “will build, Zion,” [Augustine] that is, the Church. This is now taking place, and at last, in Zion when built, “he shall be seen in his glory.” This does not happen now; then he will be seen as glorious, he who was first seen in that weakness. Hence: “We saw him as having neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53). He built Zion because:

### Verse 18.—“He has regarded the prayer of the humble, and has not despised their supplication.”

“He has regarded the prayer of the humble,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] who, filled with the Spirit, prayed that he might come. This happens in the building of Zion: the builders pray and groan; they are one poor man and many poor persons. Therefore the title speaks in the singular, but here in the plural. They are called one because of the unity of the Church’s peace; many because of its breadth. Therefore now prayer is made, now people run, now ashes are eaten as bread, and now drink is mingled with weeping, lest in the future one seek too late, ask in vain, knock fruitlessly, and remain outside with the five foolish virgins. “And he has not despised their supplication.” [Cassiodorus] To regard is precisely not to despise.

### Verse 19.—“Let these things be written for another generation; and the people which shall be created shall praise the Lord.”

“Let these things be written.” [Cassiodorus, interlinear gloss] He who above was made foul by repentance is now adorned with the honor of a prophet. He commands that what he has said be established by the testimony of Scripture, [Col. 0912C] so that a future age may learn it. As though he said: I have said that restoration is through Christ and destruction through Adam. And these things—namely, that restoration is through Christ and destruction through Adam—are to be written [Augustine, Cassiodorus] so that they may be firmly held or possessed “for another generation,” that is, for the work of the new generation. For when these things were written, they were not thus beneficial to the generation of the Old Testament; but they benefit another generation, that is, the new one. Hence he adds: “And the people which shall be created”—a new creation in Christ, not, I say, a people already created—“shall praise the Lord” who aided it. Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone is a new creation in Christ, old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (2 Cor. 5).

### Verse 20.—“For he looked down from his holy height; the Lord looked from heaven upon the earth.”

“For he looked down,” etc. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Alcuin] After the groans of the sufferer, these are now words of consolation; the poor man now rejoices. Note that he had said above, “The Lord has built Zion,” and likewise, “Let these things be written.” He now explains both: what he said was to be written, and how he built Zion. For this is what he said should be written: namely, that “he looked down,” [Augustine and Cassiodorus] that is, had mercy, “from his holy height,” in order to come humble to the humble; and thus he built Zion. Note that the Prophet speaks as past events of things that were still future. [Interlinear gloss] He then more clearly opens what he had said: “The Lord looked from heaven [Col. 0913A] upon the earth.” Why did he look down? He adds, namely:

### Verse 21.—“That he might hear the groaning of those in fetters, that he might loose the children of the slain.”

“That he might hear the groaning of those in fetters,” [Augustine] that is, of the saints, who are fettered by the fear of God and his discipline. For the fear of God is a set of fetters in which the saints groan to obtain mercy. Unless martyrs had been bound in the fetters of fear, they would not have endured harsh and painful things from persecutors. Of these fetters, the book of Wisdom says: “Hear, my son, and receive my judgment; do not reject my counsel; put thy foot into her fetters and thy neck into her chains; and her fetters shall be to thee a protection of strength, [Col. 0913B] and her chains a robe of glory” (Ecclus. 6).

Those who kill martyrs loose these fetters, and the freed persons are transformed into glory, “that he might loose the children of the slain,” [Augustine] or “of those put to death.” [Note: [Col. 0913D] From Gregory, on this psalm.] We, however, are the children of those persons put to death, and are loosed from the knots of sins and the bonds of desires. Therefore the Lord looked down upon the earth in order to hear the groaning of those in fetters of his fear and discipline. Or, “those in fetters” means those bound by sins or mortality. “That he might loose the children of the slain,” that is, us from sins. Hence elsewhere: “Thou hast broken my bonds” (Ps. 115). To what end did he hear and loose them? To this:

### Verse 22.—“That they may proclaim in Zion the name of the Lord, and his praise in Jerusalem.”

“That they may now proclaim,” [Augustine] what they were not permitted to proclaim when those in fetters were being slain, “the name of the Lord”—that is, praise concerning God’s essence—“in Zion,” that is, in the Church; “and his praise,” [interlinear gloss, Gregory] according to his works, proclaim “in Jerusalem,” that is, in the Church. Thus they may proclaim it:

### Verse 23.—“When peoples are gathered together into one, and kings, to serve the Lord.”

“When peoples and kings of the earth are gathered together,” [Cassiodorus] that is, so that they may cause peoples and kings to gather into one, into unity of faith and conduct, [Augustine] through the blood of those put to death and the groans of those in fetters which were heard. To what end? “To serve the Lord.”

[Cassiodorus] Or otherwise, from the words, “That he might hear the groaning of those in fetters.” Those in fetters are said to be the saints of the Old Testament, who, bound by legal restraints, did not employ harmful freedom. They prayed with groaning that God might loose the world from sins, and “that he might loose the children of the slain”—that is, free from their ancestral errors the children of those whom the devil had killed by deceit: namely, the apostles and other good persons of that people, who were children of those slain by the devil. Thus, once freed, they might proclaim the name of the Lord in Zion. He foretells future things. For this took place in Zion when the apostles first spoke there in various tongues the mighty works of God (Acts 2). From there their word ran throughout the universal Church. Hence he adds: [Col. 0914A] “And they may proclaim his praise in Jerusalem,” that is, in the universal Church, proclaiming it “when peoples are gathered into one, and kings, to serve the Lord.” These points are unchanged.

### Part IV. Verse 24.—“He answered him in the way of his strength: Make known to me the fewness of my days.”

“He answered.” [Alcuin, Augustine] The fourth part, in which, after assurance of pardon, he says that he passes from his own brevity to eternity. As though he said: “That they may proclaim the name of the Lord and his praise in Jerusalem. And he answered him”—that is, the praise or Jerusalem answered the Lord. The preceding words indicate that either praise or Jerusalem answered him. For above he had mentioned both praise and Jerusalem, peoples and kings. But it cannot refer to peoples or kings, since, if it did, he would have said, “They answered.” Since he says “he answered” in the singular, it is understood that praise or Jerusalem answered. Praise answers when those called by him give thanks, believing well or living well; or Jerusalem—not that reprobate Jerusalem which kills the prophets, but that which bears many children—when called, answers, does not despise, but yields fruit.

See what answered, to whom it answered, and where it answered: “in the way,” that is, in Christ, in the unity of faith in him; it did not answer in itself, that is, out of its own merits. For from itself it would have no voice but that of sin. And how did it answer? “In the way of his strength,” that is, in the faith by which it believes that Christ rose again. For Christ became the way of his strength after the resurrection, when [Col. 0914C] he was no longer weak as before, when he was the way of weakness; but, strong in heaven, he calls the Church. The praise of faith does not consist in believing that he died—which even a pagan believes—but in believing that he was glorified. Therefore it answered him not with the voice but with the heart, not with the tongue but with life; in the way not of weakness but of his strength—that is, in the faith of Christ, by which it believes him not merely dead but risen and ascended to equality with the Father.

I have said that the Church answered the Lord, and where and how. But because he foresaw some saying: “Once there was indeed a Church gathering all into one, but it has now ceased,” he says: “Make known to me the fewness,” or shortness, “of my days”—not the eternity of those days in which I shall be, but the temporal days during which I shall be in this world. He says this [Col. 0914D] because of those who say that the Church no longer exists. This utterance is not idle; this petition is not empty. For that Way itself announced: “I am with you unto the consummation of the world” (Matt. 28). The entire period until the end of the world is that shortness of days, because everything that comes to an end is short, in order that one may pass thence to eternity. I say, “Make known to me.” And:

### Verse 25.—“Do not call me back in the midst of my days; thy years are unto generation and generation.”

“Do not call me back in the midst of my days,” [Augustine] [Col. 0915A] that is, grant that I may not cease during all that short span. Let it not happen as heretics say; lead me on until the end of the world. Do not therefore call me back in the midst of my days, but complete for me these short days until the end of the world, that afterwards thou mayest give eternal days. Why do you ask concerning shortness? Because “thy years are unto generation and generation”: that is, although those days endure until the end of the world, they are nevertheless short in comparison with thine, which do not change and are eternal.

[Cassiodorus] Or thus, from the words “He answered,” etc. As though he said: They proclaim his praise in Jerusalem, and Jerusalem itself—that is, the Church—answers him by rejoicing in the Lord and obeying his commands. Where? “In the way of his strength,” [Gregory] that is, of its steadfastness, not turning aside from good. Christian religion is here briefly defined in the phrase “in the way of strength.” I say that it answered, [Cassiodorus] and in answering prayed thus: “O God, make known to me the fewness,” or shortness, “of my days,” that is, make me consider this brief time of the whole age until the end.

It desires to know the end of the age so that it may soon come to blessedness. It does not ask to know the day or the hour of the consummation, which no one can know. Hence the Lord says: “But of that day and hour no one knows, neither angel nor Son, but the Father alone” (Matt. 15). Yet it desires to know whether the age will quickly end, so that it may pass into life. Therefore he adds: “Do not call me back in the midst of my days,” [Gregory] that is, into the life already passed, or the age of sins, from which [Col. 0915C] I have been delivered. Or: “Do not call me back in the midst of my days”; do not permit me to be recalled from the course of heavenly things, so that I cleave to the care of temporal matters, rather than continuing these half-days and the days to come.

He calls these present days “the midst,” or half, “of my days.” [Alcuin] Or “days” means those which the holy man spends in the good in the present life, in which he earns the reward of life. For he has days who spends them here in the light of a good life; but they are only half-days if eternal days are not added. The sense is: Because I strive toward eternal things, “do not call me back in the midst of my days,” [Augustine] that is, do not let me remain in these half-days, but add days of joy.

“In the generation of generations,” according to another reading, “are thy years.” The generation of generations is that generation which does not pass away, gathered from all generations—that is, the saints. For the holy offspring of every generation are gathered together, and from them is made one generation of generations which does not go or pass away. In it will be the Lord’s years, which do not pass away: namely, God’s eternity. For God’s years are not one thing and he another; the years of God are God’s eternity. Eternity itself, moreover, is God’s substance, having nothing mutable, where nothing is past and nothing future. The sense is: My days are short, but thy years—that is, thy eternity—are in the generation of generations.

### Verse 26.—“In the beginning thou, O Lord, hast founded the earth; and the heavens are the works of thy hands.”

“In the beginning, thou, O Lord,” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine] as though he said: Do not call me back, for I strive toward eternity, [Col. 0916A] which he explains by saying: “O Lord, thou hast founded the earth.” And this “in the beginning,” because by thy eternity thou precedest all that thou hast made. For thou didst exist without beginning before created things. “And the heavens are the works of thy hands,” literally. Elsewhere it is said: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. 32). But what he does by his word, he also does by his hand—that is, by his power. For he is not divided into bodily members. The Word of God, moreover, is his hand.

### Verse 27.—“They shall perish, but thou remainest; and all shall grow old like a garment.”

“The heavens themselves shall perish,” [Augustine] meaning the heavens near the earth. It is certain that these will perish with respect to their quality. Hence Peter also says: “The earth and the heavens which now are, by the same word are stored up for fire, reserved” (2 Pet. 3). But concerning the higher heavens of heavens it is not certain; yet, if they remain, they remain not in themselves but in God.

Or, mystically, the heavens are the righteous, who are the works of his hands. They shall perish according to the garment—that is, according to the body—but shall be changed for the better. “But thou remainest” unchangeable. [Cassiodorus] As he showed God’s eternity by creating all things, so he shows it by remaining after things are changed. “And all,” or “all things,” “shall grow old like a garment.” As though he said: This cannot be understood of angels, but of mutable things—namely, literally of the heavens; or of saints, who grow old like a garment, that is, according to the body, which is worn away in the manner of clothing.

### Verse 28.—“And as a covering thou shalt change them, and they shall be changed; but thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail.”

[Col. 0916C] “And as a covering thou shalt change them.” Understand the heavens, which cover all things and which themselves shall be changed. Hence he adds: “And they shall be changed.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] They are rightly said to be changed, or about to be changed, because they will no longer be subject to corruption as before. But thou who hast said, “I am who am” (Exod. 3), “art the same”: that is, unchangeable and almighty. Although all things are from thee, through thee, and in thee, they are not what thou art: thou who changest and art not changed, who makest and art not made, who movest yet remainest.

“And thy years,” which shall be in the generation of generations, “shall not fail.” But shall we be able to be there? Certainly. Hear what follows:

### Verse 29.—“The children of thy servants shall dwell, [Col. 0916D] and their seed shall be established for ever.”

The children of your servants, etc. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] This is a joyful conclusion, by which we are said to be destined to dwell there. As though he said: “Your years shall not fail.” And in your years the children of your servants shall dwell—[Augustine] that is, the children of the prophets and apostles, let alone the prophets and apostles themselves. Thus Scripture says that the children dwelt there (Num. 14), since the children entered the land of promise, but their fathers did not. This signifies that new people enter into the new rest, not the old. Yet two of those fathers entered, namely Caleb and Joshua, because into the true rest enter also the One and unity—that is, Christ and the Church—with all the newness of the children. Therefore, in saying that the children shall dwell, he both alluded to the ancient history and indicated the mystery.

[Augustine.] Or the children are [Col. 0917A] good works, without which no one enters. “The children of your servants shall dwell”: that is, servants shall dwell through good works, as it were through children. Therefore do not be barren if you wish to dwell there. Send ahead the offspring of your works, which you may follow, so that they may lead you into the land of the living. Thus Joseph the son went before Jacob into Egypt; and he said to his father and his brothers: “I have gone ahead to prepare food for you” (Gen. 45). So let your children—that is, your good works—go before you, to prepare for you the feast of eternal refreshment. For such children as you have sent ahead, such shall you follow. And their seed, [Gregory] that is, their works—from which eternal fruit is reaped—shall be directed for ever, that is, into eternity. This is said because nothing crooked enters.

## Comparison on Psalm 101: “O Lord, Hear My Prayer,” etc.

[Col. 0917B]

**Verse 4.**—“They have dried up like cremium.” They express one meaning in different words. Jerome: “They have wasted away as though fried.” Others: “They have been scorched like a hearth or a burning brand.” *Moqed* derives from the root *yaqad*, “he kindled, burned up, and fried.” Hence the Roman edition, followed by Saint Augustine, has: “They have been crushed as in a frying-pan.” Moreover, according to Arnobius, *cremium* is a dry twig, although he calls it a frying-pan. This meaning fits the Hebrew and Greek especially well. The former means a scorched brand; the latter, dry wood, φύγιον (*phýgion*). Calepinus thinks *cremium* means meat fried in a pan, whose strength and moisture are drained away the more it is roasted.

**Verse 7.**—“Like a night-raven in a dwelling.” Jerome, Nebiensis, Münster, and Sanctes render *nycticorax* as “a nocturnal owl,” likewise a bird. Others agree with the Septuagint. But for “in a dwelling” all have “in solitudes,” “in ruins,” or “among ruined walls.” Let us hear Jerome’s view on these two matters in his letter to Sunnias and Fretela:

> “You ask what *nycticorax* means among the Latins. In Hebrew, the word *cos* is written in place of *nycticorax*. Aquila, the Septuagint, Theodotion, and the fifth edition rendered it *nycticorax*. Symmachus, however, rendered it ‘hoopoe’; the sixth edition, ‘owl,’ which we follow more readily. Finally, where among us and the Greeks it is read, ‘I have become like a *nycticorax* in a dwelling,’ among the Hebrews it is said, ‘I have become like an owl amid ruins.’ Most people obstinately suppose it means an eagle-owl.”

So far he. From this one may infer, even from this passage, that Jerome’s translation was published because of contentious Jews. For he translates “eagle-owl,” although he says that he does not follow that rendering. Finally, he teaches what “in a dwelling” means above, in discussing the verse “like a solitary sparrow on a roof,” where he writes:

> “And you say that you have found in the Greek ἐπὶ δώματος (*epi domatos*), which the ancient Latin manuscripts rendered ‘on a building.’ In the eastern provinces δῶμα (*dōma*) is what among the Latins is called a roof. For in Palestine and Egypt, or wherever the divine books were written or translated, roofs do not have gables but *domata*, which at Rome they call either terraces or balconies: that is, flat roofs supported by cross-beams. Thus also in the Acts of the Apostles, when Peter went up onto the *doma*, he must be understood to have gone up onto the roof of the house. And when we are commanded to make a parapet for our roof, the command is that we make certain raised structures all round the roof, so that falling headlong may not be easy. And in the Gospel: ‘What you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the *domata*,’ that is, upon the roofs (Matt. 10). And in Isaiah: ‘What has happened to you, that you all go up upon the empty roofs?’ (Isa. 22). And much else of this kind.”

Thus Jerome. It must now be carefully noted that *doma* indeed occurs in the verse, “like a solitary [Col. 0918A] sparrow on a roof.” Yet in the other verse, the manuscripts I have seen read ἐν οἰκοπέδῳ (*en oikopedō*), “in a ruined place.”

**Verse 9.**—“Those who praised me.” *Meholalai*: Jerome, “those exulting [over me].” Some others translate, “those raging against me”; others, “those mocking me.” Certainly, among the Hebrews that word has multiple meanings.

**Verse 14.**—“For the time has come.” Jerome and nearly all others likewise. The interpreters for Cajetan put “testimony” for “time”; Pratensis, “solemnity.” *Moed*.

**Verse 15.**—“They shall have pity on its earth.” Jerome renders the verb by a noun: “its pitiable dust.” *Jehonenu*. In his letter to Sunnias and Fretela, he translates, in accordance with the Septuagint, “they shall have pity,” and teaches that *aphar* can be rendered both “earth” and “dust.”

**Verse 17.**—“The nations shall fear your name, O Lord.” 221 We have taken this reading from the Roman psalmody. For in Hebrew and Greek [Col. 0918B] one reads: “The nations shall fear the name of the Lord.” The sense does not waver. וְיִירְאוּ גוֹיִם אֶת־שֵׁם אֲדֹנָי (*ve-yireʾu goyim ʾet-shem Adonai*): “The nations shall fear the name of the Lord.” Φοβηθήσονται τὰ ἔθνη τὸ ὄνομα Κυρίου (*Phobēthēsontai ta ethnē to onoma Kyriou*): “The nations shall fear the name of the Lord.”

**Verse 18.**—“Of the humble.” Jerome: “of the empty”; Pratensis and Münster: “of the solitary”; Sanctes: “of those who are like tamarisks”; Pellicanus: “of one crying aloud”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “of one sighing”; the translator for Campensis: “of the destitute”; the Paraphrase: “of this sorrowing one”; Nebiensis: “of one stirring.” If we abandon the Septuagint or Jerome, whom shall we follow? Yet, insofar as can be gathered from Hebrew lexicons concerning the word set down in Hebrew, its sense must be understood figuratively, adopting what is most fitting. Sanctes, in his *Treasury of the Holy Language*, writes that *arear* is “a tamarisk or juniper,” citing Rabbi David. But Jerome more fully and clearly satisfies us on Jeremiah 17, at the words: “For he shall be like a tamarisk in the wilderness.” He says:

> “In Hebrew it is called *arear*, or, as Symmachus rendered it, ‘an unfruitful tree in the wilderness.’”

This agrees with the interpretation of the Septuagint and with his own. For tamarisks are famously lowly trees, as in the verse:

> Not all shrubs are pleasing, nor lowly tamarisks.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogues* IV.2.)

Then, when Jerome rendered it “he looked upon the prayer of the empty,” it agrees with Symmachus’s rendering, “an unfruitful tree.” Finally, the Chaldee agrees in sound with the Vulgate: “he looked upon the prayer of the desolate.”

**Verse 24.**—“He answered him in the way of his strength.” Jerome and the more recent translators: “He afflicted my strength in the way.” Yet *anah* and *innah* in Hebrew mean both “he answered,” “he was humbled,” and “he humbled”; thus it is not unsuitable to render it in either way. As for our reading “of his strength,” in the third person, while the Hebrew has the first person: we have often noted that this happens because of the kinship of *yod* and *waw*, one of which readily passes into the other, and indeed one often serves in place of the other. Thus *coho* and *cohi* are not far apart.

“My few days.” Others take it as the verb *qitzar yamai*, “he shortened my days.” But immediately thereafter: “make known to me.” The Hebrews connect it with the following verse, in the first person future: *omar*, “I shall say.” But read *emor*, and you will have “make known,” in agreement with us; for although the pointing differs, the letters remain unchanged. Finally, where we read “to me,” the Hebrews now say “my God.” Yet in “to me” and in “my God” exactly the same letters remain; a distinction of points creates the variation. For *eli* means “my God”; and *elai*, “to me,” where the pronunciation is likewise not distinguished unless one says *elai*, which is better. Yet not a single letter is changed.

## Psalm 102

[Col. 0919]

### Title of the Psalm: “A Psalm of David Himself”

[Col. 0919A]

“Bless the Lord, O my soul.” Title: “A Psalm of David Himself.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] After the prayers of the poor man come the praises of one rejoicing. For all who are in Christ are, as it were, one person; this person speaks here and stirs up and exhorts his soul to bless the Lord, wishing to explain why He is to be blessed. For he sets forth the cause for praise, lest anyone be found sluggish in this respect. The sense of the title is: This psalm—that is, this praise which is sung here—is made to David himself, that is, to Christ, and to no other. Intention: he exhorts to praise. Method: the psalm has three parts. First, through the benefits bestowed upon himself by God, the Prophet exhorts himself to bless God. Second, through the things God bestowed upon the ancients and will bestow upon those to come, at “who performs mercies.” [Col. 0919B] Third, through the heavenly beings and all other creatures, he exhorts all to bless God, at “Bless the Lord.” [Augustine, Alcuin.] The Prophet, speaking in the person of the general righteous man according to the higher power of the soul, that is, reason, exhorts the soul to bless, saying: “O—”

**Verse 1.**—“Bless the Lord, O my soul; and let all that is within me bless his holy name.”

My soul, bless the Lord: [Augustine] that is, praise the Lord, who says: “The sacrifice of praise shall honour me” (Ps. 49). Therefore cry aloud if there is a person to hear; cry without a voice if there is no person to hear, for God hears. He then repeats more explicitly what he had said: “And all that is within me”—[Cassiodorus] that is, all thoughts and all powers; let none [Col. 0919C] be discordant—“bless his holy name.” [Augustine.] For one who hears what is inward never fails to be present; therefore let those inward things never be silent. Again he repeats:

**Verse 2.**—“Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his recompenses.”

“Bless the Lord, O my soul.” [Augustine.] The repetition serves exhortation. I say, bless him; and that you may always bless him, do not forget all his recompenses. Let not the pleasure of sin be before your eyes, but the condemnation of sin and God’s forgiveness. Consider all your evils; for as many as they are, so many are God’s good recompenses. God’s recompenses cannot all be before your eyes unless all your sins have first been before them. Note that he does not say merely “recompenses,” but “his recompenses”: one thing was owed, and another thing, not owed, was given back. Man gives evil in return for good; God gives him good in return for evil, for which good man had given evil. Behold, it is good that a person exists, lives, and was made in God’s image. Although a person ought to render God likeness to himself in return for these things, he renders unlikeness. And God returns good for these evils, inspiring repentance and granting pardon. Thus elsewhere: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. 115). He bestowed when he made me; he recompensed [Col. 0920A] when he justified me. These, then, are the recompenses: he himself is—

**Verse 3.**—“Who is merciful toward all your iniquities; who heals all your infirmities.”

He is merciful toward all your iniquities, forgiving them. [Augustine.] After forgiveness, he also heals all your infirmities, or sicknesses, because the body is weak and, from bodily weakness, many carnal desires are suggested to the soul. They tantalize it, and by some of them the soul is captured. But there is no need to fear, because he heals all your infirmities: now soothing with gentle remedies, now cutting with harsh ones. No sickness is incurable for the almighty physician. Especially at the end he will heal these sicknesses, when this corruptible thing shall put on incorruption. Hence follows:

[Col. 0920B]

**Verse 4.**—“Who redeems your life from destruction; who crowns you in mercy and compassions.”

He redeems, or shall redeem. [Augustine.] As though he said: He therefore heals all sicknesses, because he is the one who redeems your life, at the price of his blood, from destruction—that is, from the corruption so great in the body, which weighs down the soul, hinders it from thinking upon God himself, and twists it away from its lofty attention. But this will end when it puts on incorruption. He will indeed heal it, because he is the one who, if you overcome, crowns you when you are incorruptible; and this comes only from his mercy. Hence follows: I say that he crowns you in mercy and compassions.

[Col. 0920C]

**Verse 5.**—“Who satisfies your desire with good things; your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s.”

He also satisfies your desire with good things. After the crown, no struggle remains in which you need help; rather, you are satisfied with the things you desired and longed for here. When will this be? When your youth is renewed like the eagle’s. As though he said: This is not in the present life, in which no one is filled but always lacks. But when shall your youth be renewed? He adds, “like the eagle’s.” The eagle’s youth is renewed, though not unto immortality. For the likeness is given only as far as a mortal thing can resemble an immortal one. It is said that, when an eagle is weighed down by old age, the hook of its excessively grown beak prevents it from opening its mouth and taking food. It consequently grows weak; but by a certain natural means it strikes its beak against a rock [Col. 0920D] and shakes off the burden of its beak, by which it had been prevented from eating. It returns to food, everything is restored to it, and it becomes young. So too the Rock—Christ—removes what prevents us from eating our bread and shakes off old age, so that we may be renewed in him, we whose old age closes our mouths because we have forgotten to eat our bread.

**Part II. Verse 6.**—“The Lord performs mercies and judgment for all who suffer injustice.”

“The Lord performs mercies.” [Alcuin, Augustine.] The second part, in which he exhorts us to bless God through the things done for the ancients and to be done for those who follow. As though he said: In the future we shall enter and be satisfied. What is there for us here on the way? Are we abandoned? No: the Lord does not leave us in the desert, but leads us to our homeland and performs mercies. But he does so for the merciful, of whom it is said: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5). They are those who love their enemies and forgive those who sin against them. When the adulteress was accused, the Lord, writing on the ground, required this fruit of mercy (John 8). For God first wrote upon stone, marking the hardness of the Jews; but, bent down into the flesh, he wrote upon the ground the fruit which the human mind was to bear. His bending down signifies the humility of the Incarnation, through which he raised up in Christians the fruit of mercy. [Col. 0921B] This mercy, moreover, must be shown to everyone. Hence the Apostle: “Let us do good to all,” etc. (Gal. 6); and: “Give to everyone who asks of you” (Luke 6); and: “If your enemy hungers, feed him” (Rom. 12).

Yet elsewhere it is read: “Do not hand over [a person] to a sinner, and do not receive a sinner,” which seems contrary to the foregoing. But in this apparent conflict of authorities, two things must be distinguished: nature and vice. Help nature; pursue vice. Therefore, “do not hand over [a person] to a sinner, and do not receive a sinner,” means: do not receive him through love of his wickedness. Conversely, “give to everyone who asks of you,” and “if your enemy hungers, feed him”: namely, aid nature, do not assist sin; give to God’s work, not to man’s work. For that a person is human is God’s work; that he is a sinner is man’s work. Thus one who gives to a righteous person for a reason other than that he is God’s work does not give to a righteous person. Hence it is said: “Whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person shall receive a righteous person’s reward” (Matt. 10). Nor is mercy impeded if the wicked are punished. Wrongdoers must indeed be punished, not from a spirit of vengeance but of love. But when one more powerful confronts you, and you cannot correct or admonish him, endure him, secure in the knowledge that he will not go unpunished. For after mercy he adds judgment, saying: And the Lord performs judgment. Hence: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Deut. 23). But for whom? For all who suffer injustice from those who are not under their authority—that is, those who do not fall under the governing jurisdiction of the sufferer and over whom the sufferer cannot exercise discipline. Then, showing [Col. 0921D] what he did for the ancients, he adds:

**Verse 7.**—“He made his ways known to Moses, his wills to the children of Israel.”

“He made his ways known to Moses.” [Augustine.] Understand all saints through Moses: one is named, but all are included. Yet Moses is especially named because the Law was given through him, so that the sick person might be convicted, exposed in the five porticoes of the five books of the Law, and not healed there (John 5). Thus he seeks the physician, and unity is healed in the pool stirred at the angel’s descent—that is, in Christ’s Passion, since when Christ descended from heaven he suffered at the hands of the people. The Law, therefore, was given so that the proud might be humbled, the humble might confess, 222 and thus be healed. These are the hidden ways which God showed to Moses, through whom he gave the Law so that transgression might abound. [Col. 0922A] And to the true children of Israel he made his wills known. And:

**Verse 8.**—“The Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy.”

The Lord is compassionate in act and merciful by nature. [Cassiodorus.] Mercy is necessarily followed by patience. Hence follows: “And patient,” because he endures sinners for a long time; and merciful, [Augustine] because he gives good things and calls in many ways. He calls by the benefits of creation; he calls by granting time to live; he calls through the reader; he calls through the preacher; he calls through inward thought; he calls through the scourge of correction; he calls through the mercy of consolation. And he does this abundantly, because he is merciful even toward blasphemers, and truly merciful, because:

[Col. 0922B]

**Verse 9.**—“He will not be angry for ever, nor threaten unto eternity.”

“He will not be angry for ever”—[Augustine] namely, with the good. Anger is the consequence of the first sin, which we suffer in this world; but he consoles us by promising that it will end. “Nor will he threaten unto eternity”: [interlinear gloss] concerning eternal punishment. This is to be proved from the fact that:

**Verse 10.**—“He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities.”

“He has not dealt with us according to our sins.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, interlinear gloss.] As though he said: We have received what we did not deserve. This applies to all to whom he freely grants good things. “Nor has he repaid us according to our iniquities,” but, after the offense, he has absolved us. [Col. 0922C] And indeed:

**Verse 11.**—“For as the height of heaven above the earth, he has strengthened his mercy over those who fear him.”

“For he has strengthened his mercy over those who fear him.” [Augustine.] According to what measure? According to the height of heaven above earth. Can heaven depart from protecting the earth? Then God could fail to protect those who fear him. Observe the apt comparison: heaven surrounds the earth on every side. From it light comes even to the eyes of sinners; from it come air, breath, rain upon the earth, and fruits. As the earth remains fixed without God, so God’s protection remains over those who fear him. And what has he done? Behold:

[Col. 0922D]

**Verse 12.**—“As far as the east is from the west, he has removed our iniquities far from us.”

“As far as the east is from the west,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] so far has he removed our iniquities from us. As though he said: He makes light shine out of darkness. For when sin is forgiven, sins set and grace rises: sins are as though in the west; the grace by which you are delivered is in the east. Turn, therefore, away from the west of sins and stretch toward the east of grace; thus you rise and advance. He has therefore removed our iniquities far from us, as far as east is from west, [interlinear gloss] when he made sins set and grace rise. But why did he do this? Freely, not by merits. And this is:

**Verse 13.**—“As a father has compassion on his children, the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him; for he has known our formation.”

“As a father has compassion on his children,” [Col. 0923A] even by chastisements, [Augustine] so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him, because he has known our formation—that is, our weakness. He knows what he made: how it fell, how it must be restored, how it must be adopted, how it must be enriched. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] For, cast away from the work of the Creator, we ourselves have fashioned ourselves badly. He then explains “our formation,” adding:

**Verse 14.**—“He remembered that we are dust; man’s days are like grass; he shall flourish like a flower of the field.”

“He remembered that we are dust”: [interlinear gloss] although we were made in your image, O Lord, we are nevertheless dust through the dryness of sin. Or according to the other reading: “Remember that we are dust.” [Augustine.] As though he said: What formation did he know? Us, who are weak; therefore, turning to God, he says: “Remember that we are dust.” Remember—that is, may your mercy toward us endure, lest your grace forget us. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] I say that man is dust and quickly passes away. Man is like grass, which flowers today and withers soon; and his days—that is, the most beautiful thing he has—are like a flower of the field, which passes away even more quickly. “Man is like grass, and thus man shall flower,” that is, at most he will flower in this way; or “he shall flower out,” that is, he shall lose his flower. [Alcuin.] For the prefix may be intensive or privative.

Or distinguish the wording thus. He shows the condition of man, [Col. 0923C] lest he be proud, saying: This is what man has: his day is like grass. For a man comes forth like a flower and is crushed; he flees like a shadow and never remains in the same state. And all the splendor of humankind—honours, riches, and so forth—shall flower out like a flower of the field. [Augustine.] The flower of grass is that which is not perennial; what is most beautiful soon falls. Hence: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass; the grass has withered and the flower has fallen; but the word of the Lord remains for ever” (Isa. 40). What became grass for your sake—that is, flesh—is from you; therefore you are dust from yourself, but something else through his mercy. [Augustine, interlinear gloss.] Hence he adds in what follows: “But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity,” etc., as though he said: Man is grass or a flower. And indeed:

**Verse 15.**—“For the spirit shall pass through him, and he shall not remain; and he shall no longer know his place.”

“For the spirit,” [Haymo, Augustine] which is in him, “shall pass away from him.” Behold: he who feared has gone. For this is the end of those who die, and when the spirit departs, man does not remain. [Haymo.] Or thus: The spirit existing in him shall pass away from him, because, while it is in him, it changes, and afterwards departs. Hence follows: “And the spirit shall not remain in him, and he shall no longer know his place”: [Cassiodorus] that is, it shall not return to the body in this world. He says this against madmen who claim that souls will return to this world.

**Verse 16.**—“But the mercy of the Lord is from [Col. 0924A] eternity unto eternity over those who fear him.”

“But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity.” [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: Such is human nature, but through God’s mercy man shall be eternal. Here he checks presumption; there he establishes hope. And this is: “But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity”—that is, from the time the world began to be governed—“unto eternity,” that is, without end, “over those who fear him,” not over others.

**Verse 17.**—“And his justice is upon children’s children, upon those who keep his covenant.”

“And his justice is upon children’s children.” [Alcuin, Augustine.] Behold mercy and justice together: he speaks of recompense upon children’s children. Yet many righteous people have no children, much less children’s children; but children [Col. 0924B] are works, and children’s children are the rewards of works. The sense is: His mercy is over those who fear him, and his justice is upon children’s children—that is, through his mercy and justice, those who fear him shall receive an eternal reward for good works. And lest all presume, he adds: “upon those who keep his covenant.”

**Verse 18.**—“And who remember his commandments, to do them.”

“And who remember his commandments”: [Augustine] not merely in order to recite them by memory, but “to do them,” that is, to perform what they have learned. And if they seem too numerous to you, all are fulfilled in the two commandments of love (Matt. 22). Therefore hold fast the root of love, and the whole tree is in you. [Col. 0924C] For love is the end of the commandment.

**Verse 19.**—“The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven, and his kingdom shall rule over all.”

“The Lord in heaven,” etc. [Cassiodorus.] He proclaims the future judgment lest sinners grow bold. As though he said: And you ought to remember in order to act, because the Lord—[Augustine, interlinear gloss] that is, Christ, who descended and ascended—has prepared in heaven his judicial throne: that is, while in heaven, he shall judge the good and the evil, though he was formerly mocked on earth. And lest you think him powerless: “his kingdom shall rule over all.”

**Part III. Verse 20.**—“Bless the Lord, all his angels, mighty in strength, who do his word, in order to hear the voice of his words.”

“Bless the Lord.” [Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which, through heavenly beings and all other creatures, he exhorts us to bless God. He begins with the angels, saying: “his angels”—[Alcuin, Haymo] not the evil ones—“bless the Lord.” He says this in congratulation, not by command or exhortation. As though he said: “I love what you do.” And, O mighty ones—that is, all heavenly powers—who are mighty in strength, not in vice like the devil: bless him, you who do his word. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, interlinear gloss.] You are not righteous or faithful to the Word of God unless you do it. “Who do [his word],” I say, “in order to hear the voice of his words”: that is, humble in obedience, not proud; knowing and revering their Creator. Such persons are worthy to bless him, and no others. Or, “doing [his word] in order to hear the voice of his words”: that is, so that through you we may hear, being instructed by your example.

[Col. 0925A]

**Verse 21.**—“Bless the Lord, all his powers, his ministers who do his will.”

“All his powers”: [interlinear gloss] this signifies that order of angels; bless the Lord. [Cassiodorus, Haymo, Augustine.] The word, so often repeated, stirs minds. Then he adds universally concerning all: O his ministers, who do his will—not merely speak it—you, bless him. For though an evil person’s tongue is silent, his life blasphemes; and though he sings a hymn, he nevertheless drives many who observe his evil deeds into blasphemy. [Col. 0925B] [Alcuin, Augustine.] Therefore, if you wish to bless God, do his word; do his will. Hence in Leviticus the mouth of the turtledove is commanded to be bent back toward its wings (Lev. 1), so that what it has in its mouth it may show in its work. And do not boast, you who do his will, because it is not your work but God’s. For he himself works what is good through you and in you.

**Verse 22.**—“Bless the Lord, all his works; in every place of his dominion, bless the Lord, O my soul.”

“Bless the Lord, all his works.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] When you live well, all his works bless him. Or, “all [his] works,” that is, things heavenly and earthly. Bless him, I say, “in every place of his dominion”; or, his dominions are in every place. Thus where he does not rule, [Col. 0925C] there he is not blessed. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] He is everywhere; let him be blessed everywhere. No one is excused. Therefore, as no creature is excepted, so no place is excepted from praise. “Bless the Lord, O my soul.” Where he began, there he ends: blessing at the beginning, blessing at the end. We set out from blessing; let us return to blessing; let us reign in it. By this he indicates those who add a good end to good beginnings.

## 223 Comparison on Psalm 102: “Bless the Lord, O My Soul, and All,” etc.

**Verse 5.**—“Who satisfies your desire with good things.” Nearly all recent translators render “your mouth” in place of “your desire.” Yet the translator for Campensis has, with us, “your desire.” It is clear, however, that “to fill the mouth with good things” is a metaphorical expression and is more rightly applied to nothing than to desire. Jerome translated “your adornment.” For this too is the meaning of the Hebrew *ʿedyekh* (“your ornament”). But our mind is adorned with no ornaments if good desires are lacking.

“Performing mercies.” In Hebrew, *tsedaqot*, which they translate “righteous acts.” It also means almsgiving. Hence the Greek here reads ποιῶν ἐλεημοσύνας (*poiōn eleēmosynas*), “performing acts of mercy.” Add that [Col. 0926B] “performing judgment for all who suffer injustice,” the clause immediately appended, is mercy toward the godly and justice toward the ungodly.

**Verse 15.**—“The spirit shall pass through him.” Jerome, Nebiensis, Pratensis, and the interpreters for Cajetan, together with the Septuagint, say “spirit,” as in the Hebrew *ruaḥ*. Others translate: “the wind passes over it,” referring this to the flower mentioned in the preceding verse. But Catholic interpreters understand it of the soul, although it is known that *ruaḥ* among the Hebrews means both “soul” and “wind,” just as Latin *spiritus* and Greek πνεῦμα (*pneuma*) do.

“And he shall no longer know his place.” In Hebrew the order is reversed: “and his place shall no longer know him.” It is utterly certain that וְלֹא־יַכִּירֶנּוּ עוֹד מְקוֹמוֹ (*ve-lo yakirennu ʿod meqomo*) cannot attribute understanding to the place itself except figuratively. Therefore, if the place no longer knows the spirit, this means that the spirit, separated from the body, will not return again [Col. 0926C] to that corruptible body so as to live again according to this present state of the world. The sense of the statement expressed in reverse order is, however, plain when stated directly. Sanctes also sets down a rule in Book IV of his *Hebrew Institutions*: in Scripture words are often understood in the reverse sense. He gives an example from the following psalm: “The waters shall stand above the mountains,” that is, “the mountains shall stand above the waters.”

## Psalm 103

[Col. 0925]

### Title of the Psalm

[Note: [Col. 0925D] Ἀνεπίγραφος παρ’ Ἑβραίοις (*Anepígraphos par’ Hebraíois*): “Without a title among the Hebrews.”]

“A Psalm of David.”

[Col. 0925C]

“Bless the Lord, O my soul.” Title: “A Psalm of David.” It is clear. [Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] In this psalm likewise, as in the preceding one, he exhorts us to bless God. [Col. 0925D] For here he treats of God’s praises, taking the material for praise from his works: namely heaven and earth and their adornment, with which this psalm deals. The whole, however, is woven together with figures of things and mysteries. [Augustine.] Although nearly everything here can reverently be understood literally, it is nonetheless full of mysteries even in its literal sense. From the visible works spoken of here, the invisible things of God must be understood; just as, from the greatness and beauty of the structure of the world, the inestimable greatness and beauty of its Maker may be discerned and loved, so that he may at last be seen. Yet in all things the spiritual sense must be sought and examined.

Intention. [Cassiodorus.] He exhorts to praise. Method. The psalm has three parts. First, he exhorts us to bless God through heaven and earth and all their adornment. Second, he says how God brings the Church through the sea of this world to the harbour of life, at “This sea.” Third, he promises that he will always sing to the Lord, at “I will sing [Col. 0926D] to the Lord.” [Augustine.] Therefore the Prophet, about to recount the mighty deeds of God which he had conceived in his mind, pours forth in the exultation of that vision, saying: “O—”

**Verse 1.**—“Bless the Lord, O my soul; O Lord my God, you have been exceedingly magnified.”

“My soul, bless the Lord” for the great benefits and gifts recounted here. “O Lord God, you have been magnified.” He sets forth the magnificent matters he will speak of: that is, he declares here that God is magnificent, later to say in what respects he is magnificent. In all these matters, none but their author is properly to be praised. Addressing God himself, he gives the reason why he is to be blessed. As though he said: Therefore you are to be blessed, because, O Lord God—God in the proper sense, and my God—you are great by nature. “You have been exceedingly magnified” in my knowledge. You have been magnified, though always great in yourself, unable to increase or diminish because you are perfect. By this, namely:

**Verse 2.**—“You have put on confession and beauty, clothed with light as with a garment.”

“You have put on confession and beauty.” [Augustine.] For by this it is known that he is great. In a human being he is magnified through knowledge, though in himself he is unchangeably great, and his greatness neither began nor ends. The sense is: “You have put on confession and beauty, clothed with light as with a garment”: that is, you are surrounded on every side by creatures that confess you—[Haymo, Alcuin] that is, praise you—and that are beautiful and full of light. [Col. 0927B]

Or thus: let confession be understood, as above, in works; but beauty in essence. Thus: “You have put on confession,” that is, the praise of creatures, “and beauty,” which is ineffable in essence. “And you are clothed with light as with a garment”: that is, light surrounds you on every side, you who dwell in inaccessible light (1 Tim. 6), which no one can approach by himself.

Or he signifies the Incarnation when he says, “You have put on confession and beauty”: [Cassiodorus] that is, you assumed flesh, through which confession—that is, praise—and the splendour of heavenly majesty were made known. And through this you are “clothed with light as with a garment,” because through the same Incarnation people confessed him, and they are light through knowledge.

[Augustine.] Or thus: “You have put on confession and beauty,” that is, the Church, in which first comes confession of sins and afterward the beauty of virtues, that she may please the Bridegroom: that is, first there is in her confession of sins, by which she lays aside ugliness; then comes the beauty of virtues, by which she is “fairer in form than the children of men” (Ps. 44). [Col. 0927C] “And you are clothed with light as with a garment”: that is, with the Church. For she is the garment without spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5). [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] She is the seamless tunic that could not be divided (John 19). She too is light in the Lord, although formerly darkness (Eph. 5).

**Verse 3.**—“Stretching out the heaven like a skin; who covers its upper parts with waters.”

“Stretching out.” [Alcuin.] This is first understood literally. As though he said: The heaven, the earth, and the sea, with all their adornment, confess you; he subsequently treats of each of these individually [Col. 0927D], beginning with heaven, saying: You are he who stretches out the heaven. [Augustine.] Literally, God stretched out heaven as the roof, as it were, of the world; for he made the firmament broad, that it might cover the circle of the earth. He did this as a skin—that is, not by any labor, as you, O man, stretch out your roof, but as easily as someone might stretch out a skin. Yet when he says, “as a skin,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] he indicates that it too is a covering for all things, surrounding everything.

It may also be read mystically, and it depends on the statement made above that he clothed himself with the Church. As though he said: He clothed himself with the Church; but how did he do this, that he might clothe himself with her? Addressing his speech to him, he explains: You are he who stretches out the heaven as a skin. By figurative mysteries he explains how the Church was made light, without spot or wrinkle. For by “heaven” [Col. 0928A] Sacred Scripture is understood. By the skin stripped from dead animals is understood the mortality of preachers. Hence our first parents, Adam and Eve, after their transgression and becoming mortal, were clothed with garments of skins (Gen. 3).

Yet the Word of God is eternal, and is God with God. And because the world did not know God in the wisdom of God, through the foolishness of preaching—that is, through mortal preachers, who appeared foolish—God saves those who believe (1 Cor. 1), and causes the immortal Word to be known in mortal man. Preachers are fittingly compared with skins also because, just as skins are of greater use after the animals have died, so the Word of God became known not only through preachers but even more after them. For the prophets and apostles have died; what they said before still stands now. The discourse [Col. 0928B] of those dead men is stretched out, because after death they themselves became better known. For living prophets are possessed by Judea alone; dead ones by all nations, to whom their discourse is extended, so that we may read in it—afterward it will be folded up as a book.

The sense is: How did you bring it about that you might clothe yourself? Behold, you are he who stretches out heaven, that is, Sacred Scripture, so that it may cover the whole world and that through it the eternal Word of God may be known. I say, “stretching it out as a skin,” that is, through mortal preachers. For the Word of God, which was everywhere but the world did not know him (John 1), began to be known through mortals and became better known after them.

“You who cover,” or protect, “its upper parts with waters.” This too is well understood literally. For there are waters above the firmament, divided from the waters beneath it, which soak the earth [Col. 0928C].

Mystically, the upper part of Sacred Scripture, which we called heaven above, is charity: it is the more excellent way, as the Apostle says: “I show you a still more excellent way. If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 12–13). The waters are the Holy Spirit. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7). Explaining this, the Evangelist adds: “But this he said concerning the Spirit, which those believing in him were to receive” (ibid.).

Therefore the upper parts are covered with these waters: that is, through that Spirit charity is possessed; but it is not covered in others except the good. Hence in Proverbs: “Let your waters run abroad in your streets, and let no stranger share with you” (Prov. 7). [Col. 0928D] And because no stranger shares in it, or in the Spirit, with the good, as happens in baptism and the other gifts or sacraments. But strangers are all those who hear: “I do not know you” (Matt. 7). The sense is: You cover, or protect, the upper parts of Scripture with waters—that is, by giving charity through the Holy Spirit to the good; charity is concealed from the wicked.

Or, by “upper parts” are understood the two commandments of charity; by “waters,” the Holy Spirit, or charity itself. Note that what protects is sometimes supported by something else and burdens it, as a roof is supported by walls. Sometimes it is not supported or burdened by what it covers, but itself lifts it up. This is the sense here when he says: “You who protect,” that is, lift up, “its upper parts,” namely, those of Scripture, that is, the two commandments of charity, “with waters,” that is, with charity or the divine [Col. 0929A] Spirit, by which things that otherwise would be difficult become easy. For God protects and lifts up by the divine Spirit or by charity the heaven of Scripture, whose upper parts are the two commandments of charity.

[Alcuin.] Or thus: “You who cover its upper parts with waters,” that is, its surface with the spiritual sense. Or, by waters the gifts are understood, and by upper parts charity. Thus: “You who cover its upper parts with waters,” that is, you strengthen their charity by spiritual gifts, so that nothing may be able to separate them from it.

### Verse 4.—“Who makes the clouds your ascent; who walks upon the wings of the winds.”

“Who makes the clouds your ascent.” [Augustine.] This too is rightly understood both literally and mystically. For Christ ascended in a cloud; likewise the saints shall be caught up in clouds [Col. 0929B] to meet the Lord (1 Thess. 4). Thus also spiritually one ascends into the heaven of Scripture through preachers, when through them it is explained to those who do not understand. Scripture has been spread out, nor are clouds lacking to lead into it.

“He who walks upon the wings of the winds”: literally, wind is the movement of air, whose swiftness is signified by wings; but God surpasses this swiftness, being present everywhere. Hence: “His word runs swiftly” (Ps. 147), quickly accomplishing whatever he wills. Mystically, winds are souls; wings are virtues, which are contained in the two wings, that is, in the two commandments of charity. But the charity of Christ surpasses the charity of all; and the meaning is: “You walk upon the wings of the winds,” that is, you surpass the swiftness of the saints’ knowledge or charity.

[Col. 0929C] 224  
### Verse 5.—“Who makes your angels spirits, and your ministers a burning fire.”

“Who makes your angels spirits.” [Augustine.] Angel is the name of an office; spirit, of a nature. For in respect of what he is, he is a spirit; in respect of what he does, he is an angel. He says therefore: “You make your angels spirits.” For he makes angels spirits in substance when he sends them. [Alcuin.] “And you make your ministers a burning fire,” [Augustine] that is, so that they may be burning fire, as in the bush (Exod. 3); and in other cases he made them fulfill whatever mystery he willed.

Or, “a burning fire,” that is, the seraphim, who are the highest order, you make your ministers. Hence in Isaiah: “One of the seraphim flew to me” (Isa. 6); they are the highest order. Thus also, mystically, in the Church he makes spiritual men messengers [Col. 0929D] of his Word and, as it were, sends them down to earth to speak to carnal people, where they judge themselves to know nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2). And those who are fervent in spirit are ministers who set others aflame with the fire of charity and consume the hay of vices.

### Verse 6.—“Who founded the earth upon its stability; it shall not be moved for ever and ever.”

“Who founded the earth upon its stability.” [Augustine.] Perhaps literally there is some firmness unknown to us upon which the earth is established; but what follows cannot be said literally by God, namely, “it shall not be moved for ever and ever,” since the earth is read to be destined to pass away. Therefore the Holy Spirit [Col. 0930A] speaks in this psalm of things difficult according to the letter, so that we may seek spiritual meanings.

Spiritually, however, the Church is founded upon Christ, and it cannot be moved. For this cannot be said by God of the literal earth, which is read to be destined to pass away. The meaning is: You founded the earth, that is, the Church, upon its stability, that is, Christ. Therefore it shall not be moved for ever and ever.

### Verse 7.—“The abyss is its garment, its covering; waters shall stand above the mountains.”

“The abyss.” [Note: [Col. 0929D] From Augustine, second sermon on the Psalm.] This is first understood literally, thus: As though he said: The earth shall not be moved, although the abyss is the earth’s covering like a garment. All water spread abroad through seas, rivers, and hidden caverns is called the abyss. It surrounds the earth as a garment, and at the time of the Flood [Col. 0930B] it rose so greatly that it even covered the mountains. Hence he adds: “The waters shall stand above the mountains.” But—

### Verse 8.—“At your rebuke they shall flee; at the voice of your thunder they shall be afraid.”

“At your rebuke the waters shall flee, and at the voice of your thunder they shall be afraid” [Alcuin, Augustine], because through terrible winds they will be dried up. But because he says “they shall stand,” not “they stood,” as is usually said of past events, he announces not past things but future ones. In the Scriptures the past tense is often put for the future; but to speak of past things as a figure of the future is not easily encountered.

Mystically, he treats of the flood of persecutions which surrounds the Church like an abyss. The meaning is: The Church shall not be moved for ever and ever, although the abyss of persecutions is its covering like a garment; and even over [Col. 0930C] the mountains the waters of persecutions shall stand. For this flood of persecutions even overwhelmed the mountains. The apostles lay hidden in flight, as though beneath the waters. But this will not last long, because at your rebuke, O Lord, the waters of persecutors shall flee from pressing upon the mountains; and at the voice of your thunder—that is, at the voice of God given through the apostles, through the clouds, through the Scriptures—the waters shall be afraid. For the wicked will fear the threat of judgment.

### Verse 9.—“The mountains rise and the plains descend, to the place which you founded for them.”

“The mountains rise.” [Augustine.] This must first be continued concerning the persecutions of the Church. As though he said: Truly the abyss of tribulations surrounds the Church, because mountains—not earthly mountains, but the great waves of tribulations, like mountains—[Col. 0930D] rise. They rise like mountains when the waves rage, and descend like plains when they are calmed. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] For God permits the proud to grow when he wills, and humbles them when he wills, in fitting dispensation.

They descend, I say, to the place which you founded for them. For he founded a place for them. There is a certain fear, like a deep place, into which the hearts of the wicked have somehow been received; that is, he has restrained them by a certain fear. The hearts of servants are wicked, but are quieted. And—

### Verse 10.—“You have set a boundary which they shall not pass; neither shall they return to cover the earth.”

[Col. 0931A] “A boundary,” [Augustine] that is, an end, “you have set, which they shall not pass.” For they cannot pass beyond the end imposed upon them. “Neither shall they return,” that is, come back, “to cover the earth,” that is, the Church. Although light waves still rush upon it, they do not cover the earth of the Church with a flood, so that the Church may now freely preach. For although pagans still make a loud noise and murmur, I hear the sound of the shores; I do not dread the flood.

[Cassiodorus.] Or it may be read literally: as though the waters of the Flood had ceased through terrible winds. When these have ceased, mountains rise and plains descend; that is, the height of mountains and the levelness of plains, which previously lay hidden beneath the waters, appear. Or, they appeared in the place—or, to the place—which you founded, literally, that is, suitably [Col. 0931B] arranged, where he disposed, or you disposed, concerning each thing. Likewise he did, or you did, concerning the waters of the Flood, so that the earth is neither submerged by them nor henceforth needs them. Hence he adds: “You have set a boundary for the waters.” This concerns the waters of the Flood: a boundary which the waters shall not pass, neither shall they return—that is, come back—to cover the earth.

Or otherwise: [Haymo, Gloss.] We take “mountains” in a good sense, as above, namely, as the apostles and other prelates of the Church; “plains” are their subjects. As though he said: The waters of persecutions, which formerly covered the mountains, shall be afraid; when they flee, the mountains stand out for the salvation of the peoples. This is: “The mountains rise,” that is, the prelates have been exalted in free leadership; “and the plains descend,” that is, the subjects in voluntary submission. Both these and those are in the place which you founded [Col. 0931C] for them, that is, they act according to the gifts which you bestowed upon them; for he gave some as prophets, others as evangelists, and so forth (Eph. 4). “You have set a boundary for the waters which they shall not pass, neither shall they return to cover the earth.”

[Alcuin.] This may be understood not only of the persecutions of the Church, but also of the snares of the Gentiles, which were ended at Christ’s coming so that they might no longer occupy the world.

### Verse 11.—“You send forth springs in the valleys; waters shall pass through the midst of the mountains.”

“You send forth.” [Gloss.] From this point the mystical meaning must be pursued. As though he said: The earth, that is, the Church, has been stripped bare of the waters of persecutions or of Gentile rites. [Augustine.] What, then, is in the cleansed earth? Behold [Col. 0931D] you are he who sends forth springs of living water leaping up into eternal life (John 4), that is, of the Holy Spirit, “in the valleys,” that is, in the humble, who are called mountains because of spiritual loftiness, and valleys because of the humility of their spirit.

The meaning concerning those humble persons subject to grace is: Though they are mountains by spiritual loftiness, the springs of the Holy Spirit flow in them, for he rests upon the humble and meek (Isa. 66). “And the waters shall pass through the midst of the mountains.” By waters are understood preachings, or the very preachers, of the Word of God, who pass through the midst of the mountains, that is, through the midst of the apostles.

Note that he says “through the midst”: “middle” is called common, that which belongs equally to all and is not the special possession of anyone. Hence it is said of some people: [Col. 0932A] “They have peace among themselves” (1 Cor. 19 [an uncertain citation]), and the like—that is, it is in their midst, it is common to them. Thus the water of God, that is, doctrine, is not someone’s own or private possession, but public. Otherwise preaching is neither peaceful nor safe. Let truth not be mine or yours, but let us think the same thing, and let there be no schisms among you (1 Cor. 10 [an uncertain citation]). Hence the Apostle: “Whether I or they, so we preach, and so you believed” (2 Thess. 3 [an uncertain citation]). And elsewhere: “May the God,” he says, “of peace grant us to think and speak the same thing” (Phil. 4 [an uncertain citation]), and that you all think the same thing and that there be no schisms among us.

Therefore let none of the waters disagree with the mountains. If anyone says otherwise, he speaks from what is his own, not from the common middle. Such a mountain is not to be heard, because he departs from the waters running through the midst and strives to pour in something private. [Gloss.] The waters, [Col. 0932B] that is, doctrines, shall pass through, because they do not remain; prophecy shall cease in the future.

[Haymo, Augustine.] Or, the waters—that is, the preachers of God’s Word—shall pass from nation to nation in preaching. I say, waters running through the midst, that is, the common possession of the mountains, namely the exalted preachers, who, with respect to themselves, are valleys. Therefore he says, “through the midst of the mountains,” because the people’s faith is certain in that which the apostles held in common.

[Cassiodorus.] Or the mountains are heretics, among whom the waters, that is, the Scriptures, are rightly said to pass through, because they flow downward and do not make them fruitful, but pass away from them.

### Verse 12.—“All the beasts of the field shall drink; the wild asses shall await them in their thirst.”

“They shall drink.” [Augustine.] As though he said: The waters shall pass [Col. 0932C] through the midst of the mountains, and all the beasts of the field, or forest—that is, the nations, understood under the figure of beasts—shall drink these waters. This is evident from Noah’s ark, in which all animals were present; it figures the Church, in the unity of whose structure all nations are gathered.

Likewise all were present in Peter’s sheet, lowered to him three times by four lines; he bears the person of preachers.
