For a vessel was lowered from heaven to Peter by four lines, in which were animals of every kind; and a voice sounded to him: “Arise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts 10). Peter kills them all in what is evil in them, and eats them by transferring them into the body of the Church. It was lowered by four lines as a figure of the four parts of the world in which the Gospel was to be preached; [Col. 0932D] and it was lowered three times for people to be baptized, so that baptism might take place in the name of the Trinity.

From the ternary and quaternary, therefore, the number twelve is formed, which is the number of preachers. For twelve apostles, chosen by the Lord, were gathered, and by their preaching the whole world—whose four regions are called in the name of the Trinity—is summoned, that the Church may be assembled. For all were in the ark, all in the sheet; Peter kills and eats all; all drink the water flowing through the midst of the mountains. The wild asses shall await, or receive, this water. Wild asses are wild donkeys, by which are signified the great untamed persons from among the Gentiles, who are without the yoke of the Law; but even these wild ones shall drink these waters together with the timid.

The wild ass with the hare, the great with the small—who are signified [Col. 0933A] by the beasts, just as the great are signified by wild asses. Both, however, are understood to be from among the Gentiles. They shall drink, I say, or receive, “in their thirst,” because one has a greater capacity than another, another less; for “in their thirst” means according to each one’s thirst, each receives. This water is tempered for all; it frightens no one, like the sound of Tully’s voice and the din of philosophers.

[Cassiodorus.] Or, the beasts are all Gentiles, great and small; but the wild asses are proud Jews. The meaning is: “The wild asses shall await,” that is, the Jews, “in their thirst,” to drink these waters, because proud Jews defer drinking until the last time.

### Verse 13.—“Above them the birds of heaven shall dwell; from the midst of the rocks they shall give forth their voices.”

“Above those things which have been mentioned,” that is, the springs of the valleys [Col. 0933B] and the like. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Or, another reading has “above them,” that is, above the mountains: “the birds of heaven shall dwell.” Literally, not all birds dwell in the mountains; but by them are signified spiritual men, who dwell not in their own hearts but in the mountains, that is, in the authority of prophets and apostles.

These are the birds of sacrifice which Abraham did not divide. For it is read in Genesis that Abraham in his sacrifice took a three-year-old ram, a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old goat, a turtledove, and a dove (Gen. 15). He divided the ram, heifer, and goat, and set the parts opposite one another; but he did not divide the birds, and Abraham sat there until evening. Then a furnace and terror came, and it passed between the divided animals, placing [Col. 0933C] these on the right and those on the left.

Mystically, the ram, leader of the flock, signifies the prelates of the Church; the heifer and goat signify subjects. The heifer signifies Jews because of the yoke of the Law; the goat, Gentiles, who wandered freely and fed on the bitter wild olive of idolatry. The birds signify spiritual men, who enjoy the free air and rejoice in the serenity of heaven. Their age is not specified there, because the saints, meditating on eternity, pass beyond all temporal things in their minds. These birds were not divided, because the saints alone are not divided into heresies and schisms.

The ram signifying rulers, the heifer signifying Jews under the yoke of the Law, and the goat signifying Gentiles were three-year-old, because grace was revealed in the third age. These were divided, and their parts were set against one another, because all these are divided against one another through heresies [Col. 0933D] and schisms. But among spiritual people there is peace, and so far as they can, they preserve it among others. At evening, that is, at the end of the age, the furnace comes, and terror—that is, the day of judgment—and the furnace passes between the divided creatures, placing these on the right and those on the left.

Thus also, among the divided carnal members of the Church, whether rulers or subjects, the wood, hay, and straw are burned. Yet they themselves, because of the foundation before which they placed nothing, will be saved as through fire; but others who have destroyed the foundations will be placed on the left and condemned. This is the meaning: “Above them,” or “above those,” that is, above the mountains, namely prophets and apostles, “the birds of heaven,” that is, spiritual hearts, shall dwell. He added “of heaven” to indicate the saints, because there they find rocks, that is, the firm foundation [Col. 0934A] of the commandments.

For just as that one rock, Christ, is the Word of God, so the many words of God are many rocks; and these rocks are in the mountains. Whoever therefore wishes to be spiritual should dwell there and not wander in his own heart. But lest you think that these birds follow their own authority, “they shall give forth voices from the midst of the rocks,” that is, not from their own authority, but from the authority of the words of God, in which Christ the Rock sounds forth; from him his own are also called rocks. And as though someone asked, “Whence do the mountains and rocks themselves have this?” he adds: He is—

### Verse 14.—“Watering the mountains from your upper chambers; the earth shall be filled with the fruit of your works.”

“Watering the mountains,” [Augustine, Haymo, Gloss] that is, the apostles and prophets, “from your upper chambers,” that is, from your higher hidden mysteries, not from other rocks. Or thus the connection runs: “You send forth springs in the valleys. You, I say, watering the mountains from your upper chambers,” according to another reading. The meaning does not change, except that it speaks in the second person.

Or according to the other reading, which is, “watering,” etc.: As though he said, You send forth springs, and when you do the things mentioned above, you also water the mountains from their upper parts, that is, from the mountains higher than themselves, from those things that are higher than the mountains themselves. [Augustine, Haymo, Augustine.] From those mountains grace also descends even to the earth. Hence: “With the fruit of your works”—that is, with the works which you accomplish in all, for they are not human works—“the earth,” that is, the converts, shall be satisfied. [Col. 0934C] Therefore let no one boast in his own works, but “he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10). For the earth is filled by the grace of God; let it not therefore say that grace was given to it for its own merits. If grace is given, it is given freely; if it is rendered for works, a wage is rendered. Therefore you receive freely, because you, an ungodly person, are justified.

### Verse 15.—“Bringing forth grass for cattle, and herb for the service of men.”

“Bringing forth grass.” [Gloss.] This can be referred either to God or to the earth. To God, thus: “From the fruit of your works, O God, you who bring forth grass for cattle.” But it is referred to the earth thus: “The earth shall be filled.” [Augustine.] The earth, I say, brings forth grass, that is, temporal goods, for cattle, that is, for preachers, so that those who proclaim the Gospel may live by the Gospel (1 Cor. 9). [Col. 0934D] Unless the earth brings forth grass, that is, temporal goods, it is not watered but barren. If it does this, that itself is fruit.

He then explains what he had said: “And bringing forth herb,” that is, temporal goods, “for the service of men,” that is, for preachers, servants of men for Christ’s sake. Hence the Apostle: “Though I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all” (1 Cor. 9). This service arises from charity, which makes men humble—such as the apostles were not when the Lord said to them: “You shall indeed drink my cup; but to sit at my right hand is not mine to give to you” (Matt. 20), that is, not to the proud men you now are, but to the humble, who for Christ’s sake become servants of men and devote themselves to the benefit of their brethren.

These are the cattle to whom grass is owed as wages, because they serve. Of them it is said: “You shall not muzzle the ox when it treads out the grain” [Col. 0935A] (Deut. 25), and: “The laborer is worthy of his wage” (Matt. 10). Temporal goods are owed to preachers who distribute spiritual goods. Hence the Apostle: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. 9). Of them it is said: “Blessed is he who anticipates the voice of one who will ask,” that is, who understands the needy and poor person (Ps. 40).

For you ought not deal with an ox treading grain as with a passing beggar. To the latter, that is, to a beggar, you give because it is written: “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke 6). But to the latter you ought to give even when he does not ask. See, therefore, that a soldier of Christ does not become so needy that he must ask you and thereby judge—that is, show you to be blameworthy—before he asks. For just as it is said concerning one who seeks you, “Give to everyone who asks,” so concerning that preacher whom you ought to seek, it is said: “Let almsgiving sweat in your hand until you find a righteous man to whom you may give” (Ecclus. 24 [uncertain citation]).

Therefore give to everyone who asks, whoever he may be, recognizing in him the one to whom you give. But give much more to the servant of God, the soldier of Christ, even if he does not ask. Thus the Lord also had, or kept, a money bag (John 12), for the use of those who were with him—both his own companions and devout women in the company who ministered to him from their substance (Mark 15). In these matters he chiefly assumed the person of the weak; for he foresaw that many weak persons would be in his company and would seek such things. Thus he also assumed their person where he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26), although Paul sought no such things from his own people and desired to die.

Yet Christ acted more sublimely because more mercifully: lest he condemn the weak who would seek such things, he gave them an example of receiving necessities from those subject to them. For the earth to bring forth herb for the service of men, to what end is this necessary?

### Verse 16.—“That it may bring bread forth from the earth, and that wine may gladden the heart of man.”

“That the earth itself may bring forth bread.” [Augustine.] That is, Christ from the earth, namely, from the stewards of truth—that is, the apostles and others who still bear an earthly body and still walk upon earth.

Or thus: O God, you are he who brings forth grass for cattle, in order that, through their preaching, you may bring forth bread, that is, Christ, from the earth, that is, from those preached to, who believe and confess through the teaching of their elders. And the earth brings forth wine from the preachers. [Remigius, [Col. 0935D] Haymo, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Or you, O God, bring forth from the earth—that is, from subjects—wine, not wine that confuses a person, but wine that may gladden the heart of man. This wine so intoxicates as to make men sober. This intoxication appears in the mind’s being transported away from earth to heaven. Therefore this is not actual wine, by which some are wickedly intoxicated, but spiritual wine, refreshing the inner person with spiritual joy—that is, Christ.

### Verse 17.—“That he may make the face cheerful with oil, and that bread may strengthen the heart of man.”

“That he may make cheerful.” After he has spoken of the bread and wine which the earth brings forth from preachers, or God from those preached to, he adds also concerning oil. [Augustine.] He shows its effect, saying: “That he may make cheerful,” where it must be understood, as we showed or distinguished above, that the earth may also bring forth oil. Or: You, O God, bring forth grass in order that you may also bring forth oil.

For what end do you bring forth oil? That a person may make his face cheerful, that is, gladden his mind, in oil, that is, in a certain grace of the Holy Spirit by which he becomes pleasing to others. For to each person the Spirit is given, as the Apostle says, for manifestation (2 Cor. 4 [uncertain citation]). This grace is a certain beauty and radiance by which holy affection is won among people; this grace is called oil. It was pre-eminent in Christ, and hence he is praised by all, even by those who say that they cannot follow his commands. He is loved by all and proclaimed by all, because he was supremely anointed. Hence he is called Christ, that is, Anointed One. [Col. 0936B] Behold Christ: wholly anointed in himself and in his members, from whom all the rest receive.

“That the face may be made cheerful with oil, and bread is brought forth.” After stating what wine and oil accomplish, he adds what bread accomplishes, whose effect he had not shown above. As though he said: Wine is brought forth to gladden the heart, and oil to make the face cheerful. Bread is brought forth to strengthen the heart of man. Temporal bread strengthens the stomach and fills the belly; but this is spiritual bread, which strengthens the heart, because it is bread for the heart. This is the bread which came down from heaven (John 6). Therefore the bread and wine are the same: this bread is justice, that wine is justice; truth is Christ. It gladdens and strengthens them always.

### Verse 18.—“The trees of the field and the cedars of Lebanon which he planted shall be filled; there the sparrows shall make their nests.”

“The trees of the field shall be filled.” [Augustine.] Here he shows what becomes of all these things brought forth. As though he said: From the things brought forth from the earth, namely bread, wine, and oil, the trees shall be filled—that is, first the humble peoples; and afterward the cedars of Lebanon, that is, the powerful in this world. For the despised and ignoble were chosen before the wise and noble.

Lebanon means “whitening,” yet these are not other cedars but those which the Lord planted in faith. But why does he leave to those whom he planted the whiteness of the world? Because there, that is, in the cedars, that is, in the powerful of the world, sparrows shall make their nests. These are small birds, by which are understood [Col. 0936D] certain spiritual persons, namely, those poor in this world who left even their little possessions so that, naked, they might follow Jesus—as did the apostles, who left not only whatever they had but also whatever they desired to have. Though possessing nothing, they possess all things. Peter utterly left the whole world and received the whole world.

For the cedars of Lebanon, namely the noble and exalted of this world, hear with fear: “Blessed is he who understands the needy and poor person” (Ps. 40). They attend to their possessions, superfluous estates, and riches, and provide them to the servants of God. Thus they gather the sparrows, so that they may nest in the cedars of Lebanon.

### Verse 19.—“The house of the heron is their leader; the high mountains are for the deer, the rock a refuge for hedgehogs.”

“The heron’s”—[Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine]—“or the coot’s,” according to another reading—“house,” etc. Sparrows build in cedars; and although sparrows nest in the cedars of Lebanon, that is, in the rich of the world, the cedars are nevertheless not above them, because the coot’s house, not the cedar itself, is their leader—the leader of the sparrows, or of those cedars, since that too was stated before. Yet this cannot be said in Latin, because *cedri* is feminine in gender. But this can in no way be said literally. For how is the house, that is, the nest, of the coot—a sea or marsh bird—the leader of sparrows?

By this he indicates that spiritual meanings must be sought. It should be known, therefore, that the coot’s house is a rock in the water, which, beaten by waves, breaks them but is not broken. This house is strong, yet it is not on high. So also our Rock, Christ: having suffered so much from the Jews, he remained whole; nothing is stronger, nothing humbler. The Jews dashed themselves against him and were broken; he remained whole. Behold the coot’s house.

Therefore spiritual persons nest among the cedars, that is, among the wealthy of the world who support them, because of present necessity; but they have Christ the Rock as their leader, imitating his passion. And if perhaps the cedars are shaken, the sparrows will fly away but will not perish, because the coot’s house, that is, Christ the Rock, is the leader of those sparrows.

[Cassiodorus.] Or, as we have said, the coot is a bird that lives in waters. These are those who remain in the grace of baptism, whose house is baptism. The meaning is: As though he said, Who are the cedars? Who are the sparrows? Those who are baptized. Thus, the coot’s house, that is, baptism, which is the house [Col. 0937C] of the regenerated, is the leader of them—the sparrows, that is, Christians—toward heaven.

Or otherwise, according to our text, “the heron’s house.” [Note: [Col. 0937D] From Jerome here and on Zechariah.] The heron is a most rapacious bird, larger than all flying creatures, and it even defeats the eagle. [Alcuin.] By it are understood rapacious persons; but the Lord does not abandon even such persons. The sense is: Although the sparrows nest in cedars, their leader—the leader of the sparrows—is the heron’s house, that is, Christ, who is the house of the most rapacious persons, [Col. 0937D] because he does not abandon even them.

Or otherwise: by the heron, which is a rapacious bird, the tribe of Benjamin may be understood; Paul was from it, and of him it is said: “Benjamin, a ravening wolf: in the morning he shall eat the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoils” (Gen. 49). For Paul persecuted the Church in his youth, and in the evening of his life seized spoils from the devil by preaching. The meaning is: It is no wonder if cedars are planted and sparrows nest, because the house—that is, the race, that is, the generation—of the heron, namely Paul, who was from the tribe of Benjamin and was called a ravening wolf, is the leader of those sparrows and cedars, because after his conversion he converted many others to the faith.

“The high mountains.” [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: The heron’s house is the leader of the sparrows, and the high mountains, that is, the higher commandments of Scripture, are the support of deer. Deer are great spiritual persons, passing in their course beyond all the thorns of the world. These are the high mountains, namely the higher commandments standing out in Scripture: for they think lofty things, hold fast to exalted things, and are justified [Col. 0938A] on the heights.

Or the mountains are the apostles, prophets, and Christ himself, who are the support of deer, that is, of spiritual persons. [Augustine.] But for humble beasts, the Rock—that is, Christ—is a refuge for hedgehogs. Or, according to another reading, for hedgehogs and hares: that is, for timid persons, covered with small and daily sins. The hedgehog is a spiny animal and signifies sinners; the hare is a timid animal and signifies the fearful. Therefore Christ became a refuge for hares and hedgehogs, who cannot hold to lofty things.

This Rock has manifold use. For in the sea this rock is the coot’s house, because Christ amid the fluctuations of the world is the house of those who persevere in the grace of baptism. On earth it is the refuge of the hedgehog and hare, that is, of those who cling by some affection to earthly things [Col. 0938B] and are like the hedgehog and hare. It is a refuge for hedgehogs; on the mountains, that is, among the great and spiritual, it is their support. For this is the Rock from which, as said above, the birds of heaven give forth their voices.

### Verse 20.—“He made the moon for seasons; the sun knew its setting.”

He made the moon, literally. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] After earthly things he passes to heavenly things, which nevertheless serve the earth. And because the historical sense of the letter is plain, let us pursue the allegorical sense. We must therefore know that, after so many classes of Christians, which he signified through kinds of animals, and after the aforesaid ordering of prelates and subjects, he rises higher and adds concerning Christ and the Church: namely, how the Church is here in time [Col. 0938C], and waxes and wanes; and what the rising and setting of the true sun—that is, Christ—accomplish. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As though he said: God ordered the aforesaid things thus. And he himself made the moon, that is, the Church, for times, because it passes through time and will not always be so. Nor is it strange that it passes away; for the sun also, that is, Christ, knew—that is, approved; it pleased him—or knew beforehand, his setting, [Augustine] that is, his Passion, which is aptly compared to the setting of the sun. For the sun so sets as to rise again; thus shall he who sleeps—that is, Christ—not rise again? He set because he willed it; no one takes away his soul. But when he set, darkness arose among the apostles, because their hope failed.

**VERSE 21.**—“You appointed darkness, and night came to be; [Col. 0938D] in it all the beasts of the forest shall pass through.”

You appointed darkness. [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: The sun truly set, because, when it set, you appointed darkness, and night came to be among the apostles, as in Peter, who denied him. Literally also, you appointed darkness at the sixth hour, when the Lord was crucified (Matt. XXVII). And night came to be, that is, obscurity, because that darkness was as dense as night. [Alcuin, Augustine.] Or thus: when the true sun set, you appointed darkness, that is, blindness among the Jews. And night came to be in them, that is, dark obstinacy of mind. And in that night all the beasts of the forest shall pass through. “Beasts of the forest” are not understood here as above. Above, the beasts of the forest [Col. 0939A] are converts; here they are demons, just as Christ is called a lion and the devil a lion (1 Pet. V). [Haymo.] Those whom he had spoken of generally as beasts he finally divides into whelps and lions, saying:

**VERSE 22.**—“The lion’s whelps roaring to seize prey, and to seek food for themselves from God.”

The lion’s whelps shall pass through roaring, that is, raging. [Augustine.] For there are princes of demons, and there are also whelps, that is, contemptible demons, which seek in the darkness to seduce souls. He is the greater lion, who continually goes about seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. V); but they feed upon human errors. For the serpent’s food is earth (Gen. III). [Cassiodorus.] The beasts and whelps, therefore, are demons, who at the time of Christ’s Passion found the hearts of the wavering apostles [Col. 0939B] in order to seize them. [Augustine.] As though he said: They shall indeed pass through for this purpose, that they may seize prey and seek food for themselves from God, because they cannot even tempt unless God permits it.

**VERSE 23.**—“The sun has risen, and they have gathered together, and shall be placed in their dens.”

The sun has risen. [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Having said what the setting of the true sun did, he adds concerning its rising and what that rising itself accomplishes. As though he said: In the night the whelps shall pass through; but when Christ rises again, they cannot prevail over all, or they remain in their dens, that is, in the hearts of the stubborn. And this is what he says: the sun has risen, that is, Christ received back the soul which he had laid down; and the lion’s whelps have gathered together, because they withdraw from persecuting the Church when Christ has been glorified throughout the whole world [Col. 0939C]. For those upon whom the sun has risen are not dared to be attacked by the lions: they have the sign of the tau written upon their foreheads, like those who were delivered by this sign in Ezekiel (Ezek. XIX). [Alcuin.] Note that, just as at Christ’s setting the lion’s whelps pass through and at his rising they gather together, so, when Christ sets in someone through sin, evils prevail; when he rises again in that person through grace, they flee. And they shall be placed in their dens, [Augustine] that is, in the hearts of unbelievers, unless they now make assaults upon the saints.

**VERSE 24.**—“Man shall go out to his work, and to his labour until evening.”

Man shall go out to his work, [Jerome] so that he may begin to work well; and to his labour, so that he may continue [Col. 0939D] by persevering until evening, that is, until the end of the age. For it is now permitted, in the security of peace, to work good; but in the evening, that is, at the end of the world, there will be darkness and a severe assault.

**VERSE 25.**—“How magnified are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom; the earth is filled with your possession.”

How magnified, etc. [Augustine.] Having considered all these things, every believing person exults with great joy, marvels, and cannot express it. Therefore, in wonder, he cries out: Because you have made these aforesaid things, O Lord, your works are magnified—that is, great and many. And, how magnified!—something that cannot be explained. Your works, which in the literal sense were expounded above. Or where were these mystical things made? Whence came these so [Col. 0940A] great things? Behold: you have made all things in wisdom, that is, in Christ. And because they are many, the earth is filled with your possession; or, “your creation,” according to another reading. Literally, through Christ God the Father created whatever is on earth, in the sea, and in heaven (2 Cor. V). But what is said here is better understood mystically of the new creation, which Christ rescued from the old man, and with which he filled the whole earth—that is, the Church. For the grain of wheat falling into the earth bore much fruit (John XII). Before, it was alone until it passed over (Ps. CXL); but when it passed over through the Passion, it found the lost drachma and brought the wandering sheep back to the flock; hence there is joy (Luke XV). Yet there is still pilgrimage; the age is still shaken by the waves of temptations and the storms of tribulations. [Col. 0940B] Therefore he adds:

**PART II. VERSE 26.**—“This great sea, broad of hands; there are creeping things there without number.”

This sea. [Alcuin, Augustine, Haymo.] The second part, in which he says how the Lord leads the Church through the sea of this age to the shore of the homeland. As though he said: The earth is filled with your creation; but we are not yet in the land of the living, where our portion is. Rather, the sea—that is, the age—still has to be crossed. This sea is great and broad for the exercise of hands. [Augustine.] For it is difficult to work there. And there, that is, in that sea, are creeping things, that is, evil spirits, whose snares crawl; they are without number, because innumerable snares creep about in this age and seize the unwary [Col. 0940C] while they are still in these bitter waters.

**VERSE 27.**—“Small animals with great; there ships shall pass through.”

Small animals with great, [Augustine] that is, unbelievers, both small and great. For many rulers of this age and many of its insignificant people have not yet believed. They hate the Church and are constrained by Christ’s name; they do not rage because they are not permitted to do so. Their cruelty does not break out into action, but is shut up in the heart. And though there are so many dangers in this sea, the wood of the cross has nevertheless been given to us, by which we may sail across. This is what follows. Yet, although it is great, there—that is, in that sea—ships, that is, Churches, shall pass through, or travel to and fro. Christ pilots these ships by the wood of the cross. Therefore let Christ keep watch in our heart, [Col. 0940D] and we shall be safe.

**VERSE 28.**—“This dragon, which you formed to be mocked by it; all things await you, that you may give them food in due season.”

This dragon. [Augustine.] Besides these animals there is also in that sea one which surpasses them all: namely, the dragon, who is also called a lion, that is, the ancient serpent who cast down the first parents. The Church crushes his head—that is, his first suggestion—and thus escapes his other movements. He watches her heel, that is, a slipping from the way of God, in order thereby to possess her. Hence in Genesis it is said to the serpent: “I will put enmities between you and the woman” (Gen. II); “she shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel.” [Alcuin.] This dragon is elsewhere [Col. 0941A] called Lucifer, elsewhere Leviathan; made higher than the rest in essence, he became greater in malice. Yet the ships will not fear even this dragon; indeed, they will mock him.

> [Note: [Col. 0941] From Augustine here and in *On Genesis*, book II, chapter 22; and Strabo, as reported in 2 Sentences, distinction 2.]

And the sense is: Besides the other animals, in this sea is this dragon, whom you, O God, formed according to the substance in which he was good, having been placed in the empyrean; but, falling thence through his own fault, he was made here to be mocked—that is, having fallen from heaven, he was made here, in this lower dwelling-place, in order that God’s angels might mock him. For in Job Satan is said to be mocked by God’s angels, who are set over the aerial powers so that they may not harm us (Job XL). “All things”: as though he said, These aforesaid things are in the sea; but all these things—that is, the new creation, the creeping things, the animals, and the dragon—await you, that you may give them food in due season [Col. 0941B], because they can do nothing unless you permit it. What do they await? That you may give them food at a fitting time. [Augustine.] Some interpreters add: The righteous person has his food; the dragon has his food. The dragon’s food is earth, because it was said to him: “You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. III). [Alcuin, Augustine.] For those who love earthly things are the devil’s food. But the food of the righteous is the word of God. Hence: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV). If, therefore, you live well, you will have Christ’s food. But if you depart from Christ, you will be the dragon’s food.

**VERSE 29.**—“When you give to them, they will gather; when you open your hand, all things shall be filled with goodness.”

When you give. [Augustine.] As though he said: They await you to give [Col. 0941C], and when you give to them—or, according to another reading, “when you have given to them,” that is, to the demons—they will gather; before that they cannot gather or even tempt. Then he adds concerning our food. As though he said: When you give, that one will gather; but when you open your hand, etc. The hand is Christ, which is opened when he is revealed. Hence: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII). For revelation is an opening. And when you open him—that is, reveal him—all things will be filled with goodness, which they do not have from themselves. This is sometimes proved to them: namely, that they do not have it from themselves but from you, because, when you turn away, they are troubled. Therefore he adds:

**VERSE 30.**—“But when you turn away your face, they shall be troubled; you shall take away their spirit, and they shall fail; and they shall return to their dust.” 227

[Col. 0941D] But when you turn away your face, they shall be troubled, etc. [Cassiodorus.] Or the hand is God’s power, which abundantly fills all things. Therefore, when you open your hand, that is, your power, all things shall be filled with goodness; but when you turn away your face, they shall be troubled. [Augustine.] Many, filled with God’s goodness, attributed what they possessed to themselves and became pleasing in their own eyes. But God, wishing to prove to them that they possess it not from themselves but from God, sometimes troubles them, turns his face away from them, and they fall into temptation, so that together with goodness they may have humility. Thus he shows them that their righteousness and upright conduct came about through his governance. But why do you trouble them? Behold: through this you will take away [Col. 0942A] their spirit, that is, their pride; and they will utterly fail, so that they may be converted and cry: “My spirit has failed.” And, repenting of sins, they will return to their dust—that is, they will recognize that they are dust. For a person repenting of sin finds himself to be earth; and when their spirit has been taken away—

**VERSE 31.**—“Send forth your spirit, and they shall be created; and you shall renew the face of the earth.”

Send forth—or, “you shall send forth”—your Spirit, [Cassiodorus] that is, the Holy Spirit, who creates people anew. Note that their dust is called their own because they have from themselves that they are dust. But the Spirit of the Lord—behold, the remedy for those returned to dust. [Augustine.] I say: send forth your Spirit. And when he is sent forth, they shall be created in good works. Hence the Apostle: “We are his workmanship, [Col. 0942B] created in good works” (Eph. II). And you shall renew the face of the earth with new people confessing that they are good from you, not from themselves. And because every good thing is from God, therefore—

**VERSE 32.**—“May the glory of the Lord endure for ever; the Lord shall rejoice in his works.”

May the glory of the Lord endure. [Augustine, Gloss, interlinear.] Not merely for a time, but for ever—that is, eternally. And God shall rejoice in his works, not in yours but in his: namely, those which he performs in them. What this reading accomplishes, he adds, namely:

**VERSE 33.**—“He who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble; who touches the mountains and they smoke.”

He looks in mercy upon the earth of the human mind, [Col. 0942C] [Augustine] which exulted in its own goodness and attributed to itself the powers of its own abundance. God looks upon it and makes it tremble. The trembling of humility is better than the confidence of pride. Hence the Apostle: “Work out your salvation with trembling” (Phil. II). For God is he who works all things in us. He himself touches, by compunction or loss of possessions, the mountains—that is, those who had been proud and boasted of themselves—and, touched, they smoke: that is, they offer prayer to God, whereas before they wanted others to petition them and did not petition one greater than themselves. [Augustine.] But now they petition, and the sacrifice of the heart sends up smoke to God. They also begin to weep, because smoke draws forth tears.

**PART III. VERSE 34.**—“I will sing to the Lord in my life; I will make melody to my God as long as I am.”

[Col. 0942D] I will sing to the Lord. [Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which he promises always to sing. [Alcuin.] As though he said: The Lord has done these aforesaid things; and having considered them, I will sing to the Lord—that is, praise the Lord—in my present and future life, in the life of hope and of sight. [Augustine.] For now hope is our life; afterward eternal life will be the life of this mortal life. For hope is of immortal life. Whatever, therefore, it sings, it sings in life. I will make melody to my God as long as I am, because in him I am without end. “As long as,” namely, means without end. He says this lest it be thought that the activity of that life is something other than making melody, since the one who is praised cannot become tiresome: praising him does not become tiresome, but he is always praised and always loved. And so:

**VERSE 35.**—“May my speech be pleasing to him; but I shall delight in the Lord.”

My speech. [Augustine.] By it I make myself known to him who knows me, in order that he may make himself known to me who do not know him. May it be pleasing to him—and indeed it is, because your confession is sweet to God. Another reading has: “My discourse is sweet to him,” with the same sense. For a person’s discourse with God is confession of sins, which is sweet to God. Therefore confess to God what you are; perform good works, and you are in discourse. Hence Isaiah: “Put away evils from your souls; learn to do good; judge for the fatherless; and come, let us reason together, says the Lord” (Isa. IX). Your discourse, therefore, is the sacrifice of your humility, which is pleasing [Col. 0943B] to God. But I. As though he said: This is pleasing to him; what is pleasing to you? Behold: but I shall delight in the Lord. Behold the good exchange. His grace is sweet to you, as yours is to him. I mean your speech: I shall delight in the Lord, and by my example.

**VERSE 36.**—“Sinners shall fail from the earth, and the wicked, so that they are no more; bless the Lord, O my soul.”

Sinners, [Augustine, Gloss, interlinear] namely, those who sin against themselves, should fail from the earth—that is, from sins—so that they may no longer be what they once were. Let their spirit be taken away, that they may be renewed by the Spirit of God. And the wicked, who sin against their neighbours, should likewise fail so that they are no longer the wicked persons they once were. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] This man saw this—that the wicked and sinners fail—and, filled with joy, repeats the beginning, saying: “Bless the Lord, O my soul.” By this he indicates that the end of good things resembles their beginning.

## Collation on Psalm CIII: “Bless the Lord, O my soul; O Lord,” etc.

**VERSE 3.**—For *sicut pellem CAIERIAH* (“like the skin of CAIERIAH”), more recent translators render “like a curtain.” Jerome agrees with the Septuagint. In the end there is no discrepancy, since tents used to be covered with skins because of the inconveniences of the weather.

**VERSES 4 and 5.**—Why the Latins express verses 4 and 5 in the second person, while among the Hebrews and Greeks the pronouns are in the third person, St Jerome explains to Sunia and Fretela as follows:

> “ ‘Who makes your angels spirits’: for this, you say that you have found in Greek, ὅ ποιῶν ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ, that is, ‘he who makes his angels spirits.’ [Col. 0943D] Ask them briefly how, when the address is to God, the Prophet, as though speaking to another, suddenly changes, especially since he begins thus: ‘O Lord, my God, you have been greatly magnified; you have put on confession and beauty; and you cover its upper parts—that is, those of heaven—with waters; you make clouds your ascent; you walk upon the wings of the winds’; and immediately follows: ‘He who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers burning fire; who founded the earth upon its stability.’ And a little later: ‘At your rebuke they shall flee, and at the voice of your thunder they shall be afraid, and in the place which you founded for them.’ ‘You send forth springs in the valleys.’ And: ‘That you may bring bread from the earth.’ If, therefore, all these things are in the second person—that is, addressed to God—how is the third person suddenly introduced in one verse, out of sequence?”

Thus far he. Even if the present Greek copies, insofar as they could be inspected, do not agree in every respect.

**VERSE 11.**—“In the valleys.” Münster and the interpreters for Cajetan render “into rivers”: “who sends forth springs into rivers or streams.” Jerome and the other writers often mentioned stand by the Vulgate reading. For *NEHALIM* is ambiguous.

**VERSE 12.**—“The wild asses shall wait in their thirst.” This shows that the Septuagint read *IESABERU*, a reading indicated by the point placed in the left horn of the letter *shin*: that is, “they shall wait.” Otherwise, *IISCHBERU*: that is, “they shall break” or “quench.” Or, as Jerome rendered it, “they may refresh their thirst.”

**VERSE 13.**—“From the midst of the rocks.” Why the Septuagint changed “foliage” into “rocks,” the mystical sense pursued by Augustine may answer for the devout reader. For Jerome renders, “from the midst of the groves they shall utter a sound,” and the others, “from the midst of the foliage”—renderings which well suit in many ways the songs of the birds, of which the preceding clause spoke. Nor is it otherwise unusual for birds to nest in the holes of rocks and to send forth sounds from there. In Hebrew, indeed, [Col. 0944B] one reads *APHAIM*, which all interpret as branches or foliage, groves, trees, in which birds delight. Jerome in his Commentaries expounds “from the midst of the rocks” as meaning “from the midst of the Churches.” There are now innumerable places in which the Septuagint, by the authority of the Holy Spirit, as is believed, have altered the text far from the Hebrew reading; thus it should not seem surprising when they depart a little, or rather when the sense remains constant, as in this place. We shall offer two examples, in which the Septuagint have nothing in common with the Hebrew.

Jonah III: the Hebrew has, “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.” The Septuagint has, “Yet three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown”—so much so that St Jerome wondered why they had done this. Yet St Augustine, *City of God*, XVIII.44, reconciles them, referring the forty days to the intermediate time between the Resurrection and the Ascension, but the three days to the three-day period of death, taking Nineveh typologically for the Church, overthrown through repentance. Finally [Col. 0944C] he concludes: “I avoid prolixity, lest I demonstrate here at length the many places in which the Septuagint translators are thought to differ from the Hebrew truth, yet, when well understood, are found to agree. Therefore I too, according to my small measure, following in the footsteps of the apostles—for they themselves cited prophetic testimonies from both, that is, from the Hebrews and from the Septuagint—have thought that both authorities should be used, since both are one and divine.”

We shall adduce another example from Isaiah, chapter IX, where the Hebrews say: “At the first time the land of Zebulun was relieved”; the Septuagint has something quite different: “Drink this first; act quickly.” Jerome interprets this as prophetically said of the first sign performed by Christ, namely, the turning of water into wine at Cana of Galilee. Thus he says: “Jesus performed this beginning of signs at Cana of Galilee, and manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him.” Therefore it is also said in the Septuagint: “Drink this first; [Col. 0944D] act quickly,” because the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali were the first to see Christ’s miracles, so that the land which first saw the Lord performing signs might first drink the draught of faith.” Thus Jerome.

**VERSE 18.**—“The trees of the field shall be filled.” In place of “field,” the Hebrew has the tetragrammaton, the name of the Lord. Hence Jerome renders “the trees of the Lord.” Yet Sanctes and Münster interpret it as “magnificent and lofty trees.” And indeed these are found in wooded fields, where they grow tall; moreover, in their own nature they take the singular [name] from the Lord.

**VERSE 19.**—“Of the heron,” *HASIDAH*. Modern translators render “stork.” The Roman edition has “coot,” a sea bird. Augustine and Arnobius retain and interpret this reading. Jerome varies. For in Job XXIX he renders *herodion*: “The ostrich’s wing is like the wings of the heron.” Again, in Leviticus XI, he rendered the same word “heron.” Yet in this place and elsewhere he called it “kite,” so that [Col. 0945A] he seems to have doubted what bird it was. In Zechariah V he reports differing opinions in such a way that he rejects none, but adapts an interpretation to each, concerning the prophet’s words: “They had wings like the wings of a kite” (Zech. V). He says: “They had wings, according to the Hebrew *HASIDAH*, which Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion render ἐρώδιον, that is, ‘heron.’ The Septuagint alone rendered it ἔποπα, that is, ‘hoopoe.’ The Hebrews think *hasidah* is a kite, a most rapacious bird, always lying in wait for domestic birds. Those who have written on the natures of birds, however, maintain that there are three kinds of heron: one white, another speckled, and a third black, which is also very fierce, bloodthirsty, combative, and intolerant of mating, so that blood bursts from their eyes. The hoopoe, which we have adopted from the resemblance of the Greek name—for the Greeks too call it ἔποπα, because it frequents human dung—is said to be a most filthy bird, always dwelling in tombs, always in human excrement.” These things occur there. But [Col. 0945B] Jerome himself, writing to Sunia and Fretela, prefers “kite,” in these words:

> “For ‘heron,’ which in Hebrew is called *HASIDAH*, Symmachus rendered ἰκτῖνον, that is, ‘kite.’ Accordingly, we too rendered it thus 228 in Latin: ‘There birds shall build their nests; the fir tree is the house of kites,’ because it is accustomed always to make its nests in high and lofty trees. Hence the Sixth Edition rendered it more plainly: ‘For the kite, the cypress is for nesting.’ But in place of ‘fir trees’ and ‘cypresses,’ the Hebrew has *BEROSCHIM*, which signifies fir trees more than cypresses.”

Thus Jerome.

**Their leader.** [Jerome and others have “fir trees” in this place, which has nothing in common with “their leader.” However, if you take *BEROSCHIM* such that the letter *beth* is servile and not part of the substance of the word, and write an inserted quiescent *aleph*, without changing the sound of the syllable, thus *BEROSCHAM*, you have “in their leaders”; and accordingly, that the heron’s house is in the leaders of their sparrows means the same as “their leader.”

**High mountains for the deer.** Thus Jerome and Campensis. Others render, instead of “deer,” “fallow deer,” “roe deer,” or “ibexes.” *IEELIM* are wild goats. The Septuagint has ἐλάφοις, “deer”; approaching them would not be dangerous.

**For the hedgehogs.** Or, as others wish, “for rabbits”; others, “for hares.” Jerome writes of this to Sunia [Col. 0946B] and Fretela as follows:

> “In the Hebrew stands *SCHEPANNIM*, and all have rendered it by the similar word χοιρογυλίους. The Septuagint alone rendered ‘hares,’ τοῖς λαγωοῖς: that is, ‘the rock is a refuge for hares.’ But it must be known that this is an animal no larger than a hedgehog, resembling a mouse and a bear. Hence in Palestine it is called ἀρκτόμυς, ‘bear-mouse.’ There is great abundance of this kind in those regions, and they are always accustomed to dwell in caves of rocks and hollows of the ground.”

Thus far Jerome.

# PSALM CIV

[Col. 0945]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “ALLELUIA.”

[Col. 0945B]

Give thanks to the Lord. Title: Alleluia. [Cassiodorus.] Here, for the first time, the word “Alleluia” is found; it had not previously been used by any Hebrew writer, and no language has presumed to alter it, just as with “Amen” in the Gospel. It is interpreted, however, “Praise God.”

> [Note: [Col. 0945] From Jerome, in the Letter to Marcella on the Ten Names of God.]

For *alleluia* means “praise,” while *jah* is the name of the invisible God—that is, it signifies the Invisible One, a name appropriate to him alone. This title is prefixed to twenty psalms, all of which speak of God’s mighty works. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] Great exultation is in them, as in this psalm God’s benefits bestowed upon the spiritual seed of Abraham are recounted. For here the Prophet commends the good people in that Israel, who, together with other faithful people, are the true seed of Abraham, children of promise. [Augustine.] This, therefore, is the first psalm bearing the heading *Alleluia*. And its sense is: “Alleluia,” that is, “Praise God.” Hence the psalm also begins thus.

> [Note: [Col. 0945] From Augustine, at the end of the psalm and in the recapitulation.]

[Col. 0945D] **Purpose:** He exhorts to praise. **Method:** There are six divisions. Augustine divides this psalm in this manner, and Cassiodorus agrees with him, except that he makes the sixth division in a different place from Augustine. This will be shown in its place in the exposition of the psalm. First, so that you may see the inward understanding in the outward words, he exhorts, as it were, the soul within the body—the seed of Abraham, that is, the children of promise, belonging to the inheritance of the eternal covenant—to choose God himself as their inheritance and worship him freely, not for something external to him. They are to do this by praising, invoking, and proclaiming; by working well through faith, not in their own glory but in his [Col. 0946B]; by rejoicing in hope and being fervent in charity. The whole psalm expresses this, in the words, “Give thanks,” etc., down to “Remember his wonderful works,” where the division occurs, which we shall also pursue elsewhere in its proper places. Therefore the Prophet, beginning with the praise announced by the title, says:

**VERSE 1.**—“Give thanks to the Lord, and call upon his name; declare his works among the nations.”

Give thanks to the Lord, [Augustine, Gloss, interlinear, Augustine] that is, praise God, which is done by one who loves. “For praise is not becoming in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. XV). Praise having been offered first, invocation follows, that one may ask for what is desired: “and call upon his name,” because one who praises is heard. This is the fitting order: praise first, invocation afterward. Hence elsewhere: “We will give thanks to you, O God, we will give thanks, and we will call upon your name” (Ps. LXXIV). And elsewhere: “Praising, I will call upon the Lord” (Ps. XVII). In the Lord’s Prayer a brief winning of favour is promised: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. VI); afterward [Col. 0946D] the petitions follow. Then he adds: “Declare his works among the nations,” because love for the Lord is shown especially in feeding his sheep. Thus the Lord said to Peter: “Simon, do you love me?” And when he answered, “Lord, you know that I love you,” he said: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI).

**VERSE 2.**—“Sing to him; make melody to him; recount all his wonders.”

Sing to him with words, [Augustine] because one sings with the mouth; and make melody to him, that is, praise him in works, because one makes melody with the hands. Then he gives two further expressions corresponding to these two. For in regard to “Sing,” he adds, as though determining how they should sing, “Recount all his wonders.” Nothing should be kept silent through shame. Or he says this because everything that they say of him is wondrous. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] For no one can recount them all. Then he adds what he had said, “Make melody,” as is set forth in what follows.

**VERSE 3.**—“Be praised in his holy name; let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice.”

Be praised. [Augustine, Gloss, interlinear.] As though he said: Make melody in this manner: praise—that is, work—in such a way that you are praised, as those who work well may deservedly be. And this, “in his holy name,” is added lest a person glory in himself for a good work, but in the Lord. [For he does not forbid their being praised if they are good, but only being praised except in the Lord, who makes them good, to whom they ought to ascribe every good thing [Col. 0947B] and whose glory they ought to seek in all things. This is what is said elsewhere: “My soul shall be praised in the Lord” (Ps. XXXIII). And what is added there: “Let the meek hear and rejoice.” Here too he seems in some manner to add the same thing, saying: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice,” etc.] [Jerome.] Or thus: “Be praised in his holy name,” that is, rejoice to be called Christians after Christ. And let the heart rejoice, [Haymo, Augustine, Jerome] even if not the body, of those who seek the Lord, who emulate those who work well. And if the heart of those seeking the Lord rejoices, how much more that of those who find him? Therefore, while you work:

**VERSE 4.**—“Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always.”

Seek the Lord, [Cassiodorus, Augustine] as your reward, [Col. 0947C] and thus be strengthened; for from him they are strong and enlightened [Jerome, Augustine] so that they may know what must be done and be able to accomplish it. But those who turn away from him are both weak and blind. Always seek his face in this life—that is, his presence. Although it is found through faith, it must nevertheless always be sought in this life, so that afterward it may be possessed by sight. [Jerome.] The Jews, as little children, were commanded in the old Law to appear before the Lord three times in the year, not empty-handed: at Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles (Exod. XXIII). But we, who are in the year of favour, ought always to seek the face of the Trinity. [Augustine, Alcuin.] Or, “seek always,” that is, in the present and in the future. For then too he will be sought without end, because what is loved is always desired and always sought, lest it be absent, but always present. An evil person can fear his presence, which a good person loves.

**PART II. VERSE 5.**—“Remember his wonderful works which he has done, his prodigies and the judgments of his mouth.”

Remember his wonderful works. [Augustine.] The second part, in which he sets before the hearts of little children the faith of the patriarchs and God’s promises, so that we may be their seed—not from the Jews alone, but also from all nations. This he shows down to the words, “When they were few in number.” [Alcuin.] As though he said: Seek him. But because there are those who cannot bear to look at the sun in its course, who cannot understand Christ in the height of his divinity, which flies beyond understanding just as no one can look upon the sun in its course, I say to you lesser ones: at least remember his wonderful works [Col. 0948A]—or, “his wonders”—which he has done. [Augustine.] Behold, this ardent praiser now accommodates himself to the weak and nursing infants, nourishing them with God’s temporal miracles, as though he said: If it is a great thing to seek what God is—or rather, at least see the things he has done. This resembles what the Lord said to Moses: “Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you” (Exod. III), which a pure mind scarcely apprehends even for a little while. Then, mercifully accommodating his grace, he said: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob” (ibid.), which even little children could grasp. So here he first exhorts them to seek his face, which is fitting for the mature; then to attend to his works, which little children can do. And remember his greater prodigies, [Cassiodorus] namely, miracles by which something future was signified; and the judgments [Col. 0948B] of his mouth, [Alcuin] which he commanded through Moses in the Law. Note that he gradually rises: from visible prodigies he passes to judgments, then to the eternal covenant, in which there are both command and promise. For “eternal covenant” is said both of the teaching itself and of the promise of eternal inheritance. And to whom is this said? To those who live by faith.

**VERSE 6.**—“Seed of Abraham, his servants; sons of Jacob, his chosen ones.”

Seed of Abraham, his servants, [Jerome, Augustine] and those who are sons of Jacob—that is, imitators of him in wrestling against the flesh. I mean Jacob, his chosen ones. I say, remember; and you ought to do so, because:

**VERSE 7.**—“He is the Lord our God; his judgments are throughout all [Col. 0948C] the earth.”

He, Christ, is the Lord our God, [Augustine] and lest you think that Abraham’s children exist only in one nation according to the flesh: his judgments are throughout all the earth. That is, Jacob and Israel—namely, believers—are throughout all the earth; to them he makes known his judgments, but not to another nation.

**VERSE 8.**—“He remembered his covenant for ever, the word which he commanded for a thousand generations.”

He was mindful. [Cassiodorus.] Therefore you too ought to be mindful, because he was mindful in fulfilling the promises of his new covenant, [Augustine.] that is, of righteousness and eternal inheritance, which he promised in the New Testament. For “covenant” is said both of that which is promised, [Col. 0948D] and of the teaching in which the promise is declared and by which, when it has been observed, it is granted. I mean the covenant that will endure for an age, that is, forever; hence he says later, “an eternal covenant.” If this covenant is understood as the old covenant, on account of the land of Canaan, of which he goes on to speak, how is it eternal, when that earthly inheritance cannot be eternal? It must therefore not be understood of that land. Then, in order to specify that “covenant” is to be understood as the teaching of the word, he adds, “of the word.” As if to say: Of what covenant was he mindful? Behold, of “the word which he commanded for a thousand generations,” that is, all those who must live by faith. For a thousand is here taken for an indefinite number. This is the word of the Gospel, the word of faith, which extends to all generations; and for keeping it the eternal promise is granted, which he had previously signified through the covenant, [Col. 0949A] which he did not command but promised. For what we must receive is promised; what we must do is commanded. This is faith: that the righteous person may live by faith, and to this faith the inheritance is promised.

**VERSE 9.**—“Which he ordained for Abraham, and his oath to Isaac.”

“Which he ordained.” [Augustine.] As if to say: He was mindful of the word which he ordained for Abraham, and of his oath which he ordained for Isaac.

**VERSE 10.**—“And he established it for Jacob as a commandment, and for Israel as an everlasting covenant.”

And he established it, [Augustine.] namely, the word of faith, for Jacob himself as a commandment; and he established it for Israel as an everlasting covenant, that is, as an eternal promise. [Col. 0949B] Behold, that word is both in the commandment and in the promise, though in different respects. The work which he commands belongs to the commandment; but the reward of the work belongs to the promise. For he promises a reward to those who work. And the sense is: He established that word for Israel as an everlasting covenant, [Augustine, Alcuin.] that is, because from the word fulfilled he would give something eternal—namely, the land of Canaan, which is not eternal, but signifies what is eternal. Behold, the three patriarchs are named, of whom he especially declares himself to be the God: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob” (Exod. III). Behold a threefold authority. I say: he established it as an everlasting covenant.

**VERSE 11.**—“Saying: To you I will give the land of Canaan, the measuring-line of your inheritance.”

[Col. 0949C] “Saying: I will give you the land of Canaan,” [Augustine.] that is, what is signified by it. For he also gave them this land as a figure of the eternal inheritance, to which eternal inheritance not all belong. Therefore he adds, “the measuring-line of your inheritance,” namely, “I will give,” [Haimo, Gloss interlinear.] that is, the heavenly inheritance only to those marked by the measuring-line of divine predestination. Or he says “measuring-line” because, just as the land of promise was apportioned by a line into different portions, so in eternal life there are different dwelling-places, according to: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John XIV). [Cassiodorus.] Why, then, is the heavenly inheritance called the land of Canaan? Its name explains it. For Canaan is interpreted “humble,” because no one enters it [Col. 0949D] unless humble. But the same is also evident from the history. For Noah said that Canaan would be the servant of his brothers (Gen. IX). [Augustine.] That is, with Canaan excluded, the land is given to Abraham’s seed. This is servile fear, which does not remain in the house forever, because charity casts out fear, while the son remains in the house forever (John VIII; 1 John IV). Fittingly, therefore, the eternal inheritance is called the land of Canaan, because servants are driven from it and sons are received.

**PART III. VERSE 12.**—“When they were few in number, very few, and sojourners therein.”

“When they were.” [Augustine.] The third part. He had said that God must be worshipped freely; because the thought at once occurs to one of weak faith: If God is to be worshipped freely, and he himself is the inheritance, what will become of the necessities of mortal life? Here he sets forth what he bestowed on the fathers and their children, both according to the flesh and according to faith. [Augustine, Alcuin.] For he tells what aids for temporal life he bestowed on the fathers and their children, both according to flesh and faith—not that they might cling to these things, but that they might refer them to the eternal good. They do this if, being drawn by such things, they seek God’s ordinances and law. “When they were few in number.” [Augustine.] He recounts the history and briefly touches on the fact that they passed into Egypt. As if to say: God promised this when they were few in number, that is, very few, before they multiplied in Egypt; and “sojourners,” that is, strangers in it—namely, in the land of Canaan.

**VERSE 13.**—“And they passed from nation to nation, and from one kingdom to another people.”

“And they passed from nation to nation.” [Augustine.] [Col. 0950B] He briefly sets forth what he will narrate more fully later. “And from a kingdom,” that is, from the land of promise, which is called a kingdom—not because it was then one, but because the kingdom of Israel would be there. I say, they passed to another people. And how were they able to endure? Behold:

**VERSE 14.**—“He did not allow any man to harm them, and he rebuked kings for their sake.”

“He did not allow,” [Augustine.] that is, he did not permit, a man to harm them; and he rebuked kings for their sake, such as Abimelech, king of Gerar, lest he harm Isaac on account of Rebekah (Gen. XXVI), and Pharaoh, king of Egypt, lest he harm Abraham on account of Sarah (Gen. XXI). He rebuked them, saying:

**VERSE 15.**—“Do not touch my anointed ones, and [Col. 0950C] do no evil to my prophets.”

“Do not touch my anointed ones.” [Augustine.] Although these words are not found in the historical account, nevertheless God either spoke them secretly in human hearts or through an angel. Let no one be troubled that he called them “anointed ones,” for they were already Christians at that time, though secretly. Hence: “Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John VIII). For no one, either before the incarnation or after it, has been reconciled to God apart from this faith. For “there is one mediator between God and men, Jesus Christ” (1 Tim. II). “And do no evil to my prophets.” It is clearly established concerning Abraham that he was a prophet; so it must be believed concerning the others also.

**PART IV. VERSE 16.**—“And he called a famine upon [Col. 0950D] the land; he broke every support of bread.”

“And he called.” [Augustine.] The fourth part, where he begins to narrate how it came about that they passed from kingdom to kingdom. As if to say: If you ask how they passed from nation to nation and from a kingdom to another people, behold: “He called a famine upon the land,” and so on, down to “and he greatly increased his people,” as though they passed through this means. The sense is that God called a famine upon the land. He says that he “called” famine as though it were an animate person capable of obeying its caller—perhaps because God sends such evils through evil angels, who are set over such things. Therefore he called famine, that is, the angel set over famine. Or rather, he called famine, that is, he said that famine should exist; that is, [Col. 0951A] he commanded it to exist in actuality, though it already existed in his disposition. Thus he called it. And that is, because he “broke,” that is, consumed, every support of bread. And through this they passed from nation to nation and from kingdom to another people. But:

**VERSE 17.**—“He sent a man before them; Joseph was sold as a slave.”

“He sent a man before them.” [Augustine.] See how God used evils for good. Joseph, sold by his brothers, was afterwards exalted in Egypt because of righteousness (Gen. XLI). Of him he adds: “as a slave,” and so forth. As if to say: Whom did he send, and how? Behold: Joseph was sold as a slave by his brothers, [Jerome.] whom he afterwards received, together with his father, into Egypt (Gen. XXXVII), and caused Pharaoh to give them the best land (Gen. XLVII). [Col. 0951B] [Note: [Col. 0951D] From Augustine, *Repetitions on the Psalms*.] But if Joseph, humbled and exalted, made a place for God’s people among temporal goods, so that they might be strengthened against their enemies, how much more did Jesus, humbled according to the flesh and exalted in heaven, make a place for his own among eternal things. [Augustine.] Then he narrates what Joseph suffered in his humiliation and how he was exalted, saying:

**VERSE 18.**—“They humbled his feet in fetters; iron passed through his soul, until his word came.”

“They humbled his feet in fetters.” [Augustine.] We do not read of Joseph’s fetters in that history of Genesis; but we must believe that what was omitted there occurred, since the Holy Spirit says it in the Psalms. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] And although Joseph found favor [Col. 0951C] with the keeper of the prison, as is read in Genesis (Gen. XL), he was nevertheless first distressed. “Iron passed through.” As if to say: Beyond bodily evils, iron—that is, the tribulation of harsh necessity, which was in his anxious and troubled soul—passed through his soul, as is said of Mary in Luke: “And a sword shall pass through your own soul” (Luke II). [Cassiodorus.] Or, according to another reading, “his soul passed through iron,” that is, through the tribulation of harsh necessity. Yet the meaning is the same as in the former reading: Joseph remained even in this tribulation until his word came, [Augustine.] that is, the interpretation of the dream. But that word was not from him, because:

**VERSE 19.**—“The utterance of the Lord kindled him; the king sent and released him, the ruler of peoples [Col. 0951D] set him free.”

“The utterance of the Lord,” [Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus.] that is, the Spirit revealing mysteries, kindled—or set ablaze—him; that is, it vividly stirred him to speak of things to come. [Augustine.] He is said to have been kindled by the divine utterance so that he may be counted among those of whom the Apostle says: “Fervent in spirit” (Rom. XII). Thus fittingly, when the Holy Spirit was sent by the Lord to the apostles, divided tongues appeared to them (Acts II), as though of fire. From that fire depart those of whom it is said: “The charity of many shall grow cold” (Matt. XXIV). And because of this word the king, that is, Pharaoh, sent and released him from the charge, that is, from the punishment, while he was fettered; namely, [Col. 0952A] the ruler of peoples set him free, liberating him from prison.

**VERSE 20.**—“He appointed him lord of his house and ruler of all his possession.”

**VERSE 21.**—“That he might instruct his princes as himself and teach prudence to his elders.”

“That he might instruct his princes as himself, and teach prudence to his elders.” [Augustine.] We do not read this in the historical account either; but we must believe that so great a man, a worshipper of God, did not concern himself only with bodily matters.

**VERSE 22.**—“And Israel entered Egypt, and Jacob was a sojourner in the land of Ham.”

And after Joseph, Israel entered Egypt, [Augustine.] and Jacob was a sojourner, that is, a stranger and not a native, in [Col. 0952B] the land of Ham. This is Egypt, whose people descended from Ham, Noah’s son (Gen. X). For Ham was Noah’s son, the father of Canaan, from whom the Egyptians derived their origin.

**PART V. VERSE 23.**—“And he greatly increased his people and strengthened him above his enemies.”

“And he increased.” [Augustine.] The fifth part. Behold, he briefly states what happened, which he will later narrate fully. He also tells how he strengthened his people above their enemies. And all this continues down to “he spread out a cloud,” where, according to Augustine, the sixth part begins. As if to say: After Joseph, God sent Jacob into Egypt, and there he greatly increased his people by fruitfulness in childbirth, [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] and strengthened him above [Col. 0952C] his enemies. This did not take place before Moses, but through Moses’ signs. For previously the male offspring of the children of Israel were killed, and they themselves were worn down in making bricks (Exod. III); but afterwards, by the mighty hand of the Lord, through signs and wonders, they were made feared and honored, until the contempt of the hard king was overcome and he himself, with his army, was overwhelmed in the Red Sea. He now begins fully to narrate how this occurred, having first set it forth briefly:

**VERSE 24.**—“He turned their heart so that they hated his people and dealt deceitfully with his servants.”

“He turned their heart so that they hated his people.” [Augustine.] He does not say, “He turned their heart,” because God is the author of evil. For it must neither be understood nor believed that God turns the human heart to commit sins, or that it was the fathers’ sin to hate God’s people. “And that they might deal deceitfully with his servants.” God is not the author of these exceedingly grave sins, since he must not be believed to be the author even of the slightest sin. But God’s goodness is wonderful in that he uses even evil people well. For when they were evil through their own fault, he made good use of their evil. They were not good before they hated his people; rather, they were wicked and ungodly, such people as would easily envy their prosperous resident aliens. Therefore, when he increased Israel’s prosperity, by this benefit of God they were turned toward envy because they were already evil. Thus he did not turn their heart by making it evil, [Col. 0953A] but by doing good to his people. He turned their heart, evil of its own accord, by multiplying his own, so that through envy they might hate his people. For envy is hatred of another’s prosperity. God used their hatred for the training of his people and the glory of his name, as what follows shows. I say, he turned their heart so that they might hate his people, and deal deceitfully with his servants—namely, so that the servants of God might be reduced through the work of mud and brick. Then he begins to explain how he used these things for his glory, saying:

**VERSE 25.**—“He sent Moses his servant, Aaron whom he chose.”

“He sent Moses his servant.” [Cassiodorus.] He sent a servant, though he himself could do everything, in order to teach with what moderation he had accomplished all these things. And he sent Aaron [Col. 0953B] whom he chose. It would have been enough to say “whom he chose”; but nothing need be sought in the addition of *him*. It is a customary feature of divine speech, used for explanation. And:

**VERSE 26.**—“He placed in them the words of his signs, and of his wonders in the land of Ham.”

“He placed in them,” [Cassiodorus.] namely, in Moses and Aaron, the words of his signs and of his wonders in the land of Ham; that is, the words by which they proclaimed what signs and wonders the Lord would perform among Ham’s people. [Augustine.] Or thus: “words of signs” does not mean words by which signs were made. For many things were done without words, whether by a rod or an outstretched hand. But because the deeds themselves were not empty of meaning, like the words that we speak, they too are called words. “Words,” [Col. 0953C] therefore, not of voices or sounds, but of signs and wonders: through them he performed signs. And the sense is: He placed in them words of signs, that is, through them he performed signs, because they signified something as words do. And he placed words of his wonders, [Cassiodorus.] that is, through them he performed wonders which portended something. And this was in the land of Ham. What signs he performed follows:

**VERSE 27.**—“He sent darkness and made it dark, and did not embitter his words.”

“He sent darkness and made it dark.” [Augustine.] This is read literally among the plagues of Egypt, because they suffered darkness among the other plagues (Exod. X); but what is said here is better understood as the darkening of the hearts of those who despised God’s commands. And [Col. 0953D] it is a fitting beginning of the plagues: blindness, without which they would not have incurred the others. “And did not embitter,” [Haimo, Augustine.] that is, he fulfilled and confirmed his words by miracles. Or according to another reading, “they embittered”—namely, the Egyptians, by their objections—God’s words. Or as is found in certain manuscripts: “And they did not embitter,” namely Moses and Aaron, God’s words, because they patiently endured even those most hardened people, the Egyptians, on account of the Lord’s command, until everything which God had ordained should be done among them.

**VERSE 28.**—“He turned their waters into blood and killed their fish.”

“He turned their waters into blood.” [Cassiodorus.] This is the second plague, which Exodus puts first [Col. 0954A] (Exod. VII); it signified that he would turn the waters of the Red Sea into death for them. “And he killed their fish,” so that there might be no hope of life for those people in the waters, when that which is naturally nourished there dies in the water.

**VERSE 29.**—“Their land produced frogs, in the inner chambers of their kings.”

“And their land produced frogs.” [Augustine.] Behold the third plague. According to another reading, “their land gave frogs,” that is, it turned their land into frogs, because there were so many frogs that this may be said hyperbolically; and frogs were in the inner chambers of their kings (Exod. VIII). The princes, who were afterwards to be placed beneath the waters, became companions of frogs.

**VERSE 30.**—“He spoke, and the dog-fly came, and gnats throughout all their borders.”

[Col. 0954B] “He spoke, and the dog-fly came, and gnats throughout all their borders.” [Augustine.] Behold, this is the fourth plague, a humiliation of the king’s boasting, since he was not even a match for flies (Exod. VIII). If it is asked when God spoke this, we answer that this existed timelessly in his Word before it came to pass in time through that Word itself; although in a certain manner he spoke through angels, or through Moses and Aaron, so that it should occur then when it was to be done. Then follows the fifth plague.

**VERSE 31.**—“He made their rains hail, burning fire in their land.”

“He made their rains hail,” [Cassiodorus.] that is, instead of rain, which makes fruitful, there came hail, which scorches what it touches (Exod. X). This is said similarly to the preceding statement, “their land gave frogs”; and “burning fire,” that is, lightning—namely, he placed it [Augustine.] in their land.

**VERSE 32.**—“And he struck their vines and their fig trees, and broke the trees of their borders.”

And with hail and fire, [Cassiodorus.] that is, with lightning, he struck their vines and their fig trees, and broke their trees. Therefore do not doubt that their crops were destroyed where greater things perished. Then follows the sixth plague.

**VERSE 33.**—“He spoke, and the locust came, and the caterpillar, without number.”

“He spoke and the locust came,” [Augustine.] which is the mother of the caterpillar, of which it continues: “and the caterpillar,” of which—namely, of the locust [Col. 0954D] and caterpillar—there was no number. The locust and caterpillar are one plague, because one is the parent and the other its offspring.

**VERSE 34.**—“And it devoured every herb in their land and devoured every fruit of their land.”

“And it devoured every herb,” [Gloss interlinear.] that is, vegetation in their land; and it devoured every fruit of the crops of their land. [Augustine.] Then follows the seventh plague, which in Exodus is the tenth.

**VERSE 35.**—“And he struck every firstborn in their land, the first fruits of all their labor.”

And he struck every firstborn among humans in their land, and the first fruits of all their labor. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] By this he means the firstborn of cattle, which he struck likewise. This is the last plague in Egypt, [Col. 0955A] by which the Egyptians, defeated, yield. [Augustine.] It should be noted that, although Moses presents ten plagues in Exodus, the prophet neither mentions them all here nor gives them in the order in which they are narrated there. For the praise with which this psalm is concerned is free from the law of historical sequence; and here he adds something which the history does not contain and passes over some things which it does contain, by the authority of the same Spirit who spoke through the historian. [Cassiodorus.] Here, therefore, he gives the Egyptians seven evils, opposed to the seven benefits which he will later say were given to the Hebrews. Hence he adds:

**PART VI. VERSE 36.**—“And he led them out with silver and gold, and there was none feeble among their tribes.”

“And he led them out.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] This is the sixth part according to Cassiodorus. Having stated above the evils which God’s justice inflicted on the Israelites’ enemies, he now sets beneath them the temporal goods which God’s mercy gave to the Israelites, so that, helped by these, they might seek God’s law. “And he led them out in silver and gold,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] that is, with silver and gold. For, in Scriptural usage, *in* is put for *with*. This is the first benefit. [Note: [Col. 0955] From Augustine, here and in *Questions on Exodus*, questions 39, 83, 53; and book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 40.] Observe that here too he adds to the praises of God that he led the Hebrews, enriched with gold and silver, out of Egypt, because they were such people as could not despise the reward of their labors, even though temporal. God commanded them to borrow gold and silver vessels and precious garments from the Egyptians and carry them away with them. Yet because they deceived the Egyptians, God must not be thought either to command or approve deceit in those whose heart is set on things above; for in them this was not deceit, since they did not act from greed, but in obedience to God’s command. And those feeble persons whose desires God was testing were more permitted to do this to those—that is, the Egyptians—who justly suffered such things, than commanded to do it. For just as there was a command for the good, so for the greedy there was permission in one respect and command in another.
