He commanded that they act, but he permitted, not commanded, that they act in that particular manner. Thus the character of the deed belonged to the permission, but the deed itself to the command. Yet God did not permit this to occur without some benefit to the carnal soul. For because carnal people acquired something carnal from their neighbor, they afterwards received God’s law and ordinances more readily. And though they acted by deceit, they nevertheless took from the unjust what was owed to themselves, [Col. 0955D] and God made divine use both of the Egyptians’ wickedness and of the Israelites’ weakness to signify what needed to be signified by these actions. For this spiritually signified that philosophers or heretics should be despoiled by Catholics of those things found fitting for God’s tabernacle—that is, the Church—in their words or writings. Then follows the second benefit. “And there was none feeble,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] in body, not in mind, among their tribes. This was a great benefit for those about to migrate. And:

**VERSE 37.**—“Egypt rejoiced at their departure, because fear of them fell upon them.”

“Egypt rejoiced at their departure.” [Augustine, [Col. 0956A] Cassiodorus.] This was after the drowning of their army. Why did Egypt rejoice? Because fear of Israel fell upon them. Having heard of so great a slaughter of the dead in the Red Sea, Egypt feared that Israel would return and consume their survivors. Here was fulfilled what he had said above: “And he strengthened him above his enemies.” Then follows the third benefit.

**PART VII. VERSE 38.**—“He spread out a cloud for their protection, and fire to give them light by night.”

“He spread out a cloud.” [Augustine.] This is the sixth division according to Augustine, where he sets forth the temporal goods which God’s mercy gave them, after the evils which God’s justice inflicted on their enemies had been stated above. Here he now begins to tell the benefits of God that occurred while they were journeying [Col. 0956B] in the wilderness. He spread out a cloud for their protection, [Cassiodorus.] to protect them from the sun’s heat, and fire to give them light against darkness by night. Then follows the fourth benefit.

**VERSE 39.**—“They asked for meat, and the quail came; and he filled them with the bread of heaven.”

“They asked.” [Augustine.] Certainly they did not ask for quail, but for meat; and what came to them was not just any meat, but quail (Exod. XVI; Num. XI), which is meat. Since he speaks here not of the bitter complaint of the wicked, in whom God was not well pleased (Exod. XVII), but of the faith of the elect, who are the true seed of Abraham, therefore those must be understood to have asked so that something might come by which the murmurs of the bitter complainers [Col. 0956C] would be silenced (Num. XX). Then follows the fifth benefit: with the bread of heaven, that is, manna, he filled them.

**VERSE 40.**—“He broke open the rock, and waters flowed; rivers ran in the dry land.”

“He broke open the rock, and waters flowed.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] This is the sixth benefit: “rivers ran in the dry land.” By all these benefits God commends the merit of Abraham’s faith. Hence he adds:

**VERSE 41.**—“For he remembered his holy word, which he had made with Abraham his servant.”

“For he remembered his holy word, which he had spoken to Abraham his servant,” [Jerome.] that is, he remembered the promise made to Abraham, in fulfilling which figuratively he foreshadowed eternal things.

[Col. 0956D] **VERSE 42.**—“And he brought out his people in exultation, and his chosen ones in gladness.”

“And he brought out his people in exultation, and his chosen ones in gladness.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] This is the people who were in gladness, because the murmurers were struck down.

**VERSE 43.**—“And he gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labors of peoples.”

“And he gave them the regions of the nations.” [Cassiodorus.] This is the first benefit, in which the fulfillment of the promises lies. “And they possessed the labors of peoples,” that is, the fruits of the regions. [Augustine.] He gave these things not so that they might worship him for their sake, but so that they might refer them to the eternal good, that is:

[Col. 0957A] **VERSE 43.**—“That they may keep his ordinances and seek his law.”

That the elect, namely the true seed of Abraham, may keep his ordinances, and so forth. [Augustine.] As if to say: He did not give these temporal things so that they should be regarded as the highest good, but he referred them to that end where the highest good must be sought: “that they may keep his ordinances.” For these earthly goods were not given them by God so that they might dissolve in luxury or grow torpid in perverse security, but so that they might have leisure for acquiring the eternal good; namely, that the elect may keep his ordinances. [Cassiodorus.] Ordinances are those matters in which the command is plain and absolute, such as “Love God and neighbor”; these must be kept. “And seek his law.” The law concerns things that must now be fulfilled not bodily but spiritually [Col. 0957B] [Note: [Col. 0957D] From Augustine, here and in Psalm LXV.]. Therefore the law must be sought, because it is a shadow of things to come. By the example of those to whom temporal things were given so that through them they might seek God, the true seed of Abraham is taught how it ought to use temporal prosperity, just as it is instructed by the example of Joseph and Christ how patiently it ought to bear temporal adversity—prosperity and adversity, the two things by which the elect are tested. Hence: “We passed through fire and water” (Ps. LXV). [Augustine.] Therefore, you children of God, who have the promise of the present and the future life: if the temptations of the world seem harsh to you, consider Joseph in prison and Christ on the cross. If prosperity is present, use it not for its own sake toward God, but for God’s sake; nor think that he is necessary to his own because of those things which he gives even to his blaspheming wicked people. But first seek the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you (Matt. VI).

## Comparison on Psalm CIV: “Give thanks to the Lord, and call upon,” etc.

**VERSE 6.**—“The seed of Abraham, his servants.” From the Hebrew it appears that *servi* (“of [his] servant”) is singular genitive, so that Münster translated, to remove the ambiguity: “You, the seed of Abraham his servant.” In Greek, however, it is plural nominative, δοῦλοι, “servants,” although in one copy I found δούλου. From the Hebrew *ABDO* it may be said “his servant”; and the use of the singular for the plural is not unprecedented. Indeed, Campensis’s paraphrase has “the descendants of Abraham, his worshippers.” Finally, the difference matters little for the sense.

**VERSE 16.**—“Support,” *MATTHEH*, that is, “staff,” “rod.” “It is a Hebraism,” says Münster, “for the support of bread.”

**VERSE 21.**—“That he might instruct his princes.” So Jerome and the edition according to Campensis. Others render *instruct* as “bind” or “have power over.” Münster explains in his scholia why this is so. Some take *LEESOR* to mean “to bind and cast into prison”; others take it as *IASAR*, “to chastise and instruct.”

“As himself.” In Hebrew, *BENAPHSCHO*, that is, “in his soul,” which is interpreted “according to his will.” The Septuagint seem to have read *kaph* for *beth*, for the letters are very close. “According to his soul” has the same force as “as himself,” although, if one reads it also with *beth*, it can easily be reduced to the same sense.

**VERSE 27.**—“They did not embitter his words.” The master records three readings: the Vulgate reading, which differs from the Hebrew only in the number of the verb, expressed as *LO MARU*, “they did not embitter,” or, as Jerome has it, “they were not unbelieving.” Next comes the reading, “his words,” or “they did not embitter his words.” The pronoun is ambiguous in Hebrew. Another reading, without the negation, is “they embittered his words”; this is the reading of the Roman edition, which Augustine mentions. It is also found in Greek codices: παρεπίκραναν τοὺς λόγους αὐτοῦ, “they embittered his words.” Thus it is explained in three ways.

**VERSE 30.**—“The dog-fly came.” The dog-fly and the *coenomyia* have been discussed at Psalm 77, verse 50. Even Jerome, in his Commentary, here interprets it “dog-fly,” following the Greeks.

“Gnats,” *KINNIM*, which some maintain are either lice or mosquitoes.

**VERSE 35.**—“The first fruits of all their labor.” Jerome: “the first fruits of all their offspring.” Here Faber and Caecus err in supposing that Jerome understands this clause of the final plague upon the children of Israel in Egypt, Exodus XI, and therefore that our reading is not sufficiently suitable. This is false, as the first clause seems to show: “And he struck every firstborn in their land.” Thus the second clause must be understood of their chief possessions. For other translators render it either “labor” or “strength.” This is what *ON* means. Hence the translator according to Campensis: “He struck the foremost things among their possessions.” His paraphrase: “the chief things of all their labors, for which they had sweated in cultivating the fields.” Münster, however, says in his scholion: “the first fruits of all their strength”; the Hebraism calls that which first opens the parent’s womb “the first strength,” or “the first fruits of strength.”

**VERSE 41.**—“Mindful of his holy word, which he had with Abraham his servant.” Münster translated as though God had not spoken to Abraham: “He remembered,” he says, “his holy word, and Abraham his servant”; although the Hebrew reads *ETH ABRAHAM ABDO*, that is, “with Abraham his servant,” as Jerome and the others attest.

# PSALM CV

[Col. 0957]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “ALLELUIA, ALLELUIA.”

[Col. 0957D]

“Give thanks to the Lord.” Title: [Augustine, Jerome, Cassiodorus.] “Alleluia, alleluia.” Some say that one *alleluia* belongs to the end of the preceding psalm and the other to the following psalm. Jerome says that this rule must be maintained: wherever two *alleluias* are prefixed to a psalm, we should know that one belongs to the end of the prior psalm and the other to the psalm that follows; Cassiodorus also agrees with this assertion. [Augustine.] [Col. 0958D] But the majority assign every *alleluia* to the following psalm; sometimes it is placed once and sometimes twice, just as the Lord in the Gospel sometimes says “Amen” and sometimes “Amen, amen.” This is done for greater certainty of the matter. Augustine agrees with these, because what others say is not supported by convincing evidence, and especially because no one has found Greek codices that have *alleluia* at the end of any psalm. This psalm is joined to the preceding one not only in title but also [Col. 0959A] in subject. For this psalm concerns the same people Israel as the preceding one; but this treats of the wicked among them, whereas the preceding treats of the elect among the same people. For Paul implies that some in that people were true children of Abraham when he says: “But God was not well pleased with all of them” (1 Cor. II). Since the preceding psalm commends these people, it says nothing there of the iniquities of the bitter complainers. But this following psalm concerns the wicked; and because not only God’s justice but also his mercy was shown to them, it speaks of them with God’s praises, in the person of those who, converted, pray for pardon. Their examples are recalled—people in whom, even while they sinned, the abundant mercy of God appeared. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Hence this psalm, like the former, begins: “Give thanks [Col. 0959B] to the Lord.” Its purpose is to exhort to a twofold confession: of praise and of sins. Its method has six divisions. First, the Hebrew in whose person the prophet speaks, having turned from the faithlessness of the fathers to God’s mercy, urges others to turn to the same mercy, praying that they may be joined to the people of God’s good pleasure, [Cassiodorus.] which was to be gathered at Christ’s advent. Second, he recounts the sins which the fathers committed in Egypt, though the Lord nevertheless delivered them: “We have sinned.” Third, he states the sins they committed after the exodus: “They quickly failed.” [Augustine.] We shall pursue the other divisions in their places. Therefore, speaking in the person of a Hebrew converted from bitter rebellion to God’s mercy and exhorting others to the same mercy, he says:

[Col. 0959C] **VERSE 1.**—“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.”

“Give thanks to the Lord.” [Augustine.] Behold, the opening of this psalm and of the preceding one is the same; but there it follows, “and call upon his name,” while here it follows, “for he is good.” Hence confession of sins may be understood here, because it also follows: “We have sinned with our fathers,” and so forth. But confession of praise may also be understood, because that God is good belongs to his praise, and praise includes confession. We have thus distinguished confession of sin and of praise, although confession of sins is not devout without the praise of God. Therefore the person who confesses sins has God’s praise, whether in words, when he calls him good and merciful, or in inward disposition alone, when he believes this. The sense is: Give thanks to the Lord, confessing sins and praises, because he is good by nature. [Cassiodorus.] This is said lest anyone be frightened because of guilt and despair of him, rather than seek his mercy. And also because “his mercy endures forever,” [Augustine.] that is, until the end of the age. His mercy, which is shown to the miserable by consoling them in misery or delivering them from it, does this until the end of the age. Or he speaks here of that mercy by which a human being is blessed. Since this blessedness is eternal, “age” here is understood as “eternal,” as is clear in Greek. The sense is: Therefore give thanks, because his mercy—that is, the blessedness given through his mercy, since no one can be blessed without God—endures forever.

[Col. 0960A] **VERSE 2.**—“Who shall speak of the powers of the Lord, make all his praises heard?”

**Who shall speak?** [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The one who asks for mercy is filled by contemplation of the divine works, and in wonder says: And who shall speak—that is, who is sufficient to speak—of the powers of the Lord, that is, of the works which he performs mightily? And who shall make all his praises heard—that is, who can cause others to hear everything in which God is to be praised? For they ought to be spoken in such a way as to be proclaimed to listeners. But who can do all this? As if he said: No one. Or because—

**VERSE 3.**—“Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at every time.”

**Blessed are those who keep**, etc. [Augustine.] By the praises of God he means [Col. 0960B] the works of his commandments, which he himself performs in his own people. For God works in us both the willing of good and its accomplishment, as the Apostle says (Phil. 2). Who, then, shall speak of the powers of the Lord? How shall he speak of the things which God powerfully performs in his people? For he performs these ineffably. As if he said: No one is able to speak, etc. Who shall make all his praises heard [Augustine]—that is, who, having heard, shall perform all the praises, that is, the works of his commandments? Even if not all are performed when heard, nevertheless, insofar as they are performed, he himself who works in them is to be praised. Therefore he preferred to say *his praises* rather than *his commandments* or *the works of his commandments*, because, as has been said, insofar as they are performed, he himself is to be praised. Yet who is sufficient either to perform or to speak all these praises? No one.

[Alcuin.] And the sense is: His mercy [Col. 0960C] is for ever; and who is sufficient, either inwardly to conceive its effect, or to impart it to others, or to fulfil it in deed? Here he takes “powers” and “praises” in the same sense. But the two expressions are distinguished: namely, *shall speak* and *shall make heard*.

**Blessed**, etc. [Cassiodorus.] As if he said: Since no one is sufficient either to speak the powers or to perform all the praises, let him do this: let him keep judgment and righteousness. For blessed are those who keep judgment, by judging rightly and distinguishing good from evil; and who do righteousness [Augustine], by acting rightly—and both at every time, certainly from the time they begin. For “he who perseveres to the end, he shall be saved” (Matt. 24). And because God makes people righteous, he prays and says:

[Col. 0960D] **VERSE 4.**—“Remember us, O Lord, in the good pleasure of your people; visit us with your salvation.”

**Remember us, O Lord** [Augustine, Cassiodorus], so that we may be in the good pleasure of your people: that we may be among those in whom you are pleased, a pleasure not found in all, and that we may not be among the rebellious. And, that this may be so, visit us with your salvation—that is, in Jesus—so that, healed by him, we may be able to keep judgment and act justly, and thus be blessed. Visit us, I say, for this purpose:

**VERSE 5.**—“To behold in the goodness of your chosen ones, to rejoice in the joy of your nation, that you may be praised with your inheritance.”

**To behold in the goodness of your chosen ones** [Augustine]: that is, that we may behold you in that goodness which you bestow [Col. 0961A] upon the elect; that is, through your grace may we see, lest we remain blind. And visit us also *to rejoice*: that is, that we may rejoice in the joy which is God himself. Elsewhere he says to him: “My rejoicing, redeem me” (Ps. 31). I mean the joy of your nation, that is, of the children of Abraham, all of whom are one nation. Visit us also, *that you may be praised*, or, according to another reading, *to praise*: that is, that we may praise you with your inheritance.

It is remarkable that in many manuscripts it is written, “that you may be praised,” whereas in Greek there is one construction used for these three verbs; and the interpretation ought to be alike: namely, that we may see, rejoice, and praise with your inheritance. Or, according to the other reading, “that you may be praised,” it may be understood thus; and again the construction will be alike: visit us *to behold*, that is, so that you may behold us in the goodness of your elect—that is, make us to be there [Col. 0961B] and behold us there. And visit us *to rejoice*: that is, so that you may rejoice in the joy of your nation—that is, make your nation rejoice in you. And, “that you may be praised with your inheritance”: that is, make it praised in you, because it is praised only on account of you.

232 **PART II. VERSE 6.**—“We have sinned with our fathers; we have acted unjustly; we have committed iniquity.”

**We have sinned.** [Cassiodorus, Haimo.] The second part, in which he recounts the sins committed by the fathers in Egypt, though he says that they were nevertheless delivered by the Lord. As if he said: I say, “Visit,” and it is necessary that you should visit, because we have sinned with our fathers [Augustine, Jerome, Haimo], because we were materially in them when they sinned; or rather, *with our fathers* means, like our fathers, we have acted unjustly in relation to [Col. 0961C] God; we have committed iniquity in relation to our neighbour.

[Cassiodorus.] See how they state the same thing three times—that they sinned—so that their confession may appear pure. For the more vigorously a person condemns himself, the more quickly he is released. [Augustine.] And as though someone asked, “What did our fathers do?” he adds:

**VERSE 7.**—“Our fathers in Egypt did not understand your wonders; they did not remember the multitude of your mercies.”

**Our fathers in Egypt**, where many things were done for them, did not understand your wonders [Augustine]: that is, what you wished to give them through those things—not a temporal good, but an eternal one, which is awaited through patience. Therefore, being impatient, they murmured and provoked bitterness [Col. 0961D]; and they wished to be made happy by temporal goods, deceptive and fleeting as they were.

[Cassiodorus.] Note that there are two things which commend God’s benefits to us, that is, show them to be worthy of commendation: understanding and memory. He rebukes both in them. First, their understanding, when he says, “They did not understand your wonders.” [Augustine.] For understanding was needed, so that through those temporal things they might seek other goods, namely eternal ones. And “they did not remember the multitude of your mercies”: that is, the many miracles which he had performed for them in Egypt. Here he rebukes their memory, because they did not even recall things done in time, so as to believe, from the power they had experienced, that they would be delivered from their enemies.

**VERSE 8.**—“And they provoked him as they went up to the sea, [Col. 0962A] the Red Sea; and he saved them for his name’s sake, that he might make known his power.”

**And therefore, as they went up to the sea** [Augustine], namely the Red Sea. He says “went up” in reference to the configuration of the land. These men, I say, as they went up, provoked God, fearing and despairing after all that they had seen in Egypt.

[Alcuin.] This provocation occurred when, leaving Egypt, they reached the Red Sea. There they were so enclosed that on one side stood a mountain, extremely steep and impassable to anyone; on the other side was the Red Sea; and behind them were the pursuing Egyptians. On this account they began to murmur bitterly, forgetting God’s power. But then the sea was divided into twelve divisions, and no tribe dared to enter first except the tribe of Judah; for which reason it deserved among the others to obtain [Col. 0962B] the privilege or pre-eminence of kingship.

**And he saved them.** As if he said: They thus murmured [Augustine, interlinear gloss], and nevertheless the Lord saved them from the pursuing Egyptians, without following their unbelief. And this was not because of their merits, but solely for his own name’s sake, to be glorified: namely, that he might make known his power. How did he save them? Behold:

**VERSE 9.**—“And he rebuked the Red Sea, and it was dried up; and he led them through the depths as through a desert.”

**And he rebuked the Red Sea.** [Augustine.] This rebuke was not effected by a voice sent down from heaven, but by divine power, which even things devoid of sense perceive and obey. And the Red Sea was dried up, and he led [Col. 0962C] them through the depths, or through many waters—for this is the same thing—as through a desert. For where the depths had been, dryness made it like a desert, where there are no waters.

**VERSE 10.**—“And he saved them from the hand of those who hated them, and redeemed them from the hand of the enemy.”

**And thus he saved them.** [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] This was great; and, to magnify the gift, he adds what is more grievous—that is, greater: from the hand of those who hated them, namely the Egyptians, who hated them because they had been struck with plagues on their account; and he redeemed them from the hand of the enemy, namely Pharaoh. But at what price did he redeem them? As if he said: At none. Yet this was said as a figure of baptism, in which we are redeemed from the hand of the devil by Christ’s blood. Thus he named the Red Sea, [Col. 0962D] whose colour figured the blood of Christ.

**VERSE 11.**—“And the water covered those who afflicted them; not one of them remained.”

**And the water covered those who afflicted them** [Augustine], namely Pharaoh and the Egyptians; and not one remained of them, namely of those who pursued them. I do not mean, not one of the Egyptians. For those Egyptians who did not pursue them remained.

**VERSE 12.**—“And they believed in his words and sang his praise.”

**And then they believed in the words of God.** [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] It is an idiom when he says, “they believed in his words,” for “they believed his words,” which would be more idiomatic Latin. Observe the hard hearts of the Jews: they do not believe before miracles but after them. It would have been better [Col. 0963A] to believe the one making the promise. And they sang his praise, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified” (Exod. 15). [Augustine.] This is an idiom like the expression, “he lives a living life.”

**PART III. VERSE 13.**—“They acted quickly: they forgot his works; they did not wait for his counsel.”

**They acted quickly.** [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which he expounds the sins they committed after the exodus; nevertheless, God’s mercy did not fail them, being appeased through Moses. Or it concerns God’s correction, whereby in justice he exacted punishment from some through Moses.

As if he said: They believed and sang praise; yet they quickly did this—namely, they forgot his works. As if changed with utmost speed from cruelty and praise, they began to murmur [Col. 0963B]; and they did not wait for his counsel: that is, they did not patiently wait until God gave them provisions, which were delayed by God’s counsel. For God was going to give them provisions, but in excessive haste they anticipated him, asking in distrust and not awaiting his counsel. God delayed giving in order to test them.

Or, according to another reading [Augustine], “They hastened,” which is clearer. As if he said: God did these things for them, by which he called them to eternal things; but they hastened to become happy in temporal things, forgot his works, and did not wait for his counsel: that is, they did not consider for what purpose God had performed these works toward them. They ought to have reflected that such great works of God done for them were not empty, but called them to eternal things, which must be awaited patiently. But they hastened to become happy in earthly things, in which is the water-jar of desire: “whoever drinks of it shall thirst again” (John 4). Therefore he adds:

[Col. 0963C] **VERSE 14.**—“And they desired desire in the wilderness, and tempted God in the waterless place.”

**And they desired desire in the wilderness.** [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] This is an idiom like the earlier expression, “they sang his praise.” The excess of their desire is indicated by the doubling of the word. And they tempted God in the waterless place, that is, in the wilderness (Num. 11; Exod. 17).

**VERSE 15.**—“And he gave them their request, and sent abundance into their souls.”

**And he gave them their request** [Augustine], that is, the thing [Col. 0963D] they asked for; and thus, that is, because he sent abundance. Yet they were not therefore blessed, because this is not the abundance of which it is said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5). He sent it, I say, into their souls: that is, into that animate principle which is sustained by food, the principle that gives life to the body which is sustained by food. For *soul* is not taken here in respect of its rational nature, but in respect of its making the body an animate body; drink and food pertain to its sustenance. Hence the Gospel says: “Is not the soul more than food?” (Matt. 6). Or, “into their souls” means, according to their own will, so that the will which had asked in despair might be overcome by abundance. But abundance is followed by sedition:

[Col. 0964A] **VERSE 16.**—“And they provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord.”

**And, desiring honour through envy, they provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord.** [Cassiodorus.] This provocation concerned the priesthood held by Aaron and his sons.

**VERSE 17.**—“The earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered over the assembly of Abiram.”

**The earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered over the assembly of Abiram.** [Cassiodorus.] The book of Numbers plainly records how this happened. Here is God’s praise: he avenged his own. The nature of the punishment reveals what was done: those who savoured earthly things were swallowed by the earth.

[Col. 0964B] **VERSE 18.**—“And fire blazed up in their synagogue; flame consumed sinners.”

**And fire blazed up in the synagogue** [Cassiodorus], which was theirs rather than God’s: that is, among the two hundred and fifty who held censers. For Korah and the two hundred and fifty with him, wishing to possess Aaron’s priesthood, took censers in order to burn incense, and were therefore consumed by divine fire. Hence he adds: Flame consumed sinners. Those who sinned by incense perished by fire. [Augustine.] Observe that he does not say *those sinning*, for even good people are such, but *sinners*: that is, those very wicked and burdened with heavy loads of sins.

**VERSE 19.**—“And they made a calf in Horeb, and [Col. 0964C] worshipped a graven image.”

**And moreover they made a calf in Horeb** [Cassiodorus], unable to endure Moses’ absence while he remained on the summit of Mount Sinai in order to receive the law (Exod. 32). Horeb is interpreted “Calvary,” where the Lord’s crucifixion took place. Thus they sinned in Horeb, so that, already faithless then, they sinned in the name under which their descendants were to crucify the Lord: that is, in the place which, according to the interpretation of its name, indicates the place where the Jews were to crucify the Lord.

[Cassiodorus.] This arose from failure to endure those who were delayed, just as all evils arise from it. And afterwards they worshipped a graven image. Yet the calf was not carved, but cast.

**VERSE 20.**—“And they exchanged their glory for [Col. 0964D] the likeness of a calf that eats grass.”

**And they exchanged their glory** [Augustine], that is, God, who would have been their glory had they waited for him, for the likeness of a calf. He does not use the accusative construction, but the ablative, “in the likeness”; it is an idiom like the earlier phrase, “they believed in his words.” I mean a calf eating grass, so that they might be eaten by it, since they are grass—that is, flesh. For “all flesh is grass” (Isa. 40). And thus:

**VERSE 21.**—“They forgot God, who saved them, who performed great deeds in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, terrible things in the Red Sea.”

**They forgot God who saved them.** [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] A great forgetfulness! For what is retained in memory if not deliverance? *Who performed*: as if he said, How [Col. 0965A] did he save them? Behold, he is the one who performed great deeds in Egypt, deeds which could be recalled because of their greatness; and he performed wonders in the land of Ham. Such things do not ordinarily slip from the mind. And he performed terrible things in the Red Sea: that is, wonderful things, because wonder is not without a certain fear.

[Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Or they can be called terrible because they afflicted their adversaries and showed these people what they ought to fear. Such events adhere more firmly to minds, yet they forgot them.

233 **VERSE 22.**—“And he said that he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen one stood in the breach before him.”

**And, on account of these crimes, he said in threat that he would destroy them** [interlinear gloss, Augustine], because they deserved to perish. Would he utterly destroy them all? Certainly—had not Moses his chosen one [Col. 0965B] stood in the breach before him [Augustine], that is, prayed for them unceasingly. He stood, I say, in the breach—that is, in the blow by which they were to be struck—by offering himself for them, saying: “If you forgive them this sin, forgive it; but if you do not forgive them, blot me out of your book” (Exod. 32). This shows how much the intercession of saints can accomplish. For Moses, secure in God’s justice, by which God could not blot him out, obtained God’s mercy for those who would justly perish. Moses therefore stood in the breach.

**VERSE 23.**—“That he might turn away his wrath, lest he destroy them.”

**PART IV. VERSE 24.**—“And they accounted the desirable land as nothing.”

[Col. 0965C] **And they accounted it as nothing.** [Alcuin, Augustine.] The fourth part. Again he recounts other sins, and says that God was appeased through Phinehas. As if he said: They did the things just mentioned, and they also accounted the desirable land as nothing—not because they had seen it, but they accounted it as nothing in this respect, namely that—

**VERSE 25.**—“They did not believe his word, and murmured in their tents; they did not heed the voice of the Lord.”

**They did not believe his word**, or *his words* [Haimo, Alcuin]: namely, that he would bring them in. Or thus: They accounted the desirable land as nothing [Augustine], that is, they despised the eternal good signified by it. It was truly desirable. And therefore [Col. 0965D] they did not believe his word, calling them from small things to great things. Certainly, unless that land signified something great, to which they were invited, those who accounted it as nothing would in no way be blamed. For even saints account its temporal kingdom as nothing, so that they may love Jerusalem which is in heaven and truly desirable. But their unbelief is rightly rebuked, because in accounting the land as nothing, they did not believe the words of God, who leads from small things to great. And, hastening to be happy here, they did not wait for his counsel; and they murmured, saying: “Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt,” and this in their tents.

[Haimo, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As if he said: While they were at ease; for this befell them not in labour but in idleness. Thus the blameworthiness of the crime is increased; and [Col. 0966A] while they murmured, they did not heed the voice of the Lord, vehemently forbidding them to murmur.

**VERSE 26.**—“And he raised his hand over them, to cast them down in the wilderness.”

**And he raised [his hand].** [Cassiodorus.] Here God’s justice is set forth first, so that the mercy which follows may be more glorified; that mercy is shown in the following passage, where God is said to have been appeased through Phinehas’ intervention. Here, however, God’s justice is shown when he says: And he raised his hand over them, threatening punishment [Augustine, Cassiodorus], to cast them down in the wilderness. As if he said: Those formerly glorious became contemptible.

**VERSE 27.**—“And to cast down their seed among the nations, and scatter them through the regions.”

**And to cast down their seed** [Cassiodorus], that is, [Col. 0966B] their children, among the nations; and to scatter them through the regions, lest they presume any longer upon their assembly.

**VERSE 28.**—“And they were initiated into Baal-peor, and ate sacrifices of the dead.”

**And they were initiated** [Augustine]—before saying that someone appeased this indignation of God, he adds: They were initiated, or consecrated, to Baal-peor; they were consecrated to the idol of the nations. [Cassiodorus.] As if he said: They did not merely worship for a time, which indicates a more serious transgression. And, in consequence of a more vehement wrath, they ate sacrifices of the dead: things sacrificed to dead human beings as though they were gods.

**VERSE 29.**—“And they provoked him by their inventions, and ruin was multiplied among them.”

[Col. 0966C] **And they provoked him by their inventions, and ruin was multiplied among them.** [Augustine.] After he had said that God raised his hand because of their grave sins and punished them severely, before saying that he was appeased, he inserts these matters concerning the greatness of their guilt and punishment. As if he said: He deferred the execution for which he had raised his hand to cast them down, so that, given over to a reprobate mind, they might commit even this crime of idolatry and be punished in manifest justice for so great a crime. And their wickedness was so great that God was unwilling to be appeased otherwise than as Phinehas appeased him, when he killed together the man and woman engaging in intercourse. He did so not from hatred of them but from zeal for God; by this deed he delivered the people, for whom a greater destruction was impending.

[Col. 0966D] **VERSE 30.**—“Phinehas stood and appeased him, and the plague ceased.”

**Phinehas stood.** [Cassiodorus.] He stood with a steadfast mind, so that amid the general disturbance he alone might assume the confidence of intercession. And he appeased him; or he could have said, “he entreated him and pierced the adulterers”; but “he entreated him” was better, because the piercing of the adulterers, done from zeal for God, ought rather to be called prayer than action. For one who acts rightly prays; and thus the plague ceased. [Augustine.] He stated the whole matter briefly, because he is not teaching those who are ignorant but reminding those who know. The *plague* here is what above was called the *breach*, that is, the blow upon the people.

**VERSE 31.**—“And it was reckoned to him as righteousness [Col. 0967A] from generation to generation for ever.”

**And it was reckoned to him as righteousness.** [Augustine.] For God, who knew with what great love for the people this was done, reckoned it as righteousness to his priest, not merely from generation to generation—that is, as long as there is generation—but for ever.

**PART V. VERSE 32.**—“And they provoked him at the waters of Contradiction, and Moses was troubled because of them, for they embittered his spirit.”

**And they provoked him.** [Alcuin.] The fifth part, in which he treats of the water of Contradiction and the sacrifice of children. Therefore God was more vehemently angered, yet afterwards had mercy. As if he said: They so provoked him by their inventions [Col. 0967B], as was said above; and again they provoked him—that is, stirred him to anger—at the waters of Contradiction; and Moses was troubled because of them. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] That is, he was troubled in mind so as to hesitate. And this happened because they embittered his spirit: because, inflamed by the people’s excessive importunity, he rebuked them distrustfully, saying: “Can we bring forth water for you from this rock?” (Num. 20).

**VERSE 33.**—“And he spoke doubtfully with his lips; they did not destroy the nations which the Lord God had told them [to destroy].”

**And** [Augustine], because they embittered him, he distinguished this miracle from the earlier steadfastness he had shown in other miracles, in his words. For he spoke ambiguously here, though in every other case he had promised with certain faith. [Col. 0967C] Disturbed by the murmuring of an unbelieving people, he did not retain the confidence which he ought to have had, as though God could not do this, he who had already done so much. For he struck the rock doubtfully, whereas in other instances he had not doubted. For this he was corrected only by this punishment: he did not enter that land, though he was not alienated from the kingdom of God’s grace.

But those of whose iniquities this psalm speaks, when they entered the promised land, did not destroy the nations which the Lord had told them to destroy: namely, those seven peoples who possessed the land of promise.

**VERSE 34.**—“And they mingled among the nations, learned their works, served their graven images, and it became a stumbling block to them.”

[Col. 0967D] **And they mingled among the nations.** [Cassiodorus.] God had commanded that the nations be killed lest this happen. And they learned their works and served their graven images (Num. 33), and thus it became a stumbling block to them. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] This was because they did not destroy the nations but mingled with them. Or, the promised land which had been given to them as a reward was turned into ruin for those who transgressed, because by conformity to the nations they became idolaters there.

**VERSE 35.**—“And they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons.”

**And they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons** [Augustine, Cassiodorus], that is, to idols, as was the custom of the nations. Although that history does not narrate this, the prophet cannot lie here; [Col. 0968A] and, if it did not happen in the first generation, it did at least happen in the following one.

**VERSE 36.**—“And they poured out innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the graven images of Canaan.”

**And they poured out innocent blood** [Augustine, Cassiodorus], namely, the blood of little children, who were strangers to consenting to that crime. I mean their own sons, lest you suppose they were strangers, and their daughters, whom they sacrificed to the graven images of Canaan.

**VERSE 37.**—“And the land was slain by bloodshed and defiled by their works, and they committed fornication by their inventions.”

**And the land was slain by bloodshed.** [Augustine.] This is a figurative expression in which the container is put for [Col. 0968B] what it contains. The sense is: The land was slain by bloodshed—that is, human beings, almost all of whom died through this sin. For by sacrificing their children they killed their own souls. And it was defiled by their works: that is, they were defiled by their works. And they committed fornication by their inventions [Cassiodorus, Augustine]: that is, they were polluted by their adulterous superstitions, which he calls their inventions—not because they first devised or had devised them, but because they imitated others. This is more plainly expressed by the Greek word *epitēdeumata* (ἐπιτηδεύματα), here and above where he said, “they provoked him by their inventions.” Hence other translators render it “pursuits,” “affections,” or “wills.”

**VERSE 38.**—“And the Lord was angry in wrath against his people, and abhorred his inheritance.”

**And the Lord was angry in wrath against his people.** [Augustine.] There is no anger in God; this is said by analogy, as though the power of avenging had been stirred up. And he abhorred [Col. 0968C] his inheritance: that is, he turned away from them, not for their destruction but for discipline, as is suggested by calling them his inheritance. [Cassiodorus.] God’s turning away from them is the worst of all present evils. Hence follows the account of that turning away and ruin.

**VERSE 39.**—“And he delivered them into the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them.”

**And he delivered them into the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them.** [Cassiodorus.] Behold: those who gloried in idols were subjected to the reproach of slavery, serving their enemies—which is hard. For it is grievous to serve one who is hostile and is appeased by no service.

**VERSE 40.**—“And their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled under their hands; often he delivered them.”

**And their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled under their hands** [Cassiodorus]; but the Lord often delivered them. Here God’s twofold mercy is expounded. Above he first set forth God’s benefits, yet their iniquity did not cease; afterwards he introduced punishment, and again had mercy on them in their affliction.

[Col. 0969A] **VERSE 41.**—“But they embittered him by their counsel, and were humbled in their iniquities.”

**But they embittered him by their evil counsel.** [Augustine.] For a human being’s counsel directed to himself is evil when he seeks his own interests, not God’s (Phil. 2). This is what he said above: “They did not wait for the counsel,” namely, of God, which concerns eternal things. And therefore, because they embittered him, they were humbled in their iniquities. Yet though they were wicked, God, full of mercy, did not neglect them; indeed:

**VERSE 42.**—“And he saw when they were afflicted, and heard their prayer.”

**And he saw** [Haimo] with the regard of mercy when they were afflicted [Col. 0969B], and heard their prayer.

**VERSE 43.**—“And he remembered his covenant and repented according to the multitude of his mercies.”

**And he remembered his eternal covenant** [Augustine, Cassiodorus], which he had established with Abraham. Observe that the New Covenant, in which is the coming of the Lord promised to Abraham, is the reason why Israel did not perish under the debt of sin. And he repented according to the multitude of his mercies [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine]. He says “repented” not because repentance can occur in God, but because he changed what he appeared about to do—that is, to destroy them. For then he repents when he sees us repent. He is toward us as we are toward him. Yet God does nothing suddenly; rather, he had eternally foreknown [Col. 0969C] what would happen. He is said to change what seems, according to the causes of things, bound to follow, when contrary causes intervene; but he immutably foresaw both the causes and what would result.

**VERSE 44.**—“And he gave them over to mercies in the sight of all who had taken them captive.”

**And he gave them** [Augustine, Cassiodorus], namely those predestined from that people, over to mercies. He says this in the plural because each person has his own gift (1 Cor. 5 [as cited]), and the whole is of God who has mercy (Rom. 9). Thus he said “mercies” in the plural because of the differing gifts. For prophets, apostles, martyrs, and confessors came from the Jews.

[Cassiodorus.] He gave them over to mercies, and this in the sight of all who had taken them captive [Col. 0969D], that is, of the nations, so that the nations who had previously despised them might marvel at them. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Or, “in the sight of all who had taken them captive” means in the sight of the devil and his angels, who had formerly held them captive. [Augustine.] For they were made free in the presence of demons, beneath whom they had been held captive; after casting these out, Christ perfected healings. Hence the prayer here that he may perfect these healings, when it adds:

**PART VI. VERSE 45.**—“Save us, O Lord our God, and gather us from the nations.”

**Save us.** [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The sixth part. Now that the fullness of praise has been completed, he prays for what he sees will come to pass: that the Church may be gathered from all nations and sing eternal praises. As if he said: You gave us over to mercies in the sight of demons; and, once they have been cast out [Col. 0970A] from us, save us, O Lord our God.

[Alcuin.] Observe that the order is preserved here which the Lord preserves in the Gospel. Here he first speaks of the casting out of demons, then of healing, and thirdly of glorification, when he adds: “And may we glory in your praise.” [Augustine.] For the Lord said in the Gospel: “Behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am consummated” (Luke 13): that is, I am perfected, when all meet in a perfect man, in the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ (Eph. 4). These signify the three states of the Christian religion: two in the present, in which we earn merit; the third in the future, in which we shall triumph.

[Alcuin.] The first is in repentance; the second, in righteousness; the third, in glory. To signify these, the Old Testament celebrates three principal feasts: Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Tabernacles (*Cenopegia*) (Lev. 23). At Passover the lamb was sacrificed; unleavened bread was eaten with bitter lettuces; and ears of grain were roasted in fire (Exod. 12). These signified the mortification of the flesh and the bitterness of repentance. At Pentecost new loaves from the new harvest were offered, through which is understood the state of righteousness, by which we walk in newness of life. At the Feast of Tabernacles, which was the festival of booths, offerings from all the fruits of the year were made in the Temple; this signifies the state of future consummation, when the saints, consecrated in immortality, shall come rejoicing, carrying their sheaves.

These same three states are signified by what the Samaritan did for the wounded man. [Col. 0970C] He first poured in wine, then oil, and afterwards the man was made well. Wine signifies the fervour of repentance; oil, the gentleness of righteousness; and his being made well, the consummation of eternal glorification. They are also signified by Christ’s three days: those of crucifixion, burial, and resurrection. Thus these three states are marked by those three things which the Lord stated. By the casting out of demons is understood repentance, through which we are cleansed from sins; by the perfecting of healings, righteousness; and by the consummation of the third day, the perfection of future glorification.

The same three states are also signified by what is said here. The first state, that of repentance, is marked by the words, “He gave [Col. 0970D] them over to mercies in the sight of all”; the second, the state of righteousness, by “Save us”; and the third, the state of glorification, by “that we may confess and glory.” And gather us from the nations [Augustine], that is, from the Gentiles. Hence the Lord says: “I have other sheep” (John 10), namely from the Gentiles—that is, children of God dispersed among the Gentiles.

Thus John the Evangelist says of Caiaphas, who prophesied: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people, lest the whole nation perish.” But he did not say this of himself; rather, being high priest that year, he prophesied that one was to die for the nation, and not for the nation only—that is, for the Jews—but that he might gather into one the children of God who had been scattered (John 2 [as cited]): that is, gather the children of God dispersed among the Gentiles together with the Jews, [Col. 0971A] so that there might be one flock and one shepherd (John 10). This is what he prays for here when he says: “Gather us from the nations.” But the Jews falsely suppose that this will be fulfilled through Antichrist. Gather us, I say:

**VERSE 46.**—“That we may confess your holy name and glory in your praise.”

**That we may confess** [Cassiodorus, interlinear gloss, Augustine], in the present and in the future, your holy name, and glory in your praise—not in human boasting. Then he briefly sets forth praise itself:

**VERSE 47.**—“Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, from age to age; and all the people shall say: Amen, amen.”

Blessed [Cassiodorus]: as though he said, Let us confess to the Lord, saying: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel.” This is that praise which he desires those who have been gathered together to sing. The Church now sings it, rejoicing in so great a good. Blessed, I say, from age to age. [Augustine] That is, from eternity and unto eternity, because he will be praised without end by those of whom it is said: “Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ages upon ages they shall praise you” (Ps. 83). This is that third consummation of Christ’s body, which shall be in immortality after the casting out of the demons and the completion of healing. For then shall be fulfilled what was prayed at the beginning of the psalm: “Remember us, O Lord, in the good pleasure of your people, that we may see, that we may rejoice, that you may be praised with your inheritance.” — “And all the people shall say.” This is the predestined people, both from the Jews and from the Gentiles: “So be it, so be it”; as though he said: [Col. 0971C] All the predestined will consent to this praise.

## Comparison on Psalm 105: “O give thanks unto the Lord, for he is good, because,” etc.

**Verse 5.** “That we may see the prosperity of your chosen ones, rejoice in the joy of your nation, and be praised with your inheritance.” In the Greek and Hebrew there are three infinitives, where the Latin translator first used two gerunds and then another mood, “that you may be praised,” so that the sense should not be ambiguous. But *ad videndum*, “for seeing,” may be understood either as “that you may see” or “that we may see.” So too in Greek, *τοῦ ἰδεῖν*, “to see”; Hebrew, *LIREOTH*, “to see.” Likewise, Greek *τοῦ εὐφανθῆναι*, “to rejoice,” Hebrew *LISMOAII*, “to rejoice,” may mean either “that you may rejoice” or “that we may rejoice.” Finally, Greek *τοῦ ἐπαινεῖσθαι*, “to be praised,” Hebrew *LEHITHHALLEL*, “to glory or exult”: consequently it ought to have been rendered “for praising” or “for exulting.” This too was ambiguous: either “that you may be praised,” or “that I may glory,” or “that I/we may exult or praise.” Yet Augustine’s exposition suggests that the translator preferred, in the third instance, to say “that you may be praised,” in order to imply that the two preceding expressions should likewise be understood as “that you may see” and “that you may rejoice,” although he brings them into agreement.

**Verse 16.** “He sent fullness into their souls.” Jerome, instead of “fullness,” has “leanness,” and nearly all the others have “emaciation,” which seem contrary to fullness. For the Hebrew has *RAZON*, that is, “leanness.” Münster nevertheless judges the sense to agree. He calls the death itself “leanness of souls.” They thought to fatten their souls with flesh; but the opposite happened to them. Hence Sanctes translates, “destruction in their soul.”

**Verse 30.** “And he appeased.” *VAIEPHALLEL* (“and he prayed”). Jerome: “He judged,” which in the translation of Pagninus is, “he executed justice.” Therefore the Septuagint gave the result: for from the vengeance exercised by Phinehas, appeasement followed. Münster and the Neapolitan, however, translate “he prayed,” which most closely corresponds to “he appeased.”

**Verse 33.** “He distinguished with his lips.” Jerome, instead of “he distinguished,” translates “he commanded,” *VAIEBATTE* (“and he spoke” or “uttered”). Most others translate simply, “he spoke.” Münster, however, has “he spoke rashly.” Campensis agrees: “he wavered,” so that this is understood of Moses hesitating at the waters of contradiction. Augustine further follows this interpretation, although Münster seems to understand it of the people themselves. Jerome, however, takes Moses’ speaking as commanding, or, as in the Commentary, as continually interceding for them. The translator, however, gives the opposite sense to Campensis, referring this to God: because they provoked the Spirit of God, so that he spoke with his lips.

**Verse 37.** “And the land was slain.” Jerome: “It was defiled,” followed by all the others. *VATEHENAPH* might seem to be an error, with “was slain” written in place of “was stained.” Yet the Greek plainly protests: *ἐφονοκτονήθη*, that is, “was slain.” *VATEHENAPH* means “and it was defiled.” Moreover, Jerome, on Isaiah 24, translates this Hebrew word: “the earth was slain by its inhabitants.” Indeed, thus read both our manuscripts and others said to be more correct, from Froben; and meanwhile this is sufficiently apparent from his interpretation of that passage in Jerome. Hence he says: “The first sentence is against those who are lofty on the earth, so that all things now strong may be weakened, because of those who mingled blood with blood and, after the manner of Abel’s blood, caused the blood of the slain to cry out to God.” Thus he writes in the Commentary. There he interprets the two clauses: “the loftiness of the people of the earth was weakened,” and “the earth was slain by its inhabitants.” I therefore wonder that Sanctes says Jerome, in that place in Isaiah, translated, “the earth was defiled by its inhabitants,” and discusses this also in his *Thesaurus*. Augustine likewise discusses it: “We might suppose there to be a scribal error here, and say that he made ‘was slain’ in place of ‘was stained,’ unless we had the benefit of God, who willed his Scriptures to exist in many languages, and thus, on consulting the Greek manuscripts, we saw that it was written: ‘the earth was slain in bloods.’”

## Psalm 106

[Col. 0971]

### Title of the Psalm: “Alleluia, alleluia.”

[Col. 0971D]

“Give thanks to the Lord, because he is good.” Title: “Alleluia, alleluia.” This psalm commends the mercy of God, having “alleluia” twice in its title, just as the preceding psalm, concerning the people of Israel, likewise had it twice. Here too it fittingly occurs twice, because it concerns the universal Church, which consists of a double wall, namely Gentiles and Jews, gathered into one cornerstone (Eph. 2). Therefore it rightly has two alleluias, so that we may say, “Abba, Father,” although *abba* itself means “father”: that is, through the two alleluias we understand the two peoples signified by those two names, though they have the same meaning, which the Apostle used to mark this distinction, saying: “In whom we cry, Abba, Father” (Gal. 4; Rom. 8). This psalm teaches what we are through ourselves—weak and evil—and what we are through God’s mercy—good and children of God. Here human pride is crushed and God’s grace is glorified, grace which delivers from four temptations [Aug.], described in what follows, from which we cannot free ourselves. Intention: it exhorts to confession.

Method. [Cassiodorus, Augustine] There are seven divisions. First, the redeemed are urged to confession. Second, the first temptation is set forth: error, in which there is also hunger—at “They wandered.” Third, the second temptation is set forth: the difficulty of overcoming desires—at “Those sitting in darkness.” Fourth, the third temptation is set forth: weariness in doing good—at “Every food.” Fifth, the fourth temptation is set forth: the storm of the world, shaking the Church and disturbing its ruler—at “Those who go down.” Sixth, the Church, saved through God’s grace, is commended—at “He made rivers.” Seventh, it concerns heretics: when they are destroyed, the Church is raised up—at “And they were made few.” Augustine divides this psalm as we have said. [Note: [Col. 0973] From Cassiodorus, in the discussion of the psalm and in the title.] Hence Cassiodorus says that he has authority to divide the other psalms. Yet he distinguishes this psalm differently. [Augustine] Therefore, the prophet, intending to commend God’s mercy, which delivers from four temptations, first urges all believers to confession, saying:

**Verse 1.** “Give thanks to the Lord, because he is good; because his mercy is forever.”

“Give thanks to the Lord,” [Cassiodorus] in both ways, namely for sins and with praises. No one can do this most fully who has not tasted. [Augustine] Hence elsewhere: “Taste and see, because the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33). Give thanks, I say, by saying this: “Because the Lord is good,” [Col. 0973C] that is, because he is sweet; and truly, “because his mercy is forever,” [Haymo] that is, eternal; and this is what I say concerning his mercy.

**Verse 2.** “Let all who have been redeemed by the Lord now say so: those whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy and gathered from the regions.”

“Let all who have been redeemed,” [Cassiodorus] by Christ’s blood, “by the Lord” [Augustine] say so: those whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy, that is, the devil, and gathered from the regions. He gathered them gradually, not all at once, into one city—[Cassiodorus] into the one people of God, who before were being carried off through altars and groves of demons. From where did he gather them?

**Verse 3.** “From the rising and setting of the sun; from the north and from the sea.”

[Col. 0973D] “From the rising and setting of the sun; from the north and from the sea,” [Cassiodorus] that is, from the south. For by “sea” he means the Ocean on that side; this may be understood of any quarter. Here it is clear that he does not speak of the Jews alone.

### Part II. Verse 4. “They wandered in a wilderness, in a waterless place; they found not the way of an inhabited city.”

“They wandered in a wilderness.” [Augustine] The second part, in which the first temptation—error, in which there is hunger—is expounded. This error concerned the fact that they did not know the way of truth, that is, Christ; there they also suffered the lack of true bread. Notice [Col. 0974A] that the same order is maintained in the remaining temptations: first comes the exposition of the temptation; then the cry for deliverance; third, the hearing of the cry; fourth, in return for being heard, confession, that is, praise. Thus: he redeemed and gathered them, as was necessary, because they wandered, having no way of truth. They wandered, I say, in a wilderness, that is, without God, and in a waterless place, [Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, without true teaching, because they did not find the way which is Christ—the way, I say, of the city of habitation, that is, the way leading to the heavenly city, [Augustine] Jerusalem, where one must dwell. Thus they wandered. And besides error, they suffered want, because they were:

**Verse 5.** “Hungry and thirsty; their soul failed within them.”

[Col. 0974B] “Hungry and thirsty,” [Cassiodorus] because they lacked the word of God as food and the drink of grace. By “hungry and thirsty,” he signifies worldly inquirers, who sought truth among diverse opinions and did not find it; therefore their soul failed from inward good. [Augustine, Haymo, Augustine] And this was because it remained in them—that is, it did not go beyond itself, but considered itself sufficient to itself. Note that when he says, “their soul failed within them,” God’s cruelty is not shown; rather, it is shown how God commends himself—that is, makes himself worthy of commendation—by permitting a person to fail, which is expedient for us. For we fail so that we may ask, and may love him when he comes to help. Therefore, after this error, hunger, and thirst, it is added:

**Verse 6.** “And they cried to the Lord when they were troubled, and he delivered them from their necessities.”

“And they cried.” [Augustine, Haymo] As though he said: And, that is, because their soul failed, therefore, now brought together, they cried to the Lord when troubled by error and hunger; and he delivered them from their necessities, that is, unavoidable evils. What did he do for them? Behold:

**Verse 7.** “And he led them out by the right way, that they might go to a city of habitation.”

And he led out those who wandered into the right way, [Augustine] which is Christ, who says, “I am the way” (John 14). As though he said: He delivered them from ignorance, showing them Christ as the way, so that through this way, by doing good, [Col. 0974D] they might go into the city of habitation, whose way they had not previously found. Behold, he delivered them from error. How he delivered them from the hunger and thirst which burdened them he will say afterward; but first he introduces confession:

**Verse 8.** “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders toward the children of men.”

“Let them give thanks.” [Augustine, Remigius] As though he said: Because he delivered them from error. Therefore let them give thanks for his mercies—not for our merits, strength, or wisdom—and for his wonders shown to the children of men, [Haymo] that is, for those same mercies given through the wondrous manner of redemption. Let these be a cause and matter [Col. 0975A] for all to praise the Lord. [Augustine] As though he said: You who are already experienced, who have been set on the way and directed toward the city, delivered from hunger and thirst, tell those who have not experienced it. For the deliverance follows:

**Verse 9.** “Because he satisfied the empty soul, and filled the hungry soul with good things.”

“Because he satisfied.” [Augustine] As though he said: He not only led them into the way, but delivered them from hunger, because he satisfied the empty soul, [Cassiodorus] which was void and without God; and the hungry soul—that is, one desiring knowledge, when visited by God and longing for a physician—he filled with spiritual good things. [Alcuin] Or “the hungry soul” means one not desiring to know, but failing through excessive starvation. He filled it with good things; and he speaks by analogy with what commonly happens to a person exhausted by extreme hunger: he does not desire to eat, but fails through excessive starvation. [Augustine] Carefully note that in this temptation the stated order is preserved.

### Part III. Verse 10. “Those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in poverty and iron.”

“Those sitting.” [Augustine] The third part, in which the second temptation is set forth: the difficulty of overcoming desires. For one now set in God’s way knows how he ought to live, which before, in error, he did not know; but if he tries to do what he knows, he cannot, bound by evil habit. Therefore he should not strive in his own strength, but cry to the Lord; and what was difficult, namely abstaining from evils, will then become easy. The Lord could give this without difficulty; but then we would not recognize the giver of this good unless we first felt desires prevail and considered that we ourselves could do this. As though he said: He satisfied the empty and hungry soul, namely those sitting—[Cassiodorus] that is, remaining low—because they were bound by evil habit. Sitting, I say, in darkness, that is, in sins, and in the shadow of death, that is, in a vicious life, which is an image of future death: those bound in poverty, because they were poor through want of good, and in iron, because the bonds of sins that bind them are iron and invincible.

**Verse 11.** “Because they provoked the words of God and spurned the counsel of the Most High.”

“Because they provoked.” [Augustine] This again defeats one who tries to overcome: because, not recognizing grace, he attributed things to himself, wishing to establish his own righteousness and rejecting God’s counsel concerning himself. Hence he adds, “Because they provoked.” As though he said: Therefore they are bound in poverty and iron, because they provoked God’s words through pride, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own (Rom. 10). The sense is: [Cassiodorus] acting against God’s words, they refused to live under his rules. Hence he was angry with them. And they spurned the counsel of the Most High. For God’s counsel was that those who were proud should be humbled in distress: this was healthful counsel, that the disease of the world, namely pride, should be healed by the contrary remedy, humility. But they first despised this. Therefore:

**Verse 12.** “And their heart was humbled by labors; they became weak, and there was none to help.”

“They became weak in labors,” [Augustine] powerless by themselves to resist vices, and there was no other to help. For the commandment increases sin, and in these labors at last [Col. 0976A] their heart was humbled. When God withholds help, you may struggle against vices, but you cannot conquer. And when you are oppressed by your evil habit, your heart will be humbled, that it may learn to cry out. Hence he adds:

**Verse 13.** “And they cried to the Lord when they were troubled, and he delivered them from their necessities.”

“And they cried to the Lord when troubled, and he delivered them from their necessities.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus] In a similar case, the same statement as above follows: deliverance follows the cry.

**Verse 14.** “And he led them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke their bonds.”

And he led them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke the bonds of their difficulty. [Augustine] Then praise follows for their deliverance:

**Verse 15.** “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders toward the children of men.”

“Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and for his wonders toward the children of men.” [Augustine] This has been explained above: why they ought to give thanks.

**Verse 16.** “Because he broke the brazen gates and shattered the iron bars.”

Because he conquered these difficulties: [Augustine, Haymo, Cassiodorus] [Col. 0976C] namely, he broke the brazen gates, that is, natural desire, and shattered the iron bars, that is, diabolical suggestions. The brazen gates are people’s vicious habits, which do not permit those shut in to go out. The bars are unclean spirits, which bolt the gates. He uses brazen gates and iron bars to signify strength; but God’s power breaks them.

**Verse 17.** “He took them up from the way of their iniquity; for because of their injustices they were humbled.”

“He took them up,” [Gloss] into the height of good work, from the way of their iniquity. He says “took them up,” [Cassiodorus] because he had formerly been far from the proud. They were humbled to the overthrow of destruction; hence he adds: “For because of their injustices”—as though he said: I rightly said, “from the way of their iniquity,” for because of their injustices, [Augustine] that is, because through pride they rendered the credit to themselves, not to God, establishing their own injustice—they were humbled, that is, cast down to destruction; and this is understood in a bad sense. [Cassiodorus, Augustine] Or it may be understood in a good sense: “They were humbled,” that is, they found that they could do nothing without God.

### Part IV. Verse 18. “Their soul abhorred every food, and they drew near even to the gates of death.”

“Every food.” [Augustine] The fourth part, in which the third temptation, weariness, is set forth. For after one has come from ignorance to truth, from error to the way, from hunger for wisdom to the word of faith, and after he has overcome difficulties so as to live without reproach, weariness still remains: at times he may take no pleasure in reading or praying. He has escaped ignorance and desire, but dies of weariness. Therefore those who earlier languished with hunger are likewise endangered by loathing. Do not therefore think them safe because they are full, for they also die through loathing. This is the meaning of “every food,” etc. As though he said: He took them up from the way of iniquity, yet their soul abhorred every food, [Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, God’s word, by which the soul lives. Lest you suppose this slight, he adds: “And they drew near even to the gates of death,” that is, the soul’s failing. [Augustine] Therefore, if God’s word delights you, do not attribute even this to yourself, nor become puffed up with arrogance on that account; and, eagerly consuming food, do not proudly attack those endangered by loathing. Understand that this is not from yourself to yourself; feel also your own fault and weakness; cry out, and do what follows:

**Verse 19.** “And they cried to the Lord when they were troubled, and he delivered them from their necessities.”

“And they cried to the Lord when troubled, and he delivered them from their necessities.” [Augustine] He then adds how he delivered them.

**Verse 20.** “He sent his word and healed them, and delivered them from their destructions.”

“He sent his word and healed” [Augustine] those whose weakness was caused by loathing; he healed them and delivered them, not from error or hunger, nor from the difficulty of overcoming [Col. 0977C] sins, but from their destructions, that is, from the corruption of mind which loathes what is sweet. Therefore, also from this:

**Verse 21.** “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders toward the children of men.”

“Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and for his wonders toward the children of men.” [Note: [Col. 0977D] Jerome, Book I against the Pelagians.] What has been explained, do not explain again, lest you do a thing already done.

**Verse 22.** “That they may offer a sacrifice of praise and proclaim his works with exultation.”

“That they may offer a sacrifice of praise.” [Augustine] For now the Lord is sweet so that he may be praised; and “that they may proclaim his works with exultation,” not with weariness and sorrow.

### Part V. Verse 23. “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing works in many waters.”

“Those who go down.” [Augustine] The fifth part, in which the fourth temptation is explained: the storm of the world. For one delivered from the three temptations may now perhaps be worthy to have a people entrusted to him, to be appointed in the tabernacle of the ship, that is, the Church. There the fourth temptation occurs: the storm of the world, shaking the Church and troubling its ruler. This danger especially concerns rulers: the more they are honored, the more they are endangered. Yet subjects will not be free of this danger if the whole ship is endangered. As though he said: “Let them proclaim his works”—[Col. 0978A] [Haymo, Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine] namely, those who descend from the contemplative life into the sea, that is, into the laborious active life; or into the sea, into the storm of the world, so as to suffer the waves of temptations for Christ. They are in ships, that is, in the churches which they govern; these are called ships because they are struck by the waves of the world but not broken. They do works—while they preach and do such things—in many waters, that is, among many peoples.

**Verse 24.** “They saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.”

They, in a special sense. As though he said: More than others, they saw the Lord’s works and his wonders in the deep of the world, [Augustine, Haymo] that is, they saw what God wonderfully works in human hearts. For the deep of the world is the heart of human beings, from which winds burst forth and storms of seditions and dissensions arise, by God’s permission.

**Verse 25.** “He spoke, and the spirit of the tempest stood forth; and its waves were raised.”

“He spoke, and it stood.” [Augustine] As though he said: And what happens in this deep? Behold, persecution arises by God’s permission. This is the meaning: God, willing that both the ruler and the passenger, or the one being guided, should cry to him, spoke, that is, permitted it; and the spirit of the tempest arose, [Augustine, Haymo] that is, tyrannical persecution or the devil.

[Cassiodorus] Or otherwise, from “They saw.” As though he said: Those rulers themselves saw—that is, understood spiritually—the works of the Lord: for example, baptism in the Red Sea, and likewise in other things; so that they may see his wonders in the deep, because they consider his works with profound judgment. But lest they should become swollen with this, he sets forth their storms, adding: “He spoke, and the spirit of the tempest stood forth.” This does not change. And what did the spirit do? Behold: its waves were raised. He shows how:

**Verse 26.** “They go up to the heavens and go down to the depths; their soul was wasting away in evils.”

The persecutors [Augustine, Cassiodorus] go up in daring to the heavens, when they raise themselves against God through worldly exaltations. And they go down in fear to the depths, [Cassiodorus, Gloss] when they fall into despair and fear; or, to the depths, [Augustine] that is, to hell. And amid these evils the soul of the rulers wasted away.

**Verse 27.** “They were troubled and moved like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up.”

“They were troubled” in confusion of mind, [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine] and were moved: experienced rulers feel this. Moved, I say, like a drunken person. As drunkards stagger, so their prosperity or adversity proves greater than their powers. In calm they appear wise, when they speak or read; but when the storm comes, every human counsel fails, and they do not see what ought to be done. Hence he adds: “And all their wisdom was swallowed up.” Thus the Apostle says: “We were burdened beyond measure, so that we were weary even of life; and we had within ourselves the answer of death, that we might not trust in ourselves” (2 Cor. 1). For whichever way they turn, waves roar, the tempest rages, their arms fail; they cannot see where the prow should strike, where the ship should be driven or allowed to go, or from what rocks it should be held back lest it perish. [Cassiodorus] It remains, then, to cry out, that God may make their heart firm, lest it be tossed about by temptations.

**Verse 28.** “And they cried to the Lord when they were troubled, and he brought them out of their necessities.”

**Verse 29.** “And he made its storm a breeze, and its waves were still.”

And he made its storm into a breeze of the sea, [Haymo, Gloss] that is, of the world: he made the storms endured by preachers into a breeze, a light wind—that is, moderate and bearable storms. Or, “into a breeze,” that is, into the serenity of eternal rest. And its waves were still.

**Verse 30.** “And they rejoiced because they were still, and he led them to the haven of their desire.”

And the weary rulers rejoiced because the waves were still; this is what the weary do after labor: [Cassiodorus] they rejoice. And the Lord led them to the haven of their desire, [Gloss] that is, to desired tranquillity or eternal blessedness. Therefore:

**Verse 31.** “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders toward the children of men.”

**Verse 32.** “That they may exalt him in the assembly of the people and praise him in the seat of the elders.”

That all may exalt him in the assembly, [Gloss] that is, for the assembly of the people: that all may praise him for those well governed. And that all may praise him in the seat, that is, for the seat of the elders: that all may praise him for those who govern well. Or thus: [Augustine] let those who are in the assembly of the people exalt him—that is, let the lesser people who are governed praise him. And let those who are in the seat of the elders praise him—that is, let the elders who govern praise him. Behold, when he says “in the assembly,” he plainly shows that he speaks of the Church, in which all the foregoing things occur.

### Part VI. Verse 33. “He turned rivers into a wilderness and springs of water into thirst.”

“He turned rivers.” [Alcuin] The sixth part. Up to this point he has said how he brings a person to the city, teaches him how to live, feeds him, and governs him. [Augustine] Next the Church herself is commended, so that in all things God’s grace may be proclaimed to us: he resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (Jas. 4). And so that it may clearly appear of whom the psalm has spoken from the beginning, it is further commended where it says how he even makes the evil of enemies profit the Church. Here, then, is the commendation of the Church saved by God’s grace, not by her own merit; subsequently the affliction of enemies due to their pride is recalled. When they have been extinguished, [Col. 0980A] the Church is raised up, and has advanced through snares and domestic injuries inflicted by heretics. Thus God’s benefits toward the Church are plainly shown. [Augustine] As though he said: “Let them exalt him in the Church.” And if you ask why—what did he do in the Church? Behold: he resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. First he says how he resists the proud: “He turned rivers,” that is, the Jews, where there were waters, namely teachings, and prophets exercised healing, “into a wilderness,” because now there is among them no prophet, no faith in Christ, no priest, sacrifice, or temple.
