He says the same again in different words: “He turned springs of water,” that is, the Jews, from whom waters of teaching flowed to others, “into thirst.” Again he says the same:

**Verse 34.** “A fruitful land into saltiness, because of the wickedness of those who dwell in it.”

“A fruitful land,” [Cassiodorus] formerly according to the good works it did, he turned into saltiness, that is, barrenness. This is understood through saltiness because salty moisture, where it prevails, removes fertility. And by what desert? Behold: he did this “because of the wickedness,” that is, on account of the wickedness, of those dwelling in it—namely, the ruling scribes and Pharisees—because of the wickedness of those who inhabited that land, [Augustine] that is, the tabernacle of the Lord, with deceitful minds. Behold how he resists the proud. Then he says how he gave grace to the humble.

**Verse 35.** “He turned a wilderness into pools of water, and waterless land into springs of water.”

[Col. 0980C] He turned the wilderness, [Haymo, Gloss] that is, the Gentiles, into pools of water, so that waters might remain in them. He repeats the same thing: he turned land formerly without water into springs of water, from which living waters might flow to others.

**Verse 36.** “And there he placed the hungry, and they established a city of habitation.”

And there he placed [Augustine, Cassiodorus] the hungry—that is, in grace—those who would receive it eagerly. Hence: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied” (Ps. 21). And such persons, firmly obeying God’s commandments, established a city of habitation, that is, the Church, in which for the present they dwell in hope.

**Verse 37.** “And they sowed fields and planted vineyards, and produced the fruit of increase.”

And they sowed fields with God’s word and planted [Col. 0980D] vineyards. [Cassiodorus] They sow fields and plant vineyards who purify their bodies by heavenly instruction so that they may bear the fruit of good works. Hence he adds: “And they produced the fruit of increase,” that is, natural, not degenerate, fruit.

**Verse 38.** “And he blessed them, and they were multiplied exceedingly; and he did not diminish their beasts of burden.”

And therefore he blessed them, [Cassiodorus, Gloss, Alcuin] in contrast to the barren fig tree which is cursed. They were multiplied in number or merit through blessing, and this “exceedingly,” that is, greatly. Or he says “exceedingly” because many are called but few are chosen. And “their beasts of burden,” [Augustine] that is, the simple but useful persons, not taught by God but nevertheless full of faith, he did not diminish; because the foundation of God stands firm, since “the Lord knows those who are his” [Col. 0981A] (2 Tim. 2), and the righteous person cares for the lives of his beasts.

### Part VII. Verse 39. “And they were made few and afflicted by the distress of evils and sorrow.”

“And they were made few.” [Augustine] The seventh part, in which something is also said concerning heretics, by whom the Church is shaken, as it were, by civil wars. Thus divine benefits toward the Church are also commended. Notice that he joins the words as though he spoke of those mentioned before, although above he treated of the good and here of heretics. He speaks of them as if they were the same as those previously mentioned because of common sacraments and an appearance of piety, not because of spiritual power. Hence John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2). [Augustine, Alcuin] That is, they went out from the multitude of the called, but were not of the small number of the chosen. As though he said: The good were multiplied exceedingly, while heretics, presuming upon themselves, were made few. For all who are divided from the unity of faith are few, not so much in number as in merit. [Jerome] Many, however, persevere in the unity of faith. Therefore the prophet Hosea says concerning heretics: “Give them, O Lord” (Hos. 9)—what will you give them? “A womb without children and dry breasts.” And they were afflicted, namely the heretics, by the distress of evils and sorrow, [Cassiodorus] that is, by the snares of the devil and his angels. For distress is sorrow to those who forsake the author of salvation.

**Verse 40.** “Contempt was poured out upon princes, and he caused them to wander in a pathless place and not in a way.”

“Contempt was poured out,” [Augustine, Alcuin] or, according to another reading, “he poured out contempt,” upon the princes of the heretics, that is, upon heresiarchs and teachers of heresies. For they were rejected by the Church and were more despised because they wished to be princes. Of them the Lord says through the prophet Hosea: “They reigned, but not through me; they became princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. 8). [Augustine, Alcuin] These became salt that lost its savor, cast out and trodden underfoot by men; what is more worthless and despised than this?

Or otherwise: “And they were made few” concerns those same good persons of whom he spoke before. As though he said: They were multiplied, and then those good persons were made few, that is, diminished through those people, namely the heretics. And the good who persevered in faith were afflicted by the distress of evils, namely heretics—that is, by distress brought about [Col. 0981D] by heretics—and by sorrow felt for those who fell. Therefore the good were afflicted because contention was poured out over their princes, namely the heretics: [Augustine] that is, because proud heresiarchs contend against Catholics. And the Lord caused those princes to wander, or led them astray, by leaving them to themselves. Hence: “God gave them over to a reprobate mind.” Thus he led them astray by giving them to themselves. For, strictly speaking, they lead themselves astray: whoever thinks himself something when he is nothing deceives himself. Therefore he led them astray by abandoning them. And this occurred “in a pathless place and not in a way.” Those good persons of whom he spoke above were set in the way and directed toward the city of habitation. But these proud persons, abandoned by God, were led astray in a pathless place and are in no way on the way. For how can one be on the way who holds a part and abandons the whole? And what did he do with those led astray? Behold:

**Verse 41.** “And he helped the poor out of want, and made families like sheep.”

And from among them he helped the poor person. [Augustine] God could have allowed them always to remain within, but we would not profit from them. Yet when, separated by controversies, they trouble us, in us arises a zeal for investigation and an example of fear, so that one who stands may see that he does not fall, as they fell. The sense is: the proud were cast down and the humble instructed. This he says thus: “And he helped the poor out of want,” or out of poverty—that is, the one who considers himself a beggar and needy person, who gives nothing to himself but expects everything from God’s mercy, crying and knocking at the Lord’s door so that it may be opened to him. He is greatly helped by the very separation [Col. 0982B] of heretics. And what comes to pass in the poor person helped by those led astray? Many families. Hence he adds: “And he made that poor person families.” The poor person, I say, existing—or the families existing—like sheep, [Cassiodorus, Augustine] because of simplicity and innocence. Behold, you thought him one poor person, but this poor person is many families, that is, many churches; yet the Church is also one, and one sheep. [Haymo, Augustine] Or thus: He helped the poor person, and through the poor person who was helped made families like sheep, that is, he preserves families in innocence. These mysteries, however, lay hidden for a long time and are therefore found sweetly.

### Verse 42. — “The righteous shall see and rejoice; and all their iniquity shall stop its mouth.”

[Col. 0982C] The righteous shall see and rejoice. [Aug.] Behold the goal toward which the psalm tends: namely, to show that the good are exalted through the mercy of God, and the evil crushed through pride. Hence it adds: And all iniquity, chattering against the truth when convicted, shall stop its mouth.

### Verse 43. — “Who is wise and will keep these things, and understand the mercies of the Lord?”

Who is wise? [Aug.] Behold the conclusion of the psalm. As if he said: Since the Lord helps the poor man in every way, who then is wise and will keep these things?—that is, so as to be poor, and not rich; not proud, not puffed up. As if he said: Whoever is wise will keep these things. Why will he keep them? That is, because he will understand—not his own merits, not his own powers, glorying in these—but [Col. 0982D] the mercies of the Lord: namely, that He delivers from error, from evil habit, from weariness, and from shipwreck; and finally establishes him among the people, not where He resists the proud, but where He gives grace to the humble (James 4). He also understands what God has done, so that one who remains within may be multiplied rather than diminished by going out. The righteous see these things and rejoice, and iniquity stops its mouth.

## Comparison on Psalm 106: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good,” etc.

### Verse 17. — “He received them.”

For these two words Jerome gives one word only: “fools.” The other translators do likewise. Hebrew: **EVILIM**. The Septuagint seem to have diverged from the root **ILLEM**, “he gathered,” so that it is **ILLAMAM**, “he gathered,” and thus, “he received them,” even if that verb properly denotes gathering sheaves.

[Col. 0983A]

### Verse 25. — “The spirit of the storm stood.”

Faber, together with his Blind Man, attacked this passage with three darts, by which he tries to show that this reading opposes the Hebrew truth. First, because Jerome translated: “The wind of the tempest arose.” I add also what Münster translated: “He raises a stormy wind.” Yet for the spirit of the storm to stand, and for the wind of the tempest to arise or be stirred up, are mutually contradictory.

The answer is ready. Since the Hebrew says **VAJAAMED**, and this is the verb called *hiphil*, it properly means “he caused to stand,” as the interpreters for Cajetan also translated it. Nebiensis, Sanctes, and Pellicanus likewise gave a term wholly similar to our reading: “it stood.” If you had seen Augustine’s exposition, you would have understood what it means for the spirit of the storm to stand. He says: “What is ‘it stood’? It remained; it endured.”

The second objection is: How can the spirit of the storm stand, when it immediately follows, “and its waves were lifted up”? If it stood, then it was calmed. If its waves were lifted up, where was the calm? But hear Augustine again: [Col. 0983B] “It still disturbs, tosses for a long time, rages, and does not pass away.” Yet it would not even have been contrary to Hebrew truth if we understood it thus: “He caused the wind of the storm to stand,” that is, He calmed it. For to set a wind in place has two senses: either to stir up one which was not there, or to restrain one already stirred up. Nor does what follows protest against this: “and its waves were lifted up.” Indeed, in several ways the sovereignty of divine power is signified by the phrase, “the spirit of the storm stood”; and again, when it pleased Him, “its waves were lifted up.”

The third objection, taken from verse 29—“And He made its storm into a breeze”—as though it contradicted the earlier statement that the spirit of the storm stood, is removed by what has just been said.

### Verse 40. — “Contestation was poured out upon princes.”

[Col. 0984A] Here *contentio* (“contention” or “disputation”) may seem to have been written through a copyist’s error in place of *contemptio* (“contempt”). For Augustine has and expounds “contempt.” In Greek likewise one reads ἐξουδένωσις, “contempt” or “despising.” Moreover, Jerome and the other Hebraists translated “despising.”

I do not wish, by a foolish contention over the word *contentio*, to defend the error of copyists; nevertheless, I find several ancient commentators who formerly read and explained *contentio*. For St Gregory, *Morals*, book IX, chapter 4, on Job 29, “Princes ceased to speak,” says: “Who else can be understood in this passage as these leaders or princes, except the authors of heretical perversity? Of them it is said through the psalm: ‘Contestation was poured out upon their princes, and they led them astray in a trackless place and not in a way.’ Contestation is rightly said to have been poured out upon them, because they contradict one another in their reciprocal arguments.” And Cassiodorus, somewhat earlier, briefly says: “The priests of heretics are indicated and marked, concerning whom ‘contestation was poured out’ is deservedly said, because they contend not with saving doctrine but only with deadly talkativeness.” Finally, Arnobius, earlier than these, reads [Col. 0984B] and interprets *contentio*, though not so explicitly.

Accordingly, it is worth investigating whether anything may be found in Hebrew corresponding to *contentio*, and not merely to “despising,” although despisings commonly arise from disputes, and conversely. Come then. Here we read the Hebrew **BUZ**. Next, we find two words: **BAZAH**, which means “he despised,” etc.; and **BUZ**, which means “he plundered,” “he despoiled.” Hence I do not see what prevents **BUZ** from being able to mean “plundering,” in which contention sometimes has its proper place. Yet, as I said before, I would not have confidence placed in my own judgment. At last, however, the Chaldee translation clearly supports us: “He sent contention upon the princes.”

## Psalm 107

[Col. 0983]

### Title of the Psalm: “A Song of a Psalm, for David himself.”

[Col. 0983C]

“My heart is ready.” Title: “A song of a psalm, for David himself.” [Cassiod.] This is the sixth psalm concerning the two natures in Christ, in which many of the same things are contained that were stated above in two other psalms; but the things which differ are only slightly different. [Aug.] For this psalm is composed from the final portions of the two preceding psalms, namely Psalms 56 and 59, whose titles differ. The final part of Psalm 56 is the first part of this psalm, down to the verse where it says, “And thy glory over all the earth.” From there, “over the earth,” to the end, is the final part of Psalm 59. [Aug.]

Therefore it should be known that titles which appear to be based on history should be understood according to prophecy, that is, according to spiritual understanding; [Col. 0983D] and that those two psalms converge upon a single meaning, their parts being joined in this psalm not by the surface of history but by the depth of prophecy. Its title is unlike that of either of those psalms, except that here also it says “for David himself,” as there. This psalm, composed from the two whose titles differ, is therefore entitled “for David himself,” in order to signify that, although God spoke to the fathers long ago in many portions and in many ways through the prophets, He has at last spoken to us in the Son (Hebrews 1), whom He sent so that the utterances of the prophets might be fulfilled; and so that, wonderfully, things said in different psalms [Note: [Col. 0983D] From Cassiodorus, at the conclusion of the psalm.] might come together in this psalm in a single harmony, [Col. 0984C] like diverse flavors combined for food for the soul.

Thus even singers may still compose many things together. So David too is read in Chronicles to have sung the praises of God before the ark by gathering diverse portions of psalms into one (1 Chronicles 6). And things which in no way conflict are fittingly joined. But the words taken from the two aforesaid psalms are directed in this psalm to another sense than that which they contain there according to the surface of history. [Aug., Alcuin.] For the first treats of David’s flight; the second, of his victory and strength. But this psalm treats of something else: namely, Christ’s humility according to his humanity and his exaltation according to his divinity. This is shown by the changed title.

The meaning of the title is this: this song of a psalm is called a song [Cassiod.] because it concerns [Col. 0984D] the gladness of the mind, and a psalm because it exhorts to good works. For song pertains to divine things; psalm, to active works. It is attributed to David himself, that is, to Christ, who speaks here. Its intention is to admonish us to believe that Christ is God and man.

Method. The psalm has two parts. First, Christ gives thanks to the Father because, having undergone the Passion, he rose into glory. Second, he declares what salvation has been wrought for the whole earth, over which the glory of the Lord is spread, beginning, “That thy beloved may be delivered.” Therefore Christ, insofar as he is man, giving thanks to the Father, says:

### Verse 1. — “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody in my glory.”

[Col. 0985A] O God, my heart is ready for praises, [Cassiod.] because it is not delayed by sins. And he repeats: My heart is ready. Therefore I will sing within myself and among those who are mine, and I will make melody. He joins these two because good works ought always to be joined with spiritual song. [Haymo.] And this is “in my glory,” that of the resurrection: that is, in contemplation of the glorious resurrection.

Above, in the psalm from which this is taken, it says: “I will sing and make melody. Arise, my glory.” [Aug.] But the sense there is no different from what is said here, since there too “Arise, my glory” is said in order that singing and psalmody might take place in it.

### Verse 2. — “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp; I will arise at dawn.”

Arise. [Gloss, interlinear.] The Father says this to the Son, or the Son says it to the body united to himself. As if he said: I will sing and make melody. [Cassiod.] But in order that this may happen, arise—you who are the psaltery in respect of uprightness of conduct, and the harp in respect of the Passion. Then the Son answers the Father: I shall rise at the dawn of the Lord’s Day, and then:

### Verse 3. — “I will give thanks to thee among the peoples, O Lord; I will make melody to thee among the nations.”

I will give thanks to thee among the peoples, O Lord, and I will make melody to thee among the nations. [Cassiod.] And rightly so:

### Verse 4. — “For thy mercy is great above the heavens, and thy truth even unto the clouds.”

For thy mercy is great above the heavens, [Cassiod.] that is, above spiritual beings, because angels there also enjoy his benefits. In the other preceding psalm it says: “Thy mercy has been magnified unto the heavens,” [Col. 0985C] [Aug.] namely, so that it may be great even in the heavens, which is also what is said here. For the meaning of these words and of those is the same. And thy truth is great unto the apostolic clouds, [Cassiod.] by which he makes the peoples rain-soaked. Then he supplies two further things in response to the two previously mentioned. As if he said: Because thy mercy is above the heavens, therefore, O:

### Verse 5. — “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let thy glory be over all the earth, that thy beloved may be delivered.”

O God the Word, be exalted, [Haymo, Cassiod.] that is, show thyself high above the heavens. For he whose mercy the heavens possess ought rightly to be exalted above the heavens. And because thy truth reaches unto the clouds, therefore [Col. 0985D] thy glory ought rightly to be exalted over all the earth.

“That thy beloved may be delivered.” This is the second part, where he states what salvation has been wrought for the whole earth over which the Lord’s glory is spread. [Cassiod.] Here too are shown the humility of Christ’s humanity and the power of his majesty. [Alcuin.] As if he said: Be exalted; and, so that thy beloved may be delivered in the future, do this in the present:

### Verse 6. — “Save me by thy right hand, and hear me; God has spoken in his holy one.”

Save me. [Gloss, interlinear.] Christ says this for his members: that is, save those who are one with me, lest they fall. And do this by thy right hand, that is, by thy favor and propitiation; and hear me as I pray for them. [Col. 0986A] [Cassiod.] Or Christ speaks of himself and asks to be saved in the resurrection, so that the faithful may be delivered, since through such a sign they perceived his divinity. As if he said: That I may sing and make melody, save me [Alcuin, Gloss, interlinear] in the resurrection, by thy right hand, that is, through the Word who is the arm of the Father. Thus may thy beloved be delivered, and hear me.

The order of the words is reversed. For he says, “Save me and hear,” in place of “Hear and save me.” “God has spoken.” As if he said: I pray to be heard, which is beyond doubt, because God has spoken in me, his Holy One. [Cassiod.] He does not say “through the holy one,” lest he be thought to speak through him as through prophets and apostles. For in the man Christ he is present through the grace of union, but in them through the grace of adoption. [Note: [Col. 0985D] From Augustine, on Psalm 89.] Or the prophet says this concerning Christ. As if [Col. 0986B] he said: Thus he prayed, and what he prayed shall happen, because God has spoken in his Holy One, that is, in Christ.

### Verse 7. — “I will rejoice, and divide Shechem, and measure out the valley of tabernacles.”

I will rejoice. [Alcuin.] Here Christ speaks in the person of the Church and says, “I will rejoice,” [Aug.] or, according to another reading, “I shall be exalted.” In the other psalm above he said, “I shall be glad,” but here, “I shall be exalted.” This is quite fitting, since joy concerns exaltation. “And I will divide Shechem, and measure out the valley of tabernacles.”

### Verse 8. — “Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; and Ephraim is the taking up of my head.”

Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine. These things were fully expounded above. And Ephraim is mine, [Aug.] [Col. 0986C] that is, my fruitfulness, which is the taking up of my head: that is, this fruitfulness comes both from the fact that the head took me up, or that I took it up. Above, in the other psalm, “strength” occurs, where here “taking up” is read. This fits well, because by taking us up it makes us strong—namely, when Christ himself takes us up, or when we take him up. [Cassiod.] Or thus: Ephraim, that is, fruitfulness, is the taker-up of my head, because when my head took up the crown of thorns, it became fruitful beyond all measure. For it gained the whole world.

### Verse 9. — “Judah is my king; Moab is the vessel of my hope.”

Judah, from whom Christ came. Therefore Christ is understood through Judah, [Aug.] as “my king”; Moab is “the vessel of my hope.” [Col. 0986D]

### Verse 10. — “Upon Idumea I will stretch out my sandal; foreigners have become my friends.”

### Verse 11. — “Who will lead me into the fortified city? Who will lead me even unto Idumea?”

Who will lead me into the fortified city? [Cassiod.] Christ speaks here. And who will lead me even unto Idumea? Christ asks as a man, so that in reply he may deny that this can be accomplished by man. The fortified city is hell, which no one could open. Idumea denotes the Gentiles, to whom he became known after the resurrection. These things could be done by divinity alone.

### Verse 12. — “Wilt not thou, O God, who hast cast us off? And wilt thou not go forth, O God, with our armies?”

[Col. 0987A] Wilt not thou, O Lord, do this—thou who hast cast us off? [Cassiod.] He says “us” in the plural, because Christ suffers these things with his members; for he himself too is cast off when they are exposed to tribulations. Above, however, he spoke in the singular, saying, “Who will lead me?” and so forth. And thou wilt not go forth, O God, with our armies.

### Verse 12. — “Give us help in tribulation, for vain is the salvation of man.”

### Verse 13. — “In God we shall do valiantly, and he himself shall bring our enemies to nothing.”

In God we shall do valiantly, and he himself shall bring our enemies to nothing, [Aug.] those who in the other psalm above were called “tribulators.” I refer all the expositions of these matters to Psalm 69.

## Comparison on Psalm 107: “My heart is ready, O God,” etc.

[Col. 0988A]

### Verse 1. — “My heart is ready.”

The phrase is repeated although it is not in the Hebrew, but is in the Septuagint, for emphasis, as has been noted on several occasions. The other matters which seem to create variation have been reconciled as far as we could in Psalm 59, where the same verses occur as here from verse 5 to the end.

### Verse 10. — “One point should be noted.”

Jerome, writing to Sunia and Fretela, says that the phrase *mihi alienigenae subditi sunt*—“foreigners have been made subject to me,” as it is read here in Latin—stands in Greek and Hebrew as “they became friends to me”; whereas in Psalm 59 it is “they were made subject.” For he says that here he reads ἐφίλωσαν, that is, “they became friends,” and that this occurs in all translators; but there, ὑπετάγησαν, that is, “they were made subject.” Yet in the manuscripts which it has been possible to see, we have ὑπετάγησαν in both places.

## Psalm 108

[Col. 0987]

### Title of the Psalm: “Unto the end, a psalm for David himself.”

[Col. 0987B]

“O God, my praise.” Title: “Unto the end, a psalm of David.” [Note: [Col. 0987D] From Cassiodorus, at the conclusion of the psalm.] The title is clear. This psalm is the fifth among those which treat more fully of Christ’s Passion. For that this is prophecy concerning Christ is shown in the Acts of the Apostles, [Aug.] where Peter says that what is read here was prophesied about Judas: namely, “Let another receive his bishopric” (Acts 1).

Yet not everything said here can be understood of Judas alone, but rather of the class of Christ’s enemies and of the ungrateful Jews. For just as Peter bears the type of the Church, so Judas bears the persons of Christ’s enemies; and the things expressly said about Judas also suit them, such as, “Let another receive his bishopric.” [Cassiod.] Intention: it admonishes us to avoid Judas’s wickedness [Col. 0987C] and imitate Christ’s humility.

Method: the psalm has three parts. First, Christ begins with prayer and rebukes the Jews, who render evil for good. Second, he prophesies what the wicked will receive for their impiety, beginning, “Set thou a sinner over him.” Third, he prays that he may attain the resurrection and that his enemies may suffer disgrace, beginning, “But thou, O Lord.” [Cassiod.] Therefore Christ, insofar as he is man, praying to the Father, says:

### Verse 1. — “O God, do not be silent concerning my praise, because the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful man have been opened against me.”

O God, [Aug.] who alone art true of thyself, do not be silent concerning my praise which is from thee, since one must believe thee when thou praisest. For the praise of the truthful God is true. And his prayer was fulfilled when the only-begotten Son was proclaimed [Col. 0987D] to be the Son of God, because the mouth of the sinner—[Cassiod., Aug.] behold the beautiful contrast! As if he said: Therefore do not be silent concerning praise, because the wicked do not keep silence concerning reproach. And this is what follows: “Because the mouth of the sinner and of the deceitful man has been opened against me.” While my power was concealed, as though what was covered with deceit burst forth into speech from the deceitful man. Yet he is not to be believed, because the false reproach of a lying man [Col. 0988B] is false. But that deceit bursts out into speech is shown when he says:

### Verse 2. — “They have spoken against me with a deceitful tongue, and surrounded me with words of hatred; and they have attacked me without cause.”

They spoke with a deceitful tongue, saying: [Aug.] “Master, we know that thou art true,” etc. (Matthew 22). And this was against me, because they said it in order to entrap me. Then they surrounded me with open words of hatred, crying: “Crucify, crucify” (John 19). And they attacked me gratuitously, without just cause. For as uprightness pleases the godly for its own sake, so injustice pleases the ungodly.

### Verse 3. — “In return for my love, they slandered me; but I gave myself to prayer.”

[Col. 0988C] “In return for my love,” [Aug.] that is, in return for the fact that they ought to have loved me, they slandered me, denying that I was the Son of God and saying that I cast out demons by Beelzebub (Luke 11). Or according to another reading: “In return for my love, they killed me and slandered me.” They killed me because they slandered me. For those who slander Christ in his members do greater harm, killing the souls of believers, than those who killed his flesh, soon to rise again. The meaning is: They rendered evil for good, which is the worse thing. They slandered; but I, on the contrary, prayed—even for them, and not only for the faith of the disciples.

### Verse 4. — “And they rendered me evil for good, and hatred for my love.”

[Col. 0988D] And they rendered. [Aug.] As if he said: I rendered good for evils; they slandered me, though I prayed for them. Thus they rendered evil for good. What evils for what goods? Behold: “and hatred for my love.” Here lies all their great guilt. For their persecution could not harm one who died not under necessity but willingly; yet the whole crime of the persecutors [Col. 0989A] is hatred, even though the suffering of the one endured it voluntarily.

[Aug.] Here it should be noted that, in rendering good or evil, there are six distinctions, which can easily be recognized when listed. Namely: to render good for evil, and not to render evil for evil. These two belong to the good, and the former is indeed better. Again: not to render good for good, and to render evil for good. These two belong to the wicked, and the latter is worse. Again: to render good for good, and evil for evil. These two belong to those in the middle, that is, those who are either moderately good or moderately bad. The former is near to the good, and Christ does not condemn it in the Gospel; but he says that more is required, because even the Gentiles do this (Matthew 5). For they love those who love [Col. 0989B] them. The latter, however—rendering evil for evil—is near to the wicked, though it is also found among the good.

Thus the law sets a limit to vengeance: “eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Exodus 21), and the like. If this may be called the justice of the unjust, it is not so because the vengeance established by the law is unjust, but because the desire which seeks it from longing for revenge is vicious. It pertains more to a judge to discern this among human beings than for a good man to seek vengeance for himself. For the latter will render evil for evil; the judge, however, will not, but from delight in justice will render what is just for what is unjust—which is to render good for evil—and this is also what God the Judge does.

[Cassiod.] Therefore all sin in such renderings is contracted in three ways. The first degree is not to render good for good. The second is to render evil for evil. The final degree is to render evil for good. The Jews chose this worst course: namely, to slander Christ and render hatred for love. Opposed to these are three other courses. The first is to give good for good. The second, not to render evil for evil. The perfect course is to render good for evil, which Christ did when he prayed for the Jews (Luke 23).

## Part II. Verse 5. — “Set thou a sinner over him, and let the devil stand at his right hand.”

Set thou. [Cassiod., Aug.] This is the second part, where he begins to prophesy what the wicked will receive for impiety; [Col. 0989D] and this is first read specifically of Judas. Above, therefore, he spoke of many: “They spoke,” “they surrounded,” and so forth. But now, foretelling what they deserve, he speaks of one. Direct your attention to him—that is, to Judas, who delivered him, namely Christ, over to such men as those of whom he had spoken before.

As if he said: Because the sinner and deceiver opened his mouth against me, therefore set a sinner, that is, the devil, over him who was unwilling to be subject to Christ. And as though someone should ask, “What sinner?” he adds: “And let the devil stand at his right hand.” That is at each person’s right hand which he prefers to other things. Here Judas preferred the works of the devil to the works of God, and greed to his salvation. Therefore the devil stood at his right hand when he preferred greed to wisdom and money to his salvation, so that he might betray him [Col. 0990A] by whom he ought to have been possessed, lest he be possessed by the devil. This is a prediction, not a wish.

### Verse 6. — “When he is judged, let him go forth condemned; and let his prayer become sin.”

When he is judged, let him go forth condemned: that is, because he was unwilling to be such a person as would hear, “Enter into the joy of thy Lord” (Matthew 25), let him be one of whom it is said, “Cast him into the outer darkness” (Matthew 22). And lest he be thought capable of escaping impending condemnation through the prayer he had learned among the apostles, he says: “And let his prayer become sin,” [Aug.] because it is not through Christ, whom he does not wish to follow but to persecute.

It should be noted that no prayer is righteous unless it is made through Christ. It not only fails to erase sin, but itself becomes sin. But that prayer is not made through Christ which is not made with a good affection, nor does it ask for what is good; and conversely. That prayer is made through Christ in which one asks what ought to be asked, and in the manner in which it ought to be asked. Yet prayer is sometimes such that it is in part through Christ and in part not through Christ: when something good is not sought well, or something not good is sought well. Judas, however, asked neither for good nor in a good manner.

[Aug.] It may be asked when Judas could have prayed in such a way that his prayer became sin. I think it was before he betrayed the Lord, when he was already planning to betray him; for he could no longer pray through Christ.

### Verse 7. — “Let his days be few, and let another receive his bishopric.”

Let the days of his apostleship be few, [Aug.] and, lest the sacred number of twelve be diminished, let another receive his bishopric. For Matthias was substituted in his place, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 1). [Cassiod.] Observe that here the name *episcopate* or “bishopric” is first found in the Old Testament. And:

### Verse 8. — “Let his children be fatherless, and his wife a widow.”

Let his children be fatherless, and his wife a widow. [Cassiod., Aug.] Observe that Judas had a wife and children, and it happened as is said here. Certainly, when he died, his children were fatherless and his wife a widow. But someone may ask whether we should believe that what his family suffered belongs to Judas’s punishment; whether any pain also touches the dead because of events occurring among their own after death; or how the spirits of the dead know the things done around us.

In answer, this is indeed a great question and is not to be discussed now. Yet one may briefly say that the dead have concern for their dear ones, as is read of the rich man. While he suffered torments in hell, he lifted his eyes to Abraham and, among other things, said: “For I have five brothers; that he may testify to them, lest they also come into this place of torment” (Luke 16). For the dead have concern for the living whom they know to be alive. They do not see them in places of punishment, where the rich man was without his brothers, nor in the rest of the blessed, where Abraham recognized Lazarus although far away. Yet it does not therefore follow that they know what cheerful or sorrowful things happen here to those dear to them. [Col. 0991A] [Aug., Alcuin.] If, then, the dead feel these things—that is, the sorrows of their own—what is said here is an accumulation of evils. But if they do not feel them, it is a terror for the living. For they may fear that similar things will happen to them because of their own sins or those of their parents.

### Verse 9. — “Let his children be driven about and beg; let them be cast out of their dwellings.”

Let his children be driven about, [Aug.] that is, uncertain where to go; let them be cast out of their dwellings, deprived of every protection; and let them beg. How all this befell his wife and children he indicates, saying:

### Verse 10. — “Let the moneylender search out all [Col. 0991B] his substance, and let strangers plunder his labors.”

Let the moneylender search out all his substance, and let strangers plunder his labors. [Note: [Col. 0991D] From Augustine, at the end of the first exposition of the psalm.] But how did he have substance when he followed the Lord with the apostles? He left everything he possessed to his wife and children in such a way that his heart still remained in those possessions; he did not tear away the bond of greed, and he thought he could deceive the Lord when he took from the money-box what was put into it (John 12).

### Verse 11. — “Let there be none to help him, nor any to pity his fatherless children.”

Let there be none to help him. [Cassiod.] He adds this because even the good are tested, but they have God as their helper. Yet of him it is said, “Let there be none to help him,” namely, to preserve his descendants. Hence he adds: “Nor any to pity his fatherless children.” [Aug., Cassiod.] *Pupilli*, “fatherless children,” are so called as though from *pusilli*, “little ones”; hence the pupil of the eye is called *pupilla*, because it is small. [Aug.] But because his children could grow up, even in miseries, without help, and preserve the line of descent, he adds:

### Verse 12. — “Let those born of him be for destruction; in one generation let his name be blotted out.”

Let those born of him be for destruction. [Cassiod.] By this he removes every hope of posterity. “And in one generation let his name be blotted out.” [Aug.] As if he said: Let what has been begotten from him not beget, and let it quickly pass away. And:

### Verse 13. — “Let the iniquity of his fathers return to remembrance before the Lord, [Col. 0991D] and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out.”

Let the iniquity of his fathers return to remembrance before the Lord, and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out. [Aug.] The sins of fathers are repaid to those who do not depart from their fathers’ evils, but not to those changed in Christ, who are no longer children of the wicked because they no longer imitate their ways.

If, therefore, Judas had retained the adoption he had received, his past iniquity or that of his fathers would not have concerned him. But because he returned to the evils of his old stock, the iniquity of his fathers returned before the Lord, [Col. 0992A] so that it might be punished in him. Hence Exodus rightly says: “I will repay the sins of fathers upon children,” etc. (Exodus 20). This was said concerning those who imitate their fathers’ iniquity. But what is said through Ezekiel the prophet—“The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezekiel 18)—must be understood of those converted to God. And:

### Verse 14. — “Let them be always before the Lord, and let their memory perish from the earth, because he did not remember to show mercy.”

Let his father and mother always be before the Lord, [Aug.] not that they may oppose the Lord, but that God may not forget their evil merits in this man. The meaning is: “Let them be before the Lord,” that is, in the sight of the Lord, as others also translated it. “And let their memory,” [Col. 0992B] that is, the memory of his parents, perish from the earth, their offspring having been destroyed, because Judas did not remember to show mercy.

### Verse 15. — “And he persecuted the poor and needy man, and the broken in heart, to put him to death.”

And he persecuted the poor and needy man, [Cassiod.] namely Christ. To persecute the poor is sheer cruelty; others, however, sometimes suffer such treatment for the sake of wealth or honor.

[Note: [Col. 0992D] From Augustine, in the second exposition.] Or all these things may be understood of the Jewish people. For the same things suit the Jews, whose person Judas bore. As if he said: Because they rendered hatred for love, therefore set a sinner over him—that is, over the people. And let the devil stand at his right hand, as in the case of Judas.

Thus these words are understood of the Jews: “When he is judged, let him go forth condemned,” because the Jews, remaining in their wickedness, store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and revelation of righteous judgment (Romans 2). “And let his prayer become sin,” because it is not made through Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and men. “Let his days be few” should be understood of this kingdom, which did not endure long afterward. And “let another receive his bishopric”—the Gentile people received the bishopric of the Jews, that is, Christ, who had been sent to them. Hence: “God sent the Word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel.”

“Let his children be fatherless,” their kingdom, as it were their father, having been lost; or God the Father having been lost. “And let his wife,” that is, the Jewish people, [Col. 0992D] “be a widow,” their kingdom having been lost. “Let his children be driven about and beg, and be cast out of their dwellings.” This happened often in captivity; and let them beg under kings of the Gentiles.

Let the moneylender—that is, the devil, who lends evil things, or God, who lends good things—search out all his substance, [Aug.] that is, his life, punishing individual sins. For their debts are not forgiven, because they are forgiven in Christ alone, whom they rejected. And let strangers, that is, the devil and his angels, plunder his labors, because they do not lay up treasure in heaven. “And let there be none to help him”: there is no helper for one who lacks Christ. And for “his fatherless children,” [Col. 0993A] who remained so after losing their kingdom or God the Father, let there be none to pity them—not, I mean, so that they may possess temporal things, but eternal things.

“Let those born of him be for destruction,” everlasting destruction. “And let his name be blotted out,” because it remained “in one generation,” that is, because they were not regenerated. “And let the iniquity of his fathers return to remembrance before the Lord,” an iniquity repaid by these evils to those who persevere in wickedness. “And let not the sin of his mother be blotted out,” that is, of earthly Jerusalem, which is in bondage with her children and killed the prophets. “Let them be always before the Lord”: that is, let their sin not be removed from the sight of the Lord but always be punished. “And let their memory perish from the earth of the living,” that is, from the Church, because, though they were natural branches, they were broken off (Romans 11).

“Because he did not remember,” [Col. 0993B] whether Judas or the people itself, “to show mercy.” But this is better said of the people, which did not remember through repentance to show mercy, at least to the members of Christ, but persecutes them. Hence he says: “And he persecuted the poor and needy man”—or Judas persecuted Christ himself with the utmost cruelty—“and the broken in heart, to put him to death,” that is, in order to put him to death. This is said of Christ in his members. For one is not usually called “broken in heart” except one wounded by the stings of sins in the sorrow of repentance. But because such persons also are members of Christ, the Jews persecuted in his members the one whom they crucified.

### Verse 16. — “And he loved cursing, and it shall come upon him; and he did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him.”

[Col. 0993C] And he loved cursing. [Aug.] Judas did so by stealing from the money-box and selling the Lord (John 12); or the Jews did so by saying, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 26). And it shall come upon him. And he did not desire blessing, [Aug.] as when they cursed the man born blind who had been given sight, saying: “Be thou his disciple” (John 9). And blessing shall be far from him, passing to the Gentiles.

### Verse 17. — “And he put on cursing like a garment; and it entered like water into his inward parts, and like oil into his bones.”

And Judas, or the people, clothed himself—or themselves—in the curse—that is, in sins—which now delight them, but are called a curse because they prepare torments. He adds, “like a garment,” which, because it belongs to the body and is worn upon it, signifies the corrupted body. [Col. 0993D] And the same curse entered like water into his inward parts, by which the corrupted soul is understood; for outwardly in the body and inwardly in the soul he had the curse, falling under the judgment of Him who destroys both body and soul in Gehenna. And the same curse was in his bones, by which the corrupted reason is denoted. He adds, “like oil,” thereby showing that it now delights them to do evil. Or he says “like oil” because people think themselves strong: since they are presently allowed to do evil with impunity, as athletes are anointed with oil so that they may be stronger.

**VERSE 18.**—“Let it be to him like the garment with which he is covered, and like the belt with which he is always girded.”

[Col. 0994A] Let that very curse be to Judas or to the people like the garment with which he is covered. [Aug.] He seems to say here the same thing as above, where he said, “He clothed himself in cursing like a garment”; but there is a difference. Above he spoke of the garment with which one is clothed as with a tunic; here he speaks of the garment with which one is covered as with a cloak—namely, glorying before people in iniquity. And let the curse be to him like the belt with which he is always girded. People gird themselves with a belt in order to be more ready for work, unimpeded by the folds of their garments. Therefore he is girded with cursing like a belt who does not do evil suddenly, but undertakes it deliberately; and thus he learns to act wickedly so as always to be ready. Hence he says here, “with which he is always girded.”

**VERSE 19.**—“This is the work of those who slander [Col. 0994B] me before the Lord, and who speak evil against my soul.”

“This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord.” [Aug.] He did not say, “This is their reward,” but “work.” For it is evident that by garment and water, oil and belt, he describes the works by which the eternal curse is acquired. He says “of those” in the plural, “who slander,” because there is not only one Judas but many, of whom he says: “who slander me before the Lord,” saying that I am not He whom the Law of the Lord and the prophets foretold; [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine] or, more particularly, they slander Christ before the Lord who say that He is not from the Father, or is less than the Father, “and who speak evil against my soul,” saying that He could not rise again when [Col. 0994C] He willed.

**PART III. VERSE 20.**—“But you, Lord, Lord, deal with me for your name’s sake, because your mercy is sweet.”

“But you, Lord.” [Cassiod.] The third part, in which He prays that, having been delivered, He may attain the resurrection and His enemies’ disgrace. As though He said: They indeed are thus; but you, Lord, Lord. The repetition denotes the earnestness of prayer. [Aug.] Note that He says “and you,” because the conjunction “and” is not prefixed without reason, as if He said: Therefore I say, “And you,” because I too act. Hence follows: “Deal with me,” because the works of the Father and the Son are the same. The sense is: “Deal with me,” that is, work as I do upon vessels of mercy. Or, “deal with me,” that is, help [Col. 0994D] me according to my humanity; and this not because of my preceding merits, but for your name’s sake. By this He commends grace. For human nature was raised to so great a height by no preceding merits of works that the Word and flesh together—that is, God and man—should be called the only-begotten Son. This was done so that by Him who had created, through that which had not perished, that which had perished might be sought. Hence follows here: “because your mercy is sweet.” For through me you seek that which had perished.

**VERSE 21.**—“Deliver me, because I am needy and poor, and my heart is troubled within me.”

“Deliver me.” [Aug.] As though He said: Indeed, deal with me in this way—deliver me from the Passion—because I am needy and poor. [Col. 0995A] Christ’s need and poverty are the weakness through which He was crucified. “And my heart is troubled within me.” Hence: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. XXVI). [Cassiod.] For the heart could be troubled just as the flesh could be crucified; in these things the true nature of man is revealed. And:

**VERSE 22.**—“Like a shadow when it declines, I have been taken away; and I have been shaken off like locusts.”

“Like a shadow when it declines I have been taken away,” that is, I have died. For as night comes from a declining shadow, so death comes from mortal flesh. “And I have been shaken off like locusts.” [Aug.] I think this is more fittingly understood now in His members, that is, in the faithful. Hence He says more plainly in the plural, “like locusts,” rather than “like a locust.” Therefore the faithful, who are many like locusts, have been shaken off—that is, driven away—by persecutors; [Col. 0995B] or they leap from place to place, after the manner of locusts. And:

**VERSE 23.**—“My knees have been weakened through fasting, and my flesh has been changed because of oil.”

“My knees have been weakened through fasting.” [Aug.] This too is more plainly understood in His members. The meaning is: “My knees have been weakened through fasting,” that is, my strong ones, deprived of bread—that is, of Christ—failed; this appeared in Peter. But lest they utterly succumb, what follows took place: “And my flesh has been changed for the better,” into the glory of immortality, so that those failing in death might be strengthened when the Spirit was sent, “because of oil,” that is, spiritual grace, from which Christ receives His name. For Christ is so called from *chrism*; *chrism* means anointing. [Col. 0995C] Therefore Christ’s flesh was changed so that, when the Holy Spirit was sent, He might anoint the disciples; the Spirit would not have come to them if Christ had not departed. Hence He himself says: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John XVI). And the Evangelist says: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII).

**VERSE 24.**—“And I became a reproach to them; they saw me and shook their heads.”

“And I became a reproach to them,” [Aug.] because through the death of the cross I became a curse. “They saw me and shook their heads,” because they saw when my knees were weakened, but not when my flesh was changed. And therefore they shook their heads, [Cassiod.] threatening like madmen by the movement of their heads. [Col. 0995D] Therefore, O:

**VERSE 25.**—“Help me, O Lord my God; save me according to your mercy.”

“O Lord my God, help me” wholly, [Aug., Cassiod.] namely head and body. Note that Christ, who grants as God, prays as man: “Save me according to your mercy”; [Aug.] help me not according to the due reward of works.

**VERSE 26.**—“And let them know that this is your hand, and that you, O Lord, have made it.”

And thereby they will know—or, let him know—[Aug.] namely those for whom He prayed, who were among the mockers. What will they know? “That this is your hand, and that you, O Lord, have made it.” Christ is the hand of the Father. Hence: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII). This hand is [Col. 0996A] and was, because He is the Word with God; and He made it when the Word became flesh. According to divinity He was without time, and according to the flesh He was made in time.

**VERSE 27.**—“They will curse, but you will bless; let those who rise up against me be put to shame, but your servant will rejoice.”

241 They will curse, heaping insults upon that your hand, Christ. [Aug.] Therefore the curse of the wicked is vain. But when God blesses, He brings about what He says. And you, who are good, will bless. Let those who rise up against me, thinking to prevail against me, be put to shame; this will occur when I have been exalted above the heavens and my glory begins to be over all the earth. “But your servant will rejoice,” either at the Father’s right hand, or in His rejoicing members. And:

[Col. 0996B] **VERSE 28.**—“Let those who slander me be clothed with shame, and let them be covered as with a double cloak in their own confusion.”

Let those who slander me be clothed with shame, [Aug.] that is, let them be ashamed that they slandered me. This may be understood in a good sense, when they are corrected. “And let them be covered as with a double cloak in their own confusion.” A *diplois* is a double cloak. Hence others translate “double cloak” for *diplois*. The meaning is: “Let them be covered as with a double cloak in their own confusion,” [Gl. int.] that is, let them be confounded inwardly and outwardly, before God and before people. Hence elsewhere: “Crush them with a double destruction, O Lord our God” (Jer. XVII). But I:

**VERSE 29.**—“I will confess the Lord exceedingly with my [Col. 0996C] mouth, and in the midst of many I will praise him.”

“I will confess praise to the Lord.” [Aug.] This is understood in His members. *Nimis* (“exceedingly”) is usually explained as “more than is fitting,” but it is also used for “very greatly,” as here. “I will confess,” I say, “with my mouth,” because confession with the mouth is made unto salvation (Rom. X). “And in the midst of many I will praise him,” that is, in the assembly. This is what He says elsewhere: “In the midst of the Church I will praise you” (Ps. XXI). Or, “in the midst of many I will praise him,” that is, in the hearts of many, because with the heart one believes unto righteousness (Rom. X).

**VERSE 30.**—“Who stood at the right hand of the poor, to save my soul from its persecutors.”

“Who stood.” [Aug.] As though He said: I will confess the Lord, who stood at the right hand of the poor. The devil stood at the right hand [Col. 0996D] of Judas, who wished to increase his riches by selling Christ; but the Lord stood at the right hand of the poor, so that the Lord himself might be the poor man’s riches. He stood there not to increase the years of this life, or to make him strong, safe, or rich, but to save his soul from persecutors. Hence He adds: “to save my soul from its persecutors,” lest it succumb through poverty, that is, weakness. This help was given to Christ’s body in all the holy martyrs.

## Comparison on Psalm 108: “O God, do not keep silence at my praise,” etc.

**VERSE 1.**—“O God, do not keep silence at my praise.” The Hebrews relate “my praise” to the name “God,” not to the following verb, making it “God of my praise,” which, according to Jerome’s translation, is [Col. 0997A] “God praiseworthy to me.” Or, as Münster renders it, “God in whom is my praise.” Then, with a pause inserted, follows, “do not be silent.” Yet the Hebrew is *Elohe tehillathi*. The Septuagint took it as though it were not in the construct state, like *Elohim*. Nevertheless, the meaning agrees.

**VERSE 3.**—“In return for their loving me.” Since the Hebrew reads *tahat ahabathi*, literally “in place of my love,” it is ambiguously understood either as the love by which I love, or the love by which I ought to be loved. Jerome translates: “because I loved them.” So too the Greek is ambiguous: ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀγαπᾷν με, “in return for loving me.” In either case the ingratitude of the faithless Jews is aptly expressed.

**VERSE 9.**—“Let them be driven out of their dwellings.” Jerome: “let them seek among their ruins.” Faber reconciles these correctly. Jerome gives the antecedent; the Septuagint, the consequence. The more recent Hebraizing translators, however, actively render *dareshu*: “let them seek” or “search among their devastations,” or desolate places. It may be reconciled if “let them seek” is referred to those whose duty it was to drive out such sons, although this may seem more forced.

**VERSE 10.**—“Let him search.” Jerome and the Nebiensian likewise. Others: “Let him ensnare” or “destroy,” although “to search” is used here in the sense that one who does it acts with the purpose of destroying, and entangles with his deceitful snares everything [Col. 0998A] that is not his. Yet it is not far from the truth that the letter *nun* has been written in place of *beth*, which sometimes is not dissimilar, so that it should be *yebaqqesh* where we have *yenaqqesh*.

**VERSE 12.**—“Let his offspring come to an end.” Jerome and most others: “Let his end be,” *aharitho*. It may also be understood as “posterity,” as Münster and the translators for Cajetan rendered it.

**VERSE 12.**—“This is their work.” Jerome: “This is their recompense.” *Pe‘ullath* indeed means and is translated “work,” but “reward” is understood, Münster testifying from Kimhi, even though Augustine explains it otherwise.

“Before the Lord.” This corresponds to the preceding expression, “they slander me,” or, as the Hebrews have it, “those who oppose me.” Then they place “from the Lord,” as though the recompense were from the Lord. The Hebrew has *me’eth*, which is both an ablative and an accusative marker.

**VERSE 23.**—“My flesh has been changed because of oil.” [Col. 0998B] Jerome renders the last phrase “without oil,” which they understand as fatness or sap, and say: “My flesh has dried up” or “withered for lack of fatness.” Or, as Münster says, “because of failing fatness.” Yet word for word *mishamen* means “from oil” or “because of oil,” so that Faber’s claim that it should be read “apart from oil,” rather than “because of oil,” has no force. For the Greek has δι’ ἔλαιον, “because of oil.”

# PSALM 109

[Col. 0997]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF DAVID”

[Col. 0997B]

“[The] Lord said to my Lord.” Title: “A Psalm of David.” The title is clear. [Cassiod.] This psalm is the seventh of those which treat of Christ’s two natures; it speaks fully and briefly of Christ’s incarnation and [Col. 0997C] almighty divinity, as John says in the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word became flesh” (John I). Everything contained in either Testament concerning Christ’s two natures is here stated in summary.

Purpose. [Cassiod.] The prophet exhorts men to submit to Christ. Method: the psalm has three parts. First, the prophet reports the Father’s words concerning the Son, where the divine and human nature of Christ are expounded. Secondly, the Father indicates, to some extent, the divine nature, at “With you is the beginning.” Thirdly, the prophet treats Christ’s humanity, at “The Lord has sworn.” Therefore the prophet, first disclosing the divine nature, says:

> “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.” [Col. 0997D]

The Lord the Father said: [Cassiod.] The prophet speaks in our customary manner when he says, “said,” so that man may be instructed. For He did not utter it with His mouth, but said it in reality, that is, in effect. [Gl. int., Haymo, Cassiod.] Or rather, in reality, that is, in generation. Or “said” means that He eternally ordained concerning my Lord, namely the Son, who is my Lord even according to his humanity—that is, the man himself [is my Lord], and not merely insofar as he is man. By saying, “Lord to Lord,” distinguish the persons by the repetition of the same name, and understand the one nature and power of the persons. Likewise, the expression “to my Lord” indicates divinity. But “sit,” and “the Lord will send forth the rod of your strength from Zion,” indicate humanity.

What did the Father say to the Son? [Col. 0998B] This: “Sit,” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, after labor rest, and reign jointly according to your humanity. Sit not only on high, so as to rule in excellence, but also in concealment, so that you may be believed as hidden and unseen; for there is no reward of faith unless that which we believe remains hidden. Those who are withdrawn, namely those who are here below and do not yet hope for what is above, [Col. 0998C] believe what they do not see. This is the righteousness of faith of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “When the Paraclete comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, because it does not believe; and concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father and you will see me no longer” (John XVI). That is, this will be your righteousness: to believe in Him whom you will not see. For then the righteous person lives by faith (Rom. I), if he does not see what he believes.

Therefore, in saying “Sit,” He indicates two things: that He rests and reigns after the labor of the Passion, and that He is concealed. “Sit,” I say, “at my right hand,” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus] that is, in my greater goods. Or, “sit at my right hand,” that is, reign jointly as my equal, so that the right hand signifies the equality Christ has with the Father.

**VERSE 2.**—“Until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.”

“Until I make.” [Aug., Cassiod.] As though He said: Sit hidden until you reign openly. This is: “until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet,” that is, subject through faith to your divinity. He speaks by likeness when He says “footstool,” by which complete subjection is denoted. By “feet” eternal stability is understood. [Aug.] This is done and accomplished daily, though gradually, in those who are converted. Or *until* is understood as eternal. The meaning is: Sit until I make—that is, eternally, just as eternally I will make—your enemies, willing or unwilling, the footstool of your feet, [Col. 0999A] that is, subject to you either willingly or by necessity. Christ’s reign, moreover, begins from Zion, that is, from the Jews. Hence follows:

**VERSE 3.**—“The Lord will send forth the rod of your strength from Zion; rule in the midst of your enemies.”

“The rod.” [Cassiod.] The prophet sings to Christ this praise, namely the subjection of enemies, speaking to Him in his own person and showing the order in which His kingdom began: it began among the Jews and passed to the Gentiles, among whom it is consummated. Thus the prophet proceeds to the end of the psalm speaking in his own person. As though he said: The Lord will make your enemies the footstool of your feet; this will happen in such a way that it begins among the Jews. This is: “The Lord will send forth the rod of your strength from Zion,” [Jerome] that is, the kingdom of your power [Col. 0999B] will begin from Jerusalem. Hence: “Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II).

[Aug.] The prophet does not speak of that kingdom of Christ in which Christ always reigns with the Father, but of that dispensational and temporal kingdom by which, through the mediation of His flesh, He called us into eternity and reigns in us—though this kingdom shall have no end. It begins from Jerusalem. Hence the Lord himself says: “It was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke XXIV). [Jerome, Cassiodorus] Therefore the rod of strength is the scepter of royal power, by which the good are sustained and the evil broken.

Note that He says “of strength” and adds “your,” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin] because this power belongs properly [Col. 0999C] to Christ by virtue of His divinity. “Rule,” or “you will rule,” or “he will rule.” As though He said: Send forth the rod, and when the rod has been sent forth, the Father himself will rule. Or: You, Christ, rule—or will rule—in the midst, that is, in the inmost hearts of any of your enemies whatsoever. [Cassiod.] As though He said: You will rule over those converted from whatever peoples. He does not say, “You will take vengeance,” as if He were to strike the ungrateful with the severity of vengeance; rather He says, “You will rule,” so that He may lead the faithful by benefits and correction. Or: “Rule in the midst of your enemies,” that is, in the Church established among the wicked.

**PART II. VERSE 4.**—“With you is the beginning in the day of your strength, in the splendors of the saints; from the womb before the morning star I begot you.”

[Col. 0999D] “With you is the beginning.” [Cassiod.] The second part, in which the Father indicates, as far as our capacity permits, the divine nature of Christ. As though He said: Father, I, the Lord, will send forth the rod of your strength, because “with you is the beginning” for me. [Alcuin.] As though this were granted to you more than to others, because you are Son by nature, because “with you is the beginning” for me. I will not say to you, “with me,” lest you seem in some respect posterior to me: you and I are one beginning of all things. This is not seen here, but will be seen “in the day of your strength, in the splendors of the saints,” [Aug.] that is, in eternity, where divine power is contemplated not by others but by the saints, when in the resurrection they will be radiant as the angels of God.

Or thus—and the Father again speaks: [Aug.] As though He said: You already rule, O [Col. 1000A] Christ the Son; your power has already been sent forth. But on the day of your special power, namely in the future, “with you is the beginning” for me. This always is so, but is not seen; then, however, it will be seen, when Christ, formerly seen in the form of a servant, will be seen by pure hearts in the form of God, from whose vision the wicked person is removed lest he see the glory of God. I say, “in the day of your strength, in the splendors of the saints,” that is, when the saints shine in splendor like the sun in the kingdom of the Father. Then the beginning will be with Him; and now the beginning is, namely, the Father with the Son is the beginning, but then it will be seen how the beginning is with Him, because then, being like Him, they will see Him as He is.

Philip had seen according to the form of a servant, and was rebuked because in the Son he did not recognize the Father whom he sought to see, saying: [Col. 1000B] “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John XIV). He hears: “He who sees me”—not the form of a servant, but such as I have concealed for those who fear me and such as I bring to sight for those who hope in me—“sees the Father also” (ibid.). This must now be believed so that it may then be seen. Thus Philip is also told: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father in me?” (ibid.). As though He said: What you cannot yet see, believe, so that you may deserve to see the Son with the Father and in the Father, in what manner the Father is the beginning with Him. This vision is eternal life. Hence: “And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII).

“From the womb.” As though He said: This will then be seen, but now, “from the womb,” that is, from my hidden and secret substance, I begot you ineffably. And this was “before the morning star,” [Col. 1000C] [Cassiod., Aug.] that is, before all times. The morning star, which announces day to the world, is here taken as the preeminent star in place of all stars and heavenly bodies, part for the whole; through these stars times are understood, because they were set for signs and seasons, as is written in Genesis (Gen. I). Thus: “Before the morning star I begot you,” that is, before every creature, before all times.

Or it may be understood as spoken by the prophet addressing the Son: “With you,” [Alcuin.] as though he said: The Lord will send forth the rod of strength, and He is the beginning with you, that is, coeternal with you—not, however, according to your humanity, but “in the day of strength,” that is, in the brightness of divinity. I say, “your strength,” as though He were also consubstantial with you. And He is also the beginning “in the [Col. 1000D] splendors of the saints,” that is, with the Holy Spirit, who makes the saints radiant. [Aug.] And I, David, say, “from the womb I begot you.” As though he said: Since Mary is descended from me, I begot you from the womb of the Virgin. And this was “before the morning star,” that is, at night, for Christ was born before day. But He was born of her in order that He might be a priest forever, offering Himself:

**PART III. [Col. 1001A] VERSE 5.**—“The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

“The Lord has sworn.” [Alcuin.] The third part, in which the prophet treats of Christ’s humanity. Behold, the Word became flesh. It should be noted that above, “the rod of your strength” through “with you is the beginning,” were words of the prophet treating Christ’s humanity; there, however, God the Father or the prophet speaks, according to the different readings, treating Christ’s divinity. Here likewise the prophet speaks to the end of the psalm, treating Christ’s humanity. As though he said: The Lord said to the Lord, the Son, “Sit at my right hand,” etc.; He also gave Him an eternal priesthood. For the Lord has sworn to you—that is, firmly promised you—according to your humanity. [Aug.] God’s oath is the confirmation of His promise. “And he will not repent,” that is, He will not change, as happened with Aaron’s priesthood, which, contrary to our expectation, He changed.

This is said of God after our human manner, though repentance cannot occur in Him. For He knows what He does and does not change His counsel; but by the word “repentance” is signified the change of things which come about otherwise than expected. As though He said: When you repent of something you have done, you grieve over what you did; similarly, when God changes something into another thing contrary to what people expect, He is [Col. 1001B] said to repent—so much so that He is said to repent even of our punishment if we repent of our evil life. Therefore He “will not repent,” because it does not turn out otherwise than was expected. And since all things have rejoiced at this, what did He swear? This: “You are a priest forever,” that is, an eternal priest, according to the order of Melchizedek, [Cassiod.] because Christ consecrated bread and wine into His body and blood, and Melchizedek previously set forth the likeness of this sacrifice. Hence it is evident that the victims according to Aaron’s order have passed away.

**VERSE 6.**—“The Lord at your right hand has broken [Col. 1001C] kings in the day of his wrath.”

“The Lord.” Here there is a turn toward the Father. [Aug.] As though he said: And, O Lord Father, who swore this, this priest who is the Lord, seated at your right hand—to whom you said, “Sit at my right hand”—has broken or shattered kings, namely those who wish or wished to destroy Christ’s name. He shattered them, that is, made them weak so that they could not do what they wished. He did this in the day of his wrath, [Alcuin.] that is, in the time of hidden wrath, when those who fall upon the lowly stone are shattered, either unto blindness or unto conversion. [Aug.] In the future judgment, however, the falling stone will more openly crush them. Hence: “Whoever falls upon that stone will be broken to pieces; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him” (Matt. XXI). [Col. 1001D] And now:

**VERSE 7.**—“He will judge among the nations; he will fill the ruins; he will shatter heads in the land of many.”

“He will judge among the nations,” [Cassiod.] that is, among the Gentiles. Observe the precision of the expressions: He breaks kings because of pride; He judges—that is, punishes—peoples because of common sins; yet He does so to both, that they may be humbled unto conversion. Hence He adds: “He will fill the ruins,” that is, the humble, not those standing erect—those who have fallen from the height to which they raised themselves against Christ. Rightly does He say “ruins,” because “He will shatter the heads of many,” or “many heads, in the land,” [Aug.] that is, in this life. For here He makes many proud people humble. [Cassiod., Haymo] Or: “in a rich land,” another reading, namely the land which abundantly [Col. 1002A] nourishes sinners. But whence does He have power to do this? From the humility of the Passion, of which He adds:

**VERSE 8.**—“He drank from the torrent in the way; therefore he lifted up his head.”

“From the torrent,” [Aug.] that is, from the flow of our mortality, and from the transitory and turbulent Passion, He drank by being born and by dying. [Cassiod., Aug.] And this was on the way which He ran as a giant, the way by which one goes to another dwelling-place. “And therefore,” because He humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, God lifted up—or will lift up—His head; that is, for this reason God exalted Him and gave Him the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father [Col. 1002B] (Phil. II).

## Comparison on Psalm 109: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit,” etc.

**VERSE 4.**—First, no Christian doubts, on the authority of Matthew XXII, that this psalm concerns Christ, the Son of God. Yet because the first verse according to the Septuagint differs very widely from the surface of the Hebrew text, it will be worthwhile to set before us the entire verse according to the various translations of all the versions, and then to examine each word in turn, if we can determine without contention whence so great a discord has arisen, and how, departing from the sound of the words, they have brought forth so great a mystery of faith in a mystical and profoundly meaningful sense. This could not have happened without divine revelation, beyond flesh and blood; moreover, it has [Col. 1002C] above been sufficiently proved at length that the Septuagint were full of the Holy Spirit.

Thus Jerome’s Hebrew version reads: “Your people shall be willing in the day of your strength, in holy mountains; as from the womb there shall arise for you the dew of your youth.” Nicholas of Lyra: “Your people, your princes, in the day of your strength, in holy beauty; from the womb of the dawn, for you is the dew of your youth.” Sanctes: “Your people will come willingly in the day of your strength, in the beauties of holiness; from the womb, from the dawn, there was for you the dew of your birth.” Pratensis: “Your people with offerings, in the day of your strength, in the adornments of holiness; from the womb there arose for you the dew of your generation.” The translators for Cajetan: “Your people, willing ones, in the day of your strength, in the adornments of holiness; from the womb of the dawn, for you is the dew of your birth.” Pellicanus: “Your people, free offerings, in the day of your strength, in the adornments of holiness; from the womb of the dawn, for you is the dew of your generation.” Münster: “Your people are of willing dispositions, in the day of your army, in the magnificences [Col. 1002D] of holiness; from the womb of the dawn, for you is the dew of your birth.” The translator for Campensis: “But your people, on the day of your triumph, will offer vows with holy pomp. For the dew of your birth is from the womb of the dawn.” His paraphrase: “Your people will offer you voluntary and generous offerings at the time when your omnipotence and all that splendor which accompanies you appears; for before dawn the dew of your birth fell, which will make you most gracious to all.” Nebiensis: “Your people [shall be] willing in the day of your strength, in the adornments of the sanctuary; from the womb, from the dawn, for you is the dew of your youth.”

See how, among these, not everything agrees, even though they agree little or not at all with the Septuagint. Let us now reconsider the individual points.

“With you.” All translate this phrase “your people” or “your peoples.” Certainly, in Hebrew, “with you” and “your people” differ by not one single letter. For if the word is written without vowel points, it is “with you” or “your people”: *‘immekha*, “with you”; *‘ammekha*, “your people.” [Col. 1003A] Nor is it improbable that the Jews corrupted this passage, as they falsified some other principal passages of the faith; this we partly proved in the prologue. Nor will it be idle to bring in here that passage from Isaiah II: “For he is reckoned exalted.” Jerome, interpreting this passage, says: “Where we said, ‘He is reckoned exalted,’ Aquila translated, ‘In what is this one reckoned?’ The Hebrew word is either called ὕψωμα, that is, ‘a height,’ as we read in the books of Kings and Ezekiel; or certainly it means ‘in what,’ and it is written with the same letters. According to the context, if we wish to read ‘in what,’ we say *bammeh*; but if we read ‘height’ or ‘exalted,’ we say *bamah*. Therefore the Jews, understanding that the prophecy concerned Christ, interpreted the ambiguous word in the worse sense, so that they might appear not to praise Christ but to despise him.” Jerome then proceeds to disprove such an interpretation, showing that it cannot stand.

[Col. 1003B] The second phrase is “is the beginning.” The Hebrew is *nedaboth*, derived from the root *nadab*, that is, “it pleased,” “he was willing,” “he offered voluntarily.” Thus Jerome rendered it “willing leaders,” supplying, as in Faber’s copy, the verb “shall be,” which was not present in the Hebrew. Sanctes expressed it with an adverb, adding the verb “will come.” But we believe that the Septuagint followed Hebrew usage in the other word *rosh*, which means “head,” and therefore “chief,” and therefore “beginning.” Similarly, *nadib* properly signifies a prince, especially a generous one. Why, then, should we not also say *nedabith*, like *reshith*? Certainly there is analogy in their commonality, correspondence, and meaning.

For Jerome, at the beginning of Zechariah V, relates that *yod* and *waw* frequently interchange. And he says: “This error has frequently become established in the Vulgate edition: because the letters *yod* and *waw* have the same form but differ in size, one is read for the other. Nor should you wonder that he calls it an error; for he means ‘error’ in the same way as [he means] the obelus in the prologue to Chronicles. ‘But where,’ he says, [Col. 1003C] ‘the obelus—that is, a transverse stroke—has been placed before [a passage], there it is indicated what the Septuagint translators added for the sake of elegance or by the authority of the Holy Spirit, although it is not read in the Hebrew volumes.’” These are his words.

In the third phrase, “in the day of your strength,” there is no disagreement. In the fourth, “in the splendors of the saints,” or “in holy beauty,” “adornments,” “beauties,” or “magnificences,” there is only a slight difference.
