Jerome, however, rendered “in mountains” because of the similarity of the letters *daleth* and *resh*: *harre*, “mountains,” and *hadre*, “beauties.” In the fifth phrase they almost agree: “from the womb before the morning star.” For this is equivalent to “from the womb of the dawn,” or, closer to the words, “from the womb, from the dawn,” and “from the womb before the morning star.” Some render it “shall arise” or “arose,” which does not answer so closely to *merehem mischar*.

The final clause: “The dew of your begetting,” or “of your natural generation.” Dew is fittingly said of the Son of God, in accordance with that passage in Isaiah 45: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One.” Moreover, the generation of the Son is called eternal, because dew indicates morning, which in God is eternal, and the beginning in which the Word was. This morning has no evening; and as dew conceived on high descends, so it is sung of the Son of God: “His going forth is from the summit of heaven” (Psalm 18).

Someone may say, if he can maintain it, that the Jews corrupted this reading, as we charged at the beginning, since Jerome nevertheless translated “of your people,” not “with you.” Although an answer to a similar question ought already to have been sufficiently given several times, this passage has a particular vindication from Jerome himself, even against the calumnies of the Jews and their forced interpretations.

“For, in interpreting Matthew 22, where Christ the Lord confronted the Jews, who did not know how Christ could be David’s son, with the beginning of this psalm, Jerome says: David gives the testimony set forth, taken from Psalm 109. Therefore he will be called David’s Lord, not according to that whereby he was born from him, but according to that whereby he was always born from the Father, preceding [Col. 1004B] the father of his flesh. The Jews, to evade the force of the question, invent many trifles, maintaining that Damascus Eliezer was Abraham’s household servant and son, and that the psalm was written in his person: that after the slaughter of the five kings, the Lord God said to his lord Abraham, ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.’ Let us ask them how God could have said to Abraham what follows: ‘With you is the beginning in the day of your power; in the splendours of the saints, from the womb before the morning star I begot you’; and, ‘The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek.’ And let us compel them to answer how Abraham was begotten before the morning star and was a priest according to the order of Melchizedek—for whom Melchizedek offered bread and wine, and from whom he received tithes of the spoil.”

So far Jerome. Certainly, if the Vulgate and ecclesiastical edition were less than correct in this matter, Jerome would have achieved nothing, especially against the Jews, who would immediately have ridiculed an objection based on a corrupted context rather than Hebrew truth. Besides, from this passage of Jerome it is clear that Felinus attacks the Latin translator without cause because he translated ἀρχή (*archē*) as “beginning,” whereas, in keeping with the truth of the Hebrew idiom, he ought to have translated it “dominion.” For ἀρχή has that meaning too—to say nothing of what Augustine most plainly argues concerning “beginning.”

Finally, the Chaldean Paraphrast differs greatly from all the others, especially in the final clause: “Your people, the house of Israel, who devote themselves to the Law—in the day of the contest of your battle you will help them; with the splendours of holiness, God’s mercies will be ready for you; your offspring will sit confidently like descending dew.”

**VERSE 7.—“He will fill the ruins.”** Jerome: “the valleys.” Therefore he read *GEOTH*, from the root [uncertain OCR], that is, “valley”; but we now have *GEUIOTH*, that is, as others explain it, “corpses,” undoubtedly so called from falling, just as “ruins” are so called from collapsing. Yet since simply saying “he will fill corpses” would be absurd, Münster added: “He will fill the places with corpses.”

## PSALM 110

[Col. 1003]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “ALLELUIA.”

[Col. 1003D]

“I will give thanks.” Title: Alleluia. [Cassiodorus.] This is the first psalm written through all the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, signifying the perfect worshippers in the Church, just as those not written through all the letters signify the less perfect. [Note: [Col. 1003D] From Hilary on Psalm 18.] Or, as Hilary [Col. 1004D] says, in psalms of this kind, arranged according to the alphabet, the beginners are given, as it were, their elementary letters. Hence we are urged to hasten toward the pursuit of learning.

The name of angelic praise, *Alleluia*, although suitable to all psalms, is especially placed where great rejoicing is expressed. [Cassiodorus.] Thus [Col. 1005A] in this psalm the people of God, delivered from every evil, praise God and invite others to praise him for his works; this praise bears the figure of future praise.

Purpose: it exhorts to praise. Method: the psalm has three parts. First, the faithful people declare that they will give thanks in the assembly of the righteous, where praise is eternal. Second, it says that the faithful are filled with a spiritual gift, promising Christ’s coming: “He has made a memorial of his wonders; the Lord is gracious and compassionate; he has given food to those who fear him.” Third, it declares that these same persons are redeemed and that the new covenant will endure: “He has sent redemption to his people; he has commanded his covenant for ever.” [Augustine.] Therefore, beginning with praise, he says in the person of the faithful people: O Lord—

### VERSE 1

> “I will give thanks to you, O Lord, with my whole [Col. 1005B] heart, in the council of the righteous and in the congregation.”

“I will give thanks to you,” that is, “I will praise you.” This is not confession of sins, but confession of praise. The former mourns; the latter rejoices. The former shows its wound to the physician; the latter gives thanks for healing. I shall praise, I say, and this “with my whole heart”; [Jerome, Glossa interlinearis] I shall not be near with my lips but far away in heart, like those of whom it is said: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matthew 15).

I shall give thanks also “in the council of the righteous and in the congregation,” [Alcuin] that is, not rashly, but reasonably—namely, on account of eternal things—as all the righteous do. And this whole statement is understood of the present. Or the faithful people say this in hope: as though they said, “May it now be in the company of angels.” Thus, “in the [Col. 1005C] council of the righteous and congregation, I shall praise you,” here in hope. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] For here they never praise in actuality among all the righteous, where evil persons are intermixed; but already they seem to sing psalms in the future fellowship, carried upward in hope.

### VERSE 2

> “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out in all his wills.”

“Great are the works of the Lord.” [Cassiodorus.] This is the subject and cause of confession. As though he said: Therefore I will give thanks, because great is the Lord’s work, which makes a righteous person out of an ungodly one. And they are “sought out,” having nothing like them, when he permits the devil to rage for the good of his own. And lest you think his work is praised only in part, he adds, “in all his wills”: that is, his work is sought out because [Col. 1005D] whatever he wills, he does excellently. What this work is, he explains by adding:

### VERSE 3

> “Confession and magnificence are his work, and his righteousness endures for ever and ever.”

“Confession,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] namely the public confession of sins—that is, of praise and of sin—and the magnificence of a good work are his work. Or, as Jerome says, “glory and beauty are his work,” [Cassiodorus] because what he does is praiseworthy and beautiful. And his righteousness, by which he will judge, remains unchangeable for ever and ever, when he says to some, “Go into eternal fire,” and to others, “Come, blessed of my Father,” etc. (Matthew 25).

[Alcuin, Haymo.] Or, from the words “Great are the works,” he speaks generally concerning every kind of God’s work: as though he said, Therefore I will give thanks, because the works of the Lord are great; any of his works are great if they are [Col. 1006A] “sought out in all his wills,” that is, if in them the intention and will of God their maker are seen—if it is understood with what intention God willed to make them. Then he reveals God’s intention and will in his works by adding: Confession of sins and the magnificence of good works are his work; and his righteousness, that is, the reward justly bestowed, endures for ever and ever. As if he said: This is his will, that through his works there should be in human beings confession of sins, magnificence of good works, and righteousness—that is, the reward justly given.

## PART II. VERSE 4

> “He has made a memorial of his wonders; the Lord is gracious and compassionate; he has given food to those who fear him.”

[Col. 1006B] “He has made a memorial.” [Cassiodorus.] Second, he says that the faithful are filled with an abundant gift, promising the Lord’s coming, so that the inheritance may be eagerly sought. As though he said: We ought therefore to give thanks, because the Lord, gracious by nature and compassionate in his bestowal, when he came made a memorial of his wonders. [Haymo.] With the reality accomplished, he supplied the remembrance of the signs that had been in the old Law. Thus he made a memorial because he gave food to those who fear him—[Augustine, Cassiodorus] not bodily food, which he gives even to evil persons, but spiritual food: namely, his body and blood. Thus he calls Christ food, he who is the form of righteousness for believers. By Christ’s coming he feeds those who fear him, in whom are forgiveness and salvation; and, so that you may understand this of his coming, he adds:

### VERSE 5

> “He will remember his covenant [Col. 1006C] for ever; he will declare the power of his works to his people.”

“He will remember.” [Glossa interlinearis.] As though he said: And through them, or because of them—namely, those who fear him—he will remember his covenant. [Cassiodorus.] For what was promised in the Old Testament is fulfilled in the New. I mean the covenant that exists for ever and ever, that is, eternally, because he keeps the words of the covenant with firm truth so that all may be fulfilled. Thus he will remember, so that he will declare the power of his works. The power of his works is that the blind see, the lame walk, and so forth (Matthew 11). He makes these known to his Christian people for this end:

### VERSE 6

> “That he may give them the inheritance of the nations; the works of his hands are truth and judgment.”

[Col. 1106D] “That he may give them the inheritance of the nations.” [Augustine.] This indeed was the purpose of the miracles Christ performed: that the nations might believe.

Alternatively, from the words “He has made a memorial”: as though truly great and sought out are God’s works, because the Lord is gracious and compassionate—this does not change. He made a memorial of his wonders, that is, he did many new things contrary to the ordinary course of events, through which it became evident that he governs all things. “He gave food to those who fear him.” [Alcuin.] As though he said: He brings about confession and magnificence, because he gave food—that is, he inspired a good will through the Holy Spirit—to those who fear him; and through them I shall remember his covenant, that is, the promise made to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 22).

[Remigius, Haymo.] I mean the covenant [Col. 1007A] that will endure for ever, because no other follows it. For that promise was repeated in the Gospel, not altered. Thus he will remember, so that he declared the power, that is, the fulfilment, of his works—that is, of the signifying figures of the Law—to his Jewish people, as he did to the apostles. He will certainly declare it in order that he may give them, namely the apostles, the inheritance of the nations: that is, the nations to be cultivated, namely the Church promised to Abraham from all nations. To these you will give the inheritance, that is, the nations. Yet the works of his hands are truth and judgment—[Glossa interlinearis] that is, true judgment—by which he himself foretold that the disciples would suffer, saying: “A servant is not greater than his lord. And if they persecuted me, they will persecute you also” (John 15). And the meaning is: [Alcuin.] Although he gives them the inheritance, yet they will suffer much.

[Col. 1007B] Or thus: The works of his hands are judgment, by which he will judge, 244 and truth, that is, the execution of judgment. Or, “the works of his hands,” [Cassiodorus] that is, of his power, “are truth,” while he gives the promises to those who have been converted; and judgment, which he threatens against the ungodly. And likewise:

### VERSE 7

> “All his commandments are faithful, confirmed for ever and ever, made in truth and equity.”

All his commandments are faithful to those, [Glossa interlinearis] namely, who fulfil them and do not distrust the promises. They are called faithful, [Cassiodorus] because they preserve those who keep them; they are not falsehoods. And they are confirmed for ever and ever: they were not sent in vain like human words. They are made—that is, fulfilled, not merely spoken—in truth, because what is spoken is fulfilled; and in equity, because he does everything with the balance of justice. Or, they are made in truth and equity, [Glossa interlinearis] that is, they are given by one who does not lie and commands nothing but what is equitable.

## PART III. VERSE 8

> “The Lord has sent redemption to his people; he has commanded his covenant for ever.”

“Redemption.” [Cassiodorus.] Third, he declares that they are redeemed, and that the new covenant is consecrated by eternal grace. As though he said: He gave the things just mentioned; for the Lord sent redemption—[Glossa interlinearis, Cassiodorus] that is, Christ, who gives redemption to captives. He sent him [Col. 1007D] to his Jewish people. Hence: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15). And through the apostles he commanded his new covenant, which will endure for ever, because none will succeed it, because it promises eternal things, and because he does this; therefore:

### VERSE 9

> “Holy and terrible is his name; the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”

His name, [Glossa interlinearis, Cassiodorus] that is, his power and might, is holy to the good and terrible to the ungodly. [Cassiodorus.] Or his name is holy and terrible: that is, the Son, who is holy in his humanity and terrible in the power of his divinity. Therefore let him be loved, because he is advocate; let him be feared, because he is judge. Do not be negligent; do not despair. [Glossa interlinearis.] I say that he is terrible, and [Col. 1008A] fear is indeed beneficial, because the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.

### VERSE 10

> “Good understanding belongs to all who practise it; his praise endures for ever and ever.”

“Understanding,” [Glossa interlinearis, Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Haymo, Cassiodorus, Glossa interlinearis] that is, if it is understood, so that it may be held with discernment and love. For fear of judgment is the gateway of conversion if discernment of love is added. And this fear itself is good understanding for all who practise it.

Or distinguish thus: His name is terrible, and fear is beneficial, because the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, being the gateway of conversion and the way to wisdom. And this understanding, which is in the fear of the Lord—by which the way and gateway are understood—when held attentively, that is, [Col. 1008B] intensely, is good, that is, true and useful, for all who practise it: namely, those who understand it so as to do it, those who ascend from fear to wisdom.

Then he adds what ought to be rendered to the Lord for the things stated: “His praise,” that is, the Lord’s praise, “endures for ever and ever.” [Jerome, Cassiodorus.] Behold the purpose of the psalm, and for this reason *Alleluia* is prefixed. The faithful people began with praise and end in praise. Delivered from the devil, giving thanks, they set forth what the devout ought to do here and what they shall perform in heaven: here, because he delivers; there, because he crowns.

[Cassiodorus.] Alternatively, the whole psalm from its beginning, “I will give thanks,” is understood as the confession of praise that will be in the future. Thus the delivered people say: “I will give thanks to you, O Lord, in the future, with my whole heart,” because then, in reality, they will be delivered from all [Col. 1008C] evils. For then God will be praised and loved with the whole heart, when he is seen face to face. And this will occur “in the council of the righteous,” [Augustine] that is, at the judgment, when the saints will judge with the Lord, sitting on twelve seats and judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 19); and “in the congregation,” that is, when the righteous from the whole world have been gathered into one, among whom there will then be no wicked person, no one covered in sheepskin proudly practising false brotherhood, no endurance of Judas’s thefts, no Simon Magus baptized while wishing to buy the Holy Spirit because he intends to sell him. But now the Church groans among evil people, who, when the righteous have been gathered together, will be shut out of the kingdom.

And these are the great works of the Lord: [Col. 1008D] the gathering of the good and the exclusion of the evil from the kingdom. These works are sought out in all his wills, so exquisitely accomplished that in them some will of God concerning humanity is fulfilled, if all his wills concerning us are weighed: by them mercy abandons no one who confesses, and no one’s wickedness remains unpunished, when he even scourges the son whom he receives. For God does not will any human being to sin. But just as he does not will a person to sin, so he wills to spare the sinner if he repents, so that he may live; likewise he wills to punish the person who persists in sin, so that the obstinate may not escape the power of justice.

Nothing therefore established in free choice surpasses God’s will, even though it acts against his will. For if he does not will you to sin, he nevertheless does not prevent it by effective power, though he does so by a saving and just command. If he wills to spare the repentant, he also wills to punish the unrepentant. Thus God always fulfils his own will concerning humanity, because a human being does nothing from which God does not work what he wills. Great indeed are the works of the Lord, sought out in all his wills.

And truly great are the Lord’s works, because his work is magnificence—that is, the justification of the ungodly. For what is more magnificent than to justify the ungodly? This is rightly called magnificence, because where sin abounded, grace abounded still more. But lest you think that human work precedes this magnificence of God by confessing sins: confession too—that is, the condemnation of one’s offence—which is not yet a work of righteousness, is his work. Therefore let no human being glory in himself, since he does not work righteousness [Col. 1009B] unless justified. But one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly begins with faith, so that good works may show forth—not works preceding what one has deserved, but works following what one has received. “For what do you have that you did not receive?” That confession, therefore, which is not yet a work of righteousness, like the magnificence by which the ungodly are justified, is God’s work, not a human being’s.

What then shall we say? Is God unjust, who has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills? No (Romans 9). For his righteousness endures for ever and ever. “He made a memorial.” As though he said: God has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills, and so he made a memorial of his wonders, humbling one and exalting another. We should know that although his works are wonderful every day, he nonetheless fittingly reserves certain unusual works, which human weakness, intent upon novelty, may remember. For such a miracle will cling most firmly to attentive hearts, whereas continual repetition would make it cheap.

But what good are miracles unless God is feared? And what use is fear unless the gracious God gives food to those who fear him? None. But the gracious and compassionate Lord gave food to those who fear him. The food is the bread that came down from heaven, which no one deserved but which God’s mercy gave. If, for this life alone, he gave such a gift that the sinner needing justification might receive the Word made flesh, what will the glorified person receive in the future? Truly much, because he will remember his covenant for ever—that is, his promise to be fulfilled for ever, [Col. 1009D] that is, eternally.

As though he said: He who gave a pledge has not yet given all; and let not the saints who hear this be saddened. It is easier for a camel to pass through a needle’s eye than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven, because he declared to his people Israel, as to the apostles, the power of his works: that things impossible to human beings are possible to God, so that he may make even the rich enter the kingdom of heaven. He will declare this, indeed, in order to give them the inheritance of the nations. For the journey has been made to the nations. Many are called. The inheritance of the nations is occupied, [Col. 1010A] and camels, humbling themselves through the needle’s eye—that is, through the piercing straits of suffering—enter.

And the works of his hands are the truth which holy martyrs hold, for which they are judged here; and the judgment by which, in the future, they will judge those by whom they are judged here. Therefore let truth be held by those who are judged, so that they may judge those judging them, and even the angels against whom they struggle here. Let nothing separate them from Christ, because all his commandments are faithful. He does not deceive; he gives what he promised. Yet one must not hope to possess it here: rather, they are confirmed for ever and ever and made in truth and equity—that is, they command and promise what is true and just, because it is true and just that here one should labour at what is commanded and there rest in what is promised.

And we shall be able to rest there because he sent redemption to his people from the captivity of this age, so that rest may be there. He commanded his covenant for ever, new, not old. Long ago he did indeed give the Jews the land of promise, but this is the old covenant, belonging to the old person. But he commanded the new covenant for ever, where nothing carnal is to be hoped for. Whoever you may be who wish to be its heir, I do not want you to deceive yourself or imagine that you will attain something like what the eye of avarice commonly desires here; rather, seek that which the eye of man has not seen.

But first flee punishments; avoid Gehenna before you desire the God who promises. Beware of him who threatens, since holy and terrible is his name. Above all the delights of this world, desire wisdom, the mother of the delights of immortality; [Col. 1010C] but the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. “Understanding.” Wisdom will delight you in the chaste embraces of truth; but debts must first be forgiven you before rewards are requested, and do not be exalted, because fear—which is understanding—is the beginning of wisdom and is good for those who practise it. He says this because it is dangerous to understand and not to do. And his praise, whose fear is the beginning of wisdom, endures for ever and ever. This is the whole reward, this the end, this the everlasting dwelling, these the confirmed commandments, this the inheritance of the New Covenant.

## COMPARISON ON PSALM 110: “I WILL GIVE THANKS TO YOU, O LORD, WITH MY WHOLE [HEART],” etc.

### VERSE 2.—“Sought out in all his wills.”

The Hebrew word *HEPHTZEHEM* has an attached pronoun which could ambiguously be translated “their” or “his.” Jerome therefore rendered it, “to be sought out in all his wills.” In the same sense, we say “in all his wills,” namely, God’s. Nebiensis agrees. Other Hebraists reverse the sense: “The great works of the Lord are sought out by all who desire them,” so that the pronoun refers to God’s works, which people ought to investigate and praise with admiration. They thus follow Kimhi, who, they say, takes *HEPHETZ* here as a substantive used adjectivally: *HOPHETZ*.

## PSALM 111

[Col. 1011]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “ALLELUIA OF THE RETURN OF HAGGAI AND ZECHARIAH.”

[Note: [Col. 1011] In the Hebrew and Greek texts the title is simply ἀλληλουϊα, “Alleluia.”]

[Col. 1011A]

“Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.” Title: “Alleluia of the return of Haggai and Zechariah.” [Augustine.] Haggai and Zechariah lived long after David, when the seventy years of the exile had been completed, under Darius king of the Persians (Jeremiah 25). These two prophesied what appeared to concern the restoration of the temple (Haggai 1; Zechariah 1). And, as is read in Ezra, they were also helpers in rebuilding the temple (1 Ezra 5). Yet this passage does not deal with the rebuilding of that material temple, but rather with the restoration of the spiritual temple, which we are. Hence the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3).

For the restoration of that material temple signifies the renewal [Col. 1011B] of the new people from Adam’s ruin, so that it may bear the image of the new person as it formerly bore the image of the old person (1 Corinthians 15); and so that, after the captivity of this age, which revolves in the recurrence of seven days, and the misery of its long pilgrimage, it may be built as a structure not destined to collapse, as though after seventy years, but may be established eternally in blessed immortality.

[Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The aforementioned prophets understood that this spiritual restoration of the spiritual temple was prefigured by that material restoration, 245 and for this great joy they praised the Lord. Thus the title of this psalm contains their names, not because they wrote this psalm, but because they praised the Lord for the restoration of the spiritual temple discussed in this psalm, as was said. And the sense of the title is: This is *Alleluia*, [Col. 1011C] that is, praise of God—the praise, I say, of Haggai and Zechariah. Of what? Of the return, because those prophets sang God’s praises for the spiritual return of the Christian people, as David does here.

[Alcuin.] Or according to the interpretation of the names: Haggai means “mountainous”; Zechariah, “solemn.” By them the faithful are signified, who are mountainous—that is, lofty in virtues—and solemn—that is, rejoicing even in tribulations. [Cassiodorus.] Therefore, just as those prophets praised the Lord for this spiritual return, so Christians signified through them praise the Lord after the remission of sins, as persons delivered from captivity and joyful in the good things they possess. For this psalm shows, after deliverance from sins, [Col. 1011D] how great are the goods of believers and what is the recompense of the faithless. This psalm too is arranged through all the letters of the Hebrew alphabet.

In purpose it exhorts to praise. Method: the psalm has three parts. First, the Prophet teaches what the blessed man does and how great are the goods he merits by grace. Second, he treats the coming of the Lord, through whom people are blessed: “A light has arisen.” Third, he declares that adverse things befall the ungodly: “The sinner shall see.” [Augustine.] The perfection of the aforesaid building is the ineffable [Col. 1012A] peace of wisdom, whose beginning is the fear of the Lord; and with this it begins, saying:

### VERSE 1

> “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; in his commandments he will delight exceedingly.”

“Blessed is the man who fears the Lord,” not the world, [Cassiodorus] because fear of the world makes people miserable, whereas fear of the Lord makes a person desire those things through which one is blessed. “In his commandments he will delight,” or desire, exceedingly or greatly. Fear of God causes this willing. [Alcuin, Augustine.] Notice that he does not say, “he will do,” but “he will greatly will,” because willing is sufficient if the ability to fulfil the commandments is lacking. For “peace is for people of good will” (Luke 2), even if one does not make much progress in fulfilling them, since, as Job says, human life on earth is a temptation (Job 7): “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wisdom 9). And because he fears the Lord and delights exceedingly:

### VERSE 2

> “His seed shall be mighty upon the earth; the generation of the upright shall be blessed.”

“His seed shall be mighty upon the earth,” [Glossa interlinearis] so that neither death nor life may separate him from the love of God: like a harvest which no storm can cast down. Or it may be understood of the future. [Cassiodorus.] Since above he said that the one who fears the Lord is blessed, he now shows the rewards of that blessedness, saying that his seed—that is, the reward of good work—will be mighty upon the earth, not on this earth, where the saints are objects of derision, but upon the heavenly earth, where they shall shine like the sun.

[Augustine.] Or even in this present time, though it appears less so: his seed means works of mercy, from which an eternal harvest is gathered. It shall be mighty, because heaven is bought with a small thing as though with a great one: with a cup of cold water, the widow’s two small coins, and half of Zacchaeus’s goods. And “the generation of the upright,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] is not generation of the flesh but of imitation: that is, the imitators of the righteous. Or “the generation of the upright” means the works of the upright, which shall be blessed by eternal recompense.

The upright are those who do not resist a correcting father and who believe one who promises; they do not believe that their works have perished when they are not recompensed for them in temporal things. For some are bent toward earthly things, doing such good deeds while hoping for their reward from God here or seeking to please people. The blessed man does neither, for he desires neither human glory nor earthly riches. Yet:

### VERSE 3

> “Glory and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures for ever and ever.”

“Glory and riches are in his house,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, in the secret chamber of his heart, where he dwells in the hope of eternal life, where holy riches and eternal glory are laid up. And his righteousness—this is his glory and these are his riches, though he has them from God—endures for ever and ever: that is, they are laid up eternally, because he is not blessed merely for a time.

## PART II. VERSE 4

> “Light has arisen in darkness for the upright in heart: gracious and compassionate and righteous.”

“Light has arisen.” [Cassiodorus.] Second, he treats the coming of the Lord, through whom people have been eternally delivered from sins. As though he said: All these things come from this: because light, that is, the sun of righteousness, has arisen in darkness for the upright in heart. [Glossa interlinearis, Haymo.] That is, it arose in order to drive away darkness and make people upright. What is that light? The Lord: gracious by nature and while he waits, compassionate in bestowal while he justifies, and righteous in rewarding.

Or thus: “Light has arisen.” Above he spoke of the goods of the blessed person; now he says whence that person is blessed: [Cassiodorus] because light has arisen in darkness. That light is more welcome which rises in darkness, but it has risen for none except the upright in heart. What light? The Lord, gracious and compassionate, [Augustine] who is merciful toward those who confess and righteous toward those who despise him. But lest his righteousness terrify you, because:

### VERSE 5

> “The man who is gracious and lends is pleasant; he will order his words in judgment, because he shall not be moved for ever.”

That man is pleasant or sweet, [Augustine] that is, acceptable to God, who is compassionate, forgiving others in spirit and thereby earning forgiveness for himself; and who lends, [Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, gives to others in hope of the future, whether money expended or the labour of his skill. This is lending: that he may receive in the future. [Augustine.] These are the two duties of kindness: forgiving sins and distributing benefits. Hence: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven; give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke 6).

These words depend on the preceding verse: “Glory and riches are in his house.” [Cassiodorus.] Or, the compassionate person gives to the needy; the lender makes a loan, intending to receive the same amount back. He “will order,” or “orders, his words in judgment”: [Augustine] these deeds are like words by which he will defend himself at the future judgment, which will not be without mercy for him because he himself showed mercy. [Alcuin.] This is said by comparison with someone who prepares his case in advance so as to fortify it at judgment with firm pleas.

[Jerome, Cassiodorus, Glossa interlinearis.] Or, here he orders his words in judgment—that is, he speaks and arranges everything with discernment. And truly so, because when placed at the right hand in the future, [Col. 1013D] he shall not be moved for ever: that is, he shall never be separated from the Lord’s glory, even if he falls here, as Peter fell. I say he shall not be moved, but:

### VERSE 6

> “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance; he shall not fear an evil report.”

“The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance,” [Augustine] so as to hear, “Come, blessed of my Father,” etc. (Matthew 25), because then the generation of the upright will be blessed, as was said above. And he shall not fear the evil report spoken to those who are condemned: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (ibid.). This will be said to those at his left hand; and because these things shall belong to the righteous in the future, it is clear that he does not seek his own interests but those of Christ. He patiently bears hardships and confidently awaits what is promised. Therefore he adds:

### VERSE 7

> “His heart is ready to hope in the Lord; his heart is strengthened; he shall not be moved until he despises his enemies.”

“His heart is ready to hope in the Lord,” [Augustine, Alcuin] not in the world, nor is it broken by any temptations, because his heart is strengthened. Or, “he shall not fear an evil report”: that is, if someone threatens evil, he is not afraid, [Cassiodorus] because his heart is ready to hope in the Lord, not in the world; and because he hopes, his heart is strengthened, because no thing of this age softens it. He shall not be moved when he sees others rejoice in the land of the dying and himself mocked. [Augustine.] He shall not be moved from his hope until the reality comes. Hence he adds: Until, being in the land of the living, he despises all his enemies. And because of this future event:

### VERSE 8

> “He has scattered abroad; he has given to the poor. His righteousness endures for ever and ever; his horn shall be exalted in glory.”

“He has scattered abroad,” [Jerome, Haymo] to many people, and has given freely to the poor, not the rich. Behold, this person was buying what he did not see; but he was storing up treasure in heaven, who deigns on earth to hunger and thirst in the poor.

Or continue thus: [Augustine, Alcuin.] With the rest unchanged, the righteous person hopes, and not rashly, because “he has scattered abroad,” etc. It follows: “And his righteousness.” As though he said: He gave what was his, and his righteousness endures for ever and ever; that is, he lived justly and devoutly. Or thus, because he scattered abroad and gave, [Cassiodorus] therefore his righteousness is—that is, he works righteousness. For one who gives his own goods works righteousness. [Col. 1014C] And this righteousness endures for ever and ever, because under God’s guardianship nothing perishes. And his horn, [Augustine, Cassiodorus] whose humility was despised by the proud, shall be exalted in glory. For one who was humble here shall have power there.

## PART III. VERSE 9

> “The sinner shall see and be angry; he shall gnash his teeth and waste away; the desire of sinners shall perish.”

“The sinner shall see.” [Cassiodorus.] Third, he declares that, in contrast to what befalls the righteous, adverse things will come upon the ungodly. Notice that as above he enumerated the goods of the blessed, so here he enumerates the evils of the wicked. By the goods of the blessed he exhorts; by the evils of the wicked he frightens. This psalm instructs the faithful.

As though he said: The horn of the humble shall be exalted, [Col. 1014D] and the sinner will see it—[Augustine] namely, that the horn of the humble is exalted—and will be angry in late and fruitless repentance, saying: “What profit did pride and boasting in riches bring you?” He shall gnash his teeth and waste away. [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: He retains within himself the evil of envy, but, unable to harm anyone, he torments himself with the same things by which he formerly harassed the good. Or, by saying “he shall gnash,” [Augustine] he simply marks a sign of anguish, according to the words: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8). And he shall waste away because he cannot be restored to life through repentance; for the desire of sinners shall perish, with no consolation succeeding, when all things have passed away like a shadow.

## COMPARISON ON PSALM 111: “BLESSED IS THE MAN WHO FEARS THE LORD,” etc.

[Col. 1015A]

### Verse 7

**Until he looks down upon his enemies.** The interpreters have rendered it correctly. Others simply translate *looks upon* for *looks down upon*, so that you may understand vengeance, or something similar. Hence Sanctes said, “until he sees in his enemies what he desires”; or, as Münster has it, “vengeance.” Yet it is certain that among the Hebrews also *RAAH* carries the sense “to despise,” as Pellican understood, adding this interpretation: “he shall despise all their schemes and persecutions, which they pursue with fruitless toil.”

## Psalm 112

[Col. 1015]

### Title of the Psalm: “Alleluia.”

[Col. 1015A]

**Praise the Lord, you servants.** Title: *Alleluia*. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] This psalm is given the same word of praise as the preceding one, because he who receives the nations by the merit of humility is rightly praised; and the psalm itself expounds its title. For *Alleluia*, as we have said, means “Praise the Lord,” and so the psalm begins. Its intention is to exhort to praise. Its structure is in two parts. [Cassiodorus.] First, the Prophet exhorts the devoted continually to praise and everywhere proclaim God. Second, he himself does what he urges upon others—that is, he praises God—at the words, “Who is like the Lord?” [Augustine, Alcuin.] Thus, exhorting to praise, he shows who should praise, whom, for how long, where, and why, saying:

**Verse 1.—“Praise the Lord, you children; praise the name of the Lord.”**

“Praise the Lord,” O you children, simple and pure, [Augustine.] because those who are pure ought to praise—that is, little children, not in understanding but in malice, especially pride; that is, the humble. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not become children in understanding, but be little children in malice, that you may be mature in mind” [Col. 1015C] (1 Cor. 14). [Augustine, Alcuin, Ordinary Gloss.] Therefore, when a dispute had arisen among the apostles as to which of them was greatest, Jesus took a little child, set him in the midst of the disciples, and said: “Unless one humbles himself like this little child, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18), because such persons can enter through the narrow gate (Matt. 7).

You children, therefore, who are received, praise the Lord in his essence. “Praise the name of the Lord.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] He praises the name who proclaims God’s virtues. And this is done by children—that is, by the humble and pure—who enter through the narrow gate. Therefore no one except a child enters the kingdom of heaven. Such persons worthily praise, since pride does not stand in their way. For, once pride has been cast down and extinguished, praise is perfected out of the mouths of infants. But those who think themselves great sing these things unworthily: those who, though knowing God, do not glorify him as God or give thanks. And because only those who are pure, like little children, praise worthily, the child says after all else: “Let us bless the Lord.” [Alcuin, Augustine.]

Or: “Praise the name of the Lord,” that is, act in such a way that others, seeing your good works, may glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5). Behold, he has said who ought to praise and whom they ought to praise; he next adds how long he is to be praised, namely always, saying:

**Verse 2.—“Blessed be the name of the Lord, from this time forth and for evermore.”**

“Blessed be the name of the Lord.” [Cassiodorus.] As though he said: Do not suppose that I command praise only for an hour; rather, let the name of the Lord always be blessed. [Ordinary Gloss, Jerome, Augustine.] Let it not be blasphemed “from this,” that is, from the moment you begin; [Col. 1016A] “and now,” that is, in your progress; “and for evermore,” that is, unto eternity. I say “from this,” and add “for evermore,” because you begin when this is said to you; but praise him without end, not yourselves, even when you have become great.

**Verse 3.—“From the rising of the sun unto its setting, the name of the Lord is praiseworthy.”**

[Col. 1016B] “From the rising of the sun.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Here he says that God ought to be praised everywhere. As though he said: I do not command praise only for an hour, nor only in one place, but let the name of the Lord be praiseworthy, even from the rising of the sun to its setting. [Cassiodorus.] That is, everywhere—not among the Jews alone. By the circuit of the sun, as by a kind of line, he signifies the world, [Haymo.] throughout which God is to be praised; and he next adds why he is to be praised.

**Verse 4.—“The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory above the heavens.”**

“The Lord is exalted.” [Haymo.] As though he said: Therefore praise him, because the Lord is exalted above all nations and his glory is above the heavens. [Cassiodorus.] By “nations” he denotes all earthly things, and by “heavens” all heavenly things, so that by these two he indicates that all creatures are subject to him. Or, [Col. 1016C] by “nations” he signifies the carnal, and by “heavens” the spiritual, above whom God is exalted. Or thus: the Lord is exalted above all nations—that is, human beings. [Augustine.] And his glory is above the heavens, where people see the gods whom they worship gleaming—the sun, moon, and the like. Thus the heavens have above themselves him whom the humble have with themselves in their hearts. [Alcuin.] Or he calls the apostles “heavens,” through whom he reigns among the nations, which he signifies by his own name. And the sense is: I invite all to praise because he shall reign over all.

### Part II. Verse 5.—“Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly things in heaven and on earth?”

“Who is like?” [Cassiodorus.] Second, he himself does what he urges upon others, so that he may teach others by his deed as well. As though he said: The Lord is indeed exalted. For who is like the Lord our God? That is, no one can do by himself as he does. He is the one who dwells on high, [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] that is, in the holy angels, whom he exalts in such a way that he does not make them proud; and although he is high, he nevertheless does not despise the humble. And that is, because he looks with the gaze of mercy upon the lowly—those who are high through his gift, and in whom he sits. He looks upon the lowly things in heaven—that is, humble angels—and on earth—that is, humble saints; he looks upon them thus, just as conversely he hates the proud.

Or thus, he is the one [Augustine.] who dwells on high—that is, in the saints, whom he exalts without pride. And he looks upon the lowly, namely those same persons in whom he dwells, because their humility [Col. 1017A] in flesh and spirit is regarded. Hence he adds: “In heaven,” as though he said: I call them lowly in heaven because of the freedom of the spirit, and on earth because of the servitude of the body. That is, they possess humility in spirit and display it in deed.

Or he looks upon some in heaven—that is, those whom he has already called and in whom he dwells—and he looks upon others on earth, namely those whom he calls in order to dwell in them. For he possesses the former, who think heavenly thoughts; the latter he awakens while they dream earthly things.

Or, rather, the heavens are those who will judge with the Lord; the earth is the remaining multitude of saints, who will be placed at the right hand, so that they may be received by those into eternal dwellings whom they made their friends by means of unrighteous mammon. Yet both are humble, because each remembers what they did through their own wickedness and what they became through the Lord’s grace. The meaning is: he looks upon the lowly in heaven—that is, the saints who will sit with the Lord as judges of others, who here sowed heavenly things—and on earth—that is, those who will be judged and saved, who here rendered earthly things. The humble are rightly called heavens, because he is:

**Verse 6.—“Raising up the needy from the earth, and lifting the poor from the dung-hill.”**

Raising up by grace alone from the earth, [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] that is, from the stain of the body, the formerly needy—those who were formerly needy and still are so long as they groan in the body. And he raises the poor person from the dung-hill of carnal pleasure. For one is raised from the dung-hill when the vices of the flesh rule him. For what end does he raise him?

[Col. 1017C]

**Verse 7.—“That he may place him with princes, with the princes of his people.”**

[Col. 1018A] “That he may place him with princes,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] that is, with angels, “and with the princes of his people,” that is, with the apostles. That is, he raises the poor in order to add him to the orders of heaven, which consist of angels and human beings.

**Verse 8.—“Who makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a joyful mother of children.”**

“Who makes dwell.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Here he explains where he raises and exalts: in the Church, which before the bridegroom’s coming was barren (Gal. 4), but now is a glad and fruitful mother of many. [Augustine, Alcuin.] As though he said: Not only does he raise those whom he places as judges with princes; but he is the one who makes the barren woman—namely Sarah, that is, the Gentile Church, formerly barren; and Sarah signifies her—[Col. 1018B] dwell in the house, that is, in the Church of the Jews, among the Jews themselves, so that the two walls may be joined in the cornerstone (Eph. 2), and there may be one fold (John 10).

[Augustine.] I mean, he makes her a joyful mother of children—that is, of believers among all nations—because the children of the forsaken woman are many. Though they do not leave everything, they nevertheless make for themselves friends from unrighteous mammon (Luke 16), that is, by works of mercy. These words are spoken in the person of such people, concerning whom Isaiah, speaking to the Church, says: “The children whom you had lost shall say in your ears: ‘This place is too narrow for us; make room for us now, that we may dwell.’ But you shall say in your heart: ‘Who has begotten these for me? Who, then, has brought these up for me, when I know myself to be childless and a widow?’” [Col. 1018C] (Isa. 49).

## Psalm 113

[Col. 1017]

### Title of the Psalm: “Alleluia.”

[Col. 1017C]

**When Israel went out.** Title: *Alleluia*. Here again *alleluia* is used for a different subject. [Cassiodorus.] For just as God is praised for different actions, so this title is assigned for various matters. Here, beginning from the origin of the Hebrew people, the Prophet announces Christ given to the world through the great miracles bestowed upon that people. By these likenesses—that is, by what they signify—every Christian too is set free. [Augustine.] [Col. 1017D] For those miracles were figures of the spiritual mysteries of Christ and the Church, as will become clear in the exposition of the psalm. Thus past events alone are not narrated here; future things are proclaimed, because future things were signified in those acts. Therefore not everything that happened there is said here, but some things differently, lest one suppose that the Prophet merely recalls past events.

Its intention is [Cassiodorus.] to invite to the worship and praise of the true God. The psalm is in three parts. First, the Prophet says what wonders God gave to the Hebrews figuratively and to Christians spiritually. Second, he asks why these things happened, at “What ails you, O sea?” Third, he proves the nations’ images empty and commends the worship of God, at “Their idols.” Therefore the Prophet, beginning his account of wonders, says:

[Col. 1018C]

**Verse 1.—“When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people.”**

“When Israel went out of Egypt,” namely the house of Jacob from a barbarous people, [Alcuin.] when the people of Israel went out of Egypt—that is, from a barbarous people.

**Verse 2.—“Judah became his sanctuary; Israel his dominion.”**

“Judah became his sanctuary,” [Alcuin.] that is, that people was sanctified in Judah, that is, in the promised land, by worshipping the true God; this land had formerly been polluted by idolatry. “And Israel became his dominion over the land,” that is, it became powerful in it. For those who had been slaves in Egypt became masters there in the Church. Therefore:

**Verse 3.—“The sea saw and fled; Jordan turned backward.”**

The Red Sea saw the people coming out of Egypt and fled, [Jerome.] that is, it was divided, so that the people might pass through on dry ground. “And Jordan turned backward.” [Augustine.] He says this otherwise than it happened. For there it is read that the Jordan stood still on the side from which the waters flowed down; nor is anything said there about mountains leaping, as is said here: “The mountains leaped.” But both the deeds there and the words here are figures. [Col. 1019A] [Jerome, Augustine.] Therefore Israel and Jacob are rightly understood as the Christian people, which is first Jacob, that is, “wrestler,” and afterwards Israel, that is, “one who sees God.” Egypt, which means “affliction,” signifies the world.

[Alcuin.] Therefore, just as that people, in departing from Egypt, was sanctified and made powerful in Judah, so confession sanctifies Christians departing from sins. [Augustine.] For Judah means “confession.” In the spiritual departure, accomplished by the mind and God’s help, Israel—that is, those seeing God—departs from Egypt, that is, from the affliction of the world which they renounce; namely, the house of Jacob, that is, the Church, the house of wrestlers, which we are before becoming Israel, departs from a barbarous people. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] That is, we ought to be separated in mind from the blasphemies of the Gentiles. [Col. 1019B] [Augustine.] Or from the crowd of demons; for a barbarous language is one that does not praise God.

In that departure, I say, Judah—that is, confession—became his sanctification, a sanctification existing in the heart which confession cleanses; and through it, those made Israel can resist vices and become children of God. Hence he adds: “Israel his dominion.” That is, through confession one is sanctified, and through it becomes Israel, “seeing God”; and for those made Israel belongs the power of resisting vices and becoming a child of God, according to the saying: “He gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1).

And this the sea of the world saw, that is, the sinners of the world, and fled—that is, it withdrew, so that a way without opposition toward spiritual freedom might lie open. [Col. 1019C] And Jordan, which means “descent,” that is, humble persons who have been baptized, turned backward—that is, returned to him from whom they had sprung. It is therefore good for them to turn backward, so that God may be before their face, whom they had been able to have behind them; and thus, forgetting the things behind, they may stretch forward to the things before them.

[Cassiodorus.] Or because Jordan runs into the sea, it signifies those who, through various desires, drag others into the great sea—that is, into the bitter wickedness of this world. But at the Lord’s coming these things cease, as though turned backward. This is what is meant by “Jordan turned backward.” And then:

**Verse 4.—“The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock.”**

[Col. 1019D] “The mountains,” [Augustine.] that is, the stewards of the word of God, namely the apostles, “leaped” or rejoiced. They are like rams, that is, leaders of the people, who with the horns of both Testaments defeat heretics and overthrow superstitions. Hence elsewhere: “Bring to the Lord, O sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. 28). [Note: [Col. 1019D] From Jerome here and in Psalm 28; and Alcuin.]

And the sixth station of the children of Israel coming from Egypt was Elim [Note: [Col. 1019D] From Jerome, *To Fabiola on the Forty-Two Stations*; and Alcuin.], which means “rams,” where there were twelve springs and seventy palms (Exod. 15). These signify the twelve apostles and the seventy disciples, whom the Lord chose in the sixth age, that through the four parts of the world they might bear the palm of Christ’s victory, destroying with the double horn of both [Col. 1020A] Testaments every knowledge raising itself against Christ.

“And the hills,” so called from cultivating, [Cassiodorus.] that is, those of middling rank, “leaped”—those who received the seed of faith (1 Cor. 4). They are “like lambs of the flock,” [Augustine.] that is, begotten through the Gospel by the rams, not envious but innocent, generated in faith by the rams. These things, then, must not be understood only literally. Hence you should not doubt that the Jordan—that is, the ancient events—signifies here what takes place spiritually today.

### Part II. Verse 5.—“What ails you, O sea, that you fled? And you, O Jordan, that you turned backward?”

“What ails you, O sea?” [Augustine.] Second, he asks why these things occur in order to stir up wonder, and answers at “At the presence of the Lord.” [Col. 1020B] As though he said: The sea flees and Jordan turns backward; but those seeing these things wonder and say: “What ails you, O sea?” that is, O world, that you fled? That is: What has happened, O world, that your obstacles have given way, so that many thousands of people renouncing the world turn to the Lord? And this is what follows: “And you, O Jordan,” [Cassiodorus.] namely, O you who flow away in various desires, why have you turned backward? That is, away from your purpose. Why have you abandoned your customs? Likewise, O you:

**Verse 6.—“Mountains, that you leaped like rams; and hills, like lambs of the flock?”**

“Mountains,” [Augustine.] to whom at the end it will be said: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” [Col. 1020C] (Matt. 25)—what is it that you leaped like rams? And you hills, to whom it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father,” etc. (ibid.)—what is it that you leaped like lambs of the flock? Behold why:

**Verse 7.—“At the presence of the Lord the earth was moved, at the presence of the God of Jacob.”**

“At the presence of the Lord.” [Cassiodorus.] He who had asked now answers; and one answer is given to the two preceding questions, because one author made both the sea and the Jordan—that is, the ages—stand amazed, and made his own—that is, mountains and hills—rejoice. For when Christ appeared, people were moved from their superstition to the worship of the Lord. That is, these things happened because the earth, formerly sluggish in doing good, was moved [Col. 1020D]—or shaken—from its superstition to the worship of God, in order to be established more firmly.

And this was “at the presence of the Lord,” that is, through the Lord’s presence, who says: “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). Or, “at the presence of the Lord,” [Haymo, Ordinary Gloss.] that is, through the knowledge of the Lord which they possess. Or, “at the presence of the Lord,” that is, through the Lord’s mercy, namely from his wrath which they foresee to come. And as though someone asked, “Who is God?” he adds: “At the presence of the God of Jacob.” [Jerome, Alcuin.] That is, the Lord at whose presence the earth is moved is the God of Jacob; he is not a new God. Or, he who makes his own wrestle is also:

[Col. 1021A]

**Verse 8.—“Who turned the rock into pools of water, and the cliff into springs of water.”**

“Who turned the rock into pools of water, and the cliff into springs of water,” [Augustine.] that is, he who, formerly hard because unknown, melted himself to water the faithful, so that in them there might be a fountain of living water springing into eternal life (John 4). This occurred when, after rising again, he opened their understanding so that they understood the Scriptures (Luke 24). Thus the Lord himself was formerly as a rock and a cliff, until, with the Scriptures opened, he flowed forth like a spring and flooded all believers, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7).

Or thus: he is the one who turned the rock—that is, the hard hearts of the Jews—into pools of water, [Cassiodorus.] that is, to the water of baptism; and the cliff—that is, the Gentiles—[Col. 1021B] into springs of water, so that they too might pour forth abundant springs of preaching.

**Verse 9.—“Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name.”**

“Not to us.” [Cassiodorus.] Having said that God gives good things, he asks that he give them for his name’s sake, because he sees no merits in human beings. As though he said: Thus water flows from the rock, and it has not been given for our merits but through your mercy. And this is: O Lord, not to us Jews, not to us Gentiles, [Haymo.] that is, not for our merits; but give glory to your name. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] For this grace of water bursting from the rock was granted, not for our merits, but through his mercy. Hence he does not say, “Give good things”; but in place of this he says, “Give glory,” [Col. 1021C] because, for good things freely given to us, he appears glorious. For glory is when he gives in accordance with merits; therefore, give glory to your name—that is, grant us through the mercy of your name the good things for which your name is glorified. I mean glory proceeding:

**Verse 10.—“Because of your mercy and your truth, lest at any time the nations say: ‘Where is their God?’”**

“Because of”—that is, concerning—your mercy, by which you call the impious and spare sinners; and concerning your truth, by which you judge those who do not come and restore promised rewards to the good. In mercy he calls the impious and spares sinners; in truth, he judges and punishes the impious and those who do not come, and restores promised rewards.

[Alcuin.] Or thus: I mean glory proceeding [Col. 1021D] because of your mercy—that is, from the restoration of humankind—and from your truth, that is, from the fulfilled promise by which you promised the coming of the Son. Therefore give glory, lest the nations at any time say: “Where is their God?” [Note: [Col. 1021D] From Augustine, second sermon on the Psalm.] The impious often cast this in the teeth of afflicted good people. The nations which have visible gods are also accustomed to say this to us because we worship an invisible God. Lest they always say it, he says, “Lest at any time,” etc. [Augustine.] That is, give glory lest the nations say, “Where is their God?” This will be fulfilled when the sign of the Son of Man appears in heaven: when he is still proclaimed to them as not to be believed, but is already shown as to be feared.

[Col. 1022A]

**Verse 11.—“But our God is in heaven; he has done whatsoever he willed.”**

“But our God.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] As though he said: The nations ask where he is; but we answer: our God is in heaven, that is, in Christ the man, according to the saying: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5). [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Or, “in heaven” means powerful over all creatures. Or, according to another reading, “in heaven above,” because he transcends all heavenly and earthly bodies. And he has done whatever he willed, whether in bodily or spiritual things, by which he appears almighty.

### Part III. Verse 12.—“The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands.”

“The idols.” [Cassiodorus.] Third, he rejects the empty idols of the nations [Col. 1022B] and shows how useful the worship of God is. [Augustine.] Here is a complete demonstration, in blame and praise. Having shown the power of our God from his works, he turns to the visible gods of the nations. That is, our God is such; but the idols of the nations, certainly not true gods, are silver and gold in the material from which they are made. The Gentiles indeed have wooden and earthen ones also; but he names the more precious, to which greater reverence is paid, so that whoever is ashamed in their case may more readily be ashamed in the rest.

[Alcuin, Augustine.] I say they are silver and gold; but since God made these materials, he says that they are the work of human hands in their form. That is: they worship what they have made from them. For God created the material, but human folly [Col. 1022C] added the form. [Augustine.] Therefore do not add your hands so as to wish, from the metal which the true God made, to make a false god; indeed, a false human being whom you might worship as the true God. If anyone received such an image as a true human being even into friendship, he would be insane.

Therefore they are the works of human hands because fashioned by human hands; but they do not possess the functions of limbs. Hence he adds:

**Verse 13.—“They have a mouth and shall not speak; they have eyes and shall not see.”**

“They have a mouth and shall not speak.” [Augustine.] A human being who speaks is better than they are. For speaking is proper to human beings. The other things that follow, however, are common to humans and beasts, so that you may know that not merely human beings but even beasts are to be preferred to idols. [Col. 1022D] Yet for the affections of the wretched, an image resembling a living creature has greater force—namely, that it has a mouth, and so forth—than the fact that it does not live and cannot perform the functions of limbs. “They have eyes and shall not see.”

**Verse 14.—“They have ears and shall not hear; they have nostrils and shall not smell.”**

“They have ears and shall not hear; they have nostrils and shall not smell.” [Augustine.] These things are plain and utterly evident. What child, if asked, would not answer with certainty that idols have mouths and do not speak, eyes and do not see, and so forth, as the divine discourse sets forth? Why then does the Holy Spirit [Col. 1023A] repeatedly impress, in many places of Scripture, what everyone knows? Because an image resembling a living being deceives people into thinking that some hidden divinity is in it and that it is not without a living inhabitant.

Therefore demons also invite people to possess idols; and through the manifold deceit of those demons who preside over them, deadly errors are sown and multiplied. Elsewhere the Prophet condemns these things, saying: “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. 95). More prudent persons say that they worship neither idols nor demons in them, but the things signified by idols—for example, the air by one, the earth by another, and so forth. Others go further, saying that they worship not the bodies themselves, but the deities which preside over their governance, such as Jupiter, Mercury, and the like. The Apostle condemns all these things, saying: “They changed [Col. 1023B] the truth of God into a lie and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Rom. 1).

**Verse 15.—“They have hands and shall not touch; they have feet and shall not walk; they shall not cry out with their throat.”**

“They have hands and shall not touch.” [Augustine.] Even monkeys can do this, handling things with their hands; they are therefore better than idols. “They have feet and shall not walk; they shall not cry out with their throat.” A beast is better, for although it does not speak, it has a cry in its throat. Note that after speaking, which is peculiar to the human being, he adds something shared with beasts, so that you understand him to mean beasts by “and so forth,” and do not refer the things above that are common to beasts to human beings alone. For beasts too see, hear, smell, and walk, [Col. 1023C] so that you may know that not only humans but even beasts are to be preferred to idols. Thus, if you are ashamed to worship a beast possessing all these faculties, you should be much more ashamed to worship a mute idol devoid of life and sense.

**Verse 16.—“Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.”**

“Let them become like them.” [Ordinary Gloss.] That is, since idols are such, let all who make them and all who trust in them, worshipping them, become like them. [Augustine.] Let them see idols with open, living eyes, yet worship images that neither see nor live with minds shut and dead. [Alcuin.] See, then, the shamefulness of such worship when he says, “Let them become like them,” which they truly are, as has been said. Or, “let them become like them,” that is, let them understand themselves to be like idols, so that they may strive to become unlike them.

**Verse 17.—“The house of Israel hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and their protector.”**

“The house of Israel.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] Here he commends the usefulness of the Christian religion. As though he said: The nations trust in idols, which cannot help. But the house of Israel, [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] that is, the universal Church, has hoped in the Lord, whom it does not see, having cast away the world; and so that endurance may last to the end, he is their helper, and so forth. [Haymo, Cassiodorus.] Or the connection is this: I say that it hoped, because the Lord is their helper in doing good and their protector against diabolical deceits. [Augustine.] Lest it seem [Col. 1024A] that what is hope for the lesser is already possession for the greater, he adds:

**Verse 18.—“The house of Aaron hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and their protector.”**

“The house also of Aaron,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] that is, the order also of priests, hoped in the Lord; and the Lord is their helper, so that they too may persevere, and their protector, so that they may not be harmed. The Lord is the helper of lesser and greater alike because both fear the Lord. And:

**Verse 19.—“Those who fear the Lord hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and their protector.”**

“Those who fear the Lord,” among every nation, [Haymo, Cassiodorus.] hoped in the Lord. These two things, namely hope and fear, make people blessed; and the Lord is their helper and protector. [Augustine.] For we do not anticipate God’s mercy by our own merits, but:

**Verse 20.—“The Lord has remembered us and has blessed us.”**

“The Lord has remembered us.” [Jerome, Haymo, Cassiodorus.] Or the connection is this: he is truly a helper, for the Lord, who for a long time seemed almost to have forgotten, remembered us, in order to turn us through the Son whom he sent; and, once we had been turned, he blessed us through the same Son. He repeats those whom he blessed:

**Verse 21.—“He has blessed the house of Israel; he has blessed the house of Aaron.”**

“He has blessed the house of Israel,” that is, the Church. “He has blessed [Col. 1024C] the house of Aaron,” that is, the chief priests.

**Verse 22.—“He has blessed all who fear the Lord, the small with the great.”**

“He has blessed all who fear the Lord.” [Cassiodorus.] No class of people is excluded: he has blessed the small with the great.

**Verse 23.—“May the Lord add to you—upon you and upon your children.”**

“May the Lord add blessing to you,” [Augustine.] O Jews, “and upon you,” O Gentiles, “and upon your children.” Or he distinguishes fathers from children, that is, teachers from disciples, saying: O fathers, O teachers, may the Lord add to you—that is, add others to your number. And so it happened, because [Col. 1024D] the number of teachers increased. And may he add to your children; this too happened, because the number of followers increased, when children of Abraham are raised up from stones (Matt. 3). For the faith of all nations was added, and the number increased, not only of wise overseers but also of obedient peoples. Therefore:

**Verse 24.—“You are blessed by the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”**

“You,” [Augustine.] both fathers and children, are blessed by the Lord, who made you heaven in the greater and earth in the lesser. Yet because these lesser ones also, by growing, become great heavens, they are the heaven of the earth, whom they nourish with the milk of simple teaching, so that they may also be:

**Verse 25.—“The heaven of heaven is for the Lord, but he gave the earth to the children of men.”**

[Col. 1025A] “The heaven of heaven,” [Augustine.] while they hope that it may be turned into heaven. This heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord because those great ones alone are taught by the Lord: they now receive the purity and abundance of wisdom not from a human being or through a human being, but from God himself. Nor are they only the heaven of heaven, but also children of men, to whom he gave the earth in which to work—that is, subjects whom they may cultivate so as to bear fruit.

Since these things are so, both, namely heaven and earth—that is, greater and lesser—should live from him who made them and praise him; otherwise they will die, and from one dead, confession perishes as though he did not exist. Hence, turning his speech to the Lord, he says:

**Verse 26.—“The dead shall not praise you, O Lord, nor all who descend into hell.”**

[Col. 1025B] “The dead,” [Augustine.] that is, those dead in sins, shall not praise you, O Lord. Or thus: he calls those “heaven of heaven,” as we said before, whose minds he so exalted that they became teachable not by any human being but by God himself. In comparison with them, all visible things—that is, heaven and earth—are called earth. He gave this earth to the children of men—that is, to the lesser—so that, through contemplating it, they might infer the Creator, whom the weak cannot yet see without this aid.

And this is what he says: “The heaven of heaven is for the Lord,” because those greater persons are taught by the Lord alone. The meaning is the same as before. “But the earth,” that is, all visible things, “he gave to the children of men,” that is, the weak, so that through them they might know the invisible things of God. “The dead,” etc.: these words are not changed.

Or thus, from the words “You are blessed”: [Cassiodorus.] What he had above wished to be blessed, he now says confidently: “Blessed,” as though he said: I said, “May he add,” and so it will be, because you will be blessed “by the Lord,” that is, to the Lord’s honor. For this pertains to the Lord, [Alcuin.] that you serve him as well. And *Domino* is in the dative case. I mean the Lord who made heaven and earth, [Cassiodorus.] that is, every creature. You ought to belong to the Lord, because also the heaven of heaven—that is, Christ—belongs to the Lord, that is, to the Lord’s honor. [Note: [Col. 1025D] From Strabo and Bede on Genesis 1, distinction 2 of the second book of the *Sentences*.]

But he gave the earth—that is, the people to be instructed—to the children of men, namely the preachers, according to the saying: “As the Father sent me, so I send you into the world” [Col. 1026A] (John 20), that you may go and bear fruit (John 15).

Or thus: the Lord made heaven and earth, but the heaven of heaven—that is, the *empýrean* heaven, which, immediately upon its creation, was filled with holy angels, called *empýreon*, “fiery,” from its brightness, not its heat, for Greek πῦρ (*pyr*) is called *ignis*, “fire,” in Latin—[Cassiodorus, Haymo] he gave to the Lord, Christ according to his humanity. But he gave this lower earth to the children of men, so that in it they might purify themselves.

Since these things are so, O Lord, the dead in sins shall not praise you, because “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15). Nor shall all—that is, anyone at all among those who descend into hell—[Jerome.] that is, into the depth of vices; for when a sinner comes into the depth of vices, he despises, as Scripture says elsewhere [Col. 1026B] (Prov. 18). [Cassiodorus.] Or he means hell literally: the place of punishments [Note: [Col. 1025D] Understand “place of punishments” generally.], into which not only the impious but also the saints descended before Christ’s coming. Therefore he does not say universally, “none who descend,” but particularly: “nor all who descend into hell shall praise you,” because saints too descended there, but were not in the lower hell. Those impious persons will not praise:

**Verse 27.—“But we who live bless the Lord, from this time forth and for evermore.”**

“But we who live” by the life of grace, [Jerome.] bless the Lord—that is, praise the Lord—from this, that is, from the time we begin; and now, namely in progressing, [Col. 1026C] and for evermore, without end.

### Collation on Psalm 113: “When Israel went out of Egypt,” etc.

**Verse 26.—“Into hell.”** The Hebrews have “into silence,” by which is understood the grave or hell, where there is silence and the memory of a human being passes into oblivion: *DUMAH* (“silence”).

**Verse 27.—“But we who live.”** In Hebrew it stands absolutely: “but we.” Yet it is clearly to be understood in this way, since “the dead shall not praise you” had just preceded; he immediately introduces the adversative conjunction, “but we,” namely, “who live.”

## Psalm 114

[Col. 1025]

### Title of the Psalm: “Alleluia.”

[Col. 1025D]

“I have loved, because.” Title: Alleluia, that is, “Praise God.” [Cassiodorus.] This title is frequently repeated, because the praise of God is both the dignity of works and the price of labours—that is, both merit and reward. The Prophet says what this psalm contains as one like a sheep that had strayed and has been carried back to the flock on the shoulders of the merciful shepherd, and like the prodigal son, returned after a long captivity, yet still a pilgrim in this world (Luke XV). [Cassiodorus.] This psalm is the consolation of the faithful against the sufferings of the world.

Intention. He exhorts to praise.

Method. The psalm has two parts. First, the sinner, delivered from the pit of sins and set upon a rock [Col. 1026D], gives thanks because he has been heard, and says that he called upon God amid every danger. Secondly, he cries again, that, being delivered, he may come to rest: there, “O Lord, deliver.” [Augustine.] Therefore the Prophet, in the person of a captive returned home, giving thanks to God, says:

VERSE 1.—“I have loved, because the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer.”

I have loved, [Cassiodorus.] not because temporal goods have been given me, as also to unbelievers; [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] but because the Lord will hear: hope of the future kindles love. Or, according to another reading, “has heard the voice of my prayer”; the love of this man differs greatly from the love of unbelievers. For God is loved even by unbelievers because he gives them good things [Col. 1027A]. Hence elsewhere: “He will praise thee when thou hast done him good” (Ps. XLVIII). But God is loved perfectly when the mind is not shaken by adversities but is more inflamed in charity through hope. This man explains that manner in himself, saying: “I have loved,” not because he made me king or gave me prosperity, but because he will hear, or has heard, the voice of my prayer in distress. “Will hear”:

VERSE 2.—“Because he has inclined his ear to me; and in my days I will call upon him.”

Because he has already inclined, [Augustine,] therefore I have hope: “his ear to me,” when he gave his Son for us. [Cassiodorus.] In this he indicates that he believes those things which pertain to salvation. He inclined his ear in the incarnation and in the passion of the Son; having experienced mercy in him, I will call upon him, [Augustine,] which is not without faith. [Col. 1027B] Hence the Apostle: “How shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” (Rom. X.) Therefore, when he says, “I will call,” he indicates that one who loves is not idle. And this will be “in my days,” that is, in the days of my misery, which I made for myself by sinning: days full of labour, sorrow, and old corruption. In those days:

VERSE 3.—“The pains of death surrounded me, and the perils of hell found me.”

“The pains of death surrounded me.” [Augustine.] Or: “I will call in my days,” that is, in the days of my salvation, in the time of fullness. Hence: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI). “The pains surrounded me,” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] as though he said: I have loved, I will call, and these are the reasons for loving. These make me cry out, because the pains of death surrounded me—that is, sins, from which arise pain and the death of the soul, or eternal death. And this, namely eternal death, will be in hell. Hence follows: “And the perils of hell,” [Augustine, Alcuin.] that is, the debts and liabilities to the punishments of hell, found me when I was wandering from you and exposed to evils. I did not find them while rejoicing in the prosperity of this world; for, immersed in carnal pleasure, I did not notice the evils surrounding me.

VERSE 4.—“I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord.”

“Tribulation and sorrow.” [Augustine, Alcuin.] As though he said: Evils first found me, but afterwards I found tribulation—what he had formerly called “perils,” he here calls “tribulation”—and sorrow—what he had formerly called “pains” [Col. 1027D]—that is, I recognized them, though they lie hidden from others.
