Or [Augustine] by “sorrow and tribulation” he means this penal condition and the pain of scourges, which God inflicts upon a person for usefulness. Hence: “Give us help from tribulation”; for through these outward things a person recognizes his inward misery, namely the pains of death and the perils of hell.

The sense is: those things first surrounded me when I did not know it, and found me; but afterward I found that tribulation and sorrow—that is, outward affliction—are useful. For useful tribulation and sorrow, from which help comes to us, had previously been hidden from me; then vain things deceived me. But through that pain I found the inward misery which I had without knowing it. Therefore I called upon the name of the Lord—that is, I strove to be delivered by the Lord.

[Col. 1028A] PART II. VERSE 5.—“O Lord, deliver my soul. The Lord is merciful and just, and our God has compassion.”

“O Lord, deliver my soul.” [Cassiodorus.] Secondly, he again cries out that, once delivered, he may come to rest. As though he said: Since these evils are mine, O Lord, deliver my soul, because without God it is captive. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] The Apostle cries for deliverance from this captivity: “Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. VII.) “The Lord is merciful”: this is what the same Apostle adds, “The grace of God through Jesus Christ.” As though he said: I deliver, and let no one doubt, because the Lord is merciful, [Augustine,] since he first inclined his ear and called me; and just, because he scourges. For “he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII). And “our God has compassion” [Col. 1028B] again, because he receives us into blessedness. What he scourges ought not to seem so bitter as what he receives is sweet, because:

VERSE 6.—“The Lord preserves little ones; I was humbled, and he delivered me.”

The Lord preserves little ones as a shepherd does, [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Remigius,] that is, the humble, whom he seeks as grown heirs. Believe one who has experienced it, because I was humbled; and therefore he delivered me. [Augustine, Glossa interlinearis.] As though he said: That pain is not punitive but saving, like the pain caused by a physician when he cuts. Or the connection may be thus: The Lord is just and merciful, and therefore I was humbled and he will deliver me.

VERSE 7.—“Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has done you good.”

[Col. 1028C] “Return.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] He exhorts his soul to return to God, from whom it has rest. As though he said: Since the Lord is merciful, therefore, O my soul, return to your rest—that is, to God, where even here there is rest of mind—yet let no idleness be present, so that anyone should cease from working. Return, I say, not by your own merits or powers, but because the Lord has done you good: because he first gave gifts to the one delivered; otherwise he would not have been delivered. Thus he does good:

VERSE 8.—“Because he has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from falling.”

Because through faith he has delivered my soul from death. [Augustine.] Death is unbelief. Hence the Lord in the Gospel: [Col. 1028D] “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. VIII); and: “The dead shall not praise thee, O Lord” (Ps. CXIII). This man already possesses this, namely a soul delivered from death, by the very fact that from an unbeliever he has become a believer; for, as the Lord says: “He who believes passes from death to life” (John V). And he has delivered my eyes from tears and my feet from falling. These things have taken place in hope, not yet in reality, because tears still exist now, and there is still falling because of the weakness of the flesh; and in the feet, as it were in the lowest parts of the soul—that is, in sensuality—there is still slipperiness. But in the future:

VERSE 9.—“I shall please the Lord in the land of the living.”

I shall please the Lord perfectly, [Jerome, Augustine,] because there will be no falling feet in those who walk, no slipperiness of weak flesh. And this will be in the land of the living [Col. 1029A] [Augustine, Jerome, Augustine,] who live eternally—something I shall not do while I live in mortal flesh. And it should be noted that above he said, “He has delivered from falling,” not “He will deliver”; and yet here he does not say, “I do not please,” but “I shall please”: certainly then, not now.

COLLATION ON PSALM CXIV: “I HAVE LOVED, BECAUSE HE WILL HEAR,” etc.

VERSE 3.—“Perils”: METZARE. Jerome [Col. 1030A] translates “fortifications”; others, “sieges,” or “straits,” namely of hell. Nothing is said that does not convey the sense of perils.

VERSE 9.—“I shall please the Lord.” The Hebrews have: “I shall walk before the Lord,” ETHHALLEC LIPHNE ADONAI. But it is a figure of speech: to walk before the Lord means to please him in all things, as in Genesis V, “Enoch walked with God.”

PSALM CXV.

[Col. 1029]

TITLE OF THE PSALM: “ALLELUIA.”

[Col. 1029A]

“I believed, therefore I spoke.” Title: Alleluia. [Col. 1029B] [Cassiodorus.] This psalm is fittingly entitled with a voice of praise, because it contains the words of martyrs, who were strong in confession and obtained the rewards of God.

Intention. He exhorts to praise.

Method. The psalm has two parts. First, they recall the benefits of God; while doubting what worthy return they might make, the cup of passion, given by God, presents itself. Secondly, they declare themselves servants of Christ and children of the Church: there, “O Lord, because I am thy servant.” Therefore the Prophet, in the person of martyrs recalling God’s benefits, sets down first the benefit of faith and second that of confession, saying:

VERSE 1.—“I believed, therefore I spoke; but I was humbled exceedingly.”

[Col. 1029C] “I truly believed,” [Augustine,] namely sincerely and perfectly, “therefore I spoke,” because one who believes must speak. For he does not believe perfectly who does not speak what he believes. That servant is slothful or fearful; but the faithful servant spends what he has received and gains others. Therefore he enters into the joy of his Lord, who says to him: “Well done, good and faithful servant, enter into the joy of thy Lord” (Matt. XXV).

This is the true and fitting order: [Cassiodorus.] first one must believe, afterward speak, lest one who does not yet believe dare to speak; rather, confession should follow faith. [Augustine, Alcuin.] And it should be noted that he does not say, “I believed and spoke,” but, “I believed, therefore I spoke”: he not only believed the other things which faith requires, but together with them believed both what reward he might hope for by speaking and what punishment [Col. 1029D] he ought to fear by keeping silent. Thus love of speaking is instilled by the reward and necessity imposed by the punishment.

“But I,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus,] as though he said: I spoke; but I—not the very word which I believed, nor the utterance which I brought forth—“was humbled exceedingly,” that is, I suffered many tribulations for the word of God which I faithfully held. [Cassiodorus.] Thus the truth shines more brightly, because those who suffer are not those who love human glory more than God’s. Hence the Apostle: “The word of the Lord is not bound in me” (II Tim. II). And lest true confession be ascribed to human powers, he says that what is proper to man is falsehood, which he could not readily have known unless, in an elevation of mind, he had been carried up to things above. Hence he adds:

[Col. 1030A] VERSE 2.—“I said in my ecstasy: every man is a liar.”

[Col. 1030B] “But I,” [Cassiodorus,] not attributing confession to myself, “said in my elevation,” or “in my ecstasy”—that is, with my mind carried away to eternal things—what? “Every man is a liar” of himself. This he learned in ecstasy. For it is a great thing if anyone recognizes himself as unwise. Ecstasy here is when the mind is not alienated by fear but is raised upward through some inspiration of revelation. And since man has no good thing of his own:

VERSE 3.—“What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?”

“What therefore shall I render to the Lord?” [Augustine.] In saying, “What shall I render to the Lord,” etc., he may speak in ecstasy; or “in my ecstasy,” as fear, is the anguish or death which human weakness suffers when persecutors threaten and the sufferings of martyrdom press upon it. As though he said: “I was humbled” [Col. 1030C]; but in that humiliation I said in my elevation—or, as others say, in my ecstasy—that is, in fear of sufferings: what? “Every man is a liar,” of himself; from God, truthful. For being terrified, he looks to his own weakness and sees that he ought not to rely on himself. Of himself man is a liar, as Peter too, when he presumed upon himself, was found to be a lying man; but it is God’s power if he does not yield.

Seeing this accomplished in himself by God’s grace, he says: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” For my evils? He does not say, “for all that he has given,” but “for all that he has rendered.” What then had preceded on man’s part, so that the giving of all God’s gifts could be called not a giving but a repayment? What had preceded except sins? Therefore God repays people good for evil, suffering for them; while people repay him evil for good.

[Col. 1030D] VERSE 3.—“I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the Lord.”

“The cup of salvation,” as though he said: [Augustine, Alcuin.] I say what I shall render: behold, made truthful by God’s gift, I shall receive in desire the cup—that is, passion—which is called a cup by comparison, because it is a pleasing drink. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] It is also called a cup because it is drunk in measure. Hence: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able” (I Cor. X). Of this cup the Lord asks his disciples: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Matt. XX.) I mean the cup of salvation, that is, of Jesus, which is offered for eternal salvation. Or “of salvation,” [Augustine,] that is, of Jesus, who first suffered and gives us to imitate his sufferings. Therefore the death of his saints is precious in the sight of the Lord, as is said afterward. Behold, this man found nothing to render except from those things which the Lord himself had first rendered. “And I will call upon the name of the Lord,” trusting not in myself but in God.

VERSE 4.—“I will render my vows to the Lord in the presence of all his people; precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.”

“Vows.” [Jerome.] As though he said: I shall take the cup, which is in desire; and afterward I shall render my vows to the Lord in the act itself. And this “in the presence of all his people,” so that they may take an example. Why do you do this? Because precious—that is, dear—is the death of his saints [Col. 1031B] in the sight of the Lord, however cheap it may be to anyone else. [Augustine.] Or, the death of his saints is precious, that is, purchased at the price of his death, because he bought it with the blood he shed for them, so that they might not hesitate to die for him. Purchased at this price, he therefore acknowledges his condition, saying:

PART II. VERSE 5.—“O Lord, because I am thy servant; I am thy servant and the son of thy handmaid.”

“O Lord, I am thy servant.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] Secondly, the martyrs call themselves servants and sons of the Church, lest anyone think that the martyrdom of heretics pleases God, [Augustine,] because there is no place of true sacrifice outside the catholic Church. Since you bought us with a price, therefore, O Lord, I confess my condition: namely, that I am thy servant, that is, obedient. The word “because” is not in the text according to Augustine; and he repeats, “I am thy servant” [Col. 1031C] in all things. “And the son of thy handmaid,” that is, of the Church, which is a handmaid while she serves, but a bride while she is united to her bridegroom. [Cassiodorus.] Otherwise he would not be a martyr unless he were the son of the handmaid—that is, of the heavenly Jerusalem, free from sin and a handmaid of righteousness.

But those outside the Church are not sons of the handmaid, even if they call themselves servants and martyrs, as heretics do, because they have Christ’s name but are not truly such. For it is not they, but I, who am the son of thy handmaid. [Alcuin.] I am not a schismatic, but am obedient in every respect to the doctrine of the Church. [Alcuin.] Or: I am the son of the handmaid, so that, as the handmaid bears children not for herself but for her Lord, so I too may bear some for you in my death, as she too, even unwillingly, [does]; all of which is through you, because it is you, not my merits.

[Col. 1031D] VERSE 7.—“Thou hast broken my bonds: to thee I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise, and I will call upon the name of the Lord.”

“You have broken,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus,] by the power of martyrdom, my bonds of sins; those bonds are broken because all things are washed away by blood. This verse is believed to have such power that sins are forgiven to a person if, at the end of life, it is recited with a threefold confession. Since you have broken them, therefore “I will sacrifice” to you, gratefully, “a sacrifice of praise,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus,] namely myself. “And I will call upon the name of the Lord,” not relying upon my own powers.

Or, with the same sense remaining, the text may be read differently, with “because” there. Because the death of his saints is precious, therefore, O Lord, I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise. Speaking to God, he affirms what he had said above; and this is great and wonderful to me, because I, O Lord, am your servant. He marvels that he has received such things as the Lord did for the redemption of the world. And to increase his wonder, he repeats: “I am thy servant.” The rest does not change.

VERSE 8.—“I will render my vows to the Lord in the sight of all his people, in the courts of the house of the Lord, [Col. 1032B] in the midst of thee, Jerusalem.”

“My vows.” [Augustine.] As though he said: I shall sacrifice a sacrifice of praise, certainly in this way: that I shall render to the Lord my vows, that is, myself, who am his image. For the image of God must be rendered to God. Hence: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII). But because he is not only a servant but also the son of the handmaid, he says that he renders vows not everywhere, [Augustine, Cassiodorus,] but in the courts of the house of the Lord—not made by hands—that is, of the handmaid, that is, in the catholic Church, not among heretics.

And he explains what the house of God is: “in the presence of all his people,” that is, his people. For he who was willing to suffer for all ought to be publicly praised, so that more may be edified. And still more openly he names our mother herself, saying: “In the midst of thee, [Col. 1032C] Jerusalem,” where there is peace and the saints rejoice in the vision of God. But those who are not sons of her handmaid loved war rather than peace. Yet lest anyone suppose that “Jerusalem” means the Jews alone, who glory in this name, let him hear the following psalm:

COLLATION ON PSALM CXV: “I BELIEVED, THEREFORE I SPOKE,” etc.

VERSE 2.—“In my ecstasy.” Jerome: “in my stupor”; others: “in my haste,” BEHAPHZI. Augustine understands this ecstasy as fear arising from imminent sufferings and the torments of death. Thus the haste which others mention signifies complete trembling. If, however, this is the voice of martyrs, it must be referred to the weakness of the flesh.

“Every man is a liar.” Jerome translated “falsehood.” In his commentaries he teaches that it is not *mendax* (“a liar”) but *mendacium* (“falsehood”), CAZAB; although everyone now reads COZEB, that is, “one who lies” or “a liar,” as Jerome himself also cites it in Book II Against Jovinianus. Indeed, in the Commentary he defers to the Church, which you ought to imitate. He says, therefore: “But we say this according to the Hebrew truth. Yet let us speak also according to the Seventy Interpreters. For someone may say: What is it to me what is contained in the Hebrew? I follow the Church: ‘I said in my ecstasy: Every man is a liar.’”

PSALM CXVI.

[Col. 1031]

TITLE OF THE PSALM: “ALLELUIA.”

[Col. 1031D]

“Praise the Lord, all nations.” Title: Alleluia. [Cassiodorus.] This psalm is brief; because of its brevity [Col. 1032D] it admits no divisions—the first of all to be indivisible, that is, without division—yet it surpasses all others by the conciseness of its speech. It is, as it were, [Col. 1033A] the point of the psalms. From it various forms are produced; and there is a wonderful variety, against the weariness of saying salutary things, now briefly and in measured form. [Augustine.] Therefore, lest anyone should think, as we said, that by Jerusalem only the Jews are signified, he exhorts all nations to praise, speaking in the person of the martyrs:

VERSE 1.—“Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples.”

“Praise the Lord, all nations,” [Jerome,] that is, Gentiles. And “praise,” or “praise together,” him, all peoples, that is, Jews. He says “praise together” so that the praise of all may be united as one: this is the catholic Church. Therefore he truly says, “all nations, all peoples,” lest anyone from the whole world be passed over. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] These are those courts of the Lord’s house and that [Col. 1033B] entire people of which he spoke in the preceding psalm, not the Jews alone, who attempt to claim them for themselves. I say, praise, for this reason:

VERSE 2.—“Because his mercy has been strengthened over us, and the truth of the Lord remains for ever.”

Because the mercy [Jerome, Augustine, Cassiodorus,] of Christ has been strengthened over us through the gift of the Holy Spirit, while even enemies yield to the Name through which we have been delivered, to whom the raging mouths of hostile nations [Col. 1034A] have yielded. And the truth of the Lord, that is, Christ, remains for ever, both in what he has promised to the godly and in what he threatens to the ungodly.

Or thus: his mercy, that is, God’s mercifully promised restoration of humankind, has been strengthened over us because he fulfilled by Christ’s coming what he promised through the prophets. He established mercy so that it may never be moved, because he who gave it preserves it. And the truth of the Lord, that is, Christ, who is the Father’s truth, remains for ever. For if there was ever a time when the Son was not, there was once a Father without truth.

COLLATION ON PSALM CXVI: “PRAISE THE LORD, ALL NATIONS,” etc.

VERSE 1.—“Praise him, all peoples.” Origen, in chapter XV of Romans, says that the Apostle wrote, when citing this psalm, “Magnify,” as the Latin edition has it, and that in the psalm “praise together” is read; whereas the Greek manuscripts consistently have ἐπαινέσατε, “praise,” in both places, so that Origen’s copy must have had μεγαλύνατε, “magnify,” in the Apostle. Moreover, in Hebrew the word may be interpreted either “to praise” or “to glorify.” Münster translates: “honour him,” SCABEHUHU.

VERSE 2.—“Remains.” It is not expressly present in Hebrew, but only “the truth of the Lord for ever” is read. Yet the Septuagint did not add it without reason; Münster too did so among the modern translators.

PSALM CXVII.

[Col. 1033]

TITLE OF THE PSALM: “ALLELUIA.”

[Col. 1033C]

“Give thanks to the Lord, because he is good.” Title: Alleluia. [Note: [Col. 1033D] From Cassiodorus, on the title and conclusion of the psalm.] This is the fifth psalm concerning the first coming, adorned with many figures. It has some verses ending alike, some beginning alike, some alternating, and ornaments of this kind.

Intention: He exhorts to praise.

Method: [Cassiodorus.] There are four divisions. First, the faithful people, released from sins, exhorts all to give thanks to the Lord; and because it was heard through mercy in tribulation, it says that man is not to be feared. Secondly, it says that trust is to be placed in God alone: there, “It is good to trust.” Thirdly, it desires that the gates of Jerusalem be opened to it: there, “Open.” Fourthly, rejoicing in Christ’s coming, it urges the courts of God to be filled: there, “Blessed”; therefore, exhorting to praise [Col. 1033D], it says:

VERSE 1.—“Give thanks to the Lord, because he is good, because his mercy is for ever.”

“Give thanks to the Lord,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus,] that is, praise the Lord, because he alone is good through himself; this belongs properly to God, who is good through himself and from himself, as he himself says: “None is good save God alone” (Mark X). His goodness is evident in this: “because his mercy is for ever,” because he grants the gifts of mercy eternally.

VERSE 2.—“Let Israel now say that he is good, because his mercy is for ever.”

“Let [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Glossa interlinearis] Israel say.” As though I exhort you to give thanks, and, just as I exhort you, so exhort one another. This means: let Israel—that is, the whole blessed people—say to others what I say, and say it now, as though there is no delay to be made. Or “let [Israel] say,” that is, let it confess, what? “That he is good, because his mercy is for ever.”

VERSE 3.—“Let the house of Aaron now say that his mercy is for ever.”

Let the house of Aaron also, [Jerome, Cassiodorus,] namely the priests, who are mentioned separately because of reverence, now say the same thing: “because his mercy is for ever.”

VERSE 4.—“Let those who fear the Lord now say that his mercy is for ever.”

“Let those who fear [Col. 1034D] the Lord now say” [Augustine] the same thing. He says this to include the faint-hearted with the greater ones, from every nation. [Cassiodorus.] He says “those who fear the Lord” because such persons are fit to confess that his mercy is for ever. Behold four verses alike in their endings.

VERSE 5.—“Out of tribulation I called upon the Lord, and the Lord heard me in spaciousness.”

“Out of tribulation.” [Cassiodorus.] He gives an example from himself in order to stir others to God’s mercy. As though he said: Behold God’s mercy toward me, because out of tribulation I called upon the Lord, and the Lord heard me in spaciousness, because he frees from the straits of this world and sets one in the spaciousness of rewards. And because he heard:

[Col. 1035A] VERSE 6.—“The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man may do to me.”

“The Lord is my helper.” [Cassiodorus.] Therefore I will not fear what man—that is, any carnal enemy—may do to me. Then he repeats:

VERSE 7.—“The Lord is my helper, and I shall look down upon my enemies.”

“The Lord is my helper.” [Cassiodorus.] Behold the same beginning in two verses. And therefore, because the Lord is my helper, I shall look down upon my enemies—which is more than not fearing. Or, according to another reading, “I shall see my enemies,” namely at the future judgment, where the devil with his own will be seen destroyed. Or here I shall see my enemies, who are to be condemned, so that I may become safer and more watchful.

[Col. 1035B] PART II. VERSE 8.—“It is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man.”

“It is good to trust.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] Secondly, he says that trust must be placed in God alone, through whom one escapes the hostility of nations and comes to true life. [Cassiodorus, Jerome.] As though he said: Since the Lord is a helper, it is good to trust in the Lord against the evils of the world, rather than to trust in carnal man, whose salvation is vain.

VERSE 9.—“It is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in princes.”

It is good to hope for good things in the Lord rather than to hope in princes, [Augustine,] that is, angels who are called princes. Hence Michael is called a prince in Daniel (Dan. XII). It is clear that one should not hope in them [Col. 1035C] but in the Lord. For when a human being or angels appear to help, it is he who acts through them, who made them good according to their measure.

VERSE 10.—“All nations surrounded me; and in the name of the Lord, because I was avenged upon them.”

“All nations”: here he explains the tribulation he mentioned above. [Glossa interlinearis, Alcuin.] Behold from what he delivers: namely, from hidden or open tribulation. He delivers either by not allowing one to fall, or by raising one after a fall. As though one ought to hope in the Lord [Haymo,] because all nations surrounded me, probing not openly but with flatteries, threats, and other hidden devices. This happened in the beginning of the Church; and this occurred in the name of the Lord, because I was avenged upon them—or against them. [Cassiodorus.] [Col. 1035D] Other interpreters say: “In the name of the Lord I was avenged upon them,” while they themselves, converted, endure in repentance the punishments which they had inflicted on others. Then, as though giving the reason why he could overcome so greatly, he says what he first suffered in his Head, adding:

VERSE 11.—“Surrounding me, they surrounded me; in the name of the Lord, because I was avenged upon them.”

“Surrounding me, they surrounded me.” [Glossa interlinearis, Augustine.] As though he said: In the siege endured in its Head, the devout people, which is Christ’s body, felt persecutors; and on its behalf was done whatever the inward power of the Godhead accomplished through the outward flesh. It should be noted that he does not repeat “nations” here, because this was done by the Jews alone. “And in the name of the Lord, because I was avenged upon them.” This does not change.

[Col. 1036A] VERSE 12.—“They surrounded me like bees, and they blazed like fire among thorns; and in the name of the Lord, because I was avenged upon them.”

“They surrounded me like bees.” [Augustine.] Others say, “like bees [around] a honeycomb,” which was done in mystical subtlety by those who did not understand. The Holy Spirit here foretells. Bees indeed make honey in honeycombs, but for others, not for themselves: thus the Jews, unknowingly, made for us the sweetest thing of all through the Lord’s very passion. Like bees, while they think they are storing it for themselves, they make honey for others.

The Church, speaking in the person of the Head, says: “They surrounded me like bees [around] a honeycomb,” [Cassiodorus,] that is, by their bitter efforts they prepared sweet food for others. Or, according to our text, which does not have “a honeycomb,” read it thus: “They surrounded me,” Christ said. [Alcuin.] [Col. 1036B] Like bees which, by stinging others, disembowel themselves, so the Jews, by killing Christ, inwardly perished. “They blazed like fire among thorns.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Alcuin.] Thorns are sins, by which the Jews, incited, burned against Christ.

Or this is better understood of the Church. After the Lord’s passion, nations blazed against the Church like fire among the thorns of sins; for those things, that is, sins, they burned up in the faithful people with the fire of persecution. Though wishing to harm it, they advanced it. And this occurred in the name of the Lord, because I was avenged upon them. [Augustine.] Either when, after the malice in them was extinguished, they were converted and joined to the Christian people; or when, judged at the end, they will experience the judgment of truth without mercy.

[Col. 1036C] VERSE 13.—“Driven, I was overthrown so that I might fall, and the Lord received me.”

“Driven.” [Alcuin, Glossa interlinearis.] After showing that he delivers by not allowing one to fall, he also shows that he delivers by raising one after a fall. As though he said: I was avenged upon them; yet at times I was driven—that is, I wavered—and overthrown, or thrown from the horse of virtues, so that I might fall into eternal death; and the Lord received me, [Cassiodorus,] that is, raised me from my fall.

Or thus: I was driven, or thrown about, with the purpose that I should fall, as occurs when the good are given over to punishments so that they may fall from faith. [Augustine.] And then the Lord received me. Hence he adds: “And the Lord received me,” because one whose strength and praise is the Lord no more falls [Col. 1036D] than the Lord falls. But those fall who wish to be their own strength and praise. Hence he adds:

VERSE 14.—“The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation.”

The Lord is also my strength and my praise. Therefore the Lord has become salvation to me: he not only makes dangers turn aside, but also grants salvation. He does not say “has become” because he himself became something which he had not been before, but because those who believed in him became what they had not been. Therefore God does not become what he was not to himself, but to them. For salvation began to exist for those converted, which had not existed for those turned away from him. I say, “He has become my salvation”; hence those who seemed to fail rejoice amid evils.

[Col. 1037A] VERSE 15.—“The voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous.”

“The voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous,” [Augustine,] that is, in the secret places of good hearts. Though they are outwardly afflicted, they have joys in hope of the future. The wicked who rage against their bodies, not knowing this, suppose them sad, because they do not perceive their inward things, namely their joys. Hence the Apostle: “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (II Cor. VI), and: “We glory in tribulations” (Rom. V). [Cassiodorus.] He then shows how the Lord has become strength and salvation to him, saying:

VERSE 16.—“The right hand of the Lord has wrought strength; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me; the right hand of the Lord has wrought strength.”

[Col. 1037B] “The right hand of the Lord.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though he said: Hence is joy, because the right hand of the Lord, that is Christ, who is the Father’s right hand, has wrought strength. What strength? Behold: “The right hand of the Lord has exalted me.” It is great strength to exalt the humble, to make mortal man divine, to confer perfection out of weakness, glory out of subjection, victory out of suffering, and heaven upon earthly beings. He repeats it as a wonder: “The right hand of the Lord has wrought strength.” Man did not exalt himself, did not perfect himself, did not conquer, did not give himself glory or salvation. And since this is so:

VERSE 17.—“I shall not die, but live, and shall recount the works of the Lord.”

“I shall not die,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine,] says the Church, “as you suppose, O persecutor; but I shall live,” that is, I shall endure multiplied. [Col. 1037C] For the persecutor thinks that, by everywhere making slaughter and funerals, he is blotting out the Christian name, though he is rather increasing it. [Cassiodorus, Glossa interlinearis.] Or: “I shall not die” an eternal death, “but shall live” the life which you do not know, and, while I am here, “shall recount the works of the Lord,” so that through this the Church may increase. [Augustine.] Why the holy Church, the people of adoption, endured so much, he indicates, saying:

VERSE 18.—“The Lord chastening chastened me, and did not deliver me over to death.”

“The Lord chastening chastened me.” [Cassiodorus.] By this repetition is signified God’s custom: namely, his custom of chastening, as in “blessing he shall bless” (Ps. CXXXI). As though God permitted this to happen to me [Col. 1037D] for correction. Even overthrow serves for caution. [Augustine.] Whatever they do is the Lord’s chastening. Therefore let the wicked claim nothing for themselves. They would not have this power unless it were given them from above (John XIX). “And he did not deliver me over to death.” [Cassiodorus.] One whose vices are purged is not given over to death. Often a father corrects his children through wicked servants, while nevertheless preparing punishment for those servants and an inheritance for his children. What that inheritance is can be known from what follows.

PART III. VERSE 19.—“Open to me the gates of righteousness; entering through them I shall give thanks to the Lord. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it.”

“Open to me the gates.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Thirdly, he desires that the gates of Jerusalem be opened to him, where he also speaks of the cornerstone. Note that three things are distinguished here: that through which one enters, what is done within, and who enter. As though he said: So that that inheritance may be known, O prophets and apostles, who bear the keys of the kingdom of heaven, open to me the gates of righteousness [Col. 1038A]—that is, the teaching of Sacred Scripture which teaches righteousness. Behold, he shows by what one enters; and, as though someone asked, “What will he do within?”, he answers: “Entering through them, I shall give thanks to the Lord,” [Cassiodorus,] that is, I shall praise him. For those who enter through these gates of teaching truly praise; outside the catholic Church there is no praise of God.

All these gates lead to one gate, which is Christ. “And this is the gate of the Lord,” [Jerome,] that is, this gate is the Lord, to whom those gates lead. Hence he himself says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John X); and elsewhere: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV). This is the gate through which the righteous enter heaven. Hence he adds: “The righteous shall enter through it,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus,] that is, through it they shall enter heaven, where good and evil will no longer be mingled. Behold, he has made mention of both ages. And because Christ opened this gate:

### Verse 20

> “I will give thanks to you because you have heard me, and you have become salvation for me.”

“I will give thanks to you,” joyfully rendering grateful praise. For you heard me in the coming of the Son; for the righteous of old were asking for Christ’s advent, and thus he became—or is—salvation for me. And truly he is salvation, for:

### Verse 21

> “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.”

“The stone which the builders rejected.” Behold through whom he became salvation: namely, through the cornerstone, that is, Christ. Or this may be understood from the words, “Open [to me].” By the gates, death is meant, through which one enters to the Lord. Hence the Apostle says: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. III). For the saints find eternal life through this gate of death.

As though he said: Because the Lord did not deliver me to death, therefore, O you persecutors, press on and open for me the gates of righteousness—that is, the gates of death through which the righteous enter into rest. And I, having entered them—that is, through them into life—will give thanks to the Lord in the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting, which is the blessedness of the saints. And I will give thanks because this is the gate of the Lord—that is, this is the gate by which one goes to the Lord, or by which the Lord departed from the world. Hence elsewhere: “For the Lord God are the issues of death” (Ps. LXVII). And the righteous, imitating Christ their head, shall enter through it into life.

I said, “I will give thanks,” and truly I will give thanks, O Lord—that is, I will praise you in the present and in the future—because you heard me, and he became, or is, salvation for me. Who is this salvation? Behold, the stone—namely Christ—whom the builders rejected, that is, the Jews. For the Jews alone, worshipping the one God, were building themselves and others in divine worship, while others were being destroyed through idolatry; but they did not complete the work, because they despised Christ.

Or, “the builders” may be understood in an evil sense as the scribes and Pharisees, who, desiring to establish their own righteousness, were not subject to God’s righteousness (Rom. X), by rejecting Christ. Yet he became the head of the corner, in order to unite in himself, as the cornerstone, the two walls of Jews and Gentiles. And:

### Verse 22

> “This was done by the Lord, and it is marvellous in our eyes.”

“This was done by the Lord,” namely, that he should become the head of the corner. This was not done by those at whose hands he suffered, although it was accomplished only through the Passion; rather, it was done by the Lord, who was building secretly.

Or: This was done by the Lord—that is, this stone was made, according to his humanity; and another reading agrees with this sense: “It was made for him by the Lord,” that is, for the honour of the Father. And this is marvellous: namely, that God became man, in our inward eyes—that is, in the eyes of believers, not of the carnal persons who rejected him. And:

### Verse 23

> “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it.”

“This is the day” on which this was done, the day which the Lord made. My days are old, but this is the day which the Lord made—that is, in which he gave me salvation. Hence: “In an acceptable time I heard you, and in a day of salvation I helped you” (II Cor. VI).

This is the jubilee year, observed figuratively under the Law, which is called “releasing” or “beginning,” because then slaves were set free, debts remitted, and possessions restored to their owners; and on this day we too were redeemed from the slavery of sin (Lev. XXV). To us also eternal inheritance has been restored. Therefore he says that the Lord made this day, because, although he made all days, he made this one in a special manner—not because he loved it more than others, but because on it he did more than on others: on it the Lord came. On it it is fitting to rejoice. Therefore let us exult and rejoice in it, on which the devil lost his claim and humankind revived. And because it is a day of salvation, therefore:

### Part IV. Verse 24

> “O Lord, save me; O Lord, prosper well; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

“O Lord, save me.” Behold the longing of a great petition: save me from the disaster of this age, that is, from sins. And, O Lord, prosper well, so that these sufferings may be turned into eternal joys.

Or he speaks like the prodigal son returning to his father from the exile of a long captivity: “Save me, O Lord,” here and in the future, because, returning from a long pilgrimage, we are separated from those who hate peace and attack us. “And, O Lord, prosper well”: make prosperous the journey of those returning, because you have become the way for us. Or, “prosper [us] well”: when these have been saved, save others also.

“Blessed.” Fourthly, he urges that the courts of the Lord be thronged, rejoicing in Christ’s advent. As though he said: Prosper well, because you came for this purpose. “And blessed is he who is to come,” or, “who comes,” in the name of the Lord. But cursed is one who comes in his own name, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have come in the name of my Father, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John V). Such a one will be cursed. This, then, is praise concerning Christ’s advent.

Then, as though speaking in the person of priests to those of lesser rank, he says: And therefore we, the greater ones, as it were priests, [say to] the remaining Christians:

### Verse 25

> “We have blessed you from the house of the Lord; God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us.”

“We have blessed you”—a great benefit, beyond doubt—because we have blessed you from the house of the Lord, that is, from the Catholic Church, from which come baptism and every blessing. This is the holy land of which the Lord said to Moses: “Take off your sandals from your feet, for the land on which you stand is holy land” (Exod. III). This is the good land in the Gospel, which brings forth good fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold. On it we must stand upright toward heavenly things, not lie down, weighed by the sluggishness of earthly things; we must take the sandals from our feet—that is, remove dead works from our affections.

“God is the Lord”: as though he said, We have blessed you; indeed, God, to whom *latria* [worship] is owed, and the Lord, to whom *dulia* [service or veneration] is owed, has blessed us and shone upon us, driving away the darkness of sins. And you, now blessed:

### Verse 26

> “Keep the solemn day amid dense gatherings, even to the horn of the altar.”

“Keep the solemn day,” observing the day of the Lord’s Nativity and Resurrection, which is consecrated to God’s honour; and do this not lukewarmly or sluggishly, but “amid dense gatherings,” that is, amid an abundance of virtues or people. I mean you who press on “even to the horn of the altar,” literally, so that you may partake of Christ’s body—as is customary at festivals, but especially on the three chief solemnities: Easter, Pentecost, and the Lord’s Nativity. For under the old Law it was commanded (Deut. XVI) that at the three chief solemnities—Easter, Pentecost, and Tabernacles—no one should appear empty-handed before the Lord.

Empty is the person who does not possess Christ within himself; Christ is the foundation which no one can alter. Hence at those three solemnities the faithful people offer a coin by a manual offering, signifying the inward offering. For on a coin are the name and image of the king. Therefore let each person offer a coin spiritually, so as to bear within himself the name of the King—that is, Christ, from whom he is called a Christian—and present to God the image, that is, the soul, marked with the light of his countenance.

Or, by the altar is understood the sacrament of the body and blood. The horn of the altar is the power, that is, the efficacy, of that sacrament. For many, being evil, receive the sacrament but not the reality; but the good receive both the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, which is the spiritual flesh of Christ. Of this he himself says: “Unless anyone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have eternal life” (John VI).

The sense is as though he said: Keep the solemn day, you who press on in mind as far as the horn—that is, the power and efficacy—of the altar, namely the sacrament, so that you receive not only the sacrament but also its reality. Hence elsewhere: “I will enter in to the altar of God” (Ps. XLII).

But whatever others do, I say for myself:

### Verse 27

> “You are my God, and I will give thanks to you; you are my God, and I will exalt you.”

“You are my God, and no other; therefore I will give thanks to you,” that is, I will praise you.

Or, from the words “We have blessed”: this is the voice of the great to the little. For the great, those who surpass [others], who in mind touch the Word who is with God, accommodate themselves to the little, so that they can sincerely say: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober-minded, it is for you” (II Cor. V). What do they say to the little? “We have blessed you from the house of the Lord.” They bless them from the inward house of the Lord, namely the heavenly Jerusalem, from which descends “every good gift and every perfect gift,” where praise is for ages of ages.

But what do they announce from there? That the Lord, who came in the name of the Lord, whom the builders rejected, the mediator between God and human beings, equal to the Father, has shone upon us, so that we might understand what we believe and declare it to you, who do not yet understand but already believe. But that you may understand, “keep the solemn day,” that is, the solemnity of the mind; and do this “in gatherings,” that is, in the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting.

I say, keep it by walking “in the place of the wonderful tabernacle,” even to the horn of the altar—that is, even to the inward house of God, from which we blessed you, where are the heights of the altar; where there is a spiritual and everlasting sacrifice, namely the sacrifice of praise; an everlasting priest; and an everlasting altar, namely the very mind of the righteous.

To state it more fittingly, the sense of these words is this: Whoever desire to understand God the Word should not find sufficient the flesh which the Word became for their sake, so that they might be abundantly nourished; nor should this day on earth, on which the Lamb was slain, be sufficient. Rather, let it be kept in gatherings until they arrive, with minds exulting, even to the horn of the altar—that is, to his inward divinity—where we shall sing praises, saying: “You are my God, and I will give thanks to you; you are my God, and I will exalt you.” These words are not to be spoken with a noise of words; love itself is this voice.

Or thus:

> [Note: From Gregory, *Morals*, book IX, chapter 21.]

“Keep the solemn day,” namely, the day of eternity; and do this in gatherings—that is, let each person continually afflict himself with longing for that day—until he reaches the horn of the altar, that is, until the future; namely, until he attains the height of the heavenly sacrifice, that is, eternal joys.

Or, the altar signifies the human mind. Thus in the Law it was commanded that an altar be made square and hollow (Exod. XXVII). It was square because the human mind ought to be fortified by the four chief virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. It ought also to be hollow, to receive the Word of God and the fire of love. For what is poured in is repelled by pride. Hence in Leviticus it is commanded that the crop of the throat and the feathers be cast away when a turtledove or pigeon is offered as a burnt offering (Lev. I). The crop of the throat signifies the swelling of pride; the feathers signify vain inquiries into lofty matters. Therefore cast these away from the burnt offering, lest you be puffed up by knowledge or vainly devote yourself to inquiries into sublime things which human understanding cannot grasp; then the altar will be hollow.

The horn of this altar is the eminence of the mind, the contemplation of heavenly things. The sense is: Keep the solemn day, namely the brightness and exultation of the mind, proceeding through dense gatherings—or through an abundance—of virtues, even to the horn of the altar: that is, to the eminence of the mind which is the altar, namely to contemplation. We, I say, [do so] saying: “You are my God, and I will give thanks to you; you are my God, and I will exalt you.” These words do not change.

### Verse 28

> “I will give thanks to you because you have heard me, and you have become salvation for me.”

“I will give thanks to you because you have heard me, and he became—or is—salvation for me.” This verse was placed above, but it is fittingly placed here also, because joyful thanksgiving follows benefits. Thus, as he began with praise, so he concludes, saying:

### Verse 29

> “Give thanks to the Lord, because he is good, because his mercy is for ever.”

“Give thanks to the Lord.” As though he said: As I do, so you also do—namely, give thanks to the Lord, as I urged at the beginning, because he is good and because his mercy is for ever. The psalm ends where it began. For from the beginning, when we deserted God, to the end, when we return, nothing delights us more healthfully than the praise of God.

## Collation on Psalm CXVII: “Give Thanks to the Lord, because He Is Good,” etc.

### Verses 3–4

The Greeks repeat *hoti agathos* (ὅτι ἀγαθός), “because he is good,” as the Seventy Interpreters are known often to do for emphasis of the point.

### Verses 10–11

“Because I took vengeance on them.” The Greek manuscripts do not have “because.” Jerome, however, in his letter to Sunia and Fretella, wishes it to be restored under an asterisk. For the Hebrew has *KI*. Yet, for completeness of sense, something must then be understood: “In the name of the Lord,” I said, “because I took vengeance on them,” as Münster also indicated. Or, as the Master has it: “In the name of the Lord is this,” etc.

### Verse 12

“They burned fiercely like fire among thorns.” Jerome, with others, has: “They were extinguished like the fire of thorns.” Someone may say that burning fiercely and being extinguished are shown to conflict. But if you understand a sudden consumption to be indicated, no difficulty remains. For fire, swiftly burning among thorns, swiftly consumes and is consumed. Hence the Campensian Paraphrase: “They are extinguished as suddenly as fire flying through stubble.” And the Chaldean [version]: “They burn like fire among thorns.” The translator following Campensis, however, explains it actively: “Let him proceed to consume, as fire [consumes] thorns.”

### Verse 13

“I was thrust down, overturned, so that I might fall.” St Augustine, following I know not what, read: “I was thrust down like a heap of sand, so that I might fall.” For the Hebrews have *DAHO DEHITTHANI*, that is, “in thrusting, you thrust me.” But the Septuagint has *ōstheis anetrapēn* (ὠσθεὶς ἀνετράπην), “being thrust, I was overturned.” Perhaps Augustine’s reading expressed the force of the second verb, which, when applied to the sea, sometimes means that what is at the bottom rises and is borne upward; or perhaps, in place of *ōstheis* (ὠσθείς, “being thrust”), there was read *hōs amathoeis* (ὡς ἀμαθόεις), “as sandy.”

### Verse 22

“This was done by the Lord.” Some read “for him,” in the dative—namely, “it was done for him”—as Augustine does. This results from the variant reading of the pronoun *hautē* (αὕτη, “this”) or *hautēi* (αὑτῇ, “for/to her/it”), which refers in Greek to “the head.”

### Verse 24

“O Lord, save.” *HOSCHIAH NA.* We and the Greeks pronounce *hosanna* corruptly instead of *hosianna*, according to Jerome’s testimony in his letter to Damasus. Yet Johann Eck, a pious and learned man, holds that we pronounce *hosanna* correctly according to grammatical rule, because in the imperative of quiescent verbs in the *peal* [perhaps “period,” OCR uncertain] and in the conjugation called *hiphil*, the Hebrews say both *HOSCA* and [the text is incomplete]. For in Psalm LXXXV, “Save your servant,” one reads in Hebrew *HOSCA ABDECA*. Therefore he does not accept those who supposed that we pronounce this word corruptly.

Yet, although Jerome explicitly says this in his letter to Damasus, [Eck] wonders how he could have said it. But even if it is correct, nevertheless, if we combine into one the three words found in Hebrew, the elision is evident. Jerome gives by way of example Virgil’s “*Mene incoepto*,” where we scan *men incoepto*. Thus in the Hebrew sequence we read *HOSCIACH NA ANNA*. Hence *hosanna* coalesces, with an elision occurring in the middle.

Münster, in his scholia, says that in Matthew the Evangelist, chapter XXI, the Hebrew children going out to meet Christ cried in the Chaldean fashion, into which the Hebrew of the common people had degenerated: *hosanna*. Although this accords with Jerome’s opinion insofar as the word is corrupted, it does not correspond equally with what Jerome writes: that Matthew, who wrote in the Hebrew language, set down *HOSCHIAH NA*.

Then “the people of Israel,” or the world generally, must be understood; Münster nevertheless testifies that among the Chaldeans *Hosanna* means “save us.” Finally, what we say, “O Lord, save,” Jerome says derives from the Septuagint. Symmachus translated more plainly: “I beg you, Lord, save [us].”

### Verse 26

“Keep the solemn day amid dense gatherings.” Pellicanus has the same. Jerome: “Frequent the solemnity amid leafy branches”; Campensis and the translators following Cajetan render it, in other words: “Bind the feast with branches,” or “Crown the feast-day with branches,” or “Bind together branches for the feast-day.” Pratensis, Nebiensis, Sanctes, and Münster: “Bind the lamb or victim with cords.”

This variety of expressions arises from the homonymy of the Hebrew words. First, there are *ASAR* and *ISSER*, meaning “to bind” and “to arrange” or “to set in order.” Then *HAG* is ambiguous, referring either to a lamb or to a feast. Finally, *ABOTHIM*, if derived from the root *ABAH*, properly means “dense things”; but if from the stem *ABATH*, it means a leafy tree or a thick cord.

However one translates it, all tend to the same end, though in differing forms of speech: namely, that a frequent assembly of the faithful people in celebrating the solemnities of the Lord’s worship is signified, together with a full zeal of devotion and spiritual joy in eagerly performing sacred mysteries.

### Verse 28

“I will give thanks to you because you have heard me,” etc. This verse, which was verse 20, is repeated here in our text and in the Septuagint, though it is not in the Hebrew. Yet this causes no difficulty, although in certain Greek copies it is not found.

# Psalm CXVIII

## Title of the Psalm

> “Alleluia. [Note: *Alleluia* (Ἀλληλούϊα) added by the Greeks.] Aleph.”

“Blessed are the undefiled.” Title: “Alleluia. Aleph.”

> [Note: From Cassiodorus on the title and conclusion of the psalm.]

The psalm is an instructor of the faithful, a paradise of every kind of fruit, a storehouse of the Holy Spirit. The more open it seems on the surface, the deeper it is in the height of its mysteries. Here the righteous person speaks in general terms, at one time professing what he has received, at another merely hoping for what he has deserved.

This psalm is composed from similar words; yet it is not mingled with any confusion, but its subjects are unfolded with fresh expression as the letters change. It is entirely distinguished by moral teaching. All moral teaching is pleasant, and in this psalm it is pre-eminent. Other psalms, like lesser stars, shine somewhat; but this one, like the sun glowing with the noonday heat of full light, shines throughout with moral sweetness.

It is arranged according to the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, so that, as children acquire the practice of learning from their first letters, we too may learn through such elements the practice of living until maturity. Eight verses are set under each letter, so that eight verses begin with one letter, both to teach the unity of the Godhead which governs all things and to teach the purification of lawful sanctification. For circumcision is performed under the Law on the eighth day, and in Christ’s resurrection we have been made alive together with him.

In this psalm there are as many octonaries as there are Hebrew letters, namely twenty-two; and every octonary, in all its verses, begins in order with its respective letter. This could not be preserved in translation. It indicates that these are the elementary lessons of Christ’s school, a beneficial teaching perfect for blessedness; and the parts of that teaching are denoted by suitable interpretations of the names of the letters.

Here, certainly, all the letters designate the number of the righteous. The parts of this psalm correspond to the number of letters: as many letters as there are, so many divisions there are, so that in every octonary there is a distinct division. The octonary itself indicates in each division that every part is perfect and sufficient, so that whoever observes it during the life of seven days may attain the eighth day of resurrection, or possess the circumcision of heart signified by the number eight.

Each letter is, as it were, a title declaring the content of its verses. The title of this octonary is “Alleluia. Aleph.” “Alleluia” means “Praise of God,” because God is truly praised in those in whom there is remission of sins; this remission was perfectly accomplished for us through Christ’s advent, concerning which the preceding psalm spoke. He washed this world clean so that it might be worthy to praise God with an undefiled heart.

*Aleph*, the first letter, is interpreted “teaching.” Therefore attend carefully to the following verses, full of teaching. It is fittingly prefixed to this octonary: *Aleph*, “teaching,” is common to the whole psalm, which breathes moral instruction. For this octonary is like a prologue to the whole psalm, briefly touching upon what is contained in the following octonaries. Since it is clear that all people, even the wicked, wish to be blessed when they have obtained what they desire, it teaches what most do not know: how they may be truly blessed, lest anyone now go astray from the way of blessedness.

Here the entire choir of saints speaks, from first to last, as though saying: Different people seek different things by which to be blessed; but this is the way to blessedness. Those who wish to be:

### Verse 1

> “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.”

Let those be blessed who are undefiled—that is, without crime. They are so if they are in the way, that is, in Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life (John XIV). Or, “in the way,” that is, in the law of the Lord, which is the way to life. He says “undefiled” in the plural so that it may be understood of the faithful, not of Christ.

Or the connection is this: Once humankind was wretched and defiled; but now, by contrast, human beings are blessed and undefiled through the remission of sins. Yet I say this on the condition that they are in the way, that is, in Christ or in the law of God, and that they walk. This is what follows: “who walk,” not idly, in the law—not of the flesh but of the Lord. Those who walk do not sin mortally; or, if they sin, they repent. Such people advance and persevere. Yet they cannot accomplish this unless they search out and know the law of God. Hence he adds:

### Verse 2

> “Blessed are those who search his testimonies; they seek him with their whole heart.”

“Blessed are those who search his testimonies,” that is, the sacred Scriptures. This is a definition of the blessed by their acts. For blessed is the one who is in the way—that is, who walks without stain in Christ, in the law—and who searches in such a way as to advance. Otherwise one is not worthy to inquire diligently unless one has an approved life.

Notice that he first said, “Blessed are the undefiled in the way,” and afterwards, “Blessed are those who search.” What a beautiful order, full of teaching and grace: life comes before doctrine. Thus it is said of Christ: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I). And the Apostle, describing the bishop to be chosen, first speaks of life: “A bishop must be irreproachable, sober, chaste,” which pertain to a good life (I Tim. III); then he adds doctrine, namely, “able to teach,” so that he may first become accustomed to doing good before he presumes to teach. Thus the legal priest first put on the ephod, and then the breastpiece.

> [Note: From Jerome to Fabiola, *On the Priestly Garment*.]

A good life even by itself possesses grace; doctrine without life is not complete, because wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul. Hence it is said: “The wicked shall seek me and shall not find [me].” Therefore life must first be corrected, and then knowledge sought. Moral matters come first; mystical matters second. In the former is life; in the latter, knowledge. Without both, however, there is no perfection.

> [Note: From Jerome to Fabiola, *On the Priestly Garment*.]

Therefore under the Law the priest took from the victim the breast of elevation and the shoulder of separation; wisdom is in the breast and work in the shoulder (Lev. VII). So also, at the lower edge of the blue robe of the high priest, bells and pomegranates hung (Exod. XXVIII), so that the sound of preaching might be joined with the performance of good action.

> [Note: From Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chapter 8.]

The same order is in the first psalm as in this one. For first the blessed person is said not to have departed from the way of righteousness; then it adds that he meditates on the law with his whole heart.

As though he said: Blessed are those who search, provided that they seek him, and not something else. For testimonies had to be searched for this purpose: that God might be found. Otherwise it is of no avail, as for those who wish to be learned rather than righteous. Hence they seek glory among human beings, not before God.

And this must be done with the whole heart, not with a divided heart, as by heretics and friends of this world, to whom it is said: “You cannot serve God and mammon” (Matt. VI). Such people do not seek God with their whole heart.

It seems remarkable, however, that he says that those who search and seek are blessed. For even the ungodly can do this: scribes and Pharisees sitting in Moses’ seat, who say but do not do (Matt. XXIII), and heretics search and seek; yet they are not blessed, because they are not undefiled. But the righteous are already blessed in hope, because they will find what they seek. They are not blessed because they search and seek, but because of what will be added—as the Gospel says, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution” and “those who hunger” (Matt. V). They are not blessed because they suffer these things, but because of what follows: “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” and “they shall be filled.” Similar to this is what is said here:

### Verse 3

> “For those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways.”

“For [those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways].” As though he said: Those who walk in the law are blessed; for those who work wickedness have not yet walked undefiled in the law and therefore are not yet blessed. This is what he says: Those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways—that is, in faith. He uses the plural number because one faith embraces all ways, by which the righteous person lives.

Or, as “way” above in the singular is understood as Christ, so here “ways” in the plural are understood as the prophets, apostles, and all preachers. Of these ways Jeremiah says: “Stand in the ways, and ask for the ancient paths of the Lord, and seek which is the good way” (Jer. VI). Those who work iniquity have not walked in these.

Thus he speaks as though saying: Let whoever has sin not walk in the ways; or, let those who walk in the ways be without sin. But those are not said to work iniquity who, although through the weakness of the flesh they sin lightly every day, do not love their sin, but destroy it by the Lord’s Prayer and the sign of the cross.

Sin is indeed iniquity, as John says; yet the person who walks in the ways is not without sin (I John III). But he himself does not work that sin; rather, the sin dwelling in him does so, when he does not will what he does. For the tinder of sin, which is the sickness of nature, stirs up unlawful desires; and so we are not without sin. Hence the same John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (I John I). But a person does not work sin if he does not obey the desires of the flesh; whoever obeys departs from the ways. If, however, he confesses, this too pertains to the ways, and because of the ways sin is not imputed. Therefore those who work iniquity—that is, out of love and not unwillingly, like the one who says, “What I hate, I do” (Rom. VII)—do not walk in the ways.

### Verse 4

> “You commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly.”

“You commanded.” As though he said: Those who work wickedness do not walk in the ways. And this is true, because you commanded, etc. Or join it thus: They do not walk in the ways, but you commanded them to walk—that is, to keep the commandments—and therefore one must walk.

Or continue thus: Blessed are those who act in this and that way; and lest these things be despised, he adds the Lord’s command, saying: “You commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly,” or, “You commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly.” *Nimis* (“exceedingly”) sometimes means “more than is fitting,” but not here; it is understood as “very much.” The sense is: You commanded very earnestly through the prophets, and frequently through those same prophets, that your commandments be kept.

Or: You commanded your commandments to be kept, so that not even one iota might be passed over. Or, “to be kept exceedingly,” that is, beyond what the nature of the flesh can endure.

Distinguish the terms and note the differences mentioned before. For he spoke of three things: law, testimonies, and commandments. The law is “a shadow of things to come” (Heb. X), which must be kept spiritually, as in sacrifices and similar figurative matters. A testimony is a clear thing which reminds one of something. Thus Jacob says: “This stone shall be a testimony” (Gen. XXXI); and the Lord says to the healed leper: “Offer your gift as a testimony” (Matt. VIII). Thus God’s precepts are called testimonies because they warn us not to sin. Commandments are without shadow and require present action, as: “You shall love God with your whole heart” (Matt. XXII). Note that he understands testimonies as prohibitions and commandments as positive injunctions.

### Verse 5

> “Would that my ways might be directed to keep your statutes!”

“Would that.” Having expressed the life of the blessed, he desires it, and desires it against the pride of free choice, for which it is not enough to be taught unless one is first directed. Therefore, if a human being desires what God commands, he must ask God himself to give what he commands. As though he said: At your command I received the law; but unless you help me, it becomes death to me. For I am not sufficient for this without grace. Therefore I pray: “Would that [my ways] might be directed,” etc.

Or the connection is: Because you commanded, therefore would that my ways—that is, the actions of this life, which are crooked in themselves—might be directed. Let them be directed, I say, to keep your statutes. Otherwise statutes cannot be kept unless our ways are straight.

The statutes were many for the ancient people: for example, that a Hebrew servant should serve only six years; that a father should be reverently honoured, a son disciplined, God feared, and a priest honoured; and things like these. These statutes can be kept if the commandments are always before our eyes, so that crooked things may at once be corrected by them. Hence he adds:

### Verse 6

> “Then I shall not be put to shame, when I have looked upon all your commandments.”

“When I have looked upon.” As though he said: I will keep these statutes when I have looked upon your commandments—or at your commandments—as in a mirror. He adds “all” because a person who sins against one becomes guilty of all. For one guilty of a single sin is punished eternally. Hence James says: “Whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. II). The person who looks upon the commandments avoids this.

But the person who does not look upon them does not know in what respect he errs. “And then,” namely, when I have looked upon them, “I shall not be put to shame.” Previously you were ashamed in Adam and were made naked when you covered yourself with fig leaves (Gen. III); because you were ashamed, you hid yourself from the sight of God, because you blushed. But now, freed by grace, you come into God’s sight.

Or thus: I ask to keep the statutes because then, when I have kept them, I shall not be put to shame when I have looked upon all—or at all—your commandments, as in a mirror, because I shall not be a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work. For the person who examines the commandments but does not do them is put to shame. Hence James says: “If anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking upon the face of his birth in a mirror” (Jas. I). For he considered himself, went away, and immediately forgot what kind of person he was. And then, namely, when I have kept [them] and looked upon the commandments:

### Verse 7

> “I will give thanks to you in uprightness of heart, when I have learned the judgments of your righteousness.”

“I will give thanks to you.” I will not be ungrateful, but will praise you in uprightness of heart, because you made my heart upright; therefore I will praise you, which one who is crooked cannot do. I will praise you “in that”—that is, because—I have learned from the fathers, not discovered by myself, the judgments which are a great deep: the judgments, I say, of your righteousness. He calls them “judgments of righteousness,” by which the world is judged now and at the end. These judgments are judgments of righteousness because by them God frees his servants, labouring under persecution by the devil.

Or arrange the text thus: “I will give thanks to you,” that is, I will praise you, because I have learned the judgments of your righteousness—provided, however, that this is done in uprightness of heart, that is, if the heart is directed toward keeping [them]. Otherwise I should not rejoice in learning them, but be accused. For what would it profit me to have learned them if, with a perverse heart, I have crooked ways?

### Verse 8

> “I will keep your statutes; do not utterly forsake me.”

I shall keep your justifications, that is, I shall perform works of righteousness. Do not forsake me. [Haymo, Cassiodorus, Col. 1049A Ambrose, Augustine.] Having been granted the justifications, he asks God to preserve him, because he knows that the devil goes about seeking. As though he said: “And that I may keep them, do not forsake me utterly,” or “exceedingly,” which is the same thing. Even if you forsake me for testing, as with Job, it is the same. And if you forsake me for a time, let me appear weak in my own eyes; and, lest I boast of myself, nevertheless do not forsake me utterly. Or “exceedingly,” that is, so that I perish; and thus I shall glory in you, not in myself. Or he thus prays for Christ’s coming, before which God had forsaken the world because of sin; but he prays that he may not now forsake it utterly, or utterly abandon it. This has now been fulfilled in Christ’s coming, because “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5).

## Comparison on Psalm 118: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk,” etc.

[Col. 1049B]

### Aleph

**Verse 2. — “Who search.”** *Notzere*, that is, “those who keep.” But the Septuagint placed the antecedent; the Hebrew has the consequent. For no one keeps God’s testimonies better than one who has devoutly searched them with most diligent care. If you do not know what must be done, how will you keep it?

### Beth

[Note: [Col. 1049] Beth, that is, “house,” according to Jerome, *To Paula, a Roman lady*.]

**“Whereby does he correct.”** In the first letter he explained the parts of blessedness [Cassiodorus], in which he prays that he may be kept. In this second he discloses the time of conversion. [Ambrose.] At what time, above all, should one turn to God from the fall and confusion of a dissipated age? Accordingly, this octave is suitably introduced by the letter Beth, which is interpreted “confusion,” because here he shows that God’s precepts free a person from confusion—that is, from the fall of sin. As though he said: “I shall keep your justifications,” which must be kept, because by keeping your words, O Lord, the younger man corrects his way. But he first introduces this with a deliberative question:

**Verse 1 (9). — “Whereby does a younger man correct his way? By keeping your words.”**

**Whereby does he correct?** [Ambrose, Augustine.] For this man, as though confounded by the error and wantonness of a dissipated age, now deliberates in the sober mind of youth how he may correct his way, cast off what is shameful, and take up the way full of uprightness, saying: “Whereby does a younger man [Col. 1049D] correct his way?”—that is, his evil habit. “Younger” may be understood literally, because this should chiefly be done at that age, when a person is more prone to sin. Hence: “My son, receive instruction from your youth, and until gray hairs you shall find wisdom” (Ecclus. 6).

Or “the younger man” is understood as that younger son in the Gospel who is read to have corrupted his way—that is, the Gentile people. Or rather, “the younger man” here means the spiritual people, who bear the image of the new person, not the old. This is spiritual youth: the age of the new, not the old, person.

See: he first put forward the question with deliberation. And because better and more wholesome counsels appear after reflection, the Prophet adds, as though deliberating and then turning his speech to God: “O Lord, behold wherein the younger man corrects his way: by keeping your words of faith.” This is the conclusion of his deliberation; and, having rightly turned to God, he gives this answer as though offering a prayer to God. He received this counsel by God’s inspiration, not by human presumption.

And truly, at this age, still unacquainted with crimes, it is especially fitting to correct one’s way. [Ambrose.] For it is better to forestall youth by correction than, after recalling one’s falls, to weep and say: “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances, O Lord” (Ps. 24:7). The latter is a remedy for weakness; the former, the strength of salvation. Here the matter is in danger, because it is difficult to drive out established habits. Habit indeed possesses a great bond within itself; there, in what is good, it is otherwise. Hence it is said: “It is good for a man when he bears the yoke from his youth” (Lam. 3).

[Hilary, Augustine.] For it is easier to be drawn back from entering than to be recalled after one has taken up the path of evil habit. Notice also that he does not say, “by reading” or “by remembering your words,” but “by keeping” them—namely, in action. Thus he is old in mind, like Daniel; otherwise he cannot correct his way, because it is futile to preserve them in memory if one does not preserve them in life also. There is no corrected way in a perverse life. For some retain God’s words so as not to forget them, but do not put them into practice in life so as to be corrected.

**Verse 2 (10). — “With my whole heart I have sought you; do not cast me away from your commandments.”**

[Col. 1050C] **With my whole heart.** [Augustine, Ambrose, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Ambrose.] As though he said: “Because correction is in these things, therefore I have sought you”—which comes by God’s gift—“with my whole heart.” One who does not seek with his whole heart is negligent and is cast away. Therefore, “do not cast me away,” by failing to help me, as though I were unworthy, when I seek you with my whole heart. “Do not cast me away,” I say, “from your commandments,” that is, from understanding the Law; for one whom God does not help is cast away from it.

For human weakness is not equal to his upright and arduous commandments unless his prevenient love helps it. Therefore the one not helped by God is, as it were, barred from the tree of life by a flaming sword, as unworthy.

Or he speaks of ecclesiastical office. One who administers it negligently is cast away by God. Lest this happen to him, he prays: “Do not cast me away from your commandments,” which must be taught and proclaimed in the Church; the negligent person is cast away from these, lest he surrender his place to one better than himself.

And lest he incur a greater offense, he is lukewarm who is neither hot with the fervor of faith nor cold with the chill of unbelief. He is not snatched from the Lord’s hand, but is cast out as worse than the cold person—that is, one wholly unbelieving. Thus it is said to the angel of Laodicea in the Apocalypse: “Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. 3). Here he openly condemns negligence under a graver judgment than ignorance, and shows how great is the loss of one whom the Lord Jesus vomits from his mouth and rejects from his own inward parts. Yet how merciful he is: he both holds the righteous in his mouth and does not vomit out the unrighteous before warning that they are about to be vomited out.

**Verse 3 (11). — “In my heart I have hidden your sayings, that I may not sin against you.”**

**In my heart I have hidden.** [Haymo, Cassiodorus, Ambrose.] As though he said: “I have sought out your commandments and have also committed them to memory.” This is what it means: “I have stored away and hidden your sayings in my heart”—from swine and dogs, namely. For it is a kind of sin to preach to the obstinate; therefore I hid them, “that I may not sin against you,” who say: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine” (Matt. 7).

For it is a fault to make secret mysteries common to the unworthy, and, as it were, to show Babylon the treasures of God’s house. A person may do this through flattery, to please the one to whom he discloses them; through greed, to gain something; through vainglory, to appear more knowledgeable; or through careless talkativeness, while an irrevocable word flies forth without judgment. Therefore the discipline of silence must be adopted, so that one first keeps silence before speaking. Hence: “Let every person be swift to hear, slow to speak” (Jas. 1).

Thus Isaiah, when he heard from the Lord, “Cry out,” did not cry before he heard what he should cry, but answered, “What shall I cry?” (Isa. 40). The Lord also, in the Gospel, compares the kingdom of heaven to a treasure hidden in a field (Matt. 13). This is the treasure of wisdom and knowledge which a person, when he has found it, hides in his heart rather than publishing it abroad, like Mary, who kept all the Lord’s words, pondering them in her heart (Luke 2; the printed reference reads Gen. 2).

[Col. 1051C] **Verse 4 (12). — “Blessed are you, O Lord; teach me your justifications.”**

**Blessed are you.** [Cassiodorus.] Lest anyone attribute holy instruction to his own powers, he first says, “Blessed.” [Ambrose, Augustine, Gloss.] As though he said: “Because I possess your sayings, I give thanks, saying: Blessed—that is, praised—are you, O Lord, who give freely. And henceforth teach me to do, that is, grant that I may do, your justifications,” namely, the works of the saints which God commands, so that I may demonstrate in deeds what I have learned in words. For one hides the sayings in his heart in vain unless works of righteousness follow.

Or thus: [Augustine, Gloss, Augustine, Ambrose.] Above he said that the Law had been given to him; here he asks that the blessing by which the Law is fulfilled may be given him. As though he said: “He who gave the Law will also give the blessing. And, O Lord, you are blessed in your nature, [Col. 1051D] or in those of yours whom you bless; therefore teach me your justifications.” As though he said: “Because I have hidden your sayings in my heart, you have given the Law; give also the blessing of grace—namely, teach me your justifications—so that I may learn by doing, or may know the secrets of the Law; and, instructed by these—”

**Verse 5 (13). — “With my lips I have proclaimed all the judgments of your mouth.”**

**With my lips.** [Gloss, Augustine.] Or the connection may be made thus: “I have hidden your sayings in my heart; and when I saw the time of grace, I proclaimed to others with lips fitted to my heart all the judgments of your mouth.” He does not say “all your judgments,” but “all those of your mouth”—that is, those which you told me through your sayings. “The judgments of your mouth,” then, are those spoken through prophets and apostles, who are the mouth of God. I proclaimed [Col. 1052A] them all, not universally, but all that have been written or spoken.
