These judgments are those by which the world is judged both now and at the end. They are a great deep and inscrutable. Yet I kept silent about none of those things which you wished to make known to me through your sayings. And—

**Verse 6 (14). — “I have delighted in the way of your testimonies, as in all riches.”**

**I have delighted** in this life in the way of your testimonies. [Augustine.] God’s testimonies are those by which he shows how greatly he loves us, such as his birth and passion. Thus: “I have delighted in the way of your testimonies,” that is, in the humility of his birth and passion, by which we also hope for what is to come; and therefore they are fittingly called testimonies.

Or “in the way of your testimonies” means Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge [Col. 1052B] (Col. 2). [Cassiodorus, Ambrose.] Therefore Christ is called the way of testimonies, because the testimonies which speak of him lead to him, and are fulfilled in him. “Testimonies” means the sayings of Scripture.

“As in all riches” means spiritual riches; for he does not compare them with earthly riches, which he counts as filth. Or: “I have delighted,” as people delight in all temporal riches. Such temporal riches are not comparable to spiritual riches in grace, though they are pleasant to people.

**Verse 7 (15). — “I shall be exercised in your commandments, and I shall consider your ways.”**

**In your commandments.** [Alcuin, Hilary, Augustine.] As though he said: “I have proclaimed and delighted in your testimonies, [Col. 1052C] and I shall remain in them still further.” This is what it means: “I shall be exercised in your commandments” by the practice of good work; and then, by the merit of good work, “I shall consider,” that is, know, your ways. For no one reaches the inner chambers of understanding unless he has first drawn near through purity of life.

Or thus: “Teach me your justifications; and if you teach me further, I shall chatter about your commandments”—another reading—that is, against all enemies of the Christian and catholic faith I shall argue fluently with abundant reasons. Yet disputations are useful only if nothing is considered in them except the Lord’s ways. Hence he adds: “And I shall consider your ways,” which are mercy and truth, the fullness of both of which is found in Christ. And through this exercise there also comes about what follows.

[Col. 1052D] **Verse 8 (16). — “I shall meditate on your justifications; I shall not forget your words.”**

**I shall meditate on your justifications.** [Cassiodorus, Hilary, Cassiodorus.] Meditation is opposed to the forgetfulness arising from the weakness of original sin. This man knew the defect of human nature, and found a remedy against it.

“Justifications” include such things as this: a Hebrew servant serves under the Law for no more than six years; in the seventh he goes out free. This signifies that a faithful person serves in this world, distinguished by six ages, only for a time, and will be free in the resurrection. Meditation is appropriate to such matters and others stated enigmatically. But moral commandments—such as, “You shall not commit adultery,” and the like (Exod. 20)—require action alone. He therefore fittingly distinguished his expressions: “I shall be exercised in your commandments,” [Col. 1053A] and “I shall meditate on your justifications.” Therefore I shall meditate, so that I may not forget your words—that is, so that I may not be able to forget what it is expedient to retain.

## Comparison on Beth

**Verse 2 (10). — “Do not cast me away.”** *Al taschgeni*: this means, according to those who hold this view, “Do not make me wander.” The sense is the same; for to be cast away from God’s commandments is not to be helped by him. Without God’s help we never fail to wander. This is what he had previously said, as Augustine interprets it: “Would that my ways were directed!”

[Note: [Col. 1053D] Gimel, according to Jerome: “recompense.”]

**“Reward your servant.”** [Cassiodorus.] In this third letter he shows human need and asks God’s grace against it. Human need is manifold: weakness, ignorance, exile, and enemies. [Col. 1053B] Against this he seeks the help of manifold grace. Therefore the letter Gimel, interpreted “recompense,” is fittingly set before this octave, because he asks that grace may be bestowed upon him in many ways.

For above he had said, “Whereby does a younger man correct his way?” Then he added, “By keeping your words.” Now, that this may happen, he asks for help, saying:

**Verse 1 (17). — “Reward your servant: give me life, and I shall keep your words.”**

**Reward** [Cassiodorus] does not mean, “Pay back for good merits which preceded,” since none preceded; rather, “reward” means “give again and again.” Or: repay my evils with good. [Augustine.] For before faith, nothing but evils for evils is due to a person. But God, through undeserved grace, repays good for evils. For unless God repaid good for evils, there would by no means be people to whom he might repay good for good. He is certainly just in repaying good for good because he was first merciful in repaying good for evils—although even that justice by which good things are repaid to us is not without mercy.

Observe that there are four kinds of repayment: evils for evils, goods for goods, goods for evils, or evils for goods. The first two belong to justice; the third to mercy. God knows nothing of the fourth. Therefore God repays good for evil, and this is the repayment for which this man asks when he says, “Reward your servant,” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Ambrose] who attributes nothing to merits but everything to grace. What does he ask? Namely: “Give me life” through faith, by which the righteous lives.

[Col. 1053D] He is not wholly dead, but already has the beginning of good desire, who can pray: “Give me life.” Once dead and unable to know or do anything, let me be made alive through faith, by which “I shall keep your words.” For the living person keeps them, and by keeping them lives.

Or this is not the voice of a sinner, but of one already corrected and righteous, established in the progress of virtues, who with a good conscience asks for the rewards of good work. Thus the letter Gimel, interpreted “recompense,” is suitably prefixed, because here fulfilment and knowledge of the Law are said to be repaid to one already corrected. As though he said: “Because I have been so corrected as I showed above, reward me, your servant.”

Already established in the progress of virtues, he asks that recompense may be given him according to the merit of faith and work. It should not appear arrogant or foreign for him to seek a reward from God for outstanding labors. For it is the prerogative of faith and righteousness to hope for a reward from the Lord’s favor. In Matthew 14, Peter, walking upon the waves, is reproved because he doubted as a human being, not because he presumed as an apostle. We are also commanded in the Gospel to have faith and not hesitate about deeds beyond human capacity.

The Apostle too, who had earlier said, “I am not worthy to be called an apostle” (1 Cor. 15), later said: “There is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord will render to me” (2 Tim. 4). Therefore it belongs to the conscience of an innocent person, not to insolent arrogance, to seek a reward from the one whom he serves. To despair supplies material for sloth; to hope is an incentive to labor. Ask confidently, then, if your merits support you, and say: “Reward your servant,” namely, “give me life,” [Augustine] in the present and in the future, “and I shall keep your servants”—the printed text apparently reads *servos* (“servants”) for *sermones* (“words”).

But because they cannot be kept in obedience unless they are first seen in understanding, he adds:

**Verse 2 (18). — “Unveil my eyes, and I shall behold wondrous things from your law.”**

**Unveil my inner eyes** [Ambrose, Cassiodorus], the veil of which is removed in Christ. See human weakness and God’s mercy. A person is covered by the veil of ignorance; God removes it so that you may see. This is what he asks, understanding himself to be burdened by it. I say, “Unveil,” and then I shall behold wondrous things. What things? Those from your Law. The Law is where there is shadow, as in the matter of the paschal lamb and the like.

[Col. 1054C] [Alcuin, Augustine.] He therefore asks that he may see what lies concealed in these things. Or understand the new Law, namely the Gospel, in which wondrous things are considered, such as: “Unless a person renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14); and: “Love your enemies” (Matt. 5). Nothing in the commandments is more wonderful than loving enemies—that is, giving good for evils.

**Verse 3 (19). — “I am a sojourner on the earth; do not hide your commandments from me.”**

**I am a sojourner.** [Cassiodorus, Haymo, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Behold exile. As though he said: “Reward me, unveil my eyes; and you ought to do so, because I am a sojourner on earth,” or an inhabitant without citizenship. I am not a citizen of Babylon, having my heart, if not my body, in heaven. This belongs only to the righteous, to whom an eternal homeland has been promised. Hence elsewhere: “I am a stranger—not like all people, but like all my fathers,” that is, the righteous (Ps. 38).

Therefore, because I am a sojourner, do not hide your commandments from me—that is, do not withhold them from me. You can know the will of the one whom you serve. The commandments are hidden from those who think earthly thoughts, even if they hear and know them. He calls “commandments” those through which he will be freed from sojourning, and in which love is commanded, either alone or supremely.

[Augustine.] But because nothing deserving love is loved unless love itself is loved, this man, wishing to possess love for that very love, cries out:

[Col. 1055A] **Verse 4 (20). — “My soul has longed to desire your justifications at every time.”**

**My soul has longed to desire your justifications** [Augustine], that is, works of righteousness. It longed for this formerly, not only now; for when he was a sojourner on earth, he did not desire to desire them, but merely desired them. Formerly, indeed, he did not yet desire them, but languished in weariness. The love by which what should be loved is loved must be loved just as much as that love must be hated by which what should not be loved is loved.

Observe that *concupiscence* is desire, but not every kind of desire, since there is concupiscence both for things possessed and for things not possessed. Desire properly so called, however, concerns only absent things in this life. Notice also that he says, “It has longed to desire,” not “It has desired.” For we sometimes see by reason [Col. 1055B] how useful God’s justifications—that is, works of righteousness—are, yet through weakness sometimes do not desire them. Thus understanding flies ahead, while affection follows slowly, or not at all. We know what is good, but do not delight in doing it; and we desire to delight in it.

Thus this man formerly longed to desire those things whose goodness he saw, wishing to possess delight in things whose reason he had been able to perceive. He therefore shows, as it were, by what steps one arrives at them. First, one must see what things are useful and honorable; next, one must long for their desire; finally, as light and health increase, their practice becomes delightful, whereas their reason alone had been delightful. These things, then, he longed to desire at every time—not for a season, like the wicked, but always, even amid adversity. Therefore I longed to desire them because—

**Verse 5 (21). — “You rebuked the proud; cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments.”**

**You rebuked the proud** [Augustine], the first human beings, whom the saying “You shall be like gods” delighted (Gen. 3). You rebuked them, saying, “Adam, where are you?” The Lord was not ignorant, but rebuked the proud man because he had come down to such misery. Indeed, the whole inherited misery of mortals is a rebuke of the proud, and through this pride they turned aside.

[Ambrose, Augustine.] And all are cursed—not those alone—who turn aside from your commandments, as from straight paths to crooked ones. Observe that he does not say, “those who turned aside,” as though recalling the sin of those first human beings; [Col. 1055D] rather, he says, “those who turn aside.” By this not they alone are rebuked, but all are warned by their example lest they turn aside through pride; rather, let them love righteousness at every time, so that here they may receive what those people lost in paradise.

Note also that he does not say, “Cursed are those who do not fulfil the commandments,” but “those who turn aside.” For it is one thing to turn aside through pride, another not to fulfil through weakness or ignorance. But because the proud are not humbled even by such great rebuke, the choir of martyrs prays for them, saying:

**Verse 6 (22). — “Remove from me reproach and contempt, because I have sought out your testimonies.”**

**Remove.** [Augustine.] As though he said: “And because those who turn aside are cursed, I pray: remove from me the reproach that I hear and the contempt by which I am despised.” I suffer reproach and contempt because I have sought out your covenants. It is on this account that I am reproached and despised: because I have sought out your testimonies, which are called in Greek *martyria* (μαρτύρια); for these things he suffers.

Thus those who contended for truth, humbled even to death, are called not *testes* (“witnesses”), though we could certainly call them so in Latin, but in Greek *martyres* (“martyrs”). The martyrs say these things, being a reproach and a mockery to those who despise Christ’s cross and the whole Christian humility by which pride alone is healed.

What they ask is not that these things be removed from themselves as evils, since by them they attain the crown; rather, they ask this because the reproach is harmful to those who inflict it, so that those people too may be converted and love the martyrdom which has taken place. Then it is no longer [Col. 1056B] reproach, but honor. For one who has sought out the testimonies is not worthy of reproach; but those who prayed such things suffered them. Hence he adds:

**Verse 7 (23). — “For princes sat and spoke against me; but your servant was exercised in your justifications.”**

**For. Behold the enemies.** [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Ambrose, Gloss.] As though he said: “Remove reproach; yet many wish to inflict it.” For princes sat in judicial fashion, lingering as though scheming; and they openly spoke against me. The same persons were both accusers and judges, which is more grievous. And as these openly devise harm, so demons secretly plot to injure.

They acted thus; but your servant—namely, I—was exercised [Col. 1056C] not in wrongdoing but in your justifications. As though he said: “In these he meditates and conquers, because the enemy strives through wars to draw him away from them.”

[Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though he said: “Amid dangers I had not torment but advancement.” He then explains how he was exercised:

**Verse 8 (24). — “For your testimonies are my meditation, and your justifications are my counsel.”**

For your testimonies are my meditation [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine], that is, the martyrdoms which, when meditated upon, lessen sufferings. Thus this man was exercised by martyrdoms: he meditates on and loves them, looking to the crown; and he loves his enemies. Hence follows: “And your justifications are my counsel.” As though he said: “My counsel is to keep the justifications in which loving enemies consists.”

Behold counsel set against counsel. The counsel of the princes who sat was to destroy the martyrs whom they found; the counsel of the suffering martyrs was to gain those who were lost.

## Comparison on Gimel

**Verse 4 (20). — “My soul has longed,” etc.** *Garsaii.* But modern translators render it “has been broken.” Jerome, however, has “has desired”; and the sense is expressed truly. For it is plain that a soul cannot be broken by an outward breaking. It must consequently be understood of spiritual breaking—that is, of desire itself, which, when great, nearly takes the life out of the soul. The Chaldee agrees with us: “My soul desired to desire.”

**Verse 8 (24). — “My meditation.”** Jerome: “my will.” Others: “my delights,” or something similar, which are gained with little effort. For we continually meditate on things that please and delight us, and in them lies the continual exercise of our attention.

**“Your justifications are my counsel.”** Jerome: “as men most dear to me”; the Praetorian edition: “men of my counsel.” So too the others. Yet that expression was metaphorical, and therefore the Septuagint aptly explained the figure. For just as a person ignorant or doubtful about what should be done needs the counsel of godly and skilled men, whom he asks to direct the erring person into the right way, so we, ignorant by ourselves, inquire what God’s justifications are, so that in true equity we may be led to the kingdom toward which we tend by virtues and holy works, which we regulate according to God’s justifications, as according to friendly men of good counsel. *Ansche atzathi* (“men of my counsel”).

### Daleth

[Col. 1057B] **“My soul has cleaved to the pavement.”** [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] In this fourth letter he says that he is bound by bodily necessity, so that he is weary of praying or working. For “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9). [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] Yet he says that he is to be saved by God’s compassion alone; and because, placed in this necessity, he always fears falling back, the letter Daleth, interpreted “fear,” is suitably prefixed to this octave. Here it is taught that the law of faith strengthens one who fears relapse and is sufficient for him in all things.

Daleth is interpreted not only “fear” but also “birth,” which also fits well. Birth here is understood not spiritually but temporally—that is, the birth of things generated in the world [Ambrose], which are bodily and perishable. From this birth comes fear, which the person here laments, cast down from heaven to earth; previously most blessed, he breathed the air of heaven. He knew neither the cares nor the weariness of this life.

[Haymo.] As though he said: “Now your justifications are my counsel. Now I am thus disposed—but formerly—”

**Verse 1 (25). — “My soul has cleaved to the pavement; give me life according to your word.”**

**My soul has cleaved** [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Haymo, Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine] by consent to the pavement—that is, to the body, whence comes death. For “the flesh desires against the spirit” (Gal. 5), to which the soul formerly did not resist. Or it has cleaved to the pavement—that is, to earthly things—in order to care for things that ought to be trodden underfoot, like pavement. Thus earth is pavement. For in the universe as a whole, as in a certain house, heaven is the ceiling and earth the pavement; it is trodden by striking, so that it becomes a smooth, shining, firm pavement.

The human body too is compared with pavement because it is polished with similar smoothness. He says that his soul has cleaved to this pavement—that is, to the body or to earthly things. This does not contradict the earlier statements in which he said that he delighted in the testimonies and was exercised in the justifications. For however much one progresses here, one still has an affection of mortal flesh toward these earthly things, and from this death one is daily revived.

Therefore he adds: “But you, O Lord, will give me life, so that my mind may be in heaven.” And this is “according to your word” [Col. 1058A] [Cassiodorus, Augustine], that is, through Christ, who is the Word of the Father. Or “according to your word” means according to your promise, so that I may be a child of promise, not a child of self-exaltation. He does not ask this arrogantly, because he confesses here what he was in himself, saying:

**Verse 2 (26). — “I have declared my ways, and you heard me; teach me your justifications.”**

**My ways.** [Augustine, Ambrose.] As though he said: “Give me life—and you ought to do so. For I have declared my ways,” that is, I have confessed my sins. “And you heard me” by forgiving them. “Teach me.” As though he said: “You have blotted out my ways; teach me yours.” This is what he means: “Teach me your justifications.”

He says this because he wishes to progress, though he is already exercised in them. By progressing from these to others, as though by growing, he desires to arrive at the point of doing them, not merely knowing them. For one truly knows justifications who performs them; conversely, it is said of the Lord, “He knew no sin” (2 Cor. 5), that is, he did not commit it.

Or: “Teach me your justifications,” that is, make me perceive the figurative observances according to their spiritual meaning. Observe that he thinks one must reach God’s justifications in a beautiful order: first confess one’s sins. Thus it is said elsewhere: “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Isa. 43); and elsewhere: “The righteous person at the beginning of his speech is his own accuser” (Prov. 18). For if the righteous person accuses himself, he excludes the voice of the ready accuser, who is accustomed to accuse sins and aggravate everyone’s punishments; the one who confesses concerning himself stops his mouth. For shame excuses the accused; modesty accuses its own prosecutor. And, O Lord—

**Verse 3 (27). — “Teach me the way of your justifications, and I shall be exercised in your wonders.”**

**Teach me the way of your justifications** [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Ambrose], because I condemn my own ways; therefore teach me your way, so that I may understand the mysteries. Other manuscripts have, “make it known to me,” which more explicitly represents the Greek *synelison* (Συνέλισον): “make me understand.”

“The way of your justifications.” Observe the order: one must first learn the justifications, which he requested earlier here; then one must learn their stages and order—what ought to come first and what afterward. For one sins who acts out of order. To know what one should do but not to know the order of doing it is not perfect knowledge. Ignorance of order confuses the nature of affairs and the form of merits.

But once the mysteries and their order are known, I too shall be exercised in the practice of work and in spiritual understanding, as one exercises in a wrestling-school to gain strength. And this will be “in your wonders,” which lie hidden in figures. [Augustine.] He calls the justifications themselves God’s wonders, some of which are so wonderful that the inexperienced believe that they cannot be reached, either in understanding or in performance. Therefore this man, laboring and wearied by their difficulty, adds:

**Verse 4 (28). — “My soul has slumbered because of weariness; strengthen me in your words.”**

**It has slumbered.** [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As though he said: [Col. 1059A] “I say, ‘Teach me, instruct me’; but because the petition is delayed, I have slumbered like a weary watcher.” This is what it means: “My soul has slumbered,” that is, it has grown cold in hope of attaining these things, and this “because of the weariness” of delay.

Observe that he does not say “it slept” but “it slumbered.” To sleep belongs to one who is forgetful and sluggish; slumber belongs to a weary watcher, and is called *acedia*. But you, “strengthen me in your words,” so that, if the petition is still delayed, I may stand firm in the meditation of your Law.

[Haymo.] Or thus I say that I shall be exercised in wonders; yet formerly my soul slumbered from fear, doing little or no good, and therefore teach me. And because I formerly slumbered, now that I have reached these things, strengthen me in your words [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine], which I already possess, lest I fall away from them, but may press on from them to others.

See: in this octave he prays against two dangers. First, against the necessities of the flesh, saying, “Give me life”; here, against weariness. As though he said: “I pray that you may give me life, in view of the first danger, from which you have delivered me. I also pray that you may strengthen me, in view of the other danger, namely weariness, from which I have escaped through you.” Then, as though someone asked, “What prevents this?” he adds:

**Verse 5 (29). — “Remove from me the way of iniquity, and have mercy on me through your law.”**

**The way of iniquity, etc.** [Haymo, Ambrose, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Or: “That I may be able to be strengthened, O Lord, remove from me the way of iniquity,” trodden by the Fathers and still threatening. This is necessary in this age. And because the law of works entered in so that transgression might abound, [Col. 1059C] he adds: “And have mercy on me through your law,” namely the law of faith, the law of mercy and grace, through which we fulfil what we cannot fulfil by ourselves.

In the law of works, in which God commands, there is justice; in the law of faith, which gives aid, there is mercy. This man asks through faith when he says: “Remove from me the way of iniquity, and have mercy on me through your law.” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] As though he said: “Remove evils; grant good things.” He asks for mercy because no one is justified by the Law, but by faith in Christ.

**Verse 6 (30). — “I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments.”**

**The way of truth.** [Augustine.] Having said, “Have mercy on me through your law,” he sets forth the benefits he has received, so that he may obtain the rest. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though he said: “Have mercy, because I have now chosen the way of truth in which I might run”—that is, Christ, whose worship he chose, who is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). “And I have not forgotten your judgments,” so that I might run. And while I ran—

**Verse 7 (31). — “I have cleaved to your testimonies, O Lord; do not put me to shame.”**

**I have cleaved, O Lord, to your testimonies** [Cassiodorus, Ambrose, Alcuin, Augustine, Ambrose, Cassiodorus], whereas I had earlier cleaved to the pavement. One cleaves to the testimonies who renounces the world, despises the cares and weariness of this life, and is not bent by the pursuit of luxury or desire for money. Therefore, “do not put me to shame”; rather, make me attain the goal toward which I run and arrive where I tend. Hence the Apostle: “So run that you may obtain” (1 Cor. [Col. 1060A] 9). Observe that this man is not secure, but humbly asks that he may be preserved.

**Verse 8 (32). — “I have run the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart.”**
I ran in the way of your commandments, [Ambrose, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] which is narrow, like a good horse. For Christ has his horses, of whom the prophet says: “You mounted your horses, and your riding is salvation” (Habakkuk 3). And I did this when—that is, because—you enlarged my heart. For I would not run unless you had enlarged it. The enlargement of the heart is delight in righteousness, so that one acts not from fear but from delight; this is God’s gift. Or enlargement is breadth of knowledge, without which I cannot run. These are the waters of which it is said: “Let your waters flow abroad in your streets” (Proverbs 5). Concerning these the Lord cries: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7); and: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (ibid.). Note that this verse explains how it was said above, “I chose” and “I have not forgotten.” When he says, “when you enlarged my heart,” he means that it was not through myself, but by your gift, that I did the things just mentioned.

## Comparison in Daleth

**Verse 4 (28).—“It slumbered.”** Those who follow Hebrew render it: “it dripped,” “flowed away,” “melted,” “was in anguish”: *dalephah*. The sense is the same. For a soul exhausted by long waiting, or by the burden of the body, is as though dissolved both outside itself and within itself.

**“And have mercy on me according to your law.”** Similarly Nebiensis, Pratensis, the interpreters for Cajetan and Campensis, Jerome, and Sanctes: “Grant me your law”; Pellicanus [col. 1060C] and Münster: “May your law be pleasing, or gracious, to me.” Although all these converge upon one meaning, *ḥānan* signifies “he had mercy,” “he gave,” “he showed favor.” Therefore *ḥonnēnî* likewise has a varied sense.

**Verse 6 (30).—“I have not forgotten.”** Hebrew: “I set before myself.” Thus most render it, “I set before myself,” meaning to have before one’s eyes, and therefore not to forget. The interpreters for Cajetan translate “I made equal,” and Pratensis, “I did.” For *shāwāh* and *shiwwāh* sometimes bear that meaning. In the end, the interpretation comes to the same thing.

## He

[Note: Col. 1059D: Jerome interprets *He* as “these things.”]

**“Set down the law.”** In this fifth letter, he prays that, Christ having come, the One who retained the old law may establish for him the new law—a law always to be sought, because it is so ardently desired. And because through it he possesses true being, the letter *he*, [col. 1060D] interpreted “to be,” is suitably prefixed to this octonary: strengthened by the new law, he now prays for true being. [Ambrose] *He* is also interpreted “is” or “I live,” which is fitting. For whoever is, lives; and whoever lives, truly is. Such being or living is found in Christ, “who is the same yesterday and today and for ever” (Hebrews 13). Therefore one who lives in Christ speaks here, declaring how he lives—that is, how he desires to live. As though saying: “Do not put me to shame, but—”

**Verse 1 (33).—“Set before me, O Lord, the law, the way of your statutes; and I shall seek it always.”**

Set before me, O Lord, a law—[Augustine, Ambrose] not the old law, as once for subjects, but the new law, written by the Holy Spirit in the hearts of children, so that they may understand it and fulfill it [col. 1061A] from love. For one who acts unwillingly would not wish to be commanded; and one whose will is unclean is not clean in deed. This law is the way of your statutes. Hence he adds, “the way of your statutes,” namely, set it before me. As though saying: “Let the law for my journey be the way of your statutes, so that I may turn aside nowhere.” Thus an emperor prescribes to his soldiers where and by which route they are to go, lest they take the road according to their own judgment, seek self-chosen shortcuts, or leave the standards by turning to the right or left. So too the Lord gave the children of Israel, as they journeyed, a law for traveling: he went before them in a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night; when it went ahead, they followed, and when it stood still or vanished, they remained in the camp (Exodus 13). Thus the pillar of fire and cloud was their law for traveling.

“And I shall seek.” [Augustine] As though saying: “Set before me the law, and I shall seek it.” He seeks the law which he already possesses by making progress in it. And this always—that is, as long as he lives here, because progress is made for that long. After this life, one who made progress here is made perfect there, where, perfected, he abides without end. Therefore he seeks by progressing in the law which he possesses by acting upon it. Or it is always sought by observing it here and in the future, as it is said: “The Spirit searches all things” (1 Corinthians 2), not in order to discover what it does not know, but because it leaves nothing unknown. So here, one always seeks the law who never leaves any part of the law unexamined.

Or he says, “Set down the law,” concerning the old law, because this man also wishes to know the old law. He asks that it be set before him, not in order to know it according to the letter, but to understand what usefulness it has and why it was given—[col. 1061C] namely, “so that trespass might abound.” Hence he adds:

**Verse 2 (34).—“Give me understanding, and I shall search your law; and I shall keep it with my whole heart.”**

Give me understanding. [Augustine] As though saying: “I say that I shall seek it; and, in order to seek it, give me understanding, because it is not enough to seek unless you understand what you seek.” Give me understanding, therefore, so that I may reach its heights, on which the whole law depends. And, having received understanding, I shall search your law, since otherwise I cannot search it; and I shall keep it with my whole heart—that is, I shall love God with my whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind, and my neighbor as myself. And because I am less able to do this by my own powers—

[col. 1061D] **Verse 3 (35).—“Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I have desired it.”**

Lead me in the path [Augustine] of your commandments, because the way is narrow, though it is run with an enlarged heart. He then states why he asked: “for I have desired it.” For this new grace is pleasing in itself, and it leads to heaven. Therefore he says, “I have desired it”; but my will is insufficient unless you lead me in what I desire. Yet because this very will is from you, I pray:

**Verse 4 (36).—“Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to avarice.”**

Incline my heart, [Cassiodorus] so that I may desire more. He fittingly says “incline,” for those inclined through humility see better than those lying on their backs through vanity. Behold: through every minute and subtle detail he shows that all good is bestowed by God, [col. 1062A] preserved through him, and continually increased by his grace. Incline it, I say, to your testimonies. [Augustine] Something is proved by testimony; and God persuades and proves to us his statutes and commandments by his testimonies—that is, by precepts and examples—so that he may be worshiped freely. Indeed, by his testimonies he brings this about in us: that we may worship him freely. This is hindered by avarice, “the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6); therefore he adds, “and not to avarice,” so that he may worship God freely—that is, for God’s own sake—as Job did, not for earthly things (Job 1). For every form of avarice is cut away from us if God is worshiped freely. And because all things under the sun are vanity (Ecclesiasticus 1), he therefore adds generally:

**Verse 5 (37).—“Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity; give me life in your way.”**

[col. 1062B] Turn away the eyes of my body, [Cassiodorus] because we desire the things seen by them, lest they see—or lest I see—vanity. For we sin through the eyes when we covet what we see. “Death has entered through the windows of our senses” (Jeremiah 6); this is indicated here. [Ambrose, Augustine] What is asked here is thus more ours in hope than in present possession, since even now many of us are subject to vanity. Therefore he prays for what will be fulfilled not here but in the future, when creation shall be freed from its bondage to corruption (Romans 8) and shall cleave to Truth itself, entering the liberty of the glory of the children of God, where it shall no longer see the vanity of the world.

Here is another interpretation, which I confess pleases me more: let us understand the inward eyes by which we consider why we do what we do. Since our service—that is, our work—is evaluated not by the service itself but [col. 1062C] by its end, so that consideration is given not only to whether what we do is good, but especially to whether that for which we do it is good, this man prays that when he does something, the inward eyes which see why it is done may not see vanity, so as to do a good deed for its sake. In this vanity, love of human praise holds the chief place; the Lord prohibits it everywhere in the Gospel and commands that good works be done solely for God’s glory (Matthew 6). Thus he does not see vain things whose mind is fixed upon him who is above all things, whose mind is above. But whoever thinks upon these things lives under the sun, where vanity is. Therefore he says, “Turn away my eyes”—he means the mystical eyes of the mind—“lest they see vanity,” [Ambrose, Augustine] that is, the vain things of the world. Christ, however, is Truth, [col. 1062D] and he is the Way in which he asks to be given life, saying: “Give me life in your way,” that is, in Christ, who is Life. He then teaches by what means he may be turned away from vanity, adding:

**Verse 6 (38).—“Establish your word for your servant, in your fear.”**

Establish your word for your servant, in fear, [Augustine] that is, grant him to do what you speak. For it is established only in one who acts. Establish the word immovably, lest it slip; fear is useful for this. Hence he adds, “in your fear,” where there is neither fault nor negligence. [Cassiodorus, Hilary, Ambrose] He says this because many receive God’s words negligently and turn aside from them as from fables. But the holy fear of God is like a foundation in which the word is established; and the word itself is instruction in fear, lest there be zeal for God but not according to knowledge [col. 1063A] (Romans 10). [Augustine] This fear is not servile fear, by which punishment alone is feared, but chaste fear, by which offense is feared. For an adulteress fears her husband in one way, a chaste wife in another: the adulteress, lest he come; the chaste wife, lest he leave. This is the fear of the Lord which “endures for ever and ever” (Psalm 18); [Ambrose] it turns one away from vanity. Therefore he prays that the word may be established in him in this fear, lest the birds come and take it away from a careless and pretended disposition (Luke 8).

**Verse 7 (39).—“Cut off my reproach, which I have suspected, because your judgments are delightful.”**

Cut off. [Augustine] This sense is taken from the preceding verse: one whose eye sees vanity suspects the same of others, so that he believes another person acts for the motive for which he himself performs good deeds. Because the hidden things of human beings are not seen, occasion is given to suspicions, so that a person often dares to suspect what is false—or, if true, still unknown. Therefore, after the Lord had instructed people about the end of their works—not to perform their righteousness for human praise, money, or even food and clothing—because we might suspect others of performing good works for these motives, he added: “Do not judge” (Matthew 7). This is what the psalmist prays may be cut off from him. Then he added: “And you shall not be judged” (ibid.). Thus here he says: “Cut off my reproach, which I have suspected,” and adds: “because your judgments are delightful.” As though saying: “Turn away my eyes and cut off the reproach which I have suspected.” He calls his own reproach that which he suspects concerning others, because he more readily supposes in another [col. 1063C] what he feels in himself. He therefore prays that the reproach he feels in himself and suspects in others may be removed.

[Cassiodorus] Suspicion is indeed a grave vice of human nature: it thinks otherwise than the truth is, so that we call evil things good and good things evil; it leads to reproach by making us think otherwise than the matter stands. This lover of truth wishes this fault removed from himself, for God’s judgments please him: God’s word is true and his sentence firm. Hence he adds, “Because your judgments are delightful.” [Augustine, Ambrose] As though saying: “I suspect, but you judge all things truly, because your judgments are delightful,” that is, true. They are true and pleasant to a lover of truth; but human judgments about hidden matters are not pleasant, because they are rash.

Or by “reproach” is understood sin, from which reproach follows. The meaning is: “Cut off my reproach,” that is, my sin, “which I have suspected,” because, even if I do not possess it, I do not know; you know it better than I myself do. Hence the Apostle says: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified” (1 Corinthians 4). To you, the Judge, I dare confess it. “Because your judgments are delightful,” that is, sweet to one confessing, not severe. And because the judgments are sweet:

**Verse 8 (40).—“Behold, I have desired your commandments; give me life in your righteousness.”**

Behold, I have desired your commandments, [Ambrose, Augustine] as a lover of the One who loves me. Or, according to the first interpretation, connect it thus. As though saying: “Cut off the reproach which I have suspected.” But since it belongs to the envious [col. 1064A] readily to suspect another’s reproach when they cannot gnaw at an outstanding work—as the devil did concerning Job, alleging that he did not worship God freely (Job 1)—charity must be maintained against this, for charity “does not envy” (1 Corinthians 13). Hence he adds: “Behold, I have desired your commandments” (Matthew 22), which are all gathered into the two commandments of charity; that is, I have desired with my whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind to love you and my neighbor. And do you give me life, not in my own equity but in your equity or righteousness—that is, fill me with the charity I have desired, for in myself I die.

Or: “Give me life in your equity,” or “in your righteousness,” that is, in Christ, who is God. And because he is human, he is my neighbor. For he is the Word who is God, and “the Word became flesh” (John 1), so that he might be [col. 1064B] my neighbor.

## Comparison in He

**Verse 1 (33).—“And I shall seek it always.”** Since the Hebrew word *ʿēqeb* signifies “heel,” “end,” and “reward,” it supplied varied material for interpretation, although the matter itself is not difficult to reconcile. Jerome therefore has: “I shall keep it by the track.” The interpreter for Cajetan, Pratensis, Münster, and Nebiensis follow: “unto the heel,” or “unto the end.” The Campensis edition and the paraphrase agree. Sanctes, however, has: “for the reward.” I think Jerome understands “track” as perseverance, or, as Pellicanus translates it, “to the fingernail,” i.e. exactly or completely. Reward likewise is the end of labors and the prize of perseverance.

## Vav

[col. 1064C] **“And may [it] come.”** [Cassiodorus, Ambrose] In the sixth letter he prays that the Savior may come—the mercy of sinners and life of believers—to put enemies to shame and to make progress in the law, that is, to cause his own people to make progress. Since Christ is always present to worthy petitioners, saying to them while they are still speaking, “Behold, I am here,” the letter *Vav*, interpreted “he” or “that one,” is therefore prefixed to this octonary: that is, the Savior Christ, who says to us while we are still speaking, “Behold, I am here.” As though saying: “Give me life in your righteousness—”

**Verse 1 (41).—“And let your mercy come upon me, O Lord; your salvation according to your word.”**

And may your mercy come upon me, O Lord—that is, Christ. [Augustine, Haimo, Augustine] Nor is he other than the righteousness in which the psalmist had asked to be given life. “Upon me,” that is, let your Son become my head by assuming flesh, according to which he will be head. He then explains “mercy,” adding: “And your salvation,” that is, Christ, “may come according to your word,” that is, according to your promise, because all is grace.

Or, in this letter he asks that through mercy he may fulfill the commandments of God which he has desired above. [Ambrose, Alcuin, Augustine] Because he cannot fulfill them except by the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit, the letter *Vav*, interpreted “he” or “that one”—as though denoting the notable Spirit—suitably stands at the beginning. He asks this Spirit’s help against enemies and heretics, who draw people back from keeping the commandments and from true being. As though saying: “I have desired your commandments, and, that I may fulfill them, let your mercy come [col. 1065A] upon me, O Lord,” that is, the help of your grace; and that I may obtain it, “let your salvation,” that is, Christ, “come according to your word.” This does not change.

**Verse 2 (42).—“And I shall answer a word to those who reproach me, because I have hoped in your words.”**

And I shall answer. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] As though saying: “I say, Let your mercy come upon me; and if it is upon me as a protector, not crushing me, I shall answer a word to those reproaching me.” He rightly says, “I shall answer,” because it is insufficient to have Christ in the heart unless one outwardly confesses with the mouth. For “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10). Note that we ought not to be silent against evil people who can nevertheless receive an answer, lest they appear superior.

It is uncertain, however, whether it says, “I shall answer those reproaching me with the Word,” or, “I shall answer the Word to those reproaching me”; but whichever is meant, it signifies Christ. For he himself is reproached to us by those by whom he was crucified, or to whom he is a stumbling-block or foolishness (1 Corinthians 1), because “the Word became flesh,” though “in the beginning [he] was with God” (John 1). But if those who reproach the cross are ignorant of this, because they do not recognize the divinity whose weakness is despised on the cross, it is better understood: “I shall answer with the Word,” namely, the Word who was in the beginning with God, from whom one lives, in answer to those reproaching me with their reproach—neither terrified nor confounded. But because it is not he himself who speaks, but the Spirit of God, he adds: “Because I have hoped.” [col. 1065C] As though saying: “Therefore I shall answer, because I have hoped in your words,” that is, in the promises which say: “Do not consider what you are to say, for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10). That is, I shall answer because you promised this. But because many deny under the pressure of evils, he adds:

**Verse 3 (43).—“And do not take from my mouth the word of truth utterly, because I have hoped exceedingly in your judgments.”**

And do not take away—[Augustine, Ambrose, Augustine] that is, do not permit the word of truth to be taken from my mouth. It is taken from the mouth also through an evil conscience. For the Lord forbids one persisting in sin from the office of preaching, saying: “Why do you recount my righteous acts?” (Psalm 49). Eloquence is itself silenced if conscience is sick. One must therefore beware lest deeds fail to accord with words, and lest works of iniquity disfigure the teaching of discipline. The word is also taken from the mouth by birds of heaven and in many ways, but not from the heart if it is fixed there. Therefore he does not say “from my heart,” but “from my mouth.”

“Do not take it away,” I say, and this “utterly,” that is, ever; even if you take it away for a time, as in Peter, who, though for an hour troubled by fear, denied, yet was restored through weeping (Luke 22). Or: “very greatly,” as some manuscripts have. The body of Christ—that is, the Church—prays this and obtains that it may not fail very greatly, that is, altogether. For even if some members of the Church deny, the strong remain; or they are restored to the same body, [col. 1066A] because “I have hoped exceedingly in your judgments.” As though saying: “Do not take it away, because I have hoped exceedingly in your judgments,” that is, in the scourges by which you correct. Although this is a less commonly compounded word, it nonetheless fulfills the need of rendering the truth. Therefore the meaning of this passage must be examined more attentively. For he who before said, “I have hoped in your words,” here makes, as it were, an increase by saying, “I have hoped exceedingly in your judgments”: that is, the scourges by which you correct do not remove hope but increase it.

Or he says, “I have hoped exceedingly,” [Alcuin, Ambrose] because we hope for a reward greater than our merit and beyond what we ask. Hence: “The sufferings of this present time are not comparable with the future glory,” and so forth (Romans 8). Or: “in your judgments,” that is, in fear of your judgments, “I have hoped exceedingly.” For one who fears punishment keeps grace; therefore he says:

**Verse 4 (44).—“And I shall keep your law always, for ever and ever.”**

And I shall keep. [Augustine] As though saying: “Do not take the word from my mouth, and, if you do not take it away, I shall keep your law”—not the precepts of Mosaic law, but charity. And this, always. He then defines “always”: “for ever,” that is, in the present age, “and for ever and ever,” that is, in the future. For charity is the fullness of the law, [Hilary] and is kept both in this age by the saints and in the future, where angels and saints have their laws of praising God.

**Verse 5 (45).—“And I walked in a broad place, because I sought your commandments.”**

And I walked. [Augustine] Up to this point these were the words [col. 1066C] of one praying; now they are the words of one narrating, now of one petitioning, who, as though all sins had been pardoned, confesses in praise of God what God has made him. Note the unusual conjunction “and,” used as though in sequence. For he does not say, following the form of the previous words, “and I shall keep,” “and I shall walk.” Nor does he say optatively, “and may I walk,” as he had said, “and may it come,” and, “do not take away.” Rather, he says, “and I walked,” thereby intending us to understand what he did not say: namely, that he was heard; and he adds what he became. As though saying: “When I prayed these foregoing things, you heard me; and, having been heard, I walked in a broad place,” that is, in charity, on which the whole law and the prophets depend (Matthew 22). This charity has also been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit; therefore it is called breadth. [col. 1066D] In this breadth walked the one who said: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (2 Corinthians 6). And this was because “I sought your commandments.” I say that I walked in breadth; he here states the reason: “because I sought your commandments” by asking, seeking, and knocking, and God gives the Spirit by whom the love of God is poured into our hearts, so that good deeds may proceed from it.

Or thus: “And I walked.” As though saying: “May it now happen as I pray, because I also”—[Alcuin, Cassiodorus] that is, even—“walked long ago,” lest anyone think that I have only now begun; but as I began, so grant that I may now act. I walked, I say, in the breadth of knowledge which he obtained by seeking. For the heart which has received him who fills heaven and earth must be spacious.

[col. 1067A] **Verse 6 (46).—“And I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and was not put to shame.”**

And I spoke. As though saying: Above he asked that he might answer a word to those reproaching him, and that the word might not be removed from God’s mouth; now he contends for it even unto death, saying: “And I spoke of your testimonies”—in Greek, *martyria*, a word which we use in Latin—[Hilary, Ambrose] and this even in the presence of kings who could terrify him. Hence: “You shall be brought before kings and governors” (Matthew 10). “And I was not put to shame” by the scandal of the cross, which is my glory; or, I was not put to shame so as to yield. Sweet is the voice that spoke in divine testimonies; beautiful the face that was not ashamed before kings, that does not blush for its author and is not confounded by its redeemer.

[col. 1067B] **Verse 7 (47).—“And I meditated on your commandments, which I loved.”**

And I meditated on your commandments, [Augustine, Cassiodorus] considering what I should say. Behold the contemplative virtue. Why on the commandments? Behold: “which I loved”; this was given to me through the Spirit.

**Verse 8 (48).—“And I lifted up my hands to your commandments, which I loved; and I shall exercise myself in your statutes.”**

And, by acting, I lifted up my hands to your commandments, [Augustine, Ambrose, Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, I showed by works what I taught. This is a most beautiful order: first meditate, then act. For through meditation upon heavenly commandments, the practice of good work [col. 1067C] is made gentle. Here the active virtue is indicated. He says, “I lifted up my hands,” because that toward which hands are lifted is above, when works are done for God himself; but when they are done for earthly things, the hands are lowered. Thus the hands of Moses are said to have been heavy, and Hur and Aaron supported them (Exodus 17), because [Note: Col. 1067D, from Gregory, Homily 33 on the Gospels] the end of legal works was the reward of temporal things. But Christ and the Holy Spirit turn them toward spiritual use.

“Which I loved.” [Augustine] Here again the same reason which was given above is repeated. He suitably adds “which I loved” to both, because “the end of the commandment is charity” (1 Timothy 1), when a commandment is performed with charity as its object; then the work is truly good. “And I shall exercise myself,” as though saying, “I shall meditate.” “I lifted up,” and “I shall exercise myself” by repeated practice, [Ambrose, Augustine] by turning them over with the disposition of an attentive mind, in your statutes [col. 1067D]—that is, in delight in both contemplation and action.

## Comparison in Vav

**Verse 7 (47).—“I meditated.”** *Eshtaʿashʿa*: that is, “I shall delight.” Yet this strongly encourages diligent exercise.

**Verse 8 (48).—“I shall exercise myself.”** Some say “I shall speak,” others “I shall meditate.” For *sôḥâ* means to meditate, pray, or speak; these agree in one meaning. Very many expressions of this kind suggest agreement of sense to the devout and fair-minded reader, although the wording differs slightly.

## Zain

**“Remember.”** [Cassiodorus] In this seventh letter he treats of hope in God’s promises, which causes all things to be endured peacefully. Through it the human mind is raised from visible and temporal things to invisible and future goods, where true rest exists. [Note: Col. 1067D, from Ambrose here and from *On the Death of Theodosius*.] This octonary is therefore rightly placed seventh. For the number seven signifies rest because of the Sabbath, on which the Lord rested. Hence also the seventh day is observed for the dead, because true rest is then desired and prayed for them; and because hope concerns not present things but future things. Therefore the letter *Zain*, interpreted “hither” or “lead yourself,” appropriately heads this octonary, because it treats of hope, which is not concerned with present things but tends toward the future. As though saying: “Tend hither; direct your path hither, as though you were your own guide and ruler,” whither the word of God calls you—namely, to grace and eternity—when it says: “Come to me, all who labor [col. 1068B] and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11). Hastening, therefore, to enter that rest (Hebrews 4), he asks for it, saying:

**Verse 1 (49).—“Remember your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope.”**

Remember your word. [Ambrose, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Ambrose] As though saying: “This is why I act thus and thus: because, as God promises, I hope for eternal things and for help in tribulation. And you, O Lord, remember your word, made to your servant”—that is, your promise, by which you often call me to yourself, you who never deceive.

[Note: Col. 1068D, from Ambrose on the following verse.] Note that by a moral and customary manner of speaking, intended to move human feeling, he says, “Remember.” Forgetfulness does not befall God. But just as God is said to repent when, without any change in counsel, he changes events beyond human expectation, so he is said to forget when he delays and to remember when he gives quickly. Yet God does this by a sure dispensation, not through failing memory, obscure understanding, or a changed will. The sense is: “Remember your word,” that is, quickly grant what you promised to your servant, whose eyes are in his master’s hand. He modestly shows himself worthy, as though saying: “I do not hope and ask presumptuously. I am a servant; I await food from my Lord. I am a soldier; I demand pay from my emperor.” “In which,” namely in the word of promise, “you gave me hope.” You who promised made me hope for eternal things and despise present things.

Note that in this octonary the sevenfold purpose of the holy man is distinguished. The first purpose of the holy man is reward: that he may remember the promise according to which recompense is due to one living faithfully. The second is that he may console himself with hope even amid adversities. Of this he next adds:

**Verse 2 (50).—“This has comforted me in my humiliation, because your word has given me life.”**

This hope, [Augustine] which befits the humble and came to me through your word, has comforted me in my humiliation. By “humiliation” he means that which a person makes for himself by confessing sins and not arrogating righteousness to himself. Or he also means some tribulation or weakening endured from the devil, deserved through one’s pride, or in which patience is exercised and proved. Or by “humiliation” he means being cast down into death for Adam’s sin, committed most unhappily amid the happiness of paradise. Hope has comforted me because your word has given me life. [Cassiodorus, Ambrose, Cassiodorus] The promise of so great a Judge strengthens the mind and gives life to the afflicted. For in time of temptation one lives by God’s word, by which eternal things are promised. Whoever hopes for better things is never broken by lesser things. Our soul is humbled when it is handed over to the tempter to be tested by hard labors, struggling and fighting as it experiences an encounter with an opposing power; but in these temptations it is given life by God’s utterance. For this is the life-giving substance of our soul: by it the soul is nourished, fed, and governed. Therefore, just as God’s word [col. 1069B] increases in the soul as it is received, understood, and comprehended, so its life also increases. Hence in the Lord’s Prayer we ask: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke 2). Moses was sustained by this bread during the forty days in which he remained with the Lord on the mountain to receive the law (Exodus 24). He then continues concerning the humiliation in which hope comforted him, adding:

**Verse 3 (51).—“The proud acted wickedly exceedingly; but I did not turn aside from your law.”**

The proud, [Augustine, Ambrose] that is, persecutors whom even this mortality has not subdued, acted wickedly exceedingly, or very greatly. Great is the force of evil in the proud. It is not enough for them that they are ungodly; they also make others ungodly. They therefore acted wickedly very greatly, because they were not only ungodly but also compelled the godly, through persecution, to become ungodly. Pride is the greatest human sin, because from it flowed the origin of our transgression. With this weapon the devil first wounded and struck us. For unless the human being, deceived by the serpent’s persuasion, had wished to be like God and, not content with his own bounds, rashly violated what was forbidden, the deadly inheritance of guilt would never have passed to us.

Indeed, the devil himself fell through this sin. When he says, “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14), he fell from angelic fellowship. Condemned with the deserving penalty for this crime, he sought a human being as his companion, into whom he might transfer participation in his own offense. Nothing can therefore be worse than this sin. For pride began from an injury done to God; it inhabits minds lofty by celestial origin, hiding beneath ashes and sackcloth. Against it the Lord especially fought, girded with the strength of humility. “But from your law”—as though saying: “The proud pressed upon me thus, but in vain,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Ambrose] “because I did not turn aside from your law,” as the proud compelled me to do. God’s law is the remedy of the Church, so that the prosperity of the proud need not concern us and the overthrow of the saints is not to be feared. God’s law alone, therefore, can avoid the poison of pride. Here the holy man’s third purpose is indicated: if he sees the ungodly prosper, he does not therefore turn aside from the law, but avoids their contagion.

[col. 1070A] **Verse 4 (52).—“I remembered your judgments from of old, O Lord, and was comforted.”**

I remembered. [Ambrose, Augustine, Cassiodorus] As though saying: “I did not turn aside from the law, but I remembered, O Lord, your judgments, which are always true, which you also exercised upon vessels of wrath.” It is useful to retain these in memory, because fear of punishments recalls one from evils. I say, existing “from of old,” that is, from the time humankind began, from the time the world began to be governed; this is fitting for the universal righteous person to say. I remembered your judgments, which you inflict upon vessels of wrath, and was comforted, because through these also you show the riches of glory in vessels of mercy: for I have never seen the righteous forsaken.

Or thus: “I remembered your judgments which were from of old,” that is, which began from the Lord with the first righteous person, and I was comforted. [col. 1070B] [Ambrose, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Ambrose] Or, as other manuscripts read: “I was exhorted,” that is, I received exhortation, understanding that he chastises those whom he loves. Here the fourth purpose is noted: that he remembers the heavenly judgments, which, because they have been true in every age from Adam onward, comfort him; otherwise he would turn aside from the law. Evil persons fear human judgments, not to mention divine ones; but good persons desire them.

**Verse 5 (53).—“Faintness seized me because of sinners who forsake your law.”**

Faintness. [Augustine, Ambrose] As though saying: “I was comforted in myself, but faintness”—or “weariness,” according to another reading—“seized me because of sinners who forsake your law.” For he is weary because he lives among them until the threshing-floor is winnowed. Or weariness and faintness come upon him because of sinners’ transgressions, because the guilt of tyrants weighs more heavily upon the holy man than his own punishment; he faints from grief for them—so great is the power of compassion. Here the fifth purpose is indicated: to grieve over another’s fault, not one’s own injury; indeed, to pray even for them.

**Verse 6 (54).—“Your statutes were songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage.”**

Songs. [Ambrose, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] As though saying: “Faintness seized me; yet, although this is so, your statutes were songs to me,” and so forth. Or connect it thus: “All the foregoing things are mine because your statutes were songs to me,” as I continually considered them without care for or love of earthly things. And this was through the mercy of the healing Samaritan, [col. 1070D] who cared for the man wounded by robbers (Luke 10). Therefore he fittingly says “songs,” because song lightens labors and removes weariness. Thus, specifying where they are songs, he says: “in the place of my pilgrimage,” that is, in this miserable life, called a place of pilgrimage because man was cast out of paradise, where he had been endowed with royal honor, into these miseries, to lament the punishment of his wickedness. This is the humiliation of which he spoke above.

[Ambrose, Augustine] Here the sixth purpose is noted: that God’s statutes are songs to him. These two verses may also be fitted to the respective parts of a single preceding verse: to “I remembered your judgments” may be referred “weariness,” or “faintness, seized me”; while to “I was comforted” may be referred “your statutes were songs to me,” and so forth.

**Verse 7 (55).—“I remembered your name in the night, O Lord, and kept your law.”**
I remembered your name, O Lord. [Augustine, Ambrose.] So that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10). And this even in the night. “Night” denotes mortality and misery, the wrongdoing of the proud, the weariness of sins, and the place of pilgrimage. Therefore I remembered your name in the night—that is, in the present affliction, whatever its source—where thanks are to be given more than in prosperity, and where one must cling more closely to God. For it is no great thing to do this in prosperity. Or: “I remembered in the night,” literally—not only in the day—[Col. 1071B] and this is the seventh purpose of the holy man: that he attends to the praises of God not only by day but also by night, that is, at every time; and this all must do. For Judas betrayed the Lord at night, and Peter denied him (Matt. 26). At that time, therefore, prayer must be pursued more earnestly. Moreover, I remembered because it is from God that I also kept your law; otherwise I would not have remembered. Or the connection may be made thus: [Augustine] I remembered, and so I kept your law—which he would not have kept had he trusted in his own strength.

### VERSE 8 (56)

> “This came to pass for me, because I sought out your ordinances.”

“This came to pass for me.” [Augustine.] It is ambiguous whether this is said of “this law” or “this night,” since both have preceded; but the Greek idiom from which this was translated [Col. 1071C] sufficiently indicates that it was not said of the law. “This came to pass for me.” For among the Greeks this pronoun is feminine:

> [Note: [Col. 1071D] Αὕτη νόμος νύξ.]  
> “This”: law, night.

Among them “law” is masculine in gender; and thus it is clear that the text does not say “this law,” but “this night”: this is the night in which the beasts of the forest come forth and seek their food from God, in which Satan asked to sift the apostles like wheat. This night can not improperly be understood as the humiliation of this mortality and pilgrimage, where human hearts are hidden from one another, and where innumerable and grave temptations arise.

And the sense is: deservedly I remembered and kept your law, because this night, in which many temptations arise, came to pass for me—that is, for my benefit—so that I might profit, and thus learn not to be proud, through which vice man fell [Col. 1071D] into this night. Hence he later says: “It is good for me that you humbled me, that I may learn your ordinances.” But why so? Because I sought out your ordinances, not my own. “I was justified freely by grace” (Rom. 3).

Or the pronoun *haec* (“this”) may be understood as though *hoc* (“this”) had been said, so that there too the feminine may be taken for the neuter, where it says: “One thing I have asked of the Lord” (Ps. 26), though this is more commonly expressed in the neuter. Thus here also it could be said in that manner, “This came to pass for me,” as though it had said, “This thing came to pass for me.” And the sense is: that which I said above—namely, that I remembered and kept your law—came to pass for me; that is, I did not keep the law through myself, [Col. 1072A] but it was brought about for me by you, because I sought out your ordinances, not my own.

## Comparison in Zain

### VERSE 3 (51)

“Iniquitously they acted.” *Helitzuni*: that is, “they mocked me.” This is a Hebrew word from the same root as the term for scoffers in Hebrew and in the first verse of the first Psalm, concerning which something was said above. But according to Kimhi it also means “to devise cunningly” and “to behave insolently toward one’s neighbor.” Hence the Chaldee: “they slandered me.”

### VERSE 8 (56)

“This came to pass for me.” Faber and Caecus do not wish *haec facta est* to be said in the feminine gender, for they argue that the expression is absurd unless one supplies something from outside—namely, “this remembrance,” or something similar—when nothing has preceded to which it can be referred. Therefore, with Jerome, one must say: “This thing came to pass for me.” Certainly in Hebrew the word is most plainly feminine in gender: *zoth*, “this” or “that,” even though [Col. 1072B] it is sometimes used for the neuter, and some translate it “this way,” others “that way.” Moreover, in Greek it is feminine, *αὕτη*.

And you were asking to what “this came to pass” should be referred. I am surprised that Faber did not notice the verse immediately preceding: “I remembered your name in the night, and I kept your law.” That Caecus did not see it is tolerable. Yet we cannot refer it to the law, as St Augustine testifies; for the Greeks would object, since they use *nomon* in the masculine. But, as the same authority indicates, it will refer to the night, so that the meaning is: “This night came to pass for me,” that is, it benefited me. Or the feminine stands for the neuter, according to the manner of speech in Psalm 26: “One thing I have asked of the Lord,” as is explained more fully in the exposition. But St Ambrose also has: “this remembrance.”

## HETH

“My portion, O Lord.” [Cassiodorus, Ambrose, Alcuin.] In this eighth letter he desires to see the face of the Lord, because he has obeyed his commandments. And since he diligently strives to obtain what he desires [Col. 1072C] to possess, the letter *heth*, which is interpreted “fear,” is fittingly prefixed. It is understood as the fear of falling back, but also as the solicitude of acquiring that good for which he hopes; and because this will be granted in the eighth, resurrection, this group of eight is set here. As if to say: “I sought out your ordinances, because I—”

### VERSE 1 (57)

> “My portion, O Lord, I have said, is to keep your law.”

O Lord, you are my portion. [Ambrose, Augustine.] “Portion” is derived from “part”; hence some books read, “My part, O Lord.” As if to say: Others choose this or that from which to live; but my portion, or part, is God, from whom I shall live forever without end. How far removed from vices, how set apart from every stain of sin, [Col. 1072D] how rare upon earth is the person who can say this! He loves nothing of the world or of vice. He says this as Levi, to whom no lot is given among his brothers: in him there is no desire for bodily portions; lust does not inflame him, avarice does not prick him, wantonness does not effeminate him, luxury does not discolor him, ambition does not cast him down, envy does not waste him away, nor does any care of secular affairs make him anxious.

And he is truly a *levi*, that is, “one taken up,” that he may be an advocate for me and an intercessor with God. Such was he who said: “Silver and gold I do not possess, but what I have I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk” (Acts 3).

Or this may be understood of the present: “My portion, O Lord,” [Col. 1073A] that is, I share in him by adhering through faith, hope, and charity. Hence: “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Ps. 72). For human beings do not become gods by existing by nature, but by participating in the one who is true God. Thus he is my portion, because I said, “to keep.” Or the connection may be made thus: Because he is my part, I have said that I would keep your law; but I do not keep it unless the Spirit helps me, while the letter kills.

### VERSE 2 (58)

> “I entreated your face with my whole heart; have mercy on me according to your word.”

I entreated in my heart to see your face, [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Gloss interlinear] that is, Christ, whom he desired to behold; and he prays that the mercy of the first coming may be fulfilled, as promised through the prophets, so that the grace of the Gospel may abound, where faith obtains what the law commands. Thus I prayed: “Have mercy on me according to your word,” that is, according to your promise, of which I am a son. And, as though heard and helped, he adds:

### VERSE 3 (59)

> “I considered my ways, and turned my feet toward your testimonies.”

“I considered my ways,” [Ambrose, Augustine] my former evil ways; or I thought beforehand about future ways, namely what ought to be done, and how, and what ought not to be done. Hence follows: “I was ready.” And I turned my feet from my own ways, which were evil, toward your testimonies, which do not allow one to go astray. Then, having obtained this benefit of grace:

### VERSE 4 (60)

> “I am ready and have not been troubled, to keep your commandments.”

“I am ready, to keep your commandments,” [Cassiodorus] that is, I resolved to suffer for the sake of keeping your commandments. And therefore I have not been troubled. Unforeseen things disturb; the person who does not fear adversities keeps them fully. And I am so ready that:

### VERSE 5 (61)

> “The cords of sinners have encircled me; and I have not forgotten your law.”

“The cords of sinners,” [Augustine] that is, the hindrances of carnal or spiritual enemies, “have encircled me”—I who with the flesh serve the law of sin, but with the mind the law of God. Sins are like a long rope, which those who wish to entangle the saints draw along; but they cannot entangle those [Col. 1073D] who have not forgotten the law. Hence this man adds: “And I have not forgotten your law.” I say, I have not forgotten it, but:

### VERSE 6 (62)

> “At midnight I rose to confess to you concerning the judgments of your righteousness.”

“At midnight,” [Augustine, Ambrose, Augustine] that is, in the heavier tribulation I was not cast down, but rose more strongly to confess to you. Thanks must be given to God for all that happens to us, and thus the Lord can be held fast. “To confess,” I say, “concerning the judgments of your righteousness”: that is, I shall confess to you, knowing that even the fact that the cords encircle me is by the just judgment of God, which begins with his household.

But because the foregoing good things are done by God’s grace through Jesus Christ, the voice of the Savior himself is here joined to his members. For what follows belongs properly to the Head:

### VERSE 7 (63)

> “I am a partaker with all who fear you and keep your commandments.”

“I,” [Augustine] namely Christ, “am a partaker,” through human nature and divine grace, “with all,” etc. He says this in the sense in which the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one; therefore he is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Heb. 2). And he himself shared in the same things. For we would not be partakers of his divinity unless he had become a partaker of our mortality. Through this participation of his, grace is given to us, that we may fear chastely and keep your commandments. Hence follows: “of those who fear you” in heart, “and keep” in deed “your commandments.” And the sense is: [Col. 1074B] [Ambrose, Augustine] I am a partaker with all, in order that through this they may fear and keep—two things fittingly joined, because one who fears keeps. And because, through becoming a partaker with his brothers, the grain of wheat bore much fruit (John 12), he adds concerning that fruit:

### VERSE 8 (64)

> “Your mercy, O Lord, fills the earth; teach me your ordinances.”

“Your mercy, O Lord, fills the earth,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus] because the ungodly person is justified. In order that one may advance in the knowledge of this grace, he adds: “Teach me your ordinances”; because the earth is full of grace and mercy, teach me your ordinances.

[Cassiodorus.] Alternatively, from the words “I entreated”: he speaks of the second coming, when he desires to see Christ in majesty [Col. 1074C]. As if to say: Because you are my portion, O Lord, therefore I entreated in my heart to see your face, that is, the majesty of divinity. He asks to see this face not here, but in the future resurrection. Thus the Lord says to Moses: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). But because this man is a sinner, he asks that by mercy he may have what he cannot have by merits. Hence he adds: “Have mercy on me according to your word,” by which you promise the saints the vision of divinity; and you ought to have mercy, because “I considered,” etc.

Or the connection may be made thus: “I said, to keep your law.” Therefore I considered my ways—that is, what my ways were—and, having seen, I turned my feet toward your testimonies. This is the order of conversion. “I am ready and have not been [Col. 1074D] troubled, to keep your commandments”: this does not change. I have not been troubled, even though the cords of sinners encircled me. The snares are as numerous as sins. These encircle us according to the body, by which we serve the law of sin, if the resisting mind does not forget the law. Hence he adds: “And I have not only not forgotten your law, but at midnight I rose.”

[Ambrose, Cassiodorus.] The day alone is not enough for preaching; indeed one must also pray in the night, lest one be caught sluggish in sleep. For then the enticement of the flesh burns; then the tempter deceives; and the Lord himself spent the night in prayer (Luke 6), that by his own example he might invite you to pray. Then the tempter spreads or casts nets by which he may trouble an unwary mind. Then spiritual wickednesses strive to urge every crime [Col. 1075A] when there is no judge of the fault, no one conscious of the crime, no one who can be a witness of the error. Then they instill diverse dissensions in the sinner who is asleep. Therefore care must be taken that, at the time when you can conquer, you do not lose the time for conquering.

Rise, then, to proclaim God at the hour when the tempter is accustomed to attack, when the heavenly remedy is accustomed to come against grave temptations: namely, at midnight, when the firstborn of Egypt were struck down (Exod. 12), and when the bridegroom will come. Therefore rise then, lest you remain among the foolish virgins (Matt. 25). “To confess,” as if to say: I rose for this purpose, certainly to confess to you concerning the judgments of your righteousness, [Haymo, Gloss interlinear, Ambrose, Cassiodorus] that is, to praise you [Col. 1075B] for the judgments of your righteousness, by which you chastise the sons whom you receive.

Or thus: I rose to confess, I say, longing for that good which is above the judgments of your righteousness—that is, which the chastisements by which you justify cannot merit. And, to summarize the foregoing briefly: “I am a partaker with all.” Or the connection may be made thus: Though I am such a one, I do not become proud, but “I am a partaker with all.” For a member shares in the whole body. Thus the Lord is his portion in such a way that he is a partaker not of one church but of all churches. Such is the power of unity, since he is a partaker of Christ. He humbly calls himself a partaker with the servants; this is also to be a partaker of Christ. Hence the Apostle: “We have become partakers of Christ” (Heb. 3).

“Of those who fear [Col. 1075C] you.” [Ambrose, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus, Ambrose.] Behold, he humbly places himself among the unlearned.
