For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; yet they are not idle: “and who keep your commandments.” And this whole thing is your mercy, as is everything, because, O Lord, the earth is full of your righteousness, both spiritual and temporal: for he has spread faith everywhere and “makes his sun rise upon good and evil” (Matt. 6). And because I am a partaker, and every good is from you, therefore “teach me your ordinances.” He has already said that he kept them, yet here also he asks to be taught more, because they must always be sought for growth. There is never satiety in a good thing. He says “teach,” moreover, because there is no other who teaches. For he alone is the teacher, as he himself says: “One is your teacher” (Matt. 23).

[Col. 1075D] ## Comparison in Heth

### VERSE 4 (60)

“Ready and not troubled.” Jerome and the Nebiensis have: “I hastened and did not neglect.” The others: “I hastened and did not delay,” or “I was not slow.” As to the sense, they differ little. For one who is ready hastens eagerly and promptly carries everything out, neglecting nothing, without any disturbance. In Hebrew it is *hashti velo hithmāhmāhti*. Perhaps the last word was read literally as *hithhamāhti*, “I was troubled,” from the root *hamah*.

### VERSE 5 (61)

“Cords.” Jerome, Campensis, the interpreters for Cajetan, Pellicanus likewise, Pratensis, Sanctes, the Chaldee, Nebiensis, and Münster translate “assemblies” or “bands.” For *hebel* is an ambiguous word.

## TETH

“You have shown goodness.” [Ambrose, Cassiodorus.] In this ninth letter he gives thanks to God for his humiliation and patience, through which he came to righteousness. And because it is good to be humbled and to have patience, and because patience brings gladness even in tribulations, the letter *teth* is fittingly set over this group of eight, [Note: [Col. 1075D] Jerome, to Paula of Rome.] which is interpreted “good” or “exclusion,” because here he treats of patience, which excludes sadness at adversities and makes suffering good and joyful. [Ambrose, Alcuin.] Martyrs who truly serve Christ, fearing neither persecutions, swords, nor fires, even offered themselves to hostile kings and excluded the disposition of impatience. As if to say: Teach me your ordinances, because already—

### VERSE 1 (65)

> “You have shown goodness to your servant, O Lord, according to your word.”

You have shown, O Lord, goodness, or gladness, or sweetness, to your servant. [Augustine.] That is, you have caused good to delight, by making a son of one who had been a servant. It is a great gift of God that a good work is done not out of fear of punishment but out of love for righteousness—not slavishly but freely. For the servant, what he formerly was, does not remain in the house forever; the son remains, which he now is (John 8). From a servant he has been made a son.

[Gloss interlinear, Augustine.] Or “servant” may also be understood in its present sense: humble, not proud. And the sense “You have shown goodness” does not change. “To your servant,” which I now am: you previously dealt lovingly with the freedman, when a human being, wishing to emancipate himself from God’s service, [Col. 1076C] became his own master and acquired an evil liberty. For there is a good and an evil liberty, just as there is a good and an evil servitude. You did this, I say, “according to your word,” that is, according to your promise, which according to faith is secure for all the seed.

Then he asks that what he confesses he has received may be increased and perfected, saying:

### VERSE 2 (66)

> “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, because I have believed your commandments.”

“Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge.” [Augustine.] He who has already said, “You have shown goodness,” how does he say, “Teach me goodness,” unless that God’s grace may be increased in him more and more? He teaches this when he inspires charity, so that one may work not from fear [Col. 1076D] but from love, and may find delight in goodness. And the sense is: Teach me goodness, that is, inspire charity; teach me discipline, that is, grant patience, so that, by the sweetness of goodness being from God, I may endure any sufferings through love of God and neighbor; and teach me knowledge, that is, enlighten my mind.

For when charity is so great that it cannot be extinguished by tribulation, then knowledge—which previously puffed up—is useful: by it a person comes to know himself, because he knows what he deserved and what he received, and what he can do—or cannot do. Note that he says “teach.” Teaching is one thing, saying another. There is no teaching or saying where no one learns, unless he is taught. Therefore, if a pupil does not grasp what he hears, the teacher cannot say, “I taught him,” but “I spoke to him.” And so, when God wishes to teach, [Col. 1077A] he first gives understanding, without which no one would learn. Hence it is said: “He opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24).

Therefore he teaches goodness by inspiring love. For this is not taught unless it is given. He teaches discipline by regulating corrective tribulation, which is not learned by hearing, reading, or reflection, but teaches through experience. He teaches knowledge by instilling cognition; for this is given by teaching. For what else is teaching but giving knowledge? God teaches both to know what ought to be known, by inspiring truth, and to do what ought to be done, by inspiring sweetness. Thus he teaches us to do the latter and to know the former. Therefore he teaches because “I have believed your commandments.” It might seem more fitting to have said, “I have obeyed your commandments.” For commandments are to be obeyed, because we have received commands to perform; promises are to be believed. [Col. 1077B] Yet he fittingly says, “I have believed your commandments”: namely, that you commanded them, not some human being, even though they were administered through a human being. And the sense is: May the faith by which I believed that these were your commandments obtain from you the grace by which I may perform what you command.

[Alcuin, Jerome, Ambrose, Alcuin, Ambrose.] Or thus: You have shown goodness; I say, teach me your ordinances. Which ordinances? I seek no others, but those which you have bestowed on others. For you have shown gladness to your servant, O Lord, namely to any other person whatever. As if to say: You have made others glad. And this “according to your word,” that is, through your Son. For nothing is truly glad except according to the Word of God. Many things in this age appear pleasant that are not greatly sweet, and that serve our use; but the same things can profit the dead in no way. And because you have made others glad, make me glad also, lest I grow weary.

And this is what he says: “Teach me goodness,” or gladness, “and discipline and knowledge”; deservedly, because I have believed your commandments. For one who believes the commandments can have knowledge of the things taught in the commandments. Behold: through faith one has knowledge, which is the true cognition of the things that are. Hence Solomon: “God gave me true knowledge of the things that are” (Wis. 7). Through knowledge discipline is truly taken up or received. For the way of life itself, in which we know that we can please God, delights us; this is discipline. Though it be bitter to the flesh, it ought to be pleasant to the mind, because the Lord is sweet, who says: “Take my yoke, because it is light, and my burden, because it is sweet” (Matt. 11). Through faith in the commandments their knowledge is received; through knowledge, discipline; through discipline, goodness and gladness come about. Therefore he referred this one point—“because I have believed your commandments”—to those three.

### VERSE 3 (67)

> “Before I was humbled, I transgressed; therefore I kept your word.”

“Before I was humbled.” [Gloss interlinear, Augustine, Ambrose.] As if to say: You have already shown goodness, and again I have said, “Teach me goodness.” For this purpose the humiliation of correction and discipline, which I seek, is useful; but before I was humbled, I transgressed in Adam, in whom every human being was corrupted as in a root and made subject to vanity. This is useful to experience, so that, pride having been cast down, [Col. 1078A] obedience may be loved and misery may perish, never to return. Hence he adds: “Therefore”—namely, lest I be humbled again—“I kept your word.” Behold, humiliation is correction. I say, I kept it, and:

### VERSE 4 (68)

> “You are good; and in your goodness teach me your ordinances.”

“You are good,” [Ambrose, Augustine, Ambrose] that is, sweet. He praises the Judge in order to obtain his request, saying: You are good—properly good in yourself and from yourself—and good because you give good gifts to those who ask you (Luke 11). “And in your goodness,” that is, in your sweetness, teach me your ordinances. He truly wishes to perform the ordinances when he wishes to learn them in God’s sweetness. Thus weak humanity does not wish to be judged by the harshness of the law, to have the severity of remedies applied, or to have the tissues of wounds cut by the knife; [Col. 1078B] rather, it wishes to be healed by God’s goodness, so that, even if sharper measures are needed, this may be done moderately and God may lessen the force of pain. An ordinance is a work of righteousness, by which we are better taught in the goodness of the Gospel than in the severity of the law. There is condemnation there; here, remission.

### VERSE 5 (69)

> “The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me; but I will search out your commandments with my whole heart.”

“It has been multiplied.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus.] As if to say: Teach me; and there is need, because struggle is present, in which I shall show in deed what I have learned. And this is the sense: The iniquity of the proud, whom your humiliation has not yet humbled, has been multiplied against me in force and number. Iniquity has been multiplied in me; yet charity does not grow cold, because I learned the ordinances in sweetness. And this is: “But I will search out,” or “I searched out,” your commandments as one who loves. For this purpose he searches them out: that he may perform what he knows, and by performing may know more perfectly, because they are known more perfectly when they are done. “I will search out,” I say, “with my whole heart,” so that I may cling to the commandments as much as those proud persons wish to seduce me. And further:

### VERSE 6 (70)

> “Their heart has curdled like milk; but I have meditated on your law.”

“The heart of those proud persons has curdled like milk,” [Ambrose, Augustine] that is, it has grown hard through the intrusion of vice. For milk is naturally beautiful and pure, but it curdles through corruption; so too the nature of the human heart and mind is pure and clear before it curdles through the admixture of vices. Therefore their heart has curdled through envy and pride, which have spoiled the purity of nature by the corruption of malice. But I—as if to say: They are thus; I, however, have meditated on your law. This he sets against their hardness, because meditation on the law is refreshment against their obstinacy. Therefore:

### VERSE 7 (71)

> “It is good for me that you humbled me, that I may learn your ordinances.”

“It is good for me that you humbled me,” [Ambrose, Augustine] because you turned punishment into instruction. Hence the Apostle: “I take pleasure in my weaknesses” (2 Cor. 12). And the sense is: You humbled me, that is, you exercised me through diverse temptations, that I might learn to perform your ordinances, [Col. 1079A] that is, works of righteousness. But because this does not happen except through love, where sweetness is present:

### VERSE 8 (72)

> “The law of your mouth is good for me, beyond thousands of gold and silver pieces.”

“It is good for me.” [Cassiodorus, Hilary, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Here he frequently repeats “good,” because it always grows sweeter. As if to say: Humiliation is good, because what is gained from it is good. The law of your mouth is also good. The law is the Gospel spoken by Christ’s mouth. It is good, I say, beyond thousands of gold and silver pieces. By “thousands” he means without limit, because goodness could find no comparable comparison. He placed this first and afterward added “gold and silver,” so that the comparison with gold and silver—things most prized by the covetous—might be made cheap. Therefore he says “beyond,” because charity loves the law [Col. 1079B] of God more than covetousness loves thousands of gold and silver pieces.

## Comparison in Teth

### VERSE 2 (66)

“Discipline.” Jerome and Sanctes translate “word”; Pratensis and Pellicanus, with us, “discipline”; the translator according to Campensis likewise. Münster has “taste,” though he intends this to be understood as right judgment. The interpreters for Cajetan say “intention.” Now *taam* in Hebrew means reason, counsel, utterance, argumentation, and the like.

### VERSE 3 (67)

“Before I was humbled.” *Terem ‘eneh*. Jerome translated: “before I heard.” Campensis agrees: “before I carefully listened to your commandments”; Nebiensis: “before I answered.” *‘Anah* is ambiguous.

### VERSE 5 (69)

“The iniquity has been multiplied against me.” Jerome and the others rendered: “They applied,” or “fashioned for me,” or “against me, falsehood.” *Taphal* means “he added” or “he applied.” But one who adds multiplies, so that the versions do not differ in this point. Finally, every iniquity is a kind of falsehood, vanity, and lie; this is *sheqer*.

### VERSE 6 (70)

“Like milk.” Jerome: “like fat.” *Heleb* is fat, but *halab* is milk. The sense does not change.

## JOD

“Your hands.” [Cassiodorus, Ambrose, Alcuin.] In this tenth letter he asks that understanding of God’s commandments be given to him, so that he may enjoy the true life. Since no one can possess this unless he confesses sins—which happens especially in adversities—the letter *jod*, interpreted “confession” or “desolation,” is therefore prefixed; and it is fitting. Those who are desolate in adversities confess more readily. [Col. 1079D] For in favorable circumstances a person is usually exalted. When pressed by adversities, one then calls upon divine help; when prosperity first succeeds, the mind grows more proud.

> [Note: [Col. 1079D] The beginning of Jod from Jerome, *To Paula of Rome*.]

*Jod* is also interpreted “knowledge” or “beginning,” and for this reason it is rightly prefixed to this group of eight as well: here a person is taught to have been created impassible and immortal, and in the fullness of knowledge—a state to which the good person desires to return and whose beginning in this life is understanding. As if to say: Your law is good to me beyond thousands; and deservedly, because:

### VERSE 1 (73)

> “Your hands made me and formed me; give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments.”

[Col. 1080A] “Your hands made me,” [Augustine, Ambrose] according to the soul in your image and likeness; “and formed me,” or “prepared me,” or “fashioned me,” according to the body, according to which he made all people in Adam. Or he makes all in the generation of each individual. The hands of God are understood as the power of operation; or, since he says “your hands” in the plural, they are understood as power and wisdom, both of which are Christ. Or the hands of God the Father are the Son and the Holy Spirit, who work together. Thus this is not contrary to what is said in the Gospel concerning the Word of God: “All things were made through him” (John 1). For the Word of God and the hand of God are the same.

It should be noted that he has employed an opening of great commendation when he calls himself God’s work, yet mentions both his own natures, so that the Author’s favor might more readily be inclined toward the grace of his work, [Col. 1080B] and the great prerogative of humanity might also be shown. For the human being is a precious work of God. Of the other works, it is written: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 148); but he formed the human being with his hands, as though working more attentively in the creation of humanity. Concerning this creation he deliberates, as it were, beforehand, and a special counsel precedes its making: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). It is as if God labors here, so that careful workmanship may be recognized in this.

Finally, such is the dignity of humanity that the human being—not an angel—is read to sit at the right hand of God, and that the human being is honored by angels. He is the only-begotten Son of God, who is the image of God, begotten and not created according to his deity. [Col. 1080C] Insofar as he is human, he was created in the image of God; but according to the nature of deity, he is a begotten image. The human being, however, is not so: he is only made in the image, possessing something of the image according to the immaterial element. But insofar as he was formed, he is from the material of dust.

Learn, therefore, O human being, in what respect you are great and precious. The earth shows you to be lowly, but divine power shows you glorious; the image makes you precious. For what is so precious as the image of God? While you retain it, you are rightly called a human being and do not lose the name “human”; but when, neglecting it, you fall into vices, Scripture is accustomed to call you not a human being but a serpent, fox, beast of burden, or the like. Hence: “Do not become like horse and mule” (Ps. 31). And concerning Herod it says: “Tell that fox” (Luke 13). Therefore [Col. 1080D] Ezekiel uses the doubled designation: “O man, man” (Ezek. 14), so that one who outwardly has the form of a human being may inwardly preserve God’s image.

For God vindicates his image upon one who has wronged that image, so that through malice the human being may cease to be what he was and become, from a human being, a mule. For after you sinned, you began to be something else; you ceased to be what you had been. Stripped of the adornment of the heavenly image, you also lose the name of human being, since you do not retain the grace of humanity. You are a great work of God, O human being; great is what God gave you. Here he recalls this human dignity, saying: “Your hands made me [Col. 1081A] and formed me.”

[Gloss interlinear, Augustine, Gloss interlinear, Cassiodorus.] As if to say: Let your work move you, a work distinguished in the human being by the recalled dignity of its origin. He asks that understanding, darkened by sin, be restored, saying: “Give me understanding.” I ask it from no one but you: you who made me, remake me. Give me pure understanding. For although all possess by nature a pure understanding, by which a human being is distinguished from cattle, yet it has been deformed by sinning and is renewed daily. Hence the Apostle: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. 4).

[Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine.] Therefore he asks that understanding be given him so that the inner eyes may be made clearer. This happens through faith, by which hearts are purified. For although no one can believe in God unless he understands something, since faith comes from hearing the preaching [Col. 1081B] (Rom. 10), nevertheless through faith one is healed so as to understand greater things. Some things we do not believe unless we understand them; other things we do not understand unless we believe them. Therefore he adds: “that I may learn.” Give me understanding so that I may learn your commandments. If I cannot see the deity, let me at least learn the commandments.

See how profoundly the commandments are to be understood, for which this man asks understanding, though he has already kept them, and is not wholly without that understanding while asking it from God. For he alone gives understanding, even if at times through the ministry of an angel, as he gave it to Daniel, to whom the angel said: “I have come to give you understanding” (Dan. 2). Yet God himself, who is light, illuminates devout minds, even if he sometimes uses an angel’s ministry. For an angel is said to give a human being understanding in the same way that someone is said to give light to a house by making it a window, although he does not penetrate and illuminate it with his own light.

### VERSE 2 (74)

> “Those who fear you shall see me and rejoice, because I have hoped exceedingly in your words.”

Who fear thee. [Ambrose, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Ambrose.] As though he said: Grant understanding; for, if thou grant it, all who fear thee will see me—not merely outwardly here, but inwardly, and especially in the world to come—and all who fear thee will rejoice. They rejoice if what one person asks is granted; and the merciful God willingly does what delights all. Therefore those who fear see the righteous man and rejoice. To others the righteous man is hateful and burdensome to behold, as is read in the Gospel concerning the many who could not see the Lord, while others also denied him passage [Col. 1081D] (Luke VIII). Therefore he says that those who fear God see him and rejoice.

There is great power in the eyes, as is evident in natural things. The sight of an animal is beneficial to one suffering from jaundice; a wolf which sees first takes away one’s voice; the basilisk, if it sees first, kills, but if it is seen first, is killed. Why, then, should there not be power in the eyes of the righteous man who is seen with faith? Since he is the image of God, he is honoured by men; the rays of his eyes seem indeed to infuse a certain power into those who faithfully desire to see him. For it is natural to good persons to love their virtues in others. Thus the sight of the righteous is a joy to the more perfect, but to most it is an admonition to correction.

But how ought one to see the righteous man? Not in his body, not in his clothing, nor in his face alone, but inwardly. For one does not see him [Col. 1082A] unless one sees his mind and attends to his speech. Then one will rejoice when one has understood these things. [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine.] Note that he used *fear*, a verb in the present tense, but *will see* and *will rejoice* in the future tense, because in the present there is fear where temptation exists; whereas rejoicing and seeing will be perfect in the future. They will rejoice because I have hoped beyond hope in thy words—that is, in what thou hast promised—that I may be a son of promise. Note that he did not say simply, “I have hoped,” but “I have hoped beyond hope,” because God can do beyond what is understood. It is too little to hope for what we understand or ask; rather, we ought always to hope.

Or this may be understood of the angels: “Those who fear thee will see me and rejoice, because I have hoped beyond hope in thy words.” For angels [Col. 1082B] rejoice over men if they hope in the words of God. But the Church, considering that it still fears amid the misery of this life, and that the flesh desires against the spirit, says:

**VERSE 3 (75).—“I have known, O Lord, that thy judgments are equity, and in thy truth thou hast humbled me.”**

I have known, O Lord. [Haymo, Cassiodorus.] As though he said: Therefore grant understanding, because I have now known, O Lord, that thy judgments are equity—that is, that the punishment of Adam is just. For it is the highest equity that those who sin through pride should be purified by humility. Hence he adds: “And in thy truth,” that is, by thy just judgment, “thou hast humbled me” unto death; but now:

**VERSE 4 (76).—“Let thy mercy come to console me, according to thy word unto thy servant.”**

[Col. 1082C] Let thy mercy come, etc. [Augustine, Ambrose and Augustine, Ambrose.] First truth humbled unto death; then mercy restores unto life, God having promised this. This mercy is regeneration, faith, hope, and charity, which come from God’s mercy. These are consolations in this misery, not the joys of the blessed: “to console me.” He does not ask that the troubles which serve purification be removed, but that he be consoled. Let it come, I say, according to thy word given to thy servant—that is, according to what thou hast promised thy servant.

Or thus: “I have known, O Lord.” As though he said: Therefore understanding is needed, because by the understanding given I have known, O Lord, that thy judgments are equity in all that happens, even when thou scourgest thy children, because rewards are given through labours. [Col. 1082D] Note that he says, “I have known,” not “I have believed.” For believing is one thing and recognizing another: faith belongs to one who fears; recognition to the wise. The person who fears does not seek a reason. Where faith is, knowledge is not immediately present; where knowledge is, faith goes before. Thus this man knew perfectly enough to be humbled in truth, for to be humbled is unto salvation. For he knew that prosperity and adversity are given for testing. Hence he adds: “And in thy truth.” As though he said: I have known, and therefore thou hast humbled me in thy truth, that I may bear prosperity or adversity well. The self-exalted person does not see true judgments; but now let thy mercy come to thy servant. The sense is unchanged, but the order of the words is: “That it may console me.” For amid labour the perfect man asks not for the end of labour, but for the word of consolation, that he may endure well. Let it come, I say, according to thy word [Col. 1083A]—that is, as thou hast promised. But after these things, and through them:

**VERSE 5 (77).—“Let thy compassions come unto me, and I shall live; for thy law is my meditation.”**

Let thy compassions come unto me, [Augustine] in the future, and through them I shall truly live. He expresses what is given through mercy, namely eternal life, which alone is life without qualification. On what merit? Because thy law is my meditation. This meditation is the thought of one who loves: he thinks in order to work through love and not grow cold through the iniquity of the proud. This meditation, then, is in the faith which works through love (Galatians V).

**VERSE 6 (78).—“Let the proud be confounded, because unjustly they have committed iniquity against me; but I will be exercised in thy commandments.”**

[Col. 1083B] Let the proud be confounded. [Ambrose, Cassiodorus.] As though he said: Let thy compassions come to me, but let the proud be confounded—that is, let them be ashamed—because they have committed iniquity unjustly, that is, without judgment. But I will be exercised, or “was exercised,” in thy commandments, that I may do good even to my enemies. This is the remedy against enemies who rage. Behold what he said above: “Thy law is my meditation.”

**VERSE 7 (79).—“Let those who fear thee turn unto me, and those who have known thy testimonies.”**

Let them turn. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] This is properly spoken by our Head, that is, Christ; for he is the one to whom those who fear turn. As though he said: Let the proud be confounded; but let those who fear thee—that is, those beginning to turn—turn unto me; and let those who have known, those whom reading [Col. 1083C] has already imbued, although not yet action, thy testimonies concerning Christ, foretold through the prophets and displayed in him through miracles.

**VERSE 8 (80).—“Let my heart be undefiled in thy justifications, that I may not be confounded.”**

Let my heart be undefiled. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] After all this he does not dare to say that he is undefiled, but asks to be made so. Here the righteous man speaks. As though he said: Let mercy come and let me live; and, that I may obtain this, let my heart be undefiled—not by my own powers, but in thy justifications. For regeneration having been given, confession joined to it, and prayer poured forth, let this come to pass. Let it be so undefiled that I may not be confounded. As though he said: Let the proud be confounded for correction; but I not [Col. 1083D] for punishment.

*(In Iod we have found nothing of importance requiring annotation.)*

**CAPH** [Note: [Col. 1083] According to Jerome, *Caph* means “hand.”]

**My soul hath failed for thy salvation.** [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Ambrose, Alcuin.] In this eleventh letter the pilgrim of this world first ardently desires the Lord’s advent, according to the ancient Fathers; secondly, with reference to modern people, he declares how much he has endured from the proud during this expectation, while desiring to persevere in God’s commandments. Since in this expectation he has grown weary through the delay of his desire, the letter *caph*, meaning “bent,” is placed before this octonary: weary from a long campaign, he longs to be dissolved and return to the beginning [Col. 1084A] which he mentioned a little earlier. Yet he does not refuse labour if it is necessary to remain in the flesh. As though he said: “Let thy compassions come unto me, and I shall live,” because:

**VERSE 1 (81).—“My soul hath failed for thy salvation, and I have hoped beyond hope in thy word.”**

My soul hath failed for thy salvation. [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine, Ambrose.] There is a failing that is praiseworthy and desirable; and there is a failing that is blameworthy and condemnable. To fail from good into evil is bad; to fail from evil into good is good. Yet “failing,” without qualification, is ordinarily taken in a bad sense, just as “progress” is taken in a good sense, unless something is added—as when it is said, “They progress for the worse.” Here it says “for thy salvation,” not “from salvation.” This failing, therefore, is good.

Such failing [Col. 1084B] indicates an excessive desire for a good not yet possessed but most eagerly sought, as in Simeon and the ancients who desired Christ’s coming. Hence the seven sacramental antiphons before Christmas: “O Adonai! O Root of David!” and so forth, in which the Saviour’s advent is sought. They are all in the second tone because he who is invoked is God and man. They are seven because in him is the fullness of sevenfold grace. Even now all the righteous desire him who is to come. Nor has this desire of the Church rested at all from the beginning of the world, except while he dwelt here bodily with his disciples. Thus this may be the voice of Christ’s entire body: “My soul hath failed”—that is, it has grown weary through prolonged expectation—while holding fast in affection and desire “for thy salvation,” that is, for Jesus in Hebrew.

[Col. 1084C] For what is intensely desirable, as it were, causes the very soul of the one who desires it to depart; yet, if a nearer hope arises, it gives strength. Accordingly, the farther away the desired thing is, the more the one desiring it fails. Thus to fail for salvation is to pass wholly into it by every desire, even to be transfused through a kind of failing of the soul. Behold the bending of humility.

Or thus: My soul has failed from itself—that is, from the desire of its animal nature—stretching toward thy salvation, that is, toward Jerusalem. Or in this way it becomes one spirit with God: “He who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit with him” (I Corinthians VI). Therefore the soul cleaving to the Spirit fails from being soul and becomes one spirit. Hence, the more it desires to cleave to salvation, the more [Col. 1084D] it fails from itself. This failing, then, effects a diminution of frailty but an assumption of strength. [Ambrose, Augustine.] Note that here he is shown to be active (*practicus*): as the soul gives life to the body, so here he performs good works outwardly. And lest you doubt what he called “salvation,” he adds, “and in thy word,” that is, in the Son. Or, “in thy word,” that is, in thy promise, I have hoped beyond hope. This hope makes one await patiently what is not seen. He does not say simply, “I have hoped,” but “I have hoped beyond hope,” because what is to come is more than can be said.

**VERSE 2 (82).—“Mine eyes have failed for thy word, saying: When wilt thou console me?”**

[Col. 1085A] Mine eyes have failed. [Ambrose, Augustine, Ambrose, Augustine.] As though he said: My soul has failed, and so also my inner eyes, by which prophets are called seers, who can speak inwardly with God. Likewise, not from weakness but from the strength of desire, they have failed from the contemplation of temporal things, tending toward thy word—that is, thy promise.

Observe that “eyes” is said in the plural, though there is but one eye, namely the inward understanding of the mind by which God is seen. But because that one eye sees God in two ways, namely through mystical and moral understanding, the Church is said to have two eyes. Thus the Church’s two eyes are the mystical and the moral. The mystical is keener; the moral sweeter. Therefore the bridegroom says to the bride: “Thou hast taken us to heart [reading uncertain], with one of thine eyes” (Song of Songs IV), because with the mystical [Col. 1085B] eye the bride sees Christ more than with the moral eye. Perhaps these are the eyes by which Paul saw eternal things, when he began not to see bodily things. For he saw when he said, “Who art thou, Lord?” He certainly saw Christ, whom he also confessed to be Lord. By these eyes too the prophets were called seers, because through revelation they mentally discerned things that were hidden.

These eyes, then, have failed for the word through excessive longing and vehement desire, as though wearied by work. For one who devotes himself so greatly to God’s word is not idle; nor is the person who works outwardly of greater worth than one who pursues the study of knowing divinity. Wisdom itself is a supreme work and is preferred: Mary who listened is preferred to Martha who served (Luke X). Note that here he is shown already to be contemplative (*theoricus*), whose eyes [Col. 1085C] have failed for the word of God. I say, eyes “saying, When wilt thou console me?” As though he said: I endure delays. This happens so that the thing delayed may come more sweetly. Note that he says “saying.” The tongue, not the eyes, ordinarily speaks; but their voice is groaning and prayer. While spiritual desires burn, carnal desires grow cold. Hence he adds:

**VERSE 3 (83).—“For I am become as a bottle in the frost; I have not forgotten thy justifications.”**

For I am become as a bottle in the frost. [Augustine, Ambrose, Augustine, Remigius.] The flesh of this death is as frost by the heavenly benefit, through which, like frost, the concupiscence of the flesh grows numb and is contracted. As though he said: Therefore console me, because I have become as a bottle in the frost; that is, by the divine benefit—namely, the frost of continence—I have quenched all bodily heat and the burning of carnal concupiscence. This frost cools but does not burn; it makes crops fruitful but does not destroy them.

Therefore perhaps, when on the mountain the Lord displayed the glory of the resurrection in his transfiguration, his garments became white as snow (Matthew XVII), because not he alone will be free from the contagion of sin, but whoever rises again with frozen desires will rise cold. Hence: “In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew XXII). Therefore good bottles are cold—that is, constricted by frosts in freezing cold—not loosened by the heat of lust; and thus God’s justifications do not slip from memory. Hence he adds: “I have not forgotten thy justifications,” because the mind is not occupied elsewhere: concupiscence is numb, [Col. 1086A] charity burns.

Or thus: I desire this because, in comparison with the future, I have become like a bottle in the frost—that is, vile and fit for no liquid; and yet I have not forgotten thy justifications. [Haymo, Ambrose, Cassiodorus.] Or frost signifies the wicked, who do not burn with charity but are cold in unbelief. The sense is: Therefore console me, because I have become like a bottle in the frost—that is, among the wicked—retaining what was entrusted to me, thy justifications, with which the bottle is full; I have not forgotten them.

Or because a bottle is made from the skin of a dead animal, by it is understood the righteous person who chastises his body together with its vices and concupiscences; who, like a dead skin, does not feel the cold of sin; who is not broken by necessities; who is pliant to the commands of the soul. The sense is: Therefore console me, because I have become like a bottle in [Col. 1086B] the frost. Frost is the sins of the world, which the bottle does not feel—that is, I have extinguished carnal desires in myself, so that, being extinguished, I no longer feel them. And therefore I have not forgotten thy justifications.

But because he knows that temptations are not to end before the end of the world, he asks concerning this, adding:

**VERSE 4 (84).—“How many are the days of thy servant? When wilt thou execute judgment upon them that persecute me?”**

How many are the days? As though he said: Thus I desire to see salvation; but how many are the days of thy servant in this world? He says “days,” not “years,” lest there be year-long delays in this life. “When wilt thou execute judgment upon them that persecute me?” [Ambrose] That is, when will vengeance come against those who persecute me—that is, the devil and his ministers? He adds this concerning judgment, after asking concerning the days, lest anyone think that the Church will not exist for some period before the judgment. It will not end before judgment.

But why does he ask this, when the Gospel says, “It is not for you to know the times or seasons” (Acts I)? [Alcuin, Ambrose, Alcuin.] Here he prophesies that future question of the apostles in which, namely, this prophecy was fulfilled. He says “upon them that persecute” in order, as it were, to indicate that he wishes his days to be closed, that they may be delivered from these persecutors. Or this may be understood of the present: “When wilt thou execute judgment upon them that persecute me?” that is, upon demons—judgment, that is, vengeance (Romans XVI). For here God crushes Satan beneath our feet.

Or thus, so that one clause refers to the good and the other to the wicked: “How many are the days of thy servant?” That is, how long dost thou defer doing for thy servants what is expedient? As though he said: Act toward thy servants in mercy when it is necessary; and, “When wilt thou execute judgment upon them that persecute me?” As though he said: Act also toward the ungodly in justice. For in order that they may persecute:

**VERSE 5 (85).—“The wicked have told me fables, but not according to thy law.”**

The wicked have told me fables to impede faith, [Ambrose, Augustine, Ambrose] namely things that delight only in words. Hence some render “delights”: that is, such as the delight found in secular literature and among Jews and heretics—that is, in the various sects of Jews and heretics—who tell trifles as though they were some tale. But such things are not to me as thy law, because:

[Col. 1087A] **VERSE 6 (86).—“All thy commandments are truth; the wicked have persecuted me; help thou me.”**

All thy commandments are truth, unlike those things in which there is vanity. Therefore truth, not words, delights me; vain and wandering [the text is uncertain at this point] is the talkativeness of heretics, which is devoid of truth. “The wicked,” as though he said: Thy truth delights me, and because of this the wicked have persecuted me—or unjustly, because in me they persecute nothing but truth. Therefore help me.

Or the connection is: “The wicked”—as though he said—not only have they told fables, but the wicked have also persecuted me in order to corrupt truth. But help me, as against a beast, that I may contend against them for the truth. When the Church does this, it suffers torments. He adds this also:

[Col. 1087B] **VERSE 7 (87).—“They had almost consumed me upon earth, but I did not forsake thy commandments.”**

Almost. [Augustine, Ambrose, Augustine.] As though he said: Therefore help me, because they had almost consumed me upon earth, having made great slaughter among the martyrs—so excessive was the persecution against carnal frailty. But because “Help me” is not said in vain, he adds: “But I did not forsake thy commandments.” Yet, that he may be able to persevere unto the end, he adds:

**VERSE 8 (88).—“According to thy mercy quicken me, and I will keep the testimonies of thy mouth.”**

According to thy mercy, [Ambrose, Augustine] not according to my merit, quicken me, lest by loving temporal life I deny thee and so lose spiritual life. [Col. 1087C] I say, quicken me, and thus I will keep the testimonies of thy mouth—that is, the martyr-witnesses.

**COLLATION ON CAPH**

**VERSE 4 (84).—“In the frost.”** The more recent Hebraists have “in smoke,” *BEQITOR*. According to Kimhi, the word signifies everything that rises like smoke, such as vapour or mist; nor is “frost,” as Jerome also has it, a bad rendering. In either sense the quenching of desires is aptly represented.

**VERSE 5 (85).—“The wicked have told me fables”:** *CARU LI ZEDIM SCHIHOTH*, that is, “the proud have dug pits for me.” The Septuagint expressed the sense, which suits heretics and perverse sects or verbose doctrines: these cast the unwary, bewitched by fables of this kind, into deep precipices. Add that *CARAH*, according to Rabbi Abraham, sometimes means to seek out falsehood; and *SIAH*, with a left dot, means speech, but with a right dot, a pit, *SCHIAH*.

[Col. 1087D] **VERSE 6 (86).—“The wicked.”** In this word one may accuse the copyist of the fault of using a noun for an adverb: *iniqui* (“the wicked”) for *inique* (“unjustly”). For the Greek is ἀδίκως, “unjustly.” Hilary, Ambrose, and Augustine, commentators on this psalm, interpret it in that manner. Indeed, the Hebrew reads *SCHEQER*, which Jerome and nearly all the others translated “falsely,” “impiously,” “vainly,” or “gratuitously,” although it may also be taken collectively as “lying men,” as the translator for Campensis and Pellicanus rendered it. Yet we have found two of the older writers who read and expounded, “The wicked have persecuted me.” One is the very ancient author Arnobius, who interpreted the wicked as persecuting demons; the other, much later, is Cassiodorus, who interprets them as unbelievers. Finally, whether you sing it in this way or that, there is no danger.

**LAMED** [Note: [Col. 1087] Jerome interprets *Lamed* as “of discipline” or “of the heart.”]

[Col. 1088A] **For ever, O Lord.** [Augustine, Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Ambrose.] The weary expectant, who above desired that his days be closed and that he be with Christ, here shows that he does not refuse labour; indeed, he is ardent to serve him whom angels, all good persons, and every creature serve. In this twelfth letter he describes God’s power and works, saying that temporal things end but his commandments do not, according to: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Luke XXI).

Because these commandments must be carefully understood and investigated, the letter *lamed*, meaning “heart,” or “word,” or “heart of service,” is appropriately placed before this octonary, because these precepts are to be understood wisely or observed diligently. For God’s utterances are heavenly and chaste; nothing of adulterated opinion should be mixed with them, but everything should shine with sincere and spiritual truth. Therefore let the circumcised heart be raised to them; for it is fitting that what endures in heaven should remain in thee, and that thou shouldst always meditate upon it. Hence in what follows: “Unless thy law is my meditation”; and: “For ever I will not forget thy justifications.” Therefore keep God’s word and keep it diligently in thy heart.

The sense of this letter is thus connected with what precedes. Above he said, “They had almost consumed me upon earth”; but because God did not permit him to be consumed upon earth, he marvels at God’s power and exclaims:

**VERSE 1 (89).—“For ever, O Lord, thy word remaineth in heaven.”**

For ever, O Lord, thy word remaineth in heaven. [Ambrose.] Literally: the solemn order of the heavenly ordinances remains. The year passes through days and months; the cycle of the sun and moon returns in the same revolutions; and the law once established for all things remains unchangeable. Imitate this in thy mind. Take an image from the heaven of thy mind: Satan, in whom the Word did not remain, fell from heaven to earth, because he had no place in heaven, where the one obedience of all, amid distinct offices, maintains an undivided harmony of the ordained constitution. Therefore God’s word remains there for ever.

Having been cast out from there, Satan came against us more fiercely and inflicts temptations harsher than usual, as one enraged, because he has come wholly here. Therefore evils occur here, but in heaven the word remains. Yet because there too is a place for vices, as is apparent in those who fell, and because heaven itself changes and passes away, it does not remain for ever. This seems not to have been said concerning the element of heaven, but concerning the powers of heaven. Therefore the heavens are the angels, in whom nothing is unstable. There are also heavens on earth which declare God’s glory, namely the saints: though they are bodily on earth, they are in heaven in mind. Hence: “Our conversation is in heaven” (Philippians III). Yet the word of God remains more in God’s angels than in human beings, because human affection is changeable. Still, here I understand “heaven” as the disposition of the righteous rather than the element.

The sense is: I say, Help me, quicken me, [Col. 1089A] and I will keep thy testimonies—testimonies which must surely be kept, because for ever, [Augustine, Ambrose] that is, without interruption, O Lord, thy word—that is, the observance of thy commandments—remains in heaven, that is, in any righteous person or in heavenly spirits, because the supercelestial and lower rational creatures keep them. And:

**VERSE 2 (90).—“Thy truth endureth from generation to generation; thou hast founded the earth, and it remaineth.”**

From generation to generation. [Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] That is, in the two peoples, namely of the Law and of the Gospel, thy truth—that is, Christ—remains. For he was first in the faithful of the Old Testament, and afterwards in the faithful of the New Testament. This is so because thou hast founded the earth—that is, the Church, namely the saints—in faith, in which they remain. Hence he adds: thy truth remains in it; or conversely, it remains in thy truth. Literally, however, the earth is to be moved.

**VERSE 3 (91).—“By thy ordinance the day endureth; all things serve thee.”**

By thy ordinance the day endureth. [Ambrose, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The one eternal day, which has no night, is understood in the singular. That day is the one upon which Christ, the true sun, never sets. For our day is closed by night. Nor should it be doubted that the word remains in heaven and from generation to generation, since all things, temporal and eternal alike, serve thee. For he orders all things according to his will, though in different ways.

Alternatively: “For ever.” The righteous man who had said above, “They persecuted me and consumed me upon earth,” as though weary of this changeableness and these temptations, inflamed with desire for the heavenly Jerusalem and looking toward it, says: “For ever, O Lord, thy truth remaineth in heaven,” that is, in the angels who keep their eternal service. After heaven he speaks of earth, saying: “Thy truth remaineth from generation to generation.” He finds generations on earth which are not in heaven when he says, “from generation to generation.” By this repetition he indicates either all successions, among whom God’s truth is never absent from the saints, or the people of the Law and of the Gospel.

Then he gives the reason why truth remains: “For thou hast founded the earth, and it remaineth”; that is, thou hast founded on Christ, the foundation, those dwelling on earth, and they remain in the house for ever, unlike the sons [Col. 1089D] of the bondwoman. “By thy ordinance the day endureth,” because all these things are the day which the Lord has made. I rightly say, “by thy ordinance,” since all things serve thee—namely all the things of which he speaks, which belong to this day; for the ungodly do not serve.

Or thus: “For ever.” [Ambrose, Augustine, Remigius.] As though he said: I have hoped beyond hope in thy word, that is, in the Son; and rightly so, because thy word, O Lord—that is, thy Son—remains in heaven, that is, in the Church, namely in the good, but not in earth, that is, in the evil. The Church, indeed, is called paradise, in which was the tree of life. It remains, I say, for ever, according to: “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever” (Psalm XLIV).

[Augustine, the Interlinear Gloss, Haymo, the Interlinear Gloss, Ambrose.] Then, because he explains what he had said, he adds: “From generation to generation,” as above, “thy truth,” that is, God, remains. Yet it does not have this from itself but from thee, because thou hast founded the earth—that is, the soul or body—lest it be dispersed through concupiscences. It remains in good; nor do even the greater ones have this from themselves, because the day—that is, the greater ones called “days” on account of knowledge—endures by thy ordinance, whatever presses upon it. And the day’s knowledge is rightly subject to thy ordinance, since all things serve thee. This will be fulfilled in the future, when all things are subject to him; now many are slaves of sin.

**VERSE 4 (92).—“Unless thy law had been my meditation, I should perhaps then have perished in my humiliation.”**

Unless thy law. [Augustine, Ambrose, Alcuin.] Above he said, “Thou hast founded the earth, and it remaineth.” But here he explains how the earth is freed so that, once founded, it remains: “unless thy law …” As though he said: Such art thou, and thy law is so strong that its meditation delivers from such great dangers. For unless, etc.

Or join it thus: “All things serve thee,” and rightly, because if this were not so—that thy law is my meditation for knowing and doing, as it was for Job when they had almost consumed him—then [the sense follows]. [Interlinear Gloss, Ambrose, Augustine, Ambrose.] Or *then* means “therefore”: because I did not meditate, I should perhaps have perished in my humiliation, that is, in abasement and affliction. This is the law of faith which works through love, by which grace is obtained, making persons strong so that they do not perish in mortal humiliation. In this he meditates continually lest he be overcome. Hence he rightly says “unless.” For one who has not first been trained in meditation on the law is ignorant in battle.

**VERSE 5 (93).—“For ever I will not forget thy justifications; for in them thou hast quickened me.”**

For ever I will not forget. [Cassiodorus, Ambrose, Augustine.] As though he said: Unless I meditated on the law, I should have perished; but because through the law I live, it cannot slip from memory. This means “for ever,” that is, throughout my whole life. Or “for ever,” that is, if I were always to live, I would not forget thy justifications, namely the law which cleanses from sin.

Or thus: Just as the Israelites in their promised land, remembering their deliverance from Egypt, gave thanks, so this man, mindful of his own deliverance from spiritual captivity, says: “For ever,” that is, in eternal life, “I will not forget thy justifications.” As though in the true land of promise we shall remember from what thou hast delivered us [Col. 1090D] and shall give thanks. Therefore I will not forget thy justifications, because in them thou hast quickened me when I sought nothing outside thee—whom Adam lost. Behold how it comes about that he did not perish in humiliation: God, namely, justifying him. And because thou hast quickened me:

**VERSE 6 (94).—“I am thine; save me, for I have sought thy justifications.”**

I am thine. [Ambrose, Augustine.] Not the property of vices, nor of two masters. Formerly I wished to be my own, and I perished; now I am thine, and therefore save—make me safe—and thou oughtest to do so, because I have sought thy justifications, etc. Or connect it thus: I am thine because I have not sought my own wills, by which I was my own, but thy justifications, that I may be thine. Others seek other things; but I have sought thy justifications.

[Ambrose, Augustine.] He calls “justifications” those things which signified future realities, such as the paschal lamb and so forth. These are the beginnings of faith, without which no one perfectly knows grace. Therefore no one should suppose that the significations of the Old Testament, which this man seeks so diligently, are to be neglected. Therefore save me, because:

**VERSE 7 (95).—“Sinners waited for me to destroy me; I understood thy testimonies.”**

Sinners waited for me, [Augustine] hiding, as it were, in ambush and awaiting his passing so that they might kill him. “To destroy me,” by making me consent to evil. But I did not perish thereby, because I understood thy testimonies—that is, thy martyr-witnesses. For although they pressed me while I confessed, I did not yield, looking to the end without end, that is, eternal blessedness.

**VERSE 8 (96).—“I have seen the end of all perfection; thy commandment is exceeding broad.”**

I have seen the end of all perfection. [Augustine, Alcuin, Ambrose.] This man had entered God’s sanctuary; he had seen the last things, he had seen God’s heights, which cannot be explained. Yet he sums up what must be said in a brief statement: “I have seen the end of all perfection.” Perfection is the complete fulfillment of all virtues: namely, doing all things for the highest good and striving for truth even unto death. Its end is to excel in Christ’s kingdom, namely Christ himself, whom he saw with his mind as one who was to come. As though he said: I understood the testimonies, and I saw the end of all perfection, that is, Christ, who is our recompense and blessedness.

Therefore thy commandment, which is exceedingly broad, is broad to me—as though easy to perform. That broad commandment is charity, without which one could not confess martyr-witnesses amid whatever torments. In it are a thousand narrow straits, yet it makes one walk the narrow way, and on it hang the whole Law and the Prophets. Therefore the commandment of charity is broad. What is broader than that on which the whole Law and the Prophets hang?

Or thus: I say that I understood thy testimonies, and truly so. For I have seen the end of all perfection—that is, I have understood in what the end of every good action ought to consist: namely, that no one should glory in himself but in the Lord. And I have so seen this because thy commandment is exceedingly broad: for I love even my enemies. For the narrow way through grace is exceedingly broad, so as to make one love even one’s enemies.

[Col. 1091D] Or, I have seen the end of all perfection because I understood that God’s precepts must be fulfilled not for the sake of earthly but eternal things; thy commandment is exceedingly broad. Or there is a perfection of wickedness and a perfection of righteousness, but Christ is the end of both, because he destroys wickedness and completes righteousness: he destroys the former by suffering, and completes the latter by rewarding. Thus at the first advent, when the world, set in wickedness, had already brought its wickedness to completion, Christ was the end of completed wickedness. At the second advent he will be the end of completed righteousness. Therefore he says, “I have seen the end of all perfection,” that is, I have understood Christ to be the end of the perfection of evil and of good. For when the world’s wickedness was completed, the Lamb of God came to end it through the cross; and Christ is the end of completed righteousness because he rewards it. And I have seen thy commandment of charity, exceedingly broad; this is to be understood as above.

[Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] Or thus: I have seen the end of all perfection because, by the prophetic spirit, he sees a limit set to all worldly things; but thy commandments have no end, because they are exceedingly broad. This is what he says: “Thy commandment is exceedingly broad.” Therefore, earthly things having been despised, these are to be sought. He says “exceedingly” with reference to charity, which comprises the sayings of the prophets and the whole Law.

Or thus—and the order of the words is also changed—“Thy commandment,” which is exceedingly broad, that is, love of God and neighbour, “I have seen,” that is, I have known to be the end of all perfection, because every good work is rooted and formed in charity.

[Col. 1092B] **COLLATION ON LAMED.**
### Verse 3 (91)

“By thy ordinance the day endureth.” *Lemischapateca amedu haiom* means “By thy judgments they stand today.” The permanence contained in the word *amedu*, that is, “they stood,” may be referred in three ways. First, to the continuance of the days, as in the Septuagint. Hence the Cajetan translators, rendering word for word, have: “By thy judgments they stood today”; and in smaller type they add, “all days.” Pellican likewise follows this sense: “Thou hast caused thy several days,” he says, “to subsist by thy judgments and ordinances until now.”

Secondly, it may refer to the preceding words—namely, truth, earth, and word—as Jerome seems to have done: “By thy judgment they stand unto this day”; and the Pratensian version: “By thy judgments they have endured today.” Sanctes likewise: “They have stood until this day in order to perform thy judgments.”

Finally, it may be understood as a clause looking forward to what follows. Thus Münster translated: “[Col. 1092C] According to thy decrees, all things stand today; for all things obey thee.” The Campensian paraphrase similarly says: “In whatever manner thou hast willed each thing to subsist, so it subsists unto this present day.”

### Verse 4 (92)

“Unless thy law had been my meditation, then perhaps I should have perished in my affliction.” The particle “perhaps” does not appear to be found in the Hebrew, where only *az* is read, which all the more recent translators render simply “then” or “now.” In Greek there is *τότε ἄν*, that is, “then certainly.” And “perhaps” seems to weaken the sense. For there can be no doubt that one must perish if meditation on the divine law is removed. Hence Ambrose translates: “Otherwise, in my affliction”—which indicates certainty, not doubt.

Yet Jerome plainly translated “perhaps.” Nor is it always a sign of doubt; for, by a certain idiom of speech, it suggests something of the instability of our will. As if one said: “Unless thy law had been my meditation, then, when a strong temptation arose, it would perhaps have utterly destroyed me—weak and [Col. 1092D] unstable as I was, deprived of meditation on the law.” This is Hilary’s meaning in this place; he repeatedly uses *forsitan*, “perhaps.”

So that no one may lose confidence, he says:

> “We have frequently reminded you that ‘affliction’ signifies the condition in which the soul is subjected to temptations and, left to its own weakness, is made low. Therefore the law is its meditation; and unless it had been its meditation, it might perhaps have perished in affliction. Thus meditation on the law must not be abandoned when we are troubled and distressed; but when we are afflicted by various bodily infirmities, when we are harassed amid the conflicts of persecutions, meditation on the law ought to remain constant within us. For even if fires burn toward the destruction of faith, even if scourges tear us to the peril of salvation, even if hooks dig into bodies redeemed by God in order to extort a confession of impiety, we must nevertheless remember the prophetic saying, so that we may be partakers of it. Let us also say, enduring and conquering: ‘Unless thy law had been my meditation, then [Col. 1093A] perhaps I should have perished in my affliction.’”

Thus far St. Hilary. Had there been any question concerning the Greek expletive particle *ἄν*, which the Latin translator rendered “perhaps,” I think Hilary would not have passed over it in silence, especially since it seemed to weaken the sense. For a little later, in the same portion of the Psalm, he says: “We have frequently reminded you that adequate satisfaction for understanding cannot be supplied by a Latin translation.” Something has also been noted elsewhere concerning this word.

## MEM

### “How I have loved” [Cassiodorus]

In this thirteenth letter the righteous man speaks, who has advanced through meditation on the prophets and the Gospel. He says that he has understood more than the elders and that the Scriptures are therefore sweeter to him than honey [Ambrose and Jerome; Ambrose, Alcuin]. And since this comes to him through love, the letter *Mem*, interpreted as “inward parts” or “from themselves,” is fittingly prefixed to this octave [Col. 1093B], because it treats here of love that comes from the very marrow.

Thus manifold love is understood: he loves the law with his whole heart. Therefore he finds the New Testament in it, and surpasses those who preach only the Old. As if he said: “I have understood thy testimonies; I have seen the end.” And rightly, because:

### Verse 1 (97)

> “How I have loved thy law, O Lord! It is my meditation all the day.”

“How,” he says admiringly, “I have loved”—not feared—“thy law, O Lord.” [Interlinear Gloss, Ambrose.] Here he shows whence the commandment is broad to him. For love is the breadth of the commandment. Whoever loves what God commands also loves the command itself by which it is commanded, namely the law.

And note that when he says “O Lord,” he calls upon the very one he loves as witness [Col. 1093C]; whoever truly loves God loves his law. Then, explaining how he loves the law, he adds: “all the day,” etc. [Augustine, Ambrose, Augustine.] As if he said: “I have loved thy law in this manner: thy law is my meditation all the day,” that is, continually, even though the flesh hinders.

He rightly says “day,” not “night,” because for one meditating on the law it is always day. But for those who do not know that the New Testament is in it, it is always night. He also rightly says “all the day,” for whatever is done holily is meditation on the law. Such a one attains to the law of righteousness because he seeks to be justified by faith that works through love. Hence he has enemies—whom? The Jews, who glory in works; concerning them he adds:

### Verse 2 (98)

> “Thou hast made me wiser than mine enemies by thy commandment, because it is mine for ever.”

“Above my enemies.” [Ambrose, Augustine, Ambrose, Augustine.] As if he said: “I shall meditate in the law all day, and therefore thou hast made me wiser than my enemies”—namely Jews, pagans, and heretics, who either do not understand or do not act. “By thy commandment,” because they rest in signs, but I in truth; because they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; because they wish to establish their own righteousness, while this man seeks righteousness through faith in Christ, which is from God.

Thus thou hast made me wiser by thy commandment, “because it is mine for ever”: that is, I understand it in such a way that the commandment itself is eternal and avails for my eternity. For them, however, it is only for this age. They seek temporal rewards from the commandment, as the enslaved children of Hagar [Col. 1094A]; therefore it is not theirs for ever, as it is for this man when this age has ended. According to them, no commandment of the law can endure; according to this man, the love of God will remain written on the tablets of the heart for ever, together with the reward for the commandment kept. It will be God himself, who gave the commandment, when God shall be all in all.

### Verse 3 (99)

> “I have understood more than all my teachers, because thy testimonies are my meditation.”

“Above all who teach me.” [Ambrose, Cassiodorus.] As if he said: “Thou hast made me wiser than my enemies, because I have also understood above all who teach me”—those, namely, who were among the enemies, that is, above the Scribes and Pharisees. And this is because thy testimonies are my meditation in the Spirit. For I rest not in the letter but in the Spirit [Col. 1094B]; such meditation is not theirs, who understand and teach false things there.

### Verse 4 (100)

> “I have understood more than the aged, because I have sought thy commandments.”

“Above the aged.” [Ambrose, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As if he said: “I have understood above those who teach me, because I have also understood above the aged”—that is, elders in body, not in mind. For the new people who here speak, having received Christ, understand better than that old Jewish people which received the blessing first. And all this is because I have sought inwardly thy commandments—not human but divine commandments, which they transgressed; I did not receive them merely outwardly.

This whole passage may also be understood in the person of the Head, beginning with: “I have understood above all who teach me.” For this is said according to the Head, though the voice does not change. Christ and the Church are one speaker because of that mystery: “The two shall be one flesh” (Eph. 5). Thus they are also one in voice. He says, therefore: “I have understood above all who teach me.”

No one other than Christ understood the prophets above all their teachers; but Christ understood above all human beings, being taught by the Father, of whom he himself says: “As the Father hath taught me, I speak these things” (John 8). This is understood with greatest difficulty in the person of the Word himself, unless someone can in some measure grasp that for the Son to be taught by the Father is the same as to be begotten. For he whose being is not one thing and whose being taught another—what he is, that is also his being taught. From whom he has his being, from him he has also, together with it, his being taught [Col. 1094D].

But in the person of the man, when he took the form of a servant, it is more easily understood that he learned from the Father the things he spoke. In that form of a servant, especially as a boy, human beings of greater age could suppose that he ought to be taught. Therefore he understood above all, because thy testimonies were his meditation [Augustine]: he meditated on testimonies which he knew concerning himself better than they did.

The teachers are the elders, concerning whom he says: “I have understood above the aged.” From this note the age at which, as a boy, he sat among the elders and understood above them, as he did in the tradition of the elders concerning the washing of hands. Thus he says: “I have understood above the aged, because I have sought thy commandments”; for one taught by the Lord easily surpasses teachers and elders. These things also suit the members whom he himself taught, as we have read earlier.

### Verse 5 (101)

> “I have restrained my feet from every evil way, that I might keep thy words.”

“From every evil way.” [Cassiodorus, Ambrose, Cassiodorus.] As if he said: “I understood the commandments and fulfilled them in deed, because from every way of those very servants and teachers”—a way, I say, which is evil, that is, criminal—“I have restrained my feet,” that is, my affections; as though they were prone and willing to go into evil. But this man restrained them lest he should be overthrown by their perversity, namely that of the elders. I restrained them for this purpose: that I might keep thy words, which could not otherwise be done.

### Verse 6 (102)

> “I have not declined from thy judgments, because thou hast given me the law.”

Thus I restrained my feet from their way, “because I have not declined from thy judgments” [Cassiodorus, Ambrose, Augustine]—that is, from what thou hast established as a rule of life, from the paths of the old or new law. The reason is that thou, not Moses, hast given me the law—that is, the Gospel.

Or thus: I restrained my feet because I did not decline from thy judgments, that is, I always feared thy judgments. Hence elsewhere: “For I feared thy judgments” (Ps. 118:120). And I always believed them, because thou hast inwardly, with thy finger, given me the law—that is, written it in my heart—not that, like a servant, I might fear, but that I might love.

### Verse 7 (103)

> “How sweet are thy sayings to my palate! More than honey to my mouth.”

“How sweet to my palate.” [Ambrose, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] As if he said: “I understood with the mind, fulfilled in deed, and also proclaimed to others.” This is: “How sweet are thy sayings,” in which forgiveness and life are preached, “to the palate of my heart,” not of my flesh, for swallowing; and “to my mouth,” for speaking. For the palate swallows, while the mouth speaks; and they are sweet to the speaker—indeed, sweeter than honey.

[Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Other translators say: “More than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth.” Note that in such comparisons the text everywhere says not “like,” but “more than,” because such things cannot be compared with divine sayings. Honey is the Old Testament; the honeycomb is the New. That is, the sayings of God are compared to honey in respect of the Old Testament, and to the honeycomb in respect of the New, which is sweeter than the Old as the honeycomb is than honey.

Or again: honey, which is pressed out and strained, resembles open teaching; but the honeycomb resembles teaching about hidden mysteries, pressed out as it were from waxen cells by the mouth of one chewing, that is, expounding. Thus these are aptly spoken in comparison with divine sayings, to which the sayings themselves bear likeness and affinity.

### Verse 8 (104)

> “From thy commandments I have received understanding; therefore I have hated every way of iniquity.”

“From thy commandments I have understood.” [Augustine.] I do not say that I have understood the commandments themselves, but “from thy commandments,” because by doing them this man came to the height of wisdom. For one does not come to the wisdom of hidden things except through obedience to the commandments. Hence in the Book of Wisdom: “Hast thou desired wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will provide her for thee” (Sirach 1, according to the Greek).

If you do otherwise, it is said to you in the book of Jesus son of Sirach: “Do not seek what is too high for thee, nor search into what is too strong for thee; but always think upon those things which the Lord hath commanded thee” (Sirach 3). For they are to be pondered both before wisdom is received and after it has been received. But the more the sweetness of fuller wisdom inflames him, the more the love of righteousness grows. Hence he necessarily hates all iniquity. Therefore he adds: “Therefore I hated every way of iniquity,” etc.

*(In Mem, any minor points are easily reconciled.)*

## NUN

[Note: [Col. 1095] Nun, according to Jerome, means “everlasting.”]

“Thy word is a lamp unto my feet.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Ambrose, Alcuin.] In this fourteenth letter, he who above declared that he had understood and kept the commandments rejoices that the light of the Word shines upon his feet. From desire he seeks a reward and commends his soul from its affliction.

[Col. 1096B] Here he treats of humility, because he attributes both the beginning of good and its perfection to Christ. And because commandments are understood and fulfilled through Christ’s illumination and help, the letter *Nun* is prefixed, interpreted as “only one” or “their pastures,” that is, Christ, the unique helper and pasture of souls. Therefore *Nun* is rightly called “only one” or “their pastures,” because here there is discourse concerning the Only-begotten of God and the brightness of eternal light, who is also the pasture of the faithful. For he feeds and refreshes us.

This pasture is good, because there you pluck the new flower, because he has given the sweet fragrance of resurrection; there you pluck the lily of eternity and the rose of the Lord’s body and blood. But in this pasture—that is, in this octave, where he treats of this pasture—Christ himself, who is our pasture, teaches humility in himself [Col. 1096C]. For he, the true David, humble and strong of hand, obedient to the Father, fed his Father’s sheep by divine preaching, proving to them by sure indications according to the Scriptures his own coming.

The text continues thus: As if he said, “In such and such ways I have advanced, both for myself and for others; and this is not from myself, but from thy Word,” that is, Christ, who is the Word in the beginning with the Father.

### Verse 1 (105)

> “Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my paths.”

“A lamp unto my feet,” namely the feet of the mind [Ambrose, Interlinear Gloss], by which it shines in the night of this world like the ray of the moon; “and a light unto my paths,” that is, the paths of good works.

Observe that the same Word, Christ, is both light and lamp. Yet Christ is a lamp when he is recited by our mouth. For he shines in us as in an earthen vessel, whence the Apostle says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4). But in himself he is the inextinguishable light which enlightens every person coming into the world, etc. (John 1).

Therefore pour in oil, lest the lamp’s light fail you: the oil, I mean, of heavenly mercy and grace, by which the prophets were anointed; by which the hardness of our necks is softened; by which bodies battered upon the rocks of sins are also soothed. Note likewise the fitting distinction of the words: “a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my paths.” A lamp is enough for the feet in walking; paths require an expanded light for illumination.

Or, the Word—Christ—is called a lamp according to the Law, where he shone less clearly; and light according to the Gospel, where he shines openly. [Augustine.] Or “word” is understood as the word of all holy Scripture, which is a lamp to us. Hence Peter says: “We have the more certain prophetic word, to which ye do well to take heed, as unto a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Pet. 1).

And thy word, that is, the word of all holy Scripture—the word sown by prophets or apostles—is a lamp to the feet of my mind, shining in the night of this age, where there are snares and pits which a human being could not avoid by his own foresight. And the same word is light unto the paths of my works.

Properly speaking, however, the light that shines of itself is God alone (1 John 1), who enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1). Hence: “I am the light of the world.” A lamp, however, is a creature that shares in light. Therefore it is said of John: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Ps. 131). Since, then, the only-begotten Word is called light equal to the begetter, while a man illuminated by him is called a lamp; and since no human being is the Word that is light, nor is that Word a lamp, it is evident that this is not the subject here, where the same word is called both light and lamp.

[Cassiodorus.] Note that he first said “feet,” then “paths,” so that, first being made clear in heart, we may afterwards walk with upright steps.

### Verse 2 (106)

> “I have sworn, and have resolved, to keep the judgments of thy righteousness.”

“I have sworn and have resolved.” [Ambrose.] As if he said: “The Word is light to me; and therefore, with this light going before me, as one walking in light, I have sworn.” Otherwise, the weak man says that one ought not swear at all (Matt. 5). For no one swears well unless he can know what he swears.

He then explains “I have sworn” by “I have resolved,” that is, I have resolved as though by an oath; for he is so fixed in it that resolving is regarded as swearing. As if he said: “I, walking well by the lamp and having straight paths, have sworn and resolved,” that is, firmly resolved. What? “To keep the judgments of thy righteousness” amid whatever dangers. This is done through faith, while one believes under God, the righteous Judge, that no good is without fruit and no evil without punishment.

[Ambrose, Augustine.] Thus, he says, “I resolved to keep the judgments of thy righteousness,” in order to believe that each person shall be repaid according to merits, and that what is done here to the good and the evil is done by the just judgment of God; so that the perfect person may not be moved by anyone, but for this faith may endure grievous things.

### Verse 3 (107)

> “I have been humbled exceedingly, O Lord; quicken me according to thy word.”

“I have been humbled.” [Augustine, Ambrose.] As if he said: “And therefore, because I keep thy judgments, I have been humbled exceedingly”—or, “very greatly”—by the persecutor. I do not say, “I have humbled myself,” as though humility commanded by precept must necessarily be understood; rather, “I have been humbled” by violent persecution. But lest faith fail: “O Lord, quicken me according to thy word,” that is, according to thy promise, that I may keep the judgments of thy righteousness. Otherwise, the soul dies in tribulation unless thou quicken it.

Or he speaks of the virtue of humility when he says, “I have been humbled exceedingly.” This is what the one who keeps the judgments of thy righteousness desired. Blessed is the person who glories more in humility than in power; for power deceives, humility does not fail. Therefore: “O Lord, quicken me according to thy word,” so that I may live according to thy word and do all things with reason. And, O—

### Verse 4 (108)

> “Make the voluntary offerings of my mouth well-pleasing, O Lord, and teach me thy judgments.”

“O Lord, make the voluntary offerings of my mouth well-pleasing” [Augustine, Ambrose, Augustine], that is, sacrifices of praise offered in love, not fear; let them please thee, that thou mayest not reject them, but approve sacrifices of praise offered through confession of love, and not otherwise.

Therefore he rightly says “voluntary.” For voluntary is the confession of praise which he offers amid [Col. 1098B] tribulations. Having been propitiated by this offering, “teach me thy judgments, O Lord” [Augustine, Cassiodorus], which thou revealest to the faithful. Though he has often said that he has received them, he asks again from the ardor of love. He already knew them, but seeks increase. Therefore teach me, because:

### Verse 5 (109)

> “My soul is continually in my hands, yet have I not forgotten thy law.”

“My soul is continually in thy hands.” [Augustine.] Many books have “in thy hands.” Thus no one can seize it. Hence: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” (Wisdom 3), in whose hand are also we ourselves and our words. And, aided by thy hands, I have not forgotten thy law.

From this it may appear that the soul is placed in the hands of God; this indeed is clear. But some manuscripts read: “My soul is continually in my hands,” and how this is to be understood I do not know. That younger son seems to have held his soul in his own hands when he said to his father: “Give me the portion of substance that falleth to me” (Luke 15), whereby he perished. Thus he was dead.
