Unless it be said: “My soul is continually in my hands,” that is, in my works [Ambrose, Augustine, Ambrose], because I continually labor for my soul, since I continually offer it to thee to be quickened, as is said elsewhere: “Unto thee have I lifted up my soul” (Ps. 85). “And I have not forgotten thy law.”

Observe the order of the words and see how this man has advanced. For, being humbled, he is quickened; being quickened according to God’s promise, he is in spirit a voluntary minister, not one acting from necessity [Col. 1098D]. Then, being made such, he is taught the judgments of God, which are unsearchable. These judgments are such that he does not return evil for evil. But one can be taught them who always directs his soul toward God and has not forgotten God’s law. Hence, now joyful and secure, he says:

### Verse 6 (110)

> “Sinners have laid a snare for me, yet I have not erred from thy commandments.”

“Sinners have laid a snare.” [Ambrose, Cassiodorus.] As if he said: “I have not forgotten thy law; but although sinners lay a snare, I have not erred.” Thus: “Sinners have laid a snare for me, yet I have not erred from thy commandments.” The commandments of God are a heavenly antidote against the snares and poisons of the world. One who does not turn aside from thy commandments is not caught by them, because the snares lie alongside those commandments, not within them.

### Verse 7 (111)

> “I have acquired thy testimonies as an inheritance for ever, because they are the rejoicing of my heart.”

“I have acquired as an inheritance” [Ambrose], that is, as a firm possession from God, whose heir is this one who was previously an heir of Adam. What has he acquired? “Thy testimonies,” namely so that I might be God’s witness—that is, a martyr. And this is mine for ever, because in them there is not the temporal glory of those who seek vanity, but eternal glory for those who suffer for a time and reign without end, because they are the rejoicing of my heart, although they are an affliction to my body. And since they are rejoicing, gladly:

### Verse 8 (112)

> “I have inclined my heart to perform thy statutes for ever, for the sake of recompense.”

“I have inclined my heart.” [Ambrose, Augustine.] Or the connection may be thus: “Through humility”—for God rejects the proud—“I have inclined my heart to perform thy statutes for ever, for the sake of recompense.”

By “statutes” he means good works, which we perform in relation to the needs of our neighbors; these will not be eternal. How then shall we perform statutes for ever? But deeds done without love are not statutes of righteousness. Love itself, however, is eternal, and eternal recompense is prepared for it. Loving eternally, it merits eternally to possess the one whom it loves. Therefore “for ever” must be referred to both: to the merit of eternal love and to the reward of eternal recompense.

## COLLATION IN NUN

### Verse 3 (109)

“My soul is in my hands.” In this place Jerome teaches that the Greek manuscripts have been falsified: *ἐν ταῖς χερσί σου*, “in thy hands.” The Roman edition has this reading, and Augustine follows it, though he does not pass over the other. But it should be known—as Jerome says—that among the Hebrews, in the Septuagint, and in all other interpreters, it is written “in my hands,” not “in thy hands,” which in Hebrew is called *becappai*. And all Greek ecclesiastical interpreters explain this place thus. In brief, the sense is: “I am daily in danger and, as it were, carry my blood in my hands; nevertheless I do not forget thy law.”

### Verse 8 (112)

“For the sake of recompense.” The more recent translators have “unto the end.” Pellican, however, understands “unto the end” as meaning “to the nail,” perfectly. The Campensian paraphrase has: “unto the end of my life.” Yet the translator opposite has “for the sake of recompense,” and not without reason. For we have already said that *eqeb* signifies among the Hebrews both “end” and “reward,” because reward is the end of labor. Jerome translates: “for the sake of eternal recompense.” The translators for Cajetan have: “striving toward the eternal end”; and Nebiensis: “toward the eternal end.”

## SAMECH

[Note: [Col. 1099D] Samech is “help,” according to Jerome.]

“I have hated the unrighteous.” [Cassiodorus, Haymo, Ambrose.] He who above said that the light of the Word shone upon his feet, in this fifteenth letter treats of hatred for the unrighteous, who oppose the law of God. And because diligent caution must be exercised in hatred for enemies and love for friends, the letter *Samech* is fittingly prefixed to this octave. It is interpreted “hear” or “support,” which accords with the subject, because no one is strengthened unless inwardly, with the spiritual ears of the mind, he hears what he ought to follow.

It indicates that what he is about to say is mystical [Col. 1100A], calling the reader to hear. Hence elsewhere, inviting to a mystical understanding and diligent comprehension of the matter, the Lord says: “Hear, O my people, and Israel shall speak” (Ps. 49). And elsewhere: “He who hath ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8). The Prophet heard in this manner, who says elsewhere: “I will hear what the Lord God shall speak in me” (Ps. 84).

Therefore you are not idly admonished to hearing with the body, which is available to all by the very right of nature, but to spiritual hearing: so that you may hear the contents of the following verses not negligently through bodily use, but attentively through understanding of the mind. As if he said: “I have inclined my heart to perform thy statutes.”

### Verse 1 (113)

> “I have hated the unrighteous, but thy law have I loved.”

“But the unrighteous,” or, according to another reading, “the lawless,” “I have hated,” whoever they may be [Ambrose], because not even friends are to be listened to against God. This must be heard not with idle but attentive ears. For it seems to agree with the saying of the Lord: “Whoever does not hate father and mother, and wife and children and brothers for my sake, is not worthy of me” (Luke 14).

Yet it seems to differ from what the same Lord commands elsewhere: “Love your enemies,” etc. (Matt. 5), and from the Law’s command concerning honoring parents (Deut. 5). But the person who carefully considers the causes of love and hatred understands that these are not contrary to one another. For the nature which God created in all is to be loved and helped; but iniquity is to be hated and destroyed.

Therefore those who persecute are to be loved insofar as they are human beings, and hated because they are evil. We may devoutly both love and hate some persons, so that it is fitting to hate those whom you love and to love those whom you hate. Likewise, friends who advise evil must be avoided; they often bend those whom iron cannot conquer. This must be heard and acted on cautiously.

Parents and friends are likewise to be loved, but not more than God. Hence he himself says: “He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10). [Ambrose, Augustine.] Thus: “I have hated the unrighteous,” that is, those outside the law, not because they are human beings but because they are evil. For David did not hate Saul as a man, but as a persecutor. Why did I hate them? “And,” that is, because “I have loved thy law.” Thus he judges that he does not hate in unrighteous human beings the nature by which they are human, but that they are opposed to the law which he loves. And because I have loved the law, therefore thou art:

### Verse 2 (111)

> “Thou art my helper and my protector; I have hoped exceedingly in thy word.”

“My helper” [Augustine, Ambrose, Cassiodorus], for doing good; “and my protector,” for escaping evil. Or: thou art my helper through the Law, and my protector through the Gospel, through the incarnation, lest this man be any longer subject to the law of the flesh. Concerning this protection it follows: “And in thy word”—not in the law, not in the prophets, but in thy Word, that is, the protection of divinity—in which no one is deceived and in which we are delivered from death.

[Augustine, Ambrose.] Or “in thy word,” that is, in thy promise: as a child of promise, I have hoped exceedingly, continually adding to hope.

### Verse 3 (115)

> “Depart from me, ye malicious men, and I will search out the commandments of my God.”

“Depart from me, ye malicious men.” [Ambrose, Cassiodorus, Ambrose, Augustine.] Whoever hopes in Christ must separate himself from the society of the faithless, as this man does. He says this concerning noisy persons who tear the Scriptures apart with contention, who do not intend to be converted, and while they clash with one another we cannot search the commandments.

“I will search out the commandments of my God.” For where malice is, there is no keeping of heavenly commandments. Wisdom does not enter a malevolent soul; hence elsewhere: “The wicked seek me and shall not find me.” Christ loves the simple mind and the purified spirit. No fellowship can exist between unstained virtue and sins stained with foulness.

Notice that he says “I will search out the commandments,” not “I will do them,” because evil people exercise us in doing the commandments, but call us away from searching them out: now by persecuting, now by disputing, or by honoring us, so that we may spend on assisting their earthly affairs the time we owe to God’s law; now by oppressing the weak, so that they must flee to us. Wearied by such turbulent people and desiring God’s law, this man cries: “Depart from me, ye malicious men, and I will search out”—as one drives attacking flies away from his eyes. Once they have been driven away, he prays to be received by his helper, saying:

### Verse 4 (116)

> “Uphold me according to thy word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my expectation.”

“Uphold me.” [Ambrose, Augustine, Ambrose, Augustine.] Mingled with them, he could not be upheld. Note that above he had said, “Thou art my protector”; here he says, “Uphold me,” as if he said: “Thou who art my protector, uphold me more and more.” And do this “according to thy word,” that is, thy promise. He asks that what God promised may be done for him; therefore he is not rash in asking it.

Uphold me, I say, so that, coming to the future things for which I endure everything, I may truly live. Thus “and I shall live” is said of the future, as if he said: “At present I am not helped, because at present the body is dead because of sin.” And, so that I may then live, “do not put me to shame in my expectation,” that is, give more abundantly the Holy Spirit, through whom love is poured into our hearts (Rom. 8); when it is poured out, hope does not disappoint (Rom. 5). As if he said: “Let not those who hope in thee be overcome by adversities.”

And as though he were silently answered: “If you do not wish to be put to shame in your expectation, do not cease meditating on my statutes,” he perceives that this meditation is often hindered by the soul’s infirmities, and says:

### Verse 5 (117)

> “Help me, and I shall be saved; and I will meditate continually on thy statutes.”

“Help me.” [Ambrose.] As if he said: “Do not put me to shame, but help me.” Whoever hopes has confidence in that help in which salvation is sure. Above he said, “Thou art my helper”; here he asks to be helped, because, although we receive help here, it must always be sought, lest through negligence we lose it at some time.

Help me, I say, “and I shall be saved”; and, having received salvation, “I will meditate.” He says this lest some, having been helped in adversity, should afterwards be negligent in prosperous circumstances [probably *secundis*, “favorable circumstances”]. “I will meditate,” I say, “on thy statutes,” holding firmly that no one is righteous except through thee; and I will do this always.

He says this in order that a person may always be humble, confessing sins and not justifying himself like the Pharisee (Luke 18). And not only here, but also in the future, let him be humble, attributing glory not to himself but to God’s grace. For every creature, whatever good it has, has received it from Christ, who is the author of all creation. Thus: “I will meditate on thy statutes continually,” either while he lives or when, with the angels, he sings the praises of God. “Continually,” therefore, because:

### Verse 6 (118)

> “Thou hast despised all who depart from thy judgments, because their thought is unjust.”

“Thou hast despised all who depart.” [Augustine, Ambrose, Haymo.] Or the connection may be: “I ask this, namely that thou help me, because thou hast despised”—or, according to the Greek, “reduced to nothing”—“all who depart from thy judgments,” namely those who do not confess their sins. And rightly so, because their thought is unjust: perhaps they excuse themselves on the ground of weak nature.

[Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Or thus: they depart because their thought is unjust. An unjust thought is to wish to sin and not to wish to make satisfaction to the Judge. He has given thought as a sufficient reason for departing. For by thought one approaches God or departs from him, from whom all good and evil proceed. Therefore thou hast despised them, because:

### Verse 7 (119)

> “I have accounted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors; therefore I have loved thy testimonies.”

“They are transgressors,” [Augustine] such as I have accounted, judged, or reckoned all the sinners of the earth. For although there is no transgression where there is no law, and not everyone has the written law—that is, the law given through Moses—yet they have the natural law, saying: “What thou dost not wish to be done to thee, do not do to another” (Tobit 4). All act against it; and little children, just as they are sinners in their father, are also transgressors.

Every sinner, therefore, is a transgressor. Observe that he says “sinners of the earth,” because there are also sinners of heaven, such as the one who said: “I have sinned against heaven and before thee” (Luke 15), and anyone who diminishes the grace received from heaven, which the Holy Spirit has poured in. Thus the person who, being an inhabitant of heaven, leaves heaven sins against heaven. A sinner of earth is one entangled in earthly offenses.

“Therefore I have loved.” As if he said: “And because the law, whether given in paradise, implanted naturally, or repeated in writing, has made all persons transgressors, therefore I have loved thy testimonies which are in the law”—that is, testimonies concerning thy grace—“so that my righteousness may not be mine but thine.” For the law is useful in sending us to grace, not only by attesting it but also through the fear of transgression which it has exposed. Therefore, he says, I have loved thy testimonies because the law leads to grace, which alone sets free. Having recognized the grace of God, which alone frees from transgression of the law, he prays:

### Verse 8 (120)

> “Pierce my flesh with thy fear; for I have feared thy judgments.”

[Col. 1103A] **Pierce through.** [Aug., Ambr.] As though he said: “I have loved your testimonies. And do you pierce through my flesh with your chaste fear”—the fear which casts out servile fear (1 John IV), by which punishment is feared but righteousness is not loved—“so that I may be crucified with Christ through fear; for I have feared your judgments.” Thus fill me with fear, and perfect in me the fear which I possess, so that it may suffice to crucify my flesh; that is, so that I may be willing and able to imitate the gibbet of your cross, surrendering my flesh to be pierced with the nails of martyrdom for your name.

Or rather thus: with your chaste fear, which remains for ever, pierce through my flesh; that is, restrain carnal desires and fleshly lusts. He says *flesh* because he did not know transgression to arise from it. [Cassiod., Aug.] Note that he says, “pierce through,” as though saying: Do not merely bind it like a thief or a wild beast, [Col. 1103B] but pierce it through. Whoever loves the testimonies pierces through his flesh. I say, “with your fear,” because fear of the Law cannot accomplish this. For I had already feared your judgments when the Law threatened punishment; that is, servile fear of the Law first went before in me as a pedagogue, leading toward chaste fear. But it does not crucify the flesh, because the will to sin remains alive, and the deed would follow if impunity were hoped for. For such a person would prefer sin to be permitted, and grieves that it is not permitted because the Law forbids it; for he does not take spiritual delight in its good, but carnally fears the evil it threatens. Charity, however, fears to sin even if impunity follows.

The sense is: Grant me chaste fear, by which fleshly vices may be pierced through; to seek this fear I was led, as by a pedagogue, through fear of the Law—through which fear I feared your judgments.

## Comparison in Samech

**Verse 2 (114).—“My helper.”** In Hebrew it reads *SITHRI*, which some render “my hiding-place” or “my concealment”; it certainly denotes protection and refuge, that is, sure help. Hence Jerome translated “my protection.” The following word has a similar metaphor: *MAGINNI*, “my shield.”

**Verse 6 (118).—“From your judgments.”** This is how the more correct books read. Yet in the ancient writers we find “from your ordinances,” namely in Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, Arnobius, Hilary, and Cassiodorus. It is plainly a scribal error. For in the preceding verse, “I will meditate on your ordinances,” precisely the same words occur in Greek and Hebrew as in the present verse: Hebrew *HUQQUECA*, [Col. 1103D] Greek δικαιώμασί σου, δικαιώματάν σου, “your ordinances.”

Yet it should be known that in Scripture “judgments” also means God’s commandments. For Augustine testifies in *Questions on Exodus*, question 88: “Scripture indeed commonly calls that which is just a judgment.” Again, on Psalm LXXI, at the verse, “O God, give your judgment to the king” (Ps. LXXI), he shows at length that *judgment* and *righteousness* have the same force.

We might further establish this from the preceding verse in this Psalm: “I have not departed from your judgments, because you,” etc., where judgments are understood as God’s commandments, which are his ordinances, as Hilary and Cassiodorus explain; although they may also be understood as judgments which exact punishment or confer rewards. Hilary says:

> “The following verse teaches what sort of keeping of God’s word there ought to be. For it follows: ‘I have not departed from your judgments, because you laid down the Law for me.’ This, therefore, is true keeping: not to turn oneself aside in any direction from God’s judgments, nor to decline even by the slightest deviation, but always to remain intent and unmoved upon that in which one has taken one’s stand. He does not depart because God had established the Law for him.”

So Hilary. Now Cassiodorus:

> “He says, then, ‘from your judgments,’ that is, from what your holy will has established and has given to us as a rule of life. Not to depart from these is to stand in the straight way. Therefore it is foolish to contend anxiously over this point.”

**“Their thought.”** Nebiensis, Sanctes, Münster, Pellican, and the Campensian edition translate “fraud” or “deceit.” Jerome, Pratensis, and Campensis: “thought”; the interpreters for Cajetan: “wisdom.” *THARMITHAM.*

**Verse 7 (119).—“Transgressors.”** All translate “dross,” “drosses,” or “rusts.” It should be known that the Septuagint, as appears, distorted the Hebrew word *SIGIM*, from the root *SOG*, “he departed,” so that it might be understood as “those who depart,” namely those who transgress the Law. But if *SIGIM* is taken simply, from *SIG*, it means “dross.” The Chaldean, however, has: “You shattered idols.”

[Col. 1104B] **“I reckoned.”** Or, as Jerome and Pellican have it in the second person: “you counted” or “you considered.” Others say “you destroyed” or “you caused to cease.” The Septuagint and Jerome strongly lead us to conjecture that they read *heth*, the strong aspiration, in place of *he*, the weak aspiration, although the two have sufficient similarity; nor did Sanctes leave this unmentioned under the root *SABATH*. For *HISSCHBATA* means “you reckoned”; *HISSCHABTI*, “I reckoned,” from the root *HIISCHEB*. But *HIPSCHABAT*, from the stem *SCHABATH*, in the conjugation called *hiphil*, means “you destroyed” or “you caused to cease.” In the end, the sense is worthy in either case.

**Verse 8 (120).—“Pierce through with your fear.”** Jerome and the others read the indicative: “my flesh bristled,” or “my flesh was shaken with terror because of fear.” The Septuagint read *SEMOR*, imperative or optative, rather than *SAMAR*; especially when vowel-points are not supplied, each person remains free to pronounce it either way. Nor did the Septuagint translate outside the word’s meaning. For the noun derived from that verb, *MASMAR*, signifies “a nail,” as in Isaiah XLI: “He strengthened it with nails so that it should not be moved”; *BEMASMERIM*, “with nails.”

## Ain

**“I have done judgment.”** [Cassiod., Alcuin.] He who said above that he hated the wicked, in this sixteenth letter asks for Christ’s coming, because it is time for the proud to be destroyed. And because at that time one must watch and act shrewdly against the enemies of the Christian faith, the letter *ain*, interpreted “eye,” is fittingly set before this octonary. It is understood as the spiritual eye which foresees what must or must not be maintained, since here it is shown keen in discerning the Law against heretics [Col. 1104D] and corrupters.

[Ambr.] There is also another eye, namely that of the body; if this passage is understood of it, another interpretation of this letter is appropriate. For *Ain* is also interpreted “spring,” which agrees, because the origin of tears lies in the eyes, and the eye is, as it were, a source either of sin or of righteousness. If, when you see a woman’s beauty, you praise the work of the Creator, your eye has been a source of righteousness. Likewise, if you see the possessions of orphans and repel their invaders, your eye has been a source of righteousness. But if, seeing an orphan’s field planted with vines and rich in crops, you are kindled by the torches of avarice, cross the boundaries of the fathers, and wickedly rush upon undefended property, your eye has been a source and origin of sin and eternal death.

Therefore this man, foreseeing in the prophetic Spirit the judgment of God—in which the good person does not perish [Col. 1105A] and the evil person does not escape—relying on a good conscience, says:

**Verse 1 (121).—“I have done judgment and righteousness; do not hand me over to those who calumniate me.”**

“I have done judgment,” etc. [Ambr., Aug., Ambr., Aug.] As though he said: “Pierce through the flesh”; and, with the flesh pierced through, I have done judgment by discerning in judgments, and righteousness in works. Behold, he who above asked for his flesh to be pierced through—the flesh which hinders judgment—now performs judgment, which by its very name indicates what is right, although in ordinary speech we are accustomed to say, “The judgment is right” or “wrong.”

Righteousness, however, is more a virtue of the soul; whoever possesses it judges rightly. But because no one performs it in a human being except God, here the term *righteousness* signifies not righteousness itself but its work. Thus “I have done righteousness” means: “I have performed a work of righteousness.”

[Col. 1105B] Note that saying this is not the boast of a vainglorious and insolent person, but the rightly presumed assertion of an innocent life, lest he seem worthy of being handed over to evildoers. It is therefore a defense, not arrogance. Yet one who, having crucified the flesh, does judgment and righteousness must pray that, through fear of suffering evils, he may not yield to enemies and so commit evils. For he who granted victory over the flesh, lest one be drawn by pleasure, also grants patience, lest one be broken by pain.

“Do not hand me over.” As though he said: “I have done judgment; therefore do not hand me over by abandoning me in respect of the soul, even if you hand me over in respect of the body, to those who calumniate me”—that is, to those who oppose me for this very reason, because I have done judgment and righteousness.

[Ambr.] As a human being, he fears amid the devil’s warfare, knowing that the war against spiritual wickedness is unequal to him. Therefore, not trusting in himself, he humbly asks:

**Verse 2 (122).—“Undertake for your servant for good; let not the proud calumniate me.”**

“Undertake for your servant for good.” [Gl. int., Cassiod.] As though he said: “Do not hand me over, but rather undertake, as a patron, your servant—not another’s servant.” He fittingly calls himself a servant, since this is an indication of deliverance. A *servant* (*servus*) is so called from being preserved (*servando*), because one taken captive is preserved from impending death.

[Aug., Ambr., Aug.] “Undertake,” I say, “for good,” one whom they drive toward evil; as though saying: “May it benefit me also that I am your servant, not another’s.” Precious is this servitude, which consists in the outlay of virtues. Therefore I fear being handed over, because calumniators rise up proudly against my innocence.

[Col. 1105D] “Let not the proud calumniate me.” The expression “let them not calumniate” is a Greek idiom, less customary among us. Its sense is: “Let them not seize me by calumniating.” The greatest calumny is what the proud say: that one who has died is worshipped by us. The proud are Jews and Gentiles, heretics and schismatics; pride has cut all of them off from Christ’s body. Each has particular calumnies against Christian humility; the greatest is the one just mentioned.

The devil also calumniates, saying: “Does Job fear God for nothing?” (Job I). But the calumnies of all these people, like the poisons of serpents, are conquered if one looks with faith upon him who was crucified in the likeness of sinful flesh, prefigured by the bronze serpent which Moses raised in the wilderness, so that those struck by serpents might be healed by looking at it (Num. XXI; John III).

**Verse 3 (123).—“My eyes have failed for your salvation, and for the word of your righteousness.”**

“My eyes,” [Ambr., Aug., Ambr.] the inward eyes, have failed from themselves, thirstily and ardently gazing toward your salvation, that is, toward Christ. These are the eyes of the soul, not of the body, which fail toward Christ, foreseeing future punishments so as to proclaim the repentance sinners must perform; or seeing Christ’s grace, through which the kingdom of heaven is given with absolute certainty to those who hope.

The former are eyes of punishment; the latter, eyes of grace. Perhaps the eyes of punishment belong to the imperfect soul; but the purer and more sincere eyes of graces belong to the perfect soul. One and the same soul may also [Col. 1106B] possess an eye of punishments and an eye of grace, the one right and the other left. Therefore he said “eyes” in the plural.

But this man’s eyes have failed toward Christ, [Aug., Ambr., Aug.] while, mindful of human weakness, he desires divine grace in Christ, that he may be righteous; and they have failed “for the word of your righteousness.” By “the word of righteousness” he means the Gospel words which Christ was to speak in order to justify us. For we are God’s righteousness in Christ Jesus, as the Apostle says (2 Cor. V).

**Verse 4 (124).—“Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your ordinances.”**

“Deal with your servant.” [Ambr., Cassiod., Hilar., Cassiod.] As though he said: “Not only do not hand me over, but deal with your servant, not according to my righteousness but according to your mercy.” There is no weariness in asking where the giver’s generosity is present. Whoever seeks according to mercy asks for infinite things.

Note that he says, “Deal with your servant.” Here he indicates free will, which is joined to grace. Note also that he says “your,” as though “not another’s”; for whoever is another’s servant immediately falls. And what does he ask? “Teach me your ordinances,” [Aug., Cassiod.] by which you make people righteous, not by which a human being makes himself righteous. He continually asks for the ordinances he has already received, as in “Give us this day our daily bread,” etc. (Luke II).

**Verse 5 (125).—“I am your servant; give me understanding, that I may know your testimonies.”**

[Col. 1106D] “For I am your servant,” not a servant of sin, [Ambr., Aug., Gl. int.] because it did not go well when I was free unto myself. And because I am your servant, therefore give me understanding. He already has understanding, but seeks fuller understanding, that he may always receive and, in a sense, always drink from the spring of eternal light.

I say, “give,” certainly so that “I may know your testimonies,” because this is needed against calumniators. Therefore give understanding, because now it is:

**Verse 6 (126).—“It is time for you, O Lord, to act; they have destroyed your Law.”**

“It is time for you, O Lord”—or “for the Lord”—to act, no longer merely to command, because the commands of the Law could not benefit. [Aug., Ambr.] For the world was lame; and, with the faltering step of faith, it wavered, having spent all its substance upon physicians who achieved nothing, like that woman in the Gospel.

Therefore it is time to act, not to command. “There is a time to keep silence, and a time to speak” (Eccl. III). The time of the Law is called a time of speaking, when there was a voice of words without the working of grace. But the time of the Gospel is the time for those legal observances to be silent and for spiritual things to be done.

[Aug., Ambr., Aug.] The time of fullness, then, is the day of salvation; it is time for the Lord to act: namely, to ascend the cross for us, undergo death, take away sin and death, and restore life. It is time because the proud Jews, presuming upon themselves and wishing to establish their own righteousness, destroyed your Law by transgressing it, acting otherwise than had been commanded. Hence all who were humbled fled to the aid of grace; and thus, the Law having been destroyed, it was time for mercy to come through Christ, so that where sin abounded, grace might abound still more (Rom. V).

**Verse 7 (127).—“Therefore I have loved your commandments above gold and topaz.”**

“Therefore,” namely because it is the time of grace, “I have loved your commandments.” [Alcuin., Cassiod.] Or thus: in the prophetic Spirit this man foresees the times of Antichrist or Antiochus, when there will be tribulation and the iniquity of many will abound. Since he sees that in those times God’s Law is to be defiled, he cries that it is time to come to aid, lest the people’s salvation perish, saying: “O Lord, it is time to act”—that is, to help, not to delay what is necessary—“for they have destroyed your Law.” Therefore, because they destroy it, the more they destroy it, the more I have loved your commandments.

[Aug.] Grace has done this: that commandments, which could not be fulfilled through fear, may be fulfilled through love. I have loved them “above gold and topaz”; this is what he says elsewhere, “above gold and very precious stone.” Topaz is said to be a very precious stone. Formerly, when grace lay hidden under the veil in the Old Testament, people tried to keep the commandments for the sake of an earthly reward; yet they did not keep them, because they did not love them. But when they are loved above gold, every earthly reward is worthless and cannot be compared with them. And because I have loved them:

**Verse 8 (128).—“Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments; I hated every wicked way.”**

“Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments,” [Aug.] to which I clung by love, so that I might become upright from upright things. From this follows that “I hated every wicked way,” which is like a shipwreck of the straight way. Whoever loves the straight way necessarily hates the wicked way. Otherwise he cannot be directed toward all the commandments.

## Comparison in Ain

**Verse 2 (122).—“Undertake for your servant.”** Jerome, Pratensis, and the translator associated with Campensis have: “Pledge yourself,” or “command a pledge to be given for your servant.” Sanctes: “make your servant agreeable”; Münster: “make good sweet for your servant.” Nebiensis, Pellican, and the interpreters for Cajetan agree with these. Campensis, however: “urge your servant.” Each meaning answers the Hebrew word *AROB*. For one who pledges himself for someone else in a sense takes on the person of the one for whom he gives pledge.

[Col. 1108A] Moreover, when a servant is undertaken “for good,” he is fitted for and drawn toward that good by desiring its sweetness.

**“It is time, O Lord, to act.”** In the Hebrew the literal reading is “for the Lord,” *LADONAI*, and in Greek τῷ κυρίῳ, “for the Lord.” Jerome, however, translates it very plainly in the vocative: “It is time for you to act, O Lord,” as though we ought to cry to the Lord: “It is time to act,” or “It is time for you to act, O Lord.” Münster has added an element of his own, translating: “It is time for the Lord to execute judgment.” This does not fit equally well with the exposition of the Fathers. The Chaldean interprets thus: “It is time to do the will of God.”

## Phe

[Note: [Col. 1107] *Phe*, according to Jerome, means “mouth,” from *mouth*, not from *bone*.]

**“Your testimonies, O Lord, are wonderful.”** [Cass., Alcuin., Ambr.] In this seventeenth letter he says that he opened his mouth and drew in the spirit, so that his prayer might be heard; and that he wept because the Law was not kept by the Jews. Therefore the letter *Phe*, interpreted “he erred,” is fittingly placed before this octonary, because here he grieves with those who, by wandering from the way of truth, calumniate; to them he sets forth how he searches the Law and what understanding he has in it.

Because *Phe* means “he erred,” a tearful Psalm is rightly set under this letter: namely, “Look upon me and have mercy upon me,” “redeem me from human calumnies,” “make your face shine.” But because the Desired One comes slowly, he also adds: “My eyes have poured forth streams of waters.” In Jeremiah’s *Lamentations* too, a more tearful sequence occurs under this letter, when he says: “Zion has stretched out her hands; there is none to comfort her” (Lam. I). And likewise: “All your enemies have opened their mouth against you; they have hissed and gnashed their teeth” [Col. 1108C] (Ps. XXXIV).

Therefore, as Jeremiah under this letter wept for his nation’s destruction, so David here grieves for the people’s error, but without despair. The literal exposition is as follows. As though he said: “I am ashamed of my error. I do not dare speak to you, the living God; yet by the testimonies of your mercy you promise pardon, and by titles of many acts of forgiveness you summon me to hope for pardon. For:

**Verse 1 (129).—“Your testimonies, O Lord, are wonderful; therefore my soul has searched them out.”**

“Your testimonies are wonderful,” [Ambr., Aug.] when I see what you formerly did in Abraham, the children of Israel, and others. “Therefore my soul has searched them out.” Because it believes them wonderful, it seeks them by diligent inquiry.

Or by “testimonies” he means these created things which bear witness to God’s [Col. 1108D] goodness and greatness. As though he said: “Therefore I ask that you deal with me according to your mercy, because your testimonies are wonderful,” namely, testimonies of goodness and power. For heaven, earth, and all his visible works bear witness to God’s goodness and greatness. Although some of these have become cheap through mortal use, nevertheless, if they are properly considered, they are worthy of admiration. This admiration does not terrify but gives this man cause to search. “Therefore my soul has searched them out,” as though it had become more inquisitive through the very difficulty of investigation. For the more hidden causes anything has, the more wonderful it is.

Or he calls God’s commandments his testimonies, and the sense is: “Therefore I have loved your commandments, because your testimonies”—that is, your commandments—“are wonderful.” God’s commandments are testimonies of his goodness and are wonderful. For through them God’s power [Col. 1109A] has become known to blessed angels and to human beings. [Cassiod., Aug.] Therefore they must be searched out. Thus, because they are wonderful, my soul has searched them out. They may always be searched, because, though the Good One commanded good things, he nevertheless gave them to persons whom they cannot make alive and whom no righteousness would come from a good Law.

**Verse 2 (130).—“The unfolding of your words gives light and gives understanding to little ones.”**

“The unfolding of your words,” [Ambr., Cassiod., Aug.] I say—that is, those which my soul searched out—and the searching soul finds this: that the unfolding of your words enlightens me as I search. That is, the new Law, declaring the figures of the old Law and dispelling our darkness, enlightens the one who searches and thus enables progress.

By “words” he means those uttered in prophecy by the saints, such as: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear” (Isa. VII), and things of that kind. Their unfolding is Christ’s coming and the other things which have been visibly fulfilled in the Gospel as the prophets foretold. This unfolding gives inward understanding to the little ones—that is, the humble.

Therefore do not presume upon yourself, and you will understand why the good Law was given by the Good One, although it does not give life: it was given so that it might make the great into little ones, and that those distrustful of their own strength might flee to grace. This man has found this because he is a little one. These are the wonderful testimonies which the soul of this little one has searched out.

[Col. 1109C] [Ambr., Alcuin., Aug.] For only little ones are enlightened. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. II). And elsewhere: “I came into this world for judgment, that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind” (John IX).

No one can rightly perform God’s commandments unless love has been poured into the heart through the Holy Spirit. This man too confesses this, saying:

**Verse 3 (131).—“I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit, because I desired your commandments.”**

“I opened my mouth.” [Aug., Alcuin.] As though he said: “When I desired to perform the commandments, I had no source from which I could do so. Therefore I opened my mouth by asking, seeking, [Col. 1109D] and knocking; I opened it by confessing, expanding my reason.” And, thirsting, I drew in by good merits—that is, I drank in—the Spirit, by whom I might perform the commandments. For after the understanding which he said above had been given him, if anyone wishes to keep the commandments, he cannot do so without the Holy Spirit.

[Haym., Ambr.] This is said by comparison with someone who, in heat, catches a breath of air. Or here “mouth” is understood as the mouth of the soul, which cries to God in silence, as Moses, though silent in voice, cried in spirit (Exod. XIV). Susanna also, while praying, silently cried out; she was not heard by human beings, but her voice resounded before God (Dan. XIII). This mouth, that is, the entrance of the mind, is opened when we wish to learn.

[Cassiod.] A person draws in the Spirit when he is filled with a steadfast desire for God. Thus the weak man opened his mouth; the strong man drew in the Spirit—that is, the power to act which he could not possess by himself. And how he opened it and drew it in, he adds: “because I desired to know or to do your commandments” [Aug.]. But because the more sweetly he experiences them, the more ardently he thirsts, he still asks, saying:

**Verse 4 (132).—“Look upon me and have mercy upon me, according to the judgment of those who love your name.”**

“Look upon me,” [Gl. int., Ambr., Gl. int.] as though he said: “Because I desired your commandments, therefore look upon me”—that is, give me the Spirit. And because he sometimes looks in anger in order to destroy, as he looked upon Sodom (Gen. XVIII), he adds: “And have mercy upon me, whenever I suffer.”

Have mercy, I say, “according to the judgment of those who love your name” [Col. 1110B] [Aug., Cassiod.], that is, according to the judgment which you exercised toward those who love you, because, in order that they might love you, you first loved them (1 John IV). Or it is God’s judgment to give the help of mercy to those who love him, lest they be deceived by themselves.

**Verse 5 (133).—“Direct my steps according to your word, and let no unrighteousness have dominion over me.”**

“My steps.” [Aug., Ambr., Aug.] As though he said: “Deal with me as you are accustomed to deal with those who love you. And direct my steps according to your word,” that is, make me upright according to your promise. Or: “Direct my steps according to your word,” that is, direct the movements of my soul according to your commands, lest they be led astray by vices. The more charity reigns, the less unrighteousness will rule.

Therefore he adds: “Let no unrighteousness have dominion over me.” [Hilar., Cassiod.] He knew that one walking would be tempted. Therefore he did not say, “Let it be wholly excluded,” but “Let it not rule,” because it cannot be wholly excluded. Sin is in the body, but let it not reign. He then adds “every,” because it is of no avail to have kept the Law in other matters if one has stumbled in one. For whoever keeps the whole Law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all, as James says (Jas. II). And:

**Verse 6 (134).—“Redeem me from the calumnies of men, that I may keep your commandments.”**

“Redeem me from the calumnies of men,” [Aug., Cassiod., Ambr.] that is: having given the Holy Spirit, prevent the calumnies of men—that is, false accusations—from overcoming me through terrors and leading me from your commandments to their evil deeds, by which Christians are harassed everywhere.

Calumnies, therefore, are controversies against truth, which he prays may be turned away so that he may search out the commandments. Of these, then, is the more severe temptation: that is, the more grievous temptation is one of them. Not every temptation is calumny, but only the more severe kind. Temptation can exist without calumny; calumny, however, contains temptation within itself. There is also human temptation, lighter than we can bear; and this is not calumny. The more severe temptation which is calumny not only invents falsehoods but also discolors deeds that were done piously—as the unchaste mistress did to Joseph (Gen. XXXIX), and the two elders to Susanna [Col. 1111A] (Dan. XIII).

[Aug., Ambr.] Against these calumnies one must keep silence. “Redeem me,” I say, because if you accomplish this for me by granting patience, then amid the calumnies themselves I shall be free to keep your commandments. For one oppressed by calumnies does not easily keep the commandments. And:

**Verse 7 (135).—“Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your ordinances.”**

“Make your face shine,” [Ambr.] that is, make your presence manifest by helping, “upon your servant,” so that the servant may shine like earth beneath the sun: as this earth shines through the use of the visible sun, so may his servant’s mind shine with the light of the invisible Sun of righteousness, Christ.

Or thus: “Make your face shine upon your servant.” He prays to see the face, not veiled as it was for the Jews, [Col. 1111B] but to see the truth purely. Hence Moses put a veil over his face, upon which the children of Israel could not gaze because of the glory of his face (2 Cor. XIII); his face appeared horned to them (Exod. XXXIV). This signified that the Jews cannot see the true brightness of the Law under the veil of figures, namely the brightness found in spiritual understanding.

But this veil was removed in Christ’s passion. Hence the veil was torn at Christ’s passion (Matt. XXVII). Therefore on the day of the Passion the formerly veiled cross is uncovered, because through the cross the mysteries concealed in the Law and spiritual understanding hidden under the veil of the letter are disclosed.

The sense is: “Make your face shine upon your servant,” [Ambr.] that is, give me spiritual understanding of the Law. Or he here prays for Christ’s coming, by whose face the darkness was illumined. Thus “your face,” etc., means: “Send your Son, by whose shining grace the righteous are suffused.” “And teach me your ordinances,” so that I may perform them, [Aug.] because everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to Christ (John VI). Therefore whoever does not come—that is, does not act—has not learned. For one who hears, even if he retains what he hears in memory, must by no means be considered to have learned if he does not act.

Recalling the pain of his repentant transgression, he says:

**Verse 8 (136).—“My eyes have poured forth streams of waters, because they have not kept your Law.”**

“Streams of waters.” [Gl. int., Cassiod.] As though he said: “Do as I have prayed; and you ought to do so, because my eyes, through which death formerly entered—for death enters through the windows (Jer. IX)—have poured forth streams of waters,” [Ambr., Cassiod., Aug.] that is, outpourings of tears, hyperbolically speaking: copious tears, like the flowing waters of springs, in remembrance of sins.

This is so “because they have not kept,” namely those eyes themselves, “your Law”; eyes which, had they kept the commandments, would have had joy. That “they have not kept” should be referred to the eyes is clear from the fact that other books read: “Because I have not kept your Law.”

[Cassiod., Aug.] Or it can be referred to the calumniators, as was said at the beginning of the octonary. As though he said: “Therefore I wept, because the calumniating Jews have not kept your Law.” Or according to another reading: “My eyes descended by streams of waters.” Those eyes of mine which formerly ascended through pride descended by streams of waters; here the preposition “into” or “through” is understood, as when it is said of someone, “He descended the pool” or “the mountains,” without *into* or *through*. The eyes fittingly descend through the humility of repentance when they had formerly been raised through pride, while they wished to establish their own righteousness. Therefore, having been confounded by transgression, they descend from that exaltation by weeping, so that they may deserve God’s righteousness.

Or according to another reading found in certain manuscripts: “My eyes passed beyond streams of waters.” This is said emphatically: “My eyes passed beyond streams of waters,” that is, they wept more than the waters that remain after flowing out from their sources. He weeps thus because by such weeping grace is obtained, blotting out iniquity and assisting the will.

## Comparison in Phe

**Verse 2.—“The unfolding.”** Jerome and others translate *pethah* as “door,” “beginning,” or “opening.” The Septuagint rendered the metaphor: “The opening of God’s words.” For no one enters the inner chambers of divine meanings unless they have been clearly unfolded and understood.

## Sade

[Note: [Col. 1111D] *Sade*, according to Jerome, means “righteousness.”]

**“You are righteous, O Lord.”** [Cassiod.] The flesh conquered and pierced with nails, and sins wiped away through tears, in this eighteenth letter he praises God’s judgments and reveres his fiery words; asking for understanding by which he may live and be consoled. Therefore the letter *sade*, interpreted “consolation,” is fittingly set before this octonary. For he who above was sorrowful over error and poured forth tears here consoles himself through God’s righteousness.

[Col. 1112C] Consolation appropriately follows streaming tears and the grave weeping of pain; it is threefold. Those in sorrow need consolation, which comes through God’s mercy; those who have paid the penalties for their crimes hope for pardon; and those who have washed away sins by tears deserve rest.

[Ambr.] The first consolation belongs to those placed amid grief and misery, who consider God’s mercy, recalling: “God does not forget to have mercy” (Ps. LXXVI). The second and third consolations belong to those in sins who consider God’s righteousness. Some are in sins and do not know that they are, and God punishes them for sins hidden from themselves. Therefore they hope that, if they are in sins without knowing it, those sins will nevertheless be remitted once the price of guilt has been paid in punishments, provided they bear the punishment patiently, because he who punishes is just. This is their second consolation.

Again, others recognize their sins, make satisfaction for them, and weep. Hence they hope for pardon; theirs is the third consolation. The first consolation, therefore, is through God’s mercy, as we are taught in Jeremiah, where Jerusalem cries mournfully to the captive Jews: “Go, depart; for I have been left desolate. Be of good courage. Children, cry to the Lord, and he will deliver you from the hand of your enemies” (Baruch IV).

The second is through punishment, where—even if faith, that is, consciousness of sin, is lacking—punishment nevertheless makes satisfaction and brings relief. We are taught this kind of consolation in Isaiah’s words: “Comfort my people, priests; speak to the heart of Jerusalem: her sin has been paid, for she has received double from the hand of the Lord” (Isa. XL).

[Col. 1113A] The third is through satisfaction, when a crime is washed away by tears. Hence we are certain of pardon, as is found in this passage and in many others. As though he said: “Therefore I weep thus over my sins, because I know, O:

**Verse 1 (137).—“You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is upright.”**

“O Lord,” [Aug., Ambr.] you who punish are righteous in all things. This is said by the righteous man who, pouring forth tears and paying for sins with severe punishment, is not overcome by weariness nor exhausted by labor. At the beginning of his discourse he accuses himself. But whoever does not look upon his own sins thinks himself unjustly burdened; whereas the good person accuses himself and says that worthy things are inflicted upon him by the Just One, in whom he also hopes. For as he punishes justly, so he rewards the one who endures.

“And your judgment is upright,” you who command the sinner to afflict himself. Otherwise the sinner would arrogate pardon to himself. He fittingly says “upright.” For whatever is done by him is done by upright judgment, and this is the consolation of the righteous.

By this confession Daniel conquered the beasts (Dan. VI), and the three youths the flames (Dan. III). By this same confession Jonah, enclosed in the belly of the beast and scarcely having a passage for breath, deserved to be delivered from it (Jonah II). Holy Job too, after his children had been killed and he had been stripped of his lost estate (Job I), obtained by this same confession that his possessions should be restored to him with increase (Job XLII). And:

[Col. 1113C] **Verse 2 (138).—“You have commanded righteousness—your testimonies—and your truth exceedingly.”**
You commanded exceedingly—indeed, very greatly—[Alcuin], that is, through many persons and over a long time, for the sake of the weak—justice, namely your testimonies, and your truth [Cassiodorus, Augustine]: that justice which is your testimonies, and your truth. Many things are here impressed upon us which can terrify sinners. For upright judgment, justice, and truth are to be feared by everyone who sins, since whoever is condemned is condemned justly; nor can he complain against a just God. He calls the testimonies of God “justice,” because God proves himself just by commanding justice. This justice is also truth, because by such testimonies God becomes known—namely, by commanding justice. Truth, therefore, is that by which he is made known truly. The sense is: You have commanded justice—justice, I say, which is your testimonies—because, by commanding them, you have proved yourself just; and I call that justice your truth, because by such testimonies you are made known.

[Cassiodorus] Or thus: you commanded, that is, prescribed, your testimonies—that is, commandments issued under solemn attestation. These testimonies, I say, contain your justice and your truth. For they contain justice, because they determine all things impartially; and truth, because they fulfill the promises. “Exceedingly” applies to both. “Exceedingly,” that is, to justice and truth, so that the sense is: I call justice exceedingly impressed upon us in those testimonies; and I call truth exceedingly impressed upon us in the same. To impress justice upon us exceedingly [Col. 1114A] is strictness; to impress truth upon us exceedingly is a safeguard. That is: these two are impressed upon us for this purpose—that, fearing him who judges strictly, we may live strictly, and that we may cautiously await the promises of him who promises graciously. And because you commanded justice, therefore:

### VERSE 3 (139).—“My zeal has made me waste away, because my enemies have forgotten your words.”

My zeal, [Ambrose, Augustine, Ambrose, Cassiodorus], that is, charity. Or, “your zeal,” because he is zealous for God, not for himself; yet it is one and the same zeal, that is, charity. It is a person’s zeal because it is within him; and it is so called because he has it from God and refers it to God. That zeal, I say, made me waste away. This is what is elsewhere said of Christ: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” [Col. 1114B] (Ps. 68).

With this zeal this man wastes away bodily. [Ambrose] This zeal belongs to love, not envy: a good zeal maintained for the house of God, which he could not endure to see torn apart by the faithless. With this zeal Phinehas son of Eleazar burned, when he killed those joined in adultery through a union forbidden to them; by this act he redeemed all from punishment and appeased the Lord’s wrath (Num. 25). For it is better that many should be delivered through the condemnation of a few than that more should be endangered through their acquittal.

Then, as though someone should ask, “Why do you waste away so?” he adds: because your enemies have forgotten your words. In this they are enemies, even if in worldly terms they are friends—those for whom this man is zealous toward God.

### VERSE 4 (140).—“Your utterance is exceedingly refined by fire, and your servant has loved it.”

[Col. 1114C] “Your utterance is exceedingly refined by fire.” [Ambrose] As though he said: This zeal is mine because your utterance is inflamed by the Holy Spirit. For it purifies hearts as a furnace does gold; it kindles love for God; and, against the ungodly, it also enlightens its hearers (Luke 12). This is the fire that the Lord came to cast upon the earth. Warmed by this fire, Jeremiah says: “There was a blazing fire in my bones” (Jer. 20). With this fire the bush that Moses saw burned, yet was not consumed (Exod. 3). For the divine word burns in order to correct; it does not consume the sinner’s conscience in order to destroy it.

Warmed by this fire, Cleopas and the other disciple said: “Was not our heart burning within us?” (Luke 24). This fire descended from heaven upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2), because those who proclaim the utterances [Col. 1114D] of God ought to burn with this fire. Hence the red threads hang from the two tongues of the high priest’s mitre. For just as the two tongues signify that they ought to bring forth new things and old from the treasury of their heart (Matt. 13), so, in the red color of the threads, is represented the fire of charity which they ought to possess in themselves and kindle in others.

Hence, after Peter’s threefold profession of love for the Lord, pastoral care is entrusted to him. Hence also the Roman pontiff is clothed in a red cope, because he ought wholly to burn with the fire of charity, to do everything out of charity, and not to fail even in willingness for martyrdom. He bears the person of Christ, whose garment is like that of one treading in the winepress, who says: “I have trodden the winepress alone” (Isa. 63).

Then he adds: [Col. 1115A] “Exceedingly.” [Gloss, Augustine] As though he said: It is refined by fire exceedingly, so that it even burns the body. And therefore your servant—whoever he may be—has loved it. This man rightly is zealous against those who have forgotten God’s words, because he burned to bring them to that which he loved most ardently. And although this is so:

### VERSE 5 (141).—“I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your ordinances.”

I am young and despised, [Augustine, Ambrose], that is, younger and held in contempt; yet I have not forgotten your ordinances, as those older men—namely, my enemies—have. The person who accuses himself justifies God; this occurs through humility, and such humility is more remarkable in a young man.

This may literally apply to many saints [Col. 1115B] and especially to the people of grace. For many saints were trained in hardships from their earliest youth and despised by their own people: Joseph among his brothers (Gen. 37), and David among his sons (1 Sam. 16). So too the new people of grace, which follows the people of the Law in age but precedes it in faith. This people is despised and therefore greater, because God chose things held in contempt (1 Cor. 2). [Augustine] But he rejects those who wish to establish their own righteousness (Rom. 10).

These are the two peoples struggling in Rebekah’s womb, of whom it is said: “The greater shall serve the lesser” (Gen. 25). This lesser people has not forgotten God’s ordinances, while its greater enemies have forgotten them. Rightly so, because, not knowing God’s righteousness, they sought their own. This people [Col. 1115C] has not forgotten, because it sought not its own righteousness but God’s righteousness, of which it now also says:

### VERSE 6 (142).—“Your righteousness is righteousness forever, and your law is truth.”

Your righteousness. [Ambrose, Cassiodorus] As though he said: Rightly I have not forgotten, because your righteousness, O God, is righteousness forever. The righteousness of God alone is eternal; human righteousness is temporal, but God’s is eternal, because whoever follows it will rejoice forever. This is not true of the righteousness of the Jews. And your law is truth. The Law of God given through Moses is altogether true, because through it comes knowledge of sin (Rom. 7), and it bears witness to God’s righteousness (Rom. 3).

Or, that law is truth [Augustine, Ambrose], that is, spiritual, even if it is not so to the Jews. Or it may be understood of the law of the Gospel. And [Col. 1115D] your law—namely, that of the Gospel—is truth, not shadow or figure, as the Mosaic law was, but reality. [Cassiodorus, Augustine] Or “law” may generally mean his commandments. The sense is: your law is truth because whoever follows the law is fulfilled with truth, which is Christ. For the sake of this law the lesser suffers from the greater. Hence he adds:

### VERSE 7.—“Tribulation and anguish have found me; your commandments are my meditation.”

Tribulation, and so forth. [Ambrose, Cassiodorus, Augustine] As though he said: Your law is truth, and for the sake of this law tribulation and anguish—which are gifts to the righteous for laying aside the burdens of sins—have found me waiting and prepared. However fiercely they rage, your commandments [Col. 1116A] are my meditation: that is, my remedy against tribulations. And so that I may not fail in tribulation, give me understanding in it.

In tribulation this man asks for understanding, that he may know how insignificant is what persecutors take away. For even if they end his life, he shall live forever. Hence he adds, “and I shall live,” truly and rightly, because he sets righteousness, which remains forever, above temporal things.

### VERSE 8 (144).—“The equity of your testimonies is forever; give me understanding, and I shall live.”

Equity, or righteousness—as though he said: And rightly I shall live, because your testimonies are equity for me [Augustine, Hilary], or righteousness abiding forever, in tribulation. As though he said: Your righteousness in tribulation consists in *martyria*, that is, testimonies. That is: your eternal righteousness is the reason why, in tribulation, I keep the testimonies—that is, the martyr-witnesses.

Or thus, so that the text may be read in sequence: “Tribulation and anguish have found me,” and, when I am placed in tribulation, your testimonies are equity or righteousness—or are righteous forever—that is, they are for me a cause of eternal righteousness. [Cassiodorus] Such is this man’s hope against tribulations, which are temporal. And amid these tribulations, give me understanding and I shall live. By this—that is, by understanding—he surpasses the elders.

Observe that he who above was called younger now, more mature than the elders, seeks understanding amid adversities: that he may know these things to be passing and may know how to purchase life thereby; [Ambrose] that he may know how slippery this life is, be merciful to one who errs, know the common goods of the world, know its miseries, [Col. 1116C] and thus seek the harbor. Understanding is perfect virtue if a person carries out in deeds what he grasps by the mind.

## COLLATION ON SADE

### VERSE 4 (140).—“Your utterance is refined by fire.”

Jerome and others translate “tested,” “examined,” or “purified”: *tzeruphah*. The Septuagint aptly made clear by its translation that this testing is performed by the fire of the Holy Spirit, in order that it may kindle and inflame.

## QOPH

[Note: [Col. 1115D] According to Jerome, *Qoph* is interpreted “calling.”]

“ I cried.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] In this nineteenth letter he promises to seek God’s ordinances, adding that he knows God’s testimonies to be founded forever [Note: [Col. 1116D] From Augustine, *Sermon 85, On Time*.]. And because the more a person wishes to persist in good things, the more the devil attempts to seduce him and shut him up amid evils so that he cannot breathe [Col. 1116D], the remedy is to cry out to God.

[Alcuin, Ambrose] Therefore, after the error and the consolation received above, this man, more harshly shut in, cries here more earnestly. Accordingly, the letter *qoph*, interpreted “confinement,” is fittingly placed before this octave. Or consider that the meaning is the same: one who is shut in ought to look about himself and not disguise the cause of the danger.

A person is shut in when, through swelling of the inward parts and blockage of breath, the processes of inhaling and exhaling are constricted. So also one who is distressed in spirit and hard pressed by adversities is shut in. It is this confinement that is discussed here. This confinement is in the straits of the mind [Col. 1117A], as though someone could not breathe because the passage is blocked. A guilty conscience presses; the force of illness bears down on the mind’s perception; anguish cuts one off. Therefore the remedy of prayer must be sought. Cry out, then, to the physician who descended from heaven and heals the sick. Do not delay, for with him there is no postponement of healing. Do not be afraid, for he is accustomed to heal by a word, not by iron. Hence he says here:

### VERSE 1 (145).—“I cried with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord: I will seek your ordinances.”

“I cried,” [Ambrose, Gloss, Ambrose], as though he said: Enemies are on every side—not merely visible ones but, more grievously, spiritual ones. Therefore one must call upon him who can help. And so I cried with my whole heart, and so forth.

Or thus: As though he said: Give understanding—and you ought to do so, because [Col. 1117B] I cried with my whole heart. The cry of the heart, while the body’s voice is silent, is always heard by God; the cry of the heart is the intense concentration of thought. This cry is made through the elevation of thoughts and the harmony of virtues. He adds “whole,” which is the case when one thinks of nothing else.

[Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine] A divided mind does not obtain its request in such an affection of petition, whether it is held in silence or expressed aloud, if speech is needed for human beings; the effect is not despaired of. “Hear me, O Lord.” Then he adds the end to which his cry may profit: “Your ordinances,” and so forth. As though he said: I cried in order that I might seek your ordinances. To this end the cry was useful; this was what he had cried for, and this he adds, because it is not enough to cry to God: one must also seek his righteousnesses.

[Col. 1117C] Notice that he says, “I will seek,” because one who seeks is still far from doing. It does not follow that one who seeks will find, or that one who finds will do. Yet one cannot come to doing unless one seeks. The good, however, if they seek, find, as is promised in the Gospel: “Seek and you shall find” (Luke 11). Even evil people who seek find, provided they do not hate wisdom, which is God, and in which are all the things sought by those who wish to be blessed.

But of evil people who hate wisdom, Wisdom says: “The wicked shall seek me and shall not find me, for they hated wisdom” (Prov. 1, according to the Septuagint). But if they hate it, how do they seek it? They seek it not for its own sake but for the sake of something else which they love. They seek sayings of wisdom in order to possess them in teaching, not in life [Col. 1117D]; not in order to attain wisdom itself through their conduct. Rather, through its sayings they are puffed up unto vain glory by its words, and are thereby further alienated from it.

But this man, seeking in order to have it in life, says: “I will seek your ordinances”—certainly to perform them, not merely to know them.

### VERSE 2 (146).—“I cried to you: save me, and I will keep your commandments.”

“I cried.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Ambrose] Explaining what it is to cry with the whole heart, he adds, “to you”; this is to cry with one’s whole heart. For he does not cry with his whole heart who does not direct his petition to God. He then adds what he asks: “Save me”—namely, in the soul, which will keep the commandments—“and I will keep your commandments.” Where there is salvation of the soul, it causes what ought to be done to be done, and causes one to struggle even to death, if necessary [Col. 1118A]. Where this salvation is absent, weakness gives way.

In saying “I cried,” observe the readiness of his affection; in saying “I will keep your commandments,” observe the dutifulness of his diligence.

### VERSE 3 (147).—“I anticipated in immaturity and cried, because I hoped exceedingly in your words.”

“I anticipated in the untimely night,” [Augustine, Ambrose], or, as most manuscripts have it, “in immaturity.” Yet the sense is the same. “In immaturity” is scarcely found in any book. *Immaturitas* is untimely night, that is, night unsuitable for actions. For the ancients called *tempestivum* “opportune,” from *tempus*, “time.” He says literally that at night he keeps watch, driven by love of God and an intense desire to pray.

The sense is: I anticipated in immaturity and cried; or, in the untimely night [Col. 1118B] and cried—that is, with a great desire for prayer. By a kind of cry of the mind, I anticipated the hour suitable for human actions. And I hoped exceedingly in your word—or in your words—always increasing in hope, even amid adversities. And:

### VERSE 4 (148).—“My eyes anticipated dawn, that I might meditate on your utterances.”

“My eyes, directed toward you, anticipated dawn.” [Remigius, Augustine] This is like a vigorous laborer who rises before daylight in order to work well. He then adds what he had kept watch to do: “that I might meditate on your utterances.”

Or thus: “I rose before the untimely night.” Night is the whole age in which we cry out, forestalling the day on which the reward will be given. Hence: “Let us come before his face in confession” [Col. 1118C] (Ps. 94). The sense is: I rose before the untimely night and cried—that is, throughout this whole age, which is like night, by crying I forestalled the day of judgment—and I hoped exceedingly in your words. This does not change.

[Ambrose, Remigius, Augustine] “And my eyes, directed toward you, anticipated dawn”: that is, by the labor of the vineyard I forestalled the dawn of eternity. Or it may be read thus: My eyes, directed toward you by the dawn of virtues, forestalled the day—namely, of recompense—that I might meditate on your utterances. The meaning remains unchanged.

Or thus: “I rose before immaturity,” or “before the untimely night.” The time of night was immature before the time of grace came—that is, maturity itself, namely the fullness of time in which Christ came. Yet even then the Church did not keep silence but cried out in prophecy. Hence it says here: I rose before immaturity, or before the untimely night, and cried; that is, in the time of night which was before Christ’s coming, I cried out by prophesying of him who was to come. And that same Church hoped in the words of him who has power to do what he promised.

Hence it adds: “And I hoped exceedingly in your words.” The Church itself also says: “My eyes, directed toward you, anticipated dawn,” or morning. Morning is when light has arisen for those sitting in darkness; the eyes of the saints forestalled this, foreseeing that it would come. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Ambrose] These are the eyes of the heart, which believe in Christ before they are illumined by his coming. For dawn is the beginning of light, when Christ shone forth after the darkness of the age. The eyes rose before this in order to meditate upon God’s utterances in the Law and Prophets, which announce what was to come concerning Christ. [Col. 1119A] Hence he adds: “that I might meditate on your utterances.”

Or thus: “I rose before immaturity,” or, as it is in Greek, “I rose before the hour.” For no particular time is to be selected for this: it must always be done, so that Christ may always be in our heart, always on our lips and in our deeds. For although there is a time for every thing that is under heaven (Eccl. 3), there is not a time above heaven, nor above the Lord. The work is not above its author; rather, the author is above the beginning of the work.

But since the following verse expresses the time of prayer, here the time meant is more that of action than of prayer. The sense is: I forestalled the hour and cried; that is, by working for eternal things I forestalled the hour of other actions, cried in my heart, and hoped exceedingly in your words. This does not change. [Col. 1119B] He then adds concerning the time of prayer: “My eyes anticipated dawn, that I might meditate on your utterances in the morning,” that is, before daybreak. Above—that is, in the preceding verse—he said “before the hour,” according to the words, “At midnight I rose,” and so forth. Here he says “in the morning,” signifying another time for prayer, so that the former statement is according to: “I rose before the rising sun.” For it is shameful if the sun’s ray finds you idle in bed. Therefore sacrifice to God the first fruits of heart and voice every day; then night is changed into light for you—not the light of time, but of grace. Hence the bride says: “By night I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song 3).

Or thus, according to the moral sense: “I anticipated in immaturity,” that is, at an immature age. I forestalled maturity—that is, old age. For one in immature age forestalls or outruns mature age when, as a boy, he puts on the gravity of old age and anticipates old age in youthful years: gravity is then in the mind, though the age is wandering and tender. It is no great thing if, when the body has failed and is cold with the frost of old age, people rest from pleasure. There is no crown unless there has been the struggle of a more difficult contest.

But it is great and praiseworthy if they are temperate in the heat of life, restraining the resisting flesh by the rule of reason, chastening it by sparing frugality, and reducing it to slavery, lest it luxuriate in the unbridled freedom of sensuality. For it is good for a man if he has borne the yoke from his youth (Lam. 3:27; cited here as Thren. 5). This is expounded, as stated, concerning a person’s age. Then, with the preceding matters unchanged: “I cried [Col. 1119D] and hoped exceedingly in your words.” He adds concerning the hour of day, saying: “My eyes, directed toward you in praise, anticipated dawn,” [Cassiodorus] or morning—the hour at which Christ rose, since Christ’s resurrection occurred in the morning. Therefore the mind rises at dawn. For what purpose? “That I might meditate on your utterances,” which are so sweet.

### VERSE 5 (149).—“Hear my voice according to your mercy, O Lord; and according to your judgment give me life.”

“My voice.” [Gloss, Augustine] As though he said: Because I keep such earnest watch toward you, therefore, O Lord, hear my voice according to your mercy, and according to your judgment give me life. The order in which mercy is placed first and judgment follows is fitting. [Col. 1120A] First God removes punishment from the guilty according to mercy; afterward he will give them life according to judgment. For not without reason do I sing to you, O Lord, “Mercy and judgment,” though the present time of mercy is not without judgment, nor the future time of judgment without mercy.

[Hilary, Cassiodorus] Or thus, according to the preceding explanation concerning age. Although the holy man, overcoming his age, rises in the morning, nevertheless he trusts not in his works but in God’s mercy, saying: “Hear my voice according to your mercy, O Lord; and according to your judgment”—not that by which you will judge in the future, but that by which you spare those who entreat you and absolve those who condemn themselves—“give me life.” Give life to me, dead through the law of sin. And it is necessary that you give me life, because:

### VERSE 6 (150).—“Those who persecute me have drawn near to iniquity; but they have gone far from your law.”

Those who persecute me have drawn near, and so forth [Augustine, Gloss], because they now destroy the body. Hence elsewhere: “Tribulation is near” (Ps. 21). Not, certainly, a tribulation that still threatens: it is called near here because his passion was already present to him. Yet what is done in the flesh, than which nothing is nearer to the soul, is near in this way: “Those who persecute me have drawn near to iniquity,” or “unjustly,” according to another reading. Distinguish it thus: I mean persecutors devoted to iniquity.

[Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus] Or: those who persecute me unjustly have drawn near. He adds this because some are punished for crimes, whereas they have drawn near to me while having gone far from your law. The more they draw near to him, the farther they have gone from righteousness. He says this to show that his cause is better than theirs.

### VERSE 7 (131).—“Be near, O Lord, and all your ways are truth.”

You are near, O Lord, [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Ambrose, Augustine]. As though he said: They have drawn near, but they have not harmed me, because you, O Lord, are near—within, giving help; near as a remedy. Nor are you unaware of what we do; and all your ways are truth: even what we suffer is not undeserved. A Jew cannot truly say this, but a believer can, one who believes the truth.

It may be asked how all your ways are here called truth, whereas elsewhere one reads: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24). But it should be known that toward the saints all the Lord’s ways are mercy, all are truth: for even in judging he aids them, and thus mercy is not lacking; and in showing mercy he performs what he promised, so that truth may not be lacking. Toward all persons, however—both those whom he saves and those whom he condemns—all his ways are mercy and truth. For where he does not show mercy, the truth of retribution unto salvation is given, since he condemns no one undeserving of condemnation; but he saves and delivers many who are undeserving.

### VERSE 8 (152).—“From the beginning I knew from your testimonies that you established them forever.”

“From the beginning,” or “in the beginning,” I knew, and so forth. [Augustine] If a manuscript has *initio*, it is used adverbially, as we customarily say adverbially, “I shall do this another time.” The sense is: All your ways are truth. And “from the beginning,” that is, originally, the Church says—she who has existed from the beginning of humankind—I knew from your testimonies, by which you promised that you would give the eternal kingdom to your children, that you established them; that is, in Christ, the foundation, you showed them to be true. And this is forever, because what you promised through them is eternal.

The Church says that from the beginning she knew that the testimonies were established forever, and that she knew this from no other source than the testimonies themselves. The testimonies are those by which God promised, in word or deed, that he would give the eternal kingdom to his children. And because he testified that he would give himself in the Son, whose kingdom will have no end, they are founded forever—not because the testimonies themselves will be needed when the reality itself is given, but because what God promised through them [Col. 1121B] is eternal. They are said to be founded because in Christ they are shown true; he is the foundation which no one can alter.

The Church knew this from the beginning because she, who has not been absent from the earth since the beginning of humankind, says it. Her first fruit was holy Abel, sacrificed as a witness of Christ; and from the beginning it was said: “The two shall be in one flesh” (Gen. 2), which, as the Apostle says, is a great sacrament in Christ and in the Church (Eph. 5). [Alcuin] Behold two testimonies: one displayed in deed, the other in word.

Or he calls the commandments “testimonies,” and they are said to be established forever because eternal reward or eternal punishment is rendered for neglecting or keeping them. The sense is: I knew from your testimonies that you established them forever [Col. 1121C]. [Hilary] I knew, I say, from the beginning, or since the beginning—namely, in Adam, who was punished for neglecting them; or through the ancient fathers, who by keeping them came to eternity.

## COLLATION ON QOPH

### VERSE 2 (146).—“I anticipated in maturity.”

Jerome: “I rose while it was still dark.” Or, as others wish: “I anticipated the dawn.” *Bannesheph*; in Greek, *en aōria* (ἐν ἀωρίᾳ), that is, “before the hour,” “before the time.” Hence St Augustine has “in the untimely night,” and therefore concludes that it should be read as one word, *immaturitate*, or *in immaturitate*.

Yet I began to be greatly perplexed at how Jerome, in his *Commentaries*, could have read and explained “I anticipated in maturity” in two words.
