For he says: “He forestalls old vices by youthful chastity, who through the maturity of a lively mind never removes his hope from the words of God.” [Col. 1121D] Before St Jerome, Arnobius too, though in a different sense: “I anticipated in maturity and cried: I was a boy, then an adolescent, likewise a young man; now, behold, I have grown old, and, looking toward the end of my life, I cry while placed in this maturity.”

At last, from St Ambrose’s interpretation, we discover that *maturitas* and *immaturitas* may be said from different perspectives. For from his words you will infer that adolescence, compared with time, is still immature, but compared with disciplined conduct is considered mature. He says:

> “But because the following little verse plainly expresses the time of prayer, I judge that in this verse we should understand a time of actions and works rather than of prayer. Whoever, while still in adolescence, puts on the gravity of old age forestalls maturity of age; he governs youthful years with a certain veteran self-restraint and disciplines the heat of a flourishing body with the gray maturity of character. For what praise can there be if one turns a body exhausted by pleasures and already chilled by the frost of old age to the late duties of devotion, after the vigor of maturity has now been laid aside? There is no crown unless there has been the struggle of a more difficult contest.”

And, shortly afterward: “Therefore one is old before the hour if he practices the excessive discipline of sober maturity; one is young before the hour if he restrains the incentives of pleasure with the weight of old age and extinguishes the burning enticements of desire.” And again:

> “For whoever has borne the yoke from youth and has willingly submitted tender necks to the reins of mature self-command will sit alone, removed from the clamor of importunate passions, and will be still in peace.”

This is St Ambrose. Recall now what “gray maturity” and mature self-command mean in adolescence, which is an immature age; then you will see that neither “I anticipated in maturity” nor “I anticipated in immaturity” is wrongly expressed. Yet the Hebrew and Greek reading more strongly compel us toward the latter, although the translator at Campen rendered it *properō maturrime*, “I hasten most promptly,” perhaps in the manner of speech used by the poet: “Make haste with your flight.”

[Col. 1122B]

### VERSE 6 (150).—“They have drawn near,” etc.

Likewise St Jerome, Nebio, Pratensis, and Campensis comes rather close. Others translate so that the phrase “to iniquity” refers not to the verb “they have drawn near” but to the participle “persecuting.” Pellican says: “The persecutors of wickedness have drawn near”; Sanctes: “Those following an evil thought have drawn near.” And likewise Münster: “Those who carry out a wicked design have approached.” The interpreters for Cajetan: “The followers of a design have devised.” *Qarbu rodphe zimmāh.*

The whole difference rests on one small point: *rodphe* simply means “persecutors,” without a pronoun; but *rodphai* means “those persecuting me.” Finally, it makes little difference to the sense. The Chaldee also has: “My persecutors have drawn near in adultery.”

## RESCH

“See my humility.” He who above said that he had cried out, in this twentieth letter, *resch*, asks to be given life because he has sought God’s commandments with the utmost zeal. This is far from the wicked, because they have not done likewise. And since no one is given life except through humility, which is the head of all virtues, this letter is placed before this octave. *Resch* is interpreted “head,” that is, humility, the head of the virtues, which one who is shut in preserves as a serpent preserves its head by exposing its body.

Observe, then, that this letter, *resch*, is interpreted “head” or “preeminence,” by which is understood the rational faculty that governs all the members, just as the head directs the entire body and supplies it with senses. Hence one who acts shamefully and brutishly is punished in the head, so that he loses the human form because he has not retained the rationality of wisdom. Mystically, Christ is our head, without whom the power of living cannot be possessed. [Col. 1122D] Therefore, as a serpent preserves its head, so you too preserve the head—that is, Christ, by whom we live and from whom come all good things (Col. 2).

Morally, the head is humility, as stated above, which cherishes the whole body of our actions. The puffed-up person does not hold this head—that is, humility, which is the head of all virtues. Preeminence is also the Lord Christ, who, removed from the greater people, is given to the lesser Jacob—that is, to Christians. Hence Isaiah reads: “I will remove from Judah head and tail” (Isa. 1), that is, Christ, who is beginning and end, Alpha and Omega (Rev. 1). As though he said: You are near, O Lord; therefore:

### VERSE 1 (153).—“See my humility and deliver me, for I have not forgotten your law.”

See my humility, [Ambrose, Augustine] which is what? It is present [Col. 1123A] in our efforts and temptations, and by it pride is conquered; it is necessary for every Christian. Yet no one says this unless he knows that he pleases God. The sense is: See my humility—that is, let my humility please you—and judge me according to it. Others glory in other things; the righteous person glories in humility. It is good glory to be subject to Christ, and by this one is deservedly rescued from the flaming sword, that is, eternal death.

Hence he adds: “And deliver me.” The proud person is entangled in evils in order to be humbled; the humble person is delivered in order to be exalted. Therefore deliver me, because I have not forgotten your law, which says: “Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 18).

### VERSE 2 (154).—“Judge my judgment and redeem me; for the sake of your utterance give me life.”

[Col. 1123B] “Judge my judgment.” [Gloss, Augustine, Gloss] As though he said: I say, “See my humility”; then, accordingly, judge my judgment—that is, my cause, because he pleads a cause against the devil—and redeem me from evils. And for the sake of your utterance, that is, for the sake of the law mentioned above, which this man has not forgotten—namely, that he humbled himself in order to be exalted—give me life. This is the exaltation of the saints, namely eternal life.

Or “utterance” means the word of God generally. The sense is: for the sake of your utterance—that I may see and keep it—give me life. [Ambrose] Or thus: “Judge my judgment” concerns the future judgment, toward which he hastens innocent and himself the judge of his own innocence. For the righteous person, knowing that God is also merciful, does not fear for his condemnation the judgment in which he is acquitted. This judgment also begins here with the saints, who are not to be punished eternally. Hence the Lord says through Ezekiel to the angels, ministers of vengeance: “Begin with my saints” (Ezek. 9). And elsewhere Scripture says: “It is time for judgment to begin with the house of God” (1 Pet. 4).

Therefore, hoping in his Redeemer and wishing to be promptly acquitted, he says: “Judge my judgment,” that is, cause the judgment to occur soon; and there redeem me from evils; and for the sake of your utterance give me life. He says this modestly: one who mistrusts his merits hopes for mercy on account of God’s word. And this is that Word whom Simeon awaited to see.

[Cassiodorus] Or thus: Judge, in the present judgment, my judgment—that is, examine the discernment of my faith. For he does not arrogantly ask to be judged in the future; rather, he wishes God to examine the judgment by which he believes in God and in Christ’s incarnation. For that judgment, or on behalf of that judgment, all the saints are secure and do not fear the day of judgment; for those who judge rightly by believing know that they will be glorified—saints, because such people were to be redeemed by Christ’s blood. And redeem me by the blood of your passion. And give me life for the sake of your utterance, which says: “Whoever believes in me shall not die, but shall have eternal life” (John 11). Give life to me—but:

### VERSE 3 (155).—“Salvation is far from sinners, because they have not sought your ordinances.”

Salvation is far from sinners [Augustine, Ambrose, Cassiodorus], not from me, who have sought your ordinances. [Col. 1124A] This is said especially of the Jews, who chose the robber and rejected the Savior. Yet by it he terrifies all devout minds and faithless persons alike. Therefore salvation is far from them because they have made themselves far from it. He says this because they have not sought your ordinances. This man, seeing that he has received from God the ability to keep the ordinances, says:

### VERSE 4 (156).—“Your mercies are many, O Lord; according to your judgment give me life.”

Your mercies. [Ambrose, Augustine, Ambrose.] Or the connection may be made thus: even if salvation is far from sinners, nevertheless let no one despair, because, O Lord, your mercies are many. Those who perish through their own sin are delivered by the Lord’s mercy: he openly appeared to those who did not seek him; he called back those fleeing from him; he gathered the ignorant; he offered himself for all. [Col. 1124B] And give me life according to your judgment. He says this of the future judgment, because he knows that God’s judgment will not be without mercy toward one who has shown mercy. Or he speaks of the present judgment by which God spares penitents here. Thus: Give me life according to your judgment—not according to that judgment which all fear, concerning which elsewhere it is said: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant” (Ps. 142 [Vulgate]); but according to that by which you spare those who confess. Therefore, after mercy he adds judgment, because there is no mercy without judgment. Therefore give me life, because:

### Verse 5 (157)

> “Many are they who persecute me and trouble me; I have not turned aside from your testimonies.”

Many are those who persecute and trouble me [Ambrose, Augustine]; and evil spirits are joined to them. This indicates a severe persecution, inflicted by many upon one. It was fulfilled in the Church, which had so many persecutors of the martyrs. For the whole earth has been made ready by the blood of martyrs; heaven blooms with the crowns of martyrs; the churches are adorned with the memorials of martyrs; the seasons are marked by the birthdays of martyrs; healings abound through the merits of martyrs. Yet, although they are many, “I have not turned aside from your testimonies.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Glossa interlinearis.] It is more pleasing that these things are preserved amid dangers; and this is from God for us. Hence another psalm says: “Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell” (Ps. 93 [Vulgate]). Another psalm continues: “Unless the Lord had been in us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (Ps. 123 [Vulgate]). I did not turn aside.

### Verse 6 (158)

> “I saw the transgressors, and I wasted away, because they did not keep your words.”

I formerly saw transgressors [Augustine, Cassiodorus], that is, people turning aside from the testimonies because they do not endure tribulations. Other manuscripts read: “not keeping the covenant,” which is the same thing. A covenant (*pactum*) is so called from peace, as if “an act of peace”: that is, a condition established by the affection of grace between those who disagree. This suits both laws, in that it is called a covenant, because it was established so that humanity might be recalled into God’s grace and peace. The weak do not keep that covenant—that is, either law—yielding to persecutors; and the saints grieve for these companions whom they have lost. [Col. 1125A] Hence he adds here: “And I wasted away with the zeal of love.” [Augustine, Hilary.]

Or he means the covenant which the Jews made, saying: “All that the Lord has said, we will do” (Exod. 24); but afterward they worshipped idols. The saints mourn them as their fellow-citizens and kin. [Ambrose, Augustine.] Hence he says: “And I wasted away with the zeal of charity.” Blessed is the person who wastes away in the love of God. Then, explaining how they are transgressors, he adds: “because they did not keep your words,” but denied them in tribulation. In this they are transgressors; but I, differing from them:

### Verse 7 (159)

> “See that I have loved your commandments, O Lord; in your mercy give me life.”

I have loved your commandments, O Lord. [Augustine, Ambrose, Cassiodorus.] From this love, namely, comes the fruit of all sufferings. Therefore he says, “I have loved,” not merely, “I have not denied”—which was what martyrs were compelled to do, and, if they did not do it, they endured intolerable things. And, O Lord, see this: that I have loved your commandments; that is, may my love be pleasing to you and rewarded by you.

Or the connection is thus: “I saw transgressors and wasted away. Therefore, O Lord, see that I have loved,” etc. He spoke on account of that merit, namely, by which he wasted away. This I have deserved: to be looked upon by you. Above he said, “See my humility”; here again he says, “See,” adding, “that I have loved your commandments.” [Ambrose.]

This is said according to the old law, which commands that no one should present himself empty-handed before God three times a year. But the saint presents himself daily, not empty-handed, since [Col. 1125C] he says: “I have loved your commandments.” In this he offers what he loves. Love itself is an offering. Hence elsewhere: “Your vows are upon me, O God” (Ps. 55 [Vulgate]). Note that he says, “I have loved,” which is greater than merely to keep; for the former belongs to charity, the latter to necessity or fear. Thus in Exodus only those who come with willing heart and cheerful spirit are commanded to make an offering for building the tabernacle.

“In your mercy,” [Augustine, Haymo] as if he said: I have loved the commandments; therefore I ask this reward: give me life in your mercy. I do not trust in merits. But if mercy is shown in the reward which justice ought to render, how much more manifest is the mercy bestowed in obtaining the victory, to which the reward is surely due in victory. Therefore give me life in mercy, because [Col. 1125D] these men put me to death. [Augustine, Glossa interlinearis.] You will indeed do this, because you have said so in the Scriptures, which are true, and what you say is true; for:

### Verse 8 (160)

> “The beginning of your words is truth; all the judgments of your righteousness endure for ever.”

“The beginning of your words is truth,” [Cassiodorus] that is, from the beginning of your words you have spoken truth. The beginning of your words is the beginning of Scripture, as Genesis; from that beginning God spoke truth, and he keeps words of truth unto the end. Hence: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Luke 21). And because he has touched on what was done in the beginning, he adds what shall occur after the end of the age: “all the judgments of your righteousness shall endure for ever.” [Col. 1126A] The judgments of righteousness will stand perpetually, because neither time nor any thing will overturn the sentence given concerning the good or the evil.

Or thus: “The beginning,” [Augustine] as if he said: You will truly give me life, since you have promised. And the beginning of your words is truth; that is, your words proceed from your truth. Therefore they are not empty and deceive no one: by them life is foretold to the righteous and punishment to the ungodly. For these are “all the judgments of your righteousness unto eternity,” because God’s judgment concerning all things shall remain for ever.

## Comparison on Resch

### Verse 2 (154)

“Judge my judgment”: so precisely also Sanctes. Here *judgment* is understood as “cause,” as you have in the exposition. One might hesitate concerning the accuracy of the scribe because of Münster’s version, “vindicate my cause,” as though the scribe had written here *judge* for *vindicate*; [Col. 1126B] but this is not so, since the Hebrew word suits either sense. Jerome has, “judge my cause”; the Pagnine edition, “decree my contention,” or, as the translators for Cajetan have it, “litigate my lawsuit.” Campensis explained it as, “undertake the advocacy of my cause.” **RIBAH RIBI**, in Greek, **κρῖνον τὴν κρίσιν**: “Judge the judgment.”

## Sin

“Princes persecuted.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] He who above offered his humility to God, in this twenty-first letter says that persecutions are welcome to him, because wounds of sins are healed by them as by poultices. Hence: “Give us help in tribulation” (Ps. 59 [Vulgate]). Elsewhere the Lord says: “I will kill, and I will make alive; I will strike, and I will heal” (Deut. 32). Therefore the letter Sin, [Ambrose] which is interpreted “over a wound,” [Col. 1126C] as though a poultice, is fittingly placed before this octonary. For he says that tribulation heals the wounds of sins and gives health. Thus the wound is sin; over the wound is tribulation. Or the wound is understood as tribulation itself, and over the wound is the consolation of God’s words, the medicine of heavenly commandments. This is the spiritual *malagma* (“poultice”), by which every poison of wickedness is destroyed, and by which bruised persons are not burned but rather cherished and set free. Therefore, as one wounded by robbers, yet rejoicing in the Samaritan, he uncovers his wounds for this medicine of divine grace to heal, saying:

### Verse 1 (161)

> “Princes have persecuted me without cause; but my heart has stood in awe of your words.”

“Princes,” etc. [Ambrose, Glossa interlinearis; Ambrose.] As if he said: Give me life—and it is necessary, because the princes of this world, rulers of darkness, not merely some but many, as he said above in another octonary, have persecuted me. This is the wound: “without cause,” because they have nothing of their own in me. They do not persecute without cause one who has given himself to their power; for they rightfully claim dominion over their own, from whom they demand the wages of wickedness. Other books have, “not against the unwilling,” which is the same thing. [Augustine.]

Or, “princes of the earth,” namely people presiding over earthly kingdoms, persecuted me without cause. Christian religion had not injured the kings of the earth: for although Christians are free and possess the kingdom of heaven, they nevertheless render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s. Their king too—Christ—paid tribute from a fish’s mouth. And though they persecute, [Col. 1127A] my heart stood in awe of your word, by which you said: “Do not fear those who kill the body; rather fear him who can cast both soul and body into Gehenna” (Matt. 10). Your fear excludes fear of them. Though I be driven out, proscribed, killed, tortured with claws, scorched with fire, and torn limb from limb, I feared your words more than their threats. Thus I conquered, and therefore found many spoils. And so:

### Verse 2 (162)

> “I will rejoice over your words, as one who finds great spoil.”

I will rejoice, [Ambrose, Alcuin] as a victor; for he is not a victor who does not suffer. I will rejoice, I say, over your words. One who first fears God’s words afterward rejoices in God’s words. Therefore trembling at God’s word is good, for it produces exultation. This is “over the wound,” because by the Lord’s words we heal the hardness of the wound. I will rejoice, I say, as one who finds great spoils. The spoils are eternal things which the devil tries to take away, and the conversion of persecutors, which was found when persecutors themselves, amazed by the martyrs’ endurance, believed. [Ambrose.] This is a comparison with conquerors who strip spoils from the conquered. Or he calls the Scriptures, wisdom, righteousness, and resurrection “many spoils”—all things in Christ which this man took away from the Jews and found, as it were, without effort, though he had not possessed them before.

### Verse 3 (163)

> “I have hated and abhorred iniquity; but I have loved your law.”

“Iniquity,” etc. Take it thus. [Cassiodorus, Ambrose, Augustine.] As if he said: I will rejoice over your words, and I have loved your law; but iniquity—not a human being—I have hated and abhorred, putting it far from me. Love of good things is proved by hatred of evil things. He means the Old Law, which bears the signification of the New Testament, lest anyone think it should be neglected.

Or thus: above he said that he had feared God’s words. But lest you suppose from the fear he mentioned that he hated God’s words, he adds: “I have hated iniquity”; as if he said: I feared your words and hated iniquity, but I loved your law. Through chaste fear, love does not perish. Therefore that fear does not produce hatred of God’s words, but an unspoiled charity, so that God is loved whose words are feared. For if fathers are feared and loved by dutiful children, [Col. 1127D] and if a chaste wife both fears lest she be abandoned by her husband and loves in order to enjoy him, much more is the Father who is in heaven loved only by those who love his law. Therefore he says: “I have loved your law”; even if it sometimes corrects me, still I have loved it. Hence he adds:

### Verse 4 (164)

> “Seven times a day I have spoken praise to you because of the judgments of your righteousness.”

“Seven times,” that is, always, “in the day,” in this life, I have spoken praise to you. [Augustine.] This number denotes totality, because all times are carried out through seven days. Therefore it is rightly used for universality, as in: “The righteous falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. 24). He falls indeed, but does not fall by transgressing in sin, for then he would not be righteous. Rather, he falls under every kind of tribulation. Humbled, [Col. 1128A] he rises again: that is, he does not perish but advances. By contrast it is said of the wicked: “The ungodly shall be weakened in evils,” that is, in tribulations. [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Haymo.]

Or, “seven times a day,” that is, throughout the whole time of seven days, I have spoken praise to you; or “seven times,” that is, filled with the sevenfold Spirit; or “seven times,” that is, seven occasions, as is the custom among religious persons: in the day I have spoken praise to you because of the judgments—that is, the chastisements—of your righteousness, by which you correct and justify the children whom you receive. I have loved your law, and deservedly, because now:

### Verse 5 (165)

> “Great peace have those who love your law, and for them there is no stumbling-block.”

Great peace [Ambrose, Glossa interlinearis, Ambrose, Cassiodorus] is in the mind, even if it is not complete. Or great peace will be in the future, where it is truly great, for those who love your law. Charity drives away all tribulations. “And for them there is no stumbling-block,” though there may be disturbance; that is, they do not stumble upon the stone of stumbling (1 Pet. 2), as Jews and heretics do. Those who love are not scandalized, [Ambrose] because they are not little ones, concerning whom the Lord says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble,” etc. (Matt. 18). It is characteristic of the little to be scandalized.

[Augustine.] Or, “there is no stumbling-block for them”: the Law itself is no stumbling-block. For one who loves the Law honors what he does not understand in it; what seems to sound absurd he judges to be profound, and judges himself ignorant. Thus the Law is no stumbling-block to him. Or no stumbling-block of any sort exists for him, because his faith depends upon the Law itself, not upon human conduct, lest, when some who were held great fall, he perish through scandal. Rather, he securely loves the Law, [Col. 1128C] and has peace and no stumbling-block in that Law: even if many sin, he himself neither sins nor knows how to sin.

### Verse 6 (166)

> “I waited for your salvation, O Lord, and I loved your commandments.”

“I waited”: [Augustine] it is the Church speaking. As if she said: I loved your law, etc. O Lord, I waited for your salvation. The ancient righteous awaited the first advent; we await the second. For this salvation, both they and we love the commandments. It would not have profited the ancients to love the commandments unless Christ, who is God’s salvation, had delivered them. “And I loved your commandments”: as if she said, I waited, and therefore loved your commandments, through which I have salvation. I say that I loved your commandments, etc.

### Verse 7 (167)

> “My soul has kept your testimonies, and has loved them exceedingly.”

My soul has kept your testimonies. [Augustine, Ambrose, Cassiodorus.] One keeps the testimonies who does not deny them; this belongs to martyrs. But because suffering is worthless without charity, he adds: “and has loved them exceedingly,” which is greater than keeping them. “Has kept” belongs to endurance, lest religion lose what it possesses; “has loved” belongs to charity stronger than torments. Since I have loved commandments and testimonies, therefore:

### Verse 8 (168)

> “I have kept your commandments and your testimonies, because all my ways are before you.”

I have kept your commandments and your testimonies. [Alcuin, Augustine.] Understand “commandments” in what is enjoined, “testimonies” in what is forbidden. Or: commandments are precepts; testimonies are martyrdoms. Note that above he had said, “I have loved your commandments,” and then, “I have kept and loved your testimonies”; now he puts both together, so that you may know that both have been kept, when he says: “I have kept your commandments and your testimonies.” Whoever truly loves them keeps them gladly. But because evil enemies now exist, against whom the testimonies must be kept courageously, he who has kept both attributes this to God, saying: “Because all my ways,” etc. As if he said: I was able to keep them because all my ways are before you; that is, because God has deigned to attend to me—he who illumines and puts errors to flight. If he had turned away his face, I would have become troubled and would not have kept them. [Ambrose.] Therefore he says: “All my ways [Col. 1129B] are before you,” because otherwise no way is good unless God illumines it.

## Comparison on Sin

### Verse 6 (166)

“I loved your commandments.” The Hebrews have **ASITHA**, that is, “I did” or “I performed.” Yet God’s commandments unquestionably ought to be performed out of charity. Romans 13: “Love is the fulfillment of the law.” Thus whoever has effectively loved God’s commandments has already performed them.

## Thau

[Note: [Col. 1129D] Thau is interpreted, according to Jerome, as “signs.”]

“May it draw near.” [Cassiodorus.] He who above said that tribulations would be welcome to him, in this final letter desires to draw near to Christ, praying that he may come and call back the lost sheep. He purifies himself more earnestly in proportion as he enjoys the nearness of virtue. And because Christ, by coming, bestowed the consummation of eternal blessedness and [Col. 1129C] led him back from error to his homeland, [Ambrose] therefore the letter Thau is rightly prefixed to this octonary. It is interpreted “he wandered” or “he completed,” because here he says that he has consummation—that is, eternal life. Or he says that he wandered long ago, not that he is wandering now; now he says that he is to be brought back to his homeland by the merciful shepherd. Thus it is appropriately interpreted “he wandered,” and not “he wanders.” For “he wandered” is past tense; “he wanders” present tense. One who has wandered ceases to wander and condemns his former error. For “he wandered” is said of one who is no longer in error. If he still is in it, he is said not to have wandered but to be wandering. For wandering belongs to one who persists in vice; having wandered belongs to one who corrects his lapse. To have renounced error is not a fault but progress; and in this too there is consummation, as the other interpretation teaches: [Col. 1129D] that is, the perfection of discipline, because it is greater to have recalled oneself from vices than never even to have known the vices closely. For to burn away and correct minds steeped in vices belongs not only to perfect virtue but to heavenly grace. As if he said: Because I have acted thus and thus:

### Verse 1 (169)

> “Let my supplication draw near before you, O Lord; according to your word give me understanding.”

May my supplication draw near to you, O Lord. [Ambrose.] The sinner is far away; this is spoken by a perfect man. For such confidence belongs only to a consummate man. Or this is the voice of a man who is not perfect. Therefore he does not say, “May I draw near,” [Col. 1130A] as the perfect say, namely, that they draw near to God; but, “May my supplication draw near.” And even if not I myself may draw near, let my supplication be made before you. [Augustine, Ambrose.]

What is that supplication? This: “Give me understanding according to your word,” that is, your promise, because above you said: “I will give you understanding.” Or “word” means God’s law. Thus: Give me understanding, that I may have wisdom, according to your word. He asks to be wise according to God’s word, lest he become vain through human prudence.

### Verse 2 (170)

> “Let my petition enter before you; according to your word deliver me.”

Let my petition also enter to you, made before you. [Ambrose, Alcuin.] He ascends step by step: he first said, “Let it draw near”; here he says, “Let it enter,” which is more. Behold the power of prayer. Note also [Col. 1130B] that here *supplication* concerns the obtaining of good things; *petition* concerns the removal of evils. Hence he adds: “According to your word,” [Ambrose, Augustine] that is, your promise, “deliver me.” For it is burdensome to struggle here so long.

Or “word” means God’s law. Thus: deliver me, namely, from the stain of the flesh, according to your word, that is, through the words of your law. [Cassiodorus.] Note that he who above asks for understanding according to the word, so that he may see heavenly things, here asks through that same word to be cleansed from the stain of concupiscence. God’s word does both. He fittingly asks these two things: “Give me understanding and deliver me”; [Augustine] for in receiving understanding one is delivered, since one who does not understand through himself is deceived. Give understanding, because then:

### Verse 3 (171)

> “My lips shall pour forth a hymn when you have taught me your justifications.”

My lips shall pour forth, [Ambrose, Hilary, Augustine] as from fullness, because he is full of the bread of heaven, namely the bread that came down from heaven, a hymn—that is, God’s praise. Filled inwardly with God’s delights, he pours forth a hymn, as though his tongue serves not human sense but the divine Spirit. I say, they shall pour forth when you have taught me your justifications. Otherwise they shall not pour forth unless he himself teaches, for there is one teacher, namely God. God teaches when the one who hears and learns comes to him, so that he not only retains the justifications in memory but also performs them; and thus, glorying not in himself but in the Lord, he pours forth a hymn. But one who has learned and praised his teacher now desires to teach. Hence he adds:

### Verse 4 (172)

> “My tongue shall declare your word, because all your commandments are righteousness.”

My tongue shall declare [Augustine, Ambrose, Cassiodorus] your word, that I may be a minister of the word—not an idle word, for which an account must be rendered, but your word, from which salvation comes and which ought to be proclaimed because it shines with righteousness. Hence he adds: “because all your commandments are righteousness,” [Augustine, Ambrose] that is, full of righteousness. But knowing what dangers follow a teacher from opponents, he adds:

### Verse 5 (173)

> “Let your hand be for my salvation, because I have chosen your commandments.”

[Col. 1131A] “Let your hand be,” [Augustine, Hilary, Augustine] that is, let your help be present, that you may save me. Or, save me from an alien hand, so that I may not be afraid; but that I may proclaim what I ask in this confidence: because I have chosen your commandments above all other things and have subdued fear by love. And:

### Verse 6 (173)

> “I have longed for your salvation, O Lord, and your law is my meditation.”

I have longed for your salvation, O Lord. [Ambrose.] Others seek other things; but I seek nothing except your salvation. Therefore your law is my meditation. One who desires God’s salvation meditates on the law and is not diverted from it by any concern of this world. His meditation on divine decrees is unceasing.

### Verse 7 (174)

> “My soul shall live and praise you; your judgments shall help me.”

[Col. 1131B] My soul shall live. [Cassiodorus, Ambrose.] As if he said: Let your hand be present, and thus my soul shall live in the future. He speaks to the one whom he desires, promising that the believing soul will live eternally and then fully praise him with a new song. And your judgments, by which you will judge—or by which he will judge in the future, when he says, “Come, blessed,” etc. (Matt. 25)—will not destroy me but will perfectly help me, because one who believes in me shall not be condemned. Faith will profit such a one and will plead for pardon, even if he has some offense.

Or thus: “Let your hand be”: he prays for the Lord’s advent, [Augustine] because Christ is the Father’s hand. Hence Isaiah: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53). And elsewhere: “The right hand of the Lord has wrought power,” etc. (Ps. 117 [Vulgate]). [Col. 1131C] As if he said: In order that these foretold things may be fulfilled, let your hand—that is, your Son—come to be from David’s seed, [Augustine] so that he who is Creator may be Savior. Hence he adds, “that you may save me.” I ask this in confidence because I have chosen your commandments; and truly, because I have longed to see, O Lord, your salvation—that is, Christ, whom the ancients desired to be born. The Church longed for him to come from his mother’s womb; the Church longs for him to come at the right hand of the Father. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Thus he calls Christ “salvation,” naming him Salvation. He states openly what he had earlier said enigmatically. Whoever desires him has him from the Scriptures. This is what follows: “Your law is my meditation,” because it bears witness to Christ. Though the flesh which proclaims you is killed, my soul nevertheless shall live and [Col. 1131D] praise you, and your judgments, which begin with the house of God, shall help me. The Church grew through blood.

### Verse 8 (175)

> “I have gone astray like a sheep that is lost; seek your servant, O Lord, because I have not forgotten your commandments.”

“I have gone astray.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] At last it is revealed who has been speaking throughout the psalm: namely, the universal righteous person. I say that your judgments will help me and I shall live; but long ago, from Adam, I went astray by the law of sin, because I turned aside from the way into vices. I went astray, I say, like a sheep. Behold the Gospel comparison, where it is said that the shepherd, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness, went to seek the hundredth lost sheep [Col. 1132A] (Luke 15). Hence he says here, “which was lost”: it was exposed to wolves, and neither flight nor its own strength could free it. He says “was lost,” not “is lost,” because it has already been redeemed in part. That this may be completed, he prays, adding: O Lord Christ, seek again your servant. [Ambrose, Augustine, Alcuin.] You, Christ, seek again, because weak humanity cannot seek you. As you have begun, bring it to completion; seek, I say, for you ought to do this, because, although I went astray, I have not forgotten your commandments. As if he said: Seek me because I seek you, in that respect in which I say, “I have not forgotten your commandments.”

The sheep was found, yet in another respect it is still being sought; and through the shed blood of the shepherd, torn by Jewish briars, it is found among all nations. Fittingly, after the stages of merits set forth above, he recalls the old accumulations of filth, [Col. 1132B] lest he become proud of his perfection. Rather, humbly he ascribes everything to God, because “not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us”; so that, when we have done everything well, we may say: “We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done” (Luke 17). By this confession of humility we deserve to be delivered.

Hence, in Ezekiel, only those are delivered on whose foreheads Thau is found written (Ezek. 9), because otherwise exhausted human nature could not be restored unless, having renounced the errors of the old life, the brow of life, renewed by the virtue of humility, is marked. Thus, after the little child says at the end of all things, “Let us bless the Lord,” the elders answer in another voice with the same meaning: “Thanks be to God”; so that the more perfect they are, the more humbly they refer everything to God, considering themselves [Col. 1132C] as little children and, with childlike simplicity, giving thanks to God after all things. Therefore Thau is placed after all.

## Comparison on Thau

### Verse 1 (169)

“May it draw near.” Thus the Chaldee, Nebiensis, Pellicanus, Pagnine edition, Sanctes, and the translators for Cajetan. Jerome: “may it enter”; Münster: “may it come before”; the translator of Campensis: “may it penetrate”; the paraphrase: “may it be admitted.” In Hebrew, **TIQRAB** is, simply and literally, “it drew near”; but in weighing the feeling of the petitioner, the same sense may be expressed in different words.

“My supplication”: **RINNATHI**. Jerome and Nebiensis: “my praise.” Likewise Pellicanus, the Chaldee, and the Campensis edition: “similarly to us.” The others: “my cry.” [Col. 1132D] The root from which the foregoing word is formed, **RANAN**, is “to praise,” “to sing,” “to lament,” “to pray.” Therefore: “May the sorrowful supplication of thanksgiving and praise draw near before you.”

### Verse 4 (172)

“Shall declare.” Sunia and Fretela, because they had read in Greek **φθέγξεται**, said that it simply meant “shall announce.” Jerome replies: “That word—whether you say *shall declare*, *shall utter*, or *shall speak*—means the same thing.” He then adds how he translated from the Hebrew: “My tongue shall speak your word.” Yet I now find in Greek manuscripts **φθέγξαιτο**, “let it declare.” There is no difference in sense.

# Psalm 119

[Col. 1133]

## Title of the Psalm: “A Song of Ascents.”

[Col. 1133A]

“To the Lord when I was troubled.” Title: “A Song of Ascents.” [Cassiodorus.] The blessedness which the preceding psalm sang in the unified variety of its merits, these following psalms unfold through fifteen ordered steps—both of psalms and of merits—as a mystery of the Old and New Testaments. [Alcuin.] The number seven pertains to the Old, eight to the New. For the fathers of the Old Testament served the hebdomad, that is, the number seven: they observed the seventh day, or Sabbath; the seventh week; the seventh month; the seventh year; and the seventh year of the seventh decade, called the Jubilee (Lev. 23, 25). But the fathers of the New Testament serve the ogdoad, that is, the number eight, because they observe the eighth day, called the Lord’s Day; the octaves of martyrs; and the octave of the resurrection which they await. Therefore the two Testaments are signified by eight and seven. Hence Solomon says: “Give portions to seven, and also to eight” (Eccl. 11).

[Hilary.] The fifteen ascents are distinguished so that through them the teaching of the two Testaments may be signified as contained in these steps. There are fifteen steps here, just as there were as many steps in Solomon’s temple, by which one ascended into the temple, a figure of the heavenly temple to which one ascends by these steps. This is Jacob’s ladder. For on the ladder Jacob saw angels ascending and descending (Gen. 28). [Augustine.] These are spiritual teachers, who ascend through these steps of merits as by certain intermediate stairways, advancing to the understanding of spiritual things; and, as though descending, they accommodate themselves to little ones without falling. One falls when one fails; one descends when one accommodates oneself to little ones. Adam fell through swelling pride; Christ descended through mercy, condescending to little ones. Thus his people too descend in humility, rather than falling through pride. Hence the Apostle: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober-minded, it is for you” (2 Cor. 5). By these steps one ascends and descends with the foot of the mind unharmed.

The name “steps” is ambiguous among us, because we call both ascending and descending movements “steps.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Among the Greeks, it is certain that “steps” belong only to those ascending. This ascent is not made by the paces of feet but by the advance of the affections: one ascends from virtue to virtue, where charity moves the foot. Therefore the more one loves, the more one ascends; and for this reason the song, which is the exultation of the mind possessed for eternal things, is fittingly prefixed. The sense is: this is “a song of ascents,” that is, the mind’s exultation in spiritual ascent, because these are spiritual steps.

Thus one ascending speaks here. But we must see who ascends, where and from where, to what, and through whom. Who? The righteous person. Where does the ascent occur? In the heart. Hence elsewhere: “He has arranged ascents in his heart” (Ps. 83 [Vulgate]). From where does he ascend? From the valley of weeping. To what? To that “which eye has not seen, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2). Through whom does he ascend? Through the incarnate Word, who descended so that through him we might ascend. For the Word made flesh, drinking the cup of suffering, became for us the valley of weeping. Yet remaining with God, he is the mountain of ascent. Thus he descended to you while remaining in himself; he descended to you to become your valley of weeping, while he remained in himself to be the mountain to which you might ascend. Therefore, from the example of his humiliation, let there be ascent to the will and height of his divinity.

The first step is to go forth from the evils of the world and renounce all vanity. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] The beginning of progress is to abandon fleshly vices and entreat the Lord. Thus in the old law, when a Gentile slave was bought, her nails were pared and her hair cut (Deut. 21), [Col. 1134B] because everyone must put off old vanity in order to be made a servant for the Lord’s service. Thus from renunciation of the world, through certain steps of merits, one reaches eternal and perfect charity, which is set upon the highest step.

Purpose: [Hilary.] He urges us to ascend; this purpose is the same in all, as there is also one title. Method: [Cassiodorus.] The psalm has two parts. First, the one beginning to ascend, because he finds many opponents, desires to be delivered from their tongues. Second, he laments his mixture with the wicked, at “Woe is me!” Therefore the righteous person, wishing to depart from the evils of the world by which he was oppressed, says that he cried to the Lord thus:

### Verse 1

> “To the Lord, when I was troubled, I cried; and he heard me.”

“When I was troubled,” [Hilary] by sins, I cried with intensity of heart to the Lord, that he might bring me out; and he heard me, [Augustine] by setting me upon the steps of ascent. There he prays against slanderous tongues, saying:

### Verse 2

> “O Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue.”

“O Lord, deliver.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] When a person begins to ascend—that is, when, despising the world and clinging to God alone, he intends to become perfect—he begins to suffer the tongues of opponents, that is, of slanderers and, what is more grievous, of those who turn him from salvation under the appearance of counsel. Whoever does not suffer these has not yet begun to strive for progress. Therefore the one who is about to ascend first prays against them. As if he said: Because you have set me upon a step, therefore, O Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips, which urge wicked things, and from a deceitful tongue, which harms more under the guise of giving counsel.

Such things immediately confront one who has converted; by them the first human being fell. For the wicked lips were those by which it was expressly said: “Eat” (Gen. 2). The deceitful tongue was that by which, under a disguised purpose of counsel, it was said: “You shall be as gods” (Gen. 3). But the Lord, as though training him, says:

### Verse 3

> “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against the deceitful tongue?”

“What shall be given to you?” [Augustine, Alcuin, Augustine.] As if he said: You say, “Deliver me”; but what shall be given or added to you, with which you may arm yourself against the deceitful tongue that urges wicked things? He uses two words, “given” and “added,” because arrows are given as weapons and coals are added as consolation. Therefore the Lord, answering his own question, adds:

### Verse 4

> “Sharp arrows of the mighty one, with desolating coals.”

Sharp arrows of the Mighty One will be given, together with desolating—or devastating—coals; the meaning is the same. [Aug.] The sharp arrows are the words of God, because by God’s words the heart is pierced toward love of God, so that there may be in it a wound of love, not of resentment. Hence in the Song of Songs: “You have wounded my heart with love” (Song IV). The coals, however, are examples of wicked people converted to God. They are rightly called coals: from the dead they return to life, [Col. 1135B] when they are kindled and, applied to the dead, kindle them. Thus those who turn to the Lord from death return to life, warmed by the fire of charity; and by their own example they kindle others, that they may live. These are rightly set forth after the arrows, because after the exhortation of words one must act by examples, so that a person may believe himself able to do what he has received in words, when many delicate persons—even women, such as Agnes and Agatha—have already fulfilled it; and if they sinned greatly, as Paul and Mary did, they loved all the more. These examples are called desolating or devastating coals because, by laying waste, they bring to desolation carnal thoughts and worldly loves which had wickedly put forth leaves, so that the place may thus be clean for God’s building. The sense is: Sharp arrows of the Mighty One will be given [Col. 1135C] together with desolating coals, that is, with the example of those converted to God.

[Cassiod.] Or they are the words of the righteous man himself, who, in the manner of one thinking excessively, hesitates and seeks a remedy, saying: “What shall be given, or what shall be added to you against a deceitful tongue?” The meaning of these words is not changed. Then he answers his own question—or God answers—saying: “Sharp arrows of the Mighty One,” etc. The meaning is unchanged.

## Part II. Verse 5

> “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged! I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a sojourner for a long time.”

Alas for me. [Cassiod.] Secondly, he complains of his sojourning and his mingling with the wicked. As though he said: “I have received arrows and coals, yet I am still among the wicked. Therefore, alas for me!” For, having received the arrows and coals, [Col. 1135D] though now made wheat, he is not yet in the granary but on the threshing-floor, where he is oppressed by much chaff. Seeing, therefore, many evils which he had not previously seen, he cries: “Alas for me!” Evils do not appear to anyone unless he has become good. For the Lord teaches this in the Gospel parable which says that, when the grass had grown and borne fruit, the tares appeared (Matt. XIII). Hence: “Alas for me, because my sojourning,” that is, the pilgrimage of this age, “has been prolonged”; because, although the time is short, it seems long through excessive longing.

[Hilar.] Why do you lament over this? Because “I have dwelt,” not with the good, but “with the inhabitants,” or in the tents, “of Kedar” [Note: [Col. 1135D] From Jerome on Ezekiel, chapter XXV.]. Kedar was a son of Ishmael, from whom the Saracens [Col. 1136A] descended. More properly they should be called Hagarites, from Hagar; but they claimed for themselves a name from Sarah, the worthier and free woman. Both are read to have dwelt in tents. [Aug., Hier., Aug.] Therefore Ishmael’s tents are rightly called Kedar’s, because Kedar belongs to Ishmael, as is found in Genesis (Gen. XXV). By Ishmael or Kedar the wicked are signified, just as by Isaac the good are signified. Thus Isaac is now with Ishmael—that is, spiritual persons with the carnal sons of the bondwoman—and suffers at their hands, just as Ishmael persecuted Isaac. The sense is: “I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar,” or “with the tent of Kedar,” that is, with the wicked signified by Kedar.

Or according to the interpretation of the name: Kedar means “darkness.” Thus, “with the inhabitants of Kedar” means with those [Col. 1136B] who inhabit darkness; yet he has not been darkened by them. This is the same meaning as before. From this observe that the unity of Christ’s body—that is, the Church—is not to be abandoned; the Church is not to be cut apart. Since the wicked cannot now be separated from the good, they must be borne with. I say that I have dwelt with the wicked—and for a long time. This is what follows: “My soul has been a sojourner for a long time,” etc.

Or connect it thus: Why are you grieved to be with them? Because “my soul has been a sojourner for a long time.” He calls the soul a sojourner, lest you suppose a bodily pilgrimage; it is spiritual. For as the body travels in places, so the soul travels in affections. If the soul loves God, it ascends to God; but if it loves the earth, the soul is exiled from God.

## Verse 6

> “With those who hate peace I was peaceful; [Col. 1136C] when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause.”

With those. [Cassiod., Aug., Cassiod.] As though he said: “My soul has been a sojourner for a long time”; and the sojourning was not merely long but grievous, because it was “with those who hate peace.” Or connect it thus: “I have dwelt with the inhabitants,” or “with the tents,” of Kedar; and “with those who hate peace”—that is, those who tear apart Catholic unity—“I was peaceful,” that is, preserving unity, not angry and not turbulent. And “when I spoke to them,” that is, when I forbade evil deeds and spoke good things, they, obstinate as they were, attacked me without cause.

## Comparison on Psalm CXIX: “To the Lord, When I Was Troubled, I Cried,” etc.

### Verse 3

> “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue?”

The modern translators render this actively: “What will a deceitful tongue give you, and what will it add to you?” Jerome, however, follows the Septuagint throughout. From this again an argument is drawn, among countless others, that here he did not make the noted addition of vowel-points. For these three letters may be read thus: `IITEN`, meaning “he will give,” or `JUTAN`, “it will be given,” in the conjugation they call Hophal. The other verb, “may be added,” is in Hebrew the Hiphil `IOSIPH`, which properly also includes some person receiving the action.

### Verse 4

> “With desolating coals.”

Jerome and the others translate: “with coals of junipers or broom-plants,” `RETAMIM`. Münster says that when juniper coals are kindled, they retain fire for a long time; and when outwardly they seem extinguished, they still burn within. Accordingly, by “juniper coals” we should understand nothing other than intensely [Col. 1137A] burning coals, which are rightly called desolating, for the reason Jerome gives in his Commentary:

> “For ‘desolating coals,’” he says, “the Hebrew has ἀρκευθίνοις, ‘juniper coals.’ I think that the coal in Isaiah, chapter VI, which is brought to his lips in order to cleanse the faults he had contracted by speaking, or the good things he had contracted by keeping silent, is also desolating. He therefore prays for a similar coal to be given to him: a coal from God’s altar, which may make a solitude of sins on his lips—that is, may render him free from vices.”

### Verse 5

> “My sojourning has been prolonged.”

Jerome likewise has this. Pratensis: “I have been a sojourner in Etruria.” [Col. 1138A] Sanctes, Münster, Campensis, and Pellican retain the Hebrew itself, `MESCHEC`, although Pellican says `MOSOC`, interpreting it as “the Cappadocians.” The interpreters before Cajetan have “at length” for `MESCHER`. The translator according to Campensis, however, has with us: “it is prolonged.” Moreover, `MASCHAH`, without dispute, means in Hebrew “he prolonged.” Hence the Septuagint turned aside to the participle `MASCHUC`, “has been prolonged,” and the sense fits far better.

# Psalm CXX

[Col. 1137]

## Title of the Psalm

> “A Song of Ascents.”

[Col. 1137A]

“I lifted up my eyes.” [Aug., Alcuin.] Title: [Col. 1137B] “A Song of Ascents.” The same title as above, and the same meaning: a song of ascent; to ascend is to make progress in God. Progress, therefore, is a step. The second step is to seek divine protection, against which nothing can be shown able to prevail; and it fittingly follows the preceding step. For one leaving the world encounters dangers and ought to seek divine help. Thus he who above lamented amid the snares of the wicked here prays to be helped against them.

[Aug.] For he is not unskilled and improvident, like that householder in the Gospel who does not know when the thief will come and sleeps (Matt. XXIV). Therefore the hour suddenly overtakes him; by him are signified those who, presuming upon their desires and swelling in the luxuriance of this age’s pleasures, rise up against the humble. These are those who in Noah’s days marry, take wives, and build (Matt. XXIV)—that is, who presume upon these things and prefer them to God. Therefore the hour overtakes them; but it does not overtake the children of light, because they are always awake, awaiting their Lord’s return (Luke XII). Such is this man, who lifts his eyes to God.

The intention is to admonish us to the same. The method: [Cassiod.] The psalm has two parts. First, he lifts his eyes and prays. Second, he affirms what he prayed for, showing the power of the aid obtained: “The Lord keeps.” Therefore, he who above cried out as though bowed down now, taking breath, lifts his eyes to the holy intercessors, saying:

## Verse 1

> “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, [Col. 1137D] from which help will come to me.”

I lifted my inward eyes to the spiritual mountains—[Hier., Aug.] to the saints, who were first illumined by the sun of righteousness, through whom the Scriptures were opened. “From which help will come to me,” because from their Scriptures we have help in this life. Yet one must not presume upon them, but rather upon their Lord, because:

## Verse 2

> “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

My help is from the Lord through them, [Aug.] because they too receive from his fullness (John I). Yet unless you lift your eyes to them through the Scriptures, you will not approach them so as to be enlightened by him. They, therefore, are ministers; but God is the author of illumination, who is the true light, enlightening every person coming into [Col. 1138A] this world, and who can help. For he is the one who made heaven and earth.

[Col. 1138B]

## Verse 3

> “May he not give your foot to be moved; nor may he who keeps you slumber.”

May he not give. [Cassiod.] Rejoicing in such help, this man speaks to himself. As though he said: “Since help is from the Lord, therefore, that you may be steadfast upon the steps: May the Lord not give your foot,” that is, your thought, “to be moved,” so that you fall through pride, by which the angel fell and from an angel became the devil. For just as charity alone moves the foot toward perfection, so pride moves it toward falling. Charity raises the humble to heights; pride inclines the exalted toward ruin. I say: “May he not give your foot to be moved,” nor even—what is less—“may he who keeps you slumber,” that is, may he not permit you to grow sluggish in faith; for if faith slumbers in you, Christ slumbers in you. Faith in your heart is Christ in your heart.

[Cassiod., Hilar.] This is said from human custom: when a weary watchman slumbers, he suffers theft. Christ slumbers when we grow lukewarm in faith: he is to us as we are to him. Then he supplies two further statements corresponding to these two, saying:

## Verse 4

> “Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.”

Behold, he will not slumber. [Aug.] To what he said, “May he not slumber,” he answers, “He will not slumber”; and to what he said, “May he not give your foot to be moved,” he answers, “Nor will he sleep.” As though he said: “In order that he may not slumber for you, be Israel; for behold, he who keeps Israel—Christ, who keeps first through faith and afterward those who see through sight—will neither slumber [Col. 1138D] nor sleep.” If, therefore, you cannot yet see by sight, see by faith; if you cannot behold his face, because there is the appearance itself, behold his back parts. For this was said by the Lord to Moses when he sought to see his face: “You cannot see my face; but stand in the cleft of the rock, and I will protect you with my right hand, and when I have passed by, you shall see my back parts” (Exod. XXXIII).

Therefore, whoever cannot see the face should see the back parts after he has passed by. For Christ passed through suffering from death to life; this passage is called in Hebrew *pascha*. Pascha is thought to be Greek, as though from *passion*; but it is truly Hebrew, that is, “passage.” In this Christ willed to be seen—that is, believed—not only in that he died, as even the wicked believe, but also in that he rose again. [Col. 1139A] The first is: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I); the latter: “The Word became flesh” (ibid.). Therefore whoever believes that he suffered and rose again is Israel; and for such a person Christ does not slumber.

Or thus: “May he not give your foot to be moved.” [Cass., Aug.] The righteous man speaks to himself, saying: “May he not give your foot to be moved.” The meaning of the words is unchanged. Then the Lord himself answers him, saying: “Nor may he who keeps you slumber.” As though he said: “You pray that your foot may not be moved. But in order that your foot may not be moved, choose for yourself, O man, a guardian who does not sleep.” This is what he says: “Nor may he who keeps you slumber.” Then the righteous man asks: Who is the guardian who does not sleep? The Lord answers: “Behold, he who does not sleep—namely, he who keeps Israel—will neither slumber nor sleep.”

Christ slumbers while still mortal; he sleeps in dying, though he is no longer Christ in that condition. For Christ, risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. VI). He, therefore, is the one who watches and never sleeps. Hence it is said to Jeremiah: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” And he says: “I see a rod of watchfulness, for I watch over my people, says the Lord” (Jer. I).

[Alcuin.] This is said by comparison with the stick which a thief carries to steal another’s apples or garments. If the owner of the garments sleeps, the thief keeps watch with his stick. But if the owner keeps watch, the thief sleeps and does not steal. Similarly, if a person guards his garments so that he may not walk naked on the way—that is, his good works—Christ sleeps, that is, he does not punish. But if the person sleeps, Christ watches, that is, he corrects [Col. 1139C] and chastises. This is the guardian of whom Isaiah says: “One cries to me from Seir: ‘Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?’ And he said: ‘The watchman comes, morning and night; if you seek, seek; turn and come’” (Isa. XXI). Thus he will neither slumber nor sleep.

[Aug.] But lest you still suppose this is said of any human being, he adds:

## Part II. Verse 5

> “The Lord keeps you; the Lord is your protection, upon your right hand.”

The Lord keeps. The second part, where he affirms what he had prayed for. As though someone asked, “Who is that guardian?” he adds: “The Lord keeps you.” How? Behold, “the Lord is your protection,” or “protects you”—another reading—[Col. 1139D] “upon your right hand.” Or others translate: “upon the hand of your right.” It is not without reason that he does not simply say “protects you,” or “your right hand,” or “your right hand’s hand”; but uses the transitive expression “the hand of your right.” Nor does he say “of your left,” although he made us wholly and gave both right and left. Something hidden, therefore, lies concealed here, to which we attain by knocking.

The left hand, then, is whatever we possess temporally, though this too is from God; the right hand is what is eternal. The former is consolation; the latter blessedness, according to: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song II), etc. And in Proverbs: “Length of days and years of life are in his right hand; riches and honor are in his left” (Prov. III). God’s right hand, therefore, is eternal happiness; his left, worldly things, which are also from God. Therefore those who sought eternal things are said to be placed at his right hand; those who sought earthly things, at his left.

But some people, in error, reverse these, regarding the left as right and the right as left, as those who said: “Blessed is the people to whom these temporal things belong” (Ps. CXLIII). Against them the Lord says: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matt. VI), that is, do not do good works for earthly things but for eternal ones. [Aug.] He says “let it not know,” so that it may not even mingle itself in the matter, serving partly heaven and partly the world.

Behold what the right hand is; by “hand,” moreover, power is understood, as in: “Death and life are in the hands of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII). The hand of the right, therefore, is the power which God gave to believers so that they might be children and might stand at the right, according to: “He gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John I). The meaning is: “The Lord is your protection upon your right hand,” that is, over the power God gave you so that you might be at the right and be a child. This power is through faith, but it avails nothing unless God protects it. Or the hand is faith itself. Therefore, “upon the hand of your right,” that is, over the faith through which people become children, the Lord protects, so that he does not permit them to be tempted beyond what they can bear. But why must he protect? Because of scandals, which arise from two things, because there are also two commandments of charity on which hang the whole law and the prophets: love of God and love of neighbor (Matt. XXII).

## Verse 6

> “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night.”

“By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night.” [Aug.] God is the sun; the day is the wisdom of God; the moon is the Church; the night is Christ’s flesh. Whoever errs concerning God is burned by the sun in the daytime, because he errs in wisdom itself, of which it is said: “Day pours forth speech to day” (Ps. XVIII), that is, the perfect declare wisdom to the perfect. “Night reveals knowledge to night” (ibid.), that is, to the little ones is preached Christ’s humble Passion, which is as it were night. Yet they are not left in the night—that is, in the humility of the flesh—but are advanced to the higher things of divinity, because the moon also shines at night: that is, through Christ’s flesh the Church is preached and makes progress, because Christ’s flesh itself is the head of the Church. Therefore whoever takes scandal in the Church, that is, in Christ’s flesh, is burned by the moon. [Col. 1140D]

The meaning is: Therefore he must protect you, because if he protects you, “the sun shall not burn you by day” [Aug., Hier., Alcuin.], that is, you will not err concerning divinity or God’s wisdom; “nor the moon by night,” that is, you will not take scandal in the Church or in Christ’s flesh. Or, according to our text: “The Lord is your protection upon your right hand,” that is, he will protect good action; and he will not only protect action but you inwardly as well. Thus “the sun shall not burn you by day,” that is, he will so protect you that Christ will not cause you scandal in your knowledge of his divinity; “nor the moon by night,” that is, that same one will not cause you scandal in your knowledge of his humanity, or of the Church’s unity. Or, “the moon,” that is, the Church, “shall not burn you by night,” [Col. 1141A] that is, it will not permit you to be held fast by the night of tribulation.

[Hier.] Or by day are understood prosperity; by the sun, the pride arising from prosperity; by night, adversities; and by the moon, the dejection sometimes arising from adversities. The meaning is: “The sun shall not burn you by day,” that is, you shall not be burned by the pride of prosperity; “nor the moon by night,” that is, you shall not succumb to the dejection of adversity. This is said by comparison with the benefit bestowed upon the ancient people: as of old he went before the Jews in the pillar of cloud and fire, so now he preserves us in prosperity and adversity. And why shall sun and moon not burn you? Because:

## Verse 7

> “The Lord keeps you from every evil; may the Lord keep your soul.”

The Lord keeps you. [Gl. int., Aug.] Or connect it thus: and, to conclude briefly concerning all things, “the Lord keeps you from every evil”—from the scandals placed in sun and moon, and from persecutions. And may the Lord keep your soul, lest it yield, even though the body is killed; for martyrs can be killed, but cannot be bent. Then he concludes everything, saying:

## Verse 8

> “May the Lord keep your entrance and your departure, from this present time and forever.”

[Col. 1142A] May the Lord keep your entrance and your departure, [Cassiod., Aug.] that is, may he join good outcomes to good beginnings. But what is our entrance and what our departure? Behold: when we are tempted, we enter. Thus the furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the temptation of tribulation tests righteous people; when we conquer, we depart. He guards those entering, so that we may enter with sound and humble faith, lest we burst from the wind of pride; and he guards us while he does not permit us to be tempted beyond our strength. He guards the departure “from this present moment”—which is now—“and forever,” because even now he makes with temptation a way of escape; and when we have departed from every temptation, nothing will ever again harm us.

## Comparison on Psalm CXX: “I Lifted Up,” etc.

### Verse 5

> “Your protection.”

Jerome likewise has this. [Col. 1142B] What recent translators render “your shade” is literally `TZILLECA`. It is clearer than the sun that Scripture takes “shade” for “protection,” as in: “Protect us beneath the shadow of your wings.”

### Verse 6

> “It shall not burn you,” `LO IAKECAH`, that is, “it shall not strike you.” But what could it mean for the sun not to strike unless its burning heat is understood? Moreover, the Septuagint themselves often explain metaphorical tropes at the same time. Hence the Chaldean: “On the day when the sun rules, daytime things shall not harm you.”

# Psalm CXXI

[Col. 1141]

## Title of the Psalm

> “A Song of Ascents.”

[Col. 1141C]

“I rejoiced.” Title: “A Song of Ascents.” This is evident. [Alcuin., Aug.] The third step is the great joy possessed by the holy man because he sees himself and others publicly living in the Church with a pure mind and worthily serving God in this pilgrimage. Therefore we sigh for the heavenly Jerusalem, to which we are lifted by the two wings of love. For love, of whatever kind, cannot be idle. If it is earthly, it inclines the soul toward desiring earthly things; but if heavenly, it raises it toward heavenly things and kindles it toward eternal things. For a soul bound by earthly love has birdlime on its wings and cannot fly; but holy love, having freed it from this birdlime, lifts it upward to the heavenly Jerusalem, where our fellow-citizens, the angels, are.

The intention: to exhort us to desire it. The method: [Cassiod.] The psalm has two parts. First, he rejoices that he has been admonished to go to the heavenly Jerusalem, where the saints are secure and will judge with the Lord. Second, he wishes an abundance of peace to those ascending: “Pray,” etc. Therefore, because this man had already heard many things from many people concerning the heavenly city, and, having heard those urging him to go there as to a solemn feast, he says with great joy:

## Verse 1

> “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord.’”

I rejoiced, [Hilar., Aug.] that is, I had hope and joy in the things said to me by the Holy Spirit, and by the prophets and apostles, who first saw the homeland and invite us to run toward it. What were those things? Namely: “We shall go into the house of the Lord,” not made with hands. And while these things were said:

## Verse 2

> “Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem.”

Our feet, [Aug., Alcuin.] that is, our affections, were standing in your courts, O Jerusalem. This is the house of the Lord, in which the feet already stood. Let one who runs think in this way. As though he said: “Let him already be there in hope and stand there.” He says “standing” because all things there stand. Nothing passes or falls; Belial does not pass there; there is no stain there; Rachel neither grieves nor fears there. Hence elsewhere: “He has made your borders peace” (Ps. CXLVII). Note that he says “in the courts,” taking the whole from a part. [Cassiod.] Courts are indeed entrances, but here they are also understood as inner chambers. In whose courts? Jerusalem, [Col. 1142D] [Aug.] not that Jerusalem which killed the prophets, which is in bondage with her children, which is raised with physical walls, but that:

## Verse 3

> “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in the selfsame.”

Jerusalem, which is built [Aug., Haym., Gl. int.] not with masses of stones but with divine stones; which rises through the solidity of virtues and is built by the fellowship of saints never to be dissolved, “as a city,” that is, in the likeness of a city. For it is not a bodily city, but like that one “whose participation is in the selfsame”—which can be said of no carnal city. Here human beings have diverse and failing goods; but there the good belonging to each person will belong to all. Therefore he says: “Its participation is in the selfsame.” What is “the selfsame”? [Col. 1143A] [Aug.] “The selfsame” is that which always remains in the same manner—that is, the eternal. He could not have said it more expressly. That city, therefore, has a share in stability, which is not found here in any creature. God is thus the selfsame, who says: “I am who I am” (Exod. III). And how do you know where we shall go?

## Verse 4

> “For thither the tribes ascended, the tribes of the Lord: the testimony of Israel, to confess the name of the Lord.”

“For” means because “thither the tribes ascended”—[Haym.] that is, the tribe ascended, not all tribes, but the tribes that are the Lord’s. Which are the Lord’s? Those in whom is the testimony of Israel, that is, who testify themselves to be Israel through good works. Or thus: the tribes ascended in which—that is, in those which ascended—is the testimony of Israel, namely, in which it is recognized that they are truly Israel. For when grain is mixed with chaff, the whole is thought to be chaff; but when they are separated, then Israel’s testimony will be manifest. And they ascended “to confess the name of the Lord,” not themselves, like the proud. For as pride presumes upon itself, so humility confesses to God. And truly we shall go into the house of the Lord, because:

## Verse 5

> “For there seats sat in judgment, seats over the house of David.”

“There seats sat,” [Aug.] that is, will sit, “in judgment”: seats, that is, righteous people in whom God sits, and from whom he judges whatever he judges. Hence in the Book of Wisdom: “The soul of the righteous is the throne of wisdom” (Wis. VII). What are these seats which are over the house of David? Because they too will sit with Christ upon twelve seats, to judge the house of David (Matt. XIX), that is, Christ’s household, to whom they gave food at the proper time. Those will judge who, following Christ, left all things (Matt. XXIV), who become friends through the mammon of iniquity, so that they may receive those who give into eternal dwellings (Luke XVI).

This is Jerusalem’s peace: giving and receiving, so that bodily works of mercy may be joined to works of preaching. Hence the Apostle: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. IX). This is the equality Paul speaks of, by which the one who had much did not abound and the one who had little did not lack. [Aug.] For spiritual people assist carnal people here and in the future, from whom they receive the hay of temporal things. Hence [Col. 1143D] he turns his words to the judges, saying:

## Verse 6

> “Ask for the things that belong to Jerusalem’s peace; and abundance for those who love you.”

Ask. [Cassiod.] The second part, in which he speaks to the judges, wishing them an abundance of peace—the peace he preached through love of the brethren. As though he said: “And because you will sit, therefore, O seats of the Lord—you who sit in order to judge—ask,” that is, interrogate. [Aug., Cassiod.] For judging is interrogating those to be judged, since a judge ought to examine everything. I say: interrogate those who performed the things belonging to Jerusalem’s peace [Aug.], that is, works of mercy. Those who perform them are admitted to Jerusalem; the others are not, because “judgment without mercy is given to the one who has not shown mercy” (Jas. II). Therefore all who are to be interrogated should beware, and should perform the things belonging to peace, by which abundance exists eternally. Here all are poor; there they are rich, because here they gave what was theirs.

But for whom is there abundance? For those who love you. He does not say, “those who give much,” but “those who love.” For whoever loves in another a good which he himself cannot possess has it credited to him as if he possessed it. Hence, if charity has nothing to give, let it give a cup of cold water (Matt. X), and as much is credited to it as to Zacchaeus, who gave half his estate to the poor (Luke XIX). Why is this? That man gave so little; this man gave so much; and the same amount was credited to each—indeed, exactly the same. Resources are unequal, but charity is not unequal. Therefore, O Jerusalem:

## Verse 7

> “Let peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers.”

[Col. 1144B] Let peace be in your strength, [Aug.] that is, in charity. Charity is a strength as strong as death, against which, when it comes, nothing resists, though kings, fires, and other things can be resisted. It also kills what we are, so that we may be something else; therefore it is compared to death. It kills in such a way as to give life. Hence the Apostle: “I live, yet no longer I” (Gal. II). Through this, the weak are governed by the strong. Therefore he says: “Let peace be in your strength,” and through this strength and peace, “let there be abundance” in number and reward “in your towers,” or “in your high places.” Few indeed are judges, but many will belong to each one, whom they will receive into eternal dwellings; then there will be abundance in your towers. But God will be the whole abundance of both those receiving and those received.

But because charity is not our own, but seeks what belongs to others, he therefore adds, when he has spoken of charity:

## Verse 8

> “For the sake of my brothers and my neighbors, I spoke peace concerning you.”

For the sake of my brothers. [Aug., Cassiod.] As though he said: “Let there be peace; and I already spoke”—that is, preached here to others—“peace concerning you, O Jerusalem,” not for my own sake but for the sake of my brothers and neighbors, that is, in order that brothers and those first joined by the bond of charity may be bound together.

## Verse 9

> “For the sake of the house of the Lord our God, I sought good things for you.”

For the sake of the house of our God, [Aug., Alcuin.] namely, not for my own sake but for the Church, for pilgrims, so that they too may ascend, “I sought good things for you,” that is, I preached good things concerning you, O heavenly Jerusalem, because you are God’s house; and thus, in loving you, I love God.

Or read it thus, so that this verse explains the preceding one. As though he said: “I spoke peace concerning you for the sake of neighbors and brothers,” namely, “I sought good things for you for the sake of the house of the Lord our God.” The meaning of the words is unchanged.

## Comparison on Psalm CXXI: “I Rejoiced in the Things That Were Said to Me,” etc.

### Verse 2

> “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me.”

Pratensis, Sanctes, and Münster render it in such a way that the community of those rejoicing and speaking is signified. But the Septuagint and others render it so that the joy concerns what was said. For they have it in this way: “I rejoiced with those saying,” or “with those who say to me”; Jerome, however: “I rejoiced because they said to me.” [Col. 1145A] The difference arises from the letter *beth*, which sometimes denotes “in,” sometimes “with.”

### Verse 2

> “In your courts,” `BISCHCARAIIC`, that is, “in your gates.”

The Septuagint attended to the sense, since a court is the first part and entrance of a house.

### Verse 3

> “Whose participation is in the selfsame.”

Pratensis and Sanctes give another reading, sufficiently obscure, I think: “which is joined together.” Münster has it more clearly: “which is joined together with itself equally.” Or, as Jerome has it: “whose participation is together,” `CHEHUBERAH LAH IACHDAU`. But because the saints also commonly interpret “the selfsame” as Christ, our reading is, in my judgment, more suitable.

### Verse 7

> “In your strength.”

They translate: “in your walls,” or “in your outer walls,” `BEHELECA`. The Septuagint aptly unfolded the figurative expression, even though `AHLHAUL` means “strength” and “army” in Hebrew. For they do not always reduce metaphors to plain language, as in what follows: “in your towers,” or, as others wish, “in your palaces,” `BEARMENOTHAIIC`.

### Verse 8

> “Peace concerning you,” `SCHALOM BAC`.
