Jerome says “peace to you”; most say “peace in you.” Sanctes agrees with us: “peace concerning you,” since Hebrew freely bears this or another sense.

# Psalm CXXII

[Col. 1145]

## Title of the Psalm

> “A Song of Ascents.”

[Col. 1145B]

“To you I lifted [my eyes].” Title: “A Song of Ascents.” [Cassiod.] The fourth step is, amid whatever distresses, steadfastly to trust in the Lord until, in mercy, he hears. The intention: to exhort us to ascend. The method: the psalm has two parts. First, it is the voice of afflicted people looking to God, not to other protections. Second, it prays for mercy against those who insult them: “Have mercy on us,” etc. Observe the progress of the one ascending, whence it is called a song of steps. He who above lifted his eyes to the mountains now lifts them to God himself—which is greater—saying: “O you.”

## Verse 1

> “To you I lifted up my eyes, you who dwell [Col. 1145C] in the heavens.”

“You who dwell in the heavens,” [Aug.] that is, in the righteous, who are called heavens because of righteousness. Ascending to you by the affection of love, I lifted up my eyes, namely, the eyes of faith and charity. Thus this person cleanses himself so that he may become heaven. The ascent, therefore, is in affection. Through good desire we are raised to heaven, just as through evil desire we are hurled down to the depths. And as a person ascends by affection, so heaven, in which God dwells, is in righteousness—that is, through righteousness.

He fittingly says: “I lifted up my eyes to you.” For to what else would he lift them than to the goal toward which he was ascending? This man does not attend to himself, like the proud person who pleases himself and therefore displeases God. God pleases the person to whom God is pleasing; but the person to whom God is pleasing displeases himself. Observe also that, although many say this, it is not said in the plural but in the singular, as though one person were speaking: “To you I lifted up.” For through charity many are one person, who cries from the ends of the earth; and through the same charity we are united to Christ, so that with him we may be, as it were, one Christ. As he himself says in the Gospel: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III). The head descended; the same head ascended with the body, namely, the Church, clothed upon him, which he presented to himself without spot or wrinkle (Eph. V). Therefore he alone ascends who is one with us, alone. Unity joins us into one. Whoever willed to be one with him through charity ascends with him; he is with us on earth through the compassion of charity, and through charity we are with him in heaven. He is below through charity’s compassion; we are above through charity’s hope. [Col. 1146B] Therefore all of us in Christ are one person, who is not troubled over earthly things like the wicked, but because he is a pilgrim and longs for his homeland. Therefore, when each of us says—because all are one in Christ—one person says: “To you I lifted up,” not “we lifted up,” “my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens.”

And as though someone asked, “How did you lift them?” he adds by comparison:

## Verse 2

> “Behold, as the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters.”

Behold, [Aug., Cassiod.] as the eyes of servants, who are commanded to be beaten, are upon the hands of their masters, so that they may command mercy to be shown. For a servant lifts his eyes to the hands of his Lord when he is in need or when he is beaten, [Col. 1146C] because both are in the Lord’s power. And
### Verse 3

> “As the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress, so are our eyes upon the Lord our God, until he has mercy upon us.”

As the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress, so are the eyes of us all, even in prosperity, upon the Lord our God. Why? “Until,” that is, in order that, he may have mercy upon us—that is, free us from every temptation and reproach; for the whole life upon earth is temptation, the whole of it affliction. Therefore we must cry out what follows: “Have mercy upon us, O Lord.” Observe the fitting comparison, serving also a mystery. For the faithful people are the servant; Christ is the Lord; the Church is the maidservant; the mistress is the power and wisdom of God. Although by grace we are now sons and friends, yet by creation we are servants [Col. 1146D], because every creature serves God. By the Lord’s “hand,” understand power, which the good heed when they feel themselves struck. “He who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Eccles. 1). But the wicked have lost the sense of pain, and for that very reason are more grievously beaten and scourged. The good, therefore, in their chastisements heed the hand—that is, the power—of the Lord, until he says, “Spare”; by whose command we are beaten, having been cast out of paradise.

[Cassiodorus.] He gives, moreover, the comparison of servant and maidservant, lord and mistress, lest the weaker female sex should suppose itself excluded. For it too is chastened here through justice, and it too is spared through mercy. Therefore the servant who is beaten, lifting his eyes to God, breaks forth into the necessary cry, saying:

## Part II. Verse 4

> “Have mercy upon us, O Lord, have mercy upon us; for we are exceedingly filled with contempt.”

“Have mercy upon us, O Lord,” etc. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The second part, in which he prays for mercy against those who insult them, saying: O Lord, have mercy upon us. These are the words of one being beaten; and he repeats, “Have mercy upon us.” He repeats it because the body suffers through afflictions and the soul through reproaches. And you must have mercy, because “we are exceedingly filled with contempt,” that is, afflictions abound in which we are despised. For the one who hopes for things unseen is mocked by one who holds what he loves, and is told: “What do you believe, madman? You see what you believe? Has anyone returned from the lower world and told you what happens there? Look: what I love I see and enjoy.” Then, amplifying the thought, he adds:

### Verse 5

> “For our soul is exceedingly filled; [we are] a reproach to those who abound, and contempt to the proud.”

“For our soul is exceedingly filled with contempt.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] No part is free from it. Then he adds by whom and why it is despised: we are a reproach to the prosperous, because we are poor in comparison with those who abound—namely, the rich [Col. 1148A] who are happy here. Therefore he calls those “prosperous” who abound in money, in supposed justice, and in wickedness. But the righteous man says: “For I am needy and poor” (Ps. 108:22). He is poor in a frail body; he is poor in righteousness while subject to temptation. And we are contempt to the proud because we are humble.

## Comparison on Psalm 122: “Unto thee have I lifted up mine eyes,” etc.

### Verse 5

> “For our soul is exceedingly filled; [we are] a reproach to those who abound and contempt to the proud.”

Languages that delight in varied case endings easily indicate the construction and order of a sentence; but Hebrew, hampered by a lack of diverse inflections, often leaves the construction ambiguous, so that each person translates what seems more coherent to him. Therefore [Col. 1148B] *laʿag* may be either nominative or ablative: “reproach” or “with reproach.” Next, *shaʾanannim*: “to the prosperous” or “of the prosperous.” Then *buz*: “contempt” or “with contempt.” Finally, *ligeʾyonim*: “of the proud” or “to the proud.” Accordingly, it could be rendered: “Our soul has been filled with the reproach of the prosperous and the contempt of the proud,” which is how Jerome translated it. So too did others.

# Psalm 123

[Col. 1147]

## Title of the Psalm: “A Song of Ascents”

[Col. 1147B]

“Unless the Lord had been in us.” Title: A Song of Ascents. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The fifth ascent is that those delivered from dangers should attribute their deliverance not to themselves but to the Lord. Note [Col. 1147C] that he sometimes introduces one person and sometimes many; nevertheless the Church is one, because in all her members there is unity, through which many human beings are one human being. Therefore the faithful sing this exultantly because they have escaped. It is to sing in hope if they are in the body, or in actuality if they have already departed from the body; yet the song of all together is one. 

Purpose: he urges us to ascribe our deliverance to God.

Method. [Cassiodorus.] The psalm has two parts. First, the saints, mindful of how great things they escaped, ascribe these to mercy alone. Second, they give thanks because they were delivered, at “Blessed.” [Augustine.] Thus, without yet stating from what they escaped, they began to sing as follows:

### Verse 1

> “Unless the Lord had been in us, let Israel now say: unless the Lord had been in us.”

“Unless the Lord.” [Augustine.] So great is their exultation that, before setting out the dangers, they say that they have been delivered, and by whom: “Unless the Lord had been in us.” Now secure, they say this as they look back upon what they suffered, how many things they passed over, and where they have arrived. This is what I say: let Israel, since it has now escaped, say with me this: “Unless the Lord had been in us.”

### Verse 2

> “When men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive.”

“When men rose up,” [Augustine] persecuting us, in whom God was. What then can they do against the Lord in us? Unless this had been so, I say, perhaps [Col. 1148B] they would have swallowed us alive—that is, knowing evil and yet doing it, like one who knowingly burns incense to an idol while knowing that the idol is nothing. For those who know that an idol is nothing are alive; those who suppose it to be something are dead. Therefore the dead are swallowed up—those who think the evil they do ought to be done.

But the living are those who indeed know that what they do is evil, yet, overcome by persecution, pass into the fellowship of the ungodly and prefer the sweetness of this life to God, as some who, through fear of death, burned incense to idols. Observe also that Peter—that is, the Church—swallows many, but not alive. To him it is said: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10). For he eats no one—that is, incorporates no one into his members—unless that person has been killed, that is, has renounced the devil. Thus one is killed in evil but made alive in good when eaten by Peter. The reverse happens to one whom the devil swallows.

### Verse 3

> “When their fury was enraged against us, perhaps the water would have swallowed us.”

“When their fury was enraged.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As above he conquered deceitful tongues through the words of God and examples of those made alive from death, so now, if the Lord is present, he conquers those who threaten, of whom he says: “When their fury”—which is without reason, because anger and envy lack judgment—“was enraged against us.” Hence Job: “Anger kills the foolish man, and envy slays the simple” (Job 5). Unless the Lord had been in us, perhaps the water would have swallowed us—that is, the sinful people. [Augustine.] It is spoken from the likeness of the Egyptians, whom the water of the sea swallowed. It is as though he said: Unless the Lord had been in us, we would have died after the manner of the Egyptians; we would not have crossed over after the example of the Israelites. But what kind of water is this? It is a torrent: it flows violently, but quickly passes away.

### Verse 4

> “Our soul passed through the torrent; perhaps our soul would have passed through intolerable water.”

“Our soul passed through the torrent.” [Augustine.] As if to say: Unless the Lord had been present, the water would have swallowed us; but through the Lord our soul passed through the torrent, from which the Head also “drank on the way” (Ps. 109), and passes through it: he did not remain there, because he suffered but rose again and ascended. Through him he granted us also to pass through.

“Perhaps our soul would have passed through,” or “has passed through,” etc. The Latins use *forsitan* (“perhaps”) for the Greek word of doubt, ἆρα, which is more intelligibly rendered, “Do you suppose?”: “Our soul has passed through.” The sense is: as though we passed through by the Lord. And “perhaps,” that is, “Do you suppose that our soul passed through intolerable water?” Or it may mean “without substance,” as though the greatness of the danger scarcely permits this to be believed.

Water without substance [Col. 1149B] is vice, sin, and the sweetness of this life: they have poverty, not substance; need, not true subsistence, because these things truly are not, but all pass away without fruit. For one who gains gold and the like through sin is without substance, because here too he loses faith, and when he descends into hell he does not carry these things with him. Therefore he lost the greater thing to gain the lesser: he increased his money but neglected—or extinguished—his faith. Something or other abounds in the chest, but something far greater has diminished in the heart. You rejoice over the chest; you do not mourn over the heart.

[Alcuin.] In this water without substance that younger son lost the substance he received from his father, and attached himself to one of the citizens of that country—that is, the devil—feeding swine, that is, delighting in earthly and unclean acts, and desiring to eat the husks of the swine, which fill the belly but do not satisfy (Luke 8). So sins, although they delight for a time, do not furnish true satisfaction, but bring in want of every good. This is the wandering sheep whom the merciful shepherd is said in the Gospel to have sought after leaving the ninety-nine in the wilderness (Luke 15). But before bringing her back from afar, he threatened her with the rod of the Mosaic law, so that the little sheep might know that she had strayed, fear to stray further, and, unable to return by herself, humbly await and desire her restorer: who, after washing her in the life-giving water of baptism, when the water without substance had dried up, might restore her to the company of angels, bringing the prodigal son, worn down by long necessity, back to his father.

Or, according to our text, “perhaps” means: through the Lord it passed through; but perhaps, if the Lord had not been in us, you might say, our soul would have passed through intolerable water—which would in no way have been possible in us.

### Verse 5

> “Blessed be the Lord, who did not give us as prey to their teeth.”

“Blessed.” [Cassiodorus.] The second part, where the saints give thanks because they were delivered and because the snare was broken, as though to say, “And because I passed through.” “Blessed be the Lord, who did not give us as prey,” or “for hunting,” “to their teeth” [Augustine, Cassiodorus], like beasts [Col. 1150A] thirsting for our blood. I say, he did not give us, but rather—

### Verse 6

> “Our soul, like a sparrow, has been delivered from the snare of the hunters.”

“Our soul has been delivered,” [Augustine] even if the body has suffered. “From the snare,” or trap, “of the hunters,” because it is not caught by the sweetness of the present life. From this follows killing. The hunters are the persecutors; the bait in the trap is the sweetness of this life. Thus bait is put in the trap when they strive to draw people into wickedness through the sweetness of this life.

I say our soul has been delivered, which formerly was like a sparrow because it had fallen heedlessly through instability; but just as, when someone makes a loud noise, a sparrow flies away from the trap of hunters, so our soul, which was formerly held by life’s sweetness, has been rescued from the trap through the Lord’s making the tremendous noise of hell. Or this is its present meaning: our soul is like a sparrow because, just as a sparrow avoids a snare, so do the saints avoid the sweetness of this life, which is like a snare. And this—

### Verse 7

> “The snare has been broken, and we have been delivered.”

“The snare has been broken.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Because after the martyrs have been killed, the sweetness of this life remains no more by which they can again be caught. But they were not broken together with it; rather, they were delivered. And we who formerly clung to the trap have been delivered. Note that he says, “The snare has been broken,” as if it were iron. He does not say “torn,” as tow is torn: so great was the strength of evil, so great the power of the deliverer. Why was the snare broken [Col. 1150C] and why were we delivered? Because—

### Verse 8

> “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

“Our help is in the name of the Lord,” [Cassiodorus] against whom no one prevails, “who made heaven and earth,” that is, all heavenly and earthly things.

## Comparison on Psalm 123: “Unless the Lord had been in us,” etc.

### Verse 4

> “Our soul passed through the torrent.”

Jerome and the others: “The torrent passed over our soul.”

“Jerome says in his commentary on this passage: ‘The latter is better, as I understand it according to the literal sense. For in regard to the sense, our soul passes through the tribulation understood by the torrent when it conquers through courageous resistance; and the torrent passes over the soul when it afflicts indeed, but does not swallow it; rather, as it runs along only at the surface, it touches it.’” [Col. 1150D]

“Intolerable water.” Jerome: “the waters of pride passed over”; and the others are nearly to the same effect. Waters of this kind, proud—or, as Münster translates, swelling—retain their force in “intolerable water.” It will not be tedious to add what St Jerome commented on this. The Greek word ἀνυπόστατον is ambiguous and can mean either “that which does not subsist” or “that which is intolerable,” that is, which no one can bear. In place of this, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and all the interpreters unanimously render “proud and arrogant waters” for ἀνυπόστατον. Thus far he. In Hebrew it is *hammayim hazzedonim*.

# Psalm 124

[Col. 1151]

## Title of the Psalm: “A Song of Ascents”

[Col. 1151A]

“Those who trust in the Lord.” Title: A Song of Ascents. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The sixth ascent is the confidence of the most faithful Christian, compared to the most solid mountains, which he has in the Lord, so that he may not envy those who are happy in this world and imitate them. For this psalm teaches us not to fix our attention upon those who prosper in this world. From such prosperity pride arises, so that through pride they set themselves above all people, though through iniquity they are inferior to them. Hence too the heart becomes hard against the rain of God’s grace, lest it bear fruit. When the weak observe such persons, they waver, as above we read that the feet of a certain weak person were moved when he saw the peace of sinners. But one must believe in God’s wisdom: he does all things well, even if [Col. 1151B] we do not see how. Thus the heart will be upright, so that we trust in the Lord and our feet will not be moved.

Purpose: he urges confidence in the Lord.

Method. [Cassiodorus.] It has two parts. First, he asserts that the one who places his confidence in God’s strength cannot be moved. Second, he prays that prosperity may come to the good and vengeance to the wicked, at “Do good.” Thus, showing that one who trusts in God cannot be moved, he says:

### Verse 1

> “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Sion; he who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever.”

“Those who trust in the Lord.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] And who are these? Those who dwell in the spiritual Jerusalem—that is, in Christ’s Church—shall not be moved; another text says, [Col. 1151C] “for ever.” Citizens of earthly Jerusalem are often taken captive; those of the spiritual Jerusalem, which is above, are not. I say they shall not be moved, as Mount Sion shall not be moved for ever—that is, Christ, upon whom the Church is founded. For that mountain will be moved at the end of the world.

Or, according to another text: “The one who trusts in the Lord is like Mount Sion,” that is, he is comparable to that most solid mountain. And “he who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever,” [Augustine] like the sparrow, which is unstable and quickly flies here and there.

[Cassiodorus.] Or, according to our text, it may be read partly in the plural and partly in the singular: “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Sion”—literally, comparable to that mountain. “He who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever.” [Col. 1151D] First he says “they trust,” in the plural; afterward, “shall not be moved,” in the singular, because the unity of this people is numerous: they are many, yet they are one.

[Augustine.] Then he briefly describes what this Jerusalem is like, adding:

### Verse 2

> “Mountains are round about her; and the Lord is round about his people, from henceforth even for ever.”

“Mountains are round about her.” [Augustine.] As though he said: He who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved, because mountains—that is, angels and prophets—are round about her as a wall and outer fortification. But lest you remain fixed upon the mountains, [Col. 1152A] he adds: “And the Lord,” who dwells in the mountains, “is round about his people.” Therefore let hope not be in the mountains, but in the summit of the mountains. Hence Isaiah: “In the last days, the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be upon the summit of the mountains” (Isa. 2).

This mountain, therefore, is great, round about his people, from henceforth even for ever. For those whom he takes to be his people, he binds together into one by the bond of charity and peace, so that they may not be moved for ever. And truly they shall not be moved.

### Verse 3

> “For the Lord shall not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands unto iniquity.”

“For the Lord shall not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous,” [Alcuin, Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, over the righteous chosen by lot, or those who are God’s lot and inheritance. Over these the Lord will not leave the rod—that is, the dominion—of sinners. For sinners sometimes rule for the discipline of the good; but this will not always be so, as the Prophet here plainly says. And why does he not leave it? “Lest the righteous stretch out their hands unto iniquity.” Understanding that this burden of tribulations is temporary, they endure it patiently. For if it seemed that this would always be so, they would abandon righteousness; but they do not fail because they know that a time will come when Christ, appearing in his glory, will gather all nations before him and divide them as a shepherd divides goats from sheep, placing the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left (Matt. 25).

## Part II. Verse 4

> “Do good, O Lord, to the good and to the upright in heart.”

“Do good, O Lord.” [Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine.] The second part, where, after confirming the people, he prays for what he knows will happen: namely, that prosperity will come to the good and vengeance to the wicked. As though he said: And because God pleases them in all things, do good, O Lord, to those upright in deed and upright in heart, who do not wish to perish but to follow.

### Verse 5

> “But those who turn aside into bonds the Lord shall bring with those who work iniquity; peace be upon Israel.”

“But those who turn aside,” from God’s commands—those who are scandalized by the ways of the Lord—“the Lord shall bring with those who work iniquity,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus] whose deeds [Col. 1152D] they imitated and whose present joys they loved. I say he shall bring them into the bonds of guilt and punishment. For iniquity binds them to evils and does not allow them to be free. See: by the same judgment perish those who turn away from the commands of the ruler and those who strive to make them willing to do evil—that is, those failing together with those who compel them to fail.

[Augustine.] But what will happen to the upright in heart? Behold: peace shall be upon Israel. In one word he declares every good thing. For the homeland and inheritance is called by the one name “peace,” and this is Christ. For he is our peace, who made both one (Eph. 2), who will give us peace upon peace.

## Comparison on Psalm 124: “Those who trust in the Lord,” etc.

[Col. 1153A]

### Verse 1

“The Hebrews end the first verse at the words ‘he who dwells,’ and immediately begin the second verse: ‘Jerusalem—mountains,’ etc. Jerome translates thus: ‘Those who trust in the Lord [are] immovable like Mount Sion, inhabitable for ever’; and he did not observe the rules of the words. Münster, by adding ‘who does not waver,’ rendered the sense quite clearly: ‘Those who trust in [Col. 1154A] the Lord shall be immovable like Mount Sion, which does not waver but stands for ever.’ The Septuagint frequently assigns the periods of the verses differently from the Hebrew, wherever it distinguishes the order of the thoughts; for in Hebrew they are written metrically. And if one rendered word for word, this little verse could scarcely be understood: *haboteḥim badonai kehar tsiyon lo yimmot leʿolam yesheb*.”

# Psalm 125

[Col. 1153]

## Title of the Psalm: “A Song of Ascents”

[Col. 1153A]

“When the Lord turned.” Title: A Song of Ascents. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] This seventh ascent signifies, through the Old Testament—which is represented by the number seven—the return, through the Christ who was to come, of the faithful from the captivity of vices, which Babylon prophesies. For this return there is now consolation, and there is sowing in works of mercy, that there may be a more abundant harvest.

[Hilary, Augustine, Cassiodorus.] Here the Prophet speaks of that return as though it were past, though it was still future, with prophetic certainty. He speaks in the person of those who were or are redeemed by Christ’s blood and converted from spiritual captivity according to the mind, because they serve the law of God. They sing these things while they are pilgrims, mourning on the way and awaiting the redemption of the body. Therefore they are already redeemed in part, and in part still to be redeemed.

Purpose: he urges joy for spiritual deliverance.

Method: the psalm has two parts. First, the greatness of the deed is shown together with the greatness of joy. Second, he prays for conversion from captivity, because it is still future, at “Turn, O Lord.” Therefore, in the person of the redeemed, as though returning from Babylon, he says:

### Verse 1

> “When the Lord turned the captivity of Sion, we became like those who are comforted.”

“When he turned the captivity of Sion,” [Augustine] as of those returning from Babylon—a conversion which the Lord accomplished—“we became,” etc. Or according to another text: “When the Lord shall turn the captivity of Sion,” which is also Jerusalem, eternal in the angels but captive in human beings, “we became like those who are comforted,” though not yet secure; that is, we rejoiced as receiving consolation. Consolation belongs only to the miserable. We groan in reality, but are comforted in hope. When reality has passed, eternal joy will come in place of groaning, where consolation will not be necessary, because no misery will wound us.

Note that he does not say “comforted,” but “like those comforted,” through which it seems that there is no true consolation but only a kind of likeness to consolation. But it should be known that *sicut* (“like”) is not always used for likeness but is sometimes employed to express a property. Here it refers to a property; and examples from ordinary speech should be given so that we may easily understand when “as” in “As the Father lives, so the Son [lives]” refers to likeness. Again, when the Lord says, “As livestock dies, so a human being dies,” it is said with reference to likeness. It refers to property when one says, “He acted as a righteous man,” in which he is not denied to be righteous, but it is not shown what his true property is. Thus these became “like those comforted,” that is, they rejoiced as receiving consolation of soul through the resurrection [Col. 1154B] of Christ, who went before so that we might follow; through whose resurrection we hope for our own. Observe also that he uses the past tense, “when he turned,” as though speaking of the past, while foretelling the future.

### Verse 2

> “Then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation.”

“Then it was filled.” [Augustine.] As though he said: The Lord turned us, and then in that conversion our mouth was filled with joy—not the joy of the world, but the joy of redemption, which rejoices in hope. Here “mouth” means the secret place of the heart: this is the mouth of the heart, from which proceeds good or evil, which cleanses or defiles us. Of it the Lord says in the Gospel: “What proceeds out of the mouth defiles a person” (Matt. 15)—not the mouth of the flesh, but [Col. 1154C] the mouth of the heart. For if you name thefts and other evils, you are not unclean; rather, you are unclean when you think them, even if you are silent. And lest anyone understand this of the bodily mouth, the Lord immediately added, as if explaining: “Evil thoughts come forth from the heart” (ibid.).

[Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Therefore the mouth of the heart is where joys are first conceived, which afterward burst forth through the service of the tongue. “And our tongue,” namely that of the body, “was filled with exultation”; or, rather, it should be understood of the inward tongue, which inwardly cries to the Lord, as Moses cried while silent (Exod. 14), and Susanna did (Dan. 13). Or “mouth” and “tongue” are understood of the same thing; and, to show by the figure of the past that he has the future in mind, he says:

### Verse 3

> “Then they shall say among the nations: The Lord has magnified his dealing with them.”

“Then they shall say.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] This is already future. Therefore afterward too, in order that these things may happen, he prays, saying: “Turn, O Lord, our captivity.” As though he said: When the conversion occurs, then they shall say among the nations. This happens when people from the whole world run to the Church. He does not say, “The nations shall say,” because not all will believe, but some among all. What will they say? “The Lord has magnified his dealing with them,” the faithful. They say this because they see them also performing miracles; and testimony from an adversary is firm. Thus they will say. And truly—

### Verse 4

> “The Lord has magnified his dealing with us; we have become joyful.”

“The Lord has magnified his dealing with us.” [Augustine.] We harmed ourselves, having sold ourselves under sin. [Col. 1155A] Therefore the Redeemer did good to us by delivering us. He says this so that you may not doubt the words of the nations. I say that the Lord did good; hence, “we became joyful,” who were formerly captives.

## Part II. Verse 5

> “Turn, O Lord, our captivity, as a torrent in the south.”

“Turn, O Lord.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The second part, in which he prays for conversion because it was future, in which there would be sowing in hope of joy. After the redemption foretold above through the Lord’s coming, they again pray for forgiveness of their sins: they rejoice in the general remission and pray for pardon for themselves. As though he said: The Lord will loose captivity; and, having sent the Redeemer, O Lord, turn our captivity, by which we are held captive under the devil. For no captivity occurred in David’s days, but the world was captive under the devil.

“Turn,” I say, “as a torrent is turned in the south,” that is, when the south wind blows, which is a warm wind through which torrents are released to run. By it the Holy Spirit is signified, as by the north wind, the cold wind, the devil is signified. Hence in the Song of Songs: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow upon the garden of the bride, that its spices may flow” (Song 4). Therefore Scripture, urging good works, says in the book of Jesus son of Sirach: “As ice in fair weather, so your sins are dissolved” (Ecclus. 3). For sins bind us so that we cannot do good works or run toward our homeland, as cold or ice prevents water from running. But when the warm south wind blows, the ice melts and the torrents are filled. Thus, when the Holy Spirit blows, we are freed from sins [Col. 1155C] and run to our homeland, though in this running there is labor. Yet we should not therefore cease, because—

### Verse 6

> “Those who sow in tears shall reap in exultation.”

“Those who sow in tears,” [Augustine] that is, in this life filled with tears, “shall reap in exultation” the fruit of eternal blessedness, which they gather from what they sow. But what do they sow? Good works, works of mercy, for which willingness is sufficient if means are lacking. Therefore do not be sad if you have good will, from which peace is reaped. For is peace said to be on earth for the rich? No, but only for people of good will (Luke 2).

Zacchaeus had this will and sowed in it no less than in deed. He joyfully received God as a guest and promised to give half his estate to the poor, saying: “Lord, I give half my goods to the poor, and if I have defrauded anyone, I restore fourfold” (Luke 19). He retained the other half not in order to have something to possess, but to have something from which to repay his debts (Matt. 18). Great willingness sowed much. In this same willingness the widow who cast in two mites (Luke 21) did not sow little; indeed, she sowed as much as Zacchaeus. She possessed lesser means but had an equal will. If you consider what they gave, you will find things different; if you consider from what they gave, you will find them equal.

But there is another, more humble thing which, when sown, reaps that harvest: namely, a cup of cold water. Hence the Lord: “Whoever gives a cup of cold water shall not lose his reward” [Col. 1156A] (Matt. 10). Thus, if the person who has it gives it to one who does not have it, he has given as much—if he gives out of full charity—as that widow in her two mites and as Zacchaeus in half his goods. But if a person has not even that, he should nevertheless be secure if willingness is present. He should fear only that he may have and fail to act. For if he has and does not act, he has frozen inwardly, because his will is cold; he does not sow in tears and therefore will not reap in exultation.

[Cassiodorus.] Note that he says, “They sow in tears.” Spiritual sowing is always done in tears. Hence: “Blessed are those who mourn” (Matt. 5). But those who sow in the flesh sow with joy; afterward weeping will follow, because “mourning occupies the end of joy” (Prov. 14).

### Verse 7

> “As they went, they went and wept, casting their seeds.”

“As they went, they went.” [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though he said: Since those who sow in tears shall reap, therefore, although they sow with weeping, they shall nevertheless exult. This is what he says: Such persons, who sow in tears, “as they went, they went,” by progress in a better life, “and wept,” because they were miserable among the miserable. For it is better that no one should be miserable than that you should perform mercy. Anyone who wishes there to be miserable people so that he may show mercy has cruel mercy, just as a doctor is cruel who wishes for many sick people in order to practise his art.

I say, they went and wept, “casting their seeds”—as though sending them beforehand into that future age. The seeds are mercy and good works: by these one ascends. [Cassiodorus.] I say, their own seeds, namely, deeds performed not from plunder but from one’s own labor. These people wept on the way:

### Verse 8

> “But when they come, they shall come with exultation, bearing their sheaves.”

“But when they come” to the judgment, [Cassiodorus, Augustine] which will be common to all, “they shall come with exultation.” This belongs only to the good, because only the good shall come to joy. I say, they shall come “bearing their sheaves,” the fruit of their sowing: namely, the crown of joys and exultation. Then will be the triumph of those rejoicing, who even mock death, over which they groaned here.

## Comparison on Psalm 125: “When the Lord turned the captivity of Sion,” etc.

[Col. 1156D]

### Verse 1

“When the Lord turned.” It is a Hebraism: *beshub*. Similarly, it is also a Greek manner of speaking, although in Greek it is ἐν τῷ ἐπιστρέψαι Κύριον, “when the Lord turned.”

“Like those comforted.” St Jerome and all the others: “like those dreaming.” *Ḥolemim*, from the root *ḥalam*, which sometimes also means “to become fat,” so that it agrees sufficiently with “consolation,” although a dream fittingly suggests the restfulness of consolation. Hence the translator for Campensis said, “we were restored to rest”; and the Chaldean translator: “we shall be like sick persons who have recovered.” Yet St Jerome, in his Commentaries, reconciles the passage by saying: “For ‘comforted,’ all the editions alike have translated ‘dreaming.’ And ‘dreaming’ is well said, for there is not yet full joy for those situated in captivity.”

### Verse 5

“As a torrent in the south.” Sanctes: “as a torrent in a dry place.” Nebiensis agrees, which amounts to the same thing. For *negeb* means the south [Col. 1157A], or the warm south wind. Nearly all the others translate “as torrents” or “living [waters],” in the accusative case. In either case something suitable must be understood: “Turn our captivity as a torrent,” or “as torrents in the south.” Hence the Chaldean paraphrast: “Turn, O God, our captivity, as the earth is turned when streams of waters abound in time of drought.”

# Psalm 126

[Col. 1157]

## Title of the Psalm: “A Song of Ascents of Solomon”

[Col. 1157A]

“Unless the Lord builds the house.” Title: A Song of Ascents of Solomon. [Augustine.] This is the eighth ascent, signifying the New Testament, which is denoted by the number eight. It treats of the building of God’s house—that is, the Church—by the true Solomon, namely Christ, who is the true peacemaker, “who made both one” (Eph. 2), and who in himself, the cornerstone, built the Church from the two walls of Jews and Gentiles. In signification of this, Solomon built the temple (1 Kings 6). Therefore “of Solomon” is fittingly added here beyond the usual title, because he built the temple as a figure of the true peacemaker, namely Christ, who, as stated, builds the Church from two walls.

Therefore, lest you should understand that Solomon, the psalm says: “Unless the Lord builds the house” (Ps. 126). Hope must be placed in him, not in any human being, because even that Solomon who built the temple fell. For Solomon was a vehement lover of women, and that desire became such a snare to him that he was compelled by women to sacrifice to idols (1 Kings 11). The sense of the title is: this is a Song of Ascents of Solomon—that is, joy concerning the ascent, namely the building and advancement of the Church, which Christ built.

Purpose: he urges ascent.

Method: [Cassiodorus.] The psalm has two parts. First, he says how those ascending ought to conduct themselves: namely, that they should learn that building is from God alone and that exaltation in the future comes only after humiliation. Second, he says what the inheritance is and how it is gathered, at “Behold, the inheritance.” Therefore, lest anyone should take another builder besides the Lord, he says:

### Verse 1

> “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain.”

Unless the Lord. [Hilary.] That is to say: Jesus has now come; he has now brought us back from captivity; the city Jerusalem is now being built. But let those who ascend learn [Col. 1157D] that building and guarding are from God alone, and that future exaltation will come only after humiliation. Although we rejoice in the grace of the New Testament, no one ought to presume upon so great a gift; for unless the Lord—that is, Christ—builds the house, those who build it labor in vain, and so forth. [Augustine.] The Lord Christ builds without anyone cooperating inwardly; preachers who speak outwardly as ministers of building, and guardians of those being built, labor in vain. The house is the people, the city of God. Everyone who makes progress ascends to it; everyone who falls away falls from it. By loving God you ascend; by loving the world you fall. [Cassiodorus.] For these are songs of those who love and burn with a certain holy longing. Therefore, unless the Lord builds [Col. 1158A] this house, those who build it labor in vain, because “neither he that planteth is anything, nor he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase” (1 Cor. 3). [Augustine.] All who preach God’s word in the Church, the ministers of God’s sacraments, labor in this building. Having spoken of building, he adds concerning guarding, saying:

**VERSE 2.—“Unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it watches in vain.”**

Unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it watches in vain. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] See how he passes from the house to the city, which has many houses, so that there may be no presumption either in individual persons or in the fortified community. Although house and city differ according to the metaphor drawn from different things, yet they are one Church, which both signify. Then, lest any should wish to be exalted before humiliation, he turns to them and says:

**VERSE 3.—“It is vain for you to rise before the light: 282 rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow.”**

It is vain. [Augustine.] That is to say: The labor and guarding of the city are vain unless the Lord works; and it is also [Col. 1158C] vain for you to rise before the light, that is, before Christ. To rise is to be exalted and secure. As though he said: It is vain for you if you rise before the light has risen. The light is Christ, “who enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). One must rise after him, not before him—as does one who sets himself above Christ, wishing to be lofty here while Christ was humble. So wished the sons of Zebedee: before they were humbled according to Christ’s passion, they chose for themselves where they would sit in the kingdom of God, one at the right hand and the other at the left (Matt. 20). They wished to rise before the light; but rising—that is, exultation—follows sitting, that is, humiliation, so that Christ may be our light. After death he rose more highly. Therefore he adds: But rise after you have sat down, namely [Col. 1158D] when the sitting—that is, humiliation—has been completed. I say, after you have sat down; I do not mean sitting in judgment or rejoicing, but sitting in humiliation. Hence he adds, “you who eat the bread of sorrow.” For sitting sometimes signifies humility, sometimes the honor of judging. Here, however, it denotes humiliation, as is shown by his words, “you who eat the bread of sorrow.” He eats the bread of sorrow who groans in this pilgrimage; who refreshes himself in the valley of weeping amid affliction, saying: “My tears have become my bread day and night” (Ps. 41). And as though someone said: We are now commanded to sit, and are now promised that we shall rise—but when will this be? He adds:

**VERSE 4.—“When he gives sleep to his beloved.”**

[Col. 1159A] When he gives sleep, [Augustine.] that is, temporal death, in which there is secure rest. He gives it, I say, to his beloved. For the beloved will rise after death. The Lord himself was exalted after death. Therefore hope also for your exaltation after death. Sit down first, then you will rise.

**PART II. VERSE 5.—“Behold, children are the inheritance of the Lord; the fruit of the womb is a reward.”**

Behold, the inheritance of the Lord. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Secondly, he says what the inheritance is and how it is gathered. As though he said: The beloved will rise after sleep. And who are the beloved? Children. What children? Those who are the fruit of the womb. And what shall be theirs? Behold, theirs then shall be the inheritance of the Lord. What is that inheritance? Behold, the reward—that is, eternal life. Notice that he says, “the fruit of the womb.” Not [Col. 1159B] all the children of the Church, which like a certain woman gives birth in pain, are fruit of the womb, but only the good. For the womb of the Church, like Eve, gives birth in pain to good and bad children, just as Rebecca bore in her womb twins contending with one another (Gen. 25); when they appeared at birth, she distinguished them and loved Jacob. Thus also the Church, of which it was said figuratively, “In pain you shall bring forth children” (Gen. 3), gives birth to good and bad. Hence the Apostle: “My little children, for whom I am again in travail” (Gal. 4). But the good are the fruit of the womb, like Jacob beloved by his mother. Their reward is to rise after sitting, to rejoice after the bread of sorrow. For now pain and groaning are theirs; but at the resurrection the inheritance of the Church’s offspring will then appear, and it will then be seen who they are. But by what means were these children acquired? By arrows, [Col. 1159C] because:

**VERSE 6.—“Like arrows in the hand of the mighty, so are the children of those who have been shaken out.”**

Like arrows in the hand, etc. [Hilary, Cassiodorus.] Or thus: Behold the inheritance. As though he said: Who are the beloved? Behold, the inheritance of the Lord, namely children reborn of water and the Holy Spirit; these are the inheritance. Such persons are “the reward, the fruit of the womb,” that is, they are the reward rendered to the man Christ, who is the fruit of the virginal womb and who acquired them by the obedience of his passion. Hence: “Ask of me, and I will give thee the nations for thine inheritance” (Ps. 2). [Augustine.] Notice that according to this reading the division of the psalm lies here.

Like arrows. As though he said: But whence came so great an inheritance? Through arrows, because arrows in the hand of the mighty are shot forth—that is, the apostles [Col. 1159D] were sent out by the hand of Christ and went to the ends of the earth. For the Lord is mighty: when he forcefully shot arrows from the bow of Sacred Scripture, those shot forth reached the ends of the earth. The apostles are called arrows because they are sent by the Lord, passing swiftly through all things like arrows and striking without error. Thus also the children of those who have been shot forth are themselves shot forth, just as those arrows were shot forth.

“So are the children.” As though he said: And, as arrows in the hand of the mighty are shot forth, so the children of those who have been shot forth—that is, of the apostles—are shot forth, that is, sent; and thus the inheritance is acquired. The apostles are therefore so called because they are sent, by comparison with arrows. Or the apostles are called those “who have been shaken out” because they are the ones to whom the Lord said: “When you go out from a city in which they have not heard you, [Col. 1160A] shake the dust from your feet” (Matt. 10). But someone may say that for this reason they seem to be called those who shake out, rather than those who have been shaken out; and according to this they ought better to be called children of those who shake out than children of those who have been shaken out.

We answer that for this reason they may indeed rightly be called those who shake out. Yet that which is shaken out, such as dust, is called shaken out; and that from which something is shaken out, such as a garment, is likewise called shaken out. In this sense the apostles are rightly called “shaken out.” Or rather, there is another meaning here which we must by no means pass over. For perhaps the expression was put more obscurely in order to generate many interpretations, so that people might depart richer because they found something closed which could be opened in many ways, than if they had found it open in only one way.

We must understand, then, that the apostles are called the children of those who have been shaken out, namely the prophets. The prophets are called “shaken out.” For something such as a sack is said to be shaken out, so that what lay hidden and enclosed within may come forth. Therefore the prophets, who contained mysteries shut up within them, were shaken out by preachers: through their diligence and through the Lord’s opening, things that had been hidden came forth openly, as in that saying of Isaiah. It was obscure: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me” (Isa. 1). A preacher, shaking out this folded saying, declared: The ox that treads out grain came from the Jewish people, for from them came the threshing apostles. Everyone who preaches the word of God exhorts, rebukes, terrifies, and threshes the floor; he performs the office of an ox. But the ass is the people coming from the Gentiles, so that Christ may sit upon it, signified in the Gospel by the colt of an ass [Col. 1160C] upon which no one had sat (Matt. 21), because neither law nor prophet had been sent to it. Christ is in the manger for both peoples; he is food on the altar for both. See how that which was folded up has been shaken out. Therefore the prophets are called those who have been shaken out; once they have been shaken out, the apostles were begotten.

Or thus: the apostles are children of those who have been shaken out, who are sent by God’s hand to the ends of the earth. And this is the sense of the text: As though he said, How were the children gathered? Behold: just as arrows are in the hand of a mighty man, that he may send them to strike, so the children of those who have been shaken out—that is, the apostles, children of the prophets—are sent by the hand of God. And:

**VERSE 7.—“Blessed is the man who has filled his desire from them; he shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate.”**

[Col. 1160D] Blessed is the man who has filled his desire from these preachers, [Augustine.] which he does when he does not love the world. For one who is full of worldly desire has no room for what they preached. Pour out, therefore, what you carry, and thus you will become capable of receiving what you do not have. And truly blessed is he who fills it, because he “shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate,” that is, in Christ. For one who speaks in Christ and seeks Christ’s honor, not his own, is not ashamed. Or, “he shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate,” that is, in public, so that all may know what he says.

## Comparison on Psalm 126: “Unless the Lord builds the house,” etc.

**VERSE 3.—“It is vain for you to rise before the light; rise after you have sat down.”** In Jerome’s Hebrew version there is no “rise”: “It is vain for you to rise early, after you have sat down.” The Pratensian version differently reads: “It is vain for you who rise beforehand at dawn to rise, and for you who delay to sit.” Nearly all the rest are similar. The translator, however, in the Campensian version comes close to Jerome’s Hebrew version: “It is futile, if after you have rested you rise very early.” In the Hebrew there is one word which by itself means “to rise early,” and immediately follows another meaning simply “to rise”: *mashkîm qûm*, literally, “rising early, rise.” The Septuagint retained the sense. Then “after you have sat down” is not foreign to the Hebrew, *me’aḥarê shebet*, as though saying, “from after sitting,” an expression Latin usage does not recognize.

**“Bread of sorrow.”** Jerome, writing to Marcella, discusses this passage in these words: “In place of ‘bread of sorrow’ I found written *leḥem ha-ʿaṣabbîm*, which Aquila translated ἄρτον διαπονημάτων, that is, ‘bread of labors.’ Symmachus: ἄρτον μακοπαθούμενον, which they explain as ‘toilsome bread.’ The Fifth Edition and Theodotion—who in other respects agrees with the translators of the Septuagint—give ‘bread of idols.’ The Sixth gives πλάνης, that is, ‘of error.’ Nor is it surprising if Aquila gives διαπονήματον, ‘labors,’ for idols, since they are works of human hands, and the people are prophetically rebuked for rising early in vain for the temple and hurrying to the sanctuary after resting, while revering idols with the honor due to God, as Ezekiel wrote that the priests sacrificed to idols in the temple itself. But that you may be more fully persuaded that idols are denoted in Hebrew by ‘sorrow,’ this very word, *ʿaṣabbîm*, also occurs in Psalm 103. The Septuagint likewise translated it ‘idols.’ For in the place where we read, ‘The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands,’ the Hebrew has *ʿaṣabbêhem*, which Aquila translates ‘their labors.’ Since the truth is so, some not without reason understand ‘bread of labor’ as either the sacraments of heretics or the toil of this wretched and miserable life, in which we eat our bread in the sweat of our face [Col. 1162A], and amid thorns and thistles the sustenance of this brief life springs up” (Gen. 3).

**VERSE 4.—“The reward, the fruit of the womb.”** From the Hebrew it appears that “fruit” should be called the nominative, because it is written *sāḵār perî*. Otherwise, according to the character of Hebrew, one would have to say *seḵar*, so that it might be in the construct state. In Greek, however, the genitive case is plain, as Augustine also interprets it: ὁ μισθὸς τοῦ καρποῦ τῆς γαστρός, “the reward of the fruit of the womb.” Therefore, according to the direct case, Christ, the fruit of the womb, is the reward of the children, who are the beloved inheritance of the Lord. But according to the possessive construction, Mother Church gives birth to children through the womb of charity and faith, and the children will be the reward of this fruit of the womb in the particular resurrection.

**VERSE 5.—“So are the children of those who have been shaken out.”** Jerome and nearly all the others have “children of youth” or “of adolescence.” But *naʿar* means “to shake out.” Hence the passive *neʿûrîm*, that is, “those shaken out.” It is also sometimes a noun meaning adolescence, as the other interpreters understood it. Jerome, writing to Marcella, moreover testifies that the Septuagint translated “those shaken out” for “young men,” so that we understand the vigorous, lively, and ready. To confirm this he cites Nehemiah chapter 4, where we read: “Half of their young men performed the work, and half were ready for battle, with spears and shields and bows and breastplates.” The Septuagint says: “Half of those shaken out performed the work, and half of them had spears and shields and bows and breastplates.” He also followed another translation, so that you may understand “the peoples of youth,” Christians of sharpened understanding.

**VERSE 7.—“His desire.”** All the others have “his quiver,” from the Hebrew *ashpātô*. But the Septuagint understood by metaphor a stored-up joy and fullness of hope, by which a person intent in spirit, as though an arrow aimed straight, pierces the heavenly places. “For our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3). Why “quiver” is put in Hebrew for “desire” Jerome explains in his Commentaries, etc.: because he had introduced arrows in comparison with the saints, he consequently introduces the quiver to be filled with arrows. The Chaldean paraphrase interprets it as “schools.”

## Psalm 127

[Col. 1161]

**283 TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A Song of Ascents.”**

[Col. 1161C]

Blessed are all who fear the Lord. Title: A Song of Ascents. [Cassiodorus.] The ninth step is that the peaceful one, who alone builds, guards, and exalts, may be feared chastely. Intention: He exhorts to chaste fear. Method: The psalm has two parts. First, it enumerates the blessings of the one who fears; secondly, it wishes blessings for the one who fears, at “May the Lord bless you.” Therefore, exhorting to the fear of God, he says:

[Col. 1161D] **VERSE 1.—“Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways.”**

Blessed are those who fear the Lord. [Cassiodorus.] Wretched are those who fear worldly things. We should know that, besides natural fear, which belongs to all, there are four kinds of fear: worldly or human, servile, initial, and chaste or filial. Human fear occurs when we fear suffering bodily dangers or losing worldly goods, and therefore sin. This fear is evil and is abandoned with the world at the first step. But divine fear accompanies us through all the steps.

[Augustine.] Servile fear occurs when a person restrains himself from sin through fear of hell, fears the presence of the Judge and punishments, and does every good thing he does out of fear—not from fear of losing the eternal good, which he does not love, but from fear of enduring the evil which he dreads. He does not fear losing the embrace of the most beautiful bridegroom, but fears being cast into hell. This fear is good and useful: through it the habit of righteousness gradually comes about, and initial fear succeeds it, when what was hard begins to be loved. Thus servile fear begins to be excluded by charity, and is succeeded by chaste fear, by which we fear that the bridegroom may delay, depart, be offended, or be absent from us. This fear arises from love. Servile fear is useful, indeed, but it does not remain for ever. But this fear, of which the Prophet speaks here, does remain: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord,” namely with chaste fear. And who are they? “Those who walk in his ways,” that is, in faith and good works. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] He says this so that we may not merely abstain from evil, but also walk in faith. Notice that he began with the plural, saying “Blessed”; but because all are one in Christ, he speaks in the singular.

**VERSE 2.—“You shall eat the labors of your hands; you are blessed, and it shall be well with you.”**

“You shall eat the labors of your hands.” [Augustine.] As though he said: Those who fear are blessed, because you shall eat the labors, etc. Or omit “because”: as though he said, Those who fear are blessed; and O you who fear—or O you who fear, singular—for either is rightly said, because all are one person. You, I say, shall eat the labors of your hands, or “your fruits,” according to another reading. He calls them “the labors of fruits” where he ought to have said “the fruit of labors”; but because labors are undertaken with joy because of hope, and are themselves delightful, they are now food. Yet their fruit will be more delightful when the saints come with exultation, carrying their sheaves. Afterwards he says concerning both: “You are blessed,” already in the present through labor; and “it shall be well with you” in the future through fruit. And there it will truly be well, where all is well and every good thing flows together for you into the joy of delight. He then adds how the one who fears is blessed:

[Col. 1163B] **VERSE 3.—“Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine within the sides of your house.”**

Your wife, etc. Though this could be taken literally, [Alcuin.] it does not suit every God-fearing person, nor that person alone; but it is suitably taken mystically and applies generally to everyone who fears. As though he said: Thus you who fear are blessed, because your wife—that is, sensuality—is like a fruitful vine within the sides of your house: that is, she is well subject to reason and, thus remaining in paradise, that is, in tranquility, abounds in good works. And:

**VERSE 4.—“Your children shall be like young olive plants around your table.”**

Your children—that is, your works—are like young olive plants, [Col. 1163C] [Hilary, Cassiodorus] because they flourish, anointed with the oil of charity; and they are around your table because those who perform such works are refreshed with heavenly bread. Or the wife is called a man’s wisdom, concerning which Solomon says: “Love wisdom as a bride, and she will embrace you” (Wis. 8). Like a vine she gives grapes, the delightful fruits of good works. The house, then, is thought, whose walls are the two Testaments, in which the mind is strengthened as within the sides of a house. And the meaning is: Your wife, that is, wisdom, is like a fruitful vine within the sides of your house—that is, she abounds in the fruits of good works, which proceed from good thought, formed and fortified by the teaching of the two Testaments. Children are born to you from wisdom as wife. He does not say daughters, using the feminine gender, but sons, because of their firmness: that is, your imitators. And these are around your table, that is, they surround the table, the altar, when they are filled with heavenly bread, namely the Lord’s body and spiritual teaching. And they are like young olive plants, [Cassiodorus.] that is, they are compared to young olive trees, which are greener, stronger, and more fruitful. Hence come both light and relief for the weary.

It should be noted that vine and olive are mentioned here, just as wine and oil are poured upon the man wounded by robbers (Luke 10). In wine is the severity of justice; [Col. 1164A] in oil, the gentleness of mercy. The former pertains to the Old Testament, the latter to the New. [Augustine.] Or by “wife” the Church is understood, and the speech is addressed to Christ the head when it says “your” and “your children.” Yet neither voice nor person is changed, because of the unity of head and body. For Christ, head and body, is one person, and in the head every believer has these things. He says therefore to Christ: “Your wife is like a fruitful vine.” Christ’s wife is the Church, a fertile vine. She is not fertile and abundant in all her members, as she is not in chaff, but in the sides of your house: that is, in those who cling to you, O Christ, and who are your sides. For we say that someone who uses bad counsel has bad sides; and likewise, of one who uses good counsel, we say that he has good sides. Thus those who adhere to Christ are called the sides of Christ’s house.

“And your children.” Christ’s children are the same as his wife, that is, the Church; for she is Christ’s bride and she is also his children. These children are like young olive plants because they are peaceful. For oil signifies peace because it signifies charity, without which there is no peace. These children are around your table because they are satisfied at the heavenly table. The conclusion concerning the blessed person follows:

**VERSE 5.—“Behold, thus shall every person be blessed who fears the Lord.”**

Behold, thus. [Augustine.] As though he said: But why is this so? Behold, it is from the fear of God: thus every person who fears the Lord shall be blessed.

**PART II. VERSE 6.—“May the Lord bless you [Col. 1164C] from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life.”**

May the Lord bless you. [Augustine.] The second part, in which he piously asks that those who fear may be blessed. Here he wishes blessings for the one who fears, but blessings not shared by the wicked. As though he said: Those who fear the Lord will be blessed; but, O you who fear, do not seek those blessings which are not from Zion and which are also possessed by the wicked. Rather, may the Lord bless you with the blessing that is from heavenly Zion—that is, with eternal blessing—and, being placed there now in hope and afterwards in reality, may you see the good things, etc.

[Cassiodorus.] Or, may the Lord, who went forth from the Zion of the Jews, bless you, and may you see good things—not those that pass away, but the good things of Jerusalem [Col. 1164D] through all the days of your life, that is, eternal things which will always be seen. Such things as these present goods cannot be; the burial-place of goods is eternity.

**VERSE 7.—“And may you see your children’s children: peace upon Israel.”**

And may you see your children’s children, [Augustine, Cassiodorus] that is, the fruit of good works, or those born from your teaching. And, to conclude or comprehend everything briefly: may you see peace upon Israel; all those good things are called peace.

*(On Psalm 127, there is nothing to be noted.)*

## Psalm 128

[Col. 1165]

**TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A Song of Ascents.”**

[Col. 1165A]

They have often assailed me. Title: A Song of Ascents. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The tenth step is that one who fears God chastely may patiently endure everything for him. This is then expedient for the Church among the wicked. For although the wicked hear the word of God, they nevertheless daily trouble the Church with scandals and tribulations. In the Gospel they are compared to stony places, where the seed withered because it had no root (Luke 8). The Church has endured such persons from Abel onward. Intention: He exhorts to patience. Method: The psalm has two parts. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] First, by showing what she has endured, he consoles the weak; secondly, he treats of the rejection of persecutors, at “The righteous Lord.” Therefore, as though the Church were answering the complaints of weak persons who murmur [Col. 1165B] that they bear so many wicked people, she begins: “O children, do not wonder at these things as though they were new, which I have endured for so long; and do not be disturbed, because:

**VERSE 1.—“They have often assailed me from my youth; let Israel now say.”**

They have often assailed me, their mother. [Augustine.] He says this because of the frequency of sufferings, and “from my youth,” namely from the first age, from Abel. For sometimes the Church existed in Abel alone, and she was assailed by his wicked and lost brother Cain (Gen. 4). “Let Israel now say this,” while there is opportunity for others to be instructed. Let Israel therefore say this and not fear it: when she is assailed in old age, she consoles herself with the past. What shall she say?

**VERSE 2.—“They have often assailed me from my youth, yet they have not prevailed against me.”**

They have often assailed me from my youth. And why have they assailed me? [Augustine.] Because I did not consent to them, as he says: “Yet they have not prevailed against me,” namely so as to draw me into consent to sin. Since they could not do this:

**VERSE 3.—“Sinners have wrought upon my back; they have prolonged their iniquity.”**

Upon my back. [Augustine.] As though he said: Because they could not make me consent, they made me bear them, and I bear them until the end. Or thus: “Yet,” as though he said, they assailed me, but did me no harm. [Cassiodorus.] “Yet,” that is, because: They could not prevail against me so as to bring me to an end and consume me. For though certain saints have been sent to heaven, the Church could not be brought to an end. Therefore he says, “They have not prevailed,” because the Church grows through adversity.

And when they could not harm her openly, sinners wrought upon my back—that is, they attempted secretly to harm me. For what the wicked cannot do publicly to everyone, they try secretly to persuade individuals to do, so that those who appeared to be coming face to face might not be felt behind one’s back. And as they often assailed, so they did so long. This he says as follows: “They have prolonged their iniquity,” or “their injustice,” because their snares are not momentary but lasting. [Augustine.] Or thus: They have often assailed me, yet they have prolonged their iniquity—that is, they have set their injustice far from me. For although the wicked are with the good in the world, and even though they are in the Church, no one should think that iniquity is close to righteousness. Though I bear them, their iniquity is far from me. Therefore no one should fear wicked persons mixed with him who are far away.

**VERSE 4.—“The righteous Lord will cut down the necks of sinners; may all who hate Zion be confounded and turned backward.”**

The righteous Lord. The second part, in which he treats of the rejection of persecutors. As though he said: Sinners have assailed me, but this will not always be so, because the Lord will cut down the necks of sinners. In this he marks proud, stiff-necked sinners. Pride is indicated in the neck. And [Col. 1166B] may they themselves be confounded, which will occur when they see themselves condemned; and may all who hate Zion be turned backward—that is, be shown ineffective. [Augustine.] They hate Zion, that is, the Church, not only those who are open persecutors but also those who enter deceptively. For those who do not wish to observe God’s word hate the Church.

**VERSE 5.—“May they become like grass on the housetops, which withered before it was plucked up.”**

May they also become like grass on the housetops. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As though he said: There is grass that grows high up, but without a root. Therefore the wicked are compared with grass on housetops because they grow on the summit of pride, where they do not stand firmly, and often perish before they are removed from life. “Which withered before it was plucked up,” [Augustine.] [Col. 1166C] because the wicked are dry before they depart from life. They have not yet been concluded in God’s judgment, and already have no sap of greenness.

**VERSE 6.—“With which the reaper did not fill his hand, nor the gatherer of sheaves his bosom.”**

With that grass—that is, with the wicked and dried-up—the reaper did not fill his hand, nor the gatherer of sheaves his bosom. [Augustine.] The angels are the reapers who will gather good fruits to offer to God, separating grain from chaff (Matt. 13); but from the wicked they will fill neither hand nor bosom. [Haymo, Hilary.] That is, they will gather from them no good work or good thought, because in such people no fruit will be found for angels to carry in hand or bosom. [Col. 1166D] The hand refers to works, the bosom to conscience; but the wicked have fruit in neither.

**VERSE 7.—“And those who passed by did not say: ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we bless you in the name of the Lord.’”**

And they did not say. [Alcuin, Augustine.] As though he said: Those whom the angels will not gather are those to whom the apostles did not preach. This is what he says: They shall not be gathered, to whom those who passed by—namely apostles and prophets—did not say, “May the blessing of the Lord be upon you.” It was especially the custom among the Jews to say this to anyone working. [Col. 1167A] “May the blessing of the Lord be upon you.” For it was customary among the Hebrews that a superior should bless workers (Ruth 2). Hence the opposite is said here: no blessing is given to those who work in vain.

Those who passed by, then, are those who hasten through this life to their homeland, as the prophets and apostles do; they bless those rooted in charity. But to the proud they say, “May the blessing of the Lord be upon you,” namely the blessing which they will have—that is, misery. And they did not say to such persons: “We bless you in the name of the Lord.” The good are blessed. Therefore, if you live well, see that you are blessed. For all who live rightly bless, certainly not in their own name, as heretics do, but in the name of the Lord, from whom they say that all good things come, not from themselves. For they say that no one sanctifies except God, and that no one is good except by God’s gift. [Col. 1167B] They bless in the Lord’s name, not their own, because they are friends of the bridegroom and do not wish to be adulterers of the bride.

## Comparison on Psalm 128: “They have often assailed me,” etc.

[Col. 1168A]

**VERSE 3.—“Sinners have wrought upon my back.”** In the Hebrew it is “they ploughed,” “ploughing,” or “ploughmen”: *ḥāreshû ḥōreshîm*. The long and enduring harassment of persecutors is signified in both ways, as also by what immediately follows: “They prolonged their iniquity,” *he’ērîḵû lemaʿănîtām*, that is, “they prolonged their furrow.” For the metaphor once begun is maintained. The Septuagint drew out the fitting sense.

**VERSE 4.—“The necks of sinners.”** The Hebrew has “cords” in place of “necks.” It should be understood that if *ʿăbōth* is the plural of the noun *ʿāb*, it rightly means dense and thick things, by which, according to the manner of Scripture, pride is signified, also indicated by a fat neck. Hence in Deuteronomy 32, where the hardness and obstinacy of the children of Israel are reproved, it says: *ʿābîtā*—“you have grown fat.” But if *ʿăbōth* derives from *ʿābath*, it means strong cords and dense bonds, as the Hebrews wish to understand it. Either sense is worthy.

## Psalm 129

[Col. 1167]

**TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A Song of Ascents.”**

[Col. 1167B]

Out of the depths. Title: [Cassiodorus.] A Song of Ascents. The eleventh step is penitential supplication, fittingly placed after the preceding steps, because no one, however much he fears God or endures all things, feels himself wholly worthy of Christ, since in the body no one is without sin. Therefore the one security is to bow in prayers. [Alcuin.] This is the sixth psalm in the order of the penitential psalms and the eleventh in the order of the songs [Note: [Col. 1167D] From Augustine, *City of God*, XV.20.]. Six signifies perfection, because God completed the world in six days. Eleven signifies transgression, because it exceeds ten and does not attain twelve. Hence there were eleven curtains of goats’ hair in the tabernacle of the Lord (Exod. 26); there are eleven psalms of Asaph; and there were eleven apostles after the most blessed Judas had been removed, but they returned to twelve when Matthias was substituted. In these things we are given to understand that, however great anyone’s perfection may be, he is nevertheless not without sin; therefore repentance is necessary, because there is six together with eleven.

Intention: [Cassiodorus.] He exhorts to repentance. Method: It has two parts. First, the penitent seeks favor from his own miserable condition [Col. 1167D] and from the mercy of the Judge, from whom he hopes for great things. Secondly comes a joyful conclusion, with certainty of forgiveness, at “Let Israel hope.” [Augustine.] Therefore this penitent, knowing himself to be in the depths, cries out after the likeness of Jonah:

**VERSE 1.—“Out of the depths I cried to you, O Lord; O Lord, hear my voice.”**

Out of the depths I cried to you, O Lord. This is the voice of one ascending. [Augustine.] Let each person therefore consider in what depth he is, from which he may cry to God. Jonah cried from the depths, namely from the belly of the whale (Jonah 2), because not even a beast’s belly could hold back the voice of one praying: it penetrated everything and reached God’s ears. So this man cries from this mortal life, which is a depth to us. Whoever knows himself to be in the depths, battered by the waves of inward and outward misery, has the image of God within him groan and cry until God frees it, so that it may be renewed and restored by God, who impressed it when he formed humankind. But when he cries from the depths, he rises from the depths; that very cry does not allow him to remain far below.

Those are deeply in the depths who do not cry when they see themselves buried under daily sins and weighed down by certain heaps and masses of iniquities, but instead mock those who urge them to pray to God. This is the depth in which a sinner despises, as Scripture says: “When the sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18). [Cassiodorus.] He then adds what he cried: “O Lord, hear my voice.” Then he repeats the same thing in other words, saying:

**VERSE 2.—“Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplication.”**

Let your ears be attentive, [Augustine.] that is, let the hearing of your mercy be attentive to the voice of my supplication. May God be pleased by prayers to hear mercifully. Then, showing from what depth he cries, he says:

[Col. 1168D] **VERSE 3.—“If you should mark iniquities, O Lord, O Lord, who shall endure?”**

If you should mark iniquities. [Augustine.] This is the depth from which he cries; for he cries beneath the weights and waves of his iniquities. Looking around everywhere and seeing no good thing, but beholding evils on every side and troops of his crimes, he cries out in terror: O Lord, if you should mark iniquity or iniquities—that is, preserve them for eternal punishment—O Lord, who shall endure you as Judge? No one. He did not say merely, “I shall not endure,” but “Who shall endure?” Because nearly all human life is barked at by its sins, every conscience is accused by its own thoughts, and there is no pure heart that may presume upon its own righteousness. Let it therefore presume upon God’s mercy, namely that with him is propitiation.

**VERSE 4.—“For with you is propitiation; and because of your law I have waited for you, O Lord.”**
For with you there is propitiation. [Aug.] As if he said: He cries because of hope, because mercy is in him; this is what he says when he says, “For with you,” etc. Or connect it thus: No one can endure if you observe iniquity; nevertheless, I do not despair, because with you there is propitiation. In this is my hope: because with you is propitiation, namely, the sacrifice offered for us, by which he remitted sins—namely, the innocent blood of Christ, poured out and offered for us, by which all the sins of the guilty are blotted out; [Col. 1169B] by which captives are redeemed from the hand of the enemy who holds them captive. Therefore in this is my hope. For if you wished to be judge only and did not wish to be merciful, you would observe all iniquities. And who would stand before you in your judgment? There is therefore one hope: that with you there is propitiation; and because of your law, namely the law of mercy—when formerly you oppressed us beneath the old law, which made us guilty—I waited for you, O Lord; that is, because of the law of mercy and charity which gives life, I waited: the law which forgives sins and thereafter warns a person not to offend. And if I have stumbled, it provides the remedy of prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI). And because you gave this law in the very midst of our need, I waited for you, expecting when you would come and free us from every necessity. Without this [Col. 1169C] law of mercy and charity, by which one bears another’s burdens, no one endures, or endures only in vain. Then, as though someone should say: [Gloss, interlinear] “Is it true that you waited because of that law?”—let the address turn to the hearers, and he says: Certainly,

### VERSE 5.—“My soul waited for his word; my soul hoped in the Lord.”

My soul waited for his word, [Aug.] which does not deceive, which promised the kingdom after pardon. We have indeed received forgiveness of sins, but we do not yet possess eternal life: debts have been cancelled, but the reward is still to come, which we hope for in his word. If it were our word, we ought to fear. But because it is God’s word, it does not deceive. Let us therefore securely [Col. 1169D] hope in his word, which cannot deceive; and therefore he adds, “My soul hoped in the Lord.”

### VERSE 6.—“From the morning watch until night; let Israel hope in the Lord.”

From the morning guard, or watch, until night. [Aug.] He says “from the morning watch,” which is the end of night, because the Lord rose then, and this too is what we hope for in ourselves.
