From that time our soul began to hope, and it hopes until night, that is, until we die. [Alcuin.] Otherwise it has no efficacy, because only “he who perseveres unto the end shall be saved” [Col. 1170A] (Matt. X). Hence, under the law, the head and tail of the victim were offered to the Lord (Lev. III); [Aug.] and because at that hour Christ rose immortal. Therefore he hopes from the morning watch who hopes from God for nothing other than immortality.

“Let Israel hope,” etc. [Cassiod.] The second part, containing a joyful conclusion, in which, secure concerning himself, he exhorts others always to hope in the Lord. As if he said: As my soul has hoped, so let Israel likewise hope in the Lord from the morning watch until night. [Aug.] But how does a sinner hope for what he possessed who was without sin? Well,

### VERSE 7.—“For with the Lord is mercy, and with him is abundant redemption.”

[Col. 1170B] For with the Lord is mercy; [Aug.] because he who went before without sin blots out the sins of those who follow. And with him is abundant redemption, namely precious blood, which redeemed the sins of the whole world.

### VERSE 8.—“And he himself will redeem Israel from all 285 his iniquities.”

And it is so abundant [Aug.] that he himself who went before without sin will redeem Israel. Israel was able to sell himself, but not to redeem himself; he who is without sin is able to redeem. [Cassiod.] Here he now says what that one whom he called merciful and abundant will do: namely, that he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities.

## COLLATION ON PSALM 126: “OUT OF THE DEPTHS I CRIED”

[Col. 1170C]

### VERSE 4.—“Because of your law.”

St Jerome carefully examined this passage in his letter to Sunia and Fretella. From his discussion we plainly observe that he read Hebrew Bibles without the distinction of points, and likewise *yod* where we read *waw*—a *waw* which, he relates, certain interpreters had previously retained, from whom we have the reading now in use. But it is preferable to hear him speaking:

“You say that you have read in Greek, ἕνεκεν τοῦ ὀνόματός σου, that is, ‘because of your name’; and we admit that many copies are found so. But because we are devoted to truth, we must simply state what is in the Hebrew. For instead of ‘name,’ without the law, they read *thira*, which Aquila translated φόβον, that is, ‘fear.’ Symmachus and Theodotion rendered it νόμον, that is, ‘law,’ supposing it to be *THORAH*, because of the resemblance and form of the letters *yod* and *waw*, though these are distinguished by their size.” [Col. 1170D] The Fifth Edition translated it “terror”; the Sixth, “word.” Thus far St Jerome. But now, with the points, we read *TIUARE*, that is, “you will be feared.”

### VERSE 6.—“From the morning watch until night.”

*MISCHOMRIM LABOQER SCHOMRIM LABOQER*, which St Jerome translates, “from the morning watch unto the morning watch”; Pagninus, “above those watching in the morning, above those watching in the morning”; Sanctes, “more than the morning watchmen, the morning watchmen”; Münster, “before the morning watchmen, before the morning watchmen, I say”; and the rest in a similar form. This translation aims to suggest a perfect, tireless, and unceasing confidence in God. Therefore, where the sense is preserved, pedantic imitation of the words is to be rejected.

# PSALM CXXX

[Col. 1171]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A SONG OF ASCENTS”

[Col. 1171A]

“O Lord, my heart has not been lifted up.” Title: A Song of Ascents. [Cassiod.] The twelfth step is humility, which he here shows that he possesses inwardly and outwardly. Intention: he exhorts to humility. Method: the psalm has two parts. First, presenting himself as humble, he pronounces punishment upon the one who is not humble. Second, by his example he exhorts to hope, at “Let Israel hope.” Therefore, showing himself humble inwardly and outwardly, he says: O

### VERSE 1.—“O Lord, my heart has not been lifted up, nor have my eyes been raised.”

O Lord, my heart has not been lifted up inwardly. [Haymo, Cassiodorus, Augustine, Haymo.] From this note the opposite: that is, my heart has been humbled, which is a sacrifice to God; nor have my eyes now been raised outwardly, because [Col. 1171B] I have not displayed outwardly the sign of pride.

### VERSE 2.—“Nor have I walked in great matters, nor in wonders above me.”

Nor have I walked proudly in great matters, nor in wonders above me; [Aug.] that is, I was not proud. I did not wish, as it were, to become known to people by wonders; I did not seek anything beyond my powers, by which I might boast among the ignorant. Thus those who desire wonders for themselves—such as Simon Magus, who wished to advance beyond himself in wonders, delighted by the apostles’ power, not by righteousness. He wanted to do what the apostles did, but not to be what they were (Acts VIII). Therefore what he desired was beyond him, that is, beyond his powers. Rather, one must take care that no one be discordant within the body of Christ, which is the Church, nor envy one greater than himself, but [Col. 1171C] rejoice in another’s good as in his own. And one who abounds in graces should humble himself the more, according to the saying: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. III).

### VERSE 3.—“If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul.”

### VERSE 4.—“As one weaned upon his mother, so is recompense in my soul.”

“If I did not think humbly,” [Gloss, interlinear; Aug.] as if he said: I did not walk in great matters, but thought humbly concerning the benefits given me by God. And I did not exalt my soul through pride. Repeat the whole in sequence: “And if I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul, so may recompense be in my soul.” Thus may it befall me as it befalls someone leaning upon his mother—that is, needing to be cherished at his mother’s breast—who perishes if he is weaned, that is, separated from his mother’s milk: this man binds himself by a curse. [Cassiod., Alcuin.] We are accustomed to say this when we have good confidence in a cause.

Or thus: “If I did not think humbly.” He employs, in a curse, the comparison of one who is weaned, dealing with the Church under the figure of a nursing mother. For just as five stages are marked in bodily generation and nourishment, so they are in spiritual life. First we are conceived in the womb; then we are nourished there until we are brought forth into the light; then we are carried in our mother’s hands and fed with milk, until, weaned, we come to the Father’s table. Thus the first stage [Col. 1172A] is conception; the second, nourishment in the womb; the third, birth; the fourth, carrying and nursing; the fifth, weaning. So also in the womb of our mother the Church: first we are conceived when we are instructed in the rudiments of faith. Then, as it were, we are nourished in her womb, professing the same first principles. Next we are brought forth into the light when we are regenerated through baptism. Then, as it were, we are carried in the Church’s hands and nourished with milk when, after baptism, we are formed in good works and are nourished as we advance by the milk of simple teaching, until, now somewhat grown, separated from our mother’s milk, we come to the Father’s table—that is, from the simpler teaching, where “the Word was made flesh” is preached, we approach the Word who was in the beginning with God. Hence we read that Abraham made a great feast, not at Isaac’s birth nor at his circumcision, [Col. 1172B] but at his weaning (Gen. XXI).

The holy Church observes these five stages. For when, on the Wednesday of the fourth week of Christian service, Christ’s combatants are called, the infancy of the Church is, as it were, conceived. At that time they are imbued through exorcism and catechesis with the rudiments of Christianity. Then, as it were, they are nourished in the Church’s womb until Holy Saturday, on which they are brought to light through baptism. [Alcuin.] Then, as it were, they are carried in the Church’s hands and fed with milk until Pentecost. During this period no difficult observances are imposed: there is no fasting, and no rising at midnight. “For our sister is little, and she has no breasts” (Cant. VIII); therefore she must be fed gradually. Hence at that time Peter’s words are sung in the Church: [Col. 1172C] “As newborn infants, rational and without guile,” etc. (II Pet. II). Afterwards, confirmed by the Paraclete Spirit, as though weaned, they begin to fast and to observe other difficult practices.

[Aug.] But many pervert this order, such as heretics and schismatics, separating themselves from milk before the time, and therefore they perish. But he says that he has observed this order, binding himself by this curse. As if he said: Not only have I been humble in other matters, but also in knowledge, because I thought humbly: first nourished with milk, which is “the Word made flesh,” so that I might thus grow to the bread of angels, namely the Word who was in the beginning with God. For he himself is the bread on which the infant feeds. Bread passes from the table through the mother’s breast [Col. 1172D] so that the same food may reach the little infant. Thus Christ, when he was the Word in the beginning with the Father, such as angels received according to their capacity, became the Word made flesh so that, in order for man to eat angels’ bread, heavenly bread might pass through flesh to infants. Accordingly that same Word was crucified, but was not changed into a human being; rather, the human being was changed in him, so as to become better than he was—not so that the very substance of the Word might be transformed. In respect of what he was as man, God died; and in respect of what he was as God, man was raised and rose again.

[Col. 1173A] Whatever the man suffered cannot be said not to have been suffered by God, because God was man; yet no one was changed into a human being. How can you say that you have not suffered an injury if your garment is torn? Although your garment is not you, much more, therefore, whatever the flesh of Christ united to the Word suffers must be said to be suffered by God, though the Word could neither die nor be corrupted nor changed. Yet whatever of these he suffered, he suffered in the flesh. Therefore the Lord Christ, incarnate and appearing to mortals, made angels’ bread into milk for us.

“And I did not exalt my soul,” as heretics do, who, if they have grasped anything at all, or seem to have grasped it, become proud because of it. Though they are still tender and upon their mother, and are carried in the Church’s hands—as those who were carried in the womb in order to be born grow—they are separated from their mother’s milk before the time. [Col. 1173B] Therefore they perish. I did not do this. And if I did not do it, but exalted my soul by departing from milk before the time, then let recompense be in my soul as it happens to one who is weaned while he still needs to lean upon his mother: he binds himself under a curse. As if he said: So let it befall me as befalls one who is leaning upon his mother and is weaned when not yet somewhat grown.

Or thus: he dealt with humility whereby one is little in malice, not great in pride. Here he deals with exaltation whereby one is great in knowledge, not humble. For there is a good and a bad loftiness, just as there is a good and a bad humility. A person ought to be humble with regard to pride, not with regard to knowledge; lofty with regard to wisdom, not pride. Hence the Apostle: “Do not become children in understanding; but be little children in malice, that you may be perfect in understanding” (I Cor. XIV). It is good, therefore, to be humble in order to avoid pride, and lofty in wisdom. But some, lest they be proud, diminish themselves: they refuse to learn anything and remain on milk. The Apostle rebukes them, saying: “You have become such as need milk, not solid food” (I Cor. III). Be nursed, then, so that you may be nourished and grow; and, when weaned, eat bread.

He therefore says: “If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul”—that is, if I was little not in understanding but in malice—“so may recompense be in my soul as it is for one who is somewhat grown and adult”; that is, let that be repaid to me which is repaid to a child weaned [Col. 1173D] from its mother, so that it may now be fit to eat bread. Here he does not bind himself by a curse, but asserts that good is rendered to him. This is a sound interpretation, but it conflicts with the addition “upon his mother”: it does not say “from his mother” or “from his mother’s milk.” If it said that, the sense would be plain; but it says, “upon his mother,” which does not fit well. For one who is weak and upon his mother, as was said above, [Col. 1174A] perishes if weaned. Therefore it is good for an adult to be weaned, but harmful for one who is upon his mother.

Therefore do not be weaned so long as you are upon your mother. But if an adult goes astray, let him return to his mother’s milk; and thus God will reveal to him what he thinks otherwise (Phil. III), because “God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble” (Jas. IV). For this interpretation to stand, the text may be read thus: “So may recompense be in my soul as it is for one who first leans upon his mother, but afterwards, having become somewhat grown and adult, is weaned,” that is, separated from his mother’s milk, so that he may be able to come to the Father’s table. Or, if the forms in the text are ablative, the same sense is clear, so that it may be said: “So may recompense be in my soul as for one who is weaned from his mother,” that is, from his mother.

[Col. 1174B]

## PART II. VERSE 5.—“Let Israel hope in the Lord, from this time forth and for ever.”

Let Israel hope. [Cassiod., Aug.] The second part, containing the conclusion of the psalm, in which by his own example he exhorts the rest. As if he said: And because I act thus, therefore by my example let Israel hope in the Lord, because in this way it will be able to endure the evils of the world. Let it hope, I say, from this present time and for ever, that is, always without end, until it comes to eternity; for afterwards there will be not hope but possession.

## 286 COLLATION ON PSALM CXXX: “O LORD, MY HEART HAS NOT,” ETC.

### VERSE 3.—“If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul.”

Other words occur in the versions, [Col. 1174C] but they express nothing other than, from the tenor of modesty, that one attributes nothing to oneself. St Jerome: “If I did not set and silence my soul.” Pagninus: “If I did not set and humble my soul.” Sanctes: “Unless I set and silence my soul.” Münster: “If I did not set and restrain my soul.” Pellicanus: “If I did not devote myself to modesty and keep silence.” The interpreters for Cajetan: “If I did not level and silence my soul.” The translator for Campensis: “But I set and restrain my soul.” Behold, you clearly see that they attained the meaning.

“As one weaned upon his mother, so is recompense in my soul.” Because in Hebrew the weaning of the soul is set beside the weaning of an infant, signifying a reciprocal correspondence of comparison, the Seventy aptly put in the second place, “so is recompense in my soul,” in place of “so my soul is weaned unto me.” For thus there is reciprocal correspondence on both sides: *KEGAMUL ALE IMMO CAGAMUL ALAI NAPHSCHI*. St Augustine interprets it in this way: “As one weaned unto his mother, so my soul is weaned unto me.” Pagninus: “As one weaned upon his mother, as one weaned upon me is my soul.” Sanctes indeed adds something of his own: “As one weaned upon his mother, as one weaned—my soul, which is in me—may God do these things to me and add these things.” The others are read much the same in the versions mentioned [Col. 1174D].

# PSALM CXXXI

[Col. 1173]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A SONG OF ASCENTS”

[Col. 1173D]

“Remember, O Lord, David.” Title: A Song of Ascents. [Aug.] On this thirteenth step, now humble and meek, he labours for the building of the spiritual [Col. 1174D] house of God, as David did literally, who wished to build God a house. Appropriately, after the step of humility, he treats of the building of the house, because through humility one becomes God’s house. Hence: [Col. 1175A] “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, but upon the humble and quiet, and upon him who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI).

Intention: [Cassiod.] He exhorts both us and others to build a house for God. Method: the psalm has three parts. First, showing the vow to build the house, he prays that it may be fulfilled. Second, he shows the house built—and where? at “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata.” Third, he states God’s promises made to the built Zion, at “The Lord swore to David.” [Aug.] Therefore, wishing to build a house for the Lord, he says in the person of the whole Christ: O

### VERSE 1.—“Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness.”

O Lord Father, remember David, [Aug.] the spiritual [Col. 1175B] strong hand, who conquered the devil in meekness; and all his meekness. Literally, David, that king, son of Jesse, was exceedingly meek. So much so that he did not return evil for evil to Saul, when Saul, entering the cave to which he had turned aside to relieve his bowels, was given into David’s hands. David spared him, unwilling to kill him, and showed such humility toward him that he called Saul king and himself a dog or a flea (I Sam. XXIV). But this passage is not about him; rather, it is about that which he signified. For through him is typologically signified that one man whose voice is often heard in the Psalms, namely the whole Christ, head and body, whose humility and meekness are commended here:

### VERSE 2.—“As he swore to the Lord, he made a vow to the God of Jacob.”

[Col. 1175C] “As he swore.” [Aug.] As if he said: Remember him for this purpose, that he may fulfill what he swore and vowed—that is, what he firmly promised and voluntarily vowed to the Lord, the God of Jacob, that is, of those who look to things to come. That is, remember David so that he may fulfill what he promised God. Let no one presume on his own strength to render what he has vowed. For he who urges you to vow himself helps you to fulfill it. The Church vows in meekness that it may be God’s house; nothing can be offered to God more pleasing than this. But it is a house if it does not seek its own things, but rejoices in what is shared. For from private possessions comes evil.

### VERSE 3.—“If I enter into the tabernacle of my house, if I ascend the bed of my couch.”

“If I enter,” etc., down to “until I find [Col. 1175D] a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.” [Alcuin.] Up to this point the sentence is suspended. It is an aposiopesis. As if he said: If I do this or that, let me never again be believed. [Aug.] As if he said: David swore to the Lord, saying: “If I enter into the tabernacle of my house,” that is, if I seek what is mine rather than what is God’s. As if he said: I shall not seek it. For he knew that he was hindered by what was his own from becoming a place for God. “And if I ascend the bed of my couch,” that is, if I yield to the flesh—as if to say, I shall not yield. He says “ascend” because private property makes people proud. And

### VERSE 4.—“If I give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids.”

“If I give sleep,” [Aug.] that is, carnal delight, to the eyes of my mind. As if he said: I shall not give it. Earthly [Col. 1176A] prosperities are the dreams of sleepers, which swiftly pass away. For just as a person who sees treasures in a dream is rich while asleep, but on waking finds nothing, so those who sleep, languishing amid the riches and pleasures of the world, will find nothing in their hands when they wake after this life. He who wishes to find a place for the Lord says that he has not done this: “If I give sleep to my eyes.” And, to say still more, “if I give slumber to my eyelids,” which is less than sleep. As if he said: I shall not give it. There is someone who does not sleep but slumbers: now he is drawn back from earthly things, now he returns to them; he frequently bows his head like one slumbering. Therefore, while he removes from himself what is less, he says more concerning himself,

### VERSE 5.—“And rest to my temples, until [Col. 1176B] I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.”

And, [Aug.] to say something even less—that is, to remove from myself what is still less—“if I give rest to my temples.” As if he said: I shall not give it. Sleep comes to the eyes from the rest of the temples, because the temples begin to grow heavy in those who are about to sleep, and when they sense that their temples are becoming heavy, sleep is already at hand. Thus, when some temporal thing begins to delight you unto sin, your temples already grow heavy. But do not yield yourself to that delight, and sleep will not come upon your eyes. With this thought, as though rubbing your forehead, you shake off sleep and hope for a place for the Lord, “until I find.” As if he said: I shall not enter the tabernacle, I shall not ascend the bed, nor do the other things that follow, until I find a place for the Lord—not that he will do those things afterwards, but that God rests in a place prepared in himself and in others. As if he said: I shall not do those things, but this. He says “find” because he sought for a long time. For he sought in himself a place for the Lord, who rests upon the humble and quiet (Isa. LXVI). God’s place is when one abandons his own possessions, or at least their love—when one does not love oneself, but God. Then, having said “place,” he calls it a tabernacle, adding, “a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.” It is called a tabernacle according to the present condition, in which we serve as soldiers. In the future there will be the house of peace, where we shall rest. In the tabernacle we still groan; in the house we shall praise, because groaning belongs to pilgrims, praise to those now dwelling together in their homeland [Cassiod., Hilary]. And [Col. 1176D] note that he says he has fulfilled his vow to the God of Jacob, just as above he said that he had made his promise.

Or it may be read in the person of Christ the head from the words “If I enter.” As if he said: David, that is, Christ, swore, saying: “If I enter into the tabernacle of my house,” namely, the heavenly dwelling. For the tabernacle and dwelling are heavenly. “And if I ascend the bed of my couch,” that is, to the right hand of the Father, where there is rest and the end of labours. “And if I give sleep to my eyes,” that is, the rest of his three-day death. Then in other words he repeats the same thing: “and slumber to my eyelids; and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob,” [Alcuin.] that is, until the holy Church is established by preaching—an aposiopesis. As if he said: Let me no longer be believed.

[Col. 1177A]

## PART II. VERSE 6.—“Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata; we found it in the fields of the forest.”

“Behold, we heard.” [Cassiod., Alcuin.] The second part, in which the house is shown to have been built, and where; and he prays that it may be exalted and that the Jews may not be wholly alienated. As if he said: David promised this and fulfilled it. For behold, we heard “it,” in the neuter, [Haymo, Gloss, interlinear] namely the place, seat, or house; or “him,” namely the place or God; or “her.” Which “her”? Namely, the Lord’s seat. In Ephrata. Ephrata means “mirror.” [Aug.] Thus God’s future house was foretold in the law and prophets, in which there was image and shadow. But it was found among the Gentiles; hence he adds: “We found him,” or “her,” in the fields of the forest—that is, among the uncultivated Gentiles, where there were [Col. 1177B] thorns of idolatry. For what was proclaimed to the Jews in image, that is, in figure, was revealed in the faith of the Gentiles. Hence: “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell in Israel” (Isa. IX).

Or literally thus: “Behold, we heard of him,” [Hilary] namely, of the Lord who was to be born, in Ephrata. This is Bethlehem, where the Lord was born. “And we found it in the fields of the forest.” For it was heard that he was born in Bethlehem, but, through the faith of the Gentiles, he was discovered in the fields of the forest. And to confirm this further, he says that he entered, adding:

### VERSE 7.—“We shall enter into his tabernacle; we shall worship in the place where his feet stood.”

“We shall enter.” [Aug.] As if he said: We too, persevering in our service, have not merely found it but [Col. 1177C] entered. Or, “we shall enter into his tabernacle,” that of the God of Jacob. He who enters in order to dwell there is indwelt by God; he belongs to this house who is joined by charity to others as living stones. Therefore one enters who loves; and one who enters becomes God’s house. And we shall also worship in the place where the feet of the Lord stood. God’s house is the place where he must be worshipped; elsewhere God does not hear unto eternal life. He belongs to God’s house who is joined to others by charity. The sense is: “We shall worship in the place where his feet stood,” that is, we shall be among those in whom his feet stand. These are those who persevere unto the end.

Or, so that “his” refers to the house itself: “We shall worship in the place where its feet,” [Col. 1177D] namely the feet of God’s house, stood. The place in which the feet of the Lord’s house stand is Christ, in whom they persevere. Then, turning to the Lord, he says:

### VERSE 8.—“Arise, O Lord, into your rest—you and the ark of your sanctification.”

“Arise, O Lord.” [Aug.] This is said to him who says, “I slept troubled” (Ps. LVI). As if he said: So that these foretold things may happen, O Lord, rise from death into your rest, that you may no longer be troubled, because death will no longer have dominion over him (Rom. VI). And, O Lord, once you have first been exalted, let the Church also afterwards be exalted—you and the ark. As if he said: Arise: you first, and then the ark. [Cassiod.] This is not Noah’s ark or the Ark of the Covenant, which was a figure, but the ark “of your sanctification,” that is, let the Church which you sanctified arise. [Aug.] It could not promise itself resurrection unless its head first rose. And, when you go to the Father,

### VERSE 9.—“Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your saints rejoice.”

Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, [Aug.] that is, let the royal priesthood be clothed with faith, because “the righteous lives by faith” (Hab. II). Hence Peter says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, and a people for possession.” And let your saints (I Pet. II), that is, your members, having received the pledge of the Holy Spirit, rejoice—that is, be glad—in the hope of resurrection. He understands the same persons as priests and saints, namely all believers. [Alcuin.] Or, by “priests” he signifies the prelates of the Church, and by “saints” their subject faithful; and he distinguishes the ark, for whose rising he had prayed, by the parts of the Church itself, saying: “Let your priests,” that is, the prelates, [Col. 1178B] “be clothed with righteousness,” and with other virtues. For as the priests in the Old Testament used various vestments, so these evangelical priests are adorned with 287 various virtues. These are the ornaments which God requires. What the legal high priests wore upon their garments, evangelical priests ought to possess in their hearts. “And let your saints,” [Alcuin.] that is, those of lesser rank and subject to them, rejoice. Then the words are added in the person of David himself, praying to God the Father:

### VERSE 10.—“For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your Christ.”

For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away your face [Aug.] utterly from the Jews, O God the Father—the face of your Christ. Since Christ turned his face from the Jews, by whom he was crucified, toward the Gentiles, prayer is made on account of Israel’s remnant that they may be saved; this was fulfilled in the apostles and many others. And note that he says, “for David’s sake,” as if to say: Remember me also, that for my sake you may not utterly reject the Jews.

## PART III. VERSE 11.—“The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not disappoint him: Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne.”

“The Lord swore.” [Cassiod.] The third part, in which he states the promises God made to the built Zion, that is, the Church. David speaks in his own person or in that of the whole Christ. As if he said: I rightly say, “for David’s sake,” because [Col. 1178D] the Lord swore truth to David, that actual son of Jesse. And he will not disappoint David. [Aug.] Or, according to another text, “he will not repent of it,” namely the Lord. The Lord is said to repent, not because his counsel changes, but because his work changes. For God neither undergoes repentance nor is deceived in anything so that he wishes to correct an error. But as a person who repents wishes to change what he has done, so, when you hear that God repents, understand the change itself. God does this in one way, you in another. You do it because you had erred; he does it because he punishes or delivers.

He swore, I say, saying: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne.” He could have said, “of the fruit of your loins,” but he says more significantly, “of the fruit of your womb,” because Christ was born solely from a woman, to whom—that is, to that woman—a man did not come. Hence also that saying from the Church’s hymn: “Light and glory came forth through the closed gate.” Christ was set upon the throne of David his father, according to the saying: “And God will give him the throne of David his father” (Luke I). [Alcuin.] For what David ruled temporally, Christ rules spiritually. And not only shall I set him upon the throne, but also,

### VERSE 12.—“If your sons keep my covenant and these my testimonies which I shall teach them.”

“If your sons keep my covenant,” [Aug.] then their sons also will sit. Parents seem to acquire merit for their children by what he says: “If your sons keep,” and “their sons will sit.” But it must be known [Col. 1179B] that people say that they beget and leave behind children as their hope; their children are their hope. Therefore he put hope under the name “sons”; but by “sons of sons” is understood the fruit of hope. The sense is: “If your sons,” that is, the hopes of your sons, “keep my covenant,” [Remigius, Haymo] namely the baptismal covenant—that is, if your sons, hoping well, keep the covenant of baptism—“and my testimonies,” that is, the commandments of life, namely those “which I shall teach them,” not those which they establish for themselves.

### VERSE 13.—“And their sons shall sit upon your throne for ever.”

“And their sons,” [Aug.] that is, their fruit, “shall sit upon your throne for ever,” that is, eternally: they will have such fruit that their hope [Col. 1179C] will not fail, but will attain what it hopes for. Or thus: understand “sons” as people, and “their sons” as imitators. The sense is: “If your sons,” that is, the people born from you, keep my covenant and these testimonies which I shall teach them. This does not change. And also, “their sons,” that is, their followers, if they keep them—and make the distinction—then supply afterwards, “for ever,” [Alcuin.] that is, as long as this age endures, your sons and their sons will sit upon your throne; that is, they will be spiritual kings of themselves and of others, as you were a temporal king. If they keep them, they will sit.

[Aug.] What then if they do not keep them? Does the promise perish? No, because, if it is not fulfilled in you, it is fulfilled in another. For David’s sons are so not by descent but by the worship of God and by faith. Therefore, if they do not keep my covenant, they are not sons. Do not, then, glory in the flesh.

[Alcuin.] Or thus, so that David is understood as Christ, and the passage treats of the promise made to Christ in this manner: The Lord Father swore truth to David, that is, Christ, and will not disappoint or repent of it, saying: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne,” that is, those whom you, O Christ, will bring to birth in faith, I will make kings—but not all of them: only those who keep the covenant. “If your sons keep my covenant and these testimonies which I shall teach them.” This does not change. And if their sons keep them, they will sit upon your throne, that is, they will share in your blessedness, so that as you possess royal authority, so they too will possess it according to their measure. And this will be for ever, that is, eternally. This is that age [Col. 1180A] which will have no end. As if he said: The reward is not temporal but eternal.

### VERSE 14.—“For the Lord has chosen Zion; he has chosen her as a dwelling for himself.”

For the Lord has chosen, [Hilary] as if he said: God promised this freely, not because of merits, because the Lord chose Zion by grace alone, that is, the Church. For what purpose did he choose her? As a dwelling for himself, that he who is everywhere might dwell spiritually. He chose her, saying:

### VERSE 15.—“This is my rest for ever and ever; here I will dwell, for I have chosen her.”

“This is my rest.” [Aug.] These are the words of God the Father, because God loves us so much that he says he rests in us if we rest in him. He himself is never at any time troubled, nor does he rest in himself; but he says that he rests in us because we have rest in him. Therefore this is my rest, [Hilary] namely, the place where I rest. And this is for ever and ever, because it endures eternally. This could not be said literally, since that earthly Jerusalem has often been overthrown. “Here,” that is, in the Church, “I will dwell,” not because of her merit, but because I have chosen her, giving blessing.

### VERSE 16.—“Blessing I will bless her widow; I will satisfy her poor with bread.”

And, blessing, I will bless her widow with an unceasing blessing. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Every soul is a widow that understands itself to be bereft of every help except that of God alone; and I will satisfy her with bread—namely, heavenly bread. For God is bread, who in the flesh made himself milk. Whom shall I satisfy? Her poor, those of Zion: that is, those who do not presume [Col. 1180C] upon themselves but upon God. Hence elsewhere: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied” (Ps. 21). But the proud are full of themselves and will not be satisfied; whereas the humbler they are, the more they hunger, the more they eat; and the more they hunger, the further they remain from the world. One who is full is disgusted and rejects whatever may be offered him.

VERSE 17.—“I will clothe her priests with salvation, and her saints shall exult with exultation.”

Her priests, [Augustine] that is, the chosen race, namely all believers, I will clothe with salvation—that is, with Christ—according to that saying: “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3). And her saints, the same persons as the priests, shall exult with exultation because they are clothed with salvation. [Alcuin.] For they are not light in themselves [Col. 1180D] but in the Lord. Or distinguish priests from saints, as above. Thus: her priests, that is, the prelates, I will clothe with salvation, that is, with Christ, so that they may be worthy to teach; and her saints, that is, those subject to them, shall exult with exultation in Christ.

VERSE 18.—“There will I bring forth the horn of David; I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.”

There, or in that place, or there I will bring forth, or raise up, the horn of David, [Augustine] that is, Christ, so that hope may be placed in Christ. For he is the height signified by the horn—not a fleshly but a spiritual height. He is the one who baptizes by power and authority. Therefore those who rightly are signified by the horn exult securely in him, because the horn surpasses the flesh; and the spiritual height of the Church, which surpasses flesh, is Christ, who grants us by grace [Col. 1181A] to conquer the flesh (John 5), for whom John is prepared as a lamp. Hence he adds: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.” This lamp is John, who proclaims him by pointing him out, saying: “This is he who baptizes” (John 1). [Alcuin.] John, going before, announces Christ and prepares the way for the Word by accustoming people to baptism. For he is the herald of the Word, the bridegroom’s friend, Christ’s lamp. Hence, on days when no feast is celebrated, one candle is carried before the Gospel. This is John, who went before Christ in preaching and baptizing. But on feast days two candles go before, because the apostles were sent out two by two to preach in Judaea before Christ’s death and resurrection (Luke 10).

VERSE 19.—“I will clothe his enemies with confusion; but upon him my sanctification shall flourish.”

But his enemies, that is, Christ’s enemies, I will clothe with confusion. [Cassiodorus.] This the Son will do, to whom all judgment has been given. [Augustine.] But note that the Father, who speaks here, does what the Son does. Upon Christ himself, however, my sanctification shall flourish. It will not merely exist, but flourish, because he alone sanctifies and no one else does. Sanctification flourishes in him unto glory, by comparison with a tree, which is more beautiful when it blooms. Therefore sanctification flourishes unto glory in Christ, in whom is the power of sanctification. But it could not flourish in a human being, who is grass and whose every glory is like the flower of grass (Isa. 40).

## Comparison on Psalm 131: “Remember, O Lord, David,” etc.

[Col. 1181C]

VERSE 1.—“His meekness.” Jerome and others translate “his affliction.” And although the affliction which David patiently endured made his meekness more than sufficiently evident, nevertheless among the Hebrews as well, who here read **UNNOTHO**, **ANAU** means “meek” and “humble,” from the root **ANAH**, that is, “he humbled” or “was oppressed.”

VERSE 5.—“And rest for my temples.” This is not found in the Hebrew codices. “But, as is evident,” says St Ambrose, “we have discovered that many things were not idly added by the seventy men to the Hebrew reading; and this has been demonstrated above by very many more examples.” Yet it should be known that here *temples* is not taken to mean spans of time, but the sides of the head, as is more clearly evident from the Greek τοῖς κροτάφοις, “the temples.”

VERSE 6.—“Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata; we found it in the fields of the wood.” Faber contends that *him* ought [Col. 1181D] to be read in the masculine because *place* preceded it. If it were read in the feminine, it would have nothing to which it could refer, unless something were borrowed from outside, as St Augustine understands *seat*. Yet the feminine is correct from both the Hebrew—**SCHEMAANUHA**, “we heard it,” **METZANUHA**, “we found it”—and the Greek αὐτήν, “it.” It is nevertheless true that St Jerome translated well with the masculine; for, as he himself often warns, word should not be rendered by word.

VERSE 7.—“In the place where his feet stood.” In Hebrew one reads **LAHADOM RAGLAU**, that is, “the footstool of his feet,” which comes to the same thing. For the place on which feet stand is naturally called a footstool; and in both expressions are fittingly suggested the humble preaching of the apostles and the perseverance of the faithful.

VERSE 8.—“Your sanctification.” In Hebrew it is **UZECA**, “the man of your strength.” Yet saints are those strengthened firmly by the love of God; and “holy” is indeed said in the sense of “firm.” Hence the Chaldaean paraphrast has: “and the ark in which is your law.”

VERSE 11.—“He shall not deceive him.” It is read in the feminine gender in Hebrew, and likewise in Greek: **MIMMENAH**, αὐτήν, “her.” But Saints Hilary and Augustine read it in the masculine. The former refers it to David; the latter to God, because he reads, “he will not repent of him.” Those who read it in the feminine refer it to truth, from which God will not turn away. There is no difference in sense. Nor is it difficult for a reciprocal transition to occur in any language because of similarity of relationship.

VERSE 16.—“Widow.” St Jerome translates “his hunting,” while others render “his provision,” “food,” “sustenance,” or something similar. But the Greek witnesses vary three ways. Some codices have θύραν, “door”; others θήραν, “hunting.” But usage prevailed, Jerome says in his *Commentaries*, and he touches on the matter in the *Questions*: by changing a single letter, χήραν, “widow,” came to be said. Yet Faber and Caecus strongly urge that henceforth it should be sung, “his provision,” etc. St Hilary protests, though he is not ignorant of the translation “hunting.” For he says:

> “One of the translators has been found to have interpreted it thus: ‘Blessing, I will bless his capture,’ as though, since the apostles were made hunters and fishers of men, this capture of theirs were blessed—especially because Bethsaida, from which the apostles came, is called, in the interpretation of the Hebrew language, ‘house of hunters.’ But we must follow that first authority of the translation, sealed under the times of the Jews before the Lord’s coming, for the Church’s teaching: ‘Blessing, I will bless her widow.’”

So Hilary. But that St Augustine read and expounded “widow” is well known. Finally, the Hebrew reads **TZEDAH**. If it is derived from the root **TZOD**, it means “hunting” or “food”; if from the root **TZADAH**, which sometimes denotes being laid waste, especially in the passive—as in Zephaniah 3, “The cities are laid waste,” **NITZDU**—it will not unreasonably mean a widow who has been made desolate and abandoned. “A widow,” says St Augustine, “is a soul which understands itself to be deserted by every aid except that of God alone.”

VERSE 19.—“My sanctification.” Hebrew: **NIZRO**—consecration, diadem, crown, sanctification. But where the Hebrews read through *waw*, “his crown,” the Septuagint read through *yod*, the sign of the first-person pronoun, [Col. 1182D] as happens very frequently. Hence Jerome, speaking of this in the *Commentaries*, rendered it simply, without any pronoun. He writes: “For ‘sanctification,’ **NEZER** stands in the Hebrew; Aquila translates it ‘consecrated,’ and it signifies the gold plate tied upon the high priest’s forehead, bearing the engraved name of the Lord.”

## Psalm 132

[Col. 1181]

### Title of the Psalm: “A Song of Ascents.”

[Col. 1181D]

“Behold how good.” Title: “A Song of Ascents.” [Cassiodorus.] The fourteenth ascent is love of neighbour, which makes brothers dwell as one. From it come blessing and life. This psalm is an *atomus*, that is, without division, in which love of neighbour is commended, [Col. 1182D] since it admits no estrangement or division of mind. Therefore the righteous man, rejoicing in the common dwelling of brothers, says:

VERSE 1.—“Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell as one.”

Behold. [Cassiodorus.] This is the word of one pointing, as though what he is about to say may be explained more by being shown than by speech. “How good,” that is, useful, “and how pleasant,” that is, delightful. [Hilary.] This is added because there are good things which do not delight. What is good and pleasant? “For brothers to dwell as one.” [Augustine.] Yet with the individual offices rightly ordered, so that they do not hinder unity but produce it: the unity which existed among those of whom it is said, “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4). What is said here, namely, “to dwell as one,” applies to all Christians, who ought to dwell as one in mind and faith; but it applies especially to monasteries and brothers living together as one, not only in heart but also in body, as did those brothers of Judaea who, having laid all that they possessed at the apostles’ feet, dwelt as one, of whom it is said: “They had one heart and one soul, and all things were common to them” (ibid.). For this verse, like a sweet sound and pleasant melody, known throughout the whole world as the trumpet of the Holy Spirit, gathered into one those divided in body and produced many monasteries. Yet from these blessing descends to the rest, who, if they do not dwell as one bodily, nevertheless do so in mind. And because he had said “behold” by way of showing, he shows how good and pleasant it is, adding:

VERSE 2.—“Like ointment upon the head, which runs down upon the beard, Aaron’s beard.”

Like ointment. [Augustine, Alcuin.] As though he said: So good and pleasant is it for brothers to dwell as one, like ointment upon the head which runs down upon the beard, Aaron’s beard. Some say that there is here a comparison between the brothers’ living together and Aaron’s literal anointing, and the dew of Hermon; but this is worthless, since that is not something great, and those mountains are separated by a great distance. Therefore these things must be understood spiritually. Aaron is the priest who offered himself, that is, Christ, who entered the Holy of Holies and was both victim and priest. Since he did not find in the world a clean offering to offer, he offered himself; and together with the Church he is the one, whole Christ. On his head is ointment, because in him “all the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” (Col. 1); the Spirit was not given to him by measure (John 3). But from Christ the head, ascending into heaven, the Holy Spirit came down upon his beard—that is, upon the strong, vigorous, eager persons [Col. 1183D] signified by the beard, which is a mark of manhood. Thus, when we describe someone strong, we say, “He is bearded.” Therefore the ointment descended first onto the beard, onto the apostles and those who sustained the first assaults but could not be conquered; and from them it descended even to the hem of the garment. Christ’s garment is the Church, without spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5); the hem of the garment is its end, at which the garment is completed. These are the perfect who dwell as one, who fulfil Christ’s law: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. 6). The sense is: This is so good and pleasant as ointment—that is, the anointing of the Holy Spirit—which was first upon Christ the head. [Jerome.] This is said by analogy with kings and priests, who in the Old Testament were anointed as a figure [Col. 1184A] of Christ. [Augustine.] The ointment afterward descended from Christ the head upon the beard. Then he specifies upon whose beard, adding, “Aaron’s beard,” namely, that of Christ the true priest. This is the specification: that is, the apostles and the other first saints who first contended for the faith but could not be conquered, because the head himself had already gone before them, from whom the ointment descended, with such an example preceding as would conquer the beard. I say that the ointment descended upon the beard.

VERSE 3.—“Which runs down upon the hem of his garment, like the dew of Hermon, which runs down upon Mount Zion.”

That ointment afterward runs down upon the hem of his garment, [Hilary] that is, Christ’s, that is, upon those perfect persons [Col. 1184B] who dwell as one. And there is a comparison between fraternal cohabitation and spiritual anointing, namely between cause and effect. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Or the hem to which the ointment descends is understood not as the hem at the sides of the garment, but as the opening of the garment’s neck. Such are those who dwell as one. For as a person’s head enters through these openings to clothe himself, so Christ enters through fraternal concord in order to be clothed by the Church; and the same thing is signified by the hem of the garment as before, though according to a different property. Or by the hem, which is the end of the garment, are understood the saints who will be in the Church’s last times, namely, at the time of Antichrist. The sense is also this: it descended upon the hem of his garment, that is, even to the extremities of the Church at the end of the world, which is the indivisible tunic. Then, expressing the same thing in other words with different signs, he says, “like dew.” As though he said: So good and pleasant is it for brothers to dwell as one, as the dew of Hermon is good and pleasant. Dew coming from heaven is grace, by which brothers dwell as one, not by their own strength or merits. Hermon, literally, is a mountain beyond the Jordan. If this is taken literally, it is strange—and indeed impossible—that dew should descend from it onto Zion; therefore it must be understood spiritually. Hermon means “exalted light,” that is, Christ first exalted on the cross and afterward in heaven, from whom the dew of grace descends upon Zion, that is, the Church. The sense is: This is as good as the dew of Hermon, that is, the grace of Christ, first [Col. 1184D] exalted on the cross and afterward in heaven; this dew descends on Mount Zion, that is, the Church. For the Church is not one except by his gift and grace. Thus Zion here signifies the same as the beard and hem of the garment above, while the dew of Hermon signifies the same as the ointment above—namely grace, by which common dwelling is brought about. Those who are together without the dew of charity are like a restless beast under a yoke: it does not pull but creates disorder. For they are hateful, troublesome, and turbulent; they disturb others with their own anxiety and look for evil things to say about them. Such persons also murmur, of whom it is said in the book of Jesus son of Sirach: “The heart of a fool is like a cartwheel carrying hay, and it is always grumbling” (Ecclus. 33). Such are those left at the mill, in the field, and in bed (Matt. 4), [Col. 1185A] who are together only bodily; but the others, who are together in heart, are taken up.

Or thus: [Haimo.] Hermon is a pasture mountain, as Mount Zion also is. By Hermon, therefore, the Gentiles are signified, who received the nourishment of the word. [Hilary, Cassiodorus.] And this is good, like the dew of Hermon—that is, the grace received by the Gentiles—which first descended upon Mount Zion, that is, upon the Jews. Or by Hermon, which is interpreted “anathema,” sinners are understood; by Zion, the Church. Dew is a thin water by which the earth germinates, and it signifies grace by which sinners are converted. Therefore its dew, that is, Hermon’s dew, is the dew of grace that nourishes sinners in goodness. This dew descends upon Mount Zion when those who have been watered by this dew are converted to the Church, which receives them. The sense is: This also is good, like the dew of Hermon, that is, grace nourishing sinners, which descends upon Mount Zion—that is, by which they are converted to the Church.

[Col. 1186A] VERSE 4.—“For there the Lord commanded blessing, and life unto eternity.”

For there. [Augustine.] As though he said: Therefore it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell as one, because there—that is, among brothers who dwell as one—the Lord commanded blessing: that is, here he commanded that they should bless God. For those who are in concord bless God; those who are in discord do not. For in discord there is no true blessing: though the tongue makes sound, the heart is silent. And “he commanded” means “he promised” life in the future, enduring unto eternity.

## Comparison on Psalm 131: “Behold, how good and how,” etc.

VERSE 2.—“Like ointment.” The Hebrews call it the finest oil, because **SCHEMEN** means “oil,” and by adding the particle “best,” it becomes fragrant ointment. The Chaldaean also has “good ointment.”

## Psalm 133

[Col. 1185]

### Title of the Psalm: “A Song of Ascents.”

[Col. 1185B]

“Behold, now bless the Lord.” Title: “A Song of Ascents.” The fifteenth ascent is love of God. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Cassiodorus.] This is the third psalm concerning love of God, which it treats here as the preceding psalm treated love of neighbour—not because the grace by which God is loved differs from that by which one’s neighbour is loved, but because the same virtue has [Col. 1185C] different acts and its objects of love are different. Intention: it exhorts to love God. Method: the psalm has two parts. First, it invites a plurality to bless God. Second, it wishes them to be blessed, at “May he bless.” Therefore, exhorting them to bless, it says:

VERSE 1.—289 “Behold, now bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord.”

Behold. [Jerome, Hilary.] This is the word of one pointing, and it specifies to whom he makes this demonstration: all you servants of the Lord, gathered together as one now, having ascended so many steps. Or, “now,” that is, in this time, bless the Lord amid adversities. You, I say,

VERSE 2.—“Who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.”

[Col. 1185D] Who stand, [Cassiodorus, Jerome, Augustine] that is, who persevere, in the house of the Lord—that is, in the inner chambers, namely the greater and more perfect persons in the Church—and also you who stand in the courts of the house of our God—that is, at the entrance, namely beginners. For in this house there are different ranks of those who stand. Note that he says “you stand,” not “you sit,” because servants ought not sit in their master’s house. Or it is understood of the same persons: by “house” the Church is meant, and by “courts,” the breadth of charity. For in charity one is extended even to one’s enemies: there is breadth. In hatred there is narrowness. As though he said: Bless, you who stand, that is, persevere, in the Lord’s house—that is, in the Church—and who stand in the courts of the house of our God, that is, in the breadth of charity, where no one is hemmed in, etc.

[Col. 1186B] VERSE 3.—“In the nights lift up your hands unto the holy places, and bless the Lord.”

In the nights, [Augustine] that is, in adversities, not only in days of prosperity, lift up your hands of body and work, [Hilary] as Moses lifted up his hands while the people Israel fought against Amalek (Exod. 17). Lift them up, I say, unto the holy places, so that you may do good with the intention of eternal things. Otherwise it is of no avail. And bless the Lord, attributing no good thing to yourselves, but all to God.

PART II. VERSE 4.—“May the Lord bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth.”

May the Lord bless you. [Cassiodorus, Alcuin, Augustine.] The second part, in which he wishes believers to be blessed. As though he said: I said, “Bless,” and that you may be able to do this, may the Lord bless you with the blessing which is from Zion—he who is able, because he is the one who made heaven and earth. Note that above he exhorts many to bless one; but he himself blesses only one—that is, he exhorts and prays that one may be blessed, as is indicated by his speaking in the singular, “May he bless you.” For although they are many, they are nevertheless one, and blessing belongs to unity. Hence one was healed in the pool, [Col. 1186D] the one who first went down (John 5). Therefore be in the one, and blessing will reach you. Notice also that the righteous man who has ascended so many steps receives heavenly blessing as the place of recompense, because every gift of those who ascend is blessing.

## Comparison on Psalm 133: “Behold, now bless the Lord, all,” etc.

VERSE 2.—“In the courts of the house of our God.” This was added by the Septuagint for emphasis; for this is not unusual with them, and why they added or omitted certain things has been shown sufficiently often above. But let us state what St Hilary thinks of this:

> “I have found some who were uncertain about the phrase, ‘in the courts of the house of the Lord.’ They said that this was added by the first translators because it occurs in the same verses of the following psalm, supposing that it had been omitted from the Hebrew books through scribal error. But let the new interpreters discuss what they wish; for us, the authority and antiquity of the translations must be obeyed.”

So he speaks. The Hebrews then connect “in the nights” [Col. 1188A] with the preceding verse; but standing in the house of God at night and lifting up one’s hands at night signify exactly the same thing.

## Psalm 134

[Col. 1187]

### Title of the Psalm: “Alleluia.”

[Col. 1187A]

“Praise the name of the Lord.” Title: *Alleluia*. [Cassiodorus.] After the ascents that lead to eternity, *alleluia* is fittingly set down, so that the Church may enjoy the praises of God, for whom such a gift has been prepared. Intention: it exhorts to praise. Method: the psalm has three parts. First, using declarative speech, the prophet exhorts people to praise God, enumerating his mighty works because of his power. Second, he rebukes worshippers of idols, at “The idols.” Third, he exhorts every order to praise, at “House of Israel.” Thus the prophet, as though disclosing his intention, addresses after the aforesaid ascents those standing in the house, that after the benefits received they may praise God, saying:

VERSE 1.—“Praise the name of the Lord; praise the Lord, you servants.”

Praise the name—that is, the power—of the Lord. [Augustine.] You become better by praising him, not he. For God becomes neither better if you praise him nor worse if you blame him; but you will be better by praising and worse by blaming. Yet he remains good as he is. Then he adds who ought to praise and why: “Praise the Lord, you servants.” [Col. 1187C] As though he said: Who ought to praise, and why? Behold, you are servants; and because you are servants, praise the Lord; otherwise—that is, unless they praise—they offend, since they themselves are servants and he is Lord. Then he adds:

VERSE 2.—“You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.”

You who stand. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] As though he said: You servants, praise—you who stand, not wavering, not falling—and therefore ought to praise him. I mean, you stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God: that is, you who stand either in the inner chamber or at the entrance. Then he repeats:

VERSE 3.—“Praise the Lord, for the Lord is good; sing praises to his name, for it is sweet.”

Praise the Lord. [Augustine.] Praise for this reason: because the Lord is good. The chief reason for praise is expressed in one word, “good,” for all things are praised because they are good, but the principal cause for praise is that he is good from himself and in himself; his goodness is not a quality but his nature. He is good by his own goodness, not by a good received from elsewhere. He is good through himself, not by cleaving to another good; he did not need another in order to become good, but everything else needed him in order to become good. But because we cannot see how he is good in his nature, let us at least see his works. “Sing praises to his name, for it is sweet,” or “pleasant,” since he gave himself to be tasted by becoming flesh, so that man might live from the bread of angels; this is chief among his other works. Therefore it is put before the rest. The sense is: “Sing praises to his name,” that is, praise [Col. 1188A] him because he did what the reality of his name requires when he gave himself, incarnate, to human beings to taste. And this is so because the name, that is, the reality signified by the name, is sweet to one who tastes it. It should be noted that praise of God is so tempered in this psalm as to suit both the strong and the weak. Thus, through Moses, when he was sending him to the children of Israel, after saying, “I am who I am; thus you shall say to the children of Israel: He Who Is sent me to you” (Exod. 3), [Col. 1188B] he immediately moderated this, because human beings cannot grasp it, and said what a human being can grasp: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (ibid.). So that this name might not seem temporary because of its reference to human beings, he added: “This is my name for eternity” (ibid.), not because they themselves are eternal, but because he afterward made them eternal without end. For they had a beginning, but they will not have an end; in them the whole Church is understood, and the whole seed of Israel is contemplated.

VERSE 4.—“For the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his own possession.”

For the Lord chose Jacob. [Augustine, Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though he said: Therefore sing praise, because he did the following things, which you are able to grasp: namely, because the Lord chose Jacob by grace, not merit—that is, the Jewish people, understood by Jacob, whose name means “wrestler” and signifies those who wrestle against spiritual wickedness. In other words he repeats the same thing: he chose Israel for himself as a possession. Literally, the Lord set the other nations to be guarded under angels; but Jacob, that is, the Jewish people, he chose for himself, to cultivate, sow, possess, and preserve as a field. And as though someone asked, “How do you know this?” he adds:

VERSE 5.—“For I have known that the Lord is great, and our God above all gods.”

For I, [Augustine] caught up to the things above, have known that the Lord is great in himself. Not everyone can know this; rather, let them believe the one who knows, who entered into the sanctuary of God and perhaps heard secret and ineffable words which it is not lawful for a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12), who said what could be said to people and kept to himself what could not be said. For if we said to him, “We beg you, explain his greatness,” would he not perhaps answer: “He whom I see is not very great if he can be explained by me”? And our God is above all gods—that is, above all gods in heaven and on earth—because he made them.

VERSE 6.—“The Lord has done all things whatsoever he willed, in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the deeps.”

All things whatsoever. [Augustine.] Here he returns to works that may be understood. As though he said: He is great in essence, [Col. 1189A] and also great in works, because the Lord made in heaven and on earth all visible and invisible things whatsoever he willed. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] He briefly encompasses everything, and rightly says, “whatsoever he willed.” For his will, and no necessity, is the cause of all that he made; and not only in heaven and on earth, [Cassiodorus, Augustine] but in the sea, which is traversed, and in all the deeps, that is, in the depth of the unknown ocean. This must be firmly believed. Therefore, if we cannot comprehend all his works, let us firmly hold this concerning them: that all were made.

VERSE 7.—“Bringing forth clouds from the end of the earth, he made lightnings into rain.”

Bringing forth clouds. [Cassiodorus.] He recounts literally the things he made. He says that God administers the secrets of nature. As though he said: He made what he willed. He is the one bringing clouds forth from the end of the earth—that is, either from the lowest part of the earth, whence he brings them out, or from the encircling boundaries of the earth, whence he brings them toward the middle of the earth so that they may rain there. And he made lightnings into rain, because lightnings without rain would terrify and give nothing: lightning produces fear, rain joy. Therefore he who frightened by lightning refreshes by rain. He is also:

VERSE 8.—“He who brings winds out of his treasuries; who struck the firstborn of Egypt, from man even to cattle.”

He who brings winds out of his treasuries. [Augustine.] That is, from hidden causes: you do not know whence it comes, but you know that it blows by God’s command. You perceive that the wind blows, but the cause by which it blows, or the treasury of reason from which it is brought forth, is unknown. He is the one who struck, etc. He performed the following things among human beings for his people. If he has spoken of things you might love in created things, hear things you may fear. For he is the one who struck the firstborn of Egypt, from man even to cattle. He frequently repeats this in order to indicate God’s power, so that these events might not be thought accidental but understood as possessing great future significance.

VERSE 9.—“And he sent signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants.”

And he sent, [Augustine] or “sent forth,” signs and wonders in your midst, [Col. 1189D] O Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants. These things are so plain that exposition would rather obscure them. But when you hear what was done to the ungodly, beware lest it happen also to you. This is why these things are useful when read. Then he adds what the Lord did after the people had been led out of Egypt:

VERSE 10.—“He who struck many nations and slew mighty kings.”

He who struck many nations, [Augustine] which possessed the land he wished to give his people, and slew mighty kings.

VERSE 11.—“Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan.”

Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan. [Augustine.] This happened under Moses. It is read of these men in the book of Numbers that, when they forbade the children of Israel to pass through their borders, they were struck by him, and Israel possessed their land [Col. 1190A] (Num. 21). And he struck all the kingdoms of Canaan under Joshua, after Moses had already died. These things are plain.

VERSE 12.—“And he gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his people.”

And he gave their land. [Augustine.] As though he said: He drove out those ungodly persons and gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his people. Exultant praise follows for these deeds.

VERSE 13.—“O Lord, your name is for eternity; O Lord, your memorial from generation to generation.”

O Lord, your name. [Augustine.] As though he said: When you had done these things, my mouth was filled with praise and I said: “O Lord, your name,” etc. We have seen how these words are written in their literal sense, but they also signify something that must be explained.

Let us return, then, to that passage: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth,” etc. We may understand and recognize these things figuratively in human beings. For heaven consists of spiritual persons, earth of carnal persons. From these two, as it were from heaven and earth, the Church is constituted; among them he does whatever he wills. He also does what he wills in the sea, that is, among unbelievers, in whom nothing happens without God’s command: they do not rage unless permitted by God, nor is vengeance taken upon them unless God has commanded it; and in all the depths he did whatever he willed. The depths are the hidden hearts of mortals, the profound thoughts of human beings. And there God does whatever he wills, because he examines the righteous and the wicked: the good heart is hidden, and the evil heart too is hidden, [Col. 1190C] and in each is a depth. But God sees this, from whom nothing is hidden; he consoles the good heart and torments the evil.

And he is the one “who brings forth clouds from the farthest end of the earth.” The clouds are preachers. Hence: “I will command my clouds not to rain showers upon it” (Isa. V). And again: “Who are these that fly like clouds?” (Isa. LX). These clouds he sent not only from among the children of Israel, but raises them up from the farthest end of the earth and sends them to the ends of the world. But what does he do with these very clouds? [Alcuin.] “He made lightnings into rain,” that is, he bent threats toward mercy and watered by means of terrors. For preachers both terrify and soothe: they terrify by threatening eternal punishments; they soften by promising eternal joys. Therefore it is read of the manna that it melted in the sun [Col. 1190D] and hardened in the fire (Exod. XVI). For manna, given from heaven, is a figure of the divine word: it melts in the sun when it gladdens the minds of the faithful by the promise of future brightness, as when it says: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII). But it hardens in the fire when it scorches the consciences of sinners by the threat of future punishment, as in that saying: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. III).

For this reason, in the Old Law the garment of the high priest had scarlet twice dyed, which has the appearance of fire (Exod. XXVIII). Fire does two things, namely, it burns and shines, because a preacher ought to scorch the hearts of sinners by lightning, that is, by the terror of a threat, and to warm the minds of the godly by the promise of eternal light. Hence also [Col. 1191A] the pastoral staff is pointed at its lower end and extends forward at its upper end, because the preacher ought to prick the vices of the flesh and direct the powers of the mind toward what lies ahead. Yet he must always return to the consideration of himself, lest, after preaching to others, he himself should become reprobate (I Cor. IX). [Aug.] “At the beginning of his speech, one becomes his own accuser” (Prov. XVIII), lest he see the speck in another’s eye while carrying a beam in his own (Luke VI). Therefore it is said, “He made lightnings into rain.”

It follows: “Who brings forth winds from his treasuries.” The same preachers are both clouds and winds. They are clouds because of the flesh, winds because of the spirit. Clouds are seen; winds are felt and are not seen. And because flesh is from the earth, it is therefore said: “He raises clouds from the farthest end of the earth”; but whence the spirit of a human being comes is unknown. [Col. 1191B] Hence it is rightly said, “Who brings forth winds from his treasuries.” Or for another reason, the apostles are called winds, because they swiftly traversed the whole world.

“He struck the firstborn of Egypt.” The firstborn is faith, by which we begin what is good, and by which a person advances to what is better. Egypt is interpreted “affliction.” Therefore he struck the firstborn of Egypt, because whoever afflicts the Church and causes scandals, even if called a Christian, loses faith. He struck, I say, “from man even to beast,” that is, from the learned even to the unlearned. For “man” signifies the learned person, who draws after him unlearned crowds, that is, cattle. “And he sent signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants.” Pharaoh is interpreted “scattering”; Egypt, as we have said, “affliction.” Thus scattering goes before as king, and affliction follows. For those who are scattered afflict the Church; indeed, in order that they may afflict, they are scattered.

“He struck many nations and slew mighty kings.” What nations and what kings? He slew Sihon, king of the Amorites. Hear names laden with mysteries. Sihon is interpreted “temptation of the eyes,” and Amorites “those who embitter.” Therefore those who embitter have as king the temptation of the eyes; and the temptation of the eyes is nothing but falsehood of the eyes. It thinks it possesses a thing, but does not possess the truth. For it reckons what is not; it does not behold what is. Therefore the temptation of the eyes—that is, deceit and pretence—goes before as king, and embitterment follows. For they embitter because they feign. God slays that king in a person together with his people when the person condemns pretence [Col. 1191D] and loves truth, and ceases to embitter.

He also slew another king, namely Og, king of Bashan. Og is interpreted “closure,” by which the devil is signified, [Aug.] who shuts off the way to God so that faith may not be placed in him, just as Christ opens it—and Christ himself is the way. Therefore, when Christ comes, the one whose way is shut off so that he may not believe in God Christ will be confounded. Thus Bashan means “confusion,” because confusion follows closure. “And all the kingdoms of Canaan.” Canaan is interpreted “prepared for humiliation.” Here humiliation is understood not as the virtue, but as the punishment of which it is said: “Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke XVIII). Therefore Canaan is every proud person who now exalts his heart and who will be humbled on the day of judgment. [Col. 1192A] Yet now he is not humbled, but is prepared for humiliation, that is, for condemnation.

“And he gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his people.” By their land are signified all the nations, which are the inheritance of Israel, that is, of the faithful people; they pasture them through tribulation, teaching patience. Therefore they are called Israel’s inheritance, because Israel cultivates them by conforming them to itself.

Otherwise, from the passage, “He struck the firstborn of Egypt, from man even to beast.” Egypt is this world; the firstborn are the principal vices of the world, which he destroys among prudent people and simple people. “And he sent signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt” [Hilary, Cassiodorus], because he openly and visibly performed signs in the world: at the Passion the earth shook and the sun was darkened. And [Col. 1192B] “against Pharaoh and all his servants,” he sent signs against the devil and evil people. “He struck many nations,” that is, innumerable vices, “and slew mighty kings,” that is, ruling vices. Or the kings are unclean spirits, who are slain when they cannot do in us what they wish.

“Sihon, king of the Amorites.” The Amorites signify vices. For bitter are those things which take away blessedness; their king is the devil, who is called Sihon, who transforms himself into an angel of light. Sihon is interpreted “temptation of the eyes”; he is also the king of confusion who shuts off the way to God. “And Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan,” that is, all those who are wickedly humbled. For Canaan is called evil humiliation, when they fall away from holy honour. “And he gave their land as an inheritance, [Col. 1192C] an inheritance to Israel his people,” that is, he gave to the faithful the heavenly blessedness which demons abandoned through pride. This is the true land of promise, more truly called an inheritance because it is in peace, than that earthly land which the children of Israel often lost.

Thus these matters just mentioned are rightly understood spiritually, although they were done literally as well. Therefore, if God then killed them bodily, his hand does not cease even now. [Aug.] And so, lest you think that those deeds accomplished then have ceased, he says: “O Lord, your name,” that is, the working of your power, “is forever”; that is, your hand does not cease to do in this age the things which you then foretold in a figure. And, O Lord, your memorial is in the present generation and in the generation to come. One generation is that in which we are reborn through baptism; [Col. 1192D] the other is that in which we shall rise again. In both is God’s memorial, because God has not forgotten to call in this generation and to crown in the other.

VERS. 14.—“For the Lord will judge his people, and he will be entreated concerning his servants.”

“For he will judge.” The ground of praise is shown here. [Hilary, Cassiodorus.] As though he said: Therefore he is praiseworthy, because the Lord will judge his Jewish people, for whom he did so many things, to whom he sent prophets and afterwards even his own Son; but because they were hard, he will judge them in the future. And concerning his servants, that is, the faithful, he will be entreated, or will console them, when he renders to them eternal rewards. Behold, the ascent of praise has been carried as far as judgment.

Or it may be understood of the present: “he will judge.” [Col. 1193A] As though he said: Therefore he is to be praised, because, besides the future judgment, the Lord will judge his people, that is, the Jewish people, in the present. [Aug.] He has already fulfilled this, because the Lord has already judged the Jews, accepting some and rejecting others: for the righteous have been separated from them and the unrighteous have remained. This is the judgment of discrimination of which he himself said: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John XIX). And after judging them, he will be entreated concerning, or invoked by, his servants. For “God has not cast away his people whom he foreknew” (Rom. II). He has his own from every nation. Therefore the Prophet turns to reproach the idols, now derided by their own worshippers, saying:

PART II. VERS. 15.—“The idols of the nations [Col. 1193B] are silver and gold, the works of human hands.”

“The idols.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] The second part, in which, having filled himself with God’s praises, he rebukes idol-worshippers by mocking them, because the perfect praise of truth is to destroy falsehood. The same things were said above in another psalm, but repetition increases their shame. As though he said: Our God is great; but the idols of the nations are silver and gold as regards their material, and works of human hands as regards their form.

VERS. 16.—“They have a mouth and will not speak; they have eyes and will not see.”

VERS. 17.—“They have ears and will not hear; for there is no breath in their mouth.”

[Col. 1193C] “They have ears and will not hear.” [Cassiodorus.] Then he concludes all things by showing that they cannot be compared either with people or with cattle, when he says: “For there is no breath in their mouth.” [Aug.] That is, the craftsman could make those outward features, but could not give breath, hearing to ears, light to eyes, or voice to a mouth. Knowing this, they mock the idols; but what do they not know?

VERS. 18.—“May those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.”

“May those who make them become like them,” [Aug.] inwardly, as also all who trust in them. And so it undoubtedly happens. For a certain likeness to idols is impressed upon them, not indeed in their flesh, but in the inward person. For they have ears and do not hear God crying [Col. 1193D] to them; they have eyes and do not see by faith; they have nostrils and do not perceive the sweet odour of Christ.

PART III. VERS. 19.—“House of Israel, bless the Lord; 291 house of Aaron, bless the Lord.”

[Col. 1194A] “House of Israel.” [Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which, after the idols have been ridiculed, he exhorts every order to celebrate God’s praises. [Aug.] As though he said: Let idol-worshippers become like them; but you who are the house of Israel—that is, the house daily raised up from the stones from which God is able to raise up children to Abraham (Matt. III)—bless the Lord. And you who are the house of Aaron, that is, rulers, bless the Lord; and you who are

VERS. 20.—“House of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord.”

“House of Levi,” that is, ministers, bless the Lord; rulers and all who fear the Lord. [Aug.] That is, all peoples, bless the Lord. The rulers are the house of Aaron; the ministers, the house of Levi; all peoples who fear him; and all generally are the house of Israel. Therefore let us all say with one voice:

VERS. 21.—“Blessed be the Lord from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem.”

“Blessed be the Lord.” [Interlinear Gloss, Cassiodorus.] He speaks in the person of all the faithful; or the Prophet says this in his own person and does what he taught others to do.
