As though he said: Bless the Lord; and I, for my part, say: Blessed be the Lord who came from Zion, having become human, and who dwells in Jerusalem, where literally he preached and performed many miracles. [Aug.] Or, according to the interpretations of the names: Zion is interpreted “watching,” Jerusalem “vision of peace.” Therefore he is now blessed from Zion, that is, by us, who, as long as we live in hope, are in Zion, [Col. 1194C] because we watch until he comes. When life is ended, we shall be with him in the eternal city, because he is the one who dwells in the heavenly Jerusalem, which shall never fall, where we shall see him in eternal peace.

COLLATION ON PSALM CXXXIV: “PRAISE THE NAME OF THE LORD,” etc.

VERS. 14.—“He will be entreated concerning his servants.” According to the Hebrew, *yitneḥam*, it may be taken passively, that is, “he will be propitious,” as St Jerome translates it; or, as others wish, “he will console,” or “forgive.” Yet it is unusual among Latin writers for *deprecatur* to be taken in a passive sense. And St Augustine reads “he will be invoked.” Hilary and Arnobius read “he will console,” as the Roman psalmody also has it. In Greek it is a passive verb, although it sometimes has an active sense: παρακληθήσεται, “he will be consoled” or “comforted.” Finally, Scripture customarily uses [Col. 1194D] active verbs in such a way that the action is nevertheless a passion in another person. For example, Rom. VIII: “The Spirit intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings,” that is, he causes us to intercede. If *deprecari* is understood actively, the sense will be that God causes his servants to entreat him; thus, whichever way you turn it, the meaning of the matter agrees.

PSALM CXXXV.

[Col. 1193]

TITLE OF THE PSALM: “ALLELUIA.”

[Col. 1193D]

“Give thanks to the Lord.” Title: Alleluia. [Aug.] This psalm contains the praise of God; and although many things are said in God’s praises, his mercy is especially commended here. Hence the diverse beginnings [Col. 1194D] of the verses converge upon one ending, because whatever is said here is referred to God’s mercy, without which nothing endures, and which accomplishes all things. [Cassiodorus.] Therefore we are exhorted to persevere in mercy. The great power of this psalm is shown in Chronicles, [Col. 1195A] where it is read that when the children of Israel began to praise God and say, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever” (II Chron. V), immediately the glory of God filled God’s temple. So ready is the presence of divine grace, if the song is sung with purity.

Intention. It exhorts to praise.

Method. The psalm has three parts. First, it sets forth God’s magnificence and the creation of the whole world. Second, it states what he did in Egypt and among the Jewish people as a figure of ourselves, at “Who struck.” Third, it treats of Christians, at “And gave their land.” Therefore, inviting us to praise God, it says:

VERS. 1.—“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever.”

“Confess praises and sins to the Lord,” [Hilary] “for he is good,” because he hears praises and forgives sins. [Col. 1195B] [Alcuin.] Therefore we ought all and always to praise: let us praise now, that we may deserve to praise with the angels. Praise itself is our refreshment, so that no delight seems comparable to it. It is itself the reward, as it is also the activity. Therefore give thanks to the Lord, because “his mercy is forever”; [Cassiodorus] that is, his mercy is here and in the future, because here he spares and there he crowns. Or “forever” means “in the present age”: his mercy is that by which he frees us from the misery of sins. [Aug.] Or thus: I say, give thanks, and you are not to receive anything temporal for this thanksgiving. For “his mercy is forever,” that is, after judgment, the benefit which he mercifully bestows is eternal, because the blessedness given through mercy shall be eternal.

Then, showing the excellence of him to whom he exhorts us to give thanks, he adds:

VERS. 2.—“Give thanks to the God of gods, for his mercy is forever.”

“Give thanks to the God of gods.” [Aug.] He calls human beings gods, to whom the word of God came (John X), in the other psalm where he says: “I said, You are gods” (Ps. LXXXI). Nor are they called gods because all are good. For if all were good, he would not say in the same psalm: “But in the midst he judges the gods,” or distinguishes them, concerning whom he also adds:

VERS. 3.—“Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his mercy is forever.”

“Give thanks to the Lord of lords.” [Aug.] He speaks of gods and lords in the plural. For there are many gods and many lords, as the Apostle says (I Cor. VIII.5), over whom he himself is

VERS. 4.—“He who alone does great wonders, for his mercy is forever.”

“He who does.” [Aug.] It should be understood that, just as “for his mercy is forever” is placed everywhere at the end of the verses, so at the beginning of all, though it is not written, “give thanks” must be understood. This is clearer in Greek, as if we were to say, “to him doing wonders,” or “to him who does wonders,” where “give thanks” would necessarily be understood. Our mode of expression could not preserve this in all these cases. Therefore in Latin speech it cannot be expressed except by understanding in some places the whole phrase, “to him who does,” or “has done,” these or those things. Hence [Col. 1196A] what is said here is obscure, so that the sentence may be thought to be joined thus: “He who does wonders, who made the heavens,” etc., “for his mercy is forever.” As though he said: He did these things because his mercy is forever, whereas those whom he cleanses from sins and frees from misery properly belong to mercy. But it belongs to goodness that he created heaven, earth, and all very good things so that they might exist.

Therefore it must be said, though it is not written: “Give thanks to him who does or has done these or those things,” because his mercy toward you is eternal, so that the end of each verse may refer back to its beginning in this way: “Give thanks to him who alone does great wonders”; therefore give thanks, “because his mercy is forever”; and likewise in the rest. God alone is said to perform wonders, because he does the things done through human beings or angels, and he alone does without the ministry of human being or angel certain great things, which he goes on to recount:

VERS. 5.—“He who made the heavens in understanding, for his mercy is forever.”

“He who made the heavens in understanding,” [Interlinear Gloss] that is, the intelligible heavens, namely the empyrean; although it is corporeal, it is nevertheless so subtle that it cannot be seen by a mortal person.

VERS. 6.—“He who established the earth upon the waters, for his mercy is forever.”

“He who established the earth upon the waters.” [Aug.] Therefore he made the whole creation by himself, not through a creature. He has mentioned certain more excellent parts of it, from which all things may be conceived: namely, the intelligible heavens [Col. 1196C] and the visible earth. But because there are visible heavens as well, he teaches us to understand the entire bodily heavens through their lights, adding:

VERS. 7.—“He who made the great lights, for his mercy is forever.”

“He who made the great lights,” [Aug.] namely, the sun, moon, and stars. Or let us understand by “the heavens” the heavenly structure. The meaning is: He who made the heavens did not follow another’s work, but made them in his own understanding, that is, in his own wisdom. Hence: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII). What was said of the heavens must be understood of all other things in this way: “He who established the earth upon the waters”—understand, “in understanding.”

But how is the heavier earth borne by waters that are lighter? [Col. 1196D] Yet, whether it is so or otherwise, lest we seem to dispute contentiously against those who think that they have discovered these matters by certain proofs, we have a ready interpretation. For the earth is said to be founded upon the waters because it rises above the surrounding waters, just as a particular city is said to be founded upon the sea, not because the sea is beneath it, but because it rises above the sea; just as the Lord sat “upon the well,” that is, beside the well (John IV).

What great lights did he make?

VERS. 8.—“The sun to rule the day, for his mercy is forever.”

“The sun to rule the day.” [Aug., Cassiodorus.] These things he alone does by himself. The sun is the power of the day, by which all things are made manifest.

[Col. 1197A] VERS. 9.—“The moon and stars to rule the night, for his mercy is forever.”

“He made the moon and stars to rule the night,” [Aug.] that is, that they might be the light of night. Or these things may be understood figuratively. Therefore he made “the heavens in understanding,” that is, spiritual saints, to whom he granted not merely belief but understanding of divine things. But the simple, who hold the sun of faith, are called earth, as though beneath the heavens; because they stand firm in the faith of the baptism they have received, he “established the earth upon the waters.”

“He made the great lights,” that is, he bestowed the gifts of graces upon his faithful. What gifts? “The sun to rule the day; the moon and stars to rule the night.” By the sun is understood the gift of wisdom, given to the day—that is, to spiritual persons—so that they may shine. By the moon, the spirit of knowledge; [Col. 1197B] by the stars, other lesser gifts, given to the night—that is, to lesser persons—so that they too may shine in the night of this age. This is what the Apostle says: “To one through the Spirit is given the word of wisdom” (I Cor. XII): this is the sun; to another, knowledge: this is the moon; to another, faith, healing, and so forth: these are the stars. For none of these is unnecessary in the night of this age; afterwards they will cease, when this night has passed and day has come.

He made these “to rule the day,” or “the night,” that is, in order that the day might have power to shine, or the night. Wisdom differs from knowledge, however, as holy Job testifies, who in a sense defines each separately when he says: “Wisdom is piety” (Job XXVIII), that is, the worship of God, which consists in knowing and delighting in him who always is and remains unchangeable, who is God. But knowledge is “to abstain from evils” (Phil. II), that is, prudently to conduct oneself amid a crooked generation, as in the night of this age, so that each person, by abstaining from iniquity, may not be confused by darkness, being distinguished by the light of his own office.

It may also be said mystically otherwise, from the passage: “He who made the great lights,” that is, heavenly spirits, who shine before all things. And he made the sun, [Cassiodorus] that is, the wise, to rule the day, so that through them the greater may shine; and the moon, that is, the Church, and the stars, that is, the various orders, to rule the night, so that through these also the lesser may shine.

PART II. VERS. 10.—“He who struck Egypt with their firstborn, for his mercy is forever.”

[Col. 1197D] 292 “He who struck.” [Cassiodorus, Aug.] The second part, in which he states what he did in Egypt and among the Jewish people as a figure of ourselves. Note that above he spoke of what he did alone; now he begins to show what he did through angels or human beings. As though he said: Give thanks to him who struck Egypt with their firstborn. Figuratively, he likewise struck the world with those things considered chief in the world. [Cassiodorus.] For he struck the firstborn of Egypt when he condemned the glory of the world, which was thought to be pre-eminent. Luxury, pride, and avarice are things which the belly first begets and embraces as dear children; but God excludes them from himself.

[Col. 1198A] VERS. 11.—“He who brought Israel out from their midst, for his mercy is forever.”

“He who brought Israel out from their midst.” [Aug.] Thus he also leads saints out from the society of the wicked. I say, he brought them out:

VERS. 12.—“With a mighty hand and uplifted arm, for his mercy is forever.”

“With a mighty hand and uplifted arm.” [Cassiodorus, Aug.] The hand of God is invincible action, which comes from the arm, that is, from his whole singular power. This is the arm of which it was said: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII).

VERS. 13.—“He who divided the Red Sea into divisions, for his mercy is forever.”

[Col. 1198B] “He who divided the Red Sea into divisions.” [Cassiodorus, Aug.] Literally, into twelve divisions, according to the number of the tribes, so that each tribe might have its own route for passage. Figuratively, people pass from the world to God by diverse paths; for the Red Sea signifies the world. Or the Red Sea means baptism, which God now divides, so that one and the same baptism may be unto life for some and unto death for others.

VERS. 14.—“And brought Israel through the midst of it, for his mercy is forever.”

“And brought Israel through the midst of it.” [Aug.] Thus he also brings the renewed people through the waters of regeneration.

VERS. 15.—“And shook off Pharaoh and his power in the Red Sea, for his mercy is forever.”

“And shook off Pharaoh and his power in the Red Sea.” [Aug., Cassiodorus.] Thus he destroys the sins of his own through baptism. Or he quickly shook off Pharaoh and his power in the Red Sea—that is, the devil with his ministers—in baptism, like dust which is quickly shaken off. In this swiftness both the power of his divinity is displayed and those people are shown to be earthly filth, which we are accustomed to shake off. [Note: [Col. 1197D] From Origen, Homily 2 on Exodus.] And the devil is suitably understood through Pharaoh. For Pharaoh kills males and preserves females: thus the devil stifles virtues and nourishes concupiscence.

VERS. 16.—“He who led his people through the wilderness, for his mercy is forever.”

“Who led his people through the wilderness.” [Aug.] Thus he has also led us through this age, lest we perish in it or cling to it.

VERS. 17.—“He who struck great kings, for his mercy is forever.”

VERS. 18.—“And slew mighty kings, for his mercy is forever.”

“He who struck great kings and slew mighty kings.” [Aug.] Thus he strikes and slays in his faithful the devilish and harmful powers.

VERS. 19.—“Sihon king of the Amorites, for his mercy is forever.”

[Col. 1199A] “Sihon king of the Amorites.” [Aug.] Thus he slays the useless offspring, or the burning temptation, of those who embitter.

VERS. 20.—“And Og king of Bashan, for his mercy is forever.”

“And Og king of Bashan.” [Aug.] Thus also he slays the heaping-up devil, king of Bashan, that is, of confusion. For what does the devil heap up except confusion?

PART III. VERS. 21.—“And gave their land as an inheritance, for his mercy is forever.”

“And gave their land as an inheritance.” [Cassiodorus.] The third part, in which he descends to Christians, setting forth the benefits given to them, so that you may know the one author of all things.

[Col. 1199B] VERS. 22.—“As an inheritance to Israel his servant, for his mercy is forever.”

“As an inheritance to Israel his servant.” [Aug.] As though he said: Thus he struck the kings mentioned above, and gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his servant. Thus also what the devil possessed he gives as an inheritance to Abraham’s seed, which is Christ. And he understands Christ as Israel the servant. Or by Israel the servant he understands Christians, to whom the promise made to the Jews was given. [Cassiodorus.] The meaning is: He literally bestowed the benefits just mentioned upon the Jews, and gave their land as an inheritance. The promise made to them in figure, as an inheritance to Israel his servant, he gave to Christians. For although this seems to be said of the Hebrews, it properly belongs to Christians, to whom the promise made to them is given, and to whom humility, which Christ taught, properly belongs.

VERS. 23.—“For in our humiliation [Col. 1200A] he remembered us, for his mercy is forever.”

“For in our humiliation,” [Cassiodorus] namely inward humility, which belongs especially to Christians. Or “in humiliation” means “in our low estate”: he remembered us when he came.

VERS. 24.—“And redeemed us from our enemies, for his mercy is forever.”

“And redeemed us from our enemies.” [Aug., Cassiodorus.] This applies properly to Christians, whom he redeemed by the blood of his only-begotten Son. For the Hebrews he gave no price to the Egyptians.

VERS. 25.—“He who gives food to all flesh, for his mercy is forever.”

“He who gives food,” [Aug.] spiritual food, of which it is said: [Col. 1200B] “My flesh is truly food” (John VI), “to all flesh,” that is, to every race of human beings, namely Israel and the nations; not as he gave manna only to the Jews. And because he does this, therefore:

VERS. 26.—“Give thanks to the God of heaven, for his mercy is forever.”

“Give thanks to the God of heaven.” [Aug.] This is what he said above, “to the God of gods”; therefore here also he repeats what he there added:

VERS. 27.—“Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his mercy is forever.”

“Give thanks to the Lord of lords.” Therefore give thanks, because his mercy is forever.

COLLATION ON PSALM CXXXV: “GIVE THANKS TO THE LORD, FOR HE IS GOOD,” etc.

[Col. 1200C]

For the title the Greek has: Alleluia. In the Hebrew it is the ending of the final verse in the preceding psalm. This is a very small matter. The rest has been sufficiently reconciled.

PSALM CXXXVI.

[Col. 1199]

TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF DAVID CONCERNING JEREMIAH.”

[Col. 1199C]

“By the rivers of Babylon.” Title: A Psalm of David concerning Jeremiah. [Cassiodorus.] This is the third psalm concerning the lamentation of Jerusalem, because it was destroyed by the Babylonians. Two others precede it: namely, “Why, O God, have you cast us off?” (Ps. LXXIII), which concerns the captivity brought about by the Romans; and “O God, the nations have come” (Ps. LXXVIII), which concerns the devastation under Antiochus (I Macc. I). But this psalm concerns the captivity brought about by Nebuchadnezzar (IV Kings XXV), which Jeremiah bewailed in a fourfold alphabetic acrostic; for that reason the title of this psalm contains his name.

The meaning is: This psalm belongs to David the prophet, [Aug.]; the intervening words are uncertain (“being or composed”); “for” means “according to” Jeremiah, because it concerns the captivity of the Jews, which Jeremiah bewailed as a figure of ourselves, who are held spiritually captive. For just as there were two cities, Jerusalem and Babylon, of which one afflicted and took the other captive, so now there are two cities, one of the good and the other of the evil, mingled in body but separated in heart: namely Jerusalem and Babylon.

Therefore Jerusalem is held captive in Babylon, but not wholly. For its citizens include angels, free from every misery; but it is held captive in respect of human beings predestined to glory, who through sin are captives and exiles from their homeland. Thus this psalm treats of that captivity through sin; above it treated of the return, in that psalm, “A hymn is fitting for you, O God, in Zion” (Ps. LXIV). Here it says: [Col. 1200D] “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept.” For if we are citizens of Zion, we stand in the courts of Jerusalem by hope; but here, in this Babylon—that is, in the confusion of this age—we do not dwell as citizens, but are held captive and sit in humility, repenting and confessing.

There are also others who will be citizens of Jerusalem in mind, and who already are so by predestination; but in body and heart they are still citizens of Babylon and serve it. For Babylon has its lovers, who look after temporal peace, hope for nothing beyond it, fix all their joy there, and whom we see labour greatly for the earthly commonwealth. But whoever conduct themselves in it not proudly but faithfully, so that, insofar as they understand, they show such faith as they can and to whom they can, God does not permit them to perish [Col. 1201A] in Babylon; for he has predestined them as citizens of Jerusalem. He understands their captivity and shows them another city for which they may labour, for which they may long, and to which they may exhort others. Hence Jesus says: “He who is faithful in a little is faithful also in much” (Luke XVI). And again: “If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own?” (ibid.).

Yet this psalm does not concern such persons, but those who are citizens of Jerusalem in mind and desire.

Intention. It exhorts people not to conform to Babylon but to long for the heavenly Jerusalem.

Method. The psalm has two parts. [Cassiodorus.] First, it presents, as a figure of ourselves, those who were long afterwards to be taken captive by Nebuchadnezzar, and whom Jeremiah bewailed, as weeping over their evils and not forgetting Jerusalem amid evils. Second, there is a turning toward God against the enemies, at “Remember.” Therefore the Prophet, in the person of the captive—one who, as if stirred by the praises of those standing in the house—pours out this lament from longing for his homeland, saying:

VERS. 1.—“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered you, O Zion.”

“By the rivers of Babylon, there,” [Aug.] namely, in so notable a place, “we sat,” humbled, not raised up through pride nor lying down through ruin. The rivers of Babylon are all the things loved here which pass away. Seeing this, the saints do not mingle with them in love, but sit above them in contempt and weep either for those swept away by them or for themselves, who are captives there. Hence follows: 293 “And we wept,” namely over our sojourning. I say, we sat and wept when we remembered [Col. 1201C] you, O Zion, where nothing flows away. We did not weep for anything except Zion, as many people do. For many weep with Babylonian weeping and rejoice with Babylonian joy, because they rejoice over gains and weep over temporal losses. Both are of Babylon. [Cassiodorus.] Certainly each person ought to weep, but in remembering Zion. For in a hostile land the remembrance of one’s homeland is sweet. And:

VERS. 2.—“On the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments.”

In the willows, [Aug.] that is, among the evils which are in the midst of Babylon—willows which, to be sure, are watered by the rivers of Babylon, yet are barren of good works, and are in the midst of Babylon, that is, are very evil: namely, the covetous and avaricious. For some are in the outer parts of Babylon [Col. 1201D], that is, not so overwhelmed by desires. Upon those willows, I say, which are in the midst of Babylon—that is, upon those very evil persons—we suspended, that is, deferred and withheld, our instruments: that is, the Scriptures and the promises of God. For we turn the Scriptures away from these swine and dogs; we do not bind them upon them by presenting them, but suspend them by postponing them. [Cassiod.] And it should be known that the force of grief is heightened when the enjoyment by which they were accustomed to console themselves is suspended. And because we suspended our instruments:

**VERSE 3.**—“For there those who led us captive asked us for words of songs.”

For there, [Aug.] that is, in Babylon, those who led us captive asked us—not in order to profit, but to test us—namely the devil and his angels, who are said to ask when those in whom they work ask. What did they ask? Words of songs, or canticles: that is, reasons for our joyful praise and profession; as when they ask such questions as these: “What good is Christ?” or “What is this other life?” “Have not worldly affairs been worse since Christ came than they were before? Were not human affairs happier then than now? Let Christians tell us: what good has Christ brought? Why do you command me to believe concerning Christ and another life which I do not see?”

**VERSE 4.**—“And those who carried us away: Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion.”

And those who carried us away [Aug.] from the society of angels, or, in another reading, *brought us* into these miseries—understand, asked us for words of songs [Col. 1202B], saying: “Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion.” “Sing to us.” But we answer them: “Babylon carries you, Babylon holds you, Babylon feeds you. You cannot grasp anything except what shines for a time; you do not know how to meditate upon eternal things; you are full of evil desires.” Yet for those who are full of evils, we ought not to strike the instrument so that it may sound, but to suspend it. For the devil shrewdly seeks this through his own people in order to mock. Therefore they must be answered thus:

**VERSE 5.**—“How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?”

How shall we sing? [Aug.] As though he said: “They say this.” But we answer them: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” Care must be taken lest anyone, fearing to displease such people, seek their friendship [Col. 1202C] and begin to delight in Babylon. But this sufferer, pressed on every side by questioners who flatter, mockers, and reproachers, as though endangered among them, raised his mind to the remembrance of Zion and bound himself by an oath, saying:

**VERSE 6.**—“If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand be given over to forgetfulness.”

If I forget. [Aug.] As though he said: “I did not sing to them; but if, amid their words, I forget you, Jerusalem, so as to wish to please them, let my right hand be given over to forgetfulness—or, in another reading, let my right hand forget me.” That is, let eternal life, which is our right hand, forget me. Hence elsewhere: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song of Songs 2). Our left hand is temporal life. Whatever you do for eternal life is performed by the right hand; but if you also direct yourself elsewhere, the left hand has intruded, and, delighting in it as though in the right hand, one loses eternal life. Note that he lays down a condition which necessarily comes to pass: namely, that one who has forgotten Jerusalem be given over to forgetfulness. Again he says:

**VERSE 7.**—“Let my tongue cleave to my jaws, if I do not remember you.”

Let my tongue cleave to my jaws, if I do not remember you, [Aug.] that is, let me be silenced and become mute in the praises of God if I am not mindful of you—which is the consolation of tears and miseries. Thus it happens as he declares. For one who is not mindful of it becomes mute: for to what end does one sound forth, to what end does one speak, who does not sound the song of Zion? The song of Jerusalem is our tongue [Col. 1203A], namely the tongue of the faithful; the song of delight in this world is a barbarian tongue. He is mute toward God who has forgotten Jerusalem. Thus he fittingly says: “If I do not remember you,” namely, with love. Hence he adds:

**VERSE 8.**—“If I do not set you, Jerusalem, at the beginning of my joy.”

If I do not set you—or you, O Jerusalem—at the beginning of my joy, [Hilar., Haym.] that is, if my chief joy is not from you and in you, O Jerusalem. [Note: [Col. 1203D] Ἐὰν μὴ προανατάξωμαι τὴν Ἱερουσαλήμ: “if I do not place Jerusalem before [all else].”] For there is supreme joy, where we shall enjoy God fully, where we are—or shall be—secure in the fellowship of brethren united together. [Aug.] For nothing except the good will delight there. Every necessity will die, and supreme happiness will arise.

## PART II. VERSE 9.—“Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom, in the day of Jerusalem.”

Remember. [Cassiod., Gl. int.] The second part, in which there is a turning to God against the enemies. As though he said: “I am thus disposed; but, O Lord, remember the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem.” Edom is the same as Esau. For Esau is called Edom and Seir (Gen. 36). But the children of Edom, [Alcuin.] that is, the Idumaeans, hindered the Jews rebuilding Jerusalem after their return from Babylon; or they joined the Babylonians in the destruction of Jerusalem. Hence he later says, “Daughter of Babylon.” And the sense is: “I shall remember them,” that is, punish them, for what they did, on the day of Jerusalem’s restoration, which they hinder. Or: on the day when they wish to overthrow Jerusalem, having joined [Col. 1203C] the Babylonians. Behold what they do:

**VERSE 10.**—“Who say: ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundation.’”

Who say: “Lay bare, lay bare,” [Gl. int.] whatever is in it, even to the foundation—that is, let not even one person remain in Jerusalem.

**VERSE 11.**—“O miserable daughter of Babylon; blessed is he who repays you your repayment, which he will repay to us.”

Daughter of Babylon. [Gl. int., Aug., Alcuin.] As though he said: “They act thus; but, O daughter of Babylon—or you also, daughter of Babylon—you are miserable in your exultation and presumption.” He calls Idumaea the daughter of Babylon, because she allied herself with the Babylonians. But blessed is he who repays you the repayment which you repaid us. Namely, God [Col. 1203D] will repay it. What repayment?

**VERSE 12.**—“Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock.”

Blessed, [Aug.] namely, is he who shall seize and dash his—or your—little ones against the rock.

[Aug.] Or it may be read mystically. Esau signifies all carnal persons, Jacob spiritual persons. Esau was called Edom from a certain red lentil dish, for which he sold his birthright to his younger brother Jacob (Gen. 25). The latter gave food of pleasure and received the honor of dignity. Thus he who was lesser in age became greater in dignity. The carnal man, therefore, is the elder; the spiritual man, the younger [Col. 1204A], because “that which is animal comes first, afterward that which is spiritual” (1 Cor. 15). Every human being, when born, begins as carnal and animal. But if one turns from captivity, he is renewed in Jerusalem upon his return, and a certain renewal takes place according to the inward person. And just as Esau, the elder brother, was Jacob’s enemy, so all carnal persons are enemies to spiritual persons. Hence he says: “I shall remember, O Lord, the children of Edom,” that is, carnal persons who are enemies of the saints: “deliver us from them, on the day of Jerusalem’s separation,” that is, when they are separated from Jerusalem; in other words, so that the evil may be punished and the good crowned. “Who say: ‘Lay bare, lay bare, even to its foundation, in her’”—namely, in Jerusalem, that is, in the Church. This is said by comparison with a cistern: if its water is drawn out, one reaches [Col. 1204B] the foundation. But what good is it even to take life from such persons, whose eternal life is in the foundation, which is Christ? While the wicked think they are harming them, they confer crowns upon them.

[Aug.] Then, turning his speech toward the city of the wicked itself, he says: “But, O daughter of Babylon, you are miserable in your very exultation, your very presumption, and your hostilities.” Note that the city of the wicked is called Babylon and daughter of Babylon, just as God’s Church is Zion and daughter of Zion. Yet through succession and change she became daughter of Babylon, as the Church through succession becomes daughter of Zion. “Blessed is he who repays you your repayment,” namely spiritual dashing in return for carnal dashing, “which you repaid to us,” namely hatred in return for our love. [Col. 1204C] What repayment? “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock,” that is, against Christ: he who brings your citizens back to the way of truth while they are little and can be brought back, not yet wholly hardened in wickedness.

Or the whole may be understood in a moral sense. For Edom, which is interpreted “earthly” or “bloody,” is carnality, which seduces us by illicit impulses as though by its own illicit children. And the sense is: “Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom,” [Hilar.] that is, the illicit impulses of the flesh, “so that you may dash them on the day of Jerusalem,” that is, among the good things which are the days of the Church. Hence: “Day pours forth speech to day” (Ps. 18). “Who say: ‘Lay bare, lay bare, even to her foundation.’” For through an accumulation of vices distrust creeps in. But the daughter of Babylon is miserable. The daughter of Babylon [Col. 1204D] is the flesh which brings on the confusion of sins; and a fitting recompense is given to it, so that, as it incites to vices, so, when repressed, it may be subjected to virtues. “Blessed is he who repays you your repayment, which you repaid to us.” To repay the flesh is the work of the blessed, who also restrain the little ones born from the flesh—that is, evil impulses—before they grow, lest they become free, and dash them against Christ the rock, so that, shattered, they perish. “Blessed is he who shall seize your little ones,” or “his little ones,” “against the rock.” [Aug.] Behold a fitting repayment. For just as Babylon stifles those born into the world while still little through the errors of their parents and of this age, so those who are now grown, having received the knowledge of God, dash Babylon’s little ones [Col. 1205A]—their nascent desires—before they acquire strength. Thus they are more easily overcome while still little; but even those grown larger must be put to death against the rock.

## COMPARISON ON PSALM 136: “BY THE RIVERS OF BABYLON, THERE WE SAT,” etc.

**VERSE 3.**—“Those who carried us away: Sing us a hymn.” St. Jerome: “Those who afflicted us, [asked for] joy”; the Pratensian: “those mocking us, [asked for] joy”; Pellicanus: “those who seized us, [asked for] joy”; the translators for Cajetan: “our howlings, [asked for] joy,” so that these words may refer to the preceding verb, namely, “they asked”; Campensis: “those who openly insulted us commanded us to give signs of joy.” Sanctes and Münster differ: the former has, “He [asked for] words of joy while the harps were suspended”; the latter, “when we had suspended the instruments of joy.” Yet all agree in joining *SCHIMEAH*, that is, “joy,” where we say “hymn,” to what precedes, whereas we join it to what follows. For when we read “Sing a hymn” [Col. 1205B], they simply say “Sing,” because they had already joined the particle denoting “hymn” or “joy,” as stated, to the preceding words. There is controversy concerning another word, *TOLALENU*, as Münster still testifies among the Hebrews. Some derive it from the root *IALAL*, “he howled.” A howl, however, sufficiently denotes either affliction, mockery, or insult. Others take it to be [an uncertain word], that is, “we suspended,” [p. 294] from the form *TALAH*. But we follow what is more certain.

**VERSE 6.**—“Let my right hand be given over to forgetfulness.” Sanctes and Münster added something of their own making, which is wholly arbitrary. They seem to have done so because “to forget” in Hebrew is active, so that some object had to be understood. Yet active and passive do not differ with respect to the affixing of the vowel points: it can be read *TISCHCAH* or *TISCHACAH*. Again, if anything had to be supplied, this could be done as in the Roman translation, which Saints Hilary and Augustine follow: “let my right hand forget me.” Its meaning is the same as “let my right hand be given over to forgetfulness.” That is what St. Hilary attests in these words: “But what he says, ‘let my right hand forget me,’ is obscure owing to the nature of Latin usage. For according to the characteristic usage of Greek, in which it is said, ἐπιλησθεύη ἡ δεξιά μου, it is shown not that the right hand itself forgets, but that forgetfulness of it may occur; and it is a matter of great danger if forgetfulness of our right hand occurs.” Finally, St. Jerome, the Pratensian, and Pellicanus agree with our reading. Likewise the Chaldee and Nebiensian versions.

**VERSE 12.**—“He shall dash his little ones against the rock.” In Hebrew, Greek, and Latin the text has “your,” and thus all the ancients read, *OLALALIIC*. But if we expound it tropologically, as St. Jerome does in the *Commentaries* and in his work to Eustochium *On the Guarding of Virginity*, and as Augustine, Hilary, and Arnobius do, the sense is the same: “Blessed is he who shall dash his own little ones,” that is, who restrains the first stirrings of his own desires. And: “Blessed is he who shall dash, O daughter of Babylon, your little ones against the rock,” so that we understand our outer person to be addressed. Historically, however, it would not fit so well that the vengeance here foretold should be inflicted on the Babylonians by others at God’s command, so that he should be blessed who dashed Babylon’s little ones against the rock, as compensation for the wrongs which the Babylonians themselves had committed against the Jewish children in their cruel captivity. Therefore it seems to have arisen from scribal error that we read *his* for *your*, unless we choose to misuse the reflexive pronoun for the non-reflexive, as though it meant: “Blessed is he who shall dash her little ones against the rock.” Nevertheless, as I have said, according to the interpretation handed down by the saints, there is no difficulty.

# PSALM 137

[Col. 1205]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF.”

[Col. 1205C]

“I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart.” Title: “A Psalm of David himself.” [Alcuin.] The captive who above wept while sitting beside the rivers of Babylon, now, as though Jerusalem had been rebuilt and the Temple restored, and as though made a fellow citizen of that part of Jerusalem which was not captive—that is, of the angels—exults and praises Christ, to whom this psalm is addressed. And this is the meaning: this psalm is made to David himself, that is, to Christ, to whom the whole confession of this psalm is offered.

**Purpose.** [Cassiod.] It urges praise.

**Method.** The psalm has two parts. First, it commends the benefits granted to the speaker. [Aug.] Second, it states how these benefits are extended to all, at “Let them confess,” etc. Thus, in the voice of the Church, which in the preceding psalm is in Jerusalem by hope and awaits being there in reality, he says:

[Col. 1205D]

**VERSE 1.**—“I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart, because you have heard all the words of my mouth.”

I will confess to you, O Lord, [Aug.] that is, I will praise you, with my whole heart. I lay my whole heart upon the altar of your confession; set it all aflame with the fire of your love. Therefore I will confess, because you have heard the words of my inward mouth, to which God is near. Nothing makes one far from God except iniquity alone. One who clings to it does not cry inwardly to God, even if outwardly he raises his voice.

[Col. 1206C]

**VERSE 2.**—“In the sight of angels I will sing psalms to you; I will worship toward your holy temple, and confess to your name.”

In the sight of angels I will sing psalms to you. [Aug., Alcuin.] For in the presence of angels I have the psaltery and joy that are from things above, not in the presence of people who rejoice in lower things and do not know the joy of the righteous, but think miserable the person whom they see being scourged. Or thus: “In the sight of angels I will sing psalms to you,” that is, in praising I set angels before myself to imitate them; I expect hereafter to be made their equal, as I am now in praise, so then in dignity. In the praise of God, they set before themselves nothing other than God himself. Therefore, “in the sight of angels,” that is, in the purity in which angels behold and praise you—namely, so that they rest content in you alone [Col. 1206D]—I will sing psalms to you.

Hence Moses too is commanded to build the tabernacle for the Lord according to the pattern shown him on the mountain (Exod. 25). “And I will worship toward your holy temple,” that is, in your holy temple. For there is within us that in which we may worship. Hence the Apostle: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3). For God’s temple is God’s dwelling-place; and the dwelling-place of God is the soul of the righteous person (Wisdom 7). Yet angels also may be understood as God’s temple, [Aug.] because God dwells in angels as well: the angels are above [Col. 1207A], the faithful below. Thus there is a Church above and a Church below. But if they rejoice in spiritual things rather than earthly ones, those who are to become their fellow companions worship toward that angelic temple where the angels are, for whose sake the Lord of angels came. And the sense is: “I will worship toward your holy temple,” that is, I will worship for eternal things, namely, that I may be a companion of angels. “And I will confess to your name,” that is, I will praise you.

**VERSE 3.**—“For your mercy and your truth, because you have magnified your holy name above every name.”

For, [Aug.] that is, because of your mercy, by which you call and look upon the sinner; and your truth, by which you reward and fulfill your promises. These are all the ways of the Lord: mercy and truth [Col. 1207B] (Ps. 24), for there are no other ways by which he comes to us, nor others by which we come to him. Let us therefore render these things to God: mercy in giving aid, truth in judging. By these two we are helped; by these we earn God’s favor.

He next gives the reason why he confesses. [Haym.] Namely, because you have magnified the Holy One—that is, Christ—above every name in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2). [Cassiod.] Or, in another reading: “You have magnified your holy name above us,” when your worship became known to us. And because you have done this:

**VERSE 4.**—“On whatever day I call upon you, hear me; you will multiply strength in my soul.”

[Col. 1207C] On whatever day, [Cassiod., Aug.] that is, at whatever time, or when I am without the cloud of desire, I call upon you, hear me, because, instructed by the New Testament, I no longer ask for earthly things. But what follows—“you will multiply,” that is, “multiply”—I ask not in the flesh but in my soul. And because a carnal multiplication can occur in the soul, he adds “strength,” as though saying: “I ask for nothing else in my soul except strength”; in this he fully expresses a holy desire. For if he simply said, “You will multiply me,” he could be understood to have thought of earthly possession. Therefore he adds, “in my soul.” Again, lest you should suppose he meant vices in the soul, he adds, “strength.”

## PART II. VERSE 5.—“Let all the kings of the earth confess to you, O Lord, because they have heard all the words [Col. 1207D] of your mouth.”

Let them confess. [Cassiod., Hilar., Aug.] The second part, in which he says how these good things are to be extended to all, as though through my example. “Let all the kings of the earth confess to you, O Lord,” that is, self-controlled persons who govern the flesh and subject it to the spirit. This already occurs daily and will occur thus. It is now shown that the prediction was not made in vain. Why should they confess? Because they have obediently heard all the words of your mouth, which were formerly hidden among the one Jewish nation, to whom the oracles of God were entrusted (Rom. 3); but now they have been revealed everywhere and sent to all nations.

This was signified in Gideon’s fleece. When he was about to go against the Midianites, he asked the Lord for a sign: that the fleece might be wet while the threshing-floor remained dry. Then he asked that, once the fleece was dry [Col. 1208A], the threshing-floor might be drenched (Judg. 6). The threshing-floor is the world; the fleece, the Jewish nation in the midst of the world, possessing the sacrament of grace not openly but in the cloud of mystery, like rain in the fleece, while the threshing-floor around the fleece was dry—that is, the whole world around the Jewish nation. But when the fleece was pressed out—that is, when the mystery of the figures was revealed—the rain became manifest in the threshing-floor, that is, throughout the whole world, and was not covered over. Christ alone is the sweetness of that rain, namely grace. You alone, therefore, O Jew, do not recognize in the Scriptures him through whom all things were made, whom the world receives, and by whom the threshing-floor was watered. Thus, when the fleece had been dried, all the kings of the earth shall hear all the words of your mouth. I say, let the kings confess:

**VERSE 6.**—“And let them sing in the ways of the Lord, because [Col. 1208B] great is the glory of the Lord.”

And let the kings of the earth sing, [Aug.] so that, as travelers sing, they may hasten to reach the destination toward which they are going. Let them sing, I say, in the ways of the Lord, which are mercy and truth. What should they sing? This: “Because great is the glory of the Lord,” not the glory of kings. If they are humble, this is what they love and sing; but if they have exalted themselves, let them fear what follows:

**VERSE 7.**—“Because the Lord is high, and looks upon the lowly; and he knows the lofty from afar.”

Because the Lord is high. [Aug., Cassiod., Aug.] And although he is high, nevertheless he looks upon the lowly with the eye of mercy. Therefore, if they wish to be looked upon, let them be humble. For this is not the human condition, in which the humble person is despised [Col. 1208C] and the proud person regarded; rather, the Lord looks upon the humble. But if some are proud, they do not escape his notice; rather, they are seen from afar. Hence he adds: “And he knows the lofty,” that is, the proud, “from afar,” or “at a distance,” because he is not with them through grace, though he sees them perfectly. The proud person therefore does not bring it about that he is seen less perfectly by God, but that he is not with him by whom he is seen. “He knows the lofty from afar.”

[Cassiod.] But if tribulation comes upon the righteous, God the giver of life is present. This is what he says, turning toward the Lord:

**VERSE 8.**—“If I walk in the midst of tribulation, you will give me life; and over the wrath of my enemies you have stretched out your hand, and your right hand has saved me.”

If I walk in the midst of tribulation, [Aug.] which is always at hand, at least from the devil, you will give me life. Or thus: “And [he knows] the lofty from afar,” in another reading—that is, those who are exceedingly proud. He says this by comparison with the proud, who, because of excessive pride, do not look down at their feet but walk with lifted head. Thus the lofty are far off: that is, very proud people who have not truly found the tribulation and sorrow of this worldly pilgrimage, thinking that this place is their homeland and happiness, because they do not know or do not love the true homeland. Tribulation therefore comes upon them as upon people who do not know it, because they do not recognize it.

Conversely, those are in the midst of tribulation who, living in this life, recognize it to be wholly tribulation and misery, reading that this is an exile. “If I walk.” As though he said: “Those people are thus; but if I walk in the midst of tribulation”—that is, if I am in this life [Col. 1209A] as though in the midst of tribulation, judging it all misery and seeking the true homeland—“you will give me life.” But he gives life to no one otherwise unless that person is in the midst of tribulation. Hence: “Blessed are those who mourn”; and, “Woe to those who laugh” (Matt. 5; Luke 6).

“And over the wrath of my enemies you have stretched out your hand,” that is, your hand is above what enemies can do. For they can do no more than kill, but they cannot separate me from you. Or thus: “Over the wrath of your enemies you have stretched out your hand,” that is, you exact fuller vengeance upon my enemies; they are no longer permitted to crush me for long, because they either die or are converted, so that few now openly attack the Christian name. [p. 295] What wrath of enemies raged when the blood of martyrs was shed! But behold: those who persecuted the martyrs now seek the memorial shrines [Col. 1209B] of martyrs.

[Alcuin.] Or thus: “Over the wrath of my enemies you have stretched out your hand,” that is, the very fact that they are angry with me is your judgment upon them, that is, their punishment. For their anger is a penalty to them, not merely a fault. Therefore, in promising this, you stretch out the hand of vengeance over them. “And your right hand has saved me,” not the left hand, which saves temporarily. [Aug.] There is one kind of salvation in the right hand and another in the left. Temporal salvation is in the left hand; eternal salvation is in the right. God does not have a right or left hand in himself, but the right hand of God means eternal blessedness and the left hand temporal blessedness. Thus he sometimes does not save his saints with the left hand, but he always saves them with the right; the ungodly, however, he often saves with the left but not with the right. And [Col. 1209C] as though someone should say, “Why do you not take vengeance?” he answers:

**VERSE 9.**—“The Lord will repay for me. O Lord, your mercy is forever; do not despise the works of your hands.”

The Lord will repay, [Aug.] or, in another reading, “you will repay,” or “repay.” As though he said: “I do not repay, but the Lord will repay for me, because I cannot, nor ought I to.” Hence the Apostle: “Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath” (Rom. 12). Hence: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Deut. 32).

Or there is another interpretation here, not to be neglected and perhaps more to the point. It touches upon what is read in the Gospel concerning Christ, [Col. 1209D] who, when he wished to pay the tax for himself and Peter to those collecting tribute, said to Peter: “Go, cast a hook into the sea; take the first fish that comes up, open its mouth, and you will find a stater,” that is, two didrachmas (Matt. 17). A stater, however, is a unit of weight containing four drachmas. And he added: “Give it to them for me and for you” (ibid.). Christ did this particularly, he who paid for us what he had not taken away (Col. 1).

Christ, therefore, is the first fish, caught by the hook of death and first to rise from the sea, because he is the firstborn from the dead. In his mouth we find two didrachmas, that is, four drachmas: namely, the four Gospels, by which we are delivered from the vexations of this age, so that we do not remain debtors any longer. For in them all our sins are paid. Therefore he paid for us, though he himself owed nothing, and in him the prince of this world found no sin for which to kill him (John 14). Thus this man humbly says: “O Lord, repay,” etc., as though saying: “You have saved me, and this is by your grace, by which you will pay for me the price of redemption.” And, O Lord, “your mercy is forever,” that is, eternally. Therefore I do not desire the day of man, which is temporal, but eternity through your mercy. And, O Lord, “do not despise the works of your hands,” that is, do not despise us because we are human, because we were created by you, or because we were justified by you and created for good works (Eph. 2). Therefore see your works in us: for if you see our works, you condemn; if you see yours, you crown.

## COMPARISON ON PSALM 137: “I WILL CONFESS TO YOU, O LORD, WITH MY WHOLE HEART,” etc.

[Col. 1210B]

**VERSE 1.**—“Because you have heard the words of my mouth.” This clause is not found in Hebrew. It was added by the Septuagint, not immediately after the words, “I will confess to you with my whole heart,” but after the intervening verse, “In the sight of angels I will sing psalms to you.” The reason for such matters has been discussed at length. The ancient writers plainly read and adorned by their interpretations the words, “because you have heard the words of my mouth”; among them are Arnobius, St. Augustine, and Hilary. Jerome indeed indicates that it is not found in Hebrew. Nonetheless, he translates it.

**VERSE 3.**—“You have magnified your holy name above every name.” In the Hebrew, in place of “your holy [name],” there stands “your word.” Some of the later scholars also judge that a division should be made after the particle “every,” and that a copulative conjunction should be inserted between “name” and “your word.” If this is true, let them see to it. To make the matter clearer, let us set out several translations [Col. 1210C]. St. Jerome: “You have magnified your word above every name”; the Pratensian: “You have magnified your word above every name of yours”; Pellicanus and Sanctes similarly. But Münster: “You have magnified your name and your word above all things.” The translators for Cajetan do not depart from him. The translator for Campensis: “You magnify your word according to your name.” The paraphrase: “For that most august name of yours has bestowed upon us far more than you had promised in your words.”

What we should think concerning this, let us hear from Jerome in his letter to Sunia and Fretela: “You say that you found in Greek, ἐπὶ πάντας, that is, ‘above all.’ But in the Septuagint one reads: ὅτι ἐμεγάλυνας ἐπὶ πᾶν τὸ ὄνομα τὸ ἅγιόν σου, ‘because you have magnified your holy name above every name,’ as we too translated it into Latin. But know that in Hebrew it is thus: ‘because you have magnified your word above every name.’ According to the Latin edition, however, this is the meaning: ‘Because you have magnified above every name’—that is, every name in heaven and on earth—your holy Son may be meant.” Thus far he. In Hebrew it is *IMRATECA*, “your word.” And in Psalm 2, concerning the Son of God, one reads: “The Lord said to me,” which the Apostle interprets in its lofty sense in Hebrews 1. In Hebrew, moreover, you read the word *AMAR*. From this is derived their rendering here, “your word” or “your utterance.”

**VERSE 9.**—“He will repay for me.” Thus Sanctes. St. Jerome: “He will work for me.” Others: “He will accomplish for me.” Münster added what pleased him, namely “his mercy.” *IIGMOR* means “he will repay,” “he will accomplish,” “he will work”; the word has that force and meaning. St. Hilary interprets it as vengeance reserved for God alone. Augustine does likewise, adding nevertheless another interpretation: that we were not equal to making payment, and therefore Christ had to make satisfaction for us wretches. The Chaldee follows the first interpretation, concerning vengeance.

# PSALM 138

[Col. 1211]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “FOR THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID.”

[Col. 1211A]

“O Lord, you have tested me and known me.” Title: “For the end, a psalm of David.” [Aug.] This psalm is full of profound mysteries, and therefore it is exceedingly obscure. This obscurity of the mysteries has come upon us from the sin of our first parent, to whom it was said: “In toil and the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3). Therefore, from that first sin we undergo this punishment: that in the sweat of our face and toil we eat the bread which is Christ, who says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6). This bread is veiled in the prophets and revealed in the Gospel. Yet toil remains, even now, in apprehending its mysteries.

In this psalm the whole Christ speaks, as one complete man, because of the exceedingly close union of head and body. This union was signified in the creation of the first parents, because the woman was made from the man, and it was said: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2). Explaining this, the Apostle says that it is a great mystery in Christ and in the Church (Eph. 5). Hence it is truly said that Christ and the Church are no longer two but one flesh, because Christ took flesh from us. Yet we do not share one divinity with him, because he is Creator and we are creatures.

Therefore, whatever is spoken here in the person of assumed flesh pertains both to the head, who has already ascended into heaven, and to the members, who still wander on earth, so that they may be two in one voice, as they are two in one flesh. With regard to the members, he speaks in the person of the captive mentioned above, now restored to Jerusalem in hope, who remembers his departure, in which he could not be hidden from God and in which the hand of the Lord followed him. He resolves no longer to flee from God, but to go to him through him, and from the angry One to the appeased One. Hence he says that great goods belong to him and that the evils of the world do him no harm. He says this in the person of all human nature returning to God, as in the voice of the prodigal son returning from a far country to his Father (Luke 15).

The sense of the title is this: this psalm, directing us toward the end, that is, Christ, is attributed to David, that is, to the whole Christ, in whose person the Prophet speaks here.

**Purpose.** He urges us not to flee from God but to him through him.

**Method.** There are four divisions. First, he treats of God’s knowledge, which comprehends every work, both of the returning person and the exile; this compels him who cannot hide to return, especially because God’s hand touched him there. Second, he says that one must not flee from God but to him, at “Where shall I go?” Third, he states how great is the exultation of one returning to God, at “I will confess to you.” Fourth, he explains how evil persons do not harm him, at “If you slay.” Therefore the Prophet says in the person of the head speaking to the Father:

**VERSE 1.**—“O Lord, you have tested me and known me; you have known my sitting down and my rising up.”

O Lord. [Aug.] As though he said: Christ says this to the Father insofar as he is man. For the Father is not his Lord except because he deigned to be born according to the flesh: he is Father of God and Lord of man. Therefore, because he is both Father and Lord, he is Father with respect to the form of God and Lord with respect to the form of a servant; yet he is one and the same Son of God and of man.

Thus, insofar as he is man, he says to the Father: “O Lord, you have tested me by trials, as in the Passion, and known me, as in the Resurrection.” He does not say that God then came to know what he had not known before, but that he then made known to others him whom he had not previously made known; likewise, he showed him tested to others. “And you, O Lord, have known,” that is, you have willed and approved: it was done according to your will. What have you known? “My sitting down,” that is, my humility in the Passion; “and my rising up,” that is, my glorification in the Resurrection [Col. 1212B].

This may also be understood in the voice of the members. For as Christ the head sat down and rose again, so do his members sit down: humble in patience, they will rise upright in hope of eternal life. Again, they sit down while confessing their sins, and rise by grace when justified. Therefore let us also say: “O Lord, you have tested me and known me,” which he subsequently explains: “You have known my sitting down,” namely, that in humility I have patience and confess my sins; “and my rising up,” namely, that, justified by grace, I rise and am raised into the hope of eternal life.

**VERSE 2.**—“You have understood my thoughts from afar; you have searched out my path and my measuring-line.”

**“You understood.”** [Augustine.] This is first spoken in the person of the members, [Col. 1212C] where he begins to treat of his exile under the likeness of the prodigal son. As though he said: You have tested me and known me, and likewise you understood my thoughts from afar, or from a great distance, while I am still in pilgrimage, before I come to my homeland; just as the father met the younger son as he returned, because he understood his thoughts from afar—he who had said to himself when worn down by want: “I will arise and go to my father” (Luke 15). Foreknowing this intention, the father met him.

And you understood my path, namely the evil path which I travelled as though hidden, abandoning my father; and you investigated my cord, or boundary—that is, how far I had come. I had indeed gone far away; but you were there, from whose eyes I was not far, as the detected fugitive speaks, with the lawful vengeance of the avenging God pursuing him.

**VERSE 3.—“And you foresaw all my ways, because there is no speech upon my tongue.”**

“And you foresaw all my ways,” [Augustine.] that is, my works; and this before I travelled them. You allowed me to go into toil, so that I might return if I did not wish to labour. In this way I confess that there is no speech—namely, speech without truth—or, according to another reading, no deceit, upon my tongue; that is, upon the tongue of me now justified by your grace. And you truly foresaw all my ways, because:

**VERSE 4.—“Behold, O Lord, you have known all things, [Col. 1213A] the last things and the ancient; you formed me and laid your hand upon me.”**

Behold, O Lord, you have known all things: namely, my last things, when I fed swine, and my ancient things, when I asked for a portion of the estate. This is according to the parable; but mystically, our ancient things were when we fell through the ancient sin. This punishment is our last thing: namely, when we came into this mortality, which is the last punishment if we are willing to return; otherwise eternal punishment remains. You formed me for these labours, to which we are all born.

“And you laid,” or “weighed down,” “your hand upon me”: the avenging hand that weighs down the proud, beneficially in order to raise up the humble. And concerning this burdening hand:

**VERSE 5.—“Your knowledge has become wonderful [Col. 1213B] from me; it has grown strong, and I shall not be able to attain it.”**

“Your knowledge has become wonderful from me,” [Augustine.] that is, because of my sin: your knowledge has become wonderful and incomprehensible to me. For it is not easy for me to contemplate you, whom I abandoned in pride, as it was formerly, when I was with you, when I said: “Give me my portion of the estate.” It has become strengthened, or prevailed, so much that I cannot myself attain to it.

See how, in these words, the Gentile people recalls its own blindness, which once prevailed not only over the Jews but also over the nations. Therefore he here uses the same words which in Exodus signify the blindness of the Jews: “You laid your hand upon me.” For in Exodus the Lord says to Moses: “You shall not be able to see my face; but I will place you in the cleft of the rock and cover you with my right hand until I pass by; then I will remove my hand; and when I have passed by, you shall see my back” (Exodus 33).

Moses is the Jewish people. The hand of the Lord laid upon him, so that he did not see the face of the one passing by, is the blindness in the Jews, so that they did not recognize Christ’s divinity until, through his Passion, he passed from this world to the Father. After the passing, the Lord removes his hand, and Moses saw his back: for after the resurrection the blindness was removed from those who had crucified the Lord. Therefore, just as through the hand of God being laid upon the Gentile people the knowledge of God became incomprehensible, so, through the hand being laid heavily upon Moses—that is, the Jews—they could not see that Christ was God until he passed to the Father. For then, when Peter preached, many of them were converted. Therefore God shut up all in unbelief, in order that he might have mercy on all (Romans 2).

**VERSE 6.—“Where shall I go from your Spirit? And where shall I flee from your face?”**

“Where shall I go?” [Augustine.] The second part, in which he now determines that one must not flee from God, but flee to him—from the angry One to the appeased One; and this will be through him himself. As though he said: Since I, a fugitive, am not hidden from you, whose boundary you see, where shall I go from your Spirit, with which the world is full? For “the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world,” as is written in the book entitled the Wisdom of Solomon (Wisdom 1). And where shall I flee from your face—that is, from your wrath or presence? He turns this way and that, as though seeking a place of escape, and says:

[Col. 1214A] **VERSE 7.—“If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present.”**

“If I ascend.” [Augustine.] As though he said: Where shall I flee from you when angry? Nowhere. For if I ascend into heaven—that is, if I exalt myself through pride—I find you as my restrainer. If I become proud of my righteousness, you are there to strike, for true righteousness is yours. Likewise, if I descend into hell—that is, if by sinning I come into the depths of evils and, unwilling to confess, say, “Who sees me?”—you are present even there to punish. Where then shall I go, that I may flee your face—that is, not feel you angry? This man has found a counsel.

**VERSE 8.—“If I take up my wings at dawn, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea.”**

“If I take up my wings.” [Augustine.] As though he said: [Col. 1214B] I seek where I may flee; but I shall be able thus to flee the angry One, namely, if I take up my wings—that is, the two wings of charity, which I had lost. And this at the dawn of virtues, or “straight ahead,” according to another reading: that I may neither be raised up by proud presumption nor sunk in despair. And if in mind I dwell not in the middle, where I would be submerged, but in the uttermost parts of the sea—that is, at the end of the age—not that I may love the age, but its end, in which I may have rest.

Therefore let us now fly there in hope and desire, having the wings of twofold charity; but he himself also leads us there. Hence he adds:

**VERSE 9.—“For even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me.”**

“For even there.” [Augustine.] As though he said: And I shall be able to dwell there, for even there your hand will lead me, so that I may be raised up, as it were in the air—touching neither heaven through self-exaltation nor earth through despair. And your right hand, that is, your grace, will hold me so that I do not fall back but persevere. But considering the length of the journey, and how charity grows cold when iniquity abounds (Matthew 24), he adds:

**VERSE 10.—“And I said: Perhaps darkness will trample me down; and the night will be my illumination in my delights.”**

“And I said: Perhaps.” [Augustine.] As though he said: Thus I planned to fly, and so forth. And while I was considering it, I said to myself: Perhaps darkness—that is, so many evils of this age—will trample me down. For the iniquity of the age abounds, and through it the wings of charity [Col. 1214D] can grow cold. And because I despaired of crossing the sea in the night—that is, by myself—the night became my illumination: that is, this entire miserable life became illumination for me. And this came about “in my delights,” that is, through my delights. Christ is our delight, in whom we rejoice.

For the woman—namely, the wisdom of God—came. She had lost the drachma, in which is the image of the king, that is, humankind made in God’s image; and she lit from herself a lamp made of clay, that is, she filled the flesh with the light of divinity, and illuminated the night. And when the night was illuminated, she found the drachma (Luke 15).

Or thus: the night, which was formerly a horror, is my illumination in my delights; that is, it has been illuminated—my delight. And I rightly say that it has been illuminated by you:

**VERSE 11.—“For darkness shall not be darkened [Col. 1215A] by you, and night shall be illuminated as day; as is its darkness, so also is its light.”**

“For darkness,” [Augustine.] that is, sins and evil persons, who are surely darkness when they sin, shall not be darkened by you. Rather, by chastening you instruct people so that they confess their sins; and, when confessing, you illuminate them with true light. For one who does not confess sins darkens his own darkness; but if he confesses, God enlightens him. And, O Lord, the night of this night shall be illuminated by you, just as also is the day of this night.

It should be noted that the night mentioned above—that is, this miserable life—has both night and day. For the night of this our night, that is, of miserable human life, is the adversity of the age; its day is prosperity. But if God dwells in the soul while promising another light, he illuminates the night [Col. 1215B] of this night just as its day, teaching one neither to rejoice in prosperity nor to be broken by adversity. Then a person begins to use both indifferently. Thus the night of this night is to him as its day, and at every time he blesses God, as Job did.

“As is its darkness,” and so forth. As though he said: Since this is so, as the darkness of that night—that is, adversity—is to me, so also, indifferently, is its light—that is, prosperity. And if this is so, darkness will not trample me down, whom light does not exalt. And as though someone asked, “Whence comes this indifference to you?” he answers:

**VERSE 12.—“For you have possessed my reins; you received me from my mother’s womb.”**

“For you, O Lord, have possessed my reins.” [Augustine, *Glossa interlinearis*.] As though he said: I possess this indifference [Col. 1215C] because the inward possessor holds not only the heart—that is, thoughts—but also the reins—that is, pleasures—so that the light of night does not delight me, but the light of wisdom. I say that you have possessed me and received me. Here he speaks in reverse order: receiving comes before possessing. You received me, I say, from my mother’s womb—that is, from the custom of my Babylonian city, in which I was first born and am captive—where I did not formerly regard the light and darkness of night with indifference.

Otherwise, from the passage “If I ascend.” It is likewise read in the person of the members. As though he said: I do not know where I may flee from your face, because if I ascend in mind into heaven—that is, to the supercelestial angels—you are there, because whatever angel stood firm did so by your gift. And if I descend into hell—that is, to those angels who [Col. 1215D] did not stand firm—you are also present there, through punishment. And if I take up my wings—that is, I wish to do good—at the dawn of virtues; and if I dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea: this remains unchanged, namely, “you are present.” As though he said: I cannot do this without you; and indeed, “for even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me”: this also remains unchanged.

“And I said,” that is, I considered, even thus: “Perhaps darkness will trample me down.” By darkness he means that lower part of rational creation opposed to us and pressing upon us, namely wicked people, or the flesh; hence he fears. The sense is: perhaps darkness—that is, the lower rational creation, following the left-hand path—will trample me down. I feared thus; but “the night, having become my illumination, will be in my delights”: that is, even those who were formerly night, once illuminated, [Col. 1216A] will be among my delights.

I rightly say, “illuminated,” because darkness—that is, sinners—will not be darkened by you but illuminated; and night—that is, a sinner from among the Gentiles—will be illuminated by you as day, that is, as the saints from among the Jews. I say that night will be illuminated by God. And as is the darkness of that night, so also is its light, God’s light. For insofar as you acknowledge your darkness, to that extent God forgives you. But whence are these things foretold of me? Because you have possessed my reins and received me from my mother’s womb. These words do not change.

**VERSE 13.—“I will confess to you, because you have been magnified fearfully; your works are wondrous; and my soul will know exceedingly.”**

“I will confess to you.” [Augustine.] The third part, in which he says how great is the exultation and increase of one flying back [Col. 1216B] to God, while God illumines him and possesses his reins. As though he said: Because you received me, therefore I shall confess to you—that is, praise you—because you have been magnified fearfully, or made wondrous: that is, precisely in being marvellous to us, you are fearful. Thus we rejoice with trembling, because we fear lest, through pride, we lose what we receive through humility.

And your works are wondrous; it is not you alone who are wondrous. “And my soul will know exceedingly,” or “very greatly.” My soul now knows very greatly. Previously your knowledge was wondrous from me, and I could not attain it; but now I can, because you illuminated the night, possess my reins, and received me from the womb: that is, because your grace came to me and illuminated me. And it rightly knows, because:

**VERSE 14.—“My bone, [Col. 1216C] which you made in secret, is not hidden from you; and my substance is in the lower parts of the earth.”**

“My bone, which you made in secret, is not hidden from you.” [Augustine.] Here *os* means “bone,” not “mouth.” There is therefore a certain inward firmness hidden from human beings; but you who made it see it, and it cannot be broken. Saints can indeed be killed, but they cannot be bent. Thus outwardly they appeared sad to people; but to God, who sees within, they rejoiced. Hence the Apostle says: “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Corinthians 6). “And my substance is in the lower parts of the earth”: that is, I subsist in corruptible flesh, and yet my bone does not yield to the evils of this lower region. It is not so surprising that an angel is strong; but if flesh is strong, that comes from the hidden bone.

**VERSE 15.—“Your eyes saw my imperfection; 297 and in your book all shall be written; days shall be formed, and no one among them.”**

“My imperfection.” [Augustine.] He who has spoken thus far in the person of the body now speaks in the person of the head, in the same utterance. As though he said: You made in me a hidden bone; but what will happen to those in whom this strength is absent? Christ, who began to speak at the beginning of the psalm, after the intervening words of the members, again says to the Father in his own person: “Your eyes saw my imperfection,” because God mercifully regards even those who stagger, as he did Peter, lest they perish.

And “in your book,” namely in me, whom you gave to humanity as a pattern of righteousness, all shall be written—that is, instructed [Col. 1217A] and named—not only the perfect but also the imperfect. Therefore let them not despair.

[Hilary.] Otherwise, from the passage “You understood”: it is read in the person of the head, namely Christ, who speaks to the Father insofar as he is human, as he began in the first verse. As though he said: You tested me and knew me; you also understood my thoughts from afar. Here is shown the foreknowledge of divinity, which understands from afar, not in place but in time, because it sees all things before they exist. “You understood my thoughts; you investigated my path and my cord.” The path pertains to silent thoughts; direction to righteous judgments. [Cassiodorus, *Glossa interlinearis*.] Or he calls the path the narrower commandments which he taught people to keep, and the cord the eternal inheritance which he promised for keeping them.

“And you foresaw all my ways.” [Hilary.] The ways pertain to the human acts by which he lived in the world. I say that you knew all these things because there is no deceit upon my tongue, as there was upon the tongue of Adam and his sons. I, however, speak nothing but truth, although I have said certain things that appear contrary to one another, such as “The Father is greater than I” (John 14), and “I and the Father are one” (John 10). The person who observes in what respect each thing is said recognizes that these are not contrary. For according to his humanity, the Father is greater than the Son; according to divinity, the Son is equal to the Father and one with him.

And there is truly no deceit, because behold, O Lord, you have known all things: the last things concerning the incarnation, and the ancient things, namely those concerning eternal divinity. The last thing is “the Word became flesh” (John 1), namely, “a child is born to us” (Isaiah 9); the ancient thing is “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1).

[Alcuin.] These are the new and the most ancient things of which Moses says in Leviticus: “You shall eat the very old things of the old, and when the new comes, you shall cast away the old” (Leviticus 26). Some things are old, others new, and others most ancient. [Hilary, Cassiodorus.] The old things are the promises of the law and prophets concerning the Christ who was then to come. The new things are the fulfilment of the promises and the manifestation of truth. The most ancient things are those which belong to the eternity of divinity.

[Alcuin.] Therefore, when new things arrive, the old things are to be cast away, but the most ancient things retained; for once the truth of the Lord’s coming has been manifested, figure and promise ought to cease. Hence three Masses are celebrated at the Nativity. In the first, the eternal generation of the Son is sung: “The Lord said to me”; in the second, the promise of his coming: “The light shall shine,” and so forth; in the third, the fulfilment of the promise: “A child is born to us.”

And because the same one who is the Son of God became the son of man, in that Mass office where the eternal generation is sung, “The Lord said to me,” and so forth, the Gospel concerning Christ’s temporal birth is read: “The book of the generation.” And in the Mass where Christ’s temporal birth is sung, the Gospel treating of the eternal generation of the Word is read. For “A child is born to us” is sung, and “In the beginning was the Word” is read. And because figures ought to cease once truth has been manifested, the Mass office pertaining to the promise is not repeated on subsequent [Col. 1218A] days, but that pertaining to the fulfilment of the promise, namely “A child is born to us,” is repeated.

These, then, are Christ’s last things and ancient things, known by the Father and revealed by the Son—things which he hides from the wise and prudent (Matthew 11), that is, from those swollen with knowledge: the scribes, Pharisees, and all heretics [Hilary] who refuse to receive the last and ancient things in Christ. You formed me according to my humanity, and laid your hand upon me to help me. Hence: “My hand shall help him” (Psalm 18). You did not lay that hand upon the first human being.

“And your knowledge has become wonderful from me,” [Cassiodorus, *Glossa interlinearis*.] that is, through my preaching it has become wonderful to humankind. The Father’s knowledge, preached through Christ, became wonderful to people, to whom so many mysteries were opened. But through that other one, namely the first human being, it became contemptible. And it was strengthened in human hearts when they believed firmly; but through that one, namely Adam, it was weakened.

Yet “I shall not be able to attain it.” [Hilary, Cassiodorus.] Insofar as he is human, the truth of the human condition is shown when he says, “I shall not be able to attain it,” because the assumed human being cannot be made equal in knowledge or in anything else to the divine substance.
