Then he shows that nothing can escape God’s presence, adding: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?” That is, where shall I flee from your presence? Nowhere. For if I ascend into heaven, as he did in the Ascension, you are there, where I am to be placed at your right hand. And if I descend into hell, as he did when he expired, you are present, by whose power he conquered the powers of the air.

And if I take up my wings, which belong to my power—that is, the efficacy of my divinity by which he raised his body from the tomb—and do this at dawn, that is, before daylight, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, that is, beyond the vast end of the age, you are present. Christ indeed took up these wings before daylight, that is, at the time of the resurrection, and dwelt in the uttermost parts of the sea, beyond the farthest end of the age. And you are truly present: “for even there your hand will lead me and your right hand will hold me,” that is, your Son, namely the Word united to me.

“And I said this: Perhaps darkness will trample me down.” It is irony and mockery of those who suppose this—that he who is the light of the world should be trampled by darkness. He does not therefore say this with doubt, but in derision of those who suppose it. As though he said: Certainly they will not do this; rather, I shall trample them down, because I shall remove blindness. And, that is, because, “night shall be my illumination”: those who were formerly night will be illuminated by me, and, once illuminated, shall be among my delights.

And night is truly illumination, because darkness—that is, the mysteries of the Scriptures—shall not be obscured by you; and night, [Cassiodorus.] that is, a dark and obscure utterance, shall be illuminated as day, that is, made clear as an open utterance. And as is its darkness, that is, the darkness of Scripture, so also is its light; because in both, namely in open and hidden matters, the truth is alike, and both have been revealed through Christ.

[Hilary, Cassiodorus.] Therefore darkness will not trample me down, because you possessed my reins, so that my conception and birth might be without sin; and received me from my mother’s womb, the Virgin’s. For this entire thing was accomplished by your operation. Therefore I shall confess to you, that is, praise you, because you have been magnified fearfully through me. Through that other one, namely Adam, humankind fell; through me it became evident how magnificent you are. And your works concerning me are wondrous, as appeared in the Passion, resurrection, and other matters. “And my soul will know exceedingly,” because “no one knows the Father except the Son” (Matthew 11).

[*Glossa interlinearis*.] “And my bone,” that is, divinity, “which you made in secret,” that is, made hidden from the wicked, “is not hidden from you”; and my substance according to my humanity is in the lower parts of the earth, that is, from frail earth. [Col. 1219B] [Augustine.] That first human being was created among angels, yet did not stand firm. I, born among sinners, did not sin. And therefore, namely because of the things stated above, your eyes mercifully saw “my imperfection,” that is, the imperfect, not only the perfect. [*Glossa interlinearis*, Haymo.] And in the book, namely in me, all shall be written; this remains unchanged.

And days, that is, the greater ones, such as the apostles—of whom it is said, “Day pours forth speech to day” (Psalm 18)—shall be formed in me, from whom they receive the perfection of grace. And none of mine shall be formed in them, because they are not said to belong to Peter or Paul, but to Christ, from whom they are called Christians. Yet:

**VERSE 16.—“But your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honoured by me; their authority has been exceedingly strengthened.”**

[Col. 1219C] “But by me, exceedingly,” [*Glossa interlinearis*.] that is, very greatly, “your friends have been honoured, O God,” and their authority has been strengthened exceedingly, beyond what can be said. [Augustine.] Or *nimis* means “very greatly.”

Or thus: where the text reads “days shall be formed,” another reading has, “They shall wander by day, and there is no one among them.” Here Christ was still the abiding Day; hence he said: “Walk while you have the light” (John 12). He had performed many wonders among his own, and yet the imperfect were fearful, as Peter was, lest they should lose him in death (Matthew 26). This is what he says here: all shall be written, but nevertheless they shall wander by day. They will wander while still imperfect, that is, while having an erroneous understanding of Christ. And there was absolutely no one among them who did not wander—not even he who had said: “I will be with you unto death” (Matthew 16), namely Peter, who had confessed him to be the Son of God, but at that time feared that, as Son of Man, he might die and not rise again as Son of God.

He was indeed Son of God and also son of man. As Son of God, he was in the form of God, equal to the Father; as son of man, he was in the form of a servant, in which he is less than the Father. Peter therefore feared that in the form of a servant the form of God might perish, rather than confidently believing that the form of God would revive from the form of a servant. They therefore wandered by day when they did not understand the Lord placed here; but they did not perish, because your eyes saw my imperfection.

And yet “they have been exceedingly honoured by me.” The very same people who wandered, and among whom no one was without error, became your friends, O God, and were exceedingly honoured by me, because after the resurrection hidden bone was made in them, when they were clothed with power from on high. Strengthened by this, they preached the word of God everywhere and suffered for his name, in whose Passion they had trembled. And their authority was exceedingly strengthened, because they became apostles, leaders, and shepherds of the Church.

**VERSE 17.—“I shall count them, and they shall be multiplied above the sand; I arose, and am still with you.”**

“I shall count them.” [Augustine.] As though he said: I strengthened them deservedly, because I—not any human being—shall count those whom they begot in faith. And, though counted, they shall be multiplied above the sand. As though he said: Those born through the persons who wandered by day are as innumerable [Col. 1220B] as the sand. By saying “I shall count,” he shows that they are countable to God; but by adding “they shall be multiplied above the sand,” he shows that they are innumerable to us.

Or: I say that their authority has been strengthened; and do you suppose that few good persons have been born through them? [Hilary.] Do not suppose so, because I shall count them who are stars—that is, the good—and they shall be multiplied above the sand, that is, above the Jews, who are called sand because of barrenness. Hence Abraham was told in the promise: “I shall multiply your seed as the stars of heaven and as the sands of the sea” (Genesis 22). By the stars is understood the people of Christians, a people more numerous than the Jews, who are compared to sand because of barrenness.

And all this is so because, “I arose from death and am still with you,” [Augustine.] not yet with them in their knowledge, because they do not yet recognize me; for they did not recognize Christ immediately after the resurrection, as is written in the Gospel. Or: “I arose, and am still”—that is, throughout the entire present life—“with you,” that is, hidden at your right hand until I am seen by all in judgment. For throughout this time Christ is hidden at the Father’s right hand, before he is revealed in the glory in which he will come.

Or: “I arose from death”; this remains unchanged. [Alcuin.] “And I am still with you,” that is, after death as before death—though the Jews thought that they had taken me away. Or: “And I am still with you,” namely in death itself, which does not appear to be true of one who is dead. Or: I arose, and although the resurrection is a sign of divinity, [Col. 1220D] I am nevertheless still hidden from many, “with you,” that is, as you are.

Then, in the person of the members, he adds what he suffers in the meantime through the mixture of the wicked in the Church and the separation of heretics:

**PART II. VERSE 18.—“If you kill sinners, O God—men of blood, depart from me.”**

“If you kill.” [Augustine.] The fourth part, in which he says how the wicked do him no harm. The order of the words is this: As though he said: I am with you; yet I still suffer from heretics in my body, which is the Church. For, O God, if—that is, when—you kill sinners, namely heretics, who in proud arrogance bodily separate themselves from others, they are killed when, through the pride in which they swell, they lose grace. Let those slain in vanity receive, or they shall receive, their cities—that is, their vain peoples, following their vanity—who follow those inflated under the name of righteousness, after unity has been broken apart.

But this is the occasion for inflated heretics, deceiving peoples, to separate themselves and those peoples from unity: namely, because there are wicked people there, in the Church, with whom they are unwilling to mix. And there truly are in the Church not only good people whom they slander but certainly also wicked people. On this pretext, they bodily divide themselves and others from the good. They do so also because God warns the good to separate themselves from the wicked. Therefore he inserts: “Men of blood, depart from me.”

**VERSE 16.—“Because you say in thought: Let them receive their cities in vanity.”**

[Col. 1221B] “Because you say,” according to another reading, “in thought.” [Augustine.] As though he said: Therefore heretics shall receive their cities in vanity—that is, shall deceive peoples in their own separate communion—because you, O God, shall say, that is, implant in the thought of the righteous, so that they say this to the wicked: “Men of blood, depart from me.” That is, because you warn the good to separate themselves from the wicked, not in place or bodily, but in mind; not openly yet, lest they also abandon the good, but by purity of life.

What God now says to the wicked in the thought of the good, he will say openly in judgment: “Amen I say to you, I do not know you” (Matthew 7). Heretics, therefore, who often slander the innocent whom they pretend to flee as wicked, seeing wicked persons among whom the wheat groans, usurp this authority. They tell the unlearned to separate bodily from the wicked who are with the good, because God warns the righteous to say, “Men of blood, depart from me.” They say that those who do not do what God warns are not righteous; but God does not give that warning in the sense heretics suppose. For he does not warn them bodily to separate themselves from the wicked before the final winnowing, as heretics think; rather, he tells them to separate themselves from men of blood by difference of life. Men of blood are those who hate their brothers, as John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3).

**VERSE 20.—“Did I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and waste away over your enemies?”**

“Did I not hate those who hate you?” [Augustine.] As though he said: Heretics, failing to understand, accuse the good of communion with the wicked. But what accusation do they bring against me, says the body of Christ, concerning the mixture of the wicked? Even while mixed with them, have we not been separated from them? This is what he says: “Did I not, O Lord, hate those who hate you?” Why do they demand of me a bodily separation from the wicked before the time of harvest, so that before the time of winnowing I may lose the patience needed to endure chaff? Why should I break the nets of peace and unity before all kinds of fish arrive at the end of the age, as it were at the shore, to be separated? (Matthew 13.)

And did I not waste away over your enemies whom I saw transgressing your law? Certainly, in zeal for your house I saw the senseless, and I wasted away. As though he said: I share in the sacraments of the wicked, not in their deeds. I waste away over them in zeal for your house; yet:

[Col. 1222A] **VERSE 21.—“I hated them with perfect hatred; they became enemies to me.”**

“I hated them with perfect hatred,” [Augustine.] that is, I hate their iniquities, not their nature. This is to hate with perfect hatred: neither to hate people because of their vices nor to love vices because of people. How then am I defiled by the mixture of the wicked, as heretics slanderously allege? Of them he adds: “They became enemies to me.” They are enemies not only of God but also of me; and in this respect I hate them.

**VERSE 22.—“Test me, O God, and know my heart; question me, and know my paths.”**

“Test me, O God.” [Augustine.] Up to this point he has dealt with heretics and the others following them who have separated from the Church. Now he also treats of wicked or false persons joined to the Church, whom the Church endures and mourns over. As though he said: Heretics separate themselves and others. Therefore, since wicked persons inseparable from the Church remain, among whom the Church groans and whom it endures, what does the Church say? See what: “Test me, O God, and”—that is—“know my heart,” because I do not consent to the deeds of the wicked.

You, O God, test me; you know what a person who is not a heretic cannot know, for such a person does not know how to test or know my heart. But you alone search the secrets of hearts. See what Christ’s beloved among the daughters says. These are her words: “Test me, O God, and know my heart.” This conscience is clean, and the king’s daughter is glorious within; she is among the daughters as a lily among thorns (Song of Songs 2). As though she said: They are enemies; but you, O God, test me and know my heart. Question me [Col. 1222C] so that I cannot deny it. As though he said: A person questioned concerning acts performed cannot deny them; and know my paths, that is, search out my counsels and thoughts. For what purpose? Behold:

**VERSE 23.—“And see whether a way of iniquity is in me, and lead me in the eternal way.”**

“And see whether a way of iniquity is in me,” [Augustine.] whether in doing evil or consenting to it. But if you find anything in my way displeasing to your eyes, because my way is mortal, lead me in the eternal way, which is Christ. For Christ is eternal, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). In that way, therefore, there is no iniquity, because if anyone sins, “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ” (1 John 14).

[Col. 1222D] Or it may be taken in the person of the head from the words “If you kill.” [Haymo, *Glossa interlinearis*.] As though he said: Because I arose and am with you, therefore, O God the Father, if you kill sinners in the future, saying, “Men of blood, depart from me,” it is because you say concerning my preachers in thought—which is worse than saying it with the mouth—this: “Let them receive cities in vanity,” not cities in eternity, their cities, that is, their peoples. If, I say, you kill them, did I not hate those who hate you, O Lord? Certainly: that is, if you kill, I also shall kill. And did I not waste away over your enemies in anger at their sins? Certainly. “I hated them with perfect hatred”: the sense remains unchanged. “They became enemies to me”: this also remains unchanged.

“Test me, O God,” [Jerome, Cassiodorus.] to see how freely I have done all things; and know my heart; question me and know my paths by which I passed through the world. And see whether there is a way of iniquity in me. He says this confidently, he in whom the ruler of this world found—or had—nothing. And lead me, as man, to your right hand in the eternal way, that is, through the Word coeternal with you.

## Collation on Psalm 138: “Lord, You Have Tested Me and Known Me,” etc.

**VERSE 2.—“My thoughts.”** Hebrew: *REI*. St Jerome derived this word from *ROA*, because he translates “my evil.” The interpreters on Cajetan’s side do the same. Pellican derived it from the root *REAH*, that is, “he joined,” for he translates “my friend.” He seems to have followed the Chaldean interpreter, who has: “I have been traced out as to where I am in fellowship with your Church.” The translator following Campensis derived it from the theme *RAAH*, because he translated: “You look ahead to my sustenance.” The Septuagint, supported by Pratensis, Nebiensis, Sanctes, Münster, and Campensis, derive it from the same theme in another sense.

**“My cord.”** St Jerome and the other more recent interpreters render it “my reclining” or “my repose.” Yet God is said to know my cord when he knows how far I shall go before I rest there; that is what it means to recline. Thus the sense emerges, although perhaps the Septuagint understood the word through metathesis, which is sometimes customary, so that it is *IRBI* instead of *RIBEI*. For *EREB*, meanwhile, denotes a covering or the thread woven into the warp.

You have investigated. St Jerome and several others: “you have sifted”; Pratensis and Münster: “you have encompassed” (*zerîthā*). Yet “to sift out” and “to investigate” have the same force for the present purpose; and both in turn indicate God’s providence in reclaiming sinners.

[Col. 1223C] VERSE 3.—There is no speech. The Roman psalmody, which St Augustine follows, reads, “there is no deceit.” Thus Greek manuscripts now read, οὐκ ἔστι δόλος, “there is no deceit.” Yet St Jerome, in his letter to Sunia, judges this to derive from the Sixth Edition. Among the Septuagint and all the other interpreters it is said to stand otherwise.

VERSE 4.—You knew all things. Here the Hebrew makes a division, and the later translators render, “the whole of it”; St Jerome and Nebiensis, “all things”; the Chaldean paraphrast, “all the thoughts of my heart.” Then what follows, “the last things and the ancient,” is joined to the following verb, and they say, “you formed me behind and before.” The whole difference depends on the Septuagint’s taking *’āḥôr* and *qedem* in the sense of nouns: as though it said, “You knew all things that are last, and those which were before.” In that sense the second clause had to be punctuated differently in the other ordering. For the division of pauses in Hebrew does not always make a division of meanings. If, following the authority of the Septuagint’s rendering, “before and behind,” the Kabbalists dream that man was created with two faces, one anterior and one posterior.

VERSE 8.—If I should take up my wings at dawn. St Jerome likewise has the plural, “my wings.” The others, however, render “the wings of dawn” or “of the morning light,” because the Hebrew is in the construct state: *kanpê shaḥar*. I do not doubt that the Septuagint read, or vocalized, *kenāfay*, that is, “my wings”; for this is also how the Greeks render it. In Hebrew these letters can be pronounced in either way. Therefore Faber’s complaint and rhetorical flourish—that “my” here is superfluous, indeed absurd—is pointless. St Hilary considers it a great mystery, interpreting it of Christ, who soared to immortality by his own power. St Augustine, instead of “at dawn,” read “straightforwardly”; this belongs to the Old Latin translation.

At the ends of the sea. For “sea,” Sanctes and Campensis put “the west”; *yām* signifies both “sea” and the western region [Col. 1224A]. “Because,” Sanctes says, “the great sea lies westward in relation to the land of Israel.” All the others retain the Vulgate reading. In the end, the sense is not changed in the slightest.

VERSE 10.—And night is my illumination in my delights. In Hebrew, “in my delights” does not appear to be present. But one must know that the word placed here, if written simply without vowel-points, can plainly be understood as “in my delights.” For if pronounced *baʿădānay*, the letter *nun* is radical, from the root *ʿādan*, “to delight in pleasure.” Nor do I doubt that the Septuagint understood it in this way; otherwise, what could they have imagined? But the Hebrews now read *baʿădēnî*, where the *nun* is a servile letter; and St Jerome renders “around me,” or, as most others prefer, “for me.” Sanctes even adds from his own resources the word “will conceal”: “Night,” he says, “will conceal the light for me.” Others understand it differently: that nothing can be hidden from God. Hence St Jerome on this passage:

> “In Hebrew the sense is this: ‘And I said: Perhaps darkness will trample me down; but, conversely, night itself was light with you, because nothing can conceal you.’”

Symmachus rendered it better, and so forth: “and night, light, sits around me.”

VERSE 11.—As is its darkness, so also is its light. Here it should be observed that the pronoun “its” is feminine in both places and refers to the night immediately preceding. This is clear from the Greek: ὡς τὸ σκότος αὐτῆς, οὕτως καὶ τὸ φῶς αὐτῆς, “as its darkness, so also its light.” St Augustine’s view—that both expressions refer to the night—is more pleasing than Faber’s, who wishes the first to refer to night but the second to day. These relative pronouns are not now read in Hebrew; but the Septuagint took the aspirate *he* as a feminine relative, as Hebrews commonly do when they add the point called *mappiq*. Hebrew scholars, however, take that *he* as a paragogic ending: *kaḥăšēkāh, kā’ôrāh*, or thus [uncertain printed form].

VERSE 13.—You have been fearfully magnified. In Hebrew [Col. 1224C] it is obscure if one translates word for word: *nôrā’ôth niplēthî*, that is, “I have been fearfully made wonderful.” St Jerome read it with an active sense, taking the *yod* as the sign of the first-person pronoun, or else he had read two *yods*. For he says, “You have fearfully magnified me,” though he expressed the sense differently from the sound of the letters. Indeed, others virtually follow the same understanding in suitable words. Pratensis: “I have been fearfully and wonderfully formed”; likewise Münster and Campensis. Sanctes somewhat differently: “Your works are terrible; I am wonderful.” It remains only that the Septuagint read *niplēthā*, with the omission of *yod*. Nebiensis and the Latin version corresponding to the Chaldean agree with Jerome.

VERSE 14.—My bone is not hidden from you, which you made in secret. Almost all interpreters agree. Sanctes and Münster, however, put “my body,” or “the substance of my body,” for “my bone”; Nebiensis, “my essence.” Münster asserts [Col. 1224D] that he did this following Kimhi’s opinion, who takes *ʿeṣem* for *gûph*, that is, “body.” But the meaning tends to the same point: the formation of the human body, which does not subsist without bones. Hence the Chaldean: “My bones are not hidden from you.”

And my substance in the lower parts of the earth. Because the word *ruqqamtî* properly means “I was marked out with varied colours,” the translators have expressed the metaphor in various ways. They ultimately arrive at the sense that the wondrous formation of man in the mother’s womb is signified. Thus St Jerome: “I was imagined in the lowest parts of the earth”; Pratensis: “I was formed in the lower parts of the earth”; Pellicanus, ingeniously: “I was woven together in the lower parts of the earth.” Sanctes: “I was adorned with varied limbs like a Phrygian embroidered work in the womb, which is like the lower part of the earth”; Münster: “I was distinguished by varied limbs in the lower parts of the earth.” The interpreters for Cajetan and Nebiensis [Col. 1225A]: “I was embroidered with a needle in the lower parts of the earth.” Campensis’s paraphrase: “Like a tapestry woven from sinews and veins, I was woven in my mother’s womb, a place more hidden than any cavern of the earth.”

VERSE 15.—My unformed substance, *golmî*: all interpret it as a rough, unformed mass, or an unshaped foetus in the womb. Hence St Jerome in his Commentaries says that “unformed” here is used for “unshaped”: God knows even the elements of a human being before they are formed in the womb. Meanwhile, I do not know on what basis the translator for Campensis rendered it “my errors.” For neither does the paraphrase correspond to it, as often elsewhere. Sanctes nevertheless says in his *Thesaurus* that this term denotes an uncultivated human being, one without wisdom.

In your book all shall be written. Because the Hebrew may indifferently be rendered “all” or “all things,” in masculine or neuter; and again, “all” may refer to persons, days, or eyes, there follows [Col. 1225B] a diversity of interpretations. St Jerome entirely follows our reading and explains that no one is born without God’s will, nor does anyone escape his knowledge. Münster, Sanctes, and Campensis refer it to the limbs of the body, of all of which God takes account. St Hilary takes “all” to refer to eyes, which he interprets as the apostles. The Hebrew has *kullām*, “all those” or “all those things.”

Days shall be formed, and no one among them. This passage is rendered variously from the Hebrew, varies in Greek, and differs among Latin writers. Pratensis and the translator for Campensis agree in sound with the Septuagint: the sense is that days were formed before anyone was born, although he was foreknown by God as one to be born. But if we follow the deeper sense according to the Septuagint, as interpreted by St Jerome, it is expounded thus: You form all in the day; you desire all to be children of the day; but [Col. 1225C] among human beings there is no one who does not become subject to sin and thereby begin to be a child of night, nor does any one of them accomplish deeds worthy of the light of that day throughout the whole course of life. Hence the Apostle speaks to those who had ceased to be children of night: “But we, brethren, are not children of night, but children of day” (1 Thess. 5).

From this is proved what we said: that the Greek varies. For from Jerome’s words it is gathered that the Septuagint rendered ἡμέρας, “in the day,” since the Greeks lack a sixth case; and we find that several manuscripts have this reading. According to these, St Augustine and Hilary have their respective texts as far as this part is concerned. Other manuscripts plainly have ἡμέρᾳ, “day,” followed by Arnobius, an ancient author. Yet one point must be observed: when it says “no one among them,” “them” should not be referred to days but to people—if one wishes to retain the Greek and the Septuagint. For it is clear that in them the phrase is masculine, ἐν αὐτοῖς. It is otherwise in Hebrew [Col. 1225D] with respect to “days.” Accordingly Jerome rendered it: “The days were formed, and not one is among them.” In the Commentaries he explains its meaning thus, and so forth:

> “Symmachus translated this passage: ‘The days in which they were formed—not even one of them is lacking.’ The sense is: Every period of life, whose course has been allotted from the beginning of this life, runs on to a fixed end. Not one day is either more or less than you, Creator, willed it to be.”

Pellicanus is not far from this interpretation: “The days,” he says, “will be observed, and not one among them”—that is, no single day is assigned to us at our own choice, but the fixed period of life established by God cannot be overstepped by us. Sanctes and Münster offer another interpretation, in which they agree. The former says: “The limbs were formed over many days, and not one of them was unknown to you.” The latter: “Those things which were formed over days, while none of them yet existed.” Campensis’s paraphrase differs somewhat: “Although they can grow to their proper size only over many days, yet with you, O Lord, there is not this diversity of days, but one perpetual day.” St Hilary reads, “they shall be filled in the day,” indicating that some manuscripts have, “they shall be formed in the day.” St Augustine has an altogether different reading: “they shall wander by day.” In the second part, however, they agree: “no one among them.” According to Hilary, the apostles shall be filled in the day, that is, in Christ; and according to Augustine, there is no one among them apart from the day. “They shall wander by day,” namely the weak, abandoning the day, Christ; “and no one among them,” because all fled. The Chaldean paraphrast gives another sense: on the day when the world was created, all creatures were created from the beginning, and not on one day alone among them.

VERSE 16.—But to me your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honoured. Nearly all agree, except Sanctes, Münster, Campensis, and Nebiensis, who say, “How precious to me were your thoughts.” Münster does not, however, pass over or reject the other interpretation; in his scholium, *rēʿekā* is ambiguous, common to “thoughts,” “companions,” or “friends” [Col. 1226B].

Their rule has been exceedingly strengthened. Those who render “heads” or “princes” instead of “rule” differ only slightly. But those who rendered “thoughts” in the preceding clause, persisting in that sense, say “their sums,” namely of the thoughts; or, according to Nebiensis, “their number.” Jerome alone rendered “the poor.” From this it is plainly argued that he read *rāšêhem* (“their poor”) without *aleph*, where we have *rāʾšêhem* (“their heads”); Eugubinus also noticed this. But since Jerome interprets it of the apostles, the same sense returns: they were princes and leading guides of poverty.

VERSE 17.—I shall number them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand. There is no disagreement among the translators, except that those who said “thoughts” in the preceding verse apply this verse to them, changing only gender and the underlying subject.

VERSE 18.—If you slay sinners, O God: men of blood, depart from me. I find only Sanctes and Campensis willing to depart from the Vulgate reading. Yet Hebrew idiom did not compel this. They therefore say: “If you slay, O God, the wicked man and men of blood, to whom I say: Depart from me.”

VERSE 19.—Because you say in thought. Pratensis: “because they will speak of you in wickedness”; Sanctes: “who have spoken abomination against you”; likewise Münster and Campensis. But perhaps St Jerome, Pellicanus, the translator for Campensis, and Nebiensis took *yōmerûkā* from the root *mārāh*, “to be rebellious,” because they render, “they will wickedly contradict you,” or “they rebel in audacity,” although the grammatical rule requires *yimrûkā*. Others derive it from *’āmar*, with the *aleph* omitted. Then *limzimmāh* comes from the root *zāmam*, “to devise wickedness.” And the “thought” of our reading is understood, according to Cassiodorus, as depraved.

But [Col. 1226D] we have the second person, and although the sense is not damaged—because the preceding address was directed to the men of blood and it suitably followed, “because you speak,” etc.—nevertheless we gather that the Greek manuscripts varied, both from Hilary’s words and from the reading now found in Greek copies. St Hilary, therefore, interpreting this passage, says:

> “The Latin translation, because it does not know the force of the saying, has introduced great obscurity by failing to distinguish the proper meaning of an ambiguous expression. What is written among us, ‘because you will speak in thought,’ is in Greek ὅτι ἐρεῖς εἰς διαλογισμόν, ‘because you will speak into thought’; and the word ἔρεις is distinguished by pronunciation, so that either ‘you speak’ or ‘contentions’ may be understood. For both are signified by the same written words. But those who acquired knowledge of the Hebrew language have reported that it is rendered not ‘you speak,’ but ‘contentions,’ in the word ἔρεις. And reason and meaning show that this is indeed so. ‘Men of blood,’ he says, ‘depart from me’; and after a few intervening words: Thus, as there are men of blood whose teaching is flattering, so too there are men of blood whose teaching is deceitful. The deceitful teaching of heretics is blasphemous under God’s name, impious under the pretext of religion, and deceptive under the appearance of truth. In their mind and thought there persists only the pursuit of contention: they labour in nothing for human salvation, gain nothing for hope, devise nothing peaceful; so that their labour is in all these thoughts, and they meditate conflict.”

Thus St Hilary. But the reading in the Greek copies which it was possible to inspect is otherwise, though it tends to the same meaning: ὅτι ἐρισταί εἰσι εἰς διαλογισμούς, “because they are contentious in their thoughts”; or, as others have it, ἔστε, “you are.” Finally, the text used by St Augustine is, “you will speak in thought,” which he takes in a favourable sense, as the Master adduces it.

May they take, or shall they take, in vain. *Nāsû laššāw’* is rendered differently by different persons. St Jerome: “they have been lifted up in vain”; similarly Pratensis and [Col. 1227B] Nebiensis. Pellicanus renders, “under the name, vain exaltation.” The interpreters for Cajetan render it actively and literally: “they took up,” “they lifted up in vain.” But Sanctes, Münster, and Campensis add what seemed fitting to them, namely “your name.” Sanctes says, “They took up your name in vain”; Münster, “and your name is taken up in vain”; Campensis, “they contemptuously used your name”; the Chaldean: “those who swear vainly, the patrons of your enmity.” Finally, our reading corresponds to the Hebrew truth, though the tense of the verb is not preserved. Yet, as Sanctes says, *nāsû* may here stand for *nāśe’û*.

Your cities. All translations except Pellicanus’s have “your enemies” or “your adversaries,” in the case appropriate to the construction. Certainly *ʿārekā* can be from *’ôr*, “enemy,” or from *ʿîr*, “city.” Pellicanus indeed has “cities,” but “your,” not “their,” as in Hebrew. Yet just as Greek manuscripts must have varied—for we now read τὰς πόλεις σου, “your cities,” whereas the old Latin writers, St Augustine, Hilary, Arnobius, and Cassiodorus, read “their cities”—so it is no less probable that the same happened in Hebrew [Col. 1228A].

VERSE 22.—Question me. The Latin translator appears to have read in Greek αἴτησον, “ask,” instead of ἔτασον, “examine, search.” Hebrew: *beḥōnēnî*. But Hilary and Arnobius write “interrogate me,” with the Vulgate reading.

My paths. *Sarkappay*, that is, “my thoughts.” And these are indeed dispositions of the mind, which are not improperly called the paths of the heart. For the soul advances by its affections as by certain feet. Hence the Chaldean interpreter: “Know my affections.”

[Col. 1228B] VERSE 23.—In the eternal way. Thus St Jerome and several others. Pratensis, Sanctes, and the interpreters for Cajetan render “through the way of the age” or “of the world,” although Jerome testifies on Galatians chapter 1 that *ʿôlām*, especially with *waw*, signifies eternity. Finally, I do not know what Campensis’s paraphrase means: “May I patiently be punished, so that, after the manner of other wicked persons, you may slay me.” But Eugubinus teaches that this is a Hebrew idiom, making it an imprecation: “If I think with the wicked, lead me into the way of the world,” that is, into the death toward which the whole world hastens. This is what the Chaldean says: “Lead me in the way of the righteous of the world.” Yet these do not adequately accord with Jerome’s sense or with the exposition of the saints.

## PSALM 139

[Col. 1227]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “FOR THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID”

[Col. 1227C]

Deliver me. Title: “For the end, a psalm of David.” [Aug.] By David here is understood the Church, which is Christ’s body. This is the complaint, groaning, and prayer of Christ’s body, placed among evil persons and not yet possessing its good in reality but in hope, where there is full exultation. Therefore in this psalm the voice of Christ’s body is heard: this is our voice, provided that we are in Christ’s body. Whoever is not in that body will be among those amid whom that body groans: he will be either a member of Christ or an enemy of Christ. The title means: This psalm, directing us to the end, that is, to Christ, belongs to David, that is, to the Church which here speaks.

Purpose: [Cassiod.] It urges us to pray to God against the evils of the world. Method: The psalm has three parts. [Col. 1227D] First, it sets out the enemies and the evils they stir up, opposing prayers to them. Second, it says that it has help against evils, at “I said to the Lord.” Third, it discloses what the enemies’ evils are, at “the head of their encompassing,” and so forth. Thus the Church, suffering among evil people, cries:

VERSE 1.—“Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man; rescue me from the unjust man.”

O Lord, deliver me from the evil man, [Aug.] not from one person but from the whole race of evil persons, along with their prince, the devil, who is also figuratively called “man.” Hence: “The enemy, a man, has done this,” he who oversowed tares (Matt. 13); and he is called a “man” in the sense of a strong male, because he is powerful to harm. Hence it adds, “Rescue me from the unjust man.” An unjust man is one who harms; and every evil person harms. [Col. 1228C] Therefore, after saying “from the evil man,” it adds, as though explaining it, “from the unjust man,” meaning that every evil person is unjust, harming either himself or another.

He harms another either as soon as he becomes evil, or later. For some evil persons do not seem unjust because they are not cruel, harsh, persecuting, or oppressing people; nevertheless they are licentious, drunken, devoted to pleasures. Even if they do not appear to harm others, they harm themselves, and therefore are not innocent. For innocent is the person who harms neither himself nor another. Yet if anyone considers more deeply, such a person also harms others, at least by example: because he lives with you and invites you to do what he does. Later he will harm by deed as well. When he has consumed by luxurious living what he possesses, [Col. 1228D] he then seizes from others what he can squander. Thus from pleasure and luxury, by which he did not seem to harm others, proceeds that which pricks you—just as thorns are soft at the root, but from it grows what pricks. Let the root, then, be burned up, and there will be nothing from which the thorn may grow. So while someone lives luxuriously, he appears to harm no one; but later he steals what he squanders. Let pleasure therefore be corrected as a root, and the robbery that pricks like a thorn will not be born.

He then explains how the wicked persecute. [Alcuin.] They attack in three ways: with tongue, hand, and heart; and he begins with the heart, saying:

VERSE 2.—“Who have devised injustices in their heart; all day long they prepared battles.”

[Col. 1229A] Who have devised. [Aug.] As though saying: Deliver me from the people of the wicked, who, although they often display good things on their lips, have nevertheless devised injustices in their heart. Deliver me especially from these, for open enmity is more easily avoided than concealed enmity. He is difficult to avoid who bears good things on his lips and conceals evil in his heart, because no plague is more effective than a familiar enemy. Such persons “prepared battles all day,” that is, continually: schisms and heresies against which I might fight. For wars always arise from the hearts of such people, even if their words are peaceful. By saying “all day,” [Cassiod.] he indicates their continual wickedness, not wearied by delay. He then shows how they persecute with the tongue:

VERSE 3.—“They sharpened their tongue like [Col. 1229B] serpents; the venom of asps is beneath their lips.”

They sharpened their tongues, [Cassiod.] that is, they defiled them with words of wickedness; he adds, “like serpents.” [Aug.] He aptly compares them to serpents. In the serpent there is cunning and deceit for harming. It also crawls, having no feet by which its coming may be heard. Its movement is smooth along the way, but not straight. Thus the wicked crawl in order to harm: beneath the smooth contact of their words they have hidden venom. “The venom of asps,” that is, incurable venom, is beneath their lips. They have something else upon their lips. [Hilar.] He then adds concerning persecution effected by the hand, that is, in deed:

VERSE 4.—“Guard me, O Lord, from the hand of the sinner; rescue me from unjust men.”

[Col. 1229C] Guard me, O Lord, from the hand of the sinner, [Cassiod.] that is, of the devil, because he is powerful to harm and is therefore called the prince of this world (John 12). For this reason the psalmist asks to be guarded from him: the devil deceives in many ways, which the psalmist cannot by himself guard against. And “rescue me from unjust men,” that is, from the devil’s members, through whom he attempts what he cannot accomplish by himself, so that they may not harm me. I do not mean in worldly affairs, but on the Lord’s way. Therefore it adds:

VERSE 5.—“Who have devised to supplant my steps: the proud have hidden a snare for me.”

Who have devised to supplant my steps, [Cassiod., Aug.] that is, to deceive me away from God’s way, namely to draw me back. By saying “supplant,” note that they prepare pits beside the way of God. Then, showing who the enemies are, it adds: “The proud have hidden a snare,” or “a trap, for me.” By this name, “the proud,” it briefly identifies and explains the entire body of the devil. From pride comes the fact that they often call themselves just when they are unjust. From it comes their refusal to confess sins; from it also their envy of the truly just. Every proud person is envious, as the devil envied man what he himself had lost. Because he had lost the kingdom, he did not wish—and does not wish—that man should attain it; and he now works to prevent man from reaching the place from which he himself was expelled.

VERSE 6.—“And they stretched cords into a snare; beside the way they laid a stumbling-block for me.”

[Col. 1230A] And what did those proud people do? Behold, they “stretched cords,” or ropes, “into a snare for me,” [Aug.] that is, their sins, which they urge me to commit. Of these Isaiah says: “Woe to those who draw sins like a long rope” (Isa. 5). Sins are called ropes because those who persist in sins add sin to sin; and whereas they ought to be corrected by the accusation of their sin, they double it by defence. One who defends what he has done badly often wants to be fortified by other sins because of those he has committed. He committed adultery; lest he be killed, he prepares homicide. He adds sin to sin, namely homicide to adultery, and perhaps poison again for that; and so the rope is drawn out, not, of course, from straight but from twisted strands, so that there may be something by which his hands and feet are bound at the end and he is cast [Col. 1230B] into outer darkness.

This righteous man therefore says, “They stretched these cords for me.” Where did they stretch them? Behold: “Beside the way,” or “paths, they laid a stumbling-block for me.” He says “beside the way,” not “in the way.” The way is God’s commandments. Therefore do not depart from God’s way—that is, from God’s commandments—and you will not fall into stumbling-blocks.

PART II. Διάψαλμα, “interlude.” VERSE 7.—“I said to the Lord: You are my God; hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication.”

I said to the Lord. [Aug.] The second part, where he states what help he has against the evils mentioned: as though saying, “The wicked attack in so many ways; what remedy remains for you among so many evils, in these dangers?” To cry to the Lord. Therefore I, crying out, said to the Lord: “You are my God.” Those are human beings and not mine; but you are God, and mine. He says this with great confidence. Although God is the God of all by re-creation, he is properly the God of those who enjoy him. He then asks: “Hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication.” I ask nothing else. He does not simply say “my supplication,” but, more plainly expressing the affection of his soul, says “the voice of my supplication.” For there are supplications of evil persons without a voice, because they do not proceed from the good affection of the heart. But the just person’s supplication has a voice, because, proceeding from the marrow of love, it is worthy to be heard. Voice properly belongs to human beings and living creatures; other things have sound. Those, therefore, who pray to God but do not think rightly of God have sound, [Col. 1230D] not voice, because there is no life there—that is, no affection of charity. But those who think rightly of God have a supplication with voice, which is the life and soul of supplication. Such a person therefore says:

VERSE 8.—“O Lord, Lord, strength of my salvation, you have overshadowed my head in the day of battle.”

O Lord, Lord, [Aug.] that is, most truly Lord—not as men are lords, who purchase with money, whereas you purchase with your blood. You, I say, hear me, for you are “the strength of my salvation”: you give strength to my salvation, namely perseverance, by which I am saved. He says this because he saw dangers and an abundance of evils, through which charity grows cold and iniquity abounds (Matt. 24); but he also saw the comfort, namely that “he who perseveres unto the end shall be saved” (ibid.). Perseverance therefore belongs to strength. Since it is difficult to persevere on a long journey, he says: “You are the strength of my salvation,” that is, you give strength to persevere, that by persevering I may be saved. And why do I hope that you are strength? Because “in the day of battle”—while I fight against the sons and against the law of the members—“you have overshadowed my head,” that is, in the battle in which I struggle outwardly against hypocrites and inwardly against the law of the members, your grace refreshes me. This shelter will avail me so that:

VERSE 9.—“Do not hand me over, O Lord, from my desire to the sinner; they have devised against me—do not forsake me, lest perhaps they be exalted.”

Do not hand me over, O Lord, to the sinner, [Aug.] that is, to the devil, “from my desire”: do not allow me to suffer the heat arising from myself, from my desire, by which room is made for the devil, without which he can do nothing, however fiercely the enemy rages. To make this clearer by an example: behold, the devil offers gain in order to draw you into fraud. He will have no gain unless you commit fraud. Gain is bait; fraud is the snare by which you are caught if you commit fraud. The person conquered by desire falls into the snare; but God’s shade tempers the heat of desire, and there is nowhere room for the devil except through your own desire. Therefore the psalmist says: “Do not hand me over, O Lord, from my desire to the sinner,” that is, do not allow me to be handed over to the devil through my desire. [Cassiod.] “To hand over” here is said in the way in which the Apostle says: “God handed them over to the desires of their heart” (Rom. 1). He handed them over by abandoning them and permitting them to be handed over, not by imparting wickedness.

That this may not occur—namely, that he may not be handed over from his desire to the sinner—the following is plausible: just as they devise an evil plan, so may God’s power give help. “The enemies have devised against me; and you, O Lord, do not forsake me, lest perhaps they be exalted,” [Aug.] that is, lest they triumph and rejoice over me once conquered. For when a person is deceived, the devil and his followers rejoice and triumph. Hence elsewhere: “They will exult if I am moved” (Ps. 12).

PART III. Διάψαλμα, “interlude.” VERSE 10.—“The head of their encompassing; the labour of their lips shall cover them.”

The head of their circuit. [Aug.] The third part, where he states the evils of the enemies: as though saying, “Your shade covers me in the day of battle, but the head of their circuit covers them,” that is, pride. The wicked go round in the cycle of error, where the path has no end. Pride is the head of this circuit, because “pride is the beginning of every sin.” And because every proud person is hypocritical and every hypocrite a liar, it adds: “The labour of their lips,” that is, falsehood, “shall cover them,” that is, shield and defend them. Falsehood is rightly called labour: one who invents what to say labours, but truth is easily spoken. Or, “the labour of their lips,” that is, their false and lying assertion, “shall cover them,” [Cassiod.] because they are overcome by their own false assertion. Or thus: You, O Lord, are a shelter to me; but the head of those who devise evils against me is circuit, that is, [Col. 1232A] the devil, who never walks straight, together with error and temporal things. And “the labour of their lips shall cover them”: this is unchanged. Moreover:

VERSE 11.—“Coals shall fall upon them; you will cast them into fire; they shall not endure in miseries.”

Coals shall fall upon them. [Haymo.] Here on earth, before the eternal fire comes, namely the coals of the fire of concupiscence, anger, and lust. “And you will cast them into fire,” that is, into those coals: you will permit them to be cast down. Thus he calls the same things both coals and fire. [Aug.] Or, according to another reading: “Fiery coals shall fall upon them on earth, and you will cast them down,” that is, in this life, before eternal fire comes. “Fiery coals shall fall upon them,” namely the saints who have risen again from the dead. Though once darkness, they are now light in the Lord (Eph. 5); as they kindle some, they cast down others. And you will cast down the wicked. For when the wicked see the saints shining, they envy them; and thus the saints fall upon them, because through the saints’ good life and preaching the wicked incur ruin. Hence the Apostle: “To some we are an odour of life unto life; to others an odour of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2). Such persons will not endure in the miseries of this world because, being impatient, they fall—that is, fail—in these miseries which the good endure patiently. Truly they will not endure, because:

VERSE 12.—“A man of tongue shall not be directed upon the earth; evils shall seize the unjust man unto destruction.”

A man of tongue, [Aug.] whose pleasure is to speak and who does not consider what he says, shall not be directed on this earth, that is, in this life. For a man of tongue loves lies, taking no care what he says. Therefore it cannot happen that he should be directed. Whoever wishes to be directed, therefore, ought rather to listen than to speak, as James says: “Let every person be swift to hear, but slow to speak” (Jas. 1). Even if someone speaks what is true, but without necessity, he is a man of tongue. It would therefore be more perfect for all to listen to the Bridegroom, like John, who rejoiced not so much because he taught as because he heard; he says: “The friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3). But for the sake of the unlearned it is sometimes necessary to speak so that they may be taught. Therefore one who always wishes to teach always wishes to have unlearned people whom he can teach.

[Aug.] Let joy, then, consist in silence and in hearing the Bridegroom; let the voice of teaching belong to necessity, not to desire. Thus one will not be a man of tongue, who is never directed. Within, truth must be heard, that we may enter into the joy of the Lord, as was said to the faithful servant: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25). But one who delights in going outward by speaking is puffed up; and because what he loves is outside, he will be sent into outer darkness. Let joy therefore be in inward things, and necessity—not desire—in outward things.

“The unjust man”: as though saying, Not only shall the man of tongue not be directed, but evils shall seize the unjust man, and even the just. But they shall seize the unjust unto destruction. As though saying: All wish to hide from evil; even the good flee it. But evil seizes all good people, not unto destruction, because now their soul is crowned and later their flesh shall be restored. [Col. 1233A] But it seizes the wicked unto destruction because they do not endure in miseries. This does not happen to the poor person, who, although seized by evils, is not seized unto destruction. “For God chastises every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12). These evils are now for the wicked, but they also concern the future.

VERSE 13.—“I know that the Lord will execute judgment for the needy, and vengeance for the poor.”

I know what they do not foresee, [Cassiod.] namely that the Lord will at last act, even though he does not act now. He will execute judgment for the needy person who hungers for righteousness, seeks, and knocks; and he will execute vengeance—or, in another reading, “causes”—for the poor in spirit. [Aug.]

VERSE 14.—“Nevertheless the just shall confess to your name, and the upright shall dwell with your countenance.”

Nevertheless, the righteous. [Aug.] This is the conclusion of the psalm, [Col. 1233B] where he says that, if the good have been delivered and vengeance taken on their enemies, they ascribe this not to themselves but to God. Hence they shall also dwell with Him. [Cassiod.] As though he said: Although the good are now afflicted, nevertheless the righteous shall give thanks—here amid severe troubles, which is more praiseworthy, and especially in the future, when You shall render both judgment and the causes pertaining to them. They shall give thanks, I say, to Your name, [Aug.] because they will attribute nothing to their own merits, but to Your mercy. Or, they are upright in this way: whoever bends his heart toward himself twists it; but whoever directs it toward God makes it straight. Therefore their rest is where they have their heart. Hence he adds: And they shall dwell. Those who had fared badly in their own countenance, in whose sweat they ate peace, shall dwell with Your countenance, because they shall see the triune God as He is; and then, their sweat wiped away and their labours ended, they shall be filled with everlasting [Col. 1233C] joy. Therefore they fear nothing in the world.

## Comparison on Psalm 139, “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man, from the violent man,” etc.

**Verse 9.** “Do not hand me over, O Lord, from my desire to the sinner.” Jerome and almost all the others translate: “Do not give, O Lord, the desires of the ungodly,” or, “Do not bring to completion, O Lord, the desires of the ungodly.” But because the Septuagint wished the pronoun *me* to be understood—a thing which not infrequently occurs among the Hebrews—or some other word, if appropriate, they consequently rendered the sense somewhat differently. Pellican agrees with the Septuagint: “Do not give me, O Lord, to the desire of the ungodly.” Yet the Septuagint also seem to have understood the initial *mem* as a servile letter and the final *yod*, where we read *MAAUAIE*, from the root *IVA*, “he desired.”

“They devised against me.” Jerome: “his wickedness”; or, as others have it, “his criminal design,” or something similar. Certainly the Septuagint appear to have read *ZEMAMAI*, which may mean “thoughts against me.” But we now have, with *vau*—a letter whose form differs slightly from *yod*—*ZEMAMO*.

“Do not forsake me.” Hebrew: *AL TAPHEQ*. However one may wish to translate it, according to the different meanings of the word in the *hiphil* conjugation, something suitable must be borrowed from outside. Jerome translates, “do not pour out,” or “let them not be poured out,” namely into action. Sanctes translates, “do not bring to completion”; Pratensis, “do not consummate”; Münster, “do not allow [them] to advance.” [Col. 1234B] And because this verb in the conjugation called *Qal* sometimes means “to strike against,” you may therefore rightly translate it here literally: “do not cause me to strike against,” that is, “do not forsake me.”

**Verse 10.** “The head of those surrounding them.” Modern translators render: “the head or leader of those surrounding me,” and thus agree with the sense of our reading. Jerome followed another meaning when he said: “the bitterness of my companions at table.” For *ROSCH* is a homonym meaning “head,” “leader,” and “bitterness.” Whether you understand it of pride or of the devil himself, everything fits. Further, if you derive *MESIBAI* from the stem *SABAB*, it rightly means “those surrounding me”; but if from the sense given by Jerome, it means “my table-companions.”

**Verse 11.** “They shall not stand in miseries.” Others have “into pits,” referring it to the preceding verb, “You shall cast down.” They then say, “they shall not rise,” or “that they may not rise.” The meaning does not vary: hopeless [Col. 1234C] misery is indicated by deep pits from which no one can rise: *BEMAUAMOROTH BAL IAQUMU*.

**Verse 12.** “Evils shall seize the unjust man unto destruction.” Jerome likewise translates this literally. Others, changing the wording, give the same sense: “Evil shall hunt the wicked man into banishments or headlong falls.” This hunting is a seizure resulting in a headlong fall, eternal condemnation. Hence the Chaldean paraphrast: “The angel of death shall hunt the perverse and malignant man and thrust him down into Gehenna.”

## Psalm 140

[Col. 1233]

### Title of the Psalm: “A Psalm of David.”

[Col. 1233C]

“O Lord, I have cried.” Title: A Psalm of David. [Aug.] [Col. 1233D] This psalm is somewhat obscure. For in the Holy Scriptures there are profound mysteries, hidden so that they may not become cheap, sought so that they may exercise us, and opened so that they may nourish us. If Sacred Scripture were nowhere open, it would not feed you; if nowhere hidden, it would not exercise you. Yet nothing is said here which has not been said in other psalms; the same things are said, though in a different manner. They are the same because that which the world compels us to forget ought to be recalled frequently. Divine matters are also expressed in many ways, so that variety of expression may remove weariness with the truth.

But that which is treated here and in the other psalms is charity. Charity indeed is love, but not every kind of love. There is a heavenly love, and there is also an infernal love. For the wicked love one another; but that love is infernal. Different is the charity of Christians, by which they love God for His own sake and their neighbours for God’s sake, which Paul defines when he says: “The end of the commandment is charity, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and unfeigned faith” (Phil. I). Elsewhere, speaking as though to persons who know this, he says: “The end of the law is charity” (Rom. XIII); and there he does not say what charity it is, because he has said so elsewhere. For not everything can or ought to be said everywhere. Therefore he did not there say what kind of charity it is, but determined this where he added: “out of a pure heart and a good conscience and unfeigned faith.”

You have a pure heart in charity according to God when you love a person as you ought to love yourself; this is not found among the wicked. This charity joins us together with Christ. For through charity the head and body are, as it were, one man; and it is proper to the head to speak for all the members, just as our tongue [Col. 1235A] takes on the person of all the members. For it performs speech for all, saying for the foot, “You tread on me,” and for the hand, “You wounded me.” Thus Christ also, who is the head, speaks for the members, with whom He is one. For charity makes us one with Christ. Therefore, whether the head speaks or the members speak, whether what is said suits the head or the members, Christ speaks; but in His voice let each recognize his own, as one adhering to Christ’s body. At times He says what belongs to Himself alone, yet He does not separate Himself from our words; rather, He returns from what is properly His to what is ours, and sometimes passes from what is ours to what is properly His.

Thus Christ speaks throughout this psalm, either in His own person or in the person of His members. [Cassiod.] Intention: he urges us to cry to God. Method: [Col. 1235B] The psalm has two parts. First, the Prophet, knowing that a human being is entangled in sins, prays to be heard, adding those things from which he especially wishes to be delivered. Secondly, he says that, when reproved by a righteous man, he will reject false flatterers, at “The righteous man shall correct,” etc. Therefore, in the person of a man surrounded by sins, he says:

### Verse 1. “O Lord, I have cried to You; hear me: attend to my voice when I cry to You.”

“O Lord, I have cried,” [Cassiod., Aug.] for a long time now, to You. What have I cried? “Hear me”; and again I still cry, “Attend to my voice.” When? When I shall cry to You with the intention of my heart. For the cry has not yet ended, because the tribulation has not yet ended. If the tribulation has ended, let the cry also end. But if it remains until the end of the age, the cry has never ceased, O Lord.

[Col. 1235C]

### Verse 2. “Let my prayer be directed as incense in Your sight; the lifting up of my hands, the evening sacrifice.”

“My prayer,” [Cassiod.] kindled with the fire of charity, “let it be directed in Your sight like incense”; that is, let it be incense to You, that is, a sweet fragrance. In its figure, incense was said under the old law to be offered to God as a sweet-smelling odour (Exod. XXIX). “And the lifting up of my hands,” [Alcuin.] that is, my good action, which is done for eternal things, “let it be to You an evening sacrifice,” that is, let it please You as the sacrifice offered under the old law, which was more acceptable (Num. XXVIII), because it was the figure of that ancient sacrifice which was offered upon the cross at the end of the world.

[Cassiod.] Under the Law the priest indeed offered continually, both morning and evening; that which was offered in the evening was more worthy. Or, since our evening is the end of life, repentance may be called an evening sacrifice, because at the end we are cleansed. The meaning is: “Let the lifting up of my hands be an evening sacrifice to You,” that is, may my good works be acceptable to You as is repentance performed in the evening, namely at life’s end; if we offer it perfectly, we are rightly cleansed. He says this so that no one may despair who repents at the end.

[Aug.] Or this may be understood of Christ. All understand this of the Head, who at evening gave up His soul in order to receive it again; He did not lose it unwillingly. Yet we are represented there. For what hung upon the wood was taken from us. Therefore the evening sacrifice is Christ’s Passion, the offering of the saving victim, which made the Resurrection a morning gift. Thus prayer, directed purely from a faithful heart, rises like incense from a holy altar. And the lifting up of my hands, stretched out upon the cross, is the evening sacrifice, because then He laid down His soul. Then he adds in the voice of the body: And, O—

### Verse 3. “Set, O Lord, a guard upon my mouth, and a door of restraint upon my lips.”

“O Lord, set a guard upon my mouth,” [Cassiod.] or “upon my heart,” lest it devise wicked things; “and set a door of restraint upon my lips,” lest they utter foolish things. [Alcuin.] This is said by comparison with one who stands around a door, so that no one may enter or leave who is not permitted. For Jeremiah says: “Death has entered through our windows” (Jer. IX). And Peter says: “Our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (I Pet. V). [Cassiod.] Note that he asks for a guard to be placed both upon heart and mouth. A double defence is needed, so that neither may wicked thought relish evil nor perverse will burst forth into foolish words.

Or thus: “Set a guard upon my mouth,” lest unsuitable words go out; and “a door of continence,” another reading, “upon my lips.” He did not say “a bar of continence,” but “a door.” A door is both shut and opened: likewise, the door of the lips should be opened for confession of sin and shut against excuse; and so it will be a door of continence, not of ruin. What is the purpose of this door? It is this:

### Verse 4. “Do not incline my heart to words of malice, to make excuses in sins.”

[Col. 1236C] “Do not incline my heart, O God.” Christ says this in the person of the Church. [Aug.] For when one of the members prays this, He Himself prays it, just as elsewhere He says in the person of His members: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” (Acts IX); and again: “I was hungry, and you did not give Me food” (Matt. XXV). Thus here also: “Do not incline my heart,” that is, the heart of my Church—indeed, the heart of my body—“to words of malice,” namely, “to make excuses in sins,” as though everything happened by chance.

### Verse 5. “With men who work iniquity; and I will not share with their chosen ones.”

“With men who work iniquity,” [Cassiod.] that is, as men who work iniquity make excuses. The sense is: Set the door for this purpose, that I may not [Col. 1236D] excuse my sin—the chief vice which rules human beings and makes them slower to repent. Hence it is said in the Book of Kings: “To rebel is as the sin of divination, and unwillingness to submit is as the crime of idolatry” (I Kings XV). Note that he says: “to make excuses in sins.” [Aug.] This is the habit of the imprudent: when caught, they first excuse themselves by falsehoods; then, when convicted, they seek other excuses, blaming their evils on time or necessity, lest they ever yield to the truth.

“And I will not share.” As though he said: “Do not incline my heart.” If this is so, I shall not share—or, in another reading, “be bound together”—with their chosen ones, not God’s chosen ones; that is, I shall not be their companion. Their chosen ones are those who justify themselves and despise others, like the Pharisee who said, “I am not as other men,” etc. (Luke [Col. 1237A] XVIII), who defend sins by whatever means. He does not wish to be bound together with such persons—that is, associated with them—lest they hinder him. [Cassiod.] For persons are properly said to be “bound together” when two accused persons are tied by one bond, so that one hinders the other and escape cannot be free.

## Part II. Verse 6. “The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head.”

“The righteous man shall correct me.” [Cassiod., Aug.] The second part: here this faithful person, now corrected on the contrary by a righteous man, rejects false flatterers, intending to benefit the wicked by word and conduct; in this part he also asks to be guarded. As though he said: I shall not share with those who defend sins; rather, a righteous man shall correct me and rebuke me [Col. 1237B] in mercy. For one who rebukes does not hate, and rebukes all the more because he does not hate. This righteous man is Christ, or any brother, or the same person himself, who according to the inner man corrects himself according to the flesh, as though she were a wife.

“But let not the oil of the sinner,” that is, the false praise of a flatterer and pretended affection, which softens minds from the rigour of truth into harmful things, “fatten”—or, in another reading, “shall fatten”—“my head,” that is, my mind. My head does not grow from false flattery; the sinner’s oil does not delight me. Hence, when people have mocked someone with false praise, they say of him: “I anointed his head.” Therefore let the faithful person love to be reproved mercifully by a righteous man, and not praised mockingly by a sinner. Let him keep with him the oil of conscience which the prudent virgins carried with them (Matt. XXV); let him not seek the sinner’s oil.

### Verse 7. “For even yet my prayer is in their good pleasures; their judges have been swallowed up, joined to the rock.”

“For even yet.” [Rem.] As though he said: Let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head; and it will truly not do so, because what I am about to say is still future. What is that? Behold, “even my prayer shall be in their good pleasures,” that is, those sinners shall pray for eternal things as I do. [Aug.] Or join it thus: I shall not share with the wicked; the righteous man shall correct me; “for even yet”—wait—and “my prayer shall be in their good pleasures.” In the early times Christians were reviled; but wait still. “And my prayer shall be in their good pleasures,” that is, [Col. 1237D] the time will come when my prayer shall please them, so that they will say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI); and again: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus” (I John II).

“And my prayer,” that is, the prayer of my Head—namely, the prayer which He Himself taught, or by which He Himself intercedes for us—“shall be in their good pleasures,” that is, it shall please them. And even “their judges,” that is, the powerful and learned men who judge concerning morals, such as Plato, Aristotle, and Pythagoras, “have been swallowed up, joined to the rock,” that is, compared with Christ crucified. Or, another reading: “they have been swallowed up beside the rock.” The sense is the same: beside Christ, that is, compared with Christ, they seem in themselves to say something; but join them—[Col. 1238A] that is, compare them—to Christ, and they are nothing; they lie dead; their wisdom is foolish.

> [Note: [Col. 1237D] Origen, Homily 14 on Exodus.]  
> [lacuna] For Christ comes forth, and all worship Him. Christ conquers; Christ reigns; Christ commands. In figure of this, Moses’ serpent devoured the magicians’ dragons, because Christ’s wisdom made foolish the wisdom of this world (I Cor. I).

[Aug.] What then will become of them? Behold, they themselves at last:

### Verse 8. “They shall hear my words, because they have prevailed; as the richness of the earth has been broken up upon the ground.”

“They shall hear my words.” Why shall they hear? “Because the words themselves have prevailed,” [Aug.] or “have been strong”; that is, my words have power and have prevailed over their words. If they spoke eloquently, I spoke truly. [Col. 1238B] It is one thing to praise an eloquent speaker, another to commend one who speaks truth. Moreover, those who do not fear even to die for them preach my words, according to the saying: “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves” (Matt. X); and, “Do not fear those who kill the body,” etc. (ibid.); as though He said, “Do not fear death.”

What, then, did their deaths accomplish? Behold, “as the richness of the earth,” etc. As though he said: My words benefit them; their deaths also benefit them. He shows this by a comparison: just as the richness of the earth has been broken up, or torn open, upon the ground, from which a yield of fertility results, although the matter is of little account, so—

### Verse 9. “Our bones have been scattered beside hell, because my eyes are toward You, O Lord, Lord; in You have I hoped: do not take away my soul.”

[Col. 1238C] “Our bones,” that is, the bodies of Christ’s witnesses, “have been scattered.” [Aug.] That is, from the scattering of our bones comes the greatest benefit. The comparison is fitting. For the richness of the earth is something contemptible, from which nevertheless the earth receives fertility; so from what the world despised it received fertility, so that the crop of the Church might spring up more abundantly. This is the death of the saints: contemptible to the world, but precious to the husbandman—that is, Christ—who knows the usefulness and rich sap there, from which the Church grew. For God chose the contemptible things of the world, and things which are not, that those which are might be brought to nothing through them (I Cor. I).

Now the earth has already been enriched, as the Church’s crop rises up. Observe indeed how what was noble and eminent [Col. 1238D] in the world has been humbled. The emperor comes to Rome: whither does he hasten? To the emperor’s palace, or to the memorial of a fisherman? Surely he makes supplication to the fisher of men.

“Beside hell.” [Gl. int.] As though he said: “Our bones have been scattered,” and this “beside hell,” that is, according to the will of those who are in the depths, namely those who are hell, that is, deep in vices. Or he says “beside hell,” not “in hell,” because although they perhaps die the common death, they nevertheless do not descend into hell as the wicked do, but eternal life is given them.

Or thus from the passage, “They have been swallowed up,” where he speaks of those opposing Christ and the Church—namely heretics and schismatics. As though he said: My prayer shall please them; but if there are any [Col. 1239A] who oppose, they are swallowed up. This is what he says: “Their judges,” namely the teachers of heretics, “have been swallowed up by the depth of vices,” being beside the rock—that is, beside Christ—and not upon the rock, because they share in the sacraments yet are not in Christ. Therefore they are plunged into the depth of sin. And deservedly, because they shall hear my words and shall not be corrected. This is remarkable, since the words themselves have prevailed, or proved stronger, than all other words. Therefore they are more guilty because they contend.

“And as the richness of the earth has been broken up upon the ground,” from which disease comes into bodies, so, through the wasting sickness of their malice, our bones—that is, the bodies of Christ’s martyrs—have been scattered. For when the richness of the earth erupts, it corrupts the air, and then plague spreads widely among human beings; so their pride, by the wasting sickness of its malice, wounds the bodies of the martyrs, who are the bones and supports of the faithful.

[Alcuin.] Or thus from “They shall hear,” with what precedes otherwise unchanged: as yet my prayer will please them, and truly, because they themselves shall hear my words with the ear of obedience—not like Adam, who heard the Lord saying, “You shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Gen. II), but did not obey. Those predestined to life, however, shall hear my words with an ear capable of hearing. For my words “have prevailed,” that is, they have power to penetrate hearts. Therefore they shall hear them; and, turning back to Adam and recalling his transgression, they shall say: “Adam was our destruction, because he did not stand; let us stand, that we may return to our homeland.” And they shall say: “Adam is as the richness of the earth broken up upon the ground,” because, just as [Col. 1239C] rich soil produces thorns through excess abundance, so Adam, through the riches of free choice, like luxuriant ground, appropriated the forbidden tree. But as a farmer ploughs it up lest it luxuriate further, so “our bones have been scattered by God”; that is, God scattered our inward parts, where we ought to be bony—that is, firm—making us weak and unstable.

I mean us, [Cassiod.] cast down “beside hell,” that is, close to the curse. Because of the stated frailty of man, he flees to divine remedies. As though he said: These things predicted have occurred in us; but, O Lord, “do not take away”—that is, do not allow to be taken away from Your good things—“my soul,” even if the body is destroyed.

[Aug., Cassiod.] He asks this because he knew that many yield to adversities. Therefore, “do not take [Col. 1239D] away,” because “my eyes are toward You, O Lord,” not toward the threats of persecutors. For I know what You suffered for me and what You promised; through this I have securely hoped in You. Therefore do not take me away from Your good things, but let my hope always be in You and let my eyes always look toward You. For this man does not ask contrary to what the saints desire, namely to be taken from the world and to be with Christ.

### Verse 10. “Keep me from the snare which they have laid for me, and from the stumbling-blocks of those who work iniquity.”

“Keep me,” [Aug., Cassiod.] as though he said: Do not take away my soul; rather, keep me from the snare—or trap—which the wicked have set for me through deception, where bait leads to the snare; and from the stumbling-blocks [Col. 1240A] of those who work iniquity, that is, from the manifest disturbances of the restless. By snares and stumbling-blocks he briefly denotes all the evils of the world. Snares are the seductive bonds of those wishing to deceive, and the desires of the flesh. If the devil does not accomplish his purpose through these, he attempts it by stumbling-blocks, which he raises through the restless.

### Verse 11. “Sinners shall fall into his net; I am alone until I pass over.”

“They shall fall.” [Cassiod.] As though he said: Keep me, but sinners, falling from vice into vice, shall fall into the net—or into the net—of his iniquity. By saying, “Sinners shall fall into the net,” he sets out words plainly suited to the comparison. For they are enclosed as though by a kind of circuit of sins, while they tumble from vice into vice; with persons such as these, this man does not wish to be bound together. [Col. 1240B] Hence he adds: “I am alone,” or “I am solitary,” because he does not walk with the worst of men and has no agreement with them. “I am alone,” I say, until, as a traveller, I pass through the way of this world, which he crosses with unoffended step because no pleasure ensnares him.

[Aug.] Or otherwise from “Keep me.” He calls those laying the snare open persecutors; but those working iniquity are persons consenting to them, who fail through fear of persecution. The sense is: Do not take away my soul; rather, keep me from the snare of persecution which they have set for me. Persecutors do this, placing the bait of this life, as it were, in a trap. If the bird loves this bait, it falls into the trap, because through fear of death it yields to persecution. [Col. 1240C] And keep me from the stumbling-blocks of those who work iniquity, that is, from the stumbling of those who fall by consenting to them and so work iniquity. This, therefore, is said concerning those who consented to those who apostasized.

From both groups this man wishes to be guarded: from those who terrify and from those who have fallen. As though he said: Keep me from persecutors who terrify, and from those who have fallen because they were terrified, so that I may neither fear the former nor imitate the latter. And not only do others work iniquity: even those first ones themselves—namely the apostles clinging to His mouth—failed. This is what is meant: “Sinners,” that is, the apostles, “shall fall into his net,” namely the net of iniquity. They were sinners to the degree that they so loved this life as to prefer it to eternal life. For what is said in another psalm had not yet been done in them: “I have strengthened its pillars” (Ps. LXXIV).

Then, in the person of the Head, there follows: “I am alone,” etc. The voice does not change because of the unity of Head and body. As though He said: Why did this occur, namely, that they failed? Because “I am alone,” or “I am solitary”—that is, because I alone am in the time of the Passion, because no one with Him or before Him suffered for His name, the apostles failed, and while hanging on the cross He received only one thief. “I am alone,” I say, until I pass from the world to the Father. Then I shall strengthen the pillars, because at Christ’s resurrection they learned not to fear death. “I am alone until I pass over”; but when I have passed over, I shall be multiplied.
