This is the same as what He says in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John XII). And again: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to Myself” (ibid.). Thus He was alone before He had been put to death and raised from the earth.

Therefore the apostles did not yet have such strength. They were to receive strength to follow, because they did not have strength to go before. For no one is killed for Christ before Christ—that is, for confession of Christ’s name—lest anyone, by dying for Christ’s name, precede Christ. Although many died, they are martyrs. And although many prophets suffered such things, they nevertheless did not die because they foretold Christ; rather, because they spoke to men against their sins and resisted their iniquities, [Col. 1241B] and some of them are counted among the martyrs. Nor was John, than whom none greater has arisen among those born of women (Matt. XI), killed for Christ’s testimony; rather, for Herod’s adultery, because he said: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Matt. XIV). He died for the law of truth, was a martyr for righteousness, but not for Christ’s name. So too the other ancients; yet those who suffer for confession of Christ’s name are properly called martyrs.

## Comparison on Psalm 140: “O Lord, I have cried to You; hear me; attend to my voice,” etc.

**Verse 3.** “A door of restraint upon my lips.” Nearly all translate, “Guard the door of my lips,” which has the same force. But Jerome translated, [Col. 1241C] “Guard the poverty of my lips.” For without vowel points it can be pronounced with *qamets*, and means “poor man” or “poverty”; or as *dal*, with *pataḥ* and with the final *taw* lacking, and means “door, gate.” The interpreters for Cajetan said “pride.”

**Verse 4.** “To make excuses in sins.” Jerome: “to roll about wicked thoughts”; Münster: “lest I be occupied in works of impiety.” The others nearly all translate in a similar manner. Pellican, however, approaches the meaning of the Vulgate reading: “that I may not invent devices in impiety.” For *ALAL* means “to devise,” *LEHITHOLEL*, “to devise”; further, *ALILOTH*, “devices,” correctly indicates excuses in sins.

**Verse 5.** “I will not share with their chosen ones.” Jerome: “nor eat amid their delights.” The others also translate similarly; for example, Sanctes: “I will not eat the food of their pleasures”; [Col. 1241D] Münster: “I will not eat of those things which are pleasant to them.” Yet the sense comes to the same thing if you say, “I shall not share in the things which are choice,” or, “I shall not share in the things which are pleasant to them,” or, “I shall not share with those who are chosen by them,” or “with those who are pleasant or delightful to them.” For the exposition of the saints concerns the persons themselves, not things.

**Verse 6.** “The oil of the sinner.” Jerome: “the oil of bitterness.” Others: “desired oil”; others, “first” or “chief oil.” It was said in the preceding psalm that *ROSCH* is ambiguous. Because meanwhile it denotes gall, the Septuagint and Jerome take it as “sinner” or “sin.” What is more bitter than that?

[Col. 1242A] “Let it not fatten my head,” *AL IANI ROSCH*. Jerome agrees with us, where the verb is rendered according to the appropriateness of the matter. For others translate, “let it not break,” or “let it not prevent,” or “it shall not prevent my head.” Thus the sentence is ambiguous. It may mean that the sinner’s pleasures should not disturb the righteous man’s head; or, with the sense reversed, that the “chief oil,” as they call it, should be received by a devout man as a benefit, although in reality it would be a severe wound. So far is he from returning injury for injury that he embraces with a candid heart what is in itself troublesome. But as regards our reading, nothing disturbs or maddens the head—that is, a person’s mind—more than deceptive flattery. Thus “let it not fatten my head” has aptly been translated according to the proper sense.

**Verse 7.** “My prayer is in their good pleasures.” Jerome: “my prayer [is] for their evils.” The others tend in the same direction. Pratensis: “amid their evils.” Sanctes translates paraphrastically: “that He may deliver me from their evils.” [Col. 1242B] Münster: “against their evils,” *BERAOTHEHEM*. If it is derived from the root *ROA*, it undoubtedly means “their evils.” If from *RAAH*, or if it is plural, it meanwhile denotes wishes, which indeed are good pleasures.

“They have been swallowed up.” Jerome: “they have been taken away”; Pratensis: “let them be torn apart”; Sanctes and the interpreters for Cajetan: “they have been forsaken.” Others: “they have been cast down,” or something similar, which corresponds to our reading. But *NISCHMETU*, from the stem *SCHAMAT*, meaning “he cast down, let go, hurled headlong, shook off,” can be rendered in various ways.

“Joined to the rock.” Pratensis: “upon the tops of rocks.” Sanctes and Münster: “in rocky places.” Literally one would have to say: “in the hands of a cliff or rock,” *BIDE SELA*. But according to Hebrew idiom, *IAD*, that is, “hand,” is applied to every thing according to the appropriateness of its function. Jerome said, “beside the rock.” Nebiensis agrees.

**Verse 8.** “They shall hear my words, because they have prevailed.” [Col. 1242C] Others translate in place of “have prevailed,” “they were pleasant,” “sweet,” or “beautiful,” because the Hebrews say *NAEMU*. Certainly, where words please, there they achieve their effectiveness; and this is for words to be powerful and prevail. Sanctes rightly observes that the Latin translator read in Greek ἐδυνήθησαν, “they were able/strong,” instead of ἡδύνθησαν, “they were made pleasant.”

“As the richness of the earth has been broken up upon the ground.” Jerome gives the same sense: “as when a farmer splits the ground.” Whether you connect it with what precedes or refer it to what follows—namely, either that God’s words will be heard as the earth becomes fertile or bears fruit, or that martyrs’ bones, like split ground, will be contemptuously scattered—[the sense remains]. Sanctes and Münster inserted whatever pleased them, and Campensis follows: “as one who breaks and cuts wood upon the earth.” Others, without adding “wood,” seem also to take the second sense which we have just indicated, because of a different division of the verses.

**Verse 11.** “I am alone.” Thus Pellican also, [Col. 1242D] following the Chaldean: “I am solitary.” The others translate “together,” *IAHAD ANOCHI*. It is indifferent; nevertheless, by translating “together,” it will be ambiguous whether “together” looks upward—“they shall fall together”—or downward—“I shall pass over together,” since in Hebrew there is a pausal division at *RESCHAIM*.

“Until I pass over.” Sanctes and Münster say, “I shall pass over for ever.” Jerome gives neither, but only, “but I shall pass over together.” Yet the point is one: *AD* is ambiguous, meaning either “until” or “for ever.” Hence the Chaldean: “until the time passes”; and Nebiensis: “until I pass over.”

## Psalm 141

[Col. 1243]

### Title of the Psalm: “A Maskil of David, when he was in the cave; a prayer.”

[Col. 1243A]

“With my voice.” Title: A Maskil of David, when he was in the cave; a prayer. [Aug.] This psalm is the fifth among those entitled “prayer.” Nothing is said here other than what has been said in other psalms; but the same things are repeated because common repetition provides for weakness, and they are not repeated superfluously, so that what is repeated may be more firmly commended to memory. Hence it is written in Proverbs: “Desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. XXI); but a foolish man gulps it down, because the wise person reflects on what he has heard and chews it over by reconsidering it, while the foolish person gulps it down—that is, does not reflect, but consigns it to forgetfulness. These are the clean animals in the Law which chew the cud, and those unclean ones which do not chew the cud.

But the statement, “when David was in the cave,” is plain in its literal sense. [Alcuin.] For David, fleeing Saul, hid in a cave; nevertheless the matter here is not David, but what he signifies. David signifies Christ; the cave signifies the flesh, or the world, or the tomb. Therefore David in the cave is Christ with His members in the world, or Christ in the flesh, or in the tomb. The sense of the title is: This is the understanding of David—that is, of the whole Christ—which He had when He was in the cave, that is, in the world, or in the flesh, or in the tomb. [Cassiod.] And this is a prayer. Intention: he urges us to pray. Method: the psalm has two parts. First, a prayer against evils is set forth. Secondly, it treats the end of evils, at “I cried.” Therefore, in the person of the whole Christ, crying to God as though from the cave, he says:

### Verse 1. “With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice I made supplication to the Lord.”

“With my inward voice, not with the noise of the lips, I cried to the Lord.” [Aug.] He then explains what he had said, adding: “With my voice I made supplication to the Lord”; what he called “I cried,” he calls “I made supplication.” He adds this because even those who blaspheme cry to the Lord; as though he said: My cry is supplication, not murmuring, not blasphemy. And further:

### Verse 2. “I pour out my prayer before Him, and declare my tribulation before Him.”

[Col. 1243D] “I pour out” abundantly, as a pure fountain, “my prayer made before Him,” [Cassiod.] that is, where God sees—namely, in the hidden place of conscience, where He alone sees who will repay. Therefore pour out your prayer there; if human beings are to repay, pour it out before them. But if God is to repay, pray in secret, as He commands in the Gospel: “But when you pray, enter into your chamber and, having shut the door, pray to your Father; and He who sees in secret shall repay you” (Matt. VI). “And I declare my tribulation,” that is, the prayer which is offered in tribulation, “before Him,” that is, inwardly from the conscience. [Col. 1244A] Or, secure in innocence, I direct it to Him in secret. And the Church says that she does this.

### Verse 3. “When my spirit fails within me, You knew my paths.”

In failing of my spirit within me, [Aug.] or, “while my spirit failed from me,” another reading: that is, while strength failed from me. This happens so that one may not presume upon one’s own powers, nor attribute to oneself the strength one has, but may know that another works within him, according to that saying: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10). If therefore your own spirit fails, the Spirit of God speaks in you. And perhaps people, hearing, “My spirit has failed,” think him cast down. And he adds: And you knew my paths, that is, the paths of righteousness and of the commandments, [Col. 1244B] which those who think me captive do not see, and along which, while they fall, I walk safely.

VERSE 4.—“In this way in which I walked, the proud hid a snare for me.”

In this way, [Aug.] as though he said: If they think me cast down because my spirit has failed, you see me standing, whose spirit gives me life; and those who persecute me because I belong to Christ hid a snare for me in this way in which I walked—that is, in Christ. For this is what they resent: that I belong to Christ. They set the snare in this way, not according to the reality of the matter but so far as concerns themselves—that is, according to their own opinion—because they intend to set it in the way; but they set it outside the way, like heretics. They do not hide the snare in the way as they wish, but outside it. Hence elsewhere: “Set a stumbling-block for me beside the way” (Ps. 139). Thus the snare is set in the way according to their intention, but beside the way according to the reality of the matter. For Christ is the way, and he does not allow them to set a snare in the way, so that we should have no way by which to go. Yet he allows them to set it beside the way, lest we turn aside from the way.

He who says, “You worship a crucified God,” thinks that he sets a stumbling-block in the way. For he reproaches Christ’s cross because he does not understand it. To one who understands, however, it is not a stumbling-block but glory. Or “way” here is understood as charity. Note that above he said in the plural, “my paths,” but here in the singular, “way,” because there are many ways and one way: many ways, because there are many commandments; one way, because all are reduced to one thing, namely charity. Therefore, in this way, [Col. 1244D] that is, in charity, which bears all things in me, in which I walked by suffering for you, the persecutors hid a snare for me, according to their own opinion. But while they rage on every side and reproach me with frequent exultation, I, despising present things,

VERSE 5.—“I looked to the right hand and saw; and there was none who knew me.”

I looked to the right hand, [Aug.] that is, I looked toward eternal things, and saw that very right hand, which the wicked did not see. For he who fixes his attention on the right hand sees; but he who fixes it on the left is blinded. [Col. 1245A] Therefore the wicked, attending to the left hand, do not see the right. And this is what follows: And there was none who knew me. For when you endure all things, who knows what you are looking toward—whether you direct your eye to the right or to the left?

VERSE 6.—“Escape has perished from me; and there is none who seeks my soul.”

Escape has perished, [Aug.] as though he said: The persecutors hid a snare for me; nevertheless I did not flee—indeed, escape has perished from me. Escape perishes for two kinds of person: one who is enclosed, or one who is strong. The enclosed person cannot flee; the strong person does not wish to. There is also a twofold flight. One is bodily flight, which the Lord permits when he says: “When they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 10). The other is flight of the mind, which the Lord rebukes in the Gospel when he says: “But the hireling, and he who is not a shepherd, sees the wolf coming and flees” (John 10). Such flight has perished from this man.

Therefore he says, escape has perished from me, that is, I did not flee. Escape has perished from one who does not flee. He speaks as though he were enclosed, because, just as one enclosed does not flee bodily because he cannot, so this man does not flee in mind because he will not. Escape therefore has perished from him because he never flees in mind, although at times he does so bodily. And among those persecutors there is none who seeks my soul—not, I say, in order to persecute it, but in order to imitate it. For the soul is sought in two ways, either by persecutors or by lovers, just as flight perishes in two ways, both for the captive and for the strong.

[Col. 1245C] PART II. VERSE 7.—“I cried to you, O Lord; I said: You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living.”

I cried. [Cassiod., Aug., Hilar., Cassiod.] The second part, in which he treats of the end of evils. As though he said: Such is my condition. And therefore I cried to you, O Lord, and said: You are my hope. For this reason I endure all things. And you are my portion, not here, but in the land of the living, where he will grant that he himself may be seen.

Or it may be understood in the person of Christ from the words, “I looked,” who in his Passion, abandoned even by his disciples, said: “I looked to the right hand,” literally, “and saw,” whether my apostles were there. And there was none there who knew me. For the apostles were not standing at the right hand as they had been accustomed to do, because they had been scattered by carnal fear; but I remained steadfast. [Col. 1245D] Hence follows: Escape has perished from me—escape, namely, both of body and of mind. And there is none who seeks my soul, because no consolation was given him; he was left alone for his Passion. Hence elsewhere: “I looked for one to comfort me, and I found none.” And therefore I cried to you, O Lord, and said: You are my hope, because I choose you out of all things, and you are my portion in the land of the living.

He humbly and in common terms says that this land of the living is his portion, though it is wholly his. This is clear from what he said to the thief: “Today you shall be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23), which is eternally the land of the living. Then there follows, in the person of the whole Christ:

VERSE 8.—“Attend to my supplication, for I have been greatly humbled.”

Attend, [Aug.] as though he said: Because you are my hope. [Col. 1246A] Therefore attend to my supplication; and it is necessary, because I have been greatly humbled. For I humble myself inwardly, invisibly; and outwardly, visibly, I am made more humble by persecutors. And:

VERSE 9.—“Deliver me from those who persecute me, for they have become strong against me.”

Deliver me from those who persecute me, [Aug.] not so that the body may not fall, but the soul. For the devil, through his vessels—that is, through the children of unbelief—carries on bodily persecution in order that there may be inward ruin of heart. If then the soul stands while the body falls, the trap has been broken. And it is necessary that you should deliver me, because they have become strong against me. For the number of persecutors has increased; iniquity abounds and charity grows cold (Matt. 24). Then, speaking in the person of the Church, he explains from what he must be delivered, saying:

VERSE 10.—“Bring my soul out of prison, that it may confess your name; the righteous await me until you repay me.”

Bring my soul out of custody—or “prison,” another reading. [Aug.] This custody, or this prison, may perhaps be that cave mentioned by the title. Yet this world may be called a prison, where all things are vain, because all things under the sun are vanity. Hence he asks that the soul, which suffers much there, may be brought out—that is, he prays to be brought out of this world, from under the sun, where all things are vanity.

Or the human body is called a prison; but it is no great matter to depart from the body, since the wicked also possess this, and all, sooner or later, undergo it. Nor is it charity if a righteous person is too eager for this. For he ought to wish to remain in the flesh if this is necessary for the brethren. Or rather, the body is a prison, not indeed in respect of that which God made good, but in respect of that by which it is corrupted and weighs down the soul: that is, its corruption, which comes from sin, is the prison. From this corruption he wishes to be brought out, so that he may become incorruptible and the soul may rest in incorruptible flesh, whereas now it groans and is constrained in corruptible flesh.

Thus the body is now a prison to the soul because of corruption; in the future it will be a house because of incorruption and freedom. For merits make a prison: just as one dwelling is a prison to the person confined but a house to the guard, freedom makes a house and slavery a prison. Thus it is not the flesh that God made, but corruption and temptation, which are the prison from which [Col. 1246D] he prays to be brought out, saying: Bring my soul out of custody, or prison, that is, out of bodily corruption, because it is constrained in the corruption which is the body’s punishment. After these constraints, in God’s house all life will be confession—that is, praise of God. Hence he adds, that it may confess, that is, that it may confess your name.

At present the prison hinders confession. The righteous await me. He adds this from the head—that is, in the person of the Head—without changing his voice, as in that statement above at the end of the preceding psalm: “I am alone until I pass over.” [Cassiod.] Or the whole may be understood in the person of the Head from the words, “Deliver me from those who persecute me”—namely, the Jews—“for they have become strong against me,” by killing me. And, O Lord, bring my soul out of the custody, or prison, namely of the tomb—that is, the flesh to be restored to the soul. [Col. 1247A] For what purpose? That it may confess your name: that I may bring forth those who confess you. And you must bring it out, because the righteous await me, until you repay me by raising me on the third day. I say, repay me; for the resurrection itself is the recompense of the Passion.

## Comparison on Psalm 141: “With my voice I cried to the Lord, with my voice,” etc.

VERSE 6.—“Escape has perished from me.” Jerome, the Nebian, Pellican, and Sanctes, as likewise the other translators, render: “Refuge has perished from me.” They undermine the exposition of the saints and establish the opposite, because the saints interpret this of Christ or of the righteous person, who does not flee but freely offers himself in defense of truth; and yet there is none who seeks his soul, either by imitation or by attaining it. But if you say, “Refuge has perished from me,” nothing could be more remote from Christ or from the righteous person. Besides, *manos* means “refuge” or “flight.”

[Col. 1248A] VERSE 10.—“The righteous await me until you repay me.” In Hebrew stands *kiter*, which more often means “he surrounded” or “he crowned.” The words joined with it are rendered variously, according to this or that connection of the sense. Jerome says: “The righteous shall be crowned in me, when you repay me.” Nearly so the Nebian and the interpreters for Cajetan. Pellican: “The righteous shall surround themselves in me, because you will repay upon me.” Pratensis: “The righteous shall surround me when you repay me.” Sanctes: “For my sake the righteous shall crown themselves when you repay me.” Münster: “The righteous shall surround me, because you are about to make recompense to me.” The translator for Campensis: “If you give to me, the righteous shall join themselves to me.” The Paraphrase: “The righteous shall surround me like a crown when they perceive that you have avenged my injury.”

Moreover, since *kiter* can meanwhile mean “he waited,” as in Job 36, where near the beginning of the chapter we read, “Wait”: in Hebrew stands *katar*, and Münster has “Wait.” Therefore the Septuagint rendered it correctly.

# PSALM 142

[Col. 1247]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF DAVID, WHEN HIS SON ABSALOM WAS PERSECUTING HIM.”

[Col. 1247B]

“O Lord, hear my prayer.” Title: “A Psalm of David, when his son Absalom was persecuting him.” [Cassiod.] This psalm is the seventh of the penitential psalms, which are seven so that by the same number in which we sin, our sins may be washed away. For as we sin in the week of this world, so by this number of psalms the remedy of repentance is set against sins. These psalms have this pattern: they begin with tears and end in joy, lest anyone despair of pardon.

[Aug.] The history touched upon by the title is also known from the book of Kings, where we read that Absalom became an enemy to his father and waged against him not only a civil war but also [Col. 1247C] a domestic one (2 Sam. 15). Yet the psalm does not treat of him, but of what he signifies. David therefore signifies Christ and his body; Absalom signifies Judas, or persecutors, or evil impulses. Thus, as Absalom persecuted David, Judas persecuted Christ; false brethren persecute his body, which is the Church; and unlawful impulses, desires of the flesh, and evil action persecute each faithful person. And this is the sense of the title: This psalm, spoken by David, treats of what is signified when his son Absalom persecuted him.

[Cassiod., Alcuin., Aug.] Intention: it exhorts to repentance and prayer. Method: there are four divisions. First, he wins attention by the opening. Second, he recounts his evils and what he has done against them, at “For the enemy has persecuted.” Third, the supplication of the flesh is set forth and confirmed, at “Hear me speedily.” Fourth, a joyful conclusion is given, at “Your Spirit.” Therefore, exhorting to prayer in the person of the whole Christ, he says:

VERSE 1.—“O Lord, hear my prayer; receive my supplication with your ears; hear me in your truth, in your righteousness.”

O Lord, hear my prayer. [Aug.] Then he repeats the same thing in different words, saying: Receive my supplication—or petition—with your ears, that is, with the hearing of your mercy; and he repeats it again, because repetition is [Col. 1248B] confirmation: Hear me in your truth, that is, so that you may appear true and just, you who promised; in your righteousness, [Greg.] that is, because of your righteousness which is in me, which through faith in your Son’s Passion I have from you. For a human being’s righteousness comes from you.

[Aug.] Here grace is commended when he says, “in your righteousness,” not in that righteousness which is from the law, which some, wishing to establish, are not subject to God’s righteousness (Rom. 10). [Cassiod.] Or he means righteousness and truth by which God spares penitents and absolves those who condemn themselves; and he takes truth and righteousness as the same thing. The sense is: Hear me in your truth, in your righteousness—that is, according to the righteousness and truth by which you pardon penitents and those who accuse themselves. This does not conflict with the humility by which he asked to be heard; rather, it is God’s truth and righteousness not to contend in judgment against one who prays to him, nor to judge one who condemns himself. Hence he adds:

VERSE 2.—“And do not enter into judgment with your servant, because every living person shall not be justified in your sight.”

And do not enter into judgment—or into a judgment—with your servant, [Rem., Aug.] that is, do not deal strictly with me in the future, because I am your servant. For it is unworthy to enter into judgment with a servant—not to speak of doing so with a friend. Even if you call me friend, I call myself servant; I need mercy. I return to you as a fugitive; I seek peace; I am not worthy to be called your son. Therefore do not enter into judgment with me, because I too do not wish to enter into judgment with you.

Those enter into judgment with the Lord who establish their own righteousness; this humble man does not do so. Of them the prophet says: “What do you wish to contend with me in judgment? You have all forsaken me, says the Lord” (Jer. 2). [Cassiod., Aug.] See how his words here, “Do not enter into judgment,” show that above he did not ask for the righteousness of the future judgment when he said, “Hear me in your righteousness.” Why do you fear this? Because, though a person may be righteous in his own estimation, every living human being will not be justified in your sight—that is, inwardly, where you see. No one living here is wholly clean before God, who sees within, even if some appear holy to human beings. Therefore Solomon says: “Do not praise a man before death” (Ecclus. 11); nor does Paul call himself perfect, saying: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4).

And note that he says, “every living person.” [Cassiod.] By this every human being is understood universally, even an infant bound by original sin. No one, therefore, can be delivered through himself, except by grace. Or thus: “Every living person shall not be justified in your sight,” that is, in comparison with you. [Hilar., Hier.] He does not say “every human being,” but “every living being”: not an apostle, not a prophet, not angels, not thrones, not the other powers. For God alone is one in whom sin does not fall—that is, cannot fall. Since the others have free will, they can be bent in either direction; before him even the stars are not clean.

[Col. 1249B] PART II. VERSE 3.—“For the enemy has persecuted my soul; he has humbled my life to the ground.”

For the enemy has persecuted. [Alcuin., Aug.] The second part, in which is the account of evils, divided up, and he says what he has done against them. As though he said: Hear me; deliver me. And it is necessary, says the Church, because the enemy—that is, the devil, or anyone whatsoever—has persecuted my soul openly or secretly. We say this; the Head says it on our behalf. And he has humbled, so far as he was able, my life to the ground—that is, to earthly things. For this is what anyone who persecutes does: that, abandoning heavenly hope, we may savour earthly things. So far as lies in him, this is what he does; yet it does not happen to me. There follows first the person of the body. And:

[Col. 1249C] VERSE 4.—“He has placed me in darkness like the dead of the age; and my spirit has been distressed over me, my heart has been troubled within me.”

The enemy has placed me, [Hier., Cassiod., Gl. int.] so far as he was able, in darkness, that is, in the darkness of vices, like the dead of the age—that is, the other despairing persons. And my spirit has been distressed by the nearness of danger. I mean the spirit stretched forth over me, seeing misery and seeking refuge with God. [Cassiod., Hier.] Or it has become, as it were, outside me, and my heart has been troubled—that is, wisdom has been thrown into confusion within me; or, “my heart has been troubled unto repentance.” Why has it been troubled? Because:

VERSE 5.—“I remembered the days of old; I meditated on all your works; I was meditating on the works [Col. 1249D] of your hands.”

I remembered the days of old, [Cassiod.] in which Adam was punished; hence I have fear. Yet, recalling that God made heaven and earth and all things, and that he dealt kindly with the ancient fathers, this man almost forgets the miseries of the world. He consoles himself from what God has done, saying: And I meditated on all your works; and without ceasing, I was meditating on the works of your hands. For, considering what you made among natural things, and how great were the benefits you bestowed on the ancient fathers, I find consolation from your goodness and take up hope of pardon.

[Aug.] Or it may be understood in the person of Christ from the words, “He has placed me in darkness,” etc. For Christ too was placed in darkness, namely in the Passion and in the tomb; but not as one of the dead of the age in respect of himself, since he had no cause for dying. Rather, according to the opinion of those crucifying him, he was placed like those dead from of old, because they thought they would hold him in death. In the same person: “My spirit has been distressed,” or “has suffered weariness within me,” according to: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26); and again: “Jesus began to fear and to be weary” (ibid.). In him we are figured, for he transformed into himself the body of our lowliness.

Note that he does not say “from me,” but “within me,” as though he said: Not among others, because all abandoned him; and those who had clung to him withdrew. Because they saw him dying, they thought something else, and they were surpassed by the thief, who confessed at the moment when they failed. “I remembered”: the members say this, [Col. 1250B] not the Head in his own person. For how does he remember days through whom every day was made, and who never forgets? The body therefore speaks, cleaving to him in charity and devout humility. It says: “I remembered the days of old,” when you began to do good things, but did not begin to be; and “I meditated on all your works,” because all things are certainly good. In this it perceives that whatever good is in itself is from God. “And I was meditating on the works of your hands”: as though it said, “I sought the craftsman in the work, and the Creator in all created things.” Your creature was made a spectacle for me; and when I saw that every good thing is from you, the Church says:

VERSE 6.—“I stretched out my hands to you; my soul is to you like earth without water.”

[Col. 1250C] I stretched out my hands to you in prayer, [Cassiod., Rem., Aug.] signifying the form of the cross, which is salvation. Or: I stretched out my hands to you, that is, I enlarged my affections or works, which had previously been contracted. And my soul, which by itself is like earth without water, clings to you—not to me, for I cannot water it. Therefore rain upon it, that it may bear fruit.

PART III. VERSE 7.—“Hear me speedily, O Lord; my spirit has failed.”

Hear me speedily. [Cassiod., Aug.] The third part, in which the confirmed supplication of the flesh is set forth. As though he said: Because I thirst thus, therefore hear me speedily, O Lord—that is, hear me quickly. God delayed in order to inflame desire, as though rain were delayed in order to inflame thirst. If therefore you delayed for this reason, give now, because the soul thirsts in you. Therefore hear me, because my spirit has failed. Let your Spirit therefore fill me, because mine has failed; for now I am poor in spirit. The person in whom his own spirit lives is proud: he is lifted up by his own spirit against God. Hence elsewhere: “You will take away their spirit, and they shall fail” (Ps. 103). And because my spirit has failed—that is, because I am not proud—

VERSE 8.—“Do not turn your face away from me, and I shall become like those descending into the pit.”

Do not turn your face away from me, now humbled. [Aug.] Formerly you turned away from the proud man, and I became troubled; you did this so that I might discover what it was to be without you. Therefore what you took away from the proud, now restore to the humble. [Col. 1251A] Therefore do not turn away. And this is why: if you turn away, I shall become like those descending into the pit, that is, into the depth of sin, in which people despise and confession perishes. For he descends into the deep who even loses confession, as one who proposes to himself a license for sinning without hope of pardon, having loosed the reins of iniquity. Such a person does not hear God saying: “Return to me, and I will return to you” (Mal. 3). I say, do not turn away, but rather:

VERSE 9.—“Make me hear your mercy in the morning, because I have hoped in you.”

Make me hear your mercy. And this in the morning, [Cassiod., Aug.] that is, after the night of sins. For it is morning when sins are forgiven. Or “in the morning” means after the end of the age, when we shall see [Col. 1251B] what we now believe. Therefore show mercy, because I have hoped in you. We are indeed in the night, but I have hoped in you until nocturnal iniquity passes away. Night requires patience in waiting; day will give joy. And because it is not enough to hope during this night, but something must be done which I cannot do by myself, therefore I pray:

VERSE 10.—“Make known to me the way in which I should walk, because I have lifted up my soul to you.”

Make known to me the way in which I should walk. [Aug.] God did this when he kindled the prophetic word. As Peter says, we ought to attend to it as to a lamp in a dark place, until day should dawn (2 Pet. 1). Therefore he also placed himself as light in the earthen vessel of the flesh, that we might walk toward that light; and, walking toward the form of a servant, we shall reach the form of God, the pure light—namely, the Word in the beginning with God.

He adds the confidence with which he asks this: I have not inclined my soul toward the world, but lifted it to you—not against you—because with you is the fountain of life; I have brought the vessel to the fountain. Fill it, then. And therefore:

VERSE 11.—“Rescue me from my enemies, O Lord; I have fled to you. Teach me to do your will, because you are my God.”

Rescue me from my enemies, O Lord, [Aug.] namely from the devil and those whom he fills. For he did not enter Judas alone; indeed, there are many Judases whom Satan fills, and in them Satan himself is overcome. I fight against that unseen enemy; I endure these visible ones. [Col. 1251D] Therefore rescue me, because I have fled not from you but to you. Adam fled from you and hid himself among the trees of Paradise. Of him Job says: “Like a servant fleeing his master, he has attained the shadow” (Job 7). For he fled from you to a shadow; but I flee to you. And therefore teach me to do your will, because you are my God. If you do not teach me, I shall do my own will, and my God will leave [Col. 1252A] me. Therefore teach me, because you are my God. I would run to another if I had been made by another; you are my whole possession, not only the giver of the inheritance but the inheritance itself. You created me through the Word of the Lord abiding with you; you also re-created me through the Word made flesh for our sake. Therefore you are my God; and therefore teach me as my teacher.

PART IV.—VERSE 12.—“Your good Spirit will lead me into a right land; for your name’s sake, O Lord, you will give me life in your righteousness.”

Your Spirit. [Alcuin., Aug.] The fourth part, containing the joyful conclusion. As though he said: Teach me—which you will certainly do—because your good Spirit will lead me into a right land, not my evil spirit, which led me into a crooked land. Yet I have in no way deserved to be led there, because, [Col. 1252B] O Lord, it is not for my merits but for your name’s sake, [Haim., Cassiod.] that is, in order to fulfil the reality of your name, which is Jesus, that you will give me life. I killed myself, but you will give me life; and this in your righteousness, not mine.

Here the grace of God is commended, because he says that he will be given life not from merits but from the name which is Jesus. Yet he mentions this grace of righteousness because, although God does all things freely, it nevertheless belongs to his justice to give life to suppliants whom he sees assailed by demons. [Aug.] Or thus: “You will give me life in your righteousness.” This does not change. “For your name’s sake, O Lord,” means that you may thereby be praised. Hence elsewhere: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113).

VERSE 13.—“You will bring my soul out of tribulation; and in your mercy you will destroy all my enemies.”

VERSE 14.—“And you will destroy all who afflict my soul, because I am your servant.”

You will bring my soul out of the tribulation of this age. [Cassiod.] This happens when, pardon having been granted, God commands it to leave the world as though from a prison; and in your mercy, not by my merit, you will destroy all my enemies here, because they will be able to do nothing against me; and in the future judgment you will destroy all who afflict my soul—that is, the devil and all the obstinate. I say, “who afflict,” because I am your servant. Or: you will deservedly destroy those afflicting me, because I am your servant.

## Comparison on Psalm 142: “O Lord, hear my prayer; receive with your ears,” etc.

[Col. 1252D]

VERSE 4.—“Like those dead from of old.” Jerome: “like the ancient dead.” Münster likewise: “like those who died long ago.” Campensis too is not at variance. Others agree with us. It may be rendered either way from the Hebrew *kemēthê*, although the sense differs little or not at all.

# PSALM 143

[Col. 1251]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PSALM OF DAVID AGAINST GOLIATH.”

[Col. 1251D]

“Blessed be the Lord my God.” Title: “A Psalm of David against Goliath.” [Aug.] The title of this psalm is brief in number of words but weighty in its burden of mysteries. It is taken from the history in the book of Kings, where [Col. 1252D] we read that, when the Philistines were fighting against the people of God, a certain man named Goliath came out from the Philistine camp. Reproaching the Israelites, he said: “Choose one man from among yourselves to enter into single combat with me. If he conquers me, we shall be your servants; but if I conquer, you shall serve us” (1 Sam. 17). When Saul and the men of Israel heard this, they were greatly afraid.

Then David, who happened to be tending his father’s flock, was sent by him to carry loaves and certain other things to his brothers, who were in Saul’s army. When David arrived, he heard the Philistine saying the things just mentioned and said to those standing by: “What shall be given to the man who strikes down this Philistine?” (ibid.). When these words had been heard, he was brought to Saul and said to him: “I, your servant, will fight against this Philistine.” Saul said to him: “You will not be able, because you are a boy and he a mighty warrior” (ibid.). David said: “I, your servant, have killed a lion and a bear; and the Lord who delivered me from the mouth of the lion and the bear will himself deliver me from the hand of the Philistine” (ibid.).

Then Saul said: “Go; the Lord be with you,” and handed him his own weapons. Because these were too heavy, David laid them aside. He took five stones from the stream, put them in a shepherd’s pouch, and took a sling in his hand; thus armed, he went out against the Philistine. When the Philistine saw him, he despised him. And when he advanced against David, David hastened, put his hand into his bag, and took one stone, which he hurled with the sling. He did not strike the Philistine with the first stone nor with the second [Alcuin.], but with the cast of the third stone he struck him in the forehead and threw him down. [Cassiod.] When he had fallen, David ran, stood over him, took his sword, cut off his head, and thus gained the victory.

He did not become proud because of this victory, but attributing everything to God he gives thanks in this psalm. [Aug.] He understood that in that figurative victory was signified Christ’s and the faithful’s spiritual victory over the devil, because “all these things happened to them in figure” (1 Cor. 10); and in this psalm he gives thanks for both victories.

David, then, is the whole Christ, namely Head and body. Goliath is the devil. Saul’s weapons are the legal sacraments with which the Jewish people were burdened: circumcision, sacrifices, and the other visible sacraments. But because the law cannot give life—as burdensome rather than helpful—in the time of grace Christ, both Head and body, laid aside the sacraments of the law. The five stones—that is, the law itself, namely the five books of Moses—he took from the stream, that is, from that people signified by the stream, because every age flows away. [Col. 1253D] For the stream signifies the age. Thus in that stream, that is, among that people, the stones lay idle and useless.

But, so that the law might become useful, David took the shepherd’s vessel—that is, grace—without which the law could not be fulfilled, because “the fulfilment of the law is charity” (Rom. 13), which is from the Holy Spirit. This, therefore, is to place the stones in the shepherd’s vessel, with which he was accustomed to milk milk: namely, to mingle grace with the law. Thus armed, the whole Christ advances against the proud one. He sent one stone, by which he threw him down, because unity conquers the devil. He struck him in the forehead because he fell from that part of his body—that is, in those members—in which he did not have Christ’s sign.

Then, once he had been struck and cast down, David cut off his head with his own sword, because when Goliath’s great men—whom he held in his hand and by whom he slaughtered souls—believe, they speak against him. Thus his head is cut off by his own sword. Therefore, just as little David overcame proud Goliath, who trusted in himself, so Christ killed the proud devil: that is, humility killed pride. God becomes humble in order to overthrow the devil’s pride, and so that proud persons, who disdained to follow humble saints, might at least be willing to imitate him.

This victory, then, is treated of here. And this is the sense of the title: This psalm belongs to David the prophet, who here speaks in his own person or in that of the whole Christ. [Cassiod.] I call it a psalm directed against Goliath—that is, against the figurative and spiritual Goliath—because David here treats of his own figurative victory and Christ’s mystical victory, from which David’s victory itself proceeded. Therefore, giving thanks to God for his victory, as a human being does, [Col. 1254B] he also prays for the coming of him who will conquer the devil and free the faithful. David does not grow insolent through victory, as a human being commonly does, but attributes it to God’s power. This is a triumphal psalm.

Intention: it exhorts to thanksgiving for the victory, namely that David figuratively conquered Goliath. Method: the psalm has two parts. First it treats of the victory: that David figuratively conquered Goliath and, spiritually, he together with the other saints conquered the devil. The whole victory is said to arise from this: Christ will come from David’s seed to conquer the pride of the world; therefore David prays for his coming. Second, he promises to sing to the victor in the New and Old Testaments, praying to be delivered through him, at “A new song.” Therefore David, not becoming insolent because of the victory but humbly giving thanks to God, says:

“Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war.”

VERSE 1.—Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle, [Haim.] which is fought at close quarters, and my fingers for war, which is fought from afar. Then, showing that this comes to him by grace, he adds:

VERSE 2.—“My mercy and my refuge, my upholder and my deliverer.”

My mercy and my refuge. [Haim.] Whence comes this to me? From my God, because he himself is my mercy and my refuge, my upholder and my deliverer, and:

VERSE 3.—“My protector, and in him I have hoped, who subjects my people under me.”

[Col. 1254D] My protector, [Cassiodorus.] Since it would be too lengthy to explain many causes fully, he briefly touches on each one in individual words. He was mercy to him when, the last of his brothers, he was raised to be king. He was a refuge to him when, against Goliath, he gave him the counsel to cast him down with a stone, since he could not fight him otherwise. He was his supporter when he made him the king’s son-in-law; his deliverer when he freed him from the danger of the royal wrath; he was his protector when David, in the cave, gained the upper hand over Saul. “And in him I have hoped,” or “I shall hope,” “who subjects,” or “you subject,” etc. After so many benefits bestowed on him, David ought not to cease from such hope. Therefore, after recounting these benefits, he fittingly adds this; as though saying: The Lord has done these good things for me, and therefore I shall hope in him, who subjects—[Col. 1255A] or because you are he who subjects—my people beneath me. This may be understood literally of the future, because he was to rule over peoples; or he foretells that peoples will be subjected to his seed, Christ.

Then, after so many benefits, he not only confesses himself insignificant, but also declares the whole human race unworthy of God’s benefits, saying: “Lord, what is man,” etc. [Interlinear Gloss.] Or the whole may be understood in the person of Christ’s body. And humble David says, as it were: Blessed be the Lord, the God of all, yet especially mine, to whom I have subjected and given myself, “who teaches my hands for battle.” There is an appropriate order here: he first says, “my God,” and then adds, “who teaches,” etc. [Augustine.] For if you first give yourself to God, then, with him teaching and helping you, you will fight. “And my fingers for war”: he did not mention hands and fingers without reason. For just as [Col. 1255B] there are many fingers on one hand, so in one Spirit there are divisions of graces. Therefore, in the fingers is denoted the division of activity which lies in the root of unity, as the Apostle says: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge through the same Spirit, to another faith, to another this, to another that, but in one Spirit. For one and the same Spirit works all things, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12). Behold the root of unity.

With these fingers, therefore, the body of Christ fights and proceeds skilfully into war. The sense is: “Who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war,” that is, through the Holy Spirit he gives me gifts of grace, by which he makes and teaches me to fight and to go into battle against the princes of darkness and against the flesh, [Col. 1255C] to whose desires those [princes] also propose evil things. But he conquers who puts a stone into the milk-vessel, that is, who attends to grace and is led by the Spirit of God. And because in fighting you are endangered—that is, you undergo the danger of being defeated—say what follows: “You are my mercy,” that is, you grant that I may be merciful and thus conquer, because the enemy, the devil, is conquered by nothing so much as by mercy, which consists in two things: giving and forgiving. For whoever forgives, even if he has sinned, will be forgiven; and to whoever gives, it is given. Of this James says: “Mercy exalts itself over judgment,” or “mercy is set above judgment” (Jas. 2), that is, it is placed beneath judgment; because wherever a work of mercy is found, even if someone has something for which he might be punished in judgment, the flood of mercy, like water, extinguishes the fire of sin. [Col. 1255D] In this God is not unjust, nor does he abandon the truth of judgment when he pardons such persons, because it is justice that what a person has done to others should be done to him. Hence the Lord says: “With the measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Matt. 7), as though saying: If you forgive, I forgive; if you possess a measure for granting pardon, you will find with me a measure for receiving pardon; if you possess a measure for giving what you have, you will find with me a measure for receiving what you do not have. Forgive, therefore, and I forgive; give, and I give. You are my refuge, like a tower in tribulation; my deliverer, lest I fall; my supporter, lest I remain stuck on the way; and my protector, lest I be struck.

Then, turning his speech toward others, he says: “And in him I have hoped,” amid all labours and battles. Then, in the person of the head, “who subjects,” etc. Behold [Col. 1256A] the head speaking to us, or speaking to the Father, saying: “You who subject my people beneath me.” [Cassiodorus.] Then, in the joint person of David and the Church, confessing that the human race is unworthy of God’s benefits, he adds with humility and wonder:

**VERSE 4.**—“Lord, what is man, that you have made yourself known to him? Or the son of man, that you account him of value?”

“Lord, what is man,” [Augustine.] as though saying: You bestow these benefits. And, O Lord, what is man—who of himself is frail and sinful—that he should be anything, that is, anything great, because you have made yourself known to him through assumed humanity? As though saying: Of himself he is nothing; through you he is something worthy. For all that he is comes from this, that you have made yourself known to him. Then, as though explaining to whom he has made himself known, he adds: “or,” that is, “and the son of man”—what [Col. 1256B] is he, even because you reckon, or esteem, him to be of some worth? What is this, that you make him of such value? You show him to be surely something precious. For what God esteems is great, and he makes man so valuable that he sent, or gave, his Son for him—the Son who becomes food to him, the bread of angels. For God does not value man as man does: a man buys a horse more dearly than a human being.

**VERSE 5.**—“Man has been made like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow.”

“Man [is made] like vanity,” [Augustine.] as though saying: Do you esteem so highly one who of himself is like vanity and shadow? For man, who formerly was like truth, afterward, by sinning, became like vanity. When man was created, he was made like truth; but by sinning he became like vanity. For all transitory things [Col. 1256C] are vain in comparison with the Deity that abides forever. And though he has become such, nevertheless you have made yourself known to him and esteem him. Here he says what man is in himself when he says, “like vanity.” That is vain which, falling away from its own substance, vanishes, as smoke and shadow do; so also man himself wastes away. “His days,” that is, his life in motion, pass away like a shadow. It is indeed seen, but has no firmness for remaining, like a shadow; and while it exists, it is in night.

**VERSE 6.**—“Lord, bend your heavens and come down; touch the mountains and they shall smoke.”

“Lord, bend your heavens.” [Cassiodorus.] This is first understood in the person of David praying for the Incarnation. Here he now makes plain what he said above, “you have made yourself known to him,” because [Col. 1256D] God then made himself known to man when he appeared incarnate. As though saying: Such is man in himself; but that he may be restored from himself, O Lord, bend your heavens and come down to us, since these things could not happen unless the Deity stooped down. The heavens were bent when the power and honour of the heavenly beings descended to humanity and the form of God took the form of a servant.

[Augustine.] Or this may be said in the person of the Church. For humble David, full of grace—that is, the body of Christ, trusting in God and fighting—here calls upon God’s help. As though saying: We are in a struggle; but lest we fail, O Lord, bend your heavens, that is, accommodate the apostles to humankind, so that they may humbly declare your excellence to others. Through them come down into the knowledge of others; and touch by your grace the mountains, that is, the lofty ones of earth, [Col. 1257A] swollen greatnesses—that is, the proud—and they shall smoke, that is, confess their sins. But against those who have conspired against you:

**VERSE 7.**—“Flash forth lightning, and you shall scatter them; send out your arrows, and you shall throw them into confusion.”

“Flash forth lightning,” [Augustine.] or “lightnings,” or “make lightning flash,” that is, make the flashes clear, or the flash clear; that is, abound in miracles, and their conspiracy will be dissolved, because, terrified by frequent miracles, they will dare nothing, and you will scatter them from one another. Behold Christ’s warfare against the devil; and he adds concerning the same: “Send out your arrows,” that is, your words, “and you shall throw them into confusion” unto repentance.

[Cassiodorus.] Then the Prophet prays for Christ’s coming and directs his words to the Father, saying:

[Col. 1257B]

**VERSE 8.**—“Send forth your hand from on high; snatch me away and free me from many waters, and from the hand of alien children.”

“Send forth your hand.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] As though saying: In order that these things may occur, send forth your hand—that is, Christ—from on high, where he is with the Father, that he may put on flesh. Or he speaks of the second coming in the person of the Church. As though saying: Do this now. But at the end, send forth your hand from on high, that is, Christ from heaven for judgment. For the Lord himself will come with the voice of an angel, and with the trumpet of God will descend from heaven (1 Thess. 4). Then he adds in the person of the Church, “snatch me away.” As though saying: Send forth your hand, and by that hand snatch me away and free me from many waters, that is, from many peoples, fighting either outwardly or inwardly. These are the waters of contradiction, from which [Col. 1257C] God draws David’s humility. And what are “many waters”? Behold: “from the hand of alien children,” namely, those born of the devil, their perverted father. Who are they?

**VERSE 9.**—“Whose mouth has spoken vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity.”

“Whose mouth has spoken vanity”: he heightens their wickedness. Hence he adds: “And their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.” [Hilary.] That is, their right hand is their left.

## PART II. VERSE 10.—“O God, I shall sing to you a new song; upon a ten-stringed psaltery I shall make music to you.”

“O God, [I shall sing] a new song.” [Cassiodorus.] This is the second part, in which, as though he whom he had entreated as victor and deliverer has now come, he promises to sing to him in the New and Old Testaments, and through him prays to be delivered from those who place blessedness in earthly things.

[Augustine.] As though saying: You say that their mouth has spoken vanity. What, then, do you do among them, holding five stones in a shepherd’s vessel? How do you conduct yourself among them? Behold how: O God, amid their words I shall sing to you a new song, that is, the song of the new man, namely the song of the New Testament, a song concerning new grace. The noise of the waters of contradiction does not make me mute. After saying what he sings, he adds upon what instrument he sings: “and upon a ten-stringed psaltery I shall make music to you.” By another name this signifies the law, which he designated by the five stones. The sense is: “Upon a ten-stringed [Col. 1258A] psaltery I shall make music to you,” that is, in the law of the Ten Commandments I shall make music to you; I shall rejoice in you; I shall sing a new song to you, because “love is the fulfilment of the law” (Rom. 13). Whoever lacks love may carry the psaltery, but cannot sing.

**VERSE 11.**—“You who give salvation to kings, who redeemed your servant David: rescue me from the evil sword.”

“You who give salvation.” [Augustine.] As though saying: I shall sing to you, who give salvation to kings, that is, to mountains now smoking; who redeemed David your servant, namely, the whole Christ—head and body. And you who do these things, rescue me from the evil sword. He adds “evil,” because there is a good sword with which God speaks truth, of which the Lord says: “I came not to send peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10). This is the two-edged sword, mighty with both edges, namely those of the Old and New Testaments, by which every corruption is cut away from Christ’s members. Thus the good sword is that by which they speak vanity. Hence elsewhere: “Their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. 56). Therefore, what he called waters above, he here calls a sword. Thus he adds here what he said there:

[Col. 1258B]

**VERSE 12.**—“And draw me out from the hand of alien children, whose mouth has spoken vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity.”

“Draw me out from the hand of alien children.” [Cassiodorus.] By this repetition he makes the wicked more detestable: their mouth has spoken vanity, namely that earthly things are blessedness; and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity, because they hold earthly things to be their right hand [Augustine]. Then he explains who these aliens are, what their right hand is—which is called a right hand of iniquity—and how they have spoken vanity, saying:

[Col. 1258C]

**VERSE 13.**—“Whose sons are like new plantings in their youth.”

“Whose sons,” etc. [Augustine.] Here he enumerates their prosperity. This is their right hand; this is the vanity which they speak, when they say that these things are blessedness. First, therefore, showing what their right hand is, he says: “Whose sons are like new,” or “a new,” “plantings,” or “planting,” or, in another rendering, “newly established [plants] in their youth.” And:

**VERSE 14.**—“Their daughters, arrayed and adorned all around, are like the likeness of a temple.”

[Col. 1258D] “Their daughters,” [Augustine.] are arrayed and adorned all around, like the likeness of a temple. And:

**VERSE 15.**—“Their storehouses are full, pouring forth from this thing into that.”

“Their storehouses,” or “cellars,” are full, pouring forth from this thing into that. And:

**VERSE 16.**—“Their sheep are fruitful, abundant in their goings forth; their oxen are fat.”

“Their sheep,” [Augustine.] are fruitful, abundant in their goings forth; their oxen are fat, or “fat ones.” And:

**VERSE 17.**—“There is no breach in their wall, no passage out, and no cry in their streets.”

“There is no breach in their wall,” [Augustine.] or hedge; “nor passage,” or exit, “nor cry in their streets,” that is, there is no disturbance, but quiet peace in their streets. [Col. 1259A] Behold what their right hand is. Then he shows what vanity they speak, adding:

**VERSE 18.**—“They have called blessed the people to whom these things belong; blessed is the people whose Lord is its God.”

“They have called [blessed].” [Augustine.] As though saying: I do not condemn these things which they have as though they were evil; but I condemn them for calling blessed the people to whom these things belong, putting what belongs on the left hand on the right. It is indeed happiness to have healthy sons, adorned daughters, and the other temporal goods; nor are the righteous commanded to flee these things, but not to regard them as the right hand. For he does not rebuke them because they abound in these things, but because they hold them to be the right hand, that is, blessedness. This is the vanity which they have spoken. Abraham and Jacob abounded in these things without loss to their righteousness. Happiness is in these things, as stated; but it is left-hand happiness, that is, temporal, mortal, bodily.

Thus these things can be understood literally, as has been said [Jerome]. Or, beginning with the words “whose sons,” they may be understood mystically. He treats of the errors of the wicked and their most evil thoughts, showing that they are heretics, of whom some points are also expounded literally. “Whose,” that is, of the aforesaid persons, “sons are like new plantings in their youth”: their sons are a new planting, not founded upon the apostles but produced from the perversity of novelty. Behold: after enumerating their evils above, he now also accuses their supposed goods, saying that their sons are born from corrupt doctrine. They did not flourish in the ancient customs of the Fathers, but sprouted up in new errors. [Col. 1259C] “And their daughters,” who lack the strength of steadfastness, “are arrayed,” because they are not beautiful by nature but made up by men, “and adorned all around like the likeness of a temple.” These daughters are their thoughts or preachings, which do not possess the true Church but only its likeness. “And their storehouses,” that is, their hearts, “are full,” that is, crammed with diverse things; and they are “pouring forth,” because from them they breathe out most evil exhalations, which stink and corrupt the simple. I say, “pouring forth from this thing into that,” [Cassiodorus,] because, defeated in one matter, they flee unstably to another, since they have no root of truth.

“And their sheep are fruitful.” This may be understood literally, because he wishes to show that they cling to perishable things. As though saying: Their livestock is fruitful, although they themselves are barren in faith. Or mystically, their sheep are their disciples. These sheep are fruitful because they themselves generate many others in error, “abundant in their goings forth.” He does not say, “in their comings in,” because all that they seem to possess goes forth from them, soon to perish. “And their oxen are fat,” literally. Their oxen are not lean from labour, but fat from idleness, like those who abound in riches though they themselves fast from truth. Or mystically: their oxen are teachers, who are fat because they abound in earthly things.

“There is no breach in their wall, nor passage, nor cry in their streets,” literally. A wall is one made only of stones, in gardens or vineyards. But not even that falls down for them: so prosperous are they; nor does a passage or a disturbing cry [Col. 1260A] interrupt their peace. Or mystically, the wall is the philosophers’ art, which cannot be destroyed in them [Jerome] so that, having become righteous, they may pass over to Christ. Nor is the cry of God, which is upon the narrow way that leads to life, in their streets—that is, upon their broad way, which leads to death. These things aforesaid belong to them. And “they have called blessed the people to whom these aforesaid things belong”: the alien children have said this.

But you, David, what do you say? What do you say, body of Christ? What do you say, you who are not alien children? Behold: “Blessed is the people whose Lord is”—by will—“he who is its God”—by power. It should be known that, concerning this victory which this triumphal psalm celebrates, the Prophet has made it, as it were, the end of all worldly matters. For after this he will say nothing about persecutors of the Church, the miseries of the age, penitence, pious lamentation, or the exaltation of Antichrist; rather, the remaining seven psalms are full of divine proclamations and heavenly joy, so that, as though the clouds of sins had been driven away, one may come with serene minds to the praises of God. As though all things by which human ignorance needed instruction had been completed, one must now attend only to God’s praises. Hence the following psalm is specially entitled *Praise*.

## COLLATION ON PSALM 143: “BLESSED IS THE LORD MY GOD WHO TEACHES,” etc.

**VERSE 4.**—“You have made yourself known to him.” Hebrew: “you have known him.” *VATEDAEHU* has the same sense. For God knows us, and we know him, through his benefits.

**VERSE 13.**—From verse 13 through the penultimate verse inclusive, [Col. 1260C] where we read the third-person relative pronoun, the translations have “us” or “our,” according to the demands of construction, so that this interpretation yields the contrary sense. For according to us, these verses are spoken unfavourably, as though evil people place their happiness in such earthly things. According to others, they would be spoken as though all things prosperously befell the good.

The difference arises from two things. First, in the first verse of all those of which we speak, *ASCHER* occurs, which St Jerome, Nebiensis, Sanctes, and Münster translate as “as,” while others translate it “because,” “since,” or “how”; and the Septuagint renders it as a relative, “whose.” For that particle most frequently signifies this, and they retained its force in each verse: that is, “their daughters,” and “whose daughters”; “their storehouses,” and “whose storehouses”; and so on.

Then, where the pronominal sign *NU* is read—that is, “our,” according to the required different cases—the Septuagint appears to have read it with a dagesh point, making it “his,” “to him,” or “him.” And although it is singular in number, it may nevertheless be taken as referring to him, to each one of them. Such, therefore, seems to have been the interpretation they followed. Let us now descend to the individual matters which create particular difficulty.

**VERSE 14.**—“Daughters arrayed and adorned all around like the likeness of a temple.” The Septuagint adapted the metaphor found in the Hebrew to the meaning itself. For St Jerome has: “like adorned corners after the likeness of a temple”; Pratensis: “like tessellated corners,” etc.; Sanctes: “like carved corners of a palace”; the paraphrase: “like corner-columns, most carefully adorned, such as are seen in temples and royal houses.” The others likewise render it in a similar manner.

**VERSE 15.**—“Storehouses full, pouring forth from this thing into that.” Likewise St Jerome and Pratensis: “corners full, overflowing from food to food”; Sanctes: “corners full, bringing forth from kind to kind”; Münster: “let the storehouses be full, so that they may bring forth from kind to kind.” Nearly all the others agree. Regarding the first word, we concur; for those who translate “corners” understand recesses of the house and store-rooms. But we differ in the final part. For where we say, “from this thing into that,” they put “from food to food,” or “from kind to kind.” Although the sense does not differ, whether in this or that manner—since abundance of every kind is signified in either case—yet the Septuagint and St Jerome read *ZU* for *ZAN*, that is, “this [thing]” for “food” or “kind.” Indeed, without the distinction of vowel-points, the final *nun* and *waw* differ little in form. Pellicanus also seems to have read it thus, for he translates: “making expenditures from this thing into that.”

[Col. 1261A]

**VERSE 16.**—“Fruitful sheep, abundant in their goings forth.” Our translators have retained the sense while abandoning the verbal surface. St Jerome says: “Livestock by the thousands and innumerable in our open places.” The others resort to the same rendering.

“Fat oxen.” In a similar way St Jerome. Others translate: “strong for bearing.” *MESUBALIM*, literally “laden,” where “with flesh” must be supplied, and thus “fat.” This is what Sanctes indicated. Yet those who translate “fit to carry burdens” do not disagree, although “strong to endure labours” would fit better, since oxen more properly serve agriculture or draw carts. However it may be, the good condition of the beasts of burden is signified.

[Col. 1261B]

**VERSE 17.**—“There is no breach in the wall, nor passage out.” [Col. 1262A] *EN PERETZ VEEN IOTZETH*, literally: “no breaking, no going out.” It may be understood to mean that there is no captivity in which the fabric of cities and buildings is shattered. St Jerome says nearly the same: “There is no interruption, and there is no going out.” Hence Münster added “into captivity”; others refer it to barrenness, which does not occur. Thus Sanctes translates: “there is no barren woman and none that goes forth”; Pratensis: “there is no breaking, and none causing miscarriage.”

**VERSE 18.**—“They have called blessed the people to whom these things belong.” The Hebrew has *ASCHRE HAAM SCHECACHA LO*: “Blessed the people to whom it is thus.” This appears to establish true happiness, whereas our reading merely suggests a painted or pretended happiness and one proclaimed by men. But if it is understood of temporal things themselves, as the letter sounds, it is beyond doubt contrary to Christian faith if you establish blessedness in transient riches. Therefore “they have said” had to be supplied, as the Septuagint correctly interpreted it—a thing very frequently done in Hebrew. Thus Münster, on Psalm 117: “All nations surrounded me”; then in the following clause he wishes this to be supplied: “And I said: In the name of the Lord, because I have taken vengeance on them.” Likewise in the following two verses. So too Sanctes on Psalm 9: where we say, “His sin shall be sought and shall not be found,” he translates: “You will seek his impiety, which he said you would not find.” In Hebrew, “which he said” is not present.

# PSALM 144

[Col. 1261]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “A PRAISE, OF DAVID HIMSELF.”

[Col. 1261B]

“I shall exalt you.” Title: “A praise, of David himself.” [Note: [Col. 1261D] From Cassiodorus, in the preface and conclusion to the psalm.] This psalm briefly contains those matters pertaining to God’s praise which are broadly set forth in the divine Scriptures, [Col. 1261C] and in it nine topics of praise are distinguished, from which all praise of God is drawn. For wherever God’s praise is discussed, one reads either of his works, his power, or one of the other matters. The following psalms belong to the praises of this psalm, and together with it they number seven. For as there are seven penitential psalms, so there are seven psalms of praise by which God is to be praised in the day (Exod. 37). As the Prophet says: “Seven times in the day I shall declare praise to you.” Likewise there are seven spirits of graces which sing God’s praises, as is read in the Apocalypse (Apoc. 5). According to this mystery, God commanded Moses to place seven lamps in the tabernacle, shining with perpetual light.

In these seven psalms God sufficiently taught how he wishes to be praised, so that no one might err in his praise [Col. 1261D] [Augustine]. For this purpose God fills the saints with the Holy Spirit, that they may praise him; and, lest we err in praising, he established in Scripture the way of praise. In order to be well praised by man, he praised himself, so that man might find how to praise him. For what was said to man cannot be said to God: “Let not your own mouth praise you” (Prov. 27). For if man praises himself, it is arrogance; if God praises himself, it is mercy, because in praising himself he makes himself lovable, and by loving him we become better, not he. Therefore his Spirit praises him in his servants; and then he praises himself, because he causes himself to be praised.

The sense is: This praise is made to David himself, that is, to Christ, who was born of David’s seed. [Col. 1262B] [Cassiodorus.] Intention: he exhorts to praise. Method: it has three parts. First, the Prophet sets forth infinite praise. Second, he says that all will fulfil God’s praise in nine ways, at “generation,” etc. Third, [Col. 1262C] he explains these same matters more fully, at “merciful,” etc. Therefore the Prophet, in the person of the Church filled with the sevenfold Spirit, promises praise, saying: O—

**VERSE 1.**—“I shall exalt you, my God the King; and I shall bless your name for ever, and for age upon age.”

King, [Augustine, Cassiodorus,] Christ, who were born from Judah—whence there were kings in the Old Testament—and who are also my God, namely my creator and re-creator: I shall exalt you, that is, by preaching I shall make known what you are; and I shall bless your name, that is, I shall praise you, for ever, namely here, and for age upon age, namely eternally. For whoever does not begin here will be mute in the future. Then he explains what he had said:

[Col. 1262D]

**VERSE 2.**—“Every day I shall bless you, and I shall praise your name for ever, and for age upon age.”

“I shall bless you every day.” [Augustine.] Behold what he had said: “for age upon age,” without interruption in joys or sorrows; and thereby “I shall praise your name for ever, and for age upon age.” [Cassiodorus, Alcuin.] For whoever praises God here every day will deserve to praise him in the eternal day with continual exultation. Of this praise it is elsewhere said: “They shall praise you unto ages of ages” (Ps. 83), because they will always love him whom they will always see; and nothing is more delightful than that vision. [Augustine.] Therefore I shall bless now, [Col. 1263A] every day, so that, when the one day without end comes, you may go from praise to praise, just as from strength to strength. Then he adds, as it were, the cause of praise:

**VERSE 3.**—“Great is the Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy; and there is no end to his greatness.”

The Lord is great in essence and exceedingly, or greatly, praiseworthy. [Augustine.] By this one word he has given us something to ponder which cannot be fully grasped. And never cease from praises. Therefore he is greatly praiseworthy, and that is because there is no end to his greatness: he is incomprehensible in thought or place. And because his greatness has no end, one cannot bring his praise to an end.

## PART II. VERSE 4.—“Generation and generation shall praise your works, and they shall proclaim your power.”

[Col. 1263B] “Generation.” [Cassiodorus.] Second, he promises that all will fulfil God’s praise in nine ways. The nine ways of praise are: works, power, magnificence, holiness, wonders, the might of fearful deeds, greatness, remembrance, and righteousness; these will be explained below. From these, as from topics and seeds, all praise is drawn, just as all arguments are taken from a small number of topics.

[Augustine.] As though saying: I shall praise, and generation and generation—that is, every generation—will praise also. For the repetition of the speaker sends the mind of the hearer into infinity. Or two generations are suggested by this repetition: the generation in which God’s children are born in the present, and the future generation in which they will be children of the resurrection. Of this it is said in the Gospel: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his majesty” (Matt. 19). He called the resurrection “regeneration.” Therefore “generation and generation shall praise your works,” which may be contemplated so that you may be praised, you who work such things. If, then, we fail before greatness that has no end—or, that is, at least—let us praise the worker from his works, the Maker from created things, the Creator from creation. Let us see what he has made here, things known to us: “and your power.” This is the second topic of praise. As though saying: They shall praise your works; and in praising these works they shall proclaim your power. For they do not praise the works except to announce the power of the worker. Yet some eloquent people praise creation and forget its Creator. But holy praisers, [Col. 1263D] if they love works, praise the worker more; they love and praise these things for his sake, which is certainly what must be done. For if in created things some beauty, usefulness, or power is perceived, it is praised more in him who made it. For what is more beautiful than he who made all things? What more useful? What more powerful? Praise, therefore, the things made for the sake of their maker.

But if you praise works, you praise yourself too, since you are God’s work; and that saying occurs: “Let not your own mouth praise you,” and you seem arrogant (Prov. 27). But it is not arrogance, because you do not praise yourself but God in yourself. The third topic of praise follows:

**VERSE 5.**—“They shall speak of the magnificence of the glory of your holiness, and they shall recount your wonders.”

“The magnificence of glory.” [Cassiodorus.] Then the fourth topic: “They shall speak of the magnificence of the glory of your holiness.” [Col. 1264A] Other books have more plainly: “They shall speak of the magnificence of your majesty and of your holiness.” The fifth topic of praise follows: “And they shall recount your wonders.” Then the sixth:

**VERSE 6.**—“And they shall speak of the might of your fearful deeds, and they shall recount your greatness.”

“And they shall speak of the might of your fearful deeds.” [Augustine.] For he not only appeals gently, but also threatens. He appeals gently in order to exhort; he threatens in order to frighten and correct. For if he did not threaten, there would be no correction; if he did not entreat, there would be no exhortation. Thus he is lovable and fearful. Therefore they shall speak of the power by which he disciplines and punishes. If they preach the eternal kingdom, they do not keep silent about eternal fire. The seventh topic of praise follows: “And they shall recount your greatness,” which has no end; but they shall recount it when they praise him as such. The eighth topic of praise follows: “And—

[Col. 1264B]

**VERSE 7.**—“They shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, and they shall exult in your righteousness.”

“They shall pour forth outwardly the memory of your sweetness; inwardly they are full of it.” [Augustine.] By “the memory of the abundance of sweetness” he means that God has not forgotten us though we have forgotten him, and that, though we do not remember him, he causes us to remember him. For through his abundant sweetness he first remembers us by calling us, preceding us by his grace; then we remember him. Note that he does not say, “they shall eat,” but “they shall pour forth.” The one who learns eats; the one who teaches pours forth; yet he pours forth what he has eaten.
