Therefore this memory, because it is very sweet, must be eaten and poured forth. Thus eat so that you may pour forth.

The ninth topic of praise follows: “And they shall exult in your righteousness,” not their own, which those who remember you receive from you. To him, therefore, to whom they owe their being, they also owe their justification. Let no one, then, attribute to God that he exists and attribute to himself that he is righteous. For what he wishes to attribute to himself is better than what he attributes to God. Give the whole to him; praise him in everything.

## PART III. VERSE 8.—“The Lord is compassionate and merciful, patient and exceedingly merciful.”

“Compassionate.” [Cassiodorus.] Third, he explains more fully what he had briefly set forth in the second part. As though saying: They rightly praise him in these things, because the Lord is compassionate in effect and merciful by nature. The parts of praise set out above are presented here, though not every individual one can be fully explained. For who could fully explain his works or his power? And, as above, so here he begins with works, so that he is called compassionate when he restores those who have fallen; merciful by nature, and also when he creates. And he is patient. This is taken from the second topic of praise: the patience that he praises here, not because he suspends the earth, restrains the seas, and painted the heaven with stars, etc., but because he tolerates sinners so that they may be converted.

[Augustine.] Or “merciful” and “compassionate” may be taken as the same. As though saying: You, Lord, have made what they praise and proclaim, and the things for which they praise and exult; their merits are your gifts, bestowed on them through mercy. For the Lord is compassionate and merciful to those to whom he has already given forgiveness, and through this they praise and exult. [Col. 1265A] And he is patient toward those to whom he has not yet given it, but waits in order to give it. He repeats the matter of mercy: “and exceedingly merciful,” and this universally.

**VERSE 9.**—“The Lord is gracious to all, and his compassions are over all his works.”

The Lord is gracious to all, [Cassiodorus, Augustine,] namely to the good and evil, and most of all to those who taste him. This is taken from magnificence, because nothing is more magnificent than to be gracious to those who taste him and to extend mercy to all his works—not, however, to those things which the devil does, for he rather condemns them, but he grants mercy to his own works. Hence he adds: “And his compassions are over,” or “in,” all his works, because he is the one who makes his sun rise upon the good and evil (Matt. 5), and similarly in such matters. And in waiting for those who persist in sin, and warning them to turn, he does good to all and extends mercies to all.

But if he punishes, severity is exercised not upon his works but upon yours. For if you remove your evil works, and no works but his remain in you, his mercy will not abandon you. But if you do not abandon your works, his severity will be upon your works, when he says: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25). And because your compassion is over all your works:

[Col. 1265B]

**VERSE 10.**—“Let all your works confess you, O Lord, and let your saints bless you.”

Lord, let your works confess you, [Augustine] that is, praise you. Everything that exists confesses you, either in itself or through rational creatures; even things without the capacity to praise are material for praise, because [Col. 1265C] when you examine them, you discover in them the great power that comes from God. And let your saints—that is, angels and human beings, contemplating your works in confession—bless you, or bless you. Let them contemplate your confessing creation and bless you. This is drawn from holiness. For this is God’s holiness, that is, what it requires. He is called holy so that the saints ought to confess him. Then he adds what they say in confessing:

VERS. 11.—“They shall speak of the glory of your kingdom, and shall tell of your power.”

They shall speak of the glory of your kingdom, etc. [Augustine] As though he said: “For what do they say? They shall speak of the glory of your kingdom and tell of your power”—that is, they shall declare how powerfully and wonderfully you do whatever you do and order within your kingdom. [Col. 1265D] They shall say how glorious and wonderful is God, who made heaven and earth and filled them with diverse goods; how powerful is God, who made and sustains these things. This is drawn from wonders.

VERS. 12.—“That they may make known to the children of men your power, and the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom.”

That they may make known. [Augustine] As though he said: “They will surely speak for this purpose: to make known to the children of men your power and glory”; or, as others say, “the beauty of the magnificence of your kingdom,” or “the glory of the greatness of the beauty of your kingdom.” [Cassiodorus] This is drawn from the power of terrible deeds. For through the preaching of the saints the power of God, by which he will take vengeance on the wicked, has been made known. And the glory of the kingdom, by which he will crown the good, has been made known, lest it be sought less eagerly [Col. 1266A] through being unknown. It was also made known when the apostles performed miracles; and through knowledge of both, some are converted by fear of punishment, others by hope of glory. Note that after commending power, he commends the beauty of the kingdom; he does so lest power, once named, terrify the lover. For he has a kingdom in which we may delight, and that kingdom has a beauty with which nothing magnificent may be compared. Of the greatness of that kingdom he adds:

VERS. 13.—“Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages, and your dominion endures through every generation and generation.”

Your kingdom, etc. [Augustine] As though he said: “Of what kingdom will they proclaim the beauty? Not of this age.” I say that the kingdom proclaimed by them has beauty; [Col. 1266B] but the greatness of its beauty belongs not to this world but to your kingdom, because your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages—that is, eternal—and your dominion is through every generation and generation, by succession. Or, it is in this generation and the future one, by which the kingdom is shown to be mighty. [Cassiodorus] For he praises the kingdom for its perpetuity and the effectuality of its dominion; this is drawn from greatness. For if it is great to rule for a time, it is greater for dominion to have no end.

VERS. 14.—“The Lord is faithful in all 310 his words, and holy in all his works.”

The Lord is faithful in all his words, [Augustine] because he fulfilled the gifts of his coming and gave whatever he promised; and by the things given he established faith concerning the other things which he promised and, as it were, caused this to be written in a bond. [Col. 1266C] This is drawn from abundant sweetness. Hence above he said: “They shall utter the memory of the abundance of your sweetness”; and he is holy in all his works: as he is true in his promises, so he is holy in his working.

VERS. 15.—“The Lord upholds all who are falling, and raises up all who have been cast down.”

The Lord upholds all who are falling, [Cassiodorus] namely, not those who have not yet fallen, but those who are beginning to fall. He is said to uphold them all, not because he upholds everyone, but because whoever is upheld is upheld by him. And he raises up all who have been cast down, namely those who have already suffered the ruin and fall of sin. Thus by “those falling” he means those beginning to slip; by “those cast down,” those already fallen. This too belongs to abundance: namely, that he lifts up those falling and raises those cast down; hence the remembrance of sweetness is received and poured forth in his praises. [Augustine] Or otherwise, according to another reading: “The Lord upholds all who fall away from their evils,” that is, from vices and sins; the Lord upholds all such, and this is understood in a good sense. Or the passage concerns not falling away from vices, but the fact that people fall away here from temporal things. For saints such as Job, who lose something in this world and are brought low, are those who fall. Thus Job fell from the glory of the former splendor of temporal possessions, by which he shone for a time; he fell from the glory of his household and sat upon a dung-heap. So too did many other saints. Yet God upholds and strengthens them all, because [Col. 1267A] “the righteous falls seven times in a day and rises again” (Prov. XXIV). But the ungodly are weakened in evils. And he raises up all who have been cast down who belong to him, since he resists the proud. And because you do these things:

VERS. 16.—“The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord; and you give them their food in due season.”

The eyes, [Cassiodorus] that is, the intentions of all, hope in you, O Lord. Here he treats more fully of justice, so that one who hears that he is merciful may fear that he is just; and it belongs to justice that he should satisfy those who hope in him, bodily and spiritually. [Augustine] Hence he adds: “And you give them their food,” bodily or spiritual, not indiscriminately, but in due season. Food is not always to be given, but at the fitting time. For many who ask are beneficially delayed. [Col. 1267B] Therefore he gives as a physician gives to the sick person what is suitable, and when it is suitable—not as the human being desires and asks, lest its being given do harm. The Apostle asked that the angel of Satan be removed from him, and did not receive it; yet this was for his perfection, because the time had not yet passed for infirmity to be exercised. The devil asked to tempt Job and received permission, but to his own condemnation. Christ himself had come to die, yet, taking the weak into himself, he said: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI). And although he did not receive what he seemed to ask, he said: “Not what I will, but what you will” (ibid.), blessing at every time.

VERS. 17.—“You open your hand, and fill every living thing with blessing.”

[Col. 1267C] You open, etc. [Cassiodorus] As though he said: “What food do you give?” Behold, you open your hand—that is, the kindness of your power, because all things are in his power—and fill every rational living creature, namely that which can be blessed, with blessing. As though he said: “Although you do not sometimes give, yet you give in due season. You delay indeed, but do not take away.”

VERS. 18.—“The Lord is just in all his ways, and holy in all his works.”

The Lord is just. [Cassiodorus, Augustine, Cassiodorus] By the very name he makes justice plain, so that it may be manifest that this is praise concerning justice. I say that he is just in all his ways. His ways are the dispositions and wills, all of which are just, even when he strikes. Thus he is just both when he wounds and when he heals. So Daniel and all the saints confessed in tribulations that God’s judgments are just. [Col. 1267D] And he is holy in all his works: merciful, patient, giver of all good things. One should know that “ways” pertain to disposition, “works” to effect. These are distinguished according to us; but with him, to will is to do, because things have existence from his will. And:

VERS. 19.—“The Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth.”

The Lord, [Cassiodorus] who is near everywhere—that is, gracious—is near to all who call upon him, [Col. 1268A] even though he does not immediately do for them what they ask. For this is precisely why he does not do it: because he is truly near; and this is drawn from justice. But to which callers upon him? [Augustine] To all who call upon him in truth, not according to vain desires that seek something other than God himself. And he:

VERS. 20.—“He will fulfill the desire of those who fear him, and will hear their prayer; and he will save them.”

He will fulfill, at some time, [Augustine] even though not immediately when they ask, the desire of those who fear him—provided, however, that they fear him in order to do his will—and he will hear their prayer for salvation and save them. Then he concludes concerning justice, saying:

VERS. 21.—“The Lord keeps all who love him, and will destroy all sinners.”

The Lord keeps all who love him, and will destroy all sinners, [Augustine] that is, those who persevere in sins. In both there is justice. It is right both to preserve those who love him and to destroy sinners. Note that by saying “keeps,” he shows that sweetness is in him; by saying “will destroy,” he shows that truth is in him.

VERS. 22.—“My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord; and let all flesh bless his holy name for ever and ever.”

Praise. [Cassiodorus] Having set forth all the grounds of praise, a brief conclusion follows, by which he concludes what cannot be unfolded. As though he said: “Since all things [Col. 1268C] are thus, my mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord.” Behold, he concludes in praise; and by that example let all flesh—that is, humanity, converted to God—bless his holy name, both for ever, that is, in the present age, and for ever and ever, in the future.

## Comparison on Psalm CXLIV: “I WILL EXALT YOU, MY GOD, O KING,” etc.

VERS. 3.—“Of his greatness there is no end.” Therefore the Chaldean Jerome, for “there is no end,” says “there is no searching out.” Nearly all the others have *HEQER*; the sense is the same. For God’s greatness is such that the more you investigate, the more remains to be discovered. In several verses where we have the third person plural, the Hebrews have the first person singular without injury to the sense; for example, where our text has “they shall tell of wonders,” Jerome has “I shall speak,” others “I shall meditate,” and the like. [Col. 1268D] Certainly the Psalmist recounted God’s wonders, as we too shall recount them afterward; indeed, in Hebrew the singular and plural occur alternately, making it plain that they are equivalent.

VERS. 8.—“They shall exult,” Jerome; and others, “they shall praise” or “sing,” *JERANNENU*, or “they shall rejoice aloud.” These indeed plainly signify exultation in the praises of God.

VERS. 14. “The Lord is faithful.” This verse is not in the Hebrew. I think it was inserted by the Septuagint, because this psalm is written in alphabetical order, and, if this verse were not placed here, the letter *nun* would be lacking. For “faithful” in Hebrew begins with that letter: *NEEMAN*.

# PSALM CXLV

[Col. 1269]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “ALLELUIA.”

[Col. 1269A]

“Praise the Lord, O my soul.” Title: “Alleluia.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] This utterance is like saving music, heavenly harmony, delighting not only human beings but angels as well, and expressing the praise of God. It is suitably prefixed to this psalm, in which the righteous man exhorts his soul to praise God; for amid adversities the soul is sometimes troubled, whether it wishes to be or not. Hence above he said: “Why are you sad, O my soul, and why do you trouble me?” (Ps. XLI). But in order to remove its disturbance, he suggests the joy of hope, if not of present possession, saying to the troubled and sorrowing soul: “Hope in God, for I shall yet confess him” (ibid.). [Cassiodorus] Therefore, raised by this hope, the soul here praises God.

Purpose: he exhorts to praise. Method: it has three parts. First, the Prophet counsels himself, as though counseling all, to praise rather than be idle over vain things; and, as though assenting to the counsel, he declares that he will praise where he can do so fully. Second, he exhorts others not to hope in human beings, at “Do not trust.” Third, he teaches that all hope must be placed in the Almighty, at “Blessed.” Thus the righteous man, exhorting his soul to praise, says:

VERS. 1.—“Praise the Lord, O my soul; I will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing to my God as long as I exist.”

“Praise the Lord, O my soul.” [Augustine] As though he said: “Why are you anxious about others? Stand with me in the praise of God.” But why, by whom, and to whom is this counsel given? If the flesh is said to counsel the soul, this does not seem true, since counsel is usually given by the superior and worthier to the inferior. [Col. 1269C] But the flesh is inferior to the soul. For although the soul is blameworthy because sinful, yet by nature it is said to be better than a body praised in its own kind, because spiritual nature excels bodily nature, which it moves, rules, and endows with sensation; and the soul, being spiritual nature, is akin to God’s infinite substance. Thus gold, though blameworthy because dirty, surpasses lead praised for its purity; so too a bad person surpasses an excellent horse.

Therefore counsel is not given to the soul by the flesh, however greatly tamed and pacified it may be; the flesh is nevertheless dead because of sin. Rather, the soul, now also made immortal, counsels itself: for the soul is always on earth, but its purer part, namely the mind, which contemplates divine wisdom and clings to it and breathes it into the soul, sees certain parts of the soul—namely, the sensual faculty—disturbed [Col. 1269D] by the movements of the world and dragged outward by desire for earthly things. It calls it back from these to what is higher and inward. Thus the soul, exhorting itself according to its lower part, says according to reason: “Praise the Lord, O my soul.” What pleases you in this world, divided as you are among so many loves of worldly things? What concern for mortal things occupies you? Gather yourself to your Maker. Here are your peace and security. Stand with me, therefore, and praise the Lord.

Then the soul answers the mind, as though weighed down here and unable to stand thus as fully as is fitting: “I shall praise perfectly in my eternal life,” which is truly life—namely, when I have perfectly cleaved to him, from whom to be separated, as now happens, is death. Here, in this death, I praise faintly, that is, weakly, because the body weighs down the soul and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things (Wis. IX). But here hope consoles and feeds us; in it one praises while in some fashion alive. Life will be in the future. Therefore I groan here; there I shall praise fully. And how will you praise? Thus: “I will sing to my God as long as I exist,” or “as long as I am.” Here a person is concerned with other things, and therefore does not always sing or do so perfectly; but in eternity he is so occupied. [Cassiodorus] “I shall not sing thus”—rather, “as long as I shall be,” or “as long as I am.” He does not say this because he will at some point not exist, for he will exist eternally and therefore truly for a long time. Or it may be understood of the present: “I will sing.” As though he said: “In the future I shall praise perfectly, [Col. 1270B] and even here, where I shall not always remain, I will sing to my God as long as I exist.”

311 PART II. VERS. 2.—“Do not trust in princes, in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation.”

“Do not trust.” [Augustine] In the second part, having given counsel and affirmed that he will praise where he can do so fully, he now exhorts those far removed—while the evils by which the soul is troubled still remain—not to hope in human beings but in God. As though he said: “I shall praise and sing; but you little ones, who not yet—or rather, who also—hope in God, while evils are still present, hope not in human beings but in God.” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] He says this as follows: “Do not trust in princes of darkness,” that is, demons; nor in the sons of men, that is, baptizers, [Col. 1270C] in whom there is no salvation. In the one Son of Man there is salvation; hope in him, not because he is Son of Man, but because he is Son of God—not on account of what he took from you, but on account of what he preserved in himself, because salvation belongs to the Lord. And in another psalm it is said: not in the rulers of the age, nor in baptizers, who boast that they give holy things though they are only their instruments. For if a human being could give anything, less would be asked from God.

[Cassiodorus] Or thus, “Do not trust”: the Prophet looks toward the last times, at the consummation of the age, and, as though mentally placed at the end of the quickly ending world, teaches that things are not to be loved as eternal. As though he said: “I am disposed as I have said; and by my example, do not you others—especially you of the last times—trust in princes and in the sons of men,” that is, in those who especially urge the love of temporal things. First, like a saving physician, he cleanses hearts by prohibiting harmful things, so that afterward he may pour in health-giving things by exhorting them to what is wholesome. “In whom,” that is, in the sons of men, “there is no salvation.” For see what they are.

VERS. 3.—“His spirit shall depart, and he shall return to his earth; on that day all their thoughts shall perish.”

His spirit, [Augustine] that is, his soul—that is, the human being’s soul—will depart suddenly, when he neither wishes nor knows it; and when the spirit departs, the flesh will return to its earth, from which it took its beginning. And on that day, namely the day of death, all their thoughts will perish—that is, will be frustrated—which were directed toward the various circuits of the world. [Col. 1271A]

PART III. VERS. 4.—“Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all things that are in them.”

“Blessed is he whose…” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] The third part teaches that all hope must be placed in the Almighty, whom it describes from his works, so that paganism, so often defeated, may be at rest. It should be noted that, after removing harmful things above, it now teaches what brings salvation, namely, in whom hope ought to be placed. And as though someone asked, “In whom, then, should one hope?” he answers: “In the Lord, because blessed is he whose God is not an angel or a human being, but the God of Jacob”—that is, of the one who hopes in him, who was Jacob’s God. I say that he is his helper, Jacob’s helper—that is, this man Jacob’s helper, just as he was helper of the historical Jacob. He was that Jacob’s helper in such a way that he made Israel out of Jacob, one who now saw the help. [Col. 1271B] That is, Israel saw God, who is the help. Thus, if you do not see here but have God as your helper, you too will finally become Israel from Jacob, seeing; and every groaning and sorrow will cease.

He says, therefore, that blessed also is the one whose God is the God of Jacob, his helper—that is, the helper of this man Jacob, just as of that one. Why is he blessed? Because his hope is in the Lord his God. And because worshipers of demons also place hope in their own god, he defines in whom hope ought to be placed, saying: “Who made…” As though he said: “In what Lord God? In him who made heaven and earth, [Col. 1271C] sea…” [Cassiodorus, Augustine] that is, in Christ; and the psalm shows this to the end by describing him through his works. For though there are many gods and lords, yet for us there is one God, from whom are all things (I Cor. VIII). This is praise from works, because though our knowledge cannot grasp his substance, it can in some measure grasp his acts. He adds concerning these: “And he made all things that are in them,” namely in heaven, on earth, and in the sea. Thus he cares for you also among the rest. He says “all things,” lest you think another to be Creator. Or, that is, even of lesser things; and beyond the rest he adds this other thing relevant to us: he is:

VERS. 5.—“Who keeps truth for ever, executes judgment for those suffering wrong, and gives food to the hungry.”

[Col. 1271D] “Who keeps truth for ever,” that is, eternally. [Cassiodorus, Augustine] This is Christ, who is truth. Every human being is a liar. By these words he proclaims both the one to be loved and the one to be feared, in whom he keeps truth. Behold, he executes judgment—for whom? For those suffering wrong. Not every trouble is an injustice; what one suffers justly is not injustice, as in the case of a thief and other criminals. Therefore to suffer injustice is one thing; to suffer punishment another. For a person suffers punishment justly, but injustice is contrary to right. He also gives both kinds of food, bodily and spiritual, to the hungry, of whom it is said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. V). Therefore let no person boast. As though he said: God alone gives these two things: he executes judgment and gives food. This belongs to justice. [Col. 1272A] For Christ, the just judge, vindicates those who suffer for his name’s sake and gives food to those who love him.

VERS. 6.—“The Lord releases the bound; the Lord enlightens the blind.”

VERS. 7.—“The Lord raises up those cast down; the Lord loves the righteous.”

“The Lord releases the bound,” [Augustine, Cassiodorus] bound by a mortal body. He releases them from mortality, making them immortal. Or, the Lord releases those bound by faults from sins. And the Lord enlightens with wisdom those blind through ignorance; [Augustine] that is, he makes wise those who are blind. These things belong to the abundance of sweetness. And the Lord raises up through humility those cast down through pride. Those whom the devil casts down, God sets upright. And the Lord [Col. 1272B] loves the righteous, whom he places in eternal blessedness. And because he loves them, he therefore executes judgment for those suffering wrong. Who are the righteous, and how does he love them? Behold, the orphan and widow are righteous; he loves them by guarding them. And this is what he says:

VERS. 8.—“The Lord guards strangers; he will receive the orphan and widow, and will destroy the ways of sinners.”

“The Lord guards strangers,” [Augustine] namely those who say: “We have no abiding city here” (Heb. XIII). “He will receive the orphan and widow,” that is, those wholly bereft of support and aid in this world, so that they may hope in God; and even those who possess earthly things but do not trust in them are God’s orphans and widows. Or by “strangers” is understood the Church of the Gentiles. [Col. 1272C] For the whole Church of the Gentiles is a newcomer in relation to the Fathers, whose daughter she is not by flesh but by imitation. All believers in this pilgrimage are orphans, whose Father is absent; and every faithful soul is a widow while her Bridegroom is absent—that is, as long as the Bridegroom is away. Hence they desire Father and Bridegroom all the more, and God protects all these: unseen, yet desired. And he will destroy the way, or broad ways, of sinners, who here mock our narrow way. When their way has been destroyed, what remains for us? Certainly the kingdom, concerning which he adds:

VERS. 9.—“The Lord will reign for ever, your God, O Zion, from generation to generation.”

The Lord will reign in his saints for ever. [Cassiodorus] This is drawn from magnificence. The Lord will reign [Col. 1272D] when our hearts are firm in him, which is not yet the case. What Lord? Your God, O Zion, will reign. As though he said: “It pertains to you, O Church, because you are his kingdom, not Babylon.” Then he explains what he had said, “for ever”: “from generation to generation,” that is, always.

## Comparison on Psalm CXLV: “PRAISE THE LORD, O MY SOUL; I WILL PRAISE THE LORD IN MY LIFE,” etc.

VERS. 3.—“His spirit shall depart and he shall return to his earth.” Faber and Caecus wish it to read, “their spirit shall depart and they shall return to earth,” since the plural “sons of men” has preceded, and likewise “their thoughts shall perish” follows. Add that it is not fitting for the spirit, which is incorruptible, to return to earth. Yet all interpreters, Greek and Latin alike, translate it in the singular, and in Hebrew it is read *IASCHUB*, which Faber marvels at. But let him cease to marvel when “the flesh shall return” is understood. Hence Münster translated: “The human being shall return to his earth.” And their argument that a plural has preceded, especially in Greek, presents no obstacle, since we understand it thus: “His spirit shall depart from the human being, and he shall return to his earth,” as the translator for Campensis rendered it. The paraphrase, however, expounded it in the plural. Nor is there any need to contend further about this, when the matter lies in syllables.

# PSALM CXLVI

[Col. 1273]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “ALLELUIA.”

[Col. 1273A]

“Praise the Lord.” Title: “Alleluia.” [Augustine] Here again he treats of the praise of God, in which the Prophet exhorts people to praise the one who gathers Israel. Purpose: he exhorts to God’s praise. Method: the psalm has two parts. First, he shows whom he gathers and how. Second, after what has been said, he rebukes those who still cling and doubt, showing whence [Col. 1273B] they can praise: namely, if they are humble, at “Sing before.” Therefore, inviting all, both greater and lesser, to praise, he says:

VERS. 1.—“Praise the Lord, for psalmody is good; let praise to our God be pleasant and fitting.”

“Praise the Lord.” [Augustine] This is said to all nations. And as though we asked why we should praise, he gives the cause of praise: “For psalmody is good.” This is the entire reward of those who praise. As though he said: “Praise, therefore, because it is good to praise.” For the praise of God itself is our blessedness. Note that he did not say, “For praise is good,” but, to express the manner of praise, he said, “For psalmody is good.” [Col. 1273C] Psalmody itself is the praise of God performed not by voice alone but with an instrument, with hands in accord with the voice. This signifies that works ought to harmonize with the voice, and that their praise must not cease even when vocal praise is interrupted. Therefore one always praises who always acts well. But the one who acts badly blasphemes.

This praise will be perfected in eternal glory, for which we who are to arrive there should now train ourselves in the praise of good works. Psalmody, then, is good because praise of God is good. In the praise of God, the very act is the reward, which will also be ours in the future. And because psalmody is good, therefore let our praise be pleasant and fitting to God. This is surely so if it is fitting—that is, beautiful in the conduct of life. For praise is pleasing to God when it is beautiful, unlike the practice of sinners, who spoil a good melody with evil morals.

[Col. 1273D] VERS. 2.—“The Lord, building Jerusalem, will gather the dispersions of Israel.”

“Building.” [Cassiodorus] As though he said: “God deserves praise because the Lord is building”—that is, he builds the spiritual Jerusalem, namely the heavenly Church. He builds it in this way: he will gather to the kingdom the dispersions of Israel—that is, faithful persons scattered throughout the whole world. [Augustine] Or the term Jerusalem is understood as the universal Church, one part of which triumphs in heaven and one part wars on earth. For there is an eternal Jerusalem in heaven, whose citizens are angels; and the people of Israel also belong to it, though now exiles through sin. All those [Col. 1274A] in that great heavenly city rejoice, because God himself is their spectacle; but we are exiled from that city, expelled by sin, lest we remain there, and weighed down by mortality, lest we return there. Yet God has looked upon our exile.

Or he who builds Jerusalem also restores its fallen part and long ago gathered the dispersed in Christ, [Col. 1274B] whom he sent to redeem our captivity at the price of his blood. It is as though he said: “You tell us to praise God. Who is our God?” [Interlinear Gloss] The Lord has built the heavenly Jerusalem, which he constructs from living stones, repairing the angelic ruin; and he who builds Jerusalem will gather [Augustine] in one faith and charity the dispersions of Israel—that is, faithful people once scattered, whom he gathers so that the heavenly building may be formed from them. Thus—that is, through such works—God commends himself to his worshippers, that is, he commends his love to the faithful. What, then, will he give them as their reward? Himself. But how does he gather? What does he do in order to gather? Behold, he is:

VERS. 3.—“Who heals the broken in heart, and binds up their wounds.”

“He heals.” [Augustine] Partly here, fully in the future, he heals the broken in heart—that is, those who offer God the sacrifice of a troubled spirit. He heals these; he humbles the proud; but in the future health will be perfect, when this corruptible body puts on incorruption. Now, however, he binds their wounds as a physician binds fractures. Hence he adds, “and now binds their wounds,” by the comparison with a physician. For what is crooked is broken by physicians so that it may afterwards become straight; so the perverse heart, displeased with God in whatever happens, ought to be broken and crushed so that it may be made straight. If it cannot make itself straight or break itself, God will make it straight. Break it, I say, through confession, penitence, and punishment; this is signified by beating the breast. [Col. 1274D] Hence elsewhere: “Rend your hearts” (Joel II). For the heart is crushed in order that, when broken, it may be straightened and healed. That which is not first corrected by crushing is raised up badly. [Jerome] Therefore crush your own heart, and the Lord binds its wounds, as the Samaritan did to the man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, when he saw him lying wounded on the road: “he bound up his wounds” (Luke X). But concerning those who have not crushed their heart, Isaiah says: “There is no poultice to apply, nor oil, nor bandages” (Isa. I). [Augustine] God’s bandages are the temporal sacraments, by which we have consolation for the present; they will then be removed when health is perfect, just as a physician removes a fracture’s bandage when health is complete. He is:

[Col. 1275A] VERS. 4.—“Who counts the multitude of the stars, and calls them all by name.”

“Who counts the multitude of the stars.” [Augustine] Literally this is not so great a thing, if God counts all the stars, for the hairs of heads are numbered by him. But the stars are certain lights in the Church which shine among all the perverse, namely those of whom the Apostle says: “You appear in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation as lights in the world” (Phil. II). The Lord counts such persons among his own, because “the Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II). If someone inserts himself among them under the shadowy appearance of faith, he who counts knows that he is beyond the number. Hence elsewhere: “They have been multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXXIX), because within the walls of the present Church there are more persons than will be in God’s kingdom. Therefore he says, “who counts,” that is, distinguishes, the multitude of stars, that is, of the elect. For the Lord knows those who are his; and he calls by name, or calls, all those whom he has counted, because their names are written in the book of life, that is, in God’s predestination. [Col. 1275B] He knows these; this is our whole reward.

Therefore we ought not to rejoice in other things or in certain spiritual gifts, as some do. To some who have wrongly used certain gifts of the Holy Spirit he will say at the end: “I never knew you” (Matt. VII). He also said to the disciples: “Do not rejoice because spirits are subject to you, but because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X). This joy in predestination arises in us through charity, without which the other gifts of the Holy Spirit too, possessed only for a time, are removed, as the Lord says: “To him who has, it shall be given; and from him who does not have, even what he has shall be taken away” (Matt. XIII). For he has the grace of possessing the name, but does not have the charity to use it.

Or it may be said literally: “Who counts the multitude of the stars”—this is evident—“and calls them all by name.” [Cassiodorus] Or, as another translation has it: “He calls all by his own name,” not by another’s, as astrologers call them Jupiter, Venus, and the like. Or it may be understood typologically of the saints. Nor does this alter the first interpretation: “Who counts the multitude of stars,” that is, saints, “and calls them all by name,” that is, gives each one a proper gift, calling some through humility, others through chastity. [Col. 1275D] Or, “calling them all by name,” that is, all are in his household. This is said by comparison with a master who knows the names of his servants. What more need I say?

VERS. 5.—“Great is our Lord, and great is his power; and of his wisdom there is no number.”

“Our Lord is great.” [Augustine] The Prophet, full of joy, pours forth what cannot be explained. As though he said: “Yet he reflected as much as he could”; and his power is great. This is praise from greatness. And there is no number—that is, no limit—to his wisdom or understanding. For it cannot be comprehended by anyone. [Col. 1276A] He himself who counts the stars cannot be counted. No one can measure, count, or weigh God himself—the number, measure, and weight by which he ordered all things—that is, God’s wisdom itself.

As it is said in the Book of Wisdom: [Note: [Col. 1275D] From Augustine, *On Genesis*, book IV, chapter 3.] “God arranged all things in number, measure, and weight” (Wis. II): that is, in himself, who is measure, setting bounds for every thing; number, giving form to every thing; and weight, drawing every thing toward stability—that is, determining, forming, and ordering all things that are incomprehensible. [Augustine] Therefore let human voices fall silent; let human thoughts rest before the incomprehensible things of God. Let no one stretch himself out as though he were going to comprehend, but as one who is going to participate. For we shall be participants, and we shall not be what we comprehend, nor shall we comprehend the whole. But of what shall we be participants, and how shall we participate, when there are no parts in God, nor is he divided into parts? Who, then, can explain how many partake of one simple being? I do not think it can be spoken before it is seen. Confess, therefore, your weakness, if you wish to arrive at strength—[Col. 1276B] at him whose understanding has no number. But amid this difficulty of understanding, be gentle. Why? He adds:

VERS. 6.—“The Lord supports the gentle, but humbles sinners even to the ground.”

The Lord supports the gentle unto the understanding of mysteries. [Augustine] Therefore, if you wish to understand, be gentle. Do not accuse the obscurities of Scripture, which God made in order to exercise you; nor say, “It would have been better said this way.” For it was said as it ought to have been said. Let not the sick person correct the medicines which the physician has prepared. The physician knows how to regulate them; trust the one who heals you. Therefore, before you know why something has been said, do not judge; believe that it ought to have been said as it has been said. Such piety makes you capable.

But if you resist God’s hidden things, see what follows: “humbling,” etc. As though he said: “He supports the gentle, but humbles sinners”—that is, the harsh, who are opposed to the gentle—“even to the ground,” so that they think only earthly things concerning God. Because they criticize intelligible things, they therefore perceive earthly things, thinking bodily thoughts about the incorporeal God. God does this to those who wish to mock the law before they know it. Therefore, because it is a great thing to advance to intelligible and spiritual things, let us be gentle; let us knock; let us do what follows:

PART II. VERS. 7.—“Sing before the Lord in confession; sing psalms to our God upon the harp.”

Sing beforehand, or begin, to the Lord in confession. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The second part, in which, from what has been said, he rebukes and urges on those who still, as it were, remain attached to such things, showing whence they may be able to understand—namely, if they are humble and not proud. As if to say: And that you may be able to understand, sing beforehand, or begin for, the Lord in confession of sins and of praise. Accuse yourself first; then praise God. Thus one will arrive at a clear understanding of truth. [Col. 1277A] Thus the image of God will be restored in you. After confession, however, good works follow; hence he adds: Make music by works to our God on the harp, where the hand follows the voice: so let works follow the voice of praise. And as though someone were to ask, “To what God?”

### VERSE 8.—“Who covers heaven with clouds, and prepares rain for the earth.”

Who covers heaven with clouds. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Literally, he recalls works through which power is displayed. Or rather, mystically: he covers heaven with clouds—that is, he veils sacred Scripture with figures and sacraments, so as to incite us to seek. And do not be afraid on account of Scripture’s being covered, because from it he prepares rain for the earth, freely, not obtained by merits. For this purpose he willed that certain things in the Scriptures should be obscure: so that [Col. 1277B] the servants of God might have something which, by interpreting, they might pour forth upon the ears and hearts of people, receiving from God’s clouds the rich nourishment of spiritual joy. And he himself is

### VERSE 9.—“Who brings forth hay upon the mountains, and grass for the service of men.”

Who brings forth hay and grass. [Augustine.] Behold the fruit of the rain—not only upon the lowly earth, but also on mountains, that is, among those exalted in this age, who love riches more. Behold whence he has produced it and for whom he has produced it: for the service of men, that is, for preachers who serve people. Hence the Apostle says: “But ourselves your servants through Jesus Christ” (2 Cor. 4). These sow spiritual things and receive from those exalted in the age hay and grass, that is, temporal goods. For everything [Col. 1277C] given to the Church by the rich is hay. And he himself is

### VERSE 10.—“Who gives their food to the beasts, and to the young ravens that call upon him.”

Who gives to beasts, or cattle—that is, to the simple members of the Church, namely the Lord’s flocks—their food, [Augustine] that is, the pasture of the divine word; because God feeds them through men: who receive hay, that is, through preachers who distribute spiritual things to them, from whom they reap carnal things. And he gives food to the young ravens that call upon him. Ravens are Gentiles, black in sins. Hence the Jews, who called themselves alone righteous, called all Gentiles sinners. And truly our fathers were ravens, because sinners and idolaters; but we do not remain so. Yet we are rightly called [Col. 1277D] young ravens, and are such. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] For young ravens are said to feed on the dew of heaven, and, through the benefit of their age, not to know their fathers’ food—that is, the stench of corpses. So children of pagans who do not imitate their fathers’ rites are innocent and call upon him; the raven does not call upon him. But we, having been forgiven, call upon him. Therefore he gives food to the young ravens, that is, the children of pagans, who call upon him.

### VERSE 11.—“He will not take pleasure in the strength of a horse, nor will he delight in the legs of a man.”

Not in the strength of a horse, [Gloss, interlinear] as though he feeds beasts and young ones, but he will not have pleasure—that is, delight—in the strength or power of a horse, that is, in the pride of the stubborn. For pride is understood through the horse, because a man rides higher upon a horse. [Col. 1278A] Its neck also truly indicates pride, and it is swift in running. Nor will he take delight in the legs of a man, that is, in the disorderly bearing of one presumptuous and bold. [Alcuin.] By “man” he denotes bold presumption; by “legs,” a disorderly gait. Or according to another reading: “nor in the tents of a man,” that is, in the conventicles of heretics, will he take pleasure. [Augustine.] Observe that he does not say “in the tents of God,” but “of a man,” thereby indicating the tents of bold heretics. For there is also a tent of God, namely the Church; separating themselves from it, heretics have set up tents for themselves. Hence perhaps a young raven in the Church, lacking temporal honor, says: “I have chosen to be lowly in the house of my God, rather than dwell in the tent of a sinner” (Ps. 83). [Col. 1278B] For he does not make himself a tent outside the Church, in which God has no pleasure.

### VERSE 12.—“The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him, and in those who hope 313 in his mercy.”

Pleasure. [Gloss, interlinear.] As if to say: In the proud, the heretical, and the disorderly, he has no pleasure. The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him, and in those who hope in his mercy: that is, the Lord takes pleasure in those who fear and hope. He joined hope to fear because fear has no force without hope of pardon. [Augustine.] Judas indeed, when repentant, feared; but he did not hope in mercy. Therefore, despairing, he ran to the noose and hanged himself. Whoever therefore fears God should hope, and flee from him to him: from the angry one [Col. 1278C] to the appeased one. You will appease him, moreover, if you hope in his mercy; and thereafter take such care not to sin that you beg forgiveness for past sins, that they may be remitted to you.

## COMPARISON ON PSALM 146: “PRAISE THE LORD, FOR PSALMODY IS GOOD,” etc.

### VERSE 1.—“Praise the Lord, for psalmody is good. Let it be pleasant for our God,” etc.

The Hebrew punctuates differently, so that the words “for our God” belong to what precedes in this manner: “for it is good to sing to our God.” Yet what follows makes it abundantly clear that it can be referred either way, and not all translators assign the same hypostigme [pointing] everywhere. For Sanctes says: “Praise the Lord, because it is good to sing to our God, because praise is sweet and fitting.” But Münster: “Because it is good and pleasant to sing to our God; praise is desirable.” Why, however, does he translate, [Col. 1278D] “praise is desirable,” where others say “it is beautiful”? He gives the reason: because some derive the Hebrew *NAVAH* from *IVAH*, that is, “he desired,” so that it is its passive; others, however, derive it from *NAVEH*, which signifies “fitting” or “beautiful.”

### VERSE 9.—“And grass for the service of men.”

This clause is not found in the Hebrew. Very many other things were added by the Septuagint, not without the authority of the Holy Spirit or some other reason, as has been discussed above more than once at length. St. Hilary observed that some codices have it and some do not have it. The Greeks undoubtedly now read this portion.

### VERSE 11.—“Nor in the legs of a man.”

Sts. Hilary and Augustine, and the Roman Psalter, have: “nor in the tents of a man.” Arnobius, however, indicates that the Greek reads “in the legs,” ἐν ταῖς κνήμαις, which Jerome nevertheless translates as περικνημίδας, that is, “ornaments of the legs,” which he applies tropologically to a lustful gait. Arnobius takes it as standing for stability, as though we cannot [Col. 1279] stand or persevere through ourselves. Perhaps some Greek copies read σκηναῖς, “tents.” But undoubtedly the Hebrew reads “in the legs,” *BESCHOQUE*.

## PSALM 147

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “ALLELUIA OF HAGGAI AND ZECHARIAH.”

[Note: “Of Haggai and Zechariah” has been added to the title. [Col. 1279D]]

[Col. 1279A]

Praise, Jerusalem. Title: Alleluia, of Haggai and Zechariah. [Augustine.] These prophets prophesied, during the Babylonian captivity, the rebuilding of Jerusalem which, as Jeremiah foretold (Jer. 25), occurred after seventy years. In it they understood the spiritual restoration of the heavenly Jerusalem; they foretold it under the figure of that earthly restoration and praised the Lord for it. It is to be completed after seventy years—that is, after the revolution of all time, which proceeds through seven days. For it the Prophet here praises God, just as the aforementioned prophets praised God under a figure. And this is the sense of the title: This is an alleluia, that is, praise of God—praise, I say, of Haggai and Zechariah: that is, concerning the rebuilding [Col. 1279B] of the heavenly Jerusalem which they foretold, and for which they praised God. This psalm produces in us love for the future Jerusalem, which it commends in many ways. This whole psalm also proclaims God’s power.

[Cassiodorus, Augustine.] Intention: it exhorts to praise. Method: the psalm has two parts. First, it speaks of the good things of the future Jerusalem. Second, it states the good things given to the saints here, at “Who sends forth.” Therefore, still situated in the captivity of this age, the Prophet, seeing the blessed people of the eternal Jerusalem—with the joy of hope set before the joy of sight—as though joining his heart, though not his body, to the angels, says: O

### VERSE 1.—“Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion.”

[Col. 1279C] Jerusalem, now heavenly and secure, praise the Lord. This alone is your occupation. The Prophet says this so that we may now rejoice in hope and desire her, hearing him—or her—thus uttering God’s praise. And he repeats: Praise your God, O Zion. Zion and Jerusalem are the same. Jerusalem means “vision of peace”; Zion, “watching,” or “contemplation”; and it is contemplation and vision of peace: contemplation of Christ, who is our peace. Or, according to another edition: “Praise together, O Jerusalem, the Lord.” I do not say simply, “Praise,” but “Praise together,” because you consist of many. You therefore, consisting of many, praise together. And you, O Zion, praise your God. Therefore I add simply, “Praise,” because you have become one. He understands Zion and Jerusalem in the same way as before. [Col. 1279D] And as if to say, “Why shall I praise?” he answers:

### VERSE 2.—“For he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you.”

For he has strengthened, or established—not merely placed—the bars or bolts of your gates. The strengthening of bars does not occur except when the gates are shut. Thus he indicates that the gate is closed: the prudent virgins having been admitted, [Col. 1280A] and the foolish excluded, so that no one may now go out or enter. [Augustine.] Appropriately, after the exhortation to praise he adds concerning the shut gates. For Jerusalem, with its gate shut, praises securely, because no one goes out from whom it may suffer grief; no one enters whom it may fear. No friend leaves it, nor does a stranger enter there, as now happens—and hence there are scandals. And the meaning is: He has blessed your children within you, whom you once bore and who now rest within you, not wandering abroad as pilgrims. For they have flown from the nest of fear to heavenly and eternal dwellings, where they are children and secure. Who has blessed them?

### VERSE 3.—“Who has made your borders peace, and satisfies you with the fat of wheat.”

Who has made your borders peace, [Augustine] perfect peace. As if to say: Everything within enjoys peace. Outside is Gehenna; and in that peace there is fullness and no want. He satisfies you with the fat of wheat, that is, with the bread which descended from heaven, which, enclosed in flesh in the world, was known by faith alone. But then we shall see him as he is, and there will be that perfect fullness or security.

### PART II. VERSE 4.—“Who sends forth his word to the earth; his speech runs swiftly.”

Who sends forth. [Cassiodorus, Augustine.] The second part, in which he adds the gifts given here to the elect, through which the truth of the future may be recognized. As if to say: Those things mentioned before will be there; but what does he meanwhile give us in this pilgrimage? Behold, he is the one who sends his utterance to the earth, that is, the Word, having assumed flesh, to the earth, that he may be known on earth. Otherwise we should not be raised to the fat of wheat which satisfies, unless he sent [Col. 1280C] the Word to the earth by which we are weighed down and hindered from returning. For on earth we labor, weary, infirm, sluggish, cold; but he does not abandon us in the wilderness. Rather, he rains manna, because he sends his Word to the earth, and his speech runs swiftly, [Cassiodorus] because Christ’s speech, or Christ, quickly filled the world with the knowledge of truth. [Augustine.] Or according to another reading: “his speech runs unto swiftness,” or “to swiftness”—a phrase than which nothing more choice or expressive could be said. He does not say that the Word is swift; for something becomes swift by swiftness, in which it participates more or less, just as something is called hot through participation in heat and cold through participation in cold. One thing is more or less swift or hot than another according as it participates more or less in swiftness or heat. [Col. 1280D] And just as nothing is hotter than the heat by which other things are hot, so nothing is swifter than the swiftness by which other things are called swift. Therefore, just as one might say of something, “It is hot unto heat,” that is, it is so hot that it may itself be called heat, so it is said of God’s Word: “It ran unto swiftness,” that is, so that it is swiftness itself—though this is said by a certain similitude. For what is swift, such as a horse, an angel, or wind, is somewhere, not everywhere. But swiftness itself is everywhere: it is not in one part, is confined nowhere; it is not now in horses or winds but is diffused in countless other things, and at the same instants of time throughout all lands. This belongs to the Word of God: namely, not to be in one part, but to be everywhere through itself. This is the Wisdom of God, which, as is read in the Book of Wisdom, “reaches mightily from end to end” (Wis. 8), yet not by local motion but by immobility—just as if some rocky mass filled a place. [Col. 1281A] It is said to reach from one end of that place to the other, yet it does not leave one part in taking up another. That Word therefore has no motion, and that Wisdom is solid and everywhere. Yet of the spirit of Wisdom it is said in the Book of Wisdom: “mobile, certain, undefiled” (Wis. 7). But that very swiftness makes Wisdom be called a mobile activity—not so that it leaves this thing and touches that, but that it is always everywhere and is held enclosed nowhere. But who is sufficient to think these things? Surely no one. Nevertheless, there is hope of grasping the Word, because God has predestined us. And this is what he says:

### VERSE 5.—“Who gives snow like wool; he scatters mist like ashes.”

Who gives snow like wool, mist. [Augustine.] Here he says what Christ’s coming bestows. For as snow freezes above and falls to the depths, so, with love growing cold, human nature fell down to earth and, wrapped in a sluggish body, became as snow. But in this snow [Col. 1281C] are those predestined, who are like wool, from whom, namely, he will make something. For wool is the material of a garment, and from these persons, still cold in spirit, who have been predestined, is made Christ’s garment without spot or wrinkle. Hence Christ’s garment rightly shone on the mountain like snow, because Christ’s garment is made from this snow. But those predestined must be called to repentance, according to: “Whom he predestined, them he also called” (Rom. 8). Yet he did not come to call the righteous but sinners, that is, those confessing their sins and ignorance; and he calls these to repentance. And while he calls to repentance, [Col. 1281D] he scatters mist like ashes. Ash pertains to humility and repentance, because ashes and haircloth are the weapons of penitents; but mist indicates the darkness of sin and ignorance. When someone is called to understand God and told, “Grasp the truth,” he begins to wish to grasp the truth, but is not sufficient for it and suffers darkness. There is therefore still mist for him, so that he may know that he does not know and cannot grasp what he ought to know. But if he cannot penetrate truth’s mystery, let him repent of the sins through which he came into this difficulty of seeing; and so the mist will be salutary to him, which God scatters like ashes—that is, removes through the humility of repentance signified by ashes. Thus Abraham also says to God, “I am ashes” (Gen. 18): this confession is the humility [Col. 1282A] of the penitent. Therefore he scatters the mist—which stands for the darkness of sin—like ashes: that is, he removes it through humility and repentance, to which he calls those whom he predestined and has called to repentance.

### VERSE 6.—“He sends his crystal like morsels: before the face of his cold, who can endure?”

He sends his “crystal” (with masculine *suum*, or feminine *suam*) like morsels or pieces of bread. [Augustine.] By “crystal” he means the obstinate, from whom nevertheless he feeds others. The sense is: his crystal, that is, obstinate persons whom he has indeed predestined, who are not easily melted like snow. He sends them like morsels, or pieces of bread, [Augustine] that is, he makes them such that they feed others with God’s word and preach the truth which they had attacked; to others they are as bread. Hence the Apostle says: “We, though many, are one bread in Christ” (1 Cor. 10). All, therefore, are one bread; but individuals are pieces. Such was Paul. For he was crystal, that is, hard and bright: hard because he persecuted God’s Church, resisting the truth and crying out against the Gospel; bright because he was skilled in the Law. Yet afterward, when the snow, mist, and crystal had been dissolved before the face, he became bread and taught truth. Here he heightens the danger so that the grace of deliverance may be greater, as though some are snow, mist, and crystal. God dissolves these; but unless he dissolves them, who can endure or stand before the face of the cold—of vices and obstinacy? The cold, I say, is his, namely God’s. [Col. 1282C] It is called his cold, not because he produces it, but because he permits it to occur: that is, because he abandons the sinner and does not call, open the understanding, or pour in grace. Unless, therefore, he dissolves it, who can endure? No one. And who else will dissolve it but he? No one. Of this cold the Apostle says: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of the sin of death. And who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). As if he said: “I grow cold; I am wretched. No one frees from the misery of this cold except God’s grace.” Hence here also he adds:

### VERSE 7.—“He will send forth his word and melt them; his spirit will blow, and the waters will flow.”

He will send forth his word. [Augustine.] As if to say: Although no one can stand by himself before the face of cold, nevertheless there is no cause for despair, because the Lord will send forth his Word, having assumed flesh; and he will melt them, [Col. 1282D] namely, cloud, mist, and crystal. For when God’s Word comes, neither cold, darkness, nor hardness can despair. They are melted for salvation and pour spiritual streams of benefit over others. And his spirit will blow, namely the warm south wind; and the waters—[Augustine, Cassiodorus] the streams of doctrine and grace—will flow, so that others may drink from them, according to: “All you who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. 55). Thus the foregoing is rightly understood mystically. But it is also manifest literally, because God scatters snow like wool and mist like ashes; he makes crystal like fragments of white bread. Crystal is a certain substance resembling glass, but white. It is said to be snow hardened into ice over many years, so that it cannot be melted. [Col. 1283A] These three comparisons are fittingly noted here, because, in the literal sense, they display great works of God. But, mystically understood, they signify something else, which we have set forth above and have pursued thus far in the exposition.

### VERSE 8.—“Who declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and judgments to Israel.”

Who declares. [Augustine.] As if to say: His spirit will blow—the spirit, I say, of him who declares his word to Jacob, that is, to the new people of Christians, signified by Jacob; and declares his statutes and judgments, that is, his just judgments, to Israel. Israel and Jacob signify the same thing: namely, the people of believers, to whom he declares his just judgments—that not only the unrighteous but even the righteous suffer here, by the merit of God’s just [Col. 1283B] judgment. As Peter says, this judgment begins at the house of God (1 Pet. 4), presently with believers. For Christ alone paid what he did not steal; in him the ruler of the world found nothing. And if the beginning is with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel? And if the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly appear? (1 Pet. 4). This judgment of God—that the righteous and the unrighteous suffer according to their deserts, and that the righteous are delivered not by their own merits but by God’s grace—the Lord did not announce to every nation, but only to Israel, that is, to the new people, in which the Gentiles too are present.

### VERSE 9.—“He has not done so for every nation, and he has not made his judgments known to them.”

He has not done so for every nation, or people, and he has not made his judgments known to them. [Augustine, Alcuin.] For the Gentiles who have been cut from the wild olive and grafted into the good [Col. 1283C] olive [Col. 1284A] ought no longer to be called Gentiles, but one people in Christ. Or literally: he understands Jews by Jacob and Israel, to whom Christ himself declares his word; and he has not made his judgments known to them. He has not done this for others; hence he adds: “He has not done so for every nation, and he has not made his judgments known to them,” because he did not personally preach to another nation or people, according to: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15). Observe the order found in the four foregoing psalms of God’s praises. First he treated the precepts of the divine proclamation; second, the perversity of the world to be avoided; third, the gathering of the Church; fourth, he commands praise, now that it has been gathered in peace, for its security and love. To that choir gathered from the regions of the world he further connects a threefold cause for rejoicing, adding three other psalms of praise, so that in this work the grace of the Trinity may shine forth.

## COMPARISON ON PSALM 147: “PRAISE, JERUSALEM, THE LORD,” etc.

### VERSE 5.—“Mist like ashes.”

St. Jerome writes in his Commentaries that the Latin translator rendered “mist” incorrectly. For what is called ὁμίχλη in Greek, the Hebrew has *KEPHOR*, that is, “frost.” Arnobius indeed reads “mist,” but interprets “frost.” These are his words: “Mist which is scattered like ashes: frost which enriches all crops enclosed within the earth’s depths; the more it has settled upon the sown fields, the more abundantly it prospers in the ears of grain.” Yet St. Jerome himself, where he translates Amos 4, “making the morning mist,” has the Septuagint: ποιῶν [Col. 1284C] ὄρθρον καὶ ὁμίχλην, “making morning and mist.”

## PSALM 148

[Col. 1283]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “ALLELUIA OF HAGGAI AND ZECHARIAH.”

[Note: “Of Haggai and Zechariah” has been added by the Septuagint. [Col. 1283]]

[Col. 1283C]

Praise the Lord from the heavens. Title: Alleluia of Haggai and Zechariah. [Augustine.] Haggai and Zechariah, who during the Babylonian captivity foretold the liberation of the earthly Jerusalem, powerfully urge us toward the future liberation of the spiritual Jerusalem, which they understood beneath that actual one and for which they especially praised the Lord. Let us also, by their example, as though we had despised the Babylon of this pilgrimage of ours, securely meditate beforehand here upon the praise which we shall render eternally. Hence the Prophet here, by mention of a few, urges the whole creation to praise God. For all things praise God either in themselves or through others. Some have a spirit for praising God and praise him in that affection by which God pleases them; others have no understanding, but are nevertheless good in their own order and are referred to the beauty of the universe. They do not praise him by themselves, but from them God is praised by those attending to them. Thus in a certain manner they praise him, because from them there arises in us praise of God, to which the Prophet here exhorts us on account of our spiritual liberation, which the aforementioned [Col. 1283D] prophets signified in mystery as future. Therefore the title contains their names. And this is its sense: This is an alleluia, that is, praise of God, of Haggai and Zechariah—that is, for the future liberation for which the aforementioned prophets praised God. Intention: it exhorts to praise. Method: the psalm has two parts. First, he exhorts heavenly things to praise; second, earthly things, at “Praise the Lord from the earth.” And God is fittingly first praised from the heavens, afterward from the earth; for he is the one who made heaven and earth, and all things are contained in heavenly and earthly things. Thus, when we applaud some people doing good deeds, we say, “Go on, go on.” So the Prophet, rejoicing with angels who praise God, says: O you who are,

### VERSE 1.—“Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights.”

From the heavens—[Augustine] that is, you angels—praise the Lord. He does not command or urge the angels to do this, but joins his own rejoicing to them as they do it, because what they do pleases him. And, with his heart lifted up, he is with them in hope; and he repeats: O you who are in the heights, praise him. He then specifies to whom he directs this rejoicing.

### VERSE 2.—“Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers.”

[Col. 1285A] Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers. [Cassiodorus.] “Powers” is a general name for all heavenly spirits, though at times it is taken for one order; when they are sent, however, they are called angels.

### VERSE 3.—“Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light.”

Praise him, sun and moon. [Jerome.] It should be noted that he began with invisible things, which are worthier, and then sets forth visible things, which are less worthy. For the sun, moon, and all visible things yield place to invisible things, with which he begins here, saying: Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light. [Cassiodorus.] And by “light” he understands generally all things possessing light, which cannot be enumerated.

### VERSE 4.—“Praise him, heavens of heavens; and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord.”

Praise him, heavens of heavens. [Cassiodorus.] He speaks in the plural because there are several heavens. And let the waters above the heavens, divided from those beneath the firmament, praise the Lord’s name. The heavens and waters do so. For it is an exceeding praise that the tenuous heavens stand firm and sustain waters that are heavier. Unless commanded, these waters flow down as frosts; and, as is said, when heaven’s floodgates are opened, they are sent down in rain. And as if someone should ask, “What did he grant them, for which they praise?” he adds: much.

### VERSE 5.—“For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.”

[Col. 1285C] For he spoke and they were made. [Augustine.] In these words, behold, he signifies the Word through whom all things were made. Hence: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1). Therefore he spoke—that is, he begot the Word—and through him they were made. [Cassiodorus.] He says this against those who say that the world is coeternal with God. He commanded his Word, and they were created. First he said “made,” afterward “created.” For we too can make, but not create; to create properly means to make something from nothing. Therefore he alone creates, which belongs properly to deity.

### VERSE 6.—“He established them for ever and ever; he set a commandment, and it shall not pass away.”

He established them—all the things above, all heavenly things—for ever and ever. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] For though there will be a new heaven, nevertheless the things well established by God are said to stand, since they are renewed by him and remain better; and this is praise from power. For he is almighty whose works are not changed. And he set for them a commandment, that is, a law and condition, namely that they praise him; and it shall not pass away without being fulfilled, for all things praise him either in themselves or through others.

### PART II. VERSE 7.—“Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all deeps.”

Praise the Lord. [Augustine.] The second part. Having enumerated heavenly things, he descends to earthly things. Turning, therefore, toward them, as though exhorting us to praise God through consideration [Col. 1286A] of those things which, when considered, disclose God’s praise, he says: O you who are from the earth, praise the Lord—namely dragons, and so forth. Dragons dwell about water and, emerging from caves, are borne into the air, which is stirred up on their account; there are no greater living creatures upon the earth. Therefore he began with them. And all deeps. Deeps are depths of milky waters and all seas. The cloudy air also belongs to the deep: there are clouds, winds, storms, rains, lightning flashes, thunder, hail, snow, and generally whatever may arise over the earth from moist and darkened air. [Augustine.] He called all this by the name “earth,” because it is exceedingly changeable. Yet although all these things are mutable and disturbed, they have their place and order, fulfill according to their measure the beauty of the universe, and thus praise God. He therefore urges us, by consideration of them, to praise, adding:

### VERSE 8.—“Fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy winds, which fulfill his word.”

Fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy winds, [Augustine] which praise the Lord’s name. Although all these may seem disturbed and to some foolish persons to be driven by chance, nevertheless they fulfill his word. He says this because it seemed to some that God ruled things above but neglected these lower things, which were governed by accidents. Yet God also directs these, and in these least things he is praised and alleluia is sung.

### VERSES 9–10.—“Mountains and all hills, fruit-bearing trees and all cedars; beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds.”

[Col. 1286C] Mountains and all hills, fruit-bearing trees and all cedars. [Jerome.] Greater beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds, should praise him—and the rest. Then he comes to human beings, saying:

### VERSES 11–12.—“Kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth; young men and virgins, old men together with the younger, let them praise the name of the Lord, because his name alone is exalted.”

Kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth; young men and virgins, old men together with the younger—[Cassiodorus] that is, people of every sex and every age—should praise the Lord’s name. And why? He gives the reason: let them praise from his magnificence, [Augustine] namely because his name alone is exalted. For no one is exalted except under him.

### VERSE 13.—“His confession is above heaven and earth; and he has exalted the horn of his people.”

[Col. 1286D] Confession. [Augustine.] Above he spoke first of heaven, then of earth; here of all together. By heaven he understands all higher things; by earth, all lower things. And the sense is: His confession is over heaven and earth—that is, all things confess him, either in themselves or through others. The beauty of all things is the voice of those confessing him in those who attend to them: that is, those who attend to them praise him from earthly and heavenly things, than whom there is nothing better. For whatever he made is below him, and whatever pleases in these things is less than he. If, therefore, you love the visible thing he made, love much more the invisible one who made it. Through visible things his invisible things are understood. [Cassiodorus.] Or: His confession is above heaven and earth; that is, his praise from himself is greater than that from creatures, because he is more to be praised for his own sake than for creatures. “He will exalt,” or “he has exalted.” As if to say: I say that they should praise because his name is exalted; and so they should, because he will exalt—or has exalted—the horn, that is, the power and dignity, of his people. Behold what Haggai and Zechariah prophesied in captivity: namely, the exultation of God’s people. At present the horn of his people is low in tribulations; but when the Lord comes, it will be exalted.

### VERSE 14.—“A hymn for all his saints, for the children of Israel, the people drawing near to him.”

Hymn. [Augustine.] As if to say: You will exalt the horn; therefore let there now be a hymn for all his saints, for whom at the end there will also be an everlasting hymn. Hence: “For ever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83). [Col. 1287B] A hymn, however, has three things: song, praise, and God—that is, a hymn is praise of God with song. Let the saints therefore sing it now, since at the end they will receive the eternal hymn. And who are the saints for whom there ought to be a hymn? For the children of Israel, namely, let there be a hymn. Who are the children of Israel? Those who draw near to God. And this is the meaning of “the people drawing near to him”: let there be a hymn for those drawing near to him, not in flesh but in faith.

## COMPARISON ON PSALM 148: “PRAISE THE LORD FROM THE HEAVENS,” etc.

### VERSE 1.—“For he spoke and they were made.”

This clause is not in the Hebrew. What follows—“He commanded and they were created”—seemed to explain God’s speech in the beginning of Genesis. Therefore the interpreters prefaced it with the former figure of speech, so that it might cohere with the latter.

### VERSE 8.—“Ice.”

More recent translators render it “vapor,” which they understand, apparently, as hot and dry, because the translator to Campen said *camna*. Münster, however, in his lexicon observes that some also take *QUITOR* as “ice,” which is what St. Jerome did.

## PSALM 149

[Col. 1287]

### TITLE OF THE PSALM: “ALLELUIA.”

[Col. 1287B]

Sing to the Lord. Title: Alleluia. [Cassiodorus.] After all creatures, whom in the preceding psalm he exhorted to praise the Lord because they were created by him, he here invites Israel more properly and particularly to a new [Col. 1287C] song because of the newness wrought for it, which is a more wondrous work of God. [Augustine, Cassiodorus.] This is the sanctification of Israel through which it was made new from old. Intention: it exhorts to praise. Method: the psalm has two parts. First, in many ways he urges them to praise the King, because he is well-disposed and beneficent toward them. Second, he treats of the joys and power of the saints, at “They shall exult.” Therefore, exhorting the faithful to a new song, he says:

### VERSE 1.—“Sing to the Lord a new song; his praise in the assembly of the saints.”

Sing to the Lord a new song, concerning the mystery of redemption and the promise of eternity. [Aug.] As though he said: Whoever wishes to sing this song, let him love eternal things, wherein he may become new. For the old man sings an old song about earthly things. The new man sings a new one [Col. 1287D] about spiritual things: a song, that is, of peace, a song of charity. For whoever follows old hostility rather than new charity does not sing the new song. He then specifies where and by whom this song ought to be sung, saying: His praise is in the congregation of the saints, namely. For this praise is not to be sung everywhere or by everyone, but in the Catholic Church and by the saints, who are Israel.

VERSE 2.—“Let Israel rejoice in him who made him, and let the daughters of Zion exult in their king.”

Let Israel rejoice, [Aug.] even if in hope, and though it suffers many things here. Let Israel rejoice in him who made him, even a second time, that he might be Israel; and the sons, or daughters, of Zion—these are the same as Israel—and let the daughters of Zion exult in their king, that is, in Christ, who is king and priest. For as [Col. 1288B] king he fought for us, conquering the devil from the cross; as priest he offered himself for us, finding nothing in human beings which he could offer on their behalf.

VERSE 3.—“Let them praise his name in the choir; let them sing to him with timbrel and psaltery.”

[Col. 1288C] Let them praise his name. [Aug.] How? In the choir, that is, in harmony of conduct; and with the timbrel, that is, in the mortification of the flesh; and with the psaltery, that is, in spiritual activity, let them sing to him. And why they should sing, he adds:

VERSE 4.—“For the Lord is well pleased with his people, and he has exalted the meek unto salvation.”

For the Lord is well pleased with his people. [Cassiod.] In the first creation of things we read that everything pleased God; but afterwards, when their conditions had changed, we read both that he repented and that he rejoiced. Hence: “It repenteth me that I have made man” (Gen. VI). And elsewhere: “I rejoice over one sinner doing penance” (Luke XV). [Aug., Cassiod.] But here he says, “The Lord is well pleased with his people,” when he forgives sins. Or it may be understood of the future, beginning from the words, “His praise shall be in the congregation of the saints,” that is, in the future Jerusalem; and there, “Let Israel rejoice in him who made him, and let the daughters of Zion exult.” In whom? In their king, that is, in Christ, whom they will then see face to face; and “let them praise his name in the choir,” that is, in the unity of charity, because then there will be no dispersion, but a most dear unity. And “let them sing to him with timbrel and psaltery,” that is, concerning the fact that timbrel and psaltery were theirs here below. For then the saints’ exultation will be over timbrel and psaltery, not the acts themselves. Therefore let them sing, because there the Lord is well pleased with his people—a fact which will then appear, when he makes them equal to the angels. Hence he adds: “And he shall exult,” or, “He has exalted, the meek unto eternal salvation.”

[Col. 1289A] VERSE 5.—“The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their resting-places.”

They shall exult. [Cassiod.] The second part, in which he treats of the joys and power of the saints. This sequence is first read as referring to the present, up to the end of the psalm. As though he said: In the future he will exalt the meek, and therefore the saints shall exult here in glory. Glory is the frequent praise of good deeds, in which the righteous will rejoice. Where?
