Not outwardly, in popular favor, but in their resting-places, [Aug.] that is, in conscience. This is because they have so good a Lord, who gives sinners pardon and grace, and eternal life to the undeserving. The fool rejoices outwardly in the talk of men; but this is the saints’ manner of joy here: that they refer their good things to him who gave them.

[Col. 1289B] VERSE 6.—“The exultations of God are in their throat, and two-edged swords in their hands.”

The exultations of God, [Aug.] are in their throat or jaws, that is, in their tongue. For they rejoice in their resting-places and in their throat—that is, in heart and tongue—in such a way that they attribute not to themselves the fact that they are good, but to God, from whom they received what they are, and they hope for what they are not yet. And the two-edged swords—or spears, or double-sharpened, or sharp swords—that is, the word of Christ, which is sharp in the Old and New Testaments, shall be in their hands, that is, in their power, so that they may speak where they wish and to whom they wish. For what purpose?

VERSE 7.—“To execute vengeance among the nations, rebukes among the peoples.”

To execute vengeance among the nations, [Aug.] [Col. 1289C] that is, in order that by that double-sharpened sword they may kill sinners, so that they may thus be made alive, according to: “I will kill, and I will make alive” (Deut. XXXII). And lest you suppose that blood is being shed, he explains and specifies: that is, “to make rebukes,” or reproofs, among the peoples. And:

VERSE 8.—“To bind their kings in fetters, and their nobles in iron manacles.”

To bind their kings in fetters, [Aug.] that is, in the precepts of God; and to bind their nobles in manacles, or iron bonds, that is, in God’s commandments, which are called iron bonds, hard because they are unbreakable. Such are: “What God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Matt. XIX); and likewise: “Art thou bound unto a wife? seek not to be loosed” (I Cor. VII). By these bonds the kings of the nations and the nobles of the world are bound by the weak and despised of this world, whom the Lord chose in order to confound the strong. He filled these persons with the Holy Spirit and gave them double-sharpened swords, so that they might turn the hearts of nobles to the fear of Christ, and, despising secular nobility, choose poverty and nobility in Christ. For he wished an emperor to benefit from a fisherman, not a fisherman from an emperor. Through these, therefore, he bound kings and nobles with iron bonds, lest they advance to unlawful things. And this is the judgment which the saints execute among all nations. Hence he adds:

316 VERSE 9.—“That they may execute upon them the judgment written: this glory is for all his saints.”

[Col. 1290A] That they may execute. [Aug.] As though he said: For this purpose they have swords in their hands: that they may execute upon them the judgment written, that is, established by the Fathers. For these things were written beforehand and are now being fulfilled. They were once read but not done; now they are done. And he concludes thus: “This glory is for all his saints,” namely, as has been said, throughout all nations. Throughout the whole world the saints do this: thus they glory, thus they exult in their throat, thus they rejoice in their resting-places, thus they shall exult in glory, thus they sing the new song, thus they say Alleluia with heart, mouth, and life.

Or thus: “This is glory.” As though he said: Thus and thus the saints act. And “this glory is for all his saints,” that is, in this way they will attain eternal glory. [Cassiod.] Or it may be understood from the words, “They shall exult,” and the whole taken as referring to the future, [Col. 1290B] when the power and might of God are proclaimed in the glory of the saints. As though he said: He shall exalt the meek, and then the saints shall exult in glory, that is, in the vengeance upon the wicked. For the vengeance of sinners is the glory of the saints. “And they shall rejoice in their resting-places,” that is, in their separate dwellings, of which the Lord says: “In my Father’s house are many mansions” (John XIV). Then the exultations of God shall be in their throat, because in heart and tongue they do not cease to praise God, from whom they possess eternal things; and two-edged swords—that is, the word of God or the sentence of judgment concerning the good and the evil—shall be in their hands, that is, in their power. For then, receiving the authority of God’s word, they shall judge with the Lord, sitting upon twelve seats. And then vengeance and rebuke among the peoples shall truly take place. Hence he adds, [Col. 1290C] “to execute,” etc. As though he said: They shall have swords in their hands, to execute vengeance among the nations and rebukes among the peoples. Behold how great then shall be the glory and joy of the saints, when the poor, who were here an object of derision, shall have power to take vengeance on the proud.

“To bind their kings in fetters, and their nobles in iron manacles,” because then the kings of the earth and the nobles of the world shall be bound in fetters from which they shall not be free to depart; they shall bear iron bonds, heavy to carry and impossible to break, namely the torments of Gehenna. Thus the written judgment shall be carried out: “that they may execute.” As though he said: For this purpose they shall have swords, that they may execute upon them the judgment written, that is, approved by angels and all [Col. 1290D] saints, or mentioned in many passages of Scripture. Of this the Apostle says: “Know ye not that we shall judge angels?” (I Cor. VI). And lest you suppose that this authority belongs to the apostles alone, he adds: “And this glory,” namely the authority of judgment, “is for all his saints,” that is, for all the perfect, who for Christ’s sake left all earthly things.

## Comparison on Psalm 149: “Sing to the Lord a New Song,” etc.

VERSE 2.—Daughters of Zion. Although “sons of Zion” and “daughters of Zion” have the same force, it is nevertheless evident that the Hebrew and Greek have “sons of Zion,” and thus all interpreters read **BENE SION**, “sons of Zion,” Υἱοί Σίων, “sons of Zion.” Indeed, Scripture repeatedly says now “sons of Zion,” now “daughters.” But St. Jerome warns us in his letter to Sunia that, where there is no change of sense, we should avoid superfluous disputes, which he calls foolishness.

[Col. 1291A] VERSE 3.—With the psaltery. Hebrew: **CINNOR**, that is, “lyre.” But Jerome writes to Marcella, in the letter which discusses what **SELAH** means among the Hebrews, that at that time the psalms were sung in joined voice to instrumental accompaniment. Therefore it should not seem strange that they understood “psaltery” as “lyre.”

VERSE 7.—Exultations of God. The Hebrew and Greek have “exaltations,” and Arnobius reads in the same manner. Hebrew: **ROMEMOTH**; Greek: ὑψώσεις, “exaltations.” St. Augustine, however, reads “exultations.” And lest anyone allege a scribal error, he repeats it once and again in his exposition, joining it with what he had just said: “they shall rejoice in their resting-places.” However it may be, “the exultations of God” and “his exaltations” are his praises. It makes little difference.

# PSALM 150

[Col. 1291]

## TITLE OF THE PSALM: “ALLELUIA.”

[Col. 1291A]

Praise the Lord in his saints. Title: Alleluia. This psalm is the third of those which are without division. For this psalm is an indivisible unit, in which the purpose is that God should be praised because he gathered the saints, [Col. 1291B] restored them to his image after their frailty had been laid aside, and placed them, now conformed to his glory, in blessedness, where all abundance is found. Here, therefore, God’s praise in his saints is discussed: they, being glorified, praise without end. For the city of God, namely the unity of all saints, is exhorted to sing with mouth and mind. To this summit of divine praise all psalmody is brought, and this praise is sung here with bridal sweetness. Therefore, to those for whom the Prophet at the beginning of this book rightly set forth the pattern of upright conduct, now received into that heavenly Jerusalem, he says that God is to be praised in them, because he gave them all things, beginning thus:

VERSE 1.—“Praise the Lord in his saints; praise him in the firmament of his power.”

Praise the Lord in his saints, for the things which he gave [Col. 1291C] to his saints. Praise him in the firmament of his power, that is, because by his death he overcame the devil and led believers to heaven. And:

VERSE 2.—“Praise him for his mighty acts; praise him according to the multitude of his greatness.”

Praise him for his mighty acts, [Cassiod.] or for his powers, namely because all things are subjected under his feet, and every knee bends to him, of things heavenly, earthly, and infernal, as the Apostle says (Phil. II). Praise him according to the multitude of his greatness. But how can this be done, since there is no end to his greatness? Yet this is said to spiritual and holy persons, who praise without end. Since there is no end to his greatness, he is praised according [Col. 1291D] to it when he is praised without end. And “praise him according to the multitude of his greatness” means: praise him without end, just as there is no end to his greatness. [Cassiod.] He then says, by mystical comparisons until the end of the psalm, how he ought to be praised, adding:

VERSE 3.—“Praise him with the sound of the trumpet; praise him with psaltery and lyre.”

Praise him with the sound of the trumpet; praise him with psaltery and lyre. [Cassiod.] As though he said: Let the trumpet sound for the king; let the psaltery sing to God; let the lyre, along with the other instruments, sing to the bridegroom. For the trumpet is formidable, or is used in war, or is prepared for the arrivals of kings. The psaltery sounds in God’s praises and renders sound from above; [Col. 1292A] the lyre sings to the bridegroom and sounds from below. All these, compared with—that is, understood according to—human actions and the customary use of human acts, are figuratively said there to resound with the praises of God. For in the trumpet he is signified as king; in the psaltery, as God; in the lyre, [Col. 1292B] as bridegroom. The sense is: “Praise him with the sound of the trumpet,” that is, praise him as king, because he made you conquer in the devil’s war. And “praise him with the psaltery,” that is, as God, because he made you exalted. And “praise him with the lyre,” that is, as bridegroom, because he freed you from the depths.

VERSE 4.—“Praise him with timbrel and choir; praise him with strings and organ.”

Praise him with timbrel and choir, [Aug.] that is, in the changed flesh and in the harmony of voices and hearts. A timbrel is made from skin stretched upon wood. A choir, however, is an ordered gathering of voices. Praise him with strings and organ. He uses “strings” for every musical instrument that sounds through the tension of strings. An organ is like a tower constructed with different pipes, sounding by the blowing of bellows. [Cassiod.] And, so that you might understand all these things to be about [Col. 1292C] human beings, he comes to the human mouth; and, explaining what it is to praise with strings and organ, he adds:

VERSE 5.—“Praise him with well-sounding cymbals; praise him with cymbals of jubilation. Let every spirit praise the Lord.”

Praise him with well-sounding cymbals. [Aug., Cassiod.] The well-sounding cymbals are our lips, which, in accord with the heart, sound well in God’s praises; they resemble cymbals and produce harmony. Therefore they rightly stand among musical instruments. Literally, well-ringing cymbals are very small bowls made from mixed metals, which produce a high sound and make harmony. [Aug., Cassiod.] And lest you suppose that these cymbals are without a soul, he adds: “Praise him with cymbals of jubilation,” that is, with lips showing outwardly the jubilation conceived within. And because he wishes all things to be understood spiritually, he fittingly concludes: “Let every spirit,” namely angelic and human, “praise the Lord”; not flesh and blood, which shall not possess the kingdom of God, nor worldly ambition. Rather, that which is higher in the nature of things is exhorted to praise: namely spirit, which savors heavenly things and apprehends eternal things. In this psalm a brief and perfect instruction concerning the manner of divine praise is taught: namely, that all things should praise God spiritually. [Aug.] In these lies the perfection of all music: breath in the trumpet; striking in the lyre and cymbals; voice in the choir. By these musical instruments spiritual harmony is signified, perceived not by the ears but by a pure mind.

Or thus, beginning from [Col. 1293A] “Praise him in the firmament of his power”: namely, because he strengthened the saints by his power in such a way that they shall die no more. His power is in this firmament. For it is an act of great power that the saints shall now no longer die and that death shall have no more dominion over them (Rom. VI). And “praise him for his mighty acts,” or “for his powers,” that is, for the dominion which he bestowed upon his saints. For the power of God which he wrought in them is called their reigning with him forever; and these saints themselves are the multitude of his greatness. Hence he adds: “Praise him according to the multitude of his greatness,” that is, praise the saints, because he made them great and so numerous—namely, thousands of thousands. Hence: “Thousands of thousands ministered unto him, and ten hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII).

These same saints are signified in all [Col. 1293B] the musical instruments, which he employs to signify divine praise: that is, to signify the things for which and the manner in which they ought to praise. He begins with the trumpet, saying: “Praise him with the sound of the trumpet,” that is, because of the most excellent brightness of praise which is in you. “Praise him with psaltery and lyre,” that is, for heavenly and earthly things, as him who made heaven and earth. For the psaltery sounds from above, as has been said, and the lyre from below. Therefore heavenly things are signified by the psaltery and earthly things by the lyre. “Praise him with timbrel,” that is, in the changed flesh, which is without all corruption; for a timbrel is made of dried and weakened skin. “And choir,” that is, in peaceful fellowship. “And praise him with strings,” that is, in flesh now freed from corruption, which he had previously signified by the timbrel; [Col. 1293C] “and organ,” that is, in harmonious diversity. “Organ” is a general name for all musical instruments, although in common usage an organ is called that which sounds through inflated bellows. The strings, moreover, are flesh now free from corruption; to these he adds the organ, not so that they may sound individually, but so that they may sound together in most harmonious diversity, as happens in an organ. For the saints shall then have distinctions consonant, not dissonant—that is, agreeing—as a sweet song arises from diverse but not contrary voices.

“Praise him with well-sounding cymbals.” Cymbals strike one another in order to sound. Therefore they are compared by some to our lips; but I think it better to understand by cymbals those who, honoring one another, [Col. 1293D] give praise to God. Thus: “Praise him with well-sounding cymbals,” that is, in those who, mutually admonishing and honoring one another, praise God and delight. And it should be noted that there are three kinds of sound, 317 none of which is omitted here. Sound is produced by voice, as in a choir; by breath, as in a pipe; by striking, as in a lyre. All these belong to bridal hymns, but through comparisons, not literal properties, they are referred to God’s praise in his saints. Therefore, lest you suppose that lifeless cymbals are meant here, he adds: “Praise him with cymbals of jubilation.” For jubilation is ineffable praise, which proceeds only from the soul. “Let every spirit praise the Lord,” who is to be praised only spiritually.

It should be known that this is the one hundred and fiftieth psalm. [Col. 1294A] For David composed this book with the number of one hundred and fifty psalms, thereby commending to us a great mystery, which will become clear if the mystery of the number fifteen is not unknown. For what fifteen signifies in the order of single units, the same does one hundred and fifty in the order of tens, and fifteen hundred in the order of hundreds, and fifteen thousand in the order of thousands. For, as fifteen is built up from fifteen units, so one hundred and fifty is from fifteen tens, fifteen hundred from fifteen hundreds, and fifteen thousand from fifteen thousands. Therefore what is signified by fifteen is likewise signified by one hundred and fifty and by the other two numbers. Once the mystery of fifteen is known, the mystery of the rest will not be hidden.

Fifteen, then, signifies the harmony of the two Testaments. For it consists of seven and eight. Seven signifies the Old Testament, because in the Old Testament were observed the Sabbath, which is the seventh day; the seventh week; the seventh month; and the seventh year of the seventh decade, called the jubilee. Eight, however, refers to the New Testament, because in the New Testament the Lord’s Day is observed, which is the eighth after the seventh. It is also the first after the Sabbath, and the first in the first creation of things. According to this mystery is the number of the psalms. For this reason there are one hundred and fifty: that number is marked by [Col. 1294C] the same mystery as fifteen, in order that the teaching of this book may be shown to agree with both Testaments. This is why the psalms were composed in this number.

We must now consider why this work is divided into fifties and into three. It is divided by fifty because this number is marked by great and diverse mysteries. For this number, fifty, consists of the seventh of weeks—that is, seven sevens—with one added, as though the eighth itself, to complete fifty. By seven is figured the sevenfold Spirit, and likewise by fifty itself, because after this many days had been completed following the resurrection, the Holy Spirit came upon those gathered in Christ—the Spirit especially commended in Scripture by the number seven. The psalms are therefore divided by this number, to signify that we become participants in the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit if we keep the teaching of the psalms.

They are also divided by this number because fifty is divided into forty and ten. Thus Christ himself divided it: on the fortieth day after the resurrection he ascended into heaven, and ten days later he sent the Holy Spirit. By forty is indicated the temporal dwelling of this world. The law of Moses is also indicated by four, and the law by ten. For four has force in forty, and in the multiplication arising from four and ten, with respect to its signification. The world and the year have four parts, and there are four elements from which all bodies consist; but ten signifies the law because of the Decalogue of commandments written on the tablets. To this number, forty, ten is added in order to complete fifty. Ten, however, signifies eternal life. For it consists of three and seven. Three refers to the holy Trinity. Seven, however, which consists of three and four, refers to the twofold nature of man, who consists of soul and body. Three belongs to the soul because of the soul’s threefold power; four belongs to the body because of the four elements. Therefore the blessedness of eternity will be perfected in us when, having attained the sabbath-rest of both our natures, we are joined to the uncreated Trinity.

Thus, with ten added to forty as a reward rendered for fulfilling God’s law in this life, eternity itself is signified. The psalms are therefore divided by this number in order to signify that those who in the present life keep the teaching of this psalmody fulfill the law and in the future are crowned with the tenfold reward of eternal life. This gives the twofold reason why the psalms are divided by fifties. We must see why they are divided into three fifties: namely, in order that the blessed Trinity, which bestows all the things mentioned, may be intimated. For it gives sevenfold grace, helps toward fulfilling the law, and rewards in the future. Thus, when the Trinity multiplies fifty, it makes one hundred and fifty, the number which is the total and fullness of all the psalms.

[Note: [Col. 1295D] On the books of Psalms at length in the prologue.] It is also commonly asked whether the Psalms are one book or several. Jerome says that there are five books because of the five divisions made by “Let it be, let it be.” Yet this seems opposed by what is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “As it is written in the book of Psalms” (Acts I). It does not say “in the books,” but “in the book,” as though there were one book rather than several. This, however, does not conflict with the former position. For many books are rightly called one book, just as many churches are one Church and many heavens one heaven. Hence Scripture says that the waters are above the firmament, that is, heaven (Gen. I); and the same Scripture says: “And the waters that are above the heavens,” signifying the same thing by “heavens” and “firmament,” that is, heaven. “In the book of Psalms” may also mean in some one book of those five, although this usage is either absent or rare.

The Twelve Prophets too are called one book; and all the canonical Scriptures are by some called one book, because they agree in a wondrous and divine unity. Nor is this without significance, but seems worthy of great consideration: the first fifty treats of penitence; the second, of mercy [Col. 1296A] and judgment; the third, of God’s praise in his saints. These are the three states of Christian religion. For thus we advance toward eternal and blessed life. First, through penitence, we condemn sins, God calling to penitence those whom he predestined secretly with himself. Then, justified through mercy, we live rightly, lest we fear judgment in the future; God justifies those whom he has called here through mercy and fear of judgment, in which judgment all who work iniquity shall be destroyed from the city of the Lord. Finally, glorified, we enter into life, where we praise God without end.

These three states are also signified by what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Behold, I cast out devils and perform cures today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected” (Luke XIII). He casts out devils when he frees us from sins through penitence. He performs healing when through mercy he makes us live justly. In the future he shall be perfected when he crowns us. He also showed these states in his passion, sleep, and awakening. For in suffering on the cross he triumphed over the devil; in the tomb he rested; in the resurrection he exulted. Thus penitence, by which we conquer the devil, afflicts us; justice, by which we rest from evils, brings tranquility; eternal life, where God is seen as he is, glorifies and delights us. Therefore the voice of penitence is: “Have mercy on me, O God.” The voice of justice is: “I will sing of mercy and judgment unto thee, O Lord.” The voice of eternal life is: “Let every spirit praise the Lord.”

## Comparison on Psalm 150: “Praise the Lord in His Saints,” etc.

[Col. 1296C]

VERSE 1.—Praise the Lord in his saints. St. Jerome: “in his holy place”; others: “in his holiness,” or “in his sanctuary”; the Septuagint: ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις, “among his saints.” A heretic could cavil at this passage if anyone cited it in support of the honor due to saints. But although there are countless other passages which demonstrate with the greatest certainty that saints are to be venerated with due honor, this passage would nevertheless not be cited for that purpose without warrant, even according to the truth of the Hebrew. For those who translate thus intend it to be understood of the heavenly sanctuary, as Münster notes in his scholia. Yet no Catholic can doubt that a holy man is God’s temple, according to First Corinthians 3 and 6. The Chaldee also translates: “in the house of his sanctuary.” Add Psalm 113, where we sing: “Judah became his sanctification.” The Hebrews read **LEQUODSCHO**, that is, if rendered word for word, “in his sanctification”; here [Col. 1296D] is read **BEQUODSCHO**. Moreover, at the beginning of Psalm 148 it was said: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights.” I do not think that there are any heights higher than the saints themselves, apart from God, who is supremely high. Finally, St. Chrysostom, citing both readings in his exposition of this psalm, nevertheless interprets it as referring to the saints: “One,” he says, “reads ‘in his saints’; another, ‘in his sanctification.’ Either he speaks here of the people, or of holy life and holy men, or of the priesthood.” Thus he.

[Col. 1297]

# The Collections on All the Epistles of St. Paul the Apostle by Peter Lombard, Master of the Sentences and Former Bishop of Paris

Woven together with the highest skill and diligence from Sts. Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome, and certain other principal interpreters of Holy Scripture. An outstanding work, composed in the year 1140 and now first published.

(Paris: at the press of the heirs of Josse Badius Ascensius, December 1535, folio.)

# Preface of Peter Lombard

[Col. 1297A] The beginnings of things must first be sought, so that fuller knowledge of them may be obtained. For only then can the rationale of a matter be more easily explained, if its origin is learned. Therefore, if we show the manner and reason of the writings of the Epistles issued after the Gospel, the truth of what we say may become apparent.

It should therefore be known that, just as in the Old Testament, after the instruction of the Mosaic law—which contained the commandments of divine worship—prophetic teaching was necessary, in order that it might restrain the recurring sins of the people by the denunciation of punishments and exhort the same people, by promises of good things, to obey and serve the living Lord; so in the New Testament, after the Gospel, in which the order of Christian religion and the teaching of perfect holiness are handed down, there followed the very useful teaching [Col. 1297B] of the Epistles of Paul and others, in order that it might fortify the Church of God against heretical perversities, cut off vices as they arose, and exclude future controversies. These are the rags bound around ropes to draw Jeremiah out of the pit (Jer. XXXVIII). For the teaching of the Epistles, bound together with the harmonious testimonies of law, prophecy, and Gospel, as though with a threefold cord (Eccles. IV), draws the sinner from the pit of ignorance and unbelief into the light of grace and truth.

Among all writers of Epistles, Paul perhaps excels in three or more respects: namely, in the profundity of his work, in the defense of faith, and in the commendation of grace or the raising up of hope. In the profundity of his work, because this work is both more extensive than the others and more difficult to understand; in the defense of faith, because Paul, learned in the law and prophets, introduced fitting testimonies from the authoritative texts of law and prophecy in support of Catholic faith, so that he might be a foundation beneath the column; in the commendation of grace or the raising up of hope, because against the proud and arrogant, who presume upon their own works, he fought strongly, wisely, and keenly [Col. 1298A] for the commendation of God’s grace.

This grace appeared more evident and clear in him, because after, among other acts, violently persecuting the Church of God—an offence for which he was worthy of the greatest punishment—he received grace in place of a curse and mercy in place of condemnation. In him our hope is greatly raised. For just as, when we hear that David, a murderer and adulterer, recovered the spirit of prophecy through penitence, every despair of pardon is removed from the sinner; so, when we observe that Paul, formerly a persecutor of the Church, later became an apostle and preacher, our hope is raised not a little. Hence it is that these Epistles of Paul are used more frequently in the Church than the others, just as the psalms of David are used more than the other prophets.

[Col. 1298B] It should also be known that he wrote fourteen Epistles: ten to churches and four to individual persons, thereby intimating a mystery—that the sum of both Testaments is shown to be contained in this work. For ten signifies the Old Testament, while four is the mark of the New Testament. Therefore he wrote fourteen in order to indicate that he agrees with both laws and to refute the calumny of rivals who accused him of being a destroyer of God’s law given through Moses and who stirred up the hatred of the Jews against him. Wishing to have them appeased, he wrote ten to churches. Thus, just as Moses gave the people of Israel, delivered from the bondage of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, instruction in ten commandments, so the Apostle might instruct by the teaching of ten Epistles the churches of God redeemed from the devil’s power and the servitude of idolatry.

He also wrote fourteen in order to signify the harmony and agreement of the two Testaments, which Moses likewise showed in the two tablets of stone joined together, upon which the Decalogue of the law was inscribed. Our Moses also—that is, Christ—figured the same thing when he celebrated the Passover with the disciples at supper. There the rejected stone, borne by the corner and wonderful in our eyes, joined the heavenly bread with the typical lamb, ending the Old Testament and beginning the New. For by the lamb, the solemn sacrifice of the old law, and the bread, the form of the sacrament of the new law, he signified the two Testaments; and by joining these two, he declared the harmony of the Testaments mentioned above. For it is “a wheel in the midst of a wheel,” as Ezekiel saw.

From what has been said, therefore, the most evident reason of the mystery is clear: why he wrote fourteen Epistles and directed ten specifically to churches and four to persons. Thus the madness of some is refuted, who say that the Epistle [Col. 1299B] written to the Hebrews was not Paul’s, but Barnabas’s, Clement’s, Tertullian’s, or Luke’s. Such a cause led them into this error: neither is a salutation bearing his name set at its head, nor was it published in the same style as the others, but in a far more eloquent and splendid one.

They are sufficiently answered thus: if it is not to be called Paul’s because it does not have his name in its title, then neither is it Barnabas’s nor any of those mentioned, since it was written in none of their names. Nor should it be thought not to be Paul’s because it is more carefully written, since it is natural for everyone to be more capable in his own language than in a foreign one: he wrote that Epistle in Hebrew, but the others in Greek. He did not wish to prefix his name because he was hateful to the Hebrews, who regarded him as a destroyer of the law. Therefore, since he was about to treat of the abolition of the law and ceremonies, he rightly concealed his name, lest the hostility aroused by the name placed at the head should exclude the usefulness of the reading that followed. That Epistle, therefore, is Paul’s as the others are.

The order of the Epistles is also commonly asked about: why they are not arranged in the order in which the Apostle published them. It is clear that they are not, since the Epistle written to the Romans is placed first, although it was not written before all the others. For he seems to have written the Epistle to the Corinthians before this one, because it is plainly shown that he wrote this one from Corinth by what he says: “I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a minister of the Church which is at Cenchreae” [Col. 1299D] (Rom. 16). For Cenchreae is said to be a place near Corinth—indeed, the port of Corinth itself. Therefore it appears from this that it was written from Corinth, and also from his saying, “Gaius, my host, greets you” (ibid.); concerning whom, writing to the Corinthians, he mentions: “I give thanks to my God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius” (1 Cor. 1).

Therefore this Epistle, more difficult than the others to understand, and in which the Apostle appears more perfect, received the first place in the body of Epistles: not because it was first written by the Apostle, but because of the dignity of the Romans, who at that time ruled over all nations. Now *Romans* is interpreted “the lofty” or “the thunderous,” because at the time when the Apostle sent them this [Col. 1300A] Epistle they held dominion over all nations. Hence they were loftier than all peoples, and thundered forth public and private commands; and their fame resounded in the mouths of all people. Haimo says that the Apostle wrote to the Romans from Athens, in these words:

> “From Athens, a city of the Greeks, the Apostle wrote this Epistle to the Romans. Neither he himself, nor Peter, nor any of the Twelve Apostles first instructed them; rather, certain believing Jews, who, having received faith in Christ from the apostles, came to Rome, where the ruler of the world resided, to whom they themselves were subject, and evangelized to the Romans what they had learned at Jerusalem.”

Observe carefully that Haimo says that the Apostle wrote from Athens, whereas Origen says, from Corinth. Again observe [Col. 1300B] that this same Haimo says Peter first preached to the Romans, whereas ecclesiastical history contains this:

> “In the time of Claudius, the mercy of divine providence sent Peter to the city of Rome. On arriving, he first opened in the city of Rome, with the keys of his Gospel, the gate of the kingdom of heaven.”

Jerome likewise, on the Epistle to the Romans, where it is written, “That I may impart to you some spiritual grace” (Rom. 1), says:

> “Paul says that he wishes to strengthen the Romans, who held the faith through Peter’s preaching: not because they had received less from Peter, but so that their faith might be strengthened by the testimony and teaching of two apostles.”

Resolving the apparent conflict of these authorities, we say that Peter preached first [Col. 1300C] to the Romans in comparison with the other apostles, but not first in comparison with all believers. Likewise, we say that Paul wrote part of the Epistle at Athens, but completed it at Corinth, and from there sent it to the Romans.

Or rather, it is placed first because it destroys the first stage of error, namely pride, the root of all evils, as it is written: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10). By its nature it inhabits the minds of those on high, hiding under ashes and sackcloth. It had so taken possession of the Romans that, disputing among themselves and preferring themselves to one another, they produced dissensions and schisms. For the Romans had been converted to Christ from Jews and Gentiles. The Jews, however, because of the holy Fathers [Col. 1300D] from whom they traced their descent, and because of the Law which they alone had received among the other nations, despised the believing Gentiles. They said that through the observance of the Law, which they had served, they had deserved to receive the grace of Christ and faith in the Gospel; and that the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ had come to them because of the merits of works of the Law. Swollen with these claims, they preferred themselves to the Gentiles, saying:

> “We are of the Law of Abraham, to whom the promise was first made. We are God’s peculiar people. The Lord brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand and wondrous signs. He caused us to cross the Red Sea dry-shod; in the wilderness he fed us with manna; he brought water out of the rock. And, leaving other things unmentioned, we alone are worthy to receive God’s Law and to know his will. The Son of God also came especially [Col. 1301A] to us, as he himself says in the Gospel: ‘I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel’” (Matt. 15).

But the Gentiles replied:

> “The more benefits bestowed upon you that you recount, the more wicked you show yourselves to be. With the very feet by which you crossed the sea, you later danced before an idol which you had made with your own hands. And with the mouth with which, shortly before, you were offering praise to God for the drowning of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, you worshipped idols. Moreover, you despised the manna given from heaven in the wilderness, longing to return to Egypt to the pots of meat. You also often provoked the Lord to anger. Finally, you killed the Christ promised to you in the Law and the Prophets. Are we not therefore worthier than you, we who, as soon as we heard of Christ, believed in him?”

[Col. 1301B] Hence the Lord says through the Prophet: “A people whom I did not gather shall serve me; and they shall obey me at the hearing of the ear” (Ps. 17). From this it is clear that we sinned not from malice, but from ignorance. For if we had previously had prophets or apostles, we would not have worshipped idols. But as for your boasting concerning nobility of descent: if there is any glory in such things, then Ishmael and Esau can boast equally, since they were born of the same parents.

Into these disputes the Apostle therefore placed himself as a mediator, resolving all their contentions on both sides; and, like a good preacher addressing them in a ringing voice, brought them all to one concord. He showed that none of them had been saved by their own merits—for both Jews and Gentiles were held under sin [Col. 1301C]—but by the grace of God. On account of the dispute already described, then, he writes to the Romans, at one time refuting the Jews and at another the Gentiles, teaching them to humble themselves so that they may attribute everything to God’s grace, and showing [Col. 1302A] that the grace of faith in Christ’s Gospel came freely to all. He shows that it is for this reason called grace: it was not rendered as a debt of justice, but given freely. For what is grace? Something given freely, bestowed, not repaid. If it were owed to you before you had grace, a wage would have been repaid to you, not grace bestowed. This Epistle is therefore deservedly placed first, because, as stated, it destroys the root of all evils.

Having set forth the reasons for the work, number, and order of the Epistles, and also explained whence and why the Apostle wrote to the Romans, it remains to set out its subject matter, intention, and manner of treatment. The general subject of all the Epistles is the doctrine of the Gospel; their intention is to urge obedience to evangelical doctrine. [Col. 1302B] Beyond this, however, we shall seek the particular intentions and subjects in each Epistle. Thus the first Epistle has as its subject the vices of the Romans and the good things of God’s grace, to which it exhorts them; its intention is to rebuke their vices and humble them, under the hand of grace, toward true peace and brotherly concord. Its manner of treatment is as follows: according to the custom of letter writers, he prefaces a greeting, in which he does three things. For he commends his own person, the matter at hand, and the author of that matter; in these he fittingly gains goodwill. After the greeting he rebukes the vices of each party, showing that the Gentiles had departed from natural reason and the Jews from the Law. Then in many ways he shows that righteousness and salvation belong equally to both, not through the Law but through faith in Christ Jesus, in order to remove them from [Col. 1302C] the Law and establish them in faith in Christ alone. Near the end, moreover, moral instruction is added, and the Epistle concludes with thanksgiving. He therefore begins with the greeting, saying:

## ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

[Col. 1301]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1301C]

**Verses 1, 7.**—“Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, [Col. 1301D] which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh; who was predestined Son of God in power, according to the spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord; through whom we received grace and apostleship for obedience to the faith among all nations for his name’s sake, among whom you also are called of Jesus Christ—to all God’s beloved at Rome, called saints: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Thus far the construction is suspended until the sentence is completed; and “he commands” or “he writes” is understood. In this greeting he first commends his person in four ways: from his name, his condition, his rank, [Col. 1302C] and his office. From his name, when he says “Paul”; from his condition, “servant”; from his rank, “apostle”; and from his office, “set apart for the Gospel of God.” He gains praise from his name, if the force of the name itself and the reason for its imposition [Col. 1302D] are considered.

For *Paulus* means “quiet” in Hebrew, “small” in Greek, and “modest” in Latin; that is, this name *Paul*, Hebrew in origin and invention though not in its ending, was properly given to the Apostle as a mark of a twofold virtue, namely modesty and quietness. One of these the name indicates by its general designation among the Greeks, namely quietness; the other among the Latins, namely modesty. For this name *Paul*, though a common noun among Greeks, Hebrews, and Latins, was made the Apostle’s proper name. As Bede says on the Acts of the Apostles, he is reported to have come to the faith in the year of Christ’s Passion and Resurrection; but in the thirteenth year after Christ’s Passion, he received, together with Barnabas, the apostleship to the Gentiles and the name Paul. Previously he was called Saul, after Saul the persecutor, because as that Saul persecuted David, so this Saul persecuted the Church of God. But in the fourteenth year, according to the agreement of the apostles, he went forth to teach the Gentiles.

Augustine agrees with this explanation of the name Paul, saying:

> [Note: [Col. 1303D] Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, and on Psalm 71.] “For no other reason, as it seems to me, did Paul choose this name for himself than to show himself small, as the least of the apostles. He was first Saul and afterward called Paul. The Apostle did not change his name through any sort of boasting; rather, from Saul he became Paul—that is, from proud he became modest, that is, humble; for *paulum* means ‘a little.’”

[Ambrose] Thus, signifying that he had been changed, he calls himself Paul from Saul, which is interpreted “restlessness” or “temptation”: that is, “quiet.” For he who formerly brought temptations upon others afterward suffered them himself.

[Victor, bishop of Capua] Moreover, he is reported to have done this according to the custom of the holy apostles, who, as they advanced in virtues, were called by a changed name so that they might be new even in name—as Cephas, the sons of thunder, and others of that kind. Hence the holy Church has now adopted the custom of changing the names of those whom she raises to the chair of the blessed apostle Peter.

Or, as Jerome says: Paul gave himself this name from the first spoil which he brought to the holy Church, namely Sergius Paulus the proconsul, whom he converted in Cyprus. Thus, just as one who conquered the Parthians was called *Parthicus*, and one who conquered Germany *Germanicus*, so he was called Paul after that ruler whom he had first subdued.

[Origen] But since no such custom is found in the divine Scriptures, the explanation more acceptable is that which is frequently found in our own usage. For in Scripture we find some persons using two names and others three; this is so in both cases, as Solomon, who was called Ecclesiastes and Jedidiah, and Matthew, who was also called Levi, and many other examples of this sort. According to this custom, therefore, Paul too appears to us to have been called by a double name, as it is written in Acts of the Apostles: “Saul, who is also Paul” (Acts 13). There Scripture plainly shows that the name Paul was not first given to him at that time, but identifies it as belonging to his former appellation. Jerome, however, says in the book of Hebrew names that *Paul* is interpreted “wonderful” or “chosen.” The Lord himself called him a “vessel of election” [Col. 1303D] (Acts 9), and made him wonderful both in life and doctrine.

“Servant of Jesus Christ.” This is his condition.

[Origen] But one must ask why he calls himself a servant, when elsewhere he wrote: “For you have not received the spirit of slavery,” etc. (Rom. 8); and again elsewhere: “Therefore he is now no longer a servant but free” (Gal. 4). And the Lord said to the apostles: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15).

[Haimo] To this it must be said that there are two kinds of servitude. There is the servitude of fear, which is nearly servile; and there is the servitude of love, sonship, and humility, by which, after the manner of a serving son, one does not wish to offend his father. Therefore, if we understand the statement in the second sense, as referring to the servitude of humility and love, we shall not err.

[Col. 1304A] [Origen] For the truth of freedom is not injured in Paul by this, because Christ’s servitude is nobler than every freedom. Thus, in saying “servant,” he adopts a name of humility in order to summon to it the proud people to whom he wrote. And lest this servitude appear wretched, he does not simply say “servant,” but adds “of Jesus,” that is, “of the Savior,” whom all ought deservedly to serve; for to serve him is to reign. Now Jesus is called *sōtēr* (σωτήρ, “savior”) in Greek and *salvator* (“savior”) in Latin; in Hebrew, Jesus.

[Haimo] This name was bestowed by the angel upon the Son of God because he saves his people from their sins (Matt. 1). He adds “Christ,” that is, “king and priest.” For *Christos* in Greek, *Messias* in Hebrew, is called *unctus*, “anointed,” in Latin; and in the Old Testament kings and priests were anointed. But Christ was anointed not with visible oil, but with invisible oil—that is, with the oil of spiritual grace. Hence in the Psalm: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness” (Ps. 44). This name was formerly added to others, but became proper to Jesus. It is the name of a sacrament.

[Augustine, Haimo] In professing himself a servant of Jesus Christ, the Apostle shows that he has put off the law of works; and, by setting down both names, Jesus Christ, he testifies against heretics that there is one person of God and man, lest we suppose that Jesus was one person and Christ another, but may know them to be one and the same.

“Called apostle” [Note: [Col. 1304D] Irenaeus the martyr, book 4, *Against Heresies*.] This is the rank to which he was promoted; behold, from lowly he became lofty. It is as though he said to the proud people to whom he wrote: “God made me, from a servant and humble person, an apostle and exalted; so you too should be humble, that you may be exalted: [Col. 1304C] ‘For whoever humbles himself will be exalted’” (Luke 3 [probably OCR for Luke 14 or 18]).

Commending grace, he does not simply say “apostle,” but adds “called,” as though he did not come of himself and take this honor for himself; rather, he was called by God as an apostle, that is, to the apostleship, both by eternal election, which is according to purpose, and by temporal sending, by which he was sent by Christ—and from this the apostles also are called.

> [Note: [Col. 1304D] Augustine, on John.] For just as Greek *angeloi* are called *nuntii*, “messengers,” in Latin, so Greek *apostoloi* are called *missi* or *legati*, “those sent” or “envoys,” in Latin.

Or “called apostle” means called so by human beings, because of the excellence and privilege of the title—just as, in a preeminent sense, when one says “the City,” Rome is understood.

“Set apart for the Gospel of God.” This is his office.

[Col. 1304D] [Ambrose] It is as though he said: “I say Paul, set apart”—that is, from the teaching of the scribes and Pharisees and from the womb of the Synagogue, where he held the place of a teacher, as a Pharisee set apart for preaching the Gospel of God. This is said against the Jews, from whose Law he withdrew in order to preach Christ, who justified believers in what the Law could not do.

Or, “set apart,” [Haimo] means separated from the flock, namely from the other apostles, not in mind but in body. Hence the Holy Spirit says in Acts of the Apostles: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13), namely, that they might preach my name among the nations. Thus he adds here: “for the Gospel,” namely, [Col. 1305A] to be preached among the nations.

[Ambrose, Haimo] The Apostle was appointed preacher to the nations of the whole world, whereas the rest were made envoys and preachers to individual provinces. Now Gospel means “good announcement”; for εὖ (*eu*) is “good” in Greek, and ἄγγελος (*angelos*) is “messenger”; hence *Evangelium*, “good message” or “good announcement.” It is the announcement concerning matters pertaining to Catholic faith and good morals. I say, the Gospel “of God,” as not invented by man but revealed by divine inspiration.

“Which he had promised beforehand.” This is the commendation of the matter, that is, of the Gospel, which he commends in four ways: from the antiquity of time, the author, the witnesses, and the subject. He commends it from the antiquity of time and from its author together, by saying that God the Father freely promised the Gospel before its fulfillment. It did not come as something sudden, but had been promised and announced long before. Hence in the Gospel of John: “In this the saying is true, that one sows and another reaps” (John 4).

[Ambrose] “Promised,” I say, “through his prophets,” whence Jeremiah says: “Behold, days are coming, and I shall establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah” (Jer. 31). Likewise: “I shall make with you an everlasting covenant,” he says (Jer. 32). So too the others, who were great not of themselves but from God, so that they might speak not falsehood from themselves but truth from God. Behold how true and magnificent is the promise. No one announces a worthless thing through great forerunners. And for greater confirmation he adds “in the Scriptures,” as though he had promised it not only in words but also in writings, [Col. 1305C] lest it be forgotten. And to crown this true attestation he adds “holy,” not pagan. They are holy because they condemn vices and contain the mystery of the one God and the incarnation of the Son of God.

I say, Scriptures holy not concerning just anything, but “concerning the Son,” for they all lead to the Son. Concerning the Son—not an adoptive son, but “his own,” namely proper to him, consubstantial with him, coeternal and coequal. This is commendation from the subject.

“Who was made,” etc. This is commendation of the author, whom he commends in four ways: from origin, in the words “from the seed of David”; from power, in “who was predestined Son of God in power”; from grace, in “according to the spirit of sanctification,” etc.; and from generosity, in “through whom we received,” etc.

[Augustine] [Col. 1305D] It is as though he said: “The holy Scriptures treat of the Son, who was made for him”—that is, for God the Father, to his honor. He was made, I say, only according to the flesh, not according to divinity. He says this lest Christ be thought merely human. For in saying that he was made according to the flesh, he implies another nature according to which he was not made, namely the divine nature.

[Ambrose] Him who was the Son of God according to the Holy Spirit—that is, according to God, because God is spirit and is doubtless holy—he says was made according to the flesh, according to the saying: “And the Word was made flesh” (John 1), so that Jesus Christ may now be one Son of God and man. He was made according to the flesh by the work of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin, that is, born.

> [Note: [Col. 1305D] Augustine, on the Epistle to the Romans.]

Here the impiety of heretics is opposed, who, understanding this chapter with dull hearts, take Christ to be only human and do not recognize divinity in him. By adding “according to the flesh,” he preserved for divinity its dignity, by which Christ is the Word of God, through whom all things were made. For he was not made according to that by which he is the Word of God: all things were made through him. Nor could he through whom all things were made be made along with all things, nor was he made before all things so that all things might be made through him.

> [Note: [Col. 1305D] As the Arians said.]

Therefore, when the Apostle called Christ made, he added “according to the flesh,” in order to show that according to the Word, which is the Son [Col. 1306B] of God, he was not made by God but begotten.

> [Note: [Col. 1305D] Origen, on the Epistle to the Romans.]

He was indeed made, without doubt, what he had not previously been according to the flesh; but according to God he was before, and there was never a time when he was not. God was made human, if one may put it so; yet even in assuming flesh he did not cease to be God, remaining unchangeable while assuming changeable man, and not diminishing his own nature by assuming human nature.

> [Note: [Col. 1306D] Cassiodorus, on Psalm 4, book.]

Therefore, according to the flesh, he was made from the seed of David. But before the ages he was born God from God.

> [Note: [Col. 1306D] Augustine, book 4, *On the Trinity*.]

Thus, he who was, was made. But what was he? What was he made? He was the Word; he was the Son of God; he was made Son of Man. He was God; he was made man. He assumed humanity; he did not lose divinity. He was made lowly; he remained exalted.

> [Note: [Col. 1306D] Augustine, *Against Heresies*.]

[Col. 1306C] Therefore the Son of God was made the son of man: according to the truth of nature, born from God as Son of God; and according to the truth of nature, born from man as son of man. Thus through birth he possessed the name “Son” truly in each birth, not by adoption or appellation, and was true God and true man, one Son. For God the Father begot from his own nature a Son, God equal to himself and coeternal in the same divinity in which he himself is naturally eternal. But the same God the Son, though eternal and true God, was for us made true and complete man. He is true in that this God has a true human nature; he is complete in that he assumed human flesh and a rational soul. Hence the same only-begotten God is said to have been born twice: once from the Father and once from the mother. For he was born from the Father as the Word of God; he was born from the mother as the Word made flesh. Therefore one and the same is the Son of God, born before the ages and born in time.

Likewise: When the only-begotten God was conceived, he received the reality of flesh from the Virgin; and when he was born, he preserved in his mother the integrity of virginity. This, then, is the reason why God was made the son of a Virgin and the Virgin was made the mother of the only-begotten God: the one whom the Father begot from eternity, the Virgin brought forth in time when conceived. Therefore, in order to cleanse human flesh and soul, the Son of God was endowed with a rational soul by the assumption of flesh and soul, or was incarnate.

[Col. 1307A] [Note: [Col. 1307D] Augustine, book *On the Trinity*.] Hence Christ also was made less than himself by taking the form of a servant. Yet he did not take the form of a servant so as to cast off the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father; thus in the form of a servant and in the form of God he remains the same only-begotten Son. The Son of God is therefore equal to God the Father by nature, but less in condition: in the form of a servant which he assumed, he is less than the Father; in the form of God, in which he was before assuming this form, he is equal to the Father. In the form of God, he is the Word; in the form of a servant, he was made from a woman. In the form of God, he made man; in the form of a servant, he was made man.

> [Note: [Col. 1307D] Augustine, *On Faith to Peter*.] Therefore, because the form of God assumed the form of a servant, he is both God and man. Yet Christ is eternal and true God, truly conceived and born in time from the Virgin. That God [Col. 1307B] was naturally made the son of man who alone is by nature the Son of God the Father, and who, Creator and Lord of all natures, created the Virgin while about to be created from the Virgin. This God assumed human nature into the unity of his person; and, humbling himself through mercy, he filled the womb of the incorrupt Virgin, from whom he was to be born. Therefore that God took the form—that is, the nature—of a servant into his own person. He did not assume a human person, but human nature. And although the whole Trinity effected the formation of the assumed man, because the works of the Trinity are inseparable, the Son alone assumed man—that is, the form of a servant—in the singularity or unity of person, not in the unity or singularity of divine nature.

But if you still ask [Col. 1307C] how the Incarnation itself was accomplished:

> [Note: [Col. 1307D] Augustine, book 4, *On the Trinity*, on the manner of the Incarnation.]

I say that the very Word of God was made flesh, that is, was made man; yet he was not thereby transformed or changed into what he was made, but clothed with flesh so as to appear fittingly to fleshly people. Thus it was done so that there might be there not only the Word of God and human flesh, but also a rational human soul; and this whole is called God because of God and man because of man.

> [Note: [Col. 1307D] Augustine, on John.]

Let us therefore acknowledge the twofold substance of Christ: the divine, by which he is equal to the Father, and the human, by which the Father is greater. Yet both together are not two Christs but one Christ, lest God be a quaternity rather than a Trinity. Accordingly Christ is God, a rational soul, and flesh. So great is the union of the two natures that the whole is called God, the whole man, and conversely, God is man and man is God.

> [Note: [Col. 1307D] Augustine, *On Faith to Peter*.]

If this is difficult to understand, the mind should be purified more and more by faith, abstaining from sins and doing good works. For these matters are difficult.

[John of Damascus] But, to put it briefly, the emptying of the most high God was nothing other than his assumption of the servant’s form, that is, human nature. Thus both forms are in Christ, because in Christ both substances are true and complete. The natures are united to one another without conversion or alteration: the divine nature does not depart from its own simplicity; the human nature is neither converted into the nature of divinity nor divided into nonexistence; nor has one composite nature been made from the two.

> [Note: [Col. 1307D] Whether food is in the body as a drop in a furnace of [Col. 1308D] fire. Augustine, *Against Maximinus*.]

Christ, therefore, is one person of two substances; yet neither God nor man can be called a part of this person. Otherwise, before the Son of God assumed the form of a servant, he was not whole, and he increased when man was added to his divinity.

> [Note: [Col. 1308D] Ambrose, book *On the Trinity*.]

It should nevertheless be known that “was made” does not always refer to creation, as in: “Lord, you have become our refuge” (Ps. 89); and again: “You have become my salvation” (Ps. 117). Here, certainly, no definition or production by creation is declared; rather, that which was not previously a refuge or salvation to us is said to have become so for us.

> [Note: [Col. 1308D] Ambrose, book *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, which the ignorant attribute to Augustine.]

But [Col. 1308B] it may be asked, since we confess him to be our Savior, why the Apostle calls him “made from the seed of David,” when being made is one thing and being born another. Elsewhere he also said: “Made from a woman” (Gal. 4). He therefore indicated something by this expression. Because the Lord’s flesh was not formed in the Virgin’s womb and made into a body from human seed, but by the working and power of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle says “made,” not “born.” For it is one thing to be generated by the admixture of seed and a clot of blood, and another to be produced not through mixture but through power. Human beings can generate human children, but cannot make them.

Likewise, although no man’s seed intervened in the Virgin’s conception, nevertheless, because Christ was formed from that flesh of hers which undeniably derives from seed, he is rightly said to have been made from seed. Whoever asks whether he ought simply to be called a creature or a created thing should hear Augustine reason thus on this matter:

> [Note: [Col. 1308D] Augustine, book *On the Trinity*: “Whether Christ should be called a creature.”] “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1), and “the Word was made flesh” (ibid.), on account of the birth of his Incarnation, which occurred in time from the Virgin; and “all things were made through him” (ibid.). He says ‘all things’ only of things made—that is, of every creature. Hence it is plainly apparent that he through whom all things were made was himself not made. If he was not made, he is not a creature; but if he is not a creature, he is of the same substance as the Father. For every substance that is not God is a creature, and whatever is not a creature is God. If the Son is not of the same substance as the Father, then he is a made substance; and if he is a made substance, not all things were made through him. But all things were made through him. Therefore he is not a made substance.”

Yet, as the Apostle says, he was made for him—that is, for the Father’s honor—according to the flesh, but unmade according to divinity. I say, “made” particularly from the seed of David.

[Haimo] This is because Mary was of David’s stock, and from her seed the Lord’s flesh was formed by the work of the Holy Spirit in the virginal womb. But one should consider [Col. 1309A] why he here names David particularly, although it is known that the promise was made to Abraham as well as to David. The Apostle, wishing to commend grace, preferred to name David, who was also sinful, rather than Abraham, who was righteous, so that Christ may be thought to have been born from David not by merit but by grace. He also does so in order to show that a king was born according to the flesh from a human king, just as before the ages a king was born from God the King. Then, commending him from power, he adds:

“Who was predestined Son of God in power, according to the spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Here first we must see what predestination is and what predestination concerns: whether what always existed, or what came to exist in time; whether person or [Col. 1309B] nature; and, if it concerns person, then afterward we must consider according to which nature he was predestined.

> [Note: [Col. 1309D] Augustine, *On Predestination*.]

Predestination is the preparation of grace, by which from eternity God prepared, without merits, good things for Christ the man and for all whom he foreknew would be conformed to the image of his Son. For the most eminent light of predestination and grace is the mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2). For what did that man deserve, when, assumed by the Word coeternal with the Father into unity of person, he might be the only-begotten Son of God? What good of his preceded this, by which he attained this ineffable excellence? Through the act and assumption of God the Word, from the moment he began to be man, he began to be the unique Son of God. That woman, full of grace, conceived the unique Son of God by the Holy Spirit. From the Virgin Mary the unique God was born, not by the desire of flesh, but solely by God’s gift. Free will was in him, and all the more so because he was unable to sin.

Thus, in our Head, the very fountain of grace appears to us, from which grace is poured out into all his members. For any human being becomes a Christian by grace from the beginning of faith, just as that man was made Christ by grace from the beginning. This person is reborn from the Spirit; that one was born from the Spirit. By the Spirit remission of sins is effected in us; by the Spirit it was effected in him that he should have no sin.

> [Note: [Col. 1309D] Augustine, *On the Good of Perseverance*.]

He who made that man, without any preceding merits of his, to inherit no sin requiring forgiveness either from origin or by commission of his will, likewise, without any preceding merits of theirs, makes believers in him, whose every sin he forgives. He who made him such that he never had and never would have an evil will, himself makes in his members a good will from an evil will. Therefore he predestined both him and us, because he foreknew—not our merits that would precede—in him, that he should be our Head, and in us, that we should be his body, but his own works that would come to be.

> [Note: [Col. 1309D] Augustine, *On Predestination*.]

God certainly foreknew from eternity that he would do these things. This, therefore, is the predestination of the saints, which shone most brightly in the Holy of holies; no one able rightly to understand the utterances of truth can deny it. Therefore let human merits be silent here, [Col. 1310A] since they perished through Adam, and let grace reign through Jesus Christ. Whoever finds preceding merits in our Head for that unique generation should seek in us, his members, preceding merits for faith and regeneration.

> [Note: [Col. 1309D] Augustine, exposition of Psalm 118.]

For it was bestowed neither upon Christ nor upon us for any merit, but bestowed freely. He made us believe in Christ who made the Christ in whom we believe for us. He brings about in us the beginning of faith who made the man Jesus the pioneer and perfecter of faith.

> [Note: [Col. 1310D] Augustine, *On the Good of Perseverance*.]

Therefore there is no more illustrious example of predestination than the mediator himself. Whoever, then, among the faithful wishes to understand it rightly should attend to Christ, and in [Col. 1310B] him will find both it and himself: he should believe that in Christ true human nature was so exalted by the assumption of God the Word that the one who assumed and that which was assumed were one person in the Trinity. For the Trinity was not made a quaternity in the assumed man; rather, the Trinity remained Trinity, that ineffable assumption effecting the reality of one person in God and man. This is sufficient concerning predestination itself.

Next let us consider whether predestination concerns something that has always existed, or something that has not always existed; and whether it concerns a person or a nature. The same one who according to the flesh was made from the seed of David is said to have been predestined Son of God in power. Likewise: [Note: [Col. 1310D] The same author, *On the Epistle to the Romans*.] For the Son of God is rightly said not to have been predestined according to that in which he is the Word of God, [Col. 1310C] God with God. [Note: [Col. 1310D] The same author, *On John*.] For why should he be predestined, when he already was what he was—eternal, without beginning and without end? But that which did not yet exist had to be predestined, so that in its own time it might come to be as it had been predestined before the ages to come to be. Therefore whoever denies that the Son of God was predestined denies that this same one is the Son of Man. [Note: [Col. 1310D] The same author, in the book addressed to Prosper and Hilary.] Jesus, therefore, was predestined so that he who was to be David’s son according to the flesh might be the Son of God in power. Likewise, insofar as he was made man, we say that the Son of God was predestined.

From these statements it is clear that predestination concerns the person—that is, Christ Jesus—not according to that which he always was, but according to that which he was not always: that is, not according to [Col. 1310D] divinity but according to humanity. The meaning is: Christ was made according to the flesh; and Christ, insofar as he is man, is predestined—that is, chosen beforehand by grace alone—for this purpose: that this man himself might be the Son of God, not adoptive, certainly, as we are, but “in power,” that is, with the same power as the Father; not through the grace of adoption, but through the union of the Word—that is, through the grace by which his human nature is united to the Word. Therefore he is not a son through adoption, nor an adoptive son.

For Ambrose says: “I have turned and returned to the divine Scripture, and nowhere have I found the Son of God called adoptive.” But as Christ, insofar as he is God, naturally possesses the fact that he is the natural Son of God and is God, so insofar as he is man he possesses by grace the fact that he is the same natural Son of God. [Note: [Col. 1311D] Jerome, *On the Epistle to the Ephesians*.] Concerning the Son—that is, our Lord Jesus Christ—it is written that he was always with the Father, and that the Father’s will never preceded him in order that he might be. He indeed is Son by nature; we are sons by adoption. He was never not Son; we, before we existed, were predestined, and then received the Spirit of adoption when we believed in the Son of God.

[Note: [Col. 1311D] Hilary, Book II *Against Arius*.] Heretics strive to take away from the Father that whereby he is Father, while they wish to take away from the Son that whereby he is Son. They take it away when they say that he is not Son by nature. For he is not from nature when the one begotten and the one begetting do not have the same thing in themselves. Nor is he Son whose substance will be other and unlike the Father’s. And how will he be Father if he has not begotten in the Son that substance and nature which are in himself? When the Lord says, “Glorify your Son” (John 17), he attested that he is the Son of God not by name alone, but also by proper possession. We are sons of God, but this Son is not such a son. For he is the true and proper Son: by origin, not adoption; by reality, not designation; by birth, not creation.

[Note: [Col. 1311D] The same author, Book III.] He is Son by nature because he has the same nature as the one who begot him. We are sons by grace, not by nature; but the Only-Begotten is Son by nature, not by grace. Must this also be referred to the man in the Son himself? Certainly. For the fact that he is Only-Begotten, equal to the Father, belongs not to grace but to [Col. 1311C] nature; but the fact that a man was assumed into the unity of the person of the Only-Begotten belongs to grace, not nature. [Note: [Col. 1312D] Hilary, Sermon 29 on John, Sermon 20.]

Some ask whether Christ, insofar as he is man, is God or the Son of God. They attempt to prove that this is so as follows: Christ, insofar as he is man, was predestined to be the Son of God; but he was predestined to be that which he is. Therefore, since he was predestined insofar as he is man to be Son of God, he is also Son of God insofar as he is man.

We answer that Christ is that which he was predestined to be; but he is not that thing according to that in respect of which he was predestined. For he was predestined to be the Son of God. Thus he is truly Son of God; but he was predestined to this, [Col. 1311D] insofar as he is man, because he received this by grace insofar as he is man. Yet insofar as he is man, he is not that thing—unless perhaps “insofar as” expresses unity of person. For “insofar as” sometimes expresses the condition of human or divine nature, and sometimes unity of person. It expresses the condition of nature when one says, “insofar as man,” that is, “as man,” or “insofar as God,” that is, “as God.” It expresses unity of person when one says, “Christ, insofar as he is man, forgives sins”: that is, the very man who is Christ, or the person himself who is man. Sometimes, too, “according to” [Col. 1312A] denotes a cause, as when one says, “He will judge according to divinity,” that is, by the power of divinity. These distinctions must be carefully observed in their proper places.

It is also asked whether Christ, insofar as he is man, is a person. To this we say: if “insofar as” denotes cause or the condition of nature, then insofar as he is man he is not a person. For he is not a person because he is man, or insofar as he is man. If he were a person because he is man, then he would either be the third person in the Trinity or another person; but he is not another. Therefore he would be the third person in the Trinity, and hence God as well. Thus he is not called a person insofar as he is man, because insofar as he is man he is not distinguished from the Father and the Holy Spirit by a personal property; for insofar as he is man [Col. 1312B] he is not begotten by the Father, nor is he the Father’s Son. Sonship, however, is a property by which the person of the Son is distinguished from the others.

But if, insofar as he is man, he is not the third person in the Trinity, how then did Augustine say above: “He who assumed and that which he assumed are one person in the Trinity”? This authority appears to suggest that human nature together with the Word is one person in the Trinity. If this is so, then human nature together with the Word is God. Therefore some nature together with the Word is God which has not always been God. Therefore not only the divine nature is God, but another nature as well. Since this seems absurd, along with many other consequent inconveniences, Augustine’s foregoing words, and similar words wherever they are found, seem to us to be understood in this way: “He who assumed and that which he assumed are one person in the Trinity,” that is, God so assumed man that the same person which existed before remained unchanged. For the union of the one assuming and that assumed neither divided nor altered the unity of person; and then it came about that the person who had previously been God was the same person who was man.

Thus he says on John: “When the Word became flesh, the Word and man became one person”; that is, then it came about that the same person who is God was man. We are also troubled by how Augustine above said that that man was assumed by the Word, since that man is a person and a person was not assumed. Elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1312D] The same author, in the sermon *On Faith, to Peter*.] he says the same thing more explicitly, which troubles us still more: “If anyone says and believes that the man Jesus Christ was not assumed by the Son of God, let him be anathema.” And [Col. 1312D] thus it appears that a person was assumed by a person—an impious thing either to say or think.

The words of the foregoing authorities can, however, be understood thus: Christ as man, or that man, is said to have been assumed by the Word because his soul and flesh, in which the man subsists, were assumed by the Word. Thus, when you say “assumed,” look to the nature of the man Christ himself, not to his person. Likewise, it is asked whether that man began to exist or has always existed, just as we state simply that Christ or the Son of God has always existed and did not begin to exist. Augustine says of this: [Note: [Col. 1312D] The same author, *On John*.] “At one time the Son of God had what the same one, as Son of Man, did not yet have, because he was not yet man.” Likewise: “We are elected in the same way as he was glorified, because before the world existed neither we nor he—the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus—existed” (1 Tim. 2). Likewise: [Note: [Col. 1313D] Hilary, *On the Psalms*.] “Our Christ, although perhaps man only recently, is nevertheless eternal God.” Elsewhere, however, one reads that that child created the stars, and Christ himself says: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8).

Without opposing these authorities in any respect, we therefore say that that man, insofar as he is man, began to exist; insofar as he is the Word, he has always existed. For in such expressions, without an added qualification, no answer ought to be given. Hence Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1313D] The same author, *On John*.] “The Father through him, insofar as he is [Col. 1313B] his Word, made even things that were to come; but certainly according to that whereby he is man, he glorified him for us.” [Note: [Col. 1313D] The same author, *On the Predestination of the Saints*; in the book *On the Gift of Perseverance*; *On John*; *On the Epistle to the Romans*.]

Therefore he, insofar as he is man, was predestined—that is, chosen beforehand by grace alone, without merits—not only that he might be our head, that he might neither derive sin by origin nor commit it by will, and that he might be glorified from mortal nature into immortality, but also that he might be Son of God in power, that is, with the same power as the Father. That he is Son of God may be seen from the fact that he was conceived and born according to the Spirit of sanctification—that is, because he was conceived by the Holy Spirit.

But observe that the Holy Spirit was not seed for him, nor do we say that the Spirit is the father of the man Christ, lest [Col. 1313C] two fathers be said to exist. He is said to have been conceived by the Holy Spirit because this conception occurred through the operation of the Spirit, through whom all things are sanctified. [Haimo] And that conception came about through God’s gift. [Augustine] He is also proved to be Son of God from the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord—that is, of those who are his—because he caused to rise with himself dead persons who were his, because they belonged to him, according to the saying: “Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose with him” (Matt. 27).

[Haimo] Note that he used a proper name in place of a pronoun, in the Hebrew manner, an expression most customary in the Scriptures and especially frequent in the ancient books; as: “Moses did as the Lord commanded Moses” (Exod. 38). [Note: [Col. 1314D] Hilary, from the exposition of Psalm 67.]

Or it may be understood thus: “according to the Spirit”; as if he said: Christ is proved [Col. 1313D] to be Son of God according to the Spirit, that is, because he gave his own the Spirit of sanctification—sanctification, I say, begun from the resurrection of the soul, that is, from the forgiveness of sins by which the soul rises from vices. [Note: [Col. 1314D] The same author, *On the Epistle to the Romans*.] For there is a twofold resurrection, one of the soul and the other of the body.
