Of the resurrection of the soul the Apostle says later: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will give you light” (Eph. 5). “From the resurrection,” I say, “of the dead of our Lord Jesus Christ,” that is, of those who were dead in sins, who are called Christ’s because no one else could heal [Col. 1314A] them, just as someone to be healed by a physician is called that physician’s sick person.

This may also be understood of human nature, concerning which the Apostle says, “who was predestined,” so that human nature itself may truly be said to have been predestined. 4 Hence Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1314D] From the exposition of Psalm 118.] “This so great, lofty, and supreme exaltation of human nature was predestined, so that it had no higher place to which it could be raised; just as, for us, divinity itself had no lower point to which it could descend than the assumption of human nature with the weakness of flesh even to the death of the cross.”

Haimo says of the same matter: “Here the Apostle does not speak of the Word, but of the man who did not exist before he was made. For the humanity which had not previously existed—that was predestined.” Accordingly read the text thus: “Christ, insofar as he is man, was predestined”—that is, his humanity was predestined and preordained without its own merits, to be Son of God in power; that is, to be assumed by the Word, which exists in the same power of divinity as the Father, and united to him in unity of person.

“According to the Spirit of sanctification”: this relates to what was said above, “made from the seed of David according to the flesh.” Join it therefore thus: “made from the seed of David according to the flesh”; “made,” I say, “according to the Spirit of sanctification,” that is, according to the operation of the Holy Spirit, who makes human beings holy, who also formed and sanctified this man himself in the virginal womb from a woman’s seed, without a man’s seed. “From the resurrection of the dead”: this relates to what he said, “Son of God,” as though he said: That he is the Son [Col. 1314C] of God, to whom human nature is united, is apparent from the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord—that is, of his own—from the fact that he caused dead persons to rise with him. Augustine also gives this ordering of the words, but says that the other ordering appears surer and better.

Or it may be read thus: “predestined,” like “foreknown,” may be understood and referred to human knowledge, as also in the words, “I shall be their God” (2 Cor. 6), that is, “I shall be known.” The meaning is: [Ambrose] The Son of God, who lay hidden in the flesh as to what he was, was predestined—that is, eternally foreknown—to be manifested as Son of God in the power of rising, namely when he rose from the dead. For every uncertainty and distrust was trampled down and crushed by his resurrection. [Col. 1314D] For even his disciples doubted at his death, but in his resurrection the power of divinity shone forth, as he says: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12), that is, then I shall be known to be Lord of all.

He was therefore foreknown to be manifested as Son of God in the power of resurrection according to the sanctifying Spirit, that is, because he gave his own the Holy Spirit. Then he explains what power he meant, adding: “from the resurrection of the dead.” He does not say “from Christ’s resurrection,” but “of the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord,” because his resurrection brings about our [Col. 1315A] general resurrection. As if he said: The Son of God was manifested from the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord, that is, because he rose; and by this he also caused us to rise in soul and body. Hence he appears to have destroyed death in order to redeem us; for which reason he calls him our Lord, saying, “Jesus Christ our Lord.” In this he truly appears Lord: that, though dead, he conquered death. For this seems the greater power and victory in Christ, that he works while dead by the power by which he had worked while alive.

“Through whom we received.” Here he commends him for generosity. [Note: [Col. 1315D] Augustine, *On the Epistle to the Romans*.] Here is shown what the author bestowed upon him. As if he said: Such is Christ, through whom we apostles, together with the other faithful, received such gifts—that is, he who gave such grace: namely, forgiveness of sins [Col. 1315B] and patience in all labours, [Ambrose] through which we shall be rewarded in the future; and other gifts, all of which were given to us freely. We apostles alone received the apostolate, [Augustine] that is, authority and the commission to preach.

[Haimo] For the Apostle received grace through Christ together with all believers; but he received the apostolate not with all, but with the apostles alone. [Origen] Therefore he appropriately says that he received not merely the apostolate, [Note: [Col. 1315D] Ibid.] lest he prove ungrateful for the grace by which his sins were forgiven: so that no one may dare to say that by merits of a former life he was brought to the Gospel, since not even the Apostles themselves, who excel the rest, could have received the apostolate unless they had first, with the rest, received grace—the grace [Col. 1315C] which heals and justifies sinners.

[Ambrose] Therefore, appropriately preserving the order of causation, he says, “we received grace and apostleship,” that is, the power of apostleship. Where? “Among all nations.” Therefore among the Jews, because the Jews, by dwelling together, are among the nations. Or: we received the apostolate not merely among the one nation of the Jews, but also among all nations. For what purpose? “For obedience to the faith,” that is, that I, together with the other apostles, may make them obey the faith of Christ; for this we received the apostolate. And this is “for his name,” namely Christ’s: that is, in his stead, because we are his vicars. Or it is for the extension of his name—that is, for his glory, not our own—as you Romans do.

Then, to admonish them more intimately, he turns to them, saying: “Among whom,” that is, among which nations, [Haimo] you Romans too—that is, [Col. 1315D] Jews and Gentiles dwelling at Rome—are called through the grace and inward inspiration of Jesus Christ, that is, by Jesus Christ. The genitive is used for the ablative, in the Greek manner. [Augustine, Ambrose] Or: you have been called in order that you may belong to Jesus Christ, who is the salvation of all nations. When the Romans hear that they have been called among the rest, they can know that they ought not to act under the Law, because the other nations received Christ’s faith without the Law; the other peoples were called without the Law of Moses, and these too ought to observe this.

“To all who are at Rome, beloved of God, called saints.” The construction has depended upon this point up to now, as if he said: Paul, such and such a man, writes to all who are at Rome—not to others, but to God’s beloved, that is, beloved by God. [Col. 1316A] Although he writes to the Romans, he indicates nevertheless that he writes to those who abide in God’s charity. Who are these, if not those who think rightly about the Son of God? These are saints and are called.

[Augustine] Observe that here too the Apostle indicated God’s kindness rather than their merit. For he does not say “those loving God,” but “God’s beloved.” For he first loved us before all merits, so that, having been loved, we might love him. Hence he also added, “called saints,” so that no one may attribute to himself the fact that he was called.

[Ambrose] The phrase “called saints” must not be understood as though they were called because they were holy, but as meaning that they were made holy because they were called. [Haimo, Augustine] And they were called because they were beloved. Thus the sense is: he writes to God’s beloved, called saints—that is, to those whom he loved [Col. 1316B] so as to call them to holiness, by which they might be holy, sanctified through baptism. It remains for the Apostle to pronounce the greeting and complete the customary opening of an epistle; therefore he adds:

“Grace to you,” etc. Instead of what others commonly say, “Greetings,” he says, “Grace to you,” etc. As if he said: The Apostle writes to the Romans, and in writing greets them, expressing this wish: “May grace be yours,” that is, forgiveness of sins. For this is the grace by which the ungodly person is justified, and one who was formerly ungodly becomes righteous. Therefore no merits precede the reception of this grace, because punishment, not grace, is due to the merits of the ungodly. Nor would this be grace if it were not given freely, but rendered as a debt.

[Ambrose] He adds: “And peace”—may it be yours—namely reconciliation with God and tranquillity [Col. 1316C] of mind. [Note: [Col. 1316D] Augustine, in the book *Retractions*.] For as God’s grace is that by which our sins are forgiven, so peace is that by which, from enemies, we are reconciled to God. Yet we should know that both—grace and peace—belong to the general grace of God, although they are distinguished in this way.

And to show that every good is from God, he adds: “From God”; as if he said: May this grace and peace be yours from God our Father—that is, from him who is able to give, because he is God, and willing to give, because he is Father. [Ambrose] And in order to teach that apart from Christ no peace or grace exists, he added, “and from the Lord Jesus Christ,” without whom no good things are ours. [Note: [Col. 1316D] The same author, *On the Epistle to the Romans*.] That he does not join the Holy Spirit, I see no reason other than that we understand the Holy Spirit himself as God’s gift. For what else are grace and [Col. 1316D] peace than God’s gift? Hence grace, by which we are freed from sins, and peace, by which we are reconciled to God, can by no means be given to human beings except in the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Trinity itself, together with its immutable unity, is recognized in this greeting.

[Haimo] The unity appears in the words “from God.” Haimo says thus on the same point: “He did not name the Holy Spirit, because he comprehends him in his gifts”—that is, in grace and peace; for since the elect are divinely honoured through him, he is understood in his gifts.

**VERS. 8–10.**—“First indeed I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, [Col. 1317A] because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world. For God, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, is my witness that without ceasing I make remembrance of you always in my prayers, beseeching that somehow, at last, I may at some time have a prosperous journey, by the will of God, to come to you.”

After setting forth the greeting, before anything else he gives thanks for their good qualities. [Augustine] To give thanks to God is to recognize that every good thing has been given by God and to praise him for it in speech, deed, and heart. Having therefore completed the preface, he first softens those to whom he writes, though he will later rebuke these same persons severely. For here he rejoices with them over the good they have begun, and he says that he especially rejoices because their faith was spreading everywhere. Although [Col. 1317B] they had not received the faith according to the rule of truth handed down by the authorities, nevertheless, because they had begun to worship what they had heard concerning the one God, with Christ’s name introduced, the Apostle congratulates them, knowing that they could make progress. By this he also shows his love for them and exhorts them to advance, saying:

“First indeed”—as if he said: Complete what you have begun, because it is so good that before all else I give thanks to God for it; and this is what “first indeed” means, namely: before all things I give thanks to God for all of you, which you yourselves should also do. He says that he does this before all else because their faith benefits many. For those who had believed were strengthened when they saw their leaders made their brothers in faith; and those who had not believed could easily believe by their example. For an inferior readily does what he sees done by a superior.

[Haimo] Or thus: I give thanks to my God for all of you and others; and, although for others, yet “first indeed,” that is, especially for you, from whom great benefit arises, as was stated above. To whom do I give thanks? “To my God,” whom I make mine—which you Romans do not do. The words “my God” are not to be taken idly; for this expression can belong only to the saints whose God he is called, such as the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Therefore, although by nature one God is God of all, because he is Creator of all, yet he is properly called God by grace of those who, through the merit of faith and righteousness, are shown to be his worshippers.

[Ambrose] Through whom do I give thanks? Not through the Law nor prophecy, but through Jesus Christ, mediator between God and human beings, through whom God gave you all good things, because he is the minister 5 [Col. 1317D] of all God’s benefits. Then he states why he gives thanks especially, or before all else, for them, adding: “Because your faith.” As if he said: Although there are many such things in you for which I ought to give thanks—for they were remarkable in discipline, eager for good works, and more zealous to do well than to speak—yet especially for this I give thanks: because your faith, though not perfect, is proclaimed throughout the whole world. For Rome was the head of the world, and therefore the report of their faith travelled through every region, through which [Col. 1318A] many might profit.

Note that the Apostle does not praise their faith as perfect, but their readiness to believe: because they believed upon hearing; and he praises their disposition toward Christ, that is, the eager affection which they had toward Christ. “God is witness,” etc. He said that he gives thanks for them; now he says that he prays for the same persons. In this too he shows his affection toward them, so that he may commend charity to them. He calls upon as witness the God whom he serves, saying: “For God is my witness,” that what he is about to say may be more readily believed.

[Note: [Col. 1317D] Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*.] Thus authority has been set forth—that is, an oath—to establish credence for what is said. Unless perhaps someone says that he did not swear because he did not say “by God,” but said “God is witness.” It is ridiculous to think this. If you say “by God,” you swear; if you say “God is witness,” [Col. 1318B] you do not swear? For what does “by God” mean except “God is witness”? Or what does “God is witness” mean except “by God”? Behold, I tell your charity: even one who falsely swears by a stone is perjured, because he calls God the Creator as witness.

Nor does the Apostle, who here and elsewhere often swore, act contrary to the Lord’s command. For the Lord, wishing our righteousness to exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees, says in the Gospel: “I say to you, do not swear at all” (Matt. 6). And likewise: “Let your speech be, Yes, yes; No, no. What is beyond this is from evil” (ibid.). There the Lord forbade what is evil, urged the good which ought to be sought, and permitted what is necessary. For he forbade false swearing, or swearing without necessity; he urged speaking truth; he permitted an oath, which is necessary, when he said, “what is beyond this.” An oath is to be made in necessary matters, since people are slow to believe what is beneficial to them. Swearing is not good—that is, desirable—yet it is not evil—that is, forbidden—when it is necessary, although it comes from the evil of the weakness of those to whom something is said.

For if you are compelled to swear, know that it comes from the necessity arising from the weakness of those whom you are persuading; and that weakness is certainly an evil from which we pray daily to be delivered, saying: “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6). Therefore the Lord did not say, “What is beyond this is evil.” You do not do evil when you make good use of an oath to persuade another of what is beneficial; rather, it is from that person’s evil. And it should be noted that there is a great difference whether a person who demands an oath knows that the one swearing will swear falsely, or does not know it. One who does not know and therefore says, “Swear to me,” so that he may have assurance, I do not dare say commits no sin; yet it is a human temptation. But if he knows that the deed was done and compels the person to swear, he is a murderer.

Therefore the Apostle swears without sin when he says, “God is my witness,” etc.; as if he said: I attribute what you have to the Lord. And rightly so, for I pray that you may have it from him; and truly so, because “without ceasing I make remembrance of you always in my prayers.” Or thus: he said that he gives thanks; now he explains when he gives thanks, namely in prayers, and how, namely without ceasing. [Haimo] As if he said: I give thanks for you, and I do so in this way: [Col. 1319A] in my prayers, which are made for you and for others, I always have you in mind at the appointed hours for prayer. “I make remembrance,” that is, I make God remember. God is said to remember when he gives, and to forget when he ceases. And this is “without ceasing.”

[Ambrose] Or: “I make remembrance of you without ceasing.” The Apostle said that he remembered them in his prayers in order to sow charity in them—that is, so that they might love him and therefore desire to hear him. For who would not love one whom he hears remembers him? That this is so, he affirms by oath: “Witness,” etc.; as if he said: It ought to be believed that things are as I say. “For,” that is, because God is my witness, and therefore it is unsafe to lie, since nothing is hidden from him. “Whom I serve in my spirit,” not in the flesh—that is, in my will; for because God is spirit, he must be served in the mind. Or: “I serve,” not in flesh—that is, not in carnal observances—but “in my spirit,” that is, in spiritual things, namely faith, hope, and charity. In what do I serve? “In the Gospel,” by preaching; not in the Law, not in circumcision, not in what Moses the servant handed down, but in what the only Son taught. For as far as servant is from master, so far is the Gospel from the Law. I say, “the Gospel of his Son,” which his Son handed down not by writing but by inspiring minds.

“Beseeching that somehow, at last, I may at some time have a prosperous journey, by the will of God, to come to you.” As if he said: I give thanks and pray for you. I mean, beseeching—that is, attempting by entreaties. [Col. 1319C] An entreaty is an adjuration by sacred things, such as by the Nativity and Passion. I am attempting, I say, “if somehow”—that is, in some way, whether favorable or adverse, for whatever cause, easy or difficult—“I may at last,” namely after long desires, “at some time,” namely in winter or summer, have a journey to come to you; a journey, I say, that is prosperous. The Apostle does not consider a journey prosperous unless it is such that he reaches those to whom he desires to preach God’s gift. For a prosperous journey is not to undergo the labour of travel in vain.

“May I have a prosperous journey”—prosperous, I say, “by the will of God,” according to God’s will, not like evil people who consider themselves prosperous when they have committed their evil. For some, through God’s permission rather than his will, seem to obtain a prosperous journey toward evil if they have committed some crime. [Origen] The Apostle therefore wished this to be understood by adding, “by the will of God,” because a journey’s prosperity is not always effected by God’s will. Many enjoy successful outcomes in worldly affairs and exult in their prosperity, but such prosperity is not according to God’s will. [Ambrose] The Apostle, however, judges a journey prosperous only if it is in God’s will, because then the Apostle’s arrival will be useful.

**VERS. 11, 12.**—“For I desire to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual grace for your strengthening; that is, that I may be consoled together with you through the faith which is mutual—yours and mine.”

[Col. 1320A] As if he said: For this reason I entreat to come to you, because I desire to see you. He says his presence is necessary for those whom he corrected in writing and withdrew from carnal understanding, because what he writes can also be wrongly understood, since heretics are accustomed to refer sayings to another meaning. He therefore desires to see them so that, being present, he may hand on evangelical teaching in the sense in which he writes it to them, lest under the authority of his letter error should not be removed but confirmed; and also so that, by the power of miracles while present, he may persuade them of what he could not persuade by words.

Then, explaining the reason for his desire, he adds: “That I may impart something.” As if he said: I desire to see you for this purpose, that I may impart to you some spiritual grace—that is, make you sharers in God’s free gift, namely the doctrine [Col. 1320B] of the Gospel. I mean grace not carnal but spiritual, because you now understand carnally. For when he says “spiritual grace,” he indicates that they had adopted a carnal understanding. [Augustine] For under Christ’s name the Jews had handed down to them things contrary to Christ. He, providing for human weakness, decreed that the human race should be saved by faith alone added to the law of nature.

“I may impart spiritual grace for your strengthening.” [Ambrose] For you already possess something; that is, “that I may be consoled among you together,” or, according to another reading, “that we may be consoled together with you,” through the faith which is mutual—yours and mine. As if he said: I desire to impart grace to you for strengthening, and that strengthening is so pleasing to me that your being strengthened is my being consoled among you. He says this because, although he rejoices in their readiness to believe, he nevertheless grieves over their faulty faith. For he grieved over others’ vices as though they were his own.

He adds “together,” as if he said: This consolation of mine will occur together with you, because you too will be consoled. For at present I am desolate, as are you, though you do not feel it; but thus we would be consoled together. Or, according to the other reading, it can be read thus, with the same meaning: I desire to come in order that I may impart grace to you for your strengthening, that is, that we may be consoled together with you. Then he adds by what means consolation occurs: I mean consolation through that faith—not, certainly, a new faith, but yours and mine—which is mutual, that is, common. Thus consolation may occur if [Col. 1320D] we are of one and the same faith in Christ. Or: through that faith, yours and mine, which is mutual, that is, which works through love.

**VERS. 13.**—“Now I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that I have often purposed to come to you, and have been prevented until now, in order that I may have some fruit among you also, as among the other nations.”

The Apostle makes known his purpose and desire: he does not doubt that they learned certain things through brethren who came to Rome from Jerusalem or neighboring cities, whether for some business or for religion’s sake. And since he often wished to come and was prevented, it came about that he wrote the Epistle, lest, being long held in evil, they should be corrected with greater difficulty. As though someone said: “You desire to come; why then do you not come?” He says: “Because I have been prevented, although I had purposed this.”

[Col. 1321A] [Haimo] “But I do not want,” or “I do not think,” “you to be ignorant, brethren,” of this: namely, that I have often purposed—not merely wished—to come to you, and have been prevented from coming by certain hindrances, God bringing this about. [Ambrose] But you must not suppose that this happens through your fault; rather, make yourselves worthy now. Therefore he does not say idly that he has been prevented, but distinguishes the reasons for his delays. He has also urged them to prepare themselves, [Origen] so that, hearing that spiritual grace was to be ministered to them, they might make themselves worthy to receive it by abstaining from carnal vices.

“I have been prevented,” I say, “until now,” that is, up to the present. By this it is shown that God also takes care where each apostle ought, or ought not, to go; and that by a certain dispensation he permits some to preach God’s word and prevents others from doing so.

Moreover, he calls them brethren not only because they had been reborn, but also because among them were some, though few, who held right opinions; whence above he said, “called saints.” “That I may have some fruit among you, as also among the other Gentiles.” As though he said: “Therefore I desire to come, that I may have fruit among you—that is, that you may bear fruit through my preaching; or, that I may have some fruit in you—that is, that I myself may gain some reward on your account.” Therefore, for the common benefit, he declares himself eager to come to them: so that they may attain the salvation of spiritual grace by holding a right confession of faith, and that he may have before God the fruit of his ministry.

“I may have fruit among you,” I say, “as also among the other Gentiles.” By the example of the other nations he spurs them toward right faith; for a person becomes more ready to accept what is offered him if he sees many others assenting to it.

### Verses 14–15

> “I am debtor both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to wise and to foolish; so, as far as lies in me, I am ready to preach the Gospel also to you who are at Rome.”

[Haimo] As though he said: “Therefore I wish to have fruit among all, because I am indebted to preach the Gospel to all.” “To Greeks and to barbarians,” that is, to all nations. He puts Greeks first because all worldly philosophy took its beginning from them. By “barbarians” he means those who are, as it were, outside the law: neither Hebrews, Greeks, nor Latins.

And I am indebted to preach the Gospel “to the wise [Col. 1321D] and the foolish,” so that no one of either people may be excluded. [Ambrose] By “wise” he means those educated in worldly reasoning; by “foolish,” those ignorant of such matters. He declares himself debtor to all these because he was sent to all. This preaching is not owed more specially to any one people among the nations, since he was sent to preach to all, having received instruction in order to hand it on to others.

He is silent about the Jews because he was the teacher of the Gentiles. And as I owe it to others, so I owe it to you at Rome to preach the Gospel, because I am debtor to all. That is, I am ready, insofar as it lies in me, to preach the Gospel to you also. And if I am prepared for this, the fault remains another’s.

Although he says he was sent to preach to all nations, he especially declares himself ready to preach to the Romans, among whom is the head and seat of the Roman empire. For the well-being of the members depends upon the head’s not being disturbed. Therefore he desires peace for the Romans, so that Satan may not boast greatly and so that he may have better fruits of his work.

### Verse 16

> “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel. For it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.”

As though he said: “I am ready, and truly so, because I am not ashamed of the Gospel,” unlike those who preach falsehoods and think Christ’s cross a disgrace. [Haimo] By this saying he touches upon those who handed down teaching incorrectly, or who were ashamed of the cross, in which they ought rather to glory with the Apostle himself.

Therefore I am not ashamed of the Gospel, [Col. 1322B] because the Gospel itself is the power of God: that is, it proclaims God’s power, not weakness; wisdom, not folly. “For what is weak in God is stronger than men; and what is foolish in God is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1).

Or, the Gospel is God’s power for us who believe, not for others: for through Gospel teaching sin is forgiven to the believer, and, when circumstances require, miracles occur by which the teaching is commended. Since what was preached seemed incredible, it was therefore confirmed by signs and wonders performed by the apostles, lest people distrust those who said such things while doing such great deeds. [Ambrose] For no one doubts that words yield to power.

Therefore the Apostle says that he is not ashamed of God’s Gospel; but he indicates that those others are ashamed, because what they had handed down was subject to reproach, was confirmed by no testimony of power, and disagreed with Gospel and apostolic teaching.

The Gospel, then, is God’s power because it summons to faith and grants salvation to every believer, forgiving sins and justifying, so that one sealed with the mystery of the cross cannot be held by the second death. Hence he adds: “I mean the Gospel, powerful unto salvation for every believer.” What he said, “every,” he specifies: “for the Jew who believes first, and for the Greek,” that is, the Gentile—as is evident in “Greek,” for by “Greek” he means a Gentile.

Although he gives precedence to the Jew because of the fathers, he nevertheless says that the Jew too equally needs the gift of Christ’s Gospel. If, therefore, even the Jew is not justified except by faith in Christ, what need is there to remain under the Law?

[Hesychius] Or thus: “To the Jew first and also to the Greek.” As though he said: “The Gospel is effective unto salvation for every believer; I mean, the Gospel is necessary for Jew and Greek, that is, Gentile—but first, that is, especially, for the Jew.” For the Jews had very great need of this Gospel salvation and deliverance, since they were also leading others astray.

### Verse 17

> “For the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith unto faith, as it is written: But the righteous person lives by faith.”

[Haimo] As though he said: “Truly the Gospel is unto salvation for the believer, because it is unto righteousness for him—and righteousness is the cause of salvation. This is clearly shown in the Gospel itself.” And this is what he says: “For the righteousness of God is revealed in it,” [Col. 1323A] namely, in the Gospel.

[Note: Col. 1323D, Ambrose, to Opertus.] The righteousness of God is that by which he freely justifies the ungodly through faith apart from works of the Law, as the Apostle says elsewhere: “That I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness which is from the Law, but that which is through faith” (Phil. 3).

[Note: Col. 1323D, Augustine, *On the Spirit*.] This is the righteousness of God, veiled in the Old Testament and revealed in the New. It is called God’s righteousness because, by imparting it, he makes people righteous. [Ambrose] The Gospel reveals this righteousness by its very effect, [Haimo] namely, by giving faith to a person through which he is justified, who believes God to be just and true in his promises. It also reveals this righteousness by the Word, when it says: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16), that is, shall be righteous.

[Ambrose the Great] Or, it is God’s righteousness because he gave what he promised. This righteousness [Col. 1323B] is revealed in the person who believes himself to have obtained what God promised through his prophets. Whoever believes and confesses this proves God just and is a witness to his righteousness. Here the Apostle speaks against Jews who deny that this is the Christ whom God promised.

According to this interpretation, read it thus: “I rightly said that it is unto salvation for every believer, because in the one who believes—whether Jew or Greek—God’s righteousness is revealed,” that is, God appears just and true. But to the one who does not believe, God seems unjust; for one who does not believe that God gave what he promised denies that God is true. Hence he adds: “From faith unto faith.” As though he said: “God’s righteousness is revealed, extending from the faithfulness of God who promises to the faith of the person who believes him, because in the believer God appears just.”

Or, according to the other preceding interpretation, proceed thus: God’s righteousness is from faith; but this righteousness of faith belongs to the person who passes from faith unto faith. [Haimo] He says this with reference to every aspect of faith, so that everyone wishing to be justified through faith may possess all the articles of the Creed: so that the Jew, and anyone else, may pass from the faith of the Old Testament, in which one God was worshipped, to the faith of the New Testament, in which Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are worshipped; from faith in the first advent to faith in the second, believing both; from faith in the first resurrection, which is in the soul, to faith in the second, which will be in bodies; from faith in the promise to faith in its fulfillment, believing that God has promised and has fulfilled, or will fulfill, it.

[Note: Col. 1323D, Primasius, on the Apocalypse.] One must pass from the faith of the preachers [Col. 1323D] to the faith of the peoples, believing what both greater and lesser persons believe; from the faith of sowers, that is, prophets, to the faith of reapers, that is, apostles. Or the person to be justified must pass—or understand that he will pass—from faith in words and hope to faith in things and sight.

[Haimo] For faith is that by which things not seen are believed; this is properly called faith.

[Note: Col. 1323D, Augustine, in the book *Questions on the Gospels*.] Yet there is also a faith of realities, by which belief is given not to words but to the realities themselves as present. This will be when the very Wisdom of God offers herself to the saints for contemplation in manifest vision. Therefore [Col. 1324A] there would not be a righteousness of faith unless what we believed when preached were hidden, and unless by believing we came to seeing.

[Note: Col. 1324D, ibid., on Psalm 109.] He therefore says that righteousness belongs to the one who passes from faith in words, by which we believe what we do not see, to faith in realities, by which we shall obtain what we have believed: namely, from the faith in which one serves God to that in which one enjoys God. This latter, however, is improperly called faith.

And because faith is mentioned here, we must consider what faith is, in how many senses it is understood, and what things it concerns. Faith is the virtue by which things not seen are believed; things apparent do not have faith but recognition. For faith is believing what you do not see.

[Note: Col. 1324D, Augustine, in a certain homily.] Faith is understood in three ways: for that by which one believes, and which is a virtue; for that by which one believes, and which is not a virtue; and for that which is believed.

The faith [Col. 1324B] by which one believes, when joined with charity, is a virtue; it is the foundation of all good things, and in it no one perishes. It makes people faithful and truly Christian. But another faith is that of demons and of Christians only in name; for “even the demons believe—and tremble” (James 2). This is an unformed quality of the mind, called unformed because it does not have charity as its companion—charity which is the form of all virtues.

Faith is understood as that which is believed, as in: “This is the Catholic faith, which unless…” [Note: Col. 1324D, from the Athanasian Creed.] It is understood in this sense here when he says, “from faith unto faith.” The faith which is believed—that is, the faith of the Creed—has many parts, some of which have been set out here. Faith is likewise understood when it is called “the Catholic faith,” as that which must be believed universally by all.

[Col. 1324C] Some commonly ask whether the unformed quality of mind called faith in an evil Christian—by which he believes everything that a true Christian believes—remains when charity is added and becomes a virtue, or whether it is itself removed and another quality succeeds which is a virtue. For this, a divine oracle seems more properly to be sought than any definition from us. Either answer, however, may be given without danger.

Faith concerns good things and evil things, past things, present things, and future things. [Ambrose] Hope, however, concerns only future things and good things.

“As it is written”: the Apostle turns to the example of the prophet Habakkuk, [Augustine] in order to declare that it was long ago shown that a person is justified before God not by the Law but by faith. As though he said: “Righteousness is from faith, and thus salvation is from faith, not from the Law, as it is written in Habakkuk: ‘But the righteous person lives by faith.’”

Explain it thus: everyone who is righteous [Col. 1324D] is righteous by faith, [Augustine] and therefore lives—not with this present life, but with the future life, that is, eternal life, which is faith’s reward. For faith’s reward is to see what we believed before we saw it.

It should be known, however, that Habakkuk differs from the Apostle’s wording here. For in Habakkuk it reads: “But my righteous person shall live by his faith” (Hab. 2). This and many other testimonies which he cites seem to disagree with the translation of the Hebrew truth which we now use. This is because he sometimes takes from the Seventy Interpreters, and sometimes, speaking in the same Spirit as the prophets, he takes only the sense, using his own words and arrangement.

### Verses 18–19

> “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those people who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness, because what may be known of God is manifest in them. For God revealed it to them.”

[Note: Col. 1325D, Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*.] Having commended the piety of faith, by which, having been justified, we ought to be pleasing to God, he introduces its opposite with detestation, namely ungodliness. The Gentiles, puffed up and frivolous, as it were fell into the fabricated forms of idols, where they would not rest but, shattered, leap down upon [Col. 1325B] stones.

Here he specifically attacks the Gentiles in their former condition, because they boast of a good nature and excuse their shameful acts through ignorance. But the Apostle says, to the contrary, that they had formerly possessed knowledge and lost it through fault, and that the good nature left to them by God had been hurled by themselves into every evil.

As though he said: “Righteousness is from faith, and from it salvation; [Note: Col. 1325D, Augustine, *The City of God*] because unrighteousness is from ungodliness, and from it wrath—that is, punishment. This is revealed in God’s Gospel.” And this is what he means: “For in the Gospel God’s wrath is revealed,” that is, punishment. Whenever God’s wrath is read of, it must not be understood as a disturbance of his mind, but as the judgment by which punishment is inflicted for sin.

[Haimo] I mean the wrath of God who will come from heaven for judgment—the wrath which will come upon every ungodliness and unrighteousness. He does not say, “upon all ungodly persons,” but, what is more, “upon every ungodliness and unrighteousness,” that is, upon every part of ungodliness and unrighteousness.

[Origen] Ungodliness is sinning against God; iniquity is sinning against human beings. Or “ungodly” here stands for unbelieving, that is, alien to the piety of religion, such as an idolater. But an unrighteous person is one who departs from equity through the perversity of action.

[Haimo] The meaning is: God’s vengeance, of him who will come from heaven to judge the living and the dead, is revealed in the Gospel as coming upon every ungodliness and unrighteousness.

[Ambrose] Or read it thus: “The wrath of God, coming upon every ungodliness and unrighteousness, is revealed from heaven.” This accuses them because it pointed out to them the Creator or the Savior. For God is shown to be angry with them from the very structure of heaven, [Col. 1325D] since he created such beautiful stars so that from them one might recognize how great and admirable their Creator is and worship him alone.

The Apostle therefore makes the Gentile guilty through the law of nature, by which the world’s structure, testifying to its Maker, could teach that God alone ought to be loved. But unrighteousness and ungodliness appear in them when, although seeing these things, they conceal the truth and do not confess one God. Hence he adds:

“Of those who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness.” As though someone said: [Note: Col. 1325D, Augustine, in a certain sermon.] “Why is God’s wrath upon them for ungodliness, since they did not know God?” To this he replies: [Col. 1326A] God’s wrath is deservedly upon them, because they could indeed know God, and some of them even partly knew him; but they deprive themselves of this knowledge, preferring unjustly to remain in their own pleasure.

[Haimo] Read the sentence thus: “Of people,” I mean, “who hold the truth of God,” that is, true knowledge concerning God, although it freely offers itself to them—people who, I say, remain in unrighteousness, that is, in evil action.

[Note: Col. 1326D, Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*.] The thing they hold is good, but the place in which they hold it is evil. For they hold the truth, but in iniquity. You have found God, O Gentile, O philosopher, and you worship an idol. You have found truth, and hold it in unrighteousness. What you learned through God’s works, you lost through human works.

You considered the entire order of things and refuse to observe that the world is God’s work, while an idol is the work of an artisan. If, as the artisan gave the idol its shape, he also gave it a heart, the artisan himself would be worshipped by the idol. How, then, is the human being who made you not your god, if a human being is the maker of the idol? Who is your God, the one who made you? Who is the artisan’s God? The one who made him. Therefore, if the idol had a heart, would it not worship the artisan who made it? Behold how they hold God’s truth in unrighteousness.

The Apostle might, however, have been met with the objection: “How do they hold the truth, when God did not speak to them and they did not receive the Law as did the people of Israel?” He replies and shows how: “Because what may be known of God is manifest in them; for God revealed it to them.” As though he said: “They truly hold God’s truth, by which what is knowable of God—that is, what can be known concerning God—is manifest in them through the guidance of reason.” As though he said: “They have within themselves the means by which they can know it.”

What is knowable concerning God is natural reason. He says “what is knowable concerning God” because many things concerning God cannot be known through nature—for example, the mystery of redemption and incarnation.

[Origen] What is known of God is what we can attain from the ordering of this world and natural reason. What is unknown of God is the principle of his substance or nature, which is hidden from every creature; likewise, the mystery of human deliverance.

[Ambrose] And what is knowable concerning God is truly manifest in them, because not only did natural reason assist toward this, but God also revealed or manifested it to them through his work, by which he helped them. He says this lest nature alone should seem sufficient.

[Col. 1326D] For God, who is invisible by nature, made a work in order that he might also be known from visible things—a work which made its maker manifest through its own visibility. Thus the uncertain might be known through the certain, and he might be believed to be God of all who made what these things cannot make.

[Note: ibid.] Noble philosophers sought these things, as though questioning creatures concerning the Creator; and, with the beauty and arrangement of all things answering as if with a voice, they recognized the artisan from the art.

### Verses 20–23

> “For his invisible things are clearly seen from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that have been made—even his eternal power and divinity—so that they are without excuse. For when they had known [Col. 1327A] God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; but they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. For, professing themselves to be wise, they became fools; and they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed animals, and serpents.”

He shows what they could know of God and how they could know it. And as though someone asked how what is known of God could be manifest in those who had not received the Law, he adds: “For his invisible things,” etc.

It should be noted that, although God is one and a simple essence and is not composed of any diversity, he nevertheless says “invisible things” in the plural, because he is known in many ways through created things: as eternal from the permanence of creatures; [Col. 1327B] almighty from their magnitude; and so forth. His power is also perceived from their governance; and from the fact that he fills all things, his divinity—that is, goodness—is understood.

This is what he says: “Truly, what is known of God is manifest in them. For his invisible things”—that is, he himself, invisible by nature—are perceived by understanding, not by corporeal or imaginary vision, but only by that power of the mind called intellect. They are perceived through things that have been made; and, though not through the written Law which they did not have, they are clearly seen “from the creation of the world,” that is, by human beings, not by angels alone.

[Haimo] A human being is called the creation of the world preeminently because he excels among other creatures, [Col. 1327C] or because he has a correspondence with every creature. For he exists locally in a place, like any body; he senses with animals; and he understands with angels. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says: “Preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16), that is, to humanity.

Observe that he says: “Those invisible things themselves, understood through things that have been made.” [Note: Col. 1327D, Augustine, *The City of God*.] For through heaven and earth and other creatures, which they understood to be vast and enduring, they mentally perceived the incomparable, immense, eternal Creator himself.

For the greatest philosophers—whom we see not without reason set above others in reputation and glory—saw that no body is God; and so they transcended all bodies in seeking God. They also saw that whatever is mutable is not the supreme God; and therefore [Col. 1327D] they transcended every soul and mutable spirit. Then they saw that every form naturally existing in any mutable thing, and every body of the whole world, could exist only from him who exists immutably and simply: for in him to be is not one thing, to live another, to understand another, and to be blessed another; rather, for him to live, understand, and be blessed is identical with his being.

Because of this immutability and simplicity, they understood that he had made all these things and could himself be made by none. For they considered that whatever exists among substances is either body or spirit; that spirit is something better than body; that bodily form is [Col. 1328A] sensible, but spiritual form intelligible; and they preferred intelligible form to sensible form. By “sensible” we mean what can be perceived by bodily sight and touch; by “intelligible,” what can be understood by the mind’s vision.

Since, then, body and soul appeared in their sight more or less beautiful, yet could not exist at all if they could lack every form, they saw that there must be something in which was the first and unchangeable form, and therefore the incomparable form.

[Note: Col. 1328D, Augustine, *Against the Manichaeans*.] There, most rightly, they believed to be the principle of things: that which was not made and from which all things were made.

[Note: Col. 1328D, Augustine, *Against the Manichaeans*.] Thus God’s invisible things, understood through things that have been made, are clearly seen. Yet it is remarkable that he says they are invisible and again says that they are “clearly seen.” But by adding “understood,” he defines the manner of vision.

For three kinds of vision are found in Scripture: corporeal vision, spiritual or imaginary vision, and intellectual vision. This vision which the Apostle here mentions belongs to the third kind. For by this vision God is seen when hearts are purified through the piety of faith and the knowledge of excellent moral conduct.

Or read the sentence thus: “Truly, what is known of God is manifest in them, because his invisible things are seen intellectually from the creation of the world,” that is, from the constitution of the world, through the things that have been made. And so that ungodliness may be wholly without excuse, he adds: “The power which governs all things is perceived through the things that have been made, [Col. 1328C] and likewise divinity”—[Ambrose] that is, God’s goodness which fills all things—is perceived through the same things.

[Haimo; Augustine] Or, as some wish, the Trinity may be understood here: by “invisible things,” the Father; by “power,” the Son; and by “divinity,” the Holy Spirit. The meaning would be: “His invisible things,” that is, the Father; “his eternal power,” that is, the Son; and “divinity,” that is, the Holy Spirit, are understood and perceived through the things made from the creation of the world.

According to this, it seems that the philosophers of the nations had knowledge of that supreme Trinity through created things. Elsewhere, however, Augustine says that philosophers did not attain knowledge of the third person, the Holy Spirit, namely in the passage on Exodus where Pharaoh’s magicians failed at the third sign, [Col. 1328D] not at the first or second. For, he says, the greatest Gentile philosophers philosophized “περὶ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ”—“concerning the Good,” that is, the supreme Good, namely the Father—and concerning “νοῦ,” “his mind,” namely the Son. But the magicians failed at the third sign because philosophers could not reach the third person.

How, then, is it said here that they understood or knew the three persons through created things? We answer that they by no means possessed, or could have possessed, the distinction of the supreme Trinity professed by Catholic faith without revelation through teaching or inward inspiration. For revelation comes in three ways: through works, through teaching, and through inspiration.

[Col. 1329A] God revealed truth to them through works, but not through teaching or inspiration. Therefore they saw truth from afar but did not draw near through humility.

[Augustine] Thus they are not said to have understood the three persons because they understood them distinctly, truly, and properly, but because they knew that in God there were those things which sacred Scripture frequently attributes distinctly and specially to the three persons: power, wisdom, and goodness. Power is often attributed to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness to the Holy Spirit—although the power, wisdom, and goodness of the three persons are one and the same, and those three are the same goodness, wisdom, and power. It is not useless to inquire why this is so.

For just as from the movements and administration of a body you understand a soul which you do not see, so they understood the Creator from the governance of the whole world and the rule of all things.

“So that they are without excuse.” [Note: Col. 1329D, Augustine, to the monk Valentinus.] Scripture calls those persons inexcusable whom truth does not escape and in whom iniquity persists.

Concerning this, namely that by natural reason and the revelation of creation they knew God, [Haimo, Ambrose, Augustine] even to the point of confessing one principle from which all things derived their beginning, they did not glorify him as God by living and worshipping rightly; nor—or rather, and—did they give thanks for this knowledge. Instead, they attributed it to themselves, in which they were vain and false.

Hence he adds: “But they became vain in their thoughts,” thinking themselves to be something [Col. 1329C] when they were nothing; and this truly was vanity. I mean, in their own thoughts, which came from themselves, not from God. And therefore, because they did not glorify God, their heart—that is, their reason—was darkened, because they believed it to exist from themselves. Swollen pride hardened it, so that it became foolish: that is, their heart was gradually led as far as folly.

For the mist of error covered their heart, because, though they had known the Creator from creatures, they had not glorified him as God, and so they became more obtuse. Whence was their heart darkened? Behold, from this pride: saying with mouth or heart that they were wise from themselves and not from God, they became fools with respect to God.

Here he expressly marks the two things he had mentioned: how they became vain, shown in “professing themselves to be wise,” where their fault is displayed; and how their heart was darkened, shown in “they became fools,” which is their punishment. For they were wise in the natures of things, but became foolish with respect to God.

[Ambrose] They investigated physical causes, examining the courses of the stars and the quantities of the elements, but despised their God. Therefore they were foolish. For if these things are praiseworthy, how much more their Creator!

[Note: Col. 1329D, Augustine, on John.] They saw, therefore, where they ought to arrive; but, ungrateful to him who had enabled them to see, they wished to attribute to themselves what they saw.

[Note: Col. 1329D, Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*.] Becoming proud, they lost even what they saw. They were cast down—or blinded—because they were proud. Pride is the head of sin, of which it is said: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10). They grew proud by saying that they were wise. They should not have claimed for themselves what God had given, nor boasted of what they possessed not from themselves but from him.

They ought to have believed this, so that they might be healed by the one who had enabled them to see, in order that they might hold fast to what they could see. If they had done this, they would have preserved humility, could have been purified, and could have cleaved to that most blessed contemplation.

[Note: Col. 1330D, Augustine, in the *Sermon on the Mount*.] But because pride was in them, blindness overshadowed them. What they found through curiosity, they lost through pride. What God had freely given, he took away from the ungrateful.

[Note: Col. 1330D, Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*.] They turned away from truth to idols and images and the worship of demons; they worshipped the creature while despising [Col. 1330B] the Creator. Hence he adds: “And they changed.”

Behold how their heart was darkened: they changed the majesty of the invisible God, whom they had known from creatures, not merely into human beings, but—what is worse and an inexcusable offense—into the likeness of human beings. Thus they called a corruptible form “God”: that is, the image of a human being. They did not dare confer this name upon living persons, yet received images of the dead in place of God’s glory. How great their dullness! How great their folly, among whom image has more power than truth, and the dead are more important than the living! For, departing from the living God, they favor the dead.

[Ambrose] They themselves belong to their number, as it is said in Solomon’s book: “A dead man fashions a dead thing by wicked works” (Wisdom 15).

Read the sentence thus: [Col. 1330C] “They sinned not only in understanding and thought, but also in deed.” “And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God”—that is, the worship due to God, who is incorruptible—so far as concerned themselves, first into “the likeness of an image of corruptible man,” that is, into the image of one to whom it was made like; then into the likeness of images of birds. Behold greater dullness still! Then into images of four-footed animals, and finally of serpents.

[Augustine] He says this to display the height of their dullness. They so diminished God’s majesty and glory that they gave divine honor to likenesses of things that are very small and insignificant. Here, therefore, he condemns images of the ungodly, among whom some worshipped the sun, others the earth, others dead human beings, and many other such things.

He says “into the likeness of man, and birds, and four-footed animals, and serpents” because images of these were worshipped by the Romans at different times. From ancient times the Romans had the custom of worshipping images of human beings—Romulus, Jupiter, and others—especially from Aeneas’s arrival in Italy. They worshipped images of birds, four-footed animals, and serpents after Alexandria had been conquered by Augustus and subjected to Rome.

### Verses 24–25

> “Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonor their bodies among themselves, [Col. 1331A] because they changed the truth of God into a lie and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen.”

Here likewise the vengeance of God against them is shown. [Augustine, Ambrose] For because, to the dishonour of God the Creator, they deified fabricated images and likenesses of things, they were handed over to be mocked by the desires of the flesh—not so that they might do what they did not wish, but so that they might accomplish what they desired. [Origen] To hand over, however, means to permit, not to incite or instil. For, when the causes of sins have preceded, those who hold down the truth of God in unrighteousness and attribute the Creator’s glory to the creature are rightly and deservedly forsaken by God; and by this they are forsaken and handed over to desires. These sins, moreover, [Col. 1331B] because they arise from pride, are not only sins but punishments as well.

[Note: [Col. 1331D] Augustine, in a certain sermon.] For every sin which is not promptly covered by repentance is either sin and the cause of sin, or sin and the punishment of sin. [Gregory] Indeed, sin which repentance does not wash away immediately draws, by its own weight, toward another sin. Thus it comes about that it is not only sin but also the cause of sin, for the ensuing fault arises from it. But sin which arises from sin is not only sin but also the punishment of sin, because by a just judgment God darkens the sinner’s heart, so that, by the desert of the preceding sin, he may fall into others as well. The one whom He was unwilling to free, He struck by forsaking him. And this is what he says: “Therefore”—[Haimo], namely, because of idolatry [Col. 1331C] and because they surrendered God’s worship and religion to images—“God handed them over,” that is, by withdrawing grace He permitted them to be handed over. For nothing occurs without His permission, even among evils. This darkening itself was already vengeance and punishment; and yet through this punishment—that is, through the blindness of heart produced when the light of wisdom forsakes it—they fell into more numerous and graver sins.

“He handed [them] over,” I say, first “to the desires of their heart”—of their heart, I say, which was their own, that is, left by God to themselves. These desires were thus prepared by themselves, not by God. Afterward He handed them over “to uncleanness,” that is, to the act of uncleanness, so that by the act itself they might commit such great shamefulness as to subject their bodies to dishonour so far as nature is concerned: that is, so that they might, by a certain violence, apply bodies naturally resistant to it and make them more suited to vice. [Col. 1331D]

[Augustine] Here again the vengeance by which they were handed over is shown: not merely to depraved desires, but also to unclean and dishonourable actions, by which they subject and defile their bodies. I say, they have these things “in themselves,” not from elsewhere, but from themselves. [Note: [Col. 1331D] Augustine, *Against Julian*.] For a human being does not have these things from God; but he is said to be handed over to them because, forsaken by God, he yields to and consents to them: he is conquered, captured, drawn away, possessed. For whoever has been conquered by another has also become that one’s assigned slave; and the ensuing sin becomes the punishment for the preceding sin.

Or thus: “that they may subject their bodies,” I say, while they themselves act “to dishonour in themselves,” that is, within their own sex: males with males, females with females. [Col. 1332A] It must be carefully observed that here and subsequently he says, “God handed them over.” [Augustine] God does not create human wickedness, for He is not a tempter to evils. Therefore, whoever says that God does not compel people to these acts, but only forsakes those worthy of being forsaken, speaks most truly.

[Note: [Col. 1332D] Augustine, *On Free Will*.] God forsakes them by not bestowing grace, or by withdrawing grace already bestowed. For it is evident that God works in human hearts to incline their wills wherever He wills, whether toward good through His mercy or toward evil according to their deserts—[Ambrose] certainly by His judgment, sometimes manifest, sometimes hidden, but always just. Note also that God is said to work in human hearts so as to incline their will toward evil. This must not be understood as though [Col. 1332B] God imparted wickedness; rather, just as He bestows grace, by which human will is inclined toward good, so He withdraws it from some, and, once it has been withdrawn, their will bends toward evil.

“Because they exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen.”

Here he sets out their fault and punishment more fully, point by point, in order to compare them with one another; and this repeats what was said above. [Augustine] For he showed, point by point, that they had changed God’s glory: namely, that they thought a thing to be God which was not, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator. Subsequently he sets out the forms of uncleanness: namely, that females committed shamefulness with females and males with males. [Col. 1332C] In these he compares punishment with fault: just as they sinned against creating nature, so they were punished in their own nature. Hence he concludes below: “And receiving in themselves the recompense which was fitting for their error” (below, v. 27), etc. It is as if he said: They “subject,” that is, disfigure, their bodies—those who “exchanged the truth of God for a lie.”

[Ambrose] That is, they gave to an idol what is true of God—namely, that it is God. Here he calls “the truth of God” what above he called “the glory of God.” For the truth of God is the glory of God.

[Note: [Col. 1332D] Fulgentius, *To Donatus*.] To hold the truth of God is to worship one God; to turn truth into a lie is to serve the creature in place of the Creator. For true religion consists in the service of the one true God. Truth itself is indeed the true God. [Col. 1332D] For truth itself is one, and true divinity is one; therefore two true gods cannot truthfully be spoken of, just as the one truth itself cannot naturally be divided. To worship the true God, then, and to serve the true God, is certainly not to exchange the truth of God for a lie.

[Ambrose] But the person who thinks that one should serve a God who is not true exchanges God’s truth for a lie. Therefore they exchanged God’s truth for a lie when they bestowed the name of the true God upon things which are not gods. For, taking away from stones, wood, and metals what they are, and giving them what they are not, they make God’s truth into a lie: when they say that a stone is God, they do not deny God, but [Col. 1333A] “serve the creature rather than the Creator.” This is to change truth into falsehood. In order to seem to worship these things worthily, they imposed God’s name and honour upon them.

[Note: [Col. 1333D] Augustine, *On the One Baptism*.] The truth of a creature is from God, but it is not God; yet they turn it into a lie by worshipping creatures as though they were the Creator. But lest anyone should say, “I do not worship images, but the things they represent, such as the sun and moon and the like,” he adds: “and they worshipped the creature,” diligently praying to it; “and served” the works of the creature. [Ambrose] Here he condemns the things which they understood by the images. I say, they served the creature rather than the Creator, as if the former were better. Yet although He is deprived by them of His honour, He is “blessed,” that is, exalted above all things, and this “for ever,” that is, without end. “Amen”: as if to say, this [Col. 1333B] is true—that blessing belongs for ever to the true God. But the gods of the Gentiles receive honour from impiety only for a time; therefore what they say is falsehood.

VERS. 26, 27.—“Therefore God handed them over to dishonourable passions. For their females exchanged the natural use for that use which is contrary to nature. Likewise also the males, leaving the natural use of the female, burned in their desires for one another, males committing shamefulness with males, and receiving in themselves the recompense which was fitting for their error.”

Here vengeance is again repeated. It is as though he said: And because they sinned thus against creating nature, therefore God handed them over—that is, permitted them to be handed over. Here [Col. 1333C] vengeance is repeated again, just as earlier he repeated the fault. “To dishonourable passions,” that is, pleasures of the flesh which, although pleasing, are passions of a nature not to be named. [Haimo] Their dishonour is so called as being without the name of dignity. Hence a person is called dishonourable when, on being detected in some crime, he ceases to possess the name of dignity. Therefore God first handed them over to dishonourable passions, that is, to the burning heat of lust, which is a passion of nature and not to be named. Afterwards He handed them over to the very act of lust—and truly so.

“For their females exchanged the natural use of a lawful husband for that use which is contrary to nature,” namely, by acting with one another. [Haimo] Natural use is that a man and woman should unite in one act of intercourse; contrary to nature, however, is that a male defile a male and a woman a woman. [Col. 1333D] But if someone, leaving his wife, has relations with another woman, he commits shamefulness and sins, but it is not contrary to nature. Yet one who sleeps even with his own wife in a manner other than is fitting acts contrary to nature.

“Likewise also the males, leaving the natural use of the female, burned for one another in their desires”: behold, sins of the will. I say, “in their desires,” which are from themselves, not from God. [Ambrose] The Apostle testifies that these things came upon the human race through God’s anger because of idolatry: that a woman should seek a woman and a male a male with shameful desire for an improper use. For what is it to exchange natural use [Col. 1334A] for that which is contrary to nature, except, after setting aside the permitted use, to use otherwise than is permitted, when that part of the body has not been given such a use by nature? Whatever a person possesses as granted and lawful, if it is turned to another order and done otherwise than it is granted, is sin.

[Note: [Col. 1333D] Augustine, *Against Julian the Heretic*.] If you now suppose, O Julian, that the Apostle has praised lust in this passage because he called the use of the female natural, you are compelled consequently to praise every use of the female. By this argument you will also praise the illicit sexual acts committed with females, because there too the use is certainly natural, although condemnable because it is not lawful. Hence children born from such unions are called not legitimate but natural. The Apostle therefore did not praise fleshly desire in that expression, but called natural use [Col. 1334B] that use by which human nature can continue through birth. He did not call it marital use but natural use, intending that use to be understood which takes place in members created for this purpose, so that through them either sex may unite for procreation.

[Note: [Col. 1333D] The same, in the same work.] Accordingly, when someone joins with a prostitute by means of those same members, it is natural use, yet not praiseworthy but blameworthy. But if someone uses his wife by that part of the body which was not established for procreation, it is contrary to nature and shameful.

“Males with males.” It is as though he said: Not only did they burn, but males also committed shamefulness in act with males. And thus they were “receiving the recompense for their error,” that is, for their error, which was fitting—namely, recompense [Col. 1334C] appropriate to sin; that is, they received vengeance worthy of their fault. [Ambrose, Augustine] For as great as idolatry is through its impious and most grievous offence, so dreadful and foul is the compensating passion which they received: “in themselves,” namely, in their own nature, vindicating God—that is, enduring God’s vengeance in their own sex, namely, by producing deformity. [Note: [Col. 1334D] Augustine, *Against Julian the Heretic*.]

Note that he says that they ought to receive this recompense. Here, surely, you see the cause for which they were handed over shown without any ambiguity. For he stated what evil they had first done and then added, “Therefore God handed [them] over,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1334D] Augustine, *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*.] Consequently this is the punishment of preceding sin, yet it is itself sin. For they were handed over by God’s most just judgment, whether through forsaking or in some other explicable [Col. 1334D] or inexplicable way, to dishonourable passions, so that crimes might be punished by crimes and the punishments of sinners might not, however, be torments, but also increases of vices. But few perceive these punishments. Therefore the Apostle especially mentions them: he enumerates many things which are sins and punishments of sin. For between the first sin of apostasy and the final punishment of eternal fire, the intervening things are both sins and punishments.

VERS. 28–31.—“And as they did not approve having God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are not fitting; [Col. 1335A] filled with all unrighteousness, wickedness, fornication, avarice, malice; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malignity; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insolent, proud, haughty, inventors of evils, disobedient to parents, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without covenant, without mercy.”

“And as”—or, “because they did not approve having God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a reprobate mind.” [Ambrose] Behold, because they still do not come to their senses, they fall into further sins for the same fault. By saying “as,” he makes the punishment correspond to the sin: just as they sinned in their understanding of God, supposing that God did not know their evils, so they were punished in their own understanding. And this is what “as they approved” means: that is, they thought [Col. 1335B] God did not have human sins in His knowledge; thus He handed them over to a reprobate mind, etc.

Or, as it is read there, “because [they did] not,” rather than “as,” in this way: because they did not approve having God in their knowledge—that is, because they did not know God, though reason demonstrated Him to them. Or, because they approved—that is, thought—that God did not have evils in His knowledge, that is, that God was ignorant of or neglected human evils, God therefore handed them over to a reprobate mind. [Origen] That is, they understand nothing except what is far removed from uprightness, since their own blindness wholly shuts them out from the light of truth. “He handed [them] over,” I say, “to do” in deed “things which are not fitting” to reason.

I say, those “filled with all unrighteousness,” as though they did not have only a little. Then he enumerates [Col. 1335C] the parts of unrighteousness, in order to accuse them more openly. I say, those filled with wickedness. Wickedness is when someone schemes to injure another. “Fornication”: fornication is every use of fleshly intercourse outside lawful union. “Avarice”: avarice is acquiring much and not distributing one’s surplus to the poor. “Malice”: malice is rashness, when one dares what one cannot do; or malice is lack of self-restraint. I say, those full of envy, that is, pain at another’s good. [Haimo] For an envious person is one tormented by another’s happiness, and is thus divided by a double passion: either because he does not wish another to possess what he himself possesses, or because, seeing another better than himself, he grieves that he is not like him.

“Murders”: he uses the plural because there are murders of act and of will. “Strife”: strife is the assault upon [Col. 1335D] truth through the confidence of clamour. “Deceit”: deceit is when one thing is pretended and another done. “Malignity”: malignity is an evil will when it can do no further harm, or failure to return gratitude for benefits. “Whisperers”: those who sow discord among friends. “Slanderers”: those who deny or pervert others’ good qualities. And lest whispering and slander be thought trivial because they consist in words, he adds concerning them: “hateful to God,” and “insolent,” those who inflict insults and shameful things by words or deeds. “Proud in honours.” “Haughty”: the haughty are those unwilling to endure a superior or an equal. “Inventors of evils”: those who devise some new kind of evil, in word or deed. “Disobedient to parents,” whether carnal or spiritual: that is, wilder than untamed beasts. “Foolish”: those not discerning [Col. 1336A] good from evil. “Disorderly,” in dress or gait. The disorderliness of the body indicates the quality of the mind. “Without affection,” that is, without love of neighbour. “Without covenant,” that is, without fellowship; “without mercy,” because they do not suffer with the miserable.

VERS. 32.—“Though they had known the justice of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them.”

“Though they had known God’s justice,” etc. Again he shows them falling further, saying that such persons had first known by reason. “The justice of God,” that is, the just God. Yet they did not understand this: namely, that those who do such things are worthy of eternal death. Lest they should be thought afflicted only by the punishments mentioned above, in which they take delight, [Col. 1336B] he adds here the final, eternal death. And not only those who do these things are worthy of death, but also those who consent to those who do them, so that no one may be excused. [Ambrose] To consent is to keep silent when one can rebuke, or to encourage error through flattery.

CHAPTER II.

VERS. 1, 2.—“Therefore you are inexcusable, O every human being who judges. For in judging another you condemn yourself. For you do the same things which you judge. For we know that God’s judgment is according to truth against those who do such things.”

Above he spoke against the Gentiles, denouncing their pride and the shameful acts into which they were handed over because of it. [Haimo] Here, however, he treats jointly [Col. 1336C] of Gentiles and Jews, who judged one another but nevertheless did not cease from evils. It is as though he said: “Therefore”—namely, because everyone who acts or consents is worthy of death—“you are inexcusable, O human being,” namely, a person of the flesh. “Every [one],” namely, both Jew and Gentile, “who judges another,” that is, condemns him, and thereby displays himself as what he is not, namely, righteous. The Jew judges the Gentile according to the former condition, and the Gentile the Jew; and each is a human being, not spirit—that is, carnal, not spiritual—and each is inexcusable. For if a Jew judges a Gentile for idolatry, he too is an idolater; if a Gentile judges a Jew for transgressing the Law, he himself is a transgressor of the natural law. Therefore each is inexcusable.

Or he says this especially concerning the Jews, although he does not yet name them expressly: [Col. 1336D] those who boast in the Law and do the things which they condemn in others, as is shown below. And because he does not yet expressly name them, he names them below. And because not only those who sinned under the Law will perish, but those also who sinned without the Law, he therefore added there concerning the Gentiles, saying: “Wrath upon every human soul that does evil, of Jew and Greek; and glory to every one who does good, Jew and Greek.” [Haimo] It is as though he said: Therefore, namely, because the Gentiles who do the aforementioned things are inexcusable, much more are you, O every human being who judges—that is, O Jew, who, instructed by the Law, condemns others—inexcusable, because you do not keep yourself from the things for which you rebuke others.

He proves that they are inexcusable, whether speaking especially of Jews or jointly of Jews and Gentiles. It is as though he said: Truly you who judge are inexcusable. For in judging another you condemn yourself: that is, you yourself are a witness to your own condemnation when you judge another. Why is this so? For you do the same things that you judge, that is, rebuke in others. “For we know”—or, “but”—that God’s judgment is according to truth against those who do such things. Here the Apostle destroys, on his own authority, the empty excuse of Jews and Gentiles. A Jew might have said in excuse for his sin: “Even if I do the same things that I judge, my Jewish ancestry and the Law defend me.” Conversely, a Gentile might say: “Ignorance defends me.” Against this the Apostle says, “We know,” etc., showing that Jews cannot be excused by the Law or ancestry, nor Gentiles by ignorance. [Augustine] For ignorance in those unwilling to understand [Col. 1337B] is sin; in those unable to understand, it is the punishment of sin.
