“We know,” etc. [Haimo] It is as though he said: You hold such an opinion, but we know that the judgment, etc.—or, if “for” occurs there, read it thus: Truly you are inexcusable, because we know that God’s judgment is according to truth, that is, according to the equity of the matter, not according to respect of persons, against those who do such things, whether they are Jews or Gentiles: that is, against those who do the things which they rebuke in others. In judgment people take account of the persons of the powerful, the rich, and their relatives; but God’s judgment is true in this respect, because He who is truthful does not regard persons, but the merit of one’s life. [John of Damascus] Human judgment, indeed, is corrupted in many ways—by love, hatred, and fear. Often judgment is violated even by integrity, and mercy at times inclines it contrary to the rule of justice. [Col. 1337C]

[Ambrose, Origen] But God’s judgment is according to truth, because He will render to each according to the measure of good or evil. For the truth of judgment requires that the evil person receive evils and the good person receive goods. Yet this seems to be shown in this passage: that judgment according to truth belongs to God alone because it belongs to God alone to know human hearts and discern the secrets of the mind. For some things are committed in an evil deed but not with an evil intention—for example, if someone kills a person unintentionally. Other things are good in deed but not in intention—for example, if someone performs a work of mercy not because of God’s command but in order to be praised by people.

[Col. 1337D] VERS. 3–6.—“But do you suppose this, O human being, who judge those who do such things and do them yourself: that you will escape God’s judgment? Or do you despise the riches of His goodness, patience, and long-suffering? Do you not know that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart you store up wrath for yourself in the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works.”

It is as though he said: We apostles know thus; but you, O human being, namely carnal and not spiritual—every one who judges those who do such things, such as we mentioned above, and yet does them yourself—do you suppose, that is, think, this: namely, that you will in some way escape God’s judgment? And do you do this? It is as though he said: It is astonishing. [Col. 1338A] Here is rebuke with irony. For the Apostle is angry with those who promise themselves impunity while judging others.

[Ambrose] And although this chapter speaks generally against Jews and Gentiles, it can also be understood particularly against any superstitious prelate of the Church who, through hypocrisy, deceives the scrutiny of those who observe him, so that, although he ought to be punished, he appears worthy of honour. Likewise it applies to the Jew who pretends to be what he is not. Therefore he appropriately says, “you judge,” as another’s teacher: you do not accuse yourself, but others, hoping for impunity because this authority has been given you and there is no one in the world to judge you. Yet even if one who judges you is now absent, you will not be able in the future to escape the judgment of God which you escaped in the world.

And as though he should say, “Why then does He not punish?” [Col. 1338B] the Apostle says: Because God is good and waits for you. This you do not know, and therefore you despise it. And this is what follows:

“You despise the riches of His goodness”—[Origen, Haimo] that is, His abundant goodness. God’s goodness is abundant: He supplies many good things to many sinners, gently drawing them in order to attract them to repentance. You despise the riches of His patience, that is, God’s abundant patience, which endures so many and such great sinners and does not punish them quickly. He adds: and you despise the riches of His long-suffering—[Augustine, Origen] that is, God’s abundant long-suffering, which is not for an hour but is prolonged, waiting through many times. God displays this because now is the time of mercy. And do you do this? It is as though he said: It is astonishing.

Long-suffering, which elsewhere is called forbearance, seems to differ from patience [Col. 1338C] because those who sin from weakness rather than deliberate purpose are said to be sustained by long-suffering; but those who exult in their offences with a stubborn mind are said to be borne patiently. [Haimo] Patience, therefore, is that by which God does not immediately punish those who sin through pride and a stubborn mind. Long-suffering is that by which He bears for a long time those who sin through weakness and not through a settled malice of mind, awaiting repentance. [Augustine] But the person who does not use this for repentance, as God intends, but turns it toward impunity, despises it.

In order to make him anxious and rebuke him more plainly, he adds: “Do you not know why you despise God’s goodness?” And also: “Do you not know that God’s kindness leads you,” so far as lies in itself, “to repentance?” Behold, you do not know the merciful God. [Col. 1338D] And do you do this? It is as though he said: It is astonishing. He speaks sternly in all these matters because an evil mind is not recalled to life except by fear.

[Ambrose] Observe in these three verses the three stages of sin. You sin, O human being, when you promise yourself impunity; this is noted in “But do you suppose,” etc. Again, you sin more gravely because you despise God’s goodness; hence, “Or do you despise the riches of His goodness,” etc. And you sin most grievously because you do not know that you despise it; hence, “Do you not know,” etc. “And do you do this?” is a rebuke, as if he said: It is astonishing. “But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart [you] store up wrath for yourself”: it is as though he said, God’s kindness leads you to repentance, but you are not led.

Indeed, you “store up wrath for yourself,” that is, heap up vengeance for yourself; [Col. 1339A] and this according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, that is, because you are hard and stubborn in your evil, concerning which you do not even repent in heart. There are some to whom the evils they commit are displeasing and who, led by repentance of heart, strive as far as is granted them to escape from them; he is not speaking here of such persons. There are others to whom evils are pleasing and who, excessively presuming on God’s mercy and abusing patience, stubbornly persist in them. [Augustine] In this way they display His patience and accumulate their own burden by sinning more grievously.

There are others to whom evils are indeed displeasing, but because they recognize them as grave they think that they can no longer be forgiven, like Cain, who said: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon” (Gen. IV).

[Note: [Col. 1339D] Augustine on John.] And such despair insinuates itself into them, so that, as persons destined for condemnation, they do without repentance whatever pleases them. The former, therefore, through excessive hope declare God not just; the latter, through despair, judge God not good. Thus both will be endangered, both by hoping and by despairing.

[Note: [Col. 1339D] The same, *On the Words of the Lord*.] Afflicted by contrary things and contrary dispositions, they will perish. For these two things kill souls: despair and perverse hope. Through these two comes blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “Whoever sins”—that is, speaks a word of blasphemy—“against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, either in this world or in the future” (Matt. XII). Of this John also says in the Catholic Epistle: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it.” [Note: [Col. 1339D] The same, *On Sin against the Holy Spirit*.]

Sin unto death, or sin against the Holy Spirit, is committed [Col. 1339C] in two ways: through obstinacy or through despair. Obstinacy is the hardening in evil through the stubbornness of the mind, by which a person becomes unrepentant; and this unrepentance is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Despair is that by which someone wholly loses confidence in God’s goodness. Each is called sin against the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit is the love of Father and Son, and goodness so great that it has no end.

[Note: [Col. 1339D] The same, *On the Words of the Lord*.] They therefore truly sin against the Holy Spirit who suppose their own wickedness to exceed God’s goodness, thereby removing, amid this most stormy sea of iniquities, the harbour of divine pardon into which they might enter while being tossed by the waves. And by that very despair they add sins to sins, saying: “There is no mercy, and necessary condemnation is due to sinners”; as do those who also stubbornly cling to evil, who sin against the Holy Spirit—that is, against God’s goodness, which bears them with the greatest patience, gives them very many good things, and calls them from every side to correction and repentance. For He calls through the benefits of creation; He calls by granting time to live; He calls through the scourge of correction; He calls through the mercy of consolation. But take care lest, by making evil use of the length of God’s mercy, you store up wrath for yourself. Do not think God so merciful that He does not seem just, nor so just that [Col. 1340A] He does not will to show mercy. A human being is spared for this purpose: that he may be converted and not be one condemned.

[Note: [Col. 1340D] Ibid.] It is commonly asked here why sin against the Holy Spirit is called unforgivable. Different persons hold various views. Some say it is unforgivable because those who sin otherwise cannot repent, since they have hearts hardened like stones, as is said of the devil: “His heart is hardened like a stone” (Job XLI). Others say that it is called unforgivable because such sinners never repent, though they could do so, and therefore it is never forgiven them.

[Note: [Col. 1340D] Ibid.] Both sides bring forward authorities in support of their opinion. Augustine indeed says: “This unrepentance, or unrepentant heart, cannot be judged while anyone lives in this flesh. No one should be despaired of [Col. 1340B] while God’s patience leads him to repentance. Today he is a pagan; today he is an unbelieving Jew: what if tomorrow he embraces Catholic peace and follows Catholic truth? What if those whom you mark as belonging to some sort of error and condemn as altogether hopeless repent before they finish this life and find true life in the future? Therefore judge no one before the time comes.”

[Note: [Col. 1340D] The same, *Against Julian the Heretic*.] Again: “By showing patience the Lord gives room for repentance, not wishing anyone to perish,” that is, to make anyone deserving of death or to condemn him yet. But in the commentary on Matthew, the contrary is said: “So great is the stain of that sin that he cannot submit to the humility of entreaty, even if he is compelled by an evil conscience to recognize and confess his sin.” And in the commentary on Mark it is likewise said that one who sins in such a way cannot repent worthily.

Taking account, therefore, of the testimony of each authority without prejudging either side, we say that it seems to us to be called unforgivable not because such persons never repent or cannot repent, but because they repent only with difficulty, rarely, and scarcely. Hence Augustine says concerning that verse of the Psalm, “I will turn [them] into the depth of the sea,” that is, those who were most desperate. John therefore cautiously does not say, “I say that no one should pray,” but, “I do not say that no one should pray” (1 John V). And when such persons are said to be unable to repent or submit to the humility of entreaty, it must be understood that they cannot do so except scarcely, with difficulty, and rarely. Hence Augustine says: “The Lord, as though unwillingly, exacts punishment from the guilty, He who did not establish death for human beings from the beginning. For he himself brings destruction upon himself who despised the counsel of the Lord who heals.” Therefore, while there is time, let each person abandon his perversity and fear God’s patience, lest he be wholly unable later to find angry the One whom he now despises as calm. Deterring such persons, the Apostle says: “You store up wrath for yourself,” that is, you accumulate vengeance for yourself.

[Jerome] It is clear that wrath does not occur in God, but that the most merciful One is provoked by our vices to vengeance. I say, wrath to be exercised “in the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God.” [Ambrose] [Col. 1341A] He calls the time of judgment “the day of wrath and revelation.” He calls it a day, not in reference to time, but because everything then will be open which is now hidden; “of wrath,” as regards sinners, who will then be punished; “of revelation,” because then what is now unknown to us will be revealed, so that even unwillingly they will confess the righteous judgment of God, which is now denied to be future. He aptly says, “of righteous judgment,” because He is the one “who will render to each according to his works.”

[Note: [Col. 1341D] Augustine, *To Valentinus*.] For God will then render to each according to his works, whereas now He does not render to those whom He frees according to their works. Even now His goodness toward the wicked is abundant. [Gaudentius, Augustine] But in the future He will render evils for evils, because He is just; goods for evils, because He is good; and goods for goods, because He is good and just. [Col. 1341B] Only evils for goods He will not render, because He is not unjust. Thus He will render evils for evils, namely punishment for unrighteousness, as in the reprobate; goods for evils, namely grace for unrighteousness, as in little children; and goods for goods, namely grace for grace, as in adults who have merited life by doing good.

But perhaps someone will ask: How will He render according to works and recompense justly, when someone is punished perpetually for a temporal sinful act? The response is this. [Gregory] It belongs to the justice of the strict Judge that those whose minds in this life never wished to be without sin should never be without punishment; and that no limit of vengeance should be given to the wicked person who, as long as he was able, was unwilling to impose a limit upon his crime.

Finally, it is asked whether the evil will and conscience of the reprobate punished in Gehenna are sin, or punishment only; and, if sin, whether through them they merit punishment. We reply that after this life is not the time for meriting, but for receiving. For no one merits except while in the body, as is read in subsequent passages of the epistles. Therefore some concede that the evil will found in the reprobate after this life is indeed sin—that is, both fault and punishment—but that through it they merit nothing, just as the good will in the elect is indeed good and a glorious reward, but through it they merit nothing. Others say that the evil will is punishment only and not fault. For if, they say, it is fault and does not deserve punishment, it remains unpunished; and thus God leaves some sin unpunished, whereas authority says that no evil is unpunished and no good unrewarded. To this others reply that this must be understood of acts committed in the present life; yet they do not concede that it is unpunished, because that evil will is not only fault but punishment as well. Then the Apostle sets out how He renders to individuals according to their works, saying:

### Verses 7–9

> “To those indeed who, by perseverance in good work, seek glory and honor and incorruption, [he will render] eternal life; but to those who are contentious and do not submit to the truth, but believe unrighteousness, [there will be] wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress upon every soul of a human being who does evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek.”

“To those indeed,” etc. [Ambrose]: that is, to those who, making good use of God’s patience, do good works, he will render glory, because they shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father; and honor, because the saints shall be at God’s right hand; and incorruption, because what they possess will remain without end. He added this in order that a glory and honor different from those possessed in the present life might be understood. For in the present life honor and glory are often lost, because both the giver and the recipient are corruptible. But in the future incorruptible honor and glory are given.

To those who, according to God’s patience, seek eternal life by good work—that is, who have done good works with this intention, that they may possess eternal life, not that they may be seen by people, as hypocrites do. But to those who are contentious—that is, who quarrel among themselves, as you Romans do; or who contend with God, refusing to repent although he calls them to repentance in many ways—and who do not submit to the truth when it is spoken to them, but believe unrighteousness, that is, distrustfully suppose that there will be impunity rather than God’s future judgment: upon such persons, I say, after judgment there will be wrath, that is, material or spiritual punishment; and on the very day of judgment there will be his indignation, because they will be indignant against themselves. Meanwhile, before judgment, after the separation from the flesh, there will be tribulation and distress for them in the soul alone; but after judgment there will be wrath and indignation, as has been said.

Or the two following expressions explain the two preceding ones. It is as if he said: For such persons there will be God’s wrath—that is, God will appear angry, though in him there is every tranquility and no disturbance. For the divine nature is free from such passions. And lest he seem to be angry without taking vengeance, he adds: “indignation,” signifying that, beyond wrath, God will avenge the injury done to him. Thus, explaining the foregoing, he adds “tribulation and distress.” What was earlier called wrath is called tribulation; what was earlier called indignation is called distress.

“Upon every soul of a human being who does evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek.” What he had previously said indefinitely, in speaking of “those who are,” etc., he here says universally, so as to include both Jew and Gentile. [Haimo, Ambrose] It is as if he said: This punishment shall come upon every soul, both Jew and Gentile, that does evil. By “work” he signifies not only deeds but also the profession of unbelief. For he is discussing the unbeliever; and therefore he says “upon the soul,” so that you may understand spiritual punishments, because the unbeliever’s soul will be confined by spiritual punishment on account of unbelief. Upon every soul, I say—of the Jew first, that is, especially, because he also possessed the written law; and of the Greek, that is, the Gentile. [Ambrose] He always puts the Jew first because of the prerogative of the fathers: so that one who believes, being more honorable because of Abraham, may either be crowned first; or, if unbelieving, may be condemned more severely, because he has rejected the gift promised to the fathers.

### Verses 10–13

> “But glory and honor and peace [shall be] to everyone who does good, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For there is no respect of persons with God. For all who sinned without the law shall also perish without the law; and all who sinned in the law shall be judged through the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified.”

“Peace,” which above was called incorruption, shall be to everyone who does good—to the Jew first, either first in time in doing good, or first, that is, especially, in doing good; for, being better instructed, he acts better—and to the Greek, that is, the Gentile.

“For there is no,” etc. It is as if he said: I place Jew and Gentile on equal terms in punishment and glory. For—that is, because—there is no respect of persons with God: God judges not according to persons but according to merits, because he condemns both according to the measure of their sin. [Ambrose] The prerogative of lineage does not result in his accepting an unbeliever because of the fathers, or rejecting a believer because of the fathers because of his unworthiness; rather, he either rewards or condemns each person according to that person’s own merit.

And this is truly so. For—that is, because—all who have sinned without the law, namely the written law, that is, the Gentiles, shall perish, that is, be condemned, without the law: that is, not for transgressing the law. For unless he meant the written law, how could he speak of sinning without law, since all are subject to the natural law? But he speaks of the Mosaic law, to which the Jews are bound. [Augustine] For the Apostle was here speaking of that law which the Lord gave through Moses to the people of Israel. Thus he said that they, that is, the Gentiles, sinned “without the law,” because they had not received the law which the Jews boasted that they had received; and therefore he says: all who sinned without the law, namely the written law given through Moses, shall perish without the law.

> [Note: Col. 1343D. Augustine, *To Valentinus.*]

“And all who sinned in the law,” that is, possessing the written law—namely, the Jews—“shall be judged through the law,” that is, also for transgression of the law; and in this he makes their case more severe. Therefore, from those who know the divine commands is taken away the excuse which people commonly make from ignorance. Yet those who do not know God’s law shall not be without punishment either. Although it is more serious for a person to sin knowingly than unknowingly, one must not therefore flee to the darkness of ignorance in order to seek an excuse there. For it is one thing not to know, another to have refused to know.

> [Note: Col. 1343D. Id., book *On the Ignorance of Sin.*]

For ignorance that belongs not to those who refused to know, but to those who simply did not know, excuses no one so as to prevent eternal burning, though perhaps it causes one to burn more mildly if one does not believe because one has not heard what one ought to believe. Therefore every sinner is without excuse, whether by the guilt of original sin or by the addition of an improper will: whether one knows or does not know, judges or does not judge. For ignorance itself is sin in those who refused to understand; but in those who could not understand it is the punishment of sin. Therefore neither group now has an excuse; rather, just condemnation is due to both. Hence he says of both: “Those who sinned without the law shall perish without the law, and those who sinned in the law shall be judged through the law.”

> [Note: Col. 1344D. Id., *On Psalm* 118.]

But when he says, “shall be judged,” it must not be understood as though they should be saved through fire, as some say, but that they shall utterly perish. For some Catholic commentators, giving these words of the Apostle too little attention, have understood them contrary to the actual meaning, saying that those who sinned without the law perish, whereas those who sinned in the law are merely judged and do not perish—as though they were to be purified by purgatorial punishments, like the one of whom it was said: “But he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3). [Augustine] But this is rightly understood of the good foundation of which the Apostle was speaking there. Here, however, the Apostle speaks of Jews who are without Christ as their foundation. What Christian would say that a Jew who does not believe in Christ does not perish but is merely judged, when Christ himself says that it shall be more tolerable for Sodom in the judgment than for Jews who do not believe in Christ, among whom he performed so many miracles? (Matt. 10.) Likewise, he says that they shall have no excuse for the sin of unbelief because he came and spoke to them (John 15). Those to whom neither he himself nor his servants spoke have that excuse; nevertheless they shall not escape condemnation, because those who sinned without the law shall perish without the law, although they shall suffer lighter punishments. For to whom more is entrusted, more is required; and the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes (Luke 12).

“For it is not,” etc. As if someone said: “You say that those who sinned in the law shall be judged through the law; but does not the law alone save?” He says that it does not make people righteous. And this is the meaning: Truly, even those possessing the law shall be judged. For hearers of the law are not righteous before God, even if they are before people; that is, no one is righteous before God merely because of hearing the law. But doers of the law—that is, those who fulfill the law in deed [Ambrose], namely those, whoever they may be, who believe in Christ whom the law promised—shall be justified. This indeed is through grace: they shall be regarded as righteous, [Augustine] reckoned righteous before God and people.

> [Note: Col. 1344D. Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter.*]

Or read it thus: “The doers of the law shall be justified,” that is, they shall be made righteous by God so that they may be doers. It is not to be understood as though those who were already doers of the law would afterward be justified. Rather, we should know that they cannot otherwise be doers of the law except by being justified: justification is not added to doers, but justification precedes so that they become doers. Thus, if it were said, “Human beings shall be created,” it could not be understood that those who were already human beings were created; rather, by creation they come to be human beings. Therefore this is the sense here: “The doers of the law shall be justified”—that is, grace justifies them so that they may fulfill the law. They do not act in order to be justified; they are justified in order to act. [Augustine]

In certain other passages, however, the construction is found differently; as when it is said, “Those doing good shall be honored,” and “human beings shall be set free.” There honor is understood as being added to persons already good, and freedom to those who were already human beings. But that is not how it must be understood here; rather, it must be taken as stated above.

### Verses 14–16

> “For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do the things of the law, these, though not having the law, are a law to themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts among themselves mutually accusing or even defending them, on the day when God shall judge the secrets of human beings, according to my gospel, through Jesus Christ.”

He had said above that the Gentile, if he acted wrongly, would be condemned, and if he acted well, would be saved. [Remigius] But because he does not possess the law, and thus might seem not to know what is good or evil, it might appear that neither should be imputed to him. [Hilary, Augustine] Against this the Apostle says: Although he does not have the written law, he nevertheless has the natural law, by which he understands and is conscious of what is good and what is evil. For the natural law is: to inflict injury on no one; to seize nothing belonging to another; to abstain from fraud and perjury; not to plot against another’s spouse; and the like. Or, to state it briefly, it is not to wish to do to others what you do not wish done to yourself.

> [Note: Col. 1345D. Augustine, *On the Letter and the Spirit.*]

This accords with evangelical teaching. Accordingly, he does not seem here to have meant by “Gentiles” anyone other than those who belong to the Gospel. Nor should it trouble us that he says they naturally do the things of the law, not by God’s Spirit, faith, or grace. [Col. 1345C] For this is the work of the Spirit of grace: to restore in us the image of God in which we were naturally made. Vice, indeed, is contrary to nature, and grace certainly heals it. Thus the image of God in the human soul has not been so completely worn away by the stain of earthly affections that no lineaments remain in it. What was impressed there through God’s image when the soul was created has not been entirely erased. Accordingly, when vice has been healed by grace, the things of the law are done naturally. This does not mean that grace is denied by the term “nature,” as has been said; rather, nature is restored by grace. By grace, the inner person is renewed, and the law of righteousness is written there—the law that guilt had erased. For through renewal, what had been erased through oldness is written there again.

Therefore such a person, though not possessing the Mosaic written law, must be understood to act well or badly, and deservedly to be saved or condemned. I say that the person acts well and is saved; yet this is possible only through grace and faith, which renew the dormant natural image of God in a person. Without this renewal, one acts badly and is condemned, one’s conscience accusing one. [Origen, Ambrose] It is as if he said: Truly the doers shall be justified, because even the Gentiles do so. And this is the meaning: When Gentiles, who do not possess the written Mosaic law, naturally do the things of the law—that is, by natural reason enlightened through grace discern what must be done and avoided, as the law would direct—or do the things of the law, that is, believe in Christ and God, although they do not have such a law, that is, a written one, they are a law to themselves. They show, by the indications of their works, the work of the law written in their hearts—that is, firmly fixed in their reason—while they approve the acts the law commands and condemn those it forbids. [Ambrose]

Or, the work of the law is faith, which they freely possess in their hearts, that is, in their inmost affection, where faith works through love. When a person offers this to God, the person shows by a natural indication that he or she is a law to himself or herself, because he or she does what the law commands: namely, believes in Christ.

“Their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts among themselves mutually accusing or even defending them.” It is as if he said: They possess the work of the law written in their hearts; therefore they themselves will be witnesses for themselves in the future, whether for good or evil, knowing that they are deservedly condemned or saved. And this is the meaning of “they naturally do the things of the law”: their conscience bears witness to salvation or condemnation, even if this is not visible to others. [Ambrose] And not only is there consciousness of deeds, but also consciousness of thoughts—that is, of evil and good thoughts mutually accusing them. This is said of unbelievers: “accusing.” “Or even defending” is said of believers. For evil thoughts accuse unbelievers, while good thoughts defend believers. And this occurs “among themselves,” because those thoughts accuse the former and these defend the latter.

Or these are genitives in place of ablatives, in the Greek manner, since Greek lacks ablative forms. Hence in some books it is found written with ablatives thus: “And among themselves, their thoughts mutually accusing or even defending them.” Their conscience will bear witness to them on the day of the future judgment, when God shall judge the secrets of human beings—that is, what is now hidden here. He shall judge, I say, through Jesus Christ; all this is certain. “According to my gospel.” [Origen] It should be known that on that day thoughts will accuse or defend souls—not, of course, the thoughts that then exist, but these thoughts that are now in us. Certain marks and impressions of them will remain in our heart as in wax; now set within the hidden breast, they are said to be revealed on that day. “Through Jesus Christ,” because the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son. And this is “according to my gospel,” that is, the gospel proclaimed by Paul.

### Verses 17–27

> “But if you are called a Jew, and rest upon the law, and glory in God, and know his will, and approve the more excellent things, being instructed through the law; if you are confident that you yourself are a guide of the blind, a light of those in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children, having in the law the form of knowledge and truth—then you who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege? You who glory in the law, do you dishonor God through transgression of the law? For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you, as it is written. Circumcision indeed profits if you keep the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. If therefore the uncircumcised person keeps the requirements of the law, shall not that person’s uncircumcision be reckoned as circumcision? And shall not one who is uncircumcised by nature, yet fulfills the law, judge you, who through letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law?”

“But if you are called a Jew,” etc.—or, according to another reading, “But you are called a Jew.” Here he attacks the Jews particularly, accusing them more severely of sins because they possess more helps. It is as if he said: The Gentile possesses only the natural law. But you, O Jew, possess more, because you are called a Jew, from Judah the patriarch, as though this name has come to you from kinship with him. You rest upon the law: that is, you do not wander in errors, being certain what you ought to observe, unlike those who wander without the law. You glory in God: that is, in your knowledge of God. And you know his will [Haimo] concerning the redemption of the human race, which he announced to you through the prophets. And you approve the more excellent things: that is, among useful things you know how to choose the more useful, because you are instructed through the law.

And you are confident that you yourself are a guide of the blind—that is, of those who do not understand—and that you are a light to those in darkness: that is, you are confident you can also enlighten those in darkness. He calls the Gentiles blind and in darkness because they are blind through deprivation of reason and, even when they know something, nevertheless remain in darkness. [Col. 1347C] And you are confident that you are an instructor of the foolish—that is, of Jews not yet advanced—and a teacher of children: that is, of Jews who do not yet know how to reason from the law. And you are confident that you possess the form—that is, the perfection—of knowledge in the law; and not merely knowledge but also truth, so that you may be an example to others of knowledge of the law and of truth.

He did not place both, knowledge and truth, without reason. Some have knowledge and understanding of a book, and understand it as its author himself understood it. Yet they do not thereby have truth, because they do not know in what way it is true, or even that it is true. But the Jew boasts that he possesses the sense of the law and knows that that sense is truly the sense of the law, so as to be a model for others who wish to know. And when you possess all these things, O Jew, you who teach another, why do you not teach yourself? Or, if “if” occurs in the text above, read it thus: It is as if you possess these things and those. And if that is so, you who teach another, why do you not teach yourself? You who preach, as the law says, that one must not steal, why do you steal—namely, the meaning concerning Christ in the law? And you who say that adultery must not be committed, do you commit adultery? That is, do you take away from the law the truth concerning Christ and put falsehood in its place? And why do you do this? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege—by denying Christ or by giving the worship of God to idols, as the Jews often did? And why do you do this? You who glory in the law, do you dishonor God through transgression of the law: that is, because you pass over the meaning of the law concerning the incarnation and divinity of Christ. You dishonor God: that is, you are the cause why others dishonor him.

And truly so. “For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” even now, [Augustine] while you do not receive the testimony which the Father gave concerning his Son. In this the Father is disparaged, because in Christ the Father is blasphemed, as Christ himself says: “Whoever receives me receives not me alone, but him who sent me” (Matt. 10). Therefore God’s name is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of the Jews, since the Jews sought to persuade believing Gentiles that Christ should not be called God.

Notice that the Apostle uses as his own the words of the prophet Ezekiel, who said this to the Jews of his own time: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Ezek. 36). For formerly the Gentiles did not perceive that the Jews had been handed over on account of their offenses; rather, they gave their idols credit for victory, as though their gods had defeated the God of the Jews in the Jews. The Apostle shows that he took these words from elsewhere when he says, “as it is written,” in Ezekiel concerning his contemporaries.

“Circumcision indeed profits you if you keep the law,” etc. Above he showed that the law does not help them to obtain righteousness and life. Now he shows that circumcision does not help. It is as if he said: Since the Jews are such, O Jew, circumcision indeed profits you, who are of Abraham’s stock, if you nevertheless keep the law. [Haimo, Ambrose] That is, if you observe it spiritually: if you believe in Christ whom the law promised, put away all shameful things, and circumcise your heart. Thus circumcision spiritually profits toward life for one who understands it and the other sacraments of the law, because by obeying God that person makes it a sign of truth, so as to rejoice devoutly and, contemplating the truth with spiritual delight, believe in Christ. It also benefits an uneducated people following the letter of the law, while they are kept under fear of God.

It is asked how he can here say that circumcision profits, when later he says: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5). We reply that this is said according to the condition of different times. Under the former dispensation of the old law circumcision once profited, but it did not profit for salvation without observance of the spiritual law. Hence he says here: But in the time of grace, after truth has been manifested, it not only does not profit but even harms. [Col. 1348D] Therefore he says later: “If you are circumcised,” etc.

“But if you are a transgressor of the law”: it is as if he said, Circumcision profits if you keep the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law—that is, if you do not fulfill what circumcision requires, namely, belief in Christ—your carnal circumcision has become uncircumcision: that is, it has no more value than uncircumcision.

Then, arguing from the contrary, he adds: “If therefore,” etc. It is as if he said: Since your circumcision, O Jew, becomes uncircumcision if you transgress the law, then if an uncircumcised person—that is, any Gentile—keeps the righteous requirements of the law, [Ambrose] that is, the commandments through which one is justified, or faith in Christ, whom the law proclaimed as one to come for justification but could not itself give—shall not that person’s uncircumcision be reckoned as circumcision, so that he may be a son of Abraham, the father of faith? It is as if he said: No one can deny it.

And shall not the uncircumcised person—that is, the Gentile—who fulfills, that is, perfectly carries out, the law, do so by a nature enlightened and aided by grace? I say, fulfills the law by believing in Christ, promised in the law. Shall he not judge you, O Jew, who, though taught through the letter—that is, through the written law—and circumcision, which is the sign of putting away vices, are nevertheless a transgressor of the law? [Haimo] That is, will he not, by comparison with himself, show you worthy of condemnation? You have not known by nature, law, or circumcision what he has known by nature: namely, Christ. It is as if he said: He certainly shall condemn you. Thus it is clear that the law does not help. [Origen] Therefore in this passage he seems to call “uncircumcision” the Gentiles, who came to faith in Christ in the uncircumcision of the flesh. He compares and prefers them, as keepers of the spiritual law, to the Jews, who through the letter and circumcision of the flesh are transgressors of the law, and says that they shall be judged by others.

### Verses 28–29

> “For one is not a Jew who is so outwardly; nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh. But one is a Jew who is so inwardly; and circumcision is of the heart, in the Spirit, not in the letter, whose praise is not from human beings but from God.”

It is as if he said: A Jew can rightly become a Gentile, and a Gentile a Jew, as has been said. For one is not truly a Jew who is a Jew only outwardly, namely in name and nation, and who confesses with the lips while being far away in heart. For “Jew” means “one who confesses”; whoever truly believes and truly confesses is truly a Jew. Nor is that the true circumcision which is outward, namely that performed by hand in the flesh, that is, by cutting away the skin. Rather, that person is truly a Jew who is a Jew in the hidden place of the heart: one who confesses from the heart. And that is true circumcision which is circumcision—that is, cleansing—of the heart, performed in the Spirit, that is, through the Holy Spirit, not through the letter: that is, not with stone knives, as the letter of the law taught figuratively.

The praise of this circumcision—that is, of this truly praiseworthy circumcision—is not from human beings but from God: that is, from God’s grace. [Origen, Augustine] For circumcision of heart purifies the soul and cuts away the stains of vices; therefore such circumcision is not from human beings but from God.

> [Note: Col. 1349D. Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter.*]

By it unlawful desire is cut off; and this is not accomplished by the letter teaching and threatening, but by the Spirit helping and following through. [Augustine] Or thus: the praise of that person—namely, the person who is inwardly a Jew and circumcised—is not from human beings, from Jews who think earthly thoughts and glory in the flesh, but from God.

> [Note: Col. 1350D. Id., *On the Epistle to the Romans.*]

For God praises the believer, not the person circumcised in the flesh. The Jews’ praise is from people: if they do what the law commands without the Spirit, they do it from fear of punishment, not love of righteousness. [Haimo] Such persons are Jews in the flesh but pagans in the heart. [Augustine, Ambrose] [Col. 1350A] Thus what appears before a human being is not what exists before God. But whoever glories in the Spirit receives praise from God. For one believes by the Spirit, and through this is pleasing to God. That person alone is truly blessed who is righteous before God.

## Chapter III

### Verses 1–3

> “What advantage, then, has the Jew? Or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. First of all, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them. For what if some of them did not believe? Has their unbelief made the faithfulness of God void? By no means!”

Up to this point the Apostle has shown that there is no respect of persons with God, and he has proceeded so far as to say that the carnal Jew becomes a Gentile, and the spiritual Gentile becomes a true Jew. Therefore he now raises the objection which he sees may be made to him, in order to answer what dignity, under the former dispensation, the Jew has above the Gentile.

It is as if he said: Since the Jew becomes a Gentile and conversely, what advantage, under the former dispensation, does the Jew have from the law or the legal observances, he who is called God’s special people, over the Gentile, who is called an unclean dog? Or what benefit has he received from circumcision? To this he replies: It did indeed have value formerly, but Jews are not thereby more worthy in faith. And this is what he says: The Jew has much advantage over the Gentile under the former dispensation, “in every way.” Every way concerns either the administration of temporal things or the unveiling of spiritual things; in both respects God did many things for the Jews which he did not do for the Gentiles, and thus under the former dispensation they were more privileged.

“First of all”: passing over lesser matters, namely temporal matters, the Apostle sets forth an example from the chief matters, namely the spiritual things, the oracles of God. It is as if he said: Leaving aside other lesser temporal things, I state this first, that is, chief privilege, concerning the oracles: the oracles of God—that is, the law and the prophets—were entrusted to the Jews as to friends, through which they might understand the future redemption promised to come through Christ. Although, therefore, the Apostle indicates many things pertaining to the honor of Abraham’s seed, [Ambrose] he expressly mentions only this, because it is especially their glory that they were judged worthy to receive the law through which they might learn to distinguish what is right from what is perverse. Thus, under the former dispensation, the Jews had more than the Gentiles.

But you will say: No more was done for them, because some of them did not believe the oracles so as to receive Christ, the promised redeemer. He answers: “For what,” etc. It is as if he said: Even if some did not believe, this did not make it less profitable for those who believed. What harm was done to believers if some of them did not believe? Believers did not thereby receive less. For even if some did not believe, faith was not thereby rendered void. This is the meaning: “Has their unbelief made the faithfulness of God void?” that is, made God’s faithfulness unfulfilled? By no means that it has been made void! [Origen] By “the faithfulness of God” he means either that some Jews believed God, or the fulfillment of the good which God had promised to humanity. The unbelief of some did not prevent some from coming to faith in Christ, nor did it prevent God from fulfilling his promise to believers. That is, it did not prevent some Jews from being faithful to God by believing in Christ, nor prevent God from being faithful in his promises to those who believe. For because some refused to believe, this does not prejudice the remaining Jews, so that they should not be deemed worthy to receive what God promised to the faithful; since the promise was made so as to benefit believers.

[Ambrose] In order to confirm what he had said above, namely that God is faithful in his promise, the Apostle adds:

### Verse 4

> “But God is true, and every human being is false, as it is written: ‘That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged.’”

“But God is true,” etc. It is as if he said: Their unbelief has not made God’s faithfulness void; rather, God is true—that is, one who fulfills promises. But every human being is false in himself or herself, even a Jew, and so is unworthy of the promise. He says this lest the Jew seem more worthy in the new dispensation than the Gentile. [Ambrose] By this authority of the Prophet, he shows both that God is true, which confirms the preceding statements, and that the human being is false, which concerns human unworthiness. The Apostle adds “every human being is false” so that it may appear that God’s promise was made and fulfilled not because of any human worthiness, but because of God’s mercy; thus God’s grace is given to the unworthy, and God’s grace is more commendable.

[Haimo] God is called true, that is, unchangeable both in essence and in promise. A human being is called false: that is, one who neither possesses true being nor remains in the condition in which he or she was created, but dissolves through sins. It belongs to humanity to deceive and to be deceived; time and the weakness of nature make a human being mutable. A nature that is deceived is not improperly called false. But God, for whom nothing is future, remains unchangeable.

Or, every human being is false: namely, the one who does not believe what God promised and denies that God has fulfilled his promises. The Jew especially does this: distrusting God’s promises, the Jew is false and declares God false because he does not believe God’s promises. Yet God prevails over him when he grants the promises. [Ambrose] The sense of both interpretations is this: Every human being who contradicts God’s promises is false. [Haimo] Or, every human being, insofar as he or she is from himself or herself, is false: that is, unstable in essence and dissolving through sins.

That God is true he confirms by a prophetic example, adding, “as it is written”—as though to say: God is true, as is written in David (Psalm 50): “That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged.” [Haimo] It is as if David said: “I have sinned and done evil through adultery and homicide, so that you, O God, by sending the Son from my line as you promised, may be justified in your words”—the words concerning the promises of the Son—that is, may be shown to be righteous and to have fulfilled them from justice alone, not from my merits; “and that you may prevail” by fulfilling the promises, “when you are judged” by the peoples as though you ought not to fulfill the promises because of my sins, that is, as though you ought not to send the Son from my line.

For after David became an adulterer and murderer, by taking Uriah’s wife and killing Uriah with the sword of the sons of Ammon, many said: “God’s promise made to David, namely that Christ would be born from his seed, will be made void, because Christ will not be born from a murderer and adulterer. What God asserted that he had promised him will prove false.” [Ambrose] But God is true, because he sent Christ from David’s seed as he promised. Thus he prevails when judged, because he gives what he is said not to be going to give. When he gives what he is judged not about to give, he prevails, showing himself true and the one who does not believe his words false. Here “that” is consequential, not affective or causal.

Or “that” may be causal, and may refer to what David had said earlier: “Cleanse me from my sin.” It is as if he said: “Therefore cleanse me, that you may be justified,” that is, proved righteous and true in your words, [Haimo] which concern forgiveness for one who groans in repentance. For you said: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, I shall remember none of his or her iniquities any longer” (Ezek. 18). “And that you may prevail,” by granting me forgiveness of sin, “when you are judged” by people not to grant me forgiveness. For some said that David had sinned so grievously that he could not receive forgiveness of sins. [Origen] God showed them false and displayed himself true when he forgave him. [Ambrose]

Or again, it refers to what he had said: “Against you alone have I sinned.” It is as if he said: “I say that I have sinned against you alone, because you see what human beings do not see; and you are so righteous that, while I and all others sin, you alone are justified”—that is, shown righteous in all your words, namely in all your promises.

And you prevail—that is, surpass all in righteousness—when you are judged, that is, when you are compared with others in judgment. For God is of such great mercy that he is willing for a human being to be compared with himself. Hence he says through Isaiah: “Judge between me and my vineyard” (Isa. 5). [Origen.] For God surpasses the human being when compared with him in judgment. For he is found to have given human beings every disposition and every impulse by which they might strive toward and advance in the virtues. Moreover, he implanted the power of reason, by which they might recognize what they ought to do or avoid. Yet, having received these things, the human being neglected to walk in the path of virtue. Nothing was lacking to him from God, but he himself is found to have failed the things given to him by God. God is therefore rightly said to overcome such a person in judgment and to be justified in his words.

Or thus: “Against you alone have I sinned,” you who are so righteous, “so that you may be justified,” that is, proved true in all your sayings. For among human beings the God-man alone could in every respect speak the truth. And you are so righteous that you prevail—that is, surpass all human beings in righteousness—when, that is, although unjustly, you are judged by the Jews. [Augustine.] For the righteous Judge was unjustly judged by sinners; yet in this—that is, in righteousness—he overcomes all human beings. Therefore David says to him, who has no sin: “Against you alone have I sinned,” you who are so righteous that you are justified in your sayings and prevail when judged. (Ps. 5.) For you surpass all judges in righteousness: you alone judge justly, though you are judged unjustly.

Or, without changing the rest, this may be said thus: “And you prevail when you are judged.” That is: You are such that you are justified in your sayings, and also such that you prevail when judged—that is, when judged by Pilate and by the Jews. For the God-man prevailed when he was judged, because on account of that humility God the Father gave him the name above every name (Phil. 2). Yet this sense does not belong to the preceding argument, that is, to the proof of the author’s proposition—namely, to proving that God is true—but has been added by way of surplus.

VERS. 5, 8.—“But if our unrighteousness commends the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unrighteous, who inflicts wrath? I speak according to man. Far be it! Otherwise how shall God judge this world? For if the truth of God has abounded through my lie unto his glory, why am I still also judged as a sinner? And why not, as we are slanderously reported, and as some affirm that we say: Let us do evil, that good may come? Their condemnation is just.”

[Col. 1353C] [Ambrose.] Here is exposed the interpretation which carnal persons unjustly drew from the words of the prophet David, when he said, “I have sinned, that you may be justified,” understanding that our sins would be the cause of God’s justification. For there were some who said that God wished us to sin, so that he might appear righteous by comparison with us and, in forgiving our sin, might show that he is merciful. They also said that he wished us to lie, so that he alone might be found true. If this were so, we would be condemned by him unjustly.

The Apostle speaks here against such people, because this is not the sense of the Prophet’s words; rather, it is forced upon them by the perverse interpretation of malicious people, who assert that human sins and evil deeds contribute to God’s justification, that through our evils he appears righteous, and that our unrighteousness demonstrates him to be righteous. For above he said that God is true and every human being a liar, and that he gives good things to the unworthy, in which his grace and righteousness appear more praiseworthy. Thus the carnal person, saying that God uses evils as an instrument for his own glory, brings the matter to the point of calling God unrighteous for punishing sins that benefit him. For if our unrighteousness benefits him, he is undoubtedly unrighteous if he condemns the sinner.

The Apostle rejects this here, saying: “But if.” That is: God is true and every human being a liar, to whom, though unworthy, he gives good things; in this his grace and righteousness appear more praiseworthy. [Haimo.] “But if”—that is, if in this way our unrighteousness commends God’s righteousness—[Fulgentius, Haimo.] that is, makes God’s righteousness and holiness praiseworthy.

“What shall we say?” That is, what seems to follow from this? That God is unrighteous, since on account of sins he inflicts wrath—that is, vengeance and condemnation. For the Apostle here uses “wrath” for condemnation, because God is the avenger of that of which he is not the author—that is, unrighteousness—which God can punish but not produce.

There is also this sense: If our unrighteousness makes God praiseworthy, and the more we sin the more it pleases him, as the most foolish say; and if his righteousness and holiness thereby increase and become manifest in greater measure, then God is unrighteous in inflicting vengeance for the evils which he wishes us to do. For if he wishes us to sin, as some fools say, then when he condemns a sinful person he is unrighteous. [Augustine.] But is God unrighteous who inflicts wrath? To some this certainly appears so. But far be it that he should be unrighteous, or that our unrighteousness should commend him. [Haimo.] For if it commended him, he would not exact vengeance, because he is righteous.

And because it is untrue either that God is unrighteous or that our unrighteousness commends God, the Apostle adds: “I speak according to man,” that is, according to the understanding of the carnal human being; for this is a question belonging to carnal people, who are certainly both mistaken and deceived, and who deceive others. [Ambrose.] For God remains immutable; he cannot fail to love what he has made. [Col. 1354C] He does not wish us to sin; and because he is righteous, he therefore inflicts wrath upon the sinner. When, then, a just penalty is rendered to a sinner, there is not unrighteousness but righteousness with God. [Note: [Col. 1353D] Augustine, *On the Nature of the Good*.] For how will God be seen as righteous from this? Because he opposes unrighteousness; for he brings wrath upon human beings because they have made room for unrighteousness within themselves. Therefore God, who is righteousness itself, is not seen as unrighteous when he is angry against unrighteousness. He is not fittingly merciful toward those toward whom his wrath comes—even toward human beings who have made themselves ministers of that unrighteousness at which God is angry. God, therefore, is not unrighteous.

“Otherwise,” [Ambrose.] that is, unless it is the case that God is not unrighteous, “how shall God judge this world?” That is: He cannot be a righteous Judge. For how will he judge if he is unrighteous? That is: wrongly—giving evil things to the good and good things to the evil.

“For if the truth,” etc. Having inserted the rejection of God’s unrighteousness—that is, having interposed the demonstration showing that God is not unrighteous, from which it appears that the Prophet’s words are not to be understood in the sense stated—the Apostle returns to the carnal person’s attempted proof that, if God punishes the wicked, he is unrighteous. That is: Truly, if our unrighteousness commends God’s righteousness, God is unrighteous because he punishes. “For”—that is, because if through my lie, that is, through my sin, the truth, that is, the righteousness, of God has abounded—that is, increased—to his glory, that is, [Col. 1355A] if he is more glorious because of my sin—then why am I still, that is, why am I even now, and not only in the future, judged as a sinner, though I am not one?

For it is evident that, if the lie of human beings contributes to God’s glory, so that he alone may appear true, those who sin are not to be called sinners, since they will appear to sin not by their own will but by his compulsion. Far be it! [Haimo.] Here “truth” is understood as “righteousness” above, and “lie” as “unrighteousness” above. The sense is: If God appears true because of my lie, that is, my sin, why does he judge me as a sinner even in the present, not merely in the future?

Or: Why am I still judged as a sinner, even after conversion, after he has given good things to one unworthy, by which he appears glorious? For before conversion, when I deserved evil, he was not more glorious because of what was mine. The sense is as though he said: What could appear before forgiveness ought not to appear afterward—namely, that I, a sinner, am to be judged—because it is now certain that the truthfulness of forgiving would not have abounded unto glory unless I had sinned.

“And why not?” Again the Apostle infers another false conclusion from what he had said—namely, that God’s truth has abounded through my lie unto glory. That is: If this is so—if God’s truth abounds unto glory in sin—why do we not do evils so that good things may come, that is, so that God’s righteousness and glory may increase? “As we are slanderously reported”—we Apostles.

“And as some affirm that we say,” that is, as certain persons blasphemously charge us Apostles with thinking, saying, and even preaching—something which is blasphemy. [Haimo, Ambrose, Augustine.] What do they charge us with having said? Namely: “Let us do evil, that good may come.” For certain perverse people, unable to understand and inclined to censure, when they heard Paul and the other Apostles preach, “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5), said that the Apostles preached, “Let us do evil, that good may come.” [Aimo.] They said: “Therefore, the more and greater evils we commit, the more and greater good things we shall receive, and the greater grace; for God wishes us to sin so that he may have something to forgive and may himself appear merciful.”

Or this text may be connected with the preceding words—namely, “for if”—more closely than in the earlier connection. That is: “How shall God judge this world if he is unrighteous?” That is: not rightly, as is shown in part because even now he would not judge me justly as a sinner, though I am not one. And this is true: “For if the truth,” etc. The meaning of the words does not change from the first exposition.

“Their condemnation,” etc. That is: Some make this charge against us; the condemnation of such persons is just, and therefore they are not to be believed.

VERS. 9, 18.—“What then? Do we excel them? Not at all. For we have charged both Jews and Greeks alike with being all under sin, as it is written: There is no one righteous, not even one; there is no one who understands; there is no one who seeks God. All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good; there is not even one. Their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they acted deceitfully; the poison of asps is under their lips. Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood. Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace; there is no fear of God before their eyes.”

“What then?” [Origen, Ambrose.] The Apostle, as a kind of mediator between those who had believed from the circumcision and those who had come from the Gentiles, has shown above that both Jews and Greeks are guilty. There also he demonstrated that there is no respect of persons with God; there too he asked what he considered ought to be asked—namely, what advantage the Jew had in the former state. And he answered: much, showing especially in what respect. Now the question is whether, in this state of grace, the Jew has more than the Gentile; and he answers: no. Indeed, they are equal in this grace of the Gospel. That is: Although God did more for the Jew in the former state, and fulfilled good things for them, this was not through any merit of theirs.

“What then shall we say? Do we excel them?” [Haimo.] Namely, the Gentiles in this grace. “Not at all,” because there is no respect of persons with God; “but in every nation, whoever fears God is acceptable to him” (Acts 10). Truly, we Jews are not worthier than the Gentiles in this grace. “For we have charged”: above we demonstrated this by arguments—that all, Jews and Greeks alike, were under sin before this grace. For the Jews, by transgressing both the natural and the written law, and the Gentiles, the natural law, were found sinners, as was shown above. Thus neither surpasses the other even in the state of grace.

[Augustine.] By these words the Apostle settles the dispute and resolves the contention that had arisen between Jews and Gentiles, when the former thought that the reward of the Gospel had been rendered to them as due to the merits of the works of the law, while the latter, conversely, desired to set themselves above the Jews as the murderers of the Lord. Then he adds prophetic testimony, by which he shows that the Jews too are guilty—those of whom this seems less likely, since they appeared to live under God’s law—saying: “As it is written.” That is: All are under sin, as it is written of the Jews, of whom this would seem less likely: “There is no one righteous,” namely, no one who has not come to Christ. He is not righteous because “there is no one who understands,” that is, because he does not understand that Christ is God; and his failure to understand is his own fault. “There is no one who seeks God,” that is, because he does not seek God. For from the works they could have sought and found that Christ was God. I say, he does not seek him; rather, he turns away from him. And this is: “All have turned aside.”

[Ambrose.] For no one doubts that all who do not seek God turn away from him and incline toward evil. “Together,” namely, with that very turning away, “they have become useless,” because they have also caused others to turn away. [Augustine.] They have turned aside so greatly that there is none among them who does good—there is certainly not even one. Or: “There is none who does good; there is not even one,” namely, except the one Christ, because no one but Christ does good. For Christ alone works good in himself and in his own.

“An open grave.” That is: They have turned aside as we said and have been so harmful to others that “their throat is an open grave”: the stench of their words and works corrupts others, and it gapes to receive them as dead. [Ambrose.] For, enslaved to evils, they would, if possible, devour the good; just as a grave opens to receive corpses, so their throats are open against the good. And if they do not dare persecute by manifest evils, “with their tongues,” that is, with evil tongues, “they acted deceitfully,” speaking good things in words but thinking evil in their heart. For “the poison of asps,” that is, incurable hatred, was “under their lips,” that is, beneath their heart, because the words of such people are a trap. They speak for the purpose of deceiving. Thus, as lethal poison was poured forth through the serpent’s lips, so through their lips comes deceit and entrapment.

Their mouth also is abundantly “full of cursing,” [Haimo.] that is, malicious words such as “You have a demon,” and the like, and of “bitterness,” that is, bitter threats. Their feet also—that is, their affections—are swift to shed the blood of Christ and his people. That is: They are murderers by deliberate purpose; slow toward good, swift toward parricide. But this punishment will come upon them: “destruction,” that is, temporal punishment, and “misery,” that is, eternal condemnation, will be in their ways—that is, in their works. For their evil deeds will bring them destruction and misery. They do such things as will cause them to be crushed in this age by Titus and Vespasian, and in the future to be miserable, punished in soul and body.

And this is because they “have not known the way of peace,” that is, Christ. [Haimo, Origen.] Since they are always harassed by the wars of vices, they are ignorant of the way of peace—that is, Christ—through whom there is great peace for those who love the Lord’s name. Nor has even the fear of God turned them back from evil, because “there is no fear of God before their eyes.” [Ambrose.] For those who have no fear of God do not possess the beginning of wisdom.

Jeremiah says of them: “Then they all rose up against the prophet of the Lord, wishing to kill him” (Jer. 26); and he adds: “But all the people did not allow them” (ibid.). Yet it seems contradictory to say that all rose up and that all the people did not permit it. Therefore he says that all rose up—namely, the evil people—and that all the people did not permit it—namely, the good. So here too, when he says, “All have turned aside,” he does not mean the entire people without exception, but one part of the people. For there are always two peoples in one people.

This is the people whom the Lord rebukes, saying under the name of Jerusalem: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets” (Luke 13); and again: “An evil and adulterous generation” (Matt. 16). [Ambrose.] Of this people Isaiah says: “Woe to the sinful nation, the wicked seed,” etc. (Isa. 1).

VERS. 19, 20.—“Now we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and all the world may become subject to God, because by works of the law no flesh shall be justified before him.”

“Now we know,” etc. He showed by the authority of David’s Scripture that the Jews were under sin before grace; but, lest the Jews twist David’s authoritative words and divert them to another meaning, he says: “We know,” etc. That is: David says this; but we know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law—supply, “and concerning those who are under the law.” [Haimo.] For “law” is sometimes used generally for the Old Testament, and sometimes for a part of the Old Testament, as in: “The Lord opened the disciples’ understanding, that they might understand the things concerning God written in the law and the prophets and the psalms” (Luke 24). At times the Psalms are called “law,” as the Lord says: “Is it not written in your law: I said, You are gods, and all are sons of the Most High?” (John 8). And elsewhere: “That the word written in their law might be fulfilled: They hated me without cause” (John 15). Thus here also the Psalms are called law—that is, understood under the name “law”—because they instruct.

Therefore, in order to show that the things he said above from the Psalm concern the Jews, whose pride was to be broken, the Apostle said: “We know that whatever the law says,” in this passage, that is, the Psalms, “it says to those who are under the law,” that is, to Jews who possess the law; so that every mouth, even that of the Jews, may be stopped, [Note: [Col. 1357D] Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*.] from its self-glorying, and so that all the world—that is, every human being, not only the Gentile without the law, guilty of impiety, but also the Jew, guilty of transgressing the law—may become subject to God, ascribing everything to him. [Haimo.] For all are found sinners and are saved by grace, not by merits.

“Because by works,” etc. Here he begins to treat the law more fully, in order to show that righteousness does not come from it. That is: I say that all the world should be subject to God, as it ought to be, because it is certain that “by works of the law no flesh”—that is, no human being, or no person living carnally—“shall be justified before him,” namely before God, even if it may be justified before human beings. [Note: [Col. 1358D] Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*.] Therefore those who, while under the law, believed in Christ came to the grace of faith not because they were righteous, but in order to be justified.

Here the pride of those who glory in works of the law is destroyed, lest the grace of faith seem unnecessary and lest even works of the law be thought to justify. [Augustine.] “Works of the law” are those established and prescribed with the law, such as the ceremonial and figurative observances, which could never cleanse the conscience, even if performed with charity and devotion. If it is asked why those acts performed in charity did not justify, just as the good works now done in charity justify, we answer that they were not instituted for justification, but to signify future things and to display sin and weakness. Therefore no one will be justified from them before God, who sees inward things—[Haimo.] namely, whether what is done is done from love of righteousness or fear of punishment, something human beings cannot see.

Here again it is asked: Were Moses, David, and the other good persons not justified from the law? The answer is: They were indeed justified, but not by works of the law. Hence Peter says: “Why do you test us by imposing a yoke,” etc. (Acts 15). Therefore, just as we are now saved through faith in Christ, so they too were saved. And why not by works? Because the law did not come to take away sins, but to expose and punish them. [Haimo, Ambrose.] For God decreed that a human being should be justified through the sacrament of the mystery of faith which is in Christ, not through the law; for the law does not justify before God, but faith does. We speak of the law, however, with reference to ceremonial observances, as was said, not moral precepts, which certainly do justify and are fulfilled in the Gospel.

VERS. 20, 21.—“For through the law is knowledge of sin. But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been manifested, being attested by the law and the prophets.”

“For through the law”—[Note: [Col. 1359D] Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will*.] that is: Truly, righteousness does not come from the law, because through the law there is only knowledge of sin, not its removal. Therefore, if people know sin and do not avoid it, there is transgression; and thus wrath, that is, punishment, is owed. But a human being cannot avoid sin unless grace assists, so that what is recognized may be avoided; and so without doubt the law works wrath, as will be said later. [Haimo.] This is said because God’s wrath is greater against the transgressor, who knows sin through the law and nevertheless commits it.

When he says that sin is known through the law, he does not say this because sins were altogether unknown before the law. Joseph, for example, was accused of a crime and thrown into prison; and his brothers said: “We rightly suffer these things, because we sinned against our brother” (Gen. 42). But sins are said to be known through the law because some things came to be recognized as sins which had previously been unknown as sins; some things were recognized through the law as more serious than they had formerly been thought; and, generally, it became known through the law that all sins would not go unpunished before God.

“But now,” etc. [Augustine.] That is: Righteousness did not formerly come from works of the law. But now, [Ambrose.] that is, in this grace—“now” meaning at Christ’s coming, in the time of grace—the righteousness of God, not of man, has been given apart from the law, that is, without the law’s assistance. It has not only been given but also manifested—not doubtfully, but by miracles, namely, “the Lord working with them and confirming the word by signs that followed” (Mark 16). [Haimo, Augustine.] Here “the righteousness of God” means not that by which he himself is righteous, he who is essentially righteousness, but that with which he clothes the ungodly when, in mercy, he makes a believer out of an unbeliever.

And that people may believe more surely, he adds: righteousness, I say, “attested,” or having testimony, “by the law and the prophets.” [Ambrose.] For the law prefigured it through many sacraments; indeed, the law itself bears testimony to God’s righteousness precisely because no one is justified in it. [Note: [Col. 1359D] Augustine, *Against the Pelagians*.] Since the law does not justify the ungodly person convicted of transgression, it sends him to the God who justifies, and so bears testimony to God’s righteousness: by commanding, threatening, and justifying no one, it sufficiently indicates that a human being is justified by God’s gift. [Haimo.] The prophets bear testimony by foretelling what Christ’s advent fulfilled. For they foretold Christ, who “became for us wisdom and righteousness and sanctification and redemption.”

[Augustine, Ambrose.] Moreover, this is called God’s righteousness, though it might seem more properly called mercy, because it originates from a promise; and when what God promised is rendered, it is called God’s righteousness. For it is righteousness because what was promised has been paid; and when he receives those fleeing to him, it is called God’s righteousness, because not to receive them would be unrighteousness.

VERS. 22–26.—“But the righteousness of God is through faith in Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all who believe in him. For there is no distinction. For all have sinned and need the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiator through faith in his blood, for the showing of his righteousness, because of the remission of former sins in God’s forbearance; for the showing of his righteousness at this present time, that he himself may be righteous and may justify the one who is of the faith of Jesus Christ.”

“But the righteousness,” etc. That is: I have said that righteousness is from God. [Haimo.] But this righteousness of God—that is, this justification by which we are justified by God—is through faith in Jesus Christ, that is, through the faith by which Christ, the justifier of the ungodly, is believed in; for faith obtains what the law commands. [Note: [Col. 1360D] Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*.] As this is called Christ’s faith not because Christ believes, so it is called God’s righteousness not because God himself is righteous. Both belong to us; yet they are called God’s and Christ’s because they are bestowed upon us by his generosity.

Therefore the righteousness of God is apart from the law, but it is not manifested apart from the law. For how could it be attested by the law if manifested apart from the law? Rather, God’s righteousness is apart from the law because God confers it through the Spirit of grace upon the believer without the law’s aid—that is, without being aided by the law. But he does not display it apart from the law, because through the law he shows a human being his weakness, so that, fleeing by faith to God’s mercy, he may be healed. Therefore it is said of his wisdom that she bears law and mercy on her tongue: law, by which she shows the proud to be guilty; mercy, by which she justifies the humbled.

Therefore righteousness is through faith in Christ. This righteousness comes to all, and, more properly speaking, is upon all, because it is given from heaven—upon all Jews and Gentiles who believe in him. And truly, it is upon all, for there is no distinction between Jew and Gentile. For all, [Haimo.] Jews and Gentiles alike, have sinned, either in themselves or in Adam; for they are not without sin, whether it be what they inherited originally or what they added by evil habits.
