[Note: [Col. 1361D] Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*.] For the sin of the first human being corrupted not only himself but the entire human race; from him we all received together both condemnation and guilt. Thus all sinned, since from one sinner all are born sinners.

And they still daily need the glory of God—that is, God’s righteousness, not their own. [Note: [Col. 1361D] Augustine, from the *Hypognosticon*.] It is called the glory of God because through this God appears glorious. Thus Christ’s grace found all to be sinners, because he alone came without sin. And all need the glory of God—that is, that he who is able may deliver them, not you, who yourself need a deliverer. [Note: [Col. 1361D] Augustine, on Psalm 30.]

Therefore this grace of Christ, without which neither infants nor adults can be saved, is not rendered for merits but is freely given; for this reason it is called grace. [Note: [Col. 1361D] Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*.] For the whole mass owes punishment; and if the penalty of condemnation due to all were rendered to all, it would undoubtedly not be rendered unjustly. Those therefore who are delivered from it by grace are rightly called not vessels of their own merits but vessels of mercy. Let each one, then, give thanks to the mercy of God, who delivers whom he wills; for no one could rightly blame his justice if he wished to condemn all.

For all have sinned and need the glory of God—that is, pardon and forgiveness of sins. [Haimo.] Hence God appears glorious. And because all have sinned, they have therefore been justified freely, that is, without preceding merits. [Note: [Col. 1362D] Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*.] And this is through his grace, that is, through gratuitous gifts. For the grace of God is God’s gift, and the greatest gift is the Holy Spirit himself.

Therefore they were not justified through the law or through their own will, but through Christ’s grace. This does not mean that it happens without our will; rather, the law shows our will to be weak, so that grace may heal the will, and the healed will may fulfil the law—not being placed under the law or needing the law. [Note: [Col. 1362D] Augustine, *Sermons on the Words of the Lord*.] This, then, is the grace by which the ungodly person is justified; and therefore no merits precede this grace which is to be bestowed, because to the merits of the ungodly not grace but punishment is owed. Nor would this be grace if it were not freely given. [Note: [Col. 1362D] Augustine, *To Sixtus*.] It is freely given because we had previously done no good by which we might deserve it; [Col. 1361D] for nothing had preceded in our merits except that for which we deserved condemnation. Thus it found not merits for good things, but merits for punishments. Therefore they are justified freely, because they had done nothing.

“Through his grace,” [Ambrose.] because they are justified by faith, and especially “through the redemption,” which is for us in Christ Jesus and nowhere else—that is, through the price given for us by Christ Jesus. Of him Peter says: “You were redeemed not with corruptible silver or gold, but with the precious blood of the only-begotten Son of God” (1 Pet. 1). [Note: [Col. 1362D] Ambrose, on Psalm 33.] Indeed, in order that human beings might be justified by divine grace, Truth was born of Mary, so that he might offer for their justification the sacrifice of his passion and cross. For unless Christ had taken from us mortal flesh, he could not die.

It should be noted that he is rightly said to have redeemed us, not bought us. For we had previously been his by nature, but through our sins we were alienated. If, therefore, we do not return to sins, Christ’s redemption will be fruitful for us.

Whom—Christ—God the Father “set forth,” that is, arranged and foretold long beforehand; or, “set forth,” that is, openly placed before all as a propitiator, [Haimo.] that is, merciful. And this was “through faith in his blood,” that is, through faith in his passion, without which nothing pleases God. Or, “through faith in his blood,” that is, through faith and passion. He joins these together because neither has efficacy without the other. I say that he set him forth as a propitiator for this purpose, [Ambrose.] namely, “for the showing of his righteousness,” that is, to show himself true in his promises—namely, that he would free us from sins, as he had promised before. When he fulfilled this, he showed himself righteous. This showing was necessary not only for remission of present sins but also because of the remission of former sins, namely, sins preceding Christ’s coming—sins existing in God’s forbearance, God then enduring and not punishing them. For God’s forbearance is when the sinner is not punished immediately upon sinning, but is brought to repentance through God’s patience.

[Origen.] Therefore the Apostle says something lofty: God set forth his Son as a propitiator for the human race, through faith in his blood—that is, through faith and the shedding of his blood—so that by this he might show his righteousness when he remitted the former sins which they had contracted by serving most wicked tyrants, at the time when God endured and allowed this to occur. [Haimo, Origen.] For he long endures and bears human sins. If this were not so, the end of humanity would have come in judgment with the first human being. But for what purpose did he then allow and endure this? He shows by adding: “for the showing of his righteousness at this present time.” [Haimo.] Here righteousness is understood as that by which God justifies those who believe in Christ; or as Christ himself, who justifies sinners.

The sense is: He endured sins in order to show, in this time of Christ, his righteousness which makes people righteous—namely, that he himself justifies and saves. [Ambrose.] This could not occur at any other time than that in which God gave what he had long ago promised to give.

Or thus: “because of the remission of sins,” not only of present human beings, but also of those who preceded Christ’s coming—sins, I say, existing in God’s forbearance. For those righteous persons who preceded Christ’s coming were held in hell [Col. 1363A] until Christ’s passion. There they were neither oppressed by punishments nor yet saw God, which was a punishment to them. This was because of the first human being’s sin, or original sin, on account of which the entrance to the kingdom of heaven was closed; it was opened through Christ’s passion. Hence Zechariah: “You also, by the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zech. 9). Jerome says on this passage: “At Christ’s resurrection, the righteous, who were held bound in hell because of Adam’s sin, rose again.”

It is commonly asked whether the sins of the ancient righteous who were held in hell had been remitted through faith and repentance, which they are certainly known truly to have possessed; and, if all had been remitted, why they were held in the lower regions. We answer that all had been forgiven them through faith and repentance, but they had not received the complete effect of forgiveness. For there are two effects of forgiveness: freedom from punishment and enjoyment of glory. They had the one before Christ’s death, because they felt no actual punishment; but not the other, because they did not see God. Through Christ’s death, however, they were given the glory of the divine vision, from which they had been delayed while God bore with their sins.

“For the showing of his righteousness at this present time,” that is, that he might show, at the time of Christ’s death, his righteousness by which he crowns those who hope in him, “that he himself may be.” [Ambrose.] That is: He showed his righteousness so that he himself may be—that is, may appear to be—righteous in his promises, giving what he promised; otherwise he could not help. And that he may be “the justifier,” that is, the maker of righteous, of the one who is of the faith of Jesus Christ, not of the law—that is, who believes in Christ.

VERS. 27.—“Where, then, is your boasting? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we reckon that a human being is justified by faith apart from works of the law.”

Where is it, etc. Having given the reason, he speaks to those who act under the Law, showing that they boast without cause, flattering themselves on account of the Law and of Abraham’s descent, although they see that a human being is not justified before God except through faith. As though he were saying: [Note: [Col. 1363D] Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*.] Since righteousness is from faith apart from the Law, therefore, O Jew, where is your glory? You cannot boast; for that faulty boasting of yours, arising from pride, has been excluded—that is, removed. And by what law, namely, has it been excluded? [Haimo.] He questions the Jew, so that he may consider by what law proud boasting has been excluded. Is it by the law of works—that is, by the Law of Moses, which commanded carnal things? No, but by the law of faith. [Augustine.] As though he were saying: Consider by what it has been excluded: not by the labor of works, but by the ease of faith.

Or thus, and he speaks of good boasting. As though he were saying: Since righteousness is from faith [Note: [Col. 1363D] Id., *On the Spirit and the Letter*.], where then, O Jew, is your boasting—that is, what is that in which you ought to boast? Your boasting has been excluded. He means the praiseworthy boasting which is in the Lord, [Col. 1364A] and calls it “excluded,” that is, made conspicuous and expressed, not driven away or expelled. Thus certain silversmiths are called *exclusores* (“embossers”); and in this sense is also understood that passage in the Psalm: “That those who have been tested by silver may be brought forth” (Ps. LXVII), that is, that those tested by the word of the Lord may stand out. So here “has been excluded” means “has been made manifest and expressed.” Your boasting—that is, it is manifest in what you ought to boast: not in the law of works, but in the law of faith. And this is what follows: “By what law?”—that is, by what law ought you to boast? By the law of works? No, but by the law of faith.

But it is asked why the Law of Moses is called a law of works, whereas the law of the Gospel is not called a law of works, but a law of faith, of righteousness, or of the Spirit. This is worth considering, [Col. 1364B] if indeed we are able to observe and distinguish it. For it is a great matter. Although the law of the Gospel does not contain the works of the old sacraments—circumcision, namely, and the rest—it nevertheless has works in its own sacraments, suited to this time, and it has works of mercy in its moral precepts. Why then is it not itself called a law of works?

To this I shall briefly reply: the law called the law of works commanded by threatening, but did not bestow grace upon the person doing what it commanded. The law called the law of faith does indeed command works, but by believing it obtains that they may be done; and those works follow righteousness. For righteousness does not arise from the works themselves; rather, the works arise from righteousness. Therefore we speak not of the righteousness of works, but of works of righteousness. Thus it is called not a law of works, but a law of righteousness, faith, or grace, [Col. 1364C] because it bestows the grace to perform works and makes people righteous through faith. But the law of works was that in which works were commanded, while grace was not given. Through the law of works God says to man: “Do what I command.” Through the law of faith man says to God: “Give what you command.” For the Law commands in order to remind one what faith should do, so that the one commanded, if unable, may know what to ask for. But if one is immediately able and obediently does it, one should also know by whose gift one is able.

“For we judge,” then, “that the law of faith justifies”: he proves this by his own authority. As though he were saying: Truly, righteousness is through faith. For we apostles judge thus: that any human being, even a Gentile, is justified by faith without works of the Law—carnal works, [Ambrose.] that is, without circumcision, [Col. 1364D] new-moon observances, Sabbath-veneration, or without any works of the Law whatsoever, even moral ones. [Augustine.] But this must be understood of works preceding faith, not those following it, without which faith is empty, as James says: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. II). Paul himself also says: “Though I have all faith, but have not charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. XIII). [Note: [Col. 1364D] Augustine, *On Faith and Works*.]

Therefore, in preaching faith to the Gentiles, the Apostle says that a person is justified by faith without works of the Law in order to show that one does not arrive at faith by the merit of good works, but that good works follow faith. This does not mean that the believer should not afterwards work through love, [Col. 1365A] as Abraham was willing to sacrifice his son. [Note: [Col. 1365D] Id., in Book XXXIII of the *Questions*.] For works follow the justified person; they do not precede the person to be justified. Rather, by faith alone, apart from preceding works, a person becomes righteous—so that those who performed works of the Law out of fear are not more righteous—since faith works through love in the heart, even if it does not outwardly issue in a deed. [Note: [Col. 1365D] Id., *On Faith and Works*.] For faith that works through love, even where there is no opportunity for outward action, is nevertheless preserved in the heart, serving and fervent. [Note: [Col. 1365D] Id., on Psalm XXXI.]

One does not come to the righteousness of faith by merits of earlier works—the matter in which the Jews preferred themselves. Even good works before faith are empty. They seem to me to be like great strength and exceedingly swift running away from the road. Therefore let no one reckon works before faith to be truly good works: where faith was absent, [Col. 1365B] good work was absent. For intention makes a work good, and faith directs intention. Do not pay much attention to what a person does, but to what the person attends to while acting, toward what goal he directs the arms of excellent governance.

VERS. 29–31.—“Is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also. Since there is one God, who justifies circumcision by faith and uncircumcision through faith. Do we therefore destroy the Law through faith? By no means! Rather, we establish the Law.”

“Is God of the Jews only?” As though he were saying: We judge that every human being is justified by faith. This is to be believed because he is also the Creator of the Gentiles. And this is what he says: “Is he God of the Jews only?”—[Col. 1365C] that is, is he their Creator, so that on this account he is to be believed to be their justifier alone? Is he not the Creator of Gentiles as well as of Jews? Indeed, he is Creator of Gentiles as of Jews, so that he may be believed to be their justifier as he is of the Jews. And truly he is God of both, since there is one God—that is, the Creator of all.

As though he were saying: Though this can be proved in other ways, I present this one point: since he is the one God of all, he justifies all equally by the same cause, namely faith. And this is what is meant: [Augustine.] I say that there is one God, who justifies the circumcision—that is, the Jews—from faith; and justifies the uncircumcision—that is, unclean Gentiles—through faith. [Note: [Col. 1366D] Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*.] This is not said to mark any difference, as though “from faith” were one thing and “through faith” another, but for variety of expression. [Col. 1365D] [Ambrose.] For “from faith” and “through faith” mean the same thing, because the Apostle frequently changes prepositions while retaining the same sense; and because we say that all are justified through faith.

“Do we therefore destroy the Law through faith? By no means!” For the Law is not destroyed when, having been fulfilled according to the Spirit, it ceases according to the letter. Hence he adds: “Rather, we establish”—that is, confirm—the Law, because this is the grace of faith through which the Law is fulfilled, which without faith would be weak. For the Law’s standing is made firm, because its mystical and ceremonial elements are fulfilled spiritually; what it contained less fully in moral matters [Col. 1366A] is added in the Gospel; and faith testifies that what it promised as future has come. Thus its mystical and promissory elements are fulfilled in the Gospel according to spiritual understanding. But the killing letter is removed, while moral commands, in which it contained less, are fulfilled in the Gospel also according to the letter.

## Chapter IV

VERS. 1–8.—“Then what shall we say that Abraham, our father according to the flesh, found? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God. For what does Scripture say? Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. But to one who works, wages are not credited according to grace, but according to [Col. 1366B] debt. But to one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness according to the purpose of God’s grace; as David also declares the blessedness of the person to whom God credits righteousness without works: Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin.”

What he had said above, that a person is justified through faith, he proves through Abraham, in whom all put their confidence: Abraham obtained righteousness, promise, and fatherhood through faith. As though he were saying: Since no one is righteous without faith, neither, therefore, was Abraham. What then shall we say that Abraham our father—whom, namely, we ought to imitate—found according to the flesh, [Col. 1366C] that is, from works of the Law? Shall we say that he was righteous through them? No. [Ambrose.] For if Abraham was justified by works of the Law—that is, if he was truly righteous from carnal observance, which is certainly impossible—then this other impossibility follows: that he has eternal glory, which follows from righteousness, but has it from himself, not before God—that is, not from God.

[Origen.] Or thus: the Apostle often seems to show that there are two kinds of justification, one of which he calls justification from works and the other justification from faith. The justification from works, he says, has glory before human beings, but not before God; whereas the justification from faith has glory before God, who looks upon human hearts and knows [Col. 1366D] whether someone believes secretly or not. The sense is: if Abraham was justified by works of the Law, he has glory from this justification, but among human beings, not according to God. [Note: [Col. 1366D] Augustine on Psalm XXXI.] For this justification lies in human opinion, and is not before God because it is not true.

May God avert such glory; let us rather hold fast to this: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.” [Haimo.] For many boast of works while being evil, like that Pharisee who went up to the Temple with the tax collector and vaunted his works, saying: “I am not like other people,” [Col. 1367A] etc. (Luke XVIII). [Augustine.] If, then, Abraham was justified by works, he does not have glory before God, because “the one who does the Law,” he says, “shall live in it”—that is, shall not die here as guilty—yet he will not thereby have merit before God, but on account of faith. But Abraham has glory before God. Therefore he was not justified by works; and if so, then he is righteous through faith.

He proves this by adding: For what does Scripture say in Genesis? [Haimo.] As though he were saying: Attend to what it says, and from what he is righteous. Behold: Abraham believed God, who said: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII), and other such things. And that believing itself was reckoned to him as righteousness—that is, it was for him, and is for others, a sufficient cause of righteousness unto salvation. But to one who works—that is, one who [Col. 1367B] has time to work—wages are not credited, that is, will not be given, according to the grace of faith alone, but according to the debt of his own working.

But for the one who does not work—that is, who has no time to work, as Abraham had—yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, [Ambrose.] that is, if he believes in Christ, who freely forgives the sins of the ungodly, his faith alone is reckoned as righteousness: it suffices for the righteousness which works have not earned, and so it suffices for salvation. [Note: [Col. 1367D] Id., on John.] Note that he says, “believing in him,” not “believing him.” For one who believes him does not thereby believe in him. It is one thing to believe in him, another to believe him, another to believe that he is. [Note: [Col. 1367D] Bede, *On Faith*.] For the demons believed him, but did not believe in him. We believe Paul and Peter, but we do not believe in Paul [Col. 1367C] or Peter. To believe him is to believe that the things he says are true; even evil people do this. [Augustine.] To believe that he is, is to believe that he is God; evil people also do this. But what is it to believe in him? To love by believing, to cherish by believing, to go to him by believing, and to be incorporated into his members. This is the faith God requires from us; and he would find nothing to require unless he gave what he finds. [Note: [Col. 1367D] Id., on Psalm LXVI.]

By this faith the ungodly person is justified—that is, from ungodly he becomes godly—so that afterward faith itself begins to work through love. For only those works are to be called good which are done through love of God. But faith must necessarily come first, so that these other things may begin from it, rather than it from them; for [Col. 1367D] no one works well unless he first believes in God. [Note: [Col. 1368D] Augustine, *To the Romans, Earlier Expositions*.] Therefore the Apostle does not say that reward is rendered according to the merit of a work as though works rewarded by God came from us; rather, they are from God’s grace. For by grace God gave sinners faith through which they might be justified, so that through faith they might live righteously—that is, work well. Thus, when we work well after grace has been received, this must be attributed not to us but to him who justified us by grace. For if he wished to render the due reward before grace, he would render sinners the punishment due to them. [Note: [Col. 1368D] Id., *On Faith to Peter*.]

Therefore do not flatter yourself about merits when you hear that reward is given to you according to the debt of work, as though in the work there were not the grace of the one rewarding, [Col. 1368A] just as in faith there is the grace of the one justifying. [Origen.] For I can scarcely persuade myself that any work can be said to demand from God a recompense as its due, since even our ability to do, think, or speak anything comes through his gift and generosity.

“According to the purpose.” As though he were saying: The ungodly person is justified without preceding works, [Origen.] and this is according to the purpose of God’s grace—that is, according to the grace which God has purposed for believing people; or, according to what God long beforehand purposed.

Or, from the words “But to one who works,” he argues against those who said that the grace of faith had been given them by the merit of preceding works of the Law or of any kind. [Augustine.] If this were so, reward would not be credited [Col. 1368B] according to grace but according to debt. If this were so, it would no longer be grace. For if it is grace, it is given freely. What does “given freely” mean? You have done nothing good, and forgiveness of sins is given to you. Your works are examined and all are found evil. What is owed to evil works but condemnation? What is owed to good ones? Reward—namely, the kingdom of heaven.

As though he were saying: Abraham is righteous through faith; but to the one who performs those carnal works of the Law, or any good works, in order to deserve the grace of faith and justification, if there is a reward, it is not credited according to grace but according to debt—that is, it is not from grace but from the debt of his own merit. But to the one who does not perform those carnal works of the Law, but merely believes [Col. 1368C] in Christ, as a Gentile does—or who performs no good works whatever before faith but merely believes—his faith is reckoned as righteousness, that is, it suffices for righteousness.

Thus he attributes to others what he said of Abraham: if he is righteous through works, he has glory, but not before God; but Abraham has glory before God, and therefore is righteous through faith. I say that righteousness is through faith, and that this is according to the purpose of God’s grace. For God decreed thus: when the burden of the Law had ceased, faith should justify. He indicates this also by the example of the prophet David, adding: “As,” etc.

As though he were saying: I say that righteousness and salvation are from grace, just as David too speaks of the blessedness, here and in the future, of the person to whom God, at an acceptable time—that is, at the time of Christ’s coming [Col. 1368D] [Haimo.]—or, taking *accepto* adverbially, “acceptably,” that is, freely, brings righteousness to one as though unable to approach it: namely remission and good works, and this without preceding works.

“Blessed are those,” etc. Having explained the Prophet’s meaning, he briefly sets down the very words, because David speaks in these words: “Blessed are those whose iniquities, [Ambrose.] without the work and labor of penance, have been forgiven by God through baptism, so that sin no longer rules in the mortal body—even if it remains.” Here “iniquities” means original sin, namely [Col. 1369A] the tinder of sin, which is called concupiscence, or concupiscibility, or the law of the members, or weakness of nature, and by other names.

This concupiscence or concupiscibility, called the tinder of sin, is guilt and punishment before baptism; after baptism it is punishment and not guilt, making an infant capable of desiring or not desiring. [Note: [Col. 1369D] Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*.] In an adult it also produces desire; though it is no longer reckoned as sin in the regenerate, nevertheless whatever offspring is born remains bound by original sin.

Therefore the concupiscence of the flesh is forgiven in baptism, not so that it does not exist, but so that it is not imputed as sin. This is what it means not to have sin: not to be guilty of sin. [Augustine.] For just as other sins [Col. 1369B] pass away in act but remain in liability, such as murders and the like, so the converse can occur: concupiscence—that is, concupiscibility—can pass away in liability and remain in act. Augustine says of it:

> For carnal concupiscence remains in this body of death, and we are commanded not to obey its vicious desires; nevertheless, this concupiscence daily diminishes in those who make progress and practice continence. Since, when husband and wife join with one another, the intercourse of parents is not without lust, the conception of children born from that same flesh cannot be without sin. For propagation does not transmit sin, but lust; nor does the fruitfulness of human nature cause people to be born with sin, but the foulness of lust, which human beings possess from the wholly just condemnation of that first [Col. 1369C] sin.

Therefore blessed David, on account of original sin by which children are naturally bound as children of wrath, says: “In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. L). From these things it is clear that concupiscence is original sin. [Note: [Col. 1369D] Id., ibid.] It is called original because it is drawn from the defective condition of our origin. We are not held by original sin merely because we descend from Adam by carnal propagation, since Christ too descended from him and was free from every sin; but because we are conceived under the defective law of conception that arose from the first human being’s sin—that is, through the concupiscence of the flesh—we are liable for the sin called original.

Here, briefly, has been set out what original sin is, why it is called original, why it is imputed to descendants, [Col. 1369D] and how it is forgiven in baptism: namely, so that after baptism guilt does not remain, but punishment does; and what remains no longer rules, if a person perseveres in the grace of baptism. Therefore he cautiously says: “Blessed are those whose [iniquities] have been forgiven,” etc.—mitigated and destroyed insofar as guilt is concerned, though not insofar as punishment is concerned—and “whose actual sins have been covered in baptism.” He means sins existing in act, which are so covered in baptism that God no longer sees them for punishment; for this is what it means for God to see sins.

All blessed persons have what they wish; nevertheless, not everyone who has what he wishes is immediately blessed. But people are immediately miserable if they either do not have what they wish or have what they do not rightly wish. Therefore a person is not blessed unless he has all that he wishes and wishes nothing evil. And because no one is without original or venial sin, he adds: “Blessed is the man [Note: [Col. 1370D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*.] to whom the Lord has not imputed sin for punishment,” whether original sin, which comes from elsewhere, or venial sin.

[Ambrose.] Or otherwise, he establishes three degrees of offences. These sayings appear to have a threefold order because of the variety of sins. The first degree is iniquity or impiety: namely, when the Creator is not acknowledged—that is, unbelief. The second degree lies in works of grave sins. The third, in lesser sins. But “to forgive,” “to cover,” and “not to impute” are expressions of one sense and meaning: for when he covers, he forgives; and when he forgives, he does not impute. But he speaks at greater length [Col. 1370B] for the praise of God’s grace:

VERS. 9–12.—“Does this blessedness remain only in circumcision, or also in uncircumcision? For we say that faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it reckoned? In circumcision or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision but in uncircumcision. And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith which is in uncircumcision, so that he might be the father of all who believe through uncircumcision, so that it might also be reckoned to them as righteousness; and that he might be father of the circumcision, not only of those who are of the circumcision, but also of those who follow the footsteps of the faith which is in the uncircumcision of our father Abraham.”

“This blessedness,” etc. From the Prophet’s words he proved that blessedness comes from grace through faith; now he asks [Col. 1370C] in whom it is found: whether only among Jews or also among Gentiles. As though he were saying: Since it is established that blessedness comes from grace through faith, let it now be asked in whom it exists. Does this blessedness then remain only in circumcision—that is, in Jews—or also in uncircumcision—that is, in Gentiles? That is, has blessedness been granted only to Abraham’s sons, or also to those from among the Gentiles?

He then explains the reason for this question, saying: “For we say,” etc. As though he were saying: I ask this because, speaking from the meaning of the Law, we say that faith, not circumcision, was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness. That is, you who understand the Law recognize concerning Abraham that he was righteous through faith. Since this is established, how then was it reckoned—that is, in what condition was he: in circumcision or in uncircumcision? That is, after he was circumcised, or before he was circumcised? And as it is seen in him, so it can be believed in others.

Then he resolves both questions at once: This blessedness exists not only in circumcision—that is, among Jews—but also likewise in uncircumcision—that is, among Gentiles. Faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness not only in the time of circumcision but in uncircumcision—that is, in the time of uncircumcision. “And he received the sign,” etc.

The Apostle answers what could rightly be objected: since Abraham was righteous through faith before circumcision, why was he circumcised? As though someone said: [Col. 1371A] “Since Abraham was righteous before circumcision, why then was he circumcised?” [Augustine, Ambrose.] He answers: not without reason and not superfluously. Rather, he received the sign of circumcision—that is, he received circumcision as a sign, not by which he might become righteous, but by which he might be shown righteous. As though he were saying: He received circumcision, which was a sign of the righteousness already possessed. Thus circumcision had no great dignity in itself, but was only a sign for him.

For external circumcision is called a sign of internal circumcision, such a sign as is a seal—that is, one possessing a likeness of the thing sealed. As a person is stripped in circumcision of the flesh of lust, so the soul may be stripped of all filth of its first birth. And because he had not yet said of what it was a sign, he adds: “of the righteousness of faith.” As though he were saying: He received circumcision as a sign of this thing, namely the righteousness of faith—that is, righteousness from faith.

[Origen.] Or it is called a seal in another way and for another reason. As though he were saying: He received circumcision as a sign, and that sign is a seal—that is, concealing a mystery hidden from enemies, namely unbelievers, and preserved for friends, namely believers, in the likeness of a seal impressed so that what we wish to be hidden may not be open to everyone. This mystery, which circumcision contains as though hidden, is that just as a person is circumcised on the eighth day, [Col. 1371C] so in the eighth age, after the end of the seven days of the world, all oldness—of guilt and punishment alike—will be removed.

[Alcuin.] Here it must be considered in whom circumcision was first instituted, why it was instituted, what it conferred, and why it was changed in the time of grace when baptism succeeded it. Circumcision was first commended to Abraham, so that he might be under the law of the command and thus be tested whether he would fulfill it or not. So Adam received the command not to eat of the tree, for the testing of obedience; and as circumcision was received by Abraham, so also by his seed, that is, Hebrews born from him. It was done on the eighth day, with a stone knife, in the flesh of the foreskin, as commanded.

[Strabo, Augustine, Ambrose.] Circumcision was given for five reasons. First, so that Abraham might please God by obedience to the command, whereas Adam had displeased him by transgression. Second, as a sign [Col. 1371D] of Abraham’s great faith. For he believed that he would have a son in whom all nations would be blessed through faith, and through whom spiritual circumcision would be fulfilled, just as Abraham himself was justified. Third, so that by this sign that people might be distinguished from the other nations. Fourth, so that circumcision performed in the male member through which mortal creatures are generated, and in which lust commonly rules, might signify the chastity of mind and body to be preserved and indecency to be cut away. Fifth, it was commanded because original sin could not be signified more suitably as removed through Christ. For every human is born with a foreskin, just as with original sin; and the circumcised man begets one uncircumcised, transmitting to him what he himself has already lacked, just as the baptized person transmits to the child whom he generates in the flesh the liability of origin from which he himself has already been freed. [Col. 1372A]

It was commanded to be performed in the flesh of the foreskin because it was instituted as a remedy, namely against original sin, which we contract from our parents; we are conceived in concupiscence, which rules especially in that part. And because the first human being knew the guilt of disobedience in that member, it was fitting that he receive obedience in that member. It was done on the eighth day with a stone knife because, after the sevenfold number of this life, in the eighth age, which will be that of the risen, every corruption of flesh and spirit will be cut away from the elect by Christ the rock, when we shall be freed from slavery to corruption. And through Christ’s resurrection, which took place on the eighth day, the soul of every one who believes in him will be circumcised from sins. Thus there are two things in that sacrament: circumcision from sins in this present life, and circumcision from all corruption in the future.

Circumcision in its own time conferred forgiveness of sins, as baptism now does. [Bede.] For circumcision under the Law furnished the same aid of saving healing against the wound of original sin which baptism customarily performs in the time of grace now revealed, except that they could not yet enter through the gate of the kingdom of heaven: after death they were comforted by blessed rest in Abraham’s bosom and awaited in happy hope the entrance into the peace above. [Note: [Col. 1371D] Gregory, *Morals*.] Likewise, what baptismal water accomplishes among us, that among the ancients was accomplished either, for infants, by faith alone; for adults, by the efficacy of sacrifice; or, for those descended from Abraham’s stock, by the mystery of circumcision. [Col. 1372C]

From these authorities it is clear that forgiveness of sins took place through circumcision, as also through baptism. Why then was circumcision replaced by baptism? Because the sacrament of baptism is more perfect: both more universal and fuller of grace. In circumcision sins alone were forgiven; grace for working well was not bestowed through it, nor were virtues given or increased. In baptism, however, sins are forgiven, grace for cooperating is conferred, and virtues are increased.

Therefore the Apostle rightly says that Abraham received circumcision only as a sign, which is a seal—[Col. 1372D] a sign, I say, of the righteousness of faith. This righteousness of faith, or faith, belonged to Abraham in uncircumcision—that is, at the time of uncircumcision, before he was circumcised. Therefore, he had righteousness from faith while uncircumcised, so that he might be—that is, might be shown to be—the father, the author of faith by example, of all believers. He is father, I say, also through uncircumcision—that is, in the time of uncircumcision.

Or “through uncircumcision” means through what was given to him at the time of uncircumcision, that is, after faith. Note carefully the unusual preposition, placed here contrary to ordinary usage, which explains several points noted. It may be understood thus: “through uncircumcision,” that is, in uncircumcision, as one says “through that time,” [Col. 1373A] meaning “in that time”; or “through uncircumcision,” that is, through what was given to him at the time of uncircumcision. For if it were said after circumcision that he received this from it, here the discussion concerns the fatherhood which Abraham attained through faith.

[Ambrose, Haimo.] For according to the flesh he is father only of Jews; but according to faith he is father of all believers, Jews and Gentiles alike. Thus, to them also, when they believe, believing itself may be reckoned as righteousness—that is, for forgiveness of sins and good works—and thus he may be spiritual father of circumcision, that is, author by example of the righteousness which is from faith.

Abraham is father not only of those who are from carnal circumcision—that is, Jews [Haimo.]—or to whom faith is reckoned as righteousness, but also of all who follow the footsteps of Abraham’s faith, believing as fully as he believed. I mean Abraham, our father—that is, father of all believers. This faith was given to him in uncircumcision, that is, at the time of uncircumcision, as has already been said.

“For not,” etc. He said that Abraham attained righteousness and fatherhood not through the Law but through faith. Now, speaking of the promise, he adds that through the same faith he received the promise and the inheritance. [Ambrose.] As though he were saying: Fatherhood is through faith because the promise is through it, not through the Law or circumcision, which did not yet exist. And this is what follows:

VERS. 13–15.—“For the promise was not made through the Law to Abraham or to his seed, that he should be heir [Col. 1373C] of the world, but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who are of the Law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise abolished. For the Law works wrath; for where there is no law, neither is there transgression.”

For the promise was not made through the Law to Abraham or to his seed. [Ambrose, Haimo.] That is, it was made with a view to the work of his seed, namely all believers, who are Abraham’s seed not by flesh but by imitation. [Ambrose.] Or “his seed” means Christ, to whom the promise is said to have been made because it was to be fulfilled in him. What promise? Namely, that he should be heir of the world. For the Law had not yet been given when this promise was made.

Abraham is called heir of the world, that is, possessor of some people from the whole world who imitate him, [Col. 1373D] [Haimo.] because all believers are Abraham’s children through faith, and he possesses all things in Christ, who was born from him. Abraham, then, is heir of the world both in himself and in his seed, that is, Christ: in himself by example; Christ, however, is heir—that is, Lord of the world—according to power. Through Christ blessing comes to Abraham’s children; to him the Father gave the nations and the ends of the earth, as David says: “I will give him the nations,” etc. (Ps. II). Thus in him was fulfilled the promise made to Abraham: “I have made you father of many nations” (Gen. XVII); and again: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII), and other such sayings.

This promise, as has been said, was made not through the Law but through the righteousness of faith, through which people are blessed and become Abraham’s children. “For if,” etc. [Col. 1374A] He said that the promise of inheritance was made to Abraham through the righteousness of faith, not through the Law. Now he says that people become Abraham’s heirs through that same righteousness of faith, not through the Law. As though he were saying: Abraham is truly not heir of the world through the Law, because his children are not so through the Law. Who are the children here called heirs? [Ambrose.] Namely, those whom he has as possessors.

And truly they are not, because if this were true—namely, if those who are heirs are heirs only from the Law, that is, are called heirs—these consequences follow: faith, by which Abraham is known to have been righteous, has been emptied, that is, rendered fruitless; and the promise has been abolished, [Augustine] that is, left unfulfilled, so that no one is an heir. For the Law does not make anyone an heir; rather, it works wrath—that is, punishment. For it was given in order to make transgressors guilty, not as an efficient cause, but because grace did not assist. Or it works wrath in the form of temporal punishments, since it produces transgression.

[Ambrose.] He explains how this is said by adding: “For where there is no law.” As though he were saying: I say that wrath and transgression arise from the Law because without it they do not exist. For where there is no law, neither is there transgression. He says this because, when the Law is removed, pardon is granted; for the justified, there is no transgression. [Augustine.] For those who had been sinners through transgression of the Law have been justified. Note that he does not say, “Where there is no law, there is no iniquity,” but says, “there is no transgression.” For everyone who passes beyond a law is wicked, but not every wicked person passes beyond a law. Those who have not received the Law may be called wicked, [Col. 1374C] but they cannot be called transgressors. Thus he shows that transgression cannot exist at all where there has been no Law, nor wrath of so great a kind without the Law.

### Verses 16, 18

> “Therefore it is by faith, so that the promise may be secure according to grace for all the seed—not only for the one who is of the law, but also for the one who shares the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all; as it is written: ‘I have made you the father of many nations before God, whom you believed, who gives life to the dead and calls things that are not as though they were. He, against hope, believed in hope, so that he might become the father of many nations, according to what had been said to him: Thus shall your seed be, like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea.’” [Col. 1374D]

“Therefore, by faith,” etc. [Augustine.] From what has been said, he concludes that people become Abraham’s heirs by faith. As though he said: Since these incongruities would follow if they were heirs by the law, it is therefore wholly evident that they are heirs by faith, [Ambrose] which is the gift of mercy. Thus the promise is secure for all Abraham’s seed. Hence he adds: “so that the promise may be secure for all Abraham’s seed,” that is, for the Jewish and Gentile imitator alike. For the promise—that they are children of God—is secure only for those who imitate him. I say secure according to the grace of faith, not according to the merits of legal works or of any things preceding faith. For the promise cannot be secure for all the seed except by faith, because the origin of the promise is faith, through which they must be purified [Col. 1375A] so as to be worthy to be called children of God.

“Not for the one,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1375D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] As though he said: The promise, through the grace of faith, is secure for all the seed, not only for the one who is of the law—that is, not merely for the one who comes from the old law to the new, namely the Jews—but also for whoever shares Abraham’s faith, that is, whoever follows the faith which Abraham, a Gentile, possessed, so that he might be righteous. [Haimo, Ambrose.]

Or thus: the promise is secure for all the seed, and not merely for the one who alone is of the law, that is, who presumes upon the works of the law; for such a person has fallen away from God’s grace. Rather, it is secure only for the one who shares Abraham’s faith, that is, who imitates Abraham’s faith. Therefore, for the sake of faith, one must withdraw from the law, so that the promise may be secure. For the law without the grace of the promise not only does not remove sin but even increases it [Note: [Col. 1375D] Id., *On Psalm* CXVIII]; not because it becomes the efficient cause of sin, since it is holy and good, but because, once it was given, an increase of sin occurred which would not have occurred without it. Many things are said to cause certain effects, not because they themselves produce them, but because the things that occur would not occur without them. [Col. 1375B]

He—Abraham—is the father, that is, the founder by the example of faith, of us all; namely, he is the father of believers, as is written in Genesis. [Haimo.] As though he said: This is confirmed by the authority which says: “I have made you, O Abraham,” that is, “I have established you,” “a father,” that is, an originator according to faith, not merely of circumcised Jews but also of many nations. In this the pride of the Jews is struck down, for they boast of descending from Abraham’s offspring. [Augustine.] For he was not made father merely of the carnally circumcised people, [Col. 1375C] but also of uncircumcised nations that imitate Abraham’s faith.

“I have made you,” I say, “before God,” that is, you please God, “whom you believed.” [Haimo.] As though he said: By faith you please him who gives life. These are the Apostle’s words. As though he said: He is rightly to be believed, because he is the one who gives life, through faith and grace, to the dead—that is, Jews dead in sins. Therefore one may safely believe in him who justifies the dead. And he calls, through grace, things which are not—that is, Gentiles who seemed to be nothing—as though they were things which are—that is, Jews who seemed to be something. For those who adhere to him through faith and love are said to exist; but those dead in sins, as the Gentiles were, because they did not adhere to him who truly is, [Col. 1375D] are said not to exist.

[Augustine.] Or thus, according to another reading: “who calls things that are not as though they are.” He does not say, “that they may be,” but “as though they are,” because they are predestined and disposed. For things which will be are already with God; indeed, with God that is already done which will come to pass by his ordering or predestination. Hence elsewhere: “who made the things that shall be”; and elsewhere: “who chose us before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1). Who is sufficient to explain this? [Note: [Col. 1375D] Id., *On the Words of the Lord*.] Those who do not exist are chosen; and he who chooses does not err, nor does he choose in vain. Yet he chooses, and he has as chosen those whom he is going to create as chosen, whom he has with himself, [Col. 1376A] not in his nature but in his presence. Those to whom the promise was made did not yet exist; but those to whom it was promised were themselves also promised.

Therefore he calls things which are not as though they were: that is, for those who do not exist he eternally ordains and prepares the grace of justification and glorification, to be bestowed in time as though they existed—that is, as though they were already with God by predestination. In this grace alone is manifest. [Augustine.] For a human being who did not exist did not merit that he should exist, or that he should be good, or blessed. If he merited it, he already existed; but he did not yet exist; therefore he did not merit it. Rather, he received the grace of election, so that the whole body of Christ may say: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15).

[Note: [Col. 1376D] Id., *On the Saying of the Apostle*.] For nature is common to all, but grace is not—unless nature itself is considered grace because it was freely bestowed. Thus, setting aside that grace now under discussion by which human nature was created—that is, by which we are human, and which Christians and pagans share—this is the greater grace, granted to the elect alone: not that we were created as human beings through the Word, but that through the Word made flesh we have become faithful and blessed. [Col. 1376B]

Or, “he calls” means “he acknowledges”: things which do not exist in actuality, as though they did exist.

“He, against hope,” etc. Having commended him in whom Abraham believed, he begins to commend Abraham’s own faith, so that others may imitate him. As though he said: Abraham rightly is the father of all, since, against the former hope [Note: [Col. 1376D] Id., Book V, *On the Trinity*], which was according to nature—that is, according to the natural course—he believed God who promised, in hope, [Col. 1376C] that is, hoping and confidently awaiting what had been promised.

The earlier hope was according to nature: [Haimo.] namely, when, as a young man, he hoped according to nature for offspring from a young woman, yet did not have it. Now he hoped for the opposite of that hope: namely, that as an old man he would beget offspring from an old and barren woman through God’s power. This is the hope of grace. I say that he believed so that he might thus become the father of many nations. By faith he believed that this would be fulfilled according to what had been said to him—that is, promised him—in Genesis: “Thus shall your seed be, like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea.” That is, they will be innumerable: the good are signified by the stars, and the evil are understood by the sand. Abraham thus believed.

[Col. 1376D]

### Verses 19–23

> “And he was not weakened in faith, nor did he consider his own body as dead, since he was already nearly a hundred years old, nor Sarah’s womb as dead. Nor did he waver in unbelief at God’s promise; rather, he was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, fully convinced that whatever God has promised, he is able also to perform. Therefore it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”

“And he was not weakened in faith.” [Haimo.] One is weakened who wavers, even though Abraham had grounds on which he might have been weakened: namely, his own old age, and Sarah’s barrenness and old age. Hence he says: “Nor did he consider [Col. 1377A] his own body to be dead” for the work of begetting children, since he was nearly a hundred years old. Likewise, he did not consider Sarah’s womb to be dead.

God did not do these and other things contrary to nature without reason. [Ambrose.] He did such things in order to remove error and show himself to be the almighty God of all things. For some, puffed up by worldly reasoning, neglected God. Therefore God did things impossible to the world, so that those who believed through these things might be saved, made servants of God’s dominion.

It should also be noted that Isaac was promised contrary to the natural process of human generation not without representing a great reality. For this signified that the Son of God would be born from a human being contrary to human nature and reason, and that through the spirit of regeneration the children of men would be brought forth from sinners as children of God, [Col. 1377B] and from mortals as immortals.

And Abraham did not merely fail to waver at the promise, but even at God’s renewed promise—that is, when the angel promised again: “At this time I shall come, and Sarah shall have a son.” Although the fulfillment of that promise was delayed, nevertheless “he did not waver in unbelief”; rather, “he was strengthened,” that is, confirmed, in faith, giving glory to God through the steadfastness of his faith, being fully convinced through deep consideration of God’s power that whatever God promised he was able to perform, just as he was able to promise; that is, he can perform it as easily as he can promise it.

The Gentiles ought to imitate this: namely, they should believe, as Abraham believed, that God can perform whatever he has promised. [Note: [Col. 1377D] Augustine, *On Correction and Grace*.] And note that he does not say “whatever he foretold” or “foreknew,” [Col. 1377C] but “whatever he promised he is able to perform,” because he himself performs everything he promises. Even if human beings do the good things which he promised, he nevertheless does it, because he causes them to do them; they do not cause him to do what he promised. [Note: [Col. 1377D] Id., *To Prosper and Hilary*.] Otherwise, the fulfillment of God’s promises would lie not in God’s power but in human power.

Therefore he promised what he himself was to do, not what human beings were to do. For he promised not on the basis of our will’s power, but on the basis of his own predestination. Appropriately, therefore, he does not say “foretold” or “foreknew.” For he can foretell and foreknow actions done by others; but he promised in order that it might be understood that he promises what he himself does. He does not promise and another perform it; that would no longer be promising, but merely foretelling.

“Therefore,” etc. As though he said: Because Abraham [Col. 1377D] was strengthened in faith, therefore his very believing was reckoned to him as righteousness. As though he said: Through believing and receiving what was promised, he was made righteous. And as though someone should say, “What has this to do with us?” he adds:

### Verses 23–25

> “But it was not written for his sake alone that it was reckoned to him as righteousness, but also for our sake, to whom it shall be reckoned, if we believe in him who raised Jesus Christ our Lord from the dead, who was delivered up for our trespasses and rose again for our justification.”

“But it was not written for his sake alone,” [Col. 1378A] that is, merely for his praise—namely, that it was reckoned to him as righteousness—but also for our instruction. Faith will be reckoned as righteousness to us if we believe in him, namely God the Father, who raised our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Haimo.] As though he said: He who did these things will benefit us. I say, he raised him “from the dead,” that is, from the tomb, which properly is the place of the dead. The Father raised the Son, and the Son himself, insofar as he is God, raised himself. The Holy Spirit likewise performed this same work.

Christ was delivered over to death by God the Father, by Judas, and by Pilate, for the removal of our trespasses, once the devil’s legal claim had been destroyed. And he rose “for our justification,” that is, that we might live righteously, which otherwise we could not have done.

[Augustine.] Note that both Christ’s death [Col. 1378B] and resurrection remove our sins, and both justify us. Nevertheless, Christ’s death alone signifies the destruction of the old life, while the new life is signified in the resurrection alone. That life begins from justification and will be perfected in immortality. Therefore, appropriately, with respect to their differing significations, he divided his words, saying: “He was delivered up for our trespasses and rose again for our justification.”

## Chapter V

### Verses 1, 2

> “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and glory in hope of the glory of the children of God.”

[Col. 1378C] He has shown that righteousness comes from the grace of faith apart from the law. Here he shows that many other goods come from the same source. As though he said: Since justification comes by faith, therefore have peace with God. As though he said: This dissension among you is against God.

[Haimo.] For the Jews and the Gentile people disputed with one another: the Jews presumptuously boasted and vaunted the merits of works of the old law, while the Gentiles did so concerning Christ’s new calling. Therefore, restraining the boastfulness of both parties, he urges them to peace; and, lest they resent this, he counts himself among them. As though he said: Since righteousness is by faith, therefore we too have been justified by faith—not by the law, nor by ourselves, that is, not because of any merit of ours preceding faith. Let us have peace with God, a peace which you Romans do not have while you arrogate to yourselves against one another. [Col. 1378D]

[Note: [Col. 1378D] Augustine, *To Pope Boniface*.] Observe that here he says, “justified by faith.” Earlier he said, “justified freely by grace.” He says this so that faith itself may not become proud and say to itself: “If by faith, how freely? For if faith earns it, why is it not repaid rather than given?” Let no faithful person say this. For when he says, “I have faith in order that I may merit justification,” the answer is given: “What have you that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4).

Therefore, when faith obtains justification, as God has apportioned to each a measure of faith, no human merit precedes God’s grace; rather, grace itself merits to be increased, so that, increased, it may merit also to be perfected—with the will accompanying, not leading; following as a handmaid, not going before. [Col. 1379A]

[Ambrose.] Therefore we are truly justified by faith, and through it let us have peace with God. For faith, not the law, makes us have peace with God. Faith reconciles us to God by removing sins, which had made us enemies.

[Cassiodorus.] The person who has peace with God is one who does not contend against his commands with an opposing will, who follows the Lord’s commands and bends his own will to every divine precept. For true peace is agreement with good morals and warfare against vices.

[Paulinus.] By contrast, the peace of this world, which is very friendly to vices, is at variance with God; Christ came not to bring it but to remove it.

I say, let us have peace with God, [Ambrose] because we have been reconciled to him through the ministry of grace, [Col. 1379B] namely through our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, through his aid and grace.

“Through whom,” etc. He enumerates the benefits received from Christ, saying: Through Christ—that is, by whose help—we have access through faith, [Haimo] that is, entrance or approach, not only to God but also into this grace, that is, into the observance of a good life, in which we stand, [Ambrose] raised up by hope of heavenly brightness. We who formerly died in Adam also glory in hope of the glory of the children of God—that is, of angels or saints. We glory in that which we hope for: the glory possessed by God’s children, namely angels or saints.

### Verses 3–5

> “And not only so, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience; patience, proof; [Col. 1379C] and proof, hope. And hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.”

“And not only so”: we glory in the hope of glory, but we also glory, through his grace, in the tribulations which we suffer for Christ and by which we go to glory. For “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven,” or of God (Acts 14). Therefore he says that one ought to glory in them. [John Damascene.] Tribulation added to hope increases the reward, and tribulation is an indication of fixed hope. For it is no great thing to glory in happy circumstances; the upright in heart glory even in tribulations, knowing the greatness of the reward. When tribulation ends, they will acquire an infinite reward. [Col. 1379D]

“Knowing,” etc. As though he said: Why do we glory? Because we know that tribulation produces patience. [Haimo.] Through the exercise of tribulation, a person is trained to steadfastness when he bravely endures torments. [Augustine.] By this the holy martyrs conquered the cruelty of tyrants. Tribulation therefore produces patience either by increasing it, or rather by displaying it.

That tribulation does not remove patience but increases it is effected by love, which is the Holy Spirit’s distinctive gift. “Patience produces proof,” that is, purification. [Note: [Col. 1379D] Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*.] The more a person endures, the purer he is made, when the faithful soul, not resisting God’s ordering, [Col. 1380A] does not love the will of the one whose malice receives power against the good, but the will of the one from whom that power is given.

Therefore, when someone understands that neither demons nor persecutors have any power except from God and endures patiently, he is proved—that is, shown to be good—and made better, like gold which is both shown to be pure by fire and made purer. This proof produces hope, that is, certainty of future glory. [Haimo, Ambrose.] For hope is the certain expectation of future glory, which seems empty to human reason but is strengthened by the testimony of power, that is, by patience or miracles. [Haimo.] For one who, amid tribulations and adversities, is found approved through patience confidently awaits the reward of future blessedness. [Col. 1380B]

[Ambrose.] This hope, although we are judged foolish and dull by unbelievers for believing things which lack worldly rationality, nevertheless does not disappoint—that is, does not make us ashamed—because it is fulfilled. For one is disappointed who does not find what he hoped for, as happens to one who hopes in a human being. But this hope does not disappoint because it is in God, who neither deceives nor can deceive, and not in a deceitful human being. For cursed is the one who places his hope in a human being.

“Because love,” etc. As though he said: I say that hope does not disappoint—that is, it is fulfilled—and it is certain that it will be fulfilled because God’s love has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit. [Augustine.] For love is not from ourselves for ourselves. This Spirit “has been given to us,” that is, it is certain from this that hope will be fulfilled, [Col. 1380C] because we already have the Holy Spirit as a pledge, by whom, with love poured into our hearts, we love God abundantly.

[Haimo.] The word “pouring out” denotes the abundance of the gift, as also in Joel: “I shall pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2). [Ambrose, Augustine.] The Holy Spirit given to us proves that God’s promise is faithful; he is the pledge that hope will be fulfilled. Observe that the Apostle leads us step by step to God’s love, which is greater than the other things. When he says that we possess it through the Spirit’s gift, he shows that all these things must be attributed to God.

[Note: [Col. 1379D] Id., *To Julian*.] Therefore, O human being, whence do you have love, unless it has been poured into your heart through the Holy Spirit? Thus, lest anyone should think that he possesses it through [Col. 1380D] his own choice, after saying, “the love of God has been poured into our hearts,” he added, “through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” [Note: [Col. 1380D] Id., *On Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit*.] Given by whom, if not by him who ascended on high—that is, to the Father? For he gave gifts to human beings (Eph. 4).

The Father’s authority, the Son’s birth, the communion of Father and Son in the Holy Spirit, and equality in the three are made known to us. Therefore, by that which is common to Father and Son, he willed us to have communion both with one another and with himself: through the one thing both possess, namely God the Holy Spirit and the gift of God. For in him we are reconciled to the Godhead and delight in it. As we speak by truth, so we love by charity, [Col. 1381A] in order that we may know more fully and, made blessed, enjoy what we know. And because sins alienated us from the possession of true goods, love was given, which “covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4).

[Note: [Col. 1381D] Augustine, in a sermon on the Ascension.] I think, therefore, that the Holy Spirit was given twice in order that the two commandments of love might be commended to us: namely, “you shall love God,” and “you shall love your neighbor.” Love is one, and the commandments are two; the Spirit is one, and the givings are two, because no love loves one’s neighbor except that which loves God. By the very love with which we love our neighbor, we love God. But because God is one thing and one’s neighbor another, although they are loved with one love, the things loved are not one.

[Note: [Col. 1381D] Id., *On the Words of the Apostle*.] Thus perhaps they are called two commandments, one greater and the other lesser. But this love, as the Apostle says, [Col. 1381B] has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. By whom is he given? By him who, as we said, gave gifts to human beings. What gifts? The Holy Spirit, who gives a gift such as he himself is.

[Note: [Col. 1382D] Id., in the book of Prosper’s *Sentences*.] Great is his mercy. He gives a gift equal to himself, because his gift is the Holy Spirit, one God, the whole Trinity. Therefore the Spirit of Father and Son pours love into our hearts; we love him together with the Father and the Son. He gave himself to us in order to be loved, he who, though not loved, loved us.

[Note: [Col. 1382D] Id., from a sermon on the Epistle of John.] He is the fountain of which Scripture says: “Let the fountain of living water be yours alone, and let no stranger share it with you.” For all who do not love God are strangers; and he is the fountain of the Holy Spirit, whom the wicked cannot receive. [Col. 1381C] Love is that which no one can possess and be evil.

Let us therefore understand that the Holy Spirit is present in love. Yet someone can possess the name of Christ, baptism, receive the Lord’s body, possess the other sacraments, and still be evil. Love, then, is the Holy Spirit’s distinctive gift and unique fountain. Observe that, by saying that love has been poured out through the Spirit who was given to us, he shows that the Spirit is both God and God’s gift.

Or “the love of God” may be understood not as the love by which we love God, but as that by which he loves us. As though he said: Hope does not disappoint because God’s love has been poured out toward us, that is, because God loves us abundantly. [Ambrose.] And we possess this in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us and causes us to understand God’s love toward us. He granted diverse languages, so that even unlearned people spoke with interpretations. Through this both our hope is confirmed and God’s love for us is commended, so that, since it is impossible for those beloved by God to be deceived, he might make us secure concerning the promise: for God is the one who promised, and he promised to those whom he wishes to have as beloved.

### Verses 6, 7

> “For why did Christ, when we were still weak, die at the appointed time for the ungodly? For scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person; [Col. 1382A] though perhaps someone may dare to die for a good person.”

“For why,” etc. He showed above that hope will be fulfilled because Christ loves us, or because through the Spirit we love him. Now he shows the same thing from Christ’s death, which is both the effect of divine love and the cause of the fulfillment of our hope. As though he said: Since God loves us, or we love him through the Holy Spirit, it is certain that hope will be fulfilled; for otherwise Christ suffered in vain.

This is the meaning: Hope truly will be fulfilled, “for”—that is, unless hope is to be fulfilled—why did Christ die? That is, why did he do so great a thing as to die? And this was “for the ungodly,” that is, for love of the ungodly. Or, “for the ungodly” means in the place of the ungodly, who deserved to die eternally because of their ungodliness. I say, for the ungodly: not those who had once been ungodly but were not then, but rather he died for us while we were ungodly.

“While we were still weak,” in sins and therefore in need of a physician, he died—and this “at the appointed time,” [Col. 1382B] that is, only for three days, because he rose on the third day.

[Ambrose, Augustine.] Therefore do not despair of the power of him whose benevolence appears in his death, and from whom we have received such pledges: he gave his death to the ungodly and preserves his life for the righteous. He died for you, O mortal human being, so that you might live with him. He took up our death so that he might grant us his life. It is more incredible that the eternal one died than that a mortal should live eternally. We already hold what is more incredible: that God died for human beings. Will a human being, then, not live with God? Will not a mortal live eternally, for whose sake he who lives eternally died?

But how did God die, and from what source can God die? He took from you that by which he might die for you. He clothed himself so that he might die for you; he will clothe you so that you may live with him. He clothed himself in mortal flesh in the virginity of his mother; he will clothe you in everlasting life in equality with the Father. [Col. 1382C]

See how you were loved when you were not lovable. You were loved while ugly and foul, before there was anything in you worthy of love. You were loved first so that you might become worthy of being loved; you were loved first so that afterward you might love the one who loved you. For you were ungodly and had deserved condemnation; yet Christ died for you.

Or, following the sequence of the words, the text may be read thus without changing the meaning: As though he said: Hope truly will be fulfilled. For unless hope is to be fulfilled, why did Christ, when we were weak, die for us ungodly persons—that is, for us who were so weak that we were even ungodly? I say, he died “at the appointed time.” The sense is: Christ did so great a thing for nothing unless our hope is to be fulfilled.

And what he did is truly great. For scarcely does anyone die—that is, rarely does anyone die even—for a righteous person, [Haimo] that is, out of love for a righteous and good person, much less for an ungodly person. I say “rarely,” because perhaps one may be found—someone who might dare to die for a good person. [Ambrose.] As though he said: It is difficult to find someone who would do this; but Christ died [Col. 1383A] for the ungodliness of a people not yet his own.

Or thus, so that a distinction is made between “righteous” and “good.” “Righteous” here means one righteous through the exercise of virtues, and such a person is also good. But there is a good person who is not righteous: namely, one born in simplicity, innocent, who has not yet labored to increase in good qualities—as are little children cleansed in baptism. The righteous person, however, has improved the good of his nature by exercise. Although the righteous person, in the sense here used, is better than the good person, the case of innocence is nevertheless more pitiable than that of righteousness, because righteousness of this sort is not without severity.

The sense is: Christ did a truly great thing in dying for the ungodly. For scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person, one who has exercised the virtues. I say, “for a righteous person”; for perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person—that is, a simple and innocent person. [Col. 1383B] By saying “scarcely” and “anyone” of the righteous person, and “perhaps” and “someone may dare” of the good person, he shows both to be difficult and rare, but one to be more difficult and rarer than the other.

### Verses 8–10

> “But God commends his love toward us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us at the appointed time. Much more, therefore, now that we have been justified by his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him. For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, once reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.”

“He commends,” etc. As though he said: Scarcely does anyone die for a righteous or good person, but Christ died for us sinners. In this God commends [Col. 1383C] his love: that is, in this his love poured out in us, though we were unworthy of it, appears more praiseworthy. For in this a great effect of the love of the Father who sent, and of the Son who came, has been displayed to us: “while we were still.”

As though he said: I say that God commends his love toward us; he certainly commends it in this, that Christ died for us while we were still sinners. That is, he commends it in that Christ died for us sinners. And if this is so, as it certainly is, then we are now justified, once forgiveness of sins has been granted, by his blood, that is, through his death. And if this is so, as it certainly is, much more shall we, now righteous, be saved through him who lives.

For it is more difficult to die for sin and remove sin than to save those already righteous and already cooperating. I say, we shall be saved from wrath—that is, from eternal punishment, [Col. 1383D] whose only cause is sin, which he has removed.

[Haimo.] Although we read in many places of God’s wrath, we must not suppose that any disturbance can arise in him who remains always the same and judges in tranquillity. Rather, his vengeance and retribution are called “wrath.”

It should be observed that the Apostle repeatedly speaks of Christ’s death in order to commend divine love, and repeatedly speaks of human weakness in order to restrain human pride. For above he said, “Christ died for the ungodly,” and here he repeats: “Christ [Col. 1384A] died for us while we were still sinners.”

[Augustine.] See: while he hated us according to our sins, he loved us insofar as we were his work, which he also made before the foundation of the world. [Note: [Col. 1383D] Augustine, *On John*.] The love by which God loves us is incomprehensible and unchangeable. He did not begin to love us only when we were reconciled to him through his Son’s blood. Rather, before the world, before we existed at all, he loved us, so that together with his Only-begotten Son we too might be his children.

Therefore, when we say that we were reconciled to God through Christ’s death, this must not be understood as though Christ reconciled us to him so that he might begin to love those whom he hated, [Augustine] as one enemy is reconciled to another so that afterward they may become friends and love one another, whereas previously they hated one another. Rather, we were reconciled to God who already loved us, though because of sin we had enmity with him. [Col. 1384B] For he had love toward us even when we exercised hostility against him by working iniquity. [Note: [Col. 1383D] Id., in the same work.]

For as it is said to him: “You hate all who work iniquity” (Ps. 5), so it is also said to him: “You hate nothing of the things which you have made” (Wis. 11). Accordingly, in a wondrous and divine manner, even when he hated us, he loved us. He hated in us what he had not made, and, because our iniquity had not wholly consumed his work, he knew in each of us both how to hate what we had done and to love what he had made. This can indeed be understood of all human beings.

Who, then, can worthily express how greatly he loves the members of his only-begotten Son, [Col. 1384C] and how much more he loves his Only-begotten himself? Thus it is not our merit but God’s mercy that is commended, because he loved us, such as we were, so greatly that he died for us while we were ungodly. This is the testimony and pledge of his love: “He who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not also, with him, give us all things?” (Rom. 8).

This indeed had to be said: how greatly he loved us, and what sort of people we were—how greatly, lest we despair and, through despair itself, fail to dare to rise toward him; what sort of people we were, lest we become proud and, puffed up over our merits, recoil farther from him and fail more deeply through reliance on our own strength.

Moreover, it should be noted that he says that we have been justified [Col. 1384D] in Christ’s blood and reconciled to God, as though he could not reconcile and justify us in any other way than through Christ’s death [Note: [Col. 1384D] Augustine, in *On the Trinity*]. Of this we say that another way was possible for God, who can do all things, but no other was more fitting for the healing of our misery.
