For what so greatly raises our minds and frees them from despair of immortality as the fact that God valued us so highly that the Son of God, remaining immutably good in himself, retaining what he was, and receiving from us and for us what he was not, deigned—without damage to his own nature—to enter into fellowship with us; that, having no evil merit of his own, he should endure our evils by dying, and should bestow his gifts [Col. 1385A] upon believers with undeserved generosity, without any merits of ours? For even those things called our good merits are his gifts. Indeed, our merits, by which we attain the highest good, are gifts of God. [Note: [Col. 1385D] Augustine, in the same work.]

There is, further, another reason why he preferred to deliver us in this way rather than another: namely, that thus, through Christ’s death, the devil is conquered by justice, not by power. I shall explain, as I am able, how this was accomplished, so that it may be clear. By a certain justice of God, the human race was handed over to the devil’s power: the sin of the first man passed originally into all born through the union of the two sexes, binding them by the debt of the first parents; consequently, all human beings are from their origin under the prince, the devil. Hence the Apostle says: “We were by nature children of wrath” (Eph. 2). [Augustine] [Col. 1385B] “By nature,” that is, nature as corrupted by sin, not as it was created in the beginning.

Yet the manner in which man was handed over to the devil’s power must not be understood as though God did this, or ordered it to be done; rather, he merely permitted it. Nevertheless, when God justly deserted the sinner, the author of sin immediately seized him. Yet God did not restrain his mercies in his wrath, nor did he lose man from the law of his own power when he permitted him to be under the devil’s power. Rather, amid penal evils, he bestowed many good things even upon the wicked; and at last, by granting remission of sins, he rescued from the devil through Christ’s blood the man whom the intercourse of sinners had subjected to the devil, so that the devil might thus be conquered by justice, not by power.

But by what justice? By that of Jesus Christ. And [Col. 1385C] how was he conquered by it? Because, although he found in Christ nothing deserving death, he nevertheless killed him. And surely it is just that those debtors whom he held should be set free if they believe in him whom he killed without any debt. He did not wish to conquer by power because the devil, through the vice of his perversity, is a lover of power and a deserter and assailant of justice. Human beings especially imitate him in this: neglecting justice, or even hating it, they strive more after power, and either rejoice in obtaining it or burn with desire for it. Therefore it pleased God that, conquering not by power but by justice, he should rescue man, so that man might learn to imitate him in this. Afterwards, however, power followed in the resurrection. Therefore justice came first, and power afterwards. He conquered the devil by justice, because he had no sin [Col. 1385D] and was killed by that most unjust being; by power, because he rose again from the dead, never thereafter to die.

But would not Christ most justly conquer the devil if he had wished to deal with him by power alone? Certainly. But Christ set aside what he could do, in order first to do what he ought to do. For this purpose he had to be both man and God. For unless he were man, he could not be killed; unless he were God, it would not be believed that he had willingly done what he could do, but rather that he had been unable to do what he wished. Therefore the justice of humility set man free—man whom power alone could most justly have set free.

For if those three—God, [Col. 1386A] man, and the devil—were to come into court, what could the devil and man say against God? They would have nothing at all, and would utterly fail in the conduct of the case. For the devil would be convicted of having injured God, because he both deceitfully led away and violently held God’s servant, that is, man. Man too would be convicted of having injured God, because he despised God’s commands and, enslaving himself to another lord, inflicted upon himself the loss of his own servitude. The devil likewise would be convicted of having injured man, because he first deceived him by promising good things and afterwards harmed him by inflicting evils.

Therefore the devil held man unjustly, so far as the devil himself was concerned; yet man was justly held, because the devil never deserved to have power over man, whereas man deserved through guilt to suffer the devil’s tyranny. If, therefore, [Col. 1386B] God, who certainly presided over the matter, had wished to free man by power, he could most justly have freed man by the force of his command alone. But for the reason stated above, he preferred to employ the justice of humility; hence he gave up his Son to death for us, through which we have been justified and reconciled to God.

[Augustine] This is the price of our reconciliation, which Christ offered to God the Father so that he might be propitiated—not because he did not previously love us, since out of that love he gave up his Son for us; nor was the Son given up for us as though the Father did not spare him and he himself were unwilling, when it is said of him: “He gave himself.” Therefore the Father and the Son, and the Spirit of both, work this, as also all other things, together and in harmony.

But if God loved us beforehand, how are we reconciled to him through Christ’s death and delivered from wrath? To this we reply that the wrath of God, who judges with tranquility, is nothing other than just vengeance. [Note: [Col. 1386D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*.] If, then, just divine vengeance has received such a name, God’s reconciliation is rightly understood when such wrath comes to an end—namely, when we are absolved from liability to punishment. For we were enemies to God only in the way that sins are enemies to justice; and therefore, once sins are forgiven, such enmities come to an end, and those whom he himself justifies are reconciled to the Just One.

For the devil held our sins, and through them rightfully drove us toward death; but that blood had such power that Christ’s undeserved death freed from the eternal death owed by them those human beings whom he nevertheless certainly loved even as enemies. Hence it rightly follows: “For if through the death of the Son”—as if he were [Col. 1386D] saying: Truly, now living, he will be able to save those made friends. “For,” that is, because we were reconciled to God, [Augustine] though formerly we were justly under the devil’s power, our nature corrupted by sin. Understand: reconciled through the death of his Son, “while we were still enemies,” not sinners in just any sense. And if this is so, as it certainly is, then much more, being reconciled, we shall be [Ambrose] not only delivered from wrath but also saved—and this “in his life,” that is, through his life, namely because he rose from the dead.

And the sense is: From this it is certain that, living, he will be able to save his friends, because, dead, he was able to justify; once this was accomplished, those who were enemies through sin were reconciled. For they are friends of God. [Augustine] [Col. 1387A] And note that he says here, “reconciled through death,” what he said above, “justified in blood.” I say: we shall be saved.

VERS. 11.—“And not only so, but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.”

Not only shall we be saved, but we also glory already in hope concerning what we shall be in God—that is, the same as God in the future, not by nature but by love and will, because we shall love or will nothing except what God wills. Or we glory in the present, not in ourselves but in God, and this not through ourselves but through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have already now, in the present, received reconciliation to God, from whom we departed when Adam sinned.

[Col. 1387B] VERS. 12, 13.—“Therefore, as through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death, and thus death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned. For until the law sin was in the world.”

“Therefore, as.” [Ambrose] Above he said that through Christ the reconciler there are justice and life, and that this can be through him. He intends to prove this by an argument from the lesser, that is, by what is similar and less. For as through Adam, a mere man, came sin and death, so through Christ, man and God, justice and life can come. And because through Adam there came sin and death, much more through Christ can there be justice and life; so that, since the one Adam sinned in all, the one Christ, the Son of God, might conquer sin [Col. 1387C] in all.

[Note: [Col. 1387D] Augustine, book XIII of *On the Trinity*.] Therefore the Apostle here discusses at greater length two men: the first Adam, through whose sin we his descendants were bound, as it were, by hereditary evils; and the second Adam, through whom, by paying for us what he did not owe, we were freed from debts both ancestral and personal. Therefore, because through that one man the devil held all who were carnally begotten through his corrupted flesh in concupiscence, it is just that through this one man he should release all who are spiritually regenerated through his immaculate grace.

And this is what he says: “Therefore, as,” and so forth. Attend to the wording in such a way that the order of the argument from the lesser and from similarity may be made evident; as though he were saying: I say that through Christ are justice and life; and therefore [Col. 1387D] through Christ justice and life proceed to all who are regenerated by his grace—understand this—because through one man, namely Adam, from whom we are propagated, original sin entered into this miserable world on account of that same sin, that is, into all human beings.

[Note: [Col. 1387D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*.] He called the whole human race “the world.” For as they are from that one man, so they cannot be immune from that same sin unless they are absolved from its guilt through Christ’s baptism. [Note: [Col. 1387D] Augustine, in reply to Hilary’s inquiry.] See: he has proved this from the lesser. Now let the same point be shown and read from similarity, as though what had been omitted were supplied: as though he were saying, “Thus through the one Christ there are justice [Col. 1388A] and life, just as through one man sin entered into this world.” And the sense is not changed.

“And through sin, death,” [Ambrose] that is, the separation of soul and body, entered into Adam himself. And thus, through him, death passed into all human beings begotten through his corrupted flesh.

[Origen] The question is asked why the Apostle says that sin entered the world through one man, rather than through one woman, when the beginning of sin came from the woman, and before that from the serpent, or the devil. To this we reply that in these matters the Apostle followed customary usage, attributing to the man, not the woman, the succession of human posterity that succumbed to sin and the death arising from it. For posterity is customarily named not from the woman but from the man; and for this reason [Col. 1388B] mortal and bodily posterity is assigned rather to the man as author than to the woman.

[Note: [Col. 1388D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] Or because the woman is from the man, and the two are one flesh; therefore, whether it is said to be from the woman or from Adam, either expression refers to the first human being. Furthermore, it should be known that certain heretics called Pelagians said that the sin of the first transgression passed into other human beings not by propagation but by imitation. Hence they are unwilling to believe that original sin is remitted through baptism in infants, maintaining that there is absolutely none in those being born.

But if the Apostle had wished sin to be understood as sin by imitation, not propagation, he would have assigned as its leader not Adam but the devil, concerning whom it is said in the book of Wisdom: “Through the devil’s envy death entered into [Col. 1388C] the world” (Wis. 2). And because Scripture does not wish this to be understood as having occurred by propagation but by imitation, it immediately adds: “But those who belong to his party imitate him” (*ibid.*). Certainly all who transgress God’s command through disobedience imitate Adam. But one thing is an example for persons who sin voluntarily; another is an origin for persons born with sin.

For the saints imitate Christ in pursuing justice; yet beyond this imitation, his grace works our illumination and justification inwardly as well, and incorporates even baptized infants into his body, though they are not yet capable of imitating anyone. Therefore, as Christ, beyond the example of imitation, also gives believers some utterly hidden grace of his Spirit, which he secretly pours even into infants, so Adam, beyond the example of imitation, also infected within himself all who were to come from his stock with the hidden contagion of his fleshly concupiscence.

Hence he rightly adds: “In whom all sinned”; as though he were saying: Death rightly entered all through him, because through [Col. 1388D] him the cause of death entered all, namely sin. [Augustine] And this is “in whom,” namely Adam, all sinned as in their material source, not merely by his example, as some say. [Note: [Col. 1388D] Augustine, *ibid.*] For all of them had been that one man; that is, we drew original sin from him, who was the origin and material source of us all, from whom we descend according to the succession of propagation through fleshly concupiscence.

Or, “in which sin all sinned”: the Apostle said this carefully, properly, and without ambiguity—“in which they sinned”—whether “in whom,” namely the man, or “in which,” namely the sin, is understood; for the matter is clear. For there are other, personal sins, in which only those whose sins they are commit sin; but this is the one sin in which all sinned when all had been that one man. It is thus evident that all sinned in Adam, as it were in a mass. [Ambrose] Since he himself was corrupted by sin, all whom he begot were born under sin. From him, therefore, all are sinners, “until the law.”

[Note: [Col. 1389D] Augustine, *Against Julian*.] And as though someone were to ask: “Sin passed into all [Col. 1389B]; what then did the law accomplish? Could it not reconcile them so that sin would not pass into all?” “No,” he says; for until the written or natural law—that is, under the law—even original and actual sin was in the world, that is, in humankind. [Haimo] [Note: [Col. 1389D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] For neither law could take sin away, but increased it: whether the natural law, in which each person, once using reason, begins to add personal sins to original sin; or the written law, given through Moses to the people, which entered in so that transgression might abound. [Note: [Col. 1389D] Augustine, in reply to Hilary.]

Therefore the Apostle does not say that sin was in the world until the law in the sense that thereafter it existed in no one, but because what could be accomplished only by the Spirit of grace could not be removed by the letter of the law—lest anyone, trusting in his own powers, should think that free will could suffice for the law and should deride Christ’s grace.

VERS. 13, 14.—“But sin was not imputed when there was no law; yet death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a figure of the one to come.”

“But sin”; [Augustine] as though he were saying: Sin was in the world, but people did not impute it because they were blind. And this is what is meant: “Sin was not imputed,” [Note: [Col. 1389D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] that is, it was unknown and was not thought by human beings to be sin. I do not mean by God, by whose judgment those who sinned without law will perish without law. I say it was not imputed when there was no law to prohibit sin.

[Note: [Col. 1390D] Augustine, in reply to Hilary.] He does not say that sin [Col. 1389D] did not exist, but that it was not imputed, because there was neither the law of reason in an infant nor the law of the letter among the people to rebuke and reveal sin. “But death reigned,” and so forth. [Haimo] As though sin was not imputed before the law, yet death—that is, sin or condemnation—reigned from Adam until Moses, [Note: [Col. 1390D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] and until the law divinely promulgated through Moses, because even that law could not remove the reign of death.

By the reign of death he means the condition in which the guilt of sin is so condemned in human beings that it does not allow them to come to eternal life, which is truly life, but draws them to the second death, eternally penal, that is, to Gehenna. This reign of death is destroyed in each person only by the Savior’s grace, which also worked in the saints of old. Before Christ came in the flesh, they belonged to his assisting grace, not to the letter of the law, which merely commands and does not assist. For what is now revealed in the New Testament was hidden in the Old Testament by the most just dispensation of the times.

Death reigned over all except those assisted by Christ’s grace. It reigned, I say, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression—that is, who did not sin by their own personal will as Adam did, but were bound by the original fault which they drew from him and by which they would be drawn to condemnation [Col. 1390B] unless they were assisted by Christ’s grace. [Note: [Col. 1390D] Augustine, *Against Julian*.]

And note that by saying “until the law,” or “until Moses,” he includes the time in question, because even then—that is, under the law—there were sin and death, that is, condemnation. [Note: [Col. 1390D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] It should indeed be known that most Latin manuscripts read thus: “Death reigned from Adam until Moses over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.” Those who read it this way also refer it to the preceding interpretation: they take those who sinned “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” to be those who sinned in him, so as to be created like him—namely, as human beings come from a human being, so sinners from a sinner, dying persons from a mortal, and those to be condemned from one condemned. But the Greek manuscripts, from which the translation into Latin was made, all or nearly all contain the reading [Col. 1390C] first set forth.

Or, leaving the rest unchanged, the passage may be read from that point in this way: “But death reigned,” and this is understood of bodily death; as though he were saying: Sin was not imputed, that is, it was unknown before the law, but its effect showed itself, because bodily death reigned daily through various sufferings and finally by dissolution, from Adam until Moses, though it appeared less plainly. It reigned, I say, not only over those who seemed to have earned death by personally transgressing, but also over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression—that is, over children, who added nothing of their own by transgressing the law.

Or thus, from the words “until the law,” and so forth: [Ambrose] as though he were saying: I rightly said that sin passed into all, for—that is, because—[Col. 1390D] until the law, that is, even before the law, sin was in the world, though it did not appear so because the law did not teach it. I say sin was in the world; but sin was not imputed before God when there was no law. Sin was indeed imputed among human beings, but not before God, before whom it was thought that it would go unpunished because people did not know that he would exact punishment. For people maintained that God was unconcerned, and that therefore sins would go unpunished before him, though not before other people. For the natural law had not wholly grown numb, because they did not fail to know that they ought not to do to others what they did not wish to suffer themselves.

Indeed, sin was so far from unknown among human beings that Joseph, though through a false accusation, was then shut up in prison as though guilty, as were Pharaoh’s baker and cupbearer. Therefore sin was not imputed when there was no law—not, I say, among human beings, but before God. But when the law was given, they knew that God cared for human affairs and judged them.

“But death reigned”: as though he were saying, before the law sin was not imputed, but death reigned, the devil securely possessing human souls because of the supposed impunity. For, believing that they sinned with impunity, people sinned more, becoming readier for these certain sins, which the world nourished as though lawful. Satan rejoiced at this, secure in the thought that he possessed the man abandoned by God because of Adam’s cause. Death reigned, I say, from Adam [Col. 1391B] until Moses, through whom the knowledge of the one God returned, since through him the law was given in which worship of the one God was commanded.

Death therefore reigned until Moses—that is, until the law—because even then a remedy was given to human beings by which they could be freed. Yet, if under that law they were like Adam in transgression, death would reign over them. But the law was given at the beginning of the departure from Egypt, teaching concerning the one God, so that death—that is, the devil or sin—might not reign; and the reign of death first began to be destroyed in Judaea. But now it is destroyed everywhere through Christ’s grace.

And note here that “until” is to be understood exclusively: “over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.” Another text does not read *even* and *not*; as though he were saying: Death reigned until Moses, yet not over all, but over those [Col. 1391C] who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, that is, those like Adam the transgressor: namely, those who, neglecting the Creator, served the creature, establishing gods for themselves whom they might worship to God’s injury, just as Adam consented to the devil in God’s place.

For Adam’s sin is not far removed from idolatry. Despising the Creator’s command and consenting to the devil’s persuasion, he set the devil up as though in God’s place, and wished to be like God. But there were persons who sinned without abandoning God: anyone who understood God, whether through tradition or the indication of nature, and worshipped him, granting no one else the honor due to his name and majesty—if such a person sinned, since it was impossible not to sin—sinned under God, not against God. Therefore death did not reign over them, but over [Col. 1391D] those who sinned in Adam’s likeness, that is, those who served the devil under the appearance of idols.

Nearly all were such until the law; very few, such as Abraham, served the one God, and death did not reign over them, because after this death, called the first, they did not come to the second, which punishes eternally. Rather, they were kept in hope to be liberated at Christ’s coming. Thus we read of Abraham that, although he was set apart in the underworld, he was nevertheless at a great distance from sinners, so that a vast chasm lay between the righteous and sinners (Luke 16).

And it should be known that Ambrose says that texts with the other reading are corrupt, namely where it is written that death reigned even [Col. 1392A] over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression. This reading is also found in Greek manuscripts. Some understand it thus: they say that bodily death reigned over worshippers of the one God, even until Moses; but why not until the end of the age? Yet there are certain Latin manuscripts, known to have been translated from ancient Greek copies, which read, as it were, “over those who sinned,” and so forth. The simplicity of earlier times preserved and approves these as uncorrupted.

But afterward, when minds had fallen from agreement and heretics began to stir up controversy, many things in both Greek and Latin manuscripts were altered by heretics out of contentious zeal. For when they cannot use their own authority to prevail, they corrupt the words of the law so as to assert their own meaning as though it were the law’s wording, and to resist those who contradict them as though by authority.

“Who is a figure,” that is, a likeness, “of the one to come,” namely Christ, who was still future with respect to Adam at that time. Adam is called a figure of the one to come, that is, of Christ, because God had already then decreed in mystery—that is, secretly arranged—that through the one Christ he would repair what had sinned through the one Adam. Hence it is said in the Apocalypse: “The Lamb was slain from the foundation of the world.” And he is called a figure of the one to come, that is, of Christ, by contrast: because as all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ (1 Cor. 15). As that happens in the former, so this happens in the latter. [Note: [Col. 1391D] Augustine, *Against Julian the Heretic*. John, *On …* [uncertain].]

But this figure is not conformable in every respect, as is subsequently shown. Or he is called a figure of Christ because, as Adam was made by God without intercourse, [Col. 1392C] so Christ proceeded from the Virgin through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit. Or Adam is called a figure of Christ because, as he is father of all according to the flesh, so Christ is father of all according to faith. And as a rib was taken from the side of Adam while he slept, from which Eve was formed, so from Christ’s side flowed the sacraments—namely, the water of washing and the blood of redemption—through which the Church is saved.

[Remigius] Therefore, as Adam was able to communicate sin and death to his children, so Christ is able to communicate his justice and life to his own; and Christ also bestows more good upon his own than Adam inflicted evil upon his. Therefore he can save more than Adam could destroy. And this is what follows.

[Col. 1392D] VERS. 15, 16.—“But the gift is not like the transgression. For if many died through the transgression of one, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound unto many; and the gift is not like that which came through one sin: for judgment indeed came from one transgression unto condemnation, but grace from many transgressions unto justification.”

“But not as.” As though he were saying: Adam is a figure of Christ, that is, Christ and Adam are alike; but Adam’s transgression is not like Christ’s gift—that is, Christ’s gift is greater than Adam’s transgression. Therefore Adam’s sin is not as effective for condemnation [Col. 1393A] as Christ’s grace is for salvation. That is to say: their causes are not equal, nor are the effects of their causes equal. This is shown there.

“And not as through one”; but first he states what proves that the causes of Adam and Christ are unequal, saying: “For if through one”; as though he were saying: Christ’s gift is truly not like Adam’s transgression, because Adam’s transgression is one, through which many died, while Christ’s grace is manifold, through which many have been made alive. But if one transgression could put many to death, it is evident that manifold grace can much more make alive.

For Christ’s cause is abounding grace, from which come all good things to a human being, and without which one has no good. Adam’s cause is that original sin, of which all carnally begotten persons are guilty; [Note: [Col. 1393D] Augustine, in reply to Hilary.] they have many other sins from themselves, even though from that original sin they are more prone to sin. Furthermore, the form of death from Adam also has temporal force upon those redeemed through Christ; but the form of life through Christ will have eternal force. Thus, although Adam is a figure of the one to come, Christ nevertheless confers more upon the regenerate than Adam had harmed them when begotten.

And this cause of Christ rightly benefits all his own, because if Adam’s cause harmed all his own, then this cause also could benefit its own. And this is “for if,” and so forth; as though he were saying: The gift is truly not like the transgression. “For,” that is, because through the one transgression of the one man Adam—one transgression indeed, although Adam himself committed more than one—he transmitted to his descendants only one original sin. Many, namely all his children carnally begotten from him, [Col. 1393C] died, that is, were made sinners; yet then the grace of God and the gift—that is, the free gift; or grace, namely remission of sins, and the gift, namely the other gifts of the Holy Spirit—abounded much more, that is, passed over in much greater abundance, unto many, that is, all Christ’s children.

This gift is given “in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ,” that is, through Christ’s grace. [Haimo] By “grace” he means the perfection of virtues that was in Christ the man, who in his goodness grants us from his fullness. [Note: [Col. 1393D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] And note that “many” is not placed comparatively here, but absolutely, as though he had said “a great many.” For more are not justified through Christ than are condemned through Adam; rather, “abounded much more” must be said in such a way that Christ’s gift is compared with and preferred to Adam’s transgression.

For Adam, through one transgression, begot many as guilty; but Christ’s grace loosed and forgave even the sins of their own will which they added to the original guilt in which they were born. Therefore Christ’s cause is greater than Adam’s cause. And now he shows that the effects of the causes are unequal; as though he were saying: Not only are the causes unequal, but the effects also. And this is because it does not happen through one sin as it happens through the gift; rather, more is accomplished through the gift, [Col. 1394A] and he proves this.

For God’s judgment proceeds from only the one original transgression derived from Adam unto the condemnation of bodily and eternal death. But Christ’s grace proceeds, not from one transgression only, but from many transgressions unto justification, because it not only pardons but also justifies. [Note: [Col. 1394D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*.] And attend to the statement, “judgment from one unto condemnation.” This was not said because only what is drawn originally is to be condemned in judgment, but because even that alone, if it alone exists, produces condemnation.

Christ’s grace, however, remits not only what is drawn originally but also many actual sins, and in addition justifies—that is, makes the ungodly godly, and thereafter makes one advance from good to better. See: in these things he has shown that the effects of Christ’s and Adam’s causes are unequal. The effect of Adam’s cause, that is, of the sin which he introduced, is not every condemnation, but that which is owed for that one sin. For there are other condemnations arising from our added sins. But the effect of Christ’s gifts, after every original and actual sin has been removed, is complete justification and eternal life, of which he adds in the following verse:

VERS. 17.—“For if through the transgression of one death reigned through one, much more shall those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of justice reign in life through the one Jesus Christ.”

“For if”; as though he were saying: Christ’s grace proceeds unto justification, and this is well for his own through the one Christ; because if that—that is, condemnation—belongs to Adam’s own through one Adam, then Christ’s grace could also accomplish this for its own. And it truly can, because it also leads to eternal life. And rightly so. [Augustine] “For,” that is, because through the transgression of one, even if personal sins were not added, death—that is, the separation of soul and body—reigned, inflicting sufferings even before death, through the one Adam. For it exercised in all his descendants the power it had in him, whose material source he was, just as the guilt was his alone, though it was transmitted to all.

And those human beings, receiving from God and not possessing from themselves the abundance of grace—that is, remission of sins—[Haimo] “abundance” because personal sins too are forgiven—and the abundance of gifts, that is, charisms, and of justice, that is, good action, shall much more reign through the one Jesus Christ in [Col. 1394D] eternal life. [Augustine] That is, they shall reign eternally in incorruption. He says “much more” that these reign, because this is a much greater thing than the reign of death. Or they shall reign in life much more than death reigned in them, because in life they shall reign eternally, whereas death reigned in them temporarily and with an end.

VERS. 18, 19.—“Therefore, as through the transgression of one came condemnation unto all human beings, so also through the justice of one came justification of life unto all human beings. For as through the disobedience of the one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of the one [Col. 1395A] man many shall be made just.”

Therefore, “as through the trespass of one,” etc. From what has been said he draws the conclusion of his argument, bringing it to the same point which he had proposed: since Adam is a figure of Christ who was to come, and since Christ’s gift is greater and confers more, therefore, “as,” that is, in a proportionate manner, “through the trespass of one,” passing—not by imitation, but by propagation—“to all human beings,” a sentence went forth from man, or God’s judgment proceeded, unto condemnation of body and soul; so also, “through the righteousness of one,” which is efficacious, “to all human beings,” if they themselves are willing, a sentence went forth from man, or God’s judgment proceeded, unto justification, which is the cause of life. [Note: [Col. 1395D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.]

Observe that the Apostle, seeing that people become sinners not by Adam’s imitation alone but by propagation, and that they are justified not by Christ’s imitation alone [Col. 1395B] but by spiritual regeneration, said “all” and “all”—not because all who are begotten through Adam are regenerated through Christ, but because, just as no one’s carnal generation is except through Adam, so no one’s spiritual regeneration is except through Christ. If some had been begotten apart from Adam, or if some had been regenerated apart from Christ, he would not have said “all” and “all.” Just as no human being exists apart from that generation, so no righteous person exists apart from this regeneration. For no one is born except in carnal concupiscence, which has been drawn from the first human being; and no one is reborn except by spiritual grace, which was given through the second human being.

Afterward he calls these same persons “many,” though in another sense. Beginning from the passage, “But not as the trespass,” etc., he had said that [Col. 1395C] Adam is a figure of the one to come. He is a figure in this respect: one person remedies what one person sinned. Yet Adam’s causality is not such as Christ’s causality, because Adam’s trespass is one, through which many—that is, those transgressing in the same way—died; but Christ’s grace passes to more, because it reaches both these persons and those who did not transgress in the same way.

Observe that he is here dealing with Adam’s actual sin. In it he says that those died who actually sinned after Adam’s likeness. And “more” is to be read comparatively, as though he said: Truly, the gift is not like the trespass. For if, through the trespass of one, those died who imitated his transgression, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man, Christ Jesus, abound unto more. For more attain grace through Christ [Col. 1395D] than died through Adam’s trespass: through it died those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression; but Christ’s grace abounded both to those who sinned in the same manner and to those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.

For grace abounded both to many who, disregarding God, served the creature—so that, when departing this life, they might not be overtaken by the second death—and to worshippers of the one God, who by God’s sentence were held in the lower regions because of ancestral sin. In the Savior’s descent it abounded, granting pardon to all in triumph and raising them to heaven.

And the result is not through one sin in the same way as it is through the gift. For God’s judgment proceeds from one sin unto condemnation, whereas grace proceeds from many sins unto justification of life. The difference, therefore, is clear: through Adam’s one sin, those like him were condemned; but grace justified people not from one sin but from many sins, and even brought them to life—which it was well able to do. For, that is, because through the trespass of one man death reigned through one—namely, the devil or sin.

Observe that he says, “death reigned,” not “reigns,” in agreement with the earlier interpretation, where he said that death had reigned until Moses. For those who, through the Law, had fear of God because they knew his judgment were removed from death’s dominion. But before this, while there was no fear of God on earth without the Law, death prevailed over those like Adam. And if death reigned there, much more shall human beings [Col. 1396B] who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift and of righteousness reign in life through the one Lord Jesus Christ. That is, grace ought much more to reign, since it has passed to more persons than death and bestows eternal life.

But when he subsequently says “all,” he means those sinning in the same way. Again, he means all believers; and this is what he adds:

[Ambrose] Therefore, if through one person’s trespass, passing to all human beings, sin unto condemnation came upon those sinning in the same way, so also through the righteousness of one, passing to all believing human beings, justification unto life came. For condemnation or justification is not universal in all. Hence he afterward says, “Many, for as,” etc.

Here he now defines the trespass of the one, so that, as the former by the merit of sin lost, so the latter by the merit of righteousness may be seen to have delivered us. He here explains the order of exposition which he had begun above—namely, in what way Adam is a figure of the one to come—saying:

For as through the disobedience of one man, namely Adam, many were made sinners—that is, all who belong to him and are not Christ’s—so also, and deservedly, through the obedience of one man, namely Christ, many shall be made righteous—that is, all who belong to him.

And observe that he does not say that people are justified through the obedience of the one God or Word, but through the obedience of the one man, lest you suppose that the righteous of old were delivered by the Word of God alone—that is, by faith in the Word alone, without faith in the Incarnation—without which neither the ancients nor the moderns could be delivered. [Note: [Col. 1396D] Augustine, *To Optatus*.]

For this is the sound faith by which we believe that no human being, whether of mature [Col. 1396D] or tender age, is delivered from the contagion of ancient death and from the obligation of sin contracted in first birth, except through the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. By the most saving faith in this man, who is also God, even those righteous persons were saved who, before he came in the flesh, believed that he would come in the flesh.

For their faith and ours are the same. Therefore, since all righteous persons—that is, true worshippers of God, whether before or after the Incarnation—neither lived nor live except by faith in Christ’s Incarnation, and since it is consequently written that there is no other name under heaven in which we must be saved, this faith has availed for the salvation of [Col. 1397A] the human race from the time when it was corrupted in Adam.

That one man sent one sin into the world; but this one man removed not only that one sin, but all that he found added to it. Thus it has been shown how Christ’s grace surpasses Adam’s trespass: it releases not only original sin propagated from Adam, but also the actual sins mentioned above; and it grants righteousness and life. Before this grace works in a person, that person belongs to himself and is unbelieving. For by faith the ungodly person is justified. Thus, just as an adult is justified through the power of faith, so an infant is justified through the sacrament of faith: that is, from ungodly he becomes godly, and from unbelieving, believing.

[Note: [Col. 1397D] Augustine, *Against Julian the Heretic*.] But Julian asks how sin is found in an infant, saying: “This one who is born does not sin; the one who begot him does not sin; the one who believed does not sin. [Col. 1397B] Through what cracks, then, amid so many safeguards of innocence, do you imagine sin has entered?”

Holy Scripture answers him: “Through one man,” says the Apostle, “sin entered into the world”; “through the disobedience of one,” says the Apostle. What more does he seek? What could be plainer? What could be more emphatically stated? Why seek a hidden crack when he has a most open door?

Again he says: “If sin entered into the world through a human being, sin is either from the will or from nature. If it is from the will, the will that produces sin is evil; if it is from nature, nature is evil.” I answer him: Sin is from the will. Perhaps it is asked whether original sin comes from the will. I answer: indeed original sin is from the will, because it was sown by the will [Col. 1397C] of the first human being, so that it was in him and passed into all.

But as for his statement, “If sin is from nature, then nature is evil,” I ask him to answer, if he can. It is manifest that all evil works, like evil fruits, arise from an evil will, as from an evil tree; but from what will he say that the evil will itself arose, if not from good? If from an angel, what is an angel except a good work of God? If from a human being, what was that human being except a good work of God? Indeed, what were these two before an evil will arose in them, except God’s good work, and a good and praiseworthy nature? Therefore evil arises from good, and there was nothing in a human being from which it could arise except good. I say, therefore, that no evil preceded the evil will.

Again he says: “If nature is God’s work, the devil’s work is not allowed to pass through God’s work.” But was not the devil’s work, when it first existed in the angel who became the devil, produced in God’s work? Therefore, if evil, which was altogether nowhere, could arise in God’s work, why could evil, which already existed somewhere, not pass through God’s work? Human beings, moreover, are God’s work.

[Note: [Col. 1397D] The same, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] Therefore the devil’s work passed through God’s work; and because the devil is God’s creature or work, the work of God’s work passed through God’s work and came even to infants, who [Col. 1398A] committed nothing in the branch but perished in the root. They have no evil except what they drew from the spring, except what they drew from their origin. [Note: [Col. 1397D] The same, *On the Spirit and the Letter*.] Thus destruction was common, and discovery is common. For as through Adam’s disobedience many shall be made sinners by guilt, so through Christ’s obedience many shall be made righteous.

VERS. 20, 21.—“But the Law entered in, that the trespass might abound; but where the trespass abounded, grace superabounded, so that, as sin reigned unto death, so grace also might reign through righteousness unto eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

But the Law. He had shown that Christ forgives all sins, both original and actual. Here he adds [Col. 1398B] that he also delivers from the sin of the Law and from transgression, so that the Jews may be more indebted to Christ. [Note: [Col. 1397D] The same, *To Eutropius and Paulinus*.] As though he said: Justification is through Christ; but the Law of Moses entered in—that is, entered secretly—after original and actual guilt, or after natural law, in order that the trespass might abound. That is, so that a person, proudly trusting in his own powers, might receive commandments in which, failing, he also became a transgressor; and so might seek a deliverer and savior, while fear of the Law, like a pedagogue, might lead him to faith and grace in the Savior thus made humble.

It was necessary, therefore, that the Law be given to the proud, who presumed upon the freedom of their own will, so that, having transgressed it and understood their own weakness and the insufficiency of the Law, which does not consume sin, they might be humbled and run to [Col. 1398C] grace coming to their aid.

[Note: [Col. 1398D] Augustine, *On John*.] For to those born in sins and attributing much to their own strength, God gives the Law to tame pride—the pride by which they said, “There is no lack of someone to fulfil it; there is a lack only of someone to command it.” Therefore, desiring to tame their pride, God gave the Law, as though saying to human beings: “See, I give you commandments, lest you think that the one who commands is lacking; it is not one to command that is lacking, [Note: [Col. 1398D] The same, *On Psalm 102*.] but one to fulfil it. For a person born in sins cannot fulfil it; therefore Christ was born—that is, the grace which heals.”

Accordingly, by this dispensation the Law was given so that, as sin increased, the proud might be humbled; humbled, they might confess; and, confessing, might be healed. God did this not cruelly but with the design of a physician. A person sometimes seems healthy to himself but is ill; and because he does not feel the illness, he does not seek a physician. The illness worsens, the distress increases, a physician is sought, and the whole body is healed.

[Note: [Col. 1398D] The same, *To Hilary*.] Thus it was God’s great purpose that trespass should abound through the Law, so that, recognizing their own weakness in the severity of the Law, the weak might flee to the physician and seek the help of grace.

[Note: [Col. 1398D] The same, from the prologue to the Epistle to the Romans.] Trespass is said to have abounded through the Law, not because the Law commanded trespass, but because, since grace was not there, prohibition increased desire; and then, by a seeming power of its own, it became a great vice. [Col. 1399A] Thus sin abounded, because concupiscence was made more ardent by prohibition, and the charge of transgression was added to those sinning against the Law.

God’s purpose in giving the Law, however, was unknown to the Jews, as he sufficiently indicated by this expression, “the Law entered in,” etc. Or thus: “The Law entered in that trespass might abound,” that is, when the Law was given, trespass abounded. For the Apostle is here saying what resulted from the Law’s being given, not what the Law did. The Law was given to help nature, so that, because seeds of righteousness are in some way implanted in nature itself, the Law might be added, by whose authority and instruction natural capacity might advance to produce the fruit of righteousness.

[Ambrose] For just as birth perishes unless it has nourishment by which, being sustained, it may grow up, so too natural capacity for righteousness, unless it has [Col. 1399B] something to look to and reverence, does not easily advance, but languishes and yields to sins that come upon it. For through the habit of wrongdoing it is pressed down, lest it grow into fruit, and is thereby extinguished. Therefore the Law was given providently and for good; but the people, following their old practice, multiplied their sins. By that very practice they began to sin more than they had sinned before; and thus it came about that, with the Law given, sins were not diminished but abounded, the devil turning the good Law into evil, against which God forgave everything, as is shown subsequently.

Or thus: “The Law entered in that trespass might abound,” that is, it was given so that trespass might be known more abundantly through it.

[Note: [Col. 1399D] Augustine, *On Luke*.] For if the Law had not existed, sin would have lain hidden; but through the Law the human being came to know the kinds of sins and the charge of transgression, so that one who was in filth through transgression might become more filthy—that is, might recognize himself as filthy.

[Ambrose] Therefore the Law is the author of good. The ugliness of the human being’s sickness had to be shown, so that he might see that he needed not only a teacher but also a helper.

[Note: [Col. 1399D] The same, *On the Spirit and the Letter*.] Furthermore, the Law was given so that the mediocre might have a pedagogue, the perfect a sign, and the hard might feel the lash. And because a substantial discussion of the Law arises here, we must see in what senses “Law” is understood; to what people it was given; why it was given to them and not to others; to which persons among that people, and for which of them, it was given; and finally, for what reasons it was given. This must be stated briefly.

Thus “Law” sometimes means the whole Scripture of the Old Testament; sometimes the Scripture of Moses’ five books; sometimes the Decalogue written upon tablets; sometimes only ceremonial observances—that is, things figurative according to the letter; sometimes the letter together with spiritual understanding; sometimes the observance of a particular commandment. Thus the same Law often says: “This is the law of Passover”; “this is the law of leprosy”; “this is the law of burnt offerings”; and the like. Hence the holy writers, speaking variously about the Law, seem to disagree and to say contradictory things.

For the Lord says through Ezekiel: “I gave them commandments not good, and ordinances not good, by which they shall not live” (Ezek. 20). The Apostle agrees with this, [Col. 1400A] saying: “The Law brought no one to perfection” (Heb. 7); and again: “The Law works wrath.” [Bede] And here: “The Law entered in that trespass might abound,” etc. (Rom. 4). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Unless your righteousness abounds more than that of the scribes and Pharisees,” etc. (Matt. 5).

But these other statements seem contrary to them: the righteousness of the Law, when kept in its own time, conferred not only temporal goods but also eternal life. And the Apostle says: “So then, the Law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good” (Rom. 12). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “I did not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfil it” (Matt. 5).

Therefore, in order that it may be clear that these statements, though they appear so, are not contrary, we must understand that they are said according to different senses of “Law.” When it says, “I gave them commandments not good, and ordinances not good by which they shall not live,” this must be understood of the commands of legal ceremonies. They are called “not good,” not because they were evil, but because they did not make their observers good according to the letter. The other statements made on this side must be understood in the same way. Conversely, the statements said in praise of the Law are to be understood of the Law according to spiritual understanding and according to its moral precepts, which are not abolished in the Gospel but fulfilled, as Matthew shows.

The Law was given only to the Jewish people because that people alone, worshipping one God, was worthy to be entrusted with God’s oracles, while the others worshipped idols. It was also given to them because [Col. 1400C] God’s Son was to be born from that people, and the Law was given through which they might understand this and await the coming Son of God.

Though the Law was given to that people alone, it was given to every class of persons within that people, though not for all of them. For there were three kinds of persons among that people: the hard, the foolish, and the perfect. The Law was given to all these, but not for all: to the hard as a lash, to the foolish as a pedagogue, to the righteous as a sign. But the Law was not given for the righteous. For, as the Apostle says elsewhere, “Law is not laid down for the righteous” (1 Tim. 1), because righteousness gained nothing through it. Here “Law” is understood in the sense of legal observances. By “legal observances” we mean those things instituted in the Law and terminated with the Law.

The Law was given to tame the proud, to chastise the hard, to instruct [Col. 1400D] the foolish, to reveal trespass and human weakness, to manifest and bear witness to grace, and to signify future things.

But here he addresses the power of grace and shows how great are grace’s effects. As though he said: With the Law given, trespass abounded; but the Jew is not therefore to be despised because it abounded, etc. [Note: [Col. 1400D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] Or the connection may be put thus: trespass abounded through the Law, but Christ also heals this, he in whom, where trespass abounded, grace also superabounded, forgiving all things. For everything that you drew from Adam, everything that you added by your own depraved habits, he forgave; he wiped everything out; he taught prayer; he appointed the contest; [Col. 1401A] he helps the laboring person; he will crown the victor. [Origen, Ambrose.]

Or grace superabounded because it not only releases from past sins, but also gives warning against future sins. Or it superabounded because Christ’s grace benefits even those whom the devil could not overcome, and because sin reigned for a time, whereas grace reigns eternally.

“So that, as [sin] reigned,” etc. As though he said: I say that grace superabounded, yet under this condition: let no one, trusting in grace, sin more securely. Rather, let grace be strong and through righteousness lead to life, just as sin had been strong in leading to death. This is what he says: “so that, as”—that is, under this condition—I say grace superabounds: as sin, which is also apart from Adam, abounded when the Law was given, and is not from origin but from one’s own will—

[Haimo] —reigned, leading [Col. 1401B] to eternal death, so may the grace of remission of sins reign in the elect, bringing them through the righteousness of good works to eternal life; and this through Jesus Christ our Lord, without whom there is no righteousness, just as there are some sins apart from Adam.

Therefore, when he had said, “as sin reigned unto death,” he did not add “through one” or “through Adam,” because he was here dealing with that sin which people did not draw from Adam but added by their own will. [Note: [Col. 1401D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] But when he says, “let grace reign,” and adds, “through Jesus Christ our Lord,” this is because through him there was remission not only of original sins but also of voluntary sins. From Adam, however, only that which is [Col. 1401C] original is drawn.

## CHAPTER VI

VERS. 1, 2.—“What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin, that grace may abound? Far be it! For we who have died to sin—how shall we still live in it?”

“What then shall we say?” [Note: [Col. 1401D] The same, *On the Spirit*.] The Apostle raises an objection which he sees may be made by the perverse. For some perverse persons, hearing the preaching of Paul and the other apostles, received death where they ought to have received life. They said that the apostles preached that the more a person sinned, the more pleasing he would be to God and the greater grace he would receive.

[Augustine] These perverse persons derive this from the passage where it was said: “Where trespass abounded, grace also [Col. 1401D] superabounded,” as though he had said that sin is profitable because of the abundance of grace. To say this is to be ungrateful for grace. And this is what he says in objecting to himself: “What then shall we say?” As though he said: Since grace is powerful where trespass abounded, what then shall we say? Shall we say—as some accuse us of saying—that we shall remain in sin so that grace may abound? Far be it that we should say this.

[Note: [Col. 1402D] Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*.] One must not remain in sin for the sake of greater grace, as some suppose that we say. Grace did not superabound through the merit of the sinner, but through the aid of the one who comes to help, where trespass abounded. We must not remain in sin so that grace may reign. Rather, through grace itself we ought and are able to be, as it were, dead and buried to sin, and to rise in its righteousness unto eternal life.

The Apostle subsequently shows this, and first shows that we have died to sin, adding: “For we,” or “if we.” As though he said: Truly, one must not remain in sin. “For,” that is, because, we have died to sin in baptism—that is, we have been delivered from sin, so that through the grace of God it no longer rules in us. To die to sin is to be delivered from sin. And if this is so, how, etc.? Or, if “who” is read there, read it thus: “we who”—we already have this. How, that is, on what grounds, shall we still, after so great a benefit, live in it and restore strength to the enemy? For when grace has accomplished this, that we died to sin, what else do we do [Col. 1402B] if we live in it, except prove ungrateful to grace?

For one who praises the benefit of medicine does not say that the diseases and wounds from which it heals a person are beneficial. Rather, the more medicine is commended with greater praises, the more wounds and diseases from which it delivers are censured and dreaded. Thus the praise and proclamation of grace is a condemnation of trespasses.

VERS. 3–5.—“Or do you not know, brothers, that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also may walk in newness of life. For if we have been made planted together [Col. 1402C] in the likeness of his death, we shall also be in that of his resurrection.”

“Or do you not know,” etc. Here he confirms what he had said: namely, that having died to sin—which occurs in baptism—we ought not again to live in it, lest we need again to die to it. For when we are baptized, we die together with Christ. This is what he says: “Or do you not know,” etc.? And as if someone should say, “Have we died to sin?” he answers: certainly, we have, because we, “all who”—that is, of whatever condition—have been baptized, that is, cleansed from vices, “into Christ Jesus,” that is, into Christ’s institution, which is in the name of the Trinity, or into the working of Christ himself, who truly baptizes. We “were baptized into his death,” that is, into the likeness of Christ’s death, so that, as Christ died once in the flesh and lives forever, [Col. 1402D] so we, having died once to evil through baptism, may live forever to good. [Haimo.]

Or, he says that we are baptized into his death because his death is the cause of this purification. And do you not know this, brothers? As though he said: You ought not to be ignorant of this. Observe that he often reproves them for ignorance.

“For we were buried with him.” As though he said: [Augustine, Haimo.] Truly, in baptism we are made like Christ’s death, because by faith we have also been buried with him in baptism—that is, in his likeness. We, I say, were led through baptism into death, that is, into the abolishing of sins. For this purpose we died together with him [Col. 1403A] and were buried: so that, just as Christ rose—far removed from the dead—and did so through the glory of the Father, that is, through the Father’s Word united to his humanity, or through God’s grace, so we too, rising as firmly from vices, may walk in good works, advancing from good to better, established in newness of life through the righteousness of faith and hope of glory.

“For if”: as though he said, I say that we should walk in newness, which we can do. For if we have been transplanted, in the likeness of a tree, from bad soil, and made by God to be planted together—firmly adhering—to the likeness of his death; that is, if, removed from the old way of life, we firmly adhere to the good, with God bringing this about, and are like Christ’s death, then immediately we shall also be planted together in the likeness of Christ’s resurrection—that is, we shall firmly adhere to the likeness of Christ’s resurrection—so that, as Christ, having put off the old state of death, rose new, [Col. 1403B] so we too may walk in newness of life.

[Ambrose] He says that we can be made like the resurrection if we have been made planted together in the likeness of his death—that is, if, in baptism, laying aside all vices, we do not sin afterward. For this likeness of death will produce the likeness of resurrection, so that we may walk in newness of life.

[Augustine] Observe that the death by which we are said to have died to sin in baptism, and the life by which we now live in righteousness and shall afterward live eternally with Christ, are displayed in Christ’s death and resurrection. For Christ’s death and resurrection are not merely events, but also sacraments.

[Note: [Col. 1403D] Augustine, *in Euch.*] Whatever was done in Christ’s cross, burial, resurrection, ascension, and sitting at the Father’s right hand was done so that the Christian life might be conformed to these things mystically—not merely by their being spoken, but by their being enacted.

Consider, then, each thing that was done in those events and how the Christian life is conformed from them. In Christ, who had lived as the old human being—that is, with oldness contracted from the first human being, not in guilt but in punishment: namely hunger, thirst, and the like. In this way he ended and put off that oldness: enduring the pain of the cross, he had his limbs stretched out and fastened upon the cross so that they could not move toward former actions. Being buried, he likewise rested from them, removed from human sight. By these things he demands from us that we lay aside our oldness of sins with the groaning and pain of repentance; that we keep our members fastened by the nails of self-restraint and righteousness, lest we return to former evils; that we rest from them so completely that neither their sight nor their memory remains; and that, thus rising to good things, we may walk in newness of life, ascending from virtue to virtue, until, placed at God’s right hand, we see the God of gods as he is.

[Augustine] Therefore, in the cross is the pain of confessors; in burial, the rest of those absolved; in resurrection, the life of the righteous; in ascension, the progress of the perfect; and in sitting at the right hand, the glory of the blessed. Christ requires these things from us not only in the sacrament of his passion, [Col. 1404A] but also brings them about if we desire to imitate him. Hence it follows:

VERS. 6–11.—“Knowing this: that our old human being was crucified with him, in order that the body of sin might be destroyed, so that we should no longer be slaves to sin. For the one who has died has been justified from sin. But if we died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him, knowing that Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him. For in that he died, he died to sin once for all; but in that he lives, he lives to God. So also reckon yourselves indeed dead to sin, but living to God in Christ Jesus.”

“Knowing this, that the old human being,” etc. He had said that through [Col. 1404B] baptism we have died to sin and therefore ought not thereafter to live in it, but walk in newness of life. He shows through what this can be done: namely, because the old human being was crucified, etc.

[Augustine] As though he said: I say that we should walk in newness of life—I mean we who know this: that our old human being, that is, the tinder of sin and our habit, “ours,” that is, arising from us and not from God, was crucified together with Christ; that is, it was so weakened with Christ’s crucifixion that the body of sin might be destroyed, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1404D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] Or, “our old human being [was crucified with Christ,” that is, our old actions were crucified—that is, put to death—by Christ’s death, so that, with reason ruling, the body of sin might be destroyed: that is, all crimes which together form, as it were, a body and heap of sin.

But by God’s grace, he who hung upon the cross in the likeness of sinful flesh, baptism effects [Col. 1404C] the crucifixion of the old human being and destruction of the body of sin. This does not occur in such a way that concupiscence, which is scattered through and inborn in the still-living flesh, is suddenly consumed and no longer exists; rather, it occurs so that what was present in the person when born may not harm one who has died.

For if one lives in the flesh after baptism, one has concupiscence against which to fight and which, with God’s aid, to overcome—provided one has not received God’s grace in vain and does not choose to be reprobate. Baptism, therefore, does not accomplish this—except perhaps through an ineffable miracle of the Creator—that the law of sin in the members is entirely extinguished and ceases to be. Rather, it accomplishes this: everything evil done, said, or thought by a person while the mind was enslaved to that same concupiscence is wholly abolished and regarded as though it had never happened.

[Ambrose] But concupiscence itself remains for the struggle, after the bond of guilt has been loosed—the bond by which the devil, through it, held the soul and separated it from its Creator—so that we may chastise our body and subject it to slavery.

Thus our oldness of punishment and guilt, which comes from the curse of the first human being, was destroyed in Christ’s cross. He took our mortality and bore our sins in his body upon the wood. In a figure of this sin and death, Moses also lifted up the serpent upon wood in the wilderness; for by the serpent’s persuasion, humankind fell into the condemnation of death. Thus the serpent was suitably lifted up on wood as a sign of that death. For in that figure a serpent hung upon the wood. But what hung upon the wood of the cross except the Lord’s death, so that by dying he might overcome death and, having become a curse [Col. 1405A] for us, might consume the curse of our twofold oldness (Gal. 3)?

Let us consider how our oldness was consumed on the cross. Our oldness, like the curse, consists of two things: guilt and punishment. Christ assumed one of them, namely punishment. Hence he is said to have become a curse. And he consumed both in us, because by his single oldness he consumed our double oldness. Thus he rested in the tomb for one day and two nights. By the one day his single oldness is signified; by the two nights our double oldness. Therefore he rested in the tomb one day and two nights because by his single oldness he bore our double oldness.

And let us see how. Christ removed guilt—past, present, and future. He bore past sins by forgiving them; present sins by drawing people away from them and again forgiving them; but future sins he bore not by forgiving them, but by bestowing grace through which they might be avoided. Therefore he bore future sins because he brought it about that they would not occur.

He likewise consumed punishment. Punishment is twofold: Gehenna’s punishment and temporal punishment. He completely removed Gehenna’s punishment, so that those who truly repent do not experience it. But he has not yet entirely removed temporal punishment. Hunger, thirst, death, and the like remain; but he has cast down their kingdom and dominion, and at last, at the end, he will wholly destroy them. Just as one who captures a most cruel enemy does not kill him immediately, but permits him to live for a little while in disgrace and pain, so Christ first bound punishment, as it were, but will kill it in the future.

Thus death has been conquered in triumph, and with it the devil, yet it has not been wholly slain. Hence Peter, before the Passion, denied at a maidservant’s word, but afterward, brought before kings and governors, did not yield. Therefore the Apostle fittingly says: “Our old human being was crucified”—that is, wrath was weakened—“that the body of sin might be destroyed,” with flesh subjected to spirit, so that [Col. 1405C] we may no longer be slaves to sin. I do not say that sin may not exist, but that we may not be compelled to serve it; and truly we are not compelled, because we have been justified.

And truly, “the one who has died to sin”—that is, the one delivered from [Col. 1405D] sin, as we are—“has been justified from sin,” that is, is righteous and free from sin. “But if we died with Christ,” that is, if we have thus died to sin as Christ once died to punishment, “we believe that we shall also live with Christ,” that is, not elsewhere, but there with him. This means: if we have died with Christ—that is, are like his death, as stated above—then in addition to the things already mentioned, we shall have this: we shall live with him in eternal life. We shall live, I say, with a life such as his own.

Knowing that Christ, having risen, is now far removed from the dead, he no longer—that is, henceforth—dies, that is, undergoes the dissolution of soul and body [Col. 1406A]. Nor will death henceforth have dominion over him through any suffering. For in that he died, etc.; as though he said: Christ truly no longer dies, because Christ died once—once, because he died to sin, that is, in order to take away sin, which he accomplished by one death, and that suffices for this purpose. [Note: [Col. 1405D] Augustine, *Against Maximus the Heretic*.] Or, he died to sin, that is, to the likeness of sin, namely to the flesh in which there was no sin, but the likeness of sin; and he died to it when, in dying, he was stripped of mortal flesh resembling sinful flesh. In this the Apostle commends the sacrament of baptism, which is celebrated in us. [Note: [Col. 1405D] The same, *Against Julian the Heretic*.] Thus, just as he is proclaimed to have died once, by dying, to the likeness of sin, so whoever has been baptized in him may die to that reality of which that likeness was a likeness—that is, to sin [Col. 1406B]—and, whatever age the baptized person may be, may live by being reborn from the washing, just as Christ lives by rising from the tomb. [Note: [Col. 1405D] The same, *Enchiridion*.] For from a newly born infant to a decrepit old man, just as no one is to be barred from baptism, so no one fails to die to sin in baptism; infants die only to original sin, but adults also to the actual sins which they have added to original sin. [Note: [Col. 1406D] Augustine, from the book *Hypognosticon*.]

Note also that in saying this the Apostle intended it to be understood that God did not make death. God certainly did not make it; rather, man summoned it by his hands and words. Observe that here and elsewhere Augustine says that God did not make death. Yet elsewhere he says as follows: [Note: [Col. 1406D] The same, *On the Retraction of Books*.] Care must be taken lest what I said, “God is not the author of evil,” be wrongly understood—though he is the author of everything that exists, because insofar as things exist, they are good—and lest it therefore be thought [Col. 1406C] that the punishment of the wicked, which indeed is evil for those punished, does not come from him. But I said this in the same way as it is said, “God did not make death” (Wisdom 1), although elsewhere it is written, “Death and life are from the Lord God” (Sirach 11). Therefore the punishment of the wicked, which is from God, is indeed evil to the wicked, but it is to be counted among the good works of God, since it is just that the wicked be punished, and everything just is certainly good. Thus God is said not to have made death because he did not make that for which death is inflicted, namely sin. For a human being is not made worse with God as author; rather, it is the defect of the will by which a person is made worse, and that defect is far from God’s will. But when something is said to be with God as author, it is said to be by God’s will.

[Col. 1406D] But, as though he said: Death will not have dominion over Christ; rather, he lives. And he does not live merely in any fashion; he lives to God, that is, in likeness to God the Father. For as is the Father’s life, so also is Christ’s life: it admits no disturbance; and so shall ours. Whatever he said above belongs to human beings through the grace of Christ, he here attributes to the Romans, as though saying: Just as Christ died once and afterward lives forever, so you also, O Romans, consider yourselves indeed dead to sin, but living to God in virtues, that is, for God’s honor. The sense is: As Christ died once, so let sin die once in you [Col. 1407A], so that it need not be repeated; and as Christ lives forever, so may you always live in virtues—and this in Christ Jesus our Lord, that is, in Christ’s work; elsewhere there is no hope.

### Verses 12–14

> “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires. Neither yield your members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin; but yield yourselves to God, as living from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness to God. For sin shall not have dominion over you. For you are not under the law, but under grace.”

Therefore let not sin reign. [Ambrose] Because above he said that we are dead to sin and ought not to live in it, and since no one is without sin, he specifies what must especially be guarded against: namely, that we should not obey desires [Col. 1407B]. It is as though he concludes what was asked above, namely, “Shall we remain in sin?” As though he said: Because you are thus dead to sin, therefore let sin—that is, the tinder of sin—not reign in your body, although it is present; for your body is under your control through grace. I mean the body now mortal because of sin; but it will become immortal in the future if sin does not now reign. Or, let not sin reign in this mortal body unto eternity; that is, the body will die eternally through the reign of sin. [Note: [Col. 1407D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.]

The law of the flesh is what the Apostle here calls sin when he says, “Let not sin reign.” For the law, or sin, does not remain in the members of those reborn of water and Spirit as though remission of sins had not been granted them, all those sins by which we are separated from God having been slain; rather, it remains in the oldness of the flesh as something conquered and killed, unless by some unlawful consent it should in some manner revive and be restored to its own kingdom and domination. [Col. 1407C] Let it not reign, I say, so that you obey by consenting and acting upon its desires, even though through weakness you experience desire.

[Augustine] For if you consent, sin reigns. And not only should you not obey; you should not even yield your members to sin—that is, to desire—which then are weapons of unrighteousness, instruments by which unrighteousness is accomplished. The sense is: Not only should you not obey desire, but neither should you desire; for this is to yield and make the members serviceable to sin, and then they are weapons of unrighteousness.

Here observe that “desire” sometimes names the tinder of sin, namely the inborn defect; at other times it names an inward act. This occurs both in the first movement, called *propassion*; in the second, called pleasure; and in the third, called consent. But here he does not prohibit desire in its first movement, because it is not in our power to prevent its arising. Yet by God’s grace we can restrain it from reaching pleasure and consent—which he does prohibit: namely, that in your mind you should neither delight in nor consent to the desire of the flesh, which, arising from weakness, rebels against you. This weakness is a tyrant that stirs evil desires. Therefore evil desire is within us [Col. 1408A], and it must not be allowed to reign. Its desires also exist—actual concupiscences—which are the devil’s weapons.

[Ambrose] For through them an opportunity is given to him, so that, when God abandons us and he receives power, he may mock and kill us. Therefore, if you wish to be the tyrant’s conqueror, to find the enemy unarmed, and thus subject him to yourself, do not obey desire by evil action; nor even desire by taking pleasure in it or consenting to it. But rather yield—that is, make yourselves serviceable—to God: yourselves, I say, as living from the dead. It is as though he said: You ought, and are able, to yield yourselves to God, because you are alive in virtues; and you ought to do so because you were formerly dead in sins, even if you cannot accomplish in deed what is good. Or, at least be willing, whereby you will be made serviceable and prepared. This is what he says when he adds: yield [Col. 1408B] your members to God, so that they may be weapons of righteousness, by which righteousness is accomplished.

For just as we furnish our members as weapons to sin when we act wickedly—for example, when we give our members to rising anger, or our tongue for cursing, or our hands for striking—so also we give weapons to righteousness when we live uprightly, guarding our members from every shameful thing. For sin, as though he said: Do what I have said, which you can readily do. For sin will no longer have dominion over you as it once did. For you are not under the law, which did not help, but under grace, which refreshes and helps, so that each person may even become a doer of the law; without that grace, one placed under the law will be only a hearer of the law.

[Col. 1408C] ### Verses 15–18

> “What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law but under grace? By no means! Do you not know that, to whom you yield yourselves as servants for obedience, you are servants of the one whom you obey—whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness? But thanks be to God that you were servants of sin, yet from the heart you obeyed that form of teaching into which you were delivered. And, having been freed from sin, you became servants of righteousness.”

“What then?” As though he said: Because we are not under a law which terrifies, but under grace which promises good, what shall we do? Shall we sin [Haimo] in this confidence, because we are not under law but under grace? Some said this, maintaining that the law, as though joined to grace, must be observed. [Col. 1408D] Rejecting this, the Apostle says: “By no means!”

Or thus: I said that you are under grace, not under law; and because the law is from God, lest anyone perhaps oppose it on this account, he raises the objection himself. As though he said: Since the law is from God, what then shall we say?
