Shall we say, then, that we will sin because we are not under law but under grace—that is, because we have abandoned the law for grace? By no means! “Do you not know?” Lest we profess one thing but do another, and though we are called servants of God, are found by our deeds to be servants of the devil, he warns and declares that we are servants of the one whose will we fulfill by our works. As though he said: You ought not to sin, but to work well.

[Ambrose] For to whom you yield—that is, offer yourselves as servants, inclined [Col. 1409A] to obedience by consenting and acting—you are servants. That is, you will be compelled by a certain necessity brought about by habit to fulfill the will of the one whom you have obeyed, that is, after you have obeyed him; though not before you first yielded yourselves as servants. And do you not know this? You are servants, I say, whether of sin, which leads to death—that is, to a greater sin or to eternal punishment—or of obedience, that is, of righteousness, which leads to greater righteousness or to eternal life.

31. “Thanks,” etc. As though he said: You belong to the one to whom you give yourselves; but I give thanks to God because, though formerly you were servants of sin, you are so no longer. This is what he says; read the words thus: As I have said, so it appears in you, who were once servants of sin but now have obeyed, and by this have become [Col. 1409B] servants of righteousness, that is, of Christ. You obeyed, I say, not outwardly, but from the heart—that is, by the judgment of the mind—because you obeyed faith by nature rather than by law, by will rather than by fear. For this, then, I give thanks to God: that though you were formerly such, you now are not; you who are tending toward that form of teaching, that is, toward the teaching which is our form. The teaching of the Gospel is the form which restores the defaced image of God. Into that form, I say, you were delivered not by yourselves but by God’s grace; and through this you were freed, by another, from sin—that is, from the reign of the tinder of sin—and were made servants of righteousness by consenting and acting.

### Verses 19–21

> “I speak in human terms, because of the weakness of your flesh. For as you yielded your members to serve impurity and iniquity unto iniquity, so now yield your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification. For when you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness. What fruit then had you then in those things of which you are now ashamed?”

“I speak in human terms,” etc. Up to this point the Apostle has shown that one ought not to sin. Here he says what is henceforth to be done: namely, that righteousness must be served. No one can excuse himself from this, since no one is unable to do good, at least in will—which likewise comes through grace.

[Ambrose] And lest the Christian religion seem unbearable and harsh, and therefore be avoided, he commands something human—that is, easy [Col. 1409D]. [Origen] Namely, serve God in the same measure in which we previously served sin, though God ought certainly to be served more eagerly than sin, since here there is salvation and there condemnation. [Ambrose, Origen] As though he said: Because you are free from sin, therefore I say—that is, command—you something human, that is, easy and without burden, although it belongs to mature but not perfected righteousness. And I say this because of the weakness of your flesh, that is, the weakness arising from your flesh. On account of this I speak in human terms, because I ought to say greater things if you could bear them, since you owe more service to righteousness than to sin. But I spare your weakness, not requiring from you more good than [Col. 1410A] you formerly did evil.

“For as,” etc. Here he shows what that human command is, shaming them as he says that they should at least render to righteousness what they had formerly given to impurity. [Origen] What, then, is so human—that is, so easy, so free of burden—that no weakness of the flesh can possibly excuse one from it? As though he said: I truly speak in human terms, because this is human. For as you yielded—that is, prepared at the prompting of the will—your members, which would be under your own control if you wished, to serve by acting the impurity of the flesh, that is, lust, which defiles the body, and the iniquity of the mind, which, though it does not defile the body, nevertheless corrupts the soul—in­iquity, I say, leading to iniquity, that is, to the completion of evil—so now, when you have been freed from sin, yield—that is, prepare—your members, which are under your control, to serve by acting righteousness leading [Col. 1410B] to sanctification, that is, to the completion of good. This is the sense.

[Note: [Col. 1409D] Augustine, *To Anastasius*.] Just as then no fear compelled you to sin, but the lust and pleasure of sin led you, so now, for living justly, let not fear of punishment urge you, but let delight in and love of righteousness lead you. And this, as it seems to me, is not yet perfect righteousness, but in some measure mature righteousness. Hence he does not say “human” without reason. For what he says is human: “As you yielded yourselves to impurity, so now yield yourselves to righteousness”; for righteousness ought to be loved even more than iniquity then was, so that a person may endure pains for righteousness and despise everything, even death. For righteousness is sweeter [Col. 1410C] and brighter than iniquity, and therefore more worthy of love. Weigh righteousness and iniquity: is righteousness to be loved only as much as that was loved? Far from it—and would that it were loved even so! Therefore it must be loved more, altogether more. In iniquity you attained pleasure; for righteousness endure pain. Behold, this is more; yet the Apostle does not say “more,” but “as.”

[Augustine] Therefore, if righteousness is not served more—or, that is, at least let it be served as much as iniquity was then served. He says this lest faith be avoided as harsh and unbearable. Yet perhaps some are found who, just as they preferred the pleasure of sin to righteousness, [Note: [Col. 1409D] The same, in the same work.] so prefer delight in righteousness to the pleasures of the flesh, yet are afraid to suffer punishments and death for righteousness. This is human. It is too little that you despise whatever delighted you; despise also whatever terrified you: prisons, tortures, even death. In both degrees, lovers of righteousness, prepare yourselves.

“For when,” etc. As though he said: Righteousness must therefore be served. “For” means “because”: when you were servants of sin—that is, when sin ruled you—you were free from righteousness, that is, you lacked the dominion of righteousness. [Note: [Col. 1410D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*.] I ask: what sort of freedom can an enslaved servant have? The servant’s freedom exists when he delights in sinning, which comes from free choice; for one serves freely who willingly does his master’s will. [Col. 1411A] And by this he is free to sin because he is a servant of sin. Likewise, one freely serves righteousness who loves and rejoices. This is true freedom because of joy in right action, and at the same time devout service because of obedience to the command. Therefore this is good service and freedom; that other is evil.

“What fruit then,” etc. As though he said: When you were servants of sin, you lacked righteousness; and you also had such fruit as now makes you ashamed, while your end was eternal death. He says this as a question. As though he said: You lacked righteousness. What fruit then did you have? Evil, of course: I mean greater shame in those shameful sins of which—that is, at the memory of which—you are now ashamed when you are of sound mind. [Note: [Col. 1411D] Augustine, *On Psalm 30*.] For there is a certain temporal shame [Col. 1411B]: a beneficial disturbance of mind which looks back upon its sins, recoils at the recollection, blushes in recoiling, and corrects itself by blushing. Notice that the Apostle mentions former evils for this reason: this remembrance causes people to abhor their former deeds and renders them more indebted to grace.

### Verses 21–23

> “For their end is death. But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and your end eternal life. For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

“For their end,” as though he said: I ask about the fruit; for concerning the end the matter is plain, namely that their end—the outcome of their life and actions—is eternal death, which follows upon those works [Col. 1411C] and those who perform such things. [Ambrose] For one passes from the death of sin to eternal death. Behold their freedom: it is full of stains and enslaved to the filth of punishments. [Haimo] Of such people the prophet says: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1). “Beasts” means people living irrationally, without uprightness of morals and conduct. Thus for beasts to rot in dung is to end life in the stench of lust and the foulness of vices.

“But now,” as though he said: Such was your condition then, when you served sin. But now that you have been converted, you have been freed from sin, of which you were then servants. [Note: [Col. 1411D] The same, *To Boniface*.] Notice that above he said they had been *free* from righteousness, not *freed*; but now he does not call them free from sin, lest they attribute this to themselves. Rather, carefully and watchfully, he says that they have been freed, referring this to the Lord’s saying: “If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free” (John 8). But this will is free in evil because it delights in evil; therefore it is not free in good because it has not been freed. Nor can a person will any good unless helped by him who cannot will evil. Therefore here he says, with the greatest care, “freed from sin,” and above, “free from righteousness.” For free choice has not perished in the sinner to such a degree that people do not sin through it—especially [Col. 1412A] all who sin with pleasure and approve what they desire. Thus they are free from righteousness only by freedom of choice; but they are freed from sin only by the grace of the Savior.

[Note: [Col. 1411D] The same, in the same work.] “But servants,” as though he said: You have been freed from sin, but have been made servants, as it were through another, of God—you who were then free from righteousness. And you, having been freed and made servants, now have your fruit, that is, a fitting fruit; you, I say, being led toward sanctification, that is, toward the perfection of virtues. But your end will be eternal life. [Ambrose] That is, at the departure and end of life, you will have life without end.

“For the wages,” etc. As though he said: Their end is truly death, because eternal death is the wages of sin—that is, the due recompense for sin. But eternal life, which is [Col. 1412B] the end of the righteous, is given by God’s grace alone, and this in Christ Jesus our Lord, that is, through Jesus Christ. [Haimo] Observe that, in speaking of sin’s recompense, he uses the word “wages,” but in speaking of the recompense of the elect he calls it God’s grace. For those who serve under the devil receive their own reward, as though he said: wages, that is, the due payment of diabolical malice.

[Augustine, Haimo] “Wages” (*stipendium*) is so called from *stips pendenda*, “a payment to be weighed,” that is, substance to be weighed. For in ancient times money was more often weighed than counted; it was given from the public treasury to soldiers serving their country. [Note: [Col. 1411D] The same, *Enchiridion*.] Thus he said, “the wages of sin is death,” in order to show that death is inflicted on sin not undeservedly but as a debt. For wages belong, as it were, to those who have completed their service, and payment for the work of the devil’s military service is rendered as a debt, not bestowed as a gift. But grace, unless it is free, is not grace.

It must therefore be understood that even a person’s good merits are gifts of God; when eternal life is rendered for these, what is given except grace for grace? And because merits arise from grace, grace is thus rendered for grace. [Note: [Col. 1412D] Augustine, *To Valentinus*.] He could therefore rightly have said, “the wages of righteousness are eternal life,” but he preferred to say, “the grace of God is eternal life,” so that we might understand that God brings us to eternal life through his mercy, not through our merits. [Note: [Col. 1412D] The same, *To Sixtus the Presbyter*.] For what is a person’s merit before grace, since grace alone produces in us every good merit? 32. Indeed, when God crowns our merits, he crowns nothing other than his own merits. Therefore eternal life [Col. 1412D], which at the end is rendered by God for preceding merits, is rightly itself called grace, because the very merits for which it is rendered are not from us, but have been wrought in us through grace. It is given freely not because it is given without merits, but because the merits themselves for which it is given have been given.

[Note: [Col. 1412D] The same, *On Rebuke and Grace*.] It must therefore be confessed that eternal life is called grace because it is rendered for those merits which grace bestowed upon a person. Hence the Gospel also reads, “grace for grace,” that is, for those merits which grace bestowed. For it is certain that eternal life is given in return for good works, but the works [Col. 1413A] for which it will be given belong to God’s grace. Hence the Lord says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). [Note: [Col. 1413D] Augustine, Fulgentius.] We therefore receive grace for grace: the grace of glorification for the unmerited grace of justification. For the grace of justification has erased every evil merit by an undeserved benefit and strengthens by continual assistance; the grace of glorification is justly rendered to it as a reward.

## Chapter VII

### Verses 1–3

> “Or do you not know, brothers—for I speak to those who know the law—that the law has dominion over a person as long as he lives? For a woman who is under a husband is bound by the law to her husband while he lives; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. Therefore, while her husband is living, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man; but if her husband dies, she is freed from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man.”

“Do you not know, brothers,” etc. Up to this point he has dealt with the power of grace, showing that salvation comes from it and not from the law. Now he says that the law is no longer to be observed, and he deals with the law’s end and its former uselessness. The Romans, therefore, should not be surprised because the Apostle says, “You are not under law but under grace” (Rom. 6). Above, the law was said not to justify; here it is said that it ought to cease, because it was given until Christ. As though he said: Someone might ask, “Why do you say that life comes through Christ and not through observance of the law?” The answer is: because the law itself has now reached its end, and it does not give life but increases sin [Col. 1413C].

This is what he says in the form of a question. The order of the words is as follows: “Do you not know, brothers, do you not know this: that the Mosaic law has dominion over a person, so that the person obeys it, as long as it lives,” that is, as long as the law itself remains in force? You ought not to be ignorant of this. “For,” that is, because you know the law, namely the Mosaic law. For the Romans included Jews and Gentiles. And I speak to those who know the law, in which what I say is manifest if it is understood spiritually.

Then he shows this by an analogy, adding: [Note: [Col. 1413D] The same, *Eighty-Three Questions*.] “For the woman who is under a husband,” by which comparison he explains and proves what he has said. Just as a woman, while her husband lives, is bound by the law of her husband, but is released if he dies, so, while the law remains in force, a person is subject to it; but when it ceases to remain in force, the person is released [Col. 1413D].

Or thus: “Do you not know?” He is speaking of natural law. [Ambrose] In order to strengthen their minds in the teaching of the Gospel and withdraw them from the Mosaic law, he uses the example of human law, that by earthly things he may commend heavenly things. The Romans certainly know law, for they are not barbarians, but have grasped natural justice partly from themselves and partly from the Greeks, just as the Greeks did from the Hebrews. This is the sense: I say that life comes through Christ rather than through the Mosaic law because the law has an end, as is clear from the example of human law.

[Ambrose] “Do you not know, brothers, that the law of nature, though universal, is not received or observed in all its parts by everyone? It has dominion over a person [Col. 1414A] as long as it lives,” that is, as long as it remains in force. For a law is called dead when its authority ceases. You ought not to be ignorant of this because you know natural law. “And I speak to those who know the law”: this he says concerning natural law inscribed in written laws or confirmed by human custom, under which Jews, Greeks, and Latins stood. For this law is universal. Afterwards he introduces the particular law, by which he also wishes more clearly to prove his assertion. For he wishes to impart the truth to them gradually.

Hence he adds: “For the woman who is under a husband,” etc. The law has dominion while it remains in force, as I show by this example. For a woman who is under a husband is, while her husband lives, bound by the law of her husband, so that she cannot depart from him. In the same way, the Mosaic law, while it remains in force, ought to be observed. [Col. 1414B] By the following example, therefore, he more clearly teaches that a Christian is freed from the law of works, not from every law—just as a woman is freed from the law of her husband when he dies, but not from natural law. Nor ought a Christian henceforth to be under the law. For if the law lives for him, he is an adulterer; it does him no good to be called a Christian. He demonstrates this by pursuing the proposed comparison: “But if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband.” Likewise, if the law loses its force, a person is released. And because she is bound by the law of her husband while he lives, therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man: so one who transgresses while the law remains in force sins. But if her husband dies, she is freed from the law of her husband.

[Ambrose] Thus, when the law has been removed and remission of sins granted, those joined to the Gospel through grace are freed. [Col. 1414C] “So that she is not,” etc. As though he said: The woman is so free that she is not an adulteress if she is with another husband; likewise, when the law has ended, one who passes to Christ after abandoning the figures does not transgress. For, when the law is dead, those who are with Christ are not adulterers. Indeed, if anyone observes the dead law and wishes to belong to faith, he is an adulterer in both respects, and Christ does him no good.

### Verses 4–6

> “Therefore, my brothers, you also have been made dead to the law through the body of Christ, that you may belong to another—to him who rose from the dead—that you may bear fruit to God. For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sins which were through the law worked in our members so as to bear fruit unto death. But now we have been released from the law of death, in which we were held, so that we may serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.”

“Therefore, my brothers.” [Note: [Col. 1414D] Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*.] Thus far is the comparison. Thereafter he begins to speak of the matter for which he introduced the comparison, and draws an inference from the analogy. As though he said: Since this is so between husband and wife, therefore, according to this comparison, my brothers, you also, as we apostles, have been made dead to the law, your sins having been forgiven. [Ambrose] That is, you ought to be dead to the law which was given until Christ. As though he said: You have not merely abandoned the law, but have also become dead to the law, that is, to its figurative observances. For this is what is here called “law.”

You have been made dead, I say, through the body of Christ, that is, through the mystery of the incarnation or through the fulfillment of truth. [Col. 1415A] You have been made dead to the law for this purpose: that you may belong to another, namely Christ, of whom you need not be ashamed, since he is the one who rose from the dead. We are certainly his, in order that we may now bear fruit to God, whereas under the law we formerly bore fruit unto death. And we truly now bear fruit to God, not formerly. For when we were in the flesh—that is, doing the works of the flesh, which belonged to being under the law—the passions of sins, that is, desires which cause mortal sins [Augustine], namely consent to the act, under which the soul acted as under a ruling husband before grace came through faith—these passions, which were through the law, either made known or even increased by sinfulness, worked in our members [Col. 1415B]. [Ambrose] That is, they led our members to evil works, so that they bore fruit unto death, that is, produced acts deserving eternal death.

[Note: [Col. 1415D] Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*.] But now, since we belong to Christ, our sins having been forgiven, we have been released from the law which is the cause of death, namely sin. For desire was increased when the law forbade where faith was absent; and to the mass of sins was added the crime of transgression, because where there is no law, neither is there transgression. [Ambrose] Or the law is called the law of death because it kills sinners and punishes the guilty. We were held under that law and would never have been released except by God’s grace.

We have been released, I say, so that we may serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter. That is, we are to serve in the works of Christ the new man, which we attain not by our own powers or by law, but by the grace of the Holy Spirit. We are to remain in these in such a way that nothing is added [Col. 1415C] from the works of the law, which are old. Or, we serve in the newness of the Spirit, that is, in the law of faith, which is in the renewed mind, which also makes a person spiritual and is therefore rightly called the law of the Spirit; and not in the oldness of the letter, that is, not according to the letter which has grown old because it has ceased.

[Augustine] Observe that in the preceding comparison there are three things—husband, wife, and the husband’s law—and likewise in the matter for which the comparison was introduced there are three: the soul and the law of sins. The only difference is this: in the former, the husband dies, so that the wife, released from her husband’s law, may marry whom she wishes; here, however, it is not sin but the soul itself that dies to sin. [Note: [Col. 1415D] The same, in the same work.] For the soul dies to the aforesaid passions, although it already serves the law of God with the mind, while the passions themselves are not yet dead, as long as it serves the law of sin with the flesh [Col. 1415D]. Therefore something yet remains in one who is under grace, but it does not conquer or lead that person captive.

What then? Here the question arises whether the law itself is evil, because he seemed to blame the law in saying that the passions of sins were through the law and in calling it the law of death and the oldness of the letter. These words, wrongly understood, would supply fuel to the madness and fury of the Manichees. [Note: [Col. 1416D] Augustine, *Sermons of the Lord*.] For the Manichees say that the Mosaic law was not given by God and contend that it is contrary to the Gospel. When they are debated, they try to convict [Col. 1416A] Catholics by the Apostle’s aforementioned testimonies, which they do not understand. Therefore, what the Apostle perceived might be understood, he raises as an objection, so as both to deny that he meant this and to defend the law by praise of the law itself, and to explain in what sense he had spoken the foregoing words. As though he said: Since indeed it is a law of death, and increased the powers of sin by preventing good action:

### Verses 7–8

> “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means! Yet I did not know sin except through the law. For I did not know desire except the law had said: ‘You shall not covet.’ But sin, taking occasion through the commandment, worked in me every kind of desire.”

What then shall we say? Shall we say that the Law is sin—that is, that it teaches or causes sinning? Or that it is such that its giver sinned by giving it, as though it were an evil thing? By no means! [Col. 1416B] For the Law is not evil, but rather good, because I did not know sin except through the Law. [Ambrose] That is, because it made sin known: for previously some things were not known either to be sins, or to be so grave, or to deserve punishment. Thus I did not previously know sin so fully except through the Law, through which it became known either that what had been unknown was sin, or that it was grave, or that it was punishable. By this he shows that the Law is not sin, but the indicator of sin.

[Note: [Col. 1416D] Augustine, *To Simplicianus*.] Hence it is understood that the Law was given for this purpose: not that sin might be introduced or uprooted, but only that it might be shown to make the soul guilty, so that, since sin cannot be overcome without God’s grace, the very anxiety of guilt might turn the soul toward receiving grace. [Col. 1416C] That sin is made known through the Law he demonstrates in one particular instance. “For covetousness”: as though he said, “I did not know sin except through the Law, as is clear in this one case. For I did not know covetousness either to be sin or to be so grave, unless the Law said, ‘You shall not covet.’” [Augustine] To prove that sin is known through the Law, the Apostle chose what is a general sin, namely covetousness, from which all evils arise. Therefore the Law is good, because in prohibiting this it prohibits all mortal sins. The Law is not sin, but the revealer of sin. Through it a person was instructed, but, while without Christ’s grace, was overcome more grievously.

Note that when he says, “I did not know,” he does not say this concerning himself personally, but treats a general case in his own person. But it is asked what this covetousness is. [Col. 1416D] [Jerome] Some say that it is that which is prohibited in the Decalogue when it says, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property or your neighbor’s wife” (Exod. 20). Others take it generally as any covetousness for any forbidden things.

“But sin, taking occasion,” etc. Behold, it has been shown that the Law is good, since it forbids and exposes sin; yet evil nevertheless arose from it, because sin—that is, the tinder of sin, namely the vice of covetousness, which is also called carnality—[Ambrose] or sin, that is, the devil, who is the author of sin—produced in me every covetousness, that is, consent both in delight and in action. [Augustine] [Col. 1417A] For covetousness was increased by the Law’s prohibition when liberating grace was still absent; or, “every covetousness” means every sin, for in saying every covetousness he signifies all sins. [Ambrose] Sin existed before, but not every sin, when the offense of transgression was still lacking.

[Note: [Col. 1417D] Augustine, *To Simplicianus*.] But now every sin has entered, because transgression has entered as well. I say that it “produced” this, “taking occasion through the commandment,” that is, through the Law. [Augustine] The tinder takes occasion through the commandment because our carnality is such that it desires prohibited things more ardently; if these had not been mentioned, it would lie, as it were, asleep. [Ambrose] The devil too took occasion from the commandment, because, seeing that the Law was given to help human beings, he burned more fiercely with anger against [Col. 1417B] humanity and strove more insistently to turn the Law to their ruin. Previously, as if possessing them securely, he tempted less.

Or: sin—that is, the devil or the tinder—produced in me every covetousness. The sense of these words is not changed. And I say that it produced this through the commandment, having taken occasion in the things themselves, as when a woman, gold, and the like are seen. Observe that it is rightly said that sin produced every covetousness through the commandment, or took occasion through the commandment. For covetousness was less before the Law, when a person sinned without concern.

[Note: [Col. 1417D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*.] A person followed covetousness, ran wherever it drew him, and judged its pleasant enticements and the delight arising from carnal sweetness to be great happiness. But when the [Col. 1417C] Law came, like a barrier placed in its way, a person saw his evil. He wished to restrain covetousness and not follow it; he tightened his hold upon himself. Trusting in himself, he attempted to dry up the river of covetousness, but could not. The river of covetousness was indeed checked by the barriers of the Law, but not dried up. Rather, because a person trusted in himself rather than in grace, covetousness was increased when the Law opposed it; and what had formerly led him on with no barrier overwhelmed him when the barrier was broken. For, instructed through the Law, he was more grievously overcome when he transgressed it; and he became a transgressor of the Law, whereas before he had been a sinner in ignorance. Thus he rightly says, “every covetousness.” For it is complete when it transgresses the Law.

### Verses 8–11

> “For without the Law sin was dead. But I was once alive without the Law. [Col. 1417D] But when the commandment came, sin revived. Yet I died, and the commandment which was for life was found to be for death to me. For sin, taking occasion through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.”

“For without the Law,” etc. I rightly said, “through the commandment,” for without the Law—that is, when there was no Law—sin, namely the devil or the tinder of sin, was dead, that is, weak, because it did not rage so fiercely in deceiving human beings before the Law. [Ambrose, Augustine] It is clear that the Apostle speaks not in his own person but generally in the person of humanity; and here the first [Col. 1418A] condition of the human being before the Law is noted—that is, he speaks here in the person of the human being before the Law.

“But I”: as though he said, “Before the Law sin was dead. But I, a rational human being, was once—that is, in the time before the Law—alive, by comparison with this death, when I was without the Law.” Note two human beings in the same person: the inner and the outer, that is, reason and the tinder. The inner person, who is in the flesh, he says assents to the Law and by its testimony approves the Law as good; but the outer person, he says, resists the inner person and the Law, leads captive, and through the Law has greater power to sin.

“But when it came”: here the second condition, under the Law, is noted—that is, the Apostle here speaks of a human being placed under the Law. As though he said, “Without the Law I was alive; but when the [Col. 1418B] commandment of the Law came, sin, formerly asleep”—[Augustine] that is, the outer person, namely the tinder of sin—“revived,” that is, began to appear and rebel. But I, the inner person, died, sin having increased and transgression having been added.

Or from the words “without the Law” onward, he treats the sin of covetousness and other sins made known through the Law, and refers back to what he said before: “I did not know sin except through the Law.” As though he said: “And indeed, only through the Law. For without the Law sin was dead,” that is, it lay hidden and unknown; it did not appear, but was wholly unknown, as though buried.

[Note: [Col. 1417D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] “But I was once alive without the Law”: that is, I seemed to myself to live because I was not terrified by death resulting from sin, since it did not appear. As though he said, “I did not know that it was sin, and therefore lived securely,” [Col. 1418C] as though God would not judge human actions.

[Note: [Col. 1418D] Augustine, *To Boniface*.] “But when the commandment came, sin revived”: that is, it appeared and became known to me. Yet he does not say “it lived,” but “it revived,” because it had once lived in Paradise, when the commission of an act contrary to the given command was clearly evident. But when humans, born sinners, lived without a commandment, it lay hidden as though dead; they followed the desires of the flesh without awareness because there was no restraint. But when the Law was given, sin revived in the awareness of the human being who was born, though it had already once lived in the awareness of the human being who was made.

“But I died,” [Augustine] that is, I knew myself to be dead, because I saw myself guilty before God on account of my sins. [Ambrose]

[Note: [Col. 1418D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*.] For previously I was a sinner unknown to myself, but now I became a manifest transgressor to myself. Thus, to one who attends carefully, the commandment of the Law—which was for life to the obedient or observant, or was intended for life by its giver because it was good—was found to be this same thing, and not another, for eternal death to me, who did not observe it and sinned. Yet it is for death not through a defect in itself but because of the occasion mentioned above.

“For sin”: because he had said that sin was for death, he determines how this is so. As though he said, “How is the commandment for death to me?” [Ambrose] Behold: because through it I was deceived by false sweetness, whether by the devil or by the tinder. [Col. 1419A] And this is what he means: sin, that is, carnality or the devil, [Augustine] deceived or seduced me, that is, drew me from good to evil, taking occasion through the commandment. For what is desired becomes sweeter when it is forbidden, and so sin deceives through the commandment.

[Note: [Col. 1419D] Augustine, *To Simplicianus*.] For where love is lacking, prohibition increases the desire for evil; when this desire is increased, what is forbidden becomes sweeter, and so sin deceives by false sweetness. For deceptive is the sweetness followed by more numerous and greater bitterness of punishments. Sin not only seduced me through the commandment, but also through that commandment killed me, because the guilt of transgression was added.

[Note: [Col. 1419D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*.] Therefore the enemy killed you with the sword you bore; he conquered you by your own arms; he destroyed you by your own arms. You were armed with the commandment as with a sword [Col. 1419B] in order to kill the enemy. Yet you cannot do so if you trust in yourself. Be humble, therefore; do not trust in yourself, and you will be able to conquer. See then little David against great Goliath, trusting in God’s name, not in his own strength: “You come,” he says, “to me with shield and spear; I, in the name of the Lord Almighty.” Thus, and in no other way, the enemy is cast down.

Or read it thus: “I say that sin deceived me, and through it”—that is, through this very act of deceiving—“killed me,” that is, brought me to eternal condemnation.

### Verses 12–13

> “Therefore the Law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good. Has then that which is good become death to me? By no means. But sin, in order that it might appear as sin, worked [Col. 1419C] death in me through what is good, so that through the commandment sin might become sinful beyond measure.”

“Therefore the Law indeed is holy, and the commandment,” etc. [Augustine] Above he denied that the Law was sin, defending it from an accusation; here he defends it by its own praise. It is one thing to defend it from an alleged crime, another to proclaim it with the praise it deserves. The accusation was made when it was said, “Is the Law sin?” 34 The defense followed when he said, “By no means!” Truth was defended in a single word, because the authority of its defender is great. [Ambrose] But here he commends the Law with most abundant praise, lest any suspicion of opposition to it remain.

As though he said: “Because the Law is for life, commands good things and forbids evil things, and made sin known, therefore the Law indeed is holy”—that is, it teaches soundly—“and the commandment,” that is, what is commanded through it, “is holy in itself, and just,” that is, making the sinner righteous, “and good,” that is, useful in gaining life.

“What then?” Here it is asked whether the Law, even if good, is nevertheless harmful in its effect. This seemed capable of being inferred from what had been said. For he had said that the commandment was for death, and had likewise said that it was good. Thus, to those of weaker understanding, the good thing could seem to have caused death. Anticipating this objection, he rejects it and explains in what sense he had said that the commandment was for death, against certain impious persons who said that the Old [Col. 1420A] Testament was from the prince of darkness but the New Testament from the Lord.

As though he said: “It is established that the Law is good; and since it is now established that the Law is good, yet death comes to me from it, as was said above, has that which is good become death to me? That is, is this good given to me by God in such a way that it is an efficient cause of death? By no means!” For death does not arise from the Law itself, but from human vice, because not the Law but the tinder is the efficient cause of death, turning a good thing into evil.

[Note: [Col. 1419D] Jerome, *To Algasia*.] For just as medicine is not the cause of death if it identifies deadly poisons, though wicked persons may misuse them for their own death or that of others, so the Law, which exposes the poisons of sins, restrains with a kind of bridle a person abusing his freedom, and teaches him to walk with measured step, is not an efficient cause [Col. 1420B] of sin. Rather, the cause is human vice—that is, the tinder. And this is what follows: “But sin,” that is, the tinder of sin, “worked death in me,” that is, actual sin, which is the cause of death.

I say that it worked this “through what is good,” that is, through the Law, not because the Law itself is the efficient cause, but because sin took occasion from it, as was said before. I say that it worked in this way so that sin might appear as sin—that is, as the efficient cause of sin—which then appears when it draws reason into consent and action.

[Note: [Col. 1420D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*.] Or thus: sin, that is, the tinder of sin, worked death, that is, actual sin, and this through what is good, that is, through the Law; certainly not because the Law produces sin, but rather because it exposes and forbids it, so that sin may appear through it. I do not say that sin exists through the Law, but that it appears through it, [Col. 1420C] because it existed even when it did not appear. As was said above: “I did not know covetousness to be sin unless the Law said, ‘You shall not covet.’” He did not say, “I did not have it.”

[Note: [Col. 1420D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*.] Therefore the Law is good, because by its holiness and justice it shows that the covetousness which I did not recognize is evil. Thus I do not attribute sin to God’s Law but to my own vice. For the Law is good, but without grace it only exposes sin; it does not introduce it. Therefore the Law is always good: whether it harms those empty of grace, or benefits those filled with grace. For many good things are nevertheless harmful to some through their own fault; for example, the sun delights healthy eyes but increases pain in those that are sore. Likewise the Law benefits those possessing grace, which is the health of minds. It harms those empty [Col. 1420D] of grace, not by its own fault but by theirs.

I say that it worked death in me to such an extent that sin—that is, the tinder of sin—might become “sinful,” that is, cause sin, beyond measure, [Ambrose] that is, more than before, not moderately, because transgression was added. I say that it becomes sinful, and this [Augustine] through the commandment, without which the tinder did not burn so fiercely, and through which transgression increased. For the covetousness of the flesh, which is the root of evils, prevailed more through the commandment; it did not diminish. The Law did not extinguish covetousness. Where the grace of the Liberator is absent, the prohibition of sins increases the desire for sin.

[Note: [Col. 1420D] Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*.] Therefore he said “through the commandment,” because transgression was added to the desire to sin. And he said “beyond measure,” because through the Law it did not diminish but rather increased, with desires released. [Ambrose] Or here “sin” means the devil, because through God’s good gift he was inflamed with anger against humanity and persuaded people to what was contrary and unlawful, since he saw that the Lord was providing for them. In this the sin appears, that is, the enemy. And this is the meaning: sin, namely the devil, worked death in me, inflamed through what was good, namely through the Law, so that sin—that is, the enemy—might appear. Seeing that provision had been made for humanity through the Law, he persuaded them to unlawful acts, so that death might come to them from the Law instead of life. I say that it worked this to such an extent that sin became sinful, that is, caused sin, beyond measure, that is, more than before; and this [Col. 1421B] through the commandment, once given, whereby he strove more fiercely to subject humanity to graver punishments. For through the Law he took occasion to work death upon humanity.

### Verse 14

> “For we know that the Law is spiritual; but I am carnal, sold under sin.”

“For we know,” etc. As though he said: “The Law is truly not evil but good, for we know that it is spiritual,” that is, nourishing the human spirit while it instructs concerning spiritual matters; or “spiritual,” that is, given by the Holy Spirit. [Ambrose] Observe that the Mosaic Law is called both just and spiritual. The Gospel Law, however, is called the Law of the Spirit. For toward the wicked—that is, insofar as it punishes the wicked—the Mosaic Law is called just; but toward the good it is spiritual, because it forbids sin and the worship of visible things. Therefore the Mosaic Law is called spiritual because it contains the things of God and because it is to be understood spiritually. [Augustine] But the Law of the Spirit is the Gospel Law, because there God himself is present. There are words; here is the reality.

“But I”: up to this point he excused the Law, which ought not to bear blame. Here he says that blame ought not to be imputed to the principal nature, that is, reason, according to what it has from God, and consequently not to the Creator, but to human beings who have corrupted themselves and are unable to resist depraved habits. As though he said: “The Law is spiritual, but I am carnal,” that is, unable to resist the devil because of the soul’s vice, a vice I contracted through covetousness, having been born from flesh. And he adds whence this comes: [Col. 1421D] “I,” he says, “was sold in the first parent, so that I am under sin.” [Augustine]

As though he said: “Here is why I am weak: from the fault of the first human being, who for the pleasure of forbidden food sold both himself and all others.”

[Note: [Col. 1421D] Augustine, in the book *Collations*.] Adam first sold himself, and through this all his seed was subjected to sin, so that it could not employ its own power in obedience to the Law. For by Adam’s transgression and, so to speak, ruinous bargain and fraudulent eating, we were sold. Deceived by the serpent’s persuasion, he consigned all his offspring to perpetual slavery by receiving forbidden food. And this custom is observed among sellers and buyers: one who wishes to make himself the property of another master receives from his buyer some price for the loss of his own liberty and the addition of perpetual servitude. This too plainly intervened between Adam and the serpent. For Adam received from the serpent the price of a harmful liberty, namely a death-dealing fruit, and departed from natural liberty. He preferred to give himself over to the serpent’s perpetual slavery—from whom he had received the deadly price of the forbidden fruit—rather than thereafter be bound by the condition of the commandment. Thus, not without justice, he subjected the entire offspring of his posterity to the service of him whose slave he became.

[Note: [Col. 1422D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] He could sell us, but he could not redeem us. He sold us by consenting to sin; we are redeemed by the righteousness of faith. For innocent blood was given for us so that we might be redeemed. Let pride therefore blush in the seller; let grace glory in the redeemer. [Col. 1422B] A person sold himself through free choice, under the dominion of iniquity, and received as the price a slight pleasure from the tree of life. The first human being was created upright, without fault and without vice; but he did not keep himself upright, because he abandoned his ruler and turned aside to the deserter. Falling from the hand of the potter, he became a broken vessel. God permitted this so that by his misery he might prove that without God he can do nothing. Thus by voluntary covetousness he sold both himself and others, so that they might be under sin—that is, slaves of sin. Since he did not wish to restrain himself when he could, it was imposed on him that he could not do so even when he wished. By an evil willing he lost the good ability; and, made captive, he says, “I am sold under sin.” [Ambrose] Or each person has sold himself by the habit of his own will.

### Verses 15–18

> “For what I do, I do not understand. For I do not do the good that I will, but the evil that I hate, that I do. But if I do what I do not will, I agree with the Law that it is good. But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me; for I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh.”

“For what I do,” etc. He proves that he is a slave of sin, and speaks in the person of a human being under the Law. As though he said: “I am truly under sin—that is, a slave of sin—[Ambrose] because what I do according to the outer person, by omitting good or doing evil, I understand according to the inner person ought not to be done; for he sees himself know one thing through the Law and do another.” [Haimo] Note that here the Apostle assumes the person of two human beings: the inner, that is, the mind, and the outer, that is, the flesh or carnality.

“For,” etc. As though he said: “I truly do what I do not understand, because I both omit the good that I will and do the evil that I do not will.” This is proof from parts and from effect. For omitting good and doing evil are parts of doing evil. In broad and customary speech, a person who omits good is also said to do evil. “I will” and “I do not will” are effects of “I understand.” For from a person’s understanding that one thing is good and another evil, he wills the former [Col. 1423A] and does not will the latter. [Ambrose] This is what he means: “I do not do,” according to the outer person, “the good which I,” the inner person, “will,” that is, approve.

For a person subject to sin does what he does not will. By nature he indeed wills the good, but this will is without effect unless God’s grace adds its own willing, so that the good may be loved and brought into effect. There is a threefold willing: the willing of nature, the willing of grace, and the willing of vice. The willing of nature is powerless by itself, earns no crown, and is overcome and drawn away by the willing of vice unless the willing of grace comes to help. The willing of grace drives away the willing of vice and sets free the willing of nature. 35 Therefore this unredeemed person, lacking grace, says: “I do not do what I will, but I do what I hate,” that is, evil.

“But if,” etc. Above he showed that the carnal person is a slave of sin, from which evil comes. [Col. 1423B] [Ambrose] Here he shows the other point: that the nature created good by God agrees with the Law and does not naturally do the evil prohibited by the Law. Thus he proves that the Law is good, because he says that what the Law commands accords with his nature, since unwillingly he does what the Law forbids. As though he said: “I do not do what I will, and I do what I do not will. But if, though I do not will to omit it, I nevertheless omit what the Law commands; and though I do not will to do it, I nevertheless do what the Law forbids, then I, according to the inner person, agree with the Law—that is, I will the same as the Law. The Law forbids what I do not will and commands what I will. I say that I agree with the Law and testify that it is good.”

“But now”: because he agrees with the Law in not willing what it forbids, he shows that something else, namely sin, prompts him to do this. As though [Col. 1423C] he said: “I said, ‘I do evil’; but I, the inner person, do not do it. This is now clear, because I do not will it and agree with the Law.” This is what he means: “But now I, the inner person, already under the Law, before the time of grace, no longer do it; [Augustine] but sin”—that is, the law of the flesh, to which the devil comes as to his own law—“which dwells,” that is, is always, “in me,” namely in my flesh. Or “in me” means against my salvation.

[Note: [Col. 1423D] Augustine, in the prologue to the Epistle to the Romans.] Care must be taken lest anyone suppose that these words remove free choice from us. This is not so. For the human being here described is under the Law before grace. A person is then convicted of sin when he strives by his own powers to live rightly without the help of liberating grace. Grace frees free choice so that the person may believe in the Liberator and thus not sin against the Law.

“For I know”: as though he said, “This makes clear that sin dwells in the flesh, because good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh, namely in the sensual person.” [Ambrose] And I know this, because good does not dwell there. How does sin dwell in the flesh when it is not a substance but a privation of good? Behold: the body of the first human being was corrupted through sin, and that very corruption remains in the body by the condition of the offense, retaining the force of the judgment God pronounced in Adam; by association with it the soul is stained with sin. [Augustine] Therefore sin is said to dwell in the flesh because the cause of its occurrence remains in it. This is [Col. 1424A] the law of the flesh, to which the devil comes, [Ambrose] in order to deceive a person by evil suggestions and prevent him from doing what the Law commands.

### Verses 18–20

> “For to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find. For I do not do the good that I will, but the evil that I do not will, that I do. But if I do what I do not will, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me.”

“For to will”: as though he said, “Good truly does not dwell in me, because neither the willing nor the accomplishing of good is there. The willing of good is not there? For the willing of good is present with me”—that is, it lies and rests beside the flesh, powerless by itself to rise to good action. Therefore willing lies beside the flesh because it is natural, in a sense, to will [Col. 1424B] good through reason; but this willing is such that it is always overcome by the force of the flesh. God’s willing, however, overcomes the flesh. [Ambrose] Observe that the things commanded by the Law are good, so much so that a person naturally loves and wishes to do them; but the power to accomplish them is absent. Hence he adds: “But to accomplish the good I do not find at all,” because he is so pressed by sin’s dominion that he cannot go where he wishes, nor can he—or dares he—resist, because another is lord over his power.

Therefore, even if he wills, he cannot accomplish the good, because this comes from God alone, whose grace he still lacks. “For”: as though he said, “I say that I do not find the ability to accomplish good. I show this in the particular case where it would seem least likely, because I do not even find that good which I will; rather, on the contrary, I find evil, because I do even what I do not will.” And this is the meaning: “For I do not do this good which I will, but on the contrary I do this evil which I do not will.”

Or continue thus: “I do not find good; nor is this surprising, because it is not there, and indeed it is not. For I do not do what I will,” etc. He says this because many foolish persons do not find good in some thing even though it is there.

“But if I do what I do not will,” etc. He concludes the preceding argument, namely that he does not do evil. As though he said: “I do not do what I will, and I do what I do not will. But if I do what I do not will—namely, omit good and do evil—then I do not do it,” that is, I do not do the evil, from which the earlier conclusion follows: namely, that he agrees with God’s Law. “I do not do it, but sin dwelling in me”—that is, the tinder of sin or carnal [Col. 1424D] covetousness, from which all sins arise. For every mortal sin is committed through coveting. By this he is drawn into sin: pressed by sin, he accomplishes not his own will but sin’s. [Ambrose] But because he says that a person sins unwillingly, should he appear exempt from blame? Certainly not. These things began through his own vice and desire. Since he enslaved himself by consenting to sin, sin rightly rules over him. He says this to indicate from how many evils God rescues humanity and what calamities it inherited from Adam, for which not even the Law could provide help. Thus by these benefits he displays Christ, who frees people from such great evils.

### Verses 21–23

> “Therefore I find the Law, when I wish to do good, that evil is present with me. For I delight in the Law of God according to the inner person. But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members.”

“Therefore I find”: [Ambrose] he had said that the Law is good and that nature is good, since it wills the same thing and agrees with it. Here he adds that the Law helps good nature; nevertheless the outer person—that is, the tinder of sin which comes from the flesh—overcomes these two united, so that, seeing he cannot escape by either, a person may be obligated to grace.

As though he said: “Because I do not do evil—indeed, I do not will it—therefore I find the Law to be good,” that is, useful and helpful to me, namely to reason, since it [Col. 1425B] teaches what is good and what is evil—I say, to me who wish to do good. As though he said: “From this I prove the Law is good: I do not will to do what it commands, because,” etc. As though he said: “I rightly say only that I will the good, because I cannot accomplish it. This is because evil is present,” that is, lies near in ambush, “to me,” namely reason. For it is in the flesh, as it were at the soul’s door, and therefore forces a person to do otherwise than he and the Law will.

“For I delight,” etc. As though he said: “The Law is truly good for reason, because I delight in God’s Law, willing what it commands and rejoicing to be helped by it. I delight, I say, according to the inner person.” The inner person is the mind, which he says takes delight in what the Law teaches, because sin does not dwell in the soul but in the flesh. That is, the cause of sin is not from the soul but from the flesh, because flesh derives from the stock of sinful flesh, and through propagation all flesh becomes sinful. For because flesh is propagated from Adam, it has in itself sin—that is, the cause of sin. If the soul too were propagated, it would have it as well, because Adam’s soul sinned. But if the human being had sin in himself, he would not recognize himself; now, however, he recognizes himself and delights in God’s Law.

“But I see”: as though he said: “I say that I delight in God’s Law, but I see another law, namely the tinder of sin, which reigns in my members: in the eye, for coveting; in the hand, for acting; and so forth. It is warring against the law of my mind,” that is, the Law and my reason joined together as one. The tinder, which comes from flesh and wars [Col. 1425D] against the mind, is rightly called a law, because it has been justly ordained that one who did not obey his superior should not be served by what is inferior to him, namely the flesh. Your Lord is above you; your flesh is beneath you. Serve the better one, so that the inferior may serve you. You despised the superior; you are tormented by the inferior.

I say that it is warring against me and even “taking me captive,” or “leading me captive,” through consent and action, because it rules through the habit of sinning. I say that it takes me captive, or leads me captive, under the law of sin—that is, into sin, which is called a law because it rules. This law, as stated above, is in my members, that is, it arises from flesh. The nearer it is, the more dangerous it is.

[Note: [Col. 1425D] Augustine, in the prologue to the Epistle to the Romans.] This is the evil law by which each person, entangled in carnal habit, is bound. He says that it wars against the law of his mind and takes him captive. Hence it is understood that he is describing a person who is not under grace. And because it takes me captive, therefore:

### Verses 24–25

> “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Therefore I myself serve the Law with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin.”

Unhappy man that I am, [Ambrose], because he was born under sin, carrying sin with him as an enemy, through which Satan has access to him. For Adam constructed steps by which the despoiler might ascend to his children, unless the most merciful Lord protects them. Therefore he adds: “And who will deliver me?” As though he said: I am unhappy, and I cannot free myself.

[Col. 1426B] “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” That is, from the dominion of the flesh, in which death is present. No one but some great one can do this. But behold, who will deliver me? Not the law of Moses, not the native powers of free choice, but “the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord,” whom true mercy gave to us, so that, having received through him the forgiveness of sins, a person may be raised up and thereafter be able to recover his senses, sin being kept down. For a person, relieved of evils, can resist the adversary, having received power against him while aided by God.

Notice that here he introduces the fourth law, the law of faith, stronger than the law of Moses, and calls it grace. For four laws are mentioned in this sequence: the law of nature; the law of the members, [Col. 1426C] which is taken as one with the law of sin; the law of Moses; and the fourth, the law of faith. Here the third activity—that is, the state of the human being under the law of the Spirit—is indicated. For the Apostle here speaks in the person of a human being living under grace.

“Therefore I myself,” etc. Since he said that he had been freed by grace, lest anyone grow slack and secure as though sin could no longer harm him, he specifies how this liberation has taken place: namely, if he remains in grace. Otherwise sin again takes possession. As though he said: Since grace sets free, [Ambrose], therefore I—that is, the rational and inward human being—although I still have the fuel of sin as before, nevertheless “serve,” that is, am able to serve, the law of God; and I do so “with the mind,” that is, with the will. For now the mind is free; restored by grace, and with its help recalled to good habit, it can reject evil [Col. 1426D] suggestions and overcome opposing impulses.

“But with the flesh.” As though he said: With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin; and therefore we must not act more negligently, but must beware lest it reign.

It may also be read otherwise from the words, “But I am carnal.” For the Apostle speaks in his own person, or in that of some righteous person established under grace. Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1426D] The same author, *Against the Pelagians, to Boniface*.] that he had at one time thought that this discourse of the Apostle described a person under the law, as stated earlier; but, he says, it is only a person under grace who speaks here: one who delights in the law of God and assents to it; who does not do evil or will it; who “does not know,” that is, does not approve it; and for whom there is now no condemnation, [Col. 1427A] as is shown in what follows. Yet he still says that he is carnal in these words: “But I am carnal.” As though he said: “The law is spiritual, but I am carnal.” [Note: [Col. 1427D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*.]

The Apostle appropriately says this even of himself according to the flesh, so long as he lives here, because of the movements of the flesh which he feels; and every saint says the same. Thus the same person is spiritual and carnal: spiritual because he lives according to the Spirit; carnal because he feels the desires of the flesh. Yet he is not wholly carnal, because he does not consent to those desires. Therefore, in his mortal part he is carnal, and in his spiritual part spiritual. [Note: [Col. 1427D] The same author, *Eighty-Three Questions*.] In his better part he is spiritual; in his lower part, carnal.

And because this has accrued from the sin of the first man, he adds: “I,” he says, “am sold under sin,” [Col. 1427B] that is, made subject to sin—that is, to concupiscence—at the price of Adam’s evil pleasure. For he calls this by the name of sin. From it all sins arise, namely, from carnal concupiscence. [Note: [Col. 1427D] The same author, *Against Julian*.] Whatever sins there are in words, deeds, or thoughts arise only from evil concupiscence, which was produced by sin; and if it draws and entices one who consents, it conceives and gives birth to sin.

Therefore it is from sin—that is, from the fuel of sin—and, unless restrained, it generates sin. For he explains in what way he had called himself carnal: because he does not do what he approves; and this means, “I am truly under sin.” “For what I do, I do not understand,” [Note: [Col. 1427D] The same author, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] or “I do not know,” [Note: [Col. 1428D] Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*.] according to another reading: that is, I do not approve it, accept it, find it pleasing, or consent to it.

Otherwise this would seem contrary [Col. 1427C] to the statement in which he said, “that sin might appear as sin through the commandment.” For how does it appear if it is not known? But here “I do not know” means “I do not approve.” According to this manner of speaking, the Lord says to sinners: “I never knew you” (Matt. 7). Nothing, of course, is hidden from him. But because sins are not found in the rules of commandments which truth possesses, Truth itself says, “I do not know”; and the Apostle says, “I do not know”—that is, I truly do not approve.

“For I do not do the good that I will,” namely, not to desire wrongly; “but I do the evil that I hate,” that is, I experience concupiscence from the flesh. Even if I do not give consent by reason, I still struggle; I have not yet conquered. Great is my conflict, [Col. 1427D] because even if I do not consent to concupiscence, I still desire wrongly and do what I do not will. Therefore I do what I do not will; I do what I hate. What do I hate? Wrong desire.

[Augustine] It must not be understood that the Apostle wished to be chaste and was an adulterer, or wished to be merciful and was cruel, or the like. Rather, on hearing the law say, “You shall not covet,” he recognized and hated the vice. He had a war, because he wished not to covet and yet did covet. Therefore he says, “I do what I do not will,” that is, I covet. This does not mean that the Apostle follows concupiscence and is drawn by it [Col. 1428A] into evils. He was wrestling, not being subdued.

He sets these things before you concerning himself, lest you despair regarding this life. He places his own conflict before your eyes, lest you fear your own. For if the Apostle had not said this, when you saw concupiscence stirring in your members, you would despair and say: “If I belonged to God, I would not be stirred in this way.” But see the Apostle fighting, and do not make yourself despairing. [Note: [Col. 1428D] The same author, *On the Words of the Apostle*.]

“But if,” etc. As though he said: I hate what I do. But if I do, from the flesh, what I do not will in my mind—that is, if I do not will what I do, namely to covet—then I consent to the law. That is, my will, which does not consent to the flesh’s concupiscence, praises the law which says, “You shall not covet.” Since I do not will it, I consent to the law—not because I do that which it commands. For what the law hates, [Col. 1428B] I do; that is, it does not approve it, since it forbids consent. In this I agree with it: because I resist concupiscence, turn my mind away, refuse it weapons, and restrain my members. Yet what I do not will—and what the law also does not will—comes to pass in me.

I will the same thing as the law, because I do not will what it does not will; and yet I do it, but do not consent to it. Indeed, I am a witness with the law that it is good, since I will what the law wills. The law says, “You shall not covet,” and I do not will to covet. If I willed to covet, I would not agree with the law. But now I do not will what it does not will, and I will what it wills; and I do what it commands, because I do not consent to concupiscence.

[Augustine] Thus the struggle to avoid concupiscence is intense. For to have no concupiscence at all belongs to the perfect person; but not to follow one’s concupiscences belongs to one struggling and [Col. 1428C] laboring. Observe how Augustine here says that the law does not will what the Apostle did not will. What the Apostle did not will and yet did was concupiscence, which occurs in the first movement and is venial sin. If, then, the law is said not to will it—that is, to forbid it—then it forbids venial sin and commands something altogether impossible to accomplish.

Moreover, this seems contrary to what is read elsewhere, where it is said that what is not within our power is forbidden, while what we cannot avoid is permitted, in the comment on “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4). To this we reply that the law does not will any unlawful concupiscence. But concupiscence in its first movement is said not to be willed in one sense; concupiscence involving pleasure and consent in another. The former it does not will—that is, it reproves and detests it, showing that it is sin. [Col. 1428D] The latter it not only shows to be sin, but also forbids it. Thus the meaning of “You shall not covet” is: know that the concupiscence of the flesh is altogether sin, and guard against it as far as you are able. [Note: [Col. 1428D] The same author, on the same passage.]

“But now,” I say, “I do what I do not will.” But now I, the inward human being, already redeemed and having received Christ’s grace, who previously was sold under sin, do not perform it. For the mind is free, but the flesh captive. Hence he adds, “but sin”—[Augustine] that is, the fuel of sin—“which dwells in me,” that is, in my flesh. Though it dwells there, this saint nevertheless lives by faith, by not consenting to it. [Col. 1429A] For evil desires exist; but if they do not reign, he himself does not do them. He would do them if he consented. The movements of evil desires which he did not consent to for carrying out sins were not actions performed by himself. [Note: [Col. 1429D] Augustine, *Against Julian. On Marriage and Concupiscence*.]

But a person who consents to the concupiscence of his flesh, decides and determines to do what it desires, and thinks that he may still say, “It is no longer I who do it,” is greatly deceived. Even if he hates it, because he consents, both are present together: he himself hates it because he knows it to be evil, and he himself does it because he has determined to do it. If he further adds this, so that he fulfills in deed what he has determined in his heart, and says, “It is not I who do it, but the sin dwelling in [Col. 1429B] me,” merely because, when he decides and acts, it displeases him, he errs so far that he does not even recognize himself. For although it is entirely he himself—his heart determining and his body carrying out the act—he still does not think that he is himself.

Therefore, the one who says, “It is not I who do it,” speaks truly only if he merely experiences concupiscence, but does not determine it by consent of the heart or bring it to completion through the service of the body. [Note: [Col. 1429D] The same author, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] Moreover, when we do not obey the movement of unlawful desire, we do not perform it in cooperation with it; yet we are said to do it because it is not a force of another nature, but a weakness of our own nature that produces it. From this we shall be delivered in the future. But because we are not without sin here, we have desires of sin; yet we no longer perform them by obeying them, but the sin dwelling in us performs them by stirring them up. And it is a great thing [Col. 1429C] that, although concupiscence is from the flesh and the members of the body belong to the flesh, sin—that is, the flesh’s concupiscence—does not nevertheless reign.

“For I know.” As though he said: I rightly said that sin dwells in me; for I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. [Note: [Col. 1429D] The same author, in a certain sermon.] He certainly says this because a defect of the flesh is not good in a good thing. When that defect has ceased to exist, there will still be flesh, but it will no longer be damaged or defective. [Note: [Col. 1429D] The same author, *Against Julian*.] For this is the vice of concupiscence, which the mind too contracts from the flesh. Human nature was not originally established with this defect by God’s work; rather, it was wounded by the defect transmitted from the choice of will made by the first human beings.

For willing is truly good; it does not dwell in the flesh. “For to will the good is present with me,” that is, it is in me; “but to accomplish [Col. 1429D] the good I do not find,” that is, it is not in me. [Note: [Col. 1429D] The same author, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] He does not say “to do,” but “to accomplish,” because he does not do nothing: he resists concupiscence and does not consent. Another man’s wife may please him, but he does not assent; he turns his mind away, enters the inner chamber of his mind, sees concupiscence clamoring outside, and inwardly cleanses his conscience from evil. [Note: [Col. 1430D] Augustine, in a sermon *On Spiritual Combat*.]

Therefore he does good because he does not consent to concupiscence; but he does not accomplish the good, namely, so as to have no concupiscence whatever. Likewise [Col. 1430A] his enemy, namely concupiscence, does evil because it stirs up evil desire; but it does not accomplish evil because it does not drag him into evil. The whole life of the saints is spent in this warfare.

“For I do not,” etc. As though he said: I truly do not accomplish the good. “For I do not do this good which I will”—[Augustine] that is, not to covet—“but I do this evil which I do not will,” that is, I covet. “But if I do that which I do not will, it is no longer I, the inward person, who perform it, but sin,” that is, the fuel of sin, “which dwells in me.” For I do not consent with my mind, but experience concupiscence in my flesh. And because I do not perform it, therefore I find the law to be good, because it shows evil to me—that is, to reason—when I will to do good. I say “will” only, because evil lies close at hand to me—that is, the defect of concupiscence is present in me.

And I truly will the good, for I delight [Col. 1430B] in the law of God according to the inward human being—that is, inwardly in the mind, which is often called the inward or the higher person because, fecundated inwardly and from above by the Holy Spirit, it directs its attention to higher things. [Note: [Col. 1430D] The same author, *On John*.] Behold, freedom has been restored in part, namely according to the mind.

When these and similar points are considered in the context of this apostolic Scripture, it is rightly understood that the Apostle signified not only himself in his own person, but also others established under grace. Whether this is better understood as spoken in the Apostle’s own person or in the person of the universal human being established under grace is not entirely clear.

“But I see,” etc. As though he said: I delight in the law, “but I see another law in [Col. 1430C] my members.” [Note: [Col. 1430D] The same author, *On John*.] Behold, weakness still remains in part. The law in the members which wars against the mind is the defect of the flesh, arising from the punishment of sin and from the transmission of death. [Note: [Col. 1430D] The same author, *Against Julian the Heretic*.] Yet this law which is in the members has been remitted through spiritual regeneration and remains in mortal flesh. It has been remitted because the guilt has been removed by the sacrament through which believers are reborn; but it remains because it produces desires against which believers fight.

“Warring against the law of my mind”—that is, against law and reason joined together—“and making me captive,” through the flesh but not the mind, “to the law of sin,” that is, to the movement of concupiscence. [Note: [Col. 1430D] The same author, *To Valerius*.] For concupiscence itself is the law of sin. The law of the members or flesh is a certain diseased affection or weakness which stirs unlawful desire—that is, carnal concupiscence—[Col. 1430D] and this he calls the law of sin, since it keeps our flesh captive. [Note: [Col. 1430D] The same author, *On the Words of the Lord*.] Therefore the law of the flesh makes me captive under the law of sin itself, that is, under its own concupiscence. It leads me captive through the flesh, not through the mind; not wholly, but in part, because the mind resists and delights in the law of God.

This is suitably understood of the Apostle himself, who says that he is led captive through the flesh. For the mind does not consent to sin when it tickles, urges, or flatters, because it has inwardly other delights, not comparable in any degree to the delights of the flesh. Thus death strives, but the mind does not consent; and in me there is something dead and something living. [Note: [Col. 1431D] Augustine, *To Valerius*.]

Or the law of sin is understood as consent to and performance of sin. But the law of the flesh or members is the first movement of concupiscence. This is the meaning of, “I see another law,” namely a movement of concupiscence in my members: in the eye, for coveting, and likewise in the other members, “warring against the law of my mind.” This does not change. [Note: [Col. 1431D] The same author, in the same work.] “And making me captive,” that is, attempting to make me captive under the law of sin, so that I may consent in mind and fulfill sin in deed.

Or rather, the law of the members and the law of sin are the same: namely, carnal concupiscence. Thus the meaning is: “making me captive in the law of sin,” that is, under [Col. 1431B] that very law. [Note: [Col. 1431D] The same author, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] “Which is in my members.” But, as stated above, it makes me captive through the flesh, not through the mind.

What am I to hope for? Deliverance in Christ must be awaited. [Note: [Col. 1431D] The same author, *Against Adamantus*.] For I, a spiritual person because I am also carnal, am unhappy—not in my mind, but in my flesh—and so forth: “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” That is, from the gathering of impending evils, namely from the movements of concupiscence by which our body is struck, in which sin dwells. Or, “from this body of death,” that is, from this body insofar as it is mortal.

[Augustine] It will not be delivered in such a way that it no longer has this body. For it will have this body, but it will no longer be a body of this death. It will be the same body, and it will not be the same: it will be the same because the same created thing will remain; it will not be the same because it will not be mortal. It will be delivered [Col. 1431C] then, when “this mortal puts on immortality,” where no concupiscence will remain. But by whom will it be delivered? Through whom? “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.” For as death came through one human being, so through one human being will come the resurrection of the dead. But meanwhile, what will there be now? Conflict and struggle. Hence he adds: “Therefore I myself,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1431D] The same author, *On John*.]

As though he said: With my mind I delight in the law, and with my flesh I am led captive. Therefore I myself—that is, one and precisely the same person—serve with mind and flesh: with the mind I serve the law of God by not consenting to sin; but with the flesh I serve the law of sin by experiencing concupiscence. Therefore I myself serve in the flesh; I myself serve in the mind. [Note: [Col. 1432D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] For we are not two beings opposed to each other, coming from different principles; rather, I myself serve [Col. 1431D] the law of God with my mind, but serve the law of sin with my flesh, as long as weakness struggles against health. For the one in the flesh is not another than the one in the mind: I am in the mind, and I am in the flesh, and I am more in the mind than in the flesh. [Note: [Col. 1432D] The same author, *On the Words of the Apostle*.]

For there are not two opposed natures, as the Manicheans falsely claim, but one human being made from both, because there is one God by whom the human being was made. Therefore, with my mind I do not consent; with my flesh I experience concupiscence. Thus there is always conflict in this body of death, because concupiscence itself [Col. 1432A] with which we were born cannot come to an end while we live. It can be diminished daily, but cannot come to an end.

## Chapter VIII

### Verses 1–2
