> “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death.”

“There is therefore,” etc. As though he said: Because I serve the law with my mind, therefore there is now no condemnation—though there was before, there is not now—for those who are in Christ. [Note: [Col. 1432D] The same author, in a sermon *On the Concupiscence of the Flesh*.] I say that there is none for those who are in Christ Jesus, in whom all things are loosed. Therefore there is no condemnation for them, because—even though stains arising from the flesh remain—they do no harm. For although they have desires of the flesh to which they do not consent, and although the law in their members wars against the law of their mind, [Col. 1432B] still there is no condemnation, because through the grace of baptism and the washing of regeneration both the guilt with which they were born and whatever evil consent they previously gave to concupiscence—in thought, speech, or action—have been removed.

He then defines who are in Christ by saying: “Who do not walk according to the flesh.” As though he said: There is no condemnation for those who do not walk according to the flesh, that is, who do not obey the flesh, even if they sometimes fall.

“For the law.” Here he shows through what the grace of God frees: namely, through the Holy Spirit. He had said that there is no condemnation for those who do not walk according to the flesh, and someone might ask: “Can you avoid walking according to the flesh?” He replies: “I can, because the law of the Spirit,” etc.

Or the connection may be understood thus: There is no condemnation because [Col. 1432C] “the law of the Spirit”—that is, the Holy Spirit, who teaches what must and must not be done, and who is the giver of life—has freed me from the law of sin and death; that is, from the law of Moses, which, through sin—that is, transgression—is a cause of death. And this is “in Christ Jesus,” that is, through Christ, who gives that Spirit.

[Ambrose] Or, “the law of the Spirit” is understood as the law of faith, which is called spirit because God, whose faith it is, is spirit. [Note: [Col. 1432D] The same author, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] Three laws must be distinguished here, and this distinction is quite necessary. “The law,” he says, “of the Spirit of life”: behold one law. “From the law of sin and death”: behold another law. And “what was impossible for the law”: behold a third law. This is the law given through Moses on Mount Sinai.

Therefore the two laws here are good: the law of faith, which removes sin, [Col. 1432D] and the law of Moses, which reveals and forbids sin. But the law of sin is evil because it makes persons guilty. [Augustine, Ambrose] We must also observe the difference between “the law is spiritual,” said earlier about the Mosaic law, and “the law of the Spirit,” said here of the law of faith. The difference is this: the law of Moses is called spiritual because it forbids sinning, but it is not called Spirit or life because it did not give life through the remission of sins. But this is called the law of the Spirit of life because it both does not will sin and recalls from death; and because belief is by the spirit—that is, the mind—and what is believed is spirit, and the one whose faith it is, is spirit.

[Augustine, Haimo] As though he said: Therefore there is no condemnation: the law of the Spirit of life—that is, the law of faith, through which we are made alive, and which the Spirit places in the heart—has freed me. This liberation has been effected in Christ Jesus, who justifies through faith, and without faith in whom there is no justification. From what has it freed me? [Note: [Col. 1433D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] From the law of sin and death, that is, from consent to and performance of sin, which is the cause of death—something the third law, that of Moses, could not do.

The law of the flesh, as stated above, is not God’s law but the law of sin and death, and it makes persons guilty. The law of Moses, however, is holy and God’s law: it reveals evil but does not remove it. But the law of the Spirit, which is the law of faith and grace, removes evil.

### Verses 3–5

> “For what was impossible for the law, [Col. 1433B] in that it was weakened through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and concerning sin, condemned sin in the flesh, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. For those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh; but those who are according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit.”

“For what was impossible.” Here he explains how liberation was effected in Christ. As though he said: [Augustine] I rightly say that we have been freed in Christ Jesus; for God is in Christ his Son, and thus our liberation can occur through him, whereas it could not occur through the law. This is the meaning: God the Father sent his Son—that is, he made his Son visible, the Son who is consubstantial with him.

[Col. 1433C] He did not send him to a place where he was not, for he is everywhere. He came into the Virgin who had already been in the Virgin whom he created and chose; whom he chose, he created. By coming into the Virgin’s womb, he brought fruitfulness to the Virgin but did not take away her integrity. But if he was already there, how did he come? Because he began to be there in another way than he had been before. For he was there through the union of nature in a way in which he had not been before. Thus he was also in the world and is said to have come into the world because he appeared visibly to the world.

I say that he was sent “in the likeness of sinful flesh”: not into sinful flesh, but into flesh like it in capacity for suffering, mortality, and other defects. [Note: [Col. 1433D] The same author, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] All other human flesh is sinful flesh; his alone is not sinful flesh, because his mother conceived him not through concupiscence [Col. 1433D] but through grace. Yet it bears the likeness of sinful flesh, because he hungered, thirsted, slept, and so forth. [Ambrose]

Therefore, although Christ’s flesh is the same as ours, it was not made in the womb as ours is. For it was sanctified in the womb, born without sin, and he himself never sinned in it. Thus it is like ours in punishment, not in the quality of sin. [Origen] For he came to an immaculate body: he possessed the nature of a body but entirely lacked the pollution of sin conceived from the movement of concupiscence. Therefore it was not sinful flesh because it was not born from carnal pleasure; yet it was like sinful flesh because it was mortal.

[Col. 1434A] God sent his Son into this likeness in order thus to condemn sin. Hence he adds: “And concerning sin.” As though he said: He sent his Son, and in sending him—that is, by making him knowable and visible through his humanity—condemned sin, that is, destroyed the devil, “concerning sin” committed in Christ’s flesh—that is, because of the sin which he committed against Christ’s flesh. [Ambrose] For by this he lost dominion over the souls he had held, as was shown above.

Or, “he condemned sin,” that is, he weakened sin: he condemned the fuel of sin proceeding from Adam’s sin. I say, “in Christ’s flesh,” with which our old man was crucified, as was shown above.

[Augustine] Or, he condemned all sin—that is, he destroyed it—in Christ’s flesh. And he shows how it was done in the flesh: “concerning sin,” that is, because he was made [Col. 1434B] a sacrifice for sin. For he bore our sins in his body upon the wood and there destroyed them. [Augustine] He speaks in this way because in the Old Testament sacrifices for sins were called “sins”; thus through him sin is condemned.

“So that the justification of the law”—that is, the righteousness which the law of Moses promised—“might be fulfilled,” that is, brought to completion, in us. For the Mosaic law only commands, but the law of the Spirit fulfills: in us, I say, who do not walk in actions according to the flesh, even if we sometimes fall, but according to the Spirit. [Note: [Col. 1434D] The same author, *On the Same*.] One does not walk according to the flesh who does not do the works of the flesh; one walks according to the Spirit who is aided by the Spirit in the mind, so as not to follow concupiscences.

Behold, he has said that two things were accomplished through Christ: sin was condemned, [Col. 1434C] and righteousness fulfilled. To accomplish these two he says the law was powerless, adding, “what was impossible,” etc. As though he said: He condemned sin—which the law, natural or written, could not condemn—and fulfilled righteousness, in which matter, namely in accomplishing justification, the law was weakened through the flesh: either through fleshly observances, which could not justify, or through the flesh—that is, through the fuel of sin, through carnality which rebelled and, upon hearing the law, was further incited. Thus the law of the letter was weak through the flesh, and therefore unable to free from the law of sin and death.

“For those who,” etc. Truly, one who walks according to the flesh is not righteous, because neither is the one who is according to it. This is the meaning: “For those who are according to the flesh,” that is, who consent to the flesh with their mind, are not righteous. Why not? Because they set their minds on the things of the flesh—that is, they are intent and inquisitive in fleshly matters, desiring carnal things as the highest goods—which is contrary to righteousness.

“But those who.” He proves that one who walks according to the Spirit is righteous because the one who is according to it is also righteous. This is what he says: the one who is according to the flesh sets his mind on fleshly things; but those who are according to the Holy Spirit—or according to reason—by consent, that is, who consent to what the Holy Spirit teaches or reason suggests, set their minds on the things of the Spirit. [Haimo] That is, they are diligent in fulfilling what the Spirit approves.

### Verses 6–7

> “For the prudence of the flesh is death; [Col. 1435A] but the prudence of the Spirit is life and peace, because the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God. For it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be.”

“For the prudence of the flesh.” As though he said: Truly, one who sets his mind on the things of the flesh is not righteous. For the prudence of the flesh is eternal death—that is, whoever has the prudence of the flesh is worthy of eternal death. This is when a person diligently fulfills the things of the flesh, seeking temporal goods and fleeing evils, and when he follows only the natures of things. This is a grave sin.

It is called prudence, though it is foolishness, because it seems so to worldly persons. The prudence of the flesh is death. But the prudence of the Spirit, which exists when someone diligently does spiritual things, is life—that is, the cause of future life—and peace of mind here; or it is life [Col. 1435B] and peace, that is, life together with the peace which will be in the future.

Truly, the prudence of the flesh is death because the wisdom of the flesh—that is, the disposition so intent upon fleshly things—is hostile to God. That is, one who is wise according to the flesh is God’s enemy, because he does not make God his end; or because he thinks that God can do nothing beyond what appears in the natures of things. [Ambrose] And it is truly hostile to God, for it is not subject to God’s law: namely, one who is wise according to the flesh does not obey God’s good ordinances. [Note: [Col. 1435D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*.]

Observe that he frightens us away from obedience to the flesh by listing these points. And it is truly not subject to the law of God, “nor indeed can it be subject.” What does “cannot” mean? Can a human being not do so? Can the soul not do so? Can the flesh itself, God’s creature, not do so? Certainly it can. But the prudence of the flesh cannot; that is, nature can, but vice cannot. [Col. 1435C] Yet the physician came for this purpose, to drive out the vice. For the Savior came to the human race and found no one healthy: that is, the great physician came to heal the defect. Once the defect has been healed, nature is restored.

This is said against the Manicheans, who wished to posit another nature of evil opposed to God, confirming their error from this word of the Apostle. But one and the same human nature, created good by the good God, which yesterday was wise according to the flesh, today is wise according to the Spirit. While it possesses the defect, it cannot be subject to the law of God, just as lameness cannot be subject to straight walking. But remove the lameness and you will see straight walking. Thus, once the defect has been excluded, nature is healed. Why should I linger over each particular?

[Col. 1435D] ### Verses 8–11

> “But those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, provided that the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him. And if Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the Spirit lives because of justification. And if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, because of his Spirit dwelling in you.”

Those who are in the flesh, that is, who follow the desires of the flesh and delight in its pleasures, cannot please God. [Col. 1436A] But you. He turns his words to the Romans themselves and shows that he understands being “in the flesh” not as a matter of life, but of vice. As if he said: Those who are in the flesh do not please God; but you, Romans, are not in the flesh, that is, you do not perform the works of the flesh. [Ambrose] As if he said: What was said above was not said concerning you; rather, you are in the spirit, that is, in those things which reason counsels—provided, however, that the Spirit of God dwells in you. Here he teaches how one walks according to the spirit: namely, if one possesses the Spirit of God. Note that he expressed this ambiguously, because those brought under the law were not yet perfect in faith, though there is hope of progress.

But if anyone. As if he said: If anyone has the Spirit of God, he is not in the flesh. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that is, of God—for [Col. 1436B] the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ are the same Spirit—he does not belong to him, that is, he is not a member of Christ. Here is the source of walking according to the flesh: namely, that one does not possess the Spirit of Christ; this occurs when one lives according to the inclination of the flesh, or according to deeds of the flesh—that is, when the mind consents to the flesh or carries its works into action. According to these two points, a distinction was made above between walking according to the flesh and being according to the flesh.

But if. As if he said: Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him; but if Christ is in you—who is one with the Holy Spirit—this is to say, if the Spirit of Christ is in you, then the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives because of justification. That is, although the body is dead, nevertheless the spirit lives. [Augustine] [Col. 1436C] Note that he does not say “mortal,” but “dead.” Before sin it was mortal, that is, capable of dying; but after sin it became dead, that is, having within itself the necessity of dying. Accordingly he aptly added, “because of sin,” namely original sin. This is the source of this mortality. Or: “the body is dead because of sin,” namely sin to be avoided; for this weakness is retained so that, through the punishment one experiences, one may fear sinning more.

[Ambrose] Or, by the name “body” he signifies the whole human being, just as the prophet Ezekiel conversely signifies the whole human being by the name “soul,” saying: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18). One who was formerly dead in sins afterwards lives through the grace of the Spirit. The sense is: If the Spirit of Christ is in you, though the body is dead—[Col. 1436D] that is, though the human being has been dead because of sin, that is, in sins—nevertheless the spirit, that is, the soul which had been ungodly, lives because it is joined to God, who is life. And this is because of justification, that is, the remission of sins which comes from the Holy Spirit.

But if the Spirit, etc. As if he said: This already belongs to you, that the spirit, that is, the soul, lives through righteousness. “But if,” that is, if the Spirit of him, namely God the Father, who raised Christ from the dead, dwells in you—this is the reason why he will raise others, because Christ has been raised—then he who was able to do this, namely who raised Christ Jesus from the dead, as has been said, will make alive also [Col. 1437A] your mortal bodies, that is, your impassible and immortal bodies. [Note: [Col. 1437D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.]

He does not say “dead,” as they now are, although above he said that the body is dead; rather, he says “mortal,” such as the human body was even before sin. It was then mortal but not dead, because it could die if the human being sinned, but did not have within itself the necessity of dying—just as this body of ours can be capable of sickness without being sick. Thus that body was already then mortal, but through sin it became dead, that is, necessarily destined to die. Before sin, therefore, the body was animal, namely such that it was not necessary for it to die; now it is dead, namely such that it must die. “Animal” is the same as “mortal.” He therefore rightly says “mortal,” and not “dead,” [Col. 1437B] because in the resurrection, when this mortal puts on immortality, not only the necessity of dying, which it now has, but not even the mortality which the animal body had before sin, will remain. This happens not because of our worthiness nor because of our merits, [Note: [Col. 1437D] Id., *On the Baptism of Infants*.] but because of his Spirit dwelling in us, that is, because of his mercy, through which the grace of the Holy Spirit dwells in us.

It is most evident that the human being earned through sin not merely the death of the spirit but also that of the body, and that through the Holy Spirit both are delivered by Christ. [Note: [Col. 1437D] Id., *On True Religion*.] For by his gift, which is given to the soul—that is, by the Holy Spirit—not only does the soul to which it is given become safe, peaceful, and holy, but the body itself also will be made alive and will be [Col. 1437C] utterly pure in its own nature. Here is a most evident testimony concerning the resurrection, and a judgment so splendid and clear that it requires not an interpreter, but a reader.

Here also the fourth state of human life is noted. [Note: [Col. 1438D] Augustine, on Psalm 118.] In this sequence of the Apostle, four human states are indicated. The first was before the law; the second, under the law; the third, under grace; the fourth, in eternal life. In the first state, before the law, there is no struggle against the pleasures of this age. In the second, under the law, we struggle but are defeated. In the third, we struggle and conquer. In the fourth there is no struggle, but rest and eternal peace, because what is lower in us is subjected to us; it was not subjected because we had abandoned God, who is higher than we are. [Note: [Col. 1438D] Id., *Against Maximinus*.]

[Col. 1437D] Observe also that the Holy Spirit is called both the Spirit of the Father, where it reads, “If the Spirit of him who raised Christ,” and the Spirit of the Son, where it reads, “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ”; for the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. There are not two Holy Spirits, one of the Father and another of the Son; rather, there is one Spirit of the Father and the Son. Therefore, just as the Son is not from himself, but from him of whom he was begotten, so the Holy Spirit is not from himself, but from him from whom he proceeds, that is, from the Father and the Son.

But how to distinguish between that generation and this procession I do not know; I cannot do it; I am not equal to it, because both that [Col. 1438A] and this are ineffable. Therefore, just as the Prophet, speaking of the Son, says, “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53), so concerning the Holy Spirit it may most truly be said, “Who shall declare his procession?” This Trinity, then, is of one and the same substance, because the Son is not from some material, nor is he from nothing, but from him of whom he was begotten; and the Holy Spirit is not from some material or from nothing, but is from that from which he proceeds.

Therefore, brothers, etc. As if he said: Since we possess these good things from the Spirit, while from the flesh there is nothing but death.

**VERS. 12–14.—** “Therefore, brothers, we are debtors to the Spirit, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you shall die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you shall live. For all who are led by the Spirit of God are [Col. 1438B] sons of God.”

Therefore, brothers, we are debtors to the Spirit; that is, by obligation we ought to serve and obey the Holy Spirit, or reason, not the flesh, so as to live according to the flesh, that is, according to the flesh’s pleasure—although we ought to supply it with necessities, since flesh is not evil. For it is a creature of God, made by him who made the soul; neither it nor the soul is a part of God. For the whole Trinity is one God, supremely good. The soul is indeed a great good, but not the highest good. Likewise, the flesh is neither the highest good nor a great one, but a small good.

The living soul, therefore, placed between the highest and the small good—that is, between God and flesh—is lower than God and higher than flesh; it is indebted to God, to live according to him, not [Col. 1438C] indebted to flesh, to live according to the flesh’s delights. This must not be done. For if you live according to the flesh, you shall die. [Ambrose] He says this because vices arise from the bodily senses and are attributed to the flesh.

But if you put to death the deeds of the flesh—that is, if you utterly cast away what the flesh lustfully demands—and do this by the Holy Spirit, as he immediately specifies when he says, “by the Spirit of God”; or by our spirit, which nevertheless acts only through the working of the Spirit of God—if, I say, you do this, you shall live: here in righteousness, hereafter in glory. For this is our work in this life: to put to death by the Spirit the actions of the flesh, neither consenting to its desires and also reducing the desires themselves. And lest the human [Col. 1438D] mind or spirit should exalt itself and boast that it is sufficient for this, he adds: “For all who are led.”

As if he said: You who are sons can do this—and truly so. For those who are led, that is, governed, by the Spirit of God, not by their own spirit, not by a law which threatens, commands, and promises but does not help, are sons of God, that is, they serve out of love. Or he says “are led,” not “are governed,” to show the great effect of grace. For to be led is more than to be governed. [Note: [Col. 1438D] Id., in the book of Prosper’s Sentences.] We speak of someone as being led as though he himself scarcely does anything; we speak of someone as governed as though he does something. For one who is led is understood scarcely to act at all; whereas one who is governed does act, and is therefore [Col. 1439A] governed in order to act rightly. [Note: [Col. 1439D] Augustine, *On Rebuke and Grace*.]

Therefore, so that the grace of the Savior might be understood to have bestowed much, he said “are led”: not so that they do nothing, but because they are led by the impulse of grace, yet scarcely so as to act. For a person becomes a good son in proportion as the holy or good Spirit is more abundantly given him by the Father, by whom he is led and acts, and thus acts well if he is led by the Good. [Note: [Col. 1439D] Id., on Psalm 118.] Therefore, whenever he does not act—whether by doing nothing at all, or by not acting from charity—let him pray that he may receive what he does not yet possess.

**VERS. 15.—** “For you have not received again a spirit of slavery in fear; but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons.”

For you have not, etc. As if he said: You ought to be sons and not slaves. For you have not received again, as formerly under the law, a spirit of slavery in fear—that is, a spirit [Col. 1439B] which makes you serve unwillingly through fear of punishment. Rather, you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons of God, that is, the Holy Spirit, giver of the goods through which they become sons; and this is from God’s mercy. [Note: [Col. 1439D] Id., in the book *Questions on Exodus*.]

Take care not to infer, from his saying “of slavery” and “the Spirit of adoption,” that the Spirit is different, since it is one and the same Spirit—namely, he who, in the unity of the Trinity, is received as the Holy Spirit. The Apostle also shows this by saying “again.” The Spirit, therefore, is the same, but is differently received because of different works. Thus, for the Egyptians he is called a spirit of wrath, because the water divided by the Spirit harmed them; he is not called a spirit of wrath for the children of Israel, whom the divided water benefited.

Likewise, he is called the spirit of fear for the Jews because fear was instilled in them by the same Spirit by whom the law was written on the tablets: they did not yet understand grace, being convicted through the law of their weakness [Col. 1439C] and sins. But he is called the spirit of liberty for those to whom, by his work, grace and regeneration effective unto eternal life are imparted—that is, faith working through love (Gal. 5), [Note: [Col. 1439D] Id., *On the Spirit and the Letter*.] not through fear, not by dreading punishment, but by loving righteousness.

Whence, then, comes this love, except from the same source as faith itself—that is, from the Holy Spirit? It would not exist in us unless it were poured into our hearts through the Spirit. The charity of God is said to be poured into our hearts not as the love by which he himself loves us, but as that by which he makes us love him, just as the righteousness of God is called that by which we are made righteous through his gift; and the salvation of the Lord, that by which he saves us; and the faith of Christ, that by which he makes us faithful. [Note: [Col. 1440D] Augustine, on John.]

[Col. 1439D] Therefore it is one Spirit who produces two fears. For two fears are indicated here: one which is in perfect charity, namely chaste fear; the other which is not in charity, namely servile fear. In the latter, although God is believed, one does not nevertheless believe in God; and even if a good thing is done, it is not done well. [Note: [Col. 1440D] Id., in the book of Prosper’s *Sentences*.] For no one acts well unwillingly, even if what he does is good. These two fears produce two kinds of servants. There is a servant who is also a son, who fears the Lord and honors the Father. Hence the Lord says through Malachi: “If I am Lord, where is my fear? If a father, where [Col. 1440A] is my love?” (Mal. 1). And there is a servant who fears punishment but does not love righteousness.

Since fears have been mentioned, one should know that, besides natural fear, which belongs to all, there are four fears: worldly fear, which is evil and does not come from God; servile fear, which is good and from God but insufficient; initial fear, which is good and sufficient; and chaste fear, which is good and perfecting—the fear discussed here. For it begets us as sons.

**VERS. 15–16.—** “In whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’ For the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God.”

In whom. As if he said: He has given the Spirit of adoption, in whom—that is, through whom—we who are free, gathered into the Church from both peoples, cry intensely, [Col. 1440B] not ungratefully. This cry is of the heart, not of the lips; it sounds inwardly in the ears of God, as Susanna cried out with her mouth closed and her lips unmoved. The Jews indeed cried, “Abba”; the Gentiles, “Father.” Yet these mean the same thing: *Abba* is Hebrew; *Pater* means “Father” in Latin. But the Apostle used both terms because of the sacrament or mystery. Mark likewise records that the Lord uttered both in his passion.

Perhaps the Lord spoke both, in order to signify the mystery of the Church, for whom he became the cornerstone: the Church comes partly from Hebrews, to whom *Abba* belongs, and partly from Gentiles, to whom *Pater* belongs. For the Church is gathered from both peoples in the one cornerstone, who made both one, so that there might be one flock and one shepherd. In that Church the good teacher, compassionately representing its children in himself—namely, the martyrs—showed that they ought not despair if, perhaps in the time of their passion, sadness enters in through human frailty, provided that they conquer it by placing God’s will before their own. Elegantly, therefore, and not without reason, he used words from two languages, having the same meaning, because of the whole people called from Jews and Gentiles into the unity of faith.

For the Spirit himself, etc. As if he said: We truly are children; for the Spirit enables our spirit to recognize this. Thus: the Holy Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit, that is, he makes our mind recognize, while through him, remission having been effected, we do not act, that we are children of God. [Ambrose] [Note: [Col. 1440D] Id., *On Blasphemy*.] The Holy Spirit causes this to be known when remission of sins takes place in the Church through the Holy Spirit. Although the Trinity effects this remission, it is understood properly to belong to the Holy Spirit, because the Spirit is common to the Father and the Son and is the union of both; through him comes the fellowship and unity by which we become one body of the only Son of God. [Note: [Col. 1440D] Id., on John.]

For unity joins us together, and charity produces unity; charity exists only from the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Spirit is the one who makes alive, because he makes the members living. [Col. 1441A] He does not make living those which he finds separated from the body which he animates, just as the human spirit does not animate a limb which it finds severed from the body. These things are said so that we may love unity and fear separation. For nothing ought a Christian to dread so much as separation from the body of Christ. Because of this fellowship, the Holy Spirit descended upon men assembled together as one, and they spoke in all tongues, because through languages the fellowship of the human race is more harmonious. [Ambrose] Therefore the Spirit bore witness that they were children of God when, through the gift of the Spirit, the paternal mark was seen in them.

**VERS. 17–19.—** “And if children, then heirs: heirs indeed of God, and fellow-heirs with Christ, provided that we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified with him. For I reckon [Col. 1441B] that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us. For the expectation of the creation awaits the revelation of the children of God.” [Note: [Col. 1441D] Augustine, *On Eighty-Three Questions*.]

And if, etc. As if he said: We are children, and this is no small or slight thing. For if we are children, then we are also heirs, that is, participants in the same glory: heirs indeed of God, because we shall enjoy his blessedness; fellow-heirs with Christ, in whom and with whom we shall be blessed. Hence it is said: “Because we shall be like him.”

Note that, although a person is called an heir when an inheritance is secured by the death of the deceased and cannot otherwise be understood under human law, nevertheless we are called heirs of God though he does not die, because we, the children of the Bridegroom and Bride, hope for an eternal inheritance which we shall possess in the future—not through the death of the Father, who cannot die, and who is our inheritance. [Note: [Col. 1441D] Id., on John.]

Or it may be said that he will depart according to the mode in which he is now known by us. For now we know in part and see through a mirror. He will depart, therefore, so that then he may not be seen through a mirror in an enigma as now, but face to face. It may also be said that Christ our Head, departing in his passion, left us the possession of ecclesial peace, as he himself says: “My peace I leave to you” (John 14). Observe also that Christ is the inheritance of his own, and they are his inheritance. Hence: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2). Conversely: “The Lord is the portion of [Col. 1441D] my inheritance and my cup” (Ps. 15).

But by what merit are we heirs? Behold: provided that we suffer with him. As if he said: I say that we are fellow-heirs with Christ, provided that we suffer in likeness to him. This belongs to what he said above: “If you put to death the deeds of the flesh.” Yet no one can put the deeds of the flesh to death in such a way that life is free from hardship; therefore patience is necessary. I say that we suffer with this purpose: that we may be glorified.

For I reckon. As if he said: I say “if we suffer with him,” and we must suffer in order to gain glory; for I reckon, that is, I know, that the sufferings of this present time—all of them together, temporal and momentary—are not commensurate, [Col. 1442A] that is, are not sufficient, if we were dealt with strictly, to merit the future glory. For tribulation has an end; the reward will be without end, and the glory will be much greater for you than the labor here. Although that glory is now hidden—what eye has not seen nor ear heard—it will nevertheless be revealed to all, good and evil alike: not as existing in the evil, but only as existing in us, the good. Behold, the Spirit does this, which merits cannot do.

“It will be revealed,” and truly so, as he proves by the authority of those who await it. “For the expectation of the creation,” etc., as far as “for we were saved in hope.” [Note: [Col. 1442D] Id., *On Eighty-Three Questions*.] This chapter is obscure, because it is not sufficiently evident here what he now calls “creation.” According to Catholic teaching, “creation” is whatever God the Father made and formed through the Son; the Son cannot be called a creature, because all things were made through Christ.

Yet here he appears to distinguish creation from the children when he says, “The creation awaits the revelation of the children,” and “The creation will be delivered from the slavery of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God”—as though we were not creation, but children of God. Again, he says: “The whole creation groans and travails until now; and not only it, but we ourselves,” as though we ourselves were one thing and the whole creation another.

Therefore, we ourselves are called both creation and children: that we are creation is evident; but that we are children of God is not yet evident, as John says: “Beloved, we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be; when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3). [Augustine] Distinctly, therefore, before that glory [Col. 1442C] in which what we are will appear, we are called “creation” insofar as we presently suffer in soul and body while putting to death the deeds of the flesh by abstinence and enduring the stings of adversity through patience—such as we now appear. But we are called children of God according to adoption and according to what we shall be, when it appears what we shall be, which we now merit through adoption.

Thus, distinguishing the children from creation not by a difference of nature but by a difference of quality, he says: “The expectation of the creation,” that is, the creation which awaits, “awaits.” As if he said: It is continually engaged in awaiting; for the repetition denotes constancy. It awaits, I say, the revelation of the children of God, that is, when it will appear what it is to be in the future. For creation does not await the revelation of another nature, but it, being what it now is, awaits the time when it will be what it is to be. It is as though one said, when a painter is at work and colors lie beneath him ready for his work: “The expectation of the colors awaits the manifestation of the image”—not because they will then be different things or will not be colors, but because they will possess another dignity.

Or, simply, the good are called creation because they remain in God’s creation; or the same good are called creation by excellence because they are the cause of all things. This creation, therefore, awaits, because what it is does not yet appear, the revelation of the children of God; and thus all things must be endured in order that it may obtain what it awaits.

[Col. 1443A] **VERS. 20–23.—** “For the creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope; because the creation itself also shall be delivered from the slavery of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation groans and travails until now. And not only it, but we ourselves also, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, we ourselves likewise groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption as children of God, the redemption of our body.”

“For vanity,” etc. First proceed according to the interpretation in which the good are understood by “creation.” As if he said: Creation awaits, and it must await, because it has been subjected to vanity. And it can await because it does not love vain things, which are all [Col. 1443B] worldly things. This is what he says: “For creation,” that is, the good, “was subjected to vanity, not willingly,” [Augustine] that is, not loving these transient things which are vain. Hence Solomon: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. 1). For everything that is born is weak and corruptible, and therefore vain, because it cannot retain its state. Corruption itself, then, is vanity, to which creation has been subjected.

I say that it has been subjected to vanity, yet it bears this patiently because of him who subjected it in hope—that is, it patiently endures, knowing that God subjected it for the preservation of humility, but not without the consolation of this hope: namely, that this creation itself will be delivered in the future, just as Christ our Head has already been delivered.

Or: “For vanity,” etc. As stated above, “creation” denotes everything in us which presently suffers, that is, ourselves insofar as we suffer in body and soul. It is certainly creation while we put the flesh to death by fasts and adversities. And this creation, as stated above, now awaits what it shall be in the future. As if he said: It must await because creation—[Col. 1443C] that is, the human being, who now appears only as creation—has been subjected to vanity, and this unwillingly, that is, not voluntarily. For the human being sinned voluntarily, but was not condemned voluntarily. Sin, therefore, was voluntary: acting against the command of truth. But one does not voluntarily bear sin’s punishment. For one pays deserved penalties, and the punishment of sin is subjection to deception.

I say that it was not subjected voluntarily, but because of him who subjected [Col. 1443D] it, that is, because of his justice and mercy—he who both punishes sin and intends to heal the sinner—who subjected it in hope, namely this hope: that creation itself will be delivered, like us apostles. For by saying not simply “itself,” but “itself also,” he makes us understand that we must not despair even of those who have not yet believed, because they too will believe and be delivered, though they are not yet children of God. For at present they are called only creation, since they have not yet received the grace of adoption. Having lost through sin the seal of the image, the human being remained merely a creature.

And this creation itself, which is now so called since the form of sonship is not yet perfected, will be delivered [Col. 1444A] like us apostles, who are already children, although it has not yet appeared what we shall be. It will be delivered, I say, from the slavery of corruption—or inwardly, [Ambrose] that is, from the concern of seeking food, clothing, and other things by which our mortality is served—into the liberty of the glory of the children of God, that is, into the glorious liberty which the children of God shall possess. All these things will occur through the Spirit.

For we know. As if he said: Creation truly has been subjected to vanity unwillingly. “For we know”—as if he said: Believe from experience—that the whole creation groans. “The whole creation” means the human being, because the whole creation is represented in the human being; not because all angels, the exalted powers, heaven, earth, sea, and all things in them are in the human being, but because every [Col. 1444B] creature is either bodily, animate, or spiritual. Bodily creation extends through places; animate creation gives life to the bodily; spiritual creation governs the animate. And it governs well when it subjects itself to God to be governed by him.

All this creation is in the human being, because a human being understands by the spirit, like angels; senses by the soul; and exists and moves locally by the body. Therefore every creation is in the human being, because the human being understands, lives, and has a body; but not the whole of it is in the human being, because beyond the human being there are angels and other things which understand, live, and exist. This is like saying: “Every human being sees the sun,” but not the whole human being does so, because only the eye sees it. [Haimo]

Therefore the whole creation, but not the whole of creation—that is, the human being, who shares in every creation through his fallen condition—[Col. 1444C] groans. As if he said: He is constantly renewed in this, as the inchoative verb indicates, and does so out of longing for the heavenly homeland. He travails, that is, he labors with pain; as if he said, he is in labor and anxiety for the lower and upper watering-place. And this lasts “until now,” that is, until death. Or “until now,” because all the preceding fathers did this down to the present. Or he says “until now” because, although someone already established in Abraham’s bosom has ceased suffering, nevertheless, in those who have not yet been delivered, the whole creation still groans and suffers, as did that which preceded it; for in those who have not yet been delivered all pain belongs to spirit, soul, and body.

Therefore, when every human being groans and suffers, the whole creation groans and suffers. For by this universal expression he does not gather together every individual of all kinds, but all kinds of individuals. Not only, however, does that creation groan and suffer, but we apostles ourselves also, who are greater than others, because we have the firstfruits of the Spirit. Hence he adds: I say, we who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, that is, the Holy Spirit, both earlier in time and more abundantly than the rest. We ourselves, I say, groan within ourselves—or “in us.” The sense is: Not only does that creation suffer—that is, not only do body, soul, and spirit in the human being suffer from bodily difficulties—[Col. 1444D] but we ourselves, namely the apostles, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, whose spirits have already been offered as a sacrifice to God and kindled by the divine [Col. 1445A] fire of charity, groan within ourselves, apart from the body—that is, apart from bodily hardships—longing for the eternal Jerusalem.

I say that we await, confidently and bravely, unbroken either by delay or adversity, the perfect adoption as children of God: namely, that the body too may receive the benefit of adoption and that they may be children of God in every respect. For the adoption already accomplished in believers has been effected in the spirit, not in the body. The body has not yet been transformed into that heavenly change, as the spirit has already been transformed by the reconciliation of faith, turned from errors to the Lord. Therefore even in those who have believed, the body still awaits adoption. He then explains what he called adoption: “the redemption of our body,” namely that the body itself may be redeemed from mortality, [Col. 1445B] though it was previously purchased from sin. [Augustine] Or: we apostles, having misery just as others do, groan in ourselves—or within ourselves—in flesh and mind, because there is in us something over which we groan, not only on behalf of others.

If this chapter is opened up as it has been interpreted, we do not fall into those difficulties which compel many people to say certain things contrary to Catholic teaching. For I know that vain heretics have boasted many impious and foolish things about this chapter. Because the Apostle says universally, “The whole creation groans,” etc., some, such as Origen, say that even the more exalted creation, that is, the highest angels and sublime powers, suffer and groan until we are fully delivered. But this is not true. For even though they assist us, [Col. 1445C] they should be believed to do so without suffering, lest they be considered miserable—especially because he says that the very same creation which groans and suffers has been subjected to vanity. It is impious to say of the highest and most excellent angels that they are subject to vanity and must be delivered from corruption. Rather, all creation in the human being suffers, and all creation in the human being will be delivered, though not in all human beings.

Or thus: “The whole creation groans and travails,” etc. [Augustine] To travail is to suffer. [Ambrose] But the whole creation, through its daily labor, groans and suffers until now, that is, until the present time, so long as this is read. Therefore the whole creation groans and travails, that is, all the elements perform their offices with labor, as the sun and moon fulfill their appointed courses [Col. 1445D] not without labor; and this is because of us. Hence they will rest when we have been assumed; and therefore let us diligently prepare ourselves. Not only that creation of the elements groans, but we ourselves also, etc. After the worldly creation, he adds that we too await this and groan to God in order that we may be delivered from here, because for Christians this world is a sea.

**VERS. 24–26.—** “For we were saved in hope. But hope that is seen is not hope. For what a person sees, why does he hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it through patience. Likewise the Spirit also helps our weakness. [Col. 1446A] For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought; but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unutterable groanings.”

“For by hope.” As though he said: I said that we wait, and not in distrust; for we are certain, as though we were already saved. And this is what is meant by “for by hope,” as by a certain merit, we are saved—not, I say, simply “we are,” but “we have been made”; for salvation is not from ourselves. He says that we are saved by hope because the thing itself is not yet present, and thus we still remain under vanity.

“But hope.” As though he said: Hope saves; but this hope is not concerned with a visible thing. And this is what is meant: “Hope that is seen,” that is, the hoped-for thing which is seen, “is not hope,” that is, it is not subject to the virtue of hope, which concerns only things not apparent. And indeed it is not; for on what ground would this be called hope? And this is the meaning. [Col. 1446B] “For what a man sees, why does he hope for?” That is, why or how does he hope—how is he said to hope? As though he said: In no way. He says this in order that the merit of hope may appear greater and that it may therefore save.

“But if.” As though he said: What is seen is not hoped for, but rather what is not seen. But if this is so—that is, if we hope for what we do not see—this merit grows while, through patience, which bears adversities, we wait a long time, still occupied with the vain things that are under the sun. And therefore we groan, because, patiently enduring adversities, we await what we do not see; and all these things come to us from the Spirit.

“Likewise, moreover.” As though he said: The Spirit not only helps us in the matters mentioned above; but likewise, that is, by the same grace of his, while we await what we do not see, the Spirit helps our [Col. 1446C] weakness in prayer, teaching and causing us to pray as we ought. [Ambrose.] For since, as was said above, we groan and, set amid suffering, ask to be delivered, and wish things that are far off to happen immediately, or that those things by which we may come to destruction be quickly removed, the Spirit helps our weakness, lest we ask either before the proper time or for things contrary to our good. For prayer that asks contrary to reason is weak; and therefore this weakness must be helped by the Holy Spirit. He helps because he does not permit us either to ask before we ought or to ask for contrary things. [Note: [Col. 1445D] Augustine, *To Sixtus*.]

Note that not only that which prayer obtains, but prayer itself, is found among the gifts of grace. For whatever prayer obtains is plainly shown to be God’s gift, lest [Col. 1446D] a person suppose it to be from himself. For if it were in his own power, he certainly would not ask for it; rather, even praying itself is from grace. No merits precede prayer such that gifts might be bestowed not freely but as debts; for grace would then no longer be grace. And it is necessary that the Spirit should help.

[Ambrose.] “For we do not know.” Here is the weakness: “what we should pray for, as it is fitting to pray.” Here he declares that ignorance is the weakness of our prayer. For we are mistaken in thinking that what we ask is beneficial when it is not beneficial, as happened to Paul himself when he prayed that the spirit might depart from him; from God’s answer he learned that what he had asked was against his good. At times prayer is also proud and foolish, as it was in the case of the two [Col. 1447A] apostles, to whom it was said: “You do not know what you ask” (Matt. 20).

“But he himself.” As though he said: We do not know what we should pray for; but the Spirit himself intercedes—not against us, but for us—that is, he himself makes us ask, and this “with inexpressible groanings.” [Note: [Col. 1447D] Augustine, *To Proba, on Praying to God*.] He makes us groan more than can be said, both because of this exile and because of longing for the homeland; or, “with inexpressible groanings,” that is, groanings arising from an inexpressible thing. For how can that be narrated which is desired while unknown, yet not altogether unknown? For if it were wholly unknown, it would not be desired; and again, if it were seen, it would not be sought with groanings. [Note: [Col. 1447D] Id., *On the Good of Perseverance*.]

And it should be known that, according to the same figure of speech by which the Lord says to the apostles, “The Spirit speaks in you” [Col. 1447B] (Matt. 10), the Apostle here says that the Spirit intercedes with groanings. [Note: [Col. 1447D] Id., *Against the Manicheans*.] For the Holy Spirit does not groan as though he were in need or suffered distress; rather, he moves us to pray as we groan, and what we do by his moving is said to be done by him. [Note: [Col. 1447D] Id., *To Sixtus*.] Thus it is said, “the Spirit intercedes,” not because the Holy Spirit needs anything, but because he causes us to make petitions and inspires in us the disposition to intercede and groan. The assistance of the Holy Spirit is therefore expressed here. [Note: [Col. 1447D] Id., *To Sixtus*.] For the love which has been brought about in us through the Holy Spirit itself groans; it itself prays. He who gave it does not know how to close his ears against it. [Note: [Col. 1447D] Id., *On the Epistle of John*.]

Therefore what he says here must not be understood in such a way that we suppose the Holy Spirit, who is immutable God in the Trinity with the Father [Col. 1447C] and the Son, to intercede for the saints as though he were someone who was not God. Rather, it is said that he “intercedes for the saints” because he makes the saints intercede; for the Spirit, namely in himself, in the eternity of his substance, does not groan, but does so in us because he causes us to groan. This is the groaning of the dove.

By this mode of expression it is said: “The Lord your God tests you, that he may know whether you love him” (Deut. 13), that is, that he may cause you to know it. [Note: [Col. 1448D] Augustine, *Against Maximinus*.] By this trope cold is called sluggish because it makes people sluggish, and a day joyful or sad because it makes people joyful or sad. Similarly, concerning that day the Son is said not to know, because he does not cause us to know. In the same manner God said to Abraham: “Now I have known that you fear God” (Gen. 22), that is, “I have caused it to be known.” [Note: [Col. 1448D] Id., in the same work.]

[Col. 1447D] Likewise, when the Apostle says elsewhere, “But now, knowing God—or rather, being known by God,” it is so said that we understand God to have produced his knowledge in us. For what does he mean by “You have been known by God” (Gal. 4)? That is, he makes you know him. For God causes us to know him; hence we are said to be known by him. The Apostle teaches that all these statements must be understood in this way, since, when in one passage he says, “He sent the Spirit crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. 4), elsewhere, as though explaining this, he says, “In whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’” [Note: [Col. 1448D] Id., *To Sixtus*.]

[Col. 1448A] Thus here also, explaining how the Spirit helps our weakness, he says: “The Spirit intercedes for us,” etc. And it should be known that he helps differently when he does not yet dwell within, and differently when he does dwell within. Before dwelling within, he helps so that persons may become believers; dwelling within, he helps those already believers.

### Verses 27–28

> “But he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he intercedes for the saints according to God. And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called saints according to his purpose.”

“But he.” As though he said: The Spirit causes petition, and also obtains—that is, causes it to be obtained. As though he said: Not only does he intercede, but that same Spirit who searches hearts, so as to know the inexpressible groanings, knows—that is, approves and fulfills—what he desires, [Col. 1448B] that is, what he causes to be desired, because he intercedes for the saints, that is, in the place of the saints: he causes the saints to intercede for what is according to God, that is, what God wills.

The Spirit is said to search hearts not as one seeking what he does not know, but because nothing is hidden from him that he does not know. “And we know,” etc. As though he said: The Spirit not only does what has been mentioned, but that same Spirit also causes all things, prosperous or adverse, to turn to good for those who love God. We—the elders and teachers, whose authority ought to be believed—know this. Namely, we know that through the Holy Spirit all things work together for good, or lead to true good. Or, according to another reading: “The Holy Spirit works together all things unto true good.”

For whom? For those who love God, by keeping [Col. 1448C] the commandments and persevering to the end. Hence he adds: “for those,” etc. As though he said: All things work together for good for those who do not fall away—namely, for those who are called, through preachers or inwardly, saints, that is, to holiness. And this is not because of their own merit, but according to God’s purpose, that is, according to foreknowledge and predestination. (Augustine.) As though he said: Their calling comes from nothing other than God’s predestination. And from this it follows that all things work together for their good, not from their merits; for such persons all things work together for good.

For God consoles such persons by prosperity and exercises them by adversity. [Note: [Col. 1448D] Id., *On Correction and Grace*.] By their own weakness humility is exercised; by affliction, patience; by paternal contradiction, [Col. 1448D] wisdom; by hatred, benevolence. God so fully works all things together for their good that, if any of them stray and wander out of the way, he even causes this itself to advance them toward good, because they return more humble and richer. For they learn to rejoice with trembling, not arrogating to themselves confidence in persevering as though it came from their own strength. Hence: “Serve the Lord with fear,” etc. (Ps. 2), and elsewhere: “Do not be high-minded” (Rom. 12). [Note: [Col. 1448D] Id., *On the Trinity*.]

Although bodily death originally came from the sin of the first human being, [Col. 1449A] its good use has produced most glorious martyrs. Therefore not only death itself, but also all the evils of this age—the labors and pains of human beings—although they come as the due reward of sins, and especially of original sin, by which life itself was bound with the bond of death, nevertheless had to remain even after sins were forgiven, [Note: [Col. 1449D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*.] so that a person might have matters in which to contend for truth and from which the virtue of believers might be exercised; so that the new human being, amid these evils, might be prepared for the new age, wisely enduring the misery deserved by this condemned life and prudently rejoicing because it will end. These evils, therefore, which the faithful endure devoutly, are beneficial either for removing sins, for exercising and proving righteousness, or for showing the misery of this life.

Then, explaining [Col. 1449B] who those called according to the purpose are, he adds:

### Verse 29

> “For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be made conformable to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.”

“For those whom he foreknew.” As though he said: Truly all things work together for good, because he foreknows and predestines, etc. And this is the meaning. [Remigius, Augustine.] God predestined—that is, by bestowed grace prepared—that they should believe through the word of preaching, those whom he foreknew, that is, knew long beforehand. This is the purpose of which he spoke: “called according to his purpose.” He foreknew them, I say, to become conformed in purity of life now and afterward in blessedness to the image of his Son—that is, of the Son who is the image of the Father, altogether [Col. 1449C] identical with the Father. Hence it is said: “Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14).

Note that “predestination” is here taken improperly, according to the explanation just given. [Note: [Col. 1449D] Id., *On the Good of Perseverance*.] It is understood in the present sense, namely as the bestowal of grace by which persons are prepared to receive the word. Properly speaking, predestination is the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered. [Note: [Col. 1449D] Id., *On the Predestination of the Saints*.] Predestination, therefore, is the preparation of grace, which cannot exist without foreknowledge. But foreknowledge can exist without predestination. For by predestination God foreknew those things which he himself was going to do; but God also foreknew what he himself was not going to do, namely all evils. For although there are [Col. 1449D] certain things which are sins in such a way that they are also almost penalties of sin, according to the statement, “He gave them over,” etc. (Rom. 1), nevertheless sin is not God’s doing but his judgment.

Therefore God’s predestination, which pertains to good, is, as I have said, the preparation of grace; grace, as I have said, is the effect of predestination. According to this, explain the text as follows. [Augustine, Ambrose.] God predestined—that is, in his foreknowledge prepared with himself from eternity, that is, chose for the promised rewards—those whom he foreknew would become conformed to the image of his Son, so that we may bear the image of the heavenly man, that is, Christ, as we bore the image of the earthly man, Adam.

[Fulgentius.] [Col. 1450A] Therefore, whatever good things God gives to anyone, he undoubtedly foreknew that he would give them and prepared them in his foreknowledge. It must, however, be known that God has also prepared eternal fire for the wicked, namely for those whom he justly prepared to undergo punishments; nevertheless, he did not prepare them to commit sins. [Note: [Col. 1450D] Id., *On the Good of Perseverance*.] For God prepared what divine justice would render, not what human iniquity would lose. He did not prepare the unjust to lose righteousness as he prepared the saints to receive righteousness, for he has never been the author of depravity.

This rule, therefore, must be held without wavering: sinners are foreknown in their sins, not prepared for them; but punishment is prepared in accordance with what they were foreknown to be.

“So that he might be.” As though he said: I say, “conformed,” yet so that among [Col. 1450B] many brethren—that is, among many brothers—he himself may be the firstborn, that is, possessing his Father’s inheritance by right and distributing it to others, which belongs to firstborn sons. [Ambrose.] Or he is called firstborn because, before every creature, he was not made but born; because he was the first born without sin; and because he was the first to rise impassible, in whom he has brothers. [Note: [Col. 1450D] Id., *On the Creed*.] For insofar as he is the Only-Begotten, he has no brothers; but insofar as he is the Firstborn, he has deigned to call brothers all who are reborn in God’s grace through his primacy.

### Verses 30–32

> “And those whom he predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also glorified. What, therefore, shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who [Col. 1450C] is against us? He who did not spare even his own Son, but gave him up for us all—how has he not also given us all things with him?”

“And those whom.” [Augustine.] As though he said: Those whom he foreknew, he predestined. Those whom he predestined—which occurred before we existed—he also called, though formerly turned away, through preachers, because they had been prepared in foreknowledge; or he called them by an inward calling. [Note: [Col. 1450D] Ambrose, *To Opertus*.] For there is an outward calling and an inward one. The outward calling is made through preachers and is common to good and evil persons; the inward belongs only to the elect. For to call is to assist one’s knowledge of faith, or to pierce with compunction one whom God knows will hear; and this calling, as we have said, belongs only to the elect. Predestination is fulfilled by this calling.

There is another calling, performed through preachers, of which it is said: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20). “And those whom he called,” namely according to his purpose—for there are also non-elect persons called outwardly—“these he also justified” by forgiveness of sins and good works. “And those whom he justified,” while they were sinners, “them he also glorified,” [Augustine] with every kind of virtue. [Ambrose, Augustine.] Or the past tense is used for the future, so that the sense is: “He glorified,” that is, he will glorify them with eternal recompense, so that they may be like God. This [Col. 1451A] will occur in the future, but is stated in the past tense because he is said to have done what he disposed from eternity to do. Hence Isaiah says: “He who made the things that are to come.”

For such persons, as was said, all things work together for good, even their wandering, namely so that they may thereby become more cautious and not trust in themselves. This, therefore, is understood of the foreknown and not of others. For although some believe for a time and seem good, since they do not persevere, they are not glorified. [Augustine.] Note that, although four things are mentioned here—predestination, calling, justification, and glorification—one is in God and three are in us. For our predestination is not in us, but hidden with God in his foreknowledge; the other three are in us, etc. All these things belong to the foreknown.

“What, therefore, shall we say [Col. 1451B] to these things?” That is, against these things; or, what shall we say as we behold these benefits of God? Surely this: that none of our persecutors can harm us. For if God is for us, as was said, predestining us when we did not exist, calling us when we were turned away, justifying us when sinners, glorifying us when mortal, who is against us? Absolutely no one can harm us, but all things work together for good. For evil persons may indeed destroy the body further and tear it to pieces, but God our helper leads forth the soul unconquered.

“He who also.” As though he said: I say that God is for us, he who, besides other things, gave his own Son for us. This is the meaning: He did not spare even his own Son—that is, his Son consubstantial with himself—but gave him up for us all, even for sinners, which is greater; that is, he gave him up [Col. 1451C] for the restoration of all. And if he gave the Son for us, how did he not also give us all things with him—that is, righteousness in the present and eternal life in the future, which is the lesser thing? As though he said: This cannot be denied.

[Ambrose.] For it is less to give us all things than to hand him over to death for our sake. [Note: [Col. 1451D] Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels*.] Or: “With him he gave us all things,” namely things above, equal things, and things below. The higher things are ours to behold, such as God the Trinity; equal things are ours to share in fellowship, such as the angels, to whom we shall be equal in the future, though now we are inferior; lower things are ours to rule. And there are certain things now above us, such as the exalted angels and all God’s heavenly ministries; these are now ours not by dominion but by use, just as a lord’s possessions belong to servants not by power of ownership but by the ability to use them, since they use them for food, adornment, or something of that kind. Therefore angels are now superior, and in the future will be equal; thus they are ours now in one way and will be ours in another way in the future.

Note that it is said here that the Father gave up the Son. Yet the author of this cup is also he who drinks it. [Note: [Col. 1452D] Id., *On John*.] Hence the Apostle says: “Christ loved us and gave himself for us.” If, therefore, the Father gave up the Son and the Son gave up himself, what did Judas do? The Father did well in giving up the Son; the Son did well in giving up himself; Judas did evil in giving up his Master for greed. For the benefit bestowed upon us through Christ’s passion will not be credited to Judas’s wickedness. He will receive the reward of wickedness; Christ, the praise of grace. And since this is so:

### Verses 33–39

> “Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect? God is the one who justifies. Who is he who condemns? Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who also rose again—who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us. Who therefore shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or persecution, or the sword? As it is written: ‘Because of you we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we overcome through him who loved us. For I am certain that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, [Col. 1452B] nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor strength, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

“Who shall accuse?”—so that his accusation is against God’s elect, that is, so that it harms God’s elect, whom he foreknew for life? Certainly no one’s accusation harms them. The devil’s attempt, however, is called an accusation. Truly no one harms them, because neither God nor anyone else does so. Another cannot; God does not will it, because he is the one who justifies. Would he then wish to accuse his own? No.

And since no one accuses, who is he who condemns, that is, who can inflict death? No one who wishes to do so can inflict it. Christ alone could do so, but he does not will it. [Col. 1452C] Does Christ Jesus, who died for them, wish to condemn them? I say, “who died”—indeed, who also rose, which is greater, so that we too may rise; who also, what is greatest, is at the right hand of God, that is, equal to the Father, namely in the honor in which God the Father is God; or at the Father’s right hand, [Ambrose, Haimo] that is, amid God’s greater goods; who, as mediator between God and human beings, intercedes for us, not by voice, but by compassion and the presentation of his humanity, while daily offering before the Father’s gaze the human nature he assumed and the grievous kind of death he endured for us, that the Father may have mercy upon us. Since his petition is so great, it cannot be rejected.

“Who therefore.” As though he said: Since these things have been given us by God, who therefore shall separate us from God’s love? Will these adversities separate us: tribulation, that is, bodily affliction; distress, that is, anxiety of mind; persecution, which is from place to place; famine, that is, lack of food; nakedness, that is, lack of clothing; danger, that is, the onset of death; or the sword, that is, death itself? Certainly none of these will separate us.

As it is written in the Psalm in these words: “Because of you we are put to death,” by various torments, and this “because of you,” that is, because there we cling inseparably. We are put to death, I say, “all day,” that is, throughout our whole life. Or otherwise: “As it is written.” As though someone were to say: Why do you mention these things? Do these [Col. 1453A] evils happen to you? The answer: Certainly these evils happen to us, as it is written: “Because of you we are put to death all day long.” [Note: [Col. 1453D] Augustine, Sermon on the Nativity of the Lord.]

Note that he says “because of you”: by this he indicates the cause, without which the martyr’s crown is not bestowed. For punishment does not make a martyr, but the cause does. Criminals too suffered with Christ, to whom Christ was like in punishment but unlike in cause, because he suffered for us, so that we might suffer for him. In both his causes—namely, “for us” and, on our part, “for him”—provision has been made for us.

“We are reckoned,” without regard to mercy, “as sheep for slaughter,” which are useful only when killed. Behold, these evils happen to us. “But in all these things,” namely, while set amid tribulations and torments, “we overcome,” [Haimo, Ambrose] that is, we are made superior; and [Col. 1453B] this is not through ourselves, but through him who loved us, whose benefit surpasses the things mentioned. I say that we overcome, and truly: “For I am certain,” on the basis of God’s promise, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Heb. 13), “that neither death,” which they threaten, “nor life” promised to me will separate me from God; “nor angels,” the lower order; “nor principalities,” the middle order; “nor powers,” the higher order, which also works miracles. [Ambrose.] These orders are understood of evil angels, or of good angels, if that were possible; “nor things present,” namely present good or evil; “nor things to come,” good or evil; “nor strength,” that is, anyone’s violence; “nor height,” human power or Satan’s exaltation, [Augustine] namely if the devil [Col. 1453C] should display himself to us on high, equipped with the deceptions of his father, to seduce us; “nor depth,” that is, someone’s wisdom; or “nor depth,” that is, if the devil displays hell or threatens a precipice; or “neither height nor depth,” that is, neither prosperity nor adversity.

Hence Solomon says: “Give me neither riches nor poverty, lest, being filled, I become a liar, or, being poor, I steal and perjure the name of God” (Prov. 30). Many sin through elevation; many through necessity. Against this Ahaz is set forth in Isaiah: he did not wish to ask a sign from the Lord, “neither in the height nor in the depth” (Isa. 7)—a remedy in Christ, who was neither lifted up by the power by which he was equal to the Father nor troubled by the abasement of death. This is the sign in the height and in the depth, so that Ahaz might not be exalted by royal power or disturbed by affliction, as he then was because of the war of the Assyrians.

“Nor any creature,” other than those mentioned; or “other,” that is, new, namely made contrary to nature, such as a two-legged horse, if this should occur as Jannes and Mambres did, who were Pharaoh’s magicians. Nothing, I say, of these things will be able to separate us from the love of God, by which we love him, because he is better than all things. [Note: [Col. 1454D] Id., *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*.] If, therefore, no thing separates us from his love, what can be not only better but even more secure than this good?

For the very thing by which we love God cannot die, except when someone ceases to love God; and for that person death itself is not loving God, which is nothing other than preferring anything whatsoever to him in love. The love of God spoken of here is therefore the virtue which is the most upright affection of our mind and which joins us to God. This love is in us not from ourselves, but in Christ Jesus our Lord, that is, from Christ. Or he means the love by which God loves us, from which no one is separated except one divided from God; this love has been shown to us in Christ Jesus our Lord. For God showed us his love in Christ, whom he gave up for us.

## Chapter IX

### Verses 1–5

> “I speak the truth in Christ Jesus; I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit: for I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. [Col. 1454B] For I wished that I myself might be anathema from Christ for my brethren, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh: who are Israelites, whose are the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the law, and the worship, and the promises; whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.”

“I speak the truth.” [Ambrose.] Since above he seemed to speak against the Jews, who suppose themselves to be justified by the law, he now shows his wish and affection toward them. He confirms it by oath, that it may be believed more firmly; and in this way he grieves that his own race according to the flesh is deprived of Christ’s benefit. As though he said: I have spoken harshly against the Jews, but this came from love, not enmity. For I speak the truth and do not lie, being established in Christ Jesus; my conscience bears me witness—and if you do not believe me, my conscience, I say, is founded in the Holy Spirit. As though he said: The Spirit himself is witness concerning this: that I have great sorrow, that is, a stupor of mind, and continual pain in my heart, not merely outwardly but from the inmost heart.

What is the cause of this pain? My brethren—that is, Jews wandering from Christ. And I truly grieve, so greatly that “I myself wished to be anathema,” that is, separated from Christ, for these same brethren of mine. [Haimo.] That is, if it were possible, I would wish to be separated from Christ for an hour, either in this life or after death, so that my brethren [Col. 1454D] might believe.

[Ambrose.] Observe that he says, “I wished,” not “I wish,” because he knows that such an honorable member, with no preceding fault, cannot be separated from Christ. Yet he displays his feeling and love toward them, and consequently enumerates many of their distinctions, in order to awaken sorrow in all for them, because by not receiving the Savior they lost the prerogative of their fathers and of the promise, becoming worse even than the Gentiles whom they had previously abhorred. For it is more grievous to have lost dignity than never to have had it.

He then shows that he rightly grieves, adding: “who are my kinsmen according to the flesh,” and are therefore to be helped all the more; “who are Israelites,” truly according to the good, [Col. 1455A] or by descent according to all. They are those “whose is the adoption” as sons of God, that is, to whom adoption belongs because they were formerly adopted as sons; “and the glory,” because they were called God’s peculiar people, or because glory now belongs to them through the miracles they perform; “and the new covenant; and the giving of the law,” namely, what the old law conveyed figuratively; “and the worship,” that is, the worship of the one God; “and whose are the promises,” namely, those to whom the promises were made; “whose are the fathers.” Behold praise derived from their predecessors.

Then praise is drawn from their successors when he says: “from whom is Christ according to the flesh.” This is what is said in the Psalm: “A man was born in her” (Ps. 86). And although Christ was born from the fathers according to the flesh, he is nevertheless “God over all, blessed for ever.” Hence in the same psalm [Col. 1455B] it is said: “The Most High founded her.” Amen. As though he said: It is true that he himself is God.

### Verses 6–8

> “But it is not as though the Word of God had failed. For not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor are all who are Abraham’s seed Abraham’s children; but, ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called’: that is, not those who are children of the flesh are God’s children, but those who are children of the promise are reckoned as seed.”

But it is not as though it has failed—or, “but it has not failed.” [Ambrose] Because the Apostle grieved over the Jews, he consoles his grief, finding it written that not all were to be saved, but only those resembling Isaac, so that he might grieve only for those who did not believe. Yet they can believe; concerning them one need not grieve greatly, because [Col. 1455C] they are not predestined to life. For who would lament one who was long accounted dead? For God long ago decreed, foreknowing, that these would not be saved—yet He is no respecter of persons.
