For He condemns no one before he sins, and crowns no one before he conquers; but foreknowledge has determined what the future will of each person shall be, by which he is condemned or crowned.

As though he said: “The Jews do not believe in the Savior, and therefore I grieve; but this,” he says, “is what God said would happen: not all children according to the flesh would be Abraham’s seed, but those who have the faith through which Isaac was born. And this is why the Jews do not believe. Yet it is not therefore true that the word of God has failed,” or, “yet it has not therefore failed,” that is, God’s promise has not been rendered void [Col. 1455D] because not all are saved. For although some among them have gone astray, those who are true Israelites are saved, as was promised.

And this is what he says: “For not all”—[Ambrose, Augustine] as though he said: “Truly, the promise is not unfulfilled, though not all are saved; because not all who are of Israel according to the flesh are Israelites,” that is, truly belonging to Israel; “nor are all who are Abraham’s seed according to the flesh children,” that is, Abraham’s heirs. In these words he shows that grace alone, not descent, makes children of God.

Otherwise, from the passage, “I speak the truth”: above, the Apostle showed how he had been strengthened by grace, saying that nothing could separate him from Christ. Now, with sorrow, he explains how greatly [Col. 1456A] he had formerly erred when he persecuted Christ’s Church. In this God’s grace is commended. As though he said: “Now nothing can separate me from Christ, but formerly I was separated from Him; hence I now grieve.” He confirms this with an oath, saying: “I speak the truth, and do not lie,” being in Christ Jesus, while my conscience bears witness to me, founded in the Holy Spirit, who also testifies to the same thing: that I have great sorrow, that is, an astonishment of mind, and continual pain, that is, compunction, in my heart over the evils I formerly did; and thus those very evils are now turned to good.

And rightly do I grieve, because I sinned greatly. For I myself, who am now an Apostle, desired to be anathema—[Haimo] that is, separated from others—away from Christ. For *anathema* means separation [Col. 1456B] and one separated; and this was for my brethren, that is, for the Jews who are brethren in the Law, whose Law I wished to defend. Or, “for my brethren,” that is, for those whom I sought to draw back from Christ, who are now brethren in the faith, and who are also my kinsmen according to the flesh. Thus I sinned more grievously—those who are true Israelites, to whom belongs the adoption as children of God, that is, to whom it pertains, and so forth: run through what was expounded above, as far as “Amen.”

As though he said: “I, who formerly opposed this truth, now affirm it.” “But it is not,” etc. He said that the promise of the eternal inheritance had been made to the Jews; but because they, for the most part, did not believe, God’s word seemed not to have been fulfilled. He answers this objection: even if it was not fulfilled in some, it was fulfilled in others, and among the believing Gentiles [Col. 1456C] who are Abraham’s true children.

As though he said: “The Jews went astray, but God’s word did not therefore fail,” that is, the promise was not therefore unfulfilled. For God’s word fails when He does not fulfill what He promised. It truly did not fail, even though some are not saved. For not all who are from Israel are Israelites, nor are all who are Abraham’s seed Abraham’s children. These points are not changed. But Abraham’s children are those who resemble Isaac, because Scripture says thus in Genesis: “In Isaac shall your seed be called,” that is, those resembling Isaac, prefigured by him, shall be reckoned as seed. [Note: [Col. 1455D] Augustine, *Against Julian*.]

For in Isaac, Abraham’s promised son, were prefigured not those who make themselves righteous, but those whom God makes righteous. Hence He says to the Church through the prophet: “I am [Col. 1456D] the Lord who makes.” [Note: [Col. 1456D] Id., *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*.] These are the children of the free woman who is above, who is our mother. But the children of the flesh belong to the earthly Jerusalem, which is in bondage with her children. And just as Isaac did not merit the promise that he would be born, so neither did these; but by grace alone they were promised, and the adoption as children was given to them. Therefore he fittingly says, “shall be called,” because one is Abraham’s seed through God’s calling.

[Ambrose] He says “in Isaac,” not “in Jacob” or “Esau,” because Isaac’s case is different from Jacob’s and from Esau’s. Isaac was born as a type of Christ, whereas Jacob and Esau represent two peoples, namely believers and unbelievers. Yet there were good and faithful persons descended from Esau, [Col. 1457A] as Job proves, who was from Esau’s sons, fifth from Abraham, that is, Esau’s grandson. [Augustine]

Then the Apostle himself explains the authority, adding: “That is, not those who are children of the flesh are children of God.” This is the same as saying, “children of Abraham”: they are not God’s children by human activity, but those who are children of promise—that is, generated by God’s promise alone, as Isaac was—are reckoned as seed, because they are so by God’s calling. That Isaac was by God’s promise he shows from the very words of the promise, adding:

VERS. 9–13.—“For this is the word of promise: At this time I shall come, and Sarah shall have a son. And not only she, but also Rebecca, having conceived by one intercourse, by Isaac our father. For when they had not yet been born, nor had done [Col. 1457B] anything good or evil, in order that God’s purpose according to election might stand—not from works, but from Him who calls—it was said to her: ‘The elder shall serve the younger’; as it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.’”

“Of promise,” etc. And as though someone asked whether Isaac was from a promise, he answers: certainly; for this is the word of promise in Genesis: “At this time,” that is, on the same day in the returning year, “I shall come to you, O Abraham, and I shall bring this about: Sarah shall have a son,” that is, Sarah shall have a son.

“Not only she,” namely Sarah, had a promise; Rebecca also had a promise, having two sons by one intercourse with Isaac. He says this lest the parents’ merits seem to be the difference [Col. 1457C] in those born. For it cannot be said that Esau was conceived when his parents were evil, and Jacob when his parents were good. Isaac, I say, our father, that is, our founder, whom we must imitate if we wish to be children of God.

Note that the promise made to Sarah shows that no one is saved on account of lineage: Ishmael, born from Abraham, was rejected, while Isaac, born from the same Abraham, was saved by grace alone. But the promise made to Rebecca shows that no one is chosen on account of any merit of his own or of his parents, but by grace alone. [Note: [Col. 1457D] Augustine, *To Simplicianus*.] Therefore he says with the greatest care, “by one intercourse,” lest the fact that one was good and the other evil be attributed to paternal or maternal merits.

“For when,” etc. [Col. 1457D] As though he said: “Rebecca had a promise, and indeed she did, because this was said to her: ‘The elder,’ namely Esau, ‘shall serve the younger,’ namely Jacob.” And lest anyone think this came about because of their previous merit, “for,” that is, because this, was said to her, that is, to their mother, while they had not yet been born. And because they might seem to have deserved something even in the womb by struggling, he adds: “nor had they yet done anything good or evil.”

This was said so that God’s purpose, that is, God’s foreknowledge, might stand—that is, be fulfilled, or be understood to be fulfilled—according to election, that is, according to the grace which chose as it foresaw, not according to the debt of merits. For He Himself made, rather than found, those who were to be chosen. “Not from works,” as he shows: just as the saying was not because of preceding merits, so here he shows that it was not because of the future merits of either.

As though he said: “I say that this was not said because of preceding merits. Likewise I say that it was not from works”—future good or evil works, which would not have been good or evil unless grace had been added or withdrawn—“but from Him who calls,” or from calling, that is, from the grace of God who calls, that it was said to her, namely Rebecca, in Genesis: “The elder shall serve the younger.”

Literally, this can be understood of the two brothers: Esau would benefit his brother Jacob by persecuting him; for good persons benefit from the afflictions inflicted by the wicked, while their patience is exercised. [Note: [Col. 1457D] Id., *On Eighty-Three Questions*.] Or, literally, it can also be said otherwise [Col. 1458B]: the Idumeans, descended from Esau, who is also called Edom, were subject to the children of Israel and served them in David’s time. But what is chiefly intended in this prophecy is that the Jewish people, the elder—that is, earlier in the worship of the one God—would serve the younger, that is, the later people of Christians. For the Jews are our book-carriers, who carry books for us. As is written in 45.

As though he said: “Thus this was said by grace in Genesis, when they were not yet born but were to be born; just as Malachi says of the same persons after the events, namely that Jacob was chosen by grace, not merit, while Esau was rejected because grace had been withdrawn.” And this is what he says: “as it is written in Malachi.”

“Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” [Ambrose] [Col. 1458C] It should be known that foreknowledge chose the one and rejected the other. In him whom He chose, God’s purpose stands, that is, is fulfilled, because it happens as He foreknew; and likewise in him whom He rejected it stands, because it happens as He foreknew. But what is found in Malachi, namely, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated,” is God speaking now of judgment. Whereas “the elder shall serve the younger” concerns foreknowledge: foreknowing what each would become, God said this in Genesis. And in predicting this He showed Himself to have foreknowledge of future things and demonstrated that nothing can happen apart from His foreknowledge.

But the other statement in Malachi concerns events already past, from whose preceding life and works it was evident that one was to be saved and the other [Col. 1458D] condemned; judgment is ordinarily passed on deeds already done and known. Therefore God said this before the future judgment so that He might be believed to be a judge and one who renders according to merits. [Note: [Col. 1458D] Id., *To Sixtus the Presbyter*.]

God also said it so that what was later openly stated through the prophet might be understood to have been, before they were born, in God’s predestination through grace. For in Jacob, before he had been born or had done anything good, what did He love except the free gift of His mercy? And in Esau, before he had been born or done anything evil, what did He hate except original sin? For He would not in the former love a righteousness that he had not performed, nor in the latter [Col. 1459A] hate the nature which He Himself had made good.

But since he had put forward an astonishing matter concerning persons not yet born and doing neither good nor evil—namely, that God loved one and hated the other—he objects to himself the question which might trouble the hearer: how this could be right when they had done nothing. And he says:

VERS. 14–15.—“What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? By no means! For He says to Moses: ‘I shall have mercy on whom I have had mercy, and I shall show mercy to whom I shall show mercy.’”

“What then shall we say?” As though he said: “Because He chose this one without any merit and rejected that one, what then shall we say?” [Note: [Col. 1459D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*.] Shall we say that there is injustice with God, that is, that God will be called unjust? For it appears unjust [Col. 1459B] that without any merits of good or evil works He loves one and hates another. If in this matter He had considered this man’s future good deeds or that man’s future evil deeds—which God surely foresaw—he would not have said, “not from works,” but “from works.”

[Ambrose] Therefore, because He chose one without merits and rejected the other, is He unjust for this reason? By no means. He is not unjust because He loved one and hated the other, [Note: [Col. 1459D] Id., *To Sixtus*.] because He chose Jacob by mercy and rejected Esau by justice. In neither case is there injustice.

Let no one say that God chose one and rejected the other because He foresaw their future works. [Ambrose] Rather, he shows, by adding, “For He says to Moses,” that what he said serves to commend God’s grace and glory, so that no one may dare to boast of the merits of his own works. [Col. 1459C] As though he said: “Truly, He chose man through mercy, because Moses says this.” For God said to Moses—or God, introduced by Moses, said—“I shall have mercy,” by calling inwardly, “on him of whom I have mercy,” by predestining. Behold: no merits precede for which one is chosen; grace alone, by which He predestines, is the source from which one is called and saved.

Therefore he adds: “And I shall show mercy,” by giving eternal life, “to him of whom I have mercy,” by calling. Or thus: “God is not unjust but just. He knows what He does, and His judgment is not to be challenged. For He says to Moses: ‘I shall have mercy on him on whom I shall have had mercy,’” that is, I shall have mercy on him by calling and adding grace, whom I foreknew that I would give mercy to, knowing that he would be converted and remain with me.

Then he repeats it in order to confirm it more strongly through repetition: “And I shall show mercy to him to whom I shall show mercy,” that is, I shall give mercy to him whom I foreknow will return to me with his whole heart after wandering. This is to give to him to whom it should be given, and not to give to him to whom it should not be given: that He may call the one whom He knows will obey, but not the one whom He knows will not obey. For what is given ought not to rest upon the will of the person asking but upon the decision of the giver. Whether it ought to be given must be weighed by the giver’s judgment.

Although it is perilous to discern God’s judgment, nevertheless, for the sake of those who hesitate, lest they think God’s judgment unjust—though it judges not unjustly—[Col. 1460A] let us prove this by facts rather than words. There were two men, Saul and David. Let us inquire from the histories what each was found to be after the judgment of God’s foreknowledge. Let us see whether Saul conducted himself in necessity as David did, who, having received the Lord’s mercy, did not despise it and, after forgiveness of sins, persevered so well. Saul, however, when he was not heard, did not persist in prayer; rather, impatient and indignant at God’s judgment, he turned to idols which he had earlier condemned and sought help from them. [Ambrose] Hence his rejection by the One who foreknew appears just. For from this the justice of God’s foreknowing judgment is made manifest even to those unwilling to acknowledge it.

VERS. 16–17.—“Therefore it is not of one who wills nor of one who runs, but of God who has mercy. For Scripture says [Col. 1460B] to Pharaoh: ‘For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.’”

“Therefore it is not of one who wills.” As though he said: “Because by free mercy He prepares and calls whom He wills, therefore to will what is good is not of the one willing, nor to run,” that is, to work, “is of the human runner; but it is of God who has mercy.” That is, a good will or action is not from the free choice of the person willing or working, but from the mercy of God, who through imparted grace makes us will and run. [Note: [Col. 1459D] Id., *To Sixtus*.]

Behold, He did not choose because of future things which He foresaw. Where then are merits? Where are works, past or future, supposedly fulfilled or to be fulfilled by the powers of free choice? Did not the Apostle state openly concerning the commendation of gratuitous grace—that is, true grace—when he said, “It is not of one who wills nor of one who runs”? [Note: [Col. 1460D] Id., *Against Julian the Heretic*.] If you had considered this, O Julian, you would not have set the merits of the will against grace, when you hear: “It is not of one who wills nor of one who runs, but of God who has mercy.” God therefore did not have mercy on Jacob because Jacob willed and ran; rather, Jacob willed and ran because God had mercy on him. For the will is prepared by the Lord, and a person’s steps are directed by the Lord (Prov. XVI).

Therefore he fittingly says, “It is not of one who wills nor of one who runs, but of God who has mercy,” [Note: [Col. 1460D] Id., *On the Perfection of Righteousness*.] not because this happens without our will, but because our will does no good unless it is divinely helped. Hence elsewhere the Apostle says: “Not I, however, but the mercy of God with me” (1 Cor. [Col. 1460D] XV). He does not say this because he did no good, but because he would do no good if that mercy did not help him.

So also he says, “It is not of one who wills, but of God who has mercy,” [Note: [Col. 1460D] Id., *Enchiridion*.] not because there is no human will and running, but because it can do nothing unless He has mercy. For God is the one who works in us both to will and to do good. But since a person cannot believe or hope unless he wills, nor attain the prize unless he runs by his will, how does he say, “It is not of one who wills nor of one who runs,” unless because the will itself is prepared by the Lord?

Perhaps someone will understand the saying, “It is not of one who wills nor of one who runs, but of God who has mercy,” in the sense [Col. 1461A] that a human will alone is insufficient without God’s mercy. To this one may reply conversely: God’s mercy too is insufficient without the human will. Therefore, if it is rightly said that it is not of the human will because human will alone does not accomplish it, why is it not likewise rightly said conversely, “It is not of God who has mercy, but of the person who wills,” because God’s mercy alone does not accomplish it?

[Augustine] It remains, therefore, that it should be understood as rightly said for this reason: that the whole is attributed to God, who both prepares the good human will to be helped and helps it once prepared. He goes before the person willing, that he may will; He follows the person willing, lest he will in vain.

Having commended God’s mercy in the preceding words, he adds, in order also to commend God’s judgment and show that there is no injustice with Him: “For Scripture says [Col. 1461B] to Pharaoh.” As though he said: “Just as He chose Jacob by mercy, so He rejected Esau by justice.” Truly He rejected Esau by justice, because Scripture says this, introducing God speaking to Pharaoh, whom He rejected by judgment, as He did Esau. Or the connection may be made thus: willing and running are due to mercy, while the contrary is due to judgment, not injustice, as appears in Pharaoh. For Scripture says, etc.; as though he said: Good things arise from grace bestowed, which is by mercy; evil things arise when it is withdrawn, which is by justice, as appears in Pharaoh.

“For Scripture says,” etc. Or the connection may be made thus: willing and running are from mercy, as is clear in others from the same mass to which destruction is due, as is clear in Pharaoh. For Scripture [Col. 1461C] says—that is, the Lord in Scripture says to Pharaoh—“For this very thing.” This phrase is not syntactically continued here but read as though it stood alone: “I have, as it were, raised you up.” O Pharaoh, you were indeed evil, but as though asleep. I, by showing you the signs performed through Moses, raised you up “for this very thing,” that is, into this same wickedness, so that you might become worse. And this is just: the one who is in filth and refuses to repent should become still more filthy (Rev. XXII). That is, human merit requires that the person who refuses to abandon sin be further defiled by sin, as Pharaoh ought to have been corrected when he saw the signs, but through his own vice became worse.

Nor was this useless, but rather so that “in you,” who are hardened—that is, through you hardened—or “in you,” that is, against you, I might show to the good [Col. 1461D] my power, as I did in the Egyptian signs. Here it is clear that God also makes good use of the wicked. “I shall show,” I say, so that through the power shown my name may be proclaimed throughout all the earth.

Note that the example of Pharaoh, rejected by God’s just judgment, pertains to Esau, rejected by the same most equitable though hidden judgment, just as Jacob was chosen by mercy. Or thus: “For this very purpose I have raised you up.” Other manuscripts read: “For this very thing I revived you,” or “I preserved you”; and it is, “I preserved you, O Pharaoh.” God says this to him when he was liable for so many evils that he was unworthy to live, yet God reserved him precisely for this purpose [Col. 1462A]: that He might show His power in him, that is, that many signs and plagues might be displayed against him. Or, “I raised you up”: he is called raised up because, though dead before God, he was nevertheless granted a short span of life so that all nations might learn God’s power in him and learn that there is no God besides the God of the Jews.

VERS. 18.—“Therefore He has mercy on whom He wills, and hardens whom He wills.”

“Therefore, on whom He wills.” [Ambrose] Here he concludes concerning both mercy and judgment, and from the preceding examples—in which free mercy and just judgment appear—draws the conclusion. As though he said: “Because God has mercy on Jacob freely, it is clear that He has mercy freely on whom He wills; and because He rejected Esau and Pharaoh, it is clear that He hardens whom He wills by a just [Col. 1462B] judgment.” [Note: [Col. 1461D] Augustine, *To Sixtus*.]

If we seek the merit of hardening and mercy, we find a merit for hardening, but none for mercy. For there is no merit of mercy, lest grace be nullified if it is not given freely but rendered for merits. The merit of hardening is the sin of the whole condemned mass. God does not harden by imparting wickedness, but by not imparting grace, just as they are not worthy of it. Those to whom He does not impart it are not worthy, nor do they deserve it; rather, they are worthy of this and deserve this: that it not be imparted.

[Augustine] Therefore whoever is hardened should acknowledge that he is hardened deservedly, and whoever is helped should acknowledge that he is helped freely. [Note: [Col. 1461D] Id., *Enchiridion*.] Thus He has mercy in great goodness and hardens with no injustice, so that neither the delivered person may boast of his merits [Col. 1462C] nor the condemned person complain except of his own merits. For the Redeemer’s grace alone distinguishes from the lost those whom He had created together in the one mass of perdition, derived from the common cause of perdition at the beginning.

For the whole human race was condemned by God’s wholly just judgment in the apostate root, so that even if no one were delivered from it, no one could rightly criticize God’s justice. But in those who are delivered, while many more are not delivered and are left in just condemnation, it is shown what the whole mass had deserved, and to what the due judgment of God would also have led these persons, had His undeserved mercy not come to their aid. [Note: [Col. 1462D] Id., *To Simplicianus*.]

It must not therefore be understood that God hardens in such a way as to compel anyone to sin. He merely does not grant some sinners the mercy of His justification; for this reason He is said to harden them, because He does not have mercy on them, not because He impels them to sin. He does not have mercy on those to whom, by an equity most hidden and far removed from human understanding, He judges that grace ought not to be given. The Apostle does not explain this equity but marvels at it, saying: “O the depth of the riches of the knowledge and wisdom of God!” (Rom. XI.)

For God’s justice renders deserved dishonor to whom He wills from the universally and deservedly condemned mass; God’s grace grants undeserved honor to whom He wills—not through any prerogative of merits, not through fateful necessity, nor through the rashness of fortune, but through the hidden depth of His wisdom and knowledge [Col. 1463A]. [Note: [Col. 1463D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*.]

Many, seeking to account for this depth and trying by the conjectures of their own hearts to comprehend the unsearchable height of God’s judgments, have drifted into fables of vanity. They say that souls sin above in heaven and, according to their sins, are assigned to bodies on the basis of merits and confined in prisons, as it were, suitable to them. Such persons followed their own thoughts and, desiring to dispute about God’s depth, were submerged in the deep, saying that souls had lived previously in heaven, had there done something good or evil, and were cast down into earthly bodies according to their merits.

But the Catholic faith rejects this on account of the Apostle’s clear statement: “When they had not yet been born, nor had done anything good or evil.” [Note: [Col. 1463D] Id., *To Boniface*.] Faithful ignorance is therefore better [Col. 1463B] than rash knowledge.

Therefore He has mercy on whom He wills by free mercy, and hardens whom He wills by most upright justice. [Note: [Col. 1463D] Id., *Enchiridion*.] Who, moreover, is so impiously foolish as to say that God cannot turn a human being to good whenever and whomever He wills, since nothing resists His will? But when He does so, He acts by mercy; and when He does not do so, it is by judgment that He does not do so. [Note: [Col. 1463D] Id., *Against Julian*.]

He has mercy, certainly, according to grace that is given freely; but He hardens according to judgment rendered for merits. Hence we understand that God’s hardening is His unwillingness to have mercy: it is not that He inflicts something by which a person becomes worse, but only that He does not confer that by which the person becomes better. Therefore, just as it was said, “It is not of one who wills nor of one who runs, but of God who has mercy,” so it was not said, “It is not of one who wills nor of one who runs, [Col. 1463C] but of God who hardens.” [Augustine] For He does not harden by imparting something evil, but by not granting what is good. He does this in His justice, just as He gives grace from His mercy.

It is certain, therefore, that no one is delivered except by free mercy, and no one is condemned except by most equitable justice. [Note: [Col. 1463D] Id., *To Sixtus*.] But why He delivers, or does not deliver, this person rather than that, let the one who can search so great a depth of God’s judgments; yet let him beware the precipice. [Note: [Col. 1464D] Id., *On the Words of the Apostle*.] Why, then, does He deliver that person and not another? I do not wish you to ask me; I am a human being. I perceive the depth to be exceedingly great; I do not penetrate it. I tremble; I do not investigate. For God’s judgments are unsearchable.

Moreover, it should be noted that God’s hardening is only temporal. He hardens temporally, [Col. 1463D] not from eternity. Reprobation, however, is of one kind eternal and of another temporal. That which is temporal is the same as hardening, namely abandonment. That which is eternal is that God foreknows someone to be condemned. Likewise, careful distinctions must be made concerning predestination, election, love, and hatred.

VERS. 19–21.—“You will say to me, then: ‘Why does He still find fault? For who has resisted His will?’ O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does [Col. 1464A] the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ Or does not the potter have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?”

“You will say to me, then”: because he had said, “He has mercy on whom He wills, and hardens whom He wills,” it seemed to the carnal-minded person that, just as mercy is not according to merits, so hardening too is not according to merits. It also seemed that a person is wicked by God’s will, which cannot be resisted. The Apostle therefore puts this objection to himself in the person of a disputant.

As though he said: “Because it is by His will that He has mercy or hardens, you will say to me this: ‘Why does He find fault?’” that is, why is inquiry made? “Still,” that is, after it is established that hardening is by God’s will, why, I ask, is it investigated [Col. 1464B] why one person is good and another evil? There is no need to investigate this, because everyone will be such as God wishes him to be. “For who has resisted His will,” by which He hardens us? [Augustine] As though he said: no one. Thus, the carnal-minded person says, someone is good or evil by His will, and therefore God unjustly saves one and condemns another.

Or: “Why does He find fault with someone that he should do good?” That is, why does anyone strive to do good? “Still,” namely, once it is established that it is by God’s will, since one can do nothing except what God wills. “For who has resisted His will?” Or thus: since hardening is by His will, “why does He find fault?” that is, why does God complain if we offend? “Still,” that is, why does He complain of human sins, when human beings cannot avoid what God wills? [Note: [Col. 1464D] Id., *To Simplicianus*.]

For God frequently complains about human beings, [Col. 1464C] as is apparent from innumerable passages of Holy Scripture: they do not wish to believe and live rightly. Yet carnal persons, living in their pleasures, are accustomed, as stated, to murmur and speak against God, attributing their wickedness to His will rather than to their own fault.

The Apostle rebukes them, calling them back from such presumption, and thus crushes the insolence of the question: “O man,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1464D] Id., in the same work.] But he does not do this because he lacks a reason to give; rather, he calls the human being to consider his own capacity, saying, “O man.” [Note: [Col. 1464D] Id., *On the Words of the Apostle*.]

As though he said: “Consider yourself and Him. You are human; He is God. You, O man—that is, flesh, not spirit; carnal, not spiritual—you wretch whom it displeases that God complains, and who murmur against God because He rejects one and chooses another. Who are you?” That is, of what worth are you, “to answer,” that is, to understand what He does—why He has mercy on this one and hardens you? As though he said: if you were asked, you would not know how to answer, that is, understand, given your carnality; neither your wisdom nor any strength of yours aids you in this.

[Ambrose] Or: “Who are you, to answer,” that is, to contradict, “God”? Do you bring arguments against God that He chooses or rejects unjustly? It is great indignity [Col. 1465A] and presumption for a human being to contradict God: the unjust to contradict the just, the evil the good, the ignorant the perfect, the weak the most strong, the mortal the immortal, the slave the master, the creature the Creator.

The unjust person is troubled because God justifies some created from the same mass and rejects others. To show that this is rightly done, he uses Isaiah’s words and the analogy of a thing formed, which has no ground of complaint against the potter: “Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it,” that is, to the one by whom it was made and who owes it nothing, “Why have you made me thus?” As though he said: the work cannot complain against its maker. Thus you too, O human being, are formed by God, and therefore you cannot bring a case against God, asking why He made you thus or otherwise. [Note: [Col. 1465D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*.]

For if a beast could speak and said to God, “Why have you made me a beast when you made that one a human being?”, would you not rightly be angry and say, “O beast, who are you to answer God?” But because the disputant thinks his question is strongly supported by the fact that the rejected and the justified are made from one mass, he adds: “Or does not he have?” As though he said: truly the work cannot say to the maker, “Why have you made me thus?”, because the potter of clay—that is, one who works with clay—has the just authority to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor. He certainly has it.

[Ambrose] It is evident that some vessels are made for honor, being necessary for decent uses, whereas others are made for dishonor, being necessary for kitchen uses. They are, nevertheless, of one substance but differ by the artisan’s will. So too with God: though we are all of one and the same substance and all sinners, He has mercy on one and despises another, not without justice. With the potter there is will alone; with God, will joined with justice.

Just as a vessel made not for honor but for dishonor, if it is base, derives this from the clay and not from the potter, so the whole mass [Col. 1465C] of the human race is rightly corrupt and muddy not from God but through its own fault. Therefore, if from it a vessel is made for honor, this is mercy; if for dishonor, it is just, because that was its condition by nature. [Note: [Col. 1465D] Id., *On John*.]

For the whole nature, corrupted in its very root, is subject by divine judgment to deserved condemnation and, by the desert of sin, wholly condemned. [Augustine] Therefore, when vessels of wrath receive the punishment due to all, and vessels of mercy are delivered from it, justice is evident in the former and mercy in the latter. [Note: [Col. 1465D] Id., *To Boniface*.]

For if that mass were neutral, having neither goodness nor sin, it would not without reason appear unjust for vessels for dishonor to be made from it. But since the whole mass has flowed into condemnation through the free choice of the first human being, beyond doubt the making of vessels for honor from it is not due to the justice of the mass itself, which grace preceded in it, but to God’s mercy. [Note: [Col. 1465D] Id., *City of God*.] But the making of vessels for dishonor [Col. 1466A] must be attributed not to God’s injustice, which is entirely nonexistent, but to judgment. [Note: [Col. 1465D] Id., *To Boniface*.]

The Lord wisely ordered matters so as neither to condemn all nor to free all. For if all were freed, what was owed to sin by justice would be hidden; if none were freed, what grace bestows would be hidden. For, as regards original sin, all were unquestionably equal, but mercy distinguished those whom it willed. There is free pardon where vengeance could justly have been exacted. From these considerations God’s justice is evident in those who have no time to act, namely infants. Concerning those who have time to act, he adds:

VERS. 22–23.—“But what if God, desiring to show His wrath and make known His power, endured with much patience [Col. 1466B] vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order to make known the riches of His glory upon vessels of mercy, which He prepared for glory?”

What if He wills. Or, “What if God wills?” As though he said: It has already been shown that, even if God gives a human being no good thing, He is nevertheless not unjust. But what will you say if He has also given good things to some—namely, when, though they were vessels fitted for wrath unto destruction, He endured them with much patience? This is what he says. As though he said: God would not be unjust even if He gave no good thing; but He does give good to some, whereby He is shown to be good, because He endured with much patience the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction. God’s patience and forbearance consist in His enduring the wicked for as long as He does, so that, if they wish, they may be corrected, or, should they persist in their begun wickedness, He may destroy them in an orderly manner. [Note: [Col. 1466D] Id., to Sixtus.] For those long awaited are without excuse [Col. 1466C]; and therefore God waited for them, although He knew that they would not believe, so that He might use them as an instrument for the salvation of the good. [Ambrose] For God knows well how to use the wicked. He does not create human nature in them for wickedness, [Note: [Col. 1466D] Id., to Simplicianus.] but bears with them patiently for as long as He knows is fitting—not fruitlessly, but using them for the admonition or exercise of the good. [Note: [Col. 1466D] Id., on Exodus.] For God would create no angel or human being whom He foreknew would be evil, unless He likewise knew the good purposes for which He would employ them. [Note: [Col. 1466D] Id., from the book of Prosper’s Sentences.]

I say that He endured the wicked; and meanwhile, while waiting, He showed them by many indications that either they themselves would someday be punished, or that others would be punished before their eyes—that His wrath, that is, eternal punishment, [Col. 1466D] was to come—so that they might beware. In enduring them and showing them wrath, He made His power known: namely, that through the wicked He purifies the good. If, then, this is so—if God, willing to show His wrath and make His power known, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction—what answer can you give God? Or what will you say? As though he said: You can say that He justly withholds grace from such persons and condemns those who, though thus long awaited, refused to repent of their sins but abused the grace previously mentioned. Behold, here [Col. 1467A] His justice is shown in respect of those who have time for action.

“That He might show.” As though he said: For this purpose God endures the wicked, shows wrath beforehand to them, and draws them to knowledge of Himself: that He might thus show in the vessels of mercy—that is, in those chosen through mercy—the riches of His glory, that is, how rich and great His glorious mercy is. For this reason He gives so many good things to the wicked and bears with them so long: that He may prove that they are justly condemned, and that believers may love Him more, since He has kept for them a grace not shared with the wicked.

Or, “that He might show” here, in the vessels of mercy—that is, in the elect—the riches of His glory, that is, His abundant and glorious mercy, through the furnace of tribulation which they endure from the wicked; for the more they are exercised by tribulations, the purer and better they are made through the working of God’s grace.

Or it may be read concerning the future thus: “What if He wills?” As though he said: God would not be unjust even if He gave no good thing. But what will you say if He has also given good things—and certainly given them because He is God? He endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction: that is, wicked people whom, although He could have judged immediately, He endured for a long time, so that when condemned they cannot complain. [Ambrose] They were therefore awaited so that they might perish without excuse, although He foreknew that they would not believe. I say, God was willing in the future to show His wrath—that is, eternal punishment—in the lost, whom He will eternally condemn for having made evil use of His patience; and He was willing to make His power known in those being saved, whom He will then glorify when He inflicts upon the wicked vengeance for their blood. Though He was formerly thought not to be going to judge, because He long overlooked things, when He judges He will be seen to be mighty. [Col. 1467C]

“That He might show.” As though he said: He thus now endured vessels of wrath so that in the age to come He might show, by comparison with the reprobate, in the vessels of mercy—that is, in those chosen through mercy—His riches, that is, His abundant and glorious mercy. For He shows how much He has done for those whom He delivered and glorified, when those whom He abandoned have the punishment that was equally due to all.

Note that from the Apostle’s words used in this discourse—saying that Jacob was freely loved and chosen by God, but Esau, like Pharaoh, was reprobated by judgment, together with others whom God hardens by His will—it is shown that there are some to whom God does not even add grace, as to Esau and Pharaoh, while He brings it to others [Col. 1467D] as though compelling them, as to the Apostle Paul. [Ambrose] In these matters God’s foreknowledge must be sought, because nothing happens otherwise than He knew it would happen. For God’s foreknowledge is that by which He has determined what the will of each person will be, through which that person is either condemned or crowned. Therefore, foreknowing that some would have an evil will, God did not count them among the good; thus He also judged Pharaoh, in accordance with foreknowledge, to be condemned, knowing that he would not correct himself. But He chose the Apostle Paul, foreknowing that he would become faithful.

There are also certain others to whom grace was given for use: Saul, Judas, and those disciples to whom the Lord said in the Gospel, “Behold, your names [Col. 1468A] are written in heaven” (Luke 10), and who afterwards went back. But the Lord said this of them on account of the righteousness which they were serving, since it is just that each should receive according to merit. It is as though He said: “You are now worthy of eternal life,” because they were good. For often people who will become good are at first evil; and sometimes those who will be and remain evil are first good. Such were those men; and therefore their names were written in heaven on account of the righteousness which they were serving, though according to foreknowledge they were among the wicked.

For God judges according to righteousness, not according to foreknowledge, because righteousness—not God’s foreknowledge—is the reason why someone is worthy of life before God. Thus He says to Moses: “If anyone sins before Me, I shall blot him out of the book of life” (Exod. 32), so that according to the justice [Col. 1468B] of the Judge he appears to be blotted out when he sins, although according to foreknowledge he was never in the book of life. Hence John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (John 2 [i.e. 1 John 2]). Conversely, someone appears to be enrolled when he ceases to be evil, though according to foreknowledge he was never absent.

Therefore, since out of gratuitous mercy He adds grace to whom He wills and frees whom He wills, His rich and glorious goodness is plainly shown in the vessels of mercy which He prepared—waiting in the same way for them as He waits for the vessels of wrath. [Augustine] I say, He prepared them for future glory. For God endures all, knowing the end of each; and it surely benefits the good that He waits for the wicked.

**VERS. 24–26.**—“Whom He also called, not only [Col. 1468C] from among the Jews but also from among the Gentiles, as He says in Hosea: ‘I shall call not-my-people, my people; and not-beloved, beloved; and her who had not received mercy, one who has received mercy.’ And it shall be, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God.’”

“Whom He also called.” Since it has been shown that they are sons by grace alone, he begins to prove from the authorities of the prophets that these people are from both peoples. As though he said: He prepared in glory those who are vessels of mercy. [Note: [Col. 1467D] Augustine, to Optatus.] He also called them, through preachers and inwardly, though they are from the one mass of Adam from which also come the wicked, who are vessels of wrath and to whom condemnation was due. For this whole mass would justly receive [Col. 1468D] the due penalty of condemnation, unless from it the potter—who is not only just but also merciful—made other vessels unto honor according to grace, not according to what was due: while He helps infants, of whom no merits can be alleged, and goes before those older in years, so that they may be able to have some good merits. [Note: [Col. 1468D] Id., to Sixtus.] For from the stock of disobedience comes the offspring of sin and punishment—not by divine creation, but through a nature created good by God and corrupted by the perversity of the will.

If human beings live wickedly, then it comes from themselves: either from what they inherited originally or from what they have added besides. Therefore let those unwilling to live rightly not excuse themselves by saying: “What have we done, that we live wickedly, when we have not received the grace by which we might live well?” They cannot truly excuse themselves. For if they are vessels of wrath to whom the punishment due is rendered, let them ascribe this to themselves, because they are from the mass which God justly condemned on account of sin. But if they are vessels of mercy, made from that same mass, to whom He was unwilling to render punishment, let them not become puffed up, but glorify Him who has bestowed upon them undeserved mercy. [Col. 1469A]

I say that He called them not only from among the Jews but also from among the Gentiles. First he gives Hosea’s authority on behalf of the Gentiles, saying: As God says in Hosea. As though he said: Hosea does not say this from himself, but God says it in him: “I shall call not-my-people”—that is, the Gentiles, who formerly did not know Me and were not called My people—“my people,” so that they may know Me and be called My people; and “not my beloved,” namely the Gentile woman, “my beloved,” so that they may serve in love; and “her who had not received mercy, one who has received mercy,” so that they may attain eternal glory. [Haimo]

“And this which I say shall come to pass: in the place,” that is, throughout the whole world, “where it was said, ‘You are not my people,’ there,” throughout the whole world, “they shall be called sons of God.” [Ambrose] Or, “in the place,” that is, in Judaea and among the Jews themselves, who said, “You are not God’s people,” there they shall be called sons of God by those same Jews.

**VERS. 27–29.**—“But Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: ‘Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved. For He will complete and shorten the word in righteousness, because the Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth.’ And, as [Col. 1469C] Isaiah foretold: ‘Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah.’”

“But Isaiah says.” Here he gives Isaiah’s authority on behalf of the Jews. As though he said: Hosea says this concerning the Gentiles; but Isaiah openly cries out concerning Israel, that is, concerning the Jews: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea”—that is, though the children of Israel are innumerable—nevertheless only a remnant shall be saved. Thus the salvation of the Jews is spoken of in such a way that the greater part is blinded. Or, they are compared to sand because of their barrenness. [Augustine]

And the sense is: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea,” that is, though they are barren of the grace of faith and the fruit of good work, [Col. 1469D] the root of the patriarchs has not therefore perished. Or: “A remnant shall be saved in us,” that is, those whom I have left for myself when I rejected the others. Or, those abandoned by others as worthless, or as few.

The prophet next adds the means by which they are saved: namely, through the word of the Gospel, so that the glory of legal works may be excluded. As though he said: They truly shall be saved, for the Lord will make a completing and shortening word—that is, the word of the Gospel. It is called “completing” because it leads to perfection, and “shortening” because He compressed all legal matters into the one Christ. [Note: [Col. 1469D] Augustine, to Simplicianus.] Thus He saves by the concise means of faith through grace, not through the innumerable observances by which that people was oppressed in servile fashion. Although He abbreviates it in words, it is nevertheless equitable in relation to the earlier word of the Law. Hence he adds: “shortening,” I say, “in righteousness,” so that nothing required for righteousness is lacking from all the figurative matters.

Or it is called “shortening in righteousness” because it retains what is equitable, such as moral precepts, which it is right to retain, while cutting off the figures. Lest anyone doubt this, the prophet confirms it by repetition, saying: “Because the Lord,” who first made the long word of the Law, “being upon the earth”—that is, being made human upon the earth—“will make a shortened word,” in contrast with the ancient word which God is known to have made. [Jerome]

Or, the completed and shortened word is love. It is called a completing or completed word because it completes; and shortening or shortened because the Law and the Prophets hang upon it. For love compresses all things into two commandments. [Col. 1470B]

“And as He foretold.” He again gives Isaiah’s authority, commending that word. As though he said: God made the word, and that word was so necessary that, as Isaiah foretold, unless the Lord Sabaoth—that is, the Lord of powers or armies—had left us seed, that is, the word of the Gospel or Christ, who brought forth the fruit of life, we would have become like Sodom, and so forth. [Ambrose]

Or, by “seed” are understood the remnant to be saved, discussed above: namely, the apostles and other good persons. It is as though he said: “A remnant shall be saved,” because unless through them the word of God had been preached, the Gentiles would have perished. This is what he says: Unless the Lord Sabaoth, that is, of armies, when He blinded others, had left us—for our benefit—seed, that is, apostles from whom Christ’s harvest grew, we would have become [Col. 1470C] like Sodom, which is interpreted “mute”: that is, we would have been mute in confession. And we would have been made like Gomorrah, which is interpreted “rough”: that is, without grace we would have been rough, covered with the thorns of vices.

Note that he does not without reason use both “like” and “as,” though either one could have sufficed. He does this so that by one he may indicate the likeness between our guilt and theirs, and by the other the likeness of punishment. As though he said: We would be equal in punishment because we would be alike in guilt.

**VERS. 30–35.**—“What then shall we say? That Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness—but the righteousness that is from faith; whereas Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, [Col. 1470D] did not attain the law of righteousness. Why? Because not from faith, but as though from works. For they stumbled at the stone of stumbling, as it is written: ‘Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal, and everyone who believes in Him shall not be put to shame.’”

“What then?” Having heard the authorities of Hosea and Isaiah, he investigates the prophets’ meaning, lest the Jews distort it otherwise. [Ambrose] As though he said: Since Hosea and Isaiah say this, what then shall we say? That is, in what sense shall we understand the preceding words of the prophets to have been spoken? Surely this: that the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness through works of the Law—that is, who did not presume to be justified by legal observances—attained [Col. 1471A] righteousness [Note: [Col. 1471D] Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*], as it were suddenly and firmly. Not just any righteousness, but that righteousness which is from faith, which comes through grace: seeking it from God, rather than presuming upon themselves, they attained righteousness.

“But Israel, pursuing”—and this too is from Isaiah’s prophecy. As though he said: The Gentiles attained righteousness, whereas Israel, pursuing by legal works “the law of righteousness,” that is, the Law of Moses, which is a law of righteousness if rightly understood; or, pursuing “the law of righteousness,” that is, the righteousness of the Law which comes from fear of punishment rather than love of righteousness—did not attain the law of righteousness, that is, innocence and the like, which the Law truly teaches. Thus he fittingly says “pursuing.” For the Jew followed the Law, as though from behind, because he never attained the spiritual understanding by which he might be justified. [Col. 1471B]

“Why did he not attain it?” As though he said: Consider carefully why: namely, because he sought to be justified not from faith, but from works of the Law, as though these could justify. [Note: [Col. 1471D] Id., in the same work.] Therefore the Jew did not attain the law of righteousness because he did not seek righteousness from faith: he did not seek it from God; he did not believe in Him who justifies the ungodly; he did not believe that God works in a person so that the person is justified. But justification is obtained by faith.

He next gives the reason why it happened that they did not believe: “For they stumbled.” As though someone were to ask, “Why do the Jews not have faith?” He answers: Because they stumbled at the stone of stumbling; that is, because, through the swelling of their pride, they suffered stumbling—that is, blindness—in Christ, who is called a stone of stumbling by a certain likeness. For Christ, hidden in humility, was fitted to cause a stumble, like a small stone against which one does not guard. [Augustine] The Jewish people expected Him to come, but because He came humble, He was not recognized. Because He was a small stone, they stumbled against Him and were broken. But the stone grew, as Daniel says: “And it became a great mountain and filled the whole earth” (Dan. 2). [Col. 1471C]

But because He first came humble, the Jews stumbled against Him. Isaiah bears witness to this; hence it follows: “As it is written in Isaiah: Behold.” As though he said: Plainly and openly, “I place”—that is, cause to be born—“in Zion,” that is, among the Jews, “a stone of stumbling,” that is, Christ, against whom men do not guard as against a small pebble; “and a rock of scandal,” that is, the same Christ, who in the future will utterly crush and afflict the wicked. Christ is called a stone of stumbling according to the condition in which He appeared here to the wicked; He is called a rock of scandal according to what He will do to the wicked in the future. [Origen]

For “scandal” is said when an obstacle is found in the road which hinders a traveller’s steps. Therefore, because those in Zion were walking a bad road and running with swift foot on the path of destruction, they will experience Christ as avenger in the future; and for that reason He is called a rock of scandal.

Or, just as a rock is so called before polishing, and a stone after polishing, so Christ is called a rock before polishing and a stone after polishing. Christ’s polishing was His Passion, because He laid aside the misery of weakness. [Col. 1472A] Thus before the Passion Christ was a rock of scandal, because at that time the Jews were scandalized at Him, angry and indignant that He made Himself the Son of God. But Christ was a stone of stumbling in the polishing, that is, in the Passion, when they most greatly stumbled and were blinded, not believing Him to be God when they saw Him dead. Faith frees some from that stumbling. [Haimo]

Hence he adds: “And everyone who believes.” As though he said: He is not only an occasion of stumbling to the wicked, but will be a reward to the good; for everyone, whether Jew or Gentile, who believes in Him shall not be put to shame when He comes in the future.

## CHAPTER X

**VERS. 1–4.**—“Brothers, the desire indeed of my heart and my supplication to God is for them unto salvation. For I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For, ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to God’s righteousness. For Christ is the end of the Law unto righteousness for everyone who believes.”

Lest the Apostle seem to speak against the Jews out of hatred, or lest the Gentiles reject them altogether, he adds why they stumbled: and yet, O brothers, my desire indeed is that they may be saved. This desire is certainly not feigned, but is of my heart—that is, true. Moreover, supplication is made by me to God for those who stumble, and this is for salvation: that God may give them the faith through which they may be saved. [Note: [Col. 1472D] Id., *On the Words of the Apostle*.] Observe that, by the Apostle’s praying for unbelievers that they may believe, and for opponents that they may be converted, he indicates that this is given by grace, since conversion itself does not occur without God’s aid. [Note: [Col. 1472D] Id., to Paulinus.] For the will is not sufficient to move itself to believing the truths, unless God helps through grace. Hence He Himself says: “No one comes to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6).

“For I bear witness.” As though he said: I pray for them, and this is both just and necessary: just, because they have zeal for God; necessary, because it is not according to knowledge. This is what he says: I, who was once like them, bear witness to them in this matter, that they have zeal for God—that is, zeal for God. Thus it is just to pray for them; but their zeal is not according to the knowledge [Col. 1472D] of love. [Haimo] For it is foolish to venerate the Law and persecute the God of the Law; it is also foolish to confess the Father and deny the Son. The meaning is: They think they act for love of God, but they do not possess true love of God; and therefore it is necessary to pray for them.

[Ambrose] But he says this of those who handed Christ over not through envy and ill will, as the scribes and Pharisees did, but through error. To them Peter says: “I know, brothers, that you did this through ignorance” (Acts 3). Therefore, having zeal for God but not knowing His will and counsel, they acted against the God whom they professed themselves to be defending. [Augustine]

He shows how they have zeal not according to knowledge by adding: “For, ignorant,” and so forth. As though he said: They truly have zeal not according to knowledge because, ignorant of God’s righteousness—not the righteousness by which God is righteous, but that which comes to a human being from God, that is, which He gives to a human being, and which is through faith in Christ, from God who justifies the ungodly—and seeking, or wishing, in their pride to establish their own righteousness, [Note: [Col. 1473D] Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will*.] which is through carnal observances and is called their own, not because the Law was established by them, but because in the Law which is from God they established their own righteousness—[Ambrose] believing that they could fulfil that same Law in their own strength, so that merits might precede grace rather than grace might precede righteousness—[Note: [Col. 1473D] Id., in the same work] doing this, they did not submit to God’s righteousness, by which He justifies believers; that is, they do not believe that the ungodly are justified through faith. [Col. 1473B]

For this is God’s righteousness: not that which is established in the commandment of the Law, by which fear is instilled, but that which is established in the aid of grace itself. [Augustine] Hence he adds: “For Christ is the end.” As though he said: They are truly ignorant of God’s righteousness because they are ignorant of Christ. Christ is the end of the Law: that is, He fulfils in Himself and in us what the Law foretold. [Note: [Col. 1473D] Id., *On Nature and Grace*.] He is also effective unto righteousness for everyone who believes: that is, He is the giver of righteousness to every believer.

Therefore righteousness is from Christ, not from the Law. For if righteousness came through the written or natural law without faith in Christ, then Christ died gratuitously. But if He did not die gratuitously, then the ungodly are justified in Him alone, and faith is reckoned as righteousness to those who believe in Him. [Note: [Col. 1474D] Id., in the book of Prosper’s *Sentences*.] Thus all human nature can neither be justified nor redeemed from wrath—that is, from vengeance—in any way except through faith and the sacrament of Christ’s blood. [Col. 1473C]

For Christ is the end in whom the law of righteousness is not consumed but fulfilled. [Note: [Col. 1474D] Id., on John.] All perfection is in Him, beyond whom there is nothing to which hope can extend itself. Christ is also the end of believers. When the intention of one running has reached Him, it has nothing further to find, but has that in which it ought to remain. Therefore He is called the end not because He consumes, but because He perfects. He perfects righteousness through faith without works of the Law. There are works which appear good without faith in Christ, but are nevertheless not truly good because they are not referred to that end from which they are good: namely, to Christ, who is the end of the Law unto righteousness—not, indeed, human righteousness, but [Col. 1473D] divine righteousness. For there is human righteousness and divine righteousness. He speaks of the human below, at “For Moses”; but of the divine at “But the righteousness,” and so forth. Speaking first of human righteousness, he adds:

**VERS. 5–7.**—“For Moses wrote that the person who does the righteousness which is from the Law shall live in it. But the righteousness which is from faith speaks thus: ‘Do not say in your heart, Who shall ascend into heaven?’ that is, to bring Christ down; or, ‘Who shall descend into the abyss?’ that is, to bring Christ back from the dead.”

“For Moses.” [Ambrose] As though he said: Christ alone is truly righteousness unto salvation, because the righteousness of the Law is effective only for the present life. Moses shows this; for Moses wrote in Numbers and Leviticus that the person who does—without the help of grace—the righteousness which is from the Law, which comes from fear rather than love, shall live in it. [Augustine] That is, such a person shall not be punished by the legal penalty; for the Law of Moses did not make them guilty if it was observed: they lived by doing the Law. Here he calls those legal observances “the righteousness of the Law.” Thus Moses has it: “The person who does them shall live by them” (Lev. 18). They feared, certainly, that if they did not do them they would suffer stoning or something of the kind. Therefore “shall live in it” means that he shall receive this reward: not to be punished by this death. [Col. 1474A]

Therefore it is not great righteousness to fear, nor does it have merit before God. Thus not being justified before God differs from not being justified at all. Whoever is not justified at all observes neither those things which have a temporal reward nor those which have an eternal one. But whoever is justified in the works of the Law expects a temporal recompense from them and is not justified before God; nevertheless, this too is a kind of righteousness, so to speak—an earthly and carnal righteousness. [Col. 1474B]

He next adds concerning the righteousness of faith: “But the righteousness.” As though he said: Moses spoke thus concerning that righteousness of the Law; but concerning the righteousness which is from faith—that is, the righteousness of faith—Moses speaks thus in Deuteronomy: “Do not say,” and so forth (Deut. 30). [Ambrose] Or, that righteousness which is from faith itself says thus in the human heart: namely, that when observed it leads to heaven, and when not observed it leads to the abyss. This is what he says: “Do not say.” But this is the righteousness of faith: that one should not doubt the hope of God which is in Christ, and that a human being should not distrust that Christ despoiled hell and ascended to heaven with souls, by which one is made righteous. Therefore Moses says this concerning it; or righteousness itself says this in the human heart:

“O human being, do not say in your heart,” that is, do not even think: “Who shall ascend into heaven?” that is, no human being shall ascend into heaven. Do not think this, because whoever thinks it denies that Christ ascended. This is what follows: to think that is to bring Christ down, that is, to deny that Christ ascended. These words, “that is, to bring Christ,” and so forth, are the Apostle’s words, by which he explains the meaning of Moses’ preceding words.

Or: do not think, “Who shall descend into the abyss?” namely, into [Col. 1474D] hell—that is, no one shall descend there—which is the consequence of not observing the Law. Do not think this, because to think it is to bring Christ back from the dead: that is, to believe that Christ did not descend into hell. For if those who do not observe righteousness do not descend, then Abraham and the ancient fathers descended still less. But if they did not descend, then neither did Christ, who descended only to free them. Again, these are the Apostle’s words when he says, “That is, Christ.”

Or thus: “Do not say.” As though he said: When you hear it preached after the Resurrection that Christ ascended to heaven, do not say in your heart, “It is false. For who shall ascend into heaven?” Do not say this, because to say it is to bring Christ down from heaven, so far as lies in you; for this wretchedness, so far as lies in you, brings Christ down from heaven to earth. Likewise, when you hear it preached that Christ descended into hell, do not say, “It is false. For who shall descend into the abyss?” Do not say this, because to say it is to bring Christ back from the dead, so far as lies in you. [Col. 1475A]

**VERS. 8–13.**—“But what does Scripture say? ‘The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.’ This is the word of faith which we preach: because if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you shall be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. For Scripture says: ‘Everyone who believes in Him shall not be put to shame.’ For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord of all is rich toward all who call upon Him. For everyone whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.”

“But what?” As though he said: Do not say that; rather, believe this concerning the word which Scripture says concerning it in Deuteronomy. What does it say about it? [Haimo, Ambrose] Behold, “the Word”—that is, Christ, who is the Word in the beginning with the Father; or “the word,” that is, Christ’s preaching and teaching—is near, that is, useful, because it justifies and saves. The words of the old Law stood far off from justification and salvation.

Or, it is “near” because there is nothing unfitting either in saying or believing it, since what we are told to believe is not far from the nature of minds and the capacity for speech. This word ought to be in your mouth for confession and in your heart for belief. The Apostle then expounds Moses’ Scripture, saying: “This is the word of faith which we preach,” by which baptism too is consecrated. Of this word the Lord says: “Already you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” (John 15). He does not say, “because of baptism.” Why? Unless because the word cleanses even in water. Take away the word, and what is water but water? The word comes to the element. Whence comes this great power of water, that it touches the body and washes the heart, except through the working of the word—not because it is spoken, but because it is believed? For in the word itself one thing is the passing sound, another the abiding power. [Col. 1475D]

“Because if you confess.” [Augustine] As though he said: The word ought indeed to be near, because if you confess with your mouth—not works of the Law, but that the Lord Jesus has risen, when someone attacks this; or, that Christ is the Lord Jesus, that is, the Savior—and believe in your heart that God raised Him or brought Him up from the dead, you shall be saved. Behold the praise and reward of faith. The praise of faith is that you believe Jesus is Lord and that He rose again; its reward is eternal salvation.

“For with the heart.” As though he said: Believing truly gives [Col. 1476A] salvation because it gives the righteousness which is the cause of salvation. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness: that is, through faith of the heart someone is justified, that is, is made godly from ungodly. But after faith of the heart—for otherwise it is ineffective—confession is made with the mouth, not only unto righteousness but also unto salvation. This confession is added to faith, [Augustine] as in the martyrs, who confessed with their mouths amid imminent torments the faith which they held in their hearts.

Therefore it was not added in vain that confession is made with the mouth unto salvation. [Note: [Col. 1475D] Augustine, in the book *Against Lying*.] For nearly all who denied Christ before persecutors held in their hearts what they believed concerning Him, yet perished because they did not confess with their mouths—except those who returned to life through repentance, such as Peter, who in that denial held truth within and uttered falsehood without. [Col. 1476B] Why else did he wash with tears what he had denied with his mouth? What he held in his heart was working for his salvation. [Note: [Col. 1475D] Id., in the book of Prosper’s *Sentences*.]

Therefore one seeking peace from God should not have one thing in the profession of the mouth and another in the secret place of the heart. For it profits nothing that what is true is in the heart while what is false is spoken aloud, because truth must both be believed and spoken. [Note: [Col. 1475D] Id., on John.] Note that he does not simply say “one believes,” but “one believes with the heart,” because a person may unwillingly do other things—may unwillingly enter a church and approach the altar—but cannot believe unwillingly. Therefore he fittingly says, “one believes with the heart.” [Note: [Col. 1476D] Id., on Psalm 30.]

From this root of the heart, however, let confession arise. For to confess is to state what is in the heart. If one thing is in the heart and another [Col. 1476C] in the mouth, it is speech, not confession. [Note: [Col. 1476D] Id., *On the Words of the Apostle*.] Therefore what is in the heart ought to be in the mouth, because it is not without reason that the sign of the cross is made upon the forehead—that is, in the seat of shame—lest a Christian be ashamed at Christ’s reproach.

Peter sinned in denying with his mouth while believing with his heart. Let bad shame therefore depart; let salutary confession come. Let us not be ashamed of Christ’s name. Let people mock us because we believe in Christ crucified—indeed, I say, in one put to death—but in Him what was put to death was what He took from me, not that by which He made me.

“For Scripture says.” As though he said: One truly believes with the heart unto righteousness, for Scripture says through Isaiah: “Everyone”—not only Jew but Gentile also—“who believes in Him shall not be put to shame,” that is, shall not be ashamed in the future, even if here such a person seems to be put to shame. And I rightly said “everyone,” for there is no distinction between Jew and Greek: rather, in every nation whoever fears God is acceptable to Him. And truly there is no distinction. [Ambrose] For the same Lord—that is, the Creator of all—is rich toward all: that is, sufficient to enrich all who call upon Him in faith and deed. He is not rich toward others, because they do not share in His goods; but those who call upon Him will receive eternal recompense. [Col. 1476D]

He then proves from Isaiah’s authority what he had said: “For everyone,” Jew or Greek, “whoever calls upon the name of the Lord,” that is, the Son of the Father, by rightly subjecting himself to Him, “shall be saved” in eternal blessedness. Prayer, therefore, is necessary. For one who prays calls upon Him, but cannot truly do this unless he first believes. Thus those who truly call upon Him not only believe but also pray, so that after a person has believed, the soul may not cease asking for what God has promised to those who watch with their whole heart. For believing grants forgiveness of sins, whereas calling upon Him obtains God’s promises. But to show that there is no true calling upon Him without faith, he adds, “How then?” or “But,” [Augustine] having proved that persons are taken from both peoples, he shows by what means: namely, by the promise made to both, and whoever does not receive it is without excuse. As though he said: Calling upon Him saves; therefore one must believe.

### Verses 14–15

> “How then will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard? How then will they hear without a preacher? But how will they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: ‘How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things.’”

“How will they call,” etc.—or the connection may be made thus, if there is an *autem* (“but”) there. As though he said: “Whoever calls upon him shall be saved.” But no one can object to this; for how will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? They will not call unless they believe. Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard? [Col. 1477B] As though he said: They will not believe unless they hear; nor has anyone ever believed without hearing in some manner, either inwardly or outwardly.

[Ambrose] [Col. 1477C] Or: “How will they believe him whom they have not heard?”—that is, whom they have not obeyed. It is evident that one is not believed when obedience is denied him. “How then will they hear without a preacher?” That is, unless it is preached to them. As though he said: They will not hear unless it is preached. Or: “How, indeed, without a preacher?”—that is, if they resist the preacher? Nor is this obscure: whoever resists the preacher does not receive his author.

“How then will they preach unless they are sent?” This too admits of no question, because they are not true apostles unless they are sent, nor will they preach unless they are sent. For no signs of miracles bear witness to such persons. Thus it is clear that preachers were sent also to the Gentiles. In this way the Apostle refutes those who thought that the Gospel was to be preached to the Jews alone.

These words also serve to commend grace itself, so that through all this it may be shown that our whole good proceeds from grace. For he says that believing comes [Col. 1477D] from hearing; hearing, from preaching; preaching, from God’s sending: thus everything descends from the fountain of grace.

Preaching truly comes from sending, because God even sent pseudo-preachers who announced good things, for he knows how to use evil persons for good. At times he even sends evil persons to evil persons in wrath—that is, he permits evil men to preach to evil men for their mutual punishment, so that they may perish through one another, as is just according to what their merits demand.

“As it is written.” As though he said: They will not preach unless they are sent; but they have been sent, as is written in Isaiah, or in the prophet Nahum: “How beautiful are the feet!”

[Haimo] That is, the coming of the apostles who enlighten the world; in this it appears that they were sent by God. Otherwise they could not have done this.

[Col. 1478A] “Of those who proclaim the Gospel.”

[Ambrose] That is, those who announce peace: reconciliation between people and people, the barrier of Jewish legal observance and Gentile idolatry having been broken down; reconciliation also between God and the ungodly, whom he justifies through faith, and human beings who believe in him.

They proclaim also the future good things—that is, peace upon peace, because the kingdom of God is peace. As though he said: They are exceedingly beautiful, because they enlighten the world and because they proclaim the Gospel—that is, announce good news. For those announce good news well who fulfill in deed what they preach with the mouth.

### Verses 16–17

> “But not all obey the Gospel. For Isaiah says: ‘Lord, who has believed our report?’ Therefore faith comes from hearing, but hearing through the word of Christ.”

[Col. 1478B] “But not.” As though he said: All heard through the apostles; yet not all obeyed the Gospel. For although hearing is from grace, another grace is necessary to move the heart.

[Augustine] That not all obeyed he establishes by prophetic testimony: that some, not all, obeyed, in these words: “For Isaiah says, ‘Lord, who has believed our report?’”—that is, the things they heard from us, or the things that we heard from you.

[Note: [Col. 1477D] Augustine, *On John*.]

As though he said: Someone believed; not everyone did.

Some mutter among themselves, and wherever they can they cry out and contend in turbulent disputation, saying: “What did the Jews do, or what was their fault, if it was necessary for the word of Isaiah which he spoke to be fulfilled?”

[Augustine] They press this question, and make it more profound, by what is read in the Gospel [Col. 1478C] of John:

> “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said: ‘He blinded their eyes and hardened their heart’” (John 12).

We answer them that God, foreknowing the future, foretold through the prophet the unbelief of the Jews; but he did not produce it. Nor would he have foreknown their evils unless they possessed them.

[Note: [Col. 1478D] The same author, in the same work.]

For God does not compel anyone to sin because he foreknew the future sins of human beings. He foreknew their sins, not his own. Therefore, if those acts which he foreknew are not theirs, then he did not truly foreknow them as theirs. But because his foreknowledge cannot be deceived, undoubtedly it is no one else but the persons themselves who sin, those whom God foreknew would sin. Therefore, if they had wished to do good rather than evil, they would not have been foreseen as about to do evil by him who knows what each person will do and what he will repay to them according to their work. [Col. 1478D]

[Augustine] But the words of the Gospel just quoted press us more strongly than those words of Isaiah. For they say to us: If they could not believe, what sin is committed by a person who does not do what he cannot do? But if they sinned by not believing, then they could believe and did not do so. But if they could, how does the Gospel say that they could not believe, because Isaiah said, “He blinded their eyes and hardened their heart”?

They even go so far—more seriously still—as to attribute the cause to God: why they did not believe, namely because he himself blinded and hardened them.
