[Col. 1479A] You have heard the question proposed and see how deep it is; but we answer as we can. If I am asked why they could not believe, I answer: because they were unwilling. God foresaw their evil will and foretold it through the prophet. “But,” you will say, “the prophet gave another cause, not their will—namely, ‘He blinded their eyes and hardened their heart.’”

But here I answer that their will deserved this.

[Note: [Col. 1479D] Augustine, in the same work.]

For just as God blinds, so he hardens: that is, by abandoning, not by producing; and their will deserved this. For he inflicted this as the deserved punishment of blindness and hardness, on account of their proud boldness and will.

If, therefore, it is said that the Jews cannot believe because Isaiah foretold it, I answer: rather, they cannot because they will not; this God foreknew and foretold, but did not cause.

[Col. 1479B] [Augustine] It is therefore no wonder that they could not believe whose will was so proud that they attributed so much to their own powers as to deny that divine aid was necessary for them to live well. All who think so proudly cannot believe in Christ—not because human beings cannot be changed for the better, but because, so long as they think in this way, they cannot believe.

Thus, just as the fact that God cannot deny himself is praise of the divine will, so the fact that they could not believe is the fault of the human will. If anyone knows how to explain this question better, far be it from me not to be readier to learn than to teach.

Therefore, as though he said: Since someone believes the report, even if not all do, faith comes from hearing—though it is not everywhere present. For even if God teaches inwardly, nevertheless a herald announces outwardly. [Col. 1479C] Hearing, however, is not through our merits but through the word of Christ—that is, through Christ’s grace, by which he sends us teachers of the evangelical word. For unless something is spoken, it can neither be heard nor believed.

### Verses 18–21

> “But I say: Have they not heard? Indeed, their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. But I say: Has Israel not known? Moses first says: ‘I will provoke you to jealousy by that which is not a nation; by a foolish nation I will provoke you to anger.’ But Isaiah boldly says: ‘I was found by those who did not seek me; I appeared openly to those who did not ask for me.’ But concerning Israel he says: ‘All day long I stretched out my hands to a people who do not believe, but contradict me.’”

“But I say.” As though he said: They believed through hearing; but those who wish to excuse themselves for not believing say, as though they had not heard. I ask: “Have they not heard?”

[Haimo] Certainly they have heard, as David shows in the Psalm, saying: “Their sound”—that is, the fame of the apostles or of their successors—“has gone out indeed,” that is, even “into all the earth”: not only those near at hand, but those most remote, have heard.

[Note: [Col. 1479D] The same author, to Isychius.]

Or, according to another reading, *equidem* means “certainly”: “Their sound has certainly gone out into all the earth”; and thus they are without excuse. “And their words [have gone] to the ends of the world”—that is, they have been heard from every side.

[Col. 1480A] Yet this was not fulfilled even in the time of the Apostles; [Col. 1480B] but, through the Holy Spirit’s revelation, he sees that it will be fulfilled in their successors. Therefore, although he spoke with verbs in the past tense, he foretold what was to be, not what had already occurred and been completed. So too the Prophet whom he uses as witness did not say, “Their sound will go out,” but “Their sound went out,” though this had certainly not yet happened.

[Note: [Col. 1480D] The same author, in the same work.]

By saying “their,” therefore, he intended not only the apostles but also their successors to be understood. Likewise, “You shall be my witnesses to the uttermost part of the earth” (Acts 1) is not said only to the apostles; nor, “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Mark 16); nor, “When you see all these things, know that it is near, at the doors” (Matthew 24).

“But I say”: he has proved that all heard, and consequently that the Jews heard. But since they could have heard without understanding, he affirms that they also understood. As though he said: All indeed heard; but I speak specifically of the Jews: “Did Israel not know?” Certainly it knew.

For Moses, who was first—that is, greatest—among the others, says that they knew. Or “first” means: before others spoke, he says that they knew what others after him also said. Israel is said to have known the teaching of the Gospel and Christ’s coming because it could not contradict it by reason or authority; but it did not know truly, so that it might take proper root in their minds.

Then he cites the words of Moses, spoken in Deuteronomy in the person of God the Father:

> “I will lead you”—that is, permit you to be led—“to jealousy against a non-nation,” that is, against the Gentiles; namely, to envy at the conversion of the Gentiles, who were formerly called “not a nation” because they were without the Law. Or now they are “not a nation” because they do not live as Gentiles.

[Ambrose] [Col. 1480C] For the Jews are envious because the Gentiles call the Jews’ God their own, and claim that the Jews’ promises, Law, and prophets belong to them.

“By a foolish nation”—that is, against a foolish nation, namely the Gentiles who did not know the true God—“I will provoke you to anger”: I will permit you to become angry and to persecute them; and when they see this happen, let them take heed that he has come.

And not only Moses says this, but Isaiah also. Though he foresaw punishment threatening him, he nevertheless boldly says, speaking in the person of Christ:

> “I was found by those who did not seek me,” namely the Gentiles; that is, I freely offered myself to those who did not seek me of themselves, and hence comes the Jews’ envy. “And I appeared openly”—that is, manifestly—“to those who did not ask for me from others.”

“But concerning Israel,” etc. As though he said: Isaiah says this concerning the Gentiles; but concerning Israel he says this other thing in the person of Christ:

> “All day long I stretched out my hands.”

[Haimo] This is not said of hands stretched out on the cross, where he was not present all day, but of the works he bestowed upon that people. “All day long” means throughout the whole time during which I dwelt with them and enlightened the world. “My hands”—that is, my works and affections—I stretched out to the Jewish people: I displayed greater things to the Jews, because he withheld no benefit from them.

[Ambrose, Haimo] [Col. 1481A] For he raised their dead and healed various infirmities. He is said to stretch out his hands who bestows benefits liberally upon those who ask.

Or it may be understood of hands stretched out on the cross, the whole being put for a part. Thus “all day long” means a part of the whole day. I stretched out my hands on the cross to a people who did not believe, but contradicted me—which is worse.

## Chapter XI

### Verses 1–4

> “I say, then: Has God rejected his people? Far be it! For I too am an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin. The Lord has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. Do you not know what Scripture says in the case of Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel? ‘Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have dug down your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life.’ But what does the divine answer say to him? ‘I have reserved for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal.’”

“I say, then.” Since he had refuted the Jews by so many authorities, the Gentiles might have mocked them, saying that they had been entirely rejected. Against them he begins thus: “I say, then,” etc.

Since he showed the people of Israel to be unbelieving, lest he be thought to have declared all Israel unbelieving, he shows that God did not reject his inheritance. As though he said: Because I said that Israel is an unbelieving people, do I therefore say—or seem to say—that God has wholly rejected his people or inheritance, namely the Jews to whom he did good?

[Haimo, Ambrose] But do I say this? Or: “Has God rejected [his people]?” Far be it! For although I say that the Jews are unbelieving, yet not all are so; and although God has rejected them in part, he has not rejected them entirely, because he has not rejected me and others who were predestined.

“For I too am an Israelite”—that is, a Jew, not a proselyte—being from Abraham’s seed and from the tribe of Benjamin. As though he said: I descend from Abraham through Benjamin’s line. He says this lest he be thought to be from Ishmael.

“The Lord has not rejected.” As though he said: Just as he has not rejected me, likewise God has not rejected his people, whom he foreknew would be saved. For “foreknew” is here used for “predestined,” as the following words make clear. He said “whom he foreknew” so that the Jews might not again become proud because he called them unrejected and God’s people.

[Col. 1481D] “Do you not know?” As though he said: Thus the Lord did not reject the remnant in this time, but saved them, just as in Elijah’s time he reserved many for himself when Elijah thought that he alone remained. If Elijah did not know, it is no wonder that these do not know.

[Ambrose] [Col. 1481D] In Elijah’s time, when Ahab king of Samaria gave his daughter to Joram king of Judah, all the Jews appeared to be idolaters, so that Elijah thought himself the only one left in the worship of God. When Ahab king of Samaria and his wife Jezebel, trusting false prophets, persecuted God’s prophets, who hid themselves in caves, and when Ahab and Jezebel likewise urged the people toward idolatry, God showed Elijah that he had not been left alone.

[Col. 1482A] This is what he says: [Col. 1482B] “Do you not know what Scripture”—that is, the Book of Kings—“says in Elijah,” that is, where it speaks of Elijah: namely, how he “appeals”—that is, calls God as judge between himself and them—“against Israel,” saying:

> “Lord, they have killed your prophets”—this occurred under Jezebel—“and they have dug down your altars,” that is, overthrown them from their foundations; “and I alone am left in divine worship, and they seek my life,” that is, seek to take it away.

“But what?” As though he said: He thought himself alone, but what does Scripture say was the divine response spoken to him?

[Ambrose] “Behold, I have reserved”—that is, preserved by grace—“for myself seven thousand men”: that is, all the good. For universality is signified by the number seven, and perfection by a thousand: “who have not bent their knees before Baal,” the god of Ahab and Jezebel.

### Verses 5–10

> “So then, at this present time also, a remnant has been saved according to the election of God’s grace. But if by grace, no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. What then? Israel has not obtained what it sought; but the election has obtained it, while the rest have been blinded, as it is written: ‘God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes so that they may not see, and ears so that they may not hear, unto this present day.’ And David says: ‘Let their table become before them a snare, and a trap, and a stumbling block, and a recompense to them. Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see, and bend their back always.’”

“So then, at this present time,” etc. As though he said: Since there were then many good persons, even though Elijah did not know it, so also now, that is, in the same hidden manner; or, “so” means by the same grace, and in this time of grace, when it is easier.

[Col. 1482C] A remnant will be saved—or has been saved.

[Ambrose] And this is not according to merits but according to the election of grace, that is, through the grace by which they were elected. Hence the Lord says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15). For we did not first believe in him so that he might choose us. For if he chose us when already believing, he chose persons who were already chosen.

“But if.” As though he said: He said that they are saved by grace.

[Note: [Col. 1481D] Augustine, *On John*.]

“But if [they are saved] by grace,” that is, through grace, “then no longer from works of the Law.” Otherwise—that is, if they are saved through works of the Law—grace is no longer grace, but a debt. But it is agreed that grace is grace.

[Col. 1482D] “What then?” Having heard that the remnant has been saved by grace, not from works, what then is to be said? This: Israel did not attain what it sought, namely righteousness from works. But the election attained it: that is, those elected by grace received righteousness through faith. The rest, however, not only did not obtain righteousness, but were also blinded, or became so, by judgment.

[Note: [Col. 1482D] The same author, *On the Predestination of the Saints*.]

Election, therefore, is of grace, not merits; but blinding is according to merits. For they were blinded because they were unwilling to believe, just as the others believed because they were willing.

[Ambrose] [Col. 1483A] Mercy and judgment, therefore, were exercised by God upon those very wills: upon the former through mercy, grace being added; upon the latter through judgment, grace being withdrawn. Whoever, having understood, refuses to believe, ought to receive what he wills—namely, that thereafter he may be unable to believe. Therefore they were assisted in their own will, not by evil being inserted into them, but by grace being withdrawn: so that, because knowingly they said truth to be falsehood, thereafter they would not understand what is true. The envy of an evil will deserved this.

[Haimo] It is not so, however, with those who do this through error.

Then he proves by Isaiah’s authority that the Jews were blinded in part, saying: “As it is written in Isaiah,” though in different words:

> “For God gave them a spirit of compunction,” that is, an evil spirit; that is, he permitted them to have evil compunction.

Here he means evil compunction, by which even what is good often becomes burdensome to a person, just as Christ’s teaching displeased the Pharisees.

[Col. 1483B] Therefore he calls the envious mind a “spirit of compunction,” by which they envied Christ’s teaching and the salvation of the Gentiles. He also gave them “eyes”—that is, reason, which is able in itself to see, but which they have in such a way that they do not see for themselves; and “ears”—that is, reason, which understands when another teaches, but which they have in such a way that they do not hear.

The meaning is: He gave them reason, by which they nevertheless neither understand of themselves what they could understand of themselves if they wished, nor understand from another what they could know through another’s teaching.

[Col. 1483C] Their blindness continues “unto this present day,” that is, as long as a day can be called “today”: up to the present day of all to whom this writing shall come.

Then he confirms the same point by the Prophet’s authority, adding: “And David says”:

> “Let their table”—that is, the evil which they offered to me, said to have been “before them” because they knew their iniquity and nevertheless persisted in it—“become a snare for them.”

As though he said: Just as they themselves offered me vinegar, so let that iniquity itself become a snare to them, so as to hinder them; “and a trap,” to hold them; “and a stumbling block and a recompense,” that is, a cause of stumbling and eternal punishment.

Or he calls Holy Scripture “the table,” where the souls of believers are refreshed and filled with spiritual food. But the Jews, relying upon the letter of the Law and despising spiritual understanding, sit at the table hungry. This table—that is, Holy Scripture—is said to have been placed “before them,” because they delight in its carnal observances. Or it is said to have been placed before them because, if they wished to attend to reason, they could understand.

[Col. 1483D] Let this table, then, become a snare to them. Scripture, which for those who understand is the bread of refreshment, ensnares when it is understood wrongly; and for this reason Christ’s preaching is rejected. Let it become for them “a trap and a stumbling block and a recompense.”

And so it became for the Jews. Scripture of the Law was a cause of captivity to them, because through zeal for it they killed Christ; and that captivity became for them a cause of scandal and reproach, and afterward it will become the cause of eternal condemnation, which is especially called “recompense.”

[Col. 1484A] “Let their eyes be darkened”—that is, let reason, which sees, fail to see that they sin. As though he said: Since they did not see without cause, let them be made not to see. “And bend their back always”—that is, weigh down free choice, which ought to be raised upward, with sins.

[Haimo] Note that these words are spoken not as the desire of one wishing, but in the office of one foretelling.

### Verses 11–12

> “I say, then: Have they stumbled so as to fall? Far be it! But through their transgression salvation has come to the Gentiles, so that they may provoke them to jealousy. But if their transgression is the riches of the world, and their diminution the riches of the Gentiles, how much more their fullness?”

“I say, then.” As though he said: By the authority of the prophets I say that the Jews have been blinded. In saying this, then, I say—or seem and am thought to say—

[Haimo] [Col. 1484B] that they have stumbled so as not merely to fall, but to fall without restoration and without benefit.

But do you suppose that they fell irrecoverably and without benefit because I say, on prophetic authority, that they have been blinded? On the contrary, even their fall is beneficial, and they can be restored, lest anyone despise them too greatly. For did they stumble in such a way as to fall uselessly or irrecoverably? Far be it that their fall should be useless. Rather it is useful, because through their transgression—by which, being blind, they killed God—

[Augustine] or rejected the Word—salvation came to the Gentiles. Leaving the Jews, the apostles turned to the Gentiles. Thus it is said to the Jews in the Acts of the Apostles: “Because you have rejected the word of God, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13). Thus through their transgression, by which they rejected the Word, salvation came to the Gentiles.

[Note: [Col. 1483D] Augustine, *On the Judgment of God*.]

[Col. 1484C] Salvation also came to the Gentiles through the transgression by which they killed Christ, because the Jews, ravaged for the sin of Christ’s death, more miserably afflicted by the Romans, scattered throughout the world, and utterly uprooted from their kingdom, serve as a testimony that the prophecies concerning Christ, which the apostles expounded to the Gentiles, are not fabricated.

“So that they may provoke them.” As though he said: Salvation came to the Gentiles, so that the Jews, zealous for the Law and the fathers, may be provoked to jealousy of them—that is, of the Gentiles—and may envy and hate them.

Or it may be understood in a good sense. As though he said: Salvation came to the Gentiles so that the Jews may emulate them—that is, imitate the Gentiles. This has often happened and will happen more fully at the end of the age, when Jews will follow Christians in faith in Christ. Then Moses’ hand will be brought back into his bosom; then our Moses will return to his mother and his brothers.

It may also be understood thus: Salvation will come to the Gentiles, so that the Gentiles may emulate them—that is, imitate the Jews—by believing as they themselves believed. Or: so that the Gentiles may be moved by divine zeal against the evil works of the Jews.

“But if their transgression.” I said that the Jews’ transgression benefits others; if so, their conversion will benefit them still more. This is what he says. As though he said: Through their transgression salvation comes to the Gentiles.

[Augustine] “But if”—that is, “if their transgression,” by which they killed Christ or rejected the Word—

[Ambrose, Haimo] is “the riches of the world,” that is, if through their transgression the world has been enriched; and if “their diminution,” that is, their rejection, is “the riches of the Gentiles”—if the few converted Jews, such as the apostles, enriched the Gentiles—how much more will “their fullness,” which will be converted at the end of the world, be the riches of the Gentiles?

That is, if God turned their evil into good, namely into the riches of the world, much more will their good, namely when their fullness is converted at the end of the world, enrich the Gentiles through teaching and example. [Col. 1485A] In this he shows that the Jews’ fall is neither useless nor irrecoverable; and, as though someone asked whether they can be converted, he says: Certainly they can.

### Verses 13–24

> “For I speak to you Gentiles: Inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry, if somehow I may provoke my flesh to jealousy and save some of them. For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead? But if the firstfruits are holy, so also is the lump; and if the root is holy, so also are the branches. But if some of the branches have been broken off, while you, though you were a wild olive, have been grafted in among them and have become a participant in the root and richness of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches. But if you boast, it is not you who bear the root, but the root you. You say then: ‘The branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.’ Well: they were broken off because of unbelief. But you stand by faith. Do not think proudly, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps neither will he spare you. See, then, the goodness and severity of God: severity upon those who fell, but God’s goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness; otherwise you too will be cut off. And they also, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in; for God is able to graft them in again. For if you have been cut from the naturally wild olive tree and, contrary to nature, grafted into a good olive tree, how much more will these, who are according to nature, be grafted into their own olive tree?”

“I speak to you Gentiles,” that is, to Gentiles who are especially mine, concerning this: “Inasmuch as I am indeed the Apostle of the Gentiles”—and always am so, not of the Jews, because I was sent to the Gentiles—“I will honor my ministry.”

Although I am Apostle of the Gentiles, I honor my ministry by adding beyond what I owe: I labor also for the Jews, trying somehow—whether in prosperity or adversity—to provoke “my flesh,” that is, the Jews from whom I was born, to emulation, that is, to imitate me.

[Col. 1485D] I try in many ways to convert the Jews, so that, if one path does not succeed, I may undertake another. I would not do this if I despaired of their salvation. I say, I seek to provoke them to imitation, so that, God’s grace assisting, I may save at least some of them.

“For if.” As though he said: Therefore I labor for them, because their acceptance will be useful for the instruction of the Gentiles. And indeed:

[Note: [Col. 1485D] Augustine, *The City of God*.]

“If their rejection”—that is, their unbelief—“is the reconciliation of the world,”

[Col. 1486A] what will be the acceptance of the rest but life of the Gentiles from the dead, [Col. 1486B] that is, from the state in which they are dead?

That the Jews can be accepted is proved, to restrain the pride of certain Gentiles who might perhaps say that the whole Jewish people is condemned, by adding an analogy from nature: “But if the firstfruits.”

As though he said: I said that their acceptance will be very useful; lest you Gentiles say that this cannot happen because their whole people has been rejected: if the firstfruits have been made—that is, if a few of them have been accepted into faith, such as the apostles and other disciples, and made holy—then the lump also is holy, that is, the people can be sanctified.

The firstfruits are a small portion of something taken as a sample of the whole lump, as from food or drink. Since the firstfruits are of one substance with the lump, the firstfruits cannot be holy and the lump unclean; for the firstfruits are from the lump.

“And if the root is holy”—that is, if the patriarchs from whom they draw the sap of faith were holy—“then the branches,” namely those who sprang from their stock and are founded in their faith, are holy.

[Haimo] Just as a good root spreads good sap through the branches, where fruits of good flavor are produced, so the apostles and others who derived their origin from the holy fathers and imitated their faith were good and holy.

“But if some.” He further proves that the Jews can be accepted, in order to restrain the Gentiles. As though he said: The branches can be sanctified; but if some of the natural branches were broken off—that is, cut off from the promise, namely the blasphemous and ungodly persons among the Jewish people—

[Col. 1486C] while you, Gentile, though you were a wild olive,

[Note: [Col. 1485D] The same author, above on John.]

that is, naturally barren and bitter, have been grafted in—that is, joined by another’s action—among them, that is, in the place of the broken branches; and have become a companion, that is, a participant, in the root, namely the patriarchs and prophets, and in the richness, namely the apostles, who above all possess the spirit of the root—the richness of the olive tree, that is, of the Jewish people who were fruitful before Christ’s coming—if this is so:

Do not boast against the broken branches—that is, do not exult over another’s misfortune. For though the olive tree has been pruned, it has not been cut down.

[Note: [Col. 1486D] Augustine, *On Psalm 133*.]

Those proud and blasphemous persons are no longer there through their breaking off. The wild olive was not there; now it is there. They deserved to be broken off through pride; this one deserved to be grafted in through humility. They lost the root, and this one held it and became a participant in the root and in the richness of the olive tree, in the hope of promise.

[Ambrose] Since many Jews did not believe, the Gentiles also were grafted in through faith into the hope of promise, so that the Jews might feel grief. This, however, is contrary to the customary rule and law of grafting. For a good tree is normally grafted into a bad one; but here a bad tree is grafted into a good one. For he says that the wild olive was grafted in so that the shoot might bear the root’s fruit.

Do not then rejoice in their unbelief. For, as Solomon says: “He who exults over another’s misfortunes displeases God.” The Jews were not rejected on account of the Gentiles; rather, because they did not believe, they gave occasion for preaching to the Gentiles. [Col. 1487B]

[Col. 1487A] Or: Do not boast against the branches still standing. But if you boast against them, you, Gentile, are told: It is not you who bear the root, but the root bears you. That is, that people has nothing from you, but you have faith from it.

You say then, Gentile: “The branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.” As though he said: Although it is not permitted to boast against those still standing, or even against the others, the Gentile says, “They were rejected as the cause of my grafting in.” The Apostle removes this claim by saying: “Well,” that is, what you say is true, namely that they were broken off; but your addition, “so that I might be grafted in,” was not the efficient cause.

Rather, they were broken off because of their own unbelief, that is, through their own fault. Hence their breaking off gave you an opportunity for salvation, not because of you. For the Jews were not rejected by God in order that the Gentiles might enter; rather, by despising God’s gift, they made themselves rejected. Thus they also gave the Gentiles an occasion for salvation.

He wishes this arrogance to be restrained, so that one may rejoice rather in salvation and not insult weakness. For one who rejoices in others’ evils is easily deceived.

But you stand by faith. [Note: Col. 1487D, Augustine, *On Questions of Nature.*] As though he said: Consider the grace of the New Testament. Your standing is God’s gift, not your own merit. Therefore do not think highly of yourself—that is, do not think proudly—lest you too be broken off through pride, as that man was through unbelief; but fear, fear chastely: namely, fear offending God, not merely falling into punishment, but losing the benefit of so great a grace. [53] For chaste fear is present when the soul takes care lest, having deserted God, God should desert it. [Note: Col. 1487D, the same author, in a sermon on the fear of the Lord.]

And you ought to fear: for if God did not spare the natural branches—that is, the Jews—[Col. 1487C] who are in a certain sense natural branches by the prerogative of the fathers to whom the promise was made, see that perhaps this may not happen to you; it can indeed happen, that he will not spare you, an alien branch, either. [Ambrose, Haimo] For if God did not spare the Jews, who derived their origin from holy fathers and from whose people he himself assumed flesh, much less will he spare you if you fall away from faith or swell with pride.

Then, having set forth two points, he adds two corresponding ones: “See therefore.” As though he said: Because you stand by faith, see therefore God’s kindness; and because they were broken off through unbelief, see his severity—that is, his strict justice. He mentions God’s kindness and severity because by kindness he persuades and by severity he terrifies. Observe both, then, O Gentile, [Col. 1487D] and through both learn humility. Toward those indeed who have fallen, behold severity; but toward yourself behold the kindness of God, by which he confers a benefit on you. I say that God’s kindness is toward you, but on this condition: if you remain in his kindness, that is, if you attribute everything to God. Otherwise—that is, unless you remain—you too, like them, will be cut off from the holy root and will experience God’s severity.

But they also. As though he said: Not only will you be cut off if you do not remain in the good; they also—that is, the Jews—will be grafted in if they do not remain in unbelief, and therefore they are not to be despised. I say, if they do not remain—which can indeed happen. For God is able to graft them in again. For if—[Col. 1488A] as though he said—he is able to graft them in, and truly they will be grafted in. He proves this from the lesser case, speaking to the Gentile: they will truly be grafted in. For you, O Gentile, were cut from a wild olive tree—that is, from the barren rites of the Gentiles—natural to you, since you were born from it. For idolatry and things of that kind are, through practice, as it were natural to the Gentiles. And you were grafted into a good olive tree—that is, through faith you were united to the patriarchs and apostles, who possessed the richness of the Holy Spirit. [Ambrose] For here the olive tree means the faith of the patriarchs. You were grafted in, I say, and this contrary to nature, because it is natural for us to graft a shoot of a good tree into the trunk of a bad one, not a shoot of a bad tree into the trunk of a good one. And this is called grafting.

[Note: Col. 1488D, the same author, *Against Faustus.*] Yet, in ordinary human speech, something is said to be contrary to nature when it is contrary to the course of nature known to mortals—such as a shoot bearing fruit for the root. For the Apostle calls “contrary to nature” that which is contrary to the customary course of nature grasped by human knowledge. But God, the creator and founder of all natures, does nothing contrary to nature, because whatever he does is nature—or natural—for each thing; from him comes every measure, number, and order of nature. Yet it is not inappropriate to say that he does something contrary to nature when he does what is contrary to what we know in nature. For we call this known course, and customary course, of nature; and when God does something contrary to it, such things are called or termed great works or miracles. But against that highest law of nature, remote from the knowledge either of the ungodly or of the weak, God no more acts [Col. 1488C] than he acts against himself.

“How much more.” As though he said: And if this is so, as indeed it is, how much more will these who are according to nature—that is, Jews instructed by the Law in the worship of God—be grafted into their own olive tree, that is, united to their own people.

**VERS. 25–32.**—“For I do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own estimation: that blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter; and thus all Israel should be saved, as it is written: ‘There shall come from Zion one who delivers and turns impiety away from Jacob. And this is my covenant with them, when I take away their sins.’ As regards the Gospel, indeed, they are enemies for your sake; but as regards election, they are most beloved for the sake of the fathers. For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance. For just as you too once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy through their unbelief, so these too have now not believed in your mercy, that they too may obtain mercy. For God has shut up all in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all.”

“For I do not want.” As though he said: The Jews will be grafted in. And truly, because both some are being grafted in meanwhile and the fullness will be grafted in at last. And I want you to know this; this is what he says: “For I do not want you, O brothers, to be ignorant of this mystery”—that is, I do not want you to be ignorant of this hidden judgment of God; [Col. 1489A] a mystery, I say, so that you may not be wise in your own estimation—that is, I call it a mystery lest you think that you can examine it by your own intelligence.

He shows what this mystery is which he does not want them to ignore: namely, that blindness happened to Israel, not by nature but through their own fault, and only in part. For not all were blinded. It happened, I say, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter—that is, in order that it might enter; and “until it should enter” marks both a cause and a limit. And thus, namely after it has entered, all Israel will be saved through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, emulating the Gentiles. Thus, and so forth. As though he said: Israel will be saved, as it is written in Isaiah: “There shall come according to the flesh from Zion,” that is, from the Jews, “one who delivers,” as though by force—which happens even now when some Jew is scarcely converted—“and turns away,” voluntarily, [Col. 1489B] which will occur at the end when they will be converted easily, “impiety from Jacob,” that is, from the Jews: impiety meaning unbelief, or the worship of legal observance. For the worship of the Jews, since Christ’s coming, is impiety.

“And this will be my covenant with them”—that is, this promise will be fulfilled for them by me, because I myself will do what I promised. When? “When I take away,” that is, remit, “their sins.” This will occur at the end, when the Jews are converted through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch. [Note: Col. 1489D, Augustine, *The City of God.*] Hence Malachi says: “I will send you Elijah the Tishbite, who will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to the fathers, so that the children too may understand as the fathers—that is, the prophets—understood” (Malachi 4).

[Haimo] For the heart of the fathers will thus be turned to the children when their understanding is conveyed to the children; and the heart of the children [Col. 1489C] to the fathers when those fathers think what the children thought. And they, as regards the Gospel—As though he said: The Jews will then be converted, but for the present they are enemies of God and of us; and this is as regards the Gospel, that is, because of the Gospel, which is contrary to their Law, not because of their race. [Ambrose] And all this happens for your sake—that is, for your advantage, O Gentiles—so that room might be made for you to enter the faith. For the error of the Jews opened the way for the Gentiles to enter the faith before the proper time. For the Gospel first had to be preached everywhere to all Jews, and only then to the Gentiles. But because the Jews did not believe, the kingdom was taken from them and given to the Gentiles. Thus, on their occasion, the Gentiles received God’s grace sooner.

Or thus: They will then be converted, but for the present they are enemies indeed of God and of us through themselves—that is, through their own fault—yet this is as regards the Gospel and for your sake, that is, for the advance of the Gospel and of yourselves. [Augustine] For their hostility, by which they killed Christ, undoubtedly advanced the Gospel. [Note: Col. 1489D, the same author, *On the Predestination of the Saints.*] And this shows that it came about through God’s ordering. He knows how to use even evils well—not because they benefit the evildoers, but because, as he makes good use of them, they benefit the elect. Therefore it lies within the power of the wicked to sin; but that, by sinning, they should accomplish this or that result by their wickedness, does not lie in their power, but in that of God who permits it. Thus of themselves they could become enemies; yet this advances the Gospel when God uses evils for good, [Col. 1490A] so that, while they act against the will—that is, the command—of God, the will of God, wisely disposing all things, is nevertheless fulfilled concerning them and permits their action.

“But as regards election.” As though he said: Some Jews are enemies as regards the Gospel and for your sake; [Ambrose] but some of them are most beloved and elect. This is not because of their merits, but as regards election—that is, because they are chosen through grace—and for the sake of the fathers: [Augustine] that is, for the promises made to the fathers, because God’s love toward these is awakened by the remembrance of worthy fathers, through whose prerogative they received very many benefits from God. The elect, therefore, are beloved for the fathers’ sake, to whom these things were promised.

Behold: in these preceding words it has been shown why [Col. 1490B] one part of the Jews was blinded—namely, through its own fault and for the Gentiles’ sake—and why another part was enlightened—namely, by the grace of election and for the fathers’ sake. Although he seems to speak of the same people when he says “enemies” and “beloved,” since all belonged to one nation, nevertheless some are enemies of God while others are most beloved and beloved. [Note: Col. 1490D, Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints.*]

“For [the gifts and calling of God are] without repentance.” As though he said: I say that they are to be saved according to election and for the fathers’ sake, because they are not called by that calling by which many who are not foreknown are called and yet perish—the calling of which it was said, “Many are called,” etc. (Matthew 22)—but by that calling by which the elect are called. All who belong to it are taught by God, and none of them can say, “I believed in order that I might be called in this way,” because God’s mercy, by which he was called in order to believe, went before him. This calling is without [Col. 1490C] repentance—that is, without change—because whoever hears from the Father comes to the Son, who loses nothing of all that is given to him; whoever perishes was not from that company. Whoever is from it does not perish at all. Therefore John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2). [Augustine] For they belonged to the multitude of those called, but not to the small number of the elect. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.

And this is what he says. As though he said: They are truly to be saved according to election and for the fathers’ sake, because the gifts—that is, the promises—and the calling of God—that is, God’s eternal election—are without repentance, that is, without a change in God’s purpose. Or thus: I say “according to election” because God inspires faith in those to whom he gives it without any preceding repentance of theirs. And this is the meaning: the gifts and calling of God are without [54] preceding repentance; [Col. 1490D] that is, the gratuitous inward calling by which God calls one to faith, which no merit anticipates.

[Ambrose] Or thus: He had said, “There shall come one who turns impiety away from Jacob, and this will occur when I take away their sins.” But lest anyone suppose that they cannot receive mercy because he does not see them afflicted with outward repentance, he says, “Without repentance.” As though he said: Let no one despair of them, even if they do not outwardly mourn; for God’s calling, by which he calls to faith, and his gifts—that is, the remission of sins which he bestows in baptism—are without outward repentance. [Col. 1491A] This is true, because God’s grace in baptism requires neither groaning nor weeping nor any work, but only faith and contrition of heart; and it freely forgives everything. He says this lest they think that the Jews cannot receive mercy because they do not see them grieving.

“For just as.” Here he shows that impiety can be turned away from Jacob, because it was also removed from the Gentiles, who once did not believe. As though he said: Thus it was necessary that some Jews should be enemies and others elect. For you too, O Gentiles, once—that is, for a longer time than these—did not believe God. This served so that you might now believe humbly: that is, God formerly permitted you not to believe so that, after your conversion, you might have no ground for pride. But now—that is, recently—you have obtained [Col. 1491B] mercy, after it had been proved that nature fails—that is, that you cannot be helped by free choice. You have obtained it, I say, through their unbelief, which is one cause of your mercy.

So these also—that is, the Jews—have now not believed, lest after their conversion they should have material for glorying in the Law. They have not believed, I say, entering into your mercy—that is, they have not received the grace of faith through God’s mercy, as we also have. They have not believed, I say, so that they too, humbled, may obtain mercy with you—that is, the grace of faith. Therefore this happened to both—that is, to Jews and Gentiles—because God has shut up, [Haimo] that is, permitted all to be shut up, namely Jews [Col. 1491C] and Gentiles, in unbelief, [Ambrose] because otherwise they would fall through pride.

[Note: Col. 1491D, Augustine, *The City of God.*] Here he seems in some measure to explain the mystery. For God shut up all in unbelief so that, ashamed in repentance of the bitterness of their unbelief and turned in faith to the sweetness of God’s mercy, they might remain more humble; and so that the grace of the gift might be most welcome, and they might cry: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord” (Psalm 30). He shut them up, I say, nevertheless in such a way that he might have mercy on all—that is, Jews and Gentiles—not meaning that he would condemn none, as some have falsely supposed.

**VERS. 33–36.**—“O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who [Col. 1491D] has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor? Or who has first given to him, and will be repaid by him? For from him, and through him, and in him are all things. To him be glory for ages of ages. Amen.”

“O the depth,” etc. He had set forth a judgment of wonderful profundity: namely, that God shut up all in unbelief in order to have mercy on all. Struck as if with horror by its depth, and trembling as before the depth of an abyss, the Apostle cries: “O the depth,” etc. [Note: Col. 1491D, Augustine, *On Rebuke and Grace.*] For we possess a very limited understanding for examining the justice of God’s judgments, for examining gratuitous grace bestowed without any preceding merits; and we are not so disturbed that grace is granted to the unworthy as that it is equally denied to others who are unworthy. [Note: Col. 1492D, the same author, *On the Spirit and the Letter.*]

For I know that, just as impossibility, so also injustice is not with God; and I know that he resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. But why he gives to some unworthy persons and denies it to others is obscure. Something lies hidden in the deep recesses of God’s judgments. Likewise, it is not clear why he saved Jews and Gentiles in this way: by first allowing them to be shut up in unbelief. If anyone therefore asks why they are saved in this way, when there are many other modes of salvation, the Apostle indicates that he does not know this by rational reflection.

[Ambrose] As though he said: God blinded Gentiles and Jews for a time, in order that he might have mercy on all. You might think it possible to comprehend why [Col. 1492B] this was done so. For this is the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge, which by manifold providence has gained Gentiles and Jews for life. The Apostle therefore marvels at this, saying: “O the depth of riches.” He says this because God knows many things, and the profound things of wisdom, [Haimo] which concern spiritual realities, and of God’s knowledge, which concerns worldly realities. For with God is the sublime and profound knowledge of all divine and human things; he alone sees all things as they are, and before his knowledge all our understanding is blunted.

“How incomprehensible,” etc. As though he said: As his wisdom and knowledge are incomprehensible, so also are the judgments which he has made from wisdom and knowledge. And this is what he says: “How incomprehensible are his judgments,” that is, his dispositions concerning all things; “and how unsearchable his ways,” that is, the fulfillments of his dispositions, because even in their accomplishment it cannot be known what he has ordained.

Then, using Isaiah’s words, he proves that God’s wisdom is high, adding: “For who?” As though he said: His wisdom and knowledge are indeed lofty. For who, Isaiah says, has known [Col. 1492C] the mind of the Lord in wisdom and knowledge? Or who has been his counsellor in the ordering or accomplishing of things—that is, whose counsel did he follow, or who knew his counsel? [Ambrose] The counsellor of the Father is his only-begotten Son, who is also called the Angel of Great Counsel; but among human beings and angels none has been his counsellor.

“Or who has first [given]?” As though he said: Even if we cannot know God’s judgments, at least this is certain: grace alone gives good things, not preceding merit. This is what he says: “Or who has first given him faith and good works before being anticipated by his grace, and will be repaid by him”—will he receive a reward from God because he first gave his faith to him? No one. [Augustine] For rather all things are from him, the Father, from whom the Son is; [Haimo] and through him, the Son, through whom all things were made; [Augustine] and in him, the Holy Spirit, because by love alone he created and preserves all things.

[Haimo] Behold, here the Trinity of persons and unity of essence are shown. For the three distinct prepositions—“from,” “through,” and “in”—indicate the distinction of persons. [Col. 1493A] [Augustine] But the repeated pronoun “him” suggests identity of substance, as also does what follows, “to him be glory,” not “to them.” For Catholic faith proclaims not two or three gods, but the Trinity itself as one God; not so that the same Trinity may sometimes be called Father, sometimes Son, sometimes Holy Spirit, as Sabellius believes, but so that the Father is only Father, the Son only Son, and the Holy Spirit only Holy Spirit. And this Trinity is only one God. The Apostle is believed to have suggested this Trinity when he says: “From him, and through him, and in him are all things.”

[Note: Col. 1493D, Augustine, *On the Nature of the Good.*] When we hear that all things are from God, we must understand all natures and everything that exists naturally. For sins, which do not preserve nature but corrupt it, are not from him; sins arise from the will of those who sin, and although all things which he created are in God, those who sin do not defile him. Of his wisdom it is said: “She reaches to all things” (Wisdom 8), because of her purity; and nothing defiled comes into her.

We must also observe that he did not say “all things are of him,” but “all things are from him.” For “from him” does not wholly signify the same thing as “of him.” What is of him may be said to be from him, but not everything that is from him may be said to be of him, because it is not from his substance. Heaven and earth are from him because he made them, but they are not of him because they are not from his substance. [Augustine] Just as if a man begets a son and makes a house: the house is from him and the son is from him; but the son is of him, while the house is of wood [Col. 1493C] and earth. [Note: Col. 1493D, the same author, *On the Trinity.*]

Therefore, beholding the Creator in understanding through the things that have been made, we ought to understand the Trinity, whose trace appears in creatures. For in that Trinity are the highest origin of all things, the most perfect beauty, and the most blessed love. Thus those three seem to be bounded by one another and infinite in themselves. So each is in each, all are in each, each is in all, and all are one. Therefore we must not understand confusedly what the Apostle says: “From him, and through him, and in him are all things.” He says “from him” with reference to the Father, “through him” with reference to the Son, and “in him” with reference to the Holy Spirit. He does not say “from them,” “through them,” and “in them”; nor does he say “to them be glory,” but “to him,” [Col. 1493D] wishing to suggest that this Trinity is one God.

[Augustine] But take diligent care lest, because he says “from him” wishing the Father to be understood, you understand all things to be from the Father in such a way that you deny that all things are from the Son or from the Holy Spirit. For it may rightly be said that all things are from the Father, through the Father, and in the Father; similarly, this may be said of the Son and the Holy Spirit. Accordingly, when it is said, “From him, and through him, and in him are all things,” the equality of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is undoubtedly demonstrated. [Note: Col. 1493D, the same author, in the same work.]

And because he had not previously named the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit, [Col. 1494A] but had named God and Lord—which may signify the Trinity itself—he wished to refer each of these three expressions to each of the persons, adding “from him.” [Note: Col. 1494D, Augustine, *On True Religion.*] Therefore let true religion bind you to the one omnipotent God, because no creature is interposed between our mind, by which we understand him, and the Father and Truth—that is, the inner light through which we understand him.

[Augustine] Therefore let us worship Truth itself also, in no respect unlike the Father, in him and with him: that Truth which is the form of all things made from one and referred to one. Yet all these things would neither be made by the Father through the Son nor be preserved sound within their own limits unless God were supremely good, who did not begrudge any nature which was good from him; and who gave some things, as much as they willed, and others, as much as they could, that they might remain in that good. Therefore it is fitting that we worship and hold fast the gift of God itself, equally unchangeable with the Father and Son: the Trinity of one substance—the God from whom we are, through whom we are, and in whom we are; [55] [Col. 1494B] from whom we departed, to whom we became unlike, yet from whom we were not permitted to perish; the beginning to which we return, the form which we follow, and the grace through which we are reconciled; the one author by whom we were created, his likeness through which we are reformed into unity, and the peace by which we cleave to unity: namely, God who said, “Let it be”; the Word through whom everything that was made substantially and naturally was made; and the gift of his kindness, by which it pleased him, and by which that which was made from him through the Word was reconciled to its author, so that it should not perish. [Col. 1494C]

[Note: Col. 1494D, Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine.*] These are the realities to be enjoyed: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This Trinity too is one supreme reality, shared by all who enjoy it—if indeed it ought to be called a reality and not rather the cause of all realities, if indeed even “cause” is adequate. For a name suited to so great an excellence cannot easily be found. Yet it is better said thus: this Trinity is one God, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things. Thus the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are each God, and all together one God; each of them is a full substance, and all together one substance.

[Note: Col. 1494D, the same author, book VI, *On the Trinity.*] The Father is neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit; the Son is neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son. Rather, the Father is Father alone, the Son Son alone, and the Holy Spirit Holy Spirit alone. The same eternity belongs to all three, the same unchangeability, the same majesty, the same power. In the Father is unity; in the Son, equality; in the Holy Spirit, the harmony of unity and equality. These three, we say, are all one on account of the Father, all equal on account of the Son, all joined together on account of the Holy Spirit. Yet they are one: namely, the one Lord to whom that service is owed which is called *latria* in Greek. [Col. 1495A] *Latria* is owed to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

[Note: Col. 1495D, Augustine, book VI, *On the Trinity.*] The Father has no Father from whom he exists; but the Son is from the Father, both so that he exists and so that he is coeternal with him. For if an image perfectly fulfills that of which it is the image, it is equal to it, not it to its image. Here is the highest congruity, the first equality, and the first likeness: differing in no respect, unequal in no way, dissimilar in no part. Yet it corresponds identically to that whose image it is. There is the highest and first life, for which living, understanding, and being are not different things: to understand is for it to live, and this is to be.

This is one thing, as it were a perfect Word, lacking nothing; a certain art of the omnipotent and wise God, full of all the unchangeable living rational principles. [Col. 1495B] All are one in it, just as it in turn is one with him with whom it is one. There God knows all things which he made through it; and therefore, though times depart and succeed one another, nothing departs from or succeeds to God’s knowledge. Created things are not known by God because they were made; rather, were they not made because they are immutably known by God?

That ineffable embrace of the Father and the Image is not without enjoyment, love, or joy. That love, delight, happiness, or blessedness—if human speech or voice can worthily name it—is in the Trinity the Holy Spirit: not begotten, but the sweetness of begetter and begotten, flooding all creatures in abundant generosity and fullness according to their capacity, so that they keep their proper order.

All these things made by divine art [Col. 1495C] display in themselves a certain unity, form, and order. For every created thing is one thing, is formed with some kind of shape, and seeks or keeps some order. Thus, as we have said, the trace of the Trinity shines forth in creatures. For this reason we say that the nature of the highest good is simple: not because the Father alone, or the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone is in it—that is, not because this Trinity alone exists without a substance of persons, as the Sabellians supposed—but because it is what it has, except that a person is also said relatively in relation to another and is not that other. For the Father has the Son, to whom he is relatively related, yet he is not the Son; [Col. 1495D] and the Son has the Father, yet he himself is not the Father.

This nature is therefore called simple also because it is not one thing that possesses and another what it possesses, as in other things. For that which possesses liquid is not itself liquid; a body is not color; nor is air light. Therefore the Father alone is not God, nor the Son alone, nor the Holy Spirit alone; but the Trinity itself alone is one God.

“To him be glory.” As though he said: Since he is such, glory belongs to him, one singly according to substance, not to “them”; and this for ages of ages. Amen.

## Chapter XII

**VERS. 1–2.**—“Therefore I beseech you, brothers, through [Col. 1496A] the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God—your rational service. And do not be conformed to this age, but be reformed in the newness of your understanding, so that you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.”

“Therefore I beseech you.” [Ambrose] After treating of the Law and faith, and of the nature of the Jewish and Gentile peoples, he exhorts them to live rightly. For up to this point he warned them lest one should be proud against another. From here begins moral admonition, by which he urges each to work for the other’s benefit. As though he said: Because all things are in him, therefore I beseech you, brothers. As though he said: Brotherhood requires what I ask. I beseech you, I say, through the mercy of God—that is, through the apostleship mercifully entrusted to me by God, or through the mercy God has granted and shown to you.

What I ask is that you present—that is, offer—your bodies; not your minds only, but your bodies also, even though the flesh resists. Offer them, I say, as a sacrifice: in the mortification of fleshly desires; living, through good works; holy, [Col. 1496B] that is, steadfast in God; pleasing to God, by acting with a good intention.

[Note: Col. 1495D, the same author, to Maximinus.] A true sacrifice is everything done in order that we may cleave to God, when referred to that end of the good by which we can truly be blessed. Hence the human being himself, consecrated in God’s name and devoted to God, insofar as we die to the world in order to live for God, is a true sacrifice.

[Ambrose] Therefore our bodies are a sacrifice acceptable to God if we preserve them undefiled, unlike those who serve the pleasures of the flesh. Notice that he says “a living sacrifice,” because formerly, among the ancients, the victim offered was killed, so that human beings might be shown to be subject to eternal death because of sin. But because through God’s gift human beings have been purified and freed from the second death, they ought to offer a living sacrifice as a sign of eternal life. For bodies are no longer sacrificed for bodies as then; rather, the vices of bodies are put to death.

[Note: Col. 1496D, the same author, *The City of God.*] “Rational.” As though he said: Present your bodies as a sacrifice; nevertheless, let your whole service in the matters just mentioned be rational—that is, governed by discernment, lest anything be deficient; and discipline your bodies with moderation, so that they are not compelled to decay through a failure of nature, [Col. 1496D] but die to vices.

“And do not.” Here the soul is commanded to be offered as a sacrifice to God, just as bodies had previously been commanded to be offered to God. For if the body, which the soul uses as an inferior servant or instrument, is a sacrifice when its good and right use is referred to God, much more is the soul itself a sacrifice when, kindled by the fire of divine love, it loses the form of worldly desire and, referring itself to God, is reformed in submission to him as its unchangeable form.

And this is what he says. As though he said: Offer your bodies, and also your souls in this way: Do not—for it lies within your power—be conformed to this age, that is, receive the form of worldly desire. [Augustine] But be [Col. 1497A] reformed, you who were deformed in Adam, because in him the image of God was partly lost. [Note: Col. 1497D, Augustine, *On the Trinity.*] For if humankind had not lost God’s image, and again if it had lost it entirely, it would not be said, “Be reformed in the newness of your understanding” or “of your mind,” so that the image might begin to be reformed by him who formed it. For it cannot reform itself, just as it could deform itself.

Or, “be reformed”: as though he said, again and again, day by day. Such reformation occurs in those who always make progress and stretch forward to what lies ahead, imitating Christ, the new man. Hence he adds: “Be reformed,” I say, “in the newness of your understanding,” or “of your mind”; that is, reform the mind in which sins are not condemned according to the pattern of the new man.

[Note: Col. 1497D, the same author, *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness.*] Notice that here there is a general prohibition and a general command. The prohibition is: “Do not be conformed to this age.” The command is: “But be reformed in the newness of your understanding.” The former concerns not desiring; the latter, loving. The former concerns self-restraint; the latter, righteousness. The former concerns turning away from evil; the latter, doing good. For by not desiring we are stripped of oldness, and by loving we are clothed in newness.

Be reformed for this purpose: that in yourselves, through experience, you may prove what the will of God is—that is, what God wills—which will is good, because whatever God wills is good; pleasing to those who understand and have experienced it; and perfect in every goodness, so that nothing is better. Notice that “the will of God” is said either of the will by which he wills—which in God is God—or of that which he wills. Here it means God’s will [Col. 1497C] by which he wills, which is always fulfilled and is sometimes called God’s good pleasure or disposition. Of it the Prophet says: “He has done whatever he willed” (Psalm 113); and the Apostle: “Who resists his will?” (Romans 9).

Therefore God wills all good things that occur, of which he himself is the author; but he does not will evil things to occur, though he does not will that they not occur. For if he willed them not to occur and they nevertheless occurred, something would resist his will. Yet he foreknows that they occur. Furthermore, God’s will is called his operation or permission. Hence Augustine says: [Note: Col. 1497D, the same author, *Enchiridion.*] “Nothing happens unless the Almighty wills it to happen, either by permitting it to happen or by doing it himself.” Again, “will” is sometimes called his counsel, approval, command, or prohibition.

[Col. 1497D] **56 VERS. 3.**—“For I say, through the grace given to me, to all who are among you, not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think soberly, and to each according as God has apportioned the measure of faith.”

“For I say, through grace.” As though he said: “I beseech you not to be conformed to this age, but to be reformed in the newness of your understanding.” I forbid this, therefore, “for I say through the grace” of apostleship—that is, by the apostolic authority—which has been given to me, “not to think more highly,” that is, to investigate divine mysteries more than one ought to think, “but to think soberly,” or temperately; that is, without presumption and with moderation—[Col. 1498A] a precept which all heretics have transgressed. And I say this not to all of you, but to all such persons as are among you, for not all were doing this, but certain ones among them.

[Note: [Col. 1498D] Augustine, *City of God.*] And it should be known that this is the sacrifice of Christians: that many should be one body in Christ. For this is shown to the faithful, by the Church’s vow, in the sacrament of the altar, which is signified by the thing that it offers. For just as bread is made from many grains, so the holy Church consists of many members of the faithful, who rejoice together in participation in their Creator, by whose gift they are holy and one. This is shown in what follows, where he says: “We, being many, are one body in Christ” (1 Cor. 10). This cannot happen unless they think soberly, as he commands here.

“And to each one.” As he warned them not to be proud of their former [Col. 1498B] condition, so also he warns them not to be proud of the gifts received in faith. As though he said: I command you not to think more highly than you ought; and I command you to think more or less highly, according as God has apportioned the measure of faith; that is, according to the plan by which God has given measured gifts separately to each person, gifts which faith merits. He did this so that no one should lack, and so that there should be an occasion for mutual service, and thus mutual love.

[Ambrose] In these words the Apostle plainly shows that we ought to think in such a manner that we do not go beyond the bounds of justice, so that it may not be useful only to ourselves but harmful to no one.

Or thus: “And to each one I command not to think more highly, according as God has apportioned the measure of faith”; that is, according to the faith which God apportions in measure. [Augustine] For God distributes faith also in measure to each person.

[Note: [Col. 1498D] Id., *Against Julian.*] This is the faith working through love, [Col. 1498C] without which no good works of any person are to be considered such. From it all justice takes its beginning. It is not to be attributed to free choice, nor to preceding merits, because all good merits whatever begin from it. Good works, indeed, are done by a human being; but faith is made in a human being, without which those works are done by no human being. Faith, therefore, is God’s gift, which God has apportioned to each person, just as he has apportioned the other gifts of the Holy Spirit. Without that Holy Spirit it is certain that we cannot love Christ and keep his commandments; and that we are able and do these things less in proportion as we receive him less, and more in proportion as we receive him more. Therefore it is promised not only to one who does not have it, but also not in vain to one who has it: [Col. 1498D] to one who does not have it, so that it may be possessed; to one who has it, so that it may be possessed more abundantly. For if one person could have less but another could not have more, the holy Elisha would not have said to the holy Elijah: “May the Spirit which is in you be double in me” (4 Kings 2).

But to Christ, who is the Son of God, the Spirit was not given by measure, because in him dwells all the fullness of divinity. For Christ the man is not the mediator of God and human beings without the grace of the Holy Spirit. That he is the only-begotten Son, equal to the Father, belongs not to grace but to nature. But that a human being was assumed into the unity of the person of the Only-Begotten belongs to grace and not to nature. To all others, however, [Col. 1499A] it is given by measure; and what is given is increased, until the proper measure of each person is filled according to the degree of that person’s perfection. Hence John, speaking of Christ, says: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 1). To others, however, it is apportioned—not the Spirit himself, indeed, but his gifts.

And it should be known that one must obey the Apostle, who commands each person to think according to the measure of faith.

[Note: [Col. 1499D] Augustine, *City of God.*] For if an infant is fed according to its strength, it grows so as to receive more; but if it exceeds the strength of its capacity, it fails before it grows.

### Verses 4–15

> “For just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, being many, are one body in Christ; but individually we are members of one another, having differing gifts according to the grace [Col. 1499B] given to us: whether prophecy, according to the rule of faith; or ministry, in ministering; or one who teaches, in teaching; one who exhorts, in exhorting; one who gives, in simplicity; one who presides, in diligence; one who shows mercy, in cheerfulness; love without pretense; hating evil, clinging to good; loving one another with brotherly love, outdoing one another in honor; not slothful in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord, rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, constant in prayer, sharing in the needs of the saints, pursuing hospitality. Bless those who persecute you. Bless, and do not curse. Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep.”

“For just as.” As though he said: God apportioned gifts in measure because we, being many, are one body; and therefore all necessary things must be given, though not to one person. This is what he says: “For just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, being many, through diverse gifts, are one body in Christ,” serving one another. See how, by the example of the body, he teaches that none of us individually can possess everything, and that we ought therefore to care for one another, because we need one another’s services.

“But individually.” As though he said: We are all one body in Christ; but individually we are members: one person is a member of another, and so we serve others and need others. “Individually” is said because no one, whether greater or lesser, is excluded.

[Col. 1499D] “Having,” or “therefore.” As though he said: We are individually members, and for this purpose we have differing gifts—that is, distinct gifts. I say “having according to the grace given to us.” Or read it thus: As though he said: We are individually members. Therefore let this be done amid differing gifts. And this is what he says: because we are members, therefore, having gifts according to the grace given to us, let us be members of one another.

What those graces are, from whose diversity persons are called members, and how we ought in them to serve one another, he makes clear when he says: whether we have prophecy—that is, revelation of future things or of any [Col. 1500A] hidden matters—let us be members of others, so that we may prophesy to them. I say, having it according to the rule of faith, because prophecy is given as the faith of those persons—or of the hearers—requires.

[Ambrose] Note that, in the enumeration of graces, he begins with prophecy, which is the first proof that our faith is reasonable, because believers, having received the Spirit, prophesied.

Or, having ecclesiastical ministry, such as that of presbyters, let us be members of others by ministering diligently. Or let one who teaches—that is, one who has the grace of teaching—be a member of another in teaching, that is, in imparting instruction. Let one who exhorts—that is, one who has the grace of exhortation—be a member of another in exhorting. Let one who gives distribute alms not in duplicity, seeking present and future glory, but in simplicity, seeking future [Col. 1500B] glory, and thus be a member of another. Let one who presides, as a ruler, preside diligently—that is, act carefully—and thus be a member of another. Let one who shows mercy—that is, one who has the grace of compassion for the oppressed—do this cheerfully, helping with a joyful mind, and thus be a member of another.

Because “we all offend in many things” (James 3), [Augustine, Jerome] the Apostle sets before us the Lord’s and daily remedy. For this compassion is a daily remedy for daily—and, though lighter, still numerous—wounds. “For judgment without mercy will be shown to one who has not shown mercy” (James 2). Hence the Lord says: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven. Give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke 6). And it is certainly just that forgiveness be granted to one who forgives, and that something be given to one who gives. For there is in God both mercy in judging [Col. 1500C] and judgment in showing mercy. But whoever, as excessively righteous and self-assured, expects judgment without mercy provokes wrath.

[Ambrose] This mercy is manifold: namely, giving to another, forgiving one who sins, helping one who is oppressed, and so forth.

[Augustine] And therefore he does not add this concerning mercy superfluously: one member of mercy should be set forth, though another member of mercy has already been mentioned where he said, “one who gives, in simplicity”; here he says, “in cheerfulness.” Simplicity excludes hypocrisy; cheerfulness shows joy sustained by hope of the future. Therefore every act of mercy ought to be done both simply and with joy.

Let the love by which diverse gifts are united be without pretense, and thus each will be a member of another. Let yourselves be hating [Col. 1500D] evil and clinging to good, so that neither love for a friend may make you love evil, nor evil make you abandon good. Let yourselves be loving one another with brotherly love—that is, with the love that brothers have among themselves—or desiring to be loved in return by brothers. Let yourselves be outdoing one another in honor, that is, in every kind of respect.

[Ambrose] Otherwise there is no brotherly love unless they outdo one another in mutual acts of service. And let yourselves be not slothful in diligence; that is, if you are diligent in heart, do not be slothful in deed. For, as Jeremiah says, “Cursed is the one who performs the work of God negligently” (Jer. 48).

[Haimo] For those slothful in divine conduct are without hope.

[Note: [Col. 1500D] Id., *On the Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.*] And therefore, so that the chill of sloth may be driven away, [Col. 1501A] be fervent in spirit, that is, in the fire of love, even if in action you cannot fulfill what you desire. He says “fervent” because the Holy Spirit is the fire by which love burns fervently; this love is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit. The contrary of this fervor is what the Lord says: “The love of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24). Concerning this fire the Lord says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12).

“Serving the Lord,” or “serving the time.” As though he said: Although I have said that you should be fervent in spirit, nevertheless do not indiscriminately and importunately thrust the words of God upon people; rather, serve the occasion—that is, the opportunity—so that you may speak words of faith modestly and honorably, in suitable places, to suitable persons, and at suitable times. Or, in giving to your neighbor, serve the Lord. As though he said: Believe that what you bestow upon your neighbor, [Col. 1501B] you bestow upon God; and in these things be rejoicing in hope, so that you hope only for eternal things and rejoice in them. For those certain about future things rejoice because they most certainly hope that they will receive them; and therefore they are patient in tribulations. Hence he adds, “in tribulation.”

[Note: [Col. 1501D] Augustine, *On Psalm 83.*] As though he said: Do what I have said, and even if evils befall you amid these good things, be patient in tribulation. And that you may be able to endure evils, be constant in prayer, because the matter is still delayed and prayer is therefore necessary.

“Sharing in the needs.” As though he said: Endure. And share in the needs of the saints: make your own goods common to the saints who suffer, and receive saints in hospitality. This he expresses thus: “Pursue hospitality,” following the example of Abraham and Lot.

[Ambrose] Also, “bless,” that is, pray for good things, “those [Col. 1501C] who persecute you.” By this he removes them from the common custom, lest, stirred by an angry spirit, they readily curse as before; rather, having overcome anger, let them bless, so that the Lord’s discipline may be praised. He repeats it, therefore, to teach that this must always be done, saying, “Bless.” As though he said: Again and again. “And do not curse.” As though he said: Let your blessing be without an admixture of bitterness.

And you ought also to rejoice with those who rejoice over progress, and to weep with those who weep over something that ought to be mourned—for example, someone’s fall or the delay of glory. And be—

### Verses 16–21

> “Thinking the same thing toward one another, not thinking lofty things, but agreeing with the humble. Do not be wise in your own estimation; repaying evil [Col. 1501D] to no one for evil; providing things good not only before God but also before all people. If possible, so far as it depends on you, living at peace with all people; not defending yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath. For it is written: ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,’ says the Lord. But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head. Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good.”

“Thinking the same thing toward one another,” with them in joy or in weeping.

[Ambrose] And for all these things already mentioned and others, do not think lofty things, at least in your heart; [Col. 1502A] but agree with the humble, that is, imitate the humble.

[Note: [Col. 1502D] Id., *On Psalm 130.*] Note that he does not say “conversing with the humble” but “agreeing with them,” so that this may not be only in speech. For humility is true only if it is not merely on the tongue, like the hypocrite who outwardly says that he has no sin, feigns humility, and inwardly embraces vanity. Thus he has truth neither in heart nor in speech.

[Ambrose] Therefore he said, “not thinking lofty things,” lest there be pride in the soul and lest, presuming upon themselves, they profess sympathy for others but reproach them as sinners. This is the pride which offends when it sets itself above others. Then he adds, “but agreeing with the humble,” so that the cause of others may be their own, and thus they may have favor with God, “who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5).

“And do not be [Col. 1502B] wise in your own estimation”; that is, do not exercise your prudence only within yourselves, but rather among your neighbors, even if one of them offends you. Hence he adds: “Repaying evil to no one for evil,” even if persons offend you.
