[Ambrose] Then he warns that even lawful things should not be done with scandal, saying: “And provide things good, not only before God,” that is, in the secret place of the heart, “but also before all people,” so that there may be no scandal but a good example; for that ought to be done which neither displeases God nor is a scandal to a brother.

And also live at peace with all people, if it is possible—that is, if they agree. But if it cannot be done, owing to the wickedness of evil people, at least do what depends upon you, namely what pertains to you: have peace with them as far as lies within you, [Col. 1502C] so that even with those who hate peace you may be peaceable (Ps. 119). Or: have peace with all people, if possible. He says “if possible” because it is difficult. Yet, though difficult, it depends on you—that is, it lies in your power—to have peace with all people.

“And do not defend yourselves, beloved”; that is, do not retaliate against adversaries. “But give place to wrath,” that is, to God’s judgment.

[Note: [Col. 1502D] Id., *On Psalm 88.*] Observe that he does not command that saints should be unwilling for God to avenge them—as the saints cry out—but that, by not avenging themselves, they should give place to God’s wrath, he who said: “Vengeance is mine,” and to whom the saints cry in the Apocalypse: “Avenge, Lord, our blood” (Rev. 6). It must not be passed over that this should be understood otherwise, lest the saints appear to desire vengeance in order to satisfy hatred, something far removed from their perfection. Therefore they do not desire vengeance in order to satisfy hatred; yet it is written: “The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance” (Ps. 57). But the Apostle commands here, as was said, that they themselves should not avenge themselves but give place to God’s wrath.

But if a good person wishes God to punish an enemy, where then is the saying: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5), and the saying, “Not repaying evil for evil”? Is this not repaying evil for evil? Does he not fail both to love and to do good to his enemy? Since both the just person and the wicked person desire the Lord to avenge them upon [Col. 1503A] their enemies, in what are they distinguished? The good person desires more that the enemy be corrected than punished; and when God punishes, he does not delight in the enemy’s penalty, because he does not hate him, but in God’s judgment, because he loves God. What pleases him is what pleases the Lord, for God also, whom he follows in this, makes rain fall upon the just and unjust (Matt. 5); nevertheless, in this age he corrects some with hardships and at the end will condemn those who remain obstinate.

[Haimo] Vengeance, therefore, must be reserved for him. Hence he says, “Give place to wrath,” that is, to God’s vengeance, or to the wrath of adversaries. One gives place to an adversary’s wrath who allows the adversary to do what he wishes. And you ought to give place to God’s wrath. For it is written in Proverbs: “I have reserved vengeance for myself,” or “reserve it yourselves, and I will repay,” says the Lord; that is, I will avenge, [Col. 1503B] and whoever does not do so despises God.

“But if he is hungry.” Note the unusual use of the conjunction *but*; the passage must be continued as though neither conjunction had been inserted. It is as though he said without *but*: “If he is hungry,” and so forth. Or it may be read so that neither conjunction is superfluous. As though he said: Not only should you not defend yourselves, but if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink—that is, help him with the necessities of life.

“For by doing this.” As though he said: Do this because, by doing this, you will heap coals of fire—that is, the fervor of love, or of the Holy Spirit, or the burning ardor of repentance—upon his head, that is, upon his mind. And if he does not repent, nevertheless do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good, that is, by enduring; for if you strike back, you will become like that wicked person. Therefore contend against him with goodness.

[Col. 1503C]

[Note: [Col. 1503D] Augustine, *On Psalm 33.*] This is true contention and a salutary contest: that good should contend against evil, not that there should be two evil persons. If you are no longer evil, desire that the evil person become good; let it displease you that he is evil, and let it please you that he become good, lest there be two evil persons.

## Chapter XIII

### Verses 1–6

> “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. For there is no authority except from God; and those which exist have been ordained by God. Therefore, whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance; and those who resist acquire condemnation for themselves. For rulers are not a terror to good work but to evil. Do you wish not to fear authority? Do good, and you will have praise from it; for it is God’s minister [Col. 1503D] to you for good. But if you do evil, be afraid. For it does not bear the sword without cause. For it is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath upon one who does evil. Therefore be subject out of necessity, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience. For this reason you also pay taxes, since they are God’s ministers, serving for this very purpose.”

“Let every soul.” Here too he invites them to humility. For some thought that evil masters, and especially unbelieving ones, ought not to rule over believers; and that, if masters were good and faithful, they ought to be equals of good and faithful persons.

[Note: [Col. 1503D] Id., *On John.*] Here the Apostle removes this pride [Col. 1504A] beginning from the higher part—that is, the soul—signifying the whole human being. For what is “every soul” except every human being? As though he said: All the things mentioned above must be done, and although you are so perfect in the body of Christ, nevertheless let every soul be subject; that is, let every person be subject. I signify the whole person by the name “soul” so that you may serve not only bodily but also willingly.

[Haimo, Augustine] Therefore let every soul be subject, so that the person may serve even willingly, to secular authorities, good or bad: namely kings, princes, tribunes, centurions, and others of this kind. For if the one set over you is good, he is your nourisher; if he is evil, he is your tempter. Freely receive nourishment, and prove yourself in temptation. Be gold, therefore, and regard this world [Col. 1504B] as a goldsmith’s furnace.

Therefore let every soul be subject to higher authorities, that is, insofar as they are higher, namely in worldly matters. Or the reason is indicated when he says “higher,” that is, because they are higher.

“For there is no authority.” He proves that they ought to be subject in this way: because every authority is from God, and those given by God are ordained. Therefore authority is ordained; that is, whoever has authority has it by God’s ordination.

“Therefore, whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance.” This is what he says: As though he said: You ought therefore to be subject to authority because no authority is possessed by any person, good or evil, unless it has been given by God. Hence the Lord said to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19). The wickedness of human beings has in itself the desire to harm; but unless he gives it, it has no power. Therefore, before the devil took anything from Job, he said to the Lord: “Stretch out your hand” (Job 1), that is, give power; because even the power of those who harm is only from God. As it is written, Wisdom speaking: “Through me kings reign, and tyrants through me hold the earth” (Prov. 8). Hence Job says of the Lord: “He causes a hypocrite to reign because of the perversity of the people” (Job 34). And God says of the people of Israel: “I gave them a king in my wrath” (Hos. 13).

[Note: [Col. 1504D] Id., *On the Nature of the Good.*] The will to harm may come from a human mind, but power comes only from God; and this is a hidden and fitting justice. For it is not unjust that, when wicked people receive power to harm, [Col. 1504D] the patience of the good should be proved and the wickedness of the evil punished. For through the power given to the devil, Job was proved so that he might appear righteous; Peter was tempted so that he might not presume upon himself; Paul was buffeted so that he might not exalt himself; and Judas was condemned so that he might hang himself. Therefore, when God makes his righteous people through power granted to the devil, then at the end punishment will be rendered to the devil himself for his unjust will to harm.

“But those things which are” are ordained by God; that is, they are rationally disposed by him. Job says: “God does not cast away the mighty, though he himself is mighty” (Ps. 36). Gregory says that the person desires to imitate God who administers the height [Col. 1505A] of power with attention to others’ benefit rather than to his own praises; who, being set over others, desires to benefit rather than to rule. For it is pride that is feared, not the order of authority that is blameworthy. God grants power; but the pride of power is invented by the malice of our mind. Let us therefore remove what we have added from ourselves, and the things we possess by the Lord’s gift are good, because it is not just authority but wicked action that is condemned.

Therefore, whoever resists authority, whether by deceit or force—that is, the person who possesses authority, in those matters which concern authority, such as taxes and things of that kind—resists God’s ordinance, that is, one who possesses authority by God’s ordination. He therefore does not act according to God’s ordinance. In the case of good authority it is plain that God has set it over others rationally; in the case of evil authority too this can be seen, while good people are purified through it, evil people are condemned, and it itself is cast down more grievously.

Note that the term “authority” is sometimes understood to mean the authority itself which God gives someone, and sometimes the person possessing authority; the attentive reader should distinguish these. “And those who.” As though he said: Whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance. This is so serious that whoever resists it acquires condemnation for himself. Therefore no one ought to resist, but ought to be subject.

If, however, it commands what you ought not to do, then indeed disregard that authority by fearing the greater authority. Consider the very ranks of human affairs. If an official commands something, must it be done if he commands it contrary to the proconsul? Again, if the proconsul himself commands something and the emperor commands something else, is there any doubt that, disregarding the former, one must obey the latter? Therefore, if the emperor commands one thing and God another, disregarding the emperor, one must obey God.

“For rulers.” As though he said: Those who resist authority rightly acquire condemnation. For rulers, good or evil, are not a terror to good work but to evil; that is, they are not for the fear of those who act well but of those who act badly. For if a ruler is good, he does not punish one who acts well but loves him. If he is evil, he does not harm the good person but purifies him. But the evil person ought to fear, since rulers have been instituted to punish evils. He calls them rulers because they are established to correct life and restrain harmful things, bearing God’s image, so that the rest may be under one.

“Do you wish?” [Col. 1505D] As though he said: They are a terror to those who act wrongly; but do you wish not to fear authority, whether good or evil? Do good, and there is no reason to fear; indeed, you will have praise from it. Even if it is evil, it becomes for you the cause of a greater crown. If the authority is just, you will have praise from it, even as it itself praises you.

[Note: [Col. 1505D] Augustine, *Sermon on Saint Lawrence.*] If it is unjust, you will have praise from it—not because it praises you, but because it furnishes you an occasion for praise. You will truly receive praise from it, for it is God’s minister to you for good; that is, it works good for you whether it is good or evil, because it exercises you, or because it was given by God for your good, to protect you and what is yours. For it is clear that rulers were given by God [Col. 1506A] so that evil may not be done to good people.

“But if you do evil.” As though he said: The good person need not fear; but if you do evil, be afraid. And fear is appropriate because it bears the sword—that is, it has judicial power—not without cause but to punish the wicked. This he shows by adding: “For it is God’s minister,” that is, it acts as avenger in God’s place; I say, existing as an avenger for God’s wrath, that is, for the purpose of avenging the offense against God. Or: an avenger displaying God’s future wrath, that is, displaying the future vengeance of God, because this punishment shows that those who persist in evil will be punished more severely. I say that it is an avenger, and this is “upon him,” that is, for the harm of the one who does evil.

And because it is God’s minister, therefore be subject to it as if of necessity; or, according to another reading, “to necessity,” that is, to necessary ordinance, [Col. 1506B] be subject. And do this not only to avoid the wrath of the ruler or of God, but also because of conscience: namely, that your mind may be clean by loving the superior appointed by God. For although all believers, insofar as they are believers, are one in Christ—in whose faith there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, master and slave, and the like—there is nevertheless a distinction in mortal life, and the Apostles command that its order be maintained on the journey of this life. For some things are observed in the unity of faith without any distinction; others belong to the order of this life as to a journey, lest the Lord’s name and doctrine be blasphemed.

“For this reason,” this is the proof of subjection. As though he said: You ought to be subject because for this reason also—that is, to show [Col. 1506C] subjection—you pay taxes, which are a sign of subjection. He does not say “you pay” but “you render,” as though returning what you owe, because they repay by serving in defense: when they fight for their country and administer judgments. You render taxes—you who serve God; in this very matter, that is, because you give them taxes, you serve God. You truly serve God through this, for they are God’s ministers. They have been instituted so that the good may be praised and the evil punished.

Or thus: “For they are ministers.” As though he said: You ought to render taxes because they are God’s ministers. I mean, they serve you when they defend the country; “for this very purpose,” that is, for this reason, namely because of the tax, they serve you in defending the country, and because they are God’s ministers.

### Verses 7–10

> “Render therefore to all their due: [Col. 1506D] tax to whom tax is due, revenue to whom revenue is due, fear to whom fear is due, honor to whom honor is due. Owe no one anything, except to love one another. For one who loves a neighbor has fulfilled the law. For: ‘You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet’; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Love of neighbor does not work evil. Therefore love is the fullness of the law.”

“Render to all their due.”

[Haimo] Thus evangelical discipline may be praised: render tax to the person to whom you owe tax. He calls “tax” what regions [Col. 1507A] pay. To the person to whom you owe revenue, render revenue. “Revenue” is called the payment given to lords when they travel through territories; or tax is what is paid at home, while revenue is what is conveyed to the lord’s house. Render fear to the person to whom you owe fear, so that we may fear the Lord and show respect to persons. Render honor to the person to whom you owe honor, such as rising in their presence and the like.

What applies to every particular case? “Owe no one anything except to love one another”; that is, pay all other things in such a way that you owe nothing further.

[Note: [Col. 1507D] Augustine, *To Celestine.*] But pay love in such a way that you always remain indebted. For love alone is such that, even when rendered, it always keeps the person rendering it indebted. It is rendered when it is bestowed; but, even if rendered, it remains owed, because there is no time when it ought not to be given. Nor is it lost when rendered, but rather [Col. 1507B] is multiplied by being rendered. For it is rendered by possessing it, not by lacking it; like money, which cannot be paid unless it is possessed, nor possessed unless it is paid. Indeed, when it is rendered by a person, it grows in that person; and it is acquired in proportionately greater measure as it is rendered to more persons.

Here love is mentioned because it serves the humility mentioned above.

[Ambrose] Note that above he admonished us to have peace with all; here he says that love should be maintained among brothers, which he indicates by saying “one another.” Otherwise they are not truly brothers, and love must truly be maintained, because one who loves a neighbor fulfills the law. He demonstrates this in parts, saying: “For: ‘You shall not—’” As though he said: He has truly fulfilled it, for this commandment, “You shall not commit adultery”; this, “You shall not kill”; this, “You shall not steal”; this, “You shall not bear false witness”; and this, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property.” And if there is another commandment given through Moses, it is summed up—that is, contained and fulfilled—in this saying, that is, in this commandment which Moses gave in Leviticus: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

[Col. 1507C]

[Note: [Col. 1507D] Id., *On the Trinity.*] A neighbor must be loved in what is good, not in what is evil, because “one who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 11); and thus does not love himself, and neither loves his neighbor as himself. Note that although there are two commandments of love, on which the whole law and the prophets hang (Matt. 22), one is often put for both, not without reason, because neither can God be loved without a neighbor nor a neighbor without God. Here love of neighbor is mentioned because love of neighbor appears in deeds.

[Note: [Col. 1507D] Id., *On John.*] Love of God, however, is more hidden, and therefore he presents this latter in a more spiritual way. The Lord says of it: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13), where that greater commandment of love for God seems to have been omitted. But to those who understand well, both commandments are found in each, because [Col. 1508A] one who loves God cannot despise the person whom God commands to be loved. And one who loves a neighbor in a holy and spiritual way—what does that person love in the neighbor except God?

This is the love distinguished from every worldly love, which the Lord distinguished by saying: “As I have loved you” (ibid.). For what did he love in us except God—not the God whom we had, but so that we might have him? Just as a physician is said to love the sick: what does the physician love in them except the health which he desires to restore, not the disease which he comes to expel?

[Note: [Col. 1507D] Id., *On Christian Doctrine.*] Therefore, he says, let us also love one another in this way: as much as we can, let us draw one another by the care of love to possess God in ourselves. For a human being is at his best when his whole life moves toward the unchangeable life and he clings to it with his whole affection. But if he loves himself for his own sake, he does not refer himself to God; turned toward himself rather than toward something unchangeable, he therefore enjoys himself with some deficiency.

If, therefore, [Col. 1508B] you ought to love yourself not for your own sake but for the sake of him in whom lies the most upright end of your love, let no other person be offended if you also love that person for God’s sake. For this is the rule of love divinely established: that you love your neighbor for God’s sake, but God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with your whole mind—that is, that you direct all your thoughts, your whole life, and your whole understanding toward him from whom you have the very things which you direct toward him.

Therefore no one loves a neighbor unless that person loves God.

[Note: [Col. 1507D] Id., *To Jerome.*] Let each person, insofar as possible, bestow upon the neighbor whom he loves the same love as upon himself, so that the neighbor too may love God. If one does not love God, one loves neither oneself nor one’s neighbor.

[Augustine] For a lover of God is a lover of oneself; and one who does not love God does not love a neighbor because one does not love oneself.

[Note: [Col. 1508D] Id., *On John.*] Those who love themselves for the purpose of possessing God truly love themselves. Therefore, in order to love themselves, they love God. This love is not in all people. Few, indeed, love themselves so that God may be all in all (1 Cor. 15).

Love. As though he said: Truly, one who loves his neighbour does well, because love of neighbour does no evil. [Note: [Col. 1508D] Augustine, on Psalm XI.] That is, one who loves his neighbour commits no mortal evil. By “neighbour” every human being must be understood, because there is no one against whom evil ought to be done. Therefore one who loves people ought to love them either because they are righteous, or so that they may become righteous. Thus he ought also to love himself, namely either because he is righteous or so that he may become righteous. For whoever loves himself otherwise loves himself unjustly, since he loves himself in order that he may be unrighteous. Therefore, if he loves himself for these ends—that he may be evil—he no longer loves himself. For whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul. And because love does no evil: therefore love is the fulfilment of the law, that is, whoever loves fully fulfils the law. [Note: [Col. 1508D] The same author, on John.] For where charity is, what can be lacking? But where it is not, what can be of use? Why, then, do we not say that whoever possesses this virtue possesses all virtues, since charity is the fulfilment of the law, and the more it is present in a person, the more that person is endowed with virtue? [Note: [Col. 1508D] The same author, to Jerome.] But the less it is present, the less [Col. 1509A] virtue is present. The less virtue is present, the more vice is present. [Note: [Col. 1509D] Augustine, in the sermon on the ten strings.] In it the Decalogue of the law is fulfilled. For the Decalogue of the law contains ten commandments, so distributed that three pertain to God and seven pertain to man.

There is a war which a human being wages within himself: fighting against evil desires, restraining avarice, crushing pride, stifling ambition, slaying lust. Fight these battles in secret, and you will not be defeated in public. For this purpose our hands are taught for battle. In your spectacles the hunter is not the same as the lyre-player: the hunter does one thing, the lyre-player another. In God’s spectacle the two are one: you strike the same ten strings and kill wild beasts. Do you do both at once? You strike the first string, by which the one God is worshipped: the beast of superstition falls. [Col. 1509B] You strike the second string, because you do not take the name of your God in vain: the beast of error and of wicked heresies falls. You strike the third string, when, for the hope of future rest, you do whatever you do: the love of this world, more savage than the other beasts, is killed. Because of love for this world people labour in all their business; but in all your works labour, not for love of the world, but for the everlasting rest which God promises.

“Honour your father and your mother”: you strike the fourth string, so as to pay honour to your parents, and the beast of impiety falls. “You shall not commit adultery”: you strike the fifth string, and the beast of lust falls. “You shall not kill”: you strike the sixth string, and the beast of cruelty falls. [Col. 1509C] “You shall not steal”: you strike the seventh string, and the beast of rapacity falls. “You shall not bear false witness”: you strike the eighth string, and the beast of falsehood falls. “You shall not desire your neighbour’s wife”: you strike the ninth string, and the beast of adulterous thought falls. For it is one thing not to do such a deed in respect of one’s own wife, another not to desire another man’s wife. Therefore there are two commandments: “You shall not commit adultery,” and “You shall not desire your neighbour’s wife.” “You shall not desire your neighbour’s property”: you strike the tenth string, and the beast of covetousness falls. Thus, with all the beasts fallen, you move securely and innocently in love of God and in human society.

VERSE 14.—“And this, knowing the time: that it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep; for now [Col. 1509D] our salvation is nearer than when we believed. The night has passed; but the day has drawn near. Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light. Let us walk honourably, as in the day: not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies, not in strife and envy; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires.”

And this, knowing. Here is another commendation of charity. Above he said that it does no evil. Here he says that it also creates the opportunity for doing good. As though he said: We know that love does not do evil, [Col. 1510A] and we also know this: that it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep. And knowing this, let us cast off, etc. Or thus, as some books have it: “knowing this time.” As though he said: Love is the fulfilment of the law, and we, knowing this time, namely that of grace, should cast off, etc. [Ambrose.] We ought to do so because now—namely, since we have received love—there is for us an hour, that is, an opportunity, though brief, to rise from sleep, that is, from the sluggishness of doing good and from negligence or ignorance, which sleep here signifies; and we ought to rise now. For now our salvation—that is, the eternal salvation promised to us—is nearer, that is, more deserved through good works, than when we merely believed. For it is evident that after the washing [of baptism], one who acts well and applies himself to charity is close to eternal [Col. 1510B] life. For a good life is the sign and cause of future salvation; baptism is for forgiveness, but a good life is also for the crown. Therefore, since we have believed and acted, it is more shameful if we do not rise. Or: now, namely at this time, our salvation is nearer than when we believed, because we are nearer to death.

“The night has passed,” etc. [Haimo.] Here again is shown why they ought to rise. As though he said: You ought also to rise because the night of unbelief and ignorance has passed—that is, it once existed, but now does not; its memory warns you to beware. But the day—that is, eternal blessedness—has drawn near, since sins have been forgiven and you are righteous through grace. Or thus: you ought to rise because the night has passed, that is, the old man which passed away in baptism, namely the tinder of sin. But the day has drawn near, namely Christ, the sun of righteousness, by whose light they learned the truth, so that they might know what ought to be done. For before, while ignorant of Christ, they were in darkness. But when the light arose, they passed from falsehood to truth. Therefore, on account of the reasons just stated, let us cast off the works of darkness—that is, evil works which came from the darkness of ignorance, or which love darkness and lead to darkness. And let us put on, as an adornment, [Col. 1510C] the armour of light, that is, virtues which are arms, required by the light, namely faith. And, having received virtues, let us walk honourably, that is, let us be exercised in their practice, as befits the day of faith.

What the works of darkness are, he shows by adding: “Not in revelries.” [Col. 1510D] [Haimo.] As though he said: Let us walk honourably, but not in these things—namely, not in revelries, that is, luxurious banquets which are celebrated either by contributions from all or are customarily supplied in turn by companions living together; nor in drunkenness, that is, excessive drinking. For *brian*, in the masculine gender, is said to mean a cup suitable for drinking, whence is derived *ebrietas*, “drunkenness,” which is excessive drinking of wine. “Not in beds,” that is, in the sloth of sleepers, “and indecencies,” that is, in the luxury which comes through excessive food and drink. Therefore after revelry and drunkenness he placed: “Let us not walk in strife and envy,” as they used to do by preferring themselves to one another; in this the lesser envied the greater, and thus there was strife, that is, rivalry. [Note: [Col. 1511D] Augustine to Bishop Aurelian.] Note that the Romans are touched in these matters, and therefore have no right to glory. The mother of these diseases is pride and a craving for human praise, which also often produces hypocrisy. It is resisted only when fear and love of God are instilled by frequent testimonies from the divine books.

“But put on.” [Note: [Col. 1511D] The same author, in the book of the *Confessions*.] As though he said: Do not do the things aforesaid. But put on, or clothe yourselves with, our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, Christ’s pattern in all things. When you have put him on, you will not be compelled to serve the flesh. Hence he adds: “And make no provision for the flesh”—I do not mean in things necessary for sustenance, but in unlawful desires. For food must be taken as medicines are taken. [Note: [Col. 1511D] The same author, *On the Sermon on the Mount*.] Hunger and thirst burn like certain pains, and, like fevers, kill unless the medicine of food comes to the rescue. This is at hand through the consolation of God’s gifts, for he promised that all things necessary would be added to those who seek the kingdom of God. [Note: [Col. 1512D] The same author, in the book of the *Confessions*.] Therefore nourishment must be taken as medicine. Yet, while one passes from need to the quiet of satiety, in that very passage the snare of desire lies in wait; and, when health ought to be the reason for eating, dangerous pleasure joins itself as an attendant and often tries to go before, so that what should be done for health’s sake is done for its sake. Often it becomes uncertain whether the necessary care of the body seeks the aid it needs, or whether pleasure-seeking desire provides the service of deception. At this uncertainty the unhappy soul rejoices, glad that it does not appear what is sufficient for the moderation of health, so that under the pretext of health it may veil the business of pleasure. [Col. 1511C] Nor is the measure of the two the same: what is enough for health is the father of pleasure.

## CHAPTER XIV

VERSES 1–3.—“But receive one who is weak in faith, not for disputes over opinions. For one believes that he may eat all things, but one who is weak should eat vegetables. Let not one who eats despise one who does not eat; and let not one who does not eat judge one who eats, for God has received him.”

“But [receive] one weak in faith.” [Ambrose.] Since there were some from among the Jews who had received the Romans into faith in Christ with the law mixed in, certain people thought that foods ought to be distinguished as the law commanded; and these were not of perfect faith. But others, who followed Christ without the law, thought on the contrary that it was permissible to eat all foods. For it belongs to perfect faith to distinguish no food and to deem none unclean, because all things are clean to the clean. Yet some weak persons, as was said, judged or declared that some foods must be abstained from; and so there was strife among the Romans. Therefore the Apostle here commands that such people be received, not cast out, but patiently raised to faith by example and word; and, although it is unknown with what intention anyone acts, that one should not dispute on that account.

Thus the Apostle, presenting such people as sick persons to physicians, says: “But [receive] one who is weak,” etc. As though he said: [Col. 1512A] Be honourable among yourselves, as has been said. “But [receive] one weak in faith,” [Haimo.] that is, one who does not yet believe perfectly—namely, does not believe as he ought to believe—receive for healing. [Augustine.] Just as Christ received the sick in order to heal them, receive him, I say, “not for disputes over opinions,” that is, not in such a way as to judge him guilty concerning hidden matters. For one whose thought is not disclosed, or one of whom we do not know what he will later become, is not to be condemned. Therefore let us not arrogate to ourselves the judging of others’ thoughts, but let us offer our own thoughts to God; and, seeing the outward appearance of good, let us rejoice, but entrust the heart to God and pray for it.

I say, receive one weak in faith; and there are among you some who can do this. For one among you, perfect in faith, believes himself able to eat all things given for human use; [Col. 1512B] [Ambrose.] and such a person can receive others. But one who is weak—that is, one who distinguishes foods, considering some clean and some unclean—should eat vegetables. This is the person who needs to be received and is permitted to eat vegetables, concerning which there is no question and in whose use every sect agrees. Therefore the weak person is one who distinguishes foods because the Jews were forbidden to eat them; the Apostle says that this person should be left to his own judgment, lest he eat with scruple.

Or, “weak” means prone to falling: one who is easily overcome by the force of lust. As though he said: Although perfect faith is that which believes all things permissible, nevertheless one who is weak—that is, who fears falls into vices—should eat vegetables, that is, light and dry foods which do not fuel vices; and he should abstain from those by which lust is aroused. For the richness of meats [Col. 1512C] and luxurious dishes provoke the body to lust.

“One who eats.” Above he commanded that they should not dispute concerning the thoughts of others. [Ambrose.] Here he commands that they should not despise them. As though he said: Since these things are so, one who eats all things indiscriminately should not despise one who does not eat, that is, one who abstains, because it is a matter of will to eat or not to eat, and therefore no issue ought to be made of it. For all things are subject to the human will, just as they are subject to human dominion. [Note: [Col. 1512D] Id., *On the Sermon on the Mount*.] And one who does not eat all things should not judge the eater as guilty—that is, should not believe and assert that he sins—when he does not know with what intention he acts. For judgment is to be made about manifest things, not hidden things. Manifest things are those which cannot be done with a good intention, such as sexual immorality, blasphemies, thefts, and the like; [Col. 1512D] concerning these we are permitted to judge. Of these also it is said: “By their fruits you shall know them” (Matt. VII).

But matters for which it is doubtful with what intention they are done we interpret in the better sense—for example, foods, since any human foods may be taken indiscriminately with a good intention and a simple heart, without the vice of desire. Concerning such matters, which can be done with either a good or a bad intention, they wished, though they were merely human beings, to pronounce judgment upon hidden hearts, concerning which God alone judges. Hence it is said: “Do not judge before the time” (I Cor. IV). There are, therefore, certain [Col. 1513A] intermediate acts, about which we do not know with what intention they are done, because they may be done both well and badly. It is rash to judge concerning these, especially so as to condemn. “For God,” etc. As though he said: Let neither judge the other, for each is God’s servant. And this is what is meant: “For God has received him,” namely the eater, into faith, etc.; therefore [do not judge].

VERSES 4–6.—“Who are you, who judge another’s servant? To his own master he stands or falls; but he shall stand, for God is able to make him stand. For one judges one day above another day, but another judges every day alike. Let each abound in his own understanding. He who observes the day observes it for the Lord; and he who eats, eats for the Lord, for he gives thanks to God. And he who does not eat, does not eat for the Lord, and gives [Col. 1513B] thanks to God.”

“Who are you?” That is, what worth are you, who judge another’s servant—that is, assert that he should be condemned? You ought not to do so, since he is another’s servant. For it is evident that a servant ought not to judge the will of a fellow-servant. “To his own [master],” etc. As though he said: You have no right to judge the unknown heart of another’s servant, because to his own master—that is, for the honour of his own master—he who stands stands, or he falls to his own master, because even the fall of one who falls belongs to that master, who can raise him up or judge him. He says “stands or falls” because the matter is uncertain: perhaps he stands who is thought to fall. Or, he stands or falls to his own master because God, whose servant he is, is judge of the intention with which he eats or does not eat.

“But he shall stand,” that is, he can stand before his own master, because neither is he guilty if he eats [Col. 1513C] nor blameworthy if he does not eat, provided that he acts from devotion. Or thus: “But he shall stand.” Although the Apostle spoke of all the regenerate and godly living when he called him another’s servant, he immediately looked to the predestined when he said, “But he shall stand”; he says this of the predestined. And lest they arrogate standing to themselves, he adds: “For God is able to make him stand,” concerning whom no one has uncertainty. Moreover, by saying “he stands or falls,” he shows that he does not know with what intention the other acts in doubtful matters. But when he adds, “But he shall stand,” he intimates that we ought to interpret ambiguous matters in the better sense, desire the salvation rather than the death of those accused, and hold hope for good in the future, even if the present is otherwise.

“For one judges.” Above he said that some eat all things, [Col. 1513D] others not all things, speaking of kinds of food; here he says that some abstain at every time, others at a particular time, and says that each may rightly be done. As though he said: I say that he shall stand and can be believed likely to stand, because he does what he does by God’s judgment. This is what he says: for one judges that, in abstinence, a day set apart should be chosen above another day. [Haimo.] But another judges every day to be chosen for abstinence—that is, some think one ought to abstain on fixed days, others at all times. But let each of them abound in his own understanding, in his own conscience, towards what is better: so that one who eats may eat with thanksgiving, and one who abstains may do so for God. Or, let him be left in his own understanding, that he may not suffer scandal and depart from charity, the mother of all virtues.

I say that each should abound in his own understanding. And thus will act one who observes every day. [Col. 1514A] [Ambrose.] Or [one who distinguishes] between one day and another observes it for God the Lord, that is, he does it for the Lord’s honour, because he thinks that in this he pleases God. Likewise, one who eats all things eats for the Lord—that is, for the praise and honour of the Lord, whose creatures he believes all clean. Since he is sustained by them in order to serve the Lord, the result shows that he eats for the Lord: for he gives thanks to God for all the creatures by which he is sustained and fed. Likewise, one who does not eat—that is, who abstains—does not eat for the Lord’s honour, as the result shows; and that is, because he gives thanks to God for the abstinence granted him. And we ought to eat or not eat for the Lord. “For” means “because.”

[Col. 1514B] VERSES 7–13.—“For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself. For whether we live, we live to the Lord; whether we die, we die to the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s. For to this end Christ died and rose again, that he might rule both the living and the dead. But why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the judgment-seat of Christ. For it is written: ‘As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.’ Therefore each of us shall render an account of himself to God. Let us therefore no longer judge one another, but judge this rather: not to place a stumbling-block or an occasion of offence before a brother.”

[Col. 1514C] “None of us,” that is, of the faithful, lives spiritually, namely in virtues, to himself, that is, to his own will. For whoever is restrained and governed by the law does not live to himself but to God, who gave the law. If there were no law, each would live to himself. Nor does any of us die to vices, as happens in baptism, to himself, that is, so as to please himself, but to the Lord, by whose judgment he is condemned or crowned. Or: no one lives by virtues or dies to vices for himself, but for the Lord. And truly, no one [lives or dies] for himself. For whether we live the life of virtues, we live for the Lord—that is, to be judged by the Lord, or in order to please him. Whether we die to vices and sins, we die for the Lord—that is, in likeness to Christ, into whose death we were baptized: so that, as Christ died once [Col. 1514D] and lives for ever, so we too, having died once to sin in baptism, may live to God for ever.

Or thus: no one lives temporally, namely by the union of soul and body, or dies by the dissolution of soul and body, for himself—that is, for his own praise—but for God. For just as there is no end to his greatness, so there will be no end to our praise. When we have died in this flesh, we shall not cease to praise God. In this sense he speaks only of the faithful. Or, “to himself” means “to be judged by himself,” but by the Lord; in this sense it is taken of good and evil alike. And truly no one is for himself but for the Lord. This is what he means: whether we live in bodily life, we live for the Lord, that is, for the Lord’s praise or under the Lord’s judgment; whether we die temporally, we die for the Lord, that is, for the Lord’s praise or to be judged by the Lord. And because both are from the Lord, [Col. 1515A] [Ambrose.] therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s servants. [Note: [Col. 1515D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*.] Or, “the Lord’s” means “to be judged by the Lord.” Why then does a human being judge?

“For to this end.” As though he said: Truly we are the Lord’s, because he redeemed us at the price of blood; nor will death hold him for whom he died, free among the dead. This is what he says: “For to this end Christ died and rose again, that he might rule”—that is, be understood to rule—“both the living and the dead,” and judge both. Here “living” and “dead” are understood literally. He says this so that Christ may not be thought to judge only concerning the dead, as though judgment were entrusted to human beings while they live and to God after death. For the perverse teaching of foolish persons has handed down this doctrine. But it is better to say that Christ rules and judges both groups, because those to whom he gave power to become children of God reign with Christ both now and after death. [Note: [Col. 1515D] The same author, *City of God*.] But his saints reign with him now in one way, and will reign then in another. Now they reign because they set their minds on and seek the things above; finally they will reign with him so as to be in his kingdom and themselves also to be his kingdom. For the souls of the godly dead are not separated from the Church, which is even now Christ’s kingdom, since the Church now reigns with Christ among the living and the dead. Otherwise no commemoration of them would be made at God’s altar in the communion of Christ’s body. Therefore even believers who have died are his members. Thus he died and rose again in order that he might be shown to be Lord and judge of the living [Col. 1515C] and the dead.

Or thus, that we may understand “dead” and “living” mystically. As though he said: Truly we are the Lord’s. For to this end Christ died and rose again, that he might rule the living and the dead—that is, draw into his lordship those alive in virtues and those dead in sins. [Ambrose.] For through Christ the creation which, because of sin, had been estranged from its Maker and made captive, was freed. The Father sent him from heaven to earth lest his work perish. For the purpose of freeing and helping it, Christ came, died, and rose again. He died in order to free from sins those dead in sins; while he lived, he showed the way of salvation; he rose again in order to make those justified live with him. Thus from the lost he refashioned servants for himself.

[Col. 1515D] “But you.” As though he said: From these things it is clear that Christ ought to rule. But you, who eat all things, why do you judge your brother who does not eat? Or you, who do not eat, why do you despise your brother who eats? You ought not to act thus. For we shall all stand to be judged before Christ’s judgment-seat, that is, before God sitting as judge. This is said by comparison. A tribunal is the seat of judges, placed on high so that the judge may be seen by all and may himself view everyone from his elevated place. So also Christ will sit as though on a tribunal, because he will be seen by all, and he himself will see the consciences of all and [Col. 1516A] judge their cases.

And truly: for it is written in Isaiah, “As I live, says the Lord.” As though he said: I who was formerly dead now live in power, which is shown in this: “In judgment every knee shall bow to me,” even that of enemies; “and every tongue”—that is, every conscience, knowing me to be God—“shall confess to me, God, what it has done.” And because Scripture says this, therefore each of us, to be judged by the Lord, shall render to God an account of himself; there he will not evade it through evasions. And because each person will render an account for himself, let us therefore no longer, as we have hitherto done, judge one another on the basis of conjecture, as though we should not arrogate to ourselves what does not belong to us. [Note: [Col. 1516D] The same author, *City of God*.] Let us not condemn matters whose intention we do not know; or, even if they are manifest, let us not condemn them so as to despair of recovery.

[Col. 1516B] For rash judgment occurs in these two cases: when it is uncertain with what intention something was done; or when it is uncertain what one who now plainly appears good or evil will later become. To judge in these matters is either pride or envy, especially as done by those who prefer shouting and censuring to amending and correcting. Hence it is said: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged” (Matt. VII). But rather judge—that is, discern by careful observation—what is beneficial, namely this: do not place before brothers a stumbling-block, that is, something by which a brother may perish by following your example and doing the same; or an occasion of offence, that is, grief—which is the lesser thing.

VERSES 14–20.—“I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean through him, except to one who considers something unclean: to that person it is unclean. For if your brother is grieved because of food, you no longer walk according to charity. Do not destroy by your food one for whom Christ died. Therefore do not let our good be blasphemed. For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. For he who serves Christ in this is pleasing to God and approved by men. Therefore let us pursue the things that belong to peace, and let us mutually preserve the things that belong to edification. Do not destroy God’s work because of food.”

“I know,” etc. As though he said: I say that you must not place a stumbling-block before your brother—not, however, that food is unclean and therefore a stumbling-block or occasion of offence. For I know, through this—that is, because—I am persuaded in the Lord Jesus, namely by confidence in Jesus, who, after he came, released us from the law, that nothing is common, that is, unclean, through him, that is, through his coming or through his creation. [Col. 1516D] Note that he uses “common” for “unclean.” The expression is taken from vessels which were formerly common to all uses, but some of which, after being dedicated to sacrifices, were no longer called common but holy. Or it is taken from the Jews, because the Jews themselves were formerly called God’s special people. [Haimo.] All others were called common and unclean; therefore the Jews called only foods permitted by the law clean, while foods [Col. 1517A] commonly used by the Gentiles they called common, that is, unclean.

I say that nothing is unclean, except to the one who thinks something unclean; to him it is unclean because of the conscience by which he judges it so. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Not what enters the mouth defiles a person, but what proceeds from the heart defiles a person” (Matt. XV). [Ambrose.] The person who thinks this is weak, of whom he said above, “Let him eat vegetables.” For he is weak through doubting; for him what he thinks ought not to be eaten is unclean.

“For if.” As though he said: Therefore do not place a stumbling-block or occasion of offence before your brother, because if your brother, because of food, is not merely scandalized but, what is less, even grieved, it is already clear from this alone that you do not walk according to charity. In this you sin: that you do not walk [Col. 1517B] according to charity. Take care, therefore, not to grieve your brother by your food. But take still greater care not to destroy him. Hence he adds: “Do not destroy by your food one for whom Christ did so great a thing that he died.” From Christ’s death one knows how great is the value of a brother’s salvation. You ought therefore to strengthen him in good, not scandalize him, nor cause him a scruple over a trivial matter. And since your brother is grieved or destroyed by your food, “therefore let not our good be blasphemed”: that is, let not the other good things be obscured by this small matter. For one who has good works, if he is reproved in a very small matter, obscures his good and his good begins to be blasphemed on account of evil. Hence Ezekiel says: “The righteousness of the righteous will not profit him if he errs” (Ezek. XVIII).

Or, “Let not your good be blasphemed,” that is, let eating, which is in itself good, not become blasphemable. It does so when it harms another; and because it harms, abstain, because it is not the cause of God’s kingdom. If it were, you would not omit it for anyone’s scandal. He says thus that it is not the cause of God’s kingdom: “For [Col. 1517C] the kingdom of God is not food and drink.” As though he said: Therefore abstain, because food and drink are not the kingdom of God—that is, the kingdom of God is neither acquired nor lost by their use. It is not the use of foods but desire that must be restrained. It makes no difference at all what kinds or quantity of food a person receives, provided that he does so suitably to the people among whom he lives and to the needs of his own person and health. Rather, the question is with how great an ease and serenity of spirit he can do without these things whenever he ought, or indeed must, do without them, so that he may say: “I know how to abound and how to endure want” (Phil. IV).

Thus wisdom is justified by her children, who understand that righteousness lies neither in abstaining nor in eating, but in equanimity in enduring want and in not being corrupted by intemperance amid abundance, and in taking or not taking at the proper time. Thus wisdom is justified by her children, who understand that suitable times ought to exist for using earthly things; but that the readiness to do without such things and the love of enjoying eternal things ought not to vary with times, but to be retained always. Hence he adds: “But righteousness.” As though he said: Food and drink are not the cause of the kingdom, but righteousness, by which you do to your brother what you wish done to yourself; and [Col. 1518A] peace, that is, concord, which is the effect of righteousness; and joy—not, to be sure, in Epistles, as many are accustomed [to suppose], but in the Holy Spirit—that is, [the joy of] not being proud of the Holy Spirit’s gifts, but receiving them humbly and gratefully. This joy arises from brotherly peace, just as anger arises from disputation, where the Holy Spirit is absent; for he is only among the peaceful. By his grace these three things exist in someone, but not in you, O Romans.

“For he who.” As though he said: Truly righteousness and peace are the cause of the kingdom. For he who serves Christ in this, namely in righteousness, peace, and joy, pleases God, who commands this and caused scandal to no one, and is approved by human beings. [Ambrose.] Make the distinction: he pleases God, certainly, insofar as joy is in the Holy Spirit; but he is held approved by human beings insofar as [Col. 1518B] righteousness and peace are concerned. And because disputation produces discord, therefore, setting aside rash judgments, let us pursue the things of peace, not discord; and let us mutually preserve—namely Jew toward Gentile and Gentile toward Jew—the things of edification, teaching others peaceably, so that the rest may be built up or those already built up may be preserved.

“Do not,” etc. As though he said: Let us pursue these things, but let us not destroy God’s work. Or connect it thus: Therefore, again, you ought not to eat in a way that causes your brother offence, because you would destroy God’s work. And do not, because of food, whether eaten or not eaten, destroy God’s work—that is, faith and the other virtues and goods which God has wrought in them. I do not say this because food is not clean, for:

VERSES 20–23.—“All things indeed are clean, [Col. 1518C] but it is evil for the person who eats with offence. It is good not to eat meat, nor drink wine, nor do anything by which your brother is offended, or scandalized, or made weak. Do you have faith? Keep it to yourself before God. Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves. But one who distinguishes, if he eats, is condemned, because it is not from faith. But everything which is not from faith is sin.”

All things, indeed, insofar as they are created, are clean; for, as is read in Genesis, God made all things very good (Gen. 1). [Ambrose.] But it is evil for the person who eats to the offense of others—and all the more to the offense of God—as Adam did the apple, Esau the lentils, and the Jews the flesh in the wilderness. [Note: [Col. 1517D] Augustine, on John.] For in the Israelites the offense against God was by no means slight: they rejected what Wisdom gave and murmured because what concupiscence longed for was lacking. They despised what they had, and shamelessly demanded what they did not have. [Note: [Col. 1518D] Id., on Psalm 72.] They asked in culpable desire for what they obtained to their harm; they desired to eat flesh while manna was raining down upon them from heaven, so that we might know that God’s creature is not blameworthy, since every creature of God is good, but rather stubborn disobedience and disordered desire. The first human being found death not because of a pig, but because of an apple; and Esau lost his birthright not because of a hen, but because of a lentil. Therefore I do not fear the uncleanness of food [Col. 1519A], but the uncleanness of desire. [Note: [Col. 1519D] Augustine, on John.] For I know that Noah was permitted to eat every kind of flesh suitable for food; that Elijah was restored by food of flesh; that John, endowed with remarkable abstinence, was not defiled by animals—that is, locusts—serving as food. And I know that Esau was deceived through desire for a lentil, David reproved himself because of his longing for water, and that our King was tempted not concerning flesh, but concerning bread.

“It is good.” As though he said: You ought to abstain from these things because of offense, since indeed you ought to abstain even from all flesh and wine. It is good for you, O man, not to eat flesh, not to drink wine, nor to do anything by which your brother is offended—being disturbed and not knowing what he should hold to—that is, in which there would be for him a cause of condemnation. For he is offended because he departs from right faith. [Col. 1519B] Or he is scandalized, that is, grieved. Or he is made weak, so that he doubts, even if he is not offended. For the one who does not withdraw but begins to doubt is made weak.

“You have faith.” As though he said: You can well do this, because you lose nothing of your good; and this is what it means: you have faith, by which you believe all things to be clean and fit to be eaten; and hold this faith with yourself—that is, in your heart—so that no one may take it away. Hold it only before God, not before the abstainer, lest you harm him; thus preserve peace with your brother, which is beneficial before God. [Ambrose.] Therefore do this, because blessed is the one who does not judge himself—that is, does not make himself guilty—in what he approves, that is, in what he judges to be good, by harming others through his own good.

Or: blessed is the one who does not judge himself [Col. 1519C] in what he approves, that is, who does not do something other than what he considers good. Thus he calls blessed the person who does nothing other than what he approves as useful; but by his own judgment he deems worthy of condemnation the person who does what he says he ought not to do.

“But he who distinguishes.” As though he said: That person is blessed; but the one who distinguishes foods, reckoning some clean and others unclean, if he eats with that conscience, is condemned. [Haimo, Ambrose.] It is true that one who judges that he ought not to eat and yet eats is condemned. For he makes himself guilty when he does what he maintains is not beneficial for him. He is therefore condemned because he does not eat from faith—that is, according to conscience. Certainly the person who does not believe it lawful to eat eats against faith. But everything which is not from faith, even if it is good in itself, is sin—that is, whatever is done against faith, when we believe it evil. Yet not everything done with faith is good, because ignorance arising from fault causes harm. Therefore he says that everything pertaining to conscience, if done otherwise than conscience directs, is sin: even though what is done may be good, if it is believed that it ought not to be done, or ought not to be done in the manner in which it is done, it is sin. [Col. 1519D]

[Haimo.] Or thus: one converted to the faith of Christ who distinguishes foods, afterward judging some clean and others unclean, is condemned—that is, acquires condemnation for himself—especially if he eats. For he has not eaten from faith, because he acted unbelievingly, not believing all things to be clean; he doubts in faith and eats those things which he regards as unclean, and thus does not act according to faith. [Col. 1520A] For our faith requires a person to do what he rightly understands ought to be done; and what is done otherwise than has been approved is sin. [Note: [Col. 1520D] Id., in the book of Prosper’s Sentences.] Therefore the person converted to the faith sins in this, that he distinguishes foods, and especially if he eats, because he does not act from faith but as an unbeliever. But everything not from faith is sin; that is, the whole life of unbelievers is sin, because everyone living or acting in unbelief sins grievously; and nothing is good without the highest Good. Where recognition of eternal and immutable truth is absent, virtue is false even amid the best morals.

## Chapter XV

### Verses 1–7

> “But we who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each one of you please his neighbor for good, unto edification. For Christ also did not please himself, but, as it is written: ‘The reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me.’ For whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope. May the God of patience and consolation grant you to think the same thing toward one another according to Jesus Christ, so that, with one mind and one mouth, you may glorify God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore receive one another, as Christ also received you, unto the honor of God.”

“But we ought.” As though he said: If the weak person eats, he is condemned; but we who are stronger ought neither to provoke nor despise, but to bear—that is, to endure and raise up—the weaknesses of the weak, since they cannot raise themselves to us. And we ought not to please ourselves—that is, not to obey our own will, not to claim merely what pleases ourselves, but what pleases our brother, because we ought mutually to care for one another. [Col. 1520B]

[Ambrose.] One is said to please himself who so does what appears good to himself that he does not care whether it pleases or displeases his neighbor; this is unfitting. Rather, each of us, applying himself to charity, should please—or take care to please—his neighbor, that is, every person: not unto evil, but unto good, that is, toward what is beneficial, unto edification. [Haimo.]

And truly we ought not to please ourselves, for Christ also did not please himself [Col. 1520C]—that is, he did what did not please the flesh—as he himself says in the Gospel: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6). I say that he did not please himself, but God the Father, as is written in the Psalms: “The reproaches.” The psalmist, speaking in the person of the Savior, addresses God the Father thus: “The reproaches,” or slanders, “of the Jews who reproached you in me, O Father, fell upon me”; that is, they became the cause of my oppression. When I did your will, O God—in this, that I drove from the temple the wicked men who had made it a den of thieves, and in all other matters—the Jews cast reproaches upon me because they said that I sinned against you. Yet rather, by not receiving me whom you sent, they reproached you and sinned against you by not receiving me; and therefore they killed me as one sinning against God. Thus the sins of those sinning against God fell upon Christ, because the innocent one is killed by sinners as though a blasphemer. [Col. 1520D–1521A]

“For whatever things were written were written for our instruction.” As though someone asked: What relevance do these things which you say concerning Christ have for us? He answers: They have much relevance for us. [Augustine.] For whatever things concerning Christ were written in the divine books—and hence he says above, “It is written”—were written for our instruction. For Christ’s life is instruction both for our life and for our conduct. Then he adds the benefit of divine reading, saying: “That through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we may have hope”; that is, through those writings we may be taught to suffer for our neighbors, be consoled in them through Christ’s example, and thus hope for what Christ received. [Col. 1521B]

“But may the God [of patience].” As though he said: Sacred Scripture is for instruction, through which patience and consolation are obtained; but may God, who is the giver of patience and consolation, grant you to think the same thing—that is, without distinction—and this toward one another, so that what one thinks another may think; and not apart from Christ, but according to Jesus Christ, so that you may think according to Christ’s teaching. Thus, being of one mind, [Augustine] that is, of the same will, and with one mouth, that is, with the same confession of voice, you may glorify God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ: glorify him who is God by essence and also Creator, and who is Christ’s Father by nature and ours by grace, and who shows himself benevolent by sending Christ. Since, therefore, he is Creator and benevolent, glorify him by thinking the same thing. As though he said: Unless you think the same thing, you will not be able to glorify God.

“Therefore,” namely, that you may glorify God, “receive one another”: receive the weak, as Christ also received you—that is, when you were weak—unto the honor of God, that is, in order to make you immortal. [Col. 1521C]

### Verses 8–14

> “For I say that Christ Jesus was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers; but that the Gentiles should glorify God for mercy, as it is written: ‘Therefore I will confess you among the Gentiles, O Lord, and sing to your name.’ And again he says: ‘Rejoice, Gentiles, with his people.’ And again: ‘Praise the Lord, all Gentiles, and magnify him, all peoples.’ And again Isaiah says: ‘There shall be a root of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles shall hope.’ Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit. But I myself am persuaded concerning you, my brothers, that you yourselves also are full of love, filled with all knowledge, so that you are able to admonish one another.”

“For I say.” Truly Christ received the weak, because he received Jews and Gentiles. He received the Jews, indeed, so as to be their minister—that is, their apostle and preacher. This is what he says: “For I say that Christ Jesus was a minister,” that is, an apostle and preacher, “of the circumcision,” that is, of the Jews, to whom he came bodily; as he himself said: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15). That is, Christ was minister of the Jews. [Col. 1521D–1522A]

[Ambrose.] And this was for the truth of God, namely, to confirm the promises made to the fathers: that he might be true, that is, show himself truthful in his promises and fulfill the promises made to the fathers of the Jews. For he had promised Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 28); and David: “From the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131); and likewise he said: “A star shall arise from Jacob” (Num. 24). Behold, from these things it is clear that God did not reject the Jews, to whom the truth was specifically presented; but mercy was granted to the Gentiles, to whom no promise had been made. Therefore God’s truth was fulfilled in the Israelites who believed. [Col. 1522B]

One wall came from the circumcision and joined itself to the cornerstone; but that stone would not make a corner unless it received into itself another wall. That wall, therefore, pertains, as it were, to truth; the other to mercy. Hence he adds: “But the Gentiles.” As though he said: Christ did not merely receive the Jews for truth’s sake, but he also received the Gentiles for mercy’s sake. Therefore I say that the Gentiles ought to glorify God concerning—that is, because of—the mercy by which he received them, though he was neither sent for them nor sent to them, and brought them in as sheep.

He proves this by prophetic testimony, adding: “As it is written in the Psalm,” whose authority he adduces to establish concerning the Gentiles that they were received, although this might have seemed less likely. “For this reason,” or “therefore, I will confess you among the Gentiles”; that is, I will make Gentiles confess you. [Ambrose.] Confession is not only confession of sins but also praise of God. “And I will sing to your name”; that is, I will make them sing to you a new song and praise you with joy. [Col. 1522C]

And again Isaiah says: “Rejoice, O Gentiles, because you have been received, that you may be one fold with his people,” that is, with the Jews, because you are one with them. And again David says: “Praise the Lord, all Gentiles.” And while all Gentiles praise God, all peoples—namely, the twelve tribes—magnify him, who increased the number of his people by adding the Gentiles.

And again Isaiah, saying something to the same effect, declares: Jesse, who was David’s father and was also called Esai, shall be the root. David was a tree which through a branch—that is, Mary—produced the fruit Christ, because Mary bore Christ. I say that Jesse shall be the root, and from this root shall come the one who rises from death to rule the Gentiles through faith and good works. Therefore the Gentiles shall hope in him. [Col. 1522D]

“Now may the God of hope.” As though he said: I admonish you to receive one another; now may God, the giver of hope, [Haimo] that is, he who gives hope—or the God in whom we hope—fill you with every spiritual joy, so that none of you may grieve as you formerly grieved in dispute. And, that you may be able to rejoice, may he fill you with peace received in believing—that is, may he give you peace, namely mutual concord; and this will certainly occur if faith is sound—so that you may abound. As though he said: May God give you these things just mentioned, so that through possessing them you may abound in hope, that is, be more certain of eternal blessedness. And may you abound [Col. 1523A] in the power of the Holy Spirit, that is, in the strength of good action which is given through the Holy Spirit.

“But I am persuaded,” or “for.” Lest the Apostle seem to understand that all are discordant and unwise persons needing correction, he removes this impression; for he begins thus in order to admonish the more perfect concerning the correction of the lesser. Then he offers himself as an example of one who labors for others; and it is necessary that these persons do this because, hindered by other matters, he cannot come to them. As though he said: Although I thus admonish you to receive one another, not all of you need this admonition. “For I am persuaded,” etc.

Or, if the reading is *autem* (“but”), connect it thus: I admonish you to receive one another; yet I myself, who speak in this way, am persuaded concerning you, my brothers, of this: that you yourselves too, not I alone, are full of love [Col. 1523B] by which you desire good, and filled with knowledge by which you can know—all knowledge, namely of the Old and New Law. You are so filled with these two things that you can admonish one another, unless the fault remains your own—not, I say, teach one another. [Ambrose.] That is, each in turn may admonish the other.

Observe that by this praise he urges them toward better things, in the manner of an exhorter. For a person who sees himself praised labors to make true what is said of him. Hence he does not say that they should teach one another, but admonish one another; that is, he does not say that they should impart instruction, but offer admonition. For what is usually admonished is something known, but which sometimes escapes the mind or is held negligently.

### Verses 15–22

> “But I have written to you rather boldly, brothers, in part, as recalling you to remembrance because of the grace given to me by God, that I may be a minister of Christ Jesus among the Gentiles, sanctifying the Gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may become acceptable, sanctified in the Holy Spirit. Therefore I have glory in Christ Jesus toward God. For I dare not speak of anything except what Christ accomplishes through me unto the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Holy Spirit; so that from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum I have fulfilled the Gospel of Christ. And thus I have preached this Gospel, not where Christ had been named, lest I should build upon another’s foundation; but, as it is written: ‘Those to whom no announcement concerning him has been made shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand.’ For this reason I was greatly hindered from coming to you, and have been prevented until now.”

“But I have written rather boldly.” As though he said: You are full of love and knowledge; nevertheless, though you are full, I have written to you rather boldly—that is, somewhat boldly—brothers, “in part,” that is, with regard to all the perfect persons; for with regard to others it would not have been boldness. Or, “in part,” namely, on behalf of the Church of God; or “in part,” namely, of the Epistle. [Haimo.] I have written, I say, not as though I thought you unwise, but as recalling you to remembrance—that is, as making you mindful of what you ought to do. In this he indirectly rebukes them as though forgetful. [Col. 1523C]

I say that I wrote to you boldly, but not rashly, because it belongs to me to do so, on account of the grace given me—that is, on account of the apostleship given me—by God. As though he said: I could not omit it because of my office. I say that grace was given me for this purpose: that I might be a minister of Christ Jesus, whom he himself, and no other, instructs. [Ambrose.] I say, a minister among the Gentiles. Therefore he does not write rashly to them; rather, as Apostle of the Gentiles, he ventures to write to all Gentiles by the authority given him through God’s grace.

I say, “sanctifying,” that is, showing to be holy and confirming, the Gospel of God through good works and miracles, so that the offering of the Gentiles may become acceptable to God and sanctified: that is, so that the Gentiles whom I offer may be acceptable to God through perfection of faith, and sanctified through good works; and this in the Holy Spirit, whose grace is faith and good work. [Col. 1524A]

And because I act thus, I therefore have glory—that is, merit worthy of glory, as you too will have glory if you labor for your brothers—glory, I say, to be referred to God in Christ Jesus, that is, through Christ Jesus, through whose grace I do this. I say that I have glory, and rightly so: for I do not dare, as pseudo-apostles do, to speak of any of those things which Christ does not accomplish through me. That is, I speak only of those things which Christ accomplishes through me, namely through my ministry, unto the obedience of the Gentiles, so that the Gentiles may obey the Gospel. [Col. 1524B]

The Apostle says this to prove that he has been able to do no less than the apostles who were with Christ, and that no fewer works of power have been performed among the Gentiles. I say that Christ accomplishes this by word and deed, also through the power of lesser signs and greater wonders: that is, through my preaching and good works, and through the power of greater and lesser miracles [Col. 1524C] performed in the power of the Holy Spirit, who works such things in me. With him working in me, I labored so that I fulfilled—that is, preached fully—the Gospel of Christ round about, that is, everywhere, from Jerusalem as far as the Illyrian sea. In this the great power of the Holy Spirit appears: that so many nations received the Gospel through me.

But I preached this Gospel thus—that is, in such a place where Christ had not been named by pseudo-apostles. Why? Lest I should build upon another’s foundation. [Ambrose.] For if I did otherwise, this would result: I would build upon a foundation, namely teaching, handed down by pseudo-apostles. Not without reason did the Apostle do this, because he knew that pseudo-apostles proclaimed Christ otherwise than they ought and taught falsehood under Christ’s name, which afterward required the greatest labor to correct. Therefore he was careful to forestall the pseudo-apostles and deliver the truth whole where Christ had not yet been named, so that an unbroken line and an ordered surface might display the unimpaired strength of the foundation.

He proves this by the prophet’s testimony, adding: “As it is written.” Or he says this concerning good apostles: “But I preached thus, and not where Christ had been named” by other apostles. Why? “Lest I should build upon another’s foundation”; that is, lest I preach to persons already converted through others—not that I would not do this if it happened, but I preferred to lay the foundation of faith where it was not present rather than build upon another’s preaching. [Col. 1524D–1525A]

He confirms this by prophetic testimony, saying: “As it is written.” As though he said: I did this as it is written in Isaiah: “Those to whom no announcement concerning him”—that is, concerning Christ—“had previously been made shall see,” that is, believe; “and those who had not previously heard anyone’s preaching shall understand that my preaching is true.” For the Apostle hastened to imbue the Gentiles with truth so that understanding of God’s word might be true and uncorrupted.

“For this reason,” namely, because I preached to so many, “I was greatly hindered from coming to you,” as he also said at the beginning of the Epistle: “I have often,” he says, “purposed to come to you, and have been prevented until now.” He now explains this, showing the reason why he was hindered: namely, so that he might exclude the perverse inventions of pseudo-apostles. Finally, after he had preached throughout the surrounding regions, he says that he is free to come to Rome, which he had long desired; nevertheless, he promises that he will come at the time when he is going to Spain, adding thus:

### Verses 23–33

> “But now, having no further place in these regions, and having had for many years a desire to come to you, when I begin to journey into Spain, I hope that, as I pass through, I shall see you and be escorted there by you, if first I have enjoyed you in part. But now I shall go to Jerusalem, ministering to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have approved making some contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem. For it pleased them, and they are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have become partakers of their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in carnal things. Therefore, when I have completed this and assigned to them this fruit, I shall journey through you into Spain. But I know that, when I come to you, I shall come in the abundance of Christ’s blessing.
