Therefore I beseech you, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Holy Spirit, that you assist me in your prayers to God for me, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea, and that the offering of my service may be acceptable to the saints in Jerusalem, so that I may come to you with joy through the will of God and be refreshed with you. Now may the God of peace be with you all. Amen.”

“But now, having no further place,” that is, no reason to remain, in these regions, yet having had a desire for many years to come to you, when I begin to travel into Spain. [Ambrose.] He says this because he hastens also to preoccupy these persons, and because the journey to them would have been difficult for pseudo-apostles; now it was permissible to delay, when, I say, I should begin to journey there. [Col. 1525B–D]

“I hope.” As though he said: Of myself I can do nothing, but I hope in mercy that I shall see you—yet as I pass through, because you do not need a long stay, but should meanwhile prepare yourselves lest you delay me from the others. I say that I shall see you and be escorted there, namely into Spain, by you, provided that I have first enjoyed you: that is, have rejoiced concerning your fruit, with respect to that part which is now discordant. Or “in part” means with respect to time, that is, for a while. And because I have no place here and desire to see you, therefore now—that is, without delay—I shall go to Jerusalem to minister to the saints. [Col. 1526A]

[Augustine, Ambrose.] These saints had placed the prices of all their sold possessions at the apostles’ feet and had suffered from their fellow-countrymen. All the apostles shared a common care for them. I shall go to minister.

“For they approved,” I did not compel them: the Macedonians and the Achaici or Achaei (Achaeans), or Macedonia and Achaia, approved making some contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem. These people had wholly devoted themselves to divine services, caring for no worldly matter, and offered believers an example of good conduct. [Ambrose.] The Achaeans and Macedonians had at times made a collection for them; by this deed the Apostle invites the Romans to such works, because one lives by God’s mercy and has been justified; the devout person ought to be so for his brother’s sake. [Col. 1526B]

“It pleased them.” As though he said: I rightly say that they approved it. For it pleased them, and they are also their debtors. He so strongly wishes them to be more merciful that he says this is owed even by one who expects mercy; and indeed they are debtors. For if the Gentiles became partakers of their spiritual things—that is, of the preaching and sacraments of those Jews who sent preachers to them from Jerusalem—they ought certainly also to minister to them in carnal things, that is, to the Jews.

“Therefore.” As though he said: Because it pleased them to make a contribution to the saints in Jerusalem, therefore, when I have completed this—that is, fulfilled the work of service—and assigned to them, that is, shown them under the seal of each church, this fruit [Col. 1526C], I shall journey into Spain by way of you. Therefore, meanwhile, correct yourselves.

“But I know.” As though he said: I shall pass through you, but nevertheless I know, being certain of God’s grace, that although I have long been coming to you in desire, at last I shall come in actuality; and this in the abundance of Christ’s blessing, that is, in such a manner that through Christ’s blessing I shall greatly benefit you. This blessing is the power of signs, by which they are confirmed.

And because I am going to come, “therefore I beseech you, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ,” that is, if you love him, “and through the love of the Holy Spirit,” that is, if there is in you the love which the Holy Spirit causes one to possess, “that you assist me in your prayers directed to God,” that is, through prayers made by you to God. [Col. 1526D] The Apostle does not say this because he himself has less merit than they who are lesser, but he follows the order that prayer should be made by the Church for its ruler. And rightly indeed the Apostle asks lesser persons to pray for him. For many very small persons, when they gather with one mind, become great; and it is impossible that the prayers of many should not obtain their request. If, therefore, they desire to see him, let them pray that they may receive him delivered, with the joy of charity.

Hence he adds: “That I may be delivered.” As though he said: I beseech you to assist me in prayers—namely, pray for me in this: that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, lest they take away what I carry. And thus may the offering of my service—that is, the service laid upon me—be acceptable; as though he said, sufficient and undiminished, to the saints in Jerusalem. Or: may the offering be acceptable to them [Col. 1527A], so that they, understanding the Apostle’s love toward them, may with him give thanks to God in one mind. For it is great advancement for the one through whose ministry many, having become joyful, praise God.

Pray that this may happen, so that, when it is done, I may come to you with joy through God’s will. He says this to show that he does all things according to God’s will. “And that I may be refreshed with you,” which will happen when they are at peace.

“Now may the God of peace.” As though he said: I hope to come to you; but whether I come or not, may the God of peace be with you all. Christ is the God of peace, who said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave with you” (John 14), and who is with his own until the consummation of the age, as he himself says: “I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). Thus the Apostle desires him to be with these persons. [Col. 1527B] “Amen,” which is the confirmation of his desire.

## Chapter XVI

### Verses 1–16

> “Now I commend to you our sister Phoebe, who is in the ministry of the church which is at Cenchreae, that you may receive her in the Lord worthily of the saints and assist her in whatever matter she may need from you. For she herself has also assisted many, and me personally. Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow-workers in Christ Jesus, who laid down their own necks for my life; to whom not I alone give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles; and greet their household church. Greet Epaenetus, beloved to me, who is the firstfruits of Asia in Christ Jesus. Greet Mary, who labored much among you. Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsfolk and fellow-captives, who are notable among the apostles and who were in Christ before me. Greet Ampliatus, most beloved to me in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our fellow-worker in Christ Jesus, and Stachys, my beloved. Greet Apelles, approved in Christ. [Col. 1527C] Greet those who belong to the household of Aristobulus. Greet Herodion, my kinsman. Greet those who belong to the household of Narcissus, who are in the Lord. Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord. Greet Persis, my most beloved, who has labored much in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine. Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brothers who are with them. Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, Olympias, and all the saints who are with them. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.”

“I commend to you,” that is, I show to be worthy of recommendation to you, Phoebe, our—or my—sister in faith, who is in the ministry of the church at Cenchreae. [Haimo.] Phoebe was a very wealthy and very noble woman who supported from her own resources the church in the place called Cenchreae. At that time she had gone to Rome on some business, and perhaps sent this Epistle through her.

I commend her, I say, so that you may receive her in the Lord, or for the Lord, worthily of the saints, as it is fitting to receive saints. Or, as some manuscripts have it, “receive her very worthily,” that is, most honorably and respectfully; and assist her—that is, help her—in whatever matter she may need from you. And it is just: for she herself has also assisted many, including me personally. [Col. 1527D–1528A]

“Greet Prisca,” or Priscilla; for Prisca is the same person who in the Acts of the Apostles is also called Priscilla. Greet Priscilla and Aquila, my fellow-workers in Christ Jesus, that is, in the preaching of Christ Jesus. [Ambrose.] Aquila was Priscilla’s husband. They were helpers of the Apostle and had come to Rome not idly but to strengthen the Romans. Thus all the others whom he greets here are understood to have been in Rome.

He praises these two again, adding that they did not refuse to suffer dangers for him: “who for my life,” that is, for my deliverance, “laid down their necks to the sword” [Col. 1528B] in ministering to me. Not I alone give thanks to them, but all the churches of the Gentiles, because they labor for the advancement of the Gentiles, exhorting them to the faith of Christ, and did not refuse to suffer dangers for the Apostle. Therefore the Romans too ought to obey them. “And greet their household church,” that is, their family.

“Greet Epaenetus, beloved to me, who is the firstfruits of Asia in Christ,” that is, who first believed in Christ in Asia. “Greet Mary, who labored much among you,” who labored more earnestly in exhorting those whose discord she reported to the Apostle.

“Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsfolk,” because they are Jews, “and fellow-captives,” because they suffered captivity for the sake of faith. [Haimo, Augustine.] They are also spiritually kinsfolk because they were joined to the Apostle in spirit, and spiritually fellow-captives according to the saying: “While we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5). [Col. 1528C] They are “notable among the apostles,” that is, among the preachers: famous among preachers. They also “were in Christ before me,” that is, in the faith of Christ.

“Greet Ampliatus, most beloved to me in the Lord.” He was a friend of the Apostle in the Lord, but not a fellow-captive. “Greet Urbanus, our fellow-worker in Christ,” that is, one who shares the work and is my companion and that of others in exhorting to faith. “And Stachys, my beloved,” [Ambrose] who is particularly my friend, although not a helper or companion in the work.

“Greet Apelles, approved,” that is, tested, “in Christ.” For through temptations he was found faithful in Christ. The Apostle greets him [Col. 1528D], although he was neither a friend nor a fellow-worker. “Greet those who belong to the household of Aristobulus.” Aristobulus used to gather together brothers in Christ; the Apostle greets them, thus strongly approving his action.

“Greet Herodion, my kinsman. Greet those who belong to the household of Narcissus.” This Narcissus is said, as is read in other manuscripts, to have been a presbyter, who, while traveling, strengthened the holy brothers. Since he was not then present, the Apostle greets his people; and because he did not know the merits of all of them, he makes a distinction, adding: “who are in the Lord,” that is, those whom you find worthy, because not all were worthy.

“Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord,” namely, in ministering to the saints and amid hardships. “Greet Persis, my most beloved, who has labored much”—namely, more than the aforementioned women [Col. 1529A]—“in the Lord.” This labor consists both in exhortation and in ministry to the saints, and in affliction and want for Christ’s sake.

“Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord,” because he had been advanced to carry out the Lord’s affairs, namely to the priesthood; “and his mother,” his by flesh; “and mine,” by her benefactions. [Haimo.] Because of her holiness the Apostle calls her his mother, and proposes her son for an ecclesiastical office.

“Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brothers who are with them.” [Ambrose.] He greets all these together because he knew them to be united in Christian friendship. “Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, Olympias, and all the saints who are with them.” All these were likewise of one mind, and therefore he greets them together.

“Greet all of you one another [Col. 1529B] with a holy kiss.” He commands all those to whom he writes and whom he knew to greet one another with a holy kiss—that is, in Christ’s peace—so that their kisses may be religious, not carnal. “All the churches of these regions greet you,” churches, I say, of Christ, that is, which trust in Christ and not in anything else.

VERSICLES 17–21.—“Now I urge you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause dissensions and stumbling-blocks contrary to the teaching which you have learned, and turn away from them. For such persons do not serve Christ our Lord, but their own belly; and by smooth speech and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent. For your obedience has become known everywhere. I therefore rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise in what is good and guileless in what is evil. But may the God of peace [Col. 1529C] swiftly crush Satan beneath your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Timothy, my fellow-worker, greets you, and Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsmen. I, Tertius, who wrote the Epistle, greet you in the Lord. Gaius, my host, and the whole Church, greet you. Erastus, the city treasurer, greets you, and Quartus the brother. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.”

Now I urge you. [Ambrose.] As though he said: Greet and imitate those persons mentioned above; but avoid these others. And this I urge you, brothers: watch out for—that is, distinguish—those who cause dissensions and stumbling-blocks, that is, who make you disagree and offend one another. [Col. 1529D] I mean those who teach contrary to the doctrine which you learned from the true apostles, because they dealt with the Law and compelled believers to Judaize. Here he strikes at the pseudo-apostles, against whom throughout the whole Epistle he warns them to be on their guard. Watch out for them, I say, and you ought also to turn away from them. For such people do not serve Christ our Lord, but their own belly. For they flatter some and disparage others, so that they may fill their own belly. And by smooth speech and blessings they deceive innocent hearts. [Haimo.] For with carefully composed words they commended their own tradition, by which they deceived the hearts of the simple.

For your obedience. As though he said: Therefore I warn you to avoid them, because your faith and obedience are praised everywhere. And this is what he means: your obedience has become known in every place, because you are [Col. 1530A] in the capital of the world, and thus others can now be corrupted by your example. Or: I urge you to avoid them, and to do so confidently, because your obedience—that is, your readiness to obey—has become known in every place. For everywhere it is known that you obey readily, which is good; and therefore I rejoice. Hence he adds: I therefore rejoice over you, but I want you to be—that is, I want you to be—wise in what is good, by discernment, and guileless in what is evil, that is, without any share in evil.

But God. As though he said: I want you to be wise. But may God, the giver of peace, namely Christ, crush Satan—that is, false preachers, or any person or devil opposing you—beneath your feet, so that he may not be able to harm you. Rather, if he is the devil, crush his head, as was said to Eve (Gen. 3), in the figure of the Church [Col. 1530B] or of sensuality; that is, despise the first movements of his suggestions. [Ambrose.] And he will do this swiftly, namely at my coming. That this may happen, may the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. [Augustine.] Or rather: in the meantime, however, the grace of the Lord, etc. He now wishes for them the grace which he promised at his coming.

Timothy, my fellow-worker, greets you, [Ambrose.] who is as it were a co-bishop; and Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater. As though he said: You are a concern to these men, who are my kinsmen by birth or by faith. See how many and how great are those who rejoice with you in what you have begun; therefore it is fitting that you persevere. I, Tertius—by name, not by number—who wrote the Epistle, greet you in the Lord. This Tertius was the Apostle’s secretary, to whom he granted permission to greet them under his own name. Gaius, my host, greets you. This is the one to whom John [Col. 1530C] wrote in the canonical Epistle, rejoicing because he supplied provisions to the brethren; and the whole Church greets you. Above he said that all the Churches greeted them, and here he says that the whole Church greets them. I think this was said neither idly nor superfluously—for so great a man inserted nothing superfluous—but here he means the Church of another province, from which Gaius came.

Erastus, treasurer of the city of the Athenians, greets you. [Haimo.] He is called *arcarius* from *arx*, “citadel,” as though he were a ruler. Or rather, he is called so from *arca*, “chest,” because he was in charge of the treasury where the revenues from taxes and customs duties were deposited, that is, he was the city’s steward; and Quartus the brother greets you. Quartus is a proper name, as Tertius also is. Grace. As though he said: These greet you in this manner: “The grace of the Lord,” etc. Or: these persons mentioned above [Col. 1530D] greet you, and I myself subscribe in my own hand: “May the grace of the Lord be with you all. Amen.”

VERSICLES 25–27.—“Now to him who is able to strengthen you, according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal ages, but now made manifest through the prophetic Scriptures, according to the command of the eternal God, made known among all nations for the obedience of faith—to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.”

66. Now to him. As though he said: This is how I exhort you. Now to him, namely to the Godhead of the Trinity, who is able to strengthen you in perfect faith, be honour and glory, since every good thing comes from him alone. In this conclusion the sum of the Epistle is indicated: [Col. 1531A] for the Apostle chiefly intends to warn them to attribute everything to God’s grace. I mean him who is able to strengthen you, and this according to my Gospel, from which Christ’s preaching does not differ; hence he adds: and according to the preaching of Jesus Christ. This Gospel—which is also this preaching—is according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal ages; that is, according to what was revealed to me concerning God’s hidden counsel, kept silent from eternity.

[Haimo.] By “eternal ages” he means the ages preceding the beginning of the world. Or: this Gospel is according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal ages; that is, it reveals the mystery itself, which had been hidden from the world’s beginning. By “mystery” he means Christ’s incarnation and similar matters, which had been hidden through eternal [Col. 1531B] ages. For although they had been known in some measure to the ancient Fathers, still they were fully foreknown by no one until, in their own time, they were revealed through Jesus Christ, with the prophetic Scriptures opened by him and bearing witness to this preaching. This is what he says: the mystery was made manifest by Christ through the prophetic Scriptures, opened by him. It was made manifest, I say, and this according to the command—that is, the dispensation—of the eternal God, who ordained this from eternity; as though he said: it is not fabricated.

God alone is properly called eternal.

[Note: [Col. 1531D] Augustine, *On the Nature of the Good*.] Eternal fire and eternal punishment are also spoken of, but they are not eternal in the way God is called eternal. Fire is called eternal because it is without end; yet [Col. 1531C] it is not without beginning, whereas God is without beginning as well. Therefore true eternity is that which is true immortality. This is that supreme unchangeableness which God alone possesses, he who cannot be changed in any respect. For it is one thing not to change when one can change, and another thing to be altogether unable to change. Thus a human being is called good, yet not as God is, of whom it was said, “No one is good except God alone” (Matt. 19); and the soul is called immortal, yet not as God is, of whom it was said, “He alone has immortality” (1 Tim. 6). And just as a human being is called wise, yet not as God is, of whom it was said, “To the only wise God,” so fire is called eternal, yet not as God is, whose immortality alone is true eternity.

For the obedience. As though he said: that mystery [Col. 1531D] has been made manifest, and this among all nations for obedience. Or, “for obeying,” that is, so that they may obey faith by doing good works.

I say, “of the mystery kept silent,” indeed from others, but known to the only wise God; because, even if it has now been revealed to human beings, it was known to God alone, who alone perfectly knows why this was done. In this he restrains investigators who ask why God delayed his coming for so long, and why he allowed so many nations to perish. But in saying, “to the only wise God,” an error crept in among some persons:

[Note: [Col. 1531D] Augustine, *Against Maximinus*.] They suppose that the Father alone is signified here and that he alone is truly wise. Yet it is not said, “to the only wise Father,” but “to the only wise God”; and [Col. 1532A] God is one—the Trinity itself. Thus we should understand the only wise God as we understand the only mighty God: namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who are one and the only God, whom alone we are commanded to serve. Yet even if the Apostle had said, “to the only wise Father,” he would not thereby have separated the Son or the Holy Spirit. So in the Apocalypse it is written of the Son that he has a written name which no one knows except himself (Rev. 14). Yet it is not therefore said that the Father does not know that name, from whom the Son is inseparable. Therefore, just as the Father knows what no one was said to know except the Son, because the Father and Son are inseparable, so also, if it had been said “to the only wise Father,” the Son and Holy Spirit would have to be understood together with him, because they are inseparable.

I say that the mystery was made manifest [Col. 1532B] through Jesus Christ, to whom—namely, to the only God—or, to whom—namely, to Christ—belong honour from us and glory for the ages, because he himself is true glory, blessedness, and the highest good; and this for ages of ages, that is, without end. Thus it has been shown how “to him” and “to whom” can be read. Some, however, read it without “to whom.” If you remove “to whom,” the construction is complete; but blessed Augustine says that it should be added, explains how it should be understood so as not to be superfluous, and reads it differently from the way stated above, thus:

“Now to him.” As though he said: He is able to strengthen you, so that honour and glory may be to God the Father, or to the Godhead of the Trinity. I say he is able, according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal ages. These words do not change. [Col. 1532C]

[Note: [Col. 1532D] Augustine, *Against Maximinus*.] That mystery has now been made manifest through the Holy Spirit or through Christ, and this through the prophetic Scriptures, according to the command of God, made known among all nations for the obedience of faith, “to whom, the only wise God.” These words do not change. To whom, I say—that is, to the Godhead of the Trinity, or to God the Father—be honour and glory through Jesus Christ, to whom belong honour from us and glory for the ages. The addition “to whom be glory,” when “to him be glory” would suffice, is an expression unusual in our language, not an ambiguity of meaning. For to say, in an unusual order of words, “to him be glory, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory,” is the same as saying in the customary order, “to him be glory, to whom glory is through Jesus Christ.” What is lost to the sense whether it is said in this way or that?

But glory is through Christ to the Father—that is, clear knowledge accompanied by praise—[Col. 1532D] because through him the Godhead of the Trinity became known to human beings. This is the mystery kept silent from eternal ages and revealed through Christ. Therefore the inserted phrase “through Jesus Christ” should not be taken as though the meaning were, “to the only wise God through Jesus Christ,” such that God alone is understood to be wise through Jesus Christ—not by participation but by begetting Wisdom, who is Christ Jesus. Rather, it should be understood that through Jesus Christ glory belongs to the only wise God. For who would dare say that through Jesus Christ God the Father comes to be wise, when there can be no doubt that he is wise according to his own substance? Or that [Col. 1533A] the Son’s substance exists through the begetting Father rather than the Father’s substance through the begotten Son? It follows, therefore, that glory belongs to the only wise God through Jesus Christ: that is, clear knowledge accompanied by praise, by which the Godhead of the Trinity became known among the nations.

It is through Christ because, to say nothing of other things, he himself commanded the nations to be baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, where the glory of this indivisible Trinity was especially commended. Therefore God, who is the Trinity itself, is rightly called alone wise because he alone is wise according to his own [Col. 1534A] substance, not according to an added participation in wisdom, as a rational creature is wise. Therefore he said, “to the only wise God,” because God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and this Trinity is the only wise God, who could never be unwise, nor can ever become by grace a participant in wisdom, but is wise by the immobility and unchangeableness of his nature. Therefore to him be glory through Christ, to whom belong honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 1533]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 1533B]

The Corinthians are Achaeans. They likewise heard the word of truth from the Apostle, and they were subverted in various ways by false apostles: some were led astray by philosophy’s wordy eloquence; others by adherence to the Jewish Law. The Apostle calls them back to true faith and evangelical wisdom, writing to them from Ephesus through Timothy.

# CHAPTER ONE

VERSICLES 1–3.—“Paul, called as an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Sosthenes the brother, to the Church of God which is at Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called saints, together with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, both theirs and ours. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

[Col. 1533C] The Apostle writes this Epistle to the Corinthians. [Ambrose.] The Corinthians are Achaeans; they were converted by the Apostle himself, who, warned by the Lord’s command, stayed at Corinth for one year and six months, teaching the word of God among them. But afterward they were subverted in many ways through pseudo-apostles: that is, they boasted of their baptizers, thereby rending the Church’s unity and judging the power and use of the sacraments by the merits of their ministers. They thought that sacraments were of greater benefit if administered by good persons, and of greater or lesser benefit according as they were given by better or worse persons.

They were likewise subverted so as to despise the Apostle and boast of the wise people of the age, delighting in their eloquence and earthly philosophy, so that, under Christ’s name, they might be imbued with teachings contrary to the faith. [Col. 1533D] They were also puffed up because the Apostle did not come to them. They even tolerated among themselves the fornicator who had his father’s wife. There are also other topics to be noted in their places.

[Ambrose.] Concerning these and similar matters, the Apostle writes to them with great confidence and affectionate love: at one time admonishing, at another soothing, at another rebuking. For there are many reasons why the Apostle writes to them, calling them back from errors to right faith and from schisms to unity. [Col. 1534B] The Apostle’s intention in this Epistle, therefore, is to call the Corinthians back from errors and schisms to right faith, and from vices and other sins to good conduct, and to establish them therein.

His method is as follows. In this Epistle, as in the others, he places a greeting at the beginning and sets before it his own name, celebrated among all nations, so that, having heard the name of their teacher, they may submit to correction. Because they regarded him lightly, he adds titles of dignity, not of humility, such as “servant.” After the greeting, he gives thanks for the gifts of those among them who were good. Then he rebukes those who boasted about baptizers; afterward he draws them back from love of earthly wisdom. Then he reproves them concerning the fornicator whom they permitted to remain among them. Then he rebukes them because 67 they wronged and defrauded one another and sought the judgments of unbelievers. [Col. 1534C] Afterwards he instructs them concerning marriage, the reception of the Eucharist—where they greatly erred—and many other matters. Near the end, moreover, a moral exhortation is added. He begins with the greeting, saying:

Paul, called, [Ambrose.] that is, chosen by God, apostle of Christ Jesus—that is, sent by God’s will to preach Christ. Or, “called,” that is, called by human beings “apostle of Christ Jesus” by privilege of title. He begins differently here than in the Epistle to the Romans, because the occasion here differs from that there. Here he does not call himself “servant,” as he did there, because authority and commendation were more necessary here against the pride of the Corinthians, among whom he had become of little account. I say, apostle, and this not through anger but through God’s will—[Col. 1534D] unlike your pseudo-apostles, who were neither sent by God nor speak the truth.

And Sosthenes the brother. This man is said to have reported their affairs to the Apostle; therefore he associates him with himself in this greeting, thus indicating that he was greatly concerned for them. See: through the one who was living among them, he suggests that he knows their faults. He calls him “brother,” moreover, in order thereby to remove any sinister suspicion from him, showing that he did not report about them from bad motives but from love and a desire for correction.

Paul, I say, and Sosthenes write this Epistle to the Church of God, not of human beings, [Col. 1535A] as you make it, by supposing that dispensers of ministries are the authors of graces. For in that case it would be a church of human beings, not of God. Whom he calls the Church of God, he explains by adding: namely, those sanctified in baptism, and this in Christ Jesus, that is, through Christ Jesus, not through human beings—though indeed they have been overthrown by pseudo-apostles. To them, I say, who are called saints—that is, called through preachers and then made holy. Or, “called saints,” that is, chosen beforehand by God to be holy. He says this to show that nothing good comes from human beings, but everything from God.

To these, I say, the Apostle writes, together with all—that is, he writes also to the suffragans of Corinth, who suffer from the same vices. Hence he adds: those who in every place, belonging to the Corinthians, both theirs and ours—that is, first entrusted to me—call upon the name [Col. 1535B] of the Lord, not some name other than God’s; who truly call upon him while they are his servants. Of such persons it is said: “He is near to all who call upon him in truth.” For one calls upon whatever one wishes to come to oneself. What is it to invoke except to call into oneself?

[Note: [Col. 1535D] Augustine, *On Psalm 35*.] Therefore whoever calls upon God in order to become rich does not call upon God. For when you say, “God, give me riches,” you do not want God himself to come to you; rather, you want riches to come to you. But God wishes to be worshipped and loved freely. For this is to love chastely: not because he gives something besides himself, but because he gives himself.

To such persons the Apostle says: those who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, of the Saviour and King—whom they truly call upon while they believe that they are saved and ruled by him. Grace to you, etc. Here is the greeting. As though he said: Paul [Col. 1535C] and Sosthenes write this Epistle to you, and before all else greet you, wishing that grace may be with you: for those standing, that they may remain; for those fallen, that they may return. And peace, that is, tranquillity of mind. And this from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, who is distinguished from him in personal property, yet is one God with him in unity of substance. Therefore he named the Father and Christ, lest they be thought to be one person.

VERSICLES 4–12.—“I give thanks to my God always for you, because of the grace of God given to you in Christ Jesus: because in all things you have been made rich in him, in every utterance and all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed among you, so that you lack no grace as you await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will also establish you without blame until the end, on the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful, through whom you were called into fellowship with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord. But I beseech you, brothers, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you; rather, that you be made complete in the same understanding and the same knowledge. For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those who belong to Chloe, that there are quarrels among you. What I mean is that each of you says: ‘I belong to Paul’; ‘I belong to Apollos’; ‘I belong to Cephas’; ‘I belong to Christ.’”

I give thanks, etc. Here he gives thanks for the gifts of those among them who were good. For in that people some [Col. 1536A] were good and worthy of praise, while others were worthy of rebuke. After the greeting, therefore, he first sets forth the good things, so that the others may conform themselves to these, saying: “I give thanks,” etc., in heart, speech, and deed, to God, [Ambrose.] from whom I believe all things come, not from human beings. He is God of all by the power through which he creates; but he is said to be God properly of those who love him, hold fast to him, possess him, receive his aid, and are not alienated from him.

I give thanks always for you, and this because of God’s grace given to you—that is, while I consider grace, namely God’s gifts—which were given to you in Christ Jesus, that is, from Christ and from no other source. This grace also is manifold from God, because in every gift you have been made rich in him, that is, in Christ, not in a human being. And because he said that they were enriched in all things, [Col. 1536B] he sets down some parts of this: you have been made rich in every utterance, that is, in every kind of language; or, in every utterance, that is, in every manner of preaching—to ordinary, perfect, and lesser persons alike—and in all knowledge, that is, understanding of the Scriptures.

And you have been enriched in these things so that you hold them just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed among you; that is, you hold the words and knowledge concerning that which I preached about Christ just as I confirmed it by the testimony of the prophets. Or, you have been enriched, that is, filled with gifts, just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed among you; that is, because you firmly hold the faith which I preached to you. I say that you are rich, so that you lack no grace of the Holy Spirit. You, I say, are awaiting with [Col. 1536C] desire—because you are certain of it and prepared for it—the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ: that is, the vision and knowledge of Christ granted after death to each believer. Or by “revelation” he means that which will occur on the Day of Judgment, which the ungodly fear.

Who will also establish you. As though he said: You await Christ’s revelation, and you will not fail in that expectation. For he himself will establish each of you until the end, so that you may be without blame, although not without sin. He will establish you, I say, until the end—that is, until the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. His coming is understood to occur when he is made manifest to each person after death. Or thus: he will establish you, I say, while you always go in mind toward that day, namely the day of Christ’s coming, etc.

God is faithful. As though he said: He will establish you, and truly so, because God is faithful, [Col. 1536D] that is, true in his promises, through whom you were called when you had turned away. Therefore he who called you when you were turned away will more easily establish you. I say, called into fellowship not merely with angels or apostles, but with his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. But I beseech you, brothers. Up to this point he has praised the good; having praised them, he invites the others to imitate them. As though he said: I give thanks for the good, but I beseech you others, brothers, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, if you wish to belong to him after whom you are named Christians—that you all speak with one confession of the mouth, and inwardly hold in your hearts the same thing that those mentioned above say; and that there be no schisms, that is, divisions, among you. Rather, be of the same understanding—that is, [Col. 1537A] of the same will—as those mentioned above, and of the same knowledge—that is, of the same understanding—so that you may be complete.

I say this because it was reported to me about you, my brothers, by those who belong to Chloe. Chloe is the place where those were who reported it to the Apostle. Or, “those who belong to Chloe” means those belonging to that matron; for Chloe may be the name either of a place or of a person. Some think it is a place, as if it were said, “by those who are at Antioch”; others think she was a woman devoted to God, with whom many worshippers of God lived. What, then, was reported about you? Namely, that there are disputes among you concerning the Lord’s teaching.

What I mean. Here he begins to deal with the baptizers, in whom they gloried. As though he said: I know not only the disputes among you, [Col. 1537B] but also the words that you say. And this is what he means: each of you says this. For one says, “I belong to Paul”; another says, “I belong to Apollos”; another, “I belong to Cephas.” As though he said: one says, “I was baptized with this man’s baptism”; another says, “I was baptized with that man’s.” But to say this is like idolatry.

It should be understood that under his own name and those of the good apostles he indicates the pseudo-apostles. For those whom he names were undoubtedly good; but under their appearance he strikes at false apostles, lest, if he mentioned this or that person by name, he might seem to envy them and wish to attribute everything to himself. Or he inserted the names of good apostles to show that, if one must not glory in the names of greater persons, neither must one glory in the names of those whose teaching is perverse.

But among these he singles out for praise those who said that they belonged to Christ. Hence he adds: another says, “I belong to Christ,” baptized with Christ’s baptism.

[Note: [Col. 1537D] Augustine, *On John*.] He speaks rightly here, like those whom he praised above. Such persons have the door through which they must enter, which is Christ, through whom the Father is known. For no one knows the Son except the Father, nor the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. Therefore, just as he himself knows the Father through himself, while we know him through Christ, so he enters the sheepfold through himself, while we enter through that door. For Christ preaches himself, and we preach Christ; therefore he enters through himself, and we through him. Christ, then, is both door and shepherd by entering through himself; and he also gave to his own the office of shepherd. Thus Peter is a shepherd, Paul is a shepherd, and others are shepherds. But none of us calls himself the door; Christ reserved this title properly for himself. Therefore no one is the door but Christ, though others are shepherds. But because undisciplined sheep began to make schisms and set up other doors for themselves through which to enter—not in order to be gathered together, but to wander and be divided—saying, “I belong to Paul,” etc., he adds:

68. VERSICLE 13.—“Has Christ been divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?”

Has Christ been divided? As though he said: Learn how greatly you err, how greatly you presume concerning God, and how much [Col. 1538A] you attribute to human beings, when you divide glory among them. [Ambrose.] According to you, then, Christ has been divided. As though he said: You make many Christs—that is, many givers of graces. For these people erred so greatly that they believed grace was given by a human being, not merely as a minister, but as an author.

Or, they believed that in baptism Christ worked more through a better baptizer and less through one who was less good; and therefore he says: “Has Christ been divided?” As though he said: He who works the same thing in all has been divided, as far as you are concerned, while he is believed to work more in this person and less in that. Or thus: because you say these things, Christ has now been divided by you, that is, separated.

They erred grievously, because they established doors for themselves besides Christ and presumed to lay different foundations, although the Church has only one foundation, which no one can alter: Christ Jesus. [Col. 1538B] For he alone is the rock upon which the Church is founded, and Peter took his name from that rock, as the Lord said to him:

[Note: [Col. 1537D] Augustine, from a tractate on the Gospel.] “You are Peter,” etc. (Matt. 16). He had previously been called Simon; but this name, Peter, was given to him by the Lord. Peter is called so as a figure of the Christian people, from Christ the rock. For because Christ is called the rock, the Christian people too are called Peter. Thus Peter is named from the rock, not the rock from Peter, just as Christ is not named from “Christian,” but “Christian” from Christ. Therefore, he says, you are Peter, named from the rock which you confessed and recognized when you said, “You are the Christ, the Son of God”; and “upon this rock”—that is, upon myself, the Son of God, [Col. 1538C] not upon you—“I will build my Church.” I will build you and others upon myself, not myself upon you. For they are not called Peter’s, but Christ’s; not “Petrines” from Peter, but Christians from Christ, lest hope be placed in a human being. “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man” (Jer. 17).

[Note: [Col. 1538D] Augustine, *On John*.] And lest there be as many baptisms as there are servants, Christ gave his servants the ministry of baptizing, but retained its power for himself. Had he wished, he could have given that power to a servant, so that the servant might give his own baptism as acting in Christ’s place; and he could have established his power in some servant, so that the servant’s baptism would have as great a force as baptism given by the Lord. But he did not wish this. Therefore the hope of those baptized would not be in a human being. He did not wish a servant to place hope in a servant. For the servant baptizes as a minister, but the Lord baptizes as one possessing authority.

And, as has been said, he could have given this power to a servant, but did not wish to do so. For if he had given this power to servants—that is, if what belonged to the Lord had belonged to them—there would be as many baptisms as servants; just as John’s baptism was called so, one would speak of Peter’s baptism, Paul’s baptism, and the like. For that baptism was called John’s. But perhaps someone will say: “Prove to us that that baptism was called John’s.” I shall prove it by Truth itself, when he asked the Jews: “Whence was John’s baptism?” (Matt. 21). Therefore, lest there be as many baptisms [Col. 1539A] as there were servants who baptized, the Lord retained the power of baptizing for himself and gave the ministry to his servants. Therefore, if a servant says that he baptizes, he speaks correctly; but he baptizes as a minister. Thus it makes no difference whether the person to whom the ministry of baptizing has fallen is good or bad.

[Note: [Col. 1539D] Augustine, in the same work.] Hence too no one says, “my baptism,” although he may say, “my Gospel,” “my wisdom,” or “my glory,” even though these things come from God. There is a difference in these matters: one person is more learned than another, and one performs the work of evangelizing better than another; nor are all endowed with equal wisdom. But no one can be said to be baptized more or less, whether baptized by an inferior or by a greater person.

To Augustine’s statement that Christ could have given his servants the power of baptism, some object as follows. The power or might of God is the divine essence, because for God being is not one thing and being able another. Therefore, if he could not give them the ability to be what he is, neither could he give them his ability or power, namely that which he himself is. Otherwise, if he could give them his power, which he himself is, he could give them the ability to be what he is. To this we reply that Christ could not give them the ability to be what he is, and yet could give them the power which he has: namely, the power by which they could forgive sins, which he alone can do. For this is what he calls the power of baptism, namely the power of remitting sins. Therefore he could have given the authority of baptism to those to whom he conferred its ministry, while still remaining its principal author. But we do not say that he could give them the power by which he himself exists, or his ability which is his being. We speak in this way when we say that he gave us knowledge of what he himself knows, or gave prophets knowledge of future things which he possesses: not because he gave us the being which he has, or gave the prophets the knowledge which is the divine essence, but because by grace he gave us knowledge of future things which he has known by nature from eternity. Others say that he could have given the power of baptism so that baptism might be administered in their name, and remission of sins effected in it, as it was in Christ’s name; but he did not wish to do so.

Was Paul? As though he said: You say, “I belong to Paul,” “I belong to Apollos,” and so forth. But was Paul crucified for you, that he might be the author of your salvation? [Col. 1539D] Or were you baptized in Paul’s name, so that I might forgive your sins? As though he said: No.

[Note: [Col. 1539D] Augustine, *On Psalm 72*.] He calls them back to one name, since they wanted to make many names for themselves; he draws them away from love of a human being, so that Christ may be loved. As though he said: I do not want you to belong to me, but to be with me. Be with me: we all belong to him who was crucified for us. For our sins are forgiven through his name, not through the name of any human being. Hence John says: “I write to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven through his name” (1 John 2).

[Note: [Col. 1539D] Augustine, *On the One Baptism*.] Note that by means of the truth which those Corinthians held, he makes them ashamed of the false things they held. For their particular and detestable vice was that they said, “I belong to Paul.” Nor do I think that those whom he rebukes for having broken apart into schisms possessed true faith in saying, “I belong to Paul,” and so forth. For this was false. But that they knew Christ had been crucified for them, and that they had been baptized in his name rather than Paul’s, was not the result of their error but of a divine gift. They held this truth of God amid the iniquity of their schisms. By the truth, therefore, which they held, he convicts their falsehood. They had, indeed, true baptism, and from its truth they hear from him, for the correction of their falsehood: “Was Paul,” etc. It is entirely possible for some to possess true baptism and not true faith, as these persons did. By the truth [Col. 1540B] which they possessed, therefore, he corrects the falsehood which they held, just as by Christ’s resurrection, which they believed, he proves the resurrection of the dead, which they denied.

[Note: [Col. 1540D] Augustine, in the same work.] For among them were persons who did not believe that the dead would rise, although they did believe that Christ had risen.

### Verses 14–18

“I give thanks to my God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, lest anyone should say that you were baptized in my name. But I also baptized the household of Stephanas. Besides, I do not know whether I baptized any other of you. For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel—not in wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be made void. For the word of the cross is indeed foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God.”

[Col. 1540C] “I give thanks,” etc. As though he were saying: And because you take pride in baptisms, I give thanks to my God, etc., for this, that I baptized none of you who are engaged in contention. For I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, who do not belong to your factional strife. And I do not say this because baptism is not good; but lest anyone should say that you were baptized in my name, and so take greater pride in me.

[Note: Col. 1540D. The same author, *Against the Baptists*, *On Baptism.*] The Lord Jesus could indeed, as has been said, if he had wished, have given the power of his baptism to one or to several of his principal servants, so that, just as Aaron was shown to be priest by the flowering rod, ministers and dispensers of the mysteries of superior rank might be indicated by some sign, and they alone ought to baptize. But if this had been done, it would then be called their baptism, although bestowed on them by the Lord, just as John’s baptism was. Therefore the Apostle gives thanks to God that he baptized none of those who, as though forgetting in whose name they had been baptized, divided themselves by human names.

For since baptism administered through a contemptible person has as much force as baptism administered through an apostle, it is recognized as belonging neither to the one nor to the other, but to Christ—a fact which John testifies that he learned through the appearance of the dove. For I do not clearly see in what other sense he could have said, “And I did not know him” [John 1], unless he knew him in one respect and did not know him in another. He knew, certainly, that he was the Bridegroom and the Son of God; but he did not know [Col. 1541A] whether he would give others the authority to baptize, or would retain baptism as his own and receive the authority of baptism himself. But he learned this through the Spirit, as it were through the dove descending and remaining upon Christ. Hence it is said to him: “He upon whom you see the Spirit remaining and descending like a dove—this is he who baptizes” [ibid.].

“But baptized,” etc. As though he were saying: Not only did I baptize those just mentioned, but I also baptized the household of Stephanas, that is, the family of that matron, who does not belong to this contention. “Besides,” as though he were saying: Of these I am certain that I baptized them. Besides, I do not know whether I baptized any other of you who belongs to the contentious party.

“For Christ did not send me.” [Col. 1541B] Here the reason is shown why I baptized so few. As though he were saying: I baptized so few because Christ did not send me to baptize—which can be done by lesser persons—lest I should be hindered from preaching, of which he adds, “but to preach the gospel.”

[Note: Col. 1541D. Augustine, *Against Pelagius.*] Even less learned persons can baptize perfectly; but to preach the gospel perfectly is a work much more difficult and rare. Therefore the teacher of the nations, surpassing many others, says that he was sent to preach the gospel, not to baptize.

Nevertheless, when necessity pressed, he sometimes did this.

“Not in wisdom.” As though he were saying: I say that he sent me to preach the gospel, not, indeed, in wisdom of speech—that is, in the wisdom of philosophers, which is called wisdom of speech because it is called wisdom even though it is not. Or it is called wisdom of speech because it makes people verbose. [Col. 1541C] Therefore he did not send me in wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be made void.

[Note: Col. 1541D. Ambrose, *On Nature and Grace.*] For through that wisdom the cross of Christ—that is, Christ’s death—is made void, and it is judged impossible according to nature that the immortal God should die. Or the cross of Christ is made void if righteousness and eternal life are believed to exist by some means, whether through a good nature or in any other way apart from it. These things seem, indeed, to be said sharply, but in a wisdom of speech by which Christ’s cross is made void. This is not the wisdom descending from above. If, therefore, we are wise according to the Scriptures, we are not compelled to argue against Christ’s grace and to say things by which we attempt to demonstrate that human nature needs no physician in infants because it is sound, and can suffice for itself unto righteousness in older persons if they wish.

[Note: Col. 1542D. Augustine, *Against Felicianus.*] Therefore the Apostle does not presume to preach in wisdom of speech, but, content with the authority of the Scriptures, cultivates simplicity rather than swelling pride.

Or: He did not send me to preach in wisdom of speech, that is, in elegance and ornament of language, because Christian preaching does not need pomp and rhetorical adornment, lest it appear to arise from the cleverness and craftiness of human wisdom rather than from truth.

[Ambrose.] For verbal composition is sought where Truth itself does not commend itself by its own testimony, as in worldly wisdom. Therefore one who wishes to embellish [Col. 1542A] Christ’s faith with words obscures it by the brilliance of those words, so that not Christ’s faith but he himself may be praised. Therefore, showing why he did not preach in wisdom of speech, he adds: “lest the cross of Christ be made void.” Like the pseudo-apostles, lest they should seem foolish to the wise of the world, they preached Christ in human wisdom in two ways: striving after eloquence and avoiding what the world judges foolish.

“For the word,” etc. As though someone were asking whether the cross of Christ would be made void, he answers: Certainly. For the word—that is, the preaching—of the cross is indeed foolishness, that is, appears to be foolishness, to those who are perishing, that is, to the wise of this world, whose wisdom perishes and is shown false, and for that reason they themselves are condemned. Therefore, instead of saying “to the wise,” he says “to those who are perishing.”

“But to those,” etc. As though he were saying: To those who are perishing [Col. 1542B] the word of the cross is foolishness. But to those who are being saved—that is, to us, namely believers—it is the power of God, because believers understand in Christ’s cross the power of God, when they know that, though slain, he conquered the devil and freed humankind. Or, it is the power of God, that is, it gives power to believers, through which, when necessity requires, miracles are performed.

### Verses 19–22

“For it is written: ‘I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent.’ Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the inquirer of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save believers, because Jews ask for signs and Greeks seek wisdom.”

[Col. 1542C] “For it is written.” As though he were saying: Therefore he did not send me to preach in wisdom, because he had foretold that he would not receive it in evangelical preaching, but would destroy it and reject it from the company of his preachers. This is what he says: For it is written in Obadiah: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise of this age, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent,” that is, I will eliminate worldly wisdom and prudence from the preachers of the Gospel, so that I shall not receive such wise persons among the preachers; and so it came to pass.

For where is the wise person among the preachers? If he wished to be among them, he had to cast off that wisdom. And note that he first sets down the genus, then adds the species, saying: “Where is the scribe? Where is the inquirer of this age?” [Col. 1542D] “Wise person” is the genus of both, namely of the scribe and the inquirer. A scribe is one who gives precepts also concerning morals and arts. An inquirer is one who searches out the secrets of nature. God receives such persons among his preachers, but makes them foolish. Hence he adds: “Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?”

Or thus: “For it is written.” As though he were saying: I rightly say, “to those who are perishing”; for thus it is written, namely that he would destroy and render false and reprobate the wisdom of this world. This is what “I will destroy” means: “I will make void the wisdom of the wise.”

[Augustine.] Certainly I shall not destroy my own wisdom in them, but that which is theirs, which [Col. 1543A] they arrogate to themselves.

[Jerome.] For true wisdom and true prudence are not destroyed by the Lord, but the knowledge falsely so called which they store up for themselves with a lying tongue, while they fail in searching searches.

“And I will reject the prudence of the prudent”—the prudence, namely, which they have devised for proving something. He does not say this because an understanding of truth can be rejected by God, but because the prudence of those who trust in their own learning is rejected.

“Where is the wise person?” [Ambrose, Haimo.] The Apostle taunts the practitioners of approved—namely false—knowledge, saying, “Where is the wise person?” whether among Jews or Gentiles, as though he were of no account. This is an invective against Jews and Gentiles; hence he adds concerning each separately: “Where is the scribe?”—among the Jews. “Where is the inquirer of this age?”—that is, the Gentile who investigates only the natures of things.

[Col. 1543B] As though he were saying: Their wisdom has been defeated and made foolish. For the Jewish scribe and teachers of the law, although they believe that nothing is impossible to God, nevertheless, because they do not have this very plainly in the Law, hesitate to believe that the Son of God died and such things. But to Gentiles it is foolishness according to human reasoning.

“But has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” The wisdom of this world is that in which God’s weakness and foolishness are despised; it is according to worldly principles and judges impossible what it does not see in the natures of things. God made this wisdom foolish by declaring and doing possible what it judges impossible.

“For since,” etc. As though he were saying: God truly made worldly wisdom foolish, because through foolishness he saves believers; and it pleased him to do this. This is what he says: “For it pleased [Col. 1543C] God”—for it is according to his good pleasure—to save believers, and this “through the foolishness of preaching,” that is, through preachers unskilled in worldly wisdom, who seemed foolish. Or, “through the foolishness of preaching” means through the thing preached, which appears foolish, such as Christ’s passion and death, in which there is humility.

[Ambrose.] He also shows why he did this by what he had previously stated in sequence: namely, because the world did not know God through—that is, because of—its own wisdom; that is, the wise of the world did not know God because of their wisdom, in which there is pride.

[Note: Col. 1543D. Augustine, *On the Trinity.*] They did not know him, I say, through Wisdom, that is, through the incarnate Son, who, when the Son of God was manifested in flesh, was sent into this world.

[Note: Col. 1543D. The same author, *On Psalm* 33.] Therefore he is said to have come from God not by travelling through spaces, but by appearing in mortal flesh to mortals. Thus he came to the place where he already was, because he was in this world, because the world was made through him, and the world did not know him [John 1].

[Note: Col. 1544D. The same author, *On the Trinity.*] This is the light that shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it [ibid.]. But in order that it might be comprehended, the Word became flesh [ibid.].

[Note: Col. 1544D. The same author, *On John.*] For just as treatment is the path to health, so the medicine of God’s wisdom, by assumption of humanity, was adapted to our wounds, healing by certain opposites and by certain likenesses. For we were deceived by the wisdom—that is, cunning—of the serpent; [Col. 1544A] we are freed by God’s wisdom. And just as that wisdom was called wisdom, though it was foolishness, so this which is called foolishness is wisdom. Here are the opposites. The likenesses, moreover, are these: through a woman he freed those deceived through a woman; a human being freed human beings; a mortal freed mortals.

[Ambrose.] Or thus: I say that the world did not know God through its own wisdom, and this occurred in God’s wisdom; God did this by deep counsel, namely lest they should become proud, and so that faith and salvation might be recognized as coming from God, not from human wisdom. “Because Jews,” etc. As though he were saying: The world did not know God through wisdom, because Jews, accustomed from ancient times, ask for signs of power, not knowing God’s humility; and Greeks—that is, Gentiles—seek wisdom, not true wisdom, but that which seems wisdom to human ingenuity, namely whether what is preached can be [Col. 1544B] suffered by nature.

### Verses 23–31

“But we preach Christ crucified: to Jews indeed a stumbling block, but to Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. Because the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and the weakness of God is stronger than human beings. For consider your calling, brothers: not many were wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble. But God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the ignoble and despised things of the world, and things that are not, to destroy things that are, so that no flesh may boast in his presence. But from him you are in Christ Jesus, who [Col. 1544C] became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption, so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.’”

“But we,” on the contrary, preach Christ crucified, “to Jews indeed a stumbling block.” As though he were saying: What is not to the Jews a sign of power, but a stumbling block, because they rage against the preachers from shame at their own crime; “but to Gentiles foolishness.” As though he were saying: What we preach appears foolishness to the Gentiles—and likewise to you, if you belong among the wise.

Or the sense runs thus: What we preach appears foolishness because Jews ask for signs and Greeks seek wisdom. But we do the opposite: [Col. 1544D] we preach Christ to Jews, for whom he is a stumbling block, and to Gentiles, for whom he is foolishness; and yet by this foolishness God saves believers, as has been said.

“But to those who are called”: connect it thus. I say that Jews seek signs and Greeks seek wisdom. In the crucifixion which we preach there is great power of God and great wisdom of God. This is seen or made evident to Jews and Greeks—not, indeed, to all, but to those who are called.

[Augustine.] That is, to those called to life, not by the common calling but by that calling through which the foreknown are called. To them Christ’s passion appears power and wisdom, so that salvation may be from God, not from the choice of Jew or Greek, although it appears otherwise to the reprobate. Therefore, to those who are called we preach Christ, that [Col. 1545A] is, Christ crucified, namely the power of God and wisdom of God: Christ’s crucifixion, in which God’s power appears because, though dead, he conquered death—that is, the devil and the Jew—and God’s wisdom, by which he cleverly deceived the devil.

[Ambrose.] Or: To those who are called we preach Christ, that is, faith in Christ or Christ’s passion, namely the power of God, because through their faith sins are remitted, demons are driven out, and, when need arises, miracles are performed; and the wisdom of God, because those who believe in Christ crucified understand Christ to be God’s wisdom.

[Note: Col. 1545D. Ambrose, *On Psalm* 18.] For Christ is the Father’s wisdom just as he is the Father’s power; he is the Father’s Word and the Father’s hand, through whom, as by hand and word, the Father made all things. Hence: “The heavens are the works of your hands” [Hebrews 1]. [Col. 1545B] And likewise: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” [Psalm 32]. Therefore what he made by the word, he made by the hand; and what he made by the hand, he made by the word.

It can therefore be understood thus: We preach that Christ is God’s wisdom and God’s power. Take care not to understand the Son to be called God’s wisdom as though he alone were intelligent or wise for himself, the Father, and the Holy Spirit.

[Note: Col. 1545D. Augustine, *On the Trinity.*] For if in that passage the Son alone is understood to be wise for himself, the Father, and the Holy Spirit, one returns to the absurdity that the Father is not wise from himself but from the Son; that wisdom did not beget wisdom, but that the Father is said to be wise by that wisdom which he begot. For where there is no understanding, there can be no wisdom. Therefore, if the Father does not understand for himself, but the Son understands [Col. 1545C] for the Father, then the Son makes the Father wise. And if for God to be is to be wise, and if his essence is his wisdom, then it is not the Son who has his essence from the Father—which is true—but rather the Father who has his essence from the Son, which is utterly false.

Therefore God the Father is wise by that wisdom which he himself is; and the Son, the wisdom of the Father, is wise by the wisdom which is the Father, from whom the Son is begotten. Likewise, the Father is intelligent by that intelligence which he himself is; but the Son, the intelligence of the Father, is intelligent by the intelligence which belongs to the Father and from which he is begotten.

“Because,” etc. As though he were saying: There is truly God’s power and God’s wisdom in Christ’s crucifixion, because “the foolishness of God”—that is, what appears foolish concerning God to the wise of the world, such as suffering [Col. 1545D] and death—is wiser than human beings, that is, than anything human beings can perceive or be. And “the weakness of God” is stronger than human beings.

[Ambrose.] Without doubt, heavenly things surpass earthly things; therefore God’s weakness is not truly weakness but only appears so, because Christ’s weakness is a great victory. For when he was conquered, he conquered death, which no giant escaped.

“For consider,” etc. As though he were saying: God’s foolishness and weakness truly are wiser and stronger than human beings, as you can experience in yourselves. Consider your calling, brothers—that is, by whom you were called. For ignorant and weak people called you; they were counted among the foolish and weak things of the world. Such are your callers, yet they confound the wise and strong. And they truly are such, because not many of those who call are [Col. 1546A] wise according to the flesh, that is, according to human wisdom; not many are powerful, with wide authority; not many noble, in splendour of ancestry.

At first none such were among the teachers of the Christian faith, when the twelve apostles were chosen. Or he says “not many,” not “none,” perhaps on account of himself: alone among the apostles he was skilled in secular letters, rich in earthly resources, and conspicuous through relatives of Roman rank; yet he counted these things as nothing and did not use them.

“But the foolish things,” etc. As though he were saying: He did not choose the wise, but rather God chose the foolish things of the world—that is, persons ignorant of worldly wisdom—to confound, that is, to make the wise blush [Col. 1546B] and reduce them to foolishness. And God chose the weak things of the world, that is, the powerless, to confound the strong—for example, Nero. And he chose the ignoble things of the world and, what is more, the despised things; he chose things that are not, that is, the ignoble and despised, who seemed to be nothing, in order to destroy—that is, to humble through conquering—things that are, that is, those who, though they are nothing in themselves, nevertheless seem to themselves to be something.

See how those who boast of worldly wisdom openly act against God’s ordering, when God sets humility before them.

[Ambrose.] For the humble God came seeking the humble, not the lofty. Although he first chose poor, unlearned, weak people, he nevertheless did not abandon the wise, rich, and noble. But if he had chosen them first, they would rightly have seemed to themselves to be chosen for such [Col. 1546C] qualities; puffed up by them, they would not receive the salvation of humility, and thus there would be in them the pride by which humanity fell.

Therefore he did not choose kings, senators, philosophers, or orators. Rather, he chose commoners, poor people, unlearned fishermen. Unless the fisherman went faithfully before, the orator would not follow humbly. Hence the learned Nathanael was not chosen as an apostle.

To show that these things were done for the sake of humility, he adds: “So that no flesh may boast,” etc. As though he were saying: Therefore he chose weak persons rather than wise ones, so that no flesh—that is, no human being, righteous or unrighteous—might boast from himself, but from God. This is shown in the words: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.” [Col. 1546D] I say, let him not boast of himself “in his presence,” namely God’s, or in his own presence—that is, if he beholds God or attends to himself.

“But from him,” etc. [Augustine.] As though he were saying: God chose such people; nevertheless, you are in Christ Jesus, that is, in Christ’s faith. And this is “from him,” that is, through Christ himself, not through us.

Or connect it thus: I say that no one should boast from himself; yet there is another good kind of boasting, namely that from him you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, that is, enlightening you unto truth.

[Note: Col. 1546D. Augustine, *On the Trinity.*] He is said to have become wisdom for us because in time—that is, from some point in time—we turn to him, in order to remain with him [Col. 1547A] forever. Wisdom itself became flesh and dwelt among us. And he does this—that is, enlightens us—because he became for us righteousness, that is, because he first justifies us through good action.

For righteousness, which lives in itself, is undoubtedly God and lives unchangeably. Just as, though he is life in himself, he also becomes life for us when we become participants in him, so, though he is righteousness in himself, he also becomes righteousness for us when, cleaving to him, we live righteously. Thus he is righteousness for us because he is first sanctification, that is, because he first cleanses us in baptism. And this is so because he first became redemption for us, that is, because he first redeemed us by suffering.

All this was done in this way so that no one might boast except in God’s goods, as it is written in Jeremiah: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” [Col. 1547B]. Yet in Jeremiah it is written thus: “Let the one who boasts boast in this: that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord” [Jeremiah 10].

## Chapter II

### Verses 1–8

“And when I came to you, brothers, I came not in loftiness of speech or wisdom, announcing to you the testimony of Christ. For I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. And I was with you in weakness, and fear, and much trembling; and my speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of Spirit and power, so that your faith might not be in human wisdom but in the power of God. Yet we speak wisdom among the perfect—not, however, the wisdom [Col. 1547C] of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed—but we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, wisdom hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory, and which none of the rulers of this age knew. For had they known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

“And when I came to you.” As though he were saying: Just as others not wise were chosen for the apostleship, so I also—that is, even I, who had been wise—became as though I were not wise when I came to you, brothers. For I came to you not in loftiness of speech according to logic, namely so as to use logical arguments; nor in loftiness of wisdom according to physics, so as to confirm this by physical arguments—[Col. 1547D] these two being praised among the pseudo-apostles against God. Rather, I came announcing to you the testimony of Christ, that is, the things which the prophets testified concerning Christ.

“For I judged,” etc. As though he were saying: I truly did not come through that loftiness, because I did not even come through that wisdom which concerns God; and I did this by a judgment of mind. For I judged that I knew nothing among you, who were less capable, except Jesus Christ and him crucified—that is, except this: that Christ is our ruler and saviour.

[Note: Col. 1547D. Augustine, *On Faith and Works.*] And this through crucifixion. It should be known that Christ is preached not only by one who establishes faith, but also by one who instructs people in the morals by which life is lived in him. This can also be understood in what the Apostle mentions when he says: [Col. 1548A] “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.” For in the Crucified One it is said that the old human being was crucified, so that we may no longer serve sin [Romans 6]. Therefore what the Apostle says here should not be understood as though he had spoken only of those matters concerning Christ which must be believed, but also of what must be observed in life and conduct by the one who approaches the joining together of the body.

“And I,” etc. [Augustine.] As though he were saying: My preaching among you was humble, and my person also humble. This is what he says: “And I was with you in weakness,” that is, in tribulation; “and fear of mind,” that is, with an anxious mind; “and much trembling of body.” “And my speech,” which took place privately, “and my preaching,” which took place publicly, were not in persuasive words of human wisdom. [Col. 1548B] For even if my words were persuasive, they were not persuasive through human wisdom, like the words of the pseudo-apostles. Rather, they were in demonstration of Spirit and power: in my speech and preaching I showed that I had the Holy Spirit and power to perform miracles.

I did this so that your faith might not be—that is, might not be understood to be—in human wisdom, but in God’s power; that is, so that your faith might not be attributed to a human being but to God.

“Yet we speak wisdom.” As though he were saying: Among you who were incapable, we spoke simply; but among the perfect we speak wisdom, which concerns God’s secrets. Here he does not mean perfect knowers and teachers, who have no need to be taught, but hearers [Col. 1548C] already capable of receiving it.

What wisdom? Not the wisdom of this age, which rests on human arguments; nor the wisdom of the rulers of this age, that is, evil spirits or philosophers, who seemed to be rulers of the world and who are being destroyed, that is, whose wisdom is being destroyed. But we speak God’s wisdom, that is, Christ, in whom God’s wisdom concerning humanity’s redemption has been shown. We speak, I say, “in a mystery,” that is, by expounding the mysteries of the Old Testament, in which Christ is signified, as in Abel’s sacrifice or Abraham’s.

[Ambrose.] This wisdom of God is hidden, so that the pseudo-apostles may not know that it lies not in words but in power; it is not comprehensible by human reason, but is believable through the efficacy of the Spirit. This wisdom God predestined—that is, prepared—before [Col. 1548D] the ages, that is, before the world existed, for our glory: either the glory of us apostles who preach it, or the glory of all believers, so that through it all may attain eternal glory.

“Which none,” etc. As though he were saying: I rightly say that it is hidden, because it is the wisdom which none of the rulers of this age—that is, demons, philosophers, or teachers of the Law—knew. This is apparent from the following: For if demons had known God’s wisdom, concerning the redemption of the human race to be accomplished through Christ’s death, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory—that is, they would not have suggested his crucifixion, because the devil would not have suggested the crucifixion of him through whom he knew that he would lose his own right.

[Col. 1549A] Or this may be understood of the Jews. Some of them knew Christ, while others did not know him. Peter speaks of the ignorant ones: “I know, brothers, that you did this through ignorance” [Acts 3]. These did not know that he was the one promised to them in the Law. But the leaders—the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees—knew that he was the one promised in the Law; yet they did not know that he was God or the Son of God.

Thus it can be understood of both groups: if the lesser people had known him to be the Messiah promised in the Law, or if the greater ones had known him to be God or the Son of God, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.
