[Note: Col. 1549D. Augustine, *Questions on the New and Old Testament.*] For they would not have done this if they had known him to be God. If demons did not understand God made human, how much less did human beings? [Col. 1549B] Therefore demons knew him no differently than the rulers knew him. For they knew that he was the one promised in the Law, but they did not know his mystery: that he was the Son of God and eternal; nor did they know the sacrament of the incarnation, passion, and redemption.

Therefore, when demons cry out in the Gospel, “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God?” [Mark 5], they should be believed to have said it more from suspicion than from knowledge. Or: if they had known in such a manner that it was firmly settled in their minds, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

Note that he says, “They crucified the Lord of glory.”

[Note: Col. 1549D. The same author, *On the Trinity.*] He was crucified in the form of a servant, and yet the Lord of glory was crucified. For that assumption was such as to make God human and a human being God. But let the prudent, diligent, and devout reader understand what is said on account of what, and in what respect.

[Col. 1549C] For behold, we say that according to that in which God is, he glorifies his own; and according to this, namely that he is the Lord of glory, the Lord of glory was crucified. For God is rightly said to have been crucified, not through the power of divinity but through the weakness of flesh. For Christ is one person, God and human being. Therefore it is said: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” [John 3].

[Note: Col. 1550D. The same author, *Against Maximinus.*] If, therefore, you attend to the distinction of substances, the Son of God descended and the son of man was crucified; but if you attend to the unity of person, both the son of man descended and the Son of God was crucified. Because of this unity of person, he not only said that the son of man had descended from heaven, but also said that he was in heaven while speaking on earth.

[Col. 1549D] Far be it from us to suppose that Christ underwent death in such a way that life itself, so far as it lay in him, lost life.

[Note: Col. 1550D. The same author, *Against Felicianus.*] For if this were so, the fountain of life would have dried up. He therefore experienced death by participation in the human condition, which he had voluntarily assumed; he did not lose the power of his nature, by which he gives life to all things. Thus, by dying, he did not abandon his flesh in the tomb, just as, by being born, he did not abandon it when he formed it in the virgin’s womb.

Therefore he died without life departing, just as he suffered without power perishing. No one takes his life from him, because he has authority to lay it down and authority to take it up. [Col. 1550A] Behold, you have the author of the action: he will lay down his life. Behold, you have the action of authority. And, to conclude generally: whenever Christ suffers anything in the flesh, it is the action of the author, because he suffers by his own power and not because another compels him. He himself is the author of the action.

Therefore the Word’s divinity did not come to Mary by local movement, but by the undiminished fullness of his ineffable power. Nor did Christ leave the Father when he came into the Virgin: wholly everywhere, perfect everywhere. At one and the same time, therefore, he was wholly in hell and wholly in heaven, truly dead and truly alive. In him the assumption of mortality underwent death, while divinity did not lose life. Therefore the Son of God neither endured death in his soul nor experienced it in his majesty; rather, the King of glory was crucified only by participation in weakness.

### Verses 9–13

[Col. 1550B] “As it is written: ‘What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, the things which God has prepared for those who love him.’ But God revealed them to us through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God. For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the human spirit which is in that person? So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God. But we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may know what has been given to us by God; and we speak these things not in words taught by human wisdom but in the teaching of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual.”

“As,” etc. [Augustine.] As though he were saying: I say that if they had known, they would not have crucified him; but they did not know him, [Col. 1550C] as it is written in Isaiah, where this is written: “What bodily eye has not seen, because it is not a colour; nor ear heard, because it is not a sound; nor has entered into the human heart, because it is not human,” that is, carnal, but spirit—that is, spiritual—which knows it.

And the sense is: “Eye has not seen,” etc., that is, it cannot be known through bodily sight or hearing, nor by the reasoning of that human being who is not spirit. For it is not known by the reasoning of one who is carnal rather than spiritual. Or, it has not entered into the human heart because it is not something earthly.

[Ambrose.] For what enters into a human heart is below the human heart. It enters into the human heart because the heart into which it ascends is above it. For what ascends into the human heart comes from below to the human being; but that to which the human heart ascends is above the human being. Therefore what enters into the heart is below the human heart; but the eternal thing to which the heart ascends is above the heart. This is what God reserves for the good. Hence he adds: “Which God has prepared.”

Or, “it has not entered into the human heart,” that is, the heart of any carnal person. A thing is said to enter the heart when, being rightly understood, it gives pleasure.

“Which he has prepared.” As though he were saying: Eye has not seen nor ear heard those things which God has prepared as a reward for those who love him. This is God’s wisdom, that is, Christ, prepared as a reward for those who love God, whom none of the rulers knew.

“But to us,” etc. As though he were saying: They did not know, [Col. 1551A] but God has revealed to us who are spirits, not merely human beings—that is, spiritual, not carnal persons, which the pseudo-apostles are not—what he has prepared for those who love him. For we understand God to be prepared as a reward for the good. He revealed this, I say, through the Holy Spirit.

Note that Isaiah reads thus: “Eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, the things which you have prepared for those who love you” [Isaiah 64]. This is almost identical in sense with what the Apostle set down; and just as Isaiah says “apart from you,” so here the Apostle fittingly adds, “God revealed to us through his Spirit.”

And fittingly, through him. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God—that is, the very essence of God. Yet the Spirit of God is said to search all things not, of course, in order to discover what he does not know, but because he leaves absolutely nothing [Col. 1551B] unknown. [Augustine] Or he says that the Spirit of God searches all things because he makes you search them. For what you do by his gift, he himself is said to do, since without him you would not do it.

For who? As though he said: Truly the Spirit of God, and no other, knows all that belongs to God. This is proved from the lesser case. For what human being knows the things belonging to a particular person—that is, that person’s intentions and secrets—except the spirit, that is, the mind, of that person himself, and not another, which is within him? [Ambrose.]

For it is evident that our thoughts are known by no one except our own mind, which the Apostle calls “spirit.” So too, no one who is still merely a human being—that is, carnal—has known the things of God, namely God’s hidden and secret things, except the Spirit of God, that is, the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1551C] and those whom he causes to know them. Hence he adds: But we. As though he said: The Spirit of God knows them. But we have received him; we have certainly not received the spirit of this world, [Augustine] that is, the Pythian spirit, which is accustomed to divine by conjectures concerning worldly things, which spoke through the Sibyl, and which is often deceived by what seems plausible and deceives others. Or: we have not received the spirit of this world, that is, the spirit of self-exaltation, by which we might be taught the wisdom of the world; but we have received the Spirit who is from God. [Note: [Col. 1551D] Augustine, *Against Maximinus*.] Therefore the Spirit of God is the spirit of charity; the spirit of this world is the spirit of self-exaltation.

Do not be troubled that only the Holy Spirit is named here, and that he alone is said to know the things of God. For the Father [Col. 1551D] and the Son are not excluded from this knowledge; just as the Holy Spirit is not excluded when the Father and Christ are called the only and true God: “And this is eternal life: that they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent” (John 17). [Note: [Col. 1551D] Id., *On the Trinity*.] Notice also that he says, “We have received the Spirit of God.” The Spirit is certainly the Spirit of the Father and the Son, and also ours. For what is given is related both to the one who gave it and to those to whom he gave it. Thus the Holy Spirit is called not only the Spirit of the Father and the Son who gave him, but also ours who have received him. He is not that spirit of ours by which we exist—for it is the spirit of a human being that is within him—and yet we have received that spirit [Col. 1552A] which is called human. But one thing is what we received in order to exist; another, what we received in order to be holy. In Scripture, moreover, “the spirit of a human being” means the soul itself, or the rational power of that soul. For he gave us nature, that we might exist; a soul, that we might live; a mind, that we might understand.

That we may know. As though he said: We received the Spirit for this purpose, that through him we might know the things given to us by God. [Note: [Col. 1552D] Id., *On Holy Virginity*.] Therefore it is proved that we have received the Spirit of God because we know this, which it is certainly beneficial to know, since without this knowledge no one is blessed. For many possess God’s gifts and, not knowing from whom they have them, boast in impious vanity. But no one is blessed by God’s gifts who is ungrateful to the giver. Hence in the Gospel: “To the one who has, it will be given” (Luke 8). [Augustine] [Col. 1552B] For to have fully is to know from whom one has; but not to have is not to know from whom one has. Therefore whoever does not have—that is, does not know from whom he has what he has—will have it taken away from him.

Which things we also speak. As though he said: We know the things given to us by God, and we also speak them; those men, namely the pseudo-apostles, speak other things. [Jerome] I say that we speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, whether by argument or ornament. For he preferred to show these things in the sheer purity of truth rather than embellish them with the colouring of eloquence. But we speak in the teaching of the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit teaches the hearers inwardly; and we speak, I say, by fittingly comparing—that is, imparting—spiritual things to spiritual persons, which you Corinthians are not. Thus it is your fault, not ours, that we have not spoken greater things [Col. 1552C] to you.

### Verses 14–16

> But the natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are folly to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are examined spiritually. But the spiritual person judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one. As it is written: “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has instructed him?” But we have the mind of Christ.

But the natural person. As though he said: We know the things given to us, but the natural person, such as the pseudo-apostles are, does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, such as the Virgin’s childbirth and the resurrection. [Augustine] For he considers nothing capable of happening except what he knows how to happen. [Note: [Col. 1552D] Augustine, *On Eighty-Three Questions*.] A person is called “natural” [animalis], [Col. 1552D] either with respect to life or with respect to the disposition of the mind. A life is called natural when it is carried away by the unrestrained licentiousness of its own soul, which the ruling spirit does not restrain within the bounds of the natural order because that spirit does not submit itself to God’s governance. A person is called natural with respect to the disposition of the mind when he judges concerning God according to bodily images, the letter of the Law, or philosophical reasoning.

Why, then, does the natural person not receive the things of God? He adds: for they are folly to him according to human judgment, and therefore he cannot understand spiritual things. And truly the natural person cannot understand spiritual things, because the examination—that is, the testing and approval—of these spiritual things takes place only spiritually, that is, by a spiritual person. [Col. 1553A] The verb *examinatur* (“is examined”) is read impersonally.

Or thus: truly the natural person does not understand spiritual things, because the natural person is examined spiritually—that is, only through spiritual things it is proved that he is natural, because he rejects what he hears; nor are they set before him for any other reason than that he may be examined.

But the spiritual person. As though he said: The natural person cannot understand, but the spiritual person judges—that is, understands and discerns—all things: not, indeed, all things comprehended by divine knowledge, but all things that must be judged and are sufficient for righteousness and life. [Augustine] A person is spiritual either in life or in knowledge. He is spiritual in life who, having the Spirit of the Lord as ruler, governs his soul. He is spiritual in knowledge who, although he sees only in part and through a mirror, nevertheless does not think concerning God according to [Col. 1553B] bodily images, the letter of the Law, or human philosophy; but, subject to God and to the Spirit of God, he judges all things most certainly and faithfully, by a sure faith concerning hidden matters rather than by open knowledge.

And he himself is judged by no one, namely by no natural person—that is, no such person understands whether he judges rightly or wrongly. Or, “he is judged by no one” means “he is rebuked by no one.” This he proves when he says: For what natural person has known—that is, understood—the mind of the Lord, who has done these things, through whom the wisdom of the world is foolish, and whose mind we have? Therefore those people of yours cannot judge him as they customarily do. Or who has instructed him, so as to say: “Why have you done this in this manner?” As though he said: No one. But if they cannot know the mind of the Lord, neither can they know ours, because we, who are now beyond merely human beings, being one spirit with God, [Col. 1553C] have the mind of Christ, holding with sure faith the things that belong to Christ.

## Chapter III

### Verses 1–8

> And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as carnal persons; as infants in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food. For you were not yet able; indeed, even now you are not able. For you are still carnal. For while there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal and walking according to man? For when one says, “I am of Paul,” and another, “I am of Apollos,” are you not human beings? What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? Ministers through whom you believed, each as the Lord gave. I planted; [Col. 1553D] Apollos watered; but God has now given the growth. Therefore neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth. Now the one who plants and the one who waters are one.

And I, brothers. As though he said: I say that we have the mind of Christ, and yet, brothers, I—though I could have done so—could not, that is, ought not, speak to you as to spiritual persons, that is, as I am accustomed to speak to spiritual persons, but as to carnal persons. I did this with such care because I gave you milk to drink, that is, teaching that is easy, pleasant, and nourishing, as to infants in Christ, that is, in the knowledge of Christ. I did not give you solid food, that is, I did not preach higher matters to you. [Col. 1554A] Why? Because you were not yet able to receive it. Thus it is shown that the Apostle preached lesser matters, not higher ones, to them as incapable persons.

Or thus: “I could not speak to you as spiritual persons,” etc. [Augustine] The question arises whether spiritual persons possess something in teaching which they keep silent from carnal persons and tell to spiritual persons. This certainly seems to follow from these words of the Apostle. The Lord also says: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16). We expounded the Apostle’s words above in accordance with that interpretation; but there is another understanding here which must not be neglected. [Note: [Col. 1553D] Augustine, *Homilies on John*.]

For your charity ought to know that there seems to be no necessity for any secret teachings to be withheld from little believers and stated separately to those more advanced, that is, more intelligent. The Apostle preached the same things to spiritual and carnal persons, and each received them according to his capacity: the former as infants, as nourishment of milk; the latter as those more advanced, as strengthening solid food. For even if the latter heard no more, they nevertheless understood more. What is received alike by both in faith is not received equally by the mind. Therefore the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as carnal persons”; that is, you could not receive what I was saying as spiritual persons, but as carnal persons. [Note: [Col. 1554D] Id., *Homilies on John*.] “And as infants in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not solid food”: that is, what I preached to you was to you like a draught of milk, not solid food.

For just as the cross of Christ is foolishness to some and a stumbling block to others, but to those called saints it is the power and wisdom of God, so the same thing is milk to some and food to others, according as their capacity receives more or less. Thus those who say, “I belong to this man or that man,” understood the Crucified One differently from him who said, “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6). Spiritual and carnal persons hear the same things together, and each receives them according to his own capacity. It is not necessary for secret teachings to be withheld from infants and spoken to the perfect. Therefore the Apostle says, “I could not speak to you as spiritual persons,” etc.; which means: You could not understand what I was saying as spiritual persons, but as carnal persons. For if they were spiritual, they would not say: “I am of Paul.”

For not yet. As though he said: I rightly said, “as infants,” because while I was with you, you were not yet able to receive solid food as spiritual persons; indeed, [Col. 1554D] even now you are not able to receive solid food, although you have been taught by them, namely by the pseudo-apostles. For you are still carnal. [Ambrose] Here he sharply reproves those who complained that they had not long ago heard spiritual teaching, though they were still unworthy to hear it. Carnal persons are the same as natural persons: they are called carnal from flesh, natural from soul.

For while there is. As though he said: Truly you are carnal. For while there is jealousy among you—that is, envy concerning those who baptize—and contention in words, are you not carnal, because you suppose that something comes from a human being? And are you not walking according to man, that is, progressing for the worse? Certainly. For when one says. Here is the explanation [Col. 1555A] of jealousy and contention. As though he said: Are you not walking according to man when one says, “I am of Paul,” and another, “I am of Apollos”? This sin is no less than paganism. Are you not human beings—that is, carnal persons—whereas those who hope in God are gods?

And since you glory in these men, what then is Apollos? What indeed is Paul, who is greater? Are they the authors of the grace given in the sacraments? Certainly not; they are only ministers of God through whom you believed. As though he said: They are not God, who gives; they are ministers through whom he gives. Nor does he give more in baptism through better persons than through less good ones. Therefore glory must be in God, not in them.

I say that they are ministers, and they do not do this in one and the same way, but as the Lord gave to each—that is, as he allotted offices to individuals. For I, Paul, planted, that is, by preaching I converted people to faith; Apollos watered by baptism; but God, not we, has given the growth of the gift. And because God alone gives growth from himself, therefore neither the one who plants is anything in giving from himself, nor the one who waters, but God alone, who gives inward growth.

Now the one who plants and the one who waters. As though he said: Paul plants and Apollos waters; but the one who plants and the one who waters are one, that is, they are without difference. For they work only outwardly. Unless he who is within reveals it, what benefit is there in what they do? Indeed, the labourer would work all things outwardly in vain unless the Creator worked secretly within. Therefore he says, “They are one”: alike in kind of nature and in the character of their ministry. [Augustine] He says this because [Col. 1555C] it might seem that, although they give nothing from themselves, God nevertheless gives more through one than through another.

### Verses 8–13

> But each will receive his own reward according to his own labour. For we are God’s fellow-workers. You are God’s field, God’s building. According to the grace of God given to me, as a wise architect I laid a foundation; but another builds upon it. Let each take heed how he builds upon it. For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each person’s work will become manifest.

[Col. 1555D] But each. As though he said: They do not differ in giving, but in labour and reward; and this is what he says: Each will receive his own reward according to his own labour in ministering outwardly. I rightly said “reward,” for we are God’s fellow-workers in cultivating the Lord’s field, not its corrupters, as some say. And so, although we do not give growth, we nevertheless render some assistance. This is evident from the fact that you are God’s field while vices are uprooted. And you are God’s building through the imposition of virtues. [Note: [Col. 1555D] Augustine, in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*.]

It is shown most plainly by these words that God is the farmer and we are God’s field, because he cultivates us for fruit; and that we are God’s building, [Col. 1556A] because he who cultivates us dwells in us. Thus the field and the building are the same thing, which is not so in visible things. The Apostles too may be called farmers, for the farmer is the one who plants and waters. Yet, because they do not have even this from themselves, but only as God has allotted to each, he is more properly called the farmer. The Apostles are servants of that farmer, supplied with strength and grace by him.

For a human farmer cultivates a vineyard and provides the other things belonging to a farmer’s care; but he cannot give growth through the sacraments, nor can he form the fruits. But God, who can do all things, is properly the farmer. Notice that we cultivate God and God cultivates us; yet we do not cultivate God so that he becomes better thereby. We cultivate him by worshipping him, not by praying to him; but he [Col. 1556B] cultivates us in such a way as to make us better according to grace.

As though he said: You are God’s field and building, to whom I laid by preaching a foundation, that is, faith in Christ—not another faith, but that which works through love. I laid it, I say, as an architect, that is, the chief builder, wise, that is, using discernment; and I did so according to the grace given to me, that is, through the apostleship freely given to me. As though he said: I did not have this from myself.

I laid the foundation; but another builds good works upon this foundation. This certainly is not done in one manner only, but each must take heed how—that is, with what sort of works—he builds upon it. We need only consider the superstructure. [Note: [Col. 1555D] Id., *On Faith and Works*.] For no one can lay another foundation, as the pseudo-apostles appear to attempt, besides that which has been laid [Col. 1556C] by me, namely Christ Jesus—that is, faith in Christ, specifically that which works through love, through which Christ dwells in hearts. No other faith is a foundation. This faith, moreover, permits no one to perish. For faith in Christian grace—that is, the faith which works through love—laid in the foundation permits no one to perish.

But if anyone. As though he said: No one can alter the foundation, but the superstructure must be considered, because each person’s work will become manifest. This is what he says: [Note: [Col. 1556D] Id., *On Faith and Works*.] “But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each person’s work will become manifest.” Some think this is to be understood so that those seem to build gold, silver, and precious stones upon this foundation who add good works to the faith that is in Christ Jesus; while those who, although they possess the same faith, act wickedly, build wood, hay, and straw. Hence they suppose that, by the merit of the foundation, such persons can be cleansed by certain punishments of fire in order to receive salvation. [Augustine]

If this is so, then those statements which have no obscurity or ambiguity will be false: “If I have all faith, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13); and this too will be false: “Neither fornicators nor the greedy,” etc., “will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6). Finally, how can this be true: “Faith without works is dead”? [Col. 1557A] (James 2). Therefore what the Apostle says here must be understood otherwise.

If I try to discuss this too subtly, I fear that the explanation itself may be more difficult to understand. Nevertheless, so far as the Lord helps, I shall endeavour to set forth briefly and clearly, as far as I can, what I think. One person builds gold, silver, and precious stones upon the foundation of Christian faith: namely, the person who thinks of the things of God, how he may please God. Another builds wood, hay, and straw upon this foundation: namely, the person who thinks of the things of the world, how he may please the world.

For these three must not be understood as evil works, as though faith without works could save, which it cannot. Rather, wood, hay, and straw may reasonably be understood as desires for worldly things—even those lawfully permitted—of such a kind [Col. 1557B] that they cannot be lost without pain of mind. Therefore those who still love worldly things, are entangled in earthly business, and devote themselves to certain bonds and affections of the flesh—to their homes, spouses, and possessions—yet are Christians in such a way that their hearts do not withdraw from Christ and they prefer nothing to Christ, build wood, hay, and straw.

To speak more plainly: a person who clings to his wealth with a certain carnal affection, yet gives many alms from it, neither schemes fraud or any robbery in order to increase it nor, from fear that it may be diminished or lost, falls into any crime—such a person builds wood, hay, and straw. But those who live well, honour and praise God, are patient in tribulations, and desire their homeland, build gold, [Col. 1557C] silver, and precious stones. For these three are built by those who despise the world, who give all they have to the poor, or who possess as though not possessing.

Nor is it without purpose that he specified three and three. For they build gold in contemplation of God, silver in love of neighbour, and precious stones in good works, which are not consumed by fire but feel nothing, or little. They build wood, hay, and straw who, although they do not seize what belongs to another, nevertheless cling with some delight to things granted to human weakness. According to the degree in which they love these things, they will endure the fire longer as wood, less as hay, or least as straw. Because they do not prefer these things to God, they will be saved through the foundation. But those who prefer them to God [Col. 1557D] or commit crimes do not build upon the foundation but destroy it.

And the sense is this: If anyone builds upon this foundation—that is, upon faith in Christ—gold, by contemplating God; silver, by loving the neighbour; precious stones, by doing good works, that is, if they are such persons as think only of the things of God; and if anyone builds wood, hay, and straw, that is, if they use these temporal things granted to human weakness with some love, thinking in a divided way about worldly things which they cannot lack without pain—then each person’s work will at last become manifest, even if it is not so now. And truly:

[Col. 1558A] ### Verses 13–15

> For the day of the Lord will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire; and the fire will test what sort of work each person has done. If anyone’s work which he has built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire.

For the day of the Lord, that is, the day of judgment, in which hidden things will be disclosed, will declare each person’s work. This is the day of a human being acting according to his own inclination; but at judgment, or at death, each person has the day of the Lord, who judges according to merits. And it will truly declare it, because it will be revealed in fire—that is, in a person’s purgatorial punishment—though anyone now deny it; and the fire of the future judgment will test what each person’s work has been, that is, whether it is firm or perishable.

For we read that two fires will come: one eternal, by which the reprobate will be punished eternally, and which follows the judgment; the other precedes it, by which the face of this world will be burned up, and which will cleanse those who have built wood, hay, and straw. [Note: [Col. 1557D] Augustine, on Psalm 123.] Those who have built gold, silver, and precious stones are secure from both fires: not only from that eternal fire which will torment the ungodly for eternity, but also from that corrective fire by which certain persons destined for salvation will be purified. For the fire of the final judgment will last until those who were to be saved have been purified.

And if anyone’s work that he built upon it remains unconsumed in that fire, he will receive a reward, because he will lose nothing and will find what he loved. [Augustine] But if anyone’s work is burned up—that is, if it is combustible—he will suffer the loss of a lesser glory. [Note: [Col. 1557D] Id., *The City of God*.] Or, [Col. 1558C] he will suffer some punishment; but he himself will be saved because of the foundation, Christ, to whom he preferred nothing.

Yet he will be saved as one carrying a combustible thing through the fire of passing tribulation: by this fire he escapes after what is combustible has been burned. And after the death of this bodily life, until the day of condemnation and reward arrives, if during this interval the spirits of the dead who built wood, hay, and straw are said to suffer a fire of this kind—which others do not feel, because they did not carry such buildings with them—so that they encounter the fire of passing tribulation which burns up venial sins: I do not refute this, because perhaps it is true. But because it is said, “he will be saved,” that fire is treated lightly. Yet that fire will be more grievous than anything a human being can suffer in this life. [Note: [Col. 1558D] Id., on Psalm 122.]

Or the day of the Lord [Col. 1558D] may be understood as the present day, and the fire as present fire. For this too is the day of the Lord, while judgment begins with the house of God (1 Pet. 4), that is, punishment begins with those who will be saved and will be consummated in the reprobate. For the elect are punished here so that they may not be punished there. On this day there is also the fire of tribulation, by which love for temporal things is burned while people grieve over their loss. Hence it is said: “Such persons will have tribulation of the flesh” (1 Cor. 7). [Augustine] For what they do not possess without an enticing love, they do not lose without a burning pain.

As though he said: It will become manifest, for the day of the Lord, namely the day of present tribulation, [Col. 1559A] will declare it; and truly it will be declared by the fire of tribulation. For he calls the same tribulation fire, and the fire of present judgment will test what sort each person’s work is, namely whether it is firm or perishable. By this fire the work of one who did not love the things whose loss would torment him is not burned up; nothing that flows away in time was born for him. But the work of the person who loved these temporal things is burned up, since things possessed with love do not perish without pain.

If anyone’s work remains in the fire, this means the work of those whom the loss of temporal things does not torment. The one who builds upon it will receive a reward, not only after the end, when he receives the object of his thought, but also in this life, where the soul of one who despises all things has its rest. [Note: [Col. 1559D] Augustine, *On Faith and Works*.] If anyone’s work is burned up, that is, is combustible, he will suffer [Col. 1559B] loss, because he will lose what he loved and, on account of what he loved, will be punished here or in the future. But because, if either condition were proposed to him, he would rather lack such things than lack Christ, and does not abandon Christ from fear of losing them, he himself will indeed be saved, though he grieves when he loses them. Yet this will be as through fire, because, although he is burned by grief for things lost, he does not prefer them to God. Thus, although grief for what is lost burns him, it does not overthrow or consume him, being fortified by the stability and incorruptibility of the foundation. [Augustine] Therefore he will be saved, but as through fire. This fire is the trial of tribulation, concerning which it is written: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. 27).

Here one usually asks how the work of the person who builds wood, hay, and straw can be said to be burned up, [Col. 1559C] if, as stated, these are not understood as evil works. For a work is not burned, nor does it suffer loss, unless it is evil. Therefore either the works denoted by those three do not burn, or they are evil.

Some answer that by those three are not meant evil works, but good works which some persons do for the support of themselves and their own households, or for the support of the needy out of mercy. But because they perform these works with some love for temporal things, these works are said to burn—not because they are punished for doing them, but because they have some earthly affection while doing them. Nor is that earthly affection so evil as to destroy the foundation, that is, faith which works through charity. [Col. 1559D] Thus some possess both charity and such an affection. Such an affection is venial.

Or rather, wood, hay, and straw are understood not as good works nor as evil works deserving condemnation, but as venial sins. Hence Gregory [Note: [Col. 1559D] Gregory, in the *Dialogues*]: Although this may be understood concerning the fire of present tribulation, yet if anyone understands it concerning the fire of future purification, he must consider carefully that the Apostle said that a person can be saved through fire, not one who builds iron, bronze, or lead upon this foundation—that is, greater and therefore harder sins, then incapable of dissolution—but one who builds wood, hay, and straw, that is, the smallest and lightest sins, which fire easily consumes. Yet even concerning these [Col. 1560A] smallest sins, no one will obtain purification there unless, while still in this life, he has deserved it.

[Note: [Col. 1560D] Augustine, on Psalm 70.] Augustine says concerning this: Let no one who has wicked works promise himself the kingdom of God and say: “Because I have the sign of Christ and the sacraments, I shall not be blotted out forever, but I shall be saved through fire.” For the Apostle says: “A foundation has been laid,” etc. They also ask: “What does the following mean: ‘One builds gold, silver, precious stones; another, wood, hay, straw’?” This means that one who builds righteous works upon the foundation builds gold, silver, and precious stones; but if he builds sins, wood, hay, and straw.

Grillius likewise says: [Note: [Col. 1560D] Grillius on Leviticus.] “The nature of sin is like material which is quickly consumed by fire,” which the Apostle says is built by sinners [Col. 1560B] upon the foundation of Christ: wood, hay, and straw. This plainly shows that certain sins are so light that they are compared to straw, hay, and wood.

It should also be known that, just as the foundation of a bodily building is at the bottom, so the foundation of a spiritual building is at the top. Therefore, just as the weight of walls tends downward, where its foundation is, so spiritual building tends upward, where its foundation is. For there are two kinds of weights: some seek lower places, such as a stone placed upon water, and water placed upon oil; others seek higher places, such as fire and oil. For fire always seeks what is above. Oil, too, when poured beneath water, does not allow itself to remain there. So the Church, now placed below, tends toward heaven, where its foundation is [Col. 1560C] Christ, seated at the right hand of the Father.

Or it can be understood differently from the words: “As a wise architect I laid a foundation.” A wise architect is one who lays the foundation according to the instruction of the author, that is, one who evangelizes according to the tradition of the Saviour. But another builds upon it, namely those who come after the Apostles and teach, whether they are good or evil. [Augustine] But they must take care that the building corresponds to the foundation. Hence he adds: “Let each take heed how he builds upon it”: whether according to us, who are the true Apostles of Christ, or according to others, lest their crooked and frivolous superstructure cause a collapse, while the foundation nevertheless remains unharmed, because even if someone teaches wrongly, [Col. 1560D] the name of Christ remains.

Therefore the superstructure must be considered. For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, Jesus. [Ambrose] Because no one except Christ would commend his own inventions while speaking, even if some are heretics, they nevertheless teach only under Christ’s name, so that the dignity of the name may make contrary and absurd things acceptable.

“But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each person’s work will become manifest.” By gold, silver, and precious stones he signifies excellent teaching. By the other three, frivolous and vain teaching is signified, which, though it now deceives, [Col. 1561A] will nevertheless appear in the fire, because it will be burned up while good teaching remains. And it will indeed become manifest, for the day of the Lord will declare it because it is revealed in fire: that is, evil teaching will become visible to all in the fire, though it now deceives some. And the fire will test what sort each person’s work has been, because if it finds nothing in a person to burn up, it shows that person to have been a good teacher; but evil teaching is food for fire.

If anyone’s work which he built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. For when no defilement of corrupt teaching is found in him, just as fire does not consume gold, silver, and precious stones, so the good teacher will remain incorruptible, and eternal life will be his reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss. The work said to burn is evil teaching, which will perish; to suffer loss [Col. 1561B] is to undergo punishment. For who, when placed in punishment, does not feel loss? But he himself will be saved, because the substance of which he consists will not perish—that is, the good teaching in which he is grounded—just as evil teaching, which is an accident, will perish. He will be saved, I say, but as through fire, because he will not be saved without punishment. By this he shows that the person will be saved yet will endure penalties of fire, so that, purified through fire, he may be saved; and while the faithless perish eternally, it benefits such persons that they have believed in Christ in some measure.

### Verses 16–20

> Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? But if anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and that temple you are. Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish in order that he may become wise. [Col. 1561C] For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written: “I will catch the wise in their craftiness”; and again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain.”

“Do you not know that you are God’s temple,” etc. The sense is as follows: He will be saved through fire who does not depart from the foundation; but if anyone—whether a false apostle by teaching wrongly, or a person by agreeing with him—violates God’s temple, which you are, either in himself or in others, seeking to overthrow the foundation and divide the Catholic fellowship, God will destroy him in body and soul, as a sacrilegious person. [Augustine] And rightly so: for God’s temple is holy from the time of baptism, because God dwells in no one whom the Holy Spirit has not first sanctified and cleansed, as God’s temple—which you are, both in soul and in body. Therefore take heed for yourselves, because you are the temple: that is, persons in whom God sits and dwells. I call it God’s temple, that is, the temple of the Holy Spirit. Hence he adds: “And the Spirit of God,” that is, the Holy Spirit, “dwells in you,” he who perfects you in good things—and do you not know this? [Augustine] Note that the Holy Spirit is here called God. [Ambrose] For after saying, “You are God’s temple,” he does not add, “and God dwells [in you],” [Note: [Col. 1561D] Augustine, Against Maximinus.] but “the Spirit of God dwells in you,” by which he plainly shows that the Spirit of God is God.

The Holy Spirit is everywhere present, for the regeneration of human beings unto eternal life; [Col. 1562A] and is he not God to them? Indeed, he is the true God, because the true members of God are his temple, and surely the temple is subject to him whose temple it is. How, then, is he not king whose temple consists of the king’s members? How also does he not sit with the Father and the Son, he who filled the Son, and who possesses as his own house the members of the Son? Then, since he proceeds from the Father, how does he not sit with the Father? For that sitting is certainly not to be conceived carnally, especially since the Apostle says even of his members: “He raised us up and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Eph. 2). How then can anyone, whoever he may be, who confesses this, withhold from the Holy Spirit the confession that he sits with the Father and the Son—as though he were unworthy to sit with the Father and the Son, when he makes us worthy of that same seat? Therefore the Holy Spirit sits in heaven [Col. 1562B] with the Father and the Son, and dwells in his temple, namely in the saints, who are God’s temple: now walking by faith, and someday to be God’s temple also by sight, just as God’s angels are even now his temple.

[Augustine] But someone says: “Before God made heaven and earth, before he made the saints, where did he dwell?” God dwells in himself, with you, and is with himself. The saints, then, are not God’s house in such a way that, if that house were removed, God would fall. Rather, God so dwells in the saints that, if he himself departs, they fall. [Note: [Col. 1562D] Id., To Dardanus.] Moreover, it must be understood that it can be said only most foolishly that the Holy Spirit has no place in our body, which our soul wholly fills; still more foolishly is it said that the Trinity is hindered somewhere by narrowness of space, [Col. 1562C] so that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit cannot be together somewhere. But this is far more wonderful: although God is wholly everywhere, he nevertheless does not dwell in all persons.

[Augustine] Who, indeed, would dare suppose—unless he entirely ignores the inseparability of the Trinity—that the Father or the Son could dwell in someone in whom the Holy Spirit does not dwell? Or that the Holy Spirit could dwell in someone in whom the Father or the Son is absent? We must therefore observe that God is everywhere through the presence of his divinity, but not everywhere through the grace of indwelling. On account of this indwelling, where the grace of his love is acknowledged, we do not say, “Our Father who art everywhere,” though this too is true, but, “who art in heaven” (Matt. 6).

This also is wonderful: God is the indweller of some persons who do not yet know God, and is not the indweller of some persons who do know God. For those who know God but do not glorify him as God do not belong to God’s temple; while little children, sanctified by Christ’s sacrament and regenerated by the Holy Spirit, belong to God’s temple, though they are not yet able to know God. Thus those former persons were able to know him and yet not possess him; these latter were able to possess him before knowing him. But most blessed are those for whom to possess God is to know him. Therefore, speaking to Christians and believers, he says, “You are God’s temple,” etc.

[Ambrose] He said this beforehand in order to pierce those who, living shamefully, violate [Col. 1563A] their own bodies—especially the man who has his father’s wife—and, as one violating God’s temple, will be destroyed. Therefore let no one deceive himself or us, as though God disregarded this. Rather, if anyone among you seems wise in this age—that is, according to the wisdom of this age—let him become foolish in his own estimation, and believe that God can act contrary to nature, so that he may truly be wise; for one who is foolish to the world is wise to God. And he is rightly foolish in his own estimation, because this is how he is before God. For “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God”: that is, God judges that wisdom to be foolish, he who does what the world denies can be done.

Note that in Scripture “wisdom” is sometimes used for craftiness, by an improper use of the word rather than in its proper sense. That the wisdom of the world becomes foolishness he confirms by authority. For it is written [Col. 1563B] in Job: “I will catch,” that is, I will expose as false, “the wise men of the world in their craftiness,” by doing otherwise than they say. And again, it is written in the Psalm: “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise men of the world,” or of human beings, namely carnal persons, “that they are vain,” that is, false; and because the wisdom of the world is foolishness with God.

### VERSES 21–23

“Therefore let no one boast in human beings. For all things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come. For all things are yours; but you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.”

Therefore let no one boast in human beings—whether baptizers or teachers—as though he received better things from one than from another, [Col. 1563C] since they are not givers of graces, whether they are good or bad, but nevertheless ministers. “For all things are yours.” It is as though he said: You ought not to boast in human beings, because they are yours; and truly so, because all things are yours—that is, given to serve you. One ought not boast except in things more excellent.

He explains of what things he has said, “All things are yours,” by adding: “Whether Paul, or Apollos,” who are among the greater ones, “or Cephas,” who is greater than all—so that not only lesser persons are yours, but even the greater. He says this so that they may not each claim particular teachers for themselves when they make use of all of them.

[Ambrose] He then continues concerning the other things which are theirs: “Whether the world is ours, or the present life, or death.” The world, therefore, is ours if we think about it according to God’s will [Col. 1563D] and direct its course according to God’s will. The present life is ours if it is conducted moderately and for God’s glory. Death is ours if, in hope of what is to come, we willingly die for Christ. “Whether things present are ours,” by which, being sustained, they serve God; “or things to come,” in hope of which they serve. Things present are ours if we use them for sustenance in such a way as not to give offence. Things to come are ours if, believing them, we desire them more.

Or thus: “Whether the world is ours.” He says this because even the elements of the world serve us; whether the life of teachers or their death is ours. For both the life and death of teachers ought to contribute to the edification of those subject to them. Or understand by “life” holy people, teachers, and angels, [Col. 1564A] who strive for believers’ advancement; by “death,” understand the devil and his members, who, while persecuting, serve the benefit of God’s servants. The rest does not change.

“For all things,” or “but.” It is as though he said: These things are ours because all things whatever there are in the world are yours. But you are Christ’s, not a human being’s. Therefore you are not to boast in a human being, but in Christ, whose we are by creation and re-creation. The Apostle says this so that, just as these things are granted and made subject to our judgment, we may subject ourselves to Christ. But Christ is the proper Son of God the Father, doing his will, so that we too may do his will. And if we are Christ’s servants, why, then, do you expect anything from human beings to Christ’s dishonour?

[Augustine] Care must be taken [Col. 1564B] that “Christ is God’s” is not understood in the same way as “all things are yours” and “you are Christ’s.” For all things are subject to them, and they are subject to Christ, as things unlike one another and different in nature. But Christ is subject to God the Father, not as though unlike him or of another nature, but as the Father’s Son. [Note: [Col. 1563D] Augustine, in the book *Eighty-Three Questions*.] [Note: [Col. 1563D] Id., *On the Creed*.]

It should also be understood that, in this enumeration of connected things—“all things are yours; you are Christ’s; Christ is God’s”—there is no mention of the Holy Spirit, just as there is none in: “The head of the woman is the man; the head of the man is Christ; the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11). This is surely because, in things connected with one another, the connection itself is almost never counted. But the connection of the Father and the Son is the Holy Spirit, who is the divinity of the Father and the Son; and divinity itself is love, according to the saying: “God is love” [Col. 1564C] (1 John 4). Thus, with the Holy Spirit’s name unspoken, he says: “You are Christ’s; Christ is God’s”; and so, through Christ as mediator, you are God’s.

## CHAPTER IV

### VERSES 1–5

“Let a person so regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of God’s ministries. Here, moreover, it is required among stewards that someone be found faithful. But to me it is a very small matter to be judged by you, or by a human day. Yet I do not even judge myself; for I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified. But the one who judges me is the Lord. Therefore do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts; and then praise will come to each person from God.”

“Let a person so regard us.” Up to this point he has dealt with false glory; from here he deals with contempt for himself.

[Ambrose] It is as though he said: Since this is so—namely, that God is the author while we are assistants—do not think either too highly or too lowly of us. Rather, let any person so regard us, not as masters but as ministers of Christ, which the false apostles are not. The Apostle says this because they thought too little of him; but let a person think as God thinks, who chose him, and so regard us [Note: [Col. 1564D] Augustine, To Audax.] as stewards of God’s ministries, or mysteries, because we distribute the mysteries or ministries according to each person’s capacity.

And it must be understood [Col. 1565A] that not only good persons but bad persons too are stewards. For if stewardship came to us only through good persons, the Apostle would not rightly say, “Be imitators of me” (1 Cor. 4). Again, if it did not come through bad persons, the Lord would not say of some people: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23). Stewards are those through whose ministry eternal salvation is attained. For to be a steward of that salvation by word and sacrament is not the same as to be a participant in it.

“Here, moreover, it is required,” etc. It is as though he said: We ought to be regarded as I have said; but here—that is, among us and not elsewhere—now, namely in the present time, when we ought to wait until God judges, it is required which of the stewards may be found faithful, namely one to whom it may be entrusted [Col. 1565B] that he will dispense well.

“But to me,” as though he said: This is required among you, though it ought not be required; but whatever others may do, it is a very small matter to me if I am judged by you as an unfaithful steward, or by a human day—that is, human understanding, which does not see hidden things and can be deceived. Or, “by a human day,” that is, by human beings while they are in their own day and it is not the Lord’s day. He calls it human because there is a day of the Lord on which he will judge.

[Augustine] When each person will render an account for himself, then the secrets of hearts will be laid open. “Yet I do not even judge myself.” It is as though he said: It is a very small matter to me if I am judged by you or others. But neither do I, who know myself better than you do, judge myself; and therefore it is dangerous for you to judge the unknown things of my heart or another’s. For we must believe there is such a depth in a human being, hidden even from the person in whom it is, as in Peter: the depth of weakness was hidden from him when he rashly promised that he would die with the Lord. [Note: [Col. 1565D] Augustine, Book VIII, Question 83.]

Since, therefore, each person can either not at all, or scarcely, render a true judgment about himself, how can he judge another, when no one knows what happens in a human being except the human spirit? Therefore the Apostle, not presuming to give a definite judgment about himself, says: “Neither do I judge myself,” though I know myself better than they do; but God knows me better than I know myself, and therefore judgment must be left to him.

“For I am conscious of nothing against myself.” [Augustine] That is, my conscience does not reproach me in anything; “but I am not thereby justified,” that is, I do not therefore consider myself righteous, because there may be something I do not know. “For who understands transgressions?” (Ps. 18). And who boasts that he has a clean heart? The Apostle humbles himself in saying this, speaking as a human being who may unknowingly have guilt.

“But the one who judges me.” [Ambrose] It is as though he said: Neither I nor you ought to judge me; rather, “the one who judges me is the Lord”: that is, the one who can and ought to judge me is the Lord alone, who knows all things. And because the Lord is the one who can judge, “therefore do not judge before the time of judgment,” namely, until the Lord comes to judge. Otherwise an injury is done to the judge, because it is an injury to a judge if a servant issues a sentence before his judgment.

Behold, the Apostle forbids judgment because human hearts are hidden from us. [Col. 1566A] In these matters our credulity is very often deceived. [Note: [Col. 1565D] Id., On Job.] But we must take care not to be deceived by a destructive opinion: because we cannot investigate people’s consciences, we should nevertheless have a true and certain judgment about the things themselves, in this way: if we do not know whether this or that person is unchaste or chaste, righteous or unrighteous, [Note: [Col. 1566D] Id., in the same work.] let us nevertheless hate unchastity and injustice, and love chastity and justice. Let us perceive in God’s truth that the latter are to be sought and the former avoided, so that, when we seek what ought to be sought and avoid what ought to be avoided in the things themselves, we may be forgiven for sometimes—indeed, continually—not thinking truly about human beings. For such errors belong to the human trial without which this life is not lived. Hence the Apostle says: “Let no temptation overtake you except what is human” [Col. 1566B] (1 Cor. 10).

Therefore, if we cannot avoid suspicions because we are human, we must nevertheless restrain judgments—that is, definite and firm verdicts. If, then, we suspect, which is a human temptation, at least let us not judge. Thus, when there is no error about the things themselves, so that rejection of vices and approval of virtues are right, then, if there is error about human beings, it is a pardonable human temptation.

But the Apostle forbids what is destructive when he says: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light”—that is, make manifest—“the hidden things of darkness,” that is, sins, “and reveal the counsels of hearts,” that is, good thoughts.

[Ambrose] For deeds and thoughts, good or bad, will then be open. [Col. 1566C] And because then all things will be known to all, they will be able to judge themselves and others. And then each person who acts or thinks well will receive praise—that is, recompense—from God according to his measure. But here it is unknown who is worthy of praise.

Now, because above he had said that they had declared, “I am Paul’s; I am Apollos’s,” although perhaps no one had actually said this, he explains it here. It is as though he said: I said that one ought not boast in us.

### VERSES 6–9

“But these things, brothers, I have transferred in figure to myself and Apollos for your sake, so that in us you may learn not to be puffed up, one against another, beyond what is written, on behalf of one against another. For who distinguishes you? And what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it? Already you are filled; already you have become rich. You reign without us—and would that you did reign, so that we too might reign with you. For I think that God has displayed us apostles as the last, as persons appointed to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, and to angels, and to human beings.”

“But these things, brothers, I have transferred in figure to myself and Apollos,” when you did not boast in us: that is, I have set myself and Apollos forth as a figure for all, so that all may abhor this conduct, as we do.

[Ambrose] He therefore transferred these things in figure to himself and Apollos when, under his own name and Apollos’s, he refuted the glory of false apostles and perverse traditions, designating them generally rather than individually, lest greater discord arise. For no one who hears his own name, or that of the person he favours, censured is content to keep silent; but when the name is unstated, someone who hears something said about himself conceals it. And I did this “for your sake,” that is, for your benefit: namely, so that in us, who are greater, you may learn not to be puffed up, one against another, on behalf of one against another—by him, that is, one better than the other; that is, as though one person were different from another, namely better, though he is nothing in himself or in his ministry.

Or: let one be puffed up for one teacher against other ministers, that is, for a better teacher than the others. I say, “be puffed up beyond,” that is, beyond and otherwise than what is written in Jeremiah: “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” (Jer. 9; 2 Cor. 10). This is the one in whom you ought to boast, not a human being.

[Note: [Col. 1567D] Augustine, *On Rebuke and Grace*.] “For who distinguishes you from the mass of the lost?” No one but God alone: he separates you from those who perish. But because an inflated person might answer, either aloud or in thought, and say, “My faith distinguishes me, and my prayer, and my righteousness,” the Apostle anticipates him by adding: “And what?” It is as though he said: I ask, “Who distinguishes you?” But you say, “Your faith, prayer, or righteousness.” Again I ask: What good do you have that you have not received from God?

[Augustine] It must be understood that no one can be distinguished from that mass of perdition unless he has this good: to believe that whatever good he has, he received from the Saviour’s grace. It must also be understood that, just as above he forbade rash judgment, so here he seeks to warn against another kind of arrogance: lest a person become proud because of some grace given him by God, thinking that he has it from himself or from a minister. Rebuking this, the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive?” [Col. 1567C] “But if you received it from God, why do you boast in yourself or in them as though you had not received it from God, but from yourself or from them?”

Or thus: “Let not one be puffed up against another for one baptizer,” that is, one better than another. You ought not do so. For what baptizer, however good he may be, distinguishes you from one baptized by a less good person? It is as though he said: If you were baptized by Peter, how are you distinguished from one baptized by Paul? Certainly the latter has nothing from his baptizer, and neither do you.

Here he rebukes those same persons who boasted of the teaching of false apostles, despising the Apostle’s teaching.

[Ambrose] It is as though he said: You boast on their behalf. But what do you have from them that you have not received from me? He seems to speak to one person, but he speaks to a portion of the people. [Col. 1567D] “But if you received it from me, why do you boast against me, as though you had not received that very same thing from me?”

He says this against those who, having received the same things from the Apostle, boasted when they heard the teaching of false apostles. These commended themselves by eloquence and turned glory toward themselves, whereas the Apostle made himself appear contemptible in order to give glory to God. Therefore the Apostle speaks to them ironically, as though granting what they thought of themselves, when he adds: “Already you are filled.” It is as though he said: I rebuke you, asking, “Why do you boast?” etc.; but I do not seem right to do this, because you are already—that is, so quickly—filled, that is, full of the Holy Spirit. “And already you have become rich.” [Col. 1568A] It is as though he said: You can even fill others. This is irony, as though he said: It is not so. These are words of anger, not confirmation. “And you reign,” that is, you govern yourselves, “without us.”

[Ambrose] Thus those who boasted of false apostles supposed. “And would that you truly did reign!” To reign truly is to be secure concerning God’s hope and promises and to rejoice in adversity. Note that, as a loving father, he wishes good even to these ungrateful children. I say, “would that you did reign,” so that we too might reign with you. I do not say, “you with us,” since you disdain to follow us; but “we with you,” so that we may follow you if you do not wish to follow us—whom indeed you ought to follow, because we truly reign. But I fear that this will be without you.

“For I think.” It is as though he said: You think you reign without us, and this because I think—as though he said, something that should by no means be thought. [Col. 1568B] For he speaks ironically: through the evils that we suffer, God has displayed us apostles as the last, that is, the most contemptible, people for whom he cares nothing, as persons appointed to death—that is, as if reserved for death and of no use. This appears from the fact that we have become a spectacle to the world. For human beings gather to behold us, as though we were a monster; by this we are more truly proved to be God’s friends.

Or thus: “For I think”: it is as though he said, You ought to reign because I think, and am certain, that God has displayed us apostles as the last—that is, like the last saints, Elijah and Enoch, in tribulations. I mean us as persons appointed to death, because it happens to us as to those whom victors kept for death, for whose spectacle the people gathered—as they will then gather to mock Elijah and Enoch, and as evil people now gather to mock the apostles. Hence he adds: “Because we have become a spectacle to the world.”

What he means by “the world” he adds: “both to angels and human beings” [Note: [Col. 1568D] Augustine on Psalms 11.], that is, to both good and bad; to the good, that they may strengthen and praise us; to the bad, that they may insult and blame us. For good angels and good people praise, while evil ones mock. These are the right hand and the left. We employ these as weapons with which to strike the enemy, that is, the devil: those who praise and those who blame. Yet neither do the former exalt us nor the latter break us.

### VERSES 10–14

“We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are prudent in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are noble, but we are ignoble. Even to this hour, we both hunger and thirst, and are naked, and struck with fists, and homeless; and we labour, working with our own hands. When cursed, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat. We have become like the refuse of this world, the scum of all things, even until now. I write these things not to shame you, but to admonish you as my most beloved children.”

And we are fools for Christ’s sake, whose cross we preach. By keeping silent about this, you seem prudent in Christ. Hence he adds: “But you are prudent in Christ”; and this is rebuke joined with irony. It is as though he said: The whole matter is the opposite.

[Ambrose] [Col. 1569A] Again: we are weak, that is, afflicted. But you are strong in power and secure. You are noble, that is, respected. But we are ignoble, that is, despised. And “even to this hour,” that is, continually, until the present time, we hunger and thirst and are naked. For preaching the truth freely and without flattery, and reproving the deeds of a wicked life, they receive no favour from human beings. And we are struck with fists and are homeless, because persecution makes us change places. For we are driven away by unbelievers, lest we teach more persons. And we labour, working with our hands at what is necessary for ourselves, because no one gives to us.

When cursed, we bless, exhorting others to good; and we suffer persecutions, that is, torments, and endure them patiently. When slandered as magicians and evildoers, [Col. 1569B] we entreat God for them; or we entreat them not to slander us. And we have become—that is, have been considered—like the refuse of this world, by whose remaining the world is defiled, or by whose removal it is cleansed. For we have become the *peripsema* of all things. *Peripsema* is the refuse of iron or fruit, and whatever is discarded from any material in order to make it purer: such as brass filings and things of that sort, or any household sweepings. Yet through all these things we are proved prudent and strong in Christ, even though they see matters otherwise. It is as though he said: We have become more rejected than all persons, and this even until now—that is, continually until the present time.

“I write these things not to shame you”: like a healing physician, he softens harsh things with gentle ones. It is as though he said: Although I have said that you are puffed up, etc., [Col. 1569C] nevertheless I write these things not to shame you, that is, to make you blush, but I admonish you as my most beloved children, for whom I have suffered so many evils. And I rightly said that you are children, for I am a father. This is what he says:

### VERSES 15–21

“For though you have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel. Therefore I ask you: be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ. For this reason I sent Timothy to you, who is my most beloved son and faithful in the Lord. He will remind you of my ways, which are in Christ Jesus, as I teach everywhere in every church. Some have become puffed up, as though I were not coming to you. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will learn, not the speech of those who are puffed up, but their power. For the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power. What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?”

“For though you have ten thousand guardians.” He puts the finite for the infinite: that is, however great a multitude of instructors you have in Christ, they did not beget you; yet you do not have many fathers who begot you in the faith of Christ. For I alone begot you, not in myself but in Christ Jesus, that is, in faith in Christ. And this was through the Gospel, that is, through my preaching.

[Note: [Col. 1569D] Augustine, on Psalm 77.] After saying beforehand, “I begot you in Christ,” he added, “through the Gospel,” lest what belongs to God should be thought [Col. 1570A] to be his own. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Call no one your father on earth, for one is your Father, God” (Matt. 23). He did not say this in order to take this name away from others, but so that the grace of God, by which we are begotten for eternal life, may not be attributed to the nature, power, or even holiness of any human being. Others are indeed called fathers, but not as God alone is Father, who regenerates by the Holy Spirit those whom he makes children for the eternal inheritance. Human beings, however, are called fathers for the sake of honour, age, and the care of affection.

It should also be noted that, in calling the Corinthians’ teachers “guardians,” he signifies that they are children. “Therefore I ask you.” It is as though he said: Since I begot you, therefore, brothers, be imitators of me, not of false apostles, just as I am an imitator of Christ. And I ask this of you because you ought, by obligation, to obey me.

For this reason also—namely, that you may imitate me—I sent Timothy to you; through him this Epistle is believed to have been sent to them. He is my son in faith, most beloved because of his good conduct, and faithful in the Lord—that is, in preaching the Lord. He will remind you of my ways, that is, my instructions, which are in Christ Jesus and therefore must be maintained. He will remind you, I say, just as I teach them everywhere throughout the world, in every church, and therefore authoritatively.

I say that I sent Timothy, and it was necessary for him to be sent, because some of you are so puffed up over philosophers, in whose earthly wisdom they glory, as though I were not coming to you. “But I will come to you soon.”

[Ambrose] [Col. 1570C] After admonition, behold, he promises that he will go to them, if the Lord permits. Hence he adds: “If the Lord wills.” It is as though he said: I will come to you unless your fault prevents it. He says, “if the Lord wills,” in order to show that if he did not go, God had willed it because of their indignation. I say, “I will come,” and I will learn—that is, I will test and investigate—not the speech of those puffed up with the pride of profound wisdom and judging others, but their power: their faith and good works.

“For” it is as though he said, I will not seek speech because the kingdom of God—that is, the cause of God’s kingdom—is not in speech but in power: that is, not speech from human wisdom but power is the cause of the kingdom. “What do you want?” etc. It is as though he said: I truly will come. But which of these do you want: shall I come to you [Col. 1570D] with the rod of correction, where, although love is present, it does not seem to be; or with love, that is, manifest affection, so as to supply good things, and with a spirit of gentleness, so as to spare sins? He introduces words of terror so that those who were puffed up might be humbled and prepare themselves to receive him. Far be it from devout children to say: “If you are coming with a rod of correction, do not come.” It is better to be instructed by a father’s rod than to perish through a robber’s flattery.

## CHAPTER V

### VERSES 1–5

“It is altogether reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and such sexual immorality as does not exist even among the Gentiles: that someone has his father’s wife. And you are puffed up, [Col. 1571A] and did not rather mourn, so that the one who committed this deed might be removed from among you. For I, though absent in body yet present in spirit, have already judged, as though present, the one who acted in this way: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you and my spirit are assembled with the power of the Lord Jesus, to hand such a person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

“It is altogether [reported] among you,” etc. Here he rebukes the fornicator who kept his father’s wife and those who tolerated him. For they too were participants, since they allowed one guilty of so great a sin to assemble with them unrebuked. Therefore he showed not only that man, openly guilty of death, but also those adhering to him, not free from the crime.

It is as though he said: I ask whether I should come to you with a rod; and a rod is needed unless you correct yourselves. For it is altogether—that is, by everyone—reported among you, who are puffed up and do not correct it. What is reported? Sexual immorality, certainly a shameful matter; and it is such immorality as does not exist even among the Gentiles. To show the gravity of this sin, he says that not even those who do not know God commit it. He then reveals the kind of crime, saying: “That someone has his father’s wife.” And this publicly, where witnesses are not needed. For publicly he had his stepmother in the place of a wife; no evasive excuse could conceal the crime.

It must be understood that, because of this sexual immorality—namely, with the father’s wife—he begins with fornication and later will warn against every kind, both carnal and spiritual. “And you,” nevertheless. [Col. 1571C] It is as though he said: Although such a great crime is among you, nevertheless you are puffed up with the wind of pride, which drives away mercy. Yet if one member suffers, the others suffer with it. And you did not mourn—that is, grieve—for his sins, though it would have been more fitting that you should grieve in such a way that the one who did this deed, which could in no way be concealed, might be removed from among you, because you are all participants.

“For I indeed.” It is as though he said: You did not remove him, though you were present; but I, though absent in body, am present in spirit—that is, in concern of mind and forethought for you—and have already, without delay, judged the one who acted in this way as though present. I have judged, I say, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, in his stead. And I have judged in this manner: to hand such [Col. 1571D] a guilty person over to Satan, when you are assembled and in that spirit with the power of the Lord Jesus. That is, I have judged that you, assembled together without any dissension, with my authority and Christ’s power cooperating, should hand such a person over to Satan.

Or the wording may be arranged in this way: “I have judged,” namely, that when you are assembled, and with my spirit and the power of the Lord Jesus, such a person should be handed over to Satan in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; that is, that you, when assembled, should hand such a person over to Satan in the name of the Lord—that is, for the Lord’s honor and glory, whose glory lies in such a judgment. I did not judge that he should be handed over to Satan out of hatred for you. And this is for the destruction of the flesh, that is, so that [Col. 1572A] Satan may bodily afflict him and he may thus come to his senses. For the Apostle is said to have had this power: when he could not turn someone away from his folly, he would hand him over to the devil to be afflicted, until he renounced evil by professing repentance. Hence he adds: “That his spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ,” that is, that his soul may be saved—here, namely, whenever the Lord visits his heart, whenever the Lord shines upon his heart. And he calls the dawning of light, that is, the bestowal of grace, “the day of the Lord.” Or: may his soul be saved “on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ,” that is, on the Day of Judgment.

[Note: [Col. 1571D] Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*.] By these words the Apostle makes clear that he did this not from hatred, but from love. Thus the Apostle handed him over to Satan not cruelly but lovingly, and with the zeal of charity, just as Moses punished [Col. 1572B] a few worshippers of the idol in the present, thereby instilling fear and establishing discipline for the future. For that Moses did what he did with no cruelty, but with great love, is most clearly evident in his words when he prayed for the sins of the Jews and said to the Lord: “Either forgive them, or blot me out of your book” (Exod. 32).
