[Note: [Col. 1572D] Id., *On the Sermon on the Mount*.] Likewise Elijah and other good men punished certain sins by death, because in this way a beneficial fear was instilled in the living; and those punished by death were not harmed by death itself, but their sin—which might have increased had they lived—was diminished. They did not judge rashly, since God had granted them such judgment. Thus Elijah put many to death, both by his own hand and by fire obtained through divine petition. Nor did Christ rebuke this example of Elijah [Col. 1572C] when the disciples recalled what he had done and asked that they themselves be given power to call down fire from above to consume those who would not offer them hospitality (Luke 9). Rather, he rebuked the apostles’ ignorance in seeking vengeance, because they desired it from hatred rather than from love of correction. Such acts of vengeance were not absent even in the New Testament. For Peter too is recorded to have inflicted vengeance upon Ananias and his wife, when they fell lifeless and were not restored to life (Acts 5).

Or, “he handed [him] over,” etc., may be understood not of that bodily affliction but of deprivation of ecclesiastical communion, which occurs through excommunication. As though he said: I have judged that the man who is such should be handed over to Satan—that is, expelled from the Church, deprived of ecclesiastical admonition, and left free to proceed to the destruction of the flesh: namely, to do what his flesh desires, which leads him to that destruction. [Ambrose] For every carnal pleasure is from the devil; therefore, when a person is abandoned to this pleasure, he is handed over to Satan; and when the soul joins itself to fleshly desire, it suffers destruction. He does not do this, however, in the bitterness of hatred, but with the intention that this expulsion may avail to recall him. Hence he adds: “That his spirit may be saved on the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ,” that is, that his soul may be saved on the Day of Judgment.

Or, the Apostle handed him over to Satan by casting him out of the Church so that the Holy Spirit, of whom those who are defiled are stripped [Col. 1573A], might remain safe for them and not be lost. “On the day of the Lord,” namely, on the Day of Judgment. For unless he had been cast out, the spirit of the Church would not be preserved on the Day of Judgment. For because of the cause of contamination he was abandoning all, so that on the day of the Lord they would be found stripped of the Holy Spirit.

## Verses 6–8

> Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump? Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new batch, as you are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed. Therefore let us feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

“Not good.” As though he said: Since such a fornicator is among you, your boasting is not good [Col. 1573B], by which you boast that you are righteous while tolerating such a man among you. Even if you are otherwise good, this boasting is evil, because it hinders all these good things. For a little leaven—that is, consent to this sin, which, though known, is not rebuked—corrupts the whole lump. [Ambrose] That is, it defiles all those who, though able to rebuke it, conceal it. For they were participants by tolerating the guilty man. But if someone has no authority to exclude one whom he knows to be guilty, or is unable to prove the charge, he is free from guilt; nor is it for a judge to condemn without an accuser, just as Christ did not cast out Judas, because he was not accused.

Or, “a little leaven” means one fornicator, who by drawing others to sin through his example corrupts the whole lump—that is, all those [Col. 1573C] who know and do not avoid him. “And do you not know this? Purge out.” As though he said: Since a little leaven corrupts you, therefore purge yourselves by casting out from among yourselves the old leaven. [Augustine] That is, cast out the one who corrupts you, who is a member of the old man and is sour. Thus, when that fornicator is cast out, the old leaven is cast out. I say, “Purge out,” so that you may be—that is, may continue to be—a new batch: renewed in virtues and without the corruption of sin, just as you are unleavened, having been made so in baptism, that is, pure from the corruption of sin. For a batch is flour bound together with water without leaven; it is the same thing as unleavened bread. Therefore the Apostle wishes them to be a new batch, that is, one thing through love and pure from the corruption of sin, just as in baptism they were made unleavened—that is, clean and without [Col. 1573D] corruption. For *zyma* in Greek is called *fermentum*, “leaven,” in Latin.

“For.” [Note: [Col. 1573D] Augustine, *On John*.] As though he said: We ought therefore to be pure, for—that is, because—Christ, whom we ought to eat, has been sacrificed and is our Passover, through whom we ought to pass from the world to the Father. For *Pascha* is not, as some suppose, a Greek word, but a Hebrew one. Yet in this name there is a highly fitting correspondence between the two languages. Since “to suffer” in Greek is called πάσχειν (*paschein*), Passover is thought to mean “suffering,” or to have been named in this way from suffering. But in its own language—that is, Hebrew—*Pascha* means “passing over,” because the people of God first celebrated Passover when, fleeing Egypt, they crossed the Red Sea [Col. 1574A]. Now that prophetic figure has been fulfilled in truth: when Christ is led like a sheep to slaughter, and, with his blood applied to our doorposts—that is, with our foreheads marked with the sign of his cross—we are freed from the destruction of this age as though from Egyptian captivity, and make the most saving passage when we pass from the devil to Christ, from this unstable age to his most firmly established kingdom. For we pass to the abiding God so that we may not pass away with this passing world.

Passover is a sacrifice, not a passing over, as some suppose. [Ambrose] For first comes Passover and then the passage: first comes the example of the Savior, and then salvation.

“Therefore.” As though he said: Since Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed [Col. 1574B], therefore let us feast not with old leaven—that is, with the old corruption—because otherwise we would not pass over. He then distinguishes the leaven of corruption by its parts: “neither with the leaven of malice,” which is exercised against another, “and wickedness,” which one harbors in oneself. For malice is wrongdoing committed against another; wickedness is wrongdoing which one commits within oneself. But let us feast “with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth,” that is, with sincerity free from vices and with the truth of good works, which are signified by unleavened bread. Or, “with the unleavened bread of sincerity,” that is, of new life, “and truth,” so that we may be without all deceit: sincerity may produce a clean life, and truth may exclude every fraud.

## Verses 9–13

> I wrote to you in the letter: Do not associate with fornicators—not at all with the fornicators of this world, or with the greedy, or robbers, or idolaters; otherwise you would have had to leave this world. But now I have written to you not to associate: if anyone who is called a brother among you is a fornicator, or greedy, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, do not even take food with such a person. For what is it to me to judge those outside? Do you not judge those who are inside? But God will judge those who are outside. Remove the evil person from among yourselves.

“I wrote to you.” As though he said: I urge you to cleanse yourselves of this; and even without this admonition you ought to have done it, because already in another letter I wrote to you this: “Do not associate with fornicators.” [Ambrose] He indicates that he had previously written them another letter [Col. 1574D], in which he warned them not to join themselves to persons of evil life. Since they had not understood how what he wrote was to be taken, he defines it: “Not at all with the fornicators of this world,” that is, Gentiles who, pursuing their various desires, commit fornication against God. He did not forbid association with them, as they had previously understood. Nor did he forbid association with the greedy, robbers, or idolaters. He had forbidden these things also in that letter, and they must still observe them. He wrote that they must withdraw from brethren who are fornicators, greedy, robbers, or idolaters—but not from Gentiles.

“Otherwise,” that is, if I had commanded that you not associate with Gentiles, you would have had to leave this world [Col. 1575A]; that is, you would necessarily have to withdraw from worldly life, since such people are everywhere. For people living in this world cannot avoid living among such people; nor could they gain such people for Christ if they avoided their conversation and their table fellowship. Hence the Lord also ate with sinners and tax collectors.

Or he says, “Do not associate,” in this sense: otherwise—that is, if you associate [with them]—you ought to leave this world, that is, it would be better for you to die. For it is advantageous for evildoers to die sooner rather than remain longer in sins.

“But now I have written,” or “therefore.” As though he said: Since I did not write concerning those people, it is now evident that I wrote to you not to associate, etc. Or join it thus: I then wrote, and you did not understand rightly; but now I have written to you specifically not to associate in this manner [Col. 1575B], namely: if he who is called a brother, though he is not truly so, is a fornicator—publicly named and manifest, cut off or marked by the evangelical sickle. Or, according to another reading: “If anyone called a brother is a fornicator”; the sense is the same. Or if he is greedy, an idolater, a reviler—that is, a detractor—a robber, an irascible person, or habitually drunk. In all these he marks them out. With such a person—that is, with these and others like them—I wrote and write, I commanded and command, not even to take food, much less to pray, so that he may be corrected through shame.

Observe that he does not simply command that one not take food with fornicators, greedy people, and the rest, but first says: “If anyone is called a brother.” [Ambrose] For by saying “brother,” he shows that he did not forbid taking food with an unbeliever [Col. 1575C] or Gentile. Elsewhere he says: “If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner, and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you” (1 Cor. 10).

[Note: [Col. 1575D] Augustine, *On Penance*.] By saying “is called,” however, he shows that evil persons are not to be removed from communion with the Church rashly or in whatever manner one pleases, but by judgment; and if they cannot be removed by judgment, they should rather be tolerated. For we cannot forbid anyone communion unless he has either confessed voluntarily, or has been named and convicted in some judicial proceeding, ecclesiastical or civil. In saying this, therefore, he did not wish a person to be judged by another person according to arbitrary suspicion, or by a judgment presumptuously usurped outside due process; but rather according to God’s law and the order of the Church, whether voluntarily confessed or accused [Col. 1575D] and convicted.

[Ambrose] Therefore the Apostle intended here the naming which takes place against someone when a sentence is rendered according to judicial order and with integrity. For if any mere naming were sufficient, many innocent people would have to be condemned, because crimes are often falsely alleged against someone.

For here he shows that he is not speaking about Gentiles but about brethren marked by the aforesaid crimes. As though he said: I speak only of those who are brethren. “For what is it to me,” that is, what concern is it of mine, “to judge those who are outside?”—that is, outside the Church. They should rather be treated gently. As though he said: It is of no concern to me to judge them. But do you not judge those who are within, in the Church [Col. 1576A] by profession and name? Certainly. For in them the putrefaction must be cut away. But God alone will judge those who are outside; he has not entrusted us with judging them now. Since I command you not to associate with such people, therefore remove the evil person from among yourselves, by whom you are defiled.

## Chapter VI

## Verses 1–6

> Does any one of you, having a case against another, dare to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the saints? Do you not know that the saints will judge this world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters? Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more, then, worldly matters? Therefore, if you have worldly judgments, appoint as judges those who are held in contempt in the Church. [Col. 1576B] I say this to your shame: Is there not among you any wise person who can judge between his brother [and another], but brother litigates with brother—and this before unbelievers?

“Does anyone dare?” On the occasion of the judgment discussed above, he begins to deal with judicial proceedings in which they sinned in many ways: namely, by approaching unbelieving judges while despising believers; by appointing foolish judges; by litigating, defrauding, and doing other such things. As though he said: I said that you ought to judge those who are within. Although you ought to do this, does any one of you, having a case against another believer, dare to be judged before the unrighteous? [Ambrose] That is, before unbelievers, who are unrighteous toward believers in every way they can be [Col. 1576C]: they either wholly despise divine laws or interpret them falsely in order to oppress the good. Why does he not rather seek judgment before the saints, who, fearing the Lord, would serve justice in judging—preserving charity in fidelity to the truth of the law, and preserving truth in charity? As though he said: It is truly audacious and foolish to do this.

And as though someone said: “Should saints judge matters of this kind?” He says: “Do you not know that the saints will judge this world,” which is in error? The Apostle did not say “this world” idly. For he said “this world” in order to show that there is another world, one above it. The saints will judge this world because, made better by comparison, they will by the example of their faith condemn this world’s unbelief. They will also judge by authority and power. And if the world is to be judged among you [Col. 1576D]—that is, through you, because you have some saints who will judge—are you unworthy to judge these smallest matters?

As though he said: Indeed, you can judge them, since we shall also judge apostate angels. Though created worthy—that is, in dignity—they fell; whereas these frail human beings stand. Therefore angels too will be judged, because, having assaulted the saints, they were conquered by them. Do you not know this—that we shall judge angels? How much more, then, can we judge worldly matters, that is, matters concerning the world?

“Therefore, worldly judgments,” etc. Just as he had rebuked them for pursuing cases before unbelievers while despising believers, so now he rebukes them because they appointed contemptible judges [Col. 1577A], though believers. As though he said: Since you ought to judge, if you have worldly judgments—he says “if you have,” because you ought not to have them at all, but should rather forgive or disregard [such matters]—if, I say, you have them, appoint as judges those contemptible persons in the Church, that is, the undiscerning and lowly. As though he said: This is what you have done. Thus brethren are compelled to resort to them, that is, to unbelievers. The Apostle rebukes this in them, speaking ironically; and because this ought not to occur, he adds: “I say this to your shame,” or, “to your regard.” As though he said: I do not command, but remind you, that you may be ashamed. And you ought to blush that there is not among you anyone so—that is, sufficiently—wise as to judge between brother and brother, so that it is necessary [Col. 1577B] to appoint foolish people as judges. Yet these should rather be appointed than that cases should be brought before unbelieving judges, if wise persons are lacking. Thus, I say, there is no wise person; but brother litigates with brother—and that is evil—and this before unbelievers, which is worse.

Or thus: “Therefore, worldly [judgments].” Since the Apostle had said they could judge these smallest matters, he determines who should be appointed to decide such affairs: the contemptible persons in the Church, since the greater persons ought to attend to spiritual matters. As though he said: Since you ought to judge, do it in this manner. If you have worldly business, appoint as judges those in the Church who are held in contempt—that is, some wise persons who nevertheless have lesser merit.

[Note: [Col. 1577D] Augustine, *On the Work of Monks*.] For the Apostles, travelling about in preaching, did not occupy themselves with such matters. Therefore he wished faithful and holy wise persons who stayed in particular places—not those who travelled here and there for the Gospel—to be examiners of such disputes. We cannot excuse ourselves from this, even if we wish to do so.

[Augustine] For I call Christ as witness that I would prefer each day, at fixed hours, to do some manual work, and to have the remaining hours free for reading, prayer, or some undertaking concerning the divine Scriptures, rather than to endure the most tumultuous entanglements of lawsuits concerning secular affairs, whether settling them by judgment or cutting them short by intervention.

I say, “Appoint those held in contempt.” But I say this for your regard: namely, so that those who have acquired wisdom in outward matters may examine earthly cases [Col. 1577D]. Those enriched with spiritual gifts, however, ought not to become entangled in earthly business, so that, not being compelled to arrange lower goods, they may be able to serve higher goods. Yet great care must be taken that those eminent in spiritual gifts do not wholly abandon the affairs of their weaker neighbors; rather, they should entrust these matters to others suited to handle them, or manage them themselves.

“Is there not thus?” He returns to what he rebuked above: namely, that they went to unbelieving judges. As though he said: You ought not to be judged before unbelievers, because there is not among you anyone wise, etc., down to “before unbelievers.” As though he said: There certainly is among you [Col. 1578A] a wise person able to judge. [Gregory] For those whom he had called contemptible, he later calls wise when he says, “Is there not among you?”

## Verses 7–12

> Indeed, it is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather endure fraud? But you yourselves do wrong and defraud—and this to brethren. Do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God. And such indeed you once were; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1578B] and in the Spirit of our God. All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial.

“Indeed, already.” As though he said: Since you seek your own claims contentiously and before unbelievers, it is not merely a fault. Indeed, already it is altogether a fault among you—that is, in this alone there is fault among you: that you have lawsuits of this sort with one another, though this is unfitting among you. For it is sinful to litigate [80] when there ought to be peace.

[Note: [Col. 1578D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*.] From this it is apparent that it is sin to have a lawsuit against someone. But lest you excuse yourself by saying that you act justly because you suffer an injury which you want the judgment of the court to remove from you, he anticipates this and says: Why do you not rather accept injury—that is, open violence? Why do you not rather endure concealed fraud? As though he said: It is remarkable [Col. 1578C] that you do not do this instead. Hence the Lord says: “If anyone wishes to take your tunic and contend with you in court, let him have your cloak also” (Matt. 5). And elsewhere: “From him who takes what is yours, do not demand it back” (Luke 6).

Nevertheless, the Apostle permits this by way of concession to the weak, when he allows such cases to be settled within the Church among brethren by brethren acting as judges; but he sternly forbids their being conducted outside the Church. To understand soundly Augustine’s preceding words, in which he says that it is a sin to have a lawsuit against a brother, it must be stated here what is permitted or fitting for the perfect, and what is not; and what is permitted for the weak, and what is not. The perfect may reclaim their own property simply—that is, without a lawsuit or judicial process—but it is not fitting for them to bring a case concerning it before a judge. The weak, however [Col. 1578D], may reclaim their own property by bringing a case before a judge and having a lawsuit against a brother; but not contentiously or fraudulently, nor before unbelieving judges.

“But you.” As though he said: You ought to suffer injury and fraud; this you do not do. Instead, you inflict injury—that is, open violence—when you contend; and you defraud, when you corrupt judges with gifts. And you do this to brethren, whom you ought to help. You do this and thus lose the kingdom. It is worse because you do it knowingly. For do you not know that no unrighteous person will possess the kingdom of God? Therefore neither will he have salvation, since there is no salvation apart from the kingdom. Do not be deceived, as though relying on mercy: neither fornicators nor idolaters [Col. 1579A]—each of these alone is sufficient to deprive one of the kingdom—nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, that is, passive male sexual partners (*pathici*), nor men who lie with males, nor the greedy. In all these, observe that he rebukes them. Nor will thieves, drunkards, revilers, or robbers possess the kingdom of God.

“And such indeed,” that is, such persons, “you once were; but you were washed” in baptism, and therefore it is more shameful if you return [to these things]. And you were not only washed, but sanctified—that is, strengthened to do good by the gift of the Holy Spirit. And you were not merely sanctified, but justified, namely by doing good. Observe that the repeated conjunction “but” gives no small weight to the statement. “In the name.” As though he said: You were washed, and this in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God—that is, by the operation of the Holy Spirit.

“All things are lawful for me,” etc. Since I said that one ought rather to endure this than pursue lawsuits wrongly, lest anyone suppose that one’s property must never in any way be reclaimed, he adds: “All things,” etc. As though he said: One must not contend with a brother; nevertheless, all my things are lawful to me—that is, they may lawfully be reclaimed; all my property may be reclaimed by me. Yet I shall not reclaim it, because not all things are beneficial [Col. 1579B] to my course; rather, they hinder it. He shows the same point again by another reason, saying:

## Verses 12–13

> All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything. Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them.

“All things are lawful for me,” that is, they are lawful; nevertheless I shall not reclaim [them], because, though I am free, I will not be brought under the power of any person or thing. That is, I do not wish to be brought under the power of a judge, or to be under the dominion of any thing, so as to offend my brother because of it. For then a thing has dominion over us when we prefer love of it to love of our neighbor.

“Food,” etc. As though he said: Although I said that things are not to be reclaimed, nevertheless for this reason it is lawful to reclaim them: food is due to the belly, for which it was created. For by eating and drinking we repair the body’s daily decay. By “food,” understand the necessities of nature; and the belly is due food, because it cannot otherwise be sustained. Therefore it is lawful to reclaim what is ours. “But God.” [Augustine] As though he said: Food is due to the belly, and the belly to food; yet one should not labor much for these, because they will be destroyed. This is what he adds: “But God will destroy both this and that,” or, “it and them,” namely the belly and foods, according to [Col. 1579D] this present state. This will occur when “this corruptible puts on incorruption” (1 Cor. 15).

[Note: [Col. 1579D] Augustine, to Polentius.] Or thus: “All things are lawful for me.” He speaks of things pertaining to food. For among them were people who made distinctions among foods, judging some clean and others unclean. Others thought that all foods should be eaten. As though he said: Not only do you offend in lawsuits and the other things mentioned, but also in foods. Certainly all things are lawful for me—that is, I may eat all foods—not by a legal teaching, but by free authority.

[Note: [Col. 1579D] Id., in the same work.] But not all things are beneficial. Note that something may be lawful and yet not beneficial; but that which is not lawful cannot be beneficial. Consequently, not all things which are lawful—that is, which are forbidden by no command of the Lord—are beneficial. But all unlawful things are not beneficial. For just as everyone redeemed by Christ’s blood is a human being, yet not everyone who is a human being has also been redeemed by Christ’s blood, so everything that is not lawful is not beneficial; but not everything that is not beneficial is also unlawful. Therefore, in order that we may endeavor to distinguish by some definite boundary between what is lawful and beneficial, and what is not lawful and therefore not beneficial:

[Augustine] I confess that things seem lawful to me, though not beneficial, when they are permitted by the justice which is before God, but ought to be avoided because of offense to people, lest they be hindered from salvation on that account. But those things are not lawful, and therefore not beneficial, which justice itself forbids in such a way that they must not be done, even if they are praised by those to whose notice they have been brought [Col. 1580B]. If this is so, the Lord forbids only unlawful things, so that things lawful but not beneficial may be avoided, not by the bond of law, but by the free beneficence of love and the counsel of charity. These are the things given in addition to the wounded man, who was brought by mercy to the inn of that Samaritan to be healed.

[Note: [Col. 1580D] Id., in the same work.] These are not commanded by the Lord, though persons are urged to offer them to the Lord, so that they may be understood to be all the more weighty insofar as they are shown not to be owed. Therefore unlawful things are forbidden, while lawful things which are not beneficial are freely avoided.

“All things are lawful for me.” Here he repeats what he has said in order to add what he had not said, namely: “But I,” etc. As though he said: All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any thing. This would happen if I ate with offense to a brother [Col. 1580C]; for I would then offend a brother through love of food. “Food,” etc. [Augustine] As though he said: Truly all things are lawful for me, because food is due to the belly and the belly to food. These things are not altered. Hence the Apostle later says: “Eat whatever is sold in the meat market” (1 Cor. 10); but one must not eat with scandal. Hence elsewhere he says: “I will never eat meat, lest I cause my brother to stumble” (1 Cor. 8). And elsewhere again: “All things indeed are clean, but it is evil for the person who eats with offense” (Rom. 14). “But God.” As though he said: Food is due to the belly and the belly to food; but nevertheless I shall not eat with scandal, because God will destroy both this and that, or “it and them.”

[Ambrose] Or thus: “All things are lawful.” Here the Apostle anticipates what he will later discuss more fully. He says that it is lawful for him to receive support from others, just as the other apostles received it from those subject to them. But because he knew that false apostles sought an occasion to receive [support], he did not wish to receive it from them, lest the vigor of ecclesiastical truth grow slack because of the belly. Therefore, when the Apostle says, “All things are lawful for me,” it must be understood not of evil things but of good things. For some think that the Apostle said this because of the liberty of free choice, as though all things are lawful but not all beneficial. But what is forbidden is never said to be lawful. Thus John said to Herod: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6). If it were as those people say, he ought to have said: “It is lawful for you, but it is not beneficial.” Similarly, the Lord says to the Canaanite woman: “It is not lawful to throw the children’s bread to the dogs” (Matt. 15). Therefore the Apostle’s statement, “All things are lawful for me,” does not deal with evil things but with good things.

As though he said: You despise me and reckon me inferior to others because I do not receive support; but I do not abstain because it is not lawful for me to receive it. For all things are lawful to me which are lawful also to my fellow apostles, which the natural law allows, not the law of Moses, which prohibited many things because of the hardness of that people. He says this because it was lawful for him to receive support, a matter he will discuss later; but he did not wish to do so because it was not beneficial. Hence he adds, “But not all things are beneficial,” just as it is not beneficial to receive support. For if he received from those whom he rebuked for such great vices, he would undermine the authority of his teaching. A person from whom one receives cannot be rebuked earnestly [Col. 1581B], especially when that person is ready to give in order to humble his superior. But the false apostles, who preach not for religion but for gain, do not wish to be harsh toward sinners.

Hence he says: “But I will not be brought under the power of anything,” diminishing my freedom by rebuking [what I would do], as would happen if I accepted support from them. “Food,” etc. It is indeed lawful for me to receive necessary support, because food is due to the belly and the belly to food; yet I shall not receive it, because God will destroy both this and that. The sense of these words does not change.

Or thus: “All things are lawful.” As though he said: Those who have the aforementioned vices will not possess the kingdom and therefore must be avoided, because even if they were lawful they would still have to be shunned. Let it be supposed that all things are lawful—that is, let someone suppose that all things are lawful, not because they are in fact lawful, but because they seem lawful to some because legal punishments are not imposed. Yet not all things are beneficial, because they must be avoided for their own sake. Again he repeats, “All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything.” For when the mind follows conceived desires, and love of any thing obtains mastery, it is proved to be enslaved to the things by whose love it is overcome. “Food,” etc. As though he said: I will not be brought under the power of anything; and indeed, not even for food, although food is due to the belly and the belly to food. But God will destroy both this and that.

## Verses 13–17

> But the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body. And God both raised the Lord and will raise us by his power. [Col. 1581D] Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Far be it! Do you not know that the one who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, he says, “the two shall be one flesh.” But the one who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit.

“But the body.” [Ambrose] Here the Apostle returns to the earlier sense: food is due to the belly and the belly to food, but the body is not due to fornication. Therefore judgment concerning this cannot be passed over, as you Corinthians are accustomed to do. Rather, the body is due to the Lord—that is, to the Lord’s service—and the Lord is due to the body, in order to glorify and raise it. And he will raise it because God also raised the Lord [Col. 1582A]. If, then, he raised the Lord, he will also raise us by his power, to whom nothing is impossible.

“Do you not know?” As though he said: The body is not due to fornication but to the Lord, because our bodies—not merely our souls—are members of Christ, so that we may imitate him. Do you not know this? Observe that he calls our bodies members of Christ because Christ is our head.

[Note: [Col. 1581D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] Since he was made human for us, his body is the Church. If Christ had assumed only a human soul, his members would be only our souls. But because he assumed a body, through which he is also head to us who consist of soul and body, our bodies are surely his members, since he assumed a body and is the head of bodies. Therefore, if someone desiring to fornicate becomes vile in his own eyes and despises himself in himself, he should not despise Christ in himself. He should not say: “I will do this; I am nothing,” because his body is a member of Christ. Since our bodies are Christ’s members, shall I take Christ’s members away from the service of Christ? Whom ought you to spare within yourself, and make them members of a prostitute, to serve her will? Has this dignity, granted so graciously, become so worthless? Far be it that this should occur!

[Augustine] It should be noted that the bodies which the Apostle here calls members of Christ, he elsewhere calls the temple of the Holy Spirit, on account of Christ’s body, which he assumed from the stock of our body. [Note: [Col. 1581D] Id., in the same work.] Our bodies are members of Christ because of Christ’s indwelling Spirit; the same bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit. And [Col. 1582C] the body which the Spirit uses after sanctifying it cannot fail to be holy.

[Note: [Col. 1582D] Id., *The City of God*.] To say nothing of other considerations: they cannot at the same time be a member of Christ and members of a prostitute; nor should those who are members of a prostitute be said to eat the body of Christ. For this is to eat Christ’s body not merely sacramentally, but in reality: to abide in Christ, so that Christ also abides in that person.

Nor, therefore, do those remain in Christ who are not members of Christ; nor are those his members who are members of a prostitute. “Do you not know?” As though he said: Therefore it is unfitting that I should take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute, because whoever is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her. [Ambrose] For fornication [Col. 1582D] makes the two one body, so that, as they are one in nature, so too they are one in defilement. And do you not know this? And, as though someone were asking whether they are one, he answers: Certainly. For, he says, the book of Genesis says even of those lawfully joined: “The two shall be one flesh,” that is, in the carnal act, which can take place between spouses without sin; and they are also one flesh according to nature, because in nature man and woman are one. For it is evident that they are not both one flesh merely because the woman came from the man.

But whoever. As though he said: Because he who is joined to a prostitute is one with her, whoever is joined to the Lord, always doing God’s will, is not one flesh but one spirit with the Spirit of the Lord, [Col. 1583A] with whom he is one spirit—not by identity of substance. For the spirit of a human being and the Spirit of the Lord are different substances; but this spirit approaches participation in the nature of that truth and blessedness. [Augustine] Therefore one is one spirit with the Spirit of God when one clings to him in such a way as to share in blessedness. This will be complete when one’s desire is satisfied in immutable goods, namely in the Trinity itself, one’s Lord, whose image one is. Therefore the human spirit is not one, or one thing, with the Spirit of God in the way in which the Son is one with the Father and is one God. For we say of the Father and the Son, “They are one,” because the two are of one substance; and we say, “He is one,” but add what he is one—namely, one God. Observe carefully that, when “he is one” is said concerning [Col. 1583B] two or more things, and what is one is added—“one” masculine or “one” feminine—it may be said both of things that are different and of things that are of one substance. [Note: [Col. 1583D] Augustine, *Against Maximinus*.] For the spirit of a human being and the Spirit of God are different substances; and then it is said, “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit.” But when it is said of two or more, “they are one,” and what they are one is not added, they are understood not as different, but as being of one substance, as was said: “He who plants and he who waters are one” (John 10). Likewise: “I and the Father are one” (1 Cor. 3). If, therefore, it is rightly said of things that are of different substances that they are one spirit, how much more rightly are things of one substance said to be one God.

### Verses 18–20

“Flee fornication. For every sin whatever a human being commits is outside the body; [Col. 1583C] but whoever commits fornication sins against his own body. Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought at a great price. Glorify and bear God in your body.”

“Flee.” [Haimo] As though he said: Whoever is joined to a prostitute becomes one body; therefore flee fornication. With other vices, indeed, one may wait for the struggle; but flee this one, lest you even approach it, because it can be conquered in no better way. [Augustine] And you ought to flee it: for every sin whatever a human being commits, except fornication, is outside the body—that is, without contamination of the body. For other sins stain the soul alone. But whoever commits fornication sins against [Col. 1583D] his own body, because fornication contaminates not only the soul but also the body. For the soul does not desire carnally without the desire of the flesh, which has its own motion, although flesh can do nothing without the soul.

Or thus: “Every sin.” As though he said: Therefore you ought to flee fornication, because every other sin whatever a human being commits is outside the body; that is, other sins are outside the bond of carnal desire in comparison with this one, even if they are carried out through the body. [Note: [Col. 1583D] Augustine, in a sermon on the same subject.] For here the soul is subject to the body. Other sins, even if committed through the body, do not make the human mind so bound and liable to carnal desire [Col. 1584A] as happens in the act of bodily fornication alone, when the force of lust makes the mind mingle with the body itself and become, as it were, one with that to which it is glued. Hence he adds: “But whoever commits fornication sins against his own body.”

[Augustine] For here the soul properly serves the body, to such an extent that, in the very moment and experience of this very great disgrace, a person is unable to think of or attend to anything else, because that very immersion and engulfment in lust subjects the captive mind. Because of the heat of lust, than which none is greater, the pleasure of the body itself holds the mind as a slave and makes it captive. For in any other worldly matters the mind is free both to do one of them and, at the same time, to direct its thoughts elsewhere; but during the act and time of fornication [Col. 1584B] this is not permitted to the mind. Thus the whole person is swallowed up by the flesh, so that it can no longer be said, “the mind itself is its own”; rather, the whole person together may be called flesh. Thus, according to this sense, the two may rightly be said to be one flesh. These things have been said concerning the particular fornication of this body.

But because fornication in the sacred writings is understood not only particularly but also generally, let us try, with God’s help, to say this in another way as well. For the general fornication of the human soul occurs when someone, not clinging to God, clings to the world. Hence it is said: “A friend of the world is an enemy of God” (James 4). And again: “If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (John 2). Therefore, whoever clings to the world and is far from God sins against his own body, because the mind is scattered among temporal things by bodily desire, serving the creature rather than the Creator. But one who clings to God rather than the world, and through human frailty incurs any other sin foreign to carnal desire—whether through ignorance, negligence, or forgetfulness—sins outside the body, so that this is the meaning of the statement, “Every sin whatever a human being commits is outside the body”: because one sins not through bodily or temporal desire but through human temptation, which is readily forgiven. But when one clings to the world, loving and desiring temporal things, one is rightly said to sin against one’s own body, because one is given and subjected to all carnal desire, as a servant altogether of the creature and alienated from the Creator himself. Thus, so far as [Col. 1584D] it seems to me, the evil of each kind of fornication—particular and universal—can be understood in this chapter without injury to the faith.

Or it may be read thus: “For every,” etc. [Jerome] As though he said: Therefore flee fornication, because every other sin whatever a human being commits is outside the body—that is, outside one’s spouse, who is called the husband’s body, he being her head. Another sin is not committed against the honor of marriage. [Note: [Col. 1584D] Augustine, *Against Maximinus*.] But whoever commits fornication sins against his own body—that is, acts against the honor of his own body, namely his spouse.

“Do you not know?” As though he said: Likewise, fornication must be fled, because [Col. 1585A] it is certain that your members—that is, your bodies—are the temple of the Holy Spirit: that is, a temple dedicated by the work of the Holy Spirit, who also dwells in you; hence he adds, “who is in you,” who is the God of the temple. “Whom you have from God”: and thus you would offend him as both your guest and God the giver. From this it is evident that the Holy Spirit is God, which you deny. For if the Holy Spirit were not God, he certainly would not have us ourselves as his temple. Yet not only the Holy Spirit, but also the Father and the Son have us as their temple. Therefore the holy Church is the temple of God, that is, of the whole holy Trinity. And do you not know this?

“And you are not.” Here another reason is shown why they ought to flee fornication. As though he said: Flee also on this account, namely because you are not your own by right—that is, not under [Col. 1585B] your own power—but belong to God, who bought you from the devil. Hence he adds: “For you were bought at a great price,” the blood of Jesus Christ. And because this is so, therefore glorify God—namely the Holy Spirit, with the Father and the Son—that is, by good works show him glorious to others; and, though adversities press upon you, nevertheless bear God in your body: that is, endure the pains of the flesh and whatever adversities may come for God’s sake. Or, “Bear God in your body,” 82 so that you may walk according to his law. [Ambrose] For by his law he himself is seen to be in us. Therefore to bear God is to show the image of God in deeds rightly done. And the sense is: “Bear God in your body.” [Note: [Col. 1585] Ambrose, in a sermon on the two kinds of sinners.] That is, if you do not spare yourself for your own sake, at least spare yourself for God’s sake, who made you a dwelling for himself; if you overthrow it, you sin against God—[Col. 1585C] which is a grave kind of sin. The other kind is to sin against a human being. For these are the two kinds of sins: to sin against God and to sin against a human being. One sins against God also by corrupting his temple.

## Chapter VII

### Verses 1–2

“Now concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: It is good for a man not to touch a woman. But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband.”

“Now concerning the matters about which you wrote to me.” On the occasion of the fornication which he forbids, he continues with marriage, concerning which they had asked. [Ambrose] For since the pseudo-Christians, through hypocrisy, in order to appear purer than others, [Col. 1585D] condemned marriages and said that they ought to be despised, and since this did not please the Corinthians, who did not delight in this opinion, they asked the Apostle by letter about this matter alone, passing over the rest. Here he answers them, treating of the marriage of believers and unbelievers. He treats of it in three ways: according to counsel, according to concession, and according to command. The diligent reader should distinguish each in its proper place.

Here it should briefly be said what marriage is, what is the efficient cause of marriage, for what reason it ought to be contracted, what persons may lawfully contract marriage, and what are the goods of marriage by which carnal intercourse is excused. Marriage, or matrimony, is the marital union of a man and a woman between lawful persons, maintaining an indivisible sharing of life. This definition includes only the marriage of believers and lawful persons; and marriage is a good thing. For it is one of the sacraments of the Church, bearing the image of the union of Christ and the Church, as the Apostle says: “But I say that this is a great sacrament in Christ and in the Church” (Eph. 5). It is therefore established that marriage is a good thing—though certain heretics deny this, detesting marriage. Christ approved marriage by attending a wedding and commended it by a miracle. This is also apparent because he established the first marriage between the first parents. [Col. 1586B] The Apostle too says: “A virgin does not sin if she marries.”

The efficient cause of matrimony is present marital consent expressed in words, according to the statement of Pope Nicholas: “Let the consent alone, according to the law of those whose union is at issue, suffice. If that alone is lacking in a marriage, all the other things, even if celebrated with intercourse itself, are futile.” Hence also the saying: [Ambrose] “Intercourse does not make a marriage, but will does.” Likewise: “Not the deflowering of virginity, but the marital agreement makes a marriage.” The reason for which it ought to be contracted is the procreation of offspring and the avoidance of fornication. There are also other honorable reasons, such as reconciliation of enemies, restoration of a state of peace, and the like.

The persons lawful for marriage are such according to the institution [Col. 1586C] of the Church. For some persons were lawful at the beginning of our origin and before the law of Moses; others under the Law; others in the age of grace. Likewise, in the early Church some persons were lawful who are not lawful now. And among those who are now lawful or unlawful, some are fully lawful, some altogether unlawful, and some intermediate. Fully lawful are those not impeded by a vow of continence, clerical order, kinship, disparity of worship, servile condition, or natural frigidity. Altogether unlawful are those barred by a vow, by order, by kinship, or by disparity of worship. Intermediate persons—that is, neither altogether unlawful nor fully lawful—are such because of servile condition or frigidity. For if such persons, unaware of these impediments, have been joined, they may remain together if certain circumstances arise, and may be separated when those circumstances cease.

[Ambrose] The goods of marriage are three: fidelity, offspring, and sacrament. Fidelity: that one may not have intercourse with another man or woman; offspring: that it may be religiously reared; sacrament: that the marriage may not be separated. Separation is twofold: bodily and sacramental. Spouses ought not to separate bodily except by mutual consent, which sometimes occurs for the sake of religious life; but they cannot be separated sacramentally while they live, if the persons are fully lawful. Note that the third good of marriage is called sacrament not because marriage itself is that sacrament, but because it is the sign of the same reality, namely of the spiritual [Col. 1587A] and inseparable union of Christ and the Church.

By these three goods carnal intercourse between spouses is excused, so that it is either not sinful or is venial. When they come together solely for the sake of offspring, it is excused so that it is not sin; but when they come together in order to satisfy and restrain desire, it is venial. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1587D] Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*]: “Marital intercourse for the sake of begetting has no fault; but for the satisfying of desire, though still with one’s spouse, it has venial fault because of the fidelity of the marriage bed.” Likewise: “That married people, overcome by desire, use one another beyond the need of begetting children, I place among those for whom we say daily: ‘Forgive us our debts,’ etc.” (Matt. 6). Where these goods are absent, intercourse has no excuse. Hence it is said: “Every vehement lover of his own wife is an adulterer.” Yet marriage is often contracted in which these goods are not found, because neither fidelity is kept nor offspring religiously reared. Let this suffice on these matters.

As though he said: Fornication must be fled, but marriage is permitted. And this is what he says: “Now concerning the matters about which you wrote to me,” that is, concerning those things which you wrote to me. This I say: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman, because of fornication.” As though he said: It is good not to touch, but nevertheless, to avoid fornication, let each man have his own—not another’s—wife, not a concubine. This is said to exclude those who cannot have wives under divine authority. Likewise, [Col. 1587C] let each woman have her own husband, namely a lawful one. The Apostle says this by concession, not by command. [Fulgentius] For the Apostle, skilled in heavenly medicine, did not so much prescribe for the healthy as point out remedies to the sick. [Gregory] It is therefore a great good not to touch a woman, which every believer ought principally to observe. Yet if anyone is still more anxious about his own weakness than secure in the Lord’s power, and does not know continence, let him make use of a wife. [Note: [Col. 1587D] Id., *On Marriage and Married Life*.] But because marriages of this kind cannot be such as those of the first human beings could have been, let them be such as those of the holy fathers were: let them not serve the concupiscence of the flesh which necessarily exists in this body of death; rather, let that desire itself be compelled to serve only the propagation of offspring. Thus the weakness of incontinence, lest it fall into the ruin of shameful acts, is sheltered by the honorableness of marriage.

### Verses 3–6

“Let the husband render the due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. A woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise, a husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, so that you may be free for prayer; and return again to the same thing, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control. But I say this by concession, not by command.”

[Col. 1588A] “Let the husband render the due to his wife.” As though he said: I permit a man to have a wife and a woman a husband; and after they have been joined, let the husband render the due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. [Ambrose] He says that they are mutually subject to one another in this matter, so that their pleasure may be one in the law of nature. Therefore let each render to the other, because a woman has no authority over her own body for another man, but the husband does; likewise, a man has no authority over his own body for another woman, but the wife does. In this man and woman are equal, because neither husband nor wife may surrender his or her own body to another.

[Augustine] For in this matter they are mutually indebted to one another, lest an occasion for sin be given; but in other things the husband has authority. Therefore here the husband is not deprived of dominion, but of vice. [Note: [Col. 1588D] Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*. Here Augustine speaks differently than above.] Married persons therefore owe one another a kind of mutual servitude in order to avoid unlawful intercourse, so that even if perpetual continence pleases one of them, it cannot be practiced without the other’s consent. To this end, the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Thus, even if he or she seeks from marriage not the begetting of children but relief for weakness and incontinence, they should not deny one another, lest through this they fall into damnable corruptions. For rendering the marital due involves no crime; demanding it beyond the necessity of procreation is a venial fault; but fornication or adultery is a punishable crime.

“Do not,” etc. As though he said: And because neither the husband nor the wife has authority over his or her own body, therefore do not [Col. 1588C] deprive one another—that is, withhold the due—which could become a cause of adultery. [Augustine] The Apostle says this so that they may agree in the marital matter, lest discord produce fornication. I say, do not deprive one another, unless perhaps by agreement for a time, namely that you may abstain by mutual arrangement for the sake of thanksgiving; hence he adds, “so that you may be more freely available for prayer.” For God is to be entreated more purely if he is to show mercy. And although marriages are pure, one should nevertheless abstain even from lawful things, so that prayer may more readily attain its effect. “And return again to the same thing,” that is, to natural use, where, even if there is fault, it is nevertheless venial. [Ambrose] This is not so in fornication. Return, I say, lest Satan tempt you because of your intemperance or incontinence, [Augustine] lest an opportunity be given to the devil to draw you [Col. 1588D] into the snare of fornication 83 or adultery. [Ambrose] For the Apostle says this in order to exclude fornication, not to close the way for those striving toward a better life. And because the Apostle had said, “Let each have his own,” and likewise, “Return,” lest he seem to have said this as a command, he adds:

“I say all this by concession, not by command.” Therefore the person who acts otherwise—that is, who practices continence—does not sin; indeed, the person who acts thus does sin, because there is some fault in it, though slight. Because of sins of this kind one must pray to the Lord daily and often, saying: “Forgive us our debts,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1589D] Augustine, in a sermon on the words of the Apostle.] The Apostle therefore did not command this but permitted it. For one thing is permitted to weakness, another commanded to faith. He shows this by saying, “I say this by concession, not by command.” As though he said: I do not command this to chastity, but permit it to weakness; it is not praiseworthy, but venial.

But perhaps someone will say: If the Apostle granted this by way of pardon, then marriage is sin; for to whom is pardon granted except to a sinner? Where, then, is the evil of incontinence? Certainly, I dare to say that what the Apostle granted to weakness by way of pardon is sin. For in granting pardon the Apostle has in view the intercourse of married persons, in which there is the evil of incontinence. The evil of incontinence is [Col. 1589B] that a husband knows his wife even beyond the need of begetting children; but there too is the good of marriage. [Note: [Col. 1589D] Id., *On Genesis*.] For the fact that incontinence is evil does not mean that marriage apart from the intention of procreation is not good. Indeed, this good is not blameworthy because of that evil; rather, that evil becomes venial because of the marital good, which is threefold: fidelity, offspring, sacrament. Fidelity: that one may not have intercourse with another man or woman; offspring: that it may be religiously reared; sacrament: that the marriage may not be dissolved. The Apostle does not reprove this good of marriage, but the evil of incontinence. [Note: [Col. 1589D] Id., *On the Good of Marriage*.] For intercourse necessary for begetting is without fault, and it alone is properly marital. But that which proceeds beyond necessity obeys not reason but lust. Since, therefore, intercourse with the intention of begetting—which properly belongs to marriage—is not blameworthy, what does the Apostle grant by way of pardon except that spouses demand the debt of the flesh not from a wish for offspring but from the pleasure of lust? Yet this pleasure does not incur fault because of marriage, but receives pardon because of marriage. Therefore marriages are praiseworthy also for this reason: because, on their account, even that which does not belong to them is forgiven. For this intercourse, by which desire is served, is not performed in order to fulfill the offspring which marriage requires. [Note: [Col. 1590D] Id., *Against Julian the Heretic*.] Marriages, then, are altogether good in their kind, because they preserve fidelity to the marriage bed, join both sexes for the purpose of receiving offspring, and abhor the impiety of separation.

### Verses 7–11

“But I wish all people to be as I myself am. Yet each has his own gift from God: one in this way, another in that. But I say to the unmarried and widows: it is good for them if they remain thus, as I also do. But if they do not restrain themselves, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn. But to those joined in marriage I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife not depart from her husband. But if she departs, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. And let a husband not dismiss his wife.”

“But I wish.” As though he said: I grant this. Yet [Col. 1590A] I wish all people to be chaste as I myself am. So far as a kindly and concerned teacher is concerned, he wished all, if it were possible, to be like himself—that is, continent. Yet even if all are not chaste, they nevertheless have other means by which they may be saved. He says this as follows: “Yet each has a gift from God,” because marriage, like continence, is from God. I mean a gift proper to oneself—that is, suited to that person—because each is helped in what he or she seeks more eagerly. One, indeed, may be saved in marriage; another in widowed or virginal continence. [Ambrose] Therefore no one should be compelled, lest, being forbidden lawful things, one commit unlawful things. Let each choose what to follow; yet it is better to be more inclined toward this latter course. [Note: [Col. 1590D] Id., *On Marriage and Married Life*.] He shows sufficiently here that even marital chastity is a gift of God; for not only the chastity of the continent but also that of married persons is God’s gift.

“But I say.” As though he said: Let those joined in marriage render the due; but to the unmarried—that is, virgins—and widows I say that it is good for them if they remain thus, that is, chastely; or, let them go as I do. But if they are not continent, let them marry lawfully. And he adds why he says this: “For it is better to marry than to burn,” that is, to burn with lust. To burn is to be distressed or overcome by desires. [Ambrose] Therefore he does not say “better” because burning is good and marriage better; rather, he follows an ordinary manner of speaking.

“But to those.” As though he said: This I counsel to those not joined in marriage. But to those joined in marriage I command—not I, as if I had discovered this command—but the Lord, in his own person, commands that a wife not depart from her husband. Supply here: except on account of fornication. [Note: [Col. 1590D] Id., *On the Sermon on the Mount*.] For this is the reason which Christ excepted, which is left unstated here because it is very well known: namely, fornication. The Lord excepted this reason alone; all other hardships, should any perhaps arise, he commands to be endured firmly for the faithfulness and chastity of marriage. Note that departing is one thing, while living continent by mutual consent is another. The former is evil, the latter good; and this is said of a marriage in which both parties are believers.

“But if.” As though he said: She should not depart; but if she departs, namely because of fornication, I command her to remain unmarried while her husband lives, or to be reconciled to her husband if she herself is not continent. [Augustine] [Col. 1590D] For if she is not continent, a woman ought rather to be reconciled to her husband than marry another. Likewise, a husband should not dismiss his wife except for fornication. Apart from this, a husband ought not dismiss his wife, because he would make her commit adultery. But if she is an adulteress, he does not make her so, but dismisses an adulteress. What he stated previously about the wife must be supplied here: namely, that if he has dismissed her, he should not take another wife, or else should be reconciled to his wife. For the same rule is kept for husband and wife.

Ambrose, however, says: He does not add this concerning the husband as he did concerning the wife because a husband may take another wife, since the inferior does not use this law altogether in the same way as the superior. This is said to have been added by falsifiers. “But to the rest.” After treating of the marriage of believers, he passes to unequal marriages. As though he said: Where both are believers, I have given this command of the Lord.

### Verses 12–14

“But to the rest I say, not the Lord: If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her. And if any woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not dismiss her husband. For the unbelieving husband has been sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife has been sanctified through the believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean; but now they are holy.”

“But to the rest,” namely where both are not believers—as happened at the beginning of the Church, when the Gospel began to be preached to the Gentiles—“I say,” indeed from God, [Col. 1591B] “not the Lord” in his own spoken words: if any brother—that is, any believer converted to the faith while in a marriage—has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her. [Augustine] The Apostle does not command this but counsels it, so that if anyone acts otherwise, that person is not a transgressor, just as he later counsels concerning virgins. He therefore recommends what is an opportunity for gaining another, when one could lawfully leave but it is not expedient. For what is lawful is not expedient when it is indeed permitted, but the exercise of that right can bring an obstacle to others’ salvation. Such is the matter of which we have long been speaking: the departure of a believer from an unbeliever. The Lord does not forbid it, because it is not unjust before him. But the Apostle, lest it occur, advises against it by the counsel of charity, so that no one may be held to it by the necessity of concession, but may do it freely from willingness to follow counsel. This, then, seems to me to be what the Apostle says in giving this admonition. For a believing spouse may lawfully leave an unbelieving spouse.

[Note: [Col. 1591D] Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*.] For idolatry and every harmful superstition is fornication; and the Lord, in the case of fornication, permitted a wife to be dismissed but did not command it. Thus he gave the Apostle an occasion to advise that whoever wishes should not dismiss an unbelieving wife, who may perhaps become a believer; while whoever wishes may lawfully dismiss her. [Note: [Col. 1591D] Id., to Pollentius.] Because a believer may lawfully leave an unbeliever, the Lord does not forbid it. For what the Lord forbids may not be done at all; but this may be done. For if bodily fornication is detestable in a spouse, how much more is fornication of the mind, that is, unbelief. [Col. 1591D] But because it is lawful in such a way that it is not expedient, the Apostle urges and advises that it not be done, lest people, offended by the separations of spouses, recoil in horror from the doctrine of salvation itself.

Therefore believers are neither commanded by the Lord to leave unbelievers nor forbidden to do so. For if they were commanded by the Lord to dismiss such spouses, there would be no place for the Apostle’s advisory admonition that this should not be done. Nevertheless, we read that the prophet Ezra—or rather the Lord through him—not only permitted but also commanded the Israelites to dismiss foreign wives through whom they were going after foreign gods (1 Esdras 10); those women were not being won for God through their husbands. He rightly gave this command [Col. 1592A] because the Savior’s grace had not yet shone forth so greatly. And through Moses the Lord had commanded that no one should take a foreign wife (Num. 18). Rightly, therefore, those whom they had taken contrary to the Lord’s prohibition dismissed at the Lord’s command.

[Augustine] For a marriage contracted outside God’s ordinance is not to be imputed as a marriage, but, once recognized, must be corrected. [Note: [Col. 1591D] Id., in the same work.] But when the Gospel began to be preached to the Gentiles, it found Gentile spouses already joined to Gentiles. If both did not believe, but one man or woman did, and the unbeliever consented to live with the believer, the believer ought neither to have been forbidden by the Lord to dismiss the unbeliever nor commanded to do so: not forbidden, because justice permits departure from a fornicator, and an unbelieving person’s fornication is the greater [Col. 1592B] in the heart; nor commanded, because both Gentiles had not been joined contrary to a command of the Lord. It was therefore lawful by justice, but it was not fitting to do what was lawful, because of free goodwill. What he said concerning the man, he applies to the woman.

“And if any woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not dismiss him.” Then he gives the reason and end of the counsel, saying: “For the unbelieving husband has been sanctified through the believing wife,” or “in the believing wife”; and “the unbelieving wife has been sanctified through the believing husband,” or “in the believing husband.” [Note: [Col. 1592D] Id., *On the Sermon*.] I believe that it had already happened that some women came to faith through believing husbands and men through believing wives, because it often happens that one is converted to the faith through the other.

Or thus: “The unbelieving husband has been sanctified through the believing wife,” that is, the unbelieving husband is clean with respect to the believing wife, because the believing wife suffers no uncleanness from union with him; and “the unbelieving wife has been sanctified,” etc., that is, the unbelieving wife is clean with respect to the believing husband, because the believing husband is not contaminated by union with her. For the believing man has chastity even with an unbelieving spouse.

“Otherwise,” etc. [Ambrose] As though he said: I say that the believer should not dismiss an unbeliever who consents to live together. Otherwise, [Haimo] that is, if you separate, if you dismiss one another despite wishing to live together, and join yourselves to others, [Ambrose] then this is not a lawful marriage; you are adulterers, and your children, who are born from this union, would be unclean—that is, illegitimate. [Col. 1592D] But now, if you remain, your children are holy—that is, clean—because they are born from lawful marriages and are born from an equal spouse under reverence for the Creator.

Or thus, so that he speaks of children already born who remain in unbelief if their parents mutually dismiss one another. As though he said: I say that a believer should not dismiss an unbeliever. Otherwise, that is, if you dismiss one another, your children, who follow the greater party, would be unclean—that is, they will remain in unbelief; for at that time the number of unbelievers was greater than that of believers. [Note: [Col. 1592D] Id., *On the Sermon on the Mount*.] But now your children are holy—that is, Christians—whether one parent or both is the cause of it. This would not occur [Col. 1593A] if, when one believed, the marriage were dissolved and the unbelief of the spouse were not endured until an opportunity for belief.

### Verses 15–19

“But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart; for brother or sister is not subject to bondage in such cases. But God has called you in peace. For how do you know, woman, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife? Except to each as the Lord has apportioned. Let each walk as God has called him; and so I teach in all the churches. Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not draw on a foreskin. Was anyone called uncircumcised? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of God’s commandments.”

“If the unbeliever, etc.” As though he were saying: A believer must not put away an unbeliever who consents to live with him. But if the unbeliever, man or woman, departs out of hatred for the faith, let that person depart; the believer must not abandon the faith for that person’s sake. [Note: [Col. 1593D] Augustine, *On Faith*.] For in this way an unbelieving wife is most rightly dismissed if she says to her husband: “I will not be your wife unless you amass riches for me by robbery, unless you practice your customary procuring, and so forth.” [Ambrose] Then the man to whom his wife says this, if he is truly a Christian, will be bound more by love of divine grace than of his wife’s flesh, and will resolutely cut off the member that causes him scandal.

“For he is not,” etc. As though he were saying: This is why I say, “Let the unbeliever depart”: for the believing brother or sister is not subject to bondage in such matters—that is, in cohabitation and other such things. The believer is not compelled to follow an unbeliever departing out of hatred for the faith. But so long as they can remain together in peace, they should not separate; if they could be called in that condition, they should remain in it. [Col. 1593C] And therefore he says, “is not subject,” because marital reverence is not owed to one who abhors the Author of marriage. For a marriage that lacks devotion to God is not valid; and therefore one who is dismissed for God’s sake does not sin if he joins himself or herself to another. Insult to the Creator dissolves the right of marriage with respect to the one who is left, so that such a person may not be accused for joining another. But the unbeliever who departs sins both against God and against marriage. Thus marital fidelity need not be kept toward one who has departed from God so as not to hear the name of Christ. But if both come to believe through the knowledge of God, the marriage is confirmed.

Note that Ambrose appears to contradict himself. Above he said that, if a believer who puts away an unbeliever joins himself or herself to another, that person is an adulterer; here, however, he says that it is not a sin for one dismissed to join another. Some resolve this as follows. [Augustine] It is one thing to put away an unbeliever who wishes to cohabit or live together, and another to be put away for God’s sake by one who abhors Christ’s name. In the former case the law of goodwill is not observed; in the latter, truth is preserved. Therefore, although it is always permitted to put away, it is not always permitted to join oneself to another, but only when one is put away for God’s sake. Or, as others say, one may always join oneself to another believer, but not to another unbeliever.

“But God has called you in peace.” As though he were saying: The believer is not subject to bondage in such matters, but ought to preserve peace, [Col. 1594A] [Ambrose] because God has called us in peace; and therefore we ought not to be the cause of discord. Nor ought we to quarrel with one who departs, because that person departs out of hatred for the faith. [Note: [Col. 1594D] Id., to Polen.] Hence, above he urged that a believer should not leave an unbeliever on account of circumstances that may perhaps occur—that is, because “the husband is sanctified,” etc. Now, because the same circumstances may arise, he gives the same exhortation, explaining why it is not advantageous for a believer to put away an unbeliever, although it is permissible.

[Ambrose] These things are done not by a commanding law but by free charity. As though he were saying: Truly one ought to remain with an unbeliever, because how do you know, believing woman, whether you will save your unbelieving husband? He says this because those who do not abhor Christ’s name may perhaps believe. Then he says the same thing to the husband concerning the wife: Or how do you know, believing husband, whether you will save your unbelieving wife? [Col. 1594B] How, I say, do you know this, man or woman, unless you conduct yourself toward your spouse as God has apportioned to each—that is, as he has given to each, namely, to the husband authority and to the wife subjection? Or how do you know the thing stated above unless you patiently await its fulfilment, as God has apportioned to each?

[Ambrose] For he has apportioned to each when he or she is to be saved—that is, he knows when each will believe, and waits until that person believes; so you too should wait. And how do you know, man or woman, the thing stated above, unless each of you walks perseveringly, even if no immediate progress is made, as God has called each person—that is, in the state in which God called each person, not from which state; namely, so that spouse may perseveringly remain with spouse?

But lest anyone perhaps say that he preached this only to the Corinthians and not to other believers, he says: “And I preach this in your Church as I teach in all Churches”—that is, everywhere. Therefore you must hold what all hold.

“Was anyone called circumcised?” As though he were saying: Each person may remain in that state—in marriage, for example—as also in other matters which do not impede salvation. Thus, if anyone was called circumcised, let him not procure foreskin—that is, let him not be compelled to adopt Gentile rites. And if anyone was called in uncircumcision, let him not be circumcised—that is, let him not be compelled to adopt Jewish rites. The Apostle everywhere preserves what he sees to be appropriate, whether for Churches of Gentiles or of Jews. [Augustine] For he nowhere removes a custom whose observance does not hinder salvation, warning that hope of salvation should not be placed in such matters, even if they are observed so as not to offend weaker brethren. [Col. 1594D] Hence he says that they are nothing, adding: “For circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing.” For, with respect to salvation, neither this nor that—that is, neither Jewish nor Gentile observance—helps or harms; rather, what matters is the keeping of God’s commandments.

## Verses 20–28

“Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called. Were you called as a slave? Do not be concerned about it; but even if you can become free, make use of it rather. For the slave who was called in the Lord is the Lord’s freedman. Likewise, the free person who was called is Christ’s slave. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human beings. Therefore, brothers, let each person remain with God in the condition in which he was called. [Col. 1595A] Now concerning virgins, I have no command of the Lord; but I give counsel, as one who has received mercy from God to be faithful. For I judge this to be good because of the present necessity: that it is good for a person to remain as he is. Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet such persons will have tribulation in the flesh. But I spare you.”

“Let each person,” etc. As though he were saying: Let not a Gentile procure circumcision, nor a Jew uncircumcision. Rather, let each remain in the calling—that is, in the condition not opposed to one’s calling—in which, not from which, he was called. [Augustine] For he referred this to those conditions or customs of life which do no harm to faith and good morals. A spouse is called to Christ’s faith, and so is a robber; but the former is called in marriage, not from marriage, whereas the latter is called not in robbery but from robbery. For spouses need not cease to be spouses because of Christ’s faith, just as robbers must cease to be robbers.

“A slave,” etc. Above he gave one example from a manner of life; here he gives another from the duty of one’s condition. As though he were saying: Let each remain in that in which he was called. Thus, if you were called as a slave, do not be concerned, as though wishing to escape it; but if you can become free, make use of slavery rather. [Ambrose] For it is a cause of humility, pertaining to the freedom that is in the Lord: the more contemptible one is in this world for God’s sake, [Col. 1595C] the more one will be exalted in the future.

“For the one called in the Lord as a slave,” etc. As though he were saying: A person called as a slave need not be concerned, because he is Christ’s slave equally with his master. He says it thus: the one who, being a slave, was called in the Lord—that is, in faith in the Lord, or in the Lord’s work—is the Lord’s freedman.
