It is as though he said: he is the Lord’s slave, but he used the more honorable name, calling him a freedman; and this is rightly said, because he has been delivered from sins, which make people slaves. [Ambrose] Likewise, the one who was called while free—whether free from God through pride, which is a crime, or free from a human master by social condition—is Christ’s slave, which is an advancement. Therefore a slave must not be despised because of his condition, nor should a free person, lifted up in pride, set himself above a slave.

“With a price,” etc. [Col. 1595D] As though he were saying: Both are slaves of Christ, which is certainly just, because you were bought with a price—that is, Christ’s blood. And because you were bought, do not become slaves of human beings, namely in such a way as to put God’s service second. As though he were saying: Since you were bought, render a return to your purchaser, so that you may be slaves of Christ, not of human beings. They are slaves of human beings who subject themselves to human superstitions, as happens to you if you say, “I belong to Paul,” “I belong to Apollos,” and such things.

“Let each person,” etc. What he said above he repeats here, to commend it fully: let each brother remain with God—that is, in the observance of God’s commandments—in the state in which, not from which, he was called. [Col. 1596A] For no state harms a person in which that person is called.

“Now concerning virgins.” Above, when he said, “But I say to the unmarried and widows,” he gave counsel of continence not only to virgins but also to widows. Now he gives the same counsel again concerning virgins. As though he were saying: Concerning those joined in marriage, I have given the Lord’s command where both are believers, or my counsel where one is an unbeliever. But concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord—no law commanding them either to remain continent or to marry. [Augustine] Yet I give counsel inspired in me by the Holy Spirit, the same as I gave above: not to marry but to remain continent, though the other course is permitted.

I give counsel as one who has received mercy from the Lord—that is, the apostolic office—so that I may be faithful [Col. 1596B] in the stewardship entrusted to me; and from this it is clear that I am qualified to give salutary counsels.

[Ambrose] “I judge, therefore,” etc. As though he were saying: Since I am an Apostle and faithful, I give this counsel, namely not to marry, because I judge this—that is, to remain in virginity—to be good because of the impending necessity, to avoid marriage. By “necessity” he means the scarcity of the age, which married people often suffer. He puts forward a weak reason for the weak. For he could have supplied a worthier reason, commending more fully the gift of virginity.

[Note: [Col. 1595D] Ambrose, *On the Instruction of Widows*.] Virginity surpasses the condition of human nature, through which human beings are made like angels. Yet the victory of virgins is greater than that of angels. For angels live without flesh, whereas virgins triumph in the flesh. Hence in the tabernacle of the Lord the uppermost covering was of hyacinth skins, by which the life of celibates is understood. For hyacinth resembles the throne in appearance; so those who preserve virginal purity in the flesh are likened to heavenly beings. These are those “who have not been defiled with women” and “follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. 14).

“For,” etc. As though he were saying: I judge as I have said, and rightly so, because it truly is good for a person to be thus—that is, in virginity. Yet, although this is good, if you are bound to a wife, do not seek release, even if necessity presses. But if you are released from a wife, do not seek a wife, if you can remain continent. [Haimo, Ambrose] These are counsels left to one’s discretion, with no constraining command of the Lord. In these matters the Apostle is to be heard as one warning and counselling in the Spirit.

“But if,” etc. As though he were saying: Do not seek one; nevertheless, if you take a wife, you have not sinned; and likewise, if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. “Tribulation,” etc. As though he were saying: They do not sin if they marry or take wives; nevertheless, it is easier to be without marriage, because such persons—that is, married persons—will have tribulation in the flesh, [Haimo] in providing necessary things for themselves and their children.

“But I,” etc. As though he were saying: I counsel avoidance of marriage, although I nevertheless permit it. But in this I spare you: while counselling you to avoid the things that bring the aforesaid tribulations and anxieties of the flesh; or, while permitting you what you wish, I spare you, although it is burdensome. [Col. 1597A]

## Verses 29–35

“But this I say, brothers: the time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep, as though not weeping; those who rejoice, as though not rejoicing; those who buy, as though not possessing; and those who use this world, as though not using it. For the form of this world is passing away. But I want you to be without anxiety. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please God. But the married man is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife; and he is divided. And the unmarried woman and the virgin consider the things of the Lord, that they may be holy in body and spirit; but the married woman considers the things of the world, how [Col. 1597B] she may please her husband. Moreover, I say this for your benefit, not to cast a snare upon you, but for what is honorable and what affords opportunity to entreat the Lord without impediment.”

“But this,” here he exhorts to moderation. As though he were saying: You will enter into marriage, when this can be done without sin. Therefore I give you this counsel. [Augustine] I say to you, brothers, that the time is short, in which the people of God are not to be propagated by carnal generation but gathered by spiritual regeneration. And because the remaining time is short—that is, because this alone remains to be done—those who have wives should be as though they had none, [Note: [Col. 1597D] Augustine, on Psalm 147.] giving attention to God’s service, not to the work of the flesh. This is indeed done by one who has a wife: one renders the marital due but does not demand it. So too, one who marries because of personal weakness should do so weeping rather than rejoicing—grieving that one could not remain without a wife rather than rejoicing to have taken one—especially where spouses preserve continence by mutual agreement.

[Note: [Col. 1597D] Id., *On the Sermon on the Mount*.] Marriages should certainly be judged happier when, whether after the begetting of children or with offspring set aside, they can preserve continence by mutual agreement. And those who weep because of the accidents of marriage or some worldly sorrow should be as though not weeping, and should not yield or be broken by the hope of future good. Those who rejoice in some worldly prosperity should be as though not rejoicing, lest inwardly they be spiritually corrupted. Those who buy, as married people do when providing for children, should be as though not possessing—that is, they should not set their hearts on perishable things, but possess them without clinging to them in love. [Col. 1597D]

[Note: [Col. 1597D] The same author, *In the Letter for the Vindication of a Count*.] And, to put it universally: those who use this world should be as though not using it, so that they may make good things out of its goods, rather than become evil. Lest such goods be thought evil, they are given to the good; and they are taken away from them, to test them. Lest they be thought great or supreme, they are also given to the evil; and they are taken away from them, to torment them.

“For it is passing away.” [Haimo, Augustine] As though he were saying: Worldly things are to be reckoned as though they were not, because the form—that is, the beauty, not the substance—of this world passes away; that is, it grows old daily and at last will perish in the judgment amid the conflagration of worldly fires. Not its substance, but its form will perish. [Col. 1598A] Its very liberated substance will have those qualities which, through a marvelous change, suit immortal bodies. Therefore he did not say that the world perishes, but its form, because the substance does not perish, but its quality.

“But I want,” etc. As though he were saying: If you marry, I counsel you to do this. Yet I prefer that you be free from anxiety concerning a wife; when this is reduced, one watches more eagerly in God’s affairs. And rightly do I want this: the one without a wife is anxious to fulfill the things of the Lord, and how to please God with inward beauty, not how to serve him. But the married man is anxious about the things of the world—managing the household and similar concerns—and also how he may please his wife. [Haimo] For a sorrowful wife in a household is a great bitterness. And he is divided, not by nature but in action, because he serves partly God and partly [Col. 1598B] the world.

Likewise the unmarried woman—that is, the widow—and the virgin consider the things of the Lord. [Augustine] She no longer considers such things lest she be condemned by God, as does fear, the guardian against evils. [Fulgentius] But she, not fearing condemnation and secure regarding salvation, considers only the things of the Lord: namely, that she may be holy in body—that is, in actions performed through the body’s ministry—and in spirit—that is, in will.

[Note: [Col. 1598D] Id., *On Holy Widowhood*.] A faithful and chaste married woman also does this: she is holy not only in spirit but also in body, for it cannot happen that the body in which a sanctified spirit acts is not holy. But the unmarried woman does this more fully: free from worldly necessities, by which a married woman is constrained, she devotes herself more intensely to heavenly commands. But the married woman considers the things of the world and how [Col. 1598C] she may please her husband. He does not say this in order that she should not herself be holy in body and spirit, but that she is so less fully than an unmarried woman. Thus, when the Apostle speaks of unmarried and married women, he intends that the unmarried have a fuller sanctification both in body and spirit; he does not deprive married women’s bodies of all sanctification.

“Moreover, this,” etc. As though he were saying: I counsel you not to marry, but I say this for your greater benefit, namely that you may serve God more readily; not so as to cast upon you, if you are incontinent, the snare of fornication. I do not say this to cast a snare upon you, but in pursuit of what is honorable—namely, that a person may be chaste in mind and body. [Augustine] He does not say this because marriage is shameful, but because this is more honorable. And I pursue that which offers someone the means, or ease, of serving [Col. 1598D] the Lord without the impediment found in marriage.

[Note: [Col. 1598D] Id., *On Holy Widowhood*.] Therefore, when he says “for what is honorable,” he did not show marriage to be shameful; rather, under the general designation of honorable he commended what was more honorable than honorable. For what is “more honorable” except that which is more honorable? Thus, just as “better” is better than good and “more blessed” than blessed, so “more honorable” is more honorable than what he chose to call honorable.

## Verses 36–40

“But if anyone thinks that he is behaving improperly toward his virgin, because she is past the age of maturity, and it ought to happen thus, let him do what he wishes: he does not sin if she marries. [Col. 1599A] But one who has resolved in his heart, being firm, having no necessity, but having authority over his own will, and has determined this in his heart, to preserve his virgin, does well. Therefore both the one who gives his virgin in marriage does well, and the one who does not give her does better. A woman is bound by law as long as her husband lives; but if her husband has fallen asleep, she is free from the law and may marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. Yet she will be happier if she remains thus, according to my counsel. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.”

“But if anyone,” etc. As he has determined what is better and more honorable concerning virgins, so he determines what guardians of virgins should do if the virgins wish, or do not wish, to remain continent. As though he were saying: [Col. 1599B] It is more honorable and expedient to be without marriage; nevertheless, if anyone thinks that he may at some time appear dishonorable concerning—that is, on account of—his virgin, because she is past maturity, namely beyond puberty, and it must happen thus, [Ambrose] namely that she marry because the virgin does not wish to remain continent, let the guardian do what the virgin wishes, because the guardian does not sin if the virgin marries. This he says lest, though the virgin does not sin, her guardian seem to sin. Therefore I say, if it must happen, he does not sin.

For the alternative case is clear: not only does he not sin, but he does well—the one who has resolved in his heart to preserve his virgin, not putting before her the inducement to marriage. [Augustine] He has resolved, I say, firm in his intention, not caring for offspring or any other such thing. And he has no necessity, [Col. 1599C] since the virgin wishes to remain continent, but has authority, in accordance with his ward’s continence, to accomplish his own will. The one who has thus resolved does well; and that one, certainly, who has resolved not lightly but has judged in his heart—that is, discerned by judgment of mind that it is good—and because, as we said, it must happen thus: therefore, the one who gives his virgin in marriage does well, because what he does is permitted.

[Ambrose] And the one who does not give her in marriage, having authority over his own will, does better, because he lays up merit for her with God and frees her from worldly anxiety. Therefore he rightly says, “does better.” [Augustine] For what is permitted and expedient is better than what is permitted but not expedient.

[Note: [Col. 1599D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] Here a person makes good use of an evil; there a person makes good use of a good. These two things, good and evil, together with two others, good use and bad use, produce four distinctions. Someone makes good use of a good by dedicating continence to God. Someone makes bad use of a good by dedicating continence to an idol. Someone makes bad use of an evil by giving free rein to lust through adultery. Someone makes good use of an evil by restraining lust through marriage. Therefore, just as it is better to make good use of a good than to make good use of an evil, though both uses are good, so the person who gives his virgin in marriage does well, and the one who does not give her does better. For marital chastity is good, but virginal or widowly continence is better.

[Note: [Col. 1599D] Id., *On Holy Widowhood*.] “A woman is bound,” [Col. 1600A] etc. As though he were saying: A virgin may marry; likewise, a widow may marry, but it is happier to remain continent. This is what he says: a woman is bound by the law of her husband as long as her husband lives, so that she may not marry another. But if her husband has fallen asleep, she is released from the law of her husband and is permitted to marry whom she wishes.

[Augustine] He says, “whom she wishes,” because unwilling marriages are accustomed to have bad outcomes. But when he says “let her marry,” he speaks according to natural law, although only first marriages were instituted by the Lord, while second marriages are permitted. Thus first marriages are solemnly celebrated under God’s blessing, while second marriages even now lack glory. I say, let her marry, but only in the Lord: namely, let her act without suspicion of impropriety and marry a man of her own religion.

Or continue it thus: [Col. 1600B] “A woman,” etc. As though he were saying: A virgin may marry at any time; but a married woman, even if dismissed because of fornication, cannot do so while her husband lives. For a woman is bound by the law of her husband as long as he lives; but if he has fallen asleep, she is released and may marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. Yet she will be happier if she remains thus—that is, unmarried—according to my counsel.

[Note: [Col. 1599D] Id., *On Holy Widowhood*.] He sufficiently shows that a faithful woman who marries again in the Lord after her husband’s death is blessed, but that one who does not marry is more blessed. Hence the great heresies of the Cataphrygians and Novatians collapse—heresies that Tertullian puffed up with sound from lips without wisdom, while with slanderous tooth he tore apart second marriages as though unlawful—though the Apostle, with sober mind, permits them altogether lawfully. But people commonly raise a question concerning third and fourth, and still more numerous, marriages; but who would dare determine what I do not see the Apostle himself determining? For he says, “If her husband has fallen asleep,” etc. He does not say first, second, third, or whatever-numbered husband. Nor ought we to determine what the Apostle does not determine.

Therefore, to answer briefly: I ought neither to condemn any marriages nor to take away from them the modest shame attendant upon their number. Christ himself, the Apostles’ and our Master and Lord, does not condemn in the Gospel the woman who had seven husbands, nor say that she cannot exist in the resurrection; but says only: “They neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matt. 22). Therefore I do not dare, contrary to the sense of human modesty, to say, [Col. 1600D] “Let them marry as often as they wish”; nor do I dare, from my own heart and beyond the authority of Holy Scripture, to condemn marriages of any number.

[Note: [Col. 1600D] Id., to Polentius.] But what is said of the widow of one husband is said of every widow: namely, “she will be happier if she remains thus according to my counsel.” And lest anyone should suppose that this counsel was human rather than divine and therefore to be despised, he added: “But I think that I too, like the other Apostles, have the Spirit of God,” by whose inspiration I commend these things and others—something you do not suppose. [Note: [Col. 1600D] Id., on John.]

Note that, when the Apostle says “I think,” he does not doubt; rather, he rebukes despisers. Thus the Lord too does not doubt but rebukes when he says: “If you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also” (John 8). [Col. 1601A] And elsewhere: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18). By wording of doubt unbelief is rebuked; divinity does not express an opinion.

## Chapter VIII

### Verses 1–4

“Now concerning things sacrificed to idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up. But if anyone thinks that he knows anything, he does not yet know as he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, that person is known by him. Concerning foods sacrificed to idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no God but one.”

“Now concerning things sacrificed to idols,” etc. Above he treated marriage, [Col. 1601B] concerning which they had asked him. Here he treats *idolothytis*, that is, things sacrificed to idols. Some used these so indiscriminately that weaker persons were either scandalized or at least confused; moreover, those who used permitted things disorderly violated in themselves the form of the Church and shattered unity. For, knowing that all things are clean by creation, they ate in an idol-temple things sacrificed to idols in the presence of weaker persons. When the weak saw this, they supposed that they ate in reverence for the idol, and followed their example by eating in reverence for the idol. The Apostle therefore rebukes them here.

As though he were saying: You asked about the matters previously discussed, and I have taught you; but there was no need to ask concerning these others, because in these matters you know as I do. This is what he says: “Now concerning things sacrificed to idols”—whether it is permitted to eat them or not—“we know.” As though he were saying: I know, and you know equally with me, that it is permitted to eat them. Truly we, you and I, know that we all have knowledge concerning the Creator and creatures. He says this concerning the more important among them, [Col. 1601C] who, possessing knowledge, ate to the offense of the lesser; he first rebukes these, saying that they do not know sufficiently because they did not avoid giving offense to their neighbor. Others, however, ate in reverence for the idol through ignorance.

“Knowledge,” etc. [Augustine] As though he were saying: You have knowledge, but this knowledge has no value, because it makes you proud over the ignorant. For knowledge, if it is alone, puffs up—that is, exalts into pride; but charity, which is not puffed up, builds up the weak, abandoning whatever can harm them. [Note: [Col. 1601D] Augustine, *The City of God*.] Therefore possess charity, not puffing-up knowledge. Add charity to knowledge and knowledge will be useful. For knowledge is useless in itself, but useful with charity; in itself it puffs up into pride, as do demons, who are so named from knowledge in Greek, and in whom knowledge exists without charity.

For the correction of this fault, namely the pride of knowledge, Paul was given the thorn of Satan by which he is beaten lest he become exalted. [Augustine] Knowledge is also to be preferred to knowledge. For it is better to know our weakness than the nature of things. A mind that knows its own weakness is more praiseworthy than one which, ignoring this, investigates the course of the stars, [Col. 1602A] the foundations of the earth, and the heights of heaven. But better are those who apply themselves to knowing themselves, because one who applies such knowledge applies the sorrow of pilgrimage through longing for the homeland and its Creator.

“But if anyone,” etc. As though he were saying: You have knowledge concerning things sacrificed to idols, but it is not perfect knowledge. For even if anyone thinks that he knows something—namely, that it is permitted to use them—he does not yet know how he ought to know; that is, he does not yet know that he must use this knowledge in such a way as not to harm another. [Ambrose] Thus he shows that those who glory in knowledge have not known as they ought to know. For since they do not pursue charity, the mother of all goods, they do not know as they ought.

“But if anyone,” etc. As though he were saying: Such a person does not know perfectly; but one who loves [Col. 1602B] his brother truly knows, with God’s approval. This is what he says:

“But if anyone loves God, that person is known”—that is, approved—“by him.” That person loves God who, for charity’s sake, restrains knowledge so as to benefit the brother for whom Christ died. [Haimo]

“Now concerning foods,” etc. Having reproved their knowledge, he finally reveals what that knowledge is. For above he had not said what their knowledge was; here he shows it. As though he were saying: Knowledge does not avail in the ways stated above; nevertheless, it is true in this: concerning foods sacrificed to idols, you and I know that they may be eaten and are not contaminated by the idol; and we know that an idol is nothing in the world—that is, among the world’s creatures. [Note: [Col. 1601D] Augustine, on John.] For God made the material, but human folly gave it form. It indeed has a certain human form, but the human being himself was made through the Word. For whatever has been naturally made, whatever exists among creatures, was made through the Word; but the form of a human being in an idol was not made through the Word, just as sin was not made through the Word. Rather, it is nothing, and human beings are nothing while they sin.

Or, “an idol is nothing in the world” means that what they thought to be an idol is nothing. For they supposed an idol to be a subsisting person composed of an image and an indwelling spirit. Or, “an idol is nothing in the world” means that it has no likeness to anything that exists in the world. Here he calls an idol a form which the eye does not see, but which the mind imagines for itself. [Col. 1602D] For example, if someone forms with human limbs a dog’s or ram’s head, or gives one human figure two faces, and so forth: the maker makes not a likeness but an idol. For he makes something having no other thing like it, but something invented by an idle and curious mind. Therefore the Law says distinctly: “You shall not make an idol, nor any likeness of a thing” (Exod. 20; Lev. 26). A likeness, however, exists when something is fashioned from things that are in heaven, on earth, or in the waters.

“And we know that there is no God but one.” He says this lest God be thought to exist in the idol. [Note: [Col. 1602D] Id., *Against Maximinus the Heretic*.] For there is one God only: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that is, the Trinity itself is one God—and no division of parts occurs in the unity of the Godhead. For God the Father is not a part of God. There are three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. And because these three are of one substance, they are one, and are supremely one, because there is no diversity of natures there and no diversity of wills. For if they were one in nature but not in agreement, they would not be supremely one; but if they were unlike in nature, they would not be one.

[Augustine] Moreover, Christ is one person of two substances, because he is God and man; yet neither God nor man can be called a part of this person. Otherwise the Son of God was not whole before he assumed the form of a servant, and he grew when humanity was added to his divinity. But if God cannot be a part in one person, how much more can any one of the Three not be a part of the Trinity? [Col. 1603B] Thus, in this Trinity, no one is a third part, nor are all greater than the individual persons.

You have said, of course, that the one God is not composed of parts, and you wish this to be understood of the Father. “He,” you say, “is simple, unbegotten power.” But are goodness, wisdom, mercy, and power parts of that power which you have called simple? If you say that they are parts, then simple power consists of parts; and, by your own definition, this power is the one God; therefore you say that God is composed of parts. “I do not say so,” you reply; therefore they are not parts. If, then, in the one person of the Father you find those things and do not find parts, [Col. 1603C] how much more are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit one God because of their indivisible Godhead, three persons because of the property of each, and parts of no God because of the perfection of each?

The Father is power; the Son is power; the Holy Spirit is power. This you say truly. But do you deny that power begotten from power, and power proceeding from power, have the same nature? This you say falsely. This you say against the catholic faith.

### Verses 5–7

“For although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him. But not all possess this knowledge. Some, however, with consciousness of the idol until now eat as though it were a thing sacrificed to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.”

For even if, etc. [Augustine] As though he were saying: There is only one God. And truly so; for even if there are those who are called gods by participation in deity, such as the saints, whether in heaven, already received there, as those who have departed from the body, or on earth, dwelling there, as those who still wander in a mortal body; and I speak not of falsely imagined gods, but of those who are gods in truth—since indeed there are many gods, by participation in deity, such as the saints, and many lords, who are set over others: apostles on earth and archangels in heaven. Even if this is so, I say, nevertheless for us there is only [Col. 1604A] one God, the Father, who is God naturally and substantially, one God with the Son and the Holy Spirit. For “God” is said in three ways: substantially, adoptively, and by designation. The Trinity is called God substantially; the saints, who are gods through the grace of adoption, adoptively; demons and idols by designation, because they are gods in name only, not by nature or participation.

[Note: [Col. 1603D] Augustine, in the book of Questions.] Of adoptive gods it has been said: “Even if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, since there are many gods and many lords.” For he intended those to be understood who are rightly called gods, though certainly in such a way that latria—which is translated into Latin as servitude—is not owed to them; they are those whom the Law forbids men to curse, where it is written: “You shall not curse or speak evil of the gods” (Exod. 22). But they are not commanded to be honoured by sacrifices or by any services of latria.

[Ambrose, Haimo.] Or this statement—“For even if there are those who are called gods”—may also be understood of gods by designation, called gods by the Gentiles, whether in heaven, such as the sun and moon, or on earth, such as Apollo, Aesculapius, Hercules, and the like. Therefore I said “are called,” since there are many gods in pagan opinion and many lords; yet for us there is only one God, the Father, in whom we believe, and who makes us, believing in him, gods, according to the saying: “He gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in him” (John 1).

[Augustine] Therefore for us there is one God, but for the Gentiles there are many, whom our God terrifies—that is, demons. Wishing to seem gods, they demand for themselves those things which are owed to the true God: namely altars, sacrifices, and other such things. But our [Col. 1604C] God makes men gods; he himself was not made, and therefore he is the true God. We find that men are called gods in that psalm: “God stood in the assembly of gods” (Ps. 81 [82]). And again: “I said: You are gods” (ibid.).

But the question is raised: if men are called gods, should angels be called gods along with holy men, to whom equality with angels is promised as the greatest reward? In the Scriptures, indeed, I do not know whether angels can be found, or can easily be found, plainly called gods. Therefore, if this is found nowhere in the divine utterances, the principal reason that occurs to me is why angels are not called gods: lest men should think that they ought to be worshipped; lest men should incline to render to angels the service of religion called *liturgia* or *latria*. Rather, they are much more usefully called by the name of their office, angels, which in Latin means “messengers,” so that he may be worshipped whose messengers they are. Therefore what is said, “God of gods” (Ps. 49 [50]) and “a great King over all gods” (Ps. 81 [82]), is understood only of the saints, for whom there is one God, the Father.

He next shows why he is rightly called both God and Father. As though he were saying: He is truly God, because he is the one from whom we believe all things to exist. And he is truly Father, because we believe that we are cherished in him, that is, in his grace. The question is raised whether Christ or the Holy Spirit ought to be called our Father. Certainly we say that they ought, because the grace by which we are regenerated belongs as much to the Son and the Holy Spirit as to the Father; and whatever we receive from the Father, we receive from the Son and the Holy Spirit. Therefore we say that God the Trinity is one Father to us, one majesty, or one master who reigns and enlightens, just as he is one Creator.

But again the question is raised: if God the Trinity is one Father to us, is he that Father who is eternally Father by begetting the Son, or not? And if not, is he another Father? To this we say that one ought not simply say, “God the Trinity is Father,” lest the person of the Father be understood. Rather, he is Father to us; not that Father who is the third person, nor another Father, but the one God who is Father to us in time, and who is that Father, just as the Son is one God with the Father and yet is not the God who begot.

[Ambrose] And for us Jesus Christ is one God and Lord, with [Col. 1605B] the Father in substance; that is, for us the Father and Christ are one God and Lord, through whom, Christ, all things were created. For all things were created by the Father, but through the Son.

[Note: [Col. 1605D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*.] Nor were some things made through the Son and others through the Father, but the same things. Otherwise not all things would be through the Father, nor all through the Son. But if all things are through the Father and all things through the Son, then the same things were made through the Father as through the Son. Therefore the Son is equal to the Father, and the operation of both is inseparable. And we are in God through Christ, because through him we have been renewed in the knowledge of God, through whom we had been created.

“But not,” etc. As though he were saying: We know that there is one God. But this knowledge is not in everyone; that is, not all know the mystery of the one God. “But some,” or rather “for.” As though he were saying: Truly this knowledge is not in everyone, because some, etc.; or, we know that an idol is nothing. But some eat sacrificial offerings with the consciousness of the idol, because they think the idol is something divine. And this is “until now,” that is, even now after conversion, as before conversion.

[Ambrose] They eat, I say, with such consciousness, and as though it were an idol-sacrifice (*idolothytum*), that is, with reverence for the idol, as though some divinity were present there. And their conscience, being weak, is defiled by those who have knowledge of the one God but not with charity, by whom the weak were led into this error. It is not their food that is defiled, but their conscience.

[Col. 1605D]

**VERS. 8–13.—** “But food does not commend us to God. For neither, if we eat, shall we have more; nor, if we do not eat, shall we have less. But take care lest perhaps this liberty of yours become a stumbling-block to the weak. For if anyone sees one who has knowledge reclining in an idol-temple, will not his conscience, being weak, be encouraged to eat things sacrificed to idols? And the weak brother, for whom Christ died, will perish through your conscience. Thus, sinning against the brothers and striking their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat flesh, lest I cause my brother to stumble.”

“But food.” As though he were saying: Your eating harms them, but it does us no good, because food, whether eaten or not eaten, does not commend us to God; rather, it is faith concerning food, by which all things are believed to have been created clean by God. And truly, neither, if we do not eat, shall we lack—that is, have less good—nor, if we eat, shall we abound in the good of virtues or blessedness, but only by faith in it.

“But take care.” As though he were saying: As far as you are concerned, food itself is nothing.

[Haimo.] But take care lest perhaps this liberty of yours become a stumbling-block to those weak in faith, who do not yet know that an idol is nothing; and it can become a stumbling-block. For if some weak person sees one who has knowledge reclining in an idol-temple—that is, in the presence of an idol—will not his conscience, being weak, of itself be encouraged [Col. 1606B] to eat things sacrificed to idols, that is, to eat sacrificial meats as idol-sacrifices? For when someone sees a knowledgeable brother eating things sacrificed in an idol-temple, he too begins to eat; not with that consciousness by which the other, knowing through understanding that the idol is nothing, does so, but he believes that some god is there, when he sees his knowledgeable brother eat there without abhorrence. Thus the weak brother will perish through your conscience—that is, because he sees you, a wise person, eat and thinks it is done in veneration of the idol—though Christ died to save him. Thus you sin gravely.

“Thus.” As though he were saying: You sin against the brothers in this way. But by sinning thus against the brothers and striking their weak conscience, you sin in Christ, whose members they are. For when men are not imitators of the charity by which Christ set us free, they sin in Christ, [Col. 1606C] not against Christ; for to sin against Christ is to deny Christ. But to sin in Christ is to sin in those things that belong to Christ. Just as one under the Law is said to sin in the Law, so those who are in Christ are said to sin in Christ. Therefore you sin in Christ, whose kingdom you diminish. And because you sin in Christ, therefore abstain, as I too abstain even from all flesh; for if food causes my brother to stumble, I shall eat not only no meat that has been sacrificed, but no flesh at all for ever—that is, neither here nor in the future. For just as it is certain that I shall not eat after death, so I am certain that I shall not eat during life either: not because food is evil, but lest I cause my brother to stumble.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 1606D]

**VERS. 1–7.—** “Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Christ Jesus our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord? And if I am not an apostle to others, yet I am to you. For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord. This is my defence before those who question me: Do we not have the right to eat and drink? Do we not have the right to take about with us a sister, a woman, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? Or do I alone and Barnabas not have the right to do this? Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not eat of the flock’s milk?”

“Am I not free?” He begins to set himself forth as an example, so that, as he abstains from lawful things in order to avoid giving offence to the brothers, they too may abstain. For although, by apostolic rank, he had the right not to work with his hands but to live by the Gospel, nevertheless, lest he cause anyone offence by receiving support, he abstained. As though he were saying: Abstain from this lawful thing, because I too have freedom to receive maintenance, yet I do not receive it. And truly I have freedom. For am I not free to receive it? Certainly I am free to receive, since I am permitted what is permitted to the other apostles: namely, to live by the Gospel.

Although he introduced this in this way, he nevertheless intends to prove that he is an apostle, because on account of false apostles [Col. 1607B] the Corinthians thought less highly of him. Hence he adds: “Am I not an apostle?”

[Haimo.] As though he were saying: I am truly free, because I am an apostle; and I am truly an apostle, because I have seen Christ, without which—that is, if I had not seen him—I would seem less an apostle. This is what he says, speaking interrogatively as though angry: “Have I not seen our Lord Jesus Christ on the road, or in the temple at Jerusalem while I was praying? Have I not?” As though he were saying: I am truly an apostle, because you are the work of my apostleship. And he says this interrogatively: “Are you not my work, O Corinthians?” Yet this is “in the Lord,” that is, with the Lord working; or “in the Lord,” that is, for the Lord’s glory.

And because you are my work, therefore, even if I am not an apostle to others—that is, to Jews whose Law he was setting aside—yet I am an apostle to you, who were converted through me, because you are my perfected work. And I am truly an apostle to you, for you are the seal—that is, the pattern—of my apostleship in the Lord, that is, with the Lord as author, by the likeness of a seal; because in you it appears that I am an apostle, since through me you possess what others possess through the other apostles. Therefore through you I am defended before others who doubt. This is what he says: “My defence”—that is, you yourselves—before others who ask whether I am an apostle.

And because I am an apostle, do not I and my associates have the right to eat and drink what is yours—that is, to live from your maintenance?

[Augustine] As though he were saying: Certainly we have. For the Lord permitted the apostles, but did not command them, to receive necessities from those under their care, so that anyone wishing to do so might use what was permitted him by the Lord’s ordinance; but one who did not wish to use it would not act contrary to a command, but would yield his own right. To receive expenses is a right, not a command of the Lord.

And do we not have the right to take with us a sister, a woman, to minister to us, as the other apostles do, and also the brothers of the Lord—who are older—such as James, Jude, and the rest, and Cephas, that is, Peter, who is chief of the apostles?

[Haimo.] He does not find fault with this, but proves from their practice that it is permitted to him. For women, desiring the Lord’s teaching and eager for virtues, followed the apostles [Col. 1608A] and supplied support and services, just as they followed the Saviour and ministered to him from their own resources.

[Note: [Col. 1607D] Augustine, *On the Work of Monks*.] For our Lord, to whom angels ministered, had compassion on the weak and possessed money-bags into which was put money given by believers for the necessities of food. He entrusted them to Judas, so that we too might learn to tolerate thieves in the Church, if we cannot avoid them. And he chose to have women who would minister follow him, showing what peoples owed to evangelists.

[Augustine] The Lord also had women in his company, lest they should appear excluded from salvation; and they ministered to him just as they did to the apostles.

“Or I.” As though he were saying: The other apostles possessed this right by the Lord’s ordinance. Or, that is, “do I alone and Barnabas not have,” according to you, “the right [Col. 1608B] to do this?” As though he were saying: We have the right to do this, that is, to receive support. He says “to do” for “to receive,” in order to speak more decently.

Or according to another reading, which has: “Do we not have the right not to work?” As though he were saying: We certainly have the right not to work with our hands, that is, to cease from manual labour. And lest, because he abstains, he should seem to have reproved his fellow apostles, he adds: “Who serves as a soldier,” etc. Here, through human analogies, he proves that this is permitted both to himself and to others; he then adds the authority of the Law and finally that of the Lord himself.

As though he were saying: We, whether ourselves or they, rightly have this right. For who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends [Col. 1608C] a flock and does not eat its milk? Certainly no one. The milk of the flock means whatever is given by the people to their leaders. By these words the Apostle sufficiently indicates that his fellow apostles appropriated nothing beyond what was due to them; rather, as the Lord ordained, living by the Gospel, they ate bread freely given by those to whom they preached grace freely given. These things, indeed, are said according to the allowance of human custom.

**VERS. 8–15.—** “Do I say these things merely according to man? Or does not the Law also say these things? For it is written in the Law of Moses: ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain.’ Is God concerned with oxen? Or does he say this certainly for our sake? For it was written for our sake, because he who ploughs ought to plough in hope, and he who threshes, in hope of receiving fruit. [Col. 1608D] If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things? If others share in your authority, why not we even more? But we have not used this authority; rather, we endure all things, lest we give any stumbling-block to the Gospel of Christ. Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat the things from the sanctuary, and that those who serve at the altar share with the altar? Thus the Lord also ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel. But I have used none of these things.”

“But do I say these things merely according to man?” That is, do I prove this only by human analogy? Or does not the Law also say these things—that is, does not the Law of Moses prove the same thing? Certainly. For it is written in the Law of Moses: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain”—that is, you shall not forbid a preacher to live by the Gospel, that is, by preaching. But lest this seem to have been said literally, he adds: “Is God concerned with oxen?” That is, does he give a command in the Law concerning them? He says this not for oxen, but only for our sake, as he puts it: “Or does he certainly say this for our sake?” As though he were saying: Certainly he says it.

For, etc.

[Ambrose.] As though he were saying: He truly says this for our sake, because these things and others directed to the same end were written for our sake, as this itself is true: because he who ploughs—that is, the preacher who opens hearts to faith—ought to plough in hope of temporal maintenance, though not for the sake of that hope; for this ought not to be his intention or the end of his ministry. [Col. 1609B] And he who threshes—that is, distinguishes the good from the evil, like grain from chaff, by the quality of their conduct—ought likewise to do this in hope of receiving the fruit of maintenance.

“If we have sown among you.” After proving through analogies, he now proves by reasons that it is permissible for them to receive. As though he were saying: We truly have the right to receive, because if we have sown spiritual things among you—namely, things which give life to your spirit, or which have been given by the Holy Spirit—

[Augustine] namely, the word of God and the mystery of the kingdom of heaven—is it a great thing if we reap, for our support, your carnal things: that is, those temporal things granted for the life and need of the flesh?

“If others.” Again, from the lesser, he proves that it is permissible for him to receive maintenance from them, saying: If others, namely false apostles, share in your authority—that is, use your possessions [Col. 1609C] with such power that you yourselves do—why not we apostles even more, who labour for the sake of your salvation? Nevertheless, etc. As though he were saying: See, it is plain that we are permitted to receive, but nevertheless we have not used this right.

And because perhaps they might say that he did not need it, the Apostle adds against this: “But we endure all things lest we give any stumbling-block to the Gospel of Christ.” For if the Apostle received support, the false apostles would already receive it freely, and so would persist in preaching; thus an impediment would arise for the Gospel.

[Ambrose.] Therefore, in order that the right of the Christian rule might remain, he made lawful things as though unlawful. Or he says this because perhaps these Corinthians were greedy and would therefore hate the Apostle if he received anything from them. Or he says this because, if he received from them, they would think that they had bought permission to sin, and [Col. 1609D] thus the Apostle would lessen his freedom to rebuke them.

“Do you not know,” etc. He returns to what he had begun, commending it again and again—that is, showing in many ways—that he is permitted to receive, yet will not do so. Natural reason also holds that one should live from that in which one labours. Here therefore he again proves, by the analogy of pagan or Jewish priests, that he has the right to receive; natural reason agrees with this, so that he may not make light of, or treat as idle, what he commends by so many testimonies.

As though he were saying: I am truly permitted to receive, as is evident from this: those who work in the sanctuary—that is, in the temple—as craftsmen eat what belongs to the sanctuary; and those who serve [Col. 1610A] at the altar—as priests—share with the altar, because they receive a part of what is offered at the altar.

[Ambrose.] And “do you not know” this? Or the former statement refers to pagan priests, namely, “those who work in the sanctuary,” and this to the Jews, namely, “those who serve at the altar.” By “sanctuary” he means the temple of the Gentiles, and by “altar” that of the Jews; the ministers of both receive a portion of what is offered. And just as this happens here, so the Lord Christ ordained—that is, reasonably appointed—concerning preachers. For what did he appoint for those who proclaim the Gospel, that is, preachers? Namely, that they should live by the Gospel. He made this reasonable provision so that they might be freer to preach the word of God. The Lord gave them this permission when he sent them out to preach, saying: “Behold, I send you,” etc. (Luke 10). And shortly afterwards: “Remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they have. For the worker is worthy of his wages” (ibid.).

“But I.” As though he were saying: It is established in so many ways that it is permitted. But I have used none of these things—that is, none of these authorities or examples—in receiving support.

[Augustine] And lest anyone perhaps suppose that he had not received because they had not given, and that he had repeated these statements about his right for the purpose of inducing them to give hereafter, he adds:

**VERS. 15–17.—** “But I have not written these things in order that they should be so done to me; for it is better for me to die than that anyone should make my glory void. For if I preach the Gospel, it is no glory to me; for necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me, indeed, if I do not preach the Gospel! For if [Col. 1610C] I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me.”

“I have not written.” As though he were saying: I have not used this right, nor do I wish to use it; as he says: “But I have not written these things”—namely, that it is permissible to receive support—“in order that these things should be done to me,” that is, that I should receive it.

“For it is better for me.” As though he were saying: I truly did not write in order to receive, because if I received I would lose my glory. And “it is better for me to die,” that is, I prefer to die; or, I prefer to die, that is, to suffer, rather than that anyone should make my glory void. This would happen if I received support—that is, if I preached in order to receive it.

[Note: [Col. 1609D] Augustine, *On the Work of Monks*.] He calls his glory that which he has before God by having compassion on the weak. For whoever does not wish to use what is owed to him gives more abundantly to the Church. Therefore the Apostle has the greatest glory before [Col. 1610D] God in not demanding from the weak the support owed to him, but providing his daily food through his own labours. This is what the Lord says to the innkeeper to whom that wounded man who fell among robbers was brought: “If you spend anything more, when I return I will repay you” (Luke 10).

[Ambrose.] The Apostle spent more, who served as a soldier at his own expense. Or he calls his glory that which he has before God because, by receiving nothing, he kept false apostles away from preaching, since they preached only for temporal things. For this reason the Apostle abstains from maintenance, lest he become a model for rapacious false apostles in receiving it.

“For if.” As though someone asked: Would your glory be made void if you preached in such a way that these things were done to you? He answers: Certainly, because I would not preach from love, and thus there would be no glory. For if I preach only in such a way that I do not do it from love of God and neighbour and from free will, there is no glory for me before God. And indeed in this alone there is no glory, because this is necessary by injunction, as he says: “For the necessity of a command is laid upon me.” Nor do I dare omit it, because woe will befall me. Hence he adds: “For woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel,” as has been enjoined upon me.

“But if.” As though he were saying: If I act from necessity, there is no glory for me; but if I do this willingly—that is, if will is joined to necessity, so that I preach from love—I have an eternal reward. But if I do it unwillingly, only a stewardship has been entrusted to me, because even if I have no reward, I nevertheless dispense to others and benefit them. For it is clear that no one receives recompense from God for something he does unwillingly. But if he does it voluntarily, he is worthy of reward, because he consents to God, and what is done willingly is done better. But one who does something without devotion does it not from will but from necessity, because he unwillingly does what has been commanded him.

Or thus, beginning at “for if,” where he says that his glory would be void if he preached for the maintenance by which he was supported—which would indeed seem so if he did not abstain when it was expedient:

[Ambrose.] As though he were saying: My glory would truly be made void. For if I preach the Gospel in order that these things should be done to me—

[Note: [Col. 1611D] Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*.] that is, if I preach for the purpose of attaining those things, and place the end of the Gospel in [Col. 1611C] food, drink, and clothing—there is no glory for me before God. Why is there no glory if I preach in this way?

[Note: [Col. 1611D] Id., *On the Work of Monks*.] Because then it would be done from necessity. This is what is meant by: “For the necessity of sustaining this life is laid upon me.” And truly: “Woe to me”—that is, want will be mine, like that of the false apostles—if I do not preach the Gospel; that is, to my harm I shall not preach, for I shall be tormented by hunger and have no means of living. Therefore this is the necessity laid upon me to preach the Gospel: I have no means of living. Or, it is that I may gain temporal fruit from preaching eternal things. Thus there is necessity in preaching, not will.

But if I do this willingly—that is, without any necessity of this life—I have an everlasting reward. But if I do it unwillingly, as one compelled by the necessity of this life, a stewardship has been entrusted to me: that is, I provide for others, not for myself. And the sense is:

[Note: [Col. 1612D] Id., *On the Sermon on the Mount*.] If, compelled by want of those things necessary to temporal life, I preach the Gospel, others will have a reward through me, but I shall not, because I do not love the Gospel itself but place its price in those temporal things. [Augustine] It is wicked for this to happen: that a person should minister the Gospel not as a son but as a servant to whom a stewardship has been entrusted, so that, like one dispensing another’s goods, he himself receives nothing from it except provisions.

Elsewhere, however, the Apostle also calls himself a steward. For even a servant adopted into the number of sons [Col. 1612A] may faithfully dispense to his fellow-participants the same thing in which he has obtained a portion as co-heir. But here such a steward is meant as one who, like a servant, dispenses another’s property and receives nothing from it himself except provisions. Elsewhere, as has been said, he is called a steward who, as a son, ministers the Gospel to his fellow-heirs.

Therefore we ought to do good with a single heart. We ought not, then, to preach in order that we may eat; rather, we ought to eat in order that we may preach. Thus food should not be the good which we seek, but a necessity added to our work, so that this may be fulfilled: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. 6). He did not say, “First seek the kingdom of God, and then seek these things,” although they are necessary; rather, he said: “All these things shall be added to you,” that is, they will follow [Col. 1612B] if you seek those things, lest, when you seek these things, you be turned away from the former. Nor should you set up two ends, seeking both the kingdom for its own sake and these necessities for the sake of the kingdom. Therefore for the kingdom of God alone we ought to do everything, not contemplate temporal reward either alone or together with the kingdom of God.

**VERS. 18–22.—** “What then is my reward? That, preaching the Gospel, I may offer the Gospel without expense, so as not to abuse my right in the Gospel. For though I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all, that I might gain more. And I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews. To those under the Law, as though I were under the Law, though I myself was not under the Law, that I might gain those who were under the Law. To those who were without the Law, as though I were without the Law, though I was not without the Law of God but was under the Law of Christ, that I might gain those who were without the Law. I became weak to the weak, that I might gain the weak. I became all things to all, that I might make all saved.”

“What then?” As though he were saying: Since reward comes from the will, let us see how. He asks it interrogatively: “What then is my reward?” That is, by doing what, and how, shall I possess eternal reward? He answers: I shall have reward in this way, namely, if I have such love for the kingdom that, while preaching Christ’s Gospel, I offer—that is, establish—the Gospel even without expense, so that I do not abuse my right in preaching the Gospel.

[Augustine] This would occur if he received support, because then he would neither rebuke freely nor have compassion on the weak. And the meaning is: I have reward if, out of love, I act in such a way that I prefer to suffer want rather than abuse my right. I would certainly do this if, by importunately demanding or indiscreetly receiving support, I showed the Gospel to believers as burdensome. From this perhaps it would result that they thought the Gospel was preached to them so that it might be sold; through this the vigour of evangelical authority and freedom to rebuke would also grow weak.

[Ambrose.] Nor would he have compassion on human weakness; and for that reason I did many other things as well. Hence follows: “For though I was free.” As though he were saying: I shall certainly do what I have said, for I have done something greater: although [Col. 1613A] I was free from all—that is, beholden to none by their merits—I made myself servant of all, in order to serve the interests of all. He says that he made himself servant of all because through humility he showed himself like all the weak, so that by patience he might strengthen them for future salvation, cherishing their souls. And I did this “that I might gain more,” that is, might obtain the gain of my preaching.

And I even adapted myself to all, as he says: “I became to the Jews as a Jew,” in accepting or not accepting foods and things of that sort.

[Haimo.] He even circumcised Timothy; this does not seem to have been an act of pretence, such as flatterers commonly perform.

[Augustine] For a godly man and spiritual physician, knowing the causes and wounds of all, cherishes them and has compassion with great skill. Therefore he became to the Jews as a Jew because, to avoid giving them offence, he circumcised Timothy and went up to the temple after purification, lest they take occasion from him to blaspheme. And he did this in order that I might gain—or gain for Christ.

[Haimo.] And to those under the Law, namely the Samaritans, who receive only the five books of Moses, which the Jews do not use together with them, I became as though under the Law. For he does not deny that the Law is from God, but teaches Christ from it; just as the Samaritan woman, instructed by the Law, said: “I know that the Messiah is coming.” Though I myself was not under the Law in a servile manner. And why did I become such to them? In order that I might gain those who were under the Law. Those under the Law are understood to be the Samaritans. They are of Persian and Assyrian origin, [Col. 1613C] whom the king of Assyria, after removing the children of Israel, placed to inhabit the regions of Samaria.

And I became to those without the Law—that is, the Gentiles—as though I were without the Law, when I agreed with them, according to philosophical reasoning, that the world and the things made in it were created by God, that the soul is immortal, that we have our origin from him, and things of that kind. Yet I was not without the Law of God, but was under the Law of Christ, not the Jewish Law. And I became such in order that I might gain those without the Law, that is, Gentiles.

And I became weak in faith to the weak, by abstaining from lawful things. Why? In order that I might gain the weak. What follows in each case? “I became all things to all,” as though I belonged to every sect. For the prudent and spiritual Apostle yielded to all, yet did not depart from the purpose of true religion; for wherever he yielded, he yielded in order to be of benefit. Hence he adds: “That I might make all saved.”

Observe that in these words, “I became as a Jew to the Jews,” etc., Jerome and Augustine seem to disagree. Jerome holds that he was not truly a Jew and did not truly observe the legal rites, but only pretended to do so as a matter of dispensation. For he held that those legal observances could not be kept after Christ without sin. Augustine, however, says that he in no way pretended either to be a Jew or to observe those legal rites; rather, he was truly a Jew and truly observed, without placing his hope in them, those legal rites which he said could be observed after Christ without sin [Col. 1614A].

For Jerome says: “I became as a Jew to the Jews.” He says “as,” because he was not truly a Jew, just as neither was he truly a Gentile, to whom he accommodated himself in foods and matters of that sort, though not in the worship of idols; for “in Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision” (Gal. V). Thus, as a matter of dispensation, he pretended to be a Jew.

But Augustine says that this was done through the compassion of mercy, not through pretence: just as one who ministers to a sick person becomes, as it were, sick—not by falsely claiming to have fevers, but by considering with a sympathetic mind how he himself would wish to be served if he were ill. Augustine says thus: “I became as a Jew to the Jews”; he said this not with the craftiness of pretence, but with the mercy of fellow-feeling—that is, he did not say this in order to feign himself a Jew, as some [Col. 1614B] suppose. For he did those things freely, as he says: “Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised” (I Cor. VII), that is, let him not live as though he had become uncircumcised. And elsewhere he says: “Your circumcision has become uncircumcision” (Rom. II).

According to this conviction of his, therefore, he did those things which those who did not understand and paid little attention supposed he had feigned. For he was a Jew, and had been called while circumcised; he did not wish to become uncircumcised—that is, he did not wish to live as though he were not circumcised. [Note: [Col. 1613] Augustine says the same in his letter to Jerome.] For this was now within his power, and he was not under the law in a servile fashion.

Therefore he lived truly, not falsely, as the Jew that he was; just as he did not deceptively feign himself to be a Gentile, but was lawfully permitted to use every food, even those condemned by Jews—for to him every creature of God was good, not feignedly but truly [Col. 1614C]. Therefore, just as he truly adopted these Gentile practices, so he also received the Jewish sacraments without deceit, so that he might not be simple with the former and double-minded with the latter, having one thing in his heart and another in outward appearance.

For when I asked you in a letter how he could be thought to have become as a Jew to the Jews because he deceitfully adopted Jewish sacraments, when he also became as a Gentile to the Gentiles and yet did not deceitfully adopt Gentile practices, you replied: “He became as a Gentile to the Gentiles in that he permitted without distinction the eating of all foods, even those which Jews condemn.” Therefore I ask whether he did this too only in pretence. If that is utterly absurd and false, then in those matters in which he conformed to Jewish custom he acted with prudent freedom, not with servile necessity or deceitful dispensation [Col. 1614D]. Why did he preserve truth in the wild olive graft, yet spread over the natural branches some veil of dispensatory pretence?

Likewise, when he says, “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (II Cor. XI), he did not pretend another’s weakness, but grieved over it. Likewise, when he became weak to the weak, it was not a lie; rather, he spoke truly. So too in the foregoing matters, where he said that maintenance was owed him, yet he abstained lest he appear to be a seller of the Gospel and lest the course of God’s word be hindered among the unlearned by falling under evil suspicion. He did not wish to receive what was owed him by the Lord’s own ordinance; nor, because [Col. 1615A] he did not wish to receive it, did he certainly lie. For he did not say that it was not owed to him; rather, he showed that it was owed, declared that he had not used what was owed him, and that he did not wish to use it at all—thereby becoming weak to the weak.

Therefore this is not deceptive and double-faced pretence, but his merciful compassion adapts itself to all. In the likeness of compassion he bears their weakness, not deceiving them by the invention of a lie; thus he helps the Jew or pagan as he himself would wish to be helped if he were like that person, as though he himself had their weaknesses. For one who ministers to a sick person becomes, as it were, sick—not by falsely claiming to have fevers, but by considering with a compassionate mind how he would wish to be served if he were ill.

Thus he said that he was as a Jew to the Jews and as a Gentile to the Gentiles, not because he compassionately pretended those things [Col. 1615B], but because he did not pretend the things he did that resembled Jewish practice, any more than he pretended the things he did that resembled Gentile practice. 91 And so he became all things to all, not by a liar’s cunning but by a sympathizer’s affection: that is, not by deceitfully doing all their evils, but by mercifully healing the evils of all as though they were his own, doing for others what he would wish done for himself if there were need. For he considers that, as a human being, he himself might have been caught in the vices in which others are caught. Hence elsewhere he says: “Considering yourself, lest you too be tempted” (Gal. VI).

## Verses 23–27

“But I do all things for the sake of the Gospel, that I may become a partaker of it. Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it. [Col. 1615C] Everyone who strives in the contest abstains from all things; and they indeed do so in order to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible one. Therefore I run in this way, not as toward an uncertain goal; I fight in this way, not as one beating the air. Rather, I discipline my body and reduce it to servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified.”

“But I do all things.” Here is why he adapts himself to all. As though he said: “I became all things to all,” etc. But I do all these things for the sake of the Gospel, so that it may run without hindrance, and so that I may become a partaker of its promises—that is, of righteousness and eternal blessedness.

“Do you not know that those who run in the stadium,” etc.? By the comparison of athletes he shows that what he has said must be done: namely, that one must abstain from things that are contrary. As though he said: [Col. 1615D] “For the sake of the Gospel I do all the things mentioned above, and rightly so; for unless I do all these things and abstain from everything contrary to them, I shall not have the reward, as appears from the comparison. For do you not know that those who run in the stadium all indeed run? They are equal in their exertion, but one receives the prize.” The *bravium* is the reward for running.

[Augustine] Likewise, you too must run in such a way—persevering in works of charity to the end—that you may obtain the prize of the eternal calling.

Or thus: “Do you not know,” etc.? [Ambrose] By this example he shows how great is the benefit of our law, in which the palm is promised not to one person but to all—a thing not true of that stadium, that [Col. 1616A] spectacle. There only one receives the prize; the rest depart defeated, although they have labored equally. Here, however, it is not so. [Note: [Col. 1615D] Augustine, on Psalm XXVIII.] For however many run, if they run perseveringly, receive it; and the one who arrives first waits to be crowned together with the one who comes later. For it is not desire for gain but charity which makes this contest. All who run love themselves, and love itself is their running.

As though he said: “This is why I labor thus for all, because all can possess the crown, which is not so in a worldly contest. For do you not know that those who run in the stadium all indeed run, but only one receives the prize, whereas here everyone does? But you all must run in such a way that you may obtain it.”

Or thus: “Do you not know?” As though he said: “This is why I labor thus for all, because although many are called, few are chosen. Therefore I labor so that at least in this way a few out of many may be saved, as appears in this comparison. Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all indeed run, but one”—that is, as though he said, “a rare one,” not every one—“receives the prize”? And because not everyone who runs receives it, therefore run “in this way,” that is, so perfectly that you may obtain it. And note that this interpretation accords in part with the first.

“Everyone who strives,” or, “for.” As though he said: “Truly one must strive in this way, because this is evident even in a lesser matter, where one receives the prize; for everyone who competes,” etc. Or connect it thus: “Do as I have said. That these things ought to be done is apparent in a lesser matter, because everyone who competes in a contest abstains from everything that impedes the prize of the contest; so you too ought to abstain from [Col. 1616C] stumbling-blocks.”

[Note: [Col. 1616D] The same author, on Psalm LVII.] Observe that many comparisons are drawn from things not worthy of praise: as in the Gospel, from the unjust judge who would not hear the widow; and from the lazy man who lends loaves to one asking, not because of friendship, but because he has been overcome by annoyance; and in the Psalm a comparison is given from the *marsus* [a snake-charmer], who casts spells to draw an asp from a dark cave. Thus athletic and theatrical pursuits are not thereby commended, though a comparison is drawn from them.

“And they.” As though he said: “Truly we ought to abstain from stumbling-blocks, since they abstain from things contrary to their purpose; for here the matter is greater. And”—that is, because—“they indeed abstain in order to receive a corruptible crown, but we ought to abstain in order to receive an incorruptible crown.”

[Ambrose] For us a spiritual crown is reserved, not woven from earthly, withering [Col. 1616D] flowers, but set with eternal gems after the fashion of a royal diadem.

And because such a crown is reserved, therefore “I run in this way,” that is, by acting so lawfully, “not as toward an uncertain goal”—that is, so as to be uncertain of the reward. One runs toward an uncertain goal who does such things that from some he may hope, and from others despair. The Apostle says that he has not done this, and therein sets himself as an example to others.

“I fight in this way against enemies, not as one beating the air”: that is, I contend not in words but in deeds; or, I do not fight in vain like one who strikes the air instead of an enemy. “Rather, I discipline my body,” that is, I restrain the unlawful motions of the body, “and reduce it to the servitude” of reason [Col. 1617A], when it was striving in another direction. For it is subjected to servitude when it performs not its own will but that of the Spirit.

“I do this lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified,” that is, rejected by God. [Augustine] By his own fear the Apostle has made us afraid. For what does the lamb do where the ram trembles? Therefore he terrifies us by his example, saying that he fears what could quickly happen; then others must take all the more care lest, by causing offence, they become disqualified.

# Chapter X

## Verses 1–4

“For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same [Col. 1617B] spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock which followed them; and the rock was Christ.”

“For I do not want,” etc. In what precedes, he taught by analogous arguments and his own example that one must abstain even from lawful things. Here, by the example of the Jews who fell through their negligence, he makes us watchful, showing that the ancients did not escape punishment through participation in the old sacraments. As though he said: “To obtain the prize, one must act as I have said. For baptism and the other sacraments are not sufficient, as some suppose, any more than God’s benefits profited the Jews when they afterward sinned.”

“For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers,” that is, the founders of our faith, “all”—namely both good and bad—[Col. 1617C] “were under the cloud,” which protected them from heat and from the Egyptians, so that they might not be seen by them. Or, they were under the cloud because all things happened to them as a figure of us.

“And all passed through,” their enemies having been drowned, “the Red Sea; and all were baptized into Moses,” that is, under the leadership of Moses, “in the cloud and in the sea.”

[Ambrose] That is, they were purified through those visible signs; for through them they were both delivered from imminent death and cleansed from the ignorance of God which then oppressed all the nations, and they were prepared to receive the law. “And all ate the same spiritual food,” namely manna; “and all drank the same spiritual drink,” namely water from the rock.

He calls manna and the water that flowed from the rock spiritual, because they were supplied not by nature, nor by the law of the world, but by God’s power, without a mixture of elements; and because they also contained within themselves a figure of the mystery to come, which we receive in remembrance of Christ. Therefore manna was called the bread of angels, because it was created by the power through which angels subsist, signifying that he who would spiritually feed us was to come from heaven. Hence manna first came down from heaven on the Lord’s day for the people’s satisfaction. Accordingly, he rightly calls their food and drink spiritual in this sense: that they signify something spiritual.

“For they drank from the spiritual rock,” because water flowed from it by God’s power, following them—that is, [Col. 1618A] satisfying their desire, because wherever they went, abundant waters followed them. Thus Christ accompanies his own in the desert of this world. Or, “from the rock which followed,” that is, which signified the truth that was to follow. Concerning this he adds:

“And the rock was Christ,” in signification. [Augustine] For a thing which signifies is commonly called by the name of the thing it signifies. Therefore Christ was the rock, not in substance but in signification. Hence the rock which is understood to be Christ is rightly called the following rock. For where human assistance failed them, Christ was present. It was not the rock that gave them water, but Christ.

Or, “our fathers,” not theirs, because we are not like them, those proud men; and he speaks only of the good fathers: “all were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea.” These points do not change. “And all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.”

[Note: [Col. 1617D] Augustine, on John.] They are said to have been baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea because all these things bore the figure of our sacrament, that is, baptism. Moses signifies Christ, the cloud the Holy Spirit, and the Red Sea baptism consecrated by the blood of Christ. The people passing through signifies the faithful; the death of the Egyptians signifies the washing away of sins. Thus all those things were figures of us. What was then enacted figuratively is now fulfilled in our salvation, because then future things were announced, now past things are read, and present things are known.

And the sense is: “All were baptized into Moses,” that is, under that leader, “in the cloud and in the sea,” that is, they received the sign of baptism, which had the same efficacy for believers.

[Note: [Col. 1617D] The same author, on John.] Here is the meaning of what he had said, “They passed through the sea.” He explains it when he says: “All were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.” If, therefore, the figure of the sea had such efficacy, how much will the outward form of baptism avail? If that which was enacted in figure led the people across to manna, what will Christ provide in the truth of his baptism for the people brought across 92 through him? For by baptism he brought them across, after all sins, as enemies, had been slain in believers.

To where did he bring them across? To manna. What is manna? “The living bread which came down from heaven” (John VI). “And all ate the same spiritual food,” the same as we do.

[Note: [Col. 1618D] The same author, Against Faustus.] When he says “spiritual,” he shows that it must be understood spiritually in Christ; and by this he indicates the same of all the things, namely that they must be understood spiritually. When he expounds one thing—“the rock was Christ”—all the rest are illuminated. For by explaining this one thing he introduced understanding into the others.

The sense is: They ate food, certainly bodily and spiritual; but spiritual food, the same as we do. Yet their bodily food was different, namely manna, which signifies Christ and produced the same effect in believers.
