But others, namely those who did not believe, ate and died eternally—which was not so with Moses and the other good persons. Why?

[Note: [Col. 1618D] The same author, on John.] Because they understood the visible food spiritually [Col. 1619A], hungered spiritually, and tasted spiritually, so that they might be satisfied spiritually. We too today receive visible food; but the sacrament is one thing, the power of the sacrament another. Those were sacraments, and ours are sacraments too—indeed, sacraments of the same thing.

For manna signified Christ; this bread signifies the altar of God—that is, upon the altar is that which signifies him. For Christ is “the bread which came down from heaven” (John VI). “If anyone eats of this bread, he shall not die forever” (ibid.); but this pertains to the reality of the sacrament, not to the visible sacrament: the one who eats inwardly, not outwardly; who eats with the heart, not the one who presses the outward form with the tooth.

[Note: [Col. 1619D] Augustine, on John.] Therefore the Apostle carefully does not say simply, “They ate the same food,” but adds “spiritual,” because they ate the same spiritual food as we do. For their bodily food was different, since they had manna and we have something else. Thus he also carefully says, “our fathers,” not theirs, thereby signifying only the good, to whom we are like—not those who ate the same spiritual food as we do. Yet theirs was one thing and ours another in visible appearance, but different things signifying the same reality by spiritual power.

“And all drank the drink,” certainly both bodily and spiritual. But they drank the same spiritual drink as we do; their bodily drink, however, was different, namely the water which was a sign of Christ’s blood and produced the same effect in believers.

[Note: [Col. 1619D] The same author, on Psalm LXXIV.] Therefore he calls the drink which they drank and we drink spiritual, because the same thing is signified by their drink and ours. Hence theirs and ours are the same spiritual drink and food, because in mystery their food and drink are the same as ours; the same in signification, not in visible form. For the same Christ was figured for them in the rock, manifested to us in flesh, and signified on the altar under the appearance of bread.

[Note: [Col. 1619D] The same author, on John.] One faith is certainly the same under differing signs: they believe that he will come; we believe that he has come. Therefore he does not simply say, “They drank the same drink,” but adds “spiritual”; for they drank the same spiritual drink as we do, but not the same bodily drink.

What, then, did they drink? “For they drank from the spiritual rock which followed them”—spiritual, namely, because it signified Christ, and it was the same in faith. Therefore remain in the faith; observe the changed signs. For there the rock was Christ; for us, that which is placed on God’s altar is Christ. If you attend to the visible appearance, it is different; if to the intelligible signification, they drank the same spiritual drink.

[Note: [Col. 1619D] The same author, on Psalm LXXVII.] For there were among that people persons who also understood spiritually, possessing the faith later revealed, belonging not to the letter of the law but to the grace of the Spirit; and in this respect they drank the same drink from the spiritual rock. From what rock?

[Note: [Col. 1620D] The same author, on John.] “And the rock was Christ.” But in signification the rock was struck twice with the rod. The twofold striking signifies the two pieces of wood of the cross. Water was drawn from the rock when the rod came to it [Col. 1620A], because when the wood came to the rock, Christ, spiritual grace flowed forth.

[Note: [Col. 1620D] The same author, in the book *On Expressions*.] This manner of speaking must be carefully noted: things that signify something are called by the name of the things which they signify.

## Verses 5–11

“But God was not well pleased with most of them; for they were struck down in the wilderness. Now these things happened as a figure of us, that we might not be desirers of evil things, as they also desired them. Neither become idolaters, as some of them were, as it is written: ‘The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.’ Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and twenty-three thousand fell in one day. Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him, and perished by serpents. Neither murmur, as some of them murmured, [Col. 1620B] and perished by the destroyer. Now all these things happened to them as a figure; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.”

“But God was not well pleased.” He shows that temporal benefits were granted to the Jews, both good and bad, yet the evil perished. As though he said: “The Jews used all these benefits literally, but God was not well pleased with most of them”—that is, with those Jews who offended God. When he says “with most,” he shows that there were some among them with whom God was well pleased. Though the sacraments were common to all, the grace which is the power of the sacraments was not common to all. So too now baptism is common to all the baptized, [Col. 1620C] but the power of baptism—that is, grace itself—is not.

“For,” etc. As though he said: “It is apparent from this that God was not well pleased with some of them. For”—that is, because—“they were struck down in the wilderness.”

[Augustine] But lest you think that people invented these things, he adds: “Now these things happened”—I do not say were spoken or written—“as a figure of us.”

[Note: [Col. 1620D] The same author, on Psalm LXVII.] These things did not happen only for their sake, but for ours, namely for our correction. For those punishments were figures of our punishments. How great, then, are the punishments of which those were figures! For just as among good things that which is signified through a figure is far better than the figure itself—for example, the kingdom of heaven is better than the land of promise—so among evil things that which is signified is far worse than the signifying figure; for example, Gehenna is worse than any temporal punishment, however terrible. For all punishments are less than Gehenna, and must therefore be avoided with greater watchfulness.

“That we might not,” etc. As though he said: “They happened as a figure of us, so that, considering their punishments, we might not desire evil things as they desired them”—that is, lest we sin as they did and perish likewise. “Neither become idolaters” through things sacrificed to idols.

[Ambrose] He touches upon those who feasted in an idol temple, thinking themselves free from guilt. “Do not become,” I say, “as some of them” [Col. 1621A] were, “as it is written in Exodus concerning them: ‘The people’”—that is, some of the people; he puts the whole for the part—[Augustine] “‘sat down to eat and drink before the calf,’” just as you do in an idol temple. By recalling them he points to the practices found among the Corinthians, showing how severely they were punished among the Jews. “‘And they rose up to play,’” that is, to perform games in honor of the calf. Or, “to play,” that is, to worship—something like children’s play. Childhood is indeed readily given to play. What is more like childish play than worshipping idols?

[Ambrose] “Neither let us commit fornication,” as some among you do, “as some of them committed fornication with Midianite women, and therefore twenty-three thousand fell in one day. Neither let us tempt Christ,” as do those who despair of [Col. 1621B] the resurrection, “as some of them tempted him,” saying: “Can he prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Ps. XVII). Note that Christ is God, whom the Jews tempted. Therefore they perished by serpents, until the bronze serpent was raised up; those who looked upon it were healed from the serpents’ bites.

“Neither murmur,” as you do against me, or as those who possess lesser gifts of the Spirit do against God, “as some of them murmured against Moses,” and therefore “perished by the destroying angel,” who struck them outside the boundaries of the promised land.

“Now all these things.” As though he said: “These things happened to them because of their sins, and not only for that reason, but also so that it might be figured that we would perish for similar things. This is what he says: ‘Now all these things happened to them as a figure of us.’”

“But they were written for.” [Ambrose] Through these examples we are summoned to a more upright life, so that we may deserve either reward if we are obedient, or a more severe punishment if disobedient. The punishments of sinners were recorded so that we might be corrected; otherwise the punishment will be greater.

[Augustine] Here he has made clear why the writings of the Old Testament are received by us, and why it is no longer necessary for us to observe those signs in things. For when he says, “They were written for our correction,” he shows how carefully we must read and understand them. But when he says, “as a figure,” he shows that it is no longer necessary for us to serve the observance of the figures that foretold things to come, since the reality itself is manifest.

“For our correction,” I say, “upon whom”—namely us—“the ends of the ages have come,” that is, the sixth age; we are in the final age of the world and ought to be corrected all the more by so many examples of those before us. Or, “the ends of the ages have come upon us,” that is, worldliness and carnality—the love of temporal things—comes to an end in us through Christ; and therefore, if we sin, it is more shameful.

## Verses 12–15

“Therefore let him who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall. Let no temptation overtake you except what is human. But God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also make an escape, so that you may be able to endure it. Therefore [Col. 1622A], my beloved, flee from the worship of idols. I speak as to prudent persons: judge for yourselves what I say.”

93 “Therefore,” etc. As though he said: “And because they perished even though they enjoyed benefits, therefore, considering them, let him who thinks that he stands through good works take heed lest he fall through himself. For the one who stands stands by God; the one who falls falls by himself.” Therefore he says, “take heed lest he fall,” by sinning or by causing others to sin.

This concerns those who, presuming upon knowledge, ate things sacrificed to idols to the scandal of their brothers, and who, glorying in the teaching of false apostles, judged the Apostle although they themselves were guilty. Thus he cuts off pride, lest through it they be tempted as the Jews were tempted and perished. For as the Jews, disparaging Moses, tempted God, so these people, disparaging the Apostle, tempt God.

“I say lest he fall,” not because anyone is wholly without a fall, but lest temptation—that is, the delight of sin—overtake you, that is, lead reason to consent; and let there be no temptation in you except a human one, that is, one arising from matters without which this life cannot be lived.

Or: “Let no temptation overtake you except what is human.” [Augustine] He exhorts them that a human temptation, and no other, may overtake them. For human temptation is when in necessity or pressure a person does not lose trust in God by seeking human assistance.

[Ambrose] Therefore, suffering for Christ is a human temptation, through which one advances with God.

[Note: [Col. 1621D] Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*.] Or human temptation is thinking otherwise than the matter truly stands, though with a good intention. But to love one’s own opinion excessively, or to envy those who are better, until one reaches the sacrilege of breaking communion and establishing schism or heresy, is diabolical presumption. Yet to think in no respect otherwise than the matter truly stands is angelic perfection.

[Note: [Col. 1622D] The same author, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] Human temptation, then, I believe, is when someone with good intention nevertheless, through human frailty, errs in some judgment; or when in zeal to correct a brother he becomes angry more than Christian tranquillity requires. Since we are human beings but angels in hope, to whom we shall be made equal in the resurrection, if angelic perfection is not in you, let there not be diabolical presumption. Therefore he says, “Let no temptation overtake you”; and if one does arise—which God permits Satan to bring about to test or exercise the good and punish the evil—let it not overtake you except as a human temptation.

“But God is faithful.” As though he said: “I exhort you to this, but God is faithful,” that is, true in his promises, who promised that he would be the protector of his elect. He will not allow you, when afflicted for his sake, to be tempted beyond what you can bear, because he either does not permit you to fall or raises you after a fall. “But with the temptation he will also make an escape,” that is, an increase of virtue. For he who grants permission to the devil who tempts also gives mercy to those who are tempted. He makes the escape in such a way that you may endure perseveringly, not fail in the struggle, but conquer—which comes about through humility. For humility preserves one in every temptation, so that those who do not have the wind of pride do not burst [Col. 1623A] in the furnace.

“Therefore.” As though he said: “Because sacraments alone do not save; because one who falls is punished; and because God’s help is not lacking—therefore, my beloved, flee from the worship of idols,” that is, abstain from every participation in idolatry, lest through it temptation toward God arise. Let no one, therefore, be constantly present in an idol temple, nor hope anything from it. For to hope from it is to doubt God—as Saul did, who, abandoning God, who had become angry with him because of his sin, returned to idolatry in the hope of gaining something from it. It harmed him in the present and produced for him the avenging Gehenna in the future.

Therefore the Apostle urges these people to flee from the superstition of idolatry: namely, lest the knowledgeable eat things sacrificed to idols to the offence of the weak, to whom they appear to be idolaters; or lest the weak themselves [Col. 1623B] be idolaters, by eating under the veneration of an idol and thinking that the idol is something.

“And so that you may flee, I speak to you as to prudent persons,” that is, I speak something profound to you, as though to prudent persons. “Therefore judge for yourselves,” that is, carefully discern what I say, namely this: “The cup,” etc.

Or thus: “I speak as to prudent persons.” As though he said: “I warn you to flee idolatry; and in giving this warning I speak to the weak persons who are among you, as I spoke above. Speak as to prudent persons, and judge for yourselves whether the things I say are true and good.” He demonstrates this by a comparison and example from the new sacrament, that he may persuade them more easily; for those whom words do not satisfy are often persuaded by examples. Therefore he says:

## Verses 16–18

“The cup of blessing which we bless, [Col. 1623C] is it not a communion of the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of the Lord? Because we, though many, are one bread and one body, all who partake of the one bread and of the one cup. Consider Israel according to the flesh. Are not those who eat the sacrifices partakers of the altar?”

The cup of blessing, etc. As though he were saying: Therefore the worship of idols must be avoided, because one who eats food sacrificed to idols as food sacrificed to idols is one with the demon, just as, by receiving Christ’s body worthily and spiritually, one is one with Christ himself. For the cup—that is, the drink of Christ’s blood—is “of blessing,” that is, the cup by which the participant is blessed, and which we also bless, that is, which we faithful exalt by believing and giving thanks. Or: “the cup of blessing which we bless” [Col. 1623D], that is, the drink in the cup, which was not only blessed by Christ at the supper but which we priests also bless daily—“is it not a communion in Christ’s blood?” That is, does it not bring us into a certain communion with Christ’s life? As though he said: Certainly it does. And “the bread which we break” in the sacrament—that is, participation in the bread broken upon the altar—“is it not a participation in the Lord’s body?” That is, does it not make us one with him? Certainly it does. [Note: [Col. 1623D] Augustine, *On the Eucharist*.] For when Christ is eaten, life is eaten. But who would dare to eat his Lord? Yet, inviting us to eat, he says: “He who eats me lives because of me” (John 6). Nor [Col. 1624A] is Christ killed in order to be eaten; rather, when he is eaten, he gives life to the dead; he refreshes, and is not diminished. And when eaten he lives, because when killed he rose again. Nor, when we eat, do we divide him into parts. Yet this is what happens sacramentally. [Augustine] And the faithful know how they are to eat Christ’s flesh. Each receives his own portion; hence these graces themselves are called “portions.” He is eaten in portions in the sacrament, yet remains whole and entire in heaven; he remains whole and entire in your heart. For he was wholly with the Father when he came into the Virgin; he filled her and did not depart from the Father. He came into flesh so that human beings might eat him, yet remained whole with the Father so that he might feed the angels.

“Because there is one bread.” He explains how the cup of blessing and the bread become, for the recipient, [Col. 1624B] Christ’s flesh and blood. [Ambrose] As though he said: Through this we are one with Christ: because all of us who partake spiritually and worthily of the one bread, namely Christ’s body, and of the one cup, namely Christ’s blood, though we are many, are nevertheless one bread through the unity of faith, hope, and charity. And we are one body of that Head, which is Christ, through the supplying of works of charity; that is, we are one—one Church—united by the bond of faith, hope, and charity and by the mutual rendering of God’s works. [Augustine, Haimo] For by the unity of the bread and the unity of the body one must understand faith and charity; if these are absent, one receives judgment upon oneself. [Note: [Col. 1624D] Id., *On the Sacraments of the Faithful*.] And because we are one, he says that we ought to think one thing, so that one faith may have one understanding and one work.

[Col. 1624C] Figuratively, however, the one bread and one body are called Christ’s Church, because just as one bread is made from many grains and one body from many limbs, so Christ’s Church is composed from many members; so Christ’s Church is joined together from many faithful persons by charity. Christ consecrated this mystery of our peace and unity upon his table. Whoever receives the mystery of unity but does not maintain the bond of peace receives the mystery not for himself but against himself. And no one should doubt that a person then becomes a partaker of the Lord’s body and blood when he becomes a member of Christ’s body; nor is he cut off from fellowship in that bread and cup even if, before eating that bread and drinking that cup, he departs this world while established in the unity of Christ’s body. For he is not deprived of the benefit of that sacrament when he is found to possess what that sacrament signifies. For in that sacrament he who also made us ourselves commended to us his body and blood. For we too have been made his body.

“See Israel.” Here a comparison is introduced in order to understand what was said above. As though he said: Those who partake of one bread and cup are partakers of Christ’s body; and this is evident from the following comparison. See, then, Israel according to the flesh—that is, carnal Israel, observing the fleshly commands of the law and serving in the shadows of sacrifices. [Col. 1625A] He says “according to the flesh” because there is also an Israel according to the Spirit. See, I say: are not those who eat the sacrifices of that law—that is, of carnal Israel—partakers of the altar? [Augustine] They certainly are. Thus those who eat Christ’s flesh and drink his blood are his partakers.

Or it can be read so that “Israel” is in the vocative case. As though he said: Thus it is with us who receive the bread and cup; and you who are Israel—that is, people who see God—see, that is, learn how matters that are according to the flesh, namely fleshly matters such as idolatry, stand. For just as we who receive from one bread and one cup are conformed to Christ’s body, so those who eat sacrifices offered to idols are partakers of the altar of error, that is, of the demon. And are they not? Certainly [Col. 1625B] they are.

### Verses 19–23

“What then? Do I say that what is sacrificed to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything? But what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. And I do not want you to become partners of demons, because you cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot be partakers of the Lord’s table and the table of demons. Or do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he? All things are lawful for me, 94 but not all things are beneficial. All things are lawful for me, but not all things build up.”

“What then?” As though he said: What I say is, “Flee the worship of idols.” What then? Do I say—that is, do I seem to say—that what is sacrificed to idols is something great? No, [Col. 1625C] I do not say this; but rather I say that what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. [Haimo] For in the idol the devil is worshipped, and he is worse than the idol. [Note: [Col. 1625D] Augustine, *Against the Enemy of the Law*.] And because he had been forbidding idolatry, from which this passage took its beginning, lest they suppose that eating from idol-sacrifices did no harm because the idol is nothing, he confirmed both that the idol is nothing and that he did not forbid these things because an idol is something, but because they are sacrificed to demons and not to God.

Therefore let them not excuse themselves by saying that they are not devoted to insensible idols: they are rather devoted to demons, which is more dangerous. [Note: [Col. 1625D] Id., *On Psalm 26*.] For if they worshipped idols alone, just as the idols would not help them, so they would do them no harm, since neither idols nor what is offered to them are anything—that is, they have no power in themselves either to help or to harm. [Col. 1625D] But evil spirits have an innate malice and malevolent desire to harm us.

“And I do not want you.” I say that they sacrifice to demons; but I do not want you who are faithful to become partners of demons. This does not arise from the nature of the thing sacrificed, but from consciousness of the idol, or from the conscience of the brother wounded by your example. [Note: [Col. 1626D] Id., *On Christian Doctrine*.] To this kind also belong consultations and certain approved and covenantal agreements of signs with demons: such as the practices of magical arts, diviners who inspect entrails, augurs, bindings, and remedies performed with spells; and certain vows, or the hanging up and tying on of certain objects. Nor are those to be separated from this class of harmful superstition who, from consideration of birthdays, are called genethliacs, but are now commonly called mathematicians—those who attempt to foretell the outcomes of actions. [Col. 1626A]

Therefore I do not want this, because you cannot drink the Lord’s cup and the cup of demons at the same time; that is, you cannot at once be united to God and to a demon. And absolutely, you cannot be partakers of God’s table and the table of demons—that is, you cannot be one with God and with demons. Then, including himself among them, he says: “Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy?” That is, do we provoke him to anger, or envy him by eating food sacrificed to idols? As though he said: We ought not to do this. Those who eat food sacrificed to idols to the scandal of their brothers seem to provoke and envy the Lord, whose kingdom they diminish, being imitators of the devil. [Col. 1626B] For through jealous envy Satan devised idolatry, so that people, denying God, might serve idols and the Creator might lose the worship due to him. [Ambrose] Thus these persons too seem to be jealous of the Lord, and it will turn out badly for them, since they are not stronger than he. Therefore he adds: “Are we stronger than he,” so that we can resist him?

“All things are lawful for me.” Even if I call those who eat food sacrificed to idols sinners, I nevertheless do not say that these foods are unlawful, because all things are lawful for me. [Augustine] He speaks of things pertaining to food; but not all things are beneficial—that is, they do not assist me in my course, but rather hinder me. Then he qualifies the same statement differently, saying: “All things are lawful for me”—by the power of free will and the teaching of natural law. [Ambrose] For all things are lawful according to [Col. 1626C] natural law, because all things are clean; for the discussion here concerns foods and meat sacrificed to idols. Therefore he rightly says, “are lawful,” that is, they are forbidden by no command of the Lord. Or, “all things are lawful,” not because all things, including unlawful things, are lawful. Rather, let us suppose that all things are lawful. Yet not all things build up one’s neighbors, as when someone eats food sacrificed to idols and gives offense to his neighbor. And therefore:

### Verses 24–33

“Let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to another. Eat whatever is sold in the market, asking no questions because of conscience. The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness. If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions because of conscience. But if anyone says, ‘This has been sacrificed [Col. 1626D] to idols,’ do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you and for conscience’s sake. Now I mean conscience—not yours, but the other person’s. For why should my liberty be judged by another’s conscience? If I partake with thanksgiving, why am I reviled for that for which I give thanks? Therefore, whether you eat or drink or do anything else, do all things to God’s glory. Give no offense to Jews, Greeks, or the Church of God, just as I please all people in all things, seeking not what is useful to me but what is useful to many, that they may be saved.”

Let no one seek only what is his own—that is, what is useful only to himself in some way—but what is another’s; and therefore one must sometimes refrain from lawful things [Col. 1627A] so as to benefit another. [Ambrose] And because all things are lawful, yet one ought not always use them, he determines how it is lawful to eat or not eat, saying: “Eat whatever comes into the market”—that is, whatever is there or sold—if you wish, “asking no questions,” namely whether it has been sacrificed or not, or anything of that sort; and this because of the conscience of the weak bystander.

I say, eat everything. You can indeed do so safely, because, as the authority testifies, “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness”—that is, all things by which the earth is filled; and what belongs to the Lord cannot be unclean. Likewise, if one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions because of conscience. But if anyone says, “This has been sacrificed to idols,” do not eat. Why? [Col. 1627B] Not because the food is unclean, but for the sake of the one who informed you, lest he think that you eat in reverence for the idol and glory in his superstition. The one who serves idols will glory as though you revered the idols, and will be confirmed in his error because he sees you gladly desiring food sacrificed to idols; and a bad example is given to the brethren.

Therefore I speak this to the wise, who, despising the idol because it is nothing, ate of the sacrifice to the scandal of the weak. I say, for that person’s sake and for the conscience of others, namely as he immediately specifies, saying: “I mean conscience, not yours,” which is firm, “but another’s,” namely the weak person’s. “For why,” etc. As though he said: One must give it up for another, because if I acted otherwise I would be blameworthy for what is lawful and reproached for thanksgiving [Col. 1627C] by the uninstructed, who would think that I judged the idol to be something great. To prevent this, one must take great care.

“For why should my liberty be judged by another’s conscience?” That is, why do I act so that I am condemned, for another person’s sake, concerning something freely permitted, when that person suspects some dishonorable implication from it? As though he said: Since my conscience is free from devotion to the idol, why should I appear to eat for the sake of reverencing the idol? For I am judged not to differ from idolatry. “If therefore I partake with thanksgiving”—that is, by giving thanks to God—“why am I reviled?” That is, why do I fall under the blasphemy of the uninstructed for that for which I give thanks?

And because these evils result from it, “whether you eat or drink or do anything whatever, do all things [Col. 1627D] to God’s glory,” that is, to God’s praise, namely with invocation of the Creator, so that God may be praised in the actions of your conduct. For if these things are rightly done, they are praises of God.

[Note: [Col. 1627D] Augustine, *On Psalm 160*.] Therefore not only should your voice sound God’s praises; your works also should agree with your voice. When you have sung with your voice, your life may at some time fall silent; but sing in such a way that you never fall silent. For if you cry aloud with your mouth while plotting fraud, you have fallen silent in the praise of God and—what is more serious—have proceeded into blasphemy. For when God is praised because of your good work, you praise God; and when God is blasphemed because of your evil work, you blaspheme God. Therefore, if you take what you eat and drink for the refreshment [Col. 1628A] of the body and restoration of its limbs, giving thanks to him who has supplied these consolations of sustenance to you, a mortal and fragile person, your food and drink praise God. [Haimo] But if you exceed the measure due to nature through the excess of gluttony and gorge yourself with drunkenness, however much your tongue may sound God’s praises, your life blasphemes.

And “give no offense to Jews,” who abhor idols, “or Greeks,” who are not thereby reproved but confirmed in their error, “or the Church of God,” as regards the weak who are in the Church and are given offense when, following their example, they attach themselves to things hostile to God. Be so, I say, that you may please all people, just as I please all people in all things, acting without giving scandal to anyone. For this is to please all people in all things: to act without scandal to anyone, for the progress of others, so that it may be useful both to them and to oneself. [Note: [Col. 1627D] Id., *On Correction and Grace*.]

Observe that here he says, “I please all.” But elsewhere he says: “If I were pleasing people, I would not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1). He said “I would be pleasing,” however, so far as lies within himself—that is, insofar as it belongs to his own will. It is as though he said: If I wished to please, if I sought to please, I would not be God’s servant. But the one who pleases people for the sake of truth is no longer the one pleasing them; truth itself pleases them. If, however, a person pleases for his own sake—that is, seeks to please for private and personal glory—this is pride, and therefore does not please. But when he pleases people for truth’s sake, it is no longer the person but God who pleases.

Thus both statements can rightly be made: “I please,” and “I do not please.” If a good interpreter and devout seeker is present, both will be evident, and no mutual contradiction will repel the one entering. Let this also not disturb you—that I say, “I please all.” Did he please his persecutors? But he pleased every class of people for whom he gathered Christ’s Church, whether those already within it or those to be brought into it. And, to show that he pleased for truth’s sake, he adds: “Not seeking what is useful only to me, but what is useful to many”; and I seek no earthly advantage, but that they may be saved.

95

## Chapter XI

### Verses 1–3

“Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ. Now I praise you, brothers, because in all things you remember me and keep my instructions just as I delivered them to you. But I want [Col. 1628D] you to know that Christ is the head of every man; the man is the head of woman; and God is the head of Christ.”

“Be imitators of me.” As though he said: I say that you should give no offense. In this matter, so that you may offend no one, be imitators of me, as I too am of Christ; and thus through me you will be imitators of Christ, who offended no one but came to save all. [Note: [Col. 1628D] Augustine, *On Psalm 33*.] For in the Church the ranks of greater and lesser persons are ordered so that the former go before by example and the latter follow by imitation. But do those who precede by example follow no one? If they follow no one, they will go astray. Therefore they too follow someone: Christ.

“Now I praise you.” Here he begins to deal with coverings, concerning which he rebukes them for not keeping his traditions, because some of their men prayed or prophesied with covered heads, and some women without covered heads. [Col. 1629A] [Ambrose] Therefore the Apostle is angry with them because, although he was their Apostle, they had forgotten his traditions. As though he said: I blame you concerning other matters, but in this I praise you, brothers; and although I blame you concerning other matters, nevertheless I praise you in this, that in all things you remember me—that is, my authority—and keep my instructions as perfectly as I delivered them to you. It is irony that the Apostle speaks to them thus, because they were not keeping his tradition or following his authority. Accordingly, he gives them the instruction as though newly, saying: “But I want.”

As though he said: You do not keep my instructions. But I want you to know, brothers, something useful for what follows, which you do not observe: namely, that Christ is the head of every man—that is, his Lord—because, when the man did not exist, he was created through Christ. But the head of woman is man, because she was formed from his rib, though by God’s power; and therefore she ought to be subject to the man, from whom she was made through Christ. But God the Father is the head of Christ, because Christ was begotten by him. It is therefore fitting that the Father be called the Son’s head, as it were his begetter. Thus one term has different meanings. Christ is called man’s head in one way, man woman’s head in another, and God Christ’s head in another. [Note: [Col. 1629D] Augustine, *Questions*, Book 83.]

Or, by “man” here is meant the spirit—not that Holy Spirit who remains immutable with the Father and Son and is given immutably to worthy souls, but the human spirit, which, as the soul’s husband, rules its animal affection as a wife. Concerning it the Apostle says: “No one knows what belongs to a human being except the human spirit” (1 Cor. 2). And concerning it the Lord said to the Samaritan woman: “Go, call your husband” (John 4). [Col. 1629C] Therefore when this spirit is present—that is, attentive—and subjects itself devoutly to God, it understands spiritually what is said, being enlightened by the light of wisdom. [Note: [Col. 1629D] Id., *Against the Manicheans*.] Christ is the head of this man, because the human spirit is ruled by God’s wisdom, which is Christ. And as all bodily senses are in the head, so all spiritual senses—that is, the fullness of graces—are in Christ, from whom this man receives.

Through this the man is woman’s head, that is, ruler of the animal nature that is governed by the spirit as a woman by her husband. But God the Father is Christ’s head, because the Son is from and of the Father, not the Father from or of the Son. [Col. 1629D] [Note: [Col. 1629D] Id., *On the Creed*.] The Father is the Son’s principle, and is therefore called his head; Christ too is a principle, but not the Father’s. The Son is the Father’s image, in no respect unlike him and wholly equal to the Father; he owes to the Father his very being, including his equality to the Father and his being a principle. But the Father owes what he is to no one.

Or, by “God” here is understood the Trinity. [Note: [Col. 1630D] Id., *On the Trinity*.] But if “God” here means all three together, how is God the head of Christ—that is, how is the Trinity Christ’s head, when Christ is in the Trinity, so that he is the Trinity? Or is that which is Father together with the Son and Holy Spirit the head of that which is the Son alone? [Col. 1630A] For with the Son and Holy Spirit the Father is God; but the Son alone became man. According to this humility, the Father is greater even than he; and in this respect it is truly said that what he is together with the Father and Holy Spirit is the head of the human mediator, which he alone is.

For if we rightly call the mind the governing principle of a human being—that is, as it were the head of human substance—although the human being together with the mind is the human being, why should it not be much more fittingly said that the Word together with the Father is God, and that God is the head of Christ, although Christ cannot be understood as man unless together with the Word which became flesh? Therefore God—that is, the divine essence, or the Trinity—is [Note: [Col. 1630D] Id., in the same work.] Christ’s head insofar as he is man, because the divinity, being the creator, is head of the assumed creature. This interpretation does not diminish the Son’s power but proclaims mercy. [Col. 1630B]

### Verses 4–7

“Every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head. But every woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered dishonors her head; for it is one and the same as if she were shaven. For if a woman is not covered, let her also be shorn. But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaven, let her cover her head. A man indeed ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but woman is the glory of man.”

“Every man.” As though he said: And because Christ is man’s head, without any intermediary, and through Christ, God, therefore man ought not to bear a covering—the sign of subjection—since it is a mark of freedom. For every man, even one powerful or wise, praying for something from God or [Col. 1630C] prophesying—that is, expounding the Scriptures—with his head covered, as though he were not of a free mind, dishonors his head; that is, it is shameful for him to act with his head covered. In other circumstances, when appropriate, he may cover his head; but he is not yet presenting himself to, and conversing with, his Judge, where he must confess his condition.

But every woman praying, who is inferior and subject to man because man is woman’s head, praying or prophesying with uncovered head—that is, without the sign of subjection which she owes to man, as though nothing stood between her and God—dishonors her head. And indeed she does: “for it is one,” that is, it is equally shameful, “as if she were shaven.” “For if she is not covered.” As though he said: An uncovered woman is the same as one shaven; and that will indeed happen, because she will either be shaved or shorn, [Col. 1630D] which it is evident she does not wish. Thus he says: “For if a woman is not covered, let her be shorn. But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaven, let her cover her head.”

A man indeed, who is superior, ought not to cover his head—that is, to bear the sign of subjection—as though he were not free in relation to God. By “covering” here one should understand not every covering, but a certain kind, which the ancients used and many still use in some places: one by which the whole head was wrapped and which is almost like women’s veiling. “Since,” etc. [Ambrose] As though he said: A man ought not to cover his head, and honor forbids him to do so, since man is God’s image and glory, which ought not be concealed. For it is unsuitable that God’s image and glory, which is seen in man, should be hidden. [Col. 1631A]

For man was made in God’s image, not woman. But what is God’s image in man? Namely this: that the one God made one human being, so that, just as all things are from him, so all human beings might be from this one man; that the one visible man might bear on earth the image of the one invisible God; that the authority of one principle might be seen to be preserved by one God in one man, to the devil’s confusion, since he rejected the one God and wished to usurp dominion for himself. Thus man is God’s image because, just as all things are from God, so all human beings are from Adam; and so he preserves the authority of the principle that all things are from one God, against him who wished to be God.

[Haimo] Or, man has God’s likeness in this: just as the origin of the Church flowed from the side of Christ sleeping in death—namely blood and water, signifying the sacraments by which the Church is saved—so a bride was born for Adam from his side, because the rib from which Eve was formed was taken from it. [Col. 1631B] And just as Christ presides over and governs the Church, and the Church serves him, so man presides over and governs woman. Therefore man should not have the sign of subjection, but that of freedom and precedence. And man is God’s glory because he is from God and chiefly glorifies God. But woman is man’s glory because she is from him and serves him.

Or, man is called God’s image because he was chiefly created in God’s image, and reason naturally flourishes more in him than in woman, as though he himself were reason. [Col. 1631C] [Note: [Col. 1631D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*.] And observe carefully that here “man” is called God’s image, and in Genesis one reads, “Made in God’s image” (Gen. 9), where it is said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). Notice also that “let us make” and “our” are spoken in the plural, which should be understood only relationally. For it must not be understood as though gods were making, or as though man were made in the image of gods, but as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit making.

Therefore man was made in the image of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that he might subsist as God’s image; and because that image of God was not made wholly equal, being not born from him but created by him, to signify this it is called God’s image while it is not left unspoken that it was made “in the image.” For it is not equal to him, but approaches him through a certain likeness. One approaches God not by distance of place but by likeness, and departs from him by unlikeness. Therefore, though man is an image, he is also said to have been made in God’s image because of his unequal likeness. But the Son, insofar as he is God, is the Father’s image and not made “in the image,” because he is equal to the Father, whose image alone he is. But man is the Trinity’s image and is made in the image.

[Note: [Col. 1631D] Id., *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*.] Hence: God made man in his image, so that, just as God presides over all creatures by omnipotence, so man might preside over all earthly animals by intelligence. And he is God’s glory when he follows [Col. 1632A] God’s wisdom. But woman is man’s glory because she was made as man’s help, not for carnal desire—for before mortality overtook them they did not have corruptible bodies—but so that man might have glory from her when he went before her toward God and offered himself to her for imitation in holiness, just as he would be God’s glory when following God’s wisdom. Hence he adds:

### Verses 8–10

“For man is not from woman, but woman from man. For neither was man created for woman, but woman for man. Therefore woman ought to have a covering upon her head, because of the angels.”

“For man is not,” etc. As though he said: Woman is man’s glory, not man hers. The order of creation shows this, because man, namely Adam, is not from woman, namely Eve; but woman, namely Eve, is from man, namely Adam. And [Col. 1632B] there is another reason why woman is man’s glory: “For,” that is, because, man, namely Adam, was not created for woman—that is, to assist Eve—but woman, namely Eve, for man—that is, to help man. [Ambrose] And therefore, namely, to show that woman is subject to man, and because transgression began through her, woman ought to have a covering over her head, so that in the Church she may not have an uncovered head without a veil; and this “because of the angels,” that is, out of reverence for priests, because they are God’s messengers, so that, as before the Lord’s judge, she may be subject to man before his priestly representative. Or, “because of the angels,” namely lest priests, looking into her face, be aroused to lust. [Note: [Col. 1632D] Id., *On the Trinity*.]

Another interpretation from the passage, “Since he is the image,” etc. The Apostle says that man is God’s image. Therefore he removes the covering of the head from man and urges that it be placed upon woman, because she is not God’s image. But what shall we say to this? Why is woman not also God’s image? This seems certainly contrary to what Genesis says: “God made man in God’s image; male and female he made them” (Gen. 1). [Col. 1632C] [Augustine] Why, then, is man God’s image so that he should not cover his head, and woman not, so that she should cover it? But I believe that what the Apostle says belongs to the nature of the human mind. He speaks mystically of covering; for unless some hidden meaning is intended, what is said is empty.

For, as not only the truest reason but the Apostle’s own authority declares, man was made in God’s image not according to bodily form but according to the rational mind, in which, as the same Apostle says, he is renewed in the knowledge of God: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who was created according to God” (Eph. 4). And elsewhere: “Put on the new man, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him” (Col. 3). [Col. 1632D] [Note: [Col. 1632D] Id., in the same work.] Therefore, if we are renewed in the spirit of our mind, and that is the new man who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him, no one doubts that man was made in God’s image not according to the body or according to any part whatsoever of the soul, but according to the rational mind, where knowledge of God can exist and where there is no sex—in the spirit of the mind. There woman is the same as man, and woman with man—that is, the whole substance—is one image of God, because human nature itself was made in God’s image and is God’s image; the whole of it is God’s image because in both sexes God’s image is completed. Woman is not separated from that image, any more than she is excluded from the grace of renewal and the restoration of God’s image. [Col. 1633A] [Note: [Col. 1633D] Augustine, *On Genesis*.] Woman certainly possesses her own rational mind, according to which she too was made in God’s image. [Note: [Col. 1633D] Id., *On the Trinity*.] Therefore nothing excludes woman from participation in the image, since even in humanity’s first condition she had the rational mind according to which she too was made in God’s image.

Therefore God made the whole human being in his image, namely according to the spirit. But because of the unity of their union, Scripture says: “God made man in his image.” And lest anyone suppose that only the human spirit, in which God’s image is, was made, it adds: “Male and female he made them”—this according to the body, where they are recognized as two according to sex, although it had first used the singular number because of the unity of their union.

Thus there is a common nature in their minds, but in bodily sex the division of the mind is signified. For there is one eminent part of the soul or mind, which extends itself to what is eternal by contemplating truth. This is God’s image, adhering to the contemplation or consultation of eternal reasons; and therefore it is not to be restrained by a veil, as though it should be held back from them. Thus [Col. 1633C] man ought not to cover his head. There is another, lower part of the soul, directed by a certain attention toward the conduct of temporal affairs. Thus the soul, insofar as it consults and beholds truth, is God’s image; but insofar as it attends to these lower actions, it is not God’s image. Since, however, in bodily and temporal matters descent into lower things is exceedingly dangerous, it has authority over its head by which it may be restrained, as the woman’s head-covering signifies.

Therefore what belongs to the whole man is God’s image. [Note: [Col. 1633D] Id., *On Genesis*.] But what belongs only to the helper assigned to him is not God’s image, because only what adheres to unchangeable truth is God’s image. In a figure of this matter the Apostle says that man alone is God’s image and glory, but woman [Col. 1633D] man’s glory. [Note: [Col. 1634D] Id., *Against the Manicheans*.] Thus, although this is outwardly represented in two people of different sex, it is nevertheless understood within the single inner person. The person’s higher power—that is, reason—is called man, or the ruling part of the mind, because it ought to govern the lower sensuality. This man is God’s image because he adheres to the contemplation of unchangeable truth, and God’s glory when reason subjects sensuality to itself; and this is most orderly when Christ is man’s head.

The woman, however, is the glory of the man. The woman is sensuality itself, which is suitably signified by woman, because in the female it naturally predominates; by serving, it is the glory of reason. [Col. 1634A] Hence it is said: “It is not good for man to be alone” (Gen. 2). For this purpose it was good that she should be made: not only that the soul should rule the body, which occupies a servile place, but also that masculine reason should subject to itself the animal part, so that the inner mind, as masculine reason, may hold subject the animal appetite through which we pursue bodily pleasures. Thus a man ought to govern a woman and not allow her to rule over the man. [Note: [Col. 1634D] Id., *On the Trinity*.]

But if the animal part, through immoderate advance, slips too far into outward things, with the consent of its head—that is, reason, because reason does not restrain and curb it—then the house is perverse and miserable in which the woman rules over the man: she who presides over the watchtower of counsel in the masculine portion. And the inner man grows old among his enemies [Col. 1634B]—that is, demons jealous of virtue—and the vision of eternal things is withdrawn even from the man, when, with his wife, after the manner of the first parents, he eats what is forbidden. Thus the light of his eyes is not with him; and immediately both, stripped of that illumination of truth, have the eyes of conscience opened so as to see how unseemly and dishonourable they are. Like leaves of sweet fruits without the fruits themselves, that is, without good works, they weave together good words, so that by speaking well while living badly they may cover their shame.

Remember that, according to some, the sensual movement of the soul is represented by the serpent; the lower part of reason, by the woman; and the higher part of reason, by the man. To consent to enticements is to eat the forbidden food. If there is only the delight of thought, [Col. 1634C] the woman alone eats; but if an evil thought is put into action, or if there is a will to carry it out, then the man too tastes the forbidden food with the woman. Others, not implausibly, take bodily sense for the serpent, sensuality for the woman, and reason for the man.

This discussion, in which we have sought within the mind of each person a certain rational marriage, assigning the offices of contemplation and action to distinct parts while preserving the unity of the mind in both, is to be heard only so far as to make clear that the Apostle, in assigning the image of God to the man alone and not also to the woman, nevertheless intended the different sex of two human beings to signify something to be sought within one human being. For “woman,” as though he said, that is, sensuality, [Col. 1634D] is the glory of “man,” that is, of reason; she is not the source from which man proceeds. For man—that is, reason—does not come from woman—that is, sensuality—so that the rational part should be governed by the sensual; but woman—that is, sensuality—is from man, namely, so that she may be governed by him. It is as though he said: the distinction between the two indicates that what is spiritual should govern what is animal, and not the reverse. And so it is fitting; for man—that is, the rational part—was not created for woman, namely, to serve sensuality, but conversely woman for man—that is, sensuality—to serve reason. Therefore woman ought to have a covering over her head, signifying [Col. 1635A] that sensuality ought to be subject to reason.

“Because of the angels”: for this holy, consecrated, and devout signification is pleasing to the holy angels. For God does not see temporally, nor is anything new in his vision and knowledge when something happens in time and passes away, as the bodily senses of human beings—or even of heavenly angels—are affected by such things. [Note: [Col. 1635D] Bede, in a homily to be delivered at Easter.] For we must believe that angelic spirits are present with us, especially when we are engaged in divine services: that is, when we enter the church, attend with our ears to sacred readings, give ourselves to psalmody, devote ourselves to prayer, or celebrate the solemn rites of Mass. Therefore the Apostle warns women to wear a covering because of the angels. Nor may there be any doubt that, where the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood are performed, an assembly of the citizens of heaven is present—those who guarded with such vigilant watches the tomb in which the venerable body had been laid and from which it departed in rising again.

### Verses 11–17

> Nevertheless, neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man, in the Lord. For as the woman is of the man, so also the man is through the woman. But all things are of God. Judge for yourselves: is it fitting for a woman to pray to God unveiled? Does not even nature itself teach you that, if a man indeed grows his hair, it is a disgrace to him; but if a woman grows her hair, it is a glory to her, because her hair has been given to her as a covering? But if anyone seems inclined to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor has the Church of God. But in giving this instruction I do not praise you, [Col. 1635C] because you come together not for the better but for the worse.

“Nevertheless.” Although at the beginning—that is, in the first creation—the man is not from the woman, but the reverse. [Ambrose.] Nevertheless, in subsequent generation this is not so, because neither man is without woman nor woman without man in the Lord; that is, according to the Lord’s working, in whom neither is created without the other. He also created both originally from one thing—that is, from one matter—because he formed the woman from the man, and made both one in nature. The Apostle confirms that they are one in nature: for as woman was first made from man, so man is afterwards born through woman.

“But all things”: after setting forth the points one by one, in order to subject all things to God as the one first principle, [Col. 1635D] he adds, “But all things”—namely, the body and soul of each—“are from God” as author. He says this so that neither woman may grieve over subjection nor man be proud of exaltation.

Or thus: “Nevertheless.” As though he said: although transgression began through the woman and she is subject to the man, nevertheless neither man without woman nor woman without man exists in the Lord—that is, in faith in Christ. For neither stands in such a relation to the other in Christ the Lord that, if man is admitted, woman is excluded from salvation, or, if woman is admitted, man is excluded. He gives the reason why, once one is admitted, the other ought not to be excluded, adding: “For as woman is from man, so man is through woman.” This does not change.

“But you yourselves”: [Col. 1636A] because the Corinthians had not kept his tradition, and he had therefore reproved them above when he said, “I praise you,” etc., he urges the truth not from the authority of the tradition which they had neglected, but from nature. Nature teaches that women should be veiled in church, where they allowed them to be unveiled, acting against the sacramental meaning of the veil and the order of creation. As though he said: Since these things just stated are so, judge for yourselves whether it is fitting for a woman to pray to God unveiled. “Does not nature itself teach you?” Nature teaches us that, if a man grows his hair, it is a disgrace to him. [Note: [Col. 1635D] Augustine, *On the Work of Monks*.]

Here he spoke according to the law, which forbids a man to wear long hair. But if someone objects concerning Samuel and the prophets of the Old Testament, who did not cut their hair, let him consider [Col. 1636B] the difference between that mystical covering and this cutting of the hair. The case of Nazirites is different: they were specially commanded in Deuteronomy to grow their hair. For that covering—that is, the hair of the saints—signified the same thing as the veil placed over Moses’ face, namely, the veil of the reading of the Old Testament. This cutting of the hair, however, signifies the revelation of evangelical grace. Thus the hair of Samuel and the prophets, formerly retained as the veil of the Old Testament, is now laid aside in the revelation of the Gospel. Of this the Apostle says: “When you turn to Christ, the veil shall be taken away” (2 Cor. 3).

“But if a woman grows her hair, it is a glory to her.” [Augustine.] It is a glory to woman because she naturally possesses it as a covering. Hence he adds: “Because her hair has been given to her [Col. 1636C] as a covering.” [Ambrose.] Hair is an indication of a covering; therefore it is naturally fitting that a woman should be veiled and obey, so that the will of nature may be added: nature gives her a covering for this purpose, that she may know herself liable to judgment and subject; and therefore it is a glory to her if she has hair, because she has it by nature.

Natural reason agrees with this, and therefore a man is not naturally long-haired, because he is to be unveiled; the law likewise forbids a man to wear long hair. “But if anyone”: after giving the reason, in order to overcome the contentious he sets forward authority, because he does not wish to employ argument but authority. As though he said: nature too teaches what I hand down. But if anyone seems inclined to be contentious, [Ambrose] namely, one who does not wish [Col. 1636D] to yield to us, we say that we Jews—that is, we apostles who are from the Jews—have no such custom, nor has the Church of God [Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose], called from the other nations to faith in Christ. That is, neither Moses nor Christ taught thus—namely, that a man should cover his head and a woman should not.

“But this”—what has been said concerning covered heads—“I command” to be observed. The Apostle employs the authority of a command so that they may obey. For it is very unjust to wish lesser persons to obey oneself while refusing to obey greater persons. [Note: [Col. 1636D] Id., *On the Work of Monks*.] Here he shows that there are certain matters about which one must not argue, but must submit to the commanding authority. Hence he says: “But this [Col. 1637A] I command,” namely, that the cleverness of one disputing should not be sought, but the authority of one commanding should be observed; “not praising you, because you come together not for the better,” etc.

Having dealt with the covering of the head, in which they strayed greatly from the truth, he begins to address the Lord’s Supper, in which these same persons sinned greatly. As though he said: What has been said about covering or not covering the head I certainly command—not praising but reproving—the manner in which you come together for the Lord’s Supper, not for the better, but for the worse: that is, not for the use of perfection but for the harm of condemnation, as can be shown from several considerations.

### Verses 18–20

> First of all, when you come together in the church, I hear that there are divisions among you; and in part I believe it. For there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you. Therefore, when you come together in one place, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s Supper.

“First of all.” From the fact that, when you come together in the Church of God—which requires the unity of charity, so that, as people assemble bodily there, so they may also be united spiritually, namely by the affection of charity—I hear that there are divisions, that is, disagreements, among you. [Ambrose.] Note that by saying “first,” he shows that dissension is the first evil, from which the rest arise. For where there is dissension, nothing is right. I hear that there are divisions among you, and I also believe that this is so “in part,” that is, among some of you; and this is not useless to the good.

“For there must be heresies”: that is, it is even useful that heresies should exist, such as there were among those [Col. 1637C] who doubted the resurrection; but the divisions concerned spiritual gifts. [Note: [Col. 1637D] Augustine, *City of God*.] For the devil, seeing that the temples of demons were being deserted and that humankind was running to the name of the liberating Mediator, stirred up heretics who, under the Christian name, might resist Christian teaching. Those who in Christ’s Church hold some diseased and perverse view, if, when corrected so that they may hold what is sound and right, they obstinately resist and refuse to amend their destructive doctrines but persist in defending them, become heretics and are counted among the hostile armies.

[Augustine.] These too, even through their evil, benefit true Catholics, since God makes good use even of the evil, and “all things work together for good to those who love God” (Rom. 8). For all enemies [Col. 1637D] of the Church, either blinded by error or corrupted by malice, are beneficial: if they receive power to afflict her bodily, they exercise her patience; if they oppose her by erroneous thought, they exercise her wisdom. A question raised by an opponent becomes an occasion for learning. Many matters belonging to the Catholic faith, when they are agitated by the crafty disturbance of heretics so that they may be defended against them, are considered more carefully, understood more clearly, and preached more urgently.

There have arisen many who received the simplicity of heavenly words according to the sense of their own will rather than the proper exposition of the truth itself, interpreting them otherwise than the force of the sayings requires. For heresy is not a matter of the wording but of the understanding; the crime lies in the meaning, not the speech. [Note: [Col. 1637D] Id., ibid.] The kind of heretics, crafty not through the spirit of wisdom but of impatience, while disturbing Catholic peace, serves the use of those who are progressing, according to the saying: “The educated son will be wise, but he will make use of an imprudent servant.” [Note: [Col. 1637D] Id., *On True Religion*.]

Therefore let us also make use of heretics—not so as to approve their errors, but so that, in defending Catholic doctrine against their snares, we may be more watchful and cautious. Heretics benefit us, then, not by teaching the truth which they do not know, but by stirring Catholics to seek out and make known the truth. [Note: [Col. 1638D] Id., *Against the Manichaeans*.] Therefore divine providence permits many heretics to exist, so that when they assail us [Col. 1638B] and ask us things that we do not know, we may shake off sluggishness and desire to know the divine Scriptures.

Hence he says: “There must be heresies.” The Apostle neither wills nor desires that heresies should exist; rather, he says that this will happen and that it is useful. But for what is it useful? So that not only the reprobate, who say, “I am of Paul,” but also those who are approved among you—that is, among yourselves, such as those who say, “I am of Christ”—may become manifest to human beings. These are approved by God, who are able to teach well; but they cannot become manifest to people unless they teach. They do not wish to teach unless there are persons seeking instruction; but many are too sluggish to seek unless, through the troubles and attacks of heretics, they are awakened as though from sleep. [Note: [Col. 1638D] Id., *On the Usefulness of Believing*.]

A heretic, however, is one who, for the sake of some temporal advantage—and especially for the sake of his own glory and pre-eminence—either devises or follows false and novel opinions. But one who believes such things has been deceived by an appearance of truth and piety.

“When you come together,” etc. Here he rebukes them because they did not receive the Lord’s body in the order in which it ought to be received. For they received the Eucharist during meals or after meals, whereas they ought rather to do so fasting. They took occasion for doing this from the fact that the Lord, while the disciples were eating, took bread, blessed it, and gave it to them, after the old Passover had already been celebrated. As though he said: Because there are divisions among you, therefore, when [Col. 1638D] you come together in one place—which ought indeed to occur not so much by the bodily association of persons as by the joining of hearts—already, that is, from this fact alone that there are divisions among you, it is no longer lawful to eat the Lord’s Supper. Or, “already” means: at present you have this loss, namely that it is not—that is, it is not lawful for you—to eat the Lord’s Supper; in the future it will be worse for you. [Note: [Col. 1638D] Id., to Januarius.]

By “the Lord’s Supper” he means receiving the Eucharist, which they ought not to receive after eating, or mix with their own meals, as did those whom the Apostle rebukes, but fasting, in honour of so great a sacrament. Although Christ gave his body and blood to his disciples after supper, it is not therefore right to find fault with the universal Church because it is always received by fasting persons. For the Saviour wished, in order to commend more forcefully the depth of that mystery, to impress this final act upon the hearts and memories of the disciples from whom he was about to depart to his Passion. [Note: [Col. 1639D] Augustine, to Januarius.] But he reserved it for the apostles, through whom he was to order the churches, to teach in what order it should afterwards be received.

### Verses 21–22

> For each person takes his own supper beforehand in order to eat; and one indeed is hungry, while another is drunk. Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the Church of God and shame those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you.

[Col. 1639B] “For each person.” As though he said: Therefore it is not lawful for you to eat, because each one of you who are contentious takes beforehand, not to distribute to the poor but to eat, his own supper before the Lord’s Supper. One is hungry, because you give him nothing; another is drunk, though you ought to be sober. He reproves in many ways those who, after eating, received the Lord’s body, contributed nothing from their luxurious meal to the hungry, and did this in church.

“Do you not?” As though he said: You eat your own supper before the Lord’s Supper and give nothing to the poor; but do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? That is, this ought rather to be done in houses. Or do you despise the Church of God—that is, the house of prayer? [Col. 1639C] That is what you truly do, even if you do not think so. And you shame—that is, make ashamed—those who have nothing; this is certainly what you do.

[Note: [Col. 1640D] Id., in the book of Questions on Leviticus.] Note that there are people in the Church of whom it is said, “That he might present to himself a glorious Church” (Eph. 5); nevertheless, the Apostle attests that the house of prayer itself is called by this name, saying: “Do you despise the Church of God?” Daily speech has also prevailed so that no one is said to go out to church or take refuge in church unless he has gone out or taken refuge in the actual place and walls which contain the congregation of the Church.

Or it may be read otherwise. “For each person,” etc. He censures those who took back for themselves the offerings they made at the altars and would not allow them to be shared with others who had nothing. Wealthy people offered bread and wine in abundance, so that it might be consecrated by the priestly blessing and consecration, and the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood be confessed. But after the celebration of the sacred mystery and the consecration of the bread and wine, they claimed their offerings back and, without sharing with others, took them alone, so as even to become drunk from them while others were hungry.

As though he said: Therefore it is not lawful for us to eat the Lord’s Supper, because each person takes back, in order to eat, his own supper—taking back all that he offered—and one is hungry while another is drunk. Thus you act against the signification and order of the sacrament. [Ambrose.] An offering, once made, becomes that of the whole people; that is, it ought to be shared with all, because all are figured in the one bread. Since all are one, they ought to receive from the one.

He therefore censures those who, in the church where people assemble for the sake of unity and mystery, claimed their own offerings for themselves because of the dissension sown by the pseudo-teachers. For the pseudo-teachers had sown such great dissensions among them that they jealously reserved and claimed their offerings, although the offerings of all were blessed by one and the same prayer. They did this so that those who had nothing to offer might be shamed, receiving no share; and they did it so quickly that those arriving later found nothing to eat. While they acted thus, he says that such things ought rather to be done at home than in church, adding: “Do you not have houses?” etc., which extends to that point.

“What shall I say?” As though he said: Since you do these things, what shall I say to you? [Col. 1640B] I find nothing worthy of you. I praise you in other matters, but in this I do not praise you—that is, I find nothing praiseworthy in you in this matter. Or distinguish the wording thus: “Shall I praise you in this? Certainly not; I do not praise you.” But in order that they may be corrected from their error, he repeats below the pattern laid down by Christ in this matter.

### Verses 23–24

> For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night in which he was betrayed, took bread; and, having given thanks, broke it and said: “Take and eat. This is my body, which will be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: “This cup is the new testament in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”

[Col. 1640C] “For I.” As though he said: Therefore I do not praise you in this, because it is the Lord’s body that you ought to receive, and in his remembrance. This I too received—that is, learned—from the Lord and handed on to you: namely, that our Lord Jesus Christ, on the night in which he was betrayed, that is, when his Passion was already imminent—for he suffered in the night, that is, having been seized and held in order to suffer, he came to the light of the resurrection—then, I say, he took bread and, having given thanks for the restoration of humankind that was thus to come, broke it. He gave one bread to all, so that they might remain in unity; and in breaking it he showed that his Passion was voluntary.

He broke it sacramentally—that is, according to what appeared, though it was believed by the faithful to remain whole—and said: “Take and eat,” [Col. 1640D] namely, that you may be conformed to me. For this sacramental reception signifies, and when worthily celebrated effects, the union of head and members. He also said: “This,” which appears to be something else, “is my body,” the same in substance as that which will be given for us. [Augustine.] Therefore it is not less the body and blood which someone receives because he does not receive it unto salvation. “Do this”—that is, receive and eat my body—“in remembrance of me,” that is, in memory of my Passion and death, so that you may follow as I have gone before.

Likewise, for our salvation and exhortation, he took the cup after he had supped—that is, after the old Passover had ended—saying: “This cup [Col. 1641A] is the new testament in my blood.” As though he said: What this cup contains is my blood, by whose shedding the new testament—that is, evangelical teaching—is confirmed, because a testament is confirmed in the dead. Or: it is the new testament, that is, a new promise, not of a temporal but of an eternal good. For under the old law carnal things were offered, and carnal things were promised according to the letter; but in the new, where the priest is the victim, what is offered is heavenly and what is promised is heavenly.

[Col. 1641B] For in Sacred Scripture, “new” or “old testament” is understood either as the teaching in which the old or new promise is contained, or as the promise itself. And he says: “As often as you receive, do this in remembrance of me,” that is, in memory of my Passion and death. [Ambrose.] The Apostle shows by these words that the mystery of the Eucharist, celebrated while supper was in progress, is not a supper. It is spiritual medicine, which, received reverently, cleanses the one devoted to it; and it is the memorial of our redemption, so that, mindful of our Redeemer, we may deserve to obtain greater things from him.

Because we were delivered through Christ’s death, we ought in eating and drinking to remember his flesh and blood; in this we have received the new testament, which is the new law and brings the obedient into the heavenly kingdoms. The testament is therefore established by blood, because blood is the witness of the divine benefit. Hence we receive it for the protection of body and soul: Christ’s flesh is received for the salvation of the body, while his blood is received for our soul. [Col. 1641C] And it was shed as Moses prefigured when he said: “The flesh is offered for our body, but the blood for the soul” (Lev. 17). Therefore the law commands that blood is not to be eaten. Since a fuller treatment of the Lord’s body occurs here, let us briefly consider what must be known about the sacrament of the body and blood.

Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ, about to pass from this world into the invisible things of eternal majesty, celebrated the sacrament of the old Passover; and after the typical lamb, at the end, he gave his disciples his own body and blood under the form of bread and wine. Here one must carefully observe why, after the sacrament of the typical lamb, he gave the apostles the sacrament of his body and blood; why under another form; and, given that another form, [Col. 1641D] why specifically this one; and, given this one, why under a double form. Next: why water is mixed in; after what, and by the good and by the evil, it is received; and finally, whether what seem to be or happen there truly are or happen.

It must be understood, then, that after the old Passover had been celebrated, the Lord gave his body and blood to his disciples in order to show that the sacraments of the old law were to cease—among which the sacrament of the Paschal lamb was chief—and that the sacraments of the new law were to be instituted, among which the sacrament of the Lord’s body excels. He also gave it after the other rites so that it might be impressed more firmly on the memory of the disciples and thereafter be frequently celebrated by the Church.

He gave it under another form, and instituted that it should thereafter be received by the faithful, so that faith might have merit; for faith is not concerned with [Col. 1642A] things seen, because faith has no merit for one who has [*h. r. p. ex*, corrupt or uncertain reading]. He did so also lest the eye recoil from what the hand receives, and lest unbelievers mock us. For he gave it under this form [99] because the reality of this form bears an exact likeness to each of the two realities of this sacrament: that which is contained and signified, and that which is signified but not contained.

The reality contained and signified is Christ’s flesh which he drew from the Virgin, and the blood which he shed for us. The reality signified but not contained is the unity of the Church in the predestined, called, justified, and glorified. This is the twofold flesh of Christ. Hence Jerome says: “Christ’s flesh is understood in two ways: either that which was crucified and buried, or that spiritual and divine flesh of which he himself says, ‘My flesh is truly food [Col. 1642B] and my blood is truly drink’ (John 6); and likewise, ‘He who eats my flesh abides in me, and I in him,’ etc.” (ibid.).

There are therefore three things to be considered in this sacrament: one which is sacrament only; another which is sacrament and reality; and a third which is reality and not sacrament. The sacrament and not the reality is the visible form of bread or wine. The sacrament and reality are Christ’s own flesh and blood. The reality and not the sacrament is the mystical flesh of Christ. Moreover, that visible form is the sacrament of the twofold reality: namely, what is contained and signified. A sacrament is a sign of a sacred reality; and that form signifies both realities and bears an exact likeness of each.

For as bread, above other foods, refreshes and sustains [Col. 1642C] the body, and wine gladdens and intoxicates a person, so Christ’s flesh refreshes and nourishes the inner person spiritually more than other graces; and his blood gladdens spiritually and so intoxicates that it makes one sober. Hence: “How splendid is your intoxicating cup!” (Ps. 22 [23]). It also bears a likeness to the reality only signified, namely the unity of the faithful.
