For as one bread is made from many grains, and wine flows together into one from many grapes, so the unity of the Church consists of many individual believers.

Christ’s own body, which he received from the Virgin, is also the sacrament of this unity. For as Christ’s body consists of many pure members immune from every stain of sin, so ecclesial unity consists of many [Col. 1642D] clean and unstained persons. As a type of this, the ark of the Lord was made from *ligna techni*, incorruptible woods resembling white thorn. Thus we see why he gave it under this form.

But since the whole Christ is received under the form of bread and the whole under the form of wine, why did he give it not in one form but in two? In order to show that Christ assumed the whole human nature, namely soul and body, so as to redeem both. Bread refers to the body and wine to the soul, because wine produces blood, in which physicians say that the seat of the soul is found. This sacrament is therefore celebrated under two forms so that Christ’s assumption of soul and flesh, and our liberation in both, may be signified.

Water is added in order to show that our redemption was accomplished through Christ’s Passion, [Col. 1643A] and that his Passion was undertaken out of love for us. Water signifies the human race. Hence in the Apocalypse: “The waters which you saw are peoples” (Rev. 17), and nations whose salvation could not exist without the Lord’s Passion, nor the Lord’s Passion without love for the people. For if he had not loved us, he would not have surrendered himself to death for us.

After this, we must consider whether Christ’s body and blood are received by the good and the evil. [Note: [Col. 1643D] Augustine, *On the Sacraments*.] Before this, however, it must be shown that Christ’s true body is on the altar, which some unbelievers deny; but Truth himself refutes them when he says, “Take; this is my body,” as do the authorities of the saints which have been brought forward.

For Ambrose says: “Before it is consecrated, it is bread and wine; but when the words [Col. 1643B] of Christ have done their work, Christ’s body and blood come to be.” Again: “Can Christ’s word, which could make from nothing what did not exist, be unable to change things which exist into what they were not?” Eusebius also says: “The invisible priest, by the secret power of his word, changes visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood.” Again: [Note: [Col. 1643D] Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book 3.] “Even in sinners and those who receive unworthily there are Christ’s true flesh and true blood, but by essence, not with saving efficacy.” Again: [Note: [Col. 1644D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Gospel*.] “Many unworthy persons receive the Lord’s body, concerning whom the Apostle says: ‘Whoever eats the Lord’s body and drinks the blood unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.’”

By this we are taught how carefully one must avoid receiving a good thing badly. For behold, evil results when a good thing is received badly; just as, conversely, good resulted for the Apostle when an evil thing [Col. 1643C] was received well—that is, when the thorn of Satan was given to him and borne patiently. From these testimonies of the saints, then, it is clear that Christ’s true body is on the altar and is received not only by the good but also by the evil.

Certain statements, however, appear to conflict with this, and they must not be passed over in silence. Augustine says: “The good person receives the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, but the evil person the sacrament and not the reality.” We shall say in reply that “sacrament” here denotes the Lord’s body taken from the Virgin, while “reality” denotes the spiritual flesh of Christ, which is the unity of the faithful. Therefore the good person receives the sacrament—that is, Christ’s own flesh and blood—and the reality—that is, the unity of the faithful [Col. 1643D] and the increase of grace. But the evil person receives the sacrament—that is, Christ’s body under the sacrament—but not the reality, namely the unity of the Church.

Likewise: the good person eats spiritually and sacramentally; the evil person sacramentally only. Again: “The one who does not eat, eats; and the one who eats, does not eat”—that is, one who does not eat sacramentally eats spiritually, and one who eats sacramentally does not eat spiritually. The Collect also appears relevant to this: “May your sacraments, we beseech you, O Lord, accomplish in us what they contain, so that what we now perform under a form we may receive in the truth of the realities, through the Lord,” etc. That is, as we receive Christ’s flesh under the sacramental form, so may we receive Christ’s flesh in the truth of the reality—that is, spiritually [Col. 1644A].

Or otherwise: “May they accomplish in us,” etc., means: through these sacraments grant us that we who see and receive Christ under the sacrament may in the future see that same Christ face to face, as he is.

This also seems to conflict with the truth: what Truth himself said, “You are not going to eat this body which you see, nor drink that blood which those who crucify me are going to shed; but I have commended some sacrament to you.” From these words the slanderers of the truth take boldness to bark against us. So that they may no longer be permitted to err, let us unfold the difficulty. “Not this body,” etc., means: you are not going to eat it under this form, but in the sacrament—not torn apart and mangled by bites, [Col. 1644B] as you suppose, but whole and unharmed.

Since bread and wine are said by the saints, and believed by all the faithful, to pass into the substance of body and blood, it is commonly asked what sort of conversion this is: formal or substantial. That it is not formal is clear, because the form of bread and wine remains. But whether it is substantial is not evident. Some say that substance passes or is converted into substance in such a way that this becomes that, while that is not increased; nor do they grant that this can be said to be that. Others say that this passes or is converted into that because, beneath the accidents under which the substance of bread and wine previously existed, after consecration there is the substance of body and blood, though [Col. 1644C] Christ’s body itself is not affected by those accidents.

Leaving uncertainties aside, we profess what is certain from the authorities: namely, that the substance of bread and wine is converted into the substance of the Lord’s body and blood; but we do not blush to confess that we do not know the manner of the conversion. Certain things from the former substance remain—colour, taste, form, and weight—which were accidents of the former substance. They neither affect Christ’s body itself nor are grounded in it. If it is asked in what they are grounded, we say that it seems preferable to us that they exist without a subject rather than in a subject.

Concerning also that breaking which seems to take place there, it is commonly asked of what thing, or in what thing, it takes place. Since there is no other substance there than Christ’s body, if it is in any [Col. 1644D] substance, it seems to be in the body itself. But, on the other hand, since that body itself is incorruptible, because it is immortal and incapable of suffering, it seems that it cannot be in it. Hence Christ also rebukes the carnal understanding of the disciples, who thought that Christ’s flesh, like other flesh, was to be divided into parts and torn by bites. Therefore many say that there is no breaking there, but that it only appears so. To them it is objected that Ambrose says: “Nothing false is to be supposed in the sacrifice of truth,” or as happens in magicians’ tricks, where the eyes are deceived by a certain illusion so as to see what is not.

To this they reply: Sight neither deceives us nor is deceived; it would be deceived if it were believed to be broken [Col. 1645A] as it appears; nor is it an illusion, because this happens for the benefit of faith, not for deception. Others say that the breaking takes place there, not indeed in the body, but in the sacramental form of bread itself, as the Apostle seems to intend when he says, “The bread which we break.” Likewise Augustine: “When Christ is eaten, life is eaten; nor do we make parts of him, and indeed this is so in the sacrament.” Again: “Each person receives his own part; he is eaten in parts and remains whole.” Behold, from these words it is clear that Christ’s body is eaten whole and incorrupt, and that, if breaking or division is there, it is not in him, but seems to be in the sacrament.

Others say that breaking takes place there, and is the breaking of no thing, because nothing is broken there. For just as there are accidents there without a subject, so, wonderfully, [Col. 1645B] there can be breaking there in an accident, without anything whatever that is broken. For this mystery is great and inscrutable. Hence Ambrose: “Why do you seek the order of nature in Christ’s body, when the Lord’s birth itself from a Virgin takes place beyond nature? We are commanded to believe; we are not permitted to investigate.”

It should also be known that, although the species of bread and wine are different there, they should nevertheless not be called two sacraments but one, because the same thing is received under both species. It should also be known that, in the utterance of the words, “This is my body,” and “This is the cup,” the mystery is completed and the bread is converted into Christ’s body.

It is also commonly asked what sort of body he gave to the apostles. We say [Col. 1645C] that he gave it as it then was, that is, capable of suffering and mortal.

Moreover, it is commonly asked, if there is not a substantial conversion there, as some maintain, but this is said to pass or be converted into that by a figure of speech—namely because under those accidents under which the substance of bread and wine existed, it is received—what becomes of the substance of the bread or wine. They answer that it is either dissolved into pre-existing matter or reduced to nothing, which he can do who created all things from nothing.

It is also commonly asked whether, if water is not added through forgetfulness or negligence, the act is invalid. Since we have no certainty from authority on this point, we shall state without assertion what seems to us. If it is omitted not with the intention of introducing heresy but through forgetfulness, [Col. 1645D] the sacrament is nevertheless no less effected. Yet this ought to be punished severely; moreover, the Greeks do not add water.

It should also be known that Christ’s body is not received by brute animals, even if it appears to be. What, then, does the material substance receive? What does it eat? Perhaps either nothing, or the substance of bread restored to its own species.

After this, let us consider what the parts which appear to be made there signify. [Pope Sergius:] “Christ’s body is threefold: the portion of the offering placed in the chalice signifies Christ’s body now risen; the portion eaten, his body still walking upon earth; the portion remaining on the altar until the end of Mass, the bodies of the saints lying in tombs until the end of the age.”

[Col. 1646A] VERS. 26–29.—“For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you will proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. Therefore whoever eats the bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of the cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord.”

“As often as,” etc. Here he explains in remembrance of what Christ is received: namely, of his death. As though he said: Therefore you ought to receive in remembrance of the Passion, for “as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you will proclaim,” that is, represent, “the Lord’s death,” accomplished for you. This must certainly be done until the Lord comes for judgment, [Col. 1646B] because this will not be changed until then, as were the sacraments of the Jews; and because he ought to be received in remembrance of his death.

“Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 1645D] Augustine on John.] From this it is clear that holy things harm the wicked, while in the good they are for salvation and in the wicked for judgment. Certainly what we receive is holy; nor is the recipient guilty because the thing received is evil, but because that evil person receives wrongly what he receives. How carefully, then, must one avoid receiving a good thing wrongly, because what is wrongly received harms the wicked; just as, conversely, evils patiently endured benefit the good—as Satan’s angel did Paul.

[Ambrose:] Observe that he says, “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily.” Unworthy [Col. 1646C] is the person who celebrates the mystery of the Eucharist otherwise than Christ handed it down, and the person who approaches the Eucharist without a devout mind or while remaining in the will to sin. Such a person is guilty of the Lord’s body and blood because he treats its benefit with contempt. Or, “he is guilty,” etc., means that he will pay the penalties of Christ’s death and will be punished as though he had killed Christ. Or, “he is guilty,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1645D] Ibid.] means that he will incur a stain from a good thing wrongly received.

Accordingly the Apostle rightly counsels, adding: “But let a person examine himself,” that is, let him examine and cleanse himself, so that, if his sins are daily sins and not mortal sins, he may forgive his brother before approaching the altar and say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI); and then, approaching securely, let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup. The bread you eat is salutary, [Col. 1646D] not deadly poison. But see whether you forgive your debtors; for if you do not forgive, you lie—and you lie to him whom you cannot deceive. You can lie to God, but you cannot deceive him. For he looks within you and examines you.

I say: let each person examine himself; for whoever acts otherwise receives death. And this is what follows: “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily”—for example, one who is in grave sin or who handles it irreverently—“eats and drinks judgment,” that is, condemnation, “upon himself,” and this upon himself, not upon you. [Note: [Col. 1646D] Ibid.] Therefore, being good, endure an evil person securely, so that you may come to the rewards of the good: an evil person cannot defile you. Judas could associate with Peter, but could not defile him; and he approached the Lord’s [Col. 1647A] supper together with him, but Peter received it unto life and Judas unto death.

“Not,” etc. [Augustine:] As though he said: The person who eats unworthily eats judgment for this reason: because he does not discern, that is, distinguish, the Lord’s body from other foods, but receives it indiscriminately and negligently, without rendering the uniquely due reverence. By this he teaches that communion must be approached devoutly and with fear, because he is Lord whose flesh is received, so that we may appear to give thanks to the Redeemer.

[Note: [Col. 1647D] Augustine to Adrianus.] It is asked whether the Eucharist ought to be received daily, or whether days ought to be chosen on which a person, living more purely and continently, may approach so great a sacrament worthily. The proper answer to this question is given by one who advises that one should remain especially in Christ’s peace, and that each should [Col. 1647B] do what he devoutly believes, according to faith, ought to be done. For Zacchaeus and the centurion both honored the Savior, although in different and seemingly opposite ways: the former received Christ joyfully into his house (Luke XIX), while the latter said, “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Luke VII).

The following comparison also applies: among the ancient people manna tasted in the mouth of each devout person according to his own desire; so Christ’s body is received in every Christian’s mouth either daily or at fixed times. One person, out of reverence, does not dare receive daily; another, out of reverence, does not dare omit it on any day. This food wills only that it not be treated with contempt, just as manna did not tolerate loathing. Therefore the Apostle says against those who did not distinguish this food from other foods with special reverence: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself”; and he adds, “not discerning the body of the Lord.”

[Note: [Col. 1647D] Id., in the sermon *On Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit*.] Again, it is asked how someone eating here can be said to eat judgment when the Lord says, “Whoever eats me will himself live because of me” (John VI). To this we say that there are two modes of eating: one sacramental, by which both the wicked and the good eat; the other spiritual, by which the good alone eat, according to the saying: “What is it to eat Christ?” [Note: [Col. 1647D] Id., *On the Words of the Gospel*.] “It is not merely to receive his body in the sacrament, but to remain in him and to have Christ remaining in oneself.” For a person eats spiritually who remains in the unity of Christ and of the Church which the sacrament itself signifies.

[Note: [Col. 1647D] Id., in the book of sermons on Proverbs.] [Col. 1647D] For the person who is at discord with Christ neither eats Christ’s flesh nor drinks his blood, even if he daily receives the sacrament of so great a thing unto judgment. Of this spiritual eating Augustine says: “Why prepare tooth and stomach? Believe, and you have eaten.”

“Therefore among you,” etc. Here he displays an image of the future judgment upon those who receive the Lord’s body heedlessly, so that others might learn from this that the Lord’s body is not received irreverently with impunity and, terrified by their example, might amend themselves; as though he said: because they receive unworthily.

[Col. 1648A] VERS. 30–34.—“Therefore among you many are weak and sickly, and many sleep. But if we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged. Yet when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with this world. Therefore, my brothers, when you gather to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you may not gather for judgment. The remaining matters I shall arrange when I come.”

“Therefore among you many are weak,” with fevers and other illnesses, “and sickly,” with prolonged ill-health, “and many sleep,” [Ambrose:] that is, die a bodily death. This happens for the correction of others.

“But if you.” [Augustine:] As though he said: Such evils result from unworthy reception. But if, ascending the tribunal of our mind, with thought as accuser and conscience as witness, we judged ourselves by repentance and tortured ourselves with fear as executioner, so that a kind of blood of the confessing soul might flow through tears, [Col. 1648B] we would not be judged, that is, punished by God. For whoever judges himself will not be condemned.

[Note: [Col. 1647D] Id., *On Repentance*.] Therefore let the image of future judgment be before one’s eyes, and let a person mount the tribunal of his own mind against himself; let him set himself before his own face; and, judgment having been established in the heart, let accusatory thought, witnessing conscience, and executing fear be present. [Augustine:] Then let a certain blood of the confessing person flow through tears. Finally, let such a sentence be pronounced by the mind itself that a person judges himself unworthy of participation in the Lord’s body and blood, so that one who fears separation from the kingdom by the final sentence may for a time be separated by ecclesiastical discipline from the sacrament of heavenly bread.

[Note: [Col. 1648D] Id., to Januarius.] For one receives unworthily if one receives at the time when one ought to do penance. Let him therefore first judge himself and exercise himself in the severity of repentance, so that, judged by himself, he may not be judged by the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1648D] Id., *On the Book of St. Prosper*.] For sins, whether small or great, cannot go unpunished, since they are punished either when a person repents or when God judges. But divine vengeance ceases if human confession goes before it. Hence he says: “But if we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged,” that is, we would not be punished either by the aforementioned illnesses or by eternal punishment.

“But when we are judged.” [Ambrose:] As though he said: I say that we would not be judged; but neither is the judgment of temporal punishment useless to others, because, according to another interpretation, when we are judged by these temporal punishments, we are corrected by the Lord: others amend themselves through fear of our punishment, for in a few lies the correction of all.

[Note: [Col. 1648D] Id., to Bishop Paulinus.] Or we ourselves are corrected by the punishment by which we are judged, that is, punished, because even for those who suffer, their own punishment is sometimes a purification—as with the prophet Abdo, who, though forbidden by another prophet, ate, as is read in the Book of Kings:

[Note: [Col. 1648D] Otherwise in the history.] “Thus says the Lord: Because you were disobedient and did not keep the command which the Lord commanded you, [Col. 1649A] and you returned and ate bread and drank water where he commanded you not to eat or drink, your corpse shall not be brought into the tomb of your fathers” (III Kings XXIII).

For he had been told to preach in Samaria and not to eat there. Yet he ate there. Therefore the Lord threatens him through another prophet with this: although after death there is no punishment for the corpse, which feels nothing, nevertheless, according to the human affection he had for his own flesh, while alive he could be frightened or saddened about that which, when dead, he would not feel. By this, disobedience could be punished, lest his soul be carried off to Tartarean punishment. Hence he adds: “So that we may not,” etc. As though he said: Therefore we are judged or corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with this world, that is, with unbelievers.

[Col. 1649B] [Ambrose:] For a person who approaches the Lord’s table heedlessly is like an unbeliever. “Therefore, my brothers,” lest a like punishment befall you, O my brothers, when you gather, after the likeness of the Lord’s supper, to eat the Lord’s body, wait for one another, and do so fasting until all assemble, so that the offering of many may be celebrated together and ministered to all. But if anyone is hungry and, impatient, does not wish to wait, let him eat his own food at home—that is, let him be fed with earthly bread—and let him not eat after the Eucharist. You should therefore act in this orderly way and without schism, so that you may not gather for the judgment of condemnation.

“The remaining matters.” As though he said: Keep what I have said; but the remaining matters concerning the same subject, that is, those pertaining to the order of this same sacrament, [Col. 1649C] I shall arrange when I come. But you cannot dispense with these things. Behold, he shows that the chief point of your salvation must be conducted in due order, where error is no light sin. But matters which pertain to the edification of the Church he leaves to be ordered at his arrival.

## CHAPTER XII

VERS. 1–3.—“Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be ignorant. You know that when you were Gentiles, you went as you were led to dumb idols. Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Jesus be accursed’; and no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit.”

“Concerning spiritual gifts,” etc. Having dealt with how the mystery of the Eucharist ought to be celebrated, he treats of the gifts [Col. 1649D] of the Holy Spirit. Because of the greater of these gifts some were proud, while others envied and despaired as though they would never possess them. They also thought of them without distinction, because they set lesser gifts before greater ones, such as tongues. Some also attributed the gifts they possessed not to the Holy Spirit but to people or idols.

As though he said: “I shall arrange those matters afterwards, namely when I come; but concerning spiritual things,” that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, “I do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant” of what truth teaches, so that there may be no schism but peace among you. “You know”—before distinguishing the gifts of the Holy Spirit, he first treats of the one source of all of them, namely the Holy Spirit. And, intending to say that all good things [Col. 1650A] are from the Holy Spirit, he first states a corresponding contrary: “You know,” from experience, “that when you were Gentiles,” that is, living as Gentiles, “you went”—the word denotes a habitual going, marking persistence in this action—“to dumb idols,” an impiety contrary to reason, “as you were led,” by an evil spirit.

Note that, as the Apostle is about to impart spiritual things to them, he recalls their former way of life, so that, as they once were images of idols, they may now be images of God. “Therefore I make known,” etc.: because, ignorant of the rationale of spiritual things, they gave glory through individual charisms more to people than to God. [Ambrose:] Not knowing that these gifts are administered by the Holy Spirit, he therefore shows that in all things there are God’s praise and grace, so that, just as when they were an image of an idol all evil [Col. 1650B] came from humanity and no good—as they then supposed—so now all good things may be believed to come from the Spirit of God.

He therefore says: “Therefore I make known,” etc. As though he said: Since you know that an evil spirit led you, drawn away from good, into such irrational evil, namely idolatry, therefore, that is, by this means readily, I make known to you that by the Spirit of God one abstains from evil and does good. And this is what he says: “This, I say, I make known: that no one speaking in the Spirit of God”—in thought, speech, or action [Note: [Col. 1649D] Augustine, on John.], likewise in these three ways, namely heart, mouth, and deed—“says, ‘Jesus be accursed,’” that is, commits any separation from Jesus, namely any mortal sin by which he separates himself from Jesus. This is what it means to say that one abstains from evil through the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1650C] The person who breaks himself away from Christ’s body does not have this from the Holy Spirit.

[Augustine:] Or thus: no one speaking in the Spirit says in mind, word, or deed, “anathema”—that is, separation or blasphemy—against Jesus, by saying either that he is not from God or that he is less than God. And no one, however great he may be, can say truly—that is, in thought, word, and deed—“Jesus is Lord, and I am his servant,” except in the Holy Spirit, that is, except through the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 1650D] Id., *On the Sermon on the Mount*.] For he properly “speaks” who expresses by vocal sound his own will and mind. Therefore the Apostle properly used this verb “says,” signifying the speaker’s will and understanding. But the Lord used the same verb in the general manner of speaking when he said: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII). In that manner, a person is also said to give who neither wills nor understands what he says; but he properly speaks who wills and understands. No one can do this except in the Holy Spirit, which is to say, act rightly; and every good is through the Holy Spirit. Thus the greater person will not despise the lesser, because he has nothing except from the Holy Spirit.

[Ambrose:] By these words the Apostle sharply rebukes those who attributed divine benefits to people, showing that no benefit is human but a gift of God. For he says: “No one speaking in the Spirit says, ‘Jesus be accursed,’” a phrase arising from human error, like every falsehood; and “no one says, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except by the Holy Spirit,” from whom comes every truth. For every truth, whoever speaks it, is from the Holy Spirit. Jesus is not called Lord through human flattery, as happens with idols, which are called gods by people though they are not. A human being—or the devil—devised that one who is not God might be called God; but that Jesus is called Lord is a confession made in the truth by the Holy Spirit. Therefore it is not human favor or a benefit conferred on religion that Jesus is called Lord, but a gift of God, who revealed his mystery to human beings. Nor does the person who says this confer a benefit upon religion; rather, he receives one, just as people receive favor when idols are called gods although they are not. Hence their priests also are subject to people. In the Christian rule, however, it is otherwise: those who say that Jesus is God do not confer [Col. 1651B] a benefit upon religion, but receive what ought to humble them, so that they endure being corrected and do not seek to be softened by flattery.

VERS. 4–10.—“Now there are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit; and divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and divisions of workings, but the same God who works all things in all. But to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness. To one indeed through the Spirit is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healings in the one Spirit; to another, working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of utterances.”

[Col. 1651C] “Divisions,” etc. Having set forth the source of graces, he shows the graces themselves as divided. As though he said: This is common to all: no one can avoid evil and do good except through the Spirit. But there are “divisions of gifts,” that is, gifts are apportioned. Therefore the lesser person should not despair, nor the greater grow proud, when he hears of gifts. Here he calls “gifts” the various ranks and orders in the offices of the Church.

[Ambrose:] For as one who says “Jesus” and “Lord” has this from grace, so grace exists in the offices of the Church. This grace is not divided among the three persons, but is undifferentiatedly the work of the three persons—that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—whom he subsequently signifies by the three names which he gives: [Col. 1651D] Spirit, Lord, and God.

[Augustine:] Or he here calls “gifts” the virtues themselves given freely by God, such as faith, hope, and the like. The meaning is: There are divisions of gifts, that is, of the Holy Spirit’s gifts—namely, virtues which are freely given—but the same Spirit is giver of all, equally beneficent toward all in himself. There are divisions of ministries, by which some serve others, but the same Lord, namely the Son, gives to each according to his own will. And there are divisions of workings, because there are greater and lesser works, but the same giver, namely God the Father.

Note that he first signified virtues by saying “gifts,” and then signified their effects by saying [Col. 1652A] “ministries” and “workings.” For their effects are ministry in relation to one’s neighbors, and working in relation to oneself. But by saying individually “Spirit,” “Lord,” and “God,” the very same substance of deity is understood, though there is a Trinity of persons.

Lest the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit might appear to work separately and differently because he had assigned gifts to the Spirit, ministries to the Lord, and workings to God, he refers all things to the one God and adds that God works all necessary things in all. He does not bestow everything upon one person, but works all things in all, so that what one does not possess in oneself, one may possess in another; and so charity and humility may remain.

[Note: [Col. 1651D] Augustine, on John.] For if you are humble and love unity, whatever anyone has in it, you have. Take away envy, and what I possess is yours; envy separates, charity joins. As in the human [Col. 1652B] body the eye alone sees, yet not for itself alone, so you have the Holy Spirit if you love the Church. You love it if you remain in its unity and charity. This charity is the gift of the Holy Spirit, which surpasses all things, as he will say later.

“But to each.” [Ambrose:] As though he said: The gifts differ, and are not granted individually according to any person’s merit, but for the benefit of building up the Church. This is what he says: “But to each is given a manifestation of the Spirit,” that is, grace through which it is apparent that the Holy Spirit is in him, “for the benefit” of the Church; for even the lesser member who is in it is useful.

[Note: [Col. 1651D] Id., to Dardanus, *On the Presence of God*.] Note that God, being incorporeal in nature and unchangeably alive, abiding in himself in eternal stability, is wholly present to all things and wholly present to each. Yet those in whom he dwells possess him according to the diversity of their capacity, some more and some less. By the grace of his goodness he builds these as a temple most beloved to himself. The Apostle proceeds to explain them individually, defining what he had said.

“To one indeed through the Spirit”—not through merit—“is given a word of wisdom; to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit.”

[Note: [Col. 1652D] Id., *On the Trinity*.] Distinguish between wisdom and knowledge. Wisdom belongs to contemplation of eternal things. And what is among eternal things except God, whose nature alone is unchangeable? Knowledge, however, belongs to the practical handling of temporal things. Hence Job: “Behold, piety is wisdom; to abstain from evils is knowledge” (Job XXVIII). Here he calls piety the worship of God, which in Greek is called *theosebia*. And what worship is there except love and knowledge of him? But the knowledge which he calls abstaining from evils undoubtedly concerns temporal things, because evils are found among temporal things, in which one must live cautiously and prudently.

The person to whom wisdom is given is like the sun; the person to whom knowledge is given, the moon in the night of this age. Those to whom the remaining gifts are given are stars, because these too are necessary in the night. Hence in the Psalm: “The sun to rule the day, the moon and stars to rule the night” (Ps. CXXXV).

[Augustine:] Note that he does not say simply, “Wisdom is given to one, knowledge to another,” but “a word of wisdom” and “a word of knowledge,” signifying thereby that not only wisdom—that is, understanding of divine things—and knowledge of human things are given, but also the utterance of them, so that they may speak them to others.

“To another is given faith,” that is, steadfastness in faith or its utterance, “in the same Spirit.”

[Note: [Col. 1653D] Augustine, in the book of *Retractions*.] See that faith too is among God’s gifts; therefore not charity alone, but charity together with faith, is from God to us. “To another is given gifts of healings,” that is, of healing the sick; and this is in the one Spirit, the same for all. “To another, working of miracles,” that is, miracles contrary to nature; “to another, prophecy,” namely foretelling future events; “to another, discernment of spirits,” so that one discerns in what spirit, good or evil, what one hears is said, because the devil too speaks good things deceptively; “to another, kinds of tongues,” that is, speaking various languages; “to another is given interpretation of utterances,” that is, of languages or visions, as to Joseph; or “utterances” are allegorical pronouncements found in the prophets and the Gospels.

VERS. 11–17.—“But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually as he wills. For as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, although many, are nevertheless one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, whether slaves or free; and we were all made to drink in one Spirit. For the body is not one member but many. If the foot should say, ‘Because I am not a hand, I am not of the body,’ is it therefore not of the body? And if the ear should say, ‘Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body,’ is it [Col. 1653C] therefore not of the body? If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would smelling be?”

“But one and the same Spirit works all these things,” though they are diverse: one in substance with the Father and Son, and the same, that is, unchangeable.

[Ambrose:] Here, having earlier said that three work, he declares that the Holy Spirit acts, because they are of one nature: what one works, the three work. Therefore the Holy Spirit is co-worker with the Father and the Son.

[Note: [Col. 1653D] Id., on Psalm CXVIII.] He said “one and the same Spirit” lest as many spirits be thought to exist as there are works, not because the Spirit works without the Father and the Son. For the working of the Trinity is inseparable: when the Father’s working is spoken of, he is not understood to work it without the Son and Holy Spirit [Col. 1653D] [Note: [Col. 1654D] Id., *On Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.*]; when the Son’s working is spoken of, not without the Father and Holy Spirit; and when the Holy Spirit’s working is spoken of, not without the Father and Son.

[Note: [Col. 1654D] Id., *On the Trinity*.] Observe that the Apostle says here that the Holy Spirit gives gifts; elsewhere, however, he says that he was given (Rom. V). Christ too says, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” etc. (John XX). Therefore readers should be reminded that the Holy Spirit has already been called God’s gift, the Lord saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit.” Thus when they hear “the gift of the Holy Spirit,” they should recognize the manner of speech in which the Apostle says, “in the stripping off of the body of flesh” (Col. II). For just as “body of flesh” is nothing other than flesh itself, so “gift of the Holy Spirit” [Col. 1654A] is nothing other than the Holy Spirit.

Augustine, *On Faith to Peter*: “Learned and great expositors of the divine Scriptures have not yet discussed the Holy Spirit so fully and carefully that his distinctive property may be easily understood—the property by which we are able to say that he is neither Son nor Father, but Holy Spirit alone—except that they proclaim him to be God’s gift, so that we may believe that God does not give a gift inferior to himself. Therefore he is God’s gift insofar as he is given to those to whom he is given. But in God’s own being he exists even if he is given to no one, because he was God, coeternal with the Father and Son, before he was given to anyone; nor is he inferior to them because they give and he is given. For he is given as God’s gift in such a way that he also gives himself as God. For it cannot be said that he is not in his own [Col. 1654B] power, of whom it is said, ‘The Spirit breathes where he wills’” (John III).

[Augustine:] For when he is given by the Father and the Son, he is given by his own will. And he himself works all things, distributing to each—not himself divided—as he wills, as one who is God, who alone knows what is fitting and gives freely, not according to merit. Therefore the lesser should not grieve at another’s greater gift, nor should the greater be proud against the lesser.

Augustine, *On Faith to Peter*: “Learned and great expositors of the divine Scriptures have not yet discussed the Holy Spirit so fully and carefully that his distinctive property may be easily understood—the property by which we are able to say that he is neither Son nor Father, but Holy Spirit alone—except that they proclaim him to be God’s gift, so that we may believe that God does not give a gift [Col. 1654C] inferior to himself.”

“For as.” As though he said: He gives different gifts to different persons because, just as the human body is one by the union of its members and has many distinct members, and all the members of the body, although—that is, even though—they are many, are nevertheless one body through mutual service, so all believers are Christ. I do not merely say “the body of Christ,” because they are Christ himself, both the lesser and the greater.

[Augustine:] For Christ is called both head and body because of the ineffable unity of head and members.

“For all of you.” He shows how Christ’s body is one—that is, how all believers are one. As though he said: We are one by this. “For we all,” whether Jews or Gentiles, diverse in nationality, whether slaves or free, diverse in status, “were baptized,” that is, washed, “in one Holy Spirit,” and brought into one body—that is, brought into such a state that, through that one Spirit, we may with one mind be one body—as the whole human body is enlivened by one soul.

For the one Holy Spirit does all things in the members of Christ’s body just as one soul sees in the eye, hears in the ear, and does all things in all the other members. And we are one body also by this: “and,” that is, because, “we all were made to drink” in the reception of the Spirit’s various gifts, and this in the Holy Spirit, who cooperates by directing all gifts to the making of one body. Therefore no person is to be despised [Col. 1655A] or preferred as though complete in himself, nor is God’s glory to be given to human beings, because the one and same God works in all.

“For,” etc. By a comparison with the human body, he shows that the unity of Christ’s body—that is, the Church—has a variety of offices, and that this diversity does not remove unity, just as the unity of the human body consists not in a single member but in many members, so that they may provide one another what is due.

As though he said: All believers are rightly one body, for the human body, to which the Church is similar, is not one member but many. Thus in the Church not all possess one office and gift. And since the one Spirit gives all things, if the foot—that is, a person to whom an inferior gift has been given—should say, “Because I am not a hand,” that is, as worthy as the person to whom working of miracles has been given, “I am not of the body,” is it therefore not of the body? Or: is it not necessary because it is not among the foremost? Likewise, if the ear—that is, one who has knowledge—should say, “Because I am not an eye,” that is, as worthy as the one who has the word of wisdom, “I am not of the body,” is it therefore not of the body? Certainly it is, because if it is not that, it can be something else.

Again: “If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be?” that is, the ear. “And if the whole were hearing,” that is, ear, “where would smelling be?”

[Augustine:] That is, the nostrils, by which is understood the person to whom discernment of spirits is given. As though he said: If all in the Church had one office, how would the need of the body, whose governance requires diverse persons, be fulfilled?

### Verses 18–30

But now God has placed the members, each one of them, in the body as He willed. And if all were one member, where would the body be? But now there are indeed many members, yet one body. The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of your works”; nor again the head to the feet, “You are not necessary to me.” Rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are much more necessary. And those members of the body which we think less honorable, we surround with more abundant honor. And our unseemly members have more abundant comeliness; but our comely members need nothing. Yet God has harmonized the body, giving more abundant honor to that member which lacked it, so that there may be no schism in the body, but that the members may [Col. 1655D] be mutually concerned for one another. And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; or if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it. But you are the body of Christ, and members from a member. And God has indeed placed some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers; then powers, then gifts of healings, helps, administrations, kinds of tongues, interpretations of utterances. Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all powers? Do all have the gift of healings? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?

[Col. 1656A] “But now.” As though he said: In order that these inconveniences may be avoided, God has now placed—that is, by providence and rational will He has fitted—different members in the body, so that nothing may be lacking to it; and likewise in the Church He has placed different persons, to whom He has given different gifts. He has placed each of these members, whether greater or lesser, in the body—that is, in the constitution of the body—as He willed, that is, as seemed good to Him. Now there are many members in the body. But if all were one member, where would the body be, which can subsist only through diverse members? As though he said: Not only would the multiplicity of senses perish, but the body itself also. So, if all in the Church were of one office and rank, they would not be called members, nor a body.

But now, lest the body perish, there are indeed many [Col. 1656B] members, but from them all there is one body. “But the eye cannot.” As though he said: The members are diverse, but the greater cannot tell the lesser that they have no need of them. [Ambrose] And this is what he says: “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of your works,’” because, if the eye foresees, the hand works; nor can the head again say to the feet, “You are not necessary to me.” So in the Church, one of greater standing cannot say to one of lower standing, “You are not necessary to me.” For the humble person can do something which the exalted person cannot. Iron can do what gold cannot; even rank itself is not contemptible on account of those subject to it. For it is office through which rank is established. A great commander needs an army; therefore he adds:

“But much more, those members of the body which seem weaker”—that is, more righteous—“are sometimes more necessary.” And therefore those inferior members ought not to be despised by their superiors, but should be honored more. Hence he adds: “And those members of the body which we think less honorable, we surround with more abundant honor of clothing.” So also exhortation is necessary for those of lesser rank in the Church, so that some honor may be given them and they may become useful. And your unseemly members, such as the private parts, have more abundant comeliness because you conceal them. [Note: [Col. 1655D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*.]

Observe that he says “unseemly.” Far be it that there should be any ugliness in the members of the saints! But they are called unseemly because they do not possess that appearance of beauty which those parts exposed to view possess; or because of the law of the members which came from sin. It is not from the first institution [Col. 1656D] of our nature that the illicit use of the members is shameful, rather than the members themselves. So also in the Church, those who are unseemly through some sin are helped more abundantly with consolations and prayers, that they may become honorable.

Or, by the unseemly members are signified certain brethren who, although unseemly in poverty and dress, nevertheless possess abundant honor, because they are sometimes of a more pure life. But your comely members, which have enough honor in themselves, need none of those things which are done for the unseemly members; rather, by means of these, the others are to be honored. So too, nothing needs to be added by us to brethren in whom the earnest practice of skillful conduct has adorned them with honorableness.

“But God.” [Ambrose] [Col. 1657A] As though he said: Comely members need nothing, and unseemly members do need something. But God has done these things—He who has harmonized the body. How? By giving, through worthy members, more abundant—that is, greater—honor to the member which lacked honor in itself, so that there may not be schism, that is, discord, in the human body or in the Church, where unity ought to exist; but rather that all the members may be concerned in the things that must be done.

They are to be concerned for one another, I say, so that they may tend toward the same thing—that is, toward that concern which is itself one and undivided—so that they may be no less concerned for another than for themselves. Hence he adds: “And if one member suffers in adversities, all the members suffer with it”—that is, ought to suffer with it—as though it were their own evil. This is beyond doubt regarding the bodily members: for if an eye or a foot is seized by some illness, the entire body grieves with it. So it is fitting that we too should grieve with brethren if some adversity arises, and rejoice if things turn out well. Hence he adds: “Or if one member is glorified in good things, all the members rejoice with it.”

And as though someone were to say, “What have these things to do with us?” he answers by adding: “But you are the body of Christ”—that is, of Christ the Head, through the unity of faith—and members dependent upon a member, that is, upon Christ the Head and our fellow-member. Or: dependent upon me, a member by whose preaching you have been instructed. Behold, he plainly shows that he has treated our case through the analogy of bodily members.

“And some.” Here he determines which gifts of God are higher and which lower, because the Corinthians thought that what was lesser was greater, and what was greater lesser. He explains the diversity which he said exists among the members, adding: “And God has placed some”—that is, different persons—“in the Church: first,” in rank and time, “apostles,” preaching in Christ’s place and ordering and judging all things; [Augustine] “second, prophets,” namely those revealing the mysteries of Scripture or things to come. He speaks of those who were after Christ’s coming, not those who foretold Him; whoever wishes to know them should read the Acts of the Apostles. [Ambrose] “Third, teachers,” that is, those who give precepts for living, or those who instruct children in letters; “then powers,” that is, those who work miracles; “then gifts of healings,” that is, those who heal the sick; “and helps,” that is, those who provide assistance to superiors, as Titus did to the Apostle, or archdeacons [Col. 1657D] to bishops; “administrations,” namely the oversight of lesser persons, such as presbyters, who are examples to the people; “kinds of tongues.” Behold, to know many languages is a gift of God. And observe that he puts last what they put first.

“For are all?” As though he said: These things are given to different people, and rightly so, because not everything ought to be given to all; otherwise there would be no one for whom these offices might serve. He says it thus: “Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all powers? Do all have the gift of healings? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret Scriptures or languages?” Certainly not. But whoever does not have these things in himself should love them in others; and in them he already has what he does not have in himself.

## Chapter XIII

### Verses 1–2

“But desire the better gifts. And I show you yet a more excellent way. If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith so as to remove mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing.”

“But desire.” [Ambrose] Having explained, with the reason given, why they have diverse gifts and why not everything is granted to one person, and having introduced the spiritual body through the example of the human body, he has thereby shown that God should be blessed in all things. As though he said: The gifts are diverse; but among these desire—that is, seek—the better gifts, that is, the more useful ones, not tongues as you are accustomed to do.

“And yet,” he advances them gradually toward more useful things, showing that the aforesaid gifts do not always pertain to merit, but to the honor of God. Therefore he now shows them a better way, namely love. As though he said: The aforesaid gifts are in the body of Christ. And yet, that is, beyond the things mentioned, I show you a way of going to God, namely love, more excellent than those gifts. For it is the greatest gift of all, because those gifts do not always pertain to merit, but are intended to display God’s honor to the nations. Thus at the end, to those who say, “Lord, in [Col. 1658C] Your name we prophesied, cast out demons, and worked miracles,” the Lord will say, “Depart from Me. I do not know you, workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7).

“If I speak with the tongues of men.” He proves that love is more excellent than the other gifts, because the others have no value without it, while it has value without them. He begins with tongues: “If I speak with the tongues of men”—which is sometimes given to someone for God’s glory, not for merit—“and of angels.” Distinguish thus: tongues of men, those who know less; and of angels, that is, perfected human beings. Or: tongues of all men and angels, by whom angels set over lesser persons signify what they first perceive from God’s will; this is done by certain gestures or signs. Or: tongues of angels, which are used by those sent to human beings.

“If,” he says, “I do these things, but do not have love”—which one speaking in every tongue may lack—“I have become like sounding bronze,” which is struck to no use of its own, though it signifies things to others; “or a clanging cymbal,” which does not benefit itself, though it delights others who do not understand.

[Ambrose] The comparison is fitting, because just as bronze and a cymbal do not resound of themselves but through some external blow, so the speaker in tongues, not knowing what he says, utters not from himself but by the Spirit’s power those things by which he may delight his hearers. Consider the gifts of the Church, and you will recognize that the gift of love surpasses all others. [Note: [Col. 1657D] Augustine, *On Psalm 103*.] For love is the proper and unique fountain of good things, in which one who is alien does not share; [Col. 1659A] and love, like oil, cannot be pressed down to the bottom but rises above all. [Note: [Col. 1659D] Augustine, *On John*.]

Observe how great love is: if it is lacking, other things are possessed in vain; but if someone has it, that person has all things, either in himself or in others. Once he begins to possess it, he will possess the Holy Spirit; if he does not possess it, he will be without the Holy Spirit. And as the body is dead without the soul, so the soul is reckoned dead without love. This is the wedding garment in which the clothed guests recline securely. [Note: [Col. 1659D] Id., *On the Miracles of the Five Loaves*.] By this garment the cold is driven away—the cold in which Peter shivered while warming himself by Caiaphas’s coals. This alone distinguishes the children of the kingdom from the children of perdition. Other gifts are indeed given through the Spirit, but without love they profit nothing. [Note: [Col. 1659D] Id., *On the Trinity*.]

Therefore, unless the Holy Spirit is imparted to each person so greatly [Col. 1659B] that He makes him a lover of God and neighbor, he is not transferred from the left hand to the right; nor is the Holy Spirit properly called God’s gift except through the love by which the other gifts are held. Hence the Lord says: “To him who has, it shall be given; and from him who has not, even what he has shall be taken away” (Luke 8). For to one who has love, more will be added; but from one who does not have it, these gifts will be taken away even if he has them for a time. He has that by which he possesses the gracious name of Christian, but he does not have love, which is the use of the reality denoted by that name; and therefore what he has will be taken away.

[Augustine] “And if I have prophecy” of future things, which even evil men had, such as Balaam, Saul, and Caiaphas; [Ambrose] “and know all mysteries,” that is, the hidden things of the Old and New Testaments, which even evil persons know, as Judas did with the apostles, and the devil, who, as Ezekiel says, knew the divine mysteries, since he testifies that he was in God’s paradise and possessed precious stones. But this benefited him nothing, because without love he rushed into pride. “And if I know all knowledge,” divine and human, like the scribes and Pharisees. Therefore the Lord says: “You have the key of knowledge, but you neither enter yourselves nor allow others to enter” (Matt. 23). “And if I have all faith,” faith concerning every matter in which it is to be held—faith, I say, so perfect “that I remove mountains,” literally, or demons from those afflicted—“but do not have love, I am nothing,” that is, it profits me nothing toward life.

[Augustine, Ambrose] Even though those things are great, evil persons also have them; indeed, they will confess them at the judgment, where they will not dare to lie. To them it will not be said, “You did not have them,” but “I do not know you” (Matt. 7), because they possessed them without love.

### Verses 3–9

“And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I deliver up my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing. Love is patient, is kind. Love does not envy, does not behave perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own things, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices together in the truth; it bears all things, [Col. 1660A] believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails; whether prophecies are abolished, whether tongues cease, whether knowledge is destroyed. For we know in part, and we prophesy in part.”

“And if I distribute all my possessions”—that is, whatever it is lawful for me to possess—“as food,” that is, for the necessities, “of the poor,” not of the rich, who repay. Observe that he says “I distribute.” By this the prudent ordering of almsgiving is taught: it should be given not to one person but to many, so that more may benefit. “And if I deliver up my body,” as Lawrence did, “so that I may burn.” [Note: [Col. 1659D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*.] Or, “but” (*at*; the alternative reading is materially uncertain)—which is also sometimes done boastfully. “But if I do not have love, it profits me nothing.” For without love this can occur, but it cannot profit; [Note: [Col. 1660D] Augustine, *On Psalm 120*.] just as good works profit more or less not according to their quantity but according to love. [Col. 1660B] The means of one who gives much and one who gives little are unequal, but their love need not be unequal. Therefore, to give a cup of water may be as much as it was for Zacchaeus to give half his estate.

[Augustine] Christ’s disciples are recognized by love, not by prophecy, faith, or other things. For the love which is from God—and God is properly the Holy Spirit—is that through which God, who is love, is poured out in us; through Him the whole Trinity dwells in us. Therefore, most rightly, although the Holy Spirit is God, He is also called the gift of God.

“Love is patient,” and so forth. As though he said: Love is worthier also because it brings these good things. For love is patient, possessing the habit of patience in the soul; it is kind, generous toward those in need. Love does not envy, that is, it does not begrudge. Another’s good fortune does not grieve it, but it loves another’s good as its own. It does not behave perversely, that is, wrongly. It is not puffed up when things turn out prosperously. It is not ambitious, that is, it does not wish to be set above others. It does not seek only its own things, but those of others also. Or, “it does not seek its own things” means that it does not demand back what has been taken from it, because it is not a lover of money. It is not provoked, that is, stirred to anger. It not only harms no one, but does not even think evil. It does not rejoice over iniquity, but grieves when it sees someone fall into iniquity. But it rejoices together in the truth, that is, in works of righteousness or words of truth. It bears all things in action for truth’s sake, as appears in Noah, who endured much. It believes all things [Note: [Col. 1660D] Augustine, *On the Four Virtues*.] which truth urges, as appeared in Abraham, who believed God calling [Col. 1660D] and promising.

Observe that he says “believes all things,” not “believes everyone,” because it does not believe everyone, but God alone. It hopes all things which truth promises, as appears in the ancient fathers—that is, in the people of Israel, who hoped to receive what God promised. It endures all things, that is, patiently awaits all the things promised, as appears in the Head Himself, namely Christ, who patiently awaited the glory of the resurrection and ascension.

These are the weapons with which Christ’s soldier is armed. As the chief weapons of this armor, he has set forth patience and kindness. [Note: [Col. 1660D] Augustine, *On Ezekiel*.] [Col. 1661A] The one calmly bears evils inflicted by neighbors; the other desirably bestows its own goods upon neighbors. [Note: [Col. 1661D] Gregory, *Morals*.] In the battle of temptation, the mind of the saints, fortified by the shield of patience and girded with the sword of love, gains strength to endure evils and is raised to unity in repaying good things, so that it may both powerfully receive the missiles of hatred and vigorously return the darts of love. For no one goes armed to war who either takes up a shield but does not use a sword, or uses a sword but is not protected by a shield. Thus God’s soldier, overtaken in the battle of adversity, ought both to hold the shield of patience before him and, ready to preach, to send forth the darts of love, so that he may conquer.

“Love,” and so forth. As though he said: Love is worthier in this respect, because love never fails, that is, it will not end either in this age [Col. 1661B] or in the future, even though its works cease. For if in believing and hoping we love what is not yet seen, how much more shall we do so when it is seen? I say it does not fail, whether prophecies of future things cease or are abolished in the future, when all things will be present; whether tongues cease in the future—for what could one person say to another where all understand the same thing?—or whether knowledge, now by a mirror, is destroyed when it will be by the thing itself.

“For in part.” As though he said: Prophecy and knowledge will be destroyed because they are partial. For we know God in part, that is, imperfectly; and we prophesy in part, that is, imperfectly.

### Verses 10–13

“But when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be abolished. When I was a child, [Col. 1661C] I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child. But when I became a man, I put away the things of a child. We now see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then I shall know even as I have been known. But now there remain faith, hope, love—these three; but the greatest of these is love.”

“But when.” As though he said: Knowledge and prophecy are partial; but everything partial shall be abolished—that is, destroyed—when that which is perfect comes. [Ambrose] That is, our imperfection will be destroyed, not that which is true. The destruction is of imperfection, when what is imperfect is fulfilled into truth.

Some object that, by the same reasoning, love too ought to be called abolished, because it is now partial—that is, imperfect—in comparison with the future state. Some answer that knowledge itself—that is, the gift of knowledge—is not abolished, but its manner; because now we know enigmatically and through a mirror, that is, shadowily and obscurely, but then by direct sight, that is, most clearly. But they object: “So too, we now love imperfectly, but then most perfectly. Therefore the manner of loving will be abolished. Thus love can be said to be abolished as knowledge is.”

They reply: It is true that all imperfection will be removed from love as from [Col. 1662A] knowledge. But just as there are two things to be loved—God and neighbor—so there are two principal manners of loving: God for His own sake, and neighbor for God’s sake. Those manners will not be abolished in the future; rather, the manner of imperfection will be removed. But the enigmatic and mirror-like manner of knowing will be entirely removed.

Others say that not only the manner of knowledge but also its act—indeed, the knowledge itself which now exists—will be abolished in the future. That the act and use of knowledge itself will be abolished is plausible. But it is not so clear concerning knowledge itself. For knowledge is a quality of the mind itself, whose act is the very vision by which we see now and through which we are led to another vision. Hence Augustine says: “We know that, when He appears, as John says, we shall be like Him, because [Col. 1662B] we shall see Him as He is” (1 John 2). This vision is promised to us; toward this vision we are trained; toward this vision we cleanse the heart.

Or, something is said to be “in part” when another thing succeeds it. But, as Augustine says in *On Christian Doctrine*, the direct sight which we shall see succeeds faith; and blessedness itself, which we are to attain, succeeds hope. [Note: [Col. 1661D] Augustine, *On Psalm 148*.] Love, however, will rather be increased, and nothing will succeed it. Yet it will be destroyed insofar as it is partial, because it will cease to be partial; but neither it nor its act will be destroyed.

Therefore, everything partial will be destroyed: either wholly, as faith and hope; or partially, as knowledge, whose act and manner will be destroyed; and love, from which a certain manner will be removed, but not love itself, nor its act, nor a certain manner.

He demonstrates what he has said by a comparison, adding: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child,” that is, in a child’s way; “I understood human things as a child; I thought as a child. But when I became a man,” that is, of perfect age, “I put away”—that is, set aside—all the things that belonged to a child. So it is with us.

We now see something of God [Note: [Col. 1662D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*.] through a mirror, that is, through an obscure image. For we see certain creatures in which some likeness of God shines forth, and this quite obscurely. And we see in an enigma, that is, through obscure allegory. Observe that he added “in an enigma,” a thing certainly unknown to many because they do not know the literary disciplines in which there is teaching about modes of expression, which the Greeks call *tropoi*, a term which we too use instead of the Latin term. For just as we more commonly say *schemata* than “figures,” so we more commonly say *tropes* than “modes.”

Allegory is a trope; there are several kinds of this trope, that is, of allegory, one of which is called an enigma. To explain briefly, an enigma is not every allegory, but an obscure allegory. Therefore, as it seems to me, just as by the particular term “image” he signified an image, so by the term “enigma” he signified a likeness, though obscure and difficult to perceive. Thus by both names are signified likenesses which avail for understanding God, though obscurely. For now images of truth are seen by faith; then the things themselves will be seen.

Or, the mirror is the soul, in which we somehow know God. But we know Him in an enigma, [Col. 1663A] that is, obscurely; then, however, we shall see Him face to face, that is, openly, by comparison with persons looking directly at one another’s faces. There is one vision belonging to this present time and another vision belonging to the future. The former is by faith; the latter will be by direct sight.

And now, not merely others, but I myself also know in part, that is, obscurely and imperfectly. But then I shall know even as I have been known: that is, I shall see the things promised, as I am seen by the One who promises; that is, I shall know God as He Himself has known me, namely as He is. This is to be present with God, where Christ is. Or, “I shall know even as I have been known” means: as I have been foreknown to know, which is now secret.

“But now.” As though he said: Then I shall know; but now, in order that I may attain this, these three remain. As though he said: They are few things, but very useful: faith, hope, and love. Under these, knowledge and prophecy serve; without them the life of no righteous person is perfect, though even that life is imperfect by comparison with the future. [Note: [Col. 1663D] Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*.] But love is greater than these, or the greatest of them, because, when these depart, it will remain increased. Faith and hope cannot be lacking here to love; but faith and hope can exist without love, although there is no devout faith or hope without love. And because love is greater than the others, therefore—

## Chapter XIV

### Verses 1–5

“Pursue love; desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy. For one who speaks in a tongue does not speak to human beings, but to God; for no one hears. Yet in the spirit he speaks mysteries. [Col. 1663C] But one who prophesies speaks to human beings for edification, exhortation, and consolation. One who speaks in a tongue edifies himself; but one who prophesies edifies God’s Church. Now I wish you all to speak in tongues, but rather that you may prophesy. For one who prophesies is greater than one who speaks in tongues, unless perhaps he interprets, so that the Church may receive edification.”

Pursue love with your whole desire, for it is the sweet and healthful bond of minds. Without it a rich person is poor, and in it a poor person is rich. And desire also—that is, seek—other spiritual things, that is, the other gifts of the Holy Spirit. [Ambrose] But after love, especially desire that you may prophesy, rather than speak in tongues; that is, desire prophecies rather than tongues. And this is truly what should be done.

For one who speaks in a tongue [Col. 1663D] unknown and foreign does not speak to human understanding. Thus they gain no profit from this, but God does, whose praises he speaks and who understands; therefore he does not speak to human beings. “For,” that is, because, no one who is a human being—that is, carnal—hears, that is, understands, what he says. “But in the spirit.” As though he said: Because no one understands, it is certain that not the human being himself but the Holy Spirit speaks mysteries through him, namely secrets concerning God. [Note: [Col. 1663D] Augustine, *On Genesis*.]

Or thus, that “tongue” may be understood otherwise and a distinction made between spirit and mind: because, in the tongue—that is, in that bodily member which we move in the mouth when we speak—signs of things are given, not the things themselves [Col. 1664A] uttered. Therefore, by metaphor, he calls “tongue” here an utterance in which there are significations, as it were images of things; and these require the mind, that is, the understanding of the mind, in order to be understood. But when they are not understood, they are said to be in the spirit, not in the mind.

Here “mind” is understood as the higher power of the soul; “spirit” as a power of the same soul, lower than the mind, in which images of things are impressed. Therefore “tongue” is any utterance of signs. When understanding, which belongs to the mind, comes to it, either revelation, recognition, prophecy, or teaching occurs—of which he will speak subsequently.

It should be known that one speaking in tongues sometimes did not understand, and sometimes understood but was unable to explain to others. Yet someone else perhaps sometimes interpreted; and sometimes a person saw, understood, and interpreted. For example, [Col. 1664B] [Note: [Col. 1664D] Augustine, *On Genesis*.] Pharaoh saw seven ears of grain and seven cows in the spirit. Their presentation was, as it were, a tongue; but he did not understand what they signified. Therefore he was not a prophet.

Accordingly, when signs were shown to someone’s spirit through certain likenesses of bodily things, if they were not understood, he was not yet a prophet. And the person who interprets what another sees is more properly called a prophet than the one who sees, as Joseph more than Pharaoh. Pharaoh saw in the spirit; Joseph in the mind. Pharaoh’s spirit was formed so as to see images; Joseph’s mind was illuminated so as to understand the truth. Therefore in the former there was a tongue, in the latter prophecy: in the former, an imagining of things; in the latter, an interpretation of the imagining.

Thus one who foresees images of signified things by the spirit alone is a lesser prophet; one endowed with their understanding alone is more a prophet. But the greatest prophet is one who excels in both, seeing signification in the spirit and understanding it in the mind—like Daniel, who both related the king’s dream which he had seen and disclosed what it meant. For the very images were impressed upon his spirit, and their understanding was revealed in his mind.

According to this, continue the literal exposition. As though he said: Prophecy ought especially to be desired rather than tongues because one who speaks in a tongue—that is, produces signs without understanding—does not speak to human beings, but to God. This point is unchanged. And he truly does not speak to human beings, “for no one hears”; this too is unchanged. But the human spirit, not the mind, speaks mysteries. [Augustine] Or, according to another reading, “in the spirit,” not in the mind, he speaks mysteries. Spirit here may be understood as the lower power of the soul in which images of things and words are marked.

“For,” and so forth. As though he said: I rightly say of this person that he does not speak to human beings. For the one who prophesies, understanding with the mind and laying open interpretations—that is, one who expounds Scriptures hidden from many—speaks to human understanding. This serves for the edification of the ignorant, exhortation of the advanced, and consolation of the desolate. Thus it is also better to prophesy than to speak in tongues, because [Col. 1665A] the one who speaks in a tongue, which is to speak in the spirit, edifies himself—if, however, he understands. [Ambrose] But the one who prophesies, which is to speak in the mind, edifies the Church, insofar as he is concerned.

Although I thus place prophecy above tongues, I nevertheless wish you all to speak in tongues, for this too is a gift of God. Therefore I especially wish—not forbid—that you should prophesy rather than speak in tongues, because it benefits more. Why do I especially wish this? “For,” that is, because, the one who prophesies is greater, that is, worthier, than the one who speaks in tongues, unless perhaps he interprets—that is, can explain what he says, which is rare—so that the Church may receive edification.

### Verses 6–14

“But now, brethren, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what shall I profit you unless I speak to you either in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in teaching? Yet even lifeless things giving sound, whether flute or harp, unless they give distinctions of sounds, how will what is played on the flute or harp be known? For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle? So also you: unless through the tongue you give intelligible speech, how will what is spoken be known? For you will be speaking into the air. There are, for example, so many kinds of languages in this world, and nothing is without a voice. If therefore I do not know the force of the voice, I shall be a foreigner to the one to whom I speak, and the one speaking will be a foreigner to me. So also you, since you are eager for spiritual gifts, seek to abound for the edification of the Church. Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is without fruit.”

Now I said that the one who prophesies is greater [Col. 1665C] than the one who speaks in a tongue. You can see this in my own case: a tongue is of no benefit where prophecy is beneficial. For, brothers, if I should now come to you, now that you are believers, speaking in tongues, what good would I do you? None. What good, then, did a tongue do when you were unbelievers? What, I say, is the benefit unless I speak to you either in revelation—that is, so as to expound a revelation to you? Revelation is where certain mysteries are shown through figures, as in the Apocalypse. What benefit is there, therefore, unless understanding is added to the signs—that is, to the tongue—so that the action is carried on not only by the spirit but also by the mind? None. Or in knowledge—that is, so as to expound matters belonging to knowledge, those which illuminate faith, such as the nature of the Godhead; or in prophecy—that is, so as to expound Scripture which treats of future things; [Col. 1665D] or in teaching—that is, so as to expound Scriptures which form character.

[Ambrosius] Or revelation is a sudden disclosure of certain things made through the Spirit. Hence he says later: “If something is revealed to one sitting by,” etc. Prophecy is such as that of Isaiah or the other prophets, which the Holy Spirit reveals without human effort. Knowledge concerns things which one has learned by one’s own study; teaching, things one has acquired under another’s instruction.

“Yet,” etc. By comparison with certain inanimate things, he shows that tongues or prophecies are useless. As though he said: “I have shown, by my own case, that a tongue has no value without an interpreter.” By my own case, I say, though I am rational; yet I can show the same thing through inanimate objects, because “things without a soul,” etc.

Or the connection is as follows. As though he said: “Although you desire tongues, [Col. 1666A] nevertheless even things without a soul which give sound—whether flute or harp—unless they give distinctions of sounds, distinct and intelligible notes, how will what is played on the flute or harp be known?” That is, who will be able to indicate the modes or harmonies of the melody?

“For indeed.” Again he shows the same thing by another comparison. As though he said: “Truly, what belongs to these instruments will not be known, because neither will what belongs to the trumpet.” For if a trumpet gives an uncertain sound: among the Jews the trumpet was used at feasts and in war, with different sounds. Therefore, if it gives an uncertain sound, namely one which does not signify war, who will prepare himself for battle? As though he said: “That sound is not known,” that is, not understood.
