Its effect shows this, since no one prepares for battle.

So also you, speaking in a tongue of whatever signs, or in an unknown tongue, unless you give intelligible speech [Col. 1666B] through interpretation—you who ought to exhort people to battle against demons—how will they know, that is, understand, what is said by you? In no way. And truly it will not be known, for you will be speaking into the air: that is, with the empty impact of air upon human ears, not with understanding reaching human hearts. You will therefore be speaking into the air because you will be speaking so many things: for example, there are many kinds of languages in this world.

[Ambrosius] There are indeed many languages in the world, but they possess their own meaningful vocal signs, so that they may be understood. Hence he adds: “And nothing is without a voice.” The whole meaning is this: this mode of speaking has as much value as if you spoke in every language which no one ever understood, and concerning every matter in each language, because there is no thing without its own name in each language.

[Col. 1666C] Or divide the text thus: “Therefore it is not known, because you will be speaking into the air. For many, for example, many kinds of languages are in this world, and in individual languages nothing is without a voice”—that is, because you speak in all languages and concerning all things.

“Therefore, if.” As though he said: “Because others would not understand without an interpreter, therefore, if I do not know the force of a voice”—that is, the interpretation of the meaning of the voice which I utter—“I shall be a barbarian,” that is, unintelligible to the one to whom I speak, namely the one whom I ought to instruct. “And the one who speaks,” that is, the one who instructs, “will be a barbarian to me,” that is, unintelligible.

Or another reading has, “the one who hears,” to which sense even “the one who speaks” may be adapted if taken passively, so that the meaning is: “the one who speaks,” that is, the one who is instructed; or “the one who hears,” which is the same thing, will be a barbarian to me, [Col. 1666D] that is, neither does he understand me nor I him.

“So also you,” etc. As though he said: “Just as I say of myself that I shall be a barbarian without interpretation, so you too will be barbarians without interpretation. Therefore seek to abound in gifts for the edification of the Church,” which comes through interpretation. I say this because you are “emulators of spirits,” that is, you desire the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Or it may be read under one division in this way: “So”—that is, for this reason, lest you be barbarians—“you also, like me, seek to abound for the edification of the Church, since you are emulators of spirits.”

“And therefore.” As though he said: “Because you ought to edify, therefore the one who speaks in a tongue should pray to God that he may interpret,” that is, that the grace of interpretation may be given to him. Or, “let him pray” means: let him speak in such a way [Col. 1667A] that he also interprets, that is, expounds. For if another does it, it is of no value; and this is what he adds: “For if I pray,” that is, speak, “in a tongue” without interpretation, “my spirit,” namely the Holy Spirit given to me by God, “prays,” that is, makes me speak.

[Note: [Col. 1667D] Augustine, *On Genesis*.] Or “spirit,” that is, reason, prays—that is, makes me speak what it judges to be good. Or spirit here is called the power of the soul inferior to the mind, in which likenesses of bodily things are impressed. Thus, for example, Pharaoh’s spirit was formed so that he saw images, while Joseph’s mind was enlightened so that he understood.

[Ambrosius] And the meaning is: “My spirit prays,” that is, that lower power of the soul upon which images of things are impressed makes me speak; “but my mind,” that is, the other and higher power of the soul, “is without fruit,” that is, without understanding [Col. 1667B] of the things I say, and therefore is not instructed by them. This happens if someone speaks in an unknown tongue, or utters signs of certain things without understanding, just as Latin people commonly sing in Greek, delighted by the sound of the words but nevertheless not knowing what they are saying.

### Verses 15–22

“What then is it? I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the mind. I will sing psalms with the spirit; I will sing psalms with the mind. Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit, how will one who fills the place of the uninstructed person say ‘Amen’ at your blessing? For he does not know what you are saying. For you indeed give thanks well, but the other is not edified. I thank my God that I speak in the tongue of you all. But in church I prefer to speak five words with my understanding, so that I may instruct others also, rather than ten thousand words in a tongue. [Col. 1667C] Brothers, do not become children in understanding; but be little children in malice, and be mature in understanding. For it is written in the Law: ‘Because in other tongues and with other lips I will speak to this people, and not even so will they hear me, says the Lord.’ Therefore tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers; whereas prophecies are not for unbelievers but for believers.”

“What then is it?”—what is useful. What, then, ought to be done? Behold: “I will pray,” that is, speak, “with the spirit,” that is, with the will. Or, with the tongue given by the Holy Spirit: “I will pray also with the mind,” that is, with the understanding of the mind.

[Note: [Col. 1667D] Ibid.] Or: “I will pray with the spirit and I will pray also with the mind”; that is, I shall approve such speech that both the signs of things are formed in the spirit and their understanding shines forth in the mind. Likewise, “I will sing psalms with the spirit,” that is, [Col. 1667D] with the melody of song, which is the lesser thing; “and I will sing psalms with the mind,” that is, with the spiritual understanding of the mind, which is the greater thing. That is, I will sing in such a way that I understand both the harmony of the voice and, similarly, that harmony ought to exist among the members of the Church.

“Otherwise.” As though he said: “One must pray or sing psalms as I have said. But if you do otherwise—namely, if you bless,” that is, speak some good things, “with the spirit,” that is, in a tongue given through the Spirit, “who fills the place of the uninstructed person,” that is, the unlettered and untrained person? As though he said: “No one.” Not even a wise person, because he does not understand.

Then, explaining what the place of the uninstructed person is, he adds: “How will anyone say, ‘Amen’?” This is the place of the uninstructed person, even one who is very attentive: at your blessing, so that he may understand [Col. 1668A] it—by no means. “For he does not know what you are saying.”

[Note: [Col. 1668D] Augustine, *On John*.] Note that this word, *amen*, is neither Greek nor Latin, but Hebrew, and means “true.” Though “true” could have been said where *amen* is said, neither the Greek nor the Latin translator dared translate it, lest it lose value when stripped bare, but so that it might retain honor through the covering of mystery.

“For you.” As though he said: “This is why I speak of your blessing. For you,” etc. Or the connection is thus. As though he said: “I note this, that the uninstructed person has a place. But I do not note or criticize what you do, because you indeed give thanks well in a tongue.” He says this lest he seem to criticize the Spirit’s gift.

[Ambrosius] “You give thanks,” I say, “but the other is not edified.” And lest he seem to be speaking as one jealous, disparaging in others what he did not possess in himself, [Col. 1668B] he shows that he speaks in all their tongues, adding: “I give thanks.” Here he offers himself as an example: they ought not speak in tongues except for edification, just as he does, who knows all tongues. As though he said: “I do not criticize in you something I myself do not possess, because I speak the tongues of all of you,” that is, whichever tongue any one of you speaks. And for this reason, “I give thanks to my God.”

I say that I speak in the tongues of all; but in church, where I ought to be useful, I prefer to speak five—that is, few—words with my own understanding, namely so that I understand, in order to instruct others in faith and morals, rather than ten thousand words—that is, countless words—in a tongue.

So also you, brothers, act thus in church: do not become children in understanding through ignorance, children who utter words which they do not understand. [Col. 1668C] Therefore do not be children in understanding, so that you fail to understand what you say as children do; but according to the example proposed by the Lord when he says, “Become as little children” (Matt. XVIII), be little children in malice—that is, through innocence be removed from malice, as little children are—but be mature in understanding, so that you fully understand what you say and apply yourselves to what benefits your brothers. This is maturity of understanding, as Solomon says: “To know the law is the best understanding.”

“For in the Law,” or “indeed.” Here the reason is shown why they should not seek tongues: tongues are a sign for unbelievers, which they themselves are no longer. Nor are tongues for the edification which is necessary in the Church for those already believing. As though he said: “Therefore do not seek tongues, because this is written in the Law,” that is, in [Col. 1668D] the prophecy of Isaiah, here called the Law: “Because,” etc.

Or: “Indeed, it is written in the Law,” namely in Isaiah, this: “Because in other tongues and with other lips”—that is, in different kinds of languages—“I will speak through the apostles to this people,” namely the Jewish people; and I will do this so that perhaps even thus they may hear me. “And not even so,” that is, not even by the sign of a miracle, “will they hear me, says the Lord.” In this he notes that tongues were given as a sign to unbelievers. Hence he adds: “Therefore,” etc. As though he said: “Because he spoke in tongues so that by this sign they might believe, therefore tongues are a sign not for believers, who believe God able to do all things, but for unbelievers, to be moved toward faith [Col. 1669A] by the novelty of miracles.”

Or thus: he says that tongues by which truth is veiled are not to be desired, because the Lord also said through the prophet that all the veils of the old Law were to be changed, so that truth might become clear to believers in the New Testament when the veil of legal figures had been removed. By this comparison he shows that tongues in which truth is covered are not to be desired, nor given for believers, but for unbelievers; just as under the old Law there was a veil, so that truth might be veiled from the unworthy and unbelieving.

As though he said: “Therefore do not seek tongues, because this is written in the Law: ‘Because I will speak to this people in other tongues,’ namely, not about Sabbath, new moons, circumcision, and the like, but about the New Testament; ‘and with other lips,’ that is, with other words, namely concerning spiritual [Col. 1669B] things, not earthly things. ‘And not even so will they hear me, says the Lord.’” He said this concerning those whom he foreknew would not believe, to whom truth is not open—or is not pleasing—because of their sins. And thus it is evident that tongues are sometimes a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, because, when God gives speech in tongues without interpretation, it signifies that this happens because of unbelievers, so that truth may not be revealed to them.

Or thus: “to speak in other tongues and with other lips” means to speak parabolically and obscurely, as the Lord speaks to unbelievers; but to believers he speaks in the revelation of truth. Hence the Lord says to the apostles: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Luke X). And God’s sayings are obscured by the veil of an unknown tongue so that the faithless may not see them; therefore a tongue is not to be desired.

This agrees [Col. 1669C] in part with the preceding interpretation; for both are from Ambrosius. As though he said: “Therefore do not seek tongues, because this is written in the Law: ‘He speaks to this malevolent people in other tongues and other lips than to believers and well-disposed people’; they are unworthy of revelation, and so the Gospel is spoken to them in parables. ‘And thus they will not hear me, says the Lord,’ as indeed they are not worthy.”

“Therefore” is inferred by analogy. As though he said: “Because God speaks parabolically and obscurely to the faithless and ill-disposed because of their wickedness, it is therefore evident that tongues are a sign, not for believers but for unbelievers.” That is, God’s sayings in an unknown tongue are obscure so that the faithless may not see them; when they are heard, this is a sign that, [Col. 1669D] because of unbelief, it has happened that those hearing do not understand. This surely happens to unbelievers, whose minds are covered. But prophecy suits believers, not an unknown tongue. Hence he adds: “Prophecies, so that believers may be mature in understanding, are given not to unbelievers, lest what is holy be given to dogs, but to believers, that they may be edified.”

### Verses 23–33

“Therefore, if the whole Church should assemble in one place and all speak in tongues, and uninstructed persons or unbelievers enter, will they not say, ‘Are you mad?’ But if all prophesy, and some unbeliever or uninstructed person enters, he is convicted by all, judged by all. For the secrets of his heart become manifest; and thus, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you. What then is it, brothers? [Col. 1670A] When you assemble, each one of you has a psalm, has teaching, has an apocalypse, has a tongue, has an interpretation. Let all things be done for edification. If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be by two, or at most three, and in turns; and let one interpret. But if there is no interpreter, let him be silent in church; yet let him speak to himself and to God. Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge. But if something is revealed to another sitting by, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may be exhorted. And the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of dissension but of peace, as I teach in all the churches of the saints.”

“Therefore, if.” Here another reason is given why they should not speak only in tongues. As though he said: “Because tongues [Col. 1670B] are a sign and are not for edification, therefore, if the whole Church assembles in one place and all speak in tongues without an interpreter, and an uninstructed person or unbeliever enters, will he not say, ‘Are you mad?’” As though he said: “For they will seem possessed when one does not understand another.” For a certain disorderly tumult of a crowd results, like that of people suffering frenzy.

[Ambrosius] Or perhaps those who hear will think it some deception and vanity, which is sung in tongues because it would be shameful if disclosed. This is as among pagans, among whom those things called sacred rites are in some way veiled, lest they see themselves being mocked by vanities. Every imposture seeks darkness and passes off false things as true, just as pagans are deceived when their vanities are concealed. But among you nothing is cleverly disguised [Col. 1670C] or painted over; rather, one God is praised simply and openly. For if no one understood, what was sung in tongues might seem a deception, whose disclosure would be shameful.

“But if.” As though he said: “If all speak in tongues, that unsuitable consequence follows. But if all prophesy individually,” that is, expound, “and some unbeliever or uninstructed person enters, he is convicted of his own error by all; he is judged,” that is, shown by all to be liable to condemnation. And this is so because the secrets of his heart—that is, his sins, which he did not know to be sins—are made manifest to him through their expositions. And thus, falling on his face—that is, humbling himself—he will worship God, who has made himself known to him through you, declaring with his mouth what he has in his heart: [Col. 1670D] that God is truly in you.

“What then.” He now begins to determine how tongues ought to be used. As though he said: “Since these things result from speaking in tongues, what, brothers, must be done concerning them? Namely this: when you gather together, use tongues for edification, just as other things also must be done.” For each of you has some gift which he can use for edification; therefore let no one excuse himself. For example, one has a psalm, that is, praise of God by song. Or, he has a psalm, that is, by God’s grace he understands the psalms. Another has a tongue; another teaching concerning morals. Or, teaching—that is, spiritual understanding through wisdom. Another has an apocalypse, that is, revelation; another has interpretation of tongues or Scriptures. But let all these [Col. 1671A] and other things be done for edification—that is, they ought to be done.

“If,” etc. As though he said: “Other things must be done for edification in their own ways, but a tongue must be used thus: if anyone speaks in a tongue, let the speaking be by two, or at most by three.” That is, let two or three speak, and no more than three, lest they occupy the day speaking in tongues and leave no place for prophets to expound the Scriptures, who illuminate the whole Church. I say, let speech in a tongue be by two or three; and let this same thing be done in turns in the Church. Or, let one speak after another, or with intervals; and wherever or whenever someone speaks, let there be one to interpret—that is, let there be someone to expound to the people.

“But if there is no interpreter, let the one speaking in tongues be silent in [Col. 1671B] church,” where there should be nothing except edification; “but let him speak to himself,” in tongues, that is, silently pray to God. He speaks to himself who is pierced with compunction by the things he says. And here let him speak to God, that is, for the honor of God, whom he praises or honors.

Let only two or three prophets also speak, one by one; therefore there ought not to be more who speak in tongues. He says “two or three” because the speech of so many persons is sufficient. “Every word stands in the mouth of two or three” (Deut. XIX). Let the others silently judge what they say, whether it ought to be accepted or not.

But if something better is revealed through the Holy Spirit to one sitting by—that is, to one who was listening—let the first prophet be silent and give him room to speak. For sometimes something is given to an inferior person which is not given to a superior. [Col. 1671C] This is why I say that he should give place: “For you can all prophesy,” including the one sitting by who has received the grace of prophesying, though not simultaneously, lest disorder result, but one by one; so that, by this ordered use of prophecy, all, even the greater, may learn, and all, even the lesser, may exhort others.

“And the spirits.” As though he said: “The speaker ought to yield to the person sitting by, because the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets.” That is, the Holy Spirit, who is one, is subject to prophets. But he speaks in the plural because of the many prophets whom he fills, or because of his many gifts: he is subject to prophets so that, when they wish to be silent and when they wish to speak, they are able to do so. He does not compel them, as a Pythian spirit does, to cry out certain things or to keep silent. Hence, if the first does not yield, he seems not to have the Spirit of God.

The spirit is also said to be subject when it prompts and [Col. 1671D] assists good efforts. “For not.” As though he said: “Truly it is subject, because God is not the author of dissension,” that is, discord, “but of peace”; and therefore one should yield to another. But God would be a God of dissension if he compelled those whom he fills to speak at once. This he does not do; rather, he makes one yield to another. Otherwise he would be a God of dissension and not of peace.

But I teach these things about the orderly use of tongues and prophecy just as I teach in our Church. And I tell you the same as I teach in all the churches of the saints. As though he said: “What I tell you is neither new nor peculiar.” Therefore hold it firmly.

### Verses 34–40

“Let women be silent in the churches; for they are not permitted to speak, but to be subject, as [Col. 1672A] the Law also says. But if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church. Did the word of God proceed from you, or did it come to you alone? If anyone thinks himself to be a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge that what I write to you are the Lord’s commands. But if anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored. Therefore, brothers, desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But let all things be done honorably and according to order among you.”

“Women.” [Augustine] As though he said: “Although I said that you can all prophesy, nevertheless let women be silent in the churches, so that they neither speak in tongues nor prophesy. For no authority permits them to speak in church; rather, they are commanded to be subject to their husbands, as the veil indicates.” “As the Law also [Col. 1672B] says,” in Genesis: “You shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you.” But if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their husbands, and only at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church because it is contrary to ecclesiastical discipline.

[Ambrosius] And because, on account of the sin which woman introduced, she ought always to be ashamed.

“Did it proceed from you?” Since perhaps, concerning tongues and prophecy, the Apostle might seem to some to have spoken incorrectly, lest they presume to establish some other order—as they had altered his institutions in other matters—he adds a rebuke by which he reproves them. It is as though, abandoning his institutions, they wished to introduce novelties, which they could not do. For God’s word did not proceed from them, nor did they alone receive it. He says this interrogatively: “Did it proceed from you?” [Col. 1672C] As though he said: “You ought not alter what I handed down; for did the word of God proceed from you to us? Rather, it came from us to you.”

He rebukes them thus because the Corinthians boasted as though they conferred a benefit by coming to faith rather than received one, and as though other nations were called to faith through their example. Therefore he rebukes them again, adding: “Or did the word of God come to you alone?” As though he said: “No; rather, to many others.” Therefore keep what the others keep.

He reproves them thus because in the pride of their vanity they presented themselves as if, unless they obeyed the words of faith, no one would believe. “If anyone thinks himself to be a prophet or spiritual,” etc. As though he said: “For this reason also you ought to keep my commands: because what I write to you are the Lord’s commands. And if anyone truly is a prophet or spiritual, as he appears to be, he ought to recognize this.” [Col. 1672D] Otherwise, if he resists, he is neither a prophet nor spiritual.

In saying this he touches upon the false apostles, who taught not divine but earthly things according to human desires. He says “prophet or spiritual” because there are spiritual persons who are not prophets, who have no knowledge of future things.

“But if anyone.” [Haimo] As though he said: “What I write are God’s commands; but if anyone is ignorant that these are God’s commands, and refuses to believe that they are God’s commands, he will be ignored by God in the future”—that is, rejected and not recognized as being among the predestined. As is read in the Gospel, the Lord will say to the wicked: “I do not know you” (Matt. XXV), that is, “I have not known you as mine, or as among the predestined.”

[Col. 1673A] [Note: [Col. 1673D] Augustine, *On John*.] And rightly, one who does not know that what the Apostle says comes from the Lord will himself be ignored by the Lord on the day of judgment.

Or thus: the Apostle wishes the knowledge of spiritual things which he teaches to be firm, and, knowing that they must be understood spiritually, says, “If anyone.” As though he said: “Hold what I have said, and understand these things spiritually and truly.” This is what he means by saying, “If anyone thinks himself to be a prophet or spiritual”—that is, if anyone is what he appears to be—“let him acknowledge,” that is, let him truly and spiritually understand, “that what I write to you are the Lord’s commands,” because they are truly spiritual. By this he indicates that the words of the Epistles are difficult, since he commands them to be recognized by a prophet or spiritual person.

[Note: [Col. 1673D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*.] Notice that he says, “If anyone thinks himself to be a prophet or spiritual”; assuredly he is not so if he does not recognize this. For one who truly is so recognizes it. And [Col. 1673B] therefore let him recognize that they are the Lord’s commands.

“But if anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored.” The Apostle does not say this of everything he has written, as though that punishment were to be inflicted on those unable to discern the ineffable unity of the Trinity. For the little ones who glory in Christ’s cross attain glory even if they do not know what is discussed with the greatest subtlety; for not one of the little ones for whom Christ died perishes.

Therefore he does not say this concerning matters which scarcely come within the understanding of a few, and then only a slight understanding—as much as there can be, however small, in this life concerning so great a subject. Rather, he speaks of the foregoing matters which build faith and morals: namely, that prophecy be preferred to tongues; that these things not be done tumultuously, as though the spirit of prophecy compelled even unwilling people to speak; that women be silent in [Col. 1673C] church; and that all things be done honorably and in order.

Thus he restrains and recalls to peaceful order the unruly, who were all the more prone to sedition because they considered themselves eminent in a spirit of superiority while in their pride they disturbed everything. And the meaning is: “If anyone, great or small, is ignorant of these matters just mentioned, he will be ignored,” that is, disapproved.

[Augustine] For if you refer it to knowledge, God does not fail to know any persons or things; yet at judgment he will say, “I never knew you” (Matt. VII). His rejection of them is indicated by this expression.

“Therefore.” [Ambrosius] As though he said: “Because interpretation edifies, therefore, brothers, desire,” that is, seek, “to prophesy; nevertheless, do not forbid speaking in tongues,” lest dissension occur. “But let all things.” As though he said: [Col. 1673D] “I say, do not forbid it; but do all things among you, both these and the others, not childishly but honorably—that is, in peace and according to the order already given, so that what is more useful may be preferred to what is less useful.”

## Chapter XV

### Verses 1–9

“Now I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel which I preached to you, which you also received, in which you also stand, through which you are also saved—by what reasoning I preached it to you—if you hold it fast, unless you believed in vain. For I handed down to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures; that he was buried; that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures; and that he was seen by Cephas, [Col. 1674A] and afterward by the eleven. Then he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once, of whom many remain until now, but some have fallen asleep. Then he was seen by James, then by all the apostles. Last of all, as to one born untimely, he was seen also by me. For I am the least of the apostles, not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God.”

“Now I make known.” [Ambrosius] Having completed his treatment of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, he deals with the resurrection of the dead. This is because, although when he himself taught they had rightly believed in it, afterward, corrupted by the evil speech of certain persons, they had departed from this faith. He therefore first proves that it will occur through Christ’s resurrection, and then through many other arguments.

As though he said: “Up to this point I have taught concerning spiritual things; but now, brothers, I make known to you the Gospel concerning the resurrection of the dead which I have already preached to you. It is not new; you also received it,” that is, judged it worthy of acceptance; “and in it you stand,” that is, you are enabled to stand, though without it you fall; “and through it you are saved,” now in the certainty of hope, and will be saved in the future in the reality and vision of the thing itself—if nevertheless you retain the reasoning by which I preached it to you. That is, if you hold the Gospel concerning the resurrection of the dead by the reasoning through which I confirmed it to you, namely through Christ’s resurrection. I say, you hold it, “unless you believed in vain,” that is, either you hold the resurrection of the dead or faith is without effect, since it is accepted only in hope of resurrection.

Or thus: “unless.” As though he said: “You will be saved, [Col. 1674C] unless you believed in vain that same thing which I preached to you in confirmation of the resurrection of the dead.”

For I handed this down to you “first of all,” that is, among the greatest matters, and still hand down what I received from the Holy Spirit and did not invent: namely, that Christ died, not by necessity for himself but for our sins. And I say this “according to the Scriptures” of the Old Testament, which foretold Christ’s coming death. Thus Isaiah says: “He was led as a sheep to slaughter” (Isa. LIII); and again: “His life shall be taken from the earth because of the iniquities of my people” (ibid.). “He was led to death.” And I also handed down that he was buried.

[Haimo] This too was according to the Scriptures. For Isaiah says: “He shall give the wicked for his burial, and the rich for [Col. 1674D] his death” (ibid.); and again: “His tomb shall be glorious,” he says (Isa. XI). And I also handed down that he rose, his true death having been established; and so quickly, namely on the third day, that it may be believed he is able by that power to raise us. And I said this too: “According to the Scriptures.”

[Ambrosius] For Hosea says: “After two days he will revive us, and on the third day we shall rise and live in his sight” (Hos. VI). But if he died and was buried and rose, do not doubt that the dead and buried will rise. And I also handed down that, after the resurrection, he was seen by Cephas, that is, Peter, before the other men to whom he is recorded in the Gospel as appearing.

[Note: [Col. 1674D] Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*.] Otherwise this would conflict with the account that he first appeared to women. [Col. 1675A] And after this he was seen by the eleven apostles in the upper room.

[Note: [Col. 1675D] Augustine, in the book *Questions on Genesis*.] Another reading has “the twelve,” which is understood by synecdoche. For where the greater or more important part is present, what does not belong to the name itself is commonly included under that name; as in the saying, “Did I not choose you twelve?” (John VI), although Judas was not among the elect. So also here. Greek manuscripts have this number, *the twelve*, with the article, so that not any twelve, but those understood under that number, are meant.

[Note: [Col. 1675D] Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*.] But some manuscripts have “the eleven,” which, I think, people altered in confusion. Yet neither reading conflicts with the truth.

Then he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once; this is not read in the Gospel. Of these, many remain even now [Col. 1675B] and are witnesses, if you inquire of them; but some have fallen asleep, that is, have died while remaining in this testimony.

[Ambrosius] Then he was seen by James individually; this too is not in the Gospel. Then he appeared to all the apostles at the ascension. Last of all, namely after the ascension, he was seen also by me: first from heaven, afterward while I was praying in the temple. By me, I say, “as by one born untimely,” that is, like one born untimely, because he was compelled to be converted to God, just as one born untimely is compelled to be born.

Or he is called one born untimely because he received apostleship in Christ outside the proper time, after Christ had already been taken up to heaven. For one born untimely is called one born outside the lawful and suitable time, that is, before or after it ought to be.

[Haimo] So Paul here is called one born untimely because he was born in Christ later than he ought to have been. Or he is called like one born untimely because he was less than the other apostles in view of his former condition, or in time. Hence he adds: “For I,” etc. As though he said: [Col. 1675C] “He rightly appeared to me after all the others, because I am the least of the apostles,” in view of the past; and he says this for humility’s sake.

[Ambrosius] Or he was less than the others in time of calling, because he was called last; not in dignity, labor, or preaching. “Not worthy to be called an apostle,” indeed,

[Haimo] if my preceding merits are considered. Hence he adds: “Because I persecuted the Church of God.”

[Ambrosius, Haimo] Testimony from one who had formerly been an enemy is the more compelling.

### Verses 10–19

“But by the grace of God I am what [Col. 1675D] I am; and his grace in me was not empty, but I labored more abundantly than all of them—yet not I, but the grace of God with me. Whether, then, I or they, so we preached and so you believed. But if Christ is preached as raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ risen. And if Christ has not risen, our preaching is empty, and your faith also is empty. Moreover, we are found to be false witnesses of God, because we testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if the dead are not raised. For if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ [Col. 1676A] risen. But if Christ has not risen, your faith is vain. For you are still in your sins. Therefore also those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are more pitiable than all people.”

And as though someone were to ask: “If he is not worthy to be called an apostle, why then is he an apostle?” He answers: “By the grace of God I am what I am,” that is, an apostle. He gives glory to God who chose him, not to himself; and rightly he calls it grace. [Augustine] For God first gives by grace alone, when nothing but evil merits have preceded; but afterwards, through grace, good merits begin. For Paul had a merit when he persecuted the Church of God—but an evil one. [Note: [Col. 1676D] Id., *On Grace and Free Will.*] Therefore, when he possessed this evil merit, good was returned to him for evil [Col. 1676B], as he shows when he says: “By the grace of God I am what I am.” And, to show free choice as well, he adds: “And his grace,” [Augustine] that is, his apostleship, “was not void in me,” [Ambrose] that is, idle; for because he had been a persecutor, the grace given him in the apostleship was no less. “It was not void,” I say, “but I laboured more abundantly than all of them,” individually. [Note: [Col. 1676D] Id., *On John.*] For he laboured among so many peoples among whom they did not labour; yet this was more fully accomplished because he also lived by the work of his hands and did not thereby do less for the Gospel. And lest even the will itself be thought able to accomplish anything without God’s grace, he adds: “Yet not I alone work without grace, but the grace of God with me,” that is, with free choice. [Augustine] Clearly, when grace has been given, our merits begin [Col. 1676C] to be good. Yet they are good through it, because if it withdraws itself, a human being falls.

“For whether.” As though he said: “The dead man rose, and truly did so, because this is what we preach, namely, that Christ rose—whether I or they,” the other apostles. Or the connection may be understood thus: “I and the other apostles laboured, and this is true because in this preaching”—which he expresses thus—“whether I or they, we have thus preached,” namely, everywhere that Christ rose; “and thus you believed.” He rebukes them because, though this faith was manifest among all the Churches, they had departed from it. Or thus: “Truly I have this through grace, because whether I or they,” that is, I and they, “have thus,” that is, through grace, “preached; and you have thus,” that is, through grace, “believed.”

“If, however.” Up to this point he has shown that Christ rose. [Col. 1676D] Now by his resurrection he proves the resurrection of the dead. As though he said: “Thus it is established that Christ rose from death. But if”—that is, if Christ, who is the effective cause of the resurrection of the dead, rose from the dead, as is preached by all true apostles—“how do some among you say that there will be no resurrection of the dead?”

“But if.” As though he said: “Some say that it will not occur; but if this is so”—that is, if there is to be no resurrection of the dead—“it must be said that neither has Christ risen,” [Ambrose] who did everything for the sake of his own. These pseudo-apostles had handed down this teaching, denying the truth by saying that Christ neither came [Col. 1677A] in the flesh, nor suffered, nor rose.

“But if.” Lest anyone deny Christ’s resurrection, he adds the absurd consequences: “But if Christ has not risen, our preaching is empty,” that is, useless, “and your faith likewise is empty,” that is, useless, since no recompense is to come—which you do not wish. “Moreover, we are found”—and not only does this absurdity follow, but also this other—“false witnesses of God,” we apostles, whom everyone believes, since God is angered by false praise of himself, “because we have given testimony against God,” namely, that he raised Jesus Christ, whom he did not raise, if the dead do not rise.

[Note: [Col. 1677D] Augustine to Jerome.] It is utterly dreadful to say anything false about God, even if it seems to pertain to his praise, because falsehood is perhaps praised in relation to God with no lesser—indeed, with greater—wickedness than truth is censured. “For if.” As though he said: “God did not raise Jesus if the dead do not rise; for Christ did not rise if that is so,” as he says: “For if the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen.” “Which,” that is, “but if Christ has not risen, then your faith is vain,” that is, false, not merely useless. “For you are still.” As though he said: “Your faith is truly false if Christ has not risen, because you are still”—namely, after baptism—“in your sins,” which you believed would be forgiven. These are valid logical connections, though they contain false propositions. [Note: [Col. 1677D] Id., *On Christian Doctrine.*] These and other consequences are therefore drawn so that the person whose error entails them may be ashamed here, since he himself condemns these consequences. Therefore, lest they remain in this error, “therefore.”

He adds another absurdity: “And because you are in sins, therefore those also who have fallen asleep in Christ,” that is, who have died in the faith of Christ, “were in sins, and therefore have perished.” By this he instils shame and fear in them. “If in this,” etc. Here he shows another absurdity. As though he said: “And if Christ has not risen, we are people hoping in Christ,” [the text has “110”], that is, in the faith of Christ, only in this life, so that we do not hope for a future resurrection. And if this is so, then “we are more pitiable than all human beings,” who at least enjoy this present age.

### Verses 20–24

“But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep. For since death came through a human being, through a human being also came the resurrection of the dead. [Col. 1677D] And as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; then those who belong to Christ, who believed in his coming; then the end, when he has delivered the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished every rule and authority and power.”

“But now.” As though he said: “If Christ has not risen, these absurd consequences follow; but, to avoid these absurdities, it now appears that Christ has risen from the dead, who is the firstfruits of those who sleep,” that is, of the dead. They are called [Col. 1678A] sleepers because they shall easily and whole rise from death as from the sleep of slumber. Christ is called their firstfruits because he rose before the others both in time and in dignity.

“For indeed.” As though he said: “Through Christ as a human being they can rise, because death came through a human being indeed far inferior; and if this is so, therefore through a human being the resurrection of the dead can also occur. Behold: firstfruits—human being and human being: a human being unto life, a human being unto death; but that one was only human, whereas this one is God and human.” [Note: [Col. 1677D] Id., *On John.*] He then states who the one is and who the other is.

“And as.” As though he said: “Through whom came death, and through whom resurrection? Behold: as all die bodily death in Adam, because they are his children, from whom they derived death and the desert of death, so also all shall be made alive in Christ,” [Col. 1678B] because they are his children by spiritual regeneration. [Note: [Col. 1678D] Id., to Dardanus.] Observe how he says that all die in Adam and all are made alive in Christ: for no one is born unto death except through the former, and no one unto life except through the latter. [Note: [Col. 1678D] Id., to Optatus.] For as through Adam all mortals, under punishment, were made children of the age, so through Christ all immortals are made children of God by grace. No one doubts that this is said of bodily death, since the discussion concerned the resurrection of the body.

“But each.” As though he said: “All shall have this in common, namely, that they will rise; nevertheless, they will differ, because each will rise in his own order,” that is, in his own rank: martyr as martyr, apostle as apostle, and likewise the rest. “Christ the firstfruits,” etc. Here he explains the orders, both as to the certain event and as to the times when it occurred and when [Col. 1678C] the dead will rise. [Ambrose] “Firstfruits,” that is, first in time and greatest in dignity, is Christ, who rose first in order to establish faith and provide a pattern for believers. [Haimo] “Then all those who belong to Christ,” namely, those who believe in Christ, who are less worthy than he, will rise later in time and lower in dignity. He explains “those who belong to Christ” by saying: “Those who believed in his coming,” that is, who believed that he himself would come to reward the good.

Or another wording is found in the book: “Then those who are Christ’s, at his coming,” namely, shall rise—that is, when he comes for judgment. “Then shall be the end,” that is, the consummation. He says this in commendation of the resurrection: when it is accomplished, there will be both the end of the world and the consummation [Col. 1678D] of all things. And this will occur “when Christ has delivered,” that is, presented, “the kingdom,” that is, those whom he ruled in good works, “to God,” his Creator insofar as he is human, “and to his Father,” insofar as he is God.

He is said to deliver it to the Father in order to show that the Son is a different person from the Father. [Note: [Col. 1678D] Id., *On the Trinity.*] We must not therefore suppose that Christ will deliver the kingdom to God and the Father in such a way as to take it away from himself, as certain empty talkers have believed. For when it is said, “he has delivered the kingdom to God,” he himself and the Holy Spirit are not separated, since the Son and the Holy Spirit are one God together with the Father. What, then, does “when he has delivered the kingdom to God and the Father” mean, [Col. 1679A] as though God the Father did not now possess the kingdom? Rather, this is what it means: “when he has delivered the kingdom to God and the Father,” that is, when he has led believers to the contemplation of God the Father, where is the end of all things, everlasting rest, and joy.

Therefore the end will then come when he has delivered the kingdom—[Note: [Col. 1679D] Augustine, *On John.*] that is, those whom he redeemed with the blood of the Son—to God and the Father for contemplation; not that he takes it away from himself, since he is one God with the Father. “Then the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII). [Note: [Col. 1679D] Id., *On the Trinity.*] The kingdom shall shine in the kingdom, when the kingdom for which we now pray comes with the kingdom, as we say: “May your kingdom come” (Matt. VI). [Note: [Col. 1679D] Id., *On Psalm XXI.*] Therefore he will deliver the kingdom to the Father when he leads the kingdom that he sowed, when he came as less than the Father, to the vision in which, as equal, he did not depart from the Father. [Note: [Col. 1679D] Id., *On the Trinity.*]

For his faithful people, [Col. 1679B] whom he redeemed with his blood, are called here his kingdom; although every creature is also his kingdom. But “kingdom of Christ” is said in one way of every creature, in another way of the Church. [Note: [Col. 1679D] Id., in the book *Eighty-Three Questions.*] Every creature is called Christ’s kingdom according to the power of his divinity, but the Church according to the distinctive character of faith that is from him. And the meaning is: “When he has delivered the kingdom to God the Father,” that is, when he has led to the sight of the Godhead those in whom God now reigns by faith, because then the Father will be revealed by the Son. Hence: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. XI). There the essence of the Son together with the Father and the Holy Spirit will be seen; this will be granted only to pure hearts, and it is the highest blessedness. [Note: [Col. 1680D] Id., in the same work.]

Or thus: “When he has delivered the kingdom to God the Father,” that is, when he has shown [Col. 1679C] the Father to reign, which is now believed. Then indeed this will become clear through sight and manifestation; and then will be the end, “when he has abolished every rule and authority and power.” While the world endures, angels preside over angels, demons over demons, human beings over human beings, for the benefit or the deception of those living; but once all have been gathered, every pre-eminence will cease, because it will no longer be necessary. Christ is said to abolish this pre-eminence because he will exalt in the kingdom all his own who were humble here, just as he reigns from the humility which he had.

Distinguish: by “rule” he means the greater ones; by “authority,” the lesser ones; by “power,” those who work miracles, or strong human beings. [Haimo] But then every creaturely pre-eminence among angels and human beings will cease; fear will cease, love will reign, and there will be no discord between rulers and subjects. [Augustine] Or thus: “When he has abolished every rule and authority and power,” because then it will be known to all that none of these, earthly or heavenly, possessed any of these things from themselves, but from him, from whom all things are.

### Verses 25–28

“For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. But the last enemy to be destroyed is death. For he has subjected all things under [Col. 1680A] his feet. But when he says, ‘All things are subjected to him,’ undoubtedly this excludes him who subjected all things to him. And when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself also will be subjected to him who subjected all things to himself, so that God may be all in all.”

“But he must.” As though he said: “Then he will reign openly; but meanwhile he must reign secretly, because otherwise the Scriptures would be false; and he who now reigns will be able to raise his own.” I say that he must reign until he puts all enemies under his feet in the future. [Note: [Col. 1680D] Id., in the same book.]

Or thus: “He will deliver the kingdom and abolish authority; but he must reign,” that is, his kingdom must meanwhile be made manifest, “until he has put all enemies,” whether willing or compelled, [Haimo] “under his feet,” that is, under complete subjection, [Note: [Col. 1680D] Id., in the same book.] or under [Col. 1680B] his humanity, so that they may revere and honour it and acknowledge Christ the human being as God and king of all.

And the meaning is: meanwhile his kingdom must be manifested until all his enemies acknowledge that he reigns—both those who are justified from being unjust and submit to him in faith, and those who do not belong to the blessedness of the righteous, since they too, confounded by the very manifestation of his kingdom, will acknowledge that he reigns. [Augustine] Observe his words, “until he has put,” etc. They are not said as though, once he has put his enemies under his feet, he will no longer reign; rather, he will bring the kingdom to such evident clarity that his enemies will not dare deny that he reigns. Nothing can be more manifest, even if his reign continues further. It is one thing no longer to be made more manifest, another thing no longer to remain. [Col. 1680C] No longer to be made manifest means not to become clearer; no longer to remain means not to endure longer. When, however, will Christ’s kingdom be more manifest than when it has shone before all his enemies? Thus by saying “until,” he excludes a greater manifestation of the kingdom, not a longer continuance.

So also it is said: “Our eyes are upon God, until he has mercy on us” (Ps. CXXII). This does not mean that they are turned away when he has had mercy, but that they seek nothing further. Moreover, it is established among other things that he also has the power to raise the dead. Hence he adds: “But the last.” Here again is a commendation of the resurrection. As though he said: “Christ reigns now, and then he will reign. Then he will reign openly; meanwhile he must reign. But death,” [Col. 1680D] the enemy toward which we are hostile, or which is itself hostile toward us, “will be destroyed last,” because there will be nothing left to destroy after this mortal has put on immortality; for human beings will no longer be dissolved, as heretics suppose.

“For he has.” As though he said: “He will put all things under his feet; and he certainly can do this, because Scripture says that God the Father ‘subjected all things under his feet’” (Ps. VIII), that is, Christ’s, so that he may even destroy death. [Note: [Col. 1680D] Id., in the same book.] But he wishes us without doubt to understand the Father as the one who subjected all things, [Col. 1681A] just as in many places in the Gospel Christ refers to the Father what he possesses—not only because of the form of a servant, but also because of the principle from whom he is, and from whom he is equal to the one from whom he is.

He shows how this Scripture must be understood by adding: “But when Scripture says,” it is established by its authority that “all things are without doubt subjected to him,” namely, Christ, except him—that is, except the deity—who subjected all things to him. Since he is from no one, he can for no reason be subject to anyone. For he is the principle of all things.

“But when.” As though he said: “God is not subject to him; rather, he himself is subject to God insofar as he is human.” [Augustine] He expresses this thus: “When all things have been subjected to him,” that is, to the Son, “then the Son himself also,” in that very pre-eminence, insofar as [Col. 1681B] he is human, “will be subjected,” together with his body, which is the Church, [the text has “111”] “to him who subjected all things to himself.” [Note: [Col. 1681D] Augustine, in the book *Eighty-Three Questions.*] Notice that when he says “when they have been subjected,” he does not say this as though they are not subject even now. And when he says “the Son himself also will be subjected,” he does not say this as though he is not subject even now. Rather, he uses a manner of speaking frequently used by Scripture: something that always exists is said to come about at the time when it begins to be known by someone.

Thus, although the name of God is always holy seed [the reading *sanctum*, “holy,” is supplied], yet in the Lord’s Prayer it is said: “Hallowed be your name” (Matt. VI), that is, may it become known to be holy. Likewise it was said above, “when he has delivered,” namely, to God and the Father, that is, when he has shown the Father to reign. Similarly, “he will abolish [Col. 1681C] every power,” etc., because then it will be known to all that no earthly or heavenly beings possessed any power of themselves except from God, from whom all things are. For then no hope will remain for anyone in any ruler except God.

And the meaning is: “When all things have been subjected to him,” that is, when they have become known to be subject, “then he himself also will be subjected to him who subjected them to himself,” that is, he will become known to be subject according to the form of a servant, to him to whom he is equal according to the form of God. “So that he may be.” As though he said: “Then he will be subject, yet in such a way that according to the other nature, namely the divine, he is God”—[Note: [Col. 1681D] Id., *City of God.*] one with the Father and the Holy Spirit—being all things that can be desired in all his members, because the reward of virtue will be he who gave virtue, because God will be that by which they are satisfied.

[Col. 1681D] Therefore he will be all things that are honourably desired, because God will be life, salvation, strength, abundance, glory, honour, peace, the end of desires, and every good. And this will be in all. Among certain eternal beings there can be some distance, but eternity itself is without diversity of measure. There will be many dwellings in one life, namely, varying ranks of merits; but where God will be all in all, there will also be equal joy amid unequal brightness, so that what each possesses may be common to all, because even the glory of the head will belong to all through the bond of love.

[Ambrose] Or thus, so that he may be speaking of Christ according to [Col. 1682A] divinity: “When all things have been subjected to him,” that is, when all have worshipped Christ as God, “then the Son himself will be subject to him who subjected all things to himself,” that is, then Christ will show himself to be God, but God from God, so that the supreme and ineffable authority of one principle may remain. He will show himself to be God from God, while nevertheless there is one God in all, that is, in the confession of all, from whom all things are. For when every creature learns that Christ is its head and that the head of Christ is God, then not only will there be one God in all, that is, in the confession of all, but every creature will also confess him to be the one from whom all things are, because all things are from him.

But if he had said “so that God may be in all,” it would be understood that he is in all indeed either by affection or by common [Col. 1682B] perception, yet not that all things are from him. But when he said “all in all,” he signified that all things are from him, and that he is in all things from him because they were created by him—in those, however, in whose confession he will be the one God.

Or thus, “so that he may be.” As though he said: “All things will be subject to the Son, so that the Son himself may be God all in all,” that is, so that none of those who cling to him may love his own will against him. [Note: [Col. 1682D] Id., in the book *Eighty-Three Questions.*] This is the end which he mentioned above, summing everything up briefly: that is, through Christ is the consummation, which consummation he briefly called there, “then the end”; afterwards he explained in detail how there is consummation when he said, “when he has delivered the kingdom and abolished every rule,” [Col. 1682C] etc. And the meaning is: “so that God may be all in all,” that is, so that none of those who cling to him may love anything against him, and then it may be manifest what is said: “What have you that you did not receive?” For then it will be manifest that no one has or has had any good except from Christ. [Note: [Col. 1682D] Id., *On the Trinity.*] Nor should anyone suppose that the Father so subjected all things to the Son that the Son himself should not be thought to have subjected all things to himself. For the operation of the Father and the Son is inseparable.

### Verses 29–34

“Otherwise, what will those do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead do not rise at all, why are they also baptized for them? Why are we also in danger every hour? I die daily, brothers, by your glory which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord. If, according to human reasoning, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what does it profit me if the dead do not rise? Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. Do not be deceived. Evil conversations corrupt good morals. Awake, you righteous, and do not sin. For some have ignorance of God. I speak this to your shame.”

“Otherwise,” etc. He still shows another absurd consequence if the resurrection of the dead is not to come. For if the dead do not rise, then neither did Christ rise; and if he did not rise, then in baptism forgiveness of sins does not occur. As though he said: “The dead rise; otherwise,” namely, if there is to be no resurrection [Col. 1683A] of the dead, “what will those do who are baptized for the dead,” that is, for the blotting out of sins, or in order to be made dead to themselves, after the likeness of Christ’s death, when they are not to possess life? He repeats the same thing in other words: “If the dead do not rise at all,” so that not even Christ rose, “why are they also baptized for them,” that is, for sins, when these themselves are not forgiven if Christ has not risen?

[Haimo] Or thus, “otherwise”: there were certain uninstructed people who were baptized on behalf of those who had departed this life without baptism, thinking that it benefited them. For they feared either that these persons would not rise, or that they would rise badly. [Ambrose] Therefore, if any relative of one of these had departed from the world without baptism, some living person was baptized in that person’s name, thinking to benefit the dead person. [Haimo] The Apostle does not mention this without reason. [Ambrose] For he does not approve their practice, but shows their fixed faith in the resurrection. And the meaning is: “Otherwise,” namely, if the resurrection of the dead is not to come, “what will those do who are baptized for the dead,” [Haimo] that is, in the place of those who have died? What benefit will they bring to the dead? That is, what will it profit those who will not rise that living persons are baptized for them? Certainly nothing. “And if the dead do not rise at all, why are they baptized for them?” As though he said: “What is the point for those persons—that is, the dead—when sins are forgiven only on account of a future resurrection?” As though he said: “If fools are so certain of the future resurrection, you [Col. 1683C] ought not to doubt.”

“Why?” As though he said: “If the dead do not rise, why are we also”—we who do not seem foolish like those mentioned above but wise? For he distinguishes these from the foregoing when he says, “and we also.” Why, I say, are we “in danger,” that is, suffering dangers, “every hour”? And not only do I suffer dangers, but “I die daily,” [Haimo] that is, I undergo dangers of death, O brothers, “for your glory,” namely, so that you may attain eternal glory; [Note: [Col. 1683D] Augustine, in a sermon on the Epistle of James.] or, “by your glory, I swear.” Behold, the Apostle swore, so that we may know that swearing truthfully is not a sin. But one should not therefore swear in doubtful matters. It is safer not to swear than, through the habit of swearing, to commit perjury. But to swear falsely is a most grave sin. An oath does not violate the commandment when it arises not from the evil of the person swearing, but from that of the unbelieving [Col. 1683D] or weak person, who does not believe otherwise.

“Which,” etc. As though he said: “I say, by your glory or for your glory—not indeed human glory, but eternal glory—which I already possess in hope in Christ Jesus our Lord,” that is, while I consider that he himself was glorified through suffering. Again: “If the dead do not rise, what does it profit me if I fought,” that is, disputed, “with beasts at Ephesus,” namely, against people living beastially at Ephesus? [Haimo] I say that I fought, acting “according to human reasoning,” that is, rationally, because it belongs to a human being to believe, not to die like an animal. [Ambrose] Again, if the dead do not rise, this alone remains: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow,” that is, soon, [Col. 1684A] “we die.” The Apostle takes this from Isaiah. [Haimo] There it is the voice of Jews despairing in captivity. [Ambrose] The Apostle applies it to those who doubted the resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 1684D] Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount.*] For this is said concerning those who, as though nothing were to follow death, devote themselves only to the belly like cattle, and mock the faith of those who affirm the resurrection, saying: “Who has come from there? I have not heard the voice of anyone coming from there since my grandfather was placed there, since my great-grandfather was placed there, since my father was placed there; I have heard no one’s voice.” They are answered: “Fool, if your father rose, would you believe? The God of all rose, and you do not believe—the one who willed to die and rise so that we might all believe one person, lest we be deceived by many. Would you believe your father, who was going to die again, and not believe one now immortal?” [Col. 1684B] He also offered himself to be touched by the disciples, ascended into heaven while they watched, and the world received faith in him through the Spirit sent from heaven. Finally, he has testimony in heaven, testimony on earth, testimony from angels, testimony from the lower world. What, then, remains that does not cry aloud? Therefore let the murmurings of those who speak wickedly and corrupt good morals through evil conversations cease.

“Do not.” [Augustine] As though he said: “Because of all these things, do not be deceived by pseudo-teachers who seek a wound from medicine and endeavour to twist from the Scriptures a bond with which to cast the noose of death.” “For they corrupt.” As though he said: “Do not be deceived, nor even take pleasure in conversing with them, because their [Col. 1684C] evil conversations corrupt good morals,” that is, they even kill virtues by causing people not to hope for resurrection. [Ambrose] For persistent wicked speech corrupts the mind, and therefore one must beware of them.

“Awake.” As though he said: “Do not do this; rather, in opposition to them, awake from torpor, and thus you will be righteous. Afterwards, do not sin,” as God’s justice requires, namely, that you not sin by agreeing with those who are ignorant of God. [Augustine] Hence he adds: “For some have ignorance of God,” namely, those who called it foolish to believe that the dead would rise. “And I say this to you for shame,” or “for reverence,” that is, so that you may fear to agree with them, or may be ashamed, that is, so that you may be ashamed to believe the ignorant. [Ambrose] Or, “I speak to you for shame,” that is, for [Col. 1684D] your benefit.

### Verses 35–46

“But someone will say: How do the dead rise? And with what sort of body do they come? [112] Fool! What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies. And what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other kind. But God gives it a body as he wills, and to each of the seeds its own body. Not every flesh is the same flesh: one is that of human beings, another of cattle, another of birds, and another of fish; and there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. But the glory of the heavenly is one thing, and that of the earthly another. The brightness of the sun is one thing, the brightness of the moon another, and the brightness of the stars another. [Col. 1685A] For star differs from star in brightness; so also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonour; it will rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power. It is sown an animate body; it will rise a spiritual body. If there is an animate body, there is also a spiritual body, as it is written: ‘The first human, Adam, became a living soul’; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. But the spiritual is not first; rather, what is animate.”

“But someone says.” [Ambrose] Up to this point he has proved by arguments that the resurrection of the dead will occur; now he shows from the nature of things itself that this can occur, and he puts forward the words of those whose condemned opinion he said involved ignorance of God. As though he said: “The resurrection of the dead is proved by the foregoing. But nevertheless someone ignorant of God says: ‘How will the dead rise?’” That is, how can it be that the dead, who are now ashes, should rise? He says this as though it could not happen by nature. “And if they rise, with what sort of body will they come?” As though he said: “It can be no different from what it is now, namely passible and mortal.”

And because this person thinks himself wise, though he is not, in his knowledge of natural things—the knowledge by which he disproves our faith in the resurrection—the Apostle fittingly answers: “Fool, you do not observe what you see every day: the grain that you sow is not made alive,” that is, does not grow, “unless it first dies,” that is, decays. In dealing with the merely natural person, he does not proceed by the authority of Scripture, but supplies evidences by which the future re-formation of the dead [Col. 1685C] into something better may be believed, while the kind of nature remains.

“And the body that you sow, you do not sow such as will be.” [Augustine] He does not say this to deny that wheat will come from wheat, but because no one sows the grass or stalk, or the many coverings of the grains which are in the chaff, though the seeds rise with them. Therefore he adds: “But a bare grain,” for example, a grain of wheat or of any other seed. But God gives that grain a body, with chaff and an ear, as he wills. Therefore, just as a bare grain is sown and by God’s ordering rises, as it were, clothed, carrying many coverings with it, so by God’s power the dead person can live and rise with a better body.

“And to each of the seeds [Col. 1685D] he gives its own body,” the body it ought naturally to have. He does not give all seeds the same body, but to each its own, according to its kind—for example, a wheat-body to wheat. Or, he gives each seed its own body because the grain which springs from the earth does not sprout from anything other than that which was sown. So our former bodies will be re-formed for us in the future, as Job says: “Whom I myself shall see, and not another” (Job XIX).

“Not every.” This concerns the difference among those who rise, on account of the different glories of the faithful. As though he said: “The same bodies will rise, but there will be a difference in glory and dignity, although they are from the same matter, just as not every flesh is the same flesh,” that is, of [Col. 1686A] the same dignity, although it is from the same elements. This is what he says: “Not every flesh is the same flesh,” that is, of the same dignity, “but one is that of human beings, another of cattle, another of birds, and another of fish.”

The sense is this: [Note: [Col. 1685D] Augustine to Consentius.] If kinds of flesh, although all mortal, nevertheless differ among themselves according to the diversity of living creatures, it is not surprising if there is a difference of glory in the resurrection of the dead. And there are heavenly bodies, such as those of flying creatures, or such as the sun, moon, and stars; and there are earthly bodies, such as trees and other things which the earth produces. Therefore, after speaking of flesh, he adds bodies, because every flesh is indeed a body, but not conversely, as wood is.

Or heavenly bodies are those which rise; earthly bodies, on the other hand, are those before they die. Thus, because Christ is heavenly, bodies derived from him are called [Col. 1686B] heavenly bodies and are no longer called flesh; whereas bodies derived from Adam, because he is earthly, are earthly bodies.

“But one.” As though he said: “Not only do earthly things differ among themselves, but they also differ from heavenly things.” He says this thus: “But the glory of the heavenly is one thing, and the glory of the earthly another”; and even the heavenly things differ among themselves, because the brightness of the sun is one thing, the brightness of the moon another, and the brightness of the stars another. [Ambrose] And just as these, although of one nature, nevertheless have different brightness, so human beings, though of the same kind, will nevertheless have unlike glory in the resurrection: the dignity of those who have the hundredfold number will be equal to the brightness of the sun; the dignity of those who have the sixtyfold number will be compared with lunar brightness; and the dignity of those who have sought the thirtyfold number with the stars. [Col. 1686C] But the resurrection of the faithless will resemble dark and lowest stars. For unbelief cannot have a bright resurrection, because, just as a coal covered with its ash is darkened, so they, surrounded by the darkness of faithlessness and error, will lack light.

For a star differs from a star. As if he said: The stars differ from those bodies, namely from the sun and moon, because they also differ among themselves. For star differs from star in brightness; so too will the resurrection of the dead differ—that is, the dead will rise in bodies so differing. [John Damascene.] For there are many differences not only among the punishments of Gehenna but also among the rewards of the heavenly kingdom. Hence the Lord says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John 14). These are the differing dignities of merits [Col. 1686D] within the one life, even though the same denarius—that is, eternal life—is given to all.

[Note: [Col. 1686D] Id., *On Virginity*.] For the householder gave the same denarius to all who worked in the vineyard. By that denarius, certainly, something is signified which all will possess in common, such as eternal life itself, the kingdom of heaven itself, the brightness of the resurrection itself; yet one will shine more, another less. [Augustine.] Therefore there will be many dwelling-places and one denarius, [Fulgentius] because there is one blessedness which they receive, but an unequal quality of recompense; and, although they are of unequal brightness, God is nevertheless all in all. And because God is love, love will bring it about that what the individual persons have [Col. 1687A] will be common to all.

It is sown. As if he said: They will rise in differing glory; but this all will have in common, that they will be incorruptible. [Ambrose.] And this is what he says: “A body is sown,” that is, buried or put to death, “in corruption,” that is, so as to decay. Or: it is sown in corruption, that is, conceived as corruptible, and it will rise in incorruption, that is, immortal and incapable of suffering. Thus, although from the time he is conceived until dissolution a man is in corruption, and afterward teems with worms, he will nevertheless rise in incorruption.

Again: a body is sown, that is, dies and is buried, in dishonor, that is, without any honor; and it will rise in glory, that is, glorious. Again: it is sown, that is, conceived, in weakness, that is, such that any things whatever can harm it; [Col. 1687B] it will rise in power, that is, in a power which nothing can harm. [Haimo.] Or: it is sown, that is, buried, in weakness, because it is immobile and incapable of governing itself, since it cannot move or rule itself; it will rise in power, that is, truly alive and enlivened.

What is meant by each expression? “An animal body is sown,” that is, a body sustained by food in order that it may live, and having from the soul nothing except that it is made sentient through it, like animals. “A spiritual body will rise,” that is, one which no longer needs food, passing into the nature of spirit—that is, possessing certain spiritual properties natural to spirit—because it will be agile, light, and in no need of food.

[Note: [Col. 1687D] Augustine, *To Consentius*.] Note that he says, “A spiritual body will rise”; he does not say “spirit,” as though the body were changed into spirit, as some suppose. [Col. 1687C] For just as an animal body is not a soul but a body, so we must not suppose that a spiritual body is spirit, but a body. Hence the Lord too, refuting his disciples’ such opinion concerning his body, said: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24).

Therefore Christ’s body was already spiritual, yet it was not spirit. Hence here also he does not say “spirit,” but “spiritual,” because then the body will be fully subjected to the spirit and will no longer resist. And because it will be like the spirit, it will suffer no corruption and will need no food, just as man did not need food before sin. Note that when he says that the body will pass into incorruption, he mentions corruption in order that the greater dignity of the resurrection may be shown.

If there is a body. [Col. 1687D] As if he said: A spiritual body will truly rise, because if a body is now animal, it is clearly destined at some time to be spiritual also. For just as we are animal because our father Adam was made carnal, into a living soul, so in the resurrection we shall be spiritual, because our father, namely Christ, was made spiritual in his resurrection, into a life-giving spirit. He explains it thus:

[Augustine.] “Just as”—or rather, “for thus it is written in Genesis”—namely, that we, begotten from an animal father, are animal: it is written there that “the first man Adam was made into a living soul.” Here he explains what an animal body is when he says, “was made into a living soul,” able to live—that is, able to give life [Col. 1688A] to the body—yet giving it life through the support of food. “But the last Adam,” that is, Christ—this is not taken from Genesis but added by the Apostle—“was made into a life-giving spirit,” that is, one who gave life to the body in such a way that it would thereafter need no support and would not be dissoluble. Here he explains what is spiritual.

[Note: [Col. 1688D] Id., *To Consentius*.] For he intended this difference between a living soul and a life-giving spirit: there the body is animal; here it is spiritual. For the soul indeed lives in an animal body, but it does not give life so as to remove corruption. 113 But in a spiritual body, because it perfectly cleaves to the Lord, it gives life in such a way as to make the body spiritual.

Observe also why Christ is called Adam, and the last Adam. He is called Adam because he is from the same material; he is called the last because no other succeeds him [Col. 1688B] as head or author of the human race, as those two were. [Augustine.] For in a sense the whole human race is those two men, namely the first Adam and the second: from the former they are born; from the latter they are reborn. Thus each is called father of the human race.

Or, without changing the rest, this may be read thus: “If there is a body,” in order to prove, as it were from correlatives, that there is a spiritual body: “And I rightly said ‘spiritual,’ because if there is a body of the soul, there is also a spiritual body.” For when “body” is said, “animal” is added pointlessly unless there is another body, spiritual, in contrast to which it is called animal. That there is an animal body he proves by the authority of Genesis: “he was made,” and so forth; the rest is not altered.

[Col. 1688C] Or thus: “If there is a body.” As if he said: I rightly said “animal body” and “spiritual body.” For there is an animal body and there is a spiritual body. And that it is animal he proves through Genesis, where it says, “the first man was made,” and so forth; and that it is spiritual he shows there, because of “the last Adam.” The meaning of these words is not changed.

But not. He said that our bodies would become spiritual; but lest anyone doubt whether an animal body can become spiritual, he proves it by the likeness of Christ. As if he said: Christ was made into a life-giving spirit. [Augustine.] But that which is spiritual was not first in him; rather, that which is animal was first in Christ.

**VERS. 46–52.—**Then that which is spiritual. The first man was from earth, earthly; the second man, from heaven, heavenly. [Col. 1688D] As is the earthly man, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly man, so also are the heavenly. Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly. But this I say, brothers, because flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God; nor will corruption possess incorruption. Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet—for the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.

Then what is spiritual may likewise come to be in us. Therefore, having experienced this in Christ, let each person expect it for himself: namely, that from animal he may become spiritual. Then he shows whence we are animal and whence we shall become [Col. 1689A] spiritual, adding: “The first man.” As if he said: The first man was truly made into a living soul, because the first man is from earth, having been formed from the dust of the earth, and is therefore earthly—that is, by nature animal and capable of suffering.
