The second man was made into a life-giving spirit because the second man is from heaven, since the divine nature was united to the human; and is therefore heavenly—that is, spiritual in the resurrection.

Or he is called heavenly because he was conceived and born not by human custom but by divine ordinance. As the earthly father was, that is, animal and mortal, so too are the earthly: animal from animal, mortal from mortal. And as the heavenly Father is, that is, spiritual and immortal, so they too will be spiritual and immortal, and heavenly, because [Col. 1689B] they will be such heavenly persons.

Therefore, in order that we may be heavenly, just as we have borne the image of the earthly, [Ambrose] that is, just as by Adam’s example we loved earthly things, so also after baptism let us bear the image of the heavenly, by following righteousness, truth, and obedience.

“But this I say,” and so forth. As if he said: I say that we should bear the image of the heavenly; but if we do not bear it, we shall not be heavenly. This is what he says: “But this I say to you, brothers, that flesh and blood,” that is, persons given over to vices arising from flesh and blood, “will not possess the kingdom of God”; and truly so, because the corruption of sin, which is an effect of flesh and blood—that is, anyone serving the corruption of sin—will not possess incorruption, [Col. 1689C] that is, will not become immortal.

Or, by “flesh and blood” he here understands the works of the flesh. For by flesh and blood he signifies the belly and lust—that is, works of the flesh—which will not exist there; he does not want them to suppose that in the heavenly kingdom they will do things such as are done in this life, as the Jews supposed.

[Note: [Col. 1689D] Augustine, sermon *On the Rest of Death*.] For the Jews believed in a future resurrection, but after the manner of this life, so that there they would marry and beget children. Hence they could not answer the Sadducees when they proposed the question concerning the woman with seven husbands (Matthew 22), because they thought carnally concerning the resurrection. The Apostle excludes this when he says: “But this.” As if he said: It is clear from what has been said that we shall rise. But this I say, brothers: flesh and blood, that is, works of flesh and blood, will not possess the kingdom of God—that is, they will not [Col. 1689D] exist in the kingdom of God. And truly they will not, because the corruption of the flesh, whose works those are, will not possess incorruption—that is, it will not exist in the incorruptible kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 1689D] Id., in the book *Retractations*.] Or, by the expression “flesh and blood” is understood the very corruption of flesh and blood, which certainly will not exist in that kingdom, where the flesh will be incorruptible. Therefore the Apostle’s statement must not be understood as though the substance of flesh will not exist in the kingdom of God. And this is the meaning: “But this.” As if he said: It is established that we shall rise. But this I say, brothers: flesh and blood, that is, the corruption of flesh and blood, will not possess the kingdom of God.

And lest you suppose that this is said concerning substance, he clarifies it by adding: “Nor will corruption.” As if he said: I said that flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God because the corruption of mortality, indicated here by the term “flesh,” will not possess incorruption, that is, the incorruptible kingdom.

And because he said that the elect would rise in glory, and afterward said that flesh and blood do not possess the kingdom of God, he explains how this should be distinguished. As though someone were to ask, “How will there be flesh, and flesh will not be there?” he explains, saying: “Behold, I tell,” that is, I disclose to you, “a mystery,” that is, something hidden from you. [Ambrose.] For by naming a mystery he signifies obscurity. For *mysterium* is Greek, and in Latin it is called *secretum*, “a secret,” or *occultum*, “hidden.” What is it? Namely this: that all human beings, both good and evil, will rise.

[Col. 1690B] [Haimo.] This may be understood universally if we say that even the saints found alive when Christ comes will die. For only so can they rise.

[Note: [Col. 1690D] Id., *The City of God*.] For resurrection cannot occur unless death has preceded it. Therefore, if we believe that the saints who will be found alive at Christ’s coming and caught up to meet him will, in that very rapture, depart from their mortal bodies and immediately return to those same bodies made immortal, we may understand the statement universally: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” into the glory of immortality.

[Ambrose.] Or thus: all of us will rise, namely those who are found dead at Christ’s coming. But not all who are found alive will be changed into glory; only God’s saints will be.

I say that we shall rise, and [Col. 1690C] this “in a moment,” [Haimo] that is, in the briefest, smallest, and narrowest span of time. And because there is delay in a moment, however brief, he adds, “in the twinkling of an eye,” that is, as quickly as the eye strikes—that is, directs its sight—or is struck by the eyelid: in the utmost swiftness. [Ambrose.] By the twinkling of an eye he signifies extreme brevity, so that the resurrection may be shown more marvelous, and God’s power commended by its swiftness.

Therefore the resurrection will occur in the twinkling of an eye, that is, as swiftly as the eye’s ray passes to distant objects and flies over what lies between. Though there is a before and after in it, yet the whole seems to occur at once; so too will the resurrection of the dead take place. And this will occur “at the last trumpet,” that is, through a trumpet and a great or manifest voice, after which [Col. 1690D] there will be no other. The sense is: the resurrection will occur at the trumpet, that is, at the final sign which will be given for these things to be fulfilled.

This trumpet is the cry spoken of in the Gospel: “At midnight a cry was made: Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him” (Matthew 25).

[Note: [Col. 1690D] Id., *On Grace. N. T.*] The same author in the same work: He will not come when he is expected, but at midnight, that is, when it will be very dark—that is, hidden—he will come. And as though someone asked, “Will there be a sound?” he replies: Certainly. “For the trumpet will sound.” By the name “trumpet” is understood something evident and illustrious, which elsewhere is called the voice of an archangel and the trumpet of God, and in the Gospel is called Christ’s voice. The dead who are in [Col. 1691A] the tombs will hear it and come forth (John 5).

[Ambrose.] Hence he adds here also: “And the dead,” that is, sinners, or universally all the dead, “will rise incorruptible,” that is, without loss of limbs; [Augustine] and we—the good only—will be changed into the glory of immortality and impassibility. How this happens, or what this change is like, he explains by adding:

**VERS. 53–58.—**For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality. But when this mortal thing has put on immortality, then the saying which is written will come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” Now the sting of death is sin; but the strength of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, [Col. 1691B] who gave us victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not empty in the Lord.

For it must. [Ambrose.] We shall indeed be changed, because we have served well, or because this has been promised us: this corruptible body must put on incorruption as an adornment, so that it will no longer hunger or be harmed in any respect. And this mortal thing—that is, this visible mortal body—must put on immortality, so that it will no longer be dissolved.

[Note: [Col. 1691D] Augustine, *On the Creed*.] Therefore it must be believed without doubt that this visible flesh will rise. For the Apostle seems to point to it, as it were with his finger, when he says, “This [Col. 1691C] corruptible thing must…”

[Note: [Col. 1691D] Id., *On the Sermon on the Mount*.] In saying “this,” he as it were extends his finger toward it, so that the same flesh which is seen may be shown as that which will rise, though not in its present condition. This is the sense in which it was said above that “flesh will not possess”: it is because corruption and mortality will not be there. That is, flesh will not be there according to these qualities, but the same substance of flesh will be there.

“But when,” or “for.” As if he said: It will truly put on immortality, because then the saying will come to pass—that is, be fulfilled—and it could never otherwise be fulfilled. [Haimo.] Or the connection is thus: it will put on immortality. “But when this mortal thing has put on immortality, then the saying which is written will come to pass,” that is, will be fulfilled—and it could never otherwise be fulfilled—which is written in Isaiah or Hosea, where it reads thus: “I will be your death, O death” (Hosea 13). But according to the Septuagint it is: “Death has been swallowed up,” that is, bodily death has been destroyed [Col. 1691D] 114, “in the victory of Christ,” that is, in Christ’s resurrection.

That this must be understood of bodily death, not of the death of the soul, is shown by his saying, “then it will come to pass,” thereby signifying that it is future. He did not say “it has come to pass,” as though referring to something past, lest anyone suppose this was said of inward death, which has already occurred.

“Where is…?” [Ambrose.] These are the words of a prophet or Apostle rejoicing and taunting death in the person of those who rise, so that the resurrection may be more certain.

[Note: [Col. 1691D] Id., *To Marcellus*.] Thus he says in the person of the risen: “Where is, O bodily death, your victory?” that is, the power by which you dissolved all, by which you conquered all so thoroughly that even the Son of God struggled with you and overcame you not by avoiding you but by undergoing you. You conquered among the dying; you have been conquered among the rising. Your victory, by which you swallowed up the bodies of the dying, was temporary; the victory by which you have been swallowed up in the bodies of the risen will endure eternally.

“Where is, O death,” namely dissolution, “your sting?” The sting of death is understood as original sin, in which all of us sinned in one man so that all of us should die in one man; by it we have been stung and poisoned, and from it death came forth. As he himself explains by adding: “But the sting of death is sin.” For just as sin is called the sting of death, by which death was made, not a sting which death made—for we die through sin, not sin through death—so the tree of life is called such not because it made human life, but because human life was made through it; [Col. 1692B] likewise the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, through which human knowledge came to be, not which man made through his own knowledge.

Or, by the name of death the devil is signified. The meaning is: “Death has been swallowed up in victory,” that is, the devil has already been swallowed up in part; in the future he will be wholly swallowed up, because he exceeded the limit of conquering by attacking Christ, in whom he had nothing. Then, in the person of the righteous who now are and will be at the resurrection, he taunts him, saying: “Where is, O death,” namely devil, “your victory, by which you dragged the human race behind you like a flock? Where is, O death,” namely devil, “your sting?” But the sting of death is sin. Sin, however, is called the devil’s sting, which death—that is, the devil—made, not that by which he was made.

Or thus: I think that by death here is signified the pleasure of sinning and the carnal habit which kills the soul, arising from the act of sin by which we sinned in Adam. [Col. 1692C] For we earned this death by sin, which sin was entirely within free choice when, in paradise, no pain from a denied pleasure resisted the good will of man. For example:

[Note: [Col. 1692D] Augustine, *Questions*, Book 83.] If someone exists whom hunting has never delighted, he is entirely free whether he wishes to hunt or not, nor is he tormented by one who forbids it. But if, having made evil use of this freedom, he hunts against the command of the one forbidding it, a gradually creeping pleasure kills the soul, so that, should he wish to abstain, he cannot do so without distress and struggle. For “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5). Nor will the conflict cease until perfect holiness has restored the whole human being. Therefore then the saying which is written will come to pass.

[Note: [Col. 1692D] Id., *On the Words of the Apostle*.] It is not taking place now, but it will take place then. What will then take place? “Death,” that is, the pleasure of sinning, “has been swallowed up.”

[Note: [Col. 1692D] Id., on Psalm 84.] “In victory,” that is, in the fact that God’s servants will conquer the lust of the flesh. Then peace will conquer and the war will end; there will be no conflict from death, as there is now. First, following the flesh’s desire, it led us; afterward, when we resisted, it dragged us; then, when grace had been received, it began neither to lead nor drag us, but still to contend with us. [Col. 1693A]

[Note: [Col. 1693D] Augustine, *Questions*, Book 83.] After the contest will be victory, when it ceases to attack. Therefore he adds in the person of the victors: “Where is, O death, your victory—or your conflict? Where is, O death, your sting or goad?” But death’s sting is sin, because pleasure was made through sin. For sin is like a scorpion, through whose sting death came to be; but it will be swallowed up in the future, when the saints are granted neither to wish to sin nor to be able to sin.

“But the strength,” that is, the increase, “of sin is the law.” He added this lest someone say that anyone is helped by the law; rather, one is helped by God alone. For once the law was given, carnal desire grew strong and transgression was added. For by forbidding, the law increases the desire for sin, unless the Spirit pours forth love.

[Note: [Col. 1693D] Id., *On the Perfection of Righteousness*.] For all these things the Apostle gives thanks to God, saying: “But I give thanks to God, [Col. 1693B] who gave us victory over sin and death through our Lord Jesus Christ,” not through the law. For Christ says: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16).

[Note: [Col. 1694D] Id., on John.] And because we have conquered through Christ, therefore, my most beloved brothers, be steadfast in faith in the resurrection and immovable, so that you cannot be moved by false teachers. Always abound in the work of the Lord, in hope of the resurrection, knowing—that is, having hope—that your labor which you have in the Lord, that is, in the Lord’s service, is not empty, that is, without reward.

Concerning collections, after other matters, he briefly instructs them concerning collections to be made for the saints who were in Jerusalem.

[Note: [Col. 1694D] Id., *On the Sermon on the Mount*.] This is not contrary to the saying, “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matthew [Col. 1693C] 6). For it is not being anxious about tomorrow if one provides for such matters in the ordinary human way; it is so if one serves God for the sake of these things, looking in one’s works not to the kingdom of God but to acquiring such things.

## CHAPTER XVI

**VERS. 1–14.—**Now concerning the collections which are made for the saints: as I arranged in the churches of Galatia, so you also should do. On the first day of the week, let each of you set something aside at home, storing up whatever seems good to him, so that collections may not then be made when I come. When I am present, I will send those whom you approve by letters to carry your gift to Jerusalem. And if it is fitting for me to go too, they will go with me. But I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia; for I shall pass through Macedonia. Perhaps I shall remain with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may accompany me wherever I go. For I do not wish to see you now merely in passing; I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits. But I shall remain at Ephesus until Pentecost. For a great and evident door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries. If Timothy comes, see that he is with you without fear; for he performs the work of the Lord, as I also do. Therefore let no one despise him. But send him on his way in peace, so that he may come to me; for I am expecting him with the brothers. Concerning brother Apollos, I make known to you that I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers; but it was certainly not his will [Col. 1694A] to come now. He will come when he has leisure. Keep watch, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, and be strengthened; let all your things be done in love.

[Haimo, Ambrose, Haimo.] Now concerning the collections which are made, not for just anyone but for the saints—that is, for the needs of the saints—it must be observed: “As I arranged in the churches of Galatia, so you also should do,” that is, collect on the first day of the Sabbath, that is, of the week. Or, “on the first day of the Sabbath,” that is, on the Lord’s Day. For among the Jews the day which we call the Lord’s Day was called “one of the Sabbath,” “one of the Sabbaths,” or “the first of the Sabbath.”

I say, collect; but let each of you store it up at home, lest you say that there is no trustworthy minister to whom you can entrust it. Let him store up, I say, whatever seems good to him—not what burdens [Col. 1694B] him—keeping it for the saints’ use and taking care not to take it again. The sense of these words is this: the Apostle commands all the people to assemble at church on the Lord’s Day and to bring there whatever each wished to give for the work of the saints. But lest it be lost through evil ministers if they left it at the church, he commanded them to take it back with them and store it in a safe place until he came. They did this every Lord’s Day, because what is collected little by little is not burdensome, and a large amount is found.

He commands this to be prepared so that collections need not be made when he comes, since they would burden them if they had suddenly to give the whole amount at once. But when I am present, then I will send those—or these—whom you have approved, that is, judged suitable, by letters: that is, with my and your letters of praise and recommendation for those carrying and sending the gift, to convey your grace, that is, gift, to Jerusalem. If it is worthy for me to go too—that is, if the resources are substantial—they will go with me.

But I will come to you after I have passed through Macedonia, [Ambrose] that is, after I have passed through all the places as far as Macedonia. For I shall pass through Macedonia, where there is no need to remain. But perhaps I shall stay with you or even winter there, because many things need correction there, just as a physician stays where there are more sick people. I say that I shall come to you so that you may accompany me wherever I go. I say that I shall remain with you, for I do not wish to see you merely in passing. I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits.

[Col. 1694D] But I shall remain at Ephesus—from there he sent the Epistle—until Pentecost. I shall remain there because a great door has been opened to me, that is, many human hearts are ready to hear; and it is evident because they do not oppose the preaching. And as though someone said, “Why then is it necessary to remain there?” he replies: “And,” that is, because, “there are many adversaries there who try to hinder.”

But if Timothy comes to you, see that he is with you without fear; perhaps he had already been afraid there because of the disturbance caused by the false apostles. For he performs the Lord’s work as I do; therefore let no one despise him. But send him on his way in peace, so that he may come to me; for I expect him with [Col. 1695A] the brothers who are with him.

Concerning brother Apollos, I make known to you that I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers. He says this because the Corinthians had sought him, 115 since he had been appointed their bishop by the Apostle; and, unable to calm them, he had come to the Apostle at Ephesus. The Apostle answers them here, saying, “I urged him,” and so forth. And it was certainly not his will to come to you now, because he fears those who have not been corrected. But he will come when he has leisure, [Ambrose] that is, at a suitable time, namely when you have been corrected.

But you, with the eyes of your mind, keep watch against the devil’s cunning, and stand firm in faith, because sleep does not creep upon one who stands. Act manfully—for inconstancy belongs to women—and be strengthened in the Lord, so that progress may lie in your own strength. And let all your things, that is, correction, [Col. 1695B] be done in love, not from a desire for empty glory.

“But I beseech you.” The order of this passage looks back and depends upon the words, “so that you also may be subject.” As if he said: Do what I have said above; but imitate these men. And this is what follows:

**VERS. 15–24.—**But I beseech you, brothers: you know the household of Stephanas, and of Fortunatus and Achaicus, that they are the firstfruits of Achaia and have devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints, so that you also may be subject to such people and to everyone who cooperates and labors. But I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they have supplied what was lacking on your part. For they have refreshed both my spirit and yours. Therefore recognize those who are such. All the churches of Asia greet you. Aquila and Priscilla, with their house-church, among whom I also lodge, greet you warmly in the Lord. All the brothers greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. My greeting, in Paul’s own hand. If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema, maranatha. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.

But I beseech you, brothers, who know the household of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus. These men were with the Apostle in preaching to the Corinthians, so that you also may be subject to them and to such persons, and to everyone working and laboring among you. Be subject to them because they are the firstfruits of Achaia, that is, the first who believed in [Col. 1696A] Achaia, and because they devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints, that is, to ministering to the saints.

[Ambrose.] But I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, that is, because they are present with you, from whom you derive benefit. Hence he adds: “Because they have supplied,” by teaching, “what was lacking on your part.” And rightly do I rejoice, for they have refreshed both my spirit and yours: mine, certainly, by joy; yours, by love.

Or thus: I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, that is, because they came to me, as it were on your behalf, to minister to me, because they supplied what was lacking on your part, since they ministered to me in what you did not do. And rightly do I rejoice, for they refreshed both my spirit, since they fed me, and yours, [Col. 1696B] since they attended to the Apostle for you.

Therefore recognize, that is, honor, those who are such. The churches of Asia greet you. As if he said: All desire what I write. Aquila and Priscilla, among whom I lodge, warmly greet you in the Lord, with their house-church, that is, the assembly of the brothers among whom I also lodge. All the brothers greet you. Greet one another as a sign of peace, and do so with a holy kiss, that is, with a true heart.

And so that they may know that the Epistle is his, he adds: “My greeting is written in Paul’s own hand.” This greeting is the one that follows: “The grace of the Lord…” But he prefaces it with this likewise written in his own hand: “If anyone,” and so forth. As if he said: I greet the faithful; but if anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema, [Augustine] that is, separated from God or condemned, [Col. 1696C] *maranatha*, that is, until the Lord comes, or at the Lord’s coming.

[Ambrose, Augustine.] For *maranatha* is interpreted “the Lord comes,” and is compounded from Syriac and Greek, and is more Syriac than Hebrew. But *anathema* is Greek and means “condemned” or “separated.” Thus he employs an expression similar to Greek and Syriac.

[Ambrose.] Then follows the greeting: “May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you, and may my love be with all of you,” that is, love one another or God with that love with which I love you or God. And do this in Christ, that is, not according to worldly love. Amen. This statement confirms the blessing.
